issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

The Tenant [name] testified at the hearing. He described the rental unit as an apartment in an older building which had been converted to residential use. The Tenants moved into the rental unit on October 17, 2017. The Ceiling

The Tenant testified that there was dampness and staining on the ceiling of the bedroom and overtime this began to crumble and rip, and despite some attempts to repair and patch the ceiling over a number of months these repairs were unsuccessful.

He testified that he made the Landlord aware via text on [name] 2024. The Tenant tested that no one attended the rental unit until Februray 12, 2024 when they were informed that a roofer would be attending to look at on issue of the outside of the unit. The Tenant testified that the ceiling was still damp and crumbling in March 2024, and in April the Landlord directed the Tenant to his handyman but when the Tenant tried to set up a repair he was met with radio silence until April 22, 2024.

The Tenant testified that on May 9, 2024, he was informed that a roofer had attended and patched the roof once again. The Tenant testified that the spot in the bedroom was patched at the end of May 2024.

The Tenant testified that in late June 2024 the roof was repaired and the contractors realise that the current roof had been laid overtop of an existing roof. The Tenant testified that on July 30, 2024, he followed up with the Landlord because the roof was still leaking and appeared to be unfinished, he testified that during this conversation the Landlord was unaware that the strapping work had not been completed.
The Tenant testified that the exterior work was completed on August 8, 22024.
He testified that that were provided with a dehumidifier for the ongoing dampness and were offered fans and a moisture sensor, but these were never provided.

The Tenant relied on a photo of the spot on the ceiling taken in September 2024 and testified that it grew and shrunk at various times.The Tenant testified that the dampness would appear when it rained.
The Tenant testified that the ceiling was finally repaired on October 18, 2024.

During cross semination when asked if the Landlord had provided 48 hours notice to enter the unit and patch the drywall and if he had declined, the Tenant indicated that he could not speak to that’s specifically but had asked the Landlord to return in October as that was when he had time off from work. The Tenant agreed that he wanted to be present when the Landlord attended, and agreed that this would cause some delay to repairs, but indicated that they would be minimal.

The Landlord relied on a series of text messages from the Tenant including a March 4, 2024 text indicating that there had been no leaks from the ceiling but that it appeared damp and crumbling, and a text on April 2, 2024 wherein the Tenant indicates that there have Neen no further problems with the damp spot. The Landlord also relied on an April 16, 2024 text which indicated that the ceiling was damp, but this had not been the case for weeks.
The Landlord also relied on texts from May 15, 2024 and August 9, 2024 indicating that the ceiling was dry.

The Landlord testified on September 26, 2024 he requested the Tenants provide him with a key to the rental unit as he had previously tried to work around the Tenant’s schedule for repairs which was difficult as the Tenant’s always wanted additional notice. The Landlord texted that the Tenants informed him that they were out of town and would return the next week. The Window

The Tenant testified that the locking mechanism from the window had become detached when the window was locked and it could not be opened. The Tenant testified that this occurred in 2023 and they made the Landlord aware in 2023. The Tenant testified that the Landlord informed him that the Landlord’s handyman “Jake” would address the issue and source a part, however this never occurred and the window was not repaired until November 2024.

The Tenant testified that it sounded like multiple parts were ordered, and when they arrived, they would be the wrong part. The Tenant testified that the Landlord offered to break break the window in the summer months in order to repair it, but they did not want to proceed with this during the summer months due to heat.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant’s first made him aware of the damaged window on April 6, 2204 via text, and that he had not been made aware prior to this date. He testified that when he tried to replace the window, he determined that the internal mechanism was broken and looked like it had been forced off, he testified that he did not understand how this could be accomplished without excessive force and that in his view the damaged was not regular wear and tear.

He testified that while the Tenant s had previously declined to allow him to beak the widow casing to repair the widow In June 2024 they did agree in October 2024. The Landlord testified that the window was subsequently repaired around November 1, 2024. The Stove

The Tenant testified that the oven malfunctioned starting August 28, 2024. One of the elements would not turn off and if the stove was plugged in it would remain at maximum heat. The Tenant informed the Landlord when the ropable arose and were provided with the contact information for [name]. The Tenant contacted them, and they attended and repaired the oven in September 6, 2024. The Landlord confirmed that he gave the Tenant’s the contract information for [name] on August 29, 2024 he testified that he did so because it was difficult to preform repairs for the Tenants as they always requested additional notice form him before he could attend the rental unit. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord breached their miniatous obligations. With respect to the oven, the Landlord provided the Tenants with contact information for an appliance repair service and the repair was coordinated and completed by September 6, 2024. I am satisfied that this is a reasonable repair timeframe and response time for the issue, and am satisfied that it was reasonable for the Landlord to instruct the Tenants to schedule the repair directly as he had had difficulty coordinating with them in the past.

With respect to the window, I am also satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably. I am not satisfied that the Tenants have demonstrated that they made the Landlord aware of the issue in 2023. The Tenants testimony with respect to this issue was general, and I prefer the clear text message provided by the Landlord making him aware in April 2024.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to repair the window, including ordering multiple parts to complete the repair. While this may not have remedied the issue I am satisfied that it demonstrates that the Landlord was taking his obligations under the Act seriously by attempting to bring about a repair of the window. I also note that while the Landlord offered to perform the repair in June 2024 the Tenant’s declined. While it may be reasonable for them to decline as the repair required the breaming of the window frame, and they did not want to do this during the summer heat, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is now able to claim that the Landlord did not act promptly in repairing the window, as the repair was offered months earlier and delinked. I also note that the repair occurred promptly after the Tenants indicated they were ready to proceed with it in October 2024.

With respect to the ceiling, I am also satisfied the Landlord acted reasonably. While the issue was first reported in Februray 2024 and the repairs were not complete until October 2024 I note that the messaging from the Tenants appears to have been mixed, with several texts indicating that there were no further problems with the ceiling ,or that it was dry. I am also satisfied that the Landlord made efforts to repair both the ceiling and the roof, including by patching the ceiling in May 2024 and having work performed on the exterior roof including in June and August 2024. I also note that in September 2024 proposed repair dates were declined by the Tenant and that it appears the Tenants wished to be present when any reaper was completed, which made it more challenging for the Landlord to coordinate and complete the repairs. Given that it is clear the Landlord has made ongoing efforts to repair the roof and ceiling, some of which were successful, and some of which appeared to have been delayed by the Tenant’s and the roof was ultimately repaired in October 2024, I am satisfied that he Landlord acted reasonably in the circumstances when responding to the ceiling and roof.
T herefore , the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization]. (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,232.76.
The parties agree that the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord on August 4, 2025, to commence a tenancy on September 1, 2025 for a fixed term period ending on August 31, 2026.
The parties further agree that the Tenant paid to the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit of $2,195.00 at the time of entering into the tenancy agreement.

The Tenant testified that on August 5, 2025 she reached out to the Landlord indicating that she was reconciling with her husband and wanted to cancel the tenancy agreement. The Tenant further stated that the Landlord agreed that would be a valid reason to cancel the tenancy agreement. 5. [name] (‘B.C.’) disputes that he agreed to cancel the tenancy agreement and return the Tenant’s rent deposit. He stated that he wanted the Tenant to be sure that she wished to cancel the Tenancy agreement and told her to take some time to think about it. He further stated that on August 18, 2025, after the Tenant confirmed she wanted to proceed with cancelling the tenancy agreement, he advised the Tenant she would need to sign an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy and that if the Landlord was unable to rent the unit by the 1st of September, that she would not be entitled to the return of the last month’s rent deposit. 6. In an attempt to mitigate the Landlord’s losses, the Landlord listed the rental unit for rent on August 18, 2025. 7. The parties signed an N11 agreement on August 23, 2025 agreeing to end the tenancy on August 31, 2025. The parties agree that the N11 Agreement to End Tenancy was effective August 31, 2025 as the Landlord was not sure how to date it as the Tenant hadn’t moved in and the Landlord was looking to find a new tenant to commence a tenancy on September 1, 2025 the same period the Tenant’s tenancy had been set to commence. 8. The Tenant never moved into the rental unit nor was she provided with keys to the unit prior to the parties agreeing to end the tenancy. 9. On September 7, 2025, the Landlord found another tenant and entered into a new tenancy agreement to rent the unit commencing September 15, 2025, but claims that the Landlord incurred costs for credit checks on potential new tenants and advertising fees for the unit totalling $246.53. Analysis 10. Section 202(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states: In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 11. On its face the N11 Agreement to End Tenancy entered by the parties contained a termination date of August 31, 2025, a date prior to the commencement of the tenancy. 12. However, based on the testimony of the parties it becomes clear that the Tenant was attempting to end the tenancy and potentially see the return of her rental deposit and the Landlord was attempting to let the Tenant out of the tenancy while still protecting itself from the potential loss of rental income, if the unit was to remain unrented for the month of September. 13. Based on the testimony and evidence before me, I find the Tenant is responsible for rent for the period of September 1 to September 14, 2025 totalling $1,010.24 as the Landlord was able to mitigate its losses and re-rent the unit commencing September 15, 2025.The daily compensation for the rental unit is calculated as follows; $2,195.00 monthly rent amount x 12 months divided by 365 day equalling $72.16 per day x 14 days equalling $1,010.24. 14. The Tenant is entitled to compensation in the amount of $1,184.76 being the one month rent deposit of $2,195.00, less $1,010.24 for September 1 to 14, 2025. 15. Any expenses potentially incurred by the Landlord for credit checks and advertising are the cost of doing business by the Landlord and the Landlord is not entitled to offset this amount from any compensation granted to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,232.76. This amount represents: • $1,184.76 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant for the property held by the Landlord.

It is undisputed during March 2023 the Tenant installed an IKEA pantry in the rental unit. The Tenant provided an itemized receipt from IKEA (DOC-4256166). The receipt provided included other purchases other than the pantry. After reviewing the receipt with the parties, it was determined that the total amount the Tenant paid for the pantry inclusive of tax was $1,010.22.

The parties agreed to terminate the tenancy effective June 30, 2024. The Tenant provided text messages between the Tenant and the Landlord with respect to the pantry from June 18, 2024 to July 2, 2024 (DOC-4256168, DOC-4256170, DOC-4256171, DOC-4256173, DOC-4256174). Throughout these messages, the Tenant and the Landlord [name] (AV) are discussing whether the Tenant will leave the pantry in the rental unit and the Landlords will reimburse the Tenant an amount or the Tenant will remove the pantry. Several times, the Tenant insists the pantry will be removed if the Landlords do not want to buy it. On July 2, 2024, the Landlord [name] (KH) tells the Tenant “Removing the pantry isn’t an option” as KH speculates it would leave damage if removed.
KH texts the Tenant “The pantry stays to offset the clean up that I had to do” (DOC- 4256175).

The Landlords testified there is no order from the LTB that allowed the Landlords to keep the Tenant’s possessions (pantry) nor did the Landlords provide any evidence to suggest there was an agreement between the parties the Landlords could keep the pantry without providing reimbursement. The Tenant’s evidence suggests the opposite, the Tenant would have removed the pantry had the Landlords not led her to believe they would reimburse her for the item.
As of the date of the hearing, the pantry remains in the rental unit. The rental unit is currently occupied by new tenants. Analysis
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') states: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant”.

I find based on the evidence deduced at the hearing and on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords actions interfered with the Tenant’s possession of the pantry. The Landlords led the Tenant to believe she may be compensated for the pantry and the Tenant insisted she would remove the pantry should they not want to pay for it.

The Landlords have kept the Tenant’s pantry in the rental unit and that pantry is now being used by the new tenants. Therefore, while the Landlords may not have damaged or destroyed the item, I find the Landlords actions of giving the pantry to the new tenants constitutes disposing of as it is no longer in the Tenant’s possession.

Although the Tenant originally paid $1,010.22 in March 2023 for the pantry, I find that amount to be unreasonable as reimbursement. The pantry had wear and tear to it, as testified by both the Tenant and the Landlords. Further, the Tenant had offered to leave the pantry for the Landlords use for $500.00. I find this amount to be a reasonable cost to replace the property the Landlords did not return to the Tenants.
The Landlords will also be ordered to pay the filing fee paid by the Tenant for this application.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord harassed coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by giving the Tenant a notice of termination because the Landlord’s child required the rental unit for purposes of residential occupation (“N12 notice) in bad faith and thereafter constantly pressured the Tenant to move out of the rental unit, and threatened to initiate legal proceedings, if the Tenant did not move out.

The Tenant further alleged that the Landlord violated the Tenant’s privacy rights by copying third parties on her email correspondence with the Tenant, and by using her work email to correspond with the Tenant.
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The Act does not define harassment, but the Human Rights Code defines "harassment" as: engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.

By way of background, the rental unit was a three-bedroom townhouse. The Tenant had been residing in the rental unit since March 1, 2017 with her two young children. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 29, 2024 pursuant to the N12 notice.

At the beginning of March 2024, after the Tenant reported some damage to the rental unit, the Landlord’s son inspected the unit and subsequently, on March 11, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant N12 notice of termination with the termination date of May 31, 2024.

The Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination [name] claiming that the Landlord’s son and his family wished to move into the rental unit. The Tenant alleged that the Landlord gave her the N12 notice in bad faith and that there may have been another motive behind the service of the N12 notice; however, that is not an issue to be decided in this application.
The issue in this application is whether the Landlord engaged in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.
According to the Tenant, the Landlord repeatedly inquired as to the Tenant’s move out date. The Tenant felt pressured and harassed by the Landlord’s constant and frequent communications.

According to the Tenant, she did everything possible to find alternate accommodation as quickly as she could, but with two small children and after having resided int the rental unit for seven years, it was not easy, and the Landlords constant pressure caused her emotional distress.

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord violated her privacy when a “strange person” delivered the N12 notice and when the Landlord copied third parties on her email correspondence with the Tenant, and used her work email to correspond with the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that she was sensitive to the Tenant’s situation and as such did not want to pressure the Tenant and kept communications to a minimum: however, she needed to know whether and when the Tenant planned to move out, as her son’s family was under financial pressure and wished to move in.

The Tenant gave the Landlord no indication as to when she would be moving out and the Landlord periodically, about once a month, inquired whether the Tenant was successful in finding alternate accommodation. The Tenant was vague in her responses. The Landlord attempted to provide an incentive to the Tenant to move out by reducing the rent for June 2024, she also extended the move out date; however, when the Tenant provided no definite answer, the Landlord filed an L2 application to terminate the tenancy based on the N12, as was the Landlord’s right.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 29, 2024, and requested that the Landlord withdraw the L2 application scheduled for Nov 6, 2024. The Landlord was amenable to withdrawing the application if the Tenant paid the rent that the Tenant owed (3 months).

The evidence before me established that the Landlord emailed the Tenant approximately once a month asking about the status of the Tenant’s move. The Landlord did copy her son and daughter-in-law on three occasions, because they were moving into the rental unit and, as such, the Landlord wished to keep them informed. The N12 notice was personally delivered to the Tenant by the Landlord’s son, and the Landlord had informed the Tenant before hand.
The Landlord used her work email once to communicate with the Tenant when she sent the N12 notice to the Tenant, as she had a scanner at work and not at home.
It is the Tenant’s burden of proof to establish that the Landlord engaged in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant met the burden of proof, that the Landlord’s pattern of conduct amounted to harassment. On the contrary, I found the Landlord’s communications with Tenant reasonable, polite, courteous, and by no means excessive. The fact that the Landlord copied her son and daughter in-law on three communications with the Tenant and that she used her work email once also does not amount to a breach of the Act. Those communications were not made public, they were limited to the parties that had an interest in the matter. By no means were they vexatious.

The Landlord’s failure to withdraw her L2 application was due to the fact that Tenant owed rent to the Landlord and the Landlord wished to resolve all issues of the tenancy. In any case, that conduct occurred after the tenancy terminated and, as such, is not properly before me.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization]. (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,953.90. The Landlord Substantially Interfered with the Tenant’s Reasonable Enjoyment:

The Tenant filed her T2 application on September 27, 2024. She alleged that the Landlord has failed to take reasonable and appropriate steps to address the Tenant’s complaints about excessive noise from the upstairs tenant from February 2023 until December 2024, which she alleges has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she spoke to the property manager, [name] (LM), approximately 3 times between February 2023 and September 2023, and she wrote a formal email of complaint in December 2023 to the head office. The Tenant was made aware that the jurisdictional time limits prohibit a remedy beyond 1 year prior to the date the application was filed with the Board, which means I cannot grant a remedy in relation to any conduct occurring prior to September 27, 2023. The Tenant understood and wished to proceed.

The Tenant testified that her upstairs neighbour moved in around January 2023 and they got a dog in February 2023. This is when all of the ongoing noise issues started. At first the issue was the dog barking constantly when left alone, and when the Tenant spoke to her neighbouring tenant, the neighbour responded by calling her names. Then the upstairs neighbour started banging in the rental unit all night every night. The upstairs tenant would open and shut the balcony door frequently throughout the day and night, it sounded like she would drop her couch and sometimes her frames on the walls would be sideways.

The Tenant testified that after writing to the head office, one of the Landlord’s employees, [name], spoke to her and told her to keep track of the nights the noises were happening. The Tenant provided the information to the Landlord, who subsequently served an N5 notice of termination on the other tenant. The Tenant testified she had called the police on the upstairs tenant 11 times at around 2:00 a.m. or 3:00a.m. as the noise was so bad. The Tenant testified that when she would follow up with the head office, they would tell her they were working on it.

The Landlord asked the Tenant if she was aware the upstairs tenant had an autistic child that is responsible for the noise. The Tenant stated she is not aware and does not know whether the excessive noise is caused only by the child.

LM testified on behalf of the Landlord. She is the residence manager and first became aware of the noise complaints in 2024. When the Tenant would complain to her, she would pass all the information to head office about what she was told. LM also testified she tried to keep the peace and spoke to the upstairs tenant. LM also testified that she had personally heard the noises in the Tenant’s apartment and told the Tenant she would do her best, but it would be hard to take actions as the upstairs tenant has a child with a disability.

LM also testified that she is aware that 2 N5 notices were served in 2024, January and June, on the upstairs tenant in relation to the excessive noise. LM stated that the Landlord eventually moved the upstairs tenant into another building in a basement apartment. When asked why the move took so long, LM testified it took awhile for the upstairs tenant to decide what she wanted to do and she agreed to move to a new unit in November 2024.

LM testified that the Landlord offered another unit to the Tenant, however the Tenant wanted a unit with the same rent and one in which she could smoke, which was denied by the Landlord. When asked what other steps were taken by the Landlord, LM testified that they had asked the upstairs tenant to buy “puzzle tiles” for their floor to lessen the noise, but understood that they were expensive.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that they could not proceed on filing an L2 application to terminate the upstairs tenant’s tenancy as her child had a disability and the complaints related to issues caused by the disability. He further testified that there were no additional or alternative offers for sounding proofing and no actions were taken to address the excessive noise beyond offering the upstairs tenant an alternative rental unit and waiting for one to become available in December 2024.

I agree with the following statement in TNT-93077-17 (Re), 2017 CanLII 60310 (ON LTB) regarding a landlord’s obligation to respond to complaints about other tenants: 19. Section 22 of the RTA provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with a tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit. It is not sufficient for a landlord to merely refrain from conduct that substantially interferes; landlords have been held to have a positive obligation to take reasonable steps to provide tenants with reasonable enjoyment. The leading case on the issue is [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. [name]. [name].) [[name]].

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant experienced excessive noise coming from the neighbouring unit, and that they complained to the Landlord multiple times between September 2023 and December 2024. I am further satisfied that the Landlord did not respond reasonably to the Tenant’s complaints, thereby substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit. The Tenant testified that the noises were essentially a daily issue, especially at night. The Landlord did not seriously challenge the Tenant’s evidence about the frequency, duration, and intensity of the noise disturbances, and focused instead on why they did not take steps to address the noise.

Because the Landlord was aware that the excessive noise was linked to a disability, the Landlord had an obligation to accommodate the neighbouring tenant and their child short of undue hardship. However, this does not mean that regardless of the conduct, the Landlord could never proceed with filing an eviction application. I note that the LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 17: Human Rights discusses several Divisional Court cases in which a landlord has successfully established that they accommodated a tenant’s disability, which was linked to conduct that was interfering with other tenants’ enjoyment, to the point of undue hardship: see for example, Canadian Mental Health Association v. Warren, 2004 CanLII 16439 ([name]. Ct.).

However, in this case, unlike the landlord in the [name] case, the Landlord took minimal steps to address the excessive noise through accommodation. They did not seriously explore any modifications or renovations that might mitigate the noise or offer any other supports. Besides offering another unit and then waiting one year to move the upstairs tenant, the Landlord and their witness gave very little evidence regarding the steps they took to mitigate the ongoing substantial interference.

The Landlord had other options they could have considered or offered to help mitigate the excessive noise besides waiting for the upstairs tenant to agree to move, but they chose to do very little despite the significant impact the noise was having on the Tenant.

I am therefore satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, and that this interference occurred started in February 2023 and continued until the upstairs tenant moved out in December 2024. Remedies:

The Tenant has sought a total rent abatement from February 2023 to December 2024. Her rent is $967.31, and for the 23 months she claimed, that would total $22,248.13. However, as noted above, I am precluded from granting a remedy for any loss of enjoyment that took place before September 27, 2023.

The Tenant testified that the excessive noise significantly impacted her mental health. The noises took place all day and night, and she could not sleep even with noise cancelling headphones. The Tenant testified she only got a couple hours of sleep each night, and she went to a psychiatrist and asked for medical assistance in dying (MAID) as she could not continue the way things were going.
The Landlord stated that a 100% rent abatement would not be appropriate as the Tenant continued to reside in the rental unit and had access and had some enjoyment of the unit during that time.

In light of the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a 20% rent abatement from October 1, 2023 until December 1, 2024, which amount to $2,901.90. The rent abatement reflects the loss of enjoyment that the Tenant bargained and paid for but did not receive due to the Landlord’s failure properly address the excessive noise, and in arriving at this figure I have considered the impact that the noise had on the Tenant. I accept that the Tenant’s evidence that the noise had a significant impact on her mental health, and considered this when determining appropriate abatement.
ordered: The total amount Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,954.90. This amount represents: • $2,901.90 for a rent abatement; and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It was uncontested that the Landlords served the Tenants with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenants moved out because they received this notice.
The main issue between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants vacated the. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] (GT) testified that the Landlord gave them an informal N12 notice of termination giving them 90 days to vacate the unit. A copy of the email request was submitted as evidence.
GT testified that they tried to find an alternative unit but were unable to find anything affordable or comparable.
GT testified that she asked the Landlord for a reference letter to help them find a new unit, but the Landlord refused and without the letter they were unable to find a place.

GT testified that she told the Landlord that he needs to serve them with a formal N12 notice if he wanted them to move out and as a result the Landlord served them an N12 notice of termination, for personal use, on September 27, 2024, they found a place that day and vacated the unit on October 4, 2024.

GT testified that between October 2024 and January 2025, they would drive past the unit and see that no one had moved in. Photos, videos and a detailed list of observations from January 2025, through to June 29, 2025 when they seen the u-haul box, and then to May 4, 2025 showing continual signs of someone living in the unit.
GT testified that the in June 2025, the Landlord moved in, 9 months after they had vacated the unit.

GT testified that the move has caused financial hardship in many ways including rent which increased from $1,650.00 to $2,350.00, plus $300.00 pre month for electric heat, the inability to work rom home due to unreliable internet and the loss of business because the unit is too far for clients to travel to.
GT testified that above the rent differential in the amount of $8,400.00, they are seeking $200.00 in moving expenses and $723.20 in general compensation. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that he moved into the unit immediately, he did some repairs and painting and stayed in the unit except for nights he spent at his girlfriends due to paint fumes.
The Landlord testified that he works long hours, goes to the gym, visits family and friends and often gets home late.

The Landlord testified that the pictures and videos the Tenant submitted were during the day while he was at work. He further testified that the picture showing the snow not shoveled was of snow accumulation while he was at work and the photo showed previously piled snow.

The Landlord testified that the Tenants could have called, sent a text or came to his door and they would have been able to see his furniture in the unit, including the new bed for the second bedroom.
The Landlord testified that the uhaul box they seen in June 2025 was when his girlfriend was moving in with him. Analysis
The Tenants must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above.

The first and second elements of section 57(1)(a) are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of an N12 notice served by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord moved into the unit with a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, I find that the Landlord provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that he did move into the rental unit immediately after the Tenants moved out and still resides in the unit currently.

GT also gave straightforward and consistent evidence with respect to the lack of activity seen at the rental unit for the first nine months after they vacated the unit. I find this testimony consistent with the Landlord’s evidence that he moved into the unit, works late hours and may not always return directly home.

Therefore, I do not find that GT’s testimony regarding the lack of activity within the rental unit determinative on whether he moved in. For these reasons, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.
The Tenants have not proven all of the elements of the test required for their application to be successful; therefore the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] (the ‘Landlords) and [name] (the 'Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay the Tenant a total of $8,539.57 which represents: • $7,594.32 for rent differential • $892.25 for moving and storage fees • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application Evidence and Analysis

Section 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in clause 49 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) or 49 (2) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit; and • The N12 notice was given in bad faith.

There is no dispute that on or about May 16, 2023, the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act with a termination date of July 31, 2023, stating that the purchaser intends to move into the rental unit. It was also undisputed that the Tenants moved out in accordance with the notice on July 1, 2023, and returned the unit keys on July 9, 2023. The central factual dispute is whether the Purchaser occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated and whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith.

The Tenants testified that they had a good relationship with the Landlords and accepted that the Landlords needed to sell the property. After the Tenants vacated they stated they were shocked to find a listing on “condo.ca” advertising their former unit for rent. The Tenants submitted a copy of this advertisement which shows the unit was listed for rent on September 7, 2023, for $2,700.00 per month.

The Tenants further submitted a copy of the listing history for the rental unit. This document shows that the Purchaser’s contact date with her realtor to list the unit for lease was September 7, 2023, and that the unit was leased on October 1, 2023.

The Tenants testified that given the very short turn-around time of less than one month from the close date of the sale to the date the unit was listed for rent, they believe the Purchaser never moved in and that the N12 was served in bad faith.

The Landlords testified that they were experiencing financial hardship due to the increase in mortgage rates and felt their only option was to sell the rental unit. The Landlords stated they never met or spoke to the purchaser personally and that all communication was through their respective realtors. The Landlords expressly advised their realtor that the unit was tenanted. The Landlords testified that based on the information provided through their realtor, they believed the Purchaser required the unit for her own personal use and because of this belief, they served the Tenants with the N12 notice.

Both the Landlords and the Purchaser submitted a copy of the Agreement of Purchase and Sale (“APS”) for the rental unit. The close date of the purchase was August 11, 2023. The final paragraph on page 7 of 7 of the APS states: The Buyer hereby confirms that He/She is buying the Unit for His/Her own personal use as [name] and He/She will be staying in the apartment. As the [name] requires the vacant possession of the Unit, the [name] hereby is advised to go ahead with serving the N12 Notice to the Tenants.
The Purchaser does not dispute the rental unit was listed for rent as per the listing submitted by the Tenants and that she still owns the unit and still has tenants living there.

The Purchaser testified that she was only 26 years old at the time of purchasing the rental unit and she was very excited to be starting her independent life. Prior to purchasing the rental unit, the Purchaser was living with her parents.

The Purchaser stated she moved into the rental unit, but she quickly realized that living on her own made her feel anxious, disconnected from her family and very lonely; she did not enjoy living on her own as much as she thought she would. The Purchaser stated she reached out to her realtor to advise of the issue who encouraged her to give her living situation more time, but she felt she could not do so. The Purchaser testified she lived in the unit for approximately 3 weeks.

The Purchaser submitted photos date stamped on August 24, 2023, which she stated are of her family in the unit for a housewarming party. The Purchaser also submitted correspondence with the condo management to properly set up her name on the buzzer for the unit and the “Owner Registration Form” which is required for the condo management.

The Purchaser further submitted a letter from her realtor, [name] (S.A.). The letter outlines S.A.’s opinion on the good faith intention of the Purchaser and her intent to occupy the unit for her own use. It should be noted that S.A. was not present to testify and as such the letter is hearsay evidence. While hearsay evidence is admissible at the Board, it is generally given less weight than credible oral testimony that is subject to cross examination. This is particularly true when the hearsay evidence is opinion based which lacks objective verification and relies on personal bias and limited perspectives. For these reasons I gave this letter very little weight when making my determinations. Did the Purchaser move in?
Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find on the balance of probabilities that the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit. I say this for the following reasons.

The close date of the APS was August 11, 2023, and the listing history confirms the Purchaser contacted her realtor to lease the unit on September 7, 2023, just 21 days later. I find it unlikely that the Purchaser moved in all her belongings, unpacked, and then made the decision to move again in that short time.

Additionally, the Purchaser’s evidence does not assist me with making a finding that she moved in. The photos of her housewarming party are primarily taken with her family on the balcony looking outward. One photo is at the kitchen counter and none of the photos give any perspective of whether there were furniture or any personal belongings in the unit. The buzzer code information and the Owner registration form would be required even if the Purchaser never moved in as she was the new owner of the unit. The buzzer would need to be properly named so that potential tenants could be let in for viewings. Finally, the Purchaser testified she did not book the elevator for her move as she moved in over the course of several days and did not require such a service. I find this contradicts the Purchaser’s testimony of how excited she was to move into her new unit and start her independent life.

Given all of the above, I find the Tenant’s have successfully met their burden to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Was the N12 given in bad faith?

The court of appeal for Ontario recently clarified the law regarding bad faith applications when an N12 notice is served pursuant to section 49 of the Act. At paragraph 43 of Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (“Elkins v. [name]”) the court stated the following: On a plain reading of ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b), the landlord’s conduct is linked to the Purchaser’s good faith. Section 49(1) permits the landlord to, on behalf of the Purchaser, give the tenant a termination notice so long as the Purchaser, in good faith, requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. Section 57(1)(b) requires the Board to determine, among other things, whether the landlord gave the s. 49 termination notice in bad faith. When ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b) are read together, it is clear that the object of those provisions is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant. Accordingly, the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant a s. 49 termination notice…. [emphasis added]

The Court further addressed the LTB’s jurisdiction to make an order against the Purchaser if it finds that the Purchaser acted in bad faith at paragraph 58: While s. 57(3) sets out specific orders that can be made against a landlord who acts in bad faith in giving a s. 49 termination notice, it also empowers the Board to make any order it “considers appropriate”. Thus, if the Board finds that a landlord did not act in bad faith but the Purchaser did, s. 57(3) gives the Board the power to make appropriate orders against the Purchaser. This “gives teeth” to the good faith requirement on the part of Purchasers in s. 49(1).

It is clear from this decision that, depending on the specific circumstances of the case, the landlord, purchaser, or both may be held liable in a bad faith application such as this. It is also clear that the obligation of good faith is ongoing and that it is insufficient to assess only whether the Landlord acted in bad faith in giving the N12 on behalf of the purchaser. The Board must also look at the Purchaser’s intention.

In this case I find that the Landlords acted in good faith. I accept the Landlords’ testimony that they placed the rental unit on the market due to extenuating financial circumstances. This is not unusual, nor is it uncommon. The relationship between the Tenants and the Landlords was good and the Tenants stated they had no reason to believe that the Landlords were not acting in good faith on behalf of the Purchaser when they served the N12 notice.

The Landlords were provided with information that the Purchaser wanted to occupy the unit for their own use and had no reason to think otherwise. The APS contained a clause with respect to the unit being tenanted. I do not find that the Landlords could have done anything further to ascertain the true substance of the Purchaser’s intentions and as such, I find the Landlords at all material times acted in good faith.
However, for the reasons that follow and on the balance of probabilities, I find the Purchaser did not act in good faith.

The Purchaser testified that she would have kept the Tenants had her intention been to use the unit as a rental property. However, during cross-examination, she stated she could not recall whether she contacted the Tenants to offer the unit back and later clarified that she made no attempt to reach out once she realized she could not remain in the unit. This inconsistency undermines her credibility. Given that less than a month passed between the Tenants vacating the unit and it being listed for rent, the Purchaser could easily have asked her realtor to help contact the former Tenants and offer them the opportunity to return.
I find the Purchaser’s testimony that she did not remember if she contacted the Tenants was disingenuous and reflective of a possible awareness of wrongdoing.

The unit was listed for rent at a rate approximately $800.00 more per month than what the Tenants had been paying. The Purchaser’s failure to consider contacting the former Tenants, combined with her testimony that she never contemplated selling the unit, supports the conclusion that her intention was always to use the property for rental income. Evicting the Tenants enabled the Purchaser to secure a higher rent than what the Tenants were paying to the previous owners.

Since the Tenants have proven all the required elements of section 57(1)(b) of the Act the application must be granted. In accordance with the Court’s findings in [name] v. Van [name], pursuant to section 57(3), and for the reasons set out above, I find that the apportionment of liability should be placed solely at the feet of the Purchaser. Remedies

In their application the Tenants sought the following remedies: • Costs relating to the difference in rent between the Tenants old unit and their new rental unit. • Costs associated with moving and storage [name] fine.
At the outset of the hearing the Tenants submitted they are no longer seeking the administrative fine. Rent differential
The Tenants resided in the rental unit for 2 years. They moved into the unit in April 2021 and had intended on living there indefinitely.

The Tenants testified they found a new unit close to their previous rental unit that was the same size and number of bedrooms and also had parking as their previous unit had. However, the Tenants’ old unit included a storage locker and their new unit did not.

The Tenants testified their previous rent was $1,867.14 and their new rent was $2,500.00 per month. The Tenants submitted a copy of their new lease agreement to substantiate the rent differential they are claiming.

In considering a rent differential, the Board must consider whether the rental units are comparable, although they need not be exact. The units in this case are very comparable in size and parking amenities. The Tenants lost the use of a storage locker that was included with their monthly rent. The Tenants had lived in the rental unit for more than a full year and therefore I find it reasonable that they should be awarded one full year of rent differential. The Purchaser shall be ordered to pay a rent differential in the amount of $632.86 per month for 12 months totalling $7,594.32. Moving and storage costs
The Tenants are seeking reimbursement of $892.25 which consists of their costs to rent a moving truck and 1 year of storage locker fees.

The Tenants submitted receipts for their moving truck rental from U-Haul in the amount of $52.25 and also submitted their storage locker rental agreement. As stated above, the Tenants previously had use of a storage locker with their former rental unit that was not included when they had to find a new rental unit. The rental agreement states that the Tenants paid $70.00 per month for the storage locker. The rental agreement was for a fixed term from July 1, 2023, to June 30, 2024.

I am satisfied that the Tenants incurred reasonable moving and storage costs. In the circumstances, I find it appropriate to award the Tenants the full amount of out of pocket storage costs for 1 year. An order will issue for the Purchaser to reimburse the Tenants $892.25 for their moving and storage expenses.
As the Tenants were successful in proving their application, the Tenants are also entitled to the cost of filing their application in the amount of $53.00.
ordered: The total amount the Purchaser shall pay the Tenants is $8,539.57. This amount represents: • $7,594.32 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from July 1, 2023, to June 30, 2024. • $892.25 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchaser shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 10, 2026.

If the Purchaser does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 10, 2026, the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.

The parties agreed on the following issues: • mice infestation. • wasp infestation. • inadequate heat during winter months. • improperly functioning and deteriorated windows. • a rotting windowsill. • holes in the siding and exterior structure. • holes under the bathroom sink and behind the stove. • plumbing and frozen pipe concerns. • improper hydro meter allocation causing the Tenants to pay electricity for another unit.
The Tenants relied primarily on their disclosure package containing dated maintenance requests, photographs, text messages, emails, notices of entry, utility concerns, and supporting documents.

The Tenant [name] [name] gave some testimony on the mice infestation beginning on September 8, 2024. She provided photographs of dropping, for the following dates: • September 16, 2024 • September 18, 2024 • September 19, 2024 • September 20, 2024 • September 21, 2024 • September 22, 2024 • October 5, 2024 • October 6, 2024 • October 9, 2024 • October 17, 2024 • The Tenants vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2026.

Ms. [name]name] explained that the infestation worsened after the nearby house fire displace rodents. The Tenant’s deep cleaned the rental unit, removed food sources, and continued to find droppings. She stated pest control did not attend the unit until October 17, 2024, approximately 39 days after advising the Landlord.

The Landlord did not dispute the infestation. [name] stated the contractors delay were outside the Landlord’s control. Additionally, [name] stated that the Landlord knew the issue existed and acknowledged pest control attendance was delayed. Wasp Infestation

Ms. [name]name] gave testimony about the Wasp Infestation. She stated this was reported to the Landlord April 15, 2024. They found both standard wasps and black wasps inside the unit and near the crawlspace. The concern was significant because they had a dog and feared stings and nesting in hidden areas.

She stated that the issue persisted over two summer seasons. The Landlord inspected occurred, but no removal of the wasps was completed. The Tenants remained in the unit until January 2026 without resolution.

The Landlord’s evidence was that pest contractor [name] advised treatment could only be completed during certain times of year and that the landlord relied on that advice. I accept that certain pest treatments may be seasonal.

However, the evidence shows no completed resolution despite the passage of two seasons. The Landlord remained responsible for ensuring the issue was resolved. I find the Landlord failed to do so. Heat Issue

The Tenant testified that they experience significant heating problems during January 2025 and January 2026. Temperature fell as low as 11°C, 12°C, and 16°C. Despite the thermostat being set to much higher. It was discovered by the Tenants that there was cold air entering through defective windows, floor heating was not functioning properly, and insufficient insulation.

The Tenant presented evidence repeatedly requesting the Landlord for urgent assistances. The Landlord provided space heaters, but they were not suitable for all rooms and did not resolve the underlying problem.

The Landlord’s evidence was that after-hours communications were often made by text rather than emergency contact, and that contractor scheduling in the area was difficult. [name] stated, “everything just seemed to take a very long time.”
She acknowledged the issue should have been resolved sooner.

I find that the Landlord had notice of the issue and sufficient opportunity to correct it. The use of temporary space heaters was not an adequate substitute for the Tenant’s rental unit. The statement that “everything seems to take a very long time” does not excuse the Landlord from fulfilling their maintenance obligations. Hydro [name]16. The Tenants discovered that floor heating for another unit was being controlled by their breaker panel and charged to their hydro meter. This meant they were paying electricity costs for another unit. 17. This was confirmed by: • electrician attendance, • contractor verbal confirmation, • text messages from the Landlord, • the Landlord’s own acknowledgment. 18. The Tenant raised this issue repeatedly to the Landlord. The Landlord expressly admitted this problem. [name] stated, “We agree that the hydro should have been taken care of.” 19. I find that [name] statement means that the Landlord expressly agreed during the hearing that the hydro issue should have been corrected and that the floor heating for another unit was improperly connected. Resulting in the Tenants paying utility costs they should not have had too. 20. I find that this is not merely a maintenance issue; it is also improper utility allocation. I fully accept the Tenants’ claim for hydro reimbursement. Windows and Rotting Windowsill 21. The Tenants reported: • windows that would not close properly. • severe drafts. • a deteriorated living room window. • a bathroom window left unrepaired. • a rotting windowsill causing mould concerns 22. The Tenants testified they had to repeatedly bleach and manage mould concerns themselves. The Tenants admitted that only partial repairs to the windows were completed but that two windows remained unresolved at move-out date January 31, 2026. 23. The Landlord’s evidence was that contractors measured windows, scheduling was difficult, and some windows were eventually replaced. 24. I find that partial compliance does not eliminate the Landlord maintenance obligations. I find section 20 was breached. Siding, exterior holes, and structural concerns 25. The Tenants established multiple deficiencies in the rental property, including deteriorated siding, holes in the exterior structure, roof damage, insulation issues, and concerns about pest entry. Although some repairs were completed in the upper roof areas, several holes remained unaddressed, particularly those contributing to pest intrusion and inadequate insulation. 26. The Landlord acknowledged these deficiencies but stated that re-siding the entire house was not within his budget. However, financial limitations do not constitute a valid defence under section 20, as landlords are obligated to maintain the property in a good state of repair regardless of cost considerations. Accordingly, I find that a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations occurred. 27. The Landlord’s evidence was largely not a denial of the Tenants’ complaints but an explanation for delay. 28. The Landlord testified: • repairs were attempted through approved contractors. • contractor availability in the area was limited. • scheduling difficulties delayed attendance. • some contractors became reluctant to attend after learning visits had been recorded. • by-law inspections and contractor coordination created delays. • the hydro issue should have been corrected. • some pest control limitations were seasonal. • the Landlord did not believe the amount claimed was reasonable. 29. The Landlord stated the owner would be willing to pay approximately $8,000.00. 30. I accept that some delays may have been affected by contractor availability. However, those operational challenges do not displace the Landlord’s legal obligations. Analysis 31. I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex and failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. The Tenants’ evidence was detailed and supported by documents and photographs. Most importantly, when asked directly, [name] stated “I am agreeing with all of their evidence. I can’t disagree with it.” 32. She also stated, “their dates are correct.” This is highly significant. Because there was effectively no challenge to the factual record, I assign substantial weight to the Tenants’ evidence. I find that the Landlord’s evidence primarily addressed explanation and mitigation, not denial. 33. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 34. In this case, I find that the Landlord’s evidence does not rebut the existence of the maintenance failures. It primarily addresses mitigation and reasonableness of compensation. Remedies 35. Mice Infestation -The Tenants sought 100% rent abatement for September and October 2024 in the amount of $3,000.00, on the basis that an active mice infestation rendered the unit substantially unfit. I find that the mice issue was serious. Droppings were repeatedly found, multiple follow-ups were required, pest control did not attend for approximately 39 days, and the situation created sanitation concerns and significant stress. However, a 100% rent abatement is not appropriate. The unit remained habitable, and the infestation was treated. A more proportionate assessment is 60–65% of two months’ rent. I therefore award $2,000.00. 36. Wasp Infestation - The issue persisted over two summer seasons, inspections occurred, but no effective removal was completed. The Tenants had legitimate safety concerns and the issue remained unresolved at move-out. However, the issue was seasonal and did not render the entire unit unusable. I therefore award $1,500.00. 37. Heat Issue - Temperatures fell as low as 11°C to 16°C. This is below acceptable standards and affects health and safety. The issue recurred over two winters and space heaters were not adequate. Overlap with window deficiencies has been considered. I therefore award $1,868.31. 38. Hydro [name] unit’s floor heating was connected to the Tenants’ electrical panel, resulting in payment for electricity not consumed. The Landlord acknowledged the issue. I therefore award $1,889.31. 39. Window and [name]The Tenants requested 75% of rent abatement of 15 months = $16,875.00. Additionally, they requested 20% of * months for the windowsill = $2,400.00. Lastly, the Tenants requested 25% of 8 months for siding = $3,000.00. Total the Tenants are seeking in this proportion exceeds. I will acknowledge that the Tenants experienced drafts, windows that would not close, cold air infiltration, mold concerns, and exterior deterioration. Some repairs were completed but deficiencies remained. I assess the issue globally to avoid duplication. I therefore award $5,500.00. 40. [name] of $53.00 is appropriate given the Tenants are successful with their application
ordered: The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $12,810.62. This amount represents: • $12,757.62 for a rent abatement for the period ending January 31, 2026. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenant filed a T2 application on October 6, 2024. The Tenant alleges the Landlord or the Landlord agent harassed the Tenant. Tenant evidence
The Tenant stated that he had an arrangement with the Landlord and supplied postdated cheques to the Landlord to pay for his lawful rent.
The Tenant submitted documentary and photographic evidence to the Board to support his allegations of harassment.

The Tenant stated that on or around November 3, 2023 he started receiving email notices from the Landlord’s automated tenant management system ([name]) that he was in arrears of rent and to contact management.

The Tenant stated that he also received two N4 notices for nonpayment of rent and eviction form the Landlord regarding the Landlord’s claims for unpaid rent, however the Tenant had provided post dated cheques to the Landlord.
The Tenant submitted photograph copies of the N4 notices.
The Tenant stated that he would receive rent arrears reminder emails from the Landlord’s [name] system once a month despite his rent being fully paid.
The Tenant stated he suffered mental health issues and the Landlord’s monthly rent arrears reminders for almost 18 months created stress that the Tenant believes was a form of harassment.
The Tenant is seeking remedies as a result of the Landlord’s alleged harassment. Landlord evidence
The Landlord’s position is the Landlord does not dispute the Tenant was receiving email from the automated system.

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that from the fist email the Tenant received the Landlord’s employees had addressed the Tenant’s concern and assured him of the system error and to disregard the emails.

The Landlord agent testified the Landlord had acquired a tenant management system ([name]) to manage payments made by tenants. The system automatically sent out email reminders to tenants if no payment had been received within 2 to 3 days of the rent coming due.
The Landlord agent stated that the Tenant provided postdated cheques and the system had not been configured to accommodate postdated cheques.
The Landlord agent stated that [name] was not set up to handle manually deposited cheques and account for a delay in banks administration times for cheques to clear.

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that from the initial emails the Tenant received the Landlord’s staff had informed the Tenant of the issue with the automated system and to disregard the emails.

The Landlord’s legal representative submits that from the Tenant’s first contact to the Landlord the Landlord addressed the Tenant’s concerns and acted reasonably and quickly to the Tenant’s inquiries and concerns.

The Landlord’s legal representative points to the emails contained within the Tenant’s evidence package, where the Tenant makes the first inquiry on November 3, 2024 and the Landlord’s Assistant General Manager [name] responds to the Tenant’s inquiry on receiving a rent arrears reminder. The exchange between the Tenant and [name] is as follows: Friday November 3, 2023; 4:26 pm From the Tenant to the Landlord Hi there I believe that you have received post dated cheques until April could you kindly confirm that this is true? Sunday November 5, 2023; 5:16 pm I hope you had a lovely weekend. Please don’t’ worry about any emails you receive from Yardi. We have received cheques until April 2024. Cheques are cashed on the 3rd of each business day of each month and do not hit your account until 3 buisness days later. If you are ever owing any funds, we will personally contact you from this email address.
In another email dated Tuesday December 12, 2023 at 4:07 pm the Tenant notifies the Landlord of another notice to end the tenancy due to nonpayment of rent.
A Landlord employee responds to the Tenant at 11:37 am telling the Tenant to “Please disregard this notice.”

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that while the Landlord acknowledges the emails were sent every month the Landlord’s position is that the emails do not rise to the level of harassment and at best may represent a small inconvenience.
On the day of the hearing the Landlord agent stated that changes had been made to [name] that now eliminated arrears emails to the Tenant. The Act and Analysis

Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Landlord not to harass, etc. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 23.

Although the word harass is not defined in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines "harassment" as: “…engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”
While I acknowledge the first email received by the Tenant may have been a surprise, I note the Landlord took immediate and reasonable measures in responding to the Tenant.
I note that the Landlord’s employee [name], assured the Tenant the Landlord had postdated cheques and that if there were issues the Landlord would “…respond personally”.
The very next month the Tenant makes another inquiry after [name] had addressed his initial concerns and a different Landlord employee advised the Tenant to “…disregard this notice.”

I am not persuaded by the Tenant’s testimony that he believed he was at risk of being in arrears and the stress he claims it caused given the Landlord’s continuous responses of assurance that he is not in arrears and to disregard the emails.

I say this in consideration of an email, almost one year from when the emails from Yardi started dated Monday September 9, 2024 at 4:33 pm from the Tenant to the Landlord that states: Hi there I know I send this about every month but I was just making sure that you do in fact have the rent check for September if not I could come by tomorrow and give you a new one thanks in advance.

The Landlord employee responds on the same day at 4:53 pm: Hello [name], Please be advised that we have your post dated checks in the office. Due to the long weekend, we're having some delays depositing it and reflecting on your account. You are OK to ignore any reminder emails you may be receiving, they are automated messages being sent directly from the accounting software.

The email sent from the Tenant on September 9, 2024 does not appear to indicate a sense of fear from the Tenant that the Landlord may take action against him and the Tenant suggests he could, “…come by tomorrow and give you a new one.”.

I am not persuaded that the Tenant could reasonably interpret the emails as harassment given the immediate and reasonable response by the Landlord’s employees and the explanation the Tenant had received regarding the limitations of the [name] system with cheques.
I prefer the evidence submission of the Landlord and I find the Landlord agent credible in his testimony regarding the limitations of physical cheques with the Landlord’s Yardi system.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has not proved the allegations the Landlord or Landlord agent has harassed the Tenant.
Given all the above the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 13, 2026 ____________________________
