issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Jr. and [name] (the 'Landlords') altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: The Tenant filed their application on October 7, 2024.

At the hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative requested an adjournment so that the application can be amended to add additional ground(s) (substantial interference/harassment) and remedies. He submitted that the legal representative from their law firm who originally filed the application in October 2024 did not include details and particulars pertaining these grounds and they ought to have been included in the application. In other words, the application was not completed correctly. When the Board inquired as to why the amendment was not done in advance of the hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative claimed the details contained in the application had not been brought to his attention and claimed that he had been preparing (which I understand to mean preparing for the hearing) and did not consider an amendment. He also confirmed the issues he intends to add with respect to the additional ground(s) are still ongoing.

The Landlord’s legal representative opposed the adjournment and argued that it would be prejudicial to the Landlords. His position was that the Tenant’s legal representative had control over the application for 14 months and they had more than enough time to amend the application. He submitted that the Landlords had dedicated time and resources to attending the hearing and were prepared to defend the allegations as pled on the application.

Based on the submissions of the parties, and after considering the factors set out in the LTB’s Rule of Procedure 21 and Interpretation Guideline 1 pertaining to adjournments, the Board declined the adjournment request. An adjournment is not an automatic right, and the Tenant’s legal representative did not provide a sufficient explanation as to why the amendment could not have been done in advance of the hearing. The application was filed in October 2024 and any further delay in the proceedings would be unduly prejudicial to the Landlord. The Tenant and their legal representative had ample opportunity to review the application and to file an amendment. Since the newly raised issues are ongoing the Tenant may file another application to address those issues. Merits of the application
As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

In the application, the Tenant claims that the Landlord breached section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’), which reads: A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. [Emphasis Added]
The Tenant’s central allegations on their application pertain to the Tenant being locked out of a storage room.

The Tenant testified that on July 9, 2024, a noticed was posted on the storage room entry door that if the tenant wanted access to the storage, he was to contact the landlord [name] ([name]) [name]. The Tenant confirmed he did not contact the Landlords to have the lock removed from the storage room, and that lock to the entry of the storage room was removed sometime in July 2025. He claimed that the storage unit contained his tools, manuscripts, and other landscaping tools.

The Tenant further testified he had a lease agreement with the previous landlord and that that the storage unit was part his lease agreement. A copy of the lease agreement between the former landlord and the Tenant was filed as evidence with the Board, and I note that the agreement references that the service of the storage space is included with the lawful rent.
The storage room is adjacent to the rear of the Tenant’s rental unit.
The issue is whether changing the locks to a storage room is captured by s. 24 of the Act since that provision refers to the landlord changing the locking system on the “rental unit”.

The term “rental unit” is defined in s. 2(1) of the Act and it means any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises. Thus, it’s clear from the plain wording of this provision that it prohibits a landlord from altering a locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or giving entry to the residential complex, without giving the tenant a replacement key, which would prevent a tenant from accessing their rental unit. The provision is wide in its application because there are some living accommodations that have front entrances and/or lobbies/hallways, which a tenant would need to enter to obtain access to their rental unit.

The purpose of this provision is to prevent an illegal lock out situation where a tenant is denied/prevented access to their rental unit during their occupancy. This is supported by the fact that if the Board is satisfied the landlord has breached subsection 24 of the Act, then pursuant to subsection 31(3) of the Act, the LTB can order the landlord to allow the tenant to regain possession of the rental unit and refrain from renting the unit to anyone else. Under subsection 31(4) of the Act, if the landlord does not voluntarily comply with the LTB's order by allowing the tenant to regain possession of the rental unit, the tenant can obtain possession by enforcing the LTB's order through the Sheriff's office.

Based on the Tenant’s own evidence adduced at the hearing, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords have breached subsection 24 of the Act. The Tenant’s own evidence establishes that the storage unit was not part of the rental unit, since it was not used for a living accommodation. It was used to store tools. The lease agreement between the former landlord and the Tenant also references that the storage unit is a service that is provided to the Tenant and that the storage room is adjacent to the rental unit. Thus, the storage unit is not part of the rental unit and is part of the residential complex. Pursuant to section 18 of the Act, the terms in the lease agreement between the Tenant and the former landlord are deemed to continue as covenants running with the land between the current Landlords and the Tenant. This means the storage unit continued not being a part of the rental unit. The rental unit is in an apartment building (multiplex) which contains 5 units. Both parties agreed the storage unit is part of the residential complex. However, it is not part of the rental unit. Thus, the storage unit does not fall within the purview of subsection 24 of the Act as it is not an illegal lock out from a rental unit.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 02, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegation of disrepair to the washing machine. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $778.00 for their out of pocket expenses and application filing fee, on or before May 24, 2026. Request to Reschedule Filed by the Landlord

While no one was present at the hearing on the Landlord’s behalf, it appears that the Landlord wrote to the Board on April 17, 2026 requesting to reschedule the matter as they were out of the country between April 22 and May 7, 2026. A copy of their flight itinerary was submitted with the request.
Since the request was not on consent of the parties, it could not be actioned prior to the hearing. It is unclear why the Landlord did not send someone on their behalf.
At the hearing, I invited submissions from the Tenant with respect to the request to reschedule.
The Tenant submits the matter should proceed as the Landlord made no efforts to communicate this with the Tenant or seek their consent.
A similar situation arose in Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028 where the tenants requested an adjournment of the LTB hearing and did not appear at the hearing. The LTB proceeded in their absence.

In that case, the Court found at paragraph 7 the following: [7] … As of the date of the hearing, no adjournment had been granted, no evidence had been provided to support an adjournment request, and neither then tenants nor an agent on their behalf attended the hearing. There is no argument available for appeal that the LTB proceeded in a procedurally unfair manner in holding the hearing, as scheduled, in these circumstances. ..

Similarly, in this application, the Board had not granted the Landlord’s request to reschedule, the evidence submitted was a flight itinerary – it is unclear whether the Landlord actually boarded this flight nor is it clear why the Landlord was unable to attend the hearing virtually and finally, no agent of the Landlord was at the hearing to provide further clarity on this request.
Therefore, the request to reschedule was denied and I proceeded to hear the Tenant’s evidence. Interference Allegations on Disrepair Application

At the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue with respect to the allegation of interferences related to the Landlord’s behaviour, in the application for disrepair- particularly points 2, 4 and 5 on the particulars of the Tenant’s T6 application.
The Tenant understood that the application was about maintenance issues and restricted to the issue of the washing machine and the windows in the house. T6 APPLICATION
By way of background, this tenancy began on April 1, 2025 and ended on April 1, 2026 when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The lawful monthly rent was $2,400.00.
The Tenant described the residential complex as a house with two units: the main floor where he resided consisted of three bedrooms and a bathroom. The basement was rented to another tenant.
With respect to the issue of the disrepair of the windows, as the Tenant does not seek a remedy for this issue, the adjudication of this issue is not necessary.

With respect to the issue of the washing machine, the Tenant testified that in July 2025, the dryer stopped working; he explained that when it was switched to the on position, there would be no power or motion. The Tenant testified that when the Landlord was informed of the issue right away, the Landlord’s response was, it was not his responsibility and that the Tenant had to figure it out on his own. Text message correspondence between the parties was submitted into evidence in support of this assertion.

The Tenant testified that they hired a technician to attend the property and inspect the issue who recommended that the machine needed to be replaced but was able to fix the issue temporarily which led to the machine working properly for a month until the issue arose again.

The Tenant informed the Landlord again whose response did not change and so they asked the technician to find a replacement machine that was second-hand which was eventually replaced on September 29, 2025.
The Tenant seeks reimbursement for the costs they incurred related to the technician’s investigation and attendance and the eventual replacement of the washing machine.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. Once informed of the issue in July, it was the Landlord’s responsibility, no matter what the lease said, to investigate the issue and ensure it is repaired. But the Landlord failed to do so and put the onus on the Tenant.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Landlord made no effort to repair the issue or investigate it and so I find the Tenant is entitled to a remedy for the Landlord’s failure to act and for the Tenant having to resolve the disrepair issue. Remedies

Finally with respect to the remedies sought by the Tenant, at the hearing, the Tenant clarified that the Tenant seeks their out-of-pocket expenses related to the consultation of the technician for the washing machine of $180.00 for attendance and inspection on two separate occasions and the purchase of a second-hand machine of $550.00 totaling $730.00. I find this amount is reasonable and shall be awarded in full.

The Tenant confirms the claim for damages of $550.00 is the same claim for the purchase of the second-hand washing machine identified in their out-of-pocket expenses and the claim for repairs of $620.00 was put forth in error.
ordered: T he application is amend to reflect the rental unit as MAIN FLOOR.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $778.00. This amount represents: • $730.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred to fix and replaced the washing machine; and • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants filed an application alleging the Landlords failed to pay $3,500.00 as compensation pursuant to section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act).
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $3,548.00. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant testified that on August 1, 2024, the Landlords served him with an N12 Notice with a termination date of August 31, 2024. The Tenant submitted into evidence both the August 1, 2024 email and the N12 Notice.

The Tenant stated that he understood the Landlords’ elderly parents required the rental unit for their own use. As a result, he did not dispute the N12 Notice and moved out of the unit on October 2, 2024. He returned the keys to the Landlords the following day, October 3, 2024.
The monthly rent was $3,500.00. The Tenant submitted that he did not receive the compensation required under the Act and seeks this amount through the present application.
The Landlord did not ask any questions of the Tenant during cross-examination. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant confirmed that she returned the keys to the Landlords on October 3, 2024. She testified that prior to moving out the Landlords sent her numerous listings for available rental units, none of which were owned by them.
The Tenant experienced difficulty securing a new rental unit but ultimately moved into one of the units for which the Landlords had provided a listing.
The Landlord did not pose any questions to the Tenant during cross-examination. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord testified that she believed the Tenants intended to vacate on their own when the one-year lease term expired on August 31, 2024. She also stated that she had previously informed the Tenants that her parents had health issues and required the use of the rental unit.

The Landlord further testified that she received an email from the Tenant requesting an N12 Notice so that the Tenant could provide it to their employer. She stated that this was the reason she sent the August 1, 2024 email with the N12 Notice attached. Notably, the Landlord chose not to disclose this email and it was therefore not before the Board.

The Landlord submitted that the N12 Notices were “issued incorrectly.” When asked to clarify, she explained that the N12 Notices issued to the Tenants contained flaws, including incorrect termination dates and improper service on the Tenants. On this basis, the Landlord argued that the N12 Notice was invalid and therefore did not trigger any entitlement to compensation under the Act.

The Landlord also submitted that, because the Tenants ultimately moved into a rental unit for which she had provided the listing, this should be considered sufficient in lieu of providing the compensation required under the Act. Analysis

Section 48.1 of the Act states: 48.1 A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48
It is undisputed that the Landlords served the Tenants with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and did not pay the compensation required by the Act.

The Landlords submit that they should not be liable to pay compensation because: • the Tenants always intended to vacate at the end of the lease term; • the N12 Notice was invalid due to errors and improper service; and • the Tenants ultimately moved into a new unit that the Landlords had shown them.

The parties agree that the Tenants vacated because the Landlords’ parents required possession of the unit for their own use. The Landlords argue that the Tenants were leaving regardless of the N12 Notice and therefore section 48.1 does not apply. I disagree. Where a landlord serves an N12 Notice and the tenancy terminates as a result, the Act requires that compensation be paid. I find the Tenants’ evidence credible that they were exercising their rights when they sought an N12 Notice and that they vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving that notice. The Landlords elected not to submit the alleged email from the Tenants concerning their request for the N12 Notice, and I draw an adverse inference from this omission. I therefore find that the tenancy was terminated as a result of the Landlords serving the Tenants with the N12 Notice.

The Landlords also argue that the N12 Notice was invalid or improperly served, and therefore section 48.1 is not triggered. Again, I disagree. A landlord cannot rely on defects in their own notice to avoid a statutory obligation to compensate the tenant. To accept this position would allow landlords to benefit from their own errors. This concept is found in both [name] v. [organization], 2021 CanLii 146522 and [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 where the Courts found that a landlord who initiates a termination process with a statutory notice assumes legal responsibilities and cannot treat themselves simply as a passive messenger.

Lastly, the Landlords argue that because they showed the Tenants various listings, and the Tenants ultimately rented one of those units, no compensation is owing. I do not accept this interpretation. Section 48.1 contemplates the landlord offering the tenant another unit owned by the landlord they can rent directly. I find that “offer” within the meaning of the Act requires the landlord to offer a unit they own and are able to lease to the tenant, not simply showing the tenant an available unit to rent.
As the Landlords served an N12 Notice and failed to pay the required compensation, they owe the Tenants $3,500.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $3,548.00 This amount represents: • $3,500.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It was uncontested that the Landlords served the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenant moved out because she received this notice.
The central factual dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period after the Tenant vacated.
It is uncontested that the Landlord has not moved into the rental unit as of the date of the hearing, 20 months after the Tenant vacated. Tenant evidence
The Tenant testified that she moved out of the unit on September 30, 2024 and that she moved only 3 blocks away, so her and the neighbors have seen the unit vacant and renovations being done.
The Tenant testified that as a result of having to move her rent has increased from $1,400.00 to $2,500.00 per month plus utilities. She is also seeking $6,000.00 in general compensation.
The Tenant testified that the rental unit was in good condition when she moved out. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that this is his first home purchase and he bought the house to live in. He testified that the day he received possession of the house he served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination, which was dismissed for non-payment of the required compensation, and then he immediately served the Tenant with another N12 notice on February 8, 2024.

The Landlord testified that he attended the unit October 1, 2024, the day after the Tenant vacated, to clean the unit in preparation to move in, when he found mold and a hole in the floor under the flooring.

The Landlord testified that when he viewed the unit prior to purchasing it, the house was very cluttered, and he had been unable to see the extent of any damages. He further submitted that the Tenant had lived in the unit for over 10 years.
The Landlord testified that he wanted to fix the house up before moving in so he applied for permits to do the work and he was then informed that the house was an illegal duplex.

The Landlord testified that above applying for the permit for the work he also had to deal with bylaws for the for the approval of the duplex which took until October 2025, at which time it failed the fire inspection and required additional renovations.
The Landlord testified that he started the renovations in November 2025, and they are now complete and he is just waiting for the inspection to pass so he can move in.
The Landlord testified that it has always been, since the purchase of the home, his intention to move into the home and he will be moving in as soon as he receives approval. Analysis

While there has been a 20-month delay for the Landlord to move in, I find the Landlord’s explanation to be reasonable. The Landlord was unaware of the mold and the hole in the floor of the unit, and he was also unaware that the home was not legally zoned as a duplex. The rezoning and then the required renovation to both units is required by the municipality, were essential and the reason for the delay of him moving into the unit. These were issues out of his control.

Furthermore, the Landlord’s non-rental of the unit to other tenants and his testimony that he will still be moving into the unit align with his stated intentions and the conclusion that there was no bad faith in his actions.
Given the circumstances, I find that the Landlord will be moving into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time.
The Tenant has not proven all of the elements of the test required for her application to be successful. Therefore, her application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the “Seller Landlord') and/or [name] (the ‘Purchaser Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, [name] must pay $7,000.00 to the Tenant by May 25, 2026.
The residential unit is a single family dwelling located at [address]reet, Cornwall, Ontario.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the party and I have considered the party’s submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (TC)

TC provided me with a copy of the transfer of the property which closed on January 1, 2025 and the Purchaser Landlord is confirmed as [name]. The Tenant provided an evidence package, [name] that included several documents including this one. 6. [name] testified that she received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on July 3, 2024 with a termination date of September 3, 2024. The notice stated that the purchaser of the property required the rental unit for their residential occupation. 7. [name] stated that she received a text message from the Seller Landlord on July 4, 2024 where he said, “Either way place gets sold. I know it’s not ideal. But it’s a business and I don’t have a choice. The smoother transition is beneficial for everyone.” 8. The Tenant stated that she received a message from the Seller Landlord a few days later stating that the deal had fallen through but was advised again on September 16, 2024 that the property had sold. [name] told the Tenant that the closing date was December 1, 2024. 9. The Tenant attempted to find alternate accommodations for herself, her husband and their 5 children but she was unable to find another place to live. Due to these circumstances, the Tenant agreed to rent a different property owned by the Seller Landlord that was much smaller and had significant repairs to be completed prior to moving in. She said that the Landlord promised her that the work would be done in enough time for the family to move in. 10. [name] stated that she was contacted by the [name] again in late September of 2024 and he requested that she move out by November 1, 2024, a month earlier, which would help his financial situation by closing the transaction earlier. The Tenant and her family moved into the Landlord’s 2-bedroom house on November 1, 2024 and she stated that the house was in terrible shape. She stated that due to the size and the condition of the house, one of her daughters had to move in with her child’s father and the family was very distressed about this. 11. [name] stated that she discovered that the rental house was put up for sale on July 6, 2025, 8 months after she and her family vacated the house. This listing showed that the house was put up for sale in April of 2024 when the [name] owned the property and was again put up for sale on July 6, 2025. Based on my review of the land transfer documents and the real estate listing history, I am satisfied that the Purchaser Landlord put the house up for sale on July 6, 2025 and it continued to be up for sale at a lower price in September of 2025. 12. [name] stated that she was furious that the rental unit was put up for sale after she and her family had endured so much hardship and emotional distress and incurred moving expenses. She described how this situation was completely unfair to her family and herself especially with one of her daughters having to move out of the house. She stated that breaking up the family due to the lack of space was heartbreaking and the whole family was affected by the Landlord’s actions. 13. [name] is seeking a rent abatement of 30% of her monthly rent for 12 months calculated at $4,860.00. She is seeking compensation of $16,200.00 which is calculated by multiplying her monthly rent of $1,350.00 by 12 months. She is also seeking that an administrative fine be ordered against the [name] and/or the Purchaser Landlord. Analysis [name] 14. Based on the land transfer documents provided, I am satisfied that the person identified in the N12 as the person intending to move into the rental unit failed to do so within a reasonable period of time. 15. The primary issue on this application is with respect to the question of whether either or both of the two Landlords acted in bad faith in giving the Tenants the N12. 16. Because the Purchaser Landlord failed to participate in the hearing, the question of whether they acted in bad faith must be answered solely on their behaviour. For the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied that the Purchaser Landlord acted in bad faith. There is no evidence before me to support that [name] planned to move into the house for his own residential use. No declaration was provided setting out this information and I was not provided with a copy of the Agreement of Purchase and Sale. The only document that was provided (which was issued by the Seller Landlord) included the N12 notice of termination setting out that the Purchaser Landlord would be moving into the rental house. I have no evidence to corroborate that the Purchaser had any intention to reside in the rental unit. 17. Based on my review of the land transfer documents and the real estate listing history, I am satisfied that the Purchaser Landlord put the house up for sale on July 6, 2025 and it continued to be up for sale at a lower price in September of 2025. [name] 18. Because the Seller Landlord failed to participate in the hearing, the question of whether they acted in bad faith must be answered solely on their behaviour. For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied that [name] acted in bad faith. 19. The Tenant provided her uncontested evidence in a straight-forward manner and she provided me with specific dates and details. She provided documentation including a copy of the N12 notice of termination received from the Seller Landlord, copies of her text messages with that Landlord, the real estate listing for the house and the land transfer documents. 20. Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in clause 49 (1) or (2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 21. The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and the Purchaser Landlord did not move into the rental unit. 22. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 23. As I have determined that the Purchaser Landlord (who sold the house did not act in bad faith, section 57(5) does not apply to this case. 24. [name] had an obligation to the Tenants to exercise his due diligence in ensuring that the Purchaser Landlord had a good faith intention to reside in the rental house. 25. The Landlord’s text message on July 4, 2024 (stating that selling the house is a business and he does not have a choice) clearly sets out that he is treating the N12 notice as a business transaction and that there is no intention of a purchaser moving into the unit in good faith. The Landlord’s text message on November 1, 2024, requesting that the Tenants vacate one month earlier confirms again that [name] was contravening section 49 of the Act and he was looking out for his own business interests. The Landlord was apparently struggling financially and an earlier closing date would help his cash flow problems. 26. As mentioned earlier, no evidence was provided to confirm that the [name] sold the rental unit to a purchaser who planned to reside in the rental unit. Based on the information and text messages provided by the Tenant, I am satisfied that the [name] Landlord sold the house to a realtor, [name] in an effort to alleviate his financial constraints. I believe that the purchaser simply attained the property as a business transaction and this was confirmed when he listed the property for sale in July of 2025. 27. I am satisfied that the [name] knowingly served the N12 notice of termination setting out that a purchaser would be moving into the rental unit when he knew that no one would be moving into the rental unit. After the Tenants were advised that someone would be moving into the rental unit, they moved out in good faith accepting the Landlord’s words at face value. 28. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12. 29. The [name] admitted to the Tenants that he was struggling financially and provided a false notice of termination to the Tenants suspecting that they would cooperate with his plan and vacate the unit. The request for the Tenants to leave a month earlier confirmed that the Landlord’s actions directly contradicted the reasoning for the N12. 30. As such, I find that the [name] served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. A landlord’s good faith is required along the whole continuum of the process and as mentioned earlier, I believe his actions were self-serving and contrary to the Act. 31. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with their T5 application. Remedies 32. The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of 30% of her monthly rent for 12 months calculated at $4,860.00. Abatement recognizes the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for them, he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. 33. I heard no evidence from the Tenant regarding any issues with the “bundle of goods and services” at [address]reet, [name] and as such, I am not granting any abatement. 34. The Tenant is seeking substantial compensation of $16,200.00 ($1,350.00 x 12 months). The Tenant and her family were forced to move out of their home where they resided with their 5 children. The Tenant explained that she was unable to afford another unit that was of a sufficient size to house her family of 7 and that her family had to be separated due to the smaller size of the new rental unit. The Tenant provided details of how this affected all of her children. I am satisfied that this result would have been emotionally traumatic and painful for the entire family. 35. Although I was not satisfied that the Tenant’s claim for that amount was borne out of the evidence, I am satisfied based on the credible testimony of the Tenant that some amount of compensation should be awarded. The termination notice caused the Tenant and her family considerable emotional stress, serious disruption and great inconvenience due to the Seller Landlord serving the N12 in bad faith. 36. The blatant actions of the Seller Landlord caused a significant upheaval in the Tenant’s life and the amount of compensation should correlate with the Landlord’s breaches of the Act. As such, I assess the claim at $7,000.00 and shall order same. 37. The Tenant is requesting that I order that the Landlord pay a fine in this case due to the Landlord’s contraventions of the Act. 38. Given the total amount of the abatement is $7,000.00 I do not believe that a further administrative fine is required, as I believe the abatement itself serves as an adequate general and specific deterrent against the impugned conduct. No administrative fine is ordered.
ordered: The total amount the [name] shall pay the Tenant is $7,000.00. This amount represents the award for general compensation.
The [name] shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If [name] does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $307.92. T2 Application
The Tenant moved into the basement rental unit on September 1, 2023, and was out by November 29, 2023.

The Tenant testified that there were two units in the basement and the other unit was occupied by another resident, EB, who shared communal areas with the Tenant. Prior to October 10, 2023, EB sought the Tenant’s permission to have a friend visit for a few days and the Tenant consented to the request.
The friend arrived late on October 10, 2023, and during a discussion with the Tenant on October 11, 2023, she revealed to the Tenant that she is her Landlord.

The Tenant stated that she was uncomfortable with the Landlord’s presence in the shared space. The Landlord slept in a shared space on the first night and afterwards in a hallway that is not a part of the basement unit.

On November 21, 2023, the Tenant informed the Landlord that she would vacate the unit on January 1, 2024, but moved out on November 29, 2023, instead. The Tenant provided recordings of conversations between the parties on November 25, 2023, where she stated that that she did not receive a 24-hour Notice of Entry from the Landlord whose identity was not revealed to her and accused the Landlord of violating her rights. In the recording, t he Landlord opposed the Tenant’s request to terminate the tenancy earl y while EB acknowledged that she did not tell the Tenant that the Landlord was the friend because she did not wish to pressure the Tenant into saying yes.

The Landlord testified that she was informed about the Tenant’s desire to vacate the unit on November 25, 2023, and she apologized to the Tenant when she said she was uncomfortable with her in the basement. The Landlord denied entering the rental unit and stated that EB is her best friend, who she shared meals with while in the basement. The Landlord had no idea that EB, who rented the unit to the Tenant, did not tell her that she was the Landlord.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Going by the evidence, even if the Tenant was not aware that EB’s visitor was the Landlord on October 10, 2023, by October 11, 2023, the Landlord revealed her identity, and I am not satisfied that this information was intentionally withheld by the Landlord.

The parties agree d that the Landlord slept in a shared area on October 10, 2023, but subsequently slept in a hallway away from the basement. By the Landlord’s own admission in the recording, she cooked in the kitchen at least once a week.

The Tenant did not express any discomfort about the Landlord’s presence in the shared spaces until about November 21, 2023, when she expressed her intention of vacating the unit. Apart from generally stating that she was not comfortable, the Tenant did not testify to any specific actions taken by the Landlord that could be construed as substantial interference or harassment. There is no evidence to suggest that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit.

While I can understand the Tenant’s perception that she was misled by EB and having the Landlord in the shared area may have been an interference, the actions of the Landlord and the disclosed facts do not support a finding of substantial interference or harassment. T1 Application

The Tenant, who paid the rent of $900.00 for December 2023, requested a refund of the amount as well as a security deposit of $200.00; cleaning fee s of $50.00; and interest on the last month's rent deposit of $22.50.

The Landlord who did not dispute colle cting the amounts claimed, testified that the Tenant paid the rent for December 2023 and the last month's rent deposit was applied to January 2024 because the Tenant did not provide a proper notice of termination.

The Landlord further testified that on November 24, 2023 , December 10, 2023, December 17, 2023, and January 1, 2024, she posted advertisements online but was unable to re-rent the unit until February 2024. The Landlord stated that she had copies of the advertisement but as she did not provide it to the Tenant prior to the hearing, only her oral evidence was considered at the hearing.

There was no dispute that the tenancy was for a fixed term of eight months commencing September 1, 2023. In order for the Tenant to terminate the tenancy, she had to give a notice of termination under section 47.0.1 (3) of the Act which states that a Tenant who intends to terminate a yearly tenancy or a tenancy for a fixed term, shall give a Notice of Termination to the Landlord at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on t he last day of a rental period of the tenancy. In this case, the effective date of a valid Notice of Termination would have been April 30, 2024.

However, on or about November 21, 2023, the Tenant gave a verbal notice for January 1, 2024, which the Landlord did not accept. As the Tenant moved out of the rental unit without first giving a valid Notice of Termination, she terminated the tenancy in a manner that is not in accordance with the Act, and the Landlord was unable to rent the unit out until February 2024.

Therefore, the Tenant correctly paid the rent for December 2023, and the Landlord did not err in applying the last month's rent deposit to January 2024. In this circumstance, the Tenant is not entitled to a refund of the last month's rent deposit or the rent payment for December 2023.

Regarding the interest on the last month's rent deposit, section 106 (6) of the Act states that a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. The Landlord collected the last month's rent deposit of $900.00 on August 24, 2023, and did not pay any interest. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to interest on the last month's rent deposit for the period ending January 31, 2024, in the amount of $9.92 as the guideline was 2.5% in 2023 and 2024.

Section 105 (1) of the Act, states that t he only security deposit that a L andlord may collect is a rent deposit. Therefore, the Landlord must return to the Tenant, $200.00 collected as a security deposit, and $50.00 in cleaning fees.
The Tenant incurred a nonrefundable cost of $48.00 for filing the application and that amount will be reimbursed by the Landlord.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of January 31, 2024.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $307.92. This amount represents: • $9.92 interest on the last month's rent deposit • $200.00 security deposit • $50.00 cleaning fees, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 5, 2020 and moved out on December 31, 2022, the lawful rent was $1,350.00.

The Tenant filed the T2 application with the LTB on January 30, 2022, alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.

Specifically, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord in the year of 2022 issued 13 inspection notices by their property manager, [name]. That the entries were too frequent and that the repair(s) took too long to complete. The Tenant outlined the following times and dates of the notices as follow: • January 12h 11:30am-5pm, • March 4 9am-5pm and March 9 3pm-5pm, • April 18 10am-11am, • May 12 10am • June 16 10am-2pm, • July 27 10am-5pm, August 16 9am-1pm, August 23 12pm-3:30pm, August 24 12pm-3:30pm, • November 23 9am-5pm, November 25 1pm-5pm.

The Tenant submitted that what she characterized as repeat inspections were very disruptive to her household as she was at home with her young toddlers, who were napping most of the time and for which she need to amend her schedules to entertain. That many of the inspections were carried out to disrupt the household and that preparations of the rental unit were required. Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord argued that the January 12, 2022 notice of entry was statue barred on the basis that this date was more than 12 months since the T2 application filing date.
Therefore, pursuant to s. 29(2) of the Act, the date of January 12, 2022, was excluded.

The entries for the dates of March 4, April 18, May 12 and June 16, 2022, were in connection to maintenance work that was reported to the Landlord by the Tenant in October 2021 and or for a routine inspection the Landlord submits that they are permitted to perform.

The Landlord submitted that a number of the entries as provided through lawful notices were in connection to a prior T6 order LTB-T-073773-22/ SOT-25247-21, for which a hearing was held on May 18, 2022 and for which an order was issued on July 26, 2022. The order among other remedies, outlined that “the Landlord repair, replace or work on the outstanding issues by August 31, 2022.”

Further the Tenant confirmed that in addition to the T6 application, a complaint was filed with the City of [name] which resulted in the Landlord conducting an inspection of the rental unit on March 9, 2022.

The T6 order further provided that “if the Landlords do not do the repair(s), replacement(s) or work by September 1 2022, the Tenant was authorized to arrange for the repair(s), replacement(s), work to be done and may recover the cost of the by deducting the amount from the rent paid in the month(s) after the repair(s), replacement(s), work is done until there is no longer any money owing.”

The Tenant’s T6 application for maintenance included a number of issues of disrepair as follow: • Bathroom and bedroom doors did not close • Bathtub faucet leaked • Screens were missing from all windows • Hallway light can only be turned on if bathroom light is on • Flooring was separating • Kitchen drained leaked • Towel rack affixed to the cement wall fell off • Ventilation/Mould in the bathroom

The Landlord submitted that given the number of issues as pending repair from the prior T6 order and the short time frame in which they had to act, this increased the frequency of entries for the dates of July 27, August 16, August 23, August 24, 2022. The Landlord was under time pressure to compete the repairs by August 31, 2022.
It was not disputed that the Landlord entered the rental unit on the above noted dates in connection to the T6 application and resulting order
On cross examination the Tenant conceded that the November 23, 2022 entry was for an annual inspection.

The Landlord submitted that the Board consider the Tenant’s allegation in the context of s. 202 (1) of the Act where it is outlined that: In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.
The Landlord sought the dismissal of the Tenant’s application. Analysis

In addressing the entries for the period of March to June 2022, given that the totality of these account for 5 entries, one of which was in connection to a complaint raised with the City of [name], while perhaps disruptive to the Tenant, I do not find the frequency of the entries to be too often, contrary of the Tenant’s perceptions.

I also note that while an extended time range was outlined in the notices of entry, it was submitted that some of the inspections lasted no more than 10 minutes and no preparations of the rental unit were outlined for the Tenant to comply with, despite the Tenant making some preparations such as moving furniture away from the wall.

Section 27 provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry in the following circumstances: • to carry out a repair or replacement or to do work in the unit; • to allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit; • to allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998; • to carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the RTA; and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. • for any other reasonable reason for entry set out in the tenancy agreement.

LTB Interpretation Guideline 19 outlines that where a specific time of entry is known, it should be stated in the notice. Where it is not possible to state a specific time of entry, the notice may provide a reasonable window of time for entry. And that what is a reasonable window of time will depend upon the facts and circumstances in each case.

Regarding reasonable enjoyment during repairs, I turn my attention to [name]. 516/06 in which work is defined as: Definition 8. (1) In this section, “work” means maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex.

For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances. [name]. 516/06, s. 8 (2). (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant. [name]. 516/06, [name] (3).

The Landlord was required to perform repairs to the rental unit pursuant to an LTB order and complaint as filed with the City of [name]. As outlined in [name]. 516/06, s. 8 (3) (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.

On the basis of the evidence before me, I do not find that the work the Landlord was required to carry out constituted an interference that was unreasonable and given the number of issues to be addressed, that the time allocated was not disproportionate. Additionally, the evidence does not support a finding that the Landlord and or an Agent of the Landlord issued notices and entered the rental unit with the intent to harass or interfere with the Tenant.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord and or Landlord's Agent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household nor that the Landlord and or the Landlord’s Agent did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Kalum (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held by videoconference on March 26, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 9:58 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence. The Landlord did not join during the scheduled block and the LTB technical team did not advise of any related issues.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed he did not serve the Landlord with the evidence he intended to rely on at the hearing.

The Notice of ACC, sent to the parties on November 26, 2025 provided direction and support with respect to attendance at the ACC and potentially proceeding to the merit hearing, subject to the Member’s discretion. The Notice also provided instruction with service of evidence.

The Tenant confirmed he received and read the Notice and must have misunderstood the requirements for service of evidence. The Tenant did not describe any steps taken to clarify any confusion he had with respect to the Notice and direction within.
As such, the Tenant was not permitted to rely on evidence that was not properly served to the Landlord. The T2 Application
At the hearing, the Tenant was advised that his application is deficient as it did not contain the required dates and times for the claims made against the Landlord.

As explained to the Tenant, the Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931)

Although the [name] case related to a landlord’s notice of termination, it applies the long- standing common law principle of the right to know the case to be met; I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient notice and details of the case against them to allow them to determine whether to defend the claim and how to mount a defence.
As the T2 application was void of any dates with respect to the allegations of substantial interference, this portion of the application is dismissed. The T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The rental unit is a two bedroom apartment in a multi-unit complex.
The tenancy began around July 23, 2025.
The lawful rent is $1,700.00.
The T6 application was filed on October 1, 2025 and seeks a single remedy of early termination of the tenancy with a requested date of October 31, 2025.
For clarity, the tenancy commenced in July 2025 and was subject to a one-year lease.

As explained to the Tenant, termination of tenancies in general are usually ordered by the Board when there are really no other viable options left to consider, that would be tenable in respect of the parties involved. The Tenant opted to proceed with his claims.

The Tenant confirmed that the issues related to the window screens, carbon monoxide alarm, leak in kitchen and the hood fan were remedies by the Landlord. As such, a termination of the tenancy would not be considered.
The only remaining issue in the Tenant’s application relates to insufficient heating or cooling withing the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was aware of temperature issues in July 2025 and failed to take reasonable steps to repair the issue. He said that in September 2025, the Landlord installed a mini split in one of the rooms but it was inadequate to service the entire rental unit. He said he has followed up with the Landlord on multiple occasions and the Landlord refused to fix the issue.

For clarity, the Tenant does not claim there is no heat or cooling in the rental unit but rather it is insufficient. However, the Tenant did not provide any specifics related to the actual temperature within the rental unit. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The issue before me is whether the level of heat or cooling provided by the Landlord to the unit, during the material time, rendered the Landlord in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. As with all determinations, and in this regard, I cannot engage in speculation and/or conjecture. I can only make findings of fact based on the evidence before me.
As will be evident below, this case was marked, generally, by a paucity of evidence from the Tenant.

The evidence before me is that the Landlord was aware since July 2025 that the Tenant was complaining of temperature issues in the rental unit. The Landlord installed a “mini split” in one room was the Tenant states was insufficient to regulate the temperature in the entire unit.

Even in the absence of documentary evidence, I am obligated to apply the principle from [name] v. M.E.I., 1979 CanLII 4098 (FCA), [1980] 2 F.C 302 (C.A.) at 305, that when a witness swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness.

However, the Tenants did not provide any readings of temperature in the rental unit itself to show whether the various room temperatures were in compliance with subsection 15(1) of Ontario Regulation 517/06, under “Heating”.
Given the above, I cannot find that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations under the Act.
The Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenancy commenced on August 1, 2024, and ended on September 30, 2024.
The Tenant testified that he observed moisture on the floorboards of the rental unit on August 6, 2024, and the Landlord promptly sent a plumber either on August 6 or 7, 2024 to address the issue.

On August 8, and August 16, 2024, the Tenant noticed mold in the drywall of the living room and the Landlord on August 9, 2024, and about August 16, 2024, sent a contractor who removed the drywall to fix the issue.
On September 8, 2024, the Tenant observed mold in the boiler room. The contractor cut up the drywall to remove the mold.
On September 16, 2024, the Tenant observed a sulphuric smell in the unit.

On September 30, 2024, the Tenant hired a mold specialist who inspected the rental unit and provided a Mold Testing and Inspection Report. The report indicates that the Tenant had moved out of the rental unit, and they observed visible mold in the boiler room , visible water damage throughout the unit and high moisture readings. The mold remediation level was noted as level 1 with recommendations provided.
The Landlord testified that they responded to the Tenant’s complaints promptly and the mold report simply shows high moisture readings but not mold.

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with hea lth, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Applying the Court’s direction in this case, the presence of mold or moisture in the unit is not an automatic basis for finding that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act especially as they hired contractors to investigate and address the problem in a timely fashion. Although the Landlord’s efforts were insufficient as the mold report showed that mold continued to be present in the boiler room and the moisture readings in the rental unit were high, the Landlord did not neglect their obligation to maintain the unit.

Given the evidence, had the Tenant not vacated the unit, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord would have carried out further investigations and resolved the issue. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The application was scheduled for an Adjudicative Case Conference ( ‘ACC’) on September 25, 2025. Only the Tenant attended the ACC.

As the Board was not satisfied that the Landlord had been duly served with a copy of the application and the notice related to the ACC, the Tenant was therefore ordered to serve the Landlord with a copy of the Notice of Hearing related to the March 31, 2026, hearing, along with a copy of the application and the documentary evidence the Tenant intended to rely on during the proceedings, at least thirty (30) days prior to the hearing date (i.e. no later than March 1, 2026).1

The Tenant testified that they moved out of the rental unit. During the course of their tenancy, they would communicate with the Landlord in-person, as they both resided within the same residential complex.
The Tenant stated that they made no attempts to serve a copy of the application, nor a copy of the Notice of Hearing related to the March 31, 2026, hearing, to the Landlord.

The Tenant provided a copy of the Agreement to Lease they executed along with the Landlord on August 18, 2021 (DOC-7677246; Exhibit 1). The document does not reflect that the Landlord consented to being served by email, nor was an email address provided. I am therefore not satisfied that the Landlord was duly served with a copy of the Notice of Hearing.
The Board has an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding.2

The Tenant, as the applicant, is required to exercise diligence in order to ensure that their application can proceed in being heard. As the Tenant made no attempts to comply with the terms and deadlines set out in the interim order LTB -T-082586-24-IN, issued on October 1, 2025, I did not find it appropriate to adjourn the matter further.3

Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 5.17 of the Board’ s Rules of Procedure, as the Tenant failed to serve the Notice of Hearing related to the M arch 31, 2026, hearing, in accordance with the interim order LTB-T-082586-24-IN, issued on October 1, 2025, the Tenant’s application was dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application was dismissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Oakwill Non-Profit Homes Corporation (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2) and; • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.(T6)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $5,298.00 for remedies as outlined below. [name] to the proceedings
The Tenant filed the initial T2/T6 application on October 19, 2023.

The matter proceeded to an adjudicative case conference initially on November 28, 2024, the Tenant was provided oral direction that they may amend their applications and remedy request, however that they are “not able to add new allegations that were not alleged in the original application.” The Tenant submitted an amended T2/T6 application as received by the Board on August 20, 2025.
Neither the Landlord nor the Tenant was in possession of a written lease in respect of the rental unit, although both parties submitted that one would have been signed at the time of the tenancy.

I note that this order does not attempt to refer to all the of documents, videos and photos filed and as uploaded that formulate the Board’s record. In making the decision below I have considered the entirety of the relevant parts of the record. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant moved into the 4-bedroom rental property in 2016, this is the first home they share together since moving from a shelter. As of the date of the hearing the Tenant resides at the property with her now adult children in their twenties.

The rental property and only one other unit have an unfinished basement, the remaining 24 or so properties in the residential complex do not. The basement is comprised of a recreation room, bathroom and utility room.
The Tenant relies on the Tenant’s Evidence as contained in DOC-6337966 and DOC- 6309428, DOC-4550890 along with video and other documentary submissions.
On September 5, 2023, the Tenant came home to find the basement flooded with community sewage backing up into the utility room through a floor drain.

Surrounding the circumstances as arising from the incident of September 5, 2023, the Tenant testified that: • Maninder Kaur (MK), agent/ off site property manager of the Landlord was contacted at about 7:00 p.m. and advised the Tenant that a plumber would be dispatched. Was advised to save as many belongings from the basement as they could, so they brought some of their belongings upstairs. • There is no official onsite property manager residing at the residential complex, however the Tenant stressed the importance of a male resident [name] who she said is deployed by the Landlord to address various issues on the property. This individual was said to have sexually assaulted the Tenant’s daughter, was charged and was outlined as someone who could not address the Tenant’s unit in any case. • The Tenants attempted to clean up the sewage water coming out of the drain and as travelling down the hallway using a mop and bucket. • They began to feel ill almost immediately, while they waited for the plumber to come. • The odour was so bad and that when advising the Landlord’s agent that they could not stay there, they were advised to close the door to the basement. [name], the agent of the Landlord told them to pour vinegar on the drain to neutralize the odours without having a good idea of the severity of the issues. • That the temperature in the unit was above 25 degrees and the A/C unit needed to be turned off to contain the spread of the odour and that the advice was to turn off the water supply to the unit to avoid any additional water going down the drain. • The plumber arrived around 9:25 p.m. on the same evening of September 5, 2023 to snake the drain. The Tenant continued to ask for personal protective equipment ( PPE) and conveyed to the Landlord’s agent/ property manager that they could not be left to stay in the rental unit. This being a larger problem then initially thought and not entirely limited to the rental unit. • They were covered in biohazards and through the direction of the property manager contaminated the upper floor by transfer of impacted belongings and goods. • As there was no running water, they were unable to wash their hands or take a shower. • On September 6, 2023, the entire basement was now flooded with sewage. • The Tenant and family were provided alternative housing by the Landlord the following night, on September 6, 2023 despite repeated reports of illness the Tenant and family were experiencing. • The flood lasted for days, and it spread into the adjoining recreational room. • As the remediation part of the cleanup began on September 18, 2023, that their impacted personal belongings were left unattended until this time, since September 5, 2023. The Tenants were asked to signoff on an authorization to provide Service Master ability to have carriage and control of personal effects that were going to be removed and cleaned on or offsite. • The Tenants were requested to make a list of personal items and provide them to Service Master, the company hired to conduct the interior cleanup, remediation and the cleaning of the Tenants’ belongings. • The list to be provided was to include personal items to be collected and cleaned, and the Tenants were to assign a value to the items as outlined. • The items in the basement were mostly things stored, such as seasonal items, children’s clothing, artwork, sowing materials as one room was used as hobby room. Some items were stored in boxes on shelves. • That they were subsequently advised by Service Master that some items were disposed of and not returned to the Tenants. That given the economic value, the testing involved, it was determined that some items were not salvageable. On October 2, 2023, the Tenant submitted that the evidence was showing contaminated water seen by black light this despite the Tenants being advised they were able to return into the unit on September 28, 2023. • Using a black light technology – a device purchased by the Tenant on the internet, Tenant submitted that biomatter could be seen by flashing of the light on the upstairs carpets on or about September 28, 2023. And that the Landlord should have cleaned the upstairs portion of the home and had failed to do so. • Since moving in the carpets had been steam cleaned over time and that their pet dog does not go upstairs. • They took issue with the fact that reservations were made for shorter periods of time of two to three days at a time and they had to pack up again and move to another hotel locations. That this happened multiple times during the time they were displaced from the home. • “Constantly having to pack and move interfered with your family’s daily life, causing stress, disruption, and additional financial burdens.” • That the movement from one hotel to another was a traumatic experience, especially for her son who has Down syndrome and could have been avoided if Landlord booked a much longer stay at the outset i.e. for the entire period of 25 days. • The Tenant could not afford to feed her family being displaced, she is in receipt of ODSP benefits and as much of the food in fridge was lost during the time of being displaced from the rental unit, the Landlord provided them with food reimbursement on September 18, 2023. • Over 14,000 litres of waste was removed from the septic systems from the residential complex property. This representing more than 10 truck load of waste. • The Landlord was not aware of the location of one of the manholes, as it was found to be located under a fence built directly on top of the cover. With exploration of symptoms with various medical experts. • The family lost over 250 personal items such as shoes, clothing, electronics and housewares that were said to have been damaged by the sewage flood and not returned to the Tenants once collected by Service Master. • The Tenant was of the impression that she would have the final say in the way their impacted belongings were treated by Service Master, however as the Tenant signed a contract, the decision of economic value of the goods and final decisions about the feasibility to cleaning certain items and their recovery remained with the Landlord. • That both contaminated and uncontaminated items were put together by Service Master, creating additional contamination which may have been prevented. • The event of September 5, 2023 was a problem that the Landlord failed to address in a timely manner, and as a result of inadequate maintenance of the drain and septic system, the sewage backup entered the Tenant’s unit. They were the only impacted tenants. • The Tenant was not aware of the requirement to have content liability insurance and a lease copy she may have had was destroyed in the flood. • The event of September 5, 2023 has severely impacted the entire family, no longer feeling like they are a part of the community they reside in. [name] with Reasonable Enjoyment

To address the T2 portion of the application alleging [name] with Reasonable Enjoyment the Tenant referred the Board to Tab 10 of DOC-4550890 the issues raised are based on the same issues as outlined in the T6 application.

Cross-examination of [name]

The Tenant [name] (LK) confirmed that they ordered the black light used for biomatter identification from Amazon – there was no evidence of prior contamination to cross reference and that she was not formally trained for assessing biohazards.
