Regarding having to move between hotels, the second move was done because there was inadequate bedding for her family and she requested to be moved. 16. The Tenant’s children [name] and [name] testified to their own experiences of September 5, 2023 and medical impacts upon them. 21. [name] testified to the impact of losing her job, having experienced headaches, feelings of displacement and not feeling safe in the home even after they were told the home was in a good condition to return into. [name] testified to the impact of the loss of his personal items many which were disposed of as were deemed unsalvageable, items that may have held sentimental value or could no longer be replaced such as his speciality Nike shoes gifted by his brother. [name] outlined various music equipment that was submitted to have been lost in the sewage flooding, however for which he did not have invoices. And while submitting that some items have been replaced, there was no invoices or proof of payment for the replacements either. 25. Further, [name] submitted that he tried retrieving some of his music equipment however realized that it was no longer operable, it could not be salvaged. That the items he took, were left with a friend and were destroyed by him. He made suggestions about possible deductions to be attributed to the items that he provided pricing for and that he had lost. 26. On cross examination, [name] confirmed that on the day of the flood he was residing in the rental unit, he had recently moved back to commence school. He submitted that most of the items lost were his. 27. While he has purchased music equipment through various speciality stores, no documentation was available even though these may have still be under warranty. However, it was further confirmed that some of the equipment as lost was purchased on or about 2016. Landlord’s evidence 28. The Landlord relies on the their book of evidence as contained in DOC-6267088. Landlord’s witness 29. [name] (OA) contractor with DiversaTech Mechanical submitted that he is familiar with the rental unit as he received a call from [name] (MK) the property manager on September 6, 2023 to attend to clear up water. 30. (OA) explained that based on his knowledge the main line needed to be investigated to address the blockage, work done on September 6 and September 8, 2026. The issue was not connected to individual lines as connected to each individual unit. That there are 3 catch basins on the property located at 25-50 ft apart that connect to the main. That it was found that the third catch basin needed to be cleared, that a lot of soil was found to be in there, it was removed and that this was the part of the service that was done to address the blockage. 31. That with the equipment used, they were unable to clear catch basin #1 & #2 and were able to clear catch basin #3. That another company attended to assisted them due to lack of equipment, securing the services of Ultimate Drains. 32. (OA) understood that another company was dispatched for the interior part of the work and that 4 truck loads of effluent were removed that he was aware of. When questioned about 10 truckloads, he suggested this was impossible at this would have taken all day. 33. (OA) also testified to the company being dispatched to the property in April 2023, to address catch basin #2. That the complex is over 40 years old and that one of the basins was not cleaned out/serviced in a very long time. That the Non-Profit Board, providing guidance to the management of the property are the parties to make the right decisions about what needs to be done to maintain these systems. Testimony of [name] former Property Manager 34. The former property manager [name] (MK) during the time of the flood, was the point of contact to the Tenant (LK). 35. (MK) confirmed on September 5, 2023 she received a call from the Tenant (LK) that there was a flood in their rental unit. 36. That a plumber and DiversaTech Mechanical came out to the property to investigate on the same evening of September 5, 2023. 37. That the Tenants were provided alternative housing the next day September 6, 2023, booked in short increments of 3-4 days because it was being booked on (MK’s) personal credit card and being guided by not knowing how soon the rental unit would be available/ remediated. 38. That her understanding was that the sewage drain blockage was isolated only to the Tenants’ unit, that the blockage was backed up to a point where it could not be addressed by a regular plumber and therefore specialized equipment needed to be deployed to pump out the water. That this service was performed on September 8, 2023. 39. That the sewage water in the rental unit had been cleared up by Service Master on September 7, 2023. That when she provided direction to save any belongings to (LK) that she did not mean to bring up any items that were already wet. 40. (MK) submitted that the Tenants were required to move two times to the best of her understanding and that they were provided a $100.00 per diem rate for food, breakfast was inclusive of the hotel stay for which the Landlord also reimbursed the Tenants or paid for directly. 41. That the Tenant was reimbursed for all hotel stays for the period of September 6 to September 28, 2023 and for the applicable utilities for the month. That as the floor was being changed in the kitchen this created some delay with Tenants being able to reoccupy the unit. This was said not to be related to the flood. That the Tenant continued to express concern over the unit conditions and requested that the landlord conduct e-coli and air quality testing. 42. That Service Master did water extraction, left Hepa filters, sanitized the rental unit and disinfect the property completely. 43. That after the event of September 5, 2023, the Tenant (LK) made inquiries to obtain a bin and personal protective equipment (PPE) to empty the contaminated content of the rental unit. 44. As the Tenants did not have content insurance. The Board of Directors decided to pay for the Tenant’s content cleaning. The cost of this service was $4,244.48. 45. That the air quality and e-coli testing that came back confirmed that the there was no presence of any ongoing hazards, and no further recommendations were made for the Landlord to address. Samples as collected on September 14, 2023 and September 27, 2023 where the subject of the results. 46. The Tenants signed a copy of a consent to permit the content cleaning, remove belongings off site, clean and returned if can be salvaged. 47. That the Tenant (LK) was offered the opportunity to pick up any items that were deemed not to be economical to clean by Service Master, that she did not pick up the belongings for which claims are made. 48. In total the Landlord, a non-profit housing provider spent a total of $44,180.93 in plumbing, restoration, cleaning and testing costs, of which they were refunded $21,200.83 through the insurance policy for the residential complex. A policy which does not include coverage for the Tenants’ belongings. 49. That on the date of flood, this was the first time any such sewage issue arose in the complex and that there was no evidence to suggest the Tenant was responsible for the issues as arising on September 5, 2023. 50. The Landlord sought a dismissal of the Tenants’ applications, in the alternative, that the Board consider that the Landlord is non-profit housing provider and that it is the position of the Landlord that the replacement value claims as outlined are inflated, and in consideration, any award to reflect this accordingly. Analysis & Reasons: 51. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., of, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 52. Based on the evidence provided I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair, and complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. I also find that through their actions, the Landlord interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. I say this for the following reasons. 53. There is no doubt there was a sewage backup in the unit on September 5, 2023. Further it was not disputed that that there was property owned by the Tenants that was damaged and was disposed of. Included in the property were personal effects, clothing, shoes, electronics and items of sentimental value. This sewage backup was caused by the property owned and maintained by the Landlord. The backup was said to be in no way the fault of the Tenants. 54. The Landlords witness (OA) testified that the complex is over 40 years old and that one of the basins was not cleaned out/ serviced in a very long time. This may have been because the Landlord was not even aware of one the manholes, having erected a fence and garden beneath an area that was to be maintained and emptied when required. 55. Here, while it is the Landlord’s obligation to ensure the septic and drainage systems is maintained and in good working order, there was no evidence of any maintenance schedules of the systems or evidence of when the last time the septic system was pumped out. 56. While the parties differed in opinion, the Landlord paid for at lease 4 truck loads of pumped water and effluent from the holding tanks and incurred at least 20k in charges for remedial work as connect to the underground drainage and plumbing infrastructure alone. The outlying reason was a blockage to the main connecting to the Tenants rental property, but far enough removed that could not be remedied by standard plumbing methods and required specialized manpower and equipment deployment. 57. The evidence as submitted by the Tenant clearly shows sewage matter on the floor of the utility room as well as large amounts of water on the date of September 5, 2023. 58. The Tenant did not have contents insurance, and while the Landlord’s witness (MK) submitted that all lease with the Landlord have a clause which require that the Tenant have such insurance, neither party could produce a copy of the lease. 59. The Tenants testified to the impact of having to reside in hotels for over three weeks. Undoubtedly the backup caused a major inconvenience to the Tenants. And while I appreciate that there may have been acute symptoms of nausea and headaches that may have resulted from their initial cleanup efforts, I am not satisfied that any other symptoms as raised by the Tenants are directly correlated to the event. It is more likely that the event exacerbated any preexisting symptoms as testified to by the Tenants as the Tenants exposure can be described as limited, given their removal from the property almost within 24 hours of the sewage backup. 60. The evidence was that the sewer backup was expediently and reasonably dealt with by the Landlord. The Landlord took the necessary steps to provide the Tenants alternative housing, meal allowances and took additional steps to ensure the Tenants were able to move back into the rental unit such as ensuring air and e-coli testing was completed. 61. However, as the Tenants lost personal property due to the Landlord’s actions of providing a sewer system that did not work as it should and having contaminated the living space of their home, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants correspondingly. 62. In review of the Tenants remedy in seeking $35,000.00 for both applications, and while I appreciate that the loss of their items was deeply personal, the value of the Tenants assigned to their claims is not supported by the evidence. For instance, the Tenants claimed that they lost 3 pairs of orthotic insoles worth $1,200.00. They did not provide a receipt or other proof or purchase to support this claim. This was the case for over 250 items that were said to have been disposed of and for which no receipts, invoices or any other proof could be established. Rather, they provided screenshots of retail valued items from stores or specialty items sold on eBay. Even if I could find the Landlord liable for all the Tenants’ losses, the Tenants have failed to provide adequate evidence to support the value of their losses. 63. In their T6 application, part of the $35,000.00 claim the Tenants also described the remedy to include consideration for loss of income, transportation and abatement of rent. 64. As outlined at the time of hearing, the Tenants submitted that the is no documentary evidence to support their claim. As such, the loss of income and any transportation costs incurred for travel to the hotel can not be considered as there is no basis for undertaking such assessment of declared loss. 65. In addressing an abatement of rent, as the Landlord paid for the Tenants housing for the entire period of displacement from September 6 to September 28, 2026, a claim for abatement would be a form of double recovery as effectively the Tenants have been reimbursed more than the value of their loss. If I am wrong, the award of $2,750.00 as considered pursuant to the T2 portions of the application as outlined below may be attributed to this portion of the application in part. 66. Further, pursuant to section 16, of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), when a party becomes entitled to an amount from the other party the party entitled to make the claim shall minimize their losses. 67. Given that there are no receipts, that the items of loss were used items and that the Tenants may have minimized their losses if they elected to pick up and clean their own items when provided the option by Service Master, an award of $2,500.00 is what can be considered given these circumstances. In arriving at this determination, I have considered the existence of the Service Master contract, although a copy of the terms as agreed to where not evidenced. Both the Tenants and Landlord’s witness testified to different versions of contract language interpretation. Nonetheless, I have considered the options presented to the parties, both the Landlord and Tenants. Further, given the stress of the event of September 5, 2023 and timing of decisions undertaken I have considered that there may have been some miscommunication about what was expected in the context of cleaning and remediation of the Tenants’ personal belongings and effects and this in my view directly impacted the claims raised as before the Board. T2 Remedies 68. The Tenant’s T2 application claims that the Landlord substantially interfered with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to adequately maintain the sewage and drainage system. That through the Landlords’ actions they were displaced from their home for the period of September 6 to September 28, 2023, this causing “emotional, psychological and physical distress” as created by instability, exposure and loss. 69. As testified to by the Tenants the move to a hotel for a prolonged period had a profound impact upon them. They took issue with the fact that reservations were made for shorter periods of time of two to three days at a time and that they had to pack and move to another hotel location. That this happened multiple times during the time they were displaced from their home and involved packing and resettlement. This time away from home was less than ideal, it interfered with the family’s daily life, causing stress, disruption, and created additional financial burdens. 70. I take note that while the movement from one hotel to another was a traumatic experience, it was especially so for her son who has [name]’s syndrome and requires among other factors the stability of a routine and familiar surroundings. 71. And with living out of a hotel, the issues of food scarcity and ability to afford feeding a family of 5 became an issue. The Tenant submitted that she could not afford to feed her family once displaced, she is in receipt of ODSP benefits and much of the food in the fridge was lost during the time of being displaced from the rental unit. While the Landlord provided the Tenants with reimbursement for food, this did not occur until September 18, 2023. There was a certain level of stress as associated with not knowing where they would be moved to, when they could return home and what if any food related costs would be reimbursed. 72. I also take note that while the Tenant (LK) submitted that the multiple moves within the same hotel or to another property could have been avoided all together if the Landlord booked a much longer stay i.e. for the entire period of 25 days, there were many factors that were be contended with at the time. Just to name a few, the booking agent did not have a corporate card to secure an extended stay, there was a moving target with the estimated time of the initial remediation work and additional work such as testing for air quality arose at the request of the Tenants. These factors in addition to the replacement of floors that were being coordinated and while unrelated to the sewage event, created an opportunity to be completed before the Tenants moved back into the unit and created additional delays. 73. However, given the impact upon the Tenants, the Landlord by failing to maintain the residential complex, in a good state of repair, and complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards impacted the Tenants. The sewer backup created conditions necessitating the Tenants to live outside of the comfort of their home for a period of September 6 to September 28, 2023, the Landlord is therefore liable for the continuing deprivation of peaceful enjoyment of the rental property. And while the Landlord provided the Tenants with alternative accommodations, and paid them a per diem for their food, most obviously, living out of a hotel with limited personal items is not a replacement for the comforts of home, this being especially true for a family of 5 with pets and with diverse personal needs such as the parties before the Board. 74. Given all the above outlined, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants $2,750.00. 75. The Tenant also claimed the return of any of the Tenant's property in the Landlord's possession. As noted at the time of the hearing, the Landlord submitted that they do not have such possessions. And (LK) understood that the Landlord has no such property and they were offered to pick up anything that was in the possession of Service Master, an option that was not exercised for large part. Therefore, no remedy can be considered. 76. This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $5,298.00. This amount represents: • $2,500.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenants have incurred or will incur to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $2,750.00 for compensation for loss of reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount of $300.00 per month from the rent owing for a 17-month period starting June 1, 2026 and deducting $198.00 on the last 18th month to conclude the repayment of amounts as owed by the Landlord.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord s must pay to the Tenants, $1,065.24 for interfering with their vital services.
The tenancy for the rental unit commenced on May 1, 2025, and ended on November 5 or 7, 2025 when the Tenants moved out.
The lawful monthly rent was $1,800.00.

On May 2, 2025, when the Tenants viewed the rental unit in person to sign the tenancy agreement, the Landlords informed the Tenants that they would be responsible for a portion of the electricity bill. This was not contested by the Tenants who made the payments on multiple occasions.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on May 9, 2025. The Landlords, who also resided in the residential complex, introduced their puppy to the Tenants as a community dog . The Tenants informed the Landlords that their daughter was scared of dogs. In June 2025, the Tenants’ daughter allegedly stopped playing outside because of the dog.

On July 26, 2025, (amended from August 4, 2025) the Tenants heard a child screaming and went outside to investigate. They saw the Landlords laughing as their dog chased the crying child. The Tenants informed the male Landlord that the dog was a problem, and that he was not a good dog owner. The Landlord responded that the Tenants were no longer welcome there and should move out of the unit . Afterwards, the police arrived to speak with the Tenants about their alleged threats to the Landlords. The Tenants narrated the incident to the police, and the Landlords were told to keep their dog on a leash.

On September 6, 2025, the bathroom/bathtub hot water tap started to drip and did not function properly. The Tenants notified the Landlords by email on September 7, 2025. On September 23, 2025, the Tenants sent a follow-up email regarding the lack of hot water in the bathroom. On September 30, 2025, the Tenants sent the Landlord another follow-up email which he also ignored until October 3, 2025, when he responded that he does not check his emails frequently. The issue was eventually resolved on October 11, 2025.

On September 30, 2025, the female Landlord informed the female Tenant that they turned off the hot water in the bathroom manually because the Tenants failed to pay the hydro bill. The Tenants requested rent abatement of $7,200.00 for the Landlords’ conduct.

The Tenants further stated that they vacated the unit because the Landlord is a psychopath who called the police on them and kept an untrained puppy . The Landlords also caused noise disturbances by repeatedly throwing a ball against a wall and created loud banging noises. The Landlords could be heard laughing while all the noise was occurring. Analysis

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides in section 21 (1) and section 2 (1): Landlord’s responsibility re services 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligati on to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. Section 2 (1) of the Act provides: “vital service” means hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The evidence demonstrates that the hot water flow to the bathtub was significantly reduced on September 6, 2025. Although the Landlord was notified of the issue on September 7, 2025, he did not respond to the complaint. Despite follow-up emails sent on September 23, 2025, the Landlords did not take any action until October 3, 2025.

The emails presented by the Tenants indicate that on September 30, 2025, they stated amongst other things ‘… your wife informed my wife today that you have interrupted the service by turning off the hot water valve because of the non -payment for electricity’. The Landlord on October 3, 2025, denied turning off the water and stated, ‘I don’t know what my wife said but I can’t know the problem until I go into your unit to check’.

Based on all the evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords turned off the hot water to the bathtub and ignored the Tenants requests to have the issue fixed. The female Landlord expressly informed the female Tenant that the hot water had been turned off due to the non‑payment of the electricity bill, which was outstanding at the time. The male Landlord’s subsequent claim that he did not know what his wife said is not persuasive, given that he could reasonably have verified her statements before sending his delayed response to the Tenants’ email.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords withheld or interfered with [name]’ vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Landlords also substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

The Landlords will be ordered to pay the Tenants a rent abatement equal to 50% of the daily rent, in the amount of $1,065.24, for the period from September 6, 2025, to October 11, 2025. The daily rent for the rental unit was $59.18, resulting in a daily abatement of $29.59. The interruption lasted 36 days, calculated as $29.59 x 36 days, for a total abatement of $1,065.24.

Regarding the Tenants claim that they moved out of the rental unit on November 5, or 7, 2025 as a result of the Landlords ’ conduct, the evidence does not support that assertion. The Tenants stated that there were noise disturbances on unspecified dates, but it does not appear that they made a complaint to the Landlords about this issue. The Landlords’ decision to ask the Tenants to vacate the rental unit and to contact the police following the interaction between the parties on July 26, 2025, was not ideal. However, I find it more likely than not that additional comments were made during that interaction beyond what the Tenants disclosed in their evidence . In any event , the police departed the residential complex without incident after telling the Landlords to keep their dog on a leash.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlords’ actions.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,065.24 for a rent abatement.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenants focused their evidence on only the substantial interference and maintenance claim regarding how the Landlords inadequately dealt with removal of the deceased tenant of another unit and confirmed that was the only claim they were pursuing. As such, the Tenants abandoned their claims regarding altered locks, withholding vital services, and all other maintenance claims and I have made no determinations on those claims.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the remaining allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Tenants’ remaining allegations deal with what they claim to be the Landlord’s substantial inference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex for failing to properly address cleaning up after another tenant passed away in an adjoining rental unit and the Landlord’s lack of maintenance as far as it relates to the same.

The Tenant, [name] (“KS”), testified that the Tenants smelled what they thought was a gas leak in September 2022, but it turned out to be that the tenant in an adjoining rental unit had passed away and no one had discovered this. KS testified that there was blood and bodily fluids that had leaked from the deceased tenant into the Tenants’ rental unit and the Tenants ended up relocating due to the smell.

KS testified that the Landlord notified the Tenants on October 20, 2022, that the cleaning of the residential complex had started but on October 26, 2026, the Tenants raised issues with their lack of satisfaction with the cleaning. KS testified that the Tenants began insisting on a forensic certificate because they were not confident that the Landlords would complete the cleaning properly or according to by-laws regarding dealing with bio-medical waste disposal.
KS testified that as of October 26, 2022, the parties agreed to terminate the lease with a termination date of November 30, 2022.

The Tenant, [name] (“VB”), testified that the Tenants did not feel confident in the communication received from the Landlords. VB testified that the Tenants had to pull information from the Landlords. VB testified that even in November the smell remained, and many of the Tenants personal items had to be disposed of. VB testified that had the Landlords provided the forensic certificate the Tenants would have stayed as they would have had piece of mind.

The Landlords’ Agent, [name] (“MS”), testified that she is the current Property Manager for the Landlords and is familiar with this file. [name] testified that [name] (“MB”) is a previous employee of the Landlords who had been dealing with this matter. [name] testified that the Landlords were advised by the police on October 13, 2022, that the deceased tenant’s unit was released. [name] testified that the Landlords’ insurance company handled the clean up of the deceased tenant’s unit and the residential complex. [name] testified that the scene was released, and quotes were obtained within a week for appropriate cleaners.

MS testified MB was the one that handled coordinating the cleaners, and the Landlords did provide the emails between MB and the cleaners that were hired. The emails indicated the cleaning was completed by October 26, 2022, but the certification would not follow until payment had settled with the insurance company. [name] testified that the Tenants had already terminated the tenancy by the time they were seeking confirmation via forensic certification.

Both the Tenants and the Landlord provided the police report. According to the police report the police had attended the residential complex on September 28, 2022, to accompany a Landlord’s Agent to determine where the gas leak was coming from but it was determined that it was actually the smell from the deceased tenant. The police report indicates that the deceased tenant was removed from the residential complex that day, but the scene was not released until October 13, 2022 due to the police investigation.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. Although Onyskiw deals with a breach regarding a maintenance obligation, I am satisfied that the Court of Appeal provides a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches in other situations, including substantial interference.

To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

In this case, I am not satisfied that the Landlords acted unreasonably. This was an unfortunate circumstance and the Landlords’ response, while not perfect, was reasonable. While I agree with the Tenants that the communication from the Landlords could have been a little more fulsome, that would not have changed when or how soon the Landlords could have accessed the deceased tenant’s rental unit and the residential complex to begin cleaning and remediating.

I am satisfied that obtaining quotes and securing a cleaner within one week of the scene being released is a reasonable amount of time. Furthermore, the residential complex was fully cleaned and ready to be reinhabited by October 26, 2022, 13 days after being released by the police. I am satisfied that this is a reasonable amount of time based on the cleaners having to clean multiple units and multiple floors and having to remove bodily fluids.

While I appreciate that the Tenants wanted the forensic certificate, they were informed that it would take time to be provided, and the Tenants had already terminated the tenancy. Their insistence on the certificate, does not change the reasonableness of the Landlords response in this matter.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have carried their burden to demonstrate that the Landlords acted unreasonably in the circumstances and therefore somehow substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.

For the same reasons I am also satisfied that the Landlord did not breach their maintenance obligations as it pertains to the Tenants claim that the Landlord failed to adequately address the consequences arising from the deceased tenant.
Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant The Landlords also claimed compensation for each day the Tenants remained in the unit after the termination date. The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlords arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to assign the rental unit. (LTB-T-077852-24) The Tenants also applied to for an order determining that the Landlords arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to sublet the rental unit. (LTB-T-082872-24) These applications were heard by videoconference on December 4, 2025. Both Landlords, the Landlord’s legal representative, [name], both Tenants and their legal representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlords have not proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy or the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. LTB-T-077852-24 LTB-T-082872-24
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. They have sublet their mobile home and rental unit on or about September 30, 2024.

This rental unit is a site in a land lease community with four lots. The Tenants own the mobile home on the site and they rent the site from the Landlords. It is a mobile home because it has four wheels and is capable of moving. It is also for year-round occupancy.

As per the definition of a rental unit under subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the site in which the mobile home is located is the “rental unit” and not the mobile home itself because the Tenants own the mobile home, and they rent the site from the Landlords. (emphasis added)

On July 24, 2025, the Landlords gave the Tenants a first, voidable N5 notice of termination by email to their legal representative who accepted service on behalf of the Tenants. The termination date in the notice is August 13, 2025. The notice contains a single allegation in that on September 30, 2024 the Tenant assigned or sublet the rental unit without the landlord’s written consent in contravention of the Act, although it does not refer to any particular section.

On August 8, 2025 the Landlords then gave the Tenants a second N5 Notice by sending a copy to the Tenants’ legal representative by email. The termination date in the second N5 Notice is August 28, 2025.

The issue with this second notice, in part, is that it repeats the allegation in the first N5 Notice for September 30th. It then goes on to include dates of July 22, 2025 and July 24, 2025 which do not identify a behaviour of the Tenants, just that they were advised that they were in contravention of the Act by assigning or subletting the rental unit without the landlord’s consent is in contravention of the Act. They also pre-date the first N5 Notice and ought to have been included in the previous one. The only additional allegation is on August 6, 2025 which simply states that the Tenants are still in contravention of the Act as the trailer is still assigned or sublet. Again, no mention of which section they are in contravention of, and it is unduly repetitious and the identical grounds listed in the previous Notice with no substantial change.

The other issue with both notices of termination is that it appears the Landlord is attempting to circumvent section 100 of the Act by attempting to evict the Tenants alleging behavioural issues and substantial interference when in fact the actual issue on it’s face is that they allege that the Tenants have transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlords consent. The Act specifically contemplates unauthorized occupancy, and it is distinctly different from a claim of substantial interference.

Under subsection 100(2) of the Act, a landlord must file an application with the Board within 60 days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy if the Tenants had sublet the rental unit (the site) without the Landlords consent. Meaning that the Landlords had until November 29, 2024 in this case to file their A2 application. They clearly did not file an A2 application.

If the Tenants had requested to assign the tenancy because they intended to sell their mobile home and to maintain the rental of the site, then the Landlords had 15 days in which to file an A2 application with the Board pursuant to subsection 159(4) of the Act. If LTB-T-077852-24 LTB-T-082872-24 they did not file the application within 15 days of the request to assign the site, then pursuant to subsection 159(4) of the Act, there would be a deemed assignment.
The Landlord neither filed within 15 days to dispute the proposed assignment or filed within 60 days of discovering that the Tenants had sublet their rental unit without the Landlords consent.

It cannot be said that the Landlords were unaware of the transfer because on September 9, 2024 they had text communication with the Tenants as seen on page 77 of the Landlord’s evidence package denying the Tenants written request to sublet the rental unit. I say sublet because the message refers to a request from the Tenants to “have a tenant move into” their trailer to rent it. The Landlord refuses the sublet on the same date citing unpaid taxes by the Tenants.

Additionally, in part of the Landlords evidence (Book 1 Tab 2) disclosed to the Board, there is another N5 Notice dated October 1, 2024 with a termination date of October 22, 2024 identifying the Landlords awareness through this notice that the Tenant s had sublet their trailer without permission of the Landlord.
For these reasons the application must be dismissed. LTB-T-077852-24 – Tenants A2 application regarding an assignment

For the same reason that the Landlords application must fail because of the deemed assignment provision under subsection 159(4) of the Act, the Tenants A2 application under file LTB-T-077852-24 must also fail because the site is deemed assigned on the 16th day after the request is made to assign the tenancy if the Landlord has not filed an A2 application to dispute it.

Subsection 156(1) of the Act states that a tenant has the right to sell or lease his or her mobile home without the landlord’s consent. If a tenant is selling their mobile home and intend on assigning the site with the mobile home on it, then they either require a landlord’s consent, or it is deemed consent if the landlord does not file an A2 application within 15 days of their request to assign the site.

I cannot find that the Landlord refused to assign the rental unit (the site) because the Landlord did not file an A2 application within 15 days of the request to assign the rental unit and on this basis, it is deemed assigned. Accordingly, this application must be dismissed. LTB-T-082872-24 – Tenants A2 application regarding a sublet
The Tenants A2 application under file LTB-T-082872-24 regarding the Landlords refusal to allow the sublet of the rental unit to [name] and Mathieu Cortemanche, is granted.
The Tenants application is filed under section 98 of the Act.

Section 98 states that a tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board or an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. LTB-T-077852-24 LTB-T-082872-24
This application involves the latter, subtenant.

Subsection 98(2) states that tenants must file this application within one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenants filed this application on September 17, 2024 within one year of the date the Landlords refused to allow the sublet which was on September 9, 2024.
Subsection 98(3) states that if the Board determines that a landlord has unlawfully withheld consent to a sublet, the Board may order that the sublet is authorized.
In the case before me, since the Landlords did not file an A2 application regarding the sublet within 60 days of its discovery, then on the 61st day, the sublet is by statute approved.

Since the Tenants already sublet the rental unit to the proposed individuals as of September 30, 2024, and since the Landlords did not file an A2 application by November 29, 2024, then as of November 30, 2024 the proposed individuals are no longer unauthorized and on this basis I find that the sublets are approved as of November 30, 2024.

Additionally, since the Tenants are successful on one of their A2 applications I also find it appropriate that the Landlords be ordered to reimburse the Tenants the filing fee for this application in the amount of $53.00.
ordered: The Landlords’ L2 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s A2 application regarding an assignment under file LTB-T-077852-25 is dismissed.
The Tenant’s A2 application regarding their sublet to [name] and Mathieu Cortemanche, is granted and authorized as of November 30, 2024.
The Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $53.00 for the application filing fee by February 13, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Tenants by February 13, 2026, then the Landlords will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding starting February 14, 2026. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario
