issues: Limited (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (LTB-L-073730-25). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • Substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex; • Entered the unit illegally; [name], coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (LTB-T-081631-25). The Tenant also applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (LTB-T-082916-25).
reasons: The unit subject to this application is located within a campground owned by Rainbow Valley Corporation Limited and [name] [name] is the owner of the company and herein known as the Landlord.
The Tenant is the owner of his company operating as [organization] and herein known as the Tenant.

The unit was built around 1973 and historically served as the campground’s storefront and clubhouse for the park campers. There are two floors with multiple rooms. The basement contained a shower room and the main floor was a store and games room. This was known as the ‘clubhouse’. The main floor is approximately 20 x 40 feet an consists of one main area with a separate office area. There is a kitchenette with a counter and sink, a bathroom. The basement showers were removed and the room was primarily used as storage.

The Tenant states he moved in on November 19, 2022 and has used the unit as his primary residence with the approval of the Landlord. As such, the Tenant believes this landlord/tenant relationship is protected by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
The Landlord asserts that the Act does not apply to this relationship as the unit was leased for commercial use, with no residential tenancy agreement between the parties.
Both parties filed an A1 application with the Board to determine if the Act applies.
Consequently, the issue to be determined in both the T2 and A1 applications is - does the Act apply to this tenancy? The February 27, 2026 Hearing
The Landlord’s representative opposed the evidence submitted by the Tenant’s representative prior to the second hearing, stating the extreme prejudice to the Landlord.

Following party submissions, the Board declined to accept the submissions and stood the matter down for around 15 minute to allow the Tenant’s representative to review the [name] previously submitted disclosure.

The Tenant’s representative’s request to call [name] as witnesses was denied. [name] attended the previous hearing as support and was privy to the Landlord’s evidence. As such, she is a compromised witness. Being made aware of this, the Tenant’s representative understood the Board’s direction.

To avoid the rule in Browne v. Dunn (1893), 6 R. 87 (H.L. (Eng.)), the Tenant’s representative put various questions to the Landlord during cross examination in the event the Tenant’s representative intended to impeach the Landlord. The Landlord was given opportunity to provide an explanation for the intended contradictory evidence. Does the Act apply to this relationship?
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies to the rental unit or residential complex.
The Landlord’s disclosure includes: the “Camper Agreement”, commercial leases, insurance documentation, invoices, [name] report and various communications (DOC7145676).
The Tenant’s disclosure includes a summary of events, photographs, property listing, invoice, letter (DOC7145334, DOC6703130).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The Landlord’s Evidence

To summarize, the Landlords states that he is the owner of Rainbow Valley Corporation Limited that owns the campground where the unit is located. There are 28 sites and the park is deemed seasonal/recreational. Campers must provide details of their permanent residence on the seasonal rental agreement.

It was the evidence of the Landlord as per the December 5, 2025 letter from the Landlord’s registered insurance broker that relevant insurance was a commercial package policy for the seasonal campground and commercial operations. This policy has been in place for many years. Additionally, the GeoWarehouse Property Report, generated on January 9, 2026 identifies the property type as commercial.
The Tenant rented a trailer site for 2022, signed the ‘Seasonal Camping Agreement’ on May 13, 2022 and provided his permanent residence address in Orillia, Ontario.
The Tenant renewed for the 2023 season and paid a deposit to leave his trailer over the winter. The fees were paid in full in April 2023 for another camping season.

Around October 2022, the Landlord said the nature of the relationship with the Tenant changed. The Landlord had plans to hire a caretaker and made arrangements with the Tenant to do renovation work on a location to accommodate a caretaker. Based on the number of seasonal campers at that time, there was no longer a need for a store and recreational facility. The Landlord relied on various text messages to confirm the contractual relationship with the Tenant for around 20 to 40 hours per month.

The Landlord said that the Tenant was in the process of starting a business and required space to house a workshop and office. In lieu of payment for work, the parties agreed that the Tenant could use the clubhouse during renovation as a workshop and office for his business. The work was never completed by the Tenant.

The Landlord said the relationship changed again around spring 2023. The Tenant’s business was developing and he required the space for his workshop and office on a more permanent basis. The Landlord had no interest in a residential lease as the Landlord required the unit for campground purposes based on expansion plans.

It was the evidence of the Landlord that the unit was not zoned residential, the septic system insufficient for residential purposes was and he continuously carried commercial insurance on the property. However, his plan, once the septic system was approved, the space would be once again used as a camper clubhouse.
The Landlord ensured the Tenant was aware that the unit was intended for commercial purposes, zoned and insured for commercial purposes and the septic system was for temporary use.
With this in mind, the Landlord agreed to and entered in to three OREA Agreements to Lease for Commercial purposes with the Tenant on or around April 30, 2023, October 23, 2023 and May 21, 2024.
The parties negotiated the rent for commercial purposes and the Tenant provided the Landlord with his commercial insurance policy on April 30, 2023.

At all material times, rent was by to the Landlord by electronic transfer and HST was paid by the Tenant as a result of the commercial nature of the relationship. The Landlord provided the Tenant with receipts until the Tenant said they were no longer required

At the conclusion of the third lease May 31, 2025, the Landlord opted not to renew the Tenant’s commercial lease as he had received the required approvals to expand the number of camping sites and the use of the unit would be required for campground expansion purposes.
The Landlord states that the parties mutually negotiated the commercial nature of their relationship at all material times and at no time, did he consent to a transitional to a residential tenancy.
As a result, the Landlord seeks a declaration that the Act does not apply to this relationship. The Tenant’s Evidence
To summarize, to the Tenant takes the position that this landlord/tenant relationship is covered by the Act as it is a residential tenancy and has been since the Tenant moved into the rental unit.
The Tenant said that the Landlord’s own actions by serving a Board notice N13 to end the tenancy demonstrates that the Landlord too considered this to be a residential tenancy.

Although disputed by the Landlord, the Tenant said he moved into the rental unit with his partner and five children around November 19, 2022. He was previously a camper and opted to sell his home to help finance his new business development.

The Tenant provided a timeline for the sequence of events from the transition from camper to Tenant and said the Landlord was aware of his intention to make the unit his home. When he sold his home, he moved into the unit on a permanent basis and with the Landlord’s understanding of the nature of the residential tenancy. He said the Landlord provided residency letters for school enrollment and days care subsidies; the Landlord attended the unit with his child who played with the Tenant’s children. He provided furniture and offered some physical support in moving a shed and loaned tools for the Tenant to build the basement bedrooms and other projects. At all material times, the Landlord accepted the tenancy as residential.

The Tenant did not dispute that he signed three consecutive commercial leases with respect to this unit. He said he did so at the insistence of the Landlord. The Landlord explained to him that use of a commercial lease was more advantageous. The Tenant said he was in a precarious position as he had no alternative living arrangements and did not want to compromise a home for his family.

It was the evidence of the Tenant that the rental unit was far from unfinished when he moved in, as claimed by the Landlord. It contained a fully functioning kitchen, a bedroom and bathroom. In fact, there was a previous tenant who lived in the rental unit. When the Landlord wanted higher rent, he wanted to evict the previous tenant and asked the Tenant to assist with moving his possession out of the unit.

With respect to the letter provided for daycare subsidy purposes, while the Landlord states various deficiencies in the letter and denies having signed it, the Tenant asserts the Landlord did sign the letter and likely altered his signature as a preventative measure.

The Tenant takes the position the at all material times this has been a residential tenancy. The Landlord has consistently manipulated the situation with attempts to evict him using an LTB form. The Landlord also has taken extreme steps to stage a situation to avoid the protection and provisions of the Act.

The Tenant’s witness [name] (RK) said that he lived at the rental unit from the summer of 2021 to the fall of 2022. He said he paid rent to the Landlord at $1,200.00 monthly. He is employed at two different jobs and the proximity to [name] made it convenient to travel to work. He said that he did odd jobs for the Landlord and was paid accordingly. He said that he lived full time at the rental unit and slept there 7 days a week. When the Landlord evicted him and his possession were removed, he opted not to challenge the Landlord.
The Tenant requests a finding from the Board that the Act applies to this landlord and tenant relationship. Law and Analysis

In order for the Act to apply there must be a tenancy agreement between a “landlord” and a “tenant” respecting a “rental unit” or “residential premises”, as those terms are defined in the Act. The exemptions from the Act found in section 5 must also be considered. All of which have been considered in this case.

The following provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) are applicable to the determination of the case: Subsection 5(j) provides that the Act does not apply to: premises occupied for business or agricultural purposes with living accommodation attached if the occupancy for both purposes is under a single lease and the same person occupies the premises and the living accommodation; . . . Subsection 202(1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Landlord argues that the Board should consider the zoning of the property and the history of commercial leases signed between the parties. The Tenant argues that the Board must consider the nature of the use and the intention of the parties at the time the leases were entered into, regardless of the use of a commercial lease form.

Although the leases were titled commercial, this is not in itself determinative of commercial use and does not entitle the Landlord to contract out of their rights and obligations if the nature of the tenancy is residential. Further, subsection 3(4) of the Act states that in the event of any conflict with another Act the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies, with the exception of the Human Rights Code.

The fact that a landlord and a tenant sign a commercial lease does not change the true nature of a tenancy. I find that the use of a commercial lease did not reflect the actual terms agreed upon by the parties at the commencement of the tenancy, specifically that the Tenants would reside in the unit.

I am persuaded by the Tenant’s evidence that he moved into the rental unit, along with his family for residential purposes. I find that the Landlord was aware of the Tenant’s circumstances and permitted the Tenant and his family to move into the unit where the Tenant undertook renovations to comfortably accommodate his family. While a google map may reference this address as the Tenant’s place of business, I accepted that his business was growing and is mobile in nature. I prefer the Tenant’s evidence that he and family moved into the rental unit as their home. I do not find the intention of the parties at the onset of their relationship was that the unit was to be used by the Tenant for storage and an office.

Overall, there was insufficient evidence that the rental unit is operated as a place of business and the Tenant does not have any business signage on the residential complex that supports commercial use.

I considered the Landlord’s evidence that the building is zoned commercial. However, municipal by-laws and zoning cannot be used to determine the contractual relationship between a landlord and a tenant. The fact that the building is zoned commercial and that residential occupation may be a violation of the building code is irrelevant as to the application of the Act.

I have also considered the evidence that the lease agreements are on a commercial lease form and the Landlord maintains commercial insurance. However, section 202 of the Act requires the Board to ascertain the real substance of a transaction. I find the real substance of the tenancy is for residential occupation and not commercial use as the lease agreement purports to set out. The intentions of the parties when the tenancy started was for all intended purposes for residential occupation.
The next issue I must consider is the predominant use and exemption pursuant to [name]) of the Act.

The predominant purpose test as established in the case of [name] v. Kramer 1979 CanLII 2111 (ON SC) (‘Hahn’) applies to this case. In Hahn the Court held as follows: The exemption clause specifies that the premises be occupied for business purposes with living accommodation attached. To me, the wording of the section seems to indicate that the business purposes should predominate. The Act appears to specifically and carefully proceed in a manner which emphasizes the business use to be made of the combined premises so as to take them outside the definition of residential purposes.

The test in Hahn makes it clear that for the tenancy to fall outside of the parameters of the Act, the business purpose of the premise must be the primary or predominant use of the space. Therefore, in weighing the two uses of the space, the commercial use of the space would outweigh the residential use.

The evidence before the Board overwhelmingly supports the proposition that the rental unit is used solely for residential occupation. The photos of the unit show no business or commercial space open to the public. The Landlord failed to provide sufficient evidence that the Tenant is operating a business out of the rental unit. While some basic business administration may be conducted by the Tenant at the rental unit, I find it is minimal in nature. I am therefore satisfied that the predominate use of the unit is residential occupation.

The Divisional Court dealt with very similar tenancies in the Sterling Studio Lofts Incorporated v. [name], 2019 ONSC 91 (CanLII) case (Sterling). In Sterling the landlords argued: the Board was required to apply principles of contract interpretation in assessing the lease agreement; that at the time of signing the lease, the parties had turned their minds to a commercial tenancy and that it was unreasonable and incorrect for the Member to have found that the intention of the parties was to enter into a residential tenancy agreement despite the written commercial lease agreement; that it was an error of law to allow the surrounding circumstances of the tenancy to overwhelm the written contract; and the tenants could not unilaterally change the nature of the lease that they voluntarily signed. Finally, the landlords also argued that it was an error to apply the predominant purpose test from section 5(j) of the Act.

In Sterling the Divisional Court disagreed with the landlord and held that: “In accordance with s. 202, the terms of the agreement signed by the parties are not determinative with respect to the application of the RTA and, in our view, the LTB was entitled to find upon consideration of all the evidence that the true nature of the agreement was for use as a rented residential premise. To hold otherwise would result in a triumph of form over substance.”

Further, in Sterling the Divisional Court relied on the Court of Appeal case of [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corporation, 2010 ONCA 468 (CanLII), “the Court of Appeal stated that s. 202 is to be applied when determining whether a unit is intended for use as a residential premises. At paragraph 24 the Court states: Definition of a “Rental Unit” in s. 2(1) contained two components. First, the unit must be “living accommodation”. Second, it must be used or intended for use as “rented residential premises”. As I have indicated, s. 3(1) provides that the Act applies despite any term in the Lease to the contrary and s. 4 provides that “a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void”. Section 2.2 requires the Board to “ascertain the real substance of the activity” relating to the rental unit and to do so disregarding “the outward form of [the] transaction”. Accordingly, a term in the Lease providing that a site is not residential nor a rental unit will not have the effect of avoiding the application of the Act, provided that the premises otherwise fit within the statutory definition of a “rental unit”.

In consideration of the findings of the Divisional Court and the Court of Appeal, as noted above, I find that the form of the lease cannot override the true substance of the agreement of the parties and resulting use of the premises in the matter before me; the agreement was for use as a rented residential premises.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, on the balance of probabilities, I find that subsection 5(j) of the Act does not apply in this case, the tenancy is not exempt from the Act. The pre-dominate use is residential.
The merits of the Tenant’s T2 application have not been heard and will be scheduled accordingly.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.
The Tenant’s T2 application shall be scheduled to be heard. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants moved into a mobile home located at Box 16, Second Avenue, Erin, Ontario which is a land lease community. The Tenants purchased this mobile home and moved in on October 1, 2020. They own the mobile home but the land is leased by the Tenants from the Landlord. The Tenants vacated the mobile home on January 31, 2025 but they continue to own the home.

This application concerns allegations that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally without notice and that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants. Tenant’s Evidence – [name] (RM)

RM testified that she and her husband decided to sell their trailer in September of 2024 and she advised the property manager, [name] [name] of their plans. The Tenant requested that [name] let them know when he would be doing the inspection and agreed that the property manager could just pop over to complete the inspection provided he let them know the date.

RM stated that [name] did not advise them of the date that he would be doing the inspection but completed same and sent them a report on September 13, 2024. RM stated that the property manager advised her that he called them but there was no answer so he simply completed his inspection. The Tenant stated she received a list of undertakings that were required to be completed prior to selling the mobile home.

RM brought my attention to the undertaking list provided by the Landlord to the Tenants. This document states that “the above is required to bring the home into compliance with current park rules and regulations and community standards and must be completed by the closing date. The undertakings above will be subject to an inspection of completion 30 days prior to closing. Approval of a purchaser for a new lease or assignment of lease is conditional on compliance with the undertakings prior to closing.

The Tenant stated that she was not required to complete these undertakings as some of them had already been done and some of them were not listed on their own undertakings when they purchased the home. [name] stated that she received an offer but it was way too low and she refused that offer. She stated that the Landlord’s interference with these undertakings was substantially interfering with her ability to sell their mobile home. The Tenant stated that these undertakings are not necessary and the park rules are not evenly enforced around the park. She also stated that she has never been given an N5 from the Landlord regarding a failure to maintain the mobile home or the surrounding property so why is the Landlord alleging this now.

RM stated that although they have a mortgage on the house, they have taken the house off the market waiting for the results of this case. The Tenant wants the Landlord’s interference to cease immediately so that she is able to finally sell the home without these unnecessary and costly repairs.

The Tenant is seeking that the Landlord remove the undertaking list as a condition of the sale of the home, she is looking for moving and storage expenses in the amount of $1,001.04 (due to her inability to sell the unit) and she wants the Landlord to pay CMHC $25,185.60. The Tenant explained that due to the fact that they could not sell their mobile home, they did not have a sufficient deposit on a new home and they had to pay CMHC fees of over $25,000.00. [name] also is seeking that the Landlord give out a copy of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) to all new tenants at the park. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] [name] ([name])

The property manager stated that the undertakings are completed prior to the sale of any of the mobile homes and that they are based on the park’s rules and regulations. He stated that the last inspection of the rental unit was in 2020 and things can change in 5 years. 11. [name] stated that when he completed the inspection on or about September 13, 2024, he wanted to ensure that the current state of the mobile home and the area around it complied with the park rules. Based on his recollection, he stated that the skirting around the house was bending and the blocking has deteriorated causing him to believe that the house is sinking. He further noted that the siding needed to match and that fencing needed to be removed. He stated that this is the reason why these undertakings must be resolved prior to the mobile home being sold. 12. [name] stated that the sellers of the homes usually take care of the undertakings but some times the purchaser completes the undertakings. He stated that they must be completed prior to the sale going through. 13. [name] stated that he was not stopping the Tenants from selling their mobile home and that he was simply completing a necessary step when selling a property. 14. [name] stated that when he attended the mobile home in September of 2024, he did not enter the rental unit and simply walked around the home to review the condition of the home, looked at the surrounding fence, and reviewed the accessory buildings. Analysis 15. The Tenant’s T2 Application is based on the rights and obligations contained in sections 22 and 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”): 22– A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 25– A landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27. 16. The Tenants’ case to be made is that the Landlord is substantially interfering with the Tenants’ ability to sell their mobile home and because of the property manager’s actions, they have been unable to sell their home. Further, they believe that the property manager entered their home without consent. 17. Regarding the Tenants’ allegation that [name] [name] illegally entered their home in September of 2024, I am not satisfied that any illegal entry occurred. [name] testified that he inspected the outside of the house and the area around the house and the Tenants agreed that is where the inspection occurred. 18. Based on the testimony from both parties and the evidence including the undertakings, I am not satisfied that the Landlords are substantially interfering with the Tenants. Section 154 of the Act allows a Landlord within a land lease community to create park rules and regulations which the Landlord can enforce within the park. The list of undertakings created by the property manager stems from the park’s rules and regulations and according to the property manager, it is done for each house prior to being sold. 19. Section 159(1) of the Act states “If a tenant has sold or entered into an agreement to sell the tenant’s mobile home and the tenant asks the landlord to consent to the assignment of the site for mobile home to the purchaser of the mobile home, … b) the landlord may not refuse consent to the assignment unless, on application under subsection (2), the Board determines that the landlord’s grounds for refusing consent are reasonable.” 20. Section 159(2) of the Act states “The landlord may apply to the Board, within 15 days after the tenant asks the landlord to consent to the assignment, for a determination of whether the landlord’s grounds for refusing consent are reasonable.” If the landlord fails to file this application with the Board within the 15-day timeline, it is assumed that the landlord has consented to the assignment. 21. In this specific case, the Tenants have not requested an assignment of tenancy from the Landlord. The Tenants have been attempting to sell their house and they feel that the Landlord’s requests are unnecessary. The Tenants have not entered into an agreement of purchase and sale and as such, they have not requested an assignment of tenancy of their lease from the Landlord. Therefore, the Landlord’s actions are not hindering the sale of the property. 22. As such, this application is premature and must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Landlord and the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement on September 1, 2024 for a fixed term of one year ending on August 31, 2025.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025.
The Tenant filed the application with the Board on October 16, 2025.
The Tenant alleges the Landlord collected illegal rent and did not use the Tenant’s last month rent deposit for the last month of the tenancy.
The Tenant filed evidence with the Board (DOC-7618102) to support his claims in the application.

The position of the Tenant is the tenancy agreement indicates the lawful rent is $890.00, however when the Tenant was moving items into the rental unit the Landlord noticed the Tenant was moving in a small floor freezer. The Tenant alleges the Landlord insisted the Tenant pay an additional $10.00 per month to cover the cost of the electricity for the additional appliance.

The Tenant stated he paid cash for the first month then proceeded to pay the Landlord $890.00 per month consisting of his lawful rent of $880.00 and the extra $10.00 the Landlord requested for electricity.
The Tenant stated that on February 28, 2025 he texted the agent for the [name] and requested to terminate the tenancy for the end of April 30, 2025.
The Landlord agent responded back to the Tenant on the same day stating the Landlord accepted the Tenant’s request to terminate the tenancy on April 30, 2025.

The Tenant stated he had paid April 2025 rent and the Landlord is still holding the last month rent deposit that should have been applied to April 2025 given the mutual agreement to terminate the tenancy for April 30, 2025.
The position of the Landlord is the Tenant terminated the tenancy early and she is entitled to keep the last month rent deposit.

The Landlord stated that the agreement to terminate the tenancy early was based on the condition that the Tenant pay April 2025 rent and the Landlord would keep the last month rent deposit as compensation.

The Landlord stated that although another existing tenant took over the Tenant’s rental unit she was still left with a vacant room for four months because the Tenant vacated the rental unit before the end of the tenancy and she is owed compensation. Analysis

Section 3 of the Act states: Application of Act 3 (1) This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. [emphasis added]

Section 37 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Termination only in accordance with Act 37 (1) A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act. 2006, c. 17, s. 37 (1). Termination by agreement (3) A notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy. 2006, c. 17, s. 37 (3). [emphasis added]

Section 106 of the Act states: Rent deposit may be required 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (1). Rent deposit applied to last rent (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).

With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Landlord has collected an illegal charge of $10.00 for electricity charges and the Landlord did not use the last month rent deposit of $880.00 for the [name] last month.

Regarding the $10.00 the Landlord is not allowed to charge extra charges that are not covered in the tenancy agreement. Despite the Landlord’s assertion that the Tenant volunteered to pay this, this agreement is in contravention of section 3 of the Act.

Based on the text message evidence and the Tenant’s credible testimony I find the Landlord and the Tenant entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy on April 30, 2025 to terminate the tenancy in accordance with the Act. As such, the Landlord is not entitled to retain the last month rent deposit as compensation. This amount is still owing given the Tenant had paid rent for the month of August 2025.

Evidence was provided that a new tenant occupied the rental unit however this fact is not relevant to the fact the Landlord and Tenant agreed to terminate on April 30, 2025 and the new tenant moved in sometime in May 2025.
For all the reasons above the Tenant’s application is granted.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $1,008.00. This amount represents: • $80.00 for excess rent collected. • $880.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for at least one year. The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. And [name] [name] Tenant And [name] [name] Landlord [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has not proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy and the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

N12 Notice of Termination Landlord's Own Use On December 20, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination, which was deemed served on December 21, 2023, with the termination date of February 29, 2024. The Landlord claims that they require vacant possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by the Landlord, his spouse, and child.
The Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of their own residential occupation for a period of at least one year.
The Landlord has compensated the Tenant an amount equal to one month's rent by February 29, 2024. The Tenants did not dispute receiving compensation. [name] LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25

The main issue to be determined is whether the Landlord has established that he in good faith require possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation as required by s.48(1) of the Act.

Pursuant to section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’): (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by, (c) a child of the landlord… (2) The date for termination specified in the notice shall be at least 60 days after the notice is given and shall be the day a period of the tenancy ends or, where the tenancy is for a fixed term, the end of the term.

The N12 Notice of Termination gave the Tenants at least 60 days’ notice. An email- transfer of one month’s rent was sent to the Tenants on the termination date listed in the N12. Therefore, the only issue to be determined in this application is whether the Landlord has satisfied the “good faith” requirement of subsection 48(1) of the Act.

Section 48 has been interpreted by the Courts as requiring only that a landlord establish that they genuinely intend to move into the unit and live there for residential purposes for at least one year (Feeney v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), [1994] O.J. No. 2049 ([name]. Ct.)). Neither the reasonableness of the Landlords’ intention, nor the fact that the Landlords may have other motives for wanting to occupy the unit, nor the fact that there might be other available alternatives is the issue (Salter v. Beljinac,2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), [2001] O.J. No. 2792 ([name]. Ct.), and Feeney v. Noble). However, the surrounding circumstances may provide circumstantial evidence from which inferences can be drawn when deciding whether a genuine or sincere intention to occupy the unit exists ([name], [2014] O.J. No. 2678 ([name]. Ct.)). The Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord, Mr. [name]name], testified that the rental unit has been vacant since the fire on or about February 24, 2024. He claimed that he has suffered financial stress due to being unable to rent or use the unit.

Since the fire, the Landlord stated that he has been dealing with City by-law authorities, permits, and inspections. He further stated that he believes it is reasonable for him to regain possession of the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that his parents now wish to occupy the rental unit. However, upon reviewing the N12 Notice served to the Tenants, it is evident that the Landlord only selected the option indicating ‘Me, my spouse, my child’ as the intended occupants. This discrepancy raises concerns about the accuracy and consistency of the Landlord’s stated intentions. The N12 Notice is a statutory document that requires clear and truthful disclosure of who will occupy the unit. The failure to include ‘parents’ on the notice, despite later claiming that they are the intended occupants, undermines the credibility of the LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 Landlord’s testimony. Furthermore, the Landlord did not provide any supporting documentation, such as affidavits from the parents or evidence of their current living arrangements, to substantiate this claim. This inconsistency suggests that the Landlord’s stated reason for terminating the tenancy may not be genuine and casts doubt on whether the application was brought in good faith.

I note that during his testimony, the Landlord did not provide evidence of who would occupy the rental unit, when that person would commence occupation, or how the unit would be made habitable in the near future. The Landlord provided no evidence of remediation plans, given that the rental unit was deemed unsafe for occupation. In other words, the Landlord’s testimony was inconsistent regarding who would occupy the unit and for what duration. 14. [name] cross-examined the Landlord on the evidence presented. She questioned the Landlord who specifically would be moving into the rental unit. The Landlord did not clearly identify a named individual (i.e. himself, his spouse, or his child). Instead, the Landlord made reference to a general family need and future possibilities. 15. The Landlord acknowledged that significant repairs to the rental unit remain outstanding. 16. The Landlord was asked whether the unit could realistically be occupied within a reasonable time following termination. His answers were speculative and focused on future intentions rather than concrete steps. 17. Lastly, when questioned about the timing of the N12 Notice related to the Tenant’s efforts to regain access since the fire, the ongoing disputes regarding the Tenant’s belongings, and the Tenant’s filing their own application. The Landlord acknowledged that he issued the N12 after prolonged conflicts with the Tenants. Analysis 18. Based on the evidence presented by the Landlord, the evidence presented established that the unit was not habitable at the time of the notice, there is significant disputes were ongoing between the parties, and since the fire the Landlord has actively resisting the Tenant’s access. 19. The evidence presented established that a fire occurred in February 2024 rendering the rental unit temporarily uninhabitable. As a result of the fire, the Tenants were displaced and unable to return to the rental unit. 20. Since the fire, significant conflict arose between the Landlord and the Tenants regarding access to the rental unit, the Tenant’s belongings, and communication following the fire. 21. In Parris v. Laidley, 2012 ONCA 755, the Court of Appeal for Ontario stated that “drawing adverse inferences from failure to produce evidence is discretionary”, and “the inference should not be drawn unless it is warranted in all the circumstances.” 22. This is a contentious L2 application where the Landlord’s and Tenants’ credibility are central to the issues. The Landlord’s evidence regarding personal occupation was vague, inconsistent, and lacked corroboration. While the Landlord asserted that the purpose of the LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 N12 Notice was to allow for personal use of the rental unit, his testimony focused primarily on financial hardship and ongoing disputes with the Tenants rather than providing concrete details about future occupancy. The Landlord did not identify a specific individual who would occupy the unit, nor did he provide a timeline for when occupation would commence. Additionally, the Landlord failed to explain how occupation would be feasible given the extensive repairs required to make the unit habitable following the fire. The absence of a remediation plan or evidence of steps taken to restore the unit further weakens the Landlord’s position. In cases where credibility is in question, the lack of clear, reliable, and consistent evidence weighs heavily against the party bearing the burden of proof. Here, the Landlord’s shifting narrative—from initially indicating that he or his immediate family would occupy the unit to later claiming that his parents intended to move in—creates significant doubt about the genuineness of his stated intentions. 23. On a balance of probabilities, and considering the totality of the evidence presented, I find that the Landlord has not met the burden of proof required to succeed in this application. The Landlord failed to provide clear, credible, and consistent evidence regarding who would occupy the rental unit, when occupation would begin, and how the unit would be made habitable. The negative inference drawn from the absence of supporting documentation and the inconsistencies in his testimony further undermine his case. The Landlord’s emphasis on financial hardship and ongoing disputes with the Tenants indicates that the N12 Notice may have been issued as a reaction to those conflicts rather than stemming from a genuine and bona fide need for personal occupation. Given these findings, I conclude that the Landlord has not demonstrated good faith in bringing this application. Accordingly, the Landlord’s application is dismissed [name] 24. Ms. [name]name] testified that she first moved into the rental unit at [address] in February 2007, initially residing in the basement unit and later relocating to the main floor unit around 2019 or 2020, where she has continuously resided since. 25. Ms. [name]name] testified regarding a fire occurring in late February 2024, originating in the attic unit of the four-plex. She stated that she was present in her unit at the time of the fire and was forced to evacuate without adequate clothing in winter conditions. She testified that emergency responders prevented her from re-entering the building and that the Landlord attended briefly, spoke with police, and departed without speaking to the tenants. 26. The Tenant testified that following the fire, she was temporarily housed in a hotel through emergency supports and later moved to stay with a friend across the street from the rental property, where she continues to reside. She stated that she has maintained her mailing address, identification, and intention to return to [address] at all times. 27. The Tenant stated that communication with the Landlord following the fire was primarily by email. She testified that she repeatedly requested to have access to the rental unit to retrieve their belongings and return to the unit, but access was delayed and restricted. She ultimately was permitted to retrieve limited belongings months later and that many items were damaged by water and the demolition. Additionally, she repeatedly communicated LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 her intention to return to the rental unit, but the Landlord advised she could not return, providing varying explanations including financial hardship, insurance issues, and his own intention to occupy the unit himself. She stated that she expected to return within six months following the fire but never received a clear timeline from the Landlord. 28. Ms. [name]name] testified that she resides directly across the street from the rental property and has observed ongoing construction and removal of items. She described a brief interaction where the Landlord called her over regarding discarded items and subsequently appeared to contact authorities when her co-tenant attended to retrieve an item. 29. She stated that she has kept her official address, including her driver’s licence and other identification, registered to [address]. She testified that the Landlord removed all mailboxes from the property, resulting in her inability to reliably receive mail at the rental address. She has been forced to rely on redirection by mail carriers or neighbours across the street. This has caused additional administrative and personal difficulties, contributing to what she described as a ‘domino effect’ of ongoing problems. 30. The Tenant introduced photographs showing dumpsters, demolition activity, removal of contents, and the rental unit door being held open during construction. The Landlord raised no objection to the photographs and did not present any evidence to contradict them. 31. Mr. [name]name] cross-examined the Tenant on her evidence presented. 32. During cross-examination, the Landlord questioned Ms. [name] regarding the circumstances of the fire and the actions taken by firefighters. Ms. [name]name] testified that firefighters used a significant amount of water to extinguish the fire and that water entered the building and affected multiple areas of the house, including flooding the rental unit. 33. The Landlord introduced an email exchange dated April 2024 and asked Ms. [name]name] to review it. After being given an opportunity to read the document, Ms. [name] confirmed that she recognized the email and that she authored it. The Landlord put to Ms. [name]name] that the email indicated that the Tenants had removed their belongings from the unit by late April 2024, except for a limited number of items. Ms. [name]name] acknowledged the email but did not concede that this amounted to a voluntary abandonment of the tenancy. 34. The Landlord asserted that items removed from the rental unit following the fire were “garbage,” “unusable,” or abandoned by the Tenants. The Landlord referred to photographs showing items being removed and stated that the Tenants had left belongings behind unnecessarily. The Tenant, Ms. [name], denied characterizing her belongings as garbage and denied abandoning her property. 35. The Landlord further alleged that the Tenants never cooperated in arranging retrieval of their belongings. In response, documentary evidence was introduced showing that on March 12, 2024, an email was sent from the Landlord’s household (identified as [name]) to Ms. [name]name] requesting a date to retrieve belongings. Ms. [name]name] acknowledged that the email address shown was hers but testified that she did not recall seeing that email. 36. On redirect, the Tenant explained that immediately following the fire she was instructed that all communications with the Landlord proceed through her legal representative, due to the strained and contentious relationship with the Landlord. She testified that it was her LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 understanding that she should not engage directly with the Landlord and that this explained any lack of direct response to emails sent solely to her. She would forward emails sent by the Landlord directly to her legal representative, [name]. 37. The Tenant [name] testified that he has lived in the rental with Ms. [name]name] and was at work at the time of the fire. He described returning to the rental unit to find the unit inaccessible and was displaced along with Ms. [name]name]. 38. He testified that he is a drywall taper and that he relies on specialized tools for his employment. He stated that many of his tools remained inside the rental unit following the fire and had trouble accessing them. He stated this was because the Landlord would not along them access to the unit for extended periods even though the Landlord entered the unit himself. 39. Mr. [name]name] testified that as a result of being unable to retrieve his tools promptly, he was required to borrow or repurchase expensive specialty tools, work longer hours using less efficient methods, and travel frequently to storage locations. He described this as causing significant stress and financial strain. 40. Text message evidence exchanged between the Landlord and Tenant counsel was entered, showing repeated requests for access to retrieve tools and requests for clarity on timelines. The messages also demonstrate that access was often offered on short notice or subject to conditions that were difficult for the Tenants to meet given work schedules. The Landlord did not present any evidence or submissions contradicting the text messages. 41. The Landlord’s repeated assertions that he “asked for a date” to arrange retrieval of belongings do not negate the overwhelming evidence that access was delayed, conditional, and difficult to coordinate. The Tenants clearly communicated, through counsel, their reliance on legal representation for all communications due to the contentious nature of the relationship. Despite this, the Landlord continued to send direct emails and texts to the Tenants, creating confusion and further delay. The Board finds that the Landlord’s approach was unreasonable given the circumstances and contrary to the obligation to act in good faith and facilitate access promptly. The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord’s offers of access were often made on short notice, without flexibility, and subject to conditions that were impractical for the Tenants to meet, such as requiring attendance during working hours or limiting the time available for retrieval. 42. The Landlord’s evidence was not only repetitive and argumentative but also lacked probative value. Much of his testimony strayed into issues not raised during cross- examination and focused on personal opinions rather than factual rebuttal. While the Board acknowledges the seriousness of the fire and the regulatory restrictions imposed, these factors do not justify the Landlord’s characterization that the Tenants abandoned their belongings or that removed items were “garbage.” This characterization is inconsistent with the nature of the items described, particularly specialized work tools essential for employment, personal effects, and household goods. The Board finds that the Landlord’s statements were self-serving and unsupported by documentary evidence. In contrast, the Tenants provided contemporaneous communications, photographs, and LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 credible testimony that corroborated their efforts to retrieve belongings and maintain tenancy. Analysis 43. Based on the evidence presented by the Tenant’s I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord changed the locks without giving the Tenants a replacement key and has interfered with the Tenants. 44. I prefer the Tenant’s testimony as it was consistent, detailed, and corroborated by documents. The Tenant’s evidence also aligned with contemporaneous communications. The Landlord’s evidence was repetitive to the N12, and argumentative. While the Board accepts the Landlord faced regulatory and financial challenges, these do not excuse his conduct that interfered with the Tenant’s rights. 45. When I examined the evidence presented, there is no doubt a fire occurred in February 2024 affecting the rental unit, the unit was not fit for habitation. I accept that the initial displacement of the Tenants was necessary and not the fault of either party. 46. I turn to section 22 of the ‘Act’ it states: Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential co mplex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22. 47. While the fire itself does not constitute a breach, the Landlord’s post fire conduct does. I find that the Landlord unreasonably restricted access to the rental unit, failed to facilitate timely retrieval of the Tenant’s belongings, removed or disposed of the Tenant; s property without consent, and imposed conditions that were impractical and inequitable. 48. The Landlord has no authority to unilaterally deem tenant property abandoned in these circumstances. The Landlord did not provide any reasonable explanation for disposing the Tenant’s property or belongings without consent. The Landlord’s feelings about claiming it was garbage does not negate his legal obligation to obtain the Tenant’s consent before disposal. 49. The Board is particularly concerned that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenants with any clear timeline for return to the rental unit. While the Board accepts that regulatory and financial challenges may have delayed repairs, the Landlord had an obligation to communicate transparently and provide updates. Instead, the evidence shows that the Landlord gave inconsistent explanations, including financial hardship, insurance delays, and his own intention to occupy the unit. This lack of clarity created prolonged uncertainty for the Tenants, who maintained their official address and expressed a consistent intention to return. The failure to provide a timeline constitutes a significant interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment and security of tenure under section 22 of the Act. LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 50. Lastly, [name] requested that the Board impose an administrative fine against the Landlord. I am not going to impose an administrative fine against the Landlord at this time, as this is a small Landlord and the Board appears to have no prior history of the Landlord’s conduct. It is my view that the order itself serves as a sufficient warning to the Landlord that such conduct will not be tolerated should he appear before the Board in the future for similar actions or applications. Remedies 51. Mr. [name]name] credibly testified to financial loss and disruption caused by lack of access to work tools. He replaced tools that were damaged or discarded by the Landlord. These losses were directly attributable to the Landlord’s unreasonable restrictions on access and failure to safeguard the Tenants’ property. Accordingly, I order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $2,000.00 for the loss of tools and replacement costs. 52. The monthly rent for the unit was $2,000.00. Given the prolonged period during which the Tenants were deprived of reasonable enjoyment and access to their rental unit, a rent abatement is appropriate. A 25% abatement for 12 months reflects the diminished value of the tenancy during this period and compensates the Tenants for the inconvenience and loss of use. This calculation results in $500 per month for 12 months, totaling $6,000.00. Therefore, I order the Landlord to pay the Tenants $6,000.00 as a rent abatement. 53. The Tenants requested general compensation of $15,000.00 each, totaling $30,000.00, for stress, inconvenience, and interference with their rights. While the Board acknowledges the significant hardship experienced by the Tenants, including prolonged displacement, loss of property, and financial strain. After considering the seriousness of the Landlord’s conduct, the duration of interference, I find that an award of $5,000.00 per Tenant is fair and proportionate. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenants $10,000.00 in compensation. Total Award: • Compensation for tools: $2,000.00 • Rent abatement: $6,000.00 • General damages: $10,000.00 Total payable by the Landlord: $18,000.00
ordered: The Landlord’s L2/N12 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $18,000.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for rent abatement. • $2,000.00 for replacement costs of the tools. • $10,000.00 in general compensation. LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before January 17, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord' s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $1,568.83, for the cost of this application and his failure to maintain the rental unit.
The tenancy commenced on September 1, 2024, and ended in August 2025.
The lawful monthly rent was $2,800.00, with the daily rate for the unit calculated as $92.50.
The Tenants alleged that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations in several ways: Cockroaches

The Landlord promised to have the rental unit ready on September 1, 2024 , when the tenancy commenced but the Tenants were not satisfied with the state of the unit . On September 2, 2024, they sent an email to the Landlord outlining the issues of concern in the unit which included an infestation of cockroaches.
The parties agree that on September 4, September 16, and September 30, 2024, the Landlord hired professionals to treat the unit , and no live bedbug activities were observed thereafter.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Here, the Landlord responded to the Tenants’ complaints about cockroaches in a timely manner. The first complaint was made on September 2, 2024, with the first treatment taking place on September 4, 2024 . Subsequent treatments in the rental unit eradicated the problem.

Applying the Court’s direction in this case, the mere presence of cockroaches in the unit is not an automatic basis for finding that the Landlords breached s ection 20 of the Act. Therefore, on a contextual analysis, as the Landlord provided a timely response to the pest infestation, no remedy will be awarded to the Tenants. Mold / Unclean Unit

The Tenants on September 1, 2024, informed the Landlord about a dark area in one of the bedrooms of the rental unit which they believed was caused by mold. The Landlord claimed it was dirt and that the previous Tenants were untidy but took no steps to clean it . The Tenants purchased products to clean the area, $44.17 as seen in the receipts provided, and presented before and after pictures showing a noticeable difference in the area.

The entire rental unit was also unclean when the Tenants moved in on September 1, 2024, even though t he Landlord , who was present , told them that he was working on the refrigerator. The Tenants presented pictures of dirty or stained areas in the unit and testified that it took 124 hours for them and four other family members and friends to clean the unit for the first few days. The Tenants sent a text message to the Landlord notifying him about the amount of cleaning they were doing on September 1, 2024. The Tenants requested an order for $2,728.00 for the cleaning and labour calculated at $22.00 an hour.

The Landlord denied that there was mold in the rental unit and testified that on September 1, 2024, when the Tenants arrived to obtain vacant possession of the unit, he was in the process of cleaning the unit. The Landlord presented a quote, dated August 30, 2024, which he obtained from a cleaning company after they inspected the unit. The quote for ‘house regular cleaning service’ was $250.00.

While I am not satisfied from the evidence that the dark area or stain in one of the bedrooms was caused by mold, the evidence demonstrates that the unit was not thoroughly cleaned by the Landlord on September 1, 2024, when the Tenants took possession. Hence, they will be reimbursed the cost of $44.17 incurred for the cleaning supplies.

As for the time taken to do the cleaning, the Tenants requested $2,728.00 for 124hrs of work at $22.00 an hour. The Landlord disputes this amount and the invoice he provided showed he was charged $250.00 to clean the unit. In this circumstance, I find an award of $500.00 for two days of cleaning fair. As much as the Tenants claimed that they cleaned for 124 hours, the stove for example appeared untouched, and I cannot rely on that estimate. The Landlord will be ordered to pay a total of $544.17 for not ensuring the unit was cleaned prior to giving possession to the Tenants. [name]

The Tenants contacted the bylaw office, and an officer visited the rental unit in response on September 25, 2024. In an Order to Comply issued on September 26, 2024, they ordered the Landlord to install guardrails in the stairs by October 17, 2024. On October 16, 2024, the Landlord installed the guardrail which the Tenants claimed was poorly installed. However, given the evidence that it was approved by the city, I am not satisfied that the Landlord is in breach of his maintenance obligations. Stove

The Tenants testified that the stove was in poor condition and in the email from September 2, 2024, asked the Landlord for a replacement because it showed signs of fire damage. On September 11, 2024, they requested a professional inspection of the stove and by September 18, 2024, the Landlord called the request unreasonable. The Tenant presented pictures of the stove which showed filth under the stove plates and in the oven and appeared to have suffered some fire damage. On September 25, 2024, the bylaw officer told the Tenants not to use the stove because it smoked when he turned it on and he deemed it unsafe. The stove was not replaced until October 2, 2024, following a direction from the bylaw office.

The Tenants requested an order to be compensated $9 31.83 which represents the difference between the amount they spent on purchasing prepared meals from September 1, 2024, to September 27, 2024, $1,284.03, and their grocery bill in April 2025, $352.20.

The Landlord stated that the stove was in working condition although one burner smoked a bit. He was told to either clean it or replace it, but he chose to replace it on September 26, 2024, when he purchased and installed a new one.

Despite the Landlord’s statements that he was given an option on whether to replace or clean the stove, the stove was in a poor condition, dirty, melted and broken in part, and the Tenants believed it to be a safety concern. This fear was shared by the bylaw officer who ordered the Landlord to either clean the stove or replace it . The Landlord breached the Act by failing to maintain the stove, and given the condition, I am surprised by the cleaning option given by the city . Due to the Landlord’s breach of the Act, he will be ordered to pay to the Tenants, 30% of the $92.05 daily rate for the rental unit which is $745.74 ($27.62 x 27 days from September 1, 2024, to September 27, 2024). Dryer

On September 2, 2024, the Tenants informed the Landlord that the unit was not drying properly. On September 27, 2024, the Landlord tried to fix it but was unable to . By October 10, 2024, the Landlord hired a contractor who did.
The Landlord claimed that he was informed on October 1, 2024, and due to scheduling issues was not installed until October 10, 2024.

The text messages between the parties presented as evidence by the Tenant shows that sometime in October 2024, the Landlord asked the Tenants if they cancelled the service appointment for the dryer . The Tenants responded that there was some scheduling issue and that the appointment would take place the day after.

Therefore, while I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to repair the dryer from September 2, 2024, by September 27, 2024, the Landlord took steps to repair it failing which he hired a technician to have it fixed. The Tenants are entitled to 5% ($4.60) rent abatement for the period from September 2, 2024, to September 26, 2024 (25 days) at $115.00. Window Screens

The screen s in two rooms in the rental unit had holes and prevented the Tenants from opening the windows. The Landlord removed them for repairs on September 1, 2024, but they were not returned until November 2, 2024.

Although the Landlord claimed they were replaced on October 16, 2024, the Tenants presented text messages dated November 1, 2024, in which the Landlord stated that he would bring the screens tomorrow.

I am satisfied from the evidence that the screens were damaged and were not replaced within a reasonable time by the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to rent abatement of 2% ($ 1.84) rent abatement for the period from September 2, 2024, to November 2, 2024 (63 days) at $115.92. Overhead Lights
The lights did not work in one of the bedrooms as relayed to the Landlord in the email from September 2, 2024. The parties agree that this issue was resolved on September 13, 2024.
Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to rent abatement of 2% ($1.84) rent abatement for the period from September 2, 2024, to September 13, 2024 (12 days) at $20.08.
The Tenants are entitled to a total rent abatement of $1,568.83 due to the Landlord’s failure to meet their maintenance obligations.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application, and this amount must be refunded by the Landlord.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $1,568.83. This amount represents: • $544.17 for the cleaning costs and time expended by the Tenant to clean the unit • $745.74 rent abatement for the lack of a safe stove • $115.00 rent abatement for the nonfunctioning dryer • $115.92 rent abatement for the damaged screen, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by March 31 , 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $108.00.

The Tenant testified that, on September 24, 2025, she was working from home. The Landlord entered the backyard without notice, then came to the front door and knocked for around ten minutes. The Tenant explained that the backyard was for her use only, and that no one else was supposed to have access to it. As a single woman living alone, the Tenant felt uncomfortable and afraid because of the incident.

Based on the uncontested testimony of the Tenant, I am satisfied that the backyard was part of the rental unit and that the Landlord entered it without notice on September 24, 2025. Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. However, since the Landlord did not enter the basement itself, but stayed outside to knock on the front door, I am not satisfied that his actions had a significant impact on the Tenant.

I find a nominal amount of $60.00 to be an appropriate rent abatement in these circumstances. As there were no out-of-pocket costs or damaged property arising from this incident, those additional remedies are dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $108.00. This amount represents: • $60.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
