issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants applications were filed on October 9, 2024 pursuant to section 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act). Therefore, in accordance with subsection 29(2) of the Act, the Board can only award the Tenants remedies and/or consider breaches that were ongoing from October 9, 2023 as this was one-year prior to the applications being filed.

The following allegations were plead and argued at the hearings: • Lack of heat in the rental unit • Mould and Water Leaks • Water Quality • Broken Fences • Harassment / Substantial Interference – Deeming rental unit abandoned and serving N12 notice in a retaliatory manner.

The following sections of the Act are relevant to the allegations contained in the Tenant’s applications: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The rental unit is single detached dwelling located on a farm. In addition to the rental unit, the Tenants also use a portion of the land for their two horses. The monthly rent is $1,200.00 per month ($1,000.00 for the unit & $200.00 to board the horses).
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on or about July 2017 and continued to reside in the unit as of the third hearing date. Heat:
The parties agree that the rental unit has a furnace located in the basement of the rental unit and that in addition to this, the upper floor has electric baseboard heaters. Tenant’s Evidence:
The Tenant testified that she experienced concerns with heat in the rental unit as early as 2019 and stated that the furnace had to be reset or serviced several times.

The Tenant testified that from January 2022 to December 2023 the furnace was non- functional. The Tenant submitted into evidence email correspondence sent to the Landlord on January 19 & 20, 2022 advising that the house was cold and that the heat was not working (TT exhibit #1).

The Tenant testified that during the winter months of 2022 and 2023, that she had to use the wood stove on the main floor and space heaters to help heat the home. The Tenant agreed that the Landlords provided her with the wood for the main floor fireplace.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord only took her heat concerns seriously when she contacted [name] enforcement on September 24, 2023 and when an “Order to Comply” was issued by the municipality. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of the [name] order (TT exhibit #2). The order was issued on October 31, 2023 and orders the Landlords to address three maintenance concerns by December 31, 2023. One of the items addressed in the order is that the furnace is not working.
The Tenant agreed that heat in the rental unit was restored at some point in December 2023 but could not confirm the exact date as she was not residing in the rental unit during this period.

During the period of November 2, 2023 to April 27, 2024, the Tenant was living at her brothers residence located approximately two hours away from the rental unit. The Tenant stated that she decided to move out for this short period because the rental unit was too cold and to allow the Landlord to address the [name] order and other maintenance concerns (mould). Landlord’s evidence:

The Landlord testified that at the commencement of the tenancy that the furnace located in the rental unit was an oil furnace and that despite concerns being reported by the Tenants throughout the tenancy, that the concerns were addressed within a timely manner.

The Landlords submitted into evidence inspection reports of the original oil furnace from June 2017 confirming that there were no maintenance concerns when the Tenants moved into the rental unit (LL exhibit #1).
The Landlords also submitted into evidence an invoice dated January 21, 2022, confirming that the furnace was repaired after it had initially failed and reported by the Tenants (LL exhibit #2).

The Landlord agreed that on December 14, 2022, that the furnace had failed and that the technician “tagged the furnace out” and recommended a replacement. The Landlord confirmed that the furnace was shut down from this date until November 7, 2023, when a new propane furnace was installed.
The Landlords submitted into evidence documents confirming that the new propane furnace was ordered on October 11, 2023 (LL exhibit #3).

When asked why the Landlord delayed ordering a new furnace for almost a year, the Landlord responded by stating that he believed the Tenants were vacating the rental unit. The Landlord further argued that the delays were due to the Tenants not wanting a propane furnace being installed in the rental unit and wanting the original oil powered furnace to remain.

The Landlord’s representative pointed the Board to the compliance order issued by Bylaw Enforcement and pointed out that the Landlord had competed the furnace repair / replacement by the date set out in the [name] order (December 31, 2023).

The Landlord’s representative also noted that despite the delay in the furnace being installed, the wood-burning stove and baseboard heaters were still active and working during this period. Findings & Analysis:

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlords have breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the heating and ensuring that the rental unit was equipped with a working furnace.

At the hearing, the parties disagreed with and/or argued whether the furnace was working from January 2022 to November 2022. I find this to be irrelevant as it falls well outside of the Board’s one-year limitation period as the applications were filed on October 9, 2024.

I do note however, that the Landlord’s own evidence at the hearing was that the furnace failed and became inoperable in December 2022 and that despite this, a new furnace was not installed until November 2023.
Section 4 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (O. Reg. 516/06: GENERAL) states that heat is a vital service that should be provided from September 1 to June 15 of each respective year.

Therefore, the Landlord’s own testimony at the hearing confirms that the rental unit was without its primary heat source for the period prescribed in the regulations and that despite the Landlords knowing of the issue, that it was not rectified for an eleven month period.

I do not accept the Landlord’s explanation that the Tenant interfered with the installation of the new furnace as there was insufficient evidence such as specific dates or written correspondence between the parties to suggest that the Tenant was objecting to a new propane furnace being installed.

Further, although I accept that the baseboard heaters were still working, the evidence before the Board is that these heaters were only for the upstairs portion of the rental unit and therefore could not provide the same heat to the main floor and basement as the furnace would have.

I therefore find that the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations for the period of October 9, 2023 (one-year prior to the application being filed) to November 7, 2023, the date the new furnace was installed. I also find that this breach substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Mould & Water Leaks:

Although these are two separate maintenance issues being plead, the parties seemed to agree at the hearing that they closely relate / overlap with each other and therefore, the evidence and analysis of these two concerns were addressed together.

The Tenants applications allege that the rental unit has a large presence of mould, inadequate air quality and dampness due to water infiltrating into the basement portion of the home. Tenant’s Evidence:
The Tenant testified that she observed these concerns shortly after moving into the unit and that the rental unit contained a musty smell.

The Tenants take the position that these maintenance concerns are still ongoing as of the third hearing date. 34. [name] further testified that based on his findings in the inspection that he noticed that there was a lot of dust in the basement and that this portion of the home requires a cleaning, that there were some cracks on the interior brick wall in the living room and around the exterior bedroom window that should be repaired to limit moisture / water infiltration in the rental unit. 39. (TT exhibit #6). 43. The Tenant also submitted into evidence email correspondence sent to the Landlord on October 8, 2023 advising of the ongoing mould concerns and the health concerns experienced on or about this period (TT exhibit #7). 44. In addition to the mould reports, the Tenants also submitted into evidence photographs of the basement portion of the rental unit taken on March 17, 2025, confirming that water was still leaking into the basement portion of the rental unit (TT exhibit #8). The Tenant stated that water consistently leaks / pools on the basement floor and believes that this contributes to the mould / poor air quality of the rental unit. 46. The Tenant also submitted into evidence photographs from early April 2025, showing cracks on the interior brick wall of the main floor of the rental unit (TT exhibit #9). 47. The Tenant also submitted into evidence email correspondence with the Landlord on March 27, 2024 and on February 1, 2024 confirming that the water leaks / concerns were ongoing (TT exhibit #10). 48. The Tenants take the position that the Landlord took no steps to address the water infiltration into the rental unit until April 2023 by installing an eavestrough on the property and that despite this, the water leaks are still ongoing. The Tenant did however agree that the Landlord spray-foamed cracks in the foundation of the home but maintained the position that this repair was ineffective. 49. The Tenant agreed that in March 2025, the Landlord provided her with a fan and humidifier for the basement to help with dampness in the basement. Landlord’s Evidence: 50. The Landlord testified that the rental unit is over 150 years old with a stone foundation. The Landlord agrees that water leaks were reported by the Tenants in 2023 and stated that in November 2023 repairs were done. The Landlord stated that he removed the old basement staircase, and spray foamed the surrounding walls on or about the end of November 2023. The Landlords submitted into evidence photographs of the new staircase and the spray foamed walls (LL exhibit #4). The Landlord testified that on December 21, 2023, they hired their own technician to conduct an air quality test. The Landlord submitted into evidence an email received from [name] enforcement confirming that on December 19, 2023 that the compliance order issued on October 31, 2023 had been closed (LL exhibit #7) 53. The Landlord testified that when the Tenants returned to the rental unit, that the Tenant was still complaining about the air quality of the rental unit. In response to the Tenant’s complaints, the Landlords conducted an inspection on the rental unit which included removing the fireplace and surrounding drywall which confirmed that there was no visible signs of mould. 54. The Landlords conducted a subsequent air quality test of the rental unit on February 12, 2025, in response to ongoing complaints made by the Tenants. The testing was completed by [name]. The report the is the same copy that the Tenants submitted into evidence in their examination in chief. 55. Following the air quality report in February 2025, the Landlords conducted air duct cleaning in the rental unit. The Landlord was unsure however as to the exact date of this treatment, nor did the Landlords provide an invoice / receipt for this work done. 56. The Landlord testified that during his inspections of the rental unit that he did not notice a strong musty smell in the basement portion of the rental unit and stated that any smell observed was likely due to the Tenants having two cats in the rental unit. 57. With respect to the water leaks in the basement, the Landlord testified that due to the age of the house a sump pump is installed to drain excess water away from and under the home. The Landlords also submitted into evidence an invoice confirming that surrounding trees / stumps were removed from the foundation of the property on October 24, 2023 (LL exhibit # 8). 59. The Landlord further testified that in May 2025 he purchased a new de-humidifier for the basement. The Landlords submitted into evidence a copy of this receipt (LL exhibit #9) and stated that on or about the end of January 2024 that the sump-pump system was replaced to improve drainage. The Landlords submitted into evidence two receipts dated January 18 & 27, 2024 confirming that new sump pumps were purchased (LL exhibit #10) 60. The Landlord testified that on March 18, 2025, he inspected the basement of the rental unit with a municipal building inspector. During this inspection, the Landlord learned that the de humidifier was not working which is what prompted the replacement. The Landlord noted however that no compliance order was issued by [name] during this inspection and further that after the inspection was concluded that an air blower was placed in the basement to assist with any moisture in the basement of the rental unit and that the new de humidifier was installed to drain into the sump well and not overflow on the basement floor. 61. When questioned about the Tenant’s most recent photographs of water in the basement taken on March 17, 2025, the Landlord responded by stating that the water was likely coming up from the concrete floor and not through any cracks in the walls and stated that given the age of the home that “not much could be done”. The Landlord maintained the position that there is no structural damages to the property nor has an order to comply been issued by [name] enforcement with respect to foundational issues for the property. 62. On cross-examination, the Tenant’s representative referenced an email sent from the Landlord to the Tenant on October 7, 2023, in which the Landlord states that a contractor by the name of “[name]” stated that “ the only way to completely solve the problem was to excavate and put drainage around the old foundation of the home” (TT exhibit # 11). 63. Landlord reiterated on cross-examination that the rental unit is a “old house” and that not much can be done with preventing water from coming up from under the concrete floor and that “nobody lives in the basement”. Findings & Analysis: 64. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlords have breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the mould and water leaks in the rental unit. 65. Both parties at the hearing submitted into evidence mould / air quality reports conducted and gave their submissions on these reports. In reviewing each of the reports, they all seem to conclude that the rental unit contains a higher-than-normal spore count of Penicillium/Aspergillus and Chaetomium in the rental unit. Each of the reports also confirm that exposure to these types of mould spores can cause illness and/or allergic reactions to some individuals. 66. I further note that despite the oral submissions of the parties, the Tenant’s witness (Yves Levis) appeared to be the only individual present at the three hearings who had professional knowledge of the testing, the types of mould spores, the normal spore counts typically found in a residential dwelling and the effect they may have on an individual’s health. [name] ultimately confirmed that during his air quality test of the rental unit on October 28, 2024, showed that an abnormal spore count of Penicillium/Aspergillus and Chaetomium were present in the rental unit and the report further confirmed that these types of mould spores could potentially affect an individual’s health. 67. The Tenants also produced medical documentation at the hearing confirming that they have had reactions / health concerns because of the mould presence in the rental unit. 68. Further, despite the suggestions in each of the mould reports (including [name] taken prior to the first hearing date), it appears that the Landlords did not follow the recommended recommendations until after the proceedings had commenced in February 2025. 69. I therefore accept the Tenant’s testimony that as of the third hearing date on June 27, 2025, that the mould spores / issue in the rental unit is still ongoing and of a concern to the Tenants. The Landlords did not provide any reports / testing to confirm that the abnormal spore counts of Penicillium/Aspergillus and Chaetomium had been substantially reduced. 70. With respect to the water leaks in the rental unit, I also find that the Landlords are in breach of the Act with respect to this issue and further find that this issue is a contributing factor to the mould / poor air quality in the rental unit. 71. The Tenant’s photographic evidence confirms that on or about the second hearing date that a substantial amount of water was still coming into / being present on the basement floors. Although the Landlords may have taken some steps to remedy this concern, the evidence and testimony before the Board confirms that it has been ineffective. Water Quality: 72. The parties agree that the rental unit runs on well water. Tenant’s Evidence: 73. The Tenant stated that at some point during her tenancy, she began to drink bottled water only because the UV system stopped working and was not filtering the hardened water from the drinking tap. 74. The Tenant agreed that the UV system was repaired / replaced by the Landlord in May 2024, but stated that the Landlord had installed a bypass valve for the drinking water tap which has been shut off since this period. Landlord’s Evidence: 75. The Landlord testified that when in 2017 when the Tenants moved in that there was no water softener installed or UV system. The Landlord stated that a UV system was installed prior to the water softener being installed, with a separate tap to ensure that non-softened drinking water was available. The Landlord conceded that the process was done incorrectly as the UV system was to be installed after the water softener was installed. Because of this, the Landlord installed the bypass valve in May 2024. 76. The Landlord submitted into evidence water testing reports taken on June 4, 2025 for the water in the rental unit which conclude that no toxic or harmful chemicals such as coliform or E.coli are running through the water supply system (LL exhibit #11). Findings & Analysis: 77. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act or withheld a vital service from the Tenants with respect to the water quality. 78. Although there is no dispute that the bypass valve connected to the drinking tap has been turned off since May 2024, there is no evidence before the Board to suggest that the water in the unsafe for human consumption. Further, the Landlords provided evidence from the municipality confirming that the drinking water is not contaminated with any harmful chemicals and is safe to drink. 79. As such, this portion of the applications is dismissed. Fences: 80. As stated above, the rental unit is located on a farm. The total property owned by the Landlords consist of 90 acres of land. The portion of the property that the Tenants use to board their horses has cedar and wired fences separating the horse pasture from the rest of the property. Tenant’s Evidence: 81. The Tenant testified that she first noticed concerns with the fence on or about June 2022, when she noticed a tree growing through one of the fences. The Tenant claims that she advised the Landlord of this concern, but that it was never addressed. 82. The Tenant further testified that after she had temporarily vacated the rental unit, that the Landlord advised her that she was not permitted to bring back the horses and as such, no repairs were completed to address the broken / decaying fences. Despite the Landlord’s request, the Tenants still brought their two horses back to the rental property. 83. The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs of the fences taken on March 20, 2024 (TT exhibit #12). The photographs confirm that many of the wood fences have rotted and are collapsing. The Tenant stated that the fences remain in the same condition as of the hearing date. 84. The Tenant also submitted into evidence email correspondence with the Landlord’s legal representative on February 5, 2024 (TT exhibit #13). In the email correspondence, the Landlords are taking the position that they are not responsible for maintaining the fences as the horse pasture is not part of the rental unit and/or the residential complex, but a rather a “commercial space”. Landlord’s Evidence: 85. The Landlord testified that throughout the tenancy, the land had been leased out to local farmers but agreed that the Tenant was permitted to board her horses on the property for $200.00 per month. The Landlords argues that the rent for the horses is separate from the monthly rent owing for the rental unit itself and not the right to board the horses. 86. The Landlord did not dispute the condition of the fences based on the Tenant’s photographs submitted at the hearing and confirmed that the fences remain in the same state of disrepair as of the third hearing date. 87. On cross-examination the Landlord stated that he has no intentions to replace the fences. Findings & Analysis: 88. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the state of the fences. 89. The photographs submitted into evidence by the Tenants and the Landlord’s own testimony confirm that the wooden fences on the property are rotting, collapsing and not in a good state of repair. 90. I do not accept the Landlords argument that the fences are not part of the residential portion of the property or that they don’t relate to the rental unit itself. The evidence before the Board is that on or about the time the tenancy commenced that the Tenants were paying $200.00 to the Landlords for the right to board their horses on the property and that this portion of the property is located on the same land as the rental unit. 91. Section 2 of the Act defines rent as “the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing”. 92. Based on the plain reading of the definition of rent under the Act, it is clear that the Tenants are paying “rent” to board their horses on the property. 93. Further, section 2 of the Act also confirms that the “residential complex” of the property includes all common areas, services and facilities available for the use of the residents. Therefore, 94. I therefore find that the fences are part of the residential complex in which the rental unit is in and which the Tenants use / reside in. Harassment / Substantial Interference: 95. The Tenant’s T2 application alleges harassment and substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment with respect to two issues. Tenant’s Evidence: 96. The first issue is that the Landlords attempted to deem the rental unit as abandoned when the Tenants vacated on a temporary basis from November 2023 to April 2025. The Tenants submitted into evidence an email received by the Landlord’s legal representative on February 21, 2024 advising that they were “presuming the property abandoned” (TT exhibit #14). 97. The Tenant stated that she was shocked to receive this email, because she had been in active communication with the Landlords and their representative throughout the months of January and February 2024 and never once expressed that she would not be returning to the rental unit. The Tenants submitted into evidence email correspondence between the parties on January 29, 2024, February 1, 2, 5, 6, 8 & 9, 2024, confirming that the parties were discussing the maintenance and repairs on the property (TT exhibit #15). 98. The Tenant confirmed at the hearing however, that despite the Landlords advising that they were going to deem the rental unit as abandoned on February 21, 2024, that the locks to the rental unit were not changed nor were the Tenants barred from accessing the rental unit when they returned in April 2024. 99. The Tenant also agreed on cross-examination that she had cancelled her hydro account from the rental unit prior to February 2024. The Tenant stated that this was done because she believed the Landlord was using her baseboard / space heaters to heat the rental unit during the time the Tenants were out of the rental unit. 100. With respect to the second claim of harassment, the Tenant testified that shortly after reporting to the Landlords about her health concerns of mould in the rental unit that the Landlord [name] advised that his son and joint-landlord ([name]) intended to move into the rental unit. The Tenants take the position that the Landlord’s response is retaliatory. 101. The Tenant testified that the Landlords served her and her son with an N12 notice of termination on October 25, 2023. The Tenants agreed that this N12 notice was never filed with the Board on an application to terminate the tenancy. 102. On cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the Landlords had advised her at the commencement of the tenancy it was their intention to eventually move into the rental unit. 103. The Landlords then served the Tenants with a second N12 notice of termination on April 7, 2024 also stating that one of the Landlords require vacant possession of the rental unit for their own personal use. The Board’s records confirm that this N12 notice was dismissed by way of order LTB-L-029098-24 issued May 1, 2024, as the Landlords had failed to pay the required compensation pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act. Landlord’s Evidence: 104. The Landlord testified that when the Tenants vacated the rental unit on November 2, 2023 that the Tenants advised that they would return to the rental unit in mid January 2023. The Landlords submitted into evidence an email from the Tenant [name] dated December 23, 2023 stating that the Tenants would return to the rental unit mid- January 2024 (LL exhibit #12). 105. The Landlord testified that he believed that the Tenants had abandoned the rental unit because N12 was served, the Tenants did not return as per the date indicated in the prior email, because the Tenants did not pay rent for the period of October 2023 to April 2024 and because the Tenants cancelled their hydro account in January 2024. 106. On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed that he advised the Tenants that rent for October 2023 would be waived due to their concerns. Findings & Analysis: 107. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have harassed and/or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for the above noted incidents. 108. With respect to the N12 notices of termination being served, the evidence before the Board is that the Landlords served the initial N12 notice prior to [name] enforcement issuing an “order to comply” and therefore I do not accept the Tenant’s submissions that the N12 notice was served in a retaliatory manner. Further, the Landlords have the right under section 48 of the Act to serve N12 notices of termination for personal use and therefore, I find it would be unreasonable to deem a landlord in breach of sections 22 and 23 of the Act for asserting their lawful rights. If the Tenants dispute the contents / good faith of the Landlord’s N12 notice, they are ultimately afforded the right to dispute the notice at a hearing before the Board. 109. With respect to the Landlords and/or their representative asserting that the Tenants abandoned the rental unit, the evidence before the Board ultimately confirms that the Landlords never barred the Tenants access or the right to return / reoccupy the rental unit, nor were any of the Tenant’s personal items disposed of during the period that they were not in possession. Therefore, although I find that the Landlords were incorrect to assume that the Tenants had abandoned the rental unit, that there was no substantial impact on the Tenants and therefore, this portion of the application muse be denied. Remedies: 110. As the Tenants have proven some of the allegations contained in the applications, the Tenants are entitled to some or all the remedies claimed. Filing Fee: 111. The Tenants were granted a fee waiver when filing their applications and therefore there are no costs to be reimbursed to the Tenants. Administrative Fine: 112. The Tenant’s T2 application requests that the Board order the Landlords to pay a administrative fine. 113. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 entitled Administrative Fines addresses when the Board generally imposes fines: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 114. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I do not find that an administrative fine is warranted in these circumstances. Although I have found the Landlords to be in breach of the Act on some of the issues alleged, I find that the Landlords have taken and/or attempted to take steps to address the most serious of the concerns (mould / water leaks) and that the overall conduct of the Landlords does not suggest a blatant disregard for the Act. Although the Landlords own admission is that nothing has done to remedy the concerns with the fences, I do not find this to be a serous enough breach to warrant an administrative fine. 115. Finally, I find that the remedies granted as part of this order provide a sufficient deterrence to ensure future compliance with the Act by the Landlords. Cease and Desist: 116. The Tenant’s T2 application requests that the Landlords cease from attempting to remove the Tenants from the rental unit and/or serving retaliatory N12 notices. As this portion of the application was dismissed, this requested remedy must be denied. General Compensation: 117. Both the Tenant’s T2 and T6 application claim general compensation. The T2 application claims $5,000.00 and the T6 application claims $10,000.00. 118. The Board has the authority to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name].) in circumstances where the damages claimed are the result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the breach had on the tenant. 119. In both applications, the Tenants justify these amounts claimed for legal costs and disbursements, moving expenses, increased rent should they have to vacate the rental unit and pain and suffering / disruption to their lives. 120. The Tenants were represented by their local legal aid clinic on a pro bono basis and received a fee waiver from the Board and further have not terminated their tenancy or permanently moved out of the rental unit. Therefore, a large portion of these amounts claimed are moot. 121. I do find however when assessing the impact, the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenants, that the Tenants are entitled to $1,200.00 in general compensation, which is equivalent to one-months rent. The Tenants ultimately had to vacate the rental unit temporarily and re- locate approximately two hours away from their residence. Although the Tenants out-of- pocket expenses are covered under the other remedies, it is clear that the Landlord’s breach had a impact on the Tenants day-to-day lives. Rent Abatement: 122. The Tenants seek a 100% rent abatement for the period of October 1, 2023 to April 30, 2024 and a 30% rent abatement from May 1, 2024 onwards. As explained above, the lawful rent is $1,200.00 per month. 123. An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of goods and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. 124. At the hearing the parties agreed that the Landlords agreed to waive the Tenants obligation to pay rent for the month of October 2023 and as such, I find that the Tenants have already been awarded this requested abatement by the Landlords prior to the application being filed and I find it would be an abuse of process for the Tenants to request payment for this month that has already been waived by the Landlords. 125. With respect to the requested rent abatement for the months of November 2023 to April 2024, although I agree that the Tenants are entitled to a 100% rent abatement as they were not in possession of the rental unit for these months, the Tenant’s own testimony at the hearings confirm that no rent was paid to the Landlords for this period. As such, the Landlords will not be ordered to pay any funds to the Tenants for a rent abatement as the [name] requested abatement is set off from the arrears of rent owing (See: Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522). 126. With respect to the requested rent abatement for the period of May 1, 2024 to June 27, 2025 (the final hearing date), I find that the Tenant’s are entitled to a 20% rent abatement only and not a 30% abatement as the Tenants only proved some of the alleged breaches claimed on their application. 127. This amount ordered takes into consideration the number of breaches, the length of time that the breaches have been ongoing and the impact the breaches have had on the Tenants. I find that the Landlords were still in breach of the Act with respect to the mould, basement water leaks and the fence disrepair as of the third hearing date. 128. As such, the Landlords will be ordered to pay to the Tenants a rent abatement of $3,333.03, which represents a 20% rent abatement from May 1, 2024 to June 27, 2025. Out-of-Pocket Expenses Incurred: 129. The Tenant’s applications claim $13,682.63 in out-of-pocket expenses incurred from October 1, 2023 to April 27, 2024. As stated above, the Tenants did not reside in the rental unit from November 2, 2024 to April 27, 2024 and that prior to that they sometimes slept in a camper unit on the rental property. Further as explained above, the Board only has jurisdiction to award out-of-pocket expenses incurred from October 9, 2023. 130. The Tenant’s out-of-pocket expenses consists of the following: • Costs to obtain mycotoxin testing on both Tenants - $1,109.56 • Costs to obtain mould and air quality testing of rental unit - $1,762.80. • Costs to deliver / transport camper unit - $300.00 • Transportation of horses - $904.00. [name] truck rental + Fuel costs - $729.69 • Rent at temporary unit from November 2, 2023 to April 27, 2024 - $6,000.00 • Costs to board horses from November 2023 to April 2024 - $1,615.00 • Hydro costs from October 24, 2023 to January 30, 2024 - $1,173.42 • Canada Post mail forwarding from November 2023 to April 2024 - $88.16. 131. With respect to the mycotoxin testing, the Tenants submitted into evidence credit card statements confirming that they paid $555.09 on September 12, 2023, and $554.47 on October 12, 2023 (TT exhibit #16). Although I am satisfied that the Tenants incurred these out-of-pocket expenses and that these expenses were incurred because of the mould presence in the rental unit, the charge of $555.09 was incurred more than one- year prior to the application being filed and as such, the Tenants are only entitled to $554.47 for this portion of their out-of-pocket expense claim. 132. Regarding the costs the Tenants incurred to obtain their own mould testing reports, the Tenants submitted into evidence an invoice from Buller Crichton Environmental Inc. dated September 22, 2023 in the amount of 1,762.80 (TT exhibit #17). As per the terms of the invoice agreement, the Tenants paid $796.65 on September 22, 2023 and the balance of $966.15 on November 1, 2023. The Tenants submitted into evidence bank records confirming the amounts and dates of these payments. As such, I find that the Tenants are only entitled to $966.15 in these out-of-pocket expenses incurred as the payment of $796.65 was incurred more than one-year prior to the applications being filed. 133. With respect to the costs to deliver the camper unit, the Tenants submitted into evidence three e-transfer receipts sent to [name]’s brother to reimburse for gas and milage (TT exhibit #18). Each receipt is for $100.00 and are dated on October 2, 2023, October 30, 2023 and August 20, 2024. Given the dates of the receipts and the limitation period set out in subsection 29(2) of the Act I find that the Tenants are only entitled to $200.00 in reimbursement for these out-of-pocket expenses as the first payment / cost was incurred more than one-year prior to these applications being filed. 134. Regarding the costs to transfer the horses to and from the rental unit for the period of November 2023 to April 2024, the Tenants submitted into evidence two receipts dated November 4, 2023 and April 27, 2024 confirming that the Tenants were charged $452.00 each trip to bring the horses to and from the rental unit (TT exhibit #19). The Tenants are therefore entitled to $904.00 in these out-of-pocket expenses incurred. 135. With respect to the U-Haul truck rental and the fuel costs incurred, the Tenants submitted into evidence three invoices from U-Haul totaling $672.67 and two fuel receipts totalling $57.02 (TT exhibit #20). As such, I am satisfied that the Tenants incurred $729.69 in out- of-pocket expenses to move to and from the rental unit for the period of November 2, 2023 to April 27 2024 and are therefore entitled to reimbursement of these costs. 136. With respect to the rent paid from November 2023 to April 2024, the Tenant testified that she paid her brother $1,000.00 per month to reside at his residence during this period and submitted into evidence e-transfer receipts for this six-month period totaling $6,000.00 (TT exhibit #21). As I am satisfied that the Tenants had to temporarily move out of the rental unit due to the maintenance concerns with the rental unit, I find that the Tenants are entitled to these out-of-pocket expenses claimed. 137. With respect to the out-of-pocket expenses to board the horses offsite, the Tenants submitted into evidence six e-transfer receipts dated October 31 & December 1, 2023, January 1, February 1, March 1 & April 2, 2024 totaling $1,615.00 (TT exhibit #22). Although the Tenants represented these receipts as the total costs to board their horses for the months of November 2023 to April 2024, some of the receipts contain memos which confirm that additional funds were paid in addition to boarding the horses (purchasing hay). I find that the Tenants would have been responsible for these additional costs regardless of having to temporarily vacate the rental unit as it is a typical cost that comes with owing horses. Therefore, in review of the receipts and in separating the amounts specified for hay purchases, it appears that the Tenants were only paying $200.00 per month on average to board their horses. As such, the Tenants are only entitled to $1,200.00 in out-of-pocket expenses to board their horses for the period of November 2023 to April 2024. 138. With respect to the Hydro costs from October 24, 2023 to January 30, 2024, I do not find that the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement of these costs as the parties confirmed at the hearing that the Tenants were responsible for the hydro charges as per the tenancy agreement. Although the Tenants were not physically residing in the rental unit during this period and argued that the Landlords were responsible for the hydro costs incurred, the evidence before the Board is that the Landlords and their contractors were conducing repairs in the rental unit during this period as per the Tenant’s request and the [name] order. Therefore, I find that it was reasonable and essential for there to be active electricity in the rental unit during this period and as such, this claim for out-of-pocket expenses is denied. 139. Finally, regarding the costs to have the Tenant’s mail forwarded to their temporary address, the Tenants submitted into evidence receipts from Canada Post confirming that they paid $88.16 to have their mail forwarded (TT exhibit #23). The Tenants are therefore entitled to reimbursement of these costs. 140. As such, the Landlords will be ordered to pay to the Tenants $10,642.47 for the out-of- pocket expenses incurred. Order for Repairs: 141. The Tenant’s T6 application also requests that the Landlords be ordered to conduct any outstanding repairs to the rental unit / residential complex. 142. As stated above, I find that as of the final hearing date that the rental unit still contained high mould spore counts, issues with water leaking into the basement and that the fences were in a state of disrepair. 143. As such, the Landlords will be ordered to conduct these repairs by a date ordered below. 144. This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $15,175.50. This amount represents: • $3,333.03 for a rent abatement. • $10,642.47 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred. • $1,200.00 in general compensation for pain and suffering.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $1,200.00 from the rent each month from April 2026 to March 2027 and $775.50 for the month of May 2027.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

On or before May 15, 2026, the Landlords shall: • Repair the fences surrounding the rental unit [name] the appropriate repairs to ensure no water is leaking into the rental unit [name] the recommended repairs as per the mould testing reports and ensure that the air quality is improved and that any toxic mould spores are removed from the rental unit. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord, [name] (‘AT’) submits that while he is the owner of the residential complex, he is not the Landlord. The Landlord submits that the Tenant, [name] (‘MA’) has entered into a lease agreement with the tenant, [name] (‘GG’) who AT asserts is the Landlord in this application and AT denies this. For the reasons that follow, I find that AT is the Landlord. 2. [name] takes the position that AT is the true Landlord and AT’s representation of GG as the Landlord is a bad faith attempt to circumvent his responsibilities as a landlord under the LTB-T-083286-24 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). [name] submits that the real substance of all transactions and activities suggests that AT is, in fact, the Landlord. 3. AT resides in the top floor of the residential complex which is a self-contained unit. The main floor and basement share a kitchen and 2 bathrooms and is rented out as a rooming house. [name] rents a room in the lower portion of the residential complex. 4. AT does not dispute that he is the owner of the rental unit. AT submits that GG is the Landlord for the main floor and basement as the lease agreement is between GG and [name] and that MA pays rent to GG. The only document regarding the lease is an affidavit signed by [name] stating: I [name] renting a room at 48 [name] road south from [name] who is the main tenant for 650 dollar all inclusive starting Feb 2023. I understand that since I share the kitchen and bathroom with main tenant, my rental does not fall under landlord tenant act. 5. [name] testified he was required to sign the affidavit at the outset of the tenancy as a condition of entering into a tenancy agreement and moving into the rental unit. 6. [name] testified that AT was the person who listed the rental unit for rent at the outset of the tenancy. A copy of the Kijiji listing for the room for rent was entered as evidence. [name] testified that when he arranged to view the rental unit before moving in, AT picked up the Tenant and brought him to view the rental unit and assisted the Tenant to move into the rental unit. 7. The Tenant’s Witness, [name] (‘TA’), who is a diversion worker with Stepping Stone, a homelessness diversion organization, testified that he had a previous relationship with AT, who would occasionally have available rental units. TA testified he responded to AT’s ad and assisted [name] in obtaining the rental unit. TA testified that AT was present at the viewing and set the amount of the rent. 8. [name] testified that while rent was paid to GG, it was undisputed between the parties that GG provided the entirety of the rent to AT. [name] testified that AT was the person who determined when rent would increase and communicated rent increases with the residents. 9. [name] testified that when AT attempted to increase rent beyond the guideline to $750.00 in June 2024 and when the Tenant refused, AT told the Tenant to “find another place.” [name] testified that at this time, AT began to pressure GG and other residents to pressure him to leave. 10. [name] also contacted AT for issues in the rental unit, such as when he experienced issues with the internet, which was included in the lease, or when there were maintenance or other issues surrounding his tenancy. 11. AT’s position is that he has had minimal contact with MA during his tenancy. AT takes the position that as GG has disabilities, he assists GG in renting out the remainder of the residential complex, which is a rooming house, but that GG is the Landlord and AT is just a resident at the residential complex. AT submits that whatever GG is able to obtain in rent LTB-T-083286-24 monthly is provided to AT as they are friends and GG is not able to keep any rent collected as it would affect his ODSP income. 12. AT testified that while he maintains the rental unit, he does so as the Landlord for GG, not as a Landlord for the other tenants in the rental unit. 13. AT also testified that his communications with [name] regarding any rent increases were on behalf of GG. 14. AT submits that as MA’s signed declaration states that he rents a room from GG, that this document should be read at face value and supports his assertion that GG is the Landlord. 15. Section 2 of the Act states: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”) 16. Section 202 of the Act states: (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 202. 17. In my view, based on his admission that he owns the rental unit, I find that AT meets the definition of a landlord under section 2(1) of the Act. the circumstances, I am satisfied that AT is the landlord and a proper respondent to this application. 18. While GG collects rent, AT acknowledged that GG does not pay rent to AT but collects rent from his roommates and provides the entirety of the rent to AT. AT is the person responsible for maintenance and issues in the tenancy. AT was also the person who listed the units for rent, set up initial viewings, discussed rent increases. LTB-T-083286-24 19. In this case, it is clear that AT is both the owner as well as the person permitting occupancy of the unit. Based on his involvement in the operation of MA’s tenancy, there is more than enough evidence to establish that, on a balance of probabilities, AT is MA’s landlord. As a result, AT’s request to be removed as a party is denied. [name] 20. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $13,277.84 which represents the costs to replace items that were damaged or disposed of as a result of the landlord’s actions, out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Tenant as a result of the unlawful eviction, rent differential, illegal rent collected, and general compensation. The Landlord shall also pay an administrative fine of $2,000.00 to the Landlord and Tenant Board. 21. The Tenant submits that the Landlord altered the locks, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment and harassed, coerced, obstructed, and threatened the Tenant. 22. The Tenant testified that on July 2, 2024, AT had GG contact the police to have [name] removed from the rental unit. However, the police did not do so. 23. On July 3, 2024, [name] was locked out of the rental unit and the police were contacted by [name] (‘WR’), who MA says called on behalf of AT to enforce an unlawful eviction. [name] testified that when the police attended the rental unit, the Landlord stood in front of the door and barred the Tenant from gaining access to the rental unit. [name] did not stay at the rental unit that night. 24. [name] testified that he reported the incident to the police on July 4, 2024 and police contacted AT to have AT provide access to MA. The Tenant’s Witness, police constable [name] testified that he attended the rental unit on July 4, 2024 and that when the Tenant had gone for cigarettes, he had been locked out of the rental unit and his keys were left in his room. As a result of the police involvement, [name] was provided temporary access to obtain some possessions but was not allowed to stay in the rental unit. 25. A copy of the police report was entered into evidence and states that “the complainant was advised that he was allowed to obtain some necessary belongings now and he would try and arrange at a later time to gather the rest of his belongings…” 26. AT takes the position that due to issues of MA smoking in the rental unit, there was a breakdown in the relationship between GG and [name] and as a result, GG and the other residents illegally locked out MA. AT submits that he had nothing to do with the illegal lockout. 27. I found MA’s evidence to be credible that AT was present and participated in the unlawful lockout. Even if I am wrong in this, the tenancy was not lawfully terminated in accordance with the Act and AT, as the Landlord, ought to have taken steps to ensure that [name] was provided access to the rental unit. He faild to do so. LTB-T-083286-24 28. I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenant was unlawfully locked out of the rental unit on July 4, 2024 and was not permitted access to the rental unit after July 4, 2024 except to collect his possessions. 29. While the Landlord did not alter the locks, I was satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant by physically blocking their access to the rental unit. I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct constituted harassment and obstructed the Tenant’s rights to his rental unit. Remedies Out-of-Pocket Expenses 30. The Tenant claimed out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $5,577.84 because of the Landlord’s actions. The Landlod must pay the Tenant this amount for the reasons below. 31. The Tenant’s PlayStation 3 and Electro Magnetic Reader were damaged or missing as a result of the Landlord's actions. 32. The Tenant testified that as his items were left in a garbage bag outside after the eviction, his PlayStation 3 was damaged and his Electro Magnetic Reader was missing. The Tenant submits that the value of these items is approximately $500.00 based on Kijiji ads and online prices for similar items. I am satisfied that these items were damages or lost as a result of the Landlord’s breach, and that the amount sought represents out-of-pocket expanses to repair or replace the damages/missing property. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount. 33. [name] testified that as he was unlawfully locked out of the rental unit, he stayed at the Wayfare Motel from July 5, 2024 to July 23, 2024, when he was moved to a shelter. A copy of a receipt from Wayfare Motel in the amount of $1,997.84 was entered as evidence. 34. [name] testified he remained homeless until approximately October 1, 2024 as a result of the unlawful eviction. 35. [name] testified that as he was unable to store food or prepare food for the duration of time that he was unhoused, he incurred costs of approximately $35.00 per day to purchase meals. [name] seeks an order for $3,080.00 for the 88 days he was required to purchase meals as he was unable to store or prepare food. 36. I am satisfied that these reasonable out-of-pocket expenses were incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach. 37. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $5,577.84 for the out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Tenant as a result of the Landlord’s breach. Rent Differential 38. I am satisfied that in these circumstances, the Landlord’s conduct induced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit, and the Tenant may therefore claim rent differential. LTB-T-083286-24 39. The Tenant testified that they signed a new lease agreement with a tenancy start date of October 1, 2024, at a rent of $2,300.00, which was a $1,650.00 per month increase from the rent of $650.00 per month that the Tenant had been paying for the rental unit in this application. 40. The Tenant receives a subsidy from Wellington County of $1,106.00 per month. As a result, the difference the Tenant is required to pay is $544.00 per month. The Tenant seeks an order requiring the Landlord to pay the $544.00 difference in rent for a 12-month period from October 1, 2024 to September 30, 2025. 41. The rental unit the Tenant is renting is now a full basement as opposed to just a single room. Given that the rental units are not reasonably comparable, I find that The tenant is not entitled to the full amount of the rent differential but find that a nominal amount of $200.00 per month for a period of 12-months is reasonable and represents the approximate costs the Tenant would have to incur as a result of having to rent a new unit as a result of the unlawful eviction. 42. Therefore, I find that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions. The Tenant incurred increased rent of $2,400.00 for a one-year period after the Tenant left the rental unit. General Compensation 43. The Tenant also seeks general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00 for the Tenant’s pain and suffering as a result of the unlawful eviction. 44. The Board has the authority to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), in circumstances where the damages claimed are a result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the breach had on the tenant. 45. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00. The impact on the Tenant was substantial as the Tenant was rendered homeless for approximately 88 days as a result of the unlawful lockout. Fine 46. The Tenant has sought an order for an administrative fine against the Landlord be ordered. 47. Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $50,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant. 207 (1) The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 48. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00, the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. LTB-T-083286-24 31 (1) If the Board determines that a landlord, a superintendent, or an agent of a landlord has done one or more of the activities set out in paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29 (1), the Board may… d. order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court; 49. While not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. File Numbers: LTB-T-074597-22 (formerly SOT-15435-20) LTB-T-074685-22 (formerly SOT-16695-20) 50. In effect, I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors, such as the conduct of the Landlord. 51. Deterrence for egregious conduct, beyond whatever deterrent effect simple damages may provide, is an over-riding factor. 52. In my view this is an appropriate case in which to impose a fine in the amount of $2,000.00. The Landlord has blatantly attempted to circumvent his responsibilities as a Landlord under the Act and engaged in a ‘self-help’ remedy. The Tenant was locked out of the rental unit and was rendered homeless for 88 days. While the Landlord asserts that GG and the other residents locked MA out, the Landlord did not put the Tenant back in possession. I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and I was not satisfied that the amounts already ordered would sufficiently ensure future compliance. 53. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $2,000.00. T1 Application 1. The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent of $300.00, which is calculated at $50.00 per month charged for the period of December 1, 2023 to May 31, 2024, as result of an unlawful rent increase from $650.00 to $700.00.
The Tenant testified that as he moved in on January 5, 2023, the rent increase effective December 1, 2023 was not lawful as 12 months had not elapsed since the tenancy began. LTB-T-083286-24

Subsection 119 (1) (b) of the Act states that: A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed… (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply.

As less than 12 months had elapsed since the day the rental unit was first rented to the Tenant, the Landlord did not have the authority to increase the rent. In any event, the amount of the increase was beyond the guideline amount and as a result it was not a lawful increase.

The Landlord did not challenge the Tenant’s evidence that the rent had been increased by $50.00 effective December 1, 2023. As a result, I find that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent of $300.00 and the Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount back to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord / Landlord's Agent / Superintendent shall pay the Tenant is $13,277.84. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred from October 1, 2024 to September 30, 2024. • $5,577.84 for the estimated reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $300.00 for excess rent collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,000.00 by April 27, 2026. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s T1 Application was executed and filed with the Board on October 3, 2025.

This application was brought pursuant to Section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which provides a tenant may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord pay to the tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of this Act. In this Application, the Tenant sought the return of the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,233.35 and alleged illegal rent charged of $1,850.25.
The Tenant’s Application must fail, as the Application was not filed within one year that the last month’s rent deposit and the alleged illegal rents were collected in contravention of the Act.

The Tenant testified upon Board questioning that she moved into the unit on February 5, 2020, and that the tenancy terminated on May 15, 2024, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. This was confirmed by the submissions of the Landlord’s Legal Representative.

Section 135(4) of the Act is the applicable section and states: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act [emphasis added]

While the Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit for the last month of the tenancy and the Landlord charged illegal rent, section 135(4) of the Act provides that the Application must be filed within 1 year of the money being collected or retained. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 15, 2024, and brought this herein application on October 3, 2025. The Tenant was required to bring her application within a year from the date the Landlord collected or retained monies in contravention of this Act. This was not done and thus, the Tenant’s application is statue-barred.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $298.00. Evidence of the Tenant

The Tenant testified that she entered into a lease agreement with the Landlord on February 26, 2025. A day prior to entering into the lease, the Tenant was requested by the Landlord to pay $250.00, which comprised a $150.00 key deposit and $100.00 cleaning deposit. The Tenant entered a CIBC statement from February 2025 into evidence showing the payment of $250.00 being made to the Landlord.
The Tenant was informed by the Landlord that the deposits were refundable at the end of the tenancy.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2025, leaving the unit in broom swept condition and she returned the key. Despite this, the Landlord has failed to return the deposit to the Tenant. Analysis
Section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 105 (1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Section 134 of the Act states: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable

Section 17(3) of O.Reg 516/06 states: 17. The following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

Pursuant to section 134 of the Act, the Landlord was not entitled to collect a $100.00 cleaning deposit from the Tenant. The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

Pursuant to section 17(3) of the Regulations, the Landlord was entitled to collect a key deposit however it must be refundable. The evidence before the Board is that the Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord however the Landlord has not returned the deposit. As a result, this amount must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $298.00 This amount represents: • $250.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 application) • failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of their allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,126.41. Preliminary [name] to Amend/Limitation Period
Prior to the hearing, the Tenant sought to amend the application to include additional issues, including a toilet repair issue and alleged illegal entries.
Section 29(2) of the Act requires that an application be brought within one year after the alleged conduct occurred.
While amendments to clarify an existing claim or adjust quantum may be permitted, new claims cannot be introduced outside the limitation period.

I find that these additional issues constitute new causes of action and are therefore statute-barred. I have only considered issues raised in the original application that fall within the limitation period. Tree Removal/Backyard
The rental unit is a detached residential property that includes a backyard area. The tenancy began on July 1, 2023.
Prior to the commencement of the tenancy, the Landlord determined that several mature trees located in the backyard required removal due to safety concerns.
The Tenant was advised that work would be undertaken in the backyard. The Landlord engaged a contractor to perform the work.
The work began in or around July 2023 and involved removing multiple large trees in sections over time. The contractor primarily worked alone using basic equipment.
The work proceeded intermittently over several months and was substantially completed on or about October 29, 2023.
The Tenant submits that the prolonged tree removal work, including noise, debris, and safety concerns, substantially interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Landlord submits they responded to these concerns and attributed delays to weather conditions and contractor availability. The Landlord provided periodic updates to the Tenant regarding the status of the work. Analysis

Section 22 of the Act prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. However, Since this a substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit based on the Landlord’s maintenance of the rental unit or complex, the Board must consider section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 (the “Regulations”)
Pursuant to section 8(3)(b) of the Regulations, the Board shall not determine that interference was substantial unless the interference was unreasonable in the circumstances.
In this case, I find that the manner in which the work was undertaken was unreasonable for several reasons.

I find the duration of the work was excessive. The evidence suggests that approximately nine trees were removed over a period of roughly four months, from July 2023 to late October 2023. While some delay due to weather is expected, there is insufficient evidence to support that such a prolonged period was reasonably required to complete this work.

I also find that the method of completing the work contributed to the delay. The Landlord retained a single contractor who worked largely alone and used limited equipment to remove the trees incrementally.

The Landlord did not obtain evidence of qualifications, insurance, or capacity to complete the work efficiently. The Landlord’s own evidence was that the contractor selected was a retired corrections officer dabbling in tree removal upon retirement.

While the Act does not require the use of a particular type of contractor, the Landlord remains responsible for ensuring that maintenance is carried out effectively and within a reasonable time. I find the Landlord’s reliance on inexperienced handy man as opposed to hiring an experienced contributed to the delay in the work being completed in a reasonable time.

I further find the condition of the yard during the work was not reasonable. The Tenant entered pictures into evidence establishing that debris, cut timber, and equipment remained in the backyard for extended periods. The yard was left in a disrupted state for months, with uneven surfaces, materials, and partially completed work. This is not consistent with work that was done in a reasonable, timely and efficient manner.
Finally, the Landlord did not attend the property during the relevant period and relied on second-hand information. This lack of oversight contributed to the prolonged duration and

In sum, I find the Landlord’s approach reflects a lack of reasonable diligence in carrying out the work. Although the work itself was necessary, the Landlord chose a method that was slower and less efficient than would reasonably be expected. Therefore, I find the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by not removing the hazardous trees in a timely manner. Remedy

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement for the relevant period of the interference. In determining the appropriate quantum, the Board considers the nature, duration, and impact of the breach. I also considered the relevant circumstances under section 8(5) of the regulations.

The backyard remained in a disrupted condition for several months from the commencement of the tenancy July 1, 2023. Although it is an exterior amenity, it contributes to the overall value and enjoyment of the rental unit.

I find debris, timber, and equipment were present for extended periods. In these circumstances, I find that the Tenant experienced a meaningful loss of the use of the backyard. I therefore find that a 10% rent abatement for the relevant period appropriately reflects the reduced value of the tenancy attributable to the condition of the backyard.

I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the tree removal work finished October 29, 2023. Therefore, I find the Tenant is entitled to a 10% rent abatement from July 1, 2023, to October 29, 2023. Accordingly, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,309.00. Back Deck
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act by failing to maintain the deck.

The deck was in disrepair at the outset of the tenancy. Repairs were attempted in August 2023, but further issues arose in October 2023. The deck was ultimately removed and replaced with steps. Analysis
Section 20 requires that the rental unit be maintained in a good state of repair, even if the Tenant was aware of a deficiency at the outset.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (Onyskiw) (CanLII), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.
I accept that the Landlord took steps to address the issue once it was raised and that the final resolution occurred within a relatively short period after the second complaint.
However, the initial repair was inadequate, and the deck was not maintained in a good state of repair.

Rather than replace the deck the Landlord instead decided to remove the deck and replace it with stairs instead. I do not find this response to be reasonable. The deck formed part of the tenancy agreement, and the Tenant was entitled to have a deck and the lack of deck was due the Landlord’s failure to keep in a good state of repair.
The removal of the deck resulted in a reduction in the value and enjoyment of the rental unit, as it eliminated a feature that existed at the start of the tenancy.
In taking a contextual view of the circumstances, I find the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act with respect to the deck. Remedy
The deck was part of the backyard space and contributed to the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises.

While the Tenant retained access to the yard through steps, the removal of the deck reduced the functionality of the outdoor space and eliminated an elevated, usable area that had been part of the tenancy.

I do not accept the Landlord’s submission that, in the absence of a T1 application, the Tenant is not entitled to a remedy for the loss of use of the deck. The loss of the deck stems from the Landlord’s failure to maintain it in a good state of repair. Although the Landlord was entitled to remove the deck, this resulted in the permanent loss of an amenity that existed at the commencement of the tenancy.

Having regard to the circumstances, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement from August 8, 2023, being the date the Landlord was first made aware of the deficiencies in the deck, to June 30, 2024, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

In assessing the appropriate quantum of rent abatement, I find that the overall impact on the Tenant was minimal. The majority of the period without a deck occurred during months when a reasonable person would make limited use of such an amenity. Accordingly, a 5% rent abatement for the relevant period is appropriate, and the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,769.41. Incident Involving Former Contractor
The Tenant alleges that on October 17, 2023, a former contractor attended the property and engaged in aggressive behaviour.
The Landlord denies responsibility and submits that the individual was no longer acting as her agent.
I accept that an incident occurred. However, I am not satisfied that the individual was acting as the Landlord’s agent or under her control at the relevant time.
There is insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord caused or authorized the conduct.
Upon being notified of the incident, the Landlord advised the Tenant to contact the police if they felt threatened.
In the circumstances, where the individual was no longer under the Landlord’s control, I find that this was a reasonable response.
Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.
