issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because the Landlord gave a Form N12 notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The notice states the Landlord and his family require the rental unit for their own residential use.

At the hearing, the Landlord conceded that he did not intend to occupy the rental unit with his family on a full-time basis when he gave the notice of termination to the Tenant. Instead, the Landlord testified that he and his family intended to occupy both the rental unit and the principal matrimonial home on a part-time basis.

Following the Divisional Court’s reasons in MacDonald v. [name], [2008] O.J. No 6076 ([name]. Ct.), I find the Landlord was not entitled to give the Tenant a notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Act. In that decision, the Court uphold a Board order that ruled that part-time residential use of a rental unit is inadequate to end a tenancy under subsection 48(1) of the Act.

I therefore find the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith. The Landlord’s admission that he did not intend to occupy the rental unit on a full-time basis is sufficient to make the determination.

Notwithstanding my finding of the Landlord’s “bad faith” pursuant to subsection 48(1) of the Act, I stress there is no evidence the Landlord acted with malice, or any other ill-intent, when he gave the Tenant the notice of termination. The Tenant did not contest the Landlord’s description of extraordinary and highly personal circumstances that led the Landlord and his family to wish to live in the rental unit on a part-time basis. [name]

Having proven the Landlord did not have the right to give a notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to a remedy under subsection 57(3) of the Act. Rent Differential

At the hearing, the Tenant requested an order requiring the Landlord to pay the difference in rent the Tenant paid in the one-year period after vacating the rental unit, pursuant to subsection 57(3)1 of the Act.

The Tenant testified that he immediately began searching for new accommodation when he received the Form N12 notice of termination on October 1, 2024. The Tenant believed that rents were rising and that there was a low supply of adequate housing for his family. The Tenant described a sense of urgency to find a new home as quickly as possible. When he found a relatively affordable rental unit, he gave the Landlord a substantially compliant notice to end the tenancy on or about November 1, 2024, pursuant to subsection 48(3) of the Act.

On November 1, 2024, the Tenant and his family moved to a smaller rental unit that is farther from work. The Tenant gave evidence that the monthly rent at the new accommodation was $2,576.00 when his new tenancy began. A copy of his new tenancy agreement shows the base rent was $2,196.00, with additional charges for parking, a storage locker, bicycle storage and internet services.

While I am mindful of the Landlord’s legal representative’s submission that if an order is made pursuant to subsection 57(3)1 of the Act, the Board should consider only the base rent of $2,196.00 when calculating the appropriate remedy, the Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s testimony that rent at the rental unit included the use of a parking space and a storage locker adequate to store the Tenant’s bicycle. The Landlord also did not dispute the Tenant’s testimony that he could not opt out of the Landlord’s internet service.

In the circumstances, I find it is appropriate to consider the total lawful rent identified in the Tenant’s new tenancy agreement – $2,576.00 – for the purpose of determining a remedy under subsection 57(3)1 of the Act. Since the Tenant enjoyed parking and storage facilities at the rental unit, his claim for those facilities at his new accommodation is reasonable.

The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s evidence of rental advertisements for units closer to the rental unit and with lower monthly rents. I find, however, that the Tenant’s explanation for renting a smaller unit, at greater cost and distance from work, is credible and reasonable. The Tenant acted promptly to ensure his family remained housed. His decision to take the first relatively affordable rental unit that could accommodate his family was reasonable in the circumstances; and evidence of more affordable rental housing near the rental unit does not affect my exercise of discretion under subsection 57(3)1 of the Act.

The Landlord agreed the Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,850.00 when the Tenant vacated on November 1, 2024. The Landlord shall therefore pay the Tenant $8,712.00 for the increased rent the Tenant paid in the one-year period from November 1, 2024 to October 1, 2025. Compensation for Longer Commute to Work and Reduced Floor Space

The Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence of his out-of-pocket costs to commute to work. The Tenant did not, for example, submit proof of ride-share or public transportation costs. Also, since the Tenant chose to reside in his new accommodation, the Tenant’s claims for time spent traveling to work based on his hourly wage and for reduced floor space are too remote from the Landlord’s act of giving the Form N12 to merit a remedy. There shall accordingly be no order under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act. Out-of-Pocket Moving and Storage Costs

The Tenant did not have reliable evidence that a member of his household paid $150.00 in moving costs. The person who allegedly paid the amount did not participate in the hearing and the Landlord did not have a receipt or any other evidence of moving costs. In the circumstances, I find the Tenant’s evidence of out-of-pocket moving costs is not reliable, and there shall accordingly be no order under subsection 57(3)1.2 of the Act. General Damages

The Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence that showings of the rental unit to potential purchasers caused or exacerbated a medical condition among any member or members of the household. There was no evidence of a diagnosis or of any symptom, limitation or restriction that showing the rental unit could reasonably have affected.

I find the Tenant exaggerated the impact that showings had on him and his family. Although the Tenant described severe stress and anxiety, he conceded in his evidence-in- chief that he recalls only one showing that upset him. The Tenant testified that up to five people viewed the property that day, with some people opening closets to view storage space.

I find the Tenant’s description of the potential purchasers’ actions, without evidence of any underlying medical condition or other personal characteristic, inconsistent with the Tenant’s claim of extreme stress and anxiety.

The Tenant did not claim that any of the showings was done without proper notice under subsection 27(2) of the Act, and he did not introduce evidence to determine that five showings in one day was unreasonable or inconsistent with industry standards. In the circumstances, I find the Tenant did not prove losses or injuries that merit an order for general damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $8,760.00. This amount represents: • $8,712.00 for increased rent the Tenant paid for the one-year period from November 1, 2024 to October 1, 2025; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant filed a T2 Application on October 5, 2025 alleging that the Landlord, [name]'s agent or superintendent substantially interfered with my reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex or with the reasonable enjoyment of a member of my household and the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with me.

The Tenant signed a sub-tenancy agreement for the period of September 8, 2025 to December 26, 2025. This rental unit was a small basement apartment and a main floor unit where all of the roommates shared the kitchen. On or about September 21, 2025, someone broke into the upper rental unit. The Landlord, without any reason, accused the Tenant’s boyfriend of being the one who broke in. The Tenant stated that the Police was called, however no charges were laid on the Tenant or her boyfriend.

On or about September 22, 2025, the Landlord served the Tenant with a N7 Notice of Termination due to this incident, despite already investigating the incident. The Landlord told the Tenant that she must vacate the rental unit by October 2, 2025. The Tenant stated that this action was racially motivated, as this issue was already resolved as the Police were called and no charges were laid. The Landlord had no other reason to serve the Tenant with the N7 Notice.

The Tenant testified that she paid her rent on time and there were no other issues. The Tenant testified that the hydro was disconnected at the end of October 2025. The Landlord also disconnected the wi-fi for two months, from November to December 2025. The Tenant testified that the wi-fi was included in the tenancy. Legal Analysis

Section 22 of the Act states the following: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states the following: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant, and engaged in harassing behaviour. I found the Tenant’s testimony to be credible, and the Landlord was not present to contradict the evidence of the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant is requesting a rent abatement in the amount of $412.50 for the issues that took place during the end of September, October, November and December 2025. The [name] monthly rent was $825.00. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s actions caused them a lot of stress.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. In the case before me, I do not find that an abatement in the amount of $412.50 is appropriate, as the Tenant was able to access their unit other than there being the issue of the Landlord. However, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant a rent abatement as I found that the Landlord contravened Sections 22 and 23 of the Act. Based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find a 10% of rent abatement is appropriate in these circumstances, totaling to $247.50 is appropriate in these circumstances. This amount is calculated as follows: 10% of the monthly rent in the amount of $825.00 = $82.50x3 months = $247.50. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that they are requesting a rent abatement for the month of September, however I find that the Landlord’s actions commenced in October 2025. I note that the Tenant was served with a N7 Notice in September, however I do not find that this constitutes a breach of the Act. The Landlord was not present to provide submissions regarding this remedy request.

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

While the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a monetary remedy for pain and suffering, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $295.50. This amount represents: • $247.50 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing this application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.  withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay a rent abatement in the amount of $1,000.00 and the tenancy is terminated as of January 1, 2024.
The residential complex consists of two units. The Tenant lived in the upper unit and during the time of the tenancy, the lower unit was at times vacant or occupied by another tenant.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on March 1, 2023, and moved out on January 1, 2024. An N11, Agreement to End the Tenancy, with a termination date of December 31, 2023, was signed by both parties.
Based on the terms of the lease agreement, the monthly rent is $2600.00, and the Tenant was responsible for 60% of the costs related to heat, hydro, water and garbage removal.

In April 2023, the lower unit was not o ccupied. The Tenant agreed to help the Landlord by opening the basement unit for showings. The Tenant did this a couple of times, and when it became too onerous, or due to people constantly ringing the Tenant’s doorbell, informed that Landlord that he could no longer assist in this regard. The Landlord was agitated that prospective tenants and/or their agents would ring the Tenant’s doorbell calling them idiots. The ‘idiot’ statement was not directed at the Tenant, and I do not find it threatening, as alleged by the Tenant. The Landlord thereafter indicated he will add a note not to press the bell.

The Landlord made demands t hat the Tenant pay for utilities in an unprofessional and inappropriate manner. In late April the Landlord requested that the Tenant pay 100% of the gas bill for the period from March 15 to April 15, 2023, because the basement unit was not occupied by a tenant. Also in early May the Landlord demanded that the Tenant pay for 100% of the water bill because a toilet in the Tenant’s unit had broken and required maintenance. The Tenant communicated to the Landlord that he would not pay extra utility charges. In response the Landlord attended at the property on May 5, 2023, and yelled at the Tenant, calling the Tenant names, calling him cheap and threatening to make the Tenant’s life a living hell.

The Tenant also received text messages fr om the Landlord which were unprofessional in nature; swearing at the Tenant, blaming the Tenant for the Landlord’s financial issues, and calling him vulgar names. (pages 23-25). Example texts from the Landlord included, “Micheal f… you piece of sh.. I know what f…ing a..hole cheap a.. you are. I won’t have money to pay my mortgage …” (italics redact ed) Moreover, in an email dated May 18, 2023, the landlord writes to the Tenant, “After this message, I truly believe you are an a..hole.” (italics redacted) I note that in the actual texts, the words were not redacted as they are in this decision. I find this communication from the Landlord to the Tenant to be inappropriate and the unprofessional language continued even after the Tenant vacated in January 2024.

The Landlord had an ongoing dispute with t he basement tenant and would CC the Tenant in all his communications with the basement tenant. The Tenant requested not to be copied on emails related to the basement tenant. Also, the basement tenant requested via email to the Landlord on June 18, 2023, not to include the Tenant in their email communications because it was a breach of his privacy. The Landlord ignored both requests and continued to include the Tenant in the email communication. This was unnecessary and impacted on the Tenant due to the tone and number of emails being sent by the Landlord on matters that were not related to the Tenant.

The Tenant also alleged issues occu rring in October, November and December, particularly related to exterior cameras and parking at the residential complex. I do not find that these were proven on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant alleged they felt unsafe because the exterior cameras to the residential complex had been deactivated by the Landlord. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the cameras were inoperable due to the Landlord’s decision to deactivate them when the Landlord stopped paying for the service. Moreover, the Landlord testified that the camera lenses had been moved and were directed in a manner such that it would not allow the Landlord to see the exterior of the property. As such, a decision was made to stop paying the monthly fee and have them deactivated. It is unclear when the cameras were deactivated. The Tenant testified that he learned they were not working in October 2023, and from then on did not feel safe at the property. This alone does not satisfy me that the Landlord’s actions impacted on the safety of the Tenant or were in violation of the Act.
Moreover, on various occasions, the Tenant asserted that the Landlord attended at the residential complex and had the police for illegally parked cars. It was not related to the Tenant’s vehicle.

The Landlord has a right to attend at the residential complex to ensure only those permitted to park on the property are parked. The Landlord testified that the parking authority officer required the Landlord to attend at the residential complex to ensure tickets were issued only to the illegally parked vehicles. The Tenant’s actions in going outside and directing that the Landlord does not have a right to attend at the residential complex is erroneous. The Landlord’s attendance at the residential complex was appropriate. It was at the request of the parking authority officer and was to address a matter related to parking at the residential complex.

The Tenant’s application seeks a rent abatement of 5200.00 representing a full 100% abatement for the months of May 2023 and October 2023. However, the amended application and at the hearing the Tenant indicated that since the Landlord’s behaviour escalated in November and December, that a further $5,200.00 is being sought. The full rental abatement sought is $10,200.00
The Tenant also seeks an order for the Landlord to stop their behaviour, to pay a fine and to have the tenancy terminated on January 1, 2024.

The Landlord’s communication style is aggressive, unprofessional and harassing. This behaviour has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Moreover, this behaviour amounted to the Landlord harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening and interfering with the Tenant.

It is inappropriate to receive communication from the Landlord that contains language that is unprofessional, being called vulgar names and being sworn at. A landlord ought not behave or communicate in this manner, regardless, if they are charged by the police. The Landlord indicated that they had valid reasons to insult the Tenant, that he must have had a reason to attack him verbally and noted that swearing in Canada is legal. He also testified that in his view sending texts is not a serious harassment and acknowledges using bad language because he could not control his feelings. The Landlord also indicated that he can be a “good boy” when necessary, and a bad one when needed.

The Landlord noted being under stress, but I do not find that it excuses the Landlord’s behaviour and communications towards the Tenant. Moreover, his view that swearing is legal therefore acceptable also does not excuse his behaviour or change the finding that his behaviour violated the Act.

I do not accept the Landlord’s submission that they cannot be found to have violated the Act because they had not been criminally charged for their actions. One does not need a criminal charge or police involvement for a finding of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment, or to find that the Landlord’s actions were harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening and interfering with the Tenant. Moreover, I do not accept that the Tenant could have avoided the Landlord by blocking the Landlord’s texts and communication. The Tenant ought not be placed in a position to have to call police, block or avoid their landlord.

The Tenant’s claims regarding the Landlord’s actions in deactivating the camera or attending at the property to address parking issues at the residential complex were not proven. I do not find that the Landlord’s actions substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the property, nor do I find the actions to be harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening and interfering with the Tenant. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services
The Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant’s vital services, namely gas.

The Tenant heard from the basement tenant that the Landlord instructed a plumber to shut the gas at the residential complex from May 5, 2023, to October 10, 2023, thereby restricting heat to the rental unit. During the time that the heat was inoperable, the Tenant had access to other means of heating the residential unit until the Landlord was able to have the matter addressed. It is unclear how and why the gas was shut down, or if the Landlord took steps to withhold or interfere with this service. The Landlord when informed indicated that the Tenant had an electric fireplace available to use until the matter was resolved by the Landlord.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord, Landlord’s Agent, or [name] did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant’s vital services or care services and meals in a care home. Remedies
The monthly rent for the duration of the tenancy was $2,600.00 per month.
The Tenant seeks full abatement for the months of May, October, November, and December 2023.

I find a remedy is to be granted, but not a 100% abatement as claimed by the Tenant. The Tenant lived at the unit until January 1, 2024, and had full use of the unit during their occupancy. The Landlord’s verbal and written communication were harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening and interfering with the Tenant and with their reasonable enjoyment of the property.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.
I find that the abatement will be sufficient to provide adequate deterrence and compliance with the Act. As such, I will not impose a fine.
The tenancy terminated on January 1, 2024.

The Tenant withdrew their request for $500 related to moving or storage expenses. They indicated that this expense was not incurred due to moving their stuff out on their own. This remedy is not granted.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents:  $1,000.00 for a rent abatement.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by March 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy between the [name] ord and the Tenant is terminated as of January 1, 2024. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenant testified that on October 9, 2024, the towed a car belonging to her friend from a designated parking spot assigned to her. The Tenant incurred costs to retrieve the car.

The parties agree that the tenancy agreement stipulates that no guest parking is permitted unless the vehicle is first registered with the Landlord. In the past, the Tenant complied with those terms but stated that she had a medical issue on the night in question which prevented her from notifying the Landlord.

The Landlord disagreed that the Tenant always obtained permission and stated that the policy was put in place because of complaints about parking in the residential complex. The Landlord, who lives across the street, noticed the vehicle that night and had it towed.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Based on all the evidence, while I found the Landlord’s conduct excessive because he could have spoken with the Tenant later that day to confirm who occupied her parking spot overnight, the terms of the agreement were clear and understood by the parties that ‘NO guest parking allowed unless the vehicle is registered with the Landlord …. All others will be subject to being towed at the owner’s expense.’
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord' s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit and provided testimony about the issues of concern. Water Leak / Electrical Outlets
The Tenant testified that on June 13, 2022, she observed water leaking from the pipes connected to the washing machine.

On June 16, 2022, the Landlord sent someone to fix it but a month later, they discovered other issues and ordered parts to repair it. About April 13, 2023, the Tenant observed the water had turned orange and this was not resolved until July 8, 2023. Similarly, a problem with electrical outlets was only resolved about the middle of 2023.

Section 29 (1) (2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, provides that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of a number of reasons but no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

Given that the application was filed on October 10, 2024, the LTB can consider the alleged conduct if it occurred or continued after October 11, 2023. As the issue with the pipes, water and electrical outlets were resolved on or about July 8, 2023 , no further consideration is given to both issues. Smoke Detectors

The Tenant stated that the smoke detectors were not in compliance with safety codes because they were not hardwired or set off by heavy smoke . On cross examination, the Tenant confirmed that the smoke detectors were tested on June 12, 2024, and were found to be in working order.
The Landlord stated that there was no requirement that the smoke detectors be hard wired, and they inspect it periodically.

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenant has not demonstrated that the Landlord neglected their responsibility by failing to maintain the rental unit. By her own admission, the smoke detectors were found to be in compliance on June 12, 2024. Basement Seal

The Tenant claimed that the foundation of the rental unit and windows were not properly sealed and multiple times in the summer, snakes sneak into the rental unit. In the spring or summer 2024, the Tenant sent the Landlord a picture of a snake found in her washing machine.

The Landlord denied receiving any complaints about large insects or snakes entering the rental unit and had not seen the picture the Tenant referenced. The Landlord also stated that there is a procedure in filing requests for repair which involved completing a work order which the Tenant failed to do.
I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that snakes enter the rental unit or that a complaint was made to the Landlord about the foundation of the building. Heating

The Tenant stated that there was no heat in the bedrooms of the rental unit, but the issue was not rectified until April 2025. The Tenant stated that she reported this problem to the Landlord’s employees.

The Landlord stated that the Tenant did not complete a work order for the hea ting issue which they became aware of on April 25, 2025, when an employee of the Landlord visited the residential complex and spoke with the Tenant. The issue was rectified by the middle of May 2025.

Given the evidence that the issue was resolved either in April 2025, or May 2025, and the Tenant had no evidence to support the claim that the Landlord was informed on an earlier date, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was unaware of the problem prior to April 2025.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health , safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application); • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application); and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant alleges that he has experienced ongoing pest control infestation issues with mice and cockroaches and vacated the rental unit because of it. The Tenant also alleges the Landlord harassed the Tenant by sending him bill for a counter top replacement when the Tenant brought up the pest control issues to the Landlord, and that the Landlord accused him of bringing cockroaches in the rental unit. [name] and T6 for Maintenance: Pest Control
The Tenant began his tenancy on July 1, 2024, and the tenancy terminated November 30, 2025. The Tenant advised he vacated due to the pest control issues.

The Tenant says that upon him moving into the rental unit, he noticed mice traps already set up in the rental unit. The Tenant says he spoke to the Landlord about the mice traps as he has a mice phobia, and that the Landlord said there were no mice issues. The Tenant left the mice traps in the rental unit.

On October 15, 2024, the Tenant found a dead mouse in one of the mice traps and advised the Landlord of the issue on the same day. On October 17, 2024, the Landlord sent pest control services to the rental unit. The next time the Tenant told the Landlord of the mice issue was when the Tenant found another dead mouse in a mouse trap on April 18, 2025, and the Landlord sent pest control services within the week. The Landlord also attended the rental until approximately 2 weeks after this and plugged a hole that was located under the sink and the Tenant says there were no more mouse issues since.

A RegionEx pest control report was uploaded into evidence and the Tenant had the opportunity to review the document provided and indicated the report submitted was accurate. The report showed that pest control services attended on October 17, 2024, February 7, 2025 (no one home), February 26, 2025, and the last time for the mice issue on May 1, 2025, with no mice activity noted. No follow up was required after that.

The Tenant then claims there was a cockroach infestation and told the Landlord about the issue on July 28, 2025. The Tenant says that pest control services attended the rental unit within a week of the Tenant notifying the Landlord of the issue. The Tenant says that he told the Landlord about the cockroaches on three different occasions between July 28, 2025 and September 2025, and each time the Tenant advised the Landlord of the cockroach issue the Landlord responded immediately and had pest control services attend each time. The Tenant feels that the pest control services were not effective.

The [name] report indicated pest control attended the rental unit to deal with the cockroaches on August 1, and August 15 2025, and on September 2, and September 19, 2025 to conduct pest control services. On August 17, 2025 pest control attended and no one answered. On October 23, 2025, pest control attended the rental unit and noted no more cockroach activity. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act says: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Section 22 of the Act says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In the case Onyskiw v. CMJ Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (Onyskiw) (CanLII), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

Just because there is a pest control issue, that does not automatically mean the Landlord is in breach of its maintenance obligations. The breach would occur if the Landlord failed to act in a reasonable timeframe once they were notified of the issue. On the evidence before me, based on the Tenant’s own testimony, I find that each time the Tenant raised a pest control issue, the Landlord responded immediately and had pest control attended the rental unit in a timely manner. If the Tenant felt that the treatments were ineffective, the Tenant offered no evidence as to why he felt they were ineffective. It is generally accepted that pest control treatments may not rid of the pest control issue after one treatment. There was no expert evidence in front of me to establish that the pest control services were ineffective.

In accordance with [name], I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to maintain the rental unit with respect to the presence of cockroaches or mice, as the Landlord acted reasonably and in a timely manner to resolve the issues after being advised by the Tenant.
As such, the maintenance claim is dismissed.

When considering an allegation of substantial interference based on a maintenance issue, the issue itself may cause substantial interference, however it must be proven that the Landlord caused or contributed to the substantial interference.

The Landlord acted promptly, reasonably, and responsibly to the Tenant’s pest control issues. While pest control issues are concerning and troublesome to the Tenant, the Tenant must prove that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. There was no evidence that the Landlord’s response was delayed, inadequate, or that the problem was not addressed sufficiently.
Therefore, the substantial interference claim is dismissed. Harassment

The Tenant alleges two incidents of harassment. In the first incident, the Tenant claims that on April 18, 2025 the Tenant sent the Landlord an email requesting the Landlord not increase the rent due to the mice issue, and that the Landlord responded in a harassing way by telling the Tenant he would be responsible to pay to replace a countertop that he damaged by excessive humidity due to running a portable dishwasher that was not permitted. The Landlord indicated the Tenant was supposed to ask permission from the Landlord if they add a major appliance to the rental unit.
The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord accused him of bringing the pest control issue into the rental unit in an email dated September 7, 2025.

There is no definition of harassment under the Act but it is generally accepted to be a course of conduct that the landlord knows or ought to know would be most unwelcome to the tenant. I do not think that the Landlord harassed the Tenant by asking him to replace the countertop. As of the date of the hearing, the Tenant has not paid for the countertop nor has the Landlord asked again for the Tenant to pay it. As far as the email sent on September 7, 2025, I find the email would be viewed as unwelcomed and unpleasant for the Tenant and that the Landlord ought to have known this, however one incident of this nature does not amount to harassment. Therefore, the harassment claims are dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: The rental unit is a room in the basement of a single-family home. The Landlord lives on the main level of the home with her partner [name]. The tenancy commenced on April 1, 2019.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit on/around March 13, 2025, and did not give the Tenant new keys or permit him to reside in the rental unit. The Landlord did not obtain an order from the Board, and the Tenant did not agree to terminate the tenancy. As such, the Landlord was not entitled to change the locks on March 13, 2025. I am satisfied that the Landlord locked the Tenant out contrary to section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment contrary to section 22 of the Act.

I am also satisfied the Landlord did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove his property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the locks were illegally changed. Remedies

The Tenant indicated in his application he was seeking a rent abatement. The Tenant, however, acknowledged that he did not pay the Landlord rent for March 2025. As such, I do not find an abatement to be appropriate.

As a direct result of the Landlord’s actions, the following property was either damaged, destroyed or disposed of: • Queen size bed - $2,799.97 • TV 65 inch - $1,199.99 • Reclining loveseat - $2,189.99 • Vintage jewellery box - $420.99 • Dresser - $1,300.99 • Bedside table - $749.99 • Rope chain necklace - $1,200.00 • CAD cash - $2,000.00 • Tools used for his interlocking and landscaping - $202.96 • Titan tools - $110.00 • Cabinet for fish tank - $270.00 • Samsung phone – $450.50 • Straw bowl hat - $75.00 • Copper Cuban link chain - $44.93 • 4 pairs of shoes - $180.00 • Cut-off saw - $1,035.99

The Tenant testified that the amounts claimed are what he paid for each item. He explained that while he does not have the receipts, the estimates are based on research he conducted for the replacement cost.

I found the Tenant to be a credible witness. He provided his evidence in a straightforward and detailed manner with no exaggeration. While I do not find it reasonable to award the full amount claimed given the lack of supporting documentation, I do find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $10,000.00, which I believe is the reasonable cost that the Tenant will incur to replace the property.

Subsection 31(2) of the Act provides that the Board may order the Landlord to pay a specified sum to the Tenant for, (a) all or any portion of any increased rent which the tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the tenant has left the rental unit; and (b) reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses which the tenant has incurred or will incur.
The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $2,741.00, which were his reasonable costs for moving and storage.

In his application, the Tenant indicated he was seeking difference of $700.00 each month in rent. At the time the Tenant filed his application with the Board, however, he had yet to move into his new rental unit. At the hearing, the Tenant testified that he pays $650.00 month in rent at his new unit. This is less than he was paying at the former unit. As such, I do not find the Tenant has incurred increased costs.

The Tenant is claiming general damages for pain and suffering in the amount of $35,000.00, or what is commonly referred to as “non-pecuniary damages” because they are not damages directly related to a financial loss, but for pain and suffering. The object of non-pecuniary damages is to compensate a party’s pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life. In [name] v. Whitesands Apartments, [2009] O.J. No. 3198, the Court confirmed the Board’s authority to award general damages for mental distress under subsection 31(1)(f) of the Act.

I accept the Tenant’s testimony as to the profound stress he suffered because of the Landlord’s conduct. He described the impact the displacement had upon his mental and physical health. He was also unable to earn income as his work tools were disposed of during the illegal lockout.

In considering the Tenant’s claim for pain and suffering, I must look at how the Landlord’s conduct impacted the Tenant. I accept the Tenant’s testimony about the impact of the Landlord’s conduct as credible and find that the Tenant experienced tremendous stress and anguish because of the Landlord’s unreasonable conduct. Given the evidence before me, I believe an award in the amount of 7,000.00 adequately compensates the Tenant for the mental distress he endured as a result of the Landlord’s violations of their obligations. 19. The Tenant seeks an order imposing an administrative fine on the Landlord. The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 37. On or around February 18, 2025, the Landlord told the Tenant that he had to move by March 10, 2025 because she was going to sell the house. This is contrary to the Act as the Landlord did not give the Tenant proper notice in accordance with section 49 of the Act. On March 10, 2025, the Landlord vacated the home, leaving the Tenant to deal with the Purchaser who was surprised to find the Tenant residing in the home. Apparently the sale with the Purchaser fell through resulting in the Landlord’s Agent to retaliate by unlawfully evicting the Tenant the following day. 38. I find the actions of the Landlord and her agent to be completely unreasonable and contrary to the Act. I find an administrative fine of $5,000.00 is reasonable and appropriate given the nature and severity of the Landlord’s conduct. 39. In accordance with section 196(1) of the Act, the Landlord is prohibited from filing any application at the Board for any rental property until the administrative fine is paid to the Board. 40. The Landlord shall also be ordered to return any of the Tenant’s property in her possession.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $19,741.00. This amount represents: • $10,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace property that was damaged, destroy, or disposed of because of the Landlord’s actions. • $2,741.00 for moving and storage expenses. • $7,000.00 for pain and suffering.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by May 19, 2026.
The Landlord shall return to the Tenant property that is in the possession or control of the Landlord by May 19, 2026. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlords failed to address reported cockroaches, a non-functioning oven, non-functioning air conditioning, and window screens in need of repair.
Therefore, the Landlords must complete treatment for cockroaches and repair or replace the oven, air conditioning, and window screens..

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the Landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the Landlords responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a Landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I find that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords' obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit. When the Tenants moved in immediately after the last tenant vacated, the Landlords assured them that the outstanding maintenance items would be done shortly after. Painting was done, although later than the Tenants would have preferred, but no other repairs were done. The Tenants reported the problems to the Landlords using the communication/maintenance portal on the following dates: a) September 4, 2025 – water dripping from air conditioning unit, insufficient cooling b) September 4, 2025 – window screens in need of repair and/or replacement c) October 8, 2025 – cockroach infestation, treatment needed d) January 4, 2026 – oven not working
The Landlords made some commitments to comp lete repairs, however as of the date of the hearing none of the required repairs have been completed. Remedies

The Landlords must complete the follo wing repairs on the following timelines: 1. Air conditioning inspected by qualified techni cian by June 5, 2026. Identified repairs shall be completed by June 19, 2026. 2. Window screens shall be repaire d or replaced by June 5, 2026. 3. A qualified pest control technician shall in spect the rental unit by May 29, 2026 with recommended treatments to be completed in accordance with the recommendations of the technician. 4. Oven to be inspected by May 29, 2026 and repaired or replaced by June 12, 2026.
ordered: The Landlords shall complete the followi ng repairs and work by the following dates: 1. Air conditioning inspected by [name] by June 5, 2026 and identified repairs completed by June 19, 2026.
Window screens repairs or replaced by June 5, 2026.
Rental unit inspected by a qualified pest control technician by May 29, 2026 and treatment(s) completed in accordance with their recommendations.

Oven inspected by May 29, 2026 and repai red or replaced by June 12, 2026. 2. If the Landlords do not do the repair(s) and work by the dates specified above, the Tenants are authorized to arrange for the repair(s) or work to be done and may recover the cost of the repair(s) and work by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) after the repair(s) and work are done until there is no longer any money owing. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord failed to meet her maintenance obligations under the Act, which resulted in the Tenant having to vacate the rental unit. In summary the application alleges the following: • on or about September 19, 2025, the Tenant found water all over the bathroom floor of the rental unit and notified the Landlord; • the flooding continued and was observed throughout the rental unit and it was believed that sewage water was infiltrating the rental unit; • the Tenant vacated the unit temporarily with the intention of returning after the flooding issue was resolved and the rental unit was repaired; and • Instead of making the necessary repairs to the rental unit, the Landlord advised the Tenant that they would not be repairing the rental unit and that the Tenant had to find a new place to live.

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant in accordance with the order below. Tenant’s Evidence

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she woke up in the morning on September 19, 2025 and went to the bathroom. Once there, she saw water was all over the floor. The Tenant tried flushing the toilet and it flushed normally. The Tenant looked around and was not sure where the water was coming from. She then called the Landlord who told her that they would ‘get a snake’ and try to ‘clear it out’. The Tenant stated that she was not sure why the Landlord would try this course of action as the toilet was not clogged and she did not see water backing up from anywhere. The Tenant was not sure where the water was coming from but stated that it seemed to be coming out from underneath the flooring.

On September 19, 2025, the Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant asking the Tenant to move as many things the Tenant intended to keep from the living room as possible because drying equipment would need to reach all areas that water had infiltrated. A copy of the text message was tendered as evidence.

The Tenant stated that she vacated the rental unit, believing it would be temporary, to allow the clean up and repair process to unfold. The Tenant initially went to her sister’s house for the day and then booked an Airbnb.

On September 25, 2025, the Tenant received a text message from the Landlord that stated the pipe from the house to the street needed to be replaced and that it would be awhile before anyone could live in the rental unit. The Landlord then offered the Tenant her rental unit located in Goulais. The Tenant responded on October 1, 2025 to inquire about where exactly the rental unit in Goulais was located. Upon learning the location, the Tenant declined the offer. The Landlord then responded that the Tenant should look for a new place to live because the Landlord could not afford to pay the $12,000.00 it would cost to replace the pipe and that she had to sell the house. A copy of the text message correspondence was tendered as evidence.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she had to stay in Airbnb rentals from September 19, 2025 to October 6, 2025. During this time, she incurred a total of $3,591.65. Copies of the Airbnb receipts were tendered as evidence. The Tenant did not have insurance and so she paid for the Airbnb costs out-of-pocket. The Tenant stated that she started looking for rental units right away after the Landlord told her on October 1, 2025 that she should find an new place to live because the Landlord would not be replacing the pipe. However, she was not able to find an apartment until December 2025. The Landlord did not offer to pay for any of the Tenant’s costs, nor did the Landlord refund the rent the Tenant had already paid for the month of September 2025. Analysis

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit. The fact that the repairs may have been expensive does not release the Landlord of their obligations to keep the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. A landlord cannot refuse to do repairs because they are too expensive and unilaterally terminate the tenancy.

The Tenant sought reimbursement for the out-of-pocket costs she paid for Airbnb rentals in the amount of $3,591.65, for the period of September 19, 2025 to October 6, 2025. This amount is somewhat high for the time period. It was the Tenant’s evidence that the selection of Airbnb’s in the area was very limited, and she did not have any friends or family that she could stay with during this period to mitigate her costs and so she had to take whatever was available at the time.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am satisfied that, as a result of the Landlord’s failure to repair the rental unit, the Tenant was forced to find accommodation elsewhere and incurred out-of-pocket expenses. The Tenant provided sufficient evidence of her out-of-pocket costs claimed in the form of Airbnb receipts. Therefore, Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,591.65.

In the application, the Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to pay for her additional costs for food and the costs to replace items that were damaged from the flooding. However, the Tenant did not include the amount that she was seeking in her application and so no amount shall be ordered.
The Tenant withdrew her request for an order for the Landlord to do the repairs to the rental unit as she found permanent housing elsewhere in December 2025 and so this remedy is moot.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $3,639.65. This amount represents: • $3,591.65 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This file was previously before the Board on June 3, 2025 and November 26, 2025. I was not the Member on either of those dates.

At the hearing on June 3, 2025, the Member determined that the Tenant had not named the proper landlord, rather, the Tenant named the Property Manager as he was unsure of the name of the landlord. The Board determined that it would be most fair in the circumstances to permit the Tenant time to determine the identity of their landlord in order to add them as a party to the application.

The matter came back before the Board on November 26, 2025. At the hearing on November 26, the Member determined that although the Tenant had identified the names of his landlord, he had not amended the application to include them as parties to the application or otherwise provided them with notice of the application or hearing.

The Board determined it would be fair to permit the Tenant another opportunity to amend the application to name the correct parties and serve all disclosure on the added parties. As such, the Board adjourned the file and on December 3, 2025, issued an interim order requiring the Tenant to: The Tenant shall confirm the landlords’ contact information, amend his application to include those landlords and serve the amended application along with any evidence that he wishes to rely upon by December 23, 2025.
As of February 9, 2026, when the file returned before the Board, the Tenant had not complied with the interim order.

The Notice of Hearing for February 9, 2026 was issued on January 13, 2026. It names the same Landlord that was found to be incorrect on June 3, 2025 because the Tenant did not submit a request to amend their application in the two months that transpired after the interim order was issued. The Tenant also did not contact or attempt to contact the parties to be added to notify them of the hearing scheduled for February 9, 2026.
I asked the Tenant why he had not complied with the interim order, and he responded that he did not understand that he was supposed to do anything other than provide the Board with their address.

Based on my review of the file and the Tenant’s submissions, I concluded that it is unlikely that the correct landlords are aware of the proceedings at all, nor have they been provided with notice of this hearing. The incorrectly named Landlord did not attend the hearing to confirm whether he has notified the property owners of the application or hearing. In my view, it is more likely than not that they did not show up to the hearing because they are unaware of any hearing or application filed against them.

I turned my mind to Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure which addresses amendments to applications. I was not satisfied [name] or [name] had notice of a request to amend the applications to name them as the landlords. As such, I did not amend the applications.

When the file returned before the Board on February 9, 2026, I found the circumstances had not changed since November 26, 2025. The Tenant again attended the hearing in which they did not name the proper landlords or give them any notice of the hearing or proceedings. The Tenant had more than 7 months since the first appearance to comply with the interim order to ensure this precise situation was avoided.

I turned my mind to whether a further adjournment would be fair and appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant submitted that if provided the opportunity, he will send a copy of the application to the correct landlords. I do not find the Tenant was diligent in ensuring compliance with the interim order and that he was prepared to proceed today. Additionally, I do not find the Tenant’s explanation for failing to comply with the interim order reasonable. The interim order was clear on what was required of the Tenant, to put the landlord on notice. The Tenant could have mailed the documents to them at the address he located for them, but he did not. I find it is more likely than not that the Tenant’s noncompliance was due to a lack of diligence and failure to carefully read the interim order rather than a lack of understanding of what was required of him.

Considering all the circumstances, I determined that it would be unreasonable to adjourn the file. More than 7 months has elapsed since the Tenant was instructed to amend the application to name the proper parties, and the Tenant was given to adjournments to do just that. I heard no reasonable explanation that accounted for the lack of action on the part of the Tenant in amending the application and ensuring the correct parties had notice of the application and amendment sought.
Since the application was not amended to name [name] and [name] as the landlords, they have no prospect of succeeding. Therefore, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed accordingly.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant stated that when she moved into the rental unit, she signed a month-to-month lease agreement. She rents a room, and the property is a four-bedroom detached house. The Tenant testified that she had access to the entire house, however shared the common areas with the other tenants. In the lease agreement, it states that the Landlord will collect a security deposit in the amount of $150.00. A copy of this lease agreement was submitted as evidence to the Board.

The Landlord testified that the lease agreement that the Tenant presented is not accurate, as the Landlord has not given that lease agreement to any of the tenants. The Landlord states that this is only the Tenants writing and not the Landlords. There are no signatures of the Landlord on the document, and this further supports the Landlord’s position, that this is not a document that the Landlord was aware of. The Landlord testified that they are confused as to why the Tenant brought these applications before the Board, as the Landlord shares a kitchen and bathroom with the Tenant. The Landlord lives in one of the bedrooms, and has lived there before the Tenant moved in.

As stated at the hearing, the Board does not have jurisdiction to hear a matter if the Tenant is required to hare a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord. Although this issue was not specifically raised before me, as the Landlord stated that they have lived in the property prior to the Tenant moving in, this issue is live before me as it speaks to the jurisdiction of whether or not the Board can determine the application; the issue has a material impact on the outcome of this proceeding. Therefore, I proceeded to hear submissions on the preliminary matter of whether the tenancy falls under the jurisdiction of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”).

The only time that the Landlord was not occupying the rental unit was for a short period of time in November 2025 when the situation between the Landlord and Tenant escalated and the Police were called. This is a room rental, and no agreement between the parties were signed.

The Landlord submitted into evidence a photograph of their medication that her husband needed to purchase as a result of the stress that the Tenant was causing. On this medication, the rental unit’s address is listed. This supports the Landlords statement that they live there. The Landlord further submitted a video into evidence, which shows the Tenant blocking the Landlord trying to exit their driveway, which supports that the Landlord lives in the rental unit as the Landlord was trying to leave their own home.

The Tenant stated that she moved into the rental unit on or about August 1, 2025. The Tenant stated that at no point, did the Landlord live in the rental unit. She shared this property with six adults in total, and it is only a four-bedroom house. She would not have moved into the rental unit if the Landlord was living there. Regarding the document, the Tenant testified that the Landlord asked her to fill it out and said that she would sign it, however the Landlord never did. Furthermore, the Landlord listed the entire property for rent, and she would not do that if she lived in the rental unit. The Tenant stated that the address on the medication is not an indication that the Landlord lives there, nor is the video. Legal Analysis

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Landlord testified that the arrangement she has with the tenants who reside in the rental unit is that the Landlord shares a kitchen with the tenants which is located on the main floor in the house, and that it she rents the rooms out. This is why there is no lease agreement. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not live in the rental unit and she would have not moved in if the Landlord lived there.

Section 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”) states that certain rental units are exempt from the Act, including: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

After hearing both parties submissions, and based on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Act does not apply with respect to this rental unit as the Tenant was required to share the kitchen with the Landlord. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that the Landlord did not live in the rental unit, however, I prefer the testimony of the Landlord, that this is a room rental, the Landlord lives there and shares a kitchen with the Tenants. I find the Landlord’s testimony to be credible and consistent and find it believable that the Landlord would have knowledge of their rental unit, and their arrangement with the Tenants. The Tenant did not offer sufficient evidence to contradict the Landlord’s testimony regarding this.
As I find that the rental unit is exempt from the Act, the Board does not have jurisdiction to consider the Tenant’s application. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the parties agreed that the property Landlord to the action was [name].

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $1,995.18. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agree that the Landlord served an N12 Notice of Termination on the Tenant with a termination date of April 30, 2024, indicating that the Landlord personally required the rental unit for residential occupation for a period of at least one year.
The parties further agree that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 15, 2024, as a result of receiving the N12 Notice of Termination.
The Landlord does not dispute that the rental unit was listed for sale within one year of the tenant vacating.

The facts trigger the reverse onus clause in subsection 57(5) of the Act. That provision says that if a landlord gives a notice under subsection 48 and then puts the unit up for sale or rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”.
The Landlords’ position is that there was a material change in circumstances after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that he had previously resided in the rental unit until 2019 when he moved overseas for work at which time he rented the unit to the Tenant.
The Landlord further stated that he was residing in London England and that in January, 2024 he received notice from his employer that he was being transferred back to Toronto Canada.
The Landlord testified that he and his wife who were expecting their first child moved into the rental unit in May, 2024.

The Landlord testified that shortly after moving into the rental unit he and his wife determined that both the unit and the area had changed dramatically since previously residing there in 2019, and that the area would not be good for raising a child.
The Landlord stated that the area around the unit had extensive cannabis users and a number of cannabis stores had opened in the area since the Landlord had resided in the unit.
Additionally, the Landlord’s wife had been aggressively asked for money while out in the neighbourhood after moving into the rental unit.
A new 40 storey building was also scheduled for construction in the area, which the Landlord believed would create a lot of dust and noise which would not be ideal with a new baby on the way.
The Landlord didn’t realize how noisy the unit was as the bedrooms had glass sliding doors and were only two floors from a noisy common balcony in the residential complex.
The Landlord testified that as a first time parent he hadn’t previously considered these things.

The Tenant submits that there was no material change in circumstances as the Landlord knew he was expecting his first child prior to providing the Tenant with the N12 Notice of Termination. The Cannabis stores and planned construction in the area were things the Landlord ought to have known about or could have found out about prior to the Landlord giving the N12 Notice of Termination. Additionally the Tenant submits and the Landlord agreed that there had been no change to the rental unit or residential complex since the landlord had previously resided in the unit. Analysis

The reverse onus provisions of subsection 57(5) are engaged and the N12 notice is presumed to be given in bad faith. Accordingly, the Landlord must lead evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption—to establish on the balance of probabilities—that it was more likely than not—that the N12 notice was delivered in good faith.

The relevant considerations on an application under section 57 based on an N12 delivered under section 48 is whether: (a) the landlord genuinely intended that the person identified on the N12 would occupy the unit; and (b) the person identified on the N12 genuinely intended to occupy the unit. [See [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SCDC) and [name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC)]

The fact that the person identified as wanting to occupy the rental unit did not occupy the unit for a period of one year and that the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale are not the sole considerations when determining the Landlord’s good faith. A landlord may be able to establish that an unforeseen change in circumstances resulted in the person identified on the N12 being unable to occupy the unit. All other things being equal, this would be sufficient to rebut the presumption of bad faith arising under subsection 57(5) and (6). [See, for example, [name], 2021 CanLII 141438 (ON LTB)].

The Landlord’s position is that at the time the N12 notice was served he had a good faith intention to reside in the rental unit for his own residential use. The decision to vacate and list the rental unit for sale was based on an alleged change in circumstances as the Landlord had been out of the country and was not aware that the neighbourhood had changed and had not previously considered the noise of the rental unit as a new parent welcoming his first child.

My determination about the Landlord’s intentions must be made on a contextual basis, in consideration of the circumstances, events and decisions which followed the service of the N12 notice. While the Act describes the test in section 57 as being bad faith in the issuance of the notice, I must also consider the purposes of the Act, which includes to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants. More specifically, in interpreting and applying sections 48 and 57 of the Act, I must balance the rights of landlords to in good faith take occupancy of a unit for their own residential occupation for a period of at least one year with the rights of tenants to security of tenure. This latter includes tenants’ right to pursue a remedy at the Board if the landlord obtained the unit in bad faith and does not live in the unit for at least one year.

Limiting the question of good faith to an exploration of the mind of the Landlord at the instant of serving the N12 notice, and to ignore all the surrounding circumstances, would lead to results inconsistent with the objects of the Act. To require the Tenant to establish what was in the mind of the Landlord at the instant of the N12 notice being served, without regard to the surrounding circumstances and to the behaviour of the Landlord subsequent to the service of the N12 notice, would upset the balance of interests which the Act aims to achieve ([name] (Re) and TST-914-18 (Re))

A number of Board decisions have found that an unforeseen change in circumstance that prevents the person listed in the N12 notice of termination from taking possession may result in a finding that it was not served in bad faith. ([name] (Re), CET25233-12 (Re) and TST-63837-15 (Re)). The key question in the circumstances of the application before me, however, is whether the change in circumstance prevented the Landlord from maintaining possession for one year as required under section 48, further to the requisite intent behind the N12 notice. That is to say, did new, unanticipated, circumstances compel the Landlord to leave the unit – and so not maintain possession for a year?

I find that the Landlord’s change in circumstances did not constitute the type of change which compelled him to move from and sell the Unit. I find that his actions were inconsistent with a finding that he was committed, in good faith, to living in the Unit for at least one year. I find that his testimony in that regard is refuted by his own actions as he had decided to list the property shortly after moving in, and find that he has failed to establish the requisite good faith to rebut the bad faith presumption set out in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies

The Tenant seeks the Board to impose a fine on the Landlord. Although I do not find the actions of the Landlord to show that he was committed in good faith, to living in the rental unit for one year, his actions also to not warrant the imposition of a fine by the Board.

The Tenant seeks $1,947.18 in rent differential for one year being the period of May 2024 to April 2025. The rent differential is calculated at $162.27 x 12 months being the difference in his new rent and the rent he was paying at the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,947.18 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant seeks general compensation in the amount of $28,597.44 being the amount of one years rent at the rental unit. The Tenant is being compensated the rent differential between his previous unit and his current rental unit for a period of one year.
