Regardless of where the Tenant is residing they would have been responsible to pay for their housing and in the circumstances the Tenant is not entitled to 100% of one years rent as compensation.

The Tenant seeks $3,354.84 as his new rental unit is 70 square feet smaller that the previous rental unit. Although the Tenant explained how he calculated the amount being sought based on the difference in square footage. I am not satisfied on the evidence submitted by the Tenant that an additional amount of compensation based on square foot differential is appropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,995.18. This amount represents: • $1,947.18 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from May 2024 to April 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household , and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application); and • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application). This application was resolved by order LTB-T-084170-23 issued on January 13, 2025. On January 28, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Landlord alleged that they were not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. On January 30, 2025, interim order LTB-T-084170-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on January 13, 2025. Following a hearing on April 1, 2025, order LTB-T-084170-23-RV-IN2 was issued on April 4, 2025, granting the Landlord’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $18,441.02.

The tenancy for the two-bedroom rental unit commenced on July 1, 2023, but ended around September 15, 2023, following a text message from the Landlord informing the Tenant that she required vacant possession of the unit for her father. [name] Evidence

The Tenant testified that on August 9, 2023, the Landlord sent a text message stating that she drove by the rental unit and wanted to know why the lawn was not maintained. The Tenant claimed that the Landlord invaded her privacy when she drove by the rental unit to observe the lawn.

On August 19, 2023, the Landlord told the Tenant to vacate the unit so she could assess it for damages. The Landlord states in the message ‘Please be advised that I want you out of my property by September 30 th. Your rental money will be returned after any damage assessment and those damages are corrected.’

In several exchanges between the parties on the same date, the Landlord stated that the Tenant was not maintaining the lawn and that the Tenant will be required to pay to fix any cat smell in the rental unit. The Landlord also said that they left the Tenant with an immaculate garden and yard which the Tenant failed to maintain and stated, ‘Just remove yourself from my property.’

In a subsequent message on August 19, 2023, the Landlord stated ‘ September 30th out as I need it for my elderly father. I will be converting it to a fully accessible small home for him. It will be put into his name. Thank you.’

On receipt of the text message, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 15, 2023. On October 12, 2023, the Tenant observed a ‘Coming Soon’ sale sign in front of the residential complex which indicated that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith . The Tenant believes the unit was sold on March 18, 2024.

The Tenant further stated that while the rent for the unit was $2,000.00 monthly, she secured another two-bedroom unit with a monthly rent of $2,900.00. The Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to pay $10,800.00 to the Tenant, an amount representing the difference in rent, $900.00, for a period of 12 months . The Tenant provided a copy of her new tenancy agreement, dated August 25, 2023, which corroborated her testimony.

The Tenant also requested an order for the Landlord to pay the Tenant’s moving costs of $2,085.42 incurred on September 1 7, 2023. The bill provided by the Tenant shows the estimated moving cost as $2,085.42, but the actual cost, which the Tenant paid in cash, was $1,593.02.
The Tenant further requested an award of general compensation of $24,000.00 because the Landlord acted in bad faith. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2023. The additional terms of their tenancy agreement required the Tenant to maintain the lawn and gardens, remove snow, and ensure that her four cats did not cause any damage to the unit.

The Landlord stated that she drove by the rental unit daily on her way to visit her father in the hospital and although she rarely went on the street in which the unit is located, she observed that the lawns were not maintained. On August 18, 2023, the Landlord attended the unit because the Tenant reported that the lawn mower was not working. When the Tenant did not respond to her knocks, the Landlord went to the back of the unit, and turned on the lawn mower, which was functional. At this time, the Tenant came outside and was reminded to maintain the lawn.

On August 19, 2023, the Landlord asked the Tenant to vacate the rental unit with the intention that her 84-year-old father, who had been hospitalized over the summer, would occupy the unit himself after being discharged in October 2023, although the discharge date was later changed to November 2, 2023. The Landlord had hoped that her father would occupy the rental unit with the help of live in caregivers and be closer to the hospital.

The Landlord further stated that she did not anticipate the change in her father’s condition because he was doing well in September 2023, but unforeseeably, his health declined in October 2023, and he passed on October 28, 2023 . Prior to his passing, the Landlord’s husband also suffered a serious medical episode on October 23, 2023, and was also hospitalized.

The Landlord’s father was hospitalized from April 2023 to October 2023 when he passed. He lived with the Landlord prior to his hospitalization but wanted his own space with two caregivers and was unwilling to go into a conventional care home.

The Landlord renovated the rental unit following the Tenant’s move, and had the bathroom, fireplace, floors, doorway, and closets updated to accommodate her father’s needs. The Landlord provided a text message from her contractor stating that he upgraded t he rental unit in order for her father to move in.

The Landlord provided a Listing Agreement showing the rental unit was listed for sale on October 24, 2023, but acknowledged there was a ‘Coming Soon’ sign in front of the unit on October 12, 2023, and that she was in talks with the realtor prior to October 24, 2023 . The Landlord asserted that the rental unit was listed for sale due to the pressures resulting from her husband, and father’s medical condition. The sale of the unit closed on April 14, 2024. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48 (1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Based on all the evidence, I am satisfied that t he Tenant proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. An N12 notice of termination inform s a Tenant that the Landlord requires the rental unit for their own use and must provide at least 60 days to vacate. I find that the text message sent on August 19, 2023, is equivalent to an N12 notice as it contained the essential elements which includes a specified termination date and the reason for the notice . The Tenant vacated the unit on or about September 15 , 2023, as a result of that text message.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 , a case where in consideration of section 57 (1) (b) of the Act, similar to section 57(1)(a) except the notice was given on behalf of a purchaser, the court of appeal held in paragraph 42: ‘The purposes of the RTA are set out in s. 1. The first purpose listed is “to provide protection for residential tenants from…unlawful evictions”. To ignore events after a landlord gives a tenant a s. 49 termination notice limits the Board from fulfilling its responsibility to determine bad faith under s. 57(1)(b) and undermines the RTA’s stated purpose of providing tenants with protection from unlawful evictions.’

Section 57(5) of the Act provides that there is a presumption of bad faith if the Landlord advertises the rental unit, or places the building that contains the rental unit, for sale within a year after the Tenant vacates the unit. In this case, rather than the Landlord’s father occupying the unit as stated in the notice, the Landlord listed it for sale on October 24, 2023, approximately a month after the Tenant vacated the unit.

Given the legal presumption of bad faith, the Landlord bears the burden of demonstrating that the notice of termination was served in good faith. The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant, who had resided in the unit for less than two months by August 19, 2023, was served with the notice because the Landlord’s father intended to occupy the unit, even though he had been hospitalized for approximately four months prior to the service of the notice . Additionally, the Landlord was extremely dissatisfied with the Tenant’s maintenance of the lawn, as seen from the messages she sent to the Tenant on August 19, 2023. The Landlord categorically told the Tenant to remove herself from the property prior to giving the notice.

Therefore, I am satisfied that when the Landlord served the notice on August 19, 2023, requesting that the Tenant vacate the unit, the Landlord did not genuinely intend that her 84-year-old father, who had resided with her prior to his hospitalization, would occupy the unit. I find that this was a ruse employed by the Landlord to secure the Tenant’s eviction. Having succeeded in evicting the Tenant, the Landlord on October 12, 2023, advertised that the unit was coming up for sale and formally listed it for sale on October 24, 2023.

Although the Landlord claimed that she undertook repairs to the rental unit to accommodate her father’s condition, no documentary evidence was provided to substantiate th at claim. I do not accept the text message from the Landlord’s contractor, that repairs were carried out in the unit because of the Landlord’s father, as he did not attend the hearing to provide sworn testimony. In addition, no medical documentation was provided to establish that the Landlord’s father was expected to be discharged from the hospital so as to justify the service of the notice. Based on all the evidence , I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith.

Having succeeded in proving that the notice was given in bad faith, the Tenant, pursuant to section 57(3) (4) of the Act is entitled to the difference ($ 900.00) between the rent for the rental unit ($2,000.00) and the rent for her new unit ($2,900.00) for a period of twelve months in the total amount of $ 10,800.00. The evidence demonstrates that the rental unit and the new unit are comparable two-bedroom homes. The Landlord will be ordered to pay $10,800.00 to the Tenant, for the period from October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024.

Section 57 (3) (1.2) of the Act provides that the LTB can make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage, and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. The Tenant incurred moving costs of $1,593.02 and is entitled to a reimbursement of the costs.

The Tenant requested general compensation of $24,000.00. Section 57 (3) (1.1) of the Act provides that the LTB may make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses.

Given the additional rent the Tenant continued to incur monthly because of the Landlord’s bad faith eviction, I find it fair to award general compensation of $6,000.00 to the Tenant, an amount equal to three months rent ($2,000.00 x 3).

With regards to the allegations of substantial interference and harassment, section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the text messages presented by the Tenant , on August 9, 2023, the Landlord questioned the Tenant about why the lawn had not been cut. After the Tenant responded that she was undergoing physiotherapy treatments, the Landlord did not pursue the issue further at that time. However, on August 19, 2023, the parties engaged in a series of exchanges in which the Landlord stated that the Tenant would be responsible for paying for any damage to the unit and asked the Tenant to vacate the rental unit.

While the Landlord was clearly wrong in her approach , it does not appear that her conduct continued beyond August 19, 2023, and therefore does not meet the threshold for harassment, which requires persistent or repeated conduct. The Tenant’s assertion that the Landlord intruded on her privacy by driving by the property is unpersuasive, particularly as the Tenant’s indicated in one of her r esponses to the Landlord that she appreciated the Landlord keeping an eye on the property when the Tenant was not present. I am therefore not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or harassed the Tenant.
The Landlord will be ordered to pay a total of $ 18,441.02 to the Tenant , inclusive of the $48.00 cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,441.02. This amount represents: • $10,800.00 for increased rent the Tenant incurred for the one -year period from October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024, • $1,593.02 in moving costs, • $6,000.00 in general compensation, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 24 , 202 6, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The T1 application is dismissed.
The T2 application is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: entered the rental unit illegally; and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenants in the amount of $4,500.00 in illegally collected rent, plus the filing fee. Illegal rent collected

The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenants moved into the rental unit in 2018 and paid $2,000.00 per month in rent until January 1, 2024 when the rent was increased to $2,450.00.

The reason for the rent increase was that the Landlord sought more rent to help cover mortgage payments. The Landlord lives in the basement unit of the residential complex. This is not a permitted reason for an above guideline rent increase under the Act. The Tenants paid this rent for 10 months before going back to paying $2,000.00 per month until their move out date.
The parties agreed that the Landlord illegally collected $4,500.00 in rent. The Landlord shall compensate the Tenants in this amount.
The lawful rent is $2,000.00 per month.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025. T2 Application

As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenants in the amount of $4,208.28.

At the commencement of the hearing the Tenants sought to amend their application to include three new issues, and to increase the remedies claimed. The amended application was served on the Landlord prior to the hearing, and each issue was filed in time pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act. The amendment requests were granted.

In this application, the Tenants claim that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit between 5-6 times on December 27, 2023, January 18, 2024 and April 9, 2024. They also claim that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by telling them they could not have a dog as a pet, by smoking in the downstairs unit which travelled upstairs, by giving them a different and less accessible parking spot, and by routinely blocking their car with garbage bins.

The Tenants claim the following remedies: $5,000.00 related to the illegal entries; a rent abatement of $200.00 for interference related to parking and smoking; that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine in the amount of $5,000.00, out of pocket expenses totalling $208.28 for the costs incurred to purchase smoke detection equipment, and $5,000.00 in general compensation. Illegal entries

The Tenants claimed that the Landlord illegally entered their unit on the following dates: (a) 1 illegal entry on December 27, 2023; (b) 2-3 illegal entries on January 18, 2024; and (c) 2 illegal entries on April 9, 2024.

The Landlord denied ever illegally entering the rental unit. The Landlord denied entering the unit on December 27, 2023 altogether. The Landlord stated that he had the permission of the Tenants to enter on January 18, 2024 to conduct repairs to the thermostat/furnace. With respect to the April 9, 2024 allegation, the Landlord asserts that he wasn’t required to provide a notice of entry due to it being an emergency.
Section 26(1) of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, in cases of emergency, or if the tenant consents to entry at the time of entry.

Section 27 of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry to carry out a repair, and that a notice of entry must specify the reason for entry, the day, and a time of entry between the hours of 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.

The Tenants testified that they witnessed each illegal entry because they had installed a camera in their living room which has live viewing capabilities, and which also records video. The Tenants entered a number of videos into evidence which show the Landlord entering the rental unit on January 18, 2024 and April 9, 2024. December 27, 2023 entry

No video recording was produced for the December 27, 2023 date, though the Tenants testified that on this day they witnessed the Landlord entering the rental unit without notice, through remote viewing. The Landlord denied entering the rental unit. No compensation is ordered for this entry. Given the disagreement between the parties about whether an entry took place on this date, and the absence of video evidence, this claim is dismissed. January 18, 2024 entry

Regarding the January 18, 2024 entry, the Tenants submitted copies of text messages into evidence showing that the Landlord asked for permission to enter the rental unit on this date in order to inspect the heat and thermostat. The Tenants agreed to allow an entry but allege that the entry was illegal because it took place hours after they had given permission, and because the Landlord is seen walking into a variety of rooms on video. The Landlord testified that he had to walk through the rental unit in order to ensure that heat was properly emanating from the vents in different rooms, and that he had to exit and then re-enter the unit one or more times in order to adjust the thermostat which is located in the basement.

While this entry is illegal because the Tenants did not consent to it at the exact time of entry, no compensation is ordered. The Tenants expected that the Landlord would enter the rental unit on this date, and expressly provided him with permission to conduct a repair. The Landlord needed to conduct this repair in order to fulfil his maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act and I found his explanation for entering multiple rooms to be reasonable. April 9, 2024 entry

The Tenants submitted copies of text messages into evidence which show the Landlord asking to enter the rental unit in the morning on this date, in order to check the building’s thermostat after a gas meter repair. The Tenants did not consent to this entry. This constitutes an illegal entry on the part of the Landlord.
The Landlord did not provide any evidence to support that this was an emergency repair, and I was not persuaded that he was unable to provide 24 hours notice to the Tenants.

The Tenants testified that the pattern of entries by the Landlord, either without notice or on short notice created an anxious and uncomfortable living situation, given that they often took place when they were not home, or when only one of the Tenants was home with their daughter.

The Landlord shall compensate the Tenants in the amount of $1,000.00 for this illegal entry. This sum reflects the substantial stress experienced by the Tenants in having to witness an entry without notice via their camera. I consider the illegal entry on this date to constitute one prolonged entry, and not multiple entries. Because the Landlord lives in the basement unit of the complex, where the thermostat is located, any testing of the thermostat necessitates that he exits and re-enters the unit to inspect temperature levels. Pets
The Tenants testified that on October 4, 2024 the parties had a disagreement about them having purchased a dog.

The Tenants submitted a copy of a recording into evidence where the Landlord is heard telling Mr. [name]name] that he is reconsidering whether the wants to rent the unit to the Tenants given their new pet and the damage he anticipates a dog will cause.

Based on the pattern of events which followed, I am persuaded that this event caused the Landlord to engage in a pattern of retaliatory behaviour designed to pressure the Tenants to move out of the rental unit. Compensation is ordered below for the substantial interference faced by the Tenants. Parking space

The Tenants claim that beginning on February 13, 2025 the Landlord reassigned them a different parking spot in the driveway in front of the rental unit. The Tenants stated that until this date, they had a history of parking on the right side of the driveway, where all their vehicle doors are easily accessible. After February 13, 2025 the Landlord began occasionally parking on the right side of the driveway, which meant that they needed to park on the left side, near a wall.

No compensation is ordered with respect to this issue because while the Tenants were clearly inconvenienced, they did not demonstrate that they were ever assigned a parking spot or promised exclusive use of the right side. Garbage bins

The Tenants testified that beginning on March 12, 2025 to their move out date, the Landlord began routinely placing garbage bins behind their vehicle, in order to block their exit from the driveway. The Landlord denied deliberately placing the garbage bins behind the Tenants’ car and stated that it must have been garbage collection personnel who did so.

Based on a copy of an email submitted into evidence where the Tenants complain to the Landlord about this behaviour, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the unit. Compensation is ordered below. Smoking

Beginning February 14, 2025 and continuing to their move out date, the Tenants stated that the Landlord began smoking inside the rental complex, and that it coincided with them arriving home after their workday. The Tenants purchased $208.28 in equipment designed to measure the air quality in their home, and text messages to the Landlord show the Tenants complaining about being unable to breath comfortably.

The Landlord denied smoking in the basement unit. However, based on the written evidence submitted I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment. Compensation is ordered below. Remedies

The Tenants testified that they experienced a substantial level of disruption to their ability to enjoy the rental unit and live in the unit normally after the Landlord’s pattern of retaliatory behaviour began. This included being unable to breath and sleep comfortably due to smoke inhalation, fearing that the Landlord may harm their dog while they were not home during a potential illegal entry, and being inconvenienced when trying to exit their driveway. The Tenants also emphasized the anxiety experienced by their young daughter who they say became fearful of the Landlord due to the proximity of their living conditions.

The Landlord shall compensate the Tenants in the amount of $208.28 for the cost of purchasing air quality monitoring equipment. I find that this expense was taken on as a direct result of the Landlord’s conduct, so that the Tenants could monitor the ongoing impacts of inhaling second-hand smoke. $3,000.00 in general compensation is ordered payable to the Tenants for the stress and health impacts that the Tenants experienced as a result of living in a smoke-filled unit, as well as living in fear of reprisal because of having purchased a dog. The Tenants experienced tangible and routine interference with their reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenants also seek an abatement of rent for parking and smoking related interference. No additional sums are ordered as this would constitute double recovery, given the order for general compensation. The Tenants seek that a fine be paid. No fine is ordered payable, I am satisfied that the amount already ordered as compensation will serve as a sufficient deterrent to future conduct of a similar kind.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $8,756.28. This amount represents: • $4,500.00 for excess rent collected; • $1,000.00 for illegal entry; • $208.28 in out-of-pocket costs; • $3,000.00 for general compensation; • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the oust of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative requested that both the T2 and the T6 portion of the Tenant’s Application be dimissed on the basis that neither Application contains sufficient particulars to allow the Landlord to respond. The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated after the adjudicative case conference, which was held on September 23, 2025 an interim order was issued which permitted the Tenant until October 23, 2025 to amend the Application to provide particulars, but she did not do so.

As per Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”) Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met and respond.
In this case, I am satisfied that the Tenants T2 Application does not contain adequate particulars, as it lacks clear dates and times, and overall clarity.

However, I am satisfied that it is sufficiently clear that the Tenant’s T6 Application alleges that a smell was radiating from the vents of the rental unit, the Application indicates this began on May 1, 2024 and has been ongoing. I am satisfied that this allegation is clear and contains enough details for the Landlord to understand what is alleged, and respond. Therefore, I elected to dismiss the T2 portion of the Tenant’s Application and proceed on the basis of the T6 only. The T6
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2024 and became aware of an odour of dog feces coming from the basement on May 2nd or 3rd. She testified that it began to be noticeable as she walked down the first couple of steps towards the basement. She testified that the odour was initially confined to the basement but gradually began creeping its way up and expanding throughout the unit.

The Tenant testified that she reached out to [name], who had shown her the unit, and who she believed to be the Landlord, and asked hm why there was a dehumidifier running in the basement and he explained that there were issues with a prior Tenant and the basement had been repainted and advised her to leave the dehumidifier running, she did not request that he take any particular action with respect to the odour at that time.

She said that the smell began to worsen, and she was provided an email from Lydon Pearson and sent an email on August 1, 2024, asking if anything had been done about the smell on the basement. She testified that she received an email approximately two and half weeks litre from [name], in the Landlord’s maintenance department who indicated that any odour had been nebulised and the basement repainted before the Tenant moved in.

She testified that she gave the situation a month or so, then began to call a Cassandra Cook. She testified that she called approximately 9 times, and was hung up on. She testified that the smell remains and is growing by the day. She testified that if she does not have a candle burning, she can smell it, and has put tape over the ducts within the rental unit and does not enter the basement.

During cross examination the Tenant testified that she called bylaw and the officer informed her they could not smell the odour because of the weather, and did not smell it as strong as the Tenant did. The Tenant also testified that she had a bylaw odour concerning the smell, but denied to share it with the Landlord's Legal Representative.

The Tenant denied that the Landlord treated the unit on November 9, 2024 and claimed that there was dog feces on a rug within the rental unit when she moved in, but had not mentioned this on her Application or her original testimony, because she believed she would receive legal aid to assist with her Application, and did not.

The Landlord’s Agent [name] testified at the hearing. She is a [name] manager for the Landlord. She testified that the Landlord had all the ducts within the rental unit cleaned and the basement floors cleaned and painted on August 24, 2024 and the basement treated with “[name]” to neutralise smells and odours on November 9, 2024.

In support of this the Landlord relied on an email from September 24, 2024 explain this treatment to the Tenant and indicating that if the Tenant was conacred about odours the Landlord could arrange for another neutraliser treatment.
She testified that she has been responsible for the unit since December 2025 to March 2026 and during that time as received no complaints about odour from the Tenant Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
In the case I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord has failed to comply with their maintenance obligations.

I did not find the Tenants testimony to be reliable. While she claimed that she had a bylaw report detailing the smell, she did not provide this for my review or upon the request of the Landlord's Legal Representative and her own testimony on this issue seemed to suggest that when the [name] officer attended, they could not detect the odour, which matches the email the Tenant received from the Landlord on September 24, 2024 which asserts that they were informed by [name] that they were not concerned about odour in the rental unit.

Additionally, while the Tenant asserted during cross examination that there was dog feces on a rug in the rental unit when she moved in, this was not mentioned in either her initial testimony or the Application, and while the Tenant attributes this discrepancy to a lack of representation, I note that this is the Tenant’s own Application, and I am not satisfied that this accounts for the Tenants shifting testimony throughout the hearing.
Therefore, as the Tenant has relied on her testimony to substitute the dog feces odour, I am not satisfied that she has done so.

Even if I were satisfied that there was an odour in the rental unit, I am satisfied that the Landlord respond appropriately. The unit was clearly thoroughly cleaned don April 24, 2024 before the Tenant took possession, and I accept that the Landlord also performed a further neutralization treatment on November 9, 2024. While the Tenant disputes that this treatment occurred, given the thorough cleaning and treatment performed on the unit in April 24, 2024 I am prepared to accept that t was Laos performed.

I also accept that the Landlord’s Agent has not received ongoing complaints about the odour from the Tenant. While the Tenant asserted that she had followed up multiple times with [name], she did nit refer me to any documentation, or records in support of this.

Therefore, I am prepared to accept that the unit was thoroughly cleaned and tested by the Landlord prior to the Tenant taking possession, and a further treatment was performed on November 9, 2024, absent proof of further complains by the Tenant, I am satisfied that the Landlord has responded approroately, especially as they had been informed by bylaw that the odour was not a live issue.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] also known as Zhihui [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants state that the Landlord uploaded multiple single documents to TOP but only two documents were provided to the Tenants by email on November 25, 2025 which is not in accordance with the 7 day disclosure requirement set out in the Notice of Hearing.

The Landlords state that a 40-page document disclosure brief was emailed to the Tenants’ legal representative on July 6, 2024 prior to the last scheduled hearing date of July 15, 2024 in which the matter was adjourned due to there not being enough time in the scheduled hearing block to hear the matter. The Tenants legal representative states that he did not receive a copy of this disclosure. At the hearing, I directed the Landlords to forward a copy of the email to myself and the Tenant’s legal representative which shows the disclosure was sent to the Tenant’s legal representative on July 6, 2024.

I stood the matter down to allow the Landlords to forward a copy of the July 6, 2024 email. The Landlords forwarded copy of email which shows it was sent to email address for the Tenants legal representative on July 6, 2024 at 10:57 pm. The Landlords also produced a copy of a screen shot showing the attachment with the disclosure was included with the email that was sent to the Tenants legal representative on July 6, 2024 at 10:57 pm. The Tenants legal representative could not locate a copy of the email originally sent to him by the Landlords on this date.

I determined at the hearing that the Landlords document brief was emailed to the Tenants legal representative on July 6, 2024 as supported by the email produced by the Landlords, and a copy of the screen shot showing the attachment with the email. Therefore, the Landlords Document Brief was allowed to be admitted as evidence for hearing and was also provided at the hearing to the Tenants legal representative. The Tenants legal representative requested additional time to review the document brief with his clients which I did not allow because I accept that it was previously provided to the Tenants legal representative in advance of the hearing. Further, the Tenants legal representative would have the opportunity to cross examine any of the documents in the document brief.

I did not allow the other documents uploaded to the by the Landlords which were not provided to the Tenants’ legal representative at least 7 days prior to this scheduled hearing to be admitted at the hearing as they were not provided in accordance with the disclosure requirements set out within the Notice of Hearing issued and Rule 19 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules regarding disclosure. Further, the single documents uploaded by the Landlords to the Portal were not compiled in accordance with the Landlord and Tenant’s Board’s Practice Direction on Evidence which requires documents, photographs, and other items to be relied upon to have consecutively numbered pages; and include a list or table of contents identifying each item in order, and by page number, if more than one item is being submitted. Preliminary Issue#2

At the hearing the Tenants legal representative requested the following amendments to the T5 application (‘application’). The Tenants legal representative states the amendments to the application were served on Landlords on July 4, 2024. The Landlords did not oppose the following amendments. The application is amended as follows: i. One of the Landlords listed as [name] is also known as Zhihui [name]. ii. Amendment to remedy 1 to claim that the Landlords must pay the Tenants a rent abatement in the amount $21,859.20 based on twelve months rent at $1,821.60 per month. iii. Amendment to remedy 3 to claim a rent differential for twelve months in the amount of $6,700.00 based on a rent differential of $558.40 per month. iv. Amendment to remedy 5 to claim general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00. Determinations:

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. i. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $18,869.90 to the Tenants by February 6, 2026 as per the breakdown provided below: a) $10,929.60 for a rent abatement. b) $6,700.80 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from May 1, 2023 to May 1, 2024. c) $1,186.50 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. d) $53.00 for the cost of filing the application. ii. The Landlords must also pay a fine in the amount of $1,000.00 to the Landlord and Tenant Board by February 6, 2026. N12 notice of termination served in bad faith
The rental unit is a three-bedroom condominium located in Guelph.

The Tenants produced a copy of a written lease agreement for the rental unit which notes it is a 16-month fixed term lease agreement for the period January 1, 2021 – April 30, 2022. The lease agreement notes the monthly rent is $1,800.00 and does not include utilities or air conditioning. This lease agreement notes that the parties agreed to receive documents and notices by email.

It is an undisputed fact that on January 16, 2023, the Landlords served the Tenants by email an N12 Notice of Termination (“N12 notice”). The N12 notice indicates that the Landlords in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for their child for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

It is an undisputed fact that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2023 as a result of the N12 notice served by the Landlords. The Landlords state that their son, DC moved into the rental unit on May 6, 2023 and lived there until July 2024.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) for the reasons provided below.

The Tenants are retired seniors and it is their position that the Landlords attempted to illegally increase the rent above the guideline and when the Tenants did not agree to pay the illegal rent increase, one year later, the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice. The Tenants produced copies of email correspondence with the Landlords in support of their position.

The Tenants produced an email from one of the Landlords [name] which was sent to the Tenants on January 9, 2022 and notes that the cost of maintaining the rental unit is higher than the Landlords anticipated and the special assessment cost of the unit for draining the condominium is close to $1,100.00. The email further notes that the Landlords are expecting an increase in condominium fees and property taxes in 2022 and market rent for a 3 bedroom, two bathroom condominium is $2,100.00. In the email, the Landlords propose increasing the monthly rent to $1,960.00 (from $1,800.00) for the period May 1, 2022 to April 30, 2023. On January 10, 2022, the Tenants replied to the Landlords by email and requested that the Landlords confirm if they are requesting the Tenants to agree to a $160.00 per month rent increase.

Further email correspondence from the Landlords to the Tenants dated January 12, 2022 notes the proposed rent increase by the Landlords is above the guideline and it requires agreement from both parties. The Landlords also includes a link to a two-bedroom apartment listed for rent in Guelph for $2,399.00 per month plus utilities. On January 14, 2022, the Tenants replied by email to the Landlords, advising that they agree to pay up to the 1.2% guideline increase for the monthly rent. It is undisputed that the Landlord increased the monthly rate 1.2% as per the guidelines and the monthly rent increased to $1,821.60.

The Tenants produced copies of electrical utility bills which they paid while living at in the rental unit and a copy of their electrical utility statement from Priority Submetering Solutions which notes the monthly amount paid by the Tenants for their electrical utilities for the period of March 2021 – October 2021 ranged from $42.00 per month to $50.72 per month. The Tenants also produced a copy of the electrical utility bill in both of the Landlords names for the rental unit dated November 19, 2020 in the amount of $29.13 which the Tenants state, represents the amount for the electrical utilities prior to the Tenants moving into the rental unit.

The Landlords refute this evidence relating to the electrical utility bill for the rental unit dated June 26, 2023 which notes it is in [name] (one of Landlords) and DC’s name. This electrical utility bill notes the rental unit address and an amount of $188.49 ($10.10 in electricity charges + $25.00 occupancy charge + $150.00 security deposit + $3.39 taxes and rebate). The Landlords state the electrical utility bills for their son were less than what the Tenants paid because the Tenants are two retired people that spend more time at the rental unit compared to their son that spent a lot of time at the university and he ate meals outside of the rental unit.

The Tenants rely on signed statements produced for the hearing from residents residing at the residential complex in units 401, 407 and 409. The signed statements note that no one moved into the rental unit for the periods of May 1, 2023 to October 15, 2023, May 1, 2023 to November 26, 2023, and for the period May 1, 2023 to April 30, 2024.

The Landlords produced a signed statement from a resident living in unit 410 at the residential complex which notes that since the Tenants vacated the rental unit, there are noises heard of activity inside the rental unit, items are stored in the locker for the rental unit, and lighting can be seen from the patio windows and doors.

I afford no weight to these signed statements produced by the Tenants and the Landlords because none of the individuals who signed these statements were produced as witnesses for the hearing. Therefore, there was no opportunity to test or challenge any of the information contained in their statements.

The Tenants testified that they started visiting the residential complex in August 2023 to visit their friends who lived in the building and they also attended the rental unit to see if anyone had moved into it.

The Tenants produced copies of pages from a calendar for the months for August 2023 to April 2024 which note the dates and times (morning, daytime, and evening) that the Tenants knocked on the door of the rental unit, a total of 71 times during this period. The Tenants state they never heard any activity inside the rental unit, nor did anyone ever answer the door at the rental unit. The Tenants state that they did not see a vehicle parked in parking spot #21 for the rental unit after the Tenants vacated. The Tenants state they had driven by the rental unit very late at night around 1:00 am and observed lights were on in the rental unit which the Tenants state was odd that there were lights on at that time.

The Landlord produced a photograph of a grey colour vehicle parked in parking spot #21 at the residential complex. The photograph is dated January 12, 2023. The Landlord states there was someone parked in the Tenants parking sport and the Landlord did not who the vehicle belonged to. I do not find this information to be relevant as the Tenants were residing in the rental unit at this time.

The Tenants produced a copy of an unsigned lease agreement for the unit which they moved into on May 1, 2023. The Tenants state the lease agreement produced for the hearing was unsigned because the Tenants both signed a copy of the lease agreement electronically online. The lease agreement is for a fixed term for the period of May 1, 2023 to April 30, 2024 and notes the monthly rent is $2,380.00 which includes air conditioning but not utilities. The Tenants also produced a copy of a statement noting that $2,380.00 was paid each month towards the rent for the period of May 2023 - April 2024.

I accept the Tenants explanation which I find to be reasonable regarding why the lease agreement for the unit they moved into on May 1, 2023 was unsigned. It is generally accepted that since the Covid-19 pandemic, many documents are now signed electronically. The statement produced by the Tenants, noting the amounts paid towards the monthly rent at the unit they moved to, notes [name]’s name, the Landlord’s name, and the address for the rental unit which matches the lease agreement. I find this evidence further supports the Tenants moved into this unit immediately after vacating the rental unit.

The Tenants produced a copy of an invoice in the amount of $1,186.50 dated April 30, 2023 from Swan Moving and Storage Inc. to support they incurred the cost for the moving expenses. This invoice notes the Tenants names and the address for the rental unit and the address of the unit the Tenants moved to. The invoice is also signed by the Tenants. Based on the above, I accept the Tenant’s incurred this expense.

The Tenants produced a copy of a Statement of Claim dated October 25, 2021, filed with Superior Court by one of the Landlords against 3 previous tenants who were students who moved out during the Covid-19 pandemic. The Statement of Claim notes the reasons for the claim as follows. These previous tenants terminated the lease without providing 60 days notice, there are unpaid rent and utility costs, and the key fob and parking pass were not returned. The Tenants rely on this Statement of Claim to discredit the character of the Landlords. However, I afford no weight to this evidence as no one named in the Statement of Claim testified a t the hearing, and I do not find it relevant in assisting with my determination that that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Tenants also claim $300.00 for a key fob deposit that the Tenants state was collected illegally by the Landlords at the start of their lease and the Tenants claim this deposit was not returned to them. The Tenants also claim in their application that the Landlords cashed their July 2022 rent cheque a second time in April 2023 and it took the bank two weeks to return the money to the Tenants.

I stated at the hearing, that I am not able to consider the claim for the $300.00 key fob deposit collected by the Landlords, nor the Landlords depositing the Tenants cheque in the amount of $1,821.60 on two separate dates into their account. This is because the application before me relates to the Landlords giving a notice of termination in bad faith and does not relate to the illegal collection or retention of money by the Landlords. Therefore, these two allegations are dismissed.

The Landlords state that their son, DC began working in China in 2018 and that he returned from China around March 2021. The Landlord state that when he returned, he sometimes stayed with them, or at his girlfriend’s. The Landlords state DC and his girlfriend were together for about 6 years and wanted to move into the rental unit after they got married in April 2023. The Landlord’s testified that their son moved into the rental unit on May 6, 2023 and lived there until July 2024.

The Landlords state that DC currently lives in Shanghai, China and it was 2:00 am there at the time of the hearing and that is why he did not testify. The Landlord, [name] states that his mother was ill and he just returned from visiting her in China on November 30, 2025 so he could participate in the hearing as the internet in China is sporadic and is not reliable for him to participate in the electronic hearing.

The Landlords produced a copy of a water utility bill in DC’s name for the rental unit address, dated May 6, 2023 in the amount of $54.73. The Landlords also produced a copy of an Enbridge natural gas bill in DC’s name for the rental unit address for the period of May 1, 2023 – May 19, 2023 in the amount of $61.49 ($21.94 for natural gas charges + $39.55 new account charge).

The Landlords also rely on correspondence dated September 25, 2023 and September 29, 2023 between DC and someone through a Facebook chat. The Landlords state that DC was corresponding with someone through this chat to try and sell a sofa loveseat that was inside of the rental unit. The Landlords also produced a photograph of the loveseat taken to the lobby at the residential complex on September 29, 2023 prior to it being picked up by the person that purchased it from DC.

The Landlords state they are relying on evidence of items at the rental unit which required repair to support that DC was living in the rental unit. The Landlords state that the thermostat at the rental unit was not working and required repair. The Landlords produced a photograph of the thermostat taken October 7, 2023, prior to it being repaired and a photograph of the thermostat after it was repaired, taken on October 15, 2023.

The Landlords state that the kitchen faucet at the rental unit required replacement because it was leaking. The Landlord produced a photograph of the leaking kitchen faucet taken on October 15, 2023 and copy of an email dated October 17, 2023 from one of the Landlords [name] to Globe Union advising that the kitchen faucet has been leaking from some time.

The Landlords also state that the washer control board for the washing machine located inside of the rental unit required replacement and the Landlords produced a copy of an invoice dated June 15, 2024 in the amount of $356.13 for the washer control board. The Landlords also produced photographs of the washing machine inside the rental unit prior to the washer control board being replaced and after replacement of the washer control board.

The Landlords state the Tenants trespassed at the residential complex when they attended after they had moved out. The Landlords produced photographs taken in March 2024 of one of the Tenants, [name] walking in the hallway at the residential complex. The Tenants refute this and state that they have friends that still reside at the residential complex.

The Tenants put to the Landlords that on July 8, 2024, the Tenants legal representative requested proof of when DC changed his address on his drivers licence and/or his health card, and details surrounding when his job changed. The Landlords state that DC’s drivers licence and health card could not be renewed because DC held a work permit to work in China since 2018.

The Tenants provided a written statement that notes that being evicted from their home was very stressful physically, mentally, and was emotionally draining. The Tenants note that the Landlords checked with the Tenants if they would be vacationing in Florida in January 2023 as they did the previous year and the Tenants advised that they would be. The Tenants further note in their written statement that the Landlords then waited until the Tenants left for their vacation and then the Landlords emailed the N12 notice to the Tenants which they received prior to boarding the plane to take them to the port to depart on a 10-day cruise.

The Landlords state that the Tenants filed this application based on speculation. The Landlords state that the Tenants have not proven that the Landlords re-rented the rental unit to anyone else for a monthly rent amount. Remedies

The Tenants claim the following remedies: i. $21,859.20 for 1 year rent abatement based on monthly rent of $1,821.60 per month; ii. A fine to be paid by Landlords in an amount to be determined by the Landlord and Tenant Board; iii. Rent differential for 12 months in the amount of $6,700.00 based on the difference in monthly rent of $2,380.00 for the unit the Tenants moved into and the monthly rent of $1,821.60 at the rental unit; iv. General compensation in the amount of $5,000.00; and v. Moving expenses in the amount of $1,186.50. Analysis

In determining whether the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice in bad faith, I must consider the four requirements as set out within subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. The first requirement that I must consider is whether the Landlords served the N12 notice under section 48 of the Act. It is undisputed that the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice on January 16, 2023 with a termination date of April 30, 2023 and the N12 notice notes that the Landlords child intends to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year. Therefore, I find the Tenants have satisfied this first requirement.

With regards to the second requirement, I must determine if the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. I find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2023 as testified by the Tenants and supported by a copy of the new lease agreement and statement showing the Tenants paid the new rent in full starting May 1, 2023. Further, the invoice for the moving expenses dated April 30, 2023 supports the Tenants incurred moving expenses on the date they vacated the rental unit. Therefore, the Tenants have satisfied the second requirement.

Regarding the third requirement, I find that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. I have reached this determination for the following reasons provided below.

The Landlord produced a copy of the following utility bills in DC’s name. An Enbridge natural gas bill dated May 2023, an electrical bill dated June 26, 2023 from Carma Submetering and Billing Solutions, a water bill from Sandpiper Home Comfort dated May 6, 2023. While these utility bills all support that there were utilities set up in DC’s name, there were no further utility bills produced for the hearing by the Landlords to support the ongoing monthly utility consumption for which the Landlords claim their son lived inside the rental unit for the period May 2023 - July 2024. I find the lack of further utility bills beyond June 2023 supports that DC was not living at the rental unit for the period May 2023 - July 2024.

The Landlords also testified that DC worked in China in 2018 and returned in March 2021 and lived with them and also his girlfriend. The Landlords state that DC got married in April 2023 and then moved into the rental unit in May 2023. The Landlords testified that the electrical consumption at the rental unit when their son lived there was low because their son spent a lot of time at the university and ate outside of the rental unit often. There was no further evidence led by the Landlords regarding the timelines that DC attended university, nor any documentation to support when he resumed working again in China. The Landlords state that he has held a work permit to be able to work in China since 2018. Therefore, it is unclear what years DC attended university and why his health card was not reactivated during the time which DC attended university in Guelph. The Landlords provided no details regarding the reason DC moved out of the rental unit in July 2024. Based on this information which I find is missing pertinent details, I am not persuaded that DC moved into the rental unit for the period May 2023 to July 2024.

I afford little weight to the Facebook message correspondence dated September 25, 2023 and September 29, 2023 which the Landlords state was between DC and someone purchasing a sofa loveseat that was at the rental unit. The messages do not show it came from an account held by DC and the picture of the sofa loveseat is taken inside the lobby of the residential complex. Based on this evidence, I am not persuaded that DC was the one selling the sofa loveseat from the rental unit.

The Landlord also produced photographs and documentation to support a repair to the thermostat in October 2023, replacement of a kitchen faucet in October 2023, and replacement of a washer control board in June 2024. I do not find this establishes that DC was living in the rental unit during this time. This is because the Landlords own the rental unit and therefore, I find that the Landlords would have discovered these items not working at the rental unit. Other than the photographs showing these items prior to repair and after repair, there were no other photographs produced for the hearing to support someone was living inside the rental unit. There were also no copies of any mail being delivered to the rental unit in DC’s name, or a copy of an internet or telephone bill. For these reasons, I find that DC was not living at the rental unit during the period for which these photographs were taken.

While I find it odd that the Tenants visited the rental unit and knocked on the rental unit door 71 times between August 2023 to April 2024, I accept the Tenants evidence that they did do this. I find the documentary evidence produced which includes the calendar dates/times that the Tenants visited the rental unit and knocked on the door persuasive as it was corroborated by their testimony. Further, the March 2024 photographs produced by the Landlords show the Tenant [name] in the hallway at the residential complex. The Landlords never raised that DC had ever mentioned or complained about people he did not know showing up and knocking on the door of the rental unit. Based on the above evidence, I find it supports there was no one living at the rental unit during the period August 2023 to April 2024.

Based on all the reasons above, I find the Tenants have established the fourth requirement of subsection 57(1)(a) that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith. Based on a totality of the evidence and on a balance of probabilities, I find that DC did not move into the rental unit for the period of May 2023 and July 2024. While the Tenants did not establish that the Landlords evicted the Tenants so the landlords could bring in new Tenants and charge a higher monthly rent, I do not find the Tenants are required to establish this. The Tenants did establish that the Landlords wanted to increase the rent above the guideline which is undisputed by the Landlords when the Landlords sent the Tenants an email on January 9, 2022 proposing the rent increase by $160.00 per month. I accept that the Landlords did not increase the rent above the l guideline of 1.2% for that year. I find this evidence generally supports that the Landlords were motivated to try and collect a higher amount for the monthly rent than what the guideline amount would allow.

The Tenants are a retired seniors and I accept that being forced to move out of their home would create stress and frustration for them. However, they were able to find another place to move to by the termination date, they led no evidence regarding experiencing any difficulty finding another place to move to, or that they requested any extension of time from the Landlords to be able to find another place to move to. Therefore, I find that a 50% rent abatement of $10,929.60 ($1,821.60 old monthly rent x 12 months = $21,859.20 x 50% = $10,929.60) is appropriate in the circumstances.

I have determined that the Landlords served an N12 notice in bad faith which resulted in the Tenants being forced to move out of the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay a fine to the Landlord and Tenant Board in the amount of $1,000.00.

I accept that the unit the Tenants moved into for May 1, 2023 has a higher monthly rent and the amount is $2,380.00 per month. I accept this is realistically represents the market rent at the time the Tenants moved into the unit. This is because the Landlords note in their January 2022 email that market rent for a 2-3 bedroom unit in Guelph ranges from $2100.00 – $2,399.00 plus utilities and the Landlords also included a link to an advertised unit advertised on Facebook Marketplace for $2,399.00 in January 2022. The Tenants were forced to move based on the N12 notice served on them by the Landlords. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $6,700.80 ($2,380.00 new monthly rent - $1,821.60 old monthly rent = $558.40 x 12 months = $6,700.80) for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

I find it is reasonable that the Tenants hired a moving company to assist them with moving their belongings from the rental unit. I find the costs for the moving expenses to be reasonable and are supported by an invoice produced by the Tenants. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $1,186.50 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred because of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenants requested $5,000.00 for general compensation. I note that the Act references under subsection 57(3) 1.1 that an order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that because of the Landlords serving the N12 notice on them in January 2023, including the timing it was served on the Tenants, when they were leaving for vacation that this caused undue stress for them. This was a 27-month tenancy and I accept the Tenants did not want to move out of their home. However, the Tenants did not produce documentary evidence to support that they experienced any mental, emotional and physical stress because of the Landlords serving the N12 notice. Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I do not find general compensation to be warranted.
ordered: The claim for $300.00 for the key fob deposit collected by the Landlords and not returned to the Tenants is dismissed. The claim that the Landlords cashed one of the cheques in the amount of $1,821.60 provided by the Tenants on two separate dates is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $18,869.90. This amount represents: • $10,929.60 for a rent abatement. • $6,700.80 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from May 1, 2023 to May 1, 2024. • $1,186.50 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 6, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 6, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.00 by February 6, 2026. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T6 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant in the amount of $3,017.24 plus the filing fee. T1 Application
At the commencement of the hearing, the Tenant withdrew her T1 application which pertained to a $2,300.00 illegal charge that was collected at the start of the tenancy. T2 & T6 Applications

The Tenant claimed the same issue on both the T2 and T6 application. The Tenant claims that a leak in the bathroom ceiling of the rental unit started on September 27, 2024 and continued until February 6, 2025. The Tenant sought to amend her T6 application to increase the amount of rent abatement claimed to $9,200.00. The Landlord consented to this amendment.

I declined to hear the Tenant’s T2 application. The issue complained of is more appropriately categorized as a maintenance issue, and there was no prejudice to the Tenant in hearing it as a T6 issue given that the Tenant claimed a larger abatement of rent on the T6 application. The only remedy claimed by the Tenant is an abatement of rent.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant still resides in the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $2,300.00 per month. Maintenance

The Tenant claimed that she began to notice an intermittent leak in the ceiling above her bathroom shower around September 27, 2024 when black mold began to form. The Tenant advised the Landlord of the issue on the same day. The Tenant stated that the complex’s property management company attempted to fix the issue on several occasions without success, including on October 16, 2024, October 17, 2024, and January 14, 2025. The issue persisted and was considered resolved as of February 7, 2025. The Tenant also testified that between January 30, 2025 to February 6, 2025 she was not permitted to enter the washroom, her laundry room, kitchen or closet while repairs were conducted.

The Tenant stated that while the issue was ongoing, she was hesitant to use the washroom, of which there is only one in the rental unit, because she noticed changes in her breathing. The Tenant submitted a copy of a prescription into evidence for an inhaler, as well as images and video of the leak and the black staining which formed on the ceiling.
The Landlord denied being liable for the leak and stated that he made a prompt effort to reach out to the building’s property management company in order to arrange for repairs to be done.
On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

While the Landlord did reach out to property management about the leak on behalf of the Tenant, I find that the Landlord also failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate damage to the unit. The Landlord testified that maintenance is not his responsibility given that his property management company charges him monthly maintenance fees.

In this case, the Landlord never hired his own plumber to investigate the source of the leak, nor did he remove or repair the affected part of the ceiling. The Landlord is also liable for the inaction of their agent, the property management company. Remedies

The Landlord is ordered to compensate the Tenant in the amount of $3,017.24 which reflects a 30.00% abatement of rent for the period of September 27, 2024 to February 6, 2025. This abatement reflects the impact on the Tenant’s health over 133 days while the repairs were outstanding and how the Tenant’s use of the unit was substantially disrupted. A 30.00% abatement of rent is ordered because the Tenant did not lose complete use of the washroom over this period.
ordered: The T1 application is withdrawn.
The T2 application is dismissed.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $3,065.24. This amount represents: • $3,017.24 for a rent abatement for the period ending February 6, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $2,300.00 from the rent for March 2026 and the balance owing from the rent for April 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $9,301.92. Preliminary Issue – request to amend the application

At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant requested to amend the application. The Tenant sought to amend the T6 application to expand the remedy of general compensation from $8,662.80 to $23,662.80, in light of the increase to the Board’s monetary jurisdiction.
Pursuant to section 200(1) of the Act, an applicant may amend an application to the Board in accordance with the Rules. The relevant Rule is Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure.

Rule 15.1 states that where a request to amend is made prior to the hearing, it must be in writing, be served on the respondent, and filed with the Board along with proof of service on the other side.

On March 24, 2026, the Tenant uploaded into the Portal (‘TOP’) a request to amend the original application. No certificate of service was filed but she testified that she did send a copy to the Landlord by email.

Pursuant to Rule 15.3 when considering a request to amend filed prior to the hearing, the Board is to consider the following criteria: • whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; • any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; • whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; • whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and • any other relevant factors.

Given the factors set out in Rule 15.3, I am not prepared to amend the application a this point in the proceeding. The Tenant’s application was filed over 15 months’ ago; the tenancy ended nearly 16 months’ ago and claiming a significant additional remedy less than 7 days’ prior to the hearing is prejudicial to the Landlord. Additionally, the basis for the request to amend is due to medical circumstances which occurred after the hearing, which the Landlord has not been given the opportunity to review and respond to. Considering these circumstances, the Tenant’s request to amend the application is denied.

I also note that while I denied the Tenant’s request to amend the application at the hearing, the Tenant was ultimately awarded less in general compensation than she requested in her original application, therefore, had the request to amend the remedy been granted, the result would have been the same. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that she first noticed a puddle in the living room shortly after she moved in. She testified that she didn’t think anything of it at the time, thinking something might have spilled or it was from a prior leak that was fixed, so she just cleaned it up. Then, in November 2023, she started seeing mould on the baseboards. She purchased a mould testing kit from Amazon and in two days, the kit was covered in mould. The Tenant submitted photographs of the mould on the baseboards and the mould testing kit.

She testified that on January 3, 2024, after seeing the mould on the testing kit, she notified the Landlord immediately. She testified that the Landlord never did anything about the mould so she followed-up with him again on January 29, 2026 by phone. She testified that he became irate and called her names and never came to address the mould issue.

The Tenant testified that on June 20, 2024, the situation worsened after a major rainstorm caused her unit to flood. She testified that the entire floor in the boiler room was covered in water, and the water was seeping from there into her unit. She sent a video to the Landlord. On June 28, 2024, the Tenant left for a trip and when she returned on August 15, 2024, the water had dried up, but it did not appear that anything was done in the unit to rectify the issue.

The Tenant followed up with the Landlord regarding the flooding on September 3, 2024 and then, on September 12, 2024, more water was seen entering the unit. The Tenant ended up moving out of the rental unit on October 31, 2024 due to the unresolved maintenance issues.

The Landlord does not dispute that there was flooding in the rental unit on June 20, 2024. He testified that he had contractors there right away to clean up the water and then he had the foundation repaired. He testified that the foundation repair took about a month and there was no further leaking after that repair.
