The Landlord testified that the only time there was mould in the rental unit was in January 2024, when there was a link under the sink that the Tenant failed to report and any water in the rental unit was because she was not emptying the dehumidifier he provided her. He testified that the water on September 12, 2024 was from a toilet leaking and, rather than report the issue, she simply turned off the water to the toilet.

The Landlord testified that with the dehumidifier in the rental unit, the humidity was 50% and unless humidity is over 70%, there cannot be mould. He also testified that mould could grow if you leave the unit for several months in the summertime and that all basements are prone to mould.

I do not accept the Landlord’s evidence that there was no mould after the sink leaked in January 2024 or that it is not possible for there to be mould in the rental unit because a dehumidifier showed a humidity level of less than 70%, particularly when the photographs submitted by the Tenant very clearly show a significant build up of mould.

While the Landlord states that mould can only grow in humidity levels above a certain amount, the Landlord’s evidence at the hearing was inconsistent with his own statements made in text messages to the Tenant. At the hearing, he stated that it must be over 70% but in his messages to the Tenant he states that it must be over 60%. Additionally, the Landlord is not a mould specialist, and he provided no documentary evidence to support this assertion. The photographs submitted by the Tenant clearly show mould in the rental unit.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of section 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

Overall, I do not find that the Landlord’s response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances. While the Landlord responded to the initial complaint of mould by fixing a leak under the sink, the Tenant continued to report issues with mould and the Landlord failed to respond at all. The Landlord ought to have, at the very least, inspected the unit in response to the Tenant’s complaint.

I further find that the Landlord’s response to the flooding issues was unreasonable in the circumstances. The Tenant repeatedly informed the Landlord of water on the floor in the living room and bathroom. I prefer the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not respond at all to the most significant flood that occurred on June 20, 2026. The Tenant provided photographs of the dried-up water and residual dirt in support of her statements that the Landlord did not investigate or address the issue at all. While the Landlord states that he had the water in the unit cleaned up, the Landlord provided no evidence to support these statements. I would have expected to at least see a 24-hour notice of entry or an invoice from the contractor who completed the work.

Similarly, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord had the foundation repaired after the June 20, 2024 flood. The Landlord again provided no documentary evidence, such as an invoice, to support his oral testimony. I would have expected the Landlord to at least provide an invoice for such a significant project and I draw a negative inference from that lack.
Even if I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he had the foundation repaired, water continued to enter the unit after the alleged repair and therefore, this did not rectify the issue.

Additionally, while the Landlord’s position is that any mould caused was because the Tenant failed to report a leak under the sink, I am not satisfied that the Landlord submitted sufficient evidence to demonstrate this. I say this because after the Landlord allegedly repaired that leak, mould continued to appear in the rental unit. Additionally, it is unclear how mould in the bedroom window was somehow caused from a leaking sink in the kitchen. The Landlord did not call a contractor or other person with knowledge of the issues to provide evidence as to how a kitchen sink leak caused the mould issue in the rental unit.

Additionally, the Landlord gave various reasons the Tenant could have caused the mould, including vaping or failing to empty the dehumidifier. The Landlord led insufficient evidence to demonstrate that vaping can cause mould. It is unclear how vaping would cause mould in the unit. With respect to the dehumidifier, the Landlord’s evidence on this point was conflicting. In one instance, he states that the Tenant failed to empty the dehumidifier, but in another instance, he states that the dehumidifier was showing humidity levels below a level which mould go grow so mould is not possible. Iti s unclear how the Tenant’s failure to empty the dehumidifier could cause mould in an alleged humidity level that the Landlord alleges it is not possible for there to be mould in the first place. Both cannot be true. In my view, it’s more likely than not that the Landlord is positioning various reasons before the Board in an attempt to deflect blame on the Tenant. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that the mould in the rental unit was caused by the Tenant.

Even if I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the initial mould was caused by the leak in the sink, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is responsible for this. The Landlord lead no evidence that the Tenant was aware of the issue and failed or refused to report it to the Landlord. That the Tenant may not look under her sink at a frequency that satisfies the Landlord is an insufficient basis to demonstrate negligence on the part of the Tenant.

Similarly, with respect to the allegation that the last flood was caused by the Tenant due to a leaky toilet, I am not satisfied that the Landlord led sufficient evidence to prove this. The Landlord alleges that because on one occasion, he found the toilet had been shut off, this means there was a leak the Tenant failed to report. The Landlord’s evidence on this issue was also inconsistent. In one instance, the Landlord states that the water to the toilet was shut off, but in another statement states that the flooded water in the basement was from the toilet leaking. It is unclear how the water to the toilet can be both shut off and leaking in the bathroom.

Additionally, while the Landlord states that the leak was 9 months’ old because a contractor told him so, the Landlord did not call the contractor as a witness or otherwise provide evidence of a leak in the toilet that the Tenant failed to report. If the Landlord had a contractor out to address this leak, I would have expected the Landlord to at least produce an invoice to demonstrate this and I draw a negative inference from that lack.

For these reasons, I find that the Landlord was in breach of his maintenance obligations as the Landlord had been informed and was aware of the issues with flooding and mould, and their response to the issue was not timely or reasonable. T6 Remedies Rent Abatement

In her application, the Tenant requested a rent abatement of 100% from January 2024 to October 31, 2024, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. I find 100% to be unreasonable in the circumstances. A 100% rent abatement is generally only applicable if a tenant could not be in the unit at all for a period of time as would be the case in a severe fire or flood. I do not accept the Tenant’s evidence that she could not live in the unit. I find that a 40% rent abatement is reasonable in the circumstances.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a 40% rent abatement from January 3, 2024 to October 31, 2024, when the tenancy terminated, which totals $5,138.88. Costs to replace damaged property

She testified that the recurrent flooding damaged a number of her items, including her rug, television stand, and couch because they sat in water for extended periods of time. She testified that a number of her belongings were also damaged due to the mould.

I am satisfied that the Tenant led sufficient evidence to demonstrate damage to her clothing, Tupperware container, two pairs of shoes, food processor, backpack, mixer, a pair of pants, and tv stand. The Tenant provided photographs of all of the damaged items to support her oral testimony. I find that it is more likely than not that there was mould or water damage to these items and they were not able to be repaired.
I am satisfied, based on the documentary evidence provided by the Tenant, that the reasonable total cost to replace these items is $824.89.

With respect to the mattress, I am not satisfied that this item was damaged and had to be disposed of. The photograph submitted by the Tenant shows one singular small water stain. It is not clear why the Tenant had to dispose of this item rather than clean it, or whether she even attempted to clean it at all. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that this item was damaged and had to be replaced.

With respect to the memory foam pillows, I am not satisfied that these items were damaged and had to be replaced. One of the pillows shows no visible damage at all and the second pillow shows what appears to be water. It is unclear why this could not have been dried out as opposed to disposed of. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that this item was damaged and had to be replaced.

With respect to the comforter, the photograph submitted by the Tenant simply shows a comforter balled up on a bed with no visible damage at all. I find the Tenant’s evidence insufficient to demonstrate that this item was damaged at all. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that this item was damaged and had to be replaced.

With respect to the television, the Tenant alleges that she had a second 55-inch television sitting on the floor, which was damaged by one of the floods. I find the Tenant’s evidence insufficient in this regard. It is peculiar that one would have such a large television sitting on their floor. Nevertheless, none of the photographs from the flood show this item in the rental unit at all. The only visible television in the photos is sitting on top of the Tenant’s TV stand. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that this item existed in the rental unit or was damaged and had to be replaced.

With respect to the electronics’ box, while I am satisfied it was damaged and could not be repaired, the Tenant could have simply mitigated her loss by getting a new box. I am not satisfied that any remedy is reasonable for this item.

For the remaining items which the Tenant provided evidence of costs to replace, I find that the Tenant did not lead sufficient evidence to demonstrate that these items were damaged and had to be replaced. The onus is on the Tenant to prove that her belongings were damaged and had to be replaced. While the Tenant provided photos of other damaged items, there was no documentary evidence of damage to these items except for a photo showing them in the back of a truck. Considering the Tenant took significant photographs of her other items, I would have expected to see at least photographs of these items, particularly for items as significant as a mattress and an area rug, couch and bed frame to have been damaged by mould or water.

For these reasons, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that these items were damaged by either the water or the mould. No remedy will be awarded for the remaining items. Out-of-pocket expenses

The Tenant testified that the Landlord instructed her to purchase mould cleaning products to remove the mould under the sink after he repaired the leak in January 2024. She testified that she sent the products to the Landlord for approval prior to purchasing and also sent the receipts after the purchased them but the Landlord did not respond. This was not challenged by the Landlord.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses for mould cleaners because the Landlord failed to address the mould issue in the rental unit. The receipt submitted by the Tenant totals $31.59. The Landlord shall be ordered to reimburse the Tenant for this cost.

The Tenant also requested compensation for out-of-pocket expenses incurred to dispose of her mouldy belongings. She submitted a copy of her banking records showing the total amount incurred to dispose of her belongings at the dump.

Pursuant to section 16 of the Act, the Tenant has an obligation to mitigate her damages. I am not satisfied that the Tenant could not have mitigated this by disposing of the items in regular garbage pick up or had the bulky items picked up in a special pick up by the City. While the Tenant may have chosen to dispose of them at the dump, I am not satisfied that the Tenant led sufficient evidence to demonstrate that she did not have another more cost- effective alternative. Therefore, the Tenant’s request for compensation for this out-of- pocket expense is accordingly denied. T2 Application Illegal Entry

The Tenant testified that on a number of occasions, the Landlord entered her rental unit without giving her any prior notice. She testified that on February 24, 2024, she had a few friends over and the Landlord walked in unexpectedly. She testified that he was showing the unit to potential buyers, as the rental unit was listed for sale.

The Tenant testified that a similar situation occurred on March 23 or 24, 2024. She testified that she was completing an aptitude test as part of a job application process. When the Landlord entered with the potential purchasers, her friend had just exited the shower and was not clothed. RG, the Tenant’s friend, testified that she heard the door opening so she ran into the bedroom and quickly got dressed, fearing someone may see her.

The Tenant testified that on September 5, 2024, after she decided to move out, she received a text message from the Landlord indicating that he had left a dehumidifier in the rental unit. She testified that she had not been given notice that the Landlord would be going into the rental unit. Similarly, on September 20, 2024, the Tenant received a text message from the Landlord letting her know that a contractor was in her rental unit.

The Tenant testified that on September 22, 2024, the Landlord texted her screenshots of a facetime conversation he was having with a woman. In the screenshots, you can see the woman is in her rental unit. She testified that she did not receive any notice and had no idea anyone would be in her rental unit that day or why the Landlord was sending her those screenshots.

The Landlord denies that he ever entered the Tenant’s rental unit in contravention of the Act. The Landlord testified that he always gave the Tenant notice. He testified that the Tenant did work for him around the building and so their relationship was good so if he did not send her a text message with notice, he would have called her. He also denied that he showed the rental unit to potential purchases or February 24 or Marh 23 or 24, 2024. He testified that it may have been another realtor, and his office would have given the Tenant notice.
Section 26 of the Act states: A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.

Section 27 of the Act provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1.To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. (2) A landlord or, with the written authorization of a landlord, a broker or salesperson registered under the Trust in Real Estate Services Act, 2002, may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry to allow a potential purchaser to view the rental unit.

Based on the evidence and testimony before the Board, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord or their agent entered the rental unit in contravention of the Act on all 5 occasions alleged by the Tenant. I prefer the evidence of the Tenant. The Tenant and SG’s testimony was clear, consistent and supported by documentary evidence of text messages. In contrast, the Landlord’s testimony was vague, inconsistent and fraught with evasiveness.

Initially, the Landlord testified that he had always given written notice to the Tenant by text message and that he had copies of those messages. However, when given the opportunity during the hearing to produce copies of those messages, the Landlord was unable to. All of the Landlord’s testimony in defence of the allegations were generalized statements based on his beliefs of what would have been done, either by himself personally, or staff at his office. The Landlord was unable to recall specifics as to whether the Tenant was given notice at all, and how notice was given or how he obtained consent.

In my view, the lack of documentary evidence to prove the Tenant was given written notice in accordance with section 27 of the Act, suggests that it is more likely that not that the Tenant was not given written notice. Even if I accept the Landlord’s testimony that he called the Tenant and received consent to enter, there is a lack of specifics in the Landlord’s testimony to make a determination that this call was made at the time of entry, which is a requirement under section 26 of the Act. While the Tenant may not have been staying in the rental unit, she was still in possession of the rental unit and staying elsewhere does not excuse the Landlord from his obligations under the Act. Substantial interference – health issues from mould

The Tenant testified that she experienced significant, long lasting health issues due to the mould in the rental unit. She testified that she has chronic sinusitis and is still experiencing hearing issues. She testified that whenever she left the unit for an extended trip and also once she moved out, she felt significantly better. She submitted several doctor’s notes in support of these statements. One of the notes indicates that the cause of the issues is environmental. She testified that her cat also began experiencing seizures around the same time that her health issues began, which she suspects could be from the mould exposure as well.

I find that the evidence submitted by the Tenant is insufficient to prove that her health issues are caused by the mould. While one of the doctor’s states that the cause is environmental, it is unclear whether that environmental cause is in fact mould, particularly when it was the Tenant’s own evidence that her health issues have not resolved, albeit having vacated the rental unit more than a year ago. It was also the Tenant’s own testimony that no doctor has explicitly confirmed or determined that the mould caused her health issues. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Substantial interference – maintenance issues

As I have found that the Landlord was in breach of their responsibilities under section 20 of the Act with respect to the flooding and the mould, I must now consider whether this breach resulted in a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Based on my finding that the Tenant had a number of her belongings damaged due to both the flooding and the mould, and the frequency of the complaints of the issues to the Landlord, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Substantial interference & harassment

The Tenant testified that on January 29, 2026, when she had called to follow-up with the Landlord on her complaints about mould, the Landlord became very hostile and intimidating towards her. She testified that he called her a “little shit”, used profanity and told her to get out of his house. She testified that he also began accusing her of smoking in the rental unit, which she has never done since she does not smoke. She testified that following this incident, she became fearful to raise any concerns with the Landlord. She testified that he also told her to “fuck off” in a text message on September 22, 2024 when she was reiterating the requirement to give 24 hours’ notice to enter. A copy of this text message was submitted into evidence.

The Landlord did not deny that he said these things to the Tenant. He testified that after the damage in the unit due to the leak under the sink and the Tenant’s threats to bring an application, he “told her where to go”. He testified that he hounded the Tenant for 2 years about smoking in the rental unit. He knew she was smoking because he could smell it when he was in the laundry room, which is near her rental unit and he has a very sensitive nose so he can tell where the smell is coming from.

The legal test for harassment generally applied in the LTB jurisprudence is that harassment is a course of vexatious comment or conduct towards another which one knows or ought to know would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate lawful purpose (see: [name], ORTHD No 62; O’Grady v. 6891799 Canada Inc., 2023 ONLTB 25933 (Canlii), para 70).

The Landlord knew or ought to have known that his comments to the Tenant would be unwelcome. The Landlord called the Tenant a “little shit” and swore at her on at least two occasions. These comments serve no reasonable or legitimate purpose and were therefore intended to harass or vex the Tenant. Any reasonable person would find these comments hurtful and intimidating in the circumstances.

Additionally, I find that the Landlord’s continual accusations about smoking in the rental unit were unfounded and amount to harassment. The only evidence the Landlord had that the Tenant was smoking or vaping in the rental unit was his belief that smoke he smelled in the laundry room of the building was coming from her unit. The Landlord led no evidence that he or anyone else ever smelled smoke in the Tenant’s unit, or that there was any evidence of smoking found in the unit the numerous times that the Landlord entered without proper notice. The Landlord’s evidence was therefore insufficient to prove that the Tenant was smoking or vaping in the rental. Continually accusing the Tenant about smoking and vaping without sufficient evidence, particularly when the Tenant has repeatedly denied that she smokes at all, in my view, amounts to harassment. T2 Remedies Rent abatement
The Tenant requested a 100% rent abatement for the months of February, March and September 2024 for the illegal entries.

The illegal entry of a rental unit is a breach of a tenant’s privacy. An abatement of rent is the usual remedy granted in landlord and tenant matters. It reflects the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving everything being paid for, then the tenant is entitled to an abatement proportional to the difference in value of what is being paid for and what is being received.

The difficulty that arises in the context of a breach of privacy rights under the Act is that an abatement of rent is not an appropriate remedy. A single breach, such as the one here, may only deprive the tenant of his or her right to privacy for one day, which given what abatement represents, would seem to limit the available remedy to an abatement of the rent for one day. In an average tenancy, such a remedy results in an amount that is grossly inadequate. Awarding an abatement for breach of privacy fails to get at the full impact of the breach, which often results in lingering feelings of violation that can continue indefinitely into the future.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437, found that the phrase “any other order that it considers appropriate” in the remedies section of the Act (which is now found in paragraph 31(1)(f)) means that the Board has the power to award “damages for the breach of contract of lease”. For the reasons stated above, in breach of privacy cases approaching remedy as a matter of damages arising from a breach of the tenancy agreement is more logical and appropriate than describing the remedy as abatement of the rent. In this case, the Tenant also claimed general compensation for the breach of privacy and I find that is the more appropriate remedy in the circumstances. Therefore, no rent abatement will be awarded in addition to the amount awarded for general compensation. Moving costs

The Tenant claims compensation for her moving costs. I find it is appropriate to award moving costs in this case, as the unresolved maintenance issues warranted termination of the tenancy. The Tenant made substantial efforts to correct the Landlord’s behaviour and have him address the maintenance issues, to no avail. The Tenant gave her notice to the Landlord on September 4, 2024 and stated that it was because of the conditions in the rental unit.

The Tenant requested moving costs in the amount of $599.84 for a U-Haul truck, gas for the U-Haul truck, a cancellation fee for her internet and a suspension fee for suspending her wi-fi while staying with a friend.

I find that the costs for the U-Haul and the gas for the U-Haul are reasonable. The Landlord will be ordered to reimburse the Tenant for these costs, being $308.56. I am not satisfied that it is reasonable to require the Landlord to pay for the Tenant’s administrative costs for suspending and later cancelling her rogers contract because the Tenant no longer required Wi-Fi. Therefore, the Tenant’s claim for these costs is dismissed. General Compensation

In both the T2 and T6 application, the Tenant requested general compensation for the maintenance issues, illegal entries, substantial interference and harassment. In the T2 application, the Tenant requested $7,000.00 and in the T6 application, the Tenant requested $8,662.80. Health issues from mould

The Tenant testified that she experienced significant, long lasting health issues due to the mould in the rental unit. She testified that she has chronic sinusitis and is still experiencing hearing issues. She testified that whenever she left the unit for an extended trip and also once she moved out, she felt significantly better. She submitted several doctor’s notes in support of these statements. One of the notes indicates that the cause of the issues is environmental. She testified that her cat also began experiencing seizures around the same time that her health issues began, which she suspects could be from the mould exposure as well.

I find that the evidence submitted by the Tenant is insufficient to prove that her health issues are caused by the mould. While one of the doctor’s states that the cause is environmental, it is unclear whether that environmental cause is in fact mould, particularly when it was the Tenant’s own evidence that her health issues have not resolved, albeit having vacated the rental unit more than a year ago. It was also the Tenant’s own testimony that no doctor has explicitly confirmed or determined that the mould caused her health issues. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Illegal entries

In Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation (January 24, 2007) Toronto Docket No. 374/06, [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name].Ct.) (‘Wrona’), the Divisional Court replaced the decision of the Board and granted the tenant an abatement of $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry, which was well in excess of 100% of the monthly rent charged.

In Wrona there had been at least one previous application brought to the Tribunal by the tenant about the same issue. In other words, there was a history of dispute between the parties about what constituted a legal entry. Here there was no prior application between the parties or any prior issues with illegal entry brought to my attention, so there was no such history.

Based on the precedent established by Wrona, the difference between the two cases, the evidence of the impact of the illegal entry upon the Tenant, and considering that Wrona was issued more than 20 years ago, I find that a reasonable amount for damages arising out of the Landlord’s breach would be as follows: • $300.00 for the illegal entry on February 24, 2024 as the Tenant was home and had company over, which was quite intrusive. • $2,000.00 for the illegal entry on March 23 or 24, 2024 considering the impact on the Tenant on that date was significant, particularly considering that her guest was nearly caught in an extremely revealing position. • $150.00 for each entry on September 5, 20 and 22, 2025 as the Tenant was not home during the entries and, although the rental unit was disturbed, the breach of privacy was minimal. Harassment and loss of enjoyment

I am satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour in this regard had some impact on the Tenant. Considering the impact on the Tenant, that it was only two incidents, which were several months apart, and that the Tenant did not request a rent abatement for this issue, I find that general compensation in the amount of $200.00 is reasonable in the circumstances.
The Tenant also claimed general compensation for not completing an aptitude test for a job interview as she was interrupted by the Landlord during the illegal entry on March 26 or 24, 2024.

As stated in paragraph 44, the Tenant has an obligation to mitigate her damages. The Tenant led no evidence that she reached out to the company to inquire about re-doing or finishing the test considering the circumstances or otherwise made efforts to rectify the situation. As such, I am not satisfied that an award for damages in addition to what has already been awarded for this illegal entry is warranted in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,301.92. This amount represents: • $5,138.88 for a rent abatement. • $308.56 for moving expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $824.89 for the reasonable costs the Tenant incurred to replace property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $31.59 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $2,950.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') and [name] (the ‘Landlords' Agent') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $698.00 by April 24, 2026.

The Tenant’s T1 application was filed on October 6, 2025, alleging that the Landlords collected an illegal charge of $650.00 in total during the tenancy. Specifically, as the Tenant testified for a damage deposit collected on or about 2017, and further that the Landlords negotiated the said cheque after the tenancy terminated on or about July 31, 2025, in the amount of $650.00.

The Tenant further testified that although the Landlords had provided a bank draft to rectify the issue related to the alleged illegal damage deposit this bank draft was returned to the Landlords, as the Tenant wished to pursue this T1 application and seek her legal remedies and costs.

The Landlords’ Agent submitted that this matter could and should have been rectified as the Landlords provided a bank draft to remedy the situation regarding the alleged illegal damage deposit, however the same was returned by the Tenant as the Tenant also sought costs for this herein application, which the Landlords do not dispute. The Landlords’ Agent further submitted the matter could have been resolved amicably prior to this proceeding, as the Landlords are seniors who were not informed that securing damage deposit during a tenancy was not permissible. ANALYSIS: ILLEGAL CHARGE COLLECTED
The question before me is whether the Landlords are entitled to collect this additional charge pursuant to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

Subsection 134(1) of the Act states: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no Landlords shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

This reads as an absolute prohibition against a Landlord charging any kind of fee other than rent to a tenant. However, the section uses the phrase “unless otherwise prescribed” which means fees can be charged if they are specifically permitted in the regulations of the Act.
The exemptions to s.134(1) are set out in section 17 of Ontario Regulations 516/06. The list of exemptions does not include a damage deposit.
Therefore, I find that the Landlords breached section 134 of the Act by collecting from the Tenant an additional illegal charge in the sum of $650.00 for a damage deposit.
As the Tenant has been successful in their application, the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the application fee.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $698.00. This amount represents: o $650.00 for the illegal charge collected (damage deposit). o $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlords does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the applications. Therefore, the applications are dismissed.
The tenancy began February 1, 2024. The Tenant vacated the unit on August 31, 2024. T6 application

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

The Tenant testified on July 7, 2024, they came back to the apartment and found mould. The Tenant phoned the Landlord, but it went directly to voicemail because the Landlord was in the United States. The Tenant finally reached the Landlord on July 14, 2024, through an email address they got from the upstairs tenant; the Tenant included a picture of mould on the wall, panelling and a bedroom pillow. The Landlord indicated they were returning the next day and would contact a contractor to come and assess the problem. On July 15, 2024, the Tenant met the contractor at the unit; the contractor said the problem mould would be addressed through remediation. The Tenant was told to stay out of the unit until the issue was fixed; the Landlord said they could leave their furniture, which they did. On August 7, 2024, the Tenant went to the unit to see how the remediation was progressing; drywall was missing all around the apartment and insulation was exposed. While there, the contractor said that the Landlord knew there was a problem that required the sump pump being checked regularly. The Tenant returned to the unit again on August 9, 2024, to check progress and saw more panelling had been cut at the bottom of the stairs and discovered mould on the bed that necessitated it being thrown out; the contractor apologized about the mould and said all furniture should have been removed from the beginning. The Tenant did not live at the unit since the mould was discovered; they had to put their trailer at a campground and live there for 3 months. The Tenant’s testimony included reference to several pictures showing mould on: wall and panelling in basement and spare room; various shoe wear including runners, work boots, slippers, shoes; and, on furniture throughout the unit. The Landlord only returned the rent for July 2024, $1900.00; they would not cover anything else. The application should be granted along with all requested remedies; the Landlord is responsible because of the mould issues and previous flooding problems. They loved the unit but could not live in it with air quality issues related to mould.

On cross examination, the Tenant confirmed: they did not check the lease about the Landlord’s contact information; the Landlord contacted the contractor about remediation, including cleaning belongings, but this was not followed up on; the trailer was already at the campground, but they had to pay for the rest of the season; items were not taken to a laundromat to be cleaned; the bulk of the affected items discussed with the Landlord were shoes ; their were no receipts attached supporting their monetary claims for travel,, repair/replacement or moving/storage costs; and no documentary evidence of their communication with the insurance company. The Tenant also confirmed that the Landlord offered two options: the tenancy is not terminated and the rent for September to be pro- rated in accordance with the date the unit is ready; and, tenancy terminates early, the last month rent returned, and depending on when they actually vacate, any rent due will be pro-rated accordingly.

The Landlord testified after receiving the Tenant’s email, they reached out to the contractor immediately upon their return to Canada, July 14, 2024; the remediation contractor did an assessment and quote, and also had an inspection done by IMS Laboratory to determine the degree/level of spores. On July 17, 2024, the lab report was completed, and the lab technician went through the results. The technician noted that the humidity was high in the unit, but the spore count was low. The Tenant was advised not to stay at the unit during the repairs and that any items needing cleaned would be packed up and sent out; the Tenant said they could stay at their trailer while the work was being done. The remediation started immediately, including addressing the visibly affected areas and checking other areas to ensure they were not affected; they removed/cut panelling and baseboards. At the end of August 2024, the Landlord had a text discussion with the Tenant about the unit being liveable after the remediation was completed, but the Tenant said they were not comfortable living there because of breathing problems and still wanted the tenancy terminated; this was when the two options, remaining or vacating, were laid out to the Tenant with their respective terms. The application should be dismissed, the Landlord acted reasonably and did all they could, the Tenant did nothing to mitigate in respect of their belongings and chose to vacate when not necessary; the Tenant also did not provide any evidence that their insurance company would not cover their belongs or substantiation for the monetary remedies sought.

On cross examination, the Landlord testified the Tenant’s texts wanting more than return of the on-month rent were based on storage costs, but that the amount kept changing; by this time the relationship had deteriorated, which is when the two options were set out.
The Landlord referenced documents, reports, pictures, and texts contained in their document brief. Analysis

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair/maintain the residential complex, and did not fail to comply with health, safety, or maintenance standards. There was no evidence presented or argument that how the job was handled was contrary to any standards or regulations.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Landlord responded immediately, the contractor attended the unit the following day, July 15, 2024. The contractor assessed the necessary repairs and had a laboratory mould analysis done; the spore count at the time of inspection was assessed as very low to low. Although the mould was discovered a week prior, the Tenant testified they did not check for the Landlord’s contact information in the lease; therefore, the Landlord is not responsible for the delay in reporting. The Tenant was aware of the progress throughout the approximate two-month remediation process; it was completed September 2024. Although advised that once remediation was complete the unit was liveable, the Tenant chose to end the tenancy indicating they could not live in a unit that had air quality issues due to their breathing problems; the Tenant did not provide any medical documentation supporting this claim. The Tenant also did not testify to any steps they took to mitigate their property being affected, nor did they present any evidence/documentation supporting their assertion that their insurance company would not cover any losses. Further, the Tenant did not have any proof to support the monetary losses being claimed. As to living elsewhere during the repairs, the Tenant chose to live at the campground; when repairs are being addressed, particularly extensive or lengthy ones, it is inevitable that the tenant will be inconvenienced but this does not mean the landlord has breached their responsibilities.
For all these reasons, I find the Landlord acted reasonably and in a timely manner, therefore, the Tenant’s T6 application must be dismissed. T2 application

As to the T2 application, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. There was no testimony or evidence provided by either party; therefore, this application is also dismissed
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. 084355-24 In the matter of: T6 [address] ST CATHARINES ON Between: [name] [name] Tenants And [organization] Landlord [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were combined by Order of the Board and were heard by videoconference on September 10, 2025. The Landlord, represented by [name], a senior employee of the Landlord, and the Tenants attended the hearing. I enquired as to ownership of the rental unit. [name] advised that [organization] was not the owner of the rental unit but acted as the landlord within the meaning of the Act and did not dispute that [organization] was appropriately named as the respondent on these applications. The Tenants did not seek any amendment to the applications to add any other parties.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the applications that the Landlord failed to address an infestation of the rental unit by rodent, namely racoons.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the sum of $7,568.39.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on December 1, 2018 and moved out on November 30, 2024. The T6 application was commenced on October 15, 2024. The T2 application was commenced on December 12, 2024.

The Tenants first notified the Landlord that there were racoons in the attic on February 12, 2024 by email. This concerned the Tenants as they had an 8-month old child and we were concerned about the loud noises of scratching in the attic, as well as the health risks of having wild animals in their home and a newborn with no immune system.

After follow up contact to the Landlord, the Tenants received an email from the Landlord on May 6, 2024, three months after their initial notice of the rodent infestation, that the Landlord had contacted a pest control contractor. Despite follow up emails and calls to the Landlord, the Landlord did not send a pest control service to the rental unit until July 22, 2024, five months after the initial notice. The pest control service recommended remediation steps and sent a quote to Landlord for approval. After the inspection July 22, 2024, the Tenants followed up with the Landlord on July 29, 2024, August 1, 2024 and August 6, 2024. The Landlord approved the quotation in part and on August 14, 2024 Skedaddle completed the work they were authorized to perform - they sealed the existing entry point but not any other potential entry points for rodents.

The Tenants state that the [name] agent informed them that the insulation in the attic was ruined and was covered with rat and raccoon feces. The Tenants were told that the insulation needed to be repaired immediately. The Tenants stated they did not personally inspect the insulation and relied on the representative of [name] for this information.

After this repair, the rental unit was free of racoons for about two weeks. The racoon then returned through a new entry point. The Tenants notified the Landlord on September 3, 2024 about the return of the raccoons, and the Landlord arranged for [name] return on September 5, 2024 to investigate. [name] advised the Tenants that the raccoons made a new entry point and that their initial quote would have sealed that entry point but they were not approved to deal with it previously. The Tenants stated that [name] then sent a new quote to the Landlord for approval to seal this new entry point.

The Tenants followed up by email with the Landlord on September 13, 2024 as Skedaddle had not attended to seal the new entry point. As the Tenants were not satisfied with the pace at which the Landlord was proceeding to address the rodent infestation, the Tenants sent a N9 form on September 30, 2024 to end their tenancy effective November 30, 2024 as they were not prepared to live in a home with infested by rodents when the Landlord was not addressing the issue.
The Landlord responded the N9 notification immediately.

On October 16, 2024, the Landlord came to the rental unit to show the unit to a prospective tenant. The Tenants stated that the Landlord’s agent apologized for the presence of the raccoons, acknowledging that they were aware of the problem and had done nothing about it.
The Landlord had taken no additional steps to address the rodent infestation by the time the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on November 30, 2024.

In summary, the Landlord was advised of the rodent infestation on February 12, 2024, performed a repair on August 14, 2024, 6 months later, were advised of a second infestation on September 3, 2024 and did nothing for to remediate this infestation for three months until the Tenants moved out.

The Tenants described the effects the pest infestation had on them. They had a newborn child living in a home infested with rats and racoons and were concerned for their health, particularly the health of their child. The rodents were in the attic above their bedroom and their movements created noise which made it difficult to sleep. The Tenants stated that the lack of sleep was to the point of exhaustion but there was no lost time from work. The Tenants told the Landlord that the noise from the rodents was impacting their ability to sleep. They were also concerned with the cost of heating the rental unit for which they were responsible under the lease, following the advice from [name] that the insulation in the attic had been destroyed.

The Tenants stated they had no wish to move and left only because of the rodent infestation of their home. The Tenants stated that they even agreed to an above guideline rent increase from $1,775.00 to $2,000 per month in the fall of 2023 as they did not want to move. 17. [name] testified for the Landlord. She offered no credible explanation for the Landlord’s failure to address the rodent infestation, nor did she dispute the dates of the communications between the Tenants, the Landlord and [name]. It appeared to me that [name] was under the impression that once she had dispatched other staff of the Landlord to address the issue on February 12, 2024, that that was sufficient to address the problem. She stated that, until the communication from the Tenants on September 13, 2024, she thought the issue had been addressed. [name] stated that she was not in the maintenance department at the Landlord, as if that somehow excused the Landlord from performance of its obligations under the Act. 18. No other employees and no one from [name] testified. [name] stated that the Landlord was getting quotes from multiple service providers and was further delayed by the fact that approval of the quotes was needed from the owners of the rental unit and that the owners were slow in responding. I note that [name] acknowledged that [organization] was a landlord and so bears all of the responsibility of a landlord on a joint and several basis, and it is no excuse for one landlord to blame delays on another. Remedies 1. In their T6 application, filed before the Tenants vacated the rental unit but after they had delivered their N9 notice of termination, the Tenants claimed $10,000 for excess heating costs and abatement of rent of 50% for a period of 9 months and also requested that the Landlord be ordered to perform remedial work. 2. In their T2 application, filed after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Tenants repeated the claim for $10,000 and also requested that the Landlord pay the differential in rent at their new residence of $1,052 per month for a period of one year. The Tenants also claimed moving expenses of $1,822.39. The invoice from [name] the Mover states that the invoice amount is $1,472.39 and provided for a “tip” of $150. The remaining discrepancy between the invoice and the claim for $1,822.39 was not explained. 3. At the hearing, the Tenants acknowledged that the claim for $10,000 in the T2 and T6 applications was a duplication and their intention was not to claim $10,000 on each application. No evidence was led at the hearing with respect to the rent differential nor was that claim argued for in the Tenants’ submissions. 4. I find that an abatement of 40% of the Tenants’ rent for a period of 7 and one half months is appropriate. The Tenants clearly described both their communications with the Landlord and their concerns with the rodent infestation and the effect it was having on their enjoyment of their tenancy. The ability to sleep soundly and safely in the rental unit is an important element of the tenancy of which the Tenants were largely deprived. I have reduced the period of abatement of 9 months claimed by the Tenant as the Landlord should be allowed a reasonable period of time for response to the Tenants’ complaint, and as the infestation was remediated for a period of two weeks. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $6,000 ($2,000 x 40% x 7.5) is appropriate in the circumstances. I am not making a separate award for additional heating costs. The Tenants offered no evidence as to how a cost differential between their actual costs and the costs which would have been incurred had the attic been properly insulated could be calculated, and the quantification of a specific differential is a matter of speculation. 5. The Landlord is also ordered to pay the Tenants moving expenses of $1,472.39. I am satisfied that the sole reason for the Tenants’ move out was the pest infestation and the Landlord’s inaction in addressing the issue, and that the Tenants’ moving out was a reasonable response to the Landlord’s inaction. 6. The Tenants are also entitled to the filing fees for the T2 and T6 applications.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $7,568.39. This amount represents: • $6,000 for a rent abatement. • $1,472.39 for moving costs. • $96.00 for the cost of filing the applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. (T3 Application) The Tenant further applied for an order determining that the Landlords collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) The Tenant further applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. The Tenant filed numerous applications with the Board, and all the applications have been allotted a single file number. So, while this order will reflect that the Tenant’s application is dismissed, it should be noted that this is in reference to all the applications filed by the Tenant under this file number.

This matter was previously scheduled for a case conference on April 14, 2025, and the matter was adjourned to be scheduled for a hearing. As per the adjournment sheet, the Board had informed the Tenant that their applications contained no dates, lacked details/reasons, and that their remedies were unclear. The Board also advised the Tenant that these issues may be raised as a preliminary issue at the scheduled hearing.

At the hearing, the legal representative raised a preliminary issue and argued that the Tenant’s applications do not contain sufficient details and particulars for them to understand the allegations. The Tenant argued that he had filed voluminous evidence in support of his allegations with the Board, and as I understand it, his position is that the Landlords either know, or ought to know, the allegations against them. The Tenant also confirmed that he did not serve their evidence to the Landlords. The legal representative responded that the onus is on the Tenant to provide detailed particulars of the allegations on the applications, and that the respondents should not have to filter through the Tenant’s evidence to understand his allegations.

Considering the submission of the parties, I found it appropriate to dismiss the Tenant’s applications. I accepted the preliminary issue raised by the legal representative. The Tenant’s applications lacked detailed particulars, such as dates/time, reasons, to put the Landlords on notice for them to know the case to be met.

In the T1, and T2 application, no details/reasons are provided, and thus the grounds formulating the basis of the applications could not be made out. In the T3 application, the Tenant wrote “safety and maintenance issue” and does not provide any details describing the service/facility that was discontinued/reduced. Further, no remedy is selected on this application. With respect to the T6 application, there was lack of detailed descriptions as to the maintenance issue; the date when the issues started; the date when the Tenant told the Landlords about each issue; and whether the maintenance issue had been resolved. Also, the remedies on both the T2 and T6 applications are vague and not clear.

The Tenant had been previously advised at the case conference of the details missing from their applications and did not take any reasonable steps to amend their applications. The Tenant also did not serve their evidence to the Landlords which further supported the fact that the Landlords were not aware of the claims against them. Even if the Tenant had provided their evidence to the Landlords, the purpose of evidence is to corroborate the allegations. Evidence does not constitute a substitution for lack of sufficient details on the applications. Detailed particulars on the applications are what governs the grounds on the applications. In the circumstances of the case, the Landlords could not be expected to reasonably respond due to the issues noted above.
For the above noted reasons, I found it appropriate to dismiss the Tenant’s application.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) LTB-T-012364-24----[name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): (T2 Application) • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T1 application under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) for an order requiring the Landlord to repay money the Landlord collected contrary to the Act. As explained below, I find that the Tenant proved the material allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenant the amount of $2,634.84. LTB-T-012364-24
At the hearing, there was no dispute that the tenancy ended and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The termination date of the tenancy remained in dispute. Tenant’s evidence:

The Tenant testified that the tenancy began on March 1, 2021. The Tenant paid $1,530.00 as a rent deposit for the last month’s rent at the start of the tenancy. The monthly rent was $1,530.00. The Tenant testified that the parties entered into a first written lease in March 2021 for a one-year term and later entered into a second written lease beginning April 1, 2022, for a two-year term ending March 31, 2024.

The Tenant further testified that on December 1, 2023, they attempted to end the tenancy early by providing an N11 agreement to terminate, with a proposed termination date of January 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to agree to an early termination. The Tenant then served an N9 notice dated January 31, 2024, indicating an intention to terminate the tenancy at the end of the lease term on March 31, 2024.

The Tenant testified that after serving the N9, they removed their personal belongings from the rental unit and left the keys on the kitchen counter. The Tenant stated this was done because the Landlord would need access to show the unit to prospective tenants. The Tenant testified that rent for February 2024 was withdrawn by the Landlord from the [name] bank account after February 1, 2024.

The Tenant testified that on February 10, 2024, they sent their daughter to the rental unit to retrieve a security camera. The Tenant’s daughter found that the lock had been changed and the key did not work. The Tenant stated that the Landlord was inside the unit and refused entry to the Tenant’s daughter.

On February 14, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord requesting replacement keys and that the Landlord did not provide them. The Tenant submitted into evidence the N9 notice, and the emails dated February 14 and February 15, 2024. In the Landlord’s email dated February 15, 2024, the Landlord stated, “I don’t have a new key till I get a new tenant in that unit. if a new tenant gets in earlier than March 31, I will gladly reimburse you some of the money.” The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not provide replacement keys and did not return the rent for February 2024 and March 2024. Landlord’s Legal Representative submissions:

The Landlord did not attend the hearing and did not provide testimony or documents. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not cross examine the Tenant. The Landlord’s Legal Representative made submissions.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit as of January 31, 2024, because the Tenant removed personal belongings, left the keys in the unit, and permitted the Landlord to make appointments to show the unit to prospective tenants. On that basis, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord was entitled to change the locks. The Landlord’s Legal Representative further submitted that, because the Tenant served an N9 notice, the tenancy would have ended on March LTB-T-012364-24 31, 2024, pursuant to section 44 of the Act, and the Tenant is responsible for the February 2024 and March 2024 rent. Law and Analysis:

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 4: “Abandonment of a Rental Unit” explains the concept of abandonment as follows: Abandonment is a unilateral act by the tenant to relinquish their tenancy and give up possession of the rental unit without properly giving notice of the termination to the landlord. If the landlord is not sure whether or not a rental unit has been abandoned, they may file an application for determination of this issue with the Board.

Section 2(3) of the Act provides that a rental unit is not considered abandoned where the tenant is not in arrears of rent. Even if there is evidence of abandonment, such as the furniture being removed, the landlord cannot treat the unit as abandoned before the end of the rental period if the rent is fully paid.

The uncontested evidence before me is that the February 2024 rent had been paid and the Tenant was not in arrears as of February 2024. The uncontested evidence is also that the Tenant provided 60 days notice to terminate the tenancy as of March 31, 2024. In these circumstances, I do not find that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit in February 2024.

Section 24 of the Act states that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

Section 37 of the Act states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. According to section 37, a tenancy can be lawfully terminated by a notice of termination or an agreement to terminate.

Section 44(4) of the Act provides that where a tenancy is for a fixed term, a notice to terminate must be given at least sixty days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement to be effective on that expiration date. Based on the uncontested evidence, the parties had a fixed term ending March 31, 2024, and the Tenant provided at least sixty days notice for that date. There is also evidence that the Landlord refused to agree to an earlier termination. I therefore find there was no agreement to terminate before March 31, 2024, and that, but for what occurred next, the tenancy would have ended on March 31, 2024, accordance with the Act.

However, the evidence is that on February 10, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks and then refused to provide replacement keys, thereby preventing the Tenant from accessing the rental unit. There was no agreement to terminate and there was no Board order terminating the tenancy. I find that, as of February 10, 2024, the Landlord unlawfully excluded the Tenant from the rental unit and took possession. On the evidence, the Tenant was unable to exercise the right to occupy after that date. I therefore find that the tenancy ended on February 10, 2024, as a result of the Landlord’s conduct. LTB-T-012364-24

Section 134(1.1) of the Act provides: 134(1.1) No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit

Given my finding that the tenancy ended on February 10, 2024, the Landlord was not entitled to retain rent for any period after that date. I find that the Landlord collected excess rent from February 10, 2024, to March 31, 2024, because the Tenant’s rent deposit was intended to cover the last month’s rent and the tenancy did not continue to March 31, 2024. The excess amount is $2,536.00, calculated as follows: $1,530.00 × 12 months ÷ 365 days = $50.30 per day; $50.3 × 20 days = $ 1,006.00 (Feb). $1,006.00 + $1,530.00 = $2,536.00.
As the Tenant was successful on their application, the cost of filing this application is also granted. T2 Application: Illegal entry:

In the T2 application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on February 10, 2024. I have addressed the Landlord’s conduct on that date in the T1 determination, including the Landlord’s unlawful lock change and denial of access, and I have awarded a full refund of rent for the period from February 10, 2024, to March 31, 2024. In these circumstances, and given the remedy already ordered, this issue does not require a further determination for the purpose of relief, and it is dismissed. Substantial interference and harassment, etc.

At the hearing, the Tenant stated that for this claim they sought rent abatement for February 2024 and March 2024, which is the same period, and the same financial relief addressed under the T1 application. As I have awarded a full refund for the period from February 10, 2024, to March 31, 2024, under the T1, no further determination is required on the merits of the T2 allegations for that same period.

With respect to the period from February 1, 2024, to February 9, 2024, the application did not set out sufficient particulars of incidents falling within that period. As a result, the claim is dismissed for being vague and lacking sufficient details to permit the Landlord to know the case to be met and to respond. Lost Item: LTB-T-012364-24

The Tenant also stated that the Landlord took their security camera on February 10, 2024. Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord took the Tenant’s security camera.

The Tenant testified that the camera remained in the unit after January 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that on February 10, 2024, when the Tenant’s daughter attended the unit to reset the camera, she learned that the Landlord had taken it. The Tenant submitted video footage recorded by the Tenant’s daughter on February 10, 2024, which captured the interaction with the Landlord and showed a power cord to the security camera in the Landlord’s pocket. The Tenant also submitted a copy of the invoice for the camera, which indicates the cost was $50.84. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not cross examine the Tenant on this evidence. I therefore find the Tenant is entitled to $50.84 for the loss of the security camera.
The Tenant sought to withdraw the remaining cost claims in the application.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
