issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $748.00.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on July 6, 2024 in a fixed term tenancy ending December 31, 2024, and remained in the rental unit on a month to month basis until vacating the rental unit on October 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that at the time of entering into the tenancy agreement he provided a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $850.00 to the Landlord, but the amount of the deposit was later reduced pursuant to an agreement to $700.00.
The Tenant further testified that he had discussed vacating the rental unit with the Landlord in August 2025 and told the Landlord that he would provide him with an N9 Notice of Termination.

On September 1, 2025 the Tenant served an N9 Tenant’s Notice to End Tenancy (‘N9 Notice’) on the Landlord by leaving a copy on the Landlord’s desk of the Landlord at his business downstairs as well as placing a copy in the mailbox at the Landlord’s business. The N9 Notice contained a termination date of October 31, 2025.
The Tenant indicated that the main floor of [address]nue is the Landlord’s business address and was the address where the Landlord had advised the Tenant to send documents relating to the tenancy.
The Tenant further testified that he paid the Landlord rent for October on September 26, 2025. A screen capture of an e-transfer confirming the payment was produced at the hearing of this matter.

The Tenant states that he requested the return of his last month’s rent deposit from the Landlord, and that the Landlord had initially agreed to return the deposit, but later came up with excuses not to. As of the date of the hearing the Tenant testified that the last month’s rent deposit has not been returned. Analysis

Section 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.

Section 44(2) of the Act relating to a month to month tenancy sets out the notice requirement stating: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant provided 60 days notice to the Landlord before the date of termination in the N9 Notice.

The Tenant’s N9 Notice was served on the landlord in accordance with section 191(1) (d) of the Act by leaving It in the mailbox where mail is ordinarily delivered to the person, and that the tenancy lawfully terminated on October 31, 2025.
Pursuant to section 106(10) the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.

Since the Tenant paid rent of $700.00 for the month of October 2025 to the Landlord. The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and based on the uncontested evidence before me did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $748.00. This amount represents: • $700.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the 'Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $21,048.00 by May 17, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There was no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice of termination. The notice stated that the Landlord had entered into an agreement of purchase and sale for the rental unit, and that the Purchaser required vacant possession of the rental unit for their own residential use.
There was also no dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2023 as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

The Tenant testified that she was searching for rental units and came across the rental unit being listed for rent on February 28, 2024, a mere four months after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord did not dispute the listing and the Purchaser did not attend the hearing to contest or explain the listing. As such, I find it more likely than not that the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit as stipulated on the N12 notice of termination and instead rented the rental unit to new tenants after the Tenant vacated.

The Landlord submitted a copy of the Agreement of Purchase and Sale (“APS”) into evidence. The APS with a completion/closing date of November 1, 2023 was signed by the Landlord and the Purchaser on August 14, 2023. At the hearing, the Landlord testified that he had no contact with the Purchaser and that all communication regarding the sale of the rental unit was done through realtors and lawyers.
The Landlord testified that he understood that the Purchaser wanted vacant possession of the rental unit to demolish the property and rebuild their home.

The Landlord testified that he was not directed or instructed by anyone to serve the N12 notice of termination and was aware that the notice was needed to terminate the tenancy. The Landlord at no point rescinded the N12 notice of termination.

The Landlord testified that he commenced negotiations with the Tenant on September 1, 2023 for a cash for keys deal. The Landlord subsequently negotiated with the Tenant’s Legal Representative and the parties settled on a deal on September 30, 2023.

KC is the Landlord’s realtor and testified that the Landlord had no contact with the Purchaser and that he was the one who communicated with the Purchaser’s realtor, [name], via text messages and phone calls.
KC testified that there were no conditions on the APS

KC testified that [name] informed him that the Purchaser wanted to rebuild and sell the rental unit. As a result, KC requested the Purchaser to sign an affidavit that “they have no intentions to rent the property other than rebuilding and selling it” on August 23, 2023. On August 24, 2023, KC sent [name] a blank Declaration form and informed [name] that the Purchaser can fill out the form declaring that they are not renting the property for the next 12 months and that it is for their personal use. On August 25, 2023, KC informed [name] “we need to get this supplied to the tenant within this month so that we can give this to tenant 60 days before closing”. [name] responded that he understood the notice of termination was already served and is waiting for instructions from the Purchaser. KC responded informing [name] that the notice has been provided to the Tenant but the Landlord is requesting the Declaration as it “will save him from any type of question coming from tenant”. The text messages between KC and [name] were submitted into evidence. (DOC-5670839)

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord was aware or ought to have been aware that the Purchaser did not intend to use the rental unit for their own residential purposes. The Landlord testified that he was aware of the communication between KC and [name] and I find it more likely than not that KC, as the Landlord’s realtor, acted on the instructions of the Landlord. KC’s communication with [name] was clear and demonstrates that the Purchaser’s intention was to rebuild the rental unit and sell. KC was aware of this and proceeded to request the Purchaser to sign a Declaration falsely declaring that the Purchaser wants the rental unit for their personal use. There was no evidence before the Board that the Purchaser signed such Declaration.

The Landlord nevertheless continued to advance the Tenant’s move out without rescinding the N12 notice of termination or informing the Tenant that the Purchaser had no intention to move into the rental unit. In my view, the manner by which the Landlord conducted the termination of the tenancy strongly suggests an intention to circumvent the Tenant’s protections under the Act. While the Landlord submits it is not the Landlord’s responsibility to confirm the Purchaser’s intention, I disagree.

By serving the N12 notice of termination, the Landlord initiated events that had the serious consequence of ending the tenancy and compelling the Tenant to relocate which is a substantial undertaking, especially for a relatively long tenancy that commenced in 2017. In my view, the Landlord had an obligation to satisfy himself that the conditions precedent for serving an N12 notice of termination on behalf of a Purchaser had been met—namely that the Purchaser themselves required the unit in good faith for the purpose of residential occupation.

In its decision in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal quotes with approval paragraph 22 of the Board’s decision in Duarte v. [organization], 2021 CanLII 146522 (ON LTB) which says: However, in relaying the Purchaser’s intentions to terminate the tenancy, the Landlord does not serve as a mere messenger with no duties or obligations to the Tenants. By conveying the Purchaser’s stated intention to occupy the rental unit, the Landlord initiated events that had the serious consequence of ending the tenancy and compelling them to relocate their family, a substantial undertaking even in the absence of a global pandemic. As a result, I find that the Landlord had a duty to the Tenants to exercise some due diligence to confirm the good faith intentions of the Purchaser before putting the eviction in motion. Otherwise, an unscrupulous purchaser would be free to use a landlord as a straw man to divest tenants of their housing and thereby evade the statutory protections afforded to them under the Act.

In the present case, the Landlord was aware of the Purchaser’s intention to not move into the rental unit and knew, or should have known, that he was not entitled to terminate the [name] tenancy under the circumstances. Even if I considered that the Landlord was unaware of the Purchaser’s true intentions until August 23, 2023, the Landlord opted to withhold this information from the Tenant and continued the cash for keys negotiation. At best, I find that the Landlord was wilfully blind to its duties and obligations and readily exploited the Tenant’s ignorance of the Purchaser’s intentions to terminate the tenancy.
As such, I find the Landlord gave the Tenant the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies
Having proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith, the Tenant is entitled to a remedy described in subsection 57(3) of the Act.
The Tenant requested an order for the difference in rent the Tenant paid for one year after vacating the rental unit, moving and storage expenses, and general compensation.

There was no dispute that the monthly rent was $1,000.00 when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant introduced a letter from her current landlord of the accommodation she moved into after vacating the rental unit and testified that her monthly rent after vacating the rental unit was $2,500.00. The Landlord did not introduce evidence to contradict the Tenant’s evidence on this issue. I therefore find the Tenant’s evidence of the increased in rent they were required to pay to be reliable and credible.

The new accommodation is in the same neighbourhood as the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the units were similar in size and both are basement units but they vary in certain aspects. The rental unit had in-suite laundry, a gas stove, inclusion of internet and utilities, access to a backyard and shed, newer kitchen finishes and one bedroom. The new accommodation had parking included, no bedroom, shared laundry with two other units, no gas stove, no dishwasher, and was dated compared to the rental unit. There was no evidence before the Board that the rental unit was inferior to the Tenant’s new accommodation or the Tenant’s new accommodation was a betterment.

Based on the parties’ evidence, I find the Tenant paid an increase of $18,000.00 ($1,500.00 x 12) in rent for the one-year period after they vacated the rental unit. The Tenant is entitled to this amount pursuant to subsection 57(3)1 of the Act.

The Tenant is seeking moving expenses in the amount of $3,000.00. The Tenant testified she took a day or two off work to move, paid cash to her friends and family to help her move, and that her father rented a truck for the move. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence, such as receipts, for any out-of-pocket expenses incurred nor did the Tenant bring any witnesses to confirm any costs. Given that this is the Tenant’s application, I find the Tenant has failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish these costs. As such, this claim is dismissed.

The Tenant requested $12,000.00 for general compensation. It is important to note that as reference in the Act, an order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the Tenant has incurred any actual expenses. Although I accept the Tenant’ evidence that the N12 notice of termination had a negative effect on her, I do not find that general damages in the amount of $12,000.00 to be warranted in these circumstances. The Tenant provided no documentary evidence to support the proposition that the Tenant experienced any decline in mental health or an increase in stress from the service of the N12 notice of termination. Based on the evidence before the Board and given the length of the tenancy, I find that an award of $3,000.00 to be reasonable and an order for this amount will issue accordingly.
As the Tenant’s application is successful, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement for his costs of filing the application in the amount of $48.00.

The Court in [name] ruled at paragraph 52 that, “After making both those determinations, the Board must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.” [Emphasis added.] While it could be argued in some cases that the Purchaser be responsible for the bad faith notice and be ordered to pay the remedies granted, I do not find this to be the case here. There were no direction or instructions from the Purchaser to the Landlord to serve the N12 notice of termination. The evidence shows that the Purchaser was transparent and ultimately informed the Landlord that they intended to use the rental unit for investment – and not residential – purposes. As such, I do not find the Purchaser acted in bad faith and it was the Landlord who acted in bad faith. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the remedies to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $21,048.00. This amount represents: • $18,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from November 1, 2023 to October 31, 2024. • $3,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord moved to have the application dismissed because the LTB does not have jurisdiction.

Both parties agreed that there was no agreed upon regular rent rate. The parties had agreed that the Tenant would pay the utilities used in the rental unit for the right to stay in the rental unit. The utility cost fluctuated along with usage and was not a set amount for a set period of time.

Section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) defines the following: Rent “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, Tenant “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit
Rent is defined as “the amount”, which indicates a static fee. What both parties agreed was paid was not a static fee, but a rate set by a third party (a utility provider).
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, Ms. [name] does not meet the definition of a “Tenant” under the Act because they do not pay “rent” for the right to occupy the rental unit.
The Act does not apply in this circumstance. Therefore, the LTB does not have the jurisdiction to consider this matter. For that reason, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ltd (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] Askri (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owes (the ‘L1 Application’). The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants and withheld or interfered with their vital services (the ‘T2 Application’). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’). These applications were heard together by videoconference on October 8, 2025. The Landlord’s legal representative Sofia Enriquez and the Tenants attended the hearing. [name] attended the hearing, shadowing the Landlord’s legal representative.
reasons: At the hearing, it was brought to the Board’s attention that the Tenants had raised issues under section 82 with respect to various issues they experienced while living in the rental unit. The Tenants have also filed a T2 and T6 application with respect to these issues: LTB-T-084598-24. ; LTB-T-084598-24

The Tenants were informed that they would not be able to have these matters adjudicated twice by the Board. They opted to present the issues in response to the Landlord’s L1 Application on the date of the hearing.

The Landlord’s legal representative requested that the applications be combined due to the duplicative issues and the Tenants consented. Therefore, I combined the applications and heard evidence on the merits of the Tenants’ T2 and T6 Applications.

I note that the parties had participated in an Adjudicate Case Conference before another member of the Board on September 22, 2025, with respect to the Tenants’ applications and an interim order was issued. The hearing has subsequently been erroneously scheduled for a merits hearing by the Board. Since the Tenants’ applications have already been heard, however, the upcoming hearing date is cancelled. The L1 Application

The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenants was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on November 19, 2024. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit
The lawful rent is $1,741.25. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to November 19, 2024 are $11,835.25.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,650.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $66.34 is owing to the Tenants for the period from April 12, 2023 to November 19, 2024. The Section 82 Issues and the Tenant Applications

The Tenants raised the following issues in their T2 and T6 Applications: • A lack of heat in the winter: December 15, 2023 to January 17, 2024. • Issues with water access in the rental unit: September 18, 2024 and February 19, 2024. [name] and Cockroach infestations: April 15, 2024 onward. • Water and mold growth in the basement ceiling: December 27, 2023. ; LTB-T-084598-24 • Uninvited individuals entering the residential complex and knocking on the door of the rental unit. Issue 1: T2 - Heat in the Rental Unit

The Tenants testified that they noticed the baseboard heaters in their rental unit were not functioning correctly in early December 2023. They testified that they reached out to the Landlord on January 18, 2024, as the issue had persisted, and sent the Landlord a photograph of a temperature reading showing a temperature of 18.9 degrees Celsius in the unit overnight.

This photograph is included in the Landlord’s evidence and shows a thermometer with multiple temperature readings. The Tenants testified that the thermometer used shows the current temperature as well as the maximum and minimum temperature readings recorded in an area within the past 24 hours. These figures are clearly marked in the image provided to the Landlord.

The Landlord responded to the Tenants’ complaint five days later on January 23, 2024, apparently misinterpreting the image. The property manager closed the ticket as she did not understand the unit temperature had dropped to 18.9 degrees Celsius overnight and she believed that the unit temperature – which, as she understood it, was 21.5 degrees Celsius – was within the legally-required range.
The Tenant testified that she followed up with the property manager in person the day after the complaint was marked as resolved to explain the temperature readings.

The Tenant testified that no action was taken from this point forward until they received an email from their building manager on February 3, 2024, advising that the building’s boilers were experiencing maintenance issues. On February 10, 2024, and February 11, 2024, the Landlord’s agent emailed the Tenants to, advising the Tenants to purchase a space heater pending the resolution. The Tenants responded, declining to purchase a heater as it was – in their view – the Landlord’s responsibility to provide a solution. Per the Tenants’ testimony, the Landlord ultimately provided space heaters around midnight on February 11, 2024, around midnight.

Based on the evidence presented at the hearing, I am satisfied that the Landlord was in breach of its obligations under sections 21 and 22 of the Act from January 18, 2024 (the date of the Tenants’ complaint) to February 11, 2024 (the date the space heaters were provided). In my view, the Landlord did not respond appropriately to a significant issue raised by the Tenants and – as such – an abatement is owed. Issue 2: T2 - Water Issues in the Rental Unit
The Tenants testified that they experienced issues with water service to their rental unit throughout the tenancy.
The Tenants referred to two particular dates where they experienced water outages in their rental unit: September 18, 2023; October 16, 2024; and February 19, 2024. ; LTB-T-084598-24

The September 18, 2023, water outage took place more than one year prior to the Tenants’ application being filed on October 17, 2024, and therefore no remedy can be issued with respect to the Landlord’s conduct relating to this incident: subsection 29(2) of the Act.

The Tenants provided a video they filmed on October 16, 2024, which shows the bathroom sink and bathtub have no running water when the taps are opened. The Tenants did not, however, show that they communicated this issue to the Landlord on that date.

On February 19, 2024, which is during the same period the heat for the rental unit was not properly functioning, the Tenants filed a ticket in the Landlord’s portal stating that they have not had hot water in the rental unit for one week. An agent of the Landlord – Zaid [name] – responded to the complaint 2 days later, saying he would reach out to the Tenants within 72 hours. The ticket was ultimately closed without a further documented response.

The Tenants testified that they experienced frequent water disruptions without notice during the entire tenancy and that they would receive communications after-the-fact from the Landlord about any outages.

Based on the evidence presented at the hearing, I am satisfied that the Landlord was in breach of its obligations under sections 21 and 22 of the Act on February 19, 2024 (the date of the Tenants’ complaint about the hot water). In my view, the Landlord did not respond appropriately to a significant issue raised by the Tenants and – as such – an abatement is owed. Issue 3: T6 - Pest Issues

The Tenants reported a pest issue to the Landlord via the Landlord’s portal on May 24, 2023. This incident took place more than one year prior to the Tenants’ application being filed on October 17, 2024, and therefore no remedy can be issued with respect to the Landlord’s conduct relating to this incident: subsection 29(2) of the Act.

No other particular incidents regarding pest control were referred to by the Tenants in their application. While they have raised general complaints about the Landlord’s pest management strategy, they have not sufficiently detailed their allegations so that the Landlord could respond. The Tenants also testified that they submitted a ticket via the Landlord’s portal on November 19, 2024, relating to bedbugs, but this date is not mentioned in their application and no evidence in support of this testimony was provided at the hearing.

Without evidence of a particular breach by the Landlord within the limitation period, no abatement is awarded with respect to the pest issues identified in the Tenant’s application. Issue 4: The Basement Ceiling

The Tenants testified that they reported an issue regarding the presence of mold and a potential structural issue in the parking structure in the basement of the residential complex in winter of 2023. ; LTB-T-084598-24
The Tenants testified that they did not submit a ticket or written complaint to the Landlord regarding this issue as they had reported the issue to on-site staff.

The Tenants are of the view that this issue is dangerous and required a prompt response from the Landlord, and that the Landlord merely conducted a cosmetic repair to cover parts of the issue. This was not, however, supported by any evidence beyond the Tenants’ testimony and the inconclusive photographic evidence provided.

I am not satisfied that the Tenants have proven a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this issue and, therefore, no remedy is granted. Issue 5: T6 – Individuals Sleeping in Common Areas

The Tenants allege in their T6 application that unhoused individuals were sleeping in the hallway outside of their rental unit and would occasionally knock on their door looking for an individual that they don’t know. While this does not constitute a valid ground on a T6 Application, I find that there is no prejudice to the Landlord in treating this matter as a claim of substantial interference under the Tenants’ T2 Application. The Landlord was able to respond to the Tenants’ claims at the hearing.

The Tenants submitted a ticket to the Landlord on February 2, 2024, alerting the Landlord to the issue of uninvited people showing up at their rental unit. The Landlord’s agent replied to the Tenants’ complaints within minutes, seeking further information. The Tenants did not provide a response, according to the Landlord’s records presented at the hearing and the ticket was closed by the Landlord on February 27, 2024, after over three weeks without a reply from the Tenants.

The evidence shows that it is the Tenants who were not diligent in their communications about this issue to the Landlord, rather than the other way around. I am not satisfied, based on the evidence presented at the hearing, that the Landlord was in breach of its obligations under section 23 of the Act with respect to this issue and therefore no remedy is granted. Rent Abatement for Tenant Issues

Given the length of the heat outage and the Landlord’s lack of responsiveness to the Tenants’ complaints about the heat outage between January 18, 2024, and February 11, 2024, and the subsequent hot water outage on February 19, 2024, I find that a rent abatement of $918.62 – representing one-half of one month’s rent and the cost of filing the Tenants’ applications – is appropriate in the circumstances.
This amount will be deducted from the amount owing to the Landlord.
ordered: On consent of the parties, the Landlord’s L1 Application (LTB-L-060911-24) is combined with the Tenant’s T2 and T6 Applications (LTB-T-084598-24) ; LTB-T-084598-24
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated as of November 19, 2024, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $9,200.29. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit and the rent abatement/rebate awarded to the Tenants is deducted from the amount owing by the Tenants. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenants does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before February 20, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The hearing scheduled for LTB-T-084598-24 is cancelled, as the matter has been heard. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Tenants’ Legal Representative request to amend the application to include [name] as a Tenant.
An amended application had previously been served on the Landlord and filed with the Board.

Having considered the factors as set out in Rule 15.3 of the Landlord and [name] including: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors.

Having considered section 15.3 of the Landlord and Tenant Board Rule and the Landlord’s failure to attend the hearing to oppose the request, the request to amend the application shall be granted. T2 Application

The Tenants testified that they moved into the rental unit in 1999 pursuant to an oral tenancy agreement with the previous landlord. The Tenants further state that pursuant to the oral tenancy agreement a parking space was included and that $35.00 of their monthly rent went towards parking.
The Tenants stated that they had parked at the residential complex without issue since 2009 when they purchased their first car.

The Tenants testified that when the Landlord took over the property in June, 2024 he advised the Tenants that they did not have permission to park at the residential premises, and that if they wished to park at the residential premises the price for parking was $175.00 per month.

The Tenants stated that the Landlord arrived at the residential complex with parking enforcement from the City of Toronto on September 17, 18, 23, 26 and October 8, 2024 and that each time the Landlord threated to tow the Tenants’ vehicle.
The Tenants also received three parking tickets from the City of Toronto for parking on private property without consent while parking their vehicle at the residential complex during these dates.
Although two of the tickets were later withdrawn, the Tenant [name] had to take time of work to address the parking tickets.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me the Tenants have parked at the residential complex for past 15 years without issue unit the Landlord purchased the residential complex in June, 2024.

On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or a member of their household. Remedies Sought Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenants sought out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $675.00, being $75.00 for a parking ticket from October 8, 2024 as well as $600.00 for loss of wages to address the various parking ticket the Tenants received.

The Tenants shall be reimbursed $75.00 for the parking ticket they paid. However, the Tenants lead insufficient evidence to support their claim for loss of wages. As such, no compensation for loss of wages will be awarded. Rent Abatement

The Tenants also sought a rent abatement of $1,338.00 as follows: $490.00 being $35.00 per month for parking x 14 months of interrupted parking at the residential complex and $848.00 for the landlords conduct in requesting a substantial increase for parking, threatening to tow the Tenants’ vehicle and substantial interference to the Tenant’s daily life without the use of a parking space.
Based on the Tenants testimony and the uncontested evidence before me I find the Tenants’ request of $1,338.00 to be reasonable in the circumstances. [name]

The Tenants seek a determination that they have a parking space at the residential complex. I am satisfied on balance of probabilities based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants that they are entitled to a parking space at the residential complex pursuant to the oral lease agreement with the previous landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,461.00. This amount represents: • $1,338.00 for a rent abatement. • $75.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $487.00 from the rent each month from April 2026 to June 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

For the duration of the tenancy the Tenants shall have a parking space at the residential complex and are permitted to park their vehicle at the residential complex. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As a preliminary issue, this member enquired if [name] [name], who was listed as a Landlord on the application, was an employee of the Landlord or the Landlord. The Tenant advised she worked for the Landlord. As such, [name] [name] is removed as a Landlord as she is an Agent of the Landlord.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the remedy as set out below.
The Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2024. The Landlord required that they pay $2,850.00 for the Landlord’s insurance. The Tenant paid this because they are new to Canada and this was the first time they rented an apartment; they found out after paying this money to the Landlord that it is the Landlord’s responsibility to pay for their insurance, even if it is written in the tenancy agreement.

Based on the uncontested testimony before me, I do not find that the Landlord charged an illegal rent; the $2,850.00 that the Landlord required the Tenant to pay to cover the Landlord’s insurance is an illegal charge. A tenant is not responsible for paying the Landlord’s insurance costs. That this clause is contained in the lease is irrelevant; section 4 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) says a clause in a lease that is contrary to the Act is void.
As the Tenant is successful in their application, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $2,903.00. This amount represents: • $2,850.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held by videoconference on September 15, 2025. Only the Tenants and the Tenants’ agents, [name] and [name], attended the ACC. As of 1:35 PM, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, an uncontested hearing proceeded on the merits of the application with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant, [name], requested to amend the application to add the second Tenant, [name]. The application was filed by the Tenant’s former paralegal, and the Tenant did not realize until recently that the paralegal had failed to add his partner, [name] ([name]), as an Applicant.
The Tenant submitted copies of two N1 notices to increase rent received from the Landlord in 2024 and 2025. Both N1 notices indicate [name] as a Tenant.

Given that the Landlord appears to have acknowledged [name] as a Tenant in their notices of rent increase, I find little prejudice to the Landlord resulting from the Tenant’s amendment request. Therefore, the Tenant’s request to amend the application to add [name] as an [name] is granted. T2 application
In their application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed them in relation to their parking arrangements.
As explained below, the Tenants proved that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. Therefore, the total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $897.10.
The Tenants did not satisfy me, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord harassed them.
The Tenants testified that the current Landlord purchased the residential complex on or about June 23, 2024.

The Tenant [name] testified that she has resided in the rental unit since 1990 and has consistently been allocated one parking space for which she paid $20.00 per month. The Tenants did not have a written lease agreement with the former landlord.

The Tenant [name] (R.N.) testified that he moved into the unit with [name] a few months after her tenancy began. He further testified that approximately three years ago, the former landlord approved an additional parking space for his vehicle. R.N. stated that he paid the former landlord $35.00 per month for the additional space, separate from rent, from September to December 2022, and submitted receipts confirming these payments. Beginning in January 2023, R.N. testified that he and the former landlord agreed the $35.00 parking fee would be added to the monthly rent payment.

R.N. testified that issues concerning parking arose immediately after the Landlord assumed ownership of the complex. He stated that the Landlord’s son initially occupied [name]’s parking spot. When the Tenants objected, the Landlord advised them that they were entitled to only one parking space and that R.N.’s vehicle was not authorized to park on the property. The Tenants testified that the Landlord refused to review their banking records showing payment of an additional $35.00 per month added to their lawful rent for the second parking space. R.N. further testified that during this period, the Landlord attended the unit, pounded on the door with his fist, and demanded to speak with the Tenants about the parking issue. R.N. refused to engage with the Landlord, who eventually left. R.N. testified that the Landlord returned later the same day and again pounded on the unit door to confront him about parking. The Tenant could not recall the specific date but thought this incident may have taken place on the same day the Landlord took over the residential complex.

R.N. testified that the Landlord contacted parking enforcement on several occasions, resulting in three parking infraction notices being issued to R.N., each in the amount of $75.00. Copies of the notices dated September 13, 2024, September 18, 2024, and October 8, 2024, were submitted as evidence. R.N. testified that he was able to have two of the three tickets cancelled by the city after explaining the circumstances. Following the issuance of the final ticket, R.N. stated that he chose to park on the street in front of the complex to avoid further conflict with the Landlord. He continued to park on the street until the tenancy ended on August 31, 2024. The Tenant stated that he continued to pay $35.00 for parking in addition to the lawful rent despite parking on the street. Analysis

Based on the uncontested evidence before me and on the balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that by unilaterally removing the second parking spot allocated to the Tenants the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) provides that when a rental unit is sold, all covenants relating to the rental unit or the residential complex run with the land. As a result, a new landlord assumes the role of the former landlord and the existing terms and conditions of the tenancy continue unchanged. Although there was no written tenancy agreement, the Tenants established the existence of a parking agreement with the former landlord through receipts for payment and by evidence that they paid amounts in excess of the lawful rent for parking. Despite their request to consider their evidence, the Landlord refused and removed the parking spot that had been allotted to R.N. for 3 years.

Further, the Landlord repeatedly contacted parking enforcement, which resulted in the Tenant receiving multiple parking infractions and effectively compelled the Tenant to cease using the parking space and park on the street. I find that this conduct interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I also find that a reasonable tenant would consider the Landlord’s actions to constitute a substantial interference with their tenancy.
The Tenants did not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed them.

Although the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not define “harassment,” the Ontario Human Rights Code defines harassment as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.

While I find that the Landlord ought reasonably to have known that pounding on the Tenants’ door with his fist to address a parking dispute would be unwelcome, the evidence did not establish that the Landlord engaged in a continuing course of similar conduct. I find that this isolated incident supports the Tenants’ claim of substantial interference but does not rise to the level of harassment. Remedies Rent Abatement

The Tenants are seeking a 40% rent abatement for the months of September and October 2024. The Tenants have selected these specific months for their abatement request because it was when the Landlord was repeatedly calling parking enforcement to ticket R.N.’s vehicle.

Abatement of the rent is a contractual remedy. It is designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, then the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. Assessment of the quantum of abatement involves looking at the timing of the complaint and resolution, if any, and the impact on the Tenant of the Landlord’s breaches of the Act

I find that a rent abatement is an appropriate remedy in the circumstances; however, the quantum requested of 40% is unreasonable. The loss of a single parking space does not equate to 40% of the overall rental unit and amenities for which the Tenants were paying. That said, I must also consider the impact this loss had on the Tenants.
R.N. testified that interactions with the Landlord were stressful and that this stress contributed to symptoms including heart palpitations and increased blood pressure.

Taking into account the Landlord’s conduct, the loss of the parking space, and the impact on the Tenants, I find that a rent abatement of 15% for the months of September and October 2024 is appropriate. The Tenants testified that their lawful rent during this period was $947.00 per month. Accordingly, an order shall issue abating the Tenants’ rent in the amount of $284.10, calculated as follows: $947.00 × 0.15 = $142.05 per month × 2 months.

I must also consider that the Tenants continued to pay $35.00 per month above their lawful rent for a parking space they were unable to use until the end of their tenancy. In the “remedies sought” section of their schedule to the application, the Tenants requested that any illegal amounts obtained by the Landlord be reimbursed or abated. I find it reasonably clear that, in addition to the abatement for September and October 2024, the Tenants were also seeking reimbursement for the cost of the additional parking space they did not receive. Accordingly, in addition to the abatement outlined above, the Tenants shall be abated a further $490.00, representing $35.00 per month for 14 months, from July 2024 through August 2025. Out-of-pocket Expenses

The Tenants also sought reimbursement in the amount of $150.00 for two of the three parking infraction tickets issued while R.N.’s vehicle was parked in the residential complex parking lot. The Tenants provided copies of the tickets as evidence. R.N. testified that, after explaining the circumstances to the municipality, two of the three tickets were cancelled. As a result, the Tenants were only required to pay one ticket. Accordingly, I find that the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement in the amount of $75.00, representing their out-of-pocket cost for the single parking infraction ticket paid. “Other” Remedies

The Tenants also sought compensation for lost wages equivalent to five days of work. However, the Tenants did not provide any testimony that they missed work, nor did they submit evidence to support this claim. As a result, I make no order with respect to this requested remedy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $897.10. This amount represents: • $774.10 for a rent abatement. • $75.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant submitted that the Landlord’s evidence was not received 7 days prior to the hearing as required by the Board’s rules, therefore, the evidence should be excluded.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord’s evidence was mistakenly submitted a day late, but it only consists of 4 pre-existing documents that the Tenant is well aware of, therefore, nothing new is being raise or anything the Tenant is not aware of; it should be allowed.
The matter proceeded on its merits, there was no prejudice to the Tenant to allow the Landlord’s evidence as the quantity is nominal and does not contain anything the Tenant is not aware of. Merits
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the tenancy began October 1, 2025; they paid the Landlord a first month rent and a last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,250.00 each. On October 2, 2025, the Tenant went to the unit to do a pre-move-in cleaning: when they started cleaning, they noticed cockroaches in the kitchen, on the fridge, stove and floor. When they pulled the fridge out hundreds of cockroaches scattered out from underneath; underneath the floor was also very dirty and the cupboard under the kitchen sink was also dirty; indicating the Landlord did not ready the unit for move-in. The Tenant cleaned for approximately 5-hours then got fed up with the cockroach issue; they contacted the Landlord's Agent and advised the unit had a cockroach infestation; therefore, it was uninhabitable, and the tenancy must be terminated immediately. The Tenant said because they could not live there due to the condition of the unit, the Landlord had to return the last month rent deposit and the first month rent that they paid.

The Tenant relied on numerous pictures to support their position that the only option available to them was to move. The Tenant submitted the pictures were taken during the day, but the roaches were more active at night. The Tenant submitted they were not looking for perfection, but the cleanliness was terrible. The Tenant testified the pictures taken October 4, 2025, after the Landlord had done cleaning, show it was still filthy and not ready to move into. The Landlord said they would return the money and then reneged; it is contrary to the legislation for them to keep it and must be returned. Further, the Landlord should not be allowed to rely on the last month rent non-refundable clause when it is not an enforceable clause.

The Landlord's Agent testified the Tenant applied for the rental unit mid-September, shortly after viewing the unit the Tenant signed the lease. No issues were raised during the viewing, which is the exact state as when the Tenant moved in. The Landlord was not aware of any issues with the unit when it was rented to the Tenant; it had been prepared for renting as is every unit they rent out. When the complaint was received about the unit being uninhabitable, the Tenant said they wanted the lease terminated and the first and last month rent monies returned. Based on the Tenant’s description of the unit, the Landlord verbally agreed, but upon inspection the following day, consent was retracted. The Tenant was sent an email to this effect containing the inspection report and with accompanying photos which did not reveal any roach activity. As the unit was not uninhabitable, the Landlord is not required to return the first and last month rents as the Tenant did not give proper notice to terminate. The Landlord properly mitigated their losses by advertising the unit; it took approximately 2-months to rent the unit out. The same tenant lives in the unit now, and the Landlord has not received any complaints about the unit, including roaches. Analysis
Based on the testimony and evidence before me, I find the Landlord did not retain monies contrary to the legislation.

The law establishes that there is no unilateral right to rescind a contract that has been duly entered into by the parties ([name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923, [2008] O.J. No. 1934 (QL), 2008 CarswellOnt 2747, Court File No. 142/07 ([name]. Ct.) ([name], [name], and [name].)). Here, the parties entered signed a lease and the Tenant’s were given possession; the issue to be addressed is whether the unit was uninhabitable when the Tenant took possession thus leaving no other option but to terminate the tenancy. Although the Tenant provided pictures that showed cockroaches, there was generally one roach in each picture, and numerous were close-ups of the same bug/area or taken at different angles. The pictures did not demonstrate that the unit was infested to the degree that it was uninhabitable; the caselaw has long-established that unless a severe lack of compliance with health, safety or maintenance standards is established, there is no fundamental breach of the contract, and it remains intact. According to the court, a fundamental breach must be such that it frustrates the real purpose of the contract (Temlas Apartments Inc. v. Desloges [1980] O.J. No. 3624, 29 O.R. (2d) 30 ([name]. [name]. Ct.)); it must be so critical as to bring an end to the contract as a whole or repairs so protracted that occupancy is not reasonably possible (Lord Strathcona Steamship Co. v. Dominion Coal Co. [1926] 1 D.L.R. 873, [1926] A.C. 108 (P.C.)). If there are pest or cleanliness issues upon move-in, a landlord needs to be given the opportunity to rectify the issue(s); here, there is no dispute that the Landlord was not given a chance to address the issues.

Although the Landlord may have originally consented to terminating the tenancy and returning the last month rent deposit, the Tenant did not accept this offer; therefore, it is not an enforceable agreement. As such, the Tenant was required to give proper notice of termination, which is not the case as they immediately moved out. When a tenant vacates without giving a landlord proper notice of termination, the landlord is required to mitigate its losses pursuant to section 17 of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (the ‘Act’). Here, it was not contested that the Landlord had the unit re-rented approximately 2-months after the Tenant vacated, therefore, I find the Landlord mitigated its losses.

As to the clause in the lease that says the last month rent deposit is non-refundable, although not specifically raised by the Tenant, although a clause in a lease cannot be contrary to the legislation, all the above issues come into play, and the outcome of this order is not affected.
For all these reasons, the Tenant is not entitled to return of the first of last month rent deposit; accordingly, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Landlord $3,500.00.

By way of background, the tenancy began December 1, 2024. The tenancy ended on October 1, 2025. The Tenant was paying $435.00 each month in rent to rent one room. The Tenant was one of four individuals who lived in the upper portion of the Landlord’s home; they did not share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord and had their own entrance. Therefore, I find that the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) applies to this tenancy.
The Tenant states that the Landlord unlawfully terminated his tenancy and did not allow the Tenant to collect his belongings.

On September 20 or 21, 2022, the Landlord had an argument with one of the other four Tenants. As a result of this argument, the Landlord turned the power off to the upper portion of the house, telling the Tenant’s there was something wrong with the power line. However, the Landlord still had power in his area of the home, other individuals on the street still had power, and made no efforts to have this fixed.

The Tenant relocated to a friend’s house, because he did not have power. One of his roommates called him on September 30, 2025, because the Landlord was evicting all of the Tenants and removing their belongings from the house. He notes the power was returned on this date.

When the Tenant arrived, he found belongings of his being loaded into the back of a pickup truck. He asked to gather the items belonging to him, and the Landlord told him he could go to the dump if he wanted to pick these things up. The Tenant even tried to take some of his belongings from the truck bed, and the Landlord prevented him from doing so, scratching him in the process. The Tenant submitted video showing the Landlord placing belongings in the truck bed and driving away with them.

Given the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord harassed the Tenant. A reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that self-help remedies such as exercised in these circumstances are unlawful. The Board can think of few more egregious acts than unilaterally terminating a tenancy and disposing of the Tenant’s belongings. I also find the Landlord turned the power off to harass the Tenant(s) into leaving the rental unit. Remedies
The Tenant requests the following: • $3,100.00 for belongings which were disposed of by the Landlord; • $150.00 for moving and storage costs; and, • $250.00 for out-of-pocket expenses.

Although the Landlord did not clean out the Tenant’s room, the Tenant says he still lost a number of personal household items and hygiene products. He says he had lived in the rental unit for the longest period, so most everything in the kitchen was his. For example, utensils and plates, and a spare mattress which had been in the living room. The Landlord also disposed of all of his groceries.

The Tenant also lost all of his hygiene products like body wash and shampoo. He also had other items of clothing and footwear which had been in the closet, and all of this was gone too, including expensive sneakers. He estimated the costs of these items to be $3,100.00.
The Tenant also paid for a U-Haul because he still needed to move the items from his bedroom. He says he paid $150.00 for the U-Haul, although he did not have a receipt.
Finally, the Tenant asks $150.00 for the replacement of items the Landlord disposed of including hygiene products and food.

I am of the view that the costs the Tenant requests are reasonable. In my view, they fall within a range which is appropriate to replace items in a kitchen like dishes, utensils and the like, clothing and footwear, personal hygiene products, and groceries.

The Tenant does not seek a fine or abatement of rent in this matter. If the Landlord had attended such that he could have given submissions on an administrative fine, it is likely I would have ordered a fine be paid in these circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,500.00. This amount represents: • $3,100.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions; • $150.00 for moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred; and, • $250.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Starlight Investments (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (LTB-T-088044-24). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (LTB-T-084866-24).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $347.16 in rent abatement and the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant moved into the three-bedroom rental unit in March 2021 and continues to reside in the unit.
The lawful monthly rent at the time the application was filed was $1,686.00 , with the daily rate at $55.43. / LTB-T-084866-24 Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that on August 8, 2024, while she was away from the rental unit, her mother visited the unit and observed water leaking from the ceiling in the front entrance doorway, the closet , hallway, and master bedroom . The Tenant immediately made a maintenance request to the Landlord, and at the hearing, presented pic tures of the unit which corroborated her evidence.
On or about August 24, 2024, when the Tenant returned to the unit , she contacted the Landlord multiple times about the repairs.

On September 18, 2024 , the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord acknowledging information she received about the roof being replaced. She further stated that the leak was worse and there was mold in the unit: ‘I have had to move my mattress into the third bedroom because of the black mold coming through the ceiling and the wretched smell, all of this causing my asthma to be affected.’ The Landlord did not respond to the email.

On September 21, 2024, the Tenant sent an other email to the Landlord describing the conditions of the unit and attached pictures of the damage caused by the leak. The Landlord responded on September 22, 2024, stating that they were taking the issue seriously and would send someone to assess the damage and conduct repairs.

On September 24, 2024, the Tenant contacted the bylaw office who sent an officer to inspect the unit. Although the officer’s report was not provided to the Tenant, the Tenant was aware that the Landlord was given a 30-day deadline which expired, with no steps taken by the Landlord. The officer kept attending the residential complex over the problem on undisclosed dates.

On September 26, 2024, the Tenant sent another email to the Landlord because water had seeped into the fire detector and damaged it. The Landlord sent someone to remove the fire detector and provide her with a battery-operated unit.
On October 8, 2024, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord seeking an update on the repairs which were yet to commence.

At the beginning of December 2024, the city told the Landlord that if the roof were not repaired, the city would do it at their expense and bill the Landlord for it. The Landlord subsequently fixed the roof on December 19, 2024.

The Landlord on the Tenant’s request, paid for a hotel stay from February 11, 2025, to February 17, 2025, while repairs were being done inside the unit. On her return on February 17, 2025, the Tenant observed the unit was still undergoing repairs and some of her belongings were displaced. The work was not finished until February 28, 2025.

The Tenant further testified that a few repairs were not properly done but were corrected in March 2025, and that the Landlord failed to keep their promise to hire a professional to clean the unit following the repairs. / LTB-T-084866-24 Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord's witness / Residential Manager, AH, testified that there was a major storm the week the Tenant contacted him in mid August 2024. He inspected the rental unit, confirmed the Tenant’s report, and contacted the Property Manager on a suitable contractor to conduct the repairs.

The Landlord stated that the repairs were done on August 19, 2024, and presented an invoice from a construction company in support of the claim . The invoice showed the intended repair as ‘Apply tar to all areas around the chimney and vent where the leaks have been identified. Install waterproof shingles around the chimney and vent to prevent future leaks’.

About mid October 2024, the Tenant contacted AH because of a leak in her da ughter’s bedroom. The Landlord provided an invoice dated October 14, 2024, stating that the construction company addressed fix the roof on that date . The invoice showed that the contractor planned to ‘Remove all debris and damaged foam. Clean and address any water accumulation underneath the roof. Apply a barrier mat made of rubber to enhance protection.’

The Landlord also provided an invoice dated October 21, 2024, showing ‘Scope: Remove and replace drywall and insulation on the ceilings of the bedroom and stairwell. Finishing: Plaster walls and apply stipple finish.’
AH stated that when the leak stopped in one area, it began in another, but the roof was eventually replaced on or about February 14, 2025. Analysis

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.
The Tenant has not demonstrated that the Landlord completely neglected their responsibility by failing to maintain the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd ., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the leak first came to the attention of the Tenant on August 10, 2024, and she immediately notified the Landlord. By August 19, 2024, the Landlord had hired a contractor who repaired the roof. The Landlord acted reasonably in this circumstance.

Following another complaint on September 18, 2024, and September 21, 2024, the Landlord promised they would send a contractor to assess the damage and conduct all necessary / LTB-T-084866-24 repairs. However, the Landlord did not take any action until the Tenant made another complaint about mid October 2024. Given the severity of the situation, I find it unreasonable for the Landlord to wait 27 days from September 18, 2024, to October 14, 2024, before making further repairs. The Landlord will be ordered to pay to the Tenant, rent abatement of 20% or $11.08 daily for that period in the amount of $299.16 ($11.08 x 27days)

By October 14, 2024 , the Landlord had the roof repaired again and on October 21, 2024, repairs were conducted within the rental unit. But for the Tenant’s requests for temporary accommodation on December 19, 2024, no further complaints were disclosed in evidence. While the Tenant stated that the roof was replaced in December 2024, the Landlord claimed it was done in February 2025. The parties agreed that repairs were again commenced on or about February 11, 2025, and concluded by February 28, 2025. Based on the evidence, the Landlord did not neglect their maintenance obligations in this circumstance.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $347.16. this represents: • $299.16 rent abatement from September 18, 2024, to October 14, 2024, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
In the alternative, if the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 29, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $347.16 from the monthly rent in April 2026,
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Tenant’s application LTB-T-088044-24 is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________
