issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that 1001194515 Ontario Inc (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant did not prove all of the requirements of 57(1)(a) of the Act. Specifically, the Tenant failed to establish that he vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act.

I make the finding that the Tenant did not vacate as a result of the service of the N12 notice of termination based on the following: a) The Tenant began to search for a new rental unit prior to the service of the N12 by the current Landlord. The Tenant testified he began searching for a new unit because he suspected the new Landlord would serve a N12 notice of termination. These suspicions were the impetus for his search; b) The Tenant signed a new lease on June 20, 2025, well before the service of the N12 notice on July 10, 2025 by the new Landlord; c) I considered the possibility that, despite having secured a new lease, the Tenant only intended to move out if served with an N12 notice. However, at the hearing the Tenant testified that he knew the new Landlord did not want them at the rental unit and that he did not want to live in the unit as a result; and d) Finally, the Tenant testified that the N12 was served on July 10, 2025. Nonetheless, the Tenant moved out on July 14, 2025 – a mere 4 days after the service of the notice. That is, the Tenant did not delay, nor did the Tenant choose to contest the notice in any way.

Although the Tenant only vacated after the service of the N12 notice of termination, in combination the factors set out above militate in favor of finding that the Tenant had no intention of residing in the unit, even if no N12 was not served.

I find that the evidence establishes that the Tenant’s decision to leave the rental unit was made prior to receiving the N12 notice of termination. In the Tenant’s own testimony, he claimed this was due to speculation that the Landlord wanted him out.
As this is a required element under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant’s legal representative submitted that the matter had previously been adjourned and that Member [name] noted on the adjournment sheet that the sole issue to be determined was whether the Tenant had been coerced into vacating the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit in April 2019 and vacated the unit on or about May 30, 2023.

The Tenant testified that, upon moving into the rental unit, he intended to reside there permanently or, at minimum, for a significant period of time, as he considered moving to be burdensome due to the associated costs and effort. The Tenant stated that, at the commencement of the tenancy, the Landlord advised him that the property was intended solely as a rental property and that the Tenant could reside there long term.

The Tenant testified that his daughter’s school was located close to the rental unit and within a predominantly Chinese community. The Tenant further testified that his wife worked with Chinese clients in the neighbourhood and that the rental unit was also located close to his son.

The Tenant testified that the first time the Landlord informed him of the intention to sell the property was at the beginning of 2023. According to the Tenant, the Landlord advised that the property had to be sold in order to close a transaction relating to another property.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord told him he was required to vacate the rental unit so that the Landlord could decorate the property for sale.
The Tenant testified that he never received a notice of termination in relation to the sale of the property.
The Tenant testified that he received approximately 20 to 30 telephone calls from the Landlord’s agent concerning the Tenant vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant further testified that his wife agreed to vacate the rental unit and urgently searched for alternate accommodations in an effort to assist the Landlord, who had stated that funds from the sale were required to complete the purchase of another property. The Tenant stated that his wife is trusting in nature and wanted to help the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that it took approximately two to three months to secure alternate accommodations. He stated that his wife spent approximately four to five hours per day searching for accommodation options, as she wished to ensure that any new accommodation was suitable with respect to traffic, schools, and the surrounding community. The Tenant further testified that the search for alternate accommodations interfered with his wife’s employment, as she was unable to devote sufficient time to her clients.

The Tenant testified that, while completing the final cleaning of the rental unit on or around June 1, 2023, a woman attended to look at the property and advised him that the Landlord had the property listed for rent, at a monthly rent of $3,000.00.

The Tenant testified that he consistently paid his rent on time. He further testified that, although the Landlord primarily communicated with his wife, the Landlord never requested an increase in rent from him and that he would have paid more had such a request been made.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or coerced the Tenant into vacating the unit.

While the Tenant testified that the Landlord advised him in early 2023 that the property was going to be sold and that the Landlord required vacant possession in order to prepare the property for sale, there is insufficient evidence before the Board to establish that the Landlord compelled or forced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant acknowledged that neither he nor his wife were served with a notice of termination and that the Landlord never demanded an increase in rent or otherwise threatened the Tenant with eviction proceedings.

The evidence demonstrates that discussions took place between the parties concerning the Landlord’s intention to sell the property and the possibility of the Tenant vacating the unit. However, a landlord communicating a desire to sell a property or requesting that a tenant consider vacating the unit does not, in and of itself, constitute substantial interference or coercion within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord’s agent contacted the Tenant on multiple occasions regarding vacating the rental unit. However, there was insufficient evidence to establish the nature or tone of the communications and whether they were threatening, harassing, or otherwise improper. The Tenant did not testify that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent threatened eviction, withheld services, entered the unit unlawfully, or engaged in conduct that would reasonably leave the Tenant with no choice but to vacate the rental unit.

I also accept that the Tenant and his wife experienced stress and inconvenience associated with searching for alternate accommodations and ultimately relocating from the rental unit. However, the evidence establishes that the Tenant’s wife voluntarily undertook the search for another unit because she wished to assist the Landlord, who had indicated that the sale of the property was financially necessary. The Tenant’s own evidence was that his wife “wanted to help the Landlord.” This evidence supports a finding that the decision to vacate was voluntary, albeit difficult, rather than the result of coercion or substantial interference by the Landlord.

The Tenant further testified that, while cleaning the rental unit prior to vacating, a woman attended at the property and advised him that the unit had been listed for rent, at a monthly rent of $3,000.00. While this evidence may have caused the Tenant concern regarding the Landlord’s intentions, in my view, it is insufficient, on its own, to establish that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or induced the Tenant to vacate through coercion.

Accordingly, on the totality of the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or coerced the Tenant into vacating the unit. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] El- [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords: • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw their T1 application. In accordance with section 200(4) of the Act, I consented to the withdrawal of the application. [name] Moving in early

The Tenant testified that although the lease agreement states that the tenancy would commence on October 1, 2024, the Landlords agreed to allow the Tenant to move in early, on September 15, 2024. He testified that the unit was not ready on September 15 as it was not cleaned out and there was no hot water, so he had to delay his move in until September 23 or 24.

The only remedy sought by the Tenant in relation to this issue is a rent abatement. The Tenant testified that the Landlords did not charge him rent for this period nor did he pay rent for this period. Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving everything being paid for then abatement should flow in an amount proportionate to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. In this case, nothing was being paid. Therefore, even if I find in favour of the Tenant on this issue, the Tenant would not be entitled to an abatement in my view because he did not pay for the use of the unit for this period.
This portion of the Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed as no remedy can be granted for this issue. Smoking in the rental unit

The Tenant rental unit is a bedroom located in a rooming house, where the common areas are shared with other tenants. The Tenant testified that the entire house was supposed to be non-smoking and that term was in his tenancy agreement. The lease states that smoking inside is not permitted and smoking is only allowed 30 feet from the house.

The Tenant testified that he continually smelt a strong cannabis smell in his room and in the house. Hew testified that he covered the vents and under the door to try to prevent the smell from coming into his room, but the smell was so bad that he had to leave the house.

The Tenant reported the issue to the Landlords, and the Landlords informed him they would terminate that person’s lease. He informed the Landlords that he did not have evidence of anyone smoking inside but that someone was smoking right outside the door. He suggested they do inspections of all the tenants’ rooms to investigate the issue, but the Landlords never did. He testified that the issue with the smell was never resolved.

The Landlords do not dispute that the Tenant complained to them about the smell of cannabis or cigarettes in the house. The Landlord, [name] (‘TS’), testified that upon receiving the complaint, he emailed new terms and conditions to all the tenants in the house reminding them of the no smoking rules and asking them to ensure that if they are smoking, to smoke further away from the house.

TS testified that on numerous occasions, when the Tenant would message him with complaints about the smell, he would come to the rental unit to investigate but when he arrived approximately 40 minutes later, he could not smell any smoke or cannabis. He testified that they also provided the Tenant with an air purifier for his room, but the Tenant elected to have the air purifier in the hallway outside of his room.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that anyone was smoking inside the house or any such lingering smell from another person breaching the Landlords’ no smoking policy. The onus is on the Tenant to prove on a balance of probabilities that there is a strong smoke odour in the unit. The Tenant did not actually ever witness anyone smoking inside the house and the Tenant did not otherwise produce any evidence that anyone other than himself ever smelled this odour. The evidence is insufficient to establish that there was any smoke odour in the house from someone smoking inside or close to the house.

Even if someone was smoking inside, the Landlords’ response to the Tenant’s complaints were timely and reasonable. The Landlord sent reminders to other residents and provided the Tenant with an air purifier. The issue was investigated on more than one occasion by the TS, who was unable to verify that there was even any smell in the house at all. It would be unreasonable to expect the Landlord to inspect every single person’s unit in these circumstances.
For the reasons explained above, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Harassment from [name]

The Tenant testified that another resident, [name], learned about his complaints to the Landlords about smoking and started a pattern of harassing behaviour. He testified that [name] would follow him, watch his movements, and engage in prolonged and unwanted conversations with him. He testified that he told [name] he just wanted him to say hello and did not want to have a conversation with him, but [name] continued. The Tenant submitted recordings as examples of some of his conversations with [name].

The Landlords do not dispute that the Tenant complained to them about [name]’s behaviour. TS testified that on three or four occasions, he stopped by the property and spoke to [name] and let him know that the Tenant did not want to engage in conversation with him. He testified that [name] is an older gentleman who is very chatty, and he sometimes does not pick up on hints that an individual may not want to talk to him.
The Tenant’s claim in the application is based on section 23 of the Act, which states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

This claim does not amount to harassment as contemplated by section 23 of the Act because it was not the action of the Landlords but of another tenant. Nevertheless, even if the Tenant had made these claims under section 22 of the Act alleging substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment, the result would be the same. The Tenant’s own recordings demonstrate very friendly and cordial conversations with [name] in which the Tenant continues to engage and carry on the conversation. Additionally, the Landlord’s response to the complaints were reasonable.

For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. [name]18. The Tenant testified that he notified the Landlords on October 31, 2024 that he would not be able to pay his rent for November on Nov 1, 2024. The Landlords then served the Tenant with an N4 Notice of Termination using multiple different methods of service. Then, on November 7, 2024, the Landlords attended the property without notice, waited for him to leave his room and gave him and N4 Notice of Termination. He testified that they tried to coerce him into signing documents and because he felt unsafe, he contacted the police and filed a report. 19. The Tenant testified that later, on December 15 or 16, he was on his way to the laundry room when the Landlords approached him and the Landlord, [name] (‘ME’), looked at him with a horrible face before slamming his foot on the ground. He testified that ME then asked him if his water was running in his room and he told him that it wasn’t. The Tenant testified that ME was insinuating that there was running water coming from his room. 20. The Tenant testified that during the course of the tenancy, the Landlords also inspected his room approximately 15 to 20 times and had an issue with him keeping a mini fridge in his room. The Tenant did not provide any dates, times or specifics about the alleged inspections he says occurred. 21. The Landlords dispute that they have harassed or coerced the Tenant. TS testified that they visited his unit on November 7, 2024 to follow-up on the notice because they had not received any response from the Tenant and they did not want the Tenant to deny receiving the notice. He testified that when the Tenant asked them to leave him alone, they left. 22. ME denies stomping his foot or that he blocked the Tenant in with his vehicle. He testified that if they have to attend the property, they usually park, check what it is that they need to check and leave. On that particular day in December 2024, he was checking the basement because they had found a water leak coming from the wall and he was trying to find the source of the leak. 23. There is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, however prior Board decisions have defined harassment as follows: “harassment is usually considered to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome”. 24. I am not satisfied that the Landlords’ behaviour in this case amounts to harassment and a breach of section 23 of the Act. The Landlords are not required to provide the Tenant with notice whenever they will be attending the property, nor do they need to give the Tenant notice if they are going to knock on his door. Additionally, the Tenant provided recordings of the interactions with the Landlords which he complains of, and the recordings demonstrate a very reasonable and cordial conversation from the part of the Landlords. 25. The Tenant does not dispute that he was in arrears and while the Tenant may be of the view that a termination notice or follow-up is not reasonable if the Tenant notifies the Landlords that a payment will be late or not paid, I do not agree. In my view, it is not unreasonable that the Landlords would follow-up on a termination notice after receiving no payment and no response from the Tenant. It is reasonable to expect that a landlord might follow-up with a tenant to confirm they received the notice and inquire as to the status of payment or what the tenant’s plan is to pay the outstanding amount. Additionally, while serving the termination notice in more than one way may be somewhat problematic, I am not satisfied that this act in and of itself amounts to harassment but rather, indicative of landlords being overly thorough in ensuring the Tenant received the notice. 26. The Tenant also raised issues with respect to the Landlord making reports to the Credit Bureau and statements uploaded to the Portal. All of these incidents occurred after the tenancy ended so they were not considered. 27. For the foregoing reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. T6 Application 28. The Tenant testified that when he first moved into the rental unit, the shower needed to be cleaned because there was mould. He testified that he had notified TS about the issue before he even moved in and TS assured him it would be cleaned before he moved in but when he moved in, the condition was the same. The Tenant provided a copy of the text messages exchanged on September 14, 2024 in support of this statement. 29. TS testified that as soon as they were advised of the issue, they went in and cleaned it. He testified that when they met with the Tenant on October 7th to discuss all the issues he had, he did not mention any issue with the shower, so they assumed their cleaning was sufficient. He testified that when the Tenant did bring it up again, they came back and did another clean of the mould, using a stronger cleaner and more effective tools. 30. This application is brought pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act which states that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with safety, housing and maintenance standards. 31. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 32. The mere fact that there was mould in the shower does not automatically give rise to a breach of section 20 of the Act. It depends on what steps the Landlords take once made aware of the issues. It cannot be said that the Landlords breached their obligations under the Act when they responded promptly to the Tenant’s complaints, and the issues were addressed without delay. 33. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant has failed to meet the burden of proof that the Landlords failed to respond to the issue of mould in a timely manner. I say this because the evidence is essentially equal and opposite: the Tenant says the Landlord did not clean it at all until October 30, 2024 and TS says he did. Without anything further to tip the scale in the Tenant’s direction, the case must fail in this regard. 34. Additionally, I am more inclined to accept TS’ testimony in this regard. I say this because throughout the hearing, TS’ testimony has always been consistent with what can be heard in the recordings relied on in this proceeding. In contrast, the Tenant’s testimony was often inconsistent with the recordings; for example: alleging harassing behaviour when the recording demonstrates a pleasant conversation that is not harassing in nature at all. 35. For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Tenant requested to withdraw their T2 application before the board and I consented to the request. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the start of the hearing the Landlord requested that the Board dismiss the Tenants application as it was lacking in sufficient details and particulars. The Landlord submitted that the allegations in the application were vague, general, lacked particulars.

When I examine the T6 application the Tenant alleged a maintenance problem relating to mold on some furniture since July 2024, when an upstairs tenant moved out. The notice also indicates that central air for the unit was turned off and there was no heat when the weather turned cold. It is unclear if the Tenant’s maintenance issue is the central air, the mold or both. Further, the application does not indicate what repairs if any were attempted by the Landlord or whether the problem was resolved.

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (‘Ball’). The facts in [name] were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established.

The types of particulars expected in notices and applications include dates, times, and a detailed description of the alleged conduct or behaviour. This allows the responding party to know the case they have to meet and to prepare their defence

The Board’s tenant application forms have been developed with written instructions to elicit the necessary details required. For example the T6 form states at page 3: “Explaining your Reason: What is the problem? If here is more than one problem, list each problem. Give the date each problem started. Hast the problem been repaired? If so, give the date it was repaired and explain who repaired it. Explain who or what may have caused the problem. How did you inform the landlord about the problem?
The Tenant described that her evidence and disclosure for the hearing contained all the necessary details so that the Landlord could understand and respond to the claim.

I do not agree that a responding party should have to look to the supporting disclosure filed with the application, to try to piece together the claims that are being made against them as the hearing progresses and as evidence is led. As the Tenant’s application does not meet the requirements regarding specific details the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: r another tenant; • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has wilfully or negligently caused damage to the premises The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') also applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') also applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenant's conduct or that of another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. This conduct substantially interfered with the Landlord's reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or another lawful right, privilege or interest. (L2 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit as well as interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit (T2 and T6 Application). The matter was originally heard on March 25, 2024 however no order was issued by the Member prior to them leaving the Board.
reasons: The issues in the applications overlap with one another, and the evidence provided at the hearing often related to both the Landlord’s application and the Tenant’s applications.

At the outset of the hearing the Landlord sought permission to amend their application. Given the history of the file, the content of the amendment, and the timing of the amendment, pursuant to Rule 15.3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure I denied the amendment request. L2 Application
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. N5 Notice of Termination

On November 17, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N5 notice of termination deemed served the same date. The notice of termination contains the following allegations: • On July 12, 2022 at 4:00pm the kitchen wall tiles were found damaged after the Landlord inspected the rental unit. As a result, the Landlord seeks $463.81 for repairs; • On August 7, 2023 at 3:00pm the Tenant set up a user access code on the [name] thermostat without the Landlord’s consent. After a new air conditioner was installed, the Tenant did not provide the access code therefore the Landlord had to replace the thermostat. As a result, the Landlord seeks $224.85 for replacement; • On June 6, 2023 at 4:00pm, the Landlord found a mouse issue which was not reported by the Tenant. As a result, the Landlord paid $395.50 for “mouse control expense”; • Between June 29, 2023 and August 10, 2023, the Tenant obstructed the Landlord’s attempts to repair the rental unit as well as denied reasonable access to the rental unit: o The Landlord arranged a plumber to attend the rental unit to replace a leaking water valve. The Tenant sought a hotel for the day. o The Tenant refused to cooperate with the Landlord in installing a new air conditioner on July 26, 2023. o The Tenant did not allow entry for the Landlord’s energy audit scheduled for August 10, 2023. o The Tenant did not allow entry for the Landlord’s inspection on September 24, 2023. o The Tenant did not allow entry for the Landlord’s inspection on October 4, 2023. o The Tenant restricted the amount of people the Landlord attempted to bring into the rental unit on October 6, 2023. o The Tenant did not allow entry for the Landlord’s inspection on November 11, 2023. • On September 24, 2023, at 10:00am, the Landlord discovered the Tenant has not maintained the outside ground as there are weeds growing in the backyard. 2. The Tenant raised a preliminary issue regarding confusion arising from the existence of three separate N5 Notices served by the Landlord. The Landlord confirmed in their submissions that only the allegations relating to the kitchen tiles, mice, and the thermostat were being pursued, as the remaining allegations had been voided by the Tenant. Given that each of these three issues was set out in all of the N5 Notices, I found that the Tenant was reasonably aware of the case to be met. Accordingly, the presence of multiple N5 Notices did not result in any confusion or prejudice to the Tenant. 3. Despite the Landlords’ written submissions, which included issues relating to denial of entry and backyard maintenance (which were not being pursued as they were voided), this narrowing of the issues was acknowledged by both parties, and the evidence and submissions that followed were confined to these three items accordingly. Evidence of the Landlord 4. On the kitchen tile issue, the Landlord testified that during a July 12, 2023 inspection, damage was observed (warping and peeling of the tiles), and the Tenant verbally admitted that their cooking at high temperatures contributed to the damage. The Landlord’s evidence is that the tiles and adjacent hood damage indicate improper use by the Tenant. The Landlord’s cost to replace the tiles is $463.81.

For the thermostat, the Landlord stated that the device was functioning when installed prior to the tenancy commencing. Shortly thereafter, the thermostat became inaccessible to them because the Tenant set an access code and did not inform them of the new code. During installation of a new air conditioner on August 7, 2023, since the Landlord did not have access to the code, they had to replace the unit. No formal receipt for the cost of replacement was produced however a screenshot from [name] was produced showing the replacement cost in which the Landlord swore under oath they paid.

Regarding the mice infestation, the Landlord testified that the Tenant knew about the issue for months before reporting it to them on May 29, 2023. The Landlord submits that the Tenant’s delayed reporting increased the severity of the issue and ultimately led to increased costs, including a $395.50 pest control invoice which was entered into evidence. The Landlord did not allege the Tenant caused the infestation, only that the delay in reporting it aggravated the situation. Evidence of the Tenant

On the kitchen tiles, the Tenant testified that the plastic backsplash existed at move-in and was not installed by them. They denied any negligence, indicating that the damage occurred during normal cooking and that the material itself was inappropriate for use behind a stove. To prove their position, the Tenant pointed out the pictures of the tiles that are in the N5 Notice are being advertised online as “ceiling tiles”. The Tenant emphasized in their testimony that in any event the replacement of the entire area is unnecessary.

Regarding the thermostat, the Tenant testified that they were never asked for the access code before replacement and did not understand how to reset it in the first place. They maintain they never received the old unit, had limited control over the replacement thermostat, and are now improperly being asked to pay the replacement cost.
On the mice issue, the Tenant asserts they reported the problem promptly upon discovery on May 29, 2023. Of note, the affected area was infrequently accessed storage. Analysis

With respect to the kitchen tiles, I am not satisfied that the tiles were fit for their intended purpose. The Landlord’s own evidence (found in the N5 Notice) indicates that the tiles were designed for ceiling use, not for installation as a backsplash behind a heat source (stove/oven). While there is no dispute that the tiles are damaged, the issue is whether the Tenant bears responsibility for that damage.

Section 34 of the Act states: 34 The tenant is responsible for the repair of undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex caused by the wilful or negligent conduct of the tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant caused undue damage to the tiles through wilful or negligent conduct. The Landlord’s explanation that the damage resulted from high cooking temperatures is speculative and unsupported by persuasive evidence. I find it more likely than not that the tiles were inherently unsuitable for use as a backsplash and therefore not appropriate for installation in proximity to a heat source. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is not responsible for the cost of replacing the kitchen tiles.

With respect to the thermostat, the evidence establishes that the Tenant changed the access code on the Ecobee thermostat and failed to provide that code to the Landlord upon request. This issue arose in the context of the Landlord replacing the air conditioning system, at which time access to the thermostat was necessary to verify proper operation. I find the Landlord’s evidence more credible that they asked the Tenant for the access code and the Tenant’s refused to provide it in a timely manner. I make this finding as the Landlord’s evidence was clear and straightforward that they would not have incurred an unnecessary cost to purchase a new thermostat had the Tenant’s simply provided the code when first asked.

Section 64 of the Act states: 64 (1) A landlord may give a tenant notice of termination of the tenancy if the conduct of the tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant is such that it substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex for all usual purposes by the landlord or another tenant or substantially interferes with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the landlord or another tenant.

I find that the Tenant’s failure to provide the access code interfered with the Landlord’s lawful rights and interests. In the circumstances, it was reasonable for the Landlord to replace the thermostat when access could not be obtained. Although no formal receipt was produced, I accept that the replacement cost of $224.85, as reflected in the Landlord’s evidence from a Best Buy screenshot, is reasonable.

The Landlord seeks termination of the tenancy on the basis of this breach. I am not satisfied that eviction is warranted. Eviction is a remedy of last resort, and in light of the relatively modest cost of replacement, such an outcome would be disproportionate. Taking into account section 83 of the Act, I find that the Tenant shall reimburse the Landlord in the amount of $224.85 for the replacement of the thermostat and no eviction is ordered.

With respect to the mice infestation, I do not find the Tenant responsible for the cost of pest control. The Landlord acknowledged in their evidence that the presence of mice was not caused by the Tenant. Rather, the Landlord’s position was that the Tenant failed to report the issue in a timely manner.

Section 20 of the Act states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The obligation to maintain the rental unit, including addressing pest infestations, rests with the Landlord. The Landlord admitted that no pest control program was in place and provided no clear explanation as to why the issue was not identified during their prior attendances at the unit. In these circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Tenant breached the Act by failing to report the issue earlier, nor am I satisfied that the Tenant should bear responsibility for the associated pest control costs. There was no evidence, other than the Landlord’s speculation, that the Tenant knew about the mice earlier than when it was actually reported. T2 and T6 Applications

The Tenant alleges a pattern of ongoing misconduct by the Landlord throughout the tenancy, including harassment, illegal entry, failure to maintain the rental unit, and improper demands (such as providing historical proof of insurance). They claim that the Landlord repeatedly used inspections, notices, and repair issues to pressure them, while also failing to meet maintenance obligations and interfering with their reasonable enjoyment of the unit.

The allegations can be summarized as follows: • Harassment and coercion: The Landlord allegedly conducted excessive inspections, questioned and recorded the Tenants without consent, and used repeated N5 notices and demands in a threatening or coercive manner • Illegal entry: The Landlord is alleged to have entered or attempted to enter the unit without proper notice multiple times throughout the tenancy [name] denial / allegations of access: The Tenant claims the Landlord falsely alleged denial of entry despite numerous attendances for inspections and repairs throughout the tenancy • Thermostat issues: The Landlord allegedly refused to provide access to the thermostat, demanded payment for replacement, and required a deposit for access to the passcode [name] tiles: The Landlord installed improper plastic tiles behind the stove and sought compensation from the Tenants for resulting damage • Mice: The Landlord blamed the Tenants for failing to report mice and claimed resulting damages, which the Tenants dispute • Maintenance failures: The Landlord is alleged to have failed to maintain the rental unit, including the air conditioner, stair railing, and water softener, causing inconvenience and expense to the Tenant • Repair and cost disputes: The Tenant claims they were improperly required to pay for or complete repairs (such as baseboards, weed control, snow/ice removal) that were not their responsibility • Insurance and documentation demands: The Landlord demanded excessive historical proof of insurance and proof of payments • Rent receipts: the Landlord failed to provide rent receipts when requested • Service and communication issues: The Landlord allegedly failed to provide a proper address for service and gave misleading information regarding notice requirements • Utility interruption: The Tenant alleges they were left without water during repairs without adequate accommodation

During the hearing, multiple issues were identified as statute barred pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act, and subsequently withdrawn by the Tenant. These include allegations concerning the water softener, salt, and harassment allegations dating back to 2019 and 2020. Evidence of the Tenant

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s use of three overlapping N5 notices (September 14, October 7, and November 17, 2023) with similar allegations created confusion and reflected overall bad faith. While the Tenant accepts that the core issues in question (namely the tiles, thermostat, and mice) appeared across the notices, they maintain that the Landlord relied excessively on repeated notices to pressure them toward eviction. The Tenant’s position is that the multiple notices is harassing in nature.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of harassment and coercion during attendances at the unit, particularly surrounding inspections and alleged damage. They state that on October 7, 2023, the Landlord attended the unit and aggressively questioned them about the kitchen tiles, which they describe as an unwanted interrogation. The Tenant asserts that such conduct occurred repeatedly, causing them significant stress and anxiety whenever the Landlord attended the rental unit.

The Tenant further alleges other forms of harassment and tenant rights violations in the T2 application, claiming the Landlord conducted excessive attendances framed as inspections, took photos and videos throughout said inspections, and interrogated the Tenant improperly. The Tenant testified that they felt harassed as a result of the Landlord’s claims that there was a denial of entry. The Tenant feels that they have consistently allowed the Landlord entry, giving examples of: • June 1, 2023 where the Landlord entered the rental unit for 2 hours; • June 6, 2023 where the Landlord entered the rental unit for 3 hours; • July 7, 2023 where the Landlord entered the rental unit for 3 hours; • July 21, 2023 where the Landlord entered the rental unit for 3 hours; • August 7, 2023 where the Landlord entered the rental unit for 3 hours; and • October 7, 2023 where the Landlord entered the rental unit for 1 hour.

In addition, the Tenant alleged instances of illegal entry and inappropriate conduct. They testified that on October 5, 2023, the Landlord attempted to enter the unit without notice using their own keys, but was prevented from doing so due to a door chain. They also testified that the Landlord recorded and questioned them in an aggressive manner during this interaction. A further allegation of unlawful entry is made from September 1, 2023, although the Tenant had limited recollection of the circumstances.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord demanded extensive insurance records dating back to 2019 and subsequently relied on these demands in issuing an N5 notice, which they describe as excessive and intended to force termination of the tenancy.

Further allegations relate to repair disputes and financial demands. The Tenant testified that the Landlord accused them of damaging baseboards and required them to replace or pay for them, despite a lack of evidence as to what the original condition was prior to moving in. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord refused to provide access to the thermostat unless a payment was made and subsequently demanded reimbursement for its replacement. The Tenant deemed this to be harassing behaviour.

Additional concerns include the Landlord demanding payment for alleged kitchen tile damage and requiring the Tenants to manage weeds using purchased weed killer, which they dispute as their responsibility entirely.

The Tenant further alleged deficiencies in maintenance, testifying that the Landlord failed to properly accommodate them during air conditioning repairs and that they were without water for several hours during plumbing repairs.

Finally, the Tenant raised broader issues concerning the tenancy, including demands for post-dated cheques without providing rent receipts, failure to provide a proper address for service, and longstanding maintenance concerns such as a malfunctioning air conditioner (fixed in August 2023) and an unrepaired basement stair railing. They characterize these issues as part of an ongoing pattern of conduct by the Landlord that interfered with their tenancy and caused financial loss and stress.
As a result of the alleged breaches, the Tenant seeks various monetary remedies. Evidence of the Landlord

The Landlord maintains that all attendances at the rental unit were for legitimate repair or maintenance purposes and were not harassing in nature. They deny conducting excessive inspections, testifying that they only attended the rental unit for specific reasons. Notices of entry were provided in advance, outlining both the time and purpose of each visit. For example, on June 1, 2023, the Landlord attended to investigate issues in the rental unit, including the mice and dishwasher. Similarly, on July 7, 2023, the Landlord arranged for a water valve repair which required coordination with the municipality to shut off the water.

The Landlord emphasized in their testimony that the Tenant ultimately acknowledged that these attendances were for legitimate purposes, though they take issue with the Landlord’s additional actions during those visits. The Landlord denied any allegations of illegal entry. With respect to October 5, 2023, the Landlord testified that entry was not obtained because the Tenants had secured the door with a chain, and this refusal led to the service of an N5 notice. The Landlord also denied any entry on September 1, 2023, noting that no evidence was provided to support that allegation.

Regarding insurance, the Landlord explained that they had legitimate safety concerns and requested proof of tenant liability insurance. Beginning on August 13, 2023, and through multiple follow-ups, they requested documentation covering prior years. The Landlord testified that the Tenant failed to provide proof of prior years, receiving only partial records by mid-September 2023, which prompted further requests and contributed to the issuance of an N5 Notice. The Landlord denied ever requesting insurance payment records, asserting that this was a misinterpretation by the Tenant.

On the issue of alleged damage, the Landlord submitted photographs into evidence showing that certain damage in the rental unit, such as the baseboards, were beyond normal wear and tear. They note that the Tenant acknowledged responsibility in correspondence and agreed to repair the damage. The Landlord feels that they acted reasonably in pursuing compensation.

The Landlord also testified that they acted reasonably with respect to repairs and scheduling. They communicated with the Tenant regarding air conditioning repairs and provided options including the possibility of deferring work to a more appropriate date for the Tenant. Similarly, the water valve repair date was selected based on the Tenant’s availability. The Landlord indicated that they accommodated the Tenant whenever possible and that all repair-related attendances at the rental unit were necessary.

With respect to the other administrative matters in the Tenant’s applications, the Landlord testified that rent receipts were only requested once in June 2020, at which time they were provided. The Landlord further testified that their mailing address was provided in October 2023.

In cross-examination, the Landlord acknowledged certain limitations in their evidence, including the absence of a move-in condition report and any photographs of the rental unit at the start of the tenancy. They Landlord also confirmed that they did not contact the thermostat manufacturer before replacing the device, citing the urgency of the situation, and that no formal pest control program was in place. Despite these points, the Landlord maintained that their actions throughout the tenancy were reasonable, necessary, and consistent with their obligations as landlords. Analysis
Section 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord’s repeated use of N5 notices, inspections, recording, and various demands for documentation formed an overall pattern intended to pressure and intimidate the Tenant. It is uncontested that the Landlord served three N5 notices in relatively short succession during September, October, and November 2023, all of which addressed overlapping issues occurring during the tenancy.

The mere service of notices under the Act does not necessarily constitute harassment when the notices relate to legitimate tenancy concerns. The Landlord is entitled to pursue remedies available under the Act where they reasonably believe breaches have occurred. The Board has consistently held that the use of statutory notices for legitimate purposes does not amount to harassment absent evidence of bad faith, intimidation, or conduct beyond what is reasonably necessary to enforce the tenancy agreement.

The Tenant acknowledged that many of the attendances at the rental unit related to legitimate maintenance or repair concerns, including plumbing work, water valve repairs, pest concerns, and appliance issues. The Landlord provided evidence that notices of entry were served identifying the purpose and timing of the attendances, while also taking the Tenant’s availability into consideration. From the testimony of the Tenant, it appears the main issue relates to the Landlord’s behaviour during those attendances, including questioning regarding damage and the taking of photographs and/or recordings.

While the Tenant described these interactions as stressful and intimidating, the evidence does not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s conduct rose to the level of harassment or coercion prohibited by section 23 of the Act. Landlords are generally permitted to document the condition of a rental unit, investigate alleged damage, and communicate concerns regarding tenancy issues. Although the Tenant may have found the interactions unpleasant, I find that the evidence falls short of establishing a deliberate pattern of intimidation or harassment sufficient to constitute a breach of the Act.

With respect to the allegations concerning denial of entry, the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord attended the rental unit on numerous occasions between June and October 2023, often for multiple hours at a time. The Tenant relies on these attendances to argue that allegations of denied access on the N5 Notices were exaggerated or unfounded. However, the existence of prior access does not preclude the possibility that access may have been denied on other occasions. In any event, the issue before the Board is not whether the Landlord accurately characterized every interaction, but whether the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment under section 22 of the Act or constituted harassment under section 23 of the Act.

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord demanded proof of insurance and proof of payments which resulted in them feeling harassed. While the requests for documentation may have been frustrating to the Tenant, the Landlord was entitled to request proof of tenant insurance as it was required in the tenancy agreement. I do not find the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment under section 22 of the Act or constituted harassment under section 23 of the Act.

The Tenant further alleged that the Landlord improperly demanded payment for repairs and maintenance items including the thermostat, baseboards, weeds, snow and ice removal, and kitchen tiles. There is no question that landlords bear responsibility for ordinary maintenance and repair obligations, while tenants may be liable for undue damage caused wilfully or negligently.

Regarding rent receipts, the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence establishing repeated unfulfilled requests for receipts. Additionally, although the Tenant alleged the Landlord failed to provide a proper address for service, the evidence indicates that a mailing address was ultimately provided in October 2023. While this may have caused inconvenience, the evidence does not establish a substantial breach warranting compensation.

The threshold for substantial interference is higher than mere inconvenience. The Tenant testified that the repeated inspections, notices, demands for payment, and disputes caused stress and anxiety. However, the evidence suggests these were ordinary disputes arising between landlords and tenants. The evidence does not establish that the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises within the meaning of section 22 of the Act.

The Tenant also alleges unlawful entry contrary to sections 25 and 27 of the Act. The Tenant alleged that on October 5, 2023, the Landlord attempted entry without notice using their own keys but was prevented from entering because the Tenant had a chain lock on the door. The Landlord acknowledges attending on that date but denied gaining entry to the rental unit. Based on the evidence before the Board, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the Landlord entered the unit unlawfully on October 5, 2023. At most, the evidence establishes an attempted entry in disputed circumstances. The additional allegation concerning September 1, 2023 was unsupported by particulars or documentary evidence. Accordingly, the Tenant has not established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord unlawfully entered the rental unit contrary to section 25 of the Act.

When considering whether a landlord has breached section 20 of the Act, I must consider the Ontario Court of Appeal’s guidance in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) which directed the Board to look at the entirety of the factual situation before determining whether or not the Landlord committed a breach of the Act.

The Tenant’s allegations relate to the air conditioner, basement stair railing, water interruptions during repairs, pest control, and thermostat access. The evidence establishes that the air conditioner was ultimately repaired in August 2023. While the Tenant experienced inconvenience during the delay, the Landlord provided evidence that repair scheduling was discussed with the Tenant and accommodations were considered. Similarly, the water interruption associated with the water valve repair appears to have been temporary and connected to necessary repair work coordinated with the municipality. Temporary interruption of services for legitimate repair purposes does not constitute a breach of the Act, particularly where the repairs themselves are necessary. Based on the evidence of the Tenant, and taking into account [name], I cannot conclude that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act.

With respect to pest control, the Landlord acknowledged that no formal pest control program was implemented. However, the evidence before the Board is insufficient to establish that the Landlord failed to respond reasonably to the mice issue or that the condition became so serious as to amount to a breach of section 20 Act. While the Landlord may have been able to find the mice issue sooner during one of their inspections, I do not find their conduct once they become aware of the issue to be unreasonable.

The allegation concerning the basement stair railing raises a more significant maintenance concern. If a stair railing remained unrepaired for an extended period, this may constitute a failure to maintain the premises in a good state of repair. However, the evidence before the Board lacks sufficient detail regarding the severity of the missing railing, the duration of the issue, and whether the railing affects habitability of the rental unit or safety. Accordingly, the evidence is insufficient to support a monetary remedy. Of note, the T6 Application indicates the railing has been repaired as of October 27, 2023.

The Tenant bears the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached the Act as alleged in the applications. While certain aspects of the Landlord’s conduct may reasonably have caused frustration or stress to the Tenant, the evidence has not established substantial interference, harassment, unlawful entry, or serious maintenance breaches sufficient to justify the monetary remedies sought.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $410.85, which includes $224.85 for the new thermostat and $186.00 application filing fee.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before June 8, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The T2 and T6 applications are dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) an agent of the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: In her original October 9, 2025 filing, the Tenant named Del Condo Rentals, a property management company, as a party to this application. At the April 24, 2026 hearing, Del Condo Rentals’ legal representative and the Tenant’s legal representative agreed that the property management company is not a proper party to the application, and they jointly asked that Del Condo Rentals be removed as a party, per the Tenant’s March 24, 2026 request to amend the application.

The Landlord’s Agent’s legal representative and Tenant’s legal representative agreed that Del Condo Rentals did not produce or give the Tenant a Form N12 notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). At the hearing, I noted that, unlike section 31 of the Act, section 57 of the Act does not permit the Board to order a remedy against an agent of the landlord.
In the circumstances, I granted the Tenant’s March 24, 2026 request to amend the application and removed Del Condo Rentals as a party. The Landlord Gave the Notice of Termination in Bad Faith.

The Tenant introduced uncontested evidence that the Landlord gave her a Form N12 notice of termination on or about November 19, 2024. The notice states that the Landlord requires the rental unit for her parent’s residential use, pursuant to subsection 48(1)(c) of the Act.

The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit on January 28, 2025, three days before the January 31, 2025 date of termination set out in the Form N12. The Tenant confirmed that she believed the contents of the notice of termination and immediately began searching for new accommodation after receiving the notice.

The Tenant introduced reliable evidence to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent on June 20, 2025, less than one year after the Tenant vacated in accordance with the Form N12. The Tenant submitted a rental advertisement that states the rental unit was listed for rent, starting June 20, 2025 and for $2,650.00 a month. The Tenant paid $1,589.53 a month when she vacated the property in January 2025.

Based on the evidence, I find that the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5)(a) of the Act applies. The Landlord did not attend to introduce evidence to rebut the presumption, and I accordingly find the Landlord gave the Form N12 in bad faith.

The Tenant sought to introduce evidence of maintenance and repair issues at the rental unit. I declined to consider and hear evidence and submissions for matters that could have been the subject-matter of a separate application under subsection 29(1)1 of the Act; and not properly raised in this application under subsection 57(1) of the Act. Also, evidence of maintenance issues was not relevant to determine this application, based on my finding that the Landlord did not rebut the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5)(a) of the Act. Remedies
Having proven that the Landlord gave the Form N12 in bad faith, the Tenant is entitled to remedies under subsection 57(3) of the Act.

The Tenant introduced evidence of her new tenancy agreement. The Tenant confirmed that she was required to pay $1,600.00 a month at her new accommodation. The Tenant described her new accommodation as smaller than the rental unit and with fewer facilities and services. Whereas the Tenant’s former residential complex had a full fitness centre, entertainment suite, rooftop patio with barbecue and a theater, the Tenant’s new accommodation is in a row building above a commercial business and lacks facilities, both shared and in suite, such as laundry facilities and air conditioning.

Significantly, the Tenant described a loss of her sense of security and safety in her new accommodation. The Tenant testified that people have mistakenly tried to access the street-level door leading to her upstairs unit when trying to enter the commercial business on the lower floor. The Tenant spoke of the benefits of having an intercom-style security system and concierge at the rental unit, which gave the Tenant a sense of safety following a serious motor vehicle accident. The Tenant testified that, as of the hearing date, injuries sustained in the accident continue to cause pain and limit her mobility and stamina.

The Tenant testified that she incurred additional expenses at her new residence, which expenses she did not have to pay when living at the rental unit. The Tenant introduced evidence of internet charges and increased utilities charges the Tenant paid in the one- year period after she vacated the rental unit.

Based on the Tenant’s evidence and submissions, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant the increased rent the Tenant paid in the one-year period after vacating the rental unit, general compensation for expenses, compensation for moving expenses, an abatement of rent and general damages for non-pecuniary losses. Rent Differential

The Tenant introduced evidence – including copies of tenancy agreements – that she paid an increase of $10.47 a month in rent after vacating the rental unit. The Tenant is accordingly entitled to $125.64 under subsection 57(3)1 of the Act. General Compensation

The Tenant also introduced evidence of an increase in utilities charges in July 2025 and August 2025, after moving to her new residence. The Tenant submitted invoices for electricity charges at the rental unit in July and August 2024 to support her claim. The Tenant attributed the increased charges in 2025 to her use of a portable air conditioning unit and fans at the new residence.

Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I find the Tenant is entitled to $61.26 under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act for the increase in utilities charges the Tenant paid in July and August 2025 after vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant confirmed she will keep the portable air conditioning unit and fans she purchased to keep her new accommodation cool in the summer. In the circumstances, I find it is not appropriate to order the Landlord to compensate the Tenant for her cost to purchase these items, as doing so will result in unjust enrichment.

The Tenant’s tenancy at the rental unit included internet services. The Tenant introduced evidence that she was required to pay $0.00 to Bell for internet service. The Tenant also submitted evidence that, after transferring her account from the rental unit to her new residence, she was required to pay $38.42 a month for internet service. Although the Tenant did not submit copies of each Bell invoice she testified that she was required to pay the fixed amount for a number after of months, after which period the amount rose.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony and documentary evidence, I find the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that she paid $38.42 for Bell internet service from February 2025 to November 2025, and $45.20 in December 2025. The Landlord shall therefore be ordered to pay the Tenant $429.40 under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act for the increase in internet charges the Tenant paid in the one-year period after vacating the rental unit. I note the Tenant did not introduce evidence of transfer charges or of any per diem charges in January 2025.

The Tenant introduced evidence that she was entitled to use a well-equipped fitness facility at the residential complex. The Tenant testified that she used the facility as part of her physiotherapy program following the motor vehicle accident. The introduced evidence that it will cost $34.95, plus HST, payable biweekly, to join a gym located near her current accommodation.

Although the Tenant conceded that she cannot afford to join the nearby gym, and has accordingly not actually incurred an expense related to the loss of the use of the fitness facility at the residential complex, paragraph 1.1 of subsection 57(3) of the Act contemplates that the Board may make an order under the paragraph “regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses”. Since the Landlord’s action directly led the Tenant to lose access to the fitness facility she previously enjoyed under the tenancy agreement, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the cost of the gym membership for one year, or the 26 biweekly period after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord shall accordingly pay the Tenant $1,026.83 as part of the order for general compensation under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act.

The Tenant requested an order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant’s cost to rent a storage unit. However, page 4 of the tenancy agreement for the Tenant’s former rental unit does not support her claim that the agreement includes the use of a storage unit. The Tenant also did not introduce reliable evidence of any increase in her cost to commute to work. Moreover, even if the Tenant did introduce such evidence, the Tenant’s decision to live farther from work – even if the decision was made under a sense of urgency – is too remote from the Landlord’s action to merit an order against the Landlord for general compensation. There shall accordingly be no order for these claims under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act.

The Tenant did not introduce at the hearing reliable evidence of the cost to compensate the Tenant for the loss of other facilities and services at the residential complex. Out-of-Pocket Moving Expenses

The Tenant introduced evidence of her $1,014.63 out-of-pocket moving costs. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount to the Tenant, pursuant to subsection 57(3)1.2 of the Act. Abatement of Rent

The Tenant described stress and hardship from having to find and accept new accommodation that the Tenant considers inferior to the rental unit. The Tenant’s current accommodation is smaller, lacks facilities, imposes physical barriers to entry because of the Tenant’s injuries, and diminishes the Tenant’s sense of security and safety.

Other than the stress of searching for new accommodation, however, there was no evidence the Tenant was unable to use and enjoy the rental unit for all usual purposes after receiving the Form N12 notice of termination and before vacating the property.

The Act is remedial legislation, and the Tenant conceded she did not advise the Landlord of the motor vehicle accident or of her injuries, limitations and restrictions during the tenancy. The Tenant’s health status is therefore not an aggravating factor when considering an appropriate abatement of rent under subsection 57(3)2 of the Act.

In the circumstances, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant a 10 percent abatement of rent for the approximately two-month notice period the Tenant had after receiving the Form N12, or $317.91, pursuant to subsection 57(3)2 of the Act. This amount reflects the stress the Tenant experienced in the last months of her tenancy because of the Landlord’s bad faith Form N12, while recognizing that the notice of termination did not seriously affect the Tenant’s ability to use the rental unit for all usual purposes. General Damages

The Tenant’s description of her loss of relative enjoyment and diminished sense of security and safety is relevant for the purpose of exercising my discretion to award general damages pursuant to subsection 57(3)4 of the Act.

I find the remedies ordered under paragraphs 1, 1.1, 1.2 and 2 of subsection 57(3) of the Act, above, do not adequately remediate the non-pecuniary losses and injuries the Tenant described arising from the Landlord’s bad faith notice of termination. It is therefore appropriate to order general damages, as the Divisional Court did in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.). In that decision, the Court found that the Board’s award of a $900.00 abatement of rent was inadequate. The Court ruled the Board may order general damages, and the Court ordered the Landlord to pay the tenant $4,000.00 – or approximately $6,000.00 today according to the Bank of Canada’s inflation [name] – because the landlord’s associates assaulted the tenant.

Although the Landlord in this case did not commit a criminal act, I am satisfied the [name] testimony describes a non-pecuniary loss that is compensable under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. Giving the Tenant a notice of termination in bad faith was a wilful breach of the Act. However, I find the Tenant’s evidence of her diminished sense of security and general loss of enjoyment less impactful than the assault that took place in [name]. In the circumstances, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $3,000.00 in general damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act.

The Tenant’s request in paragraph 41 of the amended application, for over $19,000.00 for general damages, is therefore not reasonable. I observe that, when requesting this amount, it appears the Tenant conflated remedies under paragraph 1.1 for general compensation and 4 paragraph for any other order, including general damages, under subsection 57(3) of the Act. The provision in paragraph 1.1 that allows a tenant to claim general compensation in an amount equal to 12 months’ rent does not also refer to a claim 1 https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/related/inflation-calculator/ for general damages under paragraph 4 of the subsection. The Tenant’s claim for the amount is therefore largely arbitrary. No Order for an Administrative Fine

The Tenant did not apply for an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine, and the Tenant did not ask to amend the application to include such an order or introduce submissions on the matter. Despite my finding of bad faith, in the circumstances it is not appropriate to order an administrative fine against the Landlord.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.

This amount represents: • $125.64 for increased rent the Tenant paid for the one-year period from January 2025 to December 2025; • $1,517.49 for general compensation; • $1,014.63 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses; • $317.91 for a rent abatement; • $3,000.00 for general damages; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
