issues: ex has wilfully or negligently caused damage to the premises. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenants to pay the Landlord's reasonable out- of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenants to pay the Landlord's reasonable out- of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenant s’ conduct or that of another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. This conduct substantially interfered with the Landlord's reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or another lawful right, privilege or interest. The above all relate to the Landlord’s L2 Application. The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants; and LTB-T-085629-23 • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This is the T2 Application. These applications were heard by videoconference on January 20, 2026. The Landlord, the Tenants, and the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: On June 20, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant s a first, voidable N5 notice of termination (‘first N5 Notice’) with the termination date of July 15, 2024. The first N5 Notice contains the following allegations: • December 30, 2022 – Since the beginning of the lease on Nov 1, 2022, we’ve made it clear that we would like to share the backyard with the tenants, but not with the dog. However, the dog is often in the backyard, so we can’t use it, and the landscape is being destroyed. • May 24, 2023 – On June 5, 2023, we were made aware that a family member would benefit from air conditioning (AC). But, the central AC makes the basement very cold. Despite efforts to accommodate the tenants, I’ve also been sick due to this situation. • August 12, 2023 – A hole was made to the side of the house in order to access the internet upstairs. This was done without my consent. Cars are often driven on the lawn. Garage door has been broken. October 2023 rent not paid. Loud noise if often heard late at night.

The Landlord also indicates in the first N5 Notice that the Tenants have wilfully or negligently caused damaged to the rental unit or resident ial complex . The Landlord is seeking $10,000.00 in compensation for the undue damage.

On June 29, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant a second N5 notice of termination (‘second N5 Notice’) with a termination date of July 15, 2024. This second N5 No tice sets out the identical allegations as listed in the first N5 Notice.

As explained at the hearing, I find the first N5 Notice is unduly vague as it lacks necessary references to sp ecific dates includ ing dates and times for [name] dog being in the backyard and damag ing the property, how the Tenants caused an issue with the air conditioning and which date is the Landlord relying on, and in regards to the hole in the side of the house and damage to the g arage door , there is no indication of who caused the alleged damage. Furthermore, unpaid rent requires a different notice of term ination, and there are no dates relating to the loud noises.

While the Landlord submitted the Tenants were aware of the prohibited conduct before the first N5 N otice was served and intended to lead direct evidence of [name]’ alleged misconduct at the hearing, the problem lies in the actual text of the originating document , the first N5 Notice, which is the document against which the respondent Tenants must craft their answer. I find on the balance of probabilities that the vague allegations contained in the first N5 Notice frustrated their ability to fully and properly respond to the application. If the Tenants are deprived of the ability to know the precise dates and substance of various LTB-T-085629-23 allegations prior to the hearing, the missing information necessarily compromises their defence.

According to the Ontario Divisional Court’s decisions in both [name] v. [name] Properties1 and Ball v. Metro Capital Property2 if a notice of termination issued by a landlord is confusing to the degree that a reasonable person could not understand the precise actions or omissions that caused the landlord to pursue eviction, a Member would find it defective. Specifically, the Cour t in [name] stated that “particulars should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct engaged in by the tenant.”3 A defect in a notice of termination cannot be cured through direct evidence or clarifications offered at the subsequent merits hearing.

Having found that the first N5 notice is invalid, the Landlord cannot rely on the second N5 notice to correct the shortfall in the first notice. Section 68 of the Act requires a valid first, voidable N5 before a landlord may serve a second, non-voidable N5. A landlord cannot cure an invalid notice by ser ving a second notice or by relying on extensive evidence at the hearing to fill in missing particulars.

As there is no valid N5 n otice of t ermination given in accor dance with the Act, the Board lacks the jurisdiction to terminate the tenancy or to grant any of the re medies sought in the L2 application. As such, the Landlord’s application shall be dismissed.

At the conclusion of the Landlord’s application, the Tenants’ representative advised that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 1, 2025. The Board acknowledged that the Landlord’s application included claims for undue damages allegedly caused [name] lly or negligently by the Tenants, as well as substantial interference with the Landlord’s lawful rights, in the amounts of $5,000.00 and $10,000.00 respectively. Because the information that the Tenants had vacated the rental unit was not provided until a fter the conclusion of the hearing on the Landlord’s application, the Landlord was informed that, although the application was dismissed due to the invalidity of the first N5 Notice, she is not precluded from filing an L10 application with the Board to seek compensation. T2 Application – Preliminary Issue

In t he application, the Tenants claim substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit [name] complex, harassment, and the withholding of vital services. The details in the application are as follows: [name] interference: : Landlord regularly obstructs access to backyard of the property to tenant’s family and their pet. Landlord not allowing use of garage to the tenant and keeping his personal stuff in garage. Letters attached. • Harassment: Harassed and threatened to throw tenants out. Not accepting rent to show that we are not defaulting on rent. • Withhold vital services: Landlord switched off air condition unit in peek summer. This happened during May 2023, to September 2023 many times. Letters with this regard are attached here. 1 Toronto Docket No. 106/01, [2001] O.J. No. 5260 ([name]. Ct.) Re: TSL-18855. 2 [2002] O.J. No. 5931 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) (‘Ball’). [name]. at para. 7. LTB-T-085629-23

Upon rev iewing the fac e of the T2 application, I find th at the particulars and detaile d descriptions of the alleged conduct were not sufficiently presented in the application. A party is required to plead the material facts of their case in the application itself, rather than relying solely on supplemental evidence or documents submitted thereafter.

In the case [name] ONSC 6715 (CanLII) the Divisional Court held that a court may not determine a case on issues which have not been clearly identified or plead in a party’s pleadings. The Court stated at paragraph 28, “Absent some special circumstances it is unfair for a case to be decided on an issue not identified by the parties in the pleadings. Under such circumstances the case may be dismissed or a new trial maybe ordered where judgment has been granted on the basis of an unpleaded claim or defence: [name] ONCA 421 (CanLII), [2009] O.J. No. 2038 at para. 20 ([name]. C.A.); see also [name] supra.”

In the case before me, I find that the Tenant s’ application is so vague and lacking in particulars that it did not permit the Landlord to know the case to be met, nor to meaningfully respond. It is not sufficient for a party to rely on the presumption that the opposing party will piece together the allegations during the course of the hearing. The burden rests on the applicant to clearly set out their claim in the application.

As the Tenants’ application does not meet the legal requirements of clarity and specificity, and as no special circumstances have been established to excuse these deficiencies, the Tenants’ application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. [name]
The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________

issues: (‘MM’) (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: The Tenants’ application included the Landlord’s realtor, [name] (‘KY’), as a party.

The Board inquired whether KY should be named as a party to the application. The lease indicates the Landlord is [name], and it appears that KY was the realtor who showed the premises to the Tenants and facilitated the agreement between the parties.
The Tenants agreed that KY should not be named as a party to the application, and requested the application be amended.
I granted the request. The application has been amended to remove KY as a party. Tenants’ T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenants have proven their allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenants $11,300.00.

By way of background, the rental unit is a condominium unit. The tenancy was a one-year fixed term lease which began on August 1, 2024, and was to end on July 31, 2025. The Tenants terminated the lease on August 26, 2024. The rent was $2,750.00 monthly.

The Tenants testified that before the tenancy began, the Landlord’s agent, KY, told them that the rental unit would only be made available to them if they first paid the Landlord five months’ rent. One month would be applied to the first month of the tenancy – August 2024 – and the remainder would be applied to the last four months of the tenancy (months 9, 10, 11, and 12).

Because the Tenants were eager to rent the unit, the Tenants agreed to the Landlord’s demands. They paid the Landlord $13,750.00 for rent on or about July 4, 2024 (Doc- 5463534, pgs. 7, 24). This amount comprised three months excess rent collected ($8,250.00); first months’ rent ($2,750.00) and last month’s rent deposit ($2,750.00).

Section 106(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) states that a landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit and this amount shall not be more than the amount of rent for one month. [Emphasis added]
Thus, the Landlord was not permitted to ask for nor accept more than one month’s rent as a deposit for the last months’ rent.

The Tenants allege there was a fundamental breach of contract which led to the Tenants terminating the lease on August 26, 2024. The Tenants did not give the Landlord a notice to terminate their lease, and the notice period was not in accordance with the Act.

Section 88 of the Act states that if a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act, then a determination of arrears shall be made for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have specified in the notice.

In this case the tenancy was a fixed term to end on July 31, 2025. Section 44(4) of the Act states that notice to terminate a tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the termination date and that shall be on the last day of the fixed term. Therefore, the earliest termination date the Tenants could have specified in a termination notice pursuant to the Act was July 31, 2025. 15. However, the Landlord must demonstrate that they have made efforts to re-rent the unit pursuant to s. 88(1)(4) of the Act. The Tenants did not provide evidence to support whether the rental unit was re-rented, and the Landlord did not attend the hearing. As such, I find the tenancy ended on the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit in accordance with s. 134(1.1). The last day of the tenancy was August 26, 2024. 16. Section 134(1.1) of the Act says that a Landlord shall not collect or require from a former tenant any amount of money purporting to be rent any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. 17. As I have found the tenancy terminated on August 26, 2024, and s.134(1.1) indicates a landlord may not retain any money purporting to be rent, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenants the excess rent collected $8,250.00 ($2,750 x 3), and the last month’s rent deposit ($2,750.00). 18. Although I have found the tenancy terminated August 26, 2024, the Tenants did not seek a claim for reimbursement of the rent paid for the period between August 26 – August 31, 2024. As such, no order shall issue for these six days. 19. The Tenants also paid a $300.00 key deposit. Although the keys were returned to the Landlord, the Landlord did not refund the key deposit. 20. Section 134(1) of the Act, states that unless it is otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall collect or require from a tenant a key deposit whether or not it is refundable. 21. Therefore, the Landlord was not permitted to request a key deposit from the Tenants. The Landlord shall reimburse the Tenants the $300.00 key deposit. 22. The Landlord must reimburse the Tenants for the unlawfully collected rent, last month rent deposit, and key deposit totalling $11,300.00. [name] 23. As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. 24. The Tenants claim there was a fundamental breach of contract. They understood the rental unit had been cleaned and “disinfected” prior to their move. When they moved in, they found there was a cockroach infestation. The Tenants claim a 50% abatement for the first month of rent they paid, and out-of-pocket expenses for pest control products, lodging costs, psychological treatment, and new furniture. 25. The Tenants accessed the rental unit on July 31, 2024. At that time, the Tenants saw some dead cockroaches and one live cockroach. They inquired with KY. He said the rental unit had been cleaned and “disinfected”. KY told the Tenants the cockroaches were probably “left over” from the “disinfection” and that they could buy some cockroach spray to get rid of the remaining roaches. The Tenants say they found some chemicals to treat cockroaches in the storage locker belonging to the rental unit they used to treat the kitchen and washroom. 26. However, on the night of August 3, 2024, MM went to the kitchen and saw at least ten live cockroaches on the stove, and many more underneath the stove. This caused MM great distress, and she could not sleep because of this. DY spent the night trying to keep the roaches from entering the living room or bedroom. 27. On August 4, 2024, DY requested a call from KY. On August 5, 2024, DY wrote again explaining that the spray from the insects was not effective. He explained he would speak to building management the next day for their advice. KY replies to keep him posted. DY responds “My wife is very scared of them and couldn’t sleep in the house, so I sent her and my son to the hotel for a while” (Doc-7460722, pg 1). 28. DY purchased additional chemicals and attempted to continue treatment (Doc-5463534, pg 30). However, these chemicals were ineffective. DY also spoke to building management on August 6, 2024. They attended the rental unit and advised they would arrange for pest control. On August 13, 2024, pest control attended to inspect the rental unit (Doc-5463534). The first treatment was scheduled for August 26, 2024, the same day the Tenants vacated the rental unit. 29. MM and their son stayed in hotels or other short-term rental units for most of the month of August (Doc-5463534, pgs 44-47). DY indicates MM has a history of anxiety, and this situation was extremely upsetting to her (Doc-5463534, pg 32). She was prescribed medications (Doc-5463534, pg 31) and underwent counselling (pgs. 34-42). The Tenants replaced multiple pieces of furniture because they were fearful of bringing pests into a new rental unit (Doc-5492080). 30. Section 22 of the Act states that: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.” 31. In order to find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, there would have to be evidence suggesting that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the Tenants’ comfort. This is not borne out by the facts. The rental unit, upon the first inspection in early July, needed maintenance and the Landlord arranged for that maintenance going so far as to delay move-in so the work could be completed before the Tenants moved in. It does not accord then, that the Landlord would have then ignored pest control particularly when there was evidence the unit was treated before the Tenants moved in. Specifically, KY’s description of the unit being “disinfected” and by the treatment products found in the storage locker. There was no evidence to suggest the Landlord deliberately avoided treating the rental unit for pests. 32. Section 20(1) of the Act states that: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.” 33. The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII)(“Onyskiw”) provides me a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches of the Landlord’s duty to repair under s.20 of the Act. Rejecting the reflexive lens that an interruption of service or occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic breach of the Act, the Court of Appeal urged the Board to use a “contextual approach” to the analysis of maintenance and repair issues. 34. To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21). 35. The timeline in this case is important: • July 31, 2024 – the Tenants discover evidence of a pest problem • August 4, 2024 – Tenants tell KY problem continues • August 6, 2024 – DY calls building management • August 13, 2024 – pest control attends to evaluate • August 26, 2024 – pest control conducts first treatment 36. When applying the Court of Appeal’s guidance in Onyskiw to this situation, what I must consider is whether the Landlord responded appropriately to the Tenants’ request for maintenance. 37. In this situation, DY did not directly ask for the Landlord to intervene. Rather, DY tells KY that he will follow-up with building management. The time between the Tenants’ first request to building management and the time the first treatment is scheduled is 14 days. 38. In my view, this is a reasonable amount of time to follow-up. There was no evidence presented to suggest that the Landlord did not respond accordingly. There is evidence the unit was treated for pests before the tenancy began. I am not persuaded that the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenants’ requests for maintenance when the Tenants first found evidence of the pests on July 31, 2024. KY suggests using commercially available spray. As there had only been one live cockroach seen, whereas two were dead, it seems reasonable to me that this would be the first line of defence. When KY is told this was inadequate on August 4, 2024, DY also tells KY he will follow up with building management who do set up pest control promptly. 39. As for MM’s specific peculiarities with regard to the cockroaches, there was no evidence that this was disclosed to the Landlord. In my view, simply stating my wife is “scared” is not akin to stating that MM was suffering from a severe psychological reaction to the presence of the cockroaches. As such, I do not find it is reasonable to expect the Landlord to be responsible for MM’s therapy costs. Further, without the Landlord being made aware of MM’s specific peculiarities, I am unable to find that it was reasonable to pay for costly short-term lodging elsewhere. 40. Finally, I am not persuaded that it is appropriate to reimburse the Tenants for their furniture. The Tenants did not give the Landlord an opportunity to respond to the problem before unilaterally terminating the lease. Therefore, I find that the Tenants did not mitigate the Landlord’s damages pursuant to s.16 of the Act. Had the Tenants remained in the rental unit, it is very possible the treatments would have been effective, and it would not have been necessary to dispose of their belongings. 41. For the reasons already given, and because I find no breach of the Act, I am not of the view the Tenants should be reimbursed for the purchases of insect repellant products. 42. The Tenants submitted case law. However, I note that there was no binding case law with regard to the breaches pursuant to s. 20 and s.22 of the Act. As such, I afford these cases little weight. 43. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants is $11,348.00. This amount represents: • $8,250.00 for excess rent collected. • $300.00 for the illegal key deposit collected. • $2,750.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household (T2). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (T2). • Collected or retained money illegally, namely, the Landlord collected a rent deposit on which interest has neither been paid or credited to the Tenants’ rent ledger (T1). [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice) on November 29, 2025. The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed. The Landlord’s L1 Application was filed December 17, 2025. The rental property was sold on January 7, 2026.

The arrears of rent owing to the Landlord were not assigned to the new landlord. Therefore, this matter proceeded as an arrears only application for the rent arrears owing by the Tenant up to the date of the sale of the property.
As of the hearing date, the Tenants are still in possession of the rental unit.

This tenancy has been the subject of several L1 applications including LTB-L-014159-25 between the Tenants and the current landlord of the property. An order was made in that application dated December 12, 2025 (the “December 2025 Order”). During that hearing the Tenants contested the rent as set out in the Landlord’s N4 and the L1 hearing centred around the issue of the lawful rent. The December 2025 Order addresses the issue in detail. In short, the Member determined that the rent claimed on the N4 ($1859.00) was not the lawful rent and that the correct lawful rent is $1814.00. The application was dismissed.

The Tenants have appealed the December 2025 Order to the Divisional Court and served the current landlord with the Notice of Appeal on January 12, 2026. The Tenants are appealing that portion of the Order that establishes the monthly lawful rent not the dismissal of the application against them.

At the outset of the hearing, I questioned the Tenants about their position that the December 2025 Order did not establish the lawful monthly rent. I pointed out to the Tenants that as their T2/T1 application claimed a percentage of rent abatement for claims made against the Landlord it would not be possible to calculate percentage claims if the lawful monthly rent was not established. The Tenants agreed, that for the purpose of this L1 hearing and the T1/T2 application, the lawful rent is $1,814.00.
The rent was due on the 15th day of each month as established by agreement between the parties during the tenancy when the Tenants were having difficulty paying the rent on time.

The Tenant raised a section 82 argument in which she explained that she received an email from the Landlord on February 22, 2024 which was the culmination of a number of emails in which the parties had been speaking about accommodations that the Landlord might make because Mrs. [name] had been ill and they couple were having difficulty in paying the rent. There was discussion about a payment plan but the duration of the plan could not be agree to by the parties. In the email of February 22, 2024 which is part of an exchange dating from January 7 to February 22, 2024 (DOC 4349545) Exhibit 2 to the hearing, the Landlord advised the Tenants that she was appointing someone else to communicate with them going forward. and LTB-L-103416-24

The Tenants advanced this email as the basis for not continuing to make rental payments. Mrs. [name] testified that she did not know to whom to pay the rent and that was the reason she stopped paying it. I completely reject this a valid basis for the Tenants to withhold rent. The February 22 email did not say that rent was to be paid in any other way than what had been the practise between the parties for almost 12 years which was by e- transfer. The Landlord’s email merely said that in so far as negotiations around the issue of payment plans and late payments she was appointing someone else to take over the conversation. In my view, the Landlord’s email cannot reasonably be interpreted as changing the long-established payment method and I reject the Tenants’ position and interpretation.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $59.64. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,814.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to by the Tenants to the Landlord to January 7, 2025 is $18,138.25
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,550.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit remains with the new owner of the property and will be applied to the last month of that tenancy if and when the tenancy is terminated.

Interest on the rent deposit is owing to the Tenant for the period from May 25, 2012 to January 7, 2025 and on a going forward basis; however, as stated above that interest is now required to be paid by the current Landlord and the Tenants’ claim for interest owing lies against the current Landlord. T1 Interest on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit

The Tenants’ claim for interest on the last month’s rent deposit dates to 2012. I advised the Tenants at the hearing of the one-year limitation for claims under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, and the Tenants agreed not to proceed with this claim. T2 Application - Substantial Interference and Harassment and “Changes to the Rental Agreement”

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. T1 Application - Improper Charge for Utilities

The Tenants allege that their rental agreement provides that they pay for gas to the rental property but not for the gas water heater. The lease agreement between the parties (Exhibit 4 – DOC 4347385) clearly sets out the obligations of the Tenants, “The Tenants agree to pay all utilities with respect to the premises, including, without limitation, the following utilities: gas, electric, water/sewer, cable TV, telephones and garbage removal if applicable.” and LTB-L-103416-24

Mrs. [name]name] testified that the water heater rental was included in the Enbridge bill from the inception of the tenancy and that it was only when Enbridge and [name] split and the water heater appeared separately on the [name] bill that she realized they had been paying for the water heater. She claimed a credit for all the years of payment for the water heater and produced a chart of charges. Again, the Tenants were reminded of the one- year limitation of this issue. The Tenants accepted the limitation but pressed their argument that they should receive some compensation for this issue.

I find against the Tenants on this point as well. The lease term with respect to utilities is very clear, all utilities “without limitation” are to be paid by the Tenants this includes the water heater. [name] by Harassment regarding Changes in the Lease

The Tenants complained that the Landlord from time to time changed the terms of the rental agreement which was confusing to them and interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental property. The Tenants’ evidence on this point was vague and amounted to an assertion that the change in the date on which the rent was due was a main point of contention.

From the oral and written evidence before, Exhibit 2, changes to the date on which rent was due were as a result of requests from the Tenants because they could not pay the rent. I do not diminish the hardships that the Tenants may have faced although they were described to me and only obliquely referenced in the exchange between the parties. What I have gleaned from the evidence is that it was the Tenants who sought to change the date that the rent was due and any confusion that arose from that date was solely for their benefit until they saw an opportunity to complain about and call it a confusing change.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. [name] by Harassment and Obstruction

Essentially, the Tenants complain of the Landlord’s actions in regard to entry notices given in conjunction with the listing of the property. A number of documents were entered into evidence that form part of a larger document (DOC 7500315). Exhibit 8, pages 49 to 51, in a letter from the Landlord’s former legal representative, a line in the letter stating that the Landlord is “compelled” to bring an L1 proceeding for non-payment of rent. The Tenants assert that this statement is “obstruction and harassing”. An offer to settle the matter at the end of the letter is characterized as “coercion”.

During an attendance by a potential buyer on October 19, 2024, following a valid entry notice, photographs were taken and the Tenants were outraged that the entry notice did not specifically say that photographs were to be taken. The Tenant demanded that any photos of the interior of the home and the interior of the garage be deleted. and LTB-L-103416-24

On another attendance for a real estate showing on October 28, 2024, again following a valid notice of entry, an employee of the eventual buyer, named specifically in the notice, attended the home 6 minutes earlier than the Landlord. The Tenants had left the door unlocked and the individual opened the door and stepped inside. We do not know what was in the mind of the person when she entered but as no evidence was led on this point we can presume that she thought that the Landlord had already arrived an was inside. Nevertheless, whatever was on this person’s mind, when the Tenant came downstairs and saw the person there, she began to remonstrate them forcefully. The individual apologized profusely and went immediately outside to wait for the Landlord.

The Tenant also assert that the fact that the Landlord handed her an LTB Order for eviction for non-payment of rent during a routine inspection and replacement of the CO detectors constitutes harassment.
Finally, the Tenants complain that they were not advised of the closing of the sale of the property or the names of the new owners by the Landlord.

The interactions above were recorded by the Landlord and transcribed. The transcripts were entered into evidence as Exhibit 10. The transcript consists of the confrontations between the parties and also the third party purchaser agent.

The Tenant, Mrs. [name], repeatedly spoke sharply to me for not allowing her to read the entire transcript into the record. I assured her that I would read the transcript, and I have. What it reveals is that Mrs. [name] spoke to the Landlord and all who attended the home in a hectoring and harassing manner. It was the Tenant who was obstructionist and rude not the Landlord or any of the persons who accompanied her into the home.

In addition, I find that the written communications from the Landlord, as an example Exhibit 9, which advised the Tenants that the potential new buyer would assume the existing lease agreement and continue their tenancy to be anything but harassing. It was informative and compassionate. During cross-examination Mrs. [name] admitted that the document which she criticized was in fact not harassing. The same can be said of all the Landlord’s communications.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.
Having dismissed all of the Tenants claims in the T1/T2 application, there is no remedy to be awarded.

Despite their assertion that the only reason they did not pay their rent was because they did not know where to send it, the Tenants conceded at the hearing that they did not have any money saved to pay the arrears of rent. They asked that I give them some additional time to pay any amounts I found to be owing and I have done so.
ordered: The total amount the Tenants shall pay the Landlord is $18,342.25. This amount represents: and LTB-L-103416-24 • $18,138.25 for rent owing to January 7, 2026 plus • $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Tenants will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord the right, at any time after June 1, 2026, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. (T2 application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the amount of $10,864.41. T2/T6 Application

The Tenants claimed the same issue on both their T2 and T6 applications with the Board. The Tenants state that due to an issue with the washing machine a flood occurred in the rental unit. The Tenants claim that the Landlord failed to properly meet its maintenance obligations in addressing the flood, which resulted in the floor becoming water damaged and mold growing. The Tenants alleged that the Landlord’s failure to address this issue resulted in a substantial interference of their enjoyment of the rental property.

The Tenant [name] testified that on September 11, 2023 a water leak occurred within the rental unit due to an issues with the washing machine. The Tenants advised the Landlord of the leak on the same date and a plumber attended the unit.

The Tenants sought assistance in dealing with the flooded flooring, but were only provided some fans by the condominium corporation, but the Landlord took no steps other than advising that they would reach out to their insurance company.

The Tenants continued to follow-up with the Landlord regarding the steps the Landlord was taking to deal with the flooring, but the Landlord continuously advised the Tenants that the insurance company had been notified of the incident. The Landlord took no other action to deal with the issue.

In October the Tenants began noticing white spots of mold appearing on the dark coloured wood flooring and requested that the Landlord take action to replace the floor, but no action was taken by the Landlord.

Out of concern for their safety and well being the Tenants retain HON Environmental on September 5, 2024 to compete a mold inspection and report. The report revealed elevated concentrations of Aspergillus/Penicillium, Chrysonilia and Trichoderma in the unit.
The Tenants sent a copy of the report to the Landlord, but again no action was taken by the Landlord.

Due to the inactivity of the Landlord the Tenants felt they had no choice but to vacate the rental unit and sent an email to the Landlord on September 28, 2024 advising that they would be vacating the rental unit at the end of the month. T6 Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, I find that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Landlord took no steps to address a flood in the unit or the growth of mold that occurred as a result. T2 Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Although the Tenant [name] testified that she and the other Tenant had health concerns regarding the mold in the unit. The Tenants did not substantiate how it substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. As such the Tenants T2 application is dismissed. T6 Remedies

Under the remedies section of the T6 application, the Tenant sought a rent abatement of $11,400.00 being a rent abatement of 25% of their $3,800.00 monthly rent for 12 months from September 2023 to September 2024 when the tenants vacated the rental unit, and a declaration that the tenancy terminated on September 30, 2024 when the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

Pursuant to Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2026 (the ‘Act’) 29(2) No application may be mad under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

Although this is an ongoing issue the Tenants are outside the limitation period with respect to the portion of their application that occurred more than one year prior to October 18, 2024 the date the application was filed.
In this case I find it appropriate to order a rent abatement of $6,513.49 being 15% of the Tenants rent for the period of October 18, 2023 to September 30, 2024.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants was terminated on September 30, 2024 the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit. T1 Application

The Tenant applied to the Board, pursuant to s. 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), alleging that the Landlord has illegally collected and retained money in contravention of the Act as follows: 1. The Landlord has illegally collected and retained a key deposit of $400.00. 2. The Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants; and 3. The Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit. Key Deposit
The Tenant, [name] stated that the Tenants were required to pay a key deposit of $400.00 on August 1, 2023 upon moving into the rental unit.
The Tenants emailed the Landlord on September 28, 2024 indicating that they would be vacating the rental unit and returning the keys to the Landlord on October 1, 2024.
Despite requesting the return of the key deposit as of the date of this hearing the Landlord has not returned the $400.00 key deposit to the Tenants. Analysis

On the basis of the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a $400.00 key deposit from the Tenants on August 1, 2023. I further find that the Tenants returned the keys for the rental unit to the Landlord on October 1, 2024 after vacating the rental unit, and as of the date of this hearing, the Landlord has not returned the $400.00 key deposit to the Tenants.

Section 134 of the Act provides that a Landlord may not collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act provides for the following exceptions to the prohibition of key deposit charges in section 134: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs. [Emphasis added]

There was no evidence before me that the key deposit collected by the Landlord was equal to or less than the expected direct replacement costs to of the keys provided; the Tenants state that it is an unreasonable cost. I find that the Tenants paid a $400.00 refundable key deposit to the Landlord and the Landlord did not refund the deposit once the keys were returned. Therefore, I find that the Landlord has collected a deposit above the reasonable replacement cost contrary to the Act and Regulation and has illegally retained that key deposit after the keys were returned.
The Tenants are entitled to have the illegally collected deposit returned. Return of Last Month’s Rent Deposit
The Tenant testified that at the commencement of the tenancy the Tenants paid the Landlord $7,600.00 on July 5, 2023 representing first and last months rent.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit at the end of September, 2024 and the Landlord failed to return Tenants’ rental deposit.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied that the Landlord did not return the unused rental deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by Section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Interest on Last Month’s Deposit

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenants provided a last month’s rent deposit to the Landlord on July 5, 2023 and now interest has been paid on that amount to the Tenants annually, as required by section 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
ordered: The tenancy between the Tenants and the Landlord was terminated September 30, 2024 the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $10,864.41. This amount represents: • $6,513.49 in a rent abatement. • $400.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $3,800.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $102.92 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owes. L1 Application LTB-T-085854-25 The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. T6 Application The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them, and withheld or interfered with their vital services. T2 Application These applications were heard by videoconference on January 8, 2026 and January 14, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative, [name], and the Tenants attended the hearings. The Tenants met with Duty Counsel prior to the commencement of the hearing. LTB-T-085854-25
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenants were still in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $1,700.00. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $55.89. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,700.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to January 31, 2026 are $10,200.00.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,700.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $27.68 is owing to the Tenants for the period from April 1, 2025 to January 8, 2026. T6 Application

The Tenants allege that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the following: • Floor • Shower • Toilet • Oven • Kitchen ventilation • Washing machine [name] and water damage • Pests and bed bugs

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. LTB-T-085854-25

Subsection 20(1) does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem, then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it.

Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount because of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

In determining whether the Landlord has breached his obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. The Board must then consider whether the Landlord was informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue and whether the steps taken by the Landlord to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstances. [name]
The rental unit is a two-bedroom apartment located in the basement of a single-family home. The upper level is occupied by other tenants. The tenancy commenced on April 1, 2025.

It was the evidence of the Tenants that the tile flooring is damaged in the living area and in the bedrooms. The Tenants described the damaged as lifting, separating and cracking of tiles. The Landlord does not deny there is damage but described the damage as minor as of the date he inspected the rental unit on November 17, 2025. He believes that any significant damage was caused by the Tenants.

Both parties relied on photographs to support their positions. The Tenants presented several close-up photographs of the flooring showing gaps and cracks in between and on tiles. The Landlord relied on photographs from a rental listing. The Landlord’s photographs show the entire room and do not provide a close-up picture of the floor. Despite this, gaps in the tile could be observed in the Landlord’s photographs. Based on the Landlord’s photographs, it is clear gaps in the tile pre-dated the tenancy. The Landlord LTB-T-085854-25 did not present any compelling evidence to support his claim that the extensive damage to the flooring was caused by the Tenants.

The City of Brampton Property Standards By-law Section 31 provides the requirements for interior floors. Subsection 31.1 reads as follows: 31.1 Every floor shall be smooth and maintained so as to be free from all loose, warped, protruding, broken, or rotted boards that may create a [name] or unsanitary condition.
I am satisfied the floor in the rental unit fails to meet the requirements of subsection 31.1. Accordingly, I am satisfied the floor is in a state of disrepair.

The Landlord disputes the Tenants’ claim that they verbally reported issues with the floor in May 2025. He submits that the first he learned of the issue is when the Tenants filed their application on October 17, 2025. I am of the view that the Landlord knew or ought to have known that there was damage to the floor prior to April 1, 2025. The previous tenant vacated the rental unit on March 15, 2025, two weeks before the Tenants moved into the rental unit. Had the Landlord conducted a proper inspection of the rental unit between the tenancies, the Landlord would have observed damage to the floor.

The only repairs the Landlord has conducted on the floor was to replace a transitional piece on November 21, 2025. I find this to be unreasonable. I am satisfied the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the floor. Shower and toilet
There was no dispute that there is a leak between the shower head and the wall. I am satisfied the shower head leak constitutes a disrepair issue.
The Tenants testified that they reported the issue to the Landlord when the Landlord visited the rental unit on April 3, 2025. The leak was repaired on November 21, 2025.

The Landlord denies the Tenants reported the issue on April 3, 2025 and submits that he first became aware of the issue when he received the Tenants’ application at the end of October 2025. As explained above, there were two weeks between the occupancies of the former tenant and the Tenants. In my view, the leak would have been apparent to the Landlord had he conducted an inspection of the rental unit. It is clear to me that the Landlord either failed to inspect the unit between occupancies or had a blatant disregard to the maintenance issues. I find the Landlord knew or ought to have known about the leak on April 1, 2025.

With respect to the toilet, I am not convinced the toilet was in a state of disrepair. The Tenants described the toilet clogging two or three times. Toilets can clog for various reasons. The Tenants failed to sufficiently establish that the clogs were the result of a maintenance issue. Regardless, the Tenants confirm that any issues with the toilet have resolved. LTB-T-085854-25 Oven and kitchen ventilation

I find there is insufficient evidence to establish the oven was in a state of disrepair. The Tenants indicated that when they moved in, they found that one of the burners was not working. The Tenants acknowledged that the inspection conducted by the Landlord revealed the burner was working. There were no further reports to the Landlord of any ongoing issue.

The Tenants testified that they reported to the Landlord that there seem to be an issue with the kitchen ventilation as the unit fills with smoke when they cook. The Tenants reported this verbally to the Landlord’s wife sometime in April or May 2025. According to the Tenants, the Landlord’s wife explained that a part likely needed to be replaced and that she would order the part. The Tenants acknowledge that the Landlord provided them with the part in May 2025.

The Landlord testified that they Tenants were provided with a new filter to address the issue. He stated that he only learned the Tenants were complaining of ongoing issues when he received their application. He installed a new hood and separate vent on November 21, 2025.

I am satisfied that the steps the Landlord took to address the disrepair issue with the ventilation was reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenants do not dispute that they did not report ongoing issues to the Landlord. The Landlord cannot be held liable for issues not reported to him. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenants’ claim is dismissed. [name] machine

It was the evidence of the Tenants that the washing machine did not properly wash their clothes. They reported their concerns verbally to the Landlord on May 17, 2025 and the Landlord had the machine cleaned. The Tenants indicated that the issues persisted, and they sent a photograph of their dirty clothes to the Landlord on August 26, 2025 but no further action was taken.

The Landlord testified that he discovered the issue was with the settings the Tenants used on the machine. He explained the settings to the Tenants and how to properly operate the machine. He acknowledges the Tenants showed him some stains on clothes in August 2025 but does not believe there is a maintenance issue with the machine.

As the applicant, the onus is on the Tenants to prove their claim. I do not find that photographs of soiled clothing establish the washing machine is in a state of disrepair. I am not convinced the washing machine is in a state of disrepair. This portion of the Tenants’ claim is dismissed. LTB-T-085854-25 [name] and water damage
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to mould and water damage.

Section 26 of the City of Brampton Property Standards By-law speaks to cleanliness and mould in a rental unit. Subsections 26.4, 26.6, and 26.7 read as follows: 26.4 Every Building shall be kept free from visible mould and, or mildew. 26.6 All interior floors, ceilings, and walls shall be kept free from dampness caused by the entrance of moisture through an exterior wall, window, roof, Cellar, Basement, or Crawl Space. 26.7 All damages or defects within a Building or part thereof that may cause water damage or mould growth shall be repaired. 37. [name] presented by the Tenants establish visible mould and/or mildew on a window in the living room. The photographs also establish significant water damage on the bottom of the furnace room wall and gaps in the flooring at the bedroom door allowing dirt and water to enter the unit. It was the evidence of the Tenants that they reported these issues to the Landlord when he and his wife attended to address the washing machine. 38. Subsection 26.1 provides that every dwelling shall be delivered in a clean and sanitary condition at the time of initial occupancy. I am not convinced the Landlord met this requirement. 39. It does not appear the Landlord conducted an adequate inspection between the occupancy of the former tenants and the initial occupancy of the Tenants. Had the Landlord inspected the rental unit, he would have observed the mould and water damage throughout the rental unit. 40. It is undisputed that the Landlord addressed the surface mould on the living window on November 21, 2025. With respect to the furnace room wall, the Landlord painted the affected area on November 21, 2025. I do not find that the repairs made to the furnace room wall is adequate. I say this because evidence establishes that water damage and rot have affected the other side of the wall near the Tenants’ bedroom. The Landlord also did not address the issue with the bedroom floor/door. Pests and bed bugs 41. The Tenants testified that they found bugs in the rental unit immediately upon moving in. Tenant [name] (‘PB’) explained that she did not know what kind of bugs these were but reported the issues to the Landlord’s wife. The Landlord’s wife initially denied there was an issue but eventually provided the Tenants with bug spray when they continued to complain. LTB-T-085854-25 42. The issues with the bugs continued and PB continued to report the issues, but the Landlord took no action. On August 7, 2025, the Tenants sent photographs of the bugs to the Landlord’s wife. The Landlord finally arranged for pest control on August 16, 2025. 43. Evidence presented by the Landlord indicates the pest control technician found bedbug activity in bedrooms in the upper rental unit but no activity was noted in the rental unit. 44. The Tenants acknowledged that the Landlord tried to arrange for follow-up treatment. The Tenants explained that because they have two young children, it was difficult for them to be out of the rental unit for an extended period, which was required for the treatment. Follow-up treatment was conducted on January 9, 2026. There is no indication that the pest issue continued after this time. 45. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1). The inspection report from the pest control technician indicated there were no bedbugs in the rental unit as of August 16, 2025. The Landlord initially addressed the Tenants’ complaints by providing them with bug spray, which I find to be reasonable. When the Tenants continued to complaint, the Landlord arranged for professional pest control treatment. I find the Landlord took reasonable and adequate steps to address the Tenants’ concerns. Remedies 46. As noted above, I find the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to the floor, shower, mould, and water damage. In connection to these issues, the Tenants seek a rent abatement and an order that the Landlord make necessary repairs. 47. The Landlord indicated at the hearing that he was prepared to make any necessary repairs. The shower has been repaired as has the mould on the window. Given this, the Landlord shall be ordered to make repairs to the floor and to address any mold/mildew, water damage and/or rot to the walls throughout the rental unit. The Landlord shall also be ordered to repair the gap under the bedroom door to prevent outside elements from entering the rental unit. 48. Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that rent is for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving everything he or she is entitled to then the tenant is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference. Assessing quantum is something of an art and will vary based on several factors including the nature of the problem, the length of time or frequency of the breach, and the impact on the Tenants. 49. The Tenants placed area rugs over damaged areas on the floor. While the disrepair issue has been an inconvenience, there is no evidence suggesting the Tenants or their children have been significantly impacted. Taking into consideration the disrepair issue has been ongoing since April 1, 2025 and cosmetic in nature, I believe a 2% abatement is appropriate given there is minimal disruption to the Tenants’ ability to normally reside in the rental unit. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $340.00 in a LTB-T-085854-25 rent abatement for the damaged floor. This is calculated as follows: $1,700.00/month x .02 = $34.00/month x 10 months (April 1, 2025 to January 31, 2026) = $340.00. 50. The Tenants did not provide any evidence as to the specific impact the shower leak has had upon them. I believe any impact would be minor and likely was more of an annoyance than anything. The shower was repaired on November 21, 2025. I find a lump sum abatement of $50.00 is reasonable and appropriate given there was a minimal disruption to the Tenants and the issue was repaired within a few months. 51. Finally, I have considered an appropriate rent abatement for the mould and water damage. In their application, the Tenants state that the mould and water damage has made them sick. The Tenants, however, have not presented any evidence to support a finding that mould or mildew caused by water damage has resulted in physical illness to them or their children. There were also no submissions made by the Tenants as to specific impacts. I do accept, however, that the disrepair issue from the water damage has had some disruption on the Tenants’ ability to normally reside in the rental unit. 52. The Landlord addressed the issue of mould on the window on November 21, 2025. The Landlord’s repair to the mould and rotting window on the furnace/bedroom wall was inadequate and the Landlord has yet to address the issue with the gap at the bottom of the bedroom door. I find a 10% rent abatement is reasonable and appropriate. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $1,700.00. This is calculated as follows: $1,700 x .10 = $170 x 10 months = $1,700.00 53. The total amount the Landlord is ordered to pay the Tenants under the T6 Application is $2,090.00. T2 Application 54. The Tenants allege that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on multiple occasions. According to the Tenants, the Landlord attended to the private area outside their front door and the furnace/laundry room without written notice. For the reasons that follow, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. 55. The washing machine and dryer are located at the rear of the furnace room. This room can be accessed by a door from the rental unit and another door. The furnace room houses the furnace and breakers to the entire residential complex. Any entry the Landlord made to this area was through the secondary door and not via the rental unit. The Tenants may have had use to the laundry room, but there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the furnace/laundry room was part of the rental unit. I am satisfied this area was a common area to which the Landlord was not obligated to provide notice of entry. 56. With respect to the area outside the door to the rental unit, I am also not convinced this is a part of the rental unit to which the Landlord was obligated to provide notice of entry. The area is an enclosed area under the deck to the main upper unit and is used for common storage. LTB-T-085854-25 57. The Tenants also allege that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by installing a surveillance camera on the exterior of the residential complex. 58. I considered the evidence of the parties, which included photographs of the camera. The camera was installed on top of a window on the upper level of the residential complex. It appears the camera is pointed towards the upper deck of the complex, the back yard, and the exterior doors. I am not convinced the camera was installed to harass the Tenants or that the camera was an invasion of their privacy. The Landlord, however, removed the camera following the Tenants complaints. 59. Finally, the Tenants allege that the Landlord withheld or interfered with their vital services. In this case, the Tenants indicate that they had no heat in September 2025 and that the Landlord only turned the heat on in October 2025. 60. The Tenants presented no evidence that the Landlord intentionally withheld the heat. There is also no evidence before me that the Landlord interfered with the heat. The Tenants acknowledge that they did not specifically ask the Landlord to turn on the heat. 61. The T2 Application is dismissed. 62. The Tenants have incurred costs of $48.00 for filing their application with the Board. The Tenants are entitled to reimbursement of these costs given they were partially successfully on their claim. 63. The total amount the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants is $2,138.00. This amount shall be applied against the amount the Tenants owe the Landlord under the L1 Application. Section 83 considerations 64. The Tenants have requested that I exercise my discretion by granting them relief from eviction. 65. The Tenants have resided in the rental unit since April 1, 2025 with their 3 year old and 1 year old children. The Tenants acknowledge that they have made no payments to the Landlord since July 2025. Tenant [name] (‘RB’) testified that he lost his job on September 16, 2025. He currently works casually early approximately $1,500.00 a month. The Tenants also receive $1,200.00 a month from Canada Child Benefits. RB proposed paying the Landlord $200 to $300 a month on top of the monthly rent. 66. The Landlord testified that he is struggling financially. He stated that his credit cards and line of credit have been exhausted and that he does not have enough money to continue. He has had to borrow from the bank to make ends meet. The Landlord indicated that he could allow the Tenants to pay the arrears in three installments but that their proposed payment plan would be too financially difficult for him. LTB-T-085854-25 67. The Tenants proposal would result in a payment plan of anywhere between 2.5 to 3.5 years. I believe the duration of this plan would be extremely unfair to the Landlord. I question the credibility of RB’s statement that he could obtain money from his parents if needed. In my view, RB would have requested money from his parents prior to the hearing if this was in fact a viable option. 68. RB presented no evidence to support his claim that he earns approximately $1,500.00 a month. He also did not present any evidence to support the claim that he is employed, albeit casually. The Tenants indicated that they would pay the Landlord $1,700.00 on January 16, 2026, and that they could borrow money from their parents. 69. I share the Landlord’s concerns that this is not a viable tenancy and that the Tenants simply cannot afford to remain in the rental unit. Despite this concern, I feel it is appropriate to give the Tenants an opportunity to preserve their tenancy by paying the arrears with a three-month installment plan. As the Tenants indicated they would pay the Landlord $1,700.00 on January 16, 2026, I have made the first payment deadline January 31, 2026 for this amount.
