issues: Sebtaoui (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant alleges the Landlord is in breach of section 20(1) of the Act as there was a bed bug infestation. The Tenant believes the Landlord did nothing about the issue and the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of it. The Tenant is requesting a 100% rent abatement in the amount of $1,190.00 for the month of October 2025.

The Tenant began the tenancy on May 1, 2025, and entered into a one-year lease with the Landlord. On September 5, 2025, the Tenant discovered bed bugs. The Tenant says the Landlord responded immediately and attended the rental unit the next day and brought the Tenant bed bug powder to use. Pest control also attended the rental unit on September 22, 2025, to address the bed bugs.

The Tenant testified that on September 6, 2025, the Tenant told the Landlord that he will be vacating the rental unit by October 1, 2025 due to the bed bug issue. The Landlord did not consent to the Tenant terminating the tenancy early, but did consent to a date of termination of October 31, 2025. The Tenant paid the September 2025 rent, and because the Landlord took a last month’s rent deposit, the Landlord used the last month’s rent deposit and applied it to the October 2025 rent.

The Tenant vacated on October 1, 2025. The Landlord tried to arrange for pest control to attend the rental unit various times during the month of October 2025, however the Tenant had vacated and locked the door and would not consent for pest control to enter. The Tenant’s position was that the Landlord did not serve proper notice for entry. The Landlord’s position is that she did. The Landlord testified on October 30, 2025, she was fined $200.00 from management as pest control would attend the rental unit but could not do pest control treatments as no one would answer the door. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance obligations.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Just because there is a bed bug issue, that does not mean the Landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligations. The breach would occur if the Landlord failed to act in a reasonable timeframe once they were notified of the issue. The evidence before me is that the Tenant discovered the bed bug issue on September 5, 2025, and the following day, the Landlord attended the rental unit with bed bug powder. The Tenant told the Landlord on September 6, 2025, one day after notifying the Landlord of the issue, that he would be terminating the tenancy effective October 1, 2025. The Tenant already decided to vacate the rental unit without allowing the Landlord to remedy the situation. The Landlord also arranged for pest control services to attend the rental unit on September 22, 2025, and attempted to arrange for pest control to attend on subsequent dates in October, 2025.
Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord’s response to the bed bug issue was reasonable and addressed immediately. As such, the application shall be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges that the Landlord failed to meet its maintenances obligations with respect to the following three issues: a) Bed bug infestation in rental unit; b) A hole in the wall; and c) A gap at back door of the rental unit. Bed Bug Infestation

The Tenant testified that she and her three children were being bitten by something since moving into the rental unit. She initially thought it was mosquitos, but during a deep clean of the unit in December, 2023 she noticed bugs crawling on the bed frame.
She stated that she was hesitant to tell the Landlord as she was intimidated by him, but did notify the Landlord via a text message on March 18, 2024.

After being notified, the Landlord brought in an exterminator a few days later, on March 21, 2024 who confirmed that there were bed bugs in the unit. Based on the recommendations of the exterminator a steam cleaning was done and recommendations on cleaning were provided to the Tenant.
On April 16, 2024 the Tenant sent a text message to the Landlord advising him that the steam cleaning and recommendations of the exterminator did not resolve the bed bug issue.

The Landlord attempted to arrange for an exterminator to re-attend the property for treatment. However an alleged disagreement between the Tenant and exterminator regarding treatment and preparation of the unit resulted in the exterminator declining the job.

Arrangements were made for another exterminator to attend the property and on April 20, 2024 an exterminator from Akim Pest Control attended the rental unit and went over pre- treatment preparation an instructions with the Tenant. On April 26, 2024 the exterminator from Akim Pest Control reattended and treated the unit.
In July 2024 the Tenant advised the Landlord that the bed bugs were still present in the unit. A subsequent treatment of the unit occurred on July 28, 2024.

The Tenant requested a follow-up inspection in November, 2024, and on November 12, 2024 an exterminator attended the rental unit for an inspection and sent a text message to the Landlord that no bed bugs were found result: all okay.

The Tenant did not raise the issue of bed bugs any further with the Landlord during the remainder of the tenancy. Although she testified that the issue never full resolved. She stated that she replaced her furniture in March 2025 and purchased plug-ins which reduced the bed bugs and stopped her and her children from being bitten, but that she was still finding bugs around the baseboards until vacating the rental unit on November 29, 2025.
The Landlord submits that he believes the Tenants brought in the bedbugs and that he did everything he could with respect to the issue when it was brought to his attention. Hole in the wall

The Tenant testified that during a walk-through of the unit prior to moving in a hole was observed in the plaster on the wall of the stairwell and pointed out to the Landlord. The Tenant states that the Landlord advised her it would be fixed in the spring, but the hole was never fixed.
The Tenant’s witness [name] testified that he was present when the Tenant moved into the rental unit and there was a hole in the wall of the staircase.

The Landlord disputes that the hole was present during a walk-through of the unit as the entire unit was painted prior to the Tenant moving in. He believes that the hole was caused by the Tenant when she moved into the rental. The Landlord states he only became aware of the hole during an inspection of the unit in April 2024.
No evidence was produced by the Landlord that any action was taken on his part to address the hole in the wall, or that the hole in the wall was repaired. Gap at back door of rental unit

The Tenant testified that the back door of the rental unit which leads to the basement had a 2 ½ to 3 inch gap at the bottom of the door causing the unit to be cold in the winter and hot in the summer.
The Tenant stated that she first noticed that this was an issue in the fall of 2024 when the weather became cooler. She notified the Landlord of the issue in November, 2024.

She indicated that the Landlord looked at the door, but doesn’t believe he did anything about the issue until July 23, 2025 and that the repair completed by the Landlord at that time did not resolve the issue.

The Landlord stated that after being advised of the issue on November 16, 2024 he attended the rental unit on November 22, 2024 and worked on and adjusted the door and repainted it. After completing that work he did not receive any further complaints from the Tenant regarding the door.

He further stated that he did do additional work to the door on July 8, 2025 by adding an additional layer of plywood and weatherstripping. He states that the rental unit is an older house and the door the Tenant is referring to leads to a staircase into the basement from the exterior and that there is a secondary door at the basement level providing additional insulation. Analysis

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Bed Bug Infestation

There is no dispute between the parties that a bed bug infestation was brought to the attention of the Landlord in March 2024. In this case, the issue is whether the Landlord responded reasonably, and if he then properly addressed the problem in a timely and reasonable manner. The Landlord responded to the initial complaint of bed bugs in a timely manner and had a steam treatment implemented as suggested by the exterminator. When the initial steam treatment was unsuccessful a more aggressive treatment was implemented with respect to the issue. Months then went by without the Tenant advising the Landlord that the bed bug issue had not resolved. When the issue was again brought to the Landlord’s attention in July, further treatment occurred in a timely manner. Again after several months the Tenant reached out to the Landlord requesting an inspection of the unit for bed bugs in November 2024 as they believed the issue had not resolved. An inspection by an exterminator occurred promptly which reveal no bed bugs.

Although the Landlord could have followed-up with the Tenant regarding the issue of bed bugs during the gaps in time between complaints. I do not find it unreasonable for the Landlord to rely on the Tenant who is residing in the rental unit to keep the Landlord up to date on the existence of bed bugs in the unit. In the circumstances I find that the Landlord responded to the issue reasonably and was not in breach of their maintenance obligations under section 20(1). Hole in the wall

Based on the evidence before me I am satisfied that the Landlord took no action with respect to a hole in the wall of the staircase of the rental unit once brought to his attention. I am satisfied that the Landlord is in breach of his maintenance obligations under section 20(1) with respect to this issue. However, the Tenant sought no remedy with respect to this issue in their application. Gap at back door of rental unit

The issue was first brought to the attention of the Landlord on November 16, 2024. The evidence before me is that the Landlord attended on November 22, 2024 and performed work on the door. The Tenant does not believe any work was completed on the door, or if work was completed it had no effect on the issue. However, I heard no evidence from the Tenant that she advised the Landlord that the issue regarding the door had not been resolved after his attendance at the property on November 22, 2024. On the evidence before me I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord is in breach of his maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20(1) respecting this issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] Property Management and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The application is amended at the Tenants’ request to correct a clerical error in the date that they vacated the rental unit, from October 23, 2023 to October 23, 2022. The date was not disputed by the Landlords.

The Tenants also requested to amend the application to include additional remedies including reimbursement for a credit check, general damages, costs, and an administrative fine. A further request to amend filed January 20, 2026 requests an award for Small Claims Court fees.

These are not remedies that are available on a T1 application made under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") such as this one. To allow such an amendment would in effect be allowing the Tenants to argue a new application which they did not file which permits remedies under section 29 of the Act. This would be prejudicial to the Landlords and procedurally unfair.
The request to amend to add the remedies is denied.

The Tenants’ legal representative submitted that sections 234(l) and 238 of the Act confer jurisdiction on me to impose an administrative fine for this application. I disagree. Section 234 of the Act lists the possible offences under the Act, including collection of an illegal charge. Section 238 outlines penalties for committing an offence. Offences under the Act are investigated by the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit, not the LTB. [name] of the proceeding

The application was first before the Board on May 29, 2024. The Member dismissed the application at the hearing on the basis that the money was collected by a third party, not the Landlord, and also because it was collected or retained after the Landlord-Tenant relationship had ended.

Subsection 135(4) of the Act requires that the application be made within one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of the Act. The date that the Landlord is alleged to have collected or retained money through his agent, the collection agency, is September 18, 2023, and therefore the Tenants filed their application within the prescribed period as it was filed on October 31, 2023.

By Interim Order LTB-T-085915-23-IN dated January 29, 2025, the Member reversed their decision, found that the Board has jurisdiction, and ordered that the hearing be reconvened for reasons of procedural fairness to be heard on its merits. T1 application

The parties agree that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on October 23, 2022, but the date of termination of the tenancy is disputed. The last month’s rent deposit was applied to the month of October 2022.

The Tenants claim that they terminated the tenancy effective October 31, 2022 based on an N9 Notice to End Tenancy, in accordance with subsections 95(4)(b) and 96(2) of the Act. In their submission, the Landlord refused their request to assign the tenancy when he informed them that they needed to find a new tenant to sign a one-year lease at a higher monthly rent and then failed to respond once they directed the Landlord to the LTB information on assignments.

The Landlords’ position is that the Tenants were not entitled to rely on section 96 of the Act because he didn’t refuse the assignment, and therefore despite vacating the rental unit on October 23, 2022, the Tenants were liable for rent until the unit was re-rented. Landlord [name] (PM) first testified that he “lost a month of rent and utilities” and needed to advertise the unit and do credit checks. Later in his testimony, he stated that the unit was re-rented for February 1, 2023.

The Tenants’ application is based on the Landlords sending what they deemed to be arrears of rent to a collection agency after the Tenants moved out. Doing so was improper, as the Landlord did not first obtain an order from the LTB determining that rent was owed, but the issue to be determined is whether the Landlord was entitled to any rent after the Tenants vacated the unit.

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $2,548.00, which represents the money collected and retained by the collection agency on the Landlords’ behalf and the application filing fee. Were the Landlords entitled to collect rent after October 31, 2022?

The Tenants became aware on January 24, 2023 that the Landlords had forwarded a claim for $3,082.50 to a collection agency. It was unclear on the evidence how the Landlords arrived at this number. After several months of trying to work with the collection agency to have the charge removed, the Tenants paid $2,500.00 to the collection agency on September 19, 2023 to settle the debt. They claim that the Landlords thereby retained or collected money in contravention of the Act.
The parties entered into a tenancy agreement beginning April 1, 2022 for a one-year term ending March 31, 2023. The lawful monthly rent was $1,550.00.
On August 28, 2022, the Tenants advised Landlord [name] (PM) by email that, due to a change in their personal circumstances, they wanted to vacate the unit by November 1, 2022.

PM replied to the Tenants by email on August 29, 2022 stating that: “Unless you are able to find a suitable candidate to sign a new 1 year lease you will be responsible until next March.” On August 30, 2022, PM sent the Tenants an email stating: “Forgot to mention that the new market rent will be $1,750.00.”

On August 31, 2022, the Tenants informed PM by email that they would find a tenant to take over the remaining 5 months of the lease with the current conditions, or he could find a new tenant for whatever conditions he desired. PM responded: It doesn’t quite work that way. We are trying to help you both out. If you are looking for a prospective tenant they need to be fully aware that they would be signing a brand new lease for a minimum of 1 year with the new price. If you cannot find anyone for those terms unfortunately you will be responsible March 31st/2023 [sic].”

The Tenants responded by email the same day stating: “The RTA outlines our obligations clearly as to find a tenant to take over the remainder of the current lease,” and providing a link to the LTB website information on assignment of a tenancy.

On September 8, 2022 the Tenants emailed PM an N9 Notice to End Tenancy effective October 31, 2022 and referred to his “lack of response within seven days to allow us to assign our current lease (with current terms).” PM’s September 9, 2022 response was that “there has been plenty of correspondence” but they have been waiting for the Tenants to find a new tenant. The Tenants confirmed their position in an email on September 13, 2022 to which PM responded “We have yet to receive any candidates that you agreed to find to take over your tenancy. You have responsibilities, abide by them.” Analysis

Section 95 of the Act governs assignment of a tenancy. When a tenant requests to assign the tenancy, a landlord may consent to or refuse the assignment. Under section 95(4) of the Act: (4) A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, (a) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent; (b) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made; (c) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord refuses consent to the assignment under clause (3) (c); or (d) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made.
Subsection 95(8) states that “If a tenant has assigned a rental unit to another person, the tenancy agreement continues to apply on the same terms and conditions.”

Subsection 96(2) permits the tenant to give notice of termination of the tenancy at least a number of days after the date of the notice that is the lesser of the notice period otherwise required under this Act and 30 days.

The Landlords’ legal representative attempted to characterize the communications between the parties as a “clear miscommunication” about PM’s permission to allow assignment of the tenancy. I do not agree. The emails in evidence are clear that PM required the Tenants to find another tenant at a higher rent for a one-year term. That is not an assignment of a tenancy under subsection 95(8) of the Act, but rather a requirement for the Tenants to find a new tenancy for the Landlord. The Tenants provided PM with information from the LTB on the nature of an assignment. PM’s testimony that he had misunderstood the law about the requirements of an assignment does not make this a miscommunication.

I find that PM’s requirement that the Tenants find a new tenant to sign a new one-year lease at a higher monthly rent was not a consent to assign under the Act. I find that the Landlords therefore refused an assignment of the tenancy on August 31, 2022 and therefore the Tenants were permitted to give notice on September 8, 2022 to end the tenancy effective October 31, 2022. Even if PM reversed his position after receiving the N9 Notice and informed the Tenants that they could assign their unit, as he suggested in his testimony, this does not invalidate the N9.
I find that the tenancy is terminated as of October 31, 2022.

Subsection 134(1.1) of the Act states: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. (2) No superintendent, property manager or other person who acts on behalf of a landlord with respect to a rental unit shall, directly or indirectly, with or without the authority of the landlord, do any of the things prohibited under clause (1) (a), (b) or (c) or subsection (1.1) with respect to that rental unit.

Given that I have found that the tenancy terminated October 31, 2022, the Landlords collected $2,500.00 through the collection agency in September 2023 for a period after the tenancy was lawfully terminated and the Tenants had vacated the rental unit. The Landlords therefore collected a charge of $2,500.00 which is not allowed by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $2,548.00. This amount represents: • $2,500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,045.93.
By way of background, the rental unit is a multi-unit low-rise building. The Tenant’s rental unit is located on the basement level. He resides in the rental unit with his young child.

For the sake of clarity, the Tenant’s application is a T2/T6 application. However, the only request made in the Tenant’s T6 application is for mold and asbestos testing due to exposure. The T6 portion of the application does not specify any allegations. However, I find that a reasonable landlord could infer the allegations from the statements made in the T2 portion of the application. The Tenant clearly refers to maintenance allegations. Although the Tenant seeks compensation for the exposure to mold and/or asbestos in the T6 application, the claim does not state how much compensation the Tenant is seeking or why.

In the case of Beaugé v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, the Divisional Court states that it is an error in law to award damages where none is claimed. In other words, the Board may not assess a monetary claim when one is not stated within the claim.
Therefore, I am unable to assess any monetary compensation. However, I have considered the Tenant’s request for mold and asbestos testing in the remedies found below.

For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, some of the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,046.23.

The Tenant’s T2 application alleges that the Landlord: i. Failed to provide timely, effective, and appropriate repairs to the rental unit, specifically the bathroom ceiling, the flooring, and the heat; ii. Failed to provide the rental unit to the Tenant on the date it was promised; and, iii. Misled the Tenant as to the quality of the finishings in the rental unit. Disrepair Bathroom Ceiling

The Tenant states that in April 2025, the [name] attended the rental unit because of a leak. The [name] proceeded to cut holes in the ceiling above the shower and above the toilet. The repairs were left unattended for a month. The area was moldy and the area above the shower dripped water on the Tenant daily while he was showering. The Superintendent reattend about four weeks later to patch the ceiling. However, the sanding and painting remains incomplete. During this period of repair, the [name] also dripped sealant into the tub which was not cleaned up and has left an unsightly mark.

The Tenant states that the impact of the ceiling repair is that it is unsightly. He also says it was “gross” to have dirty water dripping on him during his shower, and that his child is afraid of spiders. Flooring

The Tenant also states that the flooring in the rental unit is in poor condition. The flooring is laminate or vinyl planks, and the planks have separated. In the bathroom, two planks have between 3 – 4 inches between them, and the other two bedrooms and living room have spaces of at least one inch between them in spots.
The Tenant states that the impact is that walking on the flooring is uncomfortable. Heat

The Tenant says the heat in his rental unit does not function correctly. First, the rental unit is uncomfortably warm throughout the winter, and the Tenant needs to have windows open at all times. Second, the heat does not turn off during the summer months. He told the Superintendent around March 5, 2025, and once a week for three additional weeks after that. However, the Superintendent did not attend the rental unit to look into the issue.

The Tenant states that in the peak of winter and summer, he estimates the rental unit was about 25 degrees. He explains that because he is in the basement unit, it was not so hot as to cause distress, but his child had suffered from symptoms of heat exhaustion.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. Given the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant has met his onus of proof. I further find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment for all usual purposes by failing to address the disrepair in the rental unit. In my view, a reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that these items should have been addressed as part of their normal maintenance protocols in the building particularly when turning the rental unit over to a new tenant. Further, the Landlord ought to have responded to the Tenant’s repeated request for maintenance to the heating system. At the very least, the Landlord ought to have been aware of these allegations after receiving a copy of the Tenant’s application. Failed to Provide Rental Unit on Time

The Tenant signed a lease and was to begin his tenancy on December 1, 2024. As the Tenant was driving to the rental unit on December 1, 2024, he called ahead to the Superintendent to let him know of his impending arrival. The Superintendent then advised him that the tenant living in Unit 103 had failed to leave the rental unit. The Tenant testified the Landlord did not make another rental unit available to him.

As a result, the Tenant had to call around to find somewhere for him and his child to stay. He was fortunate enough to find temporary accommodations with a family member. However, these accommodations were a considerable distance from the rental unit and his child’s school. The Tenant had to drive about 1.5 hours each way going back and forth from the family member’s home to his child’s school, and to his job. He also had to secure storage for his belongings while he waited for the rental unit to become available and re-rent a U-Haul on December 4, 2024.
The rental unit became available on December 4, 2024, and the Tenant was able to move in that day.

In my view, the Landlord’s failure to provide the rental unit on the day promised substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. He was forced to scramble to find alternate accommodations and storage while he waited for the unit to be made available. No effort to assist the Tenant was forthcoming. [name]

In November 2024, the Tenant went to the residential complex to look at the rental unit. He was met by someone named [name], who showed him around a rental unit which had been freshly renovated. It had a kitchen island, brand new countertops and cabinetry, and brand-new flooring. He was told that the rental unit he would be renting would be the same as the one he was viewing.

However, when the Tenant moved in on December 4, 2024, he found the rental unit was not in the same condition as the one he had seen. The cabinetry and countertops were old; there was no kitchen island, and the flooring, as described earlier, was in a state of some disrepair.

The Tenant states he felt that he was disappointed and a little angry. He was not given a rent reduction for this unit, which was clearly not the same quality or condition as the one he had been promised.

I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by effective engaging in what is colloquially known as a “bait and switch.” The Tenant was shown a pristine unit, told the unit he would be renting was in the same condition, and received a rental unit whose fixtures and finishings fell far below that standard. Further, the Landlord is responsible for representations made by their agents. Remedies
The Tenant claims, by way of remedies: • $1,700.00 for one month’s rent abatement • $400.00 for moving and storage expenses • $40,000.00 for other out-of-pocket expenses

In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], the Court remarked: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

There is no question that the Tenant is entitled to three days’ reimbursement at 100% of the rent paid for the three days he was unable to access the rental unit. He was told his tenancy was to begin on December 1, 2024, but could not move until December 4, 2024. During this period, the Tenant received no value for the money that was paid.
I find this amount to be $179.67 ($1,700.00x12/365 = $55.89/day x 3 days).

When I consider the disrepair and the effect this had on the Tenant, I am of the view that a 15% abatement is appropriate. The disrepair is predominantly unsightly rather than having a significant daily impact on the Tenant. However, having dirty shower water drip on you, stepping on an uncomfortable floor would, and heat that cannot be turned off, in my view, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes.

As the Tenant was already compensated for 100% abatement for the period between December 1 and 3, 2024, the period that the 15% abatement for the disrepair will be applied to is between December 3 and 31, 2024, a period of 27 days. I calculate this to be $226.26 ($1,700.00x12/365 = ($55.89/day x .15%) x 27 days).

With regard to the rental unit being priced at market value, despite it having lesser quality of fixtures and finishes, I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent. The Tenant has effectively paid 100% for a rental unit he believed he would be getting but received an inferior quality. The rental unit he received does not have an island, has poorly maintained flooring, old cabinetry and countertops.
I am of the view that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of $150.00, based on my experience and knowledge of market rent values of similar units.

The Tenant also requests the costs for the U-Haul for the second trip made on December 4, 2024, and storage costs for $400.00. He explains he would not have incurred this expense had the Landlord provided the rental unit to him on the agreed upon date in his lease. I agree that but for the Landlord’s failure to provide the rental unit on the date promised, the Tenant had out-of-pocket and moving and storage expenses he would not have otherwise incurred.

I am of the view the Tenant is entitled to his reasonable out-of-pocket expenses as claimed for the moving truck, storage, and gas. I find the costs are reasonable, as U-Haul is typically about $200.00 when gas is added in for the one-hour distance between the Tenant’s temporary accommodations and the rental unit. This would attribute $200.00 to the Tenant’s storage, and again I find this to be a reasonable amount and consistent with other rental storage costs. Finally, I find $30.00 of gas each day to travel back and forth is reasonable given the added distance he travelled as reflected by the travel time of 3 hours daily.
Therefore, I find the Tenant is entitled to $400.00 for moving and storage costs, and $90.00 for out-of-pocket expenses.

The Tenant also seeks $40,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses. The Tenant submits that he had a car accident which damaged his vehicle costing him $28,000.00 and subsequently had to purchase another vehicle for $10,000.00. The Tenant states that he was stressed because of the Landlord’s actions on or about December 1, 2024, and this is what led to the accident.

I am not of the view that the Tenant can be compensated for the loss of his vehicle or the cost to purchase another vehicle, as there is no connection between the Landlord’s failing to provide the rental unit to the Tenant and the Tenant subsequently having a car accident. I say this because the standard for anyone driving in Ontario is that they are responsible for operating their vehicle safely. It is unfortunate the Tenant was distracted or otherwise under emotional strain during this period; however, ultimately, it is up to the Tenant to operate a vehicle safely.

Lastly, the Tenant’s T6 application requests mold and asbestos testing. The Tenant says that because the ceiling was open for a period of four weeks, and there was evidence of mold in the hole, he and his child may have been exposed. Further, his evidence is that buildings of this age often have asbestos which is why he requests asbestos testing.

In my view, it is not superfluous to request testing of this nature, because the Tenant has a young child and both mold and asbestos carry a risk of serious, long-term health problems, particularly to children. I find this to be a reasonable request in the circumstances. As such, an order shall issue.
The total the Landlord owes the Tenant is $1,045.23.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,093.93. This amount represents: • $555.93 for a rent abatement. • $400.00 for the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred • $90.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 1, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,094.23 from the rent due and owing for the month of April 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall arrange for mold and asbestos testing with a qualified technician. Results of the testing shall be provided to the Tenant within 10 business days of their receipt and shall be provided to the Tenant no later than July 31, 2026, failing which the Tenant may make another application to the Board. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,199.95 on or before April 10, 2026.

By way of background, this application was first heard on June 18, 2025. The Landlord did not attend the hearing, and an uncontested order, LTB-T-085961-24, dated June 23, 2025 was issued partially granting the Tenant’s application.

On July 18, 2025, the Landlord filed a request to review the order on the basis of not being reasonably able to participate. The Landlord’s review was granted with order LTB-T- 085961-24-RV, dated September 2, 2025 and the matter was directed to be heard de novo.
The Tenant claims a rent abatement of $9,870.00, general compensation of $5,000.00, and for the Board to order the Landlord to repair the stove and the window crank.

At the start of the hearing, the Tenant’s representative requested to amend the application to reduce the rent abatement claim from $9,870.00 to $4,935.00. The Landlord was not opposed and there is no prejudice to the Landlord, as such, I consented to the request. Stove damage

The Tenant testified that on May 25, 2024 the stove stopped working. The Tenant testified that, as he was preparing to cook, he turned on the stove and immediately observed the cord spark. The Tenant submitted a photograph of an electrical cord showing a sliced cord, with exposed wires and burn marks in some areas. The Tenant asserts that the wire belongs to the stove.

The Tenant testified that he immediately texted the photograph to the Landlord with a message stating, “this just happened”. A copy of the text message was not submitted into evidence. The Tenant testified that the Landlord initially responded, “why are you sending me this photo?” and that he replied, “this just happened”. In cross examination, the Tenant had difficulty explaining the details of the communication with the Landlord regarding the cord but ultimately stated that he advised Landlord that the stove was damaged. The Tenant testified that he did not follow up with the Landlord as to whether the stove would be repaired or replaced.
There is no dispute that the stove was replaced by the Landlord on July 24, 2025, approximately 14 months after the alleged initial complaint.

The Landlord testified that communication between the parties is usually conducted through text message. The Landlord submitted a series of text messages between January 13, 2020 to March 23, 2024, to demonstrate that she typically responds to maintenance concerns raised by the Tenant.

The Landlord does not dispute receiving a photograph of the damaged wire from the Tenant on May 25, 2024. However, she testified that she did not understand what the Tenant was asking her to do with the photograph. She testified she responded, “what is this?”, and the Tenant replied, “let me know”, to which she responded with “okay”. The Landlord testified that she did not follow up with the Tenant or conduct an inspection, on the basis that the Tenant did not request repairs or provide further details. The alleged text communication was not submitted into evidence.

The Landlord testified that she first became aware that the stove was damage on July 2, 2025, when she followed up regarding July 2025 rent that had not been paid in full, and the Tenant advised her that he had received a Board order.

The Landlord testified that she immediately attempted to repair the stove, but that the Tenant refused entry. This is disputed by the Tenant. The Landlord did not submit any documentary evidence, such as text messages or email communications, to substantiate the alleged refusal of entry. In cross-examination, the Landlord could not recall the contractor she allegedly retained.

The Landlord takes the position that the stove was replaced on July 24, 2025, approximately 22 days after she became aware of the issue and therefore submits that she responded within a reasonable timeframe. The Landlord requests that the application be dismissed. Window crank damage

There is no dispute that the rental unit is a small 376-square-foot bachelor unit with one window. It is also undisputed that the window crank had previously been damaged and repaired by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that on or around July 3, 2024, he advised the Landlord that the window crank was damaged, preventing him from opening the window. In cross examination, the Tenant provided conflicting testimony as to when the window was last damaged. He initially stated that he had advised the Landlord of damage on March 24, 2022, and that it had not been repaired since that time. However, when directed to the T6 application, the Tenant testified that the most recent damage occurred approximately one week after May 25, 2024. The alleged text communication regarding the window issue was not submitted into evidence.

The Landlord denies receiving any communication from the Tenant with respect to the window crank. The Landlord maintains that she first learned of this issue on July 2, 2025, at the same time as the stove issue.

The Landlord testified that she inquired about repairing the window on July 4, 2025, and submitted a copy of her email communication with Hi-Lon Glass. There is no dispute that the window was repaired on July 29, 2025. Analysis

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the (“Act”), provides that, a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, there is no dispute that the Landlord received a photograph of a burnt wire on May 25, 2024. However, there is conflicting testimony between the parties as to what was communicated at that time. The Tenant provided inconsistent evidence as to what he told the Landlord and did not provide clear, direct evidence that he advised the Landlord that the stove was damaged. I find that the Tenant’s communication was not clear or specific.

The Tenant takes the position that the Landlord ought to have understood that the stove was damaged. However, I do not find that assumption to be reasonable. A burnt wire could relate to a number of items, such as an extension or computer cord. The Tenant cannot reasonably expect the Landlord to assume the stove itself was damaged based on the photograph alone. I am not satisfied that the Tenant clearly and directly communicated that the stove was not functioning.

Despite the above, I find that the Landlord had sufficient information to prompt further inquiry. The Landlord acknowledged receiving a photograph of the damaged wire and, when she asked the Tenant what it related to, the Tenant responded, “let me know”. In these circumstances, I find that the Landlord had an obligation to investigate the issue further and failed to meet her obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the stove.

With respect to the window, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet her maintenance obligations with respect to the window crank. The Tenant’s evidence with respect to when the Landlord was notified of the issue was inconsistent. The Tenant provided conflicting dates as to when the window was damaged and when the Landlord was allegedly advised. No documentary evidence, such as text messages, were submitted to corroborate that notice was provided to the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that she first became aware of the issue on July 2, 2025. I accept the Landlord’s evidence on this point, as it is consistent with the documentary evidence showing that she took steps to arrange for repairs shortly thereafter. The evidence establishes that the Landlord made inquiries regarding repair within two days and that the window was repaired on July 29, 2025. In the circumstances, I find that the Landlord responded within a reasonable timeframe once she became aware of the issue.

As the Tenant has not established that the Landlord knew or ought reasonably to have known of the issue prior to July 2, 2025, and given the Landlord’s prompt response thereafter, I find that there was no breach of section 20 of the Act. Accordingly, the window crank portion of the application is dismissed. Remedies Rent abatement

The Tenant claims a rent abatement of $4,935.00 for the period May 25, 2024 to November 24, 2025 for the loss of the stove and issues related to the window in the unit. The Tenant alleges that he was unable to cook for a 12-month period and was required to purchase a hot plate and a toaster oven, which limited the type of meals he could prepare. I find this amount to be unreasonable. No receipts were submitted to support the alleged purchase of these items. Additionally, the Tenant testified that he did not follow up with the Landlord regarding the stove until after the first order was issued and the Landlord inquired about the rent.

Based on the evidence before me, and in assessing the impact of the maintenance issue on the Tenant, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $1,151.95. This amount represents a 5% rent abatement from May 25, 2024 to July 24, 2025. [name] for repairs
As the stove has been replaced, the request for the Board to issue an order requiring the Landlord to do the repairs is moot. General compensation
The Tenant also claims $5,000.00 in general compensation.

The Board has the authority, pursuant to subsection 31(1)(f) of the Act, to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name].) in circumstances where the damages claimed are the result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the landlord’s breach had on the tenant.

In this case, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation. The Tenant testified that he was limited in what he could cook, and that the loss of the stove affected his quality of life, as he was required to use a hot plate and toaster oven. However, I am not persuaded that the impact was substantial. The Tenant did not follow up with the Landlord regarding the repair or replacement of the stove. While the Tenant may have experience some inconvenience, I am not satisfied that the impact rises to a level that would warrant an award of general compensation. Accordingly, the claim for general compensation is denied.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,199.95. This amount represents: • $1,151.95 for a rent abatement for the period ending July 24, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 10, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $600.00 for the rent owing for the month of April 2026 and $599.95 for May 2026. March 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: LTD (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) [organization] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application)
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing at 9:36 AM, the Tenant’s Legal Representative requested an adjournment as the Tenant was not in attendance and he had been trying unsuccessfully to reach them.
The Landlord was opposed to the adjournment request. They had arranged for witnesses to attend the hearing and additionally no explanation had been provided for the Tenant’s non-attendance.
The matter was held down to permit the Tenant’s Legal Representative additional time to reach his client.
The matter was recalled at 11:58 AM, and the Tenant’s Legal Representative advised that he had still not been able to reach his client.

Having considered the factors in Rule 21.8, the reason for the adjournment request, the position of the parties the prejudice to the parties, I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. The Board does not have any information as to why the Tenant is not in attendance. As such the Tenant’s request for an adjournment was denied. The Tenant’s Legal Representative did not wish to withdraw the Tenant’s applications as he had no instructions from his client to do so, and the matter proceeded to be heard. T2 and T6 Applications
In the absence of his client the Tenant’s Legal Representative called no evidence in support of the Tenant’s applications.
In the absence of any evidence in support of the Tenants applications, the applications will be dismissed.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative sought costs for their attendance at the hearing. I have considered the Board’s guidelines with respect to awarding costs. I am not satisfied that is appropriate to award costs in this situation where the Tenant did not attend. Costs are generally awarded in cases of unreasonable conduct. I do not find non-attendance to be unreasonable conduct.
ordered: The Tenants applications are dismissed. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.
In this case, the Tenant alleges that the dishwasher in the rental unit was not operational and that the Landlord failed to repair it.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on January 6, 2023 and moved out on November 15, 2024. Rent was $3,000 per month. This application was commenced on October 20, 2024.

The Tenant notified the Landlord by text message on February 9, 2024 that the dishwasher was not operational. She followed up with the Landlord on March 3, 2024. She states that the Landlord responded that he had determined that there was no warranty on the dishwasher and that a technician would attend on March 12, 2024. She states no technician attended at the rental unit on that date. The Tenant stated that she did not follow up again with the Landlord and that no one appeared to repair the dishwasher during the remainder of the tenancy. The Tenant requests a 15% rent abatement due to the non-functioning dishwasher.

The Landlord stated that the appliances in the rental unit were new at the time the Tenant moved into the rental unit. He stated that after November 6, 2023, the Tenant stopped paying rent despite ongoing follow-ups for payment.

The Landlord acknowledged that he was advised by the Tenant on February 29, 2024 that the dishwasher was not working. He stated that he gave the Tenant notice for entry on March 3, 2024 and attended at the property to inspect the dishwasher. He states he was denied entry. The Landlord stated that on March 27, 2024, the Tenant asked him if he wanted her to arrange for someone to attend to fix the dishwasher. He stated that after March 30, the Tenant stopped returning calls or responding to messages and that he assumed that the Tenant had arranged to fix the dishwasher herself.

The Landlord initiated eviction proceedings due to non-payment of rent. The application was heard on August 8, 2024 (LTB-L-031843). [name] was issued on September 17, 2024 for payment of arrears of rent of $24,186.00 but there was no eviction order due to a defect in the N4 notice. The Order indicates that the Tenant was asked about any maintenance issues under s. 82 of the Act. The issue of the dishwasher was not mentioned at the L1/L9 hearing, although the Tenant indicated she had some undisclosed issues. The Tenant commenced this T6 application and a T2 application shortly after the L9 order was issued. The T2 application was later withdrawn by the Tenant.

The Landlord stated that the Tenant told him again in September, 2024 that the dishwasher was not working. The Landlord stated that he then arranged for a technician provided by the builder of the rental unit to attend to inspect the dishwasher. The Landlord stated that he sent the Tenant notice of this intended entry but the Tenant did not co- operate. The Landlord stated that he had arranged for a technician to attend on November 1, 2024 and sent a notice of entry as required by the Act. He states that the Tenant denied entry on November 1, 2024.

The Landlord stated that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit, the Landlord tried using the dishwasher. He washed some dishes as a test and stated that the dishwasher was operational. He does not believe the dishwasher was ever broken.

I accept the evidence of the Landlord that he attempted to arrange for access to the rental unit to inspect the dishwasher and was denied entry by the Tenant. I accept the evidence of the Landlord that when he tested the dishwasher in November, 2024 that it was operational. The dishwasher was only one year old at the time the Tenant first made her complaint in February 2024. I do not believe the statements of the Tenant that the dishwasher was not working during any period of the tenancy. The Tenant stated in submissions at the hearing that she was “looking for a little help” to pay the arrears of rent.
The Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $3,625.70 Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that from February 15, 2024 to August 1, 2024, the date she vacated the rental unit she experienced excessive noise on a daily basis from the neighbouring tenant in the unit below. According to the Tenant, the noises mainly consisted of piano and violin playing for extended periods of time throughout the day and evening often past 10:00 PM. Additionally when the piano playing was occurring yelling could also be heard as if coaching was occurring. In addition to the noise from music the Tenant could also hear yelling and door slamming on a frequent basis, which escalated as her tenancy continued.

The Tenant states that the piano was situated directly below her son’s bedroom, and that the residential complex has one HVAC system and that shared ductwork between the units carries the sound from the lower unit.

The Tenant testified that the residential complex is a single family dwelling that had been converted into two rental units with one on the main floor and one in the basement. The Tenant resided in the unit on the main floor. She states that the Landlord failed to install any soundproofing between the units which contributed to the noise issues.
The Tenant testified that she worked from home and that due to the noise her work was often interrupted.

The issue of noise was first brought to the Landlord’s attention on March 21, 2024 via a text message where the Tenant inquired if there were quiet hours in the house as music and other audible things continue until 10:30 and that the sound carries through the vents. She requested that the Landlord speak with the basement Tenant.

The Landlord indicated that he would reach out to the Tenant and have her end her audible-related activities by 10pm. The Tenant states that the Landlord also suggested that the Tenants attempt to work out the issues between themselves.
The noise issue did not resolve and she continued to advise the Landlord of noise issues.

The noise from the basement tenant escalated resulting in the Tenant sending the Landlord a Letter of concern via email on June 13, 2024 setting out the issues she has been having with the basement tenant. In addition to the on-going noise issue. The basement tenant who has access to the fuse panel also shut off the electricity to the Tenant’s unit for over 12 hours. The Tenant request that the Landlord issue a N5 Notice of Termination to the basement tenant due to the ongoing interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. and suggested to the Landlord that soundproofing be installed between the units.

In response the Landlord sent an email to the Tenant on June 23, 2024 addressing the [name] concerns, but declined to take any action against the basement tenant and indicated that he was open to re-assessing the Tenant’s rental agreement.
The Landlord and the Tenant agreed to terminate their fixed term one year tenancy and the Tenant vacated the rental unit at the end of July, 2024.

The Landlord testified that he received complaints from both the Tenant and the basement tenant regarding issues that the tenants were having with each other. He would intervene which would result in an agreement for period of time before the issues between them would flair up again.

He states that the responded to complaints in a timely manner and feels that he was caught in the crossfire of the two tenants and did his best to make the situation better for both tenants, but he believes the issue was that he had two tenants with incompatible lifestyles. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act (2006) (the ‘Act’) provides that: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Section 22 addresses the behaviour of landlords, not other tenants. In the matter before me, the behaviour of the Landlord that the Tenant claims substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit is a failure to take reasonable and effective steps to address the Tenant’s complaints regarding the excessive noise from the basement tenant.

A landlord’s duty to address substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a tenant by another tenant was affirmed by the Divisional Court in Hassan v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (“[name]”). The Court held as follows: It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.”

Pursuant to [name], a landlord has the positive obligation to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment and take reasonably necessary actions against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of their premises. In other words, when a landlord receives a complaint from a tenant about offending conduct by another tenant, a landlord must take reasonable steps within a reasonable time to investigate and address the conduct. If the offending conduct does not stop, the landlord must take escalating steps up to and including issuing a notice of termination to the offending tenant.

The Landlord did not show evidence of any escalating steps with respect to the issues raised by the Tenant regarding the behaviour of the basement tenant. The most that the Landlord testified he did was to have conversations with the basement tenant regarding their behaviour and noise.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant experienced excessive noise in the rental unit coming from the basement unit on an almost daily basis. The Tenant continuously advised the Landlord of the noise issue. Although the Landlord had conversations with the basement tenant regarding the noise, The Landlord did not escalate his actions to formal letters or notices of termination despite the issue continuing.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by failing to address the noise issues of the tenant of the basement unit. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services

Section 21(1) of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.
The act defines vital services as hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat.

The Tenant testified that on June 13, 2024 the basement tenant shut off the fuses cutting electricity to the Tenant’s unit. The Tenant sent a text message on June 13, 2024 at 7:21 am to the Landlord advising that her power and been shut off by the basement Tenant.

The Tenant further stated that the Landlord advised her that he had told the basement tenant to turn the electricity back on and indicated that the basement tenant would turn it on when she got back home later that day. By 7:56 pm the Tenant again sent a text to the Landlord advising that the basement tenant had still not restored the electricity to her unit. The Landlord responding saying that the basement tenant wanted an apology before turning the electricity back on.
As a result of the electricity being shut off to her unit some of the Tenant’s groceries in the fridge/freezer spoiled.

Although the Landlord did not turn off the supply electricity to the Tenant’s unit the Landlord has a non-delegable duty to ensure vital services. The Landlord still has the responsibility to ensure vital services if another tenant interferes with electricity, the Landlord can’t sit idly by waiting for the basement tenant to turn the electricity back on. As such, I find that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant's vital services. Remedies

The Tenant testified that the remedies she seeks are in relation the ongoing noise issue with the basement tenant occurring on a daily basis from the date she moved in, February 15, 2024 to July 31, 2024 when she vacated the rental unit as well as the power being shut off in her unit on July 13, 2024. She seeks a 50% rent abatement for five and half months at $2,800.00 per month equaling the amount of $7,700.00.

The Tenant first told the Landlord about the noise issue until March 21, 2024. Given the length of time that this issue persisted, the impact on the Tenant and the Landlord’s failure to take escalating steps to address the noise effectively additionally her put was cut off by the Tenant on July13, 2024, I find that a 20% rent abatement for the period of March 21, 2024 to July 31, 2024 is appropriate in the circumstance, for a total of $2,424.10

The Tenant also seeks moving and storage expenses in the amount of $1,153.60, which the Tenant supported with invoices. The Tenant shall also be compensated for those expenses as I find that they are a direct result of the Tenant having to vacate the unit as the Landlord failed to address the noise issue in the unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,625.70. This amount represents: • $2,424.10 for a rent abatement. • $1,153.60 for all of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $10,548.00. 1. This application is brought pursuant to s.57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in cl ause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that in order to succeed on this application the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 2. The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant was given a notice under s. 48 with a termination date of July 31, 2025, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice. The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit for August 1, 2025, to a nearby rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she went back to the rental unit on two occasions, once in mid September and once in mid October 2025 to pick up mail from the mailbox at the rental unit. The Tenant submitted that on both occasions she saw that no one was living in the rental unit. On the first occasion in September, she saw contractors working in the rental unit. On the second occasion in October 2025 the place was still empty. The Tenant submitted one colored photo from September 2025 where she saw contractors working in the rental unit through the window. Based on the uncontested evidence from the Tenant I am satisfied that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a difference in rent for a 12-month period. During the hearing the Tenant testified that the rent at her new unit is $2,700.00 which represents an increase of $875.00 a month. The Tenant submitted during the hearing that she paid $1,825.00 for her previous rental unit.

The Tenant testified that it was challenging for her to find and move to another rental unit from her former unit. She submitted that she found another unit 2 blocks away and given the pressure she was under to secure alternative accommodations, she rent this unit as it would minimize the challenges of her relocations. This new rental unit is 3 bedrooms located in a house not far from her previous rental unit. The Landlord put the Tenant in the position that she had to secure housing within a short time frame. Given the Tenant’s circumstances, I find it reasonable and appropriate to find a new unit to e comparable to the former unit. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $10,500.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,548.00. This amount represents: • $10,500.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred / will incur for the one-year period from August 1, 2025, to August 1, 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
