issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'):
reasons: The Tenant’s Representative requested an adjournment because the Tenant’s Representative was unable to reach the Tenant, and the Tenant did not attend the hearing.
The Landlords oppose the Tenant’s request.

The matter was before me on October 1, 2024. The hearing was unable to be concluded at that time. I seized myself and scheduled the matter to return before me on April 15, 2025. However, unfortunately I was unable to attend this date. The matter was adjourned.

The matter was rescheduled for December 5, 2025. At the hearing scheduled December 5, 2025, the parties requested an adjournment on consent because the Tenant had surgery on December 4, 2025. The Tenant submitted a copy of medical documentation in support of the adjournment request.

As the Tenant had medical documentation and the adjournment was requested on consent, I agreed to the Tenant’s adjournment request. At this time, I canvassed the party’s availability taking into consideration a sufficient delay for the Tenant to recover from her surgery. The two Representatives and I agreed to January 30, 2026, at 10:30 a.m. The adjournment sheet included a link to the video conferencing room for the hearing January 30, 2026. The matter was not marked peremptory. 6. [name] says he spoke to the Tenant on January 9, 2026, and gave the Tenant a copy of the Notice of Hearing. During this conversation, it was presumed that the Tenant would be discharged from hospital shortly. On January 27, 2026, the Tenant’s Representative again spoke with the Tenant and learned she had not been discharged from hospital. The Tenant’s Representative requested the Tenant obtain supporting medical documentation if she would not be able to attend the hearing. 7. On January 28, 29, and 30, 2026, the Tenant’s Representative called the Tenant and left messages. However, the Tenant did not respond, and did not attend the hearing. No further medical documentation was submitted. The Tenant’s Representative submits the Board should be able to rely on the previous documentation which had been submitted to support the December 5, 2025, adjournment request. 8. The Landlords point out that the medical documentation did not support a further adjournment request. It speaks to a surgery date on December 4, 2026, and a follow-up appointment, but did not include any information about the Tenant’s ability or inability to participate in the January 30, 2026, hearing. 9. When considering the request for an adjournment, I must consider the following factors as found in the Board’s Rule 21 of the Rules of Procedure and Guideline 1 Adjourning and Rescheduling Hearings: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. 11. The Landlords referred the Board to [name], 2023 ONSC 1028, in which the Divisional Court states at par. 10: “[10] Further, the fresh evidence did not change the result. The doctor’s note is inadequate to justify an adjournment. Courts have made this point, repeatedly, about doctor’s notes. It is the court, not the doctor, who decides whether the adjournment will be granted. Thus, a doctor’s note must obtain sufficient information to enable the court or tribunal to exercise its own judgment as to whether the adjournment should be granted. This should, at a minimum, describe the diagnosis, the effect of the patient’s condition on their ability to attend and participate in the hearing, and a statement as to when, in the doctor’s opinion, the patient will be well enough to attend court and participate as required. In this case, the LTB reconsideration panel was not satisfied that the doctor’s note explained [name] inability to participate in the hearing – either by telephone or by [name] and did not further explain [name] failure to attend to request an adjournment. These are factual findings and are not amenable to appeal in this court.” [Emphasis added] 12. The Landlords also argue that granting a further adjournment would be procedurally unfair to the Landlords because the Tenant’s Representative could have sought, in advance, to request the matter be adjourned. The Landlords referred the Board to the Divisional Court case of Samson v. BCIMC, 2025 ONSC 986 (‘Samson’). Samson stands for the proposition that the individual was well-aware of the hearing date, and that the party had not exercised due diligence to seek an adjournment. 13. For the following reasons, I am not persuaded that a further adjournment is warranted in these circumstances. 14. The Board’s records confirm that the parties were sent a new Notice of Hearing on December 12, 2026. The adjournment sheet included the necessary details for participation at the next hearing date, and all parties agreed to the return date on December 5, 2026. [name] explained he advised his client of the return date on January 9, 2026. 15. Despite the Tenant Representative’s requests that the Tenant provide new medical documentation that would support the Tenant’s inability to participate on January 30, 2026, the Tenant failed to provide this information to her Representative or the Board, nor did the Tenant did not respond to her Representative’s messages or give her Representative instructions. 16. When I consider the reasons for the adjournment request, I am not satisfied that the Tenant exercised due diligence. She was not in attendance, did not respond to her Representative’s messages, or provide the requested supporting medical documents. She was well aware of the hearing having been advised on January 9, 2026. 18. I also find that a further adjournment is prejudicial to the Landlords. The Landlord attended the hearing prepared and expecting to have a resolution in this matter. The Landlord, in good faith, consented to the prior adjournment because of the Tenant’s medical issues. No request to adjourn the matter was made in advance of the hearing date. 19. Given all of the above, I find that the Tenant’s request to adjourn is denied. The Tenant has not attended the hearing to defend her application. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 1810, 7 [address] Vaughan ON [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (‘ACC’) was held by videoconference on May 20, 2026. Only the Tenants, [name] (‘MM’) and [name] (‘HM’), attended the ACC. As of 10:48 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, the application proceeded to an uncontested hearing with only the Tenants' evidence.
reasons: I raised at the hearing that the Tenants’ application contained a number of general statements about issues with the Landlord and provided a vague description of the issues with very few dates. Moreover, many of the issues were not maintenance issues. I explained that this was problematic because an application must contain sufficient particulars so that the responding party understands the case to be met and can prepare a response. In addition, dates such as when the disrepair started and when it was reported to the Landlord are important as there is a one-year limitation period set out in subsection 29(2) of the Act. The limitation period affects whether a remedy may be granted or may limit the period of time for which it may be granted.
The only maintenance issue that was clearly set out with dates and sufficient particulars was the alleged failure to repair the stove in the rental unit.

After raising the aforesaid issues with the Tenants, the Tenants stated that they still wished to proceed with their application based on the stove issue only. Accordingly, the application proceeded regarding the allegation of stove disrepair only.

As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations of stove disrepair. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenants in accordance with the order below. Failure to Maintain/Repair the Stove

MM testified on behalf of the Tenants. A summary of MM’s evidence is as follows: • The rental unit had a stove with four burners and two of the burners did not function properly. Specifically, since 2023 the two larger burners did not maintain a stable temperature during cooking and would often increase in temperature in the middle of cooking unexpectedly, which could not be controlled. As a result, the stove could not be left unattended when the two larger burners were in use. • MM’s mother, who is also a Tenant and a senior, did the majority of the cooking and was forced to work with the two larger burners that weren’t really working properly, which resulted in her experiencing issues with her knees and waist. • On January 28, 2025, MM sent an email to the Landlord and complained about the stove. Specifically, MM stated in the email that the two large burners of the stove needed a safety inspection and a technician to repair it because the temperature of the burners would increase on their own. A copy of the email was tendered as evidence. • The Tenants did not receive a response from the Landlord regarding the complaint about the stove and on February 19, 2025, MM sent a follow up email stating that the Tenants had yet to receive a response or action plan from the Landlord. A copy of the email was tendered as evidence. • On September 16, 2025, the Landlord emailed HM asking if it would be acceptable to have her professional licensed technician inspect the stove. HM responded to the Landlord’s email saying that he would prefer to book an inspector himself, to be at the Landlord’s expense. [name] stated that the Tenants did not want the Landlord’s technician to come because they were the Landlord’s friend and were no longer a licensed technician. This same technician had done other repairs in the rental unit and the Tenants did not feel that he would be able to make the repairs required. A copy of the email correspondence was tendered as evidence. • The Landlord did not agree to cover the costs of technician that HM wanted to schedule to do the repairs. • MM and HM tried addressing this issue with the building manager and made verbal complaints a few times but nothing was done. • As a result of the inaction of the Landlord, MM contacted the municipality and requested an inspection. • An inspector from the municipality inspected the unit on October 1, 2025 and confirmed that the stove was not safe and said that he would be contacting the Landlord regarding the need to repair the stove. The Tenants did not have any correspondence from the inspector or an order to comply from the municipality and were told this could not be provided for privacy reasons. • MM wrote to the building manager on October 3, 2025, to advise of the safety inspection that took place and the findings of the inspector. • Despite the involvement of the municipality, the stove was never fixed and the Tenants were told to just use the two smaller burners on the stove. This was not a reasonable solution for the Tenants as they cooked large meals three times a day and rarely had food prepared outside the home. • The only other solutions offered were for the Tenants to purchase a stove at their own expense or to move out. • On November 28, 2025 the tenants moved out.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain and repair the rental unit, which includes maintaining and repairing the appliances in the unit. The email correspondence provided establishes that the Landlord was advised of the issue with the stove in January 2025 and that this issue remained largely unacknowledged until September 2025. Although the Landlord did try to schedule a technician with the Tenants, the stove was not functioning properly and remained unrepaired up until the Tenants vacated in November 2025.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants’, I find that the Landlord did not respond reasonably. In this regard, the Tenants’ complaints regarding the stove were not responded to in a timely manner. It is not reasonable that it took several months for the Landlord to try and schedule their technician to inspect the stove. When the Tenants did not agree to the technician offered by the Landlord, the other solutions offered by the Landlord, i.e., to buy a new stove themselves or move out, were not reasonable. Remedies

In the application, the Tenants requested a rent abatement in the amount of $33,000.00. As explained at the hearing, as the Tenants were proceeding on the stove issue only, the amount sought was not appropriate and was beyond what the Board could order based on the limitation period. In light of this, the Tenant’s requested a 30% rent abatement for a 12- month period. Period of Abatement

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states that, in determining the remedy under section 30, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.

Although MM testified that she had made verbal complaints about the stove to the building manager in the past, no specifics of these verbal complaints such as dates were provided. Based on the documentary evidence tendered at the hearing, the Landlord was first notified of the issue with the stove on January 28, 2025. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on November 28, 2025. Accordingly, the period for which an abatement would be possible is January 28, 2025 to November 28, 2025, which is 10 months.

That said, it would be unreasonable to expect the Landlord to resolve the stove issue immediately upon learning of it as the issue was not urgent. It is not uncommon for it to take a couple weeks to have issues with appliances addressed and the repairs completed. This is taking into consideration scheduling a technician to assess the issue and making the necessary repairs. In some cases, parts may need to be ordered, which results in the repair taking a bit longer. Accordingly, I find a grace period of two weeks to be appropriate in the circumstance, with the resulting period of abatement being from February 12, 2025 to November 28, 2025, which is 290 days. Percentage of Abatement

While I understand that the two large burners were not functioning as they should, there was no persuasive evidence provided such as a report from an appliance technician or an order from the municipality to suggest that the two large burners were not safe to use or could not be used at all. It was MM’s evidence that her mother continued to use the burners but had to remain present while they were in use. MM acknowledged that the two smaller burners were working and there was no evidence to suggest that there were any issues with the oven.

MM asserted during her evidence that her mother’s knee and waist issues were directly attributable to the amount of time she had to spend monitoring the stove. However, there was no documentary evidence provided from a medical specialist or treating physician to support MM’s assertions. That said, I do accept that the issues with the burners created inconvenience to the Tenants as they prepared most of their food at home and relied on the stove to be able to do so.

That said, I cannot ignore the fact that the Tenants refused to allow the technician of the Landlord’s choosing to inspect and try to repair the stove in September 2025. MM claimed that this is because the technician was just the Landlord’s friend and that he was retired and/or was no longer licensed. The email from the Landlord specifically mentioned that their technician was a licensed technician. In any event, it is not for a tenant to dictate who the Landlord can hire to make repairs. There was also no evidence to suggest that the technician suggested by the Landlord was unqualified other than MM’s bald assertions that he was not.

For the foregoing reasons, I find that the rent abatement of 30% requested to be unreasonable in the circumstances. Based on my experience with similar cases and knowledge of other decisions of the Board, I find a rent abatement of 2% to be appropriate in the circumstances.
Accordingly, the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of $578.81, which is calculated as follows: $3,046.00 x 12 / 365 = $100.14 per day x 290 days = $29,040.60 x 2% = $580.81.

The Tenants had also requested other remedies such as order to repair and an order preventing the Landlord from increasing the rent until the repairs were completed. However, as the Tenants vacated, these remedies are moot and shall not be ordered.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $628.81. This amount represents: • $580.81 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $1,838.59 by February 7, 2026. The Landlords shall also pay an administrative fine to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.00 on or before February 7, 2026. T5 Application

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The rental unit is a semi-detached home with three bedrooms. The Tenants resided in the rental unit from October 15, 2022 to October 30, 2023. At the time the Tenants vacated the rental unit they were paying a monthly rent in the amount of $2,525.60.

The Landlords served an N12 notice of termination on the Tenants which stated that the Landlords in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for themselves, for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year. The N12 Notice stated a termination date of October 31, 2023.

It was undisputed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on October 30, 2023 because the Landlords gave the Tenants a N12 notice of termination claiming the Landlord required possession of the rental unit.

It was also undisputed that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit but advertised the rental unit for rent on or about November 7, 2023 and then entered into a new tenancy agreement for the rental unit within 1 week of the Tenants vacating the rental unit.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenants to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was advertised for rent and entered into a new tenancy within one year of the Tenant vacating creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlords to establish that they served the N12 in good faith. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith 11. With respect to the issue of bad faith, subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. 12. The rebuttable presumption is engaged as it is undisputed that the rental unit was advertised for rent and the Landlords entered into a new tenancy less than a year after the Tenants vacated. 13. The Landlords dispute that the N12 notice was served in bad faith as SN testified that the Landlords intended to move into the rental unit but there was a change of circumstances that lead to the rental unit being advertised and rented in a new tenancy agreement. 14. SN testified that after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Landlord [name] was unable to attain employment near the rental unit. The Landlord [name] resides in [name] and was looking to move in within the rental unit with the other Landlords, however due to not attaining employment, it became apparent that she and the other Landlords would not be able to afford the expenses of the mortgage and utilities. Therefore, the Landlords decided to advertise the rental unit and enter into a new tenancy agreement. The Landlords submitted copies of applications that the Landlord [name] had arranged with potential employers. 15. The Landlord, [name], did not attend to provide testimony on their changed circumstances and there was no evidence presented that showed there were any significant changes of circumstance during the time that the N12 notice was served and when the Landlords were expected to move into the rental unit. In my view, the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith because they failed to move into the rental unit, had advertised the rental unit and entered a new tenancy agreement within a month of the Tenants vacating. The Landlords should have known or ought to have known the requirements of serving an N12 notice, regardless of one Landlord obtaining a job near the rental unit. No explanation was provided as to why the other Landlords could not move in, other than for financial difficulties they may have encountered, and the rental unit was subsequently advertised and re-rented within a month of being vacated. The Landlords should have or ought to have reasonably been able to anticipate the potential of the Landlord, [name], not attaining a position near the rental unit and still have been able to reside within the rental unit when serving the N12 notice onto the Tenants. The circumstances in which the Landlord, [name], was not employed in the area near the rental unit is an unchanged circumstance from when the Landlords had served the Tenants the N12 notice. Therefore, I do not accept the submissions of the change in circumstances as the reason for the Landlords not moving into the rental unit. 16. In all of the circumstances, and in light of the reverse onus that applies, I find that the Landlords served the notice of termination in bad faith and the Tenants’ application must be granted. Remedies Rent abatement 17. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that rent is charged in exchange for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving those goods and services then the rent should be abated in a sum proportional to the difference between what is being charged and what is being received. 18. There was no evidence before me to suggest that Tenants use of the rental unit was diminished or hindered by the Landlords while they were still residing in the rental unit. While the Tenants submitted that this is due to the Landlords provided the N12 Notice in bad faith and should get reimbursement for a year’s worth of rent, the remedy is sought in general compensation. For these reasons, the request for rent abatement is denied. Administrative Fine 19. The Tenants are requesting that the Landlords be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligation. 20. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 21. The Landlords served an N12 notice asserting a good faith intention to occupy the rental unit, failed to move into the unit, and instead re-advertised and re-rented the rental unit within a short period of time. Despite the reverse onus imposed by section 57 of the Act, the Landlords failed to provide a credible explanation for their non-compliance as none of the circumstances at the time of serving the N12 notice changed. 22. I find that the Landlords in the present case has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and the monetary remedies of $1,838.59 being awarded, in my view, will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Therefore, I find that the Tenants’ request for an administrative fine is appropriate in all of the circumstances. An administrative fine of $2,500.00 will be imposed. Rent Differential 23. The Tenants were renting a detached house from the Landlord and the Tenants had access to the entire house. The rental unit was 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms and was equipped with a kitchen, and access to the basement. 24. The new rental unit was a detached house from the new landlord and the Tenants had access only to two floors. The rental unit was 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms and was equipped with a kitchen, and access to a basement. The Tenants had testified that this rental unit is similar. 25. In considering a rent differential, the Board must consider whether the rental units are comparable, not exact. I find that the two rental units are comparable. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to their request for a rent differential. 26. The Tenants monthly rent was $2,525.60 at their old unit and $2,550.00 at the new rental unit. The Tenant is entitled to rent differential for a 12-month period. Given the additional bedroom in comparison of the total rooms of the old unit to the new unit, the tenant is entitled to 100% of the rent differential, which amounts to $292.80 ($2,550.00- $2,525.60=$24.40 x 100% x 12 months). Moving Expenses 27. The Tenants claimed $1,097.79 in moving expenses. The Tenants testified that she incurred the following costs: • Moving Pod rental: $733.26 • Boxes/Paper: $100.00 • Gas: $160.00 • Mail forwarding: $104.53 28. The Tenants sought to withdraw their Boxes/ Papers moving expense. The Landlords did not oppose, I granted the amendment. 29. The Tenant submitted receipts and financial statements for the moving pod rental, the gas receipts and the mail forwarding receipts. I find the costs of $997.79 which represents the moving pod rental, the gas and the mail forwarding reasonable for moving 4 adults from a three-bedroom rental unit to another rental unit. The Landlords will be ordered to compensate the Tenants for these expenses. General Compensation 30. The Tenants seek general compensation in accordance with section 57(3)(1.1), in the amount of $1,904.95. It is important to note that as referenced in the Act, an order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the Tenants have incurred any actual expenses. However, in determining a reasonable quantum I must consider the impact this bad faith eviction had on the Tenants. 31. The Tenants testified that they have had financial hardships from increasing the rent from $2,525.60 to $2,550.00 per month, finding a different rental unit that was similar in space and the impact of moving 30 kilometres away from the community had impacted negatively. The Tenants claimed the general compensation of $1,904.95 due to disruption and stress. While I accept that the eviction caused disruption and stress, general compensation must be reasonable and grounded in the evidence before the Board. The Tenants did not provide documentary evidence establishing financial losses but mention 2 of the 4 Tenants must travel 40 kms extra for work. I accept this evidence as credible and find that the increased commuting distance reasonably results in ongoing inconvenience and additional expense. In all of the circumstances, and taking into account the discretionary nature of general compensation under subsection 57(3)(1.1) of the Act, I find that an award of $500.00 is reasonable and appropriate. The Landlords will be ordered to compensate the Tenants for these expenses. Other remedies 32. In submissions, the Tenants argued that while landlords are entitled to rely on an N12 notice, the misuse of such notices should be strongly penalized. The Tenants submitted that the Landlords’ conduct caused both financial and emotional hardship and urged the Board to impose consequences that would deter similar conduct in the future. I understand these submissions to be a request for an administrative fine which was granted, therefore the other remedies requested is dismissed. 33. The Landlords shall pay $48.00 to the Tenants for the cost of filing this application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,838.59. This amount represents: • $292.80 for increased rent the Tenants have for the one-year period from November 1, 2023 up to and including October 31, 2024. • $997.79 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 7, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.00 on or before February 7, 2026. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $39,048.00. Notice for Landlord’s own use

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Section 57(5) of the Act provides: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. [Emphasis added]

The Tenant moved out of the rental uni t on June 30, 2024 because the Landlord’s agent, [name], advised that the Landlord wanted to move into the rental unit. On September 10, 2024 the unit was listed for sale and it was sold on October 4, 2024. Accordingly, the reverse onus provisions of section 57(5) of the Act apply.
As the Landlord did not attend the hearing to rebut the presumption of bad faith, I find that the Landlord gave a notice in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant lived in the rental unit with the s pouse, their spouse’s parent, and their child. All three adults were named tenants on the lease. The primary characteristics of the rental unit were 5 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms, parking for 4 cars, an upper deck, and an outdoor area.
The Tenant could not find another unit to acco mmodate all family members, so they had to live separately; the Tenant, their spouse and child in one unit, and the spouse’s parent separately.

The Tenant moved into a 3-bedroom, 1 bathr oom unit with parking for 3 cars, a deck, and no other outdoor space. The rent for the unit is $2,750.00. The spouse’s parent had to relocate to a different community to find an affordable unit, which was a 1 bed/1bath apartment with a monthly rent of $2,100.00. In total the Tenants are paying an additional $3,150.00 per month in rent for smaller and less functional accommodations, or $37,800.00 over a 12-month period. The family members have been disadvantaged by having to live separately. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $37,800.00 for general compensation.

The Tenant spent $1,200.00 to move their fam ily members into new rental units. While no receipts were provided, I find the Tenant’s oral testimony to be credible and the amount claimed to be within the range of expenses often claimed at the Board.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,200.00 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the [name] ord shall pay the Tenant is $39,048.00. This amount represents:  $1,200.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.  $37,800.00 for general compensation.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by March 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘MD’) and [name] (‘RD’) (collectively, the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards and that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment, harassed the Tenant, and interfered with the supply of vital services.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the following allegations contained in the application.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant 2,069.98. Tenant’s evidence Hydro
The Tenant relied on document 7432520 in TOP.

She testified that Hydro and utilities were included in her rent based on an additional flat fee of $125.00. She pays the Landlord $1,550 a month which includes this flat fee. This arrangement was previously confirmed by the Board in order LTB-L-090247-24. This order was issued in July 2025. It was never appealed or reviewed.
The Landlord failed to pay the Hydro account leading to Hydro being disconnected. This happened 8 to 9 times since 2021. The Tenant lost her fridge contents every time.

The most recent interruption took place on June 2, 2025 and this is the one raised in this application. The Tenant had to pay the full bill to have Hydro restored instead of paying $125 to the Landlord.
The Tenant received a letter from the electricity provider, Enova.

Page 28 of the Tenant’s document package contains proof of her payment of $733.36 to Enova on June 6, 2025. The Tenant lost her food and was unable to enjoy her daily life without electricity. She has two children and their lives were seriously disrupted.
Page 29 of her document package contains a proof of her payment of $288.62 to Enova on September 22, 2025.
Page 30 contains a copy of her proof of payment of $125.00 on October 29th and page 31 contains proof of her payment of $125 on December 23rd, 2025.
All bills are addressed to the Landlord.
She testified that she paid $250 to Enova on February 23rd towards the total balance owing of some $800. There is no proof of payment, but this evidence was uncontroverted.

She has a hard time confirming exact amounts owing to Enova because the bill is not in her name. She similarly does not get notified before her power is disconnected so she has simply been making payments. Furnace and AC

The Tenant had issues with her AC and figured that the furnace would also not work. She communicated with various authorities about it. The Tenant claims that there is no air flowing through vents and the issue began around August 5, 2025. She testified that she immediately notified the Landlord of the issue but provided no corroborating evidence.

The Tenant filed many photos of temperature readings. She explained that she has an industrial thermometer intended to be used for a restaurant freezer. It has two sensors. One was placed in the kitchen, and one was in her bedroom. Pages 7 to 26 of her document package contain photos of thermometer readings between October 3, 2025 and January 2026. The thermostat is set to 22 but temperature readings are as low as 0 and often range in mid teens for the kitchen and 18-20 in the bedroom. The Tenant started using space heaters around November.
The Tenant hired an HVAC company. They attended at the property on January 27th, 2026, spent 2 hours and the property and provided a report that starts on page 37 of her document package.

Page 39 contains the following findings: “Tenant says the heat is not working well and has poor airflow. Furnace ran with one filter for 4 years, and for the last few years has had no filter. Visual inspection reveals a lot of rust, there is some on the blower wheel, on the cabinet, on the left of the inducer motor, and on the top of the furnace. The AC drain is leaking onto the top of the furnace. We inspected the furnace with an inspection camera. Found small rust spots all over the heat exchanger but no major cracks or holes. We found the evaporator coil is covered in dust which is restricting airflow Performed a combustion analysis on the flue gas, got 26 PPM. Temp rise is 47.7deg”. [emphasis added]

Page 41 contains recommendations: “Furnace should always have a clean filter, as per manufacturers instructions it should not run without one. Evaporator coil needs to be cleaned and the furnace should have a maintenance done.” I note that it does not recommend any specific or major repairs.

The Tenant testified that she alerted the Landlord to the issue as early as 2022. At that time, she heard unusual sounds from the furnace and figured that it needed to be looked at. She made an incredible statement that the furnace filter weighed 50 pounds due to dust build-up when it was removed. The 2022 application is still ongoing.

Page 63 contains a photo of the evaporator coil. According to the Tenant it shows that there is a complete wall of mold, mildew and debris in the furnace and only a small part can be penetrated by air flow. I do not find that the photo speaks for itself and not expert testified at the hearing.

The Tenant paid $122.04 for the inspection. The invoice can be found on page 68 of her document package. It indicates that a friends and family discount was applied. She explained that this discount was given to her because she found the company through Facebook.

The Tenant called this technician after the Landlord called a technician on January 21st. She observed that the technician was only at the property for 15 minutes and expected their report to be inadequate as a result. She decided it was best to call her own expert.

The Tenant filed video evidence as well (documents 6814737, 6814740, 6814759, and 6814768). In these videos she tests the air flow by placing a napkin on a vent. The napkin does not move, which she argues, proves that there is no air flow. She also narrates the temperature readings. I note that her own narrations make me question the accuracy of her thermometer readings. She can be heard explaining that the house is warm while her thermometer shows 12 or 13 degrees as one of the two readings.
She explained that the Landlord also called a house inspector to attend at the property on October 31st. The inspector was there for approximately 45 minutes. He was not a qualified HVAC technician.

Document 6855261 contains a copy of the Landlord’s inspection report. Some parts are reproduced below [emphasis added]: • Annual heating cooling insurance maintenance plan recommended. 2011 carrier installed Recommended tune up service technician call ,filter cap and filter missing , [name] and wall area around clean up remedy recommended , Noisy vibration sound further review of safety test from technician recommended , At the time of inspection room temperature 20 C* thermostat set for 25 C* • Basement. the heating furnace temperature in satisfactory, Furnace blower is functioning properly. • Limitations Determining winter comfort with specific areas is beyond the scope of a visual inspection. The heat exchanger is concealed within the furnace and cannot be reviewed. Adequacy of air flow/cooling/heating performance not determined.

Document 7482700 is a report that resulted from the Landlord’s technician’s attendance in January 2026. The Tenant takes issue with the report because of how brief the inspection was and that the report itself does not indicate the furnace type, the writer’s technician number or anything else of the sort. The technician did not leave a sticker on the furnace indicating that the furnace had been inspected. I agree. Landlord’s evidence

RD testified that he had the furnace inspected twice and no major issues were found. He asked to be informed if any actions were required and no major actions were recommended. He relies on documents 7482700, 7430087, and 7430078 which were generated by the inspector who attended in January 2026. I note that the inspection report itself is a simple unsigned letter with a visible artefact above the logo of “warmice heating and cooling”. It differs greatly from what I usually see in similar applications. I will not give this report any weight for these reasons along with the issues the Tenant herself had highlighted.
RD testified that the basement was built with permits (7123688) and in accordance with all applicable laws and standards in 2022.

He paid $352.57 to Enova on or about February 2, 2026. He says the Landlord has been paying the bills. He provided document 7430311 which is a screenshot of his utility account showing consumption of water and sewer. It is difficult to understand how this establishes that he paid Enova bills.
He testified about hiring an inspector. The inspector’s report is addressed above. This was a top-notch inspector, and RD was never told to fix the furnace.

He testified that the Tenant raised some of these issues in LTB-L-054609-25. The Tenant’s representative pointed out that the order was less than 30 days old and that the Tenant may consider requesting a review or otherwise challenging this order.
As of the date of writing this order file LTB-L-054609-25 has no record to indicate that it is being appealed or reviewed. It is now more than 30 days old.

Paragraph 34 of the order reads: “Although the Tenant alleged that the gas furnace provided inadequate heat and the Landlords were not paying the hydro bill, she admitted that there was heat in the unit and that she was paying the hydro bills and deducting that amount from the rent.” This statement is made under the header of “relief from eviction”, and I do not read it as a final determination of any issues that is raised in this application. It appears to be intended to address potential mandatory relief from eviction [name]) of the Act.

The Landlord filed proof of payment of various other bills. These bills don’t prove that Enova was paid but RD argues that an inference should be made from high utility usage that furnace was working adequately.

On cross-examination RD was questioned about his assertion that the inspections did not reveal any issues. He reiterated that even though the temperature was 20 while the thermostat was set to 25, the conclusions in the report was that no work needed to be done.

He was asked about the recommendation for a tune-up that can be found in the inspection report. RD argued that him sending a technician in January 2026 represented his attempt to tune up the furnace as recommended. He asked the inspector to fix anything that may have been wrong with the furnace and he was told that everything weas fine. He was unable to explain how his corroborating videos show that a furnace is working adequately.

RD was questioned about Enova bills and asked to explain how paying other bills prove that he paid Enova. He did not provide a satisfactory reply. He claimed that he was unsure whether Enova was separate from Kitchener utilities. He said that MD has a better understanding of this issue as she is the one who pays utility bills.

MD provided a brief testimony about the bills. She explained that the Tenant started paying $125 a month directly to Enova instead of paying it to the Landlord. The Landlord has therefore stopped paying Enova. There was never a disconnection that she was aware of. Analysis and findings
This is the Tenant’s application, and she bears the burden of proof in establishing her allegations on a balance of probabilities.

I find that she has established that it is more likely than not that the Landlord has failed to pay Enova and she has been paying Enova instead. The Landlord did not ultimately contradict this assertion, and her evidence was persuasive and well corroborated.

I also find that the power was discounted in June 2025. The Tenant provided credible testimony to this effect and said testimony was not challenged or undermined through cross-examination. The Landlord made a vague statement to the contrary and provided hearsay evidence that they may have been told that there was no disconnection. The Landlord’s evidence on this point was weak and uncorroborated. The utility account is in the Landlord’s name, and they are in the best position to provide proof of account status as any disconnection would have been reflected in the records. The Landlord failed to provide this evidence, and I draw a negative inference from the lack of this evidence.
I do not find that the Tenant established her allegations in relation to the HVAC system.

Her photographic evidence and testimony are inconsistent with her own narration in her videos. She states that the house is warm when the temperature reading is very low. The “napkin” test is entirely unpersuasive Air flow may be weak or temporarily paused even if the heating system functions perfectly.

The Tenant’s own report does not corroborate the Tenant’s claim that the furnace has major issues or that there was almost no heat at all. A report containing minor recommendations is not unusual. If anything, it would be unusual for an HVAC technician not to recommend some further work even for a well functioning furnace. The Tenant has no real explanation for the Landlord’s inspection report other than to claim that the inspector is not an expert. I note that the Tenant called no experts to testify. She filed only one expert report that she obtained months after the alleged issues began and that does not corroborate the extent of the issues she claims even though it was made during the coldest time of the year.

The Tenant’s evidence adduced at the hearing does not contain any evidence that the Tenant notified the Landlord of the lack of heat. The Landlord clearly became aware at some point, but there is no record to establish when the Tenant brought the issue to the Landlord’s attention, or that the issue was raised again after the inspection in October 2025. There is no record to support her testimony that the Landlord was made aware of any AC issues. Even the Tenant’s own testimony was rather vague and contained no dates other than 2022.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
It was incumbent on the Tenant to notify the Landlord of the alleged issues and to lead evidence corroborating her testimony about notifying the Landlord at the hearing.

The Landlord’s evidence other than the inspection report of October 2025 was similarly unpersuasive but it is hard to prove a negative, i.e. that there was no issue with the heat, especially where is no record that the issue was brought to their attention after they inspected the rental unit in October 2025.

It would appear that the HVAC system was not working perfectly, but I do not find that the Tenant established that it is more likely than not that the heat or air conditioning were ever inadequate. If they were, I am unable to find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord ought to be held liable in accordance with Onyskiw. Remedies

I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent of $500 for the impact the electricity disconnection had on her in June 2025. I accept her testimony that she had to throw out food and had to struggle to run her household when electricity was disconnected.
I also find that the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of her payments to Enova totalling $1,521.98 as set out above.

The Landlord should change Enova into their name but as the tenancy was terminated by the LTB in a final manner effective March 31, 2026 by order LTB-L-054609-25-HR, I find that it is not necessary for me to order the Landlord to do so.
I do not find that the Tenant established entitlement to any other remedies as she did not establish the corresponding claims of lack of heat/AC that would support entitlement to such remedies.
The Tenant incurred a cost of $48.00 in filing this application and I find that she is entitled to a reimbursement of this cost as she was substantially successful.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,069.98. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement for June 2025, • $1,521.98 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ouardi (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $548.00 which represents rent abatement and the application filing fee.

The Tenant alleges the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations by failing to respond to a water leak in the bathroom in a reasonable timeframe.

The Tenant moved in on August 15, 2025. On August 18, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord’s Agent [name] by text that there was an issue with the ventilation in the bathroom as there was a wide open vent that would not close. The Tenant indicates that there was water pooling in the vent and at times would drip from the vent right on the toilet.

On August 23, 2025, the Tenant sends a message in the maintenance portal indicating he has not had a response to his maintenance request. On August 25, 2025, the Landlord’s property manager [name] responded to the Tenant and advised that a technician would attend the rental unit. On August 31, 2025, the Tenant reached out again to the property manager as he had yet to be contacted by a technician.

On September 20, 2025, a technician from [name] attended the rental unit and said that this was not a ventilation issue, that it is a plumbing issue, and as such the maintenance issue was not repaired.

On September 23, 2025, the Tenant contacted the property manager to once again inquire about the water leak as it still was not repaired. The property manager responds on September 24, 2025 that 613 Plumbing will contact the Tenant to arrange an appointment. October 1 and on October 6, 2025, the Tenant contacts the property manager again to advise no one has contacted him. In the October 6, 2025 message to the property manager the Tenant says that this is a serious issue as urine is leaking from the ceiling directly in the toilet and that this is a health and safety concern.

On October 8, 2025, the property manager responds and says once again that 613 Plumbing will contact the Tenant to make an appointment. On October 13, 2025, the part of the ceiling where the vent was located and where the water was leaking from completely collapsed and fell on top of the toilet, shower area, and bathroom floor. The Tenant contacted the property manager to advise what had happened and placed urgency on the issue and wanted someone to attend the rental unit and contact him that day but no one did. It was not until October 20, 2025, that the water leak was repaired. On October 23, 2025, the ceiling was repaired. The Tenant believes the only reason why the issue was fixed was because he called the City’s Property Standards Inspector who became involved and contacted the Landlord about the issue.

The Tenant says he had to clean every day due to the water leak and the urine dripping on the toilet and that as of October 6, 2025, the smell was intolerable. The Tenant says that for 3-4 days the Tenant was unable to use his own bathroom because as of October 6, 2025 there was a constant drip of the urine coming from the ceiling so that that if he used the bathroom the urine would drip on him. The Tenant relied on neighbors during this time to use the bathroom.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative does not dispute the facts that repairs had to be done and were completed, however submits that the Landlord responded and completed the maintenance issues in a timely manner. The Landlord did not attend to provide evidence to respond to the allegations against them. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance obligations.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

What this means is that just because there is a maintenance issue, this does not mean that the Landlord is in automatic breach of the Act. The breach occurs when the Landlord fails to respond in a reasonable manner to the maintenance issue.

The evidence before me is that the Tenant contacted the Landlord numerous times starting August 18, 2025 regarding the bathroom vent and water leak and this issue was not rectified until October 20, 2025. The Tenant even placed an urgent message on October 6, 2025 to the Landlord explaining urine was leaking from the ceiling and that this was a health and safety issue. The Landlord failed to take any reasonable steps to address the issue and because of that the bathroom ceiling collapsed on October 13, 2025. The Tenant believes that it was only after he called the City after the ceiling collapsed to report the issue that the Landlord then did something about it. As the Landlord was not present, there was no explanation as to why there may have been a delay. As such, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to respond to and repair the water leak in a timely manner. Remedies

The Tenant is requesting $1,650.00 in rent abatement for the period from August 15, 2025 to October 15, 2025. The monthly rent is $1,600.00 which means the rent abatement requested is approximately 50% of his monthly rent.

There is no magic formula in awarding rent abatement. As noted in Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name] [[1997] O.J. No 1881 ([name])], a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], the Court remarked: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances…

Similarly, in Offredi v. [organization], the Divisional Court found there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate abatement can be determined. [1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC), 116 DLR (4th) 757 ([name])]

A rent abatement is meant to compensate the tenant to the degree that the tenant was deprived of what was bargained for or what is prescribed by legislation or minimum housing standards. It is only when a tenant is completely deprived of all of the benefits of a tenancy—where the rental unit is, for example, uninhabitable and cannot even be used for storage—that a 100% abatement is appropriate.

As noted by the Vice Chair in TST-56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

A rent abatement can be in the form of a lump sum or based on a percentage of the rent payable by the tenant for a past period and the Board can award an abatement against future rent. [See Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC)]

I am not satisfied the Tenant is entitled to a $1,650.00 rent abatement. The Tenant’s initial complaint started on August 18, 2025, and in the beginning the effect on the Tenant due to the maintenance issue was minimal as at that time the leak was minimal. During that time, the Tenant was still able to use all areas of the rental unit including the bathroom, although I acknowledge the Tenant had to clean the leaking water and this caused inconvenience. On October 6, 2025, the Tenant sends a more urgent request to the Landlord to repair the issue as the leak was persistent and had increased, and because of this the Tenant was unable to use the washroom for 3-4 days and had to use the neighbors. The Tenant had no access to the toilet, but did have access to the other areas of his rental unit. As such, I am going to order a lump sum rent abatement in the amount of $500.00 for the Landlord’s breach in failing to maintain and repair the rental unit in a timely manner.
The Tenant is also entitled to the application filing fee. As such, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant the $48.00 application filing fee.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending October 22, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the rent that is due on June 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
