issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. AND [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proved the allegations in part as contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,784.75 as outlined in this order. Background
The Tenant occupies the middle unit, within a detached home which is also referred to as unit # 1 by the Landlord, in a three-unit dwelling at 12 George Street West, Havelock, Ontario.
The tenancy commenced on May 15, 2015, the Tenant is a single parent to a three-year-old child.

The monthly rent is $691.87, with heat included and hydro separately metered and paid by the Tenant. The Tenant filed the T6 (maintenance) and T2 (tenant rights) applications with the LTB on October 15, 2026 and amendment on October 31, 2025 for claims alleging ongoing maintenance issues and a pattern of interference and harassment.

The Landlord’s property manager [name] (SA) confirmed review of the amended application and there was a Certificate of Service (CoS) filed with the Board to confirm service of the amendment to the Landlord.

The T2application alleges the following: a) Entry demands with incorrect purpose, refusal to reasonably reschedule, and threats to involve police; (b) Photographing the Tenant’s personal effects during entry and privacy breach by posting the unit online with a photo capturing the Tenant’s child (c) Withholding/interfering with vital services (heat); (d) Bad-faith eviction attempts, including N12 notices while advertising the unit at higher rent; (e) Discriminatory posting of rental ads. Illegal entry

On March 28, 2025, the Landlord served a notice of entry citing maintenance and inspection When the Tenant indicated she was hosting her child’s third birthday gathering and asked to reschedule and to clarify the purpose and unit, the Landlord refused and warned police would attend if entry was not allowed.

On March 29, 2025, the Landlord entered and immediately began photographing the Tenant’s belongings despite the Tenant’s objections, including regarding the bedroom. The visit culminated in the delivery of an N12 and the Tenant being advised that the place had sold.
The Tenant submitted that she believed 24 hours notice was provided based on the timing of the email in which the notice to enter was contained. The law

Section 27 provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry in the following circumstances: • to carry out a repair or replacement or to do work in the unit; • to allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit; • to allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998; • to carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the RTA; and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. • for any other reasonable reason for entry set out in the tenancy agreement. In addition, s. 27(2) of the RTA provides that the landlord, or, with the landlord's written authorization, a broker or salesperson registered under the Real Estate and Business Brokers Act, 2002, may enter a rental unit provided that they have given written notice to the tenant at least 24 hours before they enter to allow a potential purchaser to view the unit. In any case where at least 24 hours written notice has been given to the tenant, the written notice must set out: • the reason for entry; • the date the landlord will enter; and • the time of entry between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.

In the case before me, while the Landlord provided sufficient notice to enter, the notice was not entirely for the reasons as outlined. As evidenced, the Landlord attended at the rental unit to inspect the property while also taking photos and subsequently serving the Tenant an N12 notice for purchasers use. 12. (SA) the landlord’s agent submitted that the notice of entry as issued was for purposes of a unit inspection and that 24 hours notice was provided. 13. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally. While not being forthcoming about the intended service of the N12, the Landlord did provide a compliant notice and inspected the property. Therefore, no remedy shall be considered in this regard. Harassment and substantial interference Photos/ internet posting 14. The Tenant submitted that on the basis of her fiancés passing and connected circumstances, the fact that the Landlord took photos of the rental unit and property grounds in which the Tenant’s young child is seen and was used by Landlord to advertise the rental unit created a breach of her security. And that the photos were taken without consent. A photo of the ad as posted on Kijiji by the Landlord contains an image of the Tenant’s daughter in the yard of the rental property. 15. [name] or video recordings taken by a landlord within a rental unit and without the consent of the Tenant are not specifically regulated under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. While s. 27 speaks to a landlord’s rights to enter, it does not specifically address the issue of entry for the purpose of photographs. The Divisional Court has previously stated that the fact that a landlord taking photographs does not, by itself, constitute an infringement of a tenant’s privacy rights. It would only constitute an infringement if it was done for an improper purpose. The Court also specifically approved of a landlord entering a rental unit pursuant to a notice of entry for the purpose of taking photographs to be used in defence of an application brought by a tenant before the Board. ([name] v. Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management, 2015 ONSC 3893 (CanLII)). 16. In Juhasz v Hymas, 2016 ONSC 1650 (CanLII), the landlord’s realtor wanted to take photographs of the interior of the unit for the purpose of the sale of the property. The tenant refused entry on the ground because photographs of her and her children’s personal possessions would be disseminated to the public via the internet to advance the sale of the property. The Court found that in those circumstances taking photographs of a person’s home and personal belongings without their consent and posting these photographs on the internet clearly infringes privacy interests. The Court distinguished these facts from [name] on the basis that a privacy interest was clearly engaged. 17. The Court added in Juhasz v Hymas that where there is no specific clause in the tenancy agreement allowing for photographs, parties are free to work out a mutually, agreeable accommodation to address a tenant’s privacy concerns. For instance, photographs can be altered/ cropped to delete the visibility of personal items belonging to the tenant. Alternatively, personal items could be moved at the landlord’s expense to facilitate photographs being taken that would not infringe privacy interests. 18. Here, the Tenant submits that no consent was given for the Tenants child and bedroom photos to be taken by the Landlord. She made her objection known. I find that this circumstance most resembles the fact in the [name] case. In this case, the Landlord was taking the photos for purpose of an internet advertising, and as outlined above, The Court found that in those circumstances taking photographs of a person’s home and personal belongings without their consent and posting these photographs on the internet clearly infringes privacy interests. I therefore find the actions of the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant and infringed on her privacy as a result of the photos being taken and the subsequent posting of the photos on the internet for public access. Issuance of N12 notices/ threats to move out 19. The Tenant submitted that the Landlord has sent her a number of messages in which she is asked to move out, issuing various N12 notices, for Landlord’s own use and then for purchasers use. On page 49 of DOC-6702639 the Tenant evidenced a message in which the Landlord outlined that the property was sold and that she needed to move out. 20. The Tenant submitted that as of the date of the hearing, the unit was not sold based on public facing records as available to the Tenant for review. The tenant was issued an N12 for purchasers use with the date of termination of May 31, 2025. 21. In one text change the Landlord states” the place is sold you will be out sooner or later.” When the Tenant replies that the issue of access to heat can not be extinguished by threats, and asks “kindly fix my heat,” the Landlord replies, “the place is sold owner will move in papers are filles [name] is also changing I am being generous to offer you $2,000.00 for you to move on if not Tenant bimirad will move you guys out.” 22. Harassment can be defined as a course of conduct that a person knows, or should know, would be unwelcome by the other person. It is clear to me on the evidence that the Landlord understood that his sending the Tenant a notice of termination was irritating and an unwanted course of contact by the Tenant, especially where the tone suggested there were repercussions. So, while it is in the Landlord’s lawful right to issue notices, I find that the conduct of the Landlord in the course of issuing the notices and communicating with the Tenant are harassing in nature. 23. As I have found that the Landlord has been issuing N12 notices and communicating with the Tenant in a manner that can be perceived to be harassing and threatening, and that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant and infringed on her privacy as a result of the photos taken and posted on the internet, the Tenant will be awarded a combined claim of $1,000.00 in this regard. Discriminatory advertising of rental unit 24. The Tenant evidenced the Landlord’s online posting for one of the other rental units in which it was outlined that Indian or Punjabi students are preferred. The Ontario Human Rights Code, subsection 2(1) provides that everyone has the right to equal treatment with respect to housing, without discrimination because of race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed (religion), sex (including pregnancy, gender identity), sexual orientation, age, marital status, family status, disability, or the receipt of public assistance. Therefore, making it unlawful for landlords to reject tenants based on the outlined grounds. 25. While the Tenant has not alleged discrimination she has claimed in the application the consideration of a fine to be imposed upon the Landlord for his conduct as towards her and in the way he carries on his business in the capacity of landlord. As evidenced on pages 53-55 the Landlord posted a discriminatory ad on Kijiji making his preference known for students of Indian or Punjabi ethnic groups. 26. (SA) testified that the Landlord hired an external company do his advertising and that they asked that the ad be removed. 27. Given that the Landlord did not attend and I had no benefit of hearing from them as to the ad’s intentions and who the drafter was, while not imposing a fine, I am hopeful that the Landlord will take the time to educate himself in respect of the rental laws in Ontario and relevant legislation to prevent any future claims of discriminatory conduct as against himself or in his capacity as a landlord. Vital services 28. The Tenant testified that heat has been restored to the rental unit on or about Thursday of the prior week, this would be November 6, 2025 and that this is the same pattern of behaviour as in the past year where heat was restored just before another hearing was to take place. 29. The Tenant submitted that the Landlord turned off the heat in an effort to evict her, that she was told that “I need to move out” and to use an electric heater on October 3 and 9, 2025 when she complained of not having heat. A text correspondence was sent to the Landlord and the Landlord replied that “you’ve been given a notice, please consider that.” The Landlord attempted to negotiate a move out date and suggested a $2,000.00 payment to move out. 30. In evidence the Tenant submitted that she has been without heat since September 1, 2025, and that heat had been restored on or about November 6, 2025. This represents a 66 day period in during which the Tenant had no gas/ a primary source of heat in the rental unit. 31. In the year prior the Tenant submitted that she was without heat from October 16, 2024 to about December 1, 2024, coinciding with the prior LTB hearing date, the Tenant was not entirely sure but stated a few days before December 4, 2024. The claim from October 16, 2024 is reflective of the one year claim limitation as prescribed by the Act. 32. The Tenant claims a rent abatement of 30% for 49 days for the period of October 16, 2024 to about December 4, 2024 and 66 days for the period of September 1, 2025 to November 6, 2025. 33. The Tenant submitted that it was very cold in the rental unit and noting that she has a young child not having heat was of significant concern. Especially since this was an ongoing issue that had carried over from the year prior where she had found herself dealing with not having any heat again. By-law enforcement had been contacted. 34. The Landlord’s property manger [name] (SA) testified the reason there was no heat was because there was a technical issue with the furnace. That the furnace needed to be replaced and was installed in 2024, that this took a longer time because of a shortage of qualified technicians in the area. The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence to support the installation of a new furnace. 35. Additionally, that the Landlord’s bookkeeping staff did not address the payment of the gas bill on time sometime in 2025, therefore posing issues of the utility being disconnected. I find SA’s testimony provided insufficient details to explain the delay to restore the gas. 36. An abatement recognizes the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. Considering the impact on the Tenant, I find that the request is appropriate. 37. The lawful rent is $691.87. Based on the monthly rent, the per diem rate is $22.75. This amount is calculated as follows: $691.87x 12, divided by 365 days. 38. The total amount of rent for 115 days is $2,615.84. Based on the Tenant’s request of a 30% rent abatement, I find the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $784.75. T6 Application 39. The T6 application alleges the following: • No heat for extended periods across successive winters due to an unrepaired furnace; • Rodent (mice) infestation; and • Leaking kitchen sink, which the Tenant repaired herself/ personal cost 40. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Lack of Heat 41. The Tenant submitted that the lack of heat has already been addressed in that heat has been restored on or about November 6, 2025. 42. Therefore, the abatement of rent as addressed under the T2 portion of the application is awarded in consideration of this issue. [name] infestation 43. The Tenant submitted that the Landlord blocked his phone number, she was not able to contact him and while she is aware of other property managers as contacts she did not advise anyone else about this issue. That she has a cat and dog and they assist with catching of any mice, and that current day there have not been any sightings. 44. As the Tenant did not adduce any evidence to support a mice infestation and submitted that the issue was not reported to the Landlord and or his agent(s), this matter can not be considered. Kitchen sink 45. The Tenant claims for out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $230.00 that the Tenant incurred for a burst pipe and tap replacement. She came home to find a burst pipe and needed to replace the kitchen tap, the tap was replaced and she paid a friend to install it. 46. The Tenant did not notify the Landlord of this issue, as noted at the time of the hearing for this reason this claim can not be considered. Remedies 47. While the Tenant requested that the Landlord be responsible for repairs of the maintenance issues as alleged, as of the date of the hearing there are no outstanding issues as outlined in the application. And as the Tenant also sought the remedy that no rent increases be permitted until all issues are addressed, noting that this remedy is also connected to outstanding maintenance issues and there are none, no remedies will be considered. 48. Additionally, the Tenant seeks $6,000.00 in general damages for mental distress under “Other” remedies. 49. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant has provided sufficient evidence for consideration of general damages. The Tenant has had to endure two years of heat interruption, and when the issue of not having adequate heat was addressed with the Landlord, he did not respond in a manner which suggested concern, he simply stated that the Tenant has been issued a notice and “to move out”, as evidenced. I accept the Tenant’s submissions that the Landlord used these means in an effort to get her to move out voluntarily. While the Tenant claims $6,000.00 for damages as arsing from the Landlord’s conduct, I find that a lump sum of $1,000.00 to be a reasonable in this regard. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants a lump sum compensation accordingly. 50. Lastly, the Tenant requested that the Landlords pay a fine to the LTB. Guideline 16 of the Landlords and Tenant Board Interpretation Guidelines states under purpose, that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the LTB to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 51. Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the Landlord blatantly disregarded the Act and as outlined earlier, I trust the Landlord will take the time and familiarize himself with the laws governing tenancies in Ontario. I am satisfied that the remedies as ordered will provide adequate deterrence and ensure future compliance by the Landlord. 52. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,784.75. This amount represents: • $1 ,784.75 for a rent abatement of rent and • $1,000.00 in compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount of $300.00 from the lawful monthly rent owing until the amount is fully paid off.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (T1 application), and that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household and further the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background to the tenancy and the T1;T2 application.

The tenancy began on August 1, 2025. The monthly rent was $1,250.00 payable on the first of the month. The Tenants testified that they moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2025. The Tenants provided the Landlord a deposit for the last month’s rent in the amount of lawful rent, as evidence by the submitted documentary evidence.
The Tenants testified they were model Tenants and entered a fixed term lease of 6 months from August 1, 2025, to January 31, 2026.

On October 15, 2025, the Tenants filed a T1;T2 Application with the Board, alleging, the Landlords did not use their last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to them.

The Tenants provided uncontested testimony that they paid the last month’s rent, and notified the Landlord on September 1, 2025, that they would be vacating the rental unit at the end of the month, on or about September 30, 2025, and they would attempt to help mitigate the Landlord’s financial losses, by attempting to find replacement tenants, by posting advertisements on Facebook Marketplace.
The Tenants uncontested testimony was that they provided several suitable candidates, but none were accepted by the Landlords. The Tenants did in fact vacate on September 30, 2025.
The Tenants acknowledged and testified that they provided about 30 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy, on September 1, 2025, of a fixed term lease that was to end January 31, 2026.

The Tenants were adamant that the Landlord had re-rented the rental unit as of October 15, 2025, but had not provided any documentary evidence to substantiate the same, they further submitted they would be content with the return of half the last months rent and costs of this application. T1 ANALYSIS
Section 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) allows a Tenants to give notice to a landlord to terminate their tenancy.

Section 44(4) of the Act states: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a fixed term shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date. [Emphasis added.]
Based on the evidence, I find that the notice given by the Tenants on or about September 1, 2025, was short.

Section 88(1)(1) of the Act speaks to the calculation of arrears when Tenants do not give proper notice. It states: If the Tenants vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. [Emphasis added.]
Section 88(4) of the Act also requires the Board to consider whether the Landlord had established that they mitigated their damages upon being served with short notice.

The Tenants vacated on or about September 30, 2025, after giving notice that was short, so the arrears of rent owing to the Landlord would be calculated as if the Tenants had given proper notice. Had the Tenants served a proper notice in accordance with section 44, the earliest termination date they could have provided was January 31, 2026. This means the Landlord is entitled to rent arrears to January 31, 2026, subject to their duty to mitigate.

Based on the uncontested oral testimony before the Board I find that the Landlord made reasonable efforts to re-rent the rental unit effective immediately, and the Tenants believed they had done so on or about October 15, 2025, but did not provide any documentary evidence to substantiate the same, upon the Landlord receiving the Tenants’ short notice. Moreover, the reason that the Tenants’ last month rent deposit was not returned to them seems to be due to the short notice. Hence the Tenants’ T1 portion of their application must be dismissed.

The Tenants T2 portion of the application alleged harassment and substantial interference by creating a hostile environment which caused emotional distress which resulted in mental health issues of the Tenants, as the Landlord sought further funds in September 2025.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
The question to be determined by the Board is whether there was substantial interference of reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassment by the Landlord.

The Act further states that: 29(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: (3) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household.
On the evidence before me, I find the Tenants’ claims of substantial interference, were not met, as no documentary evidence was submitted to substantiate these claims.
Section 23 of the Act states “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”
The Tenants sought a rent abatement of $1,250.00 for the T2 portion of the application and out of pocket expenses which were the costs of the applications.
The Tenants testified that the Landlord sought further funds and made the tenancy difficult particularly in September 2025.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true., that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence was adduced by the Tenants, nor the Tenants’ oral testimony either in part or taken in its entirety, suffices to meet the burden of proof upon the Tenants to demonstrate that the Landlord has breached his obligations as they pertain to their T2 application.

On the evidence before me, I find the Tenant’s claims of harassment, and substantial interference were not met. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord’s behaviour on a balance of probabilities harassed the Tenants nor that the Landlord substantial interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment. The uncontested testimony of the Tenants in my opinion is self serving and without merit on a balance of probabilities.

I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants T1, T2 application is dismissed. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ing that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-087113-24 issued on December 2, 2025. The Tenants alleged that there were unable to participate in the November 25, 2025, hearing. On December 19, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On December 19, 2025 interim order LTB-T-087113-24-RV-IN was issued. The request to review was heard by videoconference on February 27, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the hearing. I was satisfied that the Landlord received the Notice of Hearing and there was no request to adjourn before me. There was no indication in the Portal that the notice of hearing had been returned as undeliverable to the Landlord. The Board records show that the Landlord logged into the Portal on November 2, 2024, updated their email address and consented to receive notices via email from the Board. Also present on February 27, 2026, was another legal representative for the Landlord, [name] for an unrelated matter. [name] confirmed that one of her colleagues would be joining the hearing as they did not have any instructions in relation to this matter. Notwithstanding, the Landlord being made aware of this hearing by the Board and one of their own legal representatives prior to the hearing being called, the Landlord was not present or represented in this hearing.
reasons: The Tenants alleged that they were not reasonably able to participate in the November 25, 2025, hearing.
They testified that on the day of the hearing, the Tenant [name] had a medical emergency and that they went to the hospital for treatment and as a result they did not attend the hearing.
After considering the testimony the Board granted the request for a review.

The Board’s power to review a decision may be exercised if a party to a proceeding was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. The case law from Divisional Court generally instructs the Board that the meaning of the phrase “not reasonably able to participate” should be interpreted broadly, to ensure natural justice, and where a party shows a genuine intent to participate in a hearing but was prevented from doing so, they should be entitled to a hearing through the review process. A party’s genuine intent to participate must be borne out by the evidence which clearly demonstrates the party’s intent to participate in the hearing. See [name] v. [name], 2011 ONSC 1557; King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., 2008 CanLII 60708, TSL-21992-11-RV (Re), 2012 CanLII 27914 (ON LTB); TEL-09087-10-RV (Re), 2011 CanLII 26960 (ON LTB); SWT-07158-10 (Re), 2010 CanLII 67967 (ON LTB).

In King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments 2008 CANLII 60708 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court stated: “Being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less”.

I was satisfied based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants that their explanation for why there were not reasonable able to participate in the hearing was reasonable in all the circumstances, and that they had a genuine intent to participate.
The re-hearing was immediately conducted. T1 Application
The T1 application was amended to include a claim that the Landlord did not return the rent deposit to the Tenants.

The Tenant’s vacated the rental unit on August 13, 2024 with termination effective as of August 31, 2024. They allege that the Landlord did not refund the rent deposit or pay interest on the rent deposit. They stated that they also paid a key deposit which had not been refunded.
The Tenants testified that they paid a rent deposit in the amount of $2,360.00 on January 1, 2023, as well as the key deposit.

The Tenants referred to DOC-4376607. This is an email to the Landlord dated August 13, 2024, confirming intention to vacate, and confirming that the Landlord had advised them they will rent out the unit as of September 1, 2024. The Tenants also requested their rent deposit to be returned.
The Tenants stated that once they vacated that the Landlord entered the unit and repainted the unit to prepare it for the next tenants.

The Tenants advised that to the best of their knowledge the Landlord has not applied for an order for any arrears of rent or arrears owing pursuant to sub-section 88(1)1. They further testified that the Landlord has reported rent owing to a collection agency and that this has affected their credit scores.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord has not refunded the rent deposit, not paid interest on the rent deposit, therefore these amounts shall be ordered. I am satisfied that the Landlord does not have an offsetting or cross-claim for any unpaid arrears or an order pursuant to sub-section 88(1)1. I am also satisfied that it is more likely than not that the Landlord had re-rented the unit as of September 1, 2024, therefore the Landlord has mitigated their potential losses.
I have calculated the interest on the rent deposit from the date collected to the date of the review hearing, total amount $157.62. T6 Application

The Tenants testified that they discovered bedbugs near the end of July 2024. They reported this to the Landlord. They stated that the Landlord did conduct a first and second treatment. However, even after that they continued to have a bed bug problem. They were still waking up with bed-bug bites or being bitten in their rental unit.

They stated that after the 2nd treatment the Landlord had advised them there was nothing further, they could do. They state that the Landlord had advised that the infestation likely may have begun in a unit next door where they had been treating for bedbugs.

They stated that they disposed on their bedframe, mattress, a duvet, curtains, bedsheets and carpets in order not to bring the bedbugs to their new rental. They stated that they have not had any bedbug problems in their new rental.
Based on the uncontested evidence, I was satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord had failed to maintain the rental unit in a safe condition fit for habitation.
The Tenant requested a rent abatement equal to one months rent for having to live with the bedbugs in July and August 2024, and for the Landlord’s failure to adequately address it.

In Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.

I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. I have reviewed all of the photos of the bedbug bites that the Tenants have suffered and while noting that the Landlord may have attempted to resolve the problem, it appears they also decided that there was nothing more they were prepared to do to resolve the problem. As a result, I am satisfied that one month rent compensation is reasonable and appropriate in all the circumstances.

The Tenants requested $3,918.00 for the costs to replace property they disposed of because the Landlord did not effectively treat for bedbugs. They stated this amount was an estimate of what they had paid.
I note that Health Canada has published online pest control tips on how to get rid of bedbugs. It does recommend that any items that cannot be washed, heated or steam cleaned should be thrown out.

As a result, based on the ineffective treatment by the Landlord it is likely that the Tenant did throw out many items including those listed above in order to avoid bringing bedbugs to their new unit, and that appears to have been successful. Therefore, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the amount requested is reasonable and appropriate in all the circumstances.

The tenants also requested compensation for out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $200.00 for their own efforts to treat the bedbugs and for medication. I am satisfied based on the uncontested evidence that this amount is reasonable and shall be ordered.

The Tenants also asked in the hearing to have their credit scores corrected to reflect that they did not owe the Landlord any money and that the Landlord did not have an order for any arrears of rent. I consented to this request. A Landlord that takes any action that negatively affects a Tenant’s credit score without lawful authority is in my view abusing their power as a Landlord.
The Tenants paid $48,00 application fee and are entitled to be reimbursed that amount.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-087113-24 issued on December 2, 2025, is granted.
The order is replaced as follows.
The [name] is terminated as of August 31, 2024, when the Tenants provided vacant possession to the Landlord.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $9,043.62. This amount represents: • Rent deposit, $2360.00 • Unpaid interest on rent deposit, $157.62 • Rent abatement, $2,360.00 • Replace property, $3,918.00 • Out of pocket expenses, $200.00 • Application fee $48.00
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord shall owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026 at 4% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall take all necessary steps to cancel any unlawful efforts to collect arrears of rent for which they do not have an order from the Board.

The Landlord shall take all necessary steps to rescind any negative notices that may have been placed on the Tenants credit history. There being no lawful authority for arrears, any negative reports amount to making a false report to a credit agency.
The Tenants may also submit this order to any credit reporting agency to have their credit history corrected. March 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: nant confirmed she was prepared to proceed without TDC consultation. The Tenant understood that TDC services are not guaranteed. The hearing commenced dealing with a preliminary matter. On May 29, 2025, the Tenant once again filed a request to amend the T2 application, adding one claim relating to an April 26, 2025 incident, adding a requested remedy (a 25% abatement of rent over three months) and a reduction in claimed general damages (from $22,896.00 to $3,816.00). This latest amendment reduced in effect the requested monetary remedies, which I was satisfied did not prejudice the Landlord. As for the added claim, it is not uncommon for parties to submit additional claims at a hearing as it takes several months typically for a hearing to be scheduled, and as this tenancy is still an active one, I did not see this additional claim out of order, especially since the monetary remedies were drastically reduced. At 10:24 am, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, Emily McGivern (‘LLR’), entered into the videoconference room to participate in the hearing. LLR also brought [name] (‘MC’) on a separate video link, who awaited in another room until she appeared as a witness for the Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved part of the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

Testimonies and exhibits/evidence of the parties are given in summary format below. It is noted the Tenant adduced six exhibits into evidence, whereas the Landlord did not submit any exhibit. Illegal entry
There were two instances that SW claimed were unlawful entries by the Landlord’s superintendent. SW provided testimony concerning an October 6, 2024 entry and an October 8, 2024 entry.

SW testified that about 5:10 pm on Sunday, October 6, 2024, the superintendent, MC, appeared at the front door without any notice, rang the doorbell, unlocked the door, and then closed the door a brief second later without MC actually entering the unit. SW stated she has a security system with cameras operating at the unit and asked that a video clip of MC at the front door be played ([name]). SW testified her 13-year old daughter, who was alone in the unit at the time, became afraid when MC unlocked the door setting off the security system, and she ran to hide further inside the unit.

SW stated her understanding that emergencies, as defined by the Landlord (exhibit TT#2), are “fire, flood and loss of heat”. SW stated this was not the first time of unlawful entry and referred to two other occurrences on September 12, 2023 and October 6, 2023 (TT#3). She said she ended up buying/installing a security camera system because of those unlawful entries.

SW then went to October 8, 2024, and stated that again without any notice, MC appeared at the door, opened the front door, yelled into the unit identifying herself and that she was with a plumber, and then proceeded up into the rental unit SW stated her belief that there was no plumbing emergency that she was aware of.

MC has been the Landlord’s superintendent since about February 2024 and she lives in a unit immediately below the Tenant’s rental unit. MC has general superintendent responsibility for 126 units in the residential complex and she confirmed her role is exclusively limited to just being a superintendent.

MC could not recall with any certainty what she did on October 6, 2024 at the rental unit door. She thought she might have been there for some work order, but apart from that she was uncertain. She could not remember unlocking the door but she was certain she did not step into the unit.

MC testified that on October 8, 2024, water flooded into her unit which appeared to come from the rental unit above. MC described water gushing through a ceiling light fixture, drenching her furniture below. She judged this to be an emergency situation that needed immediate attention. [name] said she contacted her boss about this, and was told to enter the rental unit on an emergency basis. She contacted a plumber straightaway and when the plumber arrived, she went into the unit. [name] said she called out in a loud voice as she opened the door, announced herself and the plumber. When there was no response, MC concluded the unit was empty and she led the plumber inside, going only to the kitchen and laundry room to search out the source of the flooding below. She said they found a portable [name] dishwasher on the kitchen counter and when lifted, there was a good amount of water pooled and seeping below. [name] said the plumber repaired the problem and the Landlord ended up replacing the light fixture in her unit and re-finishing/re-painting the damaged ceiling.

SW stated that the Landlord had told her a built-in dishwasher was not permitted in the rental unit, so she bought a portable countertop dishwasher which she said never leaked I the five years she has had it SW also said that MC and/or the plumber never advised her afterward of their reported findings.

Based on the submissions of both parties, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord (via MC as the Landlord’s representative) entered the rental unit on October 6, 2024 without proper notice being given in advance. MC’s recollection was poor about what had happened that day. She was unable to say whether any notice of any kind was given, but it was apparent she thought she was at the rental unit door for some “work order” which I presumed meant a regular maintenance visit. Therefore, I find MC opened the rental unit door just enough to set off MC’s security system of a door breach and this in of itself meant that “technically”, entry into the unit happened.

I do not find any unlawful entry happened on October 8, 2024 as I believe the water leaking into MC’s unit from SW’s unit met the threshold of what would be considered a emergency (i.e. flooding). I find that MC responded reasonably and responsibly by getting a plumber to SW’s unit right away. Both parties indicated that MC yelled into the unit after opening the door to identify herself and the plumber, and the work the plumber did, appeared satisfactorily restricted to finding the source of the leak downstairs.

I note that SW tried to show a pattern of unlawful entries (citing September 2023 and October 2023 entries in TT#3), but I do not find any pattern here as there was just over a year between the T2 claims here and the 2023 alleged entries (TT#3), and the entries apparently involved different Landlord employees. I must also note again that the two 2023 entries are outside the 1-year period that limits the LTB’s jurisdiction under subsection 29(2) of the Act. Substantial interference, harassment

SW testified about three alleged-to incidents that involved the superintendent, MC: i) MC yelling at the Tenant when she left the underground parking on April 22, 2024 (ii) MC kicking a Tenant’s package at the front door landing on July 16, 2024; and (iii) MC harassing/threatening a guest of the Tenant who had been parked in ‘visitors’ parking’ on April 26, 2025. 15. (i) vehicle on ramp/child:- SW described what happened to her on April 22, 2024 after she left the underground parking garage. She said she drove up the ramp to have MC run at her car, bang on the car and yell obscenities at her, all the while accusing her of hitting a child with her car. SW testified she stopped her car, stepped out and went behind her car to verify the child in question was not hit and not harmed. SW then sent her report/complaint to the Landlord by email on the same date (TT#4). 16. (ii) package:- SW submitted a video clip (TT#5b) and an email of report/complaint dated July 16, 2024 (TT#5a) in support of her testimony that MC kicked a couriered package sitting on the outdoor landing to the rental unit door. 17. (iii) guest/parked:- SW testified about MC approaching one of her guests who had been parked in ‘visitors’ parking’ at about 10:00 pm on April 26, 2025. SW stated that MC knocked on the guest’s window and shone a flashlight into his vehicle. Her guest informed MC whose guest he was and he gave a full name and address of the Tenant as proof he was indeed SW’s guest. Reportedly, MC threatened to call the police if the guest did not move his vehicle, which he did immediately. Not long after, SW stated her guest phoned her to alert her to his unpleasant encounter with MC. SW stated she then went to confront MC about this and MC did not deny she had approached that vehicle. In her view, SW said that MC’s action was very much a ‘targeting” action, and she ventured further to say it might have had something to do with her guest being a young, black male. SW emphasized that the Landlord has no published rules or regulations about guests having to register their vehicles with some Landlord authority such as MC. 18. (i) vehicle on ramp/child:- MC testified that children in the complex play in various areas and unfortunately, they sometimes play by the ramp that connects to the underground parking garage. She said she placed her own signs there to warn residents to slow down. MC could not remember the exact date, but she recounted how some children were on their scooters by the ramp when SW came up with her car. MC and two other residents witnessed one of the children almost being hit by SW’s car. MC confirmed she ran to SW’s car, banged on the car to ensure SW stopped and yelled at her about hitting a child. MC denied she used foul or demeaning language when yelling at SW, but MC did say she was very upset/concerned. MC described as SW stopped her car, got out and asked the child about whether he was hit or hurt. MC declared the child replied “yes” to being hit, but SW suggested to the child that he “was okay though”, to which he replied again, “yes”. 19. (ii) package:- MC denied kicking the couriered package with any kind of intent to damage. She declared she merely “pushed” the package aside with her foot, to make way for her to get to the rental unit door so she could place a notice in the mailbox. 20. (iii) guest/parked:- MC testified she received complaints from a couple of residents about an unknown vehicle that was parked for an unusual length of time in “visitors’ parking” with someone sitting inside. [name] said that there are many single-mothers in the complex who worry about security, so whenever she receives calls about something like this, MC tries to respond in appropriate fashion. MC testified that no one had registered their vehicle with her for the night (or for overnight), and she went out with another person to approach the vehicle. She affirmed that a man was sleeping inside the vehicle. She woke him up and asked him why he was there. She confirmed the man identified the Tenant and the Tenant’s unit number and explained that he was her guest. MC denied she uttered any threats about police or anything else, but she said that after she spoke with the man about either going to the rental unit to see the Tenant or to leave (and not sleep there), he decided drive away. MC confirmed being confronted by SW shortly afterwards and she denied it had anything to do with targeting in any way. MC confirmed there are no rules or regulations that she is aware of that sets out how visitors’ parking is to operate. She stated that she was passed the “guests must register with the superintendent” rule from her predecessor orally, but that was all. 21. In my view, the allegations of (i) and (ii) failed to persuade me that any substantial interference or harassment occurred. 22. (i) vehicle on ramp/child :- Indeed, if anyone were to see/think a child was hit, or close to being hit, by a vehicle, it would be reasonable to expect that that person would react in an upset, concerned manner. This is what I believe most likely happened on April 22, 2024 and I do not perceive MC’s actions (banging on the vehicle to get it to stop and yelling at the driver) as undue especially in respect of harassment or substantial interference claims brought under this T2 application. 23. (ii) package:- I reviewed the video clip evidence a few times and I find that the sweeping motion of MC’s foot to push aside SW’s couriered package was not an attempt to damage the package in any way, or to show some sort of disdain or disrespect. Instead, I agree more with MC that she most likely pushed the package aside simply to get a clearer passage to SW’s mailbox. 24. With regard to claim (iii) relating to a guest who was parked in the visitors’ parking area which is part of the residential complex, here I find the Landlord, via MC, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant. 25. I note that both sections 22 (substantial interference) and 23 (harassment) of the Act only apply to a tenant of a tenancy or in the case of section 22, a tenant’s household as well. As the person who was confronted by MC was a guest, and that guest obviously was not a tenant and not part of the Tenant’s household, the Landlord cannot be found to have breached sections 22 or 23 against that guest. My finding, therefore, relates to how the Landlord’s actions, through MC, impacted the Tenant during the evening of April 26, 2025. 26. MC’s actions of approaching the parked vehicle with a flashlight were arguably more those of a security person than those of a superintendent, but I did appreciate and accept MC’s testimony that many of the residents in the complex have security concerns and so contact MC when they see something questionable or out of the ordinary. I accept that MC tries to make the complex a safe place for residents. But however one may try to argue it, I find that MC acted outside her superintendent responsibilities on the night of April 26, 2025. 27. Going further, both SW and MC testified there are no Landlord rules or regulations in existence that set out for residents how visitors or guests of the complex are supposed to use “visitors’ parking”. I say this specifically about MC saying that she works on some word-of-mouth, passed-on rule that all guests are supposed to register with the superintendent. As I view it, this essentially means nothing about visitors’ parking is in place for residents of the complex, and so I find that SW’s guest did nothing wrong in parking his vehicle there late April 26, 2025. 28. As it turned out, the guest immediately informed SW of his dismay and SW confronted MC about this, and as I see it, she was justifiably shaken and upset over MC’s actions. SW testified that she felt targeted and unwelcome in the complex because of MC’s actions. 29. While SW said there was a targeting aspect to MC’s actions, I was not persuaded on a balance of probabilities that there was any targeting. SW’s guest was not present to provide any first-person account and the only person to do so was MC. I found MC’s testimony to be forthright, consistent and held up under cross-examination on this claim. As such, I relied more on MC’s testimony than SW’s indirect, hearsay submission. From this, I accept that MC responds, not just with words but with actions, to residents who may contact her for help well outside normal working hours, and I see this incident as being one of those situations, this time with an unfortunate, unintentional outcome. 30. For the breaches of unlawful entry on October 8, 2024 and of the substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment on April 26, 2025, I am ordering an abatement of rent equal to the requested 25% of one month’s rent for each incident. The rent at the time of the October 8, 2024 incident was $1,272.00 and at the time of April 26, 2025 incident, $1,298.00. This amounts to a total abatement of $642.50. 31. In the T2 application, the Tenant also asks for the following remedies: that the Landlord stop entering her unit without prior lawful notice; that MC be reprimanded by the LTB; that the Landlord pay a fine to the LTB; and general (non-pecuniary) damages in the amount of $3,316.00 (3 months of rent) for the ongoing, unsafe and uncomfortable environment SW and her daughter have been living in. 32. The order below will only include direction to the Landlord in respect of prior lawful notices, which I find proper and correct to order based on the unlawful entry of October 8, 2024. 33. I explained to the Tenant that the LTB does not have the jurisdiction to reprimand an employee of the Landlord. 34. With regard to the requested fine, I did not find the Landlord (via MC) showed any blatant disregard for the Act at any time and the order below should be sufficient to address the breaches and to ensure the Landlord adheres/complies with the Act going forward. 35. Finally, with regard to general damages, and with reference to Interpretation Guideline no. 16, I did not find any pattern of substantial interference or harassment from the valid claims made the Tenant under the T2 application (as amended). The one unlawful entry and the one visitors’ parking incident/breach were for disparate, unconnected incidents. I understand the Tenant may feel otherwise, but the evidence proffered at the hearing did not convince me of some connection between the two Landlord breaches. As a result, the general damages remedy request is denied. 36. As the Tenant is successful on part of the T2 allegations, the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the T2 filing fee. (reference: Interpretation Guideline no. 3)
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $690.50. This amount represents: • $642.50 for the Landlord’s breaches in respect of one unlawful entry and of one incident of substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment by the Tenant; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the T2 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount of $690.50 owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $690.50 from the monthly rent coming due on March 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

Effectively immediately and for the duration of the tenancy, the Landlord shall only enter the rental unit whenever proper notice of entry has been served on the Tenant, pursuant to the applicable provisions of sections 26 and 27 the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. February 17, 2026 __________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $17,400.00.
By way of background, the rental unit was a two-bedroom detached family home with one bathroom and approximately 1100 square feet. The Tenant lived in the rental unit with her child for 18 years.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’); • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

Further, section 57(5) of the Act creates a rebuttable presumption that a notice of termination given under s. 48(1) of the Act was given in bad faith if the property is advertised for sale or rent. A rebuttable presumption means that the landlord is assumed to have acted in bad faith unless the landlord can provide an explanation that satisfies the Board as to what changed after the tenancy terminated, that affected the landlord’s ability to move in or remain in the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that on June 20, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice with a termination date of September 1, 2025. He told the Tenant that he had a medical problem which required him to live closer to major hospitals and his family doctor who advised they would resume care to the Landlord and his wife. The Landlord had been living in British Colombia prior to this time.

The Tenant, feeling concerned for her Landlord’s health, agreed to move. She found another rental unit in the community. She said it was stressful, because she had lived in the rental property for 18 years.

About two weeks after moving out, she saw the rental property was being fitted for a new roof. About three weeks later, she saw a for sale sign on the front lawn of the property. The Tenant submitted a copy of the MLS listing. Her evidence is that the property is still vacant and still for sale.

The Tenant proved all of the requirements in s.57(1)(a). The Tenant was given an N12 notice of termination and the Tenant vacated the rental property in accordance with that notice. The Tenant also proved that the notice was given in bad faith because the property was put up for sale five about five weeks after she left, and the property remains vacant. Further, the Landlord did not attend the hearing to rebut the presumption of bad faith pursuant to s. 57(5) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord acted in bad faith. Remedies
By way of remedies, the Tenant seeks rent differential totalling $17,400.00 for the period between September 1, 2025, to August 31, 2026.

The Tenant told the Board that she had an agreement with the Landlord that her rent would remain $850.00 per month, but she was to pay the property taxes, which she did. Her new rent is $2,300.00 per month. The Tenant seeks $1,450.00 for 12 months as rent differential totalling 17,400.00 ($1,450 x 12). The Tenant submitted a copy of her current lease showing the current rental rate. The Tenant states that her new rental unit is in approximately the same age building and about the same size as her old rental unit.

I note that it could be argued that the Tenant paid more than $850.00 per month if the property taxes were added into the calculation. However, s. 134(1) of the Act states that no Landlord shall collect any “…fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.” Further, s. 3(1) of the Act states that the Residential Tenancies Act applies to all rental units despite any other agreement to the contrary.

What this means is that the Landlord was not permitted to charge or ask the Tenant to pay the property taxes even if the parties agreed on this. Section 3(1) specifically states that despite any agreement to the contrary, the Act prevails, and s. 134(1) prohibits the collection of any other fees, premiums, etc. such as in this case, the property taxes.

Therefore, it was not lawful for the Tenant to pay the property taxes. As a result, I am not considering these charges in the calculation of the Tenant’s lawful rent for the purposes of determining the rent differential.
I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $17,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $17,448.00. This amount represents: • $17,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant will incur for the one-year period from September 1, 2025, to August 31, 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
