issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Application names [name] and [name] and [name] as Landlords.

At the outset of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative requested that the Landlord’s [name] and [name] be removed from the Application on the basis that they had no direct relationship with the Applicant who had subleased the rental unit from a Tenant “[name]” without the Landlord’s knowledge. Therefore, the Landlord's Legal Representative suggests they are not Landlord’s. The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the Tenant [name] had always paid the rent directly, JAN 05, 2026 and the Landlord’s were not aware that he had sublet the rental unit without their consent to [name] and [name]

The Landlord's Legal Representative acknowledged that the Landlord did later become aware that the Tenant [name] had sublet the rental unit to [name] and [name] and did respond to maintenance requests in an effort to preserve their property.

The Landlord's Legal Representative also relied on a prior order by the Board LTB-L- 094078-23-RV. Wherein the [name] and [name] made a request to review the Board’s decision to decline to consider a motion to set aside brought by [name] and [name] with respect to the rental unit. She testified that this order determined that [name] and [name] were not [name], and the relationship was only between [name] and [name] as Landlord’s and the Tenant [name]

By way of background. The Landlord’s and the Tenant [name] entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the Board issued ex-parte order LTB-L-094078- 23, which terminated the tenancy. Accordingly, [name] and [name] filed a motion to set aside that ex-parte order which was declined on the basis that [name] and [name] did not have standing to bring such a motion.

In LTB-L-094078-23-RV the request to review was denied and it was indicated that the affected parties ([name] and [name]) were not named as respondents in the ex-parte order, and it was therefore reasonable for the Board to find that they did not have standing to file a motion to set aside.

LTB-L-094078-23-RV notes at Paragraph six: Any party affected by an order/decision may file a request to review that order/decision. In a situation where a person who believes they are a tenant becomes subject to eviction under an ex parte order in which they are not named as a tenant, that person must file a request to review the order. At the review hearing the Board would hear evidence and submissions as to whether the requestor is a tenant. I note that the endorsement under review tells the Affected Parties that they may file a review request and an extension of time.

LTB-L-094078-23-RV does not in my view make an explicit determination as to whether [name] and [name] are Tenant’s or whether they have standing to bring a T2 or T6 Application with respect to the tenancy. Instead, it determines that they do not have standing to bring a motion to set aside as they were not named as parties in the original ex-parte order. Instead, LTB-L-094078-23-RV indicates that if [name] and [name] believe they are Tenant’s they are able to file a request to review the ex-parte order, rather than file a motion to set aside.
Instead of removing the Landlord’s [name] and [name] outright or dismissing the Application, I allowed the parties to call evidence with respect to the relationship between the parties.

The Tenant [name] testified that she and [name] moved unto the rental unit on February 16, 2022, a move with had been delayed by a flood in the rental unit. She testified that she attended the day prior and both [name] and [name] were present, and she spoke with [name] who understood that that they were moving into the rental unit. She testified that there was no fixed date for them to vacate the rental unit, and [name] indicated that she could text him if she had any problems.

She testified that she paid the rent to [name] but reached out to the Landlord’s directly with any maintenance issues. The Tenant testified that the Landlord never filed an A2 Application during the time she resided in the rental unit.

She testified that [name] was her daughter’s boyfriend, and he had vacated the rental unit when she moved in and rented a separate unit with the Tenant’s daughter. She testified that by the time she moved in [name] had already moved out, and the Landlord was aware of that.

She testified that she did not know exactly when the Landlord became aware that she would be moving in, and that [name] had vacated but testified that they knew that he had moved out and she had taken possession.

She testified that [name] had left some furniture and some odds and ends in the rental unit such as a couch, and bed, but it was clear that he had moved out when she moved in, and his clothing was gone, She testified that the unit was empty apart from the furniture and would have been clear that [name] had vacated.

The Landlord [name] testified that he was not at the property on February 15, 2022. Instead, it was his father and suggested that the Tenant had confused the two of them. He testified that he was not aware at the time that [name] and [name] intended to move in and take over the rental unit from [name] and to his knowledge his father was not aware either.

He testified that he was not fully aware that [name] left the unit, he testified that Mr. [name] had informed him that his mother-in-law had nowhere to go, and he was going to let her move in with him. He testified that this was way after February 2022. He testified that he never provided his contact information to [name] and [name].

He testified that other than text messages with respect to maintenance issues, he never had any other communication with [name] and [name] and only responded to those messages because the property is his retirement fund and he needs to take care of it, and because he knew [name] to be related to Mr. [name]name].

He testified that “at some point” he became aware that [name] had left the rental unit because he had problems with [name]. He testified that [name] informed him that he was going to be leaving the rental unit until his mother-in-law [name] was back on her feet. He could not recall when this occurred. He testified that Mr. [name]name] indicate that he would keep paying the rent and would be back in the unit, so he took no steps after being informed that Mr. [name]name] was moving out. He did not file an A2 Application after being made aware that Mr. [name]name] had vacated. He testified that he always believed [name] and [name] to be guests of Mr. [name]name].
Ultimately, I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to remove [name] and [name] from the Application.

When I apply Section 202 of the Act, to ascertain real substance of all transactions and activities between the parties it is clear to me that there was an assignment of the tenancy. While [name] claimed that he had only ever considered [name] and [name] to be guests, it is clear that he became aware during the tenancy that [name] had vacated the rental unit while [name] and [name] remained and declined to file an A2 Application after becoming aware of this fact.

While [name] testified that he was his understanding that Stephan [name] would be returning to the rental unit, I am not satisfied that this scenario would be properly characterized as a sublet as there was no sublet agreement, and no set date on which Mr. [name] would return.

Section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: Unauthorized occupancy 100 (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. 2006, c. 17, s. 100 (1). Time limitation (2) An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. 2006, c. 17, s. 100 (2).

In this case as the Landlord never filed an A2 Application to evict the unauthorised occupants, I am satisfied that they failed to comply with the time limitation in Section 100(2) and I am satisfied that [name] and [name] are [name]. Therefore, I shall remove Stephan [name] from this Application which shall continue against remove [name] and [name]. The Particulars

In my view many of the Allegations in the T2 and T6 lack sufficient particulars. The Applications contains allegations such as a door which allows snow to enter during winter, allegations that there are no screens on the windows, and an allegation that the kitchen sink leaks, and a bathtub in the unit upstairs leaks, but no dates or times are provided fro these claims. In short, while some details are provided, the vast majority of allegations lack clear dates and times.

Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”).
The Tenant's Legal Representative indicated that the particulars including dates and times, are contained in the Tenant’s disclosure, and will be introduced during the testimony of the [name].
In the alternative the Tenant's Legal Representative sought an adjournment to amend the Application.

I am not of the view that a lack of particulars can be cured through disclosure or testimony. In my view the Application and disclosure are distinct, and while disclosure has been provided, this does not mean it shall be introduced during the hearing as evidence. I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to expect the responding party to comb through, sometimes voluminous disclosure, in order to determine the particulars of the allegations in the Application. Instead, the Application itself should clearly contain these particulars.

I am also not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate to allow the Tenant's Legal Representative additional time to amend the Application. The Application was filed on November 3, 2023, and has previously been adjourned on three occasions, prior to the hearing before me. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant has had appropriate time to prefect their Application, and it would not be an expeditious use of the Board’s resources to adjourn the matter once again so that the Application may be amended.

As many of the allegations in the Tenant’s application are vague and fail to provide dates and times for the allegations made, I find that there are insufficient particulars to allow the landlord to know the allegations made or the case to be met with respect to these issues.
Therefore, I elected to proceed with the hearing and limited the Application to those allegations with contained clear particulars, including dates and times. The T2/T6
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1048.00 The Vacuum

The Tenant testified that when she moved into the rental unit there was a shop vacuum which had been left in the laundry room, presumably to clean up from a flood. The Tenant testified that it was full of water which attracted misquotes. She testified that after some time she opened it and dumped out the water.

The Landlord [name] testified that the vacuum had been left in case there was residual water from a prior leak in the rental unit, he testified that he was never made aware that the vacuum was attracting mosquitoes. The Leak

The Tenant testified that on June 26, 2022, a pipe in the bathroom cubbyhole began to leak. She testified that this occurred around 5:00am and the Tenant did not attend to fix the leak until 10:00am, and she was forced to spend all morning catching the leak in a bucket.
The Tenant testified that this happened again on August 4, 2023, and June 25, 2023.

The Tenant confirmed that the Landlord responded within the hour and came over to address the leaks each time they occurred and acknowledged that on the first occasion it took the Landlord 5 hours to attend the rental unit because the leak began at 5:00am in the morning.

The [name] that he responded to each of the leaks promptly, all of which were caused by pinholes in separate pipes, which he attended and replaced. He testified that the leaks produced approximately a bucket of water every couple of hours. He testified that he responded within hours each time and never took more than 24 hours to respond and remedy a leak. The Bylaw Order

The Tenant testified that there were wasps in the rental unit which prompted her to call bylaw, who attended and made an order for the Landlord to make repairs within the rental unit including replacing missing caulking around the bathtub, fixing a gap under the front door, and replacing missing window screens.

The Tenant testified that she had not previously made the Landlord aware of these issues and the Landlord was given a deadline of October 20, 2023 to repair them, which they complied with. The Vital Services

The Tenant testified that on November 1, 2023, the electricity to the rental unit was shut off, she testified that she spoke to the electricity provider to have it turned back on and was informed that they had been told she was a squatter, and the company refused to restore the power. She testified that the electricity was restored on November 22, or November 23, 2023 after she called bylaw for assistance.

She testified that she was aware that the electricity was the responsibility of the Tenant in the lease agreement and had attempted to have the bills transferred into her name, but the Landlord or [name] had had informed the provider they were squatters, refused to transfer the bill without the permission of the Landlord. She testified that the electricity was originally in [name]’s name.
She testified that she was pretty sure she texted the Landlord directly with respect to the electricity shutoff.
She testified that she involved bylaw who eventually succeeded in having the electricity to the rental unit restored and was able to have the electricity bill placed under her name.

The Landlord testified that based on the lease they had with [name] the Tenant was responsible for paying the electricity and the electricity bill was in his name. He testified that to his knowledge the electricity was in Mr. [name]name]’s name. He testified that at one point during the tenancy the electric provider called him and asked him about [name] and [name], and he expressed that he did not know who they were. He confirmed during cross examination that he knew at the time of this phone call that [name] was residing in the rental unit. He testified that he never asked the electricity provider to shut off the electricity, and never had any control over this utility. He testified that he could not recall if the Tenant’s ever reached out to him with respect to the electricity.
He testified that around that time Mr. [name]name] may have told him he was leaving and turning off the electricity, then later indicated that he could not remember if this was the case. Analysis
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that they ever made the Landlord aware of the mosquitoes, and the issues appears to have been resolved after the Tenant emptied the shop vacuum of water.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably with respect to the leaks, each time the Landlord response to the Tenant promptly, and attended the rental unit within hours to repair the pipes and stop the leak. While the Tenant characterised this issue as recurring, I accept that the leaks appear to be coming separate pipes, therefore I am satisfied that each of the leaks constitute a distinct occurrence, each of which was appropriately dealt with by the Landlord. Absent the replacement of every pipe in the bathroom, I am not satisfied that there was more the Landlord could have done to respond appropriate to this issue.

With respect to the bylaw order, I am not satisfied that the Tenant had brought any of the issue identified in the order to the Landlord’s attention before the order was issued, and according to the Tenant’s own testimony the Landlord complied with the order and remedied the issues after they became aware of them, within the time allotted. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably.

With respect to the electricity, it was agreed by the parties that the electricity was the responsibility of the Tenant. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord withheld the vital service of electricity when it was shutoff to the rental unit. However, I am satisfied that the Landlord interfered with the supply of electricity to the rental unit. The Landlord initially testified that [name] had made him aware that he would be vacating and shutting off the electric, and while the Landlord later revised this testimony, this causes my to question the reliability of the Landlord’s testimony with respect to this issue.

Additionally, I am satisfied that the Landlord was well aware of the presence of the Tenant [name] within the rental unit by November 2023 and in spite of this, when he was conducted by the electricity provider he informed them that he had no idea who she was. I find that this impacted the Tenant’s ability to have the electricity placed into her own name, and contributed to the ongoing outage experienced by the Tenant from November 1, 2023 to November 22, 2023. While I am not satisfied that the Landlord himself directly withheld the service, I am satisfied that his actions nevertheless constitute a dispersion and therefore interference with the vital service of electricity.
I also accept that this action caused the Tenant to be without power for nearly one month which impacted their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord both interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, and interfered with their vital services, which respect to the electricity shutoff in November 2023. Remedies

I accept that the disruption of electricity from November 1, 2023 – November 22, 2023 impacted the Tenant’s ability to enjoy the rental unit and an abatement is appropriate. Given that the disruption lasted for nearly a full month and impacted the Tenant’s ability to enjoy the rental unit I am satisfied that an abatement of $1000.00 is appropriate. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.
As I have found in favour of the Tenant’s only in a limited manner, I am not satisfied that any further remedies are warranted.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 5, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] (the ‘Tenant’) also applied for an order determining that [name] harassed, , obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant in the amount $1,415.50. [name]
The Tenancy began on August 29, 2023.
The lawful rent was $900.00 and it was due on the first of the month.
The Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit on August 29, 2023. The rent deposit was applied to the last month’s rent in July 2025. Interest was never paid.
The Tenant vacated the unit on July 13, 2025. T1 Application – Illegal Rent
The Landlord advised the Tenant by text message that the rent would increase to $1000.00 on November 1, 2023.
No Notice of Rent Increase was provided, and the notice was less than 90 days before it took effect.
Raising the rent from $900.00 to $1000.00 represents an 11.11% increase that is higher than the Guideline, which was 2.5.%
I find that the rent increase was not given the proper notice and was above the Guideline.
Section 116(4) states that a rent increase is void if the proper notice is not given.
However, the Tenant paid the rent increase from November 2023-July 2025.
I find that this period is longer than 12 consecutive months. It is, in fact, a period of 20 months. This triggers section 135.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act).

Section 135.1 of the Act states: An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.
Therefore, I find that the rent increase, having been paid for a period of more than 12 consecutive months is, indeed a valid rent increase.
The Tenant’s T1 application is therefore dismissed. [name]
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with him.
Section 23 of the Act states that a “Landlord shall harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

There is no definition of harassment in the Act, but the Act derives its interpretation of the word from the Ontario Human Rights Code, RSO 1990, H19, that defines harassment as: “a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome,” s. 10.

On June 19, 2025, the Tenant received a photo from the Landlord of a handwritten post-it note on his door indicating he would be evicted in 24 hours. Photograph 6608035 (Exhibit 1).The Tenant testified that he only received the picture, he never actually saw the post-it note on his door in person.
On June 26, 2025, the Tenant wrote a text message back to the Landlord saying he did not understand the picture he sent. The Landlord did not reply. (Text messages DOC6608033 Exhibit 2.)

On July 11, 2025, the Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant indicating that he gave him notice on June 19, 2025 that he would evict him within 24 hours. The Tenant replied that he never received the note on the door, and was surprised by the message, but agreed to leave.
At 23:58 on July 11, 2025, the Landlord offered to help the Tenant vacate the rental unit. (Exhibit 2)
On July 12, 2025 at 7:54 AM, the Tenant asked about his last month’s rent deposit. The Landlord replied at 11:03 AM on July 12, 2025 that it was “a civil court matter”.(Exhibit 2)
On July 12, 2025 at 10:25 AM, the Landlord indicated he would move the Tenant’s belongings for him. (Exhibit 2)
The Tenant testified he was very stressed about this rapidly escalating situation, and that he had to quickly find friends in London, ON, which was more than hour away, to help him move.
On July 13, 2025 the Tenant messaged the Landlord to tell him he had returned the key and vacated the apartment. The Landlord acknowledged the message on July 13, 2025 at 16:07. (Exhibit 2)
The Landlord never replied to the Tenant’s question about the last month’s rent deposit. (Exhibit 2).

On July 13, 2025, at 16:09 the Landlord texted the tenant to apologize, saying “My apologies [name], [sic] I am not in a good spot right now drug abuse is making me,, well not be myself ???” (Exhibit 2)

I find the Landlord threatened and harassed the Tenant with an eviction beginning on June 19, 2025 and continued a pattern of harassing conduct through text messages until July 12, 2025. The eviction occurred without regard for the parameters of the Residential Tenancies Act.
I find that a reasonable person would consider the number and content of the text messages from the Landlord to be harassing and coercive.
Indeed, the Tenant vacated the premises on July 12, 2025 as a result of the Landlord’s harassing conduct.
As the Landlord did not attend the hearing, the Tenant’s testimony is unchallenged.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has proven the allegations on a balance of probabilities, so the application is granted. Remedies:

The Tenant requested the following remedies: • Return of the last month’s rent deposit and interest, $1,067.50 • Administrative Fine • Out of pocket expenses, $300.00 • General Damages $1500.00 • Cost of filing the application $48.00 • At the hearing the Tenant also asked for the rent differential in his new rental unit, however, this was not included in his original application and therefore, cannot be awarded.
I find that the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed and interfered with the Tenant, and that as a result the Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 12, 2025.
Therefore, the Landlord shall refund the last month’s rent deposit and interest, $1,067.50.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant’s out-of-pocket moving expenses to move his belongings under duress, comprising of gas and incidentals, $300.00
The Tenant shall also pay the Tenant’s cost of filing the application, $48.00. General Damages

General damages are an extraordinary remedy that is designed to compensate the Tenant and not to punish the Landlord or deter behaviour. In this way, general damages should not be confused with an Administrative Fine. Assessing the quantum of general damages is a question of mixed fact and law. (Bailey v. Capreit Limited Partnership, 2022 ONSC 5487 ([name]))

The Tenant did not elaborate on, or document, his losses incurred as a result of the Landlord’s harassment. He expressed how shocked and stressed he was at the threats of losing his apartment so suddenly, but general damages are a legal remedy meant to compensate more than shock and stress. Therefore, I do not find it appropriate in this case to award general damages. Administrative Fine
The Tenant requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine on the basis that the conduct of the Landlord was particularly egregious.

The Board’s interpretive Guideline 16, entitled Administrative Fines, states that a fine should be considered to deter the Landlord and others from similar conduct: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.
I find that the Landlord in this case behaved with blatant disregard for the RTA by failing to provide adequate notice and failing to pursue legal eviction through the RTA.
Therefore, in all of the circumstances, and considering it is a small landlord, an administrative fine will be imposed in the amount of $3,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,415.50. This amount represents: • $1067.50 for the last month’s rent and interest on the deposit • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. • $300.00 out-of-pocket moving expenses
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026.
The Landlord shall also pay an administrative fine to the Board in the amount of $3,000.00 by May 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background
The rental unit is a detached house occupied by multiple tenants. The Tenant rented a single room in the basement, where three individuals resided, while two individuals occupied the upper level.

The Tenant testified that she left the rental unit for the weekend and returned on August 5, 2024, at which time she discovered that the locks had been changed and that she had not been provided with a key. The Tenant alleged that, as a result, she was unable to access the unit, her belongings remained inside, and she subsequently became homeless and lived in her vehicle.

The Tenant further testified that she did not contact the police regarding the alleged lockout. When asked about her current housing, the Tenant stated that she secured a new rental unit on May 20, 2025 with the help of Waterloo Regional Housing.

The Landlord’s representative submitted that an N4 Notice to End a Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent was served on May 24, 2024, due to rental arrears. He personally served someone at the rental complex who identified herself as the Tenant. An order [name] was issued on October 28, 2024 wherein the Landlord withdrew the application as the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Landlord’s agent, [name] (YS), testified that in early August 2024 he inspected the Tenant’s room and found it vacant, with no belongings present. He further stated that the Tenant had not provided notice that she intended to vacate the unit. Attempts to contact the Tenant were unsuccessful, as her phone number was no longer in service.
The Landlord’s agent also testified that the Tenant had turned off the electricity at the breaker panel, which affected the entire house. Evidence

Neither party submitted documentary evidence, including photographs, correspondence, or other materials, to support their respective positions. The Tenant did not provide emails, text messages, or other records demonstrating communication with the Landlord. Similarly, the Landlord did not provide documentary evidence confirming the condition of the unit or the alleged vacancy. Analysis
Section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2026 (the Act) prohibits a landlord from changing the locks to a rental unit without providing the tenant with replacement keys.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit or residential complex by a tenant or members of the tenant’s household.
In an application under section 29 of the Act, the Tenant bears the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the alleged conduct occurred.

In this case, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord changed the locks and denied her access to the rental unit. However, the Tenant did not provide corroborating evidence to support this claim. There is no documentary evidence, witness testimony, or other objective proof demonstrating that the locks were changed or that she was denied access.

Conversely, the Landlord’s evidence is that the rental unit appeared vacant in early August 2024 and that the Tenant could not be contacted. The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant had vacated the unit without notice.

Given the absence of supporting evidence from either party, the Board must assess whether the Tenant has met the burden of proof. On the totality of the evidence before the Board, the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord changed the locks or substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] and Edith Peart (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Tenant brings this application pursuant to section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act), alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit contrary to section 22 of the Act.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant a total of $30,949.64.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2022, and moved out on July 1, 2025. The rental unit consisted of the main floor of a detached house with one bedroom, a hallway, two bathrooms, and a kitchen. The upstairs portion of the house was occupied by another tenant. The monthly rent was $1,300.00. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that throughout the entire tenancy, from July 2022 to July 1, 2025, the rental unit was not fit for habitation. He stated that the Landlord failed to remedy ongoing issues, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment, and ultimately forced him to move out.

The Tenant’s testimony, supported by photographs and documentary evidence, established the condition of the rental unit and the communication between the parties regarding the Tenant’s complaints. Two City orders were issued requiring the Landlord to address deficiencies.

The Tenant testified that when he moved into the unit in July 2022, there was no proper main entry door separating his living space. Photographs show that the entry consisted of a rough, unfinished wooden stud frame installed in a hallway opening. The structure appeared makeshift and lacked proper drywall and finishing. The Tenant testified that individuals could see through the separation into his bedroom area. He stated that for the entire tenancy he lacked privacy and did not feel secure because the entry door was incomplete and unsealed.

The Tenant further testified that from the day he moved in, he repeatedly complained about the improper door. The Landlord promised to address the issue but never completed the work. At the time the Tenant moved out, the door remained unrepaired.

The Tenant also testified that the front entry lacked proper fire separation between units. He stated there was no adequate drywall or ceiling separation, creating a fire safety concern. Toronto Fire Services conducted an inspection in November 2024 and issued an order requiring remediation. The Tenant testified that the Landlord failed to comply.

The Tenant testified that three significant leaks occurred during the tenancy. The first occurred on November 17, 2022, when water leaked from the kitchen ceiling, resulting in visible mould growth. The Tenant testified that he notified the Landlord by text message and in person beginning November 17, 2022, and continued raising the issue weekly. He stated that the Landlord did not properly address the mould before he moved out on July 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s response to the first leak was limited to painting over the ceiling without addressing the source of the water intrusion. Mould remained in the kitchen and bathroom areas.
The evidence shows mould on the kitchen ceiling and on the second bathroom floor and walls. The Tenant testified that he stopped using the second bathroom in November 2022 due to mould.

A second significant flood occurred on August 25, 2023. The Tenant testified that water covered the hallway ceiling and kitchen area, resulting in standing water and increased mould growth. After this incident, he testified that he could no longer viably use the kitchen. He stopped using the stove and refrigerator due to mould contamination and recurring water damage. He stated that he used the kitchen only to store nonperishable items and occasionally used a rice cooker.

The Tenant testified that mould developed inside the oven, refrigerator, and walls. He also testified that the refrigerator malfunctioned and that cockroaches, including dead cockroaches, were found inside it. He stated that the Landlord did not properly remediate the mould or repair the kitchen. As a result, he frequently ate outside the home or ordered takeout.
A third flood occurred on February 22, 2024, again affecting the kitchen, hallway, and bedroom. The Tenant testified that the damage worsened, and that the unit became increasingly uninhabitable.
The City issued an order by November 7, 2024, requiring remediation. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not comply.

The Tenant stated that due to mould, leaks, and infestation, he was unable to safely use the kitchen and attached bathroom from at least November 2022 onward. He described the unit as unsafe and unsustainable.

The Tenant testified that the conditions persisted for approximately three years and that the Landlord did not meaningfully address the issues. He stated that the deteriorating conditions ultimately contributed to his decision to move out on July 1, 2025.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant. The test under section 22 is objective. The interference must be significant and more than trivial. It must materially affect the tenant’s ordinary use of the premises.

Based on the uncontested evidence and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by failing to address ongoing leaks, visible mould, flooding, loss of functional kitchen facilities, loss of the second bathroom, and the absence of a secure and private main entry door. These conditions materially impaired the Tenant’s ordinary use of the premises. The Tenant is therefore entitled to remedies. Harassment, etc.

The Tenant testified that whenever he raised maintenance complaints, the Landlord responded with abusive language and told him to move out. The Tenant submitted a video recording from May 2025 in which the Landlord can be heard using offensive language toward him.
Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s conduct constituted harassment contrary to section 23 of the Act. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services
The Tenant did not establish that he was constructively evicted or that the Landlord withheld a vital service within the meaning of the Act. This claim is dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant seeks: • 50% rent abatement from November 2022 to June 30, 2025 • $1,500.00 out of pocket expenses • $9,101.64 rent differential • $14,000.00 general damages • A fine to the Board. Rent abatement:

The evidence establishes that the Tenant lost use of the kitchen, second bathroom, and secure entry throughout much of the tenancy. The Tenant repeatedly complained, and the Landlord failed to meaningfully address the issues.
Given the severity and duration of the conditions, I find that a 50% rent abatement from November 2022 to July 1, 2025, is appropriate.
The Landlord shall pay $20,800.00. This represents 50% of the monthly rent of $1,300.00 for the period from November 5, 2022, to July 1, 2025. Out-of-pocket expenses:
The Tenant did not provide documentary evidence supporting these claims. This portion of the claim is dismissed. Rent Differential:
The Tenant moved out on July 1, 2025, and began paying $2,058.47 per month for comparable accommodation. The difference is $758.47 per month.

I am satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct caused the Tenant to move. The Tenant is entitled to $9,101.64 representing the increased rent from July 1, 2025, to July 1, 2026. General Damages: Pain and Suffering
The Tenant seeks general damages for emotional distress and loss of housing stability. The Board has authority under section 31(1)(f) of the Act to award such damages.

I accept that the prolonged exposure to mould, flooding, lack of security, and harassment caused stress and mental distress. However, I find that an award of $1,000.00 is reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances. Administrative Fine

Guideline 16 provides that an administrative fine is appropriate where a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence. However, I am satisfied that the abatement awarded is significant and sufficient to encourage compliance. An administrative fine is not warranted in the circumstances
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $30,949.64. This amount represents: • $20,800.00 for a rent abatement. • $9,101.64 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred and will incur from July 1, 2025, to July 1, 2026. • $1,000.00 general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of July 1, 2025. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and Rare Roots Corporation (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord argued that the application should be dismissed as the Landlord was not properly identified. The owner of the building is [name]. Landlord [name] [name] (AB) is a director of the corporation. [name] was not listed on the lease and the Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence to support how the Tenant would know that Rare Roots owned the building.

On the lease, the Landlord’s Legal name was listed as Acquity Real Estate Inc. and was signed by Landlord [name] (NB). NB is the president of Acquity Real Estate Inc. NB said he is not a landlord as he and Acuity Real Estate Inc. are only property managers.

The Tenant testified that she has only had contact with NB and thought he was the Landlord. The Tenant had not had contact with AB until she received an N12 notice of termination that identified AB as the Landlord.

I note that the definition of “landlord” in section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) includes the owner of a rental unit “or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit.” The Act specifically contemplates that someone other than an owner of the rental unit can be a landlord.

Whether a property manager falls within the definition of “landlord” depends on the facts of the given case. Given that Acquity Real Estate was the named Landlord on the tenancy agreement and NB signed as the president of the corporation, I find that NB was a person who permitted occupancy of the rental unit, and he is therefore a Landlord and a proper respondent in this proceeding.

In terms of Rare Roots Corporation being a Landlord, NB submitted documentary evidence that shows [name] owns the building. As AB is a director of the corporation and was properly served the application, I find that the Tenant did properly serve [name] as a Landlord. All parties were present and the Tenant took no further position on whether Rare Roots Corporation should be named as a Landlord, therefore I have amended the application to include Rare Roots Corporation as a Landlord in addition to NB and AB. Preliminary Issue: Amendment Request
The Tenant sought to amend the remedies portion of her application. There were no new issues identified. The Tenant submitted the request to amend her application 7 days in advance of the hearing.
The Landlord disputed the amendment and argued it would be prejudicial.

Under Rule 15.4 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I allowed the amendment of the Tenant. As stated, there were no new issues being raised, only new remedies being sought. The issues and evidence needed to defend the alleged issues were known well in advance of the hearing by the Landlord, and therefore I did not find amending the application to add additional remedies to be prejudicial. T6 Application:

In this case the Tenant alleged the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations in relation to five different issues. As explained below, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established any of their allegations, and therefore, the application is dismissed.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligations as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Issue 1: Bulb for Stove Light:

The Tenant testified that for the entire tenancy, the Landlord never replaced the stove light in the range hood above the stove. The Tenant provided dates she notified the Landlord and testified that there were no other lights near the stove and that this significantly impacted her ability to prepare food and cook, especially in the evening.

The Landlord submitted photo evidence of the kitchen which demonstrated that there were 2 light fixtures above the cabinets, 2 pot lights in the center of the kitchen, an LED light fixture in the center of the room, and 2 light fixtures in the dining area. NB testified that he could not replace the light in the stove range as it required a special bulb that he was not able to find. He further testified that there were a total of 5 light fixtures in the kitchen and a bulb in the stove range was not needed in order to use the kitchen.
The Tenant confirmed that the photo submitted of the kitchen was the kitchen in her former rental unit, though she did not recall there being that many lights in the kitchen.

I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he attempted to find a replacement bulb but could not. I further accept that the photographs show ample lighting in the kitchen area. In the circumstances I am satisfied that the Landlord’s response was reasonable, and does constitute a breach of their maintenance obligations. This portion of the Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed. Issue 2: Sockets Exposed with no Wire Covers

The Tenant alleged that there were electrical sockets and wires not covered with a plate in the living room, her bedroom and in one of the children’s bedrooms. The Tenant alleged she was worried that her children, aged 7 and 11, or dog would be injured due to the exposed wires. To be cautious, the Tenant testified she placed a nightstand or a TV stand in front of the exposed wires. The Tenant testified that she made note of the exposed wires when she moved into the rental unit, though she did not email the Landlord. The Tenant further testified that she was not aware if the wires were live or not.

NB testified that at the move in inspection, he informed the Tenant that the wires were not electrical connections, rather were cable and internet wires. NB testified that there are no exposed electrical wires and the wires are not dangerous. He further testified that the Tenant never raised any concerns about the exposed cables.

When asked whether these were electrical connections the Tenant said she did not know. When asked if she could plug an item into the socket, the Tenant acknowledged that she could not plug something in as that was not the type of socket.

I find that the Tenant again misrepresented the facts about the alleged issue, and that she knew this was not exposed electrical wires and never notified the Landlord that she was concerned with the cable and internet connection not having a plate. As such, I find that the Landlord did not breach his maintenance obligation as he could not fix something the Tenant never notified him of. This portion of the Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed. Issue 3: Window Screen in Children’s Room

The Tenant alleged that on April 19, 2024 there was an issue with the front door code and her and her children could not enter the unit as there is only a passcode no key for the unit. The Tenant testified that her dog was in the unit panicking and she was concerned so she contacted NB. NB told her that he could cut the screen from the window and they could climb into the unit that way. The Tenant testified that after the screen was cut, the Landlord never fixed the screen. The Tenant stated that she had not sent any communication to the Landlord about fixing the screen.

NB testified that he never cut the screen. NB had previously advised the Tenant to make sure she changed the batteries in the door lock if it started to beep, so the lock would not become unfunctional. When the Tenant contacted NB, he removed the screen by prying it out. NB testified he told the Tenant that the screen would need to be re-installed from the inside of the window by pushing it back into place and he left the screen leaning against the front door. When NB was removing the screen, the Tenant was video recording him to show how it was removed. After 3 days, NB saw that the screen was still leaning against the door and put it into storage. NB testified that the Tenant never contacted him about the screen after it place did in storage.

When asked why the Tenant did not put the screen back into place as explained by the Landlord, the Tenant testified she did not think it was her responsibility and in her lease the Landlord should have to fix it.

I again find that the Tenant was not truthful in what had occurred. Her response demonstrated she knew that the screen was not cut and just needed to be pushed back into place from the inside. In addition, while she said she did not think doing so was her responsibility, she stated that she never contacted the Landlord about doing it for her. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not breach his maintenance obligation as again he could not fix something the Tenant never notified them she had an issue or wanted assistance in putting the screen back in place from inside the rental unit. This portion of the Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed. Issue 4: Smoke Alarms Going Off

The Tenant alleged ongoing issues with the fire alarms going off without a repair or remedy from the Landlord. Some of the alleged incidents were prior to 1 year before the application was filed, however there were 5 incidents of the fire alarm going off that were within the LTB’s jurisdictional time limit: October 28, 2023, October 29, 2023, March 3, 2024, March 6, 2024 and March 27, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she could not recall the exact times the fire alarm went off, but some were in the morning around 7:30am as she was getting ready for work, and others were in the evening between 5:00pm and 6:30pm. The Tenant testified that the fire alarms would go off for approximately 10 minutes on each occurrence. The Tenant testified that her children were home alone on the March 10, 2024 occurrence and that they have nightmares still because of the fire alarms.
When asked, the Tenant testified she did not know if the alarms were going off in other units, and she and her children were not forced to relocate due to the fire alarms.

NB testified that the residential complex’s fire alarms are part of the new fire code and if a alarm goes off in one unit it goes off in all of them and there is an audio and visual component with flashing lights and sound. NB further testified that on October 29, 2023, he notified the Tenant he was conducting fire alarm testing to see if he could identify a reason for the alarms going off. Between that date and March 3, 2024, the fire alarms were not an issue. During March 2024, when the fire alarms went off again, he inspected the other units and found no issue with the fire alarms. NB testified he did not inspect the fire alarm in the Tenant’s unit as she was very hostile towards him and he had limited opportunities to be able to enter the unit to inspect her fire alarms.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the fire alarm going off is a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. The Landlord did testing in October 2023 when first notified of an issue, and conducted checks of the alarms he had access to in March 2024 and no issues were identified. I find that there was not an ongoing issue with the fire alarms for the Landlord to fix. therefore I do not find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligation. Therefore, this portion of the application is dismissed. Issue 5: Issues with the air conditioner

The Tenant testified that on May 15, 2024 she noticed the air conditioner was malfunctioning and not working. She noticed that there were heating and cooling trucks outside the residential complex and thought the Landlord was completing work. When the air conditioner still did not work, the Tenant emailed the Landlord on May 25, 2024. The Landlord responded he could come and look at it that day, but the Tenant testified she asked whether he could come on May 26, 2024 instead. The Tenant testified the Landlord did not attend the rental unit until June 5, 2024, and the air conditioning was never fixed prior to her vacating the rental unit at the end of June 2024.

The Tenant testified that she could not open her windows as there was no screen on one of the windows, as discussed above, and that there was no air flow in the house. Her dog was very dehydrated, and the temperature of the rental unit was so hot that it was difficult for her and her children.

NB testified that when the Tenant emailed him on May 25, 2024 he reminded her that she is supposed to contact him with concerns immediately, not 1.5 weeks after. NB testified that he did not believe the Tenant that there was anything wrong with the air conditioning as the unit that supplies air conditioning to her unit also supplies the commercial unit that is in the same complex, and the commercial unit had air conditioning at the time of the complaint.

NB testified that he had inspected the air conditioning unit outside and the fan was running and there did not appear to be any issues with the actual unit and it was supplying cold air to the commercial unit. The Tenant uploaded videos of an air conditioning unit where the fan was not running, however NB stated that was the unit for the other rental unit and not the one that supplies her rental unit.

NB testified he made attempts to schedule a time to look at the thermostat in her unit, however he thinks the Tenant delayed him coming until she could have two individuals with her when he came into the rental unit. When NB entered the unit, he testified that the thermostat did not have a high temperature and was in the mid 70s. He thought maybe there was an issue with the connection and the wires were in the closest. NB testified he asked the Tenant to move her items in the closest so he could access the wires, and when he saw that the items in the closet were blocking the main water shutoff, he took a picture, which upset the Tenant and the individuals with her.

During the interaction, the male individual with the Tenant kept making comments to NB, and NB said he finally just cut off the thermostat as he figured something was wrong with it and he needed to get out of the house. The male individual pushed NB off the porch and NB called the police. The 2 individuals with the Tenant left before the police arrived. The Landlord provided the videos uploaded by the Tenant to the portal to the police, and the police notified him that the video was missing parts.

The Landlord provided documentary evidence that the thermostat was fixed on June 13, 2024 by Syles Mechanical, and the thermostat was relocated from the Tenant’s unit to the commercial unit so the Landlord could have access. After June 13, 2024, the Tenant did not raise further complaints about the air conditioning.

NB acknowledged that there would not have been air conditioning between June 5, 2024 and June 13, 2024 due to him cutting the thermostat, however he testified the weather was cool during this period. Except for this period, the air conditioning was never broken.

The Tenant asked for an adjournment at this point to have the male individual attend the hearing, however I denied this request as the Tenant should have brought all her witnesses for this hearing date and she was the one that had uploaded the videos that showed the male individual and the altercation with the Landlord.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant established that the air conditioning was not working from May 15, 2025 to June 4, 2025 and after June 13, 2025 as I find her testimony of events lacking credibility. I find that the Tenant demonstrated a lack of consistency throughout the hearing on all other issues alleged, and specifically misrepresented the facts on several occasions. The fact she did not provide the full video in disclosure and only parts further leads me to find that the Tenant is again trying to manipulate the facts of the alleged issue. Therefore, I find that the evidence of the Landlord is more credible.

Based on the evidence from the parties, I find that the only period of time in which the air conditioning was not working was during June 5, 2024 to June 13, 2024. The Landlord inspected the external unit and found no issue, and the unit was still supplying air conditioning to the commercial unit. I accept NB’s evidence that he had conducted a reasonable investigation and he had not identified any issue with the air conditioning prior to June 5, 2025. I also accept NB’s evidence that the air conditioning was not working due to him removing the thermometer on June 5, 2025 and he had a repair technician fix the unit on June 13, 2025.

I find that the air conditioning was not working from June 5, 2025 until June 13, 2025, though I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that NB did have the air conditioning repaired as soon as possible within 8 days of the issue commencing. Therefore, the Landlord did not breach his maintenance obligation, and this portion of the application is dismissed. Conclusion:
I find that the Tenant has not established on any of her allegations that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act, and therefore the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $9,868.10, which represents the rent differential the Tenants are required to pay as a result of the bad faith eviction, moving and other expenses, general compensation, and the costs of filing this application. Apr 2, 2026

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

The Court also agreed at paragraph 50 with the following statement made by the LTB in [name] v. [organization], 2021 CanLII 146522 ([name]. L.T.B.): [I]n relaying the Purchaser’s intentions to terminate the tenancy, the Landlord does not serve as a mere messenger with no duties or obligations to the Tenants. By conveying the Purchaser’s stated intention to occupy the rental unit, the Landlord initiated events that had the serious consequence of ending the tenancy and compelling them to relocate their family…As a result, I find that the Landlord had a duty to the Tenants to exercise some due diligence to confirm the good faith intentions of the Purchaser before putting the eviction in motion. Otherwise, an unscrupulous purchaser would be free to use a landlord as a straw man to divest tenants of their housing and thereby evade the statutory protections afforded to them under the Act.

The Tenants testified that the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act indicating that the rental unit was sold and the Purchasers intended to move into the rental unit for their own residential occupation for a period of at least one year. The N12 notice was dated April 17, 2024 with a termination date of June 30, 2024. The Tenants testified that they vacated on June 28, 2024 in accordance with the N12 notice.
The Landlord, [name] (‘DH’) did not dispute that he had served an N12 notice on behalf of the Purchasers and that the Tenants had vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenants have proven the first and second element of section 57(1)(b) of the Act.

The Tenant, [name] (‘KV’) testified that she had discovered the rental unit listed for rent on Facebook Marketplace and Kijiji on or around July 9, 2024. A copy of the listing was entered into evidence by the Tenants.

KV also testified that her former neighbour had subsequently advised somebody who was not the Purchasers had moved into the rental unit. However, the neighbour was not present at the hearing so this hearsay evidence was given little weight.

KV testified that the LH began pressuring the Tenants to sign an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy. In a text message dated September 7, 2023, LH states: You will have to sign it anyways if someone buys it for personal use if it didn’t get sold it would be null and void so it’s really not a big deal your paralegal is giving you mediocre advise we agreed you will get out so that’s what that form says it says we’ve agreed that you have 60 days from the date of sale.

In a subsequent text messages on or about February 14, 2024, [name] sent multiple text messages indicating that she intends to either have the Tenants sign an N11 or to give an N12 notice for the Tenants to vacate and to move into the rental unit until the property is sold. On April 17, 2024, [name] sent the Tenants a text message indicating that the Landlords had accepted an offer on the rental unit and the Landlords will be couriering an N12 notice to the Tenants.
The Tenants ask that I draw an inference that [name] was acting in bad faith in serving the N12 notice based on LH’s conduct leading up to the service of the N12.

DH testified that he entered into an agreement of purchase and sale with the Purchasers, which closed on June 30, 2024. He testified that he was not aware of the agreement terms between his wife, [name] (‘LH’) and the Purchasers and that they were the primarily responsible for discussing the terms of the purchase and sale of the rental unit. DH testified that he and [name] were going through a divorce at the time of the sale and had a strained relationship so he left the terms of the sale to LH, who is a real estate agent. DH did not deny that he and [name] had served an N12 for the Purchasers’ own use. DH testified that the Purchasers had advised they intended to move into the rental unit and that he and [name] had given the N12 notice on that basis. However, this was double hearsay evidence and neither [name] nor the purchasers were present to testify as to whether the purchaser indicated their intention to reside in the rental unit.

Notably, neither [name] nor the Purchasers attended the hearing to give evidence. Moreover, while DH testified that the Purchasers had indicated they required the rental unit for their own residential occupation, no evidence was entered at all in support of the assertion, such as the agreement of purchase and sale, or even a text message or email from the Purchaser to DH or LH indicating that they required the rental unit for their own use.

I am satisfied that one Landlords gave the N12 notice in bad faith in order to sell the unit vacant. This finding is supported by the text messages from LH leading up to the service of the N12 notice, as well as the fact that the rental unit was listed for rent shortly after the Tenants vacated. Based on the largely unchallenged testimony of the Tenants, I am further satisfied that nobody listed in the N12 notice moved into the rental unit as the unit was listed for rent mere days after the Tenants had vacated, and there was no evidence led that anybody listed in the N12 notice had moved into the rental unit.

As noted in Elkins, a landlord must exercise some form of diligence in determining a purchaser’s good faith. In this case, DH had very little first-hand knowledge regarding the Purchasers’ good faith intentions. The persons that did, LH and the Purchasers, did not attend the hearing. In the absence of supporting evidence such as correspondence that the Purchasers indicated a good faith intention to occupy the unit, which I would have expected to exist, I decline to accept DH’s hearsay and double hearsay evidence on this point.

In these circumstances, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords gave the N12 in bad faith. There is no credible evidence before me that the Landlords had a good faith basis to serve the N12 or that they took any steps to ascertain the Purchasers’ good faith intentions, let alone exercised some diligence. Rent Differential

The Tenants testified that a new lease agreement was signed with a start date of June 26, 2024 at a rent of $2,400.00 per month, which was a $400.00 per month increase from the rent of $2,000.00 per month that the Tenants had been paying for the rental unit in this application.
The Tenants are now paying $400.00 more per month than they were paying for the rental unit. The Tenants testified that their rental unit is comparable in size and facilities to the previous unit.

Having considered the comparison of the rental units and the amount claimed, I find that the rent differential of $4,800.00 is reasonable and an order will issue requiring the Former Landlords to pay the Tenants $4,800.00 for rent differential for a period of one year. Out-of-Pocket Expenses for Moving, Storage and Like Expenses

The Tenants also sought out-of-pocket expenses of $68.10 for the cost of a moving truck and $952.00 in lost wages. The Tenant, [name] (‘TM’) testified that as he works in Fort St. John in British Columbia, he was required to take three days off work to move out of the rental unit. A copy of his paystub was provide into evidence. I accept TM’s evidence that he took a day off work to move units, and I I find it appropriate to order the Landlords to pay the Tenants this amount pursuant to subsection 57(3) 4.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $1,020.10 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Compensation

The Tenants testified that they are now responsible for paying the utilities that were included in the rent at the rental unit. They sought general compensation in the amount of $4,000.00 which is calculated at $400.00 per month for the increased cost of utilities the Tenants are now required to incur and the stress incurred as as result of having to move due to the Landlord’s bad faith notice. As these costs are a result of the Landlords’ bad faith eviction, I find this amount to be reasonable.
Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $4,000.00 for general compensation. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines is intended to assist parties in understanding the Board’s usual interpretation of the law, and to provide guidance to Members to promote consistency in decision-making.

An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Although the Landlords’ conduct in this case does show a blatant disregard for the Act, I am of the view that the other remedies awarded should provide adequate deterrence and promote future compliance with the Act. Therefore, no administrative fine shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $9,868.10.
