issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: [address] Brampton ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on April 22, 2026 . Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 10:40 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence. Aaliyah Felicity divine [name] , Ackeilia Gabriella Christina Danie l and [name] [name] are removed as parties to the application.
reasons: The Tenant alleged that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'); did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $2,986.25.
The tenancy commenced on October 1, 2025. Ontario Works on behalf of the Tenant paid to the Landlord, $4,000.00 for the first and last month's rent deposit.

Although the rental unit is identified in the tenancy agreement, signed on September 18, 2025, as [address]. Brampton, the Tenant stated that the parties agreed that she would rent two bedrooms in the four-bedroom rental home for $2,000.00 monthly.

Prior to the commencement of the tenancy, the Landlord informed the Tenant that she had no intention of renting out the other two bedrooms in the home because of bad experiences with previous renters.

However, on September 30, 2025, when the Tenant was permitted to occupy the rental unit, she observed the Landlord and the Landlord’s husband lingering inside the rental home. When the Tenant asked when they intended to leave, the Landlord responded that it was her home, and she was not leaving.

On October 1, 2025, the Landlord thanked the Tenant for renting the unit and asked whether she and her husband could reside in the rental home. When the Tenant declined the request, the Landlord state d that she would amend the tenancy agreement , but t he Tenant also declined to sign an amendment.

On October 16, 2025, the Tenant called the police because the Landlord tried to get in a fight with her. When the police arrived, the Landlord informed them that she lives in the rental home and shared facilities with the Tenant who is merely an occupant. The police proceeded to escort the Tenant and her children out of the rental home.
The Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to re fund to the Tenant, $4,000.00 for the first and last month's rent deposit which was not fully utilized by the Tenant. Analysis
The first issue to be determined here is whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) applies to the relationship between the parties.
Section 3(1) of the Act states that the Act applies with respect to all rental units despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

The Act also contains a number of exemptions. Section 5 (i) of the Act provides that the Act does not apply with respect to living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner.

A Landlord bears the burden of proving that the exemption contained in section 5 (i) of the Act applies in this case. However, as the Landlord did not attend the hearing, I relied solely on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and the terms of the tenancy agreement.

Based on all the evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was not required to share a kitchen or a bathroom with the Landlord. The Tenant became aware of the Landlord’s intention of residing in the unit only after she moved into the unit. The Tenant’s testimony that she was not informed prior is consistent with her testimony about the meeting on October 1, 2025, where the Landlord asked her permission to reside in the unit.

Furthermore, th e tenancy agreement contains a different address for gi ving notices or documents to the Landlord. The Tenant stated that she believed the Landlord resided at that address which is located in a different city . I am satisfied that had the Landlord resided in the rental unit prior to the commencement of the tenancy, the address of the rental unit would be their address for service. I am also satisfied that the Tenant entered into the tenancy based on the Landlord’s statements that the Tenant would be the sole occupant of the rental home and that no other person would reside there.

The Landlord’s actions appear to be an attempt to circumvent the Act by claiming that the Tenant is an occupant, who shares a bathroom or kitchen facility with the Landlord. The Landlord cannot rely on th at exemption because that would be an attempt to modify the terms of the tenancy agreement after it commenced.
Based on all the evidence, I am satisfied that the exemption in section 5 (i) of the Act does not apply to the relationship between the parties.
The second issue is whether the tenant is entitled to a refund of the last month’s rent deposit and a portion of the rent paid for October 2025.

Section 106 (10) of the Act provides that any rent deposit paid by the Tenant must be applied to cover the rent for the final rental period before the tenancy ends. As the last month’s rent deposit was not applied to the rent for October 2025, the Landlord must return the full last month’s rent deposit of $2,000.00 to the Tenant.

In addition, the Landlord unlawfully evicted the Tenant on October 16, 2025, when she claimed that the Tenant was an occupant of the unit . Section 134 (1.1) (a) (b) of the Act prohibits a Landlord from collecting or attempting to collect rent from a former tenant for any period after the tenancy or the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has ended and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.

Consequently, as the Tenant was removed from the rental home on October 16, 2025, the Landlord must refund the excess rent collected for the period commencing October 17, 2025, and ending October 31, 2025.
The daily r ate for the rental unit was $65.75. Therefore, the Landlord must also refund $986.25 to the Tenant, an amount representing 15 days of rent calculated at $65.75 per day.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,986.25. This amount represents: • $986.25 for excess rent collected, and • $2,000.00 for the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove the following requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

Testified that they moved into the rental unit on June 15, 2021, and vacated October 27, 2024 after receiving an N12 Notice of Termination from the Landlord which indicated that the Landlord and the Landlord’s parent intended to occupy the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that they had concerns that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated. The Tenant testified that they frequently passed the rental unit, which is an apartment in a low rise and did not observe any signs of occupation or residence. The Tenant indicated that they observed the building a minimum of 5 or 6 times most recently in October 2025.

The Tenant also testified that on October 9, 205 they had a conversation with a security person in the building who informed the Tenant they did not believe anyone was living in the unit and did not see any signs of anyone residing in the unit.

The Tenant also referred me to emails between himself and the Landlord wherein the Landlord indicated that her presence in the building was not constant and testified that several of the maintenance reports in the Landlord’s own evidence demonstrates that the Landlord was not present at the time of these maintenance visits. The Tenant also indicated that many of the documents relied on by the Landlord were dated many months after the Tenant had vacated.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant vacated the rental unit sooner than she had expected and after the Tenant vacated, she moved into the rental unit gradually, first purchasing a bed, and bedframe and using boxes to brig her belongings to the unit over time instead of in one large move. She testified that she did need to book the elevator because her move was gradual. She testified that she began to move in on October 28, 2024 and her move was completed approximately one month later.

The Landlord directed me to an invoice for a bedframe which was delivered to the unit dated November 14, 2024, and text messages providing a rug cleaning company with delivery instructions on November 25, 2024.

The Landlord also testified that she used the utilities while in the unit, and directed me to utility bills in support of this assertion, She also indicated that she works from home and directed me to a letter from her employer which confirm the rental unit as her workplace and testified that she declared the rental unit as owner occupied for tax purposes and relied on this documentation.
The Landlord also testified that she changed the locks on March 25, 2025, because she felt unsafe as a security guard had bene following her around.

Further the Landlord testified that she has a medical issue and is required to stay home to aid her recovery and does not leave the unit frequently. The Landlord relied on a doctors note in support of this assertion.

The Landlord confirmed that she was not previously aware of the rental increase guideline, and had previously attempted to raise the rent on the unit beyond the guideline. The Landlord also confirmed that she was not aware of the elevator booking rule within the residential complex. Analysis

I accept that the Tenant received an N12 Notice of Termination and vacated as a result, however I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; or that The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant’s evidence was largely speculative and based on an assumption that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit. The mere fact that the Tenant visited the residential complex and did not see the Landlord in the unit is not itself determinative that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit, and I note that the Tenant’s assertion that the security guard/concierge did not observe the Tenant is both hearsay and not demonstrative of the Landlord failing to occupy the rental unit.

I do not accept the Tenant’s assertion that because the Landlord had testified that she was unaware of the rental increase guideline and the elevator booking policy in the complex that this undermines the reliability of testimony in this proceeding. Parties are frequently unaware of sections of the act or the rules, and I found that Landlord’s to be consistent and credible throughout and do not have concerns with respect to her reliability.

Beyond this speculation that Tenant has little clear, concrete evidence that would confirm that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit. I note that this is a Tenant’s Application, and the onus is on the Tenant to demonstrate that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time, the onus is not on the Landlord to demonstrate that they occupied the rental unit.

By contrast the Landlord has provided ample documentary evidence which suggests occupation of the rental unit including, utility bills, product invoices, a letter from her employer and a tax declaration form which list the rental unit as her home.

While much of this documentation is a comparatively recent, I note that some of it including the invoice for the bedframe, is dated shortly after the Tenant vacated the rental unit and is consistent with the Landlord’s testimony regarding moving into the rental unit in stages.

While I note that the Landlord’s own disclosure contains an email from building security asking why she had not been in the building which is consistent with the Tenants assertion, that she did not occupy the unit, I am prepared to accept that the Landlord both moved into the rental unit over a period of time and largely remained within the unit, rather than venturing out, due to medical issues. I also accept that the Landlord changed the locks because she felt threatened by a security person in the building and I find that it follows that the Landlord would be taking active steps to avoid this person where possible.

Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time, or that the N12 Notice of Termination was served in bad faith.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is granted. Facts:
The Tenancy began on June 1, 2025.
The lawful rent was $725.00 per month; it was due on the first of the month.
The Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit on June 1, 2025 in the amount of $825.00. Interest on the deposit has not been paid.

Sections 105 and 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) provides: 105 (1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. (2) In this section and in section 106, “security deposit” means money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition. 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. 5. I find that the Landlord collected $100.00 more than the legal rent for one month, which is not permissible.

The rental unit was one of five bedrooms in 5-bedroom house. The Tenant’s rental unit was on the main floor. There was one other bedroom on this floor. They were separated by a hallway. There were three bedrooms upstairs.
On August 2, 2025 at approximately 2:00 a.m., the Tenant was awakened by another tenant on his floor who was making loud outbursts and sleepwalking. The problem persisted for a month.
On September 3, 2025, the sleepwalker awoke the Tenant again. The Tenant said he was aggressive and called police.

The police attended but no report was provided in evidence. The Tenant testified that police spoke to the sleepwalker and did a soundcheck in the Tenant’s bedroom to ensure the walls were soundproof. They found that the sound traveled to the Tenant’s room and offered to issue a noise nuisance ticket the next time there was a disturbance.
On September 9, 2025, the sleepwalking noise again woke the Tenant at 2:00 a.m. The Tenant informed the Landlord the same day by email.
The Tenant said the Landlord took no action. The Landlord was not present at the hearing, so the Tenant’s evidence is uncontested.

On October 8, 2025, the sleepwalking noise occurred again and police re-attended. This time they said they were not in a position to respond to such a complaint; that it wasn’t criminal and that the Tenant had to resolve it through the Landlord.
On October 14, 2026 the Tenant sent another letter to the Landlord advising her of the ongoing problem through [name], a email communication service that provides proof of receipt. Exhibit 1.
The Landlord did not respond.
On October 21, 2025, the Landlord contacted the Tenant about showing his unit with less than 24 hours’ notice but did not mention the sleepwalking problem.
The Tenant vacated the unit on October 31, 2025. Remedies Requested

The Tenant requests the following remedies: • Refund of his last month’s rent deposit, $825.00 • The interest earned on the deposit, $8.63 • The cost of filing the application, $48.00. • Out-of-pocket expenses, $100.00 • General damages for stress. [name]

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the Act) provides that “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household”
“Interference” must rise to more than “passing” or “trifling” to be substantial.

In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No.5650, the Divisional Court confirmed that landlords have a positive obligation duty under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (The Act) to provide quiet enjoyment to tenants and must take reasonably necessary action against any other tenants in the residential complex who are intruding on the reasonable enjoyment of others.
I find that the Landlord was informed on September 9, 2025 of an issue with a sleepwalking tenant and took no action, not even an acknowledgement of the issue.
After being contacted again on October 14, 2025, the Landlord still took no action.
This lack of response is a clear violation of the positive obligation expected of landlords since [name].
At the very least, the Landlord had a duty to investigate the complaint from the Tenant.
The Tenant detailed ongoing loud noise and aggressive behaviour from another sleepwalking tenant. The Tenant testified it disrupted his sleep and made him concerned for his safety.
The effect of sudden, loud, aggressive noises and interactions in the middle of the night are destabilizing and disturbing. I find this kind of interference rises to the level of “substantial”.
The Landlord did not attend the hearing, so the Tenant’s evidence is uncontested.

Therefore, I find that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant’s complaint substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant. Remedies

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant the total of $881.63 because they substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit: • The Landlord shall refund the last month’s rent deposit, $825.00 • The interest earned on the deposit, $8.63 • The cost of filing the application, $48.00. Out-of Pocket Expenses

I decline to grant out of pocket expenses because out-of-pocket expenses must be shown to be reasonable and connected to the substantial interference. The Tenant did not detail what his out-of-pocket expenses were, nor did he provide receipts. General Damages
I decline to award general damages in this case because the Tenant did not provide evidence or documentation of losses associated with the substantial interference.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $881.63. This amount represents: • $825.00 for the last month’s rent deposit; • $8.63 for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3648.00. Charge Illegally Retained:

The Tenant testified that he paid $14,400.00 for a rent deposit for the last 4 months of rent. When the Tenant vacated on September 1, 2025, the Landlord returned $10,800.00 and did not return $3,600.00 for the last month of rent.

The Landlord at first testified that he kept the $3,600.00 as there were damages to the property when the Tenant vacated. The Landlord then testified that the Tenant only provided notice he would be vacating in mid-August 2025, so he kept the last month of rent for the lack of 60 days’ notice. The Tenant testified that he had given 30 days’ notice and the Landlord texted him that it was no problem. The Landlord then acknowledged that the Tenant did give 30 days’ notice.

When asked what he had done to mitigate his losses, the Landlord indicated he only listed the property for lease on August 26, 2025, almost 30 days after the Tenant gave their notice to terminate. The Landlord testified that he was travelling at the time so could not sign the paperwork to list the rental property, however the Landlord later testified that he had used e-signature on the documents, which could have been done at any time. The Landlord then testified that he had delayed listing the rental unit as his mother was considering moving in and he was not sure if he wanted to re-list the property at first. The Landlord also testified he wanted to paint the property and fix the grass before listing it for lease.

I find that the Landlord did not take any reasonable step to mitigate his losses under section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and the delay to re-listing the property was due to him not knowing if he wanted to re-list the rental unit. In these circumstances, it would be unfair to allow the Landlord to retain any of the Tenant’s rent deposit. As such, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did illegally retain the last months rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,648.00. This amount represents: • $3,600.00 for the last months rent deposit; • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (LTB-T-088044-24). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (LTB-T-084866-24).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $347.16 in rent abatement and the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant moved into the three-bedroom rental unit in March 2021 and continues to reside in the unit.
The lawful monthly rent at the time the application was filed was $1,686.00 , with the daily rate at $55.43. / LTB-T-084866-24 Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that on August 8, 2024, while she was away from the rental unit, her mother visited the unit and observed water leaking from the ceiling in the front entrance doorway, the closet , hallway, and master bedroom . The Tenant immediately made a maintenance request to the Landlord, and at the hearing, presented pic tures of the unit which corroborated her evidence.
On or about August 24, 2024, when the Tenant returned to the unit , she contacted the Landlord multiple times about the repairs.

On September 18, 2024 , the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord acknowledging information she received about the roof being replaced. She further stated that the leak was worse and there was mold in the unit: ‘I have had to move my mattress into the third bedroom because of the black mold coming through the ceiling and the wretched smell, all of this causing my asthma to be affected.’ The Landlord did not respond to the email.

On September 21, 2024, the Tenant sent an other email to the Landlord describing the conditions of the unit and attached pictures of the damage caused by the leak. The Landlord responded on September 22, 2024, stating that they were taking the issue seriously and would send someone to assess the damage and conduct repairs.

On September 24, 2024, the Tenant contacted the bylaw office who sent an officer to inspect the unit. Although the officer’s report was not provided to the Tenant, the Tenant was aware that the Landlord was given a 30-day deadline which expired, with no steps taken by the Landlord. The officer kept attending the residential complex over the problem on undisclosed dates.

On September 26, 2024, the Tenant sent another email to the Landlord because water had seeped into the fire detector and damaged it. The Landlord sent someone to remove the fire detector and provide her with a battery-operated unit.
On October 8, 2024, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord seeking an update on the repairs which were yet to commence.

At the beginning of December 2024, the city told the Landlord that if the roof were not repaired, the city would do it at their expense and bill the Landlord for it. The Landlord subsequently fixed the roof on December 19, 2024.

The Landlord on the Tenant’s request, paid for a hotel stay from February 11, 2025, to February 17, 2025, while repairs were being done inside the unit. On her return on February 17, 2025, the Tenant observed the unit was still undergoing repairs and some of her belongings were displaced. The work was not finished until February 28, 2025.

The Tenant further testified that a few repairs were not properly done but were corrected in March 2025, and that the Landlord failed to keep their promise to hire a professional to clean the unit following the repairs. / LTB-T-084866-24 Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord's witness / Residential Manager, AH, testified that there was a major storm the week the Tenant contacted him in mid August 2024. He inspected the rental unit, confirmed the Tenant’s report, and contacted the Property Manager on a suitable contractor to conduct the repairs.

The Landlord stated that the repairs were done on August 19, 2024, and presented an invoice from a construction company in support of the claim . The invoice showed the intended repair as ‘Apply tar to all areas around the chimney and vent where the leaks have been identified. Install waterproof shingles around the chimney and vent to prevent future leaks’.

About mid October 2024, the Tenant contacted AH because of a leak in her da ughter’s bedroom. The Landlord provided an invoice dated October 14, 2024, stating that the construction company addressed fix the roof on that date . The invoice showed that the contractor planned to ‘Remove all debris and damaged foam. Clean and address any water accumulation underneath the roof. Apply a barrier mat made of rubber to enhance protection.’

The Landlord also provided an invoice dated October 21, 2024, showing ‘Scope: Remove and replace drywall and insulation on the ceilings of the bedroom and stairwell. Finishing: Plaster walls and apply stipple finish.’
AH stated that when the leak stopped in one area, it began in another, but the roof was eventually replaced on or about February 14, 2025. Analysis

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.
The Tenant has not demonstrated that the Landlord completely neglected their responsibility by failing to maintain the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd ., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the leak first came to the attention of the Tenant on August 10, 2024, and she immediately notified the Landlord. By August 19, 2024, the Landlord had hired a contractor who repaired the roof. The Landlord acted reasonably in this circumstance.

Following another complaint on September 18, 2024, and September 21, 2024, the Landlord promised they would send a contractor to assess the damage and conduct all necessary / LTB-T-084866-24 repairs. However, the Landlord did not take any action until the Tenant made another complaint about mid October 2024. Given the severity of the situation, I find it unreasonable for the Landlord to wait 27 days from September 18, 2024, to October 14, 2024, before making further repairs. The Landlord will be ordered to pay to the Tenant, rent abatement of 20% or $11.08 daily for that period in the amount of $299.16 ($11.08 x 27days)

By October 14, 2024 , the Landlord had the roof repaired again and on October 21, 2024, repairs were conducted within the rental unit. But for the Tenant’s requests for temporary accommodation on December 19, 2024, no further complaints were disclosed in evidence. While the Tenant stated that the roof was replaced in December 2024, the Landlord claimed it was done in February 2025. The parties agreed that repairs were again commenced on or about February 11, 2025, and concluded by February 28, 2025. Based on the evidence, the Landlord did not neglect their maintenance obligations in this circumstance.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $347.16. this represents: • $299.16 rent abatement from September 18, 2024, to October 14, 2024, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
In the alternative, if the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 29, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $347.16 from the monthly rent in April 2026,
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Tenant’s application LTB-T-088044-24 is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): (a) substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex; and (b) harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them.
reasons: This application was filed on November 7, 2023. It is based on the assertion that the Landlord breached section 22 and section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’).
As described further below, this application was heard—and adjourned—on October 30, 2024.
In November of 2023, the Tenant also filed a T6 application—LTB-T-090176-23—based on the assertion that the Landlord had breached their maintenance-related obligations.

At a hearing on November 14, 2024, after issues were encountered by the Tenant uploading [name] and they were offered an opportunity to have the hearing adjourned to allow them to address those issues, the Tenant asked to withdraw LTB-T-090176-23. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

It is undisputed that the Tenant paid the Landlord $1,353.88 on April 22, 2025 for the period March 18, 2025 to December 31, 2025. This amount represented a pro-rated portion of the municipal taxes that the Tenant agreed to pay the Landlord pursuant to the lease agreement ($1,710.24 per annum).

The Tenants application rises from subsection 134(1)(a) of the Act, which states the following: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) Collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable

Section 17 of O.Reg 516/06 defines payments that are exempt from subsection 134(1) of the Act, and are therefore permissible for the landlord to collect from a tenant. For this application the relevant exemption is: 9. Payment of an amount to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the Landlord with respect to a mobile home or land lease home owned by the tenant.
The Landlord testified that the amount the Tenant pays under the terms of the lease includes the property tax for the land as well as the property tax for the mobile home.

It is undisputed the lease agreement explicitly states the Tenants “shall… pay the Tenant’s apportioned share of ‘municipal taxes and charges’ as that term is defined in the RTA and in accordance with the Landlord’s calculation…the Tenant shall reimburse the Landlord for property taxes levied with respect to the rental unit as permitted by s.134 of the RTA. The Tenant shall pay any additional taxes levied… in respect of the Tenant’s Home of the Rental Unit… the municipal taxes…payable by the Tenant hereunder shall be calculated by the Landlord and paid by the Tenant.”

Despite the explicit terms of the lease agreement, the Tenant disputes that they owe the full amount of the taxes to the Landlord and assert that the portion he pays are higher than other Tenants within the mobile home park. The Tenant submits that the higher amount is prohibited and an illegal charge.

Having heard and considered the evidence and submissions of both parties, and considered the Act and Regulations, I find that reimbursement of the property taxes paid by the Landlord is permissible. I find that the Tenant agreed to pay the taxes as calculated by the Landlord under the terms of the lease. As taxes are an exempt charge under [name], I find the Tenant has not proven the amount charged by the Landlord is illegal or above the amount that he owes. The Tenant failed to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the amounts charged were calculated or apportioned incorrectly by the Landlord.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $249.32.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord harassed him on the following occasions: • September 12, 2025 – the Landlord physically assaulted the Tenant by pulling on him during an argument. • September 10, 2025 – the Landlord harassed the Tenant verbally and by text message. • September 15, 2025 – the Landlord directed profanity toward the Tenant.

I find the Tenant’s uncontested testimony to be sufficiently reliable to ground a finding that the events occurred as described by the Tenant and that, as such, the Landlord both substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed the Tenant.

The Tenant also testified that he asked the Landlord to turn on the heat for the rental unit on September 1, 2025. The Landlord refused, citing a City of Toronto property standard that does not require heat to be provided until September 15. This bylaw was not presented at the hearing. The Tenant testified that the heat was not turned on until September 15, 2025.

Section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) defines “vital services” as follows: “vital service” means hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat.

Section 4 of O. Reg. 516/06 General (the ‘Regulation’) elaborates on the definition of “vital services” (emphasis added): 4. (1) For the purpose of the definition of “vital service” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act, September 1 to June 15 is prescribed as the part of the year during which heat is a vital service. (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), heat shall be provided so that the room temperature at 1.5 metres above floor level and one metre from exterior walls in all habitable space and in any area intended for normal use by tenants, including recreation rooms and laundry rooms but excluding locker rooms and garages, is at least 20 degrees Celsius. (3) Subsection (2) does not apply to a rental unit in which the tenant can regulate the temperature and a minimum temperature of 20 degrees Celsius can be maintained by the primary source of heat.

Regardless of any property standards imposed by a municipality, the Landlord has obligations under both the Act and the Regulation. The Regulation is clear: heat is a vital service from September 1 to June 15. As such, by refusing to turn on the heating system for the rental unit from September 1 to 14, 2025, the Landlord withheld the Tenant’s vital service contrary to section 21 of the Act. Remedies
The Tenant testified that the Landlord made him feel uncomfortable in the rental unit, both as a result of the Landlord’s harassment and the lack of heat.

Based on the evidence presented at the hearing, I have found the Landlord to have been in breach of his obligations under the act from September 1, 2025 to September 15, 2025. This period is inclusive of the particular incidents of harassment and the time that the Landlord withheld a vital service from the Tenant.

The Tenant’s rent is $1,246.61 as of the hearing date. In my view, a rent abatement of $249.32 is appropriate in these circumstances. This represents 40% of the rent charged for the period of September 1 to 15, 2025.

The Tenant also asked the Board to consider issuing an administrative fine against the Landlord. In my view, an administrative fine is not necessary in this case to deter the Landlord from repeating this conduct going forward. The finding of a breach and the abatement award are sufficient to accomplish this aim. As such, no administrative fine is ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $249.32.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $249.32 from the monthly rent payment due on May 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 26, 2026 ____________________________

Board records indicate the Tenant filed a T2 application on November 8, 2023.
An ACC hearing was held on October 24, 2024 and the application was not resolved.

The Landlord’s legal representative raised two preliminary issues: 1) The Tenant did not disclose the evidence to the Landlord prior to the hearing; and 2) The Tenant’s application is lacking sufficient reasons and details for the Landlord to know the case to be met. Landlord submissions

The Landlord’s legal representative stated the Tenant did not provide proper disclosure for evidence and as of the day of the hearing the Landlord has not received the evidence the Tenant intends to rely on.
The Landlord’s legal representative stated the Tenant failed to provide any evidence to the Landlord in accordance with the Board Rules of Procedures section 19.1.
The Landlord’s legal representative stated that evidence disclosure was raised at the ACC held on October 24, 2024 and the Tenant has not complied.

The Landlord’s legal representative also stated that the application is lacking sufficient reasons and details for the Landlord to know the case to be met. The Tenant was advised at the ACC that the Tenant had until the next hearing to amend the application and the Landlord’s legal representative stated the Tenant has failed to do so.

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that the Tenant’s application provides an alleged date of discovery of a dead squirrel in the Tenant’s chimney on March 22, 2023 and identifies the removal of the dead animal on June 5, 2023.

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that the Tenant has failed to identify any other details specifically the dates of any communication with the Landlord between March 22, 2023 and June 5, 2023. Tenant submissions

The Tenant does not dispute he did not provide evidence disclosure to the Landlord. The Tenant’s position is he understood that when he uploaded documents to the portal the Landlord was made aware of them by Board notification.
The Tenant’s position is at the ACC it was pointed out that he had an opportunity to amend the application prior to the next hearing if he chose to do so.
The Tenant stated he did not amend the application as he felt the details of his claims were sufficiently identified in the application and he did not need to amend the application. Analysis

The leading case regarding the requirement for sufficient reasons and details is [name] v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931. This case stands for the proposition that the kinds of particulars that should be contained in a notice should include “dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct engaged in by the tenant”. The Court held that the tenant needs to know the specific allegations against him/her for three purposes: a. to know the case that must be met; b. to decide whether to dispute the allegations; or c. to consider whether to void the notice.
The onus rests with the applicant, in this case the Tenant to provide sufficient details to support their claim for substantial interference.

The requirement for adequate particulars required within any notices of termination or as is in this case Board applications, has long been established by case law. The leading case regarding the requirement for sufficient reasons and details is Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931. This case stands for the proposition that the kinds of particulars that should be contained in a notice should include “dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct engaged in by the tenant”. The Court held that the tenant needs to know the specific allegations against him/her for three purposes: a. to know the case that must be met; b. to decide whether to dispute the allegations; or c. to consider whether to void the notice.

The Board’s T2 application forms have been developed with instructions to elicit the necessary details required for the Landlord to make a claim and provide sufficient reasons and details. For example, under the “REASONS FOR FILING THIS APPLICATION” section the form states: • What happened? • What were the dates and times of the events? • Who caused the problem? • What were the names and titles (such as superintendent) of all the people involved?

Although the decision in Ball v Metro applies to a Landlord’s N5 notice, I note that the same level of details like dates and times of incidents identified above are required in a tenant T2 application like this in order for the Landlord to know the case to be met.

The Tenant’s application in part states the following: “After failed attempts to get their daughter to handle it here, and after I told them it was not my responsibility to handle the squirrel (they tried to have me call someone and pay for it up fromt), the landlord hires contractor to handle the issue. This person either via ignorance or lack of IQ somehow managed to trap the [name] in chimney where it obviously proceeds to starve and die. Verbal exchanges were made both in person and on the phone regarding the near immediate and pungent smell now that the landlords had returned to Canada.” [emphasis added]

The bold sections above regarding “failed attempts”, “…the Landlord hires contractor…” and “Verbal exchanges were made both in person and on the phone”, fail to identify dates and times as indicated in the Board application form and who the Tenant was communicating with.

For procedural fairness, [name] v. Metro Capital and Board forms require applicants to be the ones to provide sufficient details for the claims that are being made. Only then can the respondent fairly have a chance to respond to those claims.
In my view the Tenant has not provided the level of detail required in the application and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

With respect to the Landlord’s legal representative’s submission regarding disclosure not being met, I find it not necessary to make a finding on this submission as the application is dismissed for the reasons above.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,313.56. Rent Deposit not applied to last month of tenancy:

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on April 15, 2025, she gave her notice on July 30, 2025, and the rental unit was re-listed for lease on July 31, 2025. The Tenant further testified that she paid rent on August 15, 2025, and her last months rent deposit was to apply from September 15, 2025 to October 14, 2025.

The Tenant testified she moved out of the unit at the beginning of August 2025, but still had the keys until the Landlord’s realtor asked that they be returned on September 17, 2025. The Tenant testified that she was informed that a new tenant had signed a lease, and as of September 17, 2025, when she returned the keys as requested, she no longer had any access to the rental unit, despite paying until October 14, 2025.

The Landlord testified that the new tenant did not move into the rental unit until October 1, 2025, but he acknowledged that the keys were collected from the Tenant on September 17, 2025. The Landlord then testified that he did not return the last months rent deposit as he was required to pay brokerage fees to find a new tenant when the Tenant terminated her lease early.

Section 88(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: Despite subsections (1) and (2), if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent that exceeds the lesser of the following amounts: 1. The amount of arrears of rent determined under subsection (1) or (2). 2. The amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit

I find that the new tenant would be entitled to occupy the rental unit from September 18, 2025 as the tenancy had been terminated on September 17, 2025 when the Landlord collected the keys from the Tenant. The fact that the Tenant did not actually occupy the rental unit until October 1, 2025 is not determinative of when the new tenant would be entitled move into the unit after the Tenant had vacated. Therefore, the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant pursuant to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. The daily compensation is $79.72 based on $2,424.00 x 12 months ÷365 days. As such, the Tenant should only pay for use to September 17, 2025, and the remainder of the last months rent deposit is to be returned.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,313.56. This amount represents: • $2,265.56 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (the ‘T2 Application’). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’). The Tenant also applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (the ‘T3 Application’).
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative withdrew both the T1 Application and the T3 Application. As such, only evidence pertaining to the Tenant’s T2 Application was heard at the hearing.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay a rent abatement and filing costs to the Tenant, pay an administrative fine the LTB, deduct ongoing rent abatements from the monthly rent as described in this order until the substantial interference ceases, and cease the conduct described in the order below. Preliminary Issue: The Limitation Period at Subsection 29(2)

The Landlord’s legal representative takes the position that the Tenant’s application is statute-barred by section 29 of the Act: 29 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: … 3. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household. … (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant takes the position that while the initial event that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and rights under the lease occurred more than one year before the T2 Application was made, the breach of section 22 is ongoing and therefore the proper subject of an application before the Board.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6: Tenant Rights speaks specifically to the question of how the limitation period at subsection 29(2) applies in the circumstances of an ongoing breach (emphasis added): Most T2 applications must be made by a tenant or former tenant within one year of the date the alleged breach occurred. When determining whether an application has been made in time under subsection 29(2), the LTB will have to determine when the alleged breach occurred. When a breach is a single event such as an illegal entry, then the limitation period begins on the day the event happened. Where the breach is not a single event but is ongoing or recurring, such as the withdrawal of a vital service, the breach occurs over a period of time and the one-year limitation period runs from the date that the vital service is restored to the tenant. However, in all cases the limitation period is one year. The fact that the tenant did not apply to the LTB when the breach first happened does not affect the right to file an application. The tenant is not required to bring an application immediately. However, the application cannot include an issue which was resolved by the landlord more than one year before the application was filed.

This approach has been applied by the Board in other cases (e.g. [name], 2023 ONLTB 66158, at paras. 48-9). While it is clear that the Board cannot issue a remedy that extends back further than one year before the Tenant filed their application and that remedies may only be granted for substantial interference during this period (Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686, at paras. 9-10), this does not bar the Board from considering applications where the alleged ongoing breach began before the limitation period but continues throughout it.

The substantial interference alleged by the Tenant in this case is ongoing: the Tenant alleges that the Landlord had been depriving him of access to part of the rental unit since renovations took place in 2020 and that this deprivation of access continued throughout the limitation period to the present day.

It is clear that the Legislature intended to limit tenants’ ability to bring applications for events that occurred over one year ago (and for the Board to issue remedies for such events). But the issues described in the Tenant’s application are anything but historical – in fact, they are live: the Tenant alleges that, as of the day of the hearing, his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit is being interfered with by the Landlord. In my view, to interpret subsection 29(2) in a manner that would deprive a tenant of the ability to apply for a remedy for an alleged continuing breach would be inconsistent with the purpose of the Act to “balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants”: section 1.

The Tenant’s application was filed October 22, 2024. Any remedy issued as a result of that application can only relate to interference that occurred on or after October 23, 2023. This is the effect of subsection 29(2) on the Tenant’s application. The Rental Agreement

A copy of the lease agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant was presented at the hearing. The address of the rental unit on the lease is “54 [address]cent”. The lease stipulates that the Tenant is “to pay for all utilities in the premises.” The lease is silent about the use of the basement of the rental unit.

The Tenant’s realtor – [name] – testified at the hearing. She testified that the Tenant approached her to assist in finding a single-family home to rent for his family. [name] testified that she assisted the parties in drafting the lease agreement. She testified that the Tenant specified that he did not want to live in a property with a basement tenant because he wanted privacy for his children. [name] testified that she attended the rental unit with the Tenant before the lease was signed but that he did not have a specific memory of the basement other than a vague recollection that it is unfinished. [name] testified that there was never, to her knowledge, an agreement to exclude the basement of the home from the rental agreement.

The Tenant testified that the basement was available to him when he moved into the rental unit in May 2019. He testified that he used the basement for storage and as a workout space for his boxing equipment.

The evidence of both [name] and the Tenant on these points is largely uncontested. I found both accounts of the content of the rental agreement to be credible and they are consistent with one another. Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities that exclusive use and access to the basement is a term of the rental agreement between the parties. Continuing Interference: The Renovation and the Loss of Basement Access

The Tenant testified that he was approached by the Landlord in October 2020 and that the Landlord proposed renovating the basement. The Tenant states that he agreed to the renovation and permitted the Landlord and his contractors access to the basement, believing the renovations to be to his benefits. The Tenant provided screenshots of text messages between himself and the Landlord’s contractor discussing the need for the basement to be cleared out before work could begin. The Tenant testified that his understanding of the project was that the Landlord intended to finish the basement, but that the basement would remain part of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord approached him after the renovations were completed and informed him of the Landlord’s intentions to move another tenant into the basement. The Tenant testified that a couple and their five children eventually moved into the basement and that the Landlord attempted to enforce a split of utility costs between the Tenant and the individuals residing in the basement of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that this family resided in the basement for about one year and then moved out. He testified that, subsequently, other individuals moved into and out of the basement, saying that there is usually “about five guys there.”

The Tenant also testified that when the basement renovation concluded, the Landlord approached him and attempted to get him to sign a new lease agreement. A copy of the unsigned agreement – which lists a new rent amount of $5,566.00 – was provided in evidence at the hearing. The Tenant testified that he never signed this agreement and did not pay the increased rent amount.

Again, the Tenant’s testimony was largely unchallenged at the hearing. I found his recounting of the events to be consistent, detailed, and supported by the documentary evidence presented at the hearing. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant’s description of the alleged events about the renovation are accurate. Continuing Interference: Continued Lack of Access to the Basement of the Rental Unit

The Tenant testified at the hearing that he continues to not have access to the basement of the rental unit and that individuals continue to occupy the basement. This is corroborated by the only evidence led by the Landlord: the testimony of [name], one of the individuals living in the basement of the rental unit. [name] testified that he has lived in the basement of the rental unit since September of 2024 and that he is an employee of the Landlord. He lives in the basement of the rental unit with three other individuals. The Tenant did not consent to their presence in the rental unit.

On cross-examination, [name] testified how he and the other basement residents access the basement. He testified that there is a side entrance to the house and that inside that space is a laundry area. Off of the laundry area – which, per [name] testimony, the Landlord informed the basement residents is a common area – are three doors: one to the upper floors of the house where the Tenant lives, one to the basement where [name] and the other residents live, and one to the garage.

I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has been continuously and substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit since at least as far back as 2022 by authorizing other individuals to live in the rental unit without the Tenant’s consent. This interference has not ceased: by the Landlord’s own evidence, there are still individuals residing in the basement. It is essentially an uncontested fact that the Landlord unilaterally purported to change the size of the rental unit, that the Tenant never agreed to a change in terms, and that the Landlord continues to permit a minimum of three individuals – none of whom know the Tenant personally – to reside in the rental unit. Continuing Interference: Laundry Facilities

The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by authorizing the individuals residing in the basement to use the Tenant’s laundry facilities in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the residents of the basement have been using the laundry facilities, that he cannot leave supplies in the laundry room without the basement residents using those supplies, and that there have been several occasions when he has wanted to use the laundry facilities, but they were in use by another party.

The Tenant testified that he had exclusive access to the laundry facilities in the rental unit until the Landlord permitted other residents to move into the basement of the rental unit. At this time, per the Tenant’s testimony, a second set of laundry facilities was installed in the basement for the other residents use, but that eventually this set broke down and the Landlord instructed the other residents to use the Tenant’s laundry room. This was corroborated again by the testimony of [name], who testified that he was instructed by the Landlord to use those facilities upon moving in. This corroborates the contents of text messages provided by the Tenant at the hearing which show conversations about the laundry issue between the Tenant, the residents of the basement, and the Landlord in June 2024. 23. [name] also testified that the Tenant did object to the basement residents using the disputed laundry facilities via text message. He testified that he was not directly involved in any disputes with the Tenant about the use of laundry room but that it is conceivable that other residents of the basement have had such disputes. 24. With respect to this issue, both the Tenant’s evidence and the Landlord’s evidence point in the same direction: the Landlord has permitted the residents of the basement to use the laundry facilities in the rental unit, and the Tenant did not consent to this arrangement. The Tenant’s uncontested testimony is that he had exclusive use of these facilities up to June 2024, when the Landlord permitted the Tenants to use the facilities when the machines in the basement broke down. 25. The Tenant also provided photos from July 2024 showing personal belongings and clothes on top of the washing machine in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that these belongings are not his and that it is a frequent occurrence that the basement residents leave items in the laundry room. 26. Again, the evidence is fairly clear: the Landlord purported to unilaterally alter the terms of the rental agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant by permitting individuals to – without the Tenant’s consent – use the laundry machines in the rental unit. The Landlord cannot unilaterally alter the terms of the rental agreement. Therefore, the Landlord’s continued permission to the basement residents to use the laundry facilities in the Tenant’s rental unit – which are not common elements, per the actual rental agreement – constitutes substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Continuing Interference: Utility Arrangements 27. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by burdening the Tenant with responsibilities associated with managing utilities payments by the individuals living in the basement of the rental unit without the Tenant’s consent. 28. The Tenant’s evidence – as described above – clearly indicates that the original terms of the agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant were that the Tenant was responsible for 100% of the utilities costs associated with the rental unit. The Tenant testified to this at the hearing and the written lease agreement corroborates his testimony. 29. The Tenant testified that the Landlord had required the Tenant to coordinate collection and reimbursement of utility costs that arose as a result of the residents residing in the basement of the rental unit. This is corroborated by the Tenant’s documentary evidence, which includes utilities bills in the Tenant’s name and text messages between the Tenant and the downstairs residents – including [name] – about utilities issues in 2024. 30. Again, the testimony given by [name] corroborates the Tenant’s position that the Landlord has downloaded responsibilities relating to the administration of utilities to the Tenant. [name] testified that the current practice for the residents of the rental unit is that the Tenant receives the bills in his name and the parties have agreed to each pay 50% of these costs. Putting these responsibilities on the Tenant despite the fact that he signed a written agreement to rent the entire rental unit himself is a clear interference with his right to reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, albeit one that is derivative of the more significant breach by the Landlord: unilaterally reclaiming part of the rental unit and installing other individuals in that space. 31. The fact that the Tenant and the downstairs residents have reached an agreement among themselves of how to manage the utilities payments in their current situation does not change the fact that it is the Landlord who put – and is continuously putting – the Tenant in a situation he should not be in. This is substantial interference. Remedies 32. As discussed above, my interpretation of the limitation period set out at section 29(2) is that any remedy issued as a result of the Landlord’s continuing substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit can only relate to interference that occurred on or after October 23, 2023. The Tenant’s uncontested testimony is that, since this time, he has not had full access to the rental unit and that other individuals are living in the basement, substantially interfering 33. The Tenant has been without full access to the rental unit that he has been paying for since that time. A rent abatement is therefore warranted on this basis alone. The loss of the unfinished basement space has had an impact on the Tenant regardless of what happened to the space subsequently. Prior to the renovations and the clawing back of the basement space by the Landlord, the Tenant used the space as an exercise room and a storage space. This loss warrants a moderate 10% abatement of the rent paid from October 23, 2023, to the hearing date. This represents the fact that the Tenant still does have access to the vast majority of the rental unit and that the space lost was of limited function. This abatement shall also be applied on an ongoing basis so long as the issue persists and the Tenant does not have full access to the rental unit. 34. However, a further rent abatement is required as a result of the events that followed. The Landlord permitted individuals to move into a part of the rental unit without the Tenant’s consent. The presence of individuals in the basement has further substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant rented a single- family home in part because he wanted the privacy that such an arrangement provides. This was disrupted when the Landlord decided to re-rent the unlawfully reclaimed basement to other individuals. The evidence shows that the presence of other individuals in the rental unit has interfered with the Tenant’s ability to use the laundry facilities that he pays for at his convenience and with the utility use in the rental unit. The Tenant also testified that the arrangement imposed by the Landlord has interfered with the Tenant’s use of the garage. Taken together, these interferences warrant an additional 15% abatement of the rent paid from October 23, 2023, to the hearing date. This abatement shall also be applied on an ongoing basis so long as the issues cited (namely, the forced sharing of the laundry facilities and the requirement to coordinate utility use and payment with unauthorized residents) persist, as described in the order below. 35. The Tenant is also seeking orders from the Board compelling the Landlord to do the following: • Install a separate suite meter or convert utility bills to the Landlord’s name to alleviate the burden of the unauthorized residents’ utilities use on the Tenant. • Restore the Tenant’s exclusive use of the laundry facilities and not authorize other individuals to use the Tenant’s laundry facilities. 36. The request for an order requiring the Landlord to cease authorizing other individuals to use the Tenant’s laundry facilities is appropriate and shall be ordered. 37. The request for an order requiring the Landlord to change the billing structure relating to the utilities would not be an appropriate exercise of the Board’s remedial jurisdiction as to do so would be a modification of the contract between the Landlord and the Tenant. That said, I recognize that the Landlord’s egregious conduct has interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit not only through the administrative burden put on him by the Landlord but also by causing increased utility usage in the rental unit. Therefore, a remedy is appropriate and an additional 5% rent abatement from October 23, 2023, to the hearing date is awarded. This abatement shall also continue on an ongoing basis until there are no longer additional users of the utilities in the rental unit. 38. The Tenant is also requesting reimbursement of utilities costs that he has paid that were not incurred by the Tenant but are a direct result of the Landlord’s conduct. In my view, this is compensated for by the rent abatements discussed above and should not be the subject of a further remedy regarding out-of-pocket expenses. 39. I note that the Tenant filed an additional request to amend the T2 application two days before the hearing that was not accepted at the hearing due to insufficient notice to the Landlord. While this amendment is not live in this matter, I do feel a need to address the request of the Tenant, falling within the category of “any other remedy” that the Board sees fit as requested by the Tenant. 40. In my view, it would be inappropriate on the basis of this application to order the Landlord to restore the Tenant’s exclusive possession of the basement of the rental unit as to do so would severely jeopardize the interests of the occupants of the basement, who were not provided with notice of this hearing and only one of whom attended – [name]. Such an order would effectively be tantamount to an eviction without notice and without an opportunity to respond. 41. It is true that if the Landlord were living up to his contractual obligations to the Tenant, there would be nobody living in the basement of the rental unit without the Tenant’s consent. But the reality of the situation is that there are individuals living in the basement and that their rights – as against the Tenant or the Landlord – have not been adjudicated. As such, it would not be appropriate to order such a remedy without these parties having notice of the proceedings and the opportunity to participate in the proceedings. Given the stakes of such an order, a significant degree of procedural fairness ought to be afforded to the basement residents before any order affecting their immediate housing arrangements could be made. In my view, an order such as the one requested by the Tenant in their amended application may have, in fact, been an unreasonable exercise of discretion and would have been vulnerable to challenge on appeal or judicial review. 42. The Tenant paid $53.00 to file this application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 43. For all relevant points regarding the rent abatements above, the monthly rent for the rental unit was $3,366.00. As such, the daily rent for the rental unit is $110.66. The total rent that was payable by the Tenant to the Landlord during this period is $90,522.34: • $40,392.00, from October 23, 2023 to October 22, 2024 • $40,392.00, from October 23, 2024, to October 22, 2025 • $9,738.34, from October 23, 2025, to the hearing date. 44. The total amount payable by the Landlord to the Tenant is $27,209.69, comprised of: • $9,052.23 (10% rent abatement for loss of use of the basement from October 23, 2023 to the hearing date) • $13,578.35 (15% abatement for the substantial interference caused by the presence of unauthorized individuals in the rental unit and the downstream issues of utility coordination and disruption of the laundry facilities) • $4,526.11 (5% abatement for the increased utilities costs caused by the present of unauthorized individuals in the rental unit) • $53.00 (the cost of filing this application) 45. I also requested submissions from the parties about whether an administrative fine would be appropriate in this case and have taken those submissions into consideration in my determinations regarding whether an administrative fine is appropriate in this case. 46. The Board’s authority to impose an administrative fine in this case is set out at subsection 57(3) of the Act. 47. When considering the amount of an administrative fine that is appropriate in a given case (if any), several factors are considered by the Board as set out in the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Guideline 16: • The nature and severity of the breach; • The effect of the breach on the Tenant; • Any other relevant factors. 48. Administrative fines issued under section 57(3) are imposed to encourage future compliance with the requirements of the Act and deter the Landlord from engaging in similar conduct going forward. Whether a fine would have a deterrent effect is to be evaluated in the context of any other remedies being ordered by the Board. 49. In this case, the nature of the Landlord’s breach is significant and severe. He unilaterally reappropriated part of a rental unit that he agreed to rent to the Tenant – and that the Tenant still pays for – and re-rented it out for a profit. He has placed many practical and financial burdens on the Tenant that are not part of the rental agreement. This is flagrant conduct that shows disregard for the Landlord’s contractual and statutory obligations. 50. As discussed above, the impact on this Tenant has been significant. All of the circumstances described above with respect to the Tenant’s other claims are relevant to the determination of whether an administrative fine is appropriate. 51. In this case, an administrative fine is appropriate. The Landlord’s conduct is egregious and there is no indication that he perceives it as such. He did not attend the hearing due to travel obligations and the evidence and arguments presented on his behalf betray a lack of understanding of the severity of his actions. Further, he has profited from his unlawful conduct: he has effectively gained an income stream at the expense of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. His conduct places the Tenant and the residents of the basement in a precarious position and the consequences wide-ranging and ongoing. Nothing presented at the hearing indicates the Landlord is conscious of this. 52. The amount payable by the Landlord to the Tenant is significant, but in my view, it is not sufficient deterrence to guarantee the Landlord will respect his obligations under the rental agreement and the Act going forward. Absent a significant deterrent, I am concerned that he would repeat the behaviour described in this order if it accrued to his benefit. As such, the deterrent effect of a significant administrative fine is warranted in this case. 53. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must also pay a fine to the LTB of $5,000.00. Taken together with the ordered abatements, I am of the view that this fine will deter the Landlord from repeating this conduct in the future.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $27,209.69. This amount represents: • $27,156.69 for a rent abatement from October 23, 2023, to January 20, 2026. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.
