issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,716.37, including the cost of filing the application.

At the hearing, the parties did not dispute the following facts: i. The parties signed a fixed term lease agreement on September 19, 2024 for the period from October 17, 2024 to October 31, 2025. ii. The Tenant was to pay $500.00 on September 19, 2024 to secure the unit, $1,750.00 on October 3, 2024 as a last month’s rent deposit, and $806.00 on October 17, 2024 as prorated rent for the month of October 2024. These dates were also listed in section 8 of the lease agreement. iii. The Tenant made the respective payments for September 19 and October 3, 2024, but did not pay any prorated rent for October 2024. The total amount the Tenant paid to the Landlord was $2,250.00 ($500.00 + $1,750.00). iv. The Tenant informed the Landlord via text on October 1, 2024 that he would have to delay moving into the unit until October 30, 2024. The Landlord reminded the Tenant that he would still be paying rent from October 17, 2024 as agreed regardless of a delayed move in date. The Tenant requested the Landlord use the $500.00 deposit paid on September 19, 2024 towards the prorated rent for October 2024, but the Landlord refused. v. The Landlord texted the Tenant on October 16, 2024 asking when the Tenant could meet to collect the keys as he was entitled to possession of the unit the next day. The Tenant replied the same day he could not meet until October 26, 2024 to which the Landlord agreed. vi. The Landlord told the Tenant via text on October 17, 2024 that if he did not pay the prorated rent for October 2024 by the end of the day the lease agreement would be void. vii. After the Tenant did not pay the prorated rent for October 2024, the Landlord and Tenant engaged in an email chain from October 18, 2024 to October 27, 2024 in which the Landlord stated the Tenant breached the lease, and the last month’s rent deposit would be held until a new tenant could be found. The Landlord then told the Tenant on October 27, 2024 that the unit was re-rented for November 15, 2024, and he would only be returning $581.63 of the $2,250.00 paid by the Tenant. The Landlord subtracted a per diem amount from October 17, 2024 to November 15, 2024 from the Tenant’s payments to arrive at the returned amount. The Landlord then paid the Tenant $581.63.

The Tenant testified he was aware of the terms of the agreement and was still willing to move in, but he did not think it was fair to pay for time he was not in the unit when his circumstances had changed. It was the Landlord who then terminated the lease before the Tenant could move in.

The Landlord argued that the parties had already negotiated and signed a lease with a set start date. The Tenant was given the opportunity to take possession on October 17, 2024 but refused. The Landlord became frustrated by the Tenant’s attempts to unilaterally change the agreed upon terms of the lease and stated that if the Tenant did not adhere to the terms then the lease was essentially void. The Landlord should be able to keep the last month’s rent deposit until the new lease started on November 15, 2024 and for the aggravation of having to find a new tenant.

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The text message exchange between the parties submitted at the hearing show that the Tenant still intended to move into the unit, but there was an issue regarding how much rent should be paid for October 2024. When the Tenant tried to change the tenancy start date to pay a lesser prorated amount for October 2024, the Landlord then told the Tenant on October 17, 2024: “Pay the $806 by the end of today or the agreement is void.” When the Tenant did not pay the amount, the Landlord then informed the Tenant on October 18, 2024 that the unit was no longer available.

Section 13 of the Act states that the tenancy begins on the day the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit under the tenancy agreement; in this instance, October 17, 2024. The Tenant was given the opportunity to collect the keys to the unit on October 17, 2024, but was unable to do so due to his own organizational issues.

The Tenant may have been in breach of the agreement by October 18, 2024 by not paying the rent owing from October 17, 2024, but he did not express the intention to terminate the agreement outright. In fact, the text exchanges show the Tenant requesting the $500.00 payment made on September 19, 2024 (which was in addition to the last month’s rent deposit and therefore contrary to sections 105 and 106(2) of the Act) be applied to October 2024’s prorated rent, but the Landlord refused. The Landlord therefore unreasonably withheld possession of the unit after issuing the Tenant an ultimatum when he had other legal avenues that could have been exercised to deal with the arrears issue for October 2024. Instead, the Landlord chose to unilaterally declare the agreement void and triggered section 107 of the Act when he stated on October 18, 2024 that the unit was no longer available and did not give vacant possession to the Tenant. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit and the additional $500.00 security deposit totaling $2,250.00
Since the Landlord has already repaid $581.63 to the Tenant, the amount outstanding is therefore $1,668.37 ($2,250.00 - $581.63).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,716.37. This amount represents: • $1,668.37 for the remaining balance of the full deposit paid by the Tenant • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 5, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for lack of particulars.

The Tenant filed the T2 application with the Board on October 1, 2024. The application alleges that the Landlord: substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. However, the Tenant failed to provide further clarification on the particulars of the case.
When I raised the above preliminary issue with the Tenant, she submit that she was going to provide details of the case to be met when presenting her evidence.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice; and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct. [Emphasis Added]
While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the test applies equally to tenant applications, including those brought under section 31, of the Act.

I find that the T2 application lacked the specific detailed information required to put the Landlord on notice to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair for the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, the [name] application is dismissed. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The T6 application is to address two issues: 1) A shower leak; and 2) A cockroach infestation. Shower Leak

The Tenant testified that in August 2023, she notified the Landlord regarding a shower leak. The next day, the Superintendent came to inspect the leak and later notified the Tenant that she would need to vacate the rental unit as there would need to be extensive repairs/ renovations completed to update the plumbing in the rental unit. The Landlord did not dispute that the shower was leaking but testified that he offered the Tenant a resolution – to move out while he updates the plumbing, but the Tenant refused. The Landlord said he also offered the Tenant another rental unit in the residential complex, but she refused that as well. The Tenant agreed that she was offered another unit in the residential complex, but that it was smaller than her current unit. The Landlord issued the Tenant an N13 notice to do renovations that were so extensive, that the Tenant had to vacate the rental unit. The Landlord submitted a copy of the N13 notice into evidence which supported his position. The Landlord testified that he had to obtain permits to conduct the repairs, but was not allowed to perform the repairs unless the Tenant vacated.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit or residential complex and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards. The Landlord responded to the Tenant’s concerns immediately, attending the rental unit the next day to address the leaking shower. Furthermore, the Landlord had plumbers attend the rental unit, something the Tenant agreed to. When the plumbers informed the Landlord that the plumbing in the residential complex was old, hence why the shower was leaking, he provided the Tenant with options, such as another rental unit, but the Tenant refused.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant understood that the leaky shower would be resolved after the plumbing in the rental unit was updated, but she failed to make this possible for the Landlord to do. The Tenant agreed that she never raised the leaky shower issue with the Landlord again because she did not want to vacate the rental unit while renovations were being performed. The Landlord adduced evidence at the hearing to support that he obtained permits to do the repair, but the repairs required the Tenant to vacate the rental unit, which she failed to do. Cockroach infestation

The Tenant testified that in May or June of 2018 she notified the Landlord regarding a cockroach infestation. The Landlord responded immediately and had several treatment sprays performed on the rental unit by contractors. However, in September 2025, the Tenant notified the Landlord regarding the cockroach infestation and again, they had a pest control specialist go out to treat the rental unit, but the Tenant refused to allow the treatment to occur, unless the whole row was treated for cockroaches. The Landlord did not dispute that there were cockroaches in the rental unit. However, the Landlord testified that the Tenant’s failure to allow treatment to be performed in her rental unit is why the issue continued. The Landlord submitted into evidence an invoice from Welcon Pest Control Inc., which supports the Landlord’s position that they attempted to treat the rental unit.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit or residential complex and did not fail to comply with health or maintenance standards. The Landlord attempted to treat the cockroach infestation, but the Tenant did not allow the treatment to occur as she was not satisfied with the manner in which the treatment was being performed. The Tenant wanted the Landlord to treat the whole row of townhouses and not just her rental unit. The Tenant denying entry to the pest control treatment contractors is what prevented the issue from being rectified, not the Landlord’s conduct.
Therefore, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 application are dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the amount of $18,095.00. [name]:

By way of background, the rental unit is a two floor, four-bedroom single detached house with two bathrooms and one kitchen. The Tenant’s family moved into the rental unit in October 2017 and moved out on February 9, 2024. The Tenant was served with an N12 notice of termination on October 4, 2023, with a termination date of January 31, 2024. The N12 states that the Landlord’s parents and child intend to occupy the rental unit.
The Landlord began to list the rental property for sale on March 21, 2024, and the rental property was sold on March 28, 2024. The Tenant’s Application:

This application is brought pursuant subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: i. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. ii. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. iii. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and iv. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties about the first, second, and third elements of this test. The Tenant was served with a notice pursuant to section 48 of the Act. The Tenant moved out on February 9, 2024, as a result of the Landlord’s notice. The Landlord’s parents and his daughter did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.
The only remaining issue to be determined is whether the notice was given in bad faith. Bad Faith:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord approached the Tenant in July 2023 and asked whether the Tenant was interested in purchasing the rental unit because the Landlord’s financial situation was not good, and the Landlord wished to sell the rental unit. When the Tenant refused, the Tenant testified that the Landlord began asking the Tenant to move out in August and September 2023 because the Landlord wanted to sell the property. The Tenant testified that they refused to move out and advised the Landlord that the Landlord could proceed with a sale while they remained in the rental unit and that they would cooperate with showings. On October 4, 2023, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice stating that the Landlord’s parents and child intended to occupy the rental unit. Text messages between the Landlord and the Tenant dated between July 24 and October 14, 2023, were submitted and entered into evidence.

The Tenant further testified that after they vacated on February 9, 2024, they learned that the rental unit was listed for sale on March 21, 2024, and sold on March 28, 2024, which was within two months after they vacated.

The Landlord did not dispute that he was trying to sell the rental unit in the summer of 2023, and confirmed that it sold on March 28, 2024. The Landlord testified that, by the fall of 2023, the family’s circumstances changed because his 17-year-old daughter planned to attend university in Toronto and had never lived alone. The Landlord testified that, because he and his wife live abroad, his parents, who were then aged 73 and 78, agreed to relocate to the rental unit with the daughter in order to support her while she attended school. The Landlord relied on a sworn declaration from his mother, evidence of WhatsApp communications between him and his parents about preparations and renovations that he says were consistent with an intention to move in.

The Landlord further testified that there was a material change in circumstances giving rise to the collapse of his plans. The Landlord testified that his 73-year-old mother slipped and fell in January 2024 and suffered a second fall near the end of February 2024, after which medical advice changed and she was advised not to go up or down any stairs. The Landlord testified that the rental unit has stairs at the entry and additional stairs leading to the bedrooms, and that following the second fall, and the medical recommendation dated March 8, 2024, his parents could no longer safely move into the rental unit as planned. The rental unit was listed for sale in March 2024 and sold on March 28, 2024. Law and Analysis:

The evidence before me is that the rental unit was sold, and the Landlord’s parents and child did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. In these circumstances, the N12 notice is presumed to have been given in bad faith pursuant to subsection 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord has the opportunity to rebut the presumption of bad faith. Once the presumption of bad faith is triggered, the burden shifts to the Landlord to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 notice was given in good faith.
The Landlord did not rebut this presumption. i. The Landlord’s parents’ and daughter’s intentions:
For the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s parents and his daughter genuinely required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation.

The test I need to apply here is found in Feeney v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), in which the Court held that “the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal”. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC) where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental [name]. The Landlord may also have additional motives for selecting a particular rental unit, but this does not affect the good faith of the Landlord’s notice.

In this case, I have limited ability to assess whether the Landlord’s parents and daughter had a genuine intention to occupy because they did not attend the hearing to answer questions about their intentions. If they intended to occupy the rental property, I would have expected the Landlord to call them to provide testimony about their plans. The Landlord relied primarily on his mother’s declaration dated on October 5, 2023. The Landlord did not submit evidence from his father or his daughter. The Landlord also relied on text messages between himself and his parents’ concerning renovations discussed in October 2023.

Normally, when a person named in an N12 says they intend to move into a rental unit, that person attends the hearing to answer questions about their intentions, including where they currently live and why they intend to move, and other circumstances that assist in assessing genuine intent. Here, because none of them attended, I cannot ask those questions or meaningfully evaluate their intentions. Although hearsay evidence may be admitted, the weight to be given to it depends on the circumstances. In this case, because the Tenant’s legal representative could not test the evidence by cross examination of the persons said to be moving in, I give the text messages every limited weight.

For these reasons, I find that the Landlord led insufficient evidence to establish that his parents and his daughter genuinely intended to reside in the rental property when the notice of termination was served. ii. The Timing of the Sale 19. It is the Landlord’s position that there was a material change in circumstances because of his mother’s condition. The Landlord testified that he served the notice in good faith because, at the time he served it, he could not have anticipated his mother’s falls. For the following reasons, I am not satisfied that the Landlord served the notice in good faith. 20. In the Court of Appeal’s recent decision in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the court held that the LTB should consider all relevant evidence when determining whether the N12 was served in bad faith and should not restrict itself to consideration of whether there was good faith at the time the N12 was served. 21. In this case, the Landlord relied on a medical note dated March 8, 2024, stating that his mother should not go up or down stairs, with a review in 8 weeks. The Landlord filed no evidence to show that his mother attended for reassessment or that the restriction was permanent. The Landlord testified that the plan changed after March 8, 2024, but provided no evidence showing steps taken between February 9, 2024, and March 8, 2024, to prepare for the parents and daughter to move into the rental property. The Landlord also testified that his parents were not in Canada from January to April 2024. Despite that, the Landlord listed the rental property for sale on March 21, 20242023, only a few weeks after the medical note and before any review or follow up. I am not persuaded that the Landlord’s evidence establishes unforeseen circumstances that explain the failure of the parents and daughter to move in after the Tenant vacated. 22. Based on the totality of the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s parents and daughter intended to occupy the rental property for at least one year at the time the N12 notice was served or when the Tenant vacated. It is more likely than not that the Landlord sought vacant possession to facilitate a sale. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. 23. Accordingly, I find that all of the elements of the legal test in section 57 of the Act have been satisfied. Remedies 24. The Tenant requests the following remedies: • Rent differential, totalling: $12,000.00. • Moving expenses, totalling: $2,153.3. • General compensation, totalling: $17,723.81. • The Landlord must pay a fine to the Board. Rent differential: 25. The Tenant testified that the rent for the subject unit was $2,800.00 per month and that she now pays $3,350.00 per month for a replacement three-bedroom upper-level unit located in a single detached house, and she must share other facilities with other tenants. The Tenant testified that the new rental unit is much smaller than the former rental unit and she could not fit all of her furniture. The Tenant moved into the new unit on February 9, 2024, and continues to live there. A copy of the lease agreement was submitted as evidence. 26. As I indicated at the hearing, when determining entitlement to a rent differential, the Board must assess whether the former and current rental units are comparable, though not necessarily identical. Since the Tenant’s current home is smaller than the former rental unit, I am satisfied that she mitigated her damages by moving to a smaller unit. However, because she is paying $550.00 more each month for a smaller unit, I find that she is entitled to 12 months. Total amount is $550.00 x12=$6,600.00 Moving Costs: 27. The Tenant seeks $2,153.30 for out of pocket moving costs. The Tenant submitted a U Haul receipt dated February 4, 2024, in the amount of $247.00, and I am satisfied that she is entitled to reimbursement for this cost. 28. The Tenant also submitted an invoice dated February 8, 2024, in the amount of $2,000.00. The Tenant testified that this was for movers on February 8, 2024. However, the invoice does not identify who issued it, does not contain sender information, and does not provide a breakdown of the work. In the absence of reliable information, I do not find this evidence sufficient. I therefore find that this cost is not proven, and I do not award it. General competition: 29. The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3) (1.1), which states: An order that the Landlords pay a specified sum to the former Tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former Tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former Tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 [Emphasis added] 30. The Tenant and her family lived in the rental property for almost 7 years and intended to remain long term but moved because of the Landlord’s notice. The Tenant testified that the unit was their first home in Canada after immigrating in 2017 following years of displacement, and that stability for her children was important. 31. The Tenant testified that the move caused significant disruption, particularly because her daughter was in her final year of high school and refused to change schools. The Tenant testified that she drove her daughter from Oakville to [name] in the mornings when she could, and that her daughter returned by Uber, while her son changed schools. In these circumstances, I find general compensation equivalent to 4 months’ rent is fair: $2,800.00 x 4 = $11,200.000 Administrative Fine: 32. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines, states that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter Landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 33. I find that the actions of the Landlords in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered. 34. This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,095.00. This amount represents: • $6,600.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from February 9, 2024, to February 28, 2025. • $247.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $11,200.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations as contained in the application that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Act. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,546.29.
The tenancy commenced on June 1, 2023 and ended on July 31, 2025 pursuant to an N9 notice as served upon the Landlord by the Tenants. The lawful rent was $1,640.00.
The rental unit is a detached house with three (3) rental units, it was said to be the former general store that is over 100 years old and that was retrofitted.
The Tenant’s filed their application on November 2, 2024 and amended it October 9, 2025 pursuant to an Interim Order direction as issued on September 26, 2025 by the LTB. Tenants evidence
The Tenants rely on their book of evidence as uploaded in the Board’s record in DOC- 6907753, comprised of text messages, emails with the Landlord and photographic evidence. Window Issues

The Tenants testified that in October of 2023 they informed the Landlord that the kitchen window is screwed shut, creating a safety hazard. And that two of the other windows had latches broken off and could not be closed properly, that the windows were drafty, but the Landlord did not address the issue.
At the hearing the Tenants submitted a photograph of one windowpane being cracked and a photo of a window screen that appears intact. Exterior Door Issues

The Tenants testified that in October of 2023 they informed the Landlord that main entrance doors to the unit do not fit properly. Tenants could see outside even when the door is closed, indicating structural and insulation problems.

At the hearing the Tenants submitted photographs of the door frame on pages 14-19, the frame appears to have some missing/ chipped off wood parts and missing isolation on the surrounding. Lack of hot water

The Tenants submitted that they were often with no hot water for dishes and showers etc. that there was only a single 175 litre hot water tank for three apartments and that at the time of their tenancy there were eight tenants residing there. It is their position that the tank is inadequate in size to provide for safe or adequate supply of hot water for the number of rental units that it was servicing. Heating / Ventilation Issues

The Tenants testified that in October of 2023 they were surprised to receive a propane invoice for $581.43 which they paid 1/3 of the cost as this bill was from the summer period. During the tenancy the Landlord insisted that the tenants must pay for shared propane tanks despite the lease stating they are responsible only for propane for Unit 3.

Tenants testified that in October of 2023 when temperatures outside became cooler, they became aware of the state the furnace and that it did not properly heat their unit. That during the peak of winter they were running out of propane ongoing and waiting for over a week in January 2024 to get the propane tanks refilled.
On February 19, 2024, in a text exchange with another Tenants state “we are without heat again for the third time in three months.”

They began to investigate what the issue was, they went to the basement of the property where the furnace was located and found that there were several open-ended pipes that were not connected to anywhere and one pipe was stuffed with a towel to close it off. That some of the pipes did not have proper connections to the furnace with gaps around them and insulating tinfoil missing. This was evidenced on pages 2-11.

The Tenants testified that they only had one working vent in the bathroom which provided them with the temperature between 52 to 68 degrees at all times. That the front bedroom temperature was 51° on going, that there was no air coming from the bedroom vent and the kitchen vent blew cold air only. One temperature reading was provided in evidence which registered approximately 18 degrees in October 2024.

That while the rental unit had a fireplace, that due to lack of controls, the fireplace can not be turned off, the room can become too hot and therefore could not be used over night due to safety concerns.

As the situation intensified, the Landlord demanded payment for propane ongoing, and threatened eviction for non-payment of utilities, this dispute arising from the Tenants advising of the inadequate heat in the rental unit. The Tenants were raising concerns in respect of the frequency of propane billing invoices and the cost of propane given the inadequacy of the heat supply. Disposition

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the Tenants’ uncontested evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the windows, and entry door frame were in a state of disrepair, that the Landlord had been aware of the window issue since July 2023 and of the other issues since October 2023, and that the Landlord has not repaired any of these issues.

I also find that as the Tenants did not have an adequate supply of hot water, and that the Landlord failed to respond to these concerns in a timely and effective manner. The evidence was that the Landlord repeatedly dismissed concerns via email/text as not factual.

Regarding the provision of heat to the rental, I find on a balance of probabilities that the rental unit got insufficient heat in the colder months and that the Landlord had been aware of this issue since October 2023. Further, based on the Tenants uncontested evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord had not investigated the issue sufficiently. The photographic evidence of the furnace as taken by the Tenants in October 2024 are indicative of widespread HVAC issues with missing pipe connections to the furnace and some pipes not being connected at all. The Tenants submitting that the Landlord took no steps to address these issues during their tenancy.
I therefore find that the Landlord has breached his obligation under s.20 of the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair. Remedies

Based on the nature and duration of the problems and their impact on the Tenants’ use of the unit, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a 3% rent abatement with respect to the windows, door/ door frame and intermittent lack of hot water for a period of November 2, 2023 to July 31, 2025, for a total of $1,030.36.

Based on the nature and duration of the heat issue and its impact on the Tenants use of the unit, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement for the periods of November 2, 2023 (1 year back to the date to the date of filing of the application) to June 15, 2024 and from September 1, 2024 to June 15, 2025. Heat is a vital service which must be provided from September 1 of each year to June 15 of the following year (as per the definition of “vital service” in the Act). Here, the evidence was that the Tenants were never without heat, given the propane fireplace in the rental unit and electric heaters that they purchased.

Notwithstanding, the Tenants submitted that they did not have adequate heat throughout the approximate 825 sq. ft unit for majority of the winter seasons. As there was no evidence of consistent temperature measures which would permit a detailed review of the temperature fluctuations, I can consider a lump sum abatement of $2,000.00 for insufficient heat for the outlined periods as noted above and in consideration of the state of the furnace and inadequacy of the HVAC system in connection to the rental unit. I also considered that given an efficient HVAC system, there was a high probability of savings as arising from lessened propane utility and a reduced chance of running out of propane in an untimely manner. Both issues that impacted the Tenants during their tenancy. Out-of-Pocket Expenses

Tenants also claim reimbursement for documented expenses related to moving and storage as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. Given the supported receipts (pg. 39-44) and incurred expenses I am able to consider all U-Haul equipment rentals and the storage unit up to the date the Tenants moved into their new rental on August 1, 2025 for at total of $467.93 of the amended $704.58 claimed. I have not considered the additional storage expenses claimed as this was a personal choice of the Tenants to move in stages, store items and unpack at their leisure.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $3,546.29. This amount represents: • $3,030.36 for abatement of rent related to all maintenance issues. • $467.93 out-of-pocket moving expenses. • $48.00 for the cost of the application filing.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $4,900, which represents two months of rent.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on January 15, 2024, and vacated the rental unit on November 14, 2024. At the time of signing the lease, the Tenant had paid first and last month rent, as well as pre-paying 4 months of rent.

By email dated August 12, 2024 (Exhibit 1: DOC 4412844), the Tenant notified the Landlord that she is looking to move out in January 2025 after the lease is done and would like to start using her prepaid rent.

The Landlord responded shortly after to the Tenant by text (Exhibit 2: DOC 4412727) and stated “To make things even more flexibility for you, you’re also open to move anytime earlier starting next month … we can always ref und you the rent. Just want to leave that third option for you so you’re flexible.” The Tenant, in the same exhibit, responded “thanks for the offer … I will give you as much not ice as possible (no less than a month if that works for you?” The Landlord responded, “Totally! Just trying to keep it as easy as possible for you. Best option for me is to have to stay on … but I know life happens”

By text on October 8 (Exh ibit 3 – DOC 4412736), the Tenant confirmed that she would move out by November 14, 2024, and the Landlord texted “Sure sounds good … thanks and really sad you weren’t able to stay on. So I’ll give back 2 month rent is that right?” The Tenant confirmed, “Yes 2 months, thank you.”
Based on this understanding, the Tenant pr ovided the Landlord with 37-days notice to vacate and moved out of the rental unit on November 14, 2024.

However, the Landlord did not return two months ‘ rent and denied every agreeing to anything less than 60-days notice. He indicated he required 60-days notice, as per the lease agreement, and would only return 1 month prepaid rent to the Tenant. Moreover, the Landlord indicated having financial concerns being a single father, not owing a car, paying monthly daycare costs of $1,200, that he did not have extra funds in his bank account, and he had a $5,000 balance owing on his credit card.
As of the date of the heari ng, the Landlord has not provided any of the prepaid rent back to the Tenant. Analysis

Subsection 202(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activiti es relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. .

The Landlord and Tenant had a mutual meeting of the minds that the Landlord would accept 1 month notice to terminate the tenancy. Both agreed that by vacating on November 14, 2024, the amount of prepaid rent to be returned to the Tenant was 2 months. The real substance of the parties’ communications was an agreement to terminate the tenancy early pursuant to section 37(3) of the Act, and for the return of the prepaid rent.

Whether the Landlord changed his mind, or circumstances arose wherein he could not longer accept shorter notice, it does not invalidate the agreement he made with the Tenant to accept 30-days notice. The Tenant was entitled to rely on the agreement, and in this case did so by giving notice to the Landlord on October 8, 2024, for a move out date on November 14, 2024.

Based on the Landlord’s actions in failing to honour his agreement to accept 30-days notice to terminate the tenancy, and the subsequent failure to return 2 months prepaid rent, I find that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant. Remedies

The Landlord failed to return prepaid rent in the amount of $4,900.00 after the Tenant vacated the rental unit in accordance with the agreement reached by the parties. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement equal to that amount.

The Tenant’s claim for out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $2,590 is denied. The Tenant indicated this amount was claimed due to having to pay rent at her other unit. At the hearing she indicated all she is seeking the two months prepaid rent.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,948. This amount represents:  $4,900 for a rent abatement.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.
The rental property consisted of a single-family home.

The Tenancy commenced on December 9, 2022 and was terminated effective October 31, 2024 by Board order LTB-L-038720-24 issued on September 24, 2024 with the Tenants vacating January 5, 2025 in accordance with the Court Enforcement Officer’s order.
The lawful monthly rent was $3,300.00

It was the Tenants testimony that at the commencement of the tenancy they noticed and informed the Landlord on December 19, 2022 that the garage door was malfunctioning as it would not close properly or lock. They supported this with pictures entered in evidence.

They then testified that the Landlord never too any step s to correct the issue during the tenancy and as a result represented a security issue, necessitating additional locks on the interior door and allowed for mice and other vermin gained access to the garage, damaging their property which they complained about on September 13, 2023. This was supported by pictures of mice excrement and their damaged property entered in evidence.
They then entered in evidence pictures purportedly taken after they moved out, claiming the Landlord had waited until they vacated to address the issue with the garage door. Remedies sought.

The Tenants testified they were seeking the following remedies: a. An abatement of rent of $3,300.00; b. Out of pocket expenses for damaged property of $449.00; and c. The application filing fee $48.00

In response the Landlord testified that they investigated upon receipt of the initial complaint on December 19, 2022 and determined that the garage door did not represent a safety issue and having communicated that received no further complaints until October 2024. Again, they testified that at that time they determined there was no safety issue and subsequent to the Tenants moving out they received no complaints from their current tenant. They supported this with a text message from their current tenant entered in evidence

They then testified that by that time the tenancy had been terminated, that the Tenants had not been paying their rent and they did not believe they had an obligation to act as the Tenants had refused to move out in accordance with the Board order.

Having considered the above testimony, evidence, and for the reasons that follow I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with health safety, housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Landlord admitted to being aware of the alleged issues, namely the garage door, mice and or rat infestation within the garage on or about October 2024. Further even if I accepted their submission that they investigated and found no issue, or the text message from their current tenant which I do not given the Tenants pictures of mice or rat excrement or very clear there was an issue and the text amounts to hearsay, I cannot overlook they testified they did not believe they had an obligation to act as the tenancy had been terminated. This is not reasonable, and a direct contravention of subsection 20 of the Act.

Regardless of the fact that the tenancy had been terminated, the Landlord had an obligation to respond to issues and maintain the rental unit up until the eviction was enforced by the sheriff, as such I am satisfied the Tenants have proven their case and are entitled to the remedies sought.

That said, given the Tenants failed prove the alleged issues were extant in September 2023, as the pictures had no date or time stamps, or that the Landlord was aware at the time due to an absence of correspondence verifying it was communicated, coupled with the issue being confined to the garage, and an absence of any receipts for the damaged property, this will affect the amount awarded. Remedies

I find that a rent abatement of $1,650.00 is appropriate in the circumstances, given, as noted above, the issues were confined to the garage, and the fact the Tenants could not establish the Landlord was aware in September 2023 as alleged.
I also find that the Tenants are entitled to the filing fee of $48.00 as sought.
As to the other remedies, again as noted above given they field to provide any receipts for the damaged property I am not satisfied they have proven the out-of-pocket expenses claimed.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $1,698.00. This amount represents: • $1,650.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending January 5, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background 1. The tenancy began on December 9, 2022. The rental unit is a single-family home and the lawful monthly rent was $3,300.00.
On September 24, 2024, the Board issued an order in file number LTB-L-038720-24 terminating the tenancy effective October 31, 2024.
The Tenants did not vacate the rental unit by that date. The Tenants ultimately vacated the unit on January 5, 2025 following enforcement by the Court Enforcement Officer (Sheriff). Tenant’s Position
The Tenants allege that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and harassed them.

The Tenants submit that a prospective Landlord attempted to contact the Landlord by telephone on October 17 and October 18, 2024 for a reference and that the Landlord did not respond. The Tenants state that as a result they lost the opportunity to rent another property.
The Tenant (DT) testified that they live with family members including two young grandchildren and a pregnant daughter and that they experienced significant stress attempting to secure housing.
The Tenant submits that the landlord’s representative advised them that a reference would only be provided if they delivered cheques for rent arrears.
The Tenant submits that this requirement was coercive and prevented them from obtaining housing.
The Tenant also submits that information relating to the Board proceedings was posted online on a forum called Opendoor and that this has negatively affected their ability to secure housing.
The Tenant testified that because of the Landlord’s conduct they experienced repeated rental denials and have continued to face housing difficulties. Landlord’s Position
The Landlord testified that the Tenants stopped paying rent in full beginning in July 2024 and that the last payment received was on July 19, 2024, leaving a portion of the July rent outstanding.
The Landlord submits that no further rent payments were received after that date.

The Landlord testified that the prior Board order provided that a reference letter would be given once the Tenants provided payment addressing the rent arrears. A copy of the order was submitted into evidence.
The Landlord submits that this condition was never satisfied and that no arrears cheques were received or deposited.
The Landlord submits that the Tenants did not dispute that they ultimately cancelled the cheques and did not pay the arrears to the Landlord.
It is the Landlord’s position that Board orders are public documents and that posting a Board order online does not alter the Tenants’ rental history.

The Landlord submits that the Tenants had several months following the September 2024 order to secure alternative housing and that their inability to do so was not caused by the Landlord as she only posted the order after the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit. Analysis 19. The Tenants allege breaches of sections 22 and 23 of the Act. These provisions prohibit a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and from harassing, coercing, threatening or interfering with a tenant. 20. The Tenants’ primary allegation is that the landlord failed to provide a reference to a prospective landlord. 21. The evidence before me indicates that order LTB-L-038720-24 issued on September 24, 2024 provides that the provision of a reference letter was conditional on the Tenants addressing the rent arrears identified in the earlier Board proceeding. The Board order states “The Landlord will give a letter of reference to the Tenants once the Tenants provide an arrears cheque.” 22. The Tenants acknowledge that the arrears were not ultimately paid. 23. In these circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Landlord was obligated to provide a reference as the condition set out in the earlier Board order had not been fulfilled. 24. Further, a landlord’s failure to provide a reference to a prospective landlord does not, in itself, constitute substantial interference with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment within the meaning of section 22 of the Act. A landlord has not positive obligation under the Act to provide a tenant with a reference. 25. The Tenants also allege that a representative of the Landlord advised that legal costs could be sought if the Tenants filed another application with the Board. 26. Even if such a statement was made, informing a party of potential legal consequences of litigation does not, on its own, amount to harassment or coercion under section 23 of the Act. 27. The Tenants further allege harassment on the basis that the Landlord posted information about the Board proceedings online. 28. Board orders are public documents, and not confidential. The Tenants provided insufficient evidence that the Landlord engaged in conduct beyond the publication of information that is already publicly available. 29. While I accept that the Tenants experienced difficulty securing housing, the evidence before me does not establish on a balance of probabilities that these difficulties were caused by conduct of the Landlord that would constitute a breach of the Act. 30. I therefore find that the Tenants have not established that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment or harassed them contrary sections 22 or 23 of the Act. 31. The Tenants’ application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ly or negligently caused undue damage to the premises (LTB-L-097350-24) The Tenant applied for an order (LTB-T-088970-24) determining that the Landlord: • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application), • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant’s household; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application), and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application). The applications were heard by videoconference on February 19, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord's witness, [name] (AW), also attended the hearing. LTB-L-024781-25 was amended to reflect the accurate amount paid and ow ed by the Tenant for the period ending November 30, 2024. / LTB-L-097350-24 / LTB-T-088970-24 On a preliminary basis, the Member at a hearing on October 23, 2025, informed the Landlord that the Notice to End your Tenancy Early For Non -payment of Rent (N4) and Notice to End your Tenancy for Interfering with Others, Damage or Overcrowding (N5) were invalid. The Landlord , aware that the tenancy cannot be terminated as a result, opted to proceed with an arrears and damages only application. The Landlord withdrew the claim about unpaid utilities because it has been resolved.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non -payment of Rent (N4 Notice).
The Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $3,015.91, due on the first day of each month.
The Tenant paid to the Landlord $1,445.22 in November 2024.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not pay the rent in full in November 2024 due to a complaint about a stove. The Landlord on October 28, 2025, informed the Tenant that she would send an agent to the unit for an inspection. In response, the Tenant stated that she would hire her own contractor and purchase a stove despite the Landlord’s entreaties that she refrain from doing so.

The Tenant testified that following her complaint about the stove not working properly on October 23, 2024, the Landlord responded in an email dated October 25, 2024, that she was not responsible for the stove. As a result, the Tenant went ahead to purchase a stove for $1,316.44 on November 2, 2024, an amount she deducted from the rent.

The emails provided by the Tenant confirms both versions of events. While the Landlord ignorantly stated that she was not responsible for the stove on October 25, 2024, by October 28, she asked to send a contractor to the unit, but the Tenant refused. The Tenant in an email on October 29, 2024, asked the Landlord to cancel the appointment and stated that if anyone showed up for an inspection, she would call the police.

I find the Tenant’s stance unreasonable, and she cannot claim that the Landlord’s failure to repair the stove caused her to purchase a new one on November 2, 2025, when s he threatened to call the police on the Landlord if she attempted to send a contractor to the unit on October 29, 2024. As a result, the Tenant is liable for the unpaid portion of the rent for November 2024.
The rent arrears owing to November 30, 2024, are $1,570.69.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. / LTB-L-097350-24 / LTB-T-088970-24 LTB-T-088970-24
The Tenant Application for a Rebate (T1), Application about Tenant Rights (T2), and Tenant Application about Maintenance (T6) did not contain the dates on which the offending conduct occurred.
The complaints about the Landlord collecting an illegal rent are based on the Tenant’s dissatisfaction with the basement of the rental home.
The complaints about the stove and mold are resolved in this order.
The Tenant’s concern that she may get evicted because the Landlord cannot afford repairs, is unfounded.
This application will be dismissed. LTB-L-097350-24

The outstanding issue in this application revolves around mold which the Landlord discovered in both washrooms in the rental unit on September 12, 2025, when she sent a contractor to inspect the Tenant’s complaint about ‘water in property everywhere’.

The Landlord testified that she incurred reasonable out of pocket expenses of $3,390.00 because she hired a contractor to clean the mold off the ceiling and floors. The Landlord believes the Tenant is responsible for the mold because she removed a glass door from the bathtub which caused water to drip to the floor.

The Landlord's witness, AW, testified that he cleaned the mold which was caused by excess steam in the bathroom due to a clogged fan. He confirmed that the Tenant had asked him why water seeps out of the bathtub in spite of the glass door, and he told her a shower curtain was a better option to prevent it.
The Tenant testified that she did not cause the mold and that she removed the glass door because it retained steam and moisture in the bathroom.

Based on all the evidence, the Landlord has failed to demonstrate that the Tenant caused the mold to grow in both bathrooms. The Landlord’s witness testified that th e cause was excess moisture because of a clogged f an, and while the Landlord asserts that the Tenant never reported the mold issue to them, the Tenant denied the assertion. This application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $1,756.69. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to November 30, 2024. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before April 5, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord’s application, LTB-L-097350-24, is dismissed. / LTB-L-097350-24 / LTB-T-088970-24
The Tenant’s application, LTB-T-088970-24, is also dismissed. March 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The tenancy commenced on October 1,2024 and the Tenant vacated on January 1, 2025.
The rental unit consisted of a two-bedroom, one bathroom apartment.
The lawful rent at time the Tenant vacated was $2,000.00.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application:
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,000.00.

It was the Tenant’s uncontested testimony and evidence, namely pictures and text messages, entered in evidence, that at the commencement of the tenancy they identified several maintenance issues to the Landlord including an exposed septic hole in the second bedroom.

It was also the Tenant’s testimony that despite promises to address all the issues identified, the septic hole never was fixed, resulting in noxious fumes, preventing use of the second bedroom and the Tenant vacating the unit. Remedies sought
Pursuant to the Tenant’s application the remedies sought are: a. Termination of the tenancy effective January 1, 2025; and b. Abatement of rent totalling $2,000.00. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, based on the uncontested testimony and evidence, I am satisfied the Tenant has proven that by failing to address the exposed septic hole, despite being informed on October 20, 2024, pursuant to the text message entered, the Landlord’s response was unreasonable, constitutes a breach of subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and therefore failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Remedies

Given the uncontested testimony and evidence that the noxious fumes went unchecked or resolved for a period of three months I am satisfied as to the necessity for the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. Therefore, the tenancy will end on January 1, 2025.

Furthermore, given t it was uncontested that the Tenant continued to pay the rent, despite the septic hole not being addressed, I find that a rent abatement of $2,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $2,000.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending December 31, 2024.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must return the Tenant’s $300.00 key deposit.

In the Tenant’s application she incorrectly checked the box asking for interest on a last month’s rent deposit rather than return of the key deposit. However, the narrative facts supporting her claim all related to return of the key deposit. Accordingly, I allowed an amendment to the application to clarify that the application sought return of that deposit illegally retained as it would have been clear to the Landlord that was the intent of the application.
The Landlords collected a key deposit of $300.00 from the Tenant. The Tenant returned the keys upon vacating the unit on June 1, 2025.

The Landlord purported to retain the key deposit in an email exchange between the parties entered into the hearing evidence as Exhibit 1 (DOC6642685). The Landlord alleged that damages had occurred to the unit which the Tenant vehemently denied at the hearing.

Irrespective of whether damage was done to the unit, which I do not accept, under the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) s. 134 a landlord may not charge a tenant for anything other than rent. Section 134 is subject to the provisions of Ontario Regulation 516/06 section 17 which allows a Landlord to charge a refundable deposit for keys. The only circumstance in which a landlord may retain this deposit is if the keys are not returned and then the funds retained may not be greater than the cost of producing replacement keys. In this case, the Landlords have not alleged that the Tenant failed to return the keys to the unit or residential complex and as such their actions in failing to return the key deposit are illegal.

If a landlord believes that a tenant has caused damage and should be required to pay compensation, the landlord must file their own application at the LTB and cannot illegally retain a refundable key deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $300.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the key deposit.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to:  a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s monthly rent is reduced by $40.00 and the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,413.00.

The Tenant says they had access to a stor age locker from the beginning of the tenancy in 2009. When they viewed the unit they asked about storage and were advised by the superintendent that it was included. When they signed the lease they were shown a locker by the superintendent and put a lock on it in their presence. They used the locker for the next 14 years up to shortly before the filing of this application.

The Landlord says storage was an additional service for an additional fee which the Tenant did not sign up for. The Tenant says everyone in the building has a locker and he is not aware of anyone else signing a separate storage agreement. The Landlord did not produce any examples of storage agreements that tenants in the building were required to sign.

I find that the Tenant had access to a storage locker for at least 14 years as part of the package of services and facilities included in the lease. A storage locker is a service or facility under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act").

The storage locker was discontinued as of Ap ril 28, 2024, which is less than 12 months before this application was filed. The discontinuance or reduction was reasonable in the circumstances; the Landlord planned to renovate the space.

The rent is reduced by $40.00 per month starting May 2023, the month that the discontinuance or reduction first occurred. The Tenant submits quotes for offsite storage at a higher price, however I agree with the Landlord’s submission that the more appropriate comparison is the cost of an onsite storage locker included with a residential lease. The Landlord says they usually charge $30-$50 and based on my experience with similar cases before the Board I believe this is a reasonable market rate. I also note that the locker provided by the Landlord is smaller than the lockers for which the Tenant obtained quotes.
In addition, the Tenant is entitled to a r ebate of the rent unlawfully collected by the Landlord for the period of time starting on May 1, 2023, when the facility was discontinued.
ordered: The lawful monthly rent effective October 8, 2025 is reduced to $1,090.00. Any subsequent rent increases shall be calculated from the reduced amount.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the T enant is $1,413.00. This amount represents:  $1,360.00 for a rent rebate for the period of time from May 1, 2023 to February 28, 2026.  $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $706.00 from the rent each month for March and April 2026 and $1.00 in May 2026. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • Entered the rental unit illegally • Changed the locks or the locking system on the rental unit or building without providing the Tenant with replacement keys The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards
reasons: The Tenant filed four T2 applications between June and November 2024, all of which contained similar allegations, and one T6 application, also within the time frame of the T2 applications.

There was an adjudicative case conference for all the files combined, held on June 23, 2025. At the case conference the parties were informed that the Act does not apply to the relationship between the parties. That finding was the result of a T3 application filed by the Tenant, LTB-T-091535-24. The order for that application, dismissing the Tenant’s application, was issued on June 4, 2025.
No request for review had been filed at the time of the adjudicative case conference, so the files were not dismissed at the case conference.
A request to review the decision in LTB-T-091535-24 was eventually filed, and there was a review order, LTB-T-091535-24-RV, denying the review request, issued on July 22, 2025.
Therefore, the determination that the Act does not apply to this relationship has been upheld on review. It is res judicata.
Despite the review decision in LTB-T-091535-24-RV, the Tenant did not withdraw his applications, and he insisted on having his applications heard in any case.
The Tenant’s application will be dismissed as the Act does not apply to this relationship.

It is before me to determine whether it is appropriate to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine on the Tenant for his failure to withdraw his applications, and his subsequent waste of Board resources and time.

Since the parties did not make submissions on this point, I find that it is not fair to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine in this matter. However, the Tenant’s applications, which were duplicative in any case, will be dismissed with prejudice.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed with prejudice. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
