issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

It was undisputed that the Tenants initially had a 6-month lease that commenced January 1, 2025, and ended June 30, 2025. It was undisputed that the lease became a month-to- month lease as of July 1, 2025. It was also undisputed that the Tenants initially provided the Landlord an N9 Tenant’s Notice to End the Tenancy (“N9 notice”) with a termination date of September 30, 2025.

The Tenant, [name] [name] (“SP”), testified that before the end of the tenancy the Tenants spoke to the Landlord about possibly extended the termination date to the end of October 2025 because one of the Tenant was interviewing for employment which would affect the move out date. SP testified that as of September 2, 2025, the Tenants were still potentially extending the move out to October 31, 2025, so the last month’s rent deposit would apply to October 2025 and they paid rent for September 2025.

SP testified that on September 13, 2025, there was a conversation with the Landlord in which the Tenants cancelled the extension to the move out and confirmed that they would honour the initial move out on the N9 notice of September 30, 2025. SP provided a text message from September 19, 2025, in which the Landlord said “per your signed N9, your move out date is 30 September 2025. Although the date was extended for 1 month upon your request, but you decided to cancel the extension over our conversation last Saturday.” SP testified that this indicated the Landlord was agreeing to cancel the extension.

SP also provided text messages from the Landlord that detailed what the Tenants would need to do to move out which SP indicated provided the Landlord was agreeing to the cancelation of the extension. SP testified that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 28, 2025, and the Landlord has retained $1,550.00 of the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord testified that he agreed to extend the Tenants’ termination date to October 31, 2025, when they asked to extend it. The Landlord testified that he did not agree to cancel the extension in September 2025 when the Tenants requested it. The Landlord testified that the cancelation of the extension was unilateral by the Tenants. The Landlord testified that when he discussed returning excess funds to the Tenants it was because the Landlord was not sure if he was holding a last month’s rent deposit or if the Tenants had already paid and once the accounting was complete upon their move out any excess would be returned. The Landlord testified that the discussion about returning excess funds was not an agreement to cancel the extension.

The Tenants’ position was that although the parties may have agreed to extend the termination date, the extension was cancelled by agreement, and the termination date was the original termination date of September 30, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord illegally retained the last month’s rent deposit when the Tenants vacated on September 28, 2025, and the last month’s rent deposit was not applied to September 2025 or returned to the Tenants.

The Landlord’s position was that there were not excess funds as the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2025, per the agreement to extend the termination date and the Tenants chose to vacate early. The Landlord’s position was that the last month’s rent deposit was appropriately applied to October 2025 which was the last rental period of the tenancy.

Subsection 37(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') directs that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. Subsection 37(3) of the Act indicates that a notice of termination need not be given if a Landlord and a Tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy.
Here, it is undisputed that the Tenants initially terminated the tenancy with an N9 notice with a date of termination of September 30, 2025.

I am also satisfied that as of early September 2025, the parties had agreed to new date of termination of October 31, 2025. This is based on testimony from both SP and the Landlord. SP testified that the Tenants paid September 2025 rent as they were planning to extend and the Landlord testified, he had agreed to extend the termination. I am satisfied that the parties had agreed to a new termination date which replaced the initial termination date of the N9 notice. Therefore, the termination date as of early September 2025, was October 31, 2025, as per agreement of the parties under subsection 37(3) of the Act.

The question before me is whether the parties then made a subsequent agreement to yet another termination date of September 30, 2025, as of September 13, 2025, as the Tenants allege or if the cancelation of the October 31, 2025, termination date was unilateral by the Tenants as the Landlord alleges.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden is the Tenants.

Both parties provided clear, consistent evidence. However, I am not convinced there was an agreement to cancel the October 31, 2025, termination date and revert back to September 30, 2025, date. While SP did provide text messages from the Landlord that the Tenants indicate demonstrate the Landlord’s agreement to cancel the extension, the texts appear to confirm the Tenants cancelation and the Landlord’s yielding to the Tenants choice to cancel.

The text messages do not indicate that there was a clear meeting of the minds between the parties that the tenancy would terminate on a specific date, specifically September 30, 2025. The text says “you decided to cancel the extension” not we decided, or I agree to cancel the extension. The texts do not clearly indicate that the Landlord was agreeing to cancel the extension, merely that he was acknowledging that the Tenants wished to cancel.

As for the continued texts about the Tenants move out and any potential excess funds, I am not convinced this indicates an agreement to cancel the October 31, 2025, termination date either. Nothing in those texts indicate that the Landlord was agreeing to change the termination date from October 31, 2025 and appears he was simply providing move out instructions to the Tenants based on their stated intent to leave as of September 30, 2025 and what would happen when or if there was any remaining funds from the last month’s rent deposit once the Tenants did vacate the rental unit as it could not be determined if there were funds remaining until the Tenants actually vacated. I do not find it inappropriate for the Landlord to point out to the Tenants on September 19, 2025, that a discussion about returning a last month’s rent deposit is premature if the Tenants are still in possession of the rental unit, as there has not been a last rental period that the last month’s rent deposit could have been applied to until there is either a last rental period or the Tenants have vacated.
As such, I am not satisfied that the termination date was changed from October 31, 2025, back to September 30, 2025.

Section 88 of the Act indicates that where a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving proper notice in accordance with the Act, the tenant is liable for the rent for the period of notice he or she could have given to the landlord to properly terminate the tenancy. Here, the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on October 31, 2025, and therefore the Tenant is liable for rent until October 31, 2025.

While section 16 of the Act directs that a party must take reasonable steps to minimize their losses resulting from the breach of a tenancy agreement, I am satisfied the Landlord would not have been able to rent the rental unit for October 2025 as the Tenants only vacated as of September 28, 2025. And in fact, the Landlord testified that he was unable to rent the rental unit for several months after the Tenants vacated.
Based on the foregoing, I am satisfied that the Landlord properly applied the last month’s rent deposit to rent owing for October 2025 as that would have been the last rental period of the tenancy.
Therefore, the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenants’ rent deposit.
As such, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a building which includes a residential unit and two commercial shops located at [address] in Woodstock, Ontario.

The Tenant was served with an N12 notice of termination in April of 2024 with a termination date of June 30, 2024. The Tenant was evicted from the rental unit on October 31, 2024 when the Sheriff took possession of the unit. This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (DC)
The Tenant testified that he is a mechanic and made a living by repairing cars in one of the shops on the property. He also created promotional items in the other shop and sold them on YouTube.

DC testified that in October of 2023, the Landlord attempted to raise the rent from $5,500.00 to $6,500.00. The Tenant refused to pay the requested increase as he stated that it was not a legal increase and at that time, he stated that the Landlords stopped maintaining the house.
DC stated that because he refused to pay the increased rent, the Landlords retaliated by serving him with the N12 notice of termination

The Tenant stated that he was not able to locate other affordable accommodations and he had no choice but to move into his recreational vehicle on November 1, 2024 which he parks in a Walmart parking lot. He stated that he has no running water in his RV and that he has had to store all of his possessions since that date.

DC stated that the Landlords only moved into the residential unit several months after he vacated the rental unit and noted that the Landlords advertised the two commercial shops for rent in July of 2025. He then stated that the building was listed for sale on September 19, 2025 which is only 11 months after he was evicted from the rental unit.

The Tenant is seeking compensation of $66,000.00 based on his previous monthly rent of $5,500.00 although he understands that $50,000.00 is the maximum that can be awarded. The Tenant stated that this whole ordeal has caused him a huge amount of pain and suffering. The Tenant is also seeking 6 months’ free rent at the rental unit so that he will have a warm place to continue his search for another place to live.

In cross-examination, the Tenant was asked why he did not provide any pictures or evidence of his current living conditions or receipts for his items that were in storage. The Tenant responded that he did not believe that was necessary.

The Tenant was asked why he was requesting the return of the last 12 months of rent when the Tenant owes rental arrears of $60,000.00 as at October 31, 2024. The Tenant responded that the Landlord failed to maintain the property which is why he withheld rent. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (SK)

SK testified that she and her husband served the N12 notice so that she and her family could move into the rental unit. They sold their house in Edmonton, Alberta and moved their family to Ontario on July 20, 2024. They resided in a friend’s basement until they were able to move into the rental house.
The Landlord stated that the Tenant failed to pay any rent from November of 2023 to October of 2024 which caused her financial situation to worsen greatly.

SK stated that when the Sheriff attended on October 31, 2024, the house was in an abysmal condition and that it had a terrible, foul odour. She stated that the house was full of jugs of liquids including feces and water, a huge amount of garbage was found in every room, torn and battered furniture was left, rice was poured in the sinks and toilets causing them to be completely clogged and the Tenant had installed temporary walls in order to rent out individual rooms.

The Landlord stated that they had to remove all of the garbage and deep clean the entire house. She stated that the temporary walls had to be removed and other renovations were required to make the house safe for habitation. The Landlord stated that she and her family moved into the house during the last week of December of 2024 and have resided there since that time.

The Landlord provided a document brief, DOC-779670, that included a copy of the L1 update form dated August 19, 2025 showing rental arrears of $64,917.00 and she provided pictures of the rental unit taken on November 26, 2024 showing the bins of garbage that had to be removed from the house.

SK provided dated pictures of herself with her family in the house during the winter of 2025. She also provided copies of their drivers’ licences, utility bills and tax assessments confirming their address at the house.

The Landlord testified that from June of 2025 to March of 2026, their financial situation worsened even more. The Landlords’ mortgage payments were not being paid due to their financial situation, they were receiving notices of mortgage arrears from the bank, they borrowed money from their families and friends and they thought that they were going to lose their house. SK provided these dated notices and emails from the bank confirming the outstanding mortgage payments during the above time period.

SK stated that they listed the house for sale in September of 2025 because of their dire financial circumstances as they thought that the bank might foreclose on their house. She stated that they were finally able to secure a second mortgage and that assisted them with keeping their mortgage current.
The Landlord stated that they continue to reside in the house with their extended family and have every intention to remain there. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant was evicted from the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

Based on the evidence that I have heard from the parties, I am satisfied that the Landlords are residing in the rental unit. I am also satisfied that the condition of the rental unit on October 31, 2024 was inhabitable and that the Landlords had no choice but to remove all of the garbage and hazardous materials, deep clean the house and renovate the unit back into a single family dwelling. The Landlords commenced residing in the rental unit during the last week of December of 2024 and continue to reside in the home. The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. 23. The presumption of bad faith set out in section 57(5) states: “For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Based on the evidence from the Landlord, the Landlords’ worsening financial circumstances from June of 2025 to September of 2025 were the reason that they put the house up for sale. The Landlords’ mortgage statements and correspondence with the bank corroborated their financial distress and listing the house for sale was a reasonable option at that point in time. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords have rebutted this presumption under 57(5) of the Act.
The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant raised four issues: mould, the fridge leaking, holes in the walls, and the stove creating a gas smell.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit had mould, providing a photograph showing the bedroom corner with black debris. According to the Tenant, the Landlord’s mould inspector told her that the mould was present throughout the unit, indicating a long build up, and that the Tenant should dispose of her mattress to avoid bringing the mould with her when she moved out.

The Landlord testified she lives on the main floor of the house. She stated that there was no mould in the rental unit and provided the mould inspector’s report which also indicates there was no mould.

The Tenant did not provide her own mould report. It is unclear from the photograph she provided if the black debris in the corner of the bedroom is dirt or mould. Considering also the Landlord’s testimony and inspector’s written report, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there was mould in the rental unit. This issue is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the fridge was leaking water toward the nearby electrical outlets, causing her to be concerned. The leak started in mid-October 2023, and the Tenant notified the Landlord immediately. The Landlord repaired the issue within several weeks.

The Landlord testified that the house and fridge are old. The fridge does not have automatic de-icing, which creates some water buildup which needs to be removed manually. The Landlord manually drained the fridge on November 16, 2023.
I find the Landlord’s repair to be timely and reasonable in the circumstances. This issue is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that there were 3-5 fist-sized holes in the walls. According to the Tenant, the Landlord promised to repair the holes before the Tenant moved in, however this was not completed. One of the holes had wires and was close to the stove, which cause the Tenant to be concerned. The Tenant confirmed that the Landlord closed the hole near the stove in late October 2023.

The Landlord testified that she was first notified of the issues on November 9, 2023, by e- mail. On November 10, 2023, the Landlord began scheduling entries to resolve the issues, but the Tenant kept requesting to re-schedule or would not secure her dog, which interfered with the Landlord’s contractors. The drywall was repaired on November 29, 2023.

No photographs of the holes were presented. Both parties’ testimonies were vague on this issue, however I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to repair the holes. This issue is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the appliances were old. Each time she used the stove, there was a gas smell, which caused her to be concerned. The Tenant notified the Landlord within the first week of moving in. The Landlord refused to inspect or change it.

The Landlord testified that the stove was brand-new when the Tenant moved in, and used electricity, not gas. The Landlord testified that the gas line was properly capped and was not connected to the stove.

No photographs were provided to show the stove’s age. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the gas was not connected to the stove. Accordingly, I find that there was no gas smell. This issue is dismissed.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (T1). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex or with the reasonable enjoyment of a member of the Tenant’s household, or that the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and that the Landlord withheld or interfered with vital services (T2). Finally, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6).
reasons: After the hearing of the Tenant’s evidence regarding this issue, the parties agreed that there was an amount owing by the Landlord to the Tenant. The parties agreed that the amount is $150.00. T2 – Substantial Interference with Reasonable Enjoyment, Harassment or Coercion
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant made three distinct claims in her T2 Application, these being that the Landlord failed to maintain the heat in her unit at a temperature that was comfortable for her ($2000.00); that the Landlord failed to attend to a water leak in her unit in January 2024 ($2000.00); and that beginning on June 28, 2024 the Landlord engaged in instances of harassment and intimidation ($15,000.00). A. Temperature in the Unit in September 2024

As for the claim regarding the temperature in the rental unit, the Tenant testified that the residential complex was a split-level home. The Tenant’s unit is in the basement but was above-ground. Much of the Tenant’s unit was under the balcony which extended from the back of the upper unit. The upper unit at the back side of the house consisted of large windows which covered most of the back of the unit. The Tenant testified that because of the physical configuration of the home, the upstairs unit was much warmer than her unit.

The Tenant testified that while the upper unit was occupied, she did not have difficulty with the temperature. She testified that after the upstairs tenant, [name], moved, the Landlord installed a Nest temperature control system. She testified that the Landlord would not allow her to have the Nest App on her phone so that she could regulate the heat. The Tenant testified about one instance where the temperature was unacceptable to her. She stated that on the Labour Day Weekend of 2024, that on September 1 and September 3, the temperature in the unit was 9 degrees Celsius because the air conditioning was on. The temperature outside the home was 23 or 24 degrees as was shown by photographs from the Nest provided by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that any time the Tenant called her to complain about the temperature in her unit, she immediately adjusted the heat. The Tenant did not challenge this evidence. Neither party testified as to how many times these calls were made. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that if calls were made about temperature she responded to them immediately.

I further do not accept that even if there was a problem with temperature on one weekend in 2024 this rises to the level or substantial interference. Finally, even if this one instance does constitute interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit, I find the claim to be unreasonable and inflated. B. Water Leak

The Tenant testified that a water leak in the unit began on January 27, 2024. The leak was fixed on January 29, 2024. The leak arose as a result of a pin hole leak in the pipe above the Tenant’s unit. The leaking only occurred while the water in the Tenant’s unit was in active use. The Landlord advised the Tenant to be sparing in her use of the water until the leak could be fixed. She suggested that the Tenant fill some buckets and the bathtub as a stop gap measure. The Tenant was highly offended by this suggestion as was apparent during her evidence.

Firstly, the claim for a leak is a maintenance issue; and, therefore improperly brought as a substantial interference claim. However, I have chosen to deal with the claim as it was before me. Even if the Tenant had brought this as a maintenance claim, I find that it has no merit. In Onyskiw v. CJM Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the court held that the reasonableness of a landlord’s conduct must be considered in evaluating a maintenance claim. In this case, there is no evidence whatsoever that the Landlord failed to maintain the plumbing system properly. Further, the Landlord took immediate and effective steps to repair the leak by hiring professional plumbers. The leak was identified on January 27th and fixed on January 29th. The speed with which the problem was repaired was entirely reasonable. [name] and Coercion
The Tenant’s claim for harassment and coercion is rooted in the delivery of the N12 Notice of Termination by the Landlord for occupation of the rental property by the Landlord’s son.

The Tenant testified that following delivery of the N12, she requested the return of $850.00 which she characterized as an illegal deposit being a deposit for keys. She stated that the Landlord’s legal representative wrote to her and advised that if she did not confirm that she, the Tenant, was leaving the unit in accordance with the termination date stated in the N12 an L2 application would be filed with the LTB. The Tenant says that the failure to address the “illegal” deposit and the reference to the L2 constitutes harassment. The Tenant testified that on August 6 to wrote to ask about the $850.00 once again and that she stated she would withhold it from her rent if it was not paid and the Landlord’s legal representative told it that doing so would affect her credit score. Again, the Tenant testified that this in her mind constituted harassment.

I do not find there to by anything harassing or coercive about this entirely normal series of interactions between the Tenant and the Landlord’s legal representative. The Landlord’s representative was focussed on the issue of the termination of the tenancy and she was retained to achieve this objective. All monies owing to the Tenant consisting of the “illegal” deposit were paid in due course.

The Tenant also has some complaints about parking. In short, the driveway of this residential complex has room to park nine vehicle in what the parties describe as three lanes. Namely three side by side lanes where three cars can be parked in tandem. There was assigned lanes of parking which did change at one point after [name] vacated the upper unit. The Tenant complained of two (2) instances in August of 2024 when the Landlord parked behind her car. On one occasion, the Tenant’s partner honked the horn and the Landlord ran out and moved her car. On the second occasion, the Landlord was not asked to move her car, the position of her car was merely noted. I find this claim to be entirely without merit. The Landlord explained that she parked in this manner because she was expecting a trade with a large truck and wanted to keep the one parking lane open for him. The Tenant was not inconvenienced at all. This is not an incident that can reasonably be interpreted as harassment or substantial interference.

There are several other complaints of harassing behaviour which include some noise from repairs being done to the upstairs unit in August 2024. These were not only not complained of at the time but are so minor in nature that I find them to be without merit.

The Tenant advised that she would no longer being cutting the grass, as was her obligation under the lease, in July of 2024. The Landlord took over this obligation and the Tenant made complaints about the way this was being done. She complained that the Landlord was using an electric lawnmower and that while she was mowing, the cord for the lawnmower was dangling over the pool momentarily. Neither the Tenant or any member of her family was in the pool at the time. The Tenant not wanting to continue with the responsibility of cutting the grass cannot now claim that the Landlord was doing it improperly. Again, this complaint is without merit.

The one complaint made by the Tenant which requires some detailed attention is an incident that occurred on September 4, 2024. The pool was being closed by a professional pool company retained by the Landlord. It was the warm weekend described above in connection with the temperature claim. The pump used to empty the pool was stationed outside the Tenant’s door as it had been every year of the Tenant’s tenancy without issue. On this day, the Tenant wanted fresh air in her unit and left the door open. Some of the fumes from the pump entered the Tenant’s unit and set of the CO2 detector. The Tenant asked the Landlord to call the fire department to attend to the detector and left the unit to pick up her daughter from school. On the Landlord’s evidence, as well as the documentary evidence of the pool company (Exhibit 12) the CO2 detector alarm was not active when they left the property.

The Tenant testified that the C02 alarm was on when she returned home and that she called the fire department. The Fire Department Report (Exhibit 13) recorded a minimal amount of CO2 in the unit which was cleared by the use of fans. On the totality of the evidence, I find that the CO2 incident was an accident contributed to by the Tenant in leaving open her door beside a running combustion engine which was in use for only a few hours. This incident in no way can be interpreted as harassment or coercion by the Landlord and the claim is entirely without merit.

The final complaint of harassment relates to the L2 filed by the Landlord. The Tenant testified that she was not made aware that the L2 would not be proceeding as scheduled because she vacated the unit. While it may be considered discourteous, it is hardly harassing. T6 – [name]
As explained below, the Tenant did prove the allegations set out in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant’s complaints about the Landlord’s maintenance failures are comprised of her complaints about snow removal, grass cutting and pool maintenance.

Regarding the grass cutting, the Lease Agreement between the parties (Exhibit 4) clearly sets out the Tenant’s obligations to cut the grass. Similarly, the lease also sets out the Tenant’s obligations to clear the snow from the property. Prior to her divorce, the Tenant lived around the corner from the rental unit in a single-family dwelling. She agreed that she was aware of the amount of snow that falls every winter in this area and the rate at which grass grows in the summer. She candidly stated that she was simply unaware of the magnitude of work that she was accepting under the lease. It may be that the Tenant took on more responsibility than she anticipated but that does not constitute a maintenance failure by the Landlord. Further, the Tenant never complained about the grass cutting or snow until July 2024 at which time the Landlord immediately took over this chore.

The Tenant complained about overgrown trees on the property and a hedge that grew quickly and impeded parking in the driveway. The Landlord provided a receipt to evidence that upon receiving the Tenant’s only complaint she retained a professional arborist to cut back the trees and shrubs in a timely manner.

The final area of contention in maintenance was the pool. The Lease Agreement at page 14 clearly states that the Landlord is responsible for the opening and the closing of the pool. The Tenant was responsible for the general maintenance, chemicals and daily pool maintenance including the cleaning of the filter and filter basket. The Tenant complained that once the pool was “opened” by the pool company about one week of intensive attention to the pool was required. This constituted regular skimming of the pool to remove large chunks of algae and repeated hourly cleaning of the filter and basket as the algae being caught by the filter would damage it burning out the pump if it was not removed. The Tenant complained at the hearing that she always had to take a day off work to attend to the pool. The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s contention, and I accepted photographs into evidence that supported her evidence; however, the lease requires the Tenant to undertake the general maintenance of the pool and I specifically find that once opened by the professional pool company the skimming of the pool falls into the general maintenance category.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $198.00 This amount represents: • $150.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a single family dwelling and the Tenant resided there from 2016 until June 2, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name], (CW)

The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental home because she received an N12 notice from the Landlord whereby he stated that he would be living in the residence. The LTB order stated that she had to vacate the rental house by May 31, 2025 however, she had a lot to pack and she remained in the unit a few days after the termination date.

CW stated that she received a call from the Landlord requesting that he be able to walk through the home for an inspection at the beginning of June of 2025. She stated that she agreed to move all of her belongings out of the house for a payment of $500.00 from the Landlord.

CW stated that she is forced to reside in her car because she is unable to find other accommodation that she can afford. She stated that she parks her car in front of the house daily and watches to see if the Landlord actually resides in the house. She stated that the Landlord put the lights on timers and that he did not take care of the property maintenance and the Municipality gave him an order to comply. She saw the order herself.

The Tenant stated that she did not see the children except for Christmas when they were there were their father. CW stated that she regularly parks in front of the house and she maintains that no one is residing there except for a lady and that the lights remain on a timer.

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $30,000.00, a rent differential of $14,400.00, storage expense of $360.00, compensation of $28,600.00 (based on her loss of ODSP due to no fixed address) and further compensation of $10,000.00 for the fact that she must live in her car. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] (LGA)

The Landlord testified that he attended the rental unit after the Tenant left and discovered broken doors, broken windows, vomit and blood on the walls, cement in the sinks and toilets and a very large amount of garbage and junk within the house and outside the house. He explained that he hired someone to remove the junk and it took 3 full trucks of garbage from the house.
The Landlord provided dated pictures of the rental house that he took when he took possession of it on June 2, 2025.

LGA stated that the house was not habitable when he took possession and he worked diligently when he was not working, to get the house ready for himself and his children. He provided receipts for garbage removal, required repairs, an invoice for the replacement of the front door, the notices from the Municipality and his responses to the Municipality confirming that the work had been done. He also provided dated invoices for furniture that was ordered on October of 2025 and delivered to the rental house.

The Landlord stated that he was able to move into the house late September of 2025 after cleaning, repairing and removing all of the garbage left by the Tenant. He provided a copy of his work schedule as a service engineer, whereby he travels for work 2-3 weeks per month and must travel out of Canada. He stated that when he is not working, he is residing at his house and his children visit him on weekends.
LGA also provided Alectra invoices showing that he has been consistently using hydro since July of 2025 through to March of 2026 at the rental address.

LGA also provided pictures of himself with his children in the rental house and showed pictures of the exterior of the house cleaned up completely. The Landlord stated that he has been residing in the house full time since September of 2025, except when he is away for work. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. I am not persuaded that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

Although the Tenant stated that she had knowledge that the Landlord was not residing in the house, based on her sitting in front of the house daily, she did not provide any pictures or corroborating evidence to support her position.

Based on the Landlord’s oral evidence, his dated pictures, his utility invoices and his work schedule, I am satisfied that the Landlord is occupying the rental unit. The Landlord had no choice but to remove the garbage, repair the house and ensure that it was habitable for himself and his children before moving into the house. I am satisfied that the Landlord is residing in the house and has been since September of 2025.
The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application lists the Landlord as “Daniels.” The Landlord’s agent confirmed the Landlord’s name as “[organization].” The Tenant requested that I amend the application to correctly name the Landlord. The Landlord’s representative did not object and I granted the amendment. T1 Application – Illegal rent

The Tenant alleges in his application that he paid the Landlord illegal rent of $613.36 for the period of “March 1, 2025 to October 23, 2025.” The Tenant claims on March 1, 2025, his rent of $3,141.36 was increased by $76.61 per month which was illegal because the Landlord did not give him a Notice of Rent Increase (‘N1’).

The Tenant testified that the rent is automatically charged to his credit card each month and up to the hearing date he has paid his rent in full which includes the 2025 increase of $76.61 per month. The Tenant requested an order requiring the Landlord to return to him $76.61 x 8 months, which is $612.88 and not $613.36.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has given the N1 notice for the previous years by regular mail. He confirmed that he has a mailbox which is accessible by a key. Although he resides with his wife, and three children, one of which is 22 years, he testified that he is the only individual in the household who has access to the mailbox and can retrieve the mail.
The Tenant referred to an email dated May 29, 2025, in which the Landlord’s account manager ([name]) states: “As discussed – here is a copy of your N1 increase for 2025”

The Tenant testified that he received the N1 notice by email on May 29, 2025 but he did not receive proof of service; therefore, he filed the T1 application. The Tenant confirmed during the hearing that he received the Landlord’s evidence which included the certificate of service for the N1 notice. He challenges the authenticity of the signature on the certificate of service asserting that the signature appears typed or different from prior handwritten signatures.

The Landlord’s agent, [name], testified that she has direct knowledge of the issues raised in this application. She stated that the N1 notice was served by Gaurav Jagtap on November 12, 2024 by regular mail, which is at least 90 days before March 1, 2025, the date the increase took effect. The notice provides that on March 1, 2025, the rent will be increased to $3,141.36 per month, which is a rent increase of $76.61 per month or 2.5% in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). 8. [name] testified that [name] signed the N1 and certificate of service. [name] is a former employee of the Landlord. [name] also confirmed that the N1 notice, mailed by [name], was not returned back to the Landlord. Analysis and Findings 9. Subsection 116 (1) of the Act provides that “a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so.” Where a notice is served by mail, it is deemed to be given five days after it is mailed in accordance with s. 191(1)(f) of the Act. 10. Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the N1 notice was properly served by the Landlord in accordance with the Act. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the N1 notice was mailed to the Tenant’s attention on November 12, 2024 and was deemed received on November 17, 2024. 11. While the Tenant testified that he did not receive the notice, this alone is not sufficient to rebut the presumption of service. The notice was deemed to have been received five days after it was mailed. Proof of actual receipt of the N1 is not required by the Act. 12. Further, the Tenant challenged the authenticity of the signature on the certificate of service asserting that the signature appears typed or different from prior handwritten signatures. I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the signature is typed on the N1 notice and the certificate of service for the N1. However, that is insufficient to establish that the document is not authentic. In addition, the Landlord’s agent, [name] testified that the N1 notice was signed and served by her colleague [name]. She also testified that the N1 notice sent to the Tenant was not returned back to the Landlord. 13. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not prove that the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act, and the rent increase effective March 1, 2025 was lawful.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord (T2 Application): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the (“Act”), provides that, a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In the case before me, the Tenant sought to raise substantial interference issues relating to: a) an alleged bedbug infestation between April 23, 2020 to October 15, 2020; b) a mold concern raised on a single occasion in 2016, with the Tenant conceding that no further allegations have been made since that time; and c) a roof leak that occurred in 2004 and was repaired in 2005.
Subsection 29(2) of the Act provides that, no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In this case, the issues raised by the Tenant occurred more than one year prior to the filing of the application. I therefore find that the Tenant is statute-barred from pursuing those claims pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act.
As a result, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application

On consent of the parties and pursuant to section 200(1) of the Act, the Application is amended to include maintenance allegations with respects to windows, mold and moisture issues within the rental unit.

The Tenant seeks the following remedies: a) an order requiring the Landlord to complete pest control treatment to eliminate any bedbugs in the rental unit; and b) an order requiring the Landlord to conduct an air quality test to determine whether mold residue is present in the unit. [name] Bedbugs

The Tenant testified that she experienced a bedbug infestation between 2020 and 2024. She acknowledged that the Landlord retained the services of Orkin Pest Control to attend at the rental unit on several occasions to conduct inspections and treatment, and no evidence of bedbugs was identified by [name] during those attendances. The Tenant further concedes that as of April 1, 2024, she has not observed bedbugs in her unit and confirmed at the hearing that none were present as of the hearing date.

As the only remedy sought with respect to this issue is an order requiring the Landlord to conduct pest control treatment, and the Tenant acknowledges that no bedbugs are presently in the unit, I find that the issue is moot. Accordingly, the bedbug allegation is not considered further in my determination. Windows

The Tenant testified that three upper-level windows in the rental unit were replaced on December 19, 2024. However, the Tenant states that the windows in her laundry room located in the basement are a concern.

The Tenant submitted a photograph of the laundry room window taken approximately one year prior to the hearing and asserts that the window has mold. Upon review of the photograph, dark discoloration is visible along the side of the window frame. The Tenant testified that the Landlord arranged for a contractor to attend the unit on November 30, 2023. She acknowledged that the window was cleaned at that time and that red tape was applied around the window frame. The Tenant is unaware of the full extent of the work completed; however, she confirmed that as of the hearing date, red tape remains around the window frame.

During the hearing, the Tenant displayed the current condition of the window through her phone camera. No dark staining or visible mold was observed around the window or frame. However, red tape remained visible around the perimeter, and the Tenant pointed to a clear plastic covering affixed over the window. The Tenant testified that she does not know why the plastic covering and tape remain in place and stated that the plastic obstructs her view to the outside. The Tenant stated that the tape and plastic covering have been in place since November 30, 2023. She further testified that she did not raise the issue with the Landlord because she believed all the windows in the unit would be replaced.

The Tenant further testified that two additional basement windows have condensation between the panes, which she states results in ice buildup during colder weather and prevents her from seeing clearly through the windows. She testified that she first raised this concern with the Landlord in June 2023 and submitted two photographs in support of this allegation. Upon review of the photographs, neither mold nor ice buildup is apparent. The Tenant was unable to recall when the photographs were taken.

In cross-examination, the Tenant conceded that, following the replacement of the three upper-level windows on December 19, 2024, she did not raise any further concerns with the Landlord regarding the remaining basement windows. She testified that she did not do so because the Landlord does not respond to her communications. The Tenant further acknowledged that on November 14, 2024, the Landlord advised her that only the three upper-level windows would be repaired. She further conceded that after this communication, she did not advise the Landlord that the additional basement windows remained a concern.

The Tenant also submitted a copy of an email sent to the Landlord dated September 29, 2015. In part, the e-mail states: “it appears there is mold in the window in the kitchen near the side door.” The Tenant testified that the Landlord conducts annual inspections of the rental unit and that, during those inspections, she shows the Landlord what she describes as mold around the kitchen window. No photographs of the kitchen window was submitted into evidence. In cross examination the Tenant conceded that as of April 1, 2025, she was aware that the Landlord took the position that all window maintenance issues had been rectified. Although the Tenant disagrees with that position, she acknowledged that she did not raise any further concerns with the Landlord after that date. Mold

The Tenant submitted two photographs taken approximately 15 years prior to the hearing and testified that mold has been present in the rental unit. She testified that holes in the roof had previously caused the ceiling to cave in, which she believes resulted in mold. The Tenant further testified that a company advised her that mold could spread through electrical outlets. However, the Tenant did not submit a mold assessment, inspection report, or any recent photographs showing mold in the unit. The Tenant was also unable to identify the company that allegedly provided this information.

In cross-examination, the Tenant testified that she believes mold has been present and growing in the unit for approximately 20 years. However, she did not submit documentary or expert evidence to substantiate this belief.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the rental unit to investigate her mold concerns and that no mold was identified during that investigation. She further testified that the investigation resulted in the Landlord leaving open holes throughout the unit and requests that the Landlord be ordered repair those holes. Damage to open holes were not alleged in the Tenant’s application, and therefore, this issue is not considered in my determination.

The Tenant testified that she has resided in the unit for 28 years, pay’s her rent on time and maintains a clean home. She stated that she wishes to live in a healthy environment. The Tenant acknowledged that she does not have proof that mold exists in the unit but testified that she believes mold is present.

The Tenant requests that an order requiring the Landlord to conduct an air quality test to confirm whether mold is present in the unit. The Tenant further requests that the Landlord inspect the basement windows, as she believes they are not properly balanced. [name] 21. [name] (LC), the Landlord’s property administrator testified that her responsibilities include responding to tenant complaints and maintenance inquires. She testified that tenants may report maintenance concerns by telephone, e-mail, or by submitting written work orders. 22. LC testified that, following receipt of the Tenant’s application, she reviewed the Landlord’s records and followed up with maintenance staff to determine whether the Tenant had submitted written workorders relating to mold or window concerns. She testified that no such work orders were found. 23. LC further testified that she had contacted the Tenant on several occasions to inquire whether there are any outstanding maintenance concerns requiring attention, and that the Tenant advised her that there were no new issues. 24. LC relied on two invoices from Service 1 Enterprises and testified that mold remediation was completed in the unit in November 2023, including work relating to basement and laundry room windows. She further testified that additional remediation was completed in March 2024, including the basement laundry room and two upper- level bedroom closets. LC testified that the Tenant has not advised the Landlord that the remediation work was unsuccessful or that mold persists in the unit. 25. LC testified that the Landlord conducts annual inspections of the rental unit, with the most recent inspection occurring on October 9, 2024. She testified that no new mold concerns were identified or raised by the Tenant during that inspection. LC further testified that no additional concerns regarding the windows have been raised by the Tenant since that time. 26. Although given the opportunity to do so, the Tenant chose not cross examine LC. 27. The Landlord requests that the application be dismissed. The Landlord submits that mold remediation was completed in the rental unit on two occasions and that, since April 2024, the Tenant has not raised any new further mold concerns. 28. The Landlord further submits that the application does not clearly identify which window requires maintenance. The Landlord notes that three upper-level windows were replaced in December 2024 and submits that the Tenant has not raised any further window related concerns since that time. Analysis 29. Section 20(1) of the Act provides that, a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 30. In order to succeed on this application, the Tenant bears the onus of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet these obligations. 31. With respect to mold, the Tenant believes mold is present in the unit and relies on photographs taken 15 years ago and historical concerns dating back approximately 20 years. However, the Tenant did not submit recent photographs, inspection reports, or expert evidence confirming the presence of mold in the unit. The Tenant also acknowledged that, when the Landlord investigated her concerns, mold was not identified. 32. The Landlord submitted invoices confirming mold remediation was completed in November 2023 and March 2024 in areas identified as concerns, including the basement laundry room and certain closets. There is no persuasive evidence before me that this remediation was inadequate or that mold persists in the unit. The Tenant also conceded that she did not raise further mold concerns with the Landlord after April 2025, despite being aware that the Landlord considered the issues resolved. 33. With respect to the windows, the evidence establishes that three upper-level windows were replaced in December 2024. Although the Tenant expressed concern abut basement and kitchen windows, the Tenant did not provide clear or contemporaneous photographic evidence demonstrating mold, structural failure, or another condition requiring repair. The photographs submitted did not show visible mold, and no objective evidence was presented confirming condensation, ice buildup, or disrepair requiring corrective action. 34. I also find it significant that the Tenant did not notify the Landlord of ongoing window concerns after being advised in November 2024 which windows would be replaced, and did not submit work orders or other communications demonstrating unresolved maintenance issues. The Landlords evidence indicates that annual inspections were conducted and that remediation and repair work was undertaken when concerns were identified. 35. With respect to the red tape and plastic covering affixed to the basement laundry room window, the evidence does not establish that these materials are mold or evidence of an ongoing mold condition. The Tenant acknowledged that the materials were installed by the Landlord’s contractor during remediation work on November 30, 2023. While there is no evidence before me that the tape and plastic covering presently pose a health or safety concern or constitute disrepair, they appear to be remnants of prior maintenance work. As these materials were installed in the course of the Landlord’s remediation efforts, I find that the Landlord is in the best position to determine whether they remain necessary. Accordingly, the Landlord is on notice of the Tenant’s concern and should assess whether the tape and plastic covering can be safely removed or whether further repair is required. 36. Based on the totality of the evidence, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord is currently in breach of section 20(1) of the Act. The Tenant’s belief that mold may be present, without supporting objective evidence, is insufficient to justify an order requiring an air quality test or further remedial work. 37. As a result, I am not satisfied that an order is warranted requiring the Landlord to conduct additional mold testing or further window repairs. 38. The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application
The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,020.50.

Although the Tenants’ application does not select reason 6 which provides that the Landlord gave an N12 notice and did not pay compensation by the termination date, the Landlord confirmed that she understood the application is about the N12 compensation and was prepared to respond.

The Tenants requested that I amend the application to select reason 6 and remove reason 2, which seeks the last months’ rent deposit. I accept the submissions of the parties and grant the Tenants’ amendment.

It is undisputed that the last months’ rent deposit of $2,972.50 was applied to the month of June 2025. The Tenants paid rent for the month of July 2025 and they moved out of the rental unit on August 2, 2025, as a result of the N12 notice. 5. [name] testified on behalf of the Tenants. She stated that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because the Landlord served an N12 notice but they did not receive the one months’ compensation from the Landlord. 6. Section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: 48.1 A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48. 2017, c. 13, s. 8. 7. In this case, the Landlord testified that she served an N12 notice with a termination date of July 31, 2025 because she required vacant possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for her own use; however, she did not pay one months’ compensation because she was not aware of the requirement. 8. I accept the Landlord’s testimony and find that the Landlord owes the Tenants one months’ compensation, in the amount of $2,972.50, because she served an N12 notice pursuant to subsection 48 of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,020.50. This amount represents: • $2,972.50 N12 compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. An interim order dated November 12, 2024, amends the application to allege that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant filed their application on the Board’s T2 application form alleging that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.

This matter was previously adjourned from October 29, 2024, and an interim order issued on November 12, 2024, amends the application to allege that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application proceeded on the basis of a “T5 Application” pursuant to section 57 of the Act. T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties’ evidence and submissions focused on the first two elements of section 57, specifically: whether an N12 notice was served to the Tenant, and if so, whether the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.
The Tenant must prove all the elements of section 57, and I do not find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of an N12 notice of termination.

The Tenant testified that after a discussion about a “lease renewal” in September 2022 (during which there was discussion of a rent increase), the Landlord subsequently called the Tenant in November 2022 asking the Tenant to move out.

The Tenant submitted a copy of his call logs for September 2022 and identified a log entry dated September 4, 2022, that he asserts is the first telephone call with the Landlord about the lease renewal and rent increase. No log entries were submitted to show any telephone conversations between the parties after September 2022.

Evidence of a text message conversation between the parties was also submitted contemporaneous to the parties’ discussions about the rent increase and renewing the lease. During the text message exchange on September 11, 2022, the Tenant requests that the lease only be renewed for a fixed term until April 2023.
The text exchange between the parties in September 2022 predates the Tenant’s recollection of when he became aware that the Landlord’s son wanted to occupy the rental unit.

The Tenant was asked why he did not request a renewed lease term for one year since all prior lease renewals were for a fixed term of one year. The Tenant explained that he did not want a month-to-month tenancy and since the Landlord had advised him that he wanted the rental unit for his son in April the Tenant “wanted that in writing”.

During this same text exchange on September 11, 2022, the Landlord writes to the Tenant, “I have no intention to evict as you are such a nice family.”, which is not consistent with the Tenant’s position that shortly after these text messages the Landlord advised the Tenant that he wants the Tenant to vacate because his son requires the rental unit.

The Landlord denied telling the Tenant that he had to move because his son intended to move into the rental unit and asserts that the plan for his son to move into the rental unit was reactionary to being advised by the Tenant during the parties’ lease renewal discussions in September 2022 that the Tenant intended to vacate the rental unit in April 2023.
The Landlord gave evidence that no formal written notice on the Board’s N12 form was served because it was never his intention to evict the Tenant.
The Landlord testified that in September 2022 it was the Tenant who requested the lease be renewed for a fixed term to April 2023, based on Tenant’s own desire to move out of the rental unit.

The parties’ evidence was consistent that there was a conversation some time in November or December 2022 in relation to the Landlord’s son occupying the rental unit. The Tenant’s position is that this conversation was verbal notice for the purpose of section 57. The Landlord’s position is that no N12 notice was served, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit of their own volition.

I do not need to determine whether the parties’ discussions constitute a notice for the purpose of section 57 of the Act because I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant intended to vacate the rental unit and effectively, gave notice to terminate the tenancy.
On September 11, 2022, the Tenant requested a renewal of their lease on a fixed term basis to April 30, 2023, despite all prior lease renewals being for one year.

The Tenant asserts that they chose April 30, 2023, as the end of the renewed lease term to codify that date as being when the Landlord wanted the Tenant to vacate however, the text messages wherein the Tenant requests a shorter lease renewal in September 2022 predate the Tenant’s best recollection of any mention that the Landlord’s son intended to move into the rental unit.
There is also a subsequent e-mail to the Landlord dated January 4, 2023, wherein the Tenant requests to delay their move to “the end of June”.

The Tenant’s representative asserts that someone making their own decision wouldn’t request permission for an extension unless they were provided with a deadline however, based on my determination that the Tenant intended to vacate on April 30, 2023, it would not be unreasonable the Tenant would request an extension of a termination date set by them.

I do not find the Tenant’s explanation of the overall circumstances to be credible. I reject the Tenant’s evidence that they chose the fixed term lease renewal date of April 30, 2023, to correspond with a request from the Landlord that the Tenant vacate the rental unit; the Landlord had not conveyed this intention to the Tenant and to the contrary, the Landlord stated they had no plans to evict the Tenant.

The Tenant’s request for a fixed term lease renewal to April 30, 2023, was in part, because they did not want to have a month-to-month tenancy. This suggests that the Tenant only required the security of a fixed term up to April 30, 2023, which is indicative of their own intention to vacate the rental unit on that date.

In the absence of the Landlord conveying an intention to terminate the tenancy contemporaneous to September 11, 2023, I find it is more likely than not that the fixed term lease renewal to April 30, 2023, was at the request of the Tenant and on the basis of their intention to vacate the rental unit.

Accordingly, I do not find that the Tenant proved that they vacated the rental unit as a result of an N12 notice served by the Landlord as required by section 57 of the Act and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit or residential complex or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant raised two principal issues: 1) that the shared kitchen of the residential unit did not have a functioning exhaust fan and 2) that broken tiles and a lack of a shower curtain made the shower in the rental unit uncomfortable to use.

I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was in breach of his maintenance obligations under the Act. It is not clear, based on the evidence presented at the hearing, that the deficiencies cited were in fact present in the rental unit or would constitute a breach of the Landlord’s obligations under the Act.

The only evidence presented by the Tenant at the hearing was his own testimony. In my view, he failed to establish that the Landlord was in breach of his obligations during the tenancy. The Tenant described the issues, the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s complaints, and the impact on the Tenant in extremely general terms. The Tenant did not submit any photographs of the alleged deficiencies nor any record of written communication with the Landlord about the issues.
Given the lack of evidence presented, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $745.00.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant submits that the Landlord charged him a $400.00 deposit for his keys which was collected at the beginning of the tenancy. In support of this allegation, the Tenant provided two photos showing $400.00 of cash with the keys.

The Tenant also seeks a refund for the amount paid for “solid waste disposal” totalling $297.00 for the 12 months between October 2024 and October 2025, when he vacated the rental unit. The Tenant states that this formed part of the water utility invoice, which he was responsible for; however, he says it was listed as “solid waste disposal” on a separate portion of the utility bill. The utility was under the Landlord’s name, but the Tenant paid 50% of the bills.

Utilities are defined pursuant to s. 2(1) of the Act as: “…heat, electricity, and water.” Utilities do not contemplate solid waste disposal, which the Board understands to be garbage, recycling, yard waste, etc.1 In my view, solid waste disposal is not akin to utilities as described in s.2 of the Act. I accept the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that he paid $297.00 for these charges between October 2024 and October 2025. Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of these charges.

The Tenant also requested the return of funds spent on pest control. However, pursuant to s. 29(2) of the Act, these costs were incurred more than one year before the application was filed on October 5, 2025. No order shall issue.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $745.00, which represents: • $400.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $297.00 for solid waste collection services. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
