issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Lopard Estates Ltd. (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $648.00. Illegally entry:

In the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord repeatedly entered the rental unit without notice. However, the Tenant did not list any specific dates or years in the application and provided only a general statement.

Upon reviewing the T2 application, I find that the particulars and detailed description of the alleged conduct must be set out in the originating document. In this case, they were not. Accordingly, this claim is dismissed as vague and lacking sufficient particulars to permit the Landlord to know the case to be met and to properly defend it. Substantial interference and Harassment, etc.

The Tenant testified that on November 1, 2023, the Landlord knocked on his door and yelled at him from outside the unit. The Tenant stated that the Landlord demanded that he move out and used offensive and abusive language. The Tenant further testified that later that same day, he encountered the Landlord in a common area of the property, and the Landlord threatened to physically remove him from the rental unit. The Tenant stated that he felt frightened and feared bodily harm.

The Tenant also testified that on November 2, 2023, the Landlord called the police and falsely stated that the Tenant was not a lawful tenant. The Tenant stated that the police attended at the rental unit while he was sleeping and attempted to remove him. After the Tenant presented his lease agreement and explained that he was a lawful tenant, the police and the Landlord left.

The Tenant testified that as a result of these incidents, he felt unsafe and moved out of the rental unit by November 15, 2023. Law and analysis: 7. [name]. Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 8. Harassment. Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 9. While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as: engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. 10. Black’s Law Dictionary (https://thelawdictionary.org/) defines harassment as “a course of conduct directed at a specific person that causes substantial emotional distress in such person and serves no legitimate purpose”. 11. Harassment in the landlord and tenant context is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate under the circumstances. 12. The Landlord’s conduct on November 1 and November 2, 2023, must be assessed in context. A landlord is entitled to communicate with a tenant and to pursue lawful remedies where disputes arise. However, a landlord is not entitled to use intimidation, threats of physical removal, abusive language, or improper police involvement to pressure a tenant to vacate. The Tenant’s uncontested evidence establishes that the Landlord attended at the rental unit, demanded that the Tenant move out, used offensive language, and threatened to physically remove the Tenant. The following day, the Landlord contacted police and attempted to have the Tenant removed despite the existence of a valid tenancy agreement. 13. The Board has consistently held that threats of physical removal and attempts to bypass the eviction process constitute serious interference with a tenant’s security of tenure. Security of tenure is a fundamental protection under the Act. When a landlord attempts to remove a tenant outside of the statutory process, that conduct strikes at the core of the Act’s purpose. 14. Even though the incidents occurred over a short period, the seriousness of threatening physical removal and involving police to remove a lawful tenant elevates the conduct beyond a minor dispute. A reasonable tenant in those circumstances would feel intimidated and unsafe. 15. Therefore, based on this analysis, I find that the Landlord breached Sections 22 and 23 of the Act, and the Tenant may be entitled to a remedy. Remedies: 16. The Tenant seeks rent abatement, rent differential, general damages, and an administrative fine. Rent Abatement 17. An abatement reflects the principle that rent is paid for a bundle of rights and services, including security of tenure and freedom from harassment. Where those rights are interfered with, a proportional reduction in rent may be appropriate. 18. I find that the Tenant is entitled to $100.00 as rent abatement for November 1 and November 2, 2023. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $600.00. Given the seriousness of the incidents but their short duration, I find that $100.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. Rent Differential 19. The Tenant seeks $1,300.00 for increased rent. He testified that after moving out he initially lived with his father and paid $550.00 per month, which was less than his previous rent. He later moved to another rental unit at a higher rent. 20. Section 31(2) of the Act permits the Board to award compensation for increased rent where a tenant is induced by the conduct of the landlord to vacate the rental unit. 21. While I am satisfied that the Tenant moved out due to the Landlord’s conduct, the Tenant initially paid less rent after moving. I am not satisfied that the later move to a higher rent unit was directly caused by the Landlord’s conduct. Therefore, no award for rent differential is granted. General Damages for pain and suffering 22. The Tenant seeks general damages for pain and suffering. The Board has authority to award such damages pursuant to section 31(1)(f) of the Act. 23. I accept the Tenant’s testimony that he experienced stress, fear, and emotional distress as a result of the Landlord’s harassment and threats. This is a reasonably foreseeable consequence and does not require medical evidence. In the circumstances, I award $500.00 in general damages. Administrative Fine 24. The Tenant also seeks the Landlord pay a fine to the Board. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter Landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 25. I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $648.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 for rent abatement • $500.00 for general damage for pain and suffering • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $5,500.00 for moving and storage fees, a rent differential, one month’s compensation, and general compensation.
The residential unit is a condo. The Tenant vacated the condo on November 1, 2024 after residing there for 3 years.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (KS)

KS testified that she received a text message from the Landlord on September 1, 2024 advising her that she had to move out of the rental unit by November 1, 2024. She provided me with the text message that stated “Due to circumstances beyond our control we are going to have to move back into the condo. I am so sorry. My realtors have offered to find a place in the area that is similar to mine if you need help finding a place. Again I am so sorry, it upsets us that we have to do this and give you the two months’ notice for November 1st.”

KS also stated that the Landlord told her that she would be required to sign documents with the Landlord and that the Landlord’s realtor would assist her with finding new accommodations. The Tenant stated that she did not receive any paperwork from the Landlord and that she did not hear from any realtor about assistance with finding another place.

KS stated that she met with the Landlord on November 1, 2024 so that the Landlord could inspect the unit for damage and she could return her keys. The Tenant stated that the Landlord was very rude and intimidating to her and she requested a friend join the meeting with her. KS stated that the rental unit was in excellent condition, she returned the keys at that time and vacated the unit on that day.

KS was able to find another condo in the same building and she noted that the Landlord appeared to be staying temporarily in the rental unit for a couple of weeks and then she noted that the unit was empty again. As she lived in the same condo building, she did walk by her previous unit several times over the next months and it appeared to be vacant.

The Tenant stated that the rental condo was put up for sale on September 9, 2025 which was 10 months after she vacated the unit. She provided a real estate listing showing the date that the condo was put up for sale and the date that the condo sold. She stated that she was very frustrated that the Landlord forced her to leave her home and the Landlord did not move into the condo. The Tenant now has to pay increased rent in her new condo.

The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $1,200.00 due to the monthly increase of rent of $100.00. KS stated that she paid $1,800.00 per month in the rental unit and now pays $1,900.00 per month and provided a copy of her recent Notice of Rent Increase as proof.

The Tenant is seeking the one month’s compensation, $1,800.00 that should have been provided by the Landlord after giving the Tenant this type of notice. She is also seeking $500.00 in moving expenses and $2,000.00 in compensation due to the Landlord’s bad faith. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I must determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence and corroborating real estate listing confirms that the Landlord advertised the rental building for sale on September 9, 2025, 10 months after the Tenant vacated. The condo sold on October 15, 2025. The Tenant’s evidence also confirms that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit as per the Landlord’s message.
Based on the above, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave this notice to the Tenant in bad faith.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with her T5 application. Remedies

The Tenant requested moving and storage costs in the amount of $500.00. Although the Tenant failed to provide receipts or invoices for these expenses, I am satisfied that the amount sought is reasonable and award same.
The Tenant requested one month’s compensation which is required under section 48 of the Act when a Landlord serves this type of notice. As such, I award $1,800.00 for this head of damage.
The Tenant requested a rent differential of $1,200.00 based on the monthly increase of $100.00 at her new residence. I award $1,200.00 for the rent differential.

The Tenant requested compensation of $2,000.00 which is a very reasonable request. Having considered the circumstances in this case, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $2,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,500.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for moving expenses; • $1,200.00 for the rent differential; • $1,800.00 for the one month’s compensation required under section 48 of the Act; and • $2,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-089853-24-RV issued on November 4, 2025. On December 3, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On December 16, 2025 interim order LTB-T-089853-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on November 4, 2025. The review request was heard by videoconference on January 14, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Landlord’s agent [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: In the review request, the Tenant claims serious errors of law in the order and procedural fairness issues related to the hearings held on September 9 and October 14, 2025. Specifically, the Tenant claims errors related to the dismissal of the T2 application, denial of his adjournment request, unreasonable discretion and misapprehension of evidence.

The initial reviewing Member reviewed the application record and listened to the hearing recording and narrowed the issue for review to whether the Member erred by not ordering the Landlord to repair and/or replace the bathtub faucet. The December 16, 2025 interim order was issued accordingly.

At this review hearing, the Tenant sought to raise various other issues as per his review request. The Landlord opposed the Tenant’s request, stating the Member reviewed and narrowed the issues and to do otherwise would be prejudicial to the Landlord and not a good use of Board time. Issue to be Determined

Rule 26.9 of the Landlord and Tenant Board Rules of Procedure establishes that the Board will conduct a preliminary review of a review request and direct a review hearing of some, or all of the issues raised in a review request. The Tenant’s review request was directed to a hearing to determine if the “hearing member seriously erred related to the bathtub faucet issue.

At the review hearing the Tenant asked me to exercise my discretion to hear all the issues in the review request. I declined to do so. I agree with the preliminary review assessment that the other grounds of review do not have the potential of raising a serious error. Additionally, the interim order directed the parties to be prepared to address bathtub faucet issue not the entire review request and I did not think it would be reasonable, fair or expeditious to add on new grounds of review regarding the Board’s other findings.

The initial reviewing Member listened to the hearing recording in relation to the Tenant’s review request and determined to narrow the issues was reasonable. I take this to mean that the initial reviewing Member, having considered the entirety of the Tenant’s request, found the majority of the Tenant’s requests did not rise to a serious error.

Additionally, I have listened to the hearing recording and agree with the initial reviewing Member’s decision to limit the scope of the issues to be determined. The other claims made in the Tenant’s request do not rise to a serious error. As such, the issue to be determined is related to the bathtub faucet. The Bathtub Faucet

There is no dispute that the Tenant’s application included the functioning of the bathtub faucet. By way of remedy, the Tenant sought an abatement of rent and an order for repair. However, the Member, having found breach with respect to the bathtub faucet, did not order repair as sought by the Tenant.
The Landlord’s representative agreed that the Member did not order repair but it was completed by the Landlord on December 9, 2025. The Tenant confirmed the reparations have been completed.

On the basis of the submissions made in the request, I am satisfied that there is a serious error related to the bathtub faucet. As per paragraph 13 of the order, the Member was satisfied that the bathtub faucet was in despair. It would have been reasonable to order the Landlord to complete the necessary repairs.
The Tenant’s review request is granted. The De Novo Hearing
The Landlord’s representative agreed that the Tenant should be awarded an abatement in relation to the bathtub faucet to the date it was repaired on December 9, 2025.
At the hearing, the abatement was calculated based on the formula set out in the November 4, 2025 order. It was agreed that the Landlord will compensate the Tenant $14.04 for the bathtub faucet.
As a result of the imposed stay, the Landlord has not paid the $150.00 abatement as ordered.

Both parties understand the total abatement ordered is $164.04. The parties agreed that this amount may be deducted from the February rent, meaning the total rent the Tenant owes for February 2026 is $932.49. The Tenant understand he is required to pay the lawful monthly rent on time and in full from March 2026 and this reduction only applies to February 2026.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-089853-24 issued on November 4, 2025 is granted.

The November 4, 2025 order is amended accordingly. It is ordered that: 1. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $164.04 representing a rent abatement for the leaking bathtub control [name] and faucet. 2. The Landlord shall deduct the amount from the February 2026 rent.
The balance of the November 4, 2025 order remains in full force and effect. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T2 and T6 application alleging that there was a flood in the rental unit on October 12, 2024, and asserts that during the course of repairs the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit, threatened the Tenant, and the repairs substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The rental unit is a townhouse with two floors. The Tenant resided on the first floor which consisted of one bedroom, a kitchen, a small living room/dining room, and a utility room. The Tenant occupied the first-floor bedroom and shared the other areas of the rental unit with three roommates/tenants. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on July 2, 2024, and moved out on October 31, 2024, after a leak originating in a utility room flooded the entire first floor of the property.

The Tenant testified that on the evening of October 12, 2024, there was a leak from the pipes in the utility room, and the issue was immediately reported to the Landlord. The Tenant began cleaning up the water and a repair person came within approximately 1-2 hours.

The Landlord sent a message in a group chat on October 16, 2024, advising that an insurance adjuster would be attending at the residential complex to do evaluations which would take approximately one hour. The Tenant sent a message on the evening of October 16, 2024, inquiring if anyone had entered the Tenant’s room.

The Landlord replied that the insurance adjuster needed to measure the floor, so it was possible they entered the Tenant’s room. The Tenant asked that the Landlord inform them the next time someone would be entering the room.

The Landlord sent another message on October 19, 2024, advising the Tenant that a further inspection would be completed on October 20, 2024, and the Landlord would be present during the 4-5 hour inspection.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord entered the Tenant’s room on October 20, 2024, and began repair work in the Tenant’s room which included removing the carpet and moving the Tenant’s belongings. The Tenant submitted photographs and video of the room showing pieces of the carpet had been removed with chunks of carpet underpad remaining

The Tenant also testified that they felt intimidated by messages sent by the Landlord on October 21, 2024, and October 23, 2024. Both messages were written in Chinese for which the Tenant had provided a translation.

The message from the Landlord on October 21, 2024, refers to repair work scheduled for the weekend and tells the Tenant that the Landlord is, “really willing to fix [your] room if you can compromise”. The Tenant gave evidence that the Landlord’s reference to a compromise was for the Tenant to pay a maintenance fee incurred by the Landlord as a result of the flood.

The Tenant translated the Landlord’s message from October 23, 2024, to read “You better leave the fan on for ventilation when you’re gone. If you don’t, the works will do the living room and storage area first, and your room will be last”.

The Tenant testified that after October 21, 2024, they did not reside in the rental unit and moved out on October 31, 2024. When the Tenant moved their belongings on October 31, 2024, there were still fans in the room, and the first floor was still under construction. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the entire first floor of the residential complex was flooded on October 12, 2024, requiring emergency service. The Landlord further testified that their insurer advised they would send an emergency service company to do an inspection, and the Landlord became aware of the inspection scheduled for October 16, 2024, on October 13, 2024.

The Landlord’s evidence is that the emergency company was slow to respond and after the initial leak was repaired there was still remediation work required to repair damage. The Landlord testified that he was advised that the carpet was wet and both the carpet and drywall should be removed however, the Landlord’s evidence is that “just a corner” of the carpet in the Tenant’s room was removed.

The Landlord asserts that any delay in completing repairs was due to the Tenant’s actions in not keeping the fans running to dry the room, and the delayed response by the insurer and emergency contractors.

The Landlord denied that the messages he sent to the Tenant on October 21, 2024, and October 23, 2024, were threatening or intimidating and testified that the Tenant’s translation of the conversation was inaccurate.

At the hearing, an online translation tool was used to obtain a more objective translation of the conversation between the parties. The translation of the text from October 21, 2024, shows that the Landlord does not use the word “compromise” but instead encourages the Tenant to keep the drying fans running and asks for the Tenant’s cooperation to expedite the completion of the repair work.

The online translation tool also translated the message from October 23, 2024, to read differently than the Tenant’s translation. The message on October 23, 2024, asks the Tenant to “please” keep the drying fans running and advises the Tenant that if the fans aren’t kept running that the living room and storage room repairs will be completed first.
The Landlord believes that the floors were finally dry on October 25 or 26, 2024, and a construction company repaired the floor some time after October 31, 2024. T6 Application
The Tenant’s application alleges that there was a flood in the rental unit and subsequent repairs were not completed promptly.

Section 20 of the Act sets out the Landlord’s statutory obligation in relation to maintenance: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In relation to the issue of the flood, a pipe began leaking on October 12, 2024, which was remedied the same day. The Landlord had a plumber attend on the evening of October 12, 2024, and the issue was resolved on the same date.

In these circumstances, I do not find that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act in relation to the leak/flood. The Landlord acted promptly to address the issue when it occurred.
In relation to the subsequent repair work, the flood occurred on October 12, 2024, and an inspection wasn’t undertaken until October 16, 2024. No repair work was completed during this time.

On October 20, 2024, the Landlord removed carpet and baseboards from the Tenant’s room without notice. The Landlord’s own evidence is that the Tenant’s room was dry on or around October 25 or 26, 2024, and the floors were not repaired when the Tenant vacated on October 31, 2024.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The evidence before me is that after the inspection October 16, 2024, repair work began on October 21, 2024, and repairs were not completed until after October 31, 2024.

Despite the Landlord testifying that this was an emergency situation, an inspection was not completed until October 16, 2024- 4 days after the leak, and remediation didn’t begin until October 21, 2024.
There was no evidence that any steps were taken to dry or remediate water damage to the Tenant’s room prior to October 21, 2024.

The Landlord’s own evidence is that the floor repair was anticipated to only take a few hours however, the Tenant’s room was not repaired for over 19 days after the flood. The only work undertaken on October 21, 2024, was providing fans to dry the room, and parts of the carpet and baseboards were removed.

The Landlord did not submit evidence to corroborate his testimony that there was delay from contractors or his insurer, nor that the Tenant’s actions caused or contributed to any delay. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to take adequate steps to perform repairs to the rental unit and residential complex within a reasonable period of time after the flood occurred. T2 Application Illegal Entry
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord illegally entered his room on October 16, 2024, and October 21, 2024, without proper notice.

The Act sets out a landlord’s ability to enter a rental unit in with, and without notice at sections 26(1) and 27(1) of the Act: 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement.

Further, section 27(3) of the Act sets out minimum requirements for a notice of entry: (3) The written notice under subsection (1) or (2) shall specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
The Landlord relies on section 26 of the Act in relation to the entry on October 16, 2024, and asserts that notice was given for the entry on October 21, 2024.

The Landlord sent a message to the Tenant on October 16, 2024, that an insurance clerk will be doing some evaluations. There was no date or time in the Landlord’s message, and the inspection took place on the same day- October 16, 2024. The Landlord takes the position that this inspection after the flood was an emergency as contemplated by section 26 of the Act and therefore, no notice of entry was required.

At the time of entry on October 16, 2024, the emergency had been resolved. The emergency situation was the leak in the utility room causing flooding and despite the need for repairs being urgent due to the water intrusion, this was no longer an emergency situation that would permit the Landlord to enter the rental unit without notice.

Further, the Landlord testified that he was aware of the scheduled inspection date on October 13, 2024, and there was no reason the Landlord could not have provided adequate and timely notice. The Landlord or their agent illegally entered the rental unit on October 16, 2024.

In relation to the alleged entry on October 21, 2024, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant on October 19, 2024, advising that a maintenance team will come for an “inspection check” on Monday (October 21, 2024) at 6:00 p.m. that will take approximately 4-5 hours.

Despite the Landlord’s notice being served at least 24 hours prior to the date of entry, the Landlord or their agent entered the rental unit on October 21, 2024, and began removing carpets and baseboards from the Tenant’s unit. [name] tendered at the hearing show the Tenant’s belongings were disturbed and there was dust and dirt on the Tenant’s bed.

The Landlord’s message advised the Tenant that an inspection would be undertaken on October 21, 2024, not that any work would be performed. The Tenant consented to the entry on the basis of an inspection but had no notice that repair work would commence.

The notice did not accurately specify the reason for entry, and the 4-5 hour timeframe exceeds the 8:00 p.m. permissible time for entry to a rental unit as set out in section 27(3). I find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on October 21, 2024. [name]
The Tenant alleges that the lack of timely repair and the repair work itself substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 (the “Regulation”) sets out criteria to be applied by the Board in determining whether there is substantial interference when a landlord does maintenance, repairs or capital improvements, criteria for determining whether to order an abatement of rent, and rules for calculating an abatement. These rules must be applied in an application for a finding that the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit by the tenant.

The regulation sets out required considerations when making a determination as to whether there was substantial interference as a result of work undertaken in the rental unit or residential complex, and the quantum of any abatement that can be ordered: (2) For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances. (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.

When the Landlord began work on October 21, 2024, a portion of the carpet and the baseboards were removed. There was exposed bare floor with pieces of carpet underlay still present. A large fan was required to run in the Tenant’s room which the Tenant found to be disruptive. The Tenant’s evidence is that he did not reside in the rental unit after October 21, 2024.

I am not satisfied that the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable. The wet carpets required removal and fans were necessary to ensure the room was dry prior to remediation. The lack of notice for the commencement of the remediation work is considered in the context of the illegal entries. Threats and Interference
Section 23 of the Act provides: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.
The Tenant relies on two messages from October 21, 2024, and October 23, 2024, in support of the allegation that the Landlord threatened or intimidated them.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s messages on October 21, 2024, and October 23, 2024, are threatening or intimidating. The translation submitted by the Tenant was disputed by the Landlord and an online translation tool showed discrepancies in the translation.

Specifically, the translation submitted by the Tenant was more terse and omitted pleasantries in the Landlord’s language such as “please”. I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s translation of the messages is accurate, nor that the language used by the Landlord was threatening or intimidating. Remedies
The Tenant requested the same remedies in both their T2 and T6 applications. Termination of the Tenancy 52. The Tenant’s application requests termination of the tenancy on October 31, 2024.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 Tenant’s Rights provides guidance in applications where a Tenant requests termination of the tenancy. Specifically: “The LTB may order that the tenancy be terminated on a specific date, either on a future date or retroactively. This remedy is used in serious cases where the tenant requests termination.” And, If the landlord's actions caused the tenant to move out of the unit, and the LTB finds the decision to move was reasonable in the circumstances, the LTB may retroactively terminate the tenancy, usually as of the date the tenant vacated the unit.

Despite the lack of haste with which the repairs were undertaken and completed, I do not find that this issue rises to a level that would entitle the Tenant to terminate their tenancy. Less than 30 days had elapsed since the issue arose and while the timeline for repairs was not reasonable, this did not rise to a level that would entitle the Tenant to terminate their tenancy.

After the Tenant’s room was dry, there was no evidence that the state of the room posed a health or safety issue, nor that the room did not comply with housing maintenance standards. The room remained aesthetically unpleasing however, there was insufficient evidence to find that the room was uninhabitable.
Further the Tenant did not submit any correspondence to the Landlord requesting immediate repairs or expressing any frustration with the length of time the repairs were taking.
Accordingly, I do not find it is appropriate to order termination of the tenancy as requested. Rent Abatement

The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications both seek a rent abatement of $888.33 which is calculated as the return of a rent deposit in the amount of $650.00, and a 100% abatement for 11 days during October 2024 when the Tenant did not occupy the rental unit.
Since the request to terminate the tenancy is denied, it would not be appropriate to order the abatement sought on the basis of the return of the Tenant’s rent deposit.

Despite this, the Tenant has proven two illegal entries by the Landlord or their agent. The Divisional Court decided in Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation 2007 CanLii 3228 (ON S.C.) an abatement of $1,000.00 for one instance of illegal entry was appropriate.

In this matter the Tenant’s rent was $650.00 per month. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 Tenant’s Rights provides: “A rent abatement cannot exceed 100% of the rent payable during the time period covered.” And, “In general, the duration of the rent abatement corresponds to the period of time that the breach occurred. However, if the breach is a single event, such as an illegal entry, the length of the breach may not be as relevant.”
The Tenant cannot be awarded an abatement that exceeds the rent for month(s) during which the issues occurred.

The Tenant’s evidence in relation to the impact of the illegal entry on October 16, 2024, was minimal. The Landlord testified that he was aware of the requirement to enter the Tenant’s unit on October 13, 2024, and there was no reason the Landlord could not have provided the required 24-hour notice.

The Tenant’s evidence in relation to the impact of the illegal entry on October 21, 2024, was more fulsome. The Tenant returned back to the rental unit to find portions of the carpet missing in their rental unit after being advised that only an inspection would take place. The Tenant’s belongings were moved and the work was undertaken without notice of the actual work.
Accordingly, given the impact of the two unlawful entries on the Tenant, I find a lump sum abatement of $650.00 for both the illegal entries is appropriate.

Since the Tenant has received the maximum abatement for the month of October in relation to illegal entries, it is not necessary to make a determination in relation to any other abatement entitlements claimed on the basis of substantial interference or breach of maintenance obligations. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2024, and I am without any evidence about the state of repairs after that date. Cost to Repair or Replace Property that was Damaged
The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications also seek reimbursement in the amount of $58.21 to replace a duvet that became soiled during the Landlord’s unexpected carpet removal on October 21, 2024.

The photographs submitted by the Tenant show construction dust and particulates on the Tenant’s duvet however, I am not satisfied that the duvet was damaged and could not have been washed or drycleaned. I decline to order the cost to replace the Tenant’s duvet. Rent Differential

The Tenant’s application requests a rent differential of $1,440.00 however, I am not satisfied the Tenant was entitled to terminate their tenancy on October 31, 2024. It would not be appropriate to order a rent differential in the absence of a determination that the Tenant was entitled to terminate their tenancy.

As decided above, the Tenant vacated less than 30 days after the flood and the Tenant’s room may have been unsightly however, there was no evidence that the room was uninhabitable after October 25, 2024, or October 26, 2024. Accordingly, the Tenant’s request for a rent differential is denied. Administrative Fine
The Tenant also requested an administrative fine.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative fines provides: “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

While this order makes findings that there were breaches of the Act by the Landlord, I do not find that these breaches constitute a blatant disregard for the Act attracting the imposition of a fine and the remedies ordered herein should encourage compliance and provide deterrence.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $698.00. This amount represents: • $650.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending October 31, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. On January 11, 2026, the Landlords requested a review of interim order LTB-T-089869-24-IN issued on December 5, 2026. The review request was heard by videoconference on March 16, 2026. The Landlords, the Landlord’s representative [name], and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing that occurred on November 26, 2025, the Landlords raised that the Tenants’ application should be dismissed because the parties signed an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy (‘N11’) that included additional terms. One of those terms was that both parties would withdraw the respective applications they had at the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘the Board’). The terms explicitly reference the file numbers of those applications and included LTB-T-089869-24 which is this file. The Landlords withdrew their application, but the Tenants did not.

Interim order LTB-T-089869-24-IN issued on December 5, 2025 denied the Landlord’s request to dismiss the application. The Landlord submits that serious errors were made by the Board in doing so. For the following reasons I agree.

Rule 26.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure establishes that any party may request review of any order which makes a final determination of the party's rights. While the order under review is an interim order it makes a final determination regarding the Landlord’s preliminary issue and ability to advance a viable defence. It therefore can be the subject of a review.

The interim order narrowly considers that the doctrine of res judicata does not apply because no Board order states that it resolves all matters between the parties. The interim order made a serious error by not considering more broadly whether it would be an abuse of process for the application to proceed in light of the written agreement between the parties to withdraw the application. Put differently the interim order made a serious error by only considering whether a Board order prohibited the Tenant’s application from proceeding and did not meaningfully engage with the question of whether the parties’ written agreement should barre the application from proceeding.

The recording reflects that the Landlord raised the terms of written agreement attached to the N11 at the hearing. The interim order also references the motion order LTB-L-009252- 25-SA issued on April 28, 2025 which also discusses those terms. As such the issue of the terms attached to the N11 agreement was before the Board.

The interim order contains no reasons about the contents of the written agreement, whether it would be an abuse of process for the tenant’s application to proceed, or why that question was not addressed. It was a serious error for the Board to unreasonably narrow the issue to purely a consideration of whether a Board order stated that it resolved all issues between the parties and it was a serious error for the Board to provide insufficient reasons for denying the preliminary issue. The review request is therefore granted. Abuse of Process

As the review was granted, the Landlord’s preliminary issue was reheard. For the following reasons I find that it would be an abuse of process for the Tenant’s application to proceed. The application is accordingly dismissed.

The parties signed an N11 agreement that contained the following additional terms: “Upon signing of the N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy all parties agree that this resolves all issues pertaining to the tenancy and will refrain from bring any further claims against each other. The Landlord shall withdraw file LTB-L-089562-24 and the Tenants shall withdraw file LTB-T-089869-24 upon the Tenants vacating the property” ([name], page 3-5).

The Board’s records reflect that the Landlord withdrew the application they said they would. The tenant application referenced in the terms agreed to by the parties is the application before me. The Tenants did not withdraw it and seek to proceed on it.
The Tenant [name] initially denied signing the N11 but then said she used DocuSign to sign it. The document is also signed by the Tenant [name]. The date by the signatures is December 23, 2024.

Emails between the parties reflect that in December 2024 the parties discussed the waiver of rent in the context of the tenancy terminating ([name], pages 17-28). In an email dated December 23, 2024, the Landlord’s representative sends the Tenants a copy of the N11 and says “If you are in agreement to these terms whereby you withdraw your LTB matter, and the Landlords will withdraw their matter. The Landlord will waive the December 2024 rent voiding the N4 notice that was served on December 21, 2024. Your last month’s rent deposit will be used for your last month’s rent being January 2025…”

The Tenants submits that the agreement to withdraw the applications was conditional, that the conditions were never fulfilled, that during the discussions for the N11 the Landlords issued a N4 notice of termination for December 2024 rent arrears (‘N4’), that the Tenants’ repudiated the agreement, and that the Landlords intimidated the Tenants into signing the agreement. None of the Tenants’ arguments satisfy me that the written agreement is invalid.

The Landlords followed through with the agreement. The Landlords withdrew their application. The Tenants did not. The N11 signed by the parties actually does not reference the waiver of rent. As such I’m not entirely satisfied it was even a conditional element of the agreement. However, even if it was, the Landlords did follow through on their promise not to collect December 2024 rent. The N4 notice was served on December 21, 2024, which is before the parties signed the N11. The Landlord never pursued an application based on the N4. The Tenants made the unilateral decision to pay December 2024’s rent but could not point to any evidence that proved the Landlords asked them to do so. The Tenants also made the unilateral decision to not vacate the rental unit by the termination date. The last month’s rent deposit was not applied to January 2025 because the Tenants refused to move out and the tenancy ended on a later date. That the Tenants changed their mind about the agreement does not satisfy me the agreement was therefore invalid. The Board already addressed the Tenants’ claim that they were pressured into signing the N11 in order LTB-L-009252-25-SA issued on April 28, 2025. The Board found that the Tenants were not pressured into signing the agreement and upheld the order terminating the tenancy based on the agreement.

Section 197 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) establishes that the Board may dismiss an application without holding a hearing or refuse to allow an application to be filed if, in the opinion of the Board, the matter is frivolous or vexatious, has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action.

The Board has consistently found that parties agreeing to resolve all issues in a tenancy prohibits parties from being able to proceed on applications covered by the agreement. See for example TST-55299-14-IN (Re), 2015 CanLII 10094 (ON LTB), [name] (Re), 2020 CanLII 61256 (ON LTB), and TST-94423-18 (Re), 2018 CanLII 123294 (ON LTB).

The written agreement between the parties has all the elements of a valid agreement, offer, acceptance, consideration, meeting of the minds etc. The terms of the agreement are extremely clear that the Tenants agreed to withdraw this application. The Landlord withdrew their application, but the Tenants failed to uphold their end of the bargain. That the Tenants’ changed their mind does not satisfy me that the agreement should not be upheld. To refuse to uphold the agreement would be fundamentally unfair and an abuse of process.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-089869-24-IN issued on December 5, 2025 is granted.
Interim order LTB-T-089869-24-IN is canceled and replaced with the following:
The application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $[name] for a rent differential and the application fee.

The residential unit is a 2-bedroom, 1 bathroom basement apartment. The house is a duplex with a basement apartment and a main floor apartment. The Tenants commenced their tenancy in the basement apartment in September of 2019 and vacated the apartment on April 30, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (JA)

JA testified that she received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord in November of 2024 with a termination date of April 30, 2025. The Landlord stated that he and his wife would be moving into the entire rental house. She stated that the upstairs tenants had also received an N12 notice of termination.

The Tenant stated that shortly after they vacated the rental unit, she noticed that the Landlord had listed the house for sale. JA provided a copy of the listing of the house which was printed on September 24, 2025 showing that 696 [name] in Burlington had been listed since August 12, 2025. 6. [name] stated that she emailed the Landlord on or about September 17, 2025 about the house’s sale listing and the Landlord told her that the house was listed on MLS to test the market. 7. JA also testified that the rental unit has been empty since she vacated the house and that the Landlord has not moved into the house. 8. [name] confirmed that her previous monthly rent at the rental unit was $1,400.00 and that she now paid $3,241.00 for a 3-bedroom townhome. She stated that she struggled to find another unit that was close to Burlington where she and her spouse worked. 9. The Tenant was very frustrated that they had to move out of their apartment after residing there for 6 years and that the move drastically interrupted their lives. She stated that she and her spouse had established friendships with other neighbours and had become good friends with the main floor tenant. She stated that it was very difficult trying to find another unit that they could afford as rent prices had increased substantially over the last 6 years. 10. The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $1,841.00 per month for a period of 12 months which is calculated as $22,092.00. She is also seeking that the Landlord pay an administrative fine due to the Landlord’s actions of failing to move into the house and listing the house for sale in August of 2025. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] (BB) 11. BB testified that he and his wife have always intended to reside in the rental house and that he is currently confirming the renovations that are necessary for them to move in. He stated that in November and December of 2024, he hired an architect who was going to prepare architectural drawings for the renovation project however that plan fell through. 12. BB confirmed that he is not residing in the rental house but that he and his wife continue to reside in their own home. 13. The Landlord stated that he made plans to consider the cost benefits of investing $350,000.00 into the rental house with the planned renovation, without affecting his savings and investments. He stated that this is why he listed the house for sale to better understand its market value and to evaluate the overall situation. He stated that he received an offer on the house but declined same and he let the listing expire. 14. BB stated that he met with a new designer in September of 2025 and that meeting convinced him that the renovations made sense and that he wanted to move forward, “full steam ahead.” He stated that a new renovation plan was developed and the plans moved forward from that point. 15. The Landlord explained that he is doing some of the renovation work himself and that this project can only be done at a certain pace due to his hip and shoulder issues. He further stated that he is waiting on contractors to confirm dates when their specific work can be done. 16. BB stated that this renovation plan is very involved and it is a substantial upgrade to the rental house. He confirmed that now that the renovations have started, he will be listing his own house for sale in the middle of May of 2026 and he plans to move into the rental unit once the majority of the work is done in the rental unit. 17. BB stated that his intention has always been to move into the rental house and that he has been working on the renovation plan since the Tenants vacated the rental unit in April of 2025. He maintains that he has acted with a good faith intention. Analysis 18. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 19. There is no question that the first and second of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenants and the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. The Landlord’s position on his occupation of the rental unit is that his upcoming move to the unit was reasonable in the circumstances. He stated that he had to investigate how the renovations would affect the value of the house prior to moving into the house with his wife. He further stated that the renovations were so extensive that he had to seek out multiple professionals to assist with the successful development of the plans. 20. The Landlord continues to reside in his current home 12 months after the Tenants vacated the rental unit and he is only now considering a move into 696 [name]. There were no unforeseen changes in circumstances involving the rental unit and the Landlord provided no extenuating circumstances that would explain a one-year delay in occupying the unit. I find that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenants vacated. 21. Therefore, I must now determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 22. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenants vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 23. According to the Landlord, he listed the rental house for sale in September of 2025 to “better understand its market value and to evaluate the overall situation.” Based on the Landlord’s evidence, I understand that he was determining whether or not it would make financial sense to substantially renovate the house. If the Landlord felt that the renovated house would not attract a sufficient market price, I suspect that he would have sold the house and remained in his current home. Only after lengthy communications and evaluations from an architect and a designer and the test of its market value, did the Landlord decide that a financial investment in the house was a viable option. 24. The Landlord’s testimony confirmed that he made the decision to move into the rental house in late fall of 2025. 25. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12. 26. I am satisfied that the Landlord did not have a good faith intention to reside in the rental house when he served the N12 notice on the Tenants. The Landlord’s intention to move into the house himself was formed after he determined that the substantial renovations in the house would be financially beneficial to him. 27. As mentioned previously, the Landlord listed the house for sale in August of 2025 and his evidence did nothing to shift the presumption of bad faith. As such, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. 28. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies 29. Although the Tenants did not provide a copy of their new lease setting out the rent differential of $1,841.00 per month, I am going to order a rent differential in an amount that I feel is reasonable. The Tenants stated that they moved into a 3-bedroom, 2 bathroom townhome which is not comparable to a 2-bedroom basement apartment. However, during the 6 years that the Tenants resided in the rental unit, rental prices have skyrocketed due to a shortage of rental accommodations. Based on the above, I am ordering a $500.00 rent differential for a period of 12 months which is $6,000.00. 30. The Tenants are also requesting that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 31. I decline to award an administrative fine based on the circumstances of this case. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 32. I believe that the rent differential award of $6,000.00 should deter the Landlord from participating in similar activity in the future. 33. The Tenants incurred a cost of $48.00 to file this application and they are entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,048.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for the rent differential; and. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord raised, as a preliminary issue, that the Board does not have jurisdiction with regard to the Tenants’ application.
However, as explained below, I find that the LTB has jurisdiction over this claim. Tenants’ T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $500.00.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenants state that they viewed the rental property on December 29, 2024. At that time, the Tenants say they paid the Landlord $500.00 because the Landlord told them she had another interested prospective tenant, and to secure their opportunity to rent the premises, she requested this fee. However, when the Tenants re-attended the rental unit on January 1, 2025, when the tenancy was to start, the Landlord presented a lease which was not on the Ontario Standard Lease and did not indicate the correct amount of rent had agreed to orally on December 29, 2024.

The Tenants say the advertised monthly rental rate was $1,300.00. However, the rental agreement reflected the rent of $650.00. The Tenants say that they believed the Landlord, who was still demanding $1,300.00, was attempting to circumvent her tax obligations stating they believed that she wanted some of the money “under the table.” Regardless, on January 1, 2025, the Tenants upon learning about the discrepancies with the lease decided not to rent the unit and did not take possession of it.

On about January 5, 2026, the Tenants asked for the return of the $500.00, but the Landlord refused. The Tenants submitted a copy of their text exchanges which they had translated, which state the rental price of the unit was $1,300.00, and also includes a reply from the Landlord, sent to the Tenants on January 5, 2025, which states: “Young lady, we made it clear; you agreed to forfeit this rent deposit and leave, correct?”.

The questions the Board needs to answer are: 1. Does the Board have jurisdiction in this matter? 2. Was the fee paid commission, bonus, fee, or premium? 3. Can the Landlord entitled to keep the funds as a result? Does the Board have jurisdiction in this matter?

The Landlord takes the position that the parties never actually entered into a tenancy. They submit that as a result the Act does not apply to their relationship, and the Board has no jurisdiction to make an order. I do not agree.

Section 134 of the Act prohibits a landlord from collecting a commission, fee, premium, or other similar charges from a tenant, former tenant, and prospective tenant. Moreover, section 135 (1.1) is clear that prospective tenant may apply to the LTB for an order that a landlord or their agent collected a charge prohibited by the Act.

This application involves an allegation made by a prospective tenant that their potential landlord collected an illegal charge. I am persuaded that the Board has jurisdiction to hear the application. Was the fee paid a commission, bonus, fee, or premium?

The Landlord submits that the funds they collected were not a “rent deposit”. Rather, she submits that the Tenants offered this money voluntarily to secure the rental unit so that the other prospective tenants would be denied. 14. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord indicated that the $500 was required to secure the unit. Even if I am wrong about this, section 134 not only prohibits a landlord from requiring a fee or premium, but it also prohibits a landlord from collecting such a charge. In the circumstances, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected the $500 from the Tenants to secure the unit and that in doing so they collected an unlawful charge. I will order it to be returned to the Tenants. Can the Landlord retain the collected funds? 15. The Landlord argues in the alternative that the amount paid was a rent deposit as evidenced in her January 5, 2025, text message. If the funds collected by the Landlord were in fact a rent deposit, the Landlord would be entitled to keep the funds, subject to the Landlord’s effort to mitigate her damages. The Landlord was in fact able to re-rent the unit, but it took two weeks, and during that time she received no income. The Landlord submits that they ought to be able to keep the deposit because the Tenants failed to take possession of the rental unit. 16. I have already found that the fee paid was a premium or a fee, and not a rent deposit. However, even if I am wrong, and the $500.00 represents a rent deposit rather than a bonus, I am still of the view that the Landlord would not be entitled to retain the amount because in my view, her losses were self-induced. 17. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that when they went to sign the lease agreement and take possession of the rental unit, the Landlord presented a tenancy agreement with terms that deviated from what the parties had agreed to. Significantly, the lawful rent stated in the lease agreement was not what had been worked out by the parties orally. The Tenants were suspicious of the changed term and decided they did not want to enter into the tenancy if it included a different amount of rent than what had been advertised and negotiated. In my view, they were entitled to do so given that the Landlord attempted to unilaterally change the terms of the lease that the parties agreed to. The Tenants are not responsible for any losses that the Landlord incurred because of the Tenants’ decision not to take possession in response, and I find that they were self-induced losses by the Landlord. 18. There was no evidence before me that the parties prepared a rental application or signed a lease. Given that, no tenancy agreement as permitted by ss. 106(1) of the Act was formed, and vacant possession was not given to these Tenants, pursuant to ss.107(1) of the Act, the Landlord must return the funds. 19. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $500.00 for the illegal charge collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, I am satisfied the Landlords have retained money illegally.
The tenancy commenced on December 1, 2022. The Tenant paid the Landlords $100.00 for a key deposit and $1,480.00 as a last month’s rent deposit (‘LMR’) on November 30, 2022.
On March 3, 2025, the Landlords served the Tenant with an N4 Notice for non-payment of rent with a termination date of March 17, 2025. The amount of arrears alleged owing was $1,711.00.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 15, 2025. The Landlords have failed to return the last month’s rent deposit and the key deposit and have not paid the Tenant interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. These facts are not in dispute.

Subsection 17(3) of Ontario Regulation 516/06 supports the premise that refundable deposits for keys are allowed but are to be refunded upon the return of the keys in question. The Landlords did not challenge the Tenant’s evidence that he returned the key to Landlord [name] on March 15, 2025. As such, the Landlords shall be ordered to reimburse the Tenant $100.00 for the key deposit.

As the Landlords gave the Tenant a N4 notice on March 3, 2025, the Tenant was not obligated to provide notice to terminate the tenancy. The tenancy would be determined to have ended on March 15, 2025, the date the Tenant gave vacation possession to the Landlords. Given this, the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent ended on March 15, 2025 when the tenancy ended.
Daily compensation is $48.66, which is calculated as follows: ($1,480.00 x 12/365). Based on this, the Tenant would have owed the Landlord $729.90 in rent from March 1 – 15, 2025 (15 days x $48.66).

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. What this means is that a landlord is not entitled to retain a deposit for damages, as claimed by the Landlords. The Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $750.10, which represents the balance owing on the last month’s rent deposit ($1,480.00 - $729.90).
The Landlords shall also be ordered to pay the Tenant $84.73 for interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit as required by s. 106(6) of the Act.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $982.83. This amount represents: • $100.00 for the illegal key deposit collected. • $750.10 for the balance of the LMR. • $84.73 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
