issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the rent deposit was illegal, only that the key deposit was illegal, so the Landlord must return the key deposit pursuant to 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’). [name]
The Tenant testified that on October 5, 2025, she signed a lease to rent the above rental unit in [name], Ontario starting November 1, 2025.
The monthly rent was $900.00 and it was due on the first day of the month.
She paid the key deposit of $200.00 by e-transfer on October 7, 2025 (Exhibit 1) and a rent deposit of $900.00 on October 9, 2025, also by e-transfer (Exhibit 2).
Her boyfriend was unable to find a job in [name], so she cancelled the lease on October 10, 2025 via text message to the Landlord and never took possession of the unit.
She requested her deposit be refunded but did not receive a response from the Landlord.
The Tenant filed this application with the Board on October 27, 2025.
The Landlord did not attend the hearing, although duly served with the Notice of Hearing, so the Tenant’s evidence remains uncontested. Rent Deposit
Sections 105, 106(1) and 106(2) provide that a Landlord may collect a rent deposit, as long as it does not exceed one month’s rent and the deposit is collected before the tenancy begins.
The tenancy was to begin November 1, 2025, and I find that the Landlord collected the rent deposit on October 9, 2025.
I find that the Landlord correctly collected one month’s rent of $900.00.

Subsection 107(1) of the Act requires that a landlord repay the amount received as a rent deposit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. In Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 5425 (CanLII), the Court found that the word “not given” suggests that it is the refusal or inability of a landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. In the present case, however, it was the Tenant’s action in refusing to take the unit that prevented her from taking possession, not any act of the landlord. As such, the Tenant is bound by the agreement with the Landlord. She is not entitled to the return of the rent deposit pursuant to subsection 107(1) because it was her act of repudiation of the agreement that prevented her from taking possession of the unit, not the action of the Landlord. Therefore, the Landlord is entitled to keep the $900.00 rent deposit.
Therefore this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Key Deposit

Key deposits are prohibited under section 134(1)(a) of the Act. The Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;
I find that the Landlord collected a $200.00 key deposit on October 7, 2025 from the Tenant.
This money shall be refunded to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00 This amount represents: • $200.00for the illegal key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Tenant testified that in January 2025 her portion of the lease was transferred to a new tenant. The Tenant testified that this was approved by the Landlord. The Tenant testified that she was initially sharing the rental unit with other roommates, and her portion of the last month’s rent deposit was $435.65, which was still being held by the Landlord at the time the lease was assigned in January 2025.

The Tenant testified that her roommates remained and as far as she knows the assignee and her former roommates continue to be in possession of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she assigned only her portion of the lease in January 2025.

Section 95(8) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that if a tenant has assigned a rental unit to another person, the tenancy agreement continues to apply on the same terms and conditions. Furthermore, section 106(10) provides that the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the last month of the tenancy. And finally, section 18 of the Act provides that covenants concerning things related to the rental unit run with the land.

The modern principles of statutory interpretation require that the words of an Act be read in their entire context, harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intent of the Legislature. See [name] v CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 at para. 39.

As such, when I consider the various sections mentioned above in their entire context and interpreted harmoniously with each other, I find that since the Tenant assigned all her rights under the tenancy agreement to the assignee (new tenant) and the tenancy continued, this included terms relating to the last month’s rent deposit. I find that the Tenant’s portion of the last month’s rent deposit was properly included with her assignment of her portion of the tenancy and was assigned to the assignee.

Furthermore, since the tenancy continued and has not ended, the last month’s rent deposit cannot be applied. As of the hearing, the Landlord has not illegally retained any money per section 135 of the Act as based on the Tenant’s testimony the tenancy continues to the best of her knowledge.

It would have been up to the assignor (the Tenant) and the assignee to come up with an agreement during the assignment of the lease to deal with the Tenant’s portion of the last month’s rent deposit. That is beyond the jurisdiction of the Board.
Therefore, based on the foregoing, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants’) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $[name] for general compensation and the application fee.
The residential unit is a 3-bedroom, 3-bath house. The Tenants vacated the house on May 31, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (JM)

JM spoke on behalf of all of the Tenants. JM stated that the Landlord advised the Tenants at a meeting on February 20, 2025 that he would be needing the rental house for his spouse’s parents. The Landlord provided them with an N9 form for each of them to sign but the Tenants advised the Landlord that he needed to provide an N12 notice.

JM stated that they received the N12 notice on March 4, 2025 which stated that the Landlord’s spouse’s parents would be moving into the rental unit. The termination date was May 31, 2025 and the Tenants vacated the unit at that time.

JM stated that within a few weeks, the Tenants noticed that the Landlord had put the rental house up for sale. They provided me with a real estate listing that showed that the house was put up for sale on June 23, 2025 and continued to be up for sale with a price change on August 21, 2025.
JM stated that in September of 2025, the house was no longer on the market and they assumed that the house sold.

JM stated that he and the other Tenants were very frustrated with the fact that they were kicked out of their home only so that the Landlord could sell the house. They felt that the Landlord purposely gave them the incorrect forms, N9, to try to prevent them from accessing their rights under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). The Tenant stated that the Landlord’s parents did not reside in the house and the Landlord simply lied to them.

The Tenant said that two of the Tenants had to move back into their parents’ home which was embarrassing, and the other Tenant had to find something else temporary. JM stated that it took them 4 months to find a new rental unit where they could all live together. He said that all of the Tenants feel that the Landlord disregarded their rights as Tenants and this whole situation was very expensive and drastically interrupted their lives.

The Tenants are seeking compensation of $12,092.00 which stems from 4 months’ rent which they feel is appropriate in the circumstances. Their previous rent was $3,023.00 per month in the rental house.
The Tenants are also seeking that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] (NW)

NW stated that his intention was for his spouse’s parents to move into the rental house but he was faced with an unfortunate situation which made the plan impossible. He stated that his wife’s parents were advised that their parents, who live in India, were very ill and the parents had to travel to India in August of 2025 to care for their own parents.

The Landlord confirmed that his spouse’s parents did not reside in the rental house and for that reason, he decided to sell the house as he said that he was having financial difficulties. He stated that he sold the rental house in October of 2025 and that he suffered a loss on the house of $150,000.00. He stated that he purchased this property as an investment and losing this large amount of money made his financial situation even worse. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenants, the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. I must determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenants vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.
It is uncontested that the Landlord’s spouse’s parents did not move into the rental unit, the house was put for sale on June 23, 2025 and the house sold in October of 2025.

The Landlord’s statement that his spouse’s parents went to India in August of 2025 does not explain why the Landlord listed the house for sale on June 23, 2025. He gave no information to corroborate a date when the spouse’s parents became aware of their family’s illness. The only other information provided by the Landlord included that he lost $150,000.00 on the sale of his investment property. The Landlord’s evidence did nothing to shift the presumption of bad faith and as such, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies
The Tenants requested compensation of $12,092.00 for the emotional distress, the serious disruption to their lives and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.

The Tenant spoke about the embarrassment of having to move back into their parents’ place, he spoke about how the Tenants had to find another comparable place that would house all three Tenants, he spoke about the moving costs that he and the other Tenants incurred and he spoke about the stress of the whole ordeal.

Although I was not satisfied that the Tenant’s claims for $12,092.00 were borne out of the evidence, I am satisfied based on the credible testimony of the Tenant that the termination notice caused them emotional distress, serious disruption and a great inconvenience by the Landlord’s bad faith notice. As such, I assess this claim at $6,000.00 and shall order same.

I decline to award an administrative fine based on the circumstances of this case. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.
I believe that the compensation award of $6,000.00 should deter the Landlord from participating in similar activity in the future.
The Tenants were successful with their application and are entitled to the application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,048.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the application fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $35,760.00. The Landlord must also pay to the Tenant $48.00, for the costs of filing this application.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
As explained below, the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
The Tenant testified they were served with an N12 Notice of Termination with a termination date of October 31, 2023 for the Landlord’s child’s own use (the “N12”). This was not disputed.

The Tenant testified that they moved out on November 4, 2023 after signing an N11 Agreement to Terminate the tenancy (the “N11”). The Tenant testified that the N11 was signed as they were offered money to be able to move, and the Tenant felt they had no choice given the N12.

The Tenant submitted screenshots of a Zillow advertisement for the upper floor of the rental unit taken on March 29, 2024 advertising it for rent for $2,980.00 per month. Some of the pictures in the Zillow advertisement show the furniture of the Tenant in the rental unit. The Tenant believes these pictures were taken when an individual the Landlord claimed was conducting an insurance inspection attended the rental unit approximately a month before they were served with the N12.

The Tenant also testified they saw an advertisement for the basement of the rental unit being separately rented. The Tenant testified they believed that it was being advertised for $2,000.00 per month, but they did not have any screenshots of this advertisement as the advertisement link had been taken down prior to the Tenant taking a screenshot.
The Tenant previously paid $2,000.00 per month in rent for the entire rental unit.

The Tenant also testified that they visited the rental unit after a package was inadvertently sent to the rental unit address in May, 2024 and upon attending the rental unit found that both the upper floors and basement of the rental unit had been rented.

Based on the above, the Tenant submitted that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith, never intended for their child to move into it, and instead intended to end a long-term tenancy to profit of the increases in the rental market that occurred during the Tenant’s tenancy.

As the rental unit was advertised for rent within a year of the Tenant vacating pursuant to the Landlord’s notice, this triggers a presumption under section 57(5) of the Act that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith unless the Landlord can prove the contrary on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord entered evidence only through putting documents to the Tenant in cross examination. No testimony was called by the Landlord in evidence, and no explanation for this advertisement of the rental unit was provided in the evidentiary portion of the hearing. The Landlord’s Legal Representative tried to submit an explanation related to why the Landlord’s child did not move into the rental unit during final submissions, but as there was no evidentiary foundation for this submission, it can be given little weight.

I find based on the above that the Landlord’s child did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period for a period of one year, and that the Landlord did not rebut the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith.

The Landlord submitted that the reason the Tenant moved out of the rental unit was not due to the N12, but because of the N11. The Landlord’s position was that the parties entered into the N11 due to rent arrears owed by the Tenant, and an agreement for compensation to be paid to the Tenant to move out of the rental unit, and this is the real reason the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant acknowledged that they signed the N11, and received compensation to do so, but testified that they entered into this agreement to terminate the tenancy because of the N12 as they believed the termination of tenancy pursuant to it was inevitable, they feared being homeless, and required the money to be able to move to a new home.

In support of this position the Tenant presented an e-mail dated September 13, 2023 from the Landlord’s Legal Representative to the Tenant that shows a discussion relating to signing the N11 that mentions both amounts of rent arrears and compensation that would be due pursuant to the service of the N12 in calculating the amounts that would be paid as compensation to the Tenant for signing the N11.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that they entered into the N11 because of the N12 served on them. In accordance with section 202(1) of the Act, I find therefore that the real substance of this agreement was that the Tenant agreed to vacate the rental unit, and did vacate, pursuant to the N12. While the Landlord submitted that the N12 had been subsequently withdrawn and did not proceed to a hearing, I find that this is irrelevant in making this finding.

I note that there was a dispute about the amount of compensation the Tenant received to sign the N11, but I find it is unnecessary to make a determination in this regard as it is irrelevant to the factual findings necessary to decide this application.

While the Landlord provided case law they submitted supported the position that in these circumstances the Tenant had not met their burden to show they moved out in accordance with the N12, this case law was distinguishable in that no N12 notice of termination had been served in the case presented. I therefore did not find it to be assistive in determining this application.
Given the above, the Tenant has proven all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act.
As the Tenant has proven their application, they are entitled to reimbursement of $48.00 for the costs of filing this application. Remedies Rent Differential
The Tenant claimed an amount of $2,000.00 per month, totalling $24,000.00 for increased rent they paid in the year after they vacated the rental unit.

In support of this, the Tenant provided the first page of a residential tenancy agreement dated November 2, 2023 with a term beginning November 5, 2023 and specifying rent as $3,950.00 per month. The Tenant testified that this is what the Tenant had been paying in rent since moving out of the rental unit.

The Tenant did not provide the signature page for this document to show the agreement was executed. The Tenant also did not provide any rent receipts, bank statements or other evidence to show that this amount of rent was paid by the Tenant on a monthly basis.

I note further that the Tenant initially testified that they moved out on November 4th or 5th, in accordance with the start of the lease presented, but presented text messages in the hearing that indicated they had not moved out of the rental unit by November 13, 2023. While the Tenant acknowledged after seeing the text messages that the move out date they testified to must not be correct, they provided no explanation this. I note that the Landlord’s position is the rental unit was actually vacated on November 26, 2023, but that a determination of the exact date is unnecessary for the determination of this application.

The Tenant has an evidentiary burden to prove the damages they have incurred. Where supporting documentary evidence would be readily available to prove a fact central to a claim being made, it is expected that a party will provide that supporting evidence. The Tenant has failed to do so.

On the basis of the above, I find the evidence presented by the Tenant in regard to what they paid in the year after vacating the rental unit to be insufficient to meet their evidentiary burden. Given this, I find that the Tenant has failed to prove they are entitled to be awarded compensation for increased rent in the year after vacating the rental unit. Administrative Fine

The Tenant requests that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16: “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find an administrative fine appropriate in this case as the only other remedy awarded in this application is the filing fee, and in my view, this does not provide sufficient deterrence to the Landlord.

The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination in bad faith. The Landlord then proceeded to split the rental unit into two units, and advertise it for rent with photographs taken shortly before that N12 notice of termination was served, renting these two new units at a considerable profit as compared to the previous rent.
This behaviour is egregious, blatantly in disregard of the Act, and a strong message of deterrence is required to encourage compliance from the Landlord in the future.

The Tenant paid $2,000.00 a month in rent. The best evidence presented in the hearing was that the total rent the Landlord is now receiving for the two new units is a total of $4,980.00, a difference of $2,980.00 per month. I find it appropriate in these circumstances to order an administrative fine equal to the increase in rent the Landlord has received over a one year period, which totals $35,760.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $48.00. This amount represents $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $35,760.00 by April 12, 2026 (see below). April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: COLMAN (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Former Tenant owes. [name] (the 'Former Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord': • collected or retained money illegally. (T1) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6) • entered the rental unit illegally. (T2 application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. These applications were heard by videoconference on April 7, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As set out below the Landlord did not prove the allegations in his application, and the Tenant did not prove the allegations in their T6 application.
Also, as set out below, the Tenant proved the allegations in their T1 and one of the allegations in their T2 application; remedy is as ordered below.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit September 1, 2021, and vacated October 31, 2024. / LTB-T-090623-24

The Tenant’s applications are subject to the one-year limitation period contained in s.29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act). The application was filed November 15, 2024, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2024. Therefore, the Board can only award remedy for issues raised in the application which occurred during the period from November 15, 2023, through October 31, 2024. L10 Application
As explained below, the Landlord did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Former Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing at least 30 days before the hearing in accordance with Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure.

The Former Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2024. The Landlord testified that he asked the Tenant for a N9 notice of termination, but the Tenant refused; the Tenant vacated without giving proper notice, therefore, the Landlord is entitled to two months rent, the 60 days the Tenant was supposed to give. Even though the rental unit was advertised on various forums, it was difficult finding a new tenant because university had already started; the unit was not re-rented until January 1, 2025. As to his responding to the Tenant about vacating on October 31, 2025, this was just to confirm what the Tenant said, it was not acceptance. Therefore, the Landlord is seeking the two months of rent for November and December 2025 and the application filing fee.

The Tenant testified the Landlord had accepted the short notice as indicated in his text dated October 30, 2025. The text said: Hi [name], Tomorrow is the last day of the month. Can you clean the room and take your stuff out. Can you send me pictures after you clean and live [sic] the keys on the desk. After I inspect the room I will e-transfer the deposit. And can you take all your food from the fridge and your stuff from the washroom. 8. The tenancy ended on because of the Former Tenant moving out in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order or agreement to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the Former Tenant's obligation to pay rent ended on that date. The Landlord’s text is clear, the Tenant is to remove all belongings, leave the keys on the desk, and upon inspection the deposit will be refunded; I do not consider this ‘just confirming’ the Tenant’s intention to vacate. On a balance of probabilities, I find this to be an agreement to end the tenancy. Accordingly, the Landlord’s L10 application is dismissed. T1 Application 13. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant the monies as set out below. / LTB-T-090623-24 14. The Landlord collected and/or retained a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). 15. Section 29(2) of the Act says a Tenant must file an application within one year; as the Tenant vacated October 31, 2024, and the Landlord retained the security deposit, the limitation period runs from the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The lease signed July 22, 2021, required the Tenant to pay $570.00 for a last month rent deposit and a refundable $200.00 security deposit upon inspection of the unit; the Landlord never returned the $200.00. Section 105 of the Act is clear; the only permissible security deposit is a rent deposit. In respect of additional charges, section 134 of the Act says such charges are prohibited unless otherwise prescribed. Prescribed exemptions are set out in s.17 of O. Reg 516/16 which permits a refundable key deposit. Therefore, the security deposit is an illegal charge, and the Tenant is entitled to return of the money. Even if the $200.00 is considered a key deposit, the Landlord did not refund the money which is contrary to the Act. As to the Landlord’s testimony that he kept the $200.00 security deposit because the Tenant’s sister moved into the rental unit, which is contrary to the lease and increased utility usage; this is irrelevant. The Landlord had not right to charge the illegal deposit, thus, the Tenant is entitled to its return. Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I find the Landlord charged and/or retained money illegally. 16. In respect of the illegal rent increase, for all the reasons set out below, I find the Landlord increased the rent illegally. 17. The Tenant testified on September 1, 2022, the Landlord increased the rent from $570.00 to $590.00, which is above the 1.2% guideline amount. On December 1, 2023, the rent increased from $590.00 to $630.00, which is also above the 2.5% guideline amount. Further, the Tenant never received a N1 notice of rent increase; all increases were done verbally. The Landlord testified that he was not aware of the guideline percentages, and the Tenant agreed to pay the new rate(s). 18. A Landlord is obligated to follow the Act; it is incumbent on the Landlord to know the rules and abide by them. Section 119 of the Act is clear that rent can only be increased once every 12-months and must be done in accordance with the Act. Section 116 sets out the requirements: 1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the rent charged is increased in accordance with an order under section 126. (3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase. 19. Here, the rent increases were done verbally, therefore the Landlord did not follow the requirements under section 116. As to the Tenant agreeing to the increase(s), this is irrelevant; the Landlord is required to raise the rent in accordance with the Act and cannot circumvent these requirements by relying on the Tenant’s consent to do so. Similarly, a / LTB-T-090623-24 landlord cannot use a new lease between the same parties as a means of circumventing the requirements under the Act. In [name] v. Grant Lake Forest Resources Ltd., 2019 ONCA 44, the Court of Appeals says at paragraph 28 that “s. 113 of the RTA expressly permits the establishment of a new rental rate with a new tenant. Recognition of a similar carve-out for an existing relationship involving the same tenant, the same landlord, and the same premises would undermine the purpose of the Act. A renewing tenant is not a new tenant.” 20. Here, although all increases are considered illegal based on not following proper procedures as required by the Act, including charging above the guideline amount, the Tenant is only entitled to return of illegal rent that complies with the limitation period. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to illegal rent for the 12-month period December 1, 2023, when the increase began, to October 31, 2024, when the Tenant vacated. The amount the Landlord owes to the Tenant is calculated as follows: $630.00 - $590.00 = $40.00 X 11 months = $440.00. 21. The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant for the illegal rent increase and money illegally charged and/or retained is $640.00. 22. As the Tenant was successful in their application, the Tenant is entitled to the application filing fee. T2 application 23. Based on the testimony and evidence before me, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on October 30, 2024. The Tenant testified when he went to start moving his belongings out of the rental unit on October 30, 2024, things were misplaced/moved around from the way he had them. The Landlord also entered while the Tenant was packing, he said he had to ‘monitor the situation’. Later that day, the Tenant received a text from the Landlord with pictures of inside his unit. Although the Landlord appears to be justifying any entry because of what he considered an unacceptable state of the unit, the Landlord had no right to enter the rental unit unless proper notice is given as per the Act. Once a tenant has given notice of termination a landlord is entitled to enter the rental unit to show it to prospective notices upon making a reasonable attempt to give the Tenant notice; this situation her is not with respect to showing the unit, therefore, even if the Landlord had tried contacting the Tenant about entry, it was for an invalid reason. In this case, minimum 24-hours notice was required per s.27. Also, Similarly, the Landlord had no right to re-enter the unit to ‘monitor’ the Tenant while he was packing; proper notice was not given, and I do not consider ‘watching a Tenant pack up their unit’ to be a valid reason in accordance with the Act. Although the Landlord testified that he was out of town on the 30th, therefore he could not have entered the rental unit, the Landlord had no evidence supporting this. It also does not explain how the Tenant’s belongings got moved around, therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities the Landlord or an agent of the Landlord entered the Tenant’s unit illegally. 24. Despite finding that the Landlord entered the unit illegally, the Tenant did not request a monetary remedy in the application or request to amend the application at the hearing to include such a remedy, therefore, no remedy is awarded. . In [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc., [2012] O.J. No. 1052 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court determined it is not / LTB-T-090623-24 open to the Board to order an amount exceeding that claimed in an application which has not been properly amended. 25. As to harassment, I find based, that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant; the allegation in the application lacks the necessary details, specifically the date. Therefore, this portion of the T2 application must be dismissed. T6 application 26. As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the T6 application is dismissed. 27. The Tenant testified the fridge first broke in August 2023, then it stopped working again on May 23, 2023; it took the Landlord 20-days to address the issue. During this time, the fridge was not usable, and the Tenant had to eat out or order in food. The Tenant is requesting $20.00 per day for meal expenses for the 20-day period, a totl of $400.00. Although the Landlord told the Tenant to use the fridge in the garage until he had a functioning fridge, this was not feasible alternative as the garage was packed full and the fridge was not accessible. As to using the other fridge in the house, this was already being used by three other tenants, therefore there was no remaining room for him. 28. The Landlord testified there are two fridges in the kitchen, the Tenant could have temporarily shared the other fridge with the other tenants or used the on in the garage; instead, the Tenant just chose to eat out, which was unnecessary. Further, the Tenant did not advise that neither of these options were viable, or that it was costing him extra money because he did not have access to a fridge. Therefore, the T6 application should be dismissed. 29. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or the residential complex. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 30. Here, the Landlord’s undisputed testimony was there were two other fridges the Tenant could have shared/used and the Tenant never advised him of these options being unworkable. Section 16 of the Act requires parties to minimize their losses; here, the Tenant did not tell the Landlord that the other fridge options were not viable. Therefore, I find the Tenant did not take the necessary steps to minimize losses; by not advising the Landlord, the Landlord was deprived of the opportunity to provide another interim option. In respect of the time-period of the repair/replacement, I find the 20-day period to resolve the issue to be timely; there was no testimony given that questioned the reasonableness of this timeframe. / LTB-T-090623-24
ordered: The Landlord’s L10 application and the Tenant’s T6 application are dismissed.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $640.00.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The full amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $688.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: During the hearing, the question arose as to whether the named Landlord was actually the Landlord.

The Tenant then requested to withdraw the application despite being made aware that he may be out of time to file his claim under section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and the Landlord’s Representative consent to amend the application.
I consented to the Tenant’s request to withdraw the application.

The Landlord’s Representative then made a request for costs against the Tenant for the wasted appearance. The Landlord’s Representative provided that the Tenant should have dealt with the issue regarding who the Landlord was well in advance of the hearing.
The Tenant submitted that the Landlord held himself out as the Landlord which is what led to the confusion and therefore the Tenant should not be liable for any costs.

The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 3 regarding costs provides: While the Board may order a party to pay the costs of another party, costs to a successful party for the preparation/representation fees paid to a legal representative are generally only awarded in cases of unreasonable conduct…

Examples of unreasonable conduct listed in Interpretation Guideline 3 do include initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith or bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find them to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, as explained below.

In this case, I cannot find that the Tenant initiated the application in bad faith or was frivolous in pursuing his claim. While the Tenant may have made an error in naming the correct party, the Tenant could have either amended his application or refiled with the correctly named parties to have the Board make determinations as to the validity of his claims. The Tenant could have taken a little more care or exercised a little more due diligence when initially filing but that is not what costs is meant to deter. The Tenant’s failure to name the correct Landlord is not inherently in bad faith, frivolous, or vexatious.
As such, I do not find there are circumstances that justify awarding costs and therefore decline to award costs in this matter.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed as withdrawn. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). The parties agreed that the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. The parties further agreed that the Tenant vacated as a result of receiving this N12 notice. The issue to be determined in this application is whether the named person on the N12 notice occupied the rental unit shortly after the Tenant vacated and whether the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Tenant did not prove the following requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit, nor am I convinced that the N12 notice was served in bad faith. I make this finding for the reasons found below.

The parties agreed that when the N12 notice was served, it stated that the Landlord’s daughter would be moving into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that when she was vacating the rental unit on May 1, 2023, she spoke with the tenant who was residing upstairs, [name] (“Z.R.”) and that [name] had informed her she would be moving into her rental unit with her three children. The Tenant submitted evidence at the hearing in the form of text messages from an individual named [name] [name] (“A.R.”) mentioning that she would be moving into a rental unit. However, I put little weight on this evidence as there was no specific mention of what rental unit A.R. would be moving into.

The Tenant called forward two witnesses, [name] (“L.S.”), and Pamlea Brand (“P.B.”) who both testified that the only information they had regarding [name] moving into the rental unit was what they were told by the Tenant. I put little weight on this evidence as this constitutes hearsay evidence. Although admissible at the Board, I put little weight on this evidence as none of these witnesses had personal knowledge of who actually moved into the rental unit when the Tenant vacated.

The Landlord testified that mid May 2023, her daughter moved into the rental unit and vacated September 2024, more than a year after living there. The Landlord also said that her daughter moved into the rental unit with her husband and their 3 children, who were having a difficult time financially. However, once their financial position had improved, they vacated the rental unit in September 2024 and moved into a larger home. The Tenant challenged the Landlord’s evidence and questioned how the Landlord’s daughter was able to move out of the rental unit if her financial position was not the best when she moved into the rental unit just 18 months prior. The Landlord testified that she moved her daughter into her rental unit so she did not have to worry about paying rent and this allowed her financial position to improve.

I find in favour of the Landlord’s evidence as the Landlord’s testimony was consistent and clear. On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s daughter moved into the rental unit, therefore, the Landlord did not serve the N12 notice in bad faith. I make this finding because the only evidence the Tenant presented in regard to the upstairs tenant moving into the rental unit was a conversation she had with her on May 1, 2023. I would have reasonable expected the Tenant to summon the other tenant to the hearing, which would have allowed the Board to hear from her directly, and this would also have provided the Landlord the opportunity to cross examine her. Also, the text messages submitted into evidence by the Tenant do not speak to which rental unit was being spoken about, so I am not convinced that another individual moved into the basement rental unit. I put little weight on the Tenant’s hearsay evidence and therefore dismiss her application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
