issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The application contains many allegations that fall outside the one year limitations period found in section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and these cannot be considered. The application also contains allegations that are not maintenance concerns. At the hearing, the Tenant stated that he wished to proceed only with the claim that the Landlords failed to address the issue of mice in the rental unit.
There was no dispute that there were mice in the rental unit and the Landlords were aware for either one or two months prior to the Tenant vacating the rental unit.

As explained below, I am not satisfied that the Landlords failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Section 46 of O.Reg. 517/06 states: (1) A residential complex shall be kept reasonably free of rodents, vermin and insects. (2) The methods used for exterminating rodents and insects shall be in accordance with applicable municipal or provincial law. (3) Openings and holes in a building containing one or more rental units shall be screened or sealed to prevent the entry of rodents, vermin, insects and other pests.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

It is uncontested that there were mice in the rental unit and there is no allegation that the Landlords’ response was not timely. The Tenant submits that the Landlords did not do enough to address the problem. The date that the Tenant reported the issue to the Landlords is contested and is central to the determination of whether the Landlords’ response was reasonable.

In this case, I find that although there were mice in the rental unit, the Landlords’ response to the issue once informed was both timely and reasonable. A landlord cannot be faulted for failure to respond to an issue before it is made aware of the issue.

The Tenant resided in the rental unit from July 1, 2023 until August 31, 2024. The Tenant clarified at the hearing that he was already living in new accommodations by August 24, 2024 but still had possessions in the rental complex. The application was filed on November 5, 2024.

The Tenant testified that in late November or early December 2023, they found mice in the rental unit and tried to use glue traps and other traps to manage the issue. He stated that he first verbally informed the Landlord [name] of the issue on June 26, 2024, and the Landlord said that he would get mousetraps but did not. The Tenant was unsure but thought it was the second week of August 2024 that the Landlord then boarded up the perimeter of the deck in an attempt to exclude mice. In the Tenant’s opinion, the Landlord “didn’t do a proper job.”

In cross-examination, the Landlords’ legal representative suggested that the Tenant’s application was correct and that the Tenant first informed the Landlords of the problem in July 2024, rather than June 26 as the Tenant testified. The Tenant maintained that he spoke with the Landlord on June 26, 2024 to inform him about the mice.

The Landlord Geraldo Salas testified that the Tenant first told him about the mice in late July 2024. When he became aware of the problem, he brought traps and steel wool to put into crevices to exclude the mice. The Tenant told him not to bring traps because they had them. The Landlord stated that he set up pest control professionals to come to the unit, but no one was home so they couldn’t enter because he did not serve a notice of entry. Pest control attended the unit on August 26, 2024. The Landlord testified that there are no mice in the unit now and submitted a declaration from the tenants that moved in on September 1, 2024 that there are no mouse or pest issues (DOC 6399969).

In cross-examination, the Landlord stated that there was never any serious complaint about the mice and when he offered traps, the Tenant said they had them. He blocked the holes where mice could enter, and if there was any maintenance complaint, he fixed the problem.

The parties agree that the Landlord boarded up the deck in August in response to the complaint. The Tenant did not adduce evidence to support his claim that the Landlord did not board up the deck to exclude mice “correctly.” The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s claim that he called professional pest control who attended August 26, 2024 when he was no longer residing in the unit but had possessions there.

If I accept the Tenant’s evidence about when he reported the issue to the Landlords, there was a problem with mice for two months that the Landlords were aware of, during which the Landlords took the above-noted action. If I accept the Landlords’ evidence, they were aware of a problem for approximately one month before the Tenant moved out.
The Landlord’s testimony was specific and unwavering that it was July 25, 2024 when the Tenant first informed him of the mice and then he took action to resolve the issue.

I give little weight to the declaration submitted by the Landlords’ new tenants that there are currently no pests and that the Landlords are responsive to maintenance concerns. The declarants were not present at the hearing for cross-examination. The declaration does, however, have some limited value in that it supports the Landlord’s testimony that he attends to maintenance complaints. It also supports the logical conclusion that the Landlords would wish to have a pest-free rental unit and made efforts to make it so.

The Tenant’s application states that he reported the mice in “July.” This is not consistent with his testimony at the hearing that he notified that Landlords on June 26, 2024. It makes sense that the Tenant’s recollection of events would be clearer two months after he moved out (when he filed the application) than on the date of the hearing (one year after filing the application.) The Tenant’s testimony was not supported by any other evidence. Because of this inconsistency, I give less weight to the Tenant’s testimony than to that of the Landlord.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that it is more likely that the Tenant informed the Landlords of the issue in late July as the Landlord testified. This means that the Landlords had one month to address the issue of mice before the Tenant vacated the unit.

Given the one-month time frame and uncontested evidence about the actions taken by the Landlords to address the Tenant’s complaints about mice, I am satisfied that the Landlords took appropriate steps to deal with the issue as reported by the Tenants. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached their obligation under s.20 of the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair.
The Tenant’s application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $11,96.49 on or before June 8, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 9. The rental unit is upper unit of a single-family home. The Tenant resided in the rental unit until May 31, 2025. At the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit, he was paying $900.00 in monthly rent. 10. It was undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 Notice on the Tenant which stated that the Landlord in good faith, required vacant possession of the rental unit , for the purpose of residential occupation by his mother for a period of at least one year. The N12 Notice provided a termination date of July 31, 2025. 11. The Tenant testified that on April 15, 2025, the Landlord personally handed him an N12 Notice of Termination and stated that his mother will be residing in the rental unit because she recently broke up with her partner. 12. The Tenant testified that after receiving the N12 Notice they decided not to challenge the Landlord’s good faith. He testified that he was able to find a new rental unit suitable for his family and vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025. This was not challenged by the Landlord. 16. The parties do not dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 Notice under s. 48 of the Act and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice. The only remaining issues to be determined are whether the Landlord’s mother moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and whether the N12 was given in bad faith. 17. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s mother did not move into the rental unit because the rental unit is empty. They also stated the Landlord’s mother still lives are her previous rental unit. 18. The Landlord testified that his mother was initially planning to move into the rental unit and she gave her landlord a notice to terminate her tenancy, and she was looking forward to moving in. However, closer to the move in date, his mother was getting anxious and decided not to move in. 19. The Landlord’s mother [name] testified that she had boxes packed and the more and more she packed, she got nervous about the move. She testified that she liked her current rental unit as it was closer to her bank and her neighbours were nice. She also provided that she was medically unfit to move, as she has blood pressure and takes medication for depression and anxiety. 20. Since the Landlord’s evidence was that his mother never moved into the rental unit, I find that the mother did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. 21. In all of the circumstances, I also find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith. The Landlord testified that his mother changed her mind about moving because she wanted to stay in her current unit/ neighbourhood and struggled to accept rental unit. I am not satisfied that this was a material change in circumstances that was not foreseeable before the Tenant vacated. The Landlord and his mother ought to have known of any differences between the two units/ neighbourhoods before the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The fact that the Landlord allowed the Tenant to vacate the rental unit in the face of these foreseeable issues is indicative of bad faith. 22. I therefore find that the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), namely that the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice, the Landlord’s mother did not move into the unit and the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies 30. The monthly rent at the end of the tenancy was $900.00. The Tenant requested a 100% rent abatement equivalent to their new monthly rent, in the amount of $2,100.00. I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent. 31. An abatement of rent is based on the principle that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. There was evidence before me that the Tenant was not able to utilize the rental unit in its entirety after the service of the notice. The Tenant submitted that the process of looking for another rental unit and moving caused them to experience a high level of stress. I find that any tenant who has to move due to a landlord’s request would experience stress and their use of the unit would have been diminished when they had to look for a new place to live, instead of enjoying their unit. The rent was $900.00, and the Tenant received the notice on April 15, 2025. The Tenant moved out May 31, 2025. I find that an abatement of 100% for the for the month of May, to be reasonable in the circumstances as they could not enjoy the rental unit during that period. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $900.00. 32. The Tenant requested the rent differential they incurred for one year after moving out of the rental unit, based on $1,200.00 per month for a total of $14,400.00 for the year. The Tenant moved into a triplex which consisted of three bedrooms, and one-bathroom as of June 1, 2025, paying $2,100.00 for the monthly rent. The parties agreed that the monthly rent for the rental unit was $900.00 at the time the Tenant vacated. The rental unit was upper unit of a house which included, 1 bedroom, 1 den and 1 bathroom, it was a bit smaller than the new unit. 33. The Tenant chose to move to another area and moved into a larger home. While the rental units are not comparable, I do find that the Tenant is entitled to a partial rent differential because the Tenant had to move as a result of the N12 notice they received. 34. Considering the fact that the Tenant’s new rental unit is bigger and hence, there was some betterment in that regard, I find that awarding a portion of the increased rent in the amount of $900.00 to be fair in the circumstances. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $10,800.00 for rent differential for a period of one year.

The Tenant incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $207.49. According to the testimony of the Tenant, the Tenant paid for a moving truck in the and gas for the moving truck, costing a total of $207.49. I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred these moving costs as a result of the Landlord’s breach.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,960.49. This amount represents: • $900.00 for a rent abatement. • $10,800.00 for increased rent the Tenant will incur for the one-year period from June 1, 2025 to June 1, 2026. • $207.49 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord’s representative raised preliminary issues, including that the allegations contained in the applications are unclear and that the Landlord has been put in the unfair position of having to respond to applications containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are, and no valid dates were included. In addition, the Tenant sent an email to the representative about an amendment filed on December 1, 2025, but there was nothing attached, and the LTB portal was blank. The Landlord’s representative also stated there were a several previous ‘Request to Amend the Application’ items filed on the portal and that none of them was a valid amendment, and they were either individual photos or empty attachments. As such, the Landlord takes the position that the Tenant has been given ample time to correct her application having been filed over a year ago and has failed to do so. Further, she stated the application fails to reflect any specific monetary relief in the requested remedies, and that the other remedies are unclear and moot as the tenancy terminated on August 7, 2024. Accordingly, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant’s T6 application should be dismissed.

The Tenant admitted that she received legal advice and some assistance from the local legal clinic. She stated she had some issues with uploading documents to the portal and said her son assisted her with some of the documents. Analysis

Applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met and determine whether to raise a defence. Natural justice and procedural fairness require nothing less.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 that, “Particulars should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, in my view, the case supports the principles of procedural fairness regarding the need for particular and details to permit one to know the case against them, which applies equally to tenant applications.

These principles are confirmed in the Court which states that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

In the matter before me, the application was not only unclear as to what the Tenant’s issues were but did not contain sufficient information to provide any detail to the Landlord to understand the claim being made with valid dates nor any clear remedies that the Board can order as the tenancy terminated. Having said that, the parties were before the Board in past, and while I have no doubt that the Landlord may have been aware of the issues raised, the remedies were unclear and there was no monetary claim included. I note that the application was filed November 5, 2024, and the Tenant received legal advice about the matter so that the Tenant was provided adequate time and opportunity to amend the application to include further information and clarify the remedies.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application was not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at a hearing or the remedies being sought. I also find that the Tenant has be given sufficient time to amend the application. As such, the Tenant’s application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the start of the hearing [name] (MB) intended to speak on behalf of the Tenant. I explained the various options for participants and MB said that she intended to represent the Tenant. MB is not licensed by the Law Society of Ontario.

As per the Board’s Practice Direction on Representation before the Landlord and Tenant Board, MB confirmed that she is appearing as a friend of the Tenant, did not receive any compensation for her representation and has not provided legal services to any other person in the last year.

While MB had some involvement in the establishment of the tenancy, she understood the distinction between a support person, a witness and a representative. MB opted to proceed as representative for the Tenant. The No Contact Order
The Landlord said that the Tenant, by court order, cannot communicate in any way with the Landlord by any physical or electronic means.

The parties attended this hearing by Zoom. As explained to the parties, the October 26, 2025 Ontario Court of Justice Form 11 in not a prohibition related to LTB matters. The Tenant and the Landlord agreed to proceed with the hearing. The Application

The Tenant filed the T1 application on October 29, 2025 where he claimed the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit for the last month of the tenancy. However, the Tenant also selected reason #4, claiming the Landlord did not allow him to move into the rental unit and did not return the money paid to the Landlord as a deposit.

There is no dispute that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on or around December 1, 2023. The Tenant said he misunderstood the Board form. He is seeking a return of $12,000.00 related to the last month’s rent deposit and a lump sum payment made to the Landlord at the onset of the tenancy. For clarity, the Tenant is seeking $3,000.00 for the last month’s rent deposit and $9,000.00 for the lump sum deposit.

The Landlord said he was confused by the Tenant’s application. While the Tenant may have selected the wrong box on the application, the total amount being sought was clearly outlined in the application. I therefore find the Landlord was put on notice of the total amount claimed in the application and had reasonable opportunity to prepare to defend his position. The application is amended to reflect the reason for the amount sought and the matter proceeded accordingly. The Disclosure

Neither party complied with disclosure requirements and did not serve each other. However, the parties had opportunity to review the evidence submitted to the Ontario Tribunals Portal (TOP), accepted the evidence and agreed to proceed.
The Tenant’s disclosure includes: lease documents, bank draft and various communications (DOC7671462, DOC6687465, DOC7209114, DOC6687513, DOC7671609, DOC7671565)

The Landlord’s disclosure includes: the agreement to lease, no contact document, lease, undertakings and various communications (DOC7671552, DOC,7209114, DOC7671417, DOC7674167, DOC7209114, 7671432,7671525, [name], DOC7671565, DOC7671609, DOC7671616, DOC7671624, [name]).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit is the main floor apartment. The Landlord lives in the lower unit.
The tenancy began on or around December 1, 2023.
The lawful rent is $3,000.00.
The Tenant was removed from the unit on October 25, 2025 as a result of a domestic altercation which resulted in a police no-contact order. [name]
To summarize, the Tenant said that he negotiated the lease agreement with the support of a real estate agent. On November 14, 2023, he paid to the Landlord $12,000.00 CAD by way of a bank draft.

The Tenant asserts that he was the contractual Tenant under the lease agreement. While he indicated his spouse and minor children on the lease agreement, he was the only person who signed the agreement. He said it was an administrative error to include them as Tenants and not occupants on the lease agreement.
On October 25, 2025, the Tenant acknowledged that he was removed from the unit by police and a no-contact order was issued by the police. His spouse and children remain in the unit.

On October 25, 2025, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord stating he was “temporarily unable to enter the property” and requested a return of $12,000.00 paid to the Landlord as a deposit. The Tenant has followed up on this request multiple times.
The Tenant asserts that he is entitled to receive the entirety of the deposit. The Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord does not dispute that he is holding a deposit, voluntarily offered by the Tenant for the last three months of the tenancy. I understood this to mean, the Landlord is holding $9,000.00 to be applied to the last three months of the tenancy upon notice to end the tenancy.

The Landlord said that the Tenant sent an email on October 6, 2025 where the Tenant said that he would be moving out but the Tenant did not provide a move out date. He understood the Tenant intended to end the tenancy, but never provided a tenant’s N9 Notice to Terminate the tenancy and the Landlord and Tenant never entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy.
The Tenant was removed from the unit on October 25, 2025, as a result of a domestic situation that resulted in a no contact order for the Tenant’s spouse and the Landlord.

The Landlord said that the Ontario Court of Justice order provides that the Tenant is permitted to make arrangements to attend the rental unit, with a uniformed police officer to retrieve his possessions but has not done so.
Additionally on February 11, 2026, a bailiff officer attended the rental unit, looking for the Tenant as the Tenant had not provided authorities with any change of address information.
The Landlord believed it was right and just to allow the Tenant’s spouse and family to continue living in the unit. He believes as a spouse, she should be permitted to continue the tenancy.
At this point, the parties were provided with opportunity to provide submissions related to the definition of spouse as it relates to this tenancy.
The Tenant maintains the position that the tenancy agreement was only between himself and the Landlord. Law and Analysis The Tenancy Agreement

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the tenancy agreement was entered into between the Tenant and the Landlord. The Tenant’s family members are occupants of the rental unit.
In making this finding I considered various communications prior to the execution of the lease agreement.
The rental application, December 1 2023 identifies the Tenant as the sole applicant and lists his family as the occupants.
The November 13, 2023 signed, Agreement to Lease is between the Tenant and the Landlord.

While the November 29, 2023 lease agreement identifies the Tenant’s family as Tenants, it is signed only by the Tenant. I accept that the Tenant made an administrative error when his family were included as Tenants rather than occupants.
Further, I also considered the Landlord’s acknowledgment in communications with the Tenant, that the lease was negotiated between the Tenant and the Landlord, not with his spouse.
Having found the lease agreement was between the Tenant and the Landlord, I turned my mind to the definition and rights of a spouse.

Subsection 2(1) of the Act defines “tenant”, in part, as follows: “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives”
In this case, while, the Tenant’s spouse lived in the rental unit, she did so as an occupant.

Subsection 3(2) of [name]. 516/06 under the Act provides that, subject to several exceptions, a spouse whose primary residence is the rental unit but who hasn’t signed the leased is considered a “tenant” under s. 2(1) of the RTA if the tenant vacates a rental unit without giving a notice of termination under the Act and without entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy.

The relevant section of [name]. 516/06 has been outlined below with respect to the definition of “tenant”: 3.(2) If a tenant vacates a rental unit without giving a notice of termination under the Act and without entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act. (3) Subsection (2) does not apply if any one or more of the following criteria are satisfied: 1. The rental unit is in a building containing not more than three residential units and the landlord resides in the building.
There is no dispute that the residential complex consists of two units and the Landlord resides in the building.
This means that in this circumstance, the Tenant’s spouse does not meet the definition of tenant in s. 3(2) of [name]. 516/06. Did the Tenant Give Notice to Vacate
Overall, both the Tenant and the Landlord gave conflicting and contradictory evidence on this issue.

The Tenant asserts that he both gave notice to the Landlord to end the tenancy but also claims he “temporarily” unable to use the property. His possessions remain in the unit; he did not arrange for a one-time visit with the police to retrieve his possessions.

On the other hand, the Landlord said the Tenant gave notice to vacate but no date was provided and his possessions remained at the unit and the Tenant provided no change of address to the authorities.

Section 37 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. According to section 37, a tenancy can be lawfully terminated by a notice of termination, agreement to terminate or an order issued by the LTB.

In the present situation, the Tenant did not provide a valid notice of termination which complies which section 44(4) of the Act. That provision states: Period of notice, tenancy for fixed term: (4) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a tenancy for a fixed term shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date. 2006, c. 17, s. 44 (4).

Based on the evidence and on a balance of probabilities, I find the tenancy was not lawfully terminated. The Tenant may have expressed an intention to move but provided no move out date to the Landlord. While he may have been prohibited from attending the unit as a result of the October 25, 2025 incident, this did not terminate the tenancy. Further, the Tenant did not return his keys to the Landlord and his possessions were not retrieved. While the Tenant may not reside at the rental unit, the Tenant has not terminated his tenancy.

As the tenancy is ongoing, the Landlord is entitled to continue to retain the Tenant’s rent deposit and the pre-paid rent intended for the last three months of this tenancy. Therefore, I find that the Tenant has failed to meet the burden of proving that the Landlord has collected or retained money illegally. The application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with vital services and did not meet its maintenance obligations.
reasons: The rental unit is an attic unit. In November, 2023, the Tenant viewed the unit and saw that it had a gas fireplace. He did not want to live in a unit heated by a gas fireplace, so he asked an employee of the Landlord how the unit was heated. The employee told him that it was heated by a furnace.
The parties then entered into a tenancy agreement to commence on January 1, 2024. The Tenant paid a deposit equal to one month’s rent.
The unit was ready a few days early, and the Landlord let the Tenant move in on December 29, 2023, but did not charge rent for December 29 to 31.
When the Tenant arrived on December 29, the temperature in the unit was 10 degrees Celsius. He promptly notified the Landlord.

On January 2, the Tenant gave the keys back to the Landlord because he felt that the unit was too cold to live in. There were some space heaters in the unit, but he did not believe / LTB-T-090956-24 that they would provide adequate heating. He told the Landlord that he would collect the keys again once the heating had been fixed. At this point, he still thought that the unit was heated by a furnace.

It turns out that the unit was not heated by a furnace. It was heated by the gas fireplace, which was connected to the duct system and provided forced air heating through vents in the same way that a furnace would.

An employee of the Landlord attended on January 2, and determined that the unit was cold because the fireplace’s pilot light was out. He returned with a technician on January 3 and fixed the pilot light.

On January 4, the Landlord notified the Tenant that the unit was heated by the fireplace, the fireplace had been repaired, and the unit was ready for occupancy. However, the Tenant did not want to live in a unit heated by a fireplace, and refused to pick up the keys and move back in. In reply, the Landlord told him that it would agree to end the tenancy, but would not agree to return his deposit.
The Tenant brings this application seeking an order that the Landlord return the deposit. Did the parties agree to end the tenancy on January 4, 2024?

The Tenant argues that the tenancy ended on or before January 4, 2024 because, on that date, the parties agreed to end the tenancy. The tenancy having ended, the Landlord would not be permitted to apply the deposit to the rent for January, and would be required to return it.

The matter was previously the subject of T1 application, LTB-T-003918-24. The argument that the parties had agreed to end the tenancy ought to have been considered in that proceeding. However, the Member did not address the question in their [name]. I will consider the question now.

If the Landlord had agreed to end the tenancy effective January 1 or January 4, then I would agree that it would be required to return the deposit. That would be true even if the Landlord did not agree to return the deposit.

However, what actually happened was that the Landlord said that it would agree to end the tenancy, but did not specify an end date. At the same time, the Landlord said that it would not return the deposit. The most reasonable interpretation of Landlord’s offer was that it would agree to end the tenancy effective January 30, once the deposit had been used up.
I do not find that the parties agreed to end the tenancy prior to January 30. Should the tenancy be retroactively terminated?

The Tenant’s main argument in this proceeding is that the Landlord did not properly maintain the unit and withheld or interfered with the supply of heat, and that the tenancy should be retroactively terminated effective January 1 or January 4 as a remedy for those contraventions. / LTB-T-090956-24

On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that that the Landlord failed to maintain the unit. The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance. It promptly repaired the heating issue two days after the tenancy began. In the interim, it provided space heaters. The Tenant did not think that the space heaters would be adequate, but he did not try them, nor did he ask the Landlord for more or better space heaters.
For the same reason, I am also not satisfied that the Landlord with withheld or interfered with the supply of heat.

In the alternative, if the Landlord’s conduct fell short of its obligations, I do not find that the conduct reasonably induced the Tenant to move. The issue was resolved promptly and there was no reason to think it would recur.

The Tenant’s real complaint is that he did not want to live in a unit heated by a fireplace. He was concerned that the fireplace might get too hot and pose a safety risk, that it might not adequately heat the unit, that it might not comply with bylaw or building code requirements, and that it might be difficult to control the temperature in the unit. Those concerns were speculative.

I take the Tenant’s point that the Landlord misled him as to how the unit was heated, and that he would not have rented the unit if he had been given accurate information. However, providing inaccurate information about the heating method does not constitute a failure to maintain the unit or a withholding of or interference with the supply of heat. The application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. I find that the Landlord, Landlord's Agent or Superintendent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. I also find that they did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant failed to prove that the Landlor d, Landlord’s Agent or Superintendent target him by not accepting the Tenant’s rent payments in the same manner as the other tenants in the residential complex, or that they do not process the Tenant’s rent payments in a timely manner.

There was insufficient evidence to prove on a balance of probability that the Landlord is making the Tenant deliver the rental payments in a different manner or that they do not process his payments in a timely manner.

Tenants are obligated to ens ure payments are delivered and received by the Landlord. If a payment is not received by a landlord, a landlord has an opportunity to provide a tenant with notice of an outstanding rental payment to allow both parties the opportunity to address the issue and have it resolved. This ensures there is a clear line of communication between the parties. The Tenant testified that he spoke with the Landlord about the March rent and felt he was being harassed. He communicated to the Landlord that he had paid the rent and they were to look for the cheque he dropped off. The Landlord’s actions were reasonable. In particular, the Tenant’s communication with the Landlord and receipt of a notice from the Landlord on March 7, 2025, which noted that the Tenant had not paid rent is not harassment, coercion, a threat or interference; nor do I find that this action constitutes substantially interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Landlord’s act of communicating with the Tenant and providing the Tenant with this letter is reasonable.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The rental unit is a single-family home. At the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit, he was paying $2,475.00 in monthly rent.

It was undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 Notice on the Tenant on October 30, 2024, which stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit, for the purpose of residential occupation by their daughter for a period of at least one year. The N12 Notice provided a termination date of January 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that in or around October 2024, the Landlord advised them that their daughter is looking to settle down and they need to move into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that after receiving the N12 Notice, he looked for another unit to move into. He testified that he was able to find a new rental unit suitable for his family and vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025. This was not challenged by the Landlord.
It was undisputed that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit. The Landlord listed the unit for sale on March 11, 2025, and sold it on September 5, 2025.

Section 57(1) (a) of the Act establishes a three-part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenant must establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • First, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 notice) in bad faith; • Second, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or Board order based on the N12 notice; • Third, that the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, pursuant to section 57(5) of the Act, the fact that the rental unit was listed for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating creates a presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. This presumption is rebuttable and the burden shifts to the Landlord to establish that they served the N12 in good faith. Rebuttal Presumption of Bad Faith

Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith; those provisions state: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale… … (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
The rebuttable presumption is engaged as it is undisputed that the rental unit was listed for sale less than a year after the Tenant vacated.

The Landlord disputes that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith as the Landlord testified that they intended for their daughter to move into the rental but there was a change of circumstances that lead to the rental unit being listed for sale.

The Landlord testified that he purchased the house in 2021 with the intention that his daughter would reside in it. The Landlord’s daughter [name] (‘MM’), had applied for medical school but was initially rejected and she re-applied an in either August 2024 or September 2024. She received an email on February 27, 2025, from Queen’s University school of medicine for a virtual live panel interview for admission into the Doctor of Medicine program. On May 21, 2025, MM received an email of acceptance for the program. The Landlord testified that his daughter was required to re-locate to Kingston on a full-time basis and it was not possible for her to move into the rental unit. The Landlord testified that they made the decision to sell the property in order to support their daughter’s education and manage their financial burden.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith.

In many other cases, the Board has found that an unforeseen change in circumstances that results in the person listed in the N12 being unable to occupy the rental unit does not constitute bad faith (see, for example, TST-66921-15, TST-87559-17, TST-80046-16). I do not agree that this is a case where an unforeseen change of circumstances resulted in MM failing to take occupancy of the rental unit Beginning in August or September 2024, the Landlord knew or ought to have known that there was a real possibility that his daughter would not be occupying the rental unit because she was applying to medical school in various places. On February 27, 2025, the Landlord’s daughter interview for medical school in Kingston. This was before the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

By serving the N12, the Landlord initiated events that had the serious consequence of ending the tenancy and compelling the Tenant to relocate which in my view is a substantial undertaking. The Landlord, as admitted, knew by the end of February 2025 that MM would potentially not be moving into the rental unit. I find the Landlord’s conduct to be unreasonable, particularly because the Landlord allowed the Tenant to move out in the face of a real possibility that his daughter would not be occupying the unit. The Landlord did not advise the Tenant of this potential change in circumstances before the Tenant moved out. This information could have changed the Tenant’s decision to vacate the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord failed to rebut the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith. As such, the Tenant have established each part of the test contained in section 57(1)(a) of the Act. Remedies Moving costs 30. The Tenant incurred reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses as a result of the Landlord’s breach in the amount of $1,500.00 According to the testimony of the Tenant, the Tenant paid for a moving truck and gas and paid cash to his friends for helping him move. He did not submit documentary evidence but I find his testimony is sufficient and this to be a reasonable amount. General compensation 31. The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $29,700.00. 32. Section 57(3) (1.1) of the Act authorizes the Board to pay general compensation in the amount of up to 12 months rent the Tenant last paid should it be determined the Landlord gave an N12 notice in bad faith. 33. The Tenant testified that the move had a detrimental effect on their mental, financial and emotional well being. He testified that his wife had recently given birth to their youngest child. Their youngest was only three months at the time the N12 was served, and his wife was scheduled for surgery, but they had to postpone to find alternative housing. It was stressful, as they took time off work and traveled to Toronto to find housing that they could afford. They submitted it was difficult to seek alternative accommodation. 34. The Landlord’s actions had a significant impact on the Tenant. Given the inconvenience faced by the Tenant by the N12 having been served in bad faith, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $4,500.00 in general compensation. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,500.00 for general compensation. Rent Abatement 35. The monthly rent at the end of the tenancy was $2,475.00 The Tenant requested a 100% rent abatement equivalent to 28 days of rent, in the amount of $2,475.00. I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent. 36. An abatement of rent is based on the principle that a tenant pays rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. There was evidence before me that the Tenant was not able to utilize the rental unit in its entirety after the service of the notice. The Tenant submitted that the process of looking for another rental unit and moving caused them to experience a high level of stress. I find that any tenant who has to move due to a landlord’s request would experience stress and their use of the unit would have been diminished when they had to look for a new place to live, instead of enjoying their unit. The rent was $2,475.00 and the Tenant received the notice on October 30, 2024. The Tenant moved out February 28, 2025. I find that an abatement of 100% for the for the month of February, to be reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,475.00. Administrative Fine 37. With respect to the Tenant’s request to impose a fine, the Board Interpretation Guideline 16, Administrative Fines, states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. The Guideline further states that that this remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 38. Not all of the Landlord’s conduct warrants a fine. I accept that the Landlord may simply have been unaware of the repercussions of serving a bad faith notice. That being said, attempting to induce the Tenant to vacate and serving a bad faith notice, constitutes a blatant disregard of the Act. A fine of $200.00 is appropriate to encourage compliance with the Act going forward. Rent differential 39. The Tenant requested the rent differential they incurred for one year after moving out of the rental unit, based on $275.00 per month for a total of $3,300.00 for the year. The Tenant moved into a house which consisted of three bedrooms, and three-bathrooms as of March 1, 2025, paying $2,750.00 for the monthly rent. The parties agreed that the monthly rent for the rental unit was $2,475.00 at the time the Tenant vacated. The rental unit was a house with three bedrooms, and two bathrooms. 40. I find that the rental units are comparable, I do find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent differential because the Tenant had to move as a result of the N12 notice they received. 41. I find that awarding an increased rent in the amount of $275.00 to be fair in the circumstances. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $3,300.00 for rent differential for a period of one year.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,823.00. This amount represents: • $2,475.00 for a rent abatement. • $3,300.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from January 30, 2025 to February 1, 2026. • $1,500.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $4,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $200.00 by June 9, 2026. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that he was seeking the return of the $200.00 key deposit but failed to include the correct math in the application.
The Landlord did not oppose this request and agreed that she would return the key deposit to the Tenant.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount set out below.

The Tenant said his puppy caused damage to the floors in the rental unit and when he negotiated a new lease with the Landlord, he paid the Landlord $1,500.00 as a damage deposit. He hired a contractor to repair the floors around October 2025. However, the Landlord was not pleased with the work done and refused to return the deposit when the tenancy ended on October 9, 2025.

There is no dispute that the Landlord collected a damage deposit from the Tenant in the amount of $1,500.00 related to floors in the rental unit. Rather, the Landlord testified that the work was not satisfactory. The Landlord was reminded that the damage allegations were not before the Board. The Landlord said that she filed an L10 application. Analysis
The question before me is whether the Landlord is entitled to collect this additional charge pursuant to the Act.

Subsection 134(1) of the Act states: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

This reads as an absolute prohibition against a landlord charging any kind of fee other than rent to a tenant. However, the section uses the phrase “unless otherwise prescribed” which means fees can be charged if they are specifically permitted in the regulations of the Act.
The exemptions to s.134(1) are set out in section 17 of Ontario Regulations 516/06. The list of exemptions does not include a damage deposit.

Given the above, I find the Landlord breached s.134 of the Act by collecting from the Tenant an additional charge in the sum of $1,500.00 as a damage deposit, irrespective of the fact that the parties negotiated and accepted the terms.
As the Tenant has been successful in his application, the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the application fee.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,748.00 This amount represents: • $1,700.00 for the illegal charge and key deposit collected; • $48.00 the cost to file the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with vital services and did not meet its maintenance obligations.
reasons: The rental unit is an attic unit. In November, 2023, the Tenant viewed the unit and saw that it had a gas fireplace. He did not want to live in a unit heated by a gas fireplace, so he asked an employee of the Landlord how the unit was heated. The employee told him that it was heated by a furnace.
The parties then entered into a tenancy agreement to commence on January 1, 2024. The Tenant paid a deposit equal to one month’s rent.
The unit was ready a few days early, and the Landlord let the Tenant move in on December 29, 2023, but did not charge rent for December 29 to 31.
When the Tenant arrived on December 29, the temperature in the unit was 10 degrees Celsius. He promptly notified the Landlord.

On January 2, the Tenant gave the keys back to the Landlord because he felt that the unit was too cold to live in. There were some space heaters in the unit, but he did not believe / LTB-T-090956-24 that they would provide adequate heating. He told the Landlord that he would collect the keys again once the heating had been fixed. At this point, he still thought that the unit was heated by a furnace.

It turns out that the unit was not heated by a furnace. It was heated by the gas fireplace, which was connected to the duct system and provided forced air heating through vents in the same way that a furnace would.

An employee of the Landlord attended on January 2, and determined that the unit was cold because the fireplace’s pilot light was out. He returned with a technician on January 3 and fixed the pilot light.

On January 4, the Landlord notified the Tenant that the unit was heated by the fireplace, the fireplace had been repaired, and the unit was ready for occupancy. However, the Tenant did not want to live in a unit heated by a fireplace, and refused to pick up the keys and move back in. In reply, the Landlord told him that it would agree to end the tenancy, but would not agree to return his deposit.
The Tenant brings this application seeking an order that the Landlord return the deposit. Did the parties agree to end the tenancy on January 4, 2024?

The Tenant argues that the tenancy ended on or before January 4, 2024 because, on that date, the parties agreed to end the tenancy. The tenancy having ended, the Landlord would not be permitted to apply the deposit to the rent for January, and would be required to return it.

The matter was previously the subject of T1 application, LTB-T-003918-24. The argument that the parties had agreed to end the tenancy ought to have been considered in that proceeding. However, the Member did not address the question in their [name]. I will consider the question now.

If the Landlord had agreed to end the tenancy effective January 1 or January 4, then I would agree that it would be required to return the deposit. That would be true even if the Landlord did not agree to return the deposit.

However, what actually happened was that the Landlord said that it would agree to end the tenancy, but did not specify an end date. At the same time, the Landlord said that it would not return the deposit. The most reasonable interpretation of Landlord’s offer was that it would agree to end the tenancy effective January 30, once the deposit had been used up.
I do not find that the parties agreed to end the tenancy prior to January 30. Should the tenancy be retroactively terminated?

The Tenant’s main argument in this proceeding is that the Landlord did not properly maintain the unit and withheld or interfered with the supply of heat, and that the tenancy should be retroactively terminated effective January 1 or January 4 as a remedy for those contraventions. / LTB-T-090956-24

On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that that the Landlord failed to maintain the unit. The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance. It promptly repaired the heating issue two days after the tenancy began. In the interim, it provided space heaters. The Tenant did not think that the space heaters would be adequate, but he did not try them, nor did he ask the Landlord for more or better space heaters.
For the same reason, I am also not satisfied that the Landlord with withheld or interfered with the supply of heat.

In the alternative, if the Landlord’s conduct fell short of its obligations, I do not find that the conduct reasonably induced the Tenant to move. The issue was resolved promptly and there was no reason to think it would recur.

The Tenant’s real complaint is that he did not want to live in a unit heated by a fireplace. He was concerned that the fireplace might get too hot and pose a safety risk, that it might not adequately heat the unit, that it might not comply with bylaw or building code requirements, and that it might be difficult to control the temperature in the unit. Those concerns were speculative.

I take the Tenant’s point that the Landlord misled him as to how the unit was heated, and that he would not have rented the unit if he had been given accurate information. However, providing inaccurate information about the heating method does not constitute a failure to maintain the unit or a withholding of or interference with the supply of heat. The application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally. (T2 Application) This application was resolved by order LTB-T-090997-24 issued on February 5, 2026. On February 5, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review request was heard by videoconference on March 16, 2026. The review was granted by way of review interim order LTB-T-090997-24-RV-IN2 issued on March 19, 2026 and a new hearing was ordered. These applications were heard by videoconference on April 21, 2026. The Tenant and both named Landlords attended the hearing. The Landlords were supported by their Vietnamese translator, [name]. The Tenant declined the opportunity to speak with [name] on the hearing date.
reasons: At the hearing, the parties took time to speak with the Dispute Resolution Officer (DRO). After their conversation, they attended the hearing room with the DRO based on an agreed statement of fact that the Landlords had reimbursed the Tenant the amount of $2,506.00 for the Tenant’s T1 application. Accordingly, the T1 application is resolved and withdrawn. T2 Application – Insufficient Particulars – Request to Adjourn Denied

The parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on June 30, 2025.In this regard and interim order was issued on July 10, 2025 outlining certain procedural requirements to be completed prior to the hearing for the merits of the applications.

The interim order reflects that the Tenant had declined to participate in the ACC and that there were deficiencies noted in their applications and that they were encouraged to seek legal counsel on this basis. The interim order also directed the Tenant to amend their application in accordance with Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure and directed the Tenant to serve a copy of the amended application on the Landlords and the LTB and to file proof of service in the form of a “Certificate of Service” with the Board.

The interim order from the ACC also directs the parties to provide disclosure to the other and to file with the LTB a copy of all of their anticipated evidence that they intend to rely on at the hearing at least ten days before the hearing date. It notes that if disclosure is not met by the deadlines, then the Member may refuse to accept the evidence or consider the issues not disclosed.

The merits hearing was scheduled to be heard on February 4, 2026. This means, that the parties ought to have served the other and filed with the LTB their disclosure evidence by January 25, 2026 at the latest and uploaded a completed Certificate of Service.

The Tenant did not attend the February 4, 2026 due to a medical condition which was noted in their request to review. Accordingly, the review was granted and a new hearing ordered. The notice of hearing for this new hearing was sent to the parties by email on March 19, 2026.

According to the Interim Review Order issued on March 19, 2026 the parties were instructed to provide disclosure at least seven days prior to this hearing. The order further notes that pursuant to Rule 19.7 of the LTB’s Rules, a party who fails to comply with an order for disclosure may not be permitted to rely on evidence that is not properly disclosed.

Despite the Review Interim order and despite the Interim Order from the ACC, neither party served the other any materials they intended to rely on at the hearing. They only upload material to the Portal without directly serving the other side. Neither party was aware of the other parties uploaded documents.

This is important to note because on October 26, 2025 the Tenant uploaded a request to amend their application and they also uploaded their respective evidence. They neither served the Landlords a copy of their amended application or their evidence despite the ACC interim order instructing them to do so.

On February 2, 2026 the Landlords uploaded a declaration to the Portal without providing the Tenant a copy of their declaration. This was also despite the ACC interim order and it was also short of the 10 day requirement to serve the Tenant and submit such evidence.

At the hearing the Landlords denied every being aware of the amended application in the portal and indicated that they uploaded their declaration based on the allegations of illegal entries and illegal charges, but they were unsure at the time what illegal charges specifically were being claimed and therefore they provided a timeline for the tenancy.

The Tenant submits that the Landlords must have been aware of the amended application on the basis that they submitted their declaration in defence of it. However, I accept that the Landlords had no knowledge of the amended application as they make no specific reference to any of the additional allegations in the Tenants amended application and for one reason or another, they make reference to garage access which is not even mentioned in the Tenant’s application or amended application.

The issue with the Tenant’s original application is that it has an essentially blank T1 application and the T2 application alleges three illegal entry dates but makes no request for any remedy on the applications are noted.

Additionally, the Tenant originally filed their application on November 5, 2024. Pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a remedy on a tenant’s application can only extend back to the one year prior to the filing of the application. In this case, that would be during the period on or after November 6, 2023.
Out of the three alleged illegal entries, two of them allegedly occurred prior to the remedy period in the Tenants application. Those being on June 30, 2023 and July 7, 2023.

Even if I were considering the allegation of an illegal entry on November 5, 2024, there is no remedy listed in the application. Allowing an amendment on this hearing date would be prejudicial to the Landlord and they declined permission for the Tenant to proceed on any amended application or proposed remedies at the hearing submitting that it would be procedurally unfair to do so.

The Tenant then requested an adjournment to be given another opportunity to correctly serve the Landlords with their amended application. The Landlords were opposed to adjournment because they have waited to have the merits of the application heard and the dispute resolved after having to wait so long.

Section 183 of the Act states that the Board shall adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.
Subsection 201(1)(f) of the Act states that the Board may amend an application if amending the application would not be unfair to any party.

The Tenant has had ample time to amend their application and to seek legal advice regarding their application since the application was filed almost one and a half years prior to this hearing and had already gone through the review process with the LTB and an ACC process. Additionally, not only was the interim order from the ACC explicit with respect to amending the application and service of the documents on the Landlords, but the Tenant still did not serve their amended application on the Landlords even though they had an additional opportunity to do so after the review was granted.

I find that adjourning the hearing in order to provide the Tenant an opportunity to amend their application would be greatly prejudicial to the Landlord and for the reasons above I denied the Tenant’s adjournment request.

Accordingly, the T2 application must be dismissed as it lacks sufficient particulars and also fails to identify any particular remedy the Tenant is seeking. Although I would not condone any conduct regarding an illegal entry, proceeding with the merits without a requested remedy would be frivolous and a misuse of the Boards limited resources.
ordered: The T1 application is resolved and withdrawn.
The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. When the capitalized word “Landlord” is used in this order, it refers to all persons or companies identified as a landlord at the top of the order. When the capitalized word “Tenant” is used in this order, it refers to all persons identified as a Tenant at the top of the order.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant a total of $148.00.

The Tenant brings this application pursuant to section 29 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) alleging the Landlord breaches of sections 21, 22 and 23 of the Act. The Tenant seeks findings that the Landlords substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment, harassed her, and withheld a vital service, namely water. The Tenant also seeks compensation and an order requiring the Landlords to cease the impugned conduct.

The Tenant moved into the rental site on April 11, 2014, and continues to reside there. The Tenant owns the mobile home and leases the land from the Landlord. The Tenant previously had a longstanding lot rental agreement with the former owner, [name]. The current owners took possession of the mobile home park in or about January 2022. The monthly rent is $347.13. Substantial interference and Harassment, etc. Incidents July 3, and July 5, 2024:

The Tenant testified that on July 3, 2024, the male Landlord attended at her rental site three times in the evening. The Tenant stated that he appeared intoxicated, made repeated demands that she pays property taxes, and delivered a handwritten note regarding surveying lot lines. The Tenant described the conduct as confrontational and intimidating. The male Landlord testified that he could not recall the events of July 3, 2024, and did not meaningfully refute the Tenant’s description.

The Tenant also submitted a recording of a telephone conversation dated July 5, 2024. The male Landlord acknowledged that it was his voice on the recording and admitted that he called the Tenant “stupid.” He testified that he was angry about a dispute concerning taxes associated with the Tenant’s trailer and that he became boisterous during the call.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant. Section 23 provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the male Landlord’s unannounced evening attendances at the Tenant’s site while appearing intoxicated, combined with demands for payment and statements regarding altering lot boundaries, would reasonably cause distress and undermine a reasonable tenant’s sense of security in her home. When considered together with the July 5, 2024, telephone call in which the Landlord used abusive language, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s conduct constituted harassment and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

While a landlord is entitled to pursue lawful disagreements about charges or lot boundaries, such disputes must be conducted in a civil and professional manner. Name calling and aggressive conduct are inconsistent with sections 22 and 23 of the Act.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlords breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act in relation to the July 3 and July 5, 2024, incidents.

The Tenant seeks an abatement of rent. Abatement is a contractual remedy that recognizes that a tenant pays rent for a bundle of goods and services and, where the tenant does not receive what is being paid for because of a landlord’s breach, the tenant may be entitled to an abatement proportionate to the reduction in value of the tenancy. Because abatement reflects a diminution in the value of the rental unit, the impact on the tenant is a relevant factor in assessing quantum. However, a tenant should not receive a greater abatement than an average tenant based on a particular sensitivity unless the landlord knew or ought to have known of that sensitivity before the tenancy began. That is not the case here. Given that the monthly rent is $347.13, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $100.00 for this breach. [name] dispute:

The Tenant testified that she constructed a deck approximately 9 years ago with the consent of the previous landlord but without a municipal permit. In July 2024, she received a municipal Order to Comply. She testified that the City would not issue a permit without the Landlord’s written consent and that the Landlord refused to provide that consent. The deck was ultimately dismantled and partially rebuilt at her expense.

The Landlord testified that he did not direct the Tenant to remove the deck and that municipal authorities issued the compliance order. The Landlord maintained that alterations to the site require written permission.

The evidence establishes that the City initiated enforcement proceedings and that the Tenant did not hold a municipal permit. The Act does not obligate a landlord to consent to structural alterations. A landlord is entitled to require compliance with municipal standards and to control alterations to the rental site, subject to the tenancy agreement.

There is insufficient evidence that the Landlord acted in bad faith or improperly interfered with the municipal process. While the Tenant incurred expense and inconvenience, those consequences flowed from municipal enforcement, not from unlawful conduct under the Act.
Accordingly, I find that the deck issue does not establish a breach of sections 22 or 23. Lot Boundary Dispute

The parties dispute whether additional space adjacent to the Tenant’s site forms part of her leased premises. The Tenant relies on a historical rent adjustment and an affidavit from the previous owner to assert that two areas were merged and incorporated into her lot. The Landlord relies on municipal and MPAC information and asserts that the Tenant is occupying land beyond her lawful site.

The evidence establishes that the Landlord told the Tenant to stop using certain portions of land and demanded additional payment if she wished to continue using them. However, there is no evidence that the Landlord physically blocked access, removed essential services, or evicted the Tenant from her primary lot.

This dispute is fundamentally a disagreement about the scope of the leased site. The Act does not prohibit a landlord from asserting what he believes to be the proper lot boundaries. On the evidence before me, the boundary dispute itself does not independently amount to substantial interference.

However, the manner in which the dispute was pursued, including the July 3, 2024, attendances and the July 5, 2024, telephone call, contributed to the harassment finding addressed above. Vital Services
Section 21 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service. Water is a vital service within the meaning of the Act.
To establish a breach of section 21, the Tenant must demonstrate that the Landlord intentionally withheld the service or failed to provide it as required.

The Tenant testified that water was shut off on July 4 and July 5, 2024, and briefly again on October 8 and October 9, 2024. The Tenant believes that the shut off was retaliatory. The Landlord denied deliberately shutting off the Tenant’s water and testified that the water system is old, that leaks occur, and that water must be shut off temporarily to conduct repairs. The Landlord admitted that he does not have documentation for the July 2024 repair because he performed the work himself.

While the timing of the July 2024 shut off coincided with the tax dispute, the Tenant failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord deliberately and selectively withheld water in violation of section 21. With respect to the October 2024 incidents, the Tenant acknowledged that she did not know the reason for the shut off and believed it was intentional. Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord intentionally withheld water or failed to provide it.
Accordingly, the claim under section 21 of the Act is dismissed. [name]:

Pursuant to section 31 of the Act, the Landlords shall refrain from engaging in verbal abuse, name calling, or intimidating conduct toward the Tenant. The Landlords shall not make repeated unannounced attendances at the Tenant’s site for the purpose of making demands unrelated to lawful rent collection or maintenance obligations. The Landlords shall conduct all future communications with the Tenant in a reasonable and professional manner consistent with their obligations under sections 22 and 23 of the Act.

The Tenant requested $1,000.00 for pain and suffering. Nonpecuniary damages are intended to compensate for distress and loss of enjoyment of life. Although I accept that the Tenant experienced stress and inconvenience, I am satisfied that the rent abatement awarded above provides adequate compensation. The claim for additional nonpecuniary damages is dismissed.

The Tenant also requested that the Landlord pay a fine to the Board. [name] 16 provides that a fine is most appropriate where a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence. While the Landlord’s conduct was inappropriate, I am satisfied that the remedies awarded are sufficient to encourage compliance. No administrative fine is ordered.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $148.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
