The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

The Landlords shall refrain from engaging in verbal abuse, name calling, or intimidating conduct toward the Tenant and shall not attend at the Tenant’s site except in accordance with the Act. February 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: gen1@[name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $69.00 to the Tenant. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that she had lived in the rental unit for 6 years until she received a call from Apex telling her that someone was coming to change the locks.

The Tenant testified that she left her house on September 24, 2025, and when she returned, the Landlord has turned off the hydro and the unit was in complete darkness and the hydro remained off until September 27, 2025, when the City forced the Landlord to reconnect it.

The Tenant further testified to events between October 15, 2025, through to October 29, 2025, all dealing directly with Apex, which included being tricked to vacate the unit and then being locked out of the unit and prevented from returning or providing her access to her property. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord [name] (RM) testified that they had lost the house and it was being taken over by the second mortgage holder.
RM testified that they had tried to sell the house to prevent losing it, but the sale was not completed because the Tenant refused to move out.
RM testified that they lost possession of the property and returned the keys to the mortgage company in early October 2025, at which time the mortgage company and Apex had control of the property.
RM testified that they did disconnect the Tenant’s hydro out of frustration as they were losing the house and the Tenant was not cooperating with them.

RM testified that they never provided the Tenant with proper notice to vacate the unit but that the Tenant knew they were losing the property and they believed the Tenant, who they thought of as family, was going to move out as they had verbally agreed.
RM further testified that they stopped collecting rent from the Tenant in July 2025, so the Tenant could use that money to help her find alternative housing.

The Landlord [name] (TM) testified that from the time they found out that they were losing the house, they kept the Tenant informed and that they were unaware of Apex’s intention of locking the Tenant out or removing her belongings. Analysis

In addressing compensation, it is uncontested that the Tenant dealt directly with Apex on behalf on the second mortgage holder who had taken over possession in October 2025. As the Tenant and [name] had resolved that portion of the application prior to the hearing, I will not be readdressing the resolved portion of the Tenant’s application, that being the illegal lockout and the removal of the Tenant’s possessions.
Based on the Landlord’s own evidence, the Landlord disconnected the hydro out of frustration in trying to have the Tenant vacate the unit.
I am satisfied that the Tenant went without hydro from September 24, 2025, through to September 27, 2025, and an abatement of 100% for that period will be granted in the amount of $69.00.

It was uncontested that the Tenant did not pay rent to the Landlord for the months of July, August, September and October, therefore, I find that the Landlord did credit the Tenant the last months rent deposit.

I have considered all the evidence and oral testimony presented at the hearing and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence, I have considered it when making my decision. This order contains all the reasons for my decision, and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $69.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026, at 4% annually on the outstanding balance.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties do not dispute the following: - The Tenant received an N12 notice for Landlord’s own use, given under section 48 of the Act, claiming the Landlord [name] required possession of the rental unit. The N12 Notice had a termination date of December 31, 2024. - The Tenant moved out as of June 7, 2025, as a result of the N12 notice.
The only issues that need to be determined are whether the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant moved out and whether the N12 notice was given in bad faith.

The Tenant discovered a for sale listing of the rental unit on August 5, 2025. The Tenant believes that that after they vacated the rental unit, the unit remained vacant for some time and then it was listed for sale.
The Landlord’s son testified that he moved into the rental unit around the second week of August as most of his furniture did not arrive until then and since then he has been living in the unit.

The Landlord [name] (‘SJ’) provided in evidence [name] receipts from the period of October 1, 2025, through to November 2025. He also provided copies of utility bills for the rental unit that span from July 15, 2025, to March 2026. SJ testified that from July 2025 to August 15, 2025, the utility consumption was low because SJ was delayed moving into the unit because of lack of the furniture.

The Landlord [name] (‘AJ’) testified that she and her husband are developers and a project they were working on went underwater because the purchasers backed out. As such, they needed to re-finance their properties to pay out the bank, investors and themselves. AJ testified that they listed their four properties for sale including the rental unit to receive offers that they could use to show value in order for the bank to approve a second mortgage. AJ testified that this was the only reason they listed the rental unit for sale, it was not their intention to sell the rental unit, and the rental unit is still under their ownership, and SJ still resides in the unit.

Based on the evidence, the presumption of bad faith in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies to this situation. This provision states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, for sale…

This provision means that, because there is evidence before me that during the one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale, it is presumed that the notice was given in bad faith. The onus then shifts to the Landlord to rebut the presumption and prove that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith.
In this case, the evidence from the Landlord SJ was that they did move into the rental unit as of August 2025, and they are still occupying the unit.
I find that the Landlord did occupy the rental unit for at least 12 months as required when a landlord terminates the tenancy with a notice of termination served under section 48 of the Act.
There is no evidence before the Board to substantiate or corroborate the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The evidence of Tenant was that the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale. I do not find that this alone establishes that the Landlord did not occupy the unit. The Tenant also did not visit the rental unit after they vacated to confirm who moved into the rental unit.

Given it was not disputed that there are charges for utilities in the name of Landlords which reflect usage. I also find the very fact that all their bills and accounts was placed in the Landlord’s name for approximately a year support a finding of residential occupation.

I find that for the utility bills show variation in electricity and water usage. Further, the utility bills show variability in thermal cooling charges in the spring, summer, and fall and thermal heating charges in the winter. Given the variable usage of utilities, I was not satisfied that no one resided in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not present any concrete evidence to challenge the Landlord’s position on these points. Therefore, I cannot find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord SJ did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

The evidence was that rental unit was listed for sale on August 5, 2025, and it failed to sell. As a result, I find the evidence supports finding the Landlord was to occupy the rental unit for the time required under the Act. The Landlord also provided a reasonable explanation for why they listed the rental unit for sale, which was not inconsistent with their own personal occupation of the rental unit.

Therefore, I find the Landlord has rebutted the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith and have proven on a balance of probabilities that the N12 was given in good faith. The Tenant’s application must therefore fail.
As the Tenant cannot establish all the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

On November 25, 2023, the Tenants filed a T2 application (T2) pursuant to s. 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') alleging that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment and harassed the Tenants. The allegations on the application were that the Landlord harassed and threatened the Tenants to pay an illegal rent increase and the Landlord interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment related to maintenance issues.
The Tenants are seeking a rent abatement in the amount of $12,480.00.
The Tenants are no longer in possession of the rental unit, having vacated on March 8, 2025. Tenant’s Evidence Threats/Harassment- Illegal Rent Increase
The Tenant, [name] testified the Tenants moved into the rental unit in November of 2011.
He testified at the time they moved in their lawful monthly rent was $900.00 per month.
He testified that sometime in 2013, the rent increased from $900.00 to $1000.00.
He testified sometime in 2016, the rent increased from $1,000.00 to $1,200.00.
He testified sometime in 2020, the Landlord wanted to raise the rent from $1,200.00 to $1,800.00, however they agreed on an amount of $1,600.00.
The Tenants later became informed that the rent increase was illegal, and they were never provided an N1 notice.
He testified in 2020, when the Landlord told them about the rent increase, he explained to the Landlord that this was an illegal rent increase, and that there was also a rent freeze during that time.
He testified the Landlord told them if he did not comply with the rent increase they would have to vacate the rental unit.

He stated that this was stressful for him and his wife, as at the time is wife was not working. He states they also have a 14-year-old child with epilepsy and an 18-yr old child with autism. DOC-4450940.

The Tenants provided text message conversations between themselves and the Landlord. This text message correspondence in part shows discussions between them regarding the rent increase, and the Tenants advising the Landlord that it may not be possible for them to pay the rent increase of $1,600.00. There was a response from the Landlord stating that he could not do anything less than the $1,600.00, as he was already losing $400.00 every month, due to his expenses and not being able to work due to his physical condition. DOC 4450903.

The Tenant testified they received a text message from the Landlord stating that if they did not pay the increase, he would evict them. The Tenants did not provide a copy of this text message as evidence.
He testified when they vacated the rental unit on March 8, 2025, the rent was $1,600.00 per month. [name] Stairs
The Tenant testified the stairs were in disrepair at the rental unit since sometime in November 2021.

He testified the stairs were the main entrance to and from the rental unit, and they were not safe and himself and his family had to be very careful climbing up and down the stairs. He was concerned that himself, his wife or his children could become injured on the stairs.

He testified he notified the Landlord of this, and the Landlord was aware of the stairs being in disrepair as he resides at the residential complex in the upper unit. He states he came to look at the stairs and said he would fix them later. The Tenant could not recall the date that he spoke to the Landlord.
He provided a photograph of the stairs which appears to show a tile/brick missing from one of the steps and the stairs also have snow on them. DOC- 4421871.
He testified that when they vacated the rental unit on March 8, 2025, the stairs were still in disrepair. [name]

He testified there was a leak in the kitchen faucet but could not recall the date but believes it was about one year before [name]. He states the leak progressively got worse over time. He stated that he spoke to the Landlord on several occasions but could not recall the date, and the Landlord said that he would fix it.
He testified the kitchen faucet was fixed sometime in 2022 but could not recall the exact date. Range
The Tenant testified when they moved into the rental unit there was a range that was provided by the Landlord.
He testified that 2 burners out of 4 burners on the range top were not working sometime in 2018, however he could not remember the exact date.
He testified that it was difficult for his family of four to only have two burners to use while cooking.

He testified they notified the Landlord and asked the Landlord to come and have a look at the range, he could not recall the date he did this. He believes they reached out to the Landlord approximately 10-15 times from the time the two burners stopped working until he replaced the range in January of 2020. He states the Landlord never came to look at the oven.
He testified he replaced the range and the amount to replace was $2,556.84. He provided a copy of the receipt. DOC-4421884. [name]
The Tenant testified the water leak in the bathroom started sometime in 2013-2014.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord approached the Tenants, as the Landlord had found some water in the basement of his rental unit and wanted to investigate where it was coming from.
He testified the Landlord looked at the shower and then put some caulking around the shower.
He testified the caulking corrected the issue was corrected and no leaks between 2014 and 2017, in the Landlord’s rental unit.
He testified when the caulking was put around their shower, they were unable to use the bathtub or shower for a 24-hour period. He testified they only have one washroom in the rental unit.
He testified that during the tenancy the caulking of the shower may have happened two times in total.

He testified the second time the Landlord experienced a leak in his unit the contractor come to investigate, and the wall in his shower needed to be opened, and this took 3-4 days to fix, and his family had to move in with his in laws during that period.
He testified the Landlord did not offer him any other alternative such as using their washroom. Landlord’s Evidence Threats/Harassment- Illegal Rent Increase

The Landlord’s daughter, [name] testified that her father did not increase the rent every year. After a few years of having the Tenant’s pay the same rent he had a discussion with the Tenants regarding a rent increase as he could not keep up with the expenses of the rental unit. She stated that there were discussions and negotiations between the parties and anytime the rent was increased it was on agreement of the parties. She stated the amount they agreed upon was often the amount the Tenants proposed they could pay.

She testified her father never threatened eviction and there was nothing in the text messages the Tenants provided that would show he did this. She states the text messages simply explain that he is retired, does not have the physical condition to be working and he is trying to maintain the expenses on his own. She states there was never an element of threat or harassment, and there was always a negotiation between the parties.

She believes the Tenants brought this application as they were upset the Landlord had filed an N12 notice for the Landlord’s son to move in, as the timing of this application was around the same time the N12 was served to the Tenants. [name] Stairs
She testified the Tenants brought up the issues of the stairs to the Landlord and he had the stairs repaired approximately three times over the period of the tenancy.
She testified she is not sure how a few brocks/tiles kept breaking on the stairs after they were repaired as they are made of very strong material, however they would break down.
She testified she believes the stairs would break down over the winter months and then the contractor would come and fix the stairs in the Spring.
She testified her father lives at the residential complex and there was no reason for him to ignore any maintenance or repair issue.
She testified the stairs were always repaired when the Tenants advised of an issue and were in good state of repair when the Tenants vacated.

She testified her father advised the Tenants that if there was ever a time over the winter months, where they felt, they did not want to access their rental unit on the stairs, they were permitted to go through his rental unit as there are two entrances and they could use that secondary entrance. [name]

She testified the Tenants told the Landlord the kitchen faucet was leaking, but he could not remember the exact date the Tenants advised him of such. However, the very next day he purchased a new kitchen faucet, and he hired a plumber to install the faucet the same day he purchased the faucet. Range

She testified the Landlord had no knowledge that two of the range top burners were not functioning and he had never been notified as such from the Tenants. She stated the Landlord was not aware that the range had been replaced and that his range had been thrown out until around the time the Tenants were vacating.
She states if the Landlord knew of this issue, he would have addressed this.

She testified when the Tenants vacated in March 2025, the Landlord told the Tenants that they could take the range that they purchased with them, but he would like to have his range returned to the rental unit. She stated the Tenants opted to leave the range behind when they left. [name]

She testified there was not a leak in the Tenants washroom, the leak was in the Landlord’s laundry room, which is adjacent to the Tenant’s washroom. The Landlord had noticed some water pooling on the floor in the laundry room.

She testified her father hired a contractor to come and look at the leak in the laundry room, and the contractor was required to access the Tenant’s washroom to see if there was any leak in the washroom that was filtering into their laundry room.
The Landlord testified the wall inside the Tenants bathroom was never taken down or opened, and it was the wall in the Landlords rental unit that was disturbed.
The Landlord testified the shower in the Tenants bathroom was never caulked as the contractor found no issue in the Tenants bathroom and the issue was isolated to the Landlord’s rental unit.
On cross examination, the Landlord stated there were no leaks in the Tenants washroom, and the water issue was inside his unit.

On cross examination, the Landlord testified that the contractor was called as water was pooling in his laundry room, the contractor accessed the Tenants rental unit to see if the water may have been coming from the Tenants washroom as it was adjacent to the Landlord’s laundry room, however, upon investigation this was not the case.
On cross examination, the Landlord testified the contractor opened the wall inside his laundry room, fixed a pipe and closed the wall back up. Analysis Threats/Harassment- Illegal Rent Increase

Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant”. While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, it is generally held that “harassment” is a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.
My order makes no determination on whether the rent increase was an illegal rent increase as that is not before me on the T2 application. The Tenants could have filed a T1 application.
I accept the Landlord and Tenants have had conversations between one and another regarding rent increases and that they were negotiating a rent increase.

I am persuaded by the Landlord’s testimony that at no time did the Landlord threaten or harass the Tenants regarding these increases. The text message string that the Tenants provided between themselves, and the Landlord does not indicate any type of threat or harassment, but rather a conversation and negotiation between the parties.

I do not accept the Tenant’s assertion the Landlord threatened or harassed the Tenants that they needed to vacate if they did not pay the increase. The Tenants did not provide any evidence that would substantiate that this was the case, and the Tenants has the burden of proof to substantiate their claim.

I accept the Landlord believes that this application was only brought as a retaliation of the Landlord serving the Tenants with an N12 notice for the personal occupation of the Landlord’s son as this application was filed around the same time the Tenants were served the N12 notice, While I accept the timing of this application was similar, I find the Tenants have the right to file their own application regarding any alleged breaches of the RTA. The filing of such application by the Tenants is an exercise of their legal right and shall not in itself be deemed as retaliation in response to a Landlord’s application.

On the basis of the evidence and testimony provided by both parties I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations pursuant to section 23 of the Act. [name], [name], Range, Bathroom Leak

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. Stairs
I accept that the Tenant’s testimony that there were some missing bricks from the stairs in the photograph that they provided.

It was undisputed by the Landlord that there was a portion on the stairs that appeared to break down over the winter months due to snow and ice and was always repaired by the Landlord in the Spring months.
The photograph that the Tenants provided has snow in the photograph.
The Tenant could not recall the dates they notified the Landlord of the issue with the stairs.
I also accept the Landlords testimony that this area would become wore down in the winter months due to ice and snow and was repaired in the Spring, if the issue was present.

I also accept the Landlord offered the Tenants use of another entrance, through his rental unit as there are two entrances, if the Tenants did not want to use the stairs where there was a missing tile/brick in the winter months.

I do not find that this interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The area of the stairs where the brock/tile was missing appears to be a small area. I find the stairs were still useable and this issue was caused by ice/snow and the Landlord promptly fixed in the Spring once the weather would allow for such repair. I also find that the Landlord provided the Tenants another option of entry to their rental unit if they did not want to use the main stairs.
On the basis of the evidence and testimony provided by both parties I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations pursuant to section 22 of the Act. [name]

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that there was a leak in the kitchen faucet. The Tenant could not recall the exact date of the leak or the exact date that it was fixed by the Landlord. He believes it started approximately one year before [name] and fixed sometime in 2022.
I am persuaded by the Landlord’s testimony that they did become aware of a kitchen faucet leak, and the Landlord bought a new faucet the following day and installed it at the rental unit.

While I accept there was a leak with the kitchen faucet, I find the leak was repaired immediately. Further, I do not find that this interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as there was no evidence before me to suggest that the faucet was not usable while leaking. Range
I am not persuaded by the Tenant’s testimony there were two burners on the range that were not working and that he notified the Landlord.

He testified they notified the Landlord and asked the Landlord to come and have a look at the range, he could not recall the date he did this. He believes he reached out to the Landlord approximately 10-15 times from the time the two burners stopped working until he replaced the range in January of 2020. The Tenants did not provide any evidence that they had reached out to the Landlord 10-15 times about this issue or any evidence that the two burners were not operating.

The Tenants then decided to replace the range on their own decision and discard the Landlord’s range, without any knowledge of the Landlord. If the Tenants were not getting a response from the Landlord as they claim, instead of buying a new range and discarding the Landlord’s, they could have hired a repair company to access whether it could be repaired.

I am persuaded by the Landlords testimony that the Landlord only became aware that the Tenants purchased a new range closer to the time the Tenants were vacating, and they told the Tenants they could take the range they purchased when they moved, even though they had discarded the Landlord’s range The Tenants declined and left the range when they vacated.

Even if I am wrong, I would not find that this interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as the range was still functioning and there were two additional burners that were operating. [name]

I am persuaded by the Landlord’s testimony that he experienced a water leak in his rental unit in his laundry room, which is adjacent to the Tenants washroom, and hired a contractor to see where the leak was coming from. This required the contractor to access the Tenants rental unit.

I am persuaded by the Landlords testimony that the contractor assessed the washroom of the rental unit, and it was determined that the water leak was not originating from the Tenants washroom, and it was later found that there was a leaking pipe in the Landlord’s rental unit.

I am not persuaded by the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord caulked around his shower, making the shower unusable for 24 hours. Even if the Landlord had caulked around the Tenants shower to address a water leak, I would not have found this to interfere with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as the shower would have only been unusable for a very short period to allow the caulking to dry. The Tenants did not provide any photographs of the shower that had been caulked.

I am also not persuaded by the Tenant’s testimony that the second time the Landlord experienced a leak in his unit and come to investigate, the wall in the shower needed to be opened and this took 3-4 days to fix, and his family had to move in with his in laws. The Tenants did not provide any photographs or evidence that show that this was the case.
I am persuaded by the Landlords testimony that at no time did any work take place in the Tenant’s rental unit regarding a leak.
On the basis of the evidence and testimony provided by both parties I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations pursuant to section 22 of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: The Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by failing to address the mould problem in a timely and appropriate manner.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,352.00.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in October 2023 and moved out on November 10, 2024. The rental unit is a detached dwelling consisting of the entire house, with monthly rent of $3,200.00. The house has three floors, three bedrooms on the upper level, laundry on the upper level, a kitchen and a half bathroom on the main floor, and a finished basement with a full bathroom but no bedroom. The basement was used as a home gym and the Tenant’s husband’s home office. Tenant’s Evidence:

The Tenant testified that mould first appeared in the basement in December 2023 as black speckling along the drywall, which later spread across the wall. The Tenant notified the Landlord in December 2023. The Tenant testified that the Landlord arranged for a mould cleaning company named ServiceMaster to inspect the rental unit in January 2024. The Tenant testified that ServiceMaster used testing equipment, identified black mould in the basement, described the problem as extensive, and advised that immediate remediation was required, including removal of drywall and investigation of the foundation. The Tenant further testified that ServiceMaster advised her to stop using the basement due to the mould.

The Tenant further testified that no one on behalf of the Landlord attended the unit and that no repairs were completed between January 2024 and late April 2024. In May 2024, the Landlord’s agent contacted the Tenant and proposed a two-day remediation plan that would have relocated the Tenant’s household of four to a two-bedroom accommodation. The Tenant testified that she refused because it was inadequate, and that no alternative accommodation was offered. The Tenant raised the issue again in June 2024. The Tenant vacated the unit on November 10, 2024.
Photographs of the basement and email correspondence between the Landlord’s agent and the Tenant in May 2024 were submitted as the Tenant’s exhibits and entered into evidence.

The Tenant described functional loss of the basement. On ServiceMaster’s advice, she avoided the basement beginning in January 2024. The Tenant’s husband moved his office upstairs and worked at the dining room table. The family stopped using the basement bathroom and used the full bathroom upstairs. The children were not permitted to exercise in the gym area. The Tenant acknowledged that she did not tell the Landlord that the basement had been taken out of use. Landlord’s evidence:

The Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant reported mould in December 2023 but testified that she did not personally inspect the basement. The Landlord testified that after ServiceMaster attended in January 2024, ServiceMaster advised that remediation would require opening walls and removing drywall. The Landlord testified that she was waiting for a quotation, but did not receive one from ServiceMaster and therefore did not arrange remediation. The Landlord testified that when the Tenant made a further complaint in April 2024, she suggested that the Tenant clean the affected area, but the Tenant refused. The Landlord testified that she proposed temporary accommodation in an Airbnb for two days while she opened and removed drywall, but the Tenant refused. The Landlord testified that she arranged for her contractor, [name], to attend, but the Tenant refused entry. The Landlord testified that no further steps were taken after that point. 9. [name] ([name]) also testified at the hearing. [name] testified that he attended the unit in November 2024, after the rental unit was vacated. He testified that he observed only minor surface mould on the basement wall, and that when the drywall was opened, he found the cavity dry with no leaking water inside the wall. Law and Analysis: 1. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with health and maintenance standards. 2. Section 20 of the Act requires the Landlord to provide and maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, and to comply with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards. 3. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 4. In this case, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there was mould in the rental unit during the tenancy. I also find that the Landlord did not respond reasonably to the reported mould condition. The Landlord acknowledged receiving complaints beginning in December 2023, yet there is no persuasive evidence of timely remediation. The Tenant’s evidence, including the photographs of the basement and the email correspondence, together with [name] testimony confirming mould on the basement wall, establishes that mould was present. The Landlord did not provide a ServiceMaster report and did not engage an alternative qualified assessor when remediation did not proceed. 5. The Landlord’s proposal in May 2024 contemplated relocating a household of four to a two-bedroom accommodation for a brief period, with no evidence of a workable plan to complete the work promptly and safely. In these circumstances, I prefer the Tenant’s evidence that the condition persisted for months without effective repair, resulting in ongoing concern about the safety of the unit. It was not reasonable to suggest that the Tenant clean the mould, as maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair, including addressing mould, is the Landlord’s obligation under the Act. 6. The Landlord also testified that the Tenant refused entry for mould remediation in May 2024. The Tenant denied this. In the absence of corroborating evidence, I am left with conflicting testimony. On an application before the Board, the party who alleges an incident occurred bears the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that their version of events is more likely than not true. The Landlord provided no corroborating evidence to support the claim that the Tenant refused entry. Accordingly, I find there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the Tenant prevented remediation before vacating the rental unit. 7. For these reasons, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached the maintenance obligation under section 20 of the Act by failing to respond to the mould issue in a reasonable manner. Remedies 8. The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 25% to 30 % from December 2023 to November 10, 2024. The Tenant testified that her husband had difficulty sleeping and experienced breathing symptoms during the tenancy, and that she and their child stayed out of the basement. The Tenant’s husband did not testify at the hearing, and the Tenant submitted no written medical evidence. Based on the lack of corroborating evidence, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant’s family members’ physical symptoms during the tenancy were caused by mould.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that ServiceMaster advised that the basement was uninhabitable because of mould. The Landlord denied that ServiceMaster told her the same thing. The Tenant submitted no corroborating evidence from ServiceMaster that the basement was uninhabitable. I find that there was insufficient evidence before me to determine, on a balance of probabilities, that the basement was uninhabitable.

It is evident from the Tenant’s testimony that she was very distressed by the mould. This situation would have been even more irksome because it was preventable. If the Landlord had addressed the condition promptly, it is not likely that the mould condition would have persisted for as long as it did.

After considering the duration of this problem and the impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment and use of the rental unit, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of 10% percent per month for the period from January 1, 2024, through to and including November 10, 2024, for a total of $3,304.00.

The Tenant also stated that mould spread to personal property in the basement, including her husband’s poster boards, a filing cabinet, and an office chair. She claimed $1,115.00 based on what had been paid for certain items but failed to provide invoices or receipts for disposal or replacement. In the absence of supporting documentation, I am not satisfied that this claim is proven. This claim is denied.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,352.00. This amount represents: • $3,304.00 for a rent abatement for the period from January 1, 2024, to November 10, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • Entered the rental unit illegally • Changed the locks or the locking system on the rental unit or building without providing the Tenant with replacement keys The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards
reasons: The Tenant filed four T2 applications between June and November 2024, all of which contained similar allegations, and one T6 application, also within the time frame of the T2 applications.

There was an adjudicative case conference for all the files combined, held on June 23, 2025. At the case conference the parties were informed that the Act does not apply to the relationship between the parties. That finding was the result of a T3 application filed by the Tenant, LTB-T-091535-24. The order for that application, dismissing the Tenant’s application, was issued on June 4, 2025.
No request for review had been filed at the time of the adjudicative case conference, so the files were not dismissed at the case conference.
A request to review the decision in LTB-T-091535-24 was eventually filed, and there was a review order, LTB-T-091535-24-RV, denying the review request, issued on July 22, 2025.
Therefore, the determination that the Act does not apply to this relationship has been upheld on review. It is res judicata.
Despite the review decision in LTB-T-091535-24-RV, the Tenant did not withdraw his applications, and he insisted on having his applications heard in any case.
The Tenant’s application will be dismissed as the Act does not apply to this relationship.

It is before me to determine whether it is appropriate to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine on the Tenant for his failure to withdraw his applications, and his subsequent waste of Board resources and time.

Since the parties did not make submissions on this point, I find that it is not fair to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine in this matter. However, the Tenant’s applications, which were duplicative in any case, will be dismissed with prejudice.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed with prejudice. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that DMJ Holdings Inc. (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,356.36. Illegal rent collected

The Tenant testified that the Landlord increased the rent twice in a 12 month period, and the second increase was above the guideline amount. The Tenant testified that the rent increased on February 1, 2024 from $2,810.00 to $2,880.97 based on a verbal agreement. The Tenant submitted supporting documents that showed that she paid $2,810.00 in January 2024, and that she paid $2,880.97 from February 2024 until October 2024.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (DJ) testified that he served a N1 notice of rent increase and the increase went into effect on November 1, 2023. DJ submitted the N1 notice as a supporting document. DJ also submitted a text message from the Tenant dated October 18, 2023 where the message from the Tenant states that the increase would not go into effect until February 1, 2024, based on counting from October 1, 2023. The Tenant also testified that she never received an N1 notice.

The Tenant further testified that on November 1, 2024 that rent increased to $2,990.00 based on a verbal conversation. The Tenant testified the lease includes utilities in the rent amount and the Landlord wanted to increase rent to reflect an increase in the utilities. DJ testified that the Tenant agreed to pay $2,990.00 even though that was above the guideline rent increase, and he submitted text messages as evidence. The Tenant testified that she felt pressured into agreeing to pay the increase of 3.82%. The Tenant further testified that she never received an N1 notice for the November 1, 2024 increase. DJ submitted a copy of an N1 notice that he testified was served on the Tenant. The copy had a handwritten note that states the increase “started November 1, 2024”, and there was no signature page included.

Based on the evidence provided by the parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has established on a balance of probabilities that a notice of rent increase was served. The start date on the first page provided was indicated to be incorrect through a hand-written note written in the past tense, implying this was not an actual copy of the potential version served. In addition, no signature page was provided, though the Landlord had provided the complete N1 notice for the 2023 rent increase. I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s supporting evidence established that an N1 notice was served when the Tenant testified she never received an N1 notice.

DJ also testified that the increase was lawful as the Tenant voluntarily agreed to increase the rent above the guideline amount. The Tenant testified that she was not aware at the time that because utilities are included in her rent that she did not have to agree when the Landlord wanted to increase the rent due to the utilities.

DJ also testified that the Tenant paid the rent increase for 12 consecutive months, therefore the lawful rent became $2,990.00 pursuant to section 136(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). However, the Landlord cannot rely upon section 136 because of the Ontario Court of Appeal’s reasoning in [name] v. [name], 2007 ONCA 408.

In any event, section 136(1) of the Act does not apply because the Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on October 28, 2025, which is within one year from November 1, 2024, the date the unlawful rent increase was first “charged”. As a result, neither section 136(1) nor 136(2) would apply due to their terms: 136 (1) Rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. (2) An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application. [Emphasis added]

While the Tenant testified she paid the 12 consecutive months of the unlawful rent, just like the deeming provisions in section 136, section 135.1(1) of the Act would not apply because section 135.1(2) states as follows: 135.1 (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. [Emphasis added]

As noted above, the Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on October 28, 2025, which was within one year of the date that the unlawful increase was first charged (November 1, 2024). As a result, neither section 136 nor 135.1 deem the increase as lawful, even if I was satisfied that the Landlord had served an N1 notice and could therefore rely upon section 136.

I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did unlawfully increase the rent above the guideline amount on November 1, 2024 and that the Tenant filed her T1 application prior to October 31, 2025. Section 110 of the Act prohibits a landlord from increasing rent except in accordance with the Act, and there is no exception for consent and parties cannot contract out of the Act. Even if the Tenant had voluntarily agreed to the increase with no pressure, the consent is void unless it can be saved by sections 135.1 or 136, which it cannot be saved by in these circumstances.
I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
I find that the lawful monthly rent is $2,880.97, and the Landlord illegally collected and retained $1,308.36. This amount is determined based on $109.03 per month illegally collected for 12 months.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,356.36. This amount represents: • $1,308.36 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $109.03 from the rent each month from July 1, 2026 to June 1, 2027.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $648.00 T1 application - Illegal charge collected
The issue in this application is whether the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed pursuant to s. 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant states that he is not responsible for the garbage removal under the lease agreement. He referred to the tenancy agreement dated February 14, 2024, paragraph 6, which is regarding services and costs.

Although the Tenant has paid both water/sewer services and solid waste management services from the beginning of his tenancy, he testified that the tenancy agreement does not make a selection with respect to garbage removal so he should be reimbursed by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that water/sewer services and solid waste management services are both set out in one “utility bill” from the City of Toronto, and because of that he claims the Tenant is responsible for the solid waste management services.

The Landlord’s representative submits that there is an implied agreed term for the Tenant to pay the garbage removal charge because the Tenant has paid for the solid waste management services from the beginning of his tenancy until October 2025. In addition, the Landlord’s representative states that page 5, paragraph e of the tenancy agreement makes the Tenant responsible for costs of all utilities.
The Tenant testified that garbage removal is a service and not “utilities” under the Act.
The parties never discussed the terms of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord stated that the Tenant was found by his real estate agent and the tenancy agreement was signed electronically. Analysis
Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
I accept the Tenant’s submission that provision e on page 5 of the tenancy requires the Tenant to pay utilities charges and not services and facilities.
Subsection 2(1)(f) of the Act defines “services and facilities” as including “garbage facilities and related services” whereas “utilities” is defined as “heat, electricity and water”.

I am not satisfied with the Landlord submission that the Tenant’s payment of the full City of Toronto utility bill from the commencement of the tenancy until October 31, 2025 demonstrates that the parties had an implied agreement that the Tenant would pay the garbage charges. While the Tenant paid the full utility bill for a period of time, this conduct alone does not override the written terms of the tenancy agreement or establish an implied term inconsistent with the lease. In the absence of a specific term assigning responsibility for garbage removal to the Tenant, I find that the solid waste management services remained the Landlord’s responsibility.
I say this because the lease lists water and sewerage charges and garbage removal as a separate service under section 6.

Further, the solid waste management services charge shown on the City of Toronto bill is the municipal equivalent of garbage removal. Just because it is listed on the “utility bill” does not make it a utility charge for the purposes of the Act. As that service was separately identified in the lease and was not selected as the Tenant’s responsibility, I find that the Tenant did not agree to pay that charge.

Subsection 135(4) of the Act provides: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997

In this case, the Tenant filed his application on October 31, 2025; therefore, the Tenant may claim illegal charges collected by the Landlord from October 31, 2024, onwards. The Tenant stated that the charge for the solid waste management services charge is $50.00 per month and he paid them from October 2024 to October 2025. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to $600.00. The amount paid by the Tenant was not challenged by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $648.00. This amount represents: • $600.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Sections 30 and 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] [organization], 2026 ONLTB 13714 Date: 2026-03-09 In the matter of: 702, 246 [address] PETERBOROUGH ON meiklejohn (the 'Tenant's) applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). This application was heard by videoconference on February 3, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, Allistair Trent, and the Landlord’s Agent, [name], a full-time employee of the Landlord, attended the hearing. The Tenants declined the opportunity to speak with Duty Counsel prior to the start of the proceeding. The Tenant [name] was the individual who testified on behalf of the Tenants and so all references to the Tenant singular in this order are to him.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I am not satisfied the Landlord collected or retained an illegal charge from the Tenants, and, in any event, I find it is more likely than not that the cost of the hot water heater rental was an implied term of the lease. Therefore, the T1 Application is dismissed.

With respect to the T6 Application, I find the Landlord was in breach of their obligations under s. 20 of the Act following a leak in the basement of the rental unit. However, I have limited the period of abatement from June 21, 2024, to December 1, 2024.
The Landlord is ordered the Landlord to pay the Tenants a total of $2,080.50 for abatement and costs. Preliminary Issue
The Landlord submitted the Tenants did not comply with orders to amend their applications and organize their evidence following an Adjudicative Case Conference held May 1, 2025.

No Interim Order issued after the ACC and the adjournment form does not direct or order the Tenants to take any steps; although, the adjournment form does indicate the Tenants were informed of issues with respect to the provision and organization of evidence and to clarify their remedies.

I was satisfied the Tenants attempted to comply with the concerns about evidence and disclosure as they compiled all of their documents and images onto two pages and emailed this to the Landlord’s Representative seven (7) days in advance of the hearing.
The Landlord’s Representative also admitted he had received and reviewed the Tenant’s disclosure; although, it was challenging to work with as the images were very small.

Further, I found the abatement remedies the Tenants were seeking were already reflected on the face of their applications; albeit, not as clearly nor in the expected location on the T6 Application and so this was clarified orally before me. The Landlord’s Representative admitted this clarification did not impact the Landlord’s defences.

I found all parties were aware of the issues and had had the opportunity to review and prepare a response to the other party’s materials. As a result, I was satisfied there was no prejudice in proceeding.

However, I concurred with the Landlord’s concerns that the Tenants’ failure to provide their evidence in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence might cause delay and the matter was held down to permit the Tenants to ensure they could accurately identify the documents on which they intended by EVID number. T1 Application

The Tenants claim the Landlord illegally placed the contract for the rental of the hot water heater into the name of the female Tenant and they then had to pay this charge, a charge to which they had not agreed.

The Landlord submits the Tenants agreed to pay for the hot water heater rental as a term of their tenancy and so it was not a charge in contravention of the Act, and secondly, that the Tenants’ claim is not properly brought under s. 135 of the Act as the Landlord did not collect or retain any funds related to the hot water heater from the Tenants.

The Tenants admitted they paid the cost to rent the hot water heater to a third-party service provider who was not an agent of the Landlord and so I do not find this was a proper claim under s. 135 of the Act.

Whether the Tenants’ claim could be amended and pursued as a T2 Application was raised as an issue. However, as I have found the Tenants and Landlord agreed the Tenants would pay the cost of renting the hot water tank, I do not find it is necessary to make this determination. Cost of hot water heater was a term of the tenancy agreement
The Tenants claim they did not agree to and did not pay to rent the hot water tank and sp were shocked when they received a bill from EnerCare in September 2025.

The Landlord claims paying for the cost of the hot water heater was always a term of the tenancy agreement, as it is for all of their tenants, that this cost was part of the Tenants’ Enbridge bill, and that the Tenants got a new bill in September 2025 because EnerCare started billing separately for the hot water heater and not because this was a new charge.

The lease agreement states it is the Tenants’ responsibility to pay for the utilities of electricity, heat and water, and that the Tenants must register with Enbridge Gas, Hydro One, and Wyse meters and provide proof of registration before March 1, 2024 [Exhibit 2 - p. 4 of EVID 7250125].

The welcome email sent by the Landlord to the Tenants on December 8, 2023, further indicates that with respect to Enbridge the Tenants are responsible for both the Gas and HWH – understood to mean hot water heater [Exhibit 3 - EVID 7286931].

I find the Tenants’ evidence that there was no charge for the hot water heater included in their Enbridge bill does not accord with the overall circumstances. The rented hot water heater was always in the rental unit and there was no evidence the cost of this rental was ever paid for by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that a customer service representative told them the Landlord placed the EnerCare account in the female [name] name. The Landlord’s Agent denied this was done. The Tenant’s evidence was hearsay. [name] is typically afforded less weight as it is not subject to cross-examination and what may have been meant and what was heard or understood can vary. As a result, I had a direct denial on one side and untested second- hand evidence on the other.

Further, I found that if the EnerCare account was set up or transferred by the Landlord as alleged by the Tenants, how the Landlord would know the female [name] name maiden name when she entered into the tenancy agreement with her married name was not explained nor why this transfer would take place 6 months into the tenancy.
The Landlord’s explanation was that there was a separation of the hot water rental charge from Enbridge to EnerCare and that this resulted in a new bill – but not a new charge.

I find the Landlord’s explanation better accords with the overall circumstances and prefer it. As a result, I find it more likely than not that the cost of the hot water tank rental was initially incorporated into the charges on the Enbridge account and, when [name] began to bill separately for the hot water tank rental it resulted in a new bill but not, I find, a new charge.
As a result, the Tenants’ T1 application is dismissed. T6 Application
On June 6, 2024, there was a flooding event in a basement room of the rental unit seemingly caused by a malfunctioning sump pump.
The Tenants reported the flooding event to the Landlord’s after-hours line, and the Landlord’s Agent attended the next day.

The Tenant testified the Landlord’s Agent told them to run a dehumidifier; but none was provided to them. The Landlord’s Agent testified she offered the Tenants fans and a dehumidifier; but, they declined the offer as they already had one. In either event, I find the Tenants had a dehumidifier that they ran to assist with the remediation.
The Tenant testified the Landlord’s Agent said they had to wait a couple of few weeks for the basement to dry out and then a contractor would attend.
In response to their concerns about mold, the Tenant testified the Landlord’s Agent dropped off a small bottle of mold remover on June 8, 2024, and said they could scrub to remove any mold.

The Landlord’s Agent testified she purchased and delivered a bottle of mold and mildew remover and wiped what was said to be mold off the face of the baseboards. The Landlord’s Agent also testified she later reconsidered whether what she had removed was mold as she determined it could not have grown overnight.

The pictures taken by the Tenant in the days after the flooding event show wet carpet, and damp baseboards [Exhibit 1 – EVID 7236819]. The Tenant testified he took steps to mitigate and, with the permission of the Landlord, removed the baseboards and removed and disposed of the bottom affected portion of the drywall.

The Tenant also testified mold was present and visible on the back of the baseboards, on the studs and on the carpet, and that he tried to use the mold remover provided by the Landlord on the studs to no effect.
The Tenant testified they were understanding of a delay in attendance for a period of time; but, ultimately no contractor attended the rental unit.

The Landlord’s Agent testified a contractor twice tried to attend the rental unit to conduct repairs but the female Tenant was verbally abusive towards him and so they did not enter. After this the Landlord’s Agent testified the Tenants told them at the end of October that they were moving and to leave them alone. As a result, the Landlord’s Agent testified they did not again seek to attend and repair the rental unit.
Whether they asked to be left alone or whether the female Tenant engaged in the alleged conduct was not put to the Tenants. Relevant law

Section 20 of the Act provides: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Landlord failed to properly investigate and remediate the flood
Although both parties provided their respective theories as to how the sump pump stopped working; I ultimately, do not find this is relevant to the issues before me.

I so find as once there is a maintenance issue, the Landlord’s obligation under s. 20 of the Act is to repair. If the Landlord believes the Tenants responsible for the cause of the disrepair, their remedy is to serve a N5 Notice to End your Tenancy For interfering with Others, Damage or Overcrowding and/or bring a claim for the cost to repair undue damage negligently caused to the rental unit by the Tenants. This was not done.
There was a flooding event, and evidence of water in carpet and on the walls.

No documentation was provided in support of the Tenants’ position there was mold in the basement as a result of the flooding event by way of testing. Nonetheless, the Tenant testified the basement was full of mold and the Landlord found the allegation of mold sufficiently plausible that they, at least initially, provided the Tenants with a bottle of mold remover after they had attended the rental unit to inspect the damage.

Given the Landlord did not attend the rental unit after the first few days following the initial flooding event, they had no evidence to suggest there was not mold in the rental unit while the Tenants were living there, and they did not testify there was no mold in the rental unit after the Tenants moved out.
As a result, I find it more likely than not that there was mold in the rental unit as a result of the flooding event.

I find it was reasonable for the Landlord to wait a few weeks for the basement to dry out before taking any steps. However, I find that after this point, it was not reasonable for the Landlord not to repair the basement.
The Landlord’s obligation is to provide a rental in a state of good repair fit for habitation.

Accepting for the moment the Landlord’s evidence that the female Tenant was verbally abusive towards their contractor when that individual attended on two occasions, and that the Tenants ultimately said they were moving and asked to be left alone, I accept that the decision to delay repair was understandable from a business perspective.

However, the Tenants did not give notice to vacate until at least 5 months after the flooding event and I do not find 2 attempts at entry during 5 months reasonable and I find it was not reasonable from the perspective of a Landlord having to comply with their obligations under the Act for the Landlord to take no further steps. As a result, I find the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act from June 21, 2024, until December 1, 2024. Remedies
The Tenants sought a monthly abatement of $400.00 from June 6, 2024, up to the date they moved out of the rental unit on December 1, 2024.

While on the Tenants’ application there were also claims for $200.00 for the costs to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of and $250.00 for the costs of the Tenant’s time spent removing drywall, these claims were not pursued at the hearing and so have not been considered. Additionally, I note what was particularised in these claims was the Tenant’s time spent removing drywall as opposed to personal property that was damaged and no out-of-pocket expenses were indicated for either of the claims.
An abatement is a monetary award that may be expressed as a lump sum for the return of rent paid and generally reflects that what has been bargained for has not been received.

As I have found it was reasonable for the Landlord to wait a few weeks for the basement to dry out before taking any steps, I limit the starting date from which any abatement may be awarded to June 21, 2024.

The rental unit was a 3-storey town home with a finished basement. The recreational room in the basement was used as a playroom for the Tenants’ children aged 6 and 9. There were also common areas on the first floor including the kitchen and bedrooms and washrooms located on the 2nd and 3rd floors.

The Tenant tarped off the playroom with a vapour barrier and testified the loss of the this room limited their enjoyment of the rental unit. Furniture from the basement was moved into the first-floor common area making this area more crowded, and his children no longer had a dedicated indoor place to entertain friends and play - particularly once it turned cold.

The Tenant also testified two of his family members had pre-existing respiratory conditions. While I accept that such conditions may make someone more susceptible to airborne irritants, they may also independently necessitate visits to the doctor and here there were no supporting medical documents that demonstrated any visits were specifically due to the presence of mold. As a result, I do not find it more likely than not that members of the Tenant’s family sought medical attention because of the presence of mold.

The Landlord disputed that the basement room was emptied of furniture or that it was set up as a dedicated pla room; however, the Landlord did not reattend the rental unit and I find a room need not be set up in a particular fashion to serve a playroom function.

While I agree with the Landlord’s submissions that the Tenants were likely not prevented from doing any activities as a result of the loss of the playroom, I nonetheless find the loss of a common space and resultant crowding in the remaining common area sufficient to warrant some award of abatement due to the resultant disruption with the Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit.

I find an abatement of 10% is warranted for the summer months starting June 21, 2024 and continuing through until the end of August and 15% for the months starting September and continuing until the Tenants moved out on December 1, 2024.

The Tenants’ rent was $2,550.00 a month of which $100.00 was for parking. In the above circumstances, I fix the amount to be awarded to the Tenants at $562.50 for the summer months and $1,470.00 for the following months for a total of $2,032.50.

The Landlord submitted that because the Landlord accepted early termination of the lease on short notice and did not pursue the Tenants for additional rent to which they may have been entitled under the Act, this should be factored in as consideration already given by the Landlord for the Tenants’ claim.

In this respect, the Landlord relied on SWT-92414-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 88158 (ONLTB) where with respect to the tenant’s claims the Member, , at para. 68, considered that the Tenant saved two month’s rent when the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy early.

Although the Landlord here may have elected not to pursue the Tenants for additional rent thinking all issues were resolved and the parties were walking, I find there was no agreement or release to this effect.

Additionally, the LTB’s records show the Landlord was advised the Tenants’ applications were commenced on November 11, 2024 – before the Tenants moved out. After this the Landlord was given Notice of an Adjudicative Case Conference and the ACC was conducted with a representative of the Landlord present on May 5, 2025. All of these events took place within one year of the Tenants vacating and were therefore within the time the Landlord had to commence a claim for unpaid rent.

Further, I find that in determining whether any arrears were owed, whether the Landlord attempted to mitigate and were not able to re-rent the rental unit despite their efforts would also be considered.

Decisions of the LTB are persuasive and not binding. Here I find the Landlord had ample notice that the Tenants were not in fact walking away from any claims and the Landlord had ample time to pursue their own claims for unpaid rent, if such were viable. As a result, I do not find it appropriate to incorporate acceptance of the Tenants’ notice as consideration already paid to the Tenants and decline to follow the reasoning in SWT- 92414-16.
The Tenants were partially successful on their applications and so I find they are entitled to the cost of filing their applications.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,080.50. This amount represents: • $2,032.50 for abatement; and, • $48.00 for their cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Saeed (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and /or [name] and [name] (the ‘Purchasers') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Board requested the Tenant provide, by way of post-hearing submissions, a copy of his current lease agreement. This was provided at 11:21 a.m. on April 28, 2026, and has been considered in my findings to corroborate the Tenant’s claim for rent differential. Amended Application
The Tenant filed a request to amend the T5 application on October 31, 2025. The amended application sought to remove a business name – [name] – and amended the Tenant’s middle name.

The Board’s Rules of Procedure 15.2 state that amending an application may be done in advance of the hearing and the amended application must be served on all parties. The Tenant advises he did not serve the Landlord nor Purchasers with a copy of the amended application.

However, I find that it is appropriate to exercise my discretion to allow the amendment even though the Landlord and Purchasers were not served with a copy of the amended application. I make this finding because I can find no prejudice to the Landlord or Purchasers. The amendments corrected the applicant Tenant’s name and does not change or amend the allegations, the remedy sought, nor affect the Landlord or Purchasers’ liability. Given this, I am satisfied it was appropriate to amend the Tenant’s application, and that this amendment is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchasers must pay to the Tenant $14,800.00.

By way of background, the rental property was a three-bedroom townhouse which had been built about five years earlier. The Tenant, his partner, and their two children moved lived in the rental unit for four years.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’) under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant submits that in April 2024, he was given an N12 notice of hearing. The N12 notice specifies a termination date of June 30, 2024, and indicates that the Purchasers intend to move into the rental unit.

The Tenant states that he opted to wait for a hearing. It is not clear to me whether the parties opted for mediation, or went before a Board member, at the hearing. However, the parties agreed on consent that the tenancy would terminate on November 30, 2024. The Tenant says the Purchaser represented during the hearing (or mediation) that they intended to move into the rental unit. Thus, I find that the Tenant has satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant was given an N12 notice pursuant to s.49 of the Act, and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of being given the N12 notice.
The Tenant submitted a copy of Purchaser Gurpreet Singh’s sworn and notarized affidavit into evidence. The affidavit indicates that the Purchasers “…intend to move into the property with my family.”

The Tenant states that he moved into another rental property nearby. As such, he has passed by the house a few times and has never seen any activity associated with daily living such as a car parked outside or curtains in the windows.

The Witness also testified. He was the Tenant’s next-door neighbour during the period of the tenancy. He continues to live in the unit immediately next door to the one that the Tenant occupied. He testified that he has only seen activity at the rental on two occasions. Shortly after the tenancy ended, in about November 2024, he saw a family attend the rental unit. After an hour or two, they left. The next time the Witness observed activity at the rental unit was during the weekend of April 25, 2026.
