An individual attended the rental unit for about 15 minutes and then left.

The Witness says he does not believe anyone lives in the rental unit. He is outside frequently and has never seen normal signs of people living in the rental unit. For example, there are no lights on in the rental unit at night and no noise typical of housing which have shared walls can be heard from the rental unit.

The Purchasers did not attend the hearing. The Board confirmed that the Purchasers were sent a copy of the Tenant’s application and notice of hearing. The best evidence before me then suggests that the Purchasers did not move into the rental unit. The Tenant and his witness both reported no activity at the rental unit typical of residential occupation, such as lights, noise, a vehicle parked in the driveway, or curtains in the windows.

I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Purchasers did not move into the rental property within a reasonable period of time. Although “reasonable” is not defined in the Act, the evidence demonstrates that the tenancy terminated on November 30, 2024, and by April 2026, there is still no evidence of anyone living in the rental unit. Given this period of nearly 18 months, I am not persuaded that this meets the test for a “reasonable” amount of time. Further, this evidence seems to contradict the Purchaser’s affidavit which stated the Purchasers intended to move into the rental unit with their family.

Given the Purchaser’s affidavit and the Tenant’s testimony that the Purchaser attended the hearing (or mediation) and represented their intention to occupy the rental unit, I am persuaded that the Purchasers directed the Landlord to give the Tenant the N12 notice in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. For the reasons already stated, I find that the liability for having given the N12 notice ought to be attributed to the Purchasers rather than the Landlord. Remedies

The Tenant seeks the following remedies: • Rent differential totalling $9,800.00; • General compensation totalling $14,000.00; • Moving expenses totalling $600.00; and, • A Board fine. Rent Differential

The Tenant states his monthly rental rate increased from $2,000.00, which included utilities, to $2,750.00 per month plus $50.00 utilities. The Tenant claims $800.00 per month for a period of 12 months. A copy of his lease was submitted to corroborate this claim.

Therefore, I find that the Purchasers must pay the Tenant $9,800.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. I calculate the rent differential to be $9,800.00 ($800.00 x 12months). An order shall issue. General Compensation
The LTB has jurisdiction to make any order that it considers appropriate, which includes awarding general compensation. [[name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC)]
General compensation involves compensating a tenant financially for, in this case, the trauma, stress and anxiety that resulted from the actions—or inactions—of the Purchasers.

When determining general compensation, the LTB should consider the effect of the breaches on the tenant. While there is no fixed formula for general compensation, the LTB should attempt to make an award that is consistent with previous awards. [See HOT- 02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB) citing Domtar Inc. v. Quebec, 1993 CanLII 106 (SCC)]

The Tenant testimony was that the move has had a significant impact on his children, particularly his eight-year-old. That child has developmental disabilities, and the move has set him back because it is challenging for him to form new friendships. Because the family had lived in the rental unit for several years, the youngster had formed good relationships with the other children in the community, and the Tenant reports both children express their sadness from missing their friends. The family occasionally go to a park which is nearby in hopes of seeing some of the neighbourhood children. 26. The Tenant also submits that his new rental unit is a brand-new townhome a few minutes away from the old rental unit and is smaller than the old rental unit although it has the same number of bedrooms, but one fewer washroom. He also states that the family feels isolated at the new property, because a large portion of the housing in the area is still under construction. He says there is not the same sense of community as there had been at the previous rental unit. Fortunately, though, the Tenant reports that neither child had to change schools because of the move. 27. Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 28. In reviewing similar orders of the Board, the quantum of award for general compensation varies greatly. However, when I consider the impact the unlawful eviction had on the Tenant and his family, contrasted with the Tenant’s evidence that the children did not have to change schools, and that the new rental unit is slightly smaller with slightly fewer amenities, I am of the view that the Tenant should be awarded $5,000.00. An order shall issue. Moving Costs 29. The Tenant’s application seeks moving costs totalling $600.00. However, the Tenant did not provide any evidence, whether oral testimony or documentary evidence, during the hearing to support this claim. As such, I find the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to support his claim. No order shall issue. Board Fine 30. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. 31. The Tenant did not provide any submissions on the request for a Board fine nor the quantum of fine sought. 32. Regardless, I am satisfied that a Board fine is not warranted in matter. In my view, the award is sufficient to act as a deterrent to the Purchasers in the future. 33. The total the Purchasers owe the Tenant is $14,800.00. 34. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Purchasers shall pay the Tenant is $14,848.00. This amount represents: • $9,800.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from December 1, 2024, to November 30, 2025. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchasers shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026.

If the Purchasers do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026, the Purchasers will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,488.00.
The Tenant applied to the Board under section 29 of the Act alleging that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20(1) of the Act.

Section 20 (1) states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1).

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Background
The Tenant has occupied the rental unit since 2017. The lawful monthly rent is $2,224.25.
The residential complex contains shared facilities including a laundry room used by multiple tenants. Tenant evidence regarding maintenance
Beginning in March 2024, the Tenant began encountering repeated cleanliness issues in the laundry room after tenants in another unit in the same complex began using the shared facilities.

The Tenant testified that on numerous occasions the Tenant found drywall debris, paint chips, dirt, and standing water in the washing machine, and debris including paper and lint inside the dryer. The Tenant also found garbage and lint scattered on the floor of the laundry room. In addition, the Tenant found pooled water in the washing machine when a washing load was terminated early by other tenants.

On June 5, 2024, the Tenant sent email communication to the Landlord, which was submitted into evidence, regarding the cleanliness of the common areas (hallways, stairs, and laundry room) and that someone needs to be hired to clean on a regular basis. The Tenant submitted one colored photo into evidence which shows the laundry room floor with debris in front of the washing machine.

On June 19, 2024, the Tenant sent the Landlord an email with a picture showing the condition of the laundry room with debris on the floor in front of the machine. This email and picture was submitted into evidence.

On June 28, 2024, the Tenant sent email communication to the Landlord which was submitted into evidence outlining the condition of the laundry room and the fact that the Tenant cleans it weekly. The [name] also explained that the washing machine needs regular cleaning, and she does not want to be responsible for it. One colored photo of the laundry room was submitted into evidence showing a full garbage can beside the washing machine.

On July 3, 2024, the Tenant reported concerns to the Landlord again regarding the state of the laundry room and included two colored photos showing the state of the laundry room. The Tenant submitted copies of the email communication and colored photos which was sent to the Landlord into evidence.
On August 20, 2024, the Landlord’s legal representative advised the Tenant that the issue would be addressed with the other tenants. This was the only response from the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that the problem continued.
On September 3, 2024, the Tenant again found debris on the laundry room floor and inside the dryer.

On September 30, 2024, the landlord’s representative advised the Tenant that the other tenants had denied responsibility and that the Tenant’s evidence was insufficient. The Tenant was advised that a general reminder letter would be sent to tenants. The Tenant submits that no letter was ever sent from the Landlord or the Landlord’s legal representative and that the condition remained the same in the laundry room. As of the date of the hearing the Landlord had not retained anyone to clean the common area.
The Tenant testified that the condition of the laundry room did not improve and that the Tenant and the Tenant’s spouse began cleaning the area weekly in order to maintain a usable space.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing and did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence. I found the Tenant’s testimony and photographs to be credible and persuasive, and therefore accept the Tenant’s claims that the shared laundry room is consistently very dirty and that the Landlord was made aware of this problem on a number of occasions but has not done anything to address the problem. I therefore find that the Landlord breached his obligation to in s. 20(1) of the Act to ensure the laundry room is in a good state of repair. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $1,440.00. A rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for the loss of the use or enjoyment of a portion of the premises resulting from a landlord’s breach of the Act.

In this case, the Tenant experienced an ongoing reduction in the benefit of the tenancy because the tenant could not rely on the landlord to maintain the shared laundry facilities in a clean and usable condition.
As a result, the Tenant and the Tenant’s spouse undertook regular cleaning of the laundry room and surrounding common areas in order to maintain the space.
The Tenant estimated that cleaning the laundry room and common areas required approximately one hour per week. The Tenant estimated the value of this work at $30.00 per hour.
This results in an estimated monthly cost of approximately $120.00.
The Tenant seeks compensation totalling $1,440.00 for approximately one year of performing this cleaning.

I find the Tenant’s estimate of the time required to clean the laundry room to be reasonable given the condition described in the evidence. I also find that the hourly rate used by the tenant represents a reasonable approximation of the value of the labour required.

In these circumstances, I find that an abatement in the amount of $1,440.00 is appropriate to compensate the tenant for the loss of the benefit of the tenancy resulting from the Landlord’s failure to maintain the common areas during the period September 2024 to the hearing date.].

The Tenant also requested an order requiring the landlord to ensure that the common areas and laundry facilities are properly maintained. I find that such an order is appropriate in order to ensure future compliance with the Act.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,488.00. This amount represents: • $1,440.00 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount of $1,488.00 from the rent owing for the month of April 2026.

The Landlord shall ensure that the common areas of the residential complex, including the laundry room, are regularly cleaned in order to maintain a clean and sanitary condition, including: a) removal of garbage and debris; b) vacuuming or sweeping as required; and c) reasonable maintenance of the laundry facilities, including running cleaning cycles on the washing machine and removing lint and debris from accessible dryer vents.

If the Landlord does not comply with paragraph 5 of this order on or before March 30, 2026, then the Tenant will be entitled to a further abatement of the rent, in the amount of $120.00 per month, for the period commencing April 1, 2026 and continuing for each month until such time as the Landlord addresses the items outlined in paragraph 5. March 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges the Landlord has retained money illegally as he has failed to return her last month’s rent deposit.
The tenancy commenced on November 29, 2023. It is the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that she paid the Landlord $1,200.00 for the first month’s rent and $2,400.00 for last two month’s rent deposit.

In her application, the Tenant indicates that with the consent of the Landlord, the tenancy was assigned to a friend at the end of May 2025. The assignee complied with the Landlord’s demand that they pay a law two month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant paid the lawful rent for April 2025 and May 2025. She vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025.
I am satisfied the Landlord has retained the last month’s rent deposit as required under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

It should be noted that the Landlord collected two months of rent as a deposit. This is prohibited by the Act. Subsection 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. Subsection 106(2) states that the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the rent for one month. Accordingly, the Landlord was not entitled to require the Tenant to pay more than $1,200.00 as a rent deposit.

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. In this case, the Landlord collected two months rent as a deposit. The Tenant paid the rent for the last two months of her tenancy. The tenancy has been assigned and the assignee has provided the Landlord with a deposit. Therefore, the Landlord was obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,400.00.

The Landlord also failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last two month’s rent deposit as required by the Act. Subsection 106(6) of the Act states: “A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline...”
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $145.12 in interest on the deposit. This is calculated 2.5% for periods ending 2023, 2024, and 2025 and 2.1% for the periods ending 2026.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $2,5,98.12. This amount represents: • Two month’s rent deposit of $2,400.00 • Interest payment on her rent deposit, $145.12 • Cost of filing the application, $53.00
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s representative requested for the application to be amended to reflect the fact the rental unit is located in Windsor instead of Chatham. I referred to the tenancy agreement which confirms that the rental property is located in the City of Windsor. Therefore, this amendment would not cause any prejudice to the Landlords because it is correcting a clerical error. I am satisfied to grant the amendment.
The Tenant requested that I amend the application to include an additional charge of $500.00 collected by the Landlords, which I have addressed below. T1 Application – Last months’ rent deposit
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $652.97.

The Tenant testified that she moved out of the rental unit on September 20, 2025 because she discovered black mould in the unit and has never returned to the unit. She confirmed that rent was paid for the period of September 1, 2025 to September 30, 2025. The Tenant explained that she found black mould on September 3, 2025, and the following day she had a mould company verify that it was black mould. The Tenant also informed the Landlord, who had their “handyman” attend at the unit but he would not touch the mould.

On September 8, 2025, the Tenant called the City of Windsor. A building bylaw officer ([name]) attended the unit and “advised that it was black mould and it was not safe to live in.” The Landlord then told the Tenant to move out.

The Tenant testified that all payments made to the Landlords were cash. She stated that she paid (first and the last months’ deposit) $1,600.00 x 2 = $3,200.00, and an additional deposit of $500.00, which is a total of $3,700.00 at the commencement of the Tenancy. The Tenant relied on the lease agreement and a handwritten document which states: “Received $2,200.00 cash (first and last) for 1414B from [name] - [name].”

I inquired as to why the lease agreement provides $500.00 instead of $1,600.00 as the last months’ rent deposit. The Tenant replied, “I don’t know.” I also asked the Tenant why she signed the lease agreement confirming $500.00, if she paid $1,600.00 for the last months’ deposit. The Tenant replied, “I don’t know. I’ve never actually signed a full lease agreement like this before, so I assume he knew what he (Landlord) was doing.” Analysis and Findings

The Tenant’s application sets out $1,600.00 as the last month’s rent deposit, the details provided does not refer to an additional $500.00 paid to the Landlord. I am not prepared to grant the amendment without notice to the Landlord. Further the Tenant has not proven that an additional $500.00 was collected or retained by the Landlords as a separate amount. I find the Tenant was unable to clearly explain the discrepancy. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.

With respect to the last month’s deposit, while the Tenant confirmed that she paid $3,200.00 for the first and last month, the handwritten receipt relied upon by the Tenant confirms a total payment of $2,200.00 cash, which aligns with the written tenancy agreement mutually signed by the parties on May 17, 2025. The Lease agreement provides $500.00 as the last months’ rent deposit and $1,600.00 is crossed out and initialed by the parties. I find the Tenant’s testimony to be inconsistent with her documentary evidence.

Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant paid $1,600.00 for the first month, and $600.00 for the last month’s deposit which totals $2,200.00. Although the lease agreement provides $500.00 as the last months’ deposit, the receipt signed by the Landlord takes into account an additional $100.00. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant paid $600.00 as the last months’ rent deposit.

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that she moved out of the rental unit on September 20, 2025, after the Landlords informed her to leave. There is no evidence before me that the Tenant was permitted to return after that date. I also accept the Tenant’s testimony that she paid rent for the month of September 2025. Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on September 20, 2025 because there was an implied agreement between the parties to end the tenancy. The Landlord asked the Tenant to vacate, and the Tenant agreed.

The Landlords did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy which was September 1, 2025 to September 30, 2025 and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by s. 106(10) the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states: “(10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).” 8. I also find that the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, interest for the period of May 22, 2025 to September 20, 2025 in the amount of $4.97 is applied to the outstanding balance owed by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $652.97. This amount represents: • $600.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • $4.97 for the interest on the last months’ rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 11, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that Aspen Apartments Limited (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The parties agreed that [organization] was the Landlord within the meaning of the Act and that the application should be amended to delete Aspen Apartments Limited and replace it with [organization] as the Landlord. The application was amended accordingly. The Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
It is undisputed that the Tenants vacated the unit on November 30, 2025. Did the Landlord collect an Illegal rent?
The Tenant testified that the Tenants’ rent was automatically withdrawn from their bank account by way of preauthorized chequing. In 2024, the lawful monthly rent was $2,164.26.

After several months , the Tenant s became aware that the Landlord was withdrawing $2,283.29 rent, which was an increase of $119.03 or 5.5%). The Tenant denied receiving a Notice of Rent Increase (‘NORI’) from the Landlord. After contacting the Landlord , the Tenants’ rent was reduced as of July 2025 to $2,218.36, representing a rent increase in the amount of rent to 2.5% (i.e. the LTB guideline amount).
The Tenants request return of the additional 3% rent (i.e. $64.93) the Landlord withdrew for rent from January 1, 2025 up to and including June 2025, in the amount of $389.58.

The Landlord’s representative submitted that the NORI was based on an above-guideline rent increase that the Landlord had applied for, which increase has not yet been approved. She produced a copy of the list of residents served with the NORI on September 30, 2024 [Doc 7381689, page 7]. The serving list indicates that the Tenants were personally served with the NORI at 3:25 p.m. on September 30, 2024.

The Landlord’s witness, Pubuduni Wickramasinghe, testified that she was the person who served the Tenants with the NORI. She said that she wedged the NORI between the door and the door frame. Depending on the unit, the NORI would either go all the way through the door or part way.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the NORI in accordance with the Board’s rules. I find it more likely than not that the Tenants received the NORI. It is evident to me that the serving list was updated with a time of service each time service was completed and the person who served the NORI attended the hearing to describe how the NORI was served. I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of her testimony.

The Landlord’s representative stated that Tenants ha d a choice to pay the above -guideline amount set out in the NORI or to pay the guideline amount. Howeve r, if Tenants d id not advise the Landlord as to which increase they wanted to pay (i.e. 2.5% or 5.5%), the Landlord automatically charged the above guideline amount for rent. Given that the Tenant did not dispute the above-guideline amount until June 2025, the Landlord legally withdrew the amount of rent set out in the NORI. She stated that if the above -guideline amount of 5.5% is not granted or a lesser above -guideline amount is granted, [name] will be refunded the difference. Analysis

Subsection 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’) provides that a NORI must be served a minimum of 90 days in advance. As explained above, I have found that the NORI was served in accordance with s.116 of the Act.

There is no evidence before me that prior to June 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord to only withdraw the guideline increase of 2.5% or that the Landlord refused to do so. As such, I find that the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: Post-hearing submissions were requested with regard to amending the Tenants’ T5 application to that of a T2 application about Tenants’ rights.
The Tenant provided post-hearing submissions on May 6, 2026. The Landlord provided submissions on May 11, 2026.

Although I do not necessarily agree with the Landlord Representative’s submissions, I am no longer of the view that an amendment to the Tenants’ application is necessary as I find my decision can be made with the facts and remedies as contained in the T5. Therefore, the determinations of this application are made pursuant to the Tenants’ T5 application, and I have not amended the Tenants’ application. Tenants’ T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $1,270.66.
By way of background, the rental unit was a single-family home with two rental units. The Tenants occupied the upper floors of the rental unit. The tenancy was about seven years in length.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; 3. The Landlord did not demolish, convert, or repair, or renovate the rental unit within a specific period of time after the Tenant vacated the rental unit; and 4. The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.

In is not contested that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N13 notice of termination (‘N13’) on or about July 26, 2024, with a termination date of November 30, 2024. The N13 states that the Landlord planned to “convert to legal duplex home” stating “secure city permit and follow all city codes to convert the single family dwelling into two legal unit home.” The N13 indicates that the Landlord will obtain the necessary building permits to convert the premises. Therefore, the Tenants have proven the first part of the test as found in s.57(1)(c).

The Tenant submits that on or about July 23, 2024, the Landlord attended the rental unit to fix the stairs at the request of the Tenants. When the Landlord attended that day, he brought up that the rental unit needed significant repairs and that it would be difficult to have the Tenants remain in the rental unit during the renovations. The Tenant says the Landlord told him that they could come back to the rental property, but that the rent would be increased.
It is not contested that the Landlord did not file an L2 application with the Board based on the N13 notice which was given to the Tenants.

Initially after receiving the N13, the Tenants searched for another rental property. However, they were unable to find anything suitable. So, after about four weeks of searching, the Tenants decided to purchase a home instead. The Tenants purchased a home around the end of December 2025. The property closed on or about February 28, 2025. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on April 14, 2025.

The Tenants new home is a short distance from the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he did not see the repairs he expected would have taken place and came to learn that new tenants were occupying the former rental unit, a fact not disputed by the Landlord. He feels the tenancy was terminated in bad faith because the Landlord did not affect the repairs as stated on the N13 notice. The Tenants submit that but for the Landlord’s N13 notice, they would have continued to live in the rental unit indefinitely and although they did purchase a home, it was an arduous process to do so and pushed up their timelines.
The Landlord argues that the Tenants did not move out in accordance with the N13 notice, and that there was a material change in circumstances such that the intended renovation did not take place.

The Landlord says that the Tenants, who he had a good relationship with, had told him numerous times that they one day planned to purchase a home. In fact, when the Landlord gave the Tenants the N13 notice, the Tenants discussed making an offer to purchase the rental unit from the Landlord.

Further, the Landlord submits that the L2 application was never filed, and the notice would have been void, so it cannot be said that the Tenants left because of being given the N13 notice. The Tenant admits he did not seek legal advice at this time.

The Landlord states he was not aware that the Tenants had purchased a home until December or January 2025. Regardless, the termination date had come and gone, and the Landlord suggests that he did not apply any pressure to the Tenants. Submitted into evidence was text messages between the parties. On October 21, 2024, the Landlord asks: “how is the home search going on?”. The next message, dated March 27, 2025, is asking if the Tenant got his keys. The Board assumes this is referencing the keys to the home the Tenants purchased.
The Tenants submitted an N9 notice on March 29, 2025, with a termination date of April 14, 2025.

The Landlord says he had planned to do extensive renovations to the rental property to change the rental property into a legal semi-detached home. The basement is already a legal unit and would remain intact. He is an experienced Landlord and had done similar renovations before and had a cost estimate of $60,000.00 for the necessary renovations (the ‘full-scale renovation’). He disputes that he told the Tenants that they could not come back, rather he says they could come back, he was just uncertain of when that would be.

The Landlord argues there was a material change in circumstances such that the intended renovation did not take place. Instead, small updates were done at a significantly lower cost, totalling $6,500.00 (the ‘small-scale renovation’) instead of the original $50-$60K budget.

The Landlord advises that in January, it became apparent he would not be able to afford the original renovation. He had two properties which were for sale and remained on the market without offers. In addition, the Landlord had several files involving other tenants before the LTB for non-payment of rent.

In my view, the Tenants have proven, on a balance of probabilities, that they vacated the rental unit because of having been given the N13 notice. The Tenants received the N13 notice and gave evidence they were aware the rental unit was in a state of disrepair, so it made sense that the unit would require extensive remediation. The Tenants did not leave by the termination date, but they purchased a home at the end of December.

The Landlord testified that although he became aware the Tenants purchased a home, he did not advise them that he would not be completing the large-scale renovation. Additionally, he stated that around the end of January or early February, it became evident that he could not afford to complete the large-scale renovation project. Again, he did not advise the Tenants at any point that the work would not be done, he says, because by this time he knew the Tenants had purchased a home.

Further, the Landlord seeks to rely on the fact that the L2 application had not been filed pursuant to giving the N13 notice, so the N13 notice was void. Thus, the Tenants should not have terminated the tenancy because they should have realized the notice was no longer in effect. However, the Landlord did not advise the Tenants that he had not filed the application with the LTB. It is unclear to me then how the Tenants were expected to know that an application was not filed with the Board and that the Landlord was rescinding the notice of termination.
The Landlord also argues his financial situation changed which was a material change in circumstances which was unforeseen and resulted in the renovation work not being conducted. Analysis
For the following reasons, I am unable to find that the Landlord gave the N13 notice in good faith.

I found the Landlord’s evidence overall lacked reliability. Specifically, the Landlord first stated in his in-chief evidence, that he realized he no longer had the money to do the large-scale renovation at the end of 2024 or beginning of 2025, and certainly before April 7, 2025. However, in cross-examination, the Landlord stated he was aware of financial burdens in as early as mid-2024. Even the Landlord’s own documentary evidence suggests that the Landlord was facing these financial challenges in “April” repeatedly referring to this period (pg. 24, Doc-7809604), where his oral testimony suggested the financial problems began anywhere from the end of December 2024 through April 2025.

The Landlord let the N13 expire without filing an L2 application with the LTB and instead abandoned the N13. No evidence was adduced that the Landlord sought the permits necessary to undertake the large-scale renovation. The Landlord’s in-chief testimony was that he realized in late December or early 2025 that he would not be doing the large-scale renovation.

However, the Landlord also testified that he knew the N13 would have expired if he did not file an L2 application with the LTB within 30 days. That means if the Landlord had intended to follow through with the L2 application with the LTB, it would have needed to be filed on or before December 30, 2025. Despite this, the Landlord still did not inform the Tenants that he abandoned the N13, nor did he advise the Tenants that he would no longer be conducting the large-scale renovation.

The Landlord’s evidence was that he did not find out that the Tenants had purchased a house until January 30, 2025. But as I have found above, the Landlord knew the N13 was void as of December 30, 2025.

Although I agree there is a significant delay between the Tenants having received the N13 (in July 2024 with a termination date of November 30, 2024), and the date the Tenants ultimately vacated the rental unit (April 2025), as the Landlord did not advise them that he had not pursued the N13 with the LTB, I am still persuaded that the Tenants vacated the rental unit in accordance with the N13 notice. They purchased their house in December 2025 and were aware their rental unit needed significant repairs. This would suggest that they believed the Landlord was intending to do the large-scale renovation and the Landlord did nothing to disabuse them of this notion.

Although the case of [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (‘Elkins’) dealt with the analysis of a bad faith eviction following the termination of a tenancy pursuant to s.57 of the Act where the purchaser wished to occupy the rental unit, I find it useful to consider this case in applications where the good faith intention of a landlord to renovate a rental unit is called into question. The Court of Appeal provides guidance in par. 45: [45] It could be argued that s. 57(1)(b) implicitly limits Board scrutiny to the Vendor Landlord’s knowledge when it gives the s. 49 termination notice. However, such an interpretation runs afoul of s. 202(1) of the RTA. Under s. 202(1), the Board is 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the “real substance of all transactions and activities relating to…a rental unit and the good faith of the participants”. Limiting the assessment of a Vendor [name] bad faith to that single point in time when the s. 49 termination notice is given precludes the Board from both ascertaining the true substance of the transaction between the Vendor Landlord and the purchaser and conducting a fair assessment of their good faith. [Emphasis added]

When I consider and apply the Court of Appeal’s decision of Elkins to the facts at hand, I can find no satisfactory reason why the Landlord, despite his clear intention to abandon the N13 application, failed to advise the Tenants of this. His testimony was that he knew the Tenants bought a house. However, the Landlord clearly stated that he found out they purchased a home on January 30, 2026, by text message. The Landlord could have told the Tenants at any time that he was not advancing the N13 application, but he did not do so.

The Landlord also argued a material change in circumstances, that being his financial situation had changed, which necessitated moving forward with the small-scale renovation rather than the original large-scale plan.

However, I am not persuaded that the change in circumstances was unforeseeable, at least in-part. Specifically, the Landlord gave evidence about two L1 applications for non- payment of rent which had been before the Board during the period. However, only one of the two applications included arrears that began in 2025, when the Landlord states he became aware he could no longer afford the renovations. The other L1 application claimed arrears which predates the N13 notice, with arrears accumulating from November 2023.

In addition, the Landlord also provided evidence about two properties he owned which lagged on the market during this period. One was listed in March 2025 but is not sold (‘property 1’). The second sold in July 2025 (‘property 2’). However, no information was led about when property 2 was listed for sale, so I cannot assess whether property 2 did in fact lag on the market. As for property 1, no evidence was led to demonstrate how the lack of this sale would have affected the Landlord’s good-faith intention to undertake the large-scale renovation in July 2024 when the N13 was given to the Tenants.

Perhaps more importantly, the Landlord led no additional corroboratory evidence that the Board might expect in these circumstances, such as financial records, tax documents, bank statements, etc., to substantiate his claim of financial burdens. I do note that the Landlord led evidence that he had re-rented the rental unit for less money than he had rented to the Tenants, suffering a loss. However, this does not reflect his entire financial picture.

The Landlord’s own evidence was that he had done several of the types of renovation projects and was “familiar” with the cost and time it would take to do this work, and he was aware as of August 2024 of the cost associated with doing the work. In my view, if the Landlord was experienced doing these types of renovations, the Landlord knew, or ought to have known whether it was financially feasible to undertake such a large-scale project.

When I consider the Court of Appeal’s guidance in Elkins, the good faith analysis cannot be limited only to the time the Landlord gave the N13 notice but also must include his behaviour following its issuance. The Landlord testified he never told the Tenants he would not be conducting the large-scale renovation despite having misgivings about his financial situation in as early as mid-2024.

Section 202 of the Act states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

Further, when I consider s.202(1) to the Act and the pattern of behaviour, I find that the eviction is more consistent with what is colloquially called a “renoviction.” I am not persuaded that the Landlord genuinely intended to conduct the large-scale renovation. He did not file an application with the Board or seek the requisite permits. Further, as early as December 30, 2024, the Landlord’s intention changed, but he failed to advise his Tenants of this and offered no reasonable explanation as to why he did not, given he also testified he was unaware they had purchased a house at that time.

Although the Tenant explained he was told the rent would be increased if he chose to return to the rental property, whereas the Landlord denies having said this, I do not find it necessary to make a determination about this given my earlier findings in paragraph 27.
As such, I find that the Tenants met their onus, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N13 notice in bad faith. Remedies

By way of remedies, the Tenants seek the following: • $4,281.00 for a 25% rent abatement for a 12-month period; • $17,124.00 for general compensation; • $26,244.00 for a rent differential, • $1,270.66 for the cost of moving; and, • a Board administrative fine.

Remedies for a bad faith termination pursuant to s.57 of the Act, are found at s.57(3): (3) The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out -of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 2. An order for an abatement of rent. 3. An order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 4. Any other order that the Board considers appropriate. [Emphasis added] Rent Abatement / General Compensation

The Tenants’ claim for a rent abatement is predicated largely on allegations of disrepair in the rental unit, rather than the inconvenience suffered because of the Landlord’s breach. In addition, the Landlord submits that the Tenants led no evidence to support their claim for rent abatement. In addition, the Tenants were able to remain in the rental unit, with little pressure from the Landlord, and were able to remain in their home until their house purchase closed.

The Tenant did refer to the difficulty securing the funds necessary to get a down-payment together. Although it was not entirely clear to me based on the Tenant’s testimony, it seems some of his funds were tied up in the United States. However, I did not hear about the impact on the Tenants except to say they were forced to purchase a house, rather than continue renting, which was not their plan.

I do not find that the Tenants led sufficient evidence to warrant a rent abatement. I agree with the Landlord’s submissions that the pleadings refer in large part to repairs which were not done. However, I find those would have been properly plead on a T6 application, rather than a T5 application. Other than the challenges of trying to free up their funds to make the downpayment, the Tenant did not leave any evidence about the impact on them, other than to have pushed up their future plans to buy a home.

For the same reasons, I also find that the Tenants led insufficient evidence to warrant general compensation. General compensation is intended to compensate for intangible losses such as pain and suffering. The Tenants did not lead evidence to suggest that they had suffered with losses often associated with bad faith evictions, such as a loss of work, excessive commutes, loss of family relationships, etc. No evidence of the losses suffered by the Tenants was led sufficient to demonstrate losses such as pain and suffering.

The Residential Tenancies Act is intended to be remedial, not punitive. In other words, the purpose of the Act is to provide protection for Tenants against unlawful evictions and rent increases, and to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants. And although I agree that the Landlord did unlawfully terminate the tenancy, not every bad faith eviction results in an order for general compensation. If it did, the Act would say so. No order shall issue. Rent Differential

The Tenants seek rent differential; that is, the difference in what they were paying to the Landlord for rent, and what they pay now. The issue here is that the Tenants are not paying rent. Rather, they are paying a mortgage payment.
Section 57(3)(1) of the Act specifically indicates that the Board can order the difference in “rent.” A mortgage payment is not rent.

Mortgage payments are not defined in the Act. However, the case of [name] v. Rizzo Shoes Ltd., provides guidance about statutory interpretation. On behalf of the Court, [name] noted: “[21] Although much has been written about the interpretation of legislation (see, e.g., [name], Statutory Interpretation (1997); [name], Driedger on the Construction of Statutes (3rd ed. 1994) (hereinafter "Construction of Statutes"); [name], The Interpretation of Legislation in Canada (2nd ed. 1991)), [name] (2nd ed. 1983) best encapsulates the approach upon which I prefer to rely. He recognizes that statutory cannot be founded on the wording of the legislation alone. At p. 87 he states: Today there is only one principle or approach, namely, the words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, and the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.”

When I consider the plain and ordinary meaning of the word rent, which is defined in the Act, I find it to be any amount paid on behalf of a tenant to a landlord. However, there is no landlord/tenant relationship in a mortgage; rather there is a mortgagor and a mortgagee. Thus, I am of the view that mortgage payments can be compensable under s.57(3) of the Act. Moving Costs
The Tenants seek moving and storage costs of $1,270.66 for moving costs.

The Landlord disputes this because the Tenant failed to lead any evidence during their in-chief about the moving costs, although it was referenced in their closing submissions. However, the Landlord also concedes that if a finding of bad faith was made, the moving costs were reasonable.

The Tenants’ application clearly seeks moving costs. Thus, I do not find it is an error in law, as stated in Beaugé v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, which found the Board cannot assess a monetary award where it was not stated within a claim.

Given that the Landlord concedes that if a bad faith finding was made, the costs of moving were reasonable, I am of the view that this is an appropriate award. I find the moving costs to be reasonable, and that but for the Landlord’s breach, the Tenants would not have incurred this expense. An order shall issue. Administrative Fine

The Tenants also seek a Board administrative fine. However, no submissions were made with regard to the fine during the hearing. As such, I am not of the view a Board fine is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,318.866. This amount represents: • $1,270.66 for the costs of moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred, and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
Subsection 57(2) of the Act requires a former tenant to file a bad faith application within one year of vacating the unit.
The Tenant testified that they received the N13 notice of termination from the Landlord on or around September 1, 2022, pursuant to section 50 of the Act.

The Tenant further testified that she moved out of the rental unit on November 22, 2022, as a result of the N13 notice. As a result, they would have until November 22, 2023 to file their application under section 57. However, the Tenant confirmed that they filed the application with the LTB on November 1, 2025, more than one year after vacating the rental unit.

Therefore, as explained at the hearing, because the application was filed beyond the one- year limitation period pursuant to subsection 57(2) of the Act, the application must be dismissed. Costs against the Tenant:
At the hearing the Landlord’s legal representative requested that the Board order costs against the Tenant for not attending the hearing and causing unnecessary legal costs for the Landlord.
Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3, costs are only awarded when a party acts unreasonably in the proceedings or if their conduct is unreasonable and causes undue expense or delay.
In my view, I do not find that it would be appropriate to order costs against the Tenant. As such, the Landlord’s request for costs is denied.

This is the first scheduled hearing by the Board and there have not been any previous adjournments. As such, I cannot conclude that the Tenant’s conduct was unreasonable and caused undue expense or delay.

Although the Landlord’s representative may have sent an email to the Tenant on or about November 3, 2025, explaining the deficiencies with the application, the likelihood of the application being dismissed at the hearing, and requesting the Tenant to withdrawal, the Tenant genuinely believed her case had merit and decided to proceed with the application.

While I understand that that the Landlord may have incurred some costs as a result of having their legal representative prepare and attend the hearing, the Tenant, who is unrepresented, admitted that she did not receive proper legal advice prior the hearing and was unclear about what to do. The Landlord’s representative admitted that he spent minimal time, under 30 minutes, preparing for the hearing and to attend the hearing.
The Landlord’s loss was minimal, and the Tenant should not be punished for attempting to enforce their legal rights by filing an application.

As such, I am unable to conclude that the Tenant has acted unreasonable during the hearing of this matter or that her conduct has willfully caused undue delays. The Landlord’s request for costs is therefore denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, [name] (‘HA’) indicated she was representing the Tenant at the hearing. I asked whether HA was licensed by the Law Society of Ontario to act in matters before the Board. HA advised she was not.
Unlicensed representatives1 may appear before the Board where they are acting for a friend or neighbour, are not being paid, and have provided “legal services” in no more than 3 matters in a year.

Although HA states she has was not being paid, she states that she had provided legal services to more than three individuals in a one-year period. When questioned about the kinds of services she has provided, she told the Board that she will read up on the area of law and explain to them their options. 1 Practice Direction on Representation before the Landlord and Tenant Board

I referred the parties to s.1(6)(1) of the Law Society Act2, which provides that legal services includes giving “…a person advice with respect to their legal interests, rights, or responsibilities of the other person….”. Given HA’s admission, I find that HA is providing legal services, and that because she is doing so more than three times per year, that this is outside of the exemptions allowed. Therefore, HA is not authorized to represent the Tenant in this matter.

HA argued that she has not “appeared” before a tribunal three times. However, I do not find that is relevant. The Law Society Act is clear that giving advice is included, not just appearances before a Board or Tribunal.

Initially, HA stayed in the room. However, it appeared that HA was continuing to advice the Tenant on her matter. As such, HA and the Tenant were cautioned at which time HA left the room, and the Tenant represented herself. Limitation Period
The Landlord’s Representative submits that the Tenant did not file her application within one year as prescribed by s.57(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’).
The Tenant’s application was filed on October 31, 2025. The tenancy terminated on October 31, 2024.
The Landlord submits that this is 366 days; therefore, it is beyond the statutory limitation period.

Initially, l had agreed with the Landlord’s submissions. However, after reviewing the Board’s LTB - Rules of Procedure Rules of Procedure, I determined that my initial analysis was incorrect. Specifically, Rule 1.13 states: “When something must be done within a specific number of days, the days are counted by excluding the first day and including the last day.”

The application must have been filed within 365 days. Thus, the first day counting towards the statutory limitation period in this case was November 1, 2024. Therefore, 365 days from November 1, 2024, is October 31, 2025. As such, I find that the Tenant’s application was brought within the limitation period. The hearing proceeded.

However, I can find no prejudice to the Landlord resulting from this omission. The Tenant sought to amend their application, and this request was granted. The Tenant’s application is amended to include “Main” in the address. Tenant’s T5 Application

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove all of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. 2 Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, [name] | ontario.ca

By way of background, the Tenant states when the tenancy began, she was living in the rental unit with her husband and four children ages 16, 13, 12, and 8. The rental unit was a four-bedroom, 2.5 bathroom detached home with a single car garage. However, the Tenant divorced in July 2024.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’); 3. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

Further, section 57(5) of the Act creates a rebuttable presumption that a notice of termination given under s. 48(1) of the Act was given in bad faith if the property is advertised for sale or rent. A rebuttable presumption means that the landlord is assumed to have acted in bad faith unless the landlord can provide an explanation that satisfies the Board as to what changed after the tenancy terminated, that affected the landlord’s ability to move in or remain in the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she was given an N12 notice of termination at the beginning of August 2024. The N12 notice indicated that the Landlord and his children would be moving back into the rental unit and listed the termination date as October 31, 2024. The Tenant did provide some testimony that she had asked for more time hoping for a termination date of October or November 2024. However, the Landlord told her he was unable to be flexible about the date. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on October 31, 2024.

The Tenant says she went past the rental unit in December 2024 or January 2025. She observed a “for rent” sign outside (Doc-670-9343). The Tenant states she called the realtor and asked, as if she was a prospective tenant, about the rental property. The realtor told her that it was a one-year lease and that the monthly rent was $3,600.00. This was $400.00 more per month than what the Tenant had been paying.

The Landlord disputes that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. Rather, he states that he had planned to move back into the rental unit, but because the Tenant failed to vacate the rental unit in time for his kids to start the school year, he was not able to follow through on his plans. Specifically, he, his wife and two children were residing overseas, in Pakistan, and had been for about one year. The plan was to have the family return to Canada in the summer of 2024 so that the children could be re-enrolled into school for September 2024. However, the Tenant was still living in the rental unit, so he had to abandon this idea for the school year in September 2024 and instead brought the family back in time for the 2025/2026 school year.

The Landlord returned to Canada on February 11, 2025. To keep the costs down while awaiting the return of the family, the Landlord advertised the upper floor rental unit while he resided in the basement. However, this was rented for only two months, not one year. After his children finished their school year in Pakistan, his family did come back home, and they are living in the rental unit as a family now. The Landlord does not know why his realtor would have told someone that the lease term was one year but thinks perhaps the realtor just “assumed” this. However, it was not his intention to rent the upper floor for a year, rather, he wanted tenants for a short term until his family returned home. Analysis

The leading case on finding good faith is [name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC). In this case, the Divisional Court instructs the Board to consider the “…the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the landlord’s proposal…”. [Emphasis Added]

Although I do find that the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination quite prematurely, I do not find that this accords to a bad faith intention on behalf of the Landlord. The Landlord’s evidence, which I accept, is that his intention was to live in the rental unit with his family. It is not disputed that this took some time, but I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the family decided to wait until the school year was over to move everyone back. The Landlord’s good faith intention was to move into the rental property, and he did. The delay in returning to the rental unit, in my view, does not affect the Landlord’s good faith intention, and I find that the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith even though he re-rented the rental unit for a short time sometime around February 2025. I accept the Landlord’s evidence it was only intended to offset some costs while he waited for his family to return.

I do accept the Tenant’s evidence that the realtor told her that the rental unit was to be a one-year term. However, beyond the conversation the Tenant had with the realtor in approximately December 2024 or January 2025, there was no evidence led to suggest that the rental unit continued to be occupied by anyone other than the Landlord. For example, the Tenant did not testify she went to the rental unit and spoke to new tenants, or made frequent observations that the rental unit was still tenanted, or spoke to multiple neighbours who reported the Landlord does not live in the rental unit. Therefore, I am unable to find that the Tenant led sufficient evidence to challenge the Landlord’s rebuttal of bad faith. For the same reason, I accept the Landlord’s testimony that he did move back into the rental unit and continues to reside there.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 13, 2026 ____________________________
