issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application). • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys (T2 Application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below and pursuant to the T2 application, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,203.00. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023, and paid her first month’s rent and last month’s rent deposit via money order. The Tenant testified that due to the effect the pest infestation was having on her mental health, the Tenant provided the Landlord with an N9 Tenant’s Notice to End the Tenancy (“N9 notice”) with a termination date of December 31, 2023, and vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2023.

The Tenant testified that she did not pay any rent for December 2023. The Tenant testified that she was indifferent about getting her last month’s rent deposit back but felt she should get it back because of the bad experience she had. The Tenant testified that the rental unit was re-rented for January 2024.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (“AA”), testified that she is the superintendent for the residential complex and the first time the Tenant provided an N9 notice the Tenant was told it had to be at least 60 days. Then when the Tenant provided the N9 notice with the termination date of December 31, 2023, which was 60 days, the Tenant was informed she would have to attempt to sublease her unit for the remainder of her lease as the earliest termination date was the end of the one-year lease.

AA provided the Tenant’s ledger which indicated the last month’s rent deposit was applied to the rent for December 2023 and testified that it was because the Tenant did not provide proper notice and vacated the rental without proper notice, because she breached her one-year lease.

Subsection 37(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') directs that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. Subsection 37(3) of the Act indicates that a notice of termination need not be given if a Landlord and a Tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy.

Here, the parties did not agree to terminate the tenancy. As such, the Tenant had to give notice to terminate in accordance with the Act. Section 44 of the Act provides the period of notice that is required for each type of tenancy. Here, I am satisfied that the tenancy was a one-year fixed term lease that commenced September 1, 2023. Section 44(3) of the Act provides that the required notice period for a fixed term tenancy is 60 days, and the termination date must be the last day of the term, which was August 31, 2024, in this case.

While the Tenant may have given a full 60 days’ notice, the date of termination was not the last day of the term, August 31, 2024, so the notice that was provided did not comply with section 44 (3). As such, the Tenant did not give notice in accordance with the Act.

Pursuant to section 88(1) of the Act, if a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving proper notice in accordance with the Act, the tenant is liable for the rent for the period of notice he or she could have given to the landlord to properly terminate the tenancy. Since the Tenant did not give proper notice, the Tenant is liable for the full rent of December 2023, and the Landlord properly applied the last month’s rent deposit to December 2023.
Therefore, the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit and the Tenant’s T1 Application is dismissed. T6 Application
The T6 Applications is centralized around the issue of a pest infestation of cockroaches and ants.

The Tenant testified that when she did her pre-move in walk through, she saw a cockroach sitting in the sink in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord prior to moving in on September 1, 2023, about the cockroaches and continuously from September 15, 2023, via email into December 2023 that there were cockroaches in her rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord had someone come and put gel in the rental unit in early September 2023. The Tenant testified that the Landlord gave her sticky pads to put in her unit and the Landlord said there was no activity so nothing else was done. The Tenant testified that the Landlord tried to have her sign a petition saying that another tenant caused the problem and also tried to blame the Tenant for bringing the cockroaches.

The Tenant also testified that there was an ant infestation at the property that was never addressed. The Tenant testified that the pest infestation was so bad that she had to make a decision to move out. The Tenant testified that she taped up all her doors and closets to prevent ants and cockroaches from entering her unit. The Tenant testified that she did not live in the rental unit and she did not cook in the rental unit because the cockroaches and ants were everywhere, in the walls, ceilings, and floors.

The Tenant testified that she was phobic and couldn’t sleep, she had to keep everything in bags and bins and her mental and physical health was greatly impacted by the Landlord’s failure to adequately address the pest infestation.

AA testified that there was no evidence of cockroaches when they keys were provided to the Tenant. AA testified that the rental unit was treated prior to the Tenant moving in. AA testified that there are yearly inspections of the residential complex and the complex is treated on average about ten times a year. AA testified that if a tenant complains about pests in their unit, they are provided with a sticky pad to place in the unit, and then it is given to head office if the sticky pad has proof of pests. Once head office provides a purchase order number, pest control is called, and the tenant is informed to prepare for a treatment.

AA testified that the Tenant’s rental unit was treated on or about September 22, 2023, with gel, and the Tenant was provided with sticky pads to monitor for further activity. AA testified that sticky pads were provided on November 22, 2023, and when they were inspected on November 28, 2023, no activity was seen as the sticky pads were empty.

AA testified that after a treatment there will sometimes be a bit of further activity, but it will taper off. AA testified that the Tenant’s unit has been re-rented and there have been no complaints of pests. AA testified that there have actually been two further new tenants in the rental unit since the Tenant and neither have complained of pests.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations, clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, as explained below.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden is the Tenant’s.

Here, I find that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s concerns of a pest infestation in an appropriate and timely manner. It was the Tenant’s evidence that after moving in on September 1, 2023, her first email complaint regarding cockroaches was September 15, 2023. The Landlord had someone attend the rental unit and treat the unit with roach gel, dust and trapping on or by September 22, 2023, within 8 days. I am satisfied that this was both timely and reasonable.

The Landlord’s evidence established that the sticky traps provided in November 2023 and left out for approximately six days provided no evidence of an active infestation. While the Tenant testified that there were cockroaches “everywhere, in the walls, ceiling, and floors”, some of the pictures provided did not support the testimony and showed a dead cockroach here or there while some of the pictures provided were unclear as to what was being shown and could have been a dead bug or a leaf or some other debris. Furthermore, the photos were mostly dated from late November 2023 to December 2023. Overall, the Tenant’s testimony of a severe pest infestation throughout her whole tenancy was not consistent with the one or two bugs shown in the photographs provided.
Based on the totality of the circumstances I do not find that the Landlord breached their responsibilities under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to any pest infestation.

As far as the Tenant’s claim regarding an ant infestation goes, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has met their burden to provide sufficient evidence to establish they informed the Landlord of their concern regarding an ant infestation. The Tenant’s testimony was that the Landlord was informed October 2023, and nothing was done. The Tenant’s evidence was vague, and the evidence was more focused on the cockroaches. As such, I am not satisfied that Tenant has established there was an ongoing issue with ants in the rental unit or residential complex.
Therefore, the Tenant’s T6 Application is dismissed. T2 Application
The Tenant’s T2 Application is also centralized around the pest infestation issue.

At the hearing, the Tenant clarified that the only claim being pursued on the T2 application was the claim of substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

Turning to the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord substantial interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex because of the Landlord’s failure to properly address the pest infestation. The Tenant’s testimony was that she informed the Landlord numerous times that she had mental health issues and that the accommodation that she required was to be let out of her lease early.

I am satisfied that what the Tenant is claiming is she required an accommodation based on a disability under the Human Rights Code, and the Landlord’s failure to accommodate was a substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Once the Tenant put the Landlord on notice of her particular mental health concerns, the Landlord had an obligation to accommodate the Tenant to the point of undue hardship, and my determination is then focused on whether there has been discrimination by the Landlord based on the Tenant’s disability. And whether the Landlord has accommodated the Tenant to the point of undue hardship.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 17: Human Rights, says: The Member must first determine whether the tenant falls within one or more of the categories contained in subsection 2(1) of the Code and has been discriminated against by the landlord. The Member must then determine whether the landlord has accommodated the tenant to the point of undue hardship. If the tenant's claim is successful, the Member has the authority pursuant to clause (f) of subsection 31(1) of the RTA to order the landlord to make necessary changes to the rental unit or residential complex to accommodate the tenant's needs.
Although the Guidelines are not binding on me, I do find them persuasive and do not see any reason to depart from the Guideline in this matter

The Tenant presented uncontested evidence that she has mental health diagnosis. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant is a person with a disability and is protected by the rights set out in subsection 2(1) of the Human Right Code R.S.O 1990 [name], (the “Code”).

The Tenant testified that she informed the Landlord several times of her mental health status and how the pest situation in her rental unit was affecting her mental health. The Tenant testified that the accommodation she was seeking was a termination of the lease.

The failure to accommodate a Human Rights issue under the Code is a serious issue, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord took any steps to accommodate the Tenant to the point of undue hardship in this matter.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

But pursuant to section 3(4) of the Act, if a provision of the Act conflicts with a provision of another Act, other than the Code, the provision of this Act applies. In the context where the Act conflicts with the Code, then the Act should be read in such a manner that there is no breach of the Code.

That means that failing to explore accommodation requirements under the Code and then failing to offer a substantive form of accommodation to a tenant constitutes a substantial interference with a tenant’s rights and a breach of section 22.

The problem that arises here is that the Tenant’s request to terminate the tenancy and insistence with the Landlord that the accommodation she sought to impose on the Landlord. But an accommodation seeker does not have the right to dictate to the Landlord the form of accommodation provided. It is up to the Landlord to craft a reasonable accommodation and then see if it works out.
However, the Landlord is still obligated to accommodate the Tenant to the point of undue hardship which has not been done here.
However, the Tenant was quite clear in her testimony that the only accommodation that she was seeking was a termination of her lease.

I am satisfied that the Landlord’s obligation to accommodate the Tenant’s disability was triggered. However, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has accommodated to the point of undue hardship. The Landlord presented no evidence on what attempts were made to accommodate the Tenant’s disability. While the Tenant could not insist on a particular accommodation, in this case termination of the lease, the Landlord presented no evidence on what attempts were made to engage in an accommodation dialogue with the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant was seeking an abatement of rent totaling $8,660.00 representing a 100% abatement for the full time she lived in the rental unit, plus $2,000.00 for the meals she had to purchase while not cooking in the unit. I am not satisfied that is appropriate for several reasons. First, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s duty to accommodate was triggered on or until the Tenant began requesting to terminate the tenancy due to the impact living in the unit was having on her mental health. At that time, I am satisfied the Landlord knew or should have known they had a duty to accommodate. As such, I am satisfied this is when the Landlord should have begun their accommodation inquiries.Therefore, any remedy flowing from the Landlord’s failure to accommodate should commence from when the Landlord’s duty to accommodate began.

Additionally, an abatement of rent is a contractual remedy that is meant to compensate a tenant for the portion of the “bundle of goods and services” that they contracted for under the tenancy agreement but was denied as a result of the landlord’s breach of the Act. The Tenant still had full use of the rental unit and therefore a 100% rent abatement plus additional sums is not appropriate.

Normally, the remedy I would order would be that the Landlord offer the Tenant a plan that reflects a reasonable accommodation of the Tenant’s disability. However, in this case, the Tenant has already vacated the rental unit and therefore the Landlord can no longer offer reasonable accommodation.

The Tenant began attempting to terminate the tenancy in October 2023 and testified about how severely living in the unit was impacting her mental health. I am satisfied that the Landlord’s reasonable accommodation could have been an agreement to terminate the tenancy given the impact of living in the rental unit was having on the Tenant.

The Tenant requests to terminate the tenancy as of December 31, 2023. I am satisfied this could have been a reasonable accommodation request and therefore the tenancy is terminated as of December 31, 2023.

I am also satisfied that a 25% rent abatement from October 2023 to December 2023 is also appropriate given the fairly significant impact the Landlord’s failure to accommodate had on the Tenant’s mental health.
Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,155.00 being a 25% rent abatement for October, November, and December 2023.
The Tenant is also requesting $500.00 to replace damaged or destroyed property however, I am not satisfied this is appropriate as this is not a result of the Landlord’s failure to accommodate.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 Application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T6 Application is dismissed.
The [name] is terminated as of December 31, 2023.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,203.00. This amount represents: • $1,155.00 for an abatement of rent for October 1, 2023, through December 31, 2023; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord submits that the Tenant’s application is statute-barred from being heard. The tenancy terminated on October 31, 2024; however, the Tenant’s application was not filed until November 1, 2025.

In reviewing the Board’s records, the Tenant’s application was not completed until November 1, 2025, although the Tenant states he began the application prior to the end of the day on October 31, 2024. The Tenant’s T5 application states the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2024.
Section 57(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) provides that no application can be made more than one year after the former Tenant vacated the rental unit.

Section 190(1) of the Act, states that the Board may extend or shorten the time requirements related to an application, but an application made pursuant to s. 57(2) of the Act is not included as one of the applications in which the Board has discretion.
Ontario Regulation 516/06, s.56(2), goes on further to state that the Board may not extend or shorten deadlines for filing applications, unless expressly permitted under s.190(1) of the Act.

Calculation of limitation periods is addressed in the Board’s Rules of Procedures: “[1.13] When something must be done within a specific number of days, the days are counted by excluding the first day and including the last day. [1.14] When the time for doing anything ends on a holiday as defined in these Rules the thing may be done on the next day that is not a holiday.”
I reviewed the calendar and found October 31, 2024, was a Thursday. Therefore, the calculation of time was not impacted by a weekend or holiday.

After explaining that his application was made beyond the limitation period thus statute- barred, the Tenant then changed his evidence to state that he was still in possession of the rental unit on November 1, 2025, because he had cleaning to do. Therefore, his application was made in time.

In considering the Tenant’s submission, the best evidence before me is the Tenant’s own application which stated the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2024. I am not persuaded that the Tenant’s oral testimony before me is credible on a balance of probabilities. I find it is more likely than not that the application accurately reflects the correct termination date because the Tenant, at the time of filing the application, would not have known his application would be statute-barred and would have not had any incentive to change his evidence.
I find that the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2024. Therefore, the one-year limitation period began on November 1, 2024, and ended on October 31, 2024.

Given the provisions of s. 57(2), the application is statute-barred, and pursuant to s. 190(1) of the Act, the Board has no authority to extend the deadline to an application made beyond that period. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
The Tenant further argues that disallowing his application will result in a miscarriage of justice.

The Board understands and appreciates the Tenant’s frustration. However, limitation periods serve several important functions as stated by [name] Robertson1, including: • create a defined time as to when potential defendants may be free of ancient obligations; • prompt claims to proceed before evidence is lost to the passage of time; • entice the plaintiff to act in a timely fashion; and • account for the plaintiffs’ own circumstances, as assessed through a subjective/objective lens, when assessing whether a claim should be barred by the passage of time (the discoverability principle). 1The Limitations Act: An Overview, 2005 CanLIIDocs 631

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Facts and Evidence:

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by failing to address the Tenant’s complaints about a tenant residing in the neighbouring unit, unit 406. According to the Tenant, the tenant in unit 406 made excessive noise, such as pounding on the wall at 2:00 a.m. or 3:00 a.m., yelling and banging. The Tenant alleged that despite having complained to the Landlord almost daily, the Landlord did not take reasonable steps to address and resolve the Tenant’s complaints.
The Tenant alleged that other residents also complained about the disruptive tenant in 406, but they did not want to get involved in the proceedings.

The Tenant further testified that police was called on several occasions; however, no police reports were submitted into evidence. According to the Tenant, the police said if the Tenant called them again, he would get arrested.
The Landlord’s position was that they did everything in their power to address the Tenant’s complaints.

According to the Landlord, the Tenant generally complained about the tenant in unit 406 when the Tenant paid rent, that is once a month, not daily as the Tenant initially testified. The Tenant subsequently confirmed the frequency of his complains to be monthly.

The Landlord’s property manager [name] testified that the Landlord posted letters and memos asking residents to be respectful of each other, and served the tenant in unit 406 several notices of termination (N5). The Landlord also considered filing an application to evict the tenant in unit 406 and sought and obtained legal advice. The Landlord was advised not to file an application with the LTB as they would not be successful. In fact the LL also served notice of termination to this Tenant.

According to the Landlord, the Tenant also complained about a previous resident of unit 406. The tenant in unit 406 at the time was an 80-year old woman. The Landlord was able to relocate her to another unit at the time.
NN stated that the tenant in unit 406 has been complaining about excessive noise coming from this Tenant’s unit as well.

The residential complex contains subsidized rental units, and as such, the Landlord required permission from the City to relocate either tenant; however the City denied the Landlord’s request. The residential complex is a newer building with fire and sound insulation. The rental unit 406 is outfitted to accommodate persons with physical disabilities.
The Tenant is currently on a waiting list to be transferred. Analysis:

The Tenant brought his application based on section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which states “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

The wording of section 22 only addresses the actions of the Landlord. However, in the present case the Landlord was not the agent by which the Tenant’s enjoyment was being disturbed. The Tenant’s enjoyment was disturbed by another tenant. When the agent of the disturbance is someone or something other than the landlord, a landlord may be held financially liable to a tenant under section 22 if it is established that the landlord failed to act reasonably in response to the tenant’s complaints about the disturbance.

The question then becomes did the Landlord respond reasonably to the Tenant’s complaints. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord acted reasonably in response to the Tenant’s complaints. The Landlord reached out to the tenants asking them to be polite and considerate of each other, gave several notices of termination, and considered filing an eviction application. The Landlord also attempted to transfer the Tenant. The Tenant is currently on a waiting list to be transferred.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
