issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on or about May 6, 2016 and still resides in the unit.

On or about October 28, 2025, the Landlord’s contractors illegally entered her rental unit, as they did not provide her with a 24-hour notice of entry. The Tenant stated that on that day, she left the rental unit around noon, and when she returned around 2:00pm, there were contractors on her balcony. The Tenant testified that she was aware the Landlord was conducting renovations to the balconies of the building, however the Superintendent assured her that they were not working on her side of the building. When she noticed this, she called the Superintendent and told him what was happening however, she did not receive a resolution from him. The Tenant testified that she was terrified this happened, as she works from home and had confidential client information on her laptop and paperwork on her desk. She did not expect anyone to enter the rental unit on that date.

The Tenant approached the contractors and asked who gave them permission to be there, and they advised her that a notice should have been given to her. The Tenant states that there was no 24-hour notice provided. The contractors destroyed various items on her balcony, which included grass that was installed, a pigeon net, lights, shoes and plants. This was a very frustrating situation as she was under the impression that no one was going to be working on her balcony, and if they were, they would give her a 24-hour notice of entry.

On or about the morning of October 29, 2025, she called [name], who is the Property Manager, and he stated that he is not involved in this however they have to put the items that were getting disposed of back on the balcony. She requested that he put this in writing however he refused. As of today, no one has repaired or replaced the items that were damaged.

The Tenant stated that this has had a negative impact on her, as she spent money on the balcony and now it is ruined. She went to the Police and reported this incident a few days later. The Tenant stated that [name] knows she works from home, and when entry is required, she receives a phone call but this time no one contacted her.

To support their application, the Tenant attempted to submit a video of the balcony. However, this video was not served on the Landlord in compliance with the Rules. The Tenant stated that it was uploaded to the Portal (“TOP”). The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that he did not review this specific document, only what was attached with the application when it was filed. He did not consent to service of evidence via TOP and therefore did not know that the Tenant was going to rely on this. Upon hearing these submissions, the Tenant was not permitted to submit this video as evidence as they did not comply with the Board’s Rules regarding disclosure.

During cross examination, the Tenant stated that she did not get any recent notice for this work. She was aware that the balconies were being repaired in August 2025, however other than this, she was not given a notice that her balcony was going to be repaired on October 28, 2025. In addition, she was advised by the Superintendent that her balcony was unaffected. The Tenant testified that she had items on her balcony, and she did not remove them prior to October 28 as she did not know that the contractors were coming on that day. She testified that she saw the contractors destroying her balcony, not working on it. Landlord’s Evidence Testimony of Tamoghna Mishra

The Landlord’s Agent, [name], who is the property manager testified that he has been working at the building for over a year and is responsible to maintain and manage the building. His duties include tenant relations, meaning if any tenants have a question or concern, he would assist in coming to a resolution. He testified that in 2025 there was a major roof leak which affected the structure of the balconies. Prior to him working for the building, there were City orders that were issued that needed to be resolved. The Landlord submitted a copy of the City Order dated March 7, 2025. Once these issues were identified, the Tenants were given a Notice that this work was going to commence. The Notice was posted on the notice board in the building. The Landlord submitted a photo of the Notice on the notice board dated September 3, 2025 as evidence to the Board, stating that starting on September 8, 2025 brick work will commence. This work included having to analyze the balconies, rectification work and water proofing. This involved the entire building, and this work was required to be done to overcome the unsafe building order from the City.

The Landlord provided a Notice of Entry dated September 4, 2025 stated that on September 9, 2025 contractors will be inspecting the balconies, the balconies must be cleared by September 8, 2025 and failure to do so may result in legal action being taken. A copy of this Notice of Entry was submitted as evidence to the Board. The Landlord submitted another Notice of Entry dated September 5, 2025 as evidence to the Board stating that balcony work will commence on September 8, 2025 and contractors will require access from the outside to the balconies. This notice also stated that the balconies must be clean for access and the work, and if they are not cleared legal action may be taken and delay charges may be issued. Furthermore, the notice stated that if there are pigeon nets, they must be removed and that it will be the responsibility of the tenant to put the pigeon nets back up at their own cost. The Landlord submitted a Notice of Entry dated September 10, 2025, as evidence to the Board, that stated the work had commenced on September 8, 2025 and reiterating what the Notice dated September 5, 2025 stated. [name] testified that these notices were also delivered on the door to each tenant. The tenants were all instructed to remove their belongings.

The Tenant was aware of this, as they were provided with the notices. The Landlord was not able to provide specific dates as the contractors were working with different sections of the building. The Tenant did not bring up any concerns with the notices, and he was not aware that the Tenant was told her balcony would not be affected. This was an ongoing process, and they were unable to specify the duration of the work.

Upon cross examination, the Tenant asked if there should have been a 24-hour notice provided, and [name] stated that the tenants were aware from September 10, 2025 that there was work going on. Testimony of Tewdros ([name]) Araya

The Landlord’s witness, [name], who is the building Superintendent testified at the hearing. He stated that he has been in this role for over 20 years, and one of his responsibilities include scheduling repairs. He was involved with the balcony repairs and the co-ordination of the contracts. He gave the Notices to the tenants advising to remove their items from their balcony. They were unable to provide exact dates and times to each tenant as to when the work would be done as this is a big job. Therefore, a blanket notice was given to all of the tenants. The Tenant called him complaining that the contractors removed her belongings, and he told the Tenant to call the office and speak with the Property Manager as he cannot make decisions regarding this issue.

Upon cross examination, when asked if he advised the Tenant that her balcony would remain untouched, he stated that he gave notice to everyone and maybe advised the Tenant what side they were currently working on however they were going to work on all of the balconies. On October 29, 2025, he stated that he may pass along the Tenant’s message to the property manager however he does not recall asking the Tenant to send an estimate.
Upon redirect examination, [name] stated that the Tenant was aware to remove all of the items from the balcony. Tenant’s Adjournment Request/Request to call witness
During the hearing, the Tenant requested an adjournment. She stated that she requires time to prepare documents, as what the Landlord’s witnesses are stating is not true.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative opposed the Tenant’s adjournment request. The T2 Application was filed in November 2025, and therefore the Tenant had plenty of time to upload and/or obtain documents for this hearing.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 outlines relevant considerations in determining whether or not an adjournment request should be granted, including: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

Having considered the factors outlined in the aforementioned Guideline, I find that the adjournment request amounts to the Tenant seeking to obtain documents hoping to potentially discredit the Landlord’s witnesses testimony. The Tenant did not request this adjournment from the onset of the hearing, but rather in the middle of the Landlord’s testimony. I do not find that the request is reasonable, it was made part way through a hearing, and I agree that the Board’s proceedings are to be managed in an expeditious manner. A change in litigation strategy, mid-way through a hearing, is not an appropriate ground for an adjournment.Accordingly, the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied.

During the Landlord’s testimony, the Tenant requested to call her witness to testify. The Tenant stated that she did not know what it meant when I asked her if she intends to call a witness to testify, and that is why she said no.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative opposed this request and stated that it would be inappropriate of the Tenant to now, during the Landlord’s testimony, call a witness.

Upon considering the Tenant’s request, I did not permit them to call their witness. The Tenant was asked after her testimony if she will be calling a witness to testify, and she stated that she will not be. I do not find it is appropriate that the Tenant call her witness, halfway through the Landlord’s testimony to provide evidence. I heard the Tenant’s submission that they may have not understood what I was asking, however the Tenant did not seek to obtain clarification and/or provide any indication that she was unaware that I was asking her if she intends to call her witness at this time. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord’s witness, [name] who is an engineer, testified at the hearing. [name] stated that his company deals with structural and restoration issues, and he has been in the field for approximately 15 years. The Landlord submitted photographs of the balconies as evidence to the Board. [name] stated that due to the state of the balconies, they had to commence their repair immediately. These repairs were significant and involved having to take off the railings of some of the balconies. The balconies were deteriorating which is a serious matter as it could be a safety concern. The reason the balconies needed to be clear of any belongings is to ensure that the work can be completed, as the contractors require access to the entire balcony. Testimony of [name]23. [name] testified as a witness for the Landlord, and he is a construction supervisor. He specializes in restoration and was involved with the balcony project at this building. He role was to oversee the project ensuring that it goes smoothly. The type of work that has been done was ordered by the City. The general conditions of the balcony resulted in them having to have major concrete repairs done. The access to the balcony was obtained through the exterior. He recalls that unit 202 did not have their items removed from the balcony as instructed, and they had to remove the net as they had to perform concrete work on the balcony. The Landlord submitted a copy of a letter from Waterbank Construction Ltd., dated April 14, 2026 which summarized the balcony repair at unit 202. The letter stated that the Tenant did not comply with the notice to remove all of the belongings in advance, and the crew was required to remove the netting in order to proceed with the scheduled work. 24. Upon cross examination, [name] testified that he was not the one that was working on this balcony, but he oversaw the entire project. He also testified that the Tenant was given additional time to remove the items from the balcony. Legal Analysis 25. Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states that: 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 27 (1). 26. Having considered the parties submissions, and based on balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit when they attended the balcony of the Tenant on October 28, 2025. I heard and considered the Landlord’s submissions, that there were notices provided, however I do not find that a notice provided on September 8, 2025, for work on October 28, 2025 is reasonable. I can appreciate that the Landlord may have not known when they will be working on a specific balcony, however I find they provided insufficient reasons as to why they were unable to provide a notice closer to the date they were able to work on the Tenant’s balcony so that they are able to prepare. I do find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord accessed the balcony through the exterior rather than through the Tenant’s rental unit, contrary to what the Tenant claimed. The Tenant was not home when the contractor accessed the balcony and I prefer the evidence of the Landlord’s witnesses, that access to the balcony was required through the exterior. Remedies Out-of-Pocket Expenses 27. The Tenant is requesting a total to $1,485.00 which represents the out of pocket expenses they will incur to replace the items that were damaged by the Landlord. The breakdown of this amount is as follows: $500.00 for the pigeon net installation, $200.00 for the pigeon net, $150.00 for the disposal, $200.00 for the lighting, $85.00 for the hanging plants, $200.00 for a grass mat and $90.00 for shoes. The Tenant did not submit any receipts regarding these amounts as they did not think this would happen and therefore did not keep receipts for these items. 28. The Landlord opposed this remedy as the Tenant did not provide any receipts to support these amounts. 29. I heard and considered the Tenant’s submissions regarding the cost to replace her belongings however I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved that they incurred and/or will incur costs on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant limited their submissions to general statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details, such as photographs of the items or estimates of the costs to replace these items. I am therefore unable to ascertain the reasonableness of the costs of these items. As such, I find the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claims in this regard. Administrative Fine 30. The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 31. While the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, I do not find that the Landlord’s actions warrant an administrative fine. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Tenant requested an adjournment. He testified that he did not receive the Notice of Hearing until January 26, 2026, and did not have time to prepare and gather evidence. The Tenant also testified that he phoned the Landlord and Tenant Board in October and was informed that his hearing date would be March 29, 2026.

The Tenant testified that he needed an adjournment to prepare and gather additional evidence. He testified that his wife had all the papers for the case, and she has passed away and he has been attempting to understand them. He also testified that he has spoken with a representative but had not yet signed a retainer. After the adjournment request was declined the Tenant revised this and testified that he had secured someone who had agreed to act as his representative if the matter were adjourned.

After considering the Tenant’s submission I elected to deny the adjournment request. Interpretation Guidelines 1 Adjourning and Rescheduling Hearings states: Parties are expected to make any necessary arrangement to proceed with a case management or merits hearing on the date set out in the Notice of Hearing. The granting of adjournments is at the discretion of the Member hearing the application or the Hearing Office conducting the case management. Pursuant to s. 21 of the SPPA, an adjournment will only be granted by the Board if it is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held. Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. Adjournment to Allow Representation Section 10 of the SPPA states that a party may be represented by a representative at a hearing. However, the right to representation is not absolute and an adjournment is not automatically granted when it is requested on this ground. The onus is on the party wishing to be represented to make all reasonable efforts to find a lawyer or paralegal able to represent them at the hearing once they become aware of the hearing date. A short adjournment may be allowed where a representative has been retained but is unavailable on the date set for the hearing, or where the party can demonstrate that they have made reasonable efforts to retain a lawyer or paralegal before the hearing but have not yet been able to do so. Adjournment to Prepare Case Both parties are expected to be prepared with their evidence, witnesses, and submissions on the scheduled hearing date, and adjournments are not generally granted because a party is not prepared to proceed. If a party requests an adjournment to acquire necessary evidence or secure the attendance of a witness, the Member may consider whether the party attempted to acquire the evidence or witness as soon as they became aware it would be required. The Member may also consider whether options other than adjournment are sufficient, such as taking a short recess, proceeding with the hearing and reconvening the hearing at a later date to consider the additional evidence or witness’s testimony, or accepting the evidence on a post-hearing basis. If the applicant's claims are unclear or not detailed enough to allow the respondent to know what evidence they must present at the hearing, the Member may consider whether the application should be dismissed or adjourned to permit the applicant to provide further details. In deciding whether the claim is sufficiently complete and clear, the Member will evaluate the application, documents filed with it and any information the respondent already has.

While the Tenant testified that he did not receive the Notice of Hearing until January 26, 2026, I note that the Boards records indicate that the Notice of Hearing was mailed to the parties on January 2, 2026. Therefore, it was be deemed received on January 7, 2026. I am satisfied that this allows the Tenant adequate time to prepare for the proceeding and gather and serve any relevant evidence.

I also note that this Application was before the Board for an Adjudicative Case Conference on June 24, 2025, where it was adjourned to a merits hearing. Therefore, the Tenant has known since June 2025 that the matter would be proceeding to a merit hearing, and has had adequate time to gather and submit evidence and secure representation.

With respect to the Tenant’s assertion that he contacted the Board in October and was informed that his hearing would be held on March 29, 2026, I see no indication of this in the Portal, and the Tenant did not provide any documentation to corroborate that he was informed of a March 29, 2026, hearing date.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for an adjournment to secure representation, I note that the right to representation is not absolute, and the Tenant has had adequate time since the Case Conference to select and retain representation, and I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that an adjournment is necessary on this basis.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant has had adequate to prepare and submit evidence and secure representation. The Board has a duty to be expeditious, and I am not satisfied that it would be an expeditious use of the Boards time to grant an adjournment in these circumstances. I also note that the Landlord intends to raise a preliminary issue with respect to whether the Act applies and find that it would be an expeditious use of both the Board and the parties time to address this preliminary issue before an adjournment is granted. The Act does Not Apply
At the hearing the Landlord’s Agent indicated that the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear this Application as the tenancy is a Commercial tenancy not a residential tenancy.
The Tenant disputed this and testified that the tenancy was both commercial and residential.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

The Landlord testified that the tenancy between the parties began November 1, 2023 and relied on a lease agreement between Konstantine Takis and [name] [name] (the [name] name prior to hyphenation after marriage). The lease agreement clearly indicates at paragraph 13 that the Tenant agrees to use the space for the re-sale of antiques (display and sell) and that any other use shall be requested in writing to the Landlord and will need approval by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that the unit is the ground floor of a building which is mixed commercial and residential, with the upper units being residential units, and the ground floor being a commercial storefront unit. He described the unit as having one large room, with two smaller rooms off of it. He testified that there was a small toilet and sink in the basement, but no kitchen or living area.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant used the space, which is a commercial storefront, to buy and sell antiques and other items including tables, chairs, and refrigerators. The Landlord testified that to his knowledge the Tenant never occupied the unit residential.

The Landlord also relied on an Enbridge gas bill in the name of “Global Humanitarian Education Missions” and [name] (the Tenant’s partner) and a letter from Wawanesa Insurance indicating the commercial property policy on the unit had been cancelled on October 24, 2024. The Landlord testified that the fact that the Tenant had placed the gas bill in the name of his business and secured commercial property insurance demonstrates that the unit was used commercially.
The Landlord also relied on an Inspection Order from the Hamilton Fire department which he indicated described the unit as commercial.

The Landlord also indicated that the Tenant had a residential property which he resided in at the time the commercial lease was signed, and where he still resides now. He testified that there was no traffic or comings and goings in the unit during the evening hours, as it was not used as a residence by the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that the unit was both commercial and residential, and that he had both used the unit as a store front and resided there. He testified that the Landlord was aware of his intention to both reside in and operate form the rental unit.

He testified that while he did have another residential unit, where he now resides, that unit had been subleased in order to free up capital to live and work in this rental unit. The Tenant disputed that the unit did not contain a kitchen and indicate that there were two kitchens within the unit.

The Tenant denied signing the lease relied on by the Landlord and testified that there had been no lease between the parties and the Landlord had demanded payment in cash from him each month. The Tenant initially testified that he first rented the unit in the spring of 2023 but later revised this to indicate that he had moved in September 2023.

He agreed that he had secured commercial property insurance and testified that he registered the gas bill in his business’s name in order to apply for tax breaks and assistance from city hall. However, he was unsuccessful in obtaining these as the unit was zoned residential and not commercial. Analysis

On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the tenancy between the parties is commercial. And therefore, the Act does not apply. Even if I were not satisfied that the tenancy is commercial, I would still find that the act does not apply by operation of Section 5(j).

I found the testimony of the Landlord to be both credible and reliable. While the Tenant was credible, I did not find his testimony to be as reliable, as it was somewhat inconsistent, for example with respect to the commencement of the lease agreement. Therefore, on the whole, I prefer the testimony of the Landlord over that of the Tenant.

The lease agreement between the parties clearly indicates the unit is to be used as a storefront. However, I am not satisfied that my analysis should end there as while the lease is relevant, I am not satisfied that it is determinative of the relationship between the parties. I note that [name], [1998] O.J. No. 3466 (‘Fiset’) the court determined that: “the form of the lease document is not irrelevant but it is not determinative.” The court also said that “if the intent was to occupy the premises as residential premises or if in fact the premises were occupied and, as I have found, known to be occupied, as residential premises, it does not matter what is said in the lease documents. Therefore, I am satisfied that further analysis is warranted.

I do not accept the Tenant’s submissions that he did not sign the lease agreement. It clearly bears his name and signature and given my concerns with the Tenant’s reliability, I am prepared to accept that the lease was signed by the parties.

I also accept that the commercial property insurance and gas bill, which has been placed into the name of the Tenant’s business, both support the conclusion that the unit was used for commercial purposes rather than residential. While the Tenant claims to have occupied the rental unit and used it for a dual purpose he did not rely on any documentation in support of this claim, and I am prepared to accept the Landlord’s testimony that he never observed the tenant occupying the unit as a residence.

Even if I were to accept the Tenant’s claims that he resided in the unit while using it as a business, I am not satisfied that the intention of the parties was ever to create a residential tenancy, and I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the property was intended to be used commercially.
Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy between the parties was commercial in nature.

I also note that even if I were to accept the Tenant’s testimony that he also resided in the rental unit, it would still be exempt from the Act under Section 5(j) which states that the act does not apply to: ( j ) premi ses occupi ed for busi ness or agri cul tural purposes wi th l i vi ng accommodati on attached i f the occupancy for both purposes i s under a si ngl e l ease and the same person occupi es the premi ses and the l i vi ng accommodati on.

Therefore, even if I were to accept the Tenant’s submissions that the unit is both commercial and residential, and that he both resided in the rental unit, and used it as business, the Act would not apply as the unit would be deemed exempt under Section 5(j).
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 24100 Date: 2026-03-25 In the matter of: 2103, 40 [address] Toronto ON Ltd. (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them. This application was heard by videoconference on March 18, 2026. [name] (JS), and the Landlord’s legal representative, Brittney-Rose Ward, attended the hearing.
reasons: This is not a care home, but it does concern the rental unit as identified. The rental unit is in a multi-residential building and the applicant before the Board is an Occupant of the rental unit and not a Tenant of the rental unit based on the following findings.
The Tenant of the rental unit is [name] as found under LTB-L-007151-25 issued on June 2, 2025 and also identified in their T2 application under LTB-T-018632-25.

The [name] was living in the rental unit at the invitation of the Tenant as evidence by the email correspondence between the Tenant, the Occupant and the Landlord starting on or about August 7, 2024 and August 12, 2024. The Tenant had permitted the Occupant to stay in their rental unit while they were away in Pakistan caring for their ailing mother. The evidence before me was that the Tenant intended to return to the rental unit after caring for their mother, however, there was no certain date of return as of early November of 2024.

On August 26, 2024 the [name] confirmed with the Landlord by email that they would be paying the rent for the month of August and September for the Tenant as discussed. After correcting the issue on the draft regarding the proper naming of the Landlord, the draft was accepted by the Landlord in September of 2024 for two months rent. The [name] also paid the rent on behalf of the Tenant for October of 2024.

According to the Occupant’s evidence, the Tenant approved for them to stay in their unit for a temporary period because they left for Pakistan to care for their ailing mother and the [name] was willing to pay the ongoing rent while the Tenant was away. I also accept that there were discussions privy to the Tenant and the Occupant about sharing the rental unit upon the Tenants return from Pakistan.

However, on or about October 21, 2024 based on the [name] email correspondence evidence, it was suggested that the [name] would be taking over the Tenant’s lease and replacing them as the Tenant to which the Landlord would not agree and rather made references to being possibly approved as a subtenant pending their application to the Landlord and signatures of the named leaseholder Tenants.

On November 7, 2024 the Landlord denied the [name] request for a lease take-over and notes that they are now an unauthorized occupant of the unit and must vacate the rental unit immediately. The [name] vacated the rental unit shortly thereafter in November of 2024.

The Landlord submits that there is no Landlord and Tenant relationship between the Occupant and the Landlord and therefore the [name] has no standing before the Board to make a T2 Application. The Landlord motions that the application be dismissed on this basis as the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply to this relationship.

It is also worth noting that the Tenant did eventually moved back into the rental unit on February 24, 2025 as per the L1 application order stating the same under LTB-L-007181- 25 issued June 2, 2025.
I agree with the Landlord for the following reasons:
The evidence before me establishes that JB was not a tenant, or a subtenant as defined by the Act.

Section 2(1) of the Act defines the following: 1. “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit… 2. “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit.
Section 97(1) of the Act stats that a tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord.

A true sublet for the purposes of section 97 of the Act is when there is a clear period of time in which the proposed subtenant is to occupy the rental unit which includes an end date of their occupancy based on a tenants date of return to the rental unit. It cannot be said that a true subtenancy exists if there is no defined end date. For example, subsection 97(5) of the Act stats that a subtenant has no right to occupy the rental unit after the end of the subtenancy. Also, with a subtenancy, the head tenant remains liable to the landlord for their obligations under their lease (subsection 97(4)). The reason the end date is important is because the Act specifically contemplates what happens when a subtenancy ends and the subtenant refuses to vacate the rental unit. In such a case the Tenant may apply to the LTB to evict the subtenant and claim compensation for unpaid rent and other specific charges (section 99 of the Act).

An assignment of the rental unit on the other hand is a complete taking over of the lease. A true assignment is where a tenant requests and receives consent from the Landlord to transfer their leasehold interests to another person. This in essence relinquishes a tenant’s rights to the unit after the assignment and the new tenant takes over the lease with the landlord.

In accordance with subsection 202(1) of the Act, in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. (Emphasis added)

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 21 titled “Landlords, Tenants, [name] and Residential Tenancies” states in part: There is no definition of "occupant" in the RTA. For the purposes of proceedings at the LTB, an "occupant" may be considered to be a person who is not a tenant but who lives in a rental unit as their principal place of residence. An occupant may be authorized or unauthorized depending on the facts of each case… If a tenant does not vacate the rental unit but allows another person to live in the rental unit with them, a sublet is not created within the meaning of the Act. In such a case there is no landlord and tenant relationship between the tenant and that person or between that person and the landlord. In that case, no consent of the landlord is required and the other person is a roommate of the tenant and/or an occupant of the tenant's rental unit. A tenant can allow people to occupy the rental unit with the tenant but the tenant cannot subdivide the rental unit into more than one rental unit. For example, if a tenant rents an entire home, the tenant may permit a person to live in and have exclusive use of the basement of that home, however, the home, including the basement, remains the rental unit. That person would be a roommate of the tenant or an occupant of the rental unit and the roommate/occupant has no protection under the Act…. (Emphasis Added)

Section 98(1) states that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.

It is clear based on the pattern of activities that the [name] is not a Tenant. They were not approved for the lease-take over as an assignment. They paid the rent on behalf of the Tenant and not as a tenant of the rental unit based on the evidence before me.

Additionally, even though the [name] was given their own parking spot and parking ticket by the Landlord, this does not make them a Tenant for the purposes of the Act. There was never an agreement or consent from the Landlord to assign the tenancy to the Occupant. In fact, this request was explicitly declined by the Landlord based on the email correspondence on November 7, 2024.

It appears based on the email correspondence that the Tenants intentions of the rental unit were unclear and so were the intentions of the Occupant. They were unclear on which date that the Tenant would return to the rental unit to maintain full time occupancy or whether they were assigning the totality of their lease to the Occupant. I would not find it to be unreasonable for the Landlord to decline the Occupants application in this respect because of the uncertain intentions of the Tenant and the miscommunications regarding the intended use of the unit by the [name] and the Tenant. More specifically, whether it was in fact a request to sublet the unit or a request to assign the unit.

Even if it were the actual Tenant that filed this T2 application, it would also likely fail on the basis that the true substance of the application is about an allegation that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refused to allow the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to another person. In this regard, the proper application would be an A2 application pursuant to subsection 98(1) of the Act and not a T2 application pursuant to subsection 29(1) of the Act.
Since I find that the Act does not apply to the relationship between the Occupant and the Landlord, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The T2 Application is dismissed. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $198.00.
The parties agreed that the rental unit is a room in a rooming house and the Tenant vacated May 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that on November 8, 2024, he received a call from the Landlord informing him that she had entered his room to turn off his fan. The Tenant testified that just previous to this he had missed a call from the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that she had entered the Tenant’s room to turn off his fan because she received several calls from other [name] who were concerned that they heard the Tenant’s fan short circuiting in his room. She testified that she called the Tenant several times and he did not answer so she messaged the Tenant to inform him he would be entering his room to turn off the fan. She testified that when she entered the fan was making a short-circuiting sound, and she turned it off.

Interpretation Guideline 19 states: Sections 26 and 27 of the RTA describe the situations in which a landlord may enter the rental unit. Entry without notice Section 26 provides that a landlord may enter the rental unit without notice: • in cases of emergency; • If the tenant consents to the landlord entering the unit at the time the landlord enters; • where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to clean the rental unit at regular intervals, the landlord may enter at the times specified in the agreement, or, if no times are specified, between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.; and • if the landlord and the tenant have agreed the tenancy will be terminated or one of them has given notice of termination to the other, the landlord may enter the unit to show it to prospective tenants between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. and, before entering, the landlord informs or makes a reasonable effort to inform the tenant of the landlord's intention to enter. A landlord must make reasonable efforts, depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case, to give the tenant advance notice in order to permit the tenant to be prepared for entry into the unit by the landlord to show the unit to prospective tenants. A landlord may not enter the rental unit without notice to perform repairs even where the tenant has requested the repairs unless the landlord obtains the tenant's consent to enter the unit at the time the landlord goes to the unit to make the repairs. Entry with notice Section 27 provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry in the following circumstances: • to carry out a repair or replacement or to do work in the unit; • to allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit; • to allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998; • to carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the RTA; and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. • for any other reasonable reason for entry set out in the tenancy agreement. In addition, s. 27(2) of the RTA provides that the landlord, or, with the landlord's written authorization, a broker or salesperson registered under the Real Estate and Business Brokers Act, 2002, may enter a rental unit provided that they have given written notice to the tenant at least 24 hours before they enter to allow a potential purchaser to view the unit. In any case where at least 24 hours written notice has been given to the tenant, the written notice must set out: • the reason for entry; • the date the landlord will enter; and • the time of entry between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.

While the guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. It does not appear to be disputed that the Landlord failed serve the Tenant with a valid notice of entry at least 24 hours in advance setting out the reason for the entry, the date, or the entry and the time of the entry.

It is also clear that the Tenant did not consent to the entry. The Landlord appears to rely on an assertion that they entered because of an emergency, however I do not accept this argument. The Landlord provided no documentation to verify that the fan was short circuiting at the time she entered or otherwise at risk of causing a fire. With the benefit of hindsight it is clear that the fan did not short circuit or cause a fire. However, I have also considered whether at the time the Landlord had a genuine belief that it was a fire risk and am not satisfied this is the case.

None of the Tenant’s who believed the fan posed a fire risk were called to testify, and while the Landlord provided a affidavit from a Tenant [name], it is vague and asserts only that the Tenant “was aware that concerns were raised by other Tenant’s about a potential fire hazard” It does not identify a date for these concerns, and does not indicate that the speaker themselves had any such concerns.

Instead, I am prepared to infer, given the Landlord’s clear aversion to utility usage, explored further in this order, that her entry was motivated not by fear of fire, but to turn off the Tenant’s fan while he was not in the room to reduce utility usage.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. The Laundry Room

The Tenant testified that the Landlord locked the laundry room from between 7:00am and 7:00pm from November 1, 2024, to November 24, 2024, when it was officially reopened, though he testified that it may have been unlocked “unofficially” earlier. The Tenant also testified that it was sometimes left locked beyond 7:00pm or locked when his clothes were inside.
The Tenant testified that the lease does not speak to laundry usage. However, he had a discussion with the Landlord and agreed not to do laundry during peak electricity hours.
The Tenant allowed that he would sometimes do laundry during these peak usage hours.

The Landlord disagreed that the laundry room was locked from November 1, 2024 to November 24, 2024. While she struggled to provide the dates that the laundry room was locked she testified that it was only locked for a total of two days.

The Landlord testified that the lease does not discuss laundry, but there was a verbal agreement before and during signing that the Tenant would not do laundry during peak hours. These being Monday – Friday from 7:00am to 7:00pm. The Landlord testified that she pays the first $400.00 of any utilities incurred by the complex and any excess charges were passed through to the Tenant’s. Therefore, all the Tenants all Tenants agreed not to do laundry during so no charges would be incurred.
The Landlord testified that she was receiving complaints from the other Tenant’s that the Tenant was breaking this agreement and doing laundry during peak hours, so she locked the laundry room.

With respect to the length of time the room was locked I prefer the evidence of the Tenant over that of the Landlord as parties had previously indicated that they agreed that the laundry room was locked from November 1, 2024, to November 24, 2024, and while the Landlord claimed it was locked for only two days she had difficulty recalling when this occurred.

With respect to substantial interference, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the locking of the room alone constitutes substantial interference as the parties had previously agreed that the laundry room would not be used between 7:00am and 7:00pm.

However, on at least one occasion it appears that the laundry room was locked while the Tenants clothing was still inside, and I am satisfied that this conduct interferes with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and ought reasonably be known to be unwelcome by the Landlord, as it prevented the Tenant from accessing his clothing.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Harassment

The Tenant testified that on November 8, 2024 the Landlord locked the laundry room while the his clothing was inside and left it locked beyond 7:00pm. He testified that he sent the Landlord a message about this, and the Landlord attended the rental unit. He testified that he could not recall who raised their voice first, but that the discussion escalated into a shouting march and the Landlord yelled at and belittled him and told him that he was the worst Tenant ever.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant asked her to come and unlocked the laundry room around 5:30pm and when she opened the door the Tenant pushed it back towards her and told her that she was not allowed to enter without notice. She testified that the Tenant was the aggressor during the interaction and while she allowed that she had raised her voice she testified that there was not shouting match between the parties and denied calling the Tenant any names, or using foul language.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord harassed him. The term harassment is not defined in the Act, however the Board often applies the definition from the Ontario Human Rights Code, which is engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. To determine whether a landlord's conduct harasses, obstructs, coerces, threatens or interferes with a tenant, the LTB will generally consider the cumulative effect of the landlord's conduct upon the tenant in the context of the landlord-tenant relationship.

In this case I found the parties to be equally credible and reliable with respect to the events of November 8, 2024, and no witnesses were called to testify as to the events of November 8, 2025. Ultimately as this is a Tenant’s application the onus is on the Tenant to demonstrate that the Landlord harassed him, which is denied by the Landlord, while I am prepared to accept that the parties engaged in a heated discussion, I note that the Tenant indicated that he could not recall who raised their voice first, and I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord was the aggressor during this interaction, or that her behaviour constitutes harassment.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant sough a rent abatement of $150.00. Given that I have found the Landlord both entered the unit illegally and interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment, I am satisfied that this modest abatement is appropriate. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $150.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also sought a fine. While I have found in the Tenant’s favour in a limited way, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour was so egregious as to warrant a fine. The illegal entry was a limited single occurrence, and the interface comparatively minor. Therefore, I am not satisfied that a fine is appropriate.

The Tenant also sought a rent differential of $150.00 and moving expense of $101.10. However, I am not stated that the Tenant has demonstrated that they vacated the rental unit because of the Landlord’s actions or that it was reasonable to do so. I note that the Landlord’s infractions were relatively minor and occurred in November 2024, and the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit until May 31, 2025. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that they moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions, and declined to award a differential or moving costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $198.00. This amount represents: • $150.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The written lease shows that the properly named Landlord is [organization]., and the named Landlord has been accordingly amended. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-092519-23 issued on July 18, 2025. On July 21, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On July 23, 2025, interim order LTB-T-092519-23-RV-IN was issued staying the order issued on July 18, 2025. On August 15, 2025, interim order LTB-T-092519-23-.RV-IN2 was issued granting the request to review the order, and sending the application to be heard de novo.
reasons: The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 28, 2023, and she moved out on October 31, 2023. The residential complex is a house divided into three different units. The applications arose because the Tenant said that she was unable to live in the rental unit because of an overpowering smell of cat pee, and she was therefore obliged to move out only a few weeks after moving in. She alleges that the Landlord refused to return her last month’s rent deposit, and he owes her expenses of moving.
The only requested remedies in the Tenant’s T6 application relate to repair, therefore, since the Tenant has already moved out the T6 application is moot, and it will be dismissed.

The Tenant said that she moved into the rental unit on September 28, 2023. The monthly rent was $1,600.00 plus $150.00 per month hydro, due on the first day of the month. She paid $3,722.60 upon moving in, which included first and last month’s rent plus a pro rata amount for three days in September 2023, plus $50.00 for a key deposit.

The Tenant said that she moved out a month later because there was a cleanliness issue, a barking dog noise, and a terrible smell of cat urine. She submitted into evidence texts to a property manager, [name] (DD) complaining about dog barking and cat urine, commencing on October 7, 2023.

The Tenant said that she did not inform the Landlord about her intention to move out because she was never given contact details for the Landlord. She said that on October 28, 2023, she told DD that she was “done” and she cancelled the November rent cheque, and moved out by October 31, 2023. She submitted into evidence a handwritten note to the Landlord, dated October 31, 2023, asking for her last month’s rent back.

The Tenant said that the Landlord told her he would return her last month’s rent if he were able to rent the unit for November 2023, and she said that new people moved into the rental unit on November 10, 2023. Nevertheless, she said that the Landlord refused to return her money for the remaining days of November 2023.

The Landlord’s agent, [name] (RB) said that the unit was re-rented for November 13, 2023. He said that he had to pay a further $988.50 to re-rent the unit by November 13, 2023, and he submitted his invoice from his rental agent into evidence. He said that the new lease was for the same rent as that paid by the Tenant. Reasons and Analysis:
As noted above, the Tenant’s T6 application is moot, and it will be dismissed.

With respect to the Tenant’s T2 application, she has asked for moving expenses and financial costs for cancelling her post-dated cheques because the Landlord’s actions, or their failure to address her concerns, forced her to terminate the tenancy early.

I find that the Tenant has not proved, on a balance of probabilities, that she was forced to move out of the rental unit because of the Landlord’s failure to act about her concerns for the reasons that follow. She is therefore not entitled to her requested remedies on the T2 application.

The Tenant testified that she first told DD about the cat urine problem on October 13, 2023, and he responded by speaking to the neighbour, as well as bringing her air fresheners the very next day. She said that as of October 26, 2023, the neighbour had told DD that she would get the cat fixed. The Tenant said that she decided to leave the next day, and she did, in fact move out by the end of October 2023.

I find that the Tenant has prime facie, failed to prove any breach of the Act on the part of the Landlord. The Landlord responded to her complaint about the neighbour immediately, and they managed to get a commitment from the neighbour to deal with the cat urine issue within a few days. The Tenant nevertheless chose to move out right away before the neighbour had an opportunity to remedy the situation.

The Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints about the neighbour in a timely, appropriate and effective manner, but the Tenant chose to move out and break her lease without giving the required notice pursuant to sections 44 and 47 of the Act.
Consequently, the Tenant’s T2 application will be dismissed.

With respect to the T1 application, the facts are undisputed. The Tenant gave insufficient notice. She told the Landlord she was moving out only a few days before she vacated the rental unit. The Landlord fulfilled their requirement under section 16 of the Act to mitigate the loss by re-renting the rental unit within two weeks, as of November 13, 2023. The Landlord did not return the pro rata amount of rent paid for the days of November 13 through November 30, 2023.

The Landlord’s evidence is that they did not return the remaining days of rent for November 2023 to the Tenant because her lack of notice forced the Landlord to spend another $988.50 to re-advertize the unit for rent.

Although there is no doubt that the Tenant’s early departure cost the Landlord extra money to re-advertize the unit a year earlier than they otherwise would have been obliged, there is no provision of the Act that permits the Landlord to unilaterally pass on advertising charges to the Tenant. The Landlord is only authorized to charge extra days of rent, after a Tenant vacates, pursuant to section 88 of the Act, when the Tenant has given insufficient notice of their departure.

Although the Tenant gave insufficient notice of her departure, the Landlord was also obliged to mitigate their loss, which they did. They re-rented the rental unit by November 13, 2023. The Landlord is therefore only entitled to rent until November 12, 2023, an extra 12 days of rent after the Tenant’s departure, because of the Tenant’s insufficient notice. The Landlord shall reimburse the Tenant for 18 days of rent in November 2023, or $57.53 X 18=$1,035.54.
ordered: All previous orders, LTB-T-092519-23 issued on July 18, 2025, and interim orders LTB-T- 092519-23-RV-IN issued on July 23, 2025 and LTB-T-092519-23-RV-IN2 issued on August 15, 2025, are cancelled. They are replaced by the following order.
The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are dismissed.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,083.54 which consists of: (a) $1,035.34 reimbursement of a portion of the last month’s rent deposit, (b) $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the amount owing on or before January 20, 2026. If the Landlord fails to pay the Tenant the full amount on or before January 20, 2026, then they shall start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: y agreement with the Tenants on July 14, 2025. PD and PH are listed as the landlords on the tenancy agreement, but SD signed the agreement as a landlord. LTB-L-078767-25 3. The Act defines a “landlord” as including, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent. 4. The Tenants only named SD as a landlord on their application while the Landlords only named PD as a landlord on their application. 5. SD clearly permitted occupancy of the rental unit. He also attempted to enforce the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement of the Act by collecting rent and a deposit. Accordingly, I am satisfied SD meets the definition of a landlord and is properly named in this proceeding. The Landlords’ application is amended to include SD as a named landlord. 6. PD and PH are the owners of the rental unit. As such, the Tenants’ application is amended to include both PD and PH as named landlords. LTB-L-078767-25
reasons: The Landlords maintain that the tenancy is exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i), which states that the Act does not apply with respect to: a. living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.
It is the position of the Landlords that the Tenants are required to share a kitchen facility with the owner. Landlords’ evidence
The rental unit is the basement of a single-family home. The rental unit has a kitchen and bathroom. The Landlords reside in the main unit of the home.

It is the evidence of the Landlords that they used the kitchen in the basement while their unit was being renovated. They argued that the rental unit was advertised as having a LTB-L-078767-25 shared kitchen and that they would provide the Tenants with advance notice as a courtesy when they wanted to use the basement kitchen.
In support of their position, the Landlords pointed to the lease agreement and rental advertisement which indicates the kitchen is a shared facility. Tenants’ evidence

The Tenants testified that the rental unit was advertised as a self-contained unit with a fully equipped kitchen, including a sink, refrigerator, oven, toaster, and microwave. The Tenants admitted into evidence a copy of their tenancy agreement which does not indicate the kitchen is a shared facility with the owner. Law and Analysis

It is important to note that the Act is remedial legislation. Section 1 of the Act provides that: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.

Given the purpose of the Act, any claim that the Act does not apply has to be examined carefully to ensure that protections provided by the Legislature to residential tenants are not easily avoided (Grenadier (Tenants of v. We-Care Retirement Homes of Canada, [1993] O.J. No.1550 (Div. Court.)). A liberal interpretation of the exemptions from the Act would undermine the objectives of the Act.
In making findings on an application, section 202 of the Act requires me to determine the real substance of all transactions and activities pertaining to a rental unit with respect to this tenancy.

The onus or burden of proving an exemption applies rests on the person claiming the exemption on a balance of probabilities. Case law dealing with section 5(i) essentially establishes a two-part test and the party relying on the exemption must establish both: a. Is the occupant required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and b. Does the owner, spouse, child or parent living in the building in which the living accommodation is located.
As the Landlords are the persons claiming the exemption, the onus is on them to prove on a balance of probabilities the two-part test outlined above. LTB-L-078767-25

There is case law standing for the proposition that the first part of the test includes establishing that the tenancy agreement must include the requirement to share a kitchen and a bathroom (see TET-82410-17 (Re), 2018 CanLII 113120 (ON LTB)).

Both parties admitted into evidence a copy of the tenancy agreement. The agreements are both signed and dated July 14, 2025 and are identical except for the description of the kitchen under paragraph 1. The Landlords’ version indicates it is a “fully equipped kitchen (shared)” while the Tenants’ version indicates it is a “fully equipped kitchen”.

I am not persuaded the Landlords’ version is the version that was presented to the Tenants. I say this because the laundry is described on both versions as “shared laundry with landlord”. I believe that had the Landlords intended for the kitchen to be shared at the commencement of the tenancy, they would have been consistent with their language and would have described it as “shared fully equipped kitchen” rather than “fully equipped kitchen (shared)”.

I am also not persuaded by the advertisement relied upon by the Landlords. The advertisement does not specify that the kitchen is to be shared with the owners. There was no evidence before me establishing that the Landlords made it clear to the Tenants that they would be required to share a kitchen with the owners. I find that it is more likely than not the Landlords modified the agreement after it had been signed by the parties.

The Landlords had a full kitchen in their main unit. The fact that their kitchen was unavailable during renovations does not change the terms of the tenancy agreement. Accordingly, I find the Tenants were not required to share a kitchen with the Landlords. The Landlords have failed to sufficient establish the tenancy is exempt pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act.

It should be noted that PD and PH seem to argue that the tenancy is not valid because SD was not authorized to rent the unit. As explained above, SD meets the definition of landlord as he permitted occupancy and collected rent and deposits. LTB-T-092542-25 Determinations
The Tenants filed a T1 application alleging the Landlords gave them an N12 notice to end the tenancy but did not pay them compensation by the termination date on the notice.
For the reasons that follow, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.

A landlord is required to compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent if a landlord gave a tenant notice under section 48 or 49 of the Act. These sections read as follows: LTB-L-078767-25 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located. 49 (1) A landlord of a residential complex that contains no more than three residential units who has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by, (a) the purchaser; (b) the purchaser’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the purchaser, the purchaser’s spouse, or a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

The tenancy commenced on July 31, 2025. PD alleges that he was unaware SD had rented the basement unit. On August 29, 2025, PD discovered the Tenants were residing in the basement and instructed SD to immediately terminate the tenancy. On September 29, 2025, SD advised the Tenants that they would have to vacate by November 1, 2025

The Tenants did not present any evidence establishing they were advised they had to vacate because of one of the reasons listed under section 48 or 49 of the Act. As such, I am not convinced the Tenants received notice to end the tenancy under section 48 or 49. Given this, the Landlords were not obligated to pay the Tenants one month’s compensation. [name]23. Having found the Act applies, and that [name] meets the definition of a Landlord under the Act, I find that he wilfully breached this Act by holding himself out as a Landlord when he did not have permission from the owners to bind the property. This represents an egregious breach of legal obligations that must be deterred. 24. The Board has the authority to issue an administrative fine to enforce compliance with the Act and deter egregious conduct pursuant to section 57(3). LTB-L-078767-25 25. To do so, I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenants, and any other relevant factors. 26. As a result of his actions, the Tenants made life decisions to move into the property, enter a lease, and then had to find alternate housing on short notice, with an impending winter. His attempt at helping out newcomers to Canada turned out to be not only an embarrassment but completely at odds with his intention. 27. His behaviour demonstrates a Landlord’s complete ignorance and disregard of his obligations and their consequences under the Act. As a result, [name] shall pay a fine to the Board in the amount of $1,000.00.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies. 2. [name] will pay an administrative fine of $1000.00 payable to the Board by May 14, 2026. LTB-T-092542-25 1. The application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
