issues: Ma (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the Adjudicative Case Conference held June 24, 2025, the Tenant was advised to organize their evidence and serve the Landlord at least 7 days prior to the hearing. The Tenant testified that the organized evidence is at line #5874345 on the portal and one new piece of evidence is at line #5874352, both of which were served to the Landlord on January 18, 26, at 9:10 p.m; the email was the one used to pay the rent and did not bounce back as undeliverable. The matter proceeded on its merits. Merits
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: .
Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant as set out below.
The tenancy began September 12, 2023; the Tenant vacated the rental unit November 15, 2024.

The Tenant testified that on September 27, 2024, there was a sewage leak in her apartment from the kitchen sink. The Tenant reached out to the property management company/Landlord immediately; she spoke to the Landlord on September 28, 2024. The Landlord said he would contact the property management company to investigate, then would decide what to do next. The property management company came to investigate after the Landlord’s initial call; as the Tenant had already cleaned up the sewage, they sprayed an anti-bacterial disinfectant. The property management company returned later that day to further investigate where the leak was coming from; they advised the Tenant the issue was most likely from a main sewage pipe problem, that the floor needed to be removed, and it was unhealthy to live there. The Tenant immediately called the Landlord to discuss what she had been told; the Landlord said ‘just wait’, that he needed to contact the management company himself and the insurance company. The Landlord also said the floor was not to be removed yet, he wanted to wait until he talked to the insurance company. The floor never got removed while the Tenant was in the unit.

The Tenant asked the Landlord if she could move and he return the last month rent deposit, as it was unhealthy to live in the unit as it was. The Landlord refused, he said she had to wait for the insurance company. The Landlord told the Tenant to sue him then he could sue the insurance company. A few days later, the Tenant asked the Landlord again about moving and was once again told to wait; she was continually in contact with the Landlord about the repair and/or moving and was always told to wait until he has a refund from the insurance company. The Tenant sent the Landlord pictures and a video of the state of the unit but even after receiving the proof, the Landlord refused to act, saying she had to wait until he received reimbursement from his insurance company.

On September 30, 2024, the Tenant gave the Landlord a notice to vacate for November 30, 2024, but ended up leaving 15 days early because of the unhealthy conditions. She could constantly hear water dripping which made her anxious, the floor lifted, and she began to have an ant problem. She was constantly cleaning the unit to try and lessen her anxiousness about living there, which almost doubled her water usage. The rank odor did not go away until about one-month after the sewage leak occurred, and she was constantly worrying about the air quality. The Tenant called #211 and #311 for help but nothing ever came of it. Apart from being forced to live in such conditions, she lost numerous items, including photo albums that were on the floor under her desk. The Tenant called her insurance company and was told it is the Landlord’s responsibility to repair the issue and compensate her; they said to bring the Landlord to the Board. After speaking to her insurance company, the Tenant called the Landlord and was still told to wait until he got a refund from his insurance company. The Landlord’s insurance company never came, only the property management attended: they cut holes in the wall to investigate the source of the problem, but the holes were not fixed until a few weeks before the Tenant moved out. The property management company fixed the problem with the main sewer pipe in the basement. While the problem was being investigated/addressed, the Landlord offered the building’s guest room, but said she could not stay there the entire time her unit was being repaired. The guestroom, however, only had a bathroom, there was no kitchen so it was not a workable interim solution because the Landlord said she would not be compensated for her eating-out costs until he received reimbursement from his insurance company. Plus, the Tenant has two children, which made the guest room even less workable.
To support her testimony the Tenant relied on pictures, video, email correspondence, water bills, and receipts for the cleaning supplies she had to purchase; the Landlord was sent a copy of all.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit and/or failed to comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, although the property management company appears to have addressed the sewage pipe problem in a timely manner, as there was no testimony to the contrary, completion of the full repair was halted by the Landlord; the Landlord refused to fix the lifting floor which had been saturated with sewage waste. Whenever the Tenant enquired about the progress of the repair, the Landlord said she had to wait until he received compensation from his insurance company. By refusing to take further steps, the Tenant was forced to live with holes in her walls until just prior to vacating, a rank odor for at least a month, a lifting floor, and generally unhealthy conditions. Although the Tenant did not have a health report, it is logical that a sewage leak that resulted in the flooring lifting would cause an unsanitary and unhealthy living condition. Therefore, it is the Landlord’s refusal to allow the issue to be fully addressed so the Tenant could live in a healthy environment, that is neither reasonable nor appropriate. The Landlord did not appear to take the issue seriously, even though it was in respect of a sewage leak in the unit. His only attempt at accommodating the Tenant was offering a guest room that did not have full facilities and was not available for the full time frame of the repair. For these reasons, the Tenant is entitled to remedy as set out below. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking one month, $3,200.00, abatement of rent, for the psychological impact of being forced to live in such unhealthy conditions, added expenses incurred for water and food, and the substantial inconvenience/interference that negatively affected the Tenant’s regular every day living and quality of life.

I find that a rent abatement of $3,200.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. The Landlord was made aware of the sewage leak immediately, and although the property management company responded in a timely manner to address the cause of the leak, the sewage- soaked floor that was lifting was never addressed. The Landlord, would not allow the full repair to be done, constantly using the excuse that he had to wait until he received reimbursement from his insurance company who, based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, does not appear to have been involved at all. It is the Landlord’s continual refusal to let the job be completed that was neither a reasonable or appropriate response. Since the Landlord refused to allow the problem to be fully addressed, the Tenant had no choice but to give notice and move out so she and her children did not have to continue living in such unhealthy conditions.

The Tenant is also seeking out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $200.00 for the excess water bill, vacuum cleaner, and cleaning materials including a mop and towels. As the Tenant included extra expenses incurred in her explanation for the requested abatement amount, I do not find it appropriate to award monies above and beyond what is already granted.
As the Tenant was successful in her application, she is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,248.00. This amount represents: • $3,200.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlords’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Notice of Termination was provided in bad faith. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.

There is no dispute that [name] is the landlord, and [name] is the Power of Attorney (which I understand to be for property) for [name]. Since the lease agreement between the parties is signed between the Tenants and [name] and the agreement references that she is the “Power of Attorney”, it’s clear that she was acting as the agent for the landlord, [name]. Thus, in the circumstances of this case, I am satisfied that [name] fits definition of landlord under Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) as she permitted occupancy of a rental unit and is the personal representative for [name].

In April 2024, the Landlords served the Tenants with a N12 Notice of termination with a termination date of June 30, 2024, pursuant to section 48 of the Act. The N12 notice states that the Landlord, [name] requires vacant possession of the rental unit because he in good faith require possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on or around June 15, 2024.

This application was filed pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, which requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: (1) The Landlords gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act in bad faith; (2) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice of termination; and (3) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

In this case, there is no dispute between the parties that the Tenants were served an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, and that the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 notice.

Regarding the third criteria of the test outlined subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, [name] [name] (‘A.G’) testified that on August 24, 2024, she observed that the rental unit was listed for sale on Condos.ca and was leased for $2,400.00 – which was higher than the Tenants’ rent. A copy of the listing was filed as evidence with the Board, and it indicates that the unit was leased on August 1, 2024, and it was listed for lease on July 30, 2024. The Tenants position is that since the rental unit was listed for lease shortly after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Landlords had served the notice of termination in bad faith. The Landlords did not dispute that the rental unit was listed for lease after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.
The central dispute between the parties is whether the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in “bad faith”.

In terms of whether the N12 notice was served in “bad faith”, subsection 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act creates a presumption of bad faith if the landlord advertises the unit for rent or sale within one year of the tenant(s) vacating the rental unit. Since the rental unit was first advertised for lease on July 30, 2024, the statutory presumption of bad faith applies in this case. The burden thus shifts to the Landlords to establish that they did not serve the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords have rebutted the presumption of bad faith.

The Landlord S.A testified that at the time the N12 notice of termination was served to the Tenants her father [name] had intention to reside in the rental unit. On April 9, 2024, she also provided confirmation to the Tenants via email that she advised her father to arrange his travel plans from Bangladesh to Canada for June 2024. A copy of the email was filed as evidence with the Board confirming her testimony.

S.A further testified that repairs were also conducted to the rental unit in anticipation of [name] moving into the rental unit. However, in July 2024, there was political disturbance (civil riots) which occurred in Bangladesh which restricted travelling. She claimed that, during this time, [name]’s health condition also deteriorated, and he was placed under medical care. A copy of the riot report, along with a hospital medical certificate for [name] were filed as evidence with the Board and they corroborate her claim. The riot report confirms that the country was on lockdown and travelling was restricted due to the riots. The riots started approximately July 2024 and lasted until early August 2024. Furthermore, the medical letter/certificate dated January 17, 2026, confirms that Mr. [name]name] is 90 years old and he was diagnosed in 2024 with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). This letter/certificate further references that the political unrest which occurred in Bangladesh around July 2024 also impacted [name] [name]’s mental health. The letter/certificate concludes by remarking that the combined impact of these issues substantially deteriorated Samuil [name]’s overall health, and he was medically advised to not undertake any air travel.

S.A further testified that, as of the hearing date, her father [name] [name] is still in Bangladesh as he not able to travel due to his health conditions. She claimed that once she learned that his father could not travel, the rental unit was listed for lease.

A.G testified that on August 26, 2024, S.A’s sister, [name] [name], wrote an email to her advising that she was taking her “father” to the hospital. A.G argued that this email implies that [name] [name] was living at the rental unit. A copy of the email was filed as evidence with the Board. S.A denied the assertion and claimed that A.G is mistaken with respect to the interpretation of the email and confirmed that Samuil [name] is still residing in Bangladesh.

In the decision of [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (“Elkins”), para 45., the court makes it clear that under s. 202(1) of the Act, the Board is required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit and the good faith of the participants. The court in Elkins in para 43., also made it clear that it an error of law for the Board to restrict their analysis of the evidence at the point in time when the landlord serves a tenant a s.49 notices of termination. While the analysis in [name] is centred upon notices of termination served for “purchaser’s own use” under section 49 of the Act, the legal principles can be applied in the context of notices provided pursuant to section 48 of the Act for “landlord’s own use”.

In applying the legal principles in Elkins and considering the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the reason for the listing of the rental unit was due to a material change in [name] [name]’s circumstances after the Tenants had vacated the rental unit. The political climate which occurred in Bangladesh in July 2024 was beyond Samuil [name]’s control, and these civil riots restricted travelling. This situation impacted his mental health, and around this time, his physical health had also significantly deteriorated. He was under medical care and was advised by a medical professional not to undertake any air travel. S.A testimony was supported by documents filed with the board, and I find her evidence to be consistent with the overall narrative of events, and I also find it to be reliable.

With respect to the Tenants evidence, the email dated August 26, 2024, does not mention where [name] [name] is residing nor does it reference whether he is in Canada. The Tenants did not summons the author of the email to the hearing to confirm the contents of the email and what the author meant by the assertions. This is evidence I would have reasonably expected the Tenant to adduce in support of their claim. The Tenants evidence pertaining to the email was based on entirely on speculation, and thus it is not reliable. Also, her email evidence, is inconsistent with her own evidence that the rental unit was leased on August 1, 2024. Thus, I place little weight on the evidence provided by the Tenants, as their evidence was inconsistent and is not reliable.
For all the above noted reasons, I find the that the Landlords’ have rebutted the presumption of bad faith. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, I raised that the T2 portion of the Tenant’s Application did not seek any remedies, and did not contain adequate particulars.
An Adjudicative Case Conference was held in this matter on May 1, 2025, where it was indicated to the Tenant that her T2 did not seek remedies and may be dismissed.
I also note that while the T2 contains allegations of harassment, there are not dates and times associated with the allegations.

Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”) dictates that applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

While [name] involved a notice of termination served on a Tenant, it is my view that the principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications, and applications should provide sufficient particulars to allow the responding party to know the allegations against them, and the case to be met.

As the Tenant’s Application does not provide dates and times for the allegations, I find that it does not contain sufficient particulars and should be dismissed. I also note that the Tenant was made aware of the potential defences in the Adjudicative Case Conference and had adequate time to amend to the Application to remedy them. Therefore, the T2 portion of the Application shall be dismissed. With Respect to the T1
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1952.00. Illegal Rent
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on August 28 2024. Prior to this, on August 1, 2024, she paid a last month rent to the Landlord of $1280.00. The Tenant also paid the lawful monthly rent for September, October, and November 2024. The Tenant testified that she was informed by the Landlord that her last month rent was being applied to the month of August 2024.
The Tenant testified that the tenancy was month to month, and she did not sign a lease agreement with the Landlord, because she was not sure when she wanted to move in.

The Tenant testified that she was being harassed by other Tenant’s within the complex, and she and the Landlord signed an N11 to Terminate the tenancy effective October 30, 2024, and she vacated the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that accordingly she had overpaid the rent, and the Landlord collected an illegal rent.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, I am satisfied that the tenancy ended effective October 30, 2024, in accordance with the N11 signed by the parties. Therefore, as the Tenant paid rent for September, October, and November, in addition to a last month rent deposit I am satisfied that the Tenant was charged an illegal rent of $1280.00. Illegal Charge
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that she also paid a separate deposit of $800.00 to the Landlord at the same time she paid her last month rent. She testified that she did not know what the deposit was for, as she was an international student, and was never informed by the Landlord of the purpose for this deposit.

She testified that she requested the deposit be returned when she vacated, and the Landlord returned only $176.00. She testified that the Landlord informed her that the rest of the deposit was being retained because of damage to the rental unit.
Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence it appears that the Landlord has collected a security deposit or damage deposit.

Section 134(1) of the Act states: Addit ion a l ch a rge s proh [name] 134 ( 1) [name] ess otherwi se prescri bed, no l andl ord [name] , di rectl y or i ndi rectl y, wi th respect to any rental unit, ( a) col l ect or requi re or attempt to col l ect or requi re from a tenant, prospecti ve tenant or former tenant of the rental uni t a fee, premi um, commi ssi on, bonus, penal ty, key deposi t or other l i ke amount of money whether or not the money i s refundabl e; ( b) requi re or attempt to requi re a tenant or prospecti ve tenant to pay any consi derati on for goods or servi ces as a condi ti on for granti ng the tenancy or conti nui ng to permi t occupancy of a rental uni t i f that consi derati on i s i n addi ti on to the rent the tenant i s l awful l y requi red to pay to the l andl ord; or ( c) rent any porti on of the rental uni t for a rent whi ch, together [name] [name] rents payabl e for al l other porti ons of the rental uni t, i s a sum that i s greater than the rent the l andl ord may l awful l y charge for the rental uni t.

While there are certain exemptions set out on Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06, based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I am not satisfied that the security/damage deposit collected by the Landlord is captured by these exemptions.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord has collected an illegal charge from the Tenant. As the Landlord has already returned $176.00, they shall be ordered to pay to the Tenant $624.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1952.00. This amount represents: • $1,280.00 for excess rent collected. • $800.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: ) applied for an order determining that [name](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application was resolved in favour of the Tenant by order LTB-T-092699-23 issued on May 2, 2025 and based on a hearing that took place by videoconference on March 20, 2024 and April 22, 2025. On May 5, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Landlord alleged that they were not reasonably able to participate in the hearing on April 22, 2025. On May 6, 2025 interim order LTB-T-092699-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 2, 2025. The review was heard by videoconference on June 10, 2025 and was granted by way of interim order LTB-T-092699-23-RV-IN2 issued on September 19, 2025 and a de novo hearing was scheduled.
reasons: At the end of the hearing on November 10, 2025, after the Tenant gave evidence regarding their application, the Tenant requested to amend their application and to proceed with an amended application at the next hearing date. The Tenant had not amended their application since it was filed and their fee waiver request was accepted on December 2, 2023.

The Tenant submits that the previous Member who heard their application the first time granted an amendment without any formal request. The Tenant clarified that the issues in their application persisted and that they should be able to recount further instances of poor conduct by the Landlord including illegal entries and other substantial interference claims.

The Landlord was opposed to granting any further amendments based on the age of the file and based on the fact that the Tenant has had ample opportunity to amend their application and had not done so. Given the age of the file, it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to have to recount historical information relating to the tenancy. Also, because this is the first time the Tenant requested to amend their application and only after they were advised of the limitation period in their application and the corresponding remedy period outlined under subsection 29(2) of the Act, which would be from the August 15, 2023 move in to the date the application was filed on December 2, 2023.

I agree with the Landlord that it would be prejudicial to allow the Tenant to amend the application after the matter has already gone through lengthy proceedings. The matter was first scheduled on an urgent basis on January 29, 2024. It was then heard over two days on March 20, 2024 and April 22, 2025. The Tenant had every opportunity to request to amend their application by serving the Landlord a copy of their proposed pleadings and by filing a copy with the LTB during that time and they did not.

Additionally, this matter has gone through the review process and at any time the Tenant could have submitted an amended application to include additional grounds, additional details and additional remedy requests, however, they took no steps to do so despite the passing of two years.

Further, it was an error for the original Member to consider amending the application to include additional grounds that were not originally pled in the application without taking submissions from the Landlord on the request. It appears that the Member permitted the Tenant to make submissions regarding illegal entries to the unit, when no such submission was made in the application and they proceeded to grant remedies for the items not claimed. The Divisional Court’s findings in Beaugé v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, at p.11, states: “In the circumstances and without any amendment to the relief claimed, it was unfair to the landlord to make such an award without adequate notice and without proper submissions. This denial of procedural fairness constitutes an error of law.”
Accordingly, the Tenant’s request to amend the application beyond December 2, 2023 was denied. [name]

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord changed the lock to the main entry door without providing the Tenant with a key in contravention of section 24 of the Act. The Tenant submits that this happened on November 23, 2023. The lock is a keypad and the Tenant submits that the Landlord changed the code after communicating with the Tenant approximately 7 days prior that the Tenant was no longer welcome in the property.

The Tenant testified that they came home and the code on the door had changed by approximately 6:00pm. He immediately sent a text to the Landlord. He submits it was snowing that day and he tried calling police, but the line was busy. He ended up gaining access to his unit by going upstairs and asking a neighbour to be let in. He told her he forgot his key and to requested entry through her door which she agreed.

The Tenant further testified that when he spoke with police the police had contacted the Landlord and he told them that the Tenant had stolen work equipment, such as the work van, and this is why he was locked out. After this the Tenant left the door unlocked in order to gain access. On December 17, 2023 the Tenant had a the code to the door and was able to gain entry using the keypad.

The Landlord agrees that he changed the keypad on November 23, 2023 as a result of an incident involving the theft of his company truck. He further testified that after he spoke with the police, he changed the code the following day and gave the Tenant the code. Aside from the Landlords oral testimony, which I find otherwise to be truthful, the Landlord provided no written correspondence of the code being given to the Tenant.

I therefore find that the Landlord altered the lock to the rental unit main door without providing the Tenant with the keycode in contravention of section 24 of the Act. Without corroborating evidence to the contrary from the Landlord, I find that the Tenant was able to access the rental unit with their code by December 17, 2023. This was a period of 24 days where the Tenant had to leave their front door unlocked to gain entry to their unit. I accordingly also find that this is substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that this conduct was most unwelcomed and harassing.
The Tenant requested an abatement equal to $500.00 regarding all of the issues noted in their T2 application which includes other items the Tenant submits they remedied themselves in the unit.

Accordingly, I find that an appropriate abatement is to be $200.00 which is the equivalent of approximately a 25% abatement over 24 days based on a monthly rent of $1,000.00. ($1,000 x 12 divided by 365 is $32.88/day. 25% is $8.22/day).
The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay a fine for locking the Tenant out of the rental unit in order to hold the Landlord accountable for their actions.

While I do accept that the Landlord admittedly changed the lock code, they did provide the Tenant the code thereafter. Aside from this, there was no further pleadings regarding a continued lockout. I therefore decline to issue a fine against the Landlord.

I am not satisfied, based on the evidence before me, that the Landlord deliberately interfered with the vital service of heat in the rental unit. In the Tenant’s application they submit that the rental unit from September 1, 2025 to November 25, 2023 that the house has never been heated past 18 degrees Celsius. Even with their own portable heater in the bedroom, it does not reach more than 16 degrees.

At the hearing the Tenant testified that they purchased their own space heater in December of 2023 and January of 2024. They had no receipts regarding their purchase. They also testified to one date of October 9, 2023 that read 17 degrees, they otherwise did not provide any temperature readings for cold temperatures between September 1, 2023 and December 2, 2023.

The Landlord submits that he recalls the Tenant complaining that it was cold in the property. The bedrooms have radiator heat and there was a cold spot noted in the common area living room. On this basis, in October of 2023 the Landlord installed a heat pump. He also testified that in the interim, he provided the Tenant with a space heater. He recalls giving the Tenant a space heater in early October after they advised it was cold in the living room and before the heat pump was installed. They could not recall the exact date the heat pump was installed but testified he received no complaints thereafter about the cold temperature.

On a balance of probabilities, I am unable to find that there was a lack of heat in the rental unit beyond October of 2023 when the Landlord installed the heat pump. I also do not accept that the Tenant purchased their own space heaters in December and January and I find the Landlord more believable that they provided the Tenant with a space heater in early October in order to supplement the heat before the installation of the heat pump as the Tenant provided no receipts corroborating their purchase and otherwise did not provide any evidence of an issue with heat beyond October 9, 2023. Accordingly, the issue with heat in the rental unit is unsubstantiated and dismissed.

Even if I were to consider the issue with heat as a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations, based on the foregoing, I find the Landlord acted within a reasonable amount of time to address the issue of heat and therefore no remedy shall be ordered.

With respect to the allegation that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant and harassed them on November 14, 2023, the Tenant failed to provide any corroborating evidence to support that the Landlord told them they were not a Canadian Citizen and to leave the rental unit in this respect. Additionally, the Tenant did not request a particular remedy in regards to this allegation. Accordingly, this part of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. T6 Application

The Tenants pleadings with respect to the work they allegedly did in the unit is insufficient as it provides no dates that they did the work. At the hearing the Tenant submits that the electrical issues they tended to relate to replacing 6 receptacle covers and placing painting tape over others. They admitted that they did not give the Landlord advance notice of the issue, and they just purchased the covers and then pointed out to the Landlord that they had done so. They gave no evidence with respect to the window sealing or baseboard opening repairs.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should consider the facts in their entire context in determining whether there was a breach of the Act. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The LTB has consistently held that a landlord should be given a reasonable opportunity to effect repairs in a rental unit after they are notified of the issue or become aware of the issue. In this case, the Tenant admittedly did not notify the Landlord of the issue and instead undertook to replace the electrical receptacle covers and then told the Landlord they had done so.

Additionally, the Tenant led no evidence with respect to the work they did or produce any documentary evidence supporting their out-of-pocket costs for any repair. Even if I were to consider the 6 electrical receptacle covers, they in no way would reach $5,000.00. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the $2,500.00 which they requested for cleaning or painting the unit as there was no evidence this was actually done or there were any costs incurred. On this basis, the Tenant’s T6 application must be dismissed entirely. Costs on Order LTB-T-092699-23-IN issued October 17, 2025

At the first de novo hearing that was scheduled to be heard on October 9, 2025, the Tenant was unprepared to proceed at the hearing and the matter was ultimately adjourned. At that hearing, the Tenant submitted that they had a visual impairment and that they could not locate relevant documents. After the hearing, the provided a medical letter confirming their vision impairment.

In the order, the Member found it appropriate, based on the Tenant’s conduct at the hearing, to make an order for costs payable to the Landlord for $200.00 and to pay LTB costs in the amount of $300.00.

This cost order was also a contention between the parties when they attended the first adjourned hearing before me on November 10, 2025 as the Tenant was required to pay Board costs on November 30, 2025 and the costs to the Landlord by this date or the Tenant’s application may be stayed or discontinued. The Landlord submitted that the hearing was premature and that the time on the interim order should expire first to see if the Tenant pays it. The Tenant was opposed to paying the costs at all.

The order that was issued with respect to costs was an interim order in these proceedings and it was based on the conduct at the hearing and the Tenant’s failure to provide medical evidence supporting a need for accommodation. It was not a final order. The Tenant has since provided medical documentation supporting their visual impairment. Accordingly, I do not find LTB costs appropriate under the circumstances.

However, based on the interim order noting that during the hearing on October 9, 2025, the Tenant would not move forward with their application, spoke over others during the hearing and became argumentative regarding their application and took up almost two hours worth of the Landlord’s time and paid representative time, I do not find it appropriate to relinquish the costs ordered of $200.00 for the Landlord.

On this basis, considering that the Tenant is successful on their application for the value of the Landlord’s costs ordered, I find it appropriate to apply a set-off of the costs against the amount the Landlord is ordered to pay. In this regard neither party owes the other with respect to the Tenant’s application.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will follow.
ordered: The order LTB-T-092699-23 issued on May 2, 2025 and the interim order issued on October 17, 2025 are replaced with the following order.
The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $200.00 as an abatement of rent for the T2 application.

The costs ordered to be paid by the Tenant to the Landlord in the amount of $200.00 under interim order LTB-T-092669-23-IN issued on October 17, 2025 is set off against the amount the Tenant owes the Landlord.
The LTB costs of $300.00 ordered to be paid by the Tenant to the LTB under LTB-T- 092669-23-IN issued on October 17, 2025 are withdrawn. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application, therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $34,471.64. [name]
The Tenant testified that she has been residing in the unit since July of 2018.
On November 9, 2024, a fire occurred in the rental unit. The fire resulted in the Tenant having to vacate the unit due to smoke damage. The Tenant started staying in a hotel shortly thereafter.
The Tenant testified that once she was able to speak with the Landlord about the fire, the Landlord took issue with the fact that she did not contact him right away.

After the fire, the Tenant testified that she kept in constant contact with the Landlord about the status of the rental unit’s repair. The Tenant had her own tenant insurance and was advised to continue paying her rent, which she did. The Tenant testified that she is currently staying at an Air BNB and had received approximately $30,800.00 for additional living expenses. The Tenant testified that this is the maximum amount she would receive for alternate accommodations from her insurance provider.
The Tenant testified that when she would contact the Landlord she would be met with various excuses with respect to the completion of the work, or she would receive no response at all.
That said, the Tenant had learned that the Landlord had received a building permit from the municipality in January of 2025, yet no work appeared to be getting done.
The Landlord was observed at the rental unit conducting cosmetic repairs to the unit’s fence and other work that appeared to the Tenant to be non-urgent. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified and confirmed that he had received a building permit from the municipality in January of 2025 and testified that he did start doing as work as possible, depending on the weather.

The Landlord testified that he did not receive his insurance payment until September 22, 2025. The Landlord explained that the funds has been deposited in July but were not cleared until September by his bank.
The Landlord testified that his insurance adjuster had advised him that the Tenant would continue paying rent. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the fire occurred in November of 2024 and the Landlord received a building permit to remediate the home in January of 2025. The Landlord’s position is that only nominal work could take place until the insurance company cut him the cheque in July, which he did not receive until September of 2025. Seemingly no work had started as of the date of the hearing.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord had a preference for specific contractors which led to more delays. Further, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the request for a rent abatement is an insurance issue and should not be addressed in the LTB. I disagree.

The Tenant continued to pay rent for the unit and as such, the issue of rent falls squarely within the purview of the LTB. While their may be insurance ramifications beyond this order means nothing to my consideration of the activities of the Landlord in this case.

Further, the Landlord’s position is that the tenancy should be terminated due to the principle of Frustrated Contracts, submitting that the fire was found to be an “act of nature” and as such, considering that no one is at fault for the fire that the date of the fire ends the tenancy. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not cite any relevant authority however, considering Professor [name] in The Law of Contract 4th ed. Carswell at pg. 677: “The key to both understanding and the application of the doctrine of frustration in modern times is the idea of a radical change in the contractual obligation, arising from the unforeseen circumstances in respect of which no prior agreement has been reached, those circumstances having come about without default by either party. What would appear essential is that the party claiming that a contract has been frustrated should establish that performance of the contract, as originally agreed, would be impossible. For example, if the subject-matter of the contract has been lost or destroyed, a court will be willing to determine that the contract is ended”.

The legal test is articulated in [name] v Salamander Opportunities et al, 2018, ONSC 5749 (‘Barnaby’). In [name], the Divisional Court held that the Board correctly identified the legal test for frustration: “An unexpected event that was not foreseeable or contemplated in the contract; and, that is not the fault of either party; and that drastically changes the nature of the contract so that it is impossible, not just difficult of expensive, to perform the obligations. The impossibility must be of a long-term nature and not temporary or transient.”

When I consider the matter before me, I do not find that the Landlord has established all parts of the test noted in Barnaby. First, the Landlord has fire insurance as was testified to during the hearing. This suggests that the unexpected event was foreseeable or contemplated. (See TET-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB), par. 12; SWT- 15411-18-AM (Re), 2018 CanLII 88487 (ON LTB)).

Even if I was to accept that neither party was responsible for the fire, the remaining parts of the test are not met. The Divisional Court noted in Dhillon v. PM Management Systems Inc. 2014, ONSC 5407, that “…an event is not a frustrating event if it is foreseen or provided for in the contract or the frustrating event was caused by the fault of a party to the contract.”

Lastly, the nature of the contract must be altered so significantly that it is impossible, not just difficult or expensive, to perform the obligations. There is no evidence before me to suggest that the rental unit cannot be repaired. Although the repairs have suffered from delays, there was no evidence to suggest that the subject matter, that is the rental unit, is destroyed.

Further, s. 37(1) of the Act, states that a tenancy may only be terminated in accordance with the Act. Section 39(1) further limits the Landlord’s ability to recover possession of the rental unit, stating: “A landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless, (a) the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit; or (b) an order of the Board evicting the tenant has authorized the possession.”

The case of Gouge and Woodland v EQB Ltd., (October 20, 2011), Court File No. DC-11- 0018-00 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) the Divisional Court further illustrates that the Landlord cannot recover possession unless it follows the statutory process, stating: “In our view, the appellant improperly regained possession and effectively evicted the respondents from their rental unit without complying with the statutory process and obtaining the requisite order. This is so even though the respondents negligently caused a fire, their second, which caused severe damage mainly to the kitchen. In these circumstances, the appellant was required to comply with s. 20(1) of the Act, make the necessary repairs and allow the respondents to continue their occupation of the unit.”
The Tenant has maintained their wish to be put back into possession of the rental unit which the Tenants’ application clearly sets out their desire to be allowed to reoccupy the rental unit.

Having considered the evidence, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit in a timely manner. The Landlord failed to account for large swaths of time after the fire occurred. The delay in receiving the building permit for two months was never explained, and the specific work that the Landlord’s contractors could not do because it was too cold could also not be explained.
That said, despite apparently waiting for insurance funds to arrive the Landlord started in inexplicably conducting exterior work to the unit’s fence and other non-fire related issues. Remedies

The Tenant had been paying the ongoing rent up to the date of the hearing, which the Landlord confirmed. The unit has been uninhabitable since November of 2024 and the Tenant has been paying rent for a unit she cannot live in due to the ongoing delays of the Landlord. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $22,752.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant testified that she had paid $41,486.64 in living costs to date since vacating the unit after the fire. The Tenant was compensated $30,832.00 from her insurance provider and the Tenant is seeking the difference of $11,671.64 that she incurred following costs and out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord’s breach. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $11,671.64 for these out-of-pocket expenses.
The Tenant also requested $1,500.00 in General Compensation. The reason for same I find was not clearly set out by the Tenant and this remedy will not be granted.

That said, the Tenant’s Legal Representative asked for a timeline to be provided by the Landlord to the Tenant with respect to the completion of the repairs and the Landlord will be ordered to provide same within 30 days of this order.
ordered: Within 30 days of this order, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant with an updated timeline with respect to the completion of the unit’s repairs.

The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $34,471.64. This amount represents: • $22,752.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending November 2025. • $11,671.64 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent owing for the months after the repairs are done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that her cat’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was substantially interfered with due to the Landlord’s construction work conducted at the residential complex on November 4, 2024. The Tenant submits that her cat is a member of their household and entitled to the protections afforded by the Residential Tenancies Act. The Tenant testified that her cat was home during the time of the construction and was traumatized by the construction noise. The Tenant testified that her reasonable enjoyment was not impacted as she was at work during the time that the work was being conducted by the Landlord.

The Tenant does not assert that her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit is an issue. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was not impacted by the construction noise because, for the most part, she was at work when the construction was being conducted. The Tenant testified that she was able to use the residential complex and her unit during the time the Landlord was addressing maintenance work at the residential complex. For the most part, when the Tenant returned from work, or shortly thereafter, the construction work would end for the day.
The Landlord submits, and I agree, that the Landlord’s responsibilities under the Residential Tenancies Act does not extend to a Tenant’s pet as being a member of a tenant’s household.

Moreover, the Landlord maintain s that the work completed at the residential complex was done with notice to the Tenant, was necessary, and resulted in a reasonable amount of noise/vibration during the work hours of the day. The Landlord work was for a brief period conducted during the day. The Landlord seeks to have the application dismissed because their duty does not extend to the Tenant’s cat, and secondly, the work was not unreasonable and the Tenant admits that it did not impact her reasonable enjoyment.

I find that the Landlord/Landlord’s Agent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was not impacted. The cat does not receive the rights and protections under the Residential Tenancies Act, and for purposes of this application is not considered a member of their household for purposes of the Residential Tenancies Act.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
