issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The parties agreed to amend the rental unit address to unit 2407, 7890 [address]reet, [name], ON .
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $16,498.84.

This application was filed pursuant to section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act'). Subsection 57(1) of the Act requires that the Tenant prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties entered into a tenancy agreement for a fixed term for the period of April 18, 2020 to March 19, 2021. The monthly rent was $1,900.00 payable on the 18th day of each month. The Tenant also paid a last month’s rent deposit of $1,900.00. A copy of the Residential Tenancy Agreement (Standard Form Lease) (the ‘Agreement) was provided into evidence by the Tenant (DOC-5807598pgs1-27). At the time of moving out of the unit the monthly rent was $1,925.00. The rental unit is a condominium unit with one bedroom and one bathroom.

There was no dispute that the Landlords served the Tenant a N12 Notice pursuant to subsection 48(1) (a) and (b) of the Act. The N12 Notice provided a termination date of September 17, 2023, and stated that the Landlord and their spouse intend to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year. A copy of the N12 Notice was provided into evidence by the Tenant (DOC-5807598pgs35-36).

Subsection 48(1)(a) and (b) of the Act provides that: A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse;

There was no dispute that the Landlords filed an application based on this N12 Notice and attended a hearing before the LTB on February 5, 2024. Only the Landlords’ Legal Representative and VR attended that hearing. On March 5, 2024, order LTB-054184-23 was issued terminating the tenancy and requiring the Tenant move out of the rental unit on or before March 18, 2024.

The Tenant testified that he moved out of the rental until on March 16, 2024, after receiving the order. He also testified that he had no alternative but to move into a small available basement unit in the area given the quick termination date in the order and put the majority of his belongings into storage. He further testified that he was eventually able to secure a condominium unit in same area as the rental unit and entered into a tenancy agreement for that new unit effective June 1, 2024.
Based on the above, we were satisfied that the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to the N12 Notice provided by the Landlords and the resulting order issued by the LTB.

Subsection 57(4) of the Act provides that: In an application under subsection (1), the Board may find that the landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith despite a previous finding by the Board to the contrary.

The Tenant asserts that the Landlords gave the N12 Notice in bad faith and did not move in the unit within the one-year period following his move out. In support of this assertion, the Tenant’s witness, and former neighbour in the residential complex, [name], SJ, testified at the hearing.

SJ confirmed that she resides in the residential complex where the rental unit was located. She testified that the rental unit was empty for some time, then a couple with two small children moved into the unit and resided there for approximately five to six months, then the unit was empty for more than one year. SJ also testified that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit until late July early August 2025. Under cross-examination, SJ confirmed that the couple living in the rental unit were not the Landlords’ family members. 13. [name], VR, testified that his wife and he had every intention of moving into the unit when the N12 Notice was given to the Tenant. He testified that it was their intention to sell the townhouse where they currently reside and move into the rental unit. VR asserted that there was a change in their circumstances because his wife had sustained an injury due to a fall in September 2023 which subsequently led to a finding of another health issue which required surgery to correct in March 2024. 14. VR also testified that due to the smell of cigarette smoke in the rental unit after the Tenant moved out, they could not live there. He testified that he tried to clear it using air fresheners, opening the windows, and then eventually painting the unit sometime in May 2024. In support of these assertions, VR provided a copy of an invoice from Gabriel Anastasis dated May 3, 2024, for painting services into evidence (DOC-5801562pg14). 15. VR did not dispute that his relatives’ friends from Israel moved into the rental unit in May 2024 as it was not possible for them to stay with the Landlords at their townhouse. VR maintained that he did not sign a tenancy agreement with these individuals. Under cross- examination, VR confirmed that these friends paid him $2,000.00 a month to reside in the rental unit which he said covered his mortgage and maintenance fees. 16. VR further testified that they started slowly moving into the unit after his relatives’ friends left in August 2024 and listed their townhouse for sale in the Spring of 2025. VR confirmed that he and his wife finally moved into the rental unit in the summer of 2025 and currently reside in the unit. 17. Based on the evidence before us, we find that the Landlords did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and that the N12 Notice was given in bad faith. 18. VR asserted that there were changes in their circumstances which prevented them from moving into the unit; in September 2023 when his wife fell and in March 2024 when his wife had to have surgery. Yet, no evidence was presented at the hearing that the Landlords took any steps to rescind the notice to the Tenant. If fact, the Landlords attended the eviction hearing for the N12 Notice in February 2024 and requested an immediate eviction despite knowing that VR’s wife was going for surgery the next month which he purported was the reason they could not move into the unit. 19. Pursuant to section 48 of the Act, a landlord must act in good faith when issuing a notice to end a tenancy for the landlord’s use. The Landlords’ actions in these circumstances were inconsistent with a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit. Additionally, the Landlords permitted friends to move into the unit from May 2024 to August 2024 and accepted $2,000.00 per month from them. 20. Section 2 of the Act defines ‘rent’ in part as the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit. 21. In this case, we were satisfied that the Landlords accepted rent from May 2024 to August 2024 from individuals who were neither the former Tenant nor occupying the rental unit for the Landlords’ use. By permitting third parties to occupy the unit and receiving rental income during this period, the Landlords effectively entered into a new tenancy agreement. 22. Section 57(5) (b) of the Act states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 23. The Landlords’ conduct is inconsistent with their stated purpose of the notice and supports a finding that the N12 Notice to end the Tenant’s tenancy was not issued in good faith. Remedies 24. In this application, the Tenant requested an abatement of rent totalling $22,800.00, $12,000.00 for the difference in rent paid for one year from the date he moved out, $10,100.00 for moving and storage expenses, general compensation in the amount of $22,800.00, and that the Landlords pay an administrative fine. 25. At the hearing, the Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of $22,800.00. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy designed to recognize the concept that if a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then they are entitled to an abatement proportionate to the difference of what is being paid for and what is being received. In this circumstance, we find that an abatement is not appropriate as the timeframe sought was not while the Tenant was residing in the rental unit. 26. The Tenant also requested $10,100.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving and storage expenses that the Tenant incurred to move out of the rental unit. The Tenant initial move into the basement unit resulted in him having to rent a storage unit for his belongings. The Tenant provided into evidence (DOC 5807598pg39) an invoice in the amount of $50.84 for the rental storage for the period of March 14, 2024 to April 12, 2024. The Tenant did not provide any further invoices with respect to any moving or storage fees. 27. Subsection 57(3) provides that: The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1.2 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 28. Therefore, based on the evidence before us, we find that the Landlords shall be ordered to pay to the Tenant $50.84 for the Tenant’s reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred for storage. 29. The Tenant also requested increased rent of $12,000.00 for the one year period after vacating the rental unit. He provided a copy of his new tenancy agreement into evidence (DOC 5807598pg 47) confirming a monthly rent of $2,950.00. Subsection 57(3) of the Act provides in part that: The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one year period after vacating the rental unit. 30. The Act is silent on whether the new unit must be comparable to the former unit when determining an order under subsection 57 of the Act. Having considered the evidence before us, the Tenant’s increased rent claim is granted, in part. We find it reasonable and appropriate to order increased rent in the amount of $500.00 for only the period of June 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025, being a ten-month period within the one year timeframe of moving out of the unit. This is because the Tenant lived in a basement unit for the first two months wherein the rent was less and because the Tenant’s new unit is larger than the former rental unit. Accordingly, the Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $5,000.00 which represents the increased rent for the stated ten-month period ($1,000 - $500 = $500 x 10). 31. The Tenant also requested general compensation in the amount of $22,800.00. Subsection 57(3) 1.1 provides that: The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 32. An order under this section may be made regardless of whether the Tenant has incurred any actual expenses. In these circumstances, we accept that having to move within a short period of time when the [name] was issued by the board and wanting to remain living in the same area although rents have increased significantly had an impact on the Tenant as presented. 33. However, we find it appropriate to award the Tenant general compensation in the amount of only $11,400.00 amounting to approximately six months of rent ($1,900 x 6 = $11,400.00) due to the N12 notice being given in bad faith. The Tenant had resided in the rental unit for approximately four years and had built a community in the area with neighbours and friends. The Tenant also had to move twice due to the short time frame requested by the Landlords and awarded in the eviction order and we accept that with any move there is additional distress, expenses, inconvenience, stress, and time lost. 34. The Tenant has further requested that the Landlords pay a fine. According to [name] 16 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guidelines, administrative fines are typically imposed where a landlord has shown “blatant disregard” for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Given the other remedies awarded in this application, we do not find that a fine is required in this circumstance. 35. The Tenant paid $48.00 for filing this application and is entitled to reimbursement of that fee. 36. This order contains all of the reasons in this matter and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $16,498.84. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for increase in rent the Tenant paid for the ten-month period from June 1, 2024 to March 1, 2025. • $50.84 for the reasonable storage expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $11,400.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal rent collected

During the hearing, the parties agreed that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') in the amount of $153.00. However, from the documents and testimony submitted this issue had already been corrected prior to the Tenant filing the T1 application by way of a correction applied to the Tenant’s ledger with a credit of $153.00. Therefore, no determinations will be made concerning this issue. A copy of the Tenant ledger was submitted into evidence. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

A central issue in this application is the Tenant’s claim that she sent an Interac e-transfer of $2,000.00 to the Landlord as a rent deposit on August 1, 2024 but that it was not applied to rent for the last month of this tenancy which ended on October 31, 2025.
During the hearing, the Tenant held up a bank statement showing that $2,000.00 was withdrawn from her bank account on August 1, 2024.

However, the Tenant did not provide: • Confirmation that the transfer was successfully completed; • Evidence that the Landlord received or accepted the transfer; or • Evidence that the funds were deposited into the Landlord’s account. Landlord evidence
The Landlord denied receiving the $2,000.00.

The Landlord called three witnesses. The Landlord called [name] (MT) who is the Landlord’s Director of Finance. MT testified that he reviewed the bank statements of the Landlord, and they did not receive the payment of $2,000.00 from the Tenant. A copy of the Landlord’s ledger of all tenants and the Tenant’s rent ledger was reviewed and submitted into evidence.

The Landlord called [name] (CW) who is the Landlord Financial Controller and testified that the Landlord does not have automatic deposits for interac etransfers. CW testified that they could not accept the etransfer as it was under investigation and submitted into evidence the August 1, 2024, Interac etransfer notification of investigation. CW testified that on March 13, 2024, she called the Landlord’s bank to ascertain if the transfer was ever accepted and the bank was unable to trace the $2,000.00 from the Tenant and explained the money was sent back to the sender.

During cross examination CW was asked what happens if the money was not deposited in the Landlord’s account. CW replied that she is not working for the Tenant’s banking institution and that the Tenant must speak with her branch to see what happened.

The Landlord called Sandy Poulio (SP) who is the Director of Administrator Services for the Landlord. SP testified that she requested confirmation from the Tenant that the $2,000.00 was received by the Landlord and the Tenant never provided any proof. The Tenant only provided her bank statement which showed the $2,000.00 was withdrawn from her account.

The Landlord submitted into evidence: • A tenant ledger showing no record of the $2,000.00 payment made on or around August 1, 2024; • Evidence that the e-transfer was under investigation; and • An email from the Tenant indicating that she contacted her bank and had the funds returned due to issues with the transaction.

In order to succeed in a T1 application, the Tenant must establish her claims on a balance of probabilities. I find that the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord received or unlawfully retained the $2,000.00 or otherwise collected illegal charges under the Act.

I accept that the Tenant attempted to make a $2000.00 payment to the Landlord on August 1, 2024. However, the documentary evidence supports the Landlord’s position that the transaction was not completed and these funds returned to the Tenant as opposed to being received by the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenant has not provided sufficient evidence to substantiate the alleged unlawful charges or that the Landlord retained funds improperly within the meaning of s. 134(1) of the Act.
While the Tenant alleges financial hardship, stress, and additional costs, these claims are not supported by sufficient evidence linking the alleged losses to a breach of the Act by the Landlord.
Similarly, as it was not proven that the Landlord retained $2,000.00, I cannot find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
As a result, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $7,501.14. Landlord Gave N12 for Own Use in Bad Faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The following facts were agreed or undisputed at the hearing: • The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of August 31, 2024; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. • The Landlord did not move into the rental unit; • The Landlord listed the building containing the rental unit for sale within 1 year of the Tenant vacating the rental unit.

The first three parts of the legal test contained in section 57 of the Act are either agreed or undisputed. Despite the submissions of the Landlord’s representative that the Tenant has the burden of proving the allegations on a balance of probabilities, section 57(5) of the Act provides: 5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;

This provision of the Act creates a rebuttable presumption and the facts in this matter engage the presumption contained in section 57(5). This means that the Landlord must prove it is more likely than not that when she gave the N12 to the Tenant she genuinely intended to move into the rental unit or that there was a material change in circumstances that would rebut the presumption. Simply put, the Landlord must prove good faith in serving the N12 notice.

The Landlord’s representative submits that the Landlord’s intention to sell the property was formed after the Landlord became aware that her son would not be moving to the property however, the reverse onus provisions of section 57(5) are not caveated by justification. Testimony of [name]

The former Landlord [name] (VF) testified that in the fall of 2023 she began having severe problems with her right knee, back pain, and hip pain. VF gave evidence that her condition “started getting critical” causing sleepless nights and difficulty maintaining her obligations at the residential complex.
VF further testified that the health issues caused her to be fearful and she called her son to tell him that she was having major problems and was afraid to continue living by herself.

VF’s evidence is that the N12 notice was served with the intention to “clear the place”, because she wanted to move into the former Tenant’s rental unit, and her son would occupy the main floor where the Landlord was residing to provide her with support and assistance.

VF testified that that her son “promised” he would move in, and she “hoped” and “believed” her son would follow through. Ultimately, VF’s son advised his mother that he could not sell his business in Gananoque and therefore, he would be unable to move.
VF also testified that her son tried to sell his business for the whole summer but when he was unsuccessful and school began in the fall, he couldn’t move into the property.

VF’s evidence is that her son told her he wouldn’t be able to move, “in the fall when school started”. VF clarified that she couldn’t remember the exact dates, but the conversation happened some time at the end of August or beginning of September.

The Landlord’s son did not testify. I am without evidence as to when VF’s son began trying to sell his business, what efforts were made, or what other discussions took place in relation to the plan for VF’s son to move into the property.

I draw a negative inference from the lack of testimony from VF’s son. It would be reasonably expected that the Landlord’s son would testify, or evidence would be submitted showing advertisements or listings for the sale of the son’s business, real estate listings for the son’s residence, or an application for VF’s son’s children to go to school in the area.

The N12 notice was served for the purpose of the Landlord’s residential occupation of the rental unit. Despite this, VF’s plan to occupy the rental unit was predicated on hope and belief that her son would also be moving in to provide support and assistance.

Ultimately, the reason VF didn’t move into the rental unit is because her son couldn’t sell his business to give effect to the plan for him to provide VF with assistance. The N12 notice was served with hope, belief, and optimism, but I do not find VF had a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit.

VF’s son hadn’t sold his business when the N12 was served, and when the termination date of the N12 notice became imminent it should have been obvious to VF that her son would not be able to move to the property to facilitate her move to the rental unit.

Based on the evidence before me I am not satisfied that the Landlord has proven, on a balance of probabilities that the N12 notice was served in good faith and therefore, the presumption contained in s. 57(5) has not be rebutted.

I also do not find that the Landlord’s son not being able to move into the property, nor that VF’s deteriorating health are a material changes in circumstances. Since the plan for VF’s son to move into the rental unit was contingent on him selling his business, when he advised VF that the business hadn’t sold this was simply maintaining the status quo that existed from the beginning.

Further, I accept the Landlord was experiencing health issues which was the catalyst for VF wanting her son to move to the property and for her to move into the rental unit however, the Landlord’s health issues were preexisting when the N12 notice was served. The deterioration of VF’s condition was a motivation to sell the property, but not a material change that prevented her from moving into the rental unit.
Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith and the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Remedies Administrative Fine
The Tenant requested a fine testifying that the Landlord has been a Landlord for “her whole life”, and should “know better”.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines considers the purpose of a fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

I do not find this to be a situation in which a fine is appropriate. Despite finding that the N12 notice was served in bad faith, there is insufficient evidence to find that the Landlord’s actions are a blatant disregard for the Act, nor that the other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Rent Differential

The Tenant testified that her monthly rent at the rental unit was $1,600.00, and her new rent is $1,950.00. The Tenant submitted a copy of the lease for her new rental unit and gave evidence that by comparison the layouts of each unit are different but estimates the square footage to be relatively similar.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the former rental unit is in a residential home, and she had 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom, laundry, and parking included. The new rental unit is a two- bedroom basement unit with laundry included. The Tenant had use of a personal outdoor space at both rental units.

I am satisfied that the Tenant’s new rental unit is comparable, and the Tenant will pay increased rent of $350.00 per month for 12 months. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,200.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one- year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. Moving Expenses

The Tenant testified that she incurred expenses for moving, supplies, and a U-Haul moving truck relying on bank statements to prove the expenses. The Tenant was asked during cross examination whether she submitted receipts however, I am satisfied that the U-Haul charges relate to the Tenant moving out of the rental unit.
The charges shown on the bank statements are contemporaneous to the period when the Tenant vacated the rental unit and coincide with the commencement date of the Tenant’s new lease.

The Tenant testified that she hired movers to assist her however, the Tenant did not submit evidence in relation to these expenses and I am without sufficient evidence to find that the Tenant incurred additional expenses for moving or storage.

The total amount of charges shown on the Tenant’s bank statement for moving expenses is $253.14, and there was no evidence that this was unreasonable. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $253.14 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Compensation

The Tenant requested general compensation pursuant to section 57 (3) 1.1 of the Act. Section 57(3) 1.1 sets out the Board’s jurisdiction to order general compensation: 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. [Emphasis added]

The Tenant testified that her claim for general compensation is quantified as lost wages for 4 days, and for the stress and inconvenience of having to move. The Tenant testified that she estimates 12 hours of apartment search time, 48 hours of packing time,

The Tenant’s evidence is that when she moved into the rental unit, she had just been evicted as a result of an N12 notice from her prior landlord and VF was aware of the Tenant’s desire for long term accommodations. The Tenant further testified that she was going to school full time and had no one to help her move.

The Tenant submitted receipts for mental health treatment in support of her testimony that having to move from the rental unit caused her stress. The Tenant also submitted an estimate for 4 days of lost wages based on her hourly rate and typical number of clientele per day.

The Landlord’s representative submits that the Tenant lacked evidence in relation to her expenses, and the quantification of general damages was speculative. Further submissions were made that the Tenant should not be entitled to compensation for “general life stress” however, the stress experienced by the Tenant was visited upon her by service of the N12 notice, and not “general life”.

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that having to move caused stress and inconvenience. The Tenant spent time looking for a new residence, packing, and moving. Section 57(3) 1.1 of the Act does not require the Tenant incur any actual expenses and I am satisfied that the Tenant’s request for, and quantum of, general compensation is appropriate. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,000.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,501.14. This amount represents: • $4,200.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after vacating the rental unit; • $253.14 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $3,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment and harassed the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord raised a preliminary issue that he is not the Landlord as listed in the Tenant’s application but rather the Landlord’s agent. The property is owned by a corporation, 35 West Avenue North Hamilton Ltd., and not by the Landlord personally. He did not make a coherent legal argument in support of his position that he should not be named as a respondent in this application. The Tenant did not consent to the amendment.

Section 2(1) of the Act defines a landlord as follows: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent;

Based on the Landlord’s submissions and argument, I am not satisfied that the application needs to be amended to name the corporate owner instead of the individual named in the application. The Landlord meets the definition of a landlord in the Act. The Landlord’s request is denied. Summary
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations in her application on a balance of probabilities.
Therefore, the Landlord must: a. Not interfere with the supply of vital services to the rental unit, and b. Pay the Tenant a total sum of $748.00. Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant filed this application on November 4, 2025 alleging, inter alia, that there was no electricity at the property. The application was scheduled to be heard on an urgent basis as a result.
Provision of vital services was restored on November 13, 2025.
There have been multiple interruptions to vital services.

Page 3 of document 6834372 in Portal contains a copy of the notice that was previously posted at the property by Enbridge. According to the notice, gas was going to be shut off on August 25, 2025. According to the notice, the owner had been advised of the impending disconnection. According to the Tenant, Gas was disconnected for non- payment.

Hot water was disconnected in September 2025. Page 4 of the same document package contains a copy of the complaint the Tenant made to the City on September 4, 2025. Page 5 is an email from ReLeaf Property Management to the Tenant confirming that the Landlord had been informed of the issue.

Gas was shut off for 33 days. The Tenant complained to the City, the City ordered the Landlord to restore gas supply to the unit, and the Landlord then paid the bills, after which gas supply was restored.

According to page 52 of Tenant’s evidence 6834372, there was no heat at the property between September 1, 2025 and November 13, 2025, no hot water between September 4, 2025 and September 18, 2025, and then again between October 16, 2025 and October 20, 2025.

There was an issue with the boiler at the property. The Landlord was ordered to address the issue but didn’t do it in a timely manner. The City then attended at the property, changed the locks on November 3 and sent a plumber on November 5. The plumber couldn’t address the issue because there was no power to the furnace.

The Tenant argues that the Landlord did not act diligently to repair the boiler in October. She complained to the city, the Landlord still took a few weeks, and subsequently interfered with the City’s attempts to repair. She claims that someone deliberately shut off hot water on October 16. Page 32 of document 6833954 is a photo of a plumber at the property taken on November 13.

The Tenant complains about bedbugs at the property. Page 61 of document 6834372 contains an email the Landlord sent the Tenant on November 19, 2025. In the email the Landlord tells the Tenant not to communicate with him about the issue because he has engaged Able Pest Control, and they are going to address the issue with the Tenant and with the City of Hamilton’s health inspector as one has been assigned to the file. He then invites the Tenant to raise further issues, if any, after the issue is resolved and the City file closed.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord has been aware of bedbug issues since May. She points to page 23 of document 6834372 in support of this position. I have reviewed that page, and I am unable to infer any knowledge on behalf of the Landlord based on this page. It makes no mention of bedbugs and there is no indication that the Landlord was advised of the bedbug issue on that page. Page 31 is similarly unhelpful as it also does not mention bedbugs.
Page 37-42 contain a summary of the Tenant’s emails to the Landlord about bedbugs. The earliest email is dated October 27, 2025.
Page 41 is the Tenant’s complain to the city about bedbugs. The email is dated November 10, 2025.

According to the Tenant, the Landlord had not found any pest control company. The Tenant hired a different company herself – same company she had hired in May. She paid for them to treat her unit, but it did not resolve the issue because the unit below her has bedbugs.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord is insolvent, doesn’t pay his contractors, won’t pay her, and can’t get legitimate contractors to work for him. The Tenant relies on page 57 of the Tenant’s document package 6834372 containing a copy of a factum filed by Home Trust Company in their proceedings for against 58 King Street East Hamilton Ltd. and [organization] to have a receiver appointed. According to the factum, the Landlord is a guarantor of the respondent’s debts. I do not find this evidence to be helpful or persuasive. It is not an order. The Landlord is not a party. The Tenant has no personal knowledge of the nature of these proceedings.
The Landlord cross-examined the Tenant.
He asked if she agreed that there was no hot water between September 4, 2025 and September 18. The Tenant was very argumentative but eventually agreed.
She did not agree that there was no heat between October 23 and November 13. She claimed that there was no heat between Spring 2025 and November 13. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord does not dispute that there was no hot water and no gas at the rental unit between September 4 and September 18, 2025. He also does not dispute that there was no hot water at the rental unit between October 16 and November 13.
The Landlord purchased the property through a corporation in December 2024. He is not related to the previous owner.
He was not aware of any issues with bedbugs until late October 2025.

When he purchased the property, he kept the existing property management in place. After some time, he noticed irregularities and started questioning the quality of their work as well as their financials. He then terminated their engagement and asked Red Leaf Property Management who manages other properties for him, to try to salvage the situation around August 2025. Red Leaf said that they could not manage this residential complex due to a number of difficult tenants and he started managing it himself.
He then learned of the issues with hot water and gas. He had previously been under mistaken belief that his previous property manager was paying utility bills.
The Landlord explained that it took him from September 4 to 18 to figure out gas issues. It was warm in September and October, so he does not believe tenants were affected.
Hot water issue was resolved when gas was restored because the boiler requires gas.

He then learned of the heat issue on October 23 when the City contacted him. It took some time to resolve. He initially sent a plumber around October 24. They diagnosed the issue and ordered parts to perform repairs. They were supposed to come in to finalize the repairs on November 3. He thought the issue was resolved but learned that someone from the City was at the property on the same date and scared the plumbers away. There was no power to the furnace, so electrician needed to be called. The Landlord had numerous calls with the City and his plumbers which caused additional delay. He was ultimately able to resolve the issue on November 13th. According to the Landlord, the issue would have been resolved faster - on or about November 3, had City of [name] not gotten involved.

The Landlord did not expect the issue of bedbugs to be raised in this application. He argues that if it started before he even purchased the property, it should not be for him to remedy. The Tenant’s application is somewhat difficult to follow and this issue is only raised in a chart attached to the application.

He testified that he only learned about the issue recently. He spoke to a pest control company and asked the Tenant to consent to him giving them her contact information so the company can coordinate an appointment with her. She informed him that it was a bigger issue that affected the entire residential complex. He asked Abell Pest Control to attend at the complex and propose a treatment plan. As of the date of the hearing he did not have an exact date when they would attend and no treatment plan was in place. He would like to have the same company deal with the entire residential complex and did not authorize the Tenant’s chosen company to do so. He heard good things about Abell Pest Control and did not wish to have the Tenant choose his pest control company.
The Landlord denied that anyone deliberately turned the heat off at any point. He denied that he does not have reputable contractors willing to work with him.
The Tenant only conducted a brief cross-examination. [name] and analysis

The Tenant brings her T6 application under sections 20(1) of the Act: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Landlords aren’t required to ensure that there are never any maintenance issues at a rental unit. They are required to act reasonably as issues arise. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant’s T2 application is brought under ss. 21, 22 and 23 of the Act: 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), a landlord shall be deemed to have withheld the reasonable supply of a vital service, care service or food if the landlord is obligated to pay another person for the vital service, care service or food, the landlord fails to pay the required amount and, as a result of the non-payment, the other person withholds the reasonable supply of the vital service, care service or food. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.
This is the Tenant’s application, and she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

I find that the following has been established on a balance of probabilities: a. There have been bedbugs at the property and the Landlord was made aware of the issue on October 27, 2025. The issue was not resolved as of the date of the hearing. b. There was no heat at the rental unit between September 4, and September 18, 2025, and c. There was no hot water between September 4 and September 18, 2025 and again between October 16 and November 13, 2025.

I do not find that the Tenant established other alleged facts on the balance of probabilities. Her other allegations are disputed and are not supported by corroborating evidence. It is possible that she is right, but it is at least as plausible that the Landlord is correct. I see no reason to prefer the Tenant’s version of the contested events. Her testimony that bedbugs have been present at the rental unit for years and that the Landlord has been aware of the issue since May 2025 was not supported by persuasive evidence. It appears inconsistent with the parties’ conduct, as the Tenant sent dozens of written complaints. None of the complaints predate late October. The Tenant filed extensive evidence, and I draw a negative inference from the lack of persuasive evidence of the Landlord’s earlier knowledge. The Tenant’s statement that the Landlord deliberately turned off the heat appears to be entirely speculative as well.

Based on the factual findings above, I find that the Landlord breached s. 21 of the Act which requires Landlords not to interfere with supply of vital services. Under s. 21(2), non- payment of utilities where the Landlord is responsible for payment, constitutes interference with vital services within the meaning of the Act. It was undisputed that the Landlord is responsible for paying the gas bill at the rental unit. Pursuant to s. 4(1) of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act, heat was a vital service at the relevant time.

I also find that the Landlord was not entirely reasonable in addressing the Tenant’s complaints. The bedbug issue was reported a month before the hearing. As of the date of the hearing, there was still no treatment plan, let alone treatment, of the rental unit or the residential complex performed by the Landlord. Similarly, it was not reasonable for the Landlord to take almost a month to fix the broken boiler. The Landlord’s testimony that the repairs were delayed by City officials was uncorroborated. The timeline appears to not be reasonable within the meaning of Onyskiw without clear and persuasive evidence from the Landlord why repairs could not have been completed sooner.
I do not find that the Tenant established a breach of any other section of the Act.

The term harassment is not defined in the Act but is usually understood to mean conduct that is known or ought to reasonably be known to be unwelcome. I do not find that the Landlord acted deliberately or that the Landlord took steps to harass the Tenant. Section 23 is distinct from sections 20 and 21, and a breach of the latter does not automatically mean a breach of the former. Similarly, I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment apart from the Landlord’s breach of ss. 20 and 21. That breach is adequately covered by sections 20 and 21 and does not automatically invoke section 22. Remedies

The Tenant’s application requests the following remedies: a. Rent abatement of $3,923.70 representing a 50% abatement of rent for 12 months, based on her monthly rent of $653.95, b. An order for the Landlord to stop activities described in the application, c. For the Landlord to pay a fine to the LTB, d. For the LTB to review prior LTB orders from 2022 and 2023, and e. For an order for the Landlord to pay a fine to the City.
No other remedies were requested in the application and no other remedies will be granted.
The Tenant withdrew her request for remedy ‘d’ at the hearing. It would not be an appropriate remedy to grant in this application even if the Tenant requested it.
Remedy ‘e’ is denied. It is outside the jurisdiction of the LTB.

Remedy ‘a’ is granted in part. The Tenant only established that it is more likely than not that the Landlord breached the Act between September 4, 2025 to September 18, 2025 and then again between October 16, 2025 and the date of the hearing. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $700. It represents a loss of approximately 1 month worth of enjoyment of her unit during this 3-month period due to the multiple issues she has had to deal with. This award represents rent abatement to November 28, 2025. This award is without prejudice to the Tenant’s right to potentially pursue further remedies in another application if the bedbug issue remains unresolved. 51. [name] ‘b’ is granted as well. The Landlord is ordered to stop interfering with the supply of vital services. This includes interfering with it by not paying utility bills the Landlord is responsible for. 52. [name] ‘c’ is denied. Fines are intended to deter misconduct and to encourage compliance by this Landlord and similar landlords. I do not find that the conduct of the Landlord was such that it would warrant a fine at this time. I do not find that the breach was egregious or deliberate or that the Landlord blatantly disregarded his obligations under the Act. A fine may be warranted if the Landlord acts similarly negligently in the future. 53. The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application and I find that she is entitled to reimbursement of this cost.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $748.00. This amount represents: • $700.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending November 28, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months of February and March 2026 until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall not interfere with the provision of vital services to the rental unit. January 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Act.
Therefore, the Landlords must compensate the Tenant in the amount of $18,000.00 and must complete the repair of the mould problems in the rental unit. Tenant’s evidence

This application is about the Tenant’s allegations of black mould (mould) in the rental unit. The Tenant says she brought this issue to the attention of the Landlords, but the Landlords were not successful in remedying the problem. The Landlords say the problem is not mould, and that they have fixed the problem.

The Tenant testified that she initially brought the issue of mould in her rental unit to the attention of the Landlords in September of 2023. She sent a text message to the Landlords at that time and subsequently sent photos detailing the problem. Text messages confirming this can be found in DOC – 2341969 filed in the portal. The Tenant testified that she was told by the Landlords to “clean it herself” and to consider moving out if she did not like it.

Although the Tenant had noticed the mould months prior to notifying the Landlords, after getting sick and believing it was due to the mould, she attempted to clean it and bleached it to try to get rid of it. She advised the Landlords that she had tried to bleach the mould many times. Pictures, time stamped November 8, 2023, found in DOC- 7388743, evidenced her attempts to fix the problem. She had forwarded these pictures to the Landlords. She testified that the mould was located in the bathroom all around the tub and then spread up to and around the sink. She noted that the sliding doors also have mould.
The Tenant testified that she was later advised that bleach does not actually stop or kill mould.
The Tenant testified that she sent follow up messages to the Landlords regarding the mould on October 22, 2023. Copies of these text messages are found in the portal.

The Tenant testified that she suffers from health problems related to the mould. Whenever she was away from the unit, she would feel fine, but upon returning to the unit, would get sick. A doctor’s note dated November 20, 2023, located at page 45 of the Tenant’s evidence package (DOC-7388743) indicates that the Tenant suffers from a lung condition for which she is undergoing investigations and treatments. At that time, the Tenant says she stayed with a friend for 1 to 2 weeks, and when she returned to her unit, stayed away from the bathroom, using her gym to shower to avoid being exposed to the mould in the bathroom.

Another medical note, dated February 24, 2026, was submitted (DOC- 7438534) which indicated that after returning from a trip when she was away from the rental unit, the Tenant developed cough episodes in her rental unit. The doctor indicated that “it is possible that mold in her apartment may contribute to her symptoms.”

The Tenant testified that in addition to her health problems, having the mould prevented her from hosting people in her unit, and she had to, and continues to, shower at her gym to avoid being exposed to the mould.

The Tenant testified that she did not receive an action plan from the Landlord to address the mould. She testified that the Landlord tried to remedy the situation by covering the mould with a sealant. This attempt was not effective in getting rid of the mould.

The Tenant submits that to the date of the hearing, it has been 908 days since she notified the Landlords of the problems with mould in her bathroom and on the sliding door, and it has still not been successfully removed. Landlords’ Evidence
The first named Landlord (OO) testified with the assistance of his daughter who translated for him.

OO testified that when the mould issue was brought to his attention, he went over to look at it, scraped it off, and removed the caulking. He denied covering up the mould. He also testified that he gave the Tenant spray for what he alleged was dirt (not mould) and said she was satisfied with his actions to address the problem.

OO said that he did not call an expert to address this problem. He said he did the repairs himself because he did not believe it was mould. He did not provide any accommodations to the Tenant for any inconvenience arising from the mould problem, and said that every time he left the premises, the Tenant was satisfied with the steps he was taking to address the mould.

OO testified that he was not aware of the evidence before the Tribunal and said that he has not been able to access the portal. He said that if he had pictures he could upload, he would be able to better argue the case. He said he was unprepared and did not have time to access and upload evidence. He acknowledged that he had previously uploaded evidence and had always previously been prepared for hearings in which he appeared. He said that if he had time, he could find emails with the building inspector. He did not detail what those emails would say. He did not seek an adjournment based on his lack of preparedness. Analysis

This application is before the Board pursuant to section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act which reads: Landlord’s responsibility to repair 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non -repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

The Board considered the testimony of both parties in outlining the alleged mould problem, including the notice provided by the Tenant to the Landlords of the problems, the Landlords’ response to the problem, and the impact on the Tenant.

I am satisfied that the Tenant provided notice to the Landlords of the problem which she identified as mould in September of 2023, based on the text messages submitted in evidence. I am also satisfied that she tried to address the problem herself by deep and extensive cleaning and bleaching the mould, efforts which did not successfully get rid of the mould. This lends credibility to the presumption that the problem was mould, because if it was just dirt, the bleach would have removed it. The Tenant’s testimony on her efforts to address the problem was credible, detailed, and supported by documentary evidence. On a balance of probabilities, it appears that the issue identified in the bathroom is mould. I am also satisfied that there may be some health issues for the Tenant arising from this unresolved problem.

I do not find that the Landlords responded in a timely and effective manner. When the Landlords attended the premises, they took the position that the mould was dirt and could be cleaned. The Landlords were not able to get rid of the problem by cleaning and other efforts they made, which suggests that this was not an issue of “dirt”. The Landlords indicated that they never consulted with any experts to confirm whether or not there was mould (as opposed to their conclusion that it was dirt) and to ascertain how to successfully address the problem. By their own testimony, their attempts to resolve the issue were not successful. In addition, they exacerbated the situation by telling the Tenant to move out if she did not like living with this problem. This was documented as noted above in the text messaging and was not refuted by the Landlords in their testimony.

The Landlords indicated that they were not prepared for the hearing. They did not seek an adjournment. I note that this matter has been longstanding with the Tenant’s issues outstanding since 2023. The text messages and pictures referred to by the Tenant had all been provided to the Landlords over 2 years ago. I find that the Landlords were well aware of the case to be met and had adequate time to file any documentation needed to support their case.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I find that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit. In addition to delayed response, they did not effectively address the problem. They failed to ascertain the true nature of the mould, taking the position that it was “dirt”, did not provide an effect plan of action to address the problem, and did not consult with experts for assistance. I do not find that the Landlords’ response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances.
This [name] contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons will be issued. Remedies

Based on the information above, I find that a rent abatement of $18,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. This has been calculated on the basis of a rent abatement of 30% per month from September 2023, the date the Tenant initially contacted the Landlord regarding the issue, to the date of the hearing. Rent amount: $2,000.00 x 30% = $600.00 x 30 months = $18,000.00.

The following additional remedies are being ordered because the problem has not yet been fixed, and the Tenant continues to have to deal with the loss of the use of her shower and the other circumstances related to the existence of the mould.
ordered: The Landlords shall repair the areas where mould is located: namely the bathroom and the sliding door by March 30, 2026.

If the Landlords do not do the repairs by March 30, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repairs to be done and may recover the cost of the repair(s) by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months after the repairs are done until there is no longer any money owing.

The Landlords shall also pay the Tenant is $18,000.00. This amount represents: • $18,000.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending February 2026: Rent amount: $2,000.00 x 30% = $600.00 x 30 months = $18,000.00.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 29, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 29, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 30, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 29, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months after the repairs are done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,998.00.
The parties agreed that on April 15, 2025, they entered into a written tenancy agreement. A copy of the lease agreement was submitted into evidence.

The parties agreed that the tenancy was to commence on May 1, 2025. The Landlord offered the Tenants an early move-in option in exchange for an additional payment of $200.00. The Tenants accepted this offer and, on April 15, 2025, paid the total sum of $1,950.00, consisting of a $1,750.00 rent deposit and the $200.00 early move-in fee.

The Tenant (WB) testified that on April 16, 2025, he attended at the rental unit to obtain a key. During this meeting, he raised a concern regarding the kitchen lighting. The Landlord became upset and, in response, offered to “tear up” the lease.

Later on April 16, 2025, the Tenants contacted the Landlord by telephone to confirm the proposed termination of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord advised that the parties would meet on April 17, 2025, at 10:00 a.m. at the rental unit to finalize the cancellation. This conversation was recorded and submitted into evidence. Although the parties did not clearly state during that conversation that the parties were agreeing to terminate the tenancy and go their separate ways, I think it would be reasonable for the Tenants to expect that all payments made in respect of the tenancy including the $200.00 would be returned. Alternatively, the Landlord’s position on the application and the way they characterized the payment would render it an illegal charge under s. 134.
Subsequently, the Landlord advised by email that he was unable to attend the scheduled meeting on April 17, 2025, due to a scheduling conflict.

On April 17, 2025, the Tenants sent a written communication confirming acceptance of the Landlord’s offer to terminate the tenancy agreement. On the same date, the Tenant’s husband returned the key to the Landlord. A copy of the April 17, 2025, email communication was submitted into evidence.

Following the cancellation, the Tenants made repeated efforts to arrange for the return of the funds paid. The Landlord scheduled multiple meetings but cancelled on at least two occasions and has not returned the funds.
The Tenant BW testified, and the Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant did not move into, occupy, or otherwise take possession of the rental unit at any time.
The Tenants returned the keys on April 17, 2025, confirming relinquishment of any access or possessory interest in the unit.
Despite the mutual termination of the tenancy, the Landlord has failed to return the sum of $1,950.00. This amount includes a rent deposit and an additional fee. Landlord testimony

During the hearing, the Landlord testified that he is not out any money, and he was able to rent the unit for May 1, 2025. Also, during the hearing, the Landlord offered a portion of the money back to the Tenant in the amount of approximately $1,400.00 believing he is entitled to a portion of the deposit due to certain administration fees, such as vetting tenants, credit checks etc.

The retention of these funds is contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), including s. 134(1), which prohibits a landlord from collecting or retaining amounts that are not permitted under the Act.

I find that the parties entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy in accordance with section 37(3) of the Act effective April 17, 2025. The question before me is whether the Act entitles the Landlord to charge or retain a fee for agreeing to terminate the tenancy.

Subsection 134(1) of the Act says that unless otherwise provided, a landlord shall not, directly, or indirectly collect certain listed charges from a tenant in addition to rent. It provides: 134. (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant or prospective tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;
The exemptions from s. 134(1) are set out in section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06:

The following payments are exempt from section 134 of the Act: 1. Payment for additional keys, remote entry devices or cards requested by the tenant, not greater than the direct costs. 2. Payment for replacement keys, remote entry devices, or cards, not greater than the direct replacement costs, unless the replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards are required because the landlord, on the landlord’s initiative, changed the locks. 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device, or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs. 4. Payment of NSF charges charged by a financial institution to the landlord. 5. Payment of an administration charge, not greater than $20, for an NSF cheque. 6. Payment by a tenant, former tenant, subtenant, or former subtenant in settlement of a court action or potential court action or an application or potential application to the Board. 7. Payment to a landlord or tenant of a mobile home park or land lease community at the commencement of a tenancy as consideration for the rental of a particular site. 8. Payment of a charge not exceeding $250 for transferring, at the request of the tenant, i. between rental units to which subsection 6 (1) or (3) of this Regulation applies, if the rental units are located in the same residential complex, or ii. between rental units in a residential complex that is described in paragraph 1, 2, 3 or 4 of subsection 7 (1) of the Act. 9. Payment of an amount to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by the tenant 17. The list of exemptions does not include a charge for entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy.

In addition, based on the documentary evidence before me, there was no evidence that the deduction of any money from the Tenant ’s deposit was in exchange of settling any potential court action. This was not a situation that involved the collection of reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred in relation to the LL’s consent to assign a lease (s. 95(7)) 19. -And given that the rental unit was rerented effective May 1st, s. 134(1.1) also applies at least with respect to any rent collected/retained for the period after April 30th. 20. Therefore, I find that the Landlord breached section 134 of Act by retaining $1,950.00 deposit for breaking the lease. 21. As the Tenant has been successful in her application, the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the application filing fee. 22. This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,998.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
