issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $382.46. Background

During the hearing, the Tenants, [name] and [name] O’Donnell both took turns to testify. The Tenants testified that they entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit municipally known as [address]ive, commencing November 1, 2024.

The Tenant, BO, testified that she gave 60 days notice on September 1, 2025, that the Tenants were vacating the rental unit. The tenancy ended on September 20, 2025, when the Tenants vacated the unit and returned the keys.
On September 2, 2025, the Tenants paid the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,750.00.
The Tenants vacated the unit substantially by September 13, 2025, and fully removed their remaining belongings by September 20, 2025.
The Tenant (BO) testified that on October 17, 2025, the Landlord re-rented the rental unit to a new tenant.

The Landlord acknowledged that the Tenants would be entitled to a refund for any period during which the unit was re-rented. The Tenants submitted a copy of text communication into evidence between the Landlord and the Tenant (BO) wherein the Landlord agreed to return a refund to the Tenants.
I find that once the Landlord re-rented the unit, the Landlord was not entitled to retain rent for the same period from the Tenants.
The Tenants were entitled to a pro-rated rent refund for the period of October 16 to October 31, 2025, totaling $1,419.35.
On November 3, 2025, the Landlord paid the Tenants $1,140.89 and deducted $334.46 described as a “lock change fee.”
The issue before the Board is whether the Landlord was entitled to charge and retain the $334.46 lock change fee. Applicable Law

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) says: 134. (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant or prospective tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

This reads as an absolute prohibition against a landlord charging any kind of fee other than rent to a tenant. However, the section uses the phrase “unless otherwise prescribed” which means fees can be charged if they are set out in regulation.

The exemptions to s. 134(1) are set out in section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06. It says in part: 17. The following payments are exempt from section 134 of the Act: 1. Payment for additional keys, remote entry devices or cards requested by the tenant, not greater than the direct costs. 2. Payment for replacement keys, remote entry devices, or cards, not greater than the direct replacement costs, unless the replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards are required because the landlord, on the landlord’s initiative, changed the locks. 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device, or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs. Analysis
I find that the lock change fee charged by the Landlord is not a lawful charge under the Act. The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Landlord did not attend the hearing to provide evidence that the fee was authorized under any provision of the Act.
The Act does not permit landlords to charge tenants for routine maintenance or unilateral lock changes, including circumstances where the tenancy has ended, unless otherwise ordered by the Board.

The deduction of $334.46 from the rent refund therefore constitutes an unlawful charge within the meaning of section 134(1) of the Act. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the sum of $334.46, representing an unlawful charge collected.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $382.46. This amount represents: • $334.46 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The rental unit is located in a high-rise condo building. The Landlord owns the rental unit and the building itself is owned by a condo corporation and managed by a property management company hired by the condo corporation. Substantial interference

It was undisputed that between September 3, 2024 and September 18, 2024, the rental unit had no clean water. Construction crews working on new condo construction adjacent to the rental unit mistakenly installed a temporary bypass connecting the building’s water supply to its irrigation system, contaminating the water for the entire building. The water was grey and had a bad odour. The property management company reached out to all residents, including the Tenant and the Landlord, by email on September 4, 2024 notifying them of the issue. VH, the Landlord’s wife, testified that she did reach out to building management for an update after becoming aware of the situation.

The Tenant submitted a letter received from legal counsel for Toronto Standard Condominium Corporation. The letter sets out all steps taken by the condo corporation between September 4, 2024, when they first received a report concerning the water, and September 18, 2024, when water was determined to be safe for residential use. It details extensive investigations into the cause, various water quality tests, flushing of chemicals from the building’s water supply as part of a sanitation and disinfection process. Clean water was restored on September 18, 2024.

This application is being brought pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act which states that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the issue is not one that could be addressed by the Landlord at all as it related to a mistake by a builder not connected to the Landlord in any way, and the condo corporation who was responsible for managing the issue. Based on the Tenant’s evidence and considering the summary of steps taken by the condo corporation which were detailed in the lawyer’s correspondence, I find that they respondent promptly and reasonably in the circumstances with respect to the water contamination. There were extensive steps required to ensure safe and clean water could be restored to the building and the condo corporation acted diligently to accomplish that.

The mere fact that there was a leak and interruption with hot water services does not automatically give rise to a breach of section 20 of the Act. It depends on what steps the Landlord takes once made aware of the issues. It cannot be said that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act when they responded promptly to the Tenant’s complaints, and the issues were addressed without delay.

Additionally, although the Landlord did not reach out to the Tenant to see how she was managing the situation, the Landlord was not required to and failing to reach out is not a breach of section 20 of the Act. Additionally, the fact that the Landlord did not independently reach out to the Tenant, in my view, does not amount to substantial interference, particularly when the Tenant never contacted the Landlord to inform them of the issue in the first place and the Tenant was regularly informed by the property management company.

The contextual approach set out in Onyskiw also applies to T2 applications where the allegations overlap with section 20(1) of the Act. Paragraph 56 of Onyskiw states: To interpret s. 20(1) as the tenants propose would result in an interpretation that places the provisions of s. 20(1) and s. 22 in conflict or disharmony with one another and disregard the intent of the legislature that where, as here, there is an overlap, both provisions should apply. The tenants' reading of the RTA does not result in the legislation functioning as an internally consistent whole.

The Court in Onyskiw found that the legislature intended both sections 20(1) and section 22 of the Act apply where the issue raised overlaps as they do here. As such, T2 application, as filed with respect to the allegation of substantial interference, cannot succeed without a breach of section 20(1) of the Act.
For the foregoing reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Withheld vital services
In the application, the Tenant also claims that the Landlord withheld vital services due to the lack of clean water between September 3, 2024 and September 18, 2024.

Section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

The difficulty with the Tenant’s application and submissions concerning the lack of hot water is that the evidence does not establish that the Landlord deliberately or intentionally withheld hot water. Rather, it was the Tenant’s evidence that there was simply a maintenance issue that caused the water to be contaminated.

Section 21(1) of the Act does not apply to disrepair or a maintenance issue. The wording of the provision shows it is intended to address the situation where a landlord deliberately interferes with or withholds a vital service. That is not what happened here. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘MZ’) and [name] (‘AZ’, the 'Landlords'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: I am satisfied AZ is properly named as a respondent Landlord to this application. AZ testified that he manages the property and tenancy for his parents, who include the landlord MZ.
The Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord AZ illegally locked the Tenant out of the residential complex

At the hearing, the Landlord AZ agreed that, on November 3, 2025, he deactivated an electronic keypad on a door that gave the Tenant entry to the residential complex. AZ’s act prevented the Tenant from entering the residential complex.

AZ explained that he deactivated the locking mechanism because he believes trespassers gained access to the rental unit on or about October 30, 2025, and AZ wanted to protect his parents who reside at the property. AZ testified he believes the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about October 30, 2025, in accordance with Board order LTB-014906-25, issued on September 17, 2025. That order terminated the tenancy and ordered the Tenant to vacate the rental unit by October 30, 2025 because the Landlords in good faith require possession of the rental unit for their own residential use.

At the hearing, the Tenant described being surprised on November 3, 2025 to discover that she was unable to use the keypad to enter the residential complex. The Landlords were at the property and, despite the Tenant’s protestations, refused to permit the Tenant to enter. The Toronto Police Service was called and [name]. [name] attended. The Tenant and [name]. [name] gave sworn testimony that AZ did not permit the Tenant to enter the residential complex. Instead, [name]. [name] was permitted to enter the rental unit to retrieve some of the Tenant’s personal items, including medicine and cash. [name]. [name] testified that, although he was able to locate medical supplies, he did not locate money in the areas of the rental unit where the Tenant instructed the officer to search.

Both Cst. [name] and the Tenant gave consistent testimony that the rental unit contained a large amount of the Tenant’s personal property. I accept the Tenant’s and [name]. [name]’s description that the rental unit remained full of the Tenant’s belongings. A person the Tenant knows removed some items of furniture from the rental unit on October 30, 2025. AZ agreed that he did not inquire who the person was, but instead assumed they were a trespasser.

The Tenant entered documentary evidence of email messages to the Landlords dated November 3, 2025. The messages, from the Tenant and the Tenant’s legal representative, advise that the Tenant remains in possession of the rental unit and assert the Tenant’s right to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant’s legal representative’s message, sent at 9:49PM, advises that only the Court Enforcement Office may enforce the September 17, 2025 Board order (see subsection 141(1), Courts of Justice Act). A November 4, 2025 letter to the Landlords from the Tenant’s legal representative demands the Landlords immediately return access to the residential complex to the Tenant.

AZ did not dispute the contents of the email messages the Tenant entered as exhibits, and AZ agreed that the Landlords did not permit the Tenant to re-occupy the rental unit. AZ also agreed with the Tenant’s evidence that the Tenant and Tenant’s legal representative were allowed to recover the Tenant’s remaining property on December 13, 2025.

Based on the evidence, I find that, even if AZ believed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit before November 3, 2025, the Tenant’s and the Tenant’s legal representative’s actions and email messages on November 3, 2025 should have dispelled that belief and caused the Landlords to give the Tenant access to the electronic keypad and residential complex. I am not satisfied that a legal authority, such as the Court Enforcement Office or the Toronto Police Service, approved of or instructed the Landlords to refuse the Tenant entry into the residential complex.

AZ’s assertion that the Court Enforcement Office later advised that what AZ had done was appropriate, and that it was not necessary to allow the Tenant to re-enter the rental property, is not credible. Without an independent witness to support AZ’s claim, I am not satisfied that the Court Enforcement Office approved of AZ’s blatant disregard for the law by personally enforcing a civil order in contravention of the Courts of Justice Act.

I am also not satisfied that another Toronto Police Services officer instructed AZ to refuse the Tenant entry into the residential complex on November 3, 2025. Again, AZ did not call the officer who gave the alleged instruction as a witness, and [name]. [name] was unable to identify the officer from AZ’s vague description of the alleged officer’s approximate age. AZ’s description of the instruction and the circumstances under which it was allegedly given was also vague and lacked probative value.

The Landlords’ failure to return possession of the rental unit and access to the residential complex to the Tenant resulted in an illegal lockout, a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the property, harassment, obstruction and interference, all of which are prohibited under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Although the electronic keypad does not require a key, as mentioned in section 24 of the Act, canceling the Tenant’s access to the keypad resulted in the Tenant being locked out of the residential complex without reasonable means to enter and occupy the rental unit. Remedies

AZ agreed that the Landlords received the Tenants’ proposed amendments to the application on December 10, 2025. The amendments clarify the remedies the Tenant seeks without materially changing the Tenant’s description of the conduct giving rise to the application. In the circumstances, I found it was appropriate to grant the Tenant’s request to amend the application, pursuant to section 200 of the Act and Rule 15.

Having proved the Landlords did not comply with sections 22, 23 and 24 of the Act, I find the Tenant is entitled to remedies described in section 31 of the Act and pled for in the amended application. I note, for example, the Tenant did not request an order requiring the Landlords to pay the difference in rent the Tenant has paid since the November 3, 2025 lockout. The Landlords were not reasonably aware of this request, and I accordingly did not consider the remedy.

The Tenant did, however, request an order for a rent abatement, general damages, reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other costs, and an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine. The Tenant also sought compensation for personal property the Tenant discovered was allegedly missing after the Tenant and the Tenant’s legal representative collected the Tenant’s items on December 13, 2023, and an order stopping the Landlords from repeating the conduct. Abatement

Board order LTB-014906-25, issued on September 17, 2025, terminated the tenancy on October 30, 2025 and ordered the Tenant to pay daily compensation for the use and occupancy of the rental unit, starting October 31, 2025 and continuing until the Tenant vacates the property. Since the Tenant was not permitted to enter the property after November 3, 2025, the Tenant’s obligation to pay compensation ended on November 3. The Tenant is entitled to an abatement if they paid the Landlords compensation for the use of the rental unit after November 3, 2025, and the Landlords shall be ordered to refund any compensation payment after that date. General Damages
The Tenant requested an order requiring the Landlords to pay $10,000.00 in general damages. The Tenant described feeling humiliated, anxious and afraid because of the Landlords’ conduct.

In [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court ruled that the Board may order a landlord to pay general damages for breaching the contractual and statutory obligation not to interfere with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rented premises. In that case, the landlord permitted people to assault the tenant to coerce the tenant to vacate the property. The Divisional Court ordered the landlord to pay the tenant $4,000.00 in general damages. Using the Bank of Canada’s inflation calculator, $4000.00 in 2007 represents approximately $6,000.00 in 2025.

As in [name], the Landlords’ conduct in this present case resulted in the Tenant’s illegal eviction from the rental unit. However, while I am mindful of the Tenant’s testimony of their personal circumstances, including testimony of their health status since the illegal lockout, the Landlords did not assault the Tenant. The Tenant’s request for $10,000.00 is, in my opinion, not reasonable in the circumstances. Instead, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlords to pay the Tenant $4,000.00. This amount takes into consideration the amount the Divisional Court ordered for the illegal eviction and assault in Mejia, adjusted roughly for inflation, and the Tenant’s evidence of how the Landlords’ conduct affected her. The amount reflects the serious nature of illegally evicting the Tenant from the rental unit without being unduly punitive. Moving and Storage Costs
The Tenant did not have reliable evidence of moving costs. There shall accordingly be no order requiring the Landlords to pay the alleged costs.

The Tenant introduced evidence showing that they rented storage space on October 30, 2025, before the Landlords illegally locked the Tenant out of the residential complex. Based on the Tenant’s testimony, I find the Tenant rented the storage space because she was required to vacate the rental unit in accordance with Board order LTB-014906-25, issued on September 17, 2025; not because of the Landlords’ actions on November 3, 2025. The Tenant’s storage costs are therefore unrelated to the conduct giving rise to this application, and there shall be no order requiring the Landlords to pay these costs. Other Out-of-Pocket Costs

I find from the Tenant’s and [name]. [name]’s sworn testimony that the Tenant had very few personal belongings when the Landlords evicted her from the rental unit on November 3, 2025. I find the Tenant is entitled to compensation for reasonable-out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant incurred because of the Landlords’ conduct.

The Tenant introduced evidence that they were required to purchase eyeglasses on November 7, 2025. Although a printed receipt shows the year 2024, I am satisfied this is an error. I believe the hand-written invoice to which the printed receipt is attached indicates the date “Nov. 7/25”. The Tenant spent $179.00 on the new eyeglasses.

On November 11, 2025, the Tenant spent $106.20 on personal items, including sleepwear and a handbag, and $81.29 socks and containers. The Tenant testified she did not have additional clothing, a bag or storage items with her when she was locked out of the rental unit on November 3, 2025. The Tenant also introduced evidence that she spent $254.23 on November 30, 2025 to replace other clothing, and $156.52 on December 1, 2025 to replace winter clothing and a home nightlight.

The Tenant introduced evidence that she spent $50.12 on November 5, 2025 to replace groceries that were left in the unit and which the Tenant was unable to access and use. The Tenant testified that although a friend provided temporary accommodation from November 3, 2025, the Tenant was required to purchase her own food and other personal items.

A receipt from Food Basics in the amount of $61.47 appears to be dated October 29, 2025 and is therefore unrelated to the Landlords’ conduct. The Tenant agreed that she would have purchased groceries described in a December 1, 2025 had she not been evicted, and I accordingly decline to order the Landlords to pay for food-related expenses on December 1, 2025.

A receipt from Dollar Tree, dated November 30, 2025, shows the Tenant purchased items the Tenant needed for her new accommodation. I find the Tenant is entitled to compensation for clothes hangers, a mop handle, [name] cleaning powder and a pill holder. The total amount for these items, including HST, is $13.28. Other items the Tenant purchased at Dollar Tree, such as food and holiday decorations, are not reasonable out-of- pocket expenses related to the Landlords’ conduct. A November 30, 2025 receipt from Rexall Pharmacy is illegible and not reliable evidence of the Tenant’s out-of-pocket expenses.

On November 29, 2025, the Tenant spent $164.90 at Winners to purchase items including beauty accessories, haircare products, athletic shoes, a handbag and a beverage. At the hearing, the Tenant testified that her beauty and haircare products remained in the rental unit. In the circumstances, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlords to pay the Tenant’s cost to replace these items. I also find it is appropriate to order the Landlords to pay the Tenant’s cost to replace athletic shoes. The Landlords, however, have already been ordered to pay for one handbag, and I am not satisfied that the expense to purchase another was reasonable or directly related to the Landlords’ conduct. The Tenant did not explain their decision to purchase the second handbag. The Landlords therefore shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $142.32 for her November 29, 2025 out-of-pocket expenses at Winners. The Tenant appropriately waived her claim for the beverage.

The Tenant testified that she incurred additional transportation costs after she was evicted from the rental unit. The Tenant gave evidence that she added funds to her public transit card on November 13, 2025, November 17, 2025, November 26, 2025 and November 27, 2025. The Tenant did not, however, adequately explain the frequent purchases or give a sufficient account of how and why she used the transit card. I am therefore not satisfied that the Tenant’s transportation costs are directly related to the Landlords’ conduct.
The Tenant is not entitled to her cost to purchase luggage on October 28, 2025. The Tenant’s decision to purchase luggage is unrelated to the conduct giving rise to this application.

The Tenant is not entitled to the cost to purchase a security camera. I am not satisfied that the Tenant introduced sufficient evidence to prove that they were required to purchase a new camera because of the Landlords’ conduct. There was also no reliable evidence of the value of the camera. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine may be ordered against a landlord to promote the landlord’s compliance with the Act and to deter other landlords from doing the same conduct. With that guidance in mind, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlords to pay an administrative fine of $3,000.00.

AZ testified that he applied to the Court Enforcement Office after he canceled the Tenant’s access to the keypad lock on the residential complex door. AZ was therefore aware, or should have been aware, that the Court Enforcement Office exercises exclusive jurisdiction to enforce civil remedies, including Board eviction orders. AZ’s spurious belief that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit on October 30, 2025, his decision to cancel the Tenant’s access to the electronic keypad, and his refusal to permit the Tenant to re-occupy the rental unit subject to proper enforcement of the September 17, 2025 Board order were wilful breaches of the Act and of the Landlords’ obligations under it. It is appropriate in the circumstances to order the Landlords to pay an administrative fine. With the order requiring the Landlords to pay the Tenant $4,000.00 in general damages, I am satisfied that an administrative fine of $3,000.00 will promote future compliance with the Act. Items Allegedly Missing

The Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence of missing items among the personal property the Tenant collected on December 13, 2025. The Tenant’s claim for these alleged items is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $5,030.96. This amount represents: • $4,000.00 for general damages; • $982.96 for the reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Tenant has incurred as a result of the Landlords’ actions; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $3,000.00 by January 19, 2026.
The Landlords shall refund to the Tenant any per diem compensation the Tenant paid to occupy and use the rental unit after November 3, 2025.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons shall be given. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $300.00. Illegal charge collected
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenants filed a T1 – Tenant Application for a [name] pursuant to section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act), alleging that the Landlord collected and retained an illegal charge in the amount of $300.00 for keys, cards, or fobs.

The tenancy began on September 1, 2024. The Tenant (SG) testified that, as a condition of moving into the rental unit, they paid the Landlord $300.00 for keys/cards/fobs. The Tenant submitted a copy of the lease agreement into evidence.
The tenancy ended on September 30, 2025, when the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant, [name] (CB), testified that upon vacating the unit, they returned the keys by leaving them with the concierge desk in the residential complex. CB submitted an text message they sent the Landlord into evidence confirming that the keys were left with the concierge. CB further testified that they contacted the Landlord regarding the return of the key deposit, but the Landlord did not respond and did not return the $300.00.
The written lease agreement was submitted into evidence. It states that the Tenant agreed to provide $300.00 refundable key deposit.
Section 134(1) of the Act prohibits a landlord from collecting or requiring any charge from a tenant unless the charge is specifically permitted under the Act.

Section 17 of the General Regulation allows a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit, provided it is no more than the expected direct replacement cost of the keys, cards, or fobs, and provided it is returned when the keys are returned.
Section 135 of the Act authorizes the Board to order a landlord to repay money collected in contravention of the Act.

I accept that a refundable key deposit is permitted under the Act. When read together, section 134 of the Act and section 17 of O.Reg 516/06 prohibit a landlord from retaining a key deposit after the key has been returned at the end of a tenancy.

The lease expressly states that the $300.00 deposit is to be returned upon termination of the tenancy and the return of the keys. The Tenants provided credible evidence, including contemporaneous text message correspondence, that the keys were returned to the concierge upon vacating the unit.
In the absence of reliable evidence that the keys were not returned or that replacement costs were incurred, I find that the Landlord was not entitled to retain the $300.00 key deposit.

I therefore find that the Landlord retained money to which they were not entitled, contrary to section 134 of the Act, and that the Tenants are entitled to a rebate under section 135 of the Act. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenants $300.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $300.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2) and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.(T6)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit is located in a 2-storey complex comprised of 12 bachelor type rental units.
The Tenant has resided in the complex since May 31, 2018.
On October 24, 2024 the Tenant filed a combined T2/T6 application with the LTB.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has not maintained the rental unit or residential complex, and has not complied with health and safety standards, specifically fire safety requirements. The T2/T6 applications were filed on the basis of a fire in the complex on September 24, 2024 that started in unit #5.

The Tenant testified that: • September 24, 2024, at approximately 6:00 p.m. he observed smoke coming from Unit #5, that it was visible from the back door and bathroom window and that he called 911, and the fire department attended. • The cause of the fire originated from a pot left on the stove unattended, with the tenant of unit #5 being reportedly unconscious when the fire started. • The smoke detector had been removed from the wall, rendering it useless. • The Tenant became aware that the building did not have accessible fire extinguishers. • On September 26, 2024 the Tenant attended at the Orillia Fire Department to make a formal complaint regarding lack of fire safety compliance. • On October 5, 2024 two (2) [name] attended at the residential complex however that he was unsure of the outcome of their inspection as nothing was provided to him. • On October 1, 2024, he sent a letter to the Landlord advising him of the situation however no response was received. • On October 2, 2024, he once more addressed his concerns with the property manager, “Martin” but that he the dismissed his safety concerns. • He and other residents are concerned for safety due to the neighbour’s history of mental health concerns and the risk of recurrence of fire in the complex as it is his belief that the complex does not have adequate fire safety protocols.

The Tenant submitted that he purchased a fire extinguisher on October 1, 2024, and two smoke detectors on October 4, 2024, and incurred $230.31out of pocket expenses for which he claims reimbursement from the Landlord. Additionally, that the Landlord be directed to ensure the residential complex is compliant with fire code safety standards in respect of the provision of fire extinguishers, hard-wired smoke alarms and any other fire safety requirements. And that the Landlord submit a fire department inspection report once upgrades are completed.

The Landlord testified that the fire of September 24, 2024 was minor in nature resulting in smoke damage only. That the building is equipped with a central smoke alarm system which is compliant with the Fire Code. And while the Tenant alleges non-compliance that there were no orders for compliance issued as against the Landlord in respect of the October 5, 2024 Fire Marshals attendance at the residential complex.
That he became aware that the Tenant bought battery operated smoke detectors and taped them to the outside of the building, this being an ineffective method and posed an eyesore for the complex.
Since then, two smoke detectors have been added to the outside of the building by the Landlord, while not required by-law, were installed as a safety precaution given the concerns raised.

At the time of the hearing both parties submitted opposing oral evidence with respect of fire code and fire safety compliance in respect of the residential complex, however, both parties failed to adduce any evidence to support their positions.

On any application before the Board the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant.

Here, w hile the Tenant may have relied upon photographic evidence, expert witness testimony or any order(s) for compliance as issued to the Landlord, no such evidence was provided. I am more compelled to accept the Landlord’s oral submissions when noting that while the Tenant attended at the Orillia Fire Department on September 26, 2024 to file a formal report concerning compliance which resulted in an inspection of the residential complex, if there were any issue of non-compliance the Tenant as the reporting party would have been in a position to access any such report or order.

In summary, the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2) or that they failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6).
Given the outlined above, I find that the Tenant has failed to meet his burden of proof, and the application shall be dismissed accordingly.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application claims that the Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,650.00 which should be returned. At the hearing, the Tenant requested that I amend the application to include an additional $2,650.00 collected by the Landlord.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Whether the Landlords collected or retained money illegally

The Tenant signed a lease agreement on December 4, 2024. The tenancy was to begin on January 1, 2025 for a fixed term of one year. The Tenant testified that she paid a total of $5,300.00 to the Landlord which is for the first and last month of the tenancy.

The Tenant never moved into the rental unit. On December 12, 2024, she contacted the Landlord and told him she would not be moving into the unit because of safety concerns in connection to the location in which the property was located.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord initially agreed to return the money but later told her he would only provide her with a refund after he finds a new prospective tenant. The Tenant assisted the Landlord by advertising the unit for rent.
The Tenant was informed by a neighbour (residing near the rental property) that someone moved into the rental unit.

On February 22, 2025, the Tenant testified that she spoke with the new occupant who confirmed their tenancy commenced in January 2026. The Tenant did not know this individual’s name and they did not attend the hearing to testify. Analysis and Findings

Subsection 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states “a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

In Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 542, para 22, the Divisional Court held: “When one looks at the words of s. 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is “not given” to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective Tenant.”

In this case, a binding tenancy agreement was formed between the parties on December 4, 2024. The Tenant’s decision on December 12, 2024 not to proceed with the tenancy agreement constitutes a unilateral repudiation of the agreement before the tenancy began. In addition, there is no evidence before me that the Landlord refused or was unable to provide vacant possession. To the contrary, the Tenant’s own evidence was that she chose not to move in due to personal safety concerns.

Consistent with the reasoning provided in Opara v. [name], [2008] O.J. No. 1934 ([name]. Ct.) and Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 542, where the tenant repudiates a binding tenancy agreement prior to taking possession, the tenant is not entitled to return of the rent deposit because it was their own actions, not the Landlords, that prevented possession from being taken. Therefore, s.107(1) of the Act does not apply on these facts because the Landlord was prepared to provide vacant possession of the rental unit but it was declined by the Tenant.

However, the Landlord has a duty to mitigate losses in accordance with sections 16 and 88(4) of the Act by attempting to re-rent the unit once informed that the Tenant would not be taking possession. If the Landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, then the Tenant who failed to take possession of the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new Tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit per to s. 88(3)(2) of the Act.

In this case, while the Tenant believes a new Tenant moved in, there is insufficient evidence establishing when the tenancy began. In the absence of reliable evidence, either direct or documentary, I am unable to determine that the Landlord has illegally retained the Applicant’s rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations on a balance of probabilities as contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $550.00 in abatement of rent and comply with other terms as outlined in this order.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2023, the rental unit is a bedroom in a detached home with shared common spaces with up to 4 other tenants at any given time. The lawful rent is $630.00. The Tenant filed the T6 Application on October 24, 2024 and filed a subsequent amendment on January 11, 2026 per an Interim Order direction dated June 23, 2025.

In their T6 Application the Tenant alleges the following issues: a) Heat was not provided on two separate occasions due to failure to maintain the furnace: • October 28–29, 2024 • December 25, 2023 – January 3, 2024 (approximately 10 days) b) Rats present on the property since 2023 c) lack of carbon monoxide detectors and smoke alarms d) oven is missing a rack e) obstructed egress windows f) snow removal

The Tenant testified that: • He notified the Landlord that there was no heat, a vital service, on two separate occasions. October 28 to October 29, 2023, and from December 25, 2023 to January 3, 2024. The cause was a malfunctioning furnace. • The Landlord did not respond and did not take timely steps to restore heat or investigate the malfunctioning furnace resulting in no heat. • There is an ongoing rat infestation stemming back to 2023 which has resulted in property damage (wiring). • Carbon monoxide detectors near the bedrooms, a carbon monoxide detector near the furnace are required by code and are not installed, inclusive of a smoke alarm in the basement which the Tenant submits should be installed. • While there are egress windows in the basement, as these are covered with shields, egress is prohibited, window size may be of issue. • Since moving into the rental unit, the oven rack has been missing causing him to improvise in the way he uses the oven.

In summary, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental property in a good state of repair and fit for habitation under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act and failed maintain a vital service. Heat

That Tenant testified that he was not sure why there was a heat interruption October 28 to October 29, 2023, the Landlord simply did not reply to him. However, he acknowledged that this was a short-term interruption.

Regarding the second outage from December 25, 2023 to January 3, 2024 the Tenant stated that he did not advise the Landlord of the interruption until December 30, 2023 as he had assumed the Landlord was already aware by being notified by another tenant(s). He sent a message stating the furnace was broken and that the thermostat is showing 14 degrees internal temperature. That three additional messages were sent to the Landlord in this regard on December 31, 2023, January 1, 2024 and January 2, 2024. That the Landlord finally replied on January 6, 2024 but that the context of the message was not in respect to the issue addressing the lack of heat.

The Landlord submitted that when she became aware of the lack of heat in the residential complex, she started calling around various HVAC places, however as it was during the holiday season, it was difficult to find someone to investigate on short notice. That she bought space heaters for the Tenants and delivered them on or about January 2, 2024.

On January 4, 2024 the Landlord had a new furnace installed after it was determined that the other could not be fixed given the useful life, an invoice for $10,243.45 as provided by Spring Home Tech was evidenced in DOC#7191061 for a purchase of a heat pump, furnace and installation costs.
I find that the Landlord failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards for the following reasons.

On the basis of the evidence, the first time the Landlord was advised of the Tenant not having heat was on December 30, 2023, on the January 2, 2024, the Landlord provided space heaters and on January 4, 2024 a new furnace was installed. Given these circumstances, while the Tenant makes a claim for $280.00 in respect of dates as outlined, I can only consider the dates the Landlord was aware of the issue, here that is from December 30, 2023 to January 3, 2024.

As there was no heat for some of the time and reduced heat for part of the time, a lump sum amount of $100.00 is reasonable given the circumstances, this in recognition that while there was an interruption earlier the Landlord may not have been advised. Ultimately, the Tenant endure temperatures which were below the required as outlined by the Act as evidenced. And while the Landlord may have been working behind the scenes to restore heat to the property, the lack of communication added to the frustration and discomfort of living in a property without sufficient heat and when heat would be restored. Rat Infestation and Property Damage

The Tenant evidenced a photo of one dead rat outside of the rental unit. And a video of holes abutting the home that he suggests are rat dens. He submits that the internet cable was damaged/ chewed by a rodent which he then replaced without the Landlord’s knowledge. The Landlord refutes that there is an infestation of rats on the property and that the Tenant is speculative only in his submission about rat dens. That there is no evidence to confirm this.

On the basis of the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that there is an ongoing infestation of rats on the property as alleged, the sighting of one dead rat outside of the residential complex is not indicative of an infestation. The Tenant has not led sufficient evidence to establish an infestation or presence of rodents in the residential complex. And as noted by the Landlord, it is not uncommon to find at least one rat given the location of the complex. For this reason, no remedies can be considered. Egress windows

The Tenant suggests he has use of the basement to do the laundry, that the windows in the basement are not large enough to be egress windows and the ones that are there are covered with plastic covers as evidenced.

The Landlord testified that at some periods of time there are rooms in the basement that are also rented. Given the concern as raised as there was insufficient evidence adduced about the bylaws of the City, and requirements to have egress windows conforming with the current standards, I am not able to make a monetary award in this regard.

The same comments apply for the requirements of fire alarms, carbon monoxide detectors, specifically how many are required and locations of each. The Tenant while raising awareness to the issue did not have any supporting expert evidence for the Board’s review such as report from a fire department or an order for compliance as issued by an appropriate authority. However, given the seriousness of the issues, the Landlord will be ordered to engage the services of the Fire Department of Barrie to have the complex inspected for compliance in respect of all required alarms, egress points and follow through on any recommendations as arising from the inspection. Missing oven rack

It was undisputed that there is a missing oven rack, and the Landlord only recently became aware of this issue. The Landlord testified that there was a rack there when the unit was rented out to the Tenant. However, given that there are other tenants residing there, it is difficult to ascertain how the missing rack came to be. Given the hazard posed of the oven being used without the rack insert, it is in the best interest of all parties’ that it be replaced. The Landlord will be ordered accordingly. Snow removal

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord failed to perform required snow removal and salting on the grounds of the residential complex. That while the Landlord had a snow removal contract in place for winter 2023-2024 to clear the driveway, the Tenant shoveled the walkway and steps leading to the residential complex door entry points.

That in the winter of 2024–2025, the Tenant shoveled the entire driveway, steps, and walkway and applied salt to these areas. There was no snow removal contract in place for this period. The Tenant says the Landlord did not respond to his request for snow removal on December 23, 2024, December 23, 2024, December 26, 2024, January 2, 2025 and January 10, 2025 as evidenced. When noting the conditions and advised the Landlord that he is doing the snow removal himself he received no responses. He seeks compensation of $1,000.00 for the two winter seasons combined.

The Landlord does not dispute that she did not hire her usual snow removal service for winter of 2024-2025, as there were issues of cars being parked in the driveway that the plough could not go around. That the Tenant was provided a number of warnings in this regard and failed to park his vehicle in a direction and location that would permit access to snow removal.

As outlined in the Tenant’s submissions the Ontario Court of Appeal in Montgomery v. Van, 2009 ONCA 808 has confirmed that snow removal in common areas remains the landlord’s responsibility even where tenants perform the work. Generally, a landlord cannot transfer its statutory maintenance obligations to a tenant without offering specific compensation for the work performed.

In [name] v. Van, 2009 ONCA 808, the tenant was injured after slipping and falling on an ice-covered walkway leading to her basement apartment. The lease contained a one- line clause stating that “tenants are responsible for keeping their walkway and stairway clean (including snow removal).” Despite this clause, the court found the landlord liable for the tenant’s injuries, holding that the maintenance obligation could not simply be shifted to the tenant through the lease.

More recently, the Ontario Court of Appeal addressed this issue in Crete v. Ottawa Community Housing Corporation, 2024 ONCA 459, drawing an important distinction between common areas and exclusive-use areas in a residential complex.

In Crete, a tenant slipped and fell on ice on the front step of their townhouse. The lease required the tenant to clear snow and ice from the front step to the main walkway. The Court considered [name]. 517/06 s. 26(1) under the RTA, which requires landlords to maintain “exterior common areas” free from unsafe accumulations of snow and ice.

The Court held that because the lease required the tenant to clear snow and ice from areas used exclusively by the tenant and not from exterior common areas, the tenant was responsible for clearing the area where the fall occurred.

In the case before me, the areas the Tenant complained of are not for his exclusive use, and there is no agreement between the parties through the lease agreement or any other agreement that the Tenant be responsible for snow removal.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex by not providing snow removal services. And while appreciate that in a multitenant complex parking of vehicles can pose to be challenge especially where City by-law precludes parking on city roads, this is not a sufficient reason to discontinue the Landlord’s obligations. While I am satisfied that the Landlord has hired someone to remove/ plough snow for the 2025-2026 season, the issue of past conduct warrants a consideration of claims as arising from the work that the Tenant submits to have done and evidenced to the Landlord through the various text messages and screenshots. The evidenced showed a significant amount of snowfall and the Tenant having shovelled pathways for access points to the complex.

The Tenant is seeking $1,000.00 for his snow removal and salting completed in part for 2023-2024 and for all areas as completed for 2024-2025. The Landlord disagrees with the amount of $800.00 for the 2024-2025 season noting that the entire snow removal contract she usually has in place costs less, and is done with professional means. The Tenant in pricing the contract using numbers he believes are reasonable for the effort and time involved and equates this to a paid for service. I understand both parties’ positions, while I am not of the opinion that the Tenant is entitled to a cost that is more or equivalent to a outsourced contractor in that there could have been some assistance from other tenants as suggested by the Landlord, and other factors, I believe a lumpsum of $450.00 abatement is reasonable in this regard.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $550.00 This amount represents: • $100.00 for a rent abatement (heat). • $450.00 for rent abetment (snow removal).
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount of $110.00 from the rent owing for the months of April through August 2026 or until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

On or before April 9, 2026, the Landlord shall contact the Fire Department of Barrie, conduct an inspection of the residential complex for compliance with the governing fire and safety standards and implement any remedial actions or recommendations as arising.
The Landlord shall also replace the oven rack as outlined. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (File LTB-T-093549-24, filed November 13, 2024) [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (File LTB-T- 030755-25, filed April 12, 2025) These applications were heard by videoconference on January 28, 2026. The Landlord, the LLR [name], and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative raised as a preliminary issue that the Tenants are in a joint tenancy, they both signed the lease as joint tenants, therefore only one application, with both Tenants named, can be filed. The Representative suggested that application LTB-T-093549-24, the earliest filed application, was able to proceed as it could be amended to add the Tenant Mabel Wang. The Landlord’s Legal Representative agreed this amendment, but not any others, specifically, adding more issues and/or remedies.

The Tenants did not dispute signing the lease as joint tenants. The Tenants requested that application LTB-T-093549-24 be amended to add [name], and that it also be amended to add the abatement requested in [name] application.

This Member explained that pursuant to the Divisional Court’s decision in [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 the Board has no jurisdiction to award damages unless a request for damages is made in the application or the respondent is given notice and an opportunity to respond to a request to amend the application. Here, the respondent/Landlord has agreed to amend the application to add [name] as a Tenant, however, the Landlord is not agreeing to add an additional remedy. As the Landlord is not consenting to amend the remedies, I do not have the jurisdiction to amend same unless on consent. If I do have the jurisdiction to amend remedies if not consented to, I find it is not appropriate in these circumstances; this issue was raised at the Adjudicative Case Conference held June 19, 2025, and the Tenants took no steps to remedy the problem.

The Tenants then requested an adjournment to merge the two applications into one application. This request was denied, the Tenants have known since the Adjudicative Case Conference that they could not proceed separately, and did not take the necessary steps to address the issue. Lack of due diligence and/or ignorance of the law is not reason to grant an adjournment.

The Tenants were given more opportunities to discuss between themselves and request to amend application LTB-T-093549-24 by adding [name] as a Tenant. The discussions were not fruitful, and the Tenants continued to request the remedy from application LTB-T- 030755-25 be added to LTB-T-093549-24. It was re-explained to the Tenants numerous times that the only amendment being allowed was adding [name], however the option was not accepted. Therefore, as applications LTB-T-093549-24 and LTB-T-030755-25 were filed separately with only one Tenant names as the tenant, whereby the Tenants should have filed one application in both names, both applications shall be dismissed without prejudice.
ordered: The Tenants applications LTB-T-093549-24 and LTB-T-030755-25 are dismissed. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. (T6 application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.(T2 application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the beginning of the hearing, the Tenant’s Legal Representative raised that he provided the Landlord and the Board a copy of the Tenant’s consolidated evidence brief the morning of the hearing; the evidence was accepted as it was a consolidation of the evidence previously disclosed.
The Tenant’s request to amend application on August 8, 2025, is approved; the request was made prior to the hearing.

Agreed upon facts: the tenancy began July 21, 2023; the Tenant vacated August 21, 2024; the rent was due the 21st of the month; the lawful monthly rent was $2,200.00; the Tenant paid $8,800.00 for a rent deposit,4 months of rent, and a $300.00 key deposit.

This application is subject to the one-year limitation period contained in s.29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act). The application was filed November 24, 2024, 2023, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 21, 2024. Therefore, the Board can only award remedy for issues raised in the application which occurred during the period from November 24, 2023, through August 21, 2024. T1 application and Analysis
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant as ordered below.
There is no dispute that the Tenant paid a total rent deposit of $8,800.00 when the lease was signed and the Tenant did not pay rent for the 2 months of prior to the last month of the tenancy.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). In violation of the Act, the Landlord also charged the Tenant 3-months rent above the allowable 1-month rent deposit. The $4,400.00 of unpaid rent shall be subtracted off the total deposit paid $8,800.00; therefore, the Tenant is entitled to return of $4,400.00.

There was also no dispute that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'); this is contrary to section 106(6) of the Act. The Tenant is entitled to the interest owed.

Interest on the deposit is owing to the date of the hearing, in the amount of $482.18 calculated as follows: • July 21, 2023 to August 20, 2024: 2.5%; $8,800.00 X 2.1% = $220.00. • July 21, 2024 to August 20, 2025: 1.6%; $8,800.00 X 1/6% = $140.80. • July 21, 2025 to March 16, 2026: 2.1%; $8,800.00 X 1.6% = $184.80; ÷ 365 days = $$0.51 X 238 days = $121.38. o As 2-months of the deposit is being applied rent for the 2-month period prior to the last month of the tenancy, May 21, 2024 through July 20, 2024, interest is not payable on this amount for those periods. Therefore: 61 days is subtracted from the interest due in 2026; 61 X $0.51 = $31.11; $121.38 - $31.22 = $90.27. o
The total amount of interest owing to the Tenant is $451.07. T6 and T2 applications
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the T6 and T2 applications. Therefore, the applications are dismissed.

The Tenant testified to unresolved maintenance issues that began early in the tenancy; whenever the Tenant reported an issue, the Landlord would defer to the Property Manager who did nothing. On July 31, 2023, the Tenant emailed the Property Manager and [name] the Landlord about: clogged dishwasher; washing machine water dispenser collects water every time after washing; stove knob for baking is loose; the patio door wheels need replaced; bathroom door lock not working; bathroom towel bar is loose; heater and AC setting issues; and the bathroom shower. The Tenant was told he could ‘live with’ the issues raised about the stove knob and washing machine softener dispenser; the Tenant stopped using the affected burner on the stove and used the washing machine as little as possible to avoid leaking. The Tenant reached out to the condominium superintendent who said he could fix the balcony door, bathroom drawer, and bathroom doorknob; the Tenant paid for these repairs to be done. The Landlord ordered a dishwasher from Costco and asked the Tenant to remove the old one so the technician could instal the new one. The Tenant said that was not his responsibility and told the Landlord he found someone who would do the removal; the Landlord agreed, and the Tenant paid $90.00 out-of-pocket for its removal. The new dishwasher broke a few months after it was installed; the Landlord asked the Tenant to to call the Costco service centre; the service centre said it would take a few months for the part. On January 3, 2024, the Landlord told the Tenant to call Costco support to log the issue since he had first-hand information. The Tenant stopped using the dishwasher.

On August 13, 2023, the Tenant emailed the condominium board about the soundproofing issues with the windows/glass as the noise heard when inside the unit from the [name] Expressway was increasing. The Tenant followed up on September 20, 2023, and included screen shots of noise measurements taken with a website application. The Landlord blamed the patio door not being shut tightly, but this was not the case. On October 17, 2023, the Tenant reached out to JAD Soundproofing to handle the issue; an appointment was made for October 25, 2023. On November 3, 2023, the Landlord's Agent said the problem was an issue for the condominium to handle and refused to approve or pay for any related expense. Once again, the Tenant had to take matters into his own hands. The Tenant had to pay for prescription cream medication to address the rash he broke out into because of the noise and related stress it caused. In cross examination the Tenant agreed that the condominium Board investigated but they did not send a sound technician. The people who came to investigate pointed the issue out to the Landlord.

On January 24, 2024, the Tenant reported the constant smell of cannabis smoke that emanates throughout the rental unit when the furnace is on which interferes with his ability to enjoy his living space comfortably. The Tenant followed up numerous times via email and/or [name], but neither the Property Manager nor the Landlord responded/investigated the cannabis issue. When the fridge sensor began malfunctioning, it kept beeping, the Tenant reported the problem, but no action was taken. Therefore, the Tenant paid out-of-pocket $112.99 on August 16, 2024, for Star Appliance to do a diagnostic on the fridge.

On August 21, 2025, during a phone call and subsequent meeting, the Property Manager was abusive, condescending in a way that was meant to intimidate and harass him. This all happened because the Tenant was insisting the Landlord return the monies that were overpaid/unlawfully kept .

The Tenant submitted he did not want to move but had no choice because of the Landlord’s behaviour/lack of response to issues. His new unit, on the opposite of the [name], is similar in size but costs $2,800.00 per month, which is $600.00 more monthly. He should be fairly compensated for the stress the Landlord put him through. He is seeking: • Rent abatement of 25% for maintenance issues from July 2023 to August 2024, being 25% of $30,800 = $7,700. • Rent abatement of 50% for harassment and a history of negligence from July 2023 to August 2024, being 50% of $30,800 = $15,400. • Rent abatement of 25% for loss of peaceful enjoyment of the unit from July 2023 to August 2024, being 25% of $30,800 = $7,700. • Administrative penalty for the Landlord up to the maximum of $50,000.00. • Any other order this Board deems just.

The Landlord testified although he never visited the unit, he worked together on issues with the Tenant. Despite all the emails the Tenant sent, the collaboration was working, except sometimes the Tenant would not respond to his inquiries. The condominium concierge investigated the cannabis odour and found nothing was out of the ordinary. The dishwasher was replaced then repaired; it took a while for this because it was just post- COVID 19. The bathroom doorknob and towel bar also took a while to get addressed. When the Tenant paid for something out-of-pocket, the expenses were deducted from the following month’s rent. The Landlord solved as many of the problems that he could, those that were within his hands; he believed they had a good working relationship/way to do things even though there were constant emails from the Tenant. The Landlord understands he has responsibilities to the Tenant, but many things have to be approved by the condominium board before being addressed/repaired. The Landlord also realizes now that deferring issues to his Property Manager was not the best way to handle; it is now apparent that the Property Manager was not responding responsibly. He did his best to collaborate with the Tenant to have issues addressed, often there was a delay in communication.

The Landlord submitted he could not do anything about the noise, it was an issue the condominium board had to handle. There were delays because of the Landlord's Agent, but he his best to work with the Tenant to address things and reimbursed any expenses incurred by the Tenant; the abatement amounts requested by the Tenant are excessive/not warranted; he is asking for full rent for his entire tenancy. Issues were never intentionally delayed being addressed; once brought to light they were dealt with as best he could, a fine is not warranted/justified.
The Tenant referenced a 21-page document brief when testifying; the Landlord did not provide and documentary evidence to support his testimony. Analysis T6 application

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Tenant notified the Landlord about 9 issues on July 31, 2023, all of which are dismissed. The Tenant did not testify about the AC/heater setting issues or the problem with the shower. Although the Tenant testified about the washing machine water dispenser collecting water after a washing is done, there was no explanation as to how this was a repair issue or how the appliance and/or its use was negatively affected. It appears, according to the Tenant’s documentation, the dishwasher was replaced, and the bath towel bar, bathroom door lock, and patio door were repaired sometime prior to the Landlord and Tenant’s communication on September 21, 2023; the Tenant did not testify to any specific dates issues were resolved or explain why the relatively short timeline was unreasonable. The stove knob was reported as being loose, there was no testimony or evidence that the Tenant ever reported that it was broken/not usable. In respect of the new dishwasher breaking, the Tenant testified that the repair was delayed pending the necessary part being received. That the appliance was a cheaper model from Costo is irrelevant, the old one was replaced and the Landlord acted when a problem arose with this one. Any involvement the Tenant had with these issues is dealt with in the T2 portion of the order. There was also no testimony about the bulbs needing changed that were referenced in the Tenant’s email dated December 20, 2023, and no specifics/dates as to when the fridge sensor began beeping. For all these reasons, these issues on the T2 application are dismissed.

As to the noise from the Gardiner Expressway, the Tenant’s first documented complaint was sent to the condominium concierge, not the Landlord's Agent/Landlord. On September 23, 2023, the Tenant asks the Landlord/Landlord's Agent to forward his email to the Condominium Board of Directors. The Landlord testified that he advised the Tenant there was nothing he could action in respect of this problem as it was the condominium’s domain. The Tenant’s correspondence is directed to the condominium and the Landlord's Agent letter dated November 3, 2023, support that the Tenant was aware any complaints about the building’s soundproofing were the condominium’s responsibility. Although the Tenant included screenshots of decibel/noise levels there are no details; the readings are not dated or explained, and there was no evidence/testimony as to what an acceptable or unacceptable level is. Therefore, this issue is also dismissed. Analysis T2 application

The applicable sections in the Act are: • Section 22: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. • Section 23: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Black’s Law Dictionary defines harassment as “a course of conduct directed at a specific person that causes substantial emotional distress in such person and serves no legitimate purpose”. Harassment in the landlord and tenant context is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate.

The allegations of harassment are with respect to the communication/meeting with the Landlord's Agent on August 21st, there was nominal testimony given and the supporting document the Tenant referenced indicated the incident occurred in 2025, well after the tenancy ended. Therefore, this issue is dismissed.

As to the allegation of substantial interference , the Tenant reported constantly smelling cannabis in his rental unit to the Landlord on January 23, 2024; although the Tenant testified to following up with the Landlord and/or Landlord's Agent about the problem not being addressed, the Landlord testified he asked the condominium concierge to investigate and it was reported there was nothing out of the ordinary/no evidence of a persistent odour. Based on the lack of details/dates in the Tenant’s testimony and the Landlord testimony that the condominium concierge reported that an existing problem was discovered, I find the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities there was an evasive odour that affected his daily living. Although the result of the investigation may not have been relayed to the Tenant, this does not affect the fact that this issue must be dismissed due to the Tenant not meeting the evidentiary burden.

Although the maintenance application has been dismissed, the T2 application element of substantial interference remains; issue of the Tenant having to be involved, follow-up, and/or pay for some things out-of-pocket. There is no dispute that the Tenant facilitated/assisted in some repairs and was reimbursed for those his incurred expenses. The Landlord testified he believed they had a collaborative working arrangement to get things addressed; I accept the Landlord’s testimony. The Landlord’s interpretation of the Tenant’s assistance is supported by the Tenant’s letter about the noise where he says, “I am willing to collaborate and cooperate in any way possible”. Apart from refusing to remove the dishwasher himself, there is no evidence that the Tenant raised what he felt as his ‘having to handle issues’ as a problem or concern with the Landlord. I find it reasonable for the Landlord to believe the Tenant was willingly helping to facilitate things. There was no evidence the Tenant was ‘forced’ to take the actions he did; it is more akin to him being asked to assist.

Therefore, based on the above, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. The Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”.

Also based on the above, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
Accordingly, the T2 application is dismissed.
