issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants, $4,816.16.

The tenancy for the two-bedroom rental unit commenced on August 1, 2023, and the Tenants vacated the unit on November 12, 2024. Although the tenancy agreement was for a three-year term ending July 31, 2026, the parties signed an Agreement to End the Tenancy (N11) with a termination date of November 15, 2024. Compensation
The Tenants requested compensation because the Landlord asked them to vacate the rental unit.

The Tenant s claimed that the Landlord’s real estate agent contacted her agent on September 10, 2024, stating that the Landlord was unwell and there were plans to sell the rental unit. The Tenants understood this communication to mean that they were required to vacate the rental unit . The Tenants contacted the Landlord’s daughter, and over several discussions, asked to vacate the rental unit in June 2025. The Landlord denied asking the Tenants to vacate the unit.

A copy of the message from the Landlord’s real estate agent indicates that the agent asked whether the Tenants were interested in vacating the rental unit. However, the message does not request that the Tenants vacate the unit , and no other d ocumentary evidence was provided to support the Tenants’ assertions. As a result, the Tenants are not entitled to compensation as I am not satisfied that they received a notice of termination from the Landlord. Last month's Rent Deposit / Excess Rent
The lawful monthly rent was $3,100.00.

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenants’ claim that they paid two deposits toward the last month’s rent, totaling $6,200.00. The first deposit was applied to the rent for December 2023, and the second deposit is still held by the Landlord.

Furthermore, the parties agreed that on or about November 12, 2024, the Landlord cashed the Tenants’ prepaid cheque. The Landlord stated that this was done because the Tenants terminated the tenancy earlier than June 2025, as initially requested. As a result, the Landlord applied the last month’s rent deposit to the rent for December 2024.

Based on all the evidence, I am satisfied that t he Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord also collected rent in excess of the lawful rent and failed to pay interest on the last month's rent deposit.

Section 106 (10) of the Act provides that a Landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a Tenant has paid to the Landlord or to a former Landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. As the tenancy ended on November 15, 2024, and the last month's rent deposit was not applied to November 2025, the Landlord must return the full last month's rent deposit of $3,000.00 to the Tenant.

In addition, the tenancy lawfully ended on November 15, 202 4, on consent of the part ies. Pursuant to section 134 (1.1) (a) (b) of the Act, the Landlord is prohibited from collecting or attempting to collect rent from a former tenant for any period after the tenancy or the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has ended and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.
Consequently, the Landlord has no basis to retain the rent for the period commencing November 16, 2024, and ending November 30, 2024.

The daily r ate for the rental unit was $ 101.91. As a result, the Landlord must refund $1,528.65 to the Tenants, representing 15 days of rent calculated at $101.91 per day. Interest on the last month's rent deposit

Section 106 (6) of the Act states that a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

The Tenant s moved into the rental unit on July 1, 20 23, and paid two last month's rent deposit totalling $6,200.00. In December 2023, one of the deposits was applied to that month’s rent , and the Landlord continues to hold the other deposit. [name] are therefore entitled to interest of $139.51 on the last month's rent deposit calculated as: a. $64.98 - July 1, 2023, to November 30, 2023, and b. $74.53 - December 1, 2023, to November 15, 2024
The Landlord must pay to the Tenants, $ 4,816.16 inclusive of $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,816.16. This amount represents: • $3,100.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $1,528.65 for the excess rent collected. • $139.51 for interest on the last month's rent deposit, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 7, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved one of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $248.00 for the key deposit, and for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024, and vacated the unit on [name] 15, 2025. The Tenant paid $200.00 to the Landlords for a refundable key deposit. The Tenant provided a text message from the Landlord ’s Agent dated about June 1, 2024, where the Landlord ’s Agent confirmed the email address to which the Tenant should pay the deposit.
The Tenant further presented a screenshot of an interac transaction from his bank which showed that $200.00 was auto deposited to ‘winter trail’ on June 1, 2024.

The Landlords’ Agent argued that the screenshot did not show that the payment was made to the Landlord because it did not contain any identifying information for the Landlord. He did not know if the Landlords received the payment.

Section 105 (1) of the Act, states that the only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit and section 134(1) specifically prohibit the collection of a key deposit. Section 17 of O’Reg. 516/06 to the Act provides for certain exceptions from section 134(1) including “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.

In this case, the deposit of $200.00 is more than “the expected direct replacement costs” for the keys and was not refunded to the Tenant at the end of the tenancy . Although the screenshot provided by the Tenant did not include the Landlords’ name or email address, the payment was made on June 1, 2024, following the Tenant’s conversation with the Landlord’s agent and the agent’s confirmation of the email address to which the payment was to be sent. As the Landlord’s Agent did not categorically deny that the Landlords received the payment, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant paid the $200.00 key deposit to the Landlords. Accordingly, the Landlords are required to refund the deposit to the Tenant.

The Tenant further claimed that the Landlord collected a $229.50 charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). While the Tenant claimed that the charge was for solid waste/garbage which he was not required to pay based on the terms of the tenancy agreement, the Landlord argued that it was contained in the same bill as the water charges which the Tenant is required to pay. In any event, even if I were to accept the Tenant’s position, the Tenant provided insufficient evidence to support the amount claimed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: videoconference on January 22, 2026 at 09:00 am. The Landlord Representative [name], the Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. Preliminary issues: 1. At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant attempted to raise several procedural issues that were either non-relevant or non prejudicial which I addressed by clarifying Board procedures and practices. 2. The Landlord Representative submitted that there were issues raised in the applications that were outside the Boards jurisdiction. Reviewing the applications I confirmed that there were several issues that allegedly occurred before October 28, 2023, the date 12 months prior to the Tenant filing their application. 3. They also submitted that the remedies sought were repeated across all three applications, making it unclear as to what was being sought. Having reviewed the applications I directed that once I canvassed the Tenant for the remedies, they were to provide the totality sought pursuant to all their applications. 4. In response the Tenant acknowledged that these issues were outside the Board’s jurisdiction, submitting that they wished to refer to them only in context of establishing an alleged pattern of behaviour. 5. Based on the above submissions I directed that the Tenant would be limited to raising issues that occurred on or after October 29, 2023. I also directed that based on the pleadings in their T2 and T6 application, the allegation in their T3 Application were redundant and as such would not consider them.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved in part the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant moved into the rental unit, March 1, 2022 and is still residing there. It’s the rear unit of a duplex, consisting of one bedroom and bathroom. The Landlord’s son and Agent resides in the front unit.
The lawful monthly rent is $1,500.00 T6 Application.
Pursuant to the amended application filed March 18, 2025 the Tenant raised the following alleged issues: Lack of AC and Heat

The Tenant testified in the summer of 2024, during a heat wave, the Landlord Agent would turn the AC off, claiming it was broken, which in their submission it was not. They supported their claims with a picture of their thermostat, and an email correspondence from August 3, 2024. They denied running the AC constantly at extreme cold temperatures or excessively storing and stacking of items that could affect the temperature inside the unit. They also testified that they denied entries due to the notices of entry (NOE) not being properly filled out or signed by the Landlord. However, they also admitted that the Landlord directed them to address issues to their son, the Landlord agent.

The Tenant testified that on September 8, 2024 they requested that the Landlord Agent turn on the heat but refused to respond until October 8, 2024 with the issue being addressed on October 9, 2024. They supported this with an email entered in evidence.

In response the Landlord Agent testified that they had an agreement to turn it on once the temperature reached 27 degrees and when they turned it on the Tenant refused to turn it down, making it uncomfortable for them and their family forcing him to turn it off.

The Landlord Agent then testified that they received the request to tur on the heat but there was an issue with the thermostat, which the Tenant delayed addressing by requesting a NOE which they provided and fixed the issue within three days. They then testified to serving another NOE to relocate the thermostat to their unit after which there were no further issues. They supported this with a copy of the NOEs entered in evidence. They then testified that the AC and heat issues were exasperated by the Tenant’s failure to address alleged excessive storing and stacking of items within the unit. Fallen tree and back steps

The Tenant testified that on October 4, 2024 they informed the Landlord by email that a tree had fallen across the back fence and the steps leading down from the back of the property were unsafe but refused to address these issues. They supported this with a picture dated April 26, 2025 entered in evidence and an email from October 4, 2024. However, they could not provide evidence that the Landlord owned the land beyond the fence line.
In response the Landlord Agent testified that the tree and steps were located outside their property line which is why they never addressed it. [name] toilet

It was the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that they informed the Landlord and Landlord agent an email on October 4 and October 14, 2024 that the toilet would constantly run but received no response. They then informed Pickering By-Law which resulted in the Landlord attending the property, without notice, on November 26, 2024, returning with a NOE fixing it on December 6, 2024. This was supported by the October 14; email entered in evidence.
The Landlord could offer no explanation for the delay in addressing the toilet, entering in evidence the NOE for the November 25, 2024 visit. Driveway

It was the Tenant’s testimony and evidence that in the same emails of October 4 and October 14, 2024 they identified that the driveway paver stones were broken representing a safety hazard, but it was never fixed. They supported this with pictures entered in evidence.
In response the Landlord Agent testified that they had no knowledge of the issue as claimed. Hot and cold water

The Tenant testified that on February 2, 2025 they discovered that they were without hot or cold water which they informed the Landlord by email. It was also their testimony that this occurred an additional two times, in each case the issue was resolved within a day.
In response the Landlord Agent confirmed receiving the complaint, but their unit was not affected so they did not investigate. [name], snow and ice removal

It was the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, supported by the lease entered in evidence, that the Landlord had delegated landscaping, snow and ice removal to them and despite informing them in June 2024 that this was in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) they refused to take responsibility resulting in the lawn being unsightly and the walkway and driveway being covered in ice, presenting a safety hazard up until the past winter. It was also their that due to the Landlord’s failure to remove the snow and ice, they were unable to access the shared laundry facility from February 12, 2025 to March 6, 2025. They also testified they were able to access the

In response the Landlord Agent didn’t deny delegating responsibility, testifying they were not aware that maintenance was their responsibility until By-Law informed them in 2025 and after that they began maintaining the property. They did testify, however, that the Tenant could have accessed the shared laundry from the front of the house which was cleared.
The Tenant testified to attempting to access from the front but claimed it was unsafe having slipped several times. [name]
Pursuant to the Tenant’s amended T2 Application field on March 18, 2025 the Tenant raised the following alleged issues: Illegal entries

The Tenant testified that due to suspecting the Landlord or the Landlord Agent were entering their unit without their knowledge they began setting traps, to include closing doors and switching the lights off whenever they left and that on May 12, 2024 and June 18, 2024 when they returned, they discovered the doors open and the lights on and in one case the thermostat had been turned off. It was their testimony that they believed the Landlord Agent had illegally entered as there was no forced entry, and the Landlord informed them that the Landlord Agent had keys to the unit.

It was also their testimony that the NOE served did not have the Landlord’s signature or in some case a photocopy thereof. It was also their submission that given that they were never provided anything in writing that authorized the Landlord Agent, that the NOE they served were invalid and the corresponding entries were illegal. They entered several NOE in evidence to support.
In response the Landlord agent denied entering the unit on May 12 or June 18, 2024 as alleged. Substantial interference and harassment

The Tenant testified that November 27, 2024 the Landlord, without providing a NOE. banged on the door and yelled at him before he granted him access out of fear of the door being damaged. They then testified that the Landlord harassed him about not maintaining the yard pursuant to the lease. They entered a video in evidence to support their submission.

They then testified that the Landlord Agent harassed them on August 13, 2024 when they threatened them after they had greeted the Landlord Agents son and wife while he was walking outside of the rental unit.

They also testified that on September 5, 2024 after he denied entry due to a NOE not being properly completed the Landlord messaged him making several false accusations regarding his conduct and failure to maintain the property. This was supported by the text message entered in evidence dated September 5, 2024.

It was also their testimony that their cable was cut by the Landlord Agent on October 29, 2023. They made this determination based on seeing the Landlord Agent around the side of the house prior, and a conversation with the [name]’s technician. It was also their submission that the Landlord Agent did this in retaliation for moving dollies that the Landlord Agent had placed at the side of the house. They submitted a [name] technician report in support.

Following this they testified that they were also harassed when the Landlord Agent sent them a text accusing them of leaving the stove unattended due to their age. This was supported by the text entered in evidence.

They the testified that after moving into the rental unit they noticed a camera was installed in the front entry inside the rental. They also testified they believed it was still active due to lights on it being on forcing them to cover it in tape. They claimed when they told the Landlord the Landlord informed them it was not working and was installed by a previous tenant.

In response the Landlord Agent didn’t deny sending the messages of September 5, 2024, again testifying they were not aware that maintenance was their responsibility until By-Law informed them in 2025 and after that they began maintaining the property. They also didn’t deny texting the Tenant about the stove, testifying they were shovelling snow when they saw through the window the ignition flame on the stove turned on left unattended and out of fear for themselves and their family.

The Landlord Agent denied cutting the Tenant’s cable as alleged. Regarding the camera the Landlord Agent testified that it is part of a security system that it wasn’t installed by them, but they haven’t removed it due to believe the camera being wired into the electrical.

They then testified to never being in receipt of a compliance order from By-Law, however they did speak to them directly regarding their responsibilities and taken over maintenance in late 2024 and had since rectified all the noted deficiencies.

The Landlord Representative then submitted that although the Tenant did suffer some interference, they still had use and or access to the facilities. They also submitted that the Tenant failed to provide any proof that the Landlord did in fact cut the cable. It was also their submission, although denied by the Tenant that the Tenant’s applications were field in retaliation to the Landlord serving a N12 Notice of termination and a failure to reach a cash for keys arrangement. On this basis they requested the applications be dismissed. Remedies sought.

Pursuant to the applications filed the Tenant was seeking the following remedies: a. Rent abatement totalling $18,000.00; b. Cessation of the alleged harassment; c. The Landlord pay a fine to the Board; d. Repair the paver stones; e. Removal of the camera; and f. General compensation totalling $15,000.00 Analysis

The Following sections of the Act are relevant: Landlord’s responsibility to repair 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. Landlord not to harass, etc. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Privacy 25 A landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
Having considered the above testimony, evidence and for the reasons that follow I am satisfied the Tenant has in part proven their case. T6 Application

First the Landlord by their own admission failed to address maintenance issues, first by delegating the responsibility on to the Tenant, which in itself is a breach, but then again by failing to address the issues, namely the toilet, hot water, AC, heat, snow removal or camera in a reasonable amount of time. Ignorance of the Act is not a defense. Accordingly, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a remedy, however, given they did not refute they still had use of the toilet, testified that the interruption to the hot water was intermittent, could still access the laundry, and they did not provide any proof that the Landlord was responsible for the grounds beyond the fence line, the amount awarded will not be as sought. T2 Application

Given the above determination, I am satisfied that the Landlord did substantially interfere with the Tenant by failing to address the maintenance issues. Same is my determination regarding the allegations of harassment as it pertains to the text messages of September 5, 2024. The Landlord ought to have known they were responsible for maintenance and sending those messages were unwanted, especially given it was uncontested that the Tenant informed them of their obligations.

Similar is my assessment regarding the events of November 27, 2024, The Landlord could be seen and heard in the video acting in an aggressive manner towards the Tenant and as such I am satisfied they did harass and intimidate the Tenant as alleged.
That said, I am not satisfied that the text regarding the stove, was intended to harass, given there was only the one instance.

As to the alleged illegal entries, the Tenant testified that the Landlord informed them at the commencement of the tenancy that their son, the Landlord Agent would be acting on their authority. Thus, I am satisfied that the Tenant was aware, even in the absence of anything in writing and the NOE served by the Agent were therefore valid.

As to the other alleged entries the Tenant offered no proof other than supposition, as such I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities they have proven their case in this regard and therefore dismissing this portion of their application.

Same is my determination regarding the allegation that the Landlord agent cut the cable. The technician report made no such finding it merely stated what the Tenant reported they believed happened. Remedies awarded

Based on the above determinations I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to the following remedies: a. Rent abatement of $2,700.00. I base this on a rate of 15.00% for a period of 12 months as the predominant of maintenance issues pertained to the outside shared space and were seasonal dependent; b. An order for the Landlord to cease harassing the Tenant over maintenance issues; c. An order for the Landlord to have the camera professionally removed; and d. General compensation of $5,000.00. I base this on the length of the tenancy, the period for which the Landlord was erroneously delegating maintenance, and the overt nature of the events of November 27, 2024.

As to the other remedy sought, namely a fine, I am not satisfied it is warranted given the remedies already awarded, the fact that it was unrefuted that the Landlord had since taken on the maintenance of the rental property pursuant to the Act and the Tenant failed to provide proof that the LAndlrod had not yet complied with By-Law enforcement.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,700.00. This amount represents: • $2,700.00 for a rent abatement; • $5,000.00 in General compensation
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 29, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,500.00 from the rent each month from April 2026 to August 2026 and $200.00 in September 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant testified on July 19, 2024, July 29, 2024, and September 25, 2024, contractors were doing work in the building; the Landlord said the contractors would not need access to the rental unit, but they had to enter the unit hallway to prop the unit door open. As there was no notice of entry given, the contractors entered the unit illegally.

The Tenant testified the Landlord is not complying with section 27(3) of the Act because they regularly give notices of entry with a minimum 8-hour window. The time periods were as follows: notices dated February 5, 2024, September 23, 2024, and November 15, 2024, 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; notice dated March 25, 2024,8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; notice dated July 19, 2023, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. On August 1, 2024, the notice of entry was dated July 29, 2024, the contractor just walked into the unit without knocking; the Tenant was in his underwear. All these events substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment.

On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that the work the contractors were doing involved painting doors and working on the hallway stoops, however, but he did not understand that they would be entering his unit to prop the door open. The Tenant also confirmed that he never expressed his concerns to the Landlord about the timeframe given for the notices of entry until November 15, 2024, at which time he filed the T2 application, and there have been no issues since.
The Tenant submitted the application should be granted and the requested remedies awarded; the jurisprudence established by the Board says the window should be maximum 4-hours.

The Landlord's Legal Representative advised he was not calling any witnesses. The Representative submitted, as set out in Guideline 19, the circumstances for entry is important. Here, the Tenant agreed that the notices of entry were for a third-party contractor. The Tenant did not advise the Landlord about his issue with the timeframe until November 15, 2024, then he immediately filed the application. The Tenant also confirmed in cross examination that the notice dated July 19, 2024, said the contractor world be starting on the 6th floor and working down from there. The Tenant also confirmed that the notice for entry on August 1, 2024, said there had to be a 2-foot clearance by the unit door and that the door would be propped open for at least 45 minutes. The Tenant further confirmed that the notice dated September 19, 2024, for entry on September 25, 2024, said the contractor was starting on the 10th floor and working down to the 6th floor, and it also says it would take approximately one-hour to complete each floor; therefore, the Tenant could do the calculation for an approximate time they would be on his floor. As the work was being done by a contractor, the Landlord gave as many particulars as possible. For all these reasons, the Landlord did not breach its obligations under the Act, and the Tenant’s application should be dismissed.

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find the Landlord/Landlord's Agent did not enter the rental unit illegally and did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Guideline 19 says a notice of entry should provide as many details as possible with respect to the proposed entry, and where a specific time of entry is known, it should be noted in the notice; where it is not possible to state a specific time of entry, the notice may provide a reasonable window of time for entry.

The guideline also says: What is a reasonable window of time will depend upon the facts and circumstances in each case. Where the landlord exercises control over the work being done and who is doing the work, the notice should be reasonably specific with respect to the time for entry. Where the landlord does not exercise control over the work being done or the person who is doing the work, the notice should set out a reasonable window of time for entry.

Here, the Landlord did not exercise control over the work being done, it was being done by a contractor. As the work being undertaken involved the entire building, basically all units/floor, I accept that it was impossible for the Landlord to give a specific or shorter timeframe. I find the Landlord provided as much detail as possible, and that due to the work being done, the timeframe could not be more specific. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: On June 19, 2025 this matter was before the Board as an adjudicative case conference. The matter was adjourned to a merits hearing, and the adjournment sheet noted that the Tenant was informed that the Application did not set out a clear cause of action or contain remedies, and the Tenant was informed of the rules for amending an Application.
The Tenant filed a request to amend on June 25, 2025, which added remedies, but did not provide any clarity with respect to the details of the allegations themselves.
At the hearing before me I raised that the Tenant’s Application was unclear, did not set out clear issues, and did not contain any dates and times for the allegations made.
The Landlord’s Agent testified that they were aware that the Tenant was seeking remedies, but did not appear to have an understanding of the issues raised by the Application.

Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”) dictates that applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

While [name] involved a notice of termination served on a Tenant, it is my view that the principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications, and applications should provide sufficient particulars to allow the responding party to know the allegations against them, and the case to be met.

As the Tenant’s Application does not provide dates and times for the allegations, or a clear cause of action I find that it does not contain sufficient particulars and should be dismissed. I also note that the Tenant was made aware of the potential defences in the Adjudicative Case Conference and had adequate time to amend to the Application to remedy them, as evidenced by the amendment the Tenant filed clarifying the remedies they were seeking. Therefore, the Application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and Ajaydeep [name] [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must provide compensation to the Tenant as set out in this [name]. Preliminary Issue

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative referred to DOC ID 7839634, Exhibit 1, and stated that this matter had already been submitted as evidence before the Landlord and Tenant Board on April 10, 2024, and the N12 Notice served on October 31, 2023, was found to have been served in good faith.

Consequently, in accordance with the Order issued on July 15, 2024, the tenancy between the Landlords and Tenant was terminated and the Tenant was ordered to move out of the rental unit on or before July 31, 2024.
The Tenant in fact vacated the rental unit on November 8, 2024, as per the Sheriff’s notice.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative went onto then say that the Tenant is raising the same issues again and that there have been no new developments and therefore asked the Board to dismiss the Tenant’s application in its entirety.
As this is a Tenant’s application, I informed the Landlord’s Legal Representative that I would hear the matter in its entirety. Relevant Law, Burden of Proof and Admissions

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant testified that she believed the N12 Notice was served in bad faith as she felt the Landlords wanted to evict her so that they could rent out the place to another tenant for a higher rent.

The Tenant expressed her concerns with respect to the original Agreement of Purchase and Sale that was brought before the Board on April 10, 2024, and said that it was not a signed Agreement. She submitted it was therefore fraudulent. However, having reviewed DOC ID 7839515, Exhibit 2, the Landlords’ Response to the Tenant, I found the Agreement of Purchase and Sale dated October 25, 2023, was signed by both parties to the Agreement.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit was still listed for sale on December 11, 2023. The “For Sale” sign was still in front of the house and was not replaced with a “Sold” sign. Furthermore, the Purchaser never came to inspect the house before entering into the Agreement with the Landlords.

The Tenant said the Landlord told her some time ago that he wanted her out because she was not paying market value rent. Her monthly rent was $1,660.00 at the time she left. Houses in that area were being rented for $800 - $1,000 more per month than what she was paying.

The Tenant stated that at the last hearing, when the Landlord was asked who the purchaser of the rental unit was, he said “a friend of a friend”. This convinced her the Agreement of Purchase and [name] was not a genuine one.

The Tenant also said that the pictures taken by the Landlord and inserted into Exhibit 2 as part of the Landlord’s response are not an accurate depiction of how the Tenant truly lived. She referred to DOC IDs 7882738,7882759,7882766 and 7882778 -Exhibits 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 respectively and said these pictures were more accurate to demonstrate how she kept her home. The Landlord’s pictures he had taken were taken just after her move when things were a mess as she was moving in a rush with her 3 children.

The Tenant claimed there were several maintenance issues during the tenancy which the Landlords would not take care of and stated that during the first 6 years of her tenancy, the Landlords never came to the rental unit.

The Tenant then referred to Exhibit 2, specifically the Landlord’s claims for damages and said that the Landlord had done very little to make material repairs to the house, so she was not able to understand where the repair and renovation estimates and claims came from. Furthermore, the recent listing pictures show that very little renovation had been done to the rental unit.

As a result of the eviction, the Tenant had to move into her mother’s 3-bedroom home which was already occupied by her mother, sister and sister’s 3 children. It was difficult to continue living there and so the Tenant moved into a shelter with her children. This move to the shelter has traumatized her children.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord had been trying to get her out of the rental unit 3 times over the course of the last few years. The first time he said he wanted to renovate the house. The second time he stated he wanted to move his elderly mother-in-law to the rental unit. She found this to be odd because the rental unit is a 3-storey townhouse which perhaps would be unsuitable for an elderly person. When the Tenant challenged the Landlord and told him he had a unit in his home that would be better suited for his mother- in-law, she says the Landlord then dropped this matter altogether. After this, she testified that the Landlord then went and listed the rental unit for sale.

Upon the Landlord’s Legal Representative’s cross-examination of the Tenant, he asked her to provide evidence that the Agreement of Sale and [name] was a fraudulent one. She responded by saying there was no realtor listed in the Agreement nor any lawyers for the buyer or seller and after speaking to a real estate agent about this, she believed that in the absence of those details, this Agreement was a fraudulent one. The Landlord’s Legal Representative reminded the Tenant that when this matter was heard the first time in April 2024, the Member did not find this Agreement to be of fraudulent nature.

The Landlord then referred to DOC ID 7883389, Exhibit 8 and demonstrated to the Tenant that even though he had asked her in 2022 to move out, he had not sold the house until a year later. The Tenant’s counterclaim was that this message proved that the Landlord was finding ways to evict her. He had been asking her since 2022 to move out and that he had not increased the rent for 3 years. He asked her to consider moving out and said he wanted the rental unit for his mother and promised the Tenant he would not re-rent the unit. She stated this was consistent with the Landlord’s constant effort to get her to leave the unit.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that all these issues were raised in the hearing in April 2024, and an [name] stating the N12 was served in good faith was issued. No new issues have come to light and consequently the Landlord could not understand why the Tenant was bringing this application before the Board for issues that had already been heard and resolved. He further went onto say that the Tenant failed to provide any evidence that the Agreement of Purchase and [name] was a fraudulent one.

The Tenant said she would like to understand how the Purchaser can purchase the rental unit without even having seen it prior to entering into the Agreement. The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the reason the Purchaser could not inspect the rental unit from inside prior to making the purchase was because the Tenant had changed the locks and not provided the Landlord with a key. The Tenant disputed this fact.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative then asked the Landlord to give evidence about the Agreement of Purchase and Sale. The Landlord testified that one of the conditions of sale was vacant possession of the rental unit. The Landlord’s Legal Representative referred to the Agreement and said it was clearly stated that if on closing the rental unit was not vacant, then the Landlord and Purchaser would have the option to either extend the Agreement or terminate it.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative then referred to page 13 in Exhibit 2 and showed there had been an Amendment to the Agreement whereby the closing date had been extended from January 11, 2024, to March 29, 2024, hoping that by then the unit would be vacant. Page 15 of Exhibit 2 was another Amendment to the Agreement extending the closing date from March 29, 2024, to May 15, 2024. Page 17 of the [name] cheque was a $10,000 deposit cheque from the Purchaser to the Landlord to be deposited into the lawyer’s account in trust.

Page 25 of the [name] pertains to the notice “delivery of vacant possession”. This was on the day of eviction when the Sheriff came to evict the Tenant. In accordance with the [name] issued on July 15, 2024, the Tenant had not vacated the rental unit on or before July 31, 2024. Finally, the Landlord called upon the Sheriff to evict the Tenant. The Landlord testified that there was a delay in the Sheriff’s office, and they did not come to the rental unit until November 2024 to evict the Tenant. The Tenant testified that even though she vacated the unit on November 8, 2024, she made arrangements with the Landlord to have a few extra days in which to move out all her belongings, which he granted. Consequently, she moved out fully of the rental unit on November 12, 2024.

The Landlord testified that the pictures depicting the state of the rental unit were taken on November 8, 2024. The estimates in his response of the repairs to be undertaken were prepared by the company after the contractor had inspected the property on the evening of November 8, 2024.

Page 53 of Exhibit 2 is another Amendment to the Agreement to extend closing of the rental unit to May 15, 2024, to July 31, 2024. Page 55 of Exhibit 2 is a further Amendment to the Agreement to amend the closing date from August 30, 2024, to September 30, 2024. Page 57 is the final Amendment to extend closing to November 30, 2024.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative then referred to Page 60 of Exhibit 2. This was an email exchange between the Landlord and Purchaser whereby the Landlord told him on November 8, 2024, that the eviction process had begun and within 72 hours the rental unit would be fully vacated, after which he would have the unit deep cleaned and repaired and they could then inspect the property as agreed upon during their earlier phone conversations.

On November 12, 2024, after the Tenant had vacated the rental unit and inspection had taken place, the Purchaser emailed the Landlord and expressed his decision to terminate the Agreement of Purchase and Sale based on the current market and condition of the rental unit. Notwithstanding the fact that, as per the Landlord’s testimony that he reduced the agreed upon sale price of the rental unit by $50,000, the Purchaser felt he would be unable to recover his losses and did not want to proceed with this transaction.

The Landlord testified that due to the constant negotiations and extensions of the closing date of the rental unit, and then the fact that the Purchaser decided not to proceed with the transaction he went through undue hardship.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative then referred to Page 62 of Exhibit 2 which was an Agreement with a broker to list the rental unit for sale. The Landlord testified that the rental unit was listed for sale for a couple of months, but he did not receive any acceptable offers. Therefore, he decided to take the rental unit off the market in February 2025 and re-rent the unit. When asked, the Landlord confirmed that the rental unit is currently rented out.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that from October 2023 to February 2025, the Landlord’s genuine intent to sell his rental unit has been consistently demonstrated.

The Purchaser was then brought into the hearing as a witness. I asked him that when entering into the Agreement of Purchase and Sale for the rental unit in October 2023, did he ever do a full site visit and inspect the property from inside. He said no he did not because he saw it from the outside and had seen the pictures of the inside. The Purchaser also stated that every time he asked the Landlord to see the rental unit, the Landlord said the unit was not currently vacant. The Purchaser testified that he still went ahead with the purchase because he had seen the pictures and believed he was getting a good deal.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative asked the Landlord to explain in the hearing if he had access to the rental unit. The Landlord testified he did not have access nor the ability to show the unit because whenever he asked, the Tenant would refuse entry by giving different excuses. The Tenant did not allow the Landlord access to the rental unit. Later, the Tenant had changed the locks, and the Landlord was not provided with a spare key.

The Landlord further testified that because the Tenant refused to allow showings of the rental unit to take place, this was the reason he had to sell the unit privately to a “friend of a friend”. The Landlord testified that for 16 months the locks had been changed, and he could not get access to the rental unit. On eviction date, a locksmith was called, and the locks were changed.

The Tenant responded to the changing of the locks claim by stating that the Landlord had asked her to change the locks because he did not want to pay for it. The lock needed to be changed because it was dangerous as is since the doorknob would not stay on nor could the Tenant open the door from the inside. She asked him numerous times to change the lock but was told by the Landlord that it was her fault and therefore she had to replace it. The Tenant referred to DOC IDs 7883411 and 78834223, Exhibits 9 and 10 respectively, which were message exchanges between the parties where the Landlord asked the Tenant to replace the lock, and they will split the difference with respect to the cost. No evidence was led by the Tenant with respect to providing the Landlord with a spare key. The Landlord did not dispute what the Tenant said.

When presenting closing submissions, the Landlord’s Legal Representative requested I take into consideration the Order issued on July 15, 2024, especially paragraph 17. He also requested I take this [name] into account because it already establishes that the N12 Notice was served in good faith.

However, subsection 57(4) of the Act states that in an application under subsection (1), the Board may find that the landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith despite a previous finding by the Board to the contrary. The Landlord did serve the N12 Notice in bad faith

I did not find the Purchaser’s evidence of intent to purchase the rental unit to be a genuine one. The Landlord testified that the Purchaser was frustrated in the end with the delay in closing and therefore decided to not proceed with the transaction. However, all the extensions with respect to the closing date were agreed upon by both parties and the final Amendment to the Agreement had a closing date of November 30, 2024. In this light the Purchaser’s evidence for the failed purchase was less reliable. Why would he agree to multiple extensions and then cancel the deal on eve of vacant possession? I did not find the explanation provided by the Purchaser to be sufficient. It was not clear what losses the Purchaser was referring to in regard to the sale of the property. The timing of the cancellation is beyond coincidental.

When the sale of the rental unit fell through, the Landlord was obligated to notify the Tenant and allow her to continue with the tenancy if she so desired. The Landlord does not deny he failed to notify the Tenant of the Purchaser’s decision not to move ahead with the transaction. The decision not to notify of the Tenant of the change in circumstances around the sale of the property goes to the heart of the Landlord’s evidence. And as referred to by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, there had already been a hearing where the Tenant had challenged the Landlord’s good faith. He knew or ought to have known of the Tenant’s interest in staying in the rental unit.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

In TSL-30516 & TSL-30517-SA, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No. 176, the purchaser was found to lack true intent to occupy the property where the purchaser entered into a purchase agreement without a complete viewing of the property.
In the above circumstances, I find that, on the balance of probabilities, the Landlord nor the Purchaser rebutted the presumption of bad faith and that the N12 Notice was not served in good faith.
As a result, I find the Tenant has demonstrated all of the required elements under s.57(1)(b). Remedies

The Tenant referred to DOC IDs 6755876, 6755878, 6755879, 6755880, 6755881, 6755882 and 6755883, Exhibits 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17 respectively, which are screenshots of the payments made to the storage company for her storage. Having reviewed these screenshots of payments made, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,918.89 for the reasonable out-of-pocket storage expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

If the Tenant meets all 3 elements of the legal test in s.57(1) of the Act, then the Board may award a general compensation of up to 12 months rent last charged for the rental unit, which in this case was $1,660.00 per month. The Tenant testified that she and her 3 children are living in a shelter and moving from shelter to shelter The Landlord’s Legal Representative’s claim is that the Landlord did not serve the N12 Notice in bad faith and therefore it would appear that his position would be that he does not owe any monies to the Tenant in the form of general compensation. Due to the fact that the N12 Notice to terminate the tenancy was served in bad faith and that the Tenant would not have moved out of the rental unit had it not been for the fact that she was served with the N12 Notice, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant some amount of general compensation. Having heard from the Landlord’s Legal Representative, the Landlord and the Tenant, I believe the general compensation should be equal to an amount of 12 months’ rent that was last charged for the rental unit which is a total of $19,920.00. This figure is reasonable, and I have based the amount on the stress and inconvenience put to the Tenant having to move and by the Landlord and Purchaser’s bad faith behaviour. The amount should also act as a deterrent should the Landlord or Purchaser decide to engage in the rental housing market again.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $26,886.89. This amount represents: • $6,918.89 for the storage expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $19,920.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $339.38 on or before [name] and must pay an administrative fine to the Board of $2,000.00 on or before June 1, 2026. Preliminary request to amend

At the hearing the Tenant sought to amend her application to include the remedy of out-of- pocket expenses in the amount of $286.38. The Tenant submits these expenses are directly related to the Tenant’s allegations in the T2 application.

The rules surrounding amending applications are found at subsection 200(1) and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure which state the following: 200 (1) An applicant may amend an application to the Board in accordance with the Rules. 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: • whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; • any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; • whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; • whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and • any other relevant factors. 15.4 The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.
Given the submissions before the Board, the Tenant’s request to amend was granted.

While I acknowledge the Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide submissions on the request to amend, the application is clear on the particulars that are alleged; further, the Landlord was served with the notice of hearing on February 13, 2026 via email and elected not to appear. I do not find the circumstances warrant adjourning the matter as I do not find the Landlord’s right to participate at the hearing is impacted. [name]
By way of background, this tenancy began in November 2024 and ended on February 1, 2026 when the Tenant vacated her unit.
The lawful monthly rent was $1,100.00. Illegal entry & Harassment
The Tenant alleges the Landlord attends the property without providing proper notice to the residents. The dates documented by the Tenant were: October 15, 2025 and October 21, 2025.

She describes the residential complex as a house with a main floor unit that consists of four bedrooms, one washroom and one kitchen. She testified that the common areas are shared with other residents, and the bedroom is her own space which she shared with her children while they resided at the property.

The Tenant testified that on October 15, 2025 she returned to the house after work to find the Landlord at the house; he was there to advise the Tenant to clear our her belongings from the kitchen sit-out area as there was work that was going to be done over the weekend.

The Tenant explains that her rental unit (the bedroom) is too small to accommodate her two children and her and their belongings so she typically leaves the laundry basket in the kitchen sit out area which is not used much by the residents.

The Tenant testified that while she removed her items, neither the Landlord or his contractors attended the property to do the proposed work and so on Tuesday morning, she returned the laundry basket to the sit-out area. That evening, the Tenant recalls the Landlord attended the unit again without notice and the next morning, she noticed her laundry basket disappeared.

The Tenant submits she called the Landlord immediately who admitted to removing the basket and having his contractor dispose of it; his contractor admitted that the Landlord asked him to throw the items despite him telling him that these were the Tenant’s belongings and that it was wrong to do so.

The Tenant testified that she is a single parent and felt so hurt by the Landlord’s conduct. She believes the Landlord should be fined for his behaviour and seeks out of pocket expenses to replace the clothing for her 12-year-old son who wears adult size small.

Based on the evidence before the Board I am not satisfied that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. The Tenant confirmed that the Landlord was always in the common areas of the residential complex.

However, I do find that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by disposing of their belongings without their knowledge or consent on October 21 -22, 2025. While no one saw the Landlord take these items, I find the Tenant’s uncontested testimony regarding the Landlord’s admission to be credible and therefore I find the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of their out of pocket expenses (for which receipts were submitted into evidence).

With respect to the request for an administrative fine to be levied against the Landlord, an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

Given the submissions and circumstances before me, I find it appropriate to levy a $2,000.00 fine against the Landlord. I say this because any reasonable person knows or ought to know that by disposing of another’s belongings without telling them is not only disrespectful but also contrary to the Act and a serious breach.
I do not find the remedies awarded will deter the Landlord from engaging in future similar conduct.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $339.38. This amount represents: • $286.38 for the out-of-pocket expenses; and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,000.00 by June 1, 2026. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
