issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background
The rental unit is a 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom apartment located on the 3rd floor of a 11 floor apartment complex containing more that 100 units.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2023 and vacated the rental unit on November 30, 2024. T6 Application
The Tenant’s T6 application alleges that the Landlord failed to meet its maintenance obligations with respect to a mice infestation within the Tenant’s unit and residential complex.

Pursuant to 20(1) of the Act a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant testified that on October 11, 2023 he saw a rodent run from his bathroom to his kitchen area under his stove. He called the Landlord’s maintenance phone number that same date to report the rodent in his unit. The Tenant stated that someone attended his unit a few days later and placed plastic boxes that held poison in his unit.

The Tenant further testified that the issued didn’t resolve and he would occasionally see mice in the unit, although he didn’t reach out to the Landlord regarding this issue again until February 8, 2024 specifically requesting pest control attend the unit. Pest control attended the rental unit within one week of his call on February 15, 2024 and indicated that the boxes were empty and refilled the poison in the boxes. The Tenant stated he was advised to call in a couple of weeks if the issue persisted.

The Tenant states that the issue didn’t resolve and called the Landlord again on March 5, 2024 and pest control attended shortly thereafter and refilled the boxes and indicated that the Tenant may want to seal the gaps around the drain and waterlines for the kitchen and bathroom sinks.
The Tenant reached out to the Landlord on March 19, 2024 requesting the gaps around the water lines and drains for the kitchen and bathroom sink to be sealed as requested by pest control.

The gaps around the water lines and drains were sealed shortly after the request by the Tenant. However, the Tenant continued to experience rodent activity and called the Landlord again on April 9 and 30, 2024 and. Pest control re-attended the Tenant’s unit and completed treatments and installed ultrasonic device which emits a sound designed to deter mice. The Landlord’s maintenance also attended the rental unit and sealed additional gaps in the walls.

The Tenant testified that the issue got better and he didn’t’ see any mice in his unit until September 25, 2024, but he could hear them in the wall. He didn’t believe the ultrasonic device was helping. Although he did not communicate any ongoing issues to the Landlord.

On September 25, 2024 the Tenant reached out to the Landlord advising a mouse was seen in his unit. The Landlord responded the following day asking if the seals in the unit needed to be replaced. An inspection occurred on October 9, 2024, but no repairs to the seals were needed.

No further complaints were made to the Landlord regarding the issue of mice and the Tenant sent an email on November 13, 2024 to the Landlord indicating his intention to end the tenancy and vacated the rental unit on November 30, 2025.
The Tenant initially testified that the issue had resolved by October, 2024, but then later indicated that the issue never fully resolved prior to him moving out of the rental unit.
The Tenant stated that he was fearful of getting sick from the mice in the unit and that his sleep was disrupted as he could hear them in the walls.

The Landlord’s Agent confirms that the Landlord first received a complaint regarding mice in the apartment on October 11, 2023, and submits that the Landlord responded promptly and appropriately to each complaint they received.

She stated that pest control initially attended the Tenant’s unit on October 12, 2023, the day after receiving the complaint. A report from Barrier Pest Control was tendered into evidence which indicated that the unit was baited and dusted.
The Landlord’s agent submits that they did not hear any further complaints from the Tenant until February 8, 2024 and had assumed that the issue had resolved.
The Landlord had Barrier Pest Control attend the unit on February 15, 2024 in response to the Tenants complaint of February 8, 2024 and the unit was again baited and dusted.
When the issue didn’t resolve the Landlord promptly sealed gaps around the water lines and drains to the kitchen and bathroom sink as recommended by Barrier Pest Control.

The Landlord again took action responding to the Tenant’s complaints on April 11, 2024 and May 9, 2024 having the unit baited and dusted and inspecting and sealing additional gaps in the walls around the electrical to the stove and radiator. Additionally an ultrasonic device was installed in the Tenant’s unit.

The Landlord attempted to follow-up with the Tenant regarding the effectiveness of the ultrasonic device on July 11, 2024 via email but received no response from the Tenant. The Landlord again assume the issue had been resolved as they did not hear from the Tenant until September 25, 2024, when the Tenant reported seeing a mouse.

The Landlord responded by conducting an inspection of the rental unit to ensure that the seals previously installed remained in place. The seals were still in place and no further complaints were received from the Tenant prior to the Tenant vacating the unit.
The Landlord’s agent submits that the Landlord responded to the issues raised by the Tenant in an appropriate and timely manner and has met its obligations under the Act.

The Landlord’s agent further submitted that on various occasions when Barrier Pest Control attended the unit for treatment it was noted that the Tenant’s rental unit had full garbage and unwashed dishes in the sink, which may have contributed to the issue. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the mice in the rental unit was an ongoing issue from October 2023 to October 2024. However, the Tenant’s evidence also reveals that the Tenant did not consistently notify the Landlord of alleged on-going issues regarding mice. Specifically the Tenant made complaints to the Landlord on October 11, 2023, February 8, 2024, March 5, 2024, April 9, 2024, April 30, 2024 and September 26, 2024.

Given the distinct gaps from October 11, 2023 to February 8, 2024 and from April 30, 2024 to September 26, 2024 and the Landlord’s Agent’s testimony that the lack of complaints on the part of the Tenant left the landlord believing that the issue had resolved. As such the legal test as set out in Onyskiw will be applied to each of the three distinct periods. October 11, 2023

On October 11, 2023 the Tenant contacted the Landlord indicating he saw a mouse in his rental unit. The Landlord arranged for and had Barrier Pest Control attend the unit and bait and dust the unit. No subsequent complaints of mice were made to the Landlord for almost 4 months.

During this period of time I find that the Landlord responded to the issue in a timely manner responding the next day. As no subsequent complaints were made the Landlord was of the belief the issue had resolved. February 8 – April 30, 2024
The Tenant reported another mouse issue to the Landlord on February 8, 2024, Barrier Pest Control attended the unit for treatment on February 15, 2024.

The issue did not resolve and Barrier Pest Control subsequently re-attended the unit on March 14, 2024 for another treatment. At this time it was suggested that gaps in the wall around the waterlines and drains for the kitchen and bathroom sink should be sealed to help prevent mouse infiltration. The work as requested was completed by the Landlord on March 26, 2024.

The issue had still not resolved and gaps around the electrical to the stove and radiator were also sealed by May 28, 2024. In addition to the regular treatment an ultrasonic device was installed in the Tenant’s unit to deal with the issue.

Again the Landlord received no complaints from the Tenant regarding the mice issue for 4 months until the complaint of September 25, 2024 was received. I find during this period the Landlord responded in a timely manner. Although the initial treatments were unsuccessful additional steps were taken by the Landlord as suggested by Barrier Pest Control to seal various gaps in the walls. As well an additional treatment method was implemented in the use of an ultrasonic device. The treatment used appeared to be effective as no complaints were received for 4 month period of time. September 25, 2024

The Tenant’s last complaint regarding mice in the unit was a call to the Landlord on September 25, 2024. In response the Landlord reached out to the Tenant to schedule an inspection of the unit to ensure the previously installed seals were still in-place. No further complaints were made to the Landlord.

As directed in Onyskiw the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations

A landlord can only address ongoing issues brought to their attention. Given the Landlord’s timely response when complaints were received from the Tenant regarding mice in the rental unit and the distinct gaps in complaints made to the Landlord regarding the issue. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord’s representative raised a preliminary issue in relation to limitation periods applicable to the Tenant’s allegations.

While exploring the limitations issue the Tenant clarified that the only allegations being raised are: T2 application- illegal entries, harassment, misuse of inspection/unauthorized photos, and T6 application- rodent infestation. Accordingly, the hearing proceeded only on these issues. T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal Entries
The Tenant’s application alleges two illegal entries by the Landlord on November 15, 2024, and November 19, 2024.

The Tenant testified that they discovered a notice of entry posted to their door when they returned home on November 14, 2024, at 5:00 p.m. The notice was for entry on the following day (November 15, 2024).

The Tenant was not present on November 15, 2024, when the Landlord’s agents entered the unit. The Tenant’s evidence is that her child had not been sleeping, and the Landlord’s entry was at an inconvenient time for her family.

The Tenant testified that her spouse was at the rental unit on November 15, 2024, when the Landlord’s agents took photographs while inside the rental unit and she felt harassed, judged, and humiliated. The Tenant acknowledged that her home was messy at the time of the entry because she was navigating challenges with her child.
The Tenant also gave evidence that during the entry her husband asked the Landlord’s agents to remove their shoes, and they replied, “In this condition?”.

The Tenant submitted a copy of an e-mail dated November 15, 2024, wherein the Tenant expresses their concern about the photographs taken on November 15, 2024, but the focus of the concern being expressed is specificity in the reason for entry and the photographs taken during the inspection.

The Landlord’s agent [name] (JS) corroborated the evidence in relation to notice being served on November 14, 2024, for entry on November 15, 2024, but clarified that the notices of entry were prepared at 8:00 a.m. and the superintendent was delivering them by 9:30 when JS was leaving.
JS explained that the notice of entry for November 15, 2024, was served to perform plumbing and unit “pre-inspections” prior to fire inspections scheduled for November 19, 2024.

JS also gave evidence that when the Tenant’s spouse asked the Landlord’s agents to remove their shoes JS replied that they can use “booties”, but it would be a safety issue to remove their shoes. The Tenant’s husband ultimately invited the Landlord’s agents to enter without requiring shoe/boot covers.
JS testified that photographs were taken during the inspection of the Tenant’s unit because there were “N5 issues” identified which the Landlord’s agent wanted to document.

The Tenant did not submit a copy of the notice of entry and neither did the Landlord’s agent. In the absence of the notice of entry being submitted I am unable to determine whether the contents of the notice complied with the requirements set out in section 27 of the Act.

Further, despite the Landlord’s agent acknowledging that a notice was served that may not have conformed with the requirement that a reasonable window of entry be provided, the [name] husband permitted entry to the rental unit on November 15, 2024.

The Tenant also testified that another notice of entry was served on November 18, 2024, and received at 11:00 a.m. [name] sent an e-mail to the Landlord complaining about the short service of the notice however, the Tenant permitted the Landlord to enter again on November 19, 2024.

The Tenant’s husband consented to entry on November 15, 2024, and the Tenant consented to entry on November 19, 2024, regardless of the sufficiency of the notices that were served. Section 26(1)(b) of the Act provides: 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.
As discussed below, the photographs taken during the entry on November 15, 2024, do not render the entry unlawful.

Accordingly, I do not find that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord illegally entered the Tenant’s rental unit on November 15, or November 19, 2024. Harassment and [name] / Photographs

The Tenant alleges that during the entry on November 15, 2024, the Landlord’s agents were asked to remove their shoes and refused. Further, on the same date, the Landlord’s agent took photographs during the entry which the Tenant asserts was solely for the purpose of humiliating and embarrassing the Tenant.

In relation to the allegation that the Landlord’s agents failed to remove their shoes before entering the rental unit, I accept the testimony of JS that the Landlord’s agents offered to wear shoe or boot coverings, and the Tenant’s husband invited them to enter without boot or shoe coverings.

Further, the Tenant did not submit evidence or testify that the requirement for the Landlord to remove their shoes was based on a religious or Code protected ground. I do not find that the Landlord’s agents’ failure to remove shoes was harassing or interfered with the Tenant.
The Tenant also alleges that during the inspection the Landlord took unauthorized photographs which the Tenant feels was harassing and humiliating.

The Divisional Court has previously considered issues in relation to photographs being taken in a rental unit in the context of illegal entry: Nickoladze v Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management, 2015 ONSC 3893 (CanLII), and [name] v [name], 2016 ONSC 1650 (CanLII).

In Nickoladze v Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management, 2015 ONSC 3893 (CanLII) the landlord took photographs during an inspection of the rental unit for use in an upcoming LTB proceeding. The Divisional Court agreed with the LTB that this was not illegal entry. The photographs were taken for a proper purpose because section 27 expressly authorizes a landlord to enter a rental unit for the purposes of conducting an inspection. The Court added that while it might be prudent for a landlord to expressly include the possibility that photographs may be taken in the notice, the failure to do so does not render the entry unlawful.

However, in Juhasz v Hymas, 2016 ONSC 1650 (CanLII), the Divisional Court found that, absent a specific term of the lease or the tenant's consent, section 27 does not authorize or require entry into a tenant's unit to take photographs for marketing purposes to advance the sale of the property.
While both decisions relate to allegations illegal entry, the Divisional Court considers different circumstances in which a landlord takes photographs in a rental unit.

The Divisional Court writes in Nickoladze v Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management: “Further, the fact that photographs were taken does not, by itself, constitute an infringement of the tenant’s privacy rights. It would only constitute an infringement if it was done for an improper purpose. In this case, the Board determined that the photographs were taken for the purpose of the inspection and for use at the hearing of the tenant’s outstanding applications. It was open to the Board, on the evidence, to reach that conclusion. In this day and age, it is not at all surprising that either a tenant or a landlord would take pictures of relevant items in order to use them at a hearing before the Board…”

In this matter, I do not find that the photographs taken by the Landlord are harassing or an interference with the Tenant. The photographs were taken for the purpose of documenting issues discovered by the Landlord’s agents during an inspection. The photographs were not taken for marketing purposes, publication, or dissemination, and do not constitute an infringement of the Tenant’s privacy rights. T6 Application

The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord did not secure the Tenant’s mailbox, refused entry to an internet service provider, and failed to perform maintenance on a bathtub. The Tenant further alleges that there was a mice infestation since December 2023.

The Tenant’s allegations in relation to the mailbox, internet service provider, and bathtub lack specific details, including dates and times. Accordingly, these issues were not considered at the hearing.
The Tenant testified that there was a mice infestation in the residential complex and submitted an e-mail dated December 29, 2023, advising the Landlord about the issue.
A further communication was sent to the Landlord on June 7, 2024, advising of the persistence of the pest problem.

The Tenant’s evidence is that she called the City many times about the issue which lasted for approximately one year. The Tenant also testified that pest control came out 2 or 3 times, but the issue wasn’t finally resolved until December 2024, or January 2025.
JS testified that the Landlord has never received a City order in relation to the issue with mice and that the Landlord performed treatments to eradicate the issue.
JS also testified that the Tenant’s rental unit was noted to have cleanliness issues which may have contributed to, or prolonged treatment for any pest issues.

JS submitted three pest control reports showing that the Landlord had pest control services perform treatments on February 8, 2024, June 27, 2024, and July 25, 2025. In each of the reports, the Tenant’s rental unit is listed as having “poor” to “moderate” sanitation. JS gave evidence that there were conversations with the Tenant about correlations between cleanliness and pest issues.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit or residential complex and did not fail to comply with health, safety, or housing maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. [Emphasis added]

In this case the Tenant complained about a rodent issue on December 29, 2024, and the Landlord engaged a pest control company to perform treatments which began on February 8, 2024. I do not find the delay of approximately four weeks to be unreasonable to engage a pest control company and begin performing treatments. Two subsequent treatments were performed, and the issue was ultimately resolved.

The only other evidence of a complaint is dated June 7, 2024, and a treatment was performed on June 27, 2024, with a follow-up treatment on July 25, 2025. I find that the Landlord acted promptly to resolve the rodent issue performing three treatments since notification of the issue on December 29, 2024, and the problem was resolved in July 2024.

Despite the Tenant testifying the issue continued until December 2024, no evidence of complaints were submitted to show there rodents were still present after July 2024, and I am satisfied that the rodent problem was remedied in July 2024.

The Landlord acted promptly and diligently to address the rodent problem performing three pest control treatments within 6 months. The evidence before me is that the condition of the Tenant’s rental unit may have contributed to the delay in eradicating the issue

Accordingly, I do not find the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations in relation to the rodent issue that occurred between December 2023, and July, 2024.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. March 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant requests to amend the application to include remedies pursuant to a T1 application. In this case, a rent deposit of $1,450.00 and $1,450.00 for an alleged illegal rent charge.
The Landlords were not opposed to the amendment and stated that they were prepared to address the additional claims.
Section 200(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the (“Act”), provides that an applicant may amend an application to the Board in accordance with the Rules.

Rule 15.4 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure provide that, the LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

This is a T6 application. A T1 application is for a rebate of money that the Landlord owes. The T6 application requests remedies consistent with those available under a T1 application. The Landlords are not opposed to the amendment and state that they are prepared to proceed with the claims alleged in the T1 application.

In the circumstances, I find that Landlords would not suffer prejudice as a result of the amendment. Pursuant to subsection 200(1) of the Act and Rule 15.4, I consented to amend the application to include a claim for illegal charges in the amount of $1,450.00 and for the return of the last months rent deposit in the amount of $1,450.00. Determinations: [name]. The Tenant requests a rent abatement for $2,900.00 because the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation with respect to mold, a sewage backup and failing to maintain a toilet. 8. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 15, 2024 and moved out of the unit on November 15, 2024. Mold 9. There is no dispute that the parties agreed for the Tenant to bring his own washer and dryer into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that on the date of move in, he observed black mold under the black rubber mats the machines were placed on. The Tenant testified that the Landlord advised them to scrub the mats with bleach which was completed by the Tenant’s mother in early July 2024. 10. The Tenant testified that the mold came back a few times between August and September 2024. When he raised the issue with the Landlord again, the Tenant testified that the Landlord advised him to spray the mats. The Tenant submitted a photo taken on or around November 15, 2024 and testified that the photo is the brick wall beside the washer and dryer. The Tenant testified that the wall was not damp, but mold could be observed. On review of the photo, there appears to be black spots extending approximately one foot from the base of the concrete wall. 11. The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the property to check for mold in November 2024 and thanked his mother for cleaning the mold off the wall. The Tenant submitted a copy of text communication between him and the Landlord and testified that the Landlord knew and agreed it was mold and therefore provided the Tenant with the option to break the lease. In the text communication between the parties, the Landlord discusses using bleach to remove the mold and to monitor it. The Tenant responds and states, in part, “So I’ve discussed it with my mother, and she’s very concerned about the probability of mold as well.” The Text communication further suggests that the Landlord offered to end the lease early which is accepted by the Tenant. An exact date to vacate the unit is not identified in the text communication. 12. In cross examination, the Tenant testified that he was not aware he could conduct his own mold inspection. He and his mother believed it was mold, but it was not guaranteed. The Tenant maintains that the Landlord knew it was mold. 13. The Landlord, [name] (KW), does not dispute that the Tenant raised the issue of mold when he moved in. KW takes the position that the dark spot on the base of the wall area is a result of the black mats that were placed on the floor and not related to mold. KW testified that he was going to clean the wall, but the Tenant’s mother insisted that she would do it herself, so he let her. 14. There is no dispute that the Tenant raised the issue again in November 2024, KW testified that he attended the unit, and that he did not observe mold. KW further testified that he was able to vacuum the residue from the mats and has not had any further concerns. 15. Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that mold was present in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that mold existed in the unit and that the Landlord was aware of the issue however, this was denied by the Landlord. 16. On review of the text communications submitted by the Tenant, the Tenant referred to the “probability” of mold rather than confirming its presence. The Tenant also did not produce any documentary evidence, such as a mold inspection report or an air quality test, to support a finding that mold was present in the unit. 17. During cross-examination, the Tenant testified that he believed the substance to be mold but was unable to confirm it was mold. In the absence of sufficient evidence to establish the presence of mold in the unit, this claim is denied. [name]-up/Toilet Issues 18. There is no dispute that the shower backed up on October 2, 2024, and that the toilet became clogged on October 6, 2024, and November 1, 2024. 19. There is no dispute that the Landlord snaked the toilet on October 6, 2024, and retained the services of Prince Plumbing to address the issue. It is also not disputed, that Prince Plumbing advised the Landlord that, in order to repair the sewage backup issue and the clogged toilet, the wall would need to be opened and the area dug down to access and repair broken or leaking pipes. 20. The Tenant testified that between October 6, 2024, and November 11, 2024, the pipes were not repaired and that the toilet continued to clog and therefore only worked intermittently. The Tenant testified that the toilet stopped flushing on November 1, 2024, and that he immediately advised the Landlord. The Tenant further testified that the plumber advised him to stop using the toilet until the pipe issue was repaired. However, written documentation confirming the plumber’s recommendation was not submitted into evidence. 21. The Tenant testified that on November 11, 2024, he followed up with the plumber, who advised him that the Landlord had cancelled the work required. The Tenant testified that he immediately contacted the Landlord, who advised that he did not want further delays but was looking for the best estimate. The Tenant testified that the Landlord, [name] (AP), attended the unit and offered to terminate the lease early. The Tenant accepted her offer as he did not have the ability to use the toilet. 22. KW testified that he was unable to find a contractor willing to complete the digging required to repair the pipe. The Landlord asserts that he contacted over ten plumbers to address the concern, but they either provided expensive quotes to complete the digging or refused to undertake the work. The Landlord did not submit any documentary evidence, such as inspection reports or quotes, with respect to the plumbers contacted. 23. KW testified that he retained the services of a plumber to complete the work on November 13, 2024; however, the plumber cancelled and did not attend. Documentary evidence such as a copy of the quote or communications confirming the cancellation was not submitted into evidence. The Landlord submitted text communication with the Tenant confirming that as of November 13, 2024, he was still “waiting on the last few estimates to come in.” 24. KW subsequently submitted a quote from Prince Plumbing dated November 13, 2024, in the amount of $4,520.00 to complete the digging and repair of the pipe. 25. As a result of the high cost associated with the digging, KW testified that he completed the digging himself on November 16, 2024, after which the plumber only charged $500.00 to repair the pipe. A copy of the repair invoice dated November 17, 2024, was submitted into evidence. 26. KW testified that the toilet issues were addressed immediately, but that it was agreed that the concern would ultimately be repaired by Prince Plumbing upon their return to town, as the plumber was out of town at the time. This is denied by the Tenant. 27. The Landlords testified that they were not aware the Tenant could not use the bathroom. KW asserts that after the toilet was repaired on October 6, 2024, no further concerns were raised until November 1, 2024, at which time he again contacted Prince Plumbing. KW further testified that the Tenant verbally advised him that there were no issues with the toilet. This is denied by the Tenant. 28. AP testified that several plumbers were contacted, and all advised that the wall would need to be opened, and the area dug to repair the pipe. However, the digging required was extremely expensive. AP testified that they wanted to repair the issue as soon as possible, but the cost of digging would cause financial hardship. 29. AP submitted an e-mail dated November 12, 2024, sent to the Tenant, in which she suggested that the Tenant could terminate the lease early provided that 60 days’ notice was given. AP testified that an official termination date was never discussed with the Tenant and that the Tenant simply abandoned the unit on November 15, 2024. In cross- examination, the Landlord testified that the Tenant responded to her e-mail on November 15, 2024, advising that he would be leaving the unit as of that date, due to the smell in the unit, but would return to collect his belongings. AP maintains that she accepted this to mean the Tenant abandoned the unit. On review of the e-mail response from the Tenant, paragraph two of the e-mail states, in part: 30. AP testified that after the repairs were completed, a new Tenant moved into the property on July 1, 2025, and no mold or plumbing issues have been raised to date. Analysis 31. This application is filed pursuant to section 20 of the Act, which states that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 32. The issue to be determined is whether the Landlords responded to the sewage and toilet issues within a reasonable time as required under section 20 of the Act. 33. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the Landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a Landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 34. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the toilet. There was no dispute that the toilet clogged on October 6, 2024 and November 1, 2024, and that on both occasions the Landlord retained the services of Prince Pluming to address the issue. Although the Tenant testified, that the toilet continued to clog between October 6, 2024, and November 11, 2024, the Tenant did not submit any documentary evidence, such as text messages or e-mails sent to the Landlords, to support ongoing complaints during this period. The Tenant also testified that the plumber advised him not to use the toilet; however, no documentary evidence was submitted to substantiate this allegation. 35. The Landlords denied being made aware of the additional toilet concerns. Considering that the Landlords addressed the toilet issues immediately after they were raised, I accept the Landlords testimony that they were unaware of any further concerns. On a balance of probabilities, I find it more likely than not that the toilet only clogged on two occasions, October 6, 2024 and November 1, 2024, and that on both occasions the issue was promptly addressed by the Landlord. 36. With respect to the pipe issue, I find that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair and maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and to comply with health and maintenance standards. 37. There is no dispute that a pipe issue was discovered on October 6, 2024, which required digging into a wall in the rental unit to complete the repair. There is also no dispute that the repair was completed on November 17, 2024. The Tenant vacated the unit on November 15, 2024. As a result, the pipe remained unrepaired for 41 days. 38. KW testified that he obtained approximately ten quotes for the digging portion of the work, but that contractors refused to complete the work, leaving him with no choice but to complete the digging himself. KW did not submit any documentary evidence with respect to the alleged multiple quotes sought. 39. The Landlords both testified that the cost of digging was too expensive and AP testified that it would cause a financial burden to retain someone to complete the digging. KW eventually submitted a quote from Prince Plumbing dated November 13, 2024, quoting a cost of $4,000.00 to complete the digging. 40. Based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlords failed to address the pipe concern within a reasonable time after becoming aware of the issue. While the Landlords testified that they contacted approximately ten plumbers, no documentary evidence was submitted to support this assertion. I find it more likely than not that the Landlords did not obtain a quote for the pipe repair until November 13, 2024, approximately 39 days after the maintenance issue was first identified. While I accept that Landlords testimony that the cost of repair was high, there is insufficient evidence before me to support a finding that reasonable efforts were made to address the issue sooner. 41. As I have found that the Landlords failed to meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act, the next issue to be determine is the appropriate abatement. 42. The Tenant testified that the sewage leak caused by the broken pipe resulted in a foul odour within the rental unit which clung to him and to his clothing and personal belongings. The Tenant testified that he was forced to have dinner in his bedroom due to the foul smell and was told by children that he smelled of sewage. 43. The Tenant testified that he spent significant time at his mother’s home due to the foul smell in the unit. He further testified that between October 11, 2024, and October 14, 2024, he remained out of the unit because the Landlords advised the pipe would be repaired but failed to do so. The Tenant testified that his bedroom was the only part of the unit he could reasonably use, as the remaining areas of the unit were affected by the odour. The Tenant testified that he ultimately decided to vacate the unit on November 15, 2024. 44. The Landlords testified that they did not notice any foul odours within the unit and submitted that the claim should be dismissed. However, on review of the e-mail communication from AP to the Tenant dated November 12, 2024, the e-mail states, in part: “ As you have mentioned, you can stay with your parents until this issue has resolved due to you being uncomfortable and the smell this broken pipe is giving off.” 45. Based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, I find it more likely than not that the broken pipe resulted in a foul odour in the rental unit that made the Tenant’s living conditions uncomfortable and that the Landlords were aware of the issue. 46. As the Tenant was completely out of his unit from October 11, 2024 to October 14, 2024, I find that a 100% rent abatement is reasonable for that time period. I further find that a 10% abatement is reasonable for the remaining 37 days during which the Tenant had to endure the foul odour in the unit. 47. In this case, the lawful rent was $1,450.00 per month. In the circumstances, I find that a rent abatement of $176.37 is appropriate for the 37 days during which the Tenant endured the odour. I also find that a rent abatement of $190.68 to be appropriate for the four days the Tenant was completely out of the unit between October 11, 2024, and October 14, 2024. I am satisfied that the Landlords were aware of the breach before the application was filed in accordance with subsection 30(2) of the Act. 48. In determining the appropriate abatement, I have considered the severity and duration of the interference with the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit, including the period during which the Tenant was unable to use the unit and the period during which the odour continued to affect the unit. T1 Application Illegal Rent Charge 49. There is no dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 15, 2024. The Tenant testified that he and the Landlords agreed to terminate the tenancy early as a result of the maintenance issues raised in the T6 application. 50. The Tenant testified that when he vacated the unit on November 15, 2024, he advised the Landlords that he would be returning to the unit periodically until December 15, 2024 to remove his personal belongings, as the last month’s rent deposit would have covered rent to December 15, 2024. 51. The Tenant testified that he attempted to return to the unit on December 7, 2024 to remove some of his personal belongings; however the Landlord had changed the locks, alleging that the Tenant had abandoned the unit and refusing to provide access to the unit until the Tenant paid for December rent. 52. The Landlord argues that there was never an agreement to terminate the tenancy on November 14, 2024. There is no dispute that the Landlords agreed to allow the Tenant to terminate his lease prior to the end of the fixed lease term; however, the Landlords maintain that the Tenant was still required to provide 60 days’ written notice to vacate. 53. AP acknowledged that the locks to the unit were changed three to four days after the Tenant vacated on November 15, 2024 because the Tenant stated in his November 15, 2024 e-mail that he was abandoning the unit, as addressed in paragraph 29 of this order. 54. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 4, Abandonment of a Rental Unit, states that: Abandonment is a unilateral act by the tenant to relinquish their tenancy and give up possession of the rental unit without properly giving notice of the termination to the landlord. If the landlord is not sure whether or not a rental unit has been abandoned, they may file an application for determination of this issue with the Board; however, it should be noted the Board has no jurisdiction to issue an order for rent or compensation if a tenant is no longer in possession of the rental unit (see section 87). In this case, the landlord may seek a remedy by applying to Court. 55. Section 87(1) of the Act provides that a Landlord may apply to the Board for an order requiring a tenant or former tenant to pay arrears of rent if, (a) the tenant or former tenant did not pay rent lawfully required under the tenancy agreement; and (b) in the case of a tenant or former tenant no longer in possession of the rental unit, the tenant or former tenant ceased to be in possession on or after the day subsection 18 (1) of Schedule 4 to the Protecting Tenants and Strengthening Community Housing Act, 2020 comes into force. 56. In this case, the Landlord has not filed an L1 application for arrears or an L10 application for arrears after the Tenant vacated the unit. 57. On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit on November 15, 2024. The Tenant’s e-mail dated November 15, 2024 clearly states that he would be returning to collect his belongings until December 15, 2024, which he believed to be the end of the rental period covered by his last months rent deposit. 58. The issue before the Board is whether the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy early. 59. The rental period is from the 15th day of the month to the 14th day of the following month. 60. There is no dispute that the parties had discussions about terminating the lease early. I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlords were aware he was vacating November 15, 2024 but would be returning to the unit until December 15, 2024 to remove his belongings, as stated in his November 15, 2024 e-mail. The Tenant submits that rent should only be owing to November 15, 2024, as the last month’s rent deposit covered the period between November 15, 2024 to December 14, 2024. 61. The Tenant takes the position that the Landlords agreed to terminate the tenancy on December 15, 2024. I do not accept the Tenant’s position. There is no evidence before me to suggest that the parties reached an agreement with respect to the date of move-out. I accept AP’s testimony that she requested 60-days’ notice to vacate and provided the Tenant with written details of what was required. Although parties may agree to terminate a tenancy at any time, there is nothing before me to suggest that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on December 15, 2024. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that such an agreement existed. Rent for the period November 15, 2024 to December 14, 2024 therefore remained owing. 62. As I have found that rent remained lawfully owing for the period November 15, 2024 to December 14, 2024, I am satisfied that the Landlords did not collect an illegal rent charge within the meaning of the Act. 63. The Tenant’s claim for an illegal rent charge in the amount of $1,450.00 is denied. 64. I note that the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit without providing the Tenant with replacement keys, which is contrary to section 24 of the Act. However, this issue was not raised in the Tenant’s application and is therefore not properly before the Board. Accordingly, the issue was not considered in my determination. Rent Deposit 65. There is no dispute that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on November 15, 2024, but intended to return to the unit until December 15, 2024 to remove his belongings. There is no dispute that the Tenant paid rent to the Landlord for the period November 15, 2024 to December 14, 2024 and the Landlord did not return the last months rent deposit. 66. Section 106(10) of the Act provides that, a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 67. Section 88(1) of the Act provides that, If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been giv en in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. 2. If the tenant abandoned or vacated the rental unit without giving any notice, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a notice of termination had the tenant, on the date that the landlord knew or ought to have known that the tenant had abandoned or vacated the rental unit, given notice of termination in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. … New tenancy (3) Despite subsections (1) and (2), if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent that exceeds the lesser of the following amounts: 1. The amount of arrears of rent determined under subsection (1) or (2). 2. The amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. Minimization of losses (4) In determining the amount of arrears of rent owing under subsections (1), (2) and (3), consideration shall be given to whether or not the landlord has taken reasonable steps to minimize losses in accordance with section 16. 68. Section 16 of the Act provides that, when a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. 69. In the case before me, no evidence or testimony was submitted by the Landlords with respect to the steps they took to minimize their losses. As I am not satisfied that the Landlords made attempts to minimize their losses, I find that the Tenant is responsible for rent only up to December 14, 2024. 70. As the Tenant paid the Landlord $1,450.00 for rent to December 14, 2024, I find that the Tenant is entitled to the return of his last month’s rent deposit of $1,450.00. The Landlord shall be ordered to return the last months rent deposit to the Tenant. 71. I have considered all of the evidence and submissions presented by the parties. Where I have not referred to specific evidence or submissions in these reasons, it is because I did not find them relevant to the issues to be determined or necessary to address in order to reach my conclusions. 72. This order includes all of my reasons within it no further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,865.05 This amount represents: • $367.05 for a rent abatement for the period ending November 15, 2024. • $1,450.00 for the last months rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenants withdrew their claim for monetary relief but submitted that the Landlord should be ordered to pay an administrative fine. The allegations against the Landlord are in substance about breach of privacy. The Tenants say they rented the whole house but the Landlord illegally entered the basement taking the position that she lived there. The Tenants say this was a rouse so the Landlords could shirk their responsibilities under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by fabricating a pretext to bring the rental unit within the exemption contained in paragraph 5(i) of the Act. The Tenants add the Landlord did not deliver the whole of the house as agreed because a third person was also living in the rental unit unbeknownst to them.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not binding on me but I accept it as the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

This remedy is not normally granted unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide an adequate deterrence and compliance. The objectives of deterrence involve both specific and general deterrence. I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors.

I find that the application must be dismissed because the remedy requested is not available on these facts. I am not satisfied that the breaches alleged against the Landlords, even if proven, could be characterised as a blatant disregard of the Landlord’s duties under the Act meriting an administrative fine because the Tenants’ testimony confirms that there appears to have been a genuine disagreement about the scope of the premises conveyed by the tenancy agreement.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant seeks refund of half his rent, the cost of buying window coverings and other ancillary relief because the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyable of the rental unit and also harasses, coerces, obstructs, etc. The Tenant’s pleadings are not clear and lack detail but the Landlord seemed aware of their substance. At the hearing, the parties joined issue on the following allegations: (1) The Landlord persisted in claiming parking charges despite a written agreement that parking would be free. (2) The Landlord falsely accused the Tenant of illegally growing cannabis. (3) The Landlord falsely accused the Tenant of being the source of a rodent infestation. (4) The Landlord falsely accused the Tenant of installing a washing machine and dryer contrary to the tenancy agreement. (5) The Landlord sent police to the Tenant’s place of worship. (6) The Landlord searches the Tenant’s household waste and falsely accuses him of not sorting it correctly. (7) The Landlord invades the Tenant’s privacy by sorting his waste. (8) The Landlord peers through the Tenant’s windows. (9) The Landlord monitors the Tenant’s movements and members of his household using the surveillance cameras installed in the residential complex. (10) The Landlord gave an N1 notice of rent increase that had mistakes. (11) The Landlord invited the Tenant to attend her church. (12) The Landlord is slow to respond to maintenance requests.

The essence of the Tenant’s complaint as revealed in the pleadings is that the landlord Precious Properties Inc. agreed in writing to give him an additional parking spot for free when his wife joined him in the rental unit but later resiled from that agreement and attempted to collect an extra charge for it. Precious Properties Inc. made two abortive attempts to terminate the tenancy on that basis, once by attempting to collect it on an improperly pleaded N5 notice of termination and again improperly claiming it as rent on a N4 notice of termination. The Tenant says this conduct is harassing and I agree. A reasonable landlord knows, or at least ought to know, that claiming a debt that does not exist would be unwelcome and bothersome to a tenant. I find the Tenant has proven this claim on a balance of probabilities because the Landlord does not deny it. At the hearing, the Landlord explained that Precious Properties Inc. was not bound by the agreement to give free parking and justified her attempts to resile from the agreement. First, the Landlord said she agreed believing the Tenant was impecunious. She later learned that he was not and feels she was coerced into the agreement by false pretences. Second, the Landlord explained that she signed the parking agreement under duress, because it was the Tenant who prepared the paperwork and presented it for signature at an inopportune moment. She was too busy to read the papers carefully and just signed them to be rid of him. These two contradictory justifications lack credibility but even if they were accepted, they would be insufficient grounds for resiling from the agreement. The Landlord will be ordered to stop demanding additional parking charges.

The Tenant understood that claims relating to conduct that occurred more than one year before the application was filed must be dismissed as disclosing no reasonable cause of action because they are barred by the one-year limitation period contained in subsection 29(2) of the Act. Of those that remain, some were withdrawn at the hearing and the remainder are trivial.

The claims that aren’t statute-barred were not proven on a balance of probabilities. I find they must be dismissed because the Tenant presented insufficient credible evidence to substantiate them, and even if proven, they are trivial and not breaches of the Act in the circumstances described.

Furthermore, the remedies the Tenant claims against this respondent are not available under the Act. In his pleadings, the Tenant describes the respondent as “property manager assistant”. In previous litigation at the LTB that forms the substance of the Tenant’s complaint, the landlord is identified as Precious Properties Inc. and this respondent is identified as the landlord’s agent. This is consistent with the evidence presented at the hearing that shows the [name] is not a “landlord” within the meaning of subsection 2(1) because she is neither the owner of the rental unit nor a person who is entitled to possession of it nor a person who permits occupancy. The tenancy agreement is with Precious Properties Inc. who is the owner of the residential unit and the true landlord. This respondent is a property manager of the Landlord. Section 31 limits monetary relief against a superintendent or agent to out-of-pocket expenses incurred.

The Tenant’s claim for buying coverings for his window are not proven on a balance of probabilities. He says he needs them to prevent the Landlord from peering through his window although he gave no evidence of that ever happening. I prefer the evidence of the Landlord that she has not, and could not, peer through the windows of this second-floor unit.
ordered: The Landlord shall stop demanding or attempting to collect additional parking charges. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant brings this application because of sewage backups in his unit. On multiple occasions, sewage came out of his toilet and bathtub and flooded his unit. His application states that backups occurred on October 26 2023, December 1 2023, March 10 2024, September 24 2024, and October 22 2024.

The Tenant previously raised the ongoing sewage backups in LTB-L-100823-23, which was an application by the Landlord respecting rent arrears. In that proceeding, the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) found that backups had occurred on October 16 2023, October 26 2023, November 17 or 28 2023, and March 9 2024. The LTB concluded that the Landlord had not met his maintenance obligations. He had sent plumbers to unclog the drain and clean up after each backup, but had failed to address the underlying cause of the backups. The LTB awarded a rent abatement, and compensation for expenses the Tenant had incurred as a result of the backups.

After the LTB had issued its decision, two more backups occurred, on September 24 2024 and October 22 2024. A few days after the October 22 backup, the Landlord finally repaired the underlying issue. The problem now appears to have been resolved.

Clearly, the Landlord is liable for the two new sewage backups. After the LTB found that he was liable for failing to repair the underlying problem, he continued to fail to repair the underlying problem. Two more sewage backups occurred as a result.

The Landlord argues that he should not be liable because he has now fixed the problem. There is no merit to that argument. The backups occurred before the Landlord fixed the problem, after he had failed to fix it for nearly a year. Remedies Rent abatement

The normal remedy for sewage backups would be a rent abatement. However, the Tenant did not claim a rent abatement in his application. Instead, under “other remedies” he wrote “unable to stay in my apartment for 9 nights and days. Not sure how to calculate these nights and days.”

I cannot award a remedy not requested in the application. The Tenant had the opportunity to amend the application following an Adjudicative Case Conference to identify potential deficiencies. He did not do so. Since he declined to provide particulars or seek an amount of compensation for being unable to stay in his apartment, no rent abatement will be awarded. Cleaning time and expenses

After the October 22 2024 sewage backup, the Landlord cleaned and disinfected the Tenant’s unit. However, the Tenant testified that he did not know that the Landlord had used disinfectant; he thought that only soap and water were used. He testified that he asked the Landlord about disinfectant, but the Landlord did not tell him he had used disinfectant.
Consequently, the Tenant purchased his own disinfectant for $38.00, and spent 4 hours disinfecting his unit. He seeks compensation of $38.00 for his expenses and $104.00 for his time.

In my view, it was reasonable for the Tenant to disinfect the unit in light of his uncontradicted testimony that the Landlord did not tell him it had already been disinfected. However, the Tenant has not explained why it took him 4 hours to apply disinfectant. The claim seems excessive. I will award $38.00 for the disinfectant and $20.00 for the Tenant’s time. Lost income
Finally, the Tenant says that when the October 22 2024 backup occurred, he had to leave work early to address it. He seeks compensation of $105.20 for lost wages.

When asked why he needed to leave work, the Tenant explained that he had to let the Landlord into the unit. Apparently, there are two locks on the Tenant’s front door. When this Landlord purchased the property, he asked the Tenant for copies of the keys to the two locks, but the Tenant refused to provide them. The Landlord then changed one of the locks and gave the Tenant a key, but left the other lock, for which the Landlord did not have a key, in place. Consequently, the Landlord could not get into the unit without the Tenant letting him in.
The Landlord is entitled to have keys to all the unit’s locks. In this case, both parties appear to be to blame for the fact that the Landlord did not have one of the keys that he should have had.

However, knowing that the Landlord could not unlock one of the front door locks, the Tenant should not have locked that lock. He could have used the other lock to secure his door. The Landlord’s inability to enter the unit in an emergency was a foreseeable consequence of the Tenant’s decision to lock both locks.
I therefore do not find the Landlord to be liable for the Tenant having to come let him in when the emergency occurred. Other orders
The application also sought an order that the Landlord repair the toilet, but at the hearing the Tenant withdrew that request.
The application also seeks an order that the Landlord remove some of the flooring to test for mould. The Tenant is concerned that the sewage backups could have caused mould growth.

The Tenant’s concern is purely speculative. He did not propose to adduce any evidence to show that there might be mould growth under the floorboards. The request for an order to test for mould is denied. Result
The Tenant will be awarded $38.00 in compensation for cleaning supplies, $20.00 in compensation for time spent cleaning, and his filing fee of $53.00 for this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $111.00, which represents compensation for expenses cleaning time and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $11,163.00, inclusive of the cost of filing the application and $5,000.00 to the LTB for an administrative fine.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;
No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and

The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 3. The rental unit contains two bedrooms and one bathroom and is located on the upper level of a quadplex building. 4. The Tenants were served with an initial flawed notice of termination under section 48 of the Act on December 29, 2023, then with a second notice of termination also under section 48 on January 15, 2024, with a termination date of March 31, 2024. The notice stated that the Landlord intended to occupy the unit for at least one year. Copies of both N12 Notices were submitted at the hearing.

The Tenants testified that they vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2024 because of the N12 notice. The Landlord informed the Tenants that his mother was very ill and both parents had mobility issues. The Landlord intended to move his parents into one of the other units he owned at 114 [address]reet and served the tenants of that unit with an N12 notice as well. The Landlord could thus move into the Tenants’ unit and be close by so that he could provide care for his parents. The Tenants submitted a copy of the Landlord’s signed Declaration and a letter from the Landlord’s employer disclosed to them confirming he was approved for compassionate care leave as evidence.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated. The Tenants discovered that the Landlord posted the Tenants’ unit for rent on May 28, 2024. The Tenants kept an eye on the rental unit and saw new tenants moving into the quadplex on July 1, 2024. The Tenants submitted a copy of the Facebook advertisement and a picture of new tenants moving in as evidence.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in s ubsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. [Emphasis added]

Though the evidence of whether the unit was re-rented is speculative, the submitted advertisement of the unit for rent within one year after the Tenants vacated and the Tenants confirming the unit address on the advertisement, is sufficient to satisfy me that subsection 57(5) of the Act applies in this situation. Therefore, it is for the Landlord to prove on a balance of probabilities that they did not give a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith. However, I may also take into consideration that bad faith is not confined to the moment in time when a landlord gives a tenant the notice of termination (see TST-94914-18 and TST-87742-17-RV). I may also take into account events during the notice period up until the date the Tenants vacated the unit.
The Landlord was not present to rebut the presumption of bad faith as set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act.

The Tenants testified that they offered the Landlord additional rent so they could stay in the unit, but the Landlord refused. The Tenants were paying the lowest rent in the residential complex and discovered that the other tenants who received the N12 notice for 114 [address]reet were also paying the lowest rent in that quadplex. The Tenants thus find it suspicious that the two units with the lowest rent were the ones served with N12 notices.

The Tenants also testified that they were made aware that the Landlord’s mother had passed away in August 2024 when they came across her obituary, however this was after the Facebook advertisement for the unit was posted in May 2024.

Having considered the uncontested submissions before me, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenants have proven the requirements under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act showing the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenants received an N12 notice, and I accept their testimony that they vacated as a result of the notice. There was no evidence that the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants moved out, and this was supported by evidence that the unit was listed for rent within three months of the Tenants vacating. As subsection 57(5) of the Act applies in this instance, it was for the Landlord to rebut the presumption of bad faith, and no such submissions were provided. Therefore, I find the Tenants have proven the allegations in the application. Remedies

The Tenants seek an order that the Landlord pay the increased rent they incurred for the one-year period after they vacated the rental unit. The difference in rent between the old unit ($840.00 per month) and the new unit ($1,310.00 per month) is $470.00 per month. Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $5,640.00 ($470.00 x 12 months) for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for the one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants request that the Landlord pay a fine to the Board for serving them a notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenants lived in the rental unit for twelve years only to discover the unit was then advertised for rent at almost double the price ($1,600.00 per month) within three months after they vacated. The Tenants perceive the Landlord’s conduct as egregious and should be strongly discouraged from happening again.

Having considered the criteria in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines, I find a fine of $5,000.00 appropriate in the circumstances to deter the Landlord from similar conduct in the future. The Landlord uprooted long-standing Tenants from their home of over a decade only to advertise the unit for rent again shortly thereafter for a significantly increased amount. There was no evidence the Landlord moved into the unit after the Tenants vacated, and it is more likely than not the Landlord chose to remove those Tenants as they were paying the lowest rent within the residential complex. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay a fine to the LTB of $5,000.00 to discourage such conduct in the future.

The Tenants claim $470.00 for out-of-pocket moving expenses as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. The Tenants’ testimony and application state that they rented a U-Haul truck and paid four of their son’s friends $100.00 each to assist with the move because of the Tenants’ mobility issues. Given the Tenants’ testimony and the amount claimed, I find $470.00 reasonable in the circumstances and order the Landlord to pay the full amount.

Pursuant to subsection 57(3)(1.1) of the Act, the Tenants also seek an order that the Landlord pay $5,000.00 as general compensation. Subsection 57(3)(1.1) provides that general compensation may be ordered regardless of whether the Tenants have incurred any actual expenses.

The Tenants testified that they received the first N12 notice when their grandchildren were visiting for the holidays. The Tenant, [name], was also recovering from knee surgery, while the other Tenant, his wife [name] [name], was recovering from cancer treatments. The Tenants were seniors who felt completely overwhelmed at the thought of having to leave their home of 12 years in their current physical state with no where else to go.

In considering the Tenants’ claim for general compensation, I have looked at how the Landlord’s breach impacted the Tenants. I accept that having to move out of the rental unit caused the Tenants significant stress relating to their health and change in environment. Given the uncontested evidence before me, I find that an award in the requested amount of $5,000.00 adequately compensates the Tenants for the mental distress they endured as a result of the Landlord’s failure to act in good faith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $11,163.00. This amount represents: • $5,640.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025. • $470.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the LTB an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by January 19, 2026. January 8, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. (T5 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) An Adjudicative Case Conference (“ACC”) was heard by videoconference on March 25, 2026. Only the Landlord and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the ACC. As of 10:07 a.m., the Tenant was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC.
reasons: Since the Tenant did not attend the ACC to support their applications, I find that these applications have been abandoned. Request for Costs
The Landlord’s Legal Representative sought costs in the amount of $200.00 for the one hour spent at the ACC and for one hour of preparation time.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 states: A Member has the discretion to require a party, a party's agent or a party's legal representative to pay, as costs, any representation or preparation expenses of another party where the conduct of the party, a party's agent or a party's legal representative was unreasonable. Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes the following: i. Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; ii. Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith;…

While the Guidelines are not binding on me, I find them informative and, in this instance, persuasive. I find the Tenant’s failure to attend the ACC, without notice to the Landlord, the Landlord’s Representative or the Board, to constitute unreasonable conduct and caused the Landlord undue expense.

Regarding the quantum of costs, Rule 23 says, “where the LTB orders a party to pay the representation/preparation fees incurred by another party, these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour for the services of a paid representative to a maximum of $700.”

The matter was called at 10:07 a.m. The Landlord’s Legal Representative is asking for costs for one hour of preparation. After reviewing the Landlord’s evidence prepared for the ACC and given that the Tenant filed two applications, a T5 application and a T6 application, I find one hour of preparation to be reasonable. Together with the one hour spent at the ACC, the total time is two hours which equals $200.00 in accordance with Rule 23.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed.
The Tenant shall pay $200.00 in costs to the Landlord.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before April 10, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 30, 2026 ____________________________
