issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • Entered the rental unit illegally • Changed the locks or the locking system on the rental unit or building without providing the Tenant with replacement keys The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards
reasons: The Tenant filed four T2 applications between June and November 2024, all of which contained similar allegations, and one T6 application, also within the time frame of the T2 applications.

There was an adjudicative case conference for all the files combined, held on June 23, 2025. At the case conference the parties were informed that the Act does not apply to the relationship between the parties. That finding was the result of a T3 application filed by the Tenant, LTB-T-091535-24. The order for that application, dismissing the Tenant’s application, was issued on June 4, 2025.
No request for review had been filed at the time of the adjudicative case conference, so the files were not dismissed at the case conference.
A request to review the decision in LTB-T-091535-24 was eventually filed, and there was a review order, LTB-T-091535-24-RV, denying the review request, issued on July 22, 2025.
Therefore, the determination that the Act does not apply to this relationship has been upheld on review. It is res judicata.
Despite the review decision in LTB-T-091535-24-RV, the Tenant did not withdraw his applications, and he insisted on having his applications heard in any case.
The Tenant’s application will be dismissed as the Act does not apply to this relationship.

It is before me to determine whether it is appropriate to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine on the Tenant for his failure to withdraw his applications, and his subsequent waste of Board resources and time.

Since the parties did not make submissions on this point, I find that it is not fair to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine in this matter. However, the Tenant’s applications, which were duplicative in any case, will be dismissed with prejudice.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed with prejudice. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under section 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $298.52 on or before April 7, 2026. Air Exchange

The Tenant testified that in May 2024, there was an issue with the toilet in the rental unit that caused sewage water to leak onto the air exchanger. She reported the issue to the Landlord some time that month and the Landlord removed the air exchanger but since the air exchanger has been removed, she has gotten a build up of mould on all the windows. The Tenant submitted photographs of the mould. She testified that she reported this to the Landlord right after they removed the air exchanger.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has replaced the air exchanger, but the new system does not work correctly. She said she often has to reset it because a light will blink and not function, so she has to unplug it for 5 minutes and then plug it back in. She testified that the Landlord has sent someone out but they just tell her to clear it from outside. She testified that she would have to deal with the error light every other day, which is not practical. She did not have these issues with the old system.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to the air exchanger.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of section 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

Overall, I do not find the Landlord’s response to the issue reasonable in the circumstances. Rather than address the issue of why the new air exchanger consistently stops running and has to be reset, the Landlord puts the onus on the Tenant to maintain the unit and reset it. This is not an adequate response to the issue. Therefore, I find that the Landlords were in breach of their maintenance obligations as they had been informed and were aware of the issue, and their response to the issue was not reasonable. No heat

The Tenant testified that because the air exchanger was connected to the duct system, any time she turns on the furnace, a sewage smell fills the rental unit. She testified that because of this, she was not able to use the heat in the unit until the Landlord fixed the issue in November 2024.

As stated in paragraph 19, the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of section 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

Applying [name], I do not find that the Landlord’s response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances. The Landlord was aware of the issue since May 2024 but did not replace the duct work until November 2024. I do not find that a delay of 6 months is reasonable, particularly when it left the Tenant without heat for months where the Landlord is obligated to provide heat. Therefore, I find that the Landlords were in breach of their maintenance obligations as they had been informed and were aware of the issue, and their response to the issue was not timely nor reasonable. [name]

The Tenant testified that the kitchen cupboards are all falling off and she has to re-drill the holes to put the doors back on. She testified that she does this for the cabinet doors, but she isn’t able to re-level the drawers. The Tenant submitted photographs of the cupboards showing the state of disrepair. The Tenant testified that she has notified the Landlord of the issue back in 2020 or 2021, but the Landlord has not ever sent anyone to repair the cupboards.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to the kitchen cupboards. They have been aware of the issue since at least 2021 but have taken no steps to repair the damaged cupboards, which is unreasonable in the circumstances. Floor Transition

The Tenant testified that the transition on the floor has screws coming up and their socks often get caught on it. She hammers them down, but they come up again. She testified that she informed the Landlord of the issue, but they have not repaired it.
I find that the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to the floor transition.

The presence of a maintenance issue in the rental unit does not automatically indicate a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. In this case, I am not satisfied that the Tenant informed the Landlord of the issue. While the Tenant testified that she informed the Landlord, she could not recall any approximate time that she informed the Landlord nor did she provide any evidence as to who it was reported to or how it was reported, such as via phone, in-person, maintenance portal, etc. As such, I find that the evidence is insufficient to establish that the Landlord was informed of the issue and given an opportunity to respond and repair the floor transition.
For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. [name]
The Tenant testified that the ceiling fan in the rental unit is droopy. The Tenant submitted a photograph of the ceiling fan.

I find that the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to the ceiling fan. There was no evidence that the ceiling fan is not operational or not functioning correctly and there is a lack of clarity from the photograph as to what the specific issue is with the ceiling fan as claimed by the Tenant.
For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Other Issues

In the application, the Tenant also claimed the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to painting, the doorbell, a kitchen outlet, bathroom fan, showerhead and the HRV system. The Tenant led no evidence with respect to these claims. As such, I find that the Tenant has presented insufficient evidence to prove that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to these remaining issues and these portions of the Tenant’s application are dismissed. Remedies Rent Abatement
The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 50% for the issue with the air exchanger and the heat.

I find that a 50% rent abatement is excessive for these two issues. I find that the mould on the windows partially affected the Tenant’s normal use and enjoyment of the rental unit. For these reasons, I find that a rent abatement of 15% for the air exchanger issue causing mould is reasonable. However, the evidence provided by the Tenant is insufficient to establish when the air exchanger was removed, when the new one was replaced and whether the mould is ongoing or if the issue was rectified. Therefore, I am unable to determine an appropriate remedy period for a rent abatement. As a result, I believe it is reasonable to award the Tenant a nominal amount by way of a lump sum of $50.00 for the issue with the air exchanger.

With respect to the issue with the heat, based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find that that a rent abatement of 25% is reasonable in the circumstances. The Tenant was unable to use the heating system from May 2024 to November 2024, although the Tenant was unable to provide any specific dates as to when the issue started and when the issue was repaired. Considering this and that pursuant to 2(1) of the Act, heat is considered a vital service only from September 1 to June 15, I find it reasonable in the circumstances to award the Tenant a rent abatement for the period of June 1 to 15, 2024 and September 1 to October 31, 2024.

The monthly rent during the relevant time period was $398.00 per month. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $248.52 for the period of June 1 to 15, 2024 and September 1 to October 31, 2024 for the heat issue. Order to repair

The Tenant requested an order requiring the Landlord to complete the repairs for the kitchen cupboards. I find the request to be reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to complete this repair within 30 days.
The Tenant obtained a fee waiver for the costs of filing this application; therefore, there will be no order for costs.
ordered: On or before April 27, 2026, the Landlord shall repair or replace the kitchen cabinet doors and drawers.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $298.52.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month of May 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ONLTB 13656 Date: 2026-03-12 In the matter of: Basement, 406 [address] Toronto ON [name] (the 'Tenant') and [name] applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] [name] (Tsiriotaki-[name]) (jointly referred to as the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and/or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them. This application was heard by videoconference on February 3, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, Demetrios [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant declined the opportunity to speak with Duty Counsel prior to the start of the proceeding.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I find the Tenant’s application does not contain sufficient particulars for the LTB or the Landlord to understand the allegations made against the Landlord.
In addition, I find the Tenant failed to comply with a peremptory [name] directing him to amend his application in accordance with the LTB’s Rules.

I was not satisfied it was appropriate to provide the Tenant with a further opportunity to amend nor that if I did so that there would be any materially different outcome and so the Tenant’s request for an adjournment was denied.
In the circumstances, I find it would be procedurally unfair for the hearing to proceed and the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Preliminary issue - who is the tenant?

It is not disputed that the Tenant and J. [name] lived in the basement of the residential complex. Nor was it disputed that each had a separate lease with the landlord, their own private bedrooms, and paid rent separately to the Landlord. Only the kitchen, bathroom, and a living space were shared.
On the basis of the above, I find the Tenant and J. [name] were not joint tenants.

Except in the case of multi-tenant applications, each tenant’s application before the LTB proceeds solely with respect to one rental unit. The question then is whether it was appropriate for there to be two tenants named on this application.

A multi-tenant application requires the payment of an additional fee for each additional unit and must be signed by a tenant from each unit. The application before me has only one signature and there was no indication in the LTB’s records that any additional fee was paid with respect to this application. Further, the LTB’s records reflect that J. [name] no longer wished to proceed with the application and had in fact filed a request to withdraw.

In the above circumstances, I did not find how or why the application named two tenants who lived in the same residential complex but had separate rental units material, as the application did not seem to have been filed in accordance with the requirements for a multi-tenant application and, in any event, one of the named individuals no longer wished to participate.

As a result, I found that the within application only related to the rental unit in which the Tenant lived, that only the Tenant was properly named as a tenant in this application, and the application was amended to remove J. [name] as a named tenant. T2 Application Insufficient particulars

The Tenant filed his T2 Application on November 5, 2024. He claimed all possible causes of action a Tenant who still lives in a rental unit can claim including that no written tenancy agreement was given for a care home or care services.
The T2 form explicitly sets out that tenants are to describe the events that led them to apply, and include what happened, the dates and times of the events, and who was involved.

The Tenant’s T2 Application contains broad allegations framed in the language of the Act largely without any accompanying identifying events, dates or times, such as that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit, abused him, harassed him, and substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment.

There is reference to some acts including refusing to provide keys, locking him out, cutting off vital services, playing loud music, installing a camera and spying on him, and failing to provide rental receipts; however, these allegations are still generalized as they refer to multiple occurrences and are not tied to specific dates, time periods, or occurrences.

Even where there is reference to specific police reports and a report of a call to the city, I find these are still within broad allegations about multiple events, and so I do not find the specifics sufficient to assist in understanding the particulars of the Tenant’s claims.

There were also issues with the Tenant’s remedies as, with the exception of a claim for mental distress, the remedies sought related to procedural issues, were claims that were more properly the subject of a different form of application, or were now moot given the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on May 31, 2025.
Finally, there was no suggestion before me that the rental unit was a care home or that care services were to be provided and so there was seemingly no basis for this claim.

In essence, as filed, the Tenant’s T2 Application was deficient and did not contain sufficient details that would allow the Landlord to know the case they had to meet and permit the matter to be heard fairly. Tenant failed to comply with [name] and his request to adjourn is dismissed
An Adjudicative Case Conference was held on June 12, 2025.

At the ACC a Member of the LTB explained to the Tenant that there were deficiencies in his T2 Application and he was directed to amend his application, and organize and re-file his evidence in an organized fashion and in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence

Following the ACC, Interim Order LTB-T-094998-24-IN issued on June 20, 2025. It states: 3. The adjourned hearing is peremptory on the Tenants to amend their T2 application by July 21, 2025, and ensure that such amendments are in compliance with Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The amendments shall detail what the issues are that they are claiming in the application, when they informed the Landlords of the issues, and any dates and times of when the issues or incidents occurred, where applicable. 4. If the Tenants fail to comply with paragraph 3 of this order, the Member may dismiss the application at the adjourned hearing. 5. The parties are directed to give to each other and to the LTB any evidence that relates to the application no later than seven (7) days before the hearing. This includes any documents, receipts, photographs, recordings or like things the party intends to rely on at the hearing. 8. For clarity, all documents, photographs and other items provided to the parties and the LTB must: 1. be readable; 2. have consecutively numbered pages; and 3. include a list or table of contents identifying each item in order, and by page number, if more than one item is being submitted.

At the outset of this hearing, the Landlord’s Representative raised that the Tenant had not complied with the Interim Order and so the Landlord was still not in a position to know the case they had to meet.

The Tenant submitted he understood his application would be dismissed by a certain date and when it was not dismissed on that date, he thought it had been accepted. He also submitted that particulars had been provided in his evidence. In the circumstances, the Tenant asked for more time to organize his evidence and amend his claim.

Firstly, leaving aside the ability of disclosure to satisfy the requirement to properly particularize a claim, I find the Tenant’s evidence was provided in such a fashion that it did not comply with the Interim Order and how this evidence related back to his claims in the T2 Application was not made clear.

I further find the Tenant’s Request to Amend an Order, that he asked me to and which I did review during the hearing, did not provide particulars for his claim and instead related primarily to the issue of the removal of J. [name] as a named tenant.
Secondly, I do not accept that the Tenant could not have obtained clarification on what was expected.

While I accept that the Tenant took some steps to seek assistance, the Tenant has had more than 7 months since the Interim Order issued to seek clarification and the Interim Order clearly stated that the Tenant had to take certain steps or his application may be dismissed on the return. [Emphasis added]

I also found the Tenant’s denial of the opportunity to speak with Duty Counsel at the outset of this hearing called into doubt the credibility of his prior unsuccessful attempts to seek assistance as it suggested he was not open to assistance even when it was available.

In the above circumstances, I was not satisfied the Tenant had provided a reasonable explanation for his failure to comply with the Interim Order, that there were steps he would now take that he was unable to take previously, that additional time would result in any material change to his claims, nor that, in the face of a peremptory order that it was appropriate to provide the Tenant with additional time.
As a result, the Tenant’s request for an adjournment was denied. Tenant’s claim is dismissed

Administrative tribunals are bound by the duty of fairness and the duty of procedural fairness includes the right of a party to know the case they have to meet. Absent this, the right to a fair hearing is denied and generally, as with any lack of procedural fairness, the resulting decision is compromised.

As held by the Supreme Court of Canada: • The duty to comply with the rules of natural justice and to follow rules of procedural fairness extends to all administrative bodies acting under statutory authority. … Moreau-Bérubé v. New Brunswick (Judicial Council), 2002 SCC 11 (CanLII), [2002] 1 SCR 249, at para. 75; and, • …the purpose of the participatory rights contained within the duty of procedural fairness is to ensure that administrative decisions are made using a fair and open procedure…with an opportunity for those affected by the decision to put forward their views and evidence fully and have them considered by the decision-maker. … [name] v Canada (Ministry of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 2 S.C.R. 817, the Supreme Court of Canada stated, at para. 22

Further, the Divisional Court has held that for administrative powers to, “be exercised in a procedurally fair way require[s] that notice be given which set[s] out the allegations sufficient to enable the parties to know the case they had to meet” and further, that, “[t]he applicants’ legitimate expectation was …to know the case that they had to meet.” In Fox North Bay Inc. v. Ontario (Alcohol and Gaming Commission, Registrar), 2022 ONSC 5898), at paras. 58 and 61.

And, in [organization] v. Corporation of City of [name], 2008 ONCA 570, when discussing how the failure of proper disclosure denied the appellant its right to a fair hearing, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held, at paras. 25 to 27: [25] Disclosure is a basic element of natural justice at common law and, in the administrative context, procedural fairness generally requires disclosure unless some competing interest prevails. As discussed in [name] and [name], Principles of Administrative Law, 4th ed. ([name], [name].: Thompson Carswell, 2004), at 258: The courts have consistently held that a fair hearing can only be had if the persons affected by the tribunal’s decision know the case to be made against them. Only in this circumstance can they correct evidence prejudicial to their case and bring evidence to prove their position. Without knowing what might be said against them, people cannot properly present their case. … [26] As noted by [name] in Waxman v Ontario (Racing Commission), [2006] O.J. No. 4226 ([name]. Ct.), at para. 11, “the failure to make proper disclosure has the effect of rendering the process ‘irretrievably tainted with unfairness from the outset’”. [27] In cases involving breaches of procedural fairness, the court will generally set aside the decision without considering whether the result would have been the same had there been no unfairness. …

Applications which make broad generalized claims and do not provide basic particulars do not allow a matter to be fairly heard. It is counter to the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness and would cause significant prejudice to the responding party if allowed to proceed.
As with all LTB applications it is the applicant, here the Tenant, who must ensure their application meets the minimum requirements.

Commencing with the prompts and direction provided on the T2 form, through an ACC before a Member of the LTB, the provision of an Interim Order, and the ability to seek assistance including the opportunity to speak with Duty Counsel at today’s hearing, the Tenant has had multiple opportunities to particularize his claims. Nonetheless, he has not done so.

I do not find the Landlord or the LTB can discern what the Tenant’s claims are and I find that it is not now for the LTB or the Landlord to correct deficiencies in the Tenant’s application, nor for the LTB or the Landlord to interpret, infer or imagine what the Tenant’s allegations might be.
In the above circumstances, I find that it would be procedurally unfair to permit a hearing on the merits to proceed. As a result, I find the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord) collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: In her application, the Tenant alleges: • The Landlord did not use her last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to her; and • The Landlord gave her an N12 Notice to End the [name] because the Landlord, a purchaser or family member requires the rental unit for residential occupation and did not pay her compensation by the termination date on the N12 Notice.

On January 30, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice with a termination date of May 31, 2024. The reason for ending the tenancy was because the Landlord signed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale of the rental unit, and the purchaser intended to move into the rental unit.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 11, 2024. One month compensation:

Subsection 49.1(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) reads as follows: 49.1 (1) (a) A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the T enant another rental unit acceptable to the T enant if, (a) the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy on behalf of a purchaser under subsection 49 (1) …
S ubsection 55.1 of the Act requires the Landlord to compensate the Tenant no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination.

I am satisfied based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that an N12 Notice was given by the Landlord and the Landlord has not paid the one-month compensation as required under section 49.1 (1)(a) of the Act.

The lawful monthly rent is $2,362.68 therefore the Landlord owes the Tenant $2,362.68. An extra 125.00 the Tenant claims is paid with rent for gas and water is not deemed as rent therefore is not considered as part of the one-month compensation. Last month rent Deposit:
Subsection 49(2) of the Act states, that a tenant who receives notice of termination under subsection 49(1) may, at any time before the date specified in the notice, terminate the tenancy earlier.

On April 30, 2024, the Tenant gave the Landlord a Notice terminating the tenancy on May 15, 2024 but she vacated earlier on May 11, 2024. Since the Notice was at least 10 days before the Tenant terminated the tenancy, the tenancy terminated lawfully. Hence, the Landlord is not permitted to retain money for per diem rent on or after May 16, 2024.

The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,362.68 which is still being held by the Landlord. Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to the last rent period of the tenancy. Thus, the last month rent deposit is applied to May 1-15 rent charges. The amount in excess of per diem rent from May 16-31, 2024 is money the Landlord collected and has retained unlawfully. Hence the Landlord is required to pay the Tenant the difference, as claimed by the Tenant in her application, in the amount of $1,181.34.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,597.02. This amount represents: • $2,362.68 for the compensation owed by the Landlord pursuant to subsection 49.1(1) • $1,181.34 the balance of last month rent deposit • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Phan (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that MTCC 1175 (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant’s application is brought pursuant to subsection 29 (1) 1. of the Act, which allows the Tenant to apply to the Board for an order determining that the Landlord has breached its maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.

At the hearing, it was raised that many of the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application were not maintenance related at all and, therefore, those allegations were not properly before the Board and ought to be dismissed.

The Tenant acknowledged that he made conduct related allegations in his application and that those allegations were not claims of disrepair. However, the Tenant’s application did claim that his washer and dryer were not working. The Tenant wanted to proceed with his application to address the washer and dryer issues only.
Accordingly, the application proceeded on the washer and dryer disrepair allegations only. Application & Evidence

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenant in accordance with the order below.

During the hearing, the following facts were not in dispute: • the rental unit came with ensuite laundry facilities, which was a GE combination washer dryer unit; • the Tenant reported to the Landlord’s Agent, AM, on September 22, 2024 that the washer and dryer had stopped working’ • AM responded the next day and arranged with the Tenant to have the superintendent inspect the washer and dryer; • A service technician attended the rental unit on October 8, 2024, but was not able to repair the washer and dryer at the time as there was a suspected electrical issue; • AM emailed the Tenant on October 9, 2024 to advise that an electrician would attend the unit on October 16, 2024; • the electrician attended the rental unit on October 16, 2024; • on October 23, 2024 AM sent an email to the TT advising that the electrician said the issue was a tripped breaker and that, once reset, power was restored to the receptacle and the dryer was able to function but the washer was still not functioning and required a replacement part; and • the washer and dryer unit was fully repaired and functioning by December 11, 2024. Tenant’s Evidence

It was the Tenant’s evidence that after emailing AM on September 22, 2024, the issue remained unresolved for an unreasonable length of time and that he had to follow up with AM multiple times, including on October 9, 2024 and November 1, 2024. The Tenant stated he was told that the delays were caused by a third party as well as the need to order replacement parts.

During cross examination it was suggested that the Tenant delayed the repairs because he was unresponsive to the technician that was trying to contact him regarding an appointment scheduled for November 22, 2024, which had to be rescheduled to November 29, 2024. The Tenant denied having been properly notified of the November 22, 2024 appointment.

The Tenant stated that, between September 22, 2024 and December 11, 2024, he had to go to a laundromat to do his laundry, which was time consuming and inconvenient. The Tenant testified that it cost him approximately $13.00 to $15.00 per load, including transportation costs. As the Tenant’s child was a baby at the time, he had to do laundry frequently and stated that he did approximately 5 loads of laundry per week. Landlord’s Evidence

AM is the property manager for the Landlord. It was his evidence that, he responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely manner and took all possible steps to try and get the washer and dryer repaired as quickly as possible. AM stated that the delay of the repairs was mostly due to the time it took to diagnose the issue. In this regard, he initially arranged for a GE appliance technician to attend to the issue, not knowing there was an issue with the power supply. He then had to arrange for an electrician to attend but this only resolved the issue with the dryer. AM then had to schedule a GE appliance technician to come back to inspect and diagnose the issue with the washer. It was determined that a part required replacement in the washer and so the appliance technician had to come back on another day to finally complete the repairs.

AM stated that he did not believe that there was anything that he could have done to make the repairs happen any quicker. AM suggested that there was some delay that was caused by the Tenant in scheduling an appliance technician to return to the unit in November as the technician was not able to reach the Tenant regarding an appointment that was scheduled and so it had to be rescheduled for a later date. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In this case, it was not disputed that the Tenant was without a functioning washer and dryer for approximately 2.5 months. However, this does not automatically mean that the Landlord was in breach of its obligations under section 20 of the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Both parties presented and relied on email correspondence between the parties as evidence at the hearing. Based on the correspondence presented at the hearing, the parties were in fairly regular communication with each other regarding the washer and dryer.

In my view, the responses of AM appear to be timely and reasonable for the most part as do the actions taken by the Landlord. In this regard, AM does provide some updates to the Tenant and explains what steps he has taken to resolve the issues. That said, there appears to be a gap between the date the electrician came on October 16, 2026 and the first scheduled appointment for the return of the GE appliance technician on November 22, 2024, which is a 38 day period.

In the October 23, 2024 email to the Tenant, AM wrote that he had reached out to GE again regarding getting a technician to come back to repair the washing machine. In this email he stated that GE’s IT system was down and that he could not reach anyone directly and so he sent an email but did not receive a response. AM followed up with GE via email on November 1, 2024 and someone from GE responded on November 5, 2024 confirming that a service request had been submitted. There was no evidence of any further follow ups by AM after November 1, 2024 and an appointment was ultimately set for November 22, 2024. In my view, given the amount of time that the Tenant had already been without a functioning washer and dryer, AM should have made further follow ups to try and get the appointment scheduled for an earlier date.

Although the Tenant denied being notified by AM of the November 22, 2024 appointment, the Tenant’s email evidence shows that the appointment details were emailed to the Tenant by AM on November 19, 2024. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the appointment had to be rescheduled due the to actions or inactions of AM or the Landlord.

Ultimately, when the GE appliance technician did attend on November 29, 2024, it was determined that a part was required, which delayed the completion of the repairs to December 11, 2024. There was no evidence provided to suggest that this period of time was unreasonable or could have occurred quicker and I accept that this period of delay was largely outside the Landlord’s control.

For the reasons set out above, I find that the repairs that were ultimately undertaken and completed were reasonable in the circumstances. However, I find that that they were not done in a reasonable period of time. While I accept that a large part of the delays were outside the Landlord’s control, the Landlord could have done more to try and get the repairs completed quicker, such as following up with GE more persistently. As such, I find that the Landlord breached its obligations under section 20 of the Act and, therefore, the Tenant is entitled to compensation. Remedies

In summary, the Tenant requested a total of $4,500.00 which they calculated as follows: • $3,000.00 for loss of use, inconvenience and health problems • $825.00 for additional costs incurred; and • $675.00 for the value of the laundry facilities included in the rent.

The Tenant provided oral testimony with respect to the loss of use and inconvenience they experienced in having to do their laundry at a laundromat. However, there was no evidence provided with respect to any health problems experienced as a result of using the laundromat. Moreover, there was no evidence provided that would substantiate a claim of $3,000.00 or a reasonable explanation as to how this amount was arrived at. Accordingly, this amount shall not be awarded.

The Tenant did not have any documentary evidence to substantiate their claim for additional costs in the amount of $825.00. While I accept that the Tenant had to go to a laundromat to do their laundry and had out-of-pocket costs as a result, the Tenant was unable to quantify those costs with any certainty or accuracy.
Although the Tenant categorized the amount claimed of $675.00 under the heading of out- of-pocket expenses in the application, the Tenant is essentially requesting a rent abatement.

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy that is based on the principle that, if you are paying 100% of the rent, you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

In other words, an abatement of rent can be viewed as compensation to the tenant for the inadequate state of repair and any inconvenience or actual loss of use of the rental unit. In determining the amount of an abatement of rent, I must consider the impact on the Tenant.

I do not doubt the Tenant’s testimony that the temporary loss of ensuite laundry was highly inconvenient, especially with having a baby whose clothing would need laundered frequently. I also accept that it would be more time consuming to have to do laundry off site.

Having considered all the evidence and submissions of the parties, the impact to the Tenant, as well as my experience and knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find that that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $251.50, which represents a 20% rent abatement for the period of November 6, 2024 to November 22, 2024, which is calculated as follows: $2,250.00 x 12 / 365 = $73.97 per day x 17 days = $1,257.49 x 20% = $251.50. The period of abatement represents the period of time during which the Landlord’s responses or actions were not reasonable and/or timely in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount that the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $299.50. This amount represents: • $251.50 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month of June 2026. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • Failed to provide and maintain the residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards pursuant to section 29(1) subsection 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. (‘the Act’). • And that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit.
reasons: At the outset, the Landlord raised the issue that the tenancy agreement has been frustrated and requested an order in accordance with s. 19 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (The Act). They stated that it applied as there had been an explosion and fire that completely destroyed E40 Chesterton Street on August 30, 2024.
Section 19 of the Act provides that the doctrine of frustration applies to tenancy agreements.

In [name] v. [name] et al, 2018 ONSC 5749 , the Divisional Court held that the following articulation of the test by the Board was correct, at paras 11 and 22: a. an unexpected event that was not contemplated in the contract or foreseeable must occur. b. the unexpected event cannot be self-induced or the fault of one of the parties. c. the event must drastically change the nature of the contract so that it is impossible (not just difficult or expensive) to perform the obligations under the contract. The impossibility of performance must be of a long term nature and not temporary or transient. Application
Both parties agreed that the explosion was unforeseeable.

For the second branch, the Landlord stated they believe that the fire is a result of arson, but no police report was filed or made an exhibit and nothing in the DFA Report concluded arson, and so I have no information before me to attribute fault in this case. I therefore conclude that there is no fault.
This case turns on the third branch of the test in determining whether the tenancy agreement was frustrated or not.

The Landlord referred to the Structural Engineering Assessment following a Fire by DFA Engineering Services Inc., dated December 27, 2024 found at DOC-5412276, which was marked as Exbibit 1, that the rental unit was completely destroyed by the explosion on August 30, 2024: It is our opinion that, due to the extent of fire damage to this building, it is not feasible to repair the building, and the superstructure should be demolished to the top of the foundation and rebuilt to match the existing.
As a social housing provider, the Landlord could not indicate when or if the rental unit would be ever rebuilt.
The Tenant argued that the Landlord has a duty to repair the rental unit, pursuant to s. 20 of the Act, and that he wished to move back in when repairs were completed.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the fire was unforeseen by the tenancy agreement, not the fault of any party, and that the building was destroyed beyond repair to the extent that the tenancy agreement was frustrated and thus terminated on August 30, 2024.

Therefore the application for the maintenance and repair of the rental unit subject to s. 20(1) of the Act cannot proceed because there is no rental unit to maintain after the explosion. The Tenant’s T6 application is moot and shall be dismissed.

As the tenancy agreement is deemed to have ended on August 30, 2024, the Board does not have jurisdiction to determine the T2 as section 23 operates within the purview of an active tenancy agreement and the behaviour alleged by the Tenant occurred after the tenancy agreement was frustrated and terminated. Accordingly, the T2 shall also be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenancy is terminated as of August 30, 2024 due to an unforeseen explosion that frustrated the tenancy agreement.
The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. February 25 , 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $248.00 for a key deposit and for the cost of filing the application.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). In September 2024, the Tenant paid a refundable key deposit of $200.00 to the Landlord and since the tenancy terminated on August 26, 2025, the Landlord has failed to refund the deposit to the Tenant.

Section 105 (1) of the Act, states that the only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit and section 134(1) specifically prohibit the collection of a key deposit. Section 17 of O’Reg. 516/06 to the Act provides for certain exceptions from section 134(1) including “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.

In this case the key deposit of $200.00 is more than “the expected direct replacement costs” for the keys and was not refunded to the Tenant at the end of the tenancy . Therefore, the key deposit was illegal, and it must be returned back to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
