issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Unlawful Entry

MC testified that the Landlord entered the rental unit without any notice to ask about rent money owing sometime around the beginning of August 2024 at 9:00 a.m. She testified that she was just waking up and rolled over in bed to see the Landlord standing at their bedroom door staring at her. She testified that this incident was very traumatic for her as she was lying there naked at the time.

The Landlord testified that there was one time when he was at the residential complex, and ran into the other Tenant, [name] [name] [name] (EJY), who asked him to look at the lock on their entrance door as the latch was not working. He testified that he went up to their unit to look at the door, which was left open, and started fixing the lock when MC, who was in the unit, saw him. He testified that he was not in the bedroom nor did he see anyone naked.

MC could not recall the date of this alleged unlawful entry by the Landlord, simply stating around the beginning of August 2024. EJY, who MC asserts was home at the time, did not attend the hearing to testify in support of this allegation. MC maintained that this incident traumatized her and was the catalyst to her vacating the rental unit approximately five months later, namely at end of December 2024. Despite MC also testifying that her relationship with EJY broke down, became abusive, and also that she lost her employment leading up to December 2024.

The Landlord testified that when the Tenants provided their notice to vacate, they stated that they enjoyed living at the premises but had to leave for other reasons. This was not disputed by MC. MC asserted that the trauma of the Landlord seeing her naked prevented her from saying the actual reason for leaving. MC did not provide any medical or professional supporting evidence regarding treatment sought for this traumatic event or have an expert testify as to how a traumatic event may make a person behave.

Given the above, the evidence before me was insufficient to find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit sometime around the beginning of August. This date/incident may or may not have been the same date the Landlord recalled going to the unit. However, the Landlord’s evidence was forth coming and candid, and I found him credible. Therefore, I find it more likely than not that MC may have just been surprised by the Landlord’s attendance at the unit to fix the door lock which was requested in person by EJY without MC knowledge and would not amount to an unlawful entry as EJY gave consent. Substantial interference/Harassment

MC testified that there was limited space for them to store their garbage outside as there were two other units and parking spaces at the front of the building where the bins were stored. She testified that when those garbage bins were full, the Landlord told them via text because the neighbours were complaining to keep their garbage inside until garbage day. MC found this to be unreasonable as other buildings in the area just had bigger bins for their residents’ garbage.

The Landlord recalled an incident where the Tenants had placed unwanted furniture in the hallway and then moved it outside. He testified that he texted them that they cannot do that as they only have two bins per unit and they can only put those out on garbage day as per the By-Laws.

The evidence before me was insufficient to find that this issue amounted to a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex. MC could not recall the date of the text message exchange with the Landlord and never really complained to the Landlord about having to store garbage in her unit after that time. Given there were no complaints, I find it unlikely that there was a substantial impact on the Tenants using the dedicated bins or waiting until garbage day.

MC testified that there were cockroaches and fruit flies in the unit and that the first floor unit had also mentioned that they had them too. MC did not believe she reported these issues to the Landlord. Given this, I find it more likely than not that if these issues were a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment they would have reported it. Since they did not, I was satisfied that most likely it was a limited time issue, resolved on its own, and did not significantly impact the Tenants.

MC also testified that there was a broken fire alarm (detector) in their unit which was pre- existing from when EJY resided in the unit before MC moved in. MC testified the EJY had told her that it was reported to the Landlord but that he was not helpful. MC confirmed that she did not report this issue to the Landlord. The evidence before me was insufficient to find that this issue was reported to the Landlord by EJY and not addressed as it was solely hearsay. Given this, I find it more likely than not that if this issue were an ongoing substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment they would have reported it. Since they did not, I was satisfied that it most likely was resolved or did not significantly impact the Tenants.

MC testified they gave their notice to vacate for the end of December 2024 on November 2, 2024 to the Landlord. She asserted that EJY and her had discussed giving notice earlier but that EJY had not texted the Landlord as discussed. She testified that she recalled the Landlord mentioning something about sub-leasing and paying one month’s rent as per their written tenancy agreement. However, she asserted that their tenancy agreement did not set out terms for sub-leasing and did not say that the Tenants must find a sub-tenant. She testified that she tried to express this to the Landlord who asked to speak to her in person.

MC asserted that when she met with the Landlord he stated that another unit in the complex is looking for a sub-lease and that he does not want two sub-leases in January and asked if they are willing to wait until February.

The Landlord confirmed that he met with MC and told her that she can either find someone to take over the lease or pay until February and he will break the lease. He testified that he told her it is hard for him to find another tenant for January at that time.

There was no dispute that the parties had signed a one-year term tenancy agreement which ended on April 30, 2025. The Tenants were looking to end the tenancy, most likely due to the breakdown in their relationship and financial issues as they had both lost employment. I was not satisfied that the information provided to the Tenants by the Landlord amounted to any form of harassment, coercion, or threat. I find it more likely than not the Tenants were simply upset that the Landlord refused to release them from their obligations under the Act.

As per subsection 44(4) of the Act, a notice by a tenant to terminate a tenancy for a fixed term shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date. A tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord as per subsection 97(1) of the Act. Based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Landlord was willing to consent to a sublet. I find it more likely than not that MC simply did not understand her obligations under the Act which even now she only partly understands.

The Landlord was entitled to assert his rights under the Act to require a proper notice of termination, be presented with a potential sub-tenant, and hold the Tenants liable for rent until the end of April. In this case, the Landlord even offered to waive the last two months of the lease if the Tenants agreed to a termination date of February 28, 2025. It is not a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit and complex to hold them to their obligations under their negotiated agreement and/or the Act.

For the above reasons, the Tenants have not proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached the Act with respect to the allegations made in this application. Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $848.00. Evidence of the Tenants

Ms. [name]name] testified that all four Tenants took possession of the rental unit on September 1, 2022. The parties executed a tenancy agreement in April 2022. The Tenants entered into evidence an email from the Landlord dated April 6, 2022, which stated that each Tenant was required to pay the Landlord $714.00 toward the last month’s rent deposit and $200.00 for a key deposit.
On April 7, 2022, the Landlord confirmed by email that each Tenant had paid $914.00. This email was also entered into evidence.
Ms. [name]name] testified that when the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Landlord provided instructions regarding the return of the keys.
Ms. [name]name] returned her keys on August 17, 2025, Ms. [name] on August 27, 2025, Ms. [name] on August 16, 2025, and [name] on August 24, 2025.
The Landlord did not return the key deposits to any of the Tenants, for a total amount of $800.00. Additionally, the Tenants paid $48.00 for the application filing fee. Analysis

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: 134(1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money, whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 provides an exception that permits a landlord to charge the actual cost of replacement keys, provided that the amount is no greater than the actual replacement cost and is refundable upon return of the keys.

The evidence establishes that the Tenants each paid $200.00, for a total of $800.00, for additional keys and that the Landlord treated this amount as a refundable key deposit. Upon the return of the keys, the Landlord was required to refund $200.00 to each Tenant, or $800.00 in total.
As all Tenants returned their keys to the Landlord, there is no juristic reason for the Landlord to retain the $800.00. The Landlord is therefore required to return $800.00 to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $848.00. This amount represents: • $800.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: At the hearing, I pointed out to the Tenants that some of their claims in the T6 application do not identify when the issue began or when the Landlord was told about it. I explained to the Tenants that this information is required to provide the Landlord a fair opportunity to adequately respond to the claims being made. For their part, the Landlord submitted they found it difficulty to prepare for these allegations given the lack of these details. Since I did not find these claims had been sufficiently pled in the application, they were not considered.
The remaining issue in the T6 involves a flood that occurred in the rental unit on October 14, 2025. This issue also forms the basis of the T2 application. T2 and T6 Applications
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the applications are dismissed
It was undisputed there was a flood in the rental unit that damaged the kitchen. This required the remediation efforts and then restoration.

The timeline of events was not in dispute at the hearing. Accordingly, I make the following findings of fact: a) The Tenants noticed a flood in the kitchen of the unit coming from the ceiling on October 14, 2025 and notified the Landlord the same day. b) The Landlord acknowledged the issue and drying the unit with dehumidifiers began by October 18, 2025. c) Based on the Landlord’s estimate that repairs would take two to three weeks, the Tenants left the unit on October 18, 2025 and stayed in hotels and an Airbnb while the work took place. d) In early November 2025, after the drying process was completed, the kitchen was gutted. The removal of the damaged kitchen was completed by November 7, 2025. e) On November 12, 2025, the Landlord provided the Tenants a copy of the insurance claim report that the Tenants required to make a claim under their own insurance policy. f) The rebuilding of the kitchen began on November 27, 2025 after the insurance company contractors were delayed for two days addressing an unrelated emergency elsewhere. g) The repairs to the unit were completed by December 4, 2025 and the Tenants were notified they could move back into the unit as of 5:00 p.m. that day.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

This contextual approach also applies to T2 applications where the allegations overlap with section 20(1) of the Act as they do in this case. Paragraph 56 of Onyskiw states: To interpret s. 20(1) as the tenants propose would result in an interpretation that places the provisions of s. 20(1) and s. 22 in conflict or disharmony with one another and disregard the intent of the legislature that where, as here, there is an overlap, both provisions should apply. The tenants' reading of the RTA does not result in the legislation functioning as an internally consistent whole.

The Tenants position was the remediation and repairs to the unit had a significant impact on them. They had to move out of the unit and stay in hotels at first. When the Landlord advised them the repairs would take longer than she originally estimated, the Tenants rented an Airbnb because they could not afford the costs of hotels. The Tenants testified they were paying for these costs on an out-of-pocket basis because they had not received the report from the Landlord’s insurance company and their own insurance company could not process the Tenants’ claim without it. These out-of-pocket costs resulted in financial strain to the Tenants. The need to move from hotels to the Airbnb required time away from work and impacted their work performance.

It was not disputed the Landlord abated the Tenants’ rent for the period they were out of the unit. The Tenants submitted evidence showing that on November 21, 2025, the Landlord transferred them $1,959.68. The Tenants also testified their insurance company reimbursed them for their accommodation costs on November 26, 2025 and December 1, 2025.

The Tenants testified the need to vacate the unit on short notice was disruptive and difficult since hotels in the areas were fully booked. They were unable to celebrate religious holidays with family in their home. They could not celebrate their anniversary on November 28, 2025 because the out-of-pocket costs had exhausted their financial resources.

The Tenants testified that the lack of communication from the Landlord caused stress because of the unpredictability concerning their housing. During cross examination however, the Tenants confirmed the Landlord did respond to their texts and emails.

The Landlord testified she was advised of the flood on October 14, 2025 at approximately 7:00 p.m. She stated she arrived at the unit approximately an hour later with her father and submitted a claim with her insurance company by midnight the same day. Her insurance company contractors were at the unit by October 18, 2025. They placed dehumidifiers in the unit, tested the area for asbestos and took readings for water damage.

The drying process concluded on October 24, 2025 and the dehumidifiers were removed. The contractors determined the kitchen would need to be entirely ripped out and the insulation in the walls would need to be checked. This process began in early November 2025 once everything had sufficiently dried and the removal of the damaged kitchen was completed by November 7, 2025.

The Landlord testified she pushed her insurance company to complete the work as soon as possible, insisting that they start with the rental unit and not her own unit directly above where the flood had also caused damage.

The rebuilding of the kitchen was supposed to begin on November 24, 2025 but did not begin until November 27, 2025 because of a two-day delay with the insurance company contractors. As stated above in paragraph 5(g), the rebuilding of the kitchen was completed on December 4, 2025. Analysis

Based on the testimony of the parties and photos submitted by the Tenants, I am satisfied there was a significant flood in the rental unit that required substantial work. The unit first had to be dried before it could be gutted and rebuilt. Despite the scope and nature of the work, the Landlord was able to fully resolve the issue in 51 days.

When a maintenance issue occurs, there is an inherent time requirement in having it addressed. Here, the Landlord responded almost immediately, having a claim filed with her insurance company within hours of the flood taking place. Work in the unit began within four days with placement of dehumidifiers and the process continued on a timely basis until repairs to the unit were completed on December 4, 2025. The lack of contractor availability for a small number of days during the repair period does not in my view amount to an unreasonable response from the Landlord.

The Tenants were abated their rent by the Landlord and reimbursed by their insurance company for their accommodation costs for the time they were out of the unit. The Tenants’ own evidence showed the Landlord communicated with the Tenants extensively throughout the process and provided them the insurance report once she obtained it.

Having considered all of the circumstances, including those faced by the Tenants and the actions of the Landlord, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord responded to the issue promptly and appropriately. Based on the work required, the steps taken and the timeline of events, I find the Landlord took reasonable steps to resolve the damage caused by the flood. Nothing in the evidence convinced me the Landlord did not take the situation seriously or that she failed to take a material step that should have been taken that would have seen the unit repaired earlier.

For these reasons, I do not find the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act to repair the flood damage in the rental unit. In applying the contextual approach set out in Onyskiw, and considering the overlap across these applications, I am also not convinced the Landlord, in responding appropriately to the flood, substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities relating to substantial interference, harassment, obstruction, and interference with the Tenant: i. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant is $[name] by March 10, 2026. This amount represents: • $2,300.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace the property that was retained by the Landlords; • $5,000.00 for general damages; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. ii. The Landlords must also pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $3,000.00 by March 10, 2026.

As explained below, the allegations claimed in the application relating to illegal entry and no 72-hour notice provided by the Landlords for the Tenant to remove their property prior to eviction by the Sheriff are dismissed.

The rental unit is a one-bedroom unit with a separate kitchen and bathroom, located in the basement of a house. The tenancy commenced in April 2024. At the time, the Tenant was 70 years old and the Landlords lived upstairs of the rental unit.

The Tenant states that in 2022 he suffered a stroke which has impacted some of his brain functioning, specifically it has been difficult for him to recall dates but he can still recall details of events. He relies on a mobility scooter to get around.

The Tenant states that he moved into the rental unit from another building that he living at and paying rent because the monthly rent was lower at the rental unit. When he moved to the rental unit he had to downsize and get rid of some of his belongings because the rental unit was furnished.

The Tenant states that the monthly rent is due on the first day of each month and he could not pay the monthly rent for July 2024 and August 2024 because he was the victim of a scam which compromised the funds in his bank account. The Tenant states that he relies on a fixed income which is money he received through his pension.

On August 23, 2024, the police attended the rental unit. The Tenant states that one of the Landlords [name] Envoy had advised the police that the Tenant was only renting a room there. The Tenant states that the police told him that the Landlords no longer want him to continue living there and that the Tenant had to leave. The Tenant states that the police telephoned the Tenant’s sister who lives in Smith’s falls.

The Tenant states that he then got his mobility scooter and drove 20 minutes to his sister’s residence. The Tenant states he was not able to return to the rental unit because the Landlords advised he could no longer live there. He states that his brother went to the rental unit one week later to pick up some of the Tenant’s belongings which could not be retrieved in a single load with his brother’s vehicle.

The Tenant states that his brother returned to the rental unit to pick up a second load of the Tenant’s belongings but was prevented from doing so by the Landlord [name]. The Tenant states that [name] advised his brother that he could not pick up any of the Tenant’s additional belongings until the Tenant paid the rent that was owing.

The Tenant states that that the Landlords have refused to return the following belongings valued at $2,450.00 as the Tenant was forced to move out of the rental unit on August 23, 2024: • One year old 50-inch Samsung smart Television, valued at $750.00; • External drive for television, valued at $150.00; • Television adaptor for use with Tenant’s hearing aids, valued at $500.00; • Three-year old, two-foot wide [name] bluetooth radio, valued at $450.00; [name] clippers valued at $100.00; [name] items including dishes, pots and pans; valued at $500.00.

The Tenant states that he cannot recall other miscellaneous items which belonged to him that the Landlords have retained beside dishes, pots, and pans. He further states that he has not replaced the above items which were retained by the Landlord due to his limited income.

The Tenant states that after he was forced to leave the rental unit, he moved into a single room on September 1, 2024 for which he pays $750.00 per month. He states the space is smaller and he shares a kitchen and bathroom. He states the room which he rents is located on the outskirts of Smith Falls. He states he could not move back to the building he previously lived at prior to moving to the rental unit because he cannot afford the market rent. He also states that he got rid of many belongings prior to moving to the rental unit as the rental unit was furnished.

The Tenant produced text message correspondence from September 2024 between the Tenant and the Landlord [name]. The text message correspondence from [name] notes “Get in touch at the end of the month. When at the end of the month you give us some money then you can have your tv”. The Tenant states [name] was referring to the money the Tenant owed to the Landlords for the July 2024 and August 2024 monthly rent.

The Tenant produced an email which was sent by his legal representative [name] to [name] on November 8, 2024 which advises that the Landlords removal of the Tenant from the rental unit on October 23, 2024 [sic] was unlawful and in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). In this email, the Landlords were asked to return the Tenants belongings identified above to the Tenant which can be arranged through the Tenant’s legal representative. The email further notes that the Tenant would like to resolve this issue amiably and not have to pursue legal action. [name] states that there was no response received from the Landlords to this email. [name] states the email incorrectly notes the date of October 23, 2024 as the date that the Tenant was illegally evicted. She states this was corrected in a follow up letter she sent to the Landlords on November 12, 2024.

The Tenant produced the follow up letter dated November 12, 2024 from Linda Tranter to the Landlords correctly notes the date the Tenant was illegally evicted from the rental unit as August 23, 2024. This letter further advises if the Landlords do not respond by November 19, 2024, the Tenant will be filing an application for illegal eviction and retention of property with the Landlord and Tenant Board. [name] states there was no response received from the Landlords to this letter.

The Tenant states after he was forced to move out of the rental unit, he began caring a lot less about things in life. He states that he became depressed and attempted suicide for which he was hospitalized in August 2025. He states that he still gets upset when he thinks about the Landlords actions which resulted be forced to move out of the rental unit, the Landlords not allowing him to move back in, and the Landlords retaining some of his belongings to date. Illegal entry

The Tenant’s claim that he was illegally evicted from the rental unit by the Landlords on August 23, 2024 is separate and distinct from an illegal entry. There was no evidence, or dates provided by the Tenant to support that the Landlords illegally entered the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlords did not enter the rental unit illegally. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed. Substantial interference
Subsection 37(1) of the Act states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act.

Subsection 37(2) stipulates that a tenancy may be terminated in accordance with a notice of termination given in accordance with the Act and the tenant vacates the rental unit in accordance with the notice, the tenancy is terminated on the termination date set out within the notice.
Subsection 37(3) of the Act allows for the termination of a tenancy based on the Landlord and the Tenant reaching an agreement to terminate the tenancy.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant when the Landlords illegally evicted the Tenant from the rental unit on August 23, 2024. I find the Tenant’s uncontested testimony persuasive. The Tenant explained the details surrounding the August 23, 2024 incident in which the Tenant was forced to move out of the rental unit and provided details surrounding its impact on him. I find the email dated November 8, 2024 and the November 12, 2024 letter sent by the Tenant’s legal representative, [name] to the Landlords which note the Tenant was illegally evicted from the rental unit and that the Landlords have items which belong to the Tenant further supports the Landlords illegally evicted the Tenant on August 23, 2024.

I find the tenancy was not terminated based on a notice of termination issued by the Landlord in accordance with the Act, nor was there an agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant to terminate the tenancy. As a result, I find the Landlords illegally terminated the tenancy which resulted in an illegal eviction of the Tenant. As a result, I find that the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant. The Tenant was also forced to move out of the rental unit without his belongings and without having another place to move to. Harassment/Obstruction/Interference
Section 40 of the Act stipulates that no landlord shall, without legal process, seize a tenant’s property for default in the payment of rent or for the breach of any other obligation of the tenant.

Pursuant to subsection 41(1) of the Act, a landlord may sell, retain for the landlord’s own use or otherwise dispose of property in a rental unit or the residential complex if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with, (a) a notice of termination of the landlord or the tenant; (b) an agreement between the landlord and the tenant to terminate the tenancy; (c) subsection 93 (2); or (d) an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord harassed, obstructed and interfered with the Tenant and his rights under the Act when the Landlords retained the Tenant’s personal belongings including a 50-inch Samsung Television, an external drive for the television, television adapter used with the Tenant’s hearing aids, two-foot wide [name] bluetooth radio, hair clippers, and miscellaneous items including dishes and pots following the illegal eviction of the Tenant on August 23, 2024. I find the September 2024 text message from [name] supports that the Landlords were refusing to return the Tenants television because the Tenant owes the Landlords money.

The action taken by the Landlords in which they retained the Tenant’s belongings is in contravention of sections 40 and 41 of the Act. This is because there was no notice of termination in accordance with the Act to terminate the tenancy, there was no agreement between the parties to terminate the tenancy, and there was no order issued by the Landlord and Tenant Board which authorizes the termination of the tenancy. No 72-hour notice

Pursuant to subsection 41(3) of the Act, a landlord must make an evicted tenant’s property available to be retrieved at a location close to the rental within 72 hours after the enforcement of an eviction order.

In the Tenant’s case, the Tenant was not legally evicted from the rental unit because of an order being issued by the Landlord and Tenant Board. Therefore, there was no enforcement from the Sheriff to evict the Tenant from the rental unit. Therefore, I find the 72-hour notice requirement for the Landlords to allow the Tenant to remove their belongings from the rental unit would not be applicable. I have already determined above why the Landlords retention of the Tenant’s belongings contravenes the Act. Remedies

At the hearing the Tenant withdrew the following remedies claimed in the T2 application: • A rent abatement in the amount of $5,000.00; • $500.00 for storage costs; and • The Tenant’s request to move back to the rental unit. Items retained by the Landlord

The Tenant requests the Landlords return the Tenant’s belongings valued at $2,450.00 which have been retained by the Landlords and include: • 50-inch Samsung Television, valued at $750.00; • External drive for the television, valued at $150.00; • Television adaptor for use with Tenant’s hearing aids, valued at $500.00; [name] bluetooth radio, valued at $450.00; [name] clippers valued at $100.00; [name] items including dishes, pots and pans; valued at $500.00 At the hearing the Tenant requested the Landlords be ordered to return the above items to the Tenant within 15 days, or compensation in the amount of $2,450.00 be awarded to the Tenant towards the cost to replace the above items.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony and the description of the items by the Tenant, I accept the Landlords have illegally retained the above noted items. As the items were retained by the Landlords in August 2024, it is unknown if the Landlords are still in possession or control of these items. The Landlords did not attend the hearing so this confirmation could not be obtained. I do not find it would be appropriate to order either the return of the items, or reimbursement to the Tenant in lieu of the items not being returned. It is unknown what the condition of these items are, or if they are still within the possession or control of the Landlords. Therefore, I find the Landlords must pay the Tenant the reasonable costs to replace the above items as set out below.

I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenant $2,300.00, which is the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace the property which was retained by the Landlords. This amount includes $750.00 for the 50- inch smart television, $150.00 for the external drive for the television, $500.00 for the television adapter for use with the Tenant’s hearing aids, $450.00 for the Dewalt Bluetooth radio, $100.00 for hair clippers, and $350.00 for dishes, pots, and pans. The Tenant claims $500.00 for the dishes, pots, and pans, but I find $350.00 is reasonable for the cost to replace these items. Administrative Fine

I find that the Landlords must pay an administrative fine to the Landlord and Tenant Board in the amount of $3,000.00. I find this amount to appropriate and to deter the Landlords from acting in a manner in the future which contravene the requirements set out within the Act. I find the behaviour of the Landlords is egregious and the Landlords have demonstrated a blatant disregard for the requirements set out within the Act. The Tenant is a vulnerable person. He is a senior citizen who has suffered a stroke and lives alone, relies on a fixed income from a pension, and requires technological aids to assist him with his hearing. I accept that the illegal eviction by the Landlords on August 23, 2024 was a traumatic experience. I accept that a police officer told the Tenant that the Landlords did not want the Tenant living there. The Tenant left the rental unit on that date on his mobility scooter with no other place to move to and without his belongings. The Tenant attempted through his legal representative to communicate with the Landlords on two occasions as supported by the November 8, 2024 email and the November 12, 2024 letter from the Tenant’s legal representative to the Landlords which request that the Landlords return the Tenant’s belongings but the Landlords were non-responsive. General damages

The Tenant claims $10,000.00 in general damages for pain and suffering caused by the Landlord’s illegal eviction. The Landlord and Tenant Board has the authority to grant such an award pursuant to section 31(1)(f) of the Act. I find the Tenant is entitled to $5,000.00 in general damages. I find this amount is appropriate because I accept that the illegal eviction and the way it was carried out by the Landlords would have caused the Tenant to experience shock and distress and also placed the Tenant in an immediate situation of placing his safety and wellbeing at risk as a result of not having another place to move to and not having all of his belongings. The Landlords refused to return some of the Tenant’s belongings and advised that one he paid the Landlords the rent he owed, they would consider returning his television. This contravenes s. 40 of the Act

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the illegal eviction and retention of the Tenant’s property by the Landlords had a negative impact on his mental health and wellbeing. While the Tenant did not produce any medical documentation, I accept the Tenant’s testimony which I found to be credible that he was hospitalized in August 2025 for a suicide attempt which was due to the illegal eviction that happened one year earlier. I accept this had a cumulative effect on the Tenant. This is because the Tenant was not able to get many of his belongings back which are retained by the Landlord. I accept that the Tenant cannot afford to pay out of pocket to replace these items because he relies on a pension. I accept that the Tenant being forced to move out of a one-bedroom apartment with a separate kitchen and bathroom and move into a place where he rents a single room and shares a kitchen and bathroom on the outskirts of Smith’s Falls was not something the Tenant ideally wanted but it was what the Tenant could afford.
The Landlords must also pay the Tenant $48.00 for the cost of the application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay to the Tenant is $[name]. This amount represents: • $2,300.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace the property that was retained by the Landlords; • $5,000.00 for general damages; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $3,000.00 by March 10, 2026. February 10, 2026 ____________________________

Not only was the Tenant able to consult individuals they trusted and relied upon, but [name] was also known to the Tenant as an experienced real estate agent, knowledgeable in the field of residential tenancies. I therefore find that the Tenant, in preparation of their second scheduled meeting with the Landlord, was able to surround themselves and consult individuals that were able to assist them in reviewing the N11 Agreement, and making an informed and rational decision. 48. The fact that M.M has been searching for alternate housing accommodations for the Tenant, following the execution of the N11 Agreement, further shows that the Tenant, and their support group clearly understood that the tenancy would be ending as a result of the N11 Agreement. 49. I did not find credible the Tenant’s testimony with respect to them feeling pressured into signing the N11 Agreement. The simple fact that the Landlord attended the rental unit with a copy of the N11 Agreement and the fact that the Tenant did not seek legal assistance does not equate to signing a document under duress, such that it would negate the N11 Agreement. This specific portion of the Tenant’s testimony seemed to be more of a boilerplate submission aimed at trying to delegitimize their own actions after agreeing to enter into the N11 Agreement after having reviewed the forms with C.L.P and [name] 50. Accordingly, on the basis of the evidence and submissions before, I am satisfied that the Tenant understood that the Landlord was seeking to terminate the tenancy and that the parties therefore entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, effective January 30, 2024, with the Tenant doing so freely, all while being informed and fully understanding that they would need to vacate the rental unit on or before January 30, 2024. 51. Despite the finding that the Tenant entered into the agreement to terminate the tenancy freely and with full understanding, subsection 77(8)(b) of the Act states that the Board may make an order setting aside an ex -parte order issued based on an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agreement, if the Board is satisfied, having regard to all the circumstances, that it would not be unfair to do so. [[name].] File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 52. While subsection 37(3) of the Act states that a “a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy,” subsection 202(1) of the Act reads as follows: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 53. After considering all of the circumstances, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 54. Indeed, while the parties entered into an agreement to end the tenancy (Exhibit 2), the Board must, pursuant to section 202 of the Act, look beyond the mere fact that an agreement was signed between the parties and consider the overall intention and conduc t of the parties when the agreement was entered into. 55. In Pinto v. [name] and White v. [name], 2021 ONSC 5502 (Pinto), the Ontario Divisional Court found that the Board erred by not applying section 202 of the Act and analyzing the true intentions of the parties when an agreement to terminate was signed. [Emphasis Added]. 56. In Pinto, the landlord approached the tenants and required them to sign an N11 agreement to terminate their tenancies for the purpose of conducting extensive repairs and renovations. The landlord did not serve the tenants with the required N13 Notice of Termination, which entitled the tenants to a compensation payment, and the tenants were led to believe that they had no alternative but to sign the N11 and without regard to their rights under the Act. I find that the present case is similar. 57. In the matter before the Board, it is clear that the catalyst to having the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement with the intent to have them vacate the rental unit, stems from the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit. This was consistently relayed to the Board through the testimony provided by the Tenant and the submissions provided by the Landlord. 58. Although the Act permits landlords to terminate tenancies because they have entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the rental unit and the purchaser intends to move into the rental unit, an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agr eement, is not intended for that purpose. 59. Indeed, an application to terminate the tenancy for a purchaser’s own use requires the landlord to serve the tenant with a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one (1) month’s rent or to offer the tenant File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 another rental unit that is acceptable to the tenant (pursuant to section 49.1 of the Act) and to swear an affidavit and/or declaration before the Board stating the purchaser’s intentions. This process also affords the tenant the right to challenge the good- faith intentions of the landlord or the person who requires the rental unit at a hearing before the Board. 60. It appears to me that the Landlord, in this case, drafted and had the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement to facilitate the process of a prospective sale and circumvent their obligations under the Act to serve the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination, to pay the required compensation prior to the termination date and from havi ng to prove their case to the Board on a balance of probabilities. In fact, by the time the hearing was concluded, the Landlord had failed to secure prospective purchasers for the rental unit, and it appears as though the Landlord had stopped the advertisements related to the rental unit. 61. The simple fact of selling (or intending to sell) the rental unit does not automatically lead to the termination of the tenancy.11 62. Thus, I find that the Landlord was not acting in good faith and was circumventing the Act when they obtained the Tenant’s signature on the N11 Agreement. 63. Accordingly, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. The Landlord would still have the opportunity to proceed with an application to terminate the tenancy, providing the appropriate notice of termination is served to the Tenant beforehand. Second T2 Application : LTB-T-097881-23 64. The Tenant testified that after being advised of the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit, the Landlord proceeded to list the unit for sale, which led to in-person showings of the rental unit being scheduled in order for prospective purchasers to view the rental unit. 65. The Tenant stated that they felt that they were being blamed by various relators (whom the Tenant described as being increasingly rude) for the Landlord’s inability to enter into an agreement of purchase and sale and therefore their inability to sell the rental unit ; despite the Landlord originally showing appreciation with respect to the Tenant’s effort to facilitate the sale of the rental unit. 66. The Tenant indicated that while the volume of the viewings increased, they believe that they were not receiving proper notices of entry for the Landlord, and their agents to conduct the in-person showings. 67. The Tenant feels that these repeated showings and blame being directed towards them made them feel uncomfortable in the rental unit, with a sense that their privacy was also being invaded as, despite their request, the Tenant was not receiving a notice of entry at least forty-eight (48) hours prior to the Landlord’s conducting showings of the rental unit. 11 Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 68. Under cross -examination, the Tenant stated that they could not recall the number of in- person showings that were conducted within the rental unit. They felt that people “were coming from all over” and that the rental unit was being treated as a “zoo” or a “circus.” 69. Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that they would receive notices from the Landlord or their various real estate agents by email with respect to showings of the rental unit, and that the Tenant had the option to decline the booking of the showing, which they exercised only a “couple of times”). 70. The Landlord submits that the Tenant failed to provide particulars with respect to the claim that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and therefore seeks for the Second L2 Application to be dismissed. 71. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by scheduling and conducting in-person showings of the rental unit through the course of their attempts to sell the rental unit. 72. Indeed, while the Tenant may have preferred to have received a notice at least forty -eight hours prior to a showing, and for only a select number of realtors to access the premises, the Landlord is only required to provide the Tenant wit h a notice “at least 24 hours before the time of [the] entry”12 in such circumstances. Additionally, nothing in the Act provides the Tenant with an ability to dictate which of the Landlord’s agents may or may not access the rental unit, when such entry is reasonable under the circumstances. 73. Furthermore, although the Tenant claimed that some showings were conducted without the Tenant being provided with proper notice, the Tenant was unable to provide any specific dates or times where such entries would have occurred, nor were they able to provide specific details with respect to comments that would have made them feel unwelcome in the rental unit. 74. As the Tenant limited their testimony and submissions to vague and general accusatory statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. 75. While conducting viewings of the rental unit in light of a prospective sale of a residential unit may be disruptive to a tenant’s day -to-day activities, a landlord is entitled to proceed in showing the rental unit to potential purchasers. The Tenant’s evidence does not lead me to conclude that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable and would amount to anything more than a “minor inconvenience,”13 for which the Tenant would not be entitled to any remedies. 76. Accordingly, the Tenant’s Second T2 Application, LTB-T-097881-23, is dismissed. 12 Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 13 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC). File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 Third T2 Application: LTB-T-095606-23 77. The Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, reiterates the grounds found in the Tenant’s motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 78. The Tenant claims the total amount of $17,000.00 as out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant would incur if the Tenant had been unsuccessful in setting aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 79. Firstly, had the motion to set aside the order LTB -L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, been denied, the Landlord would have been able to lawfully seek vacant possession of the rental unit upon the stay of the aforementioned order being lifted. As such, the Tenant would not have been entitled to further compensation or remedies on the basis of the Landlord exercising a lawful right. 80. Secondly, the motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, was granted. As such, the tenancy between the parties is not terminated pursuant to the N11 Agreement, and the Tenant is therefore not required to move out of the rental . The Tenant’s request is therefore moot. 81. I find that the Tenant’s Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, discloses no reasonable cause of action. Accordingly, the Tenant’s Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, is dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The matter was adjourned on June 12, 2025, because the hearing Member was not certain that the Landlord had been served with the notice of hearing. It had been sent by the Board to the rental unit address, and it had been emailed to an address that was different than the email address listed by the Landlord in the written lease agreement between the parties.

The Landlord was served with the notice of hearing for this hearing by email at the address listed in the lease agreement, [email]. It was not returned to the Board undelivered, so I found that the Landlord was served with the notice of hearing.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant said that he signed the lease for the rental unit on December 27, 2023. The monthly rent was $2,100.00, and he was to move in on February 1, 2024. The Tenant paid a first and last month’s rent deposit for a total of $4,200.00.

The Tenant said that he tried to contact the Landlord unsuccessfully by phone by the end of January 2024 to find out when he would get keys to move in. He said that he managed to speak to the Landlord by phone on January 24, 2024, at which time the Landlord told him he could not move in because the sitting tenant was not leaving. The Tenant submitted into evidence an email from him to the Landlord, dated January 28, 2024, in which he offers to void the lease if the Landlord returns his deposit. The Tenant said he did not hear from the Landlord until February 22, 2024. He submitted into evidence an email from the Landlord, dated February 22, 2024, in which the Landlord is defensive, and he accuses the Tenant of avoiding him, and he offers to give him his money back. That is the last response from the Landlord, who then never arranged a time to give the Tenant the money, nor did he communicate again.

Pursuant to section 13 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the period of a tenancy begins on the day the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit under the tenancy agreement. The Tenant signed a lease, and he paid the Landlord first and last month’s rent over a month prior to the commencement of the tenancy on February 1, 2024. The Landlord never provided the keys, nor did the Tenant get access to the rental unit.

Consequently, the tenancy began on February 1, 2024, and the Tenant was never permitted to move into the rental unit. The Landlord was obliged to reimburse the Tenant his deposit of $4,200.00. Instead, the Landlord was accusatory towards the Tenant, he promised to reimburse the Tenant. and then he stopped responding to any communication. To date the Landlord has not reimbursed the Tenant.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.

If the Landlord had ever permitted vacant possession, he would have been obliged to pay the Tenant interest on his last month’s rent deposit of $2,100.00. Pursuant to subsection 106(6) the Act, this is to be an annual payment at a rate equal to the guideline determined section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.
The Landlord would have owed annual interest of 2.5% on February 1 2025 and 2.1% on February 1 2026, for a total of 2.5% X $2,100.00=$52.50 plus 2.1% X $2,100.00=$44.10 or $96.60.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4.344.60. This amount represents: • $4.200 rent deposit paid to the Landlord upon signing the lease agreement • $96.60 interest on the last month’s rent deposit • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

In the Tenant’s application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not return the last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant testified that they moved out of the rental unit on August 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that he provided a notice to terminate the tenancy in June 2025. The Tenant paid their rent for the last month of the tenancy, which was August 2025.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord did not return the last month’s rent deposit. The Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,750.00 on February 8, 2024. In addition, the Landlord has not paid any interest to the Tenant on this deposit. Legal Analysis
Section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) permits a tenant to file an application against a landlord if money is being illegally collected or retained by the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord is still in possession of the last month’s rent deposit.

S ections 44 and 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allow a tenant to terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the fixed term by giving 60 days’ notice to the landlord. The Tenant testified that the provided proper notice other Landlord, as they provided notice in mid-June and vacated on August 30, 2025. Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant’s notice was in compliance with the Act. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide submissions on this matter. Therefore, I find that the Tenant proved their application on a balance of probabilities; the Landlord will be ordered to refund the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,750.00.

Subsection 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') requires that a landlord pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the rent increase guideline.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has not paid any interest to the Tenant on the deposit they collected. Therefore, I find interest on the last month’s rent deposit is payable to the Tenants for the period of February 8, 2024 to August 30, 2025, in the amount of $68.33.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,866.33. This amount represents: • $1,750.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $68.33 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not meet its maintenance obligations.
reasons: The Tenant filed this application on November 24, 2025. A hearing was scheduled for December 9, 2025, on an urgent basis, because the Tenant alleged that she had been locked out of the unit.

At the December 9 hearing, the Tenant requested an adjournment so that she could amend her application, gather evidence, and obtain legal advice and representation. The request was granted, peremptory on the Tenant, with a deadline of December 31, 2025 to amend the application.

The matter came before me on February 4, 2026. The Tenant had not filed an amended application. She said that she missed the deadline by one day, and therefore decided not to file the amendment. She asked for a further opportunity to amend the application.

I denied the request. The Tenant did not explain why she missed the December 31 deadline. Moreover, if she had wanted to pursue a request to amend despite missing the deadline, she should have filed her proposed amendment. She could have done so as early as January 1, 2026, but did not. It would not have been fair to the Landlord to allow an amendment without notice on the day of the hearing.
The matter therefore proceeded based on the Tenant’s unamended application. Evidence
During the hearing, the Tenant sought to adduce documents, photos, and videos which she had not uploaded to the Landlord and Tenant Board’s (LTB) portal.

The Tenant initially said that she believed the files had been uploaded, because she received an email from the LTB confirming receipt. However, when she read out the email, it stated that her files had not been received because she had provided the wrong file number.

The Tenant knew or ought to have known that her evidence had not been uploaded, but took no further steps to upload it. I did not allow her to adduce the evidence which had not been uploaded in accordance with the LTB’s rules. Issues

The Tenant’s application raises the following allegations: • On November 13, 2025, the Landlord entered the unit without proper notice. • On November 13, 2025, the Landlord changed the unit’s lock and did not give the Tenant a replacement key. • The Landlord failed to maintain the unit in respect of issues identified in a November 12, 2025 municipal property standards order, which were: [name] rat infestation. • Holes in the walls due to rat infestation. [name] or missing window in the front of the unit. • Missing outlet covers.

The application requests the following remedies: • An order that the Landlord repair the rat infestation, holes in the walls, window, and outlet covers. • A 100% rent abatement and compensation for living expenses for two months, on the basis that the unit was uninhabitable and the Tenant had to stay elsewhere. • Compensation of $10,000.00 for damaged belongings that were disposed of on November 25, 2025. Facts

The Tenant’s testimony was disorganized and sometimes self-contradictory. She frequently confused dates and details. Consequently, I do not find her testimony regarding the timeline of events to be reliable. The best evidence of the timeline comes from emails between the parties. The Landlord’s property manager, [name], also testified. To the extent that the evidence is inconsistent, I find the emails and [name] testimony to be more reliable than the Tenant’s testimony.

Some of [name] testimony was about steps that the Landlord’s other employees had taken, and was hearsay. I have exercised my discretion to admit it, as it is the best evidence available. I do not find it to be unfair to the Tenant to rely on the hearsay, given that the Tenant’s own evidence was so unreliable.
The Tenant testified that in the summer of 2025, there were three issues in with her unit.
First, there was a rat infestation in the unit.
Second, she had lost her key to the unit and could not unlock the front door.
Third, a window next to the front door was broken. Consequently, anyone could enter the unit by reaching through the window to unlock the front door from the inside.
At the time, the Tenant did not report any of the issues to the Landlord. She says that she came and went by reaching through the broken window to lock and unlock her door.

The first time the Tenant reported any of the issues to the Landlord was on September 29, 2025. On that date, she reported the rat infestation and the broken window, but did not mention that the broken window made her front door insecure.
The Tenant testified that on October 15, 2025, she stopped staying in the unit. She says that the unit was uninhabitable because of the worsening rat infestation.

October 16, 2025, the Landlord’s staff attend the unit to carry out pest control following 24 hours’ notice. Nobody answered the door. The Landlord’s staff would have had the right to enter the unit, but did not do so out of safety concerns because they heard a loose dog barking in the unit. Instead, they placed rat poison around the outside of the unit.

On October 29, 2025, the Landlord’s staff told the Tenant by email that they had been unable to enter on October 16 because of the dog. They said that they would return on October 30, but would not enter if nobody was home and a dog was barking inside. The Tenant replied that she was not staying in the unit, there were no pets in the unit, and the door would be unlocked.
On October 30, 2025, the Landlord’s staff attended the unit for pest control and discovered that a new lock had been installed on the door. They were unable to enter.
On October 31, 2025, the Landlord’s staff emailed the Tenant, explained the issue with the new lock, and asked to schedule a time for her to let them in to carry out pest control.

On November 10, 2025, the Tenant replied that she was not living at the unit and had left the door unlocked, and in any event that the Landlord’s staff could enter by reaching through the broken window to unlock the door.

That day, the Landlord drilled out the lock and installed a new lock. It left a letter for the Tenant telling her that she could pick up a key at its office. The Tenant did not get the letter right away, because she was not staying at the unit and was not regularly checking her mail.

On November 13, 2025, the Landlord carried out pest control in the unit, which included putting down rat poison. This was the first time its staff had been inside the unit in some time. They discovered that there was a large amount of clothing and garbage in the unit, as well as rat feces and dog urine and feces.

On November 17, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant to notify her that pest control would continue on November 20. It asked her to remove the clothing and dog feces so that pest control could be carried out. The Tenant replied that she would not touch the clothing because it was contaminated with rat feces, and that the Landlord should arrange for a cleaning crew prior to any further pest control.

On November 25, 2025, the Tenant and [name] attended the unit with a cleaning crew arranged by the Landlord. The crew cleaned up the rat feces and, at the Tenant’s direction, disposed of large amounts of clothing, furniture, and garbage. They also cleaned up a large number of dead rats resulting from the November 13 rat poison.

The Tenant initially denied that there was dog feces and urine in the unit. However, on cross-examination she admitted that there was feces in the bedroom which had been deposited by her dog, presumably before she left the unit on October 15. The cleaning crew cleaned up the dog feces as well.

The Landlord also gave the Tenant a key to the new lock on November 25. However, the Tenant has not moved back into the unit. She agrees that the rat infestation is now under control, although ongoing pest control will continue. However, she believes that other animals are living in the attic. Those possible animals are not a subject of this application. Did the Landlord enter the unit without proper notice?

On November 13, 2025, the Landlord entered the Tenant’s unit to do pest control, after giving 24 hours’ notice as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). In her application, the Tenant argues that the notice was invalid because it was placed in her mailbox, and she did not receive it because she was not staying in her unit at the time.

There is no merit to the Tenant’s argument. Section 191(1)(d) of the RTA permits a party to give a notice to a person by leaving it in their mailbox. The notice was validly given. The fact that the Tenant chose not to check her mail does not invalidate the notice. Did the Landlord change the lock and fail to provide a replacement key?

The Landlord changed the lock on November 10, 2025, and gave the Tenant a replacement key on November 25, 2025. The Tenant argues that the Landlord caused the delay, because it left a letter in her mailbox telling her to pick up the key at its office. She did not get the letter because she was not checking her mail.

Again, it is not the Landlord’s fault that the Tenant chose not to check her mail. Furthermore, even if the Tenant did not receive the letter, she could at any time have contacted the Landlord to ask for a replacement key. She did not do so, presumably because she was not staying in the unit.

The Landlord met its obligation to provide a replacement key. I do not see how it could have done so any sooner in the circumstances. Did the Landlord fail to maintain the unit in respect of the rat infestation?

The parties agree that the rat infestation in the unit was severe. However, the Tenant did not tell the Landlord about the infestation until September 29, 2025. The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance. It was not obligated to remedy an issue it could not have known about.

After being informed of the infestation on September 29, the Landlord did not begin pest control until October 16, 2025. It has not explained the delay, and I find the delay to be unreasonable. The Landlord did not know, at that point, how severe the infestation was. However, in my view, even a minor rat infestation should be considered an urgent issue.

On October 16, the Landlord was not able to carry out pest control inside the unit because its staff could not enter due to a barking dog. However, it did not inform the Tenant until October 29, and did not take any other steps to treat the unit in the meantime. I find that delay to have been unreasonable as well.

On October 31, the Landlord’s staff tried to treat the unit, but could not enter because there was a new lock on the door. They promptly informed the Tenant by email, but she did not reply until November 10. Following her reply, they promptly drilled out the lock and carried out pest control. They followed up with a thorough cleaning of the unit and ongoing pest control treatments. I find that from October 31 onwards, the Landlord followed a reasonable program of maintenance.
The Landlord was therefore in breach of its pest control obligations from September 29 to October 30.

Although the infestation was severe, the evidence does not establish that the unit was uninhabitable at any point between September 29 and October 30. The Tenant’s testimony regarding the condition of the unit was vague, and lacked dates. She did not adduce any photos or video. I am not satisfied that it was reasonable for her to stop living in the unit on October 15. Consequently, her request to be compensated for temporary accommodations and living expenses is denied.

Given the severity of the infestation, I will award a 50% rent abatement for September 29 to October 30. The Tenant’s monthly rent is $136.00, so the total abatement comes to $71.54. Should the Landlord compensate the Tenant for her belongings?

The bulk of the Tenant’s claim is a request for $10,000.00 in compensation for her belongings. She testified that when she attended the unit on November 25, there were rat feces and rotting rats throughout the unit. The smell had gotten into her clothes, mattresses, and other fabrics. She directed the Landlord’s cleaning crew to dispose of many of her belongings.
The Tenant has not established that the Landlord is liable for her belongings, for several reasons.

First, the evidence does not establish that the Landlord’s failure to act promptly between September 29 and October 30 caused the problem. The parties agree that the rat infestation already existed prior to September 29, likely for several months. If the Tenant’s belongings were damaged, there is no evidence as to whether they were already damaged before the Tenant reported the rats to the Landlord.

Second, the evidence does not establish that the rat infestation was what caused the Tenant’s belongings to smell. The Tenant admitted that her dog had defecated in her bedroom, and that she had left the feces there for more than a month. Some or all of the smell may have been caused by dog urine and feces.
Third, the Tenant made no attempt to clean her belongings. She assumed that the smell would not come out, and directed that the belongings be disposed of immediately.

For all those reasons, the Tenant has not proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s contravention of its maintenance obligations damaged or destroyed her belongings. Did the Landlord fail to maintain the window?
The Tenant told the Landlord about the broken window on September 29, 2025. She testified that the Landlord fixed it when it replaced the lock, which would have been on November 10, 2025.

There is no evidence that the Tenant provided any details to the Landlord about how the windows was broken, or explained that it allowed unsecured access to the unit. The Landlord had no way of knowing that the issue was urgent. The Tenant has not established that the delay from September 29 to November 10 was unreasonable. Did the Landlord fail to maintain the holes in the walls and missing outlet covers?

On the evidence before me, the holes in the walls and the missing outlet covers were very minor issues. It was not unreasonable for the Landlord to address the urgent issues first. I therefore do not find that the Landlord contravened its maintenance obligations.
Now that the urgent issues have been repaired, the Landlord will be ordered to investigate the holes and outlet covers and carry out any needed repairs. Conclusion

The Landlord did not act quickly enough from September 29 to October 30. A rent abatement will be awarded. Since then, the Landlord has acted promptly. The window has been repaired, the lock has been replaced, and the Tenant has a key. The rat infestation is under control, and pest control treatments are ongoing.

At this point, there is no reason for the Tenant to keep living elsewhere, and I urge her to return to the unit. Going forward, I suggest that she report maintenance issues to the Landlord, promptly and in writing, when they arise.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $71.54 for the period from September 29 to October 30, 2025.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, it will owe simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

The Landlord shall promptly inspect the unit to identify any issues regarding holes in the walls and missing outlet covers, and shall carry out repairs as needed. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
