issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. (T6 Application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T2 Application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. (T3 Application)
reasons: This matter was previously scheduled for an adjudicative case conference (“ACC”) on April 29, 2025. The Landlord’s Notice of Hearing for the ACC was returned with “No RMB” written on the envelope.

An adjournment sheet from the ACC notes, “I spoke with Tenant about bringing evidence to the hearing about why they believe they provided correct address for LL and taking steps to serve the NOH on the LL themselves”.
The Landlord’s Notice of Hearing for the merits hearing scheduled for January 22, 2026, was also returned with “No such address NSA” written on the envelope.

The Tenants testified that since the ACC they made attempts to serve the Landlord by sending messages to the Landlord’s brother on Facebook and sending documents to a marina where the Landlord keeps his boat. The Tenants also testified that they sent documents to the Landlord’s work address. The Tenants did not submit documentary evidence to corroborate their service attempts.
The Tenants’ evidence is that they did not receive a reply to any correspondence sent to the Landlord and the Landlord’s business is no longer operating at the same location.

The issue of service to the Landlord was raised at the ACC on April 29, 2025, and the Tenants did not submit evidence of what steps were taken to obtain an address for the Landlord, or why the addresses where the Notices of Hearing were served are the Landlord’s correct address.

The Tenants requested an adjournment to ensure service of the Notice of Hearing to the Landlord. The Tenants had since April 2025 to make efforts to locate the Landlord and there was no evidence that the Tenants had taken reasonable or diligent steps to determine a valid address for service to the Landlord. An adjournment is not appropriate in these circumstances, and the notice of hearing was not served to the Landlord. T2/T6 Applications
Despite the Landlord not being served with a Notice of Hearing, the Tenants’ applications lack specific reasons and details.

The Tenants filed a T2 and a T6 application that makes the same or similar allegations worded as, “Since occupancy requested repair-Deadbolts, door glass, windows, ceiling repair, drywall in hallway, light fixtures in kitchen and bath, floor covering, tile in kitchen, outlets installed wrong; front steps rail; balcony soft spots, bedroom door, mold, poorly completed repairs.”
The Tenants did not request any amendments to their applications prior to the hearing, and the Tenants has had sufficient opportunity to seek any legal advice.

The Tenants offered no dates, times, or any other factual details in relation to the allegations of disrepair. While the Tenants may have intended at the hearing to lead direct evidence of this alleged disrepair through testimony or other evidence, the problem lies in the actual text of the originating document – the application – which is the document against which the respondent Landlord must craft its’ answer.

I find on the balance of probabilities that the vague allegations contained in the application on the disrepair issues would frustrate the Landlord’s ability to fully and properly respond to the application.

According to the Ontario Divisional Court’s decisions in both [name] v. [name] and Ball v. Metro Capital Property and [name], if a Notice of Termination issued by a landlord is confusing to the degree that a reasonable person could not understand the precise actions or omissions that caused the landlord to pursue eviction, a Member would find it defective. I find that this reasoning would apply equally to applications brought by tenants.

In the present case, I find that the Tenants’ allegations of disrepair are defective due to excessive vagueness and are devoid of necessary details with regard to the allegations that provide the basis for the application.

The Tenants requested an adjournment to amend the application and correct the deficiencies. The Tenants could have sought legal advice or amended their application at any time since the ACC. The lack of reasons and details in the Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications makes adjourning the applications unreasonable because the Tenants would essentially be disclosing the substance of their claims in the amendment. The Tenants’ request to adjourn was denied.
The Tenants T2 and T6 applications lack sufficient details and are dismissed. T3 Application
The Tenants’ T3 application alleges that the Landlord reduced a service or facility and the service or facility identified in the application is “Maintenance Repairs”.

Section 2 of the Act sets out a list of services and facilities: “services and facilities” includes, (a) furniture, appliances and furnishings, (b) parking and related facilities, (c) laundry facilities, (d) elevator facilities, (e) common recreational facilities, (f) garbage facilities and related services, (g) cleaning and maintenance services, (h) storage facilities, (i) intercom systems, (j) cable television facilities, (k) heating facilities and services, (l) air-conditioning facilities, (m) utilities and related services, and (n) security services and facilities; (“services et installations”)
While section 2(g) mentions “maintenance services”, I do not find that this encompasses an allegation that the Landlord has failed to fulfill their maintenance obligations.

Since the Tenants’ T3 application does not set out an allegation that the Landlord reduced or discontinued a service or facility as set out in section 2 of the Act, the Tenants’ T3 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ T2, T6, and T3 applications are dismissed. March 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] [name] v [name] [name], 2026 ONLTB 10986 Date: 2026-02-06 In the matter of: Basement, 839 [address] Oshawa ON [name] (the 'Landlord') and [organization] (the ‘Landlord’s Agent') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on January 28, 2026. The Tenants, the Tenants’ representative [name], the Landlord, the Landlord’s representative [name], and the Landlord’s Agent’s representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenants in this matter only lived in the rental unit for nine days. They moved out because they felt that they had been misled regarding some of the facilities in the unit. They ask that the Landlord return the rent and other fees that they paid.

For the following reasons, I find that the parties agreed to end the tenancy after nine days. The Landlord can keep the rent for those nine days, but will be required to return the balance to the Tenants. Feb 6, 2026 Facts
The Landlord owns the rental unit, and [organization] manages it for him. There is no dispute that, at all relevant times, Royal York was acting as the Landlord’s agent.

On June 6, 2024, the parties entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit, at a monthly rent of $2,200.00. The rent was to be due on the first of each month, but the tenancy was to begin on June 21, 2024. The Tenants paid Royal York $733.33 in pro-rated rent for June 21 to 30, $2,200.00 for July’s rent, and a last month’s rent deposit of $2,200.00. They also paid a key deposit of $250.00 and a “verification fee” of $291.54.

Before moving into the unit, the Tenants learned that the kitchen did not have all the facilities they thought it would have. The details are unclear to me, but apparently the kitchen either did not have a working stove or did not have a working oven. In any event, the Tenants felt that they had been misled.

On June 30, the Tenants moved out of the unit. That day, they met with the Landlord. They told him that they wanted to end the tenancy because of the issue with the kitchen. The Tenants say that the Landlord agreed to end the tenancy that day. The Landlord denies making that agreement.

On July 1, the Tenants emailed Royal York. They stated that the Landlord had agreed to end the tenancy effective June 30, and asked [name] to schedule a meeting to formalize the agreement. Royal York replied stating that the parties would both need to sign an N11 form, otherwise the tenancy would not be terminated.

The Tenants then went to the Landlord and Tenant Board’s (LTB) website and downloaded an N11 form. They filled out the form with a June 30 termination date, signed it, and sent it to Royal York. The Landlord had not, at that point, signed the form.

On July 9, Royal York wrote to the Tenants “Kindly note that since the N11 Agreement to End the [name] was signed by both parties, the lease agreement is now formally terminated.” Royal York stated that it would be returning the rent deposit and key deposit.

The Tenants took the position that Royal York should also return the rent they had paid for June 21-30 and for July, and the verification fee. [name] was not willing to return those amounts. The Tenants then filed this application seeking an order for the return of the full amount. Legal framework
Section 37(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a landlord and tenant may terminate a tenancy by agreement. If they do, then no notice of termination is required.

The LTB provides an “Agreement to End the Tenancy N11” form, which landlords and tenants can use to agree to end tenancies. However, contrary to what Royal York told the Tenants, section 37(3) does not require that an agreement to terminate be executed on an N11. The N11 is provided as a convenience, but it is not a requirement. Did the June 30 conversation terminate the tenancy?

A recording of the June 30 conversation is in evidence, but it is muffled and largely inaudible. The Landlord can be heard to say that he agrees with the Tenants’ concerns regarding the kitchen. He can also be heard to say that they should meet with Royal York. I cannot hear the Landlord agree, in the recording, to end the tenancy.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord agreed to end the tenancy, but did not describe what specifically the Landlord said that would constitute an agreement. The Landlord testified that he did not agree to end the tenancy. The Landlord’s testimony is consistent with the audible part of the recording, in which he said that they should meet with Royal York.

I do not find the Tenants’ testimony to be more credible than the Landlord’s. The Tenants have not proved, on a balance of probabilities, that on June 30 the parties made an oral agreement to end the tenancy. Did the subsequent emails terminate the tenancy?

The Tenants sent Royal York an N11 form, with a termination date of June 30, signed by them. This was clearly an offer to end the tenancy effective June 30, which the Landlord could accept by signing the N11.

Royal York replied by saying that “the N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy was signed by both parties” and that the tenancy was therefore terminated. The only reasonable interpretation of that email was that Royal York was telling the Tenants that it had conveyed the N11 to the Landlord and that the Landlord had signed it.

In other words, Royal York told the Tenants that the Landlord accepted their offer to end the tenancy effective June 30. Royal York was acting as the Landlord’s agent, and had the authority to accept an offer to terminate on his behalf. [name] email therefore created an agreement to end the tenancy.

It does not matter that the Tenants never received a copy of the N11 signed by the Landlord. As discussed above, an N11 is not required to end a tenancy. Only an agreement is required. An offer to end the tenancy was made and accepted, so the requirements of section 37(3) were met.
The Landlord argues that Royal York made an error. He testified that he never signed the N11, never agreed to end the tenancy, and never told Royal York that he agreed to end the tenancy.

The Landlord’s testimony is not relevant. Royal York had the authority to act on his behalf and agree to end the tenancy. It did so. If it did so in error, that is an issue between the Landlord and Royal York.
I therefore find that the tenancy terminated effective June 30, 2024 by agreement between the parties. Remedies Rent and deposit
The tenancy ran from June 21 to 30, 2024. The Tenants paid rent of $733.33 for that period. The Landlord is entitled to retain that amount.

Royal York collected rent of $2,200.00 for July and a rent deposit of $2,200.00. It was permitted to collect those amounts at that time. Royal York has since given those amounts to the Landlord, who currently retains them.

Having agreed to end the tenancy on June 30, the Landlord is no longer permitted to retain the rent for July or the rent deposit. He is currently retaining those amounts illegally, and will be ordered to return them. Key deposit
The Landlord agrees that he should return the key deposit of $250.00. On consent, that amount will be included in the amounts he must return. Verification fee

The application also notes that the Tenants paid a verification fee of $291.54 to Royal York, but does not claim that the fee was collected illegally or seek its return. I make no order in respect of the verification fee. Filing fee
Since the Tenants’ were successful in their application, the Landlord will also be required to reimburse them for their filing fee.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $4,703.00, which represents the return of rent, a rent deposit, and a key deposit, and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 6, 2026

File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 The Landlord’s L2 application (based on N6 and N7 notices of termination) and the Tenant’s T2 application were combined by the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) to be heard together. The hearing resumed and was heard by videoconference on October 15, 2025. The Landlord [name] and the Landlords legal representatives [name] and [name] attended the hearing. reasons: The Tenants raise that the Landlords allege the same allegations in the N7 notice of termination (‘N7 notice’) forming the basis for this L2 application which were previously raised in a prior N7 notice for L2 application LTB-L-025288-24. Order LTB-L-025288-24 was issued on May 30, 2024 and reflects that the Landlords withdrew the application. The Tenants state if the LTB does not find that Res Judicata applies, then an abuse of process would be applicable. The Tenants rely on Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 79 v. City of Toronto and [name], 2003 SCC 63 at paras 25-38 and para 55. The Court references that the inherent power of the court is to prevent the misuse of procedure which would result in the administration of justice becoming dishonored. The Court further references that an abuse of process occurs when an attempt to relitigate a claim which the court has already determined and that finality in litigation must be balanced against fairness to the litigant.

The Landlords state that there was no final decision rendered making any determinations regarding LTB-L-025288-24 because the merits of the application were not heard because the Landlords withdrew the application. The Landlords states this L2 application should proceed on the merits.

I stated at the hearing that I would allow this L2 application which is based on an N6 notice of termination (‘[name] notice’) and an N7 notice to proceed on the merits. A finding of abuse of process is discretionary. I agree with the Landlords that there were no determinations on the merits in LTB-L-025288-24 because the application was withdrawn. Therefore, I find that [name] would not apply. File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 Preliminary issue#2

The Tenants raise that the Landlords filed the [name] notice and N7 notice in contravention of the Ontario Human Rights Code (the ‘Code’) and it is necessary to hear the Tenants evidence to determine if the Landlords accommodated the Tenants procedurally and substantively before adjudicating the contents of the N6 notice and N7 notice.

The Landlords state the Tenants are raising an issue with the [name] notice and N7 notice being retaliatory and this is a defense which the Tenants can raise in response to the Landlord’s application. The Landlords state that the totality of the evidence would need to be heard along with the merits of the allegations to properly address what the Tenants are raising as a preliminary issue.

I stated at the hearing that the Landlords could proceed with their L2 application based on the N6 notice and N7 notice. The issue the Tenants raise that the Landlord has failed to accommodate the Tenants as required under the Code can be addressed by the Tenants in their response to the Landlords application. L2 application

As explained below, the Landlords have proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy as it relates to an illegal act and serious impairment to safety relating to the incidents on July 31, 2023 and October 28, 2023, and an illegal act on March 5, 2024.

However, I find that the Landlords have failed to accommodate the Tenants under the Code for the reasons I provide below. The Landlords are also required to engage in a process of consultation with the Tenants and/or the Tenants legal representatives to come up with potential solutions to accommodate the Tenants up to the point of undue hardship by April 7, 2026 and the Tenants are to cooperatively engage in the process.

The Tenants are not to run the basement fan for prolonged periods as outlined further below. By April 30, 2026, the Landlords shall install soundproofing in the rental unit or the unit located above the rental unit where upper unit tenant KR resides to ensure the sound from the bathroom fan inside the rental unit does cause noise disturbance for KR.

The allegation contained in the N6 notice and N7 that from 2019 ongoing that the Tenant Mr. [name]name] persistently attacks KR verbally including profanities, racial and gender slurs, and discrimination towards KR reference no specific dates. I do not find this allegation provides sufficient detail for the Tenants to be able to properly respond to the allegation made against them. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed. November 1, 2022 incident (N6 notice)/November 1, 2023 (N7 notice) 18. The N7 notice notes an incident date of November 21, 2023 alleging that the Tenant hit KR’s bedroom door with a shovel, leaving an indentation in the door. The evidence led by the Landlords and confirmed by the Landlords witness KR supports that an incident occurred on November 1, 2022 in which Mr. [name]name] hit the entrance door of KR’s unit with a shovel and this date was undisputed by the Tenants. Therefore, I accept November 1, 2022 is the correct date that this incident occurred relating to this allegation noted in the N6 and N7 notices. 19. The Landlords produced a photograph showing the door was dented following Mr. [name]name] hitting it with a shovel. KR states she reported this to the Landlords as supported by a text message produced for the hearing. 20. Mr. [name]name] states that following this incident, he contacted Mr. [name]name] and had a conversation in the backyard at the residential complex with him and advised Mr. [name]name] that he could not smash doors. 21. Mr. [name]name] states he has sent text messages to Mr. [name]name] advising of this on the date the behaviour occurs and that he has requested that Mr. [name]name] investigate the issue as soon as possible. It was undisputed at the hearing that the allegations set out in the N6 and N7 notices specifically refer to Mr. [name]name]’s behaviour. I disagree with the Landlords position that because the Tenants did not raise a request for accommodation since the conflict commenced in 2019 with KR that this should preclude them from requesting an accommodation later. I find the medical evidence relied on by the Tenants and their testimony strongly supports that the ongoing conflict with KR adversely impacted their mental health and wellbeing. It is undisputed that the Tenants request for accommodation was made to the Landlords at least 5 months prior to the Landlords serving the Tenants with N6 and N7 notices. 87. I am satisfied that Mr. [name]name] suffers from anxiety and depression and that Ms. [name] suffers from PTSD and depression and that these are disabilities under the Code. I find the letters from their family doctor from May 2024 and June 2025 support that both Tenants have longstanding issues with their mental health. I do not accept the Landlords position that since the Tenants mental health issues were confirmed by a family doctor and not a specialist, the diagnoses are not supported. Family doctors can diagnose mental health issues, make referrals for mental health support, and prescribe medication for mental health disorders. I find this supports the diagnoses from the Tenants family doctor is a supported and valid diagnosis. Further, the family doctor has been following both Tenants for several years. I find this supports that the family doctor would have significant knowledge relating to the Tenants’ mental health status. 88. I disagree with the Landlords position that the diagnoses provided by the family doctor for both Tenants is based on information self-reported by the Tenants. The Landlord has not established that that this is the only information which the family doctor has relied upon in providing the diagnoses relating to the Tenants mental health disorders. 89. Next, I must determine whether there is a nexus between the Tenant Mr. [name]name]’s disabilities and the behaviour forming the basis for the Landlords application for which I made positive findings on some of the allegations contained in the N6 and N7 notices. It is undisputed that the allegations relating to conduct are specific to Mr. [name]name] and not Ms. [name]. This is a joint tenancy which cannot be severed. I must determine that the evidence supports a connection between Mr. [name]name]’s disabilities and the basis for eviction. Based on the reasons below, I find the evidence supports there is a nexus between Mr. [name]name]’s disabilities and the conduct at issue in the Landlords application. 90. I find the letter from Mr. [name]name]’s family doctor dated May 14, 2024 persuasive as his family doctor references his diagnosis of longstanding anxiety and depression. The letter also notes Mr. [name]name] is experiencing significant distress which is adversely impacting his mental health as a result of the conflict with another tenant. The June 28, 2025 letter references that due to Mr. [name]name] suffering from anxiety and depression, symptoms relating to insomnia and emotional regulation would be magnified due to the ongoing interpersonal conflict he is experiencing where he lives. The letter further notes this also results in Mr. [name]name] having a low resiliency and emotional volatility. File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 91. I also found Mr. [name]name]’s testimony persuasive as he described in detail the toll that the ongoing conflict is having on him and how it affects his mental health and t the conflict with KR has also caused him to worry about his mother’s health. Mr. [name]name] described not being able to sleep and that it increased his anxiety and symptoms of depression. From Mr. [name]name]’s testimony, it is strongly evident that KR constantly recording him with her phone triggers Mr. [name]name]. The evidence supports that KR recording Mr. [name]name] was often something that occurred prior to him engaging in the incidents alleged in the N6 and N7 notices. I found Mr. [name]name]’s conduct at the hearing was calm and composed. 92. Further, I find the noise emanating from the ceiling fan in the basement rental unit is a significant source of conflict between the Tenants and KR. Other than the Landlord Mr. [name] piling yoga mats three layers high in KR’s unit which did not resolve the issue with the noise, nor the conflict, the Landlords have not done anything further to explore soundproofing in the rental unit or in the unit above. 93. Based on the above, I find there is a nexus between the Tenants disabilities and the behaviour set out in the N6 and N7 notices of termination, forming the basis of the L2 application. 94. As Mr. [name]name]’s disabilities are connected to the behaviour that could result in termination of the tenancy, the Landlord has a positive duty to accommodate the Tenant up to the point of undue hardship. 95. The Code is quasi-constitutional legislation and its requirements take precedence over the Act. For the Tenants to be evicted, absent sufficient evidence which establishes that the Landlord has accommodated them up to the point of undue hardship would constitute a breach of the Code. For the reasons provided below, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has accommodated the Tenants up to the point of undue hardship. 96. The letter from Parkdale Community Legal Services dated June 10, 2024 supports that Mr. [name] was made aware that the Tenants suffered from disabilities under the Code and the letter specifically requests a meeting to discuss an accommodation process. Mr. [name] responded on June 18, 2024, confirming he received the letter but required time to obtain legal representation. 97. While Mr. [name]name] testified that he had difficulty retaining legal representation, the evidence supports there was minimal response from Mr. [name]name] from May 2024 to September 2024, despite continued follow up emails sent from Parkdale Community Legal Services to Mr. [name] up to September 2024. The evidence further supports that the Landlords did not take any further steps to engage in any consultation with the Tenants relating to their request for accommodation. The Landlords instead, served the N6 and N7 notices on the Tenants in October 2024. 98. I do not find Mr. [name]name]’s explanation to be reasonable that because the other tenant KR is experiencing issues with her mental health, it would be unfair to accommodate the Tenants. The issue is that when the Tenants requested that they be accommodated due to a disability under the Code in May 2024, the Landlords did not speak or meet or discuss File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 with the Tenants about what steps need to be taken to address their request for accommodation. 99. I do not accept Mr. [name]’s explanation that he has accommodated the Tenants when they requested they be relocated to another unit owned by the Landlords. This is because Mr. [name]name]’s testimony was contradictory as he stated there was no other unit available but then later stated he would not want to move the Tenants to a different unit and subject other tenants to Mr. [name]name]’s ongoing behaviour. I find this evidence supports the Landlords did not attempt to accommodate the Tenants request that they be relocated to another unit. 100. I am also not convinced that the Landlords would experience undue hardship by accommodating the Tenants. The Landlords raise that Mr. [name]name] has failed to comply with an undertaking to comply with conditions that include he is to immediately remove himself when he is in the presence of KR. However, I find the ongoing conflict with KR has exacerbated Mr. [name]name]’s mental health which has triggered Mr. [name]’s conduct towards KR. Mr. [name]name]’s attempt to mitigate the conflict has been minimal at best. I say this because, the correspondence between the Tenants, KR and Mr. [name]name] has mainly taken place via text message. The result has proven to be unsuccessful in reducing the conflict or its effects on the Tenants and KR. 101. Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Landlords have taken any steps to accommodate the Tenants up to the point of undue hardship. The Landlords are required to engage in a process of consultation with the Tenants and if necessary, their health professionals, to come up with a reasonable plan which either stops the behaviour complained of or reduces the impact. If the Landlords engage in that process and it proves impossible to develop such a plan or the plan does not work, then at that point, the Landlords may establish they have satisfied their burden under the Code. Section 83 considerations 102. The Landlords request termination of the tenancy. 103. Section 83 of the Act requires me to consider and apply the Code when exercising my authority to delay or refuse an eviction. 104. The Tenants state that they have been living in the rental unit for approximately 15 years and as a result, market rent would be significantly higher if they were forced to move. Mr. [name]name] states that he registered for an affordable housing list about five years ago without success of being able to find another place to move to. He states if he is forced to move, he is unsure of how it may impact both him and his Mother’s mental health. He states he is on anti-anxiety medication. He states he attended anger management therapy as an elected option through a court diversion program and voluntarily attended a Cognitive Behavioral Therapy program through a referral from his family doctor. He states that both have assisted him with managing his behaviour. Mr. [name] produced a letter dated March 20, 2025 from Women’s College Hospital which notes he was an active participant in attending weekly Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (‘CBT’) sessions from February 27, 2025 to March 27, 2025. This letter further notes that File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 during CBT, topics including depression, anxiety, anger, and conflict management were discussed and strategies outlined on how to manage them. 105. Mr. [name]name] relies on social assistance and Ms. [name] relies on Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Pension. 106. I accept the Tenants are vulnerable persons suffering from disabilities and rely on a fixed income. I accept that it would be difficult for them to find alternate housing based on market rent being significantly higher than the monthly rent they are currently paying. Having regard to all of the circumstances, in balancing the prejudice to the Landlords against the prejudice to the Tenants, I find that it would not be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act subject to conditions imposed under subsection 204(1) of the Act to provide the Tenants an opportunity to preserve their tenancy. 107. I also determined that Mr. [name]name] committed illegal acts and seriously impaired the safety of KR on July 31, 2023, October 28, 2023, and March 5, 2024. As a result, I have considered the need to ensure that Mr. [name]name] does not engage in such further serious conduct in the future. Therefore, I find a conditional order is appropriate to protect the health and safety of other tenants, occupants, and guests at the residential complex. T2 application 108. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords will proactively address concerns raised by the Tenants regarding KR’s behaviour relating to substantial interference with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment within 24 hours of the Tenants advising the Landlords in writing. The Landlords will pay $7,000.00 in general compensation and $48.00 for the application filing fee to the Tenants by April 30, 2026. 109. The Tenants claim the following allegations in their T2 application: 1) The Landlords failed to accommodate the Tenants disabilities under the Code. The Landlords issuance of the eviction notices as a response to the Tenants’ request for accommodation is discriminatory under the Code and must result in a dismissal of the Landlords application. 2) The Landlords have substantially interfered with the Tenants’ right to reasonably enjoy the rental property by failing to effectively intervene in a long running dispute between the Tenants and their upstairs neighbour, KR. Accommodation under the Code 110. I have determined already that the Landlords failed to accommodate the Tenants disability under the Code and provided my reasons for reaching this determination. File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 Substantial interference 111. For the reasons set out below, I find that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the residential complex when the Landlords failed to effectively mitigate the longstanding conflict with the other tenant KR. 112. Mr. [name]name] testified that KR has harassed him and his mother on many occasions by banging objects on the floor of her unit which starts around 4:00 am and continues throughout the day. He states that KR continuously records him at the residential complex, and bangs on the window of the rental unit at night. He states that he has advised the Landlords of this on many occasions. 113. Mr. [name]name] states that he has requested that the Landlords install cameras near the basement window of the washroom of the washroom at the rental unit but to date there are no cameras installed. He states he has also requested that the Landlords remove the bathroom ceiling fan but to date the ceiling fan remains installed in rental unit bathroom. 114. Mr. [name]name] states he has experienced issues with his mental health since he was thirteen years old. He states the conflict with KR has impacted his mental and physical health, his ability to sleep and focus. He states he either lacks sleep, or oversleeps, and will isolate himself. He states that he will often leave the rental unit to go and stay at his brother’s residence. He states he is worried about the impact that the conflict with KR has on his Mother’s health as she is a senior and has issues with her heart. He testified that he is fearful of KR. 115. DS testified that he has seen a decline in his Mother’s health. He states in 2023, he also noticed a decline with his brother, Mr. [name]name]’s health. He states that he observed him staying in his room for a period of 10 days and only coming out for food, water, or to use the washroom. 116. Ms. [name]name] testified that she advised Mr. [name]name] by telephone, text message, and a letter dated November 14, 2023 that the Tenants were experiencing noise issues which were coming from KR’s unit. Ms. [name]name] states KR’s unit is above her bedroom and that KR makes excessive noise including banging/crashing sounds and screaming between the hours of 1:00 am - 7:00 am. Ms. [name]name] states the noise the Tenants experience inside their rental unit coming from KR inside of her unit is continuous. Ms. [name]name] states that she has had to sleep on the couch inside the kitchen/living room area of the rental unit for the past few years due to the noise. 117. Mr. [name]name] states that Ms. [name] sent him letter in November 2023 which raises the Tenants concerns concerning KR stomping on the floor of her unit, smoking marijuana in the bathroom, causing noise disturbances for the Tenants and running the water in her unit which causes the temperature of the water to become extremely hot in the Tenants unit when the Tenants use their shower. 118. The Tenants produced a text message from Mr. [name]name] to Ms. [name] dated November 14, 2023 which acknowledges that he has read her letter and that he sympathizes with her situation and that he will be addressing the Tenants concerns with KR shortly. The Tenants produced a text message in which they responded to the File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 Landlord’s text message on that same date and request the Landlord not address any issues with KR at that time because things have been calm with KR and they do not want to disrupt that. 119. Ms. [name]name] references another text message from Mr. [name]name] dated January 19, 2024 which advises Ms. [name] that the Landlords only course of action is to serve KR with another notice of eviction as the first notice of eviction previously served on KR ceased the harassment. Mr. [name]name] asked Ms. [name]name] if she would like the Landlords to proceed with serving another eviction notice on KR. Ms. [name]name] responds that she hopes the Landlords will follow through with issuing KR an eviction notice. Text message correspondence produced on January 24, 2024 from Ms. [name]name] to Mr. [name]name] references a phone call with Mr. [name]name] the day before and that Ms. [name] is disappointed that the Landlords will not be pursuing an eviction notice for KR and that Mr. [name]name] and his family are fearful of any reprisal from her. 120. Ms. [name]name] states that the Tenants have gone to the police on three occasions regarding the conflict with KR but were advised by the police that it is an LTB issue. The Tenants produced copies of two applications for a Peace Bond dated August 24, 2023 and October 30, 2023 which alleges continued harassment by KR. The Tenants state both applications for the Peace Bond were not approved. 121. Mr. [name]name] has testified to the attempts to mediate the ongoing conflict with the Tenants and KR individually. The evidence supports this was done through text message correspondence. Analysis 122. For the reasons below, I find that KR has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the Landlords failed to successfully intervene in stopping this. 123. The Tenants produced video evidence that KR looks into the Tenants window of their rental unit at night, albeit, KR was requesting the Tenants turn off the bathroom fan in their unit. The prior testimony of DS also corroborates that KR looks in the windows of the rental unit at night. Mr. [name]name] testified that he leaves the bathroom fan on to discourage KR from spying on him and knocking on his window at night. 124. KR previously testified that she is able to hear when the Tenants are showering in their unit as she hears the pipes rattle and she will deliberately turn on the water which has caused Mr. [name]name] to get scaled with hot water. The text messages from Mr. [name]name] support that this issue was raised with Mr. [name]name]. Text message correspondence from Mr. [name]name] supports that he sent a text message to KR advising her not to do this but no further action was taken by the Landlords regarding this issue. 125. The testimony of Ms. [name]name] and the text message correspondence produced for the hearing supports that Ms. [name] had advised Mr. that the noise disturbance caused by KR was more than the Tenants could tolerate. I find Mr. [name]name]’s response to Ms. [name] was not helpful or proactive in addressing this situation as he asked Ms. [name] if she wanted File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 him to serve KR with another termination notice but then advised Ms. [name] that he decided not to. Mr. [name]name] states that this is because he believed Mr. [name]name] was the instigator in the conflict. 126. I find the actions taken by Mr. [name]name] to mitigate the conflict and address the concerns raised by the Tenants were ineffective. I say this because, the evidence and testimony from the Tenants and DS support that the Tenants continued to be negatively impacted by KR including noise disturbances in the middle of the night, recording Mr. [name] with her phone, and KR looking into the window of their rental unit. 127. While Mr. [name]name] testified that Mr. [name]name] was the instigator, I disagree. I find the evidence supports that the continuous behaviour engaged in by KR was disruptive and interfered with the Tenants being able to enjoy their rental unit and the residential complex. Based on this, I find this fueled the conflict between the Tenants and KR which contributed to the incidents arising in the N6 and N7 notices. The Landlord’s application alleges instances occurring between the Tenants and KR since 2019 which is nearly 5 years prior to the L2 application being filed in October 2024. I find this evidence supports that the Landlords were aware there are longstanding issues with the Tenants and KR. Further, Ms. [name]’s testimony and text message correspondence with Mr. [name]name] strongly supports that the Tenants advised Mr. [name]name] on several occasions how KR’s behaviour was interfering with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 128. I accept [name] testimony which was corroborated by DS that she has had to resort so sleeping on the couch in the rental unit due to the noise from KR’s unit at night which is directly above Ms. [name]’s bedroom. I find the Tenants testimony that the noise disturbances from KR’s unit which include banging sounds and yelling from KR’s unit in the middle of the night has adversely impacted their ability to sleep in their rental unit. The Tenants testimony and text messages support they advised Mr. [name]name] of this. 129. I find the two applications for a Peace Bond in August 2023 and October 2023 which the Tenants state were not approved support that the conflict between Mr. [name]name] and KR had escalated and was becoming more contentious. 130. The evidence supports significant ongoing conflict between the Tenants and KW which the Landlords are aware of as supported by the Landlord [name]’s testimony and text message correspondence between him and the Tenants. I find that the Landlords did not take the necessary or appropriate steps to address the conflict as it continued to ensue which resulted in substantially interfering with the Tenants rights with being able to reasonably enjoy their rental unit and the residential complex. Remedies 131. The Tenants request a dismissal of the Landlord’s application because the Landlords did not fulfill their legal obligation to accommodate the Tenants’ disabilities prior to serving them with eviction notices. I have addressed this remedy and provided reasons for determining that a conditional order is appropriate. File Numbers: LTB-L-087542-24 LTB-T-096050-24 132. I have determined the Tenants have disabilities recognized under the Code and therefore the Landlords have a duty to accommodate the Tenants disabilities under the Code up to the point of undue hardship. Therefore, it is necessary that the Landlords engage in an accommodation process with the Tenants, and if necessary, the Tenants health professionals to stop the behaviour complained of and address improving the contentious conflict between the Tenants, particularly between Mr. [name]name] and KR. 133. The Tenants request general compensation be awarded in the amount of $15,000.00 for injury to their dignity, discriminatory conduct, and pain and suffering as a result of KR’s interference with the Tenants rights and the eviction proceedings. The Landlords stated the amount claimed by the Tenants would cause financial hardship to the Landlords but no evidence was led by the Landlords further to their submission. I find an amount of $7,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. I find the Landlords have discriminated against the Tenants by not accommodating their disabilities under the Code. As a result of the ongoing conflict with KR, this has adversely affected the Tenants mental health and it rose to a level which caused pain and suffering. 134. I find the medical letters from the family doctors of both Tenants and persuasive and support that the lengthy ongoing conflict with KR has adversely affected both Tenants emotionally and physically and has exacerbated their prior issues with their mental health. I accept the Tenants testimony that they rely on fixed incomes and have resided at the rental unit for approximately 15 years. Based on this evidence, I accept that it would be difficult for the Tenants to find an alternate place to move to and has resulted in them remaining at the residential complex and continuing to endure the substantial interference from KR for a long time.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex as follows: 1. Excessive repairs to the unit 2. Failure of the Landlord to address noise complaints. Excessive Repairs to the rental unit

At the outset of the hearing the Landlord requested the Tenant’s application relating to excessive repairs be dismissed on the grounds of lack of details. Specifically, the Tenant’s application with respect to this issue does not specify times and dates of alleged issues referred to in the application.

It was explained to the Tenant at the hearing, to provide a hearing that is procedurally fair, the responding party needs to know the case to be met. The T2 application filled out by the Tenant explicitly ask the Tenant to described alleged events, provide dates and times of the alleged events, and list who was involved in the events leading to the application.

I find that the allegations in the Tenants application are vague and lack any context in terms of dates and details. Specifically, the “Explain Your Reasons” section of the application instructs the applicant to describe what happened, the dates and times of each event, who caused the problem and the names and titles of all people involved.
The Landlord would have experienced significant prejudice if expected to present a defence against unknown and unspecified allegations.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application relating to excessive repairs is dismissed. [name]

The Tenant testified that in June a new tenant moved into the building and his dog would start barking around 6:15 am when that tenant left for work until approximately 4:00 pm when the tenant returned.
The Tenant testified that this occurred on a daily basis and greatly impacted the Tenant as he mostly worked from home.

The Tenant stated that he first mentioned the issue to [name] [name] Manager for the Landlord on June 6, 2023 during a conversation and sent an email to [name] the following day regarding the issue of the dog barking.
The Tenant tendered evidence of emails he had sent to [name] regarding the barking dog on June 7, 8, 12, 14 and 15, July 11 and 28 and August 5 and 18.

The Tenant testified that he also made complaints to the City of Hamilton Animal Control and completed barking time sheets for August 12th – 17th, Although he admits that these sheets were not provided to the Landlord at the time.
The Tenant testified that he felt he had no other option but to leave the unit and vacated the rental unit at the end of November, 2023.
The Landlord’s Agent [name] testified that she is the Regional Manager for [name] and that her role is to over see property operations and site staff.
She testified to notices that the Landlord had sent to the tenant regarding his barking dog on June 7, 14, July 11 and August 3, 2023.
She stated that the Landlord also sent an N5 notice of termination to the tenant regarding his barking dog on August 18, 2023 with a termination date of September 23, 2023.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that the Landlord did not initiate and application based on the N5 as no further complaints came in regarding the dog barking and had assumed that the tenant had rectified the issue and thus voided the N5.

The Tenant confirmed that the last complaint he made to the Landlord was August 18, 2023. He stated that he didn’t see the point in continuing to complain as it did not appear to be making a difference. Analysis

A landlord’s duty to address substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a tenant by another tenant was affirmed by the Divisional Court in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”). The Court held, inter alia, as follows: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.”

In other words, a landlord has the positive obligation to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment and take the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of his premises.

In the present case after receiving complaints from the Tenant regarding another tenants barking dogs the Landlord investigated the complaints and began to issue notices to the tenant of regarding the barking dogs when complaints were received. When the barking did not stop the Landlord issued a notice of termination to the tenant of the barking dogs.

I find the actions taken by the Landlord were reasonable given the history of the complaints they had received from the Tenant. In addition the Tenant by his own admission ceased sending complaints to the Landlord after August 18, 2025. As such, the Landlord was unaware the issue had not resolved and did not take any further action after issuing a notice of termination on that date.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord has met the obligation set out in Hassan and did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
