issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenants claim that there is a lack of sufficient hot water supplied to the rental unit. The Landlord responds that there are no issues with the hot water supply, as evidenced by their investigation into the alleged disrepair.
For the reasons below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The evidence of the Tenants
The Tenant S.C. testified that she and D.J. moved into the 2-BR rental unit in December 2023. The unit is situated in the middle of the 9th floor of the residential complex.

Since then, she says, there has been insufficient hot water supply to their unit at least twice per week. The Tenants claim that the hot water significantly and unexpectedly diminishes after 3:00 p.m. and on many days is wholly unreliable after 7:00 p.m. The water temperature is lukewarm even after running the water from the bathtub faucet for several minutes. Sometimes there is no hot water. This makes bathing very unpleasant.

For example, S.C. recalls that she came home on January 27, 2024 around 5:00 p.m. and there was no hot water. This was about five weeks after taking occupancy of the unit. She reported the problem to the Landlord through a maintenance request dated the same day. The work order requested states: “No hot water. The hot water in the apartment either doesn’t get hot or doesn’t stay hot. We have been getting lukewarm water since last night. Also, every time I try to use the hot water after around 9 p.m. there is no hot water only warm which eventually turns to freezing cold after 1 minute or so. This has been going on since I moved in.”
Two days later, the Landlord sent building superintendent/resident manager A.C. to investigate. This is confirmed in her maintenance request as submitted by the Landlord.

However, she testified, the Landlord could not resolve the issue. S.C. maintains that A.C. and the Landlord’s property manager C.R. have told her that the problem is the location of the apartment – since it is an older building and because the Tenants live on the top floor, there was nothing they could do about it.

Believing this to be true, she said, at the end of January 2024 she asked the Landlord if she and her family could move to a unit on a lower floor. She stated that the Landlord informed her that a transfer was prohibited within the first year of the lease.

She testified that sometime around March 2025, she again asked the Landlord for permission to change units because of the ongoing hot water problem. The Landlord also denied that request. This time, she said, the Landlord told them that they had not given proper 60-days notice to end the tenancy. The Landlord would need at least 60 days in order to offer them a different unit.

On April 10, 2025, S.C. contacted the Landlord’s Customer Service and asked if they could “get help from someone else”. The email she sent states: “I was wondering if there is a way that I can make a complaint about the hot water issue I am having in my apartment about me not constantly having hot water available at all times of the day. I have already requested maintenance when I first moved in but all I was told was that it was because I live on the top floor and that basically there is nothing they can do. I would like to complain to someone rather than management of this building because they are not going to resolve the issue.”
Instead, on April 11, 2025, Customer Service referred the complaint back to C.R. After that, S.C. said, the Landlord promised to send a plumber but that did not happen.

On April 23, 2025, at 6:31 p.m., S.C. tested the temperature of the stream of water flowing from the bathtub faucet using a handheld thermometer while recording a video. The recording discloses that the temperature ranges from 20 to 21.5 degrees Celsius for a full minute.

S.C. testified that they had literally no hot water after 3:00 p.m. for a whole week in early November 2025. She also recorded the following videos with temperature readings: • November 4, 2025, 5:04 p.m.: 24 degrees Celsius, for about 1 minute • November 18, 2025, 6:37 p.m.: 27-28 degrees Celsius, for about 1 minute • November 23, 2025, 9:55 p.m.: the temperature is initially 22 degrees Celsius, then after about 20 seconds it drops to 21 degrees and remains steady for 30 seconds
On November 5, 2025, S.C. put a letter she wrote to the Landlord in the mailbox located outside the on-site office, where tenants were invited by signage to drop off documents and correspondence.

In the letter, she referred to two previous service requests (807141 and 832755) they had made “since moving in about the insufficient hot water”. Because of the “huge inconvenience”, S.C. asked the Landlord to reconsider transferring them to another unit “where there should be no water issues”. She wrote: “As per the Residential Tenancy Act hot water is a vital service that should have a minimum temperature of 43 degrees celsius. Most of the time we cannot take a shower at the times that we need to because we have either freezing cold or just barely warm water and as working people, we do not have all day to wait around for the water to get hot. The hot water in our unit is very inconsistent, we can have hot water and then as we are showering its turn freezing cold or like yesterday, Nov 4th, 2025, we had no hot water running from about 3:40pm when I had tried to ask my child to shower and the hot water stayed off for the rest of the night. … I have used my thermometer to test the temperature of the water coming out and have confirmed that it does not reach the minimum stated temperature above.”
S.C. says that she never received a response. The Tenants then filed this application on November 16, 2025.

She testified that it was only after the December 18, 2025 LTB hearing that the Landlord sent a plumber to investigate the water issue, on December 23, 2025. She claims that the only reason they did so was because the Member directed them to take that step.

The Landlord subsequently arranged for a second inspection on January 27, 2026. S.C. was home and made an audio/video recording of the visit. She stated that the Landlord did not send a professional plumber. A.C. attended with two others. They ran the water from the bathtub faucet for about 7-8 minutes. During this time, A.C. left the unit at least once, which she later discovered was to consult with a plumber by phone.
She noted that, overall, the Landlord’s testing always occurred during the daytime and that the Landlord has neglected to inform her of the outcome of their investigation.

According to S.C., the Tenants did not know that they could contact the municipality to inquire about a property standards inspection pursuant to City of Toronto bylaws. Neither did the Tenants hire a licensed plumber to complete an independent inspection and assessment of the problem. S.C. thought she read somewhere that they were prohibited from bringing in their own contractor.
S.C. submits that the problem has never been resolved. The evidence of the Landlord

The Landlord disputes the Tenants’ version of events. They claim that they have responded to the Tenants’ concerns promptly. In the Landlord’s opinion, there is no hot water supply issue. The Landlord submits that the Tenants are the only residents in the complex who have complained about a lack of hot water in their unit. The testimony of A.C.

The superintendent/resident manager [name] testified that he has only ever received one complaint from the Tenants in the tenant portal about issues with the hot water supply. That was on January 27, 2024. He arranged for a plumber to inspect the unit and the technician’s thermometer readings established that the water temperature was 50 degrees Celsius. He did not refer to date or the time of day the plumber conducted the inspection.

A second complaint came through the Landlord’s Customer Service on April 10, 2025. His evidence is that the Landlord arranged for a plumbing technician from LRB Contracting Service- Plumbing and Ventilation (“LRB”) to attend at the unit on April 11, 2025. A.C. stated that because the Tenants were not home, LRB was unable to enter.

He referred to an LRB work order dated the same day regarding “no hot water in whole unit”. The technician notes on the document that “No notice was given. So inspected main riser and re-circle line and found it was very hot.” The time of the inspection was not listed.

A.C. also testified that on January 27, 2026, he and two other maintenance persons performed another water temperature test in the rental unit. He maintains that he spoke to S.C. at the time and encouraged her to call him, even at night, if there was a hot water issue and that he gave her his contact information as he was leaving.
He recalls that he previously gave S.C. his contact information, possibly in April 2025, and told her that she could call at any time about a lack of hot water.

After the January 27, 2026 inspection, A.C. sent a follow up email to C.R. on February 9, 2026, as submitted by the Landlord. The email states: “We went out to talk with the plumber regarding the temperature of the water. We returned near the unit entry door to tell the tenant that the water is on normal temperature 49 C. Both me and [name] advise her that the temperature is on normal range and water is hot.” The testimony of C.R.

C.R. claims that he did not receive the letter the Tenants allegedly deposited in the onsite mailbox on November 5, 2025. He checks the mailbox regularly. He also stated that he did not see any work order requests from the Tenants about the water issue on the tenant portal, which he checks daily.

He confirmed that the Landlord sent LRB into the unit on December 23, 2025 to assess whether there was a problem with hot water. The Landlord's Legal Representative L.V. referred him to an LRB work order dated December 23, 2025.

The technician reported that when they “opened the water it was Boiling (very hot)” and that they checked relevant valves in the boiler room which “were good”. There is no mention of the time of day that the technician entered the unit.

L.V. submits that when the Landlord was informed of the alleged disrepair, the Landlord promptly investigated and made reasonable determinations based on their inspections that the supply of hot water was adequate. Analysis A landlord’s maintenance and repair obligations

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2026 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 34. [name]. 517/06: [name] states: 11. (1) Every kitchen sink, washbasin, bathtub and shower shall be provided, by safe equipment, with hot and cold running water. (2) The ordinary temperature of the hot water provided must be at least 43 degrees Celsius. 35. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The Landlord did not comply with their obligations under the Act 36. The Landlord does not refute the water temperature readings taken by the Tenants. However, the Landlord was unable to explain why the hot water temperature readings were, on average, 20 degrees lower than the mandatory temperature of 43 degrees Celsius. 37. I do not find A.C.’s evidence credible. He testified that on January 27, 2026, he offered S.C. his contact information (for the second time) and said she could call him anytime. This assertion is clearly unsupported by the video S.C. filed. At no point in the recording does A.C. converse with S.C., with the exception of saying “Thank you” as he is leaving. A.C. offered no proof, either, that he had previously given the Tenants his contact information. 38. Regarding the follow-up email A.C. sent to C.R. on February 9, 2026, in which he writes that he advised S.C. that the temperature was 49 degrees Celsius, S.C.’s recording shows the contrary. I find that A.C. was not being entirely truthful in his email. 39. What happened on January 27, 2026 is effectively as follows. Three people arrived at the unit, observably without any tools, in mid-morning. They proceeded to check the water in the bathroom for less than five minutes and then left without disclosing to S.C. their observations or conclusions. There is no evidence before me that an experienced plumbing contractor was present to personally engage in the testing process. 40. Similarly, I find C.R.‘s testimony implausible. I have no reason to doubt that S.C. placed the letter in the mailbox on November 5, 2025 as testified. 41. C.R. claims he never received the letter. I find this hard to believe because the Landlord’s agents check it regularly. I reasonably infer that the Landlord received the letter and chose to ignore it, possibly logging it as an unmeritorious complaint. 42. I prefer the evidence of the Tenants. S.C.’s testimony was given honestly, was unembellished and was internally consistent throughout. 43. In my view, there is no reason why the Tenants would not trust the Landlord when they initially informed the Tenants that there was nothing they could do to resolve the issue. 44. The Tenants felt they had no choice but to ask to transfer to another unit. The Landlord seems to have refused those requests in a cursory manner, giving questionable explanations. After more months of unabated frustration, the Tenants resumed their polite requests – not demands – for a full inspection and resolution. 45. Given the situation as S.C. describes it, I think it more likely than not that S.C. would have contacted A.C. after hours if he had truly extended such invitation. 46. I note that the Landlord led no evidence to establish that anyone informed the Tenants, in writing, of the results of the Landlord’s several inspections. 47. The question to be asked is why would the Tenants make repeated complaints about very specific disrepair if not true? A reasonable tenant in the same situation would no doubt take the same common-sense approach that the Tenants took. 48. The facts show that the Landlord neglected to conduct a properly thorough investigation. Signs of an ineffectual investigation in this case include a failure to: • properly ascertain from the Tenants the relevant details about the problem, including confirming that the issue occurred in the evenings. • attend the rental unit at the critical time(s) to perform an inspection. • engage the services of a licensed plumber to probe in more depth other possible causes for the lack of hot water. • escalate the investigation, referring the issue to a more experienced contractor. • properly document the investigative steps taken. • keep the Tenants apprised, in writing, of the reasonable steps they were taking and the results of any inspections and assessments. 49. It is widely considered common knowledge that, in general, water will heat up to the internally set temperature within 30 seconds to two minutes of a faucet being turned on. 50. The Landlord failed to explain or to present reliable evidence about why a functioning hot water recirculation system would not deliver hot water within 60 seconds to the rental unit. 51. There might be other sources of the disrepair. The Landlord led no evidence to show that they explored the possibility of a faulty pressure valve in the shower or whether a thermostatic mixing valve in the shower was defective or needed adjustment. It is unknown whether the circulation pump is running inefficiently or if a booster pump has been installed to counteract gravity. Perhaps pipes are poorly insulated, or the boiler is too old or too small to meet the high demand of residents during the late afternoon and evening. 52. I am unable to accept the Landlord’s assertion that no other tenants residing on the same floor as the Tenants have complained about the lack of hot water. The Landlord could have presented other tenants as witnesses or obtained declarations or sworn affidavits from them but chose not to do so. 53. Even if it is true that no other tenants have complained, the Landlord seems to have neglected to investigate another potential source of disrepair – that is, whether there is a faulty shower valve in the unit below the Tenants’ unit that could be allowing cold water to enter the hot water pipe, cooling it down before it reaches the upper unit. 54. For unknown reason, the Landlord’s agents and contractors never attended at the Tenants’ unit during the period of time being complained of, to test the water temperature. The parties could have agreed to entry between 8:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. In the circumstances, I assume the Tenants would be amenable to allowing entry at that time. 55. The Landlord did not present any contractors, including from LRB, to give witness testimony about the alleged disrepair and the steps taken to resolve the matter. 56. What the evidence strongly suggests is that the Landlord’s employees have adopted a blasé, perfunctory attitude in this matter. In short, if they can’t see the problem, then the problem does not exist. 57. That is an unacceptable response. If there is evidence that the hot water supply does not meet the mandatory legal standard and if the Landlord fails to make the necessary repairs, then the Landlord is in breach of the Act. And, if disrepair is established, it is not enough for the Landlord to close a work order with finality with the justification that they do not know the cause. 58. I find that the Landlords’ response to the plumbing issue was neither adequate nor timely. It fell well short of the standard the LTB expects of landlords. The Tenants waited almost two years for a remedy. They gave the Landlord every opportunity to rectify the problem. 59. Without any doubt, the Landlord failed to maintain the hot water temperature at the minimum level always required and the Landlord is, therefore, in breach of subsection 11(2) of O.Reg. 517/06. 60. Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair and maintain the rental unit and/or failed to comply with health, housing or maintenance standards. 61. By allowing the disrepair to continue without adequate resolution for more than two years, the Landlord also substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. 62. Tenants should not have to make repeated requests to landlords relating to the same issue of disrepair so they can obtain the services and facilities for which they have contracted to receive. Remedies 63. The monthly rent is $2,806.14. In their application, the Tenants seek a rent abatement of 20% of each month for the period December 2024 to November 2025. 64. Without doubt, the lack of adequate hot water supply has been ongoing since at least January 2024 as demonstrated by objective evidence. The issue has not been resolved and the impact upon the Tenants is substantial. I am satisfied that the Tenants’ request is not unreasonable. 65. Given my experience and knowledge of previous like cases before the Board, I find that the rent abatement requested of $6,721.05 is appropriate in the circumstances. 66. Other than expressing an entitlement to the filing fee, the Tenants confirmed that they are not seeking any further remedy at this time.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,769.05. This amount represents: • $6,721.05 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $2,000.00 from the rent each month from April 1, 2026 to June 1, 2026 and $769.05 from the rent due and payable on July 1, 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must provide compensation to the Tenant as set out in this [name]. Relevant Law, Burden of Proof and Admissions

On an application for service of a N12 Notice of Termination for the Landlord’s own use in bad faith, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Additionally, subsection 57(5) of the Act provides that it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a Landlord served a Notice of Termination under s.48 in bad faith if after the N12 Notice of Termination is given and within 12 months of the Tenant vacating the unit, the Landlord advertises the rental unit for sale (among other activities).

The parties agree that on May 29, 2025, the Landlord delivered an N12 Notice for Landlord’s own use claiming the Landlord required possession of the rental unit. The N12 Notice had a termination date of July 15, 2025 [Exhibit 1 – Document ID 6797100]. Accordingly, the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The N12 Notice identified the Landlord’s spouse and his child as the intended occupants of the rental unit.
The parties disagreed whether the Landlord’s spouse and child moved into the rental unit.
The parties also disagreed whether the N12 Notice was given in good faith.

I find the evidence of the parties accorded insofar as the rental unit was listed for sale within one year of the time the Tenant vacated. As a result, it is the Landlord who bears the burden of demonstrating they genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit for a period of at least one year. The Landlord did serve the N12 Notice in bad faith

The Landlord testified that he served the N12 Notice because the agreement between him and his wife was that she would take the rental unit and live there with their son who was aged 20 at the time. The Landlord’s position is that his wife and child did move into the rental unit. He testified that his wife decided on August 25, 2025, that she no longer wanted to live in the rental unit as she could not afford it, and so moved out. However, his son continued to live in the rental unit and vacated the unit shortly before it was listed for sale. The Landlord further testified that the son has some health challenges and found the divorce hard to cope with, and so it was in his best interest to remain in the townhouse in familiar surroundings for as long as was possible. All of the Landlord’s evidence about his family’s move to the rental unit was testimonial and primarily hearsay. He did not rely on any written documentation identifying that the rental unit had new occupants, such as a hydro bill or a moving invoice.

The Tenant’s position is that the spouse and child did not move into the rental unit after she vacated the unit. In support of her position that no one moved in, the Tenant testified that when she went looking for her cat who got lost during the moving period, she would go to the rental unit every evening for a few weeks and never saw any movement in the house or backyard. The time period referenced was mid July 2025. She then went on to say there was no recycling or garbage cans placed out, further confirming her belief that no one occupied the rental unit. The Tenant also said that her neighbour told her she had not seen anyone move into the unit after the Tenant had vacated. No date was provided with respect to this hearsay evidence and as such it was of little value.

The Landlord testified that on March 31, 2025, the Tenant had advised him that she was thinking of moving out of the rental unit. However, she then decided against this and continued to reside in the rental unit and did not want to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant did not dispute this. The Landlord did not dispute that after he served the notice of termination, he gave the Tenant the option to purchase the unit on May 31, 2025. [Exhibit 2 – Document ID7578998].

The Landlord testified that the N12 was not served in bad faith, but rather his circumstances changed from May 29, 2025. He described how he and his spouse were in the midst of separating and the plan was for her move into the rental unit. The Landlord testified that as a result of ongoing divorce proceeding, he needed to sell the rental unit in order to avoid filing for bankruptcy. Although his former spouse changed her mind about moving in, no evidence was provided with respect to where she was living, nor did she attend the hearing to give testimony.
The Landlord confirmed that the rental unit has been sold and that the funds are sitting in trust with the lawyer for the time being.

Having considered the evidence of the Landlord, I am not satisfied that at the time the notice was served there was a genuine intention for his spouse and son to move into the unit. He was already thinking about selling two days after he served the notice. There was little direct evidence from the Landlord to support that either his wife or child actually moved in beyond his hearsay evidence. No documents to support a lease agreement, or rental amount agreed upon, or utility accounts, or address changes were entered. And as noted above, neither the Landlord’s spouse nor son attended to testify as to what transpired. For these reasons, I am not satisfied the notice was served in good faith.

The Landlord knew or ought to have known that the unit was not affordable for his spouse and son at the time the notice was served. There was no evidence to support that his son could afford to live there. It was also implausible that the Landlord would allow his vulnerable child into the rental unit without his mother.
In the above circumstances, I find that, on the balance of probabilities, the Landlord has not rebutted the presumption of bad faith and that the N12 Notice was not served in good faith.
As a result, I find the Tenant has demonstrated all of the required elements under s.57(1)(a). Remedies

The Tenant was paying $2,665.00 per month in rent to the Landlord. The Tenant’s new rent is now $3,100.00 per month, which amounts to a $435.00 per month increase in rent. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,220.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant is incurring for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant had an alarm system in the rental unit and since moving into a new rental unit, she needed pay $200.00 to have a new alarm system installed. There was also a cost associated with the set up of Grimsby Power and although there was no change in gas company (Enbridge), there was a transfer fee associated with the move. The Tenant also had to pay to have the Internet set up. The Tenant did not have any receipts to confirm all the expenses she paid for the above. However, as opposed to the $2,000.00 the Tenant had asked for the out-of-pocket moving and other expenses, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

If the Tenant meets all 3 elements of the legal test in s.57(1) of the Act, then the Board may award a general compensation of up to 12 months rent last charged for the rental unit, which in this case was $2,665.00 per month. The Tenant has asked for 12 months rent in general compensation. The Tenant testified that the rental unit in question at $2,665.00 per month was made up of 3 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms as well as a finished basement. The current rental unit where the Tenant resides in is more costly and smaller in comparison. This unit comprises of 3 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms and no finished basement. The Landlord’s claim is that he did not serve the N12 in bad faith and therefore it would appear that his position would be that he does not owe any monies to the Tenant in the form of general compensation. Due to the fact that the N12 Notice to terminate the tenancy was served in bad faith and that the Tenant would not have moved out of the rental unit had it not been for the fact that she was served with the N12 Notice, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant some amount of general compensation. Having heard from both the Landlord and Tenant, I believe the general compensation should be equal to an amount of 3 months’ rent that was last charged for the rental unit which is a total of $7,995.00. This figure is reasonable, and I have based the amount on the stress and inconvenience put to the Tenant having to move and by the Landlord’s bad faith behaviour. The amount should also act a deterrent should the Landlord decide to engage in the rental housing market again.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $14,263.00. This amount represents: • $5,220.00 for increased rent the Tenant is incurring for the one-year period from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $7,995.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $948.28. T2 Application

The tenancy commenced on or about September 15, 2023, and the rental unit was a one- bedroom unit in the four-bedroom home. The Tenant and two others individually entered a tenancy agreement with the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that o n November 7, 202 4, the Landlord sent the Tenant an email requesting them to vacate the rental unit on November 10, 2024. The Landlord also turned off the internet, electricity, and water supply.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the short notice and requested moving and storage costs of $300.00. The Tenant testified that she made a cash payment of $300.00 to friends to help her move her belongings out of the unit.
The Tenant and her roommates signed a joint tenancy agreement for a new unit on October 27, 2024. That tenancy commenced on November 1, 2024.
The Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to pay $10,000.00 for a period of one year, an amount representing the difference in rent between the rental unit and their current unit.
The Landlord opposed the moving costs because the Tenant did not provide a receipt to substantiate the expense.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord breached the Act by substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex when he served the Tenant with a three‑day notice of termination by email, rather than providing the mandatory sixty‑day written notice. Therefore, I find that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions.

However, the Tenant is not entitled to the difference in rent for a year because the new tenancy agreement, dated October 27, 2024, was already in effect when the Landlord sent the email on November 7, 2024. In other words, irrespective of the Landlord’s email, the Tenant had already assumed the responsibility for the payment of the rent for the new unit.

Regarding the interruption to the supply of water, electricity, and internet service, the Tenant did not request any applicable remedy for this issue . I find the requested remedies for moving and storage costs, and the difference in rent, are not appropriate for this claim.

The Tenant testified that she incurred moving costs of $300.00 due to the improper notice of termination but had no invoice because the amount was paid to her friends in cash. The Landlord opposed this request and demanded a bank statement showing the amount was withdrawn. While the Tenant had no other evidence to substantiate her claim, I find on a balance of probabilities that she incurred reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses.

There is no dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit, and there are unavoidable costs associated with moving . The amount requested by the Tenant is reasonable considering that the Tenant’s roommate in file LTB-T-096507-24, incurred $316.40, as seen from her invoice, in moving from the rental unit to their newly shared unit. However, without any other corroborating evidence, I find it fair to only award the Tenant $200.00 in moving expenses. T1 Application

The parties agreed that the Tenant paid a last month's rent deposit of $1,000.00 on September 15, 2023. The Tenant requested a refund of the last month's rent deposit because it was not applied to the last month of the tenancy.
The Tenant also requested an order for the Landlord to pay the interest on the last month's rent deposit which she calculated as $69.50.
The Landlord opposed the request because the Tenant did not pay any rent in November 2024 prior to vacating the rental unit.

Section 106 (10) of the Act provides that a Landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a Tenant has paid to the Landlord or to a former Landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the last month’s rent deposit together with interest for a one-year period.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by s.106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or about July 3, 2017. The rent for the unit at the date of occupation was $1500.00 per month. The Tenant paid the Landlord $2800.00 toward first and last month’s rent by interac transfer which is confirmed by Exhibit 1 to the hearing (DOC6797935) and [name] (DOC679737) the Tenant’s bank statement. A further $200.00 was paid in cash while the two parties were sitting in the Landlord’s Jeep.

Exhibit 3 (DOC6797938) is a rent ledger created by the Tenant, and not disputed by the Landlord, shows that the Tenant paid rent for every month that he was in possession of the rental unit; including and up to the month of April 2025.
The Landlord delivered an N12 Notice to the Tenant on April 14, 2025 with a termination date of July 3, 2025. The Tenant vacated the unit on May 7, 2025.

The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant did not pay a last month’s rent deposit. He stated that he cannot access his bank records to review the transactions in his account. He further says that even if the Tenant paid the additional funds it was not a last month’s rent deposit. He testified that this is corroborated by the fact that the lease does not call for a last month’s rent deposit.

The Rental Agreement was made Exhibit 4 to the hearing ([name]). This document predates the requirement of landlords to use LTB approved forms for leases. The document consists of one page and contains the illegal term in paragraph 4(f) that if the Tenant is behind in rent for 30 days the locks to the rental unit can be changed by the Landlord. I give no weight whatsoever to the Landlord’s contention that the rent deposit doesn’t exist because it is not in the lease.

The affirmative, uncontradicted, evidence is that the Tenant provided the Landlord with $3000.00 before moving into the unit and I accept the Tenant’s evidence that half of that money was a last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord also failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). However, because of the one- year limitation for Tenant’s applications under the Act the Tenant may only claim interest for one year back from when the application was filed which is November 15, 2025. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to claim interest from October 15, 2024 to today’s date.

Because the Tenant occupied the unit for 7 days in May, 7 days of rent ($345.20) have been subtracted from the last month’s rent deposit owing to be paid to the Tenant. As well interest has been calculated on the amount of the deposit less the 7 days daily rent.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,285.53. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 minus $345.20 equals $1154.80 (7 days rent calculated as yearly rent divided by 365 equals $49.32 daily rent) for the last month's rent deposit. • $82.73 on $1154.80 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026.

If the Landlord do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must provide compensation to the Tenant as set out in this [name]. [name], Burden of Proof and Admissions

On an application for service of a N12 Notice of Termination for the Landlord’s own use in bad faith, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Additionally, subsection 57(5) of the Act provides that it is presumed, unless contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a Landlord served a Notice of Termination under section 48 in bad faith if after the N12 Notice of Termination is given and within 12 months of the Tenant vacating the unit, the Landlord advertises the rental unit for rent (among other activities).
The Tenant testified that in accordance with the N12 Notice to Terminate served and subsequent [name] dated January 30, 2025, she vacated the rental unit and moved out on February 10, 2025.
The N12 Notice identified the Landlord, his spouse and child as the intended occupants of the rental unit. The Landlord did serve the N12 Notice in bad faith

The Tenant testified that she was in the neighbourhood in August 2025 and went to see the Landlord to say hello as she felt that they had a good relationship in the past and wanted to see him. However, when she went to the rental unit expecting to find him there, he was not there and instead she found 4 new tenants were living there.
She spoke with one of the Tenants and that is how it came to her knowledge that the Landlord had rented out the unit to new tenants after she had vacated the unit.

The Tenant also testified that at some point one of her friends went to the rental unit to see her but instead found new tenants living at the rental unit. The Tenant was unable to confirm when this incident took place, but she thinks that maybe it was before August 2025.

The Landlord did not appear at the hearing today but the Tenant did direct me to DOC ID 7887059 and 788063 – Exhibits 2 and 3 whereby the Landlord had written an email to the Tenant stating that he has all the evidence and proof that his nephew and his nephew’s family are living in the unit and will bring this all to the Tribunal at the hearing. However, no evidence was presented before me today to show that the N12 Notice to Terminate was not served in bad faith. As set out above, the N12 notice identified that the Landlord, his spouse and child intended to occupy the rental unit. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that the notice was served in good faith.
As a result, I find the Tenant has demonstrated all of the required elements under subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies

The Tenant was paying $1,711.55 per month in rent to the Landlord. The Tenant’s new rent is now $2,950.00 per month, which amounts to a $1,238.45 per month increase in rent. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $14,861.40 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

DOC ID 7882955 – Exhibit 1 confirmed that the Tenant had incurred moving costs of $1,500.00. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,500.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $16,409.40. This amount represents: • $14,861.40 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from February 2025 to January 2026. • $1,500.00 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: ential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 204, 55 Talos Ottawa ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 31, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, Anne Skelly (‘LLR’), and the Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘LLA’), attended the hearing. As a preliminary matter, LLR submitted that LLA is not the Landlord as named in the T1 application. LLR stated LLA is an employee of Sleepwell Property Management, which is the Landlord’s acting property manager company. LLR then explained that the rental unit property is the subject of bankruptcy proceedings, which have placed the property under the care of the court appointed receiver, B. Riley Farber Inc. I find it is B. Riely Farber Inc and its property management company who are the landlords under this tenancy at bar. LLR sent the LTB a copy of the full name of the current landlord and sent a copy to the Tenants. With no objections being raised for consideration, I accepted the corrected name of the Landlord who should be the one named under this application, and have amended the title of proceedings above to reflect this change.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved one of two allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the claim for the $1,750.00 rent deposit is denied but the claim for the $50.00 key deposit is successful. The order below reflects this result and includes the reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee.

The parties agreed that the Tenants made their payments in respect of the rental unit to Sleepwell Property Manager who manages the rental unit property. They also agreed the Tenants paid a rent deposit of $1,750.00 and a key deposit of $50.00 to the Landlord. Documents submitted into evidence to support these facts were TT#1 (Sept 25/2026 text messages exchange) and TT#2 (Sept 26/2026 e-transfer confirmation and application approval).

LLR submitted that the $50.00 key deposit claim is not in dispute as the Landlord agrees that deposit needs to be returned; she added the Landlord is fully prepared to return that deposit to the Tenants.
MsPW provided most of the testimony for the Tenants. She was cross-examined by LLR.

MsPW testified that the Tenants viewed the rental unit before applying for a tenancy agreement. The Tenants submitted a rental application online on September 24, 2025 when they were informed (orally, not in writing) they would get extra storage as part of their tenancy. MsPW stated they told LLA that storage was a very important requirement for the Tenants if they were to live there.

When they were told their rental application was approved/accepted, MsPW said the Tenants were required to pay the two deposits in order for a lease to be drawn up and forwarded to them. MsPW confirmed that they were aware of the Landlord’s position that the rent deposit was not refundable.
MsPW also confirmed that in her discussions with LLA, LLA gave the Tenants an option to accommodate their storage needs, because the underground parking lot did not currently have any vacancy.

When they received the lease, the Tenants found that no extra storage was included. MsPW testified the Tenants then promptly informed LLA they were not going to sign the lease and requested their deposits be paid back to them. This decision was made and communicated on or about September 25, 2025. MsPW stated she viewed online advertisements for rentals in the complex on September 25th and found the rental unit was still advertised for rent (exhibit TT#3), thus leading her to conclude that the rental unit was still up for possible renting.
LLA’s testimony confirmed some of MsPW’s testimony. LLA was cross-examined by MsPW.

LLA stated that after the Tenants viewed the rental unit and asked for a rental application. They were sent two applications (one for each tenant) and the terms in the applications clearly set out the rent deposit requirement and how it would be treated (exhibit LL#2- MsPW’s filed-in/signed application). LLA confirmed that MsPW did text-message LLA three concerns about renting, as shown in exhibit TT#1. The three issues were: (i) keys; (ii) cleaning and (iii) storage. LLA referred to the reply she gave the Tenants, also set out in part in TT#1.

LLA said the Tenants wanted two sets of keys, not one, and LLA told them the Landlord would give them two sets. LLA informed the Tenants the Landlord has a dedicated cleaning staff that would attend the unit before the tenancy commenced. LLA then informed the Tenants that the only storage available would be in the underground parking lot where some parking spots had wider/larger physical space for some storage by residents. LLA informed the Tenants that no underground spots were available at that time but she would place them on a waiting list for underground parking. In the meantime, LLA indicated the Tenants could be assigned an above-ground parking spot at a discounted rate.
LLA confirmed the Landlord sent written confirmation that the Tenants had been accepted to become tenants of the rental unit (exhibit LL#1 – September 24/2026 email message).

LLA confirmed the Tenants paid the two deposits and asked for a lease. LLA confirmed the Tenants then requested a return of their deposits as they had decided they would not sign the lease and not move into the rental unit on October 1, 2025. LLA testified she did not know or was able to forecast that there would be a loss of income for the rental unit. She confirmed that when a unit is rented, it takes more than 24 hours to be able to remove rental ads from “RentSync” including all other advertisement platforms the Landlord advertises over. LLA stated she is generally aware of statutory requirements and limitations respecting deposits. LLA confirmed that the Landlord was unable to re-rent the unit for October 2025, finding new tenants only afterward.

In final arguments/submissions, LLR provided a couple of prior LTB orders and a case law citation in support of the Landlord’s position that the claim respecting the $1,750.00 deposit be denied. I noted that I am not bound by any prior LTB order but I do rely upon the Act and court decisions to provide authoritative direction on residential tenancy claims. Analysis
The T1 application claims “Reason 2” -- i.e. the Tenants paid an illegal charge to the Landlord, the total amount of that charge being $1,800.00 ($1,750.00 rent deposit and $50.00 key deposit).
The key deposit claim was not disputed by the Landlord and so the Tenants are successful with that claim.
With regard to the $1,750.00 rent deposit, I find that first, the deposit itself which was collected by the Landlord on September 24, 2025, was lawful.

To be clear, sections 105 and 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) confirm that the Landlord’s collection of a rent deposit was lawful. For easy reference, those sections are reproduced below. “105 (1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.”
The only question left to be addressed/determined under the T1 claim, then, is whether the $1,750.00 rent deposit collected by the Landlord was retained by the Landlord unlawfully.
On a balance of probabilities, I find that the answer is “no”, and thus I deny the T1 claim in respect of the rent deposit being retained unlawfully by the Landlord.
For an agreement to be a legally binding contract, it generally requires an offer and acceptance, an intention to create a legal relationship, and an exchange of consideration

Here, I was satisfied from the parties’ evidence that a binding tenancy agreement was indeed reached. This agreement started with the rental application that was filled in and signed by the Tenants after viewing the rental unit (LL#2). That rental application contained terms and conditions which the Tenants agreed with. The rental application in effect represented the offer by the Tenants to have them considered for a tenancy. The Landlord’s approval/acceptance of the Tenants’ rental application was communicated to them by email (LL#1 and TT#2), which September 24/2025 email contained specific rent- terms information about the rental unit the Tenants wanted to rent. For example, the monthly rent was $1,750.00 for the rental unit. After being accepted for tenancy, but certainly before they were able to move in, the Tenants paid a rent deposit of $1,750.00 which signified something of value being exchanged between the parties (i.e. consideration). Finally, it was clear both parties had the legal capacity to enter into the tenancy agreement (i.e. they both met landlord and tenant definitions, respectively, under the Act).

Concurrently, the Tenants raised three issues with the Landlord, which I find were reasonably and timely addressed by the Landlord so as to confirm the agreement that had been reached. With specific regard to the third storage issue, I am of the view that placing the Tenants on a waiting list for underground parking and the Landlord’s offer to give the Tenants discounted outside parking were good faith, successful efforts to help the Tenants realize a move-in on October 1, 2025 and to deal reasonably with their storage needs temporarily.
I was also satisfied that the Landlord was quite prepared to give vacant possession to the Tenants for their October 1, 2025 move-in.

To be clear, the Landlord did not, at any time, consent to cancelling the tenancy agreement the parties had reached. Basic contract law does not allow for one party to unilaterally change terms of a binding agreement, especially material terms such as was the case here.

Subsection 107(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s responsibility to return a rental deposit if vacant possession is not given to the tenant. It states: “107(1). A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant”.

Nothing in the hearing was submitted to suggest that the Tenants were unable to move into the rental unit because the Landlord denied the Tenants vacant possession or that the Landlord interfered with, or prevented, the Tenants’ ability to move in. Instead, I find it was the Tenants who decided not to proceed with the tenancy five days before the tenancy was supposed to begin.

For my findings above, I rely on Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 in which the Court of Appeal considered the proper interpretation of subsection 107(1) of the Act. In quick summary, the Court of Appeal agreed that subsection 107(1) of the Act should not apply when a landlord is willing/able to provide possession, but the tenant refuses to move in.

For the sake of completeness in my analysis, I also considered the Tenants’ communicated decision of not moving in as a “notice” of tenancy termination (the actual lease was not adduced by either party at the hearing.)
Sections 44 and 47 of the Act do allow a tenant to terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the fixed term by giving 60 days’ notice to a landlord.

As no fixed-term was identified for me to review, I assumed the tenancy at bar was going to be at least a month-to-month tenancy. I find the Tenants’ texted “notice” of termination, dated September 25, 2025, did not comply with the Act. To be clear, under month-to- month tenancies, a minimum of 60 days’ prior notice is a strict statutory requirement.
As the Tenants’ texted “notice” was not in compliance with the Act and the Landlord did not agree to terminate the tenancy, subsection 88(1)1. of the Act would apply.

Section 88 of the Act states: “88 (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. 2. If the tenant abandoned or vacated the rental unit without giving any notice, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a notice of termination had the tenant, on the date that the landlord knew or ought to have known that the tenant had abandoned or vacated the rental unit, given notice of termination in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.”

For clarity, the references to section 96 and 145 of the Act above do not apply to this case. Section 96 of the Act relates to a tenant who attempts to assign a tenancy. Section 145 of the Act relates to a tenant living in a care home who wishes to terminate a care home tenancy. Subsection 88(1)2. of the Act (as set out above) does not apply to this case because that subsection only applies when a tenant does not give any notice at all to terminate a tenancy.

In the matter before me, the Tenants’ “notice” falls under subsection 88(1)1. of the Act. As such, arrears are calculated to the earliest date that proper notice could have been given. This was at least a monthly tenancy running from the first day of each month to the last day of each month. So, the termination date must be the last day of a month and at least 60 days after notice was given. Therefore, the earliest termination date that could have properly been listed on a notice of termination that was served/given on September 25, 2025 would have been November 30, 2025.

In parallel with subsection 88(1)1., subsection 88(4) and section 16 of the Act also require the LTB to consider whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to mitigate their losses. I was satisfied that the Landlord attempted to mitigate losses by trying to re-rent the rental unit after the Tenants made their unilateral decision. (I also note as an aside that the Landlord even tried to offer the Tenants another unit to rent in another one of the Landlord’s buildings that had better storage facilities immediately available.)
Given that the tenancy was not lawfully terminated, the Tenants remained liable for rent up to the earliest proper termination date.

With the Tenants not paying anything more to the Landlord, such as rent on October 1, 2025, the Landlord lawfully was permitted to use the $1,750.00 rent deposit to cover October 2025 rent. And this is in fact what the Landlord ended up doing.
As the Tenants were successful in part with their T1 application, they are entitled to a reimbursement of their $48.00 filing fee. Reference is made to the LTB’s Interpretation Guideline no. 3.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $98.00. This amount represents: • $50.00 for the key deposit collected but not returned; and • $48.00 for the T1 application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount of $98.00 owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 20, 2026 ___________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 47, 2418 [address] BURLINGTON ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on April 22, 2026. The Tenants and the Landlord's [name], [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenants alleged that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The issue in this case is whether or not the Landlord by an email dated October 23, 2023, indicated an intention to waive the right to collect the rent for the last month of the tenancy.
As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The tenancy commenced in November 2023, and by December 1, 2025, the Tenants transferred their tenancy from the rental unit into a different unit.

Prior to the start of the tenancy, the Tenants received an email from the Landlord on October 23, 2023, stating ‘Please note the rent is $2975 and currently have a “no last month rent” incentive. The money order for the application which is generally kept as a last month rent will be used as a first month rent if you decide to take this incentive.’
The tenancy agreement dated November 1, 2023, states that ‘A rent deposit is not required’ and that the Tenants will pay a rent deposit of $0.00.

The Tenants believed that the “no last month's rent ” incentive meant that they were not required to provide a rent deposit to cover the final month of the tenancy. Hence, the Tenants interpreted that t o mean that they were entitled to a rent-free last month in the unit . The Landlord disagreed with the Tenants’ assertions.

Following discussions about the transfer to the new unit, the Landlord on November 5, 2025, sent an email to the Tenants stating, ‘I did a little bit of digging and the last month rent deferral incentive was added after the [name] was created.’

On November 6, 2025, the Landlord sent another email to the Tenants informing them that in order to transfer their tenancy from the rental unit, they were required to pay the rent for November 2025 . The Tenants complied with the request and subsequently filed this application seeking a refund of the payment.

Based on all the evidence, I find that the Landlord’s “no last month rent” incentive was simply an enticement to enable new tenants to both secure a unit, and to save an extra month’s rent by only paying for the first month of the tenancy . The payment of a rent deposit for a unit is quite different from the obligation to make the actual payment when it comes due. There is nothing i n the October 23, 2023 email that could reasonably be interpreted as an intention by the Landlord to waive their statutory right to collect the rent for the last month when it came due . A waiver of the rent payment is an uncommon practice and had the Landlord intended to do so, it would have been clearly expressed in writing, leaving no room for misunderstanding.
In addition, t he tenancy agreement simply says that a last month's rent deposit is not required, not that the rent for the last month is waived.

As the evidence does not prove that the Landlord waived the right to collect rent for the last month, the Tenants were responsible for that payment. Hence, the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order requiring [name] (the ‘Tenant') to pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of-pocket costs that are the result of the Tenant's failure to pay utility costs she was required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement (the ‘L10 application’). In the L10 application, the Landlords also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Former Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex. In file number LTB-T-096673-24, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlords collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 application’). These applications were heard by videoconference on July 29, 2025 and October 27, 2025. The Landlord [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the conclusion of the evidence presented in respect of the L10 application on July 29, 2025, the parties submitted jointly that these applications should be heard together in the interests of consistency and expediency because they have issues and evidence in common; and the Board agreed. Therefore the Tenant and the Landlord [name] returned before me on October 27, 2025 to present additional evidence and submissions in in rest of both applications.

In the L10 application, the Landlords claim that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 15, 2024 leaving them with $7,987.32 for various items of damage and $67.86 in unpaid utilities consumed for the period for the period December 1, 2024 to December 10, 2024.
In the T1 application, the Tenant seeks to recover the unused portion of prepaid rent.

The Tenant gave the Landlords an N9 notice of termination on November 15, 2024 setting out November 15, 2024 as the date of termination and vacated on that date. The Tenant acknowledges that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not allow her to unilaterally terminate the tenancy before the end of its term. As it turned out, the Landlords successfully mitigated their losses by re-renting the unit as of December 9, 2024. The Tenant accepts her liability for rent up to that date. But the Tenant prepaid the equivalent of four month’s rent at the start of the tenancy and also paid her monthly rent as it fell due each month. She would like unused portion refunded.

The substance of the dispute is the Landlords’ claim for damages and utilities. The Landlords acknowledge they must refund the unused portion of the $12,000.00 they collected as prepaid rent but they would like deduct their own expenses. 8. The following claims in the L10 application are not seriously in dispute: (a) The Tenant concedes that she did not return the two garage door openers but argued it is covered by the key deposit the Landlords collected but did not return. The Landlords agreed they received the keys and have not returned the $200.00 deposit. The Tenant did not dispute the $100.00 claimed for the garage door openers. The T1 application will be amended to include a claim for return of the key deposit. The cost of the garage door openers will be deducted and the Landlords ordered to refund the remainder. (b) The Tenant agreed that she damaged and did not replace the window covering on the front door. She did not dispute the $75.00 claimed and it shall be awarded to the Landlords. Utilities 9. The Tenant agrees that she was obliged to pay utilities under the tenancy agreement. The dispute is about whether she should pay for the period ending December 10, 2024 as claimed or until November 15, 2024 when she moved out. I can see no principled reason why the Tenant’s liability for utilities should end any earlier than her liability for rent. It could be argued that the Tenant did not consume whatever utilities were charged after she moved but I find having committed to pay them for the duration of the tenancy, she cannot avoid that liability by unlawfully terminating the lease easy. The Landlord will be awarded $67.86 for unpaid utilities. [name] 10. The Landlords claim that the Tenant damaged the lawn in the backyard when she installed her hot tub. They also claim that the Tenant neglected to care for the lawn in the front yard. They have claim $3,000.00 to resod the entire property based on a verbal quote they received from someone willing to do it for that price. They have not incurred this expense. 11. The Tenant responds that she installed the hot tub with the Landlords’ permission and repaired what little damage it caused. She has filed a receipt showing she paid $60.51 for sod. The Landlords say the repair is insufficient. 12. The Landlords showed me pictures of the lawn as it looked on the day the Tenant vacated. The pictures show a lawn that is not pristine in any sense but I am unable find that it shows signs of damage beyond normal year and tear. They did not show me pictures of what it looked like before. This claim must be dismissed because I find there is insufficient credible evidence to prove either liability or quantum on a balance of probabilities. The [name] 13. The Landlords seek $550.00 to replace a used fridge. The parties agree that the Landlords put in a new fridge when the Tenant moved in and stored the used one in the garage at the Tenant’s request for use by the Tenant and also that the Tenant took it with her without the Landlords’ permission. The Tenant says that the freezer portion of the appliance was broken and that the Landlords intended to dispose of it anyway. She said she took it away because the incoming tenant wanted it gone. 14. At the hearing, the first-named Landlord testified he had priced a used fridge of similar make and vintage and found it would cost $550.00. The Landlords gave me no particulars about the fridge and gave no corroboration for the amount claimed. 15. I find the Tenant’s version of events more probable: that the Landlords were discarding the used fridge anyway and that the Tenant removed it in keeping with her obligation to deliver vacant possession. Therefore I find this claim must be dismissed because there is insufficient credible evidence to prove either liability or quantum on a balance of probabilities. [name] 16. This claim alleges that in installing the hot tub, the Tenant damaged two of the sprinkler heads in the backyard. The Landlord had no pictures but the Tenant conceded she can’t deny this damage because she doesn’t know. The sprinkler heads were covered by grass and not readily visible. I am prepared to accept the Landlord’s unchallenged evidence and award the $150.00 claimed which I find to be a fair and reasonable cost to reinstall two sprinkler heads. [name]16. The Tenant acknowledges she had agreed to pay for duct cleaning. The incoming tenant wanted them cleaned because the Tenant had kept a pet. The Landlords say they only agreed to allow the Tenant to keep a pet on condition that she accept this expense. The Tenant later took advice and resiled from the agreement taking the position that she is not responsible for such costs. I am inclined to agree. Tenants are only responsible for the ordinary cleanliness of the rental unit, not for preparing it to the standards expected by an incoming resident. This claim must be dismissed because there was no evidence to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant or her pet caused any undue soiling to the ducts. Summary 17. The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,000.00 on March 15, 2024 and did not pay interest when the tenancy ended. Interest in the amount of $50.55 is owing to the Tenant for the period March 15, 2024 to November 15, 2024. 18. The Landlord must refund the Tenant $12,250.55 representing $12,000.00 of prepaid rent, $200.00 key deposit and $50.55 of interest on the last month’s rent deposit subject to the following deductions: (a) $67.86 for unpaid utilities. (b) $100.00 for the cost to replace garage door openers. (c) $75.00 for the cost to replace the window covering on the front door. (d) $150.00 costs to replace the damaged sprinkler heads. (e) $2,367.12 rent owing for the 24-day period from November 15, 2024 to December 9, 2024. (This amount is calculated as follows: $3,000.00 per month multiplied by 12 months divided by 365 days multiplied by 24 days) 19. Divided success. No costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $9,490.57. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing. 1. If the Landlords does no pay the Tenant $9,490.57 on or before January 17, 2026, the Landlords will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
