issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants, $4,198.00.

The tenancy for the three-bedroom rental unit commenced on August 31, 2025, and ended on October 31, 2025, after the parties signed an Agreement to End the Tenancy (N11). The termination date in the notice was October 31, 2025.
The lawful monthly rent was $3,850.00.

The Tenants paid three months rent at the commencement of the tenancy. The first month’s rent was applied to September 2025, and the second month’s rent was applied to October 2025. The Tenants requested an order for the Landlord to refund the last month's rent deposit which was not applied to any period of the tenancy.

The Tenants also requested a refund of the key deposit of $300.00 which was not refunded by the Landlord after the Tenants returned the keys . The Tenants made each of these payments on August 26, 2026.
The Landlord stated that the Tenants are not entitled to the last month's rent deposit since they did not give a 60-day notice to vacate.

The Landlord also stated that the Tenants did not return the keys to the basement area of the rental home. The parties agreed that on November 1, 2025, the Landlord in an email thanked the Tenants for returning the keys to the unit. On November 5, 2025, the Landlord informed the Tenants that the basement keys were missing. The Tenants maintained that they returned all the keys.

Section 106 (10) of the Act provides that a Landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a Tenant has paid to the Landlord or to a former Landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

In this case, the tenancy ended on October 31, 2025, but the last month's rent deposit was not returned by the Landlord even though the rent was already paid for the month. The Landlord argued that the Tenants di d not give a 60-day notice of termination . However, section 37 (3) of the Act provides that a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy . Therefore, the Landlord must return the full last month's rent deposit of $3,850.00 to the Tenants.

Section 105 (1) of the Act, states that the only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit and section 134(1) specifically prohibit the collection of a key deposit. Section 17 of O’Reg. 516/06 to the Act provides for certain exceptions from section 134(1) including “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.

Although the Landlord argued that the Tenants did not return the full set of keys, in his email to the Tenants on November 1, 2025, he thanked them for returning the keys . In his subsequent email, the Landlord stated that the basement keys were not returned but I have insufficient evidence to support the assertion. For example, no documentary evidence was provided to show that the Landlord incurred any costs to replace the keys.

Based on all the evidence , I am satisfied that the key deposit of $300.00 is more than “ the expected direct replacement costs” for the keys and was not refunded to the Tenants at the end of the tenancy . Therefore, the key deposit was illegal and must be returned to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,198.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $3,850.00 for the last month's rent deposit, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This combined T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on March 12, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant moved into the rental unit on October 15, 2021, and paid prorated rent of $600.00 for the remainder of October 2021. Pursuant to the written lease agreement the tenancy commenced on November 1, 2021. The lawful monthly rent was $1,200.00. A copy of the written lease agreement was submitted into evidence.
The tenancy was subsequently terminated by a previous Board order issued August 21, 2025, in file number LTB-L-033189-25, which terminated the tenancy effective May 8, 2025.
That order required the Tenant to pay the Landlord $7,885.68 for rent arrears owing up to May 8, 2025, and the filing fee.
The Landlord submits that this amount remains unpaid. The Tenant acknowledged that she stopped paying rent prior to the termination of the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that she stopped paying rent because the Landlord allegedly agreed to forgive rent due to ongoing maintenance issues in the rental unit. The Tenant submits that the Landlord later reneged on this agreement and served an N4 notice of termination. It was noted that at the previous L1 hearing, the Tenant did not raise any issues related to maintenance or tenants’ rights under section 82 of the Act and those issues are not addressed in that order.

The Tenant also testified that she received an N8 notice and an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy from the Landlord in October 2024, which caused confusion about whether the Landlord intended to terminate the tenancy or sell the property.

The Landlord acknowledged serving the Tenant various notices but stated that the notices were issued because the Tenant had stopped paying rent. Tenant’s Evidence Allegations that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally
Section 27 of the Act permits a landlord to enter a rental unit if the tenant receives written notice at least 24 hours before entry.
The Tenant testified that on October 12, 2024, the Landlord sent an email at approximately 6:00 a.m. advising that a real estate agent would attend the property.
The Tenant responded to the email stating that the agent should not attend; however, the agent arrived at approximately 3:00 p.m.
The agent, identified as Marina Iliuskina of Right at Home Realty Inc., attended to place a lockbox on the property.
The Tenant testified that she allowed the agent to enter the rental unit and used the opportunity to show the agent several repair issues.

The Landlord testified that she notified the Tenant via email on October 10, 2024, that an agent will be attending the property on October 12, 2204. It is the Landlord’s position that she gave the Tenant ample notice. A copy of the email to the Tenant from the Landlord was submitted into evidence which states that on October 12, 2024, between 2:40 pm and 4 pm a real estate agent would be attending the property.

Based on the documentary evidence before me, I find that the Landlord / Landlord's Agent did not enter the rental unit illegally as the Tenant was given sufficient written notice on October 10, 2024, for entry on October 12, 20024. I therefore find that the entry complied with section 27 of the Act and did not constitute an illegal entry.
Therefore, this part of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Allegations about harassment
Section 23 of the Act prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening or interfering with a tenant.

The Tenant testified that when she asked the Landlord sometime in September 2024 when she was going to do repairs to the rental unit the Landlord’s first reaction was “if you don’t like it move out.” During the hearing the Landlord did not address this allegation.

However, the Tenant did not provide sufficient details in support of these allegations. The Tenant was unable to provide the specific date when this comment was made. Further the Tenant did not provide evidence of any impact this incident had on her. While the comment described by the Tenant is not constructive communication between a landlord and tenant, a single comment without further evidence does not establish harassment within the meaning of section 23 of the Act.

Accordingly, there is insufficient evidence before me to make a finding that the Landlord engaged in a course of conduct that constitutes harassment and/or that a remedy is appropriate in the circumstances. This allegation is accordingly dismissed.
The Tenant also testified that she received an N4, N8 and N11 in October 2024, which caused uncertainty regarding the future of the tenancy.
The Landlord did not dispute giving the Tenant the notices.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant stopped paying rent in September or October 2024 and the Landlord issued an N4 notice and filed an L1 application on November 28, 2024, with file number LTB-L-097363-24. The Application was ultimately dismissed when the Landlord did not attend the hearing on March 10, 2025.
The Landlord subsequently served an N4 and filed a further L1 application on April 23, 2025, which ultimately resulted in the termination order issued August 21, 2025.
Serving notices permitted under the Act does not, by itself, constitute harassment.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, the Landlord was justified in serving in view of her success in the L1 application. In addition, the Landlord served an N8 for persistent late payment of rent and N11. Therefore, I cannot find that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Therefore, this part of the application is dismissed. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,800.00.
The Tenant applied to the Board under section 29 of the Act alleging that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act.

Section 20(1) states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s.20(1).

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Tenant evidence regarding maintenance

During the hearing, the Tenant identified, a total of four (4) maintenance issues. They are as follows: • Missing Smoke and CO2 detectors/alarms • Damaged Windows and doors • Flooding in basement • Electrical issues Missing smoke and CO2 detectors/alarms
The Tenant testified that the rental unit lacked functioning smoke and carbon monoxide alarms from the beginning of the tenancy (2021).

According to the Tenant, these alarms were not properly installed despite repeated requests. The Tenant was unable to recall dates or provide any documentary evidence wherein she alerted the Landlord to these issues.

The Tenant testified and the Landlord did not dispute, that sometime in September 2024 she requested alarms from the Landlord, and that the Landlord had shipped non-CSA approved alarms to the property in October 2024 and instructed the Tenant to install them in the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that in December 2024 she emailed the Welland Fire and Emergency Services Dept. Sometime in December 2024 a fire inspector attended the rental unit. A copy of the December 2, 2024, email was submitted into evidence.
The inspector confirmed that the rental unit did not contain proper smoke or carbon monoxide alarms.

The fire inspector temporarily installed the alarms the Landlord sent so that the Tenant would have some level of protection but informed the Landlord by email that compliant alarms needed to be installed.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not take action after receiving this communication from the Fire Inspector.

The Tenant emailed the inspector on March 3, 2025, and the inspector attended the property again on March 4, 2025, removed the non-compliant alarms, and installed CSA- approved smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.
The City billed the Landlord for the cost of the alarms and installation. A copy of the City of Welland fire and emergency services notes from March 4, 2025, was submitted into evidence.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the rental unit lacked compliant smoke and carbon monoxide alarms for a significant period.
The attendance of the municipal fire inspector and the installation of compliant alarms by the City supports the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord failed to ensure proper alarms were installed.

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenants’ submissions regarding the smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. The Landlord initially purchased the wrong alarms which she had sent to the Tenant in October. These were ultimately changed by the fire inspector in March 2025.

Based on this evidence, I find that the Landlord failed to ensure compliant smoke and carbon monoxide alarms were installed for approximately 6 months from September 2024 to March 2025 when the Fire Department installed them and sent the bill to the Landlord.
This constitutes a breach of section 20 of the Act. Electrical Issues

The Tenant also testified that she pointed out to the Fire inspector the basement and issues there concerning hanging electrical boxes. During the fire inspection, photographs were taken of electrical wiring in the basement that were the result of construction in 2021 that predated the start of the tenancy.
The Tenant stated that she told the inspector she intends to file a formal complaint with the ESA regarding these issues but will not do so until she finds a different place to stay.
An inspector from the Electrical Safety Authority later attended the property and informed the Tenant that no electrical permits had been issued for wiring modifications completed in 2021.
The Tenant testified that ESA directed the utility provider to disconnect electricity at the property.

The Tenant submits that electricity was ultimately disconnected and a final electrical bill was issued, around the time of May 2025 when she vacated the property. During the hearing the Tenant did not testify whether or not she paid the final bill.

The Tenant never reported this issue to the Landlord, and the was work was initiated by the ESA. When asked during the hearing if the Tenant ever had an issue with the electrical outlets or plugs during the tenancy the Tenant answered no she did not and was not aware of any issue until ESA informed her. The Landlord testified that after the Tenant moved out all was corrected with the electrical wiring in the unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord was aware of this issue during the tenancy or failed to address a reported electrical concern. Accordingly, I cannot reasonably find that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations in this regard and no remedy is warranted for this allegation. Therefore, this part of the application is dismissed. Basement flooding
The Tenant testified that the basement of the rental unit experienced water infiltration. The parties do not dispute that water entered the basement during the tenancy.

The Tenant provided background regarding an earlier flooding incident in 2022, stating that she notified the Landlord of a basement leak at that time but that no action was taken. The Tenant acknowledged that she did not follow up further with the Landlord and confirmed that she is not seeking remedies related to the 2022 incident because it falls outside the applicable limitation period. The Tenant provided this information for context only and testified that she stored personal belongings in the basement on pallets following the earlier incident.

The Tenant testified that the basement flooded again twice in November 2024. The Tenant was unable to recall the exact dates of these incidents or precisely when she notified the Landlord. However, the Tenant testified that she informed the Landlord and that the Landlord subsequently obtained estimates for repair work.

The evidence shows that contractors attended the rental unit on November 28, 2024, and November 29, 2024, to inspect the basement and assess the flooding. The Tenant testified that she permitted the contractors to enter the rental unit for that purpose.

In support of her evidence, the Tenant submitted an estimate dated December 2, 2024, describing the proposed repair work, including interior foundation waterproofing, crack repair, sump pump installation, waste removal, and related work.
The Tenant also testified that the sewer line was inspected by the City of Welland Water and Sewer Division on December 5, 2024.

According to the Tenant, a camera inspection conducted during that visit identified a collapsing section of sewer pipe which contributed to the water backup. The sewer line was cleared to remove debris and restore drainage. The Tenant testified that after this work was completed there were no further flooding incidents.

The Tenant also alleged that mold developed in the basement following the flooding; however, the Tenant acknowledged that no mold testing or professional assessment was conducted by the Tenant, the Landlord, or any contractor.
The evidence further shows that the Landlord and plumbers attended the property again on December 13, 2024, to conduct a further inspection.

Repair work began on December 16, 2024, and continued for approximately five days. The Tenant testified that the contractors performed significant work, including jackhammering portions of the basement floor for approximately three days in order to complete the repairs.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded to the flooding issue within a reasonable period of time after being notified. Contractors attended the property for inspection within days, estimates were obtained, and repair work commenced within approximately two weeks of the inspection.
I also note that the Tenant confirmed during the hearing that no further flooding occurred after the repairs were completed.
In these circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act in relation to the flooding issue.

Accordingly, I find that no breach of section 20 of the Act has been established with respect to the basement flooding. The Tenant also testified about water infiltration in the basement. There is no dispute about a water infiltration in the basement, but I find that it was addressed reasonably. Damaged window and Doors
The Tenant also testified that several doors and windows in the rental unit were deteriorated and contained areas of dry rot.

The Tenant testified that in September 2024, during a period of severe weather described as tornado-like conditions in the area, the exterior screen door swung open and the door chain struck the interior door glass, causing the glass pane to break.
The Tenant testified that she removed the broken glass and replaced the opening with a piece of wood as a temporary measure.

The Tenant acknowledged that she did not directly notify the Landlord about the damaged door. The Tenant testified that she instead showed the condition to Marina Iliuskina, a real estate agent acting on behalf of the Landlord, during an attendance at the property in October 2024.
The Tenant submitted one colour photograph showing the front door with a wooden panel installed in place of the broken glass.

The Landlord testified that she was not informed about the condition of the door by the Tenant and only became aware of it when she attended the rental unit on November 13, 2024, in relation to the basement flooding repairs.
The evidence indicates that the door was not repaired after the Landlord became aware of the damage.

Once the Landlord became aware that the door glass had been broken and replaced it with a temporary wooden panel, the Landlord had an obligation under section 20 of the Act to repair the door and restore it to a proper state of repair. Furthermore, there was evidence presented by the Tenant that the real estate agent was not acting as the Landlord’s agent for the purpose of satisfying her maintenance obligations under the act.
The failure to do so constitutes a breach of section 20 of the Act. Remedies
The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $14,400.00, which represents 100% abatement for twelve months of rent at $1,200.00 per month.

The Tenant also requested: • the Board order the Landlord to cease certain activities; • the Landlord pay an administrative fine; • the Board terminate the tenancy effective October 31, 2025; • compensation for a Toshiba laptop allegedly damaged during basement flooding; • $1,200.00 in moving expenses; and • $1,140.00 for increased rent she incurred after she moved out of the rental unit into a new residence.

With respect to the requests for moving expenses and increased rent, the Tenant did not provide testimony about these claims at the hearing and did not submit supporting documentation such as receipts or a new lease agreement.
Accordingly, these claims are dismissed for lack of evidence.

The request for compensation for a laptop allegedly damaged during the flooding was also unsupported by documentary evidence such as receipts, or proof of damage. Furthermore, since I dismissed the claim about the floods, I will not consider any remedies that flow from that allegation.
I therefore decline to award compensation for the laptop.

The request that the Board terminate the tenancy on October 31, 2025, cannot be granted as the tenancy was already terminated effective May 8, 2025, by a previous order of the Board. 83. The Tenant’s request for a rent abatement of $14,400.00 is significantly disproportionate to the issues proven in this application. 84. Rent abatements are intended to compensate tenants for the loss of use or enjoyment of the rental unit resulting from a landlord’s breach. 85. In this case, the proven breaches relate primarily to: • the temporary absence of compliant smoke and carbon monoxide alarms between approximately October and March 2025; and • the failure to repair the damaged door glass after the Landlord became aware of the issue in November 2024 to May 8, 2025, the date the Tenant vacated. • The failure to repair or replace the windows in the rental unit from September 2024 to May 8, 2025. 86. Considering the limited duration and scope of these issues, the amount requested by the Tenant is excessive. 91. Considering the nature and duration of the breaches, the lawful rent of $1,200.00, and the evidence before the Board, I find that a lump sum rent abatement of $1,800.00 is appropriate. 92. I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay a fine to the Board in this application. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. In my view the remedies awarded in this order will sufficiently encourage the Landlord to comply with the Act. 93. Consistent with the Divisional Court’s decision in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522, the parties may set off the amount owing by the Landlord in this order against the amount owing by the Tenant in order LTB-L-033189-25, issued by the LTB on August 21, 2025.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,800.00. This amount represents: • $1,800.00 for a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

Alternatively, the parties are authorized to deduct the amount ordered in this matter against the amount the Tenant is required to pay the Landlord in order LTB-L-033189-25 issued August 21, 2025. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue asserting that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, SO 2006, c 17 (the “Act”) does not apply pursuant to section 5(i).

The evidence and submissions in relation to the preliminary issue were concluded on April 16, 2026, and the parties were advised that the merits of the Tenants application would be scheduled on a future date if it is determined that the Act applies.
For the reasons that follow, the Act does not apply and accordingly, the Tenant’s applications are dismissed. Does the Act Apply?

Section 5 of the Act sets out exemptions from the Act, and section 5(i) provides: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located
Since it the Landlord raised the exemption and asserts that the Act doesn’t apply, the Landlord has the burden to prove their position on a balance of probabilities.

Any reference in this order to “landlord”, “tenant”, “rental unit”, “residential complex”, or other similar terms, are used for ease of understanding and are not determinative of the relationship between the parties or whether the Act applies. Landlord’s Evidence Dwayne [name]

The Landlord’s son, [name] [name] (DM) testified that the residential complex is a single family detached home with three bedrooms on the upper floor and 4 bedrooms in the basement. DM’s evidence is that he lives at the residential complex with his mother, father, grandmother, and his sister [name].

DM explained that there’s one kitchen in the basement of the residential complex that his family uses after the main floor stove was removed after purchasing the property. DM gave evidence that his sister lives in the fourth room in the basement and DM travels for work but stays in the third room in the basement on a full-time basis.
DM testified that his mother and sister use the kitchen in the basement, and he would occasionally cook there too. DM’s evidence is that it was mostly his mother and grandmother who did the cooking.

DM concluded his testimony by stating that it is made clear to anyone entering the residential complex that they are sharing spaces with the Landlord and their family. DM’s evidence is that the family moved in together and have lived there for 12 years with all of their mail and ID’s reflecting the address of the residential complex. DM further testified that he and his sister both still reside at the property.

During cross-examination DM explained that there was a chore schedule that was divided in three representing the three rooms being rented in the basement, but the Landlord’s family had other chores that were divided between themselves such as lawn care, cleaning, and mail retrieval. [name]12. [name] (GN) testified that he is a contractor that has done several projects for the Landlord beginning in approximately 2016/2017. 13. GN recalled doing a maintenance repair some time in 2024 and testified that at the time the Tenant, another gentleman, and both the Landlord’s son and daughter were living in the basement of the residential complex. 14. GN corroborated DM’s evidence that the residential complex has three bedrooms upstairs and the only kitchen with a stove is in the basement. DM also testified about the layout of the basement having one room on the left, the kitchen is on the right side, then there’s two more rooms and a door at the end of a hallway the leads to the room that the daughter of the Landlord occupies. 15. GN further testified that when he does maintenance work for the Landlord, he has seen them cooking in the basement and has been offered food by them. GN also gave evidence that he installed pot lights, hung pictures, and did painting in the room occupied by the Landlord’s daughter. 16. GN described his relationship to the Landlord as being a contractor but acknowledged that he was involved with rent collection at one point. [name]17. OC testified that he is a personal trainer and provided personal training sessions to the Landlord and her daughter. OC gave evidence that he was contacted in approximately November 2023 by the Landlord who has some mobility issues. 18. OC explained that he would provide training sessions to the Landlord a few times per week and would see the Landlord’s daughter weekly. 19. OC corroborated much of the prior testimony in relation to the layout of the interior of the property, and that there was only one kitchen in the house. OC testified that he would see DM at the house but was unaware of his circumstances or living arrangements because the extent of their relationship was described as being “acquaintances”. 20. OC testified on cross examination that he had seen the Tenant, but they were never formally introduced. OC’s evidence is that during a training session with the Landlord’s daughter the Tenant was making noise in the kitchen and they moved the training session to the Landlord’s daughter’s room. Aqeel Akhtar 21. Aqeel [name] (AA) testified that he is a mechanical engineer and knows the Landlord’s daughter because he is a client of her employer and she provides him with financial advice. 22. AA gave evidence that he would visit the Landlord’s daughter in the basement of the property and saw a small kitchen in the basement. AA testified that he recalled a with the Landlord’s daughter and the Tenant was cooking necessitating AA and the Landlord’s daughter to go to her room because it was too noisy. Tenant’s Evidence 23. The Tenant testified that there were three rooms in the basement and could not understand the testimony from the others that there were four rooms in the basement. 24. The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord has a daughter but denied knowing her name or that he shared a kitchen with her. 25. The Tenant explained that the three rooms in the basement were occupied by “[name]” and “an Indian guy”, and “some other guy from Africa”. The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord pointed at “[name]’s” room and said that her son lives here. 26. The Tenant further testified that he never saw the Landlord’s daughter walk out of her room or do anything in the basement. The Tenant believes that the Landlord and her son live upstairs but denied knowing where the Landlord’s daughter lives. 27. The Tenant also testified that there is a fourth door in the basement but doesn’t know what happens behind the door and vehemently denied sharing a kitchen with the Landlord or their family. 28. On cross examination the Tenant denied having an altercation with the Landlord’s daughter on January 9, 2024, and denied texting the Landlord to complain about her daughter using the stove on January 30, 2024. 29. The Tenant was also asked about an agreement that was signed when the Tenant took occupancy of the room. The document clearly indicates that the Tenant is required to share a kitchen with the owner of the property. The Tenant conceded that the signature resembles his but denied signing the document testifying that he wasn’t present on the date reflected on the document. 30. The Tenant first testified that he was not present on December 29, and that he did not sign any documents. The Tenant’s testimony changed to be that “if I signed something it was something to deceive me”. The Tenant then testified that he may have signed the document but not until some time in January. 31. The Tenant did not deny that he was told that he would be sharing space with the Landlord or their family, but believed he was “tricked” because the Landlord referred to “[name]” as being her son which the Tenant did not find out was untrue until after taking occupancy of the room. Analysis 32. The Act does not apply to living arrangements whose occupants are required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 33. In this matter four separate individuals testified, and their testimony was largely consistent on the following points: • The Landlord (owner) lives at the property; • The Landlord’s basement has three rooms, a kitchen, and a hallway leading to a fourth room; • The only kitchen in the property is in the basement; • The Landlord’s daughter lives in the fourth room; 34. When assessing the evidence of DM and GN their evidence was clear and largely corroborated by other witnesses. The evidence of GN is given slightly less weight because it was acknowledged he became involved in a rent dispute between the parties that goes beyond the role of just providing contractor services. 35. GN’s proximate relationship to the Landlord that was not initially disclosed during his testimony casts some doubt on the impartiality of his evidence. 36. Despite this, two other witnesses testified that they had professional relationships with either the Landlord or her daughter and much of that testimony was clear, consistent, and corroborated. 37. The Tenant’s testimony that he did not know the Landlord’s daughter, did not see her, and did not know her name lacks credibility when compared to the detailed testimony of the other witnesses. 38. The Tenant’s evidence was often inconsistent, self-serving, and unreliable. The Tenant first testified that there were three rooms in the basement but then acknowledged that there is a fourth door. When confronted with the proposition that there was another door in the basement the Tenant’s testimony then became that he didn’t know what happened behind that door. 39. The Tenant’s denial that there are four rooms in the basement contrasts with his subsequent testimony that there is another door in the basement. The Tenant conveniently relies on the position that he doesn’t know what happens behind the fourth door however, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord’s witnesses that the Landlord’s daughter resided behind the fourth door. 40. The Tenant first denied signing the agreement that indicates he would be sharing space with the Landlord, then his testimony changed to be that the Landlord must have “lifted his signature”. The Tenant denied being at the property on the date the agreement was signed but later acknowledged he was at the property on December 29. 41. The Tenant’s testimony changed again to be that he admits the signature is his and that “something was signed”, but argues that it was signed after the Landlord mislead him about “[name]” being her son. 42. The Tenant’s testimony often changed to support the narrative being asserted however, this ultimately undermined the credibility and reliability of the Tenant’s testimony. 43. It would not be unreasonable in the circumstances to draw a negative inference from the lack of testimony from the Landlord’s daughter but any negative inference that could be drawn is satisfied by the independent testimony of AA and OC. 44. The evidence before me is that the owner, her spouse, son, and daughter reside at the property. The consistent evidence is that there is only one stove (kitchen) and the Tenant was advised prior to taking occupancy that he would be required to share space with the Landlord and her son. 45. The Landlord’s son testified that his mother, grandmother and sister use the only kitchen in the house. While the Tenant argues that the Landlord deceived them that “[name]” was their son, this is still indicative that the Tenant was advised that they would also be sharing space with the Landlord’s son even if it was not “[name]”. 46. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that this property is occupied by the owner, and the occupants are required to share a kitchen with the owner. The evidence also supports a finding that the occupants are required to share a kitchen with the owner’s daughter, and to a lesser extend, the owner’s son DM. 47. In these circumstances, the rental unit is exempt from the provisions of the Act pursuant to section 5(i). Accordingly, the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Act does not apply.
The applications are dismissed. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $1,548.00. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he had to pay the Landlords a furniture deposit of $1,500.00 before the Landlord would provide him with the keys to the unit.
The Tenant testified that he vacated the unit November 16, 2025, and the Landlord told him that he would receive the return of the deposit on November 17, 2025 at 12:00 pm.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord claimed that he caused damage to the unit and the furniture and then refused to return the deposit. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord Jasmin Gill (JG) testified that they did collect a furniture deposit in the amount of $1,500.00 as they rented the Tenant a fully furnished condo.

JG further testified that the Tenant destroyed the condo and submitted pictures into evidence of the condo before the Tenant moved in and after the Tenant moved out, showing the damage and dirt left behind by the Tenant.
JG testified that they believed they were able to withhold the deposit because the Tenant was responsible for the damage he caused, which cost them over $4,000.00 to clean and repair.

The Landlord [name] testified that he had initially told the Tenant he would return the deposit but upon inspection of the unit and finding the damage, the dirt and some missing items, he did not return it. Analysis

It is uncontested that the Landlords requested a furniture deposit because they provided the Tenant a fully furnished condo. The deposit was collected for the purpose of ensuring the Tenant did not damage the furniture, so it meets the definition of a security deposit.
There is no provision of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) that would permit the Landlords to collect his kind of deposit.
Section 105(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) states: The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit in accordance with section 106.
Section 106(2) of the Act states: The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.

Section 134(1) of the Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no Landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) Collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

This means that the Landlords are not entitled to collect a deposit with respect to the furniture and they collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,500.00 which represents the return of the illegal furniture deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,548.00. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] and [organization] entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and did not meet their maintenance obligations.
reasons: The Tenant brings this application naming [name] [name], [name], and [organization] as respondent Landlords.
An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held on June 23, 2025 before Member [name]. Member [name] then directed that [name] be added to the proceeding as an additional Landlord.

At the hearing, the Tenant objected to the addition of Mr. [name]name], as she does not believe that he is a landlord of the unit, and in any event she does not want to bring this application against him.

Section 187(1) of the RTA provides that the parties to an application include “the landlord,” which necessarily means all landlords in a tenancy with multiple landlords. If Member [name] was of the view that Mr. [name]name] is a landlord of the unit, then it was appropriate to add him as a party in accordance with section 187(1).

Section 187(2) provides that I may add or remove parties as I consider appropriate. In this case, I do not find it appropriate to remove Mr. [name]name]. He objected to being removed and wished to exercise his right to participate as a party. At the hearing, he represented all the Landlords.

However, as this is the Tenant’s application, she is not required to seek any remedies against Mr. [name]name]. Hence, although he is a party to this proceeding, remedies will only be awarded against the other Landlords. Issues

The Tenant’s applications raised numerous allegations against the Landlords. The Landlords argued that some of the allegations did not contain sufficient particulars to be heard. For the reasons given orally at the hearing, I agreed with the Landlords and found that several of the allegations contained insufficient detail, especially a lack of dates. The Tenant had been warned at the ACC of the potential deficiencies in the applications, but had not amended them. I therefore found that the applications respecting those allegations would be dismissed.
Several of the other allegations occurred more than one year before the Tenant filed her application, and I also ruled that the applications respecting those allegations would be dismissed.

There remained several allegations that could have been heard. However, the Tenant only testified regarding one of the allegations, concerning maintenance of an oven. I invited her to give evidence regarding the remaining allegations, but she declined. The applications respecting the other allegations are therefore dismissed, as the Tenant has not adduced any evidence to support them.

The only issue for me to consider is the oven. The applications seek a rent abatement as compensation for the oven being in disrepair. At the hearing, the Tenant stated that she also wished to seek reimbursement for the cost of replacing the oven, as she replaced it herself on January 10, 2025. However, that remedy was not claimed in her applications, and she did not amend the applications to claim it. I therefore have no jurisdiction to consider that remedy.
Consequently, the only issue before me is whether the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period that the oven was in disrepair. Procedural issue

After the Tenant had put in her evidence, [name] testified and was cross-examined by the Tenant. Mr. [name]name] then testified briefly. At some point during Mr. [name]name]’s testimony, the Tenant disconnected from the videoconference hearing. Upon noticing her absence, I held the matter down, but she did not return. Eventually, I completed the hearing in her absence. The remainder of the hearing consisted of the Landlords’ closing arguments.

The Tenant missed her opportunity to cross-examine Mr. [name]name] and to make closing arguments, but could have done so if she had stayed connected or had reconnected after disconnecting. I am satisfied that she had the opportunity to fully participate. The oven Facts

On January 10, 2024, the oven in the rental unit malfunctioned. The Tenant says that the malfunction caused a fire inside the oven, which the Landlords deny. Nothing turns on whether there was a fire. It is common ground that the oven stopped working and needed repair.
The Landlords promptly responded and repaired the oven on January 12, 2024.

After the repair, the Tenant noticed that her food was burning when baked in the oven. On January 14, she wrote the following to the Landlords by email: Not sure if this is a concern and I can certainly turn the oven temperature down. Food is taking half the time to be done based on the recipe and I find the oven hotter than usual. My concern is there may be another problem.
On January 16, the Landlords replied to the Tenant and suggested that the oven might have previously been too cold, and that it might now be operating at the correct temperature.

On February 8, the Tenant followed up. The Landlords then offered to test the oven and asked when the Tenant would be home. The test did not happen. On March 2, the Landlords went to the unit to test the oven, but left when the Tenant did not answer the door.

The Tenant did not complain about the oven again, and the Landlords took no further action until they received notice of this proceeding in December, 2024. The Landlords then gave notice that they would test the oven on December 19. When they arrived on that date, the Tenant refused them entry on the basis that they were not certified electricians.
On January 10, 2025, the Tenant bought a new stove and installed it herself. Analysis

The Landlords were obligated to maintain the unit in a good state of repair. Having been informed on January 14 that the oven was not working properly, they should have investigated, determined whether there was an issue, and if so, repaired it.
The Tenant was not obligated to keep following up with the Landlords. The Landlords’ obligation to maintain the unit continued from the point that they knew about the disrepair.

Further, the Tenant was not required to arrange an inspection time with the Landlords. The Landlords should have given 24 hours’ notice, then entered in accordance with that notice to test the stove. The Tenant did not need to be home.

The Landlords did not meet their obligation to maintain the oven until December 19, 2024, when they gave a notice of entry and sought to test the oven pursuant to the notice. The Tenant illegally refused them entry on that date.

If the problem had persisted, the Landlords would still have been obligated to repair the oven, which would potentially have included taking legal action against the Tenant for refusing them entry. However, shortly after the December 19 incident, the Tenant replaced the oven herself. I do not find that the Landlords needed to take additional action between December 19, 2024 and January 10, 2025.
The Tenant is therefore entitled to a rent abatement from January 14 to December 19, 2024 in compensation for the disrepair.

When asked about the impact of the disrepair on her, the Tenant testified that she could not use the oven without burning her food. I do not find that testimony to be credible. If the oven was too hot, the Tenant could simply have set it to a lower temperature. She said as much to the Landlords in her January 14 email.

Given the minimal impact the disrepair ought to have had on the Tenant, I will award a 1% rent abatement. The monthly rent was $845.63, so a 340-day abatement comes to $94.53. The Tenant will also be awarded her filing fee of $53.00 for this application.
ordered: The Landlords [name] [name], [name], and [organization] shall pay the Tenant $147.53, which represents a rent abatement and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 15, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $578.15. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant [name] testified that they moved into the rental unit on December 29, 2018, and signed alone year lease at that time. The Tenant paid a last month rent deposit of $2395.00 on December 29, 2018.
The Landlord confirmed that he never paid interest on the last month rent deposit. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s are entitled to this interest. The Rent Differential

The Tenant’s also sought a differential of $115.00 on the basis that the rent was reduced during the tenancy and therefore when the last months rent was applied to the final month there were funds remaining which should be returned to them.

The Tenant testified that the tenancy became month to month after the initial lease until the parties signed a new lease with a reduced rent March 1, 2021. The Tenant testified that this was during the COVID-19 pandemic, and they had reached out to renegotiate the rent at a lower rate after comparing the unit to market rent.
The Tenant testified that they vacated October 31, 2025, at the time they vacated they were paying $2280.00 in rent. The Landlord agreed with this amount.
Therefore, the Tenant seeks the differential of $115.00 for the last month rent.

The Landlord testified that he never increased the rent for the first three years of the tenancy, and he actually lowered the rent for the Tenant’s by $300.00 during the tenancy, and even with subsequent rent increases the Tenant’s ended the tenancy paying $115.00 less than when the tenancy began.

The Landlord testified that the Tenants were not entitled to the differential because the Tenant’s ended up paying much less and the contract was for that amount. The Landlord also alleged that there were damages to the unit when the Tenant’s vacated which he was prepared to overlook until the Tenant’s filed the T1 Application.
The Landlord also encouraged me to take into account the relationship between the parties and the fact that the rent had been lowered.

Ultimately, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s are entitled to the differential sought. The last month rent deposit can only be applied to the last month of the tenancy which is October 2025. The rent for October 2025 was only $2280.00 while the last month rent deposit held by the Landlord was $2395.00. Therefore, the Tenant’s are entitled to $115.00 representing the difference.

I am not satisfied that the fact that the Landlord did not raise the rent during the first three years of the tenancy, and subsequently lowered the rent, or the allegations of damages to the rent unit entitles the Landlord to retain this differential. The Illegal Charge

The Tenant also testified that they paid a $150.00 key deposit on December 29, 2018, for two sets of keys and the garage key. The Tenant’s testified that the keys were never lost or replaced, and the deposit was never returned.
The Landlord confirmed that the key deposit was not returned after the Tenant’s vacated.
Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord illegal retained these funds and they shall be ordered returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $578.15. This amount represents: • $265.15 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $115.00 for the rent differential • $115.00 for the Illegal Charge • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background to tenancy and the application:
The tenancy began on October 24, 2023. The rental unit is a one-bedroom apartment. The lawful monthly rent is $1,485.00.
In the T6 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations with respect to a bat bug infestation and the balcony door seal in the rental unit.
In the T2 application, the Tenant alleges that the manner in which the Landlord addressed those issues substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit:

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations; it states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 6. [name]. Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 7. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that a landlord will not be held liable for breaching its maintenance obligations if it responds to a maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. 8. The sequence of events was largely undisputed. The Tenant notified the Landlord by text message on July 29, 2024, that bat bugs had been seen in the rental unit. The Landlord arranged for an inspection on August 6, 2024, at which time the infestation was confirmed. The first pest treatment took place on August 8, 2024. A second treatment took place on August 22, 2024. The Tenant reported seeing further live bat bugs on September 4, 2024. A third treatment was then scheduled for September 12, 2024. By September 26, 2024, the issue was reported to have been resolved. Tenant’s evidence: 9. The Tenant testified that he and his family were unable to comfortably use and enjoy the rental unit because they had a young child and did not believe the unit was safe while the infestation continued. The Tenant further testified that the female Tenant and the child were bitten in July and September 2024. Photographs of the bites were submitted into evidence. 10. The Tenant stated that the balcony door did not seal properly and that this allowed the bat bugs to continue entering the rental unit between July and September 2024. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not properly address caulking at the baseboards and that this also contributed to the infestation. 11. The Tenant testified that there was a bird’s nest on the balcony in July 2024 and that the nest was the likely source of the bugs. He stated that this was what he had been told by the exterminator during the inspection process. According to the Tenant, the nest contained swallows, and he was informed that these birds can carry bugs that are similar to bed bugs. However, the Tenant acknowledged that this belief was not based on his own specialized knowledge. He admitted that his understanding came from what he had been told by the exterminator, and he did not file any expert report or other documentary evidence to establish that the bird’s nest was in fact the source of the infestation. Landlord’s Evidence: 12. The Landlord called [name], the property manager, as a witness. Ms. [name]name] testified that the pest control company, [name], advised that there was a significant amount of clutter in the rental unit, which made it difficult to properly inspect and treat all affected areas. The Landlord submitted an email dated August 15, 2024, advising the Tenant to clean and declutter the unit so that treatment could be carried out effectively. 13. Ms. [name]name] also testified that [name] did not remove the bird’s nest because of environmental restrictions, and the pest control company was not legally permitted to remove it. She stated that the superintendent later removed the nest in either August or September 2024. 14. The Landlord’s evidence was also shows that the balcony door seal and issue was addressed on August 16, 2024, before the second treatment. The Landlord submitted a text message indicating that the door seal had been repaired or replaced as of that date. 15. Ms. [name]name] testified that [name] never advised management that the balcony door seal or the baseboard caulking was the cause of the infestation. She also referred to a service report dated September 26, 2024. According to Ms. [name], [name] attended on that date to inspect the unit and treat it if necessary and concluded that the issue had been resolved and that no further service was required. 16. Overall, Ms. [name]’s evidence was that the Landlord responded promptly to the complaint, arranged [name] attendances without significant delay once the issue was known, and was never advised by [name] that the unit was unsafe to occupy for an extended period. Analysis: 17. On the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord’s response was reasonable. Pest control attended within a short time after the initial report, and inspections or treatments occurred on three occasions between August and September 2024. It was undisputed that the Landlord continued to address the issue after the first treatment in accordance with the pest control technician’s recommendations. The service report dated September 26, 2024, indicated that there was no further bat bug activity. I find that the Landlord’s response to the bat bug issue was prompt, ongoing, and effective. 18. There is no evidence before me that it was necessary for the Tenant to vacate the rental unit during August and September 2024. The Tenant acknowledged that no one advised him to leave the unit and that no medical treatment was sought in relation to the bug bites. The Landlord’s evidence was that the unit was safe to re-enter approximately four hours after treatment. On the record before me, the decision to remain out of the unit for a longer period was the Tenant’s own choice. 19. I also find that the Landlord addressed each complaint raised by the Tenant within a reasonable time. The evidence shows that after the initial complaint, the Landlord arranged for professional inspection and treatment and continued with follow up attendance at approximately two-week intervals until the issue was resolved. 20. With respect to the Tenant’s position that the bird’s nest on the balcony was the source of the infestation, I find that the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to establish that fact. The Tenant did not submit expert evidence or documentary evidence confirming that the nest was the source of the bat bugs. In any event, the evidence shows that the balcony door seal was addressed by August 16, 2024, and the Landlord continued with treatment thereafter. 21. Consistent with [name], I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the bat bug issue or the balcony door seal. I find that the Landlord acted reasonably and in a timely manner after being notified by the Tenant. 22. I am also not satisfied that the Landlord breached section 22 of the Act. Although the infestation was undoubtedly frustrating for the Tenant, the evidence does not establish that any act or omission of the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlord responded reasonably to the issue and took appropriate steps to address it. 23. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 24. This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. March 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 30995 Date: 2026-04-20 In the matter of: [address] SCARBOROUGH ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on April 13, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: The application is amended to correct the spelling of the Tenant’s name.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

In the application filed on October 29, 2025, the Tenant claims that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act.
The Tenant does not state the Landlord failed to provide the required compensation. Rather, he did not cash the cheque in the required time frame and it became state dated and refused by the bank.
The Tenant said that the check was dated November 1, 2024. He attempted to deposit it around September 2025 and was advised by the bank that the 6-month validity period had expired.

The Tenant said that he negotiated a large payment with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy and the Landlord has not honoured their obligations. I note, no documentary evidence was led to support this claim.

The Landlord’s representative submits that the matter was mutually resolved by Board order LTB-L-097009-24, dated May 2, 2025. This was the hearing for the Landlord’s L2/N12 application where the parties resolved the issue with a Dispute Resolution Officer. The parties consented to an order where, amongst other things, the Landlord agreed to waive the rent owing for the month that is immediately before the month that the last month’s rent is applied.
For clarity, this means that the Tenant was provided with a month free from rent to acknowledge the compensation that the Tenant received but did not cash the cheque in a timely manner.
The Tenant confirmed that he did not pay rent for August 2025 and the last month’s rent deposit was applied to September 2025, the last month of the tenancy.

While the Tenant may believe that the Landlord agreed to pay a higher amount, the Tenant could have declined the terms discussed at the L2 hearing. However, the Tenant entered into the mutual agreement and the Tenant did not request to review the order issued May 2, 2025.
Given the above and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenant was provided with compensation for the month of August 2025. The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,655.00. Illegal Entry and [name].

The Tenant claimed the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit and changed the locks. On November 21, 2024, when the Tenant and his father returned to the rental unit to pick up his belongings after a hospital stay, the Tenant found his key to the exterior door to the residential complex non-functioning. On November 19, 2024 the Landlord sent a letter to the Tenant’s father, [name] and the Tennat stating he was being evicted summarily for breaching house rules. On November 21, 2024, the Tenant found many of his personal belongings on the front porch, placed there by the Landlord. Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, moved the Tenant’s belongings and altered the locking system of the residential complex to prevent entry by the Tenant without giving the Tenant replacement keys. Harassment
The Tenant claimed the Landlord harassed him by requiring him to contribute to group food, requiring him to engage in counselling, and by removing his belongings and placing them on the front porch.

The tenancy was a fixed term of 6 month with rent paid on a month-to-month basis. The Landlord’s letter ‘terminating’ the Tenant’s tenancy was without notice and not in proper LTB form, it was therefore not in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and given it’s impact on the Tenant, would in my view be unwelcome. The loss of housing, which was precarious for this Tenant and difficult to maintain, had a significant impact. I’m of the view this action of the Landlord rises to the level of harassment.

The Tenant testified that he was told he would be required, although he had no money, to engage in counselling offered by the Landlord and to pay for it. The Landlord sent a letter to the Tenant and his father outlining the ‘services’ offered and their exorbitant cost. The letter was not provided at the hearing. Although this was distressing to the Tenant, there was no evidence presented that this service was a mandatory requirement of the Tenancy. I cannot find based on the evidence provided that this offer of services rises to the level of harassment.

The Tenant was required to contribute to the group food costs. The residential complex is not a sanctioned group home, or a co-op, but a rooming house. The Landlord had no right to ask for and the Tenant no obligation to pay for food on a group basis. This request would be clearly unwelcome, considering that the Tenant is of low income and struggling financially. It is egregious that this ‘house rule’ if not followed could lead to the tenancy termination, and such a result is in my view harassment.

The Tenant also claimed that the Landlord charged $200.00 for a security deposit and $100.00 for internet hookup, which should have been included, according to the Tenancy Agreement. I find that these unlawful charges also harassed the Tenant, who, as noted above, is of limited means.

I find therefore that the Landlord harassed the Tenant by removing his belongings to the front porch, unlawfully entering his rental unit and requiring food to be paid at the rental unit and imposing unlawful charges contrary to the Act upon the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant claimed a rent abatement of $1,607.00 which included a portion of last month’s rent in the amount of $507.00 for November, rent paid for November in the amount of $800.00, $200.00 paid as an unlawful security deposit, and $100.00 for payment of internet services which should have been included in the tenancy according to the Tenancy Agreement.
I find that the Landlord had sufficient notice of the claim for $300.00 in unlawful charges, and I therefore grant that amount.

The Tenant paid rent for the period from November 9, 2024 to December 8, 2024. The Landlord held rent deposit in the amount of $800.00 and did not apply the rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy but retained it. The Landlord also did not return rent paid for November.

The remedy of rent abatement is appropriate in this case. Due to the illegal lockout the Tenant is obligated to pay only for the days from November 9 to November 18, 2024, when he did have access to the rental unit. The per diem amount claimed should be $526.00 for the last 20 days from November 19 to December 8, 2024 after the Tenant was locked out ($26.30 (800*12/365*10)), however the Tenant only claimed $507.00 so I will grant that amount.

In addition, I have considered that the Landlord is not entitled to retain the rent deposit for November 9 to 18 and also retain the rent paid for that month. Therefore the Tenant is entitled to a return of the $800.00 rent paid for November.
Accordingly, I find that the total rent abatement of $1,607.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant claimed replacement cost for property lost, stolen or discarded as a result of the Landlord’s actions. The Tenant and his father [name] both testified that another roommate told them another tenant had broken into Mr. [name]name]’s room and taken some of his belongings. Even on a balance of probabilities, there insufficient evidence to conclude the Landlord was responsible for the theft of Mr. [name]name]’s property from his room, or what items may have been stolen either from the room or the porch. The Tenant gave no evidence of any items missing other than his laptop. No receipts, or photos of missing objects were produced nor verbal evidence given of identifying features of the laptop or its value. I find the Tenant failed to prove the Landlord was responsible for any lost property and therefore will not award a remedy for property missing in this case.

The Tenant requested the Landlord return his property however, given it is unclear who took his property, whether the Landlord has control over it or access to it, what became of it, or what specific property was taken, I am unable to grant this request.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,655.00. This amount represents: • $1,607.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
