issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name], [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant’s household.
reasons: This matter had been adjourned on November 26, 2025, due to a scheduling overflow. An [name] was issued December 5, 2025, which itemized the issues to be addressed in the reconvened hearing.
This hearing proceeded based on the issues outlined for both the T6 and the T2 applications in the said [name].

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: frequent water shutoffs, odour of cannabis/tobacco smoke permeating the unit, renovations resulting in excessive dust in the unit, and a washroom ceiling leak/crack, occurred in the rental premises, which interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the premises and demonstrated a failure of the Landlords to meet their maintenance obligations.
Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant an abatement of rent of $8,000.00. [name]

This application address 4 areas of concern: frequent water shutoffs from December 2022 to the present, odour of cannabis/tobacco smoke from neighbouring rental units, and renovations which resulted in dust entering the rental unit and excessive construction noise (December 8, 2023 to December 15, 2023), and moving and damaging of the Tenant’s belongings during unit repairs (December 22 to December 24, 2022).

The Tenant testified on these issues as follows: (i) Frequent water shutoffs from December 2022 to present: the Tenant documented 38 times that she experienced shutdowns of water to the unit from December 2022 to the date of the hearing. A number of these dates were documented in DOC-4716442, filed in the portal. During these shutdowns, the Tenant was unable to do laundry, the water did not come through the taps in good condition, and the lack of water affected the ability to use the washroom, shower, and sinks. The Tenant testified that she works from home, and when these shutdowns occurred, she did not have water in the washroom and was unable to use the kitchen sink for food preparation. Also, she testified that the Landlords did not always provide notice of when the shutdowns would happen and often they would last a full day. (ii) Odour of Cannabis/tobacco smoke from neighbouring rental units: the Tenant testified that the smells came in through her vent. The Tenant filed an email dated June 26, 2023, in which she had complained to the Landlords about this issue (DOC-4782067). To address the situation, it appears that the vent was covered, and fans were installed, but she testified that this had not resolved the situation. She testified that keeping the fans on costs additional money for electricity. She testified that she is using medication to address her health issues arising from the smell. (iii) Renovations (December 8, 2023, to December 15, 2023) resulting in excessive dust entering the premises and excessive construction noise: the Tenant testified that the issue of excessive dust is a recurring problem, resulting from renovations undertaken by the Landlords. In the time frame noted, she dealt with layers of dust in her unit caused by the renovations, to the point where she could not have anyone else in her unit. I note that at the hearing the Tenant indicated this problem recurs every time there are renovations, but as per the [name], I am only considering the above-mentioned time frame. (iv) The Tenant did not provide details of the fourth item listed above – moving and damaging of the Tenant’s belongings during unit repairs – December 22 to December 24, 2022. T6 Application
The issues raised in the T6 application were bedbug and cockroach infestation, and a washroom ceiling leak/crack from January 16, 2023.

The Tenant testified on these issues as follows: (i) [name] and cockroach infestation: the Tenant indicated that the bedbugs are no longer a problem. She testified that every time there is construction at the residential premises, there would be a new infestation of cockroaches. There was no testimony to suggest that the Landlords did not address this problem as it arose. (ii) Washroom ceiling leak/crack from January 16, 2023: the Tenant testified that water came through the ceiling of the washroom, and the ceiling fell down. As a result of this she had to shower elsewhere, as she could not used the bathtub. She said there were 4 attempts to repair the ceiling, and her understanding is that repairs were made by “patching” the area and that those repairs did not fix the leak, causing the problem to continue. During the times when the repairs were being attempted, she stated that she had to have a fan on in the bathroom and ended up paying for the additional electricity to keep the fan going for 3 days each time a repair took place. The Tenant stated that this was finally fixed in August 2023.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I find that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair identified issues in the rental unit in a timely manner, causing this to interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. It is clear from the Tenant’s testimony that notice of each of these issues was provided to the Landlords. I note that although the washroom ceiling was finally fixed in July 2025, the 4 attempted repairs were not successful, and caused the Tenant’s further costs and inconvenience. This suggests that although the Landlords may have responded in a timely fashion, they did not address the issue successfully until several months later. The evidence presented by the Tenant demonstrated an unusual amount of dust in her unit at the time that renovations/construction was ongoing and does not appear to have ever been addressed by the Landlords. Documentation supported the Tenant’s testimony regarding the water shutoffs and the attempts to address the odour of cannabis/tobacco. The Tenant’s testimony was credible and supported by documentation. It does not appear that despite this number of ongoing issues, the Landlords reasonably addressed the problem, nor did they offer any accommodation for them to the Tenant.

In this case, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair identified issues in the rental unit in a timely and effective manner, causing this to interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. Based on the Tenant’s credible testimony and her supporting documentation, including videos, which were filed in the portal and referenced by the Tenant, the Landlords’ efforts fell short of what one would expect in addressing these problems. While a landlord does not have to meet a standard of perfection, reasonable efforts must be made, and the fact, for example, that it wasn’t until after 4 attempts to fix the ceiling crack that it was finally fixed suggests that the Landlords’ efforts were not reasonable. Also, the odour issue continues demonstrating that it has not yet been resolved.

In considering the testimony and supporting documentation, I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent. In her original application the Tenant claimed $1,650.00, which she calculated as $150.00 per time the water was shut off. For the inconvenience suffered, I find $150.00 per occasion to be reasonable. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of $5,700.00 based on 38 water shutoffs.

The Tenant also claimed an abatement of $1,000.00 calculated as 10 laundry services calculated at $100.00 each. I note that there have probably been additional times when laundry services were required, but $100.00 per service seems excessive for each laundry service. For the 38 occasions when the water was shot off, $1,000.00 appears to be reasonable, which works out to approximately $26.00 per event.

The Tenant claimed $800.00 for the attempted repairs to the washroom ceiling, based on dealing with the extra cost of the electricity for having the fans on for 3 straight days every time a repair was attempted, for the extra noise, and for having to shower elsewhere. Although the Tenant did not forward receipts showing the additional electricity costs for the time period in question, I find this to be a reasonable amount considering the time that the fans were being used.

Lastly, the Tenant claimed an abatement for the dust she has had to address in her unit every time there is construction. She did not specify an amount, and in the circumstances, considering there were a number of days and dates which have not been clearly articulated, I am ordering an abatement of $500.00 for this inconvenience.
This [name] contains all of the reasons within it. No other reasons will be issued. Remedies
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $8,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances as articulated above.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $8,064.15. This amount represents: • $8,000.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending February 25, 2026. • $64.15 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months after until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] [name], and [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.

By way of background, the parties had been before the Board on November 20, 2024. The matter was adjourned at this time. The presiding Member issued an interim order [name] on November 28, 2024. The Tenants were ordered to, on or before December 15, 2024, “…file with the Board and serve on the Landlord a copy of their amended application reflecting the correct named Landlord.” The adjournment sheet also includes the same information.
The Landlords' Representative advised he did not r eceive a copy of the Tenants’ amended application. Or der Page 2 of 3

A request to amend the Tenants’ application was filed with the Board on December 13, 2024, along with the Tenants’ Certificate of Service (‘COS’). These were e-mailed to the Board, but do not identify any other recipients.

The Tenants’ COS states that the Landlords were served on November 29, 2024, by mail to 145 Cosburn Avenue. The box entitled “Other” is checked and the name of the document that was served is identified as “order.”
The Tenant states she is certain she sent a copy not only of the Board’s Interim Order, but also the amended application to the Landlords and / or the Landlords' Legal Representative, by e-mail.

The Landlords' Representative states that he did recei ve an e-mail from the Tenant on or about November 29, 2024; however, it attached only the Interim Orde r. However, he states that neither he, nor his client, were ever provided with a copy of the Tenants’ amended T6 application.
The matter was stood down for 10 minutes to give the Tenant an opportunity to find the e-mail.

When the matter resumed, the Tenant advised that she could not find a copy of the e-mail because it was a long time ago. The Tenant was offered a further opportunity to look through her e-mail to see if she could find evidence to support that the amended application was provided to the Landlords. However, she felt she may have mailed the amended application. She then stated that she may have dropped it off to the Landlords because she lives nearby.

I am not satisfied that the Landlords were served with the amended T6 application. I say this because the Certificate of Service states that the “or der” was served by mail. However, the Landlords' Representative states he did not receive anything by mail, but did receive an e-mail on that date with the interim order. Further, the Tenant could not find a copy of the e-mail. Further still, the Tenant then stated she may have mailed it, or she may have dropped it off.

The Tenant then suggested that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, that the amended application was in the Portal ('portal'). However, I note that this is not considered service under the Board’s Rules unless both parties consented to service through the portal. There is no notation in either the adjournment sheet or the interim order that states that the parties consented to portal service.

Further, even if the Landlords could have looked in the portal for the amended application, the Tenants were subject to the Board’s interim order which clearly indicates that they must serve their amended application on the Landlords.

The Tenant states that the amendment was not of significant merit as [organization] is listed as a party to the original application. Therefore, the is little prejudice to the Landlords in proceeding. 15. The Landlords refute this argument. Because the Tenants are of the view that the current property manager, [name], were a party to the application, and because the Landlords did not get a copy of the amended application, the Landlords' Representative was not retained to represent [name]. Further, because the Landlords were unaware of the amended application, they did not take steps to sec ure witnesses who would be material to their defence, because they were unaware it would be necessary to do so. The Landlords submit that they believed, coming to the hearing this morning, that the application had been abandoned because they were never served with the amended application. 16. I am not persuaded that the Landlords would not be prejudiced by moving forward with the application despite the Tenants’ inability to provide evidence that the Landlords were properly served with the amended application. I agree with the Landlords' submissions and find it reasonable for the Landlords to have assumed the matter was abandoned having not been served with an amended application. 17. The Tenant submits that she was having difficulty recalling exactly how the Landlord was served with the amended application because it was “a long time ago.” For the same reason, this is also prejudicial to the Landlords. Witnesses have come and gone. The Tenants were given an opportunity to rectify an error in their application, but it is essential that they can prove this came to the Landlords' attention. 18. Given all of the above, I am of the view that the Tenants’ application should be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant
reasons: The Board raised a preliminary issue. Interim Order LTB-T-097224-23-RV-IN2 issued March 25, 2025, raised as a preliminary finding that the Tenant’s application may require amendments. No request to amend the Tenant’s application was uploaded to the Portal ('portal'). However, a subsequent adjournment sheet indicated that the parties had agreed that a document included in the portal (Doc-4070251) contained sufficient allegations such that the Landlord could respond to the claim.

The parties were referred to the adjournment sheet dated June 26, 2026, which states that the parties agreed that the above-noted document was to form the allegations. The Landlord advised he had not had an opportunity to review the document. Regardless, the Landlord consented to the document forming the basis of the allegations.

Given that the parties had discussed this at the prior adjourned hearing, and this had been agreed upon at the earlier date, I was satisfied that there was no prejudice to the Landlord to consent to the Tenant’s request to amend his application.
The Tenant’s application is amended to include the details found in Doc-4070251. Claim as Stated on Tenant’s T2 Application

The Board raised a further preliminary issue that the Tenant’s T2 application requested remedies that were not itemized under [name] 8 for out-of-pocket expenses. The Tenant states that these remedies relate to the moving and storage expenses. However, these are already claimed under [name] 7.

The Tenant requested to withdraw the claim on [name] 8, and I consented to that request. The Tenant’s application is amended to withdraw the claim for $2,000.00 made under [name] 8. Parties to the Application
The Landlord requests the Tenant’s application be amended to remove Nehaal Syed as a party. The Landlord indicates this was a former employee of the Landlord.
The Tenant did not object to removing Nehaal Syed as a party to the application.
The application is amended to remove Nehaal Syed; the style of cause has been updated to reflect this change. Post-Hearing Submissions

Parties were invited to provide post-hearing submissions per Interim Order LTB-T-097224- 23-RV-IN3, specific to two issues: (a) the Tenant’s request for a fine to be administered against the Landlord; (b) submissions on amending the Tenant’s application to include a request to terminate the tenancy on the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
Parties provided post-hearing submissions to the Board using the Portal ('portal'); the Tenant on February 24, 2026; the Landlord on March 3, 2026.
After reviewing the submissions, the Tenant advises that he wishes to withdraw the remedy of a fine against the Landlord.
As there is no prejudice to the Landlord in doing so, I have granted the Tenant’s request and marked the Tenant’s request for a fine against the Landlord withdrawn.
Submissions pertaining to amending the application to include a request to terminate the tenancy have been considered in my decision below.

Of note, the parties agreed I could review the Tenant’s Evidence Brief (Doc-7304215) and a list of incidents (Doc-4070251) in their entirety as part of my considerations following the conclusion of the hearing. These documents were reviewed, and relevant documents have been considered and referenced in my decision below. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant $100.00.
The Tenant claims the Landlord took a $100.00 key deposit which was not returned to him.
The Landlord agrees that he owes the Tenant this money.

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) states that no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, collect a key deposit from a tenant. Given the Landlord agrees he owes the Tenant the reimbursement of these funds, the Landlord shall reimburse to the Tenant $100.00 for the key deposit. An order shall issue.

The Tenant also requested the return of his last months’ rent deposit and interest on the deposit, and the unused portion of rent from August 17, 2023, through August 31, 2023, stating that the Landlord had not applied the last months’ rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. The parties do not dispute the Tenant paid rent in August 2023. However, I have considered this claim under the T2 portion of the application. [name]

I do not find, based on the evidence before me, that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent harassed, coerced or threatened the Tenant. Therefore, I find the Tenant did not meet their onus of proof on a balance of probabilities pertaining to the claim made pursuant to s.23 of the Act.

However, I do find that the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the application that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment for all usual purposes pursuant to s. 22 of the Act, on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $6,148.27.

By way of background, the tenancy began on January 1, 2022, and terminated on August 17, 2023. The Tenant lived alone, and residential complex unit is a mix of roughly eight apartments. The Tenant’s unit is on the ground floor facing the parking lot. However, the Tenant had other rental units above and below his.

Several parties are involved in the Tenant’s allegations. For clarity, I have listed them here with their connection to each other: • “[name]”, the Landlord’s Mother, in a relationship with Marco • “Marco”, the Superintendent or [name], who lives in or near to the residential complex • “[name]”, a tenant in the residential complex, and Marco’s son • “Nehaal Syed” (‘Nehaal’), an agent for the Landlord who was the property manager during the tenancy

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord and his agents failed to respond to his concerns that [name], and other occupants or guests in the rental complex, repeatedly threatened and harassed the Tenant, and caused excessive amounts of noise by screaming and shouting. Despite the Tenant repeatedly reporting his concerns about his safety and the harassment experienced at the hands of [name], the Landlord and his agents failed to address the behaviour of [name] and the other occupants.

The Tenant submitted copies of the text messages sent to the Landlord and Nehaal into evidence (Doc-7304215, pgs. 14-24). The noise problem started in January 2023, although the Tenant states the problems preceded this date by several months. However, he began making written records in January 2023.

The Tenant asks for assistance, by way of text message, on February 2, 19, 27, March 7, 11 (several messages), March 12, March 18, March 30, April 1, and May 14, 2023. The Tenant’s written records show that the tenants, their guests or occupants, particularly of the rental unit above the Tenant’s, frequently intentionally caused excessive noise including yelling comments such as “awwww, are people trying to sleep?”, and scraped and banged furniture with the intention of disturbing the Tenant.

The Tenant also had several incidents with [name] at the residential complex. Video evidence of an incident which occurred on August 10, 2023, shows [name] and the Tenant having a loud argument (Doc-7125126). [name] and [name] observe the argument at one point. [name] threatens that if the Tenant says one more word, he is going to “hit him.” At one point, he charges towards the Tenant and is stopped by [name]. [name] can then be heard calling the Tenant a “…piece of shit.”

Although the Tenant did not continue texting his complaints to Nehaal after May 2023, he testified that he had altercations with [name] on multiple occasions which were reported to Nehaal, including [name] behaviours. He submitted a video, taken August 11, 2023 (Doc- 4069965). In the video, [name] is outside. [name] is seen to exit his rental unit which is next door to the Tenants. [name] begins to walk away, looks towards the Tenant’s door, and then returns to slam his door shut with force in a purposeful way. A few moments later, [name] walks past the Tenant’s door and spits at it. The Tenant advises that [name] frequently urinated on or near his doorway.

The Tenant says that [name] frequently threatened him. His evidence was that “…the biker made it clear that if it wasn’t for the cameras, he would have ended me.” [name] and the Tenant had an altercation on or about August 14, 2023, in which [name] threatened him. The Tenant went to a police station to discuss the situation. He was very concerned for his personal safety and was worried that if he made a formal police report, it would have further compromised his safety. He says the police advised him to leave the situation for his own safety. He went home, packed up his belongings, and arranged to vacate the rental unit on August 17, 2023.

The Tenant’s evidence was that Nehaal was aware of, and consented to, the termination. The Tenant states that even Nehaal was wary of [name]. The Tenant’s evidence was that Nehaal and the Tenant had an understanding that he was going to have his deposit plus interest returned, the key deposit returned, and the unused rent for the period between August 17 and 31, 2023.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord failed to take appropriate measures to deal with his concerns. He states that [name]’s reports about noise are not credible because of [name]’s close relationship to Marco, and subsequently, [name]. Further, the Tenant says that neither Nehaal nor the Landlord ever attended to investigate his noise complaints.

The Landlord does not dispute that there were problems with noise in the rental complex, but states that both he and Nehaal did their best to address the concerns. He points to the text messages in evidence. On February 21, 2023, Nehaal did speak to the tenants who were making noise and followed up with the Tenant. Again, on February 27, 2023, Nehaal checks in with the Tenant asking how the noise problem was. On March 14, 2023, Nehaal advises the Tenant to knock on [name]’s door so she can investigate the next time there is a noise complaint. On March 15, 2023, [name] attended and advised she did not hear anything. On March 18, 2023, Nehaal advises he will follow up with the offending tenants again about the noise.

The Landlord also suggests that the Tenant’s own text messages stopped in mid-May 2023. The Landlord put this to the Tenant in cross-examination. The Tenant stated that he chose to meet Nehaal in person because he was worried about further threats from [name], referencing another incident in which [name] is said to have run his finger across his throat while making eye contact with the Tenant.

The Landlord agrees he did not serve any notices of termination on any of the other Tenants. He states this is because no other tenant(s) had complained of noise and [name], who had attended the complex, did not hear any noise. Further, Nehaal had addressed the Tenant’s complaints as found in the text message exchanges. The Landlord says he told the Tenant to call the police, although this point was disputed by the Tenant. The Landlord stated that he told the Tenant if there was a police report, it would allow him to move forward with a stronger case at the LTB.

The Landlord also testified that the Tenant did not give notice of termination in accordance with the Act. He testified that he only learned of the issues with the threats because of the Tenant’s application. Accordingly, the Landlord does agree with the Tenant’s submissions that he had an agreement to terminate with Nehaal. The Landlord does not believe he should have to return the deposit or the rent, which was paid for the period between August 17, 2023, and August 31, 2023. 38. In cross-examination, the Landlord asked the Tenant whether there had been any further issues between the Tenant and [name] after the event of August 14, 2023, and the Tenant admitted there had not. The Tenant was also asked why then, he chose to until August 17, 2023, to terminate the tenancy given that he “feared for his life.” The Tenant explained that he did not have a game plan. He was not expecting to flee, particularly during a pandemic, but after getting the advice of the police, he felt he needed to leave as soon as possible. Applicable Law 39. Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’), states that a Landlord shall not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes of the tenant. 40. Section 23 of the Act provides that a Landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Analysis 41. Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by failing to respond to the Tenant’s complaints in an effective or timely way. 42. The Tenant made multiple notes about the noise problems beginning in January 2023. Text messages were sent to Nehaal by the dozens over a period of four months. I am not persuaded that the Landlord took the appropriate steps nor that the steps taken were adequate. It is clear that simply speaking to the offending tenants was not addressing the [name] concerns, and no notices of termination were ever issued to any of the offending tenant(s). 43. Although it is true that a police report may have assisted the Landlord in bolstering a case against the offending tenant(s), it is not at all necessary to have a police report. A reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that they have an obligation to address tenants’ complaints in a timely and effective manner. 44. Although the case of Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority v. [name], an unreported District Court decision of October 22, 19871, was in reference to an illegal act at the residential complex, it applies to this situation as it speaks to landlords’ obligations to their tenants. The Court held: "There is an obligation upon the landlord to clean up its buildings of illegal conduct. There is an obligation on the landlord to see that there is no illegal conduct carried in its buildings in question. There is an obligation of the landlord to its other tenants." 1 Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority v. [name], an unreported District Court decision of October 22, 1987, Court File Number M153372/87 45. I am also not persuaded that having [name] attend to try to deal with the noise was appropriate because of her relationship to [name] and subsequently [name]. It was clear from the video evidence that [name] could be volatile. This too may have discouraged [name] from providing an honest reflection of the issues happening at the rental unit, which is why it was incumbent on the Landlord and or Nehaal to attend the rental unit to deal with the situation, or at the very least, issue the appropriate notice of termination. 46. I also accept the Tenant’s evidence that he was reluctant to involve police given how volatile the situation had become, and this ultimately led to the Tenant vacating the rental unit. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he began to fear for his life, given the repeated threats made to him. 47. I am not persuaded that the Landlord or his agent were not aware of the ongoing issues between the Tenant and the other individuals at the complex after May 2023. I say this because the Tenant provided ample evidence of the problems between January and May 2023. Although the Tenant’s text messages dropped off in mid-May, I am unable to find that the Landlord could reasonably believe that the problems stopped simply because the messages stopped. I say this because the Landlord admitted he had not served any notices of termination, and there was no evidence to suggest that the parties were evicted or otherwise terminated their tenancies. The earlier attempts by Nehaal prior to May 2023 to rectify the offending tenant(s) behaviour had not resulted in a significant change before May 2023. If the Landlord had done nothing further, it does not accord that the problems vanished because the Tenant stopped texting Nehaal. 48. Even if I accept the Landlord’s testimony that he was unaware of any further issues between the parties between the period of mid-May and approximately August 10, 2023, it is entirely possible that Nehaal did not tell the Landlord about the ongoing problems. Nehaal was not called to give evidence at the hearing. 49. Finally, I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he had an agreement with Nehaal to leave the rental unit, and that Nehaal told the Tenant he would be entitled to the return of the rent deposit, key deposit, interest, and the unused rent. As I found earlier, I accept the Tenant’s evidence that Nehaal was well aware of the problems with [name] at the rental unit. Even if the Landlord states he was not aware of the issue until August 14, 2023, I find the Landlord’s agent was, and the Landlord is responsible for the actions of his agents. 50. Even if I am wrong, and Nehaal did not agree to the conditions upon which the tenancy was terminated, I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he fled out of a reasonable held belief that he was in imminent danger because of the threats made to him. He spoke to police, and police advised him to remove himself, and that is what he did at his earliest opportunity. In my view, the Tenant had no intention to terminate their tenancy early or without giving proper notice. If this was true, then they would not have paid their rent due in August. Rather, I find that the Tenant’s abrupt decision to leave was precipitated by a genuine belief he would be assaulted if he remained in the rental unit. Remedies 51. The Tenant seeks, by way of remedies, $2,000.00 for moving and storage costs, and an abatement totalling $2,500.00, and requests the Board terminate his tenancy effective August 17, 2023. The Tenant’s rent was $1,125.00 at the time of termination. Moving & Storage 52. The Tenant submitted evidence of moving and storage costs (Doc-7304215, pgs. 26-31). These costs total $2,025.75. (U-Haul $657.66; Via Rail $212.44; Via Rail $124.30; Filmores $173.68; XYZ Storage $857.67). The Tenant claims $2,000.00. Per the Divisional Court matter of Beaugé v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, the Board is unable to assess a greater award than that was claimed. Thus, the Tenant’s claim is limited to the $2,000.00 as stated in the application. 53. I find the Tenant is entitled to his reasonable expenses incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $2,000.00 for moving and storage expenses. Abatement 54. The Tenant requests an abatement of $2,500.00. 55. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 56. Although the guidance in Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], refers to situations in which there was a lack of maintenance in the rental unit, I find the Court’s guidance instructive regardless: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect. 57. Given the length of time the Tenant endured the problems, the lack of effectual resolution to the Tenant’s concerns, and the impact the situation had on the Tenant, I am of the view that an abatement of $2,500.00, as requested, is appropriate in the circumstances. Termination of the Tenancy 58. The Tenant also seeks the termination of the tenancy effective August 17, 2023, the date he left the rental unit. As found above, I accept the Tenant’s evidence and find that the tenancy should terminate effective August 17, 2023. 59. Section 134(2) of the Act states that no Landlord shall collect or attempt to collect from a former tenant any amount of money purported to be rent after a tenancy has terminated. 60. Therefore, I find that the Tenant should be reimbursed for the unused rent for the period between August 17 – 31, 2023. I calculate that amount to be $517.81. ($1,125.00 x 12/365 x 14 days). 61. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $517.81 to reimburse the Tenant for rent paid between August 17 – 31, 2024. 62. For the same reasons, I am of the view the Tenant should be reimbursed his last months’ rent deposit with interest. The Tenant’s deposit was $1,100.00 (Doc-7304215, pg. 33). I calculate the interest to be $30.46. The last months’ rent deposit and interest total $1,130.46. 63. The Landlord shall reimburse the Tenant $1,130.46 for the last months’ rent deposit and interest owing for the period between January 1, 2022, and August 17, 2023. 64. The total the Landlord owes the Tenant is $6,148.27. 65. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $6,296.27. This amount represents: • $100.00 reimbursement of key deposit. • $2,500.00 for moving and storage costs. • $2,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $517.81 reimbursement of rent. • $1,100.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $30.46 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing this application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant applied for an order requiring the Landlord to return $3,000.00 rent deposit paid to the Landlord in relation to the proposed rental unit at [address]t.

The Tenant paid the Landlord $3,000.00 on October 1, 2025, in relation to the proposed rental unit. I find that this payment was a rent deposit within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’)

The first issue is whether there was a tenancy agreement between the parties. To find that there was a tenancy agreement, I must be satisfied that the parties agreed on the essential terms, including the rental unit, the rent, and the commencement date. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the parties agreed that the Tenant would rent the unit, that the monthly rent would be $3,000.00, and that the tenancy would begin on November 1, 2025. Although there were confusion and disagreement about the number of occupants and the documents required by the Landlord, I am satisfied that the essential terms of the proposed tenancy had been agreed on.

Section 105 of the Act permits a landlord to collect a rent deposit, subject to the limits set out in the Act. Section 107 of the Act requires a landlord to repay the rent deposit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

I have considered Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502. In that decision, the Court of Appeal held that section 107 of the Act does not require the automatic return of a rent deposit where the landlord was ready and able to give possession and the prospective tenant chose not to proceed. However, the Court also confirmed that a landlord may not retain a rent deposit as a penalty and that the landlord must take reasonable steps to minimize any loss.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to give vacant possession to the Tenant. The proposed move in date was November 1, 2025. The Tenant advised the Landlord on October 9, 2025, that she no longer wished to proceed. The Landlord later advised the Tenant by October 12, 2025, that she could continue with the transaction. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that, on October 23, 2025, the parties met at the property and the Landlord again told the Tenant that she could still move in at the monthly rent of $3,000.00. The Tenant declined to proceed and told the Landlord that she had found another place.

On this evidence, I find that the Landlord did not refuse to provide vacant possession to the Tenant. Rather, the Tenant chose not to proceed with the tenancy before the November 1, 2025, move in date. For that reason, I am not satisfied that section 107 requires the Landlord to return the entire $3,000.00 on the basis that vacant possession was not given.

However, that does not mean the Landlord was entitled to retain the full $3,000.00. The Landlord was not entitled to keep the deposit as a penalty. Once the Tenant withdrew from the tenancy, the Landlord was required by section 16 of the Act to take reasonable steps to minimize any loss. The Landlord’s Dut to Mitigate:

As I have found that the Landlord did not refuse to provide vacant possession to the Tenant, the next issue is whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize her losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act.

The evidence shows that the Landlord knew by October 9, 2025, that the Tenant did not intend to proceed. The intended move in date was November 1, 2025. I accept that this left the Landlord with a short period of time to find a replacement tenant. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that she reposted the rental unit on Kijiji on October 14, 2025, at the monthly rent of $3,000.00. That evidence shows that the Landlord took some steps to rent the unit again.

However, I am not satisfied that the Landlord proved that she took reasonable steps sufficient to justify retaining the full $3,000.00. The unit was not rented until March 1, 2026. Although the Landlord testified that she reposted the unit, had some showings, and later used a real estate agent, the evidence does not satisfy me that the entire delay from November 1, 2025, to March 1, 2026, was unavoidable. I also find it relevant that the unit was later advertised at different rent amounts, including amounts higher than the $3,000.00 monthly rent discussed with the Tenant.
The rental unit is a three-bedroom updated bungalow in the Scarborough area of Toronto. I accept that its size, location, and condition made it attractive to prospective tenants.

The Landlord failed to provide detailed evidence about how many showings occurred after October 14, 2025, who attended those showings, what follow up occurred, or why any prospective applicants were not accepted. On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord proved that the unit could not reasonably have been rented before December 1, 2025. I find that it is reasonable to assess the Landlord’s loss at approximately half a month of rent.

For those reasons, I find that allowing the Landlord to retain 50 percent of the $3,000.00 deposit fairly recognizes that the Tenant withdrew shortly before the proposed move in date and that the Landlord had limited time to find a replacement tenant. I also find that requiring the Landlord to return the remaining 50 percent reflects the Landlord’s failure to prove that retaining the full $3,000.00 was a reasonably mitigated loss.
I therefore find that the Tenant is entitled to a rebate of $1,500.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,548.00. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for excess rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally. (T2 Application)
reasons: The parties [name] and [name], are referred to interchangeably as “Tenants”, and “Prospective Tenants”, based on the findings in this order.

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $1,648.00 on or before February 21, 2026.
The Tenants’ T1 application seeks the return of a deposit paid in the amount of $1,600.00.

The Tenants paid a deposit to the Landlord in two payments of $300.00, and $1,300.00 in October 2025. The parties discussed a move in date of November 1, 2024, but no written tenancy agreement was signed.

The Tenants did not take possession of the rental unit on November 1, 2024. A text message from the Tenants on November 7, 2024, asks the Landlord to cancel the parties’ agreement. The Landlord does not agree to cancel the agreement, and the parties discussed a delayed move in date of November 15, 2024, which was agreed.
After the parties’ agreement that the Tenants would move in on November 15, 2024, the Landlord asks the Tenants if they have committed to moving into the rental unit.
On November 8, 2024, the Landlord send a text message asking the Tenants to confirm whether they plan to take possession of the rental unit.
Later in the evening on November 8, the Landlord asks the Tenants to pay the first month’s rent if they intend to move into the rental unit.

The Tenants reply that a landlord can only request one month as a deposit and the Landlord responds that if the Tenants are planning to move in, the agreement requires payment of the first month’s rent and a rent deposit. The Landlord asks again if the Tenants are planning to take possession of the rental unit.
There is no record of communication from either the Landlord or Tenant between November 8, 2024, and November 11, 2024.

On November 12, 2024, the Tenants send a text message to the Landlord asking for keys to the rental unit because they plan to take possession that weekend. The Landlord replies that the Tenants are too late, and because of their lack of reply the rental unit was re- rented. Analysis T1 Application
The Tenants were never given keys to the rental unit and could not take possession.

The evidence shows that after November 7, 2024, the Landlord took the position that until the Tenants confirmed their intentions and definitively provided a move in date, there was no tenancy agreement. The Landlord believes he is entitled to keep the deposit based on the loss of rent for November 2024.

Section 107 of the Act provides: 107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The Tenants did not confirm their intentions, and the Landlord treated any agreement the parties may have had as being cancelled. Accordingly, the Tenants are “prospective tenants” within the meaning of section 107 of the Act.
The Landlord did not give vacant possession of the rental unit to the prospective Tenants and accordingly, the Tenants are entitled to the return of the deposit paid. T2 Application
The Tenant’s T2 application alleges illegal entry by the Landlord and seeks a rent abatement of $1,600.00, a fine, and an order that the Landlord not “double rent” the unit.

At the hearing the Tenant clarified that they are only seeking the return of their rent deposit in the amount of $1,600.00. The Tenant did not prove the allegations in the T2 application therefore, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,600.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00 for the rent deposit; • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. [name]
The Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed. February 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally; and (T1 Application) • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. (T2 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations of illegal charge contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant claimed the Landlord collected an illegal charge because she requested a standard Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) tenancy agreement in writing and it was not provided. The Tenant testified she did not withhold the rent, and a standard form lease was never provided. She submits she is therefore owed one month’s rent of $975.00 as a remedy.

The Landlord does not dispute that he provided only a lease drafted with the assistance of his real estate agent. The tenancy agreement document was signed by the Tenant, but not the Landlord and was not the standard form tenancy agreement approved by the Board.

Section 12.1(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states that: Every tenancy agreement that is entered into in respect of a tenancy of a prescribed class on or after the date prescribed for that class of tenancies shall comply with the following requirements: 1. The tenancy agreement shall be in the form prescribed for that class of tenancies. 2. The tenancy agreement shall comply with the requirements prescribed for that class of tenancies. 2017, c. 13, s. 5.

Section 12.1(4) of the Act states that a tenant who is party to a tenancy agreement that does not comply with 12.1(1) may demand in writing that the Landlord provide a tenancy agreement that complies with subsection (1) and is signed by the Landlord.

Section 12.1(6) of the Act states that if at least 21 days have elapsed since the day the tenant made the demand and the landlord has not complied with the demand, the Tenant may withhold rent for 1 month.

Section 12.1(6) of the Act is intended to ensure that tenants have proper leases which comply with the Act. The provision is a mechanism for tenants to enforce this right under the Act by withholding rent payments until such time as the Act is complied with. Withholding rent is the only remedy available.
Accordingly, the Board has no jurisdiction to award a one month rent abatement.
Regardless, the Landlord did not collect, and the Tenant did not pay a charge which was not allowed by the Act.
I find therefore that the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act. T2 Application
The Tenant claimed the Landlord changed the locking system on the door of the residential complex unlawfully, without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that she gave notice of termination to end her tenancy to the Landlord on October 16, 2024. The termination date was October 25, 2024. The evidence is that the Landlord accepted that termination date and began to look for a new tenant. It is not disputed the Tenant had paid the rent to the end of November and the Landlord held last month’s rent in the amount of $975.00.
The Tenant testified that she and her father came to the rental unit on October 25, 2024 and found the locks changed. She alleges she was unable to access the rental unit.

It is not disputed that the Tenant’s property was removed from the unit on October 25, 2024 and placed in the garage. The Tenant picked up this property on November 22, 2024 except her dresser, which the Landlord still has in storage and is willing to provide to the Tenant.

The Tenant submits that she changed her mind on October 26, 2024 and wanted to stay in the rental unit until November 30, 2024. She notified the Landlord of this on October 31, 2024, the same day she told the Landlord she believed the locks had been changed. She requested a new key to the rental unit. She requested to know where her things were.
The Tenant submits she has the right to change her mind and she was unlawfully locked out.

The Landlord testified that he never changed the locks, and the locks are still the same locks as were on the residential complex and the Tenant’s room. He accepted her notice of termination, accepted her word that she had moved out, and entered on October 25, 2024 to prepare the room for a new Tenant. He was surprised when she emailed him on October 31, 2024 that she believed the locks were changed.
Communications between the parties contradict the Tenant’s claim.
On October 16, 2026 the Tenant told the Landlord that she was packing and the room available for showing as of ‘this Friday’, meaning October 17, 2024.

On October 23, 2024, the Landlord asked the Tenant if he could come the next day to take pictures of the room, and the Tenant gave permission. She replied that she would ask another Tenant to clean the room and stated, “I’ve moved out”. She stated the remaining items would either be picked up by her mother or discarded by another tenant. She welcomed the Landlord to enter and prepare the unit for showing to prospective new tenants.

I prefer the evidence of the Landlord in this case. The Tenant’s testimony was contradictory in many places to both her documentary evidence and the documents produced by the Landlord. She recalled no clear dates, and the dates she did give changed throughout her testimony. Her memory on specific essential points, such as when she was gone from the province, when she returned and when she attended the rental unit, was vague and without specifics and therefore unreliable. No photo or video evidence was produced that the Tenant was unable to unlock the door, or that she even attended on October 25, 2024. Her father did not testify. The Landlord’s consistent testimony and video evidence establish that he was at the rental unit from approximately 1:00 pm to nearly 7:00 p.m.

The Tenant also contradicted herself by saying she gave notice due to a job she had in Toronto, however, her own emails with the Landlord reveal she had a job out of province. Her requested remedy for reimbursement for expenses to move to Alberta supports that the original email is accurate.

The Tenant’s email on October 31, 2024 contradicts her testimony that she discovered being locked out on October 25, 2024. Waiting 6 days to request the property that had been moved, request a key, and advise that she believed the locks had been changed makes no sense. She gave no reasonable explanation why she waited 6 days, and I do not believe that she only called the Landlord. Her initial testimony was that she called and emailed repeatedly. However when asked to produce the emails or texts sent on October 25, 2024 upon discovery of the changed locks, she changed her testimony to state she had only called the Landlord. No phone records were produced to establish those calls.

The Landlord disputes he received a call on October 25, 2024. Instead he points to the Video he took on October 25, 2024 of the room, the damaged mattress and the Tenant’s property. He sent a copy of that video to the Tenant on October 25, 2024. She did not respond on that date.

Section 39 of the Act states a landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless, (a) the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit; or (b) an order of the Board evicting the tenant has authorized the possession.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex.

I find therefore that the [name] ended on October 25, 2024 and the Tenant had vacated, as the parties had agreed. A change of mind after the date of termination does not entitle a Tenant to re-possession of a rental unit. [name]29. The parties requested that I set a date for the return of the dresser but were in dispute about the deadline for doing so. Having determined that the Landlord did not unlawfully move the Tenant’s property, I have no jurisdiction to order any remedy regarding the dresser that is not on consent. The parties are open to making arrangements as between themselves regarding the dresser. Claim for Last Month’s Rent Deposit 30. Although the Tenant did not include in her T1 application a claim for last month’s rent deposit, the Landlord clearly had notice of the monetary claim from the Tenant’s T2 application, and through her disclosure. Questions were asked and evidence given regarding the last month’s rent deposit and mitigation. I therefore exercise my discretion to treat the claim regarding the retained last month’s rent deposit under the T1 application and make a determination in that regard. 31. The Landlord is still retaining last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $975.00. 32. Although the Landlord agreed to the termination date of October 25, 2024, he did not agree to waive rent owing. The Tenant was required pursuant to the Act to give 60 days’ notice which in this case would have been to December 31, 2024. The Tenant would, by that calculation owe the Landlord a further $975.00. 33. However, the Landlord mitigated his damages pursuant to section 16 of the Act, by re- renting the unit. The Landlord testified that the new tenant did not move into the rental unit until November 15, 2024. He also testified that he gave the new tenant the key on October 30 or October 31. But correspondence with the Tenant on November 4, 2024 indicates he found a qualified person to rent the room for November 15, 2024 but had not finalized the agreement yet although. I find this contradiction difficult to resolve and accept that if both facts are true, the new person has the ability to occupy the moment the key is given. When they actually moved into the rental unit is only one factor to consider when determining entitlement to occupy. That date was, in my determination, October 31, 2024. 34. The Tenant is not obligated to pay rent beyond the date the new tenant became entitled to occupy the rental unit regardless of when she moved in. 35. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord is required to return the entirety of last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,023.00 for the return of last month’s rent deposit and the application filing fee.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before April 15, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant’s T1 Application claim regarding provision of a standard form lease is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants’ T1 application did not clearly identify the reason for the claim or remedy sought. At the hearing, the Tenants requested that the application be amended to include the return of the last months’ rent deposit and a pet deposit. I granted the amendment because the Landlord confirmed that he understood the Tenants’ claim or purpose of the application and was prepared to respond at the hearing. Whether the Landlord collected or retained money illegally
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $2,048.00.

The tenancy began on April 18, 2024, and the initial one-year term ended on April 17, 2025. Thereafter the tenancy continued on a month to month basis. On August 28, 2025, the Tenants served an N9 notice to end their tenancy with a termination date of October 30, 2025. This was a valid notice of termination because it complies with sections 44 and 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

It is undisputed that the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2025 when the Tenants returned the property keys to the Landlord. The Tenants also confirmed that rent was paid for the month of October 2025, which was not disputed by the Landlord. 5. [name], testified on behalf of the Tenants. She referred to the Acknowledgement dated April 18, 2024 which confirms that the Tenants paid $7,400.00 at the beginning of the tenancy. The document sets out: $200.00 for a key deposit, $1,000.00 for a pet damage deposit, and $6,200.00 for prepaid rent for January 18, 2025 (10th month) and February 18, 2025 (11th month). The Landlord returned the $200.00 key deposit and $2,100.00 from the last months’ deposit; however, as of the hearing date, the Landlord still held $2,000.00, which consisted of $1,000.00 for the remaining balance of the last months’ rent deposit and $1,000.00 for the pet deposit. The Landlord responded that he retained these amounts because the Tenants caused damage to the rental unit. 6. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by s. 106(10) the Act, which states “a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.” 7. A Landlord is not entitled to keep a rent deposit because they believe their Tenant caused damage. A Landlord must file an application at the Board claiming compensation for damages and the Board will decide if the Landlord is entitled to compensation after holding a hearing and considering the parties’ evidence on that issue. 8. Further, it is undisputed that the Landlord collected $1,000.00 for a “pet damage deposit.” I find that the Landlord collected an additional charge prohibited by s.134(1) of the Act. Therefore, $1,000.00 is also applied to the outstanding balance owed by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • $1,000.00 for the additional illegal charge; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
