issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant testified that he found a listing for the rental unit online, which was for a room for rent and the monthly rent was $575.00 per month.
The Tenant testified that this was his first time renting and was unaware of the process of renting a unit.

The Tenant testified that he contacted the Landlord and based on the description in the ad, confirmed with the Landlord that he would rent the room. He further testified that he was not aware that he should have attended the complex to view the room before agreeing to rent it.

The Tenant testified that he asked the Landlord to accept the first month’s rent and only $250.00 of the last month rent as a deposit. He further testified that the Landlord agreed and the deposit totalling $850.00 was sent to the Landlord on August 28, 2025, and the tenancy was to begin on September 1, 2025

The Tenant testified that he went to the unit on August 31, 2025, and found the residential complex to be dirty, with mold in the sink, smelly and was not like the ad had shown. He further testified that his room did not have a bed as was shown in the ad. A copy of the ad was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that he asked the Landlord for his money to be returned but the Landlord refused and told him that the complex would be cleaned the following day. He further testified that the Landlord told him that he would return his deposit if he could find someone else to take the room.
The Tenant testified that he is sure the Landlord would have been able to find a new tenant but he was aware if the Landlord had or not. Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Act states: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the perspective tenant.

The proper interpretation of section 107(1) of the Act was addressed by the Court of Appeal in Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc.[1]: [9] Applying the Ontario Court of Appeal’s interpretation of s. 107(1) of the Act does not authorize a tenant to obtain the automatic return of a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything necessary to give the possession of the leased premises and the tenant has unilaterally repudiated the rental agreement. [10] In particular, we agree with the following observation [at para. 22]: When one looks at the words of s. 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is "not given" to the prospective tenant. The words "not given" suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. In the present case, however, it was the tenant's action in refusing to take the unit that prevented her from taking possession, not any act of the landlord. [11] This interpretation accords with common sense and fairness. To permit a tenant, who is legally obligated to take possession, to regain a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything it was required to do in order to give possession would render meaningless the concept of a rent deposit to secure the tenant's obligation to pay rent.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did provide vacant possession to the Tenant and the Tenant did not provide any evidence that the Landlord was able to rent the unit to another tenant. Therefore, I find the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleged that a rent deposit was given to the Landlord and then not returned as the Tenant did not take possession of the rental unit. Background Facts

The Tenant and the Landlord signed a tenancy agreement on October 18, 2024. The Tenant paid the Landlord $3,192.90 which was for first and last months rent in the total amount of $2,990.00 plus $192.90 for per diem rent from October 27 to 31, 2024. The tenancy agreement was for a fixed term ending October 31, 2025

Despite the tenancy starting on October 27, 2024, the Tenant was given the keys to the unit on October 25, 2024. The Tenant stated the unit was listed “as is” and she wanted to be able to clean prior to moving in her belongings.

The Tenant stated she started cleaning under the fridge and discovered what she thought was rodent urine and feces. The Tenant started to feel ill and did not finish cleaning the unit. The Tenant told the Landlord about her discovery, and the Landlord reimbursed the Tenant the cost of her cleaning supplies.

The Tenant returned to the unit on October 26, 2024, to finish cleaning but while she was at the unit she stared to feel like the unit was not suitable for her. The Tenant then advised the Landlord she was terminating the lease agreement. The Tenant stated the Landlord offered to retain pest control to attend the unit on October 27, 2024, but she was not interested in this.

The Tenant was very forthright in her testimony and stated at the time she was not on any medication for anxiety and that she may have acted out of proportion. The Tenant said she was worried about bringing her two cats into the unit if there were rodents.

The Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord by leaving them in the lock box on October 26, 2024, or October 27, 2024. The Tenant stated the Landlord did not object to her moving out of the rental unit.

The Landlord’s position is that she did not agree to terminate the tenancy and could not force the Tenant to stay once the Tenant decided she no longer wanted to live in the rental unit. The Landlord testified she listed the unit the day after the Tenant told her she was not staying and that she conducted 1 to 2 showings of the unit per week. The Landlord testified that despite her efforts to re-rent the unit, the unit remained empty until January 2025 before she could secure a new tenant. Analysis

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Musilla v Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 provides guidance on the interpretation of section 107 of the Act. Starting at paragraph 8: [8] The Board and the Divisional Court held that s. 107(1) requires a landlord to return a rent deposit only if vacant possession is refused by the landlord. Where there is an agreement for a rental of a residence and the tenant does not take possession of the residence when offered, the landlord is entitled to retain a rent deposit in accordance with the provisions of the rental agreement. [9] We agree with the reasons of the Divisional court that s. 107(1) of the Act does not authorize a tenant to obtain the automatic return of a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything necessary to give the possession of the lease premises and the tenant has unilaterally repudiated the rental agreement. [10] In particular, we agree with the following observation [at para 22]: When one looks at the words of section 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is not given to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. [11] This interpretation accords with common sense and fairness. To permit a tenant, who is legally obligated to take possession, to regain a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything it was required to do in order to give possession would render meaningless the concept of a rent deposit to secure the tenant’s obligation to pay rent.
Accordingly, the only question before the Board on the present matter is did the Tenant unilaterally repudiate the rental agreement? Did the Tenant unilaterally repudiate the rental agreement?

Based on the evidence before me, I find that there was a tenancy agreement in place when the Tenants sought the return of their rent deposit. As of October 18, 2024, when the parties signed the tenancy agreement, there was a mutual understanding and agreement by the parties on the essential terms of the tenancy. The parties agreed to the commencement date, the rental amount, and that the deposit would be used for the last month’s rent deposit, as well as 5 days of per diem rent to be paid for the right to occupy the unit on October 27, 2024. The Landlord gave the Tenant the key on October 25, 2024, at the Tenants request so she could clean. The unit was vacant and ready for the Tenant to take possession.

There was no evidence that the unit was uninhabitable. While I acknowledge some evidence of rodent activity, the Tenant’s testimony did not suggest that the unit was infested. In fact, the Tenant was not even sure she saw a live rodent but stated she may have saw one that quickly dashed off. The Landlord acted appropriately, reimbursed the Tenant for her cleaning supplies and offered to conduct immediate pest control. Additionally, the Tenant admitted that she may have acted out of proportion under the circumstances.
The Landlord’s lack of verbal objection when the Tenant advised she was leaving does not equate to an agreement to end the tenancy.
Section 106(1) of the Act states that “a landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement.

This section of the Act allows for a last month’s rent to be paid prior to or at the time of entering into a tenancy agreement. A portion of the payment the Tenant made was equivalent to one month’s rent; therefore, the deposit paid to the Landlord was lawful. Since the Tenant unilaterally repudiated the tenancy agreement, there is no obligation for the last month’s rent to be returned.

The Act further requires lawful notice when terminating a tenancy. Subsection 44(4) states that notice shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date. The Tenant agreed to a fixed term of one full year.
However, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, a landlord has an obligation to minimize their losses by taking reasonable steps to re-rent the unit.

Based on the testimony and evidence of the Landlord, I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to mitigate her losses. The Landlord placed an advertisement the following day after learning that the Tenant did not want to stay in the unit. The Landlord conducted multiple showings and made best efforts to try and rent the unit quickly. Despite these efforts, the Landlord was unable to rent the unit until January 1, 2025. Considering the time it takes to monitor responses to an advertisement, schedule showings, and the time it takes for a prospective tenant to submit a rental application and supporting documents, as well as considering the reduction in rental interest over the holidays, a 3-month delay in re-renting the unit is not unreasonable.

Since the Tenant unilaterally terminated the tenancy agreement which was to commence on October 27, 2024, and the Landlord was, despite reasonable efforts, unable to re-rent the unit until January 1, 2025, the Landlord is also entitled to retain the amount the Tenant paid for her first month rent as well as the 5 days of per diem rent. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: The Tenant testified that he regained access to the rental unit on November 22, 2025. As such, his request to be restored to possession is now moot and I will only consider his request for compensation for the alleged illegal lockout.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that on November 12, 2025, he came home to find his key for the rental unit door not to be working and that he was out of possession of the rental unit from November 12, 2025, to November 22, 2025. The Landlord denies locking the Tenant out of the rental unit. The Landlord submits that the Tenant retained possession of the rental unit throughout the period he claims to be locked out.

On the basis of the video evidence provided I am not satisfied that the Tenant was locked out of the rental unit. Surveillance video from the hallway of the rental complex on November 16, 2025, shows the rental unit door open and the Tenant passing through the door (DOC-6867430). While I have considered that the video does not have the best angle because the rental unit door is in the top left of the frame and the entire rental unit door is not shown, when I compare the video to a video taken on November 18, 2025, from the same camera, you can see a clear difference in the rental unit door position. November 16, 2025 November 18, 2025 Door Open Door Closed

I have also considered whether the rental unit door is perhaps further back than the area shown in the November 16, 2025, video, but you can clearly see the door handle and lock in the November 18, 2025 video. If the door was closed in the November 16, 2025, video I would expect to see the same door handle and lock you can see in the November 16, 2025 video.

A video provided by the Tenant (DOC-6825614) shows that his rental unit door is directly behind the black doormat you can see in the November 16, 2025, video image above. That you can see through the area behind the doormat in the November 16, 2025, also supports that the door is open.

I did not find the Tenant’s explanation for why it looks like his door is open in the November 16, 2025, video to be compelling. The Tenant testified that his bags were outside the unit, he stays in the frame, that his door is past the wall, there is a storage area, what the image is actually showing is the hinge of the door and the framing of the door. The November 16, 2025 video shows the Tenant disappearing from the frame, for the reasons already provided I find that the rental unit door is directly behind the black doormat, and a comparison of the videos taken on November 16 and 18 supports that the door is open in the November 16 video.
There was no evidence led at the hearing to support that the Landlord has manipulated the videos in any way or that the videos are not authentic.

The Landlord testified that after receiving the Board’s interim order LTB-T-097700-25-IN issued on November 21, 2025, she put a new lock on the rental unit door and gave the Tenant the key. The Tenant testified that he regained possession of the rental unit after that. I find it strange that if the Landlord never locked the Tenant out that she would replace the locks and give the Tenant a new key. However, I ultimately find the video evidence to be determinative and I accept the Landlord’s explanation for why she changed the locks on November 21, 2025. The Landlord testified that she did this because her paralegal told her she needed to do it after the Board’s interim order was issued.

While the Tenant claims he filed a police report and called [name], and that those actions support that he was locked out, I ultimately find the video evidence to be the best evidence. Additionally, when I consider all the evidence presented by the Tenant with the Landlord’s testimony that she never locked the Tenant out, I’m not satisfied that the Tenant met their burden of proof to prove the claim on a balance of probabilities.

It is possible that the Tenant might be confused about when he was locked out. His application says it happened on November 17, 2025. If that’s true it would explain why his door is open on November 16, 2025. However, at the hearing the Tenant repeatedly testified that he was locked out on November 12, 2025. If the Tenant was confused, then I find his testimony to be unreliable. The Tenant’s confusion would also not resolve the issue that the Landlord denies ever locking him out. Even if the rental unit door being open on November 16, 2025 can be explained by the Tenant’s confusion about the dates that events happen, I still find that the Tenant did not prove his claim on a balance of probabilities.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord submitted that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') does not apply, because the unit is exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act, which states 5 this Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner's spouse, child or parent or they spouses child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;
The Landlord, as the party asserting that the Act does not apply, bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities relative to this preliminary issue.

To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing and cogent evidence to establish it is more likely than not that something happened, or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanlII), paras 44-46.

The Tenant rented a room in a 3-bedroom condominium. The Tenant’s room was the master bedroom which had its own bathroom, and the other bathroom and the kitchen was shared by the Tenant, the Landlord and another roommate.

The Tenant’s Representative submitted that the Tenant, at the time of the signing of the roommate agreement, was unaware that the Landlord was one of the roommates, believed she was a tenant and protected by the Act.
The Tenant’s Representative further submitted that the Tenant believed another female was moving into the unit but instead, another male moved into the unit making her very uncomfortable.

The Tenant’s Representative submitted that the Tenant was misled by the Landlord, who is a licensed paralegal and although the Tenant was unaware that she would be sharing the unit with the Landlord, she had shared the unit with him since moving in.
The Landlord submitted that the Tenant signed a “Roommate Rental Agreement” and a copy was submitted as evidence. He further submitted that they share the kitchen.
Based on the evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply for the following reasons:
The Landlord resided in the unit and shared the kitchen with the roommates.

The Tenant signed a “Roommate Rental Agreement” prior to moving in and throughout the agreement she is referred to as a roommate and it contains such terms as: • Roommate and Landlord should respect each other’s privacy [name] and Landlord are responsible for securing their personal belongings [name] and Landlord should ask for permission before borrowing or using each other’s personal items
Since the Act does not apply, the Board has no jurisdiction to consider the merits of this application.
ordered: The Tenant application is dismissed. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Tenant’s A1 application seeks to determine that the Act applies in relation to a mobile home unit. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

The Tenant testified that she owns her mobile home, and it is situated on a leased lot. She further testified that there are 67 homes in the park, everyone lives in the park year-round, they pay property tax which reflects year-round use and there was a billboard which advertised year-round resort living.

The Landlord testified that the Act does not apply as the licence of occupation, signed by the Tenant on July 26, 2021, states the site is for vacationing purposes every day of the year during summer seasons and winter seasons and the site is not to be used for residential purposes. Analysis
The question before the Board is whether the Act applies.

Section 202(1) of the Act says: In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, a) May disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and b) May have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are relevant: 2(1) “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit … “tenant” includes: a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit … “rental unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and “rental unit” includes, (a) a site for a mobile home or site on which there is a land lease home used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and (b) a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home… “residential unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as residential premise, and “residential unit” includes, (a) a site for a mobile home or on which there is a land lease home used or intended for use as a residential premises, and (b) a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home…

In considering the real substance of the agreement, despite the licence of occupancy stating it is only for recreational purposes, the permittable seasons run from May 1 each year to October 31 and then from November 1 to April 30, equalling all 365 days of the year. Additionally, the rent is divided into 12 equal monthly payments.

Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I find that Act does apply, as the Tenant’s unit has at all times since entering into the licence of occupation been used as a residential unit with all season living.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does apply. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. LTB-T-097774-25 [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the section 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies to the rental unit and therefore the living accommodation is exempt from the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s applications are dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. and LTB-T-097774-25

At the commencement of the hearing, I confirmed with the Tenant that the Landlord’s address was the same as the rental unit to verify if I was satisfied that the Landlord had received notice of hearing. During this the Tenant began describing the living accommodations.

The Tenant testified that the residential complex was a house, and he rented a room on the main floor. The Tenant testified that there were other people also renting rooms on the main floor. The Tenant testified that the Landlord indicated that she lived upstairs and an individual the Landlord identified as her husband lived in a room on the main floor. The Tenant testified that there were multiple bathrooms but everyone in the house shared the kitchen. The Tenant testified that at some point the Landlord may have left the residential complex to visit family and he is not sure if she returned or not.

Section 5 of the Act sets out certain living arrangements where the Act does not apply. Section 5 of the Act provides: 5. This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

Based on the testimony from the Tenant I find that the occupants of the house were all required to share the kitchen with the Landlord and the Landlord’s husband (spouse). I am satisfied that the Landlord and the Landlord’s spouse lived in the house with the Tenant and other residents. Even if the Landlord at some point left the house, I am not satisfied that the Landlord permanently vacated the house. Furthermore, even if the Landlord had permanently vacated the house, the Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord’s spouse remained. Therefore section 5(i) of the Act applies, and this rental unit is exempt from the Act.
Since I am satisfied that the parties are required to share a kitchen facility, I do not find it necessary to address whether they are also required to share a bathroom facility.
Since the Act does not apply both Tenant applications shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') does not apply. April 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants’ T1 application did not clearly identify the reason for the claim or remedy sought. At the hearing, the Tenants requested that the application be amended to include the return of the last months’ rent deposit. I granted the amendment because the Landlord confirmed that she understood the Tenants’ claim or purpose of the application and was prepared to respond at the hearing. Whether the Landlord collected or retained money illegally
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $1,972.44.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on October 11, 2024, and paid a last months’ rent deposit of $1,875.00. On or about October 8-9, 2025, the rental unit flooded. The Landlord arranged temporary accommodation for the Tenants for the period of October 8 to 11, 2025. The Tenants remained in the Hotel/Airbnb provided by the Landlord while the repairs were being completed and never resumed occupation of the rental unit.

On or about October 19, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N13 with a termination date of February 28, 2026, requiring vacant possession of the rental unit for repairs. 5. [name] testified on behalf of the Tenants. He stated that they could not continue living in the Airbnb selected by the Landlord so they requested an alternative accommodation or the return of their deposit. The Tenants removed their belongings and returned the keys to the Landlord on November 1, 2025. The Landlord also testified that she did not agree to continue providing accommodation beyond October 31, 2025. She stated that the last months’ rent deposit was not applied to October 31, 2025 because she had incurred significant expenses for the Hotel and Airbnb accommodation. Analysis and Findings 6. During the hearing, the parties agreed that the last month of the tenancy was October 31, 2025. Mr. [name]name] also confirmed that rent was paid for the month of October 2025, which was not disputed by the Landlord. Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2025, and the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy which was October 1, 2025 to October 31, 2025 and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by s. 106(10) the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states “a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.” 7. A Landlord is not entitled to keep a rent deposit because they believe their tenant caused damage. A Landlord must file an application at the Board claiming compensation for damages and the Board will decide if the Landlord is entitled to compensation after holding a hearing and considering the parties’ evidence on that issue. 8. I also find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, interest for the period of October 11, 2024 to October 31, 2025 in the amount of $49.44 is applied to the outstanding balance owed by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,972.44. This amount represents: • $1,875.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • $49.44 for the interest on the last months’ rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 14, 2026. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'RTA') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: On December 22, 2025, there was an Adjudicative Case Conference convened by the LTB, which resulted in an interim order being issued on January 5, 2026 (the ‘5 Jan 26 Interim Order’). [DOC-7053745]

I surmise from the 5 Jan 26 Interim Order that the Tenant was not cooperative and that lack of cooperation is what resulted in the Member issuing the 5 Jan 26 Interim Order. The 5 Jan 26 Interim Order says, in part

At the ACC the Tenant was first engaging in the process as the Tenant and Landlords were put in separate break out rooms in order to try to resolve the dispute. However, the Tenant became uncooperative in the process when they were questioned about which issues had already been decided in previous Board orders. At one point, the Tenant put themselves on mute and refused to respond and participate in the ACC for a period of approximately five minutes. When asked how many witnesses they intended to call for the merits hearing, the Tenant demanded they be given 90 days to respond to the question as they were not prepared to provide that response as of the ACC date.

This combined T2/T6 application was filed on December 9, 2023. And while this is the first hearing regarding the application, the Tenant has engaged in the Board’s processes on at least eight other applications before the Board with the current Landlords.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit by September 30, 2024, which was more than a year prior to this ACC. The Tenant has had more than adequate time to prepare for the ACC and to determine which witnesses may be required to attend the merits hearing. Furthermore, having been involved in the previous matters, the Tenant would be in the best position to make submissions regarding which of their submissions had already been considered in previous T2 applications in order for the Board to adopt the most expeditious manner in determining the issues before it (s.183 of the Act).
An ACC is intended to support the parties in narrowing the issues in dispute and to determine the length of time that may be required to schedule the hearing of the merits of the application.

The Tenant refused to provide any details about what issues may have already been decided in a previous order of the Board when asked about them and instead pointed me to an interim decision given by Member Del Vecchio on January 16, 2025 under file 1 This is also the email provided by the tenant for the purpose of other applications filed by the Tenant —LTB-T- 012917-24, LTB-T-004855-24, LTB-T-007094-24, LTB-T-035002-23 and LTB-T-061296-22. LTB-T-012917-24 suggesting this interim order stated there should be no further preliminary issues. After the ACC, I read that interim order, and it makes no such finding. It does however determine, based on the submissions at the hearing on January 9, 2025, that the Landlords L1 application (LTB-L-04398-24) and the current T2/T6 application ought not to be heard together with the Tenant’s T2 application under LTB-T-012917-24 which was later adjourned on September 29, 2025 by Member den [name]. 3. I have no hesitation in finding that the conduct of the Tenant at the ACC was inappropriate. II. 16 Jan 26 Interim Order 4. On January 16, 2026, I issued an interim order (the ’16 Jan 26 Interim Order’). [DOC- 7163050] 5. As noted above, the Tenant consented to the delivery of documents and notices by email and there is a note on TOP indicating that the Tenant does not consent—does not want— ‘hard mail’. 6. The 16 Jan 26 Interim Order was emailed to the Tenant at [email]’. There is no indication that the email was not delivered to the Tenant. 7. In the 16 Jan 26 Interim Order, I ordered: 1. On or before January 21, 2026, the Tenant will provide to the Landlord and upload to TOP unredacted copies of: (a) all of the assignment(s) for the general benefit of creditors signed by the Tenant or bankruptcy order(s) made against the Tenant; and (b) all of the statements of affairs that the Tenant provided to the trustee or trustees administering the Tenant’s bankruptcy estate(s). 2. On or before January 21, 2026, Tenant shall provide a copy of this interim order to the trustee or trustees administering the Tenant’s bankruptcy estate(s) and shall upload to TOP evidence that this has happened. 3. On or before January 20, 2026, the Tenant shall deliver to the Landlords and upload to TOP a completed version of the chart that has been uploaded to TOP in Word format as DOC-7161792. 4. On or before January 20, 2026, the Tenant shall provide to the Landlords and upload to TOP: (a) a list of the witnesses that the Tenant intends to call on January 26, 2026 and an estimate of the time it will take each of those witnesses to provide their evidence; and (b) in the case of any witness that the Tenant expects will testify for more than 30 minutes, a document setting out what facts the Tenant expects will be introduced by that witness. … 7. Failure on the part of the Tenant to comply with this order will result in the dismissal of this application.

In the body of the 16 Jan 26 Interim Order, I was clear: 21. I wish to be very clear with the Tenant. This order is being made under subsection 201(1) of the RTA, which says, in part: 201 (1) The Board may, before, during or after a hearing, .. (d) permit or direct a party to file additional evidence with the Board which the Board considers necessary to make its decision;… 22. The information being requested is, in my view, necessary for the LTB to make a decision on this application. 23. Should the Tenant fail to provide the information as directed, I will, on January 26, 2026, dismiss this application. (emphasis in original) III. Application Dismissed
The Tenant did not comply with the 16 Jan 26 Interim Order.

I am dismissing the application as abandoned. However, had the Tenant appeared, I would have dismissed the application under subsection 201(3) of the RTA, which says, in part: 201 (3) If a party fails to comply with a direction under clause (1)(d) [of the RTA], the Board may, … (b) if the party who has failed to comply is the applicant, dismiss all or part of the application. IV. Impact of Bankruptcy

It appears, based on information provided to the Member who conducted the ACC, that the Tenant is [name], which gives rise to an issue as to whether the Tenant is a proper party to this application and ought to receive any compensation awarded by the LTB. 2 The Tenant did not comply with my order that the Tenant provide information on the Tenant’s bankruptcy. As a result, I do not know the status. In an order issued on August 6, 2024 in LTB-L-097041-23 [DOC-3837756] I found that the Tenant became bankrupt on June 23, 2024. In the 5 Jan 26 Interim Order, the Member indicates that the Tenant advised them that there was a subsequent (or previous) bankruptcy.

A Member dealing with an application where the applicant has become bankrupt should— must—consider whether the applicant remains a proper party to the application and where any compensation awarded by the LTB should be directed.

In this case, had I not dismissed the application, I would have either: (a) found that the Tenant did not have capacity to pursue the applications; or (b) directed that any of the compensation awarded to the trustee administering the Tenant’s bankruptcy.

Section 71 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (the ‘BIA’) says: 71 On a bankruptcy order being made or an assignment being filed with an official receiver, a bankrupt ceases to have any capacity to dispose of or otherwise deal with their property, which shall, subject to this Act and to the rights of secured creditors, immediately pass to and vest in the trustee named in the bankruptcy order or assignment, and in any case of change of trustee the property shall pass from trustee to trustee without any assignment or transfer.

The BIA defines ‘property’ broadly as: ‘any type of property, whether situated in Canada or elsewhere, and includes money, goods, things in action, land and every description of property, whether real or personal, legal or equitable, as well as obligations, easements and every description of estate, interest and profit, present or future, vested or contingent, in, arising out of or incident to property.’ [BIA, s. 2. and Royal Bank of Canada v. North American Life Assurance Co, 1996 CanLII 219 (SCC)]

There is case law to the effect that awards for personal injury are not ‘property’ that is available for distribution to creditors, and such actions to recover such awards can be pursued by the bankrupt and the proceeds retained by the bankrupt: It is only actions which relate directly to the bankrupt’s property and can be converted into assets for the payment of creditors that pass to the debtor’s trustee. Causes of action arising from bodily or mental suffering, such as actions for assault, seduction, criminal conversation, and damages for personal injuries, remain in the bankrupt…[Re [name], 1926 CanLII 352 (ON SC)] Not all causes of action vest in the trustee, but only those which belong to the bankrupt’s estate and which may be applied for the purpose of distribution amongst his creditors…. Consequently, the right of action does not vest in the trustee where the damages claimed are to be ‘estimated by immediate reference to pain felt by the bankrupt in respect of his body, mind or character, and without immediate reference to his rights or property…[Clement v AG of Canada and [name], 2012 ONSC 5823 (CanLII)] Certain exceptions to s. 71 [of the BIA] have been carved out by the jurisprudence. One of the exceptions is where the claim or loss is personal in nature rather than proprietary, such as where the damages claimed are to be estimated by reference to injury to the bankrupt’s person, i.e. for pain and suffering or mental distress or reputational damage. In such cases, the cause of action does not become the property of the trustee in bankruptcy and may be pursued by the bankrupt in his or her own right…[Meisels v Lawyers Professional Indemnity Company, 2015 ONCA 406 (CanLII)]

The policy underlying the findings in these cases is that the purpose of bankruptcy is not to expand the property that would be available to creditors: ‘It is not, and never has been, the policy of the law to coin into money for the profit of his creditors the bodily pain, mental anguish or outraged feelings of a bankrupt.’ [[name], 1956 CanLII 455 (AB KB)] In other words, the policy is not to make creditors better than they otherwise would have been by giving them access to ‘property’ that would not otherwise have been available to them to satisfy their claims. [See Royal Bank of Canada v. North American Life Assurance Co., 1996 CanLII 219 (SCC)]

The issue that arises in proceedings under the RTA where a bankrupt tenant (or landlord) is asserting a monetary claim is whether the claim—or the award of compensation—made is ‘property of the bankrupt’ that has vested in the trustee administering the Tenant’s bankruptcy.

I accept that an award of ‘general’ compensation is for ‘pain and suffering’ does not vest in the trustee. However, in my view, a claim by a (bankrupt) tenant for: (a) a rent abatement; or (b) out-of-pocket expenses, is the property of the bankrupt that vests in the trustee by operations of section 71 of the BIA.

The award of a rent abatement does not ‘coin into money’ the bodily pain, mental anguish or outraged feelings of the bankrupt tenant and is not ‘estimated by reference to injury to the bankrupt tenant’s person.

As was noted [name] (Re) [2017 CanLII 48926 (ON LTB)]: Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving everything being paid for then abatement should flow in an amount proportionate to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.
A rent abatement restores to the tenant money—property— that the tenant paid for rent and that would, were it not to have been paid for rent, have been available to creditors.

Similarly, a claim for out-of-pocket expenses or filing fees, in my view, constitutes property of the bankrupt that vests in the trustee. It represents reimbursement for the expenditure of money that would have been otherwise available to creditors.

In my view, the claims being made by the Tenant are ‘property’ within the meaning of the BIA and any amounts awarded to the Tenant on this application are payable to the trustee administering the Tenant’s bankruptcy and not the Tenant.
In December of 2023, the Tenant filed requests to amend the T2 application [DOC-3007955 and DOC-3007959] and T6 applications [DOC-3007968].

On the (amended) T2 application, the Tenant is asking that the LTB: (a) award $35,000.00 for the infringement of the Tenant’s ‘charter rights’ based on discrimination; (b) award $35,000.00 for harassment and interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment from February of 2023 to March of 2024; (c) award $35,000.00 for ‘assault and battery causing injury’ and ‘code discrimination’ (d) award $35,000.00 based on the issues identified in the body of the (amended) application; and (e) make an order suspending the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent.

I find that only (b) and (d) are within the jurisdiction of the LTB on a T2 application. [See RTA, s. 31] Without determining whether there is any merit to the allegations made by the Tenant, in my view, the real substance of the compensation requested by the Tenant on the (amended) T2 application is a rent abatement and not ‘general’ compensation such that claims have vested in the Trustee.

On the (amended) T6 application, the Tenant is asking the LTB to award: (a) a $34,825 rent abatement; (b) $1,904 to replace property; and (c) $35,000 based on the assertion that the Landlords: (i) breached section 26, 27, 230(6) and 231(1) and (2) the RTA and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms; and (ii) caused the Tenant bodily harm.

Without determining whether there is any merit to the allegations made by the Tenant, I find that the LTB only has jurisdiction to award (a) and (b), both of which claims have, in my view, vested in the Trustee. V. Costs

The LTB has jurisdiction to order that a party pay costs. Section 204 of the RTA says, in part: 204 (2) The Board may order a party to an application to pay the costs of another party. (3) The Board may order that its costs of a proceeding be paid by a party or the party’s paid representative. (4) The amount of an order for costs shall be determined in accordance with the Rules.

Rule 23 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure says, in part: 23.2 A member may exercise discretion to order a party to pay another party's: a. representation/preparation fees; and b. other out-of-pocket expenses. Where the LTB orders a party to pay the representation/preparation fees incurred by another party, these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour for the services of a paid representative to a maximum of $700. 23.3 A party who engages in unreasonable conduct which causes undue delay or expense may be ordered to pay costs to another party. 23.4 A party or a paid representative may be ordered to pay the LTB for its costs of a proceeding. Hearing costs will not exceed $100 per hour to a maximum of $700. 23.5 The LTB will not order a paid representative to pay its costs unless those costs result from the paid representative's conduct.

I also note that the LTB has broad jurisdiction under subsection 23(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedures Act and Rule A8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure to make any order it considers proper to prevent abuse of its processes. That, in my view, includes, in appropriate circumstances, an order that a party pay costs.

When a party acts improperly or unreasonably in a proceeding, the LTB may order them to pay to the LTB an amount that will partly cover the expenses that the LTB has incurred as a result of that conduct.
I am ordering that the Tenant pay $500.00 in LTB costs.

That, in my view, does not impact the jurisdiction of the LTB to order that the Tenant pay LTB costs. The purpose of the LTB waiving filing fees is to facilitate access to the LTB and ensure that individuals without financial means are not denied the ability to seek remedies from the LTB. Subsection 196(1) of the RTA says: 196 (1) Upon receiving information that an applicant owes money to the Board as a result of having failed to pay any fine, fee or costs, (a) If the information is received on or before the day the applicant submits an application, an employee in the Board shall, in such circumstances as may be specified in the Rules, refuse to allow the application to be filed; (b) if the information is received after the application has been filed but before a hearing is held, the Board shall stay the proceeding until the fee, fine or costs have been paid and may discontinue the application in such circumstances as may be specified in the Rules; (c) if the information is received after a hearing with respect to the application has begun, the Board shall not issue an order until the fine, fee or costs have been paid and may discontinue the application in such circumstances as may be specified in the Rules.

issues: SAUNGWEME (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,0980.00.
The Tenant testified that she became aware of the rental unit through an ad on Marketplace and when she attended the viewing, there were many people there viewing the unit.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord told her if she signed the lease and paid the deposits for the first and last month’s rent and the key deposit, she could secure the unit.

The Tenant testified that she e-transferred the Landlord $2,050.00 which was $900.00 for the first month’s rent, $900.00 for the last month’s rent deposit and $250.00 for the key deposit. Proof of the deposits and confirmation from the Landlord of receiving the deposits were submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that she was to move into the unit on November 17, 2025 but the Landlord advised her that the current AirBnB tenants might be moving out early and if so, she would be able to move in earlier also.

The Tenant testified that she contacted the Landlord on November 15, 2025 to determine if the unit was available yet and the Landlord accused her of being rude and said that he no longer felt comfortable renting the unit to her.

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord that it was okay for her not to take the unit and requested the return of her deposits. Copies of several messages of the Landlord agreeing to return the deposits were submitted as evidence.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord never returned her deposits and blocked her so she was unable to contact him. She further testified that she called the police to make a report.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected rent deposits and a key deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposits and the key deposit.

The first question before me is whether this agreement was signed by the Tenant freely, without undue pressure, and in full understanding of the consequences of entering into such an agreement. 44. Generally speaking, a contract will not be set aside except in a limited number of circumstances: common mistake, fraud, duress, misrepresentation, lack of capacity or unconscionability. With respect to motions like this, the Board may also set aside an eviction order in instances where something that could not have been anticipated occurred after the agreement was entered into that made it impossible for a party to comply with the [name]. 45. Although the Tenant pointed to their age and various medical concerns as an impediment to their ability to agree to the terms of the N11 Agreement, I note that the Tenant did not provide an adequate description of the diagnosis or clarify the effect of any such diagnosis on the Tenant’s ability to read and understand documents presented to them on August 2, 2023, or move; or when - in the opinion of a medical professional - the Tenant would be able to move out of the rental unit 10. Furthermore, the testimony provided by the Tenant and [name] was consistent. The Landlord met with the Tenant on more than one occasion to discuss their intent with respect to the rental unit and the tenancy, and the Tenant was accompanied by their support group comprised of their child and current Power of Attorney, C.L.P (who was appointed to this role after the N11 Agreement was signed) and their friend and real estate agent [name] , who both encouraged them to sign the N11 Agreement after having had an opportunity to read and review the document and ask questions to the Landlord and their agents. 47. Accordingly, on the basis of the evidence and submissions before, I am satisfied that the Tenant understood that the Landlord was seeking to terminate the tenancy and that the parties therefore entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, effective January 30, 2024, with the Tenant doing so freely, all while being informed and fully understanding that they would need to vacate the rental unit on or before January 30, 2024. 51. Despite the finding that the Tenant entered into the agreement to terminate the tenancy freely and with full understanding, subsection 77(8)(b) of the Act states that the Board may make an order setting aside an ex -parte order issued based on an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agreement, if the Board is satisfied, having regard to all the circumstances, that it would not be unfair to do so. [[name].] File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 52. While subsection 37(3) of the Act states that a “a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy,” subsection 202(1) of the Act reads as follows: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 53. After considering all of the circumstances, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 54. Indeed, while the parties entered into an agreement to end the tenancy (Exhibit 2), the Board must, pursuant to section 202 of the Act, look beyond the mere fact that an agreement was signed between the parties and consider the overall intention and conduc t of the parties when the agreement was entered into. 55. In Pinto v. [name] and White v. [name], 2021 ONSC 5502 (Pinto), the Ontario Divisional Court found that the Board erred by not applying section 202 of the Act and analyzing the true intentions of the parties when an agreement to terminate was signed. [Emphasis Added]. 56. In Pinto, the landlord approached the tenants and required them to sign an N11 agreement to terminate their tenancies for the purpose of conducting extensive repairs and renovations. The landlord did not serve the tenants with the required N13 Notice of Termination, which entitled the tenants to a compensation payment, and the tenants were led to believe that they had no alternative but to sign the N11 and without regard to their rights under the Act. I find that the present case is similar. 57. In the matter before the Board, it is clear that the catalyst to having the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement with the intent to have them vacate the rental unit, stems from the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit. This was consistently relayed to the Board through the testimony provided by the Tenant and the submissions provided by the Landlord. 58. Although the Act permits landlords to terminate tenancies because they have entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the rental unit and the purchaser intends to move into the rental unit, an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agr eement, is not intended for that purpose. 59. Indeed, an application to terminate the tenancy for a purchaser’s own use requires the landlord to serve the tenant with a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one (1) month’s rent or to offer the tenant File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 another rental unit that is acceptable to the tenant (pursuant to section 49.1 of the Act) and to swear an affidavit and/or declaration before the Board stating the purchaser’s intentions. This process also affords the tenant the right to challenge the good- faith intentions of the landlord or the person who requires the rental unit at a hearing before the Board. 60. It appears to me that the Landlord, in this case, drafted and had the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement to facilitate the process of a prospective sale and circumvent their obligations under the Act to serve the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination, to pay the required compensation prior to the termination date and from havi ng to prove their case to the Board on a balance of probabilities. In fact, by the time the hearing was concluded, the Landlord had failed to secure prospective purchasers for the rental unit, and it appears as though the Landlord had stopped the advertisements related to the rental unit. 61. The simple fact of selling (or intending to sell) the rental unit does not automatically lead to the termination of the tenancy.11 62. Thus, I find that the Landlord was not acting in good faith and was circumventing the Act when they obtained the Tenant’s signature on the N11 Agreement. 63. Accordingly, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. The Landlord would still have the opportunity to proceed with an application to terminate the tenancy, providing the appropriate notice of termination is served to the Tenant beforehand. Second T2 Application : LTB-T-097881-23 64. The Tenant testified that after being advised of the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit, the Landlord proceeded to list the unit for sale, which led to in-person showings of the rental unit being scheduled in order for prospective purchasers to view the rental unit. 65. The Tenant stated that they felt that they were being blamed by various relators (whom the Tenant described as being increasingly rude) for the Landlord’s inability to enter into an agreement of purchase and sale and therefore their inability to sell the rental unit ; despite the Landlord originally showing appreciation with respect to the Tenant’s effort to facilitate the sale of the rental unit. 66. The Tenant indicated that while the volume of the viewings increased, they believe that they were not receiving proper notices of entry for the Landlord, and their agents to conduct the in-person showings. 67. The Tenant feels that these repeated showings and blame being directed towards them made them feel uncomfortable in the rental unit, with a sense that their privacy was also being invaded as, despite their request, the Tenant was not receiving a notice of entry at least forty-eight (48) hours prior to the Landlord’s conducting showings of the rental unit. 11 Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 68. Under cross -examination, the Tenant stated that they could not recall the number of in- person showings that were conducted within the rental unit. They felt that people “were coming from all over” and that the rental unit was being treated as a “zoo” or a “circus.” 69. Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that they would receive notices from the Landlord or their various real estate agents by email with respect to showings of the rental unit, and that the Tenant had the option to decline the booking of the showing, which they exercised only a “couple of times”). 70. The Landlord submits that the Tenant failed to provide particulars with respect to the claim that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and therefore seeks for the Second L2 Application to be dismissed. 71. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by scheduling and conducting in-person showings of the rental unit through the course of their attempts to sell the rental unit. 72. Indeed, while the Tenant may have preferred to have received a notice at least forty -eight hours prior to a showing, and for only a select number of realtors to access the premises, the Landlord is only required to provide the Tenant wit h a notice “at least 24 hours before the time of [the] entry”12 in such circumstances. Additionally, nothing in the Act provides the Tenant with an ability to dictate which of the Landlord’s agents may or may not access the rental unit, when such entry is reasonable under the circumstances. 73. Furthermore, although the Tenant claimed that some showings were conducted without the Tenant being provided with proper notice, the Tenant was unable to provide any specific dates or times where such entries would have occurred, nor were they able to provide specific details with respect to comments that would have made them feel unwelcome in the rental unit. 74. As the Tenant limited their testimony and submissions to vague and general accusatory statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. 75. While conducting viewings of the rental unit in light of a prospective sale of a residential unit may be disruptive to a tenant’s day -to-day activities, a landlord is entitled to proceed in showing the rental unit to potential purchasers. The Tenant’s evidence does not lead me to conclude that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable and would amount to anything more than a “minor inconvenience,”13 for which the Tenant would not be entitled to any remedies. 76. Accordingly, the Tenant’s Second T2 Application, LTB-T-097881-23, is dismissed. 12 Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 13 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC). File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 Third T2 Application: LTB-T-095606-23 77. The Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, reiterates the grounds found in the Tenant’s motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 78. The Tenant claims the total amount of $17,000.00 as out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant would incur if the Tenant had been unsuccessful in setting aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 79. Firstly, had the motion to set aside the order LTB -L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, been denied, the Landlord would have been able to lawfully seek vacant possession of the rental unit upon the stay of the aforementioned order being lifted. As such, the Tenant would not have been entitled to further compensation or remedies on the basis of the Landlord exercising a lawful right. 80. Secondly, the motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, was granted. As such, the tenancy between the parties is not terminated pursuant to the N11 Agreement, and the Tenant is therefore not required to move out of the rental . The Tenant’s request is therefore moot. 81. I find that the Tenant’s Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, discloses no reasonable cause of action. Accordingly, the Tenant’s Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, is dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-097905-24 issued on June 11, 2025. On July 3, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on August 8, 2025 and September 22, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearings.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I am satisfied that there was a serious error in the original proceeding.

At the first hearing of this matter on March 6, 2025, both the Landlord and Tenant testified with respect to the events alleged to have occurred on September 3, 2024. The Tenant alleged that the Landlord sent an individual to the rental unit to change the locks on that date and the Landlord did not acknowledge doing so. It became apparent at the hearing that there was potentially more evidence (specifically testimony from a police constable who attended the rental unit on that date) that could help to determine the issues in dispute. The hearing was adjourned for the purpose of obtaining additional evidence to resolve the issues in dispute.

Prior to the reconvened hearing on May 29, 2025, the Tenant filed video evidence of her interactions with the individual who came to change the locks on September 3, 2024. Although the Tenant told the Member at the reconvened hearing that she had filed this video evidence, the Member did not review it. I find this to be a serious error in the proceeding. The purpose of adjourning the hearing on March 6, 2025 was to obtain evidence to help resolve the conflicting versions of events presented by the Landlord and the Tenant. The video evidence was a proverbial smoking gun that would have resolved some of the issues in the Tenant’s favour. I find it was a serious error not to review this evidence.
As a result, I cancelled the order and proceeded to hear the Tenant’s application anew. Tenant’s Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,842.19.

The Tenant testified that on September 3, 2024, she was in the process of preparing to move out because the tenancy had been terminated as of August 31, 2024 by order [name]. A man came to the rental unit that day and knocked on the front door. She did not answer the door. The man proceeded to unlock one of the locks on the front door of the rental unit. The Tenant then opened the door and confronted the man. The man told her that he had come to change the locks to the rental unit.
The Tenant submitted into evidence several videos of the incidents that occurred on September 3, 2024.

DOC-5197536 is a video taken by the Tenant on the sidewalk in front of the rental unit. In the video, the man states that he is there to change the locks. The Tenant states that she had been trying to get in touch with the Landlord. The man then makes a phone call and leaves a voice message stating “she’s still in the apartment so please call me back as soon as possible right now.”

DOC-5197563 is another video taken by the Tenant on the sidewalk in front of the rental unit. In this video, the man is speaking to someone, presumably the Landlord, on the phone saying that the Tenant is still there, discussing the keys to the rental unit, asking if the Landlord wants to speak to the Tenant (which is apparently declined), and asking for instructions on what to do.

DOC-5197584 is another video taken by the Tenant on the sidewalk in front of the rental unit. In this video, the man tells the Tenant that he must change the locks, he asks if he can take the Tenant anywhere else, and restates that he must change the locks.
The Tenant testified that she then left the rental unit because she understood that the man was going to change the locks that day.

The Tenant texted the Landlord at the time the man was at the rental unit to change the locks. The Tenant also phoned the Landlord and texted the Landlord multiple times in the following days seeking an opportunity to recover her possessions from the rental unit. The Landlord did not respond to any of the Tenant’s attempts at communication. The Tenant submitted into evidence text messages and phone records of her attempts to communicate with the Landlord after September 3, 2024 (these are attached to the Tenant’s request to review).
The Tenant said that her 2 cats were taken by Animal Control and that she stayed in a tent and shelter for several weeks after the September 3, 2024 incident.

The Tenant said that in mid October 2024 she discovered that the Landlord was not allowed to change the locks to the rental unit without Court Enforcement. She also discovered at that time that the Landlord had enforced order LTB-L-015354-24 through Court Enforcement on September 26, 2024 and that the Landlord had lawful possession of the rental unit as of that date.

The Tenant stated that she was never able to recover the possessions that were left in the rental unit on September 3, 2026 and that being abruptly removed from the rental unit was mentally distressing. She also testified with respect to the items left in the rental unit and their approximate value.
The Landlord denied anyone changing the locks on September 3, 2026. He also denied anyone unlawfully entering the rental unit on that date.

At the original hearing of this matter, the Landlord obviated addressing whether he had sent someone to the rental unit on September 3, 2024, however, at the review hearing, he did not deny sending someone to the rental unit on September 3, 2026 to see if the Tenant had moved out as he was expecting in light of order LTB-L-015354-24.

The Landlord states that he had the order lawfully enforced on September 26, 2024 and that he disposed of whatever was left in the rental unit. He submitted into evidence a video walk-through of the rental unit taken Monday, September 30, 2024 (DOC-5170534). This video showed that the Tenant had a significant amount of possessions still in the rental unit. Most of the items were packed in totes and bags, presumably in preparation to move. The Tenant acknowledged that this video, with the exception of the broken TV (see below), largely reflected how she left the unit.

The Landlord did not adequately explain why he did not respond to the Tenant’s attempts at communication after September 3, 2026. He said that he felt he had been wronged by the Tenant’s failure to pay rent and by her failure to move out in accordance with order LTB-L-015354-24 and that he did not feel obliged to respond to her.
The Landlord contested the Tenant’s testimony with respect to the value of the items left in the rental unit. Analysis

There is insufficient evidence to determine whether the locks were changed unlawfully or whether the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit prior to enforcement on September 26, 2024. As a result, these portions of the application are dismissed. I should also note that the only remedy the Tenant sought in her amended application was with respect to her lost possessions. As the Tenant will be compensated for these items with respect to the claims identified below, a finding with respect to the locks or illegal entry would have been superfluous. Similarly, a finding that the Landlord did not give the Tenant 72 hours after enforcement is not necessary given the findings below.

I am persuaded that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that they coerced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. I am also persuaded that the Tenant’s property was disposed of because of the Landlord’s actions.

The Tenant’s video evidence leaves little doubt that the Tenant was coerced to leave the rental unit on September 3, 2024. The man who attended the rental unit repeatedly told the Tenant that he had to change the locks, even after consulting with the Landlord, until the Tenant left.

The Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant between September 3, 2024 and September 26, 2024 constitutes substantial interference. I say this because of the particular nature of the Tenant’s text communications. It is clear from the Tenant’s texts that she believed the locks had been changed and that she no longer had access to the rental unit unless the Landlord let her in. The Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant’s texts to inform her that she still had lawful possession of the rental unit constitutes substantial interference. The Landlord allowed the Tenant to believe that she had been locked out of the rental unit.
The coercion and substantial interference by the Landlord caused the Tenant to vacate the rental unit and prevented her from recovering her possessions which resulted in their loss. Remedies
The Tenant’s amended application only seeks compensation for her lost possessions and I find it appropriate to grant the Tenant’s request.
To determine the appropriate quantum, it is necessary to determine what was left in the rental unit and the value of the items left in the rental unit.

With respect to what was left in the rental unit, there is clear video evidence taken by the Landlord that the Tenant left a significant quantity of items in the rental unit. While some of these items are clearly discernible in the video (e.g. pots, dishes, skateboard, radio, shelving units, TV (broken), TV not broken, bed, bedding, chair, fan, dressers, garbage can, and what appears to be several bags of clothing), it is not possible to discern from the video what was stored in the multiple bags and totes left in the rental unit.
The Tenant provided a list of the items allegedly left in the rental unit in her amended application and testified that the list accurately reflects what was left in the rental unit.
The Landlord did not provide evidence to undermine the accuracy of the Tenant’s testimony/evidence on this point.

While I accept that a significant number of items were left in the rental unit as clearly evidenced in the video, I had some difficulties with the list of items provided by the Tenant. Some of the items listed (e.g. 8,634 photographs) are unexpectedly specific and unlikely to be accurate. In addition, the volume of items identified on the list did not appear to accord with the quantity of items in the Landlord’s video, which, as noted above, the Tenant confirmed accurately represented what was left in the unit, with the exception of broken television. Having said that, and understanding that there might be some slight embellishments, I except the Tenant’s list as largely accurate.

The parties disputed whether the broken large screen TV depicted in the Landlord’s video was broken when the Tenant vacated. The Tenant testified that it was not broken when she left the rental unit while the Landlord testified that it was broken when he obtained possession of the rental unit. The video evidence, which was taken several days after the order was enforced by the Court Enforcement Office does not assist in determining this issue. While the burden of proving the application is always on the Tenant, I find that since the Landlord is alleging that the TV was broken, the burden is on the Landlord to prove this point. I also note that the Landlord had the opportunity to take video evidence when he first gained entry to the rental unit, but failed to do so. I am not satisfied, based on the evidence before me on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has proven that the TV was broken when the Tenant vacated. As a result, I conclude that this item was not broken when the Tenant vacated and the Landlord will be required to compensate the Tenant for this item.

With respect to the value of the items left in the rental unit, the Tenant requested $34,993.00. To support the amount claimed, the Tenant identified amounts and provided links to various websites for each of the items in the Tenant’s aforementioned list. I did not find this list to be particularly helpful for a number of reasons. Firstly, many of the links did not work so it was difficult to corroborate the amount claimed. Secondly, the amounts claimed, for most of the items, appeared to be for the amount it would cost to buy the items anew rather than for what it would cost to buy them used, this being the more appropriate amount to claim given that the Tenant’s lost property was used rather than new. Finally, some of the amounts claimed were just not realistic (e.g. $100.00 for a calculator, $4,000.00 for [name] bag of old phones). As a result, I do not accept the accuracy of the amount requested by the Tenant.

Given the difficulties noted above with respect to what was left in the rental unit and the value of those items, I found the best way to determine the Tenant’s overall loss was to review the video, whilst being cognizant of the Tenant’s list, and while relying on my past experience, having regard to like and similar cases, regarding value. While by no means perfect, I found this to be the best means to approximate the value. It would not have been appropriate to deny the Tenant any amount because she failed to establish value since there clearly were a large number of items left in the rental unit that did have some quantum of value. It would also not have been appropriate to grant the full amount requested by the Tenant as this overestimated the value, as identified above. Using the aforementioned method, I find the reasonable cost to replace the property that was disposed of to be $10,000.00.

The Landlord argued that the Tenant should not be compensated for all the lost items because the Tenant had expressed to the Landlord that the Tenant did not intend to take all of her items when she eventually moved out. Although the Tenant contested this to some extent, I do not find it necessary to resolve the conflicting testimony as I see no value to the Landlord’s argument on this point. Whether the Tenant did or did not intend to remove the belongings is immaterial given that the Landlord deprived the Tenant of any opportunity to remove them. We do not know, and because of the Landlord’s actions we can never know, what the Tenant would or would not have taken. Set-Off

The Tenant owes the Landlord $7,210.82 pursuant to order LTB-L-015354-24 (i.e. $3,006.00, the amount owing up to the hearing date of June 19, 2024, plus $3,485.36 for 76 days from June 20, 2024 to September 3, 2024 at $45.86 per day, plus $719.46 in interest from September 1, 2024 at 7%).
The Landlord is permitted to set off the amount owing to him from the amount he is required to pay the Tenant.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant the net amount of $2,789.18.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-097905-24 issued on June 11, 2025 is granted. The order is cancelled and replaced by this order.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,842.18 on or before April 20, 2026. This amount represents: 1. $10,000.00 for the reasonable costs the Tenant has/will incur to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions, 2. $53.00 for the cost of the application, 3. less $7,210.82 owing to the Landlord as a result of order LTB-L-015354-24 (note: order LTB-L-015354-24 is now satisfied). April 8, 2026 ____________________________
