issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The position of the Tenant is he found the rental unit listed for rent. He attended the rental unit on June 30, 2025 to view the rental unit with Landlord.
The parties entered into a tenancy agreement with lawful rent of $1,700.00 commencing on August 1, 2025 for a fixed term of one year.

The Tenant transferred a $500.00 deposit to the Landlord after viewing the rental unit, $1,200.00 on July 11, 2025 and a final $1,700.00 on July 29, 2025. The total amount the Tenant to the Landlord for a first and last month rent deposit was in the amount of $3,400.00.

The Tenant was provided keys to the rental unit and took possession of the vacant rental unit. Upon entering the rental unit the Tenant stated he suffered an panic attack, and had a feeling that he could not live in the rental unit. The Tenant left the keys in the mailbox and did not return.
The Tenant stated he attempted to settle with the Landlord and offered to allow the Landlord to keep $1,700.00 and return $1,700.00 to him to terminate the tenancy.
The Landlord filed evidence with the Board (DOC-7854625) to dispute the Tenant’s claims in the application.
The Landlord’s position is she did not prevent the Tenant from taking possession of the rental unit as the Tenant has indicated in the application.
The Landlord stated that the Landlord and the Tenant attended the rental unit on June 29, 2025 for the Tenant to view the rental unit. At that time the rental unit was rented to existing tenants.
The Tenant indicated he wished to take the rental unit and the Landlord asked the Tenant for references to perform her due diligence on the Tenant’s rental history.
The Landlord and Tenant signed a tenancy agreement (DOC-7854644).
The Landlord does not dispute she collected a first and last month rent deposit in the total amount of $3,400.00.

The Landlord stated that the Tenant picked up the keys on August 2, 2025 in the early morning to take possession of the rental unit and dropped the keys off to the Landlord on August 4, 2025 later in the evening.
The Landlord stated that she offered to return $1,700.00 to the Tenant if he signed an N11 notice to terminate the tenancy and the Tenant refused.

The Landlord submitted evidence (DOC-7854733) of an email exchange dated August 16, 2025, between the Landlord and the Tenant where the Landlord informs the Tenant of his obligation for the fixed term tenancy agreement and she was in the process of looking for new tenants.

The Landlord testified that she immediately started the process to look for new tenants on August 6, 2025 on Facebook Marketplace. The Landlord spent the next weeks interviewing approximately 20 potential tenants.

On August 23, 2025 the Landlord was able to secure new tenants for the rental unit. The new tenants made a deposit on August 23, 2025 and took possession of the rental unit on September 14, 2025. Analysis

The Tenant filed the application with the Board citing Reason 4 on the application that states: I entered into a tenancy agreement with the landlord but the landlord did not allow me to move int the rental unit and did not return the money I paid as a deposit.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find Tenant has not proved the Landlord prevented the Tenant from taking possession of the rental unit.

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Rent deposit, prospective tenant 107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 107 (1).
The Tenant’s own testimony contradicts his claim in the application as the Tenant stated he signed a tenancy agreement, received keys to the rental unit and took possession of the rental unit.
Section 107 simply means the Landlord cannot unilaterally decide to cancel the tenancy agreement and keep the last month rent deposit, but there must in fact be a tenancy agreement in place.
In this case before me there is no dispute the Landlord and Tenant had entered into a tenancy agreement and the Tenant had taken possession.

This also means that the Tenant cannot unilaterally cancel the tenancy agreement unless in accordance with the Act by way of the Landlord and Tenant agreeing to terminate, Board order or a notice of termination.
The Landlord stated the Tenant refused to sign the N11 notice to terminate the tenancy, and I find the Landlord credible that she did not agree to terminate the tenancy.

Section 16 of the Act states: When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. 2006, c. 17, s. 16.

This section means the Landlord has a positive duty to mitigate her losses and attempt to find new tenants. Based on the Landlord’s testimony, I am satisfied that the Landlord has met this requirement and was able to find new tenants to take possession on September 14, 2025.
Therefore, the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent ended on September 13, 2025.
The Tenant paid a first month rent deposit of $1,700.00 and last month rent deposit of $1,700.00.

I find the Tenant is entitled to the balance of the unused rent from September 14, 2025 to September 30, 2025, calculated as follows: • Daily compensation calculated as $1,700.00 (lawful rent) x 12 (months) / 365 (days) = $55.89. • September 14, 2025 to September 30, 2025 = 17 days x $55.89 = $950.13
Therefore the Landlord owes the Tenant $950.13 from September 14, 2025 to September 30, 2025 for the period after the Landlord secured new tenants for the rental unit.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall shall pay the Tenant is $ 998.13. This amount represents: • $950.13 for the unused portion of the last month rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The applicants requested amendment to the application dated August 20, 2025 are granted on consent for consideration.

At the onset of the hearing a preliminary issue arose regarding whether or not the applicant is a Tenant for the purposes of being able to file an application pursuant to Section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or whether they are a prospective tenant and therefore limited only to an application pursuant to section 135 of the Act.

For the reasons that follow, I do find that there was a valid tenancy agreement, however, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant is not entitled to any of the remedies being sought on the basis that I find that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.

Firstly, there is no doubt that a tenancy agreement was signed on May 15, 2023 between the parties with a commencement date of June 1, 2023. There is no dispute that the applicant arrived at the rental unit on June 5, 2023 with their belongings in a moving truck.

I also accept that the applicant transferred the utilities into their name effective June 4, 2023 and that they also obtained tenant insurance on May 19, 2023 and forwarded their mail to the new address. The applicant was moving from Alberta to Ontario to further their employment opportunities.

Secondly, I accept that the applicant paid $3,000.00 on May 19, 2023 directly to the Landlord intended to be the last month’s rent deposit. I also accept that on this same date the applicant sent a wire transfer to the Landlord’s real estate agent’s office for $1,695.00. I further accept that the applicant sent the balance of the required first month’s rent in the amount of $1,405.00 directly to the Landlord on June 2, 2023. The total amount paid by the applicant in accordance with their tenancy agreement is $6,100.00.
This relationship at the onset has all of the noted hallmarks of an enforceable contract relating to the formation of a residential tenancy agreement.

Irrespective of whatever transpired on the June 5, 2023 move-in date, the Tenant chose not to pursue their right to take possession of the rental unit and instead elected to proceed with the return of all of their deposit money paid. Which the Landlord returned to them by June 7, 2023 through the involvement of the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

What this means is that by June 7, 2023 the parties entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy. They mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy by their actions. When the deposit was returned, there was no longer a tenancy agreement.
With respect to the allegation of an illegal lockout on the move-in date, I found both the Tenants and the Landlords evidence equally believable.

The Tenant submits that it was the Landlord’s agent, MS, that took the keys from them after handing them over on the move-in date when they raised an issue about privacy regarding the installation of security cameras inside and outside of the rental unit and a comment from the Landlord’s agent, MS, that they live across the street and would be spying on them.

The Landlord submits that it was the Tenant that raised the concern about privacy and were disturbed by the close proximity of the Landlord and that it was the Tenant that stated they were not going to live there and then voluntarily gave back the keys to the Landlord’s agent on this date. The Landlord denies having security cameras inside the unit to spy on them and submits that the issue about the proximity only arose after they said that they would help them move in later because they live close by on the street over.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.
In the case before me I find both versions of events are equally believable. I am unable to find the Tenants versions of events truer than the Landlords.

Even if I were to find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on June 5, 2023 and then took the keys from the Tenant and locked them out, the Tenant failed to establish any of the requested remedies. They provided no evidence of their out-of-pocket expenses and no evidence regarding alternative accommodations.

Even so, the expense claims and rent differential are for times after the Tenant already agreed to terminate their tenancy through their actions of demanding and accepting the return of their deposits. The Tenant is not entitled to their requested remedies on the basis that they agreed to terminate the tenancy.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will follow.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant field documentary evidence (DOC-6834000) to the Board to support her claims in the application.
The Tenant’s position is the Tenant agreed to an oral tenancy agreement with the Landlord to rent a room in a rooming house for $750.00 per month commencing on November 1, 2025.
The Landlord requested the Tenant pay a first and last months rent deposit to secure the room, which the Tenant paid in one lump sum of $1,500.00.

On November 7, 2025 the Tenant texted the Landlord and informed the Landlord that her room was infested with bed bugs. She was experiencing rashes and bites as a result of the infestation and provided photos to support her claim.
The Tenant requested the Landlord schedule a treatment to remedy the issue and the Landlord refused.
On November 8, 2025 the Tenant informed the Landlord she could no longer stay in the rental unit and requested to be reimbursed for the balance of rent that was not used.

The text messages between the Tenant and the Landlord indicate the Landlord offered for the Tenant to terminate the tenancy and upon her vacating the rental unit the Landlord would return the unused portion of the Tenant’s first and last months rent deposit.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 10, 2025.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not follow through on her agreement and has not returned the last months rent deposit or the balance of November 2025 rent.
With the totality of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has proved the allegations in the application.
I am satisfied that the Landlord and Tenant entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy and the Landlord has not returned the unused portion of rent the Tenant paid to the Landlord.
The lawful rent is $750.00 per month. Daily compensation is calculated as follows: $750.00 (lawful rent) x 12 (months) / 365 (days) = $24.65.

The Landlord is holding a last month rent deposit in the amount of $750.00. The Tenant paid November 2025 rent in the amount of $750.00 and occupied the rental unit for 10 days ($24.65 x 8 = $246.50). $750.00 - $246.50 = $503.50.
The total the Landlord owes the Tenant is $503.50 (unused rent from November 11, 2025 to November 30, 2025) + $750.00 (last month rent deposit) = $1,253.50.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,296.50. This amount represents: • $1,253.50 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: For the following reasons the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
Board records indicate the Tenant filed the application with the Board on November 21, 2025.
The Tenant’s application is blank and does not indicate any claim being made or identify any remedy the Tenant is seeking.
The Tenant agent [name] submitted that the Landlord is aware of the issues and why the application has been filed and requested to proceed with the hearing.
The onus rests with the applicant, in this case the Tenant to provide sufficient evidence to support their claim.

The requirement for adequate particulars required within any notices of termination or as is in this case Board applications, has long been established by case law. The leading case regarding the requirement for sufficient reasons and details is Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931. This case stands for the proposition that the kinds of particulars that should be contained in a notice should include “dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct engaged in by the tenant”. The Court held that the tenant needs to know the specific allegations against him/her for three purposes: a. to know the case that must be met; b. to decide whether to dispute the allegations; or c. to consider whether to void the notice.

Although the decision in Ball v Metro applies to a Landlord’s N5 notice, I note that the same level of details like specifics on the claims being made and amount the Tenant is seeking is required in a T1 application in order for the Landlord to know the case to be met.

The Board’s T1 application forms have been developed with instructions to elicit the necessary details required for the Landlord to make a claim and provide sufficient reasons and details. For example, the description box under Reason 4 for a claim for damage states: “REASONS FOR FILING THIS APPLICATION”
The form then goes on to specify each allegation the Tenant can choose from by selecting the check box and provides instructions for the Tenant to explain reasons and provide a requested remedy.
In the absence of any claim the Landlord does not know the case to be met and the Board cannot issue an order in the absence of a remedy.

Board records indicate the Tenant submitted evidence and the application was filed almost five months prior and the Tenant has had ample time to review the application and prepare well in advance of the hearing.

In my view the Tenant should have been more prepared and reviewed the application with his evidence submissions. Had this been done the Tenant would have had opportunity to amend the application and provide sufficient reason and details for his claim.
For all the reasons above the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization], Brokerage (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (hereafter referred to as the ‘T6 Application’) This T6 Application was heard by videoconference on November 25, 2025. The Tenants and the Landlord’s Agent, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants partially proved, on a balance of probabilities , the allegations contained in the T6 Application. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the amount of $398.00 on or before February 28, 2026. Preliminary Issue: Named Respondent

At the start of the hearing, the Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘C.L) raised a preliminary issue, indicating that [organization], Brokerage is not a landlord, but rather a property management contracted by the owner of the rental unit o manage the rental unit on their behalf.

C.L stated that as part of their role, [organization], Brokerage, advertises the rental unit for rent, collects rents from Tenants, and coordinates with Tenants occupying the rental unit with respect to issues or inquiries relating to the rental unit.

The Tenants submit that throughout the course of their tenancy, they have only ever dealt with employees of [organization], Brokerage, and that all rent payment, questions, and inquiries were directed to [organization], Brokerage.

Section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') defines a landlord as follows: (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; [Emphasis Added]

Accordingly, the word “landlord” is not restricted solely to the property owner, as section 2 of the Act provides that the property owner can hire and name other individuals on their behalf to enforce their rights.

As such, on the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find that, while [organization], Brokerage is not the owner of the rental unit, the meet the definition of a landlord under the Act. As such, they were duly named as the respondent to this T6 Application. T6 Application: Issues with [name] a) Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenants testified that as per the terms of their tenancy agreement, the Landlord was responsible to provide the Tenants with air conditioning in the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the tenancy agreement executed on August 12, 2022 ( DOC-4656169, pages 8 to 21; Exhibit 1).
The Tenants indicated that as of August 15, 2024, their monthly rent was in the amount of $2,500.00. They described the rental unit as being a one-bedroom condo apartment.

The Tenants testified that they started encountering an issue with their air conditioning services as of May 17, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the condominium corporation to the Tenants, on May 17, 2024 (DOC-4656225, page 4 of 30; Exhibit 2).

The Tenants stated that they proceeded to contact the Landlord on June 18, 2024, to inquire about the ongoing air conditioning issue as they felt that it was “starting to be very hot and uncomfortable” in the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Tenants to the Landlord on June 18, 2024 (DOC-4656225, page 5 of 30; Exhibit 3).

The Tenants indicated that the Landlord acknowledged the air conditioning issue, and they were advised that the Landlord, in coordination with the condominium’s management (FirstService Residential), were working to resolve the issue, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenants on June 19, 2024 (DOC-4656225, page 6 of 30; Exhibit 4).

The Tenants stated that the temperature in the rental unit was as high as 31.5 degrees Celsius, as it appears from a picture of the Nest thermostat taken by the Tenant [name] (‘A.M’) on June 19, 2024 (DOC-4656225, page 7 of 30; Exhibit 4).

The Tenants proceeded to file a complaint regarding the ongoing air conditioning issues with the City of Toronto’s Municipal Licensing & Standards - Investigation Services, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences between the Tenants and the Municipal Standards Officer [name] , between June 16, 2024, and June 28, 2024 (DOC-4656225, pages 8 to 10 of 30; Exhibit 5, in bundle).

The Tenants indicated that shortly after the Landlord was contacted by [name], they proceeded to send the Tenants a cooling fan, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondence between by the Landlord , the Tenants, and [name], between June 28, 2024, and July 4 2024 (DOC-4656225, pages 11 to 14 of 30; Exhibit 6, in bundle).

The Tenants stated that despite the cooling fan provided by the Landlord, the temperature within the rental unit remained too hot. They therefore sought to terminate their tenancy on September 14, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences between the Tenants and the Landlord between July 11, 2024, and July 17, 2024 (DOC-4656225, pages 15 to 18 of 30; Exhibit 7, in bundle).
The Tenants testified that the air conditioning issue was resolved on September 13, 2024, one (1) day prior to their scheduled move out from the rental unit.

The Tenants therefore submit that the Landlord was aware of the air conditioning issue between May 17, 2024, and September 13, 2024, and that the sole step taken y the Landlord to mitigate the Tenants’ discomfort, was to send them a small cooling fan (Exhibits 3 and 6), which did not satisfy their needs.

The Tenants stated that the condominium association offered the Landlord the amount of $400.00 to purchase por table air conditioning units while the repairs to the chiller were ongoing, as it appears from the email from FirstService Residential, dated July 12, 2024 (DOC-4656225, page 12 of 30; Exhibit 8).

Based on their discussions with the Landlord, the Tenants proceeded to purchase a portable air conditioning unit in the amount of $303.18 between July 29, 2024, and August 4, 2024, which the Landlord proceeded to refund to the Tenants on September 3, 2024.

The Tenants therefore seek for the Board to award them a monthly 20% rent abatement for a period of four (4) months, due to the Landlord’s failure to be proactive in resolving the air conditioning issues, or failure to mitigate the impact felt by the Tenants within the rental unit.

The Tenants further testified that the high temperatures impacted their health as they had headaches ad difficulties sleeping in the rental unit, in addition to their work being impacted as they worked remotely and had difficulties doing so in the rental unit when the temperature crossed reached 30 degrees Celsius or more.
The Landlord did no seek to ask the Tenants questions under cross-examination. b) Landlord’s Evidence

C.L testified that the air conditioning issue the Tenants faced was actually a building- wide problem which affected close to four hundred residential units. They were only made aware of this problem on June 18, 2024, upon being contacted by the Tenants.

C.L explained that base don their exchanges with FirstService Residential, who manages the condominium on behalf of the condo association, the parts required to fix the chiller were backordered, which led to delay in the resolution of the air conditioning issue.

CL stated that they were essentially at the mercy of the condo association, as they could not take steps to resolve the issues with the chiller themselves. They submit that they took reasonable steps to address the issue by communicating with the Tenants and the condominium association and that the cooling fan originally provided to the Tenants was the only one that the condominium association had originally approved based on the electrical requirements of the rental unit.
The Landlord submits that they took reasonable steps in addressing the issue, and that therefore the Tenants are not entitled to a rent abatement. c) Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the Tenants1.

Although the rental unit is located within a condominium, the Landlord’s obligations do not change. They continue to be responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit “ in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”2

While the Tenants may have been advised as of May 17, 2024, of the building- wide chiller issue (Exhibit 2), the Tenants bear the responsibility of advising the Landlord of any ongoing issue they intend to have addressed within the rental unit. The communication provided by the Tenants (Exhibit 2) only show the Tenants as being t he recipients of this email. I 1 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name]. 2 Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. therefore accept that the Landlord was only made aware of the air conditioning issue as June 18, 2024 (Exhibit 3).

By failing to notify the Landlord of issues pertaining to the air conditioning, the Tenants unreasonably prevented the Landlord from entering the unit to assess the problem in order to take reasonable steps to repair the issue or mitigate its impact . As such, I find that the Tenants are not entitled to a rent abatement for the period starting May 17, 2024, and ending June 17, 2024.
The question therefore becomes, did the Landlord take reasonable steps to address the issue once they were notified on June 18, 2024.

I agree with the Tenants that the Landlord failed to act proactively once they became aware of the issue on June 18, 2024. While it would not be reasonable, under the circumstances, to expect the Landlord to repair or replace the chiller of an entire residential complex, of which they only own and operate one unit, the Landlord ought to have taken steps to mitigate the impact of the lack of air conditioning in the rental unit, rather than simply deferring to the condominium’s actions or inaction as the cause of the ongoing issues.

Indeed, regardless of the fact that the rental unit is located in a condominium, the Landlord obligations to the Tenants continue. I also do not find it reasonable to expect that the small cooling fan provided to the Tenants on July 3, 2024, would be sufficient to make a significant difference in the overall temperature of the rental unit (Exhibit 4), which was described as a one-bedroom apartment, nor was waiting to delegate the task of purchasing a portable air conditioning unit to the Tenants.

As such, on the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, in regard to the air conditioning issue, between June 18, 2024, and July 28, 2024, which represents a period of forty-two (42) days.

While the issue with the chiller persisted until September 13, 2024, I find that the installation of a portable air conditioning unit was reasonable under the circumstances, and as the Landlord has already refunded the Tenants the costs of the portable air conditioning unit, I find that the Tenants are only entitled to a rent abatement for the period starting June 18, 2024, and ending July 28, 2024.

Although the Tenants testified that the ongoing issues with the air conditioning impacted their medical situation, they did not submit medical notes for the Board to consider, nor did they provide an adequate description of their diagnosis or clarify the effect of any such a diagnosis on their ability to occupy the rental unit3. I therefore did not find their submissions in this regard to be pertinent. 3 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028.

Accordingly, I find - pursuant to the parties’ submissions and my knowledge of similar cases - that the Tenants are entitled to a total rent abatement in the amount of $350.00 in regard to the air conditioning issues. The amount was calculated as follows: • $250.00 for the period starting June 18, 2024, and ending July 18, 2024 (which is the equivalent to 10% of the lawful monthly rent for a period of one month). • $100.00 for the period starting July 18, 2024, and ending July 28, 2024.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the T6 Application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the amount of $398.00, which represents: • $350.00 for a rent abatement associated to the air conditioning issues. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference

The Tenant filed the application with the Board on December 2, 2024. Her claim for substantial interference relates to the Landlord substantially interfering with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to provide her a notice of entry at least 24 hours prior to attending the rental unit on November 19, 2023.

Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (‘the Act’) states: Time limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. [Emphasis Added]

T he Tenant’s application was filed with the Board on December 2, 2024, and her claim for substantial interference was brought more than a year after the date of the alleged conduct occurred, therefore, violating section 29(2) of the Act. For this reason, I dismissed the substantial interference claim and proceeded with the harassment claim only. Harassment, etc.

The Tenant’s claim for harassment relates to a June 29, 2024 incident that involved an N12 notice of termination and an N2 notice of rent increase letter being served on her by the Landlord’s legal representative. The Tenant testified that she was never paid the one- month compensation or offered any alternative accommodation. The parties agreed that the Landlord had withdrawn their application with the Board and never proceeded with the termination of the tenancy on that N12 notice. The parties further agreed that the Landlord filed an L2 application with the Board on that N12 notice, it was set to be heard by the Board on November 19, 2024, however the Tenant was notified the application was withdrawn on August 23, 2024. The Tenant testified that the N12 notice and N2 notice of rent increased impacted her mental health as the N2 notice increased the rent from $2,550.00 to $3,000.00.

I do not find that the Landlord serving an N12 notice, filing an application with the Board for eviction on that N12 notice and then withdrawing their application prior to the hearing rises to the level of harassment required to succeed in the Tenant’s claim. I make this finding because the parties agreed that the Landlord had served the N12 notice, but realized it was defective and withdrew their application before the Board. The application was withdrawn approximately 3 months prior to the hearing date and only 5 weeks after it was filed with the Board.

I also do not find that the Landlord serving the Tenant with an N2 notice for exemption rent increase rises to the level of harassment required for the Tenant to be successful in her harassment claim. I make this finding because the parties agreed that the rental unit was exempt from guideline increases and that the Landlord had provided the Tenant with 90 day notice of rent increase. While I understand the Tenant was not agreeable to the rent increase going from $2,550.00 to $3,000.00, the Landlord was legally entitled to make this rent increase under section 6.1 of the Act.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,321.35. Altered locks
There is no dispute that the Landlord changed the locking system on the rental unit townhouse sometime before November 16, 2024. The Tenant attended that day and found the locks changed.
The Landlord did not reach out to the Tenant to provide a key, nor as expected, did they arrange in advance for the locks to be changed and a key to be given.

The Landlord’s submissions and testimony are contradictory on this point. The Landlord’s property manager [name] acknowledged the mistake and testified that they often change locks in advance of the end of a tenancy to allow trades access and cleaning more easily. This makes no sense given one key opening a lock, works as well as another. No evidence was given that a special lock was installed. The Landlord’s representative submitted to the contrary that the locks were changed because the Landlord had a reasonable basis to believe the tenancy had been abandoned.
Section 79 of the Act states that: If a landlord believes that a tenant has abandoned a rental unit, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy.

A landlord must apply to the Board to terminate the tenancy. A landlord is not entitled to self-help by changing the locks if the purpose is to frustrate the tenancy. In this case, abandonment means actual complete abandonment with no intention of returning. It is not based on the Landlord’s reasonable belief that the tenant has abandoned a rental unit.

No evidence was presented that the Landlord attempted to communicate with the Tenant prior to changing the locks to see If she had abandoned the unit. They were, by all accounts, regularly in contact, and had her current phone and email address. Regardless of the reason for the Landlord to change the locks, the Tenant was not offered access to the rental unit until after she could not access the rental unit and complained to the Landlord.

Section 2(3) states: For the purposes of this Act, a tenant has not abandoned a rental unit if the tenant is not in arrears of rent. In this case rent had been paid by the Tenant to the end of November.

In this case I find no evidence that the [name] had been abandoned. The Tenant had been in regular communications with the Landlord and was clear that she was moving her possessions out slowly, and she would have the unit clean before she left. At no time did the Tenant indicate she had vacated, she did not give up the keys.

Section 24 states: A Landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

The purpose of section 24 is to ensure the Tenant’s security of tenure, that is, uninterrupted access to the unit. The Landlord violated that security of tenure by changing the locks without giving the Tenant a key to those locks immediately and without delay. The Landlord only offered the Tenant re-entry to the unit after she discovered the locks were changed and her property had been discarded, and only after several conversations regarding the situation.

Unit access must be meaningful to restore security of tenure. I accept the Tenant’s submission that the purpose for holding the rental unit was to allow a slow move over time. Once her belongings were gone, there was no further purpose for access.
For the reasons above, I find that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. Illegal Entry
The Tenant claimed the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit. She testified she did not receive any notice of entry and the property that was at the rental unit was not garbage to be thrown out.

The Landlord’s representative, at the end of [name] testimony, proposed to call a new witness to testify as to notices of entry. The Landlord’s representative stated at 4:14 p.m. that the witness had now gone home and she required an adjournment. I denied the adjournment for the following reasons.

First, this proposed witness was not present in the hearing room at any time throughout the day. No summons was on file for a witness. The Landlord’s representative did not mention at the start of the hearing that another witness would be brought in who needed to be called first due to time constraints.

Second, no notices of entry had been filed with the Board or served on the Tenant regarding entering to see if the Tenant had moved, or to change the locking system. It would have been apparent from the Tenant’s application that notices of entry and the person who gave those notices, or who actually entered the rental unit would be required in defense of this application. It is likely the Landlord did not anticipate the need for the witness, however, the desire to perfect an ill-prepared case is not a valid reason for adjournment.

Third, and in any event, the further testimony was unnecessary and not relevant to this case. The Tenant did not claim illegal entry for the lock change or for any other previous entry. She claimed unlawful entry when the Landlord’s maintenance crew removed her belongings. The Landlord entered and removed the Tenant’s belongings, from both inside and outside. Specifically from the inside, a stove, some pictures, a shower curtain and rack and boxes of personal photos that were in the closet. From the outside, there were multiple items that were in the backyard.
There was no suggestion that the entry to remove items was made “without notice” on consent or for emergency, or for some other enumerated permitted reason under section 26 of the Act.

Section 27 of the Act only permits entry with notice on certain conditions, but the removal of property is not one of the listed permitted circumstances upon which a landlord can enter the rental unit. Where entry violates a tenant’s rights, it is unlawful. No entry, however given, is valid if it’s purpose is in breach of the Act.

Where a tenant vacates the rental unit, section 41 states: A landlord may sell, retain for the landlord’s own use, or otherwise dispose of property in a rental unit or residential complex if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with, a notice of termination of the landlord or the tenant; an agreement between the landlord and the tenant to terminate the tenancy; subsection 93(2); or an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant.
The Landlord is a bailee for the goods left behind by the Tenant if the unit is properly vacated. The law of bailment applies, and most certainly does not include disposal of the property summarily.
Given no abandonment happened in this case, section 42 of the Act does not apply here.

I reiterate that proof of entry with notice, is therefore irrelevant to the validity of that notice. Even if the Landlord’s new witnesses had established the landlord gave written notice to the Tenant to ‘remove all her personal belongings’, the entry would still have been unlawful.

Finally, delaying the case, which was already 2 years old, would be overly prejudicial and not the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in this proceeding. The Landlord was afforded sufficient opportunity to prepare for and present their witnesses on the day of the hearing, and to cross examine the Tenant. I therefore denied the request to adjourn for a new witness to be called.
I note that communications between the parties demonstrate the Landlord acknowledged the mistake of entry and removal of belongings.

Considering my determination that the tenancy was clearly not abandoned, and considering the Tenant gave no permission to the Landlord to remove her belongings, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally when they entered to remove all the Tenant’s belongings. Remedies Disposed Property Compensation

The Tenant claims $6,000.00 for compensation for her discarded property. Only one photo was produced and submitted by the Landlord of the Tenant’s backyard items taken on October 28, 2024. It was not disputed that most of the possessions in the backyard were destined for the dump. Each item claimed for compensation by the Tenant is discussed below. 1. Trampoline. The trampoline was purchased in 2021 at Walmart. The Tenant claims she paid $500.00. No receipt was provided. The photo is not clear as to the condition. She acknowledges a safety net pole was broken. Left to the elements since it’s purchase, I find the depreciated value reasonably $50.00. 2. Washer/Dryer. These appliances were present in the rental unit when the Tenant moved in and were not her property. She acknowledged in her communication with the Landlord at DOC-7629584 that she would not be taking them when she moved. Therefore I find the Tenant has no entitlement to compensation for these appliances. 3. Lawnmower. No lawnmower appears in the photo of the backyard. The tenant thought she bought it in 2018. She could not say what brand or what size. She provided no receipt. I’m not satisfied that the Lawnmower was in fact in the backyard, and regardless, without knowing it’s value and condition, no order is reasonable. 4. Weight Plates. A photo of the interim shows 4-5 weight plates and kettle ball were left in the rental unit. The Tenant had no receipt. She could only estimate what they were worth new and did not know when they were purchased. I assign a nominal value of $50.00 for the plates. 5. Bicycles. The Tenant claims 5 bicycles were in the backyard, attached the back fence behind the trampoline. They could not be seen in the photo. The Tenant had no receipt for the bicycles and could not state their make, model, age or condition. Given the insufficiency of evidence no compensation is reasonable. 6. Sled Cover. The Tenant states a ‘sled cover’ was in the backyard. It does not appear in the photo provided. No receipt, or adequate evidence of description, age or condition was provided. No compensation for this item is therefore reasonable. 7. Stove. The Tenant purchased a stove and was entitled to take it with her. The Landlord discarded it when clearing her other items. She could not state the age, condition, brand or size. The Landlord has the stove available for her to pick up as it was not discarded. I find therefore that an order requiring pickup of the stove is appropriate in the circumstances. 8. Patio Table. A rectangular metal patio table with glass top and six metal chairs appears in the backyard photo. The Tenant testified she paid approximately $5- 600.00. I find the depreciated value of the table likely $250.00 and order that amount to be paid by the Landlord. 9. Jolly Jumper. The Tenant states she had a jolly jumper. The photo does not appear to show clearly this item but I am satisfied that the white item in the photo is the jolly jumper. A search of amazon during the hearing demonstrates the item is sold new for $128.00. It was purchased newly in 2022. However, exposed to the elements outside ,and used for two years, I find that it’s depreciated value likely to be $50.00. 10. Fish pump and Accessories. The photo showed a tiny pond in the backyard. The tenant claims a pump and accessories were thrown away. She claims $100.00. However, a search of amazon shows fishpond pumps value at $25.00 new. The Tenant could not articulate what other ‘accessories’ were there, or whether the pond itself was a fixture, or a removable item. No evidence of the pumps working condition or age was provided. I find therefore that no order for the accessories is reasonable, but the pump’s depreciated value is likely $5.00. 11. Pictures. A picture in the kitchen purchased at Home Sense was discarded by the Landlord. The Tenant estimates the purchase value at $60.00. However no receipt was provided. Other pictures were, according to the Tenant, outside the camera angle of the living room photo and could not be seen. Some were gifts. She could not recall more than one such picture of a tiger made of felt. She could not state the value of these other pictures. I therefore find it reasonable to compensate for the other pictures given the lack of supporting evidence, however, $30.00 is appropriate for compensation for the kitchen picture. 12. [name]. The Tenant claims a wheelbarrow was under the trampoline. It could not be seen in the photo. No evidence of age, condition or value was provided. No compensation will therefore be given for the wheelbarrow. 13. Box of Children’s Things. The Tenant claims a box of children’s photos was left in the closet of the bedroom. The Landlord produced no contrary evidence that the closet of the bedroom was empty, and [name] agreed that he did not look there. I am satisfied the box of photos was there. Although no specific value was requested by the Tenant for this item, the total amount claimed incorporates this item. Given the emotional distress and significant impact of losing photos, I find it not unfair to award $1,000.00.

Accordingly, as a result of the Landlord's actions, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,435.00, which is the reasonable cost that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was disposed. Out-Of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenant claimed future out-of-pocket expenses of $1,000.00 for gas expenses to go and buy all the things that were lost again, and the truck rental to transport those things. There were not actual current out of pocket expenses but future estimated gas expenses and possible truck rental to go out and re-purchase discarded items. The Tenant would have attended to pick them up from the rental unit if they had not been discarded, so she would not have been out of pocket. Given these are not actual out-of-pocket expenses, no compensation will be ordered. Rent Abatement

The Tenant claimed a rent abatement from the time she was locked out to the end of the Tenancy. She paid $1,700.00 for last month’s rent to November 30, 2024. Based on the Tenant’s evidence that she discovered she was locked out on November 16, 2024, I find it reasonable that the Landlord return to the Tenant rent for the 15 days from November 16 to November 30, 2024, in the amount of $838.35 (1,700*12/365=55.89 per diem amount*15). Fine

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”.

In the present case, I have considered the Landlord immediately acknowledged the mistake made and made attempts to compensate the Tenant. They were polite and apologetic. They did not dispose of the stove. I have also considered that the Tenants have been awarded a substantial monetary remedy, and so I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,321.35. This amount represents: • $1,435.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has to replace property that was damaged / destroyed / disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $838.35 for the return of last month’s rent prorated for November 16, 2024 to and including November 30, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

The Landlord shall make available the Tenant’s stove until April 27, 2026, for the Tenant or a her designate to pick it up at a mutually agreeable time. If the Tenant or her designate does not pick up the stove by end of day on April 27, 2026, the Landlord may dispose of it on or after April 28, 2026. . March 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant provide oral testimony and filed documentary evidence to the Board (DOC- 6838542) to support her claims in the application.
The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord is holding a deposit she paid to the Landlord for a rental unit and the Tenant did not take possession and the Landlord did not return the deposit.

The Tenant stated she found the rental unit and went to view the rental unit with the Landlord on September 1, 2025. The rental unit was one of two rooms in a condo. The other room was rented by another tenant.
The Tenant stated she paid a deposit of $500.00 to hold the room as the Tenant needed to provide her existing landlord with 60 days notice.
The Tenant stated the tenancy was to commence on November 1, 2025. The lawful rent was $1,350.00 per month for a fixed term of 6 months.
The Tenant submitted text messages between the Tenant an the Landlord regarding the rental details. Analysis

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Rent deposit, prospective tenant 107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 107 (1).
The Tenant’s position is there was no tenancy and therefore the Landlord has no right to hold the $500.00.
The Act defines a tenancy agreement as: “a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit;”
Section 107 prevents a Landlord from holding a deposit where the Landlord does not provide vacant possession to the Tenant.

In the case before me I am satisfied that a tenancy agreement was in place between the Landlord and the Tenant. The Tenant testified that the she and the Landlord agreed on a start date of the tenancy, the term, the day rent was due and when the tenancy was to commence.
The Tenant’s testimony was that the tenancy was to commence on November 1, 2025 so that the Tenant could given 60 days notice to her existing landlord.

The Tenant emailed the Landlord on October 26, 2025 and informed the Landlord she would not be taking the rental unit. The email from the Tenant states: “I have since decided not to proceed with the rental.”
On November 2, 2025 the Tenant follows up with another email stating that no lease was signed and she did not take possession of the rental unit and the Landlord cannot hold her deposit.

The email between the Landlord and the Tenant indicates that the Landlord was holding the rental unit for the Tenant since the Tenant gave the deposit and stated: “Hi [name], you said you wanted to rent my room I waited for you for two months. Now you don’t want to rent it anymore.”
Section 107 states a Landlord cannot unilaterally decide to cancel the tenancy agreement and keep the deposit, but there must in fact be a tenancy agreement.
Further, a prospective tenant also cannot unilaterally cancel the tenancy agreement and decline to take possession if vacant possession has been offered to the Tenant.
With the totality of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has not proved the allegations in the application.

Given the above I find the Landlord and the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord offered vacant possession to the Tenant however the Tenant attempted to cancel the tenancy agreement.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: At the start of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue and requested that the [name] application be dismissed. For reasons that follow, I agree with the Landlord that a fair and expeditious hearing is not possible and that proceeding with the application would be prejudicial.

The T2 application form lists an assortment of claims under “Reason 2 – Substantial Interference” which sound in disrepair, bad faith eviction and several other things besides but are entirely inscrutable. It includes the following notation “PLEASE REFER TO ATTACHED DOCUMENTS THAT HAVE MORE INFORMATION THAT DOES NOT FIT IN THIS BOX, THANK YOU.”

Filed contemporaneously with the application is a 17-page document entitled “November 2023 Matthew basement tenant blocked me said this is how it 2”. It continues a chronological narrative voicing disparate concerns sounding in disrepair, invasion of privacy, conflicts with a neighbour, disputes over lawn maintenance, etc.
The Tenant advised that review of her 99-page package of photographs and further 51- page chronology of events would clarify the issues.

The Board attempted to address the problem in the Tenant’s pleadings during the case management conference of October 16, 2025. By Interim order of October 20, 2025, the Board invited the Tenant to seek an amendment particularizing her claims and remedies. The Tenant’s response was to file a request to amend specifying that she seeks global compensation of $50,000.00 but without particulars. The substance of the allegations are not revised.

On discussing her concerns with the Tenant, it became apparent that she intends to raise further issues of disrepair, substantial interference and reduction of services and facilities that are not included in her pleadings and not the subject of a request to amend. Quite apart from the fact the many of the allegations rely on causes of action that are not the proper subject of a T2 application, I agree with the Landlord that it is not reasonable to expect the Landlord to examine every piece of evidence or pages of narrative in order to discern the allegations or determine what claims are being advanced.

The Board’s Rules of Procedure and processes allow for a great deal of flexibility aimed at ensuring disputes are resolved on their merits at a fair, expeditious and timely hearing. To that end, the Board will relieve a party from filing irregularities, breaches of its orders and directions or want of proper productions where it would foster the Board’s mandate contained in section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. This, sadly, is not such a case. I find the Tenant’s vague application means the Landlords are not in a position to adequately to know the case against them. I find that proceeding with the application would not result in a fair or expeditious hearing but would result in significant prejudice to the Landlords who are faced myriad, inscrutable allegations scattered across hundreds of pages seeking a substantial monetary award without particulars.

The Tenant is still in possession of the rental unit and advised that all of her concerns remain unresolved. While I make no findings, I observe that the Tenant remains at liberty to raise her issues and seek appropriate redress in properly pleaded application(s). Proper pleadings involve a concise statement of material facts identifying each issue and the cause of action being advanced.

The Tenant is encouraged to seek legal advice if she chooses to apply again. To find her local legal clinic, the Tenant may contact [name] at 1-[phone]. The Law Society of Ontario’s referral service can also assist parties in finding a suitable lawyer or paralegal. That service may be accessed by telephone at 1-[phone] or by email at [email].
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that Capreit (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards
reasons: The parties appeared before the Board on October 10, 2025 for matter LTB-T-080423-25. This was a T2T6 application filed on September 24, 2025 and primarily related to mould in the rental unit.

The order was issued on October 16, 2025 where among other things, the Landlord was ordered to conduct mould remediation. Various dates were set in the order and consequences for failure to comply. The Tenants understand they have an enforceable order.

The Tenants then filed another T2T6 application on November 21, 2025. The Tenants claims relate to the same issue and fact story. The Tenants claimed additional remedies related to a fine, costs and damages. The Tenants also claim remedies related to the costs to repair or replace property they claim was damaged, destroyed or disposed of as a result of the mould issue at the residential complex.
The Tenants’ representative states this is new information that was not available at the time of the previous application.
At the hearing, a review of the October 16, 2025 order was completed. It is clear, the Landlord has not complied with the terms of the order. The Estoppel Issue

Estoppel is a set of doctrines or principles developed by the courts. When invoked and applied, estoppel prevents a party from taking an action he or she would normally have the right to take. All of the species of estoppel are designed to achieve the same end; namely, to prevent an inequity.

The Board is not a court of common law or equity but it does consider and sometime apply estoppel principles. This is because s. 23(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act says: A tribunal may make such orders or give such directions in proceedings before it as it considers proper to prevent abuse of its processes.
The whole idea behind estoppel principles is to prevent abuses of process so sometimes the Board will look at the doctrines in the context of applying s. 23(1).

The doctrine of res judicata operates to ensure finality of decisions and prevent abuse of process. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue. In effect, it prevents a “second kick at the can”. It has two aspects, issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. The test for issue estoppel has three elements, which must all be present: (1) the same question has been decided; (2) the decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and, (3) that the parties to the prior decision were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised.

In Erschbamer v. [name], 2013 BCCA 76, the Court of Appeal for British Columbia provided a useful summary of the essential nature of each of the doctrines of res judicata as follows: “The general principles of the doctrine of res judicata were reviewed by this Court relatively recently in Cliffs Over Maple Bay. The doctrine has two aspects, issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. In brief terms, issue estoppel prevents a litigant from raising an issue that has already been decided in a previous proceeding. Cause of action estoppel prevents a litigant from pursuing a matter that was or should have been the subject of a previous proceeding. If the technical requirements of issue estoppel or cause of action estoppel are not met, it may be possible to invoke the doctrine of abuse of process to prevent relitigation of matters.”

The Court confirmed that the separate doctrine of cause of action estoppel is triggered where: • there is a final decision of a court of competent jurisdiction in the prior action; • the parties to the subsequent litigation were parties to, or are in privity with the parties to, the prior action; • the cause of action in the prior action is not separate and distinct; and • the basis of the cause of action and the subsequent action was argued or could have been argued in the prior action if the parties had exercised reasonable diligence.

The Board has a residual discretion as to whether to apply the doctrine of res judicata even if all three of these criteria are satisfied. Further, res judicata should not be applied in circumstances that would create an injustice.

As explained at the hearing, it appears that the majority of the remedies sought including a Board fine, expenses related to accommodation costs and general damages are barred by the doctrine of issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel, which are the branches of res judicata. The Tenants raised various issues related to mould and the Board made a final determination as per the October 16, 2025 order. The Tenants could have requested these remedies in the previous application.

The parties were asked for submissions on whether the doctrine of issue estoppel or cause of action estoppel applied to the various remedies as sought above. The Tenants’ representative said that she understood the issue as it relates to the Board fine and general damages. However, she believes that the Board should accept the claims related to accommodation costs. She said that the information became available a short time before the previous hearing and she did not undertake to amend the application. The presiding Member rejected the cost claim at the previous hearing. The Landlord did not provide any submissions on this issue.

Based on the submissions of the parties and in my view, the Tenants did not undertake the proper process to request to amend the application prior to the previous hearing. This was addressed by the Member and a determination made to reject the claims. In my view, the Tenants had reasonable opportunity to request to amend the application prior to the last hearing and failed to do so. I believe to include the claims in this application would be an abuse of process.
I do not find that the circumstances warrant an exercise of my residual discretion to not apply the doctrine of res judicata.

Supreme Court of Canada addressed issue estoppel in [name], 2001 SCC 44, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 460 (‘Danyluk’), para. 33: The rules governing issue estoppel should not be mechanically applied. The underlying purpose is to balance the public interest in the finality of litigation with the public interest in ensuring that justice is done on the facts of a particular case. … the court must still determine whether, as a matter of discretion, issue estoppel ought to be applied.

The Tenants did not lead sufficient evidence that would support a conclusion that they were unable to assert these claims in the previous application. I have considered all of the evidence adduced at hearing and I find the accommodation cost claims are barred by issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel.
The Tenants’ application is largely an abuse of process; most of the remedies in this application could have been included in the previous application.
However, based on the submissions of the parties, I am satisfied that the claims related to damage are not captured by the estoppel issue. The Damage Claim
The application claims $45,355.19 for costs related to the Tenants property that was damaged or destroyed by the Landlord’s failure to remediate the mould issue.

To summarize, the Tenants state that the City By-law officer and a mould technician advised them that all items in the affected area are damaged as a result of mould and should be disposed of. I note, there is no documentary evidence to support this claim and the Tenants did not call witnesses to testify.

It became clear during the Tenants’ testimony that no signs of visible mould were present. I sought submissions related to this issue. The Tenants state that they were told that their possessions were damaged by airborne mould and all items should be thrown away. The Landlord provided no further submissions.
As explained at the hearing, the Tenants’ bear the burden of proof to establish that the items were damages by mould as claimed.
In my view, there was insufficient evidence before me to establish a causal link between mould in the unit and the Tenants’ belief that their items must be disposed of.
While the Tenants’ representative argues that the presence of mould should be sufficient to establish that the Tenants’ belongings were contaminated and must be disposed of, I disagree.

I considered that the EMSL Canada Incl, report dated September 18, 2025 notes that some lab samples reported acceptable or slightly elevated levels; both Myxomycetes and Rust were reported as elevated. The Tenants were unable to provide an analysis of the elevated levels and did not call the mould remediation inspector to provide clarity. There is no indication in the report that the Tenants property was impacted by the presence of rust or mould to such a degree that disposition was required.

Additionally, I considered that the email between the EMSL Canada and the Tenants dated September 19, 2025 speaks strictly about elevated airborne mould spore presence and potential symptoms. Again, there is no indication as to the impact on the Tenants’ possessions.

In my view, the Tenants could have called the necessary experts to testify as to the impact of the airborne mould spores and their property but failed to do so. [name] there was insufficient evidence led at the hearing to support the claims related to damage.

In my view, it seems more likely that the Tenants assumed that since there was mould in the rental unit, that airborne spores damaged the items. There is no link between the mould assessment report and the damage claim. No one from the company testified on behalf of the report. Without testimony as to the findings in the report, the evidence was insufficient to find that the mould present in the rental unit caused damage to the items claimed. There was no visible presence of mould. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the report was sufficient to establish any causal link between the mould in the rental unit and the destruction of the Tenants’ belongings.

In the event I have erred in my assessment, I also considered that the Tenants failed to mitigate their losses as required by section 16 of the Act which states the following: When a landlord or a Tenants becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses.
In testimony, the Tenants acknowledged that no steps were taken to investigate the damages and potential to clean or restore the various items.

The Tenants did not provide sufficient evidence to prove their damage claim. I respect that the Tenants have lived in less-than-ideal circumstances and the Landlord has taken no reasonable steps to comply with the interim order. However, there was no evidence to establish a causal link between the mould issue and the damages claimed.
As such, I determined at the hearing, that it was not reasonable to proceed with hearing the Tenants’ evidence related to the damage claim.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $835.79. Illegal rent collected
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Application indicates that on Februray 14, 2024 the Landlord and Tenant agreed in writing to raise the lawful monthly rent to $2212.36 per month.

The Tenant testified that on [name] 8, 2025 he received an email from the Landlord indicating that the new rent in 2025 would be $2267.67 per month. The Tenant replied “confirmed, thanks [name].” The Tenant testified that he began paying this rent from March 2025 and paid it until December 2025. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not provide an N1 with respect to this increase.
The Tenant testified that the lawful monthly rent should have been $2212.36 per month rather than $2267.67 and sought $497.79 for excess rent collected by the Landlord for 9 months.

During cross examination the Tenant testified that when he received the email, he understood that it was a concerning rent increase and was for 2.5% and that he replied confirmed. He testified that at the time he did not know that the Landlord had not complied with the proper procedures to raise the rent.

The Landlord testified that on [name] 8, 2025 she sent the Tenant an email indicating the rent would be raised and he replied “confirmed”. She testified that she understood the Tenant’s reply to mean that he understood and accepted the rent increase. She testified that he would always confirm and pay afterwards. She also testified that when she followed the rent increase guideline the Tenant never questioned the increases. She testified that this had been her practice for 8 years.
Section 110 of the Act states: 110 No l andl ord shal l i ncrease the rent charged to a tenant for a rental uni t, except i n accordance wi th thi s Part .
I also note that pursuant to Section 3 of the Act, parties cannot agree to waive their rights and obligations under the Act. Therefore, parties cannot contract out of the rent rules.

Section 116 states: 116 ( 1) A l andl ord shal l not i ncrease the rent charged to a tenant for a rental uni t wi thout fi rst gi vi ng the tenant at l east 90 days wri tten noti ce of the l andl ord’ s i ntenti on to do so. 2006, c. 17, [name] (1). ( 2) [name] on ( 1) appl i es even i f the rent charged i s i ncreased i n accordance wi th an order under secti on 126. 2006, c. 17, [name]2). ( 3) T he [name] i n a form approved by the B oard and shal l set out the l andl ord’ s i ntenti on to i ncrease the rent and the amount of the new rent. 2006, c. 17, [name] (3). ( 4) A n i ncrease i n rent i s voi d i f the l andl ord has not gi ven the noti ce requi red by thi s secti on, and the l andl ord must gi ve a new noti ce before the l andl ord can take the i ncrease. 2006, c. 17, [name] (4).

In this case while the Landlord sent the Tenant an email indicating the rental would be increased, and the Tenant received this email and confirmed the new rent, the Landlord has not complied with Section 116 as they did not provide the Tenant with a notice of rent increased form approved by the Board. I also note that the increase was not sent to the Tenant 90 days in advance and the email sent by the Landlord did not indicate the date that the increase was to take effect.

I also note that in [name] v. Turnbull’s Grove Inc., 2007, ONCA 408 the court of appeal interpreted the “void” in section 116(4) to mean void ab initio, a legal nullity, as if it did not exist. It concluded that a notice that is “void” cannot be cured by section 136 as you cannot cure something that does not exist. Therefore, even if the Tenant had paid the increased rent for a period of one year the increase could not be saved by Section 136.
I also note that as the Tenant has not paid the increase for at least 12 consecutive months it cannot be saved by Section 135.1.

While the Landlord also alleged substantial compliance with the Act, I note that the requirement to provide a notice of rent increase is mandatory, and parties are not permitted to contract out of the requirements under the Act. Additionally, I note that the Landlord’s email of Februray 8. 2025 does not substantially comply as it does not indicate a date that the increase shall take effect and does not provide 90 days notice.
Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant moved in March 15 2018. He paid a last month rent deposit of $2000.00 on Februray 20, 2018. He vacated on Februray 14, 2016.
The Landlord's Legal Representative did not dispute that the Tenant was entitled to the interest owing on the last month rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $835.79. This amount represents: • $497.79 for excess rent collected. • $290.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
