issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘YZ’) and [name] (‘AW’, the ‘Landlords’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith
reasons: The Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords gave a Form N12 notice of termination for their child’s residential use under subsection 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) in bad faith.

The parties agree that, in May 2023, the Landlords gave the Tenant a Form N12 notice of termination to end the tenancy effective August 1, 2023. The notice states that the Landlords require the rental unit for the Landlords’ son WW’s residential use.

The Landlords did not dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about January 30, 2024 as a result of the Form N12 notice of termination. Although the parties entered into an intervening agreement on December 30, 2023 that gave the Tenant an additional $5,000.00 to move out by January 31, 2024, both parties’ legal representatives acknowledged the Board’s decision in Board order LTB-T-061512-23, issued on April 3, 2024. As in that case, the Tenant here introduced evidence that they would not have entered into the December 30, 2023 agreement, but for the May 2023 Form N12 notice of termination.

I am therefore satisfied the Landlords gave the Tenant a Form N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the notice. The Form N12 Notice of Termination and Terminating the Tenancy

At the hearing, WW testified that he asked his father, the Landlord AW, in the spring of 2023 if he could move to Toronto and live in the rental unit. This led AW to give the Tenant the Form N12 notice.

At the time, WW was enrolled as a student at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario. He was, however, unhappy living there and he developed mental health symptoms. WW consequently left Kingston to reside with a friend in The Netherlands. Because of immigration and visitor visa issues, WW had to return to Canada in August 2023. Since WW wanted to live in Toronto instead of Kingston, the Form N12 terminated the Tenant’s tenancy the same month [name] was to return to Canada.

The Tenant exercised her rights under the Act and did not vacate the rental unit in accordance with the Form N12 notice of termination. WW was unable to occupy the property with the Tenant present, and he instead returned to Kingston in or about August 2023. WW testified he stayed temporarily with different friends and did not maintain a permanent address. WW’s unhappiness with Kingston resurfaced, however, and he applied for an academic exchange program in Paris, France to again leave the city.

WW learned that he was accepted into the program in mid-December 2023. By then, he had personally contacted the Tenant to negotiate the Tenant’s departure from the rental unit. A December 8, 2023 email message from the Tenant to AW reads, in part: “Your son had extended an offer with a request to move out by December 29th. We appreciate the additional sum offered [$5,000.00], and this would greatly help us with leaving the property to find a new place. … However, we would accept the same offer with a move out date for January 31st instead.”
On or about December 30, 2024, the parties agreed to end the tenancy January 31, 2024, per the Tenant’s December 8, 2023 counteroffer.

WW explained at the hearing that his intention to live in the rental unit had not changed, despite applying for the academic exchange program in France. His focus at the time was on leaving Kingston. WW intended to reside in Toronto, viewing the opportunity to study in France as a way to depart Kingston.

I find WW’s decision to apply for the overseas academic exchange program is consistent with his and the Landlord’s intentions in May 2023, when the Landlords gave the Tenant the Form N12 notice for WW’s residential use of the rental unit. Indeed, WW’s reason for going on the academic exchange – to leave Kingston and live elsewhere while the rental was occupied – echoes his primary reason for wanting the rental unit and for the Landlord giving the Tenant the Form N12 notice.

WW, who was sequestered from the hearing in a separate online breakout room when AW gave evidence, corroborated AW’s testimony that WW intended to reside in the rental unit upon his return from The Netherlands in the summer of 2023. This lent credibility and reliability to both AW’s and WW’s testimony about their intentions with respect to the rental unit when the Landlords gave the Tenant the Form N12 notice under subsection 48(1) of the Act. Evidence and [name], re: Subsection 57(5)
As noted above, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about January 30, 2024.

At the hearing, the Tenant introduced evidence that the Landlords listed the rental unit for sale in May 2024. The Tenant invited me to presume the Landlords gave the Form N12 notice of termination in bad faith, pursuant to subsection 57(5) of the Act.

AW agreed he listed the property for sale, but he claimed he did not actually intend to sell it. AW explained that he had borrowed money from a family member to repay a Canada Emergency Business Account (‘CEBA’) loan AW’s business received during the COVID-19 pandemic. AW described financial hardship from poor business income and being unable to pay the CEBA loan without family assistance. When the family member visited AW from abroad in the spring or summer of 2024 and raised the matter of repaying the personal loan, AW listed the rental unit for sale to reassure the family member of his ability and willingness to honour the debt. AW testified that, despite advertising the rental unit for sale, he intended to remove the listing and proceed to have his son move in.
AW did remove the listing in September 2024. Based on evidence introduced at the hearing, I find WW moved into the rental unit in late July 2024 or early August 2024.

In the circumstances, I accept AW’s explanation for apparently advertising the rental unit for sale in May 2024. I am mindful AW admitted to being less than forthright with others, including close family members, when discussing the property listing. However, the preponderance of evidence, including evidence the Landlord endorsed WW’s direct negotiations with the Tenant in early December 2023 to end the tenancy, is consistent with AW’s evidence that he gave the Form N12 notice to the Tenant in May 2023, because he intended WW to reside in the rental unit. Information in the Tenant’s evidence of the listing for sale was also consistent with AW’s testimony that he cancelled the advertisement to sell the rental unit. By contrast, I note there was no evidence of an open house, or any other activity, during WW’s occupancy of the rental unit from the summer of 2024 that is consistent with trying to sell the property. These factors give credibility to AW’s testimony that he intended to have WW reside in the rental unit, despite any other claim or representation to AW’s creditor-family member.
The Landlords have therefore successfully rebutted the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord’s Child Moved Into the Rental Unit in a Reasonable Period

AW and WW gave consistent testimony that WW moved into the rental unit in July or August 2024, after renovations at the rental unit concluded. On July 17, 2024, AW advised WW in an email message: “Renovation of … [rental] unit all done and you can move in upon your return from France.” Later that same day, WW replied via email: “Thanks dad, noted!”. AA also introduced documentary evidence that WW received mail at the rental unit in the fall of 2024.

Although the Tenant argued that a video of the rental unit taken during an open house sometime in 2025 shows WW did not move into the rental unit in 2024, I prefer the Landlords’ evidence and find WW began occupying the rental unit in the summer of 2024. The July 17, 2024 email message between AW and WW, described above, and evidence that WW received mail at the rental unit, lend credibility and reliability to AW’s and WW’s testimony. Additionally, video of the rental unit from an unknown time in 2025 is not reliable evidence to determine whether WW resided in the rental unit in 2024.
Based on the evidence and submissions introduced at the March 3, 2026 hearing, I find that WW did move into the rental unit.

WW was overseas when the Tenant vacated the rental unit in January 2024, and the Landlords began renovating the unit approximately one month later. There was no evidence or submission to suggest the time to conclude the renovations described in the Landlords’ April 1, 2024 invoice was unreasonable. When renovations concluded in July 2024, WW returned to Canada and moved into the rental unit within weeks.
In the circumstances, I also find that WW occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

Subsections 57(1)(a) and 57(5) of the Act do not contemplate whether the person described in a Form N12 notice of termination, given under subsection 48(1) of the Act, resides in the rental unit for at least one year after the tenant vacates. Evidence of WW’s decision to move out of the rental unit in January 2025 was nevertheless relevant to a contextual approach to resolve the application.

WW conceded that he did not reside in the rental unit for one year. WW explained that he vacated the rental unit in January 2025 to temporarily return to Kingston to complete the remaining academic credit necessary to earn a degree at Queen’s University. WW testified that, as in the fall of 2023 before going on the academic exchange, he again “couch surfed” among friends and did not have a permanent address in Kingston.
The Tenant did not seriously dispute, or introduce evidence to challenge, WW’s testimony about returning to Kingston for the January 2024 semester and of his living circumstances during that period.

I find nothing in WW’s testimony about moving out of the rental unit in January 2025 affects or influences my principal findings in paragraphs 21 and 23, above. The evidence shows that, when AW gave the Form N12 notice of termination to the Tenant in May 2023, he genuinely intended to have his son [name] live at the rental unit, starting in August 2023. The evidence also shows WW moved into the rental unit, and that he did so within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated on January 30, 2024.
The Tenant has therefore not proven, on a balance of probabilities, her claim under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. The Tenant’s application must accordingly be dismissed.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: 25. The application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $71.90. Key Deposit:

At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that he paid a $150.00 key deposit and that the Landlord did not return it when the tenancy ended. However, the Landlord paid the Tenant $222.39 on November 25, 2025, in an attempt to resolve the issues raised in the Tenant’s application. That payment included the full $150.00 key deposit. As a result, the Tenant withdrew the key deposit claim from the application. Interest on rent deposit owing:
There is no dispute that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 12, 2022, and paid the Landlord $2,150.00 as a last month’s rent deposit.

There is also no dispute that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy as of September 30, 2025. The Landlord did not pay the Tenant the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the interest owing on the rent deposit is $151.29. This amount is slightly higher than the amount discussed at the hearing. My reasons for this finding are set out below.

Subsections 106 (3)(6)(10) of the Act says: (3) If the lawful rent increases after a tenant has paid a rent deposit, the landlord may require the tenant to pay an additional amount to increase the rent deposit up to the amount permitted by subsection (2). 2006, c. 17, (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (6). (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).

The parties agreed that the tenancy would terminate as of September 30, 2025. The Tenant did not pay rent for September 2025 because the Landlord applied the last month’s rent deposit to September rent. Therefore, as of September 1, 2025, the rent deposit became the rent payment for the last month of the tenancy and was no longer held as a deposit. For that reason, interest is calculated only to August 31, 2025.

After reconsidering the evidence, I find that the interest owing for the period from September 12, 2022, to August 31, 2025, is $151.29: INTEREST CALCULATOR TO 2026 Time Period From (DD- MM-YY) To (DD-MM-YY) or Anniversary Date Deposit Amount # of Days Interest Due For Period Ending in 2022 (1.2%) September 12, 2022 December 31, 2022 $2,150.00 111 $7.85 For Period Ending in 2023 (2.5%) January 1, 2023 December 31, 2023 $2,150.00 365 $53.76 For Period ending in 2024 (2.5%) January 1, 2024 December 31, 2024 $2,150.00 366 $53.90 For Period ending in 2025 (2.5%) January 1, 2025 August 31, 2025 $2,150.00 243 $35.79 For Period ending in 2026 (2.1%) January 1, 2026 February 28, 2026 FALSE $0.00 Total $151.29

The evidence also shows that the Landlord did not increase the amount of the rent deposit after September 2022. There is no dispute that the lawful rent for September 2025 was $2,205.00. Because the rent deposit remained $2,150.00, it did not cover the full September 2025 rent. I therefore find that the Landlord is entitled to deduct $55.00 from the unpaid interest.
The Landlord paid the Tenant $222.39 on November 25, 2025. Of that amount, $150.00 was applied to the unpaid key deposit. The remaining $72.39 is applied to the unpaid interest on the rent deposit.
The amount still owing to the Tenant is therefore $151.29 minus $55.00 minus $72.39, which equals $23.90.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $23.90
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $71.90. This amount represents: • $23.90 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

On June 30, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination with the termination date of August 31, 2022. The Landlord claims that he requires vacant possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by his son.

The tenancy was terminated by an LTB order on November 30, 2023, pursuant to the [name] application filing in connection to the N12 notice. The Tenants were evicted by the sheriff enforcement office on December 20, 2023. Subsequently staying for about a three month period from December 20, 2023 with friends on the same street as the rental unit, then in a tent on a property owned by an acquaintance and was finally approved for rent geared to income (RGI) housing on or about May 1, 2025.

The Tenant (GJ) stated that they have no evidence or proof that the Landlord’s son did not move into the rental unit other than that when they lived across from the rental property with friends they saw construction occurring, but that they did not see the son residing there. That after they moved out of their friends’ house, they were told by friends and neighbours that no one was residing there. And that they are aware that current day the home is still under construction however that it is their belief that no one is residing there. 5. (GJ) testified that it is their belief that the Landlord’s son had no intention of moving into the rental unit, this based on the prior hearing of the Landlord’s L2 application during which they become aware that the son lived in a condominium in Toronto. It is their belief that this is still the case as of the date of the current hearing. 6. That the Landlord effectively issued them a notice in bad faith and no one as outlined in the N12 notice moved into the rental unit in a reasonable time. Being displaced from the rental unit has had grave impact upon the Tenants, not limited to severe financial and health impacts. Above all, they submit that due to rent unaffordability they found themselves homeless living with friends and in a tent for a prolonged period incurring storage and other miscellaneous expenses. 7. The Landlord nor anyone representing the Landlord attended the hearing. Analysis 8. This application was served pursuant to Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act'). To be successful in their T5 application, the Tenants must prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 9. The first two requirements as set out in section 57(1) (a) and (b) of the Act are substantially met; however, there is no evidence before the Board to substantiate or corroborate the Tenants’ claim that the person(s) named in the N12 notice of termination did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. 10. As outlined above, the Act requires the Tenant “to prove” that no person as referred to in the N12 notice occupied the rental within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Here, the Tenants suggest that this is the case however have failed to substantiate their claims by submitting any proof which could be but is not limited to photograph(s), video or witness testimony. The Tenants’ submissions in support of their T5 application are based on “belief”, are speculative in nature and are insufficient to meet their burden of proof. 11. On the uncontested evidence before the Board, on a balance of probabilities, the Tenants did not prove that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the they vacated; and that ultimately the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 12. As the Tenants did not establish the bad faith of the Landlord and did not satisfy the third and fourth requirements of section 57(1)(a) of the Act, this application must be dismissed. 13. This order contains all of the reasons in this matter and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The application dismissed by order LTB-T-098631-24 issued on February 17, 2026 following a hearing of February 11, 2026 that the Landlord did not attend. On March 23, 2026 the Tenant requested a review of the order. On March 23, 2026, the Board granted interim order LTB-T-098631-24-RV-IN directing a hearing of the Tenant’s request for review. The request for review came before me in videoconference room 149 on May 13, 2026. As of 1:55 pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: Notice of this hearing, and of the February 11, 2026 hearing, was mailed to the Landlord at the address provided by the Tenant in his application. The envelopes were returned to the Board marked “Moved Return to Sender.” I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the address disclosed on the application is the Landlord’s current mailing address because the Tenant has personal knowledge of the fact that the Landlord lives at that address and has also observed the Landlord entering and exiting that address on a regular basis. I find therefore that notice of hearing was sufficiently given to the Landlord by mail to the last known address where the Landlord resides and that the Board has authority to proceed in the Landlord’s absence by authority of section 7 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act. Request to Review

The Tenant claimed that the Landlord repossessed the rental unit in bad faith when he gave notice of termination stating he required the rental unit for residential occupation by his son because his son never moved into the rental unit.

In order to succeed on the application, the Tenant had to prove each of the elements set out in section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; (b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith

The Board found that the Tenant had met the burden of proof with respect to parts (a) and (b) of the test but was not prepared to accept the Tenant’s evidence that no one lived in the rental unit for several months after he vacated the rental unit because it found the Tenant’s belief to be speculative and unsupported by confirmatory evidence.

The trier of fact is free to accept some, none, or all of any witness’s testimony and may draw whatever inference it deems appropriate from the evidence that has been proven. However, every witness, particularly a party whose interests are affected by the proceedings, has a right to receive reasons sufficiently detailed that allow them to understand why their evidence was rejected on a material issue.1 This is because the duty to give sufficient reasons is an essential aspect of procedural [name] The standard is not perfection, and reasons are to be read as a whole in the context of the proceedings that gave rise to them to determine whether they fulfill their intended function: (1) To justify and explain the result; (2) To explain to the unsuccessful party why they were unsuccessful; (3) To allow informed consideration of any review or appeal; and (4) To satisfy the public that justice has been done.3

In this case, the Tenant testified that he moved into his friend’s property across the road from the rental unit and monitored the comings and goings on a daily basis. He testified 1 Law Society of Upper Canada v. Neinstein, 2010 ONCA 193 at paras 80-81. 2 Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para. 127. 3 McAvany v. [name] Base Non-Profit Housing, 2025 ONSC 1164 ([name]. Ct.) at paras. 24-25. that he observed extensive renovations carried out under a building permit, construction waste being carried away, the Landlord’s son coming and going, but also observed that no one ever spent the night there. He asked the Board to infer from this circumstantial evidence that the intended occupant did not occupy the rental unit for residential purposes. The Board had no obligation to accept this evidence or draw the inference requested but it was obliged to include reasons sufficiently detailed to explain how and why it arrived at its decision. I find that the review must be granted because the Board’s reasons for rejecting the Tenant’s evidence as mere speculation are insufficient to justify and explain the result.

Based on the submissions presented, I was satisfied that order LTB-T-098631-24 issued on February 17, 2026 discloses a serious error. The request to review was granted and the application re-heard. Merits of the Original Application

The Board’s records show that the Landlord was granted termination on the strength of an N12 notice given to the Tenant in June 2022 stating that the Landlord required the rental unit for residential occupation by his son.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that: (1) He was evicted based on the Board’s order and therefore vacated the unit as a result of it within the meaning of subsection 57(1). (2) He observed no one living in the rental unit for months after he vacated the rental unit and also accept his uncontested evidence that the construction at the rental unit is ongoing as of the date of this hearing.

I therefore find that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that no person referred to in clause 48(1)(a), (b), (c) or (d) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

I accept that this delay is unreasonable, and in combination with the other evidence presented and guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith.
The application be allowed because the Tenant has proven the grounds on a balance of probabilities. Remedies
Having established the grounds for his application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies listed in subsection 57(3) of the Act that he can prove on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant testified, with reference to invoices filed, that he incurred out-of-pocket moving and storage expenses in the amount of $12,374.72. The application is amended to include that claim and the Tenant will be awarded that amount because I find it has been proven on a balance of probabilities and that it is reasonable.

The application claims loss of personal property because the Landlord did not give the Tenant access to the rental unit to recover belongings within 72 hours of his eviction by the Sheriff. He estimated the value of that property at $40,000.00 consisting of specialized tools, clothing, kitchen appliances, a snowblower, a lawnmower, an e-bike and household furnishings.

The Board accepts that these damages are recoverable under paragraph 4 of subsection 57(3). If necessary, the application will be amended to include a claim under section 41 of the Act because the Landlord did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove his property from the rental unit or from a place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.

The Tenant will be awarded $40,000.00 because I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence of his losses and based on the totality of the evidence presented I find that amount to be proven on a balance of probabilities and to be the reasonable amount for the cost that the Tenant incurred or will incur in replacing property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s breach of section 41 of the Act.

The Tenant seeks the maximum general compensation allowed under paragraph 1.1 of subsection 57(3) in the amount of $21,300.00 being the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged. This head of damages is intended to compensate for the mental distress, inconvenience and other non-pecuniary losses arising from an unlawful eviction. I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that he and his spouse lived with a friend for three months starting in December 2023 after they were evicted by the Sheriff. After that, they lived in a tent on a friend’s field until May 2025 when they eventually secured subsidized housing. During that time, the Tenant’s spouse was unable to work and lost her job. She attempted suicide. The Tenant suffered severe health and financial detriment as well. I find the claim for general compensation has been proven on a balance of probabilities and, on considering the totality of the evidence, I find $21,300.00 to be a fair and reasonable award to compensate the Tenant for his substantial losses caused by this unlawful eviction.

The Tenant confirmed that he is electing to proceed with his claims at the LTB understanding that any portion of the claim that exceeds the Board’s $50,000.00 jurisdiction will be forever extinguished by operation of subsection 207(3) of the Act once the Board issues its order.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
The Tenant did not a fee for requesting this review.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-098631-24 issued on February 17, 2026 is granted. That order is cancelled and replaced by the following.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $50,048.00. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. The Tenant also applied because the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on March 26, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord’s Agent, [name] and the Landlord’s Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenants pursuant to the terms of this order. T1 Application:

At the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw their T1 application. I consented to this request and proceeded to hear the T2 and T6 portions of the Tenant’s application. T2 Application – Substantial Interference
The Tenant, [name] (A.S.), testified that he occupied the rental unit on or about October 8, 2024.

A.S. testified that he observed a few live cockroaches in the rental unit and hundreds of dead cockroaches inside the fridge and freezer of the rental unit. He also found some cockroaches around the back of the fridge along with what appeared to be large clumps of cat hair.

A.S. sent the Landlord an email communication on October 11, 2024, notifying the Landlord of the state in which the rental unit was in at the time the Tenant took occupancy. The email included photographs of the dead cockroaches in the fridge, a photograph of his roommates’ rash from the cat hair behind the fridge causing an allergic reaction, and a photograph showing the space behind the fridge. The email requested that the Landlord immediately take action to inspect the unit for any cockroach infestation, replace the infested fridge with a new fridge, and clean and sanitize the rental unit and area in the kitchen where the fridge was located. The Tenant also requested compensation equal to one week’s rent for his time spent dealing with the issue.

The Landlord responded to the Tenant’s email on the early morning of October 12, 2024, informing the Tenant that the Landlord can send a contractor to disassemble the fridge and any other appliances that may need to be inspected, as well as a cleaner who will professionally clean the fridge after it has been disassembled. The email also apologized for the Tenant’s experience and Landlord’s surprise to hear of this after the unit had been cleaned and was only one year old. The cleaner and contractor would attend the unit at 10:00 a.m.

On October 12, 2024, the Landlord’s cleaner and contractor attended the rental unit. It was A.S.’s testimony that the Landlord’s cleaner and contractor did not do anything to resolve the issue. However, the Tenant did not tender any documentary or photographic evidence to show that state of the fridge after it was cleaned.

Shortly after the cleaning was completed, the Tenant emailed the Landlord informing them that he was not satisfied with the Landlord’s response in having the fridge professionally cleaned. The Tenant demanded that the fridge be replaced with a new one. The Tenant insisted that simply cleaning the infested fridge was not a satisfactory solution.

A.S. testified that the Landlord contacted him on October 16, 2024, and informed the Tenant that the fridge was fully functional, has now been professionally cleaned, and does not require replacement of a new fridge. The Landlord also suggested that if the Tenant is not satisfied with the Landlord’s cleaning of the fridge, the Tenant can arrange to have the fridge cleaned by their own cleaner and the Landlord will cover the costs associated with said cleaning.

A.S testified that he was unable to enjoy the use of the fridge in the unit due to the circumstances. A.S. did not testify that the fridge was not working or in a state of disrepair but rather that it was in his opinion unsanitary or unsafe to use despite the cleaning. Again, only opinion evidence was tendered to support this position.

A.S. testified that he monitored the rental unit for any signs of active cockroach infestations but did not see any signs of any. A.S. also confirmed he had access to the rental unit and full use of the bedrooms, washroom, and hallway areas. He testified that he was not fully able to use the kitchen or living room of the property which comprised of what he described to be 66% of the rental unit. This was based on his estimate.

A.S. testified that the property manager eventually agreed to inspect the unit and the fridge and upon seeing the fridge agreed to replace it as that is what was necessary. The fridge was replaced on November 1, 2024.

A.S. sought a rent abatement of 100% rent for a period of 24 days. The rent abatement is for the period of October 8, 2024, through to October 31, 2024. This is the period in which the Tenant had no use of the fridge in the rental unit.

A.S. took the position that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards by not replacing the fridge for a period of 24 days. A.S. also took the position that this substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

On cross examination, A.S. testified that he found more dead bugs in the rental unit after the cleaning on October 12, 2024, but he also confirmed that he did not upload any evidence to support his position.
A.S. also confirmed that all the issues relating to his application were resolved as of November 1, 2024, the date on which the fridge was replaced for a new fridge.
The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (A.W.), is employed by the Landlord in the capacity of a property manager.

He described the rental unit as having 2 bedrooms, 2 washrooms, with approximately 750 square feet of living space. He also described the kitchen of the rental unit to take up approximately 120 square feet and/or 20% of the rental unit space. The living room was approximately 25% of the unit being approximately 250 square feet.

A.W. confirmed that he received a copy of the Tenant’s first email on October 11, 2024, at which time the Tenant made him aware of finding the dead cockroaches in the fridge and requesting the unit be cleaned and fridge replaced. A.W. responded to the Tenant at approximately 1:00 a.m. on October 12, 2024, confirming that he can send out two individuals to inspect the appliance and have it professionally cleaned.

A.W. confirmed that the cleaner and the contractor attended the unit, and he understood the work had been completed. He did not believe that the fridge was not functioning or in a state of disrepair. The Landlord tendered two invoices from the cleaning company and contractor for the services completed on October 12, 2024.

A.W. testified that shortly after the cleaning was completed the Tenant forwarded the Landlord an email demanding the fridge be replaced and insisting that the cleaning of the fridge is not sufficient to resolve the issues. A copy of the email was uploaded to the portal by the Landlord.
A.W. testified that the Landlord did not approve the fridge being replaced because the fridge had been professionally cleaned and it was fully functional.
A.W. testified that the Tenant continued to send the Landlord emails and ultimately threatened to withhold their rent if the Landlord failed to replace the fridge.

A.W. testified that he attended the unit on October 24, 2024, at which time he observed the rental unit and the fridge. He described the fridge as being in a ordinary state of cleanliness and fully functional. He also confirmed seeing the fridge to be empty at the time of his inspection. A.W. also testified that ultimately the Landlord agreed to replace the fridge to avoid the Tenant withholding their rent and maintaining good relations as this was a new tenancy. He did not agree there was a problem with the existing fridge.

A.W. testified that the Landlord ordered a new fridge on October 25, 2024, and that the new fridge was installed in the rental unit on November 1, 2024. A copy of the invoice for the new fridge was tendered as evidence by the Landlord.
A.W. testified that when he attended the unit, he did not see a lot of furniture in the living room except for a small table and two chairs.

On cross-examination, A.W. confirmed that he saw the fridge in functional condition when he inspected it on October 12, 2024. He did not recall if the kitchen cupboards were open at the time of his inspection and confirmed he did not inspect the bedrooms as the Tenant’s concern was primarily focused on replacing the fridge.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, in that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with a functional fridge at the time of the Tenant taking occupancy of the unit. I say this because I prefer the evidence of the Tenant with respect to the state in which the fridge was initially found by the Tenant. I find the fridge was not functional at the time the Tenants occupied the unit.

Compensation that flows from this claim must be limited because the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probability that the fridge remained in a state of disrepair after the Landlord had the fridge professionally cleaned. The Tenant did not provide any evidence to prove that the fridge was not functional, and this was the Tenant’s application. The Tenant failed to upload photographs of the fridge after the cleaning was performed. His testimony alone was not sufficiently persuasive. The Landlord’s obligation under section 20 is to provide a working or functional appliance. There was no evidence to support the finding of an active infestation in the unit. I am also satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenant. The Landlord’s failure to ensure the unit was clean and free of any insects, rodents, or allergens such as large clumps of hair was unreasonable. I am not satisfied that the Landlord took diligent steps before providing the Tenant with occupancy to ensure that they have complied with their obligations such as providing the Tenant the unit free of insect or vermin.

However, the Landlord did not ignore the situation and took steps to remedy the issue within a reasonable time. It was not reasonable of the Tenant to demand a new fridge unless the fridge was no longer functional and/or unsafe to use. The Tenant did not provide persuasive evidence to support this was the case after the Landlord had the fridge professionally cleaned. This was the Tenant’s application, and the burden of proof lies with the Tenant. Remedies:
Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to pay the Tenant $750.00 compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $798.00. This amount represents: • $750.00 for substantial interference of the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit and the Landlord’s failure to maintain their obligations under section 20 of the Act. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.

The Tenant, [name] [name] (S.C.), testified that after she initially occupied the rental property, her former landlord listed and sold the property to the Purchaser/Landlord named in this application.

On or about September 28, 2023, the Tenant was served with an N12 Notice to terminate a tenancy for the Purchaser’s own use and residential occupation. The N12 notice sought vacant possession of the rental property on or before November 30, 2023.

S.C. testified that on November 30, 2023, the Landlord/Purchaser had approximately half of the Tenant’s backyard space paved with gravel. The Landlord did not communicate their intent to do this to the Tenant ahead of time. The Tenant did not consent or agree to this being done.

On or about December 1, 2023, the Landlord had a large sized wooden shed installed on a pad in the Tenant’s backyard. S.C. also testified that a large tractor was parked on her driveway preventing her from parking her motor vehicle. A photograph of the tractor and gravel was tendered as evidence by the Tenant.

S.C testified that on January 10th, and 31st, 2024, the Landlord and or their guests were causing or creating excessive noise disturbances. The excessive noise was described as loud talking, laughing, and music. S.C. also testified the Landlord and/or their guests caused or created further excessive noise disturbances on February 11th, and 19th, 2024. S.C. testified that she tried to speak to the Landlord about the noise disturbances but that each time she attempted to do so, the noise would simply be increased.

On or about March 15, 2024, the Landlord had an existing tree line in the backyard removed. S.C. testified that this tree line was a separation between the backyard of the two joined properties as the property was a duplex. S.C. testified that when she initially occupied the rental unit, she was given access to one half of the entire yard, which included a small space for her gardening and a small shed for her to maintain or store some of her personal belongings.

On or about late March 2024, the Landlord had a fence erected at the end of the Tenant’s driveway. This fence had a gate door which had a padlock and was inaccessible to the Tenant. The installation of the fence/gate resulted in the Tenant’s inability to access the backyard. The rental property had a front door and side door. Neither of the doors provided the Tenant with access to the yard. The Tenant tendered a photograph of the wooden fence/gate erected with a padlock on it.

On or about April 2, 2024, the Landlord had a large trench dug out in the yard leading to the large shed. Multiple holes were also made in the yard for the placement of posts to support the installation of a large wooden deck.

On April 11, 2024, the Landlord had additional gravel delivered to the property. S.C. also testified that the Landlord parked their motor vehicle on the Tenant’s front lawn and a truck on the Tenant’s driveway. This prevented the Tenant from accessing the front lawn or parking on their driveway. S.C. also testified that the Landlord and/or agent thereof placed a piece of plywood against the Tenant’s window to block the Tenant’s security camera. [name] of the vehicle parked on the front lawn and wooden board blocking the Tenant’s window were tendered into evidence.

On April 12, 2024, the Tenant’s driveway was blocked by a vehicle parked on her driveway. This prevented the Tenant from parking her motor vehicle in her driveway. The Tenant tendered evidence in the form of a photograph showing a vehicle blocking her driveway.

On April 19, 2024, a trailer was parked on the Tenant’s front lawn. This prevented the Tenant from accessing her front lawn. The Tenant tendered evidence in the form of a photograph showing a trailer parked on the Tenant’s front lawn. The Landlord also had a large second shed installed in the backyard. The second shed was not installed in the Tenant’s yard.

On April 21, 2024, the Tenant’s back window was sprayed with a substance that the Tenant believed to be spray foam. This action prevented the Tenant from having the ability to see through her back window and interfered with her ability to monitor the property with security cameras. The Tenant tendered a video of someone spraying her back window with a substance that looked like a foam spray.

On April 22, 2024, the Tenant’s back window was propped closed with a shovel being placed outside of the window. This prevented the Tenant from opening their window. The Tenant tendered a photograph showing a shovel placed outside of the window in such a manner as to interfere with the window being opened.

On April 23, 2024, the Tenant observed a long ladder placed against the outside of the rental property. S.C. testified that the ladder led up to the proximity of where her son’s room was located. This concerned the Tenant because she believed that the Landlord’s son had been watching her. The Tenant tendered a photograph of a ladder leaning against the rental property.
On April 24, 2024, the Landlord’s son placed his garbage on the Tenant’s driveway.

On April 27, 2024, S.C. contacted the police department and had them attend the unit so that she could peacefully remove her personal belongings from the back shed. S.C. testified that some her personal belongings had been removed by the Landlord or agent thereof.

On April 29, 2024, the Tenant’s window was blocked by a piece of plywood being placed against the window. The Tenant tendered a video of the window being blocked by a large piece of plywood. The video also shows the Tenant’s security camera being hit by the plywood causing the camera to fall and break.
On May 2, 2024, the Tenant’s back window was sprayed with a foamy substance which prevented the Tenant from looking through the window or observing the property with their security cameras.
On May 8, 2024, the Landlord’s son placed additional garbage on the Tenant’s driveway. The Tenant tendered a photograph of the garbage placed in the driveway.

S.C. testified that the Landlord also moved the Tenant’s shed in the yard from its original position to the very back corner of the yard. The Landlord also had the Tenant’s BBQ removed from the backyard and placed in the Tenant’s driveway.

On May 12, 2024, the Tenant vacated the rental unit. S.C. testified that the Landlord obtained an order form the Board for termination of the tenancy based on the Purchaser’s own use which required the Tenant to vacate the rental unit on or before June 30, 2024. S.C. testified that she felt compelled to vacate the unit prior the June 30, 2024, because of the actions taken by the Landlord.

S.C. sought a rent abatement in the amount of $2,640.00. This amount was equal to a 50% rent abatement for the period of December 2023, through to March 2024, and a 100% abatement for the period of April and May 2024.

S.C also sought general compensation in the amount of $10,000.00 for the stress caused by having to go through all these circumstances. S.C. testified that the actions of the Landlord were unreasonable, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and amounted to harassment on part of the Landlord.

On cross examination, S.C. testified to having a good relationship with her former landlord. She did concede to being irritated by the former landlord listing the property for sale not too long after her occupying the property but did maintain good relations with him.

S.C. confirmed that the rental property had originally been listed by different realtors, and the property did not sell. The property was later re-listed and sold by the current Landlord named in this application, who is also a realtor.
S.C. confirmed to be the mother of two boys who are 22, and 25 years of age. S.C. testified that one of her sons’ studies in the United States but lives with her when he is in Canada.
S.C. confirmed that the Landlord never specifically told her she could not access the backyard but did confirm that the gate was locked and that she was never provided with a key to the lock.
S.C. confirmed that her partner had a verbal confrontation with the Landlord on one heated occasion.
S.C. also confirmed and acknowledged understanding that the Landlord’s son had mental health issues which may have been the reason for some of his behavior.

The Landlord, [name] [name] [name] (K.A.H.), testified that she purchased on the property from the former Landlord and took ownership of the property on December 1, 2023. [name] also testified that she is a licensed realtor. 32. [name] testified that she assumed that the Tenant would have vacated the property on or before November 30, 2023, because this was the termination dated identified in the N12 Notice of termination that was served on the Tenant on September 28, 2023. 33. [name] confirms that on or about November 30, 2023, she had a large load of gravel delivered to the rental property and distributed in a portion of the backyard. [name] also confirms having a large wooden shed installed in the yard on a pad. [name] testified that she received the former Landlord’s consent to pour gravel on November 30, 2023. 34. [name] testified that she had the shed installed because she required a safe place to store all her personal belongings. [name] testified that she used the shed as a storage space for her personal belongings. 35. [name] testified that she was not aware that the Tenant had exclusive use of any portion of the backyard. K.A.H. also confirmed that she did not have any discussions with the Tenant or ask the Tenant what if any use of the yard she had prior to having the yard partially filled with gravel and a shed installed. The gravel and the shed were installed in the portion of the yard that was directly behind the Tenant’s unit. 36. [name] testified that the former Landlord informed her that the small shed in the yard belonged to him and the items inside were also his. The former landlord was not called as a witness to corroborate the Landlord’s testimony. 37. [name] testified that she attempted to enter the Tenant’s rental unit sometime in December 2023, but the Tenant refused to allow the Landlord entry because they disputed the lawfulness of the notice of entry provided to the Tenant. 38. [name] testified that the excessive noise that the Tenant testified to in January, and February 2023, was not intentionally caused or created by the Landlord. The Landlord was simply having conversations or listening to music with guests and did not have the intention of causing a noise disturbance. 39. [name] testified that she had the fence installed at the end of the Tenant’s driveway for the purpose of securing the backyard of the property, and more importantly the Landlord’s personal belongings located in the shed. [name] testified that she never placed or installed a lock on the fence/gate leading to the backyard and that the Tenant had access to the yard. [name] did confirm seeing a padlock on the gate in a photograph tendered as evidence by the Tenant, but she maintained that she did not install the lock, and it may have been her son who installed it. [name] testified that the gate was erected sometime in March 2024. 40. [name] testified that she removed the existing tree line in the backyard. She did not believe that the tree line was convenient and felt as a new homeowner she had the right to remove the tree line as she deemed fit. She did not speak with the Tenant prior to doing this. 41. [name] testified that she had a large deck installed in the backyard on or about April 2024. She confirmed that she did not discuss the installation of this deck with the Tenant prior to doing so. The deck as shown in the photographs clearly occupied what were previously two separate backyards. 42. [name] testified that the work that she had done on the property was to improve the home that she had just purchased and intended on occupying for her own personal use and residential occupation. She identified this as work that had to be done whether the Tenant vacated or not. 43. K.A.H. confirmed that the photographs tendered into as evidence by the Tenant show the Landlord’s motor vehicle parked in the Tenant’s driveway but maintained that she did not park it in the Tenant’s driveway. [name] testified that her son may have done this without her knowledge. She did not dispute this may have been done on multiple occasions. 44. [name] testified that the photographs also show a trailer and motor vehicle parked on the Tenant’s front lawn but maintained that she did not park them on the lawn and was not aware of this being done. [name] maintained that her son may have done this without her knowledge. 45. [name] testified that she believed that the videos tendered as evidence by the Tenant showing a wooden board being placed against the Tenant’s window was being done out of an abundance of caution and safety to prevent the window from being damaged. [name] states this would have been done when the holes in the yard for the deck posts were being dug out. [name] did not explain why the individual placing the board in front of the window did not take sufficient care to avoid hitting and breaking the Tenant’s security camera. 46. [name] testified that she believed the videos tendered by the Tenant showing the Tenant’s window being sprayed was a video of the Tenant’s window being washed with soap or a cleaner. 47. [name] testified that she did not dispose of any garbage on the Tenant’s driveway but did confirm that one of the items belonged to her son and that he may have done this without her permission. 48. [name] testified she had more gravel delivered to the property so that she could apply the gravel and extend the size of the Tenant’s driveway. She found this to be a benefit to the Tenant. She did not give the Tenant advance notice of doing this, nor did she ask the Tenant for their consent to do so. 49. [name] testified that she is a single mother who has gone though a very difficult relationship and purchased the property as her forever home and fresh start in life. She maintained that all the work was done in a very safe and professional manner. 50. [name] testified that she did not believe that the Tenant had any exclusive use of the backyard and as such felt that she was well within her rights to carry out the actions as identified above. 51. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant had exclusive use of a portion of the backyard. I am also satisfied that the Landlord unilaterally occupied the backyard space which the Tenant previously had access to. In doing so the Landlord erected a large fence and locked gate which prevented the Tenant from accessing the backyard. 52. I am also satisfied that an agent, worker, or guest of the Landlord parked their motor vehicle and trailer on the Tenant’s front lawn and in the Tenant’s driveway on multiple occasions. The Landlord had a driveway on the other side of the property as this was a duplex. Accordingly, the motor vehicle and trailer could have been parked in the other driveway which would not affect the Tenant. This was not the case and resulted in the Tenant having to park their car on the street. 53. I am also satisfied that substance sprayed on the Tenant’s window was more than likely to prevent the Tenant from having use of their security camera. I make this finding because the Tenant’s only identified the windows with cameras as being spray foamed. If this was cleaning it would have been applied to all the windows and not only the windows that have cameras. I am also satisfied that a lack of care was taken when covering the Tenant’s windows with the wooden boards. This resulted in the Tenant’s camera being broken. 54. I am not satisfied that the excessive noise disturbances that the Tenant’s testified to was intentionally done by the Landlord as it is just as probable that the noise was simply what the Landlord believed to be a conversation amongst friends or listening to music. These incidents only occurred on a handful of occasions. 55. I am mindful of the Landlord’s position that many of the actions were not done by the Landlord and that they did not have knowledge at the time. I am also mindful that the Landlord’s son has mental health issues which may have a role to play in the actions of the [name] son. Having said this, I am also mindful that the Landlord’s son was at the property as an agent for the Landlord. Accordingly, the Landlord would be responsible for the actions of her son. 56. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This includes blocking the Tenant’s access to the backyard, blocking the Tenant’s access to their driveway, and preventing the Tenant from accessing their belongings in the backyard shed. 57. Therefore, I find that the Landlord and/or Agent thereof harassed the Tenant. The harassment included spraying the Tenant’s window with a foam substance to prevent them from using their security camera, blocking the Tenant’s access to the driveway, parking in the Tenant’s front yard, and disposing of garbage onto the Tenant’s driveway. Remedies 58. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $990.00 is appropriate in these circumstances. This rent abatement is equal to a 20% rent abatement for the period of December 1, 2023, through to March 31, 2024, and a rent abatement of 35% for the period of April 1, 2024, through to May 31, 2024, the period to which rent was paid. The lawful rent was $660.00 per month. I find this amount to be more appropriate than the 50% and 100% abatement sought by the Tenant because despite incidents referenced above, the Tenant still had full use of her rental unit and living space. I am also mindful that the Tenant would not have had to access the yard in the winter as often as she would in the summer. The amounts granted are based on these factors and the severity of the substantial interference and harassment as it worsened towards the end of the tenancy. 59. Therefore, I also find that general compensation in the amount of $2,500.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. I find this amount to be appropriate because the Landlord’s actions taken had a direct impact on the Tenant’s tenancy between the period of December 1, 2023, through to May 12, 2024, the date on which the Tenant vacated the rental unit. I find that the actions substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and constituted harassment in some instances. The Tenant was treated as though she did not have any rights or authority to be in the unit, with any rights being blatantly disregarded. 60. I am mindful that many of the actions described by the Tenant were not taken by the Landlord directly but rather by someone who the Landlord authorized to be on the property, in this instance, the Landlord’s son. The Landlord is responsible for her son’s actions. I am also mindful that the Landlord’s son has a medical condition which may have impacted his judgement and that is considered when rendering this decision.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,538.00. This amount represents: • $990.00 for a rent abatement. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 19, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards(the ‘T6 application’). In file number LTB-T-075307-24, the Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 application’).
reasons: The Tenants say the rental unit was dirty when they moved in on May 1, 2023, that that the stove wasn’t functioning correctly and that rental unit was infested with bedbugs.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. (2016), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenants testified that the stove was wobbly and that controlling the temperature was a problem. They acknowledged the Landlord had the problems corrected within 2 to 3 weeks of the start of the tenancy which I find to be a reasonable response in the circumstances.

The Tenants testified that they observed bedbugs in the rental unit immediately upon moving in but did not include it in their written list of maintenance requests sent to the Landlord on May 2, 2023 because the problem wasn’t yet severe. It only became severe in the summer whereupon they lodged oral complaints with the Landlord’s superintendent. When those complaints went unanswered, they felt they had to escalate the matter by making a written request which came in September 2023. The Landlord immediately arranged for pest control technicians who did two treatments in the months of September and October. The Tenants acknowledge that they were advised the treatments had to be several weeks apart and that a third treatment would be needed. The Tenants found the conditions intolerable and vacated on October 29, 2023, before the third treatment could be done.

The Tenants accept that the Landlord responded immediately upon receiving their written complaint but submit that the Landlord fell short by not acting sooner in response to their oral complaints. I have trouble with this argument because the Tenants’ evidence in support of what they communicated to the superintendent and when was vague and lacking in detail. They had no record of when they lodged their oral complaint or complaints. I have trouble accepting the Tenants waited until the problem became severe to make their oral complaint; and waited again to make their written complaint. The [name] May 2, 2023 list of maintenance requests contains several items of a trivial nature but does not mention of pests. I find this more consistent with the probability that there were none at that time; and also consistent with the fact that the Tenants had no hesitation in voicing their concerns in writing, if they felt there was any need. Accordingly, I find the Tenants have failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that they mentioned concerns with bedbugs any earlier than September 17, 2023. I also find the Landlord’s immediate response was reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, this claim must be dismissed.

I accept the Tenants’ unchallenged evidence, confirmed by their written complaint letter of May 2, 2023, that the rental unit was not clean when they moved in and I accept that they incurred costs of $300.00 to buying supplies necessary to clean it. The Tenants will be awarded these out-of-pocket expenses because they have proven liability on a balance of probabilities and I find the quantum claimed it to be fair and reasonable in the circumstances.

I accept the Tenants’ evidence that on agreeing to allow them to assign their tenancy, the Landlord, through its superintendent, also agreed to refund their rent deposit and their key deposit. The Landlord relies on an assignment agreement of November 15, 2023 to argue that the assignment did not begin until that date and therefore the Tenants owe rent for the first fifteen days of that month. Although the assignment agreement is signed as of that date, it is silent on when the assignment takes effect.

I prefer the Tenants’ unchallenged evidence that the assignee took possession of the rental unit on November 1, 2023 and find on a balance of probabilities that the assignment began on that date. I also accept the Tenants’ unchallenged evidence that the Landlord agreed to return all of their deposit but has not. While the rent deposit must be applied to the last month of the tenancy under subsection 106(10) of the Act, the Act makes no provision for allocation of the deposit in cases of assignments. Therefore, the parties are free to allocate that money by agreement which is what happened here. This is consistent with the fact that the Landlord collected a new deposit from the assignee. The T1 application will be allowed because I find the claims have been proven on a balance of probabilities. The T6 application is allowed in part.
The Tenants incurred costs of $116.00 for filing the applications and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,146.00. This amount represents: • $1,730.00 for the last month's rent deposit and the key deposit. • $300.00 for reasonable out-of-pocket expenses. • $116.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 4, 2026. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The remainder of the claims are dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenants $1398.00. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenants uncontested evidence is that they paid $3300.00 to the Landlord on August 28, 2025 in contemplation of their tenancy on September 1, 2025: • $1500.00 for last month’s rent deposit (LMR) • $1500.00 for first month’s rent (FMR) • $300 key deposit
On September 3, 2025, there was an electrical fire in the upper levels of the house that destroyed the whole building and rendered it uninhabitable.
The Tenants were forced to find residence elsewhere, and were helped by friends and the Red Cross.
The Landlord did not provide any alternate housing or assistance.
The Tenants had contents insurance with TD Insurance and received a payment of $18,000.00 to replace their belongings. This did not include money for accommodation or rent.
The Landlord refunded the LMR and the key deposit ($1800.00), but did not refund the first month’s rent because they had already occupied the rental unit September 1-3, 2025.
The Tenants indicated that the house is presently being rebuilt, but they have ended the tenancy and are not interested in moving back. They are settled in their new home.
The Tenants are seeking a remedy from the Board to obtain the rest of the first month’s rent from the Landlord.
The Landlord did not attend the hearing, so the evidence of the Tenants is unchallenged. The Doctrine of Frustrated Contracts
A contract becomes frustrated when an event that was not foreseeable by the parties prevents the contract from being performed.
Section 19 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act), provides that the doctrine of frustration applies to tenancy contracts.

Section 3 of the Frustrated Contracts Act, RSO 1990, c. F34 states: 3(1) The sums paid or payable to a party in pursuance of a contract before the parties were discharged, (a) in the case of sums paid, are recoverable from the party as money received for the use of the party by whom the sums were paid; and (b) in the case of sums payable, cease to be payable

In the residential tenancies context, where a tenancy agreement is frustrated, the agreement to pay rent in return for occupancy is over. Any money paid for rent for the period after frustration occurs is refundable to the tenant and no further rent is owed. (TET-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB).

The jurisprudence describes two types of frustration: • Where the rental unit has been utterly destroyed or so seriously damaged that restoration will be very protracted and resumption of the tenancy is not reasonably foreseeable; or • Where an unforeseeable intervening event occurs that his not the fault of either party but so significantly changes the rights and obligations of the parties that it would be unjust to hold them to their contractual bargain. (TST-99550-18-AM (Re), 2019 CanLII 87146 (ON LTB)

The Board in TEL-10643-10(Re), 2011 Canlii 34537 (ON LTB) held that in order to successfully invoke the doctrine of frustration in the case of a tenancy agreement there must be, at a minimum, serious damage that will require a prolonged period of repair. This is determined by the facts of each case. (Spasov v Alnapa Inc., 2024 ONLTB 80945).

I find that this case before me falls in the first category of frustration. The house was uninhabitable and it had to be rebuilt, which is a long, protracted process where the resumption of the tenancy would not necessarily be foreseeable. 18. [name] et al, 2018 ONSC 5749, articulated the 3 criteria of the test for frustrated contracts at paras 11 and 22: a. an unexpected event that was not contemplated in the contract or foreseeable must occur. b. the unexpected event cannot be self-induced or the fault of one of the parties. c. the event must drastically change the nature of the contract so that it is impossible (not just difficult or expensive) to perform the obligations under the contract. The impossibility of performance must be of a long-term nature and not temporary or transient. 19. In considering the Barnaby v Salamander test, there is a line of authorities at the Board that finds having insurance means that the fire was contemplated by the parties and no frustration occurred (Haberman v Grinsaft, 2020 CanLii 119023 (ON LTB); [name] v Thunder Bay District Social Services Administration Board, 2023 ONLTB 26359; [name] v Mancini, 2025 ONLTB 62074 (CanLii). 20. I am not bound by these decisions and, given insurance is a requirement of most tenancy agreements for unforeseeable circumstances, I do not find constructive to conclude that merely having insurance means a contract is not frustrated. 21. Therefore, I find the first branch of the test is met: the electrical fire was unforeseeable event that rendered the rental unit uninhabitable. 22. Secondly, I find that the fire was not the fault of the parties. 23. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the fire drastically changed the nature of the contract so that it was difficult to perform for a time because the house was uninhabitable and rebuilding may not have been foreseeable by the parties. 24. Therefore, I find that the fire was an unforeseeable event that frustrated the contract and terminated the tenancy on September 3, 2025. 25. Pursuant to section 3(1)(a) of the Frustrated Contracts Act, I find that the unused portion of the first month’s rent paid by the Tenants is recoverable. 26. The Landlord’s proactively returning the deposits indicate to me that they deemed the tenancy to be terminated on September 3, 2025 and should have refunded the rest of September’s rent. 27. The Tenants are entitled to the rest of the rent they paid prorated for September 4-30, 2025, in the amount of $1350.00.
ordered: The Landlord pay the Tenants the total amount of $1398.00. This amount represents: • $1350 rent pro-rated for September 4-30, 2025 • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: At the hearing, I raised an issue in regard to the Tenant’s amended application. Specifically, the application lacked any particulars relating to dates and times the issues giving rise to the application occurred.

The Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931).

Although the [name] case related to the details required in a landlord’s notice of termination, it reflects the general principles of procedural fairness, which include a party’s right to know the case to be met. I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as I find it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient details of the issues to determine whether to defend the claim.
As it pertains to the T2 Application, the Tenants claimed the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I am not satisfied that the Tenants’ application contains sufficient details regarding the substantial interference. The application fails to provide a date or time or further details for that claim. As such, I find the Tenant’s claim should be dismissed for lack of details as the Landlord did not have sufficient notice to defend that claim. This claim is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
