issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Tenants claimed that the Landlord has not repaired or maintained the residential complex by failing to provide a working washing machine and dryer.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants an abatement of $2,285.84.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2016 and they continue to reside in the rental unit. This residential building provides one washing machine and one dryer in a common area so that all tenants are able to utilize the machines.
This application concerns the Landlord’s maintenance of the laundry machines. Evidence of [name] (HR)
HR testified that she and her husband have resided in their rental unit since June 1, 2015 and they continue to reside there with their children.

HR testified that she has been relying on the laundry machines throughout her tenancy and in early March of 2024, the dryer stopped working. There is one washing machine and one dryer in this residential building. Then, shortly thereafter the washing machine stopped working.

HR stated that she immediately put in a request on the maintenance application that is used by the tenants to request maintenance from the Landlord. She stated that her first requests were written in early March of 2024 and she continued on with requests for maintenance on a regular basis.

HR testified that these requests were “cancelled” by the Landlord or property management company or the response to the Tenant was changed by the Landlord to “work complete”. HR confirmed that she emailed the management company directly about this on July 31, 2024. This email was provided in Tenants’ disclosure brief.

HR stated that she continued to follow up with the management company and on August 12, 2025, they told her that there was a delay with the manufacturer and that they were working on repairing the damaged area.

HR provided multiple emails between herself and the property management company from July 31, 2024 through July 10, 2025 regarding the status of the missing washer and dryer. She explained that first the Landlord was going to arrange to have the machines fixed and then in October of 2024, the Landlord decided to install two new “Coinmatic” machines into the building.

HR stated that although the Landlord decided to replace the damaged washer and dryer in October of 2024, the new washer and dryer were not installed until July 10, 2025 and they became fully operational on July 20, 2025. The washer and dryer were not functional from March 8, 2024 to July 20, 2025, a period of 17 months and 12 days.

HR testified that during this period of time, she and her husband would gather up all of their clothes and their children’s clothes and attend at a laundromat every couple of weeks. The Tenants would then complete their loads of laundry at the laundromat and they continued this task approximately every two weeks for the period of time that the laundry machines were not functioning.

HR testified that having to attend at a laundromat was very time consuming, expensive and inconvenient but that they had no choice. HR stated that she would have loved to do laundry every day or every other day if the machines were available in the building.
HR stated that she was very frustrated with the lack of response from the Landlord and/or the property management company and felt that they did not take her complaints seriously.

HR is claiming a 10% rent abatement for the time period that the laundry machines were not functional. That time period was from March 8, 2024 to July 20, 2025. HR stated that her rent was $1,287.23 on March 8, 2024 and increased to $1,358.02 on January 1, 2025. Evidence of Elise Zerafa (EZ)
EZ testified that she is the Senior Property Manager for the Landlord for this location. She commenced this position in April of 2025.
EZ stated that as she was not employed with the Landlord when the laundry machine issues started, she reviewed the notes from the previous manager.

EZ brought my attention to the Landlord’s Document Brief which included an email dated August 15, 2024 from RTC Appliance Services and the Maintenance Coordinator for the Landlord. This email included an estimate to repair the laundry machines at the rental unit address.

EZ provided an email dated September 9, 2024 confirming that the Landlord would be moving forward with the quote to repair the machines. Further emails were provided which were dated October 3, 2024 advising the Landlord that there was a delay with the parts for the laundry machines.
EZ testified that she understood that the parts received were the incorrect parts and that is why the repairs were delayed.

EZ stated that when the Landlord decided to replace the laundry machines, after the wrong parts were received, she stated that there were problems with connecting the machines to the gas line. She stated that this connection issue caused the delay in replacing the machines.
EZ confirmed that the new laundry machines were installed on July 10, 2025 and fully functional on July 20, 2025. Law and Analysis

A T6 Application is based on the rights and obligations set out in s. 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs

The history of this issue is not contested and both parties confirmed that the laundry machines were not functional from March 8, 2024 to July 20, 2025. The real issue is whether or not the Tenants are entitled to a remedy and if the Tenants are entitled to a remedy, what should the remedy be.

The Act and the case law in this area indicate there are a number of relevant principles to consider when assessing allegations of a breach of maintenance: - First, if the Landlord responded to the disrepair in a timely and effective manner then no monetary remedy will normally flow. (See the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 Breach of [name].) - Second, the Landlord cannot be held responsible for compensation for disrepair that the Landlord was not aware of or could not reasonably have been aware of. [See s. 30(2) of the Act]. This is why the duty to mitigation in section 16 has been interpreted to include an obligation on tenants to report disrepair to a landlord. - Third, once the Landlord is aware of the disrepair, the normal obligation to repair and liability for the problem will begin.

I am satisfied that the Landlord was advised of the non-functioning laundry machines on March 8, 2024 and this issue was only remedied on July 20, 2025. The Landlord did not respond in a timely manner and did not provide adequate communication to the Tenants. The Tenants have requested a 10% abatement for the period of time that the laundry machines were not functional. This period of time was over 17 months.

Abatement of the rent is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, the rent should be abated proportional to the difference between what was being paid for and what was being received.

The Tenants did not have the use of the laundry machines and had no choice but to attend at laundromats with large loads of laundry every two weeks. These laundry machines were required to be maintained by the Landlord and the Landlord’s inaction in this case constituted a breach of section 20 of the Act.

The Tenants are seeking a 10% abatement of rent for this period of time which I believe is reasonable in the circumstances. The Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that this abatement should only be applied two days a month due to the fact that the Tenants attended the laundromat approximately twice a month. Ms. [name]name] explained in her testimony that in the circumstances, it made most sense for them to bring large amounts of laundry to a laundromat every two weeks to ensure that they and their children had clean clothes. The Tenant stated that she would have gladly done her laundry every day or every other day if the laundry machines were available. I reject [name] submission on this point.

As stated previously, it was uncontested that the laundry machines were not functional for a 17-month period. An order shall issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenants an abatement of 10% for a 17-month period which totals $2,237.84 plus the application fee. (Calculations include March 2024 – December 2024: $1,287.23 x 10% x 10 months = $1,287.23) and (January 2025 – July 2025: $1,358.02 x 10% x 7 months = $950.61)
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants a rent abatement of $2,237.84.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenants $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing of $2,285.84 by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing, it was brought to the Tenant’s attention that the allegations and remedies the Tenant wished to have determined were not included on the application itself but in a separate attached document. While I was satisfied that the allegations regarding the Landlords illegally raising the rent were sufficient for the Landlords to discern enough details to know the case to be met, and the Landlord confirmed that at the hearing, the Tenant’s allegations regarding illegal charges lacked specific dates, times, and descriptions of issues for the Landlords to be able to adequately respond. Consequently, the Tenant’s allegations regarding illegal charges were dismissed, and the application proceeded on the grounds that the Landlords collected rent in excess of the amount permitted by Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). T1 Application:

As explained below, the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $1,398.00, inclusive of the cost of filing the application.

The parties do not dispute that they entered into a one-year fixed term lease agreement that commenced on January 1, 2022. The rent was $1,550.00 as of that date and includes utilities and one parking spot. The rent is due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlords have illegally increased the rent numerous times without proper notice since 2023; however, their application was not filed until November 24, 2025.

Subsection 135(4) of the Act states: (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
Therefore, per s. 135(4) of the Act, only alleged illegal rent increases from November 24, 2024 onwards will be considered.

The Landlord submitted a rent ledger showing all payments received by the Tenant since February 2022. The Tenant also submitted their own rent ledger showing payments consistent with those in the Landlords’ ledger. Both ledgers show that the rent charged for November 2024 was $1,650.00. Whether the rent at that time was due to an illegal rent increase is beyond the Board’s jurisdiction as it falls outside the one-year limitation period in s. 135(4) of the Act. As the next rental period was December 1, 2024, the analysis of alleged illegal rent increases begins from that date with $1,650.00 as the rent charged.

The parties did not dispute the Landlords then raised the rent to $1,700.00 on January 1, 2025, $1,750.00 on April 1, 2025, $1,800.00 on January 1, 2026, and $1,816.95 on March 1, 2026. The Tenant has been paying $1,750.00 for rent consistently each month since April 2025. The Landlord only produced one N1 Notice of Rent Increase (‘N1 Notice’) which was for March 1, 2026. The Tenant would also be told about rent increases via text message.

The Landlord testified that he increases the rent for “overcrowding” when he discovers any additional occupant in the unit and decreases the rent when the extra occupant leaves. The Landlord also confirmed that previous rent increases have also included additional “utility adjustments” to account for increased utility usage when there are more people residing in the unit.

The parties also dispute whether the Tenant is using more than the single parking spot allotted to him. The Tenant was told via text that he would be charged an additional $50.00 for a second parking spot commencing January 1, 2026 until the Tenant or their occupant ceased to park their additional car. The Tenant maintains he never agreed to this additional parking charge and a copy of the text was provided in his evidence. The Landlord referred to a text from December 19, 2023 about a prior parking charge of $100.00 effective January 1, 2024; however, that charge is outside the scope of the one- year limitation period per s. 135(4) of the Act. [name]:
Section 110 of the Act states: No landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with this Part.

Section 116 of the Act states: (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the rent charged is increased in accordance with an order under section 126. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (2). Contents of notice (3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (3). Increase void without notice (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.

Subsection 119(1) of the Act states: (1) A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed, (a) since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase; or (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply.

Section 123 of the Act states: (1) A landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: 1. A parking space. 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 2006, c. 17, s. 123 (1). Application (2) Subsection (1) applies despite sections 116 and 119 and despite any order under paragraph 6 of subsection 30 (1).

Section 135.1 states: (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. 2020, c. 16, [name]. 4, s. 24. Non-application (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. 2020, c. 16, [name]. 4, s. 24. [name] compliance with s. 116 (3) For greater certainty, if subsection (1) applies with respect to an increase in rent, section 116 is deemed to have been complied with. Analysis:

The Landlord did not dispute that he has increased the rent more than once every 12 months contrary to s. 119(1) of the Act. All the increases were also above the guideline amount contrary to s. 120 of the Act. The Landlord maintained that the increases were for the guideline amount plus an additional adjustment for extra utility usage and persons in the unit. However, the rent cannot be increased unless in accordance with the Act, regardless of how many people occupy the unit. In this instance, utilities are also included in the fixed amount of monthly rent, as stated in the lease, and therefore any increases per the 12-month rule in s. 119(1) of the Act also include utilities. The Landlord is consequently not free to increase the rent when those utility amounts fluctuate. Should the parties no longer wish to continue their utilities arrangement, they are free to amend the lease by agreement.

The Landlord also did not provide proof of an N1 Notice for any rent increase other than the increase that was to take effect on March 1, 2026. Consequently, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord provided the Tenant with N1 Notices in accordance with s. 116 of the Act for the rent increases on January 1, 2025, April 1, 2025, and January 1, 2026. The Tenant also has not paid any rent increase for a consecutive 12 months since he paid $1,600.00 monthly from January 2023 to December 2023. Therefore, the above rent increases from January 1, 2025 to January 1, 2026 cannot be saved under s. 135.1 of the Act. The March 1, 2026 rent increase is also not deemed to be lawful per s. 136(1) of the Act as the Tenant had already made an application challenging the lawfulness of the rent charged on November 24, 2025.

Another issue, however, is whether the Tenant agreed to increase the rent with respect to an additional parking charge in accordance with s. 123(1) of the Act. Such an agreement would not be subject to the 12-month rule under s. 119(2) of the Act, and the charge can be added to the lawful rent. The parties do not dispute that the Landlord texted the Tenant that he would need to pay an additional $50.00 for parking effective January 2026 if the Tenant and/or anyone living with them continued to use an extra parking space on the driveway. The Tenant, however, denied ever agreeing to the additional charge, and no subsequent written communication was submitted showing that the Tenant agreed. The Landlord was the party making the claim and therefore bears the burden of proof on the balance of probabilities to substantiate that claim. Without any additional supporting evidence to contradict the Tenant, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has met the burden to show that there was an agreement between the parties to increase the rent by $50.00 for a second parking space.

As the above rent increases have been found not to be lawful and there was no established agreement to add an additional $50.00 charge to the monthly rent in accordance with s. 123(1) of the Act, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlords collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.

The lawful monthly rent is therefore $1,650.00, which was the rent charged one year before the application was filed on November 24, 2025 and before all subsequent illegal rent increases. The remedy thus extends back to the rental period following November 24, 2025, which was December 1, 2024. The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenant $1,350.00 for money collected in contravention of the Act through illegal rent increases from December 1, 2024 to March 1, 2026, for a total of 16 months. The parties’ respective ledgers confirm the amounts the Tenant has paid during this period, however, the Tenant did not lead evidence regarding how much or if rent was paid in April 2026. Therefore, the remedy is to March 1, 2026, and the Tenant is entitled to the return of $1,350.00 for rent collected in contravention f the Act calculated as follows: A – B = $1,350.00. A) Rent paid from December 1, 2024 to March 1, 2026 = $27,750.00 B) Lawful rent owing from December 1, 2024 to March 1, 2026 = $26,400.00
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,398.00. This amount represents: • $1,350.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $349.50 from the rent each month from June 1, 2026 to September 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 13, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $127.00. Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that the Landlord illegally entered her rental unit on two occasions: the first being December 5, 2023 and the second being December 11, 2023. The Tenant said that the Landlord did not provide her with notice of entry in compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) for these two occurrences. December 5, 2023:

The Landlord agreed that she entered the rental unit on December 5, 2023 without providing the Tenant with a 24-hour notice of entry as the Landlord had thought the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord testified that the Tenant texted her that she was vacating the rental unit and when the Landlord did not receive a response from the Tenant, the Landlord went to investigate if she had vacated. The Tenant did not agree with the Landlord’s version of events and testified that she never messaged the Landlord she was vacating. I find in favour of the Tenant as the Landlord was unable to adduce any of the messages she received from the Tenant, which supposedly stated the Tenant would be vacating. Furthermore, the Tenant had submitted into evidence photographs of the Landlord in the rental unit on December 5, 2023. Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on December 5, 2023. December 11, 2023:

The Landlord agreed that she entered the rental unit on December 11, 2023, but testified that she had provided the Tenant with a notice of entry on December 8, 2023. The Tenant did not agree with the Landlord’s testimony and said no such notice was ever provided. I provided the Landlord with the opportunity in the hearing to present any documentary evidence to support her claim regarding the December 8, 2023 notice of entry, but she failed to adduce such evidence. Therefore, one a balance of probability, I am satisfied the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on December 11, 2023. The Landlord agreed to entering the rental unit on this date and did not provide the Board with any evidence to substantiate a notice of entry was provided to the Tenant. Substantial interference/ Harassment, etc.

The Tenant testified that on December 7, 2023, the Landlord texted her about guests visiting her rental unit and how these visitations would result in higher utility bills. The Tenant alleges this text messages amounts to substantial interference and if it does not, then it amounts to harassment.

The Landlord did not seriously dispute that she texted the Tenant regarding an increase of utility bills as a result of her guests/ occupants visiting the rental unit. However, I do not find that the December 7, 2025 text exchanges on their own rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment required for the Tenant to be successful in these claims. The text message was a one-time occurrence, and if they were not a one time occurrence, then the Tenant failed to establish these type of messages from the Landlord were frequent or reoccurring. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with the Tenant and nor did the Landlord harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Remedies

T he Tenant submitted that she was seeking a 100% rent abatement for two months for the Landlord’s illegal entry. However, I find that $79.00 is more appropriate. I make this finding because the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on December 5, 2023 and December 11, 2023. The parties agreed the Tenant’s lawful rent during this period was $1,200.00 per month. The lawful monthly rent multiplied by 12 months in a year then amounts to $14,400.00. I then divided this number by 365 days in a year, which gives me the per diem amount of $39.45. I then take the per diem amount and multiply it by the two days of illegal entries, which amounts to a total of $79.00. It is for this reason, I find that a rent abatement of $79.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

I did not award the Tenant any other remedies for the illegal entry as the impact on the Tenant was minimal. I also did not award the Tenant any remedies under their substantial interference or harassment claim as I made my finding above that the Tenant failed to prove those claims on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant paid $48.00 for the cost of filing this application and is entitled to these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $127.00. This amount represents: • $79.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord submitted that there was no tenancy agreement between the Tenants and himself. He testified that the Tenants came to live in his home to provide help to his wife and himself as they are elderly and require assistance around the house in return the Tenants were permitted to occupy a room in the basement. He testified that the expectation of help was for them to do chores and cleaning around the property. He also testified that the Tenants never paid any rent or utilities during their stay.

The Landlord further testified that as soon as the Tenants received keys they kept making excuses why they were unable to help, such as not feeling well. He testified that eventually he had to give them notice to move out as they had reneged on their agreement to provide help. He provided copies of three notices he gave to the Tenants dated June 15, 2024, July 10, 2024, and July 22, 2024, respectively, into evidence (DOC-7755588pgs3-7).

Additionally, the Landlord asserted that the Tenants were entitled to only occupy a room in the basement which is not self-contained, and they only had access to shared facilities such as a kitchenette, bathroom, and laundry room. The Landlord provided a copy of a letter from his current care-giver, who describes the same accommodation, into evidence (DOC-7755588pg9). The relevant portion of the letter read: “I have been given the use of a large room in the lower level of the house for my use only. The lower level of the house, other than my room, is open plan. I have shared access to a small kitchen, a bathroom and laundry room area which I share with the family members from time-to-time as and when needed.”

When asked how the Tenants came to him, the Landlord testified that he had advertised for live-in helpers on the billboards at local supermarkets. Under cross-examination, when asked what criteria he was looking for in live-in helpers, the Landlord responded, “simply an ability to help around, chores.”

CL was removed from the room during LE’s testimony. [name] testified that they sold their own property and were living in an Airbnb when they decided to look for a new place to live. She also testified that they wanted to stay in the area and her husband found a listing on Kijiji describing the unit as basement apartment separate entrance, beautiful layout, private bath and kitchen, and secluded. She testified that they did not keep a copy of the advertisement and that it has since been deleted, but they were able to obtain from Kijiji the “metadata” of the existence of an advertisement and provided a copy of that into evidence (DOC-7779316pg12). The information provided in this “metadata” was the following: Ad_ID#, location, Post_User_ID#, the Ad_Title “Spacious 1,200 ft2 Studio Apartment – Lorne Park/Port Credit,” Ad_Asking_Price “2200,” Ad_Create_Date/time “2023-05-17 – 01:35:14,” Ad_Start_Date “2023-11-01” and Ad_Removal_Date “2023-11-03.”

LE testified that after seeing this advertisement, they contacted the Landlord and they arranged to meet. She testified that they met at the house and entered through a separate entrance to view the basement. She described the basement as a “quite big” room with a private bathroom and a private kitchen. She also testified that although the advertisement stated $2,200.00, the Landlord said since they were adding another person, it would be $2,300.00, which they accepted.

LE also testified that the Landlord requested first and last month’s rent plus $1,100.00 for a security deposit. She testified that she asked for a lease agreement but the Landlord said it would take too long with all the checks and that they will do this on a monthly basis. She also testified that they went to the bank immediately and gave the Landlord the cash to secure the place. In support of her assertion she provided a copy of their bank statement for the month of November 2023 highlighting a cash withdrawal on November 2, 2023 of $5,750.00 into evidence (DOC-6570575pg5).

She further testified that they moved into the unit on November15, 2023 and brought all their belongings including furniture. She testified that the Landlord had also requested for them to pay a total of six months up front, so they paid an additional $4,600.00 on December 4, 2023 and another $4,600.00 on December 29, 2023. In support of her assertions, she provided copies of their bank statement for December 2023 highlighting a cash withdrawal of $4,600.00 on December 4, 2023 and a cash withdrawal of $4,600.00 on December 29, 2023 into evidence (DOC-6570575pgs9-10). She also provided a copy of a cash withdrawal receipt from her bank dated December 29, 2023 for $4,600.00 into evidence (DOC-6570575pg13).

CL testified that they were looking for an apartment because they were paying too much for the Airbnb where they were staying and it was him who found the advertisement for this rental unit. He testified that he had a conversation with the Landlord over the telephone in which he provided his information including driver’s license, and they agreed to meet. He also testified that in early November they met with the Landlord and his wife at the rental unit and discussed a rental amount of $2,200.00. He testified that the Landlord stated that because they are two people the amount would be $2,300.00. He further testified that they agreed on this amount and were required to pay first and last month’s rent to secure the place and did so in cash that day.

CL also testified that the Landlord had requested a security deposit in the amount of $1,125.00 or $1,150.00 and that they paid the Landlord two other months twice in the amount of $4,600.00 each. CL testified that all payments were made to the Landlord in cash as requested by him and no receipts were provided. He asserted that they paid a total of six months in rent and a security deposit.

Under cross-examination, CL confirmed that when they met with the Landlord and agreed on $2,300.00 a month, they left and went to the bank to give the Landlord the cash and he knows it was $4,600.00 plus $1,150.00. Under cross-examination, CL could not provide the specific dates of any other amounts given to the Landlord but did confirm that there were two other payments of $4,600.00 each, which he asserted totals six months plus the deposit.

CL also testified that they moved in a few weeks later and described the unit as a large room in the basement which had a separate bathroom and a kitchenette, which had a laundry set, stove, fridge and microwave. He further testified that they accessed the unit through the side of the house, and there were stairs going down to a side door and when you entered you were in the unit. He did acknowledge that there was another door to go up to the main floor but that door was never used by anyone.

The Landlord submitted that the Kijiji advertisement relied upon by the Tenants simply showed there was an ad posted and he finds it unlikely that Kijiji would not be able to give the full information. He also submitted that there is no evidence that the Tenants’ cash withdrawals from their bank were received by him. He maintained that their relationship was work based, helping him in return for living in the room.

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that this was a tenancy. The Tenants moved into the unit on November 15, 2023, paid first and last month’s rent, a security deposit, and another four months rent to the Landlord in cash as demanded by him. She also submitted that while they do not have the full advertisement from Kijiji, the “metadata” is there. She further submitted that the Tenants only discovered the Landlord’s assertion that they were workers when they received the first notice from him in June 2024. She further submitted that the rental unit had its own entrance, bathroom and kitchen, and that the Tenants had no access to the upstairs. Law and Analysis

For the following reasons, I was satisfied that the parties had entered into a tenancy for this unit at a monthly rent of $2,300.00, that the Landlord received a total of $14,950.00 from the Tenants during their tenancy, and that the Act applies to this unit.

A party claiming an exemption under the Act bears the burden to prove on a balance of probabilities the living accommodation is exempt. In this case, the Landlord asserts that the bathroom and kitchen were shared facilities. Section 5(i) of the Act provides that: This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

There is no dispute that the basement is one large room that has a bathroom and a kitchen (or kitchenette). The Landlord asserts that the bathroom and kitchen were shared facilities. Other than this assertion, his supporting evidence was a letter from his current live-in caregiver. Despite the letter not being signed by the person who wrote it and that this person did not testify so the contents of the letter could not be tested, the wording in the letter also fails to support the Landlord’s assertion. On one hand, the writer states they “have been given the use of a large room in the lower level of the house for my use only” (my emphasis). Then the writer says “the lower level of the house, other than my room, is open plan. I have shared access to a small kitchen, a bathroom and laundry room area which I share with the family members from time-to-time as and when needed” (my emphasis).

The Landlord in his testimony described the room in the basement as a “large room with no door” and “open basement.” The Tenants described the basement area in a similar fashion. Given this, I was satisfied that the layout of the basement was an open plan meaning a very large room with a bathroom, kitchen area (including or not laundry machines) off of it. If this is the case, then the only way to access the bathroom and the kitchen would be through the room itself. So I find the description provided in the letter the Landlord is relying upon is inconsistent, as how can the room be only for their use but the rooms off it be shared. Given this inconsistency, along with the letter not being signed and the contents not being tested, I found it unreliable and it does not support the Landlord’s assertion.

The Landlord did not testify that he or any other member of his household used the facilities in the basement during the tenancy or provided any other supporting evidence to demonstrate that they could easily access these facility such as pictures of the area to confirm that there were no barriers or doors to the basement kitchen and bathroom. The Tenants described the unit as self-contained with the entrance being from a side exterior door. CL testified that while although at the side entrance there is another door to the main level of the house, it was not used.

Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the Tenants were required to share a kitchen or bathroom facility with the Landlord. There was no evidence provided that the Landlord or other members of his household used these facilities in the Tenants’ unit. I find it more likely than not that these facilities were exclusively used by the Tenants and that was the case from the beginning of the tenancy. Additionally, the Landlord testified that he and his wife are elderly and suffer from rheumatoid arthritis. Given this, I find it unlikely that they were going down into the basement to use these facilities.

As well, I found the Landlord’s evidence less credible than the Tenants. The second part of the Landlord’s assertion is that the Act does not apply as his arrangement with the Tenants was for them to provide help around the house, cleaning, chores, etc. for him and his wife as they are elderly in exchange for occupying the basement room. He testified that had placed an advertisement for a live-in caregiver at the supermarket and that in November 2023 when he met the Tenants and they viewed the basement this was what was discussed between them.

I find it unlikely that the Landlord would hire a couple (two people) with no experience, and no resume presented to be care-givers in his home, especially a couple who do not do this kind of work for a living. Although, the Landlord then asserted that the help was more to do with cleaning and exterior maintenance of the property, this still does not seem reasonable.

In any event, this living arrangement as described by the Landlord is not necessarily exempt from the Act as the Tenants could argue that they are paying rent in the form of work in exchange for the occupation. The Landlord’s home is not a care home or located on a farm. Rent is defined in section 2 of the Act as any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given for the right to occupy a rental unit. There does not have to be money exchanged.

As well, the Landlord asserted that there was no tenancy agreement as the Tenants did not pay any rent or utilities for their stay in his house. However, the Tenants, even after one of them was secluded, both testified that six and a half month’s rent was paid to the Landlord in cash which was supported by their bank statements showing these large cash withdrawals which amount to exactly that much. Of course, the amount of rent charged was asserted by the Tenants and only backed by this “metadata” obtained from a Kijiji advertisement that had since been deleted.

While I agree with the Landlord’s submissions that the Tenants’ supporting evidence of the “metadata” of a Kijiji advertisement is not directly linked to the Landlord or simply showing cash withdrawals on a bank statement does not mean that those amounts were given to him, however the findings before the LTB are based on a balance of probabilities.

When the “metadata” from the Kijiji advertisement is reviewed, the Ad_Title aligns with the description of this unit provided by both parties, a rental amount of $2,200.00 was requested for this unit, and the ad was removed on November 3, 2023, the day after the parties met and the Tenants assert they entered into a tenancy with the Landlord for this unit.

The parties had to come together somehow, the Landlord did not provide a copy of his alleged posting on the supermarket’s billboard for a live-in caregiver. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, I find it more likely than not that the parties found each other through a Kijiji advertisement which has since been deleted. So I find it more likely than not that the evidence presented by the Tenants is the “metadata” for that ad and this is what brought the parties together.

There was no dispute that the parties met in early November 2023 and viewed the unit together. The Tenants asserted that during this meeting the Landlord requested rent of $2,300.00 instead of the advertised $2,200.00 per month because there would be two people occupying the unit instead of only one. The Tenants also asserted that the Landlord requested first, last, and half month’s rent up front, which would amount to $5,750.00 [$2,300.00 + $2,300.00 + ($2,300.00/2 = $1,150.00)]. This was the exact cash amount that the Tenants withdrew from their bank account on this date, November 2, 2023. Therefore, I find it more likely than not that the Tenants withdrew this amount from their bank account to pay the Landlord to secure this unit.

The Tenants also asserted that they moved into the rental unit on November 15, 2023 and paid the Landlord an additional four months rent, being $4,600.00 on December 4, 2023 and $4,600.00 on December 29, 2023 in cash as the Landlord had requested six months rent to be paid in advance plus the deposit of one half month’s rent. Again the payment amounts and dates were supported by the Tenant’s bank statement showing these exact cash withdrawals. Therefore, I find it likely that these amounts were also paid to the Landlord during the tenancy.

The Landlord asserted that the Tenants never paid any moneys as their arrangement was for them to provide help. However, and although the Tenants never provided any help according to the Landlord from day one, being November 15, 2023, the first time the Landlord took issue with the Tenants not providing any help as per his alleged arrangement, was on June 15, 2024. The timeframe between the Tenants move in date and when the Landlord served them with his first notice to vacate was exactly seven months. The Landlord asserted that he was just being nice and believed the Tenants regarding their issues on why they could not fulfill their duties. I was not satisfied that was the case. I find that a reasonable person would not permit persons, who they hired to perform duties, a total of seven months to perform those duties before taking any action.

I find the timing of the Landlord’s first notice to vacate to the Tenants very telling. According to the Tenants they had paid the Landlord six and a half month’s rent, and the Landlord only took issue with these Tenants on June 15, 2023 after seven months had passed. Given this, I find it very likely that the Landlord did receive these payments from the Tenants and it was only after the Tenants began owing rent arrears in June 2024 that the Landlord took issue with them and alleged a story regarding their living arrangement.

As well, the Landlord’s third notice to vacate to the Tenants was also very telling. In that notice, the Landlord writes about the City of Mississauga Fire Department (Fire Department) considering the home a “single family dwelling” and the basement unit being unregistered and illegal. However, if the unit was not self-contained and the facilities were shared, as well as the Tenants being live-in caregivers why would the Fire Department make these determinations.

A copy of the Fire Department’s inspection report was not provided into evidence. However given the language used by the Landlord in this third notice to vacate, I find it more likely than not that the issue was that the Landlord had an illegal unregistered rental unit in his home. And perhaps this is the reason the Landlord is asserting that there was no tenancy as he may face repercussions from the Fire Department or municipality. T2 application

As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $1,198.00 to the Tenants and pay a fine of $10,000.00 to the LTB on or before May 31, 2026.
In this application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord withheld or interfered with vital services, namely electricity and water, and that the Landlord illegally locked them out of their unit.

Subsection 21(1) of the Act provides that: (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

Section 24 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. Vital Services

The Tenants each testified that sometime in June 2024 the water was shut off, CL had discovered this when trying to do laundry. They both testified that they called the police and CL testified that he spoke with the Landlord. They testified that after the police left the water appeared to be working again but would go off again and/or at times have low to no pressure during the remainder of their tenancy.

Under cross-examination of CL, the Landlord asked how he could use laundry appliances in June because they were removed by the Fire Department, and CL replied that nothing was removed until later in July 2024.

The Landlord testified that he did not shut off the water and that there is only one water valve and shutting it off would affect water to the entire house. He also submitted that there was one time where some work was being completed on a main pipe in the area and the water was shut off for a period of time. He further submitted that the Tenants’ evidence is not credible as they are asserting that they had no water from June 15 onward, several weeks yet were able to continue to reside in the unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I cannot find that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the vital service of water. The Tenants’ individual evidence of this issue was not consistent. [name] asserted that the water was completely shut off and that the Landlord would only turn it on when instructed to do so by police then turn it off again as soon as they left, but she also confirmed that she stopped contacting the police. If the water is only turned on when the police instruct it, why would the Tenants stop calling the police. CL testified that there was water but that the pressure was very low. [name] in her evidence did eventually concur that it was just low water pressure, but I was satisfied that the majority of her evidence on this issue was most likely exaggerated, inconsistent, and did not align with CL’s testimony.

LE also asserted that the Landlord shut off the electricity. She testified that as of June 15, 2024, the lights and stove in their unit were no longer working. She also testified that it was the police who made the Landlord turn the electricity back on but maintained that the stove and lights did not work for the rest of the time they resided there. CL testified that there was an issue with the washer and dryer not working so he contacted the Landlord who advised he would send someone, but no one ever came. CL also testified that they were not able to use the stove, but the refrigerator and the lights were working.
Under cross-examination, CL acknowledged that the main electrical breaker was located within their unit and admitted that on one occasion it was he who turned the power off to the whole house.
The Landlord maintained that the main electrical switch is in the unit and it was the Tenants who turned the power off in an attempt to intimidate his wife and himself.

The evidence before me was insufficient to find that the Landlord interfered with or withheld electricity. It was uncontested that the main electrical breaker was accessible by the Tenants. If this were the case, I find it unlikely that the Landlord could turn off the electricity. Additionally, CL admitted that he turned off the power one time to the whole house, so I was satisfied that the Tenants had control of the electricity. The evidence seemed to be consistent that the stove did not work, however, this is not a vital service as defined by the Act. Illegal Lock Out

There was no dispute that the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit and did not provide replacement keys to the Tenants on August 3, 2024. [name] testified that on August 3, 2024 while her husband (CL) came to pick her up from work they received a text message from the Landlord advising that he had changed the locks. [name] provided a copy of the text message into evidence (DOC-7779316pg17). The text message in part reads: “This serves to inform you that in line with our previous 3 Notices that were served on you and the City of Mississauga's Fire Department's [name] to us, the homeowners, the contents of which you were clearly made aware of in our 3rd Notice to you dated July 22nd 2024, we have changed the lock on the entry door to the room in our basement that you have been occupying for months... We ask that you do not attempt to set foot anywhere on our private property grounds... You can arrange with your movers to come and remove all your belongings from the premises anytime by prior arrangement with us in writing. Only professional movers will be allowed to enter the premises.”

LE testified that they immediately went to the property and saw the Landlord and his wife waiting outside who advised the Tenants to get out. [name] also testified that she could see pillars connected by a string with a notice saying “do not enter” on the side pathway to the rental unit’s entrance door. CL’s testimony was consistent with LE’s evidence.
There was also no dispute that a physical altercation between the Landlord and CL ensued, the Landlord’s wife was injured, and CL was charged by police.

Based on the above uncontested evidence, I was satisfied that the Landlord breached section 24 of the Act and illegally locked out the Tenants. There was no dispute that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys. Remedies

In this application, the Tenants requested an abatement of rent totalling $2,300.00, under other remedies an amount of $1,150.00 for a security deposit collected, the ability to retrieve their remaining belongings, and that the Landlord pay an administrative fine.

Section 1 of the Act sets out that one of the primary purposes is to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful evictions. The Landlord’s breach of section 24 of the Act amounts to a fundamental breach of the Tenants’ right to be protected from an unlawful eviction. This is the most egregious breach under the Act.

The Tenants testified that they had no place to go after being locked out of the unit. They also testified they had no access to their belongings. [name] testified that during the altercation at the property on August 3, 2024, she fell got hurt and called an ambulance. She also testified that she had just started a new job and they were only able to stay at a hotel for a couple of nights, as it was not cheap. She further testified that they ended up living in their car. CL testified that they went to a hotel for a couple of days and then had their car which they parked in a church parking lot. They also testified that it was only two days after the lock out that they were able to get any belongings from the unit and only with the assistance of the police.

The Landlord asserted that the Tenants testimony on where they went after being locked out was not credible. He submitted that they are testifying that they were able to pay him around $15,000.00 in a short period of time, working, but then have no money for a hotel room.

It was not disputed by the Tenants that no moneys were paid to the Landlord after those initial advance payments ending on December 29, 2024. Therefore, as found above, I was satisfied that in June 2024 when the Tenants did not pay any rent, the Landlord took issue with this tenancy. Given this, I find it likely that the Tenants may have been struggling financially.

The Landlord had also initially testified that the reason he took on the Tenants “as caregivers” was their down on their luck story about losing their property to a power of sale. Although, LE disputed that their property was sold under power of sale, there was no dispute that they had just sold their property within months of this tenancy commencing. Therefore, I find it likely that the Tenants had some funds at the beginning of the tenancy due to the sale of their property, but as the Landlord testified that he believed that CL did not work, I find it likely that the Tenants would have financial issues on only one income. Therefore, I was satisfied that the Tenants’ testimony of not being able to afford hotels or other accommodations after the illegal lock out was credible.

An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to recognize the concept that if a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then they are entitled to an abatement proportionate to the difference of what is being paid for and what is being received.

There was no dispute that the Tenants were locked out of the rental unit on August 3, 2024 and were not able to return or occupy the unit since that time. Given this, I was satisfied that the Tenants’ obligation to pay rent ceased on this date and they are entitled to the rent being abated in full from this point forward.

This tenancy commenced on November 15, 2023 on a month-to-month basis, given this I was satisfied that the monthly rental period for this tenancy is from the 15th of each month until the 14th of the next month. There was no dispute that the Tenants did not pay rent for the period of July 15, 2024 to August 14, 2024, therefore although rent is abated as of August 3, 2024, no amount shall be ordered to be paid to the Tenants from the Landlord.

The Tenants also requested the return of $1,150.00 that they say was collected by the Landlord as a security deposit at the commencement of the tenancy. Subsection 31(1)(f) of the Act provides that if the LTB has found that the Landlord breached section 24 of the Act the LTB may make any other order that it considers appropriate. I was satisfied that the amount of $4,450.00 [$5,750.00 - $2,300.00 (first month’s rent)] was paid by the Tenants as a deposit to the Landlord at the out set of this tenancy.

Subsection 106(2) of the Act provides that the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the amount of rent for one month. Since the monthly rent was $2,300.00 and the Landlord collected $4,450.00 as a deposit, I was satisfied that in accordance with subsection 106(2) of the Act $1,150.00 was collected from the Tenants illegally by the Landlord as a deposit. Therefore, in accordance with subsection 31(1)(f) I find that it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $1,150.00 as general compensation.
The Tenants further requested that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the LTB.

Guideline 16 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guidelines outlines that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the LTB to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes.

This same guideline also provides the LTB with factors to consider with respect to quantum of the fine, they are: • The nature and severity of the breach • The effect of the breach on the tenant • Any other relevant factors

The Landlord’s actions in this case showed a blatant disregard for the Act, the Landlord’s breach of illegally locking the Tenants out of the unit was harsh and severe. As stated above, the purpose of this Act is to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful evictions and so in keeping with the spirt of the legislation the LTB has a large interest to [name]’s in engaging in this behaviour in the future. The effect of this breach on these Tenants was quite substantial. They were essentially left homeless, had no access to their belongings, most likely frustrated and stressed, and therefore vulnerable.
Consequently, I find that an administrative fine of $10,000.00 to be warranted in these circumstances.

The Tenants’ request for an order to retrieve belongings is denied. There was no dispute that over the course of time since the illegal lock out on August 3, 2024, the Tenants have been given access to retrieve their belongings from the rental unit on at least two occasions. The Landlord testified that the Tenants and their Legal Representative attended the unit in December 2024 with a truck and were given the opportunity to retrieve all their belongings. He submitted that they took what they wanted and he assumed anything left behind was disposable. Since the Tenants were given the opportunity to access the rental unit and retrieve their belongings in December 2024 after this application was filed, I was satisfied that if they did not take everything it was reasonable for the Landlord to determine anything left behind could be disposed.
The Tenants are also entitled to their costs for filing the application.
