issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to a remedy.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2015, and vacated on December 20, 2024. As at the time of the application the Tenants lived in the unit with their four children aged 21, 13, 9 and 3.

The Tenants testified that they notified the Landlord of mice and cockroaches in the unit starting from November 2023. From November 2023 through to November 9, 2024, there have been numerous emails detailing mice and cockroaches in the unit.

The Tenants assert that the Landlord did not act promptly enough to address the infestation, nor did the Landlord take adequate steps to seal off the points of entry where mice were entering the unit.
The Tenants bought various mouse traps, which caught many mice. This was brought to the Landlord’s attention, with a request that the points of entry be sealed.

On August 22, 2024, a pest control company, hired by the Tenants, attended the unit to provide an inspection report. The report identified the presence of pests, as well as possible entry points, with the recommendation that the entry points be sealed.

The Tenants testified that the mice and cockroaches in their unit have impacted them. They keep their personal belongings in sealed plastic containers, they do not have visitors at the house, and it has disrupted their mental wellbeing.

The Landlord had a pest control company at tend the unit and complex a number of times. Invoices indicate treatments being conducted on November 16, 2023, April 16, 2024, May 1, 2024, June 10, 2024, July 9, 2024, August 26, 2024, October 9, 2024, and November 18, 2024. Also on October 9, 2024, an invoice was provided indicating the points of entry had been sealed.

The evidence established that the Landlord was advised of the Tenants’ concerns about mice and cockroaches and promptly hired a pest control company. The span of treatments persisted between November 2023 to November 2024.

Section 22 of the Act indicates that “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

When considering the Tenants’ allegations pursuant to section 22 of the Act in relation to the mice and cockroaches, I find that the issue leads to a finding that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.

I am satisfied that the unit and residential complex had a pest control issue with mice and cockroaches. When considering the entirety of the situation, the Landlord initially acted reasonably and promptly, but when the mice/cockroach problem continued, the Landlord ought to have investigated further or taken further remediation. The issue was concerning and impactful to the Tenants. The Tenants evidence indicated that as of late June, the pests were having an adverse impact to their whole family and noted it in an email to the Landlord “as a matter of urgency”.

There is no indication that the Landlord took any different steps to understand why, despite continued pest control treatments, the mice and cockroaches continued to be an issue at the unit and complex.

The Tenants proved, on a balance of probability, that the Landlord has substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. The evidence established that the Landlord’s treatment plan and use of a pest control company alone was not adequate to address the issue. Despite the services, the mice and cockroaches continued to enter into the unit. The Landlord’s continued response was inadequate and unresponsive to the gravity of the situation.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants as a result of the mice and cockroaches. Remedy

In terms of remedy, the Tenants seek 100% of their rent from November 2023 to November 2024. A 100% rent abatement is not warranted. Having considered all the evidence, I find a 5% abatement is granted.

Upon becoming aware of the issue in November 2023, I find that the Landlord took prompt, reasonable, and adequate steps to address the Tenants’ issue. When mice/cockroaches were reported the Landlord immediately called a professional pest control company and scheduled treatment. The Tenants first emailed the Landlord November 12, 2023, and the Landlord arranged pest control treatment on November 16, 2023. A second email from the Tenants came on April 11, 2024, and further treatment occurred on April 16, 2024. The Tenants sent a further email on April 27, 2024 and in response the pest control company attended on May 1, 2024.

The Landlord also visited the unit on May 17, 2024. At this visit, the Tenants indicated showing the Landlord the points of entry and seeking that, in addition to the pest control services, the Landlord take action to ensure the points of entry are closed up, thereby preventing mice from entering. The Landlord took no action to close the points of entry until October 9, 2024. I find this contributed to the mice/cockroach issue at the unit/complex, which in turn substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex.

The Landlord reliance on having hired a professional pest control company to address and remediate the mice/cockroaches at the unit and complex was not sufficient after he observed that there were points of entry that needed to be sealed.

Once the points of entry were sealed, the next complaint occurred in November 2024, when the Tenants notified that a new entry was made, in that the mice had chewed through the sealing foam. The Landlord did not provide evidence to indicate that he took steps to close the point of entry after the November complaint.
The Tenants resided at the unit up until they vacated on December 20, 2024. A remedy for the period from May 17, 2024, to December 20, 2024, is warranted.
The monthly rent for May and June 2024 was $1,043.45 (or $34.31 per day); and from July 1, 2024 onwards, the monthly rent was $1,069.54 (or $35.16 per day).

As the Tenants continued to reside at the unit, a 100% abatement is not warranted. I find a 5% abatement for this period is appropriate. In determining an appropriate remedy, I considered that the Tenants desire to remain at the unit, but vacated due to having received an N12, that they had to place their belongings in plastic containers, captured mice with the traps they purchased, and were limited in having visitors at their unit. However, I also considered that the Landlord was not ignorant of the issues raised. He responded by hiring a professional pest control company to attend multiple times to service the unit and complex. Moreover, he attended the residential unit and saw the points of entry in May. Once the points of entry were closed on October 9, 2024, the Tenants’ complaints were reduced.
The remedy is calculated as follows: 1. May 17 to June 30, 2024: 44 days x $34.31 x 0.05 = $75.82 2. July 1 to December 20, 2024: 172 days x $35.16 x 0.05 = $302.38
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
Having considered all the evidence presented, I find that a rent abatement of $378.20 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $426.20. This amount represents:  $378.20 for a rent abatement.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants t he full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application)
reasons: The Tenant amended the application on February 23, 2025, to include the Landlord’s contact information, specifically, the address.

The Tenant submitted, the evidence was served to the Landlord on October 4, 2025, the day the issue occurred; the evidence for the hearing is the same as what the Landlord was given. The Landlord did not raise any issue about the evidence not being received at the Adjudicative Case Conference.
I accept the Tenant’s uncontested submission that the Landlord received the necessary evidence for the hearing; the matter shall proceed on its merits. Merits

The Tenant testified they moved into the rental unit on September 29, 2024, and vacated October 4, 2024. The lease for the furnished room began October 1, 2026, but the Landlord allowed him to move in early. The Tenant paid the Landlord $2,150, as established by the e-transfers: $1,000.00 for the last month rent deposit on August 31, 2024; $1,000.00 for the first month rent on September 27, 2024; and, $150.00 for the key deposit on September 29, 2024. Two days after moving in, the Tenant noticed mouse droppings in the kitchen, mice traps all over house, bed bugs on mattress. a mouldy smell and could hear something in walls. He told the Landlord about the issues on October 4, 2025; the Landlord said she would change the mattress with one from the garage. The Tenant told him that was not a proper way to address the situation and advised he did not want to stay in the unit. The Landlord blamed the Tenant for the bed bugs and did not offer a solution.

The Tenant also testified, the Landlord admitted to not telling the Tenant about the mice problem and tried to qualify the situation by saying there are traps all-over, they are seeking a solution, and the issue will get fixed as soon as possible. The Tenant had a rash and bites on him because of the state of the unit. About leaving, the Landlord said it was the Tenant’s personal choice, he could stay, the mice issue will be addressed/fixed, and she needed 2-days to inspect about the bed bug issue. The Tenant left that day and texted the Landlord the following day that he was not returning to the unit. The Tenant told the Landlord he wanted reimbursed the first month rent minus the per diem amount for the few days he was in the unit, and the last month rent deposit; he told the Landlord she could keep the key deposit. The Landlord said she did not have the money right now and would give it back to him once the room was re-rented. Every time the Tenant followed up about the money, the Landlord just kept saying the room was not rented yet, she did not have the money, and she had to pay the mortgage; the last text between them was November 4, 2024. The Tenant did not return the key to the Landlord, he kept it because he did not want the Landlord to throw anything out.

The Tenant is seeking $2,150.00 plus compensation for clothes; 2 full suitcases that he did not take with him because he moved in with his brother who said not to bring them because of the new baby. Everyone he talked to, his brother, his manager, said bed bugs do not just get washed away, it was best to throw everything out. T1 application

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed; the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit.

The law establishes that there is no unilateral right to rescind a contract that has been duly entered into by the parties ([name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923, [2008] O.J. No. 1934 (QL), 2008 Carswell Ont 2747, Court File No. 142/07 ([name]. Ct.) ([name], [name], and [name].)). Here, the parties signed a lease and the Tenant’ was given possession of the rental unit; the issue to be addressed is whether the unit was uninhabitable when the Tenant took possession thus leaving no other option but to terminate the tenancy. Although the Tenant showed a picture of what appear to be some bed bugs on the mattress, this does not meet that of an infestation or t a level where the problem was impossible to address. The Landlord said she would take the necessary steps to have the issue fixed, the Tenant chose not to allow her this opportunity. Similarly, the Tenant did not present any evidence, for example pictures, of mice, mice droppings and mice traps in the unit, therefore, the Tenant did not establish that the problem was so extensive as to meet the level of being uninhabitable. The Tenant did not offer any detail about the mouldy smell, therefore, this issue is dismissed.

For these reasons I find the Tenant did not demonstrate that the unit was uninhabitable; as such, there was not a fundamental breach of the lease. The caselaw has long-established that unless a severe lack of compliance with health, safety or maintenance standards is established, there is no fundamental breach of the contract, and it remains intact. According to the court, a fundamental breach must be such that it frustrates the real purpose of the contract (Temlas Apartments Inc. v. Desloges [1980] O.J. No. 3624, 29 O.R. (2d) 30 ([name]. [name]. Ct.)); it must be so critical as to bring an end to the contract as a whole or repairs so protracted that occupancy is not reasonably possible (Lord Strathcona Steamship Co. v. Dominion Coal Co. [1926] 1 D.L.R. 873, [1926] A.C. 108 (P.C.)). If there are pest or cleanliness issues upon move-in, a landlord needs to be given the opportunity to rectify the issue(s); here, there the Tenant admitted that the Landlord was not given a chance to address the issues, he chose to leave instead.

Further, the Tenant retained the key, which meant the Tenant was in possession of the unit the entire time he was requesting return of the deposit. The Tenant again made a choice: to leave and not to return the key. Therefore, the Tenant made no attempt to mitigate losses as required by section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Further, by keeping the key, he is not entitled to return of the key deposit.

Therefore, I find the Landlord did not retain monies contrary to the legislation. Accordingly, the Tenant is not entitled to return of the deposit, and the application must be dismissed. T6 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair and/or maintain the rental unit. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the Board should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Tenant did not give the Landlord an opportunity to address the issues; the Tenant testified he chose to leave the unit and not return. He did so despite the Landlord’s text offering a rent discount, they needed to work together, and the issues would be addressed.

As the Tenant did not put forth any testimony with respect to the ‘mouldy smell’ or how he was affected in this regard, this issue is also dismissed in the T6 application. However, it should be noted that if the mouldy smell was an issue, the Tenant also did not allow the Landlord any opportunity to address it.

For these reasons I find there was no evidence to establish the Landlord acted contrary to the Act or any other regulation/standard that would have been required. Therefore, no remedy can flow from this application, as it is based solely on whether the Landlord breached their obligations under section 20; and they did not; the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1/T6 application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in a T1 application seeking an order determining that Ayden S Pearson (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s testimony was uncontested, and he proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,121.28 in total.

The Tenant testified that he paid a last month’s rent deposit of $1,073.00 to the Landlord at the start of the tenancy, on October 1, 2018. The Tenant testified that he moved out of the rental unit on December 3, 2023 after the Landlord gave him an eviction notice. Since he had received several eviction notices in the past, and since the rental unit had many pest infestation problems such as ants, cockroaches and bedbugs, he decided to vacate. He had already paid November 2023 rent in full. Since he moved out only 3 days into December 2023, he wanted the portion of last month’s rent deposit back for the rest of December (4th – 31st).

I note that even though the Tenant characterized the eviction as “wrongful”, during the hearing he admitted he had been evicted due to a prior LTB order from another application in which the Landlord secured an eviction. The Tenant had not requested a review of that eviction order or appealed the decision.

I did not accept the Tenant’s calculation from the T1 application for the portion of rent owing from December 4 – 31 because it was higher than the daily compensation rate. The deposit was $1,073.00. The daily compensation rate is therefore $35.28 per day. This is calculated by ($1073 times 12 months) divided by 365 days. The amount of deposit owed back for 28 days of December 2023 is $987.84.

The Tenant also submitted that he moved to a place that costs $500 more per month ($6,000 per year) in rent. The Tenant wanted “whatever you think is fair” for the bad faith eviction. A bad faith application is a T5. Based on the T1 application filed and the claims made within it, the Tenant did not properly make a bad faith claim in this application. Therefore, any remedies such as a differential of the higher rent at the new rental were not considered in this application or hearing order.
The Tenant also sought interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord owes the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit, from the date of collection to the date of vacate. However, the amount of $250 submitted by the Tenant in the T1 application for interest is inaccurate because the Tenant admitted that he included $75 for reimbursement of the application filing fee (including interest charged by the credit card company on his credit card payment).

The LTB calculates interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit using the percentages posted by the Ontario government on its website for Residential rent increases by year. Using the interest rates of 1.8% for 2018, 1.8% for 2019, 2.2% for 2020, 0% for 2021 (due to COVID19), 1.2% for 2022, and 2.5% for 2023, the total amount of interest owing on the deposit is $85.44.

The Tenant also sought reimbursement of the filing fee for this application. Since the Tenant was successful on the application, he will be reimbursed for $48.00. The LTB does not reimburse for credit card interest charges.
ordered: 10. The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,121.28. This amount represents: • $987.84 for 28 days of December, 2023 from the last month's rent deposit; • $85.44 for interest the Landlord owes on the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 11. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026 (standard 11 days from the issuance date of this order). 12. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 13. The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: allegations of no power in the bathroom from April 8-19, 2024, the removal of the only electrical outlet in the bathroom and an unsafe door damaged by the Landlord’s realtors.
Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants the amount of $3,535.68 by May 15, 2026.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on July 17, 2020 and this condo was located at Unit 72, 35 Breckenridge Drive in Kitchener, Ontario.
The Tenants had possession of the rental unit to October 31, 2025 when they vacated the rental unit.

An interim order was issued on July 7, 2025 by another Member and in that order, the Tenants withdrew their claims of illegal entries and the Landlords agreed to pay the Tenants for the electrical bill of $213.57. The Member also ordered that the Landlords initiate any investigations of the need for any repairs to supply continuous electrical power to the receptacle in the bathroom and the Landlords inspect the front door to ensure that it closed and locked properly. The Tenant’s Evidence – [name] (NN)

NN stated that although the Landlords initiated these inspections, the Landlords felt that there was nothing wrong with the electrical outlet in the bathroom which had been removed by the Landlords. The Tenant also stated that the Landlords’ investigation found that there was nothing wrong with their front door even though it was cracked.

The Tenant stated that there were two main issues including that the only electrical outlet in their bathroom stopped working and on April 8, 2024, they lost power in the bathroom. The Tenant stated that she immediately notified the Landlord on April 9, 2024 and the property manager attended on April 10, 2024 for a showing of the condo. The Tenants brought up the loss of hydro in the bathroom and the property manager claimed that they were unaware. The Tenant stated that on April 14, 2024, the property manager attended the unit to investigate the power issue and stated they would need more time to map the electrical. She stated that two more appointments were set up and then cancelled by the property manager.

NN contacted an electrician on April 19, 2024 and the electrician replaced the plug in the bathroom which also fixed the fan and the lights. The electrician also stated that there would be ongoing electrical issues until the wiring was replaced. They paid the electrician $213.57 which has now been paid by the Landlords.

NN stated that they advised the Landlords that an electrician had fixed the issue and the property manager and her partner attended on April 27, 2024 to investigate the electrical repair and the Tenants were told that they had no right to call an electrician.

NN stated that on May 7, 2024, they had not been given 24-hours’ notice of someone attending a viewing of the house and they denied the entry. They had engaged their door reinforcement lock which stopped the realtor from entering. A video was played whereby the realtor attempted to break open the door with her hip at least 10-12 times and she had been given authority by the property manager to attempt to push open the door.
NN stated that the realtors’ actions caused the door to crack and she provided pictures of the cracked door.

NN testified that they lost power in their bathroom again on June 13, 2024 and the property manager fixed the issue by restoring the lights and the fan. But, they removed the receptacle that the electrician installed and placed a plastic cover on the spot where the receptacle was located.
Since that date, they have not had the use of a receptacle in the bathroom and the Landlords failed to have an electrician check the wiring in the bathroom.
The Tenant stated that since the door was cracked on May 7, 2024, she has felt insecure and believes that the door will not stay locked if someone attempts to force it open again.

The Tenants are seeking an abatement of $63.73 for the period from April 8-19, 2024 when they had no power in the bathroom. They are also seeking a daily abatement of $5.79 a day from June 13, 2024 to October 31, 2025 as the Landlords removed the only receptacle in the bathroom which had been installed by an electrician.

Finally, the Tenants are seeking $2,000.00 for the safety and emotional turbulence that they endured due to the realtors’ actions of trying to force the door open and the resulting cracked front door. The Tenants requested that the door be fixed by the Landlords but the Landlords felt that there was nothing wrong with the door. Evidence of Landlord, [name] (AS)
AS testified that the Tenants did not start complaining until they told them that they were putting the condo up for sale.

The Landlord stated that when the Tenants’ bathroom lost power, the property manager had planned on dealing with the matter but it was apparently not fast enough for the Tenants. The Landlord stated that the Tenants had no right to call an electrician and that there were no issues with the electrical wiring in the bathroom. The Landlord stated that he told the Tenants not to use the outlet in the bathroom due to a breaker problem.
AS stated that the realtors did not cause any damage to the door and that the door was like that when the Tenants moved in a number of years ago.
AS did not agree with the abatement requested by the Tenants as he told them not to use that outlet in the bathroom. Analysis

A T6 Application is based on the rights and obligations set out in s. 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenants provided specific dates and occurrences of the issues with the electrical receptacle in the bathroom and the issues with the front door. The video of the realtors’ visit was very helpful in determining that issue.

The Landlords did not contest any of the evidence provided by the Tenants however they decided that a receptacle was not necessary in the bathroom and they felt that there were no issues with the electrical wiring. The Landlords also felt that the door had not been damaged by the realtors.
So with those two issues, the real issue is whether or not the Tenants are entitled to a remedy and if the Tenants are entitled to a remedy, what should the remedy be.

The Act and the case law in this area indicate there are a number of relevant principles to consider when assessing allegations of a breach of maintenance: 1. First, if the Landlord responded to the disrepair in a timely and effective manner then no monetary remedy will normally flow. (See the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 Breach of [name].) 2. Second, the Landlord cannot be held responsible for compensation for disrepair that the Landlord was not aware of or could not reasonably have been aware of. [See s. 30(2) of the Act]. This is why the duty to mitigation in section 16 has been interpreted to include an obligation on tenants to report disrepair to a landlord. 3. Third, once the Landlord is aware of the disrepair, the normal obligation to repair and liability for the problem will begin.

Abatement of the rent is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, the rent should be abated proportional to the difference between what was being paid for and what was being received. In terms of quantum of abatement, the Board looks primarily at the impact the breach had on the Tenants.

With respect to the time period whereby the Tenants had no power in their bathroom, I am satisfied that the Landlords were notified about the power outage in the bathroom. The Tenants had the electrical issue fixed and were advised by the electrician that the wiring required inspection. Accordingly, I am satisfied the evidence establishes that there was a breach of maintenance with respect to the loss of power in the Tenants’ bathroom for the above-mentioned period. I am awarding the requested abatement of $63.73 as that amount is reasonable in the circumstances.

With respect to the time period between June 13, 2024 and October 31, 2024, this is the time period whereby the Landlords removed the replaced receptacle and covered it with a plastic cap. The Landlords refused to address the ongoing electrical issue and simply removed the Tenants’ access to the only receptacle in the bathroom. The Tenants requested an abatement of $5.79 a day for this time period and I am awarding their requested abatement of $2,923.95 (505 days x $5.79). Again, the Tenants have requested a nominal amount to be paid for each day that the Landlords failed to maintain the rental unit.

With respect to the abatement request for the front door, I am satisfied that the realtors’ actions caused the damage to the front door. The “Ring” video showed the realtors vigorously attempting to physically force the door open after being given verbal permission from the property manager to force the door open. I cannot understand how anyone would believe that those instructions to force the door open would be reasonable or wise in any circumstance. I understand why the Tenants felt somewhat unsafe after viewing the large crack in the door. The Tenants requested abatement of $2,000.00 which I do not believe is reasonable in the circumstances. Based on the pictures of the front door and the Tenant’s few comments about the safety concern, I am awarding a global amount of $500.00 in abatement for the door.
As a result, an order shall issue requiring the Landlords to pay to the Tenants the amount of $3,535.68 which includes the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenants $3,535.68. This amount represents: • $63.73 for a rent abatement for the period April 9-18, 2024; • $2,923.95 for a rent abatement for the period June 13, 2024 to October 31, 2024; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] and Briarlane Rental Property Management Inc. (the 'Landlord') and [name] [name] [name] • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, there was uncertainty regarding who is the properly named Landlord. With the consent of the parties present, Briar Lane Rental Property Management Inc. was added as a responding landlord. T2 Application

The Tenant alleges the Landlord illegally entered or attempted to enter the rental unit, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment, and harassed him on December 9, 2022, September 22, 2023, and November 22, 2023.
For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant has not proven the allegations on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. December 9, 2022

The Tenant testified that on December 9, 2022, at approximately 10:30 a.m., the superintendent, [name] (MM), and maintenance employee, [name] [name] (RS), attended his unit, knocked repeatedly, and attempted to enter without notice.
The Tenant testified he was working from home and was not expecting anyone. He testified he heard a key inserted into the lock and believed the Landlord was about to enter without notice.
RS testified he attended to repair a plumbing issue. He testified that a notice of entry had been posted prior to attendance.
RS testified that he and the superintendent knocked repeatedly to alert the Tenant. He testified that when the Tenant objected, they did not enter the unit.

The Tenant provided a video of the interaction. The video confirms that the Landlord knocked repeatedly, announced their presence, and inserted a key into the lock. The video also confirms that once the Tenant objected, the Landlord did not proceed to enter the unit. The Tenant also submitted a copy of the notice of entry that was posted on the door. September 22, 2023
The Tenant testified that on September 22, 2023, he was asleep when loud knocking woke him. He testified that maintenance staff inserted a key and partially opened the door before he objected.
The Tenant testified that he opened the door and observed MM and RS standing outside the unit. He also observed RS recording the interaction on his smartphone.

RS testified he attended to complete outstanding repairs, including installing a tub stopper and completing caulking. He further testified that when the Tenant objected, maintenance staff did not enter and left.
The video evidence confirms that maintenance staff knocked, partially opened the door, identified themselves, and withdrew when the Tenant objected. Analysis
The Tenant submits that even though the Landlord did not enter the unit, the attempted entries constitute substantial interference and/or harassment. I do not accept this submission.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant's occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or the tenant's household.

In interpreting section 22 of the Act, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 provides that the interference must be substantial in nature to constitute a breach. Minor inconvenience or disruption for a brief period will generally not meet this threshold or warrant a remedy. See also Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name].

In both instances, the Landlord’s agents attended the rental unit for legitimate maintenance purposes and believed they were entitled to enter based on notices of entry that had been posted. When the Tenant objected, they did not enter and left. I find these were isolated incidents arising from a misunderstanding regarding notice and do not amount to substantial interference within the meaning of section 22 of the Act.

While the Tenant testified in detail about the impact these incidents had on him, I find that the Landlord’s conduct was brief and limited in nature. Consistent with Interpretation Guideline 6, I find a minor inconvenience or disruption for a short period does not meet the threshold of substantial interference under section 22 of the Act.

Moreover, Landlords are entitled under the Act to enter rental units for lawful purposes, including to perform maintenance and repairs, provided the statutory requirements are met. I find the evidence before me establishes that the Landlord’s agents attended the unit on two isolated occasions for maintenance-related purposes and withdrew when the Tenant objected. While the Tenant’s sleep was briefly interrupted, these limited and infrequent incidents, occurring several months apart, do not amount to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The term “harassment” is not defined in the Act. However, the Board has generally interpreted harassment to mean a course of conduct or comment that is vexatious and that the landlord knows or ought reasonably to know is unwelcome.

I do not find that the Landlord’s agents engaged in a course of conduct that they knew or ought reasonably to have known was unwelcome. In both instances, when the Tenant objected to their attendance, they did not enter the unit and left.

In neither case of attempted entry do I find the Landlord’s agents engaged a course of conduct to be known to be unwelcome. In both cases the upon being aware they were unwelcome in the rental unit they acted responsibly and left.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord’s practice of posting notices of entry on his door constituted substantial interference and harassment. I do not accept this submission. The Board’s Rules expressly permit a notice of entry to be served by posting it on the tenant’s door. I find there is no legal basis for the Tenant’s position that this method of service was improper or inapplicable in this residential complex. The fact that the Tenant disagrees with or does not prefer this method does not render the service improper. I find this conduct does not amount to a breach of the Act.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not illegally enter the rental unit, substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, or harass the Tenant in relation to the December 9, 2022 and September 22, 2023 incidents. This portion of the Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed. December 9, 2023

The Tenant testified that on November 22, 2023, at approximately 11:50 a.m., he was working inside the rental unit when he heard multiple loud knocks on the door. The Tenant testified that there were two separate sets of knocking, each consisting of approximately nine knocks. The Tenant testified that no one identified themselves and no one entered the rental unit.
A video provided by the Tenant confirms that knocking occurred but does not show who was present outside the door.

The Tenant further testified that the following day he heard RS performing maintenance work on the roof above his unit. The Tenant submits this supports his belief that RS was the individual who knocked on his door the previous day.
The Tenant further testified that the following day he heard RS on the roof performing maintenance and believed this confirms he had attended the unit the previous day.
RS testified that he had no recollection of attending the Tenant’s unit on November 22, 2023, and denied knocking on the Tenant’s door on that date.

This is the Tenant’s application, and the Tenant bears the burden of proving his allegations on a balance of probabilities. I find that the Tenant has not met that burden with respect to this incident.

The Tenant’s belief that RS was the individual who knocked on the door is speculative and is not supported by objective evidence. The video evidence confirms that knocking occurred but does not identify the person responsible. There is no reliable evidence before me to establish that the Landlord or its agents attended the rental unit or attempted to enter on November 22, 2023.

In the absence of sufficient evidence linking the knocking to the Landlord or its agents, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Evidence of the Tenants

On March 28, 2024, the Tenants received an N12 notice from the Landlord indicating a termination date of May 31, 2024. The Tenants requested permission from the Landlord to remain in the rental unit until the end of June, and the Landlord agreed. The Tenants ultimately vacated the rental unit on July 2, 2024.

The Tenants testified that they genuinely believed the Landlord intended to move into the rental unit; otherwise, they would not have vacated. In November 2024, they learned that the unit had been re-rented to another individual. When they confronted the Landlord, he confirmed in an email dated December 15, 2024, which was admitted into evidence, that the unit had indeed been rented to a new tenant due to a change in his circumstances.

The Tenants’ new residence is located a 20-minute drive from the rental unit. It is a three-bedroom bungalow with a monthly rent of $2,900.00 plus utilities. By comparison, the rental unit was a condominium with parking and access to a gym, rented at $2,400.00 per month inclusive of utilities.

The Tenants are seeking one year’s rent differential, general compensation in the amount of $16,020.00, and an administrative fine. In support of their claim for general compensation, the Tenants testified that they now incur additional monthly expenses, including $100.00 for a gym membership, $800.00 for daycare, $160.00 for a private tutor, and $250.00 for additional insurance. No documentation was submitted to support these claimed expenses. Evidence of the Landlord

The Landlord acknowledged that he re-rented the rental unit to a new tenant. He testified regarding the circumstances that led him to serve the N12 notice, as well as the circumstances that occurred after the Tenants vacated.

The Landlord explained that he resides in Ottawa but technically works out of Toronto. At the relevant time, he was working remotely and required to attend the Toronto office only twice per month. In the summer of 2023, his employer implemented a policy requiring a minimum of three in-office days per week. Although he sought relief from this requirement, he was only granted an extension until the end of 2023. Consequently, he began searching for fully remote work within his industry so that he could continue living in Ottawa full-time. The Landlord submitted job applications into evidence to corroborate this.

Believing that he would have to relocate to Toronto, the Landlord began preparing to sell his Ottawa home. On November 27, 2023, he contacted a realtor to initiate the process of listing the property for sale.

In January 2024, the Landlord changed jobs. His new position, located in Toronto, required mandatory in-office attendance. Although he understood there might be a limited hybrid option, the flexibility was minimal. The employer’s workplace policy was entered into evidence confirming said limited flexibility. The Landlord requested temporary remote work until the end of March to determine how to proceed regarding the rental unit, and this request was approved.

On March 21, 2024, the Landlord’s employer granted him an extension of temporary remote work until the end of May 2024. On March 28, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenants with the N12 notice. During this period, he continued working with his realtor to prepare for the sale of his Ottawa home and obtained quotes for minor renovations aimed at facilitating a quicker sale of the property.

In June 2024, the Landlord commuted daily between Ottawa and Toronto for work. After the Tenants vacated the unit on July 2, 2024, he moved in to establish a base in Toronto. Around this time, his wife became pregnant, which further complicated his plans to relocate permanently.

Shortly thereafter, the Landlord spoke with his manager and requested full-time remote work. He remained in the rental unit until August 21, 2024, when his request for full-time remote work was ultimately granted. Unable to maintain both properties, he rented the unit to a new tenant and continues to reside in Ottawa as of the date of the hearing.

The Landlord confirmed that the Tenants had offered to pay an increased monthly rent to remain in the unit. He testified that he declined their offer because his decision was not financially motivated, he genuinely intended to move into the unit at the time he served the N12 notice.

During cross-examination, the Landlord was asked whether he knew his wife was pregnant when he served the N12 notice. He confirmed that he was aware and testified that his wife planned to move into the rental unit during her second trimester. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I find that the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice, the Tenants vacated the rental unit due to the N12 notice, and that the Landlord re-rented the rental unit to another tenant. These are all not in dispute.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

In [name] v. [name], [2008] O.J. No. 6076 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court held that temporary full-time occupancy of a residential unit does not constitute “residential occupation” within the meaning of s. 48(1) of the Act. Accordingly, I cannot find that the Landlord occupied the rental unit for the purposes contemplated by the Act based on his temporary full-time stay.
It is undisputed that the Landlord re-rented the unit within one year. As a result, the burden shifts to the Landlord to rebut the presumption set out in s. 57(5) of the Act.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal clarified that, pursuant to s. 202(1) of the Act, the Board must determine the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and assess the good faith of the parties. The Court further held that the Board’s analysis should not be confined solely to the Landlord’s state of mind at the time the notice of termination was served.
The Landlord’s evidence was clear, consistent, and straightforward. There is no basis on the record to doubt the credibility or reliability of his oral testimony.

Considering the totality of the evidence, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord genuinely intended to move into the rental unit at the time the N12 notice was served. The Landlord’s evidence about his requirement to work in-office was supported by documentary evidence. Furthermore, the evidence indicates that the Landlord occupied the unit for at least one month after the Tenants vacated while attending his new job in- office. Subsequently, on August 21, 2024, he was approved for full-time remote work. This development allowed him to remain in Ottawa with his wife, particularly in light of her pregnancy, and eliminated the need for a permanent relocation to Toronto. This is a drastic change in circumstance that goes to the heart of the reason the Landlord served the N12 notice, and this was not anticipated at the time the N12 notice was served.

For these reasons, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has successfully rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I therefore find that the N12 notice was not served in bad faith.
ordered: The T5 application is dismissed. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord’s Agent') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord did not give the Tenants access to the rental unit. The Landlord also collected a rent deposit, first month’s rent and a key deposit, but did not give the prospective Tenants vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit and other funds to the Tenant. As the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $3,846.32 by March 14, 2026. Below are my reasons Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant [name] (“KC”) testified they viewed the rental unit on November 2, 2025 and entered into a tenancy agreement on November 4, 2025 with the Landlord for a tenancy to begin on December 1, 2025. KC further testified that on November 5, 2025, the Tenants paid the Landlord the rent deposit, and on November 7, 2025 paid the Landlord the first month’s rent and a key deposit due on December 1, 2025. Entered into evidence were two screenshots of interact e-transfers; the first dated November 5, 2025 from KC to the Landlord’s agent [name] for $1,895.00, and the second dated November 7, 2025 from KC to the Landlord M & J Doors Ltd. for $1,945.00 showing the funds were successfully deposited.

Shortly after the rent and the rent deposits were paid, the Landlord cancelled the lease. Entered into evidence was an email dated November 8, 2025 from the Landlord to the Tenant cancelling the lease and informing the Tenant the Landlord will be issuing a refund.

KC further testified that the Landlord nor the Landlord’s agent ever returned the funds that were deposited and never provided the Tenants with vacant possession of the unit, despite the Tenants making several attempts to recover the funds and the Landlord acknowledging their obligation to return them. The Tenant [name] provided corroborating testimony supporting KC’s account. Also entered into evidence was correspondence dated between November 15, 2025 and November 21, 2025 between the Landlord and/or the Landlord’s agent corroborating the Tenant’s testimony.
KC further testified that [name], the Landlord’s agent she was working with to recover the funds, has stopped responding to requests with the last correspondence being January 19, 2026. Analysis

Section 135(1) of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Section 107 of the Act provides that a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.
It is uncontested based on the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not give the Tenants access to rental unit because the Landlord cancelled the tenancy agreement on November 8, 2025.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I also find that the Landlord collected a rent deposit form the Tenants in the amount of $1,895.00 and an additional $1.945.00 for the rent and key deposit due on December 1, 2025 in the amount of $1,945.00 and was unable to fulfil the tenancy agreement. The Landlord did not allow the Tenants to move into the rental unit and failed to return the aforementioned funds in breach of the Act.
Accordingly, I find the Tenants are entitled to $3,840.00, the sum of the funds collected by the Landlord and never returned.
The application fee was paid by a fee waiver. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the Last Month's Rent Deposit, as required by the Act.
The Last Month’s Rent Deposit was collected by the Landlord on November 5, 2025, in the amount of $1,895.00.
KC testified that interest has never been paid on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit.
The interest on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit is owing for the period of November 5, 2025 to February 3, 2026 is $6.32.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,846.32. This amount represents: • $3,840.00 for the rent deposit, first month’s rent and the key deposit • $6.32 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

It was undisputed that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement in September 2025, for a fixed term of October 1, 2025, to September 30, 2026. The Tenant paid the first month’s rent and the last month’s rent deposit, totalling $6,300.00. The Tenant contacted the Landlord on October 2, 2025, requesting to terminate the tenancy early by agreement. The parties had some communications but did not sign an N11: Agreement to End the Tenancy. The rental unit was listed for rent on October 16, 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2025. The Landlord did not give the Tenant a notice of termination.

The Tenant, [name] [name] (‘NS’), testified that when she spoke with the Landlord’s real estate agent, he said the Landlord was agreeable to end the tenancy at the end of October 2025, but also mentioned a 60-day notice requirement. NS provided a text message from the agent sent on October 16, 2025, which indicates that the Landlord is willing to address the pest issue, and shows the Landlord’s position on the termination. The text states: Hi [name], As we discussed in detail yesterday morning, the landlord is willing to hire a pest control company for a full year to address the pest issue, should you decide to stay. He’s also open to offering a rent reduction for October and November in light of the situation. He mentioned that the same company was hired last year, and the previous tenant had confirmed that the roach problem was resolved. However, since you’ve observed otherwise, he’s provided the option to proceed with further treatment, which we discussed yesterday. That said, you mentioned that you’ve already made up your mind to move out by the end of this month. We understand and will move forward with listing the property immediately in hopes of securing new tenants by November 1st. If we’re unable to find suitable tenants by then, the landlord is prepared to accept your 60-day notice and release you from the one-year lease. We’ll also drop by on Sunday afternoon to take a look at the situation ourselves. Thanks

The Landlord, [name] (‘BK’), denied agreeing to terminate the tenancy. She acknowledged that her real estate agent spoke with the Tenant while she was out of the country but was consistent in the content of what was communicated. Specifically that, if the Landlord finds a new tenant for November 1, 2025, then the tenancy would be terminated, but if not, then the Landlord would accept a 60-day notice by the Tenant.

I am not satisfied that there was an agreement to terminate the tenancy between the parties. NS herself testified that, in her verbal conversation with the Landlord’s real estate agent, he indicated a willingness to terminate the tenancy but also mentioned a 60-day notice requirement. The portion of the agent’s text message regarding the pests shows the Landlord’s intention to continue the tenancy. The portion relating to the termination acknowledges the Landlord’s duty to mitigate their damages by looking for new tenants, but does not confirm an October 31, 2025, termination. In essence, the Tenant was seeking termination on October 31, 2025. The Landlord was only agreeable to this date on the condition that new tenants were found; otherwise, the Landlord sought termination on November 30, 2025. There was no meeting of the minds, and no specific date finalized.

Pursuant to section 47 and 44(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act (2006) (the ‘Act’), a tenant may only terminate a fixed term tenancy at the end of the fixed term. The tenant must give at least 60 days’ written notice. In this case, the Tenant’s notice of termination was not given 60 days in advance and was not effective on the end date of the fixed term tenancy. Therefore, it does not comply with the requirements of the Act and arrears of rent are calculated in accordance with section 88.

Pursuant to section 88 of the Act, arrears of rent are calculated to the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a notice of termination, had it complied with the Act. However, if a landlord enters into a new tenancy, arrears are calculated to the start date of the new tenancy. I must also consider whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize their losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act.

BK testified that she was out of the country at the beginning of October 2025. The unit was re-listed for rent on October 16, 2025, for the same price, once she returned. However, the Landlord could not find a new tenant for three months. Around the end of December 2025, the Landlord decided to sell the unit and conducted renovations. The unit was sold in April 2026.

The Tenant argued that the Landlord delayed in re-listing the unit for rent. I am not satisfied that this is the case; the Landlord was out of the country at the beginning of October 2025, and their real estate agent was still communicating with the Tenant regarding the termination at the time. The October 16, 2025, text message indicates that the Landlord was still trying to continue the tenancy but ultimately made the decision to re- rent. I am satisfied that the Landlord re-listed the unit within a reasonable time and that they incurred losses despite attempting to minimize them.

Since the Tenant owed rent for the month of November 2025, the Landlord was entitled to apply the last month’s deposit for that month. Therefore, the Landlord did not illegally retain the deposit, and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants; and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must compensate the Tenants in the amount of $578.25.

The Tenants filed a T2/T6 application which did not specify what issues constituted substantial inference, harassment, interference with vital service, or maintenance issues. However, the Landlord stated that they were prepared to address all of the issues raised in the application. T6 Application

At the commencement of the hearing, the Tenants issues were case managed. The following allegations were heard under section 20 of the Act as maintenance issues: (a) Between September 13, 2024 to October 23, 2024 several windows in the rental unit did not have screens: windows in the living room, dining room, office and second bedroom. (b) Between September 13, 2024 to September 27th or 29th, 2024 the Tenants were only provided with one key to the rental unit, and they did not have a working fob which made the parking lot of the residential complex and the complex’s front entry door inaccessible to them. (c) Around October 15, 2024 the Tenants noticed that there was some water which had pooled underneath their kitchen sink, inside of the cabinet.

In addition, an issue was withdrawn in the hearing which pertained to the Tenants not having had working electrical outlets in certain sections of the rental unit, unless overhead lights were also turned on.
The Tenants sought a 30.00% abatement of rent from September 13, 2024 to December 4, 2024 totalling $2,009.00 for all maintenance related issues. T2 Application
The following allegation was heard as instance of interference with vital services: (a) Thermostats in the rental unit were not functional between October 15, 2024 to October 23, 2024.

The following allegations were heard under section 23 of the Act as instances of harassment: (a) On October 18, 2024 the Landlord [name] sent the Tenants the following communication: “since you moved in until now, you are complaining about every single thing and we are trying our best to solve them one by one. As you know your right very well if you had any issues in the unit then you had to put this all in writing on the rental agreement before moving in and then us as owners, we would either approve or decline”. (b) On October 19, 2024 the Landlord [name] sent the Tenants the following communication: “if he leaves without fixing everything needed and you will request any additional list to be done you will have to pay the bill for his next appointments”.
The Tenants sought $35,000.00 in general damages and an administrative fine totalling $1,000.00 for all T2 related issues.
Throughout the tenancy the lawful monthly rent was $2,450.00 per month. [name] Screens

The Tenant [name] testified about all the issues outlined below. Ms. [name]name] stated that on September 13, 2024 she notified the Landlords’ property manager that there were no screens on the windows in the unit’s living room, dining room, office and second bedroom. The Tenant testified that no work was done to fix the issue until October 19, 2024 and that screens were finished being installed on October 23, [name] testified that they did not want to open the windows without having screens attached and that over this period the rental unit was very hot, and the Tenants had to constantly run fans in order to cool these sections of the unit’s interior.

The Landlord [name] testified that window technicians attended at the rental unit on October 20, 2024 to commence their work. This start date is reflected in email correspondence between the parties. On October 19, 2024 the Landlord states that their workers will attend the unit the following day on October 20th around 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. to begin conducting the work. The Tenant replies to this email indicating they are only available until 5 p.m. that day.

The parties agree that at 5 p.m. on October 20th the Tenant asked the technicians to leave the unit. Because of this, the Landlord states the technicians couldn’t return to complete the work until October 23, 2024.

The Landlord’s notice to enter the rental unit for repair work did not comply with section 27 of the Act because a window of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. was not outlined in their notice. Therefore, I do not find that it was unreasonable for the Tenant to ask the Landlord’s workers to vacate at the time they had discussed. It is also unreasonable that repair work took over one month to complete.

An abatement of rent in the amount of 10.00% is ordered for the period of September 13, 2024 to October 23, 2024 reflecting the minimal disruptions that the Tenants experienced in not being able to properly open their windows. A higher abatement is not ordered because the disrepair did not materially affect the Tenants’ normal use and enjoyment of the unit. The Landlords shall compensate the Tenants in the amount of $330.25. 2nd Key and Working Fob

The Tenant testified that only one key to the rental unit was provided to the Tenants, and that the fob they were provided with did not work, which made the parking lot and front door of the complex inaccessible. The Tenant testified that she notified the Landlord’s property manager about the fob on September 13, 2024 and was not given full fob access until September 27 or 29th.

No compensation is ordered for this issue. The Act does not mandate that a landlord provide one set of keys for each tenant that resides in the rental unit. With respect to not having fob access, the Tenant did not testify about having made any attempts to mitigate their damages, such as by speaking to security or management at their building about being given a working fob. The Tenants were required to attempt to mitigate their damages pursuant to section 16 of the Act. Leak under Sink

The Tenant testified that they noticed some water had pooled under the sink in their kitchen around October 15, 2024 and that she notified the Landlords the same day. No compensation is ordered for this issue, the Tenant testified that this had no impact on their use or enjoyment of the unit, nor was it a repeat issue. Vital Services and Harassment Thermostat/Heating

The Tenant stated that she sent the Landlords an email on October 15, 2024 about temperatures in the rental unit having dropped and that the thermostats in the unit were not fixed until October 23, 2024. No compensation is ordered for this issue.

The Tenant did not provide any testimony as to what the temperature ranges fell to in their unit over this time. Concerns about temperature readings in a unit are often subjective to the individual that is affected by them. Without actual evidence on this point, I am unable to assess the Tenants’ claims against the vital services provisions of the Act about minimal temperatures required in a unit, or if the impact on the Tenants is proportional to the damages claimed. October 18, 2024 & October 19, 2024 Communications

The Tenant testified that the communications sent to her on October 18, 2024 and October 19, 2024 felt combative and intimidating. The Ontario Human Rights Code defines "harassment" as: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”

The Landlord denied intending to harass the Tenants with their remarks, and with respect to the comment made on October 19th the Landlord explained that she was merely notifying the Tenants that additional expenses would be incurred if window technicians had to return over multiple days to fix screens. Nonetheless, I am persuaded that the Landlord’s comments would have been perceived as unwelcome or vexatious to a reasonable person, and that the Landlord harassed the Tenants.

The Landlord’s comments taken as a whole created an environment where the Tenants felt discouraged from making genuine requests for maintenance, that they would have to pay for maintenance, or that they would not have been selected as tenants if they had they voiced their concerns earlier.

While I find that the Landlord’s comments were harassing in nature, the Tenants claim for $35,000.00 in general damages and an administrative fine of $1,000.00 are excessive in the circumstances. These comments, while unwelcome, fall on the lesser end of a spectrum of possible interactions or comments that a landlord could make.

The Tenants did not provide any evidence to demonstrate that they developed a medical condition as a result of these interactions, that they incurred any costs, took time off of work, or that the comments had a prolonged or enduring affect on them. Accordingly, I order the Landlords to pay to the Tenants a nominal amount of $200.00 as general compensation. A fine is not imposed. I am satisfied that general compensation in this amount is sufficient to deter future conduct of the same kind.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $578.25. This amount represents: • $330.25 as an abatement of rent; • $200.00 in general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 19, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 19, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
