issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit and repair the source of leaks into the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenants in the amount of $5,640.00.

The only allegation in this T6 application is that the Landlord failed to repair the sources of leaks into the rental unit which caused water to pool in the Tenants’ second bedroom and laundry room between June 2024 to May 31, 2025.

The application is amended to reflect an increased claim for a rent abatement totalling $5,592.00. I was satisfied that the Landlord was served with an amended application in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure.
At all times the lawful rent of the rental unit was $1,525.00 per month.

The Tenants testified that they experienced three major water leaks into the second bedroom of their basement unit and at one point, part of their laundry room. This caused damage to flooring, baseboards, and their belongings. The Landlord did not contest that the Tenants experienced leaks in early June of 2024, November 14, 2024 and on March 15, 2025.
The parties agreed that the Tenants first notified the Landlord about a leak in the second bedroom of their unit on June 19, 2024 and that within a week a technician came to assess the source.

However, based on the evidence submitted by the parties, no meaningful repairs were conducted to address the source of these leaks throughout the time the Tenants resided in the unit. The Tenants testified that they could not use their second bedroom from the start of the first leak up to and including their move out date because of the risk of furniture being ruined, or their pets being exposed to warped flooring and possibly toxins from water damage. There was also an additional leak in their laundry room. Aside from a minor repair to the baseboards of the Tenants’ second bedroom, I have no evidence before me to suggest that other larger exterior repairs were carried out.

Written correspondence demonstrates that as early as August 6, 2024 the Landlord was aware that repairs to the exterior of the rental unit were required. The Landlord was even ordered by the City of Sudbury to repair the foundation of the rental unit after an inspection took place on December 18, 2024.

The Landlord’s agent testified in the hearing that major repairs to these areas were not conducted due to their high cost, because the Tenants only experienced leaks during “heavy rainfall” and because of weather disruptions. The Landlord’s agent did not provide any weather-related evidence in support of this latter statement which might demonstrate that construction was not possible over extended periods of time.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Landlord’s agents did not feel as though the leaks caused any inconvenience. However, the video and pictures submitted by the Tenants show otherwise. For instance, in one video, water can be seen flowing up from under the flooring of the rental unit when one of the Tenant’s applies light pressure to it with their hand. Based on the evidence submitted, I am persuaded that the Tenants had reasonable concerns about the safety of their second bedroom and property damage over the period claimed.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the source of leaks in the unit, as well as damage to flooring.

The Tenants seek one third of their rent as an abatement over the months of June 2024 to May 2025 totalling $5,592.00. In these circumstances, I find that a 33.33% abatement of rent is reasonable and reflects the substantial disruptions that the Tenants experienced in not having use of their second bedroom between June 19, 2024 to May 31, 2025. This abatement totals $5,798.95. However, the Tenants are limited to the claim in their application of $5,592.00.

This abatement commences on the date the Landlord was notified about the first leak, and ends as of the Tenants’ move out date. It also reflects the fact that the Tenants could not have guests stay over due to the presence of water in their second bedroom, that approximately one third of their space was unusable and that they had to store other belongings, including items for their pets, in other rooms over this period. The Landlord shall compensate the Tenants in this amount.
ordered: The total the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $5,640.00. This amount represents: • $5,592.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending May 31, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on March 15, 2022 and vacated the unit on November 15, 2024. This house includes one basement rental unit and one unit that includes the middle and top floor. The Tenant resided in the middle and top floor of the unit located at 396 Naim Avenue, York, Ontario.

This Application concerns allegations that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally without notice, the Landlord changed the locks, the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant and that the Landlord harassed, obstructed and/or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. [name] – Mathew [name] [name] (MWH)

MWH testified that his lease was to be terminated on November 15, 2024 and that he had left to return to Australia on November 12, 2024. He stated that he had a guest staying at the rental unit who would be vacating the unit on November 14, 2024. The Tenant provided me with text messages between himself and the Landlord regarding the guest staying there until November 14, 2024 and the Tenant explained to the Landlord that the Tenant’s own insurance would cover any issues with the guest.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord seemed to accept that and the Tenant emailed the Landlord that same statement for the Landlord’s benefit.
The Tenant stated that his friend attended on November 13, 2024 to remove most of their possessions.

On November 14, 2024, his friend attended at the rental unit to retrieve the remaining Tenant’s possessions and his own possessions and noted that two contractors were in attendance. These contractors had put a TV on the driveway and refused to allow the Tenant’s friend to retrieve their remaining possessions in the house and in the garage.

The Tenant stated his friend was prevented from entering the house or garage and the contractors stated that the house was empty. The contractors had apparently taken a video of the interior of the house.

MWH texted the Landlord on November 14, 2024 when his friend was not allowed access and reminded the Landlord that the lease was set to end on November 15, 2024. The Landlord responded with a video taken by the contractors setting out that the house was empty.

The Tenant asked me to review the Landlord’s video of the interior of the rental unit on November 14, 2024. While the video played, he pointed out some of his remaining possessions including a dustpan and broom, a blue rug and curtains, toilet paper and a toilet brush, moving box, and a mug. He stated that he also saw in the video items on the bathroom sink, dish detergent, coffee and a standing desk. He stated that his Bell Router was also in the rental unit and he had to pay $400.00 because he was unable to return it to Bell.

The Tenant’s position is that the lease was to be terminated on November 15, 2024 and that he was illegally locked out of the rental unit which prevented his friend from removing their final possessions on November 14, 2024. He stated that the Landlord had not provided 24 hour notice for the contractors, he had no right to change the locks and the Landlord failed to allow the Tenant to remove his possessions.

MWH is seeking a rent abatement of $88.83 which is one day of the rental period, $3,035.00 for the possessions that they were unable to retrieve, $500.00 for the cost of the movers who left because they had no access to the rental unit, and an order that the Landlord must return all of the Tenant’s possessions. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] (KS)

KS stated that he was not at the rental unit on November 14, 2024 but that his contractors ensured that the unit was empty and provided a video of the inside of the unit. This is the same video that was viewed earlier.

KS stated that he remembered that the Tenant’s friend removed most of their belongings on November 13, 2024. The Landlord stated that he instructed his contractors to ensure that the rental unit was empty before they changed the locks and moved forward with any construction. The Landlord’s position is that the rental unit was empty on November 14, 2024 and as such, he had a right to change the locks and take over the rental unit. Analysis

The Tenant’s T2 Application is based on the rights and obligations contained in sections 22, 23, 24 and 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”): 22– A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23– A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 24-A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 25– A landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27. 41(2) – Where an order is made to evict a tenant, the landlord shall not sell, retain or otherwise dispose of the tenant’s property before 72 hours have elapsed.

The Tenant’s case to be made is that the Landlord ended the tenancy prior to November 15, 2024 at 12 a.m. as he feels that this was the earliest time that the tenancy could end. Based on this claim, the Tenant states that the Landlord must pay him for his damages, return his possessions if they are available and pay him for one day of rent. The Tenant’s evidence included his recollection of his conversation with the friend who was going to retrieve those final possessions. The Tenant did not produce that person today to provide his evidence of the occurrences that day. The Tenant did not provide any of his text messages with his friend which could have somewhat corroborated the Tenant’s claim.

Instead the Tenant relied on the Landlord’s video that showed a few items including a moving box and cleaning supplies but the video confirmed that the house was mainly empty. I reviewed that video twice and I did not see items on the bathroom sink, dish detergent, coffee or a standing desk. The Tenant did not provide any pictures to prove that there were other items remaining in the house, the garage or on the driveway.

No evidence was provided to substantiate that the Landlord withheld any of the Tenant’s possessions, substantially interfered with the Tenant, harassed the Tenant or changed the locks prior to the termination of the tenancy.

This is the Tenant’s application and it is his case to prove. I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s evidence is more believable than the Landlord’s evidence. The video taken by the Landlord’s contractors on November 14, 2024 shows a rental unit that has been emptied by a Tenant.
As such, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal Rent

The application alleges that the rent increases on August 2023 to July 1, 2024, were illegal because they were contrary to section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”). The Tenant seeks a return of illegally collected rent payments.

This application was filed under section 135(1) of the Act. Section 135(4) states: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

The Tenant filed their application on November 20, 2024. On the basis of section 135(4) of the Act, the Board does not have jurisdiction to make an order with respect to any illegal rent collected by the Landlord more than one year before the Tenant filed the application. Therefore, I have only made a determination on the lawfulness of the rent increase charged and rent collected by the Landlord from the period starting November 1, 2023 to January 2024.

Section 135.1 of the Act, effective July 21, 2020, as a result of amendments to the Act made by the Protecting Tenants and Strengthening Community Housing Act, 2020, states the following: 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. (3) For greater certainty, if subsection (1) applies with respect to an increase in rent, section 116 is deemed to have been complied with. (4) For greater certainty, nothing in this section limits the application of section 136. (5) This section applies with respect to an increase in rent even if it was first charged before the day the Protecting Tenants and Strengthening Community Housing Act, 2020 receives Royal Assent, provided the validity of the rent increase was not finally determined by the Board before that day. (Emphasis added)

As a result of section 135.1, even if a landlord increased the rent without serving the tenant with any notice of rent increase as required by Act, the otherwise unlawful rent increase is deemed to be valid if the tenant pays the increased rent for 12 consecutive months without filing an application with the Board challenging the lawfulness of the increase.

Subsection 135.1(5) of the Act states that section 135.1 applies to rent increases levied prior to enactment of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 amendments, provided the validity of the rent increase was not finally determined by the Board before that day.
The Tenant asserts that she has been charged an illegal rent increase on February 1, 2022, through to July 31, 2024, and that he is entitled to be refunded the illegal rent paid.

However, the Tenant also testified that the Landlord began charging the Tenant a monthly rate of $400.00 effective February 1, 2022, and the Tenant paid this amount from February 1, 2022, to until the Tenant moved out on July 31, 2024, more than a 12 month consecutive period, and continued to pay that amount thereafter. As noted, the Tenant filed this application on November 20, 2024. The Tenant asserts that no notice of rent increase was served for this increase and that this amount is more than the 2021 Guideline amount.

In accordance with section 135.1 of the Act, $400.00 is deemed to be the lawful rent despite the fact no notice of rent increase was served for this increase and that this amount is more than the 2022 Guideline amount. The Tenant paid $400.00 per month for 12 consecutive months during the period of February 2022 to February 2023 and did not file this application within one year after the date the increase was first charged on February 1, 2022.
As set out above, pursuant to section 135(4) the Board cannot consider any allegedly illegal rents collected more than one year before the application was filed.
As the 2022 rent increase is deemed lawful by section 135.1 of the Act, I cannot find that the Landlord illegally collected rent and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

The Tenant also asserted that he worked for the Landlord’s jewellery store and there was a verbal agreement to offset rent with wages owed. The Tenant submits that when the wages stopped, the Tenant stopped paying rent.
The Landlord disputes that this is the case.
I do not find that the Tenant’s employment with the Landlord is connected to the Tenant’s tenancy. I find that they are two separate agreements.

Royal Bank of Canada v. MacPherson, [2009] O.J. No. 3806 ([name]. Ct.). MacPherson Act prohibits prepayment of the rent by way of the rent deposit provisions in sections 105 and 106. The bank argued that because prepayment is arguably illegal under the Act the tenant should not be able to rely on it as a defence to the bank’s demands for payment of the rent. The essential thrust of MacPherson is that the provisions that prohibit a landlord from demanding prepayment of the rent are in the Act to protect tenants against landlord demands for excessive deposits and “to treat an agreement under which a tenant has prepaid rent to his or her landlord as unenforceable would penalize the very party the provisions of the Act are meant to protect”. I would observe that here, like in MacPherson, the Landlord is prohibited to collect without the Tenant’s authorization rent from his pay.

I also find the Landlord filed a previous application with the Landlord and Tenant Board and the Board issued its decision (file number LTB-L-019927-25) dated July 31, 2025. The order requires the Tenant to compensate the Landlord for unpaid rent. Both parties attended the hearing that resulted in that order, and the Tenant raised the issue of the Landlord withholding rent payment from the Tenant’s wages. However, the Board exercised their jurisdiction and found that was not the case. I find it curious that the Tenant is now challenging the issue. In any event, it does not change my decision in that regard.
ordered: The application is dismissed. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application is filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and claims the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.

The Tenant’s claim for the return of 5.5 months rent paid upfront is granted as collection of a rent deposit for an amount that is more than one month’s rent is in direct contravention of section 106(2) of the Act.
The Tenant’s claim for the return of the Key Deposit is granted.

Notwithstanding the fact that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with an N13 Notice to vacate the rental unit for repairs to take place, the fact that the Landlord and his agent through email communications asked the Tenant to vacate the unit in order for repair work to be carried out confirms that the Tenant was asked to leave the premises. The Tribunal is satisfied as per section 202 of the Act that the real substance of the matter effectively removed the Tenant from the rental unit. The Landlord did not provide the Tenant with one month’s compensation and the Tenant’s claim for this amount is also granted.
As the Tenant was successful on his application, the Tenant is awarded his costs of filing this application. T1 Application – Determinations
The Landlord and Tenant entered into a one-year lease agreement commencing on September 10, 2025.

The monthly rent is $2,100.00. On September 8, 2025, the Tenant made two payments to the Landlord totalling to an amount of $12,900.00. This amount is for first and last month’s rent, 4 months rent upfront and includes a $300 refundable Key Deposit.
The Tenant also made monthly rent payments of $2,100.00 on October 10, 2025, and November 10, 2025.
Subsection 106(2) of the Act provides: 106(2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one period and the amount of rent for one month.
In total, the Tenant paid the Landlord $17,100 and only lived in the unit for 2.5 months before the Landlord’s Agent asked the Tenant to vacate the unit in order for repair works to be carried out.
Consequently, the Tenant claims the Landlord owes him 5.5 months of rent out of the 8 months rent that he paid upfront.
The Tenant relied upon Exhibit 1 – DOC ID 6887636 with respect to confirmation of the payments made to the Landlord and the Lease Agreement itself.

Hence, the Landlord is in direct contravention of section 106(2) of the Act as he collected 4 months rent upfront from the Tenant in addition to the first and last months’ rent payment at the commencement of the tenancy.
Despite attempts made to communicate with the Landlord and his Agent, the Tenant has yet to receive a response from the Landlord.

Subsections 135(1) and (1.1) of the Act provide: 135(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the Landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. (1.1) Without limiting the generality of subsection (1), a landlord is deemed to have retained money in contravention of this Act, if the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.2, 49.1, 52, 54, or 55 and fails to compensate the tenant as required. Key Deposit

Section 17 of the Lease Agreement states that “The keys and Fobs will be provided to tenant before closing. $300 for Key Deposit will be collected before closing and shall be returned to Tenant without deduction if all keys are returned to the Landlord.”
The Landlord has failed to return the $300 Key Deposit to the Tenant despite the Tenant asking him to do so. Compensation for N13 Notice owing
Between November 5, 2025, and November 10, 2025, the Tenant received an email asking him to vacate the unit by November 25, 2025. Consequently, the Tenant vacated on November 24, 2025.

The Landlord’s Agent did provide the Tenant options with respect to other units they could live in but because the Agent could not provide a firm date as to when the Tenant could return to the unit, he chose not to accept any of those options.
The Tenant claims the Landlord failed to pay him one month’s compensation when he was asked to vacate the premises as required under section 54.3 of the Act.

Even though no formal N13 Notice was served on the Tenant, the communication exchange that took place between the Landlord’s Agent and the Tenant does amount to an N13 for the purposes of section 57 of the Act. A tenant should not be deprived of the remedies available when a bad faith notice is served just because the Landlord failed to serve the notice in the proper form and in compliance with the Act. To decide otherwise would defeat the purpose of section 57 and produce an unjust result.
I am satisfied that the Tenant moved out as a result of the communication exchange between the Landlord’s Agent and himself.
As a result, I find that the Tenant is owed one month’s rent as compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,998.00. This amount represents: • $11,550.00 for the 5.5 months of rent paid upfront; • $300.00 for the refundable Key Deposit owing; • $2,100.00 for the compensation owing; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 26, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
lease_quotes: The keys and Fobs will be provided to tenant before closing. $300 for Key Deposit will be collected before closing and shall be returned to Tenant without deduction if all keys are returned to the Landlord.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-100174-24 issued on November 25, 2025. On December 17, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On December 17, 2025, interim order LTB-T-100174-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on November 25, 2025. This review was heard by videoconference on January 22, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenants attended the hearing. The Tenant’s were represented by [name].
reasons: The order issued on November 25, 2025 grants the T5 Tenant’s application as the presiding Member was satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice of termination in bad-faith. The order also orders the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $11,241.24 in compensation.

The Landlord’s request for review asserts that the order contains a serious error. In particular, the Landlord’s review request disputes being ordered to pay $4,100.00 in general compensation for unpaid compensation owing under section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act).

As explained below, I find that the order contains a serious error in ordering this amount and as such, the November 25, 2025 order will be varied to reduce the total amount owing to the Tenants by $4,100.00.

As explained above, the application before the Board was a T5 application only and was filed pursuant to section 57(1) of the Act. The application claims general compensation for “pain and suffering”, which was denied. The Board however granted general compensation to be paid for the one-months rent compensation owing pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act which states that “a landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48.”

No T1 application was filed by the Tenants. T1 applications are filed pursuant to section 135 of the Act which states in part: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. (1.1) Without limiting the generality of subsection (1), a landlord is deemed to have retained money in contravention of this Act, if the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55 and fails to compensate the tenant as required.

Although the parties disputed whether the required compensation was paid pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act, I find this is irrelevant and that the Board seriously erred in the November 25, 2025 order by ordering this amount as general compensation and on a T5 application filed pursuant to section 57(1) of the Act. As the application before the Board was not a T1 application filed pursuant to section 135(1) of the Act, the Board did not have the jurisdiction to make as to whether the Landlord collected or retained money illegally.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-100174-24 issued on November 25, 2025, is granted.
Order LTB-T-100174-24 issued on November 25, 2025 is varied as follows.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $7,141.24. This amount represents: • $419.18 for a rent abatement • $6,200.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024. • $474.06 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,880.08. Illegal Rent Collected:
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord had illegally collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) from December 1, 2024 to November 27, 2025.

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2021 pursuant to a short term rental agreement, and in November 2021 he signed a “rent-to-own” agreement where the rent was $2,110.66 per month, and every month $50.00 would go towards equity in the property. The Tenant then testified he was notified by email on September 27, 2024 that as of December 1, 2024 his rent would be $2,430.00. The Tenant also testified that he never received an N1 notice of rent increase. The Tenant testified that from December 1, 2024, his rent increased to $2,430.00, and that he filed his T1 application on November 27, 2025, which was within one year of the increase being first charged,

The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that as this was a rent-to-own agreement and the Tenant’s intention was to eventually own the property, this could not be a tenancy agreement. When asked how much each monthly payment went towards the total equity in the property, the Landlord’s Legal Representative did not know. The Tenant submitted as evidence the rent-to-own agreement which shows that equity was accumulating at $50.00 per month, and that as of September 2025 when the Landlord asked him to sign a new lease, emails demonstrate that the total equity was $20,025.00.

The Landlord also submitted that the Tenant had paid the rent increase for 12 consecutive months, and so the lawful rent became $2,430.00 pursuant to section 136(1) of the Act. However, the Landlord cannot rely upon section 136 because of the Ontario Court of Appeal’s reasoning in [name] v. [name], 2007 ONCA 408, which held that section 136(1) does not apply if the landlord fails to serve a notice of rent increase.

In any event, section 136(1) of the Act does not apply because the Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on November 27, 2025, 2025, which is within one year from December 1, 2024, the date the unlawful rent increase was first “charged”. As a result, neither section 136(1) nor 136(2) would apply due to their terms: 136 (1) Rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. 2006, c. 17, s. 136 (1). (2) An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application. [Emphasis added]

While the Tenant testified he paid the 12 consecutive months of the unlawful rent, just like the deeming provisions in section 136, section 135.1(1) of the Act would not apply because section 135.1(2) states as follows: 135.1 (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. [Emphasis added]

As noted above, the Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on November 27, 2025, which was within one year of the date that the unlawful increase was first charged (December 1, 2024). As a result, neither section 136 nor 135.1 deem the increase as lawful.

I find that while this originally was a rent-to-own agreement, the Tenant is a tenant pursuant to the definition of the Act and this was a tenancy agreement, therefore the Landlord was only allowed to increase rent pursuant to an N1 notice of rent increase and pursuant to the guideline. As such, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not service an N1 notice, and that the Landlord’s rent increase was above the 2.5% guideline. Therefore, the Landlord did collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,880.08. This amount represents: • $3,832.08 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $646.68 from the rent each month from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name]: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: I have find the application must be dismissed because I have determined that a fair hearing is not possible.

At the start of the hearing, the Landlord raised several preliminary issues and requested that the Tenant’s application be dismissed. First, the Landlord says the applications contain narrative allegations that seemingly sound in disrepair without the particulars necessary for understand the Tenants’ concerns. Second, the Landlord pointed out no dates are pleaded in support of the allegations and some of them at least appear to be historic and may be statute-barred by the one-year limitation period in subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). For example, one pleading claims “We had mold for a very long time. My landlord takes time to treat the mold” but without details of when the problem began and when it was treated.

Third, the Landlord says that the Tenants’ evidence is too voluminous and disorganized making it impossible for them to anticipate what is to be presented against him. And lastly, the Landlord points out that all of these frailties in Tenants’ applications were explained to them during the case management conference of June 25, 2025 and instructions given to them by the Board both orally and in interim order of July 3, 2025. On having further case management discussions with the Tenant [name], I agree with the Landlord on all these points and find that the application must be dismissed because the Board cannot resolve the disputes in a fair and expeditious hearing as mandated by section 183 of the Act.

I find the allegations lack sufficient particulars for the Landlord to be able to investigate the issues alleged and to prepare a response. Nor can the Board satisfy itself that it has jurisdiction over the dispute because the pleadings contain no dates.

Furthermore, the Tenants’ evidence is not presented in a manner conducive to a fair and expeditious hearing. The Board attempted to address this issue in its interim order issued on July 3, 2025. The Board directed the Tenant to remove repetitious materials and included the following instructions: All documents, photographs and other items provided to the parties and the LTB must: 1) be readable 2) have consecutively numbered pages; and 3) include a list or table of contents identifying each item in order, and by page number, if more than one item is being submitted.

Despite these instructions, the Tenants have not presented their evidence any discernable fashion. They advised that they were unable to do so because the Portal would not accept the volume of materials they wished to present. They have sent a series of emails containing an assortment of images and documents but without descriptive filenames or other indication of how they relate to the issues raised in the application.
The Tenants acknowledged that, during the case management hearing of June 25, 2025, they were advised on how to present their evidence and pleadings. They have not done either of those things.

I invited the Tenants to seek an adjournment to overcome the problems in the presentation of their pleadings and evidence so that their concerns can be adjudicated in a fair and expeditious hearing. The Tenant [name] [name] advised that he was unable to do so because his local legal clinic had declined to help him. He advised that his searches on Google had yielded no assistance either. He had not tried to enlist any other legal representation although instructions for doing so were given to the Tenants in the two notices of hearing as well as the Board’s interim order of July 3, 2025.

The Board’s Rules of Procedure and processes allow for a great deal of flexibility aimed at ensuring disputes are resolved on their merits at a fair, expeditious and timely hearing. To that end, the Board will relieve a party from filing irregularities and breaches of its orders and directions where it would foster the Board’s mandate contained in section 183 of the Act. The Board will also entertain requests for adjournments where it is warranted to achieve those objectives. This is not such a case.

I find the Tenants’ unparticularized pleadings coupled with the large volume of disorganized evidence means the Landlord is not in a position to adequately to know the case against it to defend himself. On considering the factors identified in Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I have determined that any further adjournments would not result in an adequate hearing but would result in significant prejudice to the Landlord. For these reasons, I find that the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
The Tenants submitted that the Landlord’s legal representative had been incorrectly named as a respondent. An order will go removing him.
ordered: The application and style of cause are amended to remove Leo Corsetti as a respondent.
The application is dismissed. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: T he Landlord’s Agent requested that they be removed as a party to the proceedings. They are an employee of [name].
Pursuant to Rule 1.6 b. of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I granted the request to removed [name] as a personal respondent.
I note that the Tenant uploaded additional documents to the portal after the hearing. Post hearing submissions were not requested and therefore not given any consideration.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant.
The parties agreed that the Tenant was put back in possession of the rental unit on December 12, 2025.

The Landlord stated that there had been a fire in the unit, that the City had issued an order to repair, and that there had not been an order to deny occupation. They alleged that a text message from the City and the order to repair amounted to an order from the City to deny occupation to the Tenants.
The City to order to repair was issued on November 7, 2025. DOC-6985589. A further order was issued on November 12, 2025. DOC-6985595.

The November 12, 2025 order indicates that there was damage due to a fire on the balcony. The order only directs the Landlord to “immediately prevent access to the balcony from within the dwelling unit.

The Landlord stated that the balcony railing, the balcony door and windows had been damaged by the fire. The photo at DOC-6988428 does appear to show the window is completely missing, and outside of the balcony door appears to be burnt. The sofa in the photo does appear to have some debris on it, however it does not appear to be burnt debris. Otherwise, the sofa does not appear to be damaged by the fire. (what cannot be determined in the absence of other evidence is the extent if any caused by smoke damage).
The Landlord therefore admitted that the Tenant had been locked out till the unit was repaired and the keys returned on December 12, 2025.
The Landlord admitted that they had removed and disposed of a sofa during the remediation of the unit.

The Tenant disagreed with the Landlord. They submitted that they had removed the sofa’s and cleaned the unit. They stated that the Landlord had placed the burnt debris inside the unit, and that is what caused the damages to the sofa, carpet and curtains.
The Tenant was seeking reimbursement for two sofas, a carpet and the curtains.
The Landlord referred to a photo at DOC-6988428 that only shows the presence of a single sofa.
The Landlord stated that any losses incurred by the Tenant the Tenant should have had tenant insurance in place to reimburse the Tenant.
The Tenant confirmed that they do not have tenant insurance.

In my view, where the Landlord locked out the Tenant, and retained full care and control of the rental unit, they became responsible for anything they or their agents do. In this case, the Landlord admitted that they had removed and disposed of the sofa. They could have stored the sofa and returned it to the Tenant, but instead they unilaterally decided to dispose of it.

The condition of the carpet as seen in the photo a DOC-6988428 does show significant debris including what appears to be smoke covered debris or ash. As a result, it is likely that the carpet was not salvageable and ought to have been disposed of.

The photo shows the extent of the damage to the window, appears to be completely destroyed, there is no frame or glass. Therefore, it is likely that the curtains were damaged or destroyed by the fire or the response to the fire.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord is responsible for the loss of the sofa that they admitted that they had disposed of. I am not satisfied that the Landlord should be responsible for the other items claimed. Remedies

The Landlord submitted that if the Tenant had tenant insurance that it would have reimbursed them. However, the Landlord did not lead any evidence to show that a tenant insurance policy would have insured the tenant for the actions of the Landlord in removing and disposing of the sofa. In para 106 Equity Builders Ltd. Et al. v. Landlord and Tenant Board et al., 2025 ONSC 759 at paragraph 109, the Divisional Court found that the Landlord failed to show that mitigation was possible. It is important to keep in mind that the damages awarded by the Board are to compensate the Tenants for the Landlords’ breaches of the RTA. The Landlords did not put forward any evidence about what types of policies were available to the Tenants and whether the policies would respond to damages caused by the Landlords’ actions. Even if a policy were to provide coverage for these types of damages, policies often include subrogation rights which would permit the insurer to pursue the Landlords for the amounts paid out under the policy. The Landlords failed to establish that mitigation was possible in the first place. (Emphasis added)
The Landlord admitted that they had removed and disposed of the sofa. I am satisfied that in all the circumstances an amount of $750.00 compensation for the sofa is appropriate.
The Tenant did not pursue a rent abatement at the hearing or any of the other remedies set out in the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $750.00. This amount represents: 2. $750.00 for the estimated costs to replace the sofa. 3. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026. 4. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 5. If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing my March 7, 2026, then commencing April 1, 2026 that Tenant shall be permitted to deduct the full amount from the lawful rent, until the full amount has been recovered. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: This application concerns a tenant who wanted to end his lease early. The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) provides a straightforward process for tenants to end their leases early. In this case, unfortunately, the Tenant did not follow the correct process.
Instead, the Tenant sent the Landlord a series of vague and confusing requests. The Landlord did not agree to the requests, but eventually agreed to end the tenancy effective November 30, 2025.

The Tenant then sent the Landlord a request to sublet his unit for 19 days in November. The request was unusual, and was only necessary because the Tenant had not followed the proper process up to that point. However, the request was valid, and the RTA required that the Landlord consider it. The Landlord arbitrarily and unreasonably refused consent to the sublet, and as a result, the Tenant lost $500.00 in rent he would have received from the subtenant.
The Landlord will be ordered to compensate the Tenant for his $500.00 loss. In the circumstances, I will not award costs to the Tenant. The first sublet request Facts
The Tenant rented the unit for a fixed term running from May 1 2025 to April 30, 2026. He paid a deposit of one month’s rent, to be applied to the final month of the tenancy.

The Tenant paid his rent through October, 2025. Then, he was offered a job in another city. On October 2, 2025, he told the Landlord that he wanted to end his tenancy early. He seems to have wanted to move out as early as October 31, 2025.

Section 95 of the RTA sets out the process for a tenant to follow when they want their tenancy to end early. The Tenant should have asked the Landlord for consent to assign the tenancy pursuant to section 95(1).
If the Landlord had consented, then the Tenant could have found someone to take over his tenancy. His liability for the rent would have ended as soon as the tenancy was assigned.

On the other hand, if the Landlord had not consented, then the Tenant could have given 30 days’ notice to end the tenancy. In this case, given the timing, he could probably have given notice for around November 1, 2025.
In either case, the Tenant would have successfully ended his obligations in the tenancy – either by terminating the tenancy, or by assigning it to someone else.
The Tenant did not ask the Landlord for consent to assign the tenancy. Instead, on October 5, 2026, he asked for consent to sublet the unit from November 1 to 30, 2025.

It is not clear to me why the Tenant requested a sublet. The proposed sublet would have helped him cover the rent for November, but after the sublet had ended, he would still have been responsible for the rent for December, January, February, March, and April.

The Landlord was, understandably, confused. He had understood that the Tenant wanted to end his tenancy, and did not know why the Tenant was now requesting a one-month sublet instead. He wrote back and asked the Tenant to clarify whether the sublet would be only for one month, or for a longer period.

On October 12, 2025, the Tenant replied that the subtenant he had in mind would “stay in the unit for the rest of the lease until April.” He did not explain why he had initially requested a sublet of only one month.
The Landlord did not consent to the sublet. Analysis
I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s request was sufficiently clear as to constitute a valid request for consent to sublet within the meaning of the RTA.

Section 2(2) of the RTA provides that subletting a rental unit refers to the situation in which: (a) the tenant vacates the rental unit; (b) the tenant gives one or more other persons the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant’s term or period; and (c) the tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit after that specified date.

The Tenant’s initial request to sublet for November 1 to 30 was clear. It would have meant that he would vacate the unit and give a subtenant the right to occupy between November 1 and 30. Starting on December 1, he would have the right to resume occupancy.

However, the Tenant subsequently said that the subtenant would stay until the end of April, which was not consistent with a subtenancy from November 1 to 30. He did not explain whether he was actually asking to sublet the tenancy from November through April, or to assign the tenancy, or something else. Effectively, the Tenant withdrew his request to sublet from November 1 to 30 but did not replace it with a new coherent request.

Since the Tenant did not make a sublet request within the meaning of the RTA, it does not matter whether the Landlord’s refusal of the request was arbitrary or unreasonable. There was no request that the Landlord was required to consider. The second sublet request Facts

At some point in October, 2025, the Tenant then gave a notice to end the tenancy effective November 30, 2025. The notice was not valid. Pursuant to section 47 of the RTA, the earliest date for which the Tenant could have given notice to end the tenancy was April 30, 2026.

On October 25, the Tenant wrote the following to the Landlord: I just wanted to follow up on my earlier notice for the end of November, just to make sure we’re on the same page. Since the last month’s rent ($1,350) was paid at the start of the lease, I just wanted to confirm that it’ll be applied to November’s rent so there’s no confusion later on.
The Landlord replied: Yes, you paid the last month rent and you don’t need to pay for November rent, you can stay till end of November.

Although the Tenant’s notice was not valid, the October 25 emails constituted a valid agreement to end the tenancy effective November 30. A few days later, the parties formalized their agreement by signing an N11 Agreement to End the [name] form.
Consequently, from October 25 onwards, the end of the term of the tenancy was no longer April 30, 2026, and was instead November 30, 2025.
In his October 25 email, the Tenant also wrote: I wanted to share that I might have found someone who’s interested in the place.
The Landlord subsequently spoke with the new applicant, but no sublet or assignment agreement was reached. Analysis

The Tenant’s second request was not a valid sublet request, either. All he told the Landlord was that he might have found someone interested in the unit. He did not say for what period the person would live in the unit, or whether he proposed to sublet or assign the unit to them. The request lacked any of the details required in a sublet request.

In this case, as well, it does not matter whether the Landlord’s refusal of the Tenant’s request was arbitrary or unreasonable. There was no request that the Landlord was required to consider. The third sublet request Facts

On November 5, 2025, the Tenant wrote to the Landlord again: I know you might say no again, but I’ve found a potential subtenant who’s a college student in Toronto. He’s looking for a place exactly from November 10th to November 29th. I wanted to check what your thoughts are on his. Even if it’s just for the last few weeks, it would at least help me recover about $500 of my total $1,400 loss. Please let me know what you think.
The Landlord refused consent, replying: As we signed the N11, we have no obligation to each other.
On November 8, 2025, the Tenant moved out of the unit. Analysis

The Tenant’s November 5 request was a valid request for consent to a sublet within the meaning of the RTA. The request addressed all the elements of section 2(2): (a) the Tenant would vacate the unit; (b) the Tenant would give another person the right to occupy the unit for a term ending on a specified date: November 29, 2025. The date was one day before the end of the Tenant’s term, November 30, 2025. (c) the Tenant would have the right to resume occupancy on November 30, 2025, for one day.

The Landlord argues that the request was not a valid sublet request, because the Tenant did not intend to move back into the unit after the sublet ended. I am not persuaded by that argument. Section 2(2)(c) does not require that a tenant move back in, or intend to move back in, after a sublet. It only requires that the tenant have the right to move back in. In this case, if the Landlord had agreed to the sublet, then the Tenant would have had the right to resume occupancy the unit on November 30, for one day. That is all that section 2(2)(c) requires.

The Landlord also argues that the sublet request was not valid, because the parties had already agreed to end the tenancy early. I am not persuaded by that argument, either. The RTA permits a tenant to request a sublet provided that the sublet ends before the end of the term of the tenancy. The parties agreed that the term of the tenancy would end on November 30. I can see no reason that agreement would restrict the Tenant’s statutory right to request a sublet ending on November 29. Did the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent?
Having received a valid sublet request, the Landlord was prohibited by section 97(2) of the RTA from arbitrarily or unreasonably withholding consent.

The Landlord told the Tenant that he was refusing consent because they had signed an N11 and therefore had no obligation to each other. As discussed above, that was an incorrect understanding of the law. The tenancy, and the parties’ RTA obligations to each other, continued until November 30. To refuse a sublet because an N11 had been signed was arbitrary and unreasonable.

On the evidence before me, it seems the Landlord may have had a second reason to refuse the request: he felt that November 10 to 29 was too short a period for a sublet. However, he has not explained why a short sublet would have been a problem. He gave no evidence of any reason for refusing a 19-day sublet. I therefore find that his refusal on that basis was also arbitrary and unreasonable. [name]

The tenancy ended on November 30, 2025. The Tenant paid his rent through October, and paid November’s rent using his rent deposit. He had to pay for the full month of November, even though he moved out on November 8.

If the Landlord had not refused the sublet request, the Tenant would still have had to pay the full rent for November. However, he would have recovered a portion of his loss by collecting rent from his subtenant for the November 10 to 29 period.

The evidence before me is vague as to what rent the proposed subtenant would have paid. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,350. That amount pro-rated for 19 days would come to $843.29. However, there is no evidence that the proposed subtenant was going to pay that amount. A tenant can sublet a unit for a lower rent than the rent they pay their landlord.

In his November 5 email, the Tenant told the Landlord that the sublet would allow him to recover “about $500.” Absent better evidence, I find that the proposed subtenant would have paid $500.00 total for November 10 to 29.
The Tenant’s rent will be abated by $500.00 to compensate him for the income he lost as of a result of the Landlord’s arbitrary and unreasonable refusal to consent to the proposed sublet. Costs

The Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) usually awards costs to a successful applicant to reimburse them for the application filing fee. The reason for this is that the respondent’s conduct caused the applicant to incur the filing fee.

Costs are a discretionary remedy. In the unique circumstances of this case, in my view it would not be fair to award costs. This application arose because the Tenant failed to follow the process set out in the RTA to end a tenancy early. Requesting consent to an assignment is simple and straightforward. Instead, the Tenant made a series of vague and confusing requests, framed as sublet requests, which did not address his goal of ending the tenancy early.

Although the Tenant eventually managed to make a valid request, which the Landlord improperly refused, the whole situation would have been avoided if the Tenant had followed the proper process at the outset.
In the circumstances, I find that primary cause of the Tenant incurring the filing fee is the Tenant’s conduct, not the Landlord’s. I decline to award costs. Conclusion
It is unfortunate that the Tenant did not simply, in early October, request the Landlord’s consent to assign the tenancy. If he had, this dispute would have been avoided.
Instead, the Tenant made several vague and confusing requests, which I do not find to have been valid sublet requests.
The Landlord then agreed to terminate the tenancy on November 30. However, the Tenant wanted to move out sooner than that, so he continued to try to find a subtenant.

On November 5, the Tenant made a valid request to sublet the unit from November 10 to 29. While the request was unusual, it was properly made in accordance with the RTA, and the Landlord was required to consider it.
The Landlord has not given any reasonable reason for refusing the Tenant’s request, so on the evidence before me, I find that the refusal was arbitrary and unreasonable.
Because of the refusal, the Tenant lost rental income of $500.00. He is entitled to reimbursed for his loss.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $500.00, which represents a rent abatement.

If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, he will owe simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Submission and Evidence

The Tenant referred to the written tenancy agreement mutually signed on May 6, 2025. He testified that he viewed the rental unit on or about April 13, 2025, and he signed the tenancy agreement on April 16, 2025. The tenancy agreement sets out a fixed term of one year, starting June 1, 2025 and ending on May 31, 2026. The lawful rent is $2,450.00.

The Tenant referred to email transfers confirming that he paid on April 18, 2025 and April 19, 2025, to the Landlord’s agent, the first month and last months’ rent deposit ($2,450.00 x2 = $4,900.00). The lease confirms that $2,450.00 is being held by the Landlord.

Prior to entering into the tenancy agreement, the Tenant saw an online advertisement indicating that the “exterior of the building will be getting redone.” The Tenant also had verbal discussions with the Landlord’s agent regarding the condition of the exterior.

In the weeks leading up to June 1, 2025, the Tenant attended the property and observed that the exterior work had not been completed. The Tenant communicated with the Landlord's agent expressing concerns about the safety and requesting for the work to be completed before moving in.

On June 1, 2025, the Landlord’s agent communicated with the Tenant via text message, “so you are not going to move in until the exterior is finished? Because the interior is completely fine and ready to go.” The Tenant responded, “yes please.” He explained at the hearing that “yes please” means that he will not be moving in until the exterior was completed because that was the agreement between the parties.

The Tenant met with the Landlord on June 10, 2025, he was provided with the keys to the unit which he retained but never took possession of or occupied the unit. The Tenant also claims that another individual is occupying the unit. Analysis and Findings

Subsection 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states “a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

In Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 542, para 22, the Divisional Court held: “When one looks at the words of s. 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is “not given” to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective Tenant.”

In this case, a binding tenancy agreement was formed between the parties on May 6, 2025. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord refused or was unable to provide vacant possession. To the contrary, the Tenant’s own evidence was that he chose not to move in on June 1, 2025. The evidence establishes that the Landlord, through the agent arranged to provide the keys to the Tenant at the start of the tenancy. While the keys were physically handed over shortly after June 1, 2025, I find that the unit was available for occupancy on June 1 and the Landlord was ready and willing to provide possession. However, the Tenant declined to attend to receive the keys and made it clear that he would not move into the unit unless the exterior work was completed.

Consistent with the reasoning provided in Opara v. [name], [2008] O.J. No. 1934 ([name]. Ct.) and Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 542, where the tenant repudiates a binding tenancy agreement prior to taking possession, the tenant is not entitled to return of the rent deposit because it was their own actions, not the Landlord’s, that prevented possession from being taken. Therefore, s.107(1) of the Act does not apply on these facts because the Landlord was prepared to provide vacant possession of the rental unit but it was declined by the Tenant.

Further, I find that the completion of the exterior work was not a term of the tenancy agreement that would justify the Tenant’s repudiation. The Tenant relies on the initial advertisement which provides “exterior of the building will be getting redone” and his verbal discussions with the Landlord’s agent as the condition that he will not take possession until the Landlord completes the exterior. However, as indicated at the hearing, this condition was not incorporated into the written lease agreement and does not constitute a binding term of the tenancy. Therefore, the Tenant’s refusal to take possession “unless new conditions are met” amounts to a unilateral refusal to perform the tenancy agreement.

The Landlord has a duty to mitigate losses in accordance with sections 16 and 88(4) of the Act by attempting to re-rent the unit once informed that the Tenant would not be taking possession. If the Landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, then the Tenant who failed to take possession of the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new Tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit per to s. 88(3)(2) of the Act.

In this case, while the Tenant believes a new Tenant moved in, there is insufficient evidence establishing when the tenancy began. In the absence of reliable evidence, either direct or documentary, I am unable to determine that the Landlord has illegally retained the Applicant’s rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
