issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit. What are the Lawful Monthly Rent and Arrears?
The lawful rent is $1,750.00. It is due on the 1st day of each month.

The Tenant disputed the amount of monthly rent. She claimed in her T1 Application (LTB- T-100733-25) and section 82 claim that the Landlord unlawfully raised the rent on April 1, 2023. While the Landlord agrees he raised the rent on April 1, 2023 above the guideline amount the effect of section 116(4), s.165 and section 165.1 of the Residential Tenancies and LTB-T-100733-25 Act, 2006 the (‘Act’) is that the rent increase is deemed not void because the Tenant paid the rent for 12 consecutive months after the illegal rent increase, and did not file any application the subject of which was a dispute of the rent increase. As a result I find that the lawful rent is $1750.00
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $57.53. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,750.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenant has paid $1,850.00 to the Landlord since the application was filed.
Based on the lawful monthly rent of $1,750.00, the rent arrears owing to January 31, 2026 are $5,150.00, and the Tenant does not dispute this amount.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,400.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.

Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $170.88 is owing to the Tenant for the period from May 31, 2019 to January 12, 2026. The Tenant claimed in in her T1 application ([name]) that interest on the rent deposit was not applied or provided. The Landlord agrees that interest was not paid.

Pursuant to section 105(6) the Landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annual on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. In this case that amount tis 2.5%.

Since the Landlord failed to pay that interest, the Tenant is entitled to deduct the amount of the payment from a subsequent rent payment. The amount owing by the Tenant in this case will be reduced by the interest the Landlord is obligated to pay. The result of this is order is that the Tenant may have to ‘top up’ their rent deposit at the end of the tenancy. Relief from Eviction.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), including whether the Landlord attempted to negotiate a repayment agreement with the Tenant and find that it would not be unfair to grant relief from eviction subject to the conditions set out in this order pursuant to subsection 83(1)(a) and 204(1) of the Act.
The Tenant has lived in the rental unit since June 1, 2019, and prior to that she resided with the Landlord’s mother. She lives in the basement apartment with her 16-year-old child.

The Tenant was without employment in the fall of 2025 but now has a stable full-time position with adequate income Based on the information provided by the Tenant regarding her income and expenses I find that while she can afford to pay the rent with her new job, and LTB-T-100733-25 she has little discretionary income. The amount the Landlord increased the rent in 2023 was the maximum the Tenant could afford.
The Tenant requests a payment plan of $200.00, which will result in repayment after 27 months, which is a long time, but not unreasonable.

The Landlord testified that he is also struggling financially but produced no documentary evidence or particulars of his financial position. He raised the rent illegally because he was starting to go into debt. He submits it is prejudicial to permit a long payment plan which would be strain on the Landlord’s finances. I fail to see how a plan that the Tenant is complying with and can afford, would be prejudicial to the Landlord. Although he testified he took a line of credit to pay the Tenant’s arrears, he did not provide evidence as to the minimum payment on $5,336.00 is more than the proposed amount the Tenant is capable of paying.

I also cannot find that the payment plan would be unfair to the Landlord given they were put in a better position financially by the above guideline rent increase, to the detriment of the Tenant. The Tenant on the other hand would experience significant prejudice if I did not grant the payment plan.
I find therefore that a conditional payment plan of $200.00 is not unfair to the Landlord.
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $5,336.00 for arrears of rent up to January 31, 2026 and costs.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord the amount set out in paragraph 1 in accordance with the following schedule: • $200.00, beginning February 20, 2026 to and including March 20, 2028. • $136.00, on April 20, 2028.

The Tenant shall also pay to the Landlord new rent on time and in full as it comes due and owing for the period February 1, 2026 to April 1, 2028, or until the arrears are paid in full, whichever date is earliest.

If the Tenant fails to make any one of the payments in accordance with this order, the outstanding balance of any arrears of rent and costs to be paid by the Tenant to the Landlord pursuant to paragraph 1 of this order shall become immediately due and owing and the Landlord may, without notice to the Tenant, apply to the LTB within 30 days of the Tenant's breach pursuant to section 78 of the Act for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant and requiring that the Tenant pay any new arrears, NSF fees and related charges that became owing after January 31, 2026. January 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • collected or retained money illegally; and • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $15,960.00 by May 8, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] [name] (JV)

JV testified that she entered into a one-year lease with the Landlord to rent the main unit at [address]nue, Welland, Ontario commencing June 1, 2024. The Tenant stated that her income was based solely on a Canada Pension Disability and for that reason, the Landlord insisted that she prepay her rent for the entire year. Although the lease stated that the Tenant “voluntarily provided the $19,000.00 payment,” JV understood that she would not be accepted as a Tenant without making that payment.

JV provided confirmation that she paid the Landlord $19,000.00 prior to moving into the rental unit. The Tenant had previously paid first and last month’s rent totalling $3,800.00. All of these funds were paid to the Landlord by June 3, 2024 and the Tenant and her family moved into the unit on June 27, 2024. The monthly rent was $1,900.00.

The Tenant provided an N9 to the Landlord on August 29, 2024 advising that she would be vacating the rental unit on September 30, 2024. JV stated that the basement tenants’ behaviour was dangerous and intolerable which caused her to terminate the tenancy.

JV testified that the basement tenants had been harassing her, trespassing in her unit to change the temperature of the air conditioner, swearing at and yelling at the Tenant and her husband, and interfering with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. She provided a number of text messages from July 15, 2024 through September 30, 2024 between her realtor, herself and the Landlord setting out multiple incidents that occurred with the basement tenants.

JV stated that she was terrified of the basement tenants and moved their fridge in front of the basement door to ensure that the tenants would not enter their unit. She further stated that the basement tenant, [name], slashed her tires on September 2, 2024 and that she witnessed him doing this. The Tenant stated that a police report was made of the incident.

JV also testified that [name] had broken into her unit multiple times after September 15, 2024 to change the temperature on the air conditioner and to generally harass her by moving her outside possessions. At that time, the Tenant was not residing in the rental unit but residing in her new rental unit while cleaning and moving her possessions.

The Tenant stated that she contacted the Landlord in November of 2024 and at other times to request the refund of the prepaid rent. She stated that as the Landlord refused to refund the prepaid rent, she filed this application.

The Tenant is seeking the return of her prepaid rent (for 10 months) in the amount of $19,000.00, a rent abatement of $3,800.00 due to the substantial interference, a rent differential of $1,200.00 and moving expenses of $1,720.71. She is also seeking that the Landlord pay an administrative fine. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (PS)

PS testified that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2024, he was unable to rent the unit until January of 2025 which is why he offered to repay 5 months of rent. He stated that the Tenant refused to accept his offer.

PS stated that after hearing about the basement tenants’ behaviour, he did contact those tenants to advise them to stop entering the main rental unit and to leave the Tenants alone. He stated that the basement tenants and the Tenants both argued with each other and he understood that they both yelled at each other.
The Landlord also stated that he was prepared to commence paying the Tenant her prepaid rent back when he started receiving rent from the new tenants in the main unit.

In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked about an email from his property manager that stated that the main unit was rented out as of November 1, 2024. PS stated that this tenancy did not work out and that he was only able to rent it out as of January 1, 2025. Analysis

Section 134(1.1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states that “No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.”

Both parties agreed that the Tenant prepaid the rent for a full year ($1,900.00 x 12 = $22,800.00) prior to moving into the rental unit. The Tenant took possession of the rental unit from June 1, 2024 (although she arrived in late June of 2024) and she vacated the unit on September 30, 2024.

The Landlord is entitled to rent for that 4-month period which is calculated as $7,600.00. The Tenant provided a 30-day notice to the Landlord that she would be vacating the unit as of September 30, 2024. I am satisfied that the Tenant was sufficiently intimidated by the basement tenants’ actions and properly ended the tenancy on September 30, 2024.

The Tenant is entitled to the return of 8 months’ rent calculated as $15,200.00 from the Landlord. The Landlord’s action of retaining these funds is contrary to section 134(1.1) of the Act. This amount also accounts for the return of the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant provided many text messages between the Tenant, the Tenant’s realtor, the Landlord and the Landlord’s realtor setting out the basement tenants’ actions which substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlord was advised repeatedly of the escalating behaviour of the basement tenants and he failed to intervene.

The Tenant sought a 100% rent abatement of $3,800.00 for the period July 1, 2024 to August 31, 2024 where the Tenant experienced substantial interference by the basement tenants. Abatement recognizes the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for them he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

I do not agree that a 100% rent abatement is reasonable and based on the evidence heard, I am ordering a 20% abatement for those two months. Monthly rent was $1,900.00 so a 20% monthly abatement is $380.00 and I am awarding that abatement for July and August which totals $760.00.

I am not satisfied that this particular case warrants a rent differential or moving expenses. Typically, those types of remedies are awarded in bad faith applications under sections 48- 50 of the Act whereby the applicable test involves a more thorough review of the Landlord’s historical behaviour. I believe that based on the amounts awarded in this matter, the Tenant will be made whole. The Tenant will have her prepaid rent fully returned and a reasonable abatement for July and August of 2024.

Given the total amount of the award is $15,960.00, I do not believe that a further administrative fine is required, as I believe the return of the prepaid rent and abatement serve as an adequate general and specific deterrent against the impugned conduct. No administrative fine is ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,960.00. This amount represents: • $15,200.00 for excess rent collected; and • $760.00 for the rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application lack sufficient detail and particulars.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the application should be dismissed as the Tenant has not provided sufficient details and particulars of allegations other than there was an issue with mice when he moved in on May 1, 2023, and the Tenant has moved out of the rental unit. Moreover, the Landlord has been put in the unfair situation of having to defend itself to an application containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are other than generalities of the allegations that there were rodent/mice issues, nor the remedies sought by the Tenant. Accordingly, the Landlord’s Representative submitted that the Tenant’s T6 application should be dismissed. Moreover, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant’s application does not disclose a reasonable cause of action.
Upon Board questioning on why the Tenant had not provided sufficient details, he testified that he could not afford private counsel, and he was a layperson.

The Board can assist parties by providing general information as needed, however the Board does not act as a legal representative for either party and consequently, it is the Applicant’s, in this case the Tenant responsibility to ensure that the application is complete and in compliance with the Act. It was further noted to the Tenant that he could have contacted Tenant Duty Counsel whose contact information was listed on the Notice of Hearing for this herein proceeding. The Tenant did not seek to amend his application during the proceeding.

An application must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital [2022] O.J. No. 5931 that, “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, I am of the view the general principle regarding the need for particular and details apply equally to Tenant application. In this leading case, the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons an details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that they can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission….’’

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted the allegations toward the Landlord are lacking any semblance of details of said issues being pleaded by the Tenant. Moreover, evidence uploaded to the Portal by the Tenant was not introduced as evidence during the proceeding and hence did not provide sufficient particulars to support the Tenant’s allegations in his application, which the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted was a general statement, and devoid of detail that simply there was an issue with mice.

I find the allegations in the Tenant’s application are vague and lack any context in terms of details. Specifically, the “Reasons for filing this Application” section of the application instructs the applicant to describe what happened, the dates and times of the events, who caused the problem and the names and titles of all people involved, which the Tenant has not done in a way that the Landlord could properly comprehend the issues at hand.
On the T6 application there simply is a statement and description that the Tenant had a mice issue since moving into the rental unit, devoid of sufficient detail.

It is not for the Landlord or the Board to assist the Tenant in completing their application or correcting deficiencies. As with all applications before the Board, it is the applicant who must bring an application that meets minimum requirements. However, the undersigned noted to the Tenant if he chooses to bring another application he should seek out legal counsel whether privately or by contacting [name], if the time limitations of the Act permit.

The Landlord’s right to present a meaningful defence in a timely fashion must also be taken into consideration. The application does not contain sufficient details on the alleged grounds that would allow the matter to be fairly heard.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application were not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met to and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at the hearing, and effectively would have experienced significant prejudice if expected to present a defence against unknown, generalized and unspecified allegations. Moreover, the Tenant did not seek an opportunitiy to amend said application and had not done so as of the date of this proceeding.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') : • entered the rental unit illegally and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application); • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application); and • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 application). This application was resolved by order LTB-T-100961-24 issued on July 14, 2025. On July 18, 2025, the Landlords requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On July 22, 2025 interim order LTB-T-100961-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on July 14, 2025. On September 8, 2025, LTB-T-100961-24-RV was issued, granting the review and sending the application to a de novo hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $3,868.94. Testimony of [name]

The rental unit is located in a new condominium located in a high-rise building. The Tenant was informed the occupancy into the condominium was on an interim basis, as the builder had not yet transferred ownership of the unit to the Landlord. The parties entered into a lease agreement.

The Tenant testified that he and his wife began occupying the rental unit on December 5, 2023, spending time there intermittently while ordering furniture throughout December. They fully moved in on January 7, 2024, at which time his wife was pregnant. Shortly after moving in, they noticed the unit was cold and lacked proper heating. On January 12, 2024, during a storm, they observed a significant draft entering the unit, which worsened the cold conditions. Videos showing airflow within the unit were submitted into evidence.

The Tenant further testified that he immediately informed the Landlords of the issue. The Landlords provided three space heaters; however, only two could be used simultaneously, as the third frequently caused the circuit to short. This resulted in a substantial increase in utility costs. The Landlords contacted building management, who scheduled an inspection for January 16, 2024, and advised that parts would be ordered for repair of the heat.

On January 12, 2024, the Tenant noticed various trades people entering and leaving the building without security accompaniment, contrary to management’s prior assurances. Despite ongoing communication between the parties, the problem persisted. On March 1, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlords reporting continued cold conditions. He testified that the Tenants avoided staying in the unit due to the temperature, only visiting during warmer days.

On March 26, 2024, the Landlords requested an inspection however no one attended. On March 28, 2024, the Landlord accessed the unit without providing notice. An email chain dated April 2, 2024, which was entered into evidence, shows the Tenant requesting proper notice for entry. Despite repeated follow-ups, the Landlord continued scheduling visits with different contractors, none of whom appeared fully informed of the issues.

On April 12, 2024, the Landlord requested access for April 15, 2024, with a broad window of entry between 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. On April 18, 2024, the Tenant complained to the Landlords about unauthorized entry. The Tenant entered emails and videos into evidence to support their position that the Landlord did not provide proper notice to enter.

The final visit appeared to address replacing the bedroom window frame and re-caulking, as the bedroom (located in a corner unit) was the main source of drafts. Repairs were completed on May 8, 2024, but the Tenant vacated the unit for two weeks due to the strong caulking odor. Upon returning on May 21, 2024, they discovered the HVAC system was not functioning, leaving the unit without air conditioning during an impending heat wave. A text message entered into evidence shows the Tenant reporting an indoor temperature of 25°C.

The Tenant continued pressing for repairs, requesting updates from the Landlord on May 24, 2024. On June 1, 2024, the Landlord advised that the issue was due to water flow problems and was still under investigation by the condominium. The Landlord requested further access to the rental unit, which the Tenant denied due to lack of 24-hour notice. These emails exchanges were entered into evidence.

On June 19, 2024, the Tenant left the rental unit again because of extreme heat. On June 24, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord for updates and were told the problem affected corner units only. This email exchange was entered into evidence.

On June 28, 2024, the Tenant texted the Landlord stating the unit was uninhabitable and requested a one-month rent waiver and reduction. This text message was entered into evidence. The Landlord responded by adding their agent to the conversation, which the Tenant perceived as rude and unhelpful. The agent’s message included demands for a doctor’s certificate to confirm health risks for an indoor temperature of 27°C, rejected rent reduction requests, and warned of potential rent increases and non-renewal of the lease. The message also referenced builder warranty issues and suggested the Tenant’s lack of cooperation could result in penalties.

On June 29, 2024, the Landlord sent an email to the Tenant as follows: “Hello [name], You were the first occupants of a brand new apartment in a building that is still under construction. Issues with the unit were unknown at that time since it had not been lived in. All new homes built in Ontario are provided with a warranty by the builder and Tarion´s role is to ensure that buyers receive the coverage they are entitled to under this warranty. This warranty is for a period of 7 years and the builder is obligated to rectify deficiencies noted by the homeowner. The homeowner cannot independently carry out any repairs during this period as this will render the warranty null and void. Further, since this is “interim” occupancy, the unit is not technically ours. It still belongs to the builder and the builder is responsible to carry out any repairs. Given that there are no assurances that there will be no further issues with the unit and there are also structural deficiencies (cracks in the ceiling and wall) that have also been identified, which will have to be rectified by the builder as part of the warranty. This will cause inconvenience to you and your family whilst the repairs are being carried out. This is not within our control or purview. Considering that you have an infant on the way it would be best for you to look for another well established home. The current lease for Suite 4310, 3883 Quartz Road, Mississauga ON , may be considered to be terminated at month end, July 2024. Please treat this as notice that your lease is being terminated and your last date of if occupancy is July 31, 2024. Your deposit of last month’s rent will be applied towards the rent for July 2024. Regards, [name]”
The Tenant asserted that the Landlord’s email amounted to an effective termination, equivalent to an N13 Notice, though he acknowledged it did not meet statutory requirements.

On July 3, 2024, the Tenant submits that the Landlord entered the unit without notice. The Tenant subsequently denied access to the Landlord on July 12, 2024 due to lack of notice. The Tenant testified that these events caused significant stress and vulnerability.

Ultimately, the Tenant signed a new lease for August 15, 2024, at a rate $450.00 higher per month than the previous rent. In total, the Tenant was unable to occupy the unit for approximately two weeks due to caulking odor, two weeks due to heating issues, and 1.5 months due to lack of air conditioning.

The Tenant claimed the unit was uninhabitable and seeks the following remedies: • Rent abatement: $3,200.00 (the full monthly rent) × 8 months • Rent differential: $450.00 (new, higher rent × 12 months • Moving expenses: $1,027.76 (an invoice for moving was entered into evidence) • General compensation for loss of enjoyment, stress caused by illegal entries, and inability to use the unit due to heating and cooling failures.

In cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed the Landlord did not personally enter without notice as entries were performed by contractors or management. The Tenant agreed that the Landlord communicated with management about giving notices to enter but believed more could have been done. No items were ever reported missing.

In cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledged understanding the rental unit was under interim occupancy and construction, and that repairs were the builder’s responsibility and under warranty. The Tenant confirmed that he denied entry to the Landlord multiple times due to a lack of 24-hour notice, even during extreme heat when the Landlord wanted to repair the air conditioning.
Finally, in cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed they moved to a larger townhouse in Oakville, citing cost considerations compared to Mississauga. Testimony of Leonel [name]

The Landlord testified that the rental unit measures approximately 900 square feet. The Landlord stated that the Tenant was aware of certain deficiencies in the rental unit at the outset, including issues with the window and a gap in the door frame, which were to be addressed by the builder under warranty.

The Landlord denied personally entering the unit without notice and explained that any entries were carried out by contractors or building management. The Landlord testified that he was not given notice by the builder prior to entry. Whenever the Landlord became aware of a scheduled entry, they forwarded the information to the Tenant, and copies of these forwarded emails were entered into evidence.

On March 28, 2024, the Tenant alleged there was an entry without notice. The Landlord explained that the builder was originally scheduled to attend on March 26, 2024, but failed to do so and instead entered on March 28, 2024 without providing any additional notice.
On April 17, 2024, the Tenant again reported unauthorized entry. The Landlord testified they had no prior knowledge of this visit and could not control who entered the rental unit.
The Landlord entered an email dated July 3, 2024 that shows the Landlord instructing building management to provide proper notice and to ensure security accompanied anyone who entered the unit.
The Landlord openly questioned how contractors accessed the unit without security present and was certain that contractors were also present with additional individuals to ensure oversight.

Regarding maintenance (including the windows), the Landlord testified that they addressed the Tenant’s concerns promptly and communicated with the builder to expedite repairs. Despite this, the Landlord acknowledged that heating was inadequate during the winter and provided portable heaters to the Tenant as a temporary measure.

The Landlord entered an email dated January 19, 2024 into evidence that shows the Landlord informing the builder that the unit was “uninhabitable during winter” and urging immediate repairs due to drafts. The builder responded the same day, marking the issue as urgent and scheduling attendance for January 22, 2024. The Landlord followed up with the builder on February 9, 2024, noting the issue remained unresolved. Further emails entered into evidence show continued follow-ups.

On March 26, 2024, the Landlord arranged for an independent contractor to fix the window and advised the builder they would bill them. The builder responded that independent work would void the Tarion warranty, preventing the Landlord from proceeding. Ultimately, the window repairs were completed on May 8, 2024.

Regarding the air conditioning, the Landlord testified that on May 24, 2024, the builder indicated that AC repairs were scheduled. The Landlord emailed the builder on May 27 and May 28, and again on May 30, stressing the urgency due to extreme heat and the [name] pregnancy. On June 3, 2024, the builder identified a water flow issue affecting cooling in corner units. The Landlord continued requesting updates on June 6, 2024, and was informed on June 17, 2024 that tradespeople would attend. However, the Tenant denied access because the Landlord gave less than 24 hours notice to enter the rental unit. The builder explained that short notice was due to efforts to expedite repairs, and the Tenants’ refusal to permit entry caused further delays. Between June 17 and June 27, 2024 the Landlord exchanged multiple emails with the builder attempting to resolve the issue.
The Landlord acknowledged sending an email to the Tenant on June 29, 2024, referencing ongoing structural cracks and unresolved AC issues.
The Landlord submitted Google reviews regarding the builder, noting that other residents had complained about similar issues.

In cross-examination, the Landlord admitted to being aware of the window gap before the tenancy began and confirmed that the Tenant was also informed. The Landlord reiterated that repairs were the builder’s responsibility under warranty and that they made consistent efforts to push for timely resolution. Analysis Regarding the T5 Application

Section 57 of the Act states: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; (b) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to i n clause 49 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) or 49 (2) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; or (c) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant argues that the email received on June 29, 2024, in which the Landlord stated that the tenancy was “terminated,” is equivalent to an N13 Notice under section 49 of the Act. After considering the evidence and submissions of both parties, I cannot accept this position. The email does not meet the statutory requirements of an N13 Notice. Its tone and content make it clear that the Landlord was not advising the Tenant that vacant possession was required to complete repairs. Rather, on its plain reading, the Landlord was expressing frustration with ongoing delays caused by the builder and unilaterally declaring the tenancy terminated.

I have also considered section 212 of the Act, which addresses substantial compliance, but even in that context, I cannot conclude that the email constitutes notice under section 49. The circumstances surrounding the tenancy do not transform this informal communication into a valid statutory notice.

Furthermore, even if I were to find that the email complied with section 49 of the Act, the evidence does not support that the Tenant vacated because of the email. I find that the Tenant left primarily due to ongoing frustration with the condition of the rental unit, not because of the Landlord’s email. Accordingly, the Tenant would fail to meet the test under section 57 of the Act in any event and the T5 application must fail. Analysis of the Entries into Rental Unit
The Act codifies tenant rights and entry restrictions in sections 22, 23, 26, and 27. In addition, Interpretation Guideline 19 issued by the Board provides detailed rules regarding lawful entry.

The Tenant alleges multiple unannounced entries and submitted videos and emails documenting entry without the required 24-hour notice. The Landlord acknowledges that contractors and/or building management sometimes entered without the Landlord’s prior knowledge and states that, when he became aware of scheduled entries into the rental unit, he forwarded notices to the Tenant. However, under the Act, entries made by builders or management acting on behalf of the Landlord as their agents are attributable to the Landlord. The Tenant’s evidence, which included videos and emails, corroborates unauthorized entry. Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord (through his agents) entered the rental unit without proper notice on at least the following occasions: prior to January 11, 2024, and again on March 28, April 17, July 3, and July 12, 2024.

There was insufficient evidence to establish that any of these entries were emergencies. I accept the Tenant’s testimony regarding the impact these entries had on them and find it credible. The Tenant experienced stress and anxiety as a result of these unauthorized entries. Accordingly, a rent abatement is warranted.

In determining the amount of abatement, I have considered that the Landlord does not dispute the lack of proper notice, although the entries were carried out by agents without the Landlord’s direct involvement. I also find that the Landlord did not act with malice. The entries occurred in the context of significant repairs requiring coordination with outside contractors, where timelines were unpredictable and, to some extent, beyond the Landlord’s control.

The circumstances do not indicate a very serious or deliberate violation of the Tenant’s rights. A reasonable remedy is $100.00 per entry resulting in a total abatement of $200.00. Based on the evidence, I do not find that an award of general damages is appropriate. The rent abatement provides sufficient compensation in the circumstances. Analysis - general

Section 20 of the Act states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that it is necessary to take a contextual approach to determining whether a landlord breached his maintenance obligations under the Act. A landlord will not be found liable if he responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. In Onyskiw, the landlord was not held liable for elevator issues due to a province-wide strike among elevator repair workers. As a result, the Court found it was unreasonable to hold the landlord liable as they could not perform inspections or repairs.

The evidence of the Tenant was that there were extended periods of cold (January– March), a caulking odour forcing a two-week absence in May 2024, and lack of AC during heat waves in June 2024 that impaired ordinary use of the rental unit. Even though the underlying causes of these issues relate to builder warranty or internal building systems, the Board must determine if the Landlord was able to perform and/or coordinate repairs in a way that is reasonable and minimally disruptive to the tenant’s enjoyment. Analysis - heating and windows

It is uncontested that the Tenant experienced significant heating issues and a pronounced draft beginning on January 12, 2024, as supported by videos and emails entered into evidence. I find that the Landlord attempted to mitigate the problem by providing space heaters and escalating the matter to building management. I find that these efforts were insufficient in the circumstances.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that only two of the three heaters could be used simultaneously, and that this temporary solution did not adequately address the lack of heat. There is no doubt that the Landlord had a duty to ensure the provision of heat as a vital service under the Act. While still using the contextual approach required in Onyskiw, the facts of the two cases are different. In this application, the Landlord chose to rely on the condominium builder to complete the repairs, and the Landlords allowed the tenancy to begin while there were known deficiencies. It is unclear from the Landlord’s evidence what the delay was in fixing the heating issue from the building’s perspective and the Landlord did not call anyone from the condominium to testify.

I do not accept that the Landlord took all reasonable steps in the circumstances, as their efforts appear limited to pressuring the building to complete the necessary repairs. While I acknowledge the issue concerning the Tarion Warranty, the evidence presented at the hearing was insufficient to establish the scope of that warranty, the specific repairs that would have affected it, or why the Landlord undertaking the repairs themselves would have voided the warranty. The only evidence before the Board was the condominium’s opinion that private work done by the Landlords would void the warranty without any further reasoning.

Similarly, it is uncontested that issues with the windows persisted from January 12, 2024, until repairs were completed on May 8, 2024. These deficiencies contributed to heat loss and airflow problems within the rental unit. The Landlord knew about these issues but they took months to resolve.

The Landlord emphasized that the Tenant was aware, or ought to have been aware, of these deficiencies given the interim occupancy status. I give this argument no weight. Section 20(2) of the Act clearly provides that a landlord must maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair even if the tenant was aware of issues prior to entering into the tenancy.

I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit as required by section 20 of the Act and that this disrepair substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises.

The circumstances surrounding the heating and window issues warrant a rent abatement. Considering the nature of the deficiencies and their impact on the Tenant, I find an abatement of 20% for the heating issue from January 12, 2024, to March 31, 2024 (which are the winter months that heat would be an issue for the Tenant) and an abatement of 5% for the window issue from January 12, 2024, to May 8, 2024. These percentages are consistent with similar Board decisions addressing comparable situations. Based on the evidence, I do not find that an award of general damages is appropriate. The rent abatement provides sufficient compensation in the circumstances. Analysis - caulking

The Tenant testified that they experienced a temporary two-week loss of enjoyment due to the caulking odor following repairs. However, based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven it was necessary to vacate the rental unit for the entire two-week period.

Having considered Onyskiw and applying a contextual approach, I find that the Landlord had no reasonable alternative but to complete the repairs as required using caulking. While I accept that the caulking may have produced an odour, I am not persuaded that it was so severe as to necessitate the Tenant’s absence for two weeks. The Tenant’s evidence about their inability to remain in the rental unit during this time was sparse. Accordingly, no remedy will be awarded in relation to this issue. Analysis - air conditioning

Air conditioning is not considered a vital service under the Act. In this case, it is undisputed that the agreement included air conditioning and that the system was inoperable during June 2024. The Landlord acknowledges that the issue was caused by a water flow problem affecting corner units and, despite repeated follow-ups, no resolution was achieved throughout the month of June.

Applying the contextual approach set out in Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord ought to have taken additional steps to mitigate the lack of airflow in the rental unit. Temporary measures such as providing fans or a portable air conditioning unit could have offered some relief until the permanent repair was completed. In Onyskiw, the landlord mitigated the affect of no elevators on the tenant by having runners help carry items up and down the stairs, therefore the Court considered the mitigating factors in their decision.

I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair as required by section 20 of the Act and that this disrepair substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises.

The circumstances surrounding the air conditioning issue warrant a rent abatement. Considering the nature of the deficiency and its impact on the Tenant, I find that an abatement of 10% for the month of June 2024 is appropriate. This award is consistent with similar decisions of the Board. Based on the evidence, I do not find that an award of general damages is warranted. The rent abatement provides sufficient compensation in the circumstances. Analysis – termination of tenancy

The Tenant’s position is that the tenancy had to be terminated prematurely due to the condition of the rental unit. Based on the totality of the evidence, I agree. The email dated June 29, 2024, demonstrates that the Landlord also recognized these ongoing issues were unlikely to be resolved in the near future. In that email, the Landlord asked the Tenant to vacate, citing persistent problems with building management and repairs. The Tenant’s decision to end the tenancy early was reasonable in light of the circumstances and the prolonged maintenance issues.

The Tenant relocated to a larger home in Oakville. Their evidence was that the housing market in [name] was tight and rents exceptionally high. The Tenant also testified that no comparable units were available within the price range of their previous monthly rent. However, the evidence before the Board was insufficient to demonstrate the steps the Tenant took to mitigate their damages or to locate a comparable rental unit at a similar price. On a balance of probabilities, I am not persuaded that the Tenant could not have found a comparable unit in a similar area or at a similar cost. The onus rests on the Tenant to prove their damages, and I am not satisfied that they have done so with respect to the increased rent they are now required to pay.

As I have found that moving was reasonable, I find it appropriate to award compensation for moving costs of $1,027.76, as supported by the evidence. The receipt for the moving expense was entered into evidence.
ordered: The T5 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $3,868.94. This amount represents: • $200.00 for a rent abatement due to illegal entries; • $1,662.16 for a rent abatement for the heat; • $615.42 for a rent abatement for the windows; • $315.60 for a rent abatement for the air conditioning; • $1,027.76 for the moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: mold throughout rental unit especially in bathrooms and kitchen, entire unit filthy requiring countless hours of cleaning by the Tenants, inoperable stove, dryer and refrigerator, kitchen drawers missing handles, leak in kitchen sink, mold in washing machine, and leak in upstairs bathroom
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the amount of $7,225.50 by May 11, 2026.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on July 5, 2024 and moved out on June 30, 2025. The rental unit located at [address]nue in Toronto, Ontario is a triplex and the Tenants resided in the second and third floors of the building. The Tenant’s Evidence – [name] (CB)

CB testified that although he and his family were supposed to move into the apartment on July 1, 2024, he and his wife refused to move their children into the unit until the Landlord cleaned the unit. The arrangement was that the Landlord would have the rental unit cleaned prior to the Tenants’ move in date. The Tenant stated that he demanded that the Landlord provide them with professional cleaners to rectify the filth, the mold throughout the rental unit and all of the maintenance issues. The Tenant stated that the Landlord could not or would not provide cleaning so he and his wife had no choice but to move in and attempt to deal with all of these issues.

The Tenant stated that they spent 5 days attempting to address all of the maintenance issues and his family moved in on July 5, 2024. CB stated that he sent countless messages to the property management company that deals with all maintenance issues with the unit and they ignored their many complaints and requests.

CB stated that they were dealing with mold in the lower level bathroom and in the upper level bathroom, there was mold on the ceiling, there was mold under the kitchen sink, there was a leak under the sink and the paint had peeled off, all rooms required deep cleaning, the fridge lacked shelving and had graffiti all over it, the fridge did not keep the items cold enough causing much wasted food and it was only replaced on August 22, 2024, the stove only had one shelf and the handle on the stove was loose, there were no working lights in the kitchen so they could not cook anything in the stove after dark with a gas stove for a period of 1.5 months, the kitchen drawers had no handles, all of the window screens were blackened, there was mold in the washing machine, there was mold and filth behind the dryer in the laundry room, and there was a leak in the upstairs bathroom causing water ingress in that bathroom. The Tenant provided several dated pictures showing the condition of the rental unit when he took possession of it.

The Tenant stated that for the first three months of their tenancy, they spent every waking minute cleaning, attempting to repair, messaging the property manager, following up with the property manager, attending laundromats to complete their laundry, purchasing ready made food or ordering prepared foods from restaurants. They are requesting a rent abatement of $14,850.00 calculated as 3 months of rent ($4,950.00 per month). The Tenant is also requesting out of pocket expenses of $10,600.00 for ready made food, laundromat expenses and cleaning supplies.

CB amended the application in early 2025 because on January 2, 2025, the stove handle broke off the stove and the door of the stove stayed open causing a tripping hazard. The Tenants were obviously unable to use the stove or the oven and it was not replaced until February 11, 2025. Further, CB stated that the dryer that had not worked since July 5, 2024 and was only replaced on February 24, 2025 which was 7.5 months after they notified the Landlord. He then stated that the stove handle broke again on May 28, 2025 and the Landlord “fixed it” with superglue and it was not fixed and remained loose and insecure. CB requested a further $5,000.00 abatement of rent on his amendment.
The Tenant provided several other dated pictures of specific incidences that occurred in 2025 including a picture of the open stove with the broken handle

CB stated that he and his wife were exhausted with having no choice but to clean the entire rental unit so that it would be a safe area for their children. They continued to send emails and text messages to the property managers to address the inoperable fridge, dryer, stove and washing machine and only temporary, minor repairs were completed that did not fully address the failing appliances. Analysis

A T6 Application is based on the rights and obligations set out in s. 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenant provided specific dates and occurrences of the many issues with the rental unit including the lack of cleanliness, the dangerous mold, the inoperable appliances and the many repairs that were required to be completed by the Landlords.
So with these issues, the real issue is whether or not the Tenants are entitled to a remedy and if the Tenants are entitled to a remedy, what should the remedy be.

The Act and the case law in this area indicate there are a number of relevant principles to consider when assessing allegations of a breach of maintenance: 1. First, if the Landlord responded to the disrepair in a timely and effective manner then no monetary remedy will normally flow. (See the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 Breach of [name].) 2. Second, the Landlord cannot be held responsible for compensation for disrepair that the Landlord was not aware of or could not reasonably have been aware of. [See s. 30(2) of the Act]. This is why the duty to mitigation in section 16 has been interpreted to include an obligation on tenants to report disrepair to a landlord. 3. Third, once the Landlord is aware of the disrepair, the normal obligation to repair and liability for the problem will begin.

Abatement of the rent is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, the rent should be abated proportional to the difference between what was being paid for and what was being received. In terms of quantum of abatement, the Board looks primarily at the impact the breach had on the Tenants.

Regarding the Tenants’ abatement request of $14,850.00, a further $5,000.00 abatement in the amending application, and the out of pocket expenses of $10,600.00, I am satisfied that there was a breach of maintenance with respect to the many items mentioned above and the Tenants are entitled to an abatement of their rent. I am not satisfied that the Tenants’ numbers are reasonable in the circumstances.

The Tenants are now requesting 4 months of rent, $19,800.00 plus $10,600.00 for their out of pocket expenses including ready made food, cleaning supplies and laundromat expenses. It is imperative to note that the Tenants resided in that rental unit for a one-year term. I am satisfied that the Landlord was given notice repeatedly of the numerous issues with this one apartment. The Landlord failed to uphold his responsibilities for maintaining the rental unit in a clean and good state of repair.

I am satisfied that the Tenants’ abatement request would be at the highest level at the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenants had to deal with the general cleaning of the whole rental unit, the specific, time-consuming mold removal work and attempting to deal with the water ingress in three areas of the house. As such, I award a 30% abatement of rent for July of 2024, calculated as $1,485.00 ($4,950.00 x 30%).

I am satisfied that the Tenants’ abatement request would continue to be at an intense level and I will award a 25% abatement of for August, September and October of 2024, calculated as $1,237.50 ($4,950.00 x 25%) for 3 months = $3,712.50.

Based on the remaining incidents relating to the stove handle and the inoperable dryer and the continuing issues mentioned previously, I am satisfied that a further abatement of 10% for November, December, January and February of 2025, calculated as $495.00 ($4,950.00 x 10%) for 4 months = $1,980.00 is reasonable.

The Tenants also requested out of pocket expenses for ready made food, laundromat services and cleaning supplies however I was provided with no invoices from the Tenants. I decline to award these expenses as I believe that the abatement awarded is a fair settlement which will encompass all of the maintenance, cleaning and repair issues that the Tenants were forced to rectify.
As a result, an order shall issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenants the amount of $7,225.50 which includes the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $7,225.50. This amount represents: • $7177.50 for a rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.

This is an application in which the named Tenant is seeking the return of their deposit in the amount of $1,300.00 which was provided to the Landlord for purposes of being used to secure the rental unit and also to be applied as the rent for the first month of the tenancy.

The Tenant and Landlord had an agreement in which the Tenant would pay the Landlord the sum of $1,300.00 to be applied as the first month’s rent for the period of December 1, 2025. The parties also agreed to execute a copy of the lease agreement at the time of the Tenant providing her last month’s rent deposit prior to taking occupancy.
The Tenant paid the Landlord the sum of $1,300.00 on November 19, 2025.

On November 21, 2025, the Tenant notified the Landlord that her personal circumstances changed and that she was no longer interested in occupying the rental unit. She demanded the return of her rent payment/deposit in the amount of $1,300.00.

The Tenant did not sign a lease agreement, nor did the Tenant receive a copy of the unit keys. The Tenant also never occupied the rental unit. The Tenant did agree that the reason for the lease not being signed, and the keys not being provided to her were based on her decision not to occupy the rental unit. Had she wanted to move forward the Landlord was not opposed to going ahead with the agreement. The Tenant also agreed that the decision not to occupy the unit was based on the Tenant’s circumstances and her decision had nothing to do with the Landlord or rental unit.

The Tenant sought the return of her deposit in the amount of $1,300.00. She believed that she was entitled to the return of this money because she’d never signed a lease agreement, never received the unit keys, and never occupied the unit.

The Landlord confirmed receiving the payment in the amount of $1,300.00 from the Tenant on November 19, 2025. The Landlord also confirmed that this payment was to be applied towards the first month’s rent. The Landlord also confirmed that the lease was to be signed prior to the Tenant taking occupancy, and at the time of her last month’s rent deposit being paid to the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that he had the unit advertised online and that he removed the advertisement when he received the $1,300.00 from the Tenant. He also testified to reposting the advertisement immediately after being notified by the Tenant that she no longer wished to occupy the unit. The Landlord confirmed that the date the Tenant notified him she would no longer occupy the unit was November 21, 2025. The tenancy commencement date was December 1, 2025.
The Landlord testified that he was unable to re-rent the unit until recently, and that the unit has now been re-rented for May 1, 2026. The Landlord’s evidence was limited to his verbal testimony.

Based on the evidence of the parties, I am satisfied that the parties had a meeting of minds, in which an implied tenancy was created by virtue of the parties’ actions. This includes the Tenant making the payment to the Landlord and acceptance of said payment by the Landlord. The parties also agreed on a term for the tenancy, a monthly rental rate, and confirmed the specific unit or room to be occupied by the Tenant. I find this to be sufficient to meet that of an implied tenancy agreement.

Despite the Landlord not filing any evidence to support their efforts to mitigate their damages and re-rent the unit. I am satisfied that the Landlord was unable to re-rent the unit for the month of December 1, 2025, being the period to which the Landlord applied said payment made by the Tenant. I am not satisfied that the nine-day notice provided by the Tenant would have allowed the Landlord sufficient time to mitigate his damages. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and that the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The uncontested facts, as recounted by the Tenant, are that the parties, at first, entered into a four month lease agreement, from January 1, 2025, to April 30, 2025, for a monthly rent of $3,100.00, due on the first day of the month. In clause #7 of that lease, the box stating that there will be a rent discount is ticked, with the explanation that the “owner has discounted the rent such that rental amount for the period January 1, 2025 to April 30, 2025 will be $2,450.00, and will then effectively return to normal rent amount of $3,100.00 on May 1, 2025.” The Tenant said that she believes the rent was $2,450.00, and it was advertised at $2,450.00. She said that she believed she had paid the full amount of lawful rent for four months at the beginning of that lease. The Tenant also testified that she signed that lease willingly and without any coercion, and she also signed it without reading all the clauses too closely.

The uncontested evidence of the Tenant is that, at the end of the first lease, the parties signed a “lease extension”, also on the standard form lease agreement, for a tenancy commencing May 1, 2025, and ending on August 31, 2025, for a monthly rent of $2,900.00. Under clause #9 about key deposits, the extended lease acknowledges that the Tenant “has already paid a refundable 200 dollar key deposit and a 1000 dollar refundable security deposit from the previous lease.”

The Tenant said that around June 2025, the Landlord started encouraging her to leave. She said that she decided to leave by the beginning of September 2025. She submitted into evidence an email exchange with the Landlord in which she informs the Landlord in early September 2025, that she will vacate the unit by September 30, 2025. The Tenant said that it was clear from their exchanges that the Landlord was unconcerned about short or insufficient notice from the Tenant because he wanted her out. Nevertheless, the Tenant was successful in having the Landlord sign a mutual agreement to end the tenancy, or an N11 form, to end the tenancy on September 20, 2025, which was the date she vacated the unit. The Tenant’s testimony is that she did not return the keys to the Landlord until September 25, 2025, because he did not return her key deposit and security deposit. She also had documentation to support her testimony that the keys were returned to the front desk of the residential complex on September 25, 2025.

The Tenant alleges that the increase from $2,450.00 on January 1, 2025, to $2,900.00 on May 1, 2025, is an illegal rent increase, as it is far above the guideline amount, and it occurred less than 12 months after the tenancy began. In addition, there was no written notice of the alleged increase 90 days prior to the increase taking effect.

The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord unlawfully withheld the return of her $200.00 key deposit and $1,000.00 security deposit, as well as the interest owed on her last month’s rent deposit. She also requests the 10 days of rent she paid for September 2025 in which she was not in possession of the rental unit. She testified that there is no last month’s rent deposit. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that there has been no illegal rent increase for the following reasons.

The first written lease clearly states that the rent is $3,100.00 and it gives the Tenant a rent discount of $2,450.00 because she paid the first four months up front, at the beginning of the lease. The Tenant said that she was not coerced nor forced into signing it, and she also said that she did not read it very carefully, even though she believes that the rent was, in fact, always $2,450.00, and it was advertised as such. I find that the binding, written and signed agreement was the actual content of the contract between the parties. Neither party was coerced into signing it. It is only the freely signed, written, agreement that constitutes the valid understanding of what the contract was between these parties. It is not for the Tenant to now come, months and months later, after having entered the written contract, paid the money stated in the contract, received the services promised in the contract, lived in the unit and vacated the unit, to submit that she did not really mean what she freely signed onto all those months ago. The written contract is the best evidence of what the agreement was, especially since the Tenant admits she signed it without coercion. The written contract clearly states that the monthly rent was $3,100.00, and the Landlord permitted a significant rent discount of over $600.00 per month because the Tenant paid all the money up front. Therefore, when the parties signed their “lease extension”, the Landlord could have validly continued to charge the Tenant $3,100.00 per month, as the lease became a month to month tenancy, but he did not. The parties, instead, agreed to a new four-month lease, with a monthly rent of $2,900.00, which was $200.00 less per month than the original contract. I find that the lease “extension” was, in fact, a new lease between the parties. The evidence for this contract is that its terms, too, was freely agreed, without any coercion. It was for a new and different fixed term, and it was for a different, lower, monthly rent, which was favourable towards the Tenant. The Landlord correctly acknowledged any deposits that were made by the Tenant in the old lease, and he applied them to the new lease.
I find that the Landlord has unlawfully retained money that he should have paid to the Tenant at the end of the tenancy for the following reasons.

The Tenant never paid a last month’s rent deposit, which the Landlord could have lawfully collected pursuant to sections 105 and 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). However, the Tenant did pay a “damage deposit” of $1,000.00, which is unlawful pursuant to section 106 of the Act, as well as a $200.00 key deposit, which is a deposit that must be reimbursed to the Tenant upon vacating the rental unit. The Tenant now claims reimbursement of these amounts, which she requested of the Landlord at the end of the tenancy, and which the Landlord did not reimburse.

I find that the Landlord is also liable to pay interest on the $1,000.00 “damage” or “security” deposit he unlawfully collected on January 1, 2025, and failed to repay at the end of the tenancy. The Landlord would have been obliged to pay interest on any last month’s rent deposit he collected pursuant to subsection 106(6) of the Act. As it happens, the Landlord did not collect a last month’s rent deposit, but rather a lesser amount of $1,000.00 which he was entitled to call whatever he wanted. However, the only lawful amount of $1,000.00 that he was entitled to collect was a last month’s rent deposit, and he is also obliged to pay interest on the amount he collected. The interest owed on $1,000.00, held for nine months in 2025, is $1,000.00 X .025=$25.00 for 12 months, or $20.83 for nine months.

Finally, I find that the Landlord should be ordered to reimburse five days in September 2025 for which the Tenant paid rent when she was no longer in possession of the unit. Although the Tenant provided insufficient notice to end the tenancy, which was a four month term tenancy to end on August 31, 2025, and which extended an extra month on a month to month, the evidence is that the parties freely signed an N11 agreement to end the tenancy on September 20, 2025. After signing the N11, the Landlord would no longer have been entitled to rent past that date. The Tenant requested 10 days of reimbursement because she, in fact, vacated the rental unit on September 20, 2025. However, it was the Tenant’s own evidence, supported by documentation, that she did not return the keys until September 25, 2025. She was therefore in possession of the unit until September 25, 2025. The Tenant is entitled to $2,900.00 X 12=$34,800.00, divided by 365 days=$95.34 times 5=$476.70.
Therefore, the total owed to the Tenant is $1,000.00 rent deposit, $200.00 key deposit, $20.83 interest on her rent deposit, $476.70 for the five days in September 2025 that the Tenant overpaid.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,750.43. This amount represents: • $200.00 key deposit collected. • $1,000.00 for the security or rent deposit collected. • $20.83 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $476.70 for days of rent paid when the Tenant was not in possession of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $525.27, inclusive of the cost of filing the application. Rent Deposit Illegally Retained:
The Tenant paid a $450.00 rent deposit to the Landlord the day the tenancy started on May 12, 2023.

The Tenant testified that he was evicted from the rental unit by the Sheriff on October 23, 2025. The Sheriff was there to give vacant possession of the residential complex to the mortgagee. The Tenant was instructed that he had to pack up and leave the premises immediately. The Tenant submitted a Notice Demanding Possession from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice dated June 25, 2025 as evidence.

The Tenant then emailed the Landlord on November 11, 2025, requesting the return of his deposit as he had paid the rent for October 2025, which became the last month of the tenancy. The Landlord replied on November 13, 2025 stating that he still had the deposit, and it might be possible for the Tenant to move back into the unit. The Tenant had already been evicted at that point and replied to the Landlord that he had no intention of returning to the unit. The tenant submitted copies of the emails as evidence.
The Tenant confirmed at the hearing that the Landlord still had not returned the deposit.

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states that “a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.”

Having considered the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on October 23, 2025, when the Tenant was evicted from the rental unit as a result of mortgage enforcement proceedings. Given that the Tenant paid the rent for October 2025, and the Landlord has not returned the deposit, I am also satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last month of the tenancy and did not return the deposit in contravention of the Act. Rent Deposit Interest:
Subsection 106(6) of the Act requires that a landlord pay interest on a last month’s rent deposit if one is collected.
As the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit of $450.00 was paid on May 12, 2023, the interest owing on the deposit up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit is $27.27.

The Tenant confirmed at the hearing that no interest was ever paid on his last month’s rent deposit and none was remitted to him after he vacated the unit. Therefore, based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit in contravention of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $525.27. This amount represents: • $450.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $27.27 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 22, 2026
