issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant vacated his unit as a result of a notice of termination the Landlord gave in bad faith. The Tenant will be awarded the increased rent he paid for a one-year period. Facts

On October 15, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a letter titled “NOTICE TO VACATE PROPERTY.” The notice was drafted so as to appear to be a legal notice. The relevant portions read as follows: TAKE NOTICE THAT: The Landlords[…] need this property for their Daughter and Son-in-law. The couple recently got married and need accommodations as soon as possible. You are hereby given 30 days notice to Vacate this property for the above mentioned reason. THIS NOTICE TO VACATE IS GIVEN IN PURSUANT TO THE APPLICABLE LAWS OF ONTARIO.

Section 48(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) provides that a landlord may give notice to terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by the landlord’s child. The October 15 notice was clearly meant to be a notice under section 48(1)(c). However, the notice was not valid. It was not given on an N12 form as required by section 43(1), and was not given 60 days in advance as required by section 48(2). The notice had no legal effect, and the Tenant would have been free to ignore it.

On November 20, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a second notice. The notice stated that it was confirmation the parties had spoken on November 13, that the Tenant had said that he had not yet found a new home, and that the Landlord had extended the deadline to November 30, 2022.
At some point, the Tenant realized that he should have been given 60 days’ notice, and asked the Landlord to provide it. In response, the Landlord verbally extended the deadline to December 31, 2022.

The parties agree that the Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2022. They do not agree on what happened after that. The Landlord says that the Tenant left some belongings behind and took another 15 days to retrieve them; the Tenant says that he could not retrieve his belongings sooner because the Landlord had changed the locks. In any case, there is no dispute that the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the notices the Landlord had given him.
After the Tenant had vacated, the Landlord’s daughter and her spouse did not move into the unit. Instead, the Landlord re-rented the unit.
The Tenant brings this application alleging that the Landlord gave him a notice of termination in bad faith. Issues

Pursuant to section 57(1)(a) of the RTA, to succeed in his application, the Tenant must establish the following: • the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48; • the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith; • the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the notice; and • the Landlord’s daughter did not occupy the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
I will consider each element in turn. Did the Landlord give a notice of termination under section 48?

The Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) has consistently held that in an application under section 57, a notice that did not comply with the RTA can be deemed to have been a notice of termination given under section 48, if it contained the essential elements of a section 48 notice (Bekkers v Bretgoltz, 2025 ONLTB 44640).

In this case, there is no dispute that the notice the Landlord gave contained the essential elements of a section 48 notice. It asserted that the Landlord required the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by his daughter, and that the tenancy was to terminate for that reason.
The Landlord’s subsequent “reminder” restated the essential elements of a section 48 notice.
I therefore find that, for the purpose of this proceeding, the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48. Did the Tenant vacate the unit as a result of the notice?

There is no dispute that the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the notice. He asked for an extension, which the Landlord gave him, and he then vacated in accordance with the extended deadline. Did the Landlord’s daughter occupy the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated?
There is no dispute that the Landlord’s daughter, [name] [name], did not move into the unit. The Landlord re-rented the unit instead. Did the Landlord give the notice in bad faith? Legal framework
The only dispute in this case is whether the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith.

“Good faith” in the context of a section 48 notice means that a landlord genuinely intends that the person identified in the notice will reside in the unit for a period of at least one year ([name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC)).

Pursuant to section 57(5), because the Landlord re-rented the unit, he bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that when he gave the notice he genuinely intended that Ms. [name] would live in the unit for at least one year. Evidence

The Landlord’s testimony was sparse. He testified that he gave the Tenant four months’ notice, but the Tenant took longer than that. After the Tenant moved, the unit needed to be repaired and repainted. Ms. [name]name] was not willing to move in until the work was done. The Landlord did the work, but by that time Ms. [name] had decided to live elsewhere.

I do not accept the Landlord’s testimony that he gave four months’ notice. The evidence is clear that he gave notice on October 15 to end the tenancy on November 14, and later extended the deadline to December 31. That is a total of two and a half months, not four months.

Ms. [name]name]’s testimony was also sparse. She testified that after she got married, she intended to move in by the end of November. When the Tenant asked for more time, she was willing to wait until the end of December. However, after the Tenant vacated, the bathrooms were not usable and half the kitchen appliances were not working. She was in a rush to move, and decided to move somewhere else. Analysis
On the evidence before me, the Landlord has not proved that he genuinely intended that Ms. [name] would move into the unit and live there for at least one year within the meaning of the RTA.

Based on the Landlord’s and Ms. [name]’s testimony, Ms. [name] was only willing to move in during a very short timeframe. If the unit became available between the end of November and December 31, she would move in. When the unit was not available in a condition satisfactory to her on December 31, she was unwilling to wait any longer for repairs. There is no evidence that the repairs took very long.

The Landlord argues that Ms. [name]name] was also prevented from moving in on December 31 because the Tenant’s belongings were still there. Ms. [name]name]’s testimony did not support that argument; she testified that she did not move in because of the condition of the unit, not because of the Tenant’s belongings. However, for the sake of argument I will accept that Ms. [name] would not have been able to move in until the Tenant’s belongings were removed on or about January 15, 2023.
In other words, Ms. [name] was only willing to move into the unit if it became available by January 15, three months after the Landlord gave notice.

Ms. [name]name]’s intentions were not consistent with the way tenancies are terminated under the RTA. Even if the Landlord had given a valid notice under section 48, the Tenant would not have been required to move. The Landlord would have had to apply to the LTB seeking an order terminating the tenancy (RTA s.43(2)(b)). Ms. [name]name] would have had no way of knowing in advance how long the application would take. The LTB might also have postponed eviction further (RTA s. 83(1)(b)).

In other words, a person who intends to move into a tenant’s unit can never predict when they will be able to move in. When a landlord gives notice stating that they intend a person to move in, they must intend that the person will move in once the unit becomes vacant. An intention that the person will move in only if the unit becomes vacant within three months is not, in my view, a valid intention within the meaning of section 48.

Furthermore, if Ms. [name]’s intention to move into the unit was conditional on the unit being in good condition, then she or the Landlord should have inspected the unit prior to giving the notice of termination. The Landlord was responsible for maintaining the unit (RTA s.20). If he did not know whether the unit was in a condition acceptable to Ms. [name], then when he gave the notice asserting that she would move in, he did not actually know whether she would move in.

I therefore find that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith. He has not proved that he meaningfully intended that Ms. [name] would reside in the Tenant’s unit. He intended that she would do so only if the Tenant were to vacate on an unrealistically short timeline, and only if the unit was in good condition which he had not checked. Remedies
The only remedy the Tenant seeks is a rent differential pursuant to section 57(3)(1) of the RTA.

In his application, the Tenant pled that his monthly rent had increased by $870.00 as a result of moving. However, at the hearing, he testified that his old rent was $1,350.00 and that his new rent was $2,000.00 plus utilities. He did not say whether his old rent included utilities. He has therefore proved a rent increase of $650.00 monthly.
There is no evidence that the Tenant’s new unit was an improvement over the old unit, so betterment does not apply.
I therefore award a rent differential of $650.00 for twelve months, $7,800.00 total. The Tenant is also entitled to his filing fee of $48.00 for this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $7,848.00, which represents a rent differential and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative raised the issue that since the Landlord was not a party to the utility contract between the Tenant and the utility provider, the LTB does not have jurisdiction to hear a contractual dispute that is essentially between the Tenant and a third party. Therefore, the application must be dismissed. The Tenant replied that the Landlord misled how the utilities were to be paid and did not respond to the Tenant’s attempts to gain clarity on the situation. I find that the application concerns the Landlord’s leasing practices and how they, and the lack of communication with the Tenant, resulted in substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the residential unit. The application thus proceeded using those parameters. T2 Application:

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,024.38, inclusive of the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant moved into the unit on September 2, 2023 and vacated on December 20, 2023.

The residential complex is described as a two-story townhouse plus basement. The Tenant rented one of five rooms, with his located in the basement. There were other tenants living in the residential complex at the time the Tenant moved in.

The Tenant testified that at the time he signed the one-year fixed term lease, he was aware that heat and electricity were the Tenant’s responsibility. The Tenant submitted a copy of the lease agreement as evidence. Prior to signing, the Landlord’s Agent provided an estimate of approximately $10.00 - $40.00 for monthly hydro costs that seemed reasonable to the Tenant. This dialogue was confirmed by an email chain between the Tenant and the Landlord’s Agent. The Landlord then emailed the Tenant on September 1, 2023 with instructions and a link on how to set up a hydro account with Enova Power.

The Tenant received his first hydro invoice dated October 11, 2023 for the period from September 2 – September 25, 2023 totaling $618.39. The Tenant paid the invoice on November 6, 2023. A copy of the bill was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant then received the second invoice dated November 8, 2023 for the period from September 25 – October 25, 2023 totaling $258.23. A copy of this bill was also submitted as evidence. The Tenant testified that the invoice amounts were higher than the estimate given to him when he signed the lease, so he emailed the Landlord on November 30, 2023 prior to paying the second invoice. The email informed the Landlord that the Tenant believed he was being charged for the entire residential complex as opposed to only his unit as well as an initiation fee. The Tenant requested the Landlord’s assistance to remedy the issue as well as reimbursement for all fees and portions of the utilities that should have been charged to the other tenants.

The Tenant then sent follow up emails to the Landlord on February 4, 2024, March 13, 2024, and June 10, 2024. After each email was sent, the Tenant would receive an automated response that one of the Landlord’s Agents would reply to the Tenant, but no one responded.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative acknowledged that a Landlord Agent should have followed up with the Tenant after the automated message was sent and could not explain why that was not done. The standard reply, however, would have been that as the Landlord is not responsible for hydro for the rental unit, the Tenant would have to speak with the utility provider to sort out the issue. The Landlord’s obligation was only to provide general guidance to the Tenant about who the existing provider was.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative also could not provide details regarding why the Tenant would have been charged hydro for the entire building or what the suite meter situation is for the residential complex, as she did not receive a reply from the Landlord regarding the issue prior to or during the hearing.
The Tenant paid the second hydro invoice on December 4, 2023.

On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that he spoke with other tenants in the residential complex and was told they did not have their own separate accounts set up with Enova Power. The Tenant later contacted Enova Power via phone and was told that the entire residential complex was assigned to his hydro account. However, the Tenant also confirmed on cross-examination that he did not contact Enova Power between September 6 to December 28, 2023. The Tenant managed to shut down the account with no assistance from the Landlord on December 28, 2023.

The Tenant received two more hydro invoices; one dated December 8, 2023 for the period from October 25 – November 24, 2023 totaling $390.67, and the final invoice dated January 15, 2024 for the period from November 24 – December 29, 2023 totaling $413.18. Copies of both bills were submitted as evidence. The Tenant did not pay the third invoice, but he did pay all outstanding amounts on February 8, 2024.

The Tenant was a student at the time with limited financial means. The Tenant testified he was incredibly stressed by the utility issue as it required him to significantly re-budget to pay the hydro bills. This was also happening during the exam period which only compounded the stress he felt. The Tenant repeatedly reached out for assistance from the Landlord only to be ignored via an automated reply.

Having considered the parties’ evidence and submissions, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for the reasons set out below.

The utility bills submitted confirm the Tenant was charged hydro for the entire residential complex, yet his lease was only for one room within the property. The Tenant was also responsible for his portion of hydro for the shared facilities such as the kitchen and bathroom, but he was not contractually obligated to pay hydro beyond that.

The Tenant was not told about how the hydro was paid prior to him moving in, only that it was estimated to be about $10.00 - $40.00 per month. The Tenant was not aware if one tenant was to pay the entire bill and be reimbursed by the others, or if there were individual suite meters that would account for each tenant’s usage and the provider would bill each directly. The Tenant also showed that he reached out to the Landlord on multiple occasions asking for help regarding the issue, yet no assistance was provided. The Landlord therefore placed the Tenant in an unreasonable situation by giving him the impression he would only be paying for his own utilities, providing no assistance or information regarding how utilities are divided or charged to other tenants in the building, and then left the Tenant to pay hydro for the entire residential complex and sort out reimbursement from the other tenants for the costs. I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by having to pay the hydro bill for the entire building. Remedies

The Tenant confirmed that he essentially assigned the lease for the remaining 7 months of the fixed term tenancy. There was no evidence to show the Landlord consented to the assignment. The assignee paid $200.00 less per month to the Tenant, so the Tenant had to make up the difference when paying the Landlord. The Tenant confirmed that he no longer seeks for the LTB to terminate the tenancy on December 31, 2023, as claimed in the application, but rather seeks to recover the $1,400.00 total rent loss from the Landlord. As the Tenant appears to have illegally assigned the tenancy, this is not a claim brought properly before me under section 22 or 29 of the Act, and the claim for this remedy is therefore dismissed.
At the hearing, the Tenant also withdrew remedies related to his last month’s rent deposit and key deposit. Therefore, these remedies were also not considered.

The four hydro statements show a period for charges from September 2, 2023 to December 29, 2023 in the amount of $1,680.47, inclusive of a $460.00 “Deposit Charge” not an “initiation fee”. The Tenant was credited the deposit amount for the last statement dated January 15, 2024 which included the outstanding balance from the previous third invoice dated December 8, 2023. Therefore the $460.00 deposit is subtracted from the total claimed by the Tenant with the remaining amount totaling $1,220.47 ($1,680.47 - $460.00).

The Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that Tenant did not mitigate his circumstances by attempting to get the other tenants to reimburse him after he paid each invoice. However, the Tenant was not aware of the terms of the other tenants’ leases including what arrangements each had for utilities with the Landlord. There was no discussion with the Tenant at the beginning of the tenancy regarding how the utilities would be paid, only that he was responsible for his own. To then place the burden on the Tenant to follow up with other tenants, all on separate leases, to reimburse his costs is not reasonable.

The Tenant argued he should only pay the estimated $40.00 per month the Landlord’s Agent quoted him in emails prior to signing the lease, meaning the Tenant should only be responsible for $160.00 of hydro costs ($40.00 x 4 months). However, the lease signed after the Tenant communicated with the Landlord’s Agent does not specify the Tenant is only responsible for a maximum of $40.00 per month for hydro. Having considered the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord should be held to an estimate that is not corroborated by the lease.

The Tenant rented one of five rooms in the residential complex and shared common areas and facilities. There were also other tenants present when the tenancy began. Thus, it stands to reason that the Tenant was responsible for 20% of the hydro costs for the 4- month period covered by the invoices which would cover his costs for his rental unit and his share of the common areas. Therefore, the Tenant is only responsible for $244.09 of hydro costs ($1,220.47 x 20%). As such, the Landlord is responsible for the remaining balance of $976.38 for the Tenant’s out-of-pocket expenses ($1,220.47 - $244.09).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,024.38. This amount represents: • $976.38 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 5, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in their application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $14,592.20.

This application is brought by the Tenants pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former Tenants vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that to succeed on this application the Tenants must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: they got a notice of termination under s. 48; they moved out of the rental unit as a result of the notice; the notice was given in bad faith meaning the Landlord had no intention of moving into the rental unit; and the Landlord did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

It is undisputed that the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 Notice of Termination on November 1, 2023, with a termination date of December 31, 2023. The N12 Notice indicates that the Landlord intends to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least 12 months.
I am satisfied that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 10, 2023, because of the N12 notice.
It is undisputed that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit and instead, advertised the rental unit for sale on or about April 16, 2024.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Pursuant to subsection 57(6), the period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that begins on the day a landlord gave the notice of termination and ends one year after a tenant vacated the rental unit. In this case, the period began on November 1, 2023, and ended on December 10, 2024. As the Landlord advertised the rental unit for sale during the prescribed period, it is presumed the N12 Notice was given in bad faith. The Landlord must establish, on a balance of probabilities, that at the time the N12 Notice was given to the Tenants, he intended to move into the rental unit.
I am not convinced the N12 Notice was given in good faith. I say this for the reasons that follow.

In January 2024, the Landlord hired a contractor to renovate the rental unit at a cost of approximately $100,000.00. According to the Landlord, these renovations were undertaken to make the rental unit comfortable for his fiancée, who was to reside in the unit with him. The Landlord claimed that he was increasingly concerned that he would be financially unable to retain the rental unit once the renovations were complete. He attributed his concerns to an unregistered mortgage of two million dollars on his primary residence and a one million mortgage on the rental unit.

The Landlord failed to sufficiently establish that there was a substantial change to his financial circumstances between the time he gave the Tenants the N12 Notice and when he advertised the rental unit for sale. No evidence was presented indicating the Landlord’s income substantially decreased or that financial institutions were making payment demands that could not be meet without selling the rental unit. There was also no evidence presented indicating the Landlord had plans to sell his primary residence of the unregistered mortgage reportedly held on this property.

The evidence before me establishes that the Landlord undertook extensive high-end upgrades that contributed to the property being sold for a record $1.6 million dollars. I believe it is more likely than not the Landlord never intended to move into the rental unit and what the Landlord really wanted to do was to have vacant possession of the rental unit so that he could renovate and sell the property. I find the N12 Notice was given in bad faith. Remedies
The Tenants seek a difference of rent in the amount of $10,000.00.

The Tenants had not found an affordable rental at the time they vacated their former unit and considered moving into a family member’s basement. However, the basement was not ready, and the Tenants immediately took residence in short-term accommodation rental located within their school boundary so their children could finish out the school year. The Tenants admitted into evidence rental receipts for the period from December 10, 2023 to July 31, 2024 totalling $31.669.89.

At the time of their eviction, the Tenants were paying a monthly rent of $3,750.00, which corresponds to a daily rent of $123.29 ($3,750.00 x12 months / 365). Therefore, the Tenants would have paid $28,973.15 at the former rental unit for the same time period (December 10, 2023 to July 31, 2024) had it not been for the bad faith conduct of the Landlord.

Based on the evidence before me, I find it reasonable and appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenants $2,696.74 in the difference in rent they paid ($31,669.89 - $28,973.15). No further award will be ordered for difference in rent as the Tenants were unable to provide evidentiary proof of the amount they paid after July 31, 2024.

The Tenants submitted receipts in the amount of $4,847.46 for their moving and storage expenses. I found these expenses to be reasonable and supported and will therefore order the Landlord to pay the Tenants $4,847.76 for their moving and storage expenses.

Pursuant to subsection 57(3) (1.1) of the Act, the Tenants seek an order that the Landlord pay $24,000.00 as general compensation. Subsection 57(3) (1.1) provides that general compensation may be ordered regardless of whether the Tenants have incurred any actual expenses.

I accept the Tenants experienced profound stress due to the bad faith conduct of the Landlord. The Tenants described the pressure they experienced from the Landlord and his realtor to vacate the rental unit. This pressure included threats that the locks would be changed, and their possessions would be put onto the street. The Tenants faced challenges finding a suitable home within the school district and ultimately had to move three times within the year. Tenant [name] (‘SS’) described having to visit the hospital to seek medical care as a direct result of the profound and the negative impact the move had upon their family and the need for ongoing counselling to manage the lasting stress.

In considering the Tenants’ claim for general compensation, I have looked at how the Landlord’s breach impacted the Tenants. I accept that having to move out of the rental unit caused the Tenants and their children significant stress. Given the evidence before me, I find that an award in the amount of $7,000.00 adequately compensates for the Tenants for the mental distress they endured as a result of the Landlord’s failure to act in good faith.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenants is $14,592.20.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $14,592.20. This amount includes the difference in rent, storage and moving expenses, general compensation, and the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (‘AM’) and [name] (‘KL’) (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord requests the application be amended to reflect the correct legal name from [name] to [name] [name] as it is now.
There was no objection from the Tenant to this requested amendment.
As there is no objection to the amendment, I consented to the requested amendment. The style of cause has been updated to reflect this amendment. Tenant’s T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

By way of background, the tenancy began in 2018 and terminated on July 15, 2023. The rental unit was a single-family dwelling occupied by the Tenant, her spouse, and young child. The Tenant’s rent was $2,000.00 monthly.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord gave her an N12 Notice of Termination (‘N12’) in bad faith (Doc-3336382). It is not disputed that the Tenant was given a N12 notice of termination on May 1, 2023, for the use of AM and the AM’s child. It is also not disputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 15, 2023. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant submits that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit in a reasonable amount of time. The Tenant provided a copy of advertisements which show the Landlord advertised rooms in rental unit for rent (Doc-3336459, pgs. 12,13,14). These advertisements indicate that the rental unit was advertised for rental occupation effective December 1, 2023.

Submitted into evidence were a series of text message exchanges between the parties dated May 16, 2023 (Doc-3336438, pg. 2). In this message, [name] asks the Tenant if she would be interested in purchasing the property. AM responded that it would help her, because then she would have “money”. The Tenant submits this is evidence of AM’s bad faith because why would AM be looking for a buyer if she had intended to move into the rental unit.

Also submitted into evidence, by the Tenant, is a copy of text message exchange between AM and the former basement tenant, identified as “JR” (Doc- Doc-3336459, pg. 5). JR was not called to testify. The text message exchange is undated. However, the message appears to be sometime around September 7, 2023. Regardless, JR inquires, with AM, how much she is asking to rent the upstairs unit (the Tenant’s rental unit). AM replies that she is asking $3,000.00 for the upper floor.

The Tenant also submitted a copy of an N12 notice which had been provided to JR (Doc- 2532403). It identifies KL as the Landlord and states that the basement unit is for use of the Landlord and their child. The Tenant submits that this does not make sense for two reasons. First, KL had told her during a conversation that AM was the actual owner of the property as the property had been signed over to her in 2021. Second, AM had told her she was escaping abuse at the hands of KL. It does not make sense that AM would be moving into her unit, while KL would then occupy the basement unit, if AM was trying to escape abuse at the hands of KL. The Tenant also raises that she did not understand why [name] was still giving notices of termination if AM is the owner of the property; therefore, she is the lawful Landlord. Landlord’s Evidence

AM’s evidence is that she had been in an abusive relationship with her ex-spouse. She gave the Tenant an N12 notice so that she could move into the rental unit. A redacted copy of her separation agreement was submitted into evidence dated April 1, 2023 (Doc- 7314904, pgs. 3,4). AM confirmed that the rental property had been put in her name in 2021 and that the Landlords had determined that KL would keep the matrimonial home, while AM would be the owner of the rental unit.

While living in the matrimonial home, AM lived on one floor of the home while KL lived on another. However, she states this situation was untenable because she and [name] were fighting in front of their son.

The intention, AM states, is that AM would move into the rental unit with her young child and the child’s nanny. She had moved most of her belongings and furniture into the rental unit on July 17, 2023. AM submitted into evidence a declaration from [name] (‘IG’) dated June 18, 2024 (Doc-7314904, pg. 17). The declaration states that IG provided moving services to AM and had moved furniture and belongings from AM’s matrimonial home to the rental unit at on July 17, 2023.

AM states that it had been her intention all along to move into the rental unit. It is her evidence she wanted to offer the Tenant a chance to purchase the rental property because she thought she may want to buy it. However, AM states she had not been feeling well then and had been under a lot of pressure because of the abusive relationship and subsequent separation from KL. AM says she does not have any family in Canada for support.

In early June, AM had a medical appointment and was diagnosed with a serious, life- threatening illness by June 27, 2023 (Doc-7314904, pgs. 18-31). The diagnosis necessitated multiple surgeries with lengthy recovery times. AM decided to remain in the matrimonial home because KL’s family lived very close by and were able to assist in taking her back and forth to medical appointments. AM also says it would be too difficult, between the ongoing medical issues, and caring for her son, to be living on her own at the rental unit. Her son’s nanny was living with KL and AM, but only provided transportation services to her son in exchange for free room and board. The nanny would not provide care services to AM unless she was paid, and AM states she was not financially able to pay the nanny particularly given that she was unable to work while dealing with her illness.

After several months of trying to manage financially, AM finally decided to put the rental unit up for rent. She had no income and the mortgage payments on the property were significant. She was worried she would lose her home by foreclosure if she did not. However, she states the rent she received was far less than the mortgage payment. When AM finally completed her medical treatments, she moved into the rental unit in July 2024 and resides there currently. She no longer rents any part of the home.

With regard to the second N12 given to JR, AM states she was aware that KL would be giving JR an N12 but had not seen it. She says because she had been feeling unwell, she had KL deal with issues pertaining to the tenancies at the rental unit. However, she believed that the N12 that JR received was not for KL to move into the rental unit, but for her, despite the N12 listing [name] as the Landlord. She agrees that [name] was acting as her agent. Applicable Sections of the Act

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Section 57(5) of the Act creates a rebuttable presumption that a notice of termination given under s. 48(1) of the Act was given in bad faith if the property is advertised for sale or rent. A rebuttable presumption means that the landlord is assumed to have acted in bad faith unless the landlord can provide an explanation that satisfies the Board as to what changed after the tenancy terminated that affected the landlord’s ability to move in or remain in the rental unit. Analysis

Although I find that the Tenant proved that the Landlord gave her an N12 notice under section 48 of the Act, and that she moved out as of a result of the notice, I do not find that the remainder of the requirements under s. 57(1)(a) were satisfied on a balance of probabilities.

I find AM’s evidence for the reason she did not move into the rental unit until July 2024 to be both credible and reliable. Her evidence was backed up by medical documentation which shows that AM was diagnosed at the end of June 2023 and that she underwent medical treatment for about one year. I also accept her testimony that it would have been difficult to care for herself and her young son without the support and assistance of KL’s family.

I do not make a negative inference that AM had no intention to move into the rental unit because AM chose to remain in the matrimonial home even where there was a potential for abuse. In my view, it is reasonable that having KL’s family’s support to care for her son and take her to medical treatments may have trumped AM’s need for security given the length and severity of the medical treatments she faced.

I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she thought the Tenant may want to purchase the property and that is why she offered the rental unit to the Tenant on May 16, 2023. I am not of the view that this singular offer negates the intention over the entire period.

I also find that AM’s evidence about why she put the rental unit back on the market, because of financial pressures, to be credible. She was not working and had applied for ODSP. However, this amount was insufficient to hold onto the rental property given the mortgage costs. In my view, it is logical that AM would have been gravely concerned about losing her home if she defaulted on the mortgage.

Additionally, the first reference to re-renting the unit was around September 7, 2023, in the text message to JR. This was about seven weeks after the termination of the tenancy, which correlates closely to AM’s recovery after her first surgery in August 2023.

Further, the only evidence that supports the unit was advertised shows that the intended date of occupation was December 1, 2023. In my view, had AM intended to immediately re-rent the unit for more money, she would not have waited to do so until December 1, 2023. There is also the declaration from IG stating that he assisted AM in moving her belongings into the rental property just a couple of days after the unit was vacated.

Although the Act does not define “reasonable”, however, reasonable is generally defined as being sensible or rational. Legislature specifically chose not to specify a timeframe in s. 57(1)(a) of the Act but chose the word “reasonable” instead. This suggests to me that I must determine whether I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the timeframes in the case before me is reasonable. In my view, AM’s actions were sensible and rational given the circumstances AM faced.

AM’s evidence is that as soon as she finished her treatment regime, she did move into the rental property as she had always intended. Again, if AM’s goal was to simply re-rent the unit for more money, or sell the rental unit, then it does not accord that as soon as she was feeling better, she moved into the rental property.

Although I would agree that [name] was acting as AM’s agent in giving the second N12 to JR, I am not persuaded that because KL indicated he was the Landlord on the form, this is indicative of bad faith on behalf of the Landlords. From the evidence before me, both KL and AM traded duties and responsibilities for the tenancies throughout the tenancy. It was clear to me, during the hearing, that AM did not even realize that KL had put his name on the second N12, rather than hers. What was clear about AM’s oral testimony was though that it was not KL who would be moving in, but her. Given that [name] and AM were going through a tumultuous time in their marriage, I find it credible that AM had not seen the second N12 and assumed it was the same as one given to the Tenant. Further, as JR was not called as a witness, I am unable to assess what JR’s understanding behind the notice.

AM’s evidence was provided in a straightforward manner; was internally consistent; and was not contradicted by any other evidence before me. In the circumstances, I am obligated to apply, to AM’s testimony the principle from Maldonado v. M.E.I., 1979 CanLII 4098 (FCA), [1980] 2 F.C 302 (C.A.) at 305, that when a witness swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness.

The Tenant also raised the issue that she believes she was coerced into signing an N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy by the Landlords. However, even if I accept this submission, I still find that the Landlord rebutted the presumption that she acted in bad faith when giving the Tenant the N12 notice.

The Tenant submits that pursuant to s.202 of the Act, I am required to consider the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the residential complex when making my determinations. I agree with this submission. The case of Elkins v Van Wissen, 2023 ONCA 789, stands for the proposition that I must consider the Landlord’s conduct before, during, and after the notice of termination was given. In this matter, I am satisfied that AM’s conduct is consistent with her stated intentions. She gave the N12 notice to the Tenant. She moved in when she was physically able to do so and continues to live in the rental unit to this day.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: Th e Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord' s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (hereafter referred to as the 'T6 Application'). This T6 Application was heard by videoconference on November 25, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness, [name] [name], and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing. The Tenant spoke with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the hearing.
reasons: While the Tenant indicated on their T6 Application that they would like the dispute resolution process to be conducted in French, they stated at the hearing that they were seeking to proceed in English only.
As both parties confirmed their preference in having the matter heard exclusively in English, both parties agreed that the order shall only be issued in English. T6 Application
The parties agree that the tenancy was terminated prior to the hearing, and that the Tenant had already moved out of the rental unit.

At the start of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue with respect to the T6 Application, as they submitted that the application was lacking in detail, and prevented the Landlord from having a fair opportunity to understand the case to be met and prepare an adequate defence.

The Landlord referenced the Divisional Court case Ball v. Metro Capital Property , [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (hereafter referred to as “Ball v. Metro Capital”), which states that a Notice of Termination which fails to provide sufficient details is void. At paragraph 10 of the case, the Court states in part that there are several purposes for requiring the landlord to provide the reasons and details in a Notice of Termination. The tenant needs to know the specific allegations in order to (1) be in a position to know the case that must be met and (2) to decide whether to dispute the allegations made against the tenant before the Landlord and Tenant Board; or (3) to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission within seven days and thereby void the notice

The Landlord also submitted that the Tenant had served the Landlord with an amended application on November 20, 2025 ([name]), which presented substantially claims from the ones previously brought forward by the Tenant ([name]).
The Landlord therefore sought for the Tenant’s proposed amendments to be denied, and for the T6 Application to be dismissed.
The Tenant agreed that they served the Landlord with an amended T6 Application on November 20, 2025, and that they intended to proceed with their amended application ([name]). Analysis

I note that [name] v. Metro Capital is in reference to a Notice of Termination served by a landlord to a tenant. I would also note that unlike an application, a Notice of Termination cannot be corrected or amended where it is lacking in detail. The [name] v. Metro Capital decision does not apply to the present case as the lack of detail arises in an application which can be sought to be amended.

I would, however, note that the principles of natural justice encapsulate the spirit of [name] v. Metro Capital, which are to afford the responding party – in this case the Landlord – the opportunity to properly understand the allegations against them, in order to know the case to be met and have the opportunity to raise a defence, if they so choose.
I agree with the Landlord that the T6 Application is not sufficiently detailed.

Indeed, the Tenant fails to provide any specific detail (such as but not limited to a detailed description of the alleged issues, the date the issues started, the date the Tenant told the Landlord about the issues, whether the issues were resolved, etc.) regarding the Landlord’s alleged failure to address the cockroach issue in the rental unit, and in addition to providing submissions to matters that do not pertain to the Landlord’s alleged failure to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failure to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards 1. For example, submissions 1 Sections 20 and 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. relating to noise complaints would be more relevant in an application submitted pursuant to section 31 of the Act.

Additionally, while the Tenant stated that they had intended to amend their T6 Application, their proposed amendments (DOC-6830324) do not clarify their existing claims. Instead, the Tenant only sought to duplicate the remedies they are also claiming through a separate and distinct application they have already filed with the Board (LTB-T-096175-25).

As the Tenant waited six (6) days prior to the hearing date to seek to amend their T6 Application, and as the proposed amendments do not bring clarity to the Tenant’s T6 Application, and rather only seek to (significantly) alter the remedies requested by the Tenant, I did not find these requested amendments to be appropriate under the circumstances, and therefore denied the Tenant’s amendment requests pursuant to section 200 of the Act and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure.
As such, the only remedy the Tenant may have been entitled to (were they to have successfully met their burden of proof ) was for the Landlord to complete certain repairs in the rental [name].
However, as the Tenant has already vacated the rental unit, these requests would be moot under the circumstances.
Accordingly, I find that the T6 Application discloses no reasonable cause of action and must therefore be dismissed3.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 Application is dismissed. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.
The rental unit is a 3-bedroom condominium unit.

The Tenant E.M. filed a T2 application because he believes that he is afforded the rights and protections of a tenant under the Act. He claims that the Landlords, who are his uncle and aunt, have violated his rights and are attempting to unlawfully evict him.

He asserts that the rental unit is akin to a rooming house operated by the Landlords. He testified that in early 2025 he began to rent a room from them. He alleges that they treat him as a trespasser: they refuse to provide him with a lease agreement although he pays rent monthly and they recently told him that he had to move out by December 6, 2025.

The [name] testified that he and his spouse purchased the condo on January 8, 2015 as a permanent home for R.F.’s mother [name] She and their six dependents (all young grandchildren of M.M.) arrived in Canada in July 2014 under the Landlords’ sponsorship. The Tenant is the Landlords’ nephew and was one of the children. He was 11 yrs. old at the time.
There is no dispute that the condo contains a singular kitchen, bathrooms and a living area. [name] and the children moved in at the same time. The Landlords live elsewhere.

The Landlords’ evidence is that [name] has resided in the unit ever since. Over the past 10 years, the children have grown up and are now adults. The Tenant, who is now 21 yrs. old, has remained living in the unit with [name]

I understand the Tenant’s evidence to be that his girlfriend lives with him and that his two brothers (one with a girlfriend) also share the unit. Some of the children decided to venture out on their own, to become independent adults.
R.F. submits that all of the adults residing in the unit share the kitchen and a bathroom.

The Landlords explain that they pay for the condo expenses. After some discussion last year, they decided that the adult children who wished to remain living at home should contribute on a monthly basis to the carrying costs of the unit as it would encourage them to become responsible adults.

On January 10, 2025, the Landlords and the remaining adult children entered into a private economic arrangement. In the case of the Tenant E.M., he agreed to pay $700.00 per month for his contribution. The Landlords assert that [name] has been delinquent in paying his share and is otherwise causing problems in the home. 12. [name] submits in response that his grandmother [name] no longer resides in the unit, having vacated when she left the country in November 2024 to begin living with her sister in Guyana. In his view, once that event occurred, he became a tenant as defined by the Act. 13. The Landlords insist that [name] continues to live in the unit. They acknowledge that she has recently been visiting her sister in Guyana. She expects to return home in March 2026. They submit that travelling or visiting relatives in another country for an extended period of time is not unusual in today’s society and does not equate to vacating the unit. 14. The Landlords’ position is that they have no landlord-tenant relationship with [name] She does not pay rent in exchange for occupying the unit and the adult children are her roommates. Neither is she a landlord. 15. They submit that the arrangement they made with [name] is exempt from the Act. That is because R.F. is the owner of the unit, [name] is R.F.’s mother, [name] lives in the condo and the occupants – being the children – must share the kitchen with R.F.’s mother. Analysis 16. Section 5(i) of the Act states that the Act does not apply to: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located; … [emphasis added] 17. I find that the owner’s parent [name] lives in the building in which the rental unit is located and that the occupant [name] is required to share the kitchen with [name] 18. There is no evidence before the Board to establish that [name] has informed the Landlords that she has vacated the unit or that she wishes to move out. I accept the Landlords’ evidence to the contrary: that the condo is [name]’s permanent home and primary residence. 19. Therefore, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that this living accommodation is exempt from the Act.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in a T2 application seeking an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. An adjudicative case conference (ACC) was held June 30, 2025. The matter did not settle at the ACC so it was directed to a hearing. The application was heard by videoconference on April 8, 2026. The Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord also attended the hearing with their legal representative [name] (paralegal).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T2 application did not contain adequate particulars and details, nor was it requested to be amended. It was determined that it would be procedurally unfair to proceed in the circumstances, so the application was dismissed.

The Tenant admitted that during the ACC, the Member provided information and recommendations regarding the application. The Tenant testified that after the ACC she had followed the Member’s instructions. She created a table of contents listing all her evidence and documents, then attached 78 pages of all her evidence.

I was not satisfied from the Tenant’s submissions or evidence package, that her claims were adequately particularized. The Tenant appears to have simply compiled her disclosure into one document, instead of relying up several separate uploads to the Portal (TOP).

The T2 application was not amended to include specific details about the allegations of substantial interference, harassment, or withholding vital services. There was no reasonable explanation provided why the Tenant had not sought legal advice and made a proper request to amend the T2 application in the 9 months since the ACC.

The Tenant advised all her claims were contained within her numerous pages of evidence. She wanted a chance to speak about her issues during the hearing and to corroborate all her claims with the evidence she had compiled and disclosed.

The Landlord’s representative submitted that it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to allow the Tenant a chance to proceed with a hearing in the circumstances. The representative argued that his client did not have adequate particulars to know what the claims were about, or how to defend against them.

I determined that the T2 application had not been requested to be amended. Instead, the Tenant had simply compiled her disclosure into one consolidated document with a table of contents added to the beginning of the document. I determined that the T2 application was minimal in description. Checkmarks had been made for certain “reasons” for the application, with some notes added to expand on the checkmarks. The notes stated things like: “See notes in the uploaded [name] tenant(s)”; “See the detailed notes uploaded. I was forced to buy a stove…” etc. None of these notes provided adequate details such as dates, times, names, or details of the incidents complained of.

Since the T2 application did not disclose adequate details regarding the claims, and since the application was not properly requested to be amended in accordance with Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure, I determined it would be procedurally unfair to adjudicate the application.
ordered: 9. The application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024, at which time the Tenant provided the Landlord with a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,100.00.

On or about mid to late October 2025, the Landlord informed the Tenant that he has defaulted on his financial obligations for the home and that he may lose the property with the Tenant being forced to vacate. It was at this time that the Landlord asked the Tenant to vacate the unit due to the circumstances.
The Tenant testified to informing the Landlord that she would be vacating the unit on November 15, 2025, a date which the Landlord was agreeable to.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 15, 2025.
The Landlord applied the rent deposit to the rental period of November 2025.

The Landlord has failed to return to the Tenant, the sum of $550.00 representing half of the rent deposit. The Tenant believes that she should be entitled to half of the deposit back because she vacated the unit on November 15, 2025, pursuant to the Landlord’s request. The deposit would have covered the rental period of November 1, 2025, through to November 30, 2025.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not use a portion of the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return that portion of the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord shall be required to return the unused portion of the deposit in the amount of $550.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $598.00. This amount represents: • $550.00 for the unused portion of the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
