issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord raised the issue that the Tenant had requested to amend the application. The Landlord opposed the request. The Landlord submitted that the proposed amendment relates solely to the addition of compensation claims, including a rent abatement in the amount of $9,470.98 and general compensation of $3,200.00. No amendments were proposed to the material facts or issues already raised in the application. The application was filed on December 10, 2024.

The Landlord relied on Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and submitted that the request to amend was not made as soon as the need for the amendment was known. The Landlord submitted that the Tenant had raised the issue of compensation and threatened legal action on the date the application was filed and continued to do so afterward. In support of this position, the Landlord filed text messages sent by the Tenant on December 10, 2024, in which the Tenant threatened to seek reimbursement of rent, as well as an email dated December 12, 2024, in which the Tenant advised that he intended to pursue the matter before the Board and seek compensation, including rent reimbursement. The Landlord also filed an email dated April 28, 2025, in which the Tenant again threatened legal action and advised that he would be seeking compensation.
The Landlord submitted that granting the amendment would be prejudicial, as the compensation being sought exceeds $10,000.00 and would significantly prejudice him financially.

The Tenant’s legal representative submitted that she was retained in September 2025. She stated that the Tenant may have forgotten to include a request for compensation in the original application and requested that the amendment be permitted in the interests of her client.

I do not find it appropriate to permit the requested amendment. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant was aware of his intention to seek compensation and communicated that intention to the Landlord on multiple occasions. I further find that the request to amend the application was made nearly ten months after the application was filed, and three months after the Tenant’s legal representative was retained, which I find to be an unreasonable delay.

Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure permits an amendment only where it is made as soon as the need for it is known and where allowing the amendment would not prejudice another party. For the reasons set out above, I find that these requirements have not been met.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s request to amend the application is denied.

The tenancy ended on October 31, 2025, when the Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord. As the only remedy sought in the application is termination of the tenancy effective January 31, 2025, and the tenancy has already ended, I find that the requested relief is moot. Accordingly, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Vendor Landlord’ or ‘VL’) and [name] (the ‘Purchaser Landlord’ or ‘PL’), gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that she had moved into the rental unit in 2018. The unit in question is a two-bedroom unit located in a house that contained three separate rental units.

On February 21, 2024, the Tenant received an N12 Notice of Termination from the VL, outlining that the VL sought to end the tenancy to permit the PL to move into the unit. The notice’s termination date was April 30, 2024.

The Tenant testified that on April 4, 2026, she had vacated the unit and had signed a new lease for a new unit, wherein the rent for that unit was $2,300.00. The rent for the unit in question was $1,089.00. The Tenant testified that her new unit is a three-bedroom house as the housing supply in her small community was limited. She testified that she required a co-signer to secure this new unit.

The Tenant testified that once she vacated the unit, she had observed that renovations had taken place to the kitchen and bathroom. This was determined by the Tenant’s mother-in-law having purchased a pantry from the Landlord in May of 2024.

The Tenant testified that from May 2024 to September 2024 she had observed work at the unit on various occasions, as her new unit was just down the street. She testified that she observed a new sliding door had been installed in the backyard. She testified that it appeared as though the PL had been digging up the backyard and that it seemed like no one was living there.

The Tenant then testified that from September 2024 to January 2025, she was not sure what was happening in the unit, but she was aware that no one had been living in the unit and that it had taken the Purchaser Landlords 17 months to move into the unit. The Tenant testified that from January 2025 to June 2025 the unit was still empty, and no renovations were taking place. Vendor [name] Evidence
The VL testified that she had purchased the residential complex in 2021 and had sold it in 2024. Each unit was occupied when she purchased it.

The VL testified that the Tenant had made her aware of various maintenance issues with the property, including the replacement of the unit’s fridge, the unit’s stove, the bathroom fan, and a broken window. The VL also testified that the municipality had also replaced the watermains. The VL testified that she sold the residential complex as she had found a four- plex which she felt was a better investment. VL testified that in December of 2023, one of the units was vacant and she felt that it was a good time to sell.
Entered into evidence was the Agreement of Purchase and Sale between the Vendor Landlord and the Purchaser Landlord dated February 7, 2024, with a closing date of March 15, 2024.

When asked about the whether the VL knew the intentions of the Purchaser Landlord when they purchased the unit, the VL responded that she knew the Purchasers and knew that they had purchased the residential complex to be used as their first home. Purchaser Landlords’ Evidence

MT testified that he is one of the Purchaser Landlords and that he is currently living in the unit. MT testified that the PLs’ intentions were always to purchase the residential complex for the purposes of starting a family. MT testified that he was aware of the fact that the residential complex had multiple units, as it had been the only affordable way to get their foot in the door to own their own property but had been living in the unit the entire time since they had purchased the unit. The PLs had been living in their parent’s home while saving up for a downpayment for a mortgage prior to moving in the residential complex.
The Purchaser Landlords were married in October of 2024, they welcomed their first child on August 31, 2025. MT testified that he works in residential and commercial construction.

MT testified that the residential complex’s proximity to his in-laws for childcare purposes, the size of the backyard for their dog and the price of the residential complex were their main reasons for choosing this unit.

MT further testified that the PLs were permitted to inspect the unit prior to making their offer, specifically inspecting the Tenant’s unit in question and had noticed maintenance issues. Generally, the unit’s amenities were dated with windows that likely dated back to the 90’s, a broken shower, mould in the attic, mildew, and cracked tiles.

Entered into evidence were photos of the unit dated April 6, 2024. Pictures of the kitchen, bathroom, hallway, and the laundry room. MT testified that when he observed the condition of the unit, he knew that he needed to inspect the unit a little more in-depth to determine what the extent of the work required might be.

MT testified that he started conducting the renovations on that day. MT testified that in order to save money, he conducted the work himself doing the work on Saturdays, Sundays and evenings while also working his own job.

On April 28, 2024, the unit’s living room and kitchen floor tiles had been removed. As well, pieces of drywall were replaced as the unit had been a wheel-chair friendly unit prior which the paneling installed for same had left dried glue on the unit’s wall.

By June 5, 2024, MT had completed sanding the entire floor and required a mask and an exhaust fan. MT testified that the floor had been completed by June 23, 2024, as the vinyl flooring that was ordered had come from London.

On June 6, 2024, MT testified that he had removed the subfloor in the unit’s bathroom after the shower had been removed after it was determined that the part of the subfloor was rotten and needed to be replaced. MT testified that it had taken him a couple of weeks to complete the sistering of the floor joists
MT testified that some of the renovations were delayed as the unit’s stairs needed to be repaired, which was completed as of June 22, 2024.

On June 8, 2024, MT had been removing the kitchen cabinets when he had found mould on the subfloor. The mould was removed by July 1, 2024. On August 9, 2024, MT had completed the installation of the drywall. On September 15, 2024, the installation of the drywall had been delayed by the fact that the PLs needed to turn off the unit’s HVAC to complete the work, which was very hot at the time.

MT testified that he had began ordering new appliances and cabinets for the unit but had also been constructing his wedding venue at the same time. By January of 2025, MT had gutted the washroom and replaced the toilet and the shower.

On February 26, 2025, the PLs had learned that the main water line which serviced all three units had been leaking worse than they had noticed. As this issue was discovered in February, the work could not be completed until June of 2025 once the ground had thawed. MT could not complete that work himself, as it required excavation.
By summer 2025, the PLs had ordered various appliances, which invoices were provided. The Purchaser Landlords moved into the unit in September of 2025. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: - The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; - The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; - No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and - The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is not dispute that the Tenant was served the N12 Notice of Termination on February 21, 2024, stating that the Purchaser Landlords intended to move into the unit. It was also not disputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. Did the Purchaser Landlord Occupy the Rental Unit in a Reasonable Amount of Time?

The Tenant in her submissions stated that she “is not seeking a finding of bad faith so much as I believe the delays were unreasonable”. The Tenant reiterated that the delay of 17-18 months was unreasonable.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that the PLs were in the unit on April 6, 2024, and that MT’s evidence with respect to the maintenance issues that were discovered and addressed was thorough and consistent and that there never a time where the PL was acting in a deceitful manner.

From April 6, 2024, on, the PLs had inspected the unit and conducted renovations as required, starting with the floor and drywall and moving into other issues that would have been discovered as the work continued, including the leaking watermain. The PLs were at all times, conducting the work themselves while simultaneously constructing a wedding venue.

On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Purchaser Landlords did not move into the unit within a reasonable amount of time. At no time during the hearing did the Tenant challenge the work that was being done by MT.

MT testified in a forthright and straightforward manner. He first knew that the unit would need work when he attended a showing of the unit in February of 2024. On April 6, 2024, as soon as the unit had been vacated, MT started work on the floor. While the work may have been delayed as the Tenant was conducting the work himself, I do not find it unreasonable to do so, considering the evidence of the Purchaser Landlords was that they had just moved out of their parents’ home, had planned on starting a family and were looking to save money by doing the renovations on their own time.

The renovations were only paused for the Purchaser Landlords’ wedding, and the weather when the work required excavation. By the time the wedding had come along, MT had already put in nearly 6 months of work on his own time. Once work started again in January, he had discovered the watermain leak which could not be addressed until warmer weather had come. By September of 2025, the Purchaser Landlords started residing in the unit full-time with their child.

That said, I am satisfied that the Purchaser Landlords had every intention to move into the rental unit and that MT had been working steadily to renovate the home to facilitate this however, explainable delays occurred which in my view, were not unreasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probability. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.

The Tenant, [name] (A.J.), testified that she signed a residential lease agreement with the Landlord on or about July 30, 2025, at which time she provided the Landlord with payment in the amount of $1,690.00. This payment included a $100.00 key deposit, and $795.00 for the first and last month’s rent deposit. The tenancy was supposed to start on September 1, 2025.

On or about August 25, 2025, the Tenant contacted the Landlord and notified him that she was no longer interested in occupying the rental unit on September 1, 2025, as per the terms of the lease agreement entered between the parties. The Landlord was not agreeable to cancelling the lease, nor was the Landlord agreeable to returning the monies provided to him. 4. [name] testified that the reason she no longer required the unit was because she initially agreed to rent the unit because her landlord at the time told her that the unit is going up for sale and that she would have to vacate the unit. The same landlord later told her that she was welcome to stay in her current unit and did not have to vacate the unit as they had previously discussed. 5. [name] testified that between the period of August 25, 2025, through to October 15, 2025, she sent the Landlord multiple potential tenants to take over her lease. The Tenant tendered evidence of messages between the parties showing the individuals being forwarded to the Landlord. The Tenant was able to do this because she placed her own advertisements of the property. 6. [name] testified that she forwarded the Landlord an individual by the name of [name], who did end up renting a room in a neighboring home. [name] was not aware as to why [name] did not rent her room that she was sent to the property to see. The Tenant tendered text communications between her and [name] to support that she was the one who found or secured [name] as a tenant. 7. [name] advertised the rental unit on Facebook marketplace, a university forum, Kijiji, and other online websites and forums to mitigate her losses and find a tenant to take over her lease. The Tenant’s efforts went on until approximately October 15, 2025, at which time the Tenant stopped forwarding the Landlord any individuals. 8. [name] testified that the Landlord was not prepared to accept any male candidates as the property was rented to all females. 9. [name] testified that she searched online and did not see any evidence of the Landlord advertising the rental unit until sometime in late October 2025. 10. The Tenant was seeking the return of her first and last month’s rent, and the $100.00 key deposit paid to the Landlord. The total amount being sought by the Tenant was $1,690.00. 11. On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she initially saw the unit in May 2025. She also confirmed that this is the same time that her landlord wanted her out to sell the unit. 12. [name] also confirmed that the only reason she did not occupy the unit as per the terms of the lease signed was because her landlord told her that she no longer had to vacate her unit and was now welcome to stay. 13. [name] confirmed not knowing why [name] took a different unit. [name] also agreed that the people who generally rented the room were university students and a lot of them would have needed occupancy by September 1, 2025. 14. [name] confirmed that she sent the Landlord 100’s of people who responded to her advertisement. [name] also testified that she sent the Landlord one or two filled out applications with potential tenants. 15. [name] also confirmed that she became aware that she was able to continue her tenancy at her current place of residence as of approximately August 15, 2025. The Landlord was informed of her decision on or about August 24, 2025. 16. The Landlord, [name] (D.M.), testified that the Tenant initially viewed the rental room in May 2025, and signed a lease agreement with a start date of September 1, 2025. The Landlord was provided with $1,690.00 for first and last month’s rent, and $100.00 for a key deposit. 17. On or about August 25, 2025, the Tenant notified the Landlord that she is no longer going to be moving into the unit, that she wants to cancel the lease and get her money back. The Landlord was only told that the Tenant’s reason for this decision was based on the Tenant’s personal circumstances. 18. D.M. confirmed that an individual by the name of [name] attended and saw the Tenant’s rental room. D.M. also testified that this person did not rent the Tenant’s room because the person was specifically looking for a room with a private bathroom. The Tenant’s room did not have a private bathroom facility. 19. D.M. testified that he did receive many names and phone numbers from the Tenant, and may have received a rental application, or two, but that none of the individuals sent to the Landlord rented the Tenant’s rental room or took over her lease agreement. 20. D.M. testified that he advertised the rental room as of August 25, 2025, and that he was unable to secure a new tenant until November 1, 2025. He attributed the delay in renting the room due to the units being for students which are not looking for a room after September 1, 2025. D.M. evidence of advertising the rental unit or mitigating his damage was limited to his verbal evidence. The Landlord failed to upload a copy of any advertisements or photographs showing a sign on the property. 21. The Landlord took the position that the Tenant should not be entitled to the return of any funds because he was unable to re-rent the unit until November 1, 2025. Accordingly, the funds paid by the Tenant should be attributed to September 2025, and October 2025. 22. On cross-examination, the Landlord agreed the Tenant may have sent him [name] but also maintained that [name] rented a different room in a different house. 23. The Landlord also confirmed that he would only accept female tenants because of the way the room was rented out. 24. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord and the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement, and that the Tenant failed to occupy the unit. I am also satisfied that the unit was available and ready for the Tenant to occupy on September 1, 2025. I am mindful of the Tenant’s efforts of securing an alternative tenant and the individual referred to the Landlord by the Tenant, who rented a room in a different house. Having said this, I am not satisfied that the Landlord unreasonably denied the Tenant’s request to assign the tenancy. Accordingly, I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to rent the unit for September 2025, or was not given the opportunity to do so, based on the Tenant’s lack of notice. The Tenant was aware as of August 15, 2025, and ought to have informed the Landlord immediately. 25. Ultimately, I am not persuaded by the Landlord’s mitigation efforts. His testimony in this regard was vague and not corroborated by documentary evidence. The Landlord instead responded to the Tenant’s efforts to mitigate rather than provide a convincing narrative of his own effort to mitigate. 26. Therefore, I find that it would be appropriate for the Landlord to pay the Tenant $895.00. This amount represents the last month’s rent deposit, and the $100.00 key deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $943.00. This amount represents: • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. • $795.00 for the return of last month’s rent deposit. • $100.00 for the return of a key deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2024, at which time she provided the Landlord her portion of a key deposit and security deposit. The total amount of the key deposit was $300.00, and the total amount provided for the security deposit was $1,000.00. These amounts were split between two tenants, one of which is the Tenant named in this application.
The total the Tenant provided the Landlord for her portion of the key/security deposit was $650.00. This amount was paid to the Landlord on July 29, 2024.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2025, at which time the Landlord failed to return the key and security deposit in the amount of $650.00 to the Tenant.
The Tenant was told that they damaged the rental unit and that the amount collected was applied to cover the cost of the damages.
To date, the Landlord has not returned to the Tenant, any portion of the key and/or security deposit.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). This charge is the $500.00 security deposit collected by the Landlord on July 29, 2024. The Landlord shall be required to return this amount. The Landlord shall also be required to return the $150.00 key deposit, as I am satisfied that the Tenant has returned the keys and the Landlord has failed to return the key deposit to the Tenant.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants H.L., 66 yrs. old, and her son, H.R. 31 yrs. old, entered into a one year fixed- term residential lease with the Landlord on May 5, 2025, expiring on April 30, 2026 and with the potential to become a month-to-month tenancy as of May 1, 2026. The Tenants paid the Landlord $1,100.00 as a last month’s rent deposit and $100.00 for a key deposit.
The rental unit is a room situated in a rooming house operated by the Landlord. The Tenants share the common areas with other tenants. The Landlord resides elsewhere.

The Tenant H.L. testified that on or about September 6, 2025, she informed the Landlord that an unrelated male tenant residing in the rooming house was substantially interfering with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex.

She had issues because that tenant, and on occasion other tenants, persistently accessed her personal storage area in the kitchen and used her items without her consent. She stated that she complained to the Landlord many times, but he refused to do anything.

On November 24, 2025, H.L. was upset about an incident in which the male tenant again took her items without permission. She had reached the end of her patience. She called the Landlord but learned that he was out of the country. She then called the Landlord’s son P.W. Neither made any efforts to resolve the conflict.

H.L. testified that when he returned from his vacation, the Landlord told her that if she could not tolerate the situation, she should look for another place that suits her better. She stated that his comment made her feel unsupported. Feeling pressured and unsafe, she began looking for another place to live.

She informed the Landlord of her intention to move on November 30, 2025, citing his neglect in addressing the conflict as the reason for considering an early departure. She also asked the Landlord to return her last month’s rent deposit and the key deposit upon them moving out.

The Landlord refused to agree to reimburse the deposits and informed the Tenants that they had to give 30-days’ notice to vacate. He then threatened to change the code to the smart lock on the entry door of the building which would bar them from entering.

On December 1, 2025, the Tenants discovered that the Landlord had disabled their access to the rental unit. They were compelled to find alternative accommodations. They were unable to retrieve personal belongings from the residence unless the Landlord let them in.

When she was able to reach the Landlord, H,[name] asked why he changed the code. Her evidence is that he falsely claimed that she had given him formal notice to end the tenancy on November 30, 2025 and asserted that he had a right to change the entry code. She maintains that he sent her several intimidating messages, including to say that if they tried to enter the house or if they returned to the property, he would call the police.
As I understand it, the Tenants tried twice more to enter the property to retrieve their possessions on December 3 and 4, 2025 but without success.
The Tenants claim that they were illegally locked out, forcing them to urgently relocate with short notice. This caused them significant hardship.

On December 7, 2025, the Landlord informed the Tenants that they could pick up their belongings from the unit. H.L. testified that when they arrived at the property, they discovered that the Landlord had removed all their possessions from the rental premises, placing them in boxes.

After sorting through the items, H.L. documented the loss of the following: • her Ontario Driver’s Licence (replacement cost $90.00) • a Costco Membership card (replacement cost $30.00) • extensive class notes from a photography course, which cannot be easily reproduced (alternative college source $500.00).
The Tenants immediately reported the loss to the Barrie Police Services as a theft.
According to the Tenants, they paid the rent in full for December 2025. They submit that the Landlord withheld their last month’s rent deposit and has declined to refund their key deposit. Analysis

I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord altered the locking system on the entry door of the residential complex without giving the Tenants a new entry code, contrary to section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
I also find that the Landlord actively prevented the Tenants from entering and occupying their rental unit after the entry code was changed. They were still in possession.

A landlord cannot unilaterally terminate a tenancy, induce a tenant to vacate or force a tenant to vacate a rental unit. I am not satisfied that this tenancy was lawfully terminated by notice of termination, by agreement or by LTB order. By failing to abide by the Act, the Landlord’s actions constitute an unlawful eviction.

The Divisional Court found in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Ct.) that it is the landlord’s legal responsibility to provide tenants with quiet enjoyment of the rental premises.

The Court determined that this responsibility imposes an obligation on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of another tenant on the tenant’s right to reasonable enjoyment of the unit or residential complex.
I accept the Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord failed to take any meaningful steps to investigate or to resolve the issues as was his obligation under the Act.

In my view, the Landlord’s lack of interest and action fell far short of the requirement. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants.

There is no uncertainty in my mind that the Landlord entered the Tenants’ unit illegally, that is without proper notice, and that he interfered with and removed their possessions without any legal authority. The entry was not in response to an emergency, the Tenants did not give their consent and the motive for entry was unreasonable. Additionally, I find that the Landlord unjustly withheld the Tenants’ possessions from them for up to 7 days after he locked them out. The Landlord is responsible for any loss of property in that regard.
Finally, the Tenants have amply established that the Landlord has unlawfully retained their last month’s rent deposit and their key deposit. Remedies

I find that a rent abatement of $1,100.00 as requested by the Tenants is appropriate in the circumstances. They paid for occupancy of the unit but had no use of it in December 2025 due to the Landlord’s grievous conduct.
The Landlord shall be ordered to pay to the Tenants the cost of replacing their lost property in the amount of $620.00.
The Landlord must also reimburse the Tenants $1,200.00 for the unlawfully retained deposits.
The Tenants’ claims for moving costs and out of pocket expenses are denied. They provided no invoices or receipts demonstrating that they incurred these costs. Administrative fine
I believe that this is an appropriate case in which to impose an administrative fine.
The Landlord’s behaviour demonstrates disrespect of the LTB processes and a troubling indifference to his responsibilities under the Act and to the Tenants’ rights.

The Landlord will be fully aware of the Act and know that he is not permitted to engage in self-help to evict tenants. He will know that he must treat his obligations seriously, exercising professional diligence in his relationships with tenants.

I am satisfied that there are no other remedies that will provide adequate deterrence and compliance in these circumstances. It is particularly important to impose a fine at this time, to ensure that the Landlord harbours no doubt that rooming houses are subject to the Act.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $2,500.00.
ordered: The tenancy is terminated as of December 4, 2025.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,968.00. This amount represents: • $1,100.00 for a rent abatement. • $1,200.00 for the return of the last month’s rent and key deposits. • $620.00 for compensation for damaged or lost property. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing the parties sought an adjournment on consent. They explained that during a private meeting between the parties the Tenant's Legal Representative became aware of LTB-L-004213-25. This is an order based on an L9 Application brought by the Landlord with respect to the tenancy.

LTB-L-004213-25 was issued on June 3, 2025, it determines that the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit on January 28, 2025, and the presiding Membre conducted an analysis under Section 88 of the Act and determined that the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent ended on Februray 26, 2025. The order determined the rent and arrears owing to Februray 26, 2025 and also deals with the last month rent deposit and interest. LTB-L-004213-25 was heard on April 16, 2025, and the Tenant’s did not attend the hearing. LTB-L-004213-25 was filed on January 15, 2025, and the Notice of hearing for LTB-L-004213-25 was sent to the Tenant by the Board by mail to the rental unit on March 2, 2025.
The Tenant’s T1 Application before me alleges that the Landlord did not return the last month rent deposit and did not pay interest on the last month rent deposit.

The Tenant's Legal Representative indicated that neither she or the Tenant’s were aware of this prior proceeding and sought an adjournment so that she could have a conversation with her clients and gather more information on the prior proceeding.
The matter was subsequently stood down so that the Tenant's Legal Representative could review the LTB-L-004213-25 and the [name] with her clients.
When the matter was recalled the Tenant's Legal Representative renewed her request for an adjournment, which was not contested by the Landlord.

The Tenant's Legal Representative indicated that the Tenant’s were never served and never received anything with respect to LTB-L-004213-25 and only received a copy of the order today. She also indicated that while the [name] was filed on January 15, 2025, the Tenant’ had provided an N9 with a termination date of January 16, 2025 and on the [name] update sheet the Landlord had completed the indicated that the Tenant vacated on January 16, 2025. She indicated that if the notice of hearing and other documents had bene mailed, they would not have been received by the Tenants.

She also indicated that the Landlord also had email addresses for the Tenant in the lease agreement but did not provide these in the L9 Application. The Tenant's Legal Representative suggested that if the Tenant’s had been aware of LTB-L-004213-25 they would have sought representation and attend the hearing.
She also indicated that the Tenant’s had been seeking to assign the tenancy which is why the N9 they provided to the Landlord did not have a termination date at the end of the rental term.
I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. While the Adjournment was requested on consent the Board must still be satisfied that is appropriate.

I note that LTB-L-004213-25 was heard on April 16, 2025, and a final order issued on June 3, 2025. This is nearly a year prior to this proceeding. While the Tenant's Legal Representative alleges that neither they or the Tenant were aware of this proceeding, I would expect the parties to do reasonable due diligence to determine whether or not the allegations in the T1 had been dealt with especially as it appears from LTB-L-004213-25 that the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit prior to the end of a fixed term tenancy, and it could reasonably be expected that the Landlord would pursue compensation.

I also note that when LTB-L-004213-25 was filed the Tenant’s were still in possession of the rental unit, and while they may have subsequently vacated before the notice of hearing was served I would expect the Tenant’s to take appropriate steps to ensure they received any subsequent documentation related to the tenancy, including by setting up mail forwarding. and making the Landlord aware of any new address.

While the Tenant's Legal Representative asserts that the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit on January 16, 2025, only one day after the Application was filed I note that LTB-L- 004213-25 amends the Landlord’s Application to note that the Tenant’s vacated January 28, 2025. Additionally, while the Tenant's Legal Representative asserts that the Tenant’s vacated after a refused assignment, this to my mind, also suggests that the Tenant’s should have been diligent in setting up mail forwarding or providing a forwarding address to ensure they were kept appraised of any proceedings related to the tenancy.

I am also not satisfied that it is an expeditious use of the Board’s time to adjourn this matter so that the Tenant's Legal Representative can file a request to review of LTB-L- 004213-25 and then continue this T1 Application. I note that the Tenant’s T1 only seeks the return of the last month rent deposit and any accumulated interest and if the Tenant does successful review LTB-L-004213-25 it is likely that this will be dealt with by a rehearing of that matter.
Therefore, as I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate, and this Application has been rendered res judicata by LTB-L-004213-25, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: On December 2, 2024 the T enant asked the Landlord for consent to assign the rental unit to [name]. This was framed as more of a fait accomplit than a request as the Tenant intended for [name] to move in almost immediately and had already collected a rent deposit from him prior to mentioning him to the Landlord.

Prior to this discussion, the Tenant had ex pressed an interest in moving and the parties had agreed that the rental unit would be listed for rent effective January 1, 2025. From this I infer that the parties agreed to end the tenancy on December 31, 2024. Any earlier transfer to a different tenant would require either an early termination of the tenancy or an assignment.

On December 2, 2024, the same day it was requested, the Landlord refused to consent to the assignment. Before refusing, the Landlord expressed concern that she had no information about [name] other than that he was a senior, and that the tenant of the other unit which shares a bathroom with this unit may not find him a suitable housemate. When refusing the assignment, the Landlord stated, ‘I waited all day for you to call me. You moved out! Where are my keys for the apt? Where are the keys??? I’m changing the locks on both doors now.’ The Tenant replied that he was still renting the unit December 31, [name] was moving in, and ‘If you change the locks you owe me the LMR’. The Landlord replied ‘you CAN NOT RENT THAT APT IM DOING RENOS NOW’.

Although the Landlord testif ied that she met with [name], determined he was not a suitable applicant because he is homeless and was able to pay first and last with money from family but had no ongoing income, and retrieved the keys from him, this contradicts her written statements which demand a return of they key. Because the Landlord makes no mention of meeting [name] in her text communication and makes no mention of her concerns about his income, it is probable that this meeting occurred after the December 2, 2024 messages. When viewed as a total package, the communications from the Landlord show that the assignment request was unreasonable denied before the Landlord obtained enough information to make a reasonable determination on the suitability of [name] as an assignee.
Further, by stating that the locks would be changed and the Tenant could not rent the unit to anyone else because renovations were being done, the Landlord cut off any further assignment requests.
The Landlord unreasonably refused consent to the assignment to [name] and arbitrarily prevented the Tenant from making any other assignment request. Remedies

Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $1,450.68. This represents a 100% rent abatement for the period of December 2-December 31, 2025 when the Tenant had moved out of the rental unit and was planning to recoup his rent through an assignment but was unable to do because of the Landlord’s unreasonable or arbitrary refusal.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlor d and the Tenant is terminated as of [Eviction date].  $1,450.68 for a rent abatement.  $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by January 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 19, 2026 _______________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • Collected or retained money Illegally (the ‘T1 Application’); • Substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complete by the Tenant or by a member of their household; [name], obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • Withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (the ‘T2 Application’); and • Failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’).
reasons: In or about December 2023, the current Landlord took ownership of the residential complex. This application is primarily about the allegation that since the current Landlord took over the building it has attempted to impose new terms and conditions for the tenancy on the Tenant without his consent. But it is also about interest the Tenant alleges is owing on his last month’s rent deposit, a lack of heat, and disrepair to his toilet.

For the reasons that follow, the Tenant’s application is granted in part and denied in part. The Landlord is ordered to pay the Tenant $6,360.10 for abatements of the rent and general compensation: and to cease and desist demanding the Tenant sign a new lease or impose charges or obligations not authorized by the tenancy agreement or by the Act. The T1 Application
The Tenant’s T1 application alleges that the Landlord failed to pay interest owing on the [name] last month’s rent deposit. The amount of interest claimed is $28.15.

The Tenant entered into an agreement for a fixed term of one-year for the period of October 1, 2015, to September 30, 2016. The Tenant says he paid first and last month’s rent (‘LMR’) of $900.00, but the lease agreement entered into evidence indicates the rent and the LMR required were $990.00.
After the expiration date of the lease, the tenancy was renewed on a month-to-month basis.
According to the Tenant, the rent increased annually by the guideline amount. On October 1, 2024, the lawful monthly rent increased to $1,154.15.

I have done the math, and if the rent was originally $990.00 as set out in the tenancy agreement and increased each year by the guideline amount starting 2016, then in 2024 the lawful rent would have risen to $1,154.15, which is the current amount being charged.
Therefore, it seems more likely than not to me that the Tenant’s initial monthly rent was $990.00 as set out in the lease agreement and not the $900.00 claimed by the Tenant.

Subsections 106(6) and (7) of the Act say: (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. (7) The landlord may deduct from the amount payable under subsection (6) the amount, if any, by which the maximum amount of the rent deposit permitted under subsection (2) exceeds the amount of the rent deposit paid by the tenant and the deducted amount shall be deemed to form part of the rent deposit paid by the tenant.

What this means is that when interest becomes payable, if the landlord has increased the rent that year by the guideline amount, the landlord is entitled to add the interest to the LMR instead of paying it out to the tenant. If a landlord takes the guideline increase every year the landlord has no obligation to pay interest to a tenant. Instead, it gets added to the LMR so when the tenancy ends the LMR will match the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.

Essentially what the Tenant says is that the current Landlord informed him that the LMR deposit it was holding needed to be topped up by $28.15 to match the new rent amount that came into effect October 1, 2024, and the Tenant was required to pay that amount to the Landlord which he did. But if the deposit was then equal to the new monthly rent, the interest that accrued October 1, 2024 of $28.15 should have been paid out to the Tenant.

The only problem with the Tenant’s position is that I do not know if the Tenant’s original deposit was $990.00, the same as the amount of rent first charged; or whether it was $900.00 as the Tenant claims.

Pursuant to s.106(3) if the lawful rent increases after the tenant pays a last month’s rent deposit the landlord may require the tenant to top up the deposit to match the new rent. If the Tenant paid a deposit of $900.00 initially and never topped it up, then the Landlord was entitled to apply any interest owing to the deposit and ask the Tenant to make up the shortfall.

Given that the Tenant says he paid an initial deposit of $900.00 and not $990.00, I cannot say that any interest is actually owing on the deposit. If the Tenant paid a deposit of $900.00 and the Landlord added the interest to the deposit each year then the Tenant’s deposit effective October 1, 2024, would stand at $1,049.24 and the Landlord was entitled to ask for a top up to the deposit of $104.91.

As a result of all of the above, I am unable to conclude that it is more likely than not that the Landlord failed to pay any interest to the Tenant that is owing on the last month’s rent deposit. As a result, the T1 part of the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. The T2 Application

The Tenant’s T2 Application alleges breaches of ss. 22 and 23 with respect to multiple demands the new Landlord has made on the Tenants with respect to signing a new lease and agreeing to new terms of the tenancy. It also alleges that the Landlord breached section 21 of the Act by withholding heat or deliberately interfering with the supply of heat for the period September 15, 2024 to October 9, 2024. [name]

The Tenant testified that since the Landlord assumed control of the building in December 2023 or early January 2024, both he and his daughter have been subjected to ongoing harassment and threats, which have substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenant says that the superintendent continuously demanded that the Tenant sign a new lease with the Landlord and that the superintendent implied that any repair work would be refused or delayed until a lease was signed.

One example of this occurred on May 6, 2024. The Tenant put in a work order to fix the toilet in his rental unit. When the superintended attended the rental unit on May 7, 2024, he told the Tenant his instructions were to refuse to do any repair work in the Tenant’s unit until a new lease was signed. Following this incident the Tenant called the police. Demanding New Terms of the Tenancy

An example of the Landlord attempting to impose terms on the Tenant that the Tenant did not consent to and are not included in his tenancy agreement is with respect to air conditioning. The Tenant’s lease does not require the Tenant to pay a charge for air conditioning. After the Tenant moved in, he routinely used his air conditioner and was not charged for doing so. But when the landlord changed in 2023, the new Landlord created leases which require tenants to pay $100.00 for the air conditioning season if they use an air conditioner. When asked to pay the charge the Tenant refused to pay it.

On September 5, 2024, the Tenant was served with a notice of termination for non- payment of the rent in Form N4 alleging the Tenant was in arrears of rent of $100.00. However, the charge of $100.00 was added to his account by the Landlord as money owed for air conditioning. It does not appear the Landlord filed an application with the Board seeking this fee.

The Landlord brought an L2 application (in Board file LTB-L-024597-25) seeking eviction of the Tenant. That application was based on an N5 alleging that the Tenant’s lease requires him to have tenant’s insurance and the Tenant’s failure to do so substantially interfered with a lawful right, privilege, or interest of the Landlord’s. The Landlord has given the Tenant four notices demanding he provide the Landlord with proof of insurance of a minimum of $1,000,000.00 liability and $50,000.00 content insurance. I can find no clause in the Tenant’s lease that requires him to have tenant’s insurance.
The Landlord’s eviction application based on the Tenant’s lack of insurance was withdrawn on September 7, 2025.

Despite the fact the Landlord withdrew the application the Tenant was then served with numerous notices that he had an outstanding amount of $186.00 on his account for L1 and L2 application fees. Some of the notices delivered to the Tenant had the word “Sheriff” on them. (See for example DOC 7008790 at pgs. 16 – 25.)

The Tenant says that the notices and demands made by the Landlord described above made the Tenant and his daughter fearful that they would be evicted. They feel unsafe, stressed and constantly worried about living in their rental unit, making it very difficult to carry out their lives in peace.

Section 22 of the Act states. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

On the basis of the evidence presented, I find that the Landlord engaged in harassment and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by demanding proof of insurance the Tenant is not required to have, improperly adding an air conditioning charge to the Tenant’s account, serving an N4 notice based on those charges, serving frivolous N5 notices with respect to the insurance issue, initiating a frivolous eviction application with the Board based on the false allegation the Tenant is required to have tenant’s insurance, issuing multiple payment demands for an application fee related to a matter that was withdrawn and not ordered by the Board, and requesting that the Tenant sign a new lease containing revised terms.
The landlord knew or ought to have known the behaviour described above was unlawful, outside the parameters of the Residential Tenancy Act, and would be most unwelcome the Tenant.
As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act.

The Tenant’s T2 application seeks: 1. Abatements of the rent totalling $5,567.90; 2. A cease and desist order; 3. Damages for pain and suffering in the amount of $5,000.00; and 4. An administrative fine of $500.00.

I find that an abatement of 30% would be reasonable in the circumstances. The harassment was by its nature ongoing and in my view caused real disruption to the Tenant’s ability to enjoy their tenancy free from harassing conduct by the Landlord.

On the evidence before me, I find that the harassing behaviour from the Landlord commenced when the Landlord charged the Tenant $100.00 for the air conditioning fee and sent demand letters. This then continued with the N4 and N5 Notices being served.

The Tenant is entitled to a 30% abatement for the period of May 1, 2024 to September 30, 2024, and for the period January 1, 2025 to October 31, 2025, a total of 15 months. I calculate the abatement as follows: • For the period May 1, 2024 to September 30, 2024: 30% x $1,126.00/month x 5 months = $1,689.00; • For the period January 1, 2025 to September 30, 2025: 30% x $1,154.15/month x 9 months = $3,116.20; and • For the period October 1, 2025 to October 31, 2025: 30% x $1,183.00 = $354.90; • For a total of $5,160.10.
Given the amount of the abatement, I do not believe that an administrative fine is required as the abatement itself serves as an adequate general and specific deterrent.
With respect to the request for damages for pain and suffering, I accept that having to be under constant threat of eviction has had a significant emotional impact on the Tenant and his daughter.

Given the impact on the Tenant, the abatement already awarded, and my knowledge of like similar cases, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant general compensation for pain and suffering in the amount of $1,000.00.

With respect to the request for a cease and desist order, an order shall issue ordering the Landlord to refrain from demanding the Tenant sign a new lease or impose charges or obligations not authorized by the tenancy agreement or by the Act. Vital Services – the Heat

Pursuant to s. 21(1) of the Act: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

As can be seen from the wording of this provision, it is not about disrepair that results in a loss of a vital service. Rather it is about a landlord deliberately doing something like turning off the heat, or otherwise wilfully interfering with it or withholding it.

Although I have no doubt the Tenant’s unit suffered from a lack of heat as he claims for the period September 15, 2024 to October 9, 2024, there is nothing in the record to suggest the Landlord did anything to deliberately interfere with it or was intentionally withholding it. As a result, the lack of heat the Tenant experienced is just as likely to have been a disrepair issue.

With respect to disrepair, the case law indicates that the simple existence of disrepair is not sufficient to support a finding that a landlord is in breach of s. 20(1) of the Act. Disrepair is an expected event that occurs in most if not all tenancies. The obligation on the Landlord is to respond to the disrepair in a timely and effective manner.

The Tenant led no evidence that he complained to the Landlord of a lack of heat during the relevant period. As it is not clear to me from the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord was even aware of the lack of heat in the Tenant’s unit, I am not satisfied the Landlord breached s. 20(1) of the Act by failing to respond in a timely and effective manner to the problem.
As a result, this part of the Tenant’s application must be denied. The T6 Application

A T6 Application is based on the rights and obligations found in s. 20(1) of the Act, which states: (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. The Toilet

The Tenant put in a work order to fix the toilet in his rental until on May 6, 2024 because it was not flushing properly. The superintendent refused to fix the toilet and told the Tenant he would need to pay for the repair. A week later, the Tenant borrowed a snake from a neighbour and fixed the problem himself.

Clearly, the refusal to address the problem with the Tenant’s toilet constitutes a breach of s. 20(1). It cannot be said the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely or effective manner.

Given the nature of the problem, the fact the Tenant was able to fix it, and the limited time in which it impacted the Tenant, it seems to me that a reasonable abatement of the rent for the disrepair to the toilet would be a lump sum of $200.00. The Leaking Shower Head
Although the Tenant led evidence about his leaking shower head, it is not a claim that he makes in his application. Therefore, the Board has no jurisdiction to address it.
This order contains all of the reasons for my order within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $6,360.10. This amount represents: • a rent abatement in the amount of $5,160.10 for harassment and substantial interference; • general compensation of $1,000.00 for pain and suffering; and • a rent abatement of $200.00 for the Landlord’s failure to attend in a timely and effective manner to the disrepair to the Tenant’s toilet.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2025.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the rent due for the period commencing June 1, 2026, and continuing until the full amount has been paid.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

The Landlord must cease and desist demanding the Tenant sign a new lease; and imposing charges or obligations on the Tenant that are not authorized by the tenancy agreement or by the Act. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. 084355-24 In the matter of: T6 [address] ST CATHARINES ON Between: [name] [name] Tenants And [organization] Landlord [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were combined by Order of the Board and were heard by videoconference on September 10, 2025. The Landlord, represented by [name], a senior employee of the Landlord, and the Tenants attended the hearing. I enquired as to ownership of the rental unit. [name] advised that [organization] was not the owner of the rental unit but acted as the landlord within the meaning of the Act and did not dispute that [organization] was appropriately named as the respondent on these applications. The Tenants did not seek any amendment to the applications to add any other parties.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the applications that the Landlord failed to address an infestation of the rental unit by rodent, namely racoons.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the sum of $7,568.39.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on December 1, 2018 and moved out on November 30, 2024. The T6 application was commenced on October 15, 2024. The T2 application was commenced on December 12, 2024.

The Tenants first notified the Landlord that there were racoons in the attic on February 12, 2024 by email. This concerned the Tenants as they had an 8-month old child and we were concerned about the loud noises of scratching in the attic, as well as the health risks of having wild animals in their home and a newborn with no immune system.

After follow up contact to the Landlord, the Tenants received an email from the Landlord on May 6, 2024, three months after their initial notice of the rodent infestation, that the Landlord had contacted a pest control contractor. Despite follow up emails and calls to the Landlord, the Landlord did not send a pest control service to the rental unit until July 22, 2024, five months after the initial notice. The pest control service recommended remediation steps and sent a quote to Landlord for approval. After the inspection July 22, 2024, the Tenants followed up with the Landlord on July 29, 2024, August 1, 2024 and August 6, 2024. The Landlord approved the quotation in part and on August 14, 2024 Skedaddle completed the work they were authorized to perform - they sealed the existing entry point but not any other potential entry points for rodents.

The Tenants state that the [name] agent informed them that the insulation in the attic was ruined and was covered with rat and raccoon feces. The Tenants were told that the insulation needed to be repaired immediately. The Tenants stated they did not personally inspect the insulation and relied on the representative of [name] for this information.

After this repair, the rental unit was free of racoons for about two weeks. The racoon then returned through a new entry point. The Tenants notified the Landlord on September 3, 2024 about the return of the raccoons, and the Landlord arranged for [name] return on September 5, 2024 to investigate. [name] advised the Tenants that the raccoons made a new entry point and that their initial quote would have sealed that entry point but they were not approved to deal with it previously. The Tenants stated that [name] then sent a new quote to the Landlord for approval to seal this new entry point.

The Tenants followed up by email with the Landlord on September 13, 2024 as Skedaddle had not attended to seal the new entry point. As the Tenants were not satisfied with the pace at which the Landlord was proceeding to address the rodent infestation, the Tenants sent a N9 form on September 30, 2024 to end their tenancy effective November 30, 2024 as they were not prepared to live in a home with infested by rodents when the Landlord was not addressing the issue.
The Landlord responded the N9 notification immediately.

On October 16, 2024, the Landlord came to the rental unit to show the unit to a prospective tenant. The Tenants stated that the Landlord’s agent apologized for the presence of the raccoons, acknowledging that they were aware of the problem and had done nothing about it.
The Landlord had taken no additional steps to address the rodent infestation by the time the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on November 30, 2024.

In summary, the Landlord was advised of the rodent infestation on February 12, 2024, performed a repair on August 14, 2024, 6 months later, were advised of a second infestation on September 3, 2024 and did nothing for to remediate this infestation for three months until the Tenants moved out.

The Tenants described the effects the pest infestation had on them. They had a newborn child living in a home infested with rats and racoons and were concerned for their health, particularly the health of their child. The rodents were in the attic above their bedroom and their movements created noise which made it difficult to sleep. The Tenants stated that the lack of sleep was to the point of exhaustion but there was no lost time from work. The Tenants told the Landlord that the noise from the rodents was impacting their ability to sleep. They were also concerned with the cost of heating the rental unit for which they were responsible under the lease, following the advice from [name] that the insulation in the attic had been destroyed.

The Tenants stated they had no wish to move and left only because of the rodent infestation of their home. The Tenants stated that they even agreed to an above guideline rent increase from $1,775.00 to $2,000 per month in the fall of 2023 as they did not want to move. 17. [name] testified for the Landlord. She offered no credible explanation for the Landlord’s failure to address the rodent infestation, nor did she dispute the dates of the communications between the Tenants, the Landlord and [name]. It appeared to me that [name] was under the impression that once she had dispatched other staff of the Landlord to address the issue on February 12, 2024, that that was sufficient to address the problem. She stated that, until the communication from the Tenants on September 13, 2024, she thought the issue had been addressed. [name] stated that she was not in the maintenance department at the Landlord, as if that somehow excused the Landlord from performance of its obligations under the Act. 18. No other employees and no one from [name] testified. [name] stated that the Landlord was getting quotes from multiple service providers and was further delayed by the fact that approval of the quotes was needed from the owners of the rental unit and that the owners were slow in responding. I note that [name] acknowledged that [organization] was a landlord and so bears all of the responsibility of a landlord on a joint and several basis, and it is no excuse for one landlord to blame delays on another. Remedies 1. In their T6 application, filed before the Tenants vacated the rental unit but after they had delivered their N9 notice of termination, the Tenants claimed $10,000 for excess heating costs and abatement of rent of 50% for a period of 9 months and also requested that the Landlord be ordered to perform remedial work. 2. In their T2 application, filed after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Tenants repeated the claim for $10,000 and also requested that the Landlord pay the differential in rent at their new residence of $1,052 per month for a period of one year. The Tenants also claimed moving expenses of $1,822.39. The invoice from [name] the Mover states that the invoice amount is $1,472.39 and provided for a “tip” of $150. The remaining discrepancy between the invoice and the claim for $1,822.39 was not explained. 3. At the hearing, the Tenants acknowledged that the claim for $10,000 in the T2 and T6 applications was a duplication and their intention was not to claim $10,000 on each application. No evidence was led at the hearing with respect to the rent differential nor was that claim argued for in the Tenants’ submissions. 4. I find that an abatement of 40% of the Tenants’ rent for a period of 7 and one half months is appropriate. The Tenants clearly described both their communications with the Landlord and their concerns with the rodent infestation and the effect it was having on their enjoyment of their tenancy. The ability to sleep soundly and safely in the rental unit is an important element of the tenancy of which the Tenants were largely deprived. I have reduced the period of abatement of 9 months claimed by the Tenant as the Landlord should be allowed a reasonable period of time for response to the Tenants’ complaint, and as the infestation was remediated for a period of two weeks. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $6,000 ($2,000 x 40% x 7.5) is appropriate in the circumstances. I am not making a separate award for additional heating costs. The Tenants offered no evidence as to how a cost differential between their actual costs and the costs which would have been incurred had the attic been properly insulated could be calculated, and the quantification of a specific differential is a matter of speculation. 5. The Landlord is also ordered to pay the Tenants moving expenses of $1,472.39. I am satisfied that the sole reason for the Tenants’ move out was the pest infestation and the Landlord’s inaction in addressing the issue, and that the Tenants’ moving out was a reasonable response to the Landlord’s inaction. 6. The Tenants are also entitled to the filing fees for the T2 and T6 applications.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord raised the following preliminary issues: that the Tenant failed to provide particulars in the applications, the Tenant failed to disclose evidence in advance, and that the issues the Tenant intended to raise are out of time.

After a review of the applications, I expressed my concern with regards to the lack of particulars in the T2 application. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, and provided the following details in support of that allegation: “Unit 6 has made my life hell since 2 months of moving in. maintenance know, Landlord knows, she’s got other no contact orders with other tenants and she’s still here, most recently she phone police to have my charges when I wasn’t even here to have done it and my phone tracked were I was. I’m tired and I have children to raise I don’t need to have to walk on eggshell because of my neighbour its not ok”

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant and: “[name] the office lady has lied to my face said I could put up the barrier between our units so I have some privacy then after unit 6 complains she threatened to fine me if I don’t remove it. I would like to have it up please for my own safety and peace of mind. The Landlord claimed its unsafe when it wasn’t I had it reinforced so it would stay up and they stated it still need to come down cause I didn’t ask permission to have it so I asked permission and was denied. [name] also told unit 8 that it was okay she also build one and has no issues with their unit doing it but because unit 6 didn’t like it she couldn’t see my every move and what time I was arriving home is why I had to remove it being harassed and stalked from unit 6”

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (“Ball v. Metro Capital”). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case involves tenant applications instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established. This is a matter of procedural fairness. The respondent landlord must have notice of the case to be met.

I find there is insufficient detail in the Tenant’ T2 application to allow the Landlord to know the case being alleged against them, as well as understanding what remedies the Tenant is seeking for the T2 application.

While the Tenant submits that her testimony will provide the Board and the Landlord all the details required, I find that allowing the application to proceed with be unfair to the Landlord as the Landlord would not have had an opportunity to prepare adequately.

I do not find that adjourning the hearing for the Tenant to amend their T2 6 application and/or submit evidence would result in the most expeditious or fair outcome. Given that the applications were filed on December 13, 2024 and the parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference hearing on October 29, 2025, I find that the Tenant has had ample time to perfect their T2 application as they were provided oral directions and an interim order was issued on October 31, 2025 from the member that there was issues with adequacy of particulars with respect to the dates and times the issues were communicated to the Landlord and issues with limitation period. The Tenant provided that she did not understand the Member’s direction and she did not have any help as such that is why she did not amend.
The dismissal of the T2 application was communicated to the parties at the hearing.
ordered: The T2 applications are dismissed. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,048.00. Illegal Charge Collected:

The Tenant testified that when they signed their lease on April 21, 2025, the Landlord requested a deposit of $2,000.00, which was not the first or last month’s rent, and it would be returned upon vacating the rental unit. The Tenant then testified that they notified the Landlord they would be vacating the unit at the end of November 2025 on November 19, 2025 and asked to schedule an inspection before leaving the unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord sent text messages that she would return the deposit once an inspection was completed, then she sent a letter stating she was withholding the deposit due to damage and the fact the Tenant had unauthorized occupants in the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that the $2,000.00 was a pet deposit and also for the pool. The Landlord also testified that she felt the deposit was necessary as the Tenant was going to be building a bus home on the property. The Landlord testified she did not return the deposit because the Tenant had overnight guests with a dog that stayed for a couple months, there was building being done in the home, and the fireplace was constantly being used. The Landlord further testified that the money was not actually a deposit, but rather she was just holding it “in trust”.

Based on the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Regardless of how the Landlord classified the money, I find this was the equivalent of a security or damage deposit, which is not allowed under the Act
