issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant seeks to amend their application to correct the name of the Landlord from “[organization]” to “Carpreit Limited Partnership.”

In reviewing the file history, the Landlord was properly served with the Tenant’s application and the Notice of Hearing. Therefore, I do not find that the Landlord is prejudiced by the Tenant’s request to amend their application to correctly name the Landlord, and I granted the Tenant’s request. The style of cause has been amended to reflect this change.
The Tenant also seeks to amend their application to include a T6 application alleging that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit based on the same facts.
Although initially I had granted the Tenant’s request to amend the application, I am no longer of the view that this is appropriate.

Rule 5.2 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure indicates that applications can be amended, but notice must be given to the affected parties. As the Landlord was not given notice of the amendment request, the Tenant’s request is denied. [name] T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $264.14.

The Tenant alleges the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and failed to maintain the rental unit, for the following reasons: • The gas fireplace was unsafe and improperly maintained; • The dishwasher was moldy; • The dryer was in disrepair; • The air conditioning failed; and, • The furnace was rusty and unsafe. [name]

When the tenancy began, the Tenant was led to believe the gas fireplace was in good working order at the commencement of the tenancy. The fireplace had been inspected in October or November of 2023, and nothing was noted. However, when the fireplace was inspected on or about November 9, 2024, it was discovered the fireplace had previously been “red tagged.” The Tenant explains that a red tag means that an appliance has been identified as unsafe by a technician and should have resulted in the gas utility being shut off to the entire house.

After this was discovered by the HVAC technician on November 9, 2024, the Tenant called the Landlord to explain that there was a potentially serious problem with the fireplace. No one answered the phone. The Tenant reported the issue using the Landlord’s online portal on approximately November 10, 2024. She followed up with the Landlord on December 3, December 10, and again on December 13, 2024. Only after the Tenant advised the Landlord that she would be filing an application with the LTB did the Landlord respond to the Tenant on December 16, 2024. It was December 17, 2024, when the fireplace was serviced and returned to a proper working condition, and.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to respond to the Tenant’s concerns in a reasonable period of time. In my view, a reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that a concern about a gas fireplace demands an immediate response because a tenant’s safety could be compromised. 12. The Tenant advises that the impact was that they were not only unable to use their fireplace, but she worried for the entire time while awaiting repairs that the gas utility company would shut off the gas to the rental unit as the Tenant describes is the normal approach in this situation. 13. By way of remedy, the Tenant requests one months’ rent abatement totalling $2,114.40. 14. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 15. The guidance offered by the Divisional Court in Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. The Divisional Court said: [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 16. The Tenant’s evidence was that the fireplace could not be used for the period between November 9, 2024, to December 17, 2024. Although the Tenant’s rental unit was still accessible, the Tenant was denied the use and enjoyment of the fireplace for this period and reasonably feared for her safety after discovering the fireplace should never have been used. However, there was no evidence before me that the Tenant was endangered by using the fireplace nor that her gas utility had been turned off. When I consider similar cases to this one, and the impact the lack of the use of the fireplace had on the Tenant, I am of the view an abatement of 10% is appropriate in the circumstances. 17. The Tenant’s rent is $2,114.40 per month. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $264.14. (($2,144.40 x 12/365) x .10 x 38 days) Dishwasher 18. The Tenant claims that the dishwasher was moldy upon move in. The Landlord replaced the dishwasher in November 2023. 19. Section 29(2) of the Act states that no application can be made more than one year after the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. 20. The Tenant’s application was filed December 16, 2024. As the dishwasher was replaced in November 2023, the Tenant’s application is beyond the limitation period of one year. No order shall issue. Dryer 21. In July 2024, the Tenant advised the Landlord that the dryer was not functioning correctly. It had a broken part which had come loose and was snagging on clothes ruining them. 22. The Tenant advises the Landlord attended the rental unit about one week later and glued the part down. This resulted in the lint trap not being able to be removed from the dryer, but it did alleviate the problem complained of. The Landlord replaced the dryer in November 2024. 23. The Tenant advises that many of her clothes were ruined while the dryer was in disrepair. However, she also advised that these clothes were not particularly important to her at this period of her life. 24. I am not persuaded, based on the Tenant’s evidence, that the Landlord failed to respond appropriately to the Tenant’s concerns. They sent someone to look at the dryer and that individual provided a repair which alleviated the problem. 25. Although “substantial” is not defined in the Act, the plain and ordinary meaning of substantial is of considerable importance, size, or worth. The Tenant testified that the destroyed clothing was of little value to her at the time. As such, I am not persuaded that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. That is, clothing which had little value to the Tenant at the time is not of considerable importance or worth. No order shall issue. Air Conditioning Failure 26. The Tenant also testified the air conditioning system failed on May 16, 2024. The Tenant logged a complaint the same day in the Landlord’s online portal. A repair person attended on May 21, 2024, and a repair was conducted. 27. The Tenant states that there had been a heat wave during this period and it was uncomfortably hot during this period. 28. In my view, the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because the air conditioning failed. Again, in this type of claim, I must consider the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s complaint. The Tenant logged a complaint and within five days the repair was affected. In my view, the Landlord responded appropriately to repair the issue. No order shall issue. Furnace Rusty & Unsafe 29. The Tenant states the furnace was very rusty to the point of being unsafe. The Landlord replaced the furnace in November 2024. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord’s agents should have replaced the furnace earlier. However, the Tenant states she did not raise this concern with the Landlord before the filing of this application, by which time the furnace had already been replaced. 30. The Ontario Court of Appeal found in [name] v. [name], 1975 CanLII 764 (ON CA), [1975] O.J. No. 2279 that there should be no compensation for items of which the Landlord was unaware of before the Tenant complained. 31. Given that the Tenant never advised the Landlord of their concern about the rusty furnace, and given the Court’s instruction in McQuestion, I am not of the view that an award should be granted in these circumstances. Further, the Tenant offered no indication of any impact the rusty furnace had on the Tenant or the tenancy. No order shall issue. 32. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, the parties agree to remove [name], who was formerly named as a tenant, as a party to the application. As such, the application is amended to reflect this change.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The T5 application alleges the Landlord gave the Tenant a N12 notice of termination (“N12”) in bad faith. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit in 2016 and vacated the rental unit in November 2021 due the rental unit being sold and the Purchaser’s child needing to move into the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she drove by the rental unit and saw a “for sale” sign at the rental unit in July 2021. The Tenant then checked the realtor site and found a listing for the rental unit. The Tenant submitted into evidence a screenshot of an MLS listing for the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she subsequently saw a “sold” sign at the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that prior to the listing, the rental unit was under construction for a long time. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that she needed funds and sold the rental unit and that her husband served the Tenant with the N12.
The Landlord testified that the N12 was served with the understanding that the Purchaser purchased the rental unit for her son.
The Landlord testified that the sale of the rental unit closed in March 2021 and there was no contact with the Purchaser. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • First, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith; • Secondly, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice; • Thirdly, that the person named in the N12 did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

It is undisputed that the Landlord served the N12 for the Purchaser’s child to move into the rental unit and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit in accordance with Board order SOL- 22517-21 issued on October 5, 2021 for the Landlord’s L2 application based on the N12.
There is no evidence before the Board to substantiate or corroborate the Tenant’s claim that the Purchaser’s son did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The evidence of the Tenant was vague and inconsistent. The Tenant submits that the rental unit was listed for sale and sold after the Tenant vacated but the Tenant’s Legal Representative stated that they served the Purchaser at the rental unit two weeks before the hearing as the Purchaser is still on title and owes the rental unit. This leads me to believe the Purchaser did not sell the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she saw the “for sale” sign in July 2021 which predates the Tenant leaving the rental unit. The only documentary evidence the Tenant submitted into evidence was a screenshot of a MSL listing that is not dated. When asked, the Tenant could not recall when she obtained the screen shot. The Tenant gave no time frames of when the rental unit was under construction. The Tenant provided no pictures of the “for sale” or “sold” signs she observed, no pictures of the rental unit under construction, and no pictures of the listing that would demonstrate the rental unit was renovated to be sold after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant did not visit the rental unit after vacating to confirm who resides in the rental unit.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

In these circumstances, the burden falls on the Tenant to establish that the Purchaser’s son did not move into rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Tenant has failed to lead sufficient evidence to establish the Purchaser’s son did not move into the rental unit. As such, the Tenant did not satisfy the third requirement of section 57(1)(b) of the Act.

Given my finding on the third requirement, there is no need for me to address the first requirement of section 57(1)(b) of the Act with regards to bad faith. As the Tenant cannot establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(b), the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,871.85 by June 9, 2026.
I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below.

The Tenant, the Landlord and their Legal Representatives resolved a number of claims in each of the T1, T2 and T6 which I will be setting out under the appropriate application. The only issues that required adjudication include the rental fee of $50.00 per month for the chicken coop and the cost of the perished birds after the Landlord disconnected the power to the chicken coop. I must determine whether the chicken coop is included in the leased premises. Chicken Coop Usage and Perished Birds

The parties provided me with a copy of the executed lease dated January 1, 2022 whereby the Tenant was to rent the premises commencing November 1, 2022. The lease, drafted by the Landlord, stated “In consideration of the rents, covenants and obligations stipulated herein the Landlord and the Tenant have agreed to enter into a Lease for part of the premises including the buildings thereon (the “Buildings”) known municipally as [name], Lyndhurst, Ontario and as outlined in red on Schedule A attached hereto (the “Premises”). For greater certainty, the Premises include with a self-contained one bedroom suite and one room of the storage shed located on the north west corner of the building.”

The Tenant’s position is that the chicken coop is squarely within the red-lined area and as such, he should not have to pay $50.00 per month to rent the chicken coop. The Landlord’s position is that the premises include the one-bedroom unit and one room of a storage shed and thus the chicken coop is not part of the Premises rented by the Tenant. Thus, the Landlord believed that he had the right to charge $50.00 per month for the Tenant’s use of the chicken coop and is entitled to the $1,100.00 he collected from the Tenant.

After reviewing the lease in its entirety and reviewing the map on Schedule A (page 14 of the lease) which detailed the buildings included in the red-lined premises, I am satisfied that the chicken coop is included in the rented premises.

Further, I note that the Landlord drafted the lease and thus any ambiguity in the lease should be interpreted against the interests of the drafter of the contract. This legal doctrine is called contra proferentem. Although the first line of the lease states that the rented premises are set out within the red lined area in Schedule “A”, the second sentence is ambiguous when it states “for greater certainty, the premises include with a self-contained one bedroom suite and one room of the storage shed located on the north west corner of the building.”
Due to the confusion with the wording in the second sentence, the “greater certainty” clause, I must interpret the contract to the benefit of the Tenant who did not create the contract.

For these reasons and the clear map that details which buildings are included in the premises, I find that the lease allows the Tenant full use of the chicken coop. Therefore, the 22 months whereby the Tenant paid $50.00 per month for the use of the chicken coop, shall be returned to the Tenant. The Landlord shall pay $1,100.00 to the Tenant.

Regarding the issue of the perished birds, both parties agreed that the Landlord shut off the power to the chicken coop on January 22, 2026. The Landlord stated that his electricity usage had gone up drastically and the Landlord determined that this increase was due to the Tenant’s electricity use in the chicken coop. At that time, the Tenant had stopped paying the $50.00 per month for the use of the chicken coop and the Landlord “turned off the power to anything he deemed unnecessary” and he locked the electrical panel area.

As soon as the Tenant realized that the power was off in the chicken coop, he immediately requested that the Landlord turn the power back on as he had live birds in the chicken coop. The Landlord stated that he refused to turn the power back on as the Tenant was not paying the $50.00 per month for the use of the chicken coop. The 12 birds in the chicken coop froze and ultimately perished.
I am satisfied that the Landlord’s actions on January 22, 2026 directly caused the death of the Tenant’s birds and I order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $240.00 for this loss.

The parties also requested that I decide the issue of the hydro payment for the chicken coop and to determine who is responsible for that payment. Based on the lease, it makes it clear that the Tenant is to pay for his own specific hydro metre, J3030215 which is connected to his rental unit. The chicken coop is not connected to the Tenant’s hydro metre and thus the Tenant must pay for his own hydro expense for his rental unit only. T1 Application
The parties agreed that the Landlord would pay the Tenant $2,437.50 for the return of the HST charged on the lease payments.
The parties agreed that the Landlord would pay the Tenant $54.00 for the snow plow maintenance.
I ordered that the Landlord pay $1,100.00 to the Tenant as reimbursement for the illegal, monthly charge of $50.00 for the chicken coop for a period of 22 months. [name]

The parties agreed that the Landlord would pay the Tenant $92.02 for the hydro expense he incurred from the pump on the filtration unit which was connected to the Tenant’s hydro metre. This should have been an expense to the Landlord and the pump has now been connected to the Landlord’s hydro metre.
I ordered that the Landlord pay $240.00 to the Tenant for the replacement of his 12 perished birds. T6 Application
The parties agreed that the Landlord pay $135.60 to the Tenant as reimbursement for the septic tank maintenance.
The parties agreed that the Landlord pay $180.00 to the Tenant as reimbursement for the chimney sweep expense.
The parties agreed that the Landlord pay $1,160.00 to the Tenant as reimbursement for the snow plowing expense.
The parties agreed that the Landlord pay $424.73 to the Tenant as reimbursement for the locksmith expense.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,871.85. This amount represents: • $3,591.50 for the T1 application; • $332.02 for the T2 application; • $1,900.33 for the T6 application; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination claiming the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit for their child’s occupation. It was also undisputed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on October 30, 2024.

It was disputed that the Tenants vacated because of the N12 notice of termination. It was the Landlord’s position that the Tenants rushed out and had plenty of time to find a suitable rental unit. The Tenants testified that they moved out because they were served an N12 notice and told that the Landlord’s daughter was moving in.

I am satisfied that the Tenant’s vacated because of the N12 notice of termination. I am satisfied that even if they rushed their move out, it was in response to being served the N12 notice of termination. As such, I am satisfied that the Tenants have proven that they vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.
It was also disputed if the Landlord’s daughter occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant’s vacated. Again, it was undisputed that the Tenants vacated on October 20, 2024.

The Tenant, [name] [name] (“TL”), testified that he did not see anyone move into the rental unit but did the rental unit listed for rent after the Tenants vacated. TL testified that he was unsure of the status of the rental unit as of the hearing date. 9. [name] (“DS”) testified that he lives about 3 houses away from the rental unit and knows the Tenants. DS testified that after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit he has not seen anyone move in. DS testified there have been no lights on and no vehicles in the driveway, but there is a garage at the rental unit. 10. The Landlord testified that his daughter moved into the rental unit February 1, 2025. The Landlord testified that his daughter changed her driver’s license and utilities to the rental unit prior to moving in so that she could enroll her child into school in the area prior to moving in. The Landlord testified that his daughter did not move in right away because some renovations took place between when the Tenants vacated at the end of October and when his daughter moved in at the beginning of February 2025. 11. The Landlord provided copies of utility bills and his daughters driver’s license all of which have the rental unit as his daughter’s address. Again, the Landlord provided that although the address was changed prior to her moving in, it was done so that the Landlord’s daughter could enroll the Landlord’s granddaughter in school, but his daughter did move into the rental unit on February 1, 2025. 12. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that it is “more likely than not” that their assertions are true. 13. It was the Tenants’ burden to show that it was more likely than not that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. 14. Here, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have carried their burden to establish that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. 15. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that his daughter moved in on February 1, 2025. I am not persuaded by the Tenants evidence that the Landlord’s daughter is not living in the rental unit. Just because DS has not seen lights or a vehicle in the driveway does not mean that the rental unit is vacant. ON the other hand, the Landlord has presented a driver’s license and utility bills as well as consistent testimony that his daughter moved in on February 1, 2025. 16. The question then becomes if the Landlord’s daughter moved in within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. While it is undisputed that the Tenants vacated on October 20, 2024, TL also testified that there was a second N12 notice that was served to the Tenants with a termination date of December 31, 2024. So, while the Tenants may have vacated the rental unit by October 30, 2024, they actually had until December 31, 2024. 17. The Landlord’s testimony was that his daughter was living with a friend and had an obligation to remain at her previous residence, and she moved in as soon as possible after the renovations and her obligations to her friend were complete. 18. I am satisfied that the Landlord’s daughter moving in on February 1, 2025, was reasonable in light of the actual termination date of December 31, 2025, the Landlord’s daughter’s obligations to her previous accommodations, and the renovations that took place. 19. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenants established that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. 20. Since the Tenants did not prove the following requirement in subsection 57(1)(a): no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, I do not have to address whether the notice was served in bad faith. 21. As such, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants application is dismissed. March 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $898.00. Rent Deposit not Applied to the Last Month of Tenancy:

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2025, and he paid first and last month’s rent in the amount of $850.00 per month. The Tenant submitted supporting documentation to prove that this was paid. The Tenant testified that there was no lease, and he notified the Landlord on November 11, 2025 that he would be vacating the rental unit at the end of November 2025 due to cleanliness issues with the other tenants.

The Tenant testified he texted the Landlord as well as his wife on November 11, 2025, however, neither responded to his messages. The Tenant further testified he saw the Landlord’s wife in person near the end of November, and she told the Tenant they did not have any money to return the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant testified that Landlord’s have not been in contact since he moved out on November 30, 2025. The Tenant also submitted supporting evidence to show that he paid the Landlord for November 2025 rent.

While the Tenant may have given inadequate notice that they intended to vacate the unit, there is no evidence of mitigation from the Landlord as they did not attend. In the absence of any evidence of mitigation, I am not prepared to find that the Landlord did mitigate their losses.

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established through his uncontested evidence that the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $428.89. Assignment Denied and LMR to be [name]rated:

The Tenant testified that they sent an email to the Landlord on October 21, 2025 indicating that they wanted to move out November 1 or November 15, 2025 or, in the alternative, that they would find an individual to assign the lease to. The Tenant then testified that on October 23, 2025 they had a phone conversation with the Landlord who verbally told them that they would not consent to any assignment and they were refusing the request.
The Landlord confirmed that she told the Tenant that she would not agree to them assigning the lease to anyone as she previously had issues.

The Tenant testified that after the phone conversation in which the Landlord refused to allow an assignment, they filed an N9 notice on October 23, 2025 with the Landlord to end the tenancy on November 23, 2025 in accordance with the N9 notice.

The Tenant testified that the last month’s rent deposit was used for November 2025, however they are seeking the return of the pro-rated amount based on their termination date of November 23, 2025, and they are seeking interest on the last month’s rent deposit as it was never paid. The Landlord testified that she has not paid any interest for the last month’s rent deposit.

Section 95(4)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: (4) A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, (a) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent;

Based on the evidence provided, and the Landlord’s testimony that she denied a general request for assignment, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established that the Landlord denied the assignment which is not allowed by the Act. Therefore, the Tenant was entitled to serve the N9 notice terminating the tenancy within 30 days.

The Tenant’s rent was $1,395.00, and the daily compensation is $1,395.00 x 12 months divided by 365 days, which is $45.86. I therefore find that the Tenant is entitled to $321.02 for 7 days of daily compensation. The interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit for 1 year is $34.87. Key Deposit Illegally Retained:

The Tenant also testified that they had paid a $25.00 key deposit that the Landlord did not return once they had vacated the rental unit and returned the keys. The Landlord testified that she had not paid the key deposit back and she did receive the returned key.

Pursuant to paragraph 17 of O.Reg. 516/06: General of the Act, refundable key deposits, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs, are permitted. Once the Tenant returned the keys, the Landlord is obligated to refund the key deposit.

I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established that the Landlord collected a key deposit and did not return it to the Tenants despite that they returned their keys to the Landlord..
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $428.89. This amount represents: • $321.02 for the Last Month’s Rent Deposit from November 24, 2025 to November 30, 2025; • $25.00 for the key deposit; • $34.87 for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord' s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on November 2, 2022.

The Tenant stated that on December 11, 2024, a water leak occurred from the roof and seeped through to the living room, bedrooms, and basement, as it appears from the picture of the basement wall taken by the Tenant on December 11, 2024, and the picture of the bedroom wall taken by the Tenant on December 13, 2024 (DOC-4708408 and DOC-4708405; Exhibit 1, in bundle).

The Tenant indicated that as parts of the ceiling were falling apart , they placed buckets in all relevant areas and proceeded to contact the Landlord by phone and email to advise them of the issue on December 11, 2024, as it appears from the picture of the living room floor taken by the Tenant on December 12, 2024 (DOC-4708407; Exhibit 2).
The Tenant stated that after advising the Landlord of the issue, the Landlord proceeded to bring additional buckets to the rental unit on December 13, 2024, in order to help in collecting the water.
While the Tenant indicated that they were unsure as to the cause of the water leak, they did not believe it was a plumbing issue.
The Tenant stated that the water leak, which started on December 11, 2024, continued for a period of twenty (20) to twenty-five (25) days, through to January 5, 2025.

The Tenant indicated that ton December 23, 2024, the Landlord had a contractor attend the rental unit to work on the ceiling. Parts of the ceiling were removed and areas of the ceiling were left exposed.
The Tenant stated that no further work was conducted by the Landlord between December 23, 2024, and December 31, 2024, with water continuing to leak through to January 10, 2025, or January 15, 2025.

The Tenant indicated that they are a technician. They purchase, repair, and resell various second-hand electronic items, such as computers and tablets. They use the basement of the rental unit as their working space.

The Tenant stated that they continuous water leak proceeded to damage: • Ten (10) laptops . They did not recall the costs they incurred to purchase these laptops, nor the date on which they were purchased. They estimate that they were in their possession for a period of one (1) month prior to the leak. • Six (6) iPads. While the Tenant recalled that the tablets were purchased a month prior to the leak, they did not recall the costs they incurred to purchase them. • Eight (8) computer monitors which were in functional order. The Landlord was unable to sell these monitors due to the damage incurred by the water leak.

The Tenant further indicated that the continuous water leak also damaged a large number of clothing items in their child’s bedroom, and furniture items, such as two (2) couches and two (2) pouffes in the living room.

The Tenant is therefore seeking for the Landlord to pay them the amount of $10,000.00 to replace the damaged items and compensate for their los t wages as they were required to stay in the rental unit throughout the cou rse of the water leak, and could therefore not supplement their income as a driver for various delivery or ride-share services.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they did not try to dry or clean the couches and pouffes. They threw out these items after determining that they were damaged.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant stated that water seeped through multiple areas of the bedroom closet, which led to their child’s clothing being damaged.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the various laptops, tablets, and computer monitors were located in the basement at the time of the leak. They were left on the floor.

Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that they did not necessarily recall all the relevant dates pertaining to the event. They maintain that the water leak was continuous for a period of twenty-five (25) days.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant indicated that they were always present in the rental unit during the times that the Landlord attended the premises with their contractors. They refrained from leaving the rental unit during is time to monitor the water leak. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘A.H’) testified that they act as the Landlord’s resident manager . They are responsible for day -to-day operations, including leasing and maintenance services.
A.H agrees that a water leak occurred on December 11, 2024, and that the Tenant contacted them on that same day to advise them of the issue.

A.H stated that they provided buckets to the Tenant on December 11, 2024, in order to try to mitigate any damages. While in the rental unit, they saw damages to the wall in the bedroom based on the water leak, which they suspected stemmed from the roof.

A.H indicated that they contacted their contractor, WasteMind Building Solutions , on December 11, 2024, in order to schedule an on- site visit of the rental unit. A.H, along with WasteMind Building Solutions , attended the rental unit on December 13, 2024, and were able to diagnose the roof issue which led to the water leak.
A.H obtained a quote from WasteMind Building Solutions on December 18, 2024, for the repairs and remediation of the rental unit.

A.H stated that the repairs started on December 18, 2024, with the removal of the drywall in the bedroom. They agreed that after the drywall was removed, they left the affected area opened in order to ensure that it was dry prior to continuing the repairs. This was done to avoid enabling the presence of mould.

A.H indicated that the water leak was addressed and resolved by December 18, 2024, and that the remaining repairs to the drywall were completed by January 3, 2025. They dispute that the water leak reached the basement area.
A.H stated that they never advised the Tenant that they were required to remain in the rental unit during the ongoing repairs.
Under cross-examination, A.H agreed that their contractor, WasteMind Building Solutions , did not enter the rental unit on December 13, 2024. They went directly to the roof to investigate the issue.
Under cross-examination, A.H agreed that the repairs to address the water leak took place on December 18, 2024. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the tenant1.

In this case, while it is not in dispute that a water leak stemming from the rook occurred on as of December 11, 2024, I find that the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the issue upon being notified.

Indeed, while the Tenant’s testimony was at times vague and at times riddled with inconsistencies with respect to the timeline of the events, the extent of the damages, and the duration of the leak, the testimony from A.H, with respect to the steps taken to investigate the leak, secure the services of a contractor and complete the repairs, was consistent and credible.

I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim and accept the Landlord’s evidence that the leak was resolved by December 18, 2024, and that the repairs to the drywall were completed by January 3, 2025.

Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to maintain the rental unit with respect to the leak, as the Landlord acted reasonably and efficiently to resolve these issues after being advised by the Tenant . The mere occurrence of the leak, while certainly inconvenient or bothersome, does not automatically equate to the Landlord failing to abide by their obligations under the Act.

Subsidiarily, I also note that while the Tenant claimed an undefined portion of the amount of $10,000.00 as reasonable costs incurred to repair or replace damaged property, they failed to provide a detailed or itemized list of the child’s clothing, which they claim were damaged by the leak, nor did they provide any documentary evidence with respect to such costs.

In accordance with section 16 of the Act, the Tenant has an obligation to mitigate their damages. They provided no reasonable explanation as to why the clothing items, or living room furniture could not be dried and kept, as opposed to needing to be disposed of. It does not appear as though they attempted to mitigate their damages.

The Tenant’s evidence with respect to their damaged electronic items (laptops, tablets, and computer monitors) was also far too vague. The Tenant could not provide an estimation of 1 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name]. the costs they had incurred to purchase these damaged second- hand items, nor did they lead any evidence as to their state at the time that the leak occurred.
Furthermore, although the Act does not define “out -of-pocket-expenses,” they are understood as being “an expense paid from one’s own funds,” 2 in order “to accomplish a result.”3

The remaining portion of the $10,000.00 sought by the Tenant appears to be akin to lost wages and a loss of further economic opportunities as opposed to out-of-pocket-expenses. Such claims do not meet the definition of out-of-pocket expenses, as these amounts are not tied to an outlay of funds from the Tenant to obtain a desired finality.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $1,898.00 to the Tenants. Preliminary Issue: Are the parties in a landlord/tenant relationship?

The named Landlord and the Tenant entered into a “sublease” agreement on January 6, 2024, with a monthly rent of $1,850.00. The agreement identifies both Tenant as “Sub- Tenant” and the Landlord as the “Principal Tenant (Landlord).” The parties signed a 10- month fixed-term “sub-lease” agreement on January 3, 2025. The Tenant paid the agreed upon rent directly to the Landlord from January 6, 2025, to October 31, 2025.
It is not disputed that the Landlord was himself a tenant in the rental unit and was responsible for paying the rent to his landlord. The Landlord and Tenant did not enter into a valid subtenancy

Sections 2(2) and 97 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) set out the four requirements for an authorized subtenancy: 1. The tenant must vacate the rental unit 2. The sub-tenant has the right to occupy the rental unit for a fixed period ending on a specified date before the end of the original tenant’s lease 3. The original tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the renal unit after that specified date 4. The landlord must consent to the subtenancy

The facts of this case are somewhat similar to those in the Divisional Court’s decision [name] v. Ogunfeibo, 2019 ONSC 7423 (‘Tremblay’). In that case, [name] rented two separate rental units from the owner of the building; she lived in one unit and rented the other out to [name]. [name] wanted her daughter to move into [name] unit, took the position that the Act did not apply, and locked [name] out.

The Court determined that the parties the parties were not in a subtenancy under section 97(1) of the Act because (1) there was no evidence that the owner had consented to the subtenancy; and (2) the agreement between [name] and [name] did not provide for [name] return to the unit or otherwise mention a subtenancy.

The Court also reviewed the Act’s definitions of “landlord”, “rent”, “rental unit”, and “tenant”, as well as the exemption in section 5(i) of the Act. Noting the Act’s remedial purpose, the Court found that that [name] and [name] had entered into a landlord and tenant relationship subject to the Act: [36] The relationship between [name] and [name] falls squarely within the words of the statute. She is a landlord because she is a “person who permits occupancy of a rental unit”. She is not permitting [name] to occupy her unit with her, so the exemption in the definition of “landlord” in paragraph (a) of the definition does not apply. [37] Similarly, [name] is “a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit”. He pays that rent directly to [name] and he gave evidence that he believed she was the landlord. So, he fits the definition of “tenant”. [38] The bedroom, kitchen, common area, and bathroom are “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises” so they meet the definition of a “rental unit.” . . .

In this case, the Agreement does not give the “Principal Landlord” the right to reoccupy the rental unit, and the rental unit’s owner has not consented to the arrangement between the Tenant and the Landlord. Therefore, with the Court’s reasoning in Tremblay and section 97 of the Act in mind, I am not satisfied that the agreement between the parties was a valid subtenancy.

Furthermore and distinct from Tremblay, the agreement between the Landlord and Tenants in this case was plainly titled as a sublease and referred to the Landlord as the principal tenant (landlord) and the Tenant’s as the subtenants. I am therefore satisfied that the parties intended to and did enter into a landlord and tenant relationship.

Looking to section 202 of the Act, it requires the Board to ascertain the substance of the agreement between the parties, and in doing so it may disregard the outward forms of a transaction and have regard to the parties’ pattern of activities. When looking at this case, I am satisfied that, like in Tremblay, the Landlord is a person who permits occupancy of the rental unit without also occupying it, and the Tenants were people who paid rent in return for the right to occupy it. Significantly, the Landlord did not specify a date for his return or his right to reoccupy of the rental unit, conversely, the Landlord was ambiguous and provided the Tenant’s the option for extension should they so choose.

Applying section 202 to the facts before me, I am satisfied that the Act does apply to the arrangement between the parties and they are in a landlord and tenant relationship. To find otherwise would give effect to what I consider to be “deliberate or abusive” misconduct within the meaning of paragraph 15 of Tremblay. T1 Application
This application is about the return of a last month’s rent deposit.

Pursuant to section 106(10) of the Act a landlord is mandatorily required to apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. This means the first question before the Board here is: when did the tenancy terminate?

It was undisputed that the parties entered into a written fixed-term tenancy agreement (DOC-7043007) commencing on January 6, 2025, and ending on October 31, 2025. Furthermore, a deposit was provided to the Landlord in the amount of $1,890.00 on the same day.

The Tenant, [name] (SW) testified that Tenant [name] (YS) responded to a text message from the Landlord in August 2025, informing him they would be vacating at the end of the lease on October 31, 2025.

YS testified that she sent a text message as well as an email to the Landlord informing him that they had vacated the rental unit on November 1, 2025. Further, she states that she requested the return of the deposit, and the Landlord did not respond.

The Tenants did not use a Board-approved form to terminate their tenancy, and instead chose to send a text. However, I am satisfied that the Tenants substantially complied with the Act because their failure to use a Board-approved did not cause significant prejudice to the Landlord within the meaning of section 212 of the Act. I am satisfied that the Tenants’ text communicated the essential elements of an N9 Notice, that they were terminating the tenancy at the end of the fixed term tenancy’s term. The Landlord did not testify that he was confused about the text. As a result, I am satisfied that, as per section 88(1) and 212, the Tenants provided lawful notice of terminating their tenancy via text message, vacated on the termination date, and notified the Landlord of doing so, and are therefore only owe arears up to the date they vacated.

First, the Landlord testified that the deposit was only collected to ensure his protection and was not intended as a last month’s rent deposit. The Landlord then testified he lost rental income for new tenants for the month of November 2025 due to the Tenant’s renting the rental unit to [name] ([name]) who was living in the rental unit when he returned to the unit on October 31, 2025. He further testified that the parties had an agreement to use the deposit for [name] for the month of November 2025. And, finally, the Landlord states that due to confusion the rental unit was left empty during the month of November 2025.

I found the Landlord to be an elusive witness generally, and did not find their evidence on these points to be credible. I am not satisfied that it is more likely than not that the Tenants agreed to extend their tenancy and have their rental deposit applied to allow [name] to stay in the unit. While [name] may have been an unauthorized occupant, I am satisfied that the Tenants had terminated their tenancy and vacated the rental unit by the time the Landlord discovered [name], and the Landlord could have brought an A2 application to evict [name] and collect any arrears stemming from her unauthorized occupancy.

As a result, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord unlawfully retained the Tenants’ rental deposit pursuant to section 106(10) if the Act, and shall order that it be returned.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants shall be $1,898.00. This amount represents: • $1,850.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must compensate the Tenants in the amount of $2,398.00.
The Tenants testified that they were never provided with N12 compensation.

As of their move in date on April 1, 2024 the Tenants lawful rent was $2,455.00. This includes sums classified as rent in the amount of $2,350.00, $60.00 in hydro related utilities paid to the Landlords, and $45.00 in internet utilities paid to the Landlords. Because these utilities did not fluctuate each month and they were paid directly to the Landlords they fall within the definition of rent. Section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) defines rent as follows: “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and f or any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, […].

The definition of “services and facilities” under section 2 of the Act includes “heating facilities and services” and “utilities and related services” hence bringing in hydro and internet payments within the definition of rent.

The Tenants testified that the Landlords raised the internet portion of the rent to $50.00 effective April 1, 2025 on approximately 60 days notice. I was not provided with any evidence that 90 days notice was given or that a Board form was used. The Tenants paid an increased rent of $2,460.00 from April 1, 2025 to their move out date which is less than 12 months. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on December 6, 2025. Pursuant to section 116(4) of the Act this increase to $2,460.00 is void because the Landlords did not provide the required amount of 90 days notice. Hence, the lawful rent remained $2,455.00. Compensation for N12 Notice owing

The Landlords gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by the Act. The N12 notice was served on October 1, 2025 and had a termination date of November 30, 2025. 7. $2,455.00 in N12 compensation is owing to the Tenants. However, on the Tenants application they only claim $2,350.00 in compensation and thus are limited to that amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $2,398.00. This amount represents: • $2,350.00 for compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
