issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The application was fil ed on December 18, 2024.
The rental unit is a single-dwelling home. The Tenants have exclusive use of the property. The Tenants moved in on November 15, 2022, and moved out on March 7, 2025.

The following issues were raised by the Tenants in their application: 1. Snow Removal: The Landlords refused to clear the snow on the driveway, sidewalk and front porch. 2022-2023, 2024-2025. 2. [name]: The Landlords failed to provide lawn maintenance in the spring and summer of 2023 and 2024. 3. Smoke Detector Testing: The Landlords failed to test the smoke detectors.
Steps in Garage: The Landlords failed to maintain the steps in the garage.
Garage Door Opener: The Land lords failed to maintain the garage door opener.
Water Softener: The Landlords failed to r epair or replace the water softener unit.

Microwave: The Landlords failed to repair or replace the microwave. 4. Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 5. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. [name] and [name] 6. The Tenants allege that the Landlords failed to provide exterior grass cutting and snow removal. The Tenants allege that the Landlords expected the Tenants to shovel the snow and take care of the grass. The Tenants assert that because the Landlords were not responsive, that they paid individuals to do the work. 7. The Landlords evidence is t hat the Tenants were responsible for exterior maintenance of the rental unit, lawn maintenance and snow removal, because it is within their exclusive use, and they had a verbal agreement to this effect. The Landlord indicated making a verbal agreement to this effect because he did not reside in Canada during the term of the tenancy.
The Tenants deny having any agreement that t hey would be responsible for the exterior maintenance. The Tenants maintain that the exterior maintenance is solely the Landlords’ responsibility.

I agree with the Landlor d that there was an agreement that the Tenants would maintain the exterior maintenance. The Tenants testified they have exclusive use of the property, that they initially conducted exterior maintenance, and that due to a back injury, the Tenants could no longer conduct the exterior maintenance. As a result of the injury, the Tenants reached out to the Landlord for help. At times, the Landlord did assist knowing that the Tenants had suffered an injury. During the time the Tenants requested help due to the Tenant’s back injury, the Landlord, within a reasonable time, would arrange for someone to attend and address the maintenance request.

The Landlords do not live in Canada. The Landlords rely on the Tenants to conduct maintenance, particularly snow removal services when there is an accumulation of snow, or if something in the exterior of the property needs to be maintained. This was as per their verbal agreement.

A landlord is responsible for complying with the Maintenance Standards regulation, [name]. 517/06, which requires that exterior common areas shall be maintained in a condition suitable for their intended use and free of hazards and further makes a landlord responsible for removing snow and ice.

The Tenants had exclusive use of the property. There was an agreement for the Tenants to be responsible for the exterior maintenance. When the Tenants had a back injury, the Tenants made requests to the Landlord for lawn maintenance, as was done on March 6, 2024, via text, the Landlords indicated that he would arrange to have someone attend for lawn maintenance. Moreover, via texts on January 23, 2024, the Tenants asked the Landlords “Could you please ask snow cleaning guy to come and do snow shoveling.” The Landlords responded, “will talk to him”. This is indicative that the Landlords responded in a reasonable manner, even if there was an agreement that the Tenants maintain the exterior of the property. I accept that the Landlords assisted to help the Tenants out due to their injury.

The Tenants claim to have paid for people to attend at the property to do the required exterior maintenance but failed to provide details as to who was hired, when were they at the property doing work and how much was paid for their services. They do not have any receipts or information about the services rendered. As such, I find the Tenants failed to prove on a balance or probabilities that they incurred expenses.

The Tenants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to this issue. Upon being notified by the Tenants of the need for lawn maintenance or snow removal, the Landlords took reasonable steps to respond and address. No remedy is granted. Smoke Detector Testing
The Tenants claim that the Landlords never tested the smoke detectors in 2 years. The Tenants indicated that the smoke detectors continued to be operational but were not tested.
The Landlords agree that the smoke detectors were operational throughout the Tenants’ tenancy.

As the smoke detectors continued to be operational, I find that the Tenants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to this issue. No remedy is granted. Steps in Garage
The Tenants assert that the garage stairs needed repair in December 2022 and informed the Landlords. The Landlords repaired the steps by February 2023.

In accordance with subsection 29(1) of the Act, this application must be made within one year of the date of the alleged breach. The steps were rectified by February 2023 and the application was filed on December 18, 2024. This claim is outside of the one-year limitation period. Garage Door Opener

The Tenants assert that the garage door opener broke in December 2022 and was fixed by the Landlords by April 2023. For the same reason noted above, the claim is outside of the one-year limitation period. [name]

The Tenants claim that the water softener unit broke in September 2023, and that they notified the Landlord about it a couple weeks afterwards. They indicated that the water had a murky yellow colour and informed the Landlord about it. Upon learning of it, the Landlord sent a technician to inspect and assess the unit, only to find out it had to be replaced. The Tenants assert the Landlords replaced the water softener unit in November 2024.

The Landlords assert they only learned about the water softener unit being broken in December 5, 2023, via email (Exh 17). The Landlords assert that the unit was replaced on January 26, 2025, as is noted by a Home Depot receipt. The Landlords assert that since the Tenants were behind in rent, it was a financial strain, and they were unable to replace it beforehand.

I find the Landlord’s became aware of the water softener unit not working via email sent by the Tenants to the Landlord on December 5, 2023. The Landlord initially sent a technician to inspect the unit. The technician disconnected the unit and informed the Landlord a new unit was needed. The Landlord replaced the unit in January 2025, as is evidenced by a Home Depot Receipt.
After having the water softener unit disconnected, no further complaints were made to the Landlord. The water was no longer a murky yellow colour. Eventually the water softener was replaced.

The Tenants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. Upon learning of the yellow murky water, the Landlord took steps to identify the problem. A technician was sent to inspect the water softener unit and disconnected it so that the Tenants had usable water in the house. The Landlords’ actions were reasonable in rectifying the issue. The Tenants were able to reside at the unit and were able to use the water and plumbing at the rental unit for all its intended purposes. Microwave
The Tenants claim the Landlords failed to repair or replace a microwave which had broken in the summer of 2023. The Tenants indicated that the microwave had not been fixed at all.

Exhibit 1 (DOC 6824470) shows that the Tenants informed the Landlord of a broken switch on the microwave on June 28, 2023, via text. The Landlord responded by permitting the Tenants to call someone to fix the microwave. On the next day, June 29, 2023, the Tenants indicated they did not know anyone who can fix it. The Landlord agreed to look into having it repaired and offered the Tenant a replacement microwave to use which was located in the basement storage room of the house.

The Tenants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords did not meet their obligations under s. 20(1) of the Act with respect to this issue. In this case the Landlords provided the Tenants with a working microwave upon learning that the Tenants microwave had broken.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed

The Tenant filed their application with the Board on December 8, 2025. The facts provided in the application referenced lack of hot water and issues pertaining to pest infestations. On March 4, 2026, the Tenant filed an amendment to his application which involved uploading a document with the Board that outlined new issues pertaining to dog feces and garbage at the rental unit/residential complex. No detailed facts were provided on these applications. In other words, both the application, and the amended application, lacked specific details pertaining to dates/time of when the issue arose, and when the Tenant advised the Landlord of the issues. Further, the amendment did not contain any remedies the Tenant sought pertaining to the new issue that were raised.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative advised that both the application and the amended application lack specific details, is confusing (difficult to understand), and that the Landlord does not understand the timeline – which I understood to mean, the Landlord does know the date range governing the issues. He further claimed that the Tenant has not served their evidence to the Landlord.

The Tenant claimed that he had served his evidence to the Landlord and relied on a copy of a text message filed with the Board to substantiate his claim. In this text message, the Landlord is expressing difficulty with obtaining the Tenant’s evidence as the Landlord is not familiar with technology. It was clear based on this documentary evidence that the Landlord did not receive the Landlord’s disclosure. The Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence whether he had served the Landlord via an alternative method of service with the evidence that he intended to rely on at the hearing. Thus, I was not satisfied on balance of probabilities that the Tenant had disclosed their evidence to the Landlord.

Considering the submission of the parties, the Board determined it was appropriate to dismiss the Tenant’s application. Both the application, and the amended application, are missing specific details to allow the Board and the Landlord to assess when the alleged events occurred, and whether the original application has been filed prior to the expiration of the limitation period as set out in subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Tenant also did not disclose their evidence. Due to the lack of specific details in these applications and the absence of the disclosure of the Tenant's evidence, the Landlord could not reasonably be expected to respond in these circumstances and does not know the case to be met. The Tenant claimed that his issues are still ongoing. Accordingly, the Board determined that the Tenant would not be prejudiced by the dismissal as they may wish to file a new application that includes specific details for grounds of the application.
For the above noted reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: [address] Ottawa ON [name] (the 'Tenants ') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was heard by videoconference on April 29, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the hearing. As of 2:23pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the total amount of $518.00 on or before June 9, 2026. Request to Amend the Application
During the hearing, the Tenants sought to amend their application in order to also claim out- of-pocket expenses related to the increased hydro costs they had incurred.

The Tenants did not seek to amend their application prior to the hearing, nor did they advise the Landlord of any such amendment request nor serve them with the corresponding documentation in advance of these proceedings.1

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord was unaware of the Tenants’ amendment request, and therefore that it would – under the circumstances – be procedurally unfair to grant such an amendment and proceed in hearing claims the Landlord was unaware were subject to be heard2.

The Tenants’ request to amend the application was therefore denied. Pursuant to the application they had filed on December 9, 2025, the Tenants were advised that the maximum amount they were subject to receive – should their application be successful – was $470.00, as a rent abatement. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenants filed their application on December 9, 2025. At the time, they had sought to raise two (2) issues related to t he allegation that the Landlord had failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, specifically a water leak near the entrance of the rental unit stemming from the ceiling (and its corresponding damages ) and a leak in the bathroom.
During the hearing, the T enants elected only to present the issue related to the water leak near the entrance of the rental unit. They no longer sought to present the issue related to the bathroom.

The Tenant [name] ( hereafter referred to as ‘M.A’ ) testified that a water leak emanating from the roof of the rental unit occurred during the month of May 2025, near the entrance of the rental unit.

M.A stated that while they had previously communicated concerns with the Landlord with respect to water leaks and the potential presence of mould, they proceeded to send the Landlord a formal email on May 30, 2025, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Tenants to the Landlord on May 30, 2025, at 8:00am (DOC-6954793 and DOC -6954751; Exhibit 1, in bundle).

M.A indicated that following consecutive days of rain showers, the leak at the entrance of the rental unit worsened, and led to parts of the ceiling falling apart on November 6, 2025. The Tenants proceeded to contact the Landlord to advise them of the worsening issue, as it appears from a copy of the WhatsApp correspondences between the Landlord and the Tenants dated November 6, 2025 (DOC-6954770; Exhibit 2).

M.A stated that the Landlord proceeded to send a maintenance technician to the rental unit on November 7, 2025. The Tenants indicated that the technician drilled a hole in the ceiling area affected by the water leak, placed a plastic cover to collect any water coming through, and left. 1 Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. 2 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160.

M.A indicate d that they proceeded to send another message to the Landlord on November 15, 2025, to advise them that no technician had returned to the rental unit following their departure on November 7, 2025, as it appears from a copy of the WhatsApp messages sent by [name] to the Landlord on November 15, 2025 ( DOC-6954783; Exhibit 3).

M.A stated that water continued to leak and as the hole drilled within the ceiling by the Landlord’s maintenance technician was not properly sealed, the temperatures within the rental unit were getting increasingly cold with the changing weather and led to an increase of the hydro costs.

M.A indicated that the Landlord never followed up with the Tenants following their November 15, 2025, WhatsApp messages (Exhibit 3) and the issue related to the ceiling and the corresponding water leak was not resolved by the time the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on January 9, 2026.

M.A stated that the ongoing issues with the water leak and the exposed ceiling caused them health issues, and impacted their holiday season, as they could not have family members in attendance at the rental unit due to the exposed ceiling and the increasingly low temperatures.

M.A indicated that “it was just cold” in the rental unit due to the exposed ceiling, and despite the heat being turned on throughout the rental unit, the heating system was not able to properly compensate and regulate the interior temperatures to comfortable levels. This contributed to M.A having a serious a prolonged flu diagnosis.

The Tenants therefore claimed the amount of $470.00 as a rent abatement as a result of the Landlord’s failure to properly address the water leak and ceiling damage near the entrance of the rental unit. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the tenants3.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before, I am satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act 3 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name]. or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, with respect to the water leak emanating from the ceiling, of which they were notified of May 30, 2025 (Exhibit 1).

Indeed, the Tenants’ testimony was consistent and credible. I therefore accept that the Tenants contacted the Landlord on multiple occasions to advise them of the issue and the worsening situation, only for the Landlord to delay addressing the matter and failing to complete the repairs (Exhibit 1 to 3).

I do not find that delaying sending a technician to the rental unit to investigate the issue of the leak to November 6, 2025 (which equates to a delay of one hundred and sixty days) equates to the Landlord taking reasonable steps to address the issue.

Furthermore, I do not find that exposing parts of the ceiling, only to leave a poorly sealed hole in the ceiling of the premises for a period of at least sixty -five days – during colder months of the year (between the month of November 2025 and January 2026) resulted in the Landlord taking adequate steps to resolve the issue.

I accept the Tenants’ testimony that the ongoing issue with respect to the water leak and the corresponding hole in the ceiling impacted the temperature within the rental unit, which in turn impeded the Tenants from benefitting from the rental unit during the holiday period, as they had originally intended.
While the Tenants may have been entitled to a greater rent abatement, they can only be awarded remedies sought within their application.4

Accordingly, pursuant to the Tenants’ uncontested evidence and submissions, t and my knowledge of similar case, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement in the amount of $470.00, as a result of the issue related to the water leak in close proximity to the entrance of the rental unit, and the corresponding damage to the ceiling.
The Tenants also incurred costs of $48.00 for the filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the total amount of $518.00, which represents: • $470.00 for a rent abatement, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 9, 2026. 4 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This application was heard with LTB-L-038594-25.
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,918.00 by June 7, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. T1 Application

The Tenant stated that he was charged an illegal rent amount (above his legal rent of $850.00/month) for July, 2024 in the amount of $20.00, August, 2024 in the amount of $350.00, September, 2024 in the amount of $450.00, October, 2024 in the amount of $450.00, November, 2024 in the amount of $450.00 and December, 2024 in the amount of $50.00 totalling $1,770.00. The Landlord agreed that he had increased the Tenant’s rent because his own expenses had risen and he required more funds to pay the bills. The Tenant stated that he paid the extra rent because the Landlord threatened to give away his room while he was away in India.

Section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states: “A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.” Further section 135(4) of the Act states: “No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act.”

The Tenant filed this application on December 18, 2024 which complies with the Act. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to pay $1,770.00 to the Tenant and the Tenant is entitled to his application fee of $48.00. [name] Evidence

The Tenant provided a very large number of dated emails from the Landlord to the Tenant which included this sample of correspondence. The Tenant left for India on June 1, 2024 to spend a few months with his family as his grandmother passed away. The Landlord arrived in Toronto on June 9, 2024 to rent out two vacant rooms in the house and remained at the house to complete some repairs. a) April 30, 2024 – “Total stupidity from guys from India. What the hell do you know? …not using your brain that God gave to you.” b) April 30, 2024 – “For fuck sake you Indian people just can not treat the ladies the right way.” c) May 28, 2024 – “If I need to fly to Toronto now because of your shallow brain… I will simply send you all out of the house. You guys are retards.” d) June 13, 2024 – “If you want to stay is $1,200.00 or you are out as well. [name] is a gay. Do not go to Russia. They would shoot you on the spot. Your hormones are messed up.” e) June 17, 2024 – “Today I am giving you notice to move out in one week. This is Canadian law. But you have a chance to apply for your place at $1,200.00 per month. It is up to you.” f) July 5, 2024 – “I’m waiting for you to come back and move you out of the house. I can pack all your things in the black bags and put them out of the house on the driveway on July 12, 2024.” g) September 11, 2024 – “Don’t be an asshole because I was paying internet for almost 3 years. I was paying for you gays to use it for your job!!” h) December 28, 2024 – “Please start packing and move to another place by January 31, 2025. There are 8,500 places to rent in Toronto” – attached notice to move i) March 22, 2025 – “It is my house. Owner. You are just the tenant. I am coming home. Because of you I lost my wife last fall!”

The Tenant stated that while he was in India with his family, he received constant emails and telephone calls from the Landlord where the Landlord continued to demand more rent from the Tenant. The Tenant stated that the Landlord yelled and screamed at him on the phone and kept calling him gay which upset his mother very much. He stated that the Landlord called him every day from June 13, 2024 to June 17, 2024 yelling at him and telling him to move out of the house and accusing him of being gay. The Landlord sent him advertisements for different properties and kept telling him that he was being thrown out.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord removed everything out of his room at the end of July of 2024, moved his possessions into another room and allowed another person to rent his room while he was away. When the Tenant returned on September 9, 2024, another woman was staying in his room so he stayed with friends for a couple of days until that woman moved out of his room.

The Tenant stated that he had a number of plants that his friend was watering for him when he was away but the Landlord threw all of the plants into the backyard where they died. The Tenant also had a gold chain that belonged to his grandmother that was in his room when he left for India along with $10,000.00 in cash. He believes that the Landlord took the chain and the cash but the police were not able to charge anyone due to the fact that so many people had access to his room.

The Tenant stated that after September 9, 2024, the Landlord remained in the house until December and the Landlord constantly harassed him, called him derogatory names and racial slurs daily and he alleged that he was assaulted by the Landlord. The Tenant stated that he could not use the kitchen to cook his food during that time period because the Landlord’s harassing behaviour made it impossible to be in the kitchen.

The Tenant stated that he lost his job in February of 2025 due to the amount of stress that he has been under dealing with the Landlord. He stated that he wrote emails to the Landlord and his son begging them to stop the Landlord from bullying him. His former legal representative also sent an email to the Landlord advising him that all communication should go through the representative, but the Landlord continued to harass the Tenant personally.

The Tenant is seeking $5,100.00 in rent abatement due to the Landlord’s continuous racist attacks, his never-ending harassment and bullying and the substantial interference to his enjoyment of the rental unit over the last year. The Tenant is claiming $425 x 12 months which is a 50% abatement of his monthly rent of $850.00.

He is also seeking $1,000.00 for the loss of his plants and $360.00 for the time period where he could not cook in the kitchen. Although he is seeking the return of the gold chain and the $10,000.00 in cash from his room, that is not a claim that can be dealt with in this tribunal.

The Tenant is also seeking that the Landlord pay an administrative fine and he is seeking an order preventing the Landlord from continuing his harassment, bullying and substantial interference. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord stated he only behaved that way because he thought that the rental house was exempt from the Act.

The Landlord stated that he moved the Tenant’s possessions because he arranged for new flooring to be installed and that the Tenant’s plants caused water damage to the floors. He stated that while the contractors were working on the floors, he stayed in the house to ensure that everyone’s possessions were safe. He stated that he had not seen a gold chain or cash in the Tenant’s room.

Regarding the use of the kitchen, the Landlord stated that the Tenant was allowed in the kitchen and he did not stop him from using it. He felt that the claim for $360.00 was nonsense. He then said, “these Indians, they don’t do anything and they don’t understand anything.” I immediately advised the Landlord that this type of comment is not acceptable and to stop.

The Landlord then stated that in June of 2024, there was a flood in the basement of the house and he felt that the Tenant caused all of this destruction and expense. He stated that the Tenant did not know how to turn off the water in the laundry room. He then stated “They are all gay-all those Indians, they have no common sense.” I advised the Landlord that his testimony was complete due to his outright, racist comments. Analysis

The pertinent section of the Act that inform the Tenant’s claims on the T2 Application is section 22: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The Tenant’s T2 Application also alleges that the Landlord harassed him. The pertinent section of the Act that inform the Tenant’s claims on the T2 Application is section 23: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

There is no definition of “harassment” under the Act but generally speaking harassment is usually considered to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be most unwelcome. [See for example, Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. Pac, 2021 CanLII 146690(ON LTB)]

The Tenant’s oral evidence was corroborated by the many, dated emails from the Landlord which confirmed that the Landlord acted abusively toward the Tenant, he used racial slurs consistently, he harassed and bullied the Tenant and he substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant was made to feel as if he did not belong in the rental unit and that he was fearful of being evicted. The Tenant’s own emotional stress and grief from the situation was visible throughout his testimony.

The Landlord did not deny any of the Tenant’s allegations except to say that he had not seen a gold chain or cash in the Tenant’s room. The Landlord felt that he had a right to treat the Tenant in the manner that he did because this tenancy was exempted from the Act. This only confirmed that the Landlord felt that he could treat the Tenant in whatever way he felt was necessary for the Landlord’s own purposes and goals to be realized. The Landlord felt that his actions did not have to comply with tenant protection legislation and/or the Human Rights Code.

The Landlord’s outbursts including racial slurs and abusive language towards the Tenant heard today in the hearing room provided a deeper look at the character of the Landlord. The Landlord’s outbursts today were completely inappropriate and were racial slurs directed towards the Tenant. I am very sorry that the Tenant had to be subjected to that inhumane treatment today.
As such, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established the Landlord’s substantial interference and harassment.

The Tenant sought a 50% rent abatement of 5,100.00 for a one-year period where the Tenant experienced harassment, bullying, racist comments and substantial interference by the Landlord. The Tenant’s application was filed on December 16, 2024 and I note that the majority of the harassment started in April of 2024 and so the one year will commence on April 30, 2024 and end on March 31, 2025.

Abatement recognizes the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for them he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

Based on the detailed emails, the aggressive bullying by the Landlord, the racial slurs clearly directed to the Tenant and the Landlord’s repetitive attempts to evict the Tenant, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the 50% rent abatement for a one-year period. The amount of $5,100.00 will be ordered as abatement.

The Tenant sought a $1,000.00 in compensation for the replacement of his plants that had been thrown out by the Landlord and they all ultimately died. I was not provided with any type of receipt for the plants to quantify their value at $1,000.00 and as such, I will not be awarding an amount for the plants.

The Tenant sought $360.00 in compensation for having to eat out during a period of time when he was not able to use the kitchen due to the Landlord residing in the house at that time. I was not provided with any type of receipt for these extra meals and as such, I will not be awarding an amount for the food.

The Tenant sought an order that the Landlord be prevented from continuing his harassment, bullying behaviour and substantial interference. This is not the type of order that can be enforced and I suggest to the Landlord that he seek out legal assistance to advise him of his rights and responsibilities which should assist both parties in the future.

The Tenant is also requesting that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

Administrative fines are generally ordered where there is egregious conduct by a landlord. In this case, the Landlord’s actions included aggressive harassment, racist slurs and personal attacks on the character of the Tenant. Despite the Tenant’s emotional condition during the hearing, the Landlord continued to verbally attack the Tenant and called him “a stupid Indian who doesn’t have any common sense” at the end of the hearing.

Based on the Landlord’s actions, I am ordering him to pay an administrative fine of $5,000.00 to the Board. I am hopeful that this fine will encourage the Landlord to comply with the Act and to deter from future, similar behaviour. T6 Application

The Tenant stated that the Landlord failed to install an exhaust fan in the kitchen at the request of all of the tenants. The Tenant explained that with 4 different people residing in the same house and cooking different types of food, the smells accumulate and make it very difficult to deal with. The Tenant stated that although there is a door and a window in the kitchen, that door and window blow the air directly into the next door neighbour’s house which is very close to the rental house. The Tenant stated that is not an option as it would cause a nuisance to the neighbours.

The Landlord stated that the tenants just have to learn to get along and cook respectfully in the kitchen. He stated that there is no law that states that he must have an exhaust fan in the kitchen and that he cannot afford to install one.

As the Tenant did not provide me with any documentation to show that an exhaust fan is required in a kitchen under the Ontario Building Code, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s actions breached the maintenance standards under the Act and regulations.
As such, I am dismissing the T6 application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,918.00. This amount represents: • $1,770.00 for excess rent collected; • $5,100.00 for rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting funds from the rent each month as necessary.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
T he Landlord shall pay an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 to the LTB by June 7, 2026. May 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: Board records indicate the Tenant requested to amend the application in writing on April 23, 2026.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord had received a copy of the amendment.
The amendment request is for the Board to find the N1 notice invalid and return the Tenant’s lawful rent to the prior amount. Analysis
The Tenant’s request to amend the application is for the Board to make a finding the notice is invalid and return the rent to the prior amount.
I make note the Tenant’s original application is also seeking compensation for the difference in rent the Landlord charged should the Tenant be successful in her application.
I see no need to amend the application given the Tenant’s requests are remedies already available to the Tenant should the Tenant be successful in her application.
In my view the application does not need amending and shall remain unchanged. Determinations:
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2009.
The Tenant is still in possession of the rental unit.

Board records indicate the Tenant filed the application on November 21, 2025 with allegations the Landlord has collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant filed evidence with the Board to support her claims in the application of the illegal rent increase / invalid N1 notice (DOC-7827423).

The Tenant stated that the Landlord served an N1 notice of increase in rent on June 1, 2024 indicating that the Landlord was applying a 5.5% rent increase in the amount of $63.68 effective December 1, 2024, making the new lawful rent $1,221.43. The Tenant submitted a copy of the N1 notice to support her claim.

The Tenant’s position is that the notice is defective pointing out the 5.5% increase is incorrect as it is above the Board order AGI amount of 1.46% combined with her 2.5% annual increase. The Tenant also points out the calculated amount of $63.68 and the total rent increasing to $1,221.45 are above the legal increase allowed by the Board.
The Tenant’s evidence contained the Landlord’s rent ledger and indicated the Tenant’s prior lawful rent as of November 1, 2024 was $1,089.87.
The Tenant is seeking compensation in the amount of $323.27, the difference of the illegally charge rent from her prior lawful rent.
The Landlord’s position is the N1 notice is not defective and the 5.5% amount indicated on the notice is a clerical error along with the total rent increase and the increased amount of $63.68.
The Landlord’s legal representative stated that the actual increase for the Tenant as of December 1, 2024 should be 2.5% and this amount was being paid by the Tenant as of December 1, 2024.

The Landlord’s legal representative submits that the Landlord ledger evidTenant’s own ledger shows she started to pay $1,117.11 as of December 1, 2024 which is a 2.5% increase from the prior $1,089.87. Analysis

Section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Notice of rent increase required 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (1). Contents of notice (3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (3).
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has proved the allegations in the application.
Although the Tenant claims the Landlord’s applied increase amount of 5.5% is above the allowable AGI amount, plus her annual increase is incorrect.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 14 states: 3% Limitation The maximum annual increase allowed in an application based on capital expenditures or security services or both is 3% above the guideline. Where more than 3% is justified, the rent is increased by 3% in the first year and any remaining increase may be taken in subsequent years, to a maximum of two additional years at 3% each year.
Nonetheless, the Landlord’s increase of rent whether combining an AGI amount or an annual guideline increase must correctly identify the amount the Landlord is seeking.
Based on the submission of the N1 notice, none of the calculations in the notice are consistent with the AGI or annual guideline increase.

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that the Tenant had started to pay the annual guideline increase of 2.5% as of December 1, 2024 in the amount of $1,117.11 up from $1,089.87 and the 5.5% increase indicated on the notice is a clerical error subject to section 212 Substantial Compliance Sufficient: Substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. 2006, c. 17, s. 212.

I disagree with this position. The Act requires the Landlord to give a valid notice of rent increase and must include particulars based on accurate percent increase of rent, the calculated amount of rent increase and the total new increase amount the Tenant is expected to pay.
The Landlord’s N1 notice is deficient with respect to all three of these requirements.

Based on the ledger the Tenant’s lawful rent on November 1, 2024, one month before the annual guideline increase was $1,089.87. The percent indicated on the notice at 5.5% does not equal the increased amount and the total amount of lawful rent indicated does ont add up with any of the calculations on the notice.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has proved the Landlord served an invalid N1 notice of rent increase. Remedy
The Tenant requested compensation in the amount of $323.27 for the illegal rent paid between December 1, 2024 and November 1, 2025.
The Tenant also seeks for the Board to make a determination on the lawful rent.

Based on the Tenant’s submissions and Landlord’s rent ledger provided by the Tenant in her evidence, I find the lawful rent is in the amount of $1,089.87 as of November 1, 2024 as the Landlord’s N1 notice for increase on December 1, 2024 is invalid.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $323.27 amount represents: • $323.27 for excess rent collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $27.04 from the June 1, 2026 rent and $26.93 each month from starting from July 1, 2026 to May 31, 2027.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
