issues: Medina (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 31, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. Also in attendance was [name], who is the Landlord’s spouse and was identified as a co-landlord. [name] did not make submissions but was present to support her husband. Tenant Duty Counsel did not enter the hearing room at any time. The Tenant was prepared to proceed understanding that [name] services are not guaranteed during the day of a hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T1 application is dismissed.

Before me, the parties agreed on the following facts: • the Tenant originally was in the basement unit as of November 1, 2024 but moved into the rental unit on May 15, 2025; • the rent for the basement unit was $2,200.00 and the Tenant had paid a $2,200.00 last month’s rent (LMR) deposit for that unit; • the tenancy for the rental unit was a month-to-month tenancy, and the rent was due on the first day of every month; • when the Tenant moved into the rental unit, she paid the Landlord an additional $600.00 to bring the LMR deposit to $2,800.00; • the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2025; • the Tenant paid all monthly rents including the month of September 2025; and • the Landlord did not return the LMR deposit to the Tenant.
From this, I find the tenancy for the rental unit, which is the subject of this T1 application, began on May 15, 2025.

The Tenant testified that when she moved into the rental unit, it was to include her then- boyfriend who joined the Tenant and the Tenant’s mother as an occupant. The Tenant stated that there were some problems between her boyfriend and the Landlord and that the Landlord essentially said if they were not happy with the rental unit, then they could leave. This was in the late September 2025 timeframe. The Tenant said that because the Landlord basically agreed to let them leave, they did so on September 30, 2025. However, the LMR deposit was never used and never returned to the Tenant after they moved out.

The Landlord testified that on September 26, 2025, he spoke with the Tenant’s boyfriend about all of the roofing materials the boyfriend had stored in the back yard and on the driveway of the rental unit property. The Landlord told the boyfriend that either they pay something extra for storage or those materials needed to be removed and stored elsewhere. He testified the boyfriend was not at all happy with the Landlord’s position, stating he needed the room for his materials. The Landlord testified he told the boyfriend that if he was not happy, and if the Tenant were not happy, then the Tenant must give the Landlord 30-60 days’ prior notice that they wanted to leave.

The Landlord led two exhibits into evidence to support his testimony. [name] is a copy of the September 26, 2025 text message sent by the Tenant to the Landlord’s wife, [name]. In that text message, the Tenant informs [name] that the Landlord told “us to leave if we didn’t like his rules” and so “we will be leaving at the end of the month”. Exhibit LL#2 is a copy of the Landlord’s September 29, 2025 text message exchange with the Tenant. In that text message, the Landlord asked for clarification whether the Tenant was leaving the end of September or the end of October, and gave the Tenant notice that he would start showing the rental unit to potential, new tenants on October 1, 2025. The Tenant’s reply in LL#2 states the Tenant was moving out September 30, 2025 and was seeking reimbursement of her LMR deposit.
The Landlord confirmed that he was able to re-rent the rental unit to new tenants with a start-date of November 1, 2025.
Based on the testimonies of the parties before me, I find that on a balance of probabilities there was no agreement between the Tenant and the Landlord to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2025.

The best evidence before me suggests the more likely situation that all along, the Landlord wanted proper prior notice of tenancy termination. The Tenant’s testimony about the Landlord agreeing to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2025, was without any evidentiary support. The Tenant’s testimony was essentially indirect evidence as she was unable to corroborate what she believed her boyfriend’s discussion with the Landlord had been about. The Landlord’s testimony was direct evidence as he recounted his exchange with the Tenant’s boyfriend firsthand. I was given no reason to believe the Landlord’s direct testimony was not credible or reliable. As well, the two exhibits submitted into evidence supported much more the Landlord’s version of events over the version the Tenant had provided.

Sections 44 and 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allow a tenant to terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the fixed term by giving 60 days’ notice to the landlord.

Here, with the tenancy being a month-to-month tenancy, I find the Tenant’s texted notice was a 60 days’ notice, therefore her claim of terminating the tenancy on September 30, 2025, did not comply with the Act. To be clear, the requirement to give a minimum of 60 days’ notice is a strict statutory requirement.

As the Tenant’s texted notice was not in compliance with the Act and the Landlord did not agree to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2025, I then looked to subsection 88(1)1. of the Act so I might determine how to deal the Tenant’s moving-out without proper notice.

Section 88 of the Act states: “88 (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. 2. If the tenant abandoned or vacated the rental unit without giving any notice, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a notice of termination had the tenant, on the date that the landlord knew or ought to have known that the tenant had abandoned or vacated the rental unit, given notice of termination in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.”

For clarity, the references to section 96 and 145 of the Act above do not apply to this case. Section 96 of the Act relates to a tenant who attempts to assign a tenancy. Section 145 of the Act relates to a tenant living in a care home who wishes to terminate a care home tenancy. Subsection 88(1)2. of the Act (as set out above) does not apply to this case because that subsection only applies when a tenant does not give any notice at all to terminate a tenancy.

In the matter before me, the Tenant vacated after giving notice that was not in accordance with the Act. As such, arrears are calculated to the earliest date that proper notice could have been given. This is a monthly tenancy running from the first day of each month to the last day of each month. So, the termination date must be the last day of a month and at least 60 days after notice was given. Therefore, the earliest termination date that could have properly been listed on a notice of termination given on September 26, 2025 was November 30, 2025.

In parallel with subsection 88(1)1., subsection 88(4) and section 16 of the Act also require the LTB to consider whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to mitigate his losses. I was satisfied that the Landlord attempted to mitigate his losses by trying to re-rent the rental unit starting on October 1, 2025 (LL#2) and the Landlord confirmed he found new tenants to start a new tenancy on November 1, 2025.

Given that the tenancy was not lawfully terminated, the Tenant remained liable for rent up to the earliest proper termination date. Since the Landlord was able to secure a new tenancy effective November 1, 2025, the Tenant’s liability is determined to extend to October 31, 2025.
Therefore, I find the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant’s LMR deposit, and applied it correctly to the month of October 2025. The Tenant’s T1 application is therefore denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. April 16, 2026 ___________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not file their application within 12 months of the date money was alleged to be collected or retained illegally by the Landlord. Consequently, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s application centred on the allegation that the Tenant paid an illegal charge to the Landlord when she was asked to provide 12 months of pre-authorized rent payments prior to the tenancy commencing on December 1, 2023. The Tenant paid $4,900.00 for the first and last month of the tenancy on October 19, 2023, then the Tenant paid $24,500.00, the equivalent of ten months’ rent, on October 24, 2023.
The Tenant’s application was filed on November 21, 2025.

Subsection 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Subsection 135(4) of the Act states: (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
Per para 2 of s. 56 of [name]. 516/06, the Board does not have the authority to extend or shorten the deadline for filing applications.

The payment at issue here is the October 24, 2023 payment. The Tenant was well out of time to file the application when the money was collected on that date. However, I examined the dates to assess if the money was also allegedly illegally retained within the limitation period. The parties confirmed that the pre-authorized monthly payments were appropriately allocated for the ten-month period from January 1, 2024 to October 1, 2024. Consequently, the Tenant received the benefit of those payments for that period, and the last portion of the $24,500.00 payment was applied on October 1, 2024. Therefore, the Tenant filed their application outside the 12-month limitation period when she filed the application on November 21, 2025.
As the Tenant did not file their application within one year after the Landlord allegedly collected or retained money in contravention of the Act, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 29, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘FSR’) and [name] (collectively, the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must make the Tenant’s belongings available to her as set out below, and must pay a fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00. Overview

This tenancy was going to be terminated effective June 30, 2026 pursuant to an LTB order. The Landlord’s L2 application LTB-L-030106-25 was heard on October 22, 2025. An order terminating the tenancy on June 30th, 2026 was issued on November 12, 2025.
The Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit without providing replacement keys between November 10th, 2025 and November 17th, 2025.
The Landlord’s daughter and her family moved into the rental unit on or about November 11, 2025.

On November 17, 2025 the Tenant attended at the rental unit and discovered that she had been locked out. Her garage remote opener did not work. She was greeted by The Landlord’s daughter and son-in-law. They had an altercation. Both parties testified about the altercation. I find the details to be inconsequential to this application and will not reproduce the parties’ detailed evidence about it. Police were called and attended at the rental unit.

The Landlord takes the position that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit before the locks were changed and was holding the unit hostage demanding cash for keys. They argue the unit had been abandoned and/or the tenancy was terminated before the Landlord changed the locks.
There is no dispute that the Tenant did not pay rent in October and November 2025.
The main issue in dispute was whether the Tenant was still residing at the rental unit on the date the locks were changed and, if she was not, what impact this has on the outcome of this application.
There is no dispute that some of the Tenant’s belongings were still at the rental unit.

As explained further below, I find that the Landlord changed the locks contrary to s. 24 of the Act but that the rental unit was no longer the Tenant’s home. I do not find that she is entitled to any remedies other than the return of her limited possessions. I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant only had a few items left at the property.

As a general comment, I would strongly encourage both parties, and any landlords and tenants who find themselves in similar circumstances, to not behave the way this Tenant and this Landlord did. A tenant who finds a new place and intends to move out, should not play games and hold their rental unit hostage demanding cash for keys for a place they have no intention of occupying long term. This is contrary to the purposes of the Act and limits supply of housing. A landlord who finds themselves dealing with a tenant who is trying to play such games, would be wise to not self help and change the locks. Both parties should instead act reasonably, and in accordance with the Act. I hope that this order will discourage misconduct, bad faith, and attempts to abuse (or at the very least misuse) the Act and the LTB process by these and similar litigants in the future. A landlord who behaves the way the Landlord did may find themselves with an even higher fine. A tenant who behaves the way the Tenant did may find themselves liable for rent up to the date the locks were changed, may have to pay fines to the LTB, and/or have their application dismissed as abuse of process pursuant to s. 23(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990. The Tenant and similar tenants may also wish to familiarize themselves with ss. 197(1) and 197(2) of the Act. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified about the circumstances leading up to November 17th. I did not find her to be a credible witness. She was argumentative and evasive. Her evidence is inconsistent with what I usually see in cases of illegal lockouts and inconsistent with independent documentary evidence.

By was of a summary, she claims that she was temporarily out of the unit when the locks were changed. She was staying with her boyfriend, returned on Monday with her children in the car planning to start her week, discovered that locks had been changed, and was subsequently displaced. She is divorced and only stays at the house when the kids are with her.

She testified about the belongings she had at the rental unit. She said she had her bed with two dressers, clothes in the wardrobe, a few pieces of furniture in her daughter’s room and her son’s room along with some clothes. She had sofas, a kitchen table, and some chairs in the living room. In response to a direct leading question from her representative, she confirmed that she had other small items such as clothes, dishes and cookware.

Evidence 6967587 contains a photo of what the Tenant claims was her bedroom furniture. She says it was worth at least $6,000 if she were to sell it. The Landlord claims that this photo was AI generated and points to some issues with it. I do not find that I need to make a determination about this issue. I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that there was no such furniture at the property when the locks were changed. It is immaterial whether this bedroom set may have been at the property at some point and subsequently moved, or whether it never existed and the photo was generated by AI.

Document 6967595 contains a recording of living room furniture taken when she moved in. It is not helpful in establishing what she had at the rental unit in November 2025. The Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant had this furniture at the property at some point. What is in dispute, is whether this furniture was still at the property when locks were changed.

After the altercation on November 17th the Tenant booked a hotel room. She submitted a copy of her Expedia booking for November 17- 24, 2025, being document 6967586. The booking indicates that the total amount payable will be $1,106.69. It directs the Tenant to “pay at the property”. There is no independent proof that payment was ever made but the Tenant claims that she paid this amount. The Tenant claims that her children had a hard time processing this eviction and hotel stay and that they were seriously impacted as a result.

Document 7044583 contains a copy of what the Tenant claims is her new lease with her friend, Nataliya Lipkin for the basement unit at 37 Newbridge Ave. It is an unsigned document. Curiously, the signature dates on page 7 are pre-filled with November 16, 2025. According to the lease, the tenancy was to begin on November 21, 2025.

Natalia Lipkin did not attend the hearing to testify. The Tenant provided no proof of moving to 37 Newbridge Ave. She provided no proof of making rent payments to Natalia Lipkin. She provided no proof that 37 [name] is her new permanent address.

The Tenant said that she moved some things out of the house before she received the L2 order. She claims that these items (basement boxes and backyard furniture) were moved to a friend’s storage. She did not explain who the friend was, what the cost was and did not provide further detail. There is no documentary evidence to corroborate this story.

The Tenant was cross-examined about the many inconsistencies and implausibility’s in her story. She was extremely argumentative, evasive and non-responsive. She could not provide a satisfactory explanation why her alleged lease was dated November 16th while she claims to have discovered the lockout on November 17th. She claims that she must have sent a wrong version to her representative. When pressed, she claimed that the lease was signed on her friend’s request because the friend had buyers for the house and the buyers needed to see a lease.

She was confronted with document page 6 of 7048047 which shows that the property where the Tenant claims to be living was sold on November 27, 2025 with a closing date of February 13, 2026. The listing makes no mention of having a basement tenant. It states that the property is owner occupied. The Tenant did not provide a plausible explanation for this discrepancy. She claimed that the sale was still conditional and there were still some issues.
She could not explain why no proof of payment for a hotel was filed into evidence. She asked the Landlord to pose this question to the Tenant’s legal representative instead.
She could not explain why her children are not in the video of November 17th altercation even though she testified that she had her children with her when she came to the house.

She was confronted with the fact that her driver’s license lists 129 Deerwood Crescent as her address, not the rental unit and not even 37 Newbridge. She provided a long convoluted explanation that completely defies belief and common sense. She claimed that she changed her address in order to help out an employee who applied to rent 129 Deerwood and that she subsequently decided to use this address to receive correspondence which caused her to update her address on the driver’s license. She was extremely evasive and argumentative at first and only provided this fantastical explanation after she was pressed on the issue. After re-direct she volunteered further fantastical detail. At that stage she claimed that using this address allowed her to obtain cheaper car insurance.

She was conveniently forgetful and argumentative when she was asked about the Landlord providing her with a reference letter in September 2025 and her telling the Landlord that she found a new place starting October 1, 2025. She was confronted with a copy of the lease on page 12 of the Landlord’s document package. She refused to answer a question.

She was asked about not paying rent in October and November 2025. She provided two self-contradictory explanations. She claimed that the Landlord must have had cheques for these months but also claimed that she needed to save money and couldn’t pay.
The Landlord attempted to serve the Tenant an N4 notice for non-payment in November 2025. It was returned to sender. The Tenant did not recall seeing the envelope.
The Tenant confirmed that she was served with a Landlord’s notice of intent to enter and that she denied entry. This exchange took place in writing.

Page 91 of document 7039580 contains a copy of the Tenant’s message to the Landlord demanding $15,000 to move out by end of November. The Tenant said that the message was taken out of context and that she won’t be commenting on it. She was asked whether she had been trying to force the Landlord to pay her money to agree to move out since the beginning. She refused to answer. Landlord’s evidence

I prefer the Landlord’s evidence on the issue of whether the rental unit was the Tenant’s home when the locks were changed. They provided detailed, internally consistent and logical evidence on this issue. It was supported by strong corroborating evidence. I find that this evidence was not seriously shaken or undermined by cross-examination.

FSR contacted the Tenant about an inspection on or about November 7th. The Tenant asked for an official notice. He sent her an official notice on November 9th. He entered the rental unit on November 10th. The Landlord noticed that the place was empty. The fridge and cupboards were empty, there was nothing in the closets. There was garbage in the kitchen. The smell was bad and there were fruit flies in the kitchen.

FSR provided persuasive corroborating video and date-stamped photographic evidence showing the state of the rental unit when he entered the unit (documents 7218723 and 7039371). The video shows a vacant main floor. Photos dated November 19th, 2025 show a mostly abandoned house with very few personal belongings left behind. FSR also provided hearsay evidence from a neighbour that the Tenant vacated on or about October 3rd. FSR claims that the neighbour did not testify out of fear of the Tenant, and that the Landlord did not speak to the neighbour until after he entered the property in November. I do not find this hearsay evidence necessary or reliable.

The Tenant never advised FSR that she had vacated the property, but she asked for a reference for a new rental. The Tenant did not pay rent in October or November 2025. He believes she left the house on or about October 3rd, on the last day of that rental period. FSR asked the Tenant to pay her rent. She did not reply and did not pay. The Tenant’s only message was asking the Landlord to pay her a substantial sum of money. The Tenant argued that she could stay until June 30th and cost the Landlord a lot more if he didn’t pay her. The Landlord prepared an N4 notice and attempted to serve it. It was issued November 6th. I do not find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant received this notice.

FSR was cross-examined about his claim that there were fruit flies. He had to admit that fruit flies are not captured in any videos or photos. He was asked about the video he took on November 10th. The Tenant argued that the video appeared staged/dramatized, in the sense that FSR clearly expected to see a vacant property before he started recording. FSR explained that he could see into the house through a transparent window near the main door. The house appeared to be empty. He admitted he didn’t knock. The video is consistent with this explanation.
He was asked about police attendance and police report. He denied that he was contacted by police on November 17th.

He was asked about LTB interim order dated December 15, 2026 ordering the Landlord not to re-rent the rental unit. He was asked why he permitted his daughter to continue to occupy the rental unit. He was asked why he didn’t make the Tenant’s possessions available to her despite the interim order. He did not provide a satisfactory explanation.

I found FSR to be a credible witness and I found his evidence to be persuasive and reliable. His testimony was logically consistent, rational, and well-supported by video and photographic evidence. It was not seriously shaken or undermined by cross-examination other than as it relates to compliance with the LTB interim order.
Sheyda testified about the events of November 17th. She corroborated FSR’s version of the events. She testified that they called the police that day. [name] and analysis

This application is brough pursuant to s. 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) : A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

There is no dispute that locks were changed and that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with a replacement key. They therefore acted contrary to s. 24 of the Act unless one of the Landlord’s arguments below succeed.

The Landlord’s defense is that the unit had either been abandoned or, in the alternative, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice of termination or the LTB order terminating the tenancy effective June 30th. The Landlord provided no authority in support of either argument other than s. 202, which they believe required the Tenant to act reasonably. 43. 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 44. Under s. 39 of the Act: A landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless, (a) the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit; or (b) an order of the Board evicting the tenant has authorized the possession. 45. Under s. 37(2) If a notice of termination is given in accordance with this Act and the tenant vacates the rental unit in accordance with the notice, the tenancy is terminated on the termination date set out in the notice. 46. Under s. 37(3) A notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy. 47. I am unable to agree that the Landlord was entitled to change the locks pursuant to s. 39(b), 37(2) or 37(3) of the Act, i.e. with the Landlord’s second argument. I do not find that the N4 was received by the Tenant. The N12 had a termination date of July 3, 2025 - earlier than the date the Tenant allegedly vacated the rental unit. The LTB order terminated the tenancy effective June 30th, 2026, not on some earlier date. I am not persuaded that a landlord may rely on such order to unilaterally change locks on a date earlier than the date indicated in such order. If such an order is to be enforced, it is to be enforced by the Sheriff, not through a landlord’s self-help. 48. The issue of s. 39(a) is more complex but I am still unable to agree with the Landlord. 49. The Tenant relies on [2002] O.J. No. 5918 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) (‘George V Apartments’). This case is binding on me. This case was decided under the prior legislation, the Tenant Protection Act, 1997 (the ‘T.P.A.’). Section 41 of the T.P.A. contained substantially identical wording as the present section 39. She argues that the unit was not abandoned as the Landlord failed to follow the proper procedures [name]) and I agree. 50. The Tenant continued to insist on her rights under the Act. She demanded proper notice of entry. She did not surrender her keys. This may have been unwise as explored elsewhere in this order, but all of this was clear evidence that she did not surrender occupancy, possession and control of the rental unit. Unlike the order of Vice-Chair Lundy below, I am unable to even find that the Landlord had good faith subjective belief that the Tenant vacated the rental unit. 51. I agree with the reasoning of Vice-Chair Lundy in SWT-94108-16 and I find that the Tenant did not abandon the rental unit for the substantially same reasons: 8. I find on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord reasonably believed that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit as of August 31, 2016. D.B. had vacated the unit pursuant to the N11 Notice and had advised him that the Tenant had already moved out before this date. 9. However, R.B.’s subjective belief, however genuine, that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit was not sufficient authority to recover possession under the Act. Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Act, a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. 10. To that end, section 39 of the Act limits the Landlord’s ability to take possession of the rental unit: 39. A landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless, (a) the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit; or (b) an order of the Board evicting the tenant has authorized the possession. 11. As R.B. never obtained an order from the Board authorizing possession, his only lawful route to recover the unit must lie in a finding of abandonment under subsection 39(a) of the Act. As the Ontario Divisional Court explained in [name]Cobb, the terms “vacated or abandoned” in subsection 39(a) effectively have the same meaning.[1] “Vacant” implies entire abandonment and a state of non-occupancy for any purpose while “abandonment” means that the tenant no longer intends to reside in the rental unit. Abandonment within the context of the Act therefore requires both an intention to abandon and clear evidence that this has in fact occurred.[2] 12. This avenue to recovery is considerably more precarious for a landlord than reliance on an order from the Board and requires clear and unambiguous evidence that the tenant has permanently vacated the rental unit with no intention of returning. As the Court noted in [name] by the tenant is not established until some action is taken by the landlord. When faced with an empty unit, a landlord re-takes possession pursuant to s. 41(a) at some risk. The tenant may be working or vacationing elsewhere, sometimes for a considerable period. The landlord must be satisfied the tenant has left the unit and obviously has no intention of returning. Non-payment of rent is certainly a factor to be considered. The safest course for the landlord is to bring an application under s. 78 [now section 79]…[3] 13. While section 79 of the Act is discretionary in that the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy, pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Act, a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. In other words, absent some action by the landlord, such as seeking an order under section 79 of the Act, the fact of abandonment in and of itself does not terminate the tenancy. In other words, even where a tenant has abandoned the rental unit, this alone does not result in termination of the tenancy. 52. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord changed the locks contrary to s. 24 of the Act. Remedies 53. The Tenant’s application requests the following remedies: a. A fine payable to the LTB, b. $20,000 for the cost of repairing or replacing property that was damaged, destroyed, or disposed of, c. $1,206.69 for out-of-pocket expenses including a hotel stay and Canada Post mail forwarding, d. An order for the Landlord to restore the Tenant in possession of the rental unit, e. An order for the Landlord to return Tenant’s belongings to her, and f. $10,000 for General Damages. 54. I do not find that the Tenant is entitled to any remedies other than remedies “a” and “e”. 55. It is undisputed that the Landlord is in possession of some of the Tenant’s belongings that were found at the rental unit following the lockout. The Landlord must make these belongings available to the Tenant. For clarity, this does not require the Landlord to return any items that the Tenant claims are in possession of the Landlord – only those items that were actually at the property on the date the locks were changed that belonged to the Tenant. I find that all of these items can be found in document 7218723. I prefer the Landlord’s version of the events, namely that these items constituted only a few items of little value as captured in the Landlord’s photographs of the property. The Tenant shall have until end of day March 24, 2026 to pick up these belongings. She can do so with written 12-hour notice to the Landlord at a time of her choosing between 8am and 8pm. 56. Other remedies require me to heavily rely on the Tenant’s testimony and claims. I would need to accept her testimony that the rental unit was her primary residence, that certain items were lost or destroyed, and that she paid certain expenses. 57. I did not find the Tenant to be a credible and reliable witness. Her explanation for adverse evidence lacked the ring of truth. Her own explanations included admissions of lying and possibly defrauding third parties (providing wrong address to insurance in order to obtain lower rates; pretending that there is a binding legal tenancy agreement for the purposes of a friend’s real estate transaction, and signing a document that does not represent their true agreement; pretending to be a tenant to assist her friend/employee to secure a rental). The Tenant clearly has a very liberal relationship with truth and facts and does not hesitate to sign misleading or even fraudulent documents when it suits her. She had no satisfactory explanation for the state of the rental unit the way it was found by the Landlord. The state of the rental unit as captured in photos/video is entirely inconsistent with the Tenant’s claim that the rental unit was her primary residence 50% of the time. 58. I also note that the Tenant did not provide a detailed testimony about the various items allegedly lost and destroyed as claimed in the application. There is no proof of actual payment to buy or replace anything or to stay at a hotel. Expedia document contains no proof of payment – to the contrary, it specifies that payment is still outstanding. 59. Overall, I do not accept the Tenant’s claim that she was still residing at the rental unit on a part-time basis when the locks were changed. I prefer the Landlord’s version of the events that the Tenant stopped paying rent, moved her belongings out, and only kept very limited connection to the rental unit for purposes that did not include using it as her home. While the tenancy was not terminated in accordance with the Act, this finding affects the remedies the Tenant is entitled to. 60. I do not find that the Tenant incurred any expenses as a result of the lockout or that any of the Tenant’s belongings were damaged or destroyed. 61. I do not find that the Tenant established that they incurred any of the expenses claimed in the application. 62. I also find that it would be inappropriate to order that the Tenant be restored in possession of the rental unit. Under s. 31(3), If the Board determines, in an application under paragraph 5 of subsection 29 (1), that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or the residential complex, or caused the locking system to be altered, during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys, and if the Board is satisfied that the rental unit is vacant, the Board may, in addition to the remedies set out in subsections (1) and (2), order that the landlord allow the tenant to recover possession of the rental unit and that the landlord refrain from renting the unit to anyone else. [emphasis added] 63. It is not a mandatory remedy, and I find that it would be inappropriate to grant it in all of the circumstances, especially considering that the Tenant was no longer living at the unit when the locks were changed. The Landlord’s daughter and her family made the rental unit their home. The tenancy would be terminated effective June 30, 2026 pursuant to an LTB order, and it would not be fair or appropriate to now have the Tenant evict the Landlord’s family, potentially with the Sheriff, occupy the unit for a few months, and then have the Landlord evict the Tenant pursuant to an LTB order, potentially with the Sheriff. 64. The Tenant sought an administrative fine in the amount to be determined by the LTB. 65. Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $35,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant: The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 66. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provide that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $35,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 67. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 68. I should therefore consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor. 69. I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00. 70. I am unable to find that the Tenant was seriously impacted by the Landlord’s actions as they weren’t living at the unit. 71. The Landlord chose to ignore requirements of the Act and simply changed the locks. The Tenant did not successfully establish their entitlement to any remedies in this application and there is therefore very little in this order to deter the Landlord and similar landlords from changing locks if a tenant behaves the way the Tenant behaved. It is important that landlords don’t take matters into their own hands even if they believe their actions are justified. I therefore find that a fine is necessary in the circumstances. 72. I considered imposing a higher fine but given that this is a small landlord, that the Tenant likely acted in bad faith, this is the first time the Landlord is found to have illegally locked a tenant out, and that the unit was largely abandoned by the Tenant, I find that a higher amount would not be appropriate at this time. 73. The Tenant requested general damages. 74. The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment. 75. The Board has previously found in cases of harassment and illegal lockouts that an amount for the illegal lockout is appropriate under general damages. See for example HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), the LTB reasoned that:…it seems to me that the quantum of general damages normally awarded to compensate a tenant for an illegal lockout is $2,500.00. That sum takes into account the inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodations while also seeking legal assistance; and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home. Some recent cases award higher damages. 76. I find that general damages would not be appropriate in the circumstances. I do not find that the Tenant was displaced or that her home was taken away. She lost nothing more than a bargaining chip and possibly a storage facility. The rental unit was no longer her home when the Landlord breached the Act. 77. As the Tenant was only minimally successful in this application, I do not find that the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the cost of filing this application. The Board typically awards the filing cost to a substantially successful party, which the Tenant is not in my view. Their application and evidence were largely misleading and unpersuasive, and they only received a minor portion of their requested remedies.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by March 31, 2026.

The Landlord shall return to the Tenant the property that is in the possession or control of the Landlord by March 22, 2026 as set out in paragraph 54 above. March 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for lack of particulars.
The Tenant filed the T2 application with the Board on November 25, 2024. However, the Tenant failed to provide sufficient clarification on the particulars of the case.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.
While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the test applies equally to tenant applications, including those brought under section 31, of the Act.

I find that the T2 application lacked the specific detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant filed an application for the return of their last month’s rent (the ‘LMR’) deposit and money paid to the Landlord for the hot water heater. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the money to the Tenant. Last Mont’s Rent
The Landlord collected $1,000 for a LMR deposit on March 30, 2025, prior to the commencement of the tenancy. This was a fixed term tenancy running May 1, 2025, to August 31, 2025.
The Landlord did not return the LMR when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. Instead, the Landlord held the LMR to apply to damages.
There is no provision in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) that allows a Landlord to apply a LMR deposit to damages.
At the hearing, the Landlord did not dispute they were holding the LMR deposit and agreed to return it to the Tenant. Hot Water Tank
The Tenant is also seeking reimbursement for the hot water tank rental payments made to the Landlord, totaling $305.10, calculated at $101.70 per month for three months.

The Tenant references section 20 of the Act in support of their position that the hot water tank rental is part of maintenance, so should be the Landlord’s responsibility. The hot water tank is powered by propane gas, and the Landlord relies on the lease, in which the Tenant agreed to pay the costs of gas for the rental unit.

The tenancy agreement does not explicitly state the Tenant will pay the rental amount for the hot water tank, nor was any evidence provided at the hearing of any oral agreement between the parties for the hot water tank rental fees.

It is a general rule of contract interpretation that any ambiguity in a contract shall be interpreted against the person who drafted the contract; in this case that would be the Landlord. The lease shows that “Gas” is not included in the lawful rent for the rental unit. There is no mention of a hot water tank rental. We find it reasonable that the Tenant was not aware of an additional hot water tank rental fee and the Landlord will be ordered to return the amount the Tenant paid.

In her application, the Tenant acknowledges $105.97 is owing to the Landlord for hydro services and requests it be deducted from the amount ordered for the hot water tank. Accordingly, the amount the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant for the hot water tank rental is $199.13. Costs
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,247.13. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the LMR • $199.13 for illegal charge collected • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 8, 421 [address] LONDON ON Ltd. (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on April 13, 2026. Only the Prospective Tenant and Prospective Tenant’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing. The Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Prospective Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Prospective Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Prospective Tenant $1,837.00. Testimony of [name] [name]

The Prospective Tenant testified that she originally found the rental unit through an online listing posted by the Landlord. The Prospective Tenant entered into evidence Facebook messages in which the Landlord accepted her application to rent the unit.

On October 17, 2025, the parties executed a written lease agreement, which was entered into evidence. The lease was to commence on November 1, 2025, at a monthly rent of $1,737.00. The lease required a deposit of $1,787.00, comprised of $1,737.00 for first month’s rent and a $50.00 refundable key deposit. APRIL 21, 2026

On October 28, 2025, the Prospective Tenant paid the Landlord a partial deposit of $700.00. On October 31, 2025, the Prospective Tenant paid an additional $1,137.00. Proof of both payments was entered into evidence. The Prospective Tenant testified that she inadvertently overpaid the deposit by $50.00 and requested the Board to return the overpayment.

On November 1, 2025, the Landlord refused to provide the Prospective Tenant with access to the rental unit, advising that the Landlord now had concerns regarding the Prospective Tenant’s application and was requiring a co-signer. The Prospective Tenant testified that she made immediate efforts to obtain a co-signer but was unable to do so.

The Landlord subsequently informed the Prospective Tenant that the lease could not commence and did not provide the Tenant with keys to the rental unit. The Prospective Tenant never obtained possession of the rental unit. Analysis

It is clear from the uncontested evidence of the Prospective Tenant that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord did not give the Tenant access to the rental unit. I am satisfied the Prospective Tenant paid the Landlord a deposit of $1,837.00 prior to commencement of the lease. This comprised of the last month’s rent, refundbale key deposit, and overpayment of $50.00.

Section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (1). (2) A prospective tenant may apply to the Board for an order under subsection 1

The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the Prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. The evidence suggests that the Prospective Tenant had no ability to move into the rental unit due to the Landlord’s actions. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenant is $1,837.00 This amount represents: • $1,837.00 for the deposit illegally retained.
The Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Prospective Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 21, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 31, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord also had her son, [name], present to assist the Landlord with English to Mandarin translation. The Tenant opted not to consult with Tenant Duty Counsel. As a preliminary issue, it was clear the tenancy in question was for a bedroom in a house that had other tenants renting other rooms- a total of four different international students with separate tenancy agreements with the Landlord. It was determined the Tenant rented a south-facing bedroom which for convenience hereto, is numbered “1”. I was satisfied to change the style of cause to more clearly identify the rental unit in question under this T1 application. That change is reflected above in the title of proceedings.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved part of the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant $400.00 for the key deposit ($100) and the utility deposit ($300). As the Tenant was successful in part, the filing fee of $48.00 will also be reimbursed to the Tenant by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that he began his rental unit tenancy on September 1, 2023 and moved out on or about August 6, 2025. The Landlord was unable to confirm a move-out date but stated she considered August 31, 2025 as the tenancy-end date. I find the tenancy did end sometime in August 2025 but no later than August 31, 2025.

The Tenant submitted two exhibits into evidence to support this part of his testimony. The first exhibit was TT#1(a and b) – a copy of signed lease from September 1, 2023 to August 31, 2024 and its Schedule A). The second exhibit was TT#2(a and b)—a copy of signed lease from September 1, 2024 to August 31, 2025 and its [name]. From the testimonies of the parties, I was able to determine the following facts: • For each of the signed leases, it was clear the Tenant paid a last month’s rent (LMR) deposit: for the first 1-year term, the LMR deposit was $840.00 and for the second 1-year term the LMR deposit was $900.00. • For both leases, the Tenant had paid the Landlord a $100.00 key deposit and a $300.00 utility deposit. A total of $400.00 has been held by the Landlord and that amount has not been returned to the Tenant. • Payments made under the tenancy (for both leases) were effected through e- transfers to the Landlord’s husband, [name]. An example of such payment was given into evidence as exhibit TT#4. • The Tenant completed his first-year term and a few months before its end, he told the Landlord he was leaving the unit and not coming back. As it turned out, the Tenant reconsidered and then entered into a second, new one-year agreement with the Landlord for the rental unit starting on September 1, 2024. • For each of the signed leases, an agreed upon provision was that the Tenant would pay ten months of rent, and if done so completely, then the last two months of the fixed term would be free (i.e. no rent payable). • The Landlord paid the Tenant $900.00 on December 28, 2025 (exhibit TT#3). 5. The only claim that was in fact contested before me was related to the two other deposits made by the Tenant in respect of keys and utilities. The Landlord’s testified position was that the keys to the rental unit were never returned to the Landlord. As the Landlord does not live at the rental address, she said anything mailed there would not reach her directly. Also, the Landlord stated she incurred cleaning fees after the Tenant moved out in August 2025. She testified that she used the utility deposit to cover the cleaning fees she incurred as well as a mattress issue she had to deal with. She also stated that the Tenant had agreed verbally with her that the utility deposit could be used to defray the Landlord’s costs. 6. The Tenant’s testified position was that after moving out, he mailed the keys back through Canada Post to the rental unit building address (to the attention of the Landlord) and as far as he was aware, the keys were successfully delivered. The Tenant maintained that he wanted the $300.00 utility deposit to be reimbursed. Analysis 7. The T1 application was filed by the Tenant with the LTB on December 13, 2025. By virtue of the one-year limitation for claims under a T1 application, the Tenant’s claim under this application can only “reach back” to December 14, 2024, which is the timeframe of the second one-year lease (TT#2a+b). This one-year limitation is a statutory limitation that is found in subsection 135(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). 8. Turning to the time-valid claim before me, I find the parties entered into a second, separate lease (tenancy agreement) for the rental unit. To be clear, the second lease created a new tenancy between the parties. 9. I was then able to determine from both parties’ submissions that under the second one- year lease, the Tenant paid all of his $900.00 monthly rents from September 1, 2025 up to and including June 1, 2025. Further, I was able to determine that the Tenant did not pay July 2025 rent (one month of free rent was credited to the Tenant) and the LMR deposit was used for August 2025. In conclusion, it was evident and I so find, the second “free” month of rent that was a provision under the TT#2 lease was not given to the Tenant, which is what the $900.00 payment on December 28, 2025 (TT#3) was meant to reconcile. 10. This means that the Landlord fulfilled her obligation under the TT#2 lease to provide the Tenant with two months of rent-free tenancy, and thus owes no money to the Tenant under this particular claim. 11. With regard to the other deposits under the T1 claim, that is the $100.00 key deposit and the $300.00 utility deposit, I find the Landlord must return the full amount of $400.00 to the Tenant. I say this for the following reasons. 12. Key deposits in general are lawful deposits according to section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06, which regulation provides an exception for key deposits that are otherwise prohibited under subsections 135(1) and (3) of the Act. 13. First, I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit and mailed back his unit keys to the rental unit building. I was satisfied with the Tenant’s testimony that he mailed the keys by Canada Post to the rental unit building, to the attention of the Landlord. Canada Post is a secure and reliable federal postal agency. Just because the Landlord did not/does not live in that building does not negate proper return of the keys to the Landlord. 14. Second, the utility deposit of $300.00 was unlawfully collected to start with. The Act is clear about what deposits are lawful and a utility deposit is not. Reference is made to sections 105 and 106 which state in summary that the only security deposit that can be collected by a landlord is a rent deposit. (The Act defines a “security deposit” as a deposit made for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of a tenant.) This means that security deposits other than rent deposits, such as damage deposits, utility account deposits and so on, are unlawful. 15. This means the unlawful $300.00 utility deposit held by the Landlord must be returned to the Tenant. Whether or not the parties talked about how that deposit was to be used does not have relevance here as parties under a residential tenancy cannot contract outside the statutory provisions of the Act. 16. As the Tenant was in part successful with his T1 application, he is entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application fee. Reference is made to the LTB’s Interpretation Guideline no. 3.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $448.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 for the key deposit that was collected. • $300.00 for the unlawful utility deposit that was collected; and. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the T1 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount of $448.00 owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 20, 2026 ____________

issues: Order under Section 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 23043 Date: 2026-03-16 In the matter of: 1, 146 [address] Toronto ON Inc. (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and withheld a vital service. This application was heard by videoconference on January 16, 2026. The Landlord’s agent, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: On consent of the parties the application is amended to add [name] as a Tenant. She testified on behalf of both tenants and I will refer to her testimony as the Tenant’s at times. I will refer to the testimony of the Landlord’s agent as the Landlord’s.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. The Landlord shall therefore pay the Tenant $948.00.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and specifically the heating system.
The Tenant testified that they did not have satisfactory heating at the rental unit starting around November 15th, 2025. The heat was finally restored on or about December 18, 2025.

On November 15 the Tenant messaged the Landlord that it was too cold inside their unit. The Tenant recorded at least 14 days with no heat and 2 days with partial heat. She did not provide exact dates. The house was as cold as 9 degrees at times. The Tenant had by-law attend at the rental unit. By-law confirmed that the house was colder than 20 degree Celsius. The Tenant typed up a summary that can be found in document 7115212 in the Portal. This summary is not a contemporaneous record of the events.

Document 6984842 shows the messages the Tenant exchanged with the Landlord’s agent between November 15, 2025 and December 14, 2025. The first message was sent on November 15th. It reads: “The heat is now off in the unit. Kian, there are some serious issues here that need to be dealt with immediately”.

November 15th was a Friday. The Landlord replies 4 days later on November 19th: “Hi [name], sorry for the late reply… We have a tech in the basement right now working on the heat issue hopefully we can fix it on site. Please always call the emergency number for no heat etc happening after hours;…”

There is a follow-up message on or about December 8th stating that the heat is off again and it is freezing in the house. The Landlord replies that they purchased a new heating unit and are waiting for it to arrive and be installed. The Landlord asks the Tenant to use space heaters in the meantime.

The Tenant then asks the Landlord about the location of space heaters and says that they never received any. The Landlord is surprised stating that heaters were provided on or about November 28th. It would appear that a tenant from another unit took the Tenant’s space heater(s) thinking that they were intended for him.

A few hours later the Tenant writes that space heaters aren’t doing much. The Landlord replies that they can’t do anything else until the new unit arrives. The Tenant then asks the Landlord to cover the cost of staying in a hotel. The Landlord’s agent replies that she can’t approve such decision and that the request would need to be made through [email].

The following day the Landlord’s agent advised the Tenant that the heating unit would be replaced on that day. She then sends a message the next day to advise the Tenant that the unit is up and running. 12. 2 days later, on Friday December 12th, the Tenant messaged the Landlord that the heat was no longer working and that the house was at 62 degree Fahrenheit. The Landlord called a technician the same day who then attended on the same day. The Tenant sent several follow-up messages complaining about continued lack of heat. As of December 14th, when the Tenant created a record of her messages, there was no reply from the Landlord’s agent. I note that December 13, 2025 was a Saturday and December 14, 2025 was a Sunday. 13. The heat issue was finally resolved by December 17th, 2025, but the Tenant testified that she had to stay home from work to make sure the heat does not turn off when their cat is along at home. The Tenant argues that the Landlord took too long to resolve the issue leaving the Tenant with intermittent heat for almost a month, including an entire weekend with no heat in December. The Tenant was unable to host friends and had to ask for exceptions to work from home. 14. The Tenant was cross-examined. She confirmed that there were 14 days when she recorded heat issues and confirmed that she did not reach out every time. She explained that she believed the Landlord was working on resolving the issue. The Tenant was somewhat evasive when asked about the Landlord answering her calls. She admitted that there was a resolution around November 18th, 2025 and that the heat was temporarily on after the repairs on December 9th. She conceded that she did not contact emergency line in the morning of December 12th. She relies on document 7115186 where she was instructed on December 8th to contact the Landlord’s agent because the issue was being addressed. The Tenant was argumentative and not responsive when asked about her ability to assess heating issues and quality of repairs and in reply to other questions. She claimed that the Landlord’s message told her that any request for a hotel stay would not be approved. I do not find this to be a reasonable interpretation of the Landlord’s agent’s message above. 15. The Landlord’s evidence was that they at all times did their best to fix the issue. After the Tenant contacted them on November 15th, they reached out to professionals on or about November 17th. The issue was resolved. The same issue reoccurred a few days later. The technician then said that the heating unit was 15 years old and needed to be replaced because fixing it would only be a temporary solution. The unit was past its useful life. 16. The Landlord then reached out to 3 different companies to obtain quotes to purchase and install a new unit. A new unit was installed on December 8th but stopped working a day later. It could not be repaired right away because parts needed to be ordered from China. The Landlord sent technicians to the residential complex more than half a dozen times during the month when the Tenant experienced issues. 17. The Landlord provided 5 space heaters to be dropped off and didn’t realize the Tenant did not receive them. They dropped off 5 more space heaters as soon as they were notified that the initial heaters were not received. 18. The issue was finally resolved on December 17th, 2025. The control board was replaced resolving all issues with the new unit. 19. The Landlord argues that they did all they could, including paying additional fees for expedited shipping. 20. The Landlord’s agent was cross-examined. She was evasive when asked about heat issues during the winter months of 2024/2025. 21. She admitted that the technicians confirmed that there were indeed issues with heat every time they attended at the rental unit. She was asked about the weekend of December 13th and why the Landlord chose not to pay for the Tenant to go to a hotel. The Landlord’s agent reiterated that she did not have authority to approve such expense and that the Tenant needed to contact the Landlord’s accounting email to have such request considered. Analysis and findings 22. This application is brought under s. 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 23. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 24. I find that the Tenant established that it is more likely than not that the Landlord breached their obligation under the Act. It would appear that the Landlord had some notice that the heating unit had issues as early as in early 2025. They then had clear written notice on November 15th. Their technician then advised them that the unit was past its useful life a few days later. The Landlord still took several weeks to find a new heating unit. This was a business decision that involved an inherent risk that the unit would fail before it is replaced. In my view, it was unreasonable for the Landlord to take that long to make the appropriate arrangements between November 17th and December 8th , including apparently doing nothing between November 17th and November 28th when space heaters were provided to residents. I do not find that the Landlord was at fault for the subsequent failure on December 12th. I accept that this was unforeseen and unforeseeable. I find that the Landlord subsequently acted reasonably by having the issue resolved in a final manner by the 17th of the same month. 25. The Tenant’s corresponding T2 alleges that the Landlord withheld vital service when there was no heat and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. This claim is dismissed. I do not find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord withheld vital services – the interruption was caused by a maintenance issue. I similarly do not find that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. It can be said that the Tenant’s enjoyment suffered as a result of the maintenance issue, but I do not find and substantial interference beyond the maintenance issue, which is properly and fully addressed through the Tenant’s T6. 26. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of 25% of monthly rent. The Tenant asked for a 100% abatement for one month. This award would require a finding that the Tenant completely lost all of their enjoyment of the rental unit for the entire month. The award is lower for two main reasons. First, the Landlord was entitled to some amount of time to deal with an urgent maintenance issue, and no remedy should be awarded during this time based on the evidence adduced at the hearing. Second, the Tenant’s evidence about the lack of heat was somewhat lacking. There are no temperature readings. There are no photos or videos of temperature readings. It is undisputed that there were issues on certain dates, but the record does not necessarily establish a persistent lack of heat for an entire month as alleged by the Tenant. There is no follow-up contact with the Landlord until December 8th. It is unclear whether there were any heat issues before that date and, if there were, it is unclear how severe these issues might have been, and what impact the space heaters had on the unit. 27. I find that this remedy is sufficient to compensate the Tenant for the Landlord’s breach of the Act as interpreted in Onyskiw. 28. The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application and I find that the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of this cost as a partially successful party in this case.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $948.00. This amount represents: • $900.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 27, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month of April 2026.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 16, 2026 ____________________________
