issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. Both applications were heard by videoconference on January 6, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord's [name], [name], and the Landlord’s Agent, [name] (PV) attended the hearing. The Tenant withdrew the claim about parking from LTB-T-068225-24 because the issue is also contained in his Tenant Application for a Rent Reduction (T3).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application s on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the applications are dismissed. / LTB-T-105407-24 Cheques

The Tenant testified that in August 2023, rental cheques for September and October 2023 were sent to an address provided by the Landlord . B y September 9, 2023, the Tenant reissued the cheques because the Landlord claimed that he had not received them.

Another cheque for the rent for December 2023, was returned to the Tenant on December 17, 2023. Since then, at the Landlord’s instruction, the Tenant has given the rent cheques to a resident of the residential complex, or the Landlord picks them up.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Section 108 of the Act provides that neither a landlord nor a tenancy agreement shall require a tenant or prospective tenant to provide post-dated cheques or other negotiable instruments for payment of rent.

The Tenant failed to demonstrate that the Landlord substantially interfere d with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant or harassed him. The Tenant did not claim during his testimony that he was forced to provide post dated cheques but appeared preoccupied that the Landlord may have given him an incorrect mailing address. Nothing in the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord acted in bad faith either in September 202 3 when they did not receive the cheques, or in December 2023 when the cheque was returned to the Tenant . To avoid a reoccurrence, the Landlord provided an alternative method of receiving the cheque rather than mailing and that resolved the issue. Self-Storage Rental

The Tenant testified that he had to rent a storage facility in March 2024 because the Landlord was infuriated at his comment over the Landlord’s alleged eviction of another Tenant. As the Landlord promised to do the same thing to him , he obtained legal advice and rented the locker.

I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant rented the storage space over comments he failed to establish were made by the Landlord. The decision to rent a storage space after speaking with counsel, rather than immediately bringing an application against the Landlord, was ill-conceived. Threats of Eviction

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s Agent, PV, repeatedly asked him when he planned to vacate the rental unit: a. March 5, 2024 – PV informed the Tenant that he required the rental unit for his nephew. / LTB-T-105407-24 b. March 18, 2024, an agent of the Landlord asked the Tenant if he had found another place. c. March 22, 2024 - PV stated that he required the rental unit even though another unit in the residential complex was vacant. d. April 2, 2024 - PV stated that he required vacant possession of the rental unit in order to change the electrical panel which is accessible only from the rental unit and repeatedly asked the Tenant when he would vacate the unit. The Tenant made a recording of this interaction. e. April 3, 2024, and April 21, 2024 – an agent of the Landlord again asked when the Tenant would vacate the unit f. May 15, 2024 - the Tenant informed PV that even though he was looking for a place, he had decided to remain in the unit g. May 23, 2024 - PV who was in the residential complex when the Tenant returned home, asked if he found a place yet. h. June 5, 2024 - PV told the Tenant that he wanted him to vacate the unit over a verbal notice given the year prior i. August 10, 2024 - the Tenant informed PV that he had no intention of moving.

PV testified that there were problems with the electrical panel in the rental unit, but it was difficult to get a hold of the Tenant by phone and he frequently returned home late. The year prior, PV had asked the Tenant if he would consider vacating the unit and the Tenant requested a year to do so.

PV denied harassing the Tenant and stated that each time he was in the residential complex, the Tenant approached him and when they spoke, the Tenant told him that he was looking for a place. The Tenant’s move would solve what PV deemed to be an emergency with the electrical panel as he accused the Tenant of changing the locks to the unit without providing a replacement key.

But for the Tenant’s undisputed statements to the Landlord that he was looking for alternative accommodation, I would have found the Landlord’s conduct to be both harassment and a substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit . The Tenant by repeatedly saying he was looking for a place, led the Landlord to believe that the unit would soon be vacant, hence the requests for updates so the Landlord could know what to do about the unit. Rent Receipts
The Tenant stated that the Landlord failed to provide rent receipts and instead provided a one-page document in December 2025 summarising the rent payments made by the Tenant.
The Tenant testified that he obtained rent receipts and provided them to PV who signed them about five times in 2024.

PV argued that they provided the Tenant with a document which covered the rent paid f or the period from January 20 18 to December 2025. PV confirmed signing and giving copies of the Tenant’s receipt to him approximately nine times in 2025. / LTB-T-105407-24

Section 109(1) of the Act provides that a landlord shall provide free of charge to a tenant or former tenant, on request, a receipt for the payment of any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent or any other amount paid to the landlord.

It is unclear from the evidence when the Tenant first made the request for rent receipts, but the Landlord did sign the copies provided by the Tenant. In this circumstance, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfere d with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant. Going forward, the Landlord must immediately provide to the Tenant a receipt for the payment of rent, as requested.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord’s representative submits that the rental address is incorrect and therefore the application must be dismissed. The Landlord’s representative submits that the rental unit is “20 Marsha [name] ” and not “[address], Scarborough, ON ”. Further the Landlord’s representative states that the Lease Agreement supports their position.

The Tenant agrees with the Landlord insofar as the rental unit address should not have included “Village Green” within the address and submits that this must have been a clerical error on the application but disagrees that the application should be dismissed due to the clerical issue.

The correct rental address is undisputed by the parties, and the Landlord suffered no prejudice as a result of the clerical error. Therefore, I do not find that the Tenant’s Application should be dismissed. I am guided by [name] of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and find there is no prejudice to either party in allowing the amendment and would be consistent with providing a fair and expeditious hearing.
Accordingly, pursuant to [name] the application shall be amended. Does the Landlord and Tenant Board have Jurisdiction to hear the Application?
On the Board’s motion I sought to clarify whether the Board had jurisdiction to hear the application.

On page 2 of the Lease Agreement (DOC- 7325745) it states, “the kitchen and washroom are shared”. Subsection 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that the Act does not apply to living accommodations where the tenant is required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, the owners spouse, child or parent.

In this case it was undisputed that the accommodations were solely shared with other tenants and not the owner, the owners spouse, child etc. Accordingly, I find that the Board has jurisdiction to hear the application. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
This application is about the return of a last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $855.00 on July 25, 2025.

Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act a landlord is mandatorily required to apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. This mean the first question before the Board here is: when did the tenancy terminate?

The parties agree that they had a written tenancy agreement with a fixed term of 12 months commencing on August 1, 2025. They also agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and returned the keys to the Landlords on December 1, 2025.
The difficulty here is that moving out of the rental unit does not legally terminate the tenancy. Under the Act a tenancy is terminated by Board order, by valid notice to terminate or by agreement.

The Tenant’s testimony was undisputed. The Tenant testified that they had an emergency that required them to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant stated they provided the Landlord 5-days notice that they were vacating the rental unit. Finally, the Tenant submits that the Landlord has a duty to mitigate and states that the Landlord has failed to fulfill their obligation to mitigate their losses as required by the Act.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant provided 3-day verbal notice that the Tenant was vacating and while he agrees that the Tenant verbally advised of a medical emergency, they received no supporting documentation regarding the emergency. The Landlord did not agree to terminate the tenancy early.

Further, the Landlord’s representative submits that they did attempt mitigate, they state that they contacted friends and family and posted the rental unit online, although could not provide specific dates that the rental unit was posted online. They state that they were able to re-rent the rental unit as of January 1, 2026. Analysis

Section 47 outlines that a Tenant may terminate a fixed-term tenancy in accordance with s.44. Even if I accept the Tenant’s testimony that they informed the Landlord they required to terminate their tenancy due to an emergency with 5-days notice, the Tenant’s notice does not comply with subsection 44(3). Furthermore, there was no agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy early.
Therefore, the tenancy did not lawfully terminate when the Tenant vacated on just a few days notice on December 1, 2025.

Pursuant to s. 88(3) of the Act the Tenant’s liability for the rent ended when the Landlords re-rented the unit for January 1, 2026. This means that the deposit should be applied to the rent due under the Lease Agreement for the month of December 2025, unless the evidence establishes the Landlords failed to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses by re-renting the unit as soon as possible. (See ss. 88(4) and 16.)

I find that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord failed to reasonably mitigate their losses and could have found a new tenant to rent the unit earlier than January 1, 2026. In this case the unit was re-rented only one month after the Tenants vacated which seems reasonable in the circumstances.

As a result, and pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, the Landlords were correct in applying the deposit to the rent due for the month of December 2025. Therefore, they are not retaining the deposit in contravention of the Act and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy
The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenants’ rent deposit.

The parties agreed that the Tenants moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2024 and that they vacated on November 29, 2025. The issue to be addressed in this application is whether the Tenants provided the Landlord with proper notice to vacate under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and whether the Landlord applied the Tenants’ rent deposit to the last month of tenancy.

The Tenants testified that they informed the Landlord that they would be vacating the rental unit at the end of November 2025. The Tenants agreed that they did not serve this notice to end the tenancy on an N9 notice, however, they sent the notice via email on September 29, 2025. A copy of this email was submitted into evidence by the Tenants. The email states that the Tenants were to vacate the rental unit on December 1, 2025. The Landlord testified that the notice provided by the Tenants was not on the Board approved form, so he did not accept December 1, 2025 as their move out date.

Section 37 of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. In accordance with sections 44(2) and 47 of the Act, the earliest termination date the Tenants could have specified on a notice of termination was December 31, 2025. While the Tenants assert that they gave the Landlord a notice of termination via email, this could not have been a valid notice as the Tenants were attempting to terminate the tenancy on the first day of the rental period, when the Act clearly states it must be the last day of the rental period.
However, Section 37(3) of the Act stipulates that a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a Tenants have agreed to terminate a tenancy.

The word “agreed” is not defined in the Act, but the meaning of an agreement is well established in the common law of contract. An agreement is formed when one party communicates an offer to the other, and the offeree communicates its acceptance.

I agree with the analysis in Dadiala v Griffin, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No 84, in which the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal recognized that while a notice of termination under the Act must be in a form prescribed by the Act, an otherwise deficient notice of termination provided by a Tenants can support a finding of the existence of an agreement to terminate a tenancy if it is accepted by the landlord. However, the landlord’s acceptance must be “unequivocal”, and it must also be clear that there is a meeting of the minds.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for December 1, 2025. The Tenants did not adduce any evidence at the hearing to support their version of events are true. I would have reasonably expected the Tenants to submit documentary evidence to support their position that the tenancy ought to have terminated at the end of November 2025. However, the only email that was submitted into evidence states the Tenants wanted to vacate in December 2025, which meant the earliest termination date could have been was December 31, 2025.

The Landlord adduced evidence at the hearing that supports his position he attempted to mitigate his losses and find a new Tenants immediately. The Landlord listed the rental unit for rent on the same day he received the September 29, 2025 email from the Tenants. The Landlord listed the rental unit for $300.00 cheaper than what the Tenants were paying. The earliest date the Landlord found another Tenants to rent the unit was January 1, 2026. On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlord incorrectly applied the last month rent deposit to the last month of tenancy. The issue of whether this is a fixed term tenancy or if a monthly tenancy are no longer relevant given my findings below.

The parties dispute if the tenancy were a monthly tenancy or a fixed term tenancy. The Landlord testified that the Tenants had signed an extension to their fixed term tenancy and had paid the post-dated cheques for an extension of the original lease. The Tenants testified that only one of the Tenants had signed the extension to the lease, so the extension was not binding on all parties. If I find in favour of the Tenants that this was a monthly tenancy rather than a fixed term one, the earliest the termination could have been, based on their September 29, 2025 email was December 31, 2025 (at least 60 days notice to terminate and last day of the rental period). The Tenants themselves in their email stated they wanted to vacate on December 1, 2025, however rent was due the first of the month, meaning the termination date ought to have been the last day of the month, bringing us to December 31, 2025. The parties agreed the Tenants had paid November 2025 rent and that they put a stop payment on their post-dated December 2025 rent, so the Landlord correctly applied the rent deposit to December 2025 rent.

And if this were a fixed term tenancy, the Tenants would have been liable to pay until the end of the fixed term, however, the Landlord would still have mitigated their losses as of January 1, 2026, as they had found a new Tenants at this time, and would have only been owed rent up to December 31, 2025.

I opt to not make a finding on whether this were a fixed term tenancy or a monthly tenancy because the outcome of both cases would still result in the earliest termination date being December 31, 2025.
Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). It was agreed between the parties that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. However, as the Tenant did not prove that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The Landlord’s L2 application to terminate the tenancy based on an N12 notice of termination for the Landlord’s own residential occupation was heard on April 24, 2024. The parties entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy on a non-voidable basis, effective May 31, 2024, and a consent order was issued resolving both the Landlord’s L2 application for termination of the tenancy because the Landlord in good faith required possession of the rental unit for the purposes of their own occupation (LTB-L-099213-23) and the Landlord’s L1 application for termination of the tenancy based on unpaid rent (LTB-L-003749-24).

The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2024, pursuant to the Landlord’s request for eviction for the Landlord’s own use. The Landlord denies that the Tenant vacated in accordance with the L2 application and submits that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2024, due to the amount of the outstanding rental arrears.

The matter before the Board was for non-voidable termination based on the Landlord’s N12 notice and the Tenant agreed to non-voidable termination in their consent order. As a result, I was satisfied that the Tenant had proven that the tenant vacated in accordance with the N12 notice of termination. Did the Landlord move into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time?
The Tenants assert that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith due to the outstanding rent arrears and did not move into the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that as his sister lived near the rental unit, he would frequently visit the rental unit while visiting his sister, and observed no signs that the Landlord ever moved into the rental unit such as a vehicle, tire tracks, shovelled snow, items in the window or other signs of occupancy of the rental unit. The Tenant also testified that he would frequently knock on doors and nobody ever answered the door to the rental unit.

The Tenant also testified that he had a conversation with a neighbour who lived near the rental unit and his neighbour had indicated that somebody who is not the Landlord or the Landlord’s family had moved into the rental unit. However, as this was hearsay evidence, it was given little to no weight.

The Landlord, [name] (‘FA’), testified that he moved into the rental unit on June 2, 2024 along with his wife and children. FA testified that he was experiencing marital issue in August 2024, and separated from his wife on September 25, 2024. After the separation FA moved out of the rental unit. A letter from FA’s wife’s legal counsel regarding negotiations for a separation agreement dated November 27, 2024, was entered as evidence by the Landlord. A divorce application was also entered into evidence by the Landlord.

FA submitted into evidence an e-transfer in the amount of $400.00 to an individual named [name] Salem (‘AS’), who he asserts is the mover who assisted the Landlord in moving into the rental unit. AS submitted a declaration that he assisted the Landlord in moving into the rental unit. However, as this was hearsay evidence, it was given little to no weight.

The Landlord’s children, [name] [name] and [name] [name] testified that they moved into the rental unit along with FA on or about June 5, 2024. The Landlord and his children testified that FA’s wife and children remain in the rental unit following the separation.

I found the testimony of the Landlord and the Landlord’s witnesses to be credible and supported by the Landlord’s supporting documentary evidence. I prefer the Landlord’s direct evidence over the Tenant’s mostly hearsay evidence. I accept that he moved in shortly after the Tenant vacated, but later vacated as a result of marital difficulties. I am further satisfied that the Landlord’s marital challenges were not reasonably foreseeable when the Tenant vacated such that the Landlord did not have a good faith intention to live in the unit for at least one year.

In my view, it is open to the LTB to find bad faith where the intended occupant moves in within a reasonable period of time after the tenant vacated, but moves out shortly thereafter and re-rents the unit with no reasonable explanation. However, this is not such a case given my finding about the Landlord’s genuine intention to occupy the unit and the fact that they did occupy it until their marriage broke down.
As a result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘NS’) and [name] (‘TN’) (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $9,353.18. T5 Application

The residential complex is a townhouse comprised of two rental units, a one-bedroom basement unit and a three-bedroom main floor unit. The Tenants resided in the main floor unit. The Tenants’ monthly rent was $2,339.00.

On October 28, 2024, the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination. The N12 notice indicates that the Landlords in good faith, personally require possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties do not dispute that an N12 notice was served, and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit due to the notice. The Landlords refute the third and fourth requirement of the legal test above.
For the reasons that follow, I find the Tenants have proven all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Burden of Proof – Rebuttable Reverse Onus

Based on the totality of evidence before me, I find it invokes the reverse onus clause under subsection 57(5)(b) of the Act. This section of the Act stipulates that if a notice is given by a landlord under s. 48 of the Act and, and the landlord enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenants, within one year of the tenants vacating, it is presumed that the landlord has given the N12 notice in bad faith. The onus of proof now shifts to the landlords to prove on a balance of probabilities that the N12 notice was served in good faith.

Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Landlords have not met their burden of proof to support that the Landlords served the N12 notice in good faith for the reasons set out below. Chain of Events Tenant’s Position
KK testified that there was a total of six people living in the rental unit at the time they received the N12 notice. Due to the notice, the Tenants vacated the unit on December 15, 2025.

KK testified that on February 1, 2026, he visited the property and spoke to an individual who stated he was renting a room in the main floor unit, and the remaining two bedrooms were also occupied by new tenants. They stated the rooms were rented out for $1000.00 a month. They also stated that the Landlord was not living with him and never mentioned an intention of moving in with them. The Tenants provided a video of this interaction which was marked as Exhibit 1 in this proceeding.

KK testified that his family of six people rented a new unit that is approximately 25 km farther away. The new rental is a four-bedroom unit, and the monthly rent is $3,100.00, however, the Tenants did not provide a copy of their new lease agreement.
The Tenant’s evidence was uncontradicted under cross examination as the Landlord stated they had no questions for KK. Landlord’s Position

NS testified that he moved into the rental unit on January 1, 2026, and that he is still residing in the rental unit. He testified that he was having marital issues at his matrimonial home, where his wife and two young children live and this is why he served the N12 notice. He testified that he stays at the rental unit approximately 5 days a month and stays at the matrimonial home approximately 5-6 days a month. He states that he did rent out the other rooms, but they are currently empty as of the date of the hearing.
Under cross-examination, NS testified that he still has personal items in the matrimonial home, and that he chose the main floor rental unit over the basement unit because “one room is enough”.

TN testified that her and her husband were continuously fighting and that she told her husband to move out. She testified that they are on speaking terms and living together some days. After approximately five months things started to resolve, and he returned to the matrimonial home. She testified that she can’t take care of the children alone without her husband. Analysis

I find the Tenant’s evidence was straightforward, concise, and credible. KK provided oral evidence that was supported by video (Exhibit 1) of an individual claiming to be the new tenant of the rental unit. This individual stated that he was renting one room in the three- bedroom unit, the other two bedrooms were each occupied by someone other than the Landlord, and the Landlord never mentioned to them that they had an intention to move into the rental unit. I accept this evidence as reliable and do not believe this individual, who has no standing in this proceeding, would have any reason to mislead KK in their conversation on February 1, 2026.

I do not find the Landlord’s evidence persuasive in supporting that he does in fact reside at the unit on a full-time basis for the purposes of residential occupation for at least one year. The Landlords both testified that because of marital problems, NS was asked to leave the rental unit by TN but continued to visit the matrimonial home and assist in taking care of his young children. NS continued to keep personal possessions at the matrimonial home and was still residing in the matrimonial home for approximately 5 days a week, the same amount of time that they are allegedly spending at the rental unit. Further, the Landlord admitted that he had in fact rented out rooms in the rental unit after the Tenants vacated. I do not find the Landlord’s evidence to be credible and find that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit, as indicated on the N12 notice.

Both Landlords were clear in their testimony that the N12 notice was served because of marital issues and a need for space between NS and TN. However, I do not accept the position that the N12 notice was served in good faith as the Landlord’s evidence was contradictory and does not support that he intended to live in the unit on full-time basis. The N12 notice requires that the Landlord, in good faith, requires the rental unit for the person identified in the notice, for the purpose of residential occupation, for at least one year. Based on the evidence before me, I do not believe that the Landlord intended on residing in the unit for the purpose of residential occupation, for at least one year. Remedies

The Tenants requested a rent abatement of $14,034.00. The Tenant’s evidence supporting the rent abatement was based on general damages they incurred post-termination of the tenancy. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement is not appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenants’ Representative was asked if they sought to amend the application to include general damages, however, the Tenants’ Representative stated they were not seeking an amendment.

The Tenants claims a rent differential of $9,132.00 ($3,100.00 - $2,339.00 = $761.00 x 12 months = $9,132.00). While the Tenants did not provide a copy of the new lease agreement, I accept the Tenant’s oral testimony that the monthly rent at their new unit is $3,100.00 and this evidence was uncontradicted by the Landlords. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $9,132.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants claimed costs of $173.18 for moving expenses incurred. This evidence was uncontradicted by the Landlords. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants s$173.18 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $9,353.18. This amount represents: • $9,132.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from December 15, 2024, to December 15, 2025. • $173.18 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not pr ove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the exterior of the property, namely the removal of snow and ice, and lawn and shrubbery/tree maintenance. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord expected them to do the work, which they did for the entirety of the tenancy.

The Landlord alleges that it is the Tenant’s responsibility to clear the snow and ice, cut the grass, and maintain the shrubs/trees. It was a term of their contract and in consideration for being responsible for the exterior cleanliness, the Landlord offered a reduced monthly rent.

Having reviewed the evidence, I find the T enant has exclusive use of the property is responsible for the ordinary cleanliness of the exterior of the property, including snow removal, maintaining the grass, trees, shrubs, and yard. Analysis
The purpose of the Act is to balance the ri ghts and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants.

Section 3 of the Act notes that this “Act … app lies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” Section 4 of the Act notes, if “a provision of this Act conflicts with a provision of another Act, other than the Human Rights Code, the provision of this Act applies.”
The Act also contemplates that both landl ords and tenants have responsibilities related to the maintenance of the rental unit and rental complex.

For landlords, subsection 20(1) of the Act provides that: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For tenants, section 33 of the Act provides that: The tenant is responsible for ordinary cleanliness of the rental unit, except to the extent that the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to clean it.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The applicable property standards bylaw for Ottawa, Property Standards (Bylaw No. 2013- 416) City of Ottawa, regulates residential properties.

The [name] defines owner as: “the lessee or occupant of the property who, under the terms of a lease, is required to repair and maintain the property in accordance with the standards for maintenance and occupancy of property.”

Section 6 of the [name] requires a yard to be kept clean and free from refuse or debris, lawns shall be kept trimmed and not overgrown, and all hedges, shrubs, trees or other plants shall be maintained in a manner that does not adversely affect the safety of the public.

The Bylaw Section 9, Safe Passage, requires all surfaced paths, walkways, patios, steps, ramps, building entrances, driveways and parking areas shall be, maintained in a hole-free condition and free of any settlements that might cause an accident or injury; maintained in a condition so as to afford safe passage by pedestrians and motor vehicles in inclement weather; and adequately illuminated at night so as to afford safe use. Rental Unit

The Tenant, together with her family, moved into the rental unit on or about May 1, 2017, and vacated on or about May 4, 2024. This application is brought 8 months following the Tenant vacating the property by eviction order issued by the LTB.

The rental unit is a single-dwelling home. It is a semi-detached two-story home with two bedrooms and a full bathroom upstairs, two bedrooms and a half bathroom downstairs, garage, laundry room, kitchen and family room. The Tenant had exclusive use of the property and lived at the rental unit for 6 years with her spouse and two children. Occasionally the Tenant had guests stay with them, but there was no point during the tenancy with the Landlord where there was another tenant at the property.
It is not contested that the Tenant had exclusive use of the property. Tenancy Agreement and Exterior Maintenance Clause

The rental agreement specifically included an exterior maintenance clause. Exhibit 1, the Rental Agreement (DOC 4754838) at clause 10 indicates that the Tenant agrees to “take care of lawn, trees and shovel snow.” (“Exterior Maintenance Clause”) Pursuant to this clause, the Tenant was responsible to clear the snow, take care of the lawn and trees.

The Landlord indicated they specifically put the clause in the agreement because the Landlord, at that time, did not live in Canada, and he provided a reduced rent because of the Tenant taking on this responsibility.

The Landlord testified that the rent charged to the Tenant was lower than market rent due to the agreement that the Tenant would maintain the exterior of the property. [name], a witness for the Landlord, testified that she lives next door to the rental unit and rents a basement apartment. The buildings are similar in that it too is a semi-detached home, but in her building, there are two 2-bedroom units. She rents the 2-bedroom basement unit for $1300.00.

In contrast and supporting the Landlord’s assertion that the Tenant’s rent was lower than market rent, the whole house occupied by the Tenant and her family when the tenancy began was $1250.00. When the Tenant vacated the property, the monthly rent was $1350.00 for the whole house.
It is not disputed that the Tenant signed the lease agreement knowing that this clause obligated them to maintain the exterior.

At all times, the Tenants had exclusive use of the property. After taking a contextual approach to the circumstances in this case, I find that the Tenants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the snow and ice removal, lawn, tree, shrubs and yard maintenance at the rental unit.

I find the Tenant was responsible to clear the snow and ice, maintain the lawn, trees, shrubs and yard because it was a term agreed to in their tenancy agreement, and at all times throughout their tenancy, they had exclusive use of the property, including the driveway and the front and back yard.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative requested an adjournment. During the submissions, it was discovered the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on August 20, 2025. The Tenant then confirmed they did vacate the rental unit on that date.

The remedies sought by the Tenant in their T2 application are as follows: 1. We respectfully request that the Landlord be prohibited from entering the premises except in emergencies or with explicit approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board and that any inspections under 27(1)(4) as state in his most recent Notice of intent to enter be done by a third party provided by the landlord and tenant board especially during the ongoing court proceedings. 2. All behaviors stated on page 4 is ended.
There are no monetary amounts sought by the Tenant. The application filing fee was waived by a fee waiver through the Board.

The parties were invited to make submissions under s. 197(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which states: The Board may dismiss an application without holding a hearing or refuse to allow an application to be filed if, in the opinion of the Board, the matter is frivolous or vexatious, has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action. [Emphasis Added]

The Tenant requests the proceeding to continue because she believes it is procedurally fair to do so and that she has the right to be heard. The Tenant argues that just because the tenancy ended, does not mean that her rights to the application terminate. The Tenant quoted sections 87.1 of the Act and section 89.1 of the Act which the Tenant feels demonstrates that applications can proceed while the Tenant is no longer in possession.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submits that the application is moot because the Tenant vacated the rental unit and the Tenant and Landlord relationship has terminated. The Landlord’s Legal Representative relies on Abara v. Hall and [name], 2022 ONSC 7093 and [name] v. Klerer, 2022 ONCA 489 that he feels point out that an application at the Board cannot proceed once the Tenant has vacated. Analysis

This application is a T2 application about tenant rights. Both parties presented cases or sections of the Act that discuss a different type of application. Each type of application has different legal tests and statutory requirements. In this case, the Tenant filed the application while she was still in possession of the rental unit. Just because the tenancy terminated during an active T2 application before the Board does not mean the application will be dismissed because the tenancy terminated. T2 applications can still be heard once the tenancy terminates. Further, subsection 29(1) of the Act states that a former tenant may file a T6 or T2 application with the Board.

However, the issue revolves around the remedies sought. The remedy sought by the Tenant involved wanting the Board to order the Landlord to not enter the rental unit unless it is an emergency, and to have the Board order the inspections done by a third party. The Tenant also wanted the behaviour of the Landlord to cease. The remedies the Tenant seeks, however, are moot because the tenancy terminated, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant did not request to amend the application.
Because the remedies are moot, there is no reasonable cause of action per section 197(1) of the Act.
Therefore, the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $411.17 by May 31, 2026. Illegal charge collected

The Landlords collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The parties agreed that the Tenant was responsible for paying 70% of all utility bills and the basement tenant was responsible for 30% of all utility bills. The Tenant testified that she would pay 100% of the utility bills and then provide the Landlords with a copy of all utility bills and deduct 30% of those bills for her lawful rent every month. However, when she vacated on September 29, 2025, the Landlords did not deduct 30% of the utility bills owed for August 2025 and September 2025, which amounts to $411.17.

The Landlords agreed that the Tenant would pay 100% of the bills and then deduct 30% off of those bills on the next month’s lawful rent. However, when the Tenant vacated on September 29, 2025, she paid 100% of August’s and September’s utility bills, but that he did not deduct the 30% of those bills from her last month rent deposit because she had damaged the rental unit.
The Landlords further agreed that 30% of the utility bills for August 2025 and September 2025 amount to $411.17.

The Landlords collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act. The Landlords withheld the amount above and treated it like a damage charge – this kind of charge is not legal under the Act. The Tenant testified that she will waive her right to collect per-diem amounts claimed for September 29, 2025 and September 30, 2025, even though the new tenants had moved in on September 28, 2025. The Tenant further waives her right to the filing fee. Therefore, the Landlords shall pay the Tenant $411.17 for the illegal charge.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $411.17. This amount represents: • $411.17 for the illegal charge collected.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant [name] testified that the Tenant’s moved into the rental unit on August 25, 202 and vacated October 24, 2025. She testified that at the time the lease agreement was signed the Tenant’s cleary refused to pay for any water heater rental charges, and indicated that while there is a box for hot water heater rental on the lease agreement it is not checked.

In spite of this there was a charge for hot water heater rental on the Enbridge Gas bill which the Tenant’s paid throughout the tenancy, and which gradually increased from $35.54 per month to $42.91. The Tenant indicated that this was part of the Enbridge Bill and was paid to [name].
She testified that they informed the Landlord of this several times and the Landlord indicated that he did not know about it.
The Tenant [name] testified that they never agreed to pay the charge and did not know what they were paying.
Under the terms of the lease agreement the Tenant’s are responsible for paying for gas, which is provided by Enridge, and the bill was in their name during the tenancy.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant’s never paid any funds directly to him for the hot water heater rental. He testified that after the Tenant’s vacated, he was contacted by [name] and Enbridge to take over the hot water heater rental. He testified that he was unaware that there was a rented hot water heater in the unit and has made more than 3 requests for the contract for the rental, but they have not been able to provide it to him.

Section 135(1) of the Act states: 135 ( 1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental uni t may appl y to the B oard for an order that the l andl ord, superi ntendent or agent of the l andl ord pay to the tenant any money the person col l ected or retai ned i n contraventi on of thi s A ct or the T enant Protection A ct, 199 7. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (1).

While I am prepared to accept that the lease agreement does not require the Tenant’s to pay for hot water heater rental, I also accept that the Landlord was unaware that there was a hot water heater rental contract associated with the property and has taken steps to secure a copy of this contract without success. 11. [name] alleges that they have paid an illegal charge to [name] via Enbridge gas, they have not paid these funds to the Landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord. Therefore, I am not satisfied that I have the authority to order the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant’s for the alleged illegal charge.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owe. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. These applications were heard by videoconference on January 30, 2026. The first named Tenant, the Tenants’ legal representative, [name], the Landlord, and the Landlord’s representative, [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenants were still in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $3,382.50. It is due on the 1st day of each month. File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $111.21. This amount is calculated as follows: $3,382.50 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenants have paid $21,637.31 to the Landlord since the application was filed.

In satisfaction of outstanding utilities and an illegal deposit of $1,000.00 owed by the Landlord to the Tenants, the parties agreed that the rent arrears and costs owing to January 31, 2026, are $18,637.10.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,300.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $182.28 is owing to the Tenants for the period from November 1, 2023, to January 30, 2026. Tenants Section 82 Claims and Application:

On an application such as this Section 82 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') allows the Tenant to raise any issue that could be the subject of an application made by the Tenant. The Tenants also filed their own application pursuant to section 29 of the Act. Therefore, I will address the Tenants claims below.

The Tenants have proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants a rent abatement of $200.00 plus the costs the Tenants incurred for filing the application. Law and Legal Test:

Section 29 of the Act limits the Tenants claim to not more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. This order shall only address those claims that are within time.

Section 22 and Section 23 of the Act says that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

There is no definition of “harassment’ under the Act but generally speaking, harassment is usually considered to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome. Section 22 of the Act contains both a subjective and objective element. The interference must be substantial; that is a subjective element as not every tenant will be equally adversely impacted by various kinds of behaviour complained of. The objective element arises from the phrase “reasonable enjoyment” meaning the Board must ask itself whether or not the reasonable person would consider the behaviour to be unreasonable. Unpaid Utilities: File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24

A persistent ongoing dispute between the parties is the issue of unpaid utilities. Paragraph 8 of the tenancy agreement says: Utilities are to be split 65%-35% with the main floor Tenants paying 65% and the Landlord paying the remaining 35%. Utilities are to be put in the main floor Tenants’ name.

The Landlord says that the Tenants failed to provide full copies of the bills which is the reason as to why they failed to remit payment to the Tenants. The Tenants say that’s not true. There was evidence presented by the Tenants as examples of instances where they sent the Landlord a full copy of the utility bill however, it was left [name]. As a result, the Tenants arbitrarily deducted it from the rent. As such, the Tenants also argue that the N4 notice of termination is invalid as it includes monies owed for utilities.

As discussed in length during the hearing, I found that the N4 included only amounts related to rent. Rent is defined as the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord. Utilities are defined as heat, electricity, and water.

Aside from the rules relating to a rent increase, rent is a fixed monthly expense where utilities fluctuate month to month. It is clear from the language of the tenancy agreement rent and utilities are separate and distinct charges/responsibilities. An N4 notice of termination is given pursuant to section 59 of the Act. Subsection 59(2) says that the notice shall set out the amount of rent due. The notice accurately did that. While I agree with the Tenants that they were owed money, arbitrarily deducting it from the rent does not render the notice invalid.
As already mentioned, in an effort of reconciliation and moving forward with this issue, the parties mutually agreed to offset the amount the Tenants owe the Landlord.

On November 17, 2025, LTB-L-051132-25-IN2 was issued. [name] 8 provided guidance in an attempt to mediate the issue until the final resolution of the applications. The Tenants were required to provide the Landlord with a full copy of any utility bill that became due and owing and the Landlord was to remit payment for their portion of the bills within 5 days.

At the hearing before me on January 30, 2026, the Tenants raised a concern that the Landlord had not followed the interim order as they remitted payment late. The Landlord says that the payment was late as they were sick.

It is clear from my interactions with the parties that they are not particularly fond of each other. However, the terms of a tenancy agreement are intended to be performed with a spirit of good faith. As mentioned at the hearing, there really is no mechanism built into the tenancy agreement that contemplates what happens in a situation (as in this case) arises when the Landlord does not pay the Tenants their portion of the utility bills.

Contra proferentem is a legal doctrine where ambiguous contract terms are interpreted against the party who drafted them (in this case, the Landlord). It encourages drafting clear 1 DOC-6131369 and DOC-6131361 File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24 terms to promote fairness in agreements and to protect the weaker party (in this case, the Tenant).

The Tenants’ recourse in a situation such as this, might be to file an application pursuant to section 29 or 135 of the Act. However, given the simplicity of the narrow issue, I do not find it to be a good use of Board resources to force the Tenants to file such applications. Therefore, terms akin to the interim order issued November 17, 2025, with the addition that if the Landlord fails to comply the Tenant may deduct it from the monthly rent shall issue. This effectively bridges the gap in the language of the tenancy agreement and the Act. Unwanted Visits:
The residential complex is a house, split into two separate residential units. The Tenants reside on the “main floor” or “upper unit”. December 4, 2024:

On December 3, 2024, the Landlord sends the Tenants an email indicating that he would like to attend the rental unit at 2:00p.m., for a home appraisal 2. On the same date, the male Tenant responds to the Landlord saying, in part: … In Ontario, a landlord cannot bring someone else into the tenant’s home without proper notice and valid reason. Under the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), landlords must provide at least 24 hours written notice before entering a tenant’s rental unit. The notice must include the reason for entry and specify the date and time of the visit, which must fall between 8 a.m and 8 p.m. If the landlord is bringing someone else into the unit (e.g., a contractor, perspective buyer, or maintenance worker), the tenant should be informed of the person’s identity and the purpose if their visit. Without such disclosure, the landlord may be violating the tenant’s rights to privacy. Kannan anyone that has not been identified nor the exact reason for coming will not be allowed to enter …

On December 4, 2024, the Landlord showed up to the rental unit and attempted to enter the rental unit however because of a child lock was not able to gain entry, and there was a disagreement over the entry.

Section 27 allows the Landlord to give notice of entry to: … 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. … 2 DOC-5110287 File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement.
Page 4 of the tenancy agreement says that the Landlord may enter between the hours of 8:00 a.m., and 8:00 p.m., to allow a potential lender or insurer to view the rental unit.

Although concise, the Landlord’s notice given on December 3, 2024, was sent at 1:23 p.m., for an inspection start time of 2:00 p.m, the following day, and it outlined a reason. There Landlord did not access the unit on that date and so I do not find that an illegal entry occurred, or that it substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, or that it was harassment. Therefore, this claim is dismissed.

The Tenant says that from the period of February 19, 2025, to February 28, 2025, the Landlord on multiple occasions showed up to the rental unit unannounced, sometimes after 9:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m. February 19, 2025:

The Tenants testified that on February 19, 2025, the Landlord kept requesting that he wanted to come to inspect a heat issue relating to the prior basement tenant complaining that there was inadequate heat. The residential complex contains one forced air furnace, the thermostat for which is in these Tenants’ rental unit. There is no evidence to suggest that the Landlord entered the rental unit on this date. The Tenants provided still photographs from what appears to be their doorbell cam3, showing the Landlord’s car parked on the street. I do not find that this instance rises to the level of substantial interference. February 22, 2025:

The Tenants testified that on February 22, 2025, the Landlord showed up to the property of the residential complex unannounced. The Landlord recalls that on this date they came to shovel snow that was completely covering the lower unit’s front entrance door. The Landlord alleges was placed there by the Tenant4. The Tenant says that it was the neighbour. February 24, 2025, to February 26, 2025:

The Tenants testified that on these series of dates the Landlord showed up to the property of the residential complex unannounced and while on the property, the Landlord was drilling after 9:00 p.m., there was some occasions where the Landlord banged on the Tenants’ door and was screaming at the Tenants. To support their claims, they provided videos of points in time showing the existence of a verbal conflict and yelling and still [name]. 3 DOC-6191758: image 2 4 DOC-7220675: Pages 8 to 11 5 DOC- 6191758 File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24
The Landlord says that for these dates he was attending the rental unit to get it ready for a prospective tenant, who would be residing in the basement unit.

The Landlord does not dispute that on February 24, 2025, he attended the rental unit to prepare the rental unit for upcoming showings. Upon arrival, they noticed that the lock on the lower unit’s main entrance door was not working properly. The Landlord also confirms that he did start drilling the lock on the door to effect a change of the lock. The Landlord felt as though this was more urgent in nature. The Landlord submitted that his involvement at the property of the residential complex had nothing to do with the Tenants upstairs- only the basement unit.

Sections 26 and 27 of the Act outline the circumstances when a landlord may enter a rental unit [emphasis added] with and without notice. A landlord need not give a notice to attend the property of the residential complex. It would appear that the Tenants’ misunderstanding of this fueled a lot of the disagreements surrounding these visits. However, the conduct of both parties is particularly concerning. 37. [name] is a 4 second, undated video, showing the male Tenant in the entry way of their rental unit, the Landlord is yelling in from outside and the Tenant opens the door and says, “what did you say?”. Video_1 is a 32 second, undated video, showing the male Tenant standing outside, on the front veranda videoing the Landlord and another individual, they appear to be shoveling snow. The Tenant says “hey, idiot. Hey, idiot- I told you to leave, right? The Landlord responds with saying “you fucking guy”. Tenant responds again “How many times did I tell you to leave? What are you doing here 4 times in one fucking week, banging on my fucking door you little bitch”. The Landlord calls the Tenant a “bastard” and the argument continues with the parties swearing and threatening one another. The Landlord does also say that they are there at the rental unit for something else and not these Tenants. 38. [name] is a 33 second, undated video and from the video it would appear that the male Tenant was standing inside the front entrance. The Landlord is banging on the door while yelling “[name], you mother fucker” the Tenant asks him what he said and the Landlord responded with “mother fucker, you’re asshole” The Tenant responds with “You’re the one slapping my door, get the fuck out” The Landlord yells back “you are asshole! You are asshole!” 39. Based on the evidence before me I do not find harassment. Although the Tenants informed the Landlord that their presence was unwelcomed and felt as though the Landlord had no right to be there- that is actually not true. As explained above, the Landlord need not give notice to attend the property. The Landlord was attending the property to ready a vacant unit for a prospective tenant or shoveling snow after a snowfall, I do not find that to be an unreasonable explanation for their presence. 40. The Landlord was also provoked by the male Tenant. The party’s behaviour is equally appalling between one another. However, it better suggests at times a genuine disagreement, not harassment. 41. However, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenant when they were drilling the lock after 9:00 p.m, on February 24, 2026. There was nothing to suggest the presence of an emergency on that date, the Landlord could File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24 have arranged to do that at a different time. The Tenants say that the noise interfered with the sleep of their young child and startled them. As the incident occurred for one night, it was not for the entire day- while also recognizing the negative impact it had on the Tenants for the night, I find an abatement of $200.00 to be reasonable given the circumstances. July 17, 2025: 42. On July 17, 2025, the Landlord attempted to gain entry into the rental unit for the purposes of carrying out an inspection because the basement tenant gave them information regarding an alleged leak in the basement. The Landlord served the Tenants a notice to [name], and the Tenants did not allow entry despite receiving notice. As a result, the Landlord called the local authorities to assist with the situation. The Tenants did not allow the inspection to be carried out because they say that this was another form of harassment. The Landlord also asserts that for the past 2 years, they have not been allowed by the Tenants to inspect the property and have engaged the assistance of the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit. 43. Section 27 allows the Landlord to give written notice for the purposes of carrying out an inspection to determine whether the rental unit is in a good state of repair. Based on the Landlord’s testimony, I find that their reason for giving the notice was reasonable. The notice itself was sufficient; therefore, I find that the Tenants were required to allow the Landlord to enter on that date. 44. The Tenants say that having police presence in the area could have a damaging effect on their relationship both professionally and personally. No evidence was supplied to support the validity of this argument. Also, I do not find it unreasonable that the Landlord felt the need to call the authorities- given the circumstances. Therefore, this claim is dismissed. Multiple N4 Notices of Termination: 45. The Tenants say that by the Landlord serving 3 N4 notices of termination it caused them confusion, and the Landlord was attempting to evict them in bad faith as they were including unpaid utilities in those notices as unpaid rent. 46. The Tenants owed rent money at the time that the notices were served. An N4 notice of termination has technical requirements that must be met. There is no dispute that the Landlord only acted on one of the notices and that is the one subject to this application. 47. I do not find that the service of the notices nor confusion surrounding the notices amounted to substantial interference. Therefore, this claim is dismissed. Heat Issue: 48. The Tenants say that this was a reoccurring event, from the heat issue in 2024, and that the same issue with the thermostat and furnace arouse again in the winter months of 2025. 6 DOC-6038040 File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24 49. The Landlord says that they were receiving complaints from the tenant in the lower rental unit stating that the rental unit had inadequate heat. The Landlord asked the Tenant to come over and investigate the thermostat and furnace. The Tenants did now allow them in, however- allowed [name] to complete an inspection. The technician noted that there may be inadequate duct supply in order for the heat to travel7. The Tenants did not feel it necessary to allow the Landlord in as they felt that this was another example of the Landlord harassing them. 50. I accept the fact that if the Landlord was receiving complaints from another tenant regarding a heat issue that he would want to come and do some sort of inspection, that is actually quite logical. The Tenants did not want the Landlord attending their rental unit and so the Landlord engaged the services of a third-party company to do the inspection on their behalf. I therefore, do not find substantial interference or harassment. Parking: 51. The tenancy agreement outlines that the Tenants receive one side of the driveway plus exclusive use of both sides of the garage. On March 12, 2024, and March 15, 2024, the Tenants complained to the Landlord that the lower unit tenant was parking their vehicles on the driveway, which was in violation of the terms of the tenancy agreement. The Tenants testified that they never loss use of the exclusive use garage and cars were still able to be parked. I agree that this may have been an inconvenience or an annoyance for the 2 days, I do not find it rises to the level of substantial interference and the impact on the Tenants was low. This claim is dismissed. Summary Remarks: 52. In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so and may have regard to a pattern of activities relating to the residential complex and the rental unit8. 53. In their closing submissions, the Tenants say that the Landlord has shown a frequent pattern of behaviour that has led to the Landlord harassing them and/or substantially interfering with their reasonable enjoyment. Aside from the events that occurred in February 2025, as per my findings set out above- what I gather from considering the evidence in this case is that the relationship between the parties has deteriorated to such a degree that neither one respects the other. 54. The Landlord and the Tenant have both engaged in disrespectful behaviour; the parties have had numerous disagreements whereby they call each other profanities and threaten one another, the Tenant has not allowed the Landlord to inspect the rental unit in over two years despite receiving written notice because the Tenants fear that he will be aggressive when on the property, the Landlord has failed to remit payment with respect to utilities owing to the Tenants. That being said, genuine disagreements, especially those that are 7 DOC-6249698 8 S.202 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24 premised on a misunderstanding of the law is not in this case harassment or substantial interference (with respect to either party). Relief From Eviction: 55. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until April 30, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. 56. The Tenant asked that the application be dismissed as the Landlord’s presentation of the rent arrears was done in bad faith. However, I have already determined that the N4 notice of termination only contained amounts pertaining to unpaid rent. The Tenants have lived in the rental unit for approximately 2.5 years and reside there with their minor child. 57. The Tenants were given an interim order to pay the on-going rent until the application was finally decided, which they complied with prior to the hearing. However, the arrears are still quite substantial. 58. Since the Tenants have not had the benefit of my order, I find a short delay of 30 days from the date of my order to be reasonable considering the circumstances. The delay is not so extensive that it shall severely prejudice the Landlord. Although an additional month may become owing, in the event the Tenants do not void the order, it would be offset by the last months rent on deposit.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants a rent abatement in the amount of $200.00 and since the Tenants are partially successful with the claims in their application the Landlord shall also pay the costs in the amount of $53.00. Therefore, the total abatement the Landlord owes the Tenants is $253.00. I have deducted that from the arrears the Tenants owe.
The Tenants shall give the Landlord a full copy of any utility bill that becomes due and owing, within 5 days of receiving it.
Within 5 days of the Tenants giving the Landlords the full copy of the utility bill, the Landlord shall remit their portion to the Tenants.

If the Landlord fails to comply with paragraph 3, above, than the Tenants may deduct the Landlord’s portion of the utilities owing from the monthly rent. Additionally, the Tenants in writing, shall set out to the Landlord which month they are deducting it from and the total amount they are deducting.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated unless the Tenant void this order.

The Tenants may void this order and continue the tenancy by paying to the Landlord or to the LTB in trust: File Numbers: LTB-L-051132-25 LTB-T-105948-24 • $28,531.60 if the payment is made on or before April 30, 2026 (less any payments made by the Tenants). See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

The Tenants may also make a motion at the LTB to void this order under section 74(11) of the Act, if the Tenants have paid the full amount owing as ordered plus any additional rent that became due after March 29, 2026, but before the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) enforces the eviction. The Tenants may only make this motion once during the tenancy.
If the Tenants do not pay the amount required to void this order the Tenants must move out of the rental unit on or before April 30, 2026.

If the Tenants do not void the order, the Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $14,790.61. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date of the hearing and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit and the abatement are deducted from the amount owing by the Tenants. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.
The Tenants shall also pay the Landlord compensation of $111.21 per day for the use of the unit starting January 31, 2026, until the date the Tenants move out of the unit
The Landlord or the Tenants shall pay to the other any sum of money that is owed as a result of this order.
If the unit is not vacated on or before April 30, 2026, then starting May 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
