issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities that [name] suffered severe allergies from pet hair and dander in the residential complex. The Landlord failed to accommodate him or fulfil their maintenance obligations under s. 20 of the Act.
Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay compensation to the Tenants.
The breach of the Landlord’s obligation was egregious and so the Landlord shall also be ordered to pay a fine. [name]
On June 18, 2021, the Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord.
They moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2021.

On May 19, 2022, the Tenant’s allergy symptoms – sneezing, runny nose and eyes, difficulty breathing - prompted him to complain to the Landlord and request the air filters in his unit be changed. The Landlord failed to respond.

The Tenant testified that he has suffered from allergies since he was 4 years old. He received allergy vaccines until he was 18. Now in his thirties, he takes oral medication to manage his condition. When the Landlord did not respond, the Tenant purchased his own air filters, air purifiers and medication to manage his symptoms.
The allergies persisted and on October 8, 2022, December 6, 2022, May 11, 2023, the Tenant contacted the Landlord by email and by phone, but on each occasion received no response.
On December 23, 2023 the Tenant telephoned the Landlord who referred him to [name] in the adjacent building, but she did not respond either.

On January 7, 2024 the Tenant’s allergies were full blown. He stated that his eyes and nose were swollen, he was tearing constantly, he could not breathe and he was forced to sleep in his car in the middle of winter to ease his discomfort.

On January 8, 2024, he telephoned the Landlord’s helpline at 5:44 AM because he was in distress. He left a message and sent an email to the Landlord, saying that the rental unit was making him physically sick and that he could no longer live there. The Landlord responded by email on January 9, 2024 that “Upper Management would accept a two months’ notice with a medical report specifying that the unit is the cause of your condition, or you can do a lease assignment.”
On January 9, 2024, again he slept in his car and telephoned the helpline and reached someone at 8:27 AM. He was told someone would call him back, but no one did.
On January 15, 2024 obtained medical note from [name] [name] confirming his allergies to animal dander in the building.

The Tenant testified that he missed 11 days of work at a crucial time when he was working on a project of national importance during the pandemic. He also testified that he had an infant at home and that he was unable to help his wife because his allergies were incapacitating him. He had numerous nights of no sleep.

The Tenant testified to their own efforts to resolve the problem by purchasing air purifiers, and filters, all of which were not helpful. He also attempted to treat the allergies but that was also unsuccessful.

There was an addendum to the lease, called Rules and Regulations, which outlined a number of responsibilities of tenants in the building. Clause 4 stipulated that: • “Dogs are permitted in the building, on the grounds and in the unit only if: …. e. The owner of a dog is responsible for all damage caused by his dog even if the owner had no control over the dog at the time of the damage. This responsibility applies to damages caused inside the unit and everywhere on the property. The landlord will be required to ask you to get rid of your dog within 7 days if: • It disturbs the neighbourhood by its continuous barking (day or night) • It interferes with the peaceful enjoyment of other tenants • You do not collect the dog’s feces in the housing unit, in the building or on the ground • It is recognized as a potentially dangerous dog after having bitten or attacked a person or a domestic animal by inflicting injuries.
The Tenants testified that they signed the Rules and Regulations on June 18, 2021 and understood that the rules would be enforced on all residents.
The Landlord did not cross-examine the Tenant.
The Landlord did not call any evidence. Landlord’s Duty to Maintain and Repair

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Section 20(1) of the Act requires landlords to maintain the residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In this case, it appears on uncontested evidence that the Landlord took no action to address air quality or offer any other solutions to assist the Tenant despite multiple requests over the course of 20 months.
In the absence of any evidence, the Board finds that the Landlord failed to respond to the request for maintenance.

The Board finds that the Landlord failed to uphold its obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex. Landlord’s duty to address substantial interference

A landlord’s duty to address substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment was affirmed by the Divisional Court in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”).
In this case, the Landlord had a duty to respond to and take reasonable steps to address the Tenant’s complaints.
Taking no action breached this obligation. Duty to Accommodate

The Human Rights Code, R.S.O 1990 c. H19 (“Code”), prohibits discrimination on grounds of race, ethnicity, religion, marital status, sex, disability, ancestry, citizenship, age, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, family status, and receipt of public assistance.1 This means that in the residential rental context, tenants and prospective tenants must be free from discrimination.

The Code at section 10 defines “disability” as “any degree of physical disability, infirmity, malformation or disfigurement that is caused by bodily injury, birth defect or illness and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, includes diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, a brain injury, any degree of paralysis, amputation, lack of physical co-ordination, blindness or visual impediment, deafness or hearing impediment, muteness or speech impediment, or physical reliance on a guide dog or other animal or on a wheelchair or other remedial appliance or device, (b) a condition of mental impairment or a developmental disability."

Landlords have a duty to accommodate Tenants in accordance with the Code up until the point of undue hardshipi and all Tenants are entitled to equal treatment free from discrimination, Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, 1992 CanLII 81 (SCC), [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970 at para. 43.

In order to trigger the duty to accommodate, a tenant is not required to inform a landlord of all the details of the tenant’s disability, but the tenant should inform the landlord that she has disability-related needs, and endeavour to provide as much information as possible to facilitate the search for accommodation. See Simpson v. Commissionaires (Great Lakes), 2009 HRTO 1382 at para. 35.

Once the duty to accommodate has been triggered, the landlord must meet its obligation. The duty to accommodate requires the landlord to show that it could not have accommodated the tenant’s disability-related needs short of undue hardship. “Accommodation” refers to what is required in the circumstances to avoid discrimination. A respondent is not required to accommodate past the point of undue hardship, and sometimes, little or no accommodation may be possible. See [name], 2009 HRTO 1306 at para. 29. The landlord has to present cogent 1 Human Rights Code, [name], [name], s. 1. evidence to support its position that it cannot accommodate the tenant’s disability-related needs because of undue hardship. See British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU, 1999 CanLII 652 (SCC), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 3 at paras. 78-79.

A duty to accommodate does not guarantee or obviate a specific course of action on the part of the Landlord; the Landlord merely must take steps up until the point of undue hardship to accommodate the Tenants.

The Landlord had a duty to accommodate the Tenant’s medical condition once it was aware of the adverse effects in the rental unit and residential complex. It was uncontested that the Tenant had allergies and there was an adverse effect on him, therefore the onus shifts to the Landlord to show it fulfilled its duty to accommodate to the point of undue hardship.

The Board finds that that the Landlord was made aware on May 18, 2022, that the Tenant suffered from severe environmental allergies due to pet hair and pet dander in the rental unit and residential complex.
The Board finds that the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s seven requests between May 18, 2022 and January 8, 2024.
On January 9, 2024, the Landlord offered that the Tenants could vacate if they provided a medical note and gave 60 days’ notice.
The Board finds this was not an accommodation, as the Act already provides that a Tenant may terminate their tenancy on 60 days’ notice.

The Board is not dictating the type of accommodation from the Landlord, but merely indicating that the Landlord must respond to the Tenant’s request for assistance, in this case, maintenance of the air quality, up until the point of undue hardship. The Board finds that the Landlord did not respond at all, and therefore did not meet its obligation under the Human Rights Code to accommodate the Tenant.
Therefore, the Board finds that the Landlord failed to accommodate the Tenant’s medical needs and discriminated against him on the basis of a medical condition. Remedies Abatement granted

The Tenants are seeking a 20% rent abatement for December 2023 to January 2024. In light of the failure of the Landlord to maintain the rental unit in a habitable state, I find that a rent abatement of $914.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. This amount shall be ordered. Out-of-pocket expenses granted
The Tenant also claimed the following costs and out-of-pocket expenses: • Air purifiers: $119.76 [name] and purifier: $922.22 • Moving costs: $1,181.73 • Medication costs: $667.60 • Total: $2,891.31

These are reasonable costs in the circumstances because they show the Tenant’s escalating efforts to manage his situation in light of the Landlord’s unresponsiveness. Receipts were submitted in evidence. He started with purifiers and air filters, moved to allergy medication. These did not help. He eventually could no longer live in the apartment and was forced to move, and so incurred moving expenses, all the while consistently contacting the Landlord for assistance.

The tenant paid rent on time and in full throughout this period, while he consistently tried to engage the Landlord. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,891.31 for these out-of-pocket expenses. General Damages granted
The Tenant was also seeking general damages in the amount of $3,000.00.
An award of general damages addresses the mental health impact upon a tenant because of a landlord’s unlawful conduct. [name] ONLTB 19346 at para 74.
I accept that the Landlord’s nonresponse throughout the tenancy caused the Tenants significant mental distress that ultimately pushed them to terminate their tenancy early.
I accept from the doctor’s note of January 15, 2024 that the Tenant suffers from severe allergies due to pet dander.

The Tenant testified that he missed 11 days of work at a crucial time when he was working on a project of national importance during the pandemic. He also testified that he had an infant at home and that he was unable to help his wife because his allergies were incapacitating him. He had numerous nights of no sleep, and suffered so much that he slept in his car in the middle of January to find some relief from his symptoms.

The Board found the Tenant’s testimony compelling and is satisfied that $3,000.00 in general damages is reasonable in all the circumstances. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $3,000.00 for the distress these tenancy issues caused and how their nonresponse exacerbated both his condition and the tenancy issues.

The Tenant requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine on the basis that the conduct of the Landlord was particularly egregious. The Board’s interpretive Guideline 16, entitled Administrative Fines, states that a fine should be considered to deter the Landlord and others from similar conduct: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

It was uncontested that the landlord took no action and made no effort to accommodate the Tenants or permit the them to terminate their tenancy sooner. The Landlord had a duty to investigate the issue, maintain the health and safety standards, and to find an accommodation to the point of undue hardship. They completely disregarded the Residential Tenancies Act and the Ontario Human Rights Act. Their inaction was an egregious breach of their obligations to the Tenant and, the Board has an interest in deterring this kind of noncompliance with the Act, so an administrative fine of $3,000.00 is appropriate in all of the circumstances.
ordered: The tenancy between the Tenants and the Landlord is terminated as of January 24, 2024.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,853.31. This amount represents: • $914.00 for a rent abatement for December 2023 to January 2024. • $2,891.31 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $3,000.00 for general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay an administrative fine of $3,000.00 by April 1, 2026
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination (‘N12); • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants’ application was filed with the LTB on February 1, 2025. Therefore, the application was filed within one year of the tenancy terminating.

The Tenants proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(b). The Tenants were given an N12 with the termination date of September 30, 2024. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2024, and returned the keys to the Landlords’ realtor on October 1, 2024.

The Tenants found a listing with the “MLS” showing that the house was for sale on October 15, 2025 (DOC-4759935). There was also a reference in the listing showing that the unit was for sale for $734,900.00. The property was not sold, so the Landlords released the property at an increased rent. This was not disputed by the Landlords. Thus, I find that the Tenants established the first three parts of the test found in s.57(1)(b).

The Landlords do not dispute that they gave the Tenants an N12 notice. However, they argue that there had been a change in circumstances which was not foreseeable. The Landlords and NK signed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale which was final. The property was to close on October 4, 2024. However, the Landlords, who currently reside overseas, got a phone call from their realtor, NM, on October 3rd, that the sale had fallen through.

NM testified that the sale was firm, and the conditions had been lifted. However, on about October 2, 2025, the purchaser told her that he would not be closing on the deal. She immediately contacted the Landlords to let them know. It was then it was decided to relist the house but also to put it up for lease on a month-to-month tenancy because the Landlords had a lot of financial uncertainty and could not afford to have the rental unit remain empty. However, they submit that they had no idea the property would not be closing until after the Tenants had already left the rental unit.

The purchaser, NK, also testified. He explained that he had planned to purchase the condominium; however, he ran into some personal financial circumstances which meant he could not close the deal. He did not recall the exact date that he told the Landlords’ realtor, but he believed it was either at the end of September or early October.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlords did not give an N12 notice of termination in bad faith. The evidence of both NM and NK closely matched and was credible. NK made a financial decision not to close the sale of the property. Although there is some minor discrepancy between NK and NM on the actual date NK advised the Landlords’ realtor, I accept NM’s evidence that it was October 2, 2024, because she had a clear and specific memory about the date she learned the deal would fall through. NM felt the delay was because NK had been hopeful that he might still be able to close the deal.

The Landlords state that they are still trying to sell their property, which is why the property is still listed for sale despite having Tenants. It is also why they chose to have a month-to- month tenancy rather than a fixed-term lease. In my view, this is consistent with the Landlords’ submissions that they always intended to sell their home. Further, this change was detrimental to the Landlords who had hoped they finally sold their property in a difficult resale market.

The evidence shows that the Landlords did not know the sale had fallen through until the Tenants had already vacated the rental unit and that it is more likely than not that the earliest date the Landlords or their agent knew the deal would not close was October 2, 2024. Given this, I find that the Landlords did not give the Tenants the N12 in bad faith. The Tenants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith.
Accordingly, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the following reasons the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
Board records indicate the Tenant filed a T6 application (DOC-4760412) on December 31, 2024.
An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was scheduled on May 22, 2025. Both the Tenant and the Landlord attended the ACC.
The application was not resolved and was sent to a scheduled hearing.

The member filed an adjournment sheet on May 22, 2025 (DOC-5664358) identifying potential deficiencies in the Tenant’s application that were raised at the hearing and states: Went through application with Tenant re potential issues. Discussed: lack of dates; test re T6; paying for common area electricity – how a maintenance issue?; justifying remedies.
At the hearing the Tenant he had not amended the application.

The Tenant’s original application claims lack sufficient reasons and details regarding the [name] claims, like date the issues occurred, if the Tenant put the Landlord on notice and if so when, and if or when the Landlord responded.
The onus rests with the applicant, in this case the Tenant to provide sufficient details in the application for the Landlord to know the case to be met.

The requirement for adequate particulars required within any notices of termination or as is in this case Board applications, has long been established by case law. The leading case regarding the requirement for sufficient reasons and details is Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931. This case stands for the proposition that the kinds of particulars that should be contained in a notice should include “dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct engaged in by the tenant”. The Court held that the tenant needs to know the specific allegations against him/her for three purposes: a. to know the case that must be met; b. to decide whether to dispute the allegations; or c. to consider whether to void the notice.

The Board’s T6 application forms have been developed with instructions to elicit the necessary details required for the Tenant to make a claim and provide sufficient reasons and details. The T6 form provides guidance for the required details as follows: The following describes the maintenance problems that led me to apply to the LTB. • What is the problem? If there is more than one problem, list each problem. • Give the date each problem started. • Has the problem been repaired? If so, give the date it was repaired and explain who • repaired it. [name] who or what may have caused the problem. • How did you inform the landlord about the problem?

Although the decision in Ball v Metro applies to a Landlord’s N5 notice, I note that the same level of details like dates and times of incidents and amounts the Tenant is seeking is required in a T6 application in order for the Landlord to know the case to be met.

For procedural fairness Board forms require applicants to be the ones to provide sufficient details for the claims that are being made. Only then can the respondent fairly have a chance to respond to those claims.
In my view the Tenant has had ample opportunity to amend the application to include specific details that are required in a T6 application.

I do not find it reasonable to adjourn the hearing and allow the Tenant to amend the application given he has had the benefit of an ACC where the member put the Tenant on notice and identified the potential deficiencies.

The Courts recognize s. 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) that means the Board is required to consider the public interest in moving applications through the Board in an expeditious manner

It is the expectation of the courts that refusal of an adjournment request is reasonable where applications are determined to be unsubstantiated, untimely, repetitive or result from a lack of preparation.

Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances.
In my view the Tenant has not provided submissions on his failure to amend the application that I consider to be exceptional in the circumstances.
For all the reasons above I find the Tenant has not met the requirements for the sufficient reasons and details in the application and therefore the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord argues that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply.

He relies on the exemption found in s. 5(i) of the Act which states that the Act does not apply to “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”
He bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.
He testified that he lives at the residential complex and shares a bathroom and a kitchen with the Tenant.
He filed a copy of his driver’s license issued December 31, 2025 with the residential complex as his address (document 7300274 in the Portal). It will expire on October 12, 2026.
He filed copies of his Bell bill and home security bill (documents 7300312 and 7300292). The bills are addressed to him.

His testimony was that the residential complex contains some 70 rooms, 1 kitchen and 4 bathrooms. Most rooms can only be used as storage but a few are rented out to individuals and he personally occupies a few other rooms.
The Tenant conducted a long cross-examination. I found that the Landlord’s testimony was seriously shaken and undermined by cross-examination.
It is not necessary for me to reproduce all of the inconsistencies and implausibility’s in this order as the Landlord fell far short from meeting his burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.
His evidence was brief and self-serving.

The documentary evidence he relies upon, other than the driver’s license, is unhelpful to his case. An owner of a 70-room boarding house/storage facility would always have Bell and home security bills in his own name whether or not he lives at the property. It would not be reasonable for such bill to be in the name of one of the tenants who may rent a room from him. These bills do not in any way suggest that he lives there.

The date of issuance of his driver’s license is incredibly suspicious. It was issued after the Tenant filed this application in mid-December. On cross-examination the Landlord claimed that he simply didn’t get around to updating his driver’s license until December after he allegedly moved into the rental unit in November. It seems at least as likely that he simply never moved into the property and therefore had no reason to change his address until it became convenient for the purposes of defending this application.

The Landlord could have called other residents as witnesses to corroborate his story. He could have filed photos and videos of his living arrangements. He could have filed some bills/invoices that only a resident of a property would have rather than bills that an owner would have. I draw a negative inference from the lack of more persuasive and more pertinent evidence from the Landlord.
The Landlord’s argument fails on multiple grounds.
First, he failed to meet the evidentiary burden of proof that he even lives at the property as set out above.

Second, even if he had established that he lives at the property, he did not lead sufficient evidence that his living at the property was part of the initial arrangement between the parties in accordance with the binding Divisional Court decision of Cowie v. Bindlish, [2010] O.J. No. 2193 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) which states, inter alia, “there was no evidence at either hearing that the [landlord] told the [tenant] prior to renting the room to him that it was her intention to move into the house.”

Finally, as the Landlord himself admitted, the property is owned by a corporation. A corporation may not rely on the exemption in 5(i) that the Landlord wishes to rely upon. See Divisional Court decision [organization] v. King, 2023 ONSC 910.
I find that the Act applies.
After I found that the Act applies, the Tenant requested an adjournment. It was the Tenant’s representative’s understanding that the Tenant was unwell and unable to attend the hearing.
I granted the request peremptory on the Tenant. Both parties confirmed that they are available on May 6, 2026.

The parties shall exchange all documents, pictures and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing by the deadlines set out below. The parties shall also provide the LTB a copy of their evidence.
ordered: The Act applies.
The hearing is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB peremptory on the Tenant.

It is expected that the next hearing will take place on May 6, 2026. If the Board is unable to schedule the hearing on said date, then the parties shall provide their unavailable dates for the months of May, June, and July 2026 to the LTB by May 6, 2026.
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.
On or before April 29, 2026, the Tenant shall provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing.
On or before April 29, 2026, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing.
If a party does not comply with the deadlines for disclosure in paragraphs 5 and 6, the Member may refuse to accept the evidence or consider the issues not disclosed.
If parties want to make disclosure through the Portal, they must sign and file the LTB's form called "Consent to Disclosure through Portal" found on the LTB's website.

Parties may give disclosed material to the LTB by uploading the material to the Tribunals Ontario Portal (‘TOP'). Uploading material to TOP does not constitute disclosure to the other party unless the parties have agreed in writing to exchange documents via TOP. Self-represented parties may also file material with the LTB by email. The LTB's e-mail address is [email].

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 39595 Date: 2026-05-19 In the matter of: Basement, [address] Brampton ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on April 22, 2026. The Landlord and the Prospective Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Prospective Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate them in the amount of $1,050.00 plus the filing fee.
On consent of the parties, the address of the rental unit is amended to reflect that it was the “basement” unit at the above address.
The application filed by the Prospective Tenants claims that the Landlord charged them $2,250.00 in illegal rent, of which $1,050.00 was still owing as of the hearing date.
Prospective Tenants are permitted to seek the return of illegally retained money pursuant to section 135(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The parties agreed that the Prospective Tenants paid the Landlord $2,250.00 on November 27, 2025. The applicants filed their application in time pursuant to section 135(4) of the Act by filing on December 16, 2025.
On a balance of probabilities, I find that the applicants were prospective tenants. This is because there was never a meeting of the minds between the parties as to what their lease would include.
In the hearing, the parties evidence differed greatly regarding what they had assumed the prospective tenancy agreement would include.

The applicants stated that after touring the unit they believed they had reached a verbal agreement to rent the unit as a household of five individuals. The terms were that they would pay $2,250.00 per month, and that this sum would include a parking spot, and all utilities – with no restrictions on how often the Prospective Tenants could do laundry each week. The Prospective Tenants sent the Landlord a deposit of $2,250.00 after viewing the unit and then received a “first draft” of a written lease.

The Landlord stated that he believed the verbal agreement reached was for a household of three individuals, and that after receiving the deposit he realized that five individuals intended to reside in the unit. This prompted the Landlord to send a “first draft” of the lease which limited the Prospective Tenants on how often they could do laundry. This “first draft” also made no mention of the applicants having use of a parking spot.

Neither party provided persuasive, corroborating evidence as to what the parties agreed to verbally. The terms of what they agreed to were never reduced to writing. Based on this lack of evidence I find that at the time of sending the Landlord a deposit of $2,250.00 the applicants were prospective tenants, and the parties were still engaged in an initial negotiation phase regarding the terms of a lease.

Given that there was no meeting of the minds as to the terms of a tenancy, no contract was formed, and the Prospective Tenants were permitted to seek out different rental accommodations which could fulfill their needs. The Landlord cannot retain the $2,250.00 provided as a deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenants is $1,098.00. This amount represents: • $1,050.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenants the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Prospective Tenants the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Prospective Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord argued that the Tenant be precluded from reliance on text messages between the Landlord and another Tenant, that the conversation is hearsay and that the exchange took place with a tenant that was not before the Board to cross-examine. And if the Board permitted the evidence, that it be regarded in a limited manner, that is attributing limited probative value to DOC-5610209 which outlines that the Landlord became aware of the presence of bedbugs in the lower-level unit on September 11, 2024.
The Tenant submitting that the Board consider the text as it establishes the Landlord’s awareness of bedbugs in the lower-level rental unit on September 11, 2024.

Hearsay evidence is admissible under s. 15 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, however the Board must first satisfy itself that the evidence is “both necessary and reliable,” as held in Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083 ([name]. Ct.). And if a decision is made that it is admissible, generally given less weight than direct, non-hearsay evidence for the reasons as outlined by the Landlord.
On the basis the above, DOC-5610209 was not excluded from the hearing and the Board’s consideration, however, was given less weight. Limitation Period
The Landlord argued that as the Tenant filed an amended application on June 13, 2025, that the limitation period be applied to the revised application.

By way of background, the Tenant filed his T6 application with the LTB on December 20, 2024 and filed the amendment on June 13, 2025. The amendment arising from a direction of an Interim Order dated June 2, 2025.
The Tenant complied with the timing of making such a submission for the Board’s consideration as they were directed to file by June 15, 2025.

Amending an application at the LTB does not automatically reset the limitation period; the original filing deadlines generally continue to apply, here there is no deviation. Therefore, the one-year limitation period flows from the original date of the T6 application filing of December 20, 2024. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The Tenant’s application concerns the Landlord’s treatment of bed bugs in the rental unit.
The rental unit is one of three units within a triplex residential complex.
It was undisputed that the Tenant discovered bed bugs in the rental unit on October 24, 2024, notified the Landlord promptly and the rental unit was treated on October 28, 2024.

The Tenant submitting that the Landlord while becoming aware of bed bugs in the lower rental unit on or about September 11, 2024, failed to act promptly therefore causing bedbugs to spread to his upper-level rental unit.
The questions before the Board are whether the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s concerns was reasonable and if the Landlord acted in a timely manner. Applicable Law/ Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Lt 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The allegations concerning bed bugs and treatments of are a common issue before the LTB. Generally, there is an initial treatment and at least one follow-up treatment for a unit before a bedbug issue is brought under control. In some instances, extra follow-up treatments are necessary given the degree of infestation.

In determining whether the Landlord has breached its obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. In this case there was no dispute that the unit was subject to a bed bug infestation which required professional treatment.

Next the Board must consider when the Landlord was informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue. In this case, the Landlord became aware of the presence of bed bugs in the complex from the tenant of the lower level on September 11, 2024. There was no evidence led that the Landlord acted on that complaint until they were informed of the same as connected to the Tenant’s unit on October 24, 2024.

The first bed bug treatment was finally performed in the complex on October 25, 2025, the report as rendered by Progressive Pest Control of the same day outlines that “two live bed bugs were produced by the Tenant. Bed bugs are coming from the lower unit.”

Follow-up treatment proceeded on November 5, 2024, as Tenant did not prepare the unit adequately for October 28, 2024. A follow-up inspection report of December 10, 2024, outlined that “both upper and front units were clear of bed bugs, with no sightings reported for approximately two weeks.”

Here, the application as before me is only in respect of the upper-level unit. The Landlord only becoming aware that there is a bed bug issue in the Tenant’s unit when notified on October 24, 2024. Unlike a multi storey residential complex where pest treatments may be conducted on the basis of regular intervals, the residential complex is comprised of three units, it may not be unusual that the Landlord would automatically draw the conclusion that the Tenant’s unit was also impacted until advised accordingly. This was only confirmed in the pest report of October 25, 2024, and after the Tenant found two bedbugs.
The Tenant submitted that after the initial treatment concluded in November 2024 there were no sightings of bed bugs noted from the period of November to March 16, 2025.

It was not disputed that the next report of bed bugs was on or about March 16, 2025, with the Landlord responding on the same day, and the unit being treated on March 24, 2025, May 8, 2025 and June 5, 2025. The May 8, 2025 report indicating that there is no bed bugs found since the last treatment.
The Tenant did not report further bed bug activity thereafter and vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2025.

Accordingly, the Board must consider the Landlord’s response to the issue once they were informed of the existence of bed bugs. The Landlord was informed of the issue in connection to the Tenant’s unit on October 24, 2024 and first treatment of the unit occurred on October 25, 2024, almost immediately. I find the Landlord’s response to issue to be reasonable and timely.

Any remedies that can be considered would arise from the date the Tenant reported the presences of bed bugs to the Landlord in that there is no evidence that there was an issue in the unit at any period prior for which the Tenant seeks an abatement of rent. And as noted above, it would be inappropriate to assume that because the lower-level unit tenant reported bed bugs on September 11, 2024, that the Tenant had them in his unit too. As such, I am satisfied that as there was no report of bed bug activity from the Tenant’s unit until October 24, 2024, it was not unreasonable for the Landlord not to treat the unit on any earlier date.

The issue of bed bugs resurfaced as reported on March 16, 2025, the Landlord acted again almost immediately in addressing the report by the Tenant and the unit was treated on the dates as outlined above.

The Tenant testified that the presence of bed bugs and resulting issues have exacerbated his mental health condition in connection to anxiety and depression causing him to restart therapeutic treatment with antidepressants. This was supported in a medical note DOC- 5616110.

Although I am sympathetic to the Tenant’s experience with the bedbugs, the fact remains that treatments were completed in a timely manner after he advised the Landlord of bed bugs in his unit. It is hard to speculate what the outcome may have been if treatment commenced in September 2024.

I also consider that the evidence suggests that this was not an ongoing infestation in that there was a long period of time from November 2024 to March 2025 where there were no sightings of bed bugs and that the emergence of the issue was not reported again until March 16, 2025. At that time treatment was commenced 8 days later and was fully completed by June 5, 2025, with no further live bed bugs being reported.

For the outlined reasons, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s bed bug complaints was reasonable and timely, therefore the Landlord did not fail to properly maintain the rental unit and residential complex and therefore did not breach section 20(1) of the Act.

Section 30(1), which speaks to the remedies requested by the Tenant, provides: “If the Board determines in an application under paragraph 1 of subsection 29 (1) that a landlord has breached an obligation under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, the Board may do one or more of the following:”…(emphasis added)
As I have not found that the Landlord has breached their obligation under subsection 20(1), no remedies can be considered, and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. LTB-T-106860-25 The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally. These applications were heard together by videoconference on April 13, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord’s Agent, [name], and the Tenant’s Agent, Marharyta Liva, attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 15, 2025. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit. Lawful Rent LTB-T-106860-25

The Tenant disputed the lawful monthly rent claimed by the Landlord of $1,362.17 effective January 1, 2025. The Tenant’s Agent submitted that the Notice of Rent Increase (N1) served by the Landlord in 2021 and effect January 1, 2022 was invalid and/or void as it claimed an unlawful amount thus all N1s from that point onward would also be invalid and/or void. She asserted that the lawful rent ought to remain at the same amount as per the last prior valid N1 which was effective January 1, 2019 being $1,164.43 (DOC- 5769554pgs1-2). There was no evidence of any rent increase in 2020 for this unit and there were no increases permitted at law in 2021.

There was no dispute that the following N1s were served on the Tenant (DOC- 5769554pgs3-10): • dated September 24, 2021, demanding a rent increase above the guideline, namely 4.2% effective January 1, 2022 in the amount of $1,213.33; • dated September 22, 2022, demanding a rent increase above the guideline namely 5.5% effective January 1, 2023 in the amount of $1,280.06; • dated September 4, 2023 demanding a rent increase above the guideline namely 4% effective January 1, 2024 in the amount of $1,331.26; and • dated September 4, 2024 demanding a rent increase equal or less than the guideline namely 2.46% effective January 1, 2025 in the amount of $1,364.00.

There was also no dispute that on October 4, 2024, order LTB-L-080033-22 (formally TSL- 24777-21) was issued which included the Tenant’s unit and name, and authorized the following rent increases above the guideline ([name]): • 2022 – 3% • 2023 – 3% • 2024 – 1.36%

The Tenant’s Agent asserts that despite the service of N1s increasing the rent above the guideline there was no order authorizing an increase until October 2024 and any charges before that order were unlawful. In support of her assertion, she relied on subsection 126(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which provides that: If an application is made under this section and the landlord has given a notice of rent increase as required, until an order authorizing the rent increase for the rental unit takes effect, the landlord shall not require the tenant to pay a rent that exceeds the lesser of, (a) the new rent specified in the notice; and (b) the greatest amount that the landlord could charge without applying for a rent increase.

She also asserted that the Tenant received a Notice to End Your Tenancy For Non- Payment of Rent (N4 Notice) on November 14, 2024, after the issuance of the Above Guideline Increase (AGI) order, LTB-L-080033-22, wherein the Landlord was permitted to LTB-T-106860-25 charge the amounts owing from the AGI order, and claimed $1,534.17 owing to November 30, 2024. She further asserted that this amount was paid to the Landlord in full thus the Tenant would have paid all outstanding amounts owing for the AGI to November 30, 2024 yet the Landlord served another N4, which this application is based upon, on February 11, 2025 and claimed an amount of $2,451.16 owing dating back to January 1, 2022.

Essentially, I was satisfied that the Tenant’s Agent’s position was that since the Tenant paid an amount claimed by the Landlord in a N4 dated November 14, 2024 which at that time the calculations for the AGI order ought to have been made, the Landlord cannot now claim additional amounts owed from the AGI order.

However, the Tenant’s position is not correct. Firstly, the AGI order LTB-L-080033-22, issued on October 4, 2024 gave 120 days to the parties to pay the other any sum owed as a result of the order. Therefore, I was satisfied that the Landlord could not claim these amounts owed for at least 120 days after October 4, 2024 which is sometime after February 1, 2025. Secondly, a N4 does not have the same effect as an LTB order. The N4 served on the Tenant in November 2024 was an allegation of rent owing and those amounts were not determined by the LTB. Therefore the Landlord is not statute barred from claiming additional amounts calculated to be owed on a later date.

In this case, there was no dispute that despite N1s being served on the Tenant in 2021, 2022 and 2023 for effective dates of January 1 the following year, the Tenant continued to only pay $1,164.43 which was the increased rent amount as of January 1, 2019. However, the Tenant was required to pay at least the guideline increase amount each year as per the N1s served. This is clearly set out in the N1 notice itself under “Important Information About the Law” which states the following: “3. If the rent increase needs approval by an order under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 the tenant is not required to pay more than the guideline increase until the order is issued. If the tenant only pay the guideline increase, the tenant may owe the landlord once the order is issued.” Emphasis Added

This is also set out in subsection 126(5) of the Act, which was relied upon by the Tenant’s Agent, and provides that a landlord shall not require the tenant to pay a rent that exceeds the lesser of the new rent specified in the notice; and the greatest amount that the landlord could charge without applying for a rent increase, which is essentially the yearly guideline amount (Emphasis Added).

Given the above, I was satisfied that the Landlord was permitted to charge and collect from the Tenant at least the guideline amount each year from 2022 to 2024 whilst serving N1s that included an amount above the guideline required by an order. Since the Landlord properly served N1s in accordance with section 116 of the Act, these guideline increase amounts were lawfully charged, and since the Tenant had not applied to challenge those rent increases within one year of them first being charged, the Landlord is entitled to rely upon subsection 136(1) of the Act which deems the rent charged for one or more years lawful. LTB-T-106860-25

Therefore, I was satisfied that the deemed lawful rent before the AGI order was issued for the following dates was: • January 1, 2022 = $1,178.40 ($1,164.43 x 1.012), guideline was 1.2% • January 1, 2023 = $1,207.86 ($1,178.40 x 1.025), guideline was 2.5% • January 1, 2024 = $1,238.06 ($1,207.86 x 1.025), guideline was 2.5%

Consequently, after the AGI order was issued, I was satisfied that the lawful rent for the following dates became: • January 1, 2022 = $1,213.33 ($1,164.43 x 1.04.2),Guideline 1.2 % AGI 3% • January 1, 2023 = $1,280.06 ($1,213.33 x 1.055), Guideline 2.5% + AGI 3% • January 1, 2024 = $1,329.47 ($1,280.06 x 1.0386), Guideline 2.5 % + AGI 1.36%

As per paragraph 5 above, the Landlord served a N1 dated September 4, 2024, demanding a rent increase equal or less than the guideline amount, namely 2.46% to take effect on January 1, 2025 in the amount of $1,364.00 (DOC-5769554pgs9-10). The Tenant has disputed this rent increase at the first hearing on November 3, 2025. Therefore, I find that this increase cannot be automatically deemed lawful by application of subsection 136(1) of the Act as it was disputed within one year of the date it was first charged.

Since the lawful rent for January 1, 2024 was $1,329.47, and the Landlord provided a N1 to the Tenant for a 2.46% increase effective January 1, 2025, the total allowable was only $1,362.17 ($1,329.47 x 1.0246). However, the Landlord’s N1 dated September 4, 2024 and served on the Tenant increased the rent to $1,364.00, which is unlawful as it is more than the allowable amount thus I find that this N1 was invalid.
Consequently, the lawful rent for January 1, 2025 remained at $1,329.47 as an invalid N1 was served on the Tenant. The lawful rent was due on the 1st day of each month.
There was no dispute that the Tenant has paid $2,728.00 to the Landlord since the application was filed.
Therefore, I find that the rent arrears owing to July 15, 2025 are $4,267.29.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,362.70 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $18.29 is owing to the Tenant for the period from January 1, 2025 to July 15, 2025. LTB-T-106860-25 LTB-T-106860-25

In this application, the Tenant sought a determination on the lawful rent which is the reason these matters were heard together. The Tenant alleged that the rent increase effective January 1, 2025 of $1,364.00 was unlawful as the prior rent increases were also unlawful. As per the above findings, the Tenant’s assertion was partly correct. Therefore, the rent is only adjusted for the period of January 1, 2025 onward at $1,329.47 per month as this was the deemed lawful rent as of January 1, 2024.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing this application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of July 15, 2025, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $3,024.30. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the difference in the costs for filing the applications. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit is deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before June 9, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal charge collected
The parties agreed that the Tenant was originally on a one year lease agreement, which began December 1, 2023 and ended on November 30, 2024, in which the tenancy went on a month to month basis.

The Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The parties agreed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025 without providing the Landlord with any written notice to vacate.

The parties further agreed the only notice provided by the Tenant was a verbal conversation with the Landlord, which occurred on July 15, 2025. The Tenant testified that the Landlord agreed to the early termination date of July 31, 2025 because there were bedbugs in the rental unit. The Landlord did not agree with the Tenant’s version of events. The Landlord testified that he never informed the Tenant that he was able to vacate the rental unit early.

Section 37 of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. In accordance with sections 44(2) and 47 of the Act, the earliest termination date the Tenant could have specified on a notice of termination given on July 15, 2025 was September 30, 2025 (60 days from the date of the notice and also on the last of the rental period). The Tenant’s notice to vacate on July 31, 2025 could not have been a valid notice as it does not comply with the Act.
However, Section 37(3) of the Act stipulates that a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy.

The word “agreed” is not defined in the Act, but the meaning of an agreement is well established in the common law of contract. An agreement is formed when one party communicates an offer to the other, and the offeree communicates its acceptance.

I agree with the analysis in Dadiala v Griffin, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No 84, in which the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal recognized that while a notice of termination under the Act must be in a form prescribed by the Act, an otherwise deficient notice of termination provided by a tenant can support a finding of the existence of an agreement to terminate a tenancy if it is accepted by the landlord. However, the landlord’s acceptance must be “unequivocal”, and it must also be clear that there is a meeting of the minds.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for July 31, 2025. What we have in this situation is a “they said – they said” situation, in which both parties do not agree on a date of termination. On a balance of probability, I am not satisfied the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy on July 31, 2025. I make this finding because the Tenant did not adduce any documentary evidence to substantiate their position. I would have reasonably expected the Tenant to adduce documentary evidence, such as email correspondences with the Landlord regarding their mutual agreement to terminate the tenancy early, or perhaps call forward witnesses that were present during the conversations the Tenant had with the Landlord regarding the early termination of the tenancy.

The Landlord testified that once the Tenant vacated the rental unit, he immediately began renovating the rental unit because of the Tenant’s assertion that there was bedbugs in the unit. The Landlord had to remove the carpet and any remaining furniture in the rental unit. I make no finding in regard to the bedbug issue as it is not an issue before me, but parties both agreed that the reason the Tenant vacated was because he stated there were bedbugs in the rental unit.

The Landlord testified the renovations had taken a month and the Landlord was unable to find a new tenant until November 1, 2025. Therefore, the Tenant’s last month rent deposit was applied to the last month of tenancy, which would have been September 2025 rent, the earliest termination date based on when the Tenant notified the Landlord they were vacating.
The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants the amount of $298.00.
The Tenant filed a T1 application on December 21, 2025, alleging that the Landlords had failed to return a $250.00 key deposit to him upon the termination of his tenancy.
The Tenant provided into evidence a signed copy of a lease, dated November 8, 2024, for the rental unit that required, at Schedule A, the payment of a refundable key deposit of $250.00.
The Tenant testified that he vacated the unit on November 30, 2025 and returned the keys at that time.
The Tenant further testified that he emailed the Landlords on December 8, 2025 and requested reimbursement of the key deposit. O rder Page 2 of 3
T he Tenant indicated that he was told by the Landlords that they were holding back the key deposit as a result of the requirement for them to deep-clean the rental unit after the Tenant vacated it.

Section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Paragraph 3 of s.17 of O.Reg. 516/05 under the Act provides that the following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs. [emphasis added]

I t was undisputed that the Tenant paid the Landlords a key deposit in the amount of $250.00. It was also undisputed that the keys were returned to the Landlords on November 30, 2025, and the Landlords did not return the key deposit.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlords received the keys to the unit on or about November 30, 2025, and the Landlords did not return the $250.00 key deposit to the Tenant. The Act does not permit a landlord to apply a refundable key deposit to cleaning costs.
As such, I find that the Landlords illegally retained this amount, and the Landlords shall pay the Tenant the amount of $250.00 for the key deposit. An order will issue accordingly.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to an order for those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $298.00. This amount represents: • $250.00 for the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 3, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
T he Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlords maintain that the Act does not apply with respect to the rental unit pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act which reads: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25

It is the position of the Landlords that Landlord [name] (‘AG) resides in one of the rooms in the basement and as such, the Tenant is required to share a bathroom and kitchen facility with the owner. Landlords’ evidence

The residential complex is a single-family home consisting of two floors and a basement. The basement has three rooms, a kitchen, and a bathroom. The main floor has three rooms, a kitchen and powder room. The upper floor consists of three rooms and two bathrooms.

The residential complex is owned by [name] (‘MR’), AG, and [name] (‘FG’). MR testified that AG resides in a room in the basement and FG resides in a room in the upper floor. MR explained that he meets and screens prospective tenants and responds to maintenance complaints for the property. He indicated that he first met the Tenant sometime the first week of August 2025 when he attended the property to look at the available room in the basement. He recalled the Tenant asking about information on the other tenants. According to MR, he told the Tenant that his 74-year-old father-in-law (AG) resides in one of the rooms and that the other room is occupied by a man from Zambia who worked in security.
MR testified that AG has resided in the basement since 2016. He described helping AG move into the room in 2016 and indicated that AG has never resided anywhere else but the basement unit.

AG testified that he has resided in the basement since 2016 and regularly uses the kitchen and bathroom facilities. He admitted into evidence documents and his government photo identification card indicating his address is the address of the residential complex.

AG explained that he is generally away from the residential complex during the day as he visits his son’s office in Mississauga but sleeps in his room almost every night. He stated that the only exception is when he is visiting his son in Richmond Hill or traveling. AG indicated that he travels to Iran once every six months and was in Iran from the beginning of September 2025 to the end of October 2025. When he is away, he often allows his friend [name] to stay in his room when [name] is doing work around the residential complex.
Finally, the Landlords tendered as evidence photographs that they say show AG’s belongings in the basement bedroom. Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant disputes that he was ever advised that AG was residing in one of the rooms in the basement. He maintains that the first he saw AG was on January 3, 2026.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on/around August 30, 2026 and resided there until February 4, 2026 when he alleges he was illegally locked out of the residential complex. It is the Tenant’s position that the Landlords are now claiming that AG resides in the basement so that they can claim that the Act is exempt thereby preventing them from being accountable under the Act. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25
The Tenant argued that the photographs of AG’s alleged room are staged and that the items were placed there to support the Landlords’ exemption claim.

In support of his position, the Tenant admitted into evidence a video (DOC-744847) which is approximately 26 minutes in length. The video shows footage recorded on February 1, 2026. The Tenant submits that the video demonstrates the Landlords’ plan to fraudulently claim that AG resided in the basement.

The Tenant also admitted into evidence a document entitled, “MLS Report (42p)_Proof of illegal rooming [name]). The Tenant referred to page 4 of the document which reads, “The basement is occupied by [name], an unidentified individual, and *** all individual tenants.” 14. [name] (‘NR’) appeared as a witness for the Tenant. NR is an Inspector with the Toronto Fire Services. NR testified that she visited the residential complex on December 1, 2025, December 2, 2025, March 10, 2026, and March 11, 2026. For the purpose of the issues to be determined in this application, NR focused on the visits of December 1, 2025 and December 2, 2025. 15. It was the evidence of NR that she attended the residential complex on December 1, 2025 at 10:18 a.m. to assess the property for fire safety issues due to a complaint regarding a lack of smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms. At that time, she met with the Tenant and Layton, an individual residing in the basement. No other individuals were present during this initial visit. 16. On December 2, 2025, NR attended the residential complex to conduct a follow-up inspection and to confirm occupancy. She explained that the confirmation of occupancy involved determining how many people resided in the home for the purpose of assessing the number of alarms required for the property. She again met with the Tenant and [name] in the basement unit. No other individuals were present in the basement during this follow- up visit. 17. The Tenant also referred to group chat messages between himself, Layton and MR. The Tenant testified that in the group chat messages, he complained about maintenance issues and explained that he would file an application with the LTB. He said that MR never responded by saying the rental unit was exempt from the Act, something he believes MR would have done if AG resided in the basement. 18. Finally, the Tenant argued that the lease agreement does not explain that he would be required to share a kitchen and bathroom with an owner. He contends that this is something that ought to have been noted had he been required to share a kitchen and bathroom with an owner. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 Law and Analysis 19. It is important to note that the Act is remedial legislation. Section 1 of the Act provides that: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. 20. Given the purpose of the Act, any claim that the Act does not apply has to be examined carefully to ensure that protections provided by the Legislature to residential tenants are not easily avoided (Grenadier (Tenants of v. We-Care Retirement Homes of Canada, [1993] O.J. No.1550 (Div. Court.)). A liberal interpretation of the exemptions from the Act would undermine the objectives of the Act. 21. In making findings on an application, section 202 of the Act requires me to determine the real substance of all transactions and activities pertaining to a rental unit with respect to this tenancy. 22. The onus or burden of proving an exemption applies rests on the person claiming the exemption on a balance of probabilities. Case law dealing with section 5(i) essentially establishes a two-part test and the party relying on the exemption has to establish both: 1) Is the occupant required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and 2) Does the owner, spouse, child or parent living in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 23. As the Landlords are the persons claiming the exemption, the onus is on them to prove on a balance of probabilities the two-part test outlined above. 24. There is case law standing for the proposition that the first part of the test includes establishing that the tenancy agreement must include the requirement to share a kitchen and a bathroom (see TET-82410-17 (Re), 2018 CanLII 113120 (ON LTB)). Having reviewed the Agreement to Lease, I am satisfied that it does. 25. Page 2 of the Agreement explains that the kitchen is a shared area and that the cleaning of the kitchen is shared with the other tenants. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant agreed that he would be required to share a kitchen at the outset. 26. AG provided direct evidence to support his claim that he has resided in the basement unit since 2016. I found AG to be a credible witness. He delivered his evidence in a straightforward manner and provided details with respect to his comings and goings at the residential complex. His evidence was not shaken by cross-examination. His testimony LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 was also supported by evidence establishing that he receives mail at the residential complex, which is the same address that appears on his government photo identification card. He also provided plausible explanations as to why the Tenant may not have seen him during the five months the Tenant resided at the residential complex, including AG’s trip to Iran and visits with his son. 27. I did not find the Tenant’s evidence sufficiently challenged the credibility of the Landlords’ evidence. 28. I reviewed the video (DOC-744847) in its entirety and, having done so, find it does little to support the Tenant’s position. The video, which was recorded on February 1, 2026, demonstrates tension between the parties. Based on their reactions, it seems that MR, FG, Layton, and [name] were bothered by being recorded by the Tenant following a dispute. The Tenant points to the portion of the video where he attends at Layton’s door to ask if he knows [name]. I am not convinced that Layton’s response is proof that [name] did not reside in the basement. In my view, [name] appears to be somewhat confused and looks as if he just woke up when the Tenant appeared at his door. 29. I am also not convinced the fact that MR went into Layton’s room to speak with Layton is proof that MR convinced Layton to lie for the Landlords. Throughout the video, Layton denies the Tenant’s accusations that he is lying for the Landlords and repeatedly states that [name] lives in the basement. 30. I also found that the MLS Report (DOC-7660517) and the testimony of NR did little to establish who were occupants of the residential complex. As explained by NR, only those individuals who were present during her inspections and chose to self-identify were noted in her report. The MLS Report does not list the names of the individuals as the report is redacted and only reflects those individuals who self-identified. 31. Finally, I find the content of the group chat messages do little in establishing whether AG resided in the basement unit. I do not believe MR’s failure to correct the Tenant indicates AG did not reside in the basement unit. 32. Based on a preponderance of the evidence, I am satisfied AG lives in a room in the basement and that he uses the kitchen and bathroom facilities shared by the other basement tenants, which includes the Tenant. Accordingly, I find the Tenant’s living accommodation is exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i). Costs 33. The Landlords’ legal representative asked the LTB to consider making an order that the Tenant’s legal representative pay the costs of the Landlords. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 34. The LTB has a discretionary power similar to that of the Courts to order costs. Generally, costs may be ordered where a party’s conduct in the proceeding was unreasonable. Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes the following: • Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; • Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith; • Taking unnecessary steps in a proceeding; • Failing to take necessary steps, such as those required by the RTA or Rules; • Any misconduct at the hearing or in the proceeding; [name] an issue which is irrelevant to the proceedings and continuing to pursue that issue after the Member has pointed out that it is irrelevant; • Asking for adjournments or delays without justification; • Failing to prepare adequately for the hearing; • Acting contemptuously toward the Member or showing a lack of respect for the process or the Board; • Failing to follow the directions of the Member or upsetting the orderly conduct of the hearing; and • Maligning another party or unreasonably slurring the character of the other party. 35. The Landlords’ legal representative submitted that the Tenant’s legal representative failed to follow the directions I provided on April 13, 2026 with respect to evidence. He stated that he first learned of the late disclosed evidence two hours before the August 16, 2026 hearing, which required him to review the evidence and have the [name] portions of the evidence translated. He seeks $100.00 in preparation costs. 36. The Tenant’s legal representative did not dispute the late disclosure of evidence despite my directions at the conclusion of the April 13, 2026. She submitted that there was value in the evidence the Tenant sought to have accepted and that she secured the services of a Farsi interpreter to minimize any prejudice to the Landlords. 37. I do not find the conduct of the Tenant’s legal representative was unreasonable. I accept that she believed there was value to the late disclosure of evidence in that she felt if supported the Tenant’s position. The request for costs is therefore denied. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
