issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 105, 955 [address] Owen Sound ON Between: [name] Tenant And [organization] Landlord [name] (‘PK’ or the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (‘SREH’ or the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 31, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name] (‘LLR’), attended the hearing. The Tenant consulted with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the commencement of the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant testified that the rental unit tenancy commenced on September 1, 2017 and is still an active tenancy. He stated the current rent the Landlord is charging as of February 1, 2026 is $989.54.

At the hearing, the Tenant informed me the Landlord is in the process of an Above- Guideline-Increase (AGI) application before the LTB, but the AGI application has yet to result in any decision or order . Nevertheless, the Landlord has continued to increase rents through the LTB’s Notice of Rent Increase (NORI) form N1, the first N1 having taken effect on February 1, 2025 and latest N1 having taken effect on February 1, 2026.
The Tenant indicated he filed the T1 application in an attempt to recover the overpayments in rent he has been making since the Landlord’s first N1 which went over the provincial guideline amount.

In support of his testimony, the Tenant led the following exhibits into evidence: • exhibit TT#1 (copy of his redacted bank statements from January 1/2024 to February 1/2026, to evidence his rent payments); • exhibit TT#2 (copy of two October 2024 letters by the Landlord, one in particular dealing with the NORI issued); and • exhibit TT#3 (copy of the Tenant’s December 10/2025 letter to the Landlord in which he stated he was not aware of any AGI application, he stated the LTB confirmed there was no AGI application, and he set out the claimed overpayments in rent he had made).

LLR submitted that the Landlord filed an AGI application with the LTB in December 2023 under case file no. LTB-L-096190-23 (the L5 application). She stated the L5 application seeks a 9% rent increase in respect of capital expenditures (CapEx) the Landlord is seeking reimbursement for. To date, the LTB has not scheduled any hearing between the parties, and the Landlord continues to wait on the LTB.

LLR stated an Adjudicative Case Conference will likely be scheduled first (which is a hearing to see whether the parties can reach a mutual settlement). If the case conference fails to produce a settlement, then the LTB will then reschedule the L5 application for a merits hearing sometime afterward.

In the meantime, LLR submitted a landlord, who is awaiting an LTB order on an L5 application, has the lawful right to issue an NORI for the higher amount which approval is being sought. Further, she stated that under subsection 126(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a tenant has the lawful right either to voluntarily pay the higher amount or to not pay it.

LLR referred to the second October 2024 letter in TT#2 which has the Landlord informing the Tenant that he can choose not to pay the higher rent amount. The Tenant replied that the wording in that letter made it unclear to him that he could refuse to pay the higher amount without leading him to breach his tenant obligation to pay rent. Analysis

I note the Tenant’s exhibit TT#3 states the Tenant was told by the LTB that the Landlord had not filed any AGI application. I am unable to understand how that might have happened as the Landlord’s L5 application LTB-L-096190-23 was filed with the LTB on December 4, 2023. I can only guess that something was misunderstood somewhere along the way.

I make reference to section 126 of the Act, which permits a landlord to claim a rent increase greater than the provincial guideline amount pursuant to section 120 of the Act, specifically in respect of AGI applications.

Subsection 126(5) of the Act provides that when a landlord has filed an AGI application and it has not yet been approved by the LTB, the landlord is entitled to seek, but may not require payment of, the AGI amount so long as proper notice of rent increase has been provided to the tenant.

Subsection 126(6) of the Act then provides a tenant the choice to either pay their rent plus the provincial guideline increase or their rent plus the AGI amount sought by the landlord. If the tenant chooses to pay the new AGI rent, and the landlord’s AGI is not approved or only approved in part, the landlord then owes the tenant any overpayments they may have made based on the underlying NORI form N1. Alternatively, if the tenant chooses not to pay the AGI amount, they may owe the landlord additional rent if an AGI order issues:

For quick reference, subsections 126(5) and 126(6) of the Act state: “126(5) If an application is made under this section and the landlord has given a notice of rent increase as required, until an order authorizing the rent increase for the rental unit takes effect, the landlord shall not require the tenant to pay a rent that exceeds the lesser of, (a) the new rent specified in the notice; and (b) the greatest amount that the landlord could charge without applying for a rent increase. 126(6) Despite subsection (5), the tenant may choose to pay the amount set out in the notice of rent increase pending the outcome of the landlord’s application and, if the tenant does so, the landlord shall owe to the tenant any amount paid by the tenant exceeding the amount allowed by the order of the Board.”

I note that a notice for an AGI rent increase must be provided in accordance with subsections 116(1) and (3) of the Act. These sections provide: “116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. 116 (3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. “

During the hearing, there was no dispute that the two NORIs (N1s) that were issued by the Landlord to the Tenant in October 2024 and in October 2025 complied fully with subsections 116(1) and (3) of the Act.

I read the Landlord’s second October 2024 letter (in TT#2) and agree with the Tenant’s submission before me that the wording was not explicit in the sense that the option to not pay the AGI increased amount was not clearly set out. That is, if the Tenant has opted not to pay the higher amount, nothing was provided in the letter about what the provincial guideline increase amount would have been.

Turning to the LTB’s N1 form, I must note that a tenant’s choice regarding payment of rent when a NORI is for an AGI amount that has not yet been approved is set out on the second page of the LTB’s N1 Notice of Rent Increase form under ‘Important Information About the Law’. It provides: “3. If the rent increase needs approval by an order under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the tenant is not required to pay more than the guideline increase until the order is issued. If the tenant only pays the guideline increase, the tenant may owe the landlord once the order is issued.”

Unfortunately, I must also note that the LTB’s N1 form does not have a space for a landlord to indicate what the provincial guideline increase will be if an AGI is not approved before the date of increase.

All this to say, I understand that the Tenant may not have understood his options clearly, but on the other hand, I find the Landlord did nothing incorrectly or unlawfully in serving the LTB’s N1 forms on the Tenant for an AGI higher amount rent increase, or in explaining as it did the Tenant’s option of not having to pay the higher amount.
Consequently, I find the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act and the claim in the T1 application must be denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. April 21, 2026 ___________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

On consent of the parties, the respondent [name] is removed as a party to the proceeding, the parties agree that Mr. [name]name] is merely an agent of the actual Landlord [name]. The application is amended to reflect this entity as being the Landlord. Illegal rent collected
The Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant filed this T1 application on December 11, 2025. This filing date is the first instance of the Tenant having challenged the lawful rent.
The Tenant moved into the unit in 2014. The rent at that time was $850.00.

The rent was increased for the first time on November 1, 2022 to $950.00 which is in excess of Ontario’s guideline rental amounts. The rental unit is not exempt from rent control. The $100.00 increase was because the Landlord wanted the rent to reflect market rent in the area. A Board form was not used to give notice to the Tenant of the increase. The Tenant paid this increase for 12 consecutive months and did not challenge the increase within one year of the first date it was charged. Therefore, the rent increase is deemed not to be void under section 135.1 of the Act. This section states: Rent increase deemed not void 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116(4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. Non-application (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue.

The next increase of $100.00 was first effective as of November 1, 2023 when rent was raised to reflect market rent in the area to $1,050.00. A Board form was not used to increase the rent. The Tenant paid this increase for 12 consecutive months and did not challenge the increase within one year of the first date it was charged. Therefore, the rent increase is deemed not to be void under section 135.1 of the Act.

The third increase of $100.00 was first effective as of November 1, 2024 when rent was raised to $1,150.00. Similarly, rent was raised to reflect market rent. A Board form was not used to increase the rent. The Tenant paid this increase for 12 consecutive months and did not challenge the increase within one year of the first date it was charged. Therefore, the rent increase is deemed not to be void under section 135.1 of the Act.

The parties discussed whether to raise the rent as of November 1, 2025 to $1,250.00 to again reflect market rent. An agreement was drafted but not signed by the parties. The Tenant never paid this sum in rent. In November of 2025 the Tenant paid $1,150.00.

On November 27, 2025 the Landlord issued the Tenant an N1 notice to increase rent by the guideline amount of 2.1% for the year of 2026, with rent being raised to $1,174.15 effective March 1, 2026. A Board approved form was used.
The parties agreed that the Tenant paid $1,150.00 for the months of December 2025 to February 2026. The parties agree that the Tenant paid $1,174.15 for the months of March and April 2026.

The Tenant’s lawful rent as of the hearing date is $1,174.15. This is because the Tenant failed to file an application in time to contest the previously illegal rent increases by the Landlord, and by paying an illegal rent consecutively over 12 months in each case, the rent became lawful pursuant to section 135.1. The Tenant has not made any overpayments of rent.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

The Landlord collected a security deposit which is not permitted by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $248.00 on or before May 25, 2026.

On December 24, 2025, the Tenant applied to the Board, pursuant to s. 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (the ‘Act’), alleging that on October 27, 2025, the Landlord illegally retained their $200.00 rent payment.

The Tenant filed this application within one-year of the date that the money was allegedly retained illegally pursuant to s. 135(4) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s allegation will be considered. Facts agreed by the parties:

On October 27, 2025, the Tenant and the Landlord verbally agreed that the rental unit would be leased to the Tenant for a fixed term from December 1, 2025 to December 1, 2026, with a monthly rent of $2,200.00. No written tenancy agreement was signed by the parties on September 22, 2020; however, it was agreed by the parties that the Tenant would sign the tenancy agreement, pick up the unit keys, and take possession of the unit on December 1, 2025, contingent on the Tenant providing the necessary documents requested by the Landlord.
On October 27, 2025, the Tenant provided the Landlord an e-transfer for a sum of $1,000.00. This payment was to apply towards the first month rent once the tenancy commenced.
Once the tenancy did not commence, the Landlord refunded the Tenant $800.00 and held onto the remaining $200.00 to use for advertising the unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord posted an advertisement on October 27, 2025, and then took it off the market. He posted the advertisement again on November 6, 2025, and it was then re-rented for December 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that on November 7, 2025, he requested clarification on the lease agreement, and the Landlord did not provide information on the existing Tenant’s lease agreement terms. He also submitted that he was not comfortable giving the Landlord his personal information such as his driver’s license. As a result of the Tenant feeling uncomfortable, he advised the Landlord on November 16, 2025, that he no longer wished to proceed with the rental. He also provided that the Landlord had marked on Facebook that the unit had already been rented to someone else as of November 11, 2025.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant requested the previous tenant’s lease agreement, and he did not want to provide it for confidentiality reasons. He also testified that the Tenant did not provide the necessary documents for the Landlord to complete a written lease agreement. Ultimately the Tenant decided not to move in. The Landlord testified that as a good faith gesture he returned a portion of the Tenant’s deposit in the amount of $800.00. However, the Landlord retained $200.00 to off set costs in relation to re- advertising the unit on Facebook. He testified that in order to boost the advertisement on Facebook, he was required to pay $50.00 a week. He testified that after the Tenant notified him that he did not want to proceed with the rental, he listed the unit right away.

The Landlord noted that there were other tenants interested in the rental unit; however, when the Tenant elected not to take possession of the unit on December 1, 2025, he was unable to secure a tenant for the remainder of the year. The Landlord stated that the unit was rented with a new tenant as of January 2026.
I must first determine whether the parties entered into a tenancy agreement.

Section 2(1) of the Act states: “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit.

A tenancy agreement exists if the parties have agreed to the essential elements of a tenancy agreement, which include, identifying the specific unit to be rented, the start date of the tenancy, the term/period, and the rent. The fact that the parties on December 1, 2025, had not yet signed the written tenancy agreement does not prevent the parties from entering into an oral tenancy agreement.

On the basis of the evidence provided, and pursuant to s. 2(1) of the Act, I am satisfied that on October 27, 2025, a valid oral tenancy agreement was established between the parties for the Tenant to occupy the rental unit for the fixed term of December 1, 2025 to November 1, 2026, with a monthly rent of $2,200.00

I am also satisfied that the Landlord provided the Tenant with the opportunity to take possession of the rental unit on December 1, 2025 as per the terms of the tenancy agreement; but the Tenant declined to take possession of the rental unit.

To determine whether the Tenant is entitled to have the remaining $200.00 returned, I must first consider whether the tenancy was lawfully terminated. A tenant’s obligation to pay rent ends once a tenancy has been terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.

Pursuant to section 37 the Act, a tenancy agreement can only be terminated according to the provisions of the Act, which means a tenancy can only be terminated by proper notice, by way of agreement between the landlord and tenant, or by way of an order issued by the Board. In other words, a tenancy cannot be terminated by one party unilaterally repudiating it.
I must consider that the Landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement, which had the effect of ending the Tenant’s tenancy.

Subsection 88(3) of the Act states: (3) Despite subsections (1) and (2), if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent that exceeds the lesser of the following amounts: 1. The amount of arrears of rent determined under subsection (1) or (2). 2. The amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit.

In addition, section 16 of the Act states: When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses.

Read together, these sections mean that the Landlord had an obligation to try to re-rent the unit as soon as he became aware of the Tenant’s intention to abandon the unit, and that the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent ends once the unit has been re-rented.
The parties disputed when the unit was re-rented.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was already advertising the unit as of November 11, 2025, and the Tenant ceased to see the unit advertised further than December 1, 2025, and it was re-rented as of this date. The Tenant submitted into evidence the Facebook marketplace posting and also text messages between the Landlord and the Tenant during November 2025.
The Landlord testified that he re-rented the unit out the unit in January 2026.

I prefer the Tenant’s evidence on this point. I note in the text messages provided by both parties that the Landlord did not deny keeping the advertisement up until December 1, 2025, nor did he deny in those text messages that the unit was re-rented out as of December 1, 2025.

In this case, I find that the Landlord re-rented the rental unit for December 1, 2025. The Landlord is not entitled to collect rent from two separate sets of tenants. Pursuant to subsection 88(3) of the Act, the Tenant is not liable for rent, and the Landlord must return the pre-payment of rent for December 1, 2025.

With respect to the Landlord’s submissions that he should be able to retain the deposit to offset his advertisement costs of $200.00, a rent deposit is not meant to be used for anything else other than rent.
For the reasons above, the Tenant’s application is granted, and the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $200.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00 This amount represents: • $200.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant, [name] (‘SNB’) testified that prior to filing the application he hired a legal representative to send a letter to the Landlord to engage the Landlord in a discussion regarding the deposit. Further, SNB stated that his legal representative sent multiple letters to the Landlord and realtor who both refused to engage in the process. SNB also hand delivered documents, as well as calling the Landlord and the Landlord’s realtor to speak about the process and the Landlord and Tenant Board process, all without success. T1 Application

As explained below, the Tenant has proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,698.00 for the illegal retention of the first and last months deposit and the filing fee.

The Application before the Landlord and Tenant Board is pursuant to subsection 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act) states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
Subsection 135(2) of the Act states: A prospective tenant may apply to the Board for an order under subsection (1).

On May 20, 2025, SNB entered into a tenancy agreement (DOC-7043451) with respect to this rental unit. On May 21, 2025, SNB paid $3,650.00 to the Landlord as a rent deposit (DOC-7043456) and the tenancy was to commence on August 1, 2025.

In or about the beginning of June 2025, SNB’s realtor, [name] (‘SR’) inquired about the SNB’s visa status. SNB advised that his work permit had expired on March 31, 2025, as such, he had ‘implied status’ while waiting for his renewal. Further, he outlined that he had a letter from the Immigration Refugee and Citizenship Canada which outlined his status.

SNB submits that the Landlord terminated the Lease Agreement as they did not want to rent to temporary residents and they would only rent to permanent residents or Canadian citizens, as a result the Landlord wished to terminate the tenancy agreement.
SNB testified that he was not provided keys to the rental unit, nor did he move into the rental unit.

Subsection 107(1) of the Act states: “A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

SNB remained a prospective tenant until such time that his tenancy commenced, and he was entitled to occupy the rental unit. Because SNB’s tenancy never commenced, the Landlord was not entitled to retain the $3,650.00 rent deposit paid by SNB as a prospective tenant.

Upon SNB’s inquiry to SR regarding the return of his deposit, he was informed that the Landlord would retain the deposit but would not be seeking additional rent for the remainder of the term of the tenancy.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Tenant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement which was to commence on August 1, 2025. As a result of the tenancy agreement, the Tenant provided a deposit to the Landlord. The Landlord unilaterally terminated the tenancy agreement and then failed to return that deposit. This is prohibited by s.107(1) of the Act. As such, the Landlord owes the (prospective) Tenant the illegally retained rent deposit in the amount of $3,650.00. Mutual Full and Final Release

SNB referenced a document dated June 25, 2025 at 1:07pm (DOC-704352) which included a message from SR which stated “Hi [name], As discussed, the landlord has decided to keep the deposit in full. Their reasoning is that they didn’t collect any rent since our agreement was finalized in May. And their plan was that you’d move in. I spoke with my office as well, and this is a decent case scenario for you as they are terminating the agreement completely without requesting for additional pay. And for your information, I won’t be receiving any commission from the deposit you made to the landlord. Since the agreement is being terminated. Please sign the mutual release and I’ll forward finalized a copy to them. Best, Surosh”.

SNB testified that he relied on SR’s knowledge regarding real estate matters and was concerned that he would be responsible to make the rental payments for the remainder of the term. SNB was (DOC-7043454) which is signed by SNB, the Landlord and individuals identified as the Listing and Co-Operative Brokerages, Brokers of Record, this document specifies that the Agreement to Lease and the transaction relating to the Agreement to Lease being terminated.

The Act is clear that you cannot contract outside of the Act. Subsection 3(1) states: Application of Act 3 (1) This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. 2013, c. 3, s. 22 (1).

Therefore, the fact that the Tenant signed the “Full and Final Release” does not excuse the Landlord from their obligation to comply with the Act, including their obligation under s.107(1) of the Act to repay the rent deposit paid by the Tenant as the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with vacant possession of the rental unit.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
All reasons for the determinations set out in this order are contained herein. No further reasons will be provided.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,698.00. This amount represents: a. $3,650.00 for the deposit; and, b. $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $298.00 for the illegal retention of the key deposit.

It was undisputed that on August 26, 2024, the Tenant paid the Landlord a key deposit in the amount of $250.00. It was also undisputed the keys were returned by hand to the Landlord on or about August 31, 2025 and the Landlord did not return the key deposit.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) provides: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of O.Reg. 516/06 under the Act provides that certain payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) of the Act, including “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.”

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord received the keys to the unit on or about August 31, 2025, and the Landlord did not return the $250.00 key deposit to the Tenants. As such, I find that the Landlord illegally retained this amount, and the Landlord shall pay the Tenants the amount of $250.00 for the key deposit.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to an order for those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord’s representative initially sought an adjournment, stating short notice and insufficient time to prepare.
However, when the Tenant described the rental unit, a preliminary issue surfaced with respect to the LTB’s jurisdiction to hear the Tenant’s application. Does the Act Apply?
The Tenant said that he shares the kitchen with the owner Landlord.

The issue before the Board is whether the Act applies. In order for the Act to apply there must be a tenancy agreement between a “landlord” and a “tenant” respecting a “rental unit” or “residential premises”, as those terms are defined in the Act. The exemptions from the Act, found in section 5, must also be considered. If the Act does not apply to this relationship, then the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear disputes between the parties.

As explained at the hearing, s.5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) describes situations where the Board does not have jurisdiction; specifically, where the tenant is required to share the kitchen or bathroom with the owner landlord.

Subsection 5(i) of the Act stipulates that the Act does not apply to living accommodation where the occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the accommodation is located (emphasis added).

The operative word with respect to the exemption under 5(i) is required. Therefore, the question to be determined is whether the Tenant was required to use and share the kitchen with the Landlord. If the answer to that question is yes, then the Act will not apply with respect to this arrangement.
At the hearing, the Tenant did not dispute that he was required to share the kitchen with the owner Landlord.
Based on the evidence before the Board, the Tenant was required to share kitchen facility with the owner Landlord.
Accordingly, the Board does not have jurisdiction as the relationship between the parties is exempt from the Act.
Having found the Act does not apply to this relationship, there was no reason to adjourn the matter.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Act does not apply. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Are the parties in a landlord/tenant relationship?

The Landlord and the Tenant entered into a “sublease” agreement on October 30, 2024, with a monthly rent of $1,600. The agreement identified the Tenant as a “subtenant” and the Landlord as the “sublessor.” The parties signed a subsequent 24-month “sublease” agreement on October 21, 2025, in which the rent was reduced to $1,500 per month for the rental unit. The Tenant paid the agreed upon rent directly to the Landlord from December 1, 2024, to December 1, 2025.

I t is not disputed that the Landlord was herself a tenant in the rental unit and was responsible for paying the rent to her landlord, a property management company called Aykler. The Landlord conceded that [name] was not aware that she had vacated the rental unit and entered into a sublease agreement with the Tenant.

In or around October 2025, the Tenant opened a notice from Aykler, advising the rent on her rental unit would be increasing by $49 per month to $1,020 per month. When the Tenant became aware that she was paying substantially more rent for the unit than the Landlord was paying to Aykler, she filed a T1 application for illegal rent against her Landlord (Ms. [name]). The Landlord and Tenant did not enter into a valid subtenancy

Sections 2(2) and 97 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) set out the four requirements for an authorized subtenancy: 1. The tenant must vacate the rental unit 2. The sub-tenant has the right to occupy the rental unit for a fixed period ending on a specified date before the end of the original tenant’s lease 3. The original tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the renal unit after that specified date 4. The landlord must consent to the subtenancy

The facts of this case are somewhat similar to those in the Divisional Court’s decision [name] v. Ogunfeibo, 2019 ONSC 7423 (‘Tremblay’), In that case, [name] rented two rooms from the owner of the building; she lived in one room and rented the other out to [name]. [name] wanted her daughter to move into [name] unit, took the position that the Act did not apply, and locked [name] out. 7. [name] sought relief from the LTB. The Hearing Member found that the parties had entered into a subtenancy pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act and ordered that [name] be put back into possession of the unit. On review, the reviewing Vice-Chair held that the Hearing Member had failed to apply the statutory test for a subtenancy but did not commit a serious error because they had discretion to find that [name] was a subtenant. [name] appealed to Divisional Court, 8. The Divisional Court held that the Hearing Member erred by finding that the parties were in a subtenancy under section 97(1) of the Act because (1) they had not made findings about whether the owner had consented to the subtenancy; and (2) the agreement between [name] and [name] did not provide for [name] return to the unit or otherwise mention a subtenancy. The court further held that the reviewing Vice-Chair erred by holding that the Hearing Member had discretion to make a finding that the Act applied and that a subtenancy existed between the parties. The Court found that the Vice-Chair’s decision ignored the statutory preconditions to finding a subtenancy. 9. By the time the matter was heard at Divisional Court [name] had already vacated the rental unit, and the Court considered it appropriate to decide the matter itself. The Court reviewed the Act’s definitions of “landlord”, “rent”, “rental unit”, and “tenant”, as well as the exemption in Section 5(i) of the Act. Noting the Act’s remedial purpose, the Court found that that [name] and [name] had entered into a landlord and tenant relationship: [36] The relationship between [name] and [name] falls squarely within the words of the statute. She is a landlord because she is a “person who permits occupancy of a rental unit”. She is not permitting [name] to occupy her unit with her, so the exemption in the definition of “landlord” in paragraph (a) of the definition does not apply. [37] Similarly, [name] is “a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit”. He pays that rent directly to [name] and he gave evidence that he believed she was the landlord. So, he fits the definition of “tenant”. [38] The bedroom, kitchen, common area, and bathroom are “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises” so they meet the definition of a “rental unit.” Although [name] shares the bathroom, kitchen and common area with others, the premises are akin to a boarding house or a rooming house, both of which are expressly included in the definition of “rental unit” above. Finally, because the bathroom and kitchen are shared with other occupants and are not required to be shared with the “owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent” the exclusion from the Act in s.5(i) does not apply. [39] [name] argues that finding that the Act applies to [name] would be contrary to the limited rights of subtenants under s. 97 and specifically contrary to the landlord’s right to evict a person who has been allowed to occupy the premises without the landlord’s consent. In this case, for example, in February of this year, the landlord/owner went to the board to evict [name] and [name]. He apparently provided notice to [name] but not to [name]. [name] consented to eviction based on an unauthorized occupancy by [name]. When the landlord succeeded in obtaining an eviction order against [name], he apparently exercised the right only against [name]. [name] daughter then took possession of the full second unit in accordance with [name] goal throughout. [40] [name] is again challenging his eviction at the board and claims that the landlord and [name] colluded to evict him unlawfully. I am not to be taken to be prejudging that ongoing proceeding. However, I do not see the fact that the landlord may have rights against an unauthorized subtenant as undermining the point that the Act applies to the relationship between the tenant, in the position of [name], and a person who rents from her in the circumstances of this case. If others are able to assert superior rights, then the outcome can be determined by the board on an analysis of each of the relationships. Specific rights set out in s. 97 in favour of tenants who sublet, and their subtenants may or may not be available where a proper subtenancy is not created as defined in s. 2(2). Moreover, if a tenant is found to have misled someone as to her capacity to rent the premises, that too may have legal consequences. The board is instructed by s. 202 of the Act to “ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit”. With this mandate, the board is well able to sort through the complexities of modern commerce to separate appropriate and necessary structure from deliberate or abusive misconduct. 10. Because [name], the rental unit’s owner and the Landlord’s landlord, was unaware of the arrangement between the Tenant and the Landlord, I am not satisfied that the agreement between the Landlord and Tenant was a valid subtenancy within the meaning of section 97 of the Act, as per the Court’s reasoning in Tremblay. 11. Unlike in Tremblay, the agreement between the Landlord and Tenant in this case was characterized as a sublease and referred to the Landlord as the sublessor and the Tenant as the subtenant. Despite this, I am nonetheless satisfied that the parties entered into a landlord and tenant relationship. 12. Section 202 of the Act requires the Board to ascertain the substance of the agreement between the parties, and in doing so it may disregard the outward forms of a transaction and have regard to the parties’ pattern of activities. In this case, I am satisfied that, like in Tremblay, the Landlord is a person who permits occupancy of the rental unit without also occupying it, and the Tenant is a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy it. The Landlord did not specify a date for her return to the rental unit. As a result, I am satisfied that the Act does apply to the arrangement between the parties because they are in a landlord and tenant relationship. To find otherwise would give effect to what I consider to be “deliberate or abusive” misconduct within the meaning of paragraph 15 of Tremblay. 13. I would note that [name] was not given notice of this proceeding. My finding regarding the relationship between the Landlord and Tenant should not be taken to preclude Aykler from asserting “superior rights” against the parties, as envisioned by the Court in paragraph 40 of Tremblay. T1 Application 14. In my view the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. The lawful rent is the rent that they agreed to when they entered into a tenancy with the Landlord, not the rent that the Landlord agreed to pay to Aykler. 15. Even if this were not the case, I must then consider section 135.1(1), which states: “An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116(4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.” As the Tenant paid $1,500 per month for twelve consecutive months from December 1, 2024, to December 1, 2025, that amount would have been deemed to the lawful rent as result of section 135.1(1). As a result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,153.00. Evidence of the Tenants

The Tenants provided oral evidence that prior to taking possession of the rental unit on December 1, 2023, they paid the Landlord $2,100.00 as a last month’s rent deposit. The Tenants further testified that from December 1, 2023 onward, they paid rent in full and on time each month.

In mid-April 2025, the Tenants advised the Landlord of their intention to vacate the rental unit effective June 15, 2025. The Landlord agreed to this termination date through both a phone call and text message. The parties further agreed that the Tenants would pay pro-rated rent in the amount of $1,100.00 for the period of June 1 to June 15, 2025. The Tenants testified that they paid this amount to the Landlord.

After vacating the rental unit on June 15, 2025, the Tenants contacted the Landlord by text message requesting the return of their last month’s rent deposit. On June 24, 2025, the Landlord responded by text message stating that he intended to return the deposit during “the first week of August.” Despite this message, the Landlord did not return the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants. Analysis

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 106(10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

The Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, the Landlord acknowledged owing the rent deposit to the Tenants however has failed to return the deposit as required. As such, this deposit is required to be returned to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,153.00 This amount represents: • $2,100.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant and the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement commencing on August 13, 2022. At the time of the tenancy agreement the Tenant provided a last month’s rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $1,100.00.
The parties came to an agreement to end the tenancy and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 14, 2024.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant.
Section 105(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: The only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Pursuant to section 106(10) of the Act: A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

Section 135(1) of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit to apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

However, pursuant to section 135(4) no order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

The Tenant filed their T1 application with the Board on January 5, 2026. That date is more than one year after the last month’s rent deposit is alleged to have been illegally retained by the Landlord. As such the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies. The Tenant also applied for a determination that the [name] and [name] (collectively, the 'Landlord') breached the Act.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex. The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
I find that the Tenant was always required to share a bathroom with the Landlord.

The unit therefore falls under the exemption found in s. 5(i) of the Act: “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.”

In the alternative, find that at the commencement of the tenancy the parties did not intend to have a tenancy governed by the Act in accordance with s. 202(1) of the Act: (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The real substance of the transaction was to allow the Tenant to occupy the Landlord’s basement until she can find a permanent place to stay. The parties never intended a tenancy within the meaning of the Act and do not meet the corresponding definitions found in s. 2(1). Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord bears the burden of proof in establishing that the Act does not apply on a balance of probabilities. I find that they met this burden.

The Landlord testified about the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant contacted [name] at work and said that she was scared to stay at her residence at the time. She was staying in her car. The two landlords discussed the situation and offered her to temporarily stay in their basement.

The Tenant paid for September 1, 2025 and moved into the basement. The basement has a wet bar, a laundry room, a washroom and a utility room. It does not have a kitchen and does not have a separate exclusive entrance. It was fully furnished with the Landlord’s existing furniture.

The Landlord testified that they never surrendered control of the basement or access thereto. Page 11 of the Landlord’s document 7467272 contains photographs filed by the Landlord. The photos aren’t very helpful as they were taken after the tenant was removed from the property. The basement came equipped with a fridge but the Landlord stored their overflow in that fridge as well.

The Landlord maintains that the entire house continued to be his home while the Tenant temporarily stayed in the basement. There was no negotiation, no lease verbal, written or implied – just an agreement for the Tenant to temporarily stay in the basement. She offered to pay $1,200 a month while she stays and the Landlord accepted the offer.

The Tenant did not and could not exclude the Landlord from any part of the basement. The Landlord never gave her keys. There was never an agreement that would prevent the Landlord from entering the basement. The basement does not have internal architecture that would permit long term use.

There were no major cooking appliances. The electrical wiring is not designed to support a full unit with major appliances. The Landlord provided other evidence about the kitchen and its inadequacy, and so did the Tenant but I will not address this issue any further as it is not a material issue.

The Landlord realized that the Tenant was planning to stay much longer than the Landlord had anticipated and sent her a notice on November 25th asking her to make sure she leaves by January 1st. The Tenant did not reply to assert her rights under the Act or otherwise challenge the Landlord’s communication until December 21st when she called the police about the notice and gave the Landlord a handwritten note outlining her protest. A police officer attended, looked at the notice, and left without telling the Landlord to do anything. The Tenant then filed an application with the LTB on December 30th, 2025. The Landlord argues that this timeline is inconsistent with someone who believes that there is an urgency or a genuine claim that she is a tenant facing illegal eviction.

The Landlord routinely exercised his right to access the basement aera. There was no way for the Tenant to keep him out. The basement can be accessed through two entry points and neither door was ever locked.
The Landlord used the basement washroom whenever it was convenient for him. As he could recall, he used it approximately 10 times between September 2025 and December 2025.

On cross-examination the Landlord confirmed that the Tenant paid $1,200 a month. He admitted that he never used the basement kitchen (the Landlord disputes this label), and the Tenant never used the upstairs kitchen. He reiterated that he never surrendered access to the basement and used the bathroom whenever he was in the basement.
I found the Landlord to be a credible witness. He admitted adverse facts and his evidence was logical, consistent, and not undermined by cross-examination. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified about the commencement of the tenancy. She was in need and was looking for a new place on an urgent basis. She told [name] that she was paying $1,200 at her previous place, and [name] agreed to let her pay the same amount. Page 9 of document 7461914 contain proof of payment. The Tenant’s description of the payments references monthly rent, and it was auto deposited into the Landlord’s account.
The Tenant’s evidence was that although there was no written lease, the Tenant and [name] verbally agreed that she would be given 60-day notice, and that parties would not step outside of the Act.
She blames her delay in replying to the Landlord’s notice of November 25th on being in complete shock, fear and disbelief when she received it.
The basement was her primary residence. It had its own kitchen area, including a fridge, a sink and cook wear. Noone else used the kitchen area while she lived there.
The Tenant’s document 7461914 contains photos the Tenant took. They clearly show that she set the wet bar area as a full kitchen.
She testified that she never saw anyone use her bathroom in the basement.

Page 19 contains a copy of the Landlord’s message of November 25, 2025. It states that the Act does not apply and that the Tenant is to vacate the property by the end of the year. It states that the parties always intended this arrangement to be temporary, that the unit is not a self-contained unit, and there was never a formal tenancy.

Page 22 contains a handwritten note containing the Tenant’s reply to the Landlord dated December 21, 2025. She states that the unit is self-contained with her own exclusive washroom and kitchen. She argues that the Act applies and demands proper process/notice under the Act.

I note that the Tenant’s own letter makes no mention of any alleged agreement she claims to have made with the Landlord at the outset of the tenancy that the Act would apply. It relies on building code and the Act itself rather than on any agreement.

The Tenant relies on texts sent by the Landlord in the Fall of 2025 where the Landlord provides her advance notice that they intend to enter. The messages reference fixing the shower, accessing the freezer etc.

Pages 20 and 21 deal with entry on November 29th, a few days after the Landlord sent their initial notice. The Tenant emphasized the fact that [name] used the term “your space” when asking to enter: “Why? I do not want to go into your space without you there. Why do you not want to be there?”.

The Tenant replies to the Landlord’s notice by saying that she disagrees. It reads: “Respectfully I will not agree. You are welcome to schedule any time you’d like to do any maintenance work you want but, I will choose not to be present.”

I note that none of the requests are a proper 24-hour notice that would comply with the Act. At no point does the Tenant demand a notice that would comply with the Act, which would have been logical had the parties in fact agreed that the Act would apply from day 1. I also note that the message somewhat contradicts the Tenant’s assertion that she took almost a month to challenge the Landlord’s claim that the Act never applied because she was too shocked to reply. She sent the Landlord a message only a few days after the notice and made no mention of shock or of her intention to challenge the notice when she is ready.

The Tenant was cross-examined. I find that her testimony and credibility were very seriously undermined by the cross-examination. She was evasive, non-responsive, and argumentative on many occasions. She did not provide persuasive, or even logical, explanations for adverse evidence. Only some of the issues are reproduced below.

She confirmed that she prepared a written declaration before the hearing. She admitted that the declaration makes no mention of the conversation that allegedly took place between the Tenant and [name] in which the parties agreed that their relationship would be governed by the Act. She could not recall the date when the conversation took place – she claimed that it was in July or August.

She did not reply whether the Landlord was ever physically prevented from entering the basement. Instead of replying directly, she argued that no landlord could be prevented from entering because they always hold a key. She did not confirm that she was never given a key but did not deny it. She argued with the Landlord instead.
She was non-responsive and/or not entirely responsive to the Landlord’s line of questioning about the Landlord’s storage in the basement and Landlord’s food in the fridge.

She denied asking for permission to use laundry in her messages. She claimed that it was merely a courtesy. I note that she characterized similar communication from the Landlord coordinating access to the basement as requesting permission.

She evaded the question about the Landlord giving her an updated Wi-Fi password that referred to her as a guest. [name], analysis and findings 37. s. 5(i) of the Act states: “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.” 38. Section 2(1) contains some definitions, including: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals “residential unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as residential premises, and “residential unit” includes,… “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex; 39. S. 202(1) of the Act: (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 40. Based on the totality of the evidence I find that the Act does not apply for multiple reasons. 41. First, the Tenant was required to share a washroom with the Landlord thus invoking exemption in s. 5(i). 42. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that he used the washroom on almost a dozen occasions and was never prevented from using it. I found the Landlord to be credible unlike the Tenant. I make this finding despite the Landlord often providing the Tenant courtesy notices before at least some of the entries. The Tenant claims that the Landlord never used her washroom, but I did not find the Tenant’s testimony to be credible nor reliable. Her evidence was very seriously undermined by cross-examination. Her own story was not entirely logical and consistent even before cross-examination. 43. I similarly find that the Landlord was never precluded from using the kitchen area. The Landlord always had some of their food stored in the fridge and while it would appear that they didn’t actually use the basement kitchen/kitchenette, I find that it was nevertheless a shared space that the Landlord was always allowed to access, even if with courtesy notice to the Tenant. 44. The arrangement was not dissimilar to having friends or family stay with the property owner for a few weeks or months, during which the property owner might attempt to give them some privacy, and the guests may attempt to compensate the property owner in some way in the meantime. 45. I note that I do not accept the Landlord’s argument that the Act does not apply because the kitchen does not have sufficient electricity or a proper stove. A landlord can’t have an otherwise genuine tenancy, had one existed in this case, not be subject to the Act simply because they choose to provide a sub-optimal kitchen to their tenant. 46. Finally, I do not find that the parties ever intended to have a residential tenancy. I find that the relationship between the parties does not fall within the purview of the Act pursuant to s. 202(1) of the Act and the relevant definitions in s. 2(1). The real substance of the arrangements was essentially that the Tenant would be permitted to “crash” in the Landlord’s basement temporarily while dealing with a personal emergency. She was never given a key and there is no record of parties treating each other as a residential tenant or a residential landlord in their communications. The record shows that the Landlord was trying to be a good Samaritan and the Tenant was grateful for assistance. The Tenant either wished to compensate the Landlord or wished to make the arrangement less one- sided and paid an amount that appears to be below market rent. Both parties agreed that the “rent” was set based solely on the amount she offered. There is indication that the “unit” was ever advertised for rent before or after. There was no landlord – just a co-worker who tried to help. There was no tenant – just a coworker who temporarily stayed in their coworkers basement and compensated their coworker for the inconvenience. There was no rental unit – just a normal basement of a residential property that said coworker temporarily stayed at. It would be perverse to now force a person who was never intended to be a landlord into a residential tenancy for a space that was never intended to be a rental unit with a person who was never intended to be a tenant. 47. The Tenant’s materials did not make a claim that parties agreed that the Act would apply to their relationship. This claim was made at the hearing for the first time and is entirely inconsistent with the balance of the evidence in this application. The parties never discuss it even though multiple messages were exchanged. The Tenant’s claim that she was too shocked to reply to the Landlord’s message of November 25th defies logic and belief. The [name] eventual reply of December 21st makes no mention of this alleged agreement. 48. Based on the totality of the evidence I find that it is more likely than not that the Act does not apply. 49. The Tenant’s application LTB-T-109372-25 is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
Application LTB-T-109372-25 is dismissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant entered into a month-to-month tenancy agreement with the Landlord and moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2025. At that time the Tenant provided the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $750.00.
The Tenant testified that he started a new job out of town and given the extended daily commute he decided to end the tenancy.
On November 11, 2025 the tenant sent a text message to the Landlord which stated: “I’m letting you know now, that I’m looking to move out in January, when my 60-day advance notice will reach”
The parties agree this text constitutes the Tenant’s 60 day notice to terminate the tenancy and vacate the rental unit at the end of January, 2026.

The Tenant testified that on December 16, 2025 the Landlord’s property manager reached out to him to inquire what date the Tenant planned to leave the unit and offered to refund January’s rent if the Tenant could vacate by the end of December to accommodate a new tenant looking to move into the unit for January 1, 2026. The Tenant stated that he did not have secure housing available and was not able to vacate the rental unit any earlier, but would advise the Landlord’s property manager if something changed.

The Landlord’s property manager [name] testified that any potential refund offered to the Tenant was conditional on the Landlord securing and new tenant to occupy the rental unit and would be based on when occupancy commenced. Additionally she stated that the potential tenant passed on the rental unit after being advised it would not be available for January 1, 2026.

The Tenant states that he advised the Landlord on December 24, 2025 that he would be vacating the rental unit early, on December 31, 2025 as he had entered into a new tenancy agreement to commence on January 1, 2026. At this time the Tenant also requested a refund of January’s rent pursuant to his earlier conversation with the property manager.

The Landlord testified that although she attempted to find a new tenant they were unable to secure a new tenancy to commence January 1, 2026 and as such offered no refund to the Tenant and applied his last month’s rent deposit to January as originally discussed with the Tenant.

Based on the evidence before me, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord and their property manager to that of the Tenant. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that any offer extended to the Tenant for a potential refund of rent was based on three criteria; 1. That the Tenant vacate the rental unit early; 2. That the Landlord was able to secure a new tenancy to commence prior to the Tenants termination date; and 3. Any potential refund would be based on when the new tenancy commenced prior to the original termination date. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there was an agreement in place to refund the Tenant solely based on the Tenant vacating the rental unit early as suggested by the Tenant.

In the circumstances the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit, and correctly applied it to January, 2026 the last month of the tenancy, based on the notice to terminate the tenancy received from the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (75) [name]. (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount of $1,266.40. Illegal rent collected

In their T1 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord charged an illegal rent. The Tenant alleges the illegal rent is based on two factors: • The City of Hamilton issued a notice of rent reduction by 0.80% to take effect on December 31, 2024, which to date has not been applied by the Landlord; and • The Landlord served the Tenant with an Above Guideline rent increase to increase the Tenants rent by 5.5% effective January 1, 2025.
The parties agree that the lawful monthly rent for the rental unit was $1,993.62 in December 2024.
The parties further agree that the Tenant has paid $2,103.26 in monthly rent for the rental unit effective January 1, 2025. Municipal Rent Reduction
The parties agree that on November 4, 2024 the City of [name] sent a notice of rent reduction effective December 31, 2024 reducing the rent payable by the Tenant by 0.80%.

Pursuant to section 131 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), if the municipal property tax for a residential complex is reduced by more than the prescribed percentage, the lawful rent for each of the rental units in the complex is reduced in accordance with the prescribed rules.
The parties further agree that the 0.80% rent reduction was to be applied to the monthly rent paid by the Tenant.
The Landlord admits that due to an error the reduction was not applied to the Tenant’s monthly rent during this period and the Tenant is entitled to compensation.
Applying a 0.80% rent reduction to the lawful monthly rent of $1,993.62 results in a reduction of $15.95 per month. Above Guideline Rent Increase
The Tenant pays his rent monthly to the Landlord via a pre-authorized automatic withdrawal from his bank account.
The Tenant asserts that beginning January 1, 2025 the Landlord began automatically withdrawing $2,103.26 from his bank account for monthly rent.

The $2,103.26 withdrawn from the Tenant’s bank account represents the 5.50% ($109.64) rent increase that the Landlord seeks as part of the Landlord’s above guideline increase application under application LTB-L-027190-24.
There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant has paid the Landlord $2,103.26 per month during this time via an automatic withdrawal agreement between the parties.
The Tenant asserts that the Landlord is not entitled to automatically take the above guideline amount.

The Landlord asserts the Notice of Rent Increase served on the Tenant advised the Tenant that they were not required to pay more than the guideline increase 2.5% until an order on the Above Guideline amount was issued. The Landlord’s Agent stated that although the Landlord increased the automatic withdrawal amount for rent commencing January 1, 2025 to the full 5.50% as claimed by the Landlord, the Tenant did not contact the Landlord and ask that this amount be reduced to the guideline increase of 2.5%. Analysis

Section 126(5) and (6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') state: (5) If an application is made under this section and the landlord has given a notice of rent increase as required, until an order authorizing the rent increase for the rental unit takes effect, the landlord shall not require the tenant to pay a rent that exceeds the lesser of, (a) the new rent specified in the notice; and (b) the greatest amount that the landlord could charge without applying for a rent increase. (6) Despite subsection (5), the tenant may choose to pay the amount set out in the notice of rent increase pending the outcome of the landlord’s application and, if the tenant does so, the landlord shall owe to the tenant any amount paid by the tenant exceeding the amount allowed by the order of the Board.

In the circumstances before me I am satisfied that the Landlord breached section 126(5) of the Act by unilaterally increasing the amount automatically withdrawn from the Tenant’s bank account to include the full 5.50% above-guideline increase without the Tenants’ consent. In doing so, the Landlord took away the Tenant’s statutory right of choice provided under section 126(6) of the Act to voluntarily pay the above-guideline increase amount pending the outcome of the application.

Although the Tenant could have contacted the Landlord and requested the automatic withdrawal amount of rent be reduced to the guideline increase of 2.5%, the onus is not on the Tenant to make that request. Any payments to the Landlord above the guideline increase are optional. As such, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of all amounts collected above the lawful guideline increase of 2.5% for the period of January 1, 2025 to the date of the hearing. Illegal Rent Collected

The lawful monthly rent for December, 2024 was $1,993.62. The lawful monthly rent was to be decreased by 0.80% pursuant to the City of Hamilton’s Notice of Rent Reduction issued pursuant to section 131 of the Act effective December 31, 2024. This would reduce the lawful monthly rent to $1,977.67.

The Landlord is entitled to at 2.5% rent increase being the guideline portion of their Notice of Rent Increase dated September 24, 2024 effective January 1, 2025. This would make the Tenant’s lawful monthly rent $2,027.11.

Although an additional rent increase may have occurred effective January, 2026. This [name] only deals with the Illegal Rent the Landlord has collected being the subject of the Tenant’s application. The difference between $2,103.26 per month and $2,027.11 per month from January 1, 2025 to the date of the hearing, equals $76.15 per month totalling $1,218.40 during this period.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,266.40. This amount represents: • $1,218.40 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,048.00 Illegal rent collected

On April 25, 2025 when entering into a tenancy agreement between the Tenant and the Landlord the Tenant paid to the Landlord $6,000.00, consisting of $4,000.00 for first and last month’s rent and $2,000.00 for a security deposit.

The Landlord does not dispute that a $2,000.00 security deposit was collected, but states it was collected at the request of the Tenant’s partner who indicated that they owned a large dog and the money could be used towards any potential future damages to the rental unit caused by the dog.
The Tenancy with respect to this rental unit ended on November 17, 2025. As of the date of the hearing the security deposit is still being held by the Landlord.
Section 105(1) of the Act states: 105(1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Sections 106(1) and 106(2) of the Act state: 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.

The amount of $2,000.00 collected as a security deposit in addition to $2,000.00 collected for a last month’s rent deposit exceeds the amount that can be collected pursuant to section 106(2) of the Act. As such I am satisfied that the Landlord collected and has retained an illegal charge.
The Tenant is entitled to the return of the illegal charge collected by the Landlord in the amount of $2,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
