issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. AND [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T6 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,867.03 This represents $3,819.03.00 for a rent abatement and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenants moved into the condominium rental unit on July 1, 2023, and pay the lawful monthly rent of $3,023.75 on the first day of each month.

It was undisputed that there was a fire in the residential complex on November 27, 2025, which caused a forced evacuation of multiple units, including that of the Tenants. As a result of the fire, the Tenants were displaced and moved in with family for the period of November 27, 2024 to January 4, 2026.

The Tenants claim that their Landlord substantially interfere with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Specifically, while the unit remained legally uninhabitable and inaccessible, the Landlord continued to demand the payment of full rent and did not grant any abatement/refund when asked.

Sections 20 and 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) provide that: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The issue before the Board is whether the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of rental unit and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards due to the fire.

It was not disputed per news reports as evidenced, a total of 408 units had to be evacuated due to life threatening carbon monoxide levels, that the conditions varied throughout the impacted buildings and return to occupancy would happen in "a phased-in approach," as determined by the authorities.

The fire source was said to be inside of the walls of the two high-rise buildings and was caused by incomplete combustion of particle board placed in an expansion joint between two buildings. The rental unit in question is located within one of the two buildings.

As the fire remained uncontrollable for a prolonged period, Tenants continued to be advised of developments and were reminded that, “Suite owners and tenants are strongly recommended to maintain appropriate insurance coverage; this is required by the condominium corporation's governing documents. The Corporation's insurance policy covers the common elements and the standard unit (as defined in the Corporation's Declaration and Standard Unit [name]). However, it does not extend to personal belongings, unit improvements/upgrades, or other non-standard items. Owners must obtain their own condominium unit owner's insurance policy to cover: • Improvements and betterments to the unit (ex. upgraded fixtures, flooring, or cabinetry); • Personal property and contents; • Personal liability And if “the unit is rented, tenants must secure tenant (renter's) insurance for their personal belongings and liability.”

The Landlord testified that the Tenants signed a lease agreement which included a clause that the Tenants must obtain personal contents insurance, this was not disputed by the Tenants. A copy of the lease agreement was produced as evidence.
It was not disputed that there was no damage sustained to rental unit as a result of the fire.

It was not disputed that the authorities permitted the re-occupation of certain units on the 6th floor where the rental unit is located on January 4, 2026, this included the permission for the Tenants to return on the same date as of 6 p.m. They were provided a time slot of 9:30 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. on January 5, 2026 to avail of scheduled elevator service for their use.

The Landlord testified that the Tenants paid for the rent to maintain the tenancy. That had they filed an insurance claim and decided to stay in alternative accommodations that those claims would have been covered in part through their insurance. On this basis, he did not believe he was in a position to consider the Tenants’ request for rent abatement. Analysis
As outlined above, it is undisputed that the fire was not the fault of the Landlord or the Tenants.

This case is similar to Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) where the Court of Appeal upheld the Divisional Court’s finding that the LTB reasonably concluded there was no maintenance breach where a Landlord took all reasonable steps to address elevator defects. The Court found the Landlord took reasonable steps to keep the tenants informed, to provide them with assistance and also to ensure that staff was ready and available to assist the tenants, occupants and guests, so as to mitigate any hardship caused to the tenants by the elevator problems.

Similarly, in this case, the Tenants were unable to return to the unit and there was nothing the Landlord could do to remedy the issues as arising from a fire which necessitated a forced evacuation, a situation not caused by or in control of the Landlord. Where this case is different however, unlike in Onyskiw, the Landlord here continued to charge the Tenants rent for a unit that was uninhabitable.

Likewise in a recent Divisional Court ruling in The Effort Trust Company v. [name], 2025 ONSC 1632 the court upheld the decision of the LTB where it was determined that following a fire in the rental unit, where the Tenant continued to pay rent while the rental unit was deemed unhabitable, the Tenant was entitled to a claim of rent abatement as awarded.

Here, the Tenants had a comprehensive insurance policy required under the terms of the lease agreement. They submitted that had they filed a claim under the policy, they would have incurred a deductible of $1,000.00 and their hotel or other alternative accommodations costs would have been covered for a period of up to two weeks. A policy outlining these terms was not evidenced.

The Landlord submitted that he did not have an insurance policy in place to protect against a possible loss of income because the condominium is insured by common elements and the Tenants are required to have their own coverage. He simply did not see a reason for it.

While the Landlord said he is unwilling to agree to an abatement of rent because the Tenants had an option to stay in accommodations that would have been paid in part by their own insurance policy, Tenants can move into any alternative housing of choice, here it was with family. The policy they have with their insurer, while required under the lease terms is separate from the Landlord’s obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

Based on the above, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, therefore dismissing the T2 application claims.

However, the Landlord’s conduct of charging rent while not being able to provide a unit that was fit for habitation was unreasonable. As the rental unit was deemed uninhabitable, at no fault and the Tenants continued to pay rent, they are owed 100% abatement for the entire period from date of evacuation to date of direction that they can safely return to the rental unit. Remedies

The Tenants claim the same remedies for both the T2 and T6 application, they claim the entitlement to the reimbursement of/ abatement of rent in the amount of $3,876.99 for the period of 39 days from November 27, 2025 to January 4, 2026.

As the lawful rent is $3,023.75 the daily compensation rate is calculated as $3,023.75 x 12/ 365 days. Daily compensation is therefore $99.41. In consideration of the 100% of abatement of rent for the period of November 27-30, 2025, the entire month of December 2025 - $3,023.75 and the period of January 1-4, 2026, the Board may consider a claim of $3,819.03.

The Tenants were forced to evacuate on November 27, 2025, the unit was uninhabitable until the Tenants were advised by building management , through the authorities that there was no longer a threat to life. The return date into the unit as provided was no earlier than 6:00 p.m. on January 4, 2026. The Landlord is required to maintain the unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, in return for which the Tenants are obligated to pay rent, given that the unit was not fit for habitation there was no rent due to the Landlord for the outlined period. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to pay $3,819.03 to the Tenants as an abatement for the rental period from November 27, 2025 to January 4, 2026.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,867.03. This amount represents: • $ 3,819.03.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 4, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $1,000.00 from the rent each month from March 1, 2026 to May 31, 2026 and $867.03 in June 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. T2 Application
The Tenants T2 application is dismissed. February 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] ([name]) [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for at least one year. (L2 Application) • applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies. (A1 Application) The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date.
reasons: The Landlord applied for a determination that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) does not apply to [name] [name]’s (CJ) occupation of the rental unit. Although CJ is identified as the “Tenant” in the application, the issue to be determined in the A1 application is whether his occupation of the rental unit is governed by the Act and whether there is a tenancy between him and the Landlord.

The Landlord submitted that CJ originally occupied the rental unit because he was in a relationship with the Landlord’s child, who also lived in the rental unit. The Landlord submitted that the arrangement was exempt from the Act under section 5. The Landlord further submitted that, after a domestic dispute, the Landlord’s child permanently vacated the rental unit on December 7, 2025. The Tenant did not dispute that the Landlord’s child previously lived in the rental unit with him, and agreed that the Landlord’s child has not lived in the rental unit since December 7, 2025.

The Landlord’s evidence was that, after their child vacated the rental unit, the Landlord took steps to notify CJ that the Landlord did not consider his ongoing occupation of the rental unit to be governed by the Act. The Landlord submitted that on December 31, 2025, CJ was hand-delivered written notice advising him that the Landlord considered the occupation of the rental unit to be exempt under section 5 of the Act and requiring him to vacate by January 31, 2026. The Landlord also sought legal advice and filed the A1 application to have the Board determine whether the Act applied.

The evidence also established that CJ continued to send payments after the Landlord’s child vacated the rental unit. However, I find that the continued payment and acceptance of money in these circumstances did not create a tenancy between CJ and the Landlord. The Landlord’s conduct after December 7, 2025 was not consistent with an intention to create a new tenancy governed by the Act. Rather, the Landlord promptly advised CJ that the Act not to apply, required him to vacate, sought legal assistance, and brought the A1 application for a determination from the Board.

I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that the N12 notice and L2 application were served and filed in the alternative, in the event the Board found that the Act applied. The fact that the Landlord took that alternative procedural step does not, in the circumstances of this case, establish that the Landlord accepted that there was a tenancy governed by the Act.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that [name] [name]’s occupation of the rental unit is exempt from the Act under section 5 of the Act. I further find that the Act does not apply to [name] [name]’s ongoing occupation of the rental unit and that there is no tenancy between [name] [name] and the Landlord that is governed by the Act. L2 application – Landlord’s own use

The Landlord also applied under the L2 application for an order terminating the tenancy based on an N12 notice, alleging that the Landlord in good faith required possession of the rental unit for residential occupation. However, I have found in the [name] application that the Act does not apply to [name] [name]’s occupation of the rental unit and that there is no tenancy between [name] [name] and the Landlord that is governed by the Act.

As a result, there is no tenancy under the Act for the Board to terminate in the L2 application. It is therefore unnecessary to determine whether the N12 notice was valid, whether the Landlord required possession in good faith, or whether compensation or daily compensation would otherwise be owing under the Act. The L2 application is dismissed because the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) does not apply to [name] [name]’s occupation or ongoing occupation of the rental unit.
There is no tenancy between [name] [name] and the Landlord that is governed by the Act.
The Landlord’s L2 application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Applicant’s Agent, [name], brings this application on behalf of the Applicant, [name]. [name] is [name]’s son, and was named as [name]’s attorney pursuant to a continuing power of attorney executed on November 6, 2022 (the “CPOA”).
It was not disputed that [name] no longer has capacity. The Respondent disputed the CPOA was valid, as in the Respondent’s view, [name] did not have capacity when the CPOA was executed.

The Substitute Decisions Act, 1992, S.O. 1992, c. 30 (the “SDA”) governs the execution and validity of continuing powers of attorney. Section 2(1) of the SDA provides that it is presumed a person of at least eighteen years has capacity to contract. Section 8(1) provides the specific requirements as to whether a person is capable of giving a continuing power of attorney. Section 10 of the SDA provides that a continuing power of attorney shall be executed in the presence of two witnesses, and excludes certain categories of people from acting as witnesses.

The CPOA is executed by [name] as well as two witnesses. I am satisfied, and it was not disputed, that those witnesses are not parties barred from serving as witnesses pursuant to section 10(2) of the SDA.

I heard evidence from [name], and [name] surrounding the execution of the CPOA and [name]’s state at the time of signing. I also heard evidence from the Respondent in respect to why she did not believe the [name] had capacity to execute the CPOA on November 6, 2022. I note that while the Respondent is [name]’s daughter, she acknowledges she had not had regular direct contact with [name] since 2016.

After hearing this evidence from both sides, I am satisfied based that [name] had capacity to execute the CPOA on November 6, 2022 in accordance with the SDA. As such, I find that [name] has capacity to bring this application on behalf of [name]. Does the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Apply?
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit.

The Applicant submits that the Act applies as in their view the Respondent has had exclusive control of the rental unit since 2003, or 2004, and has been paying condo fees for the rental unit since 2017 or 2018 when [name] asked the Respondent to pay for maintenance. The Respondent paid no amounts in respect to the rental unit prior to this time.

While these condo fees are paid directly to the condominium corporation, the Applicant submits this constituted an agreement under which a tenancy was formed and the Respondent paid this amount as rent, or as other consideration for occupation of the rental unit. The Applicant submits that even if this amount is not rent, this arrangement qualifies as a tenancy agreement under the Act in the form of a license to occupy pursuant to section 2 of the Act.

The evidence of [name] in regard to discussions surrounding an agreement for the Respondent to pay the condominium fees for the rental unit were all second hand, as he was not present for these conversations. This evidence amounts to essentially that he was told the Respondent agreed to make payments for the condominium fees in return for continuing to stay in the rental unit.

The Respondent submits that they have been living in the rental unit pursuant to a familial relationship since they moved in. The Respondent testified there was never an agreement between herself and [name] related to payments in return for staying in the rental unit.
The Respondent’s position was that as a family home, any member of the family would still be entitled to move into the rental unit with her if they wished to do so.

The Respondent testified in 2018 that automatic payments for common element fees were bouncing. The Respondent believes this was due to her mother’s cognitive decline. The Respondent received letters related to this from the condominium management including that a lien would be put on the rental unit if they were unpaid, and contacted [name] in relation to this issue. When [name] returned the Respondent’s call, she was upset and yelled at the Respondent. The Respondent testified that her sister was listening to the conversation, and stayed on the phone after [name] hung up, and told the Respondent she had to pay for these fees.

The Respondent has been paying the common element fees since this time, but considers these payments to be an informal loan to [name], who the Respondent believes remains responsible. The Respondent assumed this was a temporary issue and her mother would resume paying these fees in a few months, but never did. The Respondent also acknowledges that there was never an agreement that this amount was a loan, that was just her view of these payments.

I found the Respondent to be credible in her direct evidence as to what occurred between the parties in 2018. I find this to be the best evidence before me as to these events and I am satisfied they are an accurate version of events. While [name] testified he understood there to be an agreement to pay the condominium fees, given he had no direct knowledge of these conversations, I find I cannot imply any agreement beyond the facts as testified to by the Respondent.

While the Applicant submitted that the payment of condominium fees was the payment of rent, I find this cannot be the case. In accordance with section 2(1) of the Act: “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing,…”

The consideration paid is required to be paid to the landlord or an agent of the landlord. I cannot find that the condominium corporation who was directly paid these fees was a landlord or agent of the landlord in this scenario.

Further, it makes sense with the statutory scheme that a payment such as this would not constitute rent. The Applicant’s position in the hearing was that if the condominium fees were raised by a significant amount, the Respondent would be responsible for paying this full increase. This of course would be contrary to the Act if this amount constituted rent, as an increase above the rent increase guidelines. This definition is structured in a manner that prevents these kinds of contradictions.

However, this does not resolve the matter entirely. There is a tenancy between the parties if there is a tenancy agreement between the parties pursuant to the Act. Section 2(1) of the Act defines a tenancy agreement in the following manner: “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; (“convention de location”)

This has been interpreted by the Divisional Court as including relationships where there are no monetary payments of rent given the inclusive definition and reference to licences to occupy a rental unit being included in it (see [name] v. [name], [2000] O.J. No. 2763 paragraphs 2-4 and [name], [2006] O.J. No. 5883).

The Divisional Court has recently affirmed the basic elements required of a tenancy agreement that must be agreed upon in Fuamba et al. v. [name], 2024 ONSC 4587 (“Fuamba”) at paragraph 13, being: “(1) the parties; (2) a description of the premises to be rented; (3) the commencement of the term; (4) the duration of the term; (5) the rent (if any); and (6) all the material terms of the contract not being matters incident to the relation of landlord and tenant, including any covenants, exceptions or reservations. (see for example Londos Investments Ltd. v. [organization], [1988] O.J. No. 7 ([name]. [name]).”

I am not satisfied that all of the elements described in Fuamba were agreed on based on the testimony of the parties as to the discussions, conduct and relationship of the parties over the many years the Respondent lived in the rental unit. Particularly, I am not satisfied that the parties came to an agreement as to the payment of rent, if any, and whether or not the Respondent was entitled to exclusive use of the rental unit.
I am also not satisfied that the parties intended to create any sort of legal relationship, including a tenancy agreement on the basis of a licence to occupy.

For many years the Respondent lived in the rental unit without an expectation of payment. This was not disputed. When the Applicant submits the expectation of payment arose, the best evidence I have before me is that there was no direct agreement between [name] and the Respondent as to paying the condominium fees in return for continuing to live in the property.

Instead, the evidence is that fees previously paid by pre-authorized payments were bouncing and this was brought up to the [name]. [name] was upset and screamed at the Respondent, and following this the Respondent’s sister told the Respondent she needed to pay these fees when [name] was no longer on the phone. I find this is also insufficient to imply a tenancy agreement between the parties in these circumstances. There has to be a meeting of the minds in order to reach an agreement, even on an implied basis. The parties must also have an intention to create legal relations.

I am not satisfied that either [name] or the Respondent ever had a meeting of the minds as to what these payments constituted, or that either intended the arrangement of the Respondent paying condominium fees to constitute any sort of legal relationship, including a tenancy agreement. I note that I had no evidence before me as to the Respondent’s sister having standing to act as an agent for [name], and therefore that statements made by that party could not bind [name] to an agreement in any event.

I specifically make no findings as to what the payments made by the Respondent constituted. The parties have different positions in this respect, and I find given my other findings in this order it is both unnecessary to make that determination for the purposes of this order, and inappropriate to make such findings given my finding that the Board does not have jurisdiction over this relationship.

I am mindful in making the findings above that the definition of a tenancy agreement includes a licence to occupy pursuant to section 2(1) of the Act, and a licence is in essence a permission of use. However, in the context of a licence to occupy that qualifies as a tenancy agreement pursuant to the Act, I find that a licence still requires a certainty of terms agreed between the parties as described in Fuamba, an intention to enter into legal relations, and some form of consideration, even if that consideration is not in the form of monetary payments made directly to a landlord.

These are basic contractual principles, and whether a licence or not, section 2(1) of the Act requires tenancy agreements to be written, oral or implied agreements. Therefore, these contractual principles must be complied with to qualify under the definition. To find otherwise would result in absurdities.

For example, is a tenancy created by a parent telling their child they may stay for the week in their basement, which has its own bathroom and kitchen facilities, in exchange for cutting the lawn during their stay? If there is no requirement for an intention to create to legal relations for a licence to occupy to qualify as a tenancy agreement, this would result in a tenancy subject to the Act. The terms are certain. None of the exceptions to the Act apply. Consideration is being given, though not in the form of a monetary payment. However, it is clear that generally in these circumstances the parties did not intend to create a tenancy. It cannot be correct that the child in this scenario is then entitled to stay in the basement for an indefinite period pursuant to a weekly renewing tenancy, so long as they cut the lawn.

By way of another example, if a homeowner’s child or friend is experiencing a difficult time, and so that homeowner permits their child or friend to stay in that same basement equipped with a kitchen and bathroom for the period of a month, this is permission, or a licence, to occupy a residential unit. If nothing further were required for a licence to occupy to qualify as a tenancy agreement, this would then result in a tenancy subject to the Act. This tenancy would automatically renew for another term on an indefinite basis, and the landlord would be entitled to receive nothing, as it was clear there was no expectation of consideration. This is clearly wrong, and on reflection, I find that is because there must be a requirement for consideration and for an intent to create legal relations for a licence to occupy to qualify as a tenancy agreement under the Act.

These sorts of scenarios cannot be what the Legislature intended by their non-exhaustive definition of a tenancy agreement in section 2(1) of the Act. I find it was written broadly instead to provide protection to tenants by making clear that any contract that provides for the permission of use of land rather than a traditional leasehold interest in land will not prevent the protections of the Act from applying. The fundamental terms of a tenancy agreement, consideration, and an intention to create legal relations must still apply in order for a licence to occupy to qualify as a tenancy agreement under this definition.
I find given the above, that the licence provided to the Tenant in this case does not meet the qualifications to be a licence to occupy that qualifies as a tenancy agreement under the Act.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of the estate of [name] [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenants’ tenancy of the rental unit commenced on August 1, 2013 (DOC-7930440, pp. 4-10). [name] (‘RD’) moved out of the rental unit long ago, leaving [name] [name] [name] (‘CR’) as the only tenant living in the rental unit.

CR passed away on July 11, 2025. The application is amended to remove “[name] [name] [name] (Deceased)” as a party, and to replace him with the “Estate of [name] [name] [name]”. Unauthorized Transfer of Occupancy

The Unauthorized Occupant, [name] (‘BB’), was living in the rental unit with CR up until July 11, 2025, when CR passed away. RD was not living in the rental unit at the time, and did not occupy the unit after that time.
CR’s tenancy terminated by operation of statute on August 10, 2025, 30 days after his death: ss. 91(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. BB remained living in the rental unit after CR’s death.

An application where a landlor d alleges an unlawful transfer of occupancy of the rental unit must be field within 60 days of when the Landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy: ss. 100(2), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

When a tenant dies, that tenant ceases occu pying the rental unit. If an occupant of the rental unit remains in the unit after the tenant’s death, this amounts to an unauthorized transfer of occupancy of the unit, unless there is a lawful sublet or assignment of the unit to the occupant, with the landlord’s consent, a deemed assignment of the unit, or a new tenancy agreement is entered into between the occupant and the landlord: ss. 100(1) $ 104, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; Homestead Land Holdings Limited v. Brown, 2021 CanLII 89622 (ON LTB), paras 9-11; Jemiola v. Firchuk, [2005] OJ No 6085.

A person’s occupation of a rental unit is deemed to be an assignment of the unit with the Landlord’s consent as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if the conditions set out in ss. 104(4) are satisfied. These conditions are that a new tenancy agreement between the landlord and occupant is not entered into, and no application under ss. 100 or 101 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) is made within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy (or within 60 days of the subtenancy ending under s. 101 of the Act in the case of an overholding subtenant): ss. 104(4), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

This application was filed on October 1, 2025 by the Landlord. In the application, the Landlord claims that it discovered BB’s unauthorized occupancy on September 2, 2025. The date that the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy was disputed by BB.

Because this is the Landlor d’s application, the Landlord bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53, paras 44-46.

PA’s evidence was that the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy near the beginning of September 2025. He presented as evidence several emails to support this assertion. This included an email from BB to an employee of the landlord dated August 14, 2025 providing “tenant information” (DOC-7930440, p 20). This email belies the position that the Landlord only discovered the unauthorized occupancy in September 2025. In the email, BB identified the leaseholder as “[name] [name] [name] (DECEASED)”, and identified himself and two other individuals as “Occupants”. BB explicitly informed the Landlord in writing on August 14, 2025 that CR had died and that he was still living in the unit with two other occupants. This is consistent with BB’s evidence that he informed the Landlord that CR had died around mid-August 2025.

PA said that the Landlord did not take this email at “face value”, and waited for other confirmation from CR’s family that he had died. I do not accept the argument that the Landlord did not “discover” the unauthorized occupancy when BB explicitly informed them about it in writing. While it is reasonable to seek confirmation of this type of information, the Landlord was accurately informed about the unauthorized occupancy by BB on August 14, 2025. I find that this is when the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy, which was confirmed by CR’s family member at a later date.

Both PA and BB said that there was discussion between the Landlord and BB about entering a new tenancy agreement. PA said that BB was given the opportunity to make an application for the rental unit. BB’s application was rejected by the Landlord because BB did not have a guarantor.

Although BB said he thought he had come to an agreement over the phone with a former employee of the landlord to enter into a new tenancy agreement, no tenancy agreement was ever signed between the parties. Despite there being an application and discussion about entering into a tenancy agreement, BB and the Landlord did not enter into a new tenancy agreement.

The Landlord learned of the unauthorized occupancy on August 14, 2025 and not September 2, 2025, but the application was still filed within 60 days of when the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy.
It was not disputed that the Landlord did not give consent to the unit being sublet or assigned to BB.

PA’s evidence was that BB stayed in the unit without paying rent or compensation for use and occupation to the Landlord until February 25, 2026, when BB vacated the unit and returned the keys. BB has vacated the unit, but the Landlord seeks an order that BB pay the Landlord compensation for use and occupation of the unit for the period September 2, 2025 to February 25, 2026.

The monthly rent for the unit at the time that CR died was $1,243.96. This means the daily compensation rate is $40.90 [$1,243.96 x 12 months, divided by 365 days]. The Landlord seeks compensation for 176 days [September 2, 2025 to February 25, 2026]. This amounts to $7,198.40 [$40.90 x 176 days].

BB did not dispute that he did not pay rent or compensation for use and occupation to the Landlord for the period after CR died. He said that he attempted to pay rent to the Landlord, but the Landlord refused to accept it and returned the cheques that he provided to the Landlord.

BB disputed that he should be required to pay compensation for use and occupation for the entire period claimed by the Landlord, because there was times during this period where the Landlord deactivated his fob preventing him form accessing the unit. This is, in substance, a defence to part of the Landlord’s claim for compensation for use and occupation of the unit on the basis that the Landlord deprived BB of use and occupation of the unit during these periods. While the burden of proof remains on the Landlord relative to its application, I find it is appropriate that BB bears an evidentiary burden relative to this defence.

BB’s evidence was that his fob was deactivated for the first time in September 2025. He said that he asked an employee of the Landlord, Theresa, about why his fob was not working, and he was told that the fob was deactivated and he was not permitted to stay in the unit. BB’s possessions remained in the unit, so he asked how he can move his things if he cannot access the unit. He said that the fob was reactivated after about 2.5 weeks.

During this time, BB said he lived in his car while his children stayed with a family friend. BB said that the fob was again deactivated for approximately a week in late October or early November 2025, and then again in mid-January 2026. BB said that at this point he decided that he would just move out of the unit, and did not live in the unit after this time. He said the fob was reactivated after he spoke with Theresa again, but that it was a hassle to move and took time.
BB acknowledged that his personal property remained in the unit about February 25, 2026, when he returned the keys/fobs to the Landlord.
BB’s evidence about the fob disconnection was not contradicted by any evidence presented by the Landlord.

Although the Landlord did not present evidence contradicting BB’s claims about the fob being deactivated, EC did cross-examine BB about this issue. BB’s evidence remained consistent on cross-examination. BB did not have supporting documentary or video evidence to support his assertions about the fob deactivations, and explained that he did not document this because he was not thinking about gathering evidence for a legal proceeding.
I found BB to be a credible witness, and his evidence was cogent and consistent.

I accept that BB’s fob was deactivated by the Landlord for a total of 3.5 weeks [24 days] in September and November/December 2025. BB was effectively denied access to the unit during this time, and I agree that he should not be required to pay the Landlord compensation for use and occupation of the unit for the time that the Landlord prevented him from using or occupying the unit.

Although BB’s personal property remained in the unit during these periods, he was deprived of possession of the unit because he did not have access to, use of, control over, or occupation of the unit: see [name] v. [organization], 2004 CanLII 59995 (ON CA), para 20.

I accept BB’s evidence that he did not live in the unit after mid-January 2026, however his personal property remained in the unit, and vacant possession of the unit was not given to the Landlord until February 25, 2026. I also accept that BB’s fob was deactivated in mid- January 2026, however, BB did not give cogent evidence relative to how long this deactivation lasted. I cannot therefore determine for what period BB did not have access to, use of, or control over the unit between mid-January 2026 and February 25, 2026.

In my view, even if BB decided not to live in the unit after mid-January 2026, he still ought to be required to pay compensation for use and occupation for any period where he had control over the unit, included access to it and use of it. BB did not discharge his evidentiary burden relative to what, if any, amount of time he was actually deprived of control over, access to, or use of, the rental unit for the period of mid-January to February 25, 2026.

For these reasons, I find that BB ought be required to pay the Landlord compensation for use and occupation of the unit for 152 days [176 days, less 24 days when BB was deprived of control over, access to, and use/occupation of the rental unit]. The total amount BB must pay the Landlord for use and occupation of the unit is $6,216.80 [152 x $40.90].
The Landlord paid $201.00 to file this application, and is also entitled to recover this amount
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlor d and the Tenants is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $6,216.80 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from September 2, 2025 to the February 25, 2026, less 24 days.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the [name] ord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord filed the A2 application under section 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which authorizes the Landlord to apply to the Board for termination of the tenancy where the tenant has transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlord’s consent. Section 100(2) of the Act provides that the application must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy.

The application was filed on April 7, 2026. In the application, the Landlord indicates that he discovered the Unauthorized Tenant in the rental unit on February 2, 2026, which is more than the 60-day limitation period as set out in the Act. At the hearing, the Landlord acknowledges he knew about the Unauthorized Occupant on February 2, 2026. I do not have any jurisdiction to alter the limitation period in section 100(2) of the Act.

In addition to the above, section 104(4) of the Act states in part: (4) A person’s occupation of a rental unit shall be deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if, (a) a tenancy agreement is not entered into under subsection (1) or (2) within the period set out in subsection (3); (b) the landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 for an order evicting the person within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy; [emphasis added]

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord’s application was filed more than 60 days after the Landlord was aware that the Unauthorized Occupant was living there. As such, the current Unauthorized Occupant of the rental unit is deemed the lawful tenant of the rental unit pursuant to section 104(4)(b) of the Act and the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The rental unit is a house with a garage.

The Landlord’s father, M. [name] (MM), is the person who communicates and manages the Landlord’s Tenants. He testified that in February 2026, the Tenant owed over a year of arrears. He said that she told him she would vacate the rental unit on or around February 18, 2026, and he believed that she had left because he entered the property after that date and he discovered that all the Tenant’s belongings were gone. However, he said that he arrived at the property about a week later and found unknown people living in the rental unit and smoking [name].

MM said that he called the police to remove the unknown persons, and when the police arrived, one of the men living in the rental unit, named [name] (MH) said that he was living in the unit with the authority of the Tenant. MM said that he overheard MH tell the police that he was the Tenant’s partner, and he mentioned her by name. MM also said that he heard MH tell the police that he entered the unit by breaking into the garage.

MM said that he does not know MH, nor did he ever meet him during the tenancy. MM said that MH does not permit entry to the rental unit. He said that he attempted to have his bank visit the property for a tax assessment in April 2026, and the occupants told the assessors that they were not permitted into the rental unit. He said that he has spoken to the neighbours, and they have informed him that, up until the week before the hearing, they still observe unknown people living in the rental unit.

The Landlord filed the application on April 24, 2026. I find that the application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy at the end of February or beginning of March 2026.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, based on the Landlord’s uncontested evidence, that the Tenant transferred the tenancy to MH and other unauthorized occupants in a manner not authorized by the Act. The Tenant said to MM that she was vacating the rental unit because she had not paid rent in over a year. Although the Landlord appeared to accept her statement that she was going to leave, and they believed she had left, the tenancy never terminated as a result of a valid, written notice from the Tenant, nor a written agreement between the parties, nor as a result of an eviction order from the Board. Only a few days after the Tenant removed her belongings, there were a number of unauthorized occupants of the unit claiming a relationship with the Tenant. The Landlord did not know the unauthorized occupants, he had never met them, and the Tenant had never asked to add them as occupants of the rental unit. The Tenant had not asked for permission from the Landlord to transfer her tenancy, and none of the occupants requested a lease agreement with the Landlord. Since the tenancy never validly terminated, and since there were unauthorized occupants in the rental unit who alleged that they were there on the authority of the Tenant, I find that the tenancy was unlawfully transferred by the Tenant. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $101.92. This amount is calculated as follows: $3100.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

The Landlord has already obtained an order from the Board for the arrears owed to February 18, 2026, order LTB-L-014224-26 issued on May 5, 2026. Therefore, the Landlord is entitled to daily compensation for the unit only from that date. That order was issued against the Tenant.

Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupants, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupants paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit. Therefore, the Tenant, MH and the other unauthorized occupants will be jointly ordered to pay daily compensation for the rental unit from the date of February 19, 2026.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The same parties mentioned in paragraph #12 above will be jointly held responsible to pay the Landlord their filing costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act, for the following reasons. The uncontested evidence of the Landlord is that the Tenant has already vacated the rental unit. The only individuals who currently live in the rental unit are [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants. They did not attend the hearing to provide evidence about whether to deny or delay eviction, and they have been blocking the Landlord from any access to the property, which includes blocking entry for an essential property assessment. The Landlord said that he is on the verge of imminently losing the property as a result of the blocking of the property assessment, and I find that it is highly prejudicial to the Landlord for the tenancy or unauthorized occupancy to continue.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated. 2. [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 26, 2026. 3. If the unit is not vacated by June 26, 2026, then starting June 27, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced. 4. Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 27, 2026. 5. The Tenant, [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants shall be jointly liable to pay the Landlord $101.92 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from February 19, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit. 6. The Tenant, [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants shall also be jointly liable to pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application. 7. The Tenant, [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 26, 2026. 8. If the Tenant, [name] and/or the other Unauthorized Occupants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 26, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 27, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
