issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 Application’). [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (the ‘T2 Application’). The A1 Application and the T2 Application were heard together by videoconference on April 23, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does apply to the rental unit that was occupied by the Tenant.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit in 2018 and vacated May 25, 2024. There was no written rental agreement between the parties. The rental unit is in the basement level of the Landlord’s home.

The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant was required to share a kitchen with the Landlord under the rental agreement and, therefore, the exemption at paragraph 5(i) of the Act applies. The Tenant disputes this and takes the position that it was never contemplated that he would share a kitchen with the Landlord and that he never in fact did. ; LTB-T-025031-24

The Tenant’s testimony was unambiguous and unequivocal. He testified that he never entered the Landlord’s kitchen during the six years he resided in the rental unit. He testified that he never cooked in the kitchen, stored any food in the kitchen, or assisted the Landlord with cooking – although he acknowledges that the Landlord shared an occasional meal with him when he first moved into the rental unit. None of these facts were disputed by the Landlord, who testified that she never saw the Tenant use the kitchen. The Tenant testified that he relied entirely on the kitchenette inside the rental unit and countertop appliances for his food preparation and frequently did not eat at home.
The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant had access to the kitchen via an unlocked door, although the Tenant blocked this door when he placed a cabinet in front of the door within the rental unit.

The Tenant also provided a copy of email communication between himself and the Landlord in the lead-up to the tenancy. The email – dated June 11, 2018, and sent via Kijiji’s messaging system – lists the title of the Landlord’s rental advertisement as “Bachelor basement suit (sic) available July 1st”. The full text of the advertisement was not presented at the hearing.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the parties never contemplated that the Tenant would use the kitchen when they entered into the rental agreement. The rental unit was advertised as a bachelor suite, which typically refers to a self-contained unit rather than a room for rent. The rental unit does not contain a full kitchen, but photographs show a wet bar, cabinetry, and a refrigerator provided by the Landlord.

In my view, these facts do not correspond with the Landlord’s assertion of a shared kitchen. It is simply not credible that the parties agreed to share a kitchen, but that the Tenant never went so far as to step foot into the room over six years.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord is attempting to argue that the parties shared a kitchen to escape liability with respect to the T2 Application, which was filed approximately one month prior to the [name] application. In the absence of written terms, the Board must make a determination based on the testimony of the parties. The facts presented at the hearing clearly accord more logically with the Tenant’s description of the arrangement between the parties. The Landlord’s account of the arrangement and the parties actions during the tenancy simply do not make sense.
Therefore, I find that the Act applies to the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant. The T2 Application: No Substantial Interference or Harassment is Proven
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 Application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 Application is dismissed. ; LTB-T-025031-24

The T2 Application details several allegations of substantial interference or harassment by the Landlord. In particular, the Tenant alleges the following occurred within the one-year period before he filed his application: • In April 2023, the Landlord insisted the Tenant remain in the rental unit to supervise contractors attending to an urgent issue with respect to the residential complex’s hot water heater; • In July 2023, the Landlord reached out to the Tenant’s sister to ask about the tenancy; • In July 2023, the Landlord accused the Tenant of changing the locks to the rental unit, resulting in police attending the residential complex; and • In July 2023 and March 2024, the Landlord and the Tenant had disputes relating to parking spots in the driveway of the residential complex.

The Landlord and the Tenant both provided testimony about the above events. It is clear that each of these events was a source of contention and disagreement between the parties. However, based on the testimony presented at the hearing, I am not satisfied that the above incidents rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment.

In my view, the most serious incident – the July 2023 incident regarding the accusations that the Tenant changed the locks – amounts, essentially, to a misunderstanding. The Landlord discovered that the key she thought opened the rental unit did not in fact do so, and the Tenant did not provide his key to the Landlord so she could make a copy. The Landlord called the police non-emergency line to ask for advice – not with the intention to have the police attend the rental unit. When police attended, per the Tenant’s testimony, no action was taken. While the Tenant chose to spend the night away from the rental unit due to his feelings of stress about the circumstances, he appeared to do so of his own will.

The relationship between the parties clearly turned downhill toward the end of the tenancy as a result of several points of disagreement and conflict. However, these disagreements – in my view – are relatively benign. The parties lived in close proximity to one another and, as a result, situations arose (as they often do) that were required to be resolved. Not every point of contention between a landlord and a tenant constitutes a breach of the Act.

Even if the Tenant’s account of the events is wholly true, I am not satisfied that they amount to substantial interference or harassment. It is the Tenant’s burden to prove this is the case and, in my view, he has not done so. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Act applies to the rental unit that was occupied by the Tenant.
The T2 Application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Group (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of Upansana [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] et al (the 'Unauthorized Occupants') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] and other Unauthorized Occupants without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupants for the use of the rental unit. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupants to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex.
reasons: The Landlord filed their application alleging that they first became aware that the Tenant, U. [name] (UR) had transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to unauthorized persons on April 8, 2025. They are seeking unpaid rent. They also filed an application seeking reasonable costs to repair property damaged by the Tenant or their unauthorized occupants in the amount of $30,000.00.
The rental unit is a two bedroom new-build condo. The monthly rent, or occupancy fee, is $3,685.45.
The parties agreed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale, dated June 22, 2019. Within that agreement, in [name], are the Terms of Occupancy Licence.

The Landlord’s agent, S. [name] (SJ), is in sales and customer care for the condo sales of the Landlord. She said that when purchasers buy a condo they have a right to live in the condo prior to the closing of the sale, under an occupancy agreement. The monthly rent is charged as an “occupancy fee”. She said that the Tenant first went into default in paying their occupancy fee in February 2025, and she submitted into evidence the letter sent by the Landlord to the Tenant about the default. The date on the letter is a clerical error. SJ said that it was sent to the Tenant in February 2025. SJ said that after a purchaser defaults in paying their occupancy fee, they get reminder letters, then they are given a period of time to leave, and then their purchase agreement is cancelled, and that is what happened in this tenancy. All this is outlined in the Agreement of Purchase and Sale submitted into evidence. It is dated June 22, 2019.

SJ said that the Landlord was notified of a leak in the rental unit on April 8, 2025, by one of the neighbours. She said that the occupants of the rental unit were not at home when the Landlord’s employees went to investigate, but the occupants arrived later. She said that the occupants kept referring to themselves as “tenants”. The only name communicated to the Landlord for the unauthorized occupants was “[name]”. [name] said that when the Landlord inspected, they found defrosting food in the sink, causing water to overflow and leak into the unit. She submitted into evidence a series of photos taken on April 8, 2025, that show water on the carpet in the hallway outside the rental unit, flooding water on the floor in the unit, water leaking inside the walls in the unit directly below the rental unit, and even water leaking into the unit below that one. She said that there was water leaking through ceiling vent into a unit four floors below the rental unit. SJ submitted into evidence a video of the leaking sink taken on the day of the flooding. The video showed a sink filled with defrosting items, and the sink was overflowing with water pouring into the entire unit.

SJ said that there were other reports about occupants of the unit causing problems. She submitted into evidence an incident report, dated September 5, 2025, in which children from the rental unit were observed causing damage to a light post outside the building.

The Landlord now seeks $20,329.08 for the cost of all repairs done by the Landlord as a result of the flood on April 8, 2025, which includes floor replacement costs, removal and disposal of damaged materials, wall replacement and painting to all the units affected by the flooding, replacement of carpet in the hallway, and replacement of a front door lock damaged by the Tenant or their occupants. The Landlord amended their application to request an extra $186.45 for the cost of replacing a damaged door lock (they submitted into evidence documentary evidence of this extra cost).
The Landlord is not seeking the compensation owed by the Tenants. The Landlord is only seeking reimbursement for the damage caused.

SJ said that the named Landlord is still responsible for the rental unit, and the Landlord continues to pay condo fees. She said that the Tenant asked to be reinstated, and the Landlord replied with terms and conditions. However, she said the Tenant did not respond to the terms and conditions. Reasons and Analysis:

This matter is within the jurisdiction of the Board for the following reasons. Pursuant to subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a “tenancy agreement” includes a licence to occupy a rental unit. Subsection 58(1)4 of the Act specifically contemplates this type of agreement as coming under the Act, as it provides that notices of termination under the Act may be given to a Tenant when the tenancy arose by virtue or “collateral to an agreement of purchase and sale of a proposed unit within the meaning of the Condominium Act, 1998 in good faith and the agreement of purchase and sale has been terminated.”

The Landlord had documentary evidence that the Tenant breached the terms of the collateral agreement of purchase and sale by failing to pay the occupancy fee, even after several reminders and opportunities to pay it. This terminated the agreement of purchase and sale, and the sale was never completed.

Since the Act applies to this relationship, and the Landlord had the right to serve the Tenant with a notice of termination, section 100 of the Act relating to unauthorized transfers of tenancy also applies.

For the reasons that follow, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to [name] and other Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person/these persons.

I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant, [name] and/or the other unauthorized occupants caused wilful or negligent damage in the rental unit, and they are responsible to pay the Landlord for the out-of-pocket expenses incurred to the Landlord to repair the damage for the following reasons.

The Landlord discovered on April 8, 2025, after responding to flooding in the rental unit, that the unit was occupied by unauthorized persons, not the Tenant. The Tenant had not asked the Landlord for authorization to install these people in the rental unit. According to the Agreement of Purchase and Sale, it was only the Tenant who had the right to occupy the rental unit prior to the closing of the purchase of the rental unit, as long as the Tenant paid the occupancy fee. The Tenant had a right to request authorization to install other people, but the Tenant never did so. The Tenant defaulted on paying the occupancy fee as of February 2025, and the sale never went through.

The Landlord had video evidence and testimonial evidence about the damage caused by the leak and subsequent flooding that originated in the rental unit on April 8, 2025. They had documentary evidence of the amount the Landlord had to spend to repair the flooding in the rental unit and the other units affected by the flooding.

The Landlord’s witnesses testified that they had communication with the Unauthorized Occupants when they came home after the flooding, referring to themselves as “tenants”, and they were therefore in possession of the rental unit on the date the damage was caused. They were still in possession on the date the application was filed.
The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and they are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord has incurred reasonable costs of $20,329.08 to repair the damage, or to replace property that was damaged and cannot be repaired. I find that both the Tenant and [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants are jointly liable for this damage. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. In particular, the Tenant stopped paying their occupancy fees a long time ago, and it is prejudicial to the Landlord for this tenancy to continue. The Landlord has also suffered severe financial prejudice as a result of the unauthorized transfer of the tenancy to the unauthorized occupants. The unauthorized occupants caused extensive damage to the rental unit and other units in the building. Neither the Tenant nor the unauthorized occupants attended the hearing to explain any mitigating circumstances to delay or deny eviction.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Tenant, [name] and the Unauthorized Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 16, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 16, 2026, then starting June 17, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 17, 2026.
The Tenant, [name] and the Unauthorized Occupants shall pay to the Landlord $20,329.08, which represents the reasonable costs of repairing the damage or replacing the damaged property.
The Tenant, [name] and the Unauthorized Occupants shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Tenant, [name] and/or the Unauthorized Occupants do not vacate the rental unit on or before June 16, 2026, they shall also pay to the Landlord $121.17 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from June 17, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Tenant, [name], and/or the Unauthorized Occupants shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 16, 2026. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict (the '[name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The [name] was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant signed a lease for the rental unit on November 16, 2021.

The Landlord testified that she first became aware that the Tenant may have vacated the rental unit when an N4 Notice of Termination was returned to her with the notation “Moved” on May 31, 2025, but no keys had been returned to the building management.

The Landlord testified after receiving the returned N4 Notice, she contacted building management to confirm whether the rental unit was vacant as she could not as she did not reside in Canada. The building management advised the Landlord that the rental unit was not vacant and that an [name] was found residing in the rental unit. The building management further advised that the [name] was using the fob for the rental unit and had been regularly using the parking space associated with the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that she attempted to contact the Tenant to confirm whether the Tenant had vacated the rental unit and transferred occupancy to another person. The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not respond to the Landlord’s phone calls, messages, or emails.

Section 100 of the Act allows a landlord to apply to evict an [name] if the tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit other than by an authorized assignment or sublet (i.e. without the landlord’s consent).

Section 95 of the Act allows a tenant to assign a rental unit to another person with the landlord’s consent. Section 97 of the Act allows a tenant to sublet a rental unit to another person with the landlord’s consent. In this case, the Landlords did not consent to an assignment or a sublet. Therefore, I must determine whether the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit.

In the Ontario Court of Appeal’s decision in Samuel Property Management Ltd. V. Nicholson, [2002] CanLII 45065 (ON CA) (‘[name]’), the Court found that the determination of whether the tenant has transferred occupancy depends on whether the tenant maintains a substantial connection to the rental unit and that is a question of fact and degree. In Nicholson, the Court found that the tenant had transferred occupancy of the unit to his two friends because he had limited use of the rental unit. He occasionally stayed at the rental unit and kept clothes there, but he had handed over to his friends the day- today occupancy of the rental unit.

Based on the uncontested evidence provided by the Landlord at the hearing, I find that the [name] took over the rental unit improperly and started occupying the unit without permission from the Landlord. The N4 Notice was returned with the notation “Moved,” the Tenant did not return the keys, the Tenant did not respond to the Landlord’s attempts to contact her, and the [name] was found residing in the rental unit, using the fob, and regularly using the parking space associated with the rental unit. I am satisfied that these circumstances establish that the Tenant transferred day-to-day occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] without the Landlord’s consent.

Therefore, I find that occupancy of the rental unit was transferred to the [name], in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. The Landlords did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act requires a landlord to apply to the Board within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he first became aware of the [name] on May 31, 2025. The application was filed June 5, 2025.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. The [name] did not attend the hearing to provide the Board with evidence of their circumstances. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the [name].
The [name] owes the Landlord $21,070.14 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from May 31, 2025 to the January 6, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $95.34. This amount is calculated as follows: $2900.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the [name], the Tenant and/or the [name] paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The [name] shall pay $201.00 for the filing of the application.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The [name] shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 27, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 27, 2026, then starting June 28, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 28, 2026.
The [name] shall pay to the Landlord $21,070.14 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from May 31, 2025 to the January 6, 2026.
The [name] shall also pay to the Landlord $95.34 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from January 7, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The [name] shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The [name] shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the [name] does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 27, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Corporation (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (K.C.), is employed by the Landlord in the capacity of an investigator. He has held this position for approximately 7 years and has been employed by the Landlord for approximately 17 years.

K.C. testified that the Landlord received an anonymous letter or complaint in which the Landlord was informed that the Tenant who resides in unit 2001 does not live in the rental unit any longer and instead rents the unit out to other individuals. At the time the application was filed, the Landlord also filed and L2 application for misrepresentation of income (LTB-L-059592-24). K.C. confirmed that the sole Tenant as identified on the lease agreement is [name], an individual whom K.C. is familiar with. The L2 application was dismissed on the basis that the Tenant was not in possession on the date the application was filed.

With respect to the unauthorized transfer, K.C. identified this tenancy as an RGI unit which has specific rules that would not generally apply to standard market rent tenancy. The rules include the Tenant being required to notify the Landlord of any change in household income within 30 days of said change, the Tenant cannot assign or sublet the unit to another individual, the Tenant can have guests for a period of up to 7 days at a time without the Landlord’s consent, the Tenant can have guests for up to 30 days in a calendar year without the Landlord’s consent, and any guests staying over 30 days require the Landlord’s authorization and consent.
The Landlord assigned K.C. to investigate the status of who was occupying the rental unit based on the anonymous complaint received by the Landlord.

K.C.’s investigation documented by video surveillance and otherwise, that the Tenant was last seen in the rental unit between the period of January 24, 2024, through to February 18, 2024. The findings of the investigation also confirmed that the Tenant has not returned to the rental unit and entered it since February 18, 2024. K.C. also testified that since February 18, 2024, the only individual seen entering the Tenant’s rental unit was an unknown female who the Landlord believes the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to. This female was also seen using the laundry facilities in the complex and checking the mailbox associated with the rental unit of the Tenant. 6. [name] testified that based on video surveillance and fob reports, the [name] residing in unit 2001 was using a fob that was assigned to unit 1001, and the individual occupying unit 1001 was using the fob assigned to unit 2001. The Landlord believed that this was done deliberately to confuse the Landlord or alternatively prevent the Landlord from finding out about the unauthorized transfer of occupancy. I accept this reasoning. 7. K.C. testified he tried to speak with the [name] residing in unit 2001 but the [name] refused to allow entry or to identify themselves to the Landlord. K.C. described the [name] as rude and unwilling to share information about how they came to reside in the unit. 8. [name] testified that when reviewing the fob history and video surveillance footage, the [name] is seen entering and exiting the complex between the period of August 2023, through to the date of the hearing. K.C. testified that he believes that the Tenant did return to the unit between the period of late January 2024, through to February 18, 2024, at which time the [name] re-occupied the unit and the Tenant was no longer seen. 9. K.C. attempted to share the evidence found during his investigation with the Tenant, so that the Tenant could dispute it if he wished to do so, but the Tenant did not wish to engage in the conversation after being shown the Landlord’s findings. This attempted interaction took place during the brief period in which the Tenant occupied the unit between January 2024, through to February 2024. The Tenant at some point refused to engage in further communications with K.C. 10. The Landlord attempted to inspect the unit on or about July 3, 2024, at which time the Landlord was greeted at the door by the [name] who refused entry by the Landlord. 11. To date, the unit remains occupied by the [name]. I have no evidence to suggest that the Tenant has re-occupied the unit since February 18, 2024. 12. Based on the uncontested evidence of the Landlord, I am satisfied that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. 13. The Unauthorized [name] was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. 14. The application was not filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. The Landlord is exempt under section 7(1) of the Act. This means that the time frame permitted in section 100(2) does not apply to the Landlord. Daily Compensation 15. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized [name]. 16. The Unauthorized [name] owes the Landlord $48,279.72 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from April 18, 2024, to the May 21, 2026. 17. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $65.26. This amount is calculated as follows: $1985.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 18. Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized [name], the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized [name] paid the Landlord $1,579.12 in compensation for use of the rental unit. 19. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations 20. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized [name] shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 14, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 14, 2026, then starting June 15, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 15, 2026.

The Unauthorized [name] shall pay to the Landlord $48,279.72 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from April 18, 2024, to the May 21, 2026. This amount accounts for any payments made by the Tenant or Unauthorized [name].
The Unauthorized [name] shall also pay to the Landlord $65.26 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from May 22, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized [name] shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized [name] shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 14, 2026.

If the Unauthorized [name] does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 14, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 15, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ltd. (the ‘Landlord’) applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict the Tenant and [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy, and the claim for compensation in the application.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The monthly rent is $760.00 for the rental unit, a two bedroom house. The tenancy commenced in 2002.
The Landlord alleges that the Tenant has transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the unauthorized occupant, M. [name] (MB) without the Landlord’s consent.

The relationship between the parties has been a long-term one, and it is also complicated. A number of issues were raised by the Tenant with respect to this application. Among the issues to be addressed are the validity of the application pursuant to the time limitation period for filing it. That is, did the Landlord file this application within 60 days of first becoming aware of the transfer of the tenancy, in compliance with subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Also, if it is determined that the Landlord has proved their application, I must determine whether eviction should be denied pursuant to subsection 83(3) of the Act because the Landlord is either retaliating against the Tenant for asserting his legal rights, or because the Landlord is in serious breach because they have filed an application under section 100 of the Act, when in fact they are really seeking to sell the rental unit with vacant possession. [name]:
The Tenant was a founding Director of a medical marijuana company, which he took public. He said he retired five years ago.

The Landlord owns a row of four houses on the same street. It is undisputed that the Tenant has, on occasion, approached the Landlord’s agent, R. [name] (RJ), to secure a tenancy for one of his employees. It is undisputed that the Landlord named the Tenant as one of the parties in their application, LTB-L-080596-25, issued on December 10, 2025, and denied on review. That application involves a completely different rental unit, 152 Oxford Street, a neighbouring property to the rental unit. The Landlord’s agent, C. [name] (CJ) said that the Landlord knew that the Tenant never lived at that address, and that he was not a Tenant. She said that the Tenant was merely a guarantor for the actual Tenant of 152 Oxford Street, [name]. She said that the rent for that address always came from the Tenant, so that is why he was named on the application.

The Tenant did not dispute CJ’s evidence, nor did he allege that he was ever a valid Tenant at 152 Oxford Street. All the Tenant’s evidence was provided in the context of his being the Tenant of this rental unit, 146 Oxford Street.

It is undisputed that the tenancy at 146 Oxford Street commenced in 2002. CJ said, and it is undisputed, that the Tenant organized an authorized sublet of his rental unit from 2015 to 2023. However, CJ said that the Tenant returned to his unit in 2023. CJ and RJ do not live in any of the four houses in a row. They live outside London. CJ said that she and RJ began to suspect the Tenant was not living in the rental unit in 2024, and she started driving by the house a couple of times a week to see if his vehicle was there. She said that she never saw him, and when she texted him, he repeatedly answered that he was travelling, or he was on the west coast. CJ said that when she knocked on the door it was always MB who answered, and he said he was housesitting. She said that whenever she asked MB when the Tenant was returning, he provided vague answers.

CJ said that RJ had regular communication with the Tenant until May or June 2024. It was only after that date that they noticed they never saw him in person. They did not see him in person again. She said that they regularly reached out to him after that, and they would get a text reply like “on west coast”, “no call service”, “on the road”. CJ said that she tried a key test in June 2024, and the Landlord’s key did not work. After contacting the Tenant about it, CJ said that it was MB who gave them a valid key. CJ said that she did not know MB, except as the person who answered the door and gave the Landlord a key, and she did not even know his last name until the hearing date when he checked into the hearing.

CJ said that the Landlord wrote in the application August 6, 2025, as the date they first became aware of an unauthorized transfer of the tenancy because that was when they became certain that the Tenant was no longer living there. She said that prior to that date the Tenant repeatedly said he was away temporarily, or MB said that he was “housesitting”. However, she said that they never saw him in person after the summer of 2024, and MB had attempted to pay the rent in his own name and when the Landlord refused to take it from him, the Tenant paid it by etransfer. CJ said that even since they filed the application, on January 15, 2026, they received a call from MB in which he said that the Tenant was still away, but he had maintenance issue with the furnace.
CJ said that the Tenant responded to a call from RJ in October 2025, in which they agreed that the Tenant would vacate the rental unit by March 31, 2026.
RJ said that when he went to repair the furnace in January 2026, he asked MB when the Tenant was returning, and MB just replied “shortly”.

The Tenant said that he sublet the unit for eight years, during the period he was building a new house and living with his wife. He admits that he has, at times, secured tenancies for his employees in the four houses owned by the Landlord. However, he said that he has always, throughout the tenancy, spent lengthy periods travelling. He said that he does not travel for business, but he has competent managers that have been able to manage his business while he is away travelling.

The Tenant said that he has not stayed in the rental unit since November 2024, but he said that RJ and CJ knew that he would not be there. He said that he informed them he bought a property in Belize in 2023, and he would be spending half the year there, and half the year living in the rental unit. He said that his safety has been in jeopardy for the last two years because of his ex-wife, and he explained to RJ and CJ that he would not be living in his unit while he was still receiving threats from her.

The Tenant said that he did not ask for authorization from the Landlord to establish MB in the rental unit, but he assumed the Landlord consented to MB’s presence. He said that they knew MB was living in the unit. He said that he never asked the Landlord’s permission to sublet to MB, nor to transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to MB.

The Tenant said that he is waiting until all his divorce proceedings are final to return to the rental unit, and he did not believe he had to inform the Landlord about his intentions. He said that he has sublet before, and that was “on a handshake”. He said that he believed while the Landlord was aware that MB was living in the unit, that both parties were in agreement about it. Reasons and Analysis: Did the Tenant Transfer Occupancy of the Rental Unit:
For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to an unauthorized occupant without the Landlord’s consent.

It is undisputed that the Tenant has not lived in the rental unit, he has not stayed over night or visited it, since at least June 2024. It is undisputed that MB has lived in the rental unit since that time, and MB is paying rent to the Tenant. The Tenant never informed the Landlord that MB was going to be living in the rental unit. His own evidence is that he assumed the Landlord consented to MB’s occupancy merely because they knew about it. However, it was the uncontested evidence of the Landlord that when MB attempted to pay rent in his own name, they did not accept it, and the Tenant resumed payment of the monthly rent.
The Tenant did not provide a date of return to living in the rental unit to the Landlord for the last two years, nor did he provide a definite date of return at the hearing.

Both parties agree that the Tenant has sublet the rental unit in the past, with authorization and consent of the Landlord. Both parties agree that the Tenant never received authorization nor consent from the Landlord to sublet to MB.

I find based on the above disclosed circumstances, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant has not had a substantial connection to the rental unit for almost two years, nor has he had possession or control of the unit. His unauthorized occupant MB has even unilaterally attempted to change the locks of the rental unit. The Tenant has not stayed in the rental unit, nor has he visited or been present in the rental unit for almost two years. There is no credible evidence that the Tenant will return to the rental unit at any time in the near future, and there is no proposed date for the return.

Consequently, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the unauthorized occupant, MB. The Landlord did not consent to this transfer, and in fact, they directly objected to it when they refused to take the rent from MB. Did Landlord file the application within 60 days of first becoming aware of the transfer:

Ultimately, the Tenant does not admit that he transferred the tenancy, so it becomes important when and why the Landlord chose the date of August 6, 2025, as the date of first becoming aware of the unauthorized transfer.

CJ admits that the Landlord began to suspect the Tenant was not living in the rental unit by June of 2024. She made some unscheduled visits to the area, and she never saw the Tenant in person after that date. The Landlord received repeated texts from the Tenant saying that he was away, he was travelling, or he was on the west coast. The Tenant said that the Landlord knew he frequently travelled, and that the Landlord knew he spent lots of time at his house in Belize. If the Landlord had, in fact, been aware of the Tenant’s frequent stays in Belize, then it is, at the least, puzzling that his reply texts would constantly mention the west coast or travelling. Consequently, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence over the Tenant’s with respect to what the Landlord knew, or did not know, about the Tenant’s whereabouts. They said that the Tenant was always away, gave vague replies about where he was, someone else was living in his unit, and he also failed to provide any definite dates of return for over a year.

Although a year is a long time for the Landlord to hold a suspicion without acting, I do not find that it is unreasonable for the Landlord to hold the suspicion for a lengthy time without acting, given the relationship between the parties. The Landlord’s agents did not live on the street or even nearby, so they were not in a position to observe the rental unit on a daily or regular basis. In 2024 their belief of the Tenant’s departure from the unit was only a suspicion. The parties had a long term relationship, the Landlord had agreed to let properties to the Tenant’s employees before, the Tenant had usually honoured his position of guarantor of those employees, both parties had acted in good faith in a previous sublet relationship, the rent was getting paid, and the Landlord had not observed any damage to the rental unit. Therefore, it was not unreasonable of the Landlord to give the Tenant the benefit of a doubt for a period of a year when the Tenant consistently said he was planning to return.

Consequently, I find that it was not unreasonable of the Landlord to choose the date of August 6, 2025, as the date of first becoming certain that the tenancy had been transferred to an unauthorized occupant. They filed the application on the same date, and the application was therefore filed within 60 days of the Landlord first becoming aware of the transfer. Section 83 Considerations:
The Tenant raised a couple of issues that, if determined to be proven, would prohibit me from issuing an order for eviction.

The parties have been before the Board for a couple of matters in the past. In particular, there was [name] application launched by the Tenant, LTB-T-097258-23, in which the parties had a dispute about vacant land located behind the rental unit. The Tenant alleged that the Landlord was substantially interfering with his exclusive right to access to the land because the Landlord permitted access to it to residents from their other properties on the same street. That application was dismissed in order LTB-T-097258-23 issued on November 28, 2024. There was no review request from the Tenant.

There was also a more recent L1 application, mentioned above, for rent arrears for 152 Oxford Street. There was an attempted review of that order, LTB-L-080596-25 issued on December 10, 2025, but the review request was denied in LTB-L-080596-25-RV issued on January 14, 2026. While the Tenant’s name was on the application as a Tenant, the review request had nothing to do with [name] being named as a Tenant. In fact, the review request was filed by the other named [name]. I have found above that neither of the parties in this application has ever considered [name] a lawful Tenant of 152 Oxford Street. He was only ever a guarantor of the rent at that unit. It is impossible to know why [name] did not file the review request for that order, but there is no documentary evidence to indicate that he objected to the order, or that he attempted to review the order, which was simply an order for rent arrears. In any case, that application was filed on September 18, 2025, over a month after this application was filed. The N4 notice for that application was served on September 2, 2025, about three weeks after this application was filed. Therefore, the filing of this application could not have been in retaliation for this application.

With respect to the earlier T3/T2 application, the order dismissing the Tenant’s application was issued almost a year prior to filing this application. The fact that the Landlord then waited almost a year to file this application, as well as the fact that the Landlord, in effect, prevailed in the Tenant’s application, leads me to find, on a balance of probabilities, that this application is not retaliatory with regard to the Tenant’s application. In fact, the Landlord waiting another year, giving the Tenant the benefit of a doubt with respect to returning to his rental unit before deciding the date that they were certain that the Tenant had transferred his tenancy, all point to the Landlord’s attempt to not be retaliatory in their filing of this application.

Finally, there was the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord filed this application in bad faith because their true intention is to evict the Tenant so that they can sell the four houses in a row as their “retirement plan”. The Tenant said that the Landlord asked him to leave by March 31, 2026, because they had a tentative sale of all four houses. He had no documentary evidence to support this allegation, and the Landlord’s agents categorically denied that they want to evict the Tenant in order to sell all four houses together.

I find that the Tenant has failed to establish that the Landlord filed this application in bad faith because the true intention is to evict him and sell all four houses together. There was no documentary evidence to support the allegation, and the Landlord’s agents denied it. There was no evidence to support an allegation that the other three houses are either vacant, up for sale, or that any of the other tenants have been issued with notices of termination.
Based on the above, I find that the Landlord is not in serious breach of the Act as defined in subsection 83(3) of the Act, and it is open to me to issue an order for eviction.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act, and I find, for the following reasons, that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. The Tenant is no longer living in the rental unit, and he has not lived there for almost two years, so there is no prejudice to him in terminating the tenancy. However, I find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until July 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. The unauthorized occupant MB has now been living in the rental unit for almost two years, there are no arrears of rent, and there was no alleged damage to the unit. While the Landlord has no obligation to accept MB as an authorized tenant, the Landlord did not disclose any urgent reason to regain possession of the unit from MB immediately. Consequently, I find that it is not unfair to provide MB with a bit more time to find an alternative place to live.
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by [name].
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $24.98. This amount is calculated as follows: $760.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

There was no evidence provided to me to prove that there are any arrears of rent. The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant will owe the Landlord daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period commencing August 1, 2026.
The Landlord incurred a cost of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
I find that both the Tenant and the unauthorized occupant, [name], are jointly liable for the daily compensation and the filing fee.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of July 31, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant Marck [name] shall vacate the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated on or before July 31, 2026, then starting August 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord on or after August 1, 2026.

If the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant [name] do not vacate the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026, they shall jointly owe the Landlord daily compensation of $24.98 for the use of the rental unit commencing August 1, 2026, until they vacate the unit.
The Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name], shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name], do not pay the Landlord the full amount on or before July 31, 2026, they will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies. [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-075706-25, LTB-T-056756-25-IN3 issued on February 4, 2026. On March 5, 2026, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On March 9, 2026, interim order LTB-L-075706-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on February 4, 2026. The review request was heard by videoconference on April 16, 2026. The Landlords, the Landlords’ Agent Spinghar [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s Legal Representative Vidy Matadeen attended the hearing. Although I find that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') does not apply, for ease of reference the parties are referred to as “Landlord” and “Tenant” for the purpose of this order.
reasons: In order LTB-L-075706-25 issued on February 4, 2025, the Member found that the Landlord resided in the residential complex prior to, and throughout the time that the Tenant resided there. The parties were required to share the kitchen. However, the Member found that the exemption under section 5(i) of the Act did not apply because the Landlord did not communicate to the Tenant that she resided there. The Member referenced [name] v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628, in the decision.

The Landlord’s Agent submitted that the Member misinterpreted the Act, adding an additional element of communication to the exemption under 5(i). The Landlord’s Agent also submitted that the Member misapplied Cowie, as it does not require advance communication. The Landlord’s Agent argued that, since the Landlord proved that she resided at the residential complex at all times of the Tenant’s occupancy and they shared a kitchen, the Act does not apply.

The Tenant’s Representative took the opposing position, submitting that the order did not contain a serious error. The Representative submitted that the Member thoroughly reviewed the evidence, the parties had a fair opportunity to participate, and the order contained sufficient reasons for the decision.
Section 5(i) of the Act does not require advance communication of the arrangement to the occupant. It states:

This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 5. Cowie does not add a communication requirement either. In Cowie, the tenant rented a room in a house with a shared kitchen and bathroom. The landlord moved in after the tenancy started. The Divisional Court found that the landlord could not unilaterally change the nature of the tenancy without communicating this to the tenant.

The facts of the current case differ, as the Member determined that the Landlord resided at the residential complex before and during the Tenant’s occupancy. Therefore, there was no change that needed to be communicated. The parties were required to share the kitchen from the beginning.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Member misapplied the Act and [name] by adding a requirement of advance communication to the test under section 5(i). This is a serious error, and the review request is granted.

However, I find no error in the remainder of the order determining that the Landlord resided in the house. The Member gave extensive reasons for her determinations, referencing both parties’ evidence. I am satisfied that the Member considered the parties’ evidence and submissions when making her determinations. The Member’s findings are therefore reasonable and entitled to deference. Therefore, I do not find it necessary for the entirety of the application to be re-heard. The order will be amended.
Given that the Act does not apply to these parties, the Tenant is not entitled to file an application to the Board. Therefore, application LTB-T-056756-25 must be dismissed.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-L-075706-25, LTB-T-056756-25-IN3 issued on February 4, 2026, is granted. The order is amended as follows.
The interim order issued on March 9, 2026, is cancelled.
The Act does not apply.
The Tenant’s application, LTB-T-056756-25, is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons below, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. Background:

The Landlord. X. [name] (XC) said that the Tenant rented the rental unit, a house, in their name only. She submitted into evidence the lease agreement between the Landlords and the Tenant, which commenced on August 1, 2023. The monthly rent was $4,000.00, due on the first of each month.

XC said that the Tenant informed her that they would move out in July 2025, but they nevertheless remained in the unit until September 2, 2025. It was on that date that the Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord by placing them in a lockbox.

XC said that she went to the house on September 2, 2025, and she knocked on all the doors to ensure that the house was empty. However, she said that she found a person living in the house who said she was going to call the police. The person did not explain to XC why she was there, and XC left.

XC said that she called the Tenant the next day and asked her about the person living in the house. XC said that the Tenant told her that she let a room to the person, and that person did not want to leave when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. [name] said that the Tenant also told her that the person living in the house was not paying her rent, and that is why the Tenant vacated. XC said that the Tenant never asked for any permission or authorization to let the room, sublet the tenancy or transfer the tenancy.

XC said that she has received no rent since September 2, 2025. She said that she was informed by the Tenant that the unauthorized person is [name] [name] [name]. XC said that she saw, on camera, the unauthorized occupant vacate the rental unit on January 28, 2026.
XC said that the Tenant was only living in one of the two bedrooms in the house, so she is only seeking half the rent for the period from September 2, 2025 to January 28, 2026.
The application was filed on September 4, 2025, and therefore it was filed within 60 days after the Landlords discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Reasons and Analysis:

As stated above, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the unauthorized occupant, [name] [name] [name], without the consent of the Landlords. It is the uncontested evidence of the Landlord that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 2, 2025, but her roommate did not. The roommate was not a Tenant, nor was she an authorized occupant. The Tenant did not ask permission to have an occupant, nor to transfer the tenancy to that occupant. The Landlord came to the house to find the Tenant’s roommate living in the unit, and the Tenant’s roommate refused to leave. Instead, the roommate called the police. The Tenant’s roommate, or unauthorized occupant remained, living in the rental unit, for a further five months. The unauthorized occupant vacated the rental unit on January 28, 2026, without paying any rent to the Landlords. Daily Compensation
The Landlords are entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The tenancy and unauthorized occupancy terminated on January 28, 2026, when the unauthorized occupant vacated the rental unit.

Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $131.51. This amount is calculated as follows: $4000.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. However, the Landlords are only requesting half the daily compensation, or $65.75 for the period September 2, 2025 through January 28, 2026.

The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant owe the Landlords 148 days of daily compensation, for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from September 2, 2025 to the January 28, 2026. The total amount owed is therefore $9,731.00.
Since the Landlords became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlords $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlords incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
I find that both the Tenant and the unauthorized occupant, [name] [name] [name], are jointly liable for the daily compensation and the filing fee.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenant is terminated as of January 28, 2026, when the Unauthorized Occupant, D.S. [name], vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] [name] [name], shall pay to the Landlords $9,932.00 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from September 2, 2025 to the January 28, 2026.
The Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] [name] [name], shall also pay the Landlords $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] [name] [name], shall pay the Landlords the full amount owing by June 28, 2026.

If the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] [name] [name], do not pay the Landlords the full amount owing by June 28, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ltd (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. [name]:

The Landlord made a clerical error on their application. They inadvertently wrote that they first became aware of the unauthorized occupant on August 26, 2024, when the correct date was actually on August 26, 2025. They submitted into evidence the email from T. [name] (TK), dated August 26, 2025, that alerted them to her occupancy. The Landlord filed their A2 application on September 18, 2025. Based on the documentary evidence, I find that the Landlord made a clerical error, and it was August 26, 2025 when they first became aware of TK’s unauthorized occupancy. The application is accordingly amended.

Most of the background is undisputed. The tenancy commenced in 1989 with L. [name] (LK) listed as the Tenant. She named two children as her occupants. One of the occupants listed was TK, her daughter. TK has lived in the rental unit with her mother for most of her life, and she was an occupant of the rental unit. TK sent the Landlord an email on August 26, 2025, informing the Landlord that LK passed away in November 2024. She also said that she continues to live in the apartment, and she has been paying the rent. TK ended the email, writing “Also, do I need to provide you with further information? Please let me know and thank you very much!” She said that she believed everything was fine after sending the email, and she could remain in the unit.

The Landlord’s agent, [name] (MA), said that when the Landlord received the email, it was only then that the Landlord became aware that the Tenant had passed away, and that the Tenant’s daughter was an unauthorized occupant of the rental unit. [name] said that after they received the email the Landlord request documentation of LK’s passing. She submitted into evidence a death certificate for LK, stating that she passed away on November 23, 2024. 5. [name] said that the Landlord was unaware of LK’s passing before that email of August 2025, and that LK never requested a transfer of tenancy to her daughter TK. She said that TK has been paying the rent to date. The rent is $979.32 since January 2026. [name] said that the Landlord did not discuss the tenancy any further with TK. 6. TK said that the Landlord was aware of her mother’s passing because she had posted an announcement about it in the building. TK did not disclose this document as evidence. TK said that she has lived in the residential complex since she was born. 7. TK said that she is an early childhood educator with an annual income of approximately $45,000.00 after tax. She said that she has a very limited budget for rent. She said that she is still taking care of her mother’s debts. TK said that she wants to remain in the unit because she has nowhere else to go. 8. The Landlord submits that pursuant to subsection 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the tenancy terminated on December 27, 2024, 30 days after the death of the tenant. They submit that TK is an overholding unauthorized occupant, the Landlord never provided authorization to LK to transfer her tenancy to TK. The Landlord said that they are willing to waive the filing fee, but the last month’s rent deposit belongs to LK’s estate. Reasons and Analysis: 9. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person for the reasons that follow. 10. TK is listed as an occupant on the lease, and it is undisputed that LK never requested an authorized transfer of the tenancy to TK prior to her passing. LK passed away on November 28, 2024, and the tenancy terminated on December 27, 2024, by virtue of subsection 91(1) of the Act. Although the definition of “Tenant” in section 2(1) of the Act includes “heirs, assigns and personal representatives”, that definition of “tenant” does not include the transfer of the physical right to live in the unit. That fact is made quite clear in the wording of section 91, that is, that the tenancy is deemed terminated 30 days after the death of the Tenant. The Landlord never provided authorization for TK to become the Tenant in lieu of her mother, and TK’s occupancy in the unit is not authorized by the Landlord. There is no credible documentary evidence to support TK’s contention that she informed the Landlord of LK’s passing earlier than August 2025. The Landlord has the right to evict TK as a result of the unauthorized transfer of occupancy. 11. The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. 12. The Landlord became aware of the unauthorized transfer on August 26, 2025, and the application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Daily Compensation 13. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. The unauthorized occupant, TK, has paid the rent to the date of the hearing. She will be ordered to pay compensation from the date of the hearing to the date TK vacates the rental unit. 14. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $32.20. This amount is calculated as follows: $979.32.18 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 15. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and they are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The Landlord said that they waive the filing fee. 16. The Landlord is holding $555.00 last month’s rent deposit on behalf of the Tenant. This was collected November 21, 1989, right before the tenancy commenced. No interest has been paid on the deposit. 17. The last month’s rent deposit, and any interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit, is owed to the Tenant’s Estate. Section 83 Considerations 18. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until June 30, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act, for the reasons that follow. TK has lived in the rental unit since 1989, and she has lived in the residential complex for all her life. It is home to her. Although she is earning a sufficient income to pay more rent elsewhere, I find that it is not unfair to provide her with more time to find an alternative place to live. TK was informed at the hearing on March 24, 2026, that the Landlord was entitled to evict her because of the unauthorized transfer of tenancy, and her overholding on the tenancy long after her mother had passed away. Therefore, she has had since then to begin looking for another place to live, almost three months. I find that it is not unfair to give her a bit more time, to the end of this month, to ensure that she finds a suitable alternative place to live.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 30, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 30, 2026, then starting July 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 1, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $32.20 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from March 25, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord any amounts still owed by June 19, 2026.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant’s Estate the last month’s rent deposit of $555.00 still being held, plus any interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 19, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 8, 2026 ____________________________
