issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. The unauthorized occupant said that her last name is Gelfand. The name of the unauthorized occupant was amended accordingly.
reasons: The tenancy with the deceased, D. [name] (DF), began on May 1, 2017. Her daughter, M. Gelfand (MG) is a registered occupant of the unit. It is undisputed that the Landlord was aware that MG was living in the unit with her mother.
MG moved to dismiss the application because the Landlord misspelled her name.

I find that it is appropriate to amend the application to correctly spell the name of M. Gelfand, the unauthorized occupant, pursuant to subsection 201(1)(f) of the Act. It is not prejudicial to correctly spell the name of the unauthorized occupant. I also find that it is not unfair to any party to this application to amend the name of the unauthorized occupant, for the following reasons. It is undisputed that MG is the current occupant of the rental unit, she received the notice of hearing, and she attended the hearing to present evidence. She is the acknowledged occupant of the unit, and she knew about the hearing despite any clerical error in the spelling of her last name.
The monthly rent is $1,154.84 as of February 1, 2026. There is a last month’s rent deposit of $1,143.68, with interest paid to January 31, 2026.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] (TS), said that the Landlord became aware on August 25, 2025, that DF had passed away. TS submitted into evidence a letter dated August 26, 2025, from the Landlord to MF, advising her that since [name] passed away on August 15, 2025, the tenancy was to be terminated on September 14, 2025, pursuant to section 91 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). MG was informed that if she wished to remain in the unit, she was obliged to apply for a new tenancy at market rent. The letter also informed MG that since the tenancy was terminated, any payments past September 14, 2025, “are considered on a per diem basis and are not to be accepted as ongoing rental payments or considered the start of a new tenancy.”

TS said that rent was last paid on September 1, 2025. There have been no payments since that time. He also said that MG did not respond to the letter of August 26, 2025. TS said that the Landlord wrote in the A2 application that they first became aware that there was an unauthorized transfer of occupancy on September 14, 2025, because they were only seeking rent payment to that date.

MG said that she has lived in the unit for six years, she is still living in the rental unit, and she said that she has nowhere else to go. She said she was recently diagnosed with cancer. She said that she tried to negotiate to take over the lease and correct her name. She said that the Landlord told her they would get back to her, and they never did. MG said that she has the money set aside to pay the rent arrears owed. She said that she has no source of income other than an inheritance from her mother that amounts to one third of a million dollars. She said that she intends to apply for Ontario Works.

The Landlord submits that the unauthorized occupant MG should be evicted. They submit that [name] was at the hearing, and she had a reasonable opportunity to participate. They also submit that MG was given a number of months, prior to the hearing, to apply to be a lawful Tenant, and she did not. They submit that MG had sufficient funds to pay the rent and the arrears, but she did not pay it.
The Tenant submits that she would like to remain in the unit. She submits that she has imminent surgery for cancer, and she should be able to stay until her recovery. Reasons and Analysis:

For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to [name] Gelfand, the Unauthorized Occupant, in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

It is undisputed that the Tenant passed away on August 15, 2025. Pursuant to section 91 of the Act, the tenancy was deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the Tenant. MG was a registered occupant who lived in the rental unit, and she was informed, as of August 26, 2025, about the implications of section 91 of the Act. The Landlord was aware that MG lived in the unit, and they gave her almost three weeks to apply for a valid tenancy if she wished to remain in the unit. She failed to do so.

MG not only remained in the rental unit after she was informed that the tenancy lawfully terminated pursuant to the Act, but she chose not to apply for a new tenancy, and she failed to pay any rent after August 2025. Although MG said that she tried to negotiate with the Landlord, and the Landlord failed to respond, there was no documentary evidence of this. There is no right for a child to “inherit” the tenancy of a parent. The Landlord was within their rights to terminate the tenancy on September 14, 2025.

It is undisputed that the Landlord was aware that MG was living in the unit. However, it was not until after September 14, 2025, that the Landlord could possibly be aware that MG was an “unauthorized occupant” as described in section 100 of the Act. The tenancy with the deceased [name] continued until September 14, 2025, and the Landlord correctly informed MG that she had until that date to vacate. It was only after MG failed to vacate by September 14, 2025, that the Landlord became aware that MG was an unauthorized occupant within the meaning of section 100 of the Act. The Landlord filed the application on September 19, 2025. Therefore, I find that the Landlord filed the application within 60 days of becoming first aware of the unauthorized transfer, in compliance with subsection 100(2) of the Act.

The rent increased to $1,154.84 on February 1, 2026, and there are seven months of unpaid rent to the date of the hearing. The arrears are $7,965.18 to March 31, 2026, and that is what the Landlord requests. This is slightly less than the amount arrived at for a per diem rate, and it is therefore not prejudicial to MG to grant the Landlord’s request for this amount, rather than a per diem rate. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $37.97. This amount is calculated as follows: $1154.84 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
I find that [name] and the Unauthorized Occupant are jointly liable for the arrears, the filing fee and the daily compensation. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act, for the following reasons. The unauthorized occupant MG was informed about the law by the Landlord as of August 26, 2025. She had a number of weeks prior to the Landlord’s stated vacating date to find out her rights. She failed to vacate the rental unit, failed to pay rent, and then failed to learn about her legal rights for the next six months, up to the date of the hearing. She also had that amount of time to either negotiate a new lease with the Landlord or vacate, and she did neither. The arrears are now close to $8,000.00, and I find that it is prejudicial to the Landlord for MG to remain in the unit. However, MG has lived in the rental unit for over six years, and she is currently getting treatment for a terminal illness. Therefore, I find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until August 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by July 31, 2026, then starting August 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after August 1, 2026.
The [name] of the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $7,965.18 which represents compensation for the use of the rental unit from September 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $37.97 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from April 1, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The [name] of the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlord shall deduct the last month’s rent deposit $1,143.68, as well as any interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit from the amount owing by the [name] of the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant.
The [name] of the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the [name] of the Tenant or the Unauthorized Occupant do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-085939-25 issued on March 13, 2026 pursuant to a hearing of the Landlord’s A2 application at which only the Landlord attended. On April 8, 2026, [name], who identifies themselves as one of the previously unidentified occupants of the rental unit (the ‘Occupant’) requested a review of that order. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-085939-25-RV issued on June 12, 2026 pursuant to a hearing at which only the Landlord attended. On June 25, 2026, the [name] requested a review. The request to review refers to order [name] issued on April 14, 2025. No such order has been issued by the Board, as will be discussed below. A preliminary review of the review request was completed without a hearing.
reasons: This is the second review request by the Occupant to review an order filed in these proceedings. The original order for this matter was issued March 13, 2026. The Occupant requested a review of that order on April 8, 2026. The Occupant’s review request was denied pursuant to order LTB-L-085939-25-RV on June 12, 2026.

The request states it is a request to review order LTB-L-085939-25 issued on April 14, 2026. The only order issued on that date in relation to this matter was order LTB-L- 085939-25-IN. This was the interim order directing the previous review request to a hearing and staying the original hearing order until that hearing. This order does not make a final determination of a party’s rights and so is not subject to review in accordance with Rule 26.1.

Given the above, it is somewhat unclear as to whether the Tenant was attempting to again review order LTB-L-085939-25 issued on March 13, 2026 or instead review LTB-L- 085939-25-RV issued on June 12, 2026.
Rule 26.18 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure provides as follows: The LTB will not consider a further request to review the same order or to review the review order from the same requesting party.

Regardless of which order the [name] intended to be subject to this request to review, this request constitutes either a further request to review the same order from the same requesting party or a request to review the review order from the same requesting party.

Rule A4.2 permits the Board to waive the application of any rule. The Board will only do so in extraordinary circumstances. The circumstances in this case are not sufficiently extraordinary to warrant waiving Rule 26.18.
For the reasons above, the Board will not consider the [name]’s request to review, regardless of which order in relation to this application it was intended to relate to.
ordered: The request for review filed by the Occupant on June 25, 2026 is denied. All orders issued to date in respect of application LTB-L-085939-25 are confirmed and remain unchanged. June 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Properties (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] [name] [name] [name] [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons below, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

In this order, the Tenant’s daughter, [name] [name], is referred to as the “unauthorized occupant” within the meaning of section 100 of the Act. It is undisputed that [name] [name] is an authorized occupant of the rental unit pursuant to the lease with the named Tenant. Background:

Most of the facts in this matter are largely undisputed. The Tenant moved into the rental unit with her three daughters, [name] (the unauthorized occupant), [name] and Sama, and her son Yusuf, in 2018. At the beginning of the tenancy the Tenant’s children were, and they still are, named authorized occupants of the rental unit. The Tenant said that her husband never lived in the unit. He remained in Saudi Arabia to live and work, at all times, and he came to Canada for occasional visits. The monthly rent has been paid, and it continues to be paid monthly, by the Tenant.

The Landlord’s property manager, [name] (HF), said that the Landlord’s employees noted that there were a lot of notices piled up in front of the rental unit door in April-May 2025. HF submitted into evidence a series of correspondence between her and the Tenant in May-June 2025. At that time, the Tenant admits that she is out of the country, but she repeatedly informs the Landlord that it is for a temporary period. On June 10, 2025, she wrote to the Landlord “I would like to clarify that, due to exceptional circumstances, I am currently outside the country and expect to return within the next few months.” HF said that she understood this reply to mean that the Tenant would return some time in the summer of 2025.

HF said the Landlord was doing a number of upgrades to the building in the summer of 2025, and HF informed the Tenant, on June 2, 2025, that part of the upgrade process was to replace all locks and handles on each unit door as well as rekey the entry locks that access the building. HF wrote “[name] are being provided once request to only leaseholders for the unit.” HF said that the Tenant requested that her daughter [name] be permitted to pick up the new key. On June 11, 2025, HF replied that “unfortunately as advised by our lawyers the keys for the unit and building are only to be handed to the leaseholder or guarantor for the unit.”

It is undisputed that the Tenant never attended the residential complex to obtain new keys, and [name] (the “unauthorized occupant”) has never received a set of keys. It is also undisputed that the unauthorized occupant returned to the rental unit in the summer of 2025 and she was given access to the rental unit to get her belongings. It is undisputed that the unauthorized occupant has been living in the unit since that time, without a set of keys. The unauthorized occupant testified that she still lives in the rental unit. She said that she gets into the building by buzzing her neighbours on the intercom, and she leaves the front door unlocked when she leaves the unit.

The Tenant challenged the validity of the application, filed on October 10, 2025, pursuant to subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), alleging that it was not filed within 60 days of first becoming aware that the tenancy had been transferred.

In response to the Tenant’s challenge to the application based on subsection 100(2) of the Act, HF said that the Tenant kept changing her time of return. In the earliest communications, the Tenant said she would return in June 2025. Then, as seen above in the Tenant’s communication of June 10, 2025, she said she would return in the next “few months”. HF said that it was the Tenant’s email of September 29, 2025, that triggered the application, and it was the date upon which the Landlord became certain that the Tenant had transferred the tenancy, and the Tenant was not returning. In that email of September 29, 2025, the Tenant reiterated her request that the Landlord provide keys to the unauthorized occupant. She wrote, “…my daughter [name] [name] is residing in the unit with my full authorization as leaseholder…. While I understand your request for in-person attendance, I have made it clear that I am currently based in Saudi Arabia and am unable to attend your office in person…..” She also requested that the intercom ring be changed to the phone number of the unauthorized occupant.

The Tenant said that her trip to Saudi Arabia was necessitated by “family circumstances”. She said that she went to visit her husband and family. She said that her husband never lived in the rental unit, but he visited them in Canada. The Tenant testified that the reason she moved with her daughters to Canda was to permit them an opportunity to study here. The Tenant said that in 2025 she remained longer in Saudi Arabia than originally intended, because her mother-in-law was sick and then subsequently passed away. She said that her father-in-law also passed away in this time and she could not leave her husband alone. The Tenant said that she does not hold a rental lease for a unit in Saudi Arabia, she is currently staying with her husband in his house. She said that her home is in Canada, she pays the rent, and she still has belongings in Canada. The Tenant said that she did not transfer the occupancy to her daughter, but her daughter is permitted to remain in the unit as an authorized occupant. The Tenant’s other two daughters remain with her in Saudi Arabia. The Tenant said that the unauthorized occupant returned to Canada because she was continuing her studies.

The Tenant said that she has not yet returned to Canada because she could not find a good flight for all of the family, and she wants them all to return together. At the time of the hearing, there were travel restrictions in the middle east. Those restrictions began at the end of February 2026. The Tenant also said that her son [name] has various health conditions, and he is being treated in a hospital-run program in Saudi Arabia. He is also very attached to his father. The Tenant said that all the children who are with her in Saudi Arabia, are enrolled in schools there.

The unauthorized occupant said that she returned to Canada alone because she had a semester to finish, and she has now graduated. She said that she works as a booking coordinator for a language school for 20-25 hours per week at an hourly wage of $19.60. She said that she intends to keep this job temporarily, until she can find something in her field of computer science. The unauthorized occupant said that her father visited them about two or three times per year before 2025. She said that her sister [name] undertook about a year of university in London, but she transferred to Egypt, and is now studying in Saudi Arabia. She said that her sister Sama finished high school in London but then left to live with her father. The unauthorized occupant said that her mother was studying English and then early childhood education when she first came to Canada, but she completed those studies in the early 2020’s.

The Landlord submits that the Tenant repeatedly informed the Landlord that she was returning to the rental unit, and they believed that for many months. However, on September 29, 2025, the Landlord submits that it became apparent that the Tenant had transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the unauthorized occupant without the consent of the Landlord, and that the Tenant is now living in Saudi Arabia with her husband and three of her children.

The Tenant submits that [name] has been an authorized occupant since the beginning of the tenancy. They also submit that the Tenant is planning to return, and she fully intends to continue to reside in her home in Canada. She has continued to pay monthly rent, and she has left all her belongings in the rental unit. The Tenant submits that the unauthorized occupant is authorized to have a key to the unit, and it is not safe for her to continue to live there and leave the door unlocked. The Tenant submits that some of her children are enrolled in schools in Saudi Arabia, but that is the norm when someone is temporarily living away from home. The Tenant submits that the Landlord is merely attempting to evict the family from their home to which they fully intend to return. Reasons and Analysis:

I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') for the following reasons.

It is undisputed that the authorized leaseholder, the Tenant, left the rental unit almost a year prior to the hearing date, and she has not been back to it. The Tenant testified that she intends to return, but she said the same thing to the Landlord in the early summer of 2025, and then her return date kept changing. The Tenant testified that there were family circumstances that kept her there, but she provided no documentation of these, and no exact dates of any of the family illnesses or deaths. On the other hand, it was the Tenant’s own evidence that she has three of her four children living with her in Saudi Arabia, and the children are enrolled in schools locally. The Tenant’s son [name] is enrolled in health/medical programmes in Saudi Arabia, and it was the Tenant and [name]’s evidence that Yusuf, and at least one of the Tenant’s daughters, want to remain in Saudi Arabia with their father. It is undisputed that Canada has never been a home for the Tenant’s husband. Since 2018 the Tenant’s husband has lived and worked in Saudi Arabia.

It was also the testimony of the unauthorized occupant, as well as the Tenant, that the family moved to Canada for educational opportunities. It is also their testimony that all of them have finished their intended education in Canada, or they wish to continue their education in Saudi Arabia. Only the unauthorized occupant returned to Canada to finish her studies, and it is only she who appears to want to remain in Canada to work.

With respect to filing the application within 60 days of becoming aware of the transfer of occupancy, I find that it was wholly reasonable of the Landlord to believe the Tenant’s own words that she was returning to the rental unit. They gave her the benefit of the doubt after she had been a Tenant for almost seven years. Even though the Tenant kept pushing back the date of return, there was no reason for the Landlord to doubt that the Tenant was taking a lengthy trip back to her home country. It was only when the Tenant repeatedly insisted on the Landlord providing keys to her daughter, and perhaps more significantly, asked the Landlord to change the intercom code to her daughter’s number, that the Landlord became convinced that the occupancy had been transferred. Perhaps the most conclusive words in the Tenant’s email of September 29, 2025, were “I have made it clear that I am currently based in Saudi Arabia and am unable to attend your office in person.” That was when the Landlord reasonably concluded that the Tenant had been gone at least six months and she was not coming back.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord has complied with the time requirements of subsection 100(2) of the Act. They filed their application on October 10, 2025, only 12 days after first becoming fully aware that the tenancy had been transferred to the unauthorized occupant.

The Landlord cited the case of [name]. Mgt. Ltd. [name] (2002), 164 O.A.C. 220 (CA) (‘[name]’). In Nicholson, the Ontario Court of Appeal, upheld a Board decision that found that [name] had handed over the occupancy of his unit to two of his friends. Similar to this case, [name] left the unit to live in a different city with his wife and son. He provided occupancy to two of his friends, and they paid him rent. He testified that he stayed in the unit when his business took him to Toronto, and he still had some clothing and furniture in the unit. The decision turned on the Appeal Court’s understanding of “connection to the unit”. At Divisional Court, the court found that as long as [name] kept the unit ready for his use, and even if he used it from time to time, the “occupancy” had not been transferred. Overturning the Divisional Court decision, the Court of Appeal found that the Divisional Court based their determination on an erroneous interpretation of the decision in Toronto Transit Commission v. Toronto (City), [1969] 2. O.R. 637 (C.A.) (‘TTC’). The Court of Appeal found that not only had TTC been based on different, distinguishable, facts, (in particular, a unit in which there were no other occupants and no one to whom occupancy had been handed over), but the Divisional Court had also wrongly focused on whether [name] continued to occupy the unit, rather than whether he had transferred occupancy of it.

The Court of Appeal in Nicholson, at paragraph 20, noted “Thus, in this case, the question is whether Nicholson’s two friends were the recipients of a transfer of the occupancy of the unit even though Nicholson at times slept overnight there. The objective and common sense answer to this question is “yes”.” The court noted, further, that of course while [name] was permitted to have a roommate without transferring occupancy of the unit, that is not what happened. [name] had a family and a home elsewhere. It was clear that [name] had moved elsewhere, to that home in another city with his family and he had handed over the rental unit to his two friends without the knowledge or consent of the Landlord. I find that the facts in this case are strikingly similar to Nicholson.

Unlike [name], the unauthorized occupant here was a named and known long-term occupant of the rental unit, who is not, to our knowledge, paying any rent to the Tenant. That is really the only major difference. However, I find that the one difference becomes irrelevant in light of all the striking similarities in the facts between the cases, and the other dissimilar factors that actually strengthen the case for there having been a transfer of occupancy. Similar facts are, that the Tenant left the rental unit to live in a completely different country, with her family, in her husband’s home. She has stated, in her own words, that she is “based” in that foreign home at present. A dissimilar factor, which in fact strengthens the case for there having been a transfer, is that the Tenant does not even stay in the rental unit occasionally, as she has not been back for even a temporary time in approximately a year. As opposed to Nicholson, the Tenant does not even purport to be staying in the unit occasionally. Rather, the Tenant states that she “intends” to return at some vague, unspecified time in the future. Those latter two dissimilar facts strengthen the case for a transfer of occupancy having taken place. Finally, the Tenant has, in her own words, admitted that there is a transfer of occupancy by insisting that the Landlord provide keys to the unauthorized occupant, and also that the Landlord transfer the entry number to the unauthorized occupant.

Therefore I, too, as in Nicholson, find that the unauthorized occupant is the recipient of the Tenant’s transfer of occupancy. The Tenant no longer has a connection to the unit, except as the mother of the unauthorized occupant, paying her daughter’s rent. The Tenant left the unit a year ago, she has not been back, she has no date of return. While it is true that it would have been difficult for the Tenant to return for the date of the hearing, she could have freely returned to Canada unimpeded in the 10 months since her departure, up to the end of February 2026. In any case, her constant changes to the date of return have rendered any testimony on this point lacking in credibility. The Tenant herself has said she is based in Saudi Arabia. All her actions point to having already made a transfer of her tenancy, that she now seeks to have the Landlord accept as a fait accompli.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant intended to transfer her occupancy of the rental unit to her daughter [name], the unauthorized occupant, who is the only one amongst her children who wish to remain and work in Canada. Continued payment of the rent by the Tenant does not prove, nor does it refute or rebut, my finding that she has transferred her occupancy to her daughter. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
It is undisputed that the Tenant is not in arrears of rent at the time of the hearing.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $49.53. This amount is calculated as follows: $1506.60 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and they are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Both the Tenant and the unauthorized occupant are jointly liable for this cost. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until July 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act for the following reasons. The Tenant was a long-term Tenant, she still has belongings in the unit, and the unauthorized occupant has lived in the unit since 2018. It is, for all intents and purposes, the home of the unauthorized occupant. The rent has been paid, and the Tenant is not in arrears. The unauthorized occupant is a recent graduate making a very limited income. Therefore, I find that it is not unfair to provide the unauthorized occupant a bit more time to find somewhere suitable to live, and to also provide time for the Tenant to find a way to retrieve any belongings remaining in the unit.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by July 31, 2026, then starting August 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after August 1, 2026.

If the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant do not vacate the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026, they shall also pay to the Landlord $49.53 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from August 1, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord clarified that the lawful Tenant named in the tenancy agreement is [name] and that the Unauthorized Occupant is the Tenant’s son, [name] (‘CJ’). The application, as filed, incorrectly identifies the Unauthorized Occupant as the Tenant and does not name the lawful Tenant.

The application also describes CJ as a subtenant. However, based on the evidence before me, there was no subtenancy. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 3, 2026 after providing notice to terminate the tenancy, while CJ remained in possession of the rental unit. There is no evidence that the Tenant retained a right to reoccupy the rental unit during the alleged subtenancy period, which is an essential element of a lawful sublet. Rather, the evidence supports a finding that CJ remained in possession of the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.

The Landlord testified that he seeks possession of the rental unit and the eviction of CJ. In these circumstances, I find that the application should be amended to correctly identify [name] as the Tenant, [name] as the Unauthorized Occupant, and to reflect that the proceeding concerns the occupancy of an unauthorized occupant rather than a subtenancy.

I am satisfied that these amendments do not alter the essential nature of the application or result in any prejudice to CJ. The allegations arise from the same facts set out in the application and relate to the Landlord’s claim that CJ remained in possession of the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.

The Unauthorized Occupant was served with the Notice of Hearing and had an opportunity to participate in the proceeding but chose not to attend. There is no evidence that the errors in the application affected CJ’s ability to understand the case against him or respond to it.
Accordingly, I find it appropriate and reasonable to amend the application to correctly identify the parties and to seek the eviction of CJ rather than the termination of a purported subtenancy.

The Landlord testified that, after being advised by the Tenant that he had vacated the rental unit, he attended the unit to conduct a move-out inspection, believing that all occupants had left. During the inspection, CJ approached him and stated that he did not believe his father was actually going to move out of the rental unit.

The Landlord's uncontested evidence is that CJ requested additional time to secure alternative accommodation. In response, the Landlord permitted CJ to remain in the rental unit for a period of four weeks as a temporary accommodation and advised him that he would be required to vacate so that the rental unit could be prepared for new tenants.

The Landlord testified that, at the conclusion of the four-week period on November 1, 2025, he attended the rental unit to discuss CJ's departure. At that time, there were no indications that CJ was preparing to vacate, and CJ refused to engage in any discussion regarding his occupancy of the rental unit.

The Landlord further testified that he attended the police station on November 3, 2025 to inquire about his legal rights with respect to the occupancy. The following day, he retained a locksmith to change the locks to the rental unit. The Landlord stated that he subsequently made numerous attempts to contact CJ and arrange for the retrieval of his belongings. According to the Landlord, the only response received from CJ was that the Landlord did not have the right to remove him from the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that CJ subsequently re-entered the rental unit through a window and later requested a key. The Landlord advised CJ that a replacement key could be provided if he attended to collect it; however, CJ never did so.

The Landlord testified that, apart from an amount paid in connection with the four-week extension, CJ made no payments to the Landlord for the right to occupy the rental unit and no rent was ever paid directly by CJ.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that CJ was an unauthorized occupant of the rental unit. The evidence establishes that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit and that CJ remained in possession thereafter without the Landlord's consent to occupy the unit on an ongoing basis.

While the Landlord permitted CJ to remain in the rental unit for an additional four-week period following the Tenant's departure, I do not find that this arrangement created a tenancy agreement between the Landlord and CJ. The Landlord's uncontested evidence was that the extension was intended solely as a temporary accommodation to allow CJ time to vacate. There is no evidence that the parties entered into an agreement creating a landlord-tenant relationship, nor is there evidence that the Landlord agreed to rent the unit to CJ on a continuing basis.

In reaching this conclusion, I have considered that the Landlord advised CJ that the rental unit would need to be prepared for new tenants, that the extension was for a fixed and limited duration, and that CJ made no rent payments to the Landlord in exchange for a right of occupancy. The conduct of the parties is inconsistent with the creation of a tenancy agreement and supports a finding that CJ's occupancy after the Tenant vacated was merely tolerated for a brief period as a temporary accommodation.
Accordingly, I find that CJ remained in possession of the rental unit as an unauthorized occupant and did not acquire any rights as a tenant under the Act.
The application was filed within 60 days of the Landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy by CJ.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 to file this application and is entitled to recover those costs. I find that the Unauthorized Occupant is responsible for reimbursing the Landlord for the application filing fee, as the Landlord was required to commence this proceeding in order to obtain an order evicting CJ and recovering possession of the rental unit. In the absence of the Unauthorized Occupant’s continued occupation of the rental unit after the Tenant had vacated, the application would not have been necessary.
ordered: The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 11, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not vacate the rental unit by July 11, 2026, then starting July 12, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction of the Subtenant may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 12, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 11, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Trivedi (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $918.00.

The Tenant was going to be travelling fr om November 2023 to April 2024 and arranged an approved ‘sublet’ with the Landlord and prepaid the rent for the six-month period to the Landlord. Issues between the Landlord and the approved guest began in December 2023 and culminated in February 2024. On February 6, 2024 the Landlord told the guest that a trespassing case would be filed if they didn’t leave the rental unit. On February 8, 2024 the guest permanently vacated the rental unit on the instruction of the Landlord.

I am satisfied that the subtenant or guest was induced to leave the rental unit by the actions of the Landlord, which were not in accordance with any available procedure under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) to end a tenancy.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered wit h the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Tenant refunded their guest $870.00 for the cancelled remainder or their stay. This is less than the lawful rent for the same period. Although the Tenant claims a 100% rent abatement, they had some use of the rental unit as storage for their possessions and retained the ability to return to the same unit instead of looking for new accommodations after their travels. Therefore, I find the appropriate rent abatement is an amount equal to the amount that they refunded their paying guest, that is $870.00.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement of that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $918.00. This amount represents:  $870.00 for a rent abatement.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $98.73. Interest on rent deposit owing
The parties agree that the Tenant provided the Landlord with a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,700.00 at the time he moved into the rental unit on/or about March 1, 2022.

The parties further agree the Landlord did not pay interest on the last month’s rent deposit during the tenancy and the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The parties further agree that at the time the Tenant vacated the rental property on December 31, 2025, the lawful monthly rent was $1,793.50, and after deducting the increase for the last month’s rent deposit the Tenant is entitled to $50.73 in interest owing. Compensation for N12 or N13 Notice owing

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 50 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act.
The Tenant states that the Landlord served an N13 notice of termination on the Tenant, but that no compensation had been paid by the Landlord.

The Landlord submits that the issue of compensation was resolved under file number [name] on consent as the Tenant’s T2 application also related to the issue of the Landlord’s N13 notice of termination.
The Tenant does not agree that the consent addressed the issue of compensation.

The Landlord’s representative directed me to paragraph 3 of the consent order which states: In addition, the Landlord will compensate the Tenants’ one month rent of $1793.50 as full and final resolution of this application.

In reviewing the Tenant’s T2 application under LTB-T-045952-25 it does address the Landlord’s N13 notice of termination, but it addresses the notice from a substantial interference perspective and does not relate to the issue of compensation. Additionally the consent order indicates the payment of one month’s rent is in full and in final resolution of that application not all matters relating to the tenancy.
On a balance of probabilities I am not satisfied that the consent order does address the payment of compensation in relation to the Landlord’s N13 notice of termination.
The purpose of compensation under the Act is to help offset the loss of housing, relocation costs and disruption associated with a lawful but involuntary eviction.

The Landlord was required to pay the Tenant compensation no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination of the tenancy given by the Landlord pursuant to section 55.1 of the Act.

Section 73.1 of the Act states: If the landlord compensated the tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55, as the case may be, in connection with a notice of termination under section 48, 49 or 50 and the Board refuses to grant an application under section 69 for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant based on the notice, the Board may order that the tenant pay back the compensation to the landlord.

In the matter before the Board the tenancy was not terminated pursuant to an application in relation to a notice of termination under section 48, 49 or 50 of the Act and subsequent order. It was terminated on a consent order on an unrelated application.

If compensation had been paid by the Landlord. Pursuant to section 73.1 of the Act suggests that since the tenancy was not terminated pursuant to an application in connection with section 48, 49 or 50 of the Act, that the Board may order the return of compensation.

If the Board can order the return of compensation paid to a tenant where a tenancy is not terminated pursuant to an application in connection to section 48, 49, or 50 of the Act. It stands to reason that the Board can decline to order compensation to be paid where a tenancy is not terminated pursuant to an application in connection to section 48, 49 or 50 of the Act.

As the tenancy in the matter before the Board was terminated pursuant to a consent agreement unrelated to application in connection to section 48, 49 or 50 of the Act , I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant is not entitled to compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $98.73. This amount represents: • $50.73 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by serving an excessive number of notices of entry during the period when the rental unit was listed for sale.

The Tenant testified that the numerous showings caused her stress and inconvenience. She stated that she was required to keep the rental unit in a condition suitable for prospective purchasers, that she altered family plans on certain occasions, including an Easter gathering, and that she found the frequency of the showings disruptive. The Tenant also testified that her mobility limitations and medical conditions made preparing the rental unit for showings more difficult.

The Tenant acknowledged that each of the entries occurred in connection with the Landlord's attempt to sell the property. She also acknowledged that the notices of entry provided the required notice and that she was advised by the realtor that showings could be rescheduled if particular times created difficulties. The Tenant testified that she did not request that any showing be cancelled or rescheduled.

The Tenant also testified that she believed the Landlord was attempting to pressure her into leaving the rental unit because the property would be easier to sell if vacant. In support of this allegation, the Tenant relied upon various emails in which the Landlord discussed selling the property and the challenges associated with maintaining the tenancy while the property remained on the market. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that he decided to list the rental unit for sale because of his age, declining health, and desire to retire from property management. He testified that he was no longer able to perform many maintenance tasks himself and wished to reduce the responsibilities associated with being a landlord. The Landlord denied that the property was listed for sale for the purpose of forcing the Tenant to vacate the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that he retained real estate agent to handle the listing and showing process and that he was not personally involved in scheduling showings or issuing notices of entry.
The Landlord also testified that he offered accommodations to the Tenant during the sale process, including the opportunity to communicate concerns regarding showings through the realtor. [name]

The Landlord’s real estate agent, [name], testified at the hearing. He stated that he advised the Tenant that showings could be cancelled or rescheduled if particular dates or times posed difficulties. He further testified that, although the Tenant occasionally expressed concerns regarding the timing of certain showings, she never requested that a showing be cancelled or rescheduled.

He also testified that all showings were arranged for legitimate real estate purposes and that he did not bring family members or friends to the property under the guise of prospective purchasers. Rather, he testified that the individuals he brought to the property were prospective purchasers or persons who had expressed an interest in the property.

With respect to the Tenant's health concerns, [name] testified that he attempted to accommodate the Tenant's request that visitors wear masks by posting signage and making masks available to prospective purchasers.
He further testified that two offers to purchase the property were received but neither transaction proceeded because vacant possession could not be guaranteed. Analysis

Section 27(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that a real estate agent may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry to allow a potential purchaser to view the rental unit.

The Tenant does not allege that the entries were illegal. Rather, the Tenant argues that the frequency of the entries, together with the Landlord's motives for selling the property, substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I have reviewed the cases relied upon by the Tenant, including CET-64293-17, TNT- 07149-18, CET-13651-11, CET-77573-18, and TET-69036-16. In my view, those cases are distinguishable from the current application. Unlike the present application, those decisions involved findings that some entries did not comply with the Act, entries undertaken for improper purposes, or other circumstances beyond the mere frequency of showings.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord listed the property for sale for the purpose of harassing the Tenant or forcing her to vacate the rental unit. I find the Landlord's evidence regarding his reasons for selling the property to be credible. His evidence was generally consistent with the testimony of the real estate agent. The fact that the property was ultimately not sold does not detract from the genuineness of the Landlord's intention to market the property for sale.

There is no doubt that the relationship between the parties is acrimonious. The Tenant testified regarding historical rent increases and other disputes that occurred over the course of the tenancy. While those issues provide context regarding the parties' relationship, they are not issues before me in this application. I accept the Landlord's evidence that he no longer wishes to be a landlord and genuinely wishes to sell the rental unit, including having previously offered to sell it to the Tenant.

The Landlord acknowledged that the number of showings was significant but testified that the volume of showings reflected the realities of attempting to sell a residential property. I accept this evidence.

However, inconvenience alone is not sufficient to establish a breach of the Act. The issue is whether the Landlord's conduct amounted to substantial interference with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. While the volume of showings was significant, the evidence establishes that they were conducted for the legitimate purpose of marketing the property for sale.

The Tenant remained in possession of the rental unit throughout the listing period, received proper notice of the entries, and did not request that any showing be cancelled or rescheduled. In these circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Landlord's conduct rose to the level of substantial interference, harassment, or coercion contemplated by sections 22 or 23 of the Act.
I do accept the Board's reasoning in TST-94251-18 that a landlord has a duty to minimize the impact that showings have on a tenant.

I do accept the Board's reasoning in TST-94251-18 that a landlord has a duty to minimize the impact that showings have on a tenant. In this regard, I find the testimony of [name] to be persuasive. I accept that he advised the Tenant that showings could be cancelled or rescheduled if particular dates or times posed difficulties. He further testified that, although the Tenant occasionally expressed concerns regarding the timing of certain showings, she never requested that a showing be cancelled or rescheduled. I accept this evidence. 23. [name] also testified that all showings were arranged for legitimate real estate purposes and that he did not bring family members or friends to the property under the guise of prospective purchasers. Rather, he testified that the individuals he brought to the property were prospective purchasers or persons who had expressed an interest in the property. 24. I accept this evidence. While the Tenant may have believed some visitors were not genuine prospective purchasers, there is insufficient evidence before me to support that conclusion. 25. With respect to the Tenant's health concerns, [name] testified that he attempted to accommodate the Tenant's request that visitors wear masks by posting signage and making masks available to prospective purchasers. This supports a finding that reasonable efforts were made to address the Tenant's concerns during the showing process. 26. I accept that the volume of showings caused inconvenience to the Tenant. The Tenant testified that she was required to keep the rental unit in a condition suitable for showings, alter family plans on some occasions, and accommodate prospective purchasers entering the rental unit. 27. Having considered the evidence in its totality, I find that [name]’s testimony supports the Landlord's evidence regarding the purpose of the entries, the manner in which the showings were conducted, and the efforts made to accommodate the Tenant's concerns. His evidence does not support the Tenant's allegation that the showing process was being used as a means of harassment or to improperly pressure the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant's claim is dismissed. [name] 28. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental complex due to issues relating to the placement of a downspout and the condition of the eavestrough system. 29. The Tenant testified that the Landlord replaced an existing downspout with a longer extension that projected into an area regularly used by the Tenant and her family. The Tenant stated that the downspout reduced the available walking space, interfered with access to portions of the property, and created difficulties when mowing the lawn, shovelling snow, and moving about the yard. The Tenant further testified that water discharged from the downspout contributed to ice accumulation during the winter months and that she eventually slipped and fell on ice in the vicinity of the downspout. 30. The Tenant also testified that she repeatedly complained to the Landlord about the placement of the downspout and warned that it constituted a tripping hazard. According to the Tenant, she ultimately modified the downspout herself after obtaining the Landlord's permission. 31. With respect to the eavestroughs, the Tenant testified that they were not properly maintained and that water routinely overflowed during rainfall. The Tenant stated that overflowing water created puddles, contributed to icy conditions during the winter, and interfered with her ability to use portions of the property. The Tenant relied primarily on photographs depicting water accumulation, ice formation, and portions of the eavestrough system. 32. The Landlord acknowledged that the downspout was installed in the manner shown in the photographs. However, he testified that its placement resulted from directions provided by municipal authorities. The Landlord further testified that he responded to maintenance concerns raised by the Tenant and arranged for repairs when issues were brought to his attention. Analysis 33. I accept that the Tenant genuinely believed the downspout and eavestroughs created inconvenience and, at times, safety concerns. I also accept that the photographs demonstrate that water runoff and ice accumulation occurred on portions of the property. However, the issue before me is not whether the Tenant would have preferred a different configuration, but whether the Landlord breached his maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. 34. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established such a breach on a balance of probabilities. The photographs were largely undated and provides limited assistance in determining the duration, severity, or frequency of the alleged problems. 35. I find the evidence before me does not establish that the downspout rendered any portion of the rental complex unusable, nor does it establish that the eavestrough system was in such a state of disrepair that the Landlord failed to meet the maintenance obligations imposed by section 20 of the Act. While the Tenant clearly experienced inconvenience and frustration, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 05, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Crichlow (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: This application involves the middle unit of a triplex. Sometime in the summer of 2021 the tenants of the three separate rental units each received notice of termination pursuant to s. 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The notices all indicate the Landlord required possession for the purposes of residential occupation by the Landlord’s Daughter. The tenant of the lower unit moved out at the end of August, 2021. The Tenant who filed this application moved out of the middle unit with his family on September 30, 2021. The tenant of the top unit refused to move out and was still in possession as of the date of the hearing before the Board.

This application is brought pursuant to s 57(1)(a) of the Act. That provision requires the Tenant to prove all of the following: • The Landlord served notice to terminate pursuant to s. 48; • The Tenant moved out pursuant to the notice of termination; • The person who intended to move into the rental unit that was identified by the notice of termination failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The notice of termination was given in bad faith.
There is no dispute between the parties that the first two elements of the test have been met. An N12 was served and the Tenant moved out because of it.
That means the next question for the Board is whether the Landlord’s Daughter moved into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant believes that the Landlord’s Daughter did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time because he would drive by and see curtains and the bunkbeds he left behind through a window. He also spoke to the tenant of the upper unit about 15 months after the Tenant moved out and she told him no one was in the unit. But the upper unit tenant was not called to testify.

The Landlord has two daughters. At the time of the hearing before the Board they were 29 and 33 years old. The Landlord says that when he purchased the residential complex, he intended that it would eventually be occupied by his younger one and that she would essentially use it as her single family home. There was some delay because it was messy and there was some work the Landlord wanted to do first. He says she lived in the building with her boyfriend until January of 2023 when she moved for reasons related to her job.

According to the Landlord’s Daughter, she moved into both units in October of 2021. Her primary reason for moving was because she wanted out of her parents’ house to get more privacy. She says she and her boyfriend used various rooms in the two units for a variety of purposes. When the residential complex was first purchased her plan was to have one kitchen set aside just for baking because she loves baking and for hygienic reasons. In 2021 she typically continued to work from her parents’ home and mainly slept in unit 1. Initially she used the Tenant’s unit mostly for storage for her father’s stuff, but she also used the living room as a quiet place to study in. When she needed her laptop she always used that living room. For baking she used the kitchen in unit 1. According to her, in January of 2023 she was given a new role at her job and could no longer work from home, so she moved to [name].

In answer to a question from the Tenant, the [name] says that she could not provide documentation that she lived in the rental unit because her father paid the bills for the house and over time things like bills and licenses were lost or left with her parents.
The Tenant takes the position the [name] never moved in, and the Landlord takes the position she did.

Although the evidence of the Landlord’s Daughter about her use of the space in both units depicts an unusual type of living arrangement, her testimony was internally consistent, and corroborated by the Landlord. When inconsistencies were pointed out to her, she provided plausible explanations. In the absence of evidence to the contrary from the tenant living upstairs, I am satisfied based on the evidence provided that it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s Daughter moved into the rental unit and lived there from October 2021 to January of 2023. In this instance suspicion and uncorroborated hearsay are not sufficient to support a finding that the Landlord’s Daughter is not credible. And moving in one month after the Tenant vacated is moving in within a reasonable period of time.
As a result the Tenant’ application fails to meet the third requirement of s. 57 as set out above, and the application must be denied.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal charge collected

It is agreed that the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord for a fixed term tenancy commencing on February 1, 2024 for a period of one year. The monthly rent was $2,000.00 per month. At the time of entering into the tenancy agreement the tenant paid the Landlord $12,000.00, being $2,000.00 towards first months rent and $10,000.00 towards the last 5 months rent of the tenancy.

Based on the undisputed evidence before me, I am satisfied that the $10,000.00 collected by the Landlord is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 106(2) of the Act indicates that the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. The maximum amount the Landlord could have collected from the Tenant would have been $2,000.00 the equivalent of one month’s rent.

Pursuant to section 135(1) of the Act a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
For the purposes of this matter I am satisfied that the money in question was being retained by the Landlord in contravention of the Act.

Section 135(4) of the Act sets out the time frame in which a tenant or former tenant can apply for an order pursuant to section 135(1) as follows: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
In order to determine when the Landlord retained money in contravention of the Act it must first be determined when the tenancy ended.

The Tenant’s Agents state that the Tenant suffered a workplace accident in late September or early October, 2024 and shortly their after advised the Landlord orally that he needed to vacate the rental unit.
The Tenant’s Agents stated that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 15, 2024.
The Landlord testified that he received a txt message from the Tenant on October 15, 2024 advising that he was vacating the rental unit as of December 1, 2024.

The Landlord further testified that at that time he was leaving the country to deal with the passing of his mother-in-law and attend her funeral. He advised the Tenant that they could address the matter upon his return.
The following day the Landlord alleges that the Tenant sent another txt message to him stating that he had moved out of the rental unit and cleaned the apartment.

Upon returning from his mother-in-law’s funeral the Landlord attended the rental unit on October 31, 2024 and the unit was empty and vacant. The Landlord could not recall if the Tenant had returned the keys to the unit or not. Analysis

Section 47 of the Act states that a tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.
Section 44(4) of the Act indicates that the notice to terminate a fixed term tenancy is 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date.
On a balance of probabilities I am satisfied that the Tenant sent a txt to the Landlord on or around October 15 or 16, 2024 indicating that he was vacating the rental unit.
The notice provided by the Tenant was not valid because it did not provide 60 days notice to terminate the tenancy as required by section 44(4).

Pursuant to section 88 (1) of the Act: If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.

In accordance with section 88(1) of the Act, the earliest date the Tenant could have specified in their notice to terminate the tenancy given to the Landlord on October 15 or 16, 2024 would be December 31, 2024.

The limitation period to commence an application pursuant to section 135(1) is one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of the Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. In the case before me that limitation period would be December 31, 2025. One year after the earliest date the tenant could have terminated the tenancy pursuant to an invalid notice sent to the Landlord on October 15 or 16, 2024.
The Tenant filed their application pursuant to section 135(1) of Act, on January 6, 2026. Which is outside the time frame prescribed by section 135(4) of the Act.
For all the reasons noted above the Tenants’ application is dismissed as it is outside the time frame prescribed by section 135(4) of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Interest on rent deposit owing

At the commencement of the hearing the Tenant advised that the Tenants were no longer proceeding on their claim that the Landlord failed to pay interest on their last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
At the request of the Tenant this portion of the Tenants’ application is withdrawn. Compensation for N12 Notice owing
The Tenant testified that on September 30, 2025 the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act with a termination date of November 30, 2025.
The Tenant indicates that the Landlord did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by the Act.
On November 16, 2025, the Landlord advised the Tenants that he wished to rescind and cancel his N12 notice of termination as he no longer required the rental unit for personal use.

Notwithstanding the Landlord advised the Tenants that he wished to cancel the N12, the Tenants proceeded to look for and secured alternative housing, entering into a new tenancy agreement on or about December 7, 2025.
The Tenants proceeded to serve an N9 Notice to end tenancy on the Landlord on December 12, 2025 with a termination date of January 1, 2026.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on January 1, 2026 and moved into their new rental unit. Analysis

Pursuant to section 55.1 of the Act: 55.1 If the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55, the landlord shall compensate the tenant no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination of the tenancy given by the landlord under section 48, 49 or 50.
The Landlord advised the Tenants prior to the termination date of November 30, 2026 as contained in the N12 notice of termination, that he wished to cancel his notice of termination.

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord cancelled or attempted to cancel the N12 notice of termination on November 16, 2025 prior to the termination date contained in the notice.

Any steps taken by the Tenants to end the tenancy by serving an N9 notice of termination and securing alternative housing by entering into a new tenancy agreement were taken after the cancelation of the N12 notice of termination. At that point, the Tenants were aware that they no longer had to leave and chose to do so anyway. I find that any cost associated with their choice to leave should not have to be paid by the Landlord.
In the circumstances the Tenants are not entitled to receive compensation from the Landlord and the Tenants’ application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
