issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $9,310.50 on or before June 30, 2026. [name] to the tenancy:

The Tenant moved into a newly built residential complex in June 2020. The residential complex has 99 rental units which house seniors, families with children, physically disabled people as it has accessible units which support independent living with walkers, canes and wheelchairs etc.

The Tenant has a host of medical issues which include but are not limited to rheumatoid arthritis, chemical sensitivities, allergies, chronic fatigue and auto immune disease. [name] was exceptionally hard for the Tenant due to her low immunity levels. The Tenant is prescribed a weekly dose of an inhibitor which alters her immune system. This was especially important during [name] because it affected her immunity negatively and made her more susceptible to getting sick. The Tenant has bouts of days when she is bedridden due to her arthritis.

The Tenant was homeless in 2018, and her doctor recommended applying to Social Housing and was also in Housing First program for the region due to homelessness. The Tenant’s doctor recommended this building. All of the Tenant’s medical needs were shared with the Landlord prior to her moving in which is why she chose this non-smoking barrier- free building.
The tenancy ended on or around September 30, 2025. T2 Application
The Tenant’s T2 application alleges illegal entry, substantial interference, and harassment.
The allegations on the T2 have been grouped together as follow: a) Smoking related issues. b) Harassment by other tenants c) Safety issues.

The applicable sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’) are as follows: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The definition of harassment in the Ontario Human Rights Code is “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” The Act does not define harassment; however, the Board has relied on the definition in the Code and other similar definitions.

The Tenant’s T2 application was filed on January 21, 2022. Some of the incidents date back to 2020. The Act limits the application timeline to not more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred under section 29(2) which means the remedies granted cannot go back farther than January 21, 2021. Some of the incidents from 2020 are only referred to show continuation and do not necessarily initiate a remedy. Smoke related issues Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that since the start of her tenancy in June 2020, tobacco smoke from neighbouring units traveled to her rental unit. The Tenant complained to her Housing First worker as there was no staff on site due to [name]. She also reported the issue to the Tenant Service Coordinator, [name] (TK).

Between September 9, 2020 and May 31, 2022, the Tenant’s doctors wrote multiple letters to the Landlord documenting the impact the smoke was having on the Tenant’s health and requesting that the Landlord take steps to keep residents from smoking in the non-smoking building.

The Tenant continued to report issues with smoke to TK and other staff in writing from November 18, 2020 to May 31, 2022. The Landlord rarely responded and when they did, the response was vague. The Landlord also never provided the Tenant with any information as to measures they were undertaking to keep residents from smoking in the non-smoking building.

Between December 10, 2020 and June 3, 2022, TK advised the Tenant that she would speak to her supervisor about moving the Tenant to another building. The Tenant tried to mitigate the issue by keeping her windows open when the weather permitted, placing towels under the doors, and purchasing an air filter. Despite her efforts, the issue persisted until she moved to another building in September 2025. Landlord’s evidence

TK testified that she was the Tenant Services Coordinator until 2024. TK acknowledged receiving the Tenant’s complaints about the smell of smoke. She indicated that neither she nor staff could smell smoke when they attended the rental unit to assess the issue.

TK confirmed that the building is a non-smoking building with designated smoking areas outside. She explained that many of the Tenant’s complaints occurred during COVID when staff were not present. 17. [name] (KW) testified that she became the Tenant Services Coordinator following the departure of TK in 2024. She testified that in May 2024, the Landlord offered the Tenant a Tenant Navigator to assist her with her tenancy issues. In January 2025, the Landlord resealed the Tenant’s unit to address her concerns. She stated that the Landlord offered to transfer the Tenant on four separate occasions, but the Tenant denied all offers until September 2025. Analysis 18. In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2002] O.J. No. 5650, the Divisional Court affirmed that a landlord has a positive duty to address situations where one tenant substantially interferes with another tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. In that decision, the Court stated: It is not that the other tenant’s actions are imputed to the landlord, but rather, the landlord’s legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant’s right to quiet enjoyment. 19. It flows from [name] that a landlord faced with complaints from one tenant about another must investigate the complaints. If there is merit to the complaints, the landlord must take such reasonable steps as warnings, escalating to eviction proceedings, if the offending behaviour is not corrected. 20. In the current case, whether or not marijuana or tobacco permeated into the Tenant’s unit is not particularly important. The Tenant alleges she was disturbed by the smell of smoke in her rental unit and was denied reasonable enjoyment as a result. Accordingly, the issue that must be determined in this case is whether the Landlord acted reasonably in response to the Tenant’s complaints to provide the Tenant with reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 21. I will first state that I find it proven that tobacco and marijuana smoke permeated into the Tenant’s rental unit. The Tenant’s account of these disturbances was well documented and sufficiently convincing, particularly as it fit with the undisputed email exchanges from the relevant times and the medical records. Further, it is noteworthy that the Landlords’ agents did not deny that residents were smoking in the non-smoking building. TK testified that many of the complaints occurred during COVID when staff were not present. 22. No evidence was led by the Landlord indicating they issued warnings to residents. The extent of the Landlord’s investigation into the Tenant’s complaints was limited to visits to the rental unit in which they denied smelling smoke. I am not satisfied the Landlord objectively investigated the Tenant’s complaints. 23. I am also not convinced the Landlord took reasonable and appropriate steps to correct the issue. The Landlord was aware that the issue continued after the re-sealing of the unit. There is no indication the Landlord provided the Tenant with an air purifier equipped with HEPA or carbon filters to neutralize the smell. I find the Tenant’s denial of previous transfers were reasonable given her medical conditions. 24. Based on a totality of the evidence before me, I find the Landlord, in failing to properly investigate and correct the Tenant’s complaints of tobacco and [name], substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. [name] and safety concerns Tenant’s evidence 25. The Tenant testified that other tenants in the residential complex created an unsafe living environment by failing to adhere to COVID-19 safety protocols. She alleged that throughout her tenancy, she was harassed and verbally threatened by several tenants. She attributes these encounters to her refusal to allow non-residents or unauthorized guests entry to the building. 26. The incidents described by the Tenant included being verbally accosted when she entered or exited the building with her support dog, being spat on, excessive noise coming from the common areas at odd hours and being cursed at by other tenants. She reported these incidents to the Tenant Services Coordinator who advised her that they could not assist as the incidents occurred in areas without surveillance cameras. The Tenant also reported multiple incidents to the police, who provided her little recourse. Landlord’s evidence 27. It was the evidence of the Landlord that in addition to complaints received by the Tenant, they received complaints from other tenants about the Tenant. Given this, the Landlord arranged for mediation between the Tenant and another tenant. TK testified that they held a round table meeting with the Tenant and suggested she make audio recordings of her interactions with the offending tenants. The Tenant was also encouraged to contact police if she had safety concerns. TK stated that audio and video recordings the Tenant provided the Landlord did not establish harassment or safety concerns. Analysis 28. As explained above in Hassan, the issue that must be determined in this case is whether the Landlord acted reasonably in response to the Tenant’s harassment complaints. For the reasons that follow, I believe they did. 29. The Landlord offered mediation, held a round table discussion with the Tenant, and offered the Tenant an opportunity to transfer to another unit. When the issues persisted, the Landlord took steps to terminate the tenancies of some of the offending tenants. Remedies 1. Ontario LTB case law supports that persistent second -hand smoke and ongoing tenant harassment, combined with a landlord’s delayed or ineffective response, constitute substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment and justify compensation. 2. Guideline 6 of the Board’s Interpretation Guidelines states that, in determining the amount of an abatement for the violation of a tenant’s rights, the Board will consider factors such as a landlord’s intention in doing the action complained of by the tenant, whether the landlord was motivated by malice toward the tenant, the extent of the harm suffered as a result of the landlord’s actions, whether the tenant contributed to or aggravated the situation, and the frequency or duration of the landlord’s actions, including the number of occasions in which the conduct occurred. An abatement is not a punishment for a landlord but is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of the tenant’s rights. While the Guidelines are not binding upon me, I agree with the approach stated in the Guidelines and have considered the factors outlined above where applicable. 3. I take into consideration that the Tenant is a person with disability who requires extra care and attention who was entitled to accommodation and protection given her disability and also that a major part of this was during COVID-19 when already people were under stress and uncertainty especially a person with compromised immunity. 4. The Tenant has asked for a 25% rent abatement for each issue (Total 50% abatement). I find, based on the lack of evidence to show any reasonable efforts made by Landlord to mitigate the smoking issue, that an abatement of 25% is warranted. For the harassment issue I do find the Landlord took reasonable steps no rent abatement is being granted. The [name] monthly rent at the rental unit was $650.00 for a period between January 2021 to September 2025. his amount reflects a 25% abatement of the Tenant’s monthly rent of $650.00 over the period from January 2021 to September 2025 (25%x 650 x 4 years 9 months). The total amount of abatement granted is $9,262.50 for all the issues. 5. No other remedies are being granted as the Tenant has vacated the rental unit and other remedies are moot.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,310.50. This amount represents: • $9,262.50 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • illegally collected or retained funds from the Tenant; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant withdrew the T1 Application filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c. 17 (the ‘Act’). The Landlord consented to this withdrawal. Therefore, the only evidence presented was with respect to the Tenant’s application under section 31 of the Act pertaining to allegations of harassment.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the hearing, the Tenant presented a list of interactions with his Landlord and its agents that he characterized as a pattern of harassment. These interactions include communications about maintenance issues, asking staff about the Landlord’s online portal, disputes about use of the garage, notices of entry pertaining to maintenance of building systems, noise issues in the building, and communications about rent and insurance.

The Tenant is of the view that the series of events he described over the course of his tenancy is a targeted campaign by the Landlord to harass the Tenant and interfere with his enjoyment of the rental unit. I disagree. The materials presented by the Tenant reflect routine communications between a landlord and a tenant, in my view. Communications are all related to the tenancy and the Tenant could not point me to an instance where the Landlord or any agent of the Landlord acted unreasonably.

The Tenant did not identify any evidence of a deliberate pattern of conduct by the Landlord’s agents beyond the circumstances of the timing of various events. 6. [name], a portfolio manager for the Landlord who was the agent in communication with the Tenant during much of the relevant time, testified at the hearing. She gave clear and concise testimony about the series of events presented by the Tenant. Her explanations of the events were clear and rational. I have no reason to doubt her credibility. In every instance, a pedestrian explanation of the Landlord’s conduct was offered. 7. I am satisfied, after a thorough review of the evidence led by the parties at the hearing, that no individual allegation of conduct by the Landlord or their agents amounts to harassment, coercion, obstruction, threats, or interference with the Tenant. I am also satisfied the Landlord’s conduct does not, in aggregate, amount to harassment, coercion, obstruction, threats, or interference with the Tenant. 8. As such, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The rental unit is a single wide mobile home in a land lease community. The mobile home has 2 bedrooms, living room, kitchen and 1 bathroom. There is also an addition with 2 rooms and a loft. T2 Application - Substantial interference and withholding a vital service Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] (BH) testified that the Landlord has served an egregious number of Notices of Entry, 19 since January, which substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit.
The Tenant referred to pages 21 to 38 of the Landlord’s Document Brief 1B, which contained 21 notices of entry.

BH testified that he and his family are unable to use the addition to the trailer home because the Landlord has failed to provide heat in that area and as a result of a prior leak in the addition, there is mold, which the Landlord also refuses to address.
BH testified that due to the lack of heat and the mold in the additional that his family of five are living in only 65% of the unit, which is not enough to accommodate them.
Under cross-examination, BH agreed that the addition has never had heat and that the notices of entry were to allow contractors into the unit to complete work/repairs. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that she had bought this house so her son, BH, could afford rent after being given notice to vacate his prior unit. She further testified that BH viewed the home with her prior to the purchase.

The Landlord testified that the additional to the mobile home is 2 rooms plus a three- season room (sunroom) which has never had a source of heat was never meant to live in. Despite this, she provided BH with an electric fireplace to use in the room. It was further explained that this unheated room is comparable to an enclosed porch, not an area meant to be lived in.

The Landlord testified that each of the notices to enter were given with proper notice and were to allow contractors into the unit to complete the work required, such as renovations to the addition, mold remediation, furnace maintenance and repair/replacement of the gas range.

The Landlord testified that despite the sunroom not requiring heat, she looked into the ability to run heat to the addition, and it is impossible as the furnace is incapable and Hydro One will not permit an upgrade above the current 30 amp service, which would be required to add the additional heat. Analysis

Section 22 of the act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant. Pursuant to the Boards Interpretation Guideline 6, the interference must be substantial in nature and a minor disruption or inconvenience for a brief period of time does not normally result in an abatement of rent.

Although the tenant was inconvenienced by the frequent attendances at the unit by the Landlord’s contractors, I do not find that this inconvenience rises to the level of substantial interference, as the Landlord was required to have the contractors attend the unit to address the issues within the unit.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

In regard to the Landlord withholding heat, I find that the room without heat is a sunroom r an enclosed porch and was never intended to be heated. Despite this, the Landlord took all possible steps to try to address this issue. As the mobile home itself is heated sufficiently, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenants’ vital services. T6 Application – Maintenance Tenant’s Evidence

BH testified that the Landlord has failed to maintain the unit and as a result there is mold in the walls and insulation, windows freeze preventing them from opening and gaps or holes in the unit which were allowing wasps to enter the unit.

BH submitted pictures from January 2026, showing the following: - Condensation on a windowsill in the loft - Ceiling panels in the loft removed showing signs of mold - A hallway window with condensation and ice which makes the window inoperable - Openings allowing insects into the unit - Insulation damage caused by rodents

BH testified that the Landlord has fixed the leak, the holes insects were getting into was filled by him using spray foam, but the windows and mold are still issues the Landlord has failed to address. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that the roof was repaired in 2024 and again in 2025 resulting in the roof being completely redone.
The Landlord testified that without need, she replaced the hot water tank to a larger model and provided a new washer and dryer to help the Tenant.

The Landlord testified in January 2026 the Tenant informed her about the mold so she hired the best company she could find and had the required areas in the unit treated and cleaned, which included any of the Tenant’s belongings which may have been affected.
The Landlord testified that the unit has been tested and the air quality is good in the unit. A copy of the testing results were submitted as evidence.

The Landlord testified that the mold was caused by poor air circulation in the unit caused by the abundance of clutter in the unit and the Tenant’s growing of marijuana in the unit. A copy of the post remedial report from February 25, 2026, was submitted into evidence which stated hoarding, storage of car parts and growing marijuana in the unit were the cause of the restricted airflow and elevated humidity. Copy of photos were also submitted showing the pile of car parts and excessive belongings (hoarding) within the unit.

The Landlord testified that all of the upper-level windows have been replaced, that the unit has been cleared by the City bylaw, fire department and ESA. The only remaining item is a window that cannot be accessed because it is blocked by the Tenant’s belongings.
The Landlord testified that she additionally provided the Tenants with a water cooler due to a water advisory and dehumidifiers to help with the excess humidity. Analysis

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex and did not fail to comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards.
I find, based on the evidence before me, that the Landlord has addressed each and every one of the issues raised by the Tenant in a timely manner.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain.
For these reasons, I cannot find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was in breach of the Act with respect to the mold, leaks and windows, therefore this allegation is dismissed. Costs
The Landlord requests costs in the amount of $700.00, alleging that the Tenant is a vexatious litigant.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 speaks to ordering costs against a party and requires that, in considering a request for costs awarded against a party, the Board consider whether the party’s actions were unreasonable. A party’s actions will be considered unreasonable if they cause undue expense or delay.

Rule A8.2 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure states that the Board may find a party to be vexatious litigant when satisfied that a person has persistently instituted vexatious proceedings or conducted a proceeding in a vexatious manner.

The Tenant was self-represented throughout the proceedings and in filing the application. I do not find that the Tenant acted in bad faith, nor do I find that there is sufficient evidence to declare the applicant as a vexatious litigant.
Therefore, I do not find that costs are warranted under these circumstances.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal Entry

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord illegally entered their unit on December 6, 2024, January 5, 2025, and January 8, 2025. The Tenant testified that he believes the Landlord entered his unit illegally because on each of these days, he was sure that he locked the door to his rental unit but when he returned, the door was unlocked. The Tenant states that the Landlord is the only person with another set of keys and that on this basis, they must have been the one that entered his unit. The Tenant testified that after the incident on January 5, 2025, he started to record himself locking the door. He states that on January 8, 2025, he found his door unlocked again after he was certain he had locked it. The Tenant states that on another day shortly after he finished recording himself locking the door, the property manager’s wife exited the elevator towards his unit, appeared startled by his presence and went back into the elevator. The Tenant states that he believes she was there to unlock his door and upon seeing him in the hallway, she retreated into the elevator.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledges that he does not have proof of this aside from the fact that the Landlord is the only one to possess an extra set of keys, therefore, it must be them. The Tenant stated that his family also has a set of keys, but they live far away, and it couldn’t have been them. The Tenant stated that no items were missing from his unit, it was simply that his door was being unlocked. There was no investigation by the police.

I can understand the concern from the Tenant that he is finding his unit door unlocked, however, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord is the one who unlocked the Tenant’s door. The evidence before me is circumstantial and fails to meet the standard of proof. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally. Substantial interference and Harassment

The Tenant alleges that an individual who is not a Tenant at the building is intentionally damaging the Tenants vehicle on a regular basis. The Tenant states that this individual is from a rental building that he formerly resided in many years ago. The Tenant states that they have tried to contact the police numerous times, in addition to the Landlord, however, nobody is assisting him with the investigation. The foundation of the Tenant’s allegations is that the Landlord has failed to assist them in their investigation by failing to provide CCTV footage, so that they can then provide it to the police. The Tenant describes the damages as surface damages such as “scratches, glue marks, flat tire”.

The Tenant states that they contacted the police on October 26, 2024, after seeing the individual they believe was damaging their car in the underground parking lot where the Tenant’s car is parked. The police attended on November 9, 2024, and the CCTV footage from October 26, 2024, was already deleted. The Tenant was advised that they should contact the Landlord as soon as possible with the date and time of the incident and provide the Landlord with a USB drive so they can save the video for the Tenant.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that: • He was originally in an outdoor parking spot but was moved to an underground parking spot alleviate the issues. • He was advised to provide the Landlord with a USB drive, along with the date and time of the incident, but he did not provide one because he had no trust in giving it to the property manager because of the way he treated him

The Landlord’s Agent testified that they have moved the Tenant’s vehicle on more than one occasion to alleviate the problems he is having. Such as moving the car into underground parking from outside and placing the car directly in front of a CCTV camera. The Landlord’s Agent states that it is company policy to first obtain a police report prior to providing video to the police. They stated that there is no record of a request for recordings connected to this rental unit. They offered the Tenant the opportunity to obtain the CCTV footage by providing his own USB drive, however, there was no follow-up from the Tenant. Analysis
The issue before me is whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to resolve an issue the Tenant was having with a third-party who is not a tenant of the Landlord.

Guideline 6 states: Landlords have a positive obligation to provide quiet enjoyment and take reasonable action to address another tenant’s conduct that disturbs the complaining tenant. If the landlord fails to reasonable respond to the complaints, the Landlord may be in breach of s. 22 of the Act. While the Landlord in such a situation is not directly responsible for the actions of the offending tenant, the landlord’s responsibility is linked to a failure to take reasonably necessary actions to ensure that the complaining tenants could reasonably enjoy the premises. [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (On. [name]. Ct.), First Ontario Realty Corp. v. Appelrouth [2012] O.J. No. 3639 ([name]. [name]. Ct.).

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22.
Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 23.

As stated in Guideline 6, the Landlord only has so much control over the conduct of another tenant. In the case before me, the individual being complained of is not even a tenant, therefore, the Landlord is further limited in the actions that they can take to resolve the Tenant’s concerns.

Although it did not resolve the issue the Tenant was experiencing, the evidence before me is that the Landlord took reasonable action to address the issues. The Landlord tried to move the Tenant’s vehicle to somewhere that the Tenant felt more comfortable having it, as well as offering to provide the Tenant with the CCTV footage if they supplied a USB drive. I have heard no evidence that would amount to “harassment”. The Tenant has failed to prove their application on a balance of probabilities.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: My oral ruling to dismiss the Tenant’s claim for illegal rent is replaced with my written decision. In accordance with the Statutory Powers and Procedures Act, my decision is not final unit it’s issued in writing.

The parties came before me with a partial consent. The Landlord agreed to pay interest in the amount of $363.00 on the last month’s rent deposit. The only issue to determine was if the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Illegal rent collected

The application alleges that the rent increases on September 1, 2019, January 1, 2023, and January 1, 2025, were illegal because they were contrary to section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”). The Tenant seeks a return of illegally collected rent payments.

This application was filed under section 135(1) of the Act. Section 135(4) states: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

The Tenant filed their application on January 20, 2026. On the basis of section 135(4) of the Act, the Board does not have jurisdiction to make an order with respect to any illegal rent collected by the Landlord more than one year before the Tenant filed the application. Therefore, I have only made a determination on the lawfulness of the rent increase charged and rent collected by the Landlord from the period starting January 1, 2025.
The Tenant [name] (‘LB’) testified that the Landlord served a letter October 21, 2024, to increase rent from $1,740.00 to $1,785.00 effective January 1, 2025. The letter was submitted in evidence.
LB agreed to increase the rent to $1,785.00 and paid this amount since January 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided Notice of Rent Increase on December 30, 2025, of the rent increase effective April 1, 2026. The Tenant paid $1,820.00 each month for April 1, 2026, to May 1, 2026.
The Landlord’s representative does not dispute this evidence.

The relevant provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”) are: Landlord’s duty, rent increases 110 No landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with this Part. Landlord not to charge more than lawful rent 111 (1) No landlord shall charge rent for a rental unit in an amount that is greater than the lawful rent permitted under this Part. Notice of rent increase required 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written (N1) notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. Increase void without notice 116 (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase. Guideline increase 120 (1) No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.
The annual guideline rent increase for 2025 was 2.5%.
Based on the evidence before me, the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

I say this because the Landlord cannot increase the rent on January 1, 2025 without a proper notice of rent increase (“NORI”). In addition, the Landlord served letter purporting to raise the rent from $1,740.00 to $1,785.00 effective January 1, 2025. This rent increase is more than the guideline amount of 2.5%. It appears that the Landlord rounded up the increase to the next dollar. Rounding up rent increases is not permitted under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') as it inevitably results in an increase that is in excess of the guideline amount. As a result, the lawful monthly rent remains at $1,740.00 until the Landlord serves a valid NORI.

The increase in rent effective January 1, 2025, was contrary to sections 110 and 111 of the Act because the Landlords failed to serve a NORI at least 90 days in advance of the increase as required by section 116, and because the rent increase was greater than the rent increase guideline (section 120).

As such, I find that the $45.00 increase from $1,740.00 to $1,785.00 effective January 1, 2025, was unlawful. The lawful rent for January 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025, is $1,740.00. Therefore, the Landlords collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
The subsequent rent increase effective April 1, 2026, is therefore illegal as the rent increase was calculated based on an illegal rent amount charged.
The Tenants paid the unlawful increase each month during the 17-month period from January 1, 2025, to May 1, 2026 for a total of $745.00. Last Month’s Rent Deposit Interest
The Landlord agrees to pay the Tenant $363.00 to the Tenant for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant the total interest owing in the amount of $363.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,156.00. This amount represents: • $745.00 for excess rent collected. • $363.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $1,552.00 on or before June 16, 2026.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided them a parking spot in 2021 and charged the tenant in the amount of $80.00 for the spot. However, the Tenant believes they should not be charged for the months of August 2025 and September 2025 because they were unable to utilize the spot due to construction. As such, they allege that they should be re- imbursed in the amount of $160.00 for the two months they were unable to use the parking spot.

Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Tenant was charged an illegal charge. I say this because It is important to note that the Tenant filed a T1 application under section 135 of the Act, which addresses the collection or retention of illegal charges.

The Tenant has been charged for a parking spot since 2021; the Tenant would not be entitled to reimbursement of such charges pursuant to 136(1) which states that rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date the amount was first charged. Further, subsection 135(2) prohibits a tenant from filing an application for the retention of money retained in contravention of the Act, filed more than one year after the person collected or retained the money.

The Tenant ought to file a T2 application alleging substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment, rather than a T1 application under section 135, which addresses the collection or retention of illegal charges. Compensation for N12 owing

On July 2, 2025, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination under section 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), claiming the Landlord required possession of the rental unit for residential occupation by her spouse. The termination date in the N12 notice was December 31, 2025.
The monthly rent was $1,504.00
The Tenant submitted to the Board a copy of the signed N12 notice as evidence.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 1, 2025. Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that Tenant vacated the rental unit because they were served with the N12 notice.
The Tenant submit that the Landlord did not pay the required one month’s rent compensation.

Section 48.1 of the Act states: A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48.

Section 55.1 of the Act states: If the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55, the landlord shall compensate the tenant no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination of the tenancy given by the landlord under section 48, 49 or 50.

The Act is clear that a landlord is required to pay a tenant compensation equal to one month’s rent if the landlord serves the tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. The Act does not provide that a landlord does not have to comply with this requirement if the tenant finds new living arrangements.

Since the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant compensation for termination of the tenancy, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), I find that the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the one month’s rent compensation that is properly owed in this matter.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,552.00 This amount represents: • $1,504.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the T6 application. Therefore, the T6 application is dismissed.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the residential complex and did not fail to comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards.
The Tenant filed a T2 and T6 application but both applications include identical allegations.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on December 30, 2024. On December 31, 2024, she made a complaint to the Landlord alleging noise disturbances. The noise was described as “noises from the entrance hallway, exterior door slamming and noises from the unit above”. The Tenant also included how loud the entrance hallway and exterior door closing noises were, particularly in regard to the door slamming when it shut. The Tenant alleges that the exterior door is a fire door, and the door does not have self closing hinges as it is required to, and this is leading to the door slamming. In addition to the noise complaints, the Tenant also expressed safety concerns with a lack of lighting in the parking lot of the residential complex. The Tenant states that their complaint regarding lighting was resolved by the Landlord in early February.

The Tenant states that on January 3, 2025, she followed up by text message with the Landlord and then following that text message she received an email response to her complaint. She states the Landlord’s response was not satisfactory and simply referred her to submitting her maintenance concerns through the tenant portal. The Tenant states that she followed up with the Landlord on January 7, 10, 21, and 22, 2025, regarding the noise from the exterior door slamming. The Tenant states that the noise from the slamming exterior door was causing her to be woken up every night between 2:00 a.m. – 5:00 a.m.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledges and confirms the following: -The exterior door to the rental building that is adjacent to her unit is a fire door -Fire doors close automatically -First complaint to the Landlord was December 31, 2024, a date in which people are generally on holidays -Received response from Landlord on January 3, 2025, when staff returned from holidays -On January 8, 2025, the Tenant received an e-mail from the Landlord that they have addressed the noise complaint with the unit above. -On January 9, 2025, the Tenant thanked the Landlord for following up with the unit above and stated that their only remaining issue is the exterior fire door making a “slamming” noise when it shuts -On January 10, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant advising that the door is on self- closing hinges and meant to close firmly -On January 22, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant advising that the door is working according to how it should -On January 29, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant that they have further investigated their concerns and they have accommodated the Tenant as much as they can by making the door close as slowly as possible in order to limit the noise. The Landlord stated that the door was adjusted to close as slowly while still being able to close and be secured. -There have been no complaints made since February 2025.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I find that the Landlord acted reasonably and responded to the Tenants complaints and that their conduct does not amount to a breach of section 20 of Act. Nor does it amount to substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Landlord made attempts to address the Tenants concerns within a reasonable time and made reasonable attempts to resolve the issues. Following each complaint the Tenant made, the Landlord did respond and did engage with the Tenant, albeit it may not have been the responses that the Tenant wanted to receive, but the Landlord did engage with the Tenant and make reasonable attempts to resolve the issues they had.

The Tenant remains in the rental unit – and when asked if they have made any complaints since February 2025 they stated, “none that they can access”. The Tenant was prepared diligently for the hearing before me and with clear knowledge of the dates and correspondence she has had with the Landlord. I find it more probable than not that if there were additional complaints, she would have knowledge of them and be presenting me with this information at the hearing. The evidence before me leads me to believe that the Landlord acted promptly in addressing the Tenant’s concerns and since advising the Tenant they fixed the issue as best they could, there have been no further complaints.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. June 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 57 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] [name], 2026 ONLTB 49482 Date: 2026-06-30 In the matter of: [address] OAKVILLE ON [name] (the 'Tenants”) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was heard by videoconference on June 3, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the hearing. The Tenants advised that [name] was never a Tenant and did not reside in the rental unit. As of 9:58 a.m. the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $4,020.34 for moving and storage fees, general compensation and the application fee.
The residential unit is a single detached dwelling. The Tenants vacated the house on February 15, 2025 after residing there since November 27, 2021.

This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (XW) 4. [name] testified that he received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on October 30, 2024 with a termination date of January 26, 2025. The Tenant stated that the Landlord told him that he and his family wanted to move to Canada (from China) so that his 12-year- old son could attend school in Canada. The Tenant then signed an agreement to vacate the house by February 15, 2025 so that the Landlord and his family could move in. 5. The Tenant stated that he was not able to afford to rent another house in the same area as the prices were too expensive so he moved to Kanata with his family. He stated that Kanata has good schools and more affordable rent. 6. [name] stated that his son struggled in the new school because the Ottawa school system has a higher level of French. He stated that his son also had to move away from good friends and a school that he was comfortable in which caused him emotional stress. 7. The Tenant stated that he noted on August 14, 2025 that the Landlord had listed the house for sale and that the house sold in October of 2025. [name] was very angry to see that the Landlord did not move into the house himself and he felt that the Landlord “was cheating”. He stated that the Landlord sold the house for $1.3 million. 8. The Tenant is claiming moving expenses of $972.34 for which he provided receipts. He is requesting compensation of $43,560.00 based on 12 months of his previous rent of $3,630.00. Analysis 9. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 10. There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I must determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 11. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 12. The Tenant’s uncontested evidence and corroborating real estate listing confirms that the Landlord advertised the rental building for sale on August 14, 2025, 6 months after the Tenant vacated. The condo sold in October of 2025. 13. Based on the above, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave this notice to the Tenant in bad faith. 14. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with his T5 application. Remedies 15. The Tenants requested moving and storage costs in the amount of $972.34. The Tenants provided these receipts and I am granting this amount. 16. The Tenants requested compensation of $43,560.00 as the Act allows a Tenant to claim the maximum amount of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former Tenant. The Tenant spoke about his son’s emotional distress due to the move from Oakville to Kanata. Although it is unfortunate that the Tenants’ son is struggling with the level of French spoken in his new school, I was not provided with any school documentation to support this statement. Further, that was the only issue brought up by the Tenant about his move to another residence. 17. Having considered the circumstances in this case, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $3,000.00 to the Tenants in general compensation for the emotional distress, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,020.34 This amount represents: • $972.34 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses; • $3,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The application is amended to remove [name] as a Tenant. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Kishundoyal (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). The Tenant’s also applied for an order determining that the Landlord’s failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have proved some of the allegations contained in the application in part on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord’s must pay to the Tenant’s $3,980.78 and complete the work as ordered. Preliminary Issue: Have the claims of the Tenants already been determined by the Board?

The parties were before the Board on February 29, 2024, for a T6 application filed by the Tenant’s bearing the File Number LTB-T-034336-22 and L2 application filed by the Landlord’s bearing the File Number LTB-L-045257-22. An order addressing both applications was issued on July 3, 2024 (‘prior order’).
The Landlord, [name] (‘IM’) submits that the Tenant’s T6 application ought to be dismissed as the issues raised in the application were already addressed in the prior order.

The following issues were considered by the Board during the February 29, 2024, hearing as set out in paragraph 1 of order LTB-T-034336-22/LTB-L-045257-22: a. Automatic Garage Door b. Refrigerator c. Air Conditioning d. Shower Head e. Main bathroom fan
The issues of the showerhead and main bathroom fan are not the subject of the T2/T6 application before me and therefore will not be considered.

The principle of issue estoppel, which is a branch of res judicata prevents a party from re- litigating a matter that has already been decided previously. The principle recognizes the need for finality in the legal system. For issue estoppel to be successfully invoked, three preconditions must be met: (1) the issue must be the same as the one decided in the prior decision; (2) the prior judicial decision must have been final; and (3) the parties to both proceedings must be the same, or their privies": Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79 (2001), 2001 CanLII 24114 (ON CA)at para. 23.

In this case, the same refrigerator issue that the Tenants want to raise in the application before me is address at paragraphs 9, 15, 17, & 18 of the prior order. Therefore, applying the principle of issue estoppel, this claim cannot be relitigated and will not be addressed in this order.
I must now turn my mind to whether issue estoppel applies to the automatic garage door opener and air conditioning (‘A/C’) issues raised in this application.

The prior order addresses identical issues relating to the A/C which started on May 25, 2022 and automatic garage door opener which started on April 2, 2022 up until the date of the hearing on February 29, 2024.
Order LTB-T-034336-22 provides an analysis of the issue of the garage door opener and A/C at paragraphs 30 -25 of the order and the Tenants are awarded a remedy for these issues.

I agree that the issues regarding the garage door and air conditioning were addressed by the Board in order LTB-T-034336-22 which is a final order. With this said, the prior order does not provide a remedy if the issues were not repaired as ordered. Therefore, the Tenants are permitted to raise these issues and receive remedy if the problems continued or were not repaired after the February 29, 2024 hearing date. Issue estoppel does not prevent the Board from issuing such an order because the prior order did not address what should happen after the hearing date if the Landlord does not complete the ordered repairs to those items.

That this is the correct approach to the application of issue estoppel is confirmed by the Divisional Court’s decision in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 57092 (ON SCDC). At paragraph 36 the Court stated: When ORHT Member [name] restricted his inquiry as to what “new” issues existed after November 4th, 2005 and applied the res judicata doctrine to avoid examining any issues “raised previously” and dealt with in the November 4, 2005 order, he fell into error. The appellants were not seeking to relitigate the identified matters of disrepair identified in the tribunal’s earlier order of 2005. To the contrary, the appellants were relying on the continued existence of some of those deficiencies in 2006 to establish a breach of their s. 24(1) right as well as related expenses incurred in 2006. In terms of estoppel, this did not amount to relitigation of the same issue before [name] in November 2005. Nor could it have been anticipated at the time of the November 2005 ORHT hearing that 2006 would commence with the tribunal’s order unfulfilled. [name] judicata had no application to what Member [name] was being asked to determine.

The Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications filed on January 22, 2025 raises further issues which were not included in the prior T6 application and are properly raised at this hearing, including: a. Injury from the garage door opener [name] entries d. Harassment T2 Application

Garage Door Injury

HMM testified that the garage door had not been repaired, despite the prior Board order directing the Landlord to have it repaired by July 15, 2024. HMM stated that the Landlord was aware that the automatic garage door was not repaired. Further in March 2024 as he was manually opening the door he hurt his back. HMM referred to page 56 & 57 of the Tenant’s Book of Documents (DOC-7905660) showing doctor’s appointments that he attended and the prescriptions that he was taking as a result of his back injury. HMM further referenced page 163 of the Tenant’s Book of Documents, a doctor’s note by [name] on April 14, 2026 which speaks to his back injury, specifically it states: This is to attest that [name] injured his back in March 2024 opening a garage door…

IM’s testimony is that, HMM did not inform him that he had injured his back. Section 26 of the Act states that a landlord can enter a tenant’s unit without written notice in the case of an emergency or with the tenant’s consent. Section 27 of the Act states that a landlord can enter a tenant’s unit with written notice if it is given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under certain circumstances. The written notice must specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

Section 22 of the Act states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant.

Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Although the word harass is not defined in the Act, harassment has been found by this Board to generally be a course of conduct or behaviour that the reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.

With respect to the July 23, 2025 inspection, it was undisputed that the Landlord served a valid notice of entry to inspect the rental unit, photographs were taken during the course of the inspection, which appears to have caused the escalation.

The Landlord taking photographs of the Tenants’ unit was not improper. In [name] v. Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management, 2015 ONSC 3893 the Divisional Court found that the fact that photographs were taken did not, on its own, constitute an infringement of the tenant’s privacy rights. The Court stated that this would constitute a breach of privacy if the photographs were taken for an improper purpose. In this case, the Tenants admit that they believed the purpose of photographs was for use in a Board proceeding, namely an N13 notice that was ultimately served, thus I find the Landlord was taking photographs for a proper purpose.

I also find that the July 23, 2025 entry did not substantially interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment or constitute harassment. IM testified that the reason the inspection escalated was only due to the Tenant’s behaviour and he left once the escalation began. The Tenant’s specifically, SK, admits that she became upset when IM began taking pictures within the rental unit.

With respect to the July 23, 2025, as noted above, the entry may have been contentious, but I do not find that this interaction rose to the level of harassment as required by section 22 or is a course of conduct pursuant to section 23. The Tenants did not prove there was an impact by the entry. While the Tenants testified that they experienced stress and feel that IM engages in behaviour that ‘belittles’ or ‘demeans’. I am unable to award remedy for parties disliking the manner the other party engages with them, it must rise to a level defined in section 22 or 23, I find it does not.

I also find that the entry on July 26, 2025 was not illegal or cause substantial interference. The Landlord, [name] sent a text message to the Tenant’s informing them that he would be coming to complete maintenance in the backyard. Pursuant to subsection 26(1)(b), I am satisfied that this was a valid entry as the text messages between the parties unequivocally show that the Tenants consented to the entry. Thus, the entry was consented to by the Tenants and further the Landlord did not enter the home or interact with the Tenant’s.
I am also required to consider whether the entries and the injury from the garage door have substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment or constitutes harassment.

In terms of the HMM’s injury, I find that the Tenant’s submissions are detailed and demonstrate the injury was a result of the garage door requiring to be manually opened. Further, it is uncontested that the automatic garage door has not been repaired despite the prior Board order. I find that the Tenant’s injury is a direct result of the Landlord’s failure to complete the ordered repair and this failure also substantially interfered with the Tenants; reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. Therefore, an award shall be ordered. T6 Application

The Tenant’s failed to adduce any evidence in support of their claim with respect to the hot water tank. The Tenant’s did not provide any direct testimony on this fact.

Section 20(1) of the Act, states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Analysis

With respect to the hot water tank, the Tenant’s failed to adduce any evidence with respect to this claim, whether orally or through documentary evidence. The Landlord submitted that the issue was rectified in 3-days over the weekend. As the Tenant’s did not bring forward their own evidence about when it was brought to the attention of the Landlord and when it was repaired, I find that the Tenant’s have failed to adduce sufficient evidence establish a breach of s.20(1).

Regarding the eavestrough, I find that the Tenant’s brought this issue forward to the Landlord’s in August 2024 and it was not rectified until July 2025. However, I do not find that the water overflowing from the eavestrough amounts to substantial interference for the Tenants. I accept that the overflow of the water interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit when it rained, but not substantially, given that I was shown 1 video from August 9, 2024.

I find that the Tenants have failed to establish that the Landlords have breached their obligations under s. 20(1) of the Act or failed to act within a reasonable period of time to repair the fence. First, I find that the Tenants’ pictures of the fence do not establish that the fence was in a state of disrepair. Second, while the Tenant’s may take the position that the fence was not repaired, the Tenant’s did not adduce evidence to support the claim that the Landlords breached their obligations under s. 20(2) of the Act. The Tenant’s did not supply specific dates where they notified the Landlords of the alleged disrepair, or that the Landlord was aware of the alleged state of disrepair and refused to repair the fence. Finally, as per the testimony of the Tenant’s and agreed by the Landlord’s, the Landlord’s attended the property on July 26, 2025 and placed a new portion of the fence at the back of the property. Therefore, I find there is insufficient evidence to support the Tenants claim regarding the fence. Therefore, no order will issue.

I find that the Landlord has not acted reasonably to address the concerns relating to the automatic garage door repair. The garage door replacement took 13-months after the July 3, 2024 order. I find this is an unreasonably long period of time and therefore a breach under s. 20(1) of the Act.

The Landlord testified that he has and is not taking any steps to repair the automatic garage opener despite being ordered to repair the issue on July 3, 2024. The Landlord is required to comply with a Board order for repairs.

I find that the Landlord has not reasonably addressed the concerns relating to the A/C, as of the date of the hearing the A/C was not repaired or in working order. The Tenants provided substantial photographic evidence of the high temperatures in the home, and I do not believe, as was suggested by IM, the Tenants were removing and reinserting the disconnect to receive an award from the Board. Therefore, I find the Landlords have not taken reasonable steps to repair the A/C and therefore are in breach under s. 20(1) of the Act. Therefore, an order will issue.

However, I am not persuaded that the Landlord deliberately caused the problem with the A/c by removing the disconnect. While the HomeCare Checklist by [name] states that the Landlord had taken the disconnect, as evidenced in the video it is SK that informs the technician that the Landlord has taken the disconnect and the technician did not come to this conclusion on their own. Therefore, I place little weight on the testimony and Checklist submitted by the Tenant’s. Remedies

The Tenant’s seek the following remedies for the T2/T6 application: a. $7,793.16 being broken down as 50% rent abatement for the period of February 2024 through January (this remedy claimed separately on both T2 & T6 applications) b. $835.14 for out-of-pocket expenses for the purchase of a freezer and mini fridge in 2022 c. The Landlord to repair or replace the A/C, garage door and complete yearly eavestrough cleanings d. Order preventing rental increase until the work has been completed e. The Landlord or the Landlord’s agent to stop the following behaviour: a) Intimidation – by swearing and being disrespectful b) Be calm upon entry to the home c) Provide minimum 24-hour notice to enter the rental unit f. $5,000.00 in legal fees g. Fine to the Board h. The application filing fee
The Tenant’s legal representative abandoned the claims for out-of-pocket expenses at the hearing.
The Tenants were subject to a rental increase of $1,359.27 as of February 1, 2026 and therefore the remedies will be calculated accordingly.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

Determining appropriate remedies is often described as more of an art rather than a science. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], the Court remarked: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.

The Tenant, HMM tendered significant evidence regarding his injury. I find that it would be appropriate to order an abatement in the amount of 5% for the period of time of the injury being 6-months until fully rehabilitated. This abatement is calculated from March 1, 2024 until August 2024 and totals $389.64 [$1,298.86 x .05 x 6-months = $389.64.].

I also find that an abatement of 30% of rent for the periods May 31, 2025 – September 30, 2025 and May 1, 2026-June 30, 2026 for the A/C is appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenants provided substantial evidence to demonstrate that they continued to experience high temperatures in the summer months due to the A/C not working. I find that this substantially interfered with the Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the rental unit during warmer months
Therefore, the amount owing to the Tenant’s is $3,685.12 [($1,298.86 x 30% x 5 months = $1,948.30) + ($1,359.27 x 30% x 2 months= $815.56) = $2,763.86].

I find that the automatic garage door has not been repaired since the July 3, 2024 order. Therefore, I will order a 5% rent abatement for a 12-month from July 3, 2024 – August 2, 2025. I am awarding a relatively low amount because I find that there is minimal disruption to the Tenants’ ability for use and occupation of the rental unit due to this issue. The Tenants failed to demonstrate a significant impact on their ability to use the garage door, and I find that it did not materially affect their normal use and enjoyment of the rental unit. I do find that tenancy agreement includes a functioning automatic garage door and the Tenants should not be deprived of this benefit. Therefore, the amount to the Tenants are entitled to is $1,298.86 x 5% x 12 months = $779.28.

Given the unjustified and lengthy delay in responding to the Tenants’ requests for maintenance and repair work, I am of the view it is appropriate to include in this order for the Landlord to repair the A/C and automatic garage door opener on or before June 30, 2026.
If Landlord fails to meet this condition, the Tenants may deduct 20% of the total monthly rent from the lawful monthly rent starting July 1, 2026 until the A/C and automatic garage door are repaired.

Section 30(7) of the Act states that the where it is determined that the Landlord has breached an obligation under section 20(1), the Board can prohibit the Landlord from giving a notice of rent increase until the Landlord has completed the specified repairs or other work ordered under paragraph 4 found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1). While I find the Landlords have breached section 20(1), I do not find it meets the definition of a serious breach and therefore I will not be issuing an order prohibiting rent increases.

The Tenants’ legal representative requested $5,000.00 in legal fees. Despite seeking submissions on this request, there were no submissions provided. As such, I do not find that it would be appropriate to award this request.

The Tenants have requested that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent cease intimidation by swearing and being disrespectful, be calm upon entry to the home and provide minimum 24-hour notice to enter the rental unit. I am not prepared to order the remedy sought. While all parties within a landlord and tenant relationship are encouraged to be courteous and polite, I cannot order the remedies as requested. Additionally, as outlined in sections 26 & 27 of the Actr the Landlords are already required to provide lawful notice before entering. Administrative fine

The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine. The Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16 provides guidance about the Board’s use of fines. It states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It further provides that the remedy is not usually imposed “unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”. I find that the Landlords in this case were ordered to repair or replace issues alleged in this application in a prior Board order and did not comply with that order. The Landlords made only one attempt to attend the rental unit to repair the A/C.

At the hearing of this application before the Board the Landlords were in no way repentant for its behaviour and continued to argue it was the fault of the Tenants. I find that the Landlords showed blatant disregard for a prior Board order and a fine is necessary to discourage this type of conduct. Even though the previous orders directed the Landlords to repair or replace the A/C and automatic garage door the Landlords have failed to comply with the prior Board’s order. Therefore, I am imposing an administrative fine of $250.00.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant’s $3,980.78 by June 30, 2026. This amount represents: • $3,932.78 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant’s the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

Should the Landlord fail to make the payment in accordance with paragraph 1, the Tenant’s shall be permitted to deduct $500/month from the rent starting on July 1, 2026 and continuing until the amount has been satisfied.
The Landlord shall also ensure that the air conditioning and automatic garage door is in working condition on or before July 15, 2026.

If the air conditioning and automatic garage door are not in working condition by July 15, 2026, the Tenants may deduct 20% from their rent for the months of August and September 2026. The Tenants may deduct 5% from their lawful month rent starting on October 1, 2026 should the automatic garage door not be repaired. When the A/C and automatic garage door are repaired or replaced the Tenants must cease deducting any amounts from their lawful monthly rent.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $250.00 by June 30, 2026. June 19, 2026 ____________________________
