issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The issues in this application are: did the Tenants unilaterally try to cancel the tenancy agreement with the Landlord (and if they did, what remedy if any are they entitled to); or did the Landlord fail to give possession of the rental unit to the Tenants?
For the reasons that follow the Landlord is order to pay to the Tenants $3,650.00.

O n November 27, 2025, the Tenants entered into a fixed term tenancy agreement for the period December 29, 2025, to December 29, 2026. The lease agreement says: 1. The Tenants are entitled to serve legal notices on the Landlord by sending e-mails to [email]; 2. The lawful monthly rent is $1,800.00 and the Tenants were to pay first and last month’s rent in advance plus $50.00 for a refundable key deposit.
There is no dispute that prior to December 29, 2025, the Tenants paid to the Landlord $3,650.00 which represents first and last month’s rent and the $50.00 refundable key deposit.

On December 18, 2025, the Tenants sent an e-mail to the Landlord using the e-mail address he provided for service of documents in the lease. It says one of the Tenants was laid off unexpectedly and the Tenants wanted to negotiate an end to the lease prior to its commencement.

The Landlord says he did not see this e-mail as it went into his spam folder. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) whether the Landlord saw this e-mail or not is not legally relevant. I say this for the following reasons.

Subsection 191(1)(g) of the Act says a notice or document is sufficiently given to a person other than the Board by any means allowed in the Rules. Rule 3.1h says service by email is acceptable if the person or party receiving it has consented in writing to service by email. This means that because the Landlord consented in writing to service of documents by e-mail in the lease, the e-mail notice sent on December 18, 2025, was “sufficiently given” for all legal purposes by the Tenants even if the Landlord did not actually see it.

This conclusion is reinforced by s. 191(2) of the Act which says a notice or document that is not given in accordance with this section shall be deemed to have been validly given if it is proven that its contents actually came to the attention of the person for whom it was intended. In other words, the only time the Tenants would need to prove the Landlord actually received the e-mail was if he had not consented to service by email.

On December 22, 2025, the Tenants sent another e-mail which stated that if the Landlord would not agree to terminate the lease, the Tenants would still proceed with the tenancy, and the keys were requested.

On December 29, 2025, the Landlord says he was in the unit waiting for the Tenants to appear, but it is not clear to me if that is true or not, or even relevant. I say this because on January 10, 2026, the Landlord finally responded to one of the e-mails sent by the Tenant. It says in part: “You did not call me to get the keys for December 29th, and I could only assume you were abandoning your lease... I had to re-list the condo and it's not rented until February now.” I take this to mean that by January 10, 2026, the Landlord had re- rented the unit and was not willing to give the keys to the Tenants.

The reason this is important is because of the wording of s. 107(1) which says: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. [Emphasis added.]

The Landlord’s failure to check the email they provided led to the communication breakdown. By failing to actively offer the keys to the Tenants on or after December 29, 2025, the Landlord failed to deliver vacant possession to the Tenants and is liable to repay to the Tenants the amount received as a deposit.
The deposits paid here were the last month’s rent deposit of $1,800.00 and the refundable key deposit of $50.00. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay those amounts to the Tenants.

That leaves the first month’s rent of $1,800.00. By failing to offer the keys to the Tenants the Landlord essentially repudiated the tenancy unilaterally just like the Tenants tried to do in their original e-mail of December 18, 2025. In other words, the Landlord’s behaviour constitutes an implied agreement to terminate the tenancy. As there was no tenancy, no rent is payable.
As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants the amount requested in the application totalling $3,650.00.
Finally, the Tenants paid $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of that cost from the Landlord.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,650.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $5,048.00.
The residential unit is a single detached dwelling. The Tenant vacated the house on February 15, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] [name] (SC)

SC testified that he received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on November 29, 2024 with a termination date of February 15, 2025. The Tenant stated that the notice showed that the Landlord, her spouse, her child and her parent would be moving into the rental unit.

The Tenant, his spouse and his two teenage daughters voluntarily left the house based on the notice of termination. SC stated that they ultimately purchased a house although they did not get to save sufficient money prior to buying the house.

The Tenant stated that he attended at the rental house on March 5, 2025 to check to see if any of his mail had been delivered there and he met the new tenants who were residing in the rental unit. SC stated that the new tenants provided them with a copy of their lease showing that they moved into the unit in March of 2025. A copy of that lease was entered into as evidence.
Further, the Tenant provided a copy of a rental advertisement for the rental unit dated February 19, 2025 which showed that the unit was being rented out for $3,000.00 per month.
The Tenant stated that he was very angry that he and his family were forced out of their home and that he sent a message to the Landlord but received no response.

SC stated that when they resided in the rental unit, their daughters were bussed to and from school and now at their new house there are no buses for the girls to travel to school. SC stated that his wife must now stay up after her midnight shift to drive the girls to school every day.

The Tenant stated that they had to incur moving expenses of $1,800.00 which he paid cash for as the mover was a friend. He also stated that he had to re-wire the dog kennel at an expense of $500.00 and he provided a receipt for this cost.

The Tenant is seeking compensation of $15,000.00 due to the fact that they had to purchase a house earlier than they planned, the issues with the lack of bussing of the girls, the stress and emotional upset of moving and the girls’ emotional stress and tension. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I must determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence and corroborating rental listing confirms that the Landlord advertised the rental building for rent on February 19, 2025, 4 days after the Tenant vacated. Further, the lease with the new tenants confirmed that the Landlords are not residing in the rental unit.
Based on the above, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave this notice to the Tenant in bad faith.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with his T5 application. Remedies

The Tenant requested moving and storage costs in the amount of $1,800.00 and a dog kennel re-wiring cost of $500.00. Although the Tenant provided a receipt for the dog kennel, I am not satisfied that this expense is an appropriate claim and am denying this claim. Regarding the moving expense of $1,800.00, no invoice was provided and as such, no amount will be awarded for moving expenses. 16. The Tenant requested compensation of $15,000.00 due to the Tenant’s submission that he was forced to purchase a house before he planned, the problems he incurred with his daughters’ transportation to school, the stress and interruption of moving and the resulting effects that it had on his daughters’ emotional health. It is of course unfortunate that this move caused the Tenant’s daughters emotional stress and I am sure that everyone would have been affected in one way or another. However, no specific information was provided to substantiate such a high award for compensation. 17. Having considered the circumstances in this case, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $5,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,048.00. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant’s amended application is based on various allegations concerning interactions with other tenants on the residential complex as well as lack of heat for two days in January 2025. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant testified that in November 2024, new tenants moved into another unit located in the same house as the rental unit. At the time the new tenants moved in there was an understanding that the Tenant and new tenants would share the laundry room.

On December 25, 2024, she woke up to a loud outburst from the new tenant. On December 27, 2024, she had an interaction with the new tenant who was verbally abusive. The Tenant immediately notified the Landlord of the issue as the Tenant was scared from the incident. At the same time, the Tenant informed the Landlord that the new tenants had changed the lock to their unit which prevented the Tenant from access to the laundry room. The Landlord never subsequently provided the Tenant access to the laundry.

On December 30, 2024, the new tenant’s dog was barking and howling for a long period of time. The Tenant found out the new tenant was in the hospital and had left the dog unattended. Once the new tenant returned to the rental unit the barking and howling subsided.

In early January 2025, the heat went out for two days. The Landlord provided the Tenant with space heaters for the period but the Tenant had specifically asked for a hotel accommodation that was never provided.
On January 17, 2025, the new tenant was playing their music very loudly. The Tenant felt threatened.

On March 20, 2025, due to the new tenant’s actions and the Landlord’s inability to control the new tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant is seeking 100% rent abatement from December 25, 2024 to March 20, 2025. The Tenant is also seeking different in rent for one year and moving expenses of $1,243.00. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord testified that he did everything he could to make the Tenant happy. When he was informed of the incidents involving the new tenant, he asked the Tenant to document everything including recorded noise. The Tenant did not ever send him any records involving proof of the new tenant’s actions.

The Landlord testified that he spoke to the new tenant about lowering the noise on two occasions, assuming this corrected the problem. Additionally, the Landlord admitted to having knowledge about the new tenant changing the lock which prohibited the Tenant from access to laundry.

The Landlord also testified about the heat going out for two days, confirming that he provided space heaters to the Tenant. He had an electrician inspect the residential complex, who recommended he replace some fixtures although it was not a requirement. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the evidence and submissions at the hearing, I cannot find that Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as it relates to the altercations of the new tenant. I accept the evidence of the Landlord that he spoke to the new tenant and did not hear further complaints from the Tenant, therefore he believed the situation was resolved. Furthermore, I accept that evidence of the Landlord that he asked the Tenant to provide recordings of any further incidents, and the Tenant failed to provide any evidence of further wrongdoing by the new tenant. It is unclear from the evidence what the Tenant wanted the Landlord to do in the circumstances given the actions already taken.

Regarding the heat, I do not find that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable in the circumstances. There was no evidence that the Landlord could foresee an issue with the heat. It appears on its face that the Landlord acted reasonable by providing the Tenant space heaters for two days, and the issue was rectified in a quick timeframe.

Regarding the laundry room, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit [name] complex. The Landlord admitted that he was aware the Tenant did not have access to the laundry however did not rectify the issue. It is reasonable to conclude that failure to have access to laundry interferes with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant entered receipts for the local laundromat into evidence which totalled expenses of $208.13. Furthermore, I find it reasonable that the Tenant be awarded a rent abatement of 5% from December 27, 2024 to March 20, 2025 due to the lack of use of the laundry. The monthly rent was $800.00, therefore 5% rent abatement during this period totals $109.15.

Despite this, I do not find it appropriate to award the Tenant compensation for vacating the rental unit. The finding involving the laundry does not rise to the level of substantial interference that would terminate the tenancy early nor would it attract compensation other than what was previously described.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $365.28. This amount represents: • $208.13 for out-of-pocket expenses relating to laundry; • $109.15 as a rent abatement; and • $48.00 application fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the last month’s rent deposit (‘LMR’) and the key deposit.

The Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice with a termination date of February 12, 2026, because he was selling the rental unit.

On December 31, 2026, the Tenants notified the Landlord of their intention to move out of the rental unit on January 10, 2026. This is permitted under the Act because once a tenant receives an N12 notice, sections 49(4)-(5) provide that they may terminate the tenancy at any time with at least 10 days notice to the landlord.

Section 49.1 of the Act requires landlords to compensate tenants an amount equal to one month’s rent when terminating a tenancy on behalf of a purchaser. The Tenants last paid the $2,600 monthly rent in November 2025. Their understanding was that the one month’s rent compensation would be satisfied by providing a rent credit for December rent, with the LMR being applied to the January rent.

The Landlord argues that the LMR was applied to December and the one month’s rent compensation was applied to January. The Landlord testified that he did not return any money to the Tenants because he had to pay condominium fees, property taxes, and insurance for the month of January.

The Act does not permit rent deposits to be applied to fees, taxes, or insurance. The Act requires LMR to only be applied to the last month of the tenancy. In this case, the LMR should have been applied to January 2026.

The Tenants terminated the tenancy and returned vacant possession to the Landlord on January 10, 2026, so they are entitled to the return of the portion of the LMR for the period of January 11-31, 2026. Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $85.48. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,600 x 12, divided by 365 days. The total amount of unreturned deposit is $1,795.08.
There is no dispute that the Tenants paid a $200 key deposit to the Landlord and returned the keys to the Landlord. This deposit is to be refunded to the Tenants.

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. Therefore, the Landlord is required to pay the interest that has accrued since the deposit was collected January 1, 2022.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,169.38. This amount represents: • $1,795.08 for the portion of the last month's rent deposit that was unlawfully retained • $126.30 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $200.00 for the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 15, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $248.00.
The Tenants claim that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Evidence and Analysis

The Tenant testified that the tenancy began on February 28, 2021. The Tenants stated the rent was $1,913.82 per month and that they paid a key deposit of $200.00 prior to moving in. The Tenants submitted a copy of the cheque noting the term “key deposit” in the memo section, which was provided to the Landlord confirming that the Tenants paid this amount.

The Tenants testified that they vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025. The Tenants testified that they entered into an agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy and they vacated the rental unit in accordance with that agreement. The Tenants testified that upon moving out of the unit, their key deposit was never refunded by the Landlord. The Tenants submitted a text message confirming that they vacated the unit and a request to obtain a refund of the key deposit which was replied to and acknowledged by the Landlord.

The Tenants further testified that they have tried to get into contact with the Landlord to get a refund of their key deposit, but the Landlord informed them they were retaining the funds as a damage deposit. The Tenants then stated that upon vacating the unit, the Landlord did a walkthrough with them and stated nothing needing to be repaired was outside of normal wear and tear.

The Tenants have filed a T1 application pursuant to section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The T1 is an application for an order that the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.

Section 134(1) of the Act states that unless otherwise provided, a landlord shall not directly or indirectly collect certain listed charges from a tenant in addition to rent. The provision specifically lists a key deposit as a prohibited charge, whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of the General regulation [name]. 516/06, provides a list of exemptions from section 134 of the Act, including a “payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”. According to this provision, a key or fob deposit must be refundable.

When read together, section 134 of the Act and 17 of the regulation prohibit a landlord from retaining a key deposit after the key has been returned at the end of the tenancy. Even if the key deposit was initially collected legally pursuant to section 17 of the regulation, the deposit must be refundable.

At the end of the tenancy, the Tenants did not receive a refund of this key deposit. While refundable key deposits are permissible pursuant to the Act, the Tenants never received the refundable key deposit upon terminating the tenancy, vacating the unit, and returning the keys even after requesting the same. Accordingly, the Landlord has retained the deposit illegally and they will be required to return the $200.00 key deposit the Tenants paid.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $925.00 which represents the unlawfully retained last month’s rent deposit. However, for the reasons that follow, the Tenant’s request for the Landlord to pay the Tenants for the cost of this application is denied.

The parties agreed to the following facts: • The Tenants paid a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,500.00 at the outset of the tenancy. • The Tenants vacated the rental unit on November 30, 2025. • $1,125.00 was paid for the last month of the tenancy, November 2025 • $375.00 of the last month’s rent deposit was applied to the month of November 2025 and $200.00 was returned to the Tenants, with the remaining $925.00 being retained by the landlord.
The Landlord did not dispute that he is currently retaining an amount of $925.00 which was not returned to the Tenants or applied to the last month of the tenancy.

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that “a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a Tenant has paid to the Landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.”

As the Tenants paid short for the last month of the tenancy in the amount of $375.00, I find that it was not inappropriate for the Landlord to apply $375.00 of the last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy.

Section 134(1) of the Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

It was undisputed between the parties that the Landlord had offered to pay the Tenants in cash and had offered to deliver the cash directly to the Tenants subsequent to the Tenants vacating the rental unit. The Landlord testified that as he has had difficulties with electronic banking, he was not comfortable sending an e-transfer.

The Tenants assert they refused to accept the Landlord’s offer to pay them in cash as they were concerned about counterfeiting and not having a paper record of the payment. However, there was no evidence before me that there was any credibility to the assumption that the Landlord would provide counterfeit money or defraud the Tenants.

The Landlord submits that he should not be liable for the Tenants’ filing fee as the fee arose out of the Tenants’ unreasonable conduct. The Tenants sought an order requiring the Landlord to reimburse the Tenants for the cost of filing this application.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 states: As a general principle, a Member should not order costs of any kind in favour of a party if the conduct of that party was not proper. If both parties were responsible for the unreasonable conduct, neither should be ordered to pay the costs to the other, although one or both may be ordered to pay the Board’s costs.

In this case, the Tenants chose not to accept the return of the last month’s rent deposit without any reasonable basis for the refusal and chose to file this application. I am satisfied that the Tenants’ conduct was unreasonable in the circumstances and as a result, decline to award the filing fee.

However, the Landlord did not use the Tenants' rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and has not return the deposit to the Tenants. The Landlord shall be ordered to return the remaining balance of the filing fee in the amount of $925.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $925.00. This amount represents: • $925.00 for the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Board received numerous post-hearing submissions from the Tenant. As they were unsolicited and post-hearing, they have not been considered in my determinations.
As explained below, the Tenant’s application did not contain sufficient details or name the proper Landlord and therefore is dismissed.

The Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931).

Although the [name] case related to the details required in a landlord’s notice of termination, it reflects the general principles of procedural fairness, which include a party’s right to know the case to be met. I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as I find it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient details of the issues to determine whether to defend the claim.

In this case, the parties were before the Board on August 18, 2025, for an Adjudicative Case Conference (“ACC”) and the Tenant was informed that he had improperly named an employee as the Landlord instead of the actual Landlord, Toronto Community Housing Corporation, and that his application needed to be amended.

An interim order was issued on August 20, 2025, highlighting the improperly named Landlord. Furthermore, the order indicated at paragraph 3 of the order section that the Tenant had until October 5, 2025, to amend his application to change who was listed as the Landlord, provide dates of the events, clarify claims, or for any other reasons and that failure to do so may result in claims being dismissed.

The Tenant did not make any amendments to his application. As such, the Tenant’s application remains as it was originally filed. For example, reason 4 is checked off and the explanation says only “[name] and other tenants”. The other reasons are equally brief with no dates or details.

The Landlord’s Representative confirmed that an amended application was never received by the Landlord and Toronto Community Housing Corporation was never properly named as the Landlord on the application. The Landlord’s Representative provided that as the application stands first, the proper Landlord is not named and therefore cannot properly respond. Second, there are insufficient details contained in the application for the Landlord, whether properly named or not, to be able to know the case to be met and to properly respond.

The Tenant testified that he did not amend the application because he was told at the ACC that the Board was going to send him a “form” to change his application and was waiting for the “form” to change the application and he never received it. But he was supposed to provide all the evidence he had for his claims before the hearing, and he did so.

However, the Tenant was able to email the Board approximately 31 separate times between October 9, 2025, and June 3, 2026. The Tenant testified that he has provided the Board with over 600 pages of documents to support his claim. The Tenant could not provide anywhere in those 600 pages an amended application, with the properly named Landlord or more sufficiently detailed claims.

I am not satisfied that the Board was sending the Tenant anything other than the Interim Order and I am satisfied that the Interim Order was properly served to the Tenant. The Tenant had consented to service via email, and the Interim Order was emailed to the Tenant on August 20, 2025. Furthermore, if the Tenant was waiting for something from the Board like he claims, I find it unusual that he was able to email the Board approximately 31 times between October 31, 2025, and June 3, 2026, but not once did he follow up on whatever “form” he was apparently waiting for.

Ultimately it is the Tenant’s responsibility to perfect their own application, and the Tenant was put on notice at the ACC that he needed to take steps to amend the application to change who the listed Landlord was as well as to provide more sufficient reasons and details for each of his claims. The Tenant has failed to do so. The Tenant was unable to provide an adequate reason for failing to take the necessary steps to clarify his claims and name the proper Landlord after being made aware at the ACC that these were necessary steps. I am not persuaded that the Board was sending a “form” other than the Interim order, which was properly served to the Tenant.
As such, I find that the Tenant’s application has a complete lack of detail and does not name the proper Landlord, and it would be procedurally unfair to allow the hearing to proceed.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants are seeking the return of their last month’s rent deposit (LMR) because they believe the Landlord was receiving both rental income and applying the Tenants’ LMR for the month of December 2025.
There is no dispute that the parties entered into a one-year fixed term tenancy for the period of June 15, 2025, to June 14, 2026, and the Tenants paid a rent deposit of $2,170.
Monthly rent was due on the first of the month and the Tenants paid the November 2025 rent.
The Tenants terminated the tenancy and returned vacant possession to the Landlord on December 8, 2025.

The Tenants allege that new Tenants moved into the rental unit on December 8, 2025. Tenant JH testified the Tenants observed lights on in the rental unit when they drove past, and current tenants had sent text messages that the rental unit was occupied. The Tenants submitted screenshots of text messages, but no witnesses were present to provide evidence at the hearing. I gave this hearsay evidence very little weight.

The Landlord testified that they re-rented the unit effective January 1, 2026. Contractors were hired to clean and paint the rental unit in preparation for the new tenants and some of this work was carried out in the evenings to accommodate the holiday season.

I accept the Landlord’s direct evidence that they did not re-rent the unit until January 1, 2026, over the Tenants’ hearsay evidence that the unit was rented earlier. Because the Tenants did not terminate the tenancy in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), they were responsible for rent up until the Landlord re-rented the unit: see sections 88(1), 88(3)-(4) of the Act. The deposit was applied for the month of December, and therefore the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________

LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 These applications were heard by videoconference on May 12, 2026. The Landlord’s agent [name], the Landlord's Legal Representative Crystal Sankey, the Tenant and the Tenant's Legal Representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw the T1 application LTB-T-013071-23, without opposition, and I consented to the request.

As context, in the T1 the Tenant alleged that the Landlord had unlawfully charged him $9,898.78, representing the costs to repair damage to the garage door of the residential complex, the damage of which the Landlord blamed on the Tenant’s negligent conduct.

A tenant may file a T1 to recover amounts paid to the landlord for an illegal charge. The parties agree that the Tenant never paid any of that amount. The Tenant's Legal Representative correctly submits that there is no cause of action. T2 application [LTB-T-007915-23]

The illegal charge forms part of the basis for the T2 application. In the T2, the Tenant complained that the Landlord attempted to collect the repair costs from him without an LTB order and without legal basis, and that this conduct substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment and constituted harassment.
The following facts are not disputed.

On February 2, 2022, the Tenant’s vehicle collided with the garage door leading to residents’ underground parking. On February 4, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a letter informing him that “the reported damage may be billable to your account”.

On May 3, 2022, the Landlord mailed a demand letter, attaching repair invoices, to the Tenant requiring him to pay $9,898.78 by May 20, 2022. The Landlord then sent the Tenant a reminder on June 3, 2022, alleging he owed that amount in rent arrears.
On June 9, 2022, the Landlord gave an N4 notice of termination claiming rent arrears of $1.431.98 for June 2022. The Tenant provided proof that he had paid the rent.

On September 14, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a second N4 notice, asserting that the arrears had accumulated to $5,727.92. Although the Tenant had paid the rent from June 1, 2022 to September 30, 2022, the Landlord had applied those payments to reduce the repair costs (leaving an outstanding balance of $4,170.86 as a chargeback).

The Landlord gave the Tenant a voidable N5 notice of termination on January 27, 2023, with a termination date of February 16, 2023. By the hearing date, the Landlord had removed the $9,878.78 chargeback from the Tenant’s account ledger, choosing instead to pursue their L2 application based on the N5 notice. The T6/L2 hearing process
Some of the facts and issues in the T6 and L2 applications are in dispute.

The parties agreed to proceed with the applications in a consolidated manner given the extensive overlap in facts and issues. The Tenant testified first on the T6 and was cross- LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 examined. The Landlord’s evidence was treated as both its response to the T6 and its L2 evidence, and the Landlord’s witness was cross-examined by the Tenant’s representative. T6 application [LTB-T-007915-23]
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.

The Tenant claims that on February 2, 2022, the Landlord failed to maintain the pavement leading up to the entrance of the underground parking garage free from ice. He contends that this failure resulted in his vehicle accidentally damaging the garage door. L2 application [LTB-L-013352-23]
The Landlord claims that the Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage of $9,898.78 to the garage door.

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord asked to amend the application to solely claim financial compensation for negligent damage under subsection 89(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Accordingly, the tenancy shall continue and this order addresses only the financial liability for the damaged garage door.
For the following reasons, the Landlord’s application is dismissed. The uncontested facts
The Tenant moved into Unit #704 in the high-rise residential complex on January 1, 2016.

On February 2, 2022, when he was driving home from work, at approximately 6:40 a.m. the Tenant entered the underground parking garage from the street. But before he could enter the interior of the garage, his vehicle crashed into the closed garage door.

The Tenant reported the situation to the Landlord’s after-hours line, leaving a message that his vehicle had slid down an icy ramp into the door. He asked how he could get into the garage. He then observed a tenant exiting the garage in their vehicle, approached them and, with their assistance, was able to drive his vehicle into the garage.

There was a bucket of salt in the interior of the garage near the door; the Tenant spread salt on the driveway before proceeding to park in his allotted space. He spoke later that morning with the Landlord’s agent [name] who confirmed that the Landlord had not salted the entrance ramp the previous night or in the early morning hours.

The Tenant’s verbal report to the Landlord was transcribed to an incident report completed by the Landlord’s employee M.D. (later amended by J.C.N. to identify the Tenant). It states that, “Due to ice the tenant slid into the overhead door, as a result the door will not open”.

The Landlord’s Community Manager [name] testified that he was he was informed about “the accident” when he arrived at work at 8:00 a.m. The incident was captured on the Landlord’s surveillance camera mounted in the interior of the garage. 24. [name] viewed the surveillance camera footage and arranged to have IDS Doors Cambridge remove the door for safety reasons. He attended the scene later to take photographs; although the time was not precise, he thought it was likely around 2:00 p.m. when they applied salt to various outside areas. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 25. The Landlord's Legal Representative presented the footage of the collision. It shows the night sky, the Tenant driving onto the ramp and the moment of impact. The force of the impact caused the garage door to partially disconnect from the mechanical track and the overhead guiderails collapsed. The door then hung tenuously from the track. 26. The photos provided by the Landlord show a concrete entry ramp that slopes downward (the gradient was not readily known). Prior to the incident, the garage door was in good working condition. 27. The Landlord keeps maintenance logs. [name] presented a log which consists of data an employee recorded between February 1 and 3, 2022, as follows: • February 1st: “partly cloudy”, the outside temperature was -8 degrees Celsius in the morning, 1 degree at noon and 4 degrees in the afternoon; • February 2nd: “snow showers”, the outside temperature was 2 degrees Celsius in the morning, 1 degree at noon and 0 degrees in the afternoon; and • February 2nd: “cloudy”, the sidewalks were salted at 2:00 p.m., 4:30 p.m., 6:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. and shoveled at 6:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. 28. The Landlord salted the sidewalks four times between 2:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. on February 2nd because, according to [name], the temperature was still a bit warm and ice was melting. By 6:00 p.m. it had been snowing enough that walkways needed shoveling. 29. The Landlord uses a third-party contractor to remove snow and ice on the driveway unless there is a small amount, in which case the Landlord will shovel/salt that area. The log shows that winter maintenance was not performed on the “Driveway” (the entrance ramp) on February 1, 2 or 3, 2022. There are no entries logged for the rest of February 2022. 30. The Landlord submitted a weather summary from WeatherSpark.com for the period 5:00 p.m. on February 1, 2022 to 7:00 a.m. on February 2, 2022. It shows that at 1:41 a.m. on February 2, 2022, there was “light rain”, and the temperature was 4 degrees Celsius. From 3:33 a.m., there was intermittent light rain until 6:00 a.m., with temperatures falling to 3 degrees Celsius by 6:39 a.m. For unknown reason, the list does not describe the “Weather” (rain, snow etc.) at 6:39 a.m. in contrast to the previous entries. 31. Final repairs to the garage door were completed by Waterloo Garage Doors Inc. on February 7, 2022, at a cost of $9,605.00. The facts in dispute 32. The Tenant’s evidence is that the roads were somewhat icy and that it was dark and raining when he approached the underground garage entrance. 33. He described his usual practice of slowly driving down the ramp, applying his brakes, pressing the remote to open the garage door, and waiting the 10 to 20 seconds required for the door to open. He also testified that he had winter tires installed on his vehicle in November, approximately three months before the incident. 34. He stated that, on this occasion, when he applied his brakes the vehicle lost traction on a thin layer of ice and slid forward into the large door. He testified that he attempted to reverse several times while the vehicle continued to skid but he was eventually able to back up and drive off the ramp. He believes freezing rain created icy conditions on the LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 driveway. His position is that the Landlord failed to carry out timely winter maintenance and that this caused the collision, which he says was accidental. 35. The Landlord disputes this, arguing that the Tenant has not proven that icy conditions were present. They submit that, even if there was ice present and the Tenant had winter tires, there is insufficient evidence regarding the condition of the tires. The Landlord maintains that, with proper driving and braking, the Tenant should have been able to exercise enough control to avoid ramming the door, and that the collision resulted either from excessive speed or a failure to brake appropriately, amounting to negligence. 36. The Landlord further contends that the garage entrance was properly maintained in accordance with the weather conditions on February 2, 2022. Relying on its maintenance log, the Landlord asserts that the driveway was relatively dry and free of ice. Analysis T6 application 37. Section 20 of the Act requires the Landlord to properly maintain common areas, including driveways and ramps. This requires proactive, diligent maintenance to reduce and minimize snow and ice buildup, particularly on inclines where the risk of vehicle slippage is highly foreseeable.1 38. The Tenant gave credible evidence that the ramp was covered in nearly invisible ‘glare’ ice when he arrived at the complex in the early morning of February 2, 2022, as this became apparent when he applied his brakes. The video supports the vehicle losing traction and that the Tenant was only able to reverse with difficulty after several attempts, consistent with impaired traction and not inconsistent with the presence of ice. 39. The Landlord’s weather data is consistent with a freeze-thaw cycle capable of producing such ice. It is commonly understood that a concrete surface – such as the ramp – will absorb and retain cold for an extended time, causing water to freeze on contact even where air temperatures are just above freezing. This provides a plausible explanation for the presence of a thin layer of ice on the ramp at the time. There is also a concern that the data was capable of being edited, as someone has emphasized relevant data in bold type. 40. The surveillance video shows a reflective surface on the outside ramp, highlighted by the vehicle’s headlights, consistent with ice. I give minimal weight to the photographs the Landlord took later showing wet conditions as these are not contemporaneous. 41. The Landlord did not dispute that the ramp was not salted or sanded within a reasonable time before the incident. The log referenced shows no such work was done until approximately seven hours afterward. The absence of entries for the rest of February 2022 also raises concerns about whether the log is complete and concurrent. I find it of limited reliability; without verification by the person who completed it, the log cannot be entrusted to establish the condition of the ramp at the time of the incident. 42. The Landlord did not attend the site at the time of the incident or lead evidence from any witness who observed conditions around 6:30 a.m. I give little weight to [name]’s later 1 As reinforced by section 8 of the Occupiers' Liability Act,1990. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 observation that the ramp appeared relatively dry in photographs, as it cannot displace contemporaneous evidence of ice. 43. The Tenant’s position is that freezing rain was foreseeable had the Landlord prudently monitored the winter weather. He reasonably expected the Landlord to properly maintain the ramp to prevent ice-related mishaps. 44. I find that there was insufficient evidence produced to demonstrate that the driveway was free of ice, and the evidence points to the contrary. 45. Consequently, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to properly maintain the ramp free of ice. L2 application 46. The Landlord seeks an order requiring the Tenant to pay $9,878.78 for the cost of the garage door repairs. To succeed, the Landlord must prove on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage. 47. Finding a breach of maintenance obligations alone does not establish causation. 48. The issue to be determined is whether the damage was caused by the Tenant’s negligence, assessed against the standard of a reasonable winter driver, or by the Landlord’s failure to salt/sand the ramp leading up to the garage door. 49. The Landlord argues that the Tenant caused the damage by driving negligently. I am unable to find that the evidence supports this. 50. The Tenant’s evidence (i) that he discovered the ice only when he applied his brakes, and (ii) of his subsequent effort to salt the ramp, supports both the presence of ice and the absence of prior treatment. 51. I accept that the Tenant had winter tires on his vehicle, was driving at low speed, and reacted promptly. The Landlord’s submission that winter tires should have prevented the incident is not persuasive. While it is well-known that proper winter tires improve traction and reduce the risk of accidents, the Landlord has not introduced any objective evidence to establish that winter tires completely eliminate the risk of sliding on untreated ice. 52. In my view, loss of control due to slippery conditions, particularly on an untreated downward slope, is consistent with basic physics rather than negligence. Tires have nothing to grab onto; gravity takes over, dragging the vehicle down the icy slope towards the immovable structure – here, the garage door. 53. I place significant weight on the Landlord’s incident report attributing the collision to ice, which the Landlord did not dispute at the time, and on J.L.’s initial characterization of the incident as “an accident”. Their own evidence acknowledges the presence of icy conditions; [name] testified that salt was applied multiple times later that day beginning at approximately 2:00 p.m., to accelerate ice melting on the ground. 54. There is no evidence that the Landlord conducted a timely or thorough investigation into ice conditions or that they otherwise conducted a thorough investigation into the cause of the damage. They did not attend the scene, interview the Tenant or other witnesses, or verify conditions before alleging negligence. Instead, they relied on after-the-fact weather data and an unverified maintenance log. This further weakens the Landlord’s position. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 55. Based on all the evidence, I find that the collision resulted from the condition of the ramp, not negligence by the Tenant, and was therefore an accident. I am satisfied that, but for the Landlord’s failure to salt or sand the area, the Tenant’s vehicle would not have struck the garage door. As a tenant is not liable under the Act for damage arising from a faultless accident, the Landlord’s claim must fail. 56. The Landlord’s L2 application is dismissed. T2 portion of the T2/T6 application 57. It is undisputed that the Landlord treated the repair costs as rent, issued demands for payment, and used the threat of eviction to compel compliance. The N5 notice was served nearly one year after the incident and no reasonable explanation for the delay was given. The timing also closely follows the Tenant’s filing of his applications and raises a reasonable inference of retaliatory conduct. 58. Landlords are not entitled to engage in "self-help" financial remedies. That is, a landlord cannot unilaterally decide a tenant is liable for damage, add repair costs to a rent ledger, and characterize non-payment of the disputed damage as a lawful reason for eviction. The proper mechanism is to apply to the Board for an assessment of damage liability prior to penalizing the tenant. 59. By charging back the repair costs without an LTB order and using the eviction process to pressure the Tenant into paying for an incident caused by the Landlord's own maintenance failure, the Landlord engaged in substantial interference with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment and coercion, contrary to sections 22 and 23 of the Act. Remedies 60. The Tenant did not intend to pursue any of the remedies available under the Act, other than a request for a declaration that they are not responsible for the damage and for an order that the Landlord refrain from repeating similar breaches in future. 61. While the Act does not provide for stand-alone declaratory relief, the Board must determine liability when deciding the L2. For the reasons above, I have found the Tenant is not liable for the damage to the garage door. 62. Additionally, the Board routinely declines to order a landlord or a tenant to comply with the Act in future because the duty already exists in law and such orders would be too vague to enforce. The Board is not a supervisory authority. It is a creature of statute; once a final decision is issued, the Board is functus officio. 63. The Tenant's Legal Representative asked to amend the applications to seek a nominal rent abatement of $50.00 and, in the circumstances, such request is not unreasonable. Administrative fine 64. The [name] Interpretation Guideline 16 states that a fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter similar activity in the future. The Guideline permits a Member to order a fine even though it has not been requested in an application. 65. Although a fine was not pursued in this T2 application, I raised the issue with the parties. After hearing submissions, and in the circumstances, I am not inclined to impose a fine LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 even though the Landlord’s conduct, as an experienced corporate landlord, would ordinarily support the imposition of a significant fine. 66. I have considered that the incident appears to be isolated. The Landlord retains a third- party contractor for snow and ice removal, and it may be that it was performed inadequately or not at all in the hours leading up to the incident. While the use of a contractor does not relieve the Landlord of its responsibility to ensure that the ramp is properly treated, it is a mitigating factor. 67. The Board is satisfied that the Landlord understands that damage claims cannot be pursued without proper investigation and without an order of the Board. The Landlord is expected to ensure that proper investigations are conducted into damage claims and that those claims are pursued in accordance with the Act. Similar conduct in future may result in the imposition of a significant fine.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord submits that the wrong party has been named to the application. The Landlords named in the Tenant’s application were identified as [name] and Curran Property Management. However, the correct Landlord is [organization].
The Tenant does not contest amending the application to reflect the name of the Landlord.
Therefore, I granted the amendment to [organization]. The style of cause has been amended to reflect [organization]. Amended Application

The Tenant filed two subsequent amended applications. The most recent was filed with the Board on May 14, 2026. The first amended application sought $100.00 per month as an ongoing abatement, while the second amended application sought a total award of $2,900.00 as an abatement for the period between December 2023 and May 2026.
The Landlord was provided with a copy of the Tenant’s Requested amendment and did not make submissions about the proposed amendments.

I cannot find any prejudice in allowing the Tenant to amend their application. I find it appropriate to exercise my discretion to grant the amendment, and I am satisfied it is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.
The Tenant’s application has been amended to include a claim for abatement of $2,900.00. [name]

For the sake of clarity, the Landlord also has an application pursuant to an N5 notice of termination (File LTB-L-040882-24) which was heard at the same time as the Tenant’s application. Both applications involve the same circumstances pertaining to the kitchen countertop. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached their obligation under s.20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’); the Landlord alleges the Tenant caused the damage to the countertop pursuant to s.89(1) of the Act and substantially interfered with the Landlord’s lawful rights and privileges, pursuant to s.88.1 of the Act. Documentary evidence from both applications has been referred to in this order and identified as ‘L’ for Landlord evidence and ‘T’ for Tenant evidence.

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $152.61 and repair or replace the kitchen countertop.
By way of background, the tenancy began in August 2022. The rental unit is a one- bedroom apartment.

When the Tenant moved into the rental unit, he requested several repairs be made to the rental unit (T Doc-7988744, pg 6). These requests were made to Tyler, who was the carpenter who regularly worked for the Landlord conducting repairs such as the ones the Tenant asked for. The message was dated August 5, 2022, and reads:

When “Tyler” attended the rental unit on or about August 5, 2022, to undertake the repairs, the Tenant spoke to him about the countertop. Tyler apparently told him that the Landlord would not repair this. However, the other repairs were done which was confirmed by the Tenant during cross-examination. The Landlord also repaired items which were not listed in the August 5, 2022 text message including replacing the fridge, stove, and adding/replacing a medicine cabinet.
The Tenant says that after that, he decided to just try to deal with it. He tried to glue the piece down, but that did not work. Eventually, he used duct tape to stick the pieces down.

Over a year later, the Tenant required a new fridge. The Landlord ordered the fridge in November 2023. When the new fridge arrived, it was larger than the old fridge so it would not fit into the space between the countertop and the wall. The Tenant did not want to give up the new, larger fridge and kept it (L Doc-4556548, pg 1). However, he asked if he could have a new countertop which would extend over the space where the fridge had been. This would solve two problems, allowing him to have more counterspace, and address the problem with the seam which had lifted.

The Tenant made multiple requests for a replacement countertop in November and December 2023. Several times indicated he would replace it himself, but the Landlord refused and repeatedly warned the Tenant he was not to make alterations to the kitchen. (L Doc-4556548, pgs 1,2,5,8,9).

The Landlord’s Agent, CC, is the owner of the property management company who oversees the operations of the building, including repairs. CC says she did discuss the [name] requested repair with Tyler, but that [name] advised it was unnecessary as the entire kitchen was only about 10 years old. CC’s oral testimony was that this conversation took place on January 9, 2024. However, CC says the kitchen countertop was not broken when the fridge was ordered.

The Landlord says that the Tenant did not advise them of the needed repairs until December 7, 2023. Before this, the Landlord says the Tenant had sent about 25 e-mails between November 2023 and December 2023 asking for a new countertop but never mentioned that it was damaged. She believes the Tenant attempted to take off the old countertop which damaged the seam after which he applied the duct tape. The Tenant agrees that the duct tape worsened the damage but says that duct tape should not have pulled up the laminate unless it was damaged to begin with. He believes the damage was caused by the previous tenants because other items in the unit were damaged when he moved in.

On December 20, 2023, the Tenant wrote CC referencing the damage to the countertop. A plan was made for CC to attend the rental unit on January 9, 2024. CC observed the duct tape and saw there were “bumps” underneath the tape. She explained that the bumps, she assumed, were tiny portions of broken countertop. However, before she could take off the tape or conduct any further investigations, the Tenant told her to leave his unit. The Tenant has refused entry to CC ever since. Since the Tenant refuses entry, she cannot fix the issue.

CC asserts that when she was made aware of the issue, she responded in a timely, reasonable, and efficient manner. She learned of the requested repair on December 20, 2023, and attended January 9, 2024. She attempted again in early May 2026 to gain access and was again refused.

The questions the Board must answer are: • When was the Landlord told about the requested repair? • Did the Landlord breach s. 20(1) of the Act? • How do limitation periods apply to situation and the remedy sought? • What is the appropriate remedy? When was Landlord told about the requested repair?

I find that the Tenant told [name] about the requested repair to the countertop on August 5, 2022. I say this because the Tenant gave oral testimony about the conversation he had with Tyler about the countertop when [name] was in the rental unit. I also accept the documentary evidence of the screenshot of a text message dated August 5, 2022, sent to [name] itemizing requested repairs.
Landlord is defined in s.2 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), and includes the “heirs, assigns, personal representatives…” of the owner of a rental unit.

The Landlord denies receipt of the request for the repair before December 20, 2023. However, I am of the view that the Tenant was entitled to rely on the request he made to [name] because Tyler was an acting as an agent for the Landlord when he attended to do repairs in early August 2022. CC’s evidence was that [name] had been doing the repairs for the Landlord for about 14 years.

When [name] attended the rental unit in early August 2022, Tyler did repairs, such as replacing a broken mirror. In my view, it would be logical for the Tenant to then ask Tyler about the peeling countertop. There was logical correlation between the repairs [name] was sent to do and the Tenant’s repair request. In my view, a reasonable tenant would assume that they could ask an individual sent by the Landlord about other repairs they wanted done when they were already there doing similar repairs.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

Although CC states she was not aware until December 2023 of the damage to the countertop, I find it is more likely than not that they knew about the Tenant’s request for maintenance to the kitchen countertop as of August 5, 2022, when the Tenant sent the text message to Tyler.

I find CC’s testimony lacks reliability. I say this because her oral testimony was that she attended the rental unit on January 9, 2024, and observed the duct tape and saw “bumps” underneath which she believed to be small chips of the countertop surface. However, CC wrote to the Tenant on January 15, 2024, “Tyler has no idea what you are referring to, he said there is nothing wrong with the counter” (L Doc-4556548, pg 12). These statements contradict each other. CC observed the tape and broken pieces of countertop on January 9, 2024, but CC then says [name] is unaware of the problem when she wrote on January 15, 2024.

Another example where I find CC’s testimony lacks reliability is regarding her statement that she was not aware of the Tenant’s request to fix the countertop until December 2023. CC says that the countertop was not broken when the fridge was ordered which was in about November 2023. However, it is not clear to me how CC would know whether there was a problem with the countertop in November 2023. CC gave no evidence as to how she came to believe this.

Further, the Tenant’s evidence demonstrates that multiple other requests for maintenance were made when he moved in; for example, the mirror in the bathroom was broken, closet doors needed repair, and the medicine cabinet was repaired/replaced. [name] was aware of these repairs, and these repairs were done, including some not even noted in the August 5, 2022, text message. Yet CC says she was unaware of the damaged countertop even though this was listed in the August 5, 2022, text message along with some of the other requests.

Even if was to I find that CC was not aware until December 20, 2023, that the kitchen countertop was damaged, this does not relieve the Landlord from responsibility for their agents, and I find that [name] was an agent for the Landlord. [name]

The Tenant says the Landlord, by failing to repair the countertop, breached s.20(1) of the Act which states that the Landlord has an obligation to maintain the residential unit in accordance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the seam of the countertop had lifted and despite his efforts to glue the area, the area remained in a state of disrepair. He says the Landlord persisted in not effecting a repair even after she became aware of the problem.

I acknowledge CC was unable to complete a thorough investigation of the issue on January 9, 2024, because the Tenant told her to leave. However, CC was able to make observations about the bumps under the tape and gave testimony about her assumptions the bumps were chipped pieces of countertop.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord was in breach of s.20(1) of the Act. [name] was not called to give evidence, so I am unable to assess his evaluation of whether the countertop required repair at the time the tenancy began. Therefore, the best evidence before me is the screen shot of the August 5, 2022, text message which I accept, which corroborates the Tenant’s testimony that reported that the laminate surface was peeling and requested maintenance.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant requested maintenance on August 5, 2022. The Landlord’s agent seems to have dismissed this request outright, and it is unknown whether Tyler even reported the request to the Landlord. However, the earliest the Landlord attended the rental unit to see the countertop was January 9, 2022. I do not find that the Landlord was reasonable, timely, or efficient in its efforts to address the Tenant’s concern. Limitation Period/Remedy Sought

The Tenant requests a total abatement of $2,900.00 for the period between December 2023 and May 2026, and the repair or replacement to the damaged countertop. This was calculated at $100.00 per month for each month the Tenant’s countertop was damaged.

Section 29(2) of the Act states that no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. Where the situation is ongoing, as it is here, the limitation period does not start under the repair is done. However, the LTB is unable to grant a remedy beyond the limitation period.

The Tenant filed his application on January 25, 2024. Therefore, the limitation period began on January 26, 2023, for the purpose of calculating the time the Tenant would be entitled to an award. That is because even if the breach occurred before the limitation period, as it did here, the Divisional Court in Toronto Community Housing Corp v. [name], [2010] OJ No. 1463 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), found that remedies cannot exceed 12 months prior to when the application was filed although evidence of prior disrepair could be admissible if it helps to illustrate the cause of disrepair.

However, CC’s evidence was that on January 9, 2024, she went to the Tenant’s rental unit, and the Tenant ordered her to leave. She testified she attempted to return to the rental unit in May 2026, and the Tenant again refused to allow her inside.

Section 16 of the Act says that: “When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses.”

What this means is that as soon as the Tenant refused to cooperate with the Landlord’s efforts to conduct repairs, the Tenant is no longer entitled to a remedy, particularly when this happened again as recently as May 2026. Section 16 obligates the individual who is entitled to the claim, that is the Tenant, to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses, in this case the Landlord. In other words, you cannot demand an abatement while simultaneously refusing to allow the Landlord into the rental unit to assess or correct the problem.

Therefore, the Tenant’s remedy period is limited to the one-year period before the application was filed to the date that he told CC to leave. I find that period to be January 26, 2023, to January 9, 2024.

The Tenant seeks $100.00 per month for each month he was unable to use the countertop, which I calculate to be 7.54% of the monthly rent. The Tenant says he believes this is fair because he has not been able to use the entire kitchen countertop. He cooks a lot and there is very little counterspace.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.
In Avcan Management Inc. v. O’Laughlin, 2012 ONSC 537, the Divisional Court found that the LTB needs to analyze the impact on the Tenant’s ordinary use and enjoyment of the rental unit.

The photo of the countertop submitted after the tape was removed shows a section of laminate which appears to be about 4 inches long and 2 inches wide which is broken away, and a portion of the seam which appears to be 6 to 8 inches in length is lifted.

When I consider the Divisional Court’s findings in Avcan, and I consider the impact on the Tenant’s ordinary use and enjoyment of the rental unit, I find an appropriate abatement is 1%. The countertop is still functional albeit unsightly and the problem is largely cosmetic. The entire area affected by the lifting appears to be about 12” inches in length, and only two inches wide at its widest. In my view, the portion of the countertop affected is well below the 7.54% abatement requested. One may also assume the Tenant would have used a cutting board to prepare foods so although the Tenant complained of getting food poisoning, it seems unlikely that the countertop would have contributed to this.
I calculate this to be $152.61. The Tenant’s monthly rent at the time the application was filed was $1,327.00 ($1,327.00 x 11.5 months (x .01)).

The Tenant also seeks the repair of the countertop. Given that there is no question that the countertop is damaged, as evidenced by the photo of the countertop, and given that the Landlord agrees the countertop is damaged, I find it appropriate to award this remedy. (T Doc-7988744, pg 16). The Landlord shall repair or remediate the countertop such that the countertop is properly sealed and functions in the manner intended.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: On or before August 4, 2026, the Landlord shall repair the kitchen countertop such that the surface is sealed and the surface functions as intended.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $152.61. The Tenant may deduct this amount from the lawful monthly rent due and owing for the month of July 2026. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization], [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal entry
In their application, the Tenants alleges that on September 23, 2024, the Landlord entered the rental unit with a contractor without providing the required 24 hours’ notice.

The Landlord’s representative submitted that the September 23, 2024 incident falls within the limitation period under section 29(2) of the Act, but argued that the Tenants did not select any remedy related to this allegation. The Tenants confirmed that their requested remedies were not connected to the illegal entry claim. As a result, the illegal entry issue is moot. Even if the Tenants had succeeded on this claim, no remedy could be granted due to their failure to request one. The matter was initially heard by the Board on August 7, 2025, at which time the Tenants had an opportunity to amend their application to include a remedy for the alleged illegal entry but did not do so. Accordingly, the illegal entry claim is dismissed. Substantial interference

I raised a preliminary issue in regard to the Tenants’ substantial interference claim. Specifically, the Tenants’ claim relates to a December 19, 2023 incident. The Tenants’ application was filed on January 29, 2025, which means the Tenants’ brought the claim before the Board outside of the time limitation set under section 29(2) of the Act.

Section 29(2) of the Act states: Time limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. 2006, c. 17, s. 29 (2). [Emphasis Added]

The December 19, 2023 incident occurred more than one year prior to application filing date and therefore, the Board has no jurisdiction to hear this claim. Therefore, the substantial interference claim is dismissed. Harassment, etc.
The Tenants’ application also claimed that the Landlord and or the Landlord’s agents harassed them. However, the Tenants failed to provide any particulars related to their harassment claim.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]. [name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the Tenants to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the Tenants to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the Tenants to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.

While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the principles in [name] also apply to Tenants applications. In this case, the Landlord was not given enough specific information to know how to adequately defend the Tenants’ claims.
