When I raised the above as a preliminary issue with the Tenants, they did not dispute that details were omitted from the application, specifically dates and times of the events that gave rise to the application. I find that the T2 application lacked the detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice and to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, I find that the Tenants’ harassment claim must be dismissed. T6 Application:

The Landlord’s representative raised a preliminary issue regarding the Tenants’ T6 application. In particular, the application included claims dating back to 2012, which fall outside the limitation period prescribed by section 29(2) of the Act. Although some issues were within the applicable limitation period, the Tenants did not select any remedies in relation to those claims. Consequently, even if the Tenants had been successful, no remedy could have been awarded. The application proceeded to a case conference before the Board on August 7, 2025, at which time the Tenants were given an opportunity to amend their application to include remedies for the claims within the limitation period. However, they did not do so.
Therefore, I am dismissing the Tenants’ T6 application, as it does not include any specified remedy for the alleged breaches.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant testified that the Landlord is in violation of section 27(3) and section 22 of the Act.

The Tenant testified that he was provided on January 23, 2025, a notice of entry for January 24, 2025, between the hours of 9:00 am and 4:00 pm. A copy of the notice of entry was submitted as evidence in DOC 6560203 page 3.

The Tenant testified that the notice did not comply with the Divisional Court decision in [name] v. [organization] Corporation, [2007] O.J. No. 423, which determined that, while a landlord is not required to specify the exact hour and minute of a required entry, a six hour entry window does not comply with the requirement in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and that a landlord should specify a time of entry.
The Tenant further testified that because of the notice he had to stay home at the expense of other activities.

The Tenant testified that he contacted the contractor who was to be attending the unit and received an email back stating that the work to be completed should take about 30 minutes. A copy of the email was submitted as evidence DOC 6666719.
Under cross-examination the Tenant confirmed that he was not trained to install radiators, and he was unaware of the qualifications of [name], the author of the email.

The Tenant further confirmed that the notice of entry was served on him by the contractor and although he was aware the notice was defective when he received it, he did not bring it to the attention of the Landlord nor the contractor.
The Tenant further acknowledged that when the contractor attended his unit on January 24, 2025, he refused entry into his unit.
The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement in the amount of $4,500.00 which he puts forth is a proportionate deterrent and ordering anything less would make a mockery of the Divisional Court’s decision.

The Tenant submitted [name] v. [organization] Corporation, [2007] O.J. No. 423, in which he was awarded $1,000.00, TNT-00226 in which he was awarded an abatement in the amount of $3,000.00, TNT-34917-21 which is a settlement agreement in which he was awarded $4,000.00 and LTB-T-035166-23 in which he was awarded $4,500.00.
The Landlord is requesting the application be dismissed as there was no illegal entry, as the Tenant had denied the entry.

The Landlord's Representative submitted that the Tenant was aware the notice was defective, and he did not address the issue with the Landlord or the contractor, for the sole purpose of seeking unjust enrichment.
The Landlord's Representative further submitted that there was no evidence to support the loss of reasonable enjoyment of the unit by the Tenant and that the amount sought was unreasonable.

The Landlord’s Representative requested that, if the application is not dismissed, then a modest abatement of rent, $26.04, an equivalent of 1 day’s rent be imposed. He referred to a previous decision of the Board, which I found to be TNT-92678-17. Analysis
I am not bound by the previous decisions of the Board, but I am bound by the Divisional Court decision.

Guideline 19 of the Board’s Interpretation Guidelines provides that a Tenant may remain in the rental unit while the landlord exercises the right of entry, but the landlord’s right of entry can be exercised even if the tenant is not in the unit at the time of entry. A tenant does not have the right to deny entry simply because the time of entry is not convenient to the tenant. A tenant may not interfere with the landlord’s right of entry.
Although the Tenant testified that he remained home for the time of entry, he further testified that he denied the entry into his unit.
The Tenant is seeking an abatement of rent in the amount $4,500.00.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they're paying for, they should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that although the notice to enter may not have been in compliance with [name] v. [organization] Corporation, [2007] [name] No. 423, the difference between that decision, the other decisions of the Board and the matter currently before me, is that in this matter the Tenant denied the entry into his unit and therefore there was no illegal entry.
I find that although the Tenant chose to remain home that day, there was no evidence submitted which would support any loss of reasonable enjoyment or substantial interference to the Tenant.

I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally and that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental, therefore the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord’s Representative submitted that the Act does not apply because the Landlord’s daughter resides in the unit and shares a kitchen and/or bathroom with the other roommates, therefore exempting the unit under section 5(i) of the Act: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

The Landlord testified that his daughter lives in the unit as she goes to university in the area, and was living there previously to the TT moving in. His daughter’s room is on the main floor and the Tenant’s room was upstairs. His daughter and the other tenants shared the kitchen and a bathroom. A copy of the lease agreement for a single room, a utility bill in the Landlord’s daughter’s name and test messages between the Tenant and the Landlord’s daughter in which she refers to the Landlord as her dad, were submitted as evidence.
The Landlord’s daughter MZ testified that she was attending a local school and lived in the unit in a bedroom on the main floor, sharing the kitchen with the other tenants.
MZ testified that she met the Tenant on the day she moved in and since that day has always referred to her father as the Landlord when speaking to the Tenant.
The Tenant testified that she only became aware that MZ was the Landlord’s daughter once the Landlord was trying to evict her. Analysis

Section 5(i) of the Act requires the tenant to share the kitchen or bathroom with the owner or the owner’s immediate family. In addition, the Board must consider the living arrangements at the beginning of the tenancy and any unilateral change to the pattern of use by the Landlord after the tenancy begins will not cause a tenancy that is subject to the Act to be exempted by section 5(i) ([name] v. Bindlish, [2010 O.J. No. 2193 ([name]. [name]. Ct.)). The onus rests on the person seeking to rely on the exemption. In this case, that is the Landlord.

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find on a balance pf probability that the Tenant was required to share the kitchen with the Landlord’s daughter MZ and this means that the arrangement is exempt from the Act.
There is no dispute that the Landlord’s daughter MZ lived in the unit in a bedroom on the main floor and had been living there prior to the Tenant moving in.

I find that the Landlord, MZ and the Tenant were all equally credible, they all gave their evidence in a straightforward manner. However, I am persuaded by MZ that since the Tenant moved in, she was referring to the Landlord as her father.

Based on the evidence of the parties, I find that the Tenant was sharing the unit with the Landlord’s daughter and therefore the exemption under section 5(1) of the Act applies and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): collected or retained money illegally LTB-T-009285-25 The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on May 26, 2026 Tenant [name] attended the hearing on behalf of both Tenants with his representative, Abraar Unia. The Landlord, [name], attended the hearing on behalf of both Landlords with his representative, [name]. Imran appeared as a witness for the Landlords. LTB-T-015712-25 LTB-T-015712-25
reasons: The Tenants allege the Landlords collected illegal rent from May 2024 to February 2025. The Tenants also allege the Landlords failed to pay interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. Interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit

Subsection 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires a landlord to pay a tenant interest annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guidance determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

The Tenants paid the Landlords a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,800.00 on July 5, 2021. The Landlords have not paid the Tenants interest on the deposit. I am satisfied the Landlords have illegally retained the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. As such, the Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $276.40 for interest owing on the deposit up to the date of the Order. This is calculated as follows: • July 5, 2021 to December 31, 2021 = $0 (0%) • January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2022 = $33.56 (1.2%) • January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2023 = $69.90 (2.5%) • January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024 = $69.90 (2.5%) • January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025 = $69.90 (2.5%) • January 1, 2026 to June 22, 2026 = $33.13 (2.1%) Illegal rent collected

The tenancy commenced on October 1, 2021 for a fixed term expiring on October 1, 2022 for a monthly rent of $2,800.00. It is undisputed that the Landlord charged and collected $2,800.00 a month between October 2021 and December 2021.
There also seems to be no dispute that the parties entered into a new agreement on January 1, 2022 wherein the rent was discounted to $2,300.00 until January 1, 2023.

On September 19, 2022, Landlord [name] (‘SNS’) texted Tenant [name] (‘FM’) to advise that they will sign a new tenancy agreement on October 1, 2022 for a monthly rent of $2,500.00. FM responded as follows: “Walikumassalam ... We agreed to raise it to $2400 from 1st Oct 2022. We already have a lease. I don’t see any reason why we need to sign a new one.”

SNS replied as follows: LTB-T-015712-25 “We were agreed to for $2400 starting January 2022 but you said you misunderstood & thought it will be on starting on October 1st 2022. I honoured your misunderstanding & now it will be $2500 starting October 1st & we will do a lease contract. Period”

On October 1, 2022, a monthly tenancy agreement was executed between the parties reflecting a monthly rent of $2,500.00. It was FM’s evidence that on April 27, 2024, SNS verbally notified him that the rent would increase to $2,700.00 effective May 1, 2024. fm maintains that he paid the rent increase from May 2024 to February 2025. Analysis

Fixed term tenancies in Ontario continue month to month under the same terms unless terminated in accordance with the Act. What this means is that the Landlords were not entitled to require the Tenants to enter into a new tenancy agreement on October 1, 2022 as the fixed term was not scheduled to expire until January 1, 2023.

Section 119 of the Act provides that a landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed. What this means is that the Landlords could not increase the rent until January 1, 2023.
SNS testified that he had a “mutual understanding” with FM that when they could afford it, they would resume paying $2,800.00 a month.

I am not convinced there was a meeting of the minds between the parties as to the amount of rent charged. I say this because the written tenancy agreement stipulates that the rent is discounted to $2,300.00 until January 1, 2023. Furthermore, it is clear from the text messages between the parties on September 19, 2022 that there was not a clear understanding as to the amount of rent to be charged. The Tenants, however, do not seek the illegal rent collected for October 1, 2022 to April 30, 2024.

Subsection 116(1) requires a landlord to give a tenant at least 90 days written notice of a rent increase. Furthermore, subsection 116(3) requires that the written notice be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.

As the Landlords did not give the Tenants notice in accordance with subsection 116(4), the increase on May 1, 2024 is void. This means the lawful monthly rent remained $2,500.00 and any amount the Landlords collected in excess of that amount constitutes an illegal rent increase.

The Tenants admitted into evidence bank records supporting their position that they paid the Landlord $2,700.00 for rent between May 1, 2024 and February 1, 2025. This represents $200.00 a month collected more than what the Landlords were entitled to collect. Accordingly, the Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $2,000.00 (10 months x $200).
The Tenants incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement of these costs. LTB-T-015712-25 LTB-T-009285-23
The Tenants sought to withdraw their T2 application, and I consent to the request. T6 Application
The Tenants allege the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the toilet and washing machine.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord. Toilet
For the reasons that follow, I am not convinced the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to the toilet.

There seems to be a dispute whether the Tenants contacted the Landlord to repair a leaky toilet or upgrade the seat. The Tenant testified that the toilet leaked, but the Landord indicated the Tenant requested a fancier toilet seat for his inlaws who were visiting. The Tenant made his request on May 24, 2024 and the Landlords sent their handyman, Imran, to assess the issue on May 27, 2024.

Imran testified that he is a friend of the Landlords and is not a plumber but is handy. He explained that he pulled out what appeared to be the lid from a toothpaste which had gotten stuck in the toilet and suggested that the toilet seat be replaced. He did not provide any explanation as to what he believed caused the toilet to leak, and there is no connection between replacing the toilet seat and stopping the leak, but nonetheless, the Tenant was satisfied with the replacement seat, which confirms that he was not seeking to fix a leaky toilet, but to replace the toilet seat. LTB-T-015712-25

The Landlords purchased a new toilet seat and left it for the Tenants to install as the Tenants were on vacation, and the Tenants did not wish for the Landlords to enter the rental unit in their absence. The toilet seat was replaced by the Landlords at the end of June 2024 as the Tenant was not comfortable installing the seat on his own.

The Tenants did not present any compelling evidence to establish that the disrepair issue was not resolved by the new toilet seat. There is also no evidence before me indicating the Tenants continued to report an issue with the toilet seat after June 2024. As such, the issue to be determined is whether the steps taken by the Landlords were reasonable in the circumstances. I find that they were.

The Tenants reported the disrepair issue on a Friday and by Monday, the Landlords sent someone to address the issue. I do not believe it would be appropriate to hold the Landlords liable for the delay in the installation of the new toilet seat as the delay was due to the Tenants’ request that the Landlords not enter the rental unit in their absence. I am satisfied the steps the Landlords took to address the disrepair issue were reasonable and appropriate. Washing machine
I am also not convinced the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to the washing machine.

The Tenants reported to the Landlords on October 1, 2024 that the washing machine was vibrating and smoking. The Landlord sent a technician to assess the issue the following day. The technician determined the Tenants were responsible for the malfunction.

The Landlords explained to the Tenants that he would repair the washing machine if necessary but indicated the Tenants would be charged for the expense given they were responsible for the disrepair issue. The Tenants responded that they were prepared to share the cost for a new washing machine. The Tenants purchased their own washing machine on October 27, 2024.

The Tenants did not advise the Landlords in advance that they intended to purchase a new washing machine. In my view, the Tenants interfered with the Landlords’ ability to address the disrepair issue with the washing machine. As such, I find the Tenants have failed to establish the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenants $2,329.40, which represents: • $276.40 in interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit that was illegally retained; • $2,000.00 in illegal rent collected and retained; and • $53.00 for the application filing fee. LTB-T-015712-25
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 3, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. LTB-T-009285-25
The T2 application having been withdrawn, the LTB's file is closed.
The T6 application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that she rented the unit before she came to Canada and moved into the unit on August 15, 2024, the unit is on the top floor of the residential complex.
The Tenant testified on August 17, 2024 there was a loud party in the unit below her, a copy of the incident report was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that from her unit she continually heard crying and stomping which would shake her unit. A audio recording of a conversation she could hear late at night was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant submitted a video of her attending the unit below her asking the tenant about the crying, stomping and other loud noises. The tenant in the video denies any crying or stomping, stating that it is just her and her husband in the unit.
The Tenant also submitted videos of her stove rattling a crying noise and a bang.
The Tenant testified that the noises from the other unit prevented her from sleeping which also affected her daily life and schooling.

The Tenant testified that she moved out of the unit because she could not live like that anymore as the noise was really affecting her life and the Landlord did not investigate or respond to her complaints. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s Agent [name] Willing (AW), testified that he had spoken with the Tenant and the property manager to investigate and corroborate the Tenant’s complaints but there was no clear evidence of substantial noise.

The Landlords Agent Dustin Simons (DS), the property manager, testified that as a result of the Tenant complaint’s he had spoke with the tenants below her, requesting that the keep the noise down and although the tenants claimed they had not made any noise, the said they would try to be quieter.

DS testified that he responded to the Tenant’s complaints, and he submitted a log of dates and times from April 9 through to April 13, 2024, at different times on each date, and confirmed that he was unable to hear any noises coming from the unit below the Tenant’s unit.
DS testified that he spent 8 months trying to corroborate the Tenant’s complaints but found no evidence of substantial noise coming from the unit below the Tenant. Analysis
Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant.

A landlord who fails to take reasonable steps to address substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment by one tenant of another tenant can be found to have substantially interfered with the “victim” tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. This means that the Landlord has the positive obligation to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment and take the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of his premises. [[name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Ct.)].

Based on the testimony and the evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities, that there was not a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The recordings submitted by the Tenant at the hearing indicates some noise, but the sounds were not unusually loud and were actually so light that words or even what language was being spoken, could not be heard. The Tenant also testified that she had called the police, but no police report was submitted to substantiate her complaints.

People living in multi-unit residential complexes must accept that they will hear a certain amount of noise. The mere fact that the Tenant is hearing others does not establish substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment.

I further find that the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the Tenant’s complaints and throughout 8 months of investigation, were unable to corroborate the Tenant’s issues. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant and this claim must be dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony presented at the hearing and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence, I have considered it when making my decision. This order contains all the reasons for my decision and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] “Mike” [name] (the 'Landlords'): • Entered the rental unit illegally on November 4, 2024 by failing to give 24 hours’ notice. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have not proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name]
The tenancy began on May 13, 2023 and ended February 28, 2025 when the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
The rental unit is a two-storey single family dwelling with a backyard situated on a corner lot in the City of Caledon, ON.
The lawful rent was $3,100.00/ month. T2 – Illegal Entry
The Tenant [name] (SF) testified that she noticed the heat stopped working on October 30, 2024 and emailed the Landlord’s representative, who informed the Landlord.

On November 4, 2024, the Landlord Mike [name] (MK) sent an email to the Tenants at 1:38 p.m., saying that he would attend the rental unit at 6:00 p.m. that night because he considered the request from the Tenants was urgent (DOC-802980).
When both Landlords attended the rental unit, Tenant [name] (AF) spoke to them at the door, closed the door, and informed his wife that the Landlords were there to check the heat.
The Landlords testified that AF let them in, but SF testified that AF did not let them in and that they let themselves in, and in her words, this constitutes an illegal entry.

Since the Tenants had alerted the Landlords to an issue with the heat, I find it unlikely that they would deny them entry in that moment when they were aware they were there to investigate the problem. I therefore find the Tenants consented to the entry at the time.

The Tenants testified that then the Landlords attempted to go upstairs to do a home inspection and the Tenants protested, so the Landlords checked the thermostat, which was located on the stairs and noted that it read 22C.
Both parties agree the Landlords were refused entry to check the radiators upstairs.
The Landlords being satisfied that the thermostat was working and read 22C, departed. Application of the Law

Section 26 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, states: (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.

I find that in this case, both (a) and (b) were true in this case: The Landlord had been summoned to the property by the Tenant in her email of October 30, 2024. The issue of heat is a vital service and is urgent and so he provided 5.5 hours’ notice of his entry on November 4, 2024 even though it was not necessarily required in the circumstances.
Nevertheless, if this was not sufficient to meet the 24 hour notice period in section 27(1)(5), I find that the Tenant AF consented to the Landlords’ entry to investigate the heat issue.

The Tenants’ refusal to allow the Landlord to investigate further whether the radiators were working upstairs resulted in a brief investigation of the thermostat, and the Landlords being satisfied that it was working, immediately departed.
Therefore, I do not find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants have proven the Landlords entered the premises illegally.
This ground of the application shall be dismissed. T2 – Substantial Interference – Fence

The Tenants allege that the Landlords failed to maintain the fence in their yard from July 28, 2023-December 2024 and that this failure substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenants were evicted before the fence was completed in August 2025.
Such an application is better brought forward under s. 20 of the Act as it relates to the Landlord’s maintenance obligations.
The test for a complaint of substantial interference is whether the Landlords took reasonable steps to investigate the problem. Tenants’ Evidence

Tenant SF testified that her family had decided to rent this unit because it had a 12 ft fence around the yard that could protect her daughter. The yard abutted a ravine and perpendicular to the ravine was a bridge.
On July 28, 2023, the fence was taken down as part of City construction on the bridge.
A temporary orange fence measuring 3-4 ft high was installed.
The Tenants testified that it was insufficient and people traversed their backyard and stole items off their deck.

The Tenants could not recall when they told the Landlord that they were dissatisfied with the temporary fence, but informed him that items had been stolen from their yard. Landlord’s Evidence 27. [name] testified that he was in contact with [name], a project manager from the City of Caledon, for the entire duration of the construction. 28. He testified that the thought he had control of the situation, even though surveyors, developers, engineers and city officials were making the decisions. 29. He testified that before he could replace the fence, he had to get a survey done first, then dig posts and it was difficult to coordinate everyone. There was also a dispute with the city about the property line, so a second survey had to be completed. 30. In August 2024 fence posts were installed. 31. Then construction stopped for the winter. 32. The Landlords testified that they were in constant communication with the Tenants until the Tenants stopped communicating with them. There was an outstanding arrears issue that poisoned the relationship, and ultimately led to the Tenants being evicted in February 28, 2025. Application of the Law – Substantial Interference 33. Section 22 of the Act states that “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.” 34. Interference has to rise to a “substantial” level, and not be passing, transient or trifling. 35. The Divisional Court in Hassan v. Niagara Housing Authority [2000] O.J. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”) affirmed that a landlord has a positive obligation to take reasonably necessary actions to ensure that all tenants can reasonably enjoy the rental premises: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion … on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.” 36. I find that there is no evidence the Tenants informed the Landlord that they were dissatisfied with the state of the fence. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he sent at least 4 emails about the fence being repaired, or whether construction workers would be on the property. In order for a landlord to investigate a problem, they need to be aware the problem exists. From the Landlord’s perspective, he was working with city officials to get the fence done as soon as possible. 37. In addition, I find that the Landlord actually had little control to take any reasonable steps to secure the Tenants’ yard. 38. A construction project on the scale described would have significant timelines, delays, and interruptions as evidenced by the piecemeal approach to re-erecting the fence: a year went by between putting fence posts in the ground in August 2024 and re-erecting the fence in August 2025. 39. I find it unlikely that the Landlord had as much control as he thought he did over the situation. 40. I find there was very little he could do to satisfy the Tenants’ desire to repair the fence while ongoing construction was taking place nearby. It was an unfortunate situation. 41. Therefore, I find that he did not substantially interfere in the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, and made efforts to remain in contact about the evolution of the project until contact was refused. 42. Therefore, I find that the Tenants did not prove the allegation of substantial interference on a balance of probabilities and the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $1,754.95.

On April 9, 2021, the Tenants paid to the Landlord $1,575.00 as a 1-month security deposit. The tenancy was terminated as of May 31, 2025, by a written notice on April 1, 2025, which was accepted by the Landlord.

In early May, the Tenants did not pay their rent as they had been under the impression that they had paid a last month’s rent deposit that would be applied to their last month however, the Landlords demanded a rent payment for that month.
On June 15, 2025, after having conducted an inspection of the unit, the Landlords advised the Tenants that they would not be refunding their deposit due to alleged damages found in the unit.

Section 3(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states; This Act, except Part [name], applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

Section 106(10) of the Act states; (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

As such, based on the Tenants’ uncontested evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Act required the Landlords to apply the deposit to the Tenants’ last month’s rent. As such, the Landlords will be directed to repay the Tenants their deposit.

Having determined that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit, I am also satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, totaling $125.95 since April 9, 2021, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlords will also be ordered to repay this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,754.95. This amount represents: • $1,575.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $126.95 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 14, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 15, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord’s representative brought a motion to dismiss the application on the basis that the application did not disclose enough detail to know the case to meet.

The application states: I have reasonable belief that Landlord was discriminating and or harassing me in connection to disability. In January 2024 I requested accommodation of disability in form of rent discount 50 for 2 months due to catastrophic situation with finances in connection to different disabilities including termination from job as was later discovered due to [name] . On February 7 2024 Landlord's Lawyer declined request in allegedly high handed harassing manner. One of reasons was "Although your landlord has a duty to accommodate any disability that you may suffer from within the meaning of the Human Rights Code the landlord’s duty to accommodate does not extend to requiring it to forgive your rent in the circumstances of this matter. Requiring the landlord to provide you with rent free housing in addition to not being justified in the circumstances would also amount to undue hardship."

A close reading of these first few sentences of the application disclose sufficient particulars that I find the Landlord was put on notice about the complaint. The discrimination took place on or about January 2024 and the requested accommodation was refused by the Landlord’s lawyer on February 7, 2024 with the stated reason.

The sentences that follow, however, do not disclose any clear information, and I agree, are irrelevant. I find the application can be saved by amending and striking the sentences that follow. Therefore, the application shall proceed only on the first few sentences quoted above.
The Tenant did not describe any harassing behaviour in his application, so that element of his application is dismissed.

Therefore, the motion to dismiss is denied. Duty to Accommodate 1. The Tenant submits that the Landlord’s failure to provide him a 50% rent abatement for January 2024 and February 2024 constitutes a breach of the Landlord’s duty under the Ontario Human Rights Code (“Code”). I do not agree. 2. Under the Code, housing providers have a duty to accommodate the Code-related needs of tenants, to ensure that the housing they supply is designed to be inclusive of persons identified by Code grounds, and to take steps to remove any barriers that may exist, unless to do so would cause undue hardship. Common examples of housing-related accommodations include physical and accessibility modifications, policy adjustments related to pets, guests and parking allocations, help filling out forms or changing rent payment deadlines. A landlord’s duty to accommodate under the Code does not extend to the amount of rent charged to a tenant. As such, I am not satisfied the Landlord breached their obligation to accommodate under the Code. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,498.00.

The tenancy began in January 2023. F our post-secondary students signed a standard one-year lease. In January 2024 they renewed the lease for another year. In November 2024 the Tenant advised the Landlord that two of the original tenants planned to move out, but she and another tenant wished to stay. One tenant had already been replaced within the group, and they planned to get a fourth roommate, but they didn’t need the fourth to afford the unit. The Tenant clearly expressed to the Landlord that she was willing and able to continue the tenancy with another of the original tenants.

The Tenant was unaware at the time that pursuant to section 38(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), the lease did not terminate at the end of the initial term, and instead automatically converted to a monthly tenancy. The Landlord insisted that a new lease needed to be signed each year and would not approve a new lease without additional documentation from the newer roommates which they could not provide on the Landlord’s requested timeline. The Landlord advised that if the requirements to sign a new lease were not met by January 31, they would advertise the unit for rent – which they did, advising the Tenant on February 8 that new tenants would be moving in on April 1.

As they could not comply with the Landlord’s requirements to sign a new lease, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. They did not wish to move, and incurred extra costs and disruption by doing so, but were pressured into doing so because they were not aware that they were entitled to stay in the rental unit and the Landlord’s demands were not in accordance with the Act. While the Landlord was correct that they could not remove the names of the tenants who were choosing to leave without their consent, the Landlord was not entitled to end, or require the Tenant to end, the tenancy simply because two of the original four signees were no longer residing in the unit. The Tenant was legally entitled to remain in the unit and have any roommates of her choosing.
Therefore, I find that t he Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions. The Tenant incurred increased rent of at least $6,450.00 for a one-year period after the Tenant left the rental unit. During the tenancy the Tenant was paying one quarter of the total rent, or $712.50 per month. The rental unit was a 2-storey duplex with 5 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms and was shared by four people. The Tenant moved to a 2 bed/1 bath apartment with one roommate. The Tenant now pays slightly more than half of the monthly rent because she has the bigger of the two rooms and has a parking spot. She is now paying $1,275.00 per month. I am satisfied that the rental units are comparable in the per roommate bedroom and bathroom size and the new unit does not have significantly improved features which would justify the increased monthly rent. Because the Landlord was not present at the hearing, it would be prejudicial to amend the application to increase the amount claimed for increased rent, so the originally claimed amount is awarded despite it being lower than the actual increase amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the T enant is $6,498.00. This amount represents:  $6,450.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by June 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 29, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 30, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This Member raised as a preliminary issue that the Tenant’s evidence had not been compiled into one document brief as required by the interim order issued by the Board on August 18, 2025.

The Tenant submitted she was not aware of this requirement because it was her husband who attended the Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC). The main evidence they want to rely on is the order from the city; the Tenant requested to proceed, relying on this one document. In the alternative, the Tenant requested an adjournment so the evidence could be properly submitted.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted the matter should not be adjourned, it should be dismissed for non-compliance. Prior to the ACC, the Tenant sent an email with approximately 14 attachments; at the ACC the issue of proper disclosure was discussed, including the evidence being properly organized and served. The Tenant [name] knew this. Further, the Tenant acknowledged the Landlord’s document brief, which was in the proper format, no steps were taken to organize and resubmit/serve their evidence. An interim order is issued for a reason; parties are expected to comply, otherwise the weight of such an order is diminished. Further the matter is old, concerning issues in 2024, which prejudices the Landlord as the witness pool of those the necessary knowledge is greatly depleted.

Based on the submissions before me, the Tenant’s application is dismissed; the Tenant did not exercise due diligence. Interim order LTB-T-010232-25-IN issued by the Board on August 18, 2025, is clear; it required the parties to submit evidence by a specified deadline and set out the potential consequences if a party did not comply. Tenant did not abide by the interim order. The order says on or before September 18, 2025, the Tenant shall “provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures, and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing”. The order also says: 6. If a party does not comply with the deadlines for disclosure as detailed above, the Member may refuse to accept the evidence or consider the issues not disclosed. 8. To ensure an expeditious hearing, submissions from the parties shall follow the requirements of the Board as per Rule 19 and the Practice Direction on Evidence and can be obtained from the Landlord and Tenant Board website. 9. For clarity, all documents, photographs, and other items provided to the parties and the LTB must: 1) be readable; 2) have consecutively numbered pages; and 3) include a list or table of contents identifying each item in order, and by page number, if more than one item is being submitted.

This is a joint tenancy, as such, the joint tenants are expected to act together. It is undisputed that the issue of proper disclosure was raised at the ACC. That the Tenant’s husband did not relay the disclosure requirements to this Tenant is not a justification for non-compliance; not only should the Tenant [name] have passed on any necessary information resulting from the ACC, the Tenant, [name], should also have ensured she was properly prepared for the hearing.

As to proceeding based on the city order, there is no certificate of service on file for this 32-page document, and the document appears to have been only posted to the portal and not properly served to the other side.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name] and Agreed Statement of Facts

The Landlord and Tenants agree to the following facts: • The first lease agreement between the parties was signed on November 8, 2021. • In the first lease agreement, the rental unit only consisted of the main floor of the residential complex. • The lawful rent in the first lease agreement was $1,800.00. • There were various lease agreements presented between the parties from November 8, 2021, to May 1, 2025, with rent increases sent throughout this time. • Prior to May 1, 2025, rent was $1,845.00, however, the Tenants signed a new lease agreement on May 2, 2025, which increased rent to $2,500.00. This new amount of monthly rent took effect on May 1, 2025. • In this new lease agreement the rental unit is described for the first time as consisting of the main floor and basement. • As this new lease agreement was a brokered deal between the parties involving a mutual agent, who was the co-signor on the lease agreement, the rent was going to be split between the Tenants and the co-signor. The Tenants would be responsible for $2,300.00 and the co-signor would contribute the remaining $200.00.

With the above agreed upon, the substance of the Tenants’ application was as follows: • The Tenants allege that they paid an illegal rent increase from $1,800.00 to $2,500.00, and that the Landlord coerced them into signing the new lease agreement. • The Tenants allege that they paid an illegal charge as the Landlord required them to pay a $700.00 top up on the last month’s rent deposit due to the increase in monthly rent as set out by the lease agreement signed in May 2025. Analysis Illegal Rent Collected

As per s.123 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: • A parking space. • A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing.

In addition, pursuant to s.16(1) of O.Reg. 516/06, the following services, facilities, privileges, accommodations or things are prescribed for the purposes of subsection 123 (1) of the Act: • Cable television. • Satellite television. • An air conditioner. • Extra electricity for an air conditioner. • Extra electricity for a washer or dryer in the rental unit. [name] plug-ins. • Lockers or other storage space. [name]. • Electricity. • Water or sewage services, excluding capital work. • Floor space. • Property taxes with respect to a site for a mobile home or a land lease home. [emphasis added]
Subsection 16(1) of O.Reg. 516/06 supplements the definition of “services and facilities” in s. 2(1) of the Act, and includes floor space.

In addition, looking at s.16(3) of O.Reg. 516/06, if the agreement under s.123(1) of the Act is to provide or cease to provide floor space, the maximum increase in rent or minimum decrease in rent shall be proportionate to the change in floor space. In this case, it is clear that this new agreement was providing more floor space to the Tenants.

Furthermore, s.16(4) of O.Reg. 516/06 states that if an amount determined in accordance with subsection (3) would be unreasonable given the nature and quality of the floor space added or taken away, the maximum increase in rent or minimum decrease in rent shall be a reasonable amount based on the nature and quality of the floor space and the amount of the change in the floor space.

I find that in this case as the increase is less than double the prior monthly rent, and only a portion of what could have been attributed to a rental increase due to a sizeable increase in floor space, the increase in rent to an additional $700.00 is reasonable and compliant with s.123 of the Act. Pursuant to s.16(3) of O.Reg. 516/06, the rental agreement including the basement space falls under s.123(1) of the Act as the Tenants wanted and added more floor space for their use and enjoyment. In addition, per s.16(4) of O.Reg. 516/06, I find that the nature and quality of the basement space would effectively increase the amount of space the Tenants would have use and access to, thereby the rent was reasonably and increased to reflect this change in additional floor space.

In this case, the Tenants take the position that they have always had access to the basement after the basement was no longer being rented. Both parties admitted that while a fraudulent lease was used to evict the basement tenant, there was a disagreement as to the nature of the Tenants’ ability to use the basement as a part of their occupation of the property; however, it was admitted by the Tenants that they wanted the basement unit for their own personal use and occupation, and the Landlord advised them that because there was already a tenant in that unit, they cannot just evict them.

Regardless of the fact that a new, fraudulent lease agreement listed the basement as a part of the Tenants’ space and was signed by the Landlord for the same amount of rent, I do not find this satisfactory on a balance of probabilities to support the Tenants’ claim that they previously had lawful use of and access to the basement. This façade, which was consented to by both parties, does not lawfully terminate the tenancy of the prior basement tenant, therefore, does not grant the Tenants a lawful possession to the floor space in basement unit.

In addition, in this case, it was the Tenants’ evidence that they had the permission of the Landlord’s Agent to use and occupy the basement in the property as soon as the basement tenant vacated the property. The Landlord’s Agent then testified that she granted the Tenants 5 months of use of the basement for free, but, with the understanding that there would be a new lease signed for an increase in rent due to having use and access of more floor space in the property.

As it relates to the claim of coercion, I find that the Tenants did not present sufficient evidence to invalidate signing the new lease. The fact that this new lease agreement was brokered by a mutual agent, who also ultimately co-signed for the Tenants, thereby making himself liable for the monthly rent, does not bolster the Tenants’ claim. While there is a language barrier for the Tenants in communicating in English, the Tenants, the Landlord’s Agent, and the person who brokered the deal all speak Arabic, so with the method of communication being entirely in Arabic, there is nothing unfamiliar or lost in translation for the Tenants.

The Tenants also claimed that the Landlord’s Agent said she would give them a bad reference to any new prospective landlord, which was another factor in them feeling coerced to sign the new lease agreement. On the other hand, the Tenants testified that they were searching for another property to move into, however, due to being a family of nine, they could not find a property similarly price for what they were paying prior to the new lease agreement. While the Tenants have a sympathetic situation as well being refugees from Syria, this ultimately does not absolve them from the agreement they opted to enter into after not finding another property to suit their needs.
The Tenants bear the burden of proof and based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenants failed to meet that burden.

The Tenants failed to provide sufficient evidence specific to the alleged illegal increase in rent due to now having more floor space in the property. As a matter of fact, the Tenants initially based their claim to having access to the basement by knowingly using a fraudulent lease to evict the basement tenant, then consequently and wilfully signed a new lease agreement for a higher amount of rent for an increase in the amount of floor space they always wanted.

Ultimately, the bottom line for determining rent was what did the Tenants sign for and was the increase compliant with O.Reg. 516/06 and the Act. I find that based on a balance of probabilities, it is unreasonable that gaining more floor space in the property would not have come at in increase in rent; moreover, the Tenants agreed to an increase in floor space and actively sought out to gain the floor space in the basement, and as such the Landlord has the right to increase rent as prescribed for additional floor space added in a new lease agreement.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act as under s.123 as rent can be increased at any time where the landlord provides a new service or facility within the meaning of the Act or the regulation. Illegal Charge Collected

The Tenants allege that the Landlord collected an unlawful increase in the rent deposit as there was a top up of $700.00 for the rent deposit to match the new lawful rent as stipulated in the new lease agreement signed May 2, 2025. The Tenants assert that the Landlord has illegally collected this overpayment as an illegal charge.

As it pertains to the last month’s deposit, the applicable sections of the Act are as follows: Rent deposit may be required 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (1). Amount of rent deposit (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (2). Same (3) If the lawful rent increases after a tenant has paid a rent deposit, the landlord may require the tenant to pay an additional amount to increase the rent deposit up to the amount permitted by subsection (2). 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (3); 2013, c. 3, s. 32 (1).

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Act as based on the above. The Act contemplates that an increase in rent can be met with an increase in rent deposit held by the landlord. As such, since the tenancy never ended, and there was a signing of a new term for occupancy where the lawful monthly rent increased, the Landlord can require a top up on the rent deposit because the Landlord is entitled to have a rent deposit that matches the increased lawful monthly rent.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: It should be noted that the Tenant made an accommodation request for an ASL Interpreter which was granted and provided for, however, this request was done in error. The Tenant then said she speaks Hindi and would prefer an interpreter. During the hearing, I canvassed with the Tenant if she was comfortable proceeding in English, and she confirmed that she was. Is this Illegal Rent?

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that what the Tenant is claiming as illegal rent is not proper, accurately captured in the application, and not within the Board’s jurisdiction to consider.
The Tenant alleged that they paid the Landlord illegal rent as the rent she was paying was significantly higher that the market rate for similar units in the building.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that there is no legal basis for the application because the parties signed an agreement in which the Tenant agreed to pay the stipulated rent in exchange for the right to occupy the rental unit.

The parties agree that the rent the parties agreed to in the tenancy agreement is $2,357.00. The Tenant submitted that she asked the Landlord to reduce her rent to what the other units are listed for but received a response approximately 7 months later, denying the request. Moreover, the Tenant requested to move into another unit with a lower rent, and one was not provided.

However, upon hearing further submissions from the Tenant, she substantiated the fact that that she wilfully signed the lease for the rental unit and did not refute the fact that she intentionally entered into the tenancy agreement knowing that the Landlord was seeking $2,357.00 for this rental unit. Pursuant to s.113 of the Act, subject to s.111, the lawful rent for the first rental period for a new tenant under a new tenancy agreement is the rent first charged to the tenant. Therefore, I find that this amount is the lawful monthly rent.
The Tenant did not present any evidence to suggest that the tenancy agreement and/or its terms are invalid because she coerced into signing it or misled by the Landlord.
As such, there is no legal basis to find the rent, which the parties willingly agreed to in the tenancy agreement is unlawful.
For this reason, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the unlawfully retained rent payments to the Tenant.

The Tenant’s application was framed as a claim that the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to move into the rental unit. However, based on the evidence and submissions, I find that the central issue is whether the Landlord was entitled to retain the $7,500.00 paid by the Tenant. Both parties made submissions on that issue, and I am satisfied that they had a full opportunity to address it.
The Landlord acknowledged receiving $7,500.00 from the Tenant prior to the commencement of the tenancy. The tenancy was to begin on February 1, 2026, but the Tenant never moved into the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that they became aware on February 1, 2026, that the Tenant would not be moving in. The Landlord further testified that they made no efforts to re-rent the unit after that date. The only reason provided was that the Landlord wished to keep the unit available in case the Tenant changed their mind and returned.

Under section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), a landlord is required to take reasonable steps to minimize losses arising from a tenant’s breach. A landlord is not entitled to automatically recover rent for the balance of a fixed term or notice period. Instead, the landlord may recover only the rent actually lost during a reasonable vacancy period, and only where reasonable efforts to re-rent the rental unit are demonstrated.

In this case, the Landlord made no effort to mitigate any alleged loss. The Landlord’s decision not to re-rent the unit in case the Tenant might return does not satisfy the statutory duty to minimize losses.

As a result, I find that any ongoing loss was not minimized and cannot be attributed to the Tenant. Further, because the Tenant never took possession of the rental unit, there is no evidentiary basis to support anything more than, at most, a minimal turnover period. In the absence of any mitigation efforts, I do not find that the Landlord has established an entitlement to retain any portion of the $7,500.00.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord has retained money without lawful entitlement under the Act, and the full amount must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,548.00. This amount represents: • $7,500.00 for rent unlawfully retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $973.00.
The Tenancy commenced on November 1, 2024 and terminated on July 15, 2025.

It was the Tenant’s testimony that they had entered into an oral agreement with the Landlord on June 21, 2025, to terminate the tenancy early which they then confirmed on June 22, 2025 to terminate it effective July 15, 2025. It was also their testimony that this agreement included that the Landlord would return half of the last month’s rent deposit, $925.00. They supported their submissions with text messages entered in evidence.
They then testified they were seeking the $925.00 and the $48.00 representing the filing fee for the application.

In response the Landlord testified that there had been other messages from June 21, 2025, not reflected in the Tenant’s evidence, in that they agreed to return the $925.00 on the condition they could find another tenant which they were unable to do until November 2025. It was on this basis that they retained the $925.00. They also testified that it wasn’t until July 2, 2025 that the Tenant confirmed they would leave on July 15, 2025 which contributed to the delay in finding a replacement tenant. Analysis

The onus to prove an application lies with the applicant, in the case before me the Tenant. Having considered the above testimony, evidence and reasons that follow, I am satisfied they have proven their case.

Specifically, the June 22, 2025 correspondence clearly shows that the Landlord agreed to return half of the last month’s rent. The Landlord claimed there were conversations before this, they failed to provide any evidence in support. Furthermore, even if they had they would have predated the June 22, 2025 texts and their confirmation that they would return the monies.

Additionally, the messages between the Landlord and Tenant following July 15, 2025 wherein the Tenant was requesting the money promised, there is no mention of this previously agreed condition. Accordingly for this reason and those above I am not satisfied that the Landlord has successfully rebutted the Tenant’s case. Remedies awarded

Based on the above determination I am satisfied that the Landlord did retain the Tenant's rent deposit contrary to the agreement of June 22, 2026 and therefore the Tenant is entitled to the $925.00 representing the deposit and 48.00 representing the filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord, shall pay the Tenant is $973.00. This amount represents: • $925.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • 48.00 for the filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The tenancy began on June 10, 2023, the Tenant vacated on November 30, 2024.
The limitation period with respect to the application is June 10, 2023, when the tenancy began, to November 30, 2024, when the Tenant vacated.
The rental unit is a basement apartment in a house; the Landlord and family live on the main floor. Preliminary Issues
Item 1(a) through 1(c) are outside of the limitation; they are with respect to events pre- tenancy.

Issues in the application that do not have dates/sufficient particulars are dismissed. Only the following issues are proceeding: • Noise: September 11, 16 and 22, 2023; December 26 and 27, 2023. • Harassment: December 25 through 29, 2023. Merits

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. I further find that that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the basement apartment upon the Landlord’s assurance that they are not up late at night, and that the unit was sound-proofed. Almost immediately after moving in, the noise from the Landlord’s unit/floor started. The noise was mostly in the middle of the night from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. The Landlord said because he gets up for work so early, he needs to eat at that time. The Landlord should have advised the Tenant of such a disruptive routine; had the Tenant known, she would not have signed the lease. She spoke to the Landlord and texted numerous times, but the noise continued. The Tenant testified to noise on September 11, 16 and 22, 2023, and referred to a text sent at 5:43 a.m. on September 19, 2023, advising the Landlord there is ‘still someone walking with heavy footfall past midnight every night. Last night it was until 12:45 a.m.”. The Tenant described as stomping up and down stairs and like someone was sitting on a chair and pushing it back. When asked if she was a sensitive sleeper, the Tenant responded that she could not quantify her sleep habits.

The Tenant also testified on December 27, 2023, the Landlord’s son, [name], makes noise by walking around and talking on the phone at 4:30 a.m.; the Tenant sends the Landlord videos of the banging noises coming from the main floor. The Landlord advised he was out of town, and his son was home; he admitted that his son’s friend is at the house, but he was only supposed to be visiting twice while they were away. Later that day the Tenant sent the Landlord pictures showing that the son’s friend had his car parked at the house and reported that they made noise and banging noises for 2-hours. The Landlord again admitted the son and friend were at home but claimed they were only playing with/feeding the cat; this explanation made no sense. The Tenant sent another video recording of [name]’s friends stomping and banging at 7:00 p.m. The Tenant advises the Landlord that she feels harassed and asks for the harassment to stop as it is affecting her quality of life because her sleep is being affected; the Landlord did not respond to her text which equates to harassment. The Tenant referred to the videos in evidence.

The Landlord testified he lives on the main level of the home with his wife and 2 children. When he spoke to the Tenant prior to her signing the lease, he told her it was a basement unit, therefore, she would hear regular noises, but they are not noisy at night. He also told the Tenant the unit was no sound-proofed. Any noise he and his family make is not substantial, it is from regular everyday activities; sometimes someone will get up in the middle of the night to get a glass of water or if hungry, will microwave something. He spoke to his son about the Tenant’s noise complaints and was told he was not home on some dates the Tenant complained. Approximately In September 27, 2023, he put runners in the kitchen and hall. He also put foam pads in the living room and on the stairs. He never received any noise complaints from the previous tenant; they lived in the unit for 7-years. The Landlord also testified that he works shiftwork but never said to the Tenant that he woke up at 3:00 a.m.; his morning shifts start at 6:00 a.m. and night shifts he leaves the house by 8:30 p.m. Analysis Harassment
Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find the Landlord did not harass the Tenant.
Section 23 of the Act says landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. Black’s Law Dictionary defines harassment as “a course of conduct directed at a specific person that causes substantial emotional distress in such person and serves no legitimate purpose”. Harassment in the landlord and tenant context is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate.

The videos in evidence do not demonstrate noise to the level of harassment. The noise is very faint, barely audible at times; it does not sound like stomping or banging to the degree relayed by the Tenant, as such, it does not meet the level of ‘substantial’. In respect of the Landlord son’s friend parking/being at the house, even if more times than he was supposed to, does not amount to harassment. Accordingly, this part of the application is dismissed. [name]

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the noise she is hearing is any other than that associated to everyday living; the video evidence was of very faint noises and the Tenant only referred to one text dated September 19, 2026 about not sleeping. There was no evidence of furniture being slid across the floor or stomping and banging either through the night or during the daytime. Therefore, this part of the application is also dismissed
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove that Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

The parties do not dispute that in May, 2024 the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 Notice of Termination under 48 of the Act with a termination date of June 30, 2024. In the N12 Notice, the Landlord claimed that he required vacant possession of the rental unit because the Landlord intended to move into the unit. The Tenants did not vacate the rental unit on June 30, 2024. The Landlord did not file an L2 application based on the N12 notice.

On July 17, the Landlord filed an application with the LTB (file number [name]) based on N5 and N8 notices given to the Tenants for termination of the tenancy on September 30, 2024. On December 18, 2024 an Order (the “L2 N5 Order”) was issued for payment of the sum of $450.00 on terms with a provision that if the Tenants missed a scheduled payment, the Landlord could apply for an eviction.

The Landlord also gave the Tenants an N4 notice for arrears of rent and filed an L1 Application about non-payment of rent (file number LTB-L-058050-25). An Order (the “L1 Order”) was issued on February 7, 2025. In the L1 Order, the Tenants had until February 18, 2025 to void the Order by paying the Landlord $22,686 failing which the Landlord could pursue eviction by filing the Order with the sheriff’s office for enforcement.
The Tenants did not pay the Landlord $22,686 by February 18, 2025.
As the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit on February 18, 2025, the Landlord commenced enforcement proceedings with the [name] based on [name].

The Tenants admit that they did not move out of the rental unit on February 18, 2025. The Tenants acknowledge that they remained in occupation of the rental unit until March 1, 2025 when faced with eviction under the L1 Order in March 2025. The Tenants evidence on cross-examination is that the reason they vacated the rental unit was because of “all these Orders” and the Tenants specifically stated that they moved out because of the enforcement of the L1 Order.

The parties do not dispute that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on March 1, 2025. In their T5 application the Tenants state that they moved out of the rental unit on March 1, 2025. However, they disagree about the reason the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
