The Tenants claim that they moved out of the rental unit on March 1, 2025, shortly before the scheduled eviction, pursuant to the N12 notice given to them in May, 2024 for which no L2 application had been commenced. The Landlord’s position is that the Tenants moved out as a result of the enforcement of the L1 Order about non- payment of rent. Based on the evidence before me, I prefer the Landlord’s position on this issue.

I find that the Tenants did not intend to vacate the rental unit and remained in the rental unit until faced with eviction under the L1 Order and moved out of the rental unit as a result of the anticipated execution of the L1 Order on March 1, 2025, which is entirely unrelated to the N12 Notice.

Therefore, I do not find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice the Landlord gave them. Since one of the required parts of the test in subsection 57(1)(b) is not satisfied, I find that the T5 Application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] (the 'Tenant') to pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (L9 Application) The applications were heard together by videoconference on May 21, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant testified that she came across an online ad for the rental property, advertising the rental unit for a monthly rent of $2,450.00.

The Tenant further testified that she reached out to the listing agent with respect to the availability of the rental unit, and began negotiating a tenancy agreement. She states that after the Landlord discovered that the Tenant had a small dog, the agent on behalf of the Landlord sought a monthly rent of $2,600.00. The parties entered into a tenancy agreement on July 20, 2025, with an agreed upon monthly rent of $2,600.00 due on the Order Page: 2 of 4 15th of each month. The [name] agreement commenced on August 15, 2025 for a period of one year.

The Tenant states that she paid the Landlord $2,600.00 in monthly rent for August, September, October and November as well as a last month’s rent deposit . The Tenant now seeks the return of an increased rental amount of $150.00 above the original listing price that she paid for those months totalling $750.00

The Tenant submits that the increase in rent above the listing price for the unit was due to her having a dog and is an illegal charge pursuant to section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Further, the Tenant submits that section 14 of the Act prohibits provisions in a tenancy agreement prohibiting animals and that any such provisions in a tenancy agreement are void.
The Landlord submits that the increased amount in rent negotiated between the parties was not due to a dog fee, but due to the demand for the rental unit.

The parties agree that the tenancy agreement does not contain any provisions relating to restrictions on pets or animals, nor does it contain any additional animal or pet fees above the monthly rent. Analysis

In support of her position, the Tenant relies on section 14 of the Act, which states: A provision in a tenancy agreement prohibiting the presence of animals in or about the residential complex is void.

The tenancy agreement does not contain any provisions prohibiting the presence of animals in or about the residential complex. In fact, it is undisputed that the Tenant resides in the rental unit with her dog. Based on the evidence before me section 14 of the Act is not applicable to this matter.

Section 134 of the Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord; or [name]: 3 of 4 c) rent any portion of the rental unit for a rent which, together with all other rents payable for all other portions of the rental unit, is a sum that is greater than the rent the landlord may lawfully charge for the rental unit.

On the fact before me, I find that the parties freely negotiated and entered into a tenancy agreement with a monthly rent of $2,600.00. Although the issue of a pet may have come up during the negotiating process, the tenancy agreement contains no additional charges or premiums for a pet or any other charge in addition to the negotiated rent as agreed between the parties.

On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act. The Tenant’s application will be dismissed. L9 Application 1. As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit. 2. The Tenant did not pay the total rent they were required to pay for the period from November 15, 2025 to June 14, 2026. 3. The lawful rent is $2,600.00. It is due on the 15th day of each month. 4. The Tenant has paid $4,900.00 to the Landlord after the application was filed. 5. The Landlord alleges the rent arrears owing to June 14, 2026 are $1,050.00. 6. The Tenant disputes the arrears believing the amount sought by the Landlord is an illegal ‘pet charge’. This issue has been determined above in the Tenants L1 application. It is not an illegal charge and therefore the Tenant must pay it. 7. The rent arrears owing to June 14, 2026 are $1,050.00. 8. The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $1,236.00. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to June 14, 2026 and the cost of the application.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before June 27, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name]:

The Tenants testified that they observed a mold like substance inside of their rental unit. The substance was found inside of a closet near the front entry way, along the front door of the rental unit, and on a window near the basement stairway. The Tenants tendered evidence in the form of photographs of the mold claimed. The Tenants testified that they informed the Landlords of the mold on or about December 7, 2023.

The Tenants did not have the substance tested but believed that the substance was mold. The reason for this belief was because the Tenants attempted to clean the substance on multiple occasions, but it would return shortly thereafter. The Tenants also attempted to use products such as mold and mildew spray which proved to be ineffective for the long term.

The Tenants testified that the Landlords attended to the mold issues and concerns sometime in February 2025, with the work being completed in approximately April 2025. The Tenants do not believe that the delay of over one year was reasonable.

The Tenants also testified that the trim that was removed from the closet space by the Landlords’ contractor had visible mold and could not be re-used inside the closet space. The Tenants tendered photographs of the trim and substance observed.

The Landlord testified that the unit was built in 2020, and that the property was still under new home warranty. The Landlord also testified that the mold in the closet resulted from the construction of the home. The Landlord also had a contractor attend the unit and inspect the issue, but the Tenants and the contractor had a dispute which created delays in having the work completed. The Landlord testified that the mold in the closet was corrected and addressed by December 2025, and that any delays would have been associated with the builder and warranty program that the Landlords relied upon.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the rental unit had a substance inside the closet that on a balance of probabilities was a form of mold. I do not have sufficient evidence to make a finding of the type of mold it was, nor do I have sufficient detail to find that the mold was a dangerous versus a non- dangerous mold. None the less, the presence of mold would normally cause a reasonable person to have concern for their health and wellbeing. The Tenant was pregnant at the time and was expecting a child. I am mindful that the Landlords’ ability to carry out the necessary repairs are somewhat dependent on the warranty and builder, but I do not have any documentation to show that the Landlords took reasonable steps to contact the builder or warrant program in 2023, when being initially informed of the issue. Therefore, I find that the Landlords have failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Snow removal and salting:

The Tenants testified that the Landlords failed to clean the snow and salt the driveway throughout the winter months as necessary. The Tenants also testified that the lease agreement stipulates that the Landlords are responsible for all exterior maintenance work, which they understood to include snow removal and salting.
The Tenants testified that they had to shovel the snow and salt the driveway at the rental unit for the periods of February 2024, March 2024, December 2024, January 2025, and February 2025.

The Tenants take the position that the snow removal and salting was the responsibility of the Landlords, and the Landlords’ failure to attend to this was a breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Act.

The Landlord did not dispute that she did not have salting or snow removal services carried out at the rental property. The Landlord took the position that the unit was a self- contained unit with only the Tenants living in it and that the Tenants should be responsible for their own salting and snow removal. The Landlord did not believe that the snow removal and salting was included in the Tenants’ monthly rent. The Landlord did confirm that the lease specifically stated that the Landlords was responsible for all exterior maintenance. The Landlord also agreed that the driveway formed a part of the exterior property.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlords were responsible for salting and snow removal. I make this finding because the lease did not state that the Tenants are responsible for salting and snow removal and stated that the Landlords were responsible for all exterior maintenance. Although, the Act allows a landlord to contract out of their obligation for snow removal and salting in some circumstances, I do not find this to be the case in these circumstances. Therefore, I find that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Window and door repairs:

The Tenants testified that the back door and back window in the rental unit were not properly sealed and allowed a draft into the kitchen. The window would also show signs of ongoing condensation. The Tenants testified that the Landlords agreed to have the window replaced by the manufacturer and did so in December 2025. The Tenants notified the Landlords of the window issue in late December 2023 / early January 2024. The Tenants testified that the door was never replaced or repaired.

The Tenants testified that their utility bills would be higher for heating due to the draft in the window and door. The Tenants also did not believe that the window repair being completed one year after their initial complaint to be reasonable.

The Landlord testified that she was never notified of the door not being sealed or requiring any repairs. The Landlord did not dispute being notified of the window requiring sealing and confirmed having this work done sometime in December 2025. The Landlord testified that any delay in having this work done would have been attributed to ordering the window and supply of such, and relying on the home builder or warranty program to have the work completed. The Landlord did not tender any evidence to support that she took immediate steps to report the issue to the builder or warranty program back in December 2023, or early January 2024.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the window and door were not properly sealed and required repairs. I am also satisfied that the Tenants made the Landlords aware of both the issues at the same time. I do not find the delay in having the window repaired to be reasonable. I also do not have sufficient evidence to find that the cause of the delay was solely due to the warranty program and/or builder. Therefore, I find that the Landlords have failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') by failing to repair the window within a reasonable time and failing to repair the door.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, I am not satisfied that the Landlords took all reasonable steps available at the time of being notified of the concerns to address the issues. I do not have any evidence of the Landlords’ communication with the warranty program and/or the builder showing reasonable steps taken by the Landlords. I also do not find that one year is a reasonable time to have a unit inspected and treated for mold or have a window in the unit replaced. Remedies

The Tenants sought a rent abatement in the amount of 573.81 for the entirety of their claim. The Tenants’ lawful rent was $1,850.00 per month. Based on the evidence, I find the amount sought by the Tenants to be very reasonable given the circumstances.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $573.81 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenants also sought compensation in the amount of $2,500.00 for damaged items that the Tenants had to throw away because of the mold in the closet. The Tenants testified that they had to throw out several pieces of clothing because of mold exposure. The Tenants did not have any photographs of the damaged items, nor did the Tenants have any receipts of the costs for the damaged items. The Tenants also did not tender any evidence to support that the damaged items could not be drycleaned or professionally cleaned rather than being thrown away. A party seeking compensation for damages to their personal property bears the burden of proof and is expected to substantiate the claim on a balance of probabilities.

Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenants had $2,500.00 worth of damaged clothing and items that could not be washed or professionally cleaned because the Landlords did not repair or maintain the rental unit or the residential complex. I am making this finding for a lack of evidence on this issue. I do not have any photographs of the damaged clothing or items, nor do I have any reports showing the clothing or damaged items could not be professionally washed or salvaged. Therefore, no compensation shall flow from this claim.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenants $626.81. This amount represents: • $573.81 for a rent abatement for the period of February 2024, through to February 2025. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application came before another Member on March 27, 2023 with respect to a preliminary issue regarding changing of the locks which resulted in interim order LTB-T-012287-23-IN-2 issued on April 12, 2023. The remainder of the application was heard by videoconference before me on June 5, 2023, June 6, 2025, August 13, 2025, and October 8, 2025. The parties agreed that the Member who issued interim order LTB-T-012287-23-IN-2 was not seized of this matter. The Landlord’s agent, [name], the Landlord’s representative, [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s representative, [name], attended the hearing. [name] attended the hearing as a witness for the Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,677.09.

By way of background, it is uncontested that maintenance issues arose in the rental unit involving mould which required the Tenant to reside away from the rental unit commencing July 18, 2022 while the Landlord effected repairs. The Tenant resumed residing in the rental unit in June 2023 and subsequently moved out in November 2023.
This application was filed on February 7, 2023 and pertains to the period up to June 2023 when the Tenant resumed residing in the rental unit. Partial Resolution

At the hearing, the Landlord indicated that they had already consented to paying the Tenant $5,030.48 with respect to the following items: • $426.00 for hygiene items and clothes (line 47 on DOC-5047257) • $211.53 for pharmacy items • $398.00 for gas utilities (line 45 on DOC-5047257) • $760.00 for groceries (line 46 on DOC-5047257) • $600.00 for dog care • $790.34 for school supplies(line 35 on DOC-5047257) • $573.93 for fall clothing for child 1 (line 36 on DOC-5047257) • $450.50 for fall clothing for child 2 (line 37 on DOC-5047257) • $702.64 for shoes and rain boots (line 38 on DOC-5047257) • $117.54 for cat carriers (line 53 on [name])

During the course of the hearing, the Landlord also consented to paying the Tenant: • $398.61 for electricity the Tenant paid at the rental unit when the Tenant was unable to occupy the rental unit. • $200.00 for Rogers expenses from July to September 2022.
As a result, the total amount the Landlord consented to paying the Tenant is $5,629.09. Changing Locks

Although interim order LTB-T-012287-23-IN-2 issued on April 12, 2023 found that the Landlord unlawfully changed the locks on October 17, 2022, it acknowledged the health and safety circumstances under which this occurred. This is evidenced by the wording in the order at paragraph 13 and by the fact that the order did not require the Landlord to provide keys to the Tenant immediately, but ordered the Landlord to provide them several months later, July 31, 2023, when the Landlord expected remediation of the rental unit to be complete.

I also recognize the health and safety concerns which caused the Landlord to change the locks. The Landlord changed the locks and restricted access to the rental unit upon the recommendation of the environmental consultant the Landlord retained whose report dated October 13, 2022 states: As soon as reasonably achievable the residence should be isolated until remediation scope of work can be effectively performed. Access should be restricted to those with appropriate PPE including respirator (P-100 filters) and protective clothing.

I am also mindful that the Tenant had not been residing in the rental unit since July 18, 2026 when the locks were changed on October 17, 2022 and that the Landlord was paying for the Tenant’s alternative accommodation.

I also note that the Landlord notified the Tenant on October 14, 2026 that they would be changing the locks to the rental unit in accordance with the recommendation from the environmental consultant and that the Landlord offered to retrieve anything from the rental unit for the Tenant.

I accept that the locks were changed for the Tenant’s own protection and that the Landlord changed the locks so that they could fulfil their obligation to maintain the rental unit. I also find that the Landlord minimized the impact on the Tenant by forewarning them of their intention to change the locks, explaining their reasons for doing so, and by agreeing to retrieve anything from the rental unit the Tenant required.

In light of the above, while I find that the Landlord did not have lawful authority under the Act to change the locks, I find no compensation to the Tenant for this is warranted in the particular circumstances of this case.
As a result, while the application is granted with respect to finding that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act with respect to changing the locks, no remedy is ordered.

If I am incorrect in finding that no remedy is warranted for the Landlord’s breach, I would find the appropriate remedy to be $1.00 given the subsidy of changing the locks and the minimal impact on the Tenant. Illegal Entry

I am not persuaded that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on October 24, 2022. The Tenant was not residing in the rental unit at that time so the Landlord could effect repairs. I find that the Tenant gave the Landlord implicit consent to enter the rental unit to effect repairs and that the entry was therefore lawful.
As a result, this portion of the application is dismissed.

If I am incorrect on this point and the entry was unlawful, I find that the unlawful entry had no impact on the Tenant because they were not residing in the rental unit at that time and that no compensation for this unlawful entry is warranted.

Again, if I am incorrect in finding that no remedy is warranted for the Landlord’s breach, I would find the appropriate remedy to be $1.00 given the minimal impact on the Tenant. Substantial Interference

While the Tenant’s T2 pleadings with respect to substantial interference are not particularly clear, the Tenant argued at the hearing that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment by not properly caring for their personal property such that their personal property was damaged and needed to be replaced.

I am not persuaded on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established that their personal property was damaged. The Tenant focused much of their testimony on how the work in the rental unit was not conducted properly, however most of this is immaterial absent a finding that their personal property was damaged. Having said that, I am not persuaded that the work was not conducted properly. Shortly after the Tenant left the rental unit on July 18, 2022, the Landlord’s contractor cordoned off areas of the rental unit with tarps and tape and installed air scrubbers to create negative air pressure in the potentially contaminated areas of the rental unit. Although the Tenant testified that she did not believe this work was done properly (e.g. scrubbers were not always on, tape on the tarps coming loose), there was no evidence to suggest that the work did not achieve the desired results. That the work was not done perfectly does not mean that it was not done sufficiently.

With respect to the Tenant’s personal possessions, the Landlord employed contractors who engaged in an extensive decontamination process with respect to the Tenant’s goods. The decontamination process, including pictures, is set out in the report from Greenough Environmental Consulting dated March 9, 2023. Their preliminary report dated February 13, 2023 states that the mould sampling of personal property indicates “low counts for toxigenic mould species”, that the spore counts were not a concern, and that there was no active mould amplification associated with the items tested.
The Tenant maintained that the items were not decontaminated because they smelled bad and did not look clean.

The Landlord replied to this assertion by stating that there was a difference between decontaminating and cleaning. Decontamination involved HEPA vacuuming and wiping with a concrobium product, cleaning was a more extensive process which the Landlord did not undertake.
The Tenant submitted photos into evidence, however, these photos did not show obvious signs of mould and I did not find them to be supportive of the Tenant’s allegation that the property was damaged.

Ultimately, I found the documentary evidence from the Landlord’s contractors to be more persuasive with respect to the status of the Tenant’s goods than the Tenant’s testimony. These documents indicated that the Tenant’s property was not damaged by mould. The Tenant bears the onus of proving that the property was damaged and they have not met this burden.
As a result, I was not persuaded that the Tenant provided sufficient evidence to establish that their personal property was damaged and this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

I should also note that all the dated receipts for the replacement property the Tenant states they had to buy were dated for August and September 2022. It is not clear to me why the Tenant did not seek to retrieve items from the rental unit at that time rather than buying new items. While this raises concerns regarding mitigation, I do not need to consider this as I am not persuaded that the Tenant has established that their items were damaged.

The Tenant also alleges that the storing of their items after they were cleaned by the Landlord’s contractors was inadequate and caused damage to their property, however, there was no persuasive evidence of this. The Tenant’s photographs did not identify any noteworthy damage. Harassment, etc.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by: • ignoring the Tenant’s concerns about mould • giving the Tenant “arbitrary deadlines” for the Tenant to provide consent for the Landlord to remove items from the rental unit so remediation work could occur, failing which the Landlord would take “unilateral action” with respect to the items in the rental unit • changing the locks • inaccurately telling the Tenant in July 2022 that the mould issue had been resolved • trying to get the Tenant to sign legal release and nondisclosure agreements

I am not persuaded that any of these allegations, even if true, constitute harassment, etc. These allegations, including changing of the locks addressed more fulsomely above, lack the animus that forms the basis for this type of claim.
In addition, I am not persuaded that the Landlord ignored the Tenant’s concerns about mould in the rental unit.
There was a sewage backup in October 2021 which the Landlord rectified at that time.

On July 6, 2022, the Tenant reported a mouldy smell, damaged baseboard, and rippled wall in the bathroom by sending an email to an employee of the Landlord, [name]. The Tenant sent the email to [name] in the hopes of receiving a quicker response than going through the regular maintenance request process, however [name] was on vacation (as evidenced by the auto reply the Tenant received) and did not respond until July 11, 2022 when he returned. After consulting with the Tenant regarding attendance at the rental unit, [name] attended the rental unit on July 13, 2022 for an initial inspection and then had a professional contractor, [name], attend the rental unit that same day. 34. [name] cut an investigatory hole in the drywall and replaced a portion of the plumbing stack on July 13, 2022. 35. The Tenant requested air testing for mould on July 14, 2022 and the Landlord had testing done on July 15, 2022. The results of the mould testing were expected on July 18, 2022, but the Tenant relocated to an Airbnb on July 18, 2022 and did not reside in the rental unit again until June 2023. 36. It is clear from the Landlord’s initial response and the ongoing communication between the parties after the Tenant stopped residing in the rental unit, that the Landlord was very attentive to the Tenant’s concerns regarding mould. As a result, I see no merit to the allegation that the Landlord ignored the Tenant’s concerns regarding mould. 37. I am also not persuaded that the Landlord gave the Tenant “arbitrary deadlines” with respect to obtaining the Tenant’s consent to remove possessions from the rental unit so that remediation work could be completed. The Tenant was advised on November 24, 2022 that the contents of the rental unit would need to be removed to complete the remediation work. The parties engaged in extensive negotiations thereafter and the Tenant’s personal property was ultimately removed from the rental unit on January 30, 2023. 38. As a result, the application is dismissed with respect to the Tenant’s allegation of the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Failure to Maintain 39. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the Board should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. In this case, I am not persuaded the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act for the reasons set out below. 40. The Tenant’s T6 application states that the Landlord was first informed about the problem on July 6, 2022. 41. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on July 18, 2022 and the Landlord paid for the Tenant’s alternative accommodation from that time until the Tenant moved back in in June 2023. 42. While I acknowledge that remediation of the rental unit took an extraordinary length of time, no evidence was led or obtained on cross-examination suggesting that the Landlord did not pursue the remediation work in a reasonable manner. I cannot infer simply from the length of time itself that the Landlord took too long to complete the work. Without some evidentiary basis to find that the Landlord delayed completing repairs, I cannot find that they did so. 43. The Landlord also took steps to ameliorate the impact the maintenance issues had on the Tenant by paying for their alternate accommodation etc. 44. In light of the above, and in keeping with Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord responded to the maintenance issues reasonably in the circumstances and that the Landlord was not in breach of their maintenance obligations under the Act. If I am wrong on this point, I find that no compensation is warranted because the Landlord paid for the Tenant’s alternative accommodations until the maintenance issues were resolved. 45. As a result, this portion of the application is dismissed. Remedies 46. Given that that the Landlord agreed to pay the Tenant $5,030.48 prior to the hearing and agreed to pay an additional $598.61 during the course of the hearing, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $5,629.09. 47. I do not find it appropriate to order any of the other remedies requested. The primary reason for this is that, with the exception of the changing of the locks discussed at length above (for which I do not find any compensation warranted for the reasons stated), the Tenant has not established that the Landlord breached any of their other obligations under the Act. 48. Moreover, the Tenant’s request to be compensated for legal expenses runs contrary to Interpretation Guideline 3 which limits costs unless there is unreasonable conduct during the proceeding. Most of the legal expenses the Tenant wishes to be compensated for arose prior to the commencement of the proceeding and there was no suggestion that the Landlord conducted themselves inappropriately in the Board’s proceedings to warrant a costs award. As a result, a costs award would be inappropriate. 49. The Tenant’s request for an abatement of rent is also not warranted given that the Landlord paid (or has agreed during the course of these proceedings to pay) for the Tenant’s alternate accommodation and out-of-pocket expenses related to accommodation. 50. The Tenant’s request to be compensated for lost income is also not justified. I have no doubt that the discovery of mould in the rental unit and the sequela that followed were a horrible experience for the Tenant and that the Tenant experienced some financial loss because of what happened, however, the Tenant has not established lawful grounds by which those losses ought to be transferred to the Landlord. The Landlord responded to the problems appropriately and did their best to mitigate harm to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,677.09. This amount represents: • $5,629.09 representing the amount the Landlord conceded at the hearing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026 the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) and [name] (the 'Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination to vacate the rental unit on March 31, 2022, because the purchaser required the rental unit for their own residential use. The Landlord provided the Tenant with one month rent compensation as required by sections 49.1 and 55.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
The Tenant lived in the rental unit, a two bedroom, upper unit, of a house since 2014. Her monthly rent at the time she moved out was $1,446.00.

It is undisputed that the Tenant also signed an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy on March 31, 2022, after it was sent to her by the Landlord. The Tenant admits that she received no legal advice during the time of vacating the rental unit. She said that she signed the N11 agreement to terminate because she wanted to be on good terms with the Landlord so that he would pay her the one month’s rent compensation he had promised. She was unaware that she was entitled to receive the one month’s rent as a result of being served an N12 notice of termination. The Landlord said that he was told by his legal representative that it was appropriate to give the Tenant an N11 agreement to terminate.

All the evidence from all parties, during the hearing, was submitted on the basis that this was a T5 application filed by the Tenant alleging a bad faith eviction on the basis of an N12 notice of termination. It is undisputed that compensation of one month’s rent was paid by the Landlord to the Tenant. None of the parties asserted that the application should be dismissed because the parties had signed an N11 agreement to terminate.

As it happens, the Tenant does not dispute that she signed the N11 agreement to terminate of her own free will. If I were only to consider the N11 agreement to terminate, the application would be dismissed.

However, for the purpose of this application I will disregard the signed N11 agreement to terminate. Neither party appeared to understand the distinction between terminating a tenancy via an N12 notice of termination or terminating a tenancy with an agreement to terminate. I proceeded on the basis of a T5 application filed by the Tenant alleging that the N12 notice of termination she received was in bad faith.

The Tenant said that she had a long-term, good, relationship with her Landlord. She testified that she was shocked when her Landlord called her in January 2022 and informed her that the tenancy would be ending by March 31, 2022. He told her he was selling the house.

The Tenant said that the process of selling the house was “very aggressive” with up to nine showings per day, and there were many showings by the middle of January 2022. She said that the house was sold by January 17, 2022, after about 40 showings. She said that showing her unit was a “full-time job”. The Tenant works from home. The Tenant said that the purchaser was “aggressive” in coming to inspect the rental unit throughout February 2022.

The Tenant said that she was served the N12 and N11 notices on January 18, 2022, and she cooperated with the Landlord at all times because she wanted to ensure that she would get the one month extra rent compensation, and also that the Landlord would provide her with a good reference. She signed the N11 agreement to terminate. She also said that she immediately began to look for somewhere else to live.

The Tenant said it was extremely difficult to find a new unit. She said that she could not move “just anywhere” because her niece was coming to live with her while attending an acting academy in the Junction. She said that she looked in the Junction, but she also looked all over the city. She said there was a shortage of places, and it was like the “Hunger Games” to find a unit during [name]. The Tenant said that she required a two bedroom unit, and she had to significantly up her budget. She said she eventually found a place in March, and she moved to a main floor unit at 97 Eileen Ave, near [name] and St. Clair. It was a two bedroom unit for $3,250.00 per month.

The Tenant said that she believes the eviction was in bad faith because the purchaser, [name] [name] (ND) did not move into the rental unit. The Tenant said that she walked by the rental unit weekly and it was completely unused, and she saw no activity in either the upper or lower units. She said the bins were never out, and when she went to collect the mail there was no one there, and all the vegetation was overgrown.

The Tenant said that on August 30, 2022, she saw some grass was cut and she observed what appeared to be a showing of the unit. She said she googled her address and saw a current ad for her unit for rent, and it even used her own staging photos. The Tenant submitted into evidence the ad for her unit from August 2022, for a monthly rent of $2,800.00. She said that she messaged the renting realtor, and she was informed that the unit was leased.

The Tenant requests 12 months of the rent differential between her new unit and the old unit, or 12 X $1,804.00= $21,648.00. She also requests general compensation based on the stress and anxiety she suffered looking for a new place and having to endure so many showings of her unit, in the equivalent of $6,880.00. She also requests moving expenses of $1,400.00.

The Tenant said that she believes there is bad faith on the part of both ND and her former Landlord because the sale of the house was completely dependent upon vacant possession, and the Landlord pursued the sale quickly and aggressively, and the purchaser did not move into the rental unit.
The Former Landlord, P. [name] (PSC) said that he served an N12 notice of termination for purchaser’s own use on the basis of instructions from his real estate agent.

PSC said that he owned the property since 1987, and he was a good Landlord. He said that he decided to retire and sell the house, and he called the Tenant on January 3, 2022, in good faith, to alert her to the sale and the fact that she might have to move out. He said that he mentioned March 31, 2022, because he knew it was possible, and he just wanted her to be aware of the possibility. He said that he did not tell the Tenant that she would, for sure, be leaving by March 31, 2022.

PSC said that he never discussed with any one the possibility of selling the house as an investment property. He said that he just wanted to sell it for a good price. PSC said that he does not remember if the ad for sale of the house mentioned investment, but he believes it mentioned that there was a rental income from the house. He said that he is confident that the clause in the agreement for purchase and sell that mentions vacant possession was requested by the purchaser.

PSC’s realtor, C. Pyke (CP) said that it was the purchaser’s agent who insisted on a clause for vacant possession. CP said that it was she who informed the Landlord about an N11 agreement to terminate as well as an N12 notice of termination. CP said that the Landlord served the N12 notice in good faith, merely ensuring that the purchaser could move into the house with vacant possession. CP said that she asked the purchaser’s real estate agent if the purchaser was moving in, and she ensured CP that the purchaser required vacant possession. She did not recall if she ever discussed the house as a good investment. However, she was certain that she advised the Landlord that the property had to be sold with the sitting tenants.

ND’s husband, [name] (PSH) testified that he moved into the residential complex with ND in June 2022, and they moved out unexpectedly two months later. He said that after they moved into the residential complex he proposed to ND. PSH said that they had been a couple since 2020, and when he proposed on August 6, 2022, it was a surprise. He said that between the move out date in March 2022, and June 2022, he and ND were getting the house cleaned and planning renovations. He said they took their time acquiring things. He said that he and ND at no time told the real estate agent to serve an N12 notice of termination because they were first-time buyers and they “did not know anything.” He said that he works in film, and he knows nothing about obligations to tenants pursuant to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

PSH said that upon moving in they were planning to renovate, but after the proposal they had to take stock and figure out what made sense financially. He said that they decided in August 2022 to rent out the house and save more money. He said they moved in with his in-laws because they had space.

PSH said that he and ND eventually completed their renovation, and they have lived in the residential complex since September 2025. He submitted photos to support his testimony about the renovation, and subsequent moving into the residential complex.

ND said that she was aware there were tenants living in the residential complex when she purchased the property, but she was told they were going to leave. She said that she knows nothing about the clause for vacant possession.

ND said that when she viewed the house she was looking for a place for her family to live, she was intending to live in the whole house, and she planned to immediately renovate. She submitted into evidence her [name] receipt for moving into the residential complex on June 3, 2022. She said that when she bought the house her contractor was busy. ND said that she had a contractor in mind from before the purchase of the house. She said that an architect came to inspect in April 2022, and the contractor came to assess the job in July 2022, and it was then he said it would take a number of months before he could start the job. ND said that they slowly moved things between April and June 2022, and they were in constant discussion about what to do with the space. She said that she moved from her own condo into the residential complex, and then she and PSH moved in with her parents. ND married PS in January 2023.
ND said that once PSH proposed their plans changed.

It is undisputed that ND advertised the rental unit for rent in August 2022, and there were new tenants living in the rental unit as of September 2022. She said that the new tenants were always aware that ND intended to renovate and live in the house, that their tenancy was temporary, and then they discovered the black mould.

ND said that the tenants moved within six months because they found mould. She said that both upper and lower tenants moved out after about six months for the same reason. She said it was then that she completely gutted the residential complex and carried out a renovation. It took about six months to get permits.

ND said that the lawn may have been overgrown when the Tenant walked by because she, ND, received a notice from the City about overgrown grass, and she had to hire someone to cut the grass. However, ND said that the residential complex was never vacant for long. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that neither the Former Landlord PSC nor the Purchaser ND served the Tenant with a notice of termination in bad faith for the following reasons.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

It is true that subsection 57(5) provides a presumption of bad faith in the case where the rental unit is advertised for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating. I will not consider whether there is a presumption of bad faith that has, or has not, been rebutted in this case because subsection 57(5) applies to a notice of termination pursuant to section 48 of the Act, not an N12 notice served pursuant to section 49 of the Act. In any case, even were the presumption to apply here, I find it is rebutted for the reasons given below. In particular, the purchaser moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the rental unit, she moved out temporarily because of a sudden change of plan, and it was always the purchaser’s intention to live in the rental unit, and the purchaser does now live in it (see below).
It is undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

It is before me to determine whether a person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. That is, did either the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse move into to the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated?

The Tenant said that she walked by the house frequently in the summer of 2022, and she saw no activity and no one appeared to be living there. ND and PSH both testified that they slowly moved their belongings from April to June 2022, and then they moved more stuff on June 3, 2022. They had a UHaul receipt for a moving truck dated June 3, 2022. The pick up location of the UHaul is in the vicinity of the residential complex. ND and PSH said that they got engaged on August 6, 2022, and they had a Facebook posting to support that testimony. They had photos of some of their belongings in the residential complex in August 2022. ND said that the residential complex was inhabited at all times from at least June 2022, but she did, in fact, get an order from by law to cut the grass, and she did so by August 2022. The Tenant had no photos, nor did she supply dates she walked by the allegedly deserted residential complex to support her allegation that the residential complex was uninhabited. I am mindful that the onus is on the Tenant to prove her allegations in this application, and she had no documentary evidence to contradict either ND’s or PSH’s testimony.

ND does not deny that the rental unit was re-rented by September 2022, but she said that it was the result of a drastic change in plans, that is getting engaged, discovering that her contractor would not be able to renovate immediately, and a sudden need to save more money because of a wedding and a major renovation.

Neither ND nor PSC appear to have really educated themselves about N12 notices and the appropriate situation in which to serve one, and they both relied on real estate agents for advice about vacant possession, when they perhaps should have more intently focused on their obligations as either Landlord or Purchaser of a property with sitting tenants. Nevertheless, I find that the evidence supports ND’s evidence that she purchased the property for her own use and occupation. The fact that ND carried out a major renovation and she now lives in the property supports, on a balance of probabilities, that it was always her intention to fully move into the entire residential complex after a major renovation. There is no doubt that ND may not have completely thought through what would happen when she first bought the property in April 2022, but all the evidence supports her testimony that once she had thorough discussions with her architect and contractor, and once she was unexpectedly engaged and planning a wedding, her renovation project became a longer term plan than she may have originally considered. However, I find on a balance of probabilities, that moving into the residential complex for her own use was always ND’s plan. ND was a bit cavalier about moving in for only a few months, casually renting the property out again for a very temporary period, but I do not find that establishes that the Tenant has proved bad faith service of the N12 notice on the part of either ND or PSC.

Therefore, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that a person referred to in subsections 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Even were the rental of the rental unit in September 2022 to demonstrate a presumption of bad faith, less than a year after the Tenant moved out, ND has rebutted that presumption by establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that she always planned to renovate and live in the residential complex. She does, in fact, currently live in the residential complex. I also find that the evidence supports PSC’s submission that he gave the N12 notice of termination for purchaser’s own use which he believed to be the appropriate notice. His real estate agent, CP, testified under oath that she did in fact inquire whether the purchaser was planning to move into the residential complex.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s application was filed on February 1, 2026, and alleges that the Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlords and that the Landlords did not allow the Tenants to move into the rental unit and did not return the Tenant’s deposit.
The rental unit is in a two-storey apartment building consisting of eight rental units.

The parties agree that a tenancy agreement was signed by the Tenants on January 2, 2026 for a move in / commencement date of February 1, 2026. The Landlords entered into evidence a copy of the tenancy agreement (LL exhibit #1). The monthly rent as per the agreement was $1,295.00 per month.
The parties also agree that prior to signing the lease, that the Tenants paid to the Landlords a rent deposit of $1,295.00 on December 30, 2025.

The Tenant testified that at the time she signed the lease agreement, the Landlords promised her that she could move in on January 15, 2026 and that due to the ongoing renovations, the rental unit was not ready and a such, she advised the Landlords in February 2026 that she would not be moving into the rental unit. the Tenants request that the deposit of $1,295.00 be returned.

The Landlords take the position that the tenancy was set to commence on February 1, 2026, and that the Tenants unilaterally cancelled the tenancy agreement by not moving into the rental unit. 8. [name] appeared as witness for the Landlord. [name] is employed as an onsite superintendent / maintenance staff for the Landlord. [name] testified that at the time the Tenants signed the tenancy agreement, that another resident had recently been evicted and that the Tenants were advised that renovations / repairs to the unit had to be conducted prior to them moving in. 9. [name] confirmed that the tenancy agreement was to commence February 1, 2026, but agreed that he advised the Tenant that if the renovations were completed earlier that she could move into the unit prior to February 1, 2026. 10. [name] further stated that on or about February 1, 2026, the rental unit was habitable and that some minor maintenance repairs were required (drywall patches & baseboards being installed). [name] testified that despite this he attempted to call the Tenant on several occasions to inquire about the move in at which point the Tenant advised via text message on February 10, 2026 that she would not be moving into the rental unit. 11. The Landlord’s agent [name] [name] testified that after the Tenants cancelled the tenancy agreement, that the unit was immediately advertised for rent and that a new tenant signed an agreement on March 10, 2026 and moved into the rental unit on March 23, 2026. 12. The Tenant’s application is filed pursuant to section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act): 107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. 13. The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2011 O NCA 502 provides the Board with guidance, starting: When one looks at the words of section 107(1), It is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is not given to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. In the present case, however, it is the tenant’s action in refusing to take the unit that prevented him from taking possession, not any act of the landlord However, with respect to a landlord’s ability to retain a rent deposit, section 105(1) and 106(1) of the Act provides that a landlord may only take a deposit as security against the payment of the last month’s rent. The landlord may not take a deposit to secure any other obligation. Thus, if a tenant breaches a tenancy agreement and the landlord, in accordance with its obligations to mitigate its damages, is able to re rent the premises without suffering any loss of rent, the landlord is not entitled to retain the rent deposit. The landlord cannot realise double payment by use of a deposit, nor can it apply the funds to any other purpose. 14. In this case, I find that the Tenants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords refused and/or failed to give the Tenants possession to the rental unit and further find that the Landlords took diligent efforts to mitigate their losses by re-renting the unit as soon as possible. 15. As this is the Tenant’s application, the onus rests with the Tenants to prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. In this case, the Tenant present at the hearing led insufficient evidence such as written correspondence from the Landlords suggesting that the Tenants could not move into the rental unit as of February 1, 2026, which is the commencement date set out in the tenancy agreement. I accept the oral testimony of the Landlord’s witness that the unit was fit for residential occupation (despite some minor maintenance deficiencies) and that the Tenants unilaterally chose not to move into the unit and terminate their tenancy. The Act ultimately provides a tenant with a remedy should they move into a rental unit and allege that the landlord has not met their maintenance obligations under the Act (section 29(1) 1. of the RTA). 16. The evidence before the Board suggests that the rental unit was habitable, despite some minor maintenance concerns, and that the Tenants unilaterally terminated the tenancy and refused to move into the rental unit. The Tenant present at the hearing also did not cross- examine or challenge the Landlord’s efforts to mitigate their losses and to re-rent the unit. I therefore find that the Landlords re-renting the unit as of March 10, 2026, to suggest reasonable and diligent efforts were made to mitigate their losses and as such, the Landlords are entitled to hold the Tenant’s deposit for the month of February 2026. 17. As such, the Tenants have failed to prove that the Landlords has breached section 107(1) of the Act. The application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants T1 application alleges that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord did not give the Tenants access to the rental unit as agreed.

The Tenants testified that they made a deposit for the rental unit on January 9, 2026. They state that after they made the deposit, they continued to see the ad for the rental unit online. The Tenants being concerned that it was a scam requested a lease agreement from the Landlord and the Landlord stated that it is a verbal tenancy agreement and she assured them that it was not a scam. On January 13, 2026, the Tenants informed the Landlord that they were cancelling their lease.

Section 2(1) of the Act defines a “tenancy agreement” as follows: “Tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; (“convention de location”)

The evidence before me is that the Tenants elected not to take possession. After the Tenants withdrew their intent to occupy the unit – the Landlord did not fail to provide the Tenants with vacant possession. Based on the evidence I’ve heard I can only infer that if the Tenants did not cancel their lease agreement on January 13, 2026, that the Landlord was ready, willing and capable of providing vacant possession on the move-in date of February 1, 2026.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit and was ready to provide the Tenants with vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord is not required to repay the rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenants application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that ANAM SIDDIQUE (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the parties consented to the application being amended to reflect the proper name of the Landlord, “[name]” Preliminary Issue – Motion to Dismiss
The Tenant filed an application alleging that the Landlord excessively entered the rental unit.

The Landlord raised a preliminary issue that the application lacks sufficient particulars to permit a fair response. Specifically, the Landlord submits that the application does not identify the dates of the alleged entries, the number of entries complained of, or the period over which the alleged conduct occurred
As explained below, I agree with the Landlord’s representative and find the application is dismissed on a preliminary basis.

The Tenant's application was filed on February 12, 2025. As a result, the timing of the alleged entries is relevant both to the Landlord's ability to respond to the allegations and to determine whether any of the alleged conduct falls within the Board's jurisdiction having regard to the applicable limitation period.

The Tenant acknowledged that the application does not contain dates for many of the alleged entries. The Tenant submits that supporting documents were provided to the Landlord and that some of those documents contain descriptions of the entries.

The application alleges excessive entries but does not clearly identify the dates of the alleged entries, the number of entries being relied upon, or which specific incidents are said to constitute the alleged breach. This information is particularly important in this case because the Landlord disputes the allegations and because limitation period issues may arise.

Procedural fairness requires that a responding party be given adequate notice of the case against them. Without sufficient particulars, the Landlord cannot reasonably investigate the allegations, determine whether records exist concerning the alleged incidents, or prepare a meaningful response.

I find that it would be improper to “craft” pleadings from the Tenant’s oral and documentary evidence led in the course of the hearing. I find that it is not sufficient for the Tenant to expect the Landlord to piece together the case to be met.

I have considered whether the Tenant should be granted an opportunity to amend the application. However, the application was filed more than sixteen months before the hearing. Despite having ample opportunity to clarify the allegations, the Tenant did not amend the application or provide a concise summary identifying the dates and particulars of the alleged entries.

I am not satisfied that permitting a further amendment at this stage would be appropriate. I find the deficiencies in the application prevent the matter from proceeding on its merits. Accordingly, I find that the application lacks sufficient particulars and should be dismissed.
ordered: The application is amended to reflect the proper name of the Landlord.
The application is dismissed. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order. Illegal entry

The Tenant, [name] (P.Q.), testified that on October 8, 2024, he observed a notice posted on what he referred to as the Landlord’s door. The notice indicated that the Landlord would be sending someone to enter his rental unit for the purposes of retrieving a portable heater that he was previously given by the Landlord. The notice did not provide a specific date or time for entry and stated that someone would be attending his unit within the next few days.

On October 18, 2024, the Landlord’s Agent attended the Tenant’s rental unit and proceeded to remove the portable heater from the rental unit. The visit lasted for no more than a few minutes. The Tenant testified that he was not provided with any written notice of entry for the attendance on October 18, 2024. 4. [name] testified that on January 9, 2025, he observed a notice posted on the Landlord’s door. This notice stated that the Landlord’s Agent would be entering his rental unit for the purposes of bringing down salt for the water softener. [name] testified that the notice also stated that entry would be made on January 10, 2025. 5. [name] testified that on January 12, 2025, the Tenant observed two individuals at his door and asked who the individuals were. The individuals responded by stating that they were there to place the salt in the HVAC room for the water softener. P.Q. informed them that he was not given notice of them attending on that day and did not want to allow them access. The two individuals entered the unit, placed the salt in the HVAC room, and vacated the unit. [name] testified that he did not receive a notice of entry from the Landlord to enter his unit on this date. 6. [name] also testified that the Landlord would often leave notices of entry on the Landlord’s own door instead of his rental unit door. He also testified that the notices would often fail to provide all necessary particulars such as the reason for entry, and specific date and times of entry. 7. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 1, 2025. 8. The Tenant sought compensation in the amount of $4,560.00. 9. The Landlord, [name] (V.M.), testified that the Tenant did not agree to email service of notices, nor did the Tenant agree to notice of entry by telephone. The Tenant insisted on receiving written notices left at his door. 10. [name] testified that the door that the Tenant claims is her door on which she posted the notices was a common door which the Tenant would use or pass by daily. V.M. did not deny posting the notices on the common door rather than the door of the Tenant’s rental unit. 11. V.M. did not dispute having someone enter the rental unit on October 18, 2024, for the purpose of retrieving the portable heater that she had previously provided to the Tenant. The Landlord believes that she sent a text to the Tenant notifying him in advance of the entry but did not upload a copy of the text to support her position. 12. V.M. did not dispute that someone entered the unit on January 12, 2025. V.M. also did not dispute that the person she sent into the unit used her key to enter the unit after knocking and the Tenant failing to open the door. V.M. did not recall the specific details of the notice that she provided the Tenant prior to this entry. 13. [name] testified that she is 72 years of age and is limited in terms of what she can and cannot do. She testified to leaving the notices on the common door because of her mobility issues going up and down stairs. She also suffers from congestive heart failure. 14. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord, and/or an Agent thereof, illegally entered the Tenant’s rental unit on October 18, 2024, and January 12, 2025. I make this finding because the Landlord failed to properly serve the Tenant with the notices of entry by posting a copy of the notices on the Tenant’s door. Despite this, the Tenant did see the notices in advance of the Landlord’s entry. I am also not satisfied that the Landlord provided the Tenant with proper notice for the entries on October 18, 2024, and January 12, 2025, because the notices did not specify these as the dates on which the Landlord would be entering the unit. I am not satisfied that the Landlord notified the Tenant of any changes in advance of the entry times and dates. Therefore, I find that the Landlord’s Agent entered the unit illegally on October 18, 2024, and January 12, 2025. Remedies 15. I find an award of $400.00 for the two illegal entries to be an appropriate amount given the circumstances. I find this amount to be appropriate because Landlord’s entries were both for very brief periods of time, the entries were not carried out with any ill intent and were limited to two separate incidents. Therefore, I find this amount to be an appropriate award for the Tenant and to deter the Landlord from entering a rental unit without proper notice in the future.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $448.00. This amount represents: • $400.00 for illegal entries. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 24, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
