issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It is uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice and the Tenant moved out because of this notice.
The Tenant resided in the unit from March 2023 to February 11, 2025, when she vacated the unit pursuant to an order by the Board for occupancy by the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord fired her property management company and then tried to cancel the tenancy before she had actually moved in.
The Tenant testified that only a month into the tenancy the Landlord served her with an N5 notice, again trying to terminate the tenancy.
The Tenant testified that while she was living in the upper portion of the home, the Landlord, from March 2023 to April 2023, lived in the basement unit.

The Tenant testified that she was served the N12 notice in February 2024. The Landlord’s first application was dismissed because it was defective and the second application resulted in termination of the tenancy.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord obtained a shortened hearing date from the Board because she would be returning to Canada in 2 weeks but she does not believe the Landlord ever came back.
The Tenant testified that she went past the unto a month after moving out and the snow must not done and it appeared no one was living there.
The Tenant further testified that if the Landlord has returned she may have moved back into the basement unit.
The Tenant testified that she drove past the unit a couple of weeks ago and the house still looks empty and the grass in unkept.
The Landlord testified that she did in fact try to buy the Tenant out before the tenancy started.

The Landlord testified that after serving the Tenant with the N12 notice, there was a hearing before the Board and it was found that she required possession of the unit in good faith and the tenancy was terminated.

The Landlord testified that she had bought tickets to return to Canada in March 2025 but her flight was postponed to April 8, 2025 due to her father’s health. A copy of the ticket stub was submitted as evidence.

The Landlord testified that the home is a single family home and she had at one point made a wall to create a separate unit but she has taken the wall down and returned the home to a single family dwelling.

The Landlord testified that the unit is her only residence in Canada, and she moved back into the unit in April 2025. She submitted a copy of an email with her child’s school, confirming that her child will be returning to the school. Analysis

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In this case, the evidence from the Landlord is that she did move into the unit in April 2025 and still lives in the unit currently. Her testimony was supported by the copy of the plane ticket stub and the emails confirming her child returning to the school in the area of the rental unit.
Although the Tenant does not believe the Landlord returned to Canada and is residing in the unit, her testimony did not provide any evidence to the contrary or contradict the Landlord’s evidence.

Based on the evidence before me, I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of the Landlord’s testimony. I am therefore satisfied on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated the unit and did not serve the N12 notice in bad faith. Costs
The Landlord requested costs, alleging that this is the Tenant’s fourth application, all on the same basis, which amounts to nothing more than a fishing expedition.

The Board generally only orders costs where a party’s conduct in the proceedings was unreasonable. I am not satisfied that the Tenant conduct at the hearing was unreasonable and no evidence was presented to conform any prior hearing based on the same facts.
Therefore, the request for costs is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: es Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has wilfully or negligently caused damage to the premises. The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlord's reasonable out- of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 These applications were heard by videoconference on May 12, 2026. The Landlord’s agent [name], the Landlord's Legal Representative Crystal Sankey, the Tenant and the Tenant's Legal Representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw the T1 application LTB-T-013071-23, without opposition, and I consented to the request.

As context, in the T1 the Tenant alleged that the Landlord had unlawfully charged him $9,898.78, representing the costs to repair damage to the garage door of the residential complex, the damage of which the Landlord blamed on the Tenant’s negligent conduct.

A tenant may file a T1 to recover amounts paid to the landlord for an illegal charge. The parties agree that the Tenant never paid any of that amount. The Tenant's Legal Representative correctly submits that there is no cause of action. T2 application [LTB-T-007915-23]

The illegal charge forms part of the basis for the T2 application. In the T2, the Tenant complained that the Landlord attempted to collect the repair costs from him without an LTB order and without legal basis, and that this conduct substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment and constituted harassment.
The following facts are not disputed.

On February 2, 2022, the Tenant’s vehicle collided with the garage door leading to residents’ underground parking. On February 4, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a letter informing him that “the reported damage may be billable to your account”.

On May 3, 2022, the Landlord mailed a demand letter, attaching repair invoices, to the Tenant requiring him to pay $9,898.78 by May 20, 2022. The Landlord then sent the Tenant a reminder on June 3, 2022, alleging he owed that amount in rent arrears.
On June 9, 2022, the Landlord gave an N4 notice of termination claiming rent arrears of $1.431.98 for June 2022. The Tenant provided proof that he had paid the rent.

On September 14, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a second N4 notice, asserting that the arrears had accumulated to $5,727.92. Although the Tenant had paid the rent from June 1, 2022 to September 30, 2022, the Landlord had applied those payments to reduce the repair costs (leaving an outstanding balance of $4,170.86 as a chargeback).

The Landlord gave the Tenant a voidable N5 notice of termination on January 27, 2023, with a termination date of February 16, 2023. By the hearing date, the Landlord had removed the $9,878.78 chargeback from the Tenant’s account ledger, choosing instead to pursue their L2 application based on the N5 notice. The T6/L2 hearing process
Some of the facts and issues in the T6 and L2 applications are in dispute.

The parties agreed to proceed with the applications in a consolidated manner given the extensive overlap in facts and issues. The Tenant testified first on the T6 and was cross- LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 examined. The Landlord’s evidence was treated as both its response to the T6 and its L2 evidence, and the Landlord’s witness was cross-examined by the Tenant’s representative. T6 application [LTB-T-007915-23]
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.

The Tenant claims that on February 2, 2022, the Landlord failed to maintain the pavement leading up to the entrance of the underground parking garage free from ice. He contends that this failure resulted in his vehicle accidentally damaging the garage door. L2 application [LTB-L-013352-23]
The Landlord claims that the Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage of $9,898.78 to the garage door.

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord asked to amend the application to solely claim financial compensation for negligent damage under subsection 89(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Accordingly, the tenancy shall continue and this order addresses only the financial liability for the damaged garage door.
For the following reasons, the Landlord’s application is dismissed. The uncontested facts
The Tenant moved into Unit #704 in the high-rise residential complex on January 1, 2016.

On February 2, 2022, when he was driving home from work, at approximately 6:40 a.m. the Tenant entered the underground parking garage from the street. But before he could enter the interior of the garage, his vehicle crashed into the closed garage door.

The Tenant reported the situation to the Landlord’s after-hours line, leaving a message that his vehicle had slid down an icy ramp into the door. He asked how he could get into the garage. He then observed a tenant exiting the garage in their vehicle, approached them and, with their assistance, was able to drive his vehicle into the garage.

There was a bucket of salt in the interior of the garage near the door; the Tenant spread salt on the driveway before proceeding to park in his allotted space. He spoke later that morning with the Landlord’s agent [name] who confirmed that the Landlord had not salted the entrance ramp the previous night or in the early morning hours.

The Tenant’s verbal report to the Landlord was transcribed to an incident report completed by the Landlord’s employee M.D. (later amended by J.C.N. to identify the Tenant). It states that, “Due to ice the tenant slid into the overhead door, as a result the door will not open”.

The Landlord’s Community Manager [name] testified that he was he was informed about “the accident” when he arrived at work at 8:00 a.m. The incident was captured on the Landlord’s surveillance camera mounted in the interior of the garage. 24. [name] viewed the surveillance camera footage and arranged to have IDS Doors Cambridge remove the door for safety reasons. He attended the scene later to take photographs; although the time was not precise, he thought it was likely around 2:00 p.m. when they applied salt to various outside areas. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 25. The Landlord's Legal Representative presented the footage of the collision. It shows the night sky, the Tenant driving onto the ramp and the moment of impact. The force of the impact caused the garage door to partially disconnect from the mechanical track and the overhead guiderails collapsed. The door then hung tenuously from the track. 26. The photos provided by the Landlord show a concrete entry ramp that slopes downward (the gradient was not readily known). Prior to the incident, the garage door was in good working condition. 27. The Landlord keeps maintenance logs. [name] presented a log which consists of data an employee recorded between February 1 and 3, 2022, as follows: • February 1st: “partly cloudy”, the outside temperature was -8 degrees Celsius in the morning, 1 degree at noon and 4 degrees in the afternoon; • February 2nd: “snow showers”, the outside temperature was 2 degrees Celsius in the morning, 1 degree at noon and 0 degrees in the afternoon; and • February 2nd: “cloudy”, the sidewalks were salted at 2:00 p.m., 4:30 p.m., 6:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. and shoveled at 6:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. 28. The Landlord salted the sidewalks four times between 2:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. on February 2nd because, according to [name], the temperature was still a bit warm and ice was melting. By 6:00 p.m. it had been snowing enough that walkways needed shoveling. 29. The Landlord uses a third-party contractor to remove snow and ice on the driveway unless there is a small amount, in which case the Landlord will shovel/salt that area. The log shows that winter maintenance was not performed on the “Driveway” (the entrance ramp) on February 1, 2 or 3, 2022. There are no entries logged for the rest of February 2022. 30. The Landlord submitted a weather summary from WeatherSpark.com for the period 5:00 p.m. on February 1, 2022 to 7:00 a.m. on February 2, 2022. It shows that at 1:41 a.m. on February 2, 2022, there was “light rain”, and the temperature was 4 degrees Celsius. From 3:33 a.m., there was intermittent light rain until 6:00 a.m., with temperatures falling to 3 degrees Celsius by 6:39 a.m. For unknown reason, the list does not describe the “Weather” (rain, snow etc.) at 6:39 a.m. in contrast to the previous entries. 31. Final repairs to the garage door were completed by Waterloo Garage Doors Inc. on February 7, 2022, at a cost of $9,605.00. The facts in dispute 32. The Tenant’s evidence is that the roads were somewhat icy and that it was dark and raining when he approached the underground garage entrance. 33. He described his usual practice of slowly driving down the ramp, applying his brakes, pressing the remote to open the garage door, and waiting the 10 to 20 seconds required for the door to open. He also testified that he had winter tires installed on his vehicle in November, approximately three months before the incident. 34. He stated that, on this occasion, when he applied his brakes the vehicle lost traction on a thin layer of ice and slid forward into the large door. He testified that he attempted to reverse several times while the vehicle continued to skid but he was eventually able to back up and drive off the ramp. He believes freezing rain created icy conditions on the LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 driveway. His position is that the Landlord failed to carry out timely winter maintenance and that this caused the collision, which he says was accidental. 35. The Landlord disputes this, arguing that the Tenant has not proven that icy conditions were present. They submit that, even if there was ice present and the Tenant had winter tires, there is insufficient evidence regarding the condition of the tires. The Landlord maintains that, with proper driving and braking, the Tenant should have been able to exercise enough control to avoid ramming the door, and that the collision resulted either from excessive speed or a failure to brake appropriately, amounting to negligence. 36. The Landlord further contends that the garage entrance was properly maintained in accordance with the weather conditions on February 2, 2022. Relying on its maintenance log, the Landlord asserts that the driveway was relatively dry and free of ice. Analysis T6 application 37. Section 20 of the Act requires the Landlord to properly maintain common areas, including driveways and ramps. This requires proactive, diligent maintenance to reduce and minimize snow and ice buildup, particularly on inclines where the risk of vehicle slippage is highly foreseeable.1 38. The Tenant gave credible evidence that the ramp was covered in nearly invisible ‘glare’ ice when he arrived at the complex in the early morning of February 2, 2022, as this became apparent when he applied his brakes. The video supports the vehicle losing traction and that the Tenant was only able to reverse with difficulty after several attempts, consistent with impaired traction and not inconsistent with the presence of ice. 39. The Landlord’s weather data is consistent with a freeze-thaw cycle capable of producing such ice. It is commonly understood that a concrete surface – such as the ramp – will absorb and retain cold for an extended time, causing water to freeze on contact even where air temperatures are just above freezing. This provides a plausible explanation for the presence of a thin layer of ice on the ramp at the time. There is also a concern that the data was capable of being edited, as someone has emphasized relevant data in bold type. 40. The surveillance video shows a reflective surface on the outside ramp, highlighted by the vehicle’s headlights, consistent with ice. I give minimal weight to the photographs the Landlord took later showing wet conditions as these are not contemporaneous. 41. The Landlord did not dispute that the ramp was not salted or sanded within a reasonable time before the incident. The log referenced shows no such work was done until approximately seven hours afterward. The absence of entries for the rest of February 2022 also raises concerns about whether the log is complete and concurrent. I find it of limited reliability; without verification by the person who completed it, the log cannot be entrusted to establish the condition of the ramp at the time of the incident. 42. The Landlord did not attend the site at the time of the incident or lead evidence from any witness who observed conditions around 6:30 a.m. I give little weight to [name]’s later 1 As reinforced by section 8 of the Occupiers' Liability Act,1990. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 observation that the ramp appeared relatively dry in photographs, as it cannot displace contemporaneous evidence of ice. 43. The Tenant’s position is that freezing rain was foreseeable had the Landlord prudently monitored the winter weather. He reasonably expected the Landlord to properly maintain the ramp to prevent ice-related mishaps. 44. I find that there was insufficient evidence produced to demonstrate that the driveway was free of ice, and the evidence points to the contrary. 45. Consequently, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to properly maintain the ramp free of ice. L2 application 46. The Landlord seeks an order requiring the Tenant to pay $9,878.78 for the cost of the garage door repairs. To succeed, the Landlord must prove on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage. 47. Finding a breach of maintenance obligations alone does not establish causation. 48. The issue to be determined is whether the damage was caused by the Tenant’s negligence, assessed against the standard of a reasonable winter driver, or by the Landlord’s failure to salt/sand the ramp leading up to the garage door. 49. The Landlord argues that the Tenant caused the damage by driving negligently. I am unable to find that the evidence supports this. 50. The Tenant’s evidence (i) that he discovered the ice only when he applied his brakes, and (ii) of his subsequent effort to salt the ramp, supports both the presence of ice and the absence of prior treatment. 51. I accept that the Tenant had winter tires on his vehicle, was driving at low speed, and reacted promptly. The Landlord’s submission that winter tires should have prevented the incident is not persuasive. While it is well-known that proper winter tires improve traction and reduce the risk of accidents, the Landlord has not introduced any objective evidence to establish that winter tires completely eliminate the risk of sliding on untreated ice. 52. In my view, loss of control due to slippery conditions, particularly on an untreated downward slope, is consistent with basic physics rather than negligence. Tires have nothing to grab onto; gravity takes over, dragging the vehicle down the icy slope towards the immovable structure – here, the garage door. 53. I place significant weight on the Landlord’s incident report attributing the collision to ice, which the Landlord did not dispute at the time, and on J.L.’s initial characterization of the incident as “an accident”. Their own evidence acknowledges the presence of icy conditions; [name] testified that salt was applied multiple times later that day beginning at approximately 2:00 p.m., to accelerate ice melting on the ground. 54. There is no evidence that the Landlord conducted a timely or thorough investigation into ice conditions or that they otherwise conducted a thorough investigation into the cause of the damage. They did not attend the scene, interview the Tenant or other witnesses, or verify conditions before alleging negligence. Instead, they relied on after-the-fact weather data and an unverified maintenance log. This further weakens the Landlord’s position. LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 55. Based on all the evidence, I find that the collision resulted from the condition of the ramp, not negligence by the Tenant, and was therefore an accident. I am satisfied that, but for the Landlord’s failure to salt or sand the area, the Tenant’s vehicle would not have struck the garage door. As a tenant is not liable under the Act for damage arising from a faultless accident, the Landlord’s claim must fail. 56. The Landlord’s L2 application is dismissed. T2 portion of the T2/T6 application 57. It is undisputed that the Landlord treated the repair costs as rent, issued demands for payment, and used the threat of eviction to compel compliance. The N5 notice was served nearly one year after the incident and no reasonable explanation for the delay was given. The timing also closely follows the Tenant’s filing of his applications and raises a reasonable inference of retaliatory conduct. 58. Landlords are not entitled to engage in "self-help" financial remedies. That is, a landlord cannot unilaterally decide a tenant is liable for damage, add repair costs to a rent ledger, and characterize non-payment of the disputed damage as a lawful reason for eviction. The proper mechanism is to apply to the Board for an assessment of damage liability prior to penalizing the tenant. 59. By charging back the repair costs without an LTB order and using the eviction process to pressure the Tenant into paying for an incident caused by the Landlord's own maintenance failure, the Landlord engaged in substantial interference with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment and coercion, contrary to sections 22 and 23 of the Act. Remedies 60. The Tenant did not intend to pursue any of the remedies available under the Act, other than a request for a declaration that they are not responsible for the damage and for an order that the Landlord refrain from repeating similar breaches in future. 61. While the Act does not provide for stand-alone declaratory relief, the Board must determine liability when deciding the L2. For the reasons above, I have found the Tenant is not liable for the damage to the garage door. 62. Additionally, the Board routinely declines to order a landlord or a tenant to comply with the Act in future because the duty already exists in law and such orders would be too vague to enforce. The Board is not a supervisory authority. It is a creature of statute; once a final decision is issued, the Board is functus officio. 63. The Tenant's Legal Representative asked to amend the applications to seek a nominal rent abatement of $50.00 and, in the circumstances, such request is not unreasonable. Administrative fine 64. The [name] Interpretation Guideline 16 states that a fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter similar activity in the future. The Guideline permits a Member to order a fine even though it has not been requested in an application. 65. Although a fine was not pursued in this T2 application, I raised the issue with the parties. After hearing submissions, and in the circumstances, I am not inclined to impose a fine LTB-T-007915-23 LTB-L-013352-23 even though the Landlord’s conduct, as an experienced corporate landlord, would ordinarily support the imposition of a significant fine. 66. I have considered that the incident appears to be isolated. The Landlord retains a third- party contractor for snow and ice removal, and it may be that it was performed inadequately or not at all in the hours leading up to the incident. While the use of a contractor does not relieve the Landlord of its responsibility to ensure that the ramp is properly treated, it is a mitigating factor. 67. The Board is satisfied that the Landlord understands that damage claims cannot be pursued without proper investigation and without an order of the Board. The Landlord is expected to ensure that proper investigations are conducted into damage claims and that those claims are pursued in accordance with the Act. Similar conduct in future may result in the imposition of a significant fine.
ordered: The application LTB-T-013071-23 having been withdrawn, the LTB's file is closed. L2 application
The Landlord’s application is dismissed. T2/T6 application
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $98.00. This amount represents: • $ 50.00 as an abatement of rent. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,298.00 which represents the unlawfully retained deposits and the cost of filing this application.

The Tenant submits that the last month’s rent deposit was not applied to the last rental period nor was it returned to the Tenant. The Tenant also submits that the Landlord has unlawfully retained a key deposit in the amount of $250.00. Last Month’s Rent Deposit

A copy of the lease agreement was entered as evidence by the Tenant. The Tenant testified that on August 15, 2025, as per the lease agreement, the Tenant paid an illegal security deposit in the amount of $3,000.00 along with a key deposit in the amount of $250.00 which was unlawfully retained by the Landlord.
A copy of the Tenant’s e-transfer in the amount of $3,250.00 dated August 15, 2025 was entered into evidence by the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on December 27, 2025 and returned the keys to the Landlord’s handyman as per the Landlord’s request. The Tenant also testified that the security deposit and the key deposit have not been returned to the Tenant.
Section 105 of the Act provides that the only security deposit a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106 of the Act.
Section 106(2) of the Act states that “the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.”

While the Landlord and the Tenant may have agreed upon a security deposit in the lease agreement, section 3(1) of the Act states that “this Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.”

What this means is that it was not open to the parties to contract out of the Act with regards to the security deposit. The only security deposit the Landlord was entitled to collect in accordance with sections 105 and 106 of the Act was an amount equal to the rent for one month.

Section 134 of the Act prohibits landlords from collecting a rent deposit. However, pursuant to section 17.3 of [name]. 516/06, it is not illegal for landlords to collect key deposits provided the deposit is refundable and is no more than the actual replacement costs of the keys.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, am satisfied that the Landlord illegally collected an amount that is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). I further find that the Landlord has unlawfully retained the key deposit.
The Landlord shall refund the security deposit and the key deposit in the amount of $3,250.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,298.00. This amount represents: • $3,250.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It is uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice and the Tenant moved out because of this notice.

With respect to whether the N12 was served in bad faith, section 57 of the Act states the following: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in section 6 the landlord (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant;

Based on the uncontradicted evidence before me, I find that the presumption of bad faith under section 57(5) of the Act applies here because the Landlord acknowledged advertising the unit after the Tenant vacated the unit. Therefore, the onus is on the Landlord to provide that the N12 notice of termination was not served in bad faith. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that the Landlord served the N12 with false pretenses, that he renovated the unit after she moved out and then rented it out as an Airbnb.
The Tenant vacated the unit on June 30, 2025.
The Tenant testified that she passes the unit all the time and the house remains vacant, the neighbors do not see anyone living there, the snow is not done in the winter and the grass is not cut now.
The Tenant submitted ads for the unit to be rented as an Airbnb along with reviews from the people who stayed in the unit through the months of July, August and September 2025.

The Tenant also submitted photos of the house as follows: • December 2025 with the driveway not cleared, February 17, 2026 • February 17, 2026 no vehicle and light on • February 19, 2026 with the same light on • March 12, 2026 with the driveway clear but no vehicle • April 11, 2026 no vehicle in the driveway and no lights on
The Tenant testified that the move was very stressful as she is a single mom with 2 children and a dog, and she is a volunteer firefighter so she must remain within 10 km of the station.
The Tenant testified that she moved from an entire home to a basement unit and her children have to share a room.
The Tenant is seeking general compensation in the amount of $28,600.00 and for the Landlord to pay a fine to the Board.
The Landlord testified that the N12 notice was not in bad faith because he moved into the unit on July 3, 2025, and still resides in the unit.
The Landlord submitted letters from neighbors stating that he moved back into the unit almost a year ago and they help him with his dogs.
The Landlord also submitted his tax papers his address being listed as the address of the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that he did list the unit as an Airbnb while he was living in it to try to earn some money for repairs. He pointed out in the reviews submitted by the Tenant that there were complaints of his clothes and personal belongings in the unit.

The Landlord testified that he lives a busy life and is currently in a custody battle. He testified that he is a on the road salesman, he doesn’t come home every night, and his son’s school is an hour away. Analysis
The Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above.

The first and second elements are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination served by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord moved into their unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated, I find the Landlord provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that he had moved into the rental unit on July 3, 2025.

The Tenant also gave straightforward and consistent evidence in respect to the unit being listed as a Airbnb after she vacated. I find this evidence is consistent with the Landlord’s evidence that he listed the unit as an Airbnb while he was living in the unit to try to earn extra money.
For these reasons, I find on the balance of probabilities that the landlord did occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the tenant vacated the unit.

Therefore, I find the Landlord has rebutted the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith and proven on a balance of probabilities that his intent to move into the rental unit was genuine. The Tenant’s application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the deposit collected from the Tenant.

The application was framed as a claim that the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to move into the rental unit. However, based on the evidence, I find that the central issue is whether the Landlord was entitled to retain the $1,495.00 paid by the Tenant. I am satisfied that both parties had a full opportunity to address that issue.
The parties agree that on January 25, 2026, the Landlord provided the Tenant with the proposed terms of a tenancy, including a lawful monthly rent of $1,495.00 with utilities and internet included.
The Tenant paid $1,495.00 on that date as a deposit toward the tenancy.

On January 29, 2026, the Landlord provided a formal lease agreement containing terms that differed from the initial agreement, including: • an additional charge for air conditioning; and • a utilities arrangement that was not consistent with the earlier representation that utilities were included.

I find that these changes were material and were introduced after the Tenant had already made payment based on the earlier agreed terms. Moreover, on the basis of the evidence before the Board, I cannot find that he Landlord established that these additional charges were clearly disclosed and agreed to prior to payment.

The Tenant declined to sign the lease with the revised terms and, on January 31, 2026, advised the Landlord that they would not be moving into the unit. This occurred within two days of receiving the revised lease.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant acted reasonably in refusing to proceed with the tenancy where the Landlord materially altered the agreed-upon terms after payment was made.

In these circumstances, no final tenancy agreement was concluded on the original terms, and the Landlord has not established a lawful basis under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) to retain the $1,495.00.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord retained money without lawful entitlement, and that amount must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,548.00. This amount represents: • $1,495.00 for the rent deposit unlawfully retained. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Tenant filed a further amended application [Doc 2678668] on January 30, 2024 seeking to define the rental unit as the basement unit, withdraw a claim for harassment and modify remedies sought. There was no dispute that the proposed amended application was served on the Landlord’s representative and that the Landlord was aware of the proposed changes. As such, I exercised my discretion to amend the application as set out in the further amended application. Adjournment request – April 21, 2026 hearing

At the outset, the Landlord’s representative, [name], requested an adjournment because the Landlord had been out of the country since late 2025 dealing with storm related issues. The Landlord’s representative s ubmitted that despite had placing numerous phone calls, leaving phone messages and sending emails to the Landlord since October 2025, the Landlord only reached out to them yesterday, stating that they remained abroad , had no reliable internet and requested an adjournment in order to be able to attend the continued hearing. Given that the Landlord’s representative did not know where the Landlord was until yesterday afternoon, they have been unable to prepare for the continued hearing.

Despite the Tenant being agreeable to the adjournment request, I exercised my discretion to deny the request. I do not find it credible that almost six months after a storm caused the Landlord to leave the country , he is unable to find any location that will allow him adequate internet to attend the hearing. There was no explanation as to why the Landlord could not have phoned into the hearing if internet were not available. In my view, the Landlord chose not to attend the hearing. The Tenant, his witness and his representative were in attendance. [name] of Landlord’s representative on record

The Landlord’s representative advised that he had advised the Landlord that if the adjournment request were de nied, he would request to be removed as representative on record, given the lack of communication and instructions from the Landlord. I was satisfied that the Landlord was aware of the consequences of his non -attendance. The Landlord’s representative subsequently withdrew as representative on record and the matter proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence. The application
As explained below, the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,048.00.
The Tenant moved into the unit on June 1, 2021 and vacated the unit in or around November 2022.
The rental unit was located in the basement of the Landlord’s home, with the Landlord occupying the main level. Illegal entry

The Tenant said that the Landlord broke into his unit, stole his belongings and changing the locks. The Tenant stated that he was incarcerated from October 5, 2022 until December 15, 2022. In October, the Tenant had multiple [name], [name], [name]) attending the unit to feed his three cats and check on his unit. In or around November 30, 2022, an acquaintance (Tasha perhaps – he could not remember her name) attended at the unit but she could not get in because the back gate was locked. In or around December 5, 2022, his friend, [name], attended the unit. While she could not access the backyard, she took photographs of the unit through the front windows which showed most of the Tenants belongings were gone. Tenant’s witness – [name] (‘CW’)

CW testified that she has known the Tenant for about five years and that he asked her to keep an eye on the belongings in his apartment in November 2022. On November 17, 2022, she attended at the rental unit and found the gate to the back yard locked. The Landlord did not answer the door so she was not able to gain access to the unit. She reattended the unit on December 2, 2022, looked in the windows and saw that the unit was empty and being renovated. Analysis

For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord entered the Tenant’s unit illegally or disposed of the Tenant’s belongings. First, the Tenant’s evidence regarding not vacating the unit was inconsistent. While t he Tenant stated that that he did not abandon the unit, never tried to leave it and never told the Landlord he was leaving the unit. he also testified that he never one hundred per cent agreed that he was leaving until things were de alt with (i.e. contract signed). This indicates to me that he and the Landlord were negotiating terms for him to leave. The fact that he produced photographs of his belongings being pack up when he was preparing to move out , which he stated he took weeks or days before October 6, 2022, lead me to believe that he was indeed in the process of moving out. Lastly, the police report dated September 6, 2026 confirms “Complainant moving out in two weeks” and the Tenant admitted that his roommate had already moved out by the time he was incarcerated. As such, I find it more likely than not that the Tenant was in the process of moving out.

With respect to the removal of the Tenant’s belonging from the unit, the Tenant admitted that he had multiple people attending the unit while he was incarcerated and that he had instructed them to move certain things from the unit, including his cats. The Tenant did not produce any of those individuals to testify as to what items, if any, remained in the unit, nor did he produce any photographs of his unit during the period of his incarceration. While the Tenant’s witness confirmed that the unit was empty as of December 2, 2022, there is nothing to confirm that the Landlord, rather than the Tenants friends who were retrieving items from the unit, removed the Tenants possessions.

As such, I find that the Landlord did not enter the Tenant’s unit illegally nor did he remove and dispose of the Tenant’s belongings. This part of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Substantial interference
To establish substantial interfer ence, the Tenant must demonstrate conduct that is serious, ongoing, or reasonably likely to disrupt the Tenant’s ordinary use and enjoyment of the premises.

The Tenant testified that when his friend, [name], moved in with him around August or December 2021, the Landlord started establishing rules and not letting them use the laundry. The Tenant had to call police after the Landlord threatened his roommate . The Landlord then stopped giving the Tenant rent receipts and started banging on the floor with chairs and hammers. He would constantly harass the Tenant and his girlfriend.
On January 8, 2022, the Landlord woke up the Tenant, his girlfriend, his roommate and his roommate’s three-year-old son by banging on the door and yelling, accusing them of smoking in the unit.

On January 11, 2022, he received multiple text messages from the Landlord threatening his roommate, telling him he could not use the laundry room. The Tenant called the police who then spoke with the Landlord, which upset him further.
On January 19, 2022, the Landlord advised the Tenant that the laundry room would be locked and they would no longer have access to it even though laundry was included in the Tenant’s lease.
On January 27, 2022, the Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant telling him to find a new place to live before things got worse.

On March 6, 2022, the Tenant had to ask the Landlord to unlock the laundry room door so that he could do laundry. The Landlord was swearing at the Tenant and telling him if he stepped foot in the laundry room something bad would happen. The Tenant called police, who then assisted the Tenant to remove the laundry room door so that he could do his laundry. Thereafter, the Tenant removed the laundry room door every time he wanted access to the laundry room, claiming that he received consent from police to do so.

The Tenant stated that on March 8, 2022, the Landlord sent him a threatening text message using vulgar language, telling him that he was using his last month’s rent, that he did not have to pay rent anymore and that he would have to move out by the end of the year. The Tenant admitted that he did not pay the Landlord any rent after April 2022 because he did not know what was going to happen.

The Tenant stated that throughout the tenancy, t he Landlord always kept his kitchen door open into the common back entryway in order to keep an eye on who is entering the Tenant’s unit, despite the Tenant asking him to close it numerous times. The Tenant found this intrusive and an invasion of his privacy. He said the Landlord would also stand at the common back entry door yelling at the Tenant and accusing him of smoking in the unit . The Tenant stated he only smoked cannabis outside and the problems only started after the Landlord first saw him using a bong outside . The Tenant admitted that he and his roommate started smoking inside the unit in or around March 15, 2022.

In support of his testimony, t he Tenant produced the following police incident reports [Doc 3691311, pages 1-3, 5-6, 8-15]: January 28, 2022 [name] says last night Landlord was looking in his windows . Incident report says “Advice given to both parties. Not a police matter”. March 7, 2022 [name] having issues with Landlord who lives in same house. Says three people cam in and were in his face. Now they are upstairs. Incident report says, “Advice given, no criminal elements”. March 15, 2022 [name] says his Landlord is stomping around upstairs, just started doing it. Other Tenant in the room confirmed he is doing it. Ongoing issues with him. Says police have attended quite a few times regarding this matter. [name] believes his Landlord is getting on his hands and knees and eavesdropping on his conversations . Complainant very argumentative, roommate yelling in background, both seemed to be under the influence of a substance. Upstairs was in darkness. No answer at door. Police did not attend complainant’s address. March 31, 2022 [name] screaming at him, smashing something against the floors, says he’s going to have people com over and beat up the complainant. No grounds for charges. [name] angry with police for not charging his Landlord. April 3, 2022 [name] is using a hammer to hit the floor. [name] said this is an ongoing issue. Has been going the last 20 minutes. April 24, 2022 [name] having on -going issues with Landlord. Landlord believes complainant is smoking indoors . Threatening to physically har m complainant. Concerned things may escalate. [name] doesn’t want to speak to police. Just wanted to ask questions about his situation. May 12, 2022 [name] and girlfriend are having ongoing issues with Landlords. Landlords are harassing comp lainant and girlfriend and are currently screaming at them. Girlfriend is scared to leave unit. May 12, 2022 Complainant very worked up, saying Landlord is yelling at him, threatening him, ongoing issue. We were just there this morning. He wants criminal charges and sounds very aggravated. Not very co - operative answering questions . Advice provided for complainant to contact enforcement unit of Ministry of Housing. August 4 & 6, 2022 Complainant believes landlord is withholding his mail . He is very belligerent and sexist with call take and said if we send a female officer he will lodge a complaint. [name] advised to speak to property standards regarding a second mailbox. August 28, 2026 Complainant calling in saying Landlord is screaming at him. Complainant yelling back – hard to get info. Says Landlord is smashing on the floor. Both parties too noising, ongoing disputes, no offence committed, not a police matter at this time. September 6, 2026 Complainant understand the long history of Landlord/Tenant disputes he is having and the proper way to address them. However, now the Landlord is following complainant around and taking photos. Complainant is trying to do his best but with this harassment he needs a police report. No offence committed. [name] moving out in 2 weeks, both parties cautioned to stay away from each other.

The Tenant said it was very scary living in the unit and the Landlord wanted to make his life a living hell. Every time he was picked up to go somewhere, the Landlord would be standing at his window, staring at his friends and terrifying them. The Landlord did the same to any friends that visited. The Tenant resorted to being pick up around the corner of the street. He said that sometimes the Landlord would even follow him just to observe what vehicle he was getting into. He said that the Landlord was totally intrusive and never understood his responsibilities as a Landlord. Analysis

There is insufficient evidence for me to determine that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit by removing access to the laundry room. The Tenant did not produce a copy of his lease to confirm that laundry was included . While he may have called the police when he could not access the laundry room, I do not find it credible that police assisted the Tenant to remove the laundry room door or told him to keep it in his unit. The Tenant did not produce any witnesses (i.e. police) to co rroborate his testimony.

I do find, however that the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the unit by screaming at the Tenant and withholding his mail.

With respect to screaming, while I have no doubt that the non-payment of rent, smoking in the rental unit and removal of the laundry room door contributed to the Landlord’s outbursts, the Landlord should have known that his outbursts were upsetting for the Tenant, causing him to call the police on numerous occasions. While the Tenant stated that he had videos of the Landlord screaming at him, he did not produce those videos. Even though the police reports confirm there was no wrongdoing on the part of the Land lord, I am satisfied that the Tenant had reason to call the police on numerous occasions.

With respect to withhold some of the Tenant’s mail, I accept the Tenant’s evidence that when he made enquiries of ODSP about payment stubs, they advised that some of his mail had been returned to them, marked return to sender. The Tenant did not, however, indicate how many envelopes had been returned to ODSP.

Although none of the police reports stated there were no charges or indicated any wrongdoing on the part of the Landlord, I am satisfied that the amount of times the Tenant complained to police confirms a pattern of conduct on the part of the Landlord which the Landlord knew or ought to have known was upsetting the Tenant.

Therefore, I find that t he Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by screaming at them on a number of occasions and withholding some of the Tenant’s mail.
In the circumstances, I find a rent abatement of $1,000.00 is reasonable. Withheld or interfered with vital services

The Tenant stated that o n March 21, 2022, the Tenant’s power was shut off. Since the electrical panel was located inside the laundry room, police were called. This was the start of multiple instances of the Landlord shutting off the Tenant’s power.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord withheld his hydro at least five times and that the Landlord would turn power to certain things off just to aggravate him. For example, the Tenant might not have power to the bathroom, another day it was the fridge , another day it might be the stove. The Tenant stated he called police whenever his power was off because he and the Landlord no longer communicated with each other . The police would attend and turn the breaker switch back on. As soon as the police would leave, the Landlord would go downstairs and turn off another breaker, then yell at the Tenant.

The Tenant produced the copies of the following police incident reports [Doc 3691311, pages 4, 6, ]: March 21, 2022 Rear Door complainant has an ongoing problem with Landlord. Now the breaker has gone on complainant’s fridge and “Landlord” has not flipped it back on. Long history and complainant is dealing with [name] which is making situation worse. April 3, 2022 [name] says Landlord has now cut the power so would like police to reattend. April 19, 2022 [name] says his Landlord has shut the power off to his apartment in the basement. Does this all the time. [name] went up to figure out why and Landlord said to call the police.

The Tenant stated that there were three other times when his power went off, then on again without him having to call police (i.e. he would go into the laundry room to turn on the breaker). It was when he could not get into the laundry room, that he would call police. He said sometimes the power would be off for eight hours or four hours or one hour or half an hour , or he would get home and the power would be off. Analysis

For the following reasons, I am not satisfied that the Landlord withheld a vital service, namely hydro. While I accept that there may have been multiple instances when the Tenant’s hydro did not work, there is insufficient evidence for me to determine that the Landlord was turning off breakers in the laundry room. The Tenant denies that the breakers could trip by themselves, he did not produce any evidence that he asked the Landlord to investigate why his power was turning off or produce any witnesses, such as an electrician, to confirm that the breakers could not have tripped. There is no evidence before me about the age of the house or the status of the electrical system in order to rule out that the breakers did not trip by themselves. The Tenant did not produce any photographs or videos of the Landlord turning off breakers in the laundry room as soon as police left. None of the police reports state that the Landlord did anything to the electrical panel.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services. This part of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for substantial interference • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; • The Landlords did not demolish the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlords served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.
The parties agree that the Landlords served the Tenant with an N13 notice of termination for demolition dated January 21, 2025 with a termination date of June 30, 2025.
The parties further agree that the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to an N11 agreement as a result of the N13 notice of termination on July 1, 2025.
The Tenant testified that since vacating the rental unit demolition of the rental unit has not occurred.

The Landlord testified that it was the intention of the Landlords commence demolition as soon as possible, but there were delays due to various applications required for demolition, zoning, redevelopment and construction with the City of Clarence-Rockland (the ‘City’)
The Landlord testified that the residential complex is a duplex and that the Landlords own the adjoining properties. The Landlords intend to demolish redevelop and combine all three properties.

The Landlord further testified that he applied to the City for redevelopment of the properties under an R2 application based on a recommendation of City staff. A planning committee hearing occurred on February 26, 2025, but the application was rejected as the Landlords need to bring an R3 application for the proposed redevelopment. An R3 application was filed with the City and approved in late April, 2025.
The Landlord states that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit services were disconnected.

The Landlord testified that although a demolition permit had been applied for it was not issued by the City until November, 2025, and that due to snowfall and weather conditions demolition was delayed until the Spring of 2026.

The Landlord further testified that the demolition of the buildings on the surrounding properties has occurred and the interior of the rental unit has been removed, but was delayed due to asbestos being found. The structure of the residential unit is due to be demolished shortly.

Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Landlord served an N13 notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith. I find, based on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord had a genuine intention to demolish the rental unit at the time of serving the notice and ultimately has started demolition. I accept that the Landlord intended to demolish the rental unit as soon as the Tenant vacated based on the steps he had taken to pursue demolition while the Tenant was still living in the rental unit. While demolishing the unit is taking longer than the Landlord expected, the delays, in my view, are not a result of the Landlord’s conduct.
As the Tenant did not prove the elements of the test in subsection 57(1)(c), the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Landlords served an N12 notice of termination on the Tenant, which stated that the Landlords’ child in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year. The N12 notice of termination contained a termination date of July 31, 2024.

It is undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2025 pursuant to an Order on consent issued on December 17, 2024 in relation to the Landlords’ L2 application based on the N12 notice of termination.
It is further undisputed that the Landlord’s son [name] did not move into the rental unit.

The Tenant submits that the Landlords’ application was brought in bad faith as the Landlords’ son did not move into the rental unit as indicated on the Landlords’ N12 notice of termination and supporting declaration.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the Landlord [name] testified that the Landlords entered into a new tenancy agreement with their son’s girlfriend and her mother within one year of the Tenant vacating the rental unit, creating a rebuttable presumption that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlords to establish that they served the N12 in good faith. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

Section 57(5) and 57(6) establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant… The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
The rebuttable presumption is engaged as the Landlords admitted to entering into a tenancy agreement with their son’s girlfriend and mother.

The Landlords dispute that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith as the Landlord [name] testified that her son did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated due to an unforeseen change of circumstances that led to the rental unit being rented to someone other than the former tenant.

The Landlord [name] testified that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit the Landlords planned to perform some repairs to the rental unit including painting, and replacing the appliances and carpeting prior to their son [name] moving in. The Landlords anticipated these repairs would take approximately 2 months to complete.

She further testified that late in the evening on April 21, 2025 [name] collapsed and was taken to a hospital where it was determined that as a result of a hole in Daniel’s heart a blood clot travelled to his brain causing him to suffer a stroke. The Landlords provided medical documentation in support of Daniels medical episode.

Both [name] and [name] testified that after [name] was discharged from the hospital on April 29, 2025 he had multiple follow-up appointments, and required assistance as he could no longer manipulate stairs independently, operate a motor vehicle or live independently until he had fully recovered. 15. [name] provided testimony that he did intend to move into the rental unit to get some independence as he was residing with his parents prior to suffering a stroke. 16. [name] further testified that he currently resides with his mother as his parents have separated. He states that the stroke has affected him physically and mentally including loss of motor function, memory loss and sleep issues and that he still does not feel comfortable residing on his own. 17. The Landlords did not notify the Tenant that [name] didn’t move into the rental unit after suffering the stroke as they were still hopefully that he would be able to in time. 18. The Landlords rented the rental unit to [name] girlfriend and her mother in the fall of 2025 after it was apparent that [name] was not in a position to move in. 19. The Tenant questions [name] condition after the stroke as the Landlords went on a vacation to Portugal from July to September leaving [name] behind. 20. The Landlords testified that the vacation was booked prior to Daniel’s medical episode and they contemplated cancelling, but they had to deal with personal matters in Portugal and decided to still go as they felt comfortable leaving [name] in the care of his brother who is a medical doctor. Analysis 21. I find on the basis of the Landlords’ testimony and evidence submitted have rebutted the presumption of bad faith and that they did serve the N12 notice in good faith. In other words, the evidence establishes that at the time the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12, their son genuinely wanted to move into the rental unit for independence. This was supported by the L2 application the Landlords filed which was resolved on consent. 22. In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord may also have additional motives for selecting a particular rental unit, but this does not affect the good faith of the Landlord’s notice.” 23. I also agree with the following statement from the Board’s order TST-87742-17RV, which states: “the Landlord’s obligation to act in good faith extends beyond the time the notice of termination is served”. I take this statement to mean that bad faith is not confined to the moment in time when a landlord gives a tenant an N12 Notice. I find that bad faith can extend to the period between when the N12 Notice was given, and the time when a tenant moves out. 24. In many other cases, the Board has found that an unforeseen change in circumstances that results in the person listed in the N12 Notice being unable to occupy the rental unit does not constitute bad faith (see, for example, TST-66921-15, TST-87559-17, TST80046- 16). I agree that this is a case where an unforeseen change of circumstances resulted in the Landlords’ son [name] failing to take occupancy of the rental unit. This change of circumstances was as a result of the Landlords’ son suffering a stroke and resulting limitations after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. I am satisfied that the Landlords did not foresee this happening when they served the N12 Notice. 25. In my view, the Landlords delivered the N12 notice in good faith, and the Landlords’ son genuinely wanted move in and remain in the unit for residential occupation for at least one year, and was unable to do so due to unforeseen circumstances. As a result this application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the amount listed below by June 30, 2026. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy
The Landlord charged the Tenants an illegal charge in the amount of $3,600.00. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The parties agreed that the Tenants had paid the Landlord a first and last month rent deposit when the tenancy began on February 1, 2025. This was a fixed term tenancy ending on January 31, 2026. However, parties agreed that the Landlord consented to the Tenants vacating the rental unit on November 30, 2025 and terminating the lease early. The last month rent deposit was applied to November 2025 rent.

The parties further agreed that the Landlord charged the Tenants an illegal charge on December 1, 2025, by cashing a post-dated cheque in the amount of $3,600.00. The Landlord testified the reason he charged the Tenants this amount was because of damage caused by the Tenants.

Therefore, I find the Landlord charged the Tenants an illegal $3,600.00 charge. The post- dated cheque was for rent and rent only. The Landlord cannot arbitrarily use a post-dated cheque to pay for damages without the consent of the Tenants. The parties agreed the Tenants did not provide the Landlord with consent to do this.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,648.00. This amount represents: • $3,600.00 for the illegal charge. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant O.C. is a minor child and is, therefore, removed as an applicant party. There is no dispute that [name] is the only putative Landlord; the evidence is that the named respondent [name] is not an owner, landlord or tenant. As a result, the application is further amended to remove [name] as a respondent party. The Applicant’s standing to bring theT2 application

As explained below, the applicant L.J. did not prove that the respondent [name] is the owner of the property or her Landlord, either of which – if proven – would give her standing to bring this T2 application.

L.J. and J.J. are siblings. L.J. does not dispute that [name] is a Tenant but she is also claiming to be a Tenant. She acknowledged that she is [name]’s housemate and that she moved into the unit at the invitation of J.J. or by mutual agreement. 4. [name] disputes that he is the Landlord and that his sister is a Tenant. I accept [name]’s uncontroverted evidence that he is the proper Tenant in this tenancy. He provided a copy of a letter on company letterhead from his landlord Sterling Karamar, dated April 10, 2026, which confirms that [name] and an individual named J.D. are the only Tenants under an existing residential lease for this rental unit. I found [name]’s testimony and documentary evidence to be credible and so I give the Landlord’s letter significant weight. 5. L.J. co nfirmed that she is not listed on J.J.’s lease with Sterling Karamar. 6. The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 21 is a helpful resource for the parties to refer to, and I find it accurately explains the law: an occupant or roommate cannot file an application at the LTB relating to the tenancy against either the Landlord or the Tenant. 7. I find that L.J. is an occupant as contemplated by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and is not a Tenant as defined by the Act. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
