issues: er under Sections 30, 31 and 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 203, 3125 [address] WINDSOR ON Between: [name] Tenant And [organization] Landlord [name] (‘KA’ or the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (‘API’ or the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (the T2 application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application) These T1, T2 and T6 applications were heard by videoconference on June 4, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant’s Legal Representative, [name] (‘[name]’), the Landlord’s [name], [name] (‘LLR’) attended the hearing. [name] (‘SBDK’) and [name] (‘JS’) were called forward as witnesses for the Landlord.
reasons: The Tenant led the following exhibits into evidence during the hearing: • TT#1 – photos taken by the Tenant herself of the rental unit on September 3, 2024. • TT#2 – copy of the Landlord’s Incoming Inspection Report dated September 3, 2024.

The Landlord led the following exhibits into evidence during the hearing: • LL#1 – copy of an Incoming Inspection Report for unit 108. • LL#2 – copy of the signed lease (signed August 23, 2024) between the Tenant and the Landlord. • LL#3 – copy of September 3, 2024 “work order” for the rental unit in respect of the maintenance work needed to be done. • LL#4 – copy of September 4, 2024 dated notice to enter, to enter September 9, 2024 to conduct maintenance repairs. • LL#5 – photos taken by SBDK on September 9, 2024 of the repairs done on that date. • LL#6 – copy of September 10, 2024 dated notice to enter, to enter September 13, 2024, to conduct maintenance repairs. [name] – copy of September 13, 2024 dated notice to enter, to enter September 18, 2024, to conduct a preliminary outgoing inspection of the unit. • LL#8 – copy of the N11 agreement signed by the Tenant on September 13, 2024, with a termination date of November 30, 2024. • LL#9 – copy of the Preliminary Move-out Inspection Report conducted on September 20, 2024. • LL#10 – copy of the Final Move-out Inspection Report conducted on October 2, 2024. • LL#11 – copy of “work order” for rental unit by “turnover team”- work done in August 2024.

The parties were able to agree on the timeline of actions/events of the parties before, during and at the end of the rental unit tenancy. Specifically, they agreed to the following: • The Tenant applied online for a tenancy with the Landlord as she was moving from Edmonton to Toronto to become a student at university. • On July 16, 2024, SBDK hosted a virtual tour over a videoconference link with AK, showing AK a similar unit to the rental unit being applied for. There had been another tenant in the rental unit at the time so SBDK presented AK with a similar unit on the first floor (#108) to view. (ref: LL#1) • On July 17, 2024, AK paid a last month rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $1,096.94. AK also paid a “balance” of $2,164.59 at the outset of the tenancy which comprised a pro-rated rent for 27 days of September ($989.52), a discounted rent for October 2024 ($1,075.00) and a refundable key deposit ($100.00). • A “welcome” email from the Landlord was sent to AK on or about July 19, 2024. • The previous tenant in the rental unit moved out on or about August 5, 2024. • The Landlord’s “turnover team” began preparation work on the rental unit in advance of the rental unit being rented to AK. (ref: LL#11) • The Landlord’s administration group sent a lease to AK in August and it was signed by the parties on August 23, 2024, which confirmed the tenancy agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant. The lease was for a one-year term starting on October 1, 2024 with a monthly rent of $1,096.94. (ref: LL#2) • No direct communication concerning the rental unit was had between SBDK and AK between August 9, 2024 and September 3, 2024. • On September 3, 2024, AK went into the rental unit for the first time (moving in), with SBDK present. (ref: TT#2 – AK stated she was not present for the inspection whereas SBDK stated AK was present) • AK had communicated her displeasure with the rental unit to SBDK on September 3, 2024, which concerned the physical state of the rental unit and the alleged stench inside the unit. (ref: TT#1) SBDK opened up a “work order” on that date to have the complained-about items resolved. (ref: [name]) • AK moved to a temporary location elsewhere while the Landlord attended to the issues raised by AK. AK did not return to the rental unit to live there. [name] provided lawful notices to enter, the Landlord entered a number of times between September 9, 2024 and September 30, 2024, to address/resolve all of the complained-about items. (ref: LL#4, LL#5, LL#6) [name] informed SBDK and JS that she just could not live in the rental unit, and on September 13, 2024, she signed an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy, effective November 30, 2024. (ref: LL#8) • After receiving the N11 form, the Landlord conducted a preliminary outgoing inspection of the rental unit on September 20, 2024 (AK was not present). (ref: LL#9) • AK moved out of the rental unit on October 1, 2024, returning the rental unit keys to the Landlord on October 2, 2024, and the Landlord conducted an inspection. (ref: LL#10) • The Landlord then conducted a “turnaround” effort to have the rental unit re-rented to new tenants effective November 1, 2024. • New tenants moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2024.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations regarding the unlawful retention of the last month’s rent deposit and the key deposit, and the substantial interference claim in the T2 application, all on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant did not succeed in persuading me there was any maintenance breach by the Landlord under the T6 application. Therefore, the Landlord must return the last month’s rent deposit and the key deposit to the Tenant. As well, the Landlord will be ordered to pay a $109.69 rent abatement in respect of the T2 claim. The T6 application will be dismissed. T1 application
The parties confirmed the Tenant paid rents in full for September 2024 and October 2024.

The Tenant gave a signed N11 agreement form to the Landlord with a termination date of November 30, 2024 (LL#8) and while I was not given anything to show the Landlord signed that N11, I was satisfied the Landlord in effect accepted the N11 from the Tenant. This was evident by way of SBDK’s testimony about the preliminary outgoing inspection conducted on September 20, 2024 following the N11 service (LL#9), the efforts after the Tenant vacated on October 2, 2024 to conduct a final inspection, and then “turnaround” the rental unit for a new tenancy (LL#10). SBDK confirmed the rental unit was leased to new tenants starting on November 1, 2024.

I believe the real substance of the actions by both parties show they effectually agreed to cancel the one-year lease, move to a month-to-month arrangement and operate the tenancy in accordance with the N11 that was served. These actions also reflect the parties’ attempts to minimize their losses (according to section 16 of the Act)

In the end, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy, which ended on October 31, 2024, and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act.

While claimed under the T2 and T6 applications but not under this T1 application, the claim respecting the refundable key deposit was not contested. The Landlord confirmed having taken a $100.00 key deposit and not returning it to the Tenant. This, too, is prohibited by the Act.

Simply for the sake of completeness, I note that security deposits, or damage deposits by another name, are prohibited by the Act. I refer to section 105 of the Act which sets this out clearly and also to section 234(d) of the Act which defines the collection of a security deposit as an offence, and section 234(g) which states the failure to return a last month’s rent deposit is an offence.

With regard to any key deposit in a tenancy, reference is made to section 134 of the Act which sets out key and similar deposits are also generally prohibited, but there are exceptions. Such an exception is found in subsection 17(3) of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulations”), which supports the premise that refundable deposits for keys are allowed in tenancies but are to be refunded upon the return of the keys in question.

In final submissions, the Landlord stated their intention all along was to return the last month’s rent deposit and key deposit, but the Landlord simply wanted to await the outcome of the LTB hearing for the three applications.
As such, the order below requires the return of both deposits, that are still being held by the Landlord, to the Tenant. T2 application

Here, I find that there was a significant “mismatch” between the information given to the Tenant by the Landlord (via SBDK) during the virtual tour in July 2024, versus what the Tenant actually found on September 3, 2024 when she entered into the rental unit for the first time.

AK testified that what shocked her the most when she entered the unit was the smell of what she described as “spoilage” and the state of the bathroom. AK did say as well that there had been some kitchen cabinet-side and baseboard areas that looked beaten and deteriorated. AK immediately raised these issues with SBDK on that day. SBDK confirmed in her testimony that AK was very upset when AK first viewed the rental unit in person.
Both SBDK and JS testified that the smell that was present in the rental unit came from the cleaning and painting jobs that had been done in the unit by the “turnaround team”.
I note that both the Tenant and Landlord never presented anything that was actually found in the rental unit which could have turned rotten or had spoiled.
In my view, the photos taken by AK (TT#1) clearly show the “mismatch” between the rental unit as found on September 3, 2024 and unit 108 as it was shown to AK in July 2024.

With regard to the photos found in TT#2, I note SBDK testified the Tenant was present during the TT#2 inspection whereas AK denied being present, saying that the inspection must have been done before she first entered the unit. Whatever the case, the photos of TT#2 actually depict the state of the bathroom just like the photos in TT#1 did, but the photos were shot from a further distance away, thus de-emphasizing the problem areas that were vividly shown in the close-up photos of TT#1. Misrepresentation

AK alleged the Landlord (via SBDK) misrepresented the state of the unit, but I do not believe the Landlord (SBDK or any other Landlord staffer) tried to misrepresent anything at any time. I say this for the following reasons.

AK had elected to take a virtual tour of the rental unit in July 2024, turning down SBDK’s suggestion of an in-person tour. I fully understand why AK had elected to do so as she was in Edmonton at the time, but certainly the virtual tour was not forced upon AK by SBDK.

From SBDK’s testimony, I was also satisfied with the extent to which she had gone to give AK as thorough a tour as was possible. As the rental unit was rented at that time, SBDK stated the Landlord’s policy was that rented units could not be entered into and shown to prospective tenants due to privacy reasons. As a result, SBDK showed AK a similar bachelor unit (#108) which had been empty and had undergone a “turnaround” cleanup. SBDK explained this to AK at the time. SBDK also explained that unit 108 was on the east side of the building whereas the rental unit was on the west. SBDK walked to the rental unit door so AK could see what it looked like and also SBDK ventured into the outside parking lot to show AK the rental unit window from outside. In my view, there was nothing in SBDK’s actions to suggest there was any hint of trying to mislead or misrepresent– she tried to give AK the most complete tour that she could at the time.
While no intentional misleading or misrepresentation was at play, it was quite evident that the rental unit on September 3, 2024 failed to match what had been shown to AK in the unit 108 tour.

I reviewed the photos in TT#1 and agree that on a balance of probabilities, the Tenant was justified in feeling very disappointed about the state of the rental unit, particularly the bathroom itself. For example, the “gunk” that the Tenant had testified was prevalent – around the base of the toilet and along the baseboard under the toilet – was present and quite unsightly and off-putting. The tub was not in a good state of repair – deterioration where tub-tiles met the drywall, staining especially in the brown/yellow grouting that was quite visible, rusted tub fixtures/faucets, etc. A further example was the bathroom floor tiles (small square tiles) which were also in need of cleaning up, especially the grouting between the small tiles. The drywall between the tub and the toilet was in clear need of a patchwork / clean up job. The toilet itself appeared to be poorly cleaned around the seat and at the base. The Tenant also testified that the bathroom door itself was ill-fitted as it could not be closed fully.

I note that the remaining maintenance issues, inter alia, a chip in the bathroom sink, kitchen cabinetry and baseboards damage all represent important issues but in of themselves would not amount to someone reasonably becoming shocked by their presence. Indeed, I see these other issues as simply exacerbating what had been truly off-putting to the Tenant when she first saw the bathroom. Odour

With regard to the foul smell or smell of “spoilage”, I am unable to determine what exactly the complained-about odour was. The Tenant’s description amounted to calling the odour a stench, whereas SBDK’S and JS’ separate descriptions placed the odour as something that cleaning materials and water-based or oil-based paints leave.

Apart from the Tenant’s description, there was no evidence to show something had rotted or spoiled and there was no one brought forward by the Tenant to provide first-person corroboration of her testimony. As such, I was more persuaded by the separate testimonies of SBDK and JS, whose testimonies stood up to cross-examination. That is to say, I was more persuaded that most likely, the clean up materials and the painting of the unit left an after-odour that the Tenant found offensive, but this did not translate in my view to something wrong in the unit. Uninhabitable unit
Finally, I must also address the Tenant’s testified-to claim that the rental unit was uninhabitable, and that the Landlord was responsible for that.

In this case, I do not believe the rental unit was uninhabitable. Nothing was adduced into evidence to show the rental unit failed to meet any one or more health, safety or maintenance standards, never mind trying to show whether those failed standards made the unit uninhabitable.

I agree the rental unit bathroom lacked aesthetical cleanliness on September 3, 2024, and in fact was in a real need of clean-up repair, but the state of the bathroom did not render the rental unit uninhabitable. For example, the living area and kitchen photos in TT#2 show a bright, clean configuration with clean, newer fridge and stove appliances (compared to LL#1-unit 108).

In cases similar to the one at this hearing, I find that parties often times have different standards or expectations when it comes to finding a place suitable for living. What one person finds totally acceptable, another perceives otherwise. And when that happens, I find that differences need to be sorted out by respectful confrontation, discussion/exchanges and then resolution.

When AK made her complaints known to SBDK on September 3, 2024, the evidence shows SBDK took the complaints seriously and she promptly got her maintenance staff involved (i.e. JS et al.). The work that JS and his staff did in September 2024 was quite quick and professional, resulting in a bathroom that was clean, bright and functional around September 5, 2024 (LL#5), only two days after the Tenant first saw the unit. All taken together, I believe the rental unit was habitable all along, and certainly moreso (vis- à-vis anyone’s standard level or expectation) as of September 5th onwards. Substantial interference claim
Returning to the “mismatch” determination above, I find that this “mismatch” created a valid basis for the substantial interference claim made in the Tenant’s T2 application and during the hearing.

More specifically, substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment under section 22 of the Act can arise from maintenance issues such as there were in this case. Reference is made to section 8 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regs”). That section applies every time a tenant claims a landlord has substantially interfered with her/his reasonable enjoyment when the interference is caused by “work”. And “work” is defined as maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex. The repair work in this case meets this definition, especially as the need for that repair work was totally unknown and unforeseen by the Tenant prior to her moving in on September 3, 2024.

The Tenant expected, and quite rightfully so, that the rental unit would have been in the same or better state that unit 108 had been in when she “toured” it in July 2024. In my view, therefore, that repair work on September 3, 2024 indeed qualified as “unreasonable” work needed because of the inadvertent and unfortunate circumstance of “mismatching” that had occurred.

To be clear, section 8 of the [name] is not intended to dissuade or deter landlords from undertaking maintenance, repairs or capital improvements. It is there to deal with situations when the work under certain circumstances creates substantial interference. For sake of clarity, subsection 8(3) of the [name] says: “the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.”

I provided this finding of substantial interference at the hearing, and indicated the Tenant would be entitled to a small abatement of rent to address the breach, but nothing more as the Landlord was indeed responsive, professional and effective in resolving the issues raised on September 3, 2024. Toward this end, I am granting a 10% rent abatement for the month of September 2024. In my view, the Landlord promptly resolved all maintenance issues and any decision by the Tenant to not live in the rental unit after the Landlord’s good efforts cannot be held against the Landlord, and certainly not to the Landlord’s account in respect of the Tenant’s decision to find alternative living arrangements, etc. Harassment, obstruction, coercion, threat or interference claim

Very little was testified-to or submitted on this section 23 claim directly. Indeed, nothing from either side, either from testimonies or from evidence adduced, showed there had been any actions that would be deemed as obstruction, coercion or interference.

To be clear, the Landlord’s actions at no time forced, bullied or compelled the Tenant into taking a “virtual tour”, entering the tenancy or leaving the tenancy. As well, nothing was given to suggest the Landlord created obstacle or hindrance for the Tenant to live in the rental unit, and certainly to any meddling, intrusion or impeding of the Tenant’s ability to move in or live in the rental unit.

I do accept that when the Tenant informed the Landlord she was going to move out and wanted to break her lease, the Landlord did put up some restriction as to what the Landlord was willing to do. That is, the Landlord did agree to let the Tenant out of her one- year term lease if she signed an LTB form agreement (i.e N11) to move out. The Landlord did not have to do that, but in a cooperative effort, the Landlord did.

That form agreement resulted in an N11 that was signed by the Tenant and contained a termination date of November 30, 2024. However, the Tenant surrendered her keys to the Landlord on October 2, 2024, so when the Landlord told the Tenant her last month’s rent deposit might not be returned, the Landlord was just doing what was lawful under the circumstances at the time. The Tenant had paid rents up to October 31, 2024 and a last month’s rent deposit could have covered November 2024 rent, had the Landlord been unable to re-rent the unit for November 1, 2024. Therefore, I find that the assertion of one’s rights, respectively asserted as was done by the Landlord here, cannot be construed as some sort of threat or as a form of harassment.
This section 23 claim as a result cannot succeed and must fail. T6 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T6 maintenance application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T6 application is to be dismissed.

For me to consider the submissions of both parties, I am guided by case authority from the courts. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this T6 application, the evidence submitted made it quite evident that the Landlord promptly and reasonably responded to the Tenant’s maintenance complaints, which were first made on September 3, 2024. The Landlord’s maintenance team was actioned by SBDK on September 3rd, JS and his team began substantial repairs on September 5th and they finished their work some two visits later on or about September 30th.

This, to me, shows the Landlord gave serious regard to the Tenant’s stated feelings and concerns, and quite frankly, resolved the maintenance issues in a timely fashion so as to satisfy the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 while trying to keep the tenancy intact.

It was the Tenant who unilaterally decided to move out (in effect breaking her lease) and in this regard, I find the Landlord was understanding and accommodating of the Tenant’s desire to exit this short-lived tenancy.
ordered: The Tenant’s maintenance (T6) application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,354.63. This amount represents: • $1,096.94 for the last month’s rent deposit: • $100.00 for the key deposit; • $109.69 for the abatement of rent stemming from the substantial interference claim; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the T1, T2 and T6 applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount of $1,354.63 owing by June 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 29, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 30, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 18, 2026 _____________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order. Illegal Entry:
The Tenant, [name] (N.S.), testified that on February 21, 2025, he contacted the Landlord and notified the Landlord of his sink being clogged and asking for the Landlord to contact a plumber.
N.S. testified that the Landlord responded on February 22, 2025, asking the Tenant to try and use Drano solution to unclog the sink. The Tenant attempted to do so, but it was not helpful.

N.S. testified that the Landlord sent him an email on February 22, 2025, at approximately 2:22 p.m., notifying the Tenant that the Landlord’s daughter will be entering the rental unit on February 23, 2025, between the hours of 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. for the purposes of inspecting the clogged sink. A copy of the email was tendered as evidence by the Tenant.

N.S. testified that the Landlord sent him a text message at approximately 5:32 p.m., stating that the Landlord’s daughter will be entering the rental unit at 5:45 p.m.; to inspect the rental unit. This text was sent on February 22, 2025, approximately 3 hours after the parties agreed to February 23, 2025, between the hours of 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m.

N.S. testified that the Landlord’s daughter used a copy of the Landlord’s key and proceeded to enter the Tenant’s rental unit at approximately 5:45 p.m., on February 22, 2025. N.S. testified that he did not receive proper notice of the entry and believes that this constitutes an illegal entry on the Landlord’s part.

N.S. testified that he was startled by the Landlord’s daughter because he did not receive the text sent by the Landlord at 5:32 p.m. He also did not feel that the fifteen-minute notice period provided was appropriate. N.S. testified that the clogged sink was an ongoing issue and by no means an emergency that permitted the Landlord to enter the unit without lawful notice.
N.S. testified that the Landlord’s daughter returned to his rental unit at approximately 6:30 p.m., after sending a text at 6:27 p.m. This entry was to determine if the sink was still clogged or not.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025.
The Tenant was seeking a rent abatement in the amount of $790.00 which is 50% of the rent for one month for the Landlord illegally entering the Tenant’s rental unit.

On cross-examination, N.S. agreed that in his email to the Landlord dated February 21, 2025, he used language such as immediate when referencing a time frame in which he expects the repairs to be carried out. N.S. also maintained that he never referenced the repair as an emergency because it was not and never agreed to waive his rights to notice of entry.

The Landlord, [name] (A.G.), did not dispute that her daughter entered the Tenant’s rental unit on February 22, 2025, as per her instructions to her daughter. The Landlord testified that she texted the Tenant at approximately 4:40 p.m., she did not receive a response from the Tenant but sent her daughter to enter the unit because the Tenant wanted the repairs done immediately. She did not dispute having an agreed entry time of February 23, 2025, between the hours of 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. when sending her daughter into the unit on February 22, 2025.

A.G. testified that she believed that the repair and clogged sink was an emergency that permitted entry without notice. I disagree, at most the Tenant would have been delayed in having the ability to wash their dishes. I do not find the clogged sink to be an emergency repair that allows a landlord to enter the unit in the absence of a proper notice of entry.
A.G. denies that her daughter entered the unit a second time on February 22, 2025, at 6:30 p.m.
A.G. also testified that she is a small Landlord and that this rental unit is her only rental property. The property is a duplex, and she occupies one of the two self-contained residential units.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord and/or an Agent thereof illegally entered the Tenant’s rental unit on February 22, 2025. I make this finding because the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with proper notice in advance of said entry. The parties agreed to an entry date of February 23, 2025, between the hours of 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. Despite this arrangement, the Landlord elected to have her daughter enter the Tenant’s rental unit after providing the Tenant with insufficient notice by text less than an hour before the intended entry. A clogged sink that prevents a tenant from washing their dishes is not an emergency and a landlord entering a rental unit without proper notice is inappropriate and constitutes an illegal entry. Therefore, I find that the Landlord’s Agent (daughter of the Landlord) entered the rental unit illegally on February 22, 2025. Remedies

Therefore, I find that the sum of $200.00 is appropriate in these circumstances. I find this amount to be appropriate because the illegal entry was limited to a single date, it was not done with ill intent, and the Landlord believed that they were acting in good faith to have the repairs requested carried out ahead of schedule. None the less, proper notice was not provided to the Tenant and the entry was illegal.

I do not find that the issuance of a fine to be appropriate in these circumstances. I find the sum awarded sufficient to deter the Landlord from entering a rental unit without proper notice in the future.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for illegal entry. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] Naeem [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): collected or retained money illegally LTB-T-009285-25 The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on May 26, 2026 Tenant [name] attended the hearing on behalf of both Tenants with his representative, Abraar Unia. The Landlord, [name] Naeem [name], attended the hearing on behalf of both Landlords with his representative, [name]. Imran appeared as a witness for the Landlords. LTB-T-015712-25 LTB-T-015712-25
reasons: The Tenants allege the Landlords collected illegal rent from May 2024 to February 2025. The Tenants also allege the Landlords failed to pay interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. Interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit

Subsection 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires a landlord to pay a tenant interest annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guidance determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

The Tenants paid the Landlords a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,800.00 on July 5, 2021. The Landlords have not paid the Tenants interest on the deposit. I am satisfied the Landlords have illegally retained the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. As such, the Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $276.40 for interest owing on the deposit up to the date of the Order. This is calculated as follows: • July 5, 2021 to December 31, 2021 = $0 (0%) • January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2022 = $33.56 (1.2%) • January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2023 = $69.90 (2.5%) • January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024 = $69.90 (2.5%) • January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025 = $69.90 (2.5%) • January 1, 2026 to June 22, 2026 = $33.13 (2.1%) Illegal rent collected

The tenancy commenced on October 1, 2021 for a fixed term expiring on October 1, 2022 for a monthly rent of $2,800.00. It is undisputed that the Landlord charged and collected $2,800.00 a month between October 2021 and December 2021.
There also seems to be no dispute that the parties entered into a new agreement on January 1, 2022 wherein the rent was discounted to $2,300.00 until January 1, 2023.

On September 19, 2022, Landlord [name] Naeem [name] (‘SNS’) texted Tenant [name] (‘FM’) to advise that they will sign a new tenancy agreement on October 1, 2022 for a monthly rent of $2,500.00. FM responded as follows: “Walikumassalam ... We agreed to raise it to $2400 from 1st Oct 2022. We already have a lease. I don’t see any reason why we need to sign a new one.”

SNS replied as follows: LTB-T-015712-25 “We were agreed to for $2400 starting January 2022 but you said you misunderstood & thought it will be on starting on October 1st 2022. I honoured your misunderstanding & now it will be $2500 starting October 1st & we will do a lease contract. Period”

On October 1, 2022, a monthly tenancy agreement was executed between the parties reflecting a monthly rent of $2,500.00. It was FM’s evidence that on April 27, 2024, SNS verbally notified him that the rent would increase to $2,700.00 effective May 1, 2024. fm maintains that he paid the rent increase from May 2024 to February 2025. Analysis

Fixed term tenancies in Ontario continue month to month under the same terms unless terminated in accordance with the Act. What this means is that the Landlords were not entitled to require the Tenants to enter into a new tenancy agreement on October 1, 2022 as the fixed term was not scheduled to expire until January 1, 2023.

Section 119 of the Act provides that a landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed. What this means is that the Landlords could not increase the rent until January 1, 2023.
SNS testified that he had a “mutual understanding” with FM that when they could afford it, they would resume paying $2,800.00 a month.

I am not convinced there was a meeting of the minds between the parties as to the amount of rent charged. I say this because the written tenancy agreement stipulates that the rent is discounted to $2,300.00 until January 1, 2023. Furthermore, it is clear from the text messages between the parties on September 19, 2022 that there was not a clear understanding as to the amount of rent to be charged. The Tenants, however, do not seek the illegal rent collected for October 1, 2022 to April 30, 2024.

Subsection 116(1) requires a landlord to give a tenant at least 90 days written notice of a rent increase. Furthermore, subsection 116(3) requires that the written notice be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.

As the Landlords did not give the Tenants notice in accordance with subsection 116(4), the increase on May 1, 2024 is void. This means the lawful monthly rent remained $2,500.00 and any amount the Landlords collected in excess of that amount constitutes an illegal rent increase.

The Tenants admitted into evidence bank records supporting their position that they paid the Landlord $2,700.00 for rent between May 1, 2024 and February 1, 2025. This represents $200.00 a month collected more than what the Landlords were entitled to collect. Accordingly, the Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $2,000.00 (10 months x $200).
The Tenants incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement of these costs. LTB-T-015712-25 LTB-T-009285-23
The Tenants sought to withdraw their T2 application, and I consent to the request. T6 Application
The Tenants allege the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the toilet and washing machine.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord. Toilet
For the reasons that follow, I am not convinced the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to the toilet.

There seems to be a dispute whether the Tenants contacted the Landlord to repair a leaky toilet or upgrade the seat. The Tenant testified that the toilet leaked, but the Landord indicated the Tenant requested a fancier toilet seat for his inlaws who were visiting. The Tenant made his request on May 24, 2024 and the Landlords sent their handyman, Imran, to assess the issue on May 27, 2024.

Imran testified that he is a friend of the Landlords and is not a plumber but is handy. He explained that he pulled out what appeared to be the lid from a toothpaste which had gotten stuck in the toilet and suggested that the toilet seat be replaced. He did not provide any explanation as to what he believed caused the toilet to leak, and there is no connection between replacing the toilet seat and stopping the leak, but nonetheless, the Tenant was satisfied with the replacement seat, which confirms that he was not seeking to fix a leaky toilet, but to replace the toilet seat. LTB-T-015712-25

The Landlords purchased a new toilet seat and left it for the Tenants to install as the Tenants were on vacation, and the Tenants did not wish for the Landlords to enter the rental unit in their absence. The toilet seat was replaced by the Landlords at the end of June 2024 as the Tenant was not comfortable installing the seat on his own.

The Tenants did not present any compelling evidence to establish that the disrepair issue was not resolved by the new toilet seat. There is also no evidence before me indicating the Tenants continued to report an issue with the toilet seat after June 2024. As such, the issue to be determined is whether the steps taken by the Landlords were reasonable in the circumstances. I find that they were.

The Tenants reported the disrepair issue on a Friday and by Monday, the Landlords sent someone to address the issue. I do not believe it would be appropriate to hold the Landlords liable for the delay in the installation of the new toilet seat as the delay was due to the Tenants’ request that the Landlords not enter the rental unit in their absence. I am satisfied the steps the Landlords took to address the disrepair issue were reasonable and appropriate. Washing machine
I am also not convinced the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to the washing machine.

The Tenants reported to the Landlords on October 1, 2024 that the washing machine was vibrating and smoking. The Landlord sent a technician to assess the issue the following day. The technician determined the Tenants were responsible for the malfunction.

The Landlords explained to the Tenants that he would repair the washing machine if necessary but indicated the Tenants would be charged for the expense given they were responsible for the disrepair issue. The Tenants responded that they were prepared to share the cost for a new washing machine. The Tenants purchased their own washing machine on October 27, 2024.

The Tenants did not advise the Landlords in advance that they intended to purchase a new washing machine. In my view, the Tenants interfered with the Landlords’ ability to address the disrepair issue with the washing machine. As such, I find the Tenants have failed to establish the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenants $2,329.40, which represents: • $276.40 in interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit that was illegally retained; • $2,000.00 in illegal rent collected and retained; and • $53.00 for the application filing fee. LTB-T-015712-25
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 3, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. LTB-T-009285-25
The T2 application having been withdrawn, the LTB's file is closed.
The T6 application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-015792-25 issued on March 16, 2026. On March 25, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review request was heard by videoconference on May 26, 2026. Only the Tenant and that the Tenant’s representative [name] attended the hearing. I was satisfied that the Landlord had received the Notice of Hearing and there was no request to adjourn before me. Based on this, I proceeded to hear the review at 9:22a.m.
reasons: The Tenant did not attend the adjudicative case conference that was held on March 9, 2026 and as such the application was dismissed. The Tenant testified that on the morning of the hearing his power went down, he had no internet, and that he kept trying to connect to the hearing but was unsuccessful. The Tenant testified that he was finally able to join the case conference around 10:00a.m. but at that time the application had already been dismissed. I accept the Tenant’s testimony as it was offered in a forthright manner and was unchallenged. When I consider that not being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, as stated by the Divisional Court in King-Winton v. DoverholdInvestments Ltd., 2008 CanLII 60708, I find that the Landlord was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. As such the review was granted and the application was reheard. The Application

The Tenant testified that the Sheriff enforced order LTB-L-047330-24 issued on Oct 11, 2024 on January 22, 2025. The Tenant testified that he knew the Sheriff was coming but he lived in the rental unit for 5 years, it’s a 6-bedroom house, and he needed time to remove all his belongings. The Tenant testified that despite asking, the Landlord did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. I accept the Tenant’s testimony as it was offered in a forthright manner and was unchallenged. Remedies

The remedies section of the application is not filled out, but the Tenant does make sufficiently clear on page 5 of the application that they are looking to be reimbursed for $70,000.00 worth of items that they were not given an opportunity to retrieve from the rental unit or to have the items returned.

The Tenant testified that the following items were left in the rental unit, they cost the following amounts, and he was never given an opportunity to retrieve the items: • Elliptical Machine - $5,000.00 • Rope Machine - $15,000.00 • Leg Press Machine $10,000.00 • Weights for Machines $6,000.00 • Two Boxing Bags $800.00 • 10 Sets of Boxing Gloves – $500.00 • 5 Skipping Ropes – $100.00 • China Cabinet - $8,000.00 • Artists Merchandise T-Shirt, [name], etc $6,000.00 • Official Gold Plaques of Records – Priceless • Samsung Stereo - $2,000.00 • Play station 5 - $1,000.00 • 20 Play Station Games - $2,000.00. • Kitchen Items, pots etc - $1,500.00 - $2,000.00 • TV – $2,000.00 • Rogers Internet Box – Tenant did not give a cost • Garden Equipment and other Tools - Couple hundred dollars for the general tools and the Tenant said he could not estimate the cost of garden tools • BBQ - Couple of Thousand • Fridge - $1,200.00
The Tenant testified that most of the items were purchased in 2023, the leg press was purchased in 2024, and the Elliptical Machine, and China Cabinet were brand new.

The Tenant took a video on the day he was evicted (DOC-8030517). It shows him walking around describing the items he left behind and many of the items he mentioned at the hearing can be seen in the video, including the gym equipment. I found the Tenant to be a credible witness. As such, I accept on a balance of probabilities that the items he says were in the rental unit when he was evicted where actually there. The Tenant also tried to mitigate his damages by repeatedly following up with the Landlord about getting his items back.

On the lower end of the Tenant’s estimate for the items is $63,300. Anytime the Tenant provided a range I’ve taken the lower number as the Tenant should not be entitled to costs that exceed what he actually paid and he has the burden to prove his case on a balance of probabilities. For the BBQ I’ve interpreted a couple thousand dollars on the lower end as two thousand etc.

My concern with the Tenant’s evidence is the accuracy of the cost of the items. He provided no receipts. However I found the Tenant to be a credible witness, the items left behind such as gym equipment, a china cabinet, etc are inherently expensive, and the Tenant appeared confident in what he spent on the items. The Tenant is not entitled to the full replacement cost of the items. I’m removing 20% of the costs to reflect my concerns about accuracy. For all the items except the Elliptical Machine and the China Cabinet I’m removing a further 20% to reflect depreciation of the items. The total replacement costs awarded to the Tenant are $40,580.00.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-015792-25 issued on March 16, 2026 is granted.
Order LTB-T-015792-25 issued on March 16, 2026 is canceled and replaced with the following.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $40,628.00. This amount represents: 1. $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 2. $40,580.00 for the reasonable replacement costs for items the Landlord retained.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application is filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and claims the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue

At the outset of the hearing, I had asked the Tenant to clarify the exact address of the rental unit as the application form implied the Tenant had rented the entire house. The Tenant confirmed he had been renting the Basement Unit in the house and consented to his application form to be amended to reflect same. T1 Application -Determinations
The Landlord and Tenant entered into a lease agreement on May 12, 2025.
At the start of the tenancy, the Tenant paid the Landlord a last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,750.00.

The Tenant testified that on or around December 7, 2025, he spoke with the Landlord verbally and sent a text message stating that he wished to terminate his tenancy. The Landlord responded by saying that he would be agreeable to terminate the tenancy as of January 31, 2026.

Section 47 of the Act states that: “A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44”.

Subsection 44(2) of the Act states that: “A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.”

Notwithstanding the fact that no formal N9 Notice to Terminate was provided by the Tenant to the Landlord, it was understood by both parties that the tenancy would be terminated as of January 31, 2026.

The Tenant testified that on or around January 24, 2026, he told the Landlord that he needed more time to find a place. The Landlord said he would ask the new tenant if he could delay his move in date by an extra month and the new tenant agreed. Thus, the new termination date of the tenancy would be February 28, 2026.

The Tenant testified that on or around January 29, 2026, his rental application for another unit had been approved and advised the Landlord he would move out as per the original date of January 31, 2026. Rent deposit applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord and Tenant agreed to a revised termination date of February 28, 2026. Four days later, the Tenant advised that he could vacate on the original termination date. This change was prejudicial to the Landlord, who had already made arrangements with a new tenant, including a confirmed move-in date, in reliance on the agreed extension. The [name] last-minute reversal disrupted those arrangements and resulted in the Landlord incurring a loss of one month’s rent. I am satisfied the parties agreed to a new termination date of February 28, 2026, and on that basis the Landlord was entitled to apply the deposit to the month of February.
As a result, I find that the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants’ application is filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and claims the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.
The Tenants’ claim for the return of the last month’s rent paid upfront is granted as the Landlord is not the registered owner of the rental unit.
The Tenants’ claim for the return of the key deposit is granted.
As the Tenants were successful on their application, the Tenants are awarded their costs of filing this application. T1 Applications -Determinations
The Landlord and Tenants entered into a lease agreement on June 8, 2025.

The monthly rent is $2,500.00. On June 5, 2025, the Tenants made a payment by cheque to the Landlord for the sum of $5,000.00. This amount was for the first and last month’s rent. The cheque was made payable to the real estate company the Landlord was using for the purposes of renting out the unit.
On June 9, 2025, the Tenants received a receipt for the payment of $300.00 which they had made to the Landlord for the key deposit.

The Tenants moved into the unit on or around June 8, 2025. On December 16, 2025, they had been locked out of the condominium building. The Tenants’ fob keys had been deactivated, and they no longer had access to the common areas or the elevators.

When following up with the management office the next day, December 17, 2025, the Tenants testified that they had been advised there was an issue between the builder and the Landlord. They tried many times to contact the Landlord but to no avail. After much back and forth with the builder and property management company, the Tenants were advised that the Landlord had defaulted on the mortgage payment earlier that year and a formal notice had been sent to her on December 2, 2025.
The Tenants further testified that the Landlord had continued to collect rent from them even after having received default notices from the builder.

Consequently, the Tenants had no option but to enter into a new tenancy agreement directly with the builder and were required to pay another last month’s rent deposit. The builder was also unable to honour the key deposit that the Tenants had paid to the Landlord.

The Tenants emailed the Landlord on several occasions and tried calling her as well as the realtor. There was no response from either. However, on January 6, 2026, the Landlord did send an email to the Tenants stating she had been out of the country for a while and therefore missed the closing of her unit. She wrote she would be compiling all the documents and emails and will fully reimburse the Tenants for the funds they are entitled to. However, they have received no further communication from the Landlord since then despite their numerous attempts to contact her.
Despite the Landlord’s email confirming she will reimburse the Tenants the funds they are entitled to, the Tenants have yet to hear anything further from her or receive the funds.

Subsection 135(1) of the Act provides: 135(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the Landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Having considered all the facts before me, I find that the Landlord did illegally retain the Tenants’ rent deposit and key deposit. Having defaulted on the mortgage and the closing of the condominium, the Tenants have had to pay a second last month’s rent and key deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,848.00. This amount represents: • $2,500.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $300.00 for the Key • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has illegally retained the last month’s rent deposit. As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities and the application is dismissed.

On December 12, 2025, the Tenant sent an N9 Notice to advise her Landlord that she intended to terminate her tenancy one month early on January 30, 2026. She claimed that she prepared the N9 on December 1, 2025, but it didn’t get sent due to a computer glitch. The Landlord refused the Tenant’s N9 Notice on December 12, 2025, because it did not give the required 60 days notice of termination and because the termination date on the Notice was incorrectly stated. The Landlord sent the Tenant a new N9 Notice for her signature with a termination date of February 28, 2026, but she refused to sign it.

The Tenant was adamant that she needed to vacate her rental unit on January 31, 2026, and agreed with the Landlord to pay a nominal fee to have her rental unit advertised for rent on February 1, 2025, on a fast-track basis. The Tenant understood that this meant she would be able to vacate the rental unit on January 31, 2026, but the Landlord corrected her that she would be responsible for the February 2026 rent if it was not rented for that month.

The Landlord’s agent confirmed in testimony that the unit was advertised on their media platforms and that they paid extra for advanced search engine optimization that ensured the Tenant’s rental unit was featured prominently in their advertisements. The Landlord stated the movement on rental units is typically slow during the Christmas period and there was lots of inventory everywhere at the time. The rental unit was not leased until March 14, 2026, despite the favourable location of the rental complex. The Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit was retained to pay the rent for the last month of the tenancy (February 2026).

This is a tenancy that renewed as a monthly tenancy agreement following the end of the fixed term. Pursuant to subsection 44(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Tenant was required to give the Landlord at least 60 days notice to terminate the monthly tenancy. As the Tenant gave notice on December 12, 2025, the earliest she could have terminated the tenancy is February 28, 2026. As such, the Tenant is not entitled to the return of the last month’s rent deposit. However, that is not the end of the analysis.

Pursuant to section 16 of the Act, the Landlord also has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses resulting from the Tenant’s unilateral repudiation of the tenancy agreement. I am satisfied the Landlord took reasonable steps to re-rent the unit for February 1, 2026. As the Landlord was unable to re-rent the unit, the Landlord correctly applied the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit to the rent owing for February 2026.
The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application is filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and claims the Landlords illegally collected or retained money.
The Teant’s claim for the return of rent paid due to an illegal rent increase is dismissed as the rent increase is deemed lawful. T1 Application -Determinations:
The Tenant claims the Landlord charged him an illegal rent from February 1, 2025, to present.

Subsections 135(1) and (4) of the Act provide: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant ant money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. The February 1, 2025, rent increase of $100.00 is deemed lawful:

The Tenant testified rent was $1,900.00 a month and that on or about January 26, 2025, the Landlord told the Tenant verbally that effective February 1, 2025, the monthly rent would be increased to $2,000.00, which amounted to an increase of $100.00 per month. The Tenant referred to page 184 in DOC ID 8016273, Exhibit 1, where the Landlord had texted the Tenant on or about January 24, 2025, stating that they needed to discuss rent increase and dishwasher issues. The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s testimony.

Section 120 (1) of the Act provides: 120 (1) No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.

The guideline increase in 2025 was 2.5% which would be equivalent to $47.50 a month on a monthly rent of $1,900.00. The $100.00 rent increase on February 1, 2025, was well above the guideline increase.

Above guideline increases are permitted where the Landlord has made an application to the Board under section 126 of the Act and the increase has been granted by an order of the Board. Parties are also entitled to agree to above guideline rent increases so long as the agreed upon increase accords with sections 121 or 123 of the Act.

There was no evidence this increase was authorized by an order of the Board, nor a suggestion the rent was increased because parking or a new prescribed service was added as provided for in section 123 of the Act, nor was there an agreement reached under section 121 of the Act.

The Tenant also testified he was not provided with a Notice of Rent Increase. Sub-sections 116(1) and (4) of the Act provide: 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.
In the above circumstances, I find the increase in monthly rent from February 1, 2025, from $1,900.00 to $2,000.00 was in excess of the guideline.
Nonetheless, there are sections of the Act that provide for circumstances under which an unlawful rent increase will be deemed lawful.

Section 135.1 addresses when an increase in rent that would have been void under section 116(4) for failure to serve a Notice of Rent Increase does not apply. 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116(4) is deemed not to be vid if the tenant has paid the increased in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. (3) For greater certainty, if subsection (1) applies wit respect to an increase in rent, section 116 is deemed to have been complied with. (4) For greater certainty, nothing in this section limits the application of section 136.

At the hearing, the Tenant acknowledged that as of February 1, 2025, he paid the $2,000.00 per month for 12 consecutive months. However, he felt that he was entitled to file the application at any time during the month of February as this still fell within the “12 consecutive months” period.
The Tenant also testified that he was waiting for the dishwasher and other maintenance issues to be resolved which is why he did not dispute the rent increase earlier.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant had filed an application on or around October 14, 2025, with respect to maintenance issues. He did not raise the issue of an illegal rent increase back then. This application has not yet been heard by the Board.

When the Tenant had filed his application with the Board, he had already made 13 consecutive rent payments of $2,000.00 per month and he did not file an application disputing the increase within one year of when it was first charged. Therefore, I find the monthly rent of $2,000.00 to be deemed lawful in accordance with section 135.1 of the Act.
Therefore, the Tenant’s claim for illegally charged rent is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants claim that they entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord but the Landlord did not allow them to move into the rental unit and did not return their money.

The Tenants contacted the Landlord on Facebook marketplace regarding accommodation in Unit 3002 at the residential complex. They viewed the unit in the first week of November 2025 and entered into a written tenancy agreement on November 16, 2025. The tenancy agreement titled “Residential Sublease” provides under paragraph 23 that the kitchen, living room and den will be shared. [name] testified that [name] was not the owner of unit 3002. [name] rented unit 3002 and their arrangement under [name] was that the Tenants would sublet one room in the unit. They would share the kitchen with [name] but they would have their own washroom.

The Tenants testified that they paid to the Landlord $6,850.00 between November 17, 2025 to December 5, 2025. They referred to their bank statement and testified that they email transferred to [name] the following sums: • November 17, 2025, $2,200.00 (first and last month’s rent); • November 18, 2025, $1,100.00 (additional deposit); • December 1, 2025, $550.00 (key and garage remote deposit); • December 1, 2025, $900.00 and $1,100.00 (house damage deposit); and • December 2, 2025, $1,000.00 (elevator deposit).

In late November 2025, [name] informed the Tenants that she had obtained possession of Unit PH05 in the same building and proposed that the Tenants move into that unit instead of unit 3002. The Tenants agreed. The parties proceeded on the basis that the monies previously paid and retained by [name] would be applied to the tenancy for unit [name].

On December 2, 2025, the parties mutually signed a new written lease agreement titled “Residential Tenancy Agreement (Standard Form of Lease)” for Unit [name]. The tenancy was to commence on December 6, 2025 and the lawful rent was $1,100.00 due on the 1st day of each month. However, prior to the move in date, the Landlord claimed that a water pipe had burst in unit [name] and that possession would be delayed.

On December 6, 2025, the Tenants were not provided with possession of unit [name]. [name] informed the Tenants that she would be unable to provide the unit and indicated that the monies paid would be returned. Despite repeated requests by the Tenants, the monies collected were not refunded.

The evidence establishes that [name] was herself a Tenant occupying unit 3002 and proposed that the Tenants occupy one bedroom in that unit while sharing the kitchen and living areas with her. The arrangement contemplated occupancy of only a portion of the rental unit rather than creation of a separate rental unit. However, the issue before me concerns the subsequent tenancy agreement for unit [name] because on December 2, 2025, the parties signed a new tenancy agreement and that tenancy is subject to the Act. Unlike [name] for unit 3002, the “Residential Tenancy Agreement (Standard Form of Lease)” does not explicitly provide that the kitchen or bathroom will be shared with the Tenants.

Further, Subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’) provides that a “landlord” includes, “(a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”)”

In this case, I am satisfied that [name] meets the definition of “landlord” in s.2(1)(a) of the Act with respect to unit [name] because she entered into a tenancy agreement for PH05, agreed to provide the Tenants the rental unit for purpose of occupancy in exchange for the monthly rent of $1,100.00, and accepted money from the Tenants in connection with that tenancy. I am also satisfied that [name] is the owner of PH05 or an individual who permits occupancy of Unit PH05, other than a tenant who occupies the rental unit in the residential complex.

I also find that when the parties agreed that the Tenants would rent unit [name] instead of unit 3002, they intended for the monies previously paid by the Tenants and retained by [name] to be applied to the PH05 tenancy. The agreement sets out the $3,000.00 deposit and $550.00 key deposit. Although the remaining deposits are not set out, based on the Tenants’ bank statements, I am satisfied that 6,850.00 was paid. [name] did not refund any of the monies paid under the earlier arrangement and continued to retain those funds after the unit [name] agreement was executed. Therefore, I find that [name] has retained $6,850.00 with respect to the PH05 tenancy.

Subsection 107(1) of the Act states that “a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.” I find that subsection 107(1) applies and requires the Landlord to repay $6,850.00 because the Landlord retained those monies and did not provide the Tenants with vacant possession of Unit [name].
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $[name]; this amount includes the filing cost of $53.00. The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove that Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

The parties do not dispute that in May, 2024 the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 Notice of Termination under 48 of the Act with a termination date of July 31, 2024. In the N12 Notice, the Landlord claimed that he required vacant possession of the rental unit because the Landlord intended to move into the unit. The parties also do not dispute that the Landlord filed an application with the LTB based on this N12 Notice (file number LTB-L- 041420-25) and on October 11, 2024 a consent order (the “L2 Order”) was issued terminating the tenancy on June 30, 2025 with a [name]’s clause for enforcement on or after July 1, 2025 if the Tenant’s did not vacate.

The Landlord subsequently gave the Tenants an N4 notice for arrears of rent and filed an L1 Application about non-payment of rent (file number LTB-L- 013930-25). An Order (the “L1 Order”) was issued on May 23, 2025. On the L1 hearing, the Vice [name] noted the existence of the L2 Order and, instead of granting a standard order in the L1 application, exercised her discretion at the Tenants’ request to postpone the termination of the tenancy to June 30, 2025, the same date for termination stated in the L2 Order as that was the termination date the parties agreed to in the L2 application. In the L1 Order, the Tenants had until June 30, 2025 to pay the Landlord the total amount owing - $11,436– failing which the Landlord could pursue eviction by filing the order with the sheriff’s office for enforcement.
The parties do not dispute that the Tenants did not pay the Landlord $11,436 by June 30, 2025.

As the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit on June 30, 2025, on July 7, 2025, the Landlord commenced enforcement proceedings based on the L1 Order, the file number for which is specifically referenced in the Sheriff’s documents. The Sherrif’s Confirmation of eviction proceedings states at the Tenants will be notified of eviction scheduled for July 16, 2025 by ordinary mail and the confirmation of delivery of vacant possession by the Sherriff on July 16, 2025 references enforcement of the L1 Order.

The parties further do not dispute that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit in July, 2025. However, they disagree about the reason and the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. The Tenants claim that they moved out of the rental unit on July 15, 2025, the day before the scheduled eviction, pursuant to the LTB’s [name], which is directly connected to the N12 Notice the Landlord gave them. In their T5 application and in the accompanying [name], the Tenants state that they moved out of the rental unit on July 16, 2025, the scheduled date of eviction. The Landlord’s position is that the Tenants moved out as a result of the L1 Order about non-payment of rent. Based on the evidence before me, I prefer the Landlord’s position on this issue.

I find that the Tenants remained in the rental unit until faced with eviction and moved out of the rental unit as a result of the anticipated execution of the L1 Order on July 16, 2026, which is entirely unrelated to the N12 Notice.

The facts are similar to those in TST-00530-18 Berger v. [name] cited by the Landlord’s representative. While the reason a tenant moved out of the rental unit must be considered on the facts of each case, [name] stands for the proposition that where there are two Order’s for eviction, it is open to the Board to make a finding that a tenant moved out because of one of the Orders. In [name], the Vice Chair found that the tenant moved out because of the Landlord’s enforcement of the L1 Order in that case. I make a similar finding here.

Therefore, I cannot find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice the Landlord gave them or as a result of the L2 Order that flowed from that N12 Notice. Since one of the required parts of the test in subsection 57(1)(b) is not satisfied, I find that the T5 Application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________
