issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

This application is about an allegation that the Tenant paid a rent deposit in the amount of $3,600.00 to the Landlord and the deposit was not returned as the Tenant did not take possession of the rental unit.
The Tenant submitted evidence consisting of the rental application (DOC-7438204), and the proof of payment for the deposit (DOC-7438206). Rent deposit

The Tenant stated that she applied for a rental unit and filled out an offer to lease application with the Landlord. The application signed and dated by the Tenant indicates the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to terms for the rental unit as follows: • Rental unit address 6, 385 [address]reet, [name], ON; • Commencement of tenancy January 1, 2026 for a fixed term of one year ending December 31, 2026; • Lawful rent $1,750.00 due on the first of each month; • A first and last month rent deposit required in the amount of $3,500.00;and • Utilities to be paid by the Tenant.

The Tenant stated that she handed her application to the super intendent, [name] along with her deposit cheque. The cheque in the amount of $3,600.00 was for a first and last month rent deposit ($1,750.00 X 2) and a $100.00 key deposit.
The Landlord cashed the cheque and accepted the Tenant’s application for the rental unit.
The Tenant stated that after the Landlord approved her application and acceptance for the tenancy, her mother suffered an injury and fell ill on December 2, 2025.

The Tenant texted [name] on December 23, 2025 and requested to withdraw her application. [name] responded by instructing the Tenant to email [name] the Landlord agent. The Tenant emailed Christpher on December 24, 2025 and stated she did not get a response back from [name] until January 2, 2026 informing the Tenant she was legally responsible for the rental unit for a fixed term.

The Tenant holds the position that no tenancy agreement was signed and the Landlord failed to follow through on a condition in the application allowing the Tenant to review the tenancy agreement before taking possession of the rental unit.
The Tenant requested an order from the Board for the Landlord to return the first and last month rent deposit of $3,500.00 and the $100.00 key deposit. Analysis Was there a tenancy in place?

In Musilla v. Avcan Management [2010] ONSC 5425 the court found a tenancy agreement had been entered into when the rental application was accepted by the Landlord. The essential terms of the agreement were set out in the rental application. The [name] v. Avcan Management case resembles the decision of the court in Opara v. [name] [2008] [name] No. 1934 ([name]). There the Court upheld a decision of the Board dismissing a tenant’s application for a refund because the Court observed that the tenancy agreement came into effect the day the parties reached an agreement on the rental unit and the deposit being paid.

The issue to be determined before me is whether the parties had entered into a tenancy agreement at the time that the Tenant informed the Landlord that she no longer required the rental unit and whether the Tenant is entitled to the return of the deposit pursuant to section 107 of the Act.

Once a tenancy agreement is made, whether pursuant to the terms of a rental application (as in Musilla, supra) or in some other unspecified form (as in Opara v. [name], supra), neither party may unilaterally break the agreement, and a tenant who does so is not entitled, under subsection 107(1) of the Act, to the return of the rent deposit.

In this case I find the essential terms of a tenancy agreement were agreed upon by the Landlord and the Tenant in the rental agreement such as the rental unit address, the monthly rent, the day of the commencement of the tenancy, and defining additional terms such as parking and utilities. Did the Landlord provide vacant possession?

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act , 2006, (the ‘Act’) provides: “A Landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.” [emphasis added]

The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc. further provides the Board with guidance, regarding s. 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), stating the Act should not apply where a landlord has done everything to provide possession, but the tenant refuses to move in.

The Divisional Court, in Opara v. [name], [2008], O.J. No. 1934 ([name].[name].Ct.), also deals with the issue currently before the Board. The court held that a tenancy agreement is a contract and once the parties have entered into a tenancy agreement, unless the Landlord agrees, the Tenant cannot decide to break the agreement.

With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find that the Landlord intended to make the rental unit identified in the application available for the Tenant commencing in January 1, 2026.
The actions of the Tenant was the cause for the Tenant not taking possession of the rental unit. Was the tenancy lawfully terminated?

Section 88 of the Act states: Arrears of rent when tenant abandons or vacates without notice 88 (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.
The rental application indicates the Tenant made a payment of $1,750.00 for the first month’s rent and $1,750.00 to be held as the last month rent deposit upon acceptance of the application.
As stated above I find a tenancy agreement was in place pursuant to the Landlord’s acceptance of the Tenant’s rental application. The term was for a fixed term of one year.

Although the Tenant claims she never accepted keys to the rental unit, the rental unit application shows the Landlord’s intent to provide vacant possession of the rental unit upon commencement of the tenancy January 1, 2026.
The tenancy was not terminated in accordance with the Act, or by the Landlord providing a notice or on agreement between the parties.
The Tenant’s email evidence indicates the Landlord agent did not accept the Tenant’s request to terminate the tenancy and informs the Tenant of her legal obligation for the fixed term.

The Tenant stated that in communication with the Landlord agent she was informed that the Landlord would attempt to re-rent the rental unit and if the Landlord found a new tenant the Landlord would waive any further fees (rent). The Tenant stated the Landlord agent also informed her that she may be liable for further fees (rent) if the Landlord could not re- rent the rental unit. The Tenant stated she was never contacted by the Landlord agent again.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the tenancy was not terminated in accordance with the Act.

Pursuant to section 16 of the Act the Landlord has a duty to mitigate their losses and try to find replacement tenants however there is inconclusive evidence before me to find the Landlord is in breach of section 16 of the Act and when or if the Landlord re-rented the rental unit to a new tenant.

Based on my knowledge of similar like cases, in my view the reasonable amount of rent under section 88 of the Act the Landlord is entitled to when a Tenant vacates or abandons a rental unit, and if the rental unit was not re-rented would be two months rent. This amount is the amount the Tenant paid in the first months rent $1,750.00 and last month rent deposit $1,750.00 and I find the Landlord is not in breach of the Act.

The Tenant’s position is the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with a tenancy agreement for her review pursuant to the rental application and therefore, this entitles the Tenant to withdraw her application.
I do not find that the Tenant’s submission is supported by relevant sections of the Act or is supported by the case law for such applications.
Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Key deposit
The Tenant submitted evidence as proof of payment for a $100.00 key deposit.
The Tenant stated she never took possession of the rental unit and did not receive keys from the Landlord.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.”

With the totality of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Landlord failed to return the full rent deposit to the Tenant which is in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act. Furthermore, the Landlord’s requirement of an additional deposit from the Tenant was also in contravention of the Act.
Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is granted and the Landlord owes the Tenant $100.00.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $148.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 application fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: Did the Tenant request an assignment or propose a sublet?
Did the Landlord refuse consent arbitrarily or unreasonably deny a request for an assignment [name]) of the Act?
Is the Tenant entitled to terminate the tenancy early? Background

The following facts were undisputed: a) The Tenant entered into a fixed-term tenancy with an expiry date of April 30, 2026. A copy of the lease agreement was submitted into evidence. b) On December 18, 2025, the Tenant requested to terminate the tenancy early. c) The Landlord advised the Tenant that early termination was not permitted but that the Tenant could seek to assign the tenancy to a new tenant. d) On January 8, 2026, the Tenant notified the Landlord that she intended to vacate the rental unit and would locate a replacement tenant. The Tenant submitted email communication into evidence. e) The Landlord provided photographs of the rental unit to assist with advertising. f) On January 17, 2026, the Tenant identified a prospective occupant who wished to take possession of the rental unit on February 1, 2026, but only for a two-month period (February 1, 2026 – March 31, 2026) and paying rent to the Landlord. g) The Landlord advised the Tenant that she remained responsible for rent until April 30, 2026, the end of the fixed term. h) The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2026. The unit remained vacant for approximately three months.

The Landlord testified, and the Tenant did not dispute that the Landlord was also looking for someone to rent the rental unit. A copy of the advertisement was submitted into evidence. The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not present a candidate willing to assume the tenancy for its remaining term. The Landlord submitted that he is entitled to require that an assignee take over the lease as written until the end of the term. Law
Section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 governs assignment of a tenancy.

An assignment occurs where a tenant permanently transfers all of their rights and obligations under the tenancy agreement to another person, and the tenancy continues with the new tenant on the same terms.
Pursuant to s. 95(5) of the Act, a landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment to a potential assignee.

Under section 97 of the Act, a sublet occurs where a tenant vacates the rental unit for a temporary period and permits another person to occupy the unit, while the original tenant remains responsible for the tenancy, including paying the rent directly to the landlord during the subtenancy, and intends to return at the end of the subtenancy. Analysis
The Tenant submits that she sought to assign the tenancy, and it was arbitrarily or unreasonably refused by the Landlord.

However, the evidence establishes that the proposed tenant intended to occupy the unit for only two months, from February 1, 2026, to March 31, 2026. This person did not intend to continue with the tenancy after March 31, 2026.
An assignment requires that the incoming tenant assume the tenancy on the same terms, including the remaining duration of the lease.

As the parties here had a fixed-term tenancy ending April 30, 2026, it was not possible under the Act for there to be a valid assignment to an assignee who intended to occupy the unit for only two months and vacate before the end of the lease.
Therefore, I find that the Tenant was not proposing a valid assignment within the meaning of the Act.
The Landlord advised that the Tenant remained responsible for the lease to April 30, 2026. The Landlord’s position correctly reflects the Tenant’s obligations under tenancy agreement.

There is insufficient evidence that the Landlord refused a valid assignment request. The Landlord’s insistence that the tenancy continue to April 30, 2026, was consistent with the Act and the tenancy agreement. I am not satisfied that the Landlord imposed a condition that amounted to an arbitrary or unreasonable refusal under s. 95(5).

I have also considered whether the Landlord has unreasonably withheld consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant. However, as set out above, for there to be a valid subtenancy under the RTA, the original tenant remains responsible for the tenancy, including paying the rent directly to the landlord during the subtenancy, and intends to return at the end of the subtenancy. In this case, these requirements were not met. The Tenant had secured alternate accommodation effective February 1, 2026, and there was no intention to return to the rental unit. Further, the circumstances indicate that the proposal was not for a temporary sublet but rather a transfer of occupancy for the remainder of the lease term, which had three months remaining, with rent only being paid directly to the Landlord for two of those months. Accordingly, I find that this was not a valid request for a sublet within the meaning of the Act.
I find that the Tenant did not serve a valid notice of termination in accordance with the Act and the Tenant vacating the rental unit does not, in itself, terminate the tenancy.
As no valid assignment was refused, the Tenant was not entitled to unilaterally terminate the tenancy on the basis of s. 95 of the RTA.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 41291 Date: 2026-06-25 In the matter of: 207, 1073 [address] OTTAWA ON Group (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally; and • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This application was heard by videoconference on May 19, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord’s Agent, D. Cordero, and the Landlord’s legal representative, D. [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally and substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the property by failing to adequately respond to complaints of second-hand smoke. Illegal Entries on September 29, 2023 and February 1, 2024

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenants’ evidence that someone who works for the Landlord tried to enter the rental unit on September 29, 2023 and on February 1, 2024 without proper notice, as required by subsection 27(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Tenant SC testified that he was present in the rental unit on both days when an employee of the Landlord inserted a key in the front door lock to enter the unit. SC prevented the door from being opened, demanded the person identify who they are, and refused the person permission to enter on both days.

The parties introduced consistent evidence that the Landlord intended to install weatherstripping to the rental unit door on September 29, 2023 and replace a kitchen appliance on February 1, 2024. There was also evidence that, although the parties discussed in principle the Landlord’s attendance at the rental unit to perform those tasks, they did not agree on a firm date and time for those activities to take place. The Tenants therefore did not expect the Landlord’s attendance on those days.

The Landlord’s employee did not physically enter the rental unit on either September 29, 2023 or February 1, 2024. I find, however, that this is not a defence to the Tenants’ application for a breach of the Landlord’s obligation to give proper notice under subsection 27(1)1 of the Act to enter the rental unit. To interpret the Act differently would diminish the Act’s purpose to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and be inconsistent with privacy interests in section 25 of the Act. But for SC’s presence in the rental unit on both days, and his response to the sound of the rental unit door being unlocked, the Landlord’s employee would surely have entered the unit in a manner that is not permitted under the Act. I note that, with respect to the privacy interest in section 25 of the Act, the Tenant LG testified that, although not at home at the time, the Landlord’s actions affected her and caused her to lose her sense of security and safety at the residential complex. [name]
The Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not adequately respond to their complaints of second-hand cigarette smoke from a neighbouring rental unit.

The Landlord’s Agent gave evidence at the hearing. As the Landlord’s property manager from June 2020 to February 2026, the Landlord’s Agent has knowledge of the Tenants’ complaints of second-hand smoke and of the Landlord’s response to those complaints.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that the Landlord began receiving complaints of second- hand smoke from the Tenants in 2022. The Landlord’s Agent further testified that the Landlord installed weatherstripping to the rental unit’s door in October 2023. The Landlord’s Agent’s testimony on these matters is consistent with the Tenants’ evidence of their history of complaints and of the Landlord’s response.

I note, however, that the Landlord’s Agent did not explain why the Landlord did not respond until October 2023 to the Tenants’ complaints of second-hand smoke to install weatherstripping, or do any other thing to address second-hand smoke entering the rental unit. Also, the Landlord did not introduce evidence to show that it responded to the Tenants’ December 12, 2023 email message advising that the weatherstripping installed in October 2023 had come off; or reliable evidence that it installed an air purifier in the hallway outside the rental unit; or that anyone came to inspect the residential complex’s HVAC system before 2024. Indeed, the Landlord’s Agent testified that the Landlord waited until 2024 to inspect the HVAC system in relation to the Tenant’s complaints, because the Landlord wanted to see if the aforementioned weatherstripping, and asking the smoking tenant to stop smoking in their unit, would resolve the issue.

I find the Landlord’s response to the Tenants’ complaints of second-hand smoke was inadequate. The Landlord’s own evidence of email messages with the Tenants reveals that the Landlord only installed weatherstripping once in response to the Tenant’s complaints, and the Landlord did not replace the weatherstripping when it learned in December 2023, at the latest, that the weatherstripping had failed. In the circumstances, I find this does not satisfy the Landlord’s duty to reasonably address tenants’ complaints of substantial interference, as the Divisional Court described in [name] v. [name], [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Ct.) and, more recently, in North Avenue Road Corporation v. Travares, 2015 ONSC 6986 ([name]. Ct.), where the Court affirmed at paragraph 37 that its reasons in Hassan apply to tenant complaints about second-hand cigarette smoke.

At the hearing, the Tenants described general discomfort from the odour of second-hand cigarette smoke and being aware of its hazards. The Tenant LG testified that she is a former smoker who quit after giving birth. The Tenants described concern for their baby’s and their own health, and feeling helpless and frustrated because of the Landlord’s apparent inaction.

Based on the Tenants’ testimony, I find that there is substance to the impact the Landlord’s omission had on the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex. That is, the omission to adequately respond to the Tenants’ complaints of second-hand smoke substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, as set out in subsection 23 of the Act. Remedies

Having proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, and substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex, the Tenants are entitled to a remedy under subsection 31(1)(c) of the Act and as pled for in their application to the Board.

While I am mindful of the Tenants’ testimony of how the Landlord’s illegal entries and omission to respond to their complaints of second-hand cigarette smoke affected them, the Tenants agreed that the Landlord’s actions and omission did not prevent them from using the rental unit and residential complex for all usual purposes. The Tenants also agreed that they did not have evidence that the Landlord’s actions and omission affected their baby’s or their health, including LG’s mental health after the illegal entries in September 2023 and February 2024.

In the circumstances, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenants a five percent abatement of rent for the Landlord’s omission to adequately address complaints from second-hand smoke from March 2023, or one-year before the Tenants filed their application with the Board, to October 2024, when the Tenants vacated the rental unit. This amount is consistent with other Board decisions, including LTB-T-013516-24, issued on May 28, 2025.

I also find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to a 50 percent abatement of the daily rent payable on September 29, 2023 and February 1, 2024 to remedy the impact the Landlord’s illegal entries had on the Tenants.

The Tenants introduced evidence that their monthly rent was $1,449.42 when they terminated their tenancy in 2024. The parties, including of course the Landlord, did not introduce evidence of the monthly rent in 2023. Although page 7 of the Tenants’ application form suggests the rent in 2023 was $1,484.06, this amount is not reliable because of the Tenants’ assertion that their 2024 rent of $1,449.42 represents an increase in rent starting from January 2024. I accordingly find it is reasonable to use the Tenants’ last monthly rent to calculate the total rent abatement the Landlord must pay under this order, or $1,449.42 for the second-hand smoke and $47.67 for the illegal entries into the rental unit.

The Tenants requested an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine, pursuant to subsection 31(1)(d) of the Act. Following the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines, I find the total rent abatement the Landlords must pay the Tenants - $1,497.59 – is inadequate to deter the Landlord from omitting to respond adequately to future tenant complaints. However, I note that the Act is remedial legislation and not punitive. In the circumstances, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine of $1,000.00. Together with the amount the Landlord must pay the Tenants, the administrative fine will promote future compliance with the Landlord’s duty under section 23 of the Act and as the Divisional Court described in Hassan and North Avenue Road Corporation.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,545.59. This amount represents $1,497.59 for a rent abatement and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.00 by July 7, 2026. June 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1), of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit fail to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. [name]
The Tenant testified that her first solo tenancy began on September 1, 2020 when she moved in to the unit.
She testified that she rented the unit knowing it was a basement but had not visited the unit prior to moving in.

She testified that there were multiple issues after she moved in, such as basement dampness, an issue with the oven, windows, moisture, mold, humidity, leaks in the ceiling, plumbing, a strong odor of sewage, poor air quality and problems with the washer and dryer. The only issue before me on this T6 is the mold issue.
She testified that [name] from [name] P [organization] told her to purchase a dehumidifier on October 18, 2021.
On December 6, 2023 at 12:31 PM, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord requesting a mold test (DOC- DOC-6875459 – Exhibit 1).

The Tenant testified that this was because her clothes were molding in her closet, there was mold on her couch and chairs, near the ceiling where she stored her items, she had to replace her mattress, there were odours, she had rashes, fevers, brain fog, fatigue, body pain, joint paid, sneezing, respiratory difficulties, and bad headaches. (Tenant’s evidence book –DOC-7629001, Exhibit 2.)
On December 6, 2023 at 8:59 p.m., the Landlord responded and asked for photos, and requested entry on December 11, 2023 at 8:00 AM (Exhibit 1)
On January 2, 2024, [name] diagnosed the Tenant with a fungal infection based on mold in her house and prescribed cream and medication (DOC-7629001, Page 3 of Exhibit 2).
The Tenant testified that the Landlord housed her in a hotel at no expense from January 17, 2024 to February 1, 2024. The cost was $1806.00 and paid by the Landlord *(DOC- 6875538 Exhibit 3).
The Tenant testified she had no intention of returning to the rental unit.
The Tenant signed an N11 on January 25, 2024 and was deemed to have vacated the unit on January 31, 2024. The agreement mutually released both parties.
The Landlord refunded her last month’s rent deposit of $1136.00 on February 1, 2024.
She instructed the Landlord by email to dispose of her items that she had left behind, saying “you are allowed to dispose of them.” (DOC-6877783 - Exhibit #4).

She filed this application on July 7, 2024 after she moved out of the apartment. She also filed a T2 application, but this was withdrawn on December 1, 2025 LTB-T-055172-24, so the only application before me is the T6. Landlord’s Evidence 1. The Landlord agreed they received the Tenant’s email on December 7, 2023 and responded at 8:59 p.m., a few hours later) 2. On December 11, 2023, a plumber attended for a service call at Unit 7, 36 [address]nue (DOC-6875494, Exhibit 5) 3. The Landlord called expert witness [name]. He testified that he is a mold remediation and asbestos removal technician for Healthy Home Environment Inc. and has worked in the industry for 13 years. He is accredited by the IRCRC, MTCU, [name], Health Inspections for Home Assessments and RDQ. I am satisfied that his knowledge, training and experience qualifies him as an expert witness. 4. He was first contacted on December 7, 2023 by the Landlord, and later attended Unit 7, 36 Third Street, on December 13, 2023 in person accompanied by [name] to conduct an inspection and assessment. He spent two hours in the unit. He took Air-O-Cell samples in two places in the apartment: at the entrance/vestibule and one in the middle room. He noted that there was water seeping in from the vestibule and found visual mold growth in the area. He checked exterior walls, did moisture mapping, checked the bathroom, bedrooms and kitchen. He did not find any confirmation using equipment, but instead took an Air-O-Cell sample from the vestibule. Particle counting indicated that the area was mild to elevated. He determined that the windows were normal. He determined that water was seeping in from the vestibule near items that were stored and cautioned the Tenant about storing items. 5. He conducted a mold remediation on December 19-22, 2023. 6. The Landlord was also in touch with the City of Ottawa concerning the Tenant’s request for an investigation. Email correspondence dated January 8, 2024 with the City of Ottawa shows that the [name] officer involved, [name], said he would “hold off on the order as it seems as though you are doing everythin you can to address the concerns.” (Exhibit 8). This document is not being considered for the truth of its contents and the By- [name] officer was not called as a witness . It merely demonstrates to me that the Landlord was in communication with the responsible authorities and was taking steps to address the situation. The City of Ottawa closed the request on January 31, 2024 (DOC-6875738, Exhibit 6.) 7. On January 18, 2024, [name] returned to the unit and conducted a follow-up inspection. 8. He explained that there was a 3,833 count of spores in December 2023 in one cubic meter, which indicates a mold-elevated area. He used the December reading as a baseline. In January 2024, the number of spores had decreased to 417 count in one cubic meter in the same area. In his opinion, this reading appeared normal. 9. Similarly, the reading in the entrance on January 18, 2024 was also 315 ct/m3, and this was lower. The middle area was also 90 count/m3, which [name] testified was lower than December 2023. 10. He added that amplified mold growth is usually more than 3,000 counts/m3, and we can decrease it by using dehumidifiers, lowering the temperature in the living space, and keeping things in plastic instead of cardboard. 11. His clearance inspection report published January 29, 2024 was made Exhibit 7 - DOC- 6877755. His report made the following recommendations to the Landlord: • Consider getting your contractor to explore other exterior wall assemblies and determine if further work will be required. • It is important to keep monitoring the relative humidity levels and the seasonal use of a dehumidifier is required. • Contents should be packed at plastic containers if the storage is used. 12. The Landlord renovated the Tenant’s bathroom from 17 January-February 8, 2024. During this time, the Landlord housed the Tenant in a hotel from January 17-Feburary 1, 2024 at their expense (DOC-6875538 – Exhibit 8). 13. The Landlord testified that it was the Tenant who requested to terminate the tenancy on January 24, 2024. The N11 was signed January 25, 2024, and the Landlord refunded the last month’s rent deposit of $1136.00 on February 1, 2024 (DOC-6875550 -Exhibit 9) 14. The Landlord recalled [name] to do some additional air testing on February 13, 2024 to make sure the unit was clear. 15. The Landlord conducted further renovations in April and May 2024. Analysis 1. [name] 16. According to section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1).
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to uphold these obligations and requests remedies, including rent abatement and cost of replacing her belongings.
The Test is whether the Landlord responded took reasonable steps in a timely manner.
The Tenant has the burden of proving the allegation on a balance of probabilities. And for the foregoing reasons, I find that she has not discharged this burden.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (hereinafter “Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 21. [name] [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (hereinafter [name]) stands for the proposition that the Landlord has a duty to respond to and take reasonable steps to address a Tenant’s complaints. 22. I find that the Tenant notified the Landlord of a mold issue on December 7, 2023 and that the Landlord responded the same evening to obtain more information (photos) and schedule an assessment by a mold expert, [name]. [name] testimony confirmed this timeline. 23. Four days later, on December 11, 2023 the Landlord’s employee, [name], escorted a plumber to the unit to investigate the leak. Two days after that on December 13, 2023, [name] attended to conduct his assessment, and the mold was remediated December 19-22, 2023. He subsequently conducted follow-up investigation that showed that the presence of aspergillus was significantly decreased on January 18, 2024. The Tenant was housed at a hotel at the Landlord’s expense during this time. The report of January 29, 2024 made several recommendations. Neither his testimony, nor his report were impeached by the Tenant. The Tenant never asked if the Landlord had taken [name] advice. 24. I find that shortly thereafter, the Landlord engaged contractors to renovate the bathroom as both a responsive and preventative measure. As a result, the Landlord incurred expenses to provide alternate housing to the Tenant and sought to decrease her inconvenience by finding a nearby hotel for her to stay between January 17, 2024 and February 1, 2024. This cost the Landlord $1806.00. 25. The Landlord wishes me to consider Macdougall v. [name] et al LTB-T- 064554-22. However, I note that this is a T2 application involving harassment. I note that it involves the same residential complex and Landlord, but do not find it instructive to this case because the tests are different. 26. The Tenant asked me to consider the case of Lafleur v Marcotte 2022 Canlii 87316 (ONLTB), a similar case involving mold. I find this case is distinguishable because the Landlord in that case did not act immediately, but waited almost a month before coming to inspect the mold, and tried to fix the problem himself not having the proper equipment or expertise. 27. This was not the case with the Landlord before me. The Landlord in this case acknowledged the Tenant’s request in the same day by email and made arrangements as soon as practically possible to retain the professional services at the earliest opportunity: a plumber attended December 11, 2023 and a mold expert on December 13, 2023. 28. I therefore find that the Landlord took reasonable steps in a timely fashion to investigate the source of the mold by retaining the services of a plumber and a mold remediation expert within hours of the Tenant’s initial complaint. These dates and actions were not challenged by the Tenant. The Landlord went to great lengths to have [name] conduct an inspection, assessment, mold remediation, renovation, and an air test on 3 separate occasions in a two-month period. They took the problem seriously and responded appropriately. 29. Therefore I do not find that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to uphold her maintenance obligation. 2. The Tenant’s belongings 30. Having found the Landlord was not in serious breach of their obligations, I do not find that they are responsible for the Tenant’s belongings. 31. Furthermore, I find that the Tenant instructed the Landlord to dispose of her belongings and has no further claim to them.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Inc. (the 'Tenants’) applied for an order determining that [organization] (the ‘Landlord’) collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord illegally retained his damage security deposit, his key deposit and the accrued interest on his last month rent (LMR) deposit. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord overcharged him rent over the past 12 months. Illegally Retention Of Money

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied the Tenant paid the Landlord a damage security deposit in the amount of $2,290.00, a key deposit of $200.00, and a last month’s rent deposit of $2,290.00.

The Landlord did not return the key deposit or the security damage deposit to the Tenant after the Tenant vacated. Text messages from the Landlord admitted into evidence indicate the Landlord was retaining both deposits to cover alleged damages and cleaning costs.

Subsection 105(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. Subsection 106(2) states that the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the rent for one month. The Landlord was not entitled to require the Tenant to provide a damage security deposit in addition to a last month’s rent deposit. I am satisfied the Landlord illegally collected a damage security deposit. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $2,290.00.

The Landlord was also not legally entitled to retain the key deposit as the key was returned upon vacant possession being provided to the Landlord. There seems to be some indication that the Landlord retained these deposits because of damage to the rental unit. However, the Landlord is not entitled to retain any deposit for damages. Accordingly, the Landlord shall also be ordered to pay the Tenant $200.00. Interest on LMR

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by subsection 106(6) of the Act. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $138.35 of LMR interest calculated as follows: LMR Interest on $2.290 from Sept 1, 2023, to January 31, 2026 Period LMR Interest Accrued Interest 2023 (4 months Sept-Dec) $2,290 $2,290 x 2.5% x 4 / 12 $19.08 2024 (12 months) $2,290 $2,290 x 2.5% $57.25 2025 (12 Months) $2,290 $2,290 x 2.5% $57.25 2026 (1 Month) Jan $2,290 $2,290 x 2.5% x 1 /12 $ 4.77 Total Accrued Interest = $138.35 Overpayment of Rent

The Tenant’s application included an allegation that the Landlord overcharged him illegal rent. However, the Tenant withdrew this part of his application at the hearing because he lacked documentation to prove this allegation.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs. Finding

The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $2,676.35 which includes $2,290.00 for damage security deposit, $200.00 for the key deposit, $138.35 for interest on the last month's rent deposit, and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,676.35 which represents: • $2,290.00 for the illegal damage deposit collected. • $200.00 for the key deposit. • $138.35 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The parties entered a one-year tenancy for the period September 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026. The Landlord was reluctant to rent to the Tenant as she is an elderly woman living alone and her impression of the Tenant was not favourable. The Tenant’s aunt, who had accompanied him to view the rental, persuaded the Landlord to rent to the Tenant by offering to pay an additional two months rent over and above the first and last month’s rent deposits. The Landlord noted in her evidence that the aunt refused to be a guarantor for the Tenant.

The Tenant gave a notice of termination to the Landlord on December 19, 2025 and vacated the unit on December 31, 2025. This notice was not valid because it does not comply with sections 44 and 47 of the Act. Under those provisions, the earliest termination date the Tenant could have correctly provided was August 31, 2026, the last day of the fixed term for this tenancy.

The Tenant testified that he had paid rent for the months of September (first month’s deposit), October, November and December and that he used the last month’s rent deposit for the month of January 2026. The Tenant took until January 21, 2026 to clean out the rental unit. The Tenant then returned to China because he was struggling with mental health issues.
The Tenant argues that the two months pre-paid rent paid by his [name] at the beginning of the tenancy was illegally received by the Landlord and that it should be returned to him.

The Landlord argues that the additional two months were freely given. I find that the additional two months payment was freely given by the Tenant to secure the rental accommodation when his aunt refused to be his guarantor.

Even if the Landlord collected the additional two months illegally, which is not the case, once the Tenant violated the terms of the lease agreement by terminating the tenancy without providing a valid notice of termination.

Under section 88(1) of the Act, the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent continued until August 31, 2026 (the last day of the one year term), unless the Landlord was able to re-rent the unit prior to that date, or the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate her losses.

In this case, the Landlord told the Tenant if he assisted in securing a new tenant right away, she would refund that portion of the pre-paid rent that was covered by a new tenant. The Tenant did not assist the Landlord in finding a new tenant.

The Landlord re-rented the unit in April for occupation on May 1, 2026. She is an elderly woman and in the circumstances she was diligent in mitigating her damages. 12. entitled to apply that money to outstanding rent. 13. She was therefore entitled to retain the two months pre-paid rent and apply it to the outstanding rent owing by the Tenant for the months of February and March 2026.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed, and the LTB file is closed. June 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $290.47 on or before June 22, 2026.
In the application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord unlawfully charged and retained a $200.00 key deposit and failed to pay interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant submitted a copy of the lease agreement between four co-tenants and the Landlord. The agreement required each co-tenant to pay a $200.00 key deposit. The Tenant testified that the lawful monthly rent was $4,276.00, which was divided equally among the co-tenants at $1,069.00 each.
The Tenant stated that the rental unit was secured by a standard lock and metal key.

The Tenant testified that on or about January 24, 2024, he paid the Landlord $1,269.00 by eTransfer, representing the last month’s rent deposit and the key deposit. The Tenant stated that the rent did not increase during the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on August 25, 2025, and returned the keys to the receptionist at the Landlord’s business office. The last month’s rent deposit was applied to the final month of tenancy; however, no interest was paid. Despite repeated requests over six months following move-out, the Landlord has not refunded the key deposit. Analysis Illegal charge collected

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) prohibits illegal charges, subject to exemptions set out in section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06. Section 17 permits a landlord to collect a refundable key, remote entry device, or card deposit, provided it does not exceed the direct replacement cost.

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the key was a standard metal key that could be replaced at a nominal cost of $10.00 or less. I therefore find that the $200.00 key deposit exceeded the expected direct replacement cost and was not lawful.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that the Tenant paid the $200.00 key deposit required by the lease and that the Landlord did not refund it after the key was returned. Accordingly, the Landlord will be ordered to refund the key deposit. Interest on the rent deposit
A landlord’s obligation to pay annual interest on a rent deposit is set out in section 106(6) of the Act.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that he paid a last month’s rent deposit of $1,069.00 on or about January 24, 2024. I also accept that, although the deposit was applied to the final month of tenancy, the Landlord did not pay interest on the amount held from the start of the tenancy to August 25, 2025.
I calculate the amount of interest owing to the Tenant is $42.47. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay this amount to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $290.47. This amount represents: • $200.00 for refund of the key deposit collected. • $42.47 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant has brought this application under section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (1).

The Tenant alleges the Landlord collected illegally rent and a charge for a hot water tank rental. Both issues have been addressed in the Interim Order issued February 25, 2026. The Landlord was ordered to pay the Tenant $892.50 for the illegally collected rent and the Tenant’s claim for hot water tank rental was dismissed pursuant to the limitation period.
The parties agree that the Landlord has since paid the Tenant $892.50 for the illegally collected rent.

The Tenant attempted to raise issues with respect to the oven and closet door. These issues are not appropriate brought in a T1 application. The Tenant would be required to file an application under subsection 29(1)(1) of the Act (T6 application) for consideration of these issues.
The Tenant also raised the issue with respect to the outstanding water bill. For the reason that follows, this issue will not be considered in the application.

As indicated above, this application is brought under section 135(1) of the Act. There is no indication that the Landlord has illegally collected or retained money from the Tenant in connection to the water bill. The water utility account is in the Landlord’s name, and he advises the Tenant the amount she owes each month. The issue seems to stem from a dispute over the amount the Landlord alleges the Tenant owes him. Such issues are more appropriately addressed in an L2 or L10 application.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $53.00 for the application filing fee.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord’s legal representative raised a preliminary issue and made submissions that the Tenant’s application lacks specific reasons and details that would enable the Landlord to adequately respond to the allegations.

The Tenant’s application alleges, “I have had cockroaches since May 2024.”, and states that the issue is ongoing. The Tenant filed an amended application to include an allegation that there have been issues with mice in the rental unit since July 2025.
The Tenant’s application notes pest issues relating to cockroaches since May 2024, and mice since July 2025. The Tenant’s application notes that the issues are ongoing.
The Tenant’s amended application clearly lists the two issues being alleged and provides the date each issue is alleged to have started. The Tenant submits that the issues are ongoing.

While the Tenant’s application is not detailed, there is sufficient information that the Landlord had enough information to provide evidence and respond to the Tenant’s allegations. Therefore, the Landlord’s request that the application be dismissed for a lack of particulars was denied. Summons

The Tenant raised the issue that she had served a summons on the Landlord’s agent Anthony Pukas (AP). The Tenant did not pay the Landlord’s agent the attendance money required when a summons is served.

The Landlord’s agent is named on the Tenant’s application and attended the hearing. Documents were served by the Landlord and accordingly I am satisfied that even despite attendance money not being paid, there was compliance with the summons.
Since the Landlord’s agent was named on the application AP was called to testify by the Landlord during the proceedings, and the Tenant had the opportunity to cross examine AP. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] (PS) testified that she has had cockroaches in her rental unit since 2024 and has consistently, if not monthly, requested pest control treatments which the Landlord has refused.

PS first testified that she began complaining about cockroaches in January or February and the Landlord committed to performing pest control treatments in the entire building in March which were not completed until April. PS clarified that the issue actually began in May of 2024, and she contacted the Landlord using a work order.
PS gave evidence that historically when she had to request pest control, she would complete a work order at the office and within a week a pest control treatment would be performed.

PS submitted a letter dated July 21, 2024, which is the first evidence of any complaint to the Landlord about cockroaches that was tendered at the hearing. In the letter PS writes, “As you are aware, I have been getting treatment for cockroaches every 2 weeks for the last 2+months.”. PS also complains that the continuous treatment is unreasonable and requests an update about the Landlord’s “escalated corrective action”.
In August 2024, the Tenant made a complaint to the City of Toronto by-law in relation to the cockroach issue.

PS also submitted various e-mails and communications to the Landlord evidencing her request for pest control treatments up to November 25, 2025. E-mails from February and March 2026 were also submitted showing PS cancelled a treatment appointment in January 2026, and that there are still ongoing discussions about subsequent treatment appointments.
While not every e-mail submitted at the hearing has been addressed in this order, the entirety of the communications submitted by PS have been considered.
PS testified that she had no reason to keep track of all of her work orders or requests for treatment and could not recall how many times her rental unit was treated for cockroaches.

PS gave evidence in relation to the circumstances surrounding some of the e-mail communications and testified that the Landlord would often not reply to her e-mails. PS also testified that “Brittany” or “[name]” would commit to performing pest control treatments but, would either not schedule treatments or perform other work such as filling holes and gaps that were believed to be contributing to the issue.

PS’s evidence is that because of medical limitations she cannot move furniture and is unable to prepare her rental unit for pest control treatments without assistance or sufficient prior notice to obtain assistance.
PS also testified about an issue with mice in the rental unit and submitted an e-mail dated August 28, 2025, which is the first notification to the Landlord about an issue with mice.

PS also submitted three videos taken on July 20, August 28, August 29, and August 30, 2025, showing a mouse in the rental unit. Two e-mails from PS dated March 25 and April 23, 2026, advises that a mouse was discovered in the rental unit and requests the mouse be removed and traps replaced.

PS further testified that [name] came to fill holes and requested a dead mouse be removed from the rental unit in early 2026 evidenced by an e-mail from PS dated March 25, 2026. PS’s evidence is that the superintendent came to remove the dead mouse and also checked the living room for signs of mice.

The Landlord’s pest control treatment reports were put to PS during cross examination. PS disputed some the reports on the basis of clerical errors however, the reports reflect the following: Treatment Date Activity Level Unit Prepared Pest July 28, 2024 No live activity 50-59% Cockroaches August 16, 2024 No live activity 80-89% prepared Cockroaches October 4, 2024 “Low” 80-89% prepared Cockroaches October 29, 2024 No live activity “Few dead ones found” 70-79% prepared Cockroaches November 22, 2024 No live activity 70-79% prepared Cockroaches December 13, 2024 “No access” - Cockroaches December 16, 2024 No live activity 0% prepared Cockroaches January 3, 2025 No live activity 80-89% prepared Cockroaches April 4, 2025 No live activity 0% prepared Cockroaches July 3, 2025 No live activity 0% prepared Cockroaches and Mice July 31, 2025 No live activity “Prepared” Mice September 11, 2025 No live activity (Roaches); 2 Bait stations emptied 90-100% prepared Cockroaches and Mice October 23, 2025 Moderate 70-79% prepared Mice

The proposition was put to PS that after treatments were performed and no live activity was found by the pest control company then that must suggest that the treatments were effective. PS disputed this assertion testifying that the pest control company spends “two and a half” minutes spraying but that is not sufficient time to conclude that there are no live cockroaches in the rental unit.

During the hearing there was only one photograph submitted showing two roach traps with approximately 4 dead roaches and PS explained that the number of photographs should not be the measure by which the issue is determined, and the photograph simply proves that she did have a cockroach issue.

PS acknowledged during cross examination that in December 2025, after PS continued making complaints, the Landlord engaged a different pest control company who performed a “flush and spray” in PS’s rental unit on December 10, 2025.
The same company engaged on December 10, 2025, returned in April 2026. Landlord’s Evidence

Anthony Pukas (AP) testified that he is a property manager and has been in that capacity for approximately 3 years. The residential complex where PS resides is a multi-unit complex with 420 rental units.

AP explained that generally, when the Landlord receives a complaint about pest issues the Landlord’s pest control company is contacted and scheduled for inspections and treatments. AP’s evidence is that tenants are provided with paperwork containing instructions for preparing their rental unit for treatments.

AP also testified that the pest control company used by the Landlord has been engaged to provide pest control services since before AP became a property manager for the Landlord. AP gave evidence that the pest control company used by the Landlord has achieved “good results”, and AP has not had complaints from other rental units about cockroaches.

AP’s evidence is that the Landlord does not make determinations as to the type of treatment a rental unit receives (gel, dust, spray), and leaves the decision about the most suitable type of treatment to the pest control company.

AP further testified that during the involvement of Toronto by-law enforcement, the Landlord provided copies of the pest control invoices and queried the Landlord’s ongoing obligations to perform pest control treatments when the reports show “no live activity”. AP’s evidence is that the by-law enforcement officer’s advice was to, “leave it to pest control to make the decision”.

AP gave evidence that when PS would make a complaint the Landlord would send the pest control company monthly or sometimes twice per month, but after multiple attendances at the rental unit with reports noting, “no live activity”, AP questioned the necessity of continued treatments.

AP also provided context in relation to the clerical errors in some of the pest control reports noting that the pest control company often comes to treat multiple rental units, and some of the reports list “warranty” because the pest control company will return for a follow-up visit.

AP’s testimony also referenced the pest control reports that noted PS has not all ways prepared the rental unit for treatment as required. AP believes that PS’s lack of preparedness may have contributed to the Landlord’s ability to effectively treat and resolve the cockroach issue.

During cross examination AP’s answers were evasive and at times, confrontational. When AP was asked if he would agree that the mice and cockroach issue had not been resolved he answered, “If we’re still treating it then it’s not resolved. We can only treat if the unit is prepared properly.”.

When AP was asked about e-mail communications and PS’s perceived lack of responses, AP passed responsibility to “Brittany” for answering communications, asserted he was unaware of [name]’s responses or replies to PS, and failed to directly answer whether some of PS’s e-mails did not receive a reply.
When asked about a specific e-mail and letter, AP asserted that he was performing two roles at the time and responded to PS’s follow-up communication promptly.

AP denied that PS did not get pest control treatments in a “timely manner” testifying that in January 2025 when PS was calling regularly and insisting on treatment, the previous pest control treatments still needed time to take effect and the reports from the pest control company indicated, “no live activity”. Analysis

The Act sets out the Landlord’s maintenance obligations in section 20: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

PS’s application is brought pursuant to section 29(1), 1. of the Act which provides: 29 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 1. An order determining that the landlord has breached an obligation under subsection 20 (1) or section 161.

There was insufficient evidence at the hearing to prove on a balance of probabilities that the rental unit was not fit for habitation, nor that it failed to comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

PS did not submit evidence that the rental unit was deemed uninhabitable by any municipal or other regulatory authority. Further, the issue of pests did not cause PS to vacate the rental unit, nor was there evidence that the issue was so severe that it would render the rental unit uninhabitable.

I also do not find that PS has proven that the rental unit failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The parties did not dispute that PS called Toronto By- law enforcement however, PS did not submit copies of any by-laws that were contravened and there was no evidence that a by-law infraction notice was issued. There is insufficient evidence to find that the Landlord was not in compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

When considering whether the rental unit was in a good state of repair, PS asserts that the pest issues persist, and at times she was ignored by the Landlord when requesting pest control treatments. PS submits that the Landlord failed to respond to her and failed to follow through with treatments.

The Landlord’s representative submits that when PS requested pest control treatments, the Landlord scheduled treatments for PS’s unit. When PS requested that a different pest control company the Landlord acquiesced to the request.

The Landlord’s representative also noted PS’s inconsistent preparation of the rental unit and referenced the decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, asserting that the Landlord cannot be found to be in breach of the Act given the Landlord’s ongoing efforts to resolve any issues.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board also considered the issue of a persistent cockroach infestation in SOT-03000- 19 (Re), 2019 CanLII 126915 (ON LTB). The facts in SOT-03000-19 are strikingly similar to this matter in that the landlord attempted to address a cockroach issue in a tenant’s rental unit, there were varying degrees of preparedness, the landlord performed numerous pest control treatments over a period of three years, and many of the treatment report notes state, “no live activity”.

AP testified similarly to “D.M.”, the landlord’s witness in SOT-03000-19: “D.M. also noted that whenever a technician finds no evidence of live activity, it is not necessary to conduct a follow-up treatment. Nonetheless, the company will attend and conduct a treatment regardless of prior activity at the request of a tenant or the landlord.” SOT-03000-19 (Para. 11)

While prior orders of the Board are not binding, and the facts in SOT-03000-19 are distinguishable because the tenant in SOT-03000-19 was actively frustrating the landlord’s efforts to eradicate the issue, I find that the circumstances are similar, and the reasoning applied by the Member in that matter is persuasive to my determinations.

The Member in SOT-03000-19 also referenced Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 in their reasons, and goes on to articulate the principles of applying a contextual approach when considering the Landlord’s response to a maintenance defect. The Member also decides that issues persisting over a lengthy period of time require “a dynamic, as opposed to a fixed, interpretation.”.

In SOT-03000-19 the Member also references a section of the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 which affirms the contextual, dynamic approach stating: “If a landlord has done little maintenance for an extended period, and a serious condition results that takes some time to rectify, the landlord should be responsible for the tenants’ loss of use of their unit or the common facilities during the repairs. However, if the landlord has a reasonable program of maintenance, including preventative maintenance, and is acting responsibly to rectify a problem that requires extensive repairs, an abatement of rent should not be ordered.”

The Landlord’s pest control efforts were well documented and despite the persistence of the issue, the Landlord continues to perform pest control treatments which was evidenced by the parties’ communication in early 2026.

PS failed to submit photographs to accompany her requests for pest control that would substantiate the severity of the issue, and while I am satisfied that PS had both cockroaches and mice on occasions during the tenancy, PS’s assertion that there was an ongoing, unresolved, cockroach problem cannot be reconciled when considered against the pest control reports that consistently note, “no live activity”.

Further, when considering Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., the decision in SOT-03000-19, and Interpretation Guideline 5, the Landlord performed consistent pest control treatments since July 2024, despite reports stating there was no live activity discovered. While PS asserted that she was dissatisfied with the Landlord’s level of communication, the issue is the Landlord’s response to the maintenance problem not the sufficiency of communication to PS.

The Landlord acted promptly, reasonably, and diligently to address the pest issues. There is insufficient evidence to determine the severity of the issue and the minor delays asserted by the Tenant are not unreasonable when considered in the context of the Landlord’s ongoing efforts.
Accordingly, I do not find that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
