issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name]-Motlagh (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant filed two requests to amend her application. The first was filed on May 27, 2025; the second was filed with the Board on April 20, 2026. The second amended application was served on the Landlord’s Representative on April 20, 2026. The second amended version was largely the same as the first amended version. The second amended copy specified an amount of $25,824.00 for general compensation and clarified the request of $8,400.00 is for “disgorgement” of the Landlord’s unjust enrichment.

The Landlord did not offer any objections at the April 15, 2026, hearing but sought to clarify that this latest version superseded any prior applications or amendments. The Tenant’s Representative confirmed the April 20, 2026, amended version was the final iteration.

The Landlord was served with the amended application just about three weeks before the hearing and largely clarified the remedies sought as opposed to adding new remedies. I am not of the view that this would have prejudiced the Landlord because the same hearing preparation would have been necessary regardless of the quantum of the remedies. When I consider the reasons for the amendments, I am satisfied that the amendments are appropriate and made in good faith, did not prejudice any party, and are consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. Tenant’s T5 Application 5. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $25,395.50. 6. By way of background, the tenancy began in March 2017. The rental unit was a one- bedroom condominium unit with a den in a new building. The building also had amenities such as underground parking, free fitness classes, concierge, hot tub, etcetera. 7. The Tenant says the problems began in December 2018. The Landlord asked for an illegal rent increase and said if the Tenant refused to pay this, she would put the unit up for sale. This was followed up with multiple messages from various agents of the Landlord, or the Landlord herself, asking the Tenant to help the Landlord pay the mortgage on the property. At one point, the Landlord withheld keys necessary for storage. The Tenant called the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit and was finally given the keys after they became involved. The Tenant also states that in 2020, the Landlord accused her of not paying her rent on time although she had provided the Landlord with post-dated cheques. In the summer of 2022, the Landlord refused to conduct repairs at the rental unit. The Tenant called bylaw officers, and only once bylaw became involved did the Landlord do the necessary repairs. The Tenant adds that in May 2020 she was accused of having not paid the rent on time, although the Landlord had been provided with post-dated cheques for the period in question, but had failed to deposit the cheques. 8. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Further, section 57(5) of the Act creates a rebuttable presumption that a notice of termination given under s. 48(1) of the Act was given in bad faith if the property is advertised for sale or rent. A rebuttable presumption means that the landlord is assumed to have acted in bad faith unless the landlord can provide an explanation that satisfies the Board as to what changed after the tenancy terminated, that affected the landlord’s ability to move in or remain in the rental unit. 9. The Tenant testified that on she was given an N12 notice of termination for the Landlord’s child on October 14, 2023, with a termination date of December 14, 2023 (Doc-2913577, [name]). This was submitted into evidence, and the Landlord does not contest that she gave the N12 notice to the Tenant. 10. The parties also agree that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 1, 2023. 11. There is some contention about the circumstances surrounding the Tenant’s termination; however. After receiving the N12 notice, the Tenant found a new rental unit to move into and signed a lease on October 23, 2023, with the tenancy to begin on December 1, 2023. On November 13, 2023, the Tenant gave the Landlord an N9 notice terminating the tenancy effective December 1, 2023 (Doc-4534225, pgs 21-23). 12. However, the Landlord’s former legal representative had sent the Tenant correspondence via e-mail dated November 17, 2023 (Doc-5696165). In that correspondence, the former representative advised the Tenant that the Landlord was no longer pursuing the L2 application and will be withdrawing the application for the time being. 13. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant terminated her tenancy in accordance with the N12 notice. There was no evidence before me to suggest the Tenant had been looking for another rental unit until she was given the N12 notice. Her evidence was she signed the new lease on the 23rd of October. She was given the N12 on October 14, 2023 (Ex. 1 pg 18, 19). 14. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of an MLS listing for her rental unit (Doc- 4534225, pgs. 24-26). The details indicate the contract began on March 3, 2024, and that the rental unit was re-leased with a new tenancy commencing April 15, 2025. The rent was now $2,850.00, which was $750.00 more each month than it had been when she was living there. 15. The Landlord points to the November 17, 2023, letter to demonstrate that her needs had changed and she would no longer require the rental unit. The Landlord explains that she wanted the rental unit for her daughter to use. In August 2023, her daughter had a job offer to provide physiotherapy services to an individual in their home, and the rental unit was more conveniently located. However, the job was to start in November which then was pushed back to December, and she was still not given a contract. 16. While her daughter waited on the contract, the rental unit sat empty. After a few months, the Landlord could no longer wait for her daughter and decided to re-rent the rental unit because she still had to pay mortgage and taxes on the vacant unit. It is not clear to me whether her daughter eventually took the job, or not. Analysis 17. Section 202 of the Act states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 18. Although the case of [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (‘Elkins’) dealt with the analysis of a bad faith eviction following the termination of a tenancy pursuant to s.57 of the Act where the purchaser wished to occupy the rental unit, I find it useful to consider this case in applications where the good faith intention of a landlord to occupy the rental unit is called into question. The Court of Appeal provides guidance in par. 45: [45] It could be argued that s. 57(1)(b) implicitly limits Board scrutiny to the Vendor Landlord’s knowledge when it gives the s. 49 termination notice. However, such an interpretation runs afoul of s. 202(1) of the RTA. Under s. 202(1), the Board is 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the “real substance of all transactions and activities relating to…a rental unit and the good faith of the participants”. Limiting the assessment of a Vendor [name] bad faith to that single point in time when the s. 49 termination notice is given precludes the Board from both ascertaining the true substance of the transaction between the Vendor Landlord and the purchaser and conducting a fair assessment of their good faith. 19. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged. 20. In this matter, the Landlord bore the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that her daughter had a legitimate job offer. When I consider the evidence, I am not persuaded that the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith. It is not clear to me whether the Landlord’s daughter had a job offer or not. Her daughter was not called to testify and no corroboratory documentary evidence, such as copies of the correspondence between her daughter and potential employer, were submitted into evidence. 21. The Landlord’s oral testimony was that her daughter had a job offer. However, she also said that she had sent “them her resume.” At the very least, I find that the Landlord gave the N12 notice prematurely where her daughter had no firm offer of employment and had not signed any documentation. 22. Although not binding on me, I find the following case TET-69036-161, by Vice-Chair Ruth [name], to be instructive: “64. Landlords are professionals operating a business and are deemed to know something about the law governing their business. At a bare minimum a landlord ought to know that he or she is subject to laws and when conflict arises with a tenant there is a positive obligation to seek information and advice about those laws.” 23. What this suggests is that the Landlord had an obligation to ensure that not only was she familiar with the law, but she had an obligation to ensure that she was not giving her Tenant a premature N12 notice where there was a serious question as to whether the job 1 TET-69036-16 (Re), 2017 CanLII 49115 (ON LTB) offer would materialize. Given the Landlord’s evidence, it is not clear whether her daughter actually had a job offer, or whether she had simply sent in her resume and was waiting for a response from the employer. 24. Section 202 states that in making my determinations, I may disregard the outward form of transactions and have regard to the pattern of activities. I find that the outward form of the job offer lacks reliability. I find the pattern of activities suggests, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord wished to terminate the tenancy to rid herself of what she believed to be a problem Tenant as evidenced by the Tenant’s testimony about the history of issues between the parties going back to 2018. 25. I agree that the rental unit sat vacant for several months as evidenced by the date on the MLS listing. However, I am not satisfied the reason for this was because of the job offer. Even if this is the case, this still does not relieve the Landlord from the responsibility of giving the Tenant an N12 notice prematurely when her daughter did not have a firm job offer and contract. 26. When I consider the Court’s guidance in Elkins, and I look at the behaviour before, during, and after the N12 notice was given, I find it was given in bad faith. I also do not find the letter of November 17, 2023, advising the Tenant the Landlord was withdrawing the application to be evidence of the Landlord’s good faith or a material change of circumstances. I say this because the Tenant had already given her N9 notice, so the Landlord was aware that the Tenant had decided to move out. Further, I find the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, that the job offer was not firm, such that the N12 notice should not have been issued in the first place. Remedies 27. The Tenant seeks the following remedies: • Moving costs totalling $395.50; • Parking costs totalling $295.50; • Out of Pocket Expenses totalling $2,000.00; • General damages totalling $34,224.00; and, • An administrative fine. Moving Costs 28. The Tenant seeks $395.50 for moving costs. The Tenant provided a receipt from Takeoff Moving Company Inc. (Doc-4182643, pg 38). 29. In my view, the requested remedy is reasonable given my knowledge and experience of similar matters. 30. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $395.50 for moving expenses. Parking Costs/Out-of-Pocket Expenses 31. The Tenant seeks reimbursement for the cost of parking. She used to have underground parking included in her rent but now must pay for street parking. 32. The Tenant also seeks reimbursement of $1,011.36, for the cost of a dishwasher as an out-of-pocket expense. This is because she had a dishwasher at the old rental unit, but she did not have one at her new rental unit and purchased one. 33. I am of the view that these two claims are not properly claimed as out of pocket expenses. Rather, I find these would be more accurately claimed under general compensation. Section 57(3)(1.2) states that the Board may order the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant incurred or will incur. In my view, “other like expenses” would relate to the expenses incurred from moving as described earlier in the subsection such as moving and storage. However, the costs of parking and the loss of amenities have been considered in my assessment of general damages. General Damages 34. The Tenant is seeking $34,224.00 in general compensation. General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered by the illegal eviction. The Tenant’s evidence was that the eviction had a significant impact on her. She agreed, in cross- examination, that she signed a new lease very quickly after receiving the N12. This was because the price was affordable, and she was worried about being priced out of a very competitive market. 35. However, her new rental unit does not offer many of the amenities she had at her previous unit. The new rental unit is the main floor of a 100-year-old house. The Tenant no longer has underground parking and has to plan ahead to purchase city parking permits. She does not have a den, balcony, air conditioning, or in-suite laundry, and estimates the rental unit to be about 20 – 25% smaller than her old rental unit. 36. The Tenant used the exercise facilities regularly at the condominium building, including fitness classes, and the hot tub, but these services are no longer closer or convenient. Before she was able to walk to almost everything she needed, for example groceries, but cannot in the new unit. The Tenant recalled being able to walk to see a Blue Jays game or go to the theatre. Now she must drive. Her daily commute to work is now twenty minutes longer each way because of the traffic from her new residence. 37. The Tenant reports the most significant detriment to her well-being was losing her social circle which she had at the old rental unit during a very difficult time. Not only did she lose her housing during the Covid-19 pandemic, she was providing care to her mother during a terminal illness. 38. In cross-examination, the Tenant was asked about her utility bills, because she had brought up during her in-chief that she pays for electricity, but not for water. However, I did not find this to be an illustrative line of questioning because the Tenant did not make a claim for electricity expenses, and her testimony did not focus on this. Rather, it was a passing reference and not material to my findings, although the Tenant did indicate she pays slightly more for utilities now than she did before. 39. The Landlord submits the Tenant should not be reimbursed for the dishwasher, because it was the Tenant’s choice to select a rental unit without the same amenities. I agree the Tenant selected a rental unit with a great deal fewer amenities than she had, and I also find that the Tenant did so to limit her ongoing financial risks. In my view, the Tenant could have selected a rental unit with more included features such as she had before, and it is equally as likely the monthly rent would have been significantly higher. This is demonstrated by the increase the Landlord herself charged for the Tenant’s former unit. Had the Tenant done so, the Tenant would have been able to claim all of that as rent differential. However, since the Tenant did not, the claim is limited almost entirely to general compensation. 40. Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization],2 pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 41. When I consider the impact, this move had on the Tenant during a very stressful and emotional time in her life, the loss of the amenities, smaller rental unit, increase to commute time, and the loss of community, I am of the view the appropriate remedy is $25,000.00. This award is in keeping with other orders of this Board (See Adapa v Singh, 2026 ONLTB 7310). 42. The Tenant also argued that the Landlord should not be allowed to profit from the eviction and seeks the “income” which was over and above the old rent as part of the damages and seeks restitution. In support of this argument, the Tenant submitted an excerpt from [name] , par. 66. I am not of the view that the excerpt provided supports the Tenant’s position. The case of [name] is about the proposition of whether a tenant can be ordered back into possession in the situation where a new tenant is now occupying the rental unit. 43. The Landlord also submitted an excerpt from Atlantic Lottery Corp. Inc. v. Babstock4, at par. 23, which states (in-part): “restitution is the law’s remedial answer to circumstances in which a benefit moves from the plaintiff to the defendant, and the defendant is compelled to restore that benefit.” However, I find the head of damages claimed, that being restitution or “disgorgement” is not a head of damages found within the framework of the Act. I do agree that the Board has the jurisdiction to award “any other order that the Board considers appropriate.” 2 Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) 3 Minas v. Adler, 2022 ONSC 6706 ([name]. Ct.) 4 Atlantic Lottery Corp. Inc. v. Babstock, 2020 SCC 19 44. The case of [name] v. Becker5, pertained to a matrimonial matter, but the Supreme Court of Canada provides guidance on the application of restitution to matters at hand, stating: “It is not enough for the court simply to determine that one spouse has benefited at the hands of another and then to require restitution. It must, in addition, be evident that the retention of the benefit would be “unjust” in the circumstances of the case.” 45. I am not of the view that the retention of the benefit by the Landlord is unjust in this case. The quantum of the award is well over the $8,400.00 the Tenant claims is the earnings from the new rent after the Tenant vacated. In effect, the extra income has been accounted for in the general compensation. Further, the Act is remedial and intended to put the Tenant back in the position she would have been had the unlawful eviction not taken place, not put the Tenant in an advantageous or greater position then that been if not for the unlawful eviction. Administrative Fine 46. The Tenant also seeks an administrative fine to the maximum jurisdiction of the Board. 47. The Board’s Guideline 16 speaks to the situations in which a fine can be administered and refers to the member considering the nature and severity of the breach, the effect the breach had on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors. It goes on to state that “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.” [Emphasis added] 48. I am not persuaded that a Board administrative fine is necessary in these circumstances. I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour meets the test of “blatant disregard for the RTA”. Although I do find that the breach was serious and had a significant impact on the Tenant, I am of the view that the remedy awarded sufficiently addresses future deterrence and compliance with the Act. 49. The Tenant paid $48.00 to file the application is entitled to reimbursement of this fee. 50. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony, and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 51. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue. 5 Pettkus v. [name], 1980 CanLII 22 (SCC), [1980] 2 SCR 834
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $25,443.50. This amount represents: • $395.50 for out-of-pocket expenses for moving; • $25,000.00 for general compensation; and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing this application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The rental unit is a four-bedroom farmhouse. The monthly rent was $1,307.22. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2025.

There is no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. In the N12 notice, the Landlord stated that she required vacant possession of the rental unit for her own residential occupation. The Tenant vacated the rental unit in response to the N12 notice. Did the Landlord Occupy the Rental Unit After the Tenant Vacated?

At the hearing, the Tenant provided no direct evidence that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant stated that she believed the Landlord moved into the rental unit after the Tenant moved out.

The Landlord testified that, after the Tenant and the Tenant’s family vacated the rental unit, she moved into the rental unit on September 25, 2025. The Landlord testified that she has continued to reside in the rental unit since that date and was still living there as of the hearing date.

The Landlord testified that she relocated from a location approximately six hours away. She testified that she resigned from her previous employment before moving and relied on a resignation letter dated July 2, 2025, as evidence of her intention to relocate and occupy the rental unit.

The Landlord also testified that she incurred moving expenses and provided moving records, including a U-Haul receipt, to support her evidence that she moved into the rental unit. She further testified that she changed her driver’s licence, Canada Post address, utility accounts, car insurance, and house insurance to reflect her residence at the rental unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and continued to reside in the rental unit as of the hearing date.

As a result, the Tenant has not proven one of the required elements under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Specifically, the Tenant has not proven that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Accordingly, the application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing the Landlord requested to adjourn the hearing so that they could obtain additional evidence on the basis that the offending tenant that is being complained of had been evicted and they did not have time to submit evidence with respect to those eviction proceedings. The representative of the Landlord submits that they were retained at the beginning or March and had not read through everything, and it just became evident at the hearing after a private meeting with the Tenant’s representative, that they would require additional documentation.

The Tenant was opposed to an adjournment on the basis that they had filed their application on March 10, 2024, more than two years prior, because the Board already issued an interim order requiring disclosure by specific deadlines on November 1, 2024, and those deadlines have clearly passed.

I declined to adjourn the matter on the basis that the Landlords representative had not adequately prepared or submitted evidence prior to the hearing despite being retained more than a month prior to the hearing. I was not satisfied that they had taken reasonable steps after becoming retained to submit the documents they wanted to submit as it was evident by the plain reading of the Tenant’s application on what issues were to be litigated. The Landlords lack of preparedness is not a good reason to adjourn a matter that has been filed more than two years prior. T2 Application – the neighbouring dog in unit 105 off leash and substantial interference

The Tenant’s application has seven allegations of substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit over a period of eleven months between the dates of April 1, 2023 and February 15, 2024. The Tenant confirmed this at the hearing. The alleged dates are as follows: 1. April 1, 2023 2. June 19, 2023 3. June 21, 2023 4. September 1, 2023
December 27, 2023
February 4, 2024

February 15, 2024 April 1, 2023 5. On April 1, 2023 the tenants in unit 105 moved into the residential complex with their dog. On this date the tenants had their dog of leash at the property. The Tenant complained to the Landlord on this date regarding the dog being off leash. Unit 105 has access to the back yard from their unit. On this date the dog was off leash and lunged at the Tenant. 6. At the hearing the Tenant testified that they had a text conversation with the Landlord’s agent regarding the dog and submit that the agent told the Tenant that they would address the issue with the tenant in 105 and the Tenant also stated that they would use the stairs to avoid the dog. 7. However, the evidence provided at the hearing was not a text message at all. It was an email on this date and there is no mention of using the stairs and no response from the Landlord put into evidence by the Tenant of such a text conversation.

The Landlord’s agent testified that they spoke with the offending tenant on the same date and cautioned them to ensure that their dog would be on a leash when outside. They agree that the Tenant spoke with them on this date regarding the dog in unit 105 and unit 107.

The Landlord’s agent further submits that the Tenant did not tell them that they would use the stairs to avoid the Tenant’s dog in unit 105, but they did say that they would take the stairs because of issues they were having with the dog from unit 107. June 19, 2023

In the Tenant’s application they allege that on this date they emailed the Landlord’s property manager, [name], about the unleashed dog and that Ms. [name] stated she had seen it herself on security cameras loose out back and in the halls of the building.

However, at the hearing, the Tenant’s evidence they produced for this date was a message from another tenant in the residential complex complaining to the Tenant. He submits that the other tenant texted him this date to complain that she had been scratched by the dog. He admits that he did not interact with the Landlord or the dog on this date. Accordingly, this submission is dismissed as it relates to another tenant in the residential complex but not the Tenant. Further, I am not satisfied that the Landlord was made aware of this incident until weeks after it occurred as they testified. June 21, 2023

In the Tenant’s application they state that on this date they had a friendly talk with the dogs owner, [name] from unit 105 regarding his dog being loose/aggressive behaviour. At the hearing the Tenant testified that he spoke with [name] at the Tenant’s place of employment and that he mentioned he saw it off leash and was concerned about safety for dogs and himself and he was advised by [name] at this time that he would put the dog on a leash. Again, there is no evidence on this date that either the Landlord was notified or that there was any specific incident concerning the dog on this date. This allegation is also therefore dismissed. September 1, 2023

The Tenant submits that they texted the Landlord’s agent, Ms. [name] on this date asking why the Landlord had not contacted animal control about the dog. They responded that they had, but that nothing could be done with the dog because it is on private property. The Landlord’s agent also stated that they verbally had a conversation with the offending dog owner and that they were putting together a notice with their legal representative.

Again, this is not a specific conduct issue of the other tenant’s dog on this date, but a complaint made to the Landlord and their response. The Tenant only submitted a copy of the Landlords response and not the message they sent to the Landlord on this date. I accept that the Tenant communicated with the Landlord on this date regarding concerns with the dog in unit 105. This is the third communication I accept for a period of 5 months regarding the dog in unit 105.

I also accept that in September of 2023 the Landlord had their legal representative serve the offending tenants in unit 105 a voidable first N5 Notice. Although a copy was not submitted, I accept that it was given.

The Landlord’s agent testified that within the voiding period the offending tenant was incarcerated for unrelated issues and that his spouse was caring for the dog and using a leash on it when it was outside. This continued up until the offending tenant got out of jail in approximately December of 2023. They were advised not to file the N5 notice in this regard because the conduct had not continued during the voiding period.
I accept that the Landlord served notice and it was voided because there were no further allegations submissions from the Tenant regarding incidents about the dog between these dates.

Although the Tenant submits that the Landlord took no action to address the issue with the offending dog in unit 105 since reporting the issue on April 1, 2023, I am unable to find that they took no action. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that they had called animal control about the dog, but that they stated nothing could be done on private property.

Neither the Landlord nor the Tenant called any person from animal control to testify regarding whether the Landlord did or did not contact them after receiving complaints of the dog being off leash. Therefore, I find both parties evidence equally believable on this point. December 27, 2023

The Tenant submits that on this date they had to use the back ramp to take out their dog. When they opened the door, they were charged at by the tenant’s dog. They reported the issue to the Landlord’s agent. At the hearing the Tenant submits that the dog basically attached him again, however they led no evidence with respect to any prior attack. They submit that the Landlord’s response was that they could not do anything because animal control won’t help for issues on private property. They relied on an undated text message at the hearing under page 20 of their evidence book stating it was dated December 27, 2023.

The Landlord disputes this allegation as the text evidence submitted was with respect to unit 107 and not 105 as they had testified to. The Landlord submits that the Tenant was complaining of unit 107, which is not the dog that is subject to the Tenant’s application. Additionally, by this date the Landlord had been in contact with animal control, and she submits that she was told multiple times that they would not do anything because it related to private property.

I prefer the evidence of the Landlord on the basis that the documentary evidence provided by the Tenant indicates this is a separate incident with a different neighbour’s dog. I do not accept this was an allegation against unit 105 as it obviously isn’t. January 3, 2024

The Tenant submits that they had a conversation in the hallway with Ms. [name]name] this date regarding the interaction with the other tenant’s dog on December 27th and was told by them that the Tenant could call animal control but that it likely won’t help. This allegation is not contained in the Tenant’s application and therefore is not considered with respect to remedy. I accept that they spoke with the Landlord’s agent on this date about unit 105’s dog. February 4, 2024

The Tenant submits that on this date the weather was bad again which required that they use the back ramp to take out their dog. The Tenant’s application suggests that the Tenant and their dog were viciously attacked when entering the back ramp and that the attack was recorded on video. The application further states that the Tenant filed a police report and the Landlord was contacted via email.

At the hearing we viewed two video recordings. One recording of the Tenant exiting the back door with their dog and the other from a camera located outside the back door at the ramp. While I do see the dog come at the back door and you can see the Tenant pulling back their own dog and steadying themselves, there is no evidence of any vicious attack made by the other tenant’s dog. At the hearing, while viewing the footage, the Tenant stated that they had to yank their dog back and use their leg to shut the door to prevent being bitten or scratched. While I accept that the Tenant was fearful on this date being surprised by the other tenant’s dog on the ramp, I do not find any vicious attack happed on this date and find the Tenants application submissions misleading and exaggerated on this point. Additionally, the video evidence supports that the incident took place on February 3, 2024 at 11:35pm and they emailed the Landlord at 2:13am on February 4th.

Given that this is the only allegation that the Tenant and their dog were “viciously attacked” on this date, I do not draw any negative inference from the date difference here and accept the incident happened on February 3, 2024 with the dog from unit 105 and that access to the ramp was effectively blocked regarding this incident. February 15, 2024

The Tenant submits that on this date the tenant’s dog in unit 105 was loose and off their leash and they reported this to the Landlord’s agent on this date. They also contacted animal control and were told by them that the Landlord’s agent had made no inquiry with them about the dog. The Tenant submits that the Landlord’s ongoing statements regarding contacting animal control are a complete fallacy in this regard and that this supports a finding with respect to the substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment for not doing anything about the dog and then lying about stating they were.

The Landlord’s agent testified that she did in fact have conversations with animal control on several occasions after receiving complaints about the dog and were told by them that they could not do anything because they are on private property.

Again, neither of the parties had any person from animal control attend the hearing to confirm whether or not there were or weren’t any inquiries made by the Landlord between April 1, 2023 and February 5, 2024 despite their opportunity to do so.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

In the case before me, I find both the Tenant’s evidence and the Landlord’s evidence equally believable regarding their contact with animal control. On this basis I am unable to find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or obstructed or harassed the Tenant by falsely claiming to contact animal control about the dog.
I accept that the tenant in unit 105 moved out on or by June 1, 2024 and that there were no further incidents regarding the dog after this date.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to accommodate the Tenant based on their medical issues to ensure unimpeded access to the ramp at the back of the property. Firstly, because I am not satisfied that the Landlord was made aware of the Tenant’s condition prior to April 18, 2024 when the Tenant provided the Landlord with their medical note. The Tenant led no evidence with respect to the Landlords failure to accommodate them after receiving the medical note and no evidence of any occurrences regarding the other tenant’s dog after February 15, 2024 or their loss of use of the ramp.

Additionally, none of the evidence provided by the Tenant during the hearing was with respect to notifying the Landlord of any specific accommodation related need. For instance, they led no evidence with respect to what date they told the Landlord that they had any particular need for accommodation. No text, email or other information was provided in this respect.

The Tenant submits that on July 12, 2023 the Landlord requested a medical note from them to support giving the tenant notice for the dogs behaviour and the impact on the [name] use of the back ramp so they could use it at a hearing. The Tenant did not provide this letter until sometime on or about April 18, 2024 which is approximately nine months later. They stated that they got the letter to support with their filing of their T2 application for full disclosure. The Tenant submits that this was also in support of why they needed to use the back ramp for medical reasons.

The Tenant gave no further evidence of any other issues with the other tenant’s dog. They submit that by June 1, 2024 that they were able to freely use the back ramp because they found out the tenant in unit 105 had vacated and the dog was no longer there.

For the reasons above, while I would agree that the dog interfered with the Tenant, I do not find the interference substantial on the evidence before me. On this basis, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,171.74. Testimony of [name]
The Tenant testified that the tenancy began July 1, 2024. The lease agreement between the parties was entered into evidence. The monthly rent was $4,900.00.
Prior to the tenancy commencing, the Tenants paid the Landlords first and last month’s rent of $4,900 each on June 7, 2024. The proof of payment by way of etransfer was entered into evidence.

Furthermore, on June 30, 2024, the Tenants paid the Landlord $2,000.00 as a “cleaning and damage deposit” as well as $300.00 as a key deposit. The proof of payment by way of etransfer was entered into evidence.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 1, 2025. When they returned the keys to the Landlords, they were given the $300.00 key deposit.
The Tenants seek return of the “cleaning and damage deposit” as well as interest on the last month’s rent deposit. Analysis

Section 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.

Section 134 of the Act states: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; (b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord; or (c) rent any portion of the rental unit for a rent which, together with all other rents payable for all other portions of the rental unit, is a sum that is greater than the rent the landlord may lawfully charge for the rental unit

It is clear on its face that the Landlords collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act by requiring the Tenants to pay a $2,000.00 “cleaning and damage deposit”. As this is an illegal charge, the Landlords must return this amount to the Tenants. The cleaning and damage deposit does not fall within the exemptions found in section 17 of O.Reg 516/06.

Furthermore, based on the uncontested evidence at the hearing, I find the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by Act. Interest from June 7, 2024 to July 1, 2025 is owing by the Landlords to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $2,171.74. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the illegal charge collected; • $123.74 for interest on the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The parties agree that upon moving into the rental unit the Tenant paid the Landlord a $300.00 key deposit. The Tenant testified that on March 8, 2026, upon vacating the rental unit, she returned the main door key, mailbox key, and fob to the Landlord. To support her testimony, the Tenant entered text messages into evidence. The messages between the parties show the Landlord acknowledging receiving the “keys” from the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that when she met with the Tenant, she only received the main door key, and subsequently had to replace both the mailbox key and the fob. To support her testimony the Landlord entered into evidence a receipt for $116.21 for the replacement keys dated May 30, 2026. The Landlord admitted that she owes the Tenant $183.79 for the remaining balance of the key deposit. Analysis

The onus for proving the T1 Application lays with the Tenant on a balance of probabilities. Based on the evidence at the hearing, I am not satisfied that the Tenant returned all the keys to the Landlord. While the text messages indicated the Landlord received the “keys”, that in and of itself does not prove that all keys were returned.

I prefer the oral evidence of the Landlord, who testified that she had to pay $116.21 to replace the keys that were not returned. It would be illogical for the Landlord to incur the cost of replacement had they received all the keys. Based on this, I do not find that the Tenant met their burden to prove their application.
I find that the Landlord owes the Tenant the remainder of the balance of the unused key deposit amounting to $183.79 as well as the application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $239.71. This amount represents: • $183.79 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-021914-23 issued on March 5, 2025. On July 16, 2024, [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') requested that order LTB-T- 021914-23 issued on June 18, 2024 be reviewed and that the order be stayed until the Landlords’ request to review the order is resolved. On July 17, 2024, an interim order was issued staying the June 18, 2024, order. The Review Request hearing was held by video conference on February 11, 2025. The Landlords, the Landlords’ representative, [name], and Tenant [name] attended the hearing. [name] provided translation services to the Landlords.
reasons: Interim review order LTB-T-021914-23-RV-IN issued on February 19, 2025, granted the Landlord’s review request.
The hearing September 9, 2025, was adjourned on consent of the parties; the Landlord’s internet connection was not stable enough to proceed.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the monies as set out below.

On August 11, 2022, the Landlord served the Tenant with a N12 notice of termination based on the Landlord ‘s child moving into the rental unit. The termination date in the notice was October 31, 2022.
The tenancy began February 1, 2020; Tenant vacated on January 1, 2023.

The Tenant testified when viewing the rental unit, they told the Landlord they wanted to live there a long time and the Landlord agreed. They moved in February 2020 to the upstairs of the house; there were three other tenants in the basement. At the end of [name], the entire house received a notice of eviction. They received a N12 with a termination date of April 30, 2022; the Landlord gave a second ‘reminder’ notice on March 15, 2022, and a third on March 31, 2022. This shows that the Landlord was actively pursuing getting them out; this belief was confirmed when they overhead a conversation that they were not evicting the remaining basement tenant, the just wanted the Tenants out. On July 22, 2022, the Landlord told the Tenant, they did not want them living there, that they wanted to renovate the whole house. When the Tenant did not leave, the Landlord became hostile, fore example he cute the utilities. The Tenant started looking for a new place because the constant fighting with the Landlord was not worth it. Two-bedroom rentals for three adults are expensive, approximately $3,500 to $5,000 in most areas in the city. They ended up moving to [name] where they bought a home, because a mortgage was cheaper than renting in Toronto; it took about 8-months to find their new place. They would have stayed in their rental home if the Landlord had not continually given them N12 notices to vacate. Although the Tenant did not see the rental unit advertised or have direct knowledge that the Landlord did not move in, they were told this by neighbours whom they kept in contact with as demonstrated by the text in evidence.

The Landlord [name] testified the rental unit is the main floor of the house with 3 bedrooms and 1 bathroom; there is another rental unit in the basement. On April 20, 2022, they served the Tenant with a N12 notice; they were retiring and did not want the onus of having a rental property, so they gave the house to 2 of their children. The intention was always that their son move into the main floor unit. The tenants that were renting in the basement stayed, their son [name] [name] was to live on the main floor. Their son moved into the main floor rental unit after renovations were done, sometimes his girlfriend also stayed there. They did not re-rent to anyone else; their son still lives in the unit.

On cross examination the Landlord testified they gave the house to the children on February 7, 2023, about 1 ½ months after the Tenant vacated. After being given the house, the kids started renovating which took a few months or so. When asked if they were aware a Latin family was living in the main-floor unit, the Landlord replied he had no knowledge of this, but it is possible they were in the basement. With respect to their son living in the basement, the Landlord testified that he only lived in the basement for a short period of time, then went to the main floor. They do not know specifics because their son did not want them to visit because his girlfriend at the time did not want them to.

After the Landlord’s testimony, the Tenant requested to call a rebuttal witness because the Landlord’s dates were very vague, and their witness can give more details as to when the son moved in and who is living their now; the Tenant’s request was denied. A rebuttal witness is called to rebut unexpected testimony from the other side; that the Landlord is vague with dates does not meet this criterion. Further, this individual could have been called to testify on behalf of the Tenant at that stage in the hearing, but the Tenant did not do this; to allow their testimony going to the merits of the application after the Tenant’s case has rested is improper.

In closing submissions, the Tenant referred to evidence on the portal at lines #6165925 and #6681320; this evidence is not relied on. It was not referenced during the Tenant’s testimony, and new evidence is not permitted during closing statements. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

According to section 57(5), for the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises
The Tenants has proven all requirements in subsection 57(1).

There is no dispute about the Tenant being given N5 notices, as such, the first element of the above test has been met. As to the second element, I accept the Tenant’s testimony that had they not received the N12 notices they would have stayed in the rental unit, therefore, I find the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice(s). In respect of the third element, the Landlord’s testimony was very vague; they did not know specifics, including dates when their son moved in and who was living where. The Tenant’s testimony was detailed and established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s son did not live in the rental period for a minimum of as least one-year as is required by the Act. Although the Tenant admitted to not seeing the unit advertised for rent, and that their knowledge about the sons living arrangements, living in the basement not the main floor unit, is based on hearsay, the Landlord did not present sufficient testimony or evidence to rebut the allegation. In civil law, the balance of probabilities means that a court will decide a matter in favour of the party whose version of evets is more likely than not to be true, typically interpreted as at least a 51% likelihood of being correct. Tenant proved the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) and is entitled to remedy as set out below. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking: (1) the differential in rent for one year from January 1st, 2023, in the total amount of $20,477.76, ($1706 payable bi-weekly) together with (2) moving expenses in the amount of $1000.00. She also claims (3) $35,000 by way of damages for (a) the loss of businesses installing TV equipment (for which there was no market in [name]) and (b) the costs of the commute from [name] to Toronto where she and her partner were both employed. The new home is approximately 800 square feet larger than the rental unit, with 3 bedrooms and 1 bathroom; the rental unit was a 2- bedroom apartment with a backyard and 2 parking spaces. What they are asking for as ‘rent differential’ is actually for the cost of their mortgage.

I find the Tenant is not entitled to the difference in rent and their mortgage payments claimed in the amount of $20,477.76 pursuant to section 57(3)1 of the Act. I believe this type of relief does not encapsulate the relief that the Board can consider pursuant to section 57(3) of the Act. In my view, by using the qualifier “reasonable”, the Legislature signalled its intent that any and all losses suffered by a former tenant are not automatically compensable. In my opinion, the costs incurred by the Tenant in choosing to purchase a home upon vacating the rental unit does not meet the spirit or intent of the Legislation and will be denied.

I find the Tenant’s request for $1,000.00 compensation for moving expenses, including the renting of two moving trucks pursuant to section 57 (3)2, both of which I find to be reasonable; the Landlord did not provide any testimony as to why this amount should be considered unreasonable.

As to the Tenant’s claim for the loss of the business arising from the move to [name], I find this to be too remote as to be a foreseeable consequence of the bad faith eviction; the reality is that the eviction during COVID inevitably meant that the Tenant would face a longer and more difficult commute to attend work. Therefore, I award the Tenant $10,000.00 in general compensation in this regard pursuant to section 57(3) 1.2.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,048.00.
At hearing, the Tenant agreed to delay the due date for any monies owed to them by the Landlord to 6 months from the hearing date. Costs

The Tenant requested costs; this is the 5th hearing that they had to take ½ days off to attend. The Tenant is seeking 4 hours at $49.55 per hour for a total of $198.20 for the last hearing held on August 12, 2025; at 1:16, after sign-in, their matter was stood down and then adjourned at 3:15.

The Landlord's Legal Representative apologized for the last hearing, he was called to the other hearing room for what was supposed to be a simple consent, but it was not. Then he had technical difficulties and was not able to sign back into this hearing room.

The Landlord spoke to the Representative at 2:35 p.m. then again at 3:04 p.m.; during their first discussion, the Landlord's Legal Representative said he would only be few more minutes. The Landlord called again at 3:04 p.m. as the Representative was still not present; at this time the Landlord's Legal Representative advised that he was having technical difficulties. At 3:15 p.m., this member adjourned the hearing.

The Tenant’s request for costs to be ordered based on the Landlord's Legal Representative’s non-attendance at the last hearing is granted. Guideline 3 sets out that if the party whom the costs are being ordered against, does not attend the hearing “without notifying the person affected with the intention to do so, provided that the failure to attend the hearing delayed the process unnecessarily or caused unnecessary expense to the other party”. [Emphasis added]

Here, the matter had to be adjourned on August 12, 2025; this adjournment would not have been necessary had the Landlord's Legal Representative attended the hearing. In the least the Landlord's Legal Representative should have let the Landlord or the Board about the technical difficulties her was experiencing. I find costs in the amount of $198.20, based on lost wages, to be reasonable.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage that the Tenant has as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing, $11,048.00 by October 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from October 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $198.20 for costs as ordered in paragraph 3.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 5, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: unilaterally changed the terms of the tenancy by occupying the space for residential purposes, I find that on a balance of probabilities, the parties agreed to a residential tenancy. 3. I considered the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant was renting the space to start a small mechanic workshop but he provided no evidence for any period on or after the tenancy started in 2017 that supports the Tenant occupied the rental unit for the purposes of operating a business, nor was their evidence of any signage, advertising or other atypical indicators of business being operated from the unit. 4. There is no written tenancy agreement available to verify whether the parties agreed to a residential or commercial tenancy, but the Tenant provided a copy of a rental agreement Form (Doc-7988028) submitted to Ontario Works (OW) that contained the Landlord’s signature. The Landlord denies signing the two OW rental agreements forms in 2018 and 2020 but the signatures on these documents are consistent with signatures contained in other documents the Landlord provided in these proceedings. I find it more probable than not that the document was signed by the Landlord. I also accepted the Tenant’s testimony that the tenancy was residential which also seems consistent with the Landlord’s evidence that he hired the Tenant to do some work while also giving him possession of the rental unit after the Tenant encountered some issues having lived on another property owned by the Landlord prior to 2017.
reasons: The tenant shall give advance notice to the landlord of the tenant’s intent to raise the issue at the hearing.
The notice shall be given within the time set out in the Rules.

The notice shall be given in writing and shall comply with the Rules. 2020, c. 16, [name]. 4, s. 16. Orders (3) If a tenant raises an issue under subsection (1), the Board may make any order in respect of the issue that it could have made had the tenant made an application under this Act. 2020, c. 16, [name]. 4, s. 16. 24. On August 19, 2024, the Tenant submitted a list of issues he intended to raise about illegal rent charge. I considered the claim under Section 135 of the Act states, “A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (1).” 25. There’s no dispute the Tenant paid more than $400.00 per month starting September 1, 2024, to comply with the Board’s interim order LTB-L-030693-24-IN issued on August 13, 2024. As already referenced above in paragraph 14, hereof, the Board ordered the Tenant to pay $600.00 rather than $400.00 which based on my findings is considered an illegal rent charge that the Landlord has collected. Therefore, the amount the Tenant overpaid the Landlord to comply with the interim order is deemed to be collected and retained by the Landlord unlawfully. 26. The Landlord’s ledger (DOC-7992114) included a record of all the Tenant’s payments, and it supports a finding that the Tenant paid the Landlord $12,135.00 ($3,600.00+$5,535.00+$3000.00) for a period of 20 months starting September 1, 2024, to/and including April 1, 2026. A breakdown is as follows: • $600.00 for 6 months for the period from September 1, 2024, to February 1, 2025, for a total of $3,600.00. • $615.00 for 9 months for the period from March 1, 2025, to November 1, 2025, for a total of $5,535.00; and & LTB-T-022018-24 • $600.00 for 5 months for the period from December 1, 2025, to April 1, 2026, for a total of $3,000.00. 27. The maximum the Landlord can charge is $400.00 per month for 20 months, from September 1, 2023, to April 1, 2026, which totals $8,000.00 any amount in excess therefore is deemed unlawful. I find the Landlord collected and retained $4,135.00 unlawfully calculated as follows: $12,135.00 the Tenant paid less $8,000.00 the Landlord was legally able to retain. LTB-T-022018-24 28. As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed 29. The Tenant didn’t provide any details about threats or harassment behaviour by the Landlord. There was clearly a disagreement about the lawful rent charge between them and both parties exercised their rights and filed an application at the Board. The parties acted in accordance what they believed was lawful and the Landlord’s actions cannot be construed as harassment or a threat to end the tenancy. 30. The Tenant testified the Landlord unilaterally changed the terms of their oral tenancy agreement because the space in Unit #1 was reduced to half, whereby the Tenant occupies one side of Unit #1, and the Landlord occupies and utilizes the other half of the space for storage. The Tenant testified the partial wall divides the two spaces which initially was not there when the tenancy started back in 2017. 31. The Tenant’s application was filed on March 11, 2024, and the Tenant testified that the wall was constructed by the Landlord, with the Tenant’s help in 2019 sometime, which reduced his unit to half. 32. Section 29(2) of the Act, states that no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. 33. The issue that gave rise to the Tenant’s application occurred almost four years prior to the date the Tenant filed his application. The application is out of time, and the Board has no jurisdiction to issue any order. 34. There was no evidence led about other allegations in the application about unlawful entry and therefore the issue was not considered. 35. The T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The L1 application is dismissed.
On or before June 13, 2026, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,135.00 which represent the money the Landlord retained unlawfully. & LTB-T-022018-24

If the Landlord does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before June 13, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The T2 application is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $598.00 by June 27, 2026.

The Tenants testified that they rented 616-7 Kenaston Gardens in North York from February 22, 2024 to February 20, 2026. They provided a copy of the lease for the property that confirmed that the rent was $2,550.00 per month and that a $300.00 key deposit fee was charged by the Landlord, along with a last month’s rent deposit of $2,550.00. These amounts were paid by the Tenants to the Landlord prior to moving into the unit.
The Tenants are seeking the return of the $350.00 key deposit fee which has not been returned to them by the Landlord since the termination of their tenancy.

Further, they stated that due to constant water ingress in the apartment, the Landlord agreed to reduce the rent to $2,300.00 per month in the last year of their lease. The Tenants stated that this was done by the Landlord to entice them to remain in the rental unit for another year. The Tenants provided a copy of their email dated February 18, 2026 to the Landlord requesting the return of the key deposit and the $250.00 rent adjustment balance upon move-out. The Landlord responded to the Tenants on February 19, 2026 and stated that she felt that the Tenants had not provided proper notice of termination.

The Tenants further provided a copy of their bank statement confirming that their current monthly rent payment was $2,300.00. Due to the fact that the Tenants’ monthly rent was $2,300.00 per month and they had provided a last month’s rent deposit of $2,550.00, they are seeking the return of $250.00 from the Landlord. Law and Analysis

Section 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.”
Based on the Tenants’ uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord charged an illegal fee of $300.00 for the key deposit in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act.

Section 106(1) of the Act states “A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement and 2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.”

Further section 106(10) states “A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy termination.”

In the Landlord’s response to the Tenants on February 19, 2026, she did not correct or dispute the fact that the current rent was $2,300.00 per month. This corroborates the Tenants’ position that the current rent was $2,300.00 per month and their bank statement also confirmed that monthly amount.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord retained $250.00 more than the allowable rent deposit. The Act prohibits the Landlord from retaining this $250.00 and that amount shall be returned to the Tenants.
The Tenants are successful with their application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $598.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected; • $250.00 for the excess last month’s rent deposit illegally retained; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
