issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, I find that it is more likely than not that the Applicant is not a tenant within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Only tenants or former tenants are entitled under s.29 of the Act to file this type of application. The Application is dismissed accordingly. [name] and overview
This application is different from what I usually see in applications alleging an illegal lockout.
Some facts are not in dispute.

The application is brough t against the mortgagee in possession . The mortgagors and supposed landlords are not named in the application but assisted the Applicant in a number of ways, including providing affidavit evidence. The Applicant’s daughter, SH, was a consenting spouse to the mortgage although she claims that she did not fully appreciate or understand what she was consenting to. The Applicant is represented by the same law firm as the mortgagor landlord in the mortgagor landlord’s proceedings against the Respondent.

The mortgagors are AF, who is the Applicant’s [former] son -in-law, [name] (‘MN’) who is AF’s mother, and [organization] , a corporation controlled by MN and headquartered at the same address as AF’s [former] office.

There is no dispute that the Respondent was not the Applicant’s landlord when the tenancy allegedly commenced. The disputed lease s are between the Applicant and one of the mortgagors, [organization] No standard Ontario lease was used as is required by s. 12.1 of the Act. Instead, an Ontario Real Estate Association form of lease was entered into in January 2024 and then again in January 2025 . At the hearing the Applicant testified that MN was her landlord.
There was never an oral or a written lease between the Applicant and the Respondent.

The mortgagors defaulted on their mortgage and the Respondent enforced against them. The Respondent then became the Applicant’s landlord to the extent that the [name] was a genuine tenant. Section 47(1) of the Mortgages Act, 1990, states inter alia: 47 (1) A person who becomes the mortgagee in possession of a mortgaged residential complex which is the subject of a tenancy agreement between the mortgagor and a tenant or who obtains title to the residential complex by foreclosure or power of sale shall be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement. (2) A person who is the landlord under the tenancy agreement ceases to be the landlord while another person is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1). (3) A person who is deemed to be a landlord is subject to the tenancy agreement and to the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which apply to residential complex.

The Respondent caused Sheriffs to change the locks and evict all persons occupying the rental unit on or about March 2nd, 2026 after successfully bringing a motion to the Superior Court for an order granting leave to issue a Writ of Possession on December 30, 2025 and subsequently obtaining a writ of possession on January 6, 2026.

The people who were found at the rental unit were the Applicant’s daughter, SH, SH’s young son, and the Applicant’s son, [name]. A Range Rover with license plate CYEM 648 registered in the name of AF was found at the property. SH explains that it is her vehicle, and it is only registered in AF’s name. A second Range Rover with the license plate CWTF 831 was also found at the property. It is registered to MN. The Applicant’s explanation why MN’s vehicle was found at the rental unit is that MN was out of the country and asked the Applicant to ensure the vehicle is safe and to regularly move it.

The order pursuant to which the locks were changed was issued by the Superior Court of Justice on June 5, 2025 in a mortgage proceeding between the Respondent and the mortgagors. The mortgage is registered against the rental unit and against another property, 37 [name]. (’37 Aylin’). The parties filed motions and cross-motions in the Superior Court to address this issue.

The [name] was not at the property when the locks were changed and hasn’t attended at the rental unit since the lockout despite , according to the Applicant, spending most of her time in Canada and having her vital belongings at the rental unit. Her explanation is that she was temporarily out of the country when the locks were changed.

The Applicant’s daughter, SH, filed an application similar to this one before the Applicant filed hers. Her application LTB-T-026659-26 was heard on April 9, 2026. The written order is yet to be issued but parties agree that SH’s application was dismissed by an oral order of Vice [name] due to SH not being a tenant. The dismissal was without prejudice to the Applicant’s right to bring this application.

Under s. 29(1) of the Act, a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or the residential complex or caused the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of t he rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. [emphasis added]
The first issue in dispute is whether the Applicant was a “tenant” at the rental unit when the locks were changed March 2nd, 2026.

Section 2(1) of the Act defines a tenant as follows: “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;
Both parties provided extensive reasons and submissions on the issue.
The Applicant’s argument is found in document 7736671 in in Portal (‘TOP’). Additional oral submissions were made at the hearing.
The Respondent’s argument is found in document 7854780 in TOP. Counsel for the Respondent made additional oral submissions.

For the reasons below I find that on a balance of probabilities the Applicant was not a “tenant” within the meaning of the Act when the locks were changed March 2nd, 2026, because there was no genuine tenancy between the applicant and MN. Evidence
The Applicant relies on her affidavit (document ID 7865866 in TOP). The Applicant also provided testimony at the hearing.

She testified that she entered into a tenancy agreement with MN in January 2024 and moved into the rental unit with her son around February 2024. MN’s affidavit confirming this story is document 7866928. MN’s affidavit includes evidence that the Respondent was put on notice that there was a tenant at the premises as early as in August 2024 . At that time the Respondent was not made aware that the Applicant is not an arms -length party with the mortgagors.

The Applicant vacated the rental unit shortly after moving in. She vacated the unit in order to it to facilitate the sale of the rental unit . The sale fell through on or about April 16, 2024 . She did not provide much detail. It is unclear when she moved out or where she stored her belongings. She did not explain what her son did with his belongings. She testified that her boxes were in the basement, but they are not captured in the photos that were take on March 23, 202 4 (page 3 54 of document 7854734). She suggested that her boxes may be somewhere in a corner that is not visible in the photos.

There are no receipts or invoices for the Applicant’s move in and out of the rental unit in Spring 2024. She did not explain what her living arrangements were going to be if the property did sell. She did not address whether her landlord compensated her for th e major inconvenience of having to temporarily vacate the unit shortly after moving into it. It would appear that a month of rent was waived but this is not supported by any documentary evidence. There is no evidence of deposit or withdrawal corresponding to rent being paid , waived, or reimbursed.

According to the Applicant, she lived at the rental unit for a year under the initial lease before signing a new lease for 3-year term in January 2025. At that time, she decided to prepay rent for 2 years totalling $60,000.00. It was her idea. This allowed her to keep rent from increasing, secured her housing for years, and she was able to help out her family.

The prepayment was made in two instalments: $10,000 cash on January 30 th, 2025 and $50,000 transfer from abroad. She then clarified that the cash payment was only $9,800 because she needed to use $200 to buy a few things. She then paid $200 to her landlord the following day. There is no corroborating evidence to support the Applicant’s story about this subsequent $200 payment. No messages, no proof of payment, deposit or withdrawal. There is no proof of purchasing anything. Her recollection at the hearing was poor which is somewhat understandable given the passage of time.
She testified that she was in the Netherlands when the locks were changed, when her Superior Court motion was heard, and when this application was heard.

On cross-examination she testified that she goes back and forth between Canada and the Netherlands. She initially replied that she had been there for 3 months most recently. She then corrected herself and testified that it had been two weeks.
She acknowledged that her husband lives in the Netherlands. He doesn’t come to Canada often and she usually travels to him.

She did not deny that rent checks for 37 [name] , a rental property owned by AF, were made out to her. She explained that bank accounts of AF and/or SH were frozen as a result of civil proceedings against them, and she accepted their rent checks on their behalf. She then transferred funds to SH because 37 [name] became SH’s property after separation . There is no corroborating evidence confirming any transfers to SH.
The Applicant does not have a copy of the lease in her possession. She testified that MN has the physical copy. She did not have it available to her in electronic format at the hearing.

She testified that she was unaware of the mortgage until the mortgage was enforced . However, as made clear during the cross -examination, her own affidavit references knowledge of the mortgage in February 2024 and vacating the property so it could be sold and mortgage paid off : “ In February 2024, shortly after I took possession, [name] advised me that an offer had been received for the purchase of the Premises. I was advised that the sale was intended to pay out the mortgage held by Mr. [name]name] and discharge the mortgage from title.”. She then testified that she knew about the mortgage but didn’t know about mortgage enforcement.

She claimed that she thought it was normal to move into a property and then vacate it shortly thereafter to allow her landlord to sell the property. She admitted that the property was going to be sold with “vacant possession” meaning that she would be unable to return to the rental unit if the transaction closed. She was initially evasive when asked about the relatives she stayed with during her temporary absence. She then testified that she stayed with her husband’s brother.
She was inconsistent about the manner in which she was compensated for her absence. She said that she received a refund but also testified that she didn’t pay rent during her absence.

She confirmed that she didn’t provide any evidence of rent payments during her first year of the tenancy. She paid rent in cash. She claims that no one asked her for proof of payment. She confirmed that her tenancy was being challenged but claimed that she thought the challenge was limited to the period starting January 2025.
She testified that the source of funds to pay her rent was her savings. She confirmed that these savings were in an account.

She admitted writing an email to the Respondent in which she claimed that the Range Rover with license plate CYEN648 was rented by the mortgagor-landlord for her daughter, SH. She confirmed that this was untrue but explained that she made a mistake.

She admitted that another Range Rover was parked at the property inside of the garage and that it belonged to MN. MN left the vehicle with them while she was out of the country so they can move it to prevent the battery from dying. MN was away for 4 months.
She was asked about MN’s and MN’s husband’s whereabouts. She repeatedly referred to Canada as “here” when answering.
She did not know why the Respondent found a Mercedes registered to AF’s business (Team Immigration) at the rental unit.
She admitted that she never reached out to the Respondent to retrieve any of her belongings from the rental unit after the Sheriff enforced eviction.
The Applicant’s affidavit references and appends her previously filed “civil” affidavit sworn on March 6, 2026 in the Mortgagor’s civil proceedings.

It incorporates affidavits of Hamed Ardestani -Pourhajirm (7866939), [name] [name] (7736466), and [name] (7736517). 44. [name] is a colleague of SH at the “Agency” . His affidavit supports the Applicant’s claim that she lived at the rental unit and claims that AF was not living there. 45. [name] is a neighbour. He claims to have observed the Applicant at the property along with SH, her son, and [name] . The Applicant appeared unable to recall this neighbour’s name without referencing her materials and struggled to pronounce his name. When questioned about this, she claimed that she is not friends with this neighbour and had no conversations with them. 46. [name] -Pourhajirm is a friend of [name]. According to his affidavit, he helped [name] move into the rental unit, which he refers to as the Applicant’s residence, on or about February 2024. 47. None of the three affiants profess to have any knowledge of the disputed lease , rent payments or other tenancy arrangements. They do, however, strongly support a finding that the property has not been vacant and that the Applicant has resided at the rental unit, at least at some point(s) in time. 48. She additionally relies on document 7736524 as proof of continuous residency. The document contains a photo of a BMO letter addressed to the Applicant and SH at the rental unit, a letter from Toronto Musician’s Association addressed to SH only, and two letters addressed to [name]. I note that there is no mail addressed to the Applicant only. There is exactly one letter addressed to the Applicant and SH. It would appear that it pertains to some financial product they jointly have with BMO. 49. She testified that she had lots of mail coming to the residence and had many photographs of the family at the rental unit. No such documents were introduced into evidence. 50. AF testified that the Applicant live d at the rental unit. He is not privy to specific rental arrangements between MN and the Applicant. AF’s evidence was that he never lived at the rental unit. 51. SH relies on her affidavit 7736461 and provided additional testimony. She separated from AF and left their home with her son in October 2024. She moved into the rental unit where her mother and her brother already lived. 52. According to SH, the Applicant’s residency is in the Netherlands, and she is back and forth most of the time. The Applicant moved into the rental unit because she has no credit history or work history in Canada and couldn’t secure an alternative rental unit. 53. AF never lived in the rental unit according to SH. 54. SH testified that her mother, the Applicant, has the lease in her possession . It is with the Applicant in the Netherlands. This is inconsistent with the Applicant’s own testimony that the lease is in MN’s possession, and she does not travel with the lease. When SH was being locked out on March 2, 2026, she tried reaching the Applicant to get a copy of the lease but was initially unable to do so because of the time difference. 55. SH is a realtor but is not very active. She was seriously impacted by the lockout and the loss of her home. 56. SH confirmed that her and AF were parties to litigation brought by creditors in relation to various real properties. Financial difficulties started in 2023. She signed paperwork for mortgage renewal as a consenting spouse of AF. This was prior to their separation, and she claims that she didn’t realize it pertained to the rental unit. 57. She was questioned about her separation agreement with AF (starting on page 210 of 7854734). It is full of placeholders such as “’Cottage’ means the property described as [legal description]” and “[husband/wife]” or “ child[ren]” or “$TBD” throughout. It doesn’t have properly numbered subparagraphs. Parties did not exchange financial disclosure and did not receive independent legal advice. The agreement identifies 6 Maryvale Crescent, a site intended for development without a house, as a “matrimonial home” in clause 24. It also identifies 37 [name] as the matrimonial home in clause 25. She agreed that neither of these properties were the matrimonial home at the time the agreement was signed . 37 [name] was the matrimonial home prior to the parties’ separation and became a rental after they vacated it. She couldn’t recall details of the tenancy at 37 [name]. This is perplexing considering SH’s and the Applicant’s claim that this property became hers pursuant the separation agreement between SH and AF. 58. The separation agreement is dated January 13, 2025 but lists January 15, 2025 as the date of separation. SH explained that it was a mistake. The separation occurred in October 2024. 59. She asked AF to sign a separation agreement and he consented. She separated because she wanted to take herself and her son out of the situation that was becoming too stressful. It was unfair to them and AF had to agree to anything she wanted as part of the separation agreement. 60. Support obligations and even custody details were left as “TBD”. As of the date of the hearing they were still TBD. 61. She claimed that immediate priority was to finalize urgent matters including housing stability. 62. The rental unit is not mentioned in the separation agreement at all even though it was the place that she and her son lived at. She was unable to explain this inconsistency other than to state that AF had nothing to do with the rental unit, which is factually incorrect because he is one of the mortgagors in relation to this property. 63. She denied having any involvement with her mother’s lease renewal and the $60,000 rent prepayment. 64. SH testified that she never contacted her landlord, MN, for repairs. She explained that she had men at home and didn’t need to ask the landlord. It is unclear what “men” were at home as the only other man identified in the Applicant’s evidence as a resident of the rental unit was [name]. 65. The Respondent did not call any witnesses to testify at the hearing. He relies on affidavit s 7854734, 7854746, and 7854765 and argues that the Applicant’s story is clearly untrue and abuse of process as a collateral attack on the Respondent’s legitimate mortgage proceedings inter alia. [name] and analysis 66. Section 1 of the Act sets out its purposes as follows: “The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.” [emphasis added] 67. The Act is not designed to resolve disputes between mortgagors and mortgagees even if the mortgagor or their family occupy the mortgaged property and someone loses their home as a result of mortgage proceedings. For the Act to apply, there needs to be a genuine residential landlord-tenant relationship. 68. S. 2(1) provides some definitions, including: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, acc ommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex; 69. Under s. 18, covenants run with the land: “ Covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made.” 70. Under s. 24: “A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.” 71. Under s. 202(1), the Board is to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit: “In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.” 72. Based on the totality of the evidence, and in accordance with s. 202(1), I find that it is more likely than not that the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit does not include a genuine tenancy between the Applicant and MN. 73. There are multiple major issues with the Applicant’s version of the events. 74. Overall, I did not find the Applicant to be a credible and reliable witness. Her story was full of self -contradictions and inconsistencies. Her explanations lacked the ring of truth and defied belief at times. 75. In my view, the Applicant’s story defies logic and belief on its face. It involves untraceable cash payments, poorly drafted legal documents, conveniently timed absences from the country by multiple parties , documents not reflecting the true nature of transactions (e.g. vehicle ownership), and contracts between family members, to name a few. Any one of these irregularities could be explained away but the totality of these issues strongly suggest that the Applicant’s account of her tenancy is not credible. 76. The credibility of the Applicant’s witnesses and the reliability of their testimony was very seriously shaken and undermined by cross -examination. The witnesses were inconsistent, argumentative, forgetful and evasive. 77. The application and everything that surrounded it is inconsistent with my experience hearing similar applications involving mortgagors and mortgagees. The applicants usually name their actual mortgagor-landlord as a respondent even if legally the mortgagee in possession is the correct respond ent. It is unusual for them not to do so. They typically do not know whether the mortgagor or the mortgagee is to blame – they just know that they were locked out and want their home back. It is unusual, although not unprecedented, for the mortgagor- landlord to present a united front with the applicant-tenant. 78. It is similarly unusual for a genuine tenant, even a non-arms-length genuine tenant, to vacate the rental unit shortly after moving into it in order to facilitate their landlord’s sale of the home. 79. The Applicant’s evidence is that she paid rent by cash every month during the first year of her purported tenancy. The source of payment included her savings that were in a bank account. There is no corroborating evidence such as account statements to show that she withdrew $2,500 a month to pay her rent. 80. She then prepaid rent for two years with a $50,000 transfer to the mortgagor’s bank account and with cash payments of $9,800 and $200 for the total of $10,000 cash. 81. This story lacks the ring of truth. 82. The evidence corroborating this story is the Mortgagor’s bank statement showing a branch- to-branch transfer of $9,800 and a transfer of $50,000. There is no corroborating evidence whatsoever to connect the $50,000 to the Applicant aside from her self -serving testimony and self-serving affidavit evidence . She did not explain the source of funds and accepted the Respondent’s explanation that the funds came from her husband when it was suggested to her on cross-examination. Evidence of the funds’ origin would have been persuasive and would have been easy to obtain. 83. There is similarly no corroborating documentary evidence that she ever made any cash payments to the mortgagor. 84. There is simply no evidence to corroborate any cash payments during the first 12 months of the alleged lease. Not even proof of deposits into the mortgagor’s account. The Applicant’s incredible explanation for this lack of evidence is that she didn’t expect this to come up. 85. The only corroborating evidence of a cash payment of $9,800 at lease renewal does not show a corresponding withdrawal from the Applicant’s account. To the contrary, the Applicant’s landlord’s bank statement shows a withdrawal of the same amount of $9,800 a day before this bank-to-bank transfer was made. At best, it is unclear who made this payment to the mortgagor. At worst, it would appear that the $9,800 payment represented the mortgagor withdrawing and then depositing their own funds within 24 hours . MN who controls this bank account did not attend the hearing and was therefore not available for cross-examination. 86. I draw a negative inference from the lack of corroborating evidence to support these purported cash payments. The Applicant filed extensive evidence. She was represented by very capable counsel and supported by the mortgagor throughout the hearing. It is not believable that it would not occur to her to provide evidence of these supposed cash payments if such evidence ever existed. It is simply not believable that there is no evidence of any withdrawals from any accounts belonging to her or perhaps to her husband. 87. The Applicant similarly failed to file other corroborating evidence that would be easy to obtain and that would obviously be persuasive. There are no IDs showing the rental unit as the Applicant’s address. There are no tax returns showing the mortgagor declaring the rental income to the Canada Revenue Agency. There are no messages between the parties that would deal with maintenance or rent or any other landlord-tenant related matters. There are no photographs of the Applicant inside of the rental unit. I similarly draw a negative inference from the lack of persuasive corroborating documentary evidence proving that she treated the rental unit as her home. 88. It is unusual for a person whose residence is disputed before the LTB to be able to provide merely a single envelope addressed to her and another person as the only proof of residence. There are no IDs, no tax papers, no photos, no bills, no proof of orders or deliveries, and not a single letter addressed to the Applicant alone. Such evidence could be easily obtained online , if it existed , or requested from third parties (e.g. banks and utility providers) if necessary. This lack of evidence is entirely inconsistent with my experience hearing similar applications, even from unrepresented parties who file almost no evidence otherwise. This is the first time I see so little evidence of residence from a well -represented party who filed extensive evidence. 89. There is a significant amount of evidence that the Applicant lived at the property, including affidavits from witnesses who don’t have any obvious reason to lie. It is possible that she did in fact live there at times. This alone does not establish tenancy , especially for a family member of the owner/mortgagor. When the evidence is viewed in its totality, I find to be less likely than not is that the Applicant occupied the rental unit as a genuine rent-paying tenant within the meaning of the Act even if she lived with her son and/or her daughter at times. 90. She claimed that she was in the Netherlands on March 2, came back on March 6th and then left again on an unspecified date. Her evidence is that she spent most of her time in Canada but happened to be absent on the date of the lockout and the date of both hearings. Being absent from Canada does not mean that she is not a tenant, but the timing of the Applicant’s absences, the lack of proof of travels, her inconsistent testimony, evasiveness and forgetfulness in relation to these travels, and other factors make it difficult to believe that the travels occurred as described by the Applicant. 91. I note that there is an affidavit that was purportedly signed by her in person in Toronto on March 6, 2026. She was once again inconsistent about her presence in Canada during this period of time as she appeared to agree with the Respondent legal representative that she wasn’t in Canada between March 2 and March 10 before once again claiming that she came back on the 6th to swear her affidavit. 92. She could not recall how many times she travelled back and forth. She testified that it was 2 to 3 times. She was unable provide proof of travel dates despite the Respondent previously putting her on notice that they would question her about it and demanding proof of travels. Her recollection about her travel prior to March 2, 2026 was similarly inconsistent. She initially testified that she had been in the Netherlands for 1 month but then corrected it to one week. She claimed that she spent 3 weeks out of most recent three months in the Netherlands. She spent the total of 2 out of the last 12 months in the Netherlands. Her best estimate was that she spent maybe 3 months out of the last 3 years in the Netherlands. She claims that she lives in Canada most of the time. She takes care of her grandson. 93. AF was an unhelpful witness. He professes no personal knowledge of the disputed lease. He was evasive and argumentative on cross-examination. 94. The Applicant’s story is that there is no longer a single family unit between SH and AF. AF and SH separated over a year ago. The Applicant and SH describe their relationship with AF and MN as “not enemies”. The degree of cooperation and grace between SH’s and AF’s sides of the family is not sufficiently explained by them being former in -laws and “not enemies”. 95. The purported tenancy was entered into between the Applicant and a corporation controlled by her in-laws. It is undisputed that the tenancy agreement was “renewed” within a month of a summary judgement hearing between the mortgagor and the mortgagee. 96. The purported tenancy was renewed shortly after the Applicant’s daughter and the mortgagor-landlord’s son, AF, separated. The separation occurred because SH was too stressed as a result of AF’s conduct. She needed to keep herself and her son away from him, his drama and his family. 97. She was frustrated with AF and claims that both parties recognized that he was to blame. The separation agreement they purportedly entered into was based on her telling AF that he better give her whatever she wants. To the extent that the agreement is a comprehensible legal document, it appears consistent with this claim as it primarily benefits SH. 98. She then moved into a property controlled by AF ’s mother. She failed to mention her new home in the separation agreement. 99. SH’s mother then voluntarily provided a large lump -sum prepayment for 2 years to her daughter’s former mother-in-law. Part of her stated motivation was to help MN out. It seems highly unlikely that a spouse who is fed up with their husband’s drama and takes her child away from him would then move into a property controlled by his side of the family and watch her mother voluntarily prepay $60,000 to her [former] in-laws. 100. In my experience, this is unusual conduct between former in-laws after a separation and a family dispute. It is similarly unusual for AF to attend his former mother-in-law’s tenancy hearing and appear this invested in the safety of her tenancy. 101. The sequence of events surrounding enforcement by the Sheriff is calls into question the Applicant’s claim that she was residing in the rental unit as a Tenant. The A pplicant happened to not be at the rental unit when the locks were changed. According to her, she was only out of the country for a couple of months out of the last year and a few weeks in the last three months, but these absences happened to coincide with the hearing of this application, the hearing at the superior court, and the lockout. 102. The Applicant’s husband resides in the Netherlands. The Applicant did not explain why she does not live with him. Her evidence is that he has only travelled to Canada once and she has only spent a few months out of the last three years in the Netherlands. While spouses sometimes live apart, this is not the norm, and no explanation was provided for the Applicant’s decision to reside separate and apart from her husband. 103. The Applicant’s testimony about her location and travels was very difficult to believe. Aside from incredibly convenient timing of her travels and complete lack of corroborating evidence about it, I note that she repeatedly referred to Canada as “here” on cross - examination. This is strange for someone who claims to be in the Netherlands. 104. She testified that her belongings were in the rental unit in 2024, but they are nowhere to be found in the photos. I have reviewed the photos, and it is very difficult to imagine where someone’s personal belongings could possibly be located if they constituted more than a single storage box. There is no reason to believe that the appraiser attempted to conceal the Applicant’s belongings from their appraisal report. 105. It is still unclear what belongings she has at the rental unit in 2026. Her application addresses the belongings as follows: “To be Determined. Personal items including jewellery designer items clothing identification documents medication and a child s belongings. Full itemization to be determined upon regaining access to the unit” [sic] 106. The Applicant and her family have been given access to the unit. SH attended at the rental unit and took one of the Range Rovers. The Applicant has nevertheless failed to itemize any of her belongings that were allegedly impacted. She didn’t testify about any of her personal items. 107. As of the date of the hearing she has made no attempt to collect anything despite the interim order of the Board requiring the Landlord to provide her access to her belongings. The Applicant did not testify about any medicatio n she needed to retrieve or re-purchase. Even when her representative asked her about the belongings, she was only able to provide hearsay evidence about what her daughter reported to her. 108. The Applicant claims that she lost her home when the Sheriff changed the lock s on or about March 2 nd, 2026 . She claims that she has been back to [name] at least temporarily since the lockout. It is hard to understand why a person who lost her home would be completely uninterested in any of her belongings located at the rental unit. Her testimony is inconsistent with what the Board usually hears in cases involving genuine lockouts. She did not testify about the items that are still at the rental unit. There is no itemized list. There are no photos of items she lost. There is no update to the estimated cost. She didn’t testify about the impact the loss of her home had on her. Her testimony is not even consistent with what I usually here from a person who is locked out of a home where they occasionally reside. 109. Her application claims moving expenses of $8,000 and $1,500 per month for storage. However, there is no basis for such a claim as nothing has been moved out of the rental unit or into a storage facility as of the date of the hearing. 110. The application also claims $8,000 for the cost of temporary accommodations including hotels and for the cost of personal items directly caused by the eviction and displacement. However, no evidence of any such expenses was provided. 111. The legal burden of proof is on the Respondent to establish that the Act does not apply but it is difficult for the Respondent to prove a negative, i.e. that there was not a genuine tenancy. I am not inclined to give as much weight to the Respondent’s evidence because the Respondent failed to attend the hearing and make himself available for cross - examination. Ultimately, however, I find that the Applicant’s version of the events is untrue on a balance of probabilities even if I, arguendo, give no weight at all to the Respondent’s affidavit evidence that wasn’t confirmed by Applicant’s witnesses. 112. The application is dismissed because it is more likely than not that the Applicant is not a tenant within the meaning of the Act. 113. The Respondent argues that this application should be dismissed as abuse of process. They argue that the disputed lease is a sham and that the matter of this alleged tenancy is subject of motions and other proceedings in the Superior Court. It is not necessary for me to make a finding that this application constitutes an abuse of process, as I find that the application fails for other reasons.
ordered: The Act does not apply.
The application is dismissed.
Interim order LTB-T-022090-26-IN issued by the LTB on April 10, 2026 is cancelled. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,748.00 by June 29, 2026.

The Tenant testified that she agreed to rent [address] in Etobicoke from the Landlord commencing February 15, 2026. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,700.00 to the Landlord on February 2, 2026 and provided a copy of that email money transfer. She signed a standard, residential lease with the Landlord on February 12, 2026.

She stated that at the last walk through of the apartment on February 13, 2026 with the listing agent, she noted cockroaches in the unit and advised him that she would not be moving in. The agent advised the Tenant that he would eliminate the cockroaches and let her know when they were gone.

The Tenant stated that she was shown the unit 3 more times by the listing agent, who had apparently hired a pest control company to deal with the issue. She stated that on the last date, March 10, 2026, she continued to see the roaches. The Tenant requested that her deposit of $2,700.00 be returned as she would not be moving into the rental unit.
The Tenant stated that she was not provided with a key to the rental unit and that each time she viewed the apartment, the listing agent or Landlord unlocked the apartment. Law and Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states “A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”
The Tenant was not provided with keys for the rental unit and thus she was not given vacant possession of the rental unit. Thus, the Tenant is entitled to the return of her last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant’s application is successful.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,748.00. This amount represents: • $2,700.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 29, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 30, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 18, 2026 ____________________________
