issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in their T2 Application for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant also applied in their T6 Application for an order determining that the Landlord • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant partially proved the allegations contained in each of the T2 and T6 applications on a balance of probabilities. Where the allegations were not proved those claims are dismissed. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,982.82. T2 Application Determinations: Illegal entry, March 3, 2024

It is not disputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of entry to enter the rental unit on March 3, 2024 for “appraisal”, either mortgage or insurance. The Landlord [name] emailed notice of entry to the Tenant [name]. While the form of notice was not proper, the parties agree the Tenant permitted entry.

On March 3, 2024 there was no potential mortgagee or insurer at the rental unit. Instead, the Landlord [name] and two renovations contractors entered. The reason given was “re-purposement of the property”. I accept the Tenant’s testimony in this regard on a balance of probabilities. I note none of the people who attended that day were at the hearing to give evidence or be cross-examined. However, the Tenant’s video system picked up their discussions about drawings and permits.

While the two contractors were inspecting and discussing and waiting for her upstairs, the Landlord [name] went to the basement, picked up and looked at the Tenant’s documents in closed file folders on the Tenant’s desk and also looked behind the bar. The Tenant produced a video at the hearing taken with his security system, showing Ms. [name] picking up folders, looking through them and appearing to take photos with her cellular phone. Although there is no actual evidence of photos, the video of the Landlord doing what appeared to be taking photos is sufficient in my view to establish that she did so on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord [name] testified that before March 3, 2024 his wife had heard from a neighbour that the Tenant may be operating his business from the rental unit. Mr. [name]name] testified that his wife took the neighbour’s word because they had received some rental payments from the Tenant’s company. I note that neither [name] nor the neighbour testified, and no sufficient reason was given for their absence to require the hearsay evidence. Moreover, neither were available for cross examination. The evidence, therefore, is less reliable, and I give it less weight. However, I accept that the Landlord and his wife were concerned about their insurance, and as Mr. [name]name] testified, his wife “panicked and tried to get evidence that she could confront him with.”. They were upset, and it is clear the Landlord felt justified in looking for information to support this allegation. Their strong concern, however, is not justification for the breach of privacy.

Sections 25, 26 and 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) serve to protect Tenant’s rights and their privacy. There was no evidence that the photos taken were not disseminated. In that context it is reasonable to conclude the Tenants felt violation and a fear that personal information was exposed,. There was a complete disregard by the Landlord to the privacy intent behind those section of the Act.

Entry can be accomplished with notice to the Tenant for a limited and specific reasons under section 27 of the Act. None of those enumerated reasons allow entering for ‘re- purposement’, nor does section 27 permit changing the reason for entry once the entry is underway. Based on the Landlord’s testimony, Ms. [name] was clearly motivated to attend and seek out evidence of the Tenant’s business operations. On a balance of probabilities, she entered the rental unit for that purpose. The evidence strongly suggests there was no real intention to ‘appraise’ the property, and the people were neither mortgage brokers nor insurance providers. Even if the people at the rental unit that day were legitimate mortgage or insurance appraisers, engaging in an improper purpose after entry makes any lawful entry unlawful. The actions of Ms. [name]name] were without doubt outside of any lawfully permitted reasons in section 27 of the Act.
I am satisfied based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on March 3, 2026. Illegal Entry, Other Dates

The Tenant also claimed three other unlawful entries. The Tenant testified that on March 8, 2024 the Landlord entered for the purpose of a further ‘appraisal’. Notice of entry was given by email in the manner agreed between the parties. A man came to the property, gave his business card and observed the exterior property and garage. The Tenant remained on the property the entire time. I find the Tenant failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that this entry was unlawful, because even if the notice was by email, it was in the way the parties agreed and there is sufficient evidence at the hearing that the Tenant permitted this entry.

On March 20, 2024, pursuant to another email notice of entry in the method arranged between the parties, the Landlord and contractors attended. They had a list of work to complete. Entry was permitted by the Tenant, inspections ensued and they measured things. The Tenant did not consent to work beginning immediately, and they left. I find the Tenant permitted this entry and the purpose for which it was made was lawful.

On March 30, 2024 the Landlord re-attended to repair the front porch railing. Notice had been given on March 29, 2024. The Tenant Mr. [name]name] testified that notice had been given after sabbath hours and that he had not checked his email, however, provided no evidence of that email was produced at the hearing. He could not recall when it was received. I am not satisfied the Tenant proved the notice was not provided within 24 hours, on a balance of probabilities.

Pursuant to section 27 of the Act, a Landlord must enter by giving 24 hours’ notice of entry unless consent is given to enter sooner. Section 27 of the Act only requires notice of entry in writing to enter the rental unit. No similar notice is needed to attend the residential complex.

I accept that in addition to email notice for March 30, 2024 per the agreement between the parties, the Landlord also received permission verbally on March 29, 2024 from [name] that he could return on March 30, 2024 to finish the front porch work. [name] did not testify to the contrary. The Landlord attended pursuant to both the notice of entry and verbal permission. He then continued to secure the front railing. I note the Landlord had no reason to enter the rental unit on March 30, 2024 and did not do so.
I find therefore, that the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on March 30, 2024.

On April 8, 2024 the Landlord attended to repair the bathroom ceiling and laundry room based on a valid notice of entry. The Tenant also permitted entry. On that date, the Landlord verbally requested to access areas outside the scope of the notice, so he could complete the garage door repair as the Tenant had requested. He was refused access to the inside of the garage that day, so he remained outside, and repaired the door from the outside. As noted above, since the Landlord did not enter the rental unit to complete this repair, he was not in breach of section 27 of the Act.

Accordingly, regarding all three notices of entry, not including March 3, 2024, I find that the Landlord or Landlord’s agent did not enter the rental unit illegally. Substantial interference & Harassment

The Tenant claimed the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit by unlawfully entering and going through their papers on March 3, 2024. The Tenant further claimed that they were harassed because of that unlawful entry and the breach of privacy.

Sections 22 and 23 of the Act which read as follows: [22] A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. [23] A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The word “harass” is not defined in the Act but harassment is generally considered to be an egregious unwanted or unwelcome conduct that a landlord knows or ought to know would be unwelcome or would alarm. [name] does not have to be intentional. It could be an isolated incident if that incident is so serious that it can be labelled as harassment.

I find that the evidence discussed above regarding the March 3, 2024 unlawful entry is sufficient to make out substantial interference. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that photos were taken. Objectively, any person in the Tenant’s position, given the tense relationship between the parties, would find their enjoyment of their home interfered with knowing their private documents were photographed. The video demonstrates the Landlord using her phone in a manner that clearly indicates a photo is being taken. Although the Landlord testified no photos currently exist, that does not lessen the interference impact. Privacy was breached, and personal documents were riffled through. It is not relevant that the photos may have been deleted. Having someone who is in a trust position, with a key to your home, who enters under pretense and goes through private documents certainly undermines a tenant’s sense of security and feeling of safety in their home. Had the documents been tax or medical related, or third party private business documents, the breach is all the more egregious. I am satisfied that the degree of interference is sufficient to make it substantial.

For the reasons above, I find this March 3, 2026 incident rises to the level of harassment, despite that it was not repeated. The Landlord knew or ought to have known that intentionally viewing and photographing personal documentation would be unwelcome. However, I have considered the hearsay testimony that the Landlord was remorseful afterwards.

Although the Tenant claims the numerous entries combined to constitute harassment, I heard evidence of only lawful entries afterwards. All those entries were at the Tennat’s request, and were a result of the Tenant’s voluminous list of maintenance issues sent on March 14, 2024. They are not harassment because the Tenant requested the entries for maintenance and repair, and therefore they could not have reasonably been unwelcome.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and I also find the Landlord harassed and interfered with the Tenant for the single unlawful entry. T2 Application Remedy
As to remedy, the Tenant requested 12 month rent abatement in the amount of 25%. This is unreasonable given the event occurred solely on March 3, 2024.

I find it appropriate to grant the Tenant a lump sum rent abatement of $2,000.00 for the unlawful entry, substantial interference and harassment due to that unlawful entry. T6 Determinations: 1. The Tenant claimed the following issues in their Amended Application: 1. Outside Light Fixture Failure. 2. [name]. 3. [name]. 4. No Bathroom Fan Cover. 5. Dining Room Light Broken. 6. Basement Leak Repair Incomplete. 7. Hall Closet Door Broken. 8. Bedroom Closet Door Broken. 9. Pantry Door Broken. 10. Tree Hitting Window. 11. Basement Ceiling Light Broke. 12. [name]. 13. Basement Stair Railing Broken. 14. [name]. 15. Master [name]. 16. Laundry Room Paint Peeling. 17. Main [name]. 18. Garage Back Door Rot. 19. Crawl Space Air Leak. 20. Main Flooring Nails Exposed. 2. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 3. I will discuss each issue separately below. Outside Light Fixture Failure 4. It is not disputed that the exterior light fixture was not functioning and was hanging loose. 5. The Tenant testified that it was brought to the Landlord’s attention on March 19, 2024. This was the day after the application was filed. I discuss my consideration of section 30 requiring advance notice to a Landlord below. 6. The Landlord repaired this light fixture on March 26, 2024 by changing the light bulb and securing the fixture. 7. I find the fixture was repaired in a reasonable and timely manner. Therefore the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breach his maintenance obligations regarding the light fixture. [name]8. The Tenant claimed the front porch railing was not to code. The Tenant notified the Landlord of the problem on March 14, 2024. The Tenant can’t recall specifically when it was fixed and produced no photos of what the ratings were like before they were fixed, but testified it took 3 attempts to fix the problem and it was never properly done. The Tenant hired someone in the end to fix the disrepair, add blocks under the bottom rail, and properly fill and secure the gap between one post and the wall. 9. The Landlord agrees he came three or four times to repair the railing. The City By-Law officer required the railing to be secure, balusters to be secured, lattice to be removed and the gap near the house to be closed to smaller than four inches. The Landlord showed photos of his work. He agrees he is not a professional, and the photos of his work, despite his construction background, demonstrate that. 10. I find the Landlord’s work, although satisfactory to the By-Law officer from a safety or code perspective, was not completed in a professional manner and was of low quality, The repair was neither timely nor reasonable. Had the Landlord hired a professional, the repair would have been completed properly on one date, instead of three. Three dates attending to simply fix a railing installation is unreasonable. 11. I note that while a Tenant is only entitled to maintenance, and not improvement, to the property, there is a basic workmanlike standard to be met that includes not only safety but a reasonable attractive appearance. In my view that standard was not met regarding the railing. The balusters were reinforced by the Landlord with unsightly horizontal bars, and the bottom rail continued to sag meaning there was a risk balusters would disconnect again. Some remained barely connected. Moreover, the unsightly patch where the large gap met the wall remained wiggly. The Landlord testified the City inspector called him sometime after April 19, 2024 and he was satisfied with the fix but acknowledges the Tenant did not like the ‘aesthetics’. There is no mention of that call in the inspector’s report. On a balance of probabilities I conclude the wiggle was not fixed by the Landlord, despite his oral testimony. 12. I am satisfied the Tenant proved the Landlord failed to meet his maintenance obligations regarding the railing in a reasonable and timely manner. The out of pocket expense to repair the railing will be ordered in the amount of $552.32. 13. However, the Tenant failed to testify to any impact regarding the railing. I find that it was safe to use quickly after the complaint and the Tenant did not lose use of the railing. The Tenant failed to prove the installation was unsafe. Regarding remedy therefore, no rent abatement is appropriate. [name] 14. The Tenant claimed the basement egress window was cracked. He placed tape on the window to hold it together. He could not say when this happened. He notified the Landlord of the problem on March 14, 2024. The Tenant could not remember when it was fixed but agrees it was repaired on or before March 26, 2024. 15. The Landlord testified he hired a glass repair person to replace this window and he picked up all broken glass. 16. Although the Tenant proved the disrepair, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to repair the broken window, as the fix was done professionally and in a reasonable and timely manner. No Bathroom Fan Cover 17. The Tenant claimed the bathroom fan had no cover. No photo of the disrepair was provided. I note the Tenant was tasked in the Tenancy Agreement entered into by the parties in 2020, with renovating both bathrooms in the rental unit. Therefore the fan cover would have been the Tenant’s obligation to install. I am left to wonder if the work the Tenant undertook to complete was in fact completed. Although maintenance remains the responsibility of the Landlord, I note that the missing the fan cover was not brought to the attention of the Landlord until March 14, 2024. 18. The Tenant testified that on March 25, 2024 the Landlord replaced the fan cover, however, he claims the one provided was the incorrect size, and the Tenant bought a new one and put it in afterwards. The Tenant failed to provide a photo, receipt or date when these things happened. 19. I find therefore the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the fan cover. Dining Room Light broken. 20. The Tenant testified that one light in the tracking light system of the dining room did not work. He did not provide a photo of the light. He is unsure when he notified the Landlord. He claims the light was never repaired. 21. I find the Tenant failed to prove any disrepair. Further he failed to prove the Landlord did not meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the light. Basement Leak Repair Incomplete. 22. The Tenant claimed that repair from a leak which occurred in 2020 was never completed. The Tenant’s testimony was confusing and vague. The Tenant’s recollection was not clear. [name] were confused. I am satisfied the Landlord knew about the basement repair as early as May 2020. 23. The Landlord does not dispute the basement bedroom flooring was not completed. The bedroom was left with only plywood subflooring. He claims [name] delayed final repair steps but did not explain what efforts were made to find a contractor between 2020 and March 2024, and why one could not be obtained. 24. The Landlord arrange for a contractor to attend only after the full list of maintenance issues was brought to the Landlord’s attention on March 14, 2024, and the City by-law inspector was involved, On April 8, 2024 the work began, and by May 3, 2024 the flooring was done. 25. Given the delay of four years, and the lack of action only when a full list was given and the City was called, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the basement bedroom flooring in a reasonable and timely manner.

Regarding remedy, the Tenant failed to provide information regarding the impact to him and his family. It is unclear whether the bedroom was unusable, or if it simply didn’t have nice flooring. I cannot to conclude the room is unusable as a bedroom. The Tenant’s application was filed on March 18, 2024; therefore the Tenant is only entitled to a remedy from March 19, 2023 onwards. A nominal rent abatement of approximately 1% for the full period from March 19, 2023 to May 3, 2024 is appropriate in the circumstances in the amount of $400.00. Hall Closet Door Broken.

The Tenant claimed the hall closet door was broken. A photo was produced of a sliding door off its tracking. The Landlord was notified on March 14, 2024. The Tenant claims the Landlord repaired the door on March 25, 2024, by putting the door back on its hinges. The Landlord disputes the timeframe. He claims he does not recall notification on January 16, 2024 but he recalls he fixed the door in early February.
Regardless of which timing is accurate, I find this disrepair to be trivial, and the repair completed in a reasonable and timely manner.

Although the Tenant proved the minor disrepair, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to repair the hall closet door. Bedroom Closet Door Broken.

The Tenant claimed the bedroom sliding closet door was broken in that it was missing half the door. The Tenant testified he told the Landlord on January 16, 2024. A photo was produced showing the door. I am satisfied there was disrepair.
The Tenant states the Landlord fixed the problem on March 25, 2024. The Tenant did not provide the email proving notification, nor supporting documentary evidence regarding the repair.
The Landlord disputes the timing. He doesn’t recall any notification on January 16, 2024 but knows he was informed sometime in late January and fixed the problem in early February.

The parties do not dispute the doors were fixed shortly after notification of the problem, which I find to be in a reasonable and timely manner. No evidence that they were not repaired properly was before me. Accordingly, despite the dispute regarding timing, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not fail to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to repair the bedroom closet door. Pantry Door Broken.

The Tenant claimed the pantry door was broken. He provided a photo of the pantry cabinet door missing from the cabinet. The Landlord was notified in January, and I find that although the Tenant could not recall any date, it was in all probability the same date as the other doors, on January 16, 2024. The Tenant claims it was not fixed until March 25, 2024.
The Landlord doesn’t recall the date he was notified but agrees he fixed the problem in early February.

Given the vague recollection of the Tenant with respect to dates and times generally at this hearing, and the lack of documentary evidence contradicting the Landlord’s recollection, I find the Tenant’s recollection unreliable and prefer the testimony of the Landlord that the door was fixed in February.

Regardless, I am satisfied the Landlord repair the door in a reasonable and timely manner and therefore Landlord did not fail to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to repair the pantry cabinet door. [name].

The Tenant claimed a tree was hitting the window and causing noise. He provided a photo of a [name] adjacent to the window, which was overgrown. A small branch appears close to the window. The Tenant testified that he notified the Landlord ‘at the same time’, in January. He testified it was fixed March 25, 2024.

Regardless of who might have been responsible for lawn maintenance, the Tenant failed to prove the presence of the [name] itself is disrepair. I find the trimming of this [name] or to be a minor issue easily solved by either the Landlord or the Tenant.

Given the absence of particulars as to how the branches touching the house were ‘disrepair’, I find the Landlord, by trimming or removing the [name] on March 25, 2024, fixed the problem in a reasonable and timely way. Therefore, the Tenant failed to prove the Landlord did not meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the exterior ‘tree’.

Even if I am incorrect that the fix was timely, I find the Tenant did not testify to any significant impact from the lack of trimming of this [name], such as the number of times noise might have been caused, how it may have affected the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit, or any damage to the house or window as a result of the branches touching. Therefore, even if the Landlord failed during that time frame to trim the [name], no remedy is appropriate. Basement ceiling light broken.

The Tenant claimed the basement living room light was broken. The Tenant testified it simply didn’t function. Although he claimed it stopped functioning in 2019, the Tenant failed to prove he notified the landlord about the problem until March 14, 2024. The Tenant showed a photo of a perfectly good condition ceiling light, which did not assist in establishing the ‘disrepair’.

The Landlord doesn’t dispute that by March 25, 2024 he had attended and fixed the light. Given the large volume of issues the Tenant claimed all on March 14, 2024, and the time the Landlord needed to gather materials and assistance, 11 days is neither unreasonable nor untimely in my view.
Therefore, the Tenant failed to prove the Landlord did not meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the basement ceiling light. [name].

The Tenant claimed the doorbells did not operate. The Tenant provided no photo of broken doorbells; however, the Landlord does not dispute the disrepair. The doorbells had never been operable and the Landlord submits he did not promise the rental unit with operating doorbells.

The Landlord was notified in January, 2024 of the problem although the Tenant cannot recall the date. The Landlord failed to fix the problem properly. He only removed the bells and put the wiring into the holes that were left behind.
I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the door bells.

Regarding remedy, the impact to the Tenant, while annoying was not substantial. The Tenant testified he sometimes missed callers and packages because the doorbells were not working. He provided no dates when this occurred. Because the Landlord refused to provide a doorbell that operated, the Tenant bought and paid for a wireless doorbell in the amount of $30.50 and installed it himself. I therefore I find it reasonable to return the $30.50 to the Tenant. Basement Stair Railing Broken.
The Tenant claimed the basement stair rail was broken. He testified that one baluster was disconnected from the others and provided a photo showing the disconnected baluster.
Despite the existence of this problem the Tenant did not notify the Landlord until March 14, 2024. Despite the safety issue, the Tenant’s evidence is that it was not a high priority to him.
The Parties agree the Landlord repaired the problem 11 days later on March 26, 2024.

Given the evidence before me I am satisfied as to the disrepair, but I am not satisfied the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the stair baluster. The Landlord, in the circumstances, repaired the baluster in a reasonable and timely manner, taking into account the very large list sent by the Tenant. Downpipes Not Secure.

The Tenant claims four downpipes were not secure on the eavestroughs. In fact, the Tenant testified that it was the downpipe extensions that were disconnected. It is unclear from the evidence why they were disconnected, how they were removed, or why the Tenant simply didn’t pick them up and slip them back on.

The Tenant provided a photo of only one downpipe with extension on the ground. In the circumstances, although it was removed, I fail to see how it was ‘disrepair’. Given the absence of any photo, I also find the disrepair of the others was not proven.
Regardless of the lack of disrepair, the Landlord re-secured the downpipe extension proven to be disconnected on March 26, 2024.

Although the Tenant testified that one extension was not fixed. I accept the Landlord’s testimony, in the absence of photos proving there were other extensions to re-attached, that the Landlord fixed all downpipes that had extensions. Those that did not have extensions, there was nothing to fix.

I find therefore, that the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the downpipe extension. Master Bedroom Ceiling Damage.

He then testified at the hearing that it was the master bedroom bathroom ceiling that had paint damage. The Tenant’s claims regarding this were vague. The photo showed a bathroom ceiling, not a bedroom ceiling. [name] paint peeling is evident. The Tenant notified the Landlord of this disrepair on March 14, 2024.

The Landlord repaired the problem on April 8, 2024. The Landlord testified this was the bathroom the Tenant had renovated himself, and they had painted over the wallpaper on the ceiling. He corrected the problem. Although the Tenant claims the repair did not last and it still has problems, he failed to articulate what the continuing problem is or provide photos of that problem.

Given the vagueness of his testimony and the prompt and reasonable repair, I find the Tenant failed to prove the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the bathroom ceiling damage. Laundry Room Paint Peeling

The Tenant claims the paint on the walls and ceiling of the Laundry Room were peeling. Photos show large sections where paint was peeling and falling. The Landlord was notified of the problem on the March 14, 2024 notification email. On April 8, 2024 the Landlord attended the rental unit and fixed the problem. I accept that the problem was caused by the Tenant using inferior or improper paint when they painted that room. The Landlord scraped it all off cleaned up the problem.

Given the large list of items the Landlord received all at once, less than four days before filing of this application, I find the delay to April 8, 2024 was reasonable. In my view the problem was repaired in a reasonable and timely manner and therefore the Tenant failed to prove that the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the laundry room paint. Main Railing Broke.

The Tenant claimed the main stair railing was broken. A photo was produced of the wooden railing missing a large piece just by the joint of the handrail. No explanation was given as to how this was caused, but the Tenant testified that it happened a short while before March 14, 2024. The Landlord was notified of the disrepair on March 14, 2024. The Tenant testified the Landlord did not repair the rail until June 5, 2024 and made three attempts to do so, using different methods.

The Landlord testified he started the repair around March 25, 2024, but his first method chipped all out and he suspects someone gouged out the infill before it was dry. The Landlord agrees he tried other methods and finally finished the work around April 12, 2024.

I note the By-Law officer was not made aware of the stair rail issue by the Tenant. Given the lack of reliability with the Tenant’s recollections and given both parties appear to have vague and unsupported recollections on this point, I find there is insufficient evidence to conclude the railing was not fixed in a timely and reasonable manner. Despite the unorthodox methods of the Landlord, the Tenant provided evidence the railing was filled, painted and is secure.
I find therefore the Tenant failed to prove the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the main floor stair railing. Garage Back Door Rot.

The Tenant claimed the garage door was rotten. A photo was produced of the wooden garage door rotten and disintegrating a few inches from the ground. The Tenant reported this problem to the Landlord on March 14, 2024.

The parties agree the Landlord repaired the problem on April 8, 2024. He gave evidence that the Tenant refused to allow him access to the garage in order to repair the door. He testified that he fixed the problem from the outside by adding plywood and repainting.

Despite not having the door removed to repair, the Tenant failed to provide any evidence that this fix was insufficient or incomplete. Moreover, there was no evidence that there was safety or security concerns with the door. It cannot be concluded therefore that the three weeks timeframe to repair the door was not reasonable or timely. I have taken into account the large list of items the Tenant gave the Landlord all at once on March 14, 2024, and that given a significant amount were repaired within the first two weeks.
I find therefore that the Tenant failed to prove the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the garage door. Crawl Space Air Leak.

The Tenant claimed the crawl space door was leaking air. A photo was produced of a staircase, and a small door open to a small dark space, which was insufficient to support the Tenant’s claims. The Tenant testified a draft came around the door, which affected his heating bill. He provided one statement from April through May of 2024, after the claim was filed, and after the issue arose and was repaired of a heating bill. It would have been more persuasive if the Tenant had provided the bill from February in 2024 and the bill from February in 2025. This was not done, and without the comparison, the single bill from April is determinative of nothing. The Tenant also did not provide evidence of any impact to him of this small draft, discomfort experienced or heating bills impacted significantly.

I find therefore that the Tenant failed to prove disrepair. Even so, the Landlord testified he fixed the issue on April 12, 2024 by caulking around the door and screwing it shut. He cannot recall if he caulked the bottom.

I find the Landlord’s repair was reasonable and timely. The Tenant failed to prove that the repair did not adequately address the problem and the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the crawl space door draft. [name].
The Tenant testified that the main floor hardwood nails were exposed and there were chips. He notified the Landlord about the disrepair on March 14, 2024.

All flooring repair was begun March 25, 2024 and completed by April 4, 2024. The Landlord filled the chips, hammered the nails and stained the fill to match the floor. More chips were drawn to his attention and he hired a company to fix the rest.

In my view, the Landlord adequately addressed the problem and the fix was reasonable and timely. Therefore, I find the Tenant did not prove that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the exposed flooring nails and chips. Issues raised at the Application but not properly claimed

The Tenant raised issues within their materials and at the hearing that were not properly claimed in their T2 or T6 Application. I have denied hearing those issues. Among those issues are duct cleaning, locksmith, and mold generally. T6 Application Remedies

Section 30(2) states that in determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.
The Tenant’s application was filed on March 18, 2026.

The Tenant testified that they gave notice of all maintenance issues in 2019 before they moved into the rental unit. The Tenant could not recall the date or the method of how that notice was given. No documentary evidence was produced to support the assertion that notice was given in 2019. Similarly, there was no evidence before me of any communication between 2019 and 2024 of any maintenance issues.
The Landlord denies receiving any notice of issues before the Tenant moved in.

Given the Landlord’s denial, the Tenant is put to the onus of proving he notified the Landlord. The Tenant’s evidence was unreliable in this regard. I found the Tenant’s testimony without the necessary detail on most issues. He could frequently not recall dates or times. He testified to dates that were different than in his own materials, such as when he first notified the Landlord, which he states was ‘early March’, then ‘March 16’, then March 14. In addition, some issues didn’t arise until early 2024 according to the Tenant, therefore he could not have notified the Landlord about them in 2019. At one point in the hearing, when asked directly if he had evidence that he notified the Landlord before March 14, 2024, the Tenant agreed he did not, and that for the purposes of this application the date is March 14, 2024.

Accordingly, I accept the Landlord was notified of most maintenance issues on either January 16, 2024 or March 14, 2024 in one communication with a list. That email and list was not produced at the hearing.

Considering the Landlord received 4 days’ notice before the application was filed to complete the repairs, I find no remedy is open to the Tenant prior to March 14, 2024 or January 16, 2024 regarding maintenance issues notified on that date. Where notice is proved to have been in 2020, a remedy going back to the beginning to the Tenant’s limitation period was available.
I have addressed remedies above in each section. The total remedies that will be ordered are $2,982.82.
The Tenant is also entitled to their filing fee.

The [name] requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”.

In the present case, as the Tenants have been awarded a substantial monetary remedy, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. Given the Landlord’s remorse and lack of repetition of the breach, I find an administrative fine not appropriate. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,030.82. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for a rent abatement for the T2 Application. • $400.00 for rent abatement for maintenance issues. • $582.82 for reimbursement of out of pocket expenses. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the outstanding balance. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit in June 2024 and moved out on March 8, 2026.
There is no dispute that no person occupied the rental unit after the Tenant vacated and that the rental unit was listed for sale on March 29, 2026.

The remaining issues to be determined are whether the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice under section 48 of the Act and whether the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of that notice. Was there notice under s.48?

The Tenant testified that he received a text message from the Landlord on February 5, 2026, stating that the Landlord intended to recover possession of the rental unit by May 1, 2026, because the Landlord needed the rental unit for his parents’ residential occupation. The Tenant testified that he objected and promptly contacted the Landlord after receiving the text message. The Tenant stated that, during a telephone conversation, the Landlord explained that he required the rental unit for his mother because of her age and financial difficulties. A copy of the text message was submitted at the hearing.

The Landlord did not dispute that he sent the Tenant a text message on February 5, 2026, asking the Tenant to vacate the rental unit by May 1, 2026, because the Landlord’s mother or parents required the rental unit.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative argued that the Landlord never served the N12 notice of termination pursuant to s.48 of the Act to the Tenants. Therefore, the first requirement in s.57(1) of the Act has not been met, and the Tenants’ application should be dismissed. The Landlord’s legal representative also submitted an LTB decision for my consideration during the hearing. While Board decisions are not binding upon me, I am not obligated to agree with the approach stated in the decision.

The text message, and the Landlord’s phone conversation with the Tenant collectively constitute a notice under s.48(1) the Act. A Landlord is entitled to terminate a tenancy be- because they wish to recover possession of the unit for their own use. There is no dispute that the Landlord notified the Tenant that he needed the house back for his mother by May 1, 2026.

Section 202 of the Act requires the Board to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or rental unit and the good faith of the participants. In doing so, the Board may disregard the outward form of a transaction and consider the real substance of what occurred.

In this case, the Landlord clearly told the Tenant that he had to vacate the rental unit by May 1, 2026, because the Landlord’s family member required the unit for residential occupation. Although the Landlords never actually served a valid N12 on the Tenant, I am satisfied that for the purposes of s. 57(1)(a) the correspondence between the parties is “a notice of termination under section 48”. To find otherwise would make a mockery of the protections s. 57 is supposed to confer on tenants. In my view, it would be inconsistent with section 202 of the Act to allow the Landlord to escape the consequences of the Act simply because the notice was not given on the Board’s prescribed N12 form. I therefore find that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice under section 48 of the Act for the purpose of residential occupation by the Landlord’s parents or mother. Did the Tenant Vacate the Rental Unit as a Result of the Notice?

The Tenant testified that he moved out on March 8, 2026, because of the Landlord’s notice. The Tenant stated that, after receiving the Landlord’s message, he began looking for another place to live. He testified that he eventually moved to another house with similar features, with a monthly rent of $3,100.00 plus utilities.

During the hearing, the Tenant was asked when he secured the new rental unit and whether he had supporting documents for his moving expenses. The Tenant was given two opportunities during the hearing to submit evidence. The first time, the Tenant submitted documents related to moving expenses and a rental listing. The second time, the Tenant was given another opportunity to provide proof related to the new rental unit. He submitted a copy of the new lease agreement and a screenshot of a bank transaction. The Tenant stated that the bank transaction was proof that he had paid first and last month’s rent for the new rental unit.

The Landlord testified that, on February 5, 2026, he sent the Tenant a text message because his mother was living in Cornwall and was considering moving to Ottawa if the rental unit became available. The Landlord testified that the Tenant called him later that evening and explained that the Tenant’s family members were coming from Pakistan and that he needed to remain in the rental unit until September 2026.

The Landlord further testified that the Tenant followed up by email on February 19, 2026, asking for more time to remain in the rental unit. The Landlord testified that he then looked for alternate accommodation for his mother so that the Tenant could remain in the rental unit. The Landlord testified that, after finding alternate accommodation for his mother, he emailed the Tenant on February 26, 2026, and told him that he did not have to move out. The Landlord’s position was that, as of February 26, 2026, the Tenant had been clearly told that he could remain in the rental unit.

The Landlord also testified that, after receiving that message, the Tenant responded that he had already found another place and would be moving. The Landlord’s position was that the Tenant chose to move after being told that he no longer had to vacate. The copies of the emails had been submitting at the haring as evidence.
Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice.

The lease for the new rental unit was signed on February 28, 2026. This was after the Landlord advised the Tenant on February 26, 2026, that the Tenant did not have to move because the Landlord had found alternate accommodation for his mother.

The Tenant stated that he had paid first and last month’s rent before receiving the Landlord’s February 26, 2026, email. However, the bank transaction screenshot provided by the Tenant does not support that evidence. The Tenant testified that the new rent was $3,100.00 per month. If the Tenant had paid first and last month’s rent, the expected amount would have been $6,200.00. The bank transaction screenshot showed a total amount of $4,650.00. The amount therefore does not match the Tenant’s evidence that the payment was for first and last month’s rent.

The Tenant did not provide a receipt, rental application, confirmation from the new landlord, or other reliable evidence proving that a binding tenancy agreement had been formed before the Landlord told him that he did not have to move.

The Tenant also acknowledged that, after receiving the Landlord’s February 26, 2026 email, he did not discuss the situation with the new landlord or attempt to cancel the new lease. He also did not discuss with the Landlord whether he could remain in the rental unit after the Landlord told him that he no longer needed to move.

Because this is the Tenant’s application, the Tenant bears the burden of proving that he vacated the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice. I accept that the Landlord’s February 5, 2026, message caused the Tenant concern and led him to begin looking for another rental unit. However, the evidence does not establish that the Tenant was legally required to move or that he had already entered into a binding new tenancy before the Landlord told him that he could stay.

On the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant chose to proceed with the new rental unit after the Landlord advised him that he no longer had to move. I am therefore not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice.
As the Tenant has not proven this required element under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $739.60 by June 27, 2026.

On March 9, 2026, the Tenant filed a T1 Tenant Application for a Rebate of Money the [name]. In the application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord charged him an illegal rent and that the Tenant was overcharged in the amount of $559.78.

The Tenant testified that he received an N1 Notice of Rent Increase (the “NORI”) on January 29, 2025 from the Landlord. At that time, his legal rent was $854.70. The Tenant provided a copy of a previous LTB order, LTB-T-077429-24 whereby the Board found the [name] of November 1, 2023 was void. This order set out that the Tenant’s legal rent for the period of February 1, 2024 to January 31, 2025 was $854.70 per month.

The Tenant provided a copy of the January 29, 2025 NORI which used a base rent of $854.70 plus a guideline increase totalling $897.96 commencing April 1, 2025. He stated that he paid the new rental amount without question and then realized that his new rent should have been $876.07 (2.5% is $21.37 which calculates as $876.07), not the incorrect amount of $897.96. He also pointed out that the Landlord did not provide the required 90 days’ notice.

The Tenant stated that he received another NORI on February 1, 2026 to be effective on May 1, 2026 with a new rent of $916.81. This notice used the previous calculations which he believed were contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”).
The Tenant stated that despite suspecting that the rental amounts were illegal, he paid the rent in the amounts set out in both NORIs to the Landlord. Law and Analysis

Section 120(1) of the Act states “No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.”

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the January 29, 2025 NORI was void as it increased the rent by more than the guideline, contrary to section 120 of the Act and was based on an illegal rent. Accordingly, the lawful rent for the period of April 1, 2025 to April 30, 2026 (as 2nd NORI started May 1, 2026) was $854.70 per month. This means that the Tenant is entitled to be refunded the amounts paid for the illegal rent increase in the amount of $562.38 [($897.96 – $854.70) x 13].

I also find that the February 1, 2026 NORI was void as it increased the rent by more than the guideline and was based on an illegal rent. Accordingly, the lawful rent for the period of May 1, 2026 – June 30, 2026 is $854.70. The Tenant is entitled to be refunded the amounts paid for the illegal rent increase in the amount of $124.22 [($916.81 - $854.70) x 2].
As the Tenant was successful with his application, he is entitled to the application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $739.60. This amount represents: • $686.60 for excess rent collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,553.00 by July 3, 2026.
The Tenant testified that she contacted the Landlord by text message on January 13, 2026 regarding the rental of a condo located at [address]reet in Toronto which was to commence on April 1, 2026.

The Tenant stated that she provided a last month’s rent deposit to the Landlord on January 13, 2026 in the amount of $1,500.00. She and the Landlord agreed to contact each other in February of 2026 to arrange for a viewing of the condo.

The Tenant stated that she texted the Landlord on February 13, 2026 to arrange for the viewing and she did not receive a response. After repeated text messages to the Landlord and no response from the Landlord, the Tenant requested that her $1,500.00 deposit be returned.
The Tenant provided a copy of the text messages between the parties. Law and Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states “A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

The Tenant was not provided with keys for the rental unit and thus she was not given vacant possession of the rental unit. As such, the Tenant is entitled to the return of her last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant’s application is successful.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,553.00. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for the last month’s deposit illegally retained by the Landlord; and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants; and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was scheduled to be heard and/or was heard by videoconference on June 2, 2025, April 14, 2026, and May 19, 2026. The Tenants, the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord, the Landlord’s translator, [name], and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative requested the Tenants’ claims with respect to the reductions of space and/or size of the rental unit be dismissed on the basis that any changes to the rental unit were completed well over a year prior to the application being filed. In addition, she requested the Tenants’ claims of harassment be dismissed as she was of the view that they were already dealt with in order LTB-T-060525-22.

With respect to the first issue, The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that he believed the construction or changes to the space in the unit commenced in January 2021 and requested the application be amended to reflect the January 2021 date as a commenced date as opposed to an end date. The Landlord’s Legal Representative was opposed to this.

As explained at the hearing, even if I were to amend the application to reflect a commenced date of January 2021, a limitation issue would still likely exist and, in any event, the applications filed by the Tenants are for orders made pursuant to sections 30 and 31 of the Act. These sections do not address when there has been a reduction of a service or a facility or allow the Board to make an order regarding the reduction of a service or facility. Rather, this issue is addressed by a different application that is filed pursuant to section 130 of the Act. For these reasons, the allegation related to the reduction of the size of the rental unit was dismissed.

With respect to the second issue, the Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the previous order was based on a T1 application that did not address the harassment alleged in the applications before me. In reviewing the previous order, it appears that it dealt with very separate issues such as whether there was a rent discount and if there was an illegal rent increase and deposit. Accordingly, I found that the issue of harassment was not addressed in the previous order and so res judicata did not apply. The Application

The Tenants’ application is a combined T2 Application about Tenant Rights and a T6 Tenant Application about Maintenance (the ‘Application’). In summary, the Application alleges the following: • the Landlord refused and/or failed to install working smoke detectors on each floor of the rental unit; • there were fire safety issues in the unit for which the St. Catharines Fire Department issued an Inspection Order; • there were Ontario Building Code violations in the unit for which the City of St. Catharines issued an Order to Comply; and • the Landlord engaged in harassing and verbally abusive conduct toward the Tenants, gave the Tenants an unlawful notice of termination and tried to have the Tenants removed by the police.

As explained below, the Tenants have proven some of the allegations contained in the Application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenants in accordance with the order below. Tenants’ Evidence 7. [name] (‘GZ’) testified on behalf of the Tenants. It was his evidence that he and the other Tenant, [name], were international students who had lived in the unit since approximately January 2021. They vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2022. At that time, their rent was $1,300.00 per month. A summary of GZ’s testimony is as follows: i. When the Tenants moved in there were no smoke detectors but the Tenants were unaware that the Landlord was required to have smoke detectors in the unit until much later. ii. The Tenants told the Landlord about having no smoke detectors some time in April 2022. The unit was inspected on April 12, 2022 by St. Catharines Fire Services and smoke detectors and a carbon monoxide detector were installed by Fire Services that same day. During the inspection, the inspector also found that there was insufficient ceiling fire separation and that a two dwelling unit had been constructed without an ESA permit for electrical work. As a result, an Inspection Order was issued. A copy was tendered as evidence. iii. On or about April 26, 2022, an Order to Comply was issued by the City of St. Catharines for the reason that an accessory dwelling unit had been constructed on the main floor of the building without first obtaining a building permit. A copy of the Order to Comply was tendered as evidence. iv. As a result of the two orders being issued the Landlord was very angry with the Tenants and told them they had to move out. The Landlord swore at them on multiple occasions and called the police on the Tenants. v. On April 18, 2022, the police attended the rental unit. During this time, the Landlord was heard saying rude and offensive comments in Mandarin toward the Tenants (which the Tenants also speak) such as “I hope your parents get hit by a car as soon as they step outside” and “you will be hit by car”. After hearing the language used by the Landlord, the Tenants felt offended and upset. A copy of the recording was tendered as evidence. vi. On April 20, 2022, the Landlord sent the Tenant a text message stating that no one can live in the rental unit during construction and that, as per the City Order, the Landlord has to deconstruct the wall and the Tenants must vacate by April 30, 2022. A document was also given to the Tenants that stated in both English and Mandarin that the Tenants had to move out by April 30, 2022, when their lease expired. vii. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2022 due to the notice given by the Landlord and they would have stayed longer had they not been given notice to vacate. The Tenants found a new place with a monthly rent of $2,475.00. Landlord’s Evidence 8. It was the Landlord’s evidence that there were smoke alarms and a carbon monoxide detector in the rental unit when the Tenants moved in in January of 2021. The Landlord did not become aware that there were any issues with the detectors until around April 13, 2022. By this date, Fire Services had already attended the rental unit and installed detectors. 9. The Landlord acknowledged receiving the Fire Inspection Order and the Order to Comply and understood that she was required to remove the wall in the unit or get a permit for its lawful construction. She also understood that she had to take action as soon as possible to avoid penalties. 10. The Landlord denied forcing the Tenants to move out. She stated that the Tenants told her at the beginning of April 2022 that they would not be continuing with their lease for May as they were graduating and had other plans. Based on this, she advised the building department that the Tenants were vacating at the end of April 2022. 11. The Landlord stated that the Tenants were looking for a new place to live and asked the Landlord to provide them with a letter that stated the reason the lease was ending. The Landlord stated that this is why she gave the Tenants a letter in English and in Mandarin that said that they had to move out and why. In summary, the Letter stated: i) there were fire and building inspections completed in the unit and that immediate rectification was ordered; ii) in order to take care of the Tenants, the Landlord asked the fire and building departments to give her until May 1, 2022 to do the work required; iii) the lease agreement between the Landlord and Tenants expires on April 30, 2022; and iv) the Tenants must move out of the rental unit by April 30, 2022. The Landlord relied on text message correspondence between the parties on April 20, 2022 in support of her position that the Tenants requested the letter from her. 12. With respect to the incident that occurred on April 18, 2022, the Landlord stated that the police were called as there was a concern of an illegal resident staying in the rental unit. In this regard, there was a third person living in the unit and the Landlord did not know who they were and she wanted them removed from the property. The Landlord admitted that her she lost her temper and that her language was inappropriate but denied that she made the offensive comments to the Tenants and stated that they were directed at the unauthorized person who was staying with them. During the altercation, the police spoke with the parties and the Tenants confirmed that they were leaving at the end of the month. Analysis 13. There was insufficient evidence provided at the hearing to establish that the Tenants notified the Landlord that there were no functioning smoke detectors and/or carbon monoxide detectors in the unit. It was GZ’s evidence that he told the Landlord about the issue in April 2022 but could not recall an exact date. Based on the correspondence submitted as evidence, it appears that the first time the Landlord became aware of the issue was after the Fire Department had already inspected and replaced the detectors on April 13, 2022. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed. 14. With respect to the Inspection Order and the Order to Comply, the fact that these were issued does not automatically establish that the Landlord was in breach of her obligations under section 20 of the Act. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 15. The aforesaid orders were issued to the Landlord on or about April 25, 2022. It was not disputed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2022. It is hardly reasonable to expect the Landlord to comply with the orders within 5 days. In addition, there was no evidence to suggest that the Landlord knew or ought to have known of the deficiencies listed in the orders prior to them being issued. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached her obligations to maintain and repair under the Act and so the T6 portion of the Application is dismissed. 16. In turning to the allegations regarding the Landlord’s conduct, I find that the Landlord’s conduct on April 18, 2022, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. Both the Tenant and the Landlord’s translator translated the audio recording of what the Landlord said that day and although their translations differed slightly, the essence was the same. The fact is that the Landlord made rude and offensive comments and wished harm on the Tenants and/or their occupant. As section 22 of the Act not only includes tenants, but also members of a tenant’s household, it does not assist the Landlord to any degree if her comments were meant for the Tenant’s occupant and, in any event, the evidence of GZ was that the Tenants found the Landlord’s comments deeply offensive. Moreover, simply because the Tenants had a guest or roommate staying with them does not warrant a call to the police. In my view, this was an escalation by the Landlord that was simply not called for and totally inappropriate. 17. The Tenants also alleged that the Landlord engaged in harassing behaviour in trying to get them to vacate. Harassment is generally considered a course of conduct that is known or ought to be known to be unwelcome. Based on the evidence and submission provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of harassment with the intent to make the Tenants vacate. In looking at the text message correspondence provided, it appears to be neutral in tone and not aggressive or harassing in nature. The correspondence also supports the Landlord’s position that the letter asking the Tenants to vacate, which included the reasons why, was provided at the request of the Tenants. Of course, there was the incident that occurred on April 18, 2022, which I accept was quite unpleasant for the Tenants. However, the evidence suggests that this was an isolated incident and, as such, would not establish a pattern of harassment. 18. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Tenants vacated as a result of the conduct of the Landlord. Rather, I find it more likely than not that Tenants intended on vacating at the end of their lease term. In this regard, there was no documentary evidence provided wherein the Tenants expressed to the Landlord a desire to remain in the rental unit after April 30, 2026. 19. There was insufficient evidence to determine that the incident on April 18, 2026 was a deciding factor to move out and the correspondence between the parties in March 2022 suggests that at least one of the Tenants was already looking at places to rent. 20. For these reasons, I find it more likely than not that the parties reached an agreement to end the tenancy and that the Tenants vacated in accordance with that agreement. Remedies 21. As the Tenants were successful in proving that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, the Tenants are entitled to compensation. The Tenants sought a rent abatement in the amount of $2,600.00. 22. Although the April 18, 2022 incident took place for only a short period of time on one day, the impact to the Tenants lasted beyond this period of time and date. In this regard, GZ testified that he found the comments made by the Landlord to be very offensive and as if the Landlord was cursing them so that they or their family would experience injury. It was recognized by Divisional Court in Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] [name] No.423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) that rent abatements are not limited to a calculation that accounts only for the period of time that a breach of the Act occurs. 23. Having considered the conduct of the Landlord and the impact to the Tenants, I find a lump sum abatement of $1,000.00 to be appropriate in the circumstances. 24. The Tenants also requested that the Landlord pay an administrative fine. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 25. I am satisfied that the rent abatement ordered will serve as an adequate deterrence to the Landlord and promote compliance with the Act going forward. Accordingly, no fine shall be ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the Application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the Tenant as ordered below.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

Per the Tenants’ uncontested testimony, the Tenants paid the Landlord a $500.00 refundable key deposit at the beginning of the tenancy. The Tenants testified that they returned the keys upon moving out of the unit on February 24, 2026, and that the deposit was never returned to him.
I found the Tenants to be credible in their testimony, and their testimony was consistent with the terms of the lease provided at the hearing.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord refused to return the key deposit because of alleged maintenance issues in the unit after the Tenants vacated. This is not permitted under the Act. A refundable key deposit is precisely that: a refundable deposit to be repaid to the Tenants upon return of the keys to the rental unit. The Landlord cannot unilaterally withhold these funds and attribute them to another claim (that, it is worth noting, has not been adjudicated).
By not returning the refundable key deposit, the Landlord has illegally retained the funds. These funds must be paid to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $948.00.
The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to return the Tenants’ key deposit and rent deposit as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The tenancy began on September 8, 2024. At the beginning of the tenancy, the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent collected a key deposit of $100.00. The Tenant also paid a rent deposit of $800.00. The monthly rent was $800.00.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit and returned the key to the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent on April 6, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord asked the Tenants to move out of the rental unit in March 2025. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 6, 2025. The Tenant testified that the March and April 2025 rent had been paid in full. The Tenant further testified that, on April 6, 2025, they contacted the Landlord and requested the return of the key deposit and rent deposit. The Landlord refused to return both deposits and stated that the money would be applied to maintenance costs. The Tenant submitted text message correspondence between the parties dated April 2025 in support of this evidence.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence. I find on a balance of probability, that the tenancy ended on April 6, 2025, the Tenants returned the key, and the rent had been paid in full up to the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

Section 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) governs rent deposits. A rent deposit may be collected only for the rent for the last rental period before the tenancy ends. In these circumstances, because the Tenants paid the March and April 2025 rent in full and vacated the rental unit on April 6, 2025, the Landlord was not entitled to retain the rent deposit. The Tenant is entitled to the return of the rent deposit in the amount of $800.00.

Section 134 of the Act prohibits a landlord from collecting or retaining charges in addition to rent, except as permitted by the Act. Section 135 of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant to apply for an order requiring the landlord to repay money collected or retained in contravention of the Act.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 provides that a landlord may collect a refundable key, remote entry device, or card deposit, provided the amount is not greater than the expected direct replacement cost. A key deposit must be refundable.

When section 134 of the Act is read together with section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06, a landlord is not permitted to retain a key deposit after the key has been returned at the end of the tenancy. I find that the Tenants returned the key on April 6, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord was required to return the key deposit. The Tenant is entitled to the return of the key deposit in the amount of $100.00.
The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenants $900.00, representing $800.00 for the rent deposit and $100.00 for the key deposit.
As the Tenants were successful in their application, the Landlord must also reimburse the Tenants for the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $948.00. This amount represents: • $900.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants' application alleges that the Landlords failed to pay the one month's compensation required by section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") following the service of an N12 Notice of Termination.

The parties do not dispute that the Tenants received an N12 Notice of Termination dated February 23, 2026, with a termination date of May 1, 2026. The notice states that the rental unit was required for the residential occupation of the Landlord and the Landlord's child for a period of at least one year.

The parties also do not dispute that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on March 5, 2026. 4. [name] ("AC") testified that the Tenants paid the rent due for February 2026 together with prorated rent for the period they occupied the rental unit in March 2026. 5. [name] ("DM") testified that the Landlords returned the rent paid for March and April 2026 by e-transfer together with the Tenants' last month's rent deposit. AC testified that, at the commencement of the tenancy, the Tenants had paid the equivalent of two months' rent as a last month's rent deposit in the amount of $4,400.00, which was returned to them. Notices of termination 6. The main issue in dispute concerns the circumstances in which the N12 Notice of Termination came to be issued. 7. DM testified that the Tenants provided an N9 Notice of Termination before the N12 notice was signed. The N9 notice is dated February 23, 2026, with a termination date of March 5, 2026. 8. DM testified that she is the Landlord and that [name] ("MM") is not a landlord named on the tenancy agreement but acts as the property manager and agent for the Landlord. DM testified that she did not sign the N12 notice. Although the notice bears DM's name as the Landlord, it was signed by MM. 9. DM testified that MM had advised the Tenants that DM intended to return to Ontario and eventually occupy the rental unit. However, no date had been established for that move, and the information was provided only as a courtesy to give the Tenants additional time to find alternate accommodation. 10. The Tenant, [name] (AH) testified that, on January 26, 2026, MM verbally advised the Tenants that they would need to vacate the rental unit because the MM's son intended to move into the unit. AH testified that MM also advised the Tenants that they could remain in the rental unit until June 2026 if necessary. 11. MM testified that the Tenants had already secured alternate accommodation by February 18, 2026, and requested permission to vacate the rental unit early. MM agreed to that request. 12. MM further testified that, on February 23, 2026, the Tenants advised her through WhatsApp that they required an N12 Notice of Termination in order to secure their new rental accommodation. [name] testified that the Tenants prepared both an N9 Notice of Termination and a pre-populated N12 Notice of Termination and sent them to her for signature on the N12 notice. 13. MM testified that she did not request that the N12 notice be prepared. She understood that the Tenants required the notice solely for the purpose of securing alternate accommodation and, in an effort to assist them, signed the notice.
