[name] testified that she and AC discussed the termination date, and she amended the notice to reflect a termination date of May 1, 2026. [name] stated that she believed she was assisting the Tenants and later felt that she had been misled into signing the notice. 14. AC testified that the Tenants wished to ensure that any termination of the tenancy complied with the requirements of the Act. He testified that, between February 20 and February 23, 2026, he followed up daily with MM regarding the issuance of an N12 notice. When no notice was forthcoming, AC prepared a draft N12 notice for MM's convenience. 15. AC acknowledged that he pre-populated the N12 notice before it was signed. He testified that he initially inserted a termination date of April 23, 2026, representing approximately 60 days from the date of preparation. It was not disputed that MM amended the termination date to May 1, 2026, before signing the notice. 16. AC further testified that it was common practice during the tenancy for the Tenants to prepare documents on MM's behalf at her request, for her review and signature. As an example, AC testified that the Tenants prepared a reference letter, at MM's request, to assist them in obtaining alternate rental accommodation. 17. MM acknowledged that the Tenants had prepared documents on her behalf during the tenancy, including the reference letter. She maintained, however, that she signed the N12 notice only because she believed it was required by the Tenants to secure their new rental unit. Analysis and Determination 18. The issue before me is whether the Tenants are entitled to compensation pursuant to section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"). Section 48.1 requires a landlord who gives a tenant a notice of termination under section 48 to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one month's rent or to offer another acceptable rental unit. 19. There is no dispute that an N12 Notice of Termination dated February 23, 2026 was signed by MM and provided to the Tenants. The central issue is whether, in the circumstances of this case, the N12 notice was a notice of termination given by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act, thereby triggering the compensation requirement under section 48.1. 20. There is also no dispute that the Tenants subsequently provided an N9 Notice of Termination. AC testified, however, that the N9 Notice of Termination was served after the Tenants had already received the signed N12 Notice of Termination. 21. Having considered the evidence in its entirety, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 notice was initiated or issued by the Landlord as a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. 22. I prefer the evidence of DM and MM regarding the circumstances in which the N12 notice came to be signed. Their evidence was consistent that the Tenants had already advised they intended to vacate the rental unit, had secured alternate accommodation, and requested documentation to assist them in obtaining that accommodation. MM's evidence that the Tenants prepared both an N9 Notice of Termination and a pre-populated N12 Notice of Termination was consistent with AC's testimony that he prepared the N12 notice before it was signed. 23. I accept that MM amended the termination date on the N12 Notice of Termination prior to signing it. However, I do not find that this, on its own, establishes that the Landlord initiated a termination of the tenancy under section 48 of the Act or that the notice was given by the Landlord for the purposes of section 48.1. In assessing the evidence as a whole, I find that the circumstances surrounding the preparation and execution of the N12 notice are more consistent with it being generated at the Tenants’ request for documentation, after the Tenants had already secured alternate accommodation and believed such documentation was required for their new tenancy, rather than a notice issued by the Landlord initiating termination of the tenancy. 24. I also place weight on the evidence of AH that, prior to the execution of the N12 notice, MM advised the Tenants that they could remain in the rental unit until they secured suitable alternate accommodation, including potentially until June 2026. This evidence is inconsistent with an intention by the Landlord to terminate the tenancy on a fixed date pursuant to section 48 of the Act. 25. Further, the Tenants vacated the rental unit on March 5, 2026, prior to the termination date set out in the N12 notice, after requesting to do so. The Landlord returned the Tenants' last month's rent deposit. In my view, these actions are consistent with a mutually agreed early termination following the Tenants’ decision to relocate, rather than enforcement of a landlord-initiated termination under section 48. 26. While the Act provides for mandatory compensation where a landlord gives an N12 notice under section 48, I am not satisfied that the N12 notice in this case was given by the Landlord in that statutory sense. The evidence supports a finding that the Tenants received the signed N12 notice after it had been prepared by them at their request, and that the N9 Notice of Termination was only served after receipt of the signed N12 notice, consistent with the Tenants’ understanding that documentation was required to secure alternate accommodation. 27. In all of the circumstances, I find that the Tenants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave an N12 notice within the meaning of section 48 of the Act so as to trigger the compensation requirement under section 48.1. 28. Accordingly, and for the reasons set out above, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenants’ rent deposit because the Tenants voluntarily moved out of the rental unit without providing proper notice to the Landlords to end the tenancy.

The Tenants moved out in response to a notice that was posted to the door of the rental unit. This was not a notice of termination of tenancy issued by the Landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c. 17 (the ‘Act’). Rather, the notice was a “Notice to Vacate” order executed by the Superior Court of Justice relating to a dispute between their Landlords and the Landlords’ mortgagee.

The Landlord [name] testified about these circumstances at the hearing. She testified that she was in contact with the Tenants after they reached out about the Notice to Vacate and offered reassurance that she was seeking a stay of that order through Court processes. She testified that she explicitly told the Tenants that they didn’t have to move. She was successful in obtaining a stay on February 26, 2026, and testified that she immediately told the Tenants about this outcome, only to learn that they had decided to vacate the rental unit.

The Tenants stress is understandable: they did not know how their interests would be impacted by the dispute between the Landlords and their mortgagees and felt a need to take action to secure their living situation. However, the fact is they vacated the rental unit on February 27, 2026, without receiving a Notice of Termination from the Landlords or providing notice in accordance with the Act.

In these circumstances, section 88(1) of the rent applies, and the Tenants would have continued to have an obligation to pay rent after they vacated the unit. The Landlords attempted to mitigate their losses, as required by section 88(4): Ms. [name]name] testified that the rental unit was listed for re-rental as of late March 2026.

Given the ongoing obligation to pay rent, the Landlords were entitled to use the Tenants’ last month rent deposit for the final period rent would be owing for pursuant to section 88 of the Act. The Tenants are, therefore, not entitled to the return of the deposit.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the amounts in accordance with this order.
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Illegal Rent Collected by Landlord
The Tenant gave uncontested testimony at the hearing about the rent she paid to the Landlord, and this evidence was corroborated by the documentary evidence presented at the hearing.

Per the evidence presented, I find that the Tenant made two rent payments to the Landlord: • On June 24, 2025, the Tenant paid $17,000.00 to the Landlord, consisting of $8,500.00 in prepaid rent for the first month of the tenancy (July 15, 2025, to August 14, 2025) and a last month’s rent deposit of $8,500.00. • On July 14, 2025, the Tenant paid $85,000.00 to the Landlord, consisting of prepaid rent for the period of August 15, 2025, to June 14, 2026. The lease agreement between the parties characterizes this as a voluntary prepayment by the Tenant, but the Tenant testified that the Landlord’s agent told her it was necessary to proceed with the rental agreement.
Bank drafts for both of these payments were provided by the Tenant and corroborate her testimony about the amounts paid.

The written lease agreement between the parties is for a one-year term beginning July 15, 2025. However, the Tenant testified that she moved out of the rental unit at the end of January 2026, as the parties had mutually agreed to an early termination of the Tenancy.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord visited her at the rental unit on December 10, 2026. A copy of a text message conversation between the parties corroborating this visit was presented at the hearing. The Tenant’s uncontested testimony is that the Tenant expressed dissatisfaction with the property during this meeting, citing some maintenance issues, and that the resolution that the parties reached was to agree to conclude the tenancy early on January 31, 2026.

There was no evidence directly showing a written agreement to terminate the tenancy early. However, there is sufficient circumstantial evidence that corroborates the Tenant’s testimony, and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the parties agreed to early termination of the tenancy on January 31, 2026. The Tenant provided documentation of email conversations regarding the termination of the tenancy, and the Landlord does not – in these communications – object to the Tenant moving out in January. Nor does he express concern about the Tenant breaking the lease. The Tenant also provided screenshots of MLS listings showing that the Landlord began to advertise the rental unit in early January 2026, consistent with the timeline set out in the Tenant’s testimony.

I am satisfied that the Tenant did not have an obligation to pay further rent as of February 1, 2026, and that the unused balance of the prepaid rent – totalling $47,250.68 – ought to be returned to her. Key Deposit

The Tenant also testified that she paid $400.00, which she characterized as a refundable key deposit. She testified that the rental unit is secured by an electronic lock and that she provided the code to the Landlord shortly after vacating the rental unit, but that the $400.00 deposit was never returned to her. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord illegally retained these funds at the time the Tenant returned control of the rental unit to the Landlord and that these funds should be returned to the Tenant as well.

I am also satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Rent Deposit and Interest

The Tenant testified that, as part of the agreement to terminate the tenancy, the parties agreed that the Landlord would return the $8,500.00 rent deposit to the Tenant. She testified that the Landlord had not done so. I found her testimony on this point to be clear and consistent, and it was uncontested at the hearing. As such, the deposit should be returned to her.

The Landlord also failed to pay interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. The Tenant credibly testified that no interest was ever paid to her on the $8,500.00 rent deposit collected by the Landlord. This interest is payable to the Tenant. Monetary Jurisdiction of the Board

In her application, the Tenant is requesting the following amounts be returned to her: • $47,250.68 for excess rent collected. • $400.00 for the illegal charge retained. • $8,500.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $115.54 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The total remedy being requested by the Tenant exceeds the Board’s monetary jurisdiction of $50,000.00: s. 207(1). Consequently, the Board cannot issue an order for the full amount claimed.

I sought post-hearing submissions from the parties on whether the Tenant consents to waive the part of her claim that exceeds the Board’s monetary jurisdiction. Her legal representative wrote to the Board confirming that the Tenant is waiving the amounts claimed in excess of $50,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $50,000.00. This amount is the maximum claim available under the Board’s monetary jurisdiction and is ordered in light of my findings that the following amounts have been illegally retained by the Landlord: • $47,250.68 for excess rent collected. • $400.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $8,500.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $115.54 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 Application’). [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (the ‘T2 Application’). The A1 Application and the T2 Application were heard together by videoconference on April 23, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does apply to the rental unit that was occupied by the Tenant.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit in 2018 and vacated May 25, 2024. There was no written rental agreement between the parties. The rental unit is in the basement level of the Landlord’s home.

The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant was required to share a kitchen with the Landlord under the rental agreement and, therefore, the exemption at paragraph 5(i) of the Act applies. The Tenant disputes this and takes the position that it was never contemplated that he would share a kitchen with the Landlord and that he never in fact did. ; LTB-T-025031-24

The Tenant’s testimony was unambiguous and unequivocal. He testified that he never entered the Landlord’s kitchen during the six years he resided in the rental unit. He testified that he never cooked in the kitchen, stored any food in the kitchen, or assisted the Landlord with cooking – although he acknowledges that the Landlord shared an occasional meal with him when he first moved into the rental unit. None of these facts were disputed by the Landlord, who testified that she never saw the Tenant use the kitchen. The Tenant testified that he relied entirely on the kitchenette inside the rental unit and countertop appliances for his food preparation and frequently did not eat at home.
The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant had access to the kitchen via an unlocked door, although the Tenant blocked this door when he placed a cabinet in front of the door within the rental unit.

The Tenant also provided a copy of email communication between himself and the Landlord in the lead-up to the tenancy. The email – dated June 11, 2018, and sent via Kijiji’s messaging system – lists the title of the Landlord’s rental advertisement as “Bachelor basement suit (sic) available July 1st”. The full text of the advertisement was not presented at the hearing.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the parties never contemplated that the Tenant would use the kitchen when they entered into the rental agreement. The rental unit was advertised as a bachelor suite, which typically refers to a self-contained unit rather than a room for rent. The rental unit does not contain a full kitchen, but photographs show a wet bar, cabinetry, and a refrigerator provided by the Landlord.

In my view, these facts do not correspond with the Landlord’s assertion of a shared kitchen. It is simply not credible that the parties agreed to share a kitchen, but that the Tenant never went so far as to step foot into the room over six years.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord is attempting to argue that the parties shared a kitchen to escape liability with respect to the T2 Application, which was filed approximately one month prior to the [name] application. In the absence of written terms, the Board must make a determination based on the testimony of the parties. The facts presented at the hearing clearly accord more logically with the Tenant’s description of the arrangement between the parties. The Landlord’s account of the arrangement and the parties actions during the tenancy simply do not make sense.
Therefore, I find that the Act applies to the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant. The T2 Application: No Substantial Interference or Harassment is Proven
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 Application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 Application is dismissed. ; LTB-T-025031-24

The T2 Application details several allegations of substantial interference or harassment by the Landlord. In particular, the Tenant alleges the following occurred within the one-year period before he filed his application: • In April 2023, the Landlord insisted the Tenant remain in the rental unit to supervise contractors attending to an urgent issue with respect to the residential complex’s hot water heater; • In July 2023, the Landlord reached out to the Tenant’s sister to ask about the tenancy; • In July 2023, the Landlord accused the Tenant of changing the locks to the rental unit, resulting in police attending the residential complex; and • In July 2023 and March 2024, the Landlord and the Tenant had disputes relating to parking spots in the driveway of the residential complex.

The Landlord and the Tenant both provided testimony about the above events. It is clear that each of these events was a source of contention and disagreement between the parties. However, based on the testimony presented at the hearing, I am not satisfied that the above incidents rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment.

In my view, the most serious incident – the July 2023 incident regarding the accusations that the Tenant changed the locks – amounts, essentially, to a misunderstanding. The Landlord discovered that the key she thought opened the rental unit did not in fact do so, and the Tenant did not provide his key to the Landlord so she could make a copy. The Landlord called the police non-emergency line to ask for advice – not with the intention to have the police attend the rental unit. When police attended, per the Tenant’s testimony, no action was taken. While the Tenant chose to spend the night away from the rental unit due to his feelings of stress about the circumstances, he appeared to do so of his own will.

The relationship between the parties clearly turned downhill toward the end of the tenancy as a result of several points of disagreement and conflict. However, these disagreements – in my view – are relatively benign. The parties lived in close proximity to one another and, as a result, situations arose (as they often do) that were required to be resolved. Not every point of contention between a landlord and a tenant constitutes a breach of the Act.

Even if the Tenant’s account of the events is wholly true, I am not satisfied that they amount to substantial interference or harassment. It is the Tenant’s burden to prove this is the case and, in my view, he has not done so. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Act applies to the rental unit that was occupied by the Tenant.
The T2 Application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant. The Tenant is also entitled to an ongoing rent abatement. Request to amend
At the outset of the February 11, 2025, hearing the Landlord consented to the Tenant’s request to amend their applications found at DOC-4129739.

At the January 13, 2026 hearing The Landlord’s Legal Representative advised that they were only representing [organization]. As a result, [organization] was added as a party to this application. They are the property manager for the owners of the building, [organization].

The Tenant occupies a one-bedroom apartment on the first floor with their child and a dog. They have been Tenants for at least 12 years. They reside above the boiler room and the laundry room. Maintenance Issues Cockroaches
The Tenant reported that there was a cockroach issue in their unit. It was reported to the superintendent and in writing in January 2022. See DOC-4129739, evidence binder part 2, at page 23.
They testified that the Landlord sprayed their unit a few months later.
The Tenants testified that they reported to the Landlord on September 30, 2022, that there was still a problem with cockroaches.
They testified that the Landlord sprayed in November 2022.
They testified that they continued to have issues with cockroaches after that, at least until March 2026. See evidence binder 1 pages 8, 11-13,14,15,18.
They testified that the issue remains unresolved despite their own efforts to address it as well as the actions of the Landlord.

The Landlord’s property manager [name] testified that they could not recall if pest treatment had been called after the January 2022 maintenance request. They stated that in 2022 there had been many requests to treat for cockroaches from many tenants.

The Landlord referred to their evidence found in DOC-6145539. At page 4 is a receipt for treatment for cockroaches on November 29, 2022, for 10 units, including this one. At page 5, is a receipt for treatment on December 21, 2022, for cockroaches for 12 units, including this one. At page 13, a report dated November 16, 2023, that says that this unit was not prepared for treatment.
The Landlord testified that they still receive complaints about cockroaches. They characterized this as nothing out of ordinary since every building in Oshawa have roaches.
The Landlord testified that they stopped treating the unit after the Tenant refused to cooperate. However, they admitted that the Tenant did provide consent a few days later.

On cross-examination, the Landlord clarified that they did permit the superintendent to address emergency repairs. All other requests had to be forwarded to the property manager because the Tenant had sent 4-50 emails harassing the staff. They had also advised the superintendent not to enter the unit after the Tenant disagreed with the quality of the work. Flooring
The Tenant testified that the flooring started to lift in the summer of 2021, describing it like a speed bump in the middle of the living room.

They filed a maintenance request with the Landlord on September 30, 2022. They stated that the Landlord conducted an inspection on October 17, 2022. They stated that a repairman tried to rip up the floor and glue it back however that did not resolve the problem. They then came again on November 23, and December 9, 2022.The Landlord attempted repairs while the Tenant was absent during the period December 19-27. 2022.

The work remained unsuccessful. In January 2023, the City of Oshawa inspected on February 3, 2023 issued a property standards order for the Landlord to repair the flooring. See Tenant’s evidence binder 2 at page 24. They testified that the floor remains uneven. At page 45 is a photo with red tape marking where the floor is uneven so that the Tenant can avoid the hazard.

The Landlord testified that they felt it was the Tenant that was not satisfied with the repairs they had done, and that is why they called bylaw. They blamed the Tenant for not cooperating with the repairs. They stated that the City had closed their property standards order. Electrical Wiring
The Tenant testified that they submitted a work order to repair a switch that had caused an electrical shock to their child. They stated that this has not yet been repaired.

The Landlord denied that the Tenant has reported any electrical issues. However, at page 22, of the Landlord’s book of evidence they provided a copy of the maintenance request in which the Tenant reported that their son had been shocked by a light switch in their bedroom. Walls and [name]

The Tenant testified that there was water damage to the walls, in their son’s bedroom the walls started to crack so that they could see the concrete behind it. They stated that there were gaps between the flooring and baseboards.
They stated that it took the Landlord several months before this issue was finally resolved.
The Landlord did not respond to these issues. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, entitled Breach of Maintenance Obligations provide that timeliness of repairs depends on a number of factors including the effectiveness of the work undertaken. Timeliness of response depends on a great number of factors, but principally on the seriousness of the state of non-repair and its possible effects on the tenant and the availability of materials and possibly contractors to do the repairs. The tenant may also be alleging that the repairs attempted by the landlord were ineffective or badly done, which has reduced the value of the unit or left the same problem unremedied. These issues must be addressed directly through evidence and decided by the Member.

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair OR maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with housing OR maintenance standards.

I did not find the Landlord’s testimony to be credible nor reliable. Their testimony amounts to hearsay evidence for the most part. They did not call to testify the pest control technicians, or the handyman or any other contractor to explain they work and or repairs that they had undertaken.

The Landlord admitted that there remains a problem with cockroaches. However, they were dismissive of this on the basis of a bald statement that every building in Oshawa has cockroaches. I did not find that credible.

The Landlord attempted to shift blame to the Tenant about the floor repairs, however in my view, the fact that the City of Oshawa had to issue a property standards order supports the Tenants view that the work was not satisfactorily repaired.

It was undisputed that the repairs to the electrical and the walls and drywall had taken months to be resolved. As a result, there is a breach because of the unexplained delays of the Landlord to take immediate action to resolve the. This is particularly concerning where the Tenant’s son is being shocked from an electric switch. Interference with Reasonable Enjoyment

In the Tenant’s amended T2 application they checked the reason 3, interference with reasonable enjoyment and referred to [name], schedule A, amended as of September 11, 2024 fails to provide anything to show what the Landlord has done to interfere with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Since the Tenant did not provide any testimony on this issue, the Tenant’s T2 application must be dismissed. Remedies 1. In Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.

The Board has a one-year limitation period in accordance with section 29(2) of the Act was explained. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) the Divisional Court affirmed that the Board may not order a remedy beyond the one-year limitation period. Accordingly, we conclude that the Board erred in law in allowing an abatement of rent prior to the one-year period preceding the making of the application.
The Tenant’s applications were filed on April 6, 2023, therefore the Board can only consider a remedy going back 12 months or to April 6, 2022.
The Tenant confirms that the walls and drywall were resolved by March 2023.
The Tenant confirms that the electrical issue was resolved by February 2023.
The Landlord admits that there remains a cockroach issue in the residential complex. The Tenant states that they continue to find evidence of cockroaches in their rental unit to date.

There is a dispute as to whether or not the floors have been adequately repaired. The City of [name] advised in an email dated March 19, 2024, that they have closed their file in relation to the property standards order. In my view that is the best evidence from an independent third party that the floors have been adequately repaired.

The Landlord submitted that the applications be dismissed because of the Tenants actions to refuse to comply with the Landlord’s direction so that work could be done. In the alternative the Landlord submitted that since they could not recall what remedies had been requested that none should be awarded.

On the second point, the Landlord’s legal representative was present on August 11, 2025 when the Tenant testified regarding the remedies and was afforded every opportunity to cross-examine the Tenant on them. To suggest on January 13, 2026 that because they do not recall what was requested that none should be ordered is an absurd result.

I do not agree that the Tenant has substantially interfered in the Landlord’s ability to effect repairs. The tenant was even absent December 19-27, 2022. The repair was substandard and that led to a property standards order.

The Landlord did not provide proof of what instructions if any had been given to the Tenants to prepare a unit for cockroach treatment. They also did not have their pest control technician testify. The Landlord admits there remains a cockroach problem. As a result the pet control treatment appears to be ineffective, and not because of anything that the Tenant has done. The Tenant may have been frustrated that the Landlord kept using the same pest control company to no avail and may have preferred that the Landlord try a different company. The refusal of entry, the Landlord admitted was short-lived, a few days. Therefore, in my view this did in any meaningful way obstruct the Landlord from treating for cockroaches.
I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. The parties did not provide case law on an appropriate remedy or to show what may have been ordered by the Board in past decisions.

In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, the Divisional Court stated that the Board could not make an order for a remedy that had not been requested in the application or in an amended application. In the circumstances and without any amendment to the relief claimed, it was unfair to the landlord to make such an award without adequate notice and without proper submissions. This denial of procedural fairness constitutes an error of law. Therefore, that part of the Board’s order awarding $3,000.00 for stress damages is set aside. Rent abatement
The Tenant requested a total rent abatement. The amount is calculated based on a various percentage of rent for each issue.

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 15% for 12 months for the cockroach issue. In my view this is a reasonable amount. Since the issue remains ongoing, I would award a rent abatement from April 2022 to the date of this order; total 50 months equals $3,346.64.

The Tenant requested 25% rent abatement for one month for the electrical issue. This is a serious issue that endangered the safety of the Tenant and the occupants and ought to have been rectified as an emergency repair. It was not and the Landlord took a month to affect the repairs. In the hearing, despite evidence to the contrary they denied it had been reported to them. As a result, the delay warrants the 25% request; an amount of $209.17 shall be ordered.

The Tenant requested 20% for six months for the walls and flooring. In my view it would be more appropriate to award 15%, which is reasonable. This also required intervention by the City of Oshawa to have the flooring repaired. In my view these repairs were not timely. Therefore, an amount of $753.00 shall be ordered.
At the hearing, the Tenant did not pursue remedy 2, therefore no amount shall be ordered.

At the hearing, the Tenant requested compensation under remedy 4 in the amount of $1,131.54 for out-of-pocket expenses. This is broken down as $94.00 for a bedbug inspection, $395.50 for cockroach spray and $461.04 for caulking paid for by the Tenant. In my view, the cockroach spray is reasonable, the issue of bedbugs was not pursued and there was no explanation for why caulking was required or why the Tenant undertook this work and did not request the Landlord do it. Therefore, an amount of $395.00 shall be ordered.

At the hearing the Tenant requested compensation of $1,000.00, under remedy 5. However, this remedy is reserved to compensate a tenant for future expenses where the Board permits a tenant to do the repairs themselves. Therefore, since the Tenant did not seek permission for future repairs, no amount shall be ordered.

At the hearing, the Tenant requested compensation for out-of-pocket expenses under remedy 8. However, in the amended application the Tenant did not request compensation, therefore no amount can be ordered.

The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $7,500.00 for pain and suffering the family has suffered living in the unit. They have endured stress of never knowing the next time they would find a cockroach on their pillow. They submitted that they had to clean the unit after their holidays, and when the superintendent showed up, they stated that if it was such a big deal, then the Tenant should leave.

I accept the oral testimony of the impact of living through these issues has had on them. Although there was no medical documents to show the impact of stress, in my view this is not fatal given that the Landlord was afforded every opportunity to cross examine the Tenant on their remedies.

In my view, general damages in the amount of $5,000.00 is reasonable. The Tenant has endured a prolonged issue with cockroaches that the Landlord appears to treat on a monthly basis if required and one that the Landlord dismisses because every building in [name] has cockroaches.

In addition, I have determined that an ongoing rent abatement of 5% is warranted for the continuing cockroach issues. The Landlord admits the problem is ongoing. Therefore, until the Landlord can fully resolve the problem, or that the Tenant does not report a live siting of cockroaches in their rental unit period of three consecutive months, the Tenant shall be entitled to an ongoing 5% rent abatement.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $9,703.81. This amount represents: • $4,308.81 for a rent abatement • $395.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred; and • $5,000.00 in general damages.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the lawful rent until such time as the amount has been repaid.

Commencing July 1, 2026, the Tenant is also entitled to a further 5% rent abatement until such time as the Landlord fully resolves the cockroach issue, or that the Tenant does not report a live siting of cockroaches in their rental unit for a period of three consecutive months.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I find, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does apply to this tenancy. While the Landlords asserts that the Tenant was required to share the bathroom facility, I do not find there was genuine living situation captured by the exemption contained in s. 5(i) of the Act.

While the rental unit listing stated that the washroom facilities would be shared, it did not state that it would be shared with the Landlord. Further, the tenancy agreement signed by the parties did not state the Tenant would be required to share the bathroom facilities with the Landlord. While it stated that the rental unit would not be subject to the Landlord and Tenant Board; it did not state for what reason. In addition, the Landlord has her own bathroom on a separate floor that she utilized daily. Furthermore she stated that her use of the Tenant’s lower-level bathroom was occasional and only when required.

Section 5(i) of the Act states: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located; The Facts

It was undisputed that the Landlord is the owner of the residential complex which is a bungalow. The Landlord lives on the upper floor of the residential complex and has her own bathroom on that floor that she uses on a daily basis. The Tenant’s rental unit is on the lower level which contains a kitchenette, bedroom and bathroom.

It was undisputed that the advertisement for the rental unit which the Tenant responded to included “shared access to 3pc bathroom”. With this said, the advertisement does not state that it is required to be shared with the Landlord.

It was further undisputed that the Landlord and Tenant completed and signed a rental application (‘agreement’) on August 16, 2025. The agreement does not state that the Landlord and Tenant would be sharing the washroom facilities (DOC-8017400).
The dispute between the parties revolves around whether the Tenant was required to share the washroom facilities during the pivotal period when tenancy began.

The Landlord submits that s. 5(i) of the Act is applicable in this case as the advertisement for the rental unit expressly stated that the Tenant would be required to share the washroom which was supported through documentary evidence. Further, the Landlord stated that when the Tenant viewed the rental unit, she reinforced that the bathroom would be shared. The Landlord testified that she required the use of the bathroom due to physical health needs. She stated that she utilized the bathroom sometimes weekly and others monthly, it was dependant on her needs during the month.
The Tenant’s representative submits that s. 5(i) does not apply in this case as the Tenant was not required to share the washroom and did not share the washroom at the commencement of the tenancy.
The Tenant testified that during two walkthroughs of the rental unit prior to the tenancy beginning the Landlord stated that the bathroom would be private. Analysis

In Cowie v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628, the Divisional Court held that the Board must examine the situation between the parties at the commencement of the lease when determining whether the exemption in section 5(i) of the Act applies. The Court found that the Act: . . . explicitly creates an exemption from the general application of the Act only if the person in the category of the respondent “lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”. That means that the respondent was required to live in the building at the time when she rented the room to the appellant in order for the exemption to apply. It was not sufficient that she merely intended to move in at some subsequent time. Nor was it sufficient that she actually did move in at a subsequent time

The Landlord relies on the advertisement with respect to the rental unit being exempt under s. 5(i) of the Act. However, as per Cowie v. Bindlish, I must focus on whether the Landlord actually lived in the rental unit when the tenancy began in determining whether the Tenant was required to share the kitchen or bathroom. In this case it was undisputed that the Landlord resides within the residential complex and has a separate washroom that she used on daily basis. The Landlord acknowledged that she did not use the Tenant’s bathroom on a daily basis and only used the bathroom as required, on occasion.
The Tenant’s evidence was that he was not required to share the washroom facilities at the commencement of the tenancy and did not share the washroom on a day-to-day basis.

Looking to s. 202 of the Act, it requires the Board to ascertain the substance of the agreement between the parties, and in doing so it may disregard the outward forms of a transaction and have regard to the parties’ pattern of activities. In this case I find that the true substance of the tenancy is that the Tenant was not required to share a bathroom with the owner at the beginning of the tenancy as the Landlord use of the washroom was only occasional.

As a result, the Landlords did not meet the onus of establishing on a balance of probabilities that they shared a bathroom and/or kitchen with the Tenant and has not established that the tenancy falls under the exemption in section 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved part of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $150.00 to the Tenant. Illegal Charge

Section 134 of the Act prohibits landlords from charging tenants’ fees that are in addition to rent. That section states that unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit: (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

Section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06 under the Act provides that certain payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) of the Act, including “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.” There is no exception for a damage deposit.

It was undisputed that the Landlord collected a $150.00 key deposit from the Tenant on September 1, 2025. The keys were returned by the Tenant on March 21, 2026 but the Landlord had failed to return deposit as of the date of the hearing.

As such, I find that the Landlord illegally retained this amount, and the Landlord shall pay the Tenants the amount of $150.00 for the deposit. Did the Landlord fail to apply the last months rent to the last month of the tenancy?
The Tenant also claims that the Landlord failed to return the last month’s rent deposit.

Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, a landlord must apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. This mean the first question before the Board here is: when did the tenancy terminate?

The parties agree that they had a written tenancy agreement with a fixed term of 8-months commencing on September 1, 2025 to April 30, 2026. It was further undisputed that the Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $650.00 on September 1, 2025.
It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 21, 2026 and returned the keys to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that he has a disability and his parents assist with certain aspects of his life which included his tenancy. The Tenant stated that the conversations surrounding the termination of the tenancy occurred with his father [name] (‘HS’) and therefore the Tenant was not involved in the discussion regarding the termination of the tenancy or vacating the rental unit. Further, he stated that he could have been the individual the Landlord spoke to regarding her concerns and the termination of the tenancy.

HS testified that he is the Tenant’s father and he and his wife assist the Tenant with specific responsibilities regarding his day-to-day life, which included the Tenant’s tenancy. [name] testified that on March 9, 2026, he and the Landlord had a phone call discussing the tenancy and her concerns regarding the Tenant’s behaviour. [name] stated that during the call he suggested that the Tenant should move from the rental unit due to the late-night calls from the Landlord where she stated she would change the locks. Finally, HS testified that on March 19, 2026, he and the Landlord had a phone call where he informed the Landlord the Tenant would be vacating the rental unit on March 21, 2026. HS stated that he chose to terminate the tenancy quickly due to the statements made by the Landlord and his concerns the Tenant would be locked out of the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that she did not agree to terminate the tenancy prior to April 30, 2026, as such the Tenant did not terminate in accordance with the Act. Analysis

Section 47 of the Act provides that a tenant may terminate a fixed-term tenancy by giving the landlord a notice of termination in accordance with [name]. Even if I accept the Tenant’s testimony that they informed the Landlord that the Tenant was terminating their tenancy due to the concern that the Landlord would change the locks, the Tenant acknowledges they terminated the tenancy with 2-days notice. This notice does not comply with subsection 44(4) which states to terminate a tenancy for a fixed term the Tenant shall give at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, which would mean that the earliest date the Tenant could terminate the tenancy would be May 31, 2026. Furthermore, there was no agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy early.
Therefore, the tenancy did not lawfully terminate when the Tenant vacated on just a few days notice on March 19, 2026.

Pursuant to s. 88(1) of the Act, if a tenant provides a notice of termination that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a valid notice. In this case, the earliest valid termination date the Tenant could have provided on March 19 was May 31, 2026, as the Tenant was required to terminate the tenancy in accordance with s. 44 of the Act.
However, the Landlords re-rented the unit for May 1, 2026, which means the Tenant’s liability to pay rent ended on April 30, 2026 in accordance with s. 88(3) of the Act.

This means that the Landlord was entitled to apply the Tenant’s deposit to the rent due under the Lease Agreement for the month of April 2026, unless the evidence establishes the Landlords failed to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses by re-renting the unit as soon as possible. (See ss. 88(4) and 16.)

I find that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord failed to reasonably mitigate their losses and could have found a new tenant to rent the unit earlier than May 1, 2026. In this case the unit was re-rented only one month after the Tenants vacated which seems reasonable in the circumstances.

As a result, and pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, the Landlord was correct in applying the deposit to the rent due for the month of April 2026. Therefore, they are not retaining the deposit in contravention of the Act and this part of the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $198.00. This amount represents: • $150.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $1,398.00 on or before July 10, 2026. Does the Landlord and Tenant Board have jurisdiction to hear this application?

For the reasons set out below, I find, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does apply to the relationship between the parties. While the Landlords asserts that the Tenant was required to share both the bathroom and kitchen facilities, this is insufficient to establish a genuine living situation that is captured by the exemption contained in section 5(i) of the Act which states: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located; The Facts
It was undisputed that the Landlords are the owner of the residential complex. It was also undisputed that the Tenant paid rent to the Landlords in exchange for use and occupation of the rental unit.

The parties agree there is a formal OSL that was executed on August 13, 2024 (DOC- 8162686). Neither the OSL nor additional terms outline state that the Tenants will be required to share facilities with the Landlords. The dispute between the parties revolves around whether the Landlords resided in the rental unit during the pivotal period when tenancy began and whether the Landlords and the Tenant were required at that time to share a kitchen and washroom with each other.
It was undisputed that at the commencement of the tenancy neither Landlord lived at the rental unit.

The Landlord, [name] (‘ZJ’) submits that section 5(i) of the Act is applicable in this case for 2 reasons 1) the rental unit is the Landlords primary residence which is supported through documentary evidence which included the Landlord’s driver’s licenses being registered to the address of the rental unit, utility bills and a bank statement; and, 2) the Tenant knew that she would be required to share the kitchen and bathroom facilities when they returned from oversees.

ZJ referred to the Landlord’s evidence package (DOC-8093321) in support of their submission that the rental unit is exempt under s. 5(i) of the Act. ZJ referred to page 2 of the evidence package which showed her and her mother’s driver’s licenses which were registered to the rental unit. Further she referred to page 3-4, which showed bills from Metergy, the electricity provider with [name]’s (‘XT’) on the bill. Further, ZJ stated that the Landlords had one property registered with this company, further supporting their submission. Furthermore, ZJ referred to page 6 of the package, showing an aerial view of the layout of the rental unit. ZJ submitted that the location of the bathroom and one kitchen that was to be shared by the Landlords and Tenant.

The Tenant submits that 5(i) does not apply in this case as she was not informed that she would be required to share the facilities, did not share the facilities at the commencement of the tenancy as neither Landlord was present in the rental unit for over 6-months. The signed OSL and additional terms referred to her as a Tenant and she submits that she ought to have the protections and rights of a tenant per the Act. Furthermore, the Tenant submits that she had not seen ZJ at the rental unit during the entire tenancy. Regarding the Landlord, [name], she arrived at the rental unit without notice 6-months after the tenancy commenced and stayed in a bedroom for approximately 1-2 months and then left; she stated that she did not agree to this arrangement. Analysis

In Cowie v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628, the Divisional Court held that the Board must examine the situation between the parties at the commencement of the lease when determining whether the exemption in section 5(i) of the Act applies, it found that the Act: . . . explicitly creates an exemption from the general application of the Act only if the person in the category of the respondent “lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”. That means that the respondent was required to live in the building at the time when she rented the room to the appellant in order for the exemption to apply. It was not sufficient that she merely intended to move in at some subsequent time. Nor was it sufficient that she actually did move in at a subsequent time

The evidence from both parties establishes that neither Landlord was living in the residential complex at the commencement of the tenancy. For over 6-months the Tenant was alone within the rental unit until the Landlord, [name] arrived at the rental unit unannounced and stayed in one of the bedrooms for approximately 1-2 months and then left. Therefore, applying [name] v. Bindlish to these facts, I find the rental unit does not fall within the exemption contained in section 5(i) of the Act.

In addition, while the Landlords assert that the Tenant was aware that she would be sharing facilities with the Landlord, there is no mention of that requirement in the lease. Therefore, I prefer the Tenant’s evidence that she was not informed that she would be required to share the facilities.

As a result, the Landlords did not meet the onus of establishing on a balance of probabilities that they shared a bathroom and/or kitchen with the Tenant at the commencement of the tenancy and has not established that the tenancy falls under the exemption in section 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $1,350.00 to the Tenant.
This application is about the return of a last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant paid the Landlords a rent deposit of $1,350.00 on August 31, 2024.
Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act a landlord must apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. This mean the first question I must determine is when did the tenancy terminate?

The parties agree that they had a written tenancy agreement with a fixed term of 12 months commencing on September 1, 2024, and ending on August 31, 2025. They also agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and returned the keys to the Landlords on July 31, 2025. The Tenant had paid the rent for July 2025.
The difficulty here is that a tenancy is not legally terminated simply by the tenant vacating. Under the Act a tenancy is terminated by Board order, by valid notice to terminate or by agreement.

The Tenant testified that on May 27, 2025, she sent a text via WeChat to XT with an N9 Notice to Terminate the Tenancy (‘N9 notice’) as of July 31, 2025 (DOC – 7636090). The Tenant stated that the Landlord responded with the ���� (‘OK’) [name] which she took to mean that [name] was agreeing to the Tenant’s termination date.

ZJ first testified that the Tenant’s last month deposit was withheld due to the damage within the rental unit. ZJ further testified the Tenant failed to provide appropriate notice per the Act as she attempted to terminate the tenancy prior to the end of the fixed term using an N9 Notice to Terminate the Tenancy (‘N9 notice’) via WeChat, which is not valid notice. Finally, ZJ stated that the Landlords use of the OK emoji was not an agreement or acceptance of the Tenant’s notice to terminate. She stated that emoji meant only that she understood she was moving from the rental unit, not an acceptance of the early termination.
It was undisputed that the Landlords re-rented the unit for September 1, 2025. Analysis

Section 37(1) of the Act states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. This means to terminate the obligation to pay rent the tenancy must be terminated by proper notice, by agreement, or by Board order. In order for a tenant’s N9 notice of termination to be valid where there is a fixed-term one year leased, the termination date cannot be prior to the last day of the lease. In addition, the N9 Notice must be given to the landlord at least 60 days before the termination date: sections 44(4) and 47 of the RTA/

Here, the N9 notice the Tenant gave the Landlord on May 27, 2025 was not valid as the earliest date the Tenant could have given as a date of termination would have been August 31, 2025, in accordance with [name]).

However, I must also consider whether the parties entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy effective July 31,2026, [name]) of the Act provides that “A notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy”.

The Landlord’s testimony on this issue was contradictory. At first, the ZJ stated the last months deposit was being held due to the damage within the rental unit, then she stated that it was due t the Tenant’s non-compliance of the Act. Where the Landlord’s testimony is contradictory, I rely on the documentary evidence before me. I find that [name] responded to the Tenant’s stated intention to terminate the tenancy effective July 31, 2026 using the OK emoji which is commonly understood to mean "that's correct" or "sounds good" and is commonly used to express approval, agreement or perfection when responding to a text message.

On the issue of whether a emoji can be a sufficient basis for a finding that parties have entered into a binding agreement I am guided by the persuasive case Saskatchewan case of South West Terminal Ltd. v Achter Land, 2023 SKKB 116 at paragraphs 36 to 38: [36] I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that [name] okayed or approved the contract just like he had done before except this time he used a �� emoji. In my opinion, when considering all of the circumstances that meant approval of the flax contract and not simply that he had received the contract and was going to think about it. In my view a reasonable bystander knowing all of the background would come to the objective understanding that the parties had reached consensus ad item – a meeting of the minds – just like they had done on numerous other occasions. [37] Additionally, I find under these circumstances a �� emoji is “an action in electronic form” that can be used to allow to express acceptance as contemplated under The Electronic Information and Documents Act, 2000, SS 2000, c E-7.22 [EIDA] as per s. 18: 18(1) Unless the parties agree otherwise, an offer or the acceptance of an offer, or any other matter that is material to the formation or operation of a contract, may be expressed: (a) by means of information or a document in an electronic form; or (b) by an action in an electronic form, including touching or clicking on an appropriately designated icon or place on a computer screen or otherwise communicating electronically in a manner that is intended to express the offer, acceptance or other matter. (2) A contract shall not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely by reason that information or a document in an electronic form was used in its formation [38] I note Justice [name] in Quilichini v Wilson’s Greenhouse, 2017 SKQB 10, [2017] 8 WWR 375 [Quilichini] interpreted this provision of the EIDA as follows: [10] The legislation is clear. Agreement to contractual terms can be expressed by touching or clicking on an appropriately designated icon or place on a computer screen. The fact that the contract could have alternatively been executed by printing a hard copy and having a participant sign a hard copy form does not detract from the foregoing. The fact that there are optional ways to execute the contract does not lead to the conclusion that using only one of those options does not constitute agreement.

I find the tenancy in this instance was terminated by agreement on May 27, 2026 when [name] acknowledged the Tenant’s intention to terminate the tenancy effective July 31, 2026, by providing a response which is widely understood to communicate acceptance or agreement. So, the Tenant was liable for the rent up until July 31, 2025, the date the tenancy terminated.

As a result of the agreement to terminate the tenancy on July 31, 2026, I find that the Landlord is retaining the deposit in contravention of the Act and therefore the $1,350.00 deposit paid by the Tenant on August 31, 2024 must be returned. 28. [name] is not entitled to use a rent deposit to cover any alleged damage caused by the Tenant. The Landlord must file an application at the LTB seeking an order requiring the Tenant to pay compensation for damages. 29. This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,398.00. This amount represents: • $1,350.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The parties were before the LTB on November 29, 2024 wherein the Tenants requested an adjournment as they had vacated the unit and wished to amend the remedies in their application. At that time, the matter was adjourned to allow the Tenants to file a request to amend. On January 8, 2025, interim order, LTB-T-026805-23-IN, was issued directing the Tenants to file their amended application on or before December 20, 2024 and that they were permitted to serve the Landlords via email. The Tenants uploaded to the Tribunals Ontario Portal (‘portal’) a request to amend the application, seeking new remedies, on August 13, 2025.

At the hearing, the Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that the amended application was not served on the Landlords or provided by the deadline as directed by the LTB. She also submitted that a certificate of service has also not been filed. The Tenants’ Legal Representative could not provide information as to whether the amended application was provided to the Landlords via email at the time, but submitted that a copy was provided in the Tenants’ evidence brief given seven days prior to this hearing. He also submitted that the amended application is in the portal and has been there for over ten months, that the Landlords knew that an amended application was forthcoming, and when the parties were before the LTB in February 2026 for a case conference the amendments were discussed.

As per Rule 15.4 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure (the ‘Rules’), the LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

In these circumstances, I was satisfied that it was appropriate to grant the Tenants’ request to amend the application in order to have a fair and expeditious hearing. Although, the amended application was not served on the Landlords, they were aware that the Tenants sought to amend the remedies requested as they had vacated the rental unit, a copy of the amended application was uploaded to the portal in August 2025, and these amendments, being the remedies only, do not significantly change the Landlords’ response to this application. [name], it would be a significant prejudice to the Tenants if the amendments were not allowed as they would be out of time to file a new application.

The application is amended to include a request for the following remedies: a) $4560.00 for rent abatement; b) $900.00 for increased rent for the one year period after the Tenants vacated being a rent difference of $75.00 per month; and c) $500.00 for moving and storage expenses. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

This tenancy commenced on October 1, 2022 for a fixed term ending on October 1, 2023, at a monthly rent of $1,900.00 due on the 1st day of each month. The rental unit was a two bedroom basement unit, including its own bathroom, kitchen and living space. The Landlords lived in the upper portion of the dwelling. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2023. Illegal entry 8. [name] (VI), one of the Tenants, was the only one who testified at the hearing. She stated that she could not point out the exact date but her mother, AE, had noticed some of her paperwork missing, things misplaced, and inner doors opened within the unit. She also stated that the Landlords never provided any notices of entry and would just knock on the inner door (the one between their units) to talk to them. When asked how many times she thought that the Landlords had entered without notice, VI responded maybe once or twice as she does not know because they entered when no one was home. 9. Under cross-examination, VI could not provide any information as to the contents of a possible video recording of an illegal entry claimed in the application. [name] stated that she did not know if her mother had provided the recording to the Landlords. Under cross- examination, VI confirmed that they did not call the police regarding any illegal entries or complain to the Landlords about it in any of their written communications. 10. One of the Landlords, [name], FA, denied ever entering the rental unit and stated that he is aware that he must serve notice of entry in writing at least 24 hours in advance. He stated that he never received any complaint from the Tenants of someone entering their unit or them having missing items. 11. Under cross-examination, FA maintained that he never entered the unit during the tenancy. He also stated that he had once given a 24 hour notice of entry to do required maintenance for the internet but did not disclose a copy of that notice to the Tenants in advance to be entered into evidence. 12. The Landlords’ son, IA, testified that he never entered the unit without notice on February 21, 2023. IA also testified that AE did accuse them verbally of entering the unit on this date when they were discussing the utility bills. 13. Under cross-examination, IA confirmed that his father emailed the Tenants a 24 hour notice of entry as they needed to do maintenance on the internet but the Bell technician arrived earlier than the time provided in the notice, so they had to wait as the Tenants would not open the door. He also testified that when they did attempt to enter at the time provided in the notice, the Tenants would not allow them in the unit. 14. The evidence before me was insufficient to find that the Landlords illegally entered the rental unit. VI’s evidence was hearsay as it was information that had been told to her from her mother. As well, the Tenants’ evidence was mere suspicion that the Landlords had entered the unit, referring to moved and/or missing items. The Tenants never complained to the Landlords of anything missing. Therefore, I cannot find that the Landlords illegally entered the unit. [name] and Harassment 15. Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 16. Section 23 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 17. Harassment is not defined in the Act, however it is generally accepted that harassment is a course of conduct that a person knows, or should know, would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate, lawful purpose. Altercation – February 21, 2023 18. VI stated that on or about February 21, 2023 there was an altercation between her mother, AE, and the Landlords’ son, IA, that resulted in her mother crying and calling the police. She stated that IA had approached her mother about paying the utilities in cash without providing a copy of the bill. She also stated that her mother said that IA had threatened to take her to court. She further stated that this incident left her mother quite shaken that she had to file a police report. 19. FA stated that the Tenants’ agreement was to pay 40% of the utilities for the premises. He stated that he provided the bills with the calculations via email to AE every month, but they never paid. He also stated that he had to take them to the LTB and only then did they pay the utility costs. FA confirmed that he was not in the country when his son went to talk to AE about the outstanding utility bills in February 2023. 20. IA testified that on February 21, 2023, he knocked on the Tenants door to ask about the unpaid utilities. He testified that AE told him that she was waiting for some funds from the government for utilities, then she started to accuse and shout at him that they are entering the unit and stealing her paperwork which resulted in an argument. IA also testified that the police did attend, and resolved the situation by speaking with both of them. 21. Under cross-examination, IA maintained that he did not threaten AE, he responded that he asked her when she will pay and if she does not pay then they will have to go to the Landlord board for her to leave. Under cross-examination when asked why not just serve a N5 Notice of termination, IA responded that he did not know about that and had not received any legal advice at that time. He testified that it was after this time that he connected with the Landlords’ Legal Representative. 22. Based on the evidence before me there was no dispute that an altercation or argument occurred between AE and IA on February 21, 2023 and that the police were called. The Tenants assert that the Landlords’ son threatened AE on this date. IA confirmed that he essentially told AE if she did not pay the utilities costs they would take her to the LTB to have her evicted. I am not satisfied that this amounts to a threat as this is a landlord’s recourse for resolving this particular issue and a tenant can be evicted for not paying utility cost they are required to pay under their tenancy agreement. 23. Additionally, based on the evidence before me I was not satisfied that the Landlords’ son was the aggressor in this altercation. He testified that it was AE who began shouting at him and making false accusations. AE did not testify at the hearing. [name] was not present during this altercation so her evidence is hearsay. Therefore, the best evidence before me was that of IA who asserted that it was AE who first started shouting and making false accusations. There appeared to be no dispute that the Tenants had not paid the utility costs they were required to pay under the tenancy agreement at that time, so IA’s request for payment was not unlawful. Issues with mail 24. [name] stated that the Landlords would provide them their mail as they did not have a separate key to the mailbox. She stated she had ordered something and emailed the Landlords asking for the package and that their response was that they are not entitled to services like mail. A copy of this email was not provided into evidence. 25. FA stated that the Tenants never complained of an issue with receiving their mail but that they did request a key to the mailbox which he felt unsafe providing as it is a shared mailbox. He also stated that they provided all mail to the Tenants either by leaving it at their door or by hand. He also stated that even after the Tenants vacated he repeatedly requested that they come collect their mail and they only came months later. 26. There was no dispute that the Tenants were not provided with a mailbox key during their tenancy. However, I was not satisfied that this amounted to a substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the unit or the complex. VI did not confirm that this package was not received, or not received on time, and there was no other evidence of any issues with receiving mail during the tenancy. FA confirmed that mail was given to the Tenants at their door or by hand. In this case, I find it more likely than not the VI simply requested a mailbox key, not a package, and it was denied. I was also satisfied that the Landlords’ denial of providing a mailbox key did not impede the Tenants ability to receive their mail. 27. As per the above, the Tenants have not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords’ breached their obligations under the Act. Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the following reasons I find that the Tenant failed to prove the bulk of her application on a balance of probabilities. However, I have found that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities in three minor ways, and the Landlord is ordered to pay the Tenant a $500.00 rent abatement for those issues.

The Tenant testified that on the evening of January 24, 2024, water began coming through the ceiling vent in the rental unit bathroom. The Tenant testified that the water was originally dripping but then became a solid stream. The Tenant testified that the leak went on for an hour and that eventually the entire rental unit was flooded.

The Tenant testified that she repeatedly called the Landlord but could not get through. The Tenant testified that she called 911, the fire department assisted her to find the water shut off valve, that herself and the fire department called the Landlord and that eventually the power was shut down. An internal email from the Landlord’s office reflects that the actual leak was stopped on the same night it happened (DOC-7947174, page 3).
