I have no evidence about what caused the flood. I therefore cannot find that the flood was the result of the Landlord breaching their maintenance obligations. The question before me is whether the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations regarding repairing the damage to the rental unit following the leak. For the following reasons I find that the Landlord largely did not, with three minor exceptions. Evidence

The parties provided the following evidence about the events that took place after the flood: [name] show that on January 24, 2024 a piece of the ceiling near where the leak happened was cut open (DOC-7974863, page 55). • The Tenant testified that on January 25, 2024, the day following the flood, the Landlord visited the rental unit to assess the situation but advised the Tenant that not much could be done because everything was still wet (DOC-7974863, page 41). Photographs taken on January 25, 2024 show a lifted floorboard and water soaked items (DOC-7974863, page 56). • The Tenant was served with a notice of entry for January 26, 2024. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not attend because the drywall was still wet (DOC- 7974863, page 41). • An internal email from the Landlord’s office (DOC-7947174, page 3) and the testimony of the Landlord’s agent [name] support that the Landlord had to wait for the drying to finish before they could complete repair work. [name] testified that to avoid another flood, the leak must be monitored for at least a week to ensure that the correct pipe was fixed. [name] testified that waiting and observing was required. • The Tenant testified that she thinks the Landlord attended the rental unit again on January 29, 2024 to check on the situation. [name] taken on January 31, 2024 show that more holes were cut in the bathroom ceiling (DOC-7974863, page 57). • The Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of entry for February 5, 2024 (DOC- 7974863, page 41). • The Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of entry for February 7, 2024 (DOC- 7974863, page 42). The Tenant testified that someone checked the drywall and did some work on the washroom ceiling. [name] taken on February 8, 2024 show that repair work is underway. Part of the ceiling has been patched up but there is a remaining hole. Construction supplies and debris can be seen throughout the bathroom (DOC-7974863, page 58). • The Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of entry for February 9, 2024 (DOC- 7974863, page 42). • The Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of entry for February 12, 2024 (DOC- 7974863, page 42). The Tenant testified that a 7-member cleaning crew attended the rental unit. • A photograph taken on February 12, 2024 shows what looks like it could be mould starting to form in the corner of a room (DOC-7974863, page 59). • The Landlord supplied photographs taken on February 12, 2024 that show a repaired bathroom ceiling and a small bubble at the top of a window (DOC- 7947174, page 9). • The Tenant testified that on February 14, 2024 the people who had repainted the rental unit knocked on her door and indicated that they had come back to put up the curtains. [name] taken on February 14, 2024 show a repaired ceiling, small mark or bubble on a wall, a slightly lifted floorboard, a bubble by a curtain road, and what looks like mould on a wall by a bed (DOC-7974863, page 60). • The Tenant testified that the Landlord told her all work was done on February 14, 2024. • The Tenant testified that she contacted the City bylaw office and that they attended the rental unit on February 15, 2024 to do an inspection. • The City issued an order to comply with a number of required repairs (DOC- 7974863, page 47) including issues with the flooring, windows, mildew, mould, painting etc. The deadline for the Landlord to comply was March 19, 2024. • On February 27, 2024, the Landlord emailed the Tenant indicating that they were writing to the Tenant about the list of repairs they got from the City that needed to scheduled. The Landlord asked the Tenant for her preferred time of day to do the work ASAP so that the work can start. • The Tenant testified that on March 6, 2024 contractors came and wiped off mould next to her bed but did not disinfect. • The Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of entry for March 18, 2024 (DOC- 7974863, page 44). • The Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of entry for March 19, 2024 (DOC- 7974863, page 44). • The Tenant testified that she requested that the Landlord terminate her lease but the Landlord refused. The Tenant testified that she had not been staying in the rental unit since the flood and that she signed a lease for a new apartment on March 15, 2024, for a new tenancy to begin on March 20, 2024. However, the Tenant continued to pay rent until August 2025 and served an N9 notice of termination with August 27, 2025 as the termination date. The Tenant testified that she did not visit the rental unit from March 20, 2024 to August 26, 2025. • The Tenant testified that she returned to the rental unit on August 26, 2025 to do a move out inspection. Photographs taken on that day show that the bubble in the ceiling near the curtain rod appears to have popped as there is now a hole and debris around it, one of the floor tiles is very slightly lifted, and there is some patchwork that appears to have been done without the walls being painted afterwards (DOC-7974863, page 68). The Tenant also testified that there was peeling wallpaper and that there was still mould in the corner of one of the rooms in the rental unit, however the Tenant provided no photographs of those items.

The Tenant testified that no one actually attended the rental unit on February 5, 2024, March 18, 2024, or March 19, 2024 despite the notices of entry served by the Landlord. However, during cross examination the Tenant agreed that she was not present at the rental unit for the entire entry window on March 18, 2024 and March 19, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she never heard back from the City regarding whether the work order was cleared. The Landlord’s agent testified that he assumes the work order was cleared but he was not employed by the Landlord at the time. The Landlord’s agent testified that there are no current work orders from the City about the rental unit.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord falsely claimed the repairs were done when they weren’t, didn’t meet the timelines provided, and contradicted themselves. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s leasing agent told her the day following the flood that the repairs would be done within 5 days. In an email dated January 25, 2024 the Landlord says that “all damages to the property have been diligently addressed and repaired” (DOC- 7974863, page 37). The Tenant testified that she was initially told that the repairs would only take a week or two weeks. The Tenant testified that on February 27, 2024 she got a call from the Landlord who indicated that the work was mostly complete and would take 2- 3 days.

The Tenant testified that she did not feel safe in the rental unit because there were so many notices of entry, so many contractors showing up, and they sometimes showed up without notice. However, the Tenant agreed that no one ever entered without her permission. I also note that the Tenant filed a maintenance application not an application about tenant’s rights regarding illegal entries or substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Analysis

A flood in a rental unit is inherently undesirable and having numerous contractors attended to fix the problem is inherently disrupted. However, that does not alone establish that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The Court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the repairs could not happen immediately because the Landlord had to wait for drying to occur first and had to monitor the leak.
The evidence of both parties supports that between January 24, 2024 to March 19, 2024 the Landlord repeatedly sent contractors to the rental unit to undertake various stages of the repairs.

The photographs of both parties (DOC-7947174, page 9 and DOC-7974863, page 60) show a repaired ceiling by February 14, 2024. I do not agree with the Tenant’s assessment that the ceiling work was not done to the required standard. The hole is closed, the ceiling has been painted, and the Tenant presented no evidence from anyone with construction knowledge that the ceiling repair was subpar. There is also no evidence of any further flooding incidents.

While the City found defects in the rental unit the evidence supports that the Landlord was addressing those issues. The Landlord emailed the Tenant about the repairs and sent contractors to the unit to address the issues, including on March 6, 2024 to address the mould. I’m not satisfied by the Tenant’s testimony that no one attended the rental unit on March 18, 2024 or March 19, 2024 as she was not present during the entire entry window and its possible work occurred like an inspection that would not leave any physical changes in the rental unit. The Tenant also signed a new lease March 15, 2024, for a tenancy to start on March 20, 2024 without giving the Landlord an opportunity to resolve the problem.

The Tenant testified that there was still mould in the corner of one of the rooms and peeling wallpaper during her August 26, 2025 move out inspection. However, the Tenant provided no photographs of those issues. Without photographs I’m not satisfied by the Tenant’s assessment of those issues. It’s not that I have a concern with the Tenant’s credibility, but rather the accuracy of her assessment of outstanding issues. The Tenant submits that the bathroom ceiling was not repaired when photographs show that it was DOC-7947174, page 9). The Tenant seems to be submitting that minor aesthetic issues constitute maintenance breaches. This leads me to have a concern about the reliability of the Tenant’s testimony in the absence of photographs. The Landlord also testified that there are no outstanding work orders by the City, which supports that the City closed their file at some point.

While I agree with the Tenant that the Landlord provided her with conflicting timelines, that alone does not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations. The initial assessment was given by a leasing agent, not a contractor, and before more substantial assessment had happened. While the Landlord could have communicated with the Tenant better throughout the repairs, the Landlord did ultimately resolve the ceiling leak issue in a reasonable timeframe.

As such I find that the Landlord responded reasonably to the leak, repaired the issue, addressed the mould, and was in the process of addressing the issues identified by the city when the Tenant signed a new lease agreement. As such the bulk of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. I do however find that the Tenant proved some minor breaches of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations.

The Landlord’s photograph from February 12, 2024 (DOC-7947174, page 9) shows that some repair was made to the top of one of the windows in the rental unit but that a bubble remains. The Tenant’s photograph from August 26, 2025 shows that the bubble popped (DOC-7974863, page 64). I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations regarding the bubble near the window as the repair was clearly inadequate and did not address the problem. I’m not satisfied by the Landlord’s explanation that someone may have entered the rental unit in the Tenant’s absence and caused the damage to the bubble area around the window. The Tenant denied leaving the door open and the damage is exactly where the bubble was.
I find that the Tenant’s photographs from August 26, 2025 establish that the Landlord never addressed a crack on the rental unit floor (DOC-7974863, page 66). However, the crack is minor.

I also find that the Tenant’s photographs from August 26, 2025 establish that the Landlord patched up holes in the living room of the rental unit but did not paint over them (DOC- 7974863, page 67). Remedies

The remedies sought by the Tenant are to end her tenancy on March 20, 2024, the date she stopped living in the rental unit and a 100% rent abatement from the time she vacated to August 2025 when she terminated the tenancy with a notice of termination.

As I have found that the Landlord addressed the leak issue in a reasonable manner, I do not find the remedy of terminating the tenancy to be reasonable. The only maintenance breaches I have found are a bubble by the window, a minor crack in the floor, and some unpainted over patches. None of those issues would significantly impact the Tenant or justify ending the tenancy. The Tenant led insufficient evidence to establish that the rental unit was unfit for habitation. Additionally, the Tenant chose to stop living in the rental unit and it’s unclear what fixes the Landlord would have made to those issues had the Tenant followed up about the issues with the Landlord.

As the Tenant chose to stop living in the rental unit the maintenance issues I have found did not impact her. However, I find a nominal rent abatement of $500.00 to be reasonable. The Landlord should have fixed the bubble by the window, crack in the floor, and painted over the patches. While not living there, the Tenant was still a tenant and should have been provided with a rental unit without those issues.
The Tenant incurred costs of 48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the application is dismissed. Illegal charge collected
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenants paid the Landlord a key deposit in the amount of $1,000.00 on April 8, 2022.
The Tenants filed their application on March 27, 2026.

The Tenants testified that this $1,000.00 charge did not reflect the replacement value of the keys they were provided with. The keys are standard metal keys. No programmable fobs were provided to the Tenants.
In order for a key deposit to be legal it must reflect the expected direct replacement cost of the keys. This is according to section 17(3) of [name]. 516/06 General of the Act.

When a key deposit given at the start of a tenancy is considered legal in its amount according to this regulation, it has both a collection date and a retention date. That is, it is legally collectible at the start of a tenancy, and a landlord is legally permitted to retain it until the end of a tenancy, when it is to be returned in exchange for keys.
However, in this case the deposit was illegal in its amount when it was collected. Therefore, there is no legal retention date that the Landlord was permitted to wait until, before returning it.

This application is brought under section 135(1) of the Act which states: “A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.”

Section 135(4) states: “No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act […].”
The Tenants have filed this application over one year since the amount was first collected and thus are out of time to seek reimbursement of this sum.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: No (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The application is amended to correctly identify the Tenant as [name].

The Tenant’s application does not seek a remedy or provide an explanation regarding the claim. Upon my inquiry, the Tenant stated that his application is regarding the key deposit of $500.00. He referred to the lease agreement which confirms that $500.00 was held by the Landlord. During the hearing, the Landlord’s representative, indicated that the Landlord was prepared to respond to the Tenant’s claim. Therefore, I was satisfied to hear the merits of the application.

The Tenant testified that he was provided with two keys but he only returned one key back to the Landlord when he moved out of the rental unit on August 27, 2025. He stated that the cost for the keys are approximately $250.00 each.

The Landlord’s agent, [name], testified that one key was returned back to the Landlord on August 27, 2025. The Tenant did not return one key and one fob. The Landlord was required to change the locks. [name] stated that the Landlord incurred the cost of changing the locks to avoid safety or security issues in the future for any new Tenant.

While section 134 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 contains a general prohibition on a landlord imposing additional, non-rent charges on a tenant, section 17 of O.Reg. 516/06 under the Act provides for an exemption for “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.
Under this provision, if a Tenant has paid a key deposit to a Landlord they are entitled to have that payment refunded when they return the keys.

However, in this case the evidence establishes that the Tenant lost the second set of keys which required the Landlord to incur the cost of at least $500.00 to change the rental unit’s locks. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord incurred a reasonable expense as a result of the Tenant’s action and was not required to refund the $500.00 collected from the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must allow the Tenants to apply the illegally collected rent deposit to the arrears of rent for April and May, 2026.

The Landlord collected rent more than the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') by requiring the Tenants to pay not only a first and last month’s rent deposit but also two additional months of rent at the outset of the tenancy in the amount of $5,280.00.

The Tenants testified that they understood that these additional two months rent would be applied to the second- and third-month’s rent of the tenancy. Mrs. [name]name] testified that her husband receives Ontario Disability Support Payments (‘ODSP’) and that it was unrealistic for them to have agreed to place such a large amount of money with the Landlord to be applied to the end of tenancy when it arose.

The Landlord testified that page 35 of DOC8174640-26 (paragraph 51 of the [name] to the Lease) states that the additional two months was a voluntary payment and that it would be applied to the second and third last months of the tenancy. The Tenants did sign this document.
The Tenant testified that this payment was not made voluntarily but rather because they were desperate to secure housing.
The Landlord relied heavily on case law in support of his position that he was entitled to collect the additional two months rent and to apply that rent as he sees fit.
I disagree with the Landlord’s interpretation of the cases cited and below I have distinguished them on their facts.

Further, I return to the clear language of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’). Sections 105 and 106 of the Act clearly provide that the only rent deposit a landlord can collect is an amount equal to one month’s rent. Section 134(1)(b) states that unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord
While there are some permitted exemptions to the prohibition in Section 134(1)(b), they are not relevant to this matter.

The purpose of sections 106 and 134 is to protect prospective tenants from exactly the coercion evident in this case. The Tenants were desperate to obtain accommodation. The Landlord discerned that he might have difficulty collecting the rent on a regular basis because the husband is on ODSP. The Landlord saw an opportunity to ensure payment of rent or protection from a large amount of arrears if the Tenants were unable to pay rent. This case differs from all of the cases cited to me in which the courts and adjudicators have found that IF prospective tenants voluntarily agree to a greater deposit, it does not violate section 106 of the Act.

In LTB-L-043744-22, the adjudicator found that the tenants offered the additional months of rent to compete with other prospective tenants. In LTB-T-054124-23, the adjudicator found that the tenants did not provide any evidence of duress. In this case, the Tenants have specifically identified their reliance on ODSP as a reason they did not voluntarily provide the additional funds. In LTB-T-089244-23, the five months of additional rent collected had already been applied to arrears and therefore there was no remedy to be offered by the LTB. This is precisely the remedy sought by the Tenants in the instant case. They seek to have the additional payments applied to arrears of rent to bring their rent current as they have already paid June rent in full.
I do not accept that the Tenants made the additional payment voluntarily and find that it was an illegal payment contrary to the Act.
ordered: The Landlord shall apply the amount of $5,280.00 in excess rent collected to the months of April and May 2026 June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant’s rent deposit. The Tenant entered into a one-year tenancy with the Landlord beginning on July 1, 2025, and ending on June 30, 2026. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on March 24, 2026. This was a verbal lease. In the Tenant’s own words “I decided to break my lease.” The Tenant provided a text message to the Landlord on February 20, 2026 which purported to be a notice of termination of the tenancy (DOC 7682108) ending the tenancy at the end of March.
The Landlord wrote back to the Tenant on the same day indicating that this was not sufficient notice but that she would accept termination of the tenancy at the end of April.

The Tenant paid March rent and vacated the unit on March 24, 2026. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord re-rented the unit “in April” without providing any evidence of this or any information as to how he came to this knowledge.

As well, the chain of text messages provided by the Tenant as DOC 7682108 cuts off some of the responses by the Landlord to the Tenant’s request for return of his last month’s rent deposit causing me to be concerned about the text messages that the Tenant has not presented and what explanations they might offer for the Landlord’s position.

Section 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) provides that a tenant may terminate a fixed-term tenancy by serving a notice of termination in accordance with [name]. The text message the Tenant sent to the Landlord on February 20, 2026 does not comply with subsection 44(4) which provides that the termination date for a fixed term tenancy agreement cannot be prior to the last day of the fixed term, which in this case was June 30,2026. Furthermore, there was no agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy early.
Therefore, the tenancy did not lawfully terminate when the Tenant vacated on March 24, 2026.

Pursuant to s. 88(1) of the Act, if a tenant provides a notice of termination that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a valid notice, which in this case was June 30, 2026.

This means that the Landlord was entitled to apply the Tenant’s deposit to the rent due under the tenancy for the month of April 2026, unless the evidence establishes the Landlord either re-rented the unit for April 2026 or failed to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses by attempting re-renting the unit as soon as possible. (See ss. 88(4) and 16.)

The Tenant provided no evidence that the Landlord re-rented the unit in April 2026 or failed to take reasonable steps the mitigate their losses. In the absence of such evidence, I cannot find that the Landlord is improperly withholding the last months’ rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed, and the LTB file is closed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must refund the last month’s rent deposit with interest in the amount of $3,005.25. [name]
The [name] began March 5, 2026 and ended March 31, 2026.
The lawful rent was $3,000.00.
The Tenants paid a last month’s rent deposit on February 6, 2026 of $3000.00 and the Landlord accepted the deposit.
The Tenants never fully moved into the unit because of a cockroach infestation. There is a T2 and T6 application that is the subject of the infestation, so that issue will not be addressed here.
I find the Tenants moved in furniture on March 5, 2026 and moved the furniture out on March 9, 2026, but they never occupied the unit.
The Landlord accepted first month’s rent in a pro-rated amount of $2552.00 to reflect the Tenants moved in after March 1st and the Tenants paid this amount.
The Tenants advised the Landlord that they were not going to continue the tenancy and requested the return of their last month’s rent deposit on March 30, 2026.
I find the Landlord has refused to refund the deposit and downplayed the infestation to justify keeping the deposit. Analysis
Section 106(10) states that a landlord must apply a rent deposit to the last month’s rent before the tenancy terminates.
A Landlord cannot retain rent money after the tenancy has terminated.
As the tenancy terminated on March 31, 2026, there was no last month for which rent was owed, so the Landlord must return the rent deposit to the Tenant.

In addition, section 106(6) states “A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.”
Therefore, I also find that the Landlord owes the Tenant $5.25 in interest on the rent deposit. Remedies
The Tenants are seeking the return of the deposit plus interest.
For the above-stated reasons, the Landlord shall refund the deposit with interest.
ordered: The Landlord shall refund the rent deposit in the amount of $3,005.25 (deposit + interest) by July 6, 2026.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant in the prescribed time, he will owe interest calculated annually at 4%. June 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord's representative advised that the Landlord was not disputing the allegations contained in the application. He acknowledged that the transfer fee paid by the Tenants constituted an illegal charge under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and conceded that the Tenants are entitled to the remedy claimed in the application.

The Landlord's representative further advised that the Landlord has been in receivership since April 26, 2026. He submitted that any amount ordered by the Board would form part of the claims process in the receivership and that there are currently no funds available to reimburse the Tenants. The Tenants acknowledged that they were notified prior to the hearing that the Landlord was in receivership.

I accept the Landlord's admission that the transfer fee was collected contrary to the Act. The evidence before me establishes that the Tenants paid an amount that the Landlord was not entitled to charge. Accordingly, pursuant to the Board's remedial authority under the Act, the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement of the illegal charge in the amount claimed in the application.

The existence of the receivership does not affect the Board's jurisdiction to determine the parties' rights and obligations under the Act or to grant the appropriate remedy. Whether, and in what manner, the Board's order is enforced or satisfied is a separate matter that is governed by the applicable insolvency and receivership proceedings. The Landlord's financial circumstances do not extinguish the Tenants' entitlement to the remedy provided under the Act.

For the reasons given, an order will be issued determining the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act, and to include that the Landlord is to pay the Tenants the amount claimed in the application, representing reimbursement of the illegal charge.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name]: • collected or retained money illegally (T1 application); • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 application); and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application) This combined application was first before the Board on November 4, 2025. The Tenants were unrepresented and declined to speak with Tenant Duty Counsel. The Landlord was present and represented by [name]. The matter was adjourned, peremptory on the Tenants.
reasons: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants terminated in February 2023. The combined T1/T2/T6 application was filed on April 26, 2023.

The application was first before the Board on November 4, 2024 and I adjourned the matter on my own motion in order to permit the Tenants the opportunity to amend their application. The Tenants’ application referred to a schedule which consisted of 255 pages detailing the Tenants’ complaints and evidence. As noted by the Landlord's legal representative, it was difficult to know the Tenants’ allegations of what happened in order to properly respond.

By Interim Order LTB-T-030017-23-IN dated November 14, 2024, I provided the Tenants with specific directions on how to complete clear pleadings, including the need for them to be chronological and consist of concisely stated facts. The Tenants were permitted to specify page numbers of the evidence to support the factual allegations in the pleadings.

The Tenants were provided until December 5, 2024 to serve and file the revised pleadings and dates were provided for submission of evidence for both parties. The Interim Order stated that if a party did not comply with the deadlines, I might refuse to accept evidence or consider issues not disclosed.
No request to amend the application nor revised pleadings were served or filed, and therefore the Tenants did not comply with the Interim Order.

At the hearing on June 12, 2026, Tenant [name] stated that their legal representative was unable to attend the hearing and that he was supposed to have filed revised documents. Whether or not the Tenants’ representative was supposed to have served and filed revised documents, he did not do so. That is a matter between the Tenants and their legal representative which cannot be addressed in this forum.

The Board is required by Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") to “adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.”

The tenancy terminated in February 2023, the application was filed over three years ago on April 26, 2023, and the Tenants were provided with a chance to perfect their application more than a year and a half ago. It is impossible to proceed with the application as it stands.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenants to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenants’ conduct or that of another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. This conduct substantially interfered with the Landlord's reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or another lawful right, privilege, or interest (the ‘Section 88.1 Claim’). On April 16, 2024, the Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household, and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (the ‘First T2 Application’). On April 18, 2024, the Tenants applied for a second order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household, and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenants (the ‘Second T2 Application’). ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 The L2 Application, the Section 88.1 Claim, the First T2 Application, and the Second T2 Application were heard together by videoconference on April 23, 2026. The Landlord, the Tenant [name], and the Tenant’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The parties agree that the Tenant’s moved into the rental unit in 2019, when it was owned by a previous landlord. The Landlord bought the property in February 2024.

The core issue pertaining to all of the applications is whether the Tenants were entitled to use of the garage of the residential complex as a term of the rental agreement. The residential complex is a house and the Tenants’ rental unit is in the basement level of the building. Preliminary Issue: The Landlord’s N5 Notice is Invalid

The Tenant’s legal representative raised the validity of the N5 notice of termination (the ‘N5 Notice’) as a preliminary issue at the hearing. He submitted that the N5 Notice does not contain sufficient reasons and details to constitute a valid notice of termination, per subsection 43(2) of the Act and the leading case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931.

For a notice to contain sufficient reasons and details, a tenant must be able to know the case to be met before the Board, to decide whether to dispute the allegations, and – in the case of a voidable N5 notice – whether to take corrective action to void the notice. Dates and times of the alleged conduct – as well as a detailed description of the conduct – must be provided in the notice.
On May 22, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N5 notice of termination (the ‘N5 Notice’).

No particular dates are attached to the allegations in the N5 Notice. Rather, the Landlord generally states that the Tenants are “continuing” to have “encroached upon and unauthorizedly and illegally occupied the substantial portion of the garage of the rented premises and refused to vacate [their] illegal possession.”

Upon hearing the submissions of the parties, I considered whether the N5 Notice complies with the requirement of subsection 43(2) to provide reasons and details. I did so with a view toward subsection 212(1), which directs that substantial compliance with the Act is sufficient with respect to the contents of notices given under the Act.

In my view, the N5 Notice is not substantially compliant with the requirements of subsection 43(2). All that is clear from the notice is that the allegations are about the use of the garage and that the issue is, in the view of the Landlord, continuing. No details are provided about when this conduct began, when the Tenants “refused” to cease the conduct, or sufficient clarity as to what specific lawful right, privilege, or interest is alleged to have been interfered with by the Tenant. Rather, a broad and sweeping assertion of illegality is made. ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24

The contents of the N5 Notice do not allow the Tenants to meaningfully respond to the allegations. Therefore, I find that the N5 Notice is invalid. The L2 Application to terminate the tenancy must therefore be dismissed. The Section 88.1 Claim
The Landlord’s Section 88.1 Claim for compensation in the amount of $1,890.00 must also be dismissed.
The Section 88.1 Claim does not describe any out-of-pocket expenses arising from any substantial interference by the Tenants. Rather, it asserts a right to compensation generally.

Only out-of-pocket expenses are eligible to be claimed under section 88.1 of the Act. No such expenses have been disclosed in the Landlord’s application. Therefore, the Section 88.1 Claim is dismissed. The First and Second T2 Applications
The Tenant [name] testified at the hearing about the events detailed in the First and Second T2 Applications.

Mr. [name]name] testified that he moved into the rental unit in 2019. He testified that prior to moving into the basement unit, the previous landlord allowed the Tenants to store some of their belongings in the garage pending the completion of renovations in the basement. He testified that once the renovations were complete and the tenancy began, the Tenants continued to store personal items in the garage with the full knowledge of the previous landlord. Mr. [name]name] showed photographs of his personal items in the garage during that period. Per Mr. [name]name], the previous landlord never objected to this arranged use of the shared space.

The Landlord was not a party to the original tenancy agreement but rather stepped into the shoes of the previous Landlords when she bought the property in 2024, per section 18 of the Act. She testified that the previous landlord had told her that the items in the garage were left behind by another tenant who resided upstairs.

No evidence was offered in support of the Landlord’s position that the Tenants are not entitled to use of the garage under the terms of the rental agreement, other than her testimony about a statement made by the previous landlords to her during the course of the sale that the basement tenants did not have access to the garage. This statement from the previous landlords is hearsay. The previous landlords, [name] and [name], were summonsed by the Landlord, but did not comply with the summons and attend the hearing.

I prefer the direct evidence of Mr. [name]name] with respect to whether the Tenants had been using the garage during the tenancy with the knowledge and agreement of the former landlords. Mr. [name]name] provided extensive detail about how the arrangement came to be at the beginning of the tenancy and photographic evidence of his use of the garage throughout his years living in the rental unit. The only evidence presented by the Landlord to the contrary is a hearsay statement – no documentary evidence of what she was told by ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 the previous owners of the property was presented at the hearing. I therefore find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Tenants’ use of the garage for storage of personal belongings was an implied term of the tenancy for its entire duration and continues to be a term of the rental agreement between the Landlord and the Tenants.

Mr. [name]name] testified that, on March 13, 2024, the Tenants received a notice from the Landlord’s former paralegal that they were to remove their property from the garage within 72 hours. A copy of this notice was provided at the hearing, citing section 41 of the Act as the legal authority under which the Landlord was acting.

Section 41 is not applicable in the circumstances of this case. It speaks to the law surrounding the disposal of abandoned property when a tenant vacates a rental unit. This did not occur here. The Tenants remained in possession of the rental unit when this notice was given.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the Tenants immediately sought legal advice after receiving the notice. The Tenants provided a letter – dated March 14, 2024 – authored by a staff lawyer at the Hamilton Community Legal Clinic. In the letter, which is addressed to the Landlord’s former paralegal, the lawyer states the Tenants’ position that the use of the garage is an implied term of the tenancy and that the Tenants have a continuing right to use of the garage. It is clear, based on this letter, that the Tenants disputed the Landlord’s assertion of exclusive use of the garage. In other words, the Landlord was on notice of the Tenants’ position as of March 14, 2026.

Mr. [name]name] testified that on April 16, 2026, the Landlord’s father (acting on the Landlord’s authorization) attended the residential unit with a rented bin with the intention of disposing of the property in the garage. The Tenants objected and told the Landlord’s father to stop disposing of their belongings. The Tenants contacted the Landlord’s paralegal to reiterate their position that the property was not abandoned and that the Landlord had no right to dispose of that property. The Landlord’s paralegal asserted the Landlord’s rights to dispose of the property. At this point, the Tenants filed the First T2 Application.

Per Mr. [name]name]’s testimony, the Landlord’s father reattended the next day – April 17, 2026 – and, again, intended to dispose of the Tenants’ property. The Landlord’s father attended the property with a dumpster and three other individuals. Mr. [name]name] testified that these individuals started throwing objects into the dumpster and harassing the Tenants, who were attempting to intervene.

Police attended the unit after the Tenants called to report the conduct of the Landlord’s father and his associates. A police record documenting the attendance was provided by the Tenants. The report states that the police arrived to find a large dumpster in the driveway of the residential complex full of miscellaneous items, that the parties were advised to co-operate regarding the belongings, and that Mr. [name]name] was directed to assist in identifying which objects belonged to the Tenants and, therefore, should be removed from the dumpster pending adjudication of the First T2 Application before the Board.

The Tenants presented photographs taken by Mr. [name]name] on April 17, 2026, showing assorted household items in a dumpster. Mr. [name]name] testified that all of the objects were thrown in the dumpster by the Landlord’s father and his associates. Mr. [name]name] testified ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 that many of the items were damaged in this process. He also testified that the police told these agents that they are not permitted to dispose of the Tenants’ items and provided him with a business card and contact information for the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the next day – April 18, 2026 – the Landlord’s paralegal posted yet another notice on the dumpster sitting next to the garage, asserting notice of the Landlord’s intention to attempt disposal of the property, again citing the inapplicable provisions of section 41 of the Act. A photograph of this purported notice was provided at the hearing, visibly affixed to a dumpster sitting in the driveway.

The Landlord was not present at the residential complex during the events alleged but confirmed her father and paralegal were acting on her behalf. She did not offer any testimony that contradicted Mr. [name]name]’s testimony.

I find Mr. [name]name]’s testimony to be highly credible. It is supported by photographic evidence and documentary evidence from the police and the Landlord’s paralegal. I find, based on his testimony, that it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s agents conducted themselves as described by Mr. [name]name] from March 13, 2024, to April 18, 2024.
I am satisfied that these facts constitute both substantial interference and harassment by the Landlord and her agents.

It is clear on its face that removing tenants personal possessions from a shared area of the residential complex without lawful authorization substantially interferes with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. This is especially the case here, where the Tenants clearly asserted their right to use of the space under the rental agreement, informed the Landlord’s agents – including her legal representative – of this position, and called the police to intervene when the Landlord’s agents took matters into their own hands. By the time of the events of April 17, 2026, occurred, the Tenants had filed the First T2 Application with the Board and – per the police report – the Landlord was made aware of this. Nevertheless, the Landlord and her agents persisted.

The conduct also clearly constitutes harassment. The service of intimidating notices citing inapplicable sections of the Act is harassing behaviour, as is the continued attendances at the rental unit. Continuing to serve such purported notices after the police attended to the situation and with full knowledge of the Tenants’ intention to obtain clarity from the Board about their rights and the lawfulness of the Landlord’s conduct is a continuation of this pattern. Unilaterally asserting a right to dispose of the Tenant’s property with no lawful basis and then authorizing an agent to follow through on this assertion clearly constitutes harassment.

I am not satisfied that the situation described in the First and Second T2 Applications constitutes an illegal entry into the rental unit, as the Tenants do not take the position that the garage is an area exclusive to their use. Per the implied term of the rental unit, the garage is a shared space between the Tenants and their Landlord. ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 Remedies: The T2 Applications

The Tenants seek the following remedies with respect to the First and Second T2 Applications: • $1,233.40 in compensation for property damaged or destroyed as a result of the Landlord’s conduct; and, • $3,500.00 in general compensation.
The Tenants have also requested that the Board impose an administrative fine on the Landlord.
The Tenants obtained a fee waiver with respect to both the First T2 Application and the Second T2 Application. Therefore, no reimbursement of these costs is required.

The claim for compensation in the amount of $1,233.40 for property destroyed or damaged by the Landlord is clearly warranted. Mr. [name]name] took photographs which show a myriad of the Tenants’ personal possessions thrown carelessly into a dumpster by the Landlord’s agents. Many objects are visibly broken or damaged, and Mr. [name]name] testified that others were non-functional as a result of how the Landlord’s agents handled them. The Tenants provided an itemized list of 15 representative objects that were damaged and estimated costs of replacements for each. The estimates are conservative and represent reasonable claims on the part of the Tenants. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the amount claimed by the Tenants is reasonable and that the damage occurred as a result of the substantial interference and harassment described above. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to compensate the Tenants the full amount.

In my view, the claim for general compensation in the amount of $3,500.00 is also warranted based on the evidence presented. It is evident that the events that occurred have had a significant impact on the Tenants. The Landlord acted flagrantly throughout this process and demonstrated herself – through her agents – to be undeterred by intervention after intervention to cease the conduct and resolve the dispute through proper channels. In the Tenants’ position, it is an extremely reasonable response to these circumstances to feel insecure regarding their housing and the safety of themselves and their property.

The Tenants reside in the rental unit with three small children and endured a month of uncertainty, stress, and chaos caused by the Landlord’s conduct. The Tenants evidently experienced a loss of peace of mind during the period that the Landlord was asserting a right to dispose of their belongings and bar them from use of the garage. As a result of the conduct described above, the Tenants were compelled to obtain urgent legal advice and to call on police to intervene. Mr. [name]name] described the time as a period of stress and undue intimidation for the Tenants. In my view, the impact of the Landlord’s conduct warrants the compensation granted.

In my view, an administrative fine is also warranted in this case. The Landlord had every indication and every opportunity to cease her conduct and await proper adjudication of the issues in dispute. She chose not to, instead opting for action. She has shown repeated blatant disregard for the Act, for the Board’s processes, for law enforcement, and for her ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 Tenants’ rights and well-being. It is precisely these circumstances in which an administrative fine is required to deter the Landlord from similar conduct going forward.

As of the hearing date, the Tenants still live in the rental unit. As I found above, they still have a right to shared use of the garage as an implied term of the tenancy. At the hearing date, the Landlord reiterated the position that she acted reasonably throughout this process. In her closing submissions, she asserted that she gave the Tenants “enough time” and that they “did not act diligently” in response to the notices she provided (which, again, had no grounding in law). In my view, it is fair to say that as of the hearing date, the Landlord was still of the view that she had never acted improperly.

Deterrence is clearly of paramount importance in this case. In sum, I am ordering the Landlord to pay $4,733.40 to the Tenants in compensation for her conduct. In my view, this is an insufficient deterrent in the present case. An administrative fine is also warranted.

The Landlord’s breaches are severe. They are a repeated pattern of behaviour. The breaches took place after cautioning from the Tenants’ legal representatives and from police. All of these factors are relevant to determining the amount of the fine to be issued.

The Landlord appears to assume a right to use the residential complex as she deems fit. This is incorrect. Her use of the property is bounded by the Tenants’ rights and the terms of their pre-existing tenancy.

I am concerned about further breaches in reprisal for the Tenants’ applications, especially given that the Landlord filed the L2 Application in the weeks after the events described in the T2 Applications. I am concerned that the Landlord will not respect the finding of the Board that the Tenants are entitled to use of the garage as a shared space going forward.

In my view, a significant fine is necessary to deter future interference with these Tenants’ rights by the Landlord. Therefore, I order the Landlord to pay a fine of $5,000.00 to the Board in relation to the breaches described above.
ordered: The L2 Application and the Section 88.1 claim are dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,733.40. This amount represents: • $1,233.40 in compensation for property damaged or destroyed as a result of the Landlord’s conduct; and, • $3,500.00 in general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 12, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $900.00 from the rent each month from July 2026 to November 2026, and $233.40 from the rent in December 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by July 11, 2026. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,200.00. Charge Illegally Retained and Return of Pre-paid Rent:

The Tenant testified that she paid rent in 6-month installments. The first lump sum of $12,000.00 was paid on May 1, 2023 and she moved in on July 1, 2023, and the second installment was paid on December 1, 2023 in the amount of $12,000.00. The Tenant testified that while the tenancy agreement stated the tenancy started on May 15, 2023, the verbal agreement was that the tenancy started on July 1, 2023 and was a 1 year lease ending on June 30, 2024. The Landlord confirmed that the tenancy term was July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she notified the Landlord on March 6, 2024 that she was going to be moving out through a verbal conversation, and the Tenant vacated on March 18, 2024. The Tenant testified that the Landlord and her husband on March 6, 2024 agreed the Tenant could move out, though they initially did not consent. The Tenant is seeking the return of the rent for May and June 2024 in the amount of $4,000.00.

The Landlord testified that on February 26, 2024 the Tenant had told her that it was her intention to finish her tenancy to June 30, 2024. The Landlord then testified that she started showing the rental unit to new tenants with the start date of July 1, 2024. The Landlord said she did not agree to let the Tenant end her lease early, but said if she was successful in finding a new tenant, she would refund the rent to the Tenant.

When asked how she mitigated her loss, the Landlord testified she advertised the rental in a Wechat group and on a site called 51 Rent. The Landlord submitted a log of dates where she showed the rental unit to prospective tenants from March 2, 2024 to the end of June 2024. The Landlord’s log states she had 16 people contact her about the rental unit, though she only showed the unit twice in April 2024 and twice in May 2024, and 4 of the calls do not have a date documented. The Landlord submitted an advertisement for the unit where the identified the tenancy start date was July 1, 2024, however the Landlord testified that was from before the Tenant notified her she intended to vacate the rental unit before the end of the lease. The Landlord then testified she amended the advertisement to show an earlier start date, however this was not provided as evidence.

I find that the Landlord did take some reasonable steps to mitigate her losses under section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). However, the Landlord only listed the unit for rent on 2 websites and did not take more active steps to re-rent the unit and mitigate her loss. When the Landlord was not receiving applications through those websites alone, she could have posted to other websites or utilized a realtor, but chose not to. In these circumstances, I find it would be fair to have a partial refund of the rent that was retained. If the Landlord had reasonably mitigated their loss, I think they could have re-rented as of June 1, 2024 and as such, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $2,000.00.

The Tenant further testified that she had paid $200.00 as a key deposit and the Landlord had not returned it upon receiving the keys. The Landlord confirmed the key deposit had been paid, the keys had been returned, and she had not returned the key deposit yet, but she was willing to. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did illegally retain the key deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,200.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for June 2024 rent. • $200.00 for the key deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $2,453.00 to the Tenant.

The Tenants’ T1 application was filed on March 24, 2026, alleging that the Landlord collected an illegal charge totalling $2,400.00 by depositing and cashing a cheque in the amount of $2400.00 dated November 1, 2024 cheque twice - the first time on November 1, 2024 and then again on June 27, 2025. Excess Rent Collected in the Amount of $2,400.00
The parties agree that the tenancy began on June 10, 2023, and terminated on May 27, 2026. The monthly rent is $2,400.00 and was due on the first of each month.

It was undisputed that the Tenants made their rental payments by cheque to the Landlord during their tenancy. It was also undisputed that the Tenants paid the Landlord the lawful rent for November 2024 and June 2025 via cheque 42 & 50 respectively and cheque #42 was deposited for a second time on June 27, 2025. These cheques were deposited by the Landlord using mobile deposit and the Landlord was in receipt of the Tenants’ cheques after they were deposited into her bank.
Where the parties disagree is whether the Landlord received $2,400.00 after cashing the November 1, 2025, cheque for the second time on June 27, 2025.

The Tenant entered a 5-page document into evidence. The Tenant’s evidence includes a copy of the cashed cheques from November 1, 2024 and June 1, 2025. In addition, the Tenant referred to page 5, a statement from her bank showing a history of the cheques throughout the duration of her tenancy (DOC-7728684), the bank statement showed cheque #42 being cashed on both November 1, 2024 and June 27, 2025. Further, the Tenant testified that her bank brought the Landlord cashing the cheque twice to her attention in October 2025 and stated that an investigation would occur. The Tenant was later contacted by the bank who stated that due to the period of time since the Landlord cashed the cheque was unable to recover the money.

The Landlord’s representative testified that the Landlord had “accidentally” deposited the cheque 8-months after it had already been deposited in November 2024. He stated that as the Landlord had not labelled the cheque as deposited, the Landlord redeposited the cheque for a second time. The Landlord’s representative testified that the Landlord’s bank held the cheque for a 5-day period, flagged the cheque and it was reversed, therefore the Landlord is not in receipt of the $2,400.00. The Landlord’s representative stated that he would provide proof of the reversed cheque but needed time to send the proof of the reversal to the LTB and Tenant.

I indicated at the hearing that I was prepared to stand the mater down to permit for the Landlord’s representative to provide documentary evidence the Landlord was not in receipt of the Tenants funds, the Landlord’s representative ultimately declined the offer stating that he did not have the ability to access this information. As a result, the Landlord provided no evidence to support the submission of the Landlord’s representative that the Landlord is not in receipt of the $2,400.00 when the cheque was cashed a second time.

I note that the Notice of Hearing (‘NOH’) was mailed to the Landlord on May 7, 2026 and the NOH provides directions and references to what a party should do if they have evidence they would like to rely upon at the hearing. Further the Practice Direction on Evidence outlines deadlines for disclosing evidence, it states; …In accordance with Rule 19, all parties must provide the other parties and the LTB with a complete copy of the evidence they intend to rely upon at least 7 days before the hearing or 5 days in the case of responding evidence, unless the LTB orders or directs otherwise. Responding evidence is something that addresses an issue raised by the other party's evidence.
I am satisfied that the Landlord had sufficient time to obtain supporting evidence, and no evidence was submitted in accordance with the LTB’s Rules. Analysis

The Tenants’ evidence regarding the Landlord deposit of cheque #42 was undisputed. The Landlord’s representative did not supply documentary evidence that ought to be readily available to demonstrate that the Landlord was not in receipt of the Tenants funds. I find that the Tenant’s testimony coupled with her supporting documentary evidence supports that the Landlord not only deposited the cheque in both November 2024 and June 27, 2025 but also that the Landlord is in receipt of the funds from that cheque.
For the reasons stated above, I find that the Landlord is retaining the funds in contravention of the Act and therefore the $2,400.00 paid by the Tenant on June 25, 2025 must be returned.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,453.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for excess rent collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.

As a preliminary issue, I found that the portions of the T2 application alleging substantial interference and harassment are defective as they contain no reasonable particulars of specific incidents or conduct. Those portions of the application are therefore dismissed without the need for further analysis.
The remaining allegation under the T2 application is that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with 72 hours to retrieve their belongings following the Sheriff’s eviction on October 13, 2023.

The evidence establishes that the Sheriff enforced the eviction on October 13, 2023, at approximately 10:00 a.m. [name] contacted the Landlord later that same day and was provided access to the unit. The Tenant acknowledged that they were provided access again on October 15, 2023, and remained in the unit for approximately 11 hours, until after 1:00 a.m.

While the Tenant alleged they were limited to insufficient access time, the Tenant did not provide any documentary or corroborating evidence to support the assertion that access was restricted to less than 72 hours overall. In particular, the Tenant referenced a recording but did not disclose or produce it at the hearing. The Tenant also did not provide any detailed inventory of belongings allegedly left behind.

In my view, the Tenant’s evidence regarding whether the Landlord provided 72 hours of access to retrieve their belongings was inconsistent and unreliable. Their testimony shifted repeatedly about when they contacted the Landlord, how much time was offered, and the number of opportunities they were permitted to attend.

The Tenant initially claimed they were told they would have only four hours on October 13, 2023, but then conceded that the Landlord offered eight hours on October 14 and ultimately allowed them to attend for approximately eleven hours on October 15, remaining in the unit until after 1:00 a.m. Despite stating that the Landlord refused them access on the 15th, they later confirmed they attended for an extended period that day. The Tenant also asserted they were limited to a single attendance but provided no corroborating evidence, and their own answers demonstrated multiple opportunities to retrieve their possessions. These internal contradictions, coupled with the absence of the alleged recording and any list of missing items, undermine the reliability of their account and do not demonstrate that the Landlord failed to provide the required 72‑hour access.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was provided with meaningful access to retrieve their belongings over multiple days following the eviction. The Tenant’s evidence does not establish that the Landlord denied access in a manner that breached the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the T2 application is dismissed. The Tenant’s T1 application - last month’s rent deposit

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 106 of the Act requires a landlord to apply the rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. Retaining the deposit in these circumstances is not permitted.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,402.94 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $51.31 is owing to the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,454.25. This amount represents: • $1,402.94 for the last month's rent deposit. • $51.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6 July 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6 July 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7 July 6 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
