issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply. Below are my reasons. Agreed upon facts
The Applicant moved into the unit in June 2025 together with his partner, [name] [name] (“KW”), and their child.
The Applicant occupied the unit from June 2025 to the date of the hearing, and KW occupied the unit from June 2025 to March 22, 2026.
The Landlords did not reside at the property at any time from June 2025 to the date of the hearing.
KW is the daughter of the Landlords, Mrs. [name] (“AW”), and Mr. [name]name] (“DW”). Applicant’s evidence
The Applicant submits that he is a tenant within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and that the exemption contained in section 5(i) of the Act does not apply.

The Applicant testified that while the parties never entered into a written tenancy agreement, the rent amount was negotiated and agreed upon, thus an implied oral tenancy agreement was in place, and this is substantiated by his occupancy, and that the Applicant made regular rent payments to the Landlords.

The Applicant further testified that he paid monthly rent of $1,500.00 directly to the Landlords and entered into evidence bank records showing 8 ongoing rent payments between August 1, 2025 and March 31, 2025. The Applicant also relies on correspondence dated June 11, 2025 between the Applicant and KW in which KW writes to the Applicant that they are paying rent.

The Applicant further testified that the circumstances changed on March 22, 2026, when KW left the home following an incident. The Applicant claimed that from that point forward the Landlords' daughter no longer resided in the unit, and the Applicant remained the sole occupant, while continuing to pay the rent in full after March 22, 2026. Entered into evidence was correspondence dated March 7, 2026 between the Applicant and the Landlord, AW, where the Landlord requests the Applicant transfers ‘rent’. The Applicant claims that this correspondence corroborates his position that the Landlord acknowledges that these payments are for ‘rent’ and not simply compensation for household expenses.

The Applicant denied that the exemption in section 5(i) of the Act applied because he and KW were common-law partners. They shared a bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, and all other living facilities within the home and submits that the arrangement was not one in which he was merely sharing accommodation with the Landlords' daughter; rather, they jointly occupied the entire premises together as a family unit.

The Applicant further claimed that even if an exemption may previously have existed, this such exemption ceased to apply once KW moved out of the unit on March 22, 2026, and that he thereafter became entitled to the protections of the Act. Landlord’s evidence
The Landlords submit that the Act does not apply because the living accommodation falls within the exemption set out in section 5(i) of the Act.

The Landlord, AW testified that the property was made available to her daughter, KW, her grandson, and the Applicant after KW contacted her in distress and required housing. AW further testified that she and her husband, DW postponed plans to sell the property in order to provide accommodation to their daughter and her family. AW further testified that no tenancy agreement, written or oral, was ever created and that the arrangement was intended as a family accommodation arrangement rather than a tenancy.

KW, acting as a witness for the Landlords, testified she shared all living facilities with the Applicant including the bathroom, kitchen and bedroom. Entered into evidence were photographs showing the shared areas of the home. The Landlord’s representative submitted that because the Landlord’s daughter, continuously occupied the premises together with the Applicant until March 22, 2026 and that during that period, the Applicant shared all living facilities with the Landlords' daughter and therefore fell squarely within the exemption contemplated by section 5(i).

The Landlord further submits that KW’s departure from the property on March 22, 2026, was neither voluntary nor permanent. KW testified that she left the home because of a domestic conflict with the Applicant and because police advised that she and the child should stay elsewhere. KW further testified that she wished to return to the property and would have continued living there if the relationship had not broken down and that she currently resides in temporary accommodations with her aunt, sleeping with her son in an office space. Entered into evidence was a police report arising from the March 22, 2026 incident.

The Landlord’s representative claimed that the Applicant cannot create rights under the Act through conduct that effectively excluded the Landlords' daughter from the home and that KW’s temporary absence, caused by the breakdown of the parties' relationship and concerns for her safety, did not transform an exempt living arrangement into a tenancy governed by the Act. Analysis

Section 5(i) provides that the Act does not apply with respect to: "living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner's spouse, child or parent, or the spouse's child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located." Period between June 2025 to March 22, 2026

I am satisfied that from June 2025 until March 22, 2026, the Applicant resided in the unit together with KW, the daughter of the Landlords. The evidence on this point is not in dispute. The Applicant’s own testimony is that he and KW moved into the property together and shared a bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, and all other living facilities. KW also testified that they occupied the entire home together as a family.

The purpose of the exemption is to exclude from the Act living arrangements where an occupant shares living facilities with specified family members of the owner. During this period, the Applicant unquestionably shared the kitchen and bathroom facilities with the Landlords' daughter. Therefore, I find this relationship and living arrangement fit squarely into the exemption.

I also considered the Applicant’s position that he was a common-law partner of KW and occupied the unit together as a family. I accept this evidence; however, that fact does not assist the Applicant. The issue before me is not whether the Applicant met the definition of ‘spouse’, but whether the living accommodation was subject to the Act. As the evidence establishes that the accommodation was shared with the Landlord’s daughter, it therefore falls within the exemption in section 5(i), meaning KW herself was not occupying the premises pursuant to a tenancy governed by the Act. Accordingly, the Applicant cannot then acquire rights under the Act through his relationship with KW that neither she nor the living arrangement itself possessed in the first place.
Further, it is immaterial given these circumstances whether the Landlords themselves also resided in the unit.

Accordingly, I find that the exemption in section 5(i) applied to the living accommodation from June 2025 until March 22, 2026. During that period, the Act did not apply. The Period after March 22, 2026
The more difficult question is whether the legal characterization of the arrangement changed after KW left the unit on March 22, 2026.
The Applicant submits that once [name] ceased residing in the unit, the factual basis for the exemption disappeared and a tenancy governed by the Act came into existence.
I do not accept that submission.

The evidence establishes that KW’s departure was directly connected to the breakdown of the parties' relationship and the incident that occurred on March 22, 2026. The police report dated March 22, 2026, writes that KW left because she did not feel safe and because police recommended that she and the child stay elsewhere. KW further testified that she wishes to return to the property and would still be living there but for the break down in the parties’ relationship.

I find this evidence credible and consistent with the surrounding circumstances. Nothing in the evidence suggests that KW permanently surrendered her occupancy of the home or abandoned any intention of returning. Rather, the evidence supports a finding that her absence was temporary and arose solely because of the incident between her and the Applicant.

In my view, the Applicant's position would require a finding that a living arrangement that was exempt from the Act for approximately nine months was instantaneously transformed into a tenancy governed by the Act solely because the Landlords' daughter temporarily left the premises following a dispute. Such a result would be inconsistent with both the factual circumstances and the purpose of the exemption.

The parties' legal relationship did not materially change on March 22, 2026 as no new agreement was entered into between the Landlords and the Applicant. No new rights were granted. No new consideration was exchanged. The Applicant simply remained in possession of the same premises after the family relationship underlying the arrangement had broken down.

The Board has consistently recognized that the existence of a tenancy depends upon the true nature of the parties' arrangement and not solely upon temporary changes in occupancy. Here, the accommodation was originally provided as housing for the Landlords' daughter, the child, and the Applicant as a family unit. The subsequent temporary absence of the Landlords' daughter due to a conflict does not, in my view, create a new tenancy relationship where none previously existed.

I also considered and place considerable weight on the fact that KW expressed a continuing desire to return to the property and that her current living arrangements are plainly temporary in nature. Her absence was a consequence of the relationship breakdown rather than evidence that the original exempt arrangement had permanently come to an end.

For these reasons, I find that the Applicant has not established that a tenancy subject to the Act came into existence after March 22, 2026 and therefore, the living accommodation remains outside the scope of the Act.

Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities that the exemption contained in section 5 (i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applied to the parties' living arrangement from the commencement of occupancy in June 2025. I further find that KW’s departure from the property on March 22, 2026 was a temporary absence arising from a dispute and did not fundamentally alter the existing arrangement or create a new tenancy governed by the Act.
Accordingly, the Applicant has not established that the Act applies to the living accommodation.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. June 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the November 21, 2024 hearing, the parties requested on consent to remove “[organization]” (‘Remax”) as a named Landlord on the application. Remax is the Landlord’s former employer, and the rental unit is owned solely by the Landlord, [name]. Having considered the parties’ submissions, I found it appropriate to grant the request under Rule 15.4 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The amendment is therefore reflected in the style of cause of this order. T5 Application:

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $11,693.04, inclusive of the cost of filing the application.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; 3. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and
The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 4. The rental unit is described as a two-story townhouse with basement containing three bedrooms and one-and-a-half bathrooms.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenants a N12 notice with a termination date of June 30, 2022. The Landlord subsequently filed a L2 application that was granted via Board order on March 21, 2023 (LTB-L-035123-22). The Tenants were to vacate the unit by June 30, 2023, though they did not actually vacate until July 31, 2023. The intended occupant of the rental unit was to be the Landlord’s son, [name] (‘BF’). The parties do not dispute that BF did not move into the rental unit after the Tenants vacated. Therefore, I am satisfied that the first three parts of the test under subsection 57(1)(a) have been met. The issue then turns to whether the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Landlord testified that BF was initially to move into the rental unit with two of his friends as roommates who would then pay rent to BF. However, by the time the L2 application was heard and an order issued, BF’s intended roommates decided not to move into the unit. The parties do not dispute that, instead, the Landlord secured the daughter of a family friend to occupy the unit with her family. The new occupants moved into the unit on or about August 20, 2023 and paid $2,000.00 in rent to the Landlord each month until they vacated on or around June 30, 2024. The Landlord classifies the new occupants as BF’s roommates, whereas the Tenants submit the Landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement immediately after they vacated the unit.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. [Emphasis added]

Pursuant to subsection 57(6) of the Act, the period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that begins on the day a landlord gave the notice of termination and ends one year after a tenant vacated the rental unit. The L2 order states that the Landlord gave the N12 notice to the Tenants on April 22, 2022. Therefore, the period under consideration in this instance is April 22, 2022 to July 31, 2024.

Given that BF never moved into the unit, I am not satisfied that the new occupants could be considered as “roommates”. Subsection 2(1) of the Act defines a “tenant” to include a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit. The substance of the N12 notice and legislative tests in both subsections 48(1)(c) and 57(1) of the Act are in relation to BF as the Landlord’s son being the intended occupant of the rental unit, not anyone else. It was also not BF who located the new “roommates” but the Landlord herself, and rent was paid by the new occupants to the Landlord directly. Consequently, I am satisfied that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with someone other than the former Tenants; therefore, subsection 57(5) of the Act applies, and it is for the Landlord to prove on a balance of probabilities that they did not give a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith.

The Landlord testified that she began renovating the basement of the rental unit in August 2023 in order for her son to move in. BF’s roommates would reside on the main and second floors, and BF would live in the basement. A bathroom and bedroom were added to the basement, and the renovations were completed by the end of October 2023. The new tenants were living in the upper part of the unit while the renovations were ongoing.

The Landlord further testified that BF was to move into the unit around November 1, 2023; however, on October 27, 2023, he was physically assaulted at a Halloween party that took place at the Landlord’s residence while she was not present. BF’s jaw was broken and several of his teeth had been knocked out. A few days after the incident, BF moved into his father’s house instead without telling the Landlord. BF no longer felt safe living in the home where he was assaulted, nor did he want to live with people in the rental unit who were essentially strangers. The Landlord submitted a sworn statement by BF into evidence that reiterated her statements.

The Landlord testified that once she became aware that BF no longer intended to move into the unit, she decided to sell her home and move in instead. She updated the new tenants in the unit on the situation and then took the winter to prepare her home for sale. The home was listed in the spring and sold on or around May 16, 2024. The new tenants vacated the unit by June 30, 2024, and the Landlord and her two daughters moved in on August 13, 2024. The Landlord lived in the unit until September 26, 2025, a total of approximately 13 months, after which she moved into the new home she purchased.

The Landlord emphasized that there was an unfortunate change in circumstances that resulted in her son not moving into the unit, though there was a genuine intention for him to do so up until he was assaulted. When the plans changed, the Landlord took steps to mitigate the issue and act in her best financial interests by moving into the property herself with her two other children, thereby also complying with the intended spirit of the Act.

The Tenants reiterated that the Landlord immediately re-rented the unit for a higher rent within 20 days of them vacating. BF never moved into the unit, and the Landlord did not move into the unit herself until over a year later, which is far beyond the “reasonable time” contemplated in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Analysis:

The Ontario Divisional Court in [name] v. Salter 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), [2001] O.J. No. 2792 ([name]. Ct.), referring to Justice [name]’s reasons in Feeney v. Noble (1994), 19, O.R. (3d) ([name]. Ct.), stated that: “…the test of good faith is a genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the landlord’s proposal.” Moreover, in [name], the English Court of Appeal pronounced that a landlord need only establish a bona fide wanted and immediate intention to occupy the premises as a residence.

Here, the Landlord must prove that at the time the notice of termination was served to the Tenants, her son had a genuine intention to move into the rental unit after the Tenants vacated and remain there for at least one year. However, I may also take into consideration that bad faith is not confined to the moment in time when a landlord gives a tenant the notice of termination (see TST-94914-18 and TST-87742-17-RV). I may take into account events during the notice period up until the date the Tenants vacated the unit.

While the Landlord emphasized that she and her daughters occupied the unit after BF informed her that he would no longer be moving in, the Landlord did not do so until over a year after the Tenants had vacated the unit. Regardless, the intended occupant listed on the N12 was BF, not the Landlord, as evidenced by BF’s sworn declaration that accompanied the L2 application; therefore, the focus of the analysis remains the change in circumstances for BF between the date the N12 notice was served and when the Tenants vacated the unit.

The Landlord testified that the original plan was for BF to move into the unit with his two friends as there were three bedrooms in the unit. However, neither the L2 order nor BF’s declaration in support of the N12 makes any reference to him intending to live with anyone else in the unit; this was only brought to light once the Tenants’ application was filed. The Landlord also stated that the basement underwent extensive renovations so BF could live on that floor, however, it was not clear why that was necessary as there were already three bedrooms in the unit and only three people (including BF) who were to move in. Furthermore, neither of BF’s two friends provided evidence about when they notified BF or the Landlord about not moving into the unit, and no timeline was provided besides to say that too much time had passed after the original N12 notice termination date of June 30, 2022. Without this additional evidence, the Landlord has not shown a clear timeline of when plans first started to change after the N12 notice was served and before the Tenants vacated the unit.

BF also did not testify to provide more details as to why he needed two roommates in the first place, what other attempts he made to find other roommates once his friends said they would no longer be moving in, or why he himself did not move into the unit right after the Tenants vacated when there were three available bedrooms. Although a sworn statement by BF was submitted as evidence, this did not address the aforementioned issues and could not be cross-examined regardless, thereby carrying less evidentiary weight. BF’s testimony, as the intended occupant, would have been crucial to providing this missing information regarding his change in circumstances.

Given the above issues and the application of subsection 57(5) of the Act placing the burden of proof onto the Landlord, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord has shown that the N12 notice of termination was served in good faith. Therefore, the legal test in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act has been met, and the Tenant’s application is granted. Remedies

The Tenants submitted a copy of the rental agreement for their new residence that commenced on August 1, 2023 as evidence. The parties do not dispute the rent difference between the old unit and new unit being $931.67 per month. However, the Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that as there was an additional third tenant named in the new lease, the Tenants seek to claim rent difference for a larger unit contrary to the intent of the remedy in the Act. The Tenants maintained that the new unit is a smaller three-bedroom unit in a semi-detached house as opposed to a townhouse. The Tenants had space for two cars at the old unit, whereas the new unit only has a single-lane driveway.

Regardless of whether a third tenant was added to the new rental agreement, I am satisfied that the new unit is of a comparable size given that it contains the same number of bedrooms as the old unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $11,180.04 ($931.67 x 12 months) for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants also claimed $1,244.00 for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses they incurred as a result of having to move out of the renal unit. The parties did not dispute that the Tenants incurred $460.00 for the cost of a moving [name], but the Landlord did challenge the additional $784.00 for the Tenants’ alleged lost wages. The Tenants claimed two days of lost wages, though the Tenant, [name], testified it actually took him seven days to pack the storage bin by himself, as the other Tenant, [name], was unable to physically assist. The Tenants did not provide any supporting documentation to substantiate the cost, which work days were used, and why they had to be used for the moving process. Consequently, I find the additional $784.00 in costs too remote to claim as a moving expense. Therefore, the Tenants are granted only $460.00 for reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $11,693.04. This amount represents: • $11,180.04 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from August 1, 2023 to July 31, 2024. • $460.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 24, 2026

issues: he unit after the termination date. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenants to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenants’ conduct or that of another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. This conduct substantially interfered with the Landlord's reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or another lawful right, privilege, or interest (the ‘Section 88.1 Claim’). On April 16, 2024, the Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household, and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (the ‘First T2 Application’). On April 18, 2024, the Tenants applied for a second order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household, and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenants (the ‘Second T2 Application’). ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 The L2 Application, the Section 88.1 Claim, the First T2 Application, and the Second T2 Application were heard together by videoconference on April 23, 2026. The Landlord, the Tenant [name], and the Tenant’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The parties agree that the Tenant’s moved into the rental unit in 2019, when it was owned by a previous landlord. The Landlord bought the property in February 2024.

The core issue pertaining to all of the applications is whether the Tenants were entitled to use of the garage of the residential complex as a term of the rental agreement. The residential complex is a house and the Tenants’ rental unit is in the basement level of the building. Preliminary Issue: The Landlord’s N5 Notice is Invalid

The Tenant’s legal representative raised the validity of the N5 notice of termination (the ‘N5 Notice’) as a preliminary issue at the hearing. He submitted that the N5 Notice does not contain sufficient reasons and details to constitute a valid notice of termination, per subsection 43(2) of the Act and the leading case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931.

For a notice to contain sufficient reasons and details, a tenant must be able to know the case to be met before the Board, to decide whether to dispute the allegations, and – in the case of a voidable N5 notice – whether to take corrective action to void the notice. Dates and times of the alleged conduct – as well as a detailed description of the conduct – must be provided in the notice.
On May 22, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N5 notice of termination (the ‘N5 Notice’).

No particular dates are attached to the allegations in the N5 Notice. Rather, the Landlord generally states that the Tenants are “continuing” to have “encroached upon and unauthorizedly and illegally occupied the substantial portion of the garage of the rented premises and refused to vacate [their] illegal possession.”

Upon hearing the submissions of the parties, I considered whether the N5 Notice complies with the requirement of subsection 43(2) to provide reasons and details. I did so with a view toward subsection 212(1), which directs that substantial compliance with the Act is sufficient with respect to the contents of notices given under the Act.

In my view, the N5 Notice is not substantially compliant with the requirements of subsection 43(2). All that is clear from the notice is that the allegations are about the use of the garage and that the issue is, in the view of the Landlord, continuing. No details are provided about when this conduct began, when the Tenants “refused” to cease the conduct, or sufficient clarity as to what specific lawful right, privilege, or interest is alleged to have been interfered with by the Tenant. Rather, a broad and sweeping assertion of illegality is made. ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24

The contents of the N5 Notice do not allow the Tenants to meaningfully respond to the allegations. Therefore, I find that the N5 Notice is invalid. The L2 Application to terminate the tenancy must therefore be dismissed. The Section 88.1 Claim
The Landlord’s Section 88.1 Claim for compensation in the amount of $1,890.00 must also be dismissed.
The Section 88.1 Claim does not describe any out-of-pocket expenses arising from any substantial interference by the Tenants. Rather, it asserts a right to compensation generally.

Only out-of-pocket expenses are eligible to be claimed under section 88.1 of the Act. No such expenses have been disclosed in the Landlord’s application. Therefore, the Section 88.1 Claim is dismissed. The First and Second T2 Applications
The Tenant [name] testified at the hearing about the events detailed in the First and Second T2 Applications.

Mr. [name]name] testified that he moved into the rental unit in 2019. He testified that prior to moving into the basement unit, the previous landlord allowed the Tenants to store some of their belongings in the garage pending the completion of renovations in the basement. He testified that once the renovations were complete and the tenancy began, the Tenants continued to store personal items in the garage with the full knowledge of the previous landlord. Mr. [name]name] showed photographs of his personal items in the garage during that period. Per Mr. [name]name], the previous landlord never objected to this arranged use of the shared space.

The Landlord was not a party to the original tenancy agreement but rather stepped into the shoes of the previous Landlords when she bought the property in 2024, per section 18 of the Act. She testified that the previous landlord had told her that the items in the garage were left behind by another tenant who resided upstairs.

No evidence was offered in support of the Landlord’s position that the Tenants are not entitled to use of the garage under the terms of the rental agreement, other than her testimony about a statement made by the previous landlords to her during the course of the sale that the basement tenants did not have access to the garage. This statement from the previous landlords is hearsay. The previous landlords, [name] and [name], were summonsed by the Landlord, but did not comply with the summons and attend the hearing.

I prefer the direct evidence of Mr. [name]name] with respect to whether the Tenants had been using the garage during the tenancy with the knowledge and agreement of the former landlords. Mr. [name]name] provided extensive detail about how the arrangement came to be at the beginning of the tenancy and photographic evidence of his use of the garage throughout his years living in the rental unit. The only evidence presented by the Landlord to the contrary is a hearsay statement – no documentary evidence of what she was told by ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 the previous owners of the property was presented at the hearing. I therefore find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Tenants’ use of the garage for storage of personal belongings was an implied term of the tenancy for its entire duration and continues to be a term of the rental agreement between the Landlord and the Tenants.

Mr. [name]name] testified that, on March 13, 2024, the Tenants received a notice from the Landlord’s former paralegal that they were to remove their property from the garage within 72 hours. A copy of this notice was provided at the hearing, citing section 41 of the Act as the legal authority under which the Landlord was acting.

Section 41 is not applicable in the circumstances of this case. It speaks to the law surrounding the disposal of abandoned property when a tenant vacates a rental unit. This did not occur here. The Tenants remained in possession of the rental unit when this notice was given.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the Tenants immediately sought legal advice after receiving the notice. The Tenants provided a letter – dated March 14, 2024 – authored by a staff lawyer at the Hamilton Community Legal Clinic. In the letter, which is addressed to the Landlord’s former paralegal, the lawyer states the Tenants’ position that the use of the garage is an implied term of the tenancy and that the Tenants have a continuing right to use of the garage. It is clear, based on this letter, that the Tenants disputed the Landlord’s assertion of exclusive use of the garage. In other words, the Landlord was on notice of the Tenants’ position as of March 14, 2026.

Mr. [name]name] testified that on April 16, 2026, the Landlord’s father (acting on the Landlord’s authorization) attended the residential unit with a rented bin with the intention of disposing of the property in the garage. The Tenants objected and told the Landlord’s father to stop disposing of their belongings. The Tenants contacted the Landlord’s paralegal to reiterate their position that the property was not abandoned and that the Landlord had no right to dispose of that property. The Landlord’s paralegal asserted the Landlord’s rights to dispose of the property. At this point, the Tenants filed the First T2 Application.

Per Mr. [name]name]’s testimony, the Landlord’s father reattended the next day – April 17, 2026 – and, again, intended to dispose of the Tenants’ property. The Landlord’s father attended the property with a dumpster and three other individuals. Mr. [name]name] testified that these individuals started throwing objects into the dumpster and harassing the Tenants, who were attempting to intervene.

Police attended the unit after the Tenants called to report the conduct of the Landlord’s father and his associates. A police record documenting the attendance was provided by the Tenants. The report states that the police arrived to find a large dumpster in the driveway of the residential complex full of miscellaneous items, that the parties were advised to co-operate regarding the belongings, and that Mr. [name]name] was directed to assist in identifying which objects belonged to the Tenants and, therefore, should be removed from the dumpster pending adjudication of the First T2 Application before the Board.

The Tenants presented photographs taken by Mr. [name]name] on April 17, 2026, showing assorted household items in a dumpster. Mr. [name]name] testified that all of the objects were thrown in the dumpster by the Landlord’s father and his associates. Mr. [name]name] testified ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 that many of the items were damaged in this process. He also testified that the police told these agents that they are not permitted to dispose of the Tenants’ items and provided him with a business card and contact information for the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the next day – April 18, 2026 – the Landlord’s paralegal posted yet another notice on the dumpster sitting next to the garage, asserting notice of the Landlord’s intention to attempt disposal of the property, again citing the inapplicable provisions of section 41 of the Act. A photograph of this purported notice was provided at the hearing, visibly affixed to a dumpster sitting in the driveway.

The Landlord was not present at the residential complex during the events alleged but confirmed her father and paralegal were acting on her behalf. She did not offer any testimony that contradicted Mr. [name]name]’s testimony.

I find Mr. [name]name]’s testimony to be highly credible. It is supported by photographic evidence and documentary evidence from the police and the Landlord’s paralegal. I find, based on his testimony, that it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s agents conducted themselves as described by Mr. [name]name] from March 13, 2024, to April 18, 2024.
I am satisfied that these facts constitute both substantial interference and harassment by the Landlord and her agents.

It is clear on its face that removing tenants personal possessions from a shared area of the residential complex without lawful authorization substantially interferes with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. This is especially the case here, where the Tenants clearly asserted their right to use of the space under the rental agreement, informed the Landlord’s agents – including her legal representative – of this position, and called the police to intervene when the Landlord’s agents took matters into their own hands. By the time of the events of April 17, 2026, occurred, the Tenants had filed the First T2 Application with the Board and – per the police report – the Landlord was made aware of this. Nevertheless, the Landlord and her agents persisted.

The conduct also clearly constitutes harassment. The service of intimidating notices citing inapplicable sections of the Act is harassing behaviour, as is the continued attendances at the rental unit. Continuing to serve such purported notices after the police attended to the situation and with full knowledge of the Tenants’ intention to obtain clarity from the Board about their rights and the lawfulness of the Landlord’s conduct is a continuation of this pattern. Unilaterally asserting a right to dispose of the Tenant’s property with no lawful basis and then authorizing an agent to follow through on this assertion clearly constitutes harassment.

I am not satisfied that the situation described in the First and Second T2 Applications constitutes an illegal entry into the rental unit, as the Tenants do not take the position that the garage is an area exclusive to their use. Per the implied term of the rental unit, the garage is a shared space between the Tenants and their Landlord. ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 Remedies: The T2 Applications

The Tenants seek the following remedies with respect to the First and Second T2 Applications: • $1,233.40 in compensation for property damaged or destroyed as a result of the Landlord’s conduct; and, • $3,500.00 in general compensation.
The Tenants have also requested that the Board impose an administrative fine on the Landlord.
The Tenants obtained a fee waiver with respect to both the First T2 Application and the Second T2 Application. Therefore, no reimbursement of these costs is required.

The claim for compensation in the amount of $1,233.40 for property destroyed or damaged by the Landlord is clearly warranted. Mr. [name]name] took photographs which show a myriad of the Tenants’ personal possessions thrown carelessly into a dumpster by the Landlord’s agents. Many objects are visibly broken or damaged, and Mr. [name]name] testified that others were non-functional as a result of how the Landlord’s agents handled them. The Tenants provided an itemized list of 15 representative objects that were damaged and estimated costs of replacements for each. The estimates are conservative and represent reasonable claims on the part of the Tenants. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the amount claimed by the Tenants is reasonable and that the damage occurred as a result of the substantial interference and harassment described above. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to compensate the Tenants the full amount.

In my view, the claim for general compensation in the amount of $3,500.00 is also warranted based on the evidence presented. It is evident that the events that occurred have had a significant impact on the Tenants. The Landlord acted flagrantly throughout this process and demonstrated herself – through her agents – to be undeterred by intervention after intervention to cease the conduct and resolve the dispute through proper channels. In the Tenants’ position, it is an extremely reasonable response to these circumstances to feel insecure regarding their housing and the safety of themselves and their property.

The Tenants reside in the rental unit with three small children and endured a month of uncertainty, stress, and chaos caused by the Landlord’s conduct. The Tenants evidently experienced a loss of peace of mind during the period that the Landlord was asserting a right to dispose of their belongings and bar them from use of the garage. As a result of the conduct described above, the Tenants were compelled to obtain urgent legal advice and to call on police to intervene. Mr. [name]name] described the time as a period of stress and undue intimidation for the Tenants. In my view, the impact of the Landlord’s conduct warrants the compensation granted.

In my view, an administrative fine is also warranted in this case. The Landlord had every indication and every opportunity to cease her conduct and await proper adjudication of the issues in dispute. She chose not to, instead opting for action. She has shown repeated blatant disregard for the Act, for the Board’s processes, for law enforcement, and for her ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24 Tenants’ rights and well-being. It is precisely these circumstances in which an administrative fine is required to deter the Landlord from similar conduct going forward.

As of the hearing date, the Tenants still live in the rental unit. As I found above, they still have a right to shared use of the garage as an implied term of the tenancy. At the hearing date, the Landlord reiterated the position that she acted reasonably throughout this process. In her closing submissions, she asserted that she gave the Tenants “enough time” and that they “did not act diligently” in response to the notices she provided (which, again, had no grounding in law). In my view, it is fair to say that as of the hearing date, the Landlord was still of the view that she had never acted improperly.

Deterrence is clearly of paramount importance in this case. In sum, I am ordering the Landlord to pay $4,733.40 to the Tenants in compensation for her conduct. In my view, this is an insufficient deterrent in the present case. An administrative fine is also warranted.

The Landlord’s breaches are severe. They are a repeated pattern of behaviour. The breaches took place after cautioning from the Tenants’ legal representatives and from police. All of these factors are relevant to determining the amount of the fine to be issued.

The Landlord appears to assume a right to use the residential complex as she deems fit. This is incorrect. Her use of the property is bounded by the Tenants’ rights and the terms of their pre-existing tenancy.

I am concerned about further breaches in reprisal for the Tenants’ applications, especially given that the Landlord filed the L2 Application in the weeks after the events described in the T2 Applications. I am concerned that the Landlord will not respect the finding of the Board that the Tenants are entitled to use of the garage as a shared space going forward.

In my view, a significant fine is necessary to deter future interference with these Tenants’ rights by the Landlord. Therefore, I order the Landlord to pay a fine of $5,000.00 to the Board in relation to the breaches described above.
ordered: The L2 Application and the Section 88.1 claim are dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,733.40. This amount represents: • $1,233.40 in compensation for property damaged or destroyed as a result of the Landlord’s conduct; and, • $3,500.00 in general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. ; LTB-T-030943-24; LTB-T-031672-24

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 12, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $900.00 from the rent each month from July 2026 to November 2026, and $233.40 from the rent in December 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by July 11, 2026. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: n order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-032109-24 issued on January 10, 2025. On January 15, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Landlord alleged that they were not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. On January 17, 2026, interim order LTB-T-032109-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on January 10, 2025 Following a hearing on March 10, 2025, order LTB-T-032109-24-RV-IN2 was issued on April 11, 2026, granting the Landlord’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date. This application was heard by videoconference on April 14, 2026, and June 16, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord's Legal Representative[name], and the Landlord attended the hearing. The Landlord’s wife, and witness, [name] (NK), also attended the hearing. At the hearing on June 16, 2026, I granted t he Tenant s’ unopposed request to amend the application to reflect the accurate difference in rent between the rental unit and their new unit , $135.00 and not $100.00.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants, $17,696.48 for giving a notice of termination in bad faith.
The tenancy for the three-bedroom rental unit commenced on May 12, 2022, and ended on February 17, 2024. The lawful monthly rent was $2,650.00. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenants testified that they vacated the rental unit following the Landlord’s service of a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit (N12) with a termination date of February 28, 2024.

On December 3, 202 3, the Landlord attended the rental unit with his wife and rea l estate agent. They informed the Tenants that they intend to sell the unit and asked if the Tenants would buy it. The Tenants requested to deal with the new Landlord as they had just recently had a baby, their other children attended school in the area, and they were not in a position to purchase the rental unit or relocate.

On January 1, 2024, the Landlord sent an email stating ‘… due to some personal reason I would like to proceed with termination of our rental agreement on the property located at [address]ive, [name], Ontario, N2R, 0P9 with expiration on February 28, 2024’.

The Landlord verbally informed the Tenants that he intended to occupy the unit because his residence would undergo repairs which would impact his son’s pneumonia. At the Tenants’ request for a formal notice, the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination indicating that he intends to occupy the unit.

Following their move from the unit, the Tenants discovered on April 9, 2024, that the rental unit was listed for sale online on March 20 , 2024 . The Tenants believe that it was the Landlord’s intention from the onset to sell the unit. They visited his home on May 1, 2024, and no renovations were ongoing. The Landlord subsequently sold the rental unit on June 8, 2024, and later sold his own residence in October 2024.
The Tenants’ new tenancy agreement shows that the tenancy for the ir current three- bedroom unit commenced on March 1, 2024, and the lawful monthly rent is $2,785.00.

The Tenants stated that due to the actions of the Landlord, they had to change their children’s school in the middle of the school year, which made it difficult for the children to adapt. They lost the support of friends in the neighbourhood who helped with the children; and in addition, suffered a loss of income as the male Tenant sustained a back injury during the move and was required to take time off work.

The Tenants requested an order for the Landlord to pay the difference in rent for a period of one year, $1,620.00 ($135.00 x 12 months); [name] rental cost of $128.48; and general compensation of $30,000.00. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that he served the N12 notice because he planned to renovate his home which included painting, carpeting of the basement, and staining of stairs, but due to his son’s asthma and allergic reaction to paint, they decided to move into the rental unit.

However, after the Tenants moved out of the unit , there was a change in the Landlord’s circumstances when on February 18, 2024, his wife, NK travelled to Pakistan and was involved in a car accident on February 23, 2024. The Landlord and other family members and friends had to convince NK to return to Canada because she was traumatized by the accident. NK was unwilling to both move back to Canada and into the rental unit.
The Landlord sold the rental unit in June 2024. The Landlord s ubsequently sold their residence in October 2024 and moved into a new home because NK’s condition became stable over the summer.

NK testified that she returned to Canada on March 20, 2024, following the accident which left her with bruises, anxiety, and panic attacks. The driver, her brother was hospitalized in critical condition but has since recovered. NK told the Landlord that she would return to Canada only on the condition that they would not move into the rental unit because of her bruised hands, and she was not mentally prepared for a move. The Landlord provided a letter from a doctor dated February 28, 2024, which stated that NK was diagnosed with major depressive disorder compounded by recurrent panic attacks. The lette r is devoid of any reference to an accident.

NK further stated that on her return to Canada, she did not seek any medical attention. NK continued taking the medication prescribed by her doctor in Pakistan for a period of two months and stayed in contact with them.

The Landlord provided a video of the alleged accident which showed that the occupants of the vehicle exited without assistance and appeared unharmed as they stood beside the vehicle. While NK stated that she obtained the video to facilitate a report that she made to the authorities, a copy of that report was not provided as evidence.

On cross examination, NK acknowledged that she is a social media influencer and on March 15, March 16, March 19, March 21, and March 25, 2024, she posted videos of her reviews of restaurants in Canada which she had made weeks prior to the date they were posted. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. 3. No person referred to in subsection 48 (1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Based on all the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant s proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. The Tenants received an N12 notice of termination and vacated the unit as a result of the notice. However, the Landlord did not occupy the unit after the Tenants vacated. Rather, the Landlord listed it for sale on March 20, 2024, approximately one month later. This engages section 57(5) of the Act which provides that there is a presumption of bad faith if the Landlord advertises the rental unit, or places the building that contains the rental unit, for sale within a year after the Tenant vacates the unit.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 , a case where in consideration of section 57 (1) (b) of the Act, similar to section 57(1)(a) except the notice was given on behalf of a purchaser, the court of appeal held in paragraph 42: ‘The purposes of the RTA are set out in s. 1. The first purpose listed is “to provide protection for residential tenants from…unlawful evictions”. To ignore events after a landlord gives a tenant a s. 49 termination notice limits the Board from fulfilling its responsibility to determine bad faith under s. 57(1)(b) and undermines the RTA’s stated purpose of providing tenants with protection from unlawful evictions.’

Given the legal presumption of bad faith, in addition to the Act’s stated purpose of protecting Tenants from unlawful evictions, the Landlord bears the burden of demonstrating that the notice of termination was served in good faith. Prior to the service of the N12 notice, the Landlord on December 3, 2023, informed the Tenants of his intention to sell the unit and asked if they were interested in purchasing it. After the Tenants declined, the Landlord subsequently advised that he intended to occupy the unit himself due to planned renovations at his residence which would allegedly impact his child’s health.

The Landlord’s subsequent claim that a material change in circumstance s prevented him from occupying the rental unit , specifically the trauma his wife suffered as a result of the vehicular accident in Pakistan on February 23, 2024 , is not supported by any other meaningful evidence. There is no documentary evidence to demonstrate that his wife and her brother were the people who exited the vehicle following the accident as it was nighttime and only the silhouette of the individuals were visible from the video . The accident report which the Landlord’s wife allegedly filed, was not presented as evidence, neither were pictures showing the alleged bruises on her hands. The prescription she purportedly received from the doctor was undated, casting doubt on her claim that she took any medication for a period of two months because of the accident . Although she claimed that her brother was in critical condition following the accident, the video shows both individuals getting out of the vehicle without assistance, and appearing physically unharmed, as they stood near the vehicle.

Furthermore, despite the Landlord’s claim that NK was so distraught from the accident that it prevented them from moving into the rental unit, the evidence demonstrates that NK was able to carry on with her usual activities. NK continued to post videos of herself online on March 15, March 16, and March 19, 2024, prior to her return to Canada on March 20, 2024. Hence, I am not persuaded that the accident constituted a material change in circumstances that prevented the Landlord from occupying the unit.

In addition, no documentation was provided to establish that the Landlord’s son suffers from asthma or has an allergy to paint, or that the Landlord renovated his residence between February 2024 and June 2024.

Given the foregoing , I am satisfied that at the time the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in January 2024 , he did not genuinely intend to occupy the unit. I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the notice to secure vacant possession of the rental unit in order to facilitate its sale . Accordingly, I find that t he Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies

Having succeeded in proving that the notice was given in bad faith, the Tenant s, pursuant to section 57(3) (4) of the Act are entitled to the difference ($ 135.00) between the rent for the rental unit ($2,650.00) and the rent for their new unit ($2,785.00) for a period of twelve months in the total amount of $1,620.00. The evidence demonstrates that the rental unit and the new unit are comparable three-bedroom units. The Landlord will be ordered to pay $1,620.00 to the Tenants, for the period from March 1, 2024, to February 28, 2025.

Section 57 (3) (1.2) of the Act provides that the LTB can make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage, and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. The Tenants incurred moving costs of $128.48 and are entitled to a reimbursement of the costs.

The Tenants requested general compensation of $30,000.00. Section 57 (3) (1.1) of the Act provides that the LTB may make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses.

Given the additional rent the Tenant s will continue to incur monthly because of the Landlord’s bad faith eviction, and the impact of their move on their children and lifestyle, I find it fair to award general compensation of $15,900.00 to the Tenants, an amount equal to six months rent ($2,650.00 x 6).
The Landlord will be ordered to pay a total of $ 17,696.48 to the Tenant s, inclusive of the $48.00 cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $17,696.48. This amount represents: • $1,620.00 for increased rent the Tenants incurred for the one-year period from March 1, 2024, to February 29, 2025, • $128.48 in reasonable out-of-pocket moving costs, • $15,900.00 in general compensation, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30 , 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal charge collected

The parties agreed that on March 6, 2026, the Tenant and the Landlords entered into a verbal agreement that were to commence on March 15, 2026. The Tenant contacted the Landlords and asked if they were able to move in as of March 10, 2026, and the Landlords agreed and said they would waive the 5 day rent period from March 10, 2026 to March 15, 2026. The Tenant was going to move into the rental unit and pay $1,150.00 per month on a monthly tenancy. The parties further agreed the Tenant paid a $200.00 deposit to secure the rental unit on or about March 6, 2026. However, on March 8, 2026, the Tenant requested the Landlords return the deposit as they were no longer able to move into the rental unit on March 10, 2026. The Landlords in good faith returned $150.00 to the Tenant as they understood their financial position, but informed the Tenant that they would only return the remaining $50.00 should they find someone to move into the rental unit for March 15, 2026. The Landlords did not find anyone to move in for more than 60 days after the date the monthly tenancy had commenced.

I find that on March 6, 2026, the parties entered a verbally binding contract where the Tenant was to take possession of the rental unit on March 15, 2026. The Tenant, two days after paying $200.00 deposit, wanted to opt out of the agreement. However, the Tenant was not legally entitled to opt out of the legally binding agreement without the consent of the Landlords. The Landlords did not consent to having the Tenant opting out of their agreement unless they had found someone to move into the rental unit sooner. The Tenant did not testify that they attempted to find a replacement tenant, but the Landlords testified that they attempted to find someone to take over the monthly tenancy, but were only successful 60 days later.

Therefore, I find the Landlords did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlords returned $150.00 to the Tenant in good faith as he had made them aware of his circumstances. However, the Landlords were clear that they would only return the remaining $50.00 should they find a replacement tenant, which did not happen for another 60 days. There are legal ways to end a monthly tenancy early, which include,: 1) on the consent of all parties; 2) the Landlords issues a notice of termination; or 3) the Board issues the termination. In this case, none of the three above occurred, so the earliest date the Tenant could have terminated the tenancy was May 14, 2026, which is 60 days and the last of the rental period, which is why they are not entitled to the $50.00 remaining on the deposit and the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I raised a preliminary issue with the Tenant in regard to her application. Specifically, the Tenant’s application claims that the Landlord charged her an illegal rent charge but does not specify how much the illegal charge was for. When I raised this issue with the Tenant, she herself was uncertain of the amount of the illegal charge.

The Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931).

Although the [name] case related to the details required in a landlord’s notice of termination, it reflects the general principles of procedural fairness, which include a party’s right to know the case to be met. I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as I find it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient details of the issues to determine whether to defend the claim.
The Landlord’s representative submitted that they were unsure of the reason the Tenant had brought an application before the Board and were unsure of how to defend the [name] claims.

As it pertains to the T1 application, the Tenant claimed the Landlord charged them an illegal rent charge, but does not specify how much the illegal charge was for and when it was charged. I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s application contains sufficient details regarding an illegal rent charge and the Landlord is therefore unable to defend the claim. The Tenant ought to have included particulars related to the amount of the illegal rent charge and provided particulars as to when it was charged.

Even if I did proceed with the Tenant’s application and the Tenant was successful in her application, there would be no remedy awarded to her as no amount was selected in her application. Therefore, her application is moot.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: (sherry) (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') (T2 application): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application):
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 portion of the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s T2 application is brought pursuant to section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). Section 29(2) of the Act states that no application can be made under this provision more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. In Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich, [2010] O.J. No. 1463, the Divisional Court held that a remedy cannot go back further than the one-year limitation period in subsection 29(2). In other words, a remedy cannot go back further than one year before the application was filed.

In the present case, the Tenant filed his T2 application on April 30, 2024. The limitation period in section 29(2) prevents me from awarding a remedy in relation to any period prior to April 30, 2023, one year before the application was filed.

The allegations of breaches in the Tenant’s application are prior to April 30, 2023. Therefore, I find that the Tenant’s claims enumerated above are out of time and application must be dismissed. T5 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application o on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T5 portion of the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that they vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2023, after being served a second N12 notice of termination (N12 notice) with a termination date of December 31, 2022. The first N12 Notice had a termination date of November 20, 2022, and was defective and withdrawn. In both N12 notices the Landlord claimed they required vacant possession of the rental unit for the purpose of the residential occupation of the Landlord’s daughter, [name].

The Tenant also testified that she provided the Landlord a N9 Tenant’s Notice to End the Tenancy on April 30, 2023, after receiving a N2 Notice of Rent Increase Unit Partially Exempt, and the alleged harassing behaviour of the Landlord and the rent increase both caused her to make the decision to vacate prior to the L2 application being heard by the Board.
The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that the L2 application was not heard and withdrawn by the Landlord on or about May 11, 2023. Analysis

This application is brought pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a)the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that in order to succeed on this application the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; 3. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
There is no dispute between the parties about the first two elements of this test.
The central factual dispute between them is the allegation that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith and the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that they were aware that the Landlord’s daughter did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time and was in fact residing in another apartment. Moreover, the Landlord re-rented the unit to another Tenant, before her daughter in fact moved in. This is why the Tenant believed the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Moreover, the Tenant testified she felt as though the Landlord was attempting to have her vacate, and this behaviour was akin to harassment. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

The Landlord testified that when she served the Tenant with the N12 notices, the second with the termination date of December 31, 2022, it was the Landlord’s intention that her daughter would move into the rental unit for at least a year if not longer due to her studies at University of Toronto.

The Landlord testified this was not a ruse to simply evict the Tenant, nor was rent raised to force her to vacate. The Tenant simply did not communicate with the Landlord after receiving the N12 notices and it was obvious she would not vacate pending a Board hearing. The Landlord noted that the first N12 notice had a date of termination of November 20, 2022, which the Landlord discovered was defective, after the fact, and hence the need for the second notice with a termination date of December 31, 2022.

The Landlord further testified her daughter entered into a lease for another unit close to the university for December 1, 2022, to November 30, 2023, at 25 Carlton Street and when that lease period ended the Landlord’s daughter moved into the rental unit, given it was quite obvious the Tenant would not vacate prior to the date of termination on the first notice or second notice, and the Landlord’s daughter needed housing stability for her schooling as commuting from the Landlord’s home was no longer viable as it was time consuming and tiresome on her daughter.

The Landlord testified she filed an N2 notice as was her right to raise rent from $2,550.00 to $3,700.00 given the expenses of carrying the rental unit had increased, on January 26, 2023, and thereafter the Tenant served her N9 on February 17, 2023, regarding vacating on April 30, 2023.

The Landlord further testified and provided documentary evidence to substantiate that she wrote the Tenant on February 28, 2023 advising the Tennat that her daughter had rented another unit and would not be moving to the rental until her fixed tenancy was terminated. This correspondence was sent to the Tenant shortly after receiving the N9 notice from the Tenant, but she did not hear back from the Tenant, so the claim the Tenant was unhoused for a time being in the Landlord’s opinion was far fetched.

The Landlord further testified after the Tenant vacated on April 30, 2023 the rental unit was vacant for two months, and the Landlord was forced to re-rent the unit to another tenant for a fixed period, until her daughter could move into the rental unit (terminate her tenancy) which she in fact has done and currently resides in the rental unit as of the date of this proceeding.

The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (VC), testified it was always her and the Landlord’s intention that she would reside in the rental unit if she attended University of Toronto and in fact her mom had promised her the rental unit during her schooling, but given the Tenant did not vacate, as per the N12 notices, she was forced to rent another unit to hold her over, until she could move into the rental unit, which is what occurred. 22. [name] further testified the facts of her schooling alone precipitated the serving of the N12 notices onto the Tenant, and to her knowledge the Landlord did not harass the Tenant into vacating the rental unit, and in fact the Landlord was awaiting the L2 application to be heard, upon receiving the N9 notice from the Tenant. 23. I find that, based on the evidence before me, when the Landlord served the N12 notice, it was served in good faith. I find based on the evidence before me the intended occupant listed in the N12 occupied the rental unit once the Tenant vacated the rental unit, and once she was able to given the aforementioned circumstances, and hence I am satisfied the Landlord has rebutted the presumption that they served the N12 in bad faith. 24. Based on the above, I cannot find that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed. 25. I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 26. This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T5 applications are dismissed. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
