issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application named [name] (“SL”) as the Landlord’s Agent.
SL testified that she is not the Landlord’s Agent, that she was the Tenant’s Real Estate Agent.
The Landlord confirmed that [name] has never acted in any capacity for him.

The Tenant testified that [name] was her Real Estate Agent and the Tenant named [name] as a party because the Tenant wanted SL to attend and provide evidence on the Tenant’s behalf. The Tenant confirmed that she was not seeking repayment from SL.

Based on the submissions of the parties, I am satisfied that [name] is not a proper party and is actually a witness and should be removed as a party. Therefore, the application shall be amended to remove [name] as a party. Preliminary Issue – Landlord’s name and Application details
At the hearing, the Landlord confirmed that his last name is actually spelled Bedessee not Beddesee. As such, the application shall be amended to reflect the correct spelling of the Landlord’s name.
As explained below, the Tenant’s application did not contain sufficient details as it pertains to reason 1, charge of an illegal rent, and therefore that portion of the application is dismissed.

The Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931).

Although the [name] case related to the details required in a landlord’s notice of termination, it reflects the general principles of procedural fairness, which include a party’s right to know the case to be met. I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as I find it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient details of the issues to determine whether to defend the claim.

Here, the Tenant’s application contained two claims, a claim for illegal rent charged and a claim that the Landlord failed to pay interest on the last month’s rent deposit. The Landlord did not dispute that he understood the Tenant’s claim regarding the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit as it was clear and understandable. However, the claim regarding the charge of illegal rent was unclear.

The Tenant testified that the charge of illegal rent claiming $700.00 was a combination of $500.00 for a key deposit that was not returned and $200.00 in unpaid interest. However, under the “Explain your Reasons” section of the Tenant’s application, nowhere was it explained how the Tenant arrived at $700.00 for the illegal rent charged. The only mention of a key deposit was “I had paid the agent $500.00 for keys”. The Tenant’s application did not have dates, times, or specifics of how she arrived at what she was claiming as the illegal rent charge.
The Landlord testified that he did not understand what the Tenant was claiming as an illegal rent charge as the Tenant’s application was unclear, and he did not understand reason #1.

In this case, I am not satisfied that the Tenant provided sufficient details of her claim regarding an illegal rent charge for the Landlord to know and understand the claim being made. The application lacks sufficient specifics and details for the Landlord to understand that the Tenant was claiming the illegal rent charge was actually about the allegedly retained key deposit.
As such, the Tenant’s claim regarding an illegal charge is dismissed as not being sufficiently detailed. Interest Owing
As explained below, the Tenant proved the remaining allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $184.13.

It was undisputed that the Tenant paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit of $3,500.00 on January 4, 2021. It was also undisputed that the Landlord has never paid the Tenant any interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord testified that instead of paying interest on the last month’s rent deposit he topped up the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit. Therefore, the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit was $3,700.00 as of November 30, 2025, which was applied to December 2025 rent.

The Tenant did not dispute that she never paid the Landlord any additional money to bring her last month’s rent deposit in line with what the current rent was. However, the Tenant did provide that there were no rent increases in 2022 or 2023, and she did not receive interest in those years.

Section 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that a Landlord shall pay interest to the Tenant annually at a rate equal to the amount of the guideline increase permitted for the same year the interest is to be paid in.

Section 106(7) of the Act provides that the Landlord may deduct from the interest payable the amount needed to top up the last month’s rent deposit so that the last month’s rent deposit matches the current rent.

Here, interest is calculated up to the date the last month’s rent deposit ceased to be a deposit and became rent. As the last month’s rent deposit was used for the rent due on December 1, 2025, the Tenant is entitled to interest up to November 30, 2025. Interest is calculated as follows: • For the period January 4, 2021, to January 3, 2022: $3,500.00 x 1.2% = $42.00; • For the period January 4, 2022, to January 3, 2023; $3,500.00 x 2.5% = $87.51; • For the period January 4, 2023, to January 3, 2024; $3,500.00 x 2.5% = $87.51; • For the period January 4, 2024, to January 3, 2025; $3,500.00 x 2.5% = $87.51; and • For the period January 4, 2025, to November 30, 2025; $3,500.00 x 2.5% = $79.60 • For a total of $384.13

In this case the Tenant should have been paid a total of $384.13 in interest over the tenancy. The Landlord applied $200.00 toward the last month’s rent deposit, therefore, the Landlord owes the Tenant $184.13 in interest that was not paid during the tenancy.
As such, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $184.13 for unpaid interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $184.13 for interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the Tenant’s $2,300.00 rent deposit.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenants testified that they paid a $2,300.00 rent deposit to the Landlord when they signed a lease to move into the rental unit on March 25, 2026. The term of the lease was scheduled to commence on May 1, 2026.
On March 31, 2026, the Tenants informed the Landlord of their intention not to proceed with the lease due to concerns about pest issues.

Per the Tenants’ testimony, the Landlord confirmed that they would return the deposit to the Tenants if the Landlord was able to find a new tenant for the unit to begin paying rent on May 1, 2026. The Tenants provided an email from the Landlord dated April 15, 2026, confirming that she found a new tenant to occupy the rent starting May 1, 2026.

Section 88(1) of the Act provides that where a tenant does not give notice in accordance with the Act or there is no agreement between the parties to terminate the tenancy, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with the Act. In this case, the Tenant could have given 60 days’ notice, therefore the Tenant would be obligated to pay rent up to May 31, 2026.

However, section 88(3) of the Act relieves the Tenant of the obligation to pay rent on the day a new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. A landlord is obligated to mitigate their losses pursuant to section 8(4) of the Act and consideration must be given to whether or not the Landlord too reasonable steps to do so.

In this case, a new tenant occupied the rental unit on May 1, 2026. The Landlord suffered no loss, because the Tenants’ tenancy (and their obligation to pay rent) was to commence on that date. Therefore, I find that pursuant to section 88(3) of the Act, despite the inadequate notice, the Tenant was no longer liable to pay rent to the Landlord for any period of time.

The Tenants provided an email from the Landlord, dated April 15, 2026, where the Landlord states that she will not be returning the deposit to the Tenants because the new tenant for the unit is paying $200.00 less per month in rent than the Tenants were going to pay. This is immaterial to whether the deposit should be returned.

Per subsection 106(10), a rent deposit must be applied by the Landlord to the payment of rent for the last rental period before the tenancy terminates. There is no such period in this case. Since the Landlord was successful in their efforts to re-rent the unit, the Tenants had no rent obligations whatsoever to the Landlord by operation of subsection 88(3). Regardless of the new rent charged by the Landlord to the new tenant, the Tenants are entitled to the return of their deposit as there is no applicable rental period for the deposit to be applied to.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,348.00. This amount represents: • $2,300.00 for the last month rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $13,215.38.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; • The Landlord did not convert the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N13 Notice of Termination (DOC-3228310, page 3). The notice says that the Landlord intends to convert the rental unit to non-residential use, specifically that it will be used as a commercial rental.
There is also no dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 14, 2022, as a result of the notice.
For the following reasons I find both that the Landlord did not convert the rental unit into non-residential use and that the N13 notice was served in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that [name] used to collect the rent for the Landlord and was friends with the Landlord. [name] testified that the N13 notice was served so that she could use the rental unit to run her business ‘High End Thrifters’. [name] testified that her previous landlady was kicking her out of her shop’s previous location, so she knew she had to move the shop.

The Tenant testified that after he vacated the rental unit he would go by it. The Tenant testified that at first he saw lots of renovations happening at the rental unit but then he saw that [name] and her boyfriend were living there. The Tenant testified that he would see both of their vehicles at the rental unit and that their vehicles were there for long periods of time.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit never became a store or any other type of commercial unit. The Tenant testified that he never saw any signage that indicated that a store was being operated out of the rental unit. The Tenant provided an image from google maps to show that there is little foot traffic on the street where the rental unit is located and it would not make sense to put a store there (DOC-6256450, page 5). 9. [name] testified that the floor was redone, a bookshelf was removed, and a partition was put between the dining room and kitchen. [name] testified that the renovations were done on commercial unit by July 2022 and that she moved the items for her store into the rental unit around that same time. [name] also testified that she purchased the property in July 2022 from the Landlord. 10. [name] testified that she operated a store at the rental unit for a short period of time between July 2022 until November 2022. [name] testified that the store did not work out because there was no foot traffic and no parking. [name] testified that the pandemic also played a role. [name] testified that she did not want to operate her business into the winter because then she would have to heat the front porch. 11. There is no dispute that there were two units at the rental complex and the Tenant rented the downstairs unit. [name] testified that she lived in the upstairs unit while her shop was operating and that once she stopped running the business she took over both units as her living space. [name] testified that to convert the store back into her living space she just had to take the partition down between the living room and kitchen. 12. [name] agreed that she put no signage up at the rental unit to indicate that she was running a store but said that she had no signage at her previous location either. [name] testified that she had a foldable chalkboard. 13. [name] testified that she did not have a business licence but also that she didn’t need one. [name] said that her business is a “glorified garage sale”. [name] testified that she doesn’t give receipts to customers. 14. The Tenant pointed to the Landlord’s evidence package and suggested that the photographs it includes were potentially misleading (DOC-6256486). The Landlord’s evidence package includes photographs of renovations that were done to the rental unit and a photograph of [name] store front. I agree with the Tenant’s representative that the inclusion of the storefront photograph in the evidence book with the renovation photos seems to suggest that the storefront is what the rental unit was converted to. However, the Tenant provided photographs from Facebook Marketplace that demonstrate that the photo is of [name] previous store that was in a different location DOC- 6256450. 15. [name] testified that she has photos showing she was running a shop out of the rental unit. However, I note that no such photo was provided by the Landlord as evidence. 16. I find the following evidence of the Tenant compelling: the testimony that every time he went by the rental unit he saw no indication that a shop was being run there, that he saw [name] and her boyfriends vehicles at the rental unit for long periods of time, that the rental unit is not located in a place that makes sense to operate a shop because of the lack of foot traffic, and that the Landlord included a misleading photograph in their evidence package. I find that the Tenant’s evidence proves on a balance of probabilities that the rental unit was never converted into non-residential use and that instead [name] simply used it as her home. 17. The testimony of [name] further deepened my concern that the rental unit was never used as a shop by [name]. I found [name] testimony to be evasive. She did not want to answer a question about who moved into the rental unit with her. I was left with the impression from her testimony that she would rather not have been participating in the hearing. 18. That renovations occurred does not satisfy me that a shop existed. [name] said that the only thing that needed to be done to revert the shop into a living space after she closed her business was to remove the partition. As such the majority of the renovations that occurred were clearly not related to the conversion of the rental unit. 19. The Landlord did not provide a single photograph, receipt etc. to support that the rental unit was used as a shop. 20. [name] described her business as a glorified yard sale. Yard sales can occur at residential homes and [name] description of her business does not support that the Landlord in good faith needed to evict the Tenant so that this business could operate. 21. [name] testified that she lived in the upstairs unit while she claims to have been running a shop and then took over the entire house when her shop closed. This in the context of all the other evidence supports that the intention was always for her to use the rental unit as her personal residence. 22. As I’m not satisfied that the rental unit was ever converted into non-residential use, I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies 23. The Tenant’s request for the maximum amount of general compensation pursuant to section 57(3)1.1 is granted. The Tenant paid $800.00 in rent and therefore the maximum compensation is $9,600.00. 24. The impact on the Tenant from the bad faith eviction was enormous. The Tenant has a disability and relies on the Ontario Disability Support Program (‘ODSP’) as his source of income. The Tenant testified that he could not afford to move. The Tenant testified that he was homeless after he was evicted, lived in his SUV, and floated around Walmart parking lots etc. The Tenant testified that being homeless cost him more as ODSP reduced his payments and that he had to buy fast food. The Tenant testified that he had to sell his tools at a large loss to get money. The Tenant was homeless between May 14, 2022 to September 1, 2022 when he found a new place to live. 25. While homeless the Tenant put his stuff in storage. The Tenant’s request for storage costs between May 11, 2022, to August 31, 2022, in the amount of $1,458.13 is granted. The Tenant had to incur this costs as a direct result of the bad faith eviction. The Tenant provided a use agreement for the storage, a receipt for the first partial month, and a letter from the Tenant’s brother explaining why the storage had to be in his name and outlining the total costs (DOC-3228310 page 38-43 and DOC-3238858 page 2). While the Tenant did not have a receipt for every single month of storage, I found the Tenant to be a credible witness and he did have some supporting documentation that bolstered his testimony. 26. The Tenant’s new rental unit is $200.00 a month more expensive than the rental unit that is the subject of this application. While the only supporting documentation the Tenant had about the increase in rent is a somewhat informal signed note by his new landlord (DOC- 3228310), I find the Tenant to be credible and accept that he is paying $200.00 more monthly. The Tenant only had to incurs this expense as a direct result of the bad faith eviction and I find it reasonable to award it. 27. Pursuant to section 57(3)(1.1) of the Act I can only award the increase in rent for one year after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant was homeless from May 14, 2022 to September 1, 2022 so I can only award the increase in rent from September 1, 2022 to May 14, 2023 which is 9.5 months. As such $1,900.00 is the difference in rent that will be awarded. 28. The Tenant paid $257.25 in gasoline to move his stuff into storage and I find it reasonable to award those expenses. The Tenant had receipts (DOC-3228310, page 46-47). While some of these receipts are close together and are before the Tenant vacated the rental unit, I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the gasoline costs are all related to putting his stuff in storage. 29. The request for extra food expenses while the Tenant was homeless is denied. The Tenant does not have receipts and I’ve already factored in the impacts of being homeless on the general compensation amount awarded. 30. The request for a fine is denied. The evidence before me is that the Landlord sold all his rental properties and therefore I don’t have ongoing concerns about his conduct as a landlord in the future. The remedies already awarded will encourage compliance with the Act and operate as deterrence.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,215.38. This amount represents: • $9,600.00 for general compensation • $1,900.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after the tenancy ended. • $1,458.13 for storage costs • $257.25 for moving costs
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'):  entered the rental unit illegally.  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.  did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. T6 Application: The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. A1 Application: The Tenant also applied for an order to determine whether the Act applies.
reasons: The [name] application was withdrawn by t he Tenant on a previous hearing before the LTB (see DOC-6603035). The application having been withdrawn, the LTB’s file is closed relative to the [name] application. [name]
The T2 application wa s filed on April 18, 2024. The tenant vacated the rental unit on March 18, 2024.

The T2 application form fil ed by the Tenant does not include any allegations. In the part of the form designated for the explanation of reasons for filing the application, the Tenant wrote “… see [name] to Form T2 ..”, however the appendix was not filed with the application.

The application was scheduled for an [name] tive Case Conference (‘ACC’) on January 28, 2025. The LTB’s records indicate that the Tenant attended the ACC with a legal representative. The presiding Member’s adjournment sheet states, inter alia, that the Appendix to the T2 application was missing, and that the Tenant’s legal representative said this issue would be addressed through a request to amend the T2 application. The adjournment sheet also indicates that the Tenant and his legal represented were directed to deliver the request to amend the T2 application by March 28, 2025 (see DOC-4945223).
No request to amend the T2 application wa s served and filed until May 21, 2026 (DOC- 799881 & DOC-7998803).

I accept that the Tenant did not intentionally neglect to file the appendix when the T2 application was filed, but the result of the absence of this document is that the T2 application, as filed, made no factual allegations. This was not rectified until the Tenant delivered the request to amend the application move than 2 years later, on May 21, 2026.

The T2 application wa s filed pursuant to ss. 29(1) of the Act. Subsection 29(2) of the Act prescribes a one-year limitation period for this type of application. The LTB does not have jurisdiction to order a remedy relative to anything that happened more than one year before the application was filed: ss. 29(2), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; [name] v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII).

Although the applicat ion was originally filed about one month after the tenancy ended, because the application was devoid of allegations at the time, the limitation period ought to run from May 21, 2026, the date the request to amend the application was delivered, and the first time any allegation was made relative to this application.

Parties are not permitted to file blank applicati on to preserve a limitation period, only to add the allegations later by requesting to amend the blank application. This would amount, in my view, to an impermissible circumvention of the limitation period, and would defeat the Legislature’s intent in implementing the limitation periods in the Act.

I accept that circumvention of the limitation period was not the Tenant’s intent, but it would be the effect if I were to grant the request to amend the application and not consider the issue of the limitation period.

The Tenant’s submission was that his former legal representative was supposed to serve and file the request to amend earlier, but to the surprise of the Tenant, the legal representative failed to do so. This may be the case, but even if the Tenant was failed by his former legal representative and does not himself bear responsibility for this failure, I do not have jurisdiction to extend limitation periods: ss. 190, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; ss.50(2), General, [name]. 516/06.
The request to amend the application was filed more than two years after the tenancy ended. All allegations included in the amended application are barred by the statutory limitation period.
The request to amend the T2 application is denied because no allegations included in the amended application are within the statutory limitation period.
The T2 application is dismissed because no allegations are made in it. T6 Application
At the hearing, the Tenant, through DC, requested to withdraw the T6 application, and I consented to the request.
ordered: The T2 application is dismissed.
The A1 and T6 applications having been withdrawn, the LTB’s file is closed. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities against the Purchaser. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay the Tenant $6,036.00.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’) which alleged that the Purchaser intended to move into the rental unit, that the Tenant vacated because of the N12 notice on April 6, 2025 after a Board order was issued. There is no dispute between the parties that the purchase of the property fell through, and that the Purchaser never moved into the rental unit. The only question that remains is whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.
For the following reasons I find that the Purchaser served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith, but the Landlord did not. [name]

The Landlord spouse Tanzeela Mahmood (‘[name]’) provided testimony on behalf of the Landlord, as although he was present at the virtual hearing he was unwell and in hospital. 7. [name] testified that neither she nor the Landlord knew the purchaser prior to entering into an agreement of purchase and sale. The Landlord received a declaration of the Purchaser, which states that he and his wife personally intended to occupy the main floor rental unit. The Landlord and Purchaser signed an agreement of purchase and sale on October 29, 2024 with a closing date of January 10, 2025. Based on the representation by the Purchaser the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination. The closing date for the sale of the property was extended because the Tenant would not vacate without an eviction order. The Landlord received an email from the Purchaser’s lawyer on April 15, 2025 after the Tenant vacated requesting to extend the closing date for two weeks. The Landlord agreed to extend the closing date to April 24, 2025. On April 23, 2025 the Purchaser’s lawyer emailed the Landlord indicating that the Purchaser would be unable to complete the closing due to unfortunate reasons, but provided no further details. 8. The Landlord deemed the Purchaser in breach of their agreement and the Purchaser agreed to forfeit his deposit in the amount of $25,000.00 to the Landlord and a mutual release was signed. 9. The Landlord relisted the property on May 9, 2025, as it was critical to do so as soon as possible as the Landlord owed $200,000.00 to the Canadian Revenue Agency and over $100,000.00 in credit card bills, The Landlord’s corporation was also in debt and the Landlord needed to reduce their debt. 10. [name] testified due to their financial situation she and the Landlord needed to rent their primary residence and move in with her sister just to make ends meet. 11. The Landlord reduced the price of the rental property multiple times, but were still unable to sell the rental unit and entered into a new tenancy agreement to rent the unit commencing August 1, 2025. 12. A landlord who takes no steps to confirm that a purchaser actually wants to move into a rental unit is not serving the notice in good faith. However, that is not what happened here. In this case the Landlord did act diligently to confirm the Purchaser’s intentions. The Landlord received a written declaration from the Purchaser outlining their intentions. The Purchaser waived a condition with respect to financing on November 3, 2024, and agreed to amendments of the closing date during the eviction process showing that he was still interested. The Purchaser attended the hearing for the Landlord’s eviction application and provided testimony. The Landlord received an email from the Purchaser’s lawyer that he was not going to follow through with the sale after the Tenants vacated. I find that the Landlord took adequate steps to confirm the Purchaser’s intention and that based on the information available to the Landlord it was reasonable for the Landlord to believe that the Purchaser genuinely intended to move into the rental unit. 13. For those reasons the claim is dismissed against the Landlord. Purchaser’s Bad Faith 14. While I believe the Purchaser that he originally intended to purchase the property to live in with his family, the Court in Elkins established that the LTB should consider all relevant evidence when determining whether the N12 was served in bad faith and should not restrict itself to consideration of whether there was good faith at the time the N12 was served. 15. The Purchaser testified that he went to Pakistan at the end of December, 2024 as his father had become ill. Unfortunately, his father passed away on January 24, 2025. The Purchaser returned from Pakistan on February 2, 2025. He states that the unforeseen trip had had a financial impact on him and the money he used on the trip was supposed to go towards his down payment. Not withstanding the expenses incurred he still intended to close the deal and believed he still could. 16. The Purchaser further testified that he had planned to borrow $150,000.00 from a friend in order to complete the purchase of the property, but when he reached out to his friend as the closing date neared his friend told him that he would not be able to lend him any money. It was at this point that the Purchaser asked his lawyer to request and extension of the closing date. 17. The Purchaser states that during this extension he attempted to secure the $150,000.00 he needed from other sources including family, but was unsuccessful and could not proceed with the purchase of the rental property. 18. The Purchaser waived the financing condition on the agreement of purchase and sale on November 3, 2024, without properly securing all the financing he required to complete the purchase of the property. Additionally, the Purchaser testified that his unforeseen trip to Pakistan had an impact on the finances he was planning to use to complete the purchase. 19. Notwithstanding that he knew or ought to have known that his finances were in question he proceeded to testify at the hearing of the Landlord’s eviction application and neglected to advise the Board of his current financial situation. Additionally when he had his lawyer request an extension of the closing date he failed to provide the Landlord with the reason for the extension or any issues he was having with respect to financing that might affect the closing of the sale. 20. I do not find that the Purchaser acted diligently and maintained a genuine intention to purchase the property and move in. The Purchaser had an obligation to maintain his awareness about his financial circumstances and failed to do so. 21. For those reasons I find that the Purchaser did not maintain a good faith intention to move into the rental unit and that therefore the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Remedies 22. The Tenant seeks a difference in rent between the old rental unit and the new rental unit for a period of one year. He described the old and new rental units as being similar in size. He testified that he was previously paying $3,400.00 per month to rent the rental unit and is currently paying $3,900.00 per month in rent at the new rental unit and provided a lease agreement supporting this claim. In cross examination the Tenant agreed that his monthly rent had increased effective January, 2025 to $3,485.00. 23. The difference in rent between the agreed upon monthly rent when the Tenant vacated being $3,485.00 and his currently monthly rent $3,900.00 is $415.00 per month being $4,980.00 for one year. 24. I am satisfied that rent differential is appropriate in the circumstances. Therefore the Purchaser must pay to the Tenant $4,980.00 for the increase rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. 25. The Tenant seeks moving expenses he incurred as a result of moving from the rental unit. At the hearing he provided oral testimony that his moving expenses were $1,008.00, but did not provide any supporting documentation. Neither the Landlord, nor the Purchaser questioned the amount claimed by the Tenant for moving expenses and I find the amount claimed reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, I find that the Purchaser must pay the Tenant $1,008.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. 26. The Tenant seeks general damages in the amount of $15,000.00 for the emotional distress and impact on his child in relocating and disruption of his schooling, his own loss of work and time due to a longer commute and adjusting to a new area. The tenant also seeks reimbursement of legal fees of $2,850.00 which he paid for representation at the eviction hearing on the N12. 27. The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3)(1.1), which states: An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. [Emphasis added]. 28. The Tenant did not substantiate or expand on these claims. Without a more fulsome explanation I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant is entitled to general damages. With respect to the Tenant’s claim for legal fees it would be inappropriate to award any costs for legal fees in relation to another matter, additionally these fees were not substantiated. 29. In the circumstances I find that the Tenant is not entitled to any general damages.
ordered: The total amount the Purchaser shall pay the Tenant is $6,036.00. This amount represents: • $4,980.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred or will incur for one year after vacating the rental unit. • $1,008.00 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchaser shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Purchaser does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant’s application is based on the allegation that the Landlord permitted electricity to be disconnected.
There is no dispute that it was disconnected by the Electric Safety Authority (‘ESA’) on or about April 30, 2026.
There is no dispute that the issues that led to the disconnection have not been addressed, and the electricity continues to be disconnected.
The Landlord’s only defense is that the Tenant allegedly interfered with Landlord’s attempts to address the issues.
For the reasons below, I find this defense to be unpersuasive. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that she saw an ESA “Notice of Disconnect – Occupant” in the beginning of April. The notice advised that electricity would soon be disconnected (page 3 of document 8048250 in Portal). The notice indicates that the owner has been notified. According to the Tenant, the Landlord was first notified no later than early February 2026 but ESA waited until May to disconnect electricity as they don’t disconnect it during cold months.
Pages 14, 15, and 24 of 8048250 are notes from the ESA file. They indicate that there are multiple issues at the rental unit.
Page 17 of 8048250 shows that a notice was delivered to the Landlord on or about February 4, 2026 via Purolator. The Landlord was also notified on other dates including May 2026.

On or about April 30, 2026 the Tenant returned home and found that her rental unit had no power. She has been living without electricity ever since. She reached out to the Landlord but hasn’t heard back. Her legal representative wrote to the Landlord (document 8060513) and received no reply.

The Landlord has not done anything to address the issue. He has not attended at the rental unit and has not attempted to serve the Tenant any notice of entry. No electrician attended or attempted to attend.

On cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the Landlord served approximately 5 notices of entry in total but testified that he rescheduled and only attended at the unit twice. She said she was flexible regarding times of entry and did not have any issues with the Landlord’s notices. She denied that he ever attempted to perform any electrical repairs.
The most recent notice of entry was given to her in 2025. The Landlord has not attempted to enter the unit in 2026.
The Landlord remains in breach of LTB order LTB-T-015278-25-HR issued by the LTB on April 14, 2025. The Landlord was required to perform multiple repairs and has no performed any of them.
The Landlord’s request to review was denied by order LTB-T-015278-25-RV issued by the LTB on July 31, 2025. The Landlord did not attend the hearing of his request to review. Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord’s explanation/defense was fundamentally two-fold.

First, he argued that he can’t repair anything at the rental unit because the Tenant interferes with his attempts to repair. He called the police who advised him not to escalate. He fears attending at the rental unit to avoid the Tenant making allegations against him. She yells at him, and he doesn’t wish to communicate with her. She has previously told him that she “won the [name] lottery” and will extort as much money from him as possible. According to the Landlord, the Tenant’s strategy is to cause as much damage as possible so she can maximize what he has to pay her.
Second, according to the Landlord, the issue is not as serious as it looks and could be resolved by the Tenant if she simply flips her breakers.

He provided very brief testimony. He didn’t provide any dates. He did not explain how he arrived at the conclusion that the issue is not as serious as it appears from the ESA documents. He did not provide any evidence to corroborate his serious allegations that the Tenant intentionally causes damage/losses so she can get a payday from him.

On cross-examination he admitted that he is not a certified electrician but testified that he is an electronic technician who understands electrical work. He confirmed that he has not hired an electrician to address ESA issues.

He was asked whether he was notified of potential disconnection in February 2026. He was somewhat evasive. He admitted to receiving one envelope, but he redirects some of his mail and correspondence may gave gone to the wrong address.

He was asked whether he has any evidence that he attempted to comply with the ESA order. He said that there is no evidence because all he needs to do is serve a 24-hour notice, have the Tenant allow entry, and to preform repairs once he enters.

He was asked whether he has taken any steps to comply since April 30th. He testified that he would do work in the yard, wait to see the Tenant and then ask her if she wants him to go into her unit and do the work. According to him, the Tenant would not let him in and would demand a 24-hour notice instead. The Tenant denies this allegation.
He was specifically asked whether he has served any notices to enter the unit since April 30, 2026. He could not recall.

He was asked about his compliance with LTB order LTB-T-015278-25-HR. He could not recall seeing this order. This is a perplexing reply considering that he had previously filed a request to review this order.

His witness, CD, provided brief testimony. She is the Landlord’s friend who does not reside at the residential complex. She testified that the Landlord could not perform repairs because the Tenant would not let him into the building. She could not recall the date(s) and did not specify which repairs she was referring to. Law and analysis

This application invokes ss. 21(1), 22, and 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
This is the Tenant’s application, and she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit, including its electrical system, contrary to s. 20(1) of the Act. The Landlord has been aware of the issues since February and has not responded to the issue reasonably. He has been aware of the disconnection since it occurred, and has not acted reasonably.
There is no dispute that electricity was disconnected by the ESA due to ESA violations at the property.

Under the Act, the Landlord is responsible for addressing these issues. I find that the Landlord has not taken sufficient steps to address them. If he is to be believed, he has verbally asked for permission to enter without notice on some unspecified date(s) and was denied entry. He has not done anything else. The Tenant denied that even this has occurred.

To the extent that there is conflict between the Tenant’s version and the Landlord’s version of the events, I prefer the Tenant’s version. It was logical, supported by documentary evidence, and not shaken or undermined by cross-examination. The Landlord’s version was uncorroborated, somewhat contradicted by documentary evidence, and shaken by cross-examination.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has done nothing at all since the disconnection occurred. The Landlord provided testimony to the contrary, but it is not corroborated by any documentary evidence. The Landlord’s own testimony was that he needed to serve a 24-hour notice to enter the unit, but none have been served. His testimony was that he chose to surprise the Tenant at the residential complex to request verbal permission to enter instead. I am not persuaded that this has occurred but even if it has, this is not a reasonable response to this urgent issue. The Landlord had multiple ways to either address the issue, or to demonstrate good faith efforts to address the issue. He could have called an independent electrician, he could have served written notices, he could have recorded his attempts to enter. I draw a negative inference from the lack of any such evidence.
The Landlord has also breached sections 21(1) and 22 as a result. Remedies

The Tenant requested the following remedies: a. Fine payable to the LTB, b. 100% rent abatement until power is restored and for the time since power was disconnected, c. $30,000 for general damages, d. $4,000 for projected moving expenses so the Tenant can temporarily vacate the rental unit until maintenance issues are addressed, e. Order requiring the Landlord to comply with ESA requirements and restore electricity supply to the rental unit, [name] that the tenancy will not be terminated if the Tenant temporarily moves out until electricity is restored, and [name] for sheriff enforcement to re-enter the rental unit if necessary,
Remedy ‘b’ is granted in part. The Tenant is already entitled to an ongoing rent abatement of 50% pursuant to the previous order.

She testified about the serious impact the lack of electricity has had on her. She lives in the dark, she has had to throw out hundreds of dollars worth of groceries from her fridge and her freezer, she can’t keep food at home, she can’t shower because water is heated by electricity. She missed days of work. She is unable to enjoy the rental unit and has been looking for alternative housing. Her income is very low at some $600 a month and she is unable to afford market rent elsewhere.

I find that the Tenant is entitled to a 50% rent abatement starting April 30th, 2026 and until electricity is restored. The Tenant has not been paying rent as permitted under order [name] and this remedy does not result in an order that the Landlord must pay any amount to the Tenant. There is nothing to abate when rent has not been paid. 40. [name] ‘d’ is granted in the amount of $1,000.00. The Tenant provided no receipts and no estimates. She is a single person, and the rental unit is small. The amount of $4,000 appears to be excessive and I find that $1,000.00 represents the reasonable cost she will incur as a result of the Landlord’s misconduct. 41. Remedies ‘e’ and ‘f’ are granted. The Landlord shall immediately take all necessary steps to restore supply of electricity to the rental unit, and the tenancy shall remain in full force and effect until it is terminated in accordance with the Act. 42. Remedy ‘g’ is denied. The Tenant has a key to the rental unit. She is allowed to temporarily vacate it under the Act and she can re-enter any time using her key. Should the Landlord choose to illegally lock the Tenant out, the Tenant may bring an application to require the Landlord to restore her in possession. At this time, this remedy is purely speculative. Further, pursuant to s. 31(5) of the Act, sheriff enforcement, if granted, will likely expire because the Tenant would need to rely on it. 43. [name] ‘a’ is granted. 44. Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $50,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant: The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 45. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provide that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 46. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 47. I should therefore consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor. 48. I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00. 49. The Tenant was seriously impacted by the Landlord’s actions. 50. The Landlord chose to ignore requirements of the Act and left the rental unit in a deplorable state without electricity, a vital service. The Landlord was previously fined $500 in LTB-T-015278-25-HR. This small fine was imposed for his first egregious breach of the Act, and this fine does not appear to have deterred the Landlord. A year later the Landlord has still not complied with the previous order. He is once again found to be in breach of the Act. The breach is once again egregious. It is clear that a more substantial fine is necessary to deter the Landlord and similar landlords and to ensure compliance. An even higher fine may be appropriate if the Landlord breaches the Act again in the future. 51. The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $30,000 for the serious impact this eviction has on her mental, physical and emotional well-being. 52. The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment. 53. I find the amount of $5,000 to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s actions had on her, her work, and her mental health. She lost food that she paid for and missed days of work. She suffered mentally and financially. Her testimony on this issue was credible, uncontroverted and persuasive. On the other hand, the Tenant is already not paying rent and is compensated via rent abatement. The disconnection occurred just over a month ago. A higher award would be excessive in my view.
ordered: The Landlord shall immediately restore electricity supply to the rental unit. This includes, but is not limited to, complying with ESA requirements and orders.
The Tenant is entitled to an additional and ongoing 50% rent abatement starting April 30, 2026 and until supply of electricity is restored.
If the Landlord does not do the work by June 12, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $362.50 a month from the rent owing beginning July 1, 2026 and until the work is complete.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $6,000.00. This amount represents: 1. $5,000.00 for general damages. 2. $1,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant will incur.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing beginning July 1, 2026 and until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy shall continue until it is terminated in accordance with the Act even if the Tenant temporarily vacates the rental unit until supply of electricity is restored.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by June 19, 2026. June 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: Ilesanmi v [name], 2026 ONLTB 43421 Date: 2026-06-01 In the matter of: [address] Toronto ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on May 29, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 9:31 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,348.00.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant was locked out of their rental unit contrary to s. 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') on or about March 31, 2026.
The Tenant is entitled to a 100% rent abatement of $1,600.00 for the month of April 2026.

I also find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,700.00 and that deposit was not returned nor applied to the Tenant’s rent. The Tenant is entitled to have this deposit returned to them.
Finally, based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence, I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant incurred out-of-pocket expenses of $2,000.00 as a result of the lockout.
The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application and is entitled to a reimbursement of this cost.
The Tenant did not request any other remedies.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,348.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00 rent abatement. • $1,700.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $2,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Application for a Rebate of Money the Landlord owes (T1)

The Tenant alleges in his application that the Landlord did not use his last month’s rent deposit of $2,000.00 for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to him after the tenancy ended. The Tenant seeks an order requiring the Landlord to pay $2,000.00.

The tenancy began on February 1, 2024. The Landlord collected a last months’ deposit of $2,000.00 on February 1, 2024, and a key deposit of $250.00. The parties do not dispute that the key deposit of $250.00 was returned to the Tenant on May 2, 2026.
The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on April 28, 2026, and rent for April was paid.

The Landlord testified that she obtained vacant possession of the rental unit on April 28, 2026. She indicated that 1 additional set of keys were not returned until May 14, 2026. This was not disputed by the Tenant.

On April 9, 2026, the Tenant texted the Landlord informing her that he had accepted a job and wanted to move out before the end of the month (April 30, 2026). The Tenant asked whether the Landlord would be open to returning his May/ last month’s rent deposit if he vacated before the end of April 2026. The Landlord replied that she would be open to discussing the matter if the Tenant moved out of the unit well before the end of the month so that she could prepare the unit for a new Tenant.
The Landlord ultimately did not return the rent deposit.
The Landlord’s explanation at the hearing was that the deposit was applied to the May 2026 rent because the Tenant did not give proper notice.

The Tenant asserted that the Landlord provided several reasons for not returning his last month’s deposit. He further asserted that the Landlord’s reply to his text message on April 9, 2026 implies that she did not object to him moving out and was willing to return his deposit. Analysis and findings
The issue before me is whether the Tenant is entitled to the return of his rent deposit.

The evidence before me does not establish that the Landlord definitively agreed to return the Tenant’s deposit if the Tenant moved out on April 28, 2026. The Landlord's text message expressly states: “I would be open if you are planning to be out well before the end of the month so that I can get things ready for a new Tenant.” In my view, the wording “I would be open” suggests an invitation for a discussion and does not in any way create an agreement.

In these circumstances, the Tenant was required to either: enter into an agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy in accordance with s. 37(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'); or serve a notice to terminate his tenancy at least 60 days in advance in accordance with s. 44(2). The Tenant did neither.

Subsection 88(1)1 of the Act addresses how much rent a tenant may owe if they vacate a rental unit without having served a valid notice of termination or entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy: (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.

As the Tenant vacated the unit without having served a valid notice of termination or entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, in accordance with subsection 88(1) of the Act, the Tenant may be liable for rent up to June 30, 2026, which is the earliest valid termination date the Tenant could have specified when he gave the Landlord the invalid notice on April 9, 2026.

In accordance with subsection 88(3) of the Act, a Tenant’s liability for rent arrears in this situation can be earlier if the landlord re-rents the unit. In this case, the Landlord testified that the unit remains vacant.

I have also considered whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize its losses, as required by subsection 88(4) of the Act. The Landlord testified that she contacted her real estate agent and listed the property on May 2, 2026. However, due to the rental market the property remains vacant. There was no evidence before me that the Landlord removed the listing, delayed marketing the unit, or otherwise failed to make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord fulfilled her obligations as required by subsection 88(4) of the Act in reasonably attempting to re-rent the unit and to mitigate its losses.
For all the reasons given above, I am satisfied that the Landlord is entitled to apply the last month’s deposit to May 2026.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') or the Landlord's superintendent or the Landlord's agent substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant's household. (LTB-T-052027-25 – T2) Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord or collected or retained money illegally. (LTB-T-038969-25 – T1)
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant advised that he also had another outstanding T2 application alleging the Landlord withheld vital services on June 25, 2025. That application had yet to be heard, and I had agreed to hear that application, along with the Tenant’s T1 application as they alleged the same issues.

LTB-T-052027-25 had inadvertently not been combined with LTB-T-038969-25 after the hearing had been completed and LTB-T-052027-25 had been scheduled for an Adjudicative Case Conference on May 4, 2026, where neither party attended. The outcome of that application is reversed for the purposes of this order.

Further, LTB-T-052027-25 had alleged that the Landlord withheld vital services. Having taken submissions from the parties, I amended the Tenant’s application to reflect a claim that the Landlord had substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the unit, contrary to s. 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Tenant’s Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant testified that his unit is in a rooming house, which he had moved into in July of 2021.

When he moved into that unit, another tenant had the residential complex’s utilities in their name. Once the tenant had vacated their unit in September of 2021, the Tenant has assumed the utilities in his name. The Tenant testified that since that time, he has been responsible for collecting the utility expenses from the other tenants.

The Tenant had sent an e-mail to the Landlord on December 31, 2024, outlining to the Landlord that he does not believe that he should be responsible for collecting and paying all of the utilities, and that another one of the tenants has not been paying him his share of the utilities. The Landlord responded by e-mail on February 10, 2025, that an LTB hearing taking place on February 12, 2025, would give her a “better idea of what position we are in”.

The Tenant testified that he believes what the Landlord is doing is illegal, and that the Landlord should reimburse him $1,510.37 for amounts he was forced to pay as a result of the other tenant not paying their share. The Tenant testified that he feels he is being coerced to have taken on this responsibility

The Landlord testified that she only provided the lease terms and that she never advised the tenants as to how to sort out the utilities themselves. Further, the Landlord testified that the Tenant never asked her to assume the utilities in 2021 and that this transaction occurred amongst the tenants, and that the Landlord has provided authorization to the Tenant to switch the utilities into his name.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant may have been coerced by another tenant to assume the utility responsibilities but that the lease had always said that the tenants were responsible for their own utilities and that when the Tenant had advised the Landlord about the other tenant who had not been paying their share of the utilities, that tenant had been served N4 and N5 notices of termination, the latter being for non-payment of utility costs to the Tenant. That tenant had been evicted. Analysis

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Section 135(1) of the Act states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Having considered the evidence of both parties, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected or retained money in contravention of the Act, nor did the Landlord substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.

The Tenant raised the issue with the Landlord of the other tenant not paying their share of the utility costs to the Tenant. The Landlord followed this up by issuing a Notice of Termination to that tenant, where they had subsequently been evicted. As such, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably to the issue as raised by the Tenant with respect to the paying of the utility costs to the Tenant, by the other tenants in the residential complex.
Further, section 29(2) of the Act states: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant testified that the utilities have been in his name since September 2021. The Tenant filed this application on June 23, 2025. Had the Tenant wished to raise the assignment of the utility costs generally, the Tenant was obligated to raise that issue by way of an application within one year of those utility accounts being assigned. As such, I am not satisfied that the application for substantial interference was filed within one year after the alleged conduct took place and this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

Lastly, the Tenant’s T1 application alleges that the Landlord issued an illegal charge or illegal rent by forcing him to pay the utilities. The Landlord herself did not request or charge for these amounts and did not collect any monies from the Tenant or other tenants with respect to these issues. As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord issued an illegal charge or illegally retained or collected any money from the Tenant and the Tenant’s T1 application is also dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the applic ation on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must reimburse the Tenants f or their filing fee of $48.00 by June 23, 2026.

The Tenants alleged that the Landlord withheld the r eturn of their refundable key deposit and interest on the last month’s rent deposit pending receipt of a quote for cleaning the rental unit after they vacated.

The Tenants testified that they repeatedly advised the Landlords that it was not lawful to withhold the key deposit or interest on the rent deposit. Despite this, the Landlords refused to return these amounts until after the Tenants filed their application.
The Tenants submitted that they are entitled to reimbur sement of the filing fee because they would not have incurred this cost had the Landlords complied with the Act. Applicable law

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) prohibits illegal charges, subject to exemptions set out in section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06. Section 17 permits a landlord to collect a refundable key, remote entry device, or card deposit, provided it does not exceed the direct replacement cost.
A landlord’s obligation to pay annual interest on a rent deposit is set out in section 106(6) of the Act. Analysis

I find that the Landlords withheld the Tenants’ key deposit and the interest owing on the rent deposit pending receipt of a cleaning quote. There is no basis under the Act for withholding these amounts for this reason.

I further find that the Landlords returned the key deposit and paid the interest owing only after the Tenants filed their application with the Board. Although the Landlords are no longer in contravention of the Act, the Tenants were required to bring an application to secure compliance.

The Board may order reimbursement of an application filing fee where a tenant is required to bring an application to enforce their rights under the Act. In these circumstances, I find that the Tenants would not have incurred the filing fee but for the Landlords’ conduct
Accordingly, the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee, and an order will issue requiring the Landlords to pay this amount
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenants $48.00 for the cost of filing the application by June 23, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 23, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: the 'Landlords') applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') to pay the rent that the Tenants owe. (L9 Application) The Landlords also applied for an order requiring the Tenants to pay the Landlords reasonable out-of-pocket costs that are the result of the Tenants’ failure to pay utility costs they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement, and the Landlords reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlords incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. (L10 Application) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlords: • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 Application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) These applications were collectively heard by videoconference on April 20, 2026. The Landlord [name], the Landlords’ Legal Representative Petar Guzina and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: The parties agree that both Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlords to rent the rental unit commencing October 15, 2023 for a fixed term ending April 14, 2024.
The Tenant [name] stated that he vacated the rental unit in March, 2024. The Tenant [name] did not return his keys to the Landlords after vacating the rental unit.
The tenancy agreement continued beyond the fixed term date of April 14, 2024 as a month-to-month tenancy.
The Landlords submit that the tenancy continues for both Tenants and there was no agreement to terminate [name]’s tenancy

Based on the submissions of both parties, I am satisfied that this is a joint tenancy. Except in very specific circumstances pertaining to domestic violence, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not permit one joint tenant to sever their interest in an ongoing joint tenancy in the absence of an agreement by all the parties. In this case, there is no evidence that the parties agreed to amend the tenancy agreement to remove [name] as a Tenant.
The Tenant [name] is properly named as a Tenant in these applications. L9 Application
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 1 2024. The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenants did not pay the total rent they were required to pay for the period from February 15, 2024 to June 30, 2026.
The lawful rent is $3,400.00. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.

The tenancy ended on July 1, 2024, as a result of the Tenants moving out in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order or agreement to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the Tenant's obligation to pay rent also ended on that date.
The Landlords had collected a rent deposit of $3,300.00 from the Tenants and this deposit was applied to June’s rent.
The rent arrears and daily compensation owing to June 30, 2024 less the last months rent deposit are $8,900.00.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $58.99 is owing to the Tenants for the period from October 14, 2023 to June 30, 2026.
The Landlords incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The Landlords are entitled to $9,027.01. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to June 30, 2024 and the cost of the application minus the rent deposit and interest owing. L10 Application
As explained below, the Landlords proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 1, 2024.
The application was filed within one year after the Tenants ceased to be in possession of the rental unit. Unpaid Utilities
The Tenants failed to pay water costs that they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement.
The Landlords produced an invoice from Alectra Utilities associated with water charges in the Tenants name, dated July 29, 2024 in the amount of $938.78.

The Landlords produced a letter from the Municipality of Vaughn, dated January 27, 2025 indicating that the unpaid amount of $931.78 owing to Alectra Utilities has been added to the property taxes for the rental unit.
The Landlords incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses of $931.78 as a result of the Tenants’ failure to pay water costs that they were required to pay under the tenancy agreement. Damages
Included in the Landlords’ application is a claim for compensation in the amount of $771.83 to repair damage and or replace property that was damaged in the rental unit.
