In order for an application for compensation for damages made pursuant to section 89(1) of the Act to succeed, a landlord must establish the following: (a) there was property damage to the rental unit or residential complex; (b) the damage is “undue” meaning that it is not normal wear and tear and it is not insignificant; and (c) the damage was a result of wilful or negligent conduct by the Tenants, occupant or guest.
In this context, the word “property” refers to the physical objects such as walls, ceilings, floors, appliances and fixtures in a residential complex.
If all of these factors are met, then the Board can award the landlord the reasonable cost of repair, or the replacement if it is not reasonable for the damage to be repaired.
The Landlords allege damage to the flooring in the rental unit, missing floor vent covers as well as a cost incurred to rent a waste disposal bin to remove items left in the unit. Waste [name]

The rental of a garbage disposal [name] is not wilful or negligent undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex as prescribed in section 89 of the Act. As such, the Landlord is not entitled to compensation for the rental of the waste disposal [name]. Missing vent covers

The Landlords did not provide sufficient evidence with respect to the claim that floor vent covers were missing. No photographs of the missing covers were provided, and I am not satisfied that the Landlords have proven this component of their application on a balance of probabilities based on the evidence adduced at the hearing. Damages to Floors
The Landlords claim that the flooring of the rental unit was damaged and required cleaning and polishing to remove scratches.
The Landlords provided one photograph of a scratched floor.
The Tenants along with their witness [name] testified that the flooring depicted in the photograph was in that condition at the time they moved into the rental unit.

With respect to the evidence before me I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the alleged damage to the floor is “undue” meaning that it is not normal wear and tear and it is not insignificant, nor am I satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the scratches to the floor were a result of wilful or negligent conduct by the Tenants, occupant or guest.

The Landlords did not prove that the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Tenants permitted in the residential complex wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex. T2 Application Request to Amend
At the commencement of the hearing of the Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications the Tenants sought to rely upon amended applications filed with the Board on April 15, 2026.
The Landlords were opposed to the request to amend as the Tenants had not complied with the time frame for amendments as set out in an interim order.
An interim order was issued on February 18, 2025 in relation to LTB-T-039414-24 and combined that matter with LTB-L048859-24, LTB-L-083081-24 and LTB-T-040852-24.

The interim order also indicates that if the Tenants wished to amend their application prior to the hearing then on or before March 15, 2025 the Tenants were to serve their amended application along with all supporting documents on the Landlords, file a copy with the Board along with an affidavit of service. The Tenants did not comply with the interim order.

LTB Rule of Procedure 15 states that an applicant seeking to amend their application shall request this amendment in writing by serving the amended application to all other parties and filing the amended application and a Certificate of Service with the Board. The request to amend the application is then decided at the hearing.

However, [name] allows the Board to exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

As the Tenants had not complied with the interim order issued on February 18, 2025 and Rule of Procedure 15 the request to amend the application was denied and the Tenants proceeded on their original applications. Illegal entry

The Tenants testified that on March 2, 2024 the Landlord [name] Kimberly illegally entered the rental unit without providing notice. Both Tenants testified that a showing of the rental unit had been scheduled and the Landlords gave the Tenant [name] notice, but the Tenant [name] did not receive notification of the showing and was asleep with his girlfriend. After being awoken by the yelling of the Landlord and being advised by [name] that a showing was scheduled he sent a text message to the Landlord asking her to skip his room. After the showing ended the Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord [name] Kimberly left the rental unit but remained on the property and after a period of time she re-entered the rental unit without permission and proceeded to the bedroom where the Tenant [name] was with his girlfriend. The Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord [name] Kimberly attempted to force the door open and was yelling and swearing at him attempting to give him a document. At the time both [name] and his girlfriend were not fully clothed and were attempting to sleep. The Tenants’ witness [name], [name]’s girlfriend also confirmed the Tenants’ version of events from that day.

The Landlord [name] Kimberly testified that she had received consent from the Tenant [name] prior to showing the unit and they she never left the property before re- entering the rental unit to attempt to serve a document on [name].

On a balance of probabilities I prefer the evidence of the Tenants to that of the Landlord. Although the Landlord had permission from the Tenant [name] to show the rental unit. After the showing ended the Landlord left the unit and then re-entered without notice or permission to do so. The Landlord’s re-entry into the rental unit at this time was illegal.

Although the Tenants’ application alleges two other occasions when the Landlords illegally entered the rental unit it contained no particulars of the dates, times or particulars regarding these entries and insufficient detail for the Landlords to know how to defend these allegations, as such I considered no further evidence or submissions with respect to any further alleged illegal entries. Substantial interference and Harassment
The Tenants allegations of substantial interference and harassment relate to the illegal entry on March 2, 2024 and the conduct of the Landlord [name] Kimberly.

Sections 22 and 23 of the Act relate to substantial interference and harassment and state: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23. landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the evidence before me I am satisfied that the conduct of the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenants and constituted harassment. Remedies
The Tenants sought the following remedies 1. The Landlords pay a fine; 2. The Board end the tenancy; 3. Moving and storage expenses; and 4. A delayed eviction until August 1, 2024.
The tenancy between the parties has already ended as of the date of this hearing. The remedies the Tenants seek relating to ending the tenancy and delayed eviction are now mute.

A remedy must flow from the cause of the application. In this matter the remedy relating to moving and storage expenses does not flow from the Tenants application as the Tenants vacated the rental unit pursuant to an agreement to end the tenancy and not as a result of the Landlords’ conduct contained in the Tenants’ L2 application. As such an award for moving and storage costs would be inappropriate.
The Tenants request that a find be imposed against the Landlords, but do not suggest an amount.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline # 16 on Administrative Fines says: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA.
I am not satisfied on the evidence before me that an administrative fine against the Landlords is appropriate in the circumstances. T6 Application

The Tenant [name] testified that on May 20, 2024 an issue arose with the central air and it stopped working during a heat wave. She testified that on that same date she either called or sent a text to the Landlords, but no action was taken by the Landlords to address the issue.
The Tenant further stated that the issue resolved on its own after approximately one week.

The Landlord [name] Kimberly testified that at the time of the alleged issue with the central air the Landlords were in the woods of Quebec without cell service and upon returning were advised by the Tenant that she was able to get the central air working by fiddling with the thermostat, and that no action was required by the Landlords.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the Tenants. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to meet their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Tenants’ T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Tenants shall pay the Landlords is $9,958.79. This amount represents: • $9,027.01 for rent arrears owing and costs of the application minus the rent deposit and interest owing; • $931.78 which represents the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Landlord incurred or will incur as a result of the unpaid utility costs.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlords the full amount owing by July 7, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlords the full amount owing by July 7, 2026, the Tenants will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v Numekevor-Otoo, 2026 ONLTB 43424 Date: 2026-06-01 In the matter of: [address] Mississauga ON Numekevor-Otoo (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was heard by videoconference on May 29, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,248.00.

On consent of the parties, the application is amended to correct the Tenant’s name to [name] and [name] [name] instead of “Iremi” as listed in the application. On my own motion and on notice to the Landlord, I find it appropriate to amend the application to recharacterize the Tenant’s request for abatement of rent of $2,200 to a request for general damages. The total amount requested remains the same. The Tenant provided testimony about the impact the eviction had on them that supports a request for general damages. The Tenant is not a sophisticated party and was clearly confused about many aspects of LTB hearing and application process. The prejudice to the Landlord is minimal as the total amount requested and awarded remains the same. It is unclear what evidence, if any, the Landlord could introduce if the hearing were adjourned in order to permit the Tenant to properly amend their application on notice to the Landlord instead of the application being amended on May 29th. In accordance with s. 183 of the Act and the Board’s obligation to conduct expeditious proceedings, I find it appropriate to simply amend the application instead of adjourning the application to allow the Tenant an opportunity to amend their application.
There was no dispute that the Tenant was locked out on May 4, 2026.
There was no dispute that the Landlord resided at the residential complex, and the Tenant was required to share a kitchen and bathroom with the Landlord starting in April 2026.
The Landlord argues that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply.

She relies on the exemption contained in s. 5(i) of the Act: the Act does not apply to “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.”

It is undisputed that the Landlord moved into the property before the locks were changed. By simply moving in, however, a landlord does not convert a tenancy covered by the Act to one not covered by the Act. See: [name] v. Bindlish, [2010] O.J. No. 2193 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) which states, “there was no evidence at either hearing that the [landlord] told the [tenant] prior to renting the room to him that it was her intention to move into the house.”

What is in dispute is whether the Landlord resided at the residential complex at the commencement of the tenancy and/or whether the parties agreed that the Landlord would reside at the residential complex at the commencement of the tenancy.
The Landlord bears the burden of proof in establishing that the Act does not apply on a balance of probabilities.
I do not find that she established that it is more likely than not that the Act does not apply.

The Landlord provided brief testimony that she lived at the rental unit and had access to common areas at material times. She recently moved in on a full-time basis for personal reasons after a breakdown in her relationship.

She provided almost no detail. There are no photos and no documents to support the Landlord’s claim. She provided no mail addressed to her at the rental unit and no photos or videos of her belongings at the residential complex prior to April 2026. She didn’t even testify that the parties agreed that the washroom or the kitchen would be shared with her. Her testimony was that the Tenant only rented a bedroom on a temporary basis, and that the Landlord had access to the common areas, which they occasionally used when they visited the property. There were no dates. There was no testimony about any specific occasions when she used the kitchen or the washroom at the commencement of the tenancy. There is no written contract between the parties and no rental ad to corroborate the Landlord’s version of the events.

The Tenant categorically denied that the Landlord lived at the property or that there was an agreement that she would live at the property. They lived at the property for approximately one year before the Landlord moved in. They do not deny that they only rented a room but state that they shared the kitchen with other occupants. They did not share anything with the Landlord until recently when the Landlord moved into part of the residential complex in April 2026.
The Landlord did not cross-examine the Tenant about their living arrangements.

Case law dealing with s. 5(i) essentially establishes a two-part test and the party relying on the exemption has to establish both: 1) is the occupant required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and 2) does the owner, spouse, child or parent live in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

I note that spending an occasional night at the residential complex would likely be insufficient to satisfy the second part of the test. The term “lives” is not defined in the Act but common sense and some LTB jurisprudence suggest that accessing the house every now and again would not be sufficient (see for example [name], 2023 ONLTB 23303). It seems to me that the term “live” would require one to treat a location as their permanent residence or at least a local homebase if they split time between different cities.
The Landlord failed to establish that the exemption applies in accordance with case law above. There is almost no evidence that she lived at the rental unit until she recently moved in.
I therefore find that the Act applies.
There was no dispute that the Landlord changed the locks and locked the Tenant out. There was no dispute that the tenancy was not terminated in accordance with the Act prior to the lockout.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord breached s. 24 of the Act: “A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”
The Tenant withdrew their request for most remedies identified in their application. They no longer wish to move back into the rental unit.
The two remaining remedies are: a. Payment of $2,200, and b. Fine payable to the LTB.

I find that the Tenant established entitlement to remedy ‘a’. The Tenant labelled it as “rent abatement” representing the loss of 100% of enjoyment of the rental unit due to the Landlord’s harassment, interference with reasonable enjoyment and, ultimately, being locked out of the rental unit. The Tenant testified about the impact the illegal eviction had on them. [name] [name] was very emotional, complained that her health had deteriorated and about the serious impact the eviction had on her. [name] suddenly lost her home and had nowhere to stay. Both of them were very seriously impacted. They also testified about the Landlord’s conduct after the Landlord moved into the property but before they were ultimately evicted. I would grant the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement in the amount of $2,200 but I find that it is better characterized as general damages.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment.

The Board has previously found in cases of harassment and illegal lockouts that an amount for the illegal lockout is appropriate under general damages. See for example HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), the LTB reasoned that:…it seems to me that the quantum of general damages normally awarded to compensate a tenant for an illegal lockout is $2,500.00. That sum takes into account the inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodations while also seeking legal assistance; and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home.
Some recent cases award higher damages.

I find the amount of $2,200 to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s actions had on them. The impact on the Tenant is consistent with what I usually see in cases of illegal lockouts. A higher award may have been appropriate, but I am not inclined to award an amount higher than what the Tenant’s application requests.
I will not order the Landlord to pay a fine to the LTB.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

I should therefore consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor.
The Tenant was seriously impacted by the Landlord’s actions.

Fines are very often appropriate in cases of illegal lockouts. In the case before me, however, I do not find that the Landlord acted with blatant disregard for the Act or that she or similar landlords need to be additionally deterred. I found the Landlord to be credible and reasonable at the hearing. She admitted adverse facts and did not unnecessarily prolong the hearing of this application. She called the LTB and other authorities before she changed the locks. She received confirmation that the Act does not apply in cases where a landlord shares a kitchen and a bathroom with their tenant. This is confirmed by a recording of her call with the LTB that she filed into evidence (document 8038047 in Portal). The advice the Landlord received was partially wrong as set out above, but I accept her testimony that she genuinely believed it to be correct. She is not a sophisticated landlord. Ignorance of the law is not a valid defense, and it does not render the illegal lockout lawful. The Landlord’s genuine confusion and due diligence she conducted before changing the locks strongly suggests that a fine is not necessary, however. The correct course of action would have been to bring an application to the LTB for a determination whether the Act applies, but I do not find that a fine is overall necessary to deter misconduct or to ensure compliance by this Landlord or other similar landlords.
The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application and I find that they are entitled to a reimbursement of this cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,248.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: On March 31, 2026, the Tenant asked the Landlord for consent to assign the rental unit. The Landlord responded on April 1, 2026, and provided the Tenant with information regarding the documents required from the proposed assignee.
It is undisputed that the Tenant proposed two prospective assignees. The first prospective assignee did not complete the required application despite requests from the Landlord.

The Landlord’s agent, [name], testified that the second proposed assignee submitted an application to the Landlord on or about May 1, 2026. The Landlord acknowledged receipt of the application on May 4, 2026.
On May 5, 2026, the Landlord informed the Tenant that the proposed assignee did not satisfy the Landlord’s screening criteria.

The Tenant submits that the refusal was unreasonable because neither she nor the proposed assignee were advised of the reasons for the refusal. The Tenant also submits that the Landlord did not request additional information before denying the application. The Tenant further testified that a credit check was not identified in the April 1, 2026 email setting out the information required from a proposed assignee and was only raised after the application had already been denied.

The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2026 because the Landlord unreasonably refused the second assignee. The Tenant also testified that she served an N9 notice with a termination date of June 5, 2026. The Landlord denied receiving an N9 notice from the Tenant. The Tenant also did not refer to the notice during the hearing. The Tenant sought an order to terminate the tenancy as of June 5, 2026. [name] for the decision

This application was brought under s.98 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states: “98 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant."

Subsection 95(5) of the Act provides: “A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of a rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3)(b).” [Emphasis added.]

This reference in s. 95(5) to “clause (3) (b)” is to subparagraph 95(3)(b). Subsection 95(3) says: “(3) If a tenant asks a landlord to consent to the assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee, the landlord may, a. consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee; [name] consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee; or [name] consent to the assignment of the rental unit.”

Essentially what these provisions mean is that if a Tenant asks a landlord to consent to an assignment to a potential assignee a Landlord can refuse the particular proposed assignee or simply refuse permission to assign at all. Where the landlord refuses consent to a particular proposed assignee that the Tenant’s right to make application to the Board under s. 98 is triggered.

Thus, the issue before me is whether the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refused the second proposed assignee. According to the Landlord, the second prospective assignee did not satisfy the Landlord’s credit check and reference criteria. [name] testimony was that the Landlord reviewed the application, ran a credit check, contacted the Landlord reference, and reviewed the financial documents before refusing the Application. Although the Landlord did not provide the specific contents of the credit check or Landlord reference because of “privacy concerns,” I accept that the refusal was based on the Landlord’s screening criteria and not on an arbitrary refusal to allow an assignment. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not act arbitrarily or unreasonably. For these reason, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ndlords') applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Tenants') to pay the rent that the Tenants owe. (L9 Application) The Landlords also applied for an order requiring the Tenants to pay the Landlords reasonable out-of-pocket costs that are the result of the Tenants’ failure to pay utility costs they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement, and the Landlords reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlords incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. (L10 Application) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlords: • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 Application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) These applications were collectively heard by videoconference on April 20, 2026. The Landlord [name], the Landlords’ Legal Representative Petar Guzina and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: The parties agree that both Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlords to rent the rental unit commencing October 15, 2023 for a fixed term ending April 14, 2024.
The Tenant Noah [name] stated that he vacated the rental unit in March, 2024. The [name] [name] did not return his keys to the Landlords after vacating the rental unit.
The tenancy agreement continued beyond the fixed term date of April 14, 2024 as a month-to-month tenancy.
The Landlords submit that the tenancy continues for both Tenants and there was no agreement to terminate [name] [name]’s tenancy

Based on the submissions of both parties, I am satisfied that this is a joint tenancy. Except in very specific circumstances pertaining to domestic violence, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not permit one joint tenant to sever their interest in an ongoing joint tenancy in the absence of an agreement by all the parties. In this case, there is no evidence that the parties agreed to amend the tenancy agreement to remove [name] [name] as a Tenant.
The Tenant Noah [name] is properly named as a Tenant in these applications. L9 Application
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 1 2024. The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenants did not pay the total rent they were required to pay for the period from February 15, 2024 to June 30, 2026.
The lawful rent is $3,400.00. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.

The tenancy ended on July 1, 2024, as a result of the Tenants moving out in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order or agreement to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the Tenant's obligation to pay rent also ended on that date.
The Landlords had collected a rent deposit of $3,300.00 from the Tenants and this deposit was applied to June’s rent.
The rent arrears and daily compensation owing to June 30, 2024 less the last months rent deposit are $8,900.00.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $58.99 is owing to the Tenants for the period from October 14, 2023 to June 30, 2026.
The Landlords incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The Landlords are entitled to $9,027.01. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to June 30, 2024 and the cost of the application minus the rent deposit and interest owing. L10 Application
As explained below, the Landlords proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 1, 2024.
The application was filed within one year after the Tenants ceased to be in possession of the rental unit. Unpaid Utilities
The Tenants failed to pay water costs that they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement.
The Landlords produced an invoice from Alectra Utilities associated with water charges in the Tenants name, dated July 29, 2024 in the amount of $938.78.

The Landlords produced a letter from the Municipality of Vaughn, dated January 27, 2025 indicating that the unpaid amount of $931.78 owing to Alectra Utilities has been added to the property taxes for the rental unit.
The Landlords incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses of $931.78 as a result of the Tenants’ failure to pay water costs that they were required to pay under the tenancy agreement. Damages
Included in the Landlords’ application is a claim for compensation in the amount of $771.83 to repair damage and or replace property that was damaged in the rental unit.

In order for an application for compensation for damages made pursuant to section 89(1) of the Act to succeed, a landlord must establish the following: (a) there was property damage to the rental unit or residential complex; (b) the damage is “undue” meaning that it is not normal wear and tear and it is not insignificant; and (c) the damage was a result of wilful or negligent conduct by the Tenants, occupant or guest.
In this context, the word “property” refers to the physical objects such as walls, ceilings, floors, appliances and fixtures in a residential complex.
If all of these factors are met, then the Board can award the landlord the reasonable cost of repair, or the replacement if it is not reasonable for the damage to be repaired.
The Landlords allege damage to the flooring in the rental unit, missing floor vent covers as well as a cost incurred to rent a waste disposal bin to remove items left in the unit. Waste [name]

The rental of a garbage disposal [name] is not wilful or negligent undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex as prescribed in section 89 of the Act. As such, the Landlord is not entitled to compensation for the rental of the waste disposal [name]. Missing vent covers

The Landlords did not provide sufficient evidence with respect to the claim that floor vent covers were missing. No photographs of the missing covers were provided, and I am not satisfied that the Landlords have proven this component of their application on a balance of probabilities based on the evidence adduced at the hearing. Damages to Floors
The Landlords claim that the flooring of the rental unit was damaged and required cleaning and polishing to remove scratches.
The Landlords provided one photograph of a scratched floor.
The Tenants along with their witness [name] testified that the flooring depicted in the photograph was in that condition at the time they moved into the rental unit.

With respect to the evidence before me I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the alleged damage to the floor is “undue” meaning that it is not normal wear and tear and it is not insignificant, nor am I satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the scratches to the floor were a result of wilful or negligent conduct by the Tenants, occupant or guest.

The Landlords did not prove that the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Tenants permitted in the residential complex wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex. T2 Application Request to Amend
At the commencement of the hearing of the Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications the Tenants sought to rely upon amended applications filed with the Board on April 15, 2026.
The Landlords were opposed to the request to amend as the Tenants had not complied with the time frame for amendments as set out in an interim order.
An interim order was issued on February 18, 2025 in relation to LTB-T-039414-24 and combined that matter with LTB-L048859-24, LTB-L-083081-24 and LTB-T-040852-24.

The interim order also indicates that if the Tenants wished to amend their application prior to the hearing then on or before March 15, 2025 the Tenants were to serve their amended application along with all supporting documents on the Landlords, file a copy with the Board along with an affidavit of service. The Tenants did not comply with the interim order.

LTB Rule of Procedure 15 states that an applicant seeking to amend their application shall request this amendment in writing by serving the amended application to all other parties and filing the amended application and a Certificate of Service with the Board. The request to amend the application is then decided at the hearing.

However, [name] allows the Board to exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

As the Tenants had not complied with the interim order issued on February 18, 2025 and Rule of Procedure 15 the request to amend the application was denied and the Tenants proceeded on their original applications. Illegal entry

The Tenants testified that on March 2, 2024 the Landlord [name] Kimberly illegally entered the rental unit without providing notice. Both Tenants testified that a showing of the rental unit had been scheduled and the Landlords gave the Tenant [name] notice, but [name] [name] did not receive notification of the showing and was asleep with his girlfriend. After being awoken by the yelling of the Landlord and being advised by [name] that a showing was scheduled he sent a text message to the Landlord asking her to skip his room. After the showing ended the Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord [name] Kimberly left the rental unit but remained on the property and after a period of time she re-entered the rental unit without permission and proceeded to the bedroom where [name] [name] was with his girlfriend. The Tenant Noah [name] testified that the Landlord [name] Kimberly attempted to force the door open and was yelling and swearing at him attempting to give him a document. At the time both [name] [name] and his girlfriend were not fully clothed and were attempting to sleep. The Tenants’ witness [name], [name] [name]’s girlfriend also confirmed the Tenants’ version of events from that day.

The Landlord [name] Kimberly testified that she had received consent from the Tenant [name] prior to showing the unit and they she never left the property before re- entering the rental unit to attempt to serve a document on [name] [name].

On a balance of probabilities I prefer the evidence of the Tenants to that of the Landlord. Although the Landlord had permission from the Tenant [name] to show the rental unit. After the showing ended the Landlord left the unit and then re-entered without notice or permission to do so. The Landlord’s re-entry into the rental unit at this time was illegal.

Although the Tenants’ application alleges two other occasions when the Landlords illegally entered the rental unit it contained no particulars of the dates, times or particulars regarding these entries and insufficient detail for the Landlords to know how to defend these allegations, as such I considered no further evidence or submissions with respect to any further alleged illegal entries. Substantial interference and Harassment
The Tenants allegations of substantial interference and harassment relate to the illegal entry on March 2, 2024 and the conduct of the Landlord [name] Kimberly.

Sections 22 and 23 of the Act relate to substantial interference and harassment and state: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23. landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the evidence before me I am satisfied that the conduct of the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenants and constituted harassment. Remedies
The Tenants sought the following remedies 1. The Landlords pay a fine; 2. The Board end the tenancy; 3. Moving and storage expenses; and 4. A delayed eviction until August 1, 2024.
The tenancy between the parties has already ended as of the date of this hearing. The remedies the Tenants seek relating to ending the tenancy and delayed eviction are now mute.

A remedy must flow from the cause of the application. In this matter the remedy relating to moving and storage expenses does not flow from the Tenants application as the Tenants vacated the rental unit pursuant to an agreement to end the tenancy and not as a result of the Landlords’ conduct contained in the Tenants’ L2 application. As such an award for moving and storage costs would be inappropriate.
The Tenants request that a find be imposed against the Landlords, but do not suggest an amount.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline # 16 on Administrative Fines says: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA.
I am not satisfied on the evidence before me that an administrative fine against the Landlords is appropriate in the circumstances. T6 Application

The Tenant [name] testified that on May 20, 2024 an issue arose with the central air and it stopped working during a heat wave. She testified that on that same date she either called or sent a text to the Landlords, but no action was taken by the Landlords to address the issue.
The Tenant further stated that the issue resolved on its own after approximately one week.

The Landlord [name] Kimberly testified that at the time of the alleged issue with the central air the Landlords were in the woods of Quebec without cell service and upon returning were advised by the Tenant that she was able to get the central air working by fiddling with the thermostat, and that no action was required by the Landlords.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the Tenants. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to meet their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Tenants’ T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Tenants shall pay the Landlords is $9,958.79. This amount represents: • $9,027.01 for rent arrears owing and costs of the application minus the rent deposit and interest owing; • $931.78 which represents the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Landlord incurred or will incur as a result of the unpaid utility costs.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlords the full amount owing by July 7, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlords the full amount owing by July 7, 2026, the Tenants will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name]: • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must either: 1. return the Tenant’s belongings to her, pay $4,000.00 in general damages and pay an administrative fine, or 2. pay the Tenant $50,000.00.

The application named the Landlord and GL as the respondents. At the hearing the Tenant requested to amend the application removing GL as a respondent. The Tenant is satisfied that GL was not involved in the lockout and has done his best to assist the Tenant. GL consented to the amendment request, and the Landlord was not present at the hearing to take a position. I find it appropriate to amend the application as requested.

Based on the uncontroverted evidence of the Tenant and GL, I find that the Tenant established that it is more likely than not that the Landlord (GL’s lender) locked the Tenant out without providing a replacement key on or about December 16, 2025. At the time, the rental unit was the Tenant’s residence. She had all of her personal and business belongings at the rental unit and was renting out some parts of the house some of the time.

I therefore find that the Landlord breached section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’): “A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

The Tenant also established that it is more likely than not that she had more than $50,000 worth of belongings at the rental unit when the locks were changed. Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence I find that the Tenant’s belongings consist of personal items captured by her photos (document 8098282) and her valuable personal and business items that were stored in the basement. The Tenant’s evidence was that she had dozens of boxes and a lot of expensive furniture she uses for staging. Her evidence was that her belongings were worth close to $200,000. This evidence was uncontroverted.

She has attempted to reach out to the Landlord both before and after the interim order was issued by the LTB requiring the Landlord to give her access to her belongings, but received no reply. GL also attempted to assist but was only able to communicate with the Landlord’s lawyer and was ultimately unsuccessful. Remedies
The Tenant withdrew request for most of her remedies. I find it appropriate to grant the remedies she requested at the hearing
The Landlord must return the Tenant’s belongings that are in the Landlord’s possession on or before June 24, 2026.

If the Landlord fails to do so, then the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $50,000 representing the reasonable cost that the Tenant will incur to replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of by the Landlord in the process of the lockout. The amount is reduced to match the Board’s monetary limit of $50,000. The Tenant is aware of the monetary limit and consented to the amount sought being reduced to $50,000.
The Tenant sought an administrative fine in the amount to be determined by the LTB.

Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $50,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant: The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.
Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provide that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

I should therefore consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor.
I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00 but only if the Landlord returns the Tenant’s belongings to her.
The Tenant was seriously impacted by the Landlord’s actions.

The Landlord chose to ignore requirements of the Act and simply changed the locks. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to explain their actions. If the Landlord returns the Tenant’s belongings, then there will be very little in this order to deter other Landlord’s from behaving in a similar fashion. If the Landlord does not return the belongings, they will have to pay the Tenant $50,000 which should act as a sufficiently strong deterrent in my view and no fine will be necessary.
The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $20,000.00 for the serious impact this eviction has on her mental, physical and emotional well-being.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment.

The Board has previously found in cases of harassment and illegal lockouts that an amount for the illegal lockout is appropriate under general damages. See for example HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), the LTB reasoned that:…it seems to me that the quantum of general damages normally awarded to compensate a tenant for an illegal lockout is $2,500.00. That sum takes into account the inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodations while also seeking legal assistance; and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home.
Some recent cases award higher damages.

I find the amount of $4,000 to be appropriate in the circumstances if the Landlord returns the Tenant’s belongings to her. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s actions had on her. This evidence was uncontroverted. I find it appropriate to award an amount consistent with the “usual” award for “inconvenience and displacement” inherent in an illegal lockout case but adjusted for inflation since 2019.
ordered: The Landlord shall return to the Tenant all property that is in the possession or control of the Landlord by June 29, 2026.
The Tenant shall write to the LTB on or before June 30th, 2026 advising the Board whether the Landlord complied with paragraph 1 of this order.

If the Landlord complies with paragraph 1 of this order, then the Landlord shall: • Pay the Tenant $4,000.00 on or before June 30, 2026. • Pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by June 30, 2026.
If the Landlord fails to comply with paragraph 1 of this order, then the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $50,000.00 on or before June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $713.00.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair residential complex.

The Tenant [name] testified that they moved into the rental unit in 2023 and still reside there, he described the rental unit as a large house divided into four floors each containing its own rental unit.

He testified that in early April 2025 the lock on the main door for the complex broke and anyone was therefore able to enter the complex from the street without entering the passcode and without turning the door handle, leaving the complex accessible to anyone from the street. He testified that they sent a request through the Landlord’s portal requesting a repair on April 27, 2025.

He testified that the Landlord did not respond to this maintenance request, and they did not hear anything from the Landlord until the door was repaired on May 22, 2025. He did not know why the repair took nearly one month to complete but speculated it was a cost saving measure from the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that before the door was repaired during the night of May 7 or early morning of May 8, 2025, someone entered the complex and stole his bicycle which was stored in the hallway. The Tenant sought out of pocket expenses for his lost bicycle at the hearing.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I am satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations by failing to repair the front door in a timely manner or communicate with the Tenant about the repair. As the Landlord did not attend I did not hear evidence from them why it took nearly a month to fix the door, and while there could be a reasonable explanation for this delay none was provided to me, additionally I note that the Landlord did not communicate with the Tenant during the repair process, I do not find this to be reasonable in the circumstances as the broken door allowed access to the building to anyone, and would therefore be priority repair to all Tenants.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably and find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1). Remedies

The Tenant sought out of pocket expenses of $665.00 to replace their stolen bicycle and the U-Lock that was attached to it. The Tenant relied on a receipt indicating they had paid $699.47 for the bike and lock in September 2023.

I am satisfied that the loss of the bike is directly related to the broken front door, the Landlord was made aware of the broken front door and failed to repair it within a reasonable time. As a result, this allowed someone to enter the complex and steal the Tenants bicycle, I find that it was reasonably foreseeable that someone may enter the unsecured complex through the broken door and steal items from residents of the complex. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord took any steps to mitigate this occurrence, such as adding a temporary lock, or advising the Tenant to move his bicycle into his unit until the door was repaired.

I am also satisfied that the Tenant shall incur reasonable costs of $665.00 to replace their bicycle as a result of the Landlord’s breach. I accept the receipt relied on by the Tenant with respect to the cost of the bicycle and lock.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $665.00 for these out-of-pocket expenses.
ordered: The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $713.00. This amount represents: • $665.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant will incur. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: and (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,371.25 on or before May 17, 2026.
The Tenancy began on March 1, 2022, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025. Asbestos

There is no dispute that on June 1, 2022, the Tenant reported a water leak in the living room ceiling. The Tenant testified that she was concerned that the vermiculites falling from the ceiling may contain asbestos and told the Landlord on June 7, 2022.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to test for asbestos, and as such, the Tenant had the unit tested for asbestos on July 5, 2022 by Safe Tech at a cost of $519.80 (includes HST). The analysis result showed that the material is vermiculite, an insulating material. The Tenant testified that report found asbestos and the report recommended that the exposed arears be HEPA vacuumed, and damp wiped. The Tenant testified that the report was provided by Safe Tech to the Landlord on August 2, 2022. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not clean or remediate the asbestos.
The Tenant testified that a cleaner came to the unit and looked at the hole to investigate but did not clean it. The Landlord only proceeded to patch and close the hole rather than HEPA Vacuum it.

The Landlord testified that he offered to test the material for [name], but the Tenant refused because the Tenant preferred AHERA testing. The Landlord also testified that on July 24, 2022, the Landlord mopped and Hepa vacuumed the space, and the Tenant was not present during the clean up. As such, the Landlord’s position is that he adequately remedied the asbestos before repairing the ceiling.
The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence that he followed the recommendations contained in the report.

Neither party provided expert testimony about the level of asbestos activity in the unit or about the impact this level of asbestos activity might have on the occupant of the unit. I note however that Tenant’s evidence confirms that asbestos was present in the rental unit and recommends steps for the Landlord to take to address it.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord breached his obligation under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex and the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. The presence of asbestos particles in the living room posed a health concern to the Tenant and the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to remedy this situation.

It is clear that asbestos particles were present in the rental unit. I also find that the Landlord did not act reasonably to remedy this situation after the inspection report was provided. I prefer the evidence of the Tenant and find that it was more likely than not that the only action taken by the Landlord was to drywall and patch the hole. The Landlord’s evidence, regarding dates were at times vague and not corroborated by any documentary evidence. As such, I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abetment of rent.

The next issue before me is the impact on the Tenant of this issue of disrepair. The Tenant did not establish any specific losses as a result of the asbestos, but I take judicial notice of the fact that exposed asbestos can have has negative effects on one’s well being. I find that the Tenant was also impacted by experiencing anxiety about the presence of asbestos. The report did not establish that the presence of asbestos was such that it would significantly impact an average person and as such a higher reward would not be appropriate. I find that an award of $1,200.00 accurately represents the impact on the Tenant.
The Tenant is also entitled to out of pocket expenses for costs incurred for testing the material in the amount of $519.80. The Tenant submitted receipts from Safe Tech. Rat infestation

The Tenant testified that they informed the Landlord on February 15, 2023, about a rodent infestation in the rental unit and that rodents were persistent during the winter months. The Landlord set up traps and put down boxes of rat poison. However, the problem persisted, and the Tenant told the Landlord about the problem every month until the Tenant moved out on February 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s response was inadequate. The Landlord would either set up traps or install chicken skin for open spaces. The Tenant stated that the rats were chewing things on the ceiling and chewing through food and the problem persisted until the Tenant moved out. On May 10, 2023, a technician from Solace Pest Solutions arrived at the unit to inspect and found that there were multiple entry points for rodents and entry points around pipes and wires and they recommended an aggressive rodenticide program. The Tenant’s witness, [name] who is a licensed pest control technician hired by the Landlord who testified that there were activity and the Landlord was given recommendations for how to address the problem. However, Landlord did not hire them to complete treatments following their recommendations.

The Landlord does not dispute that the Tenant first complained of rodents on February 15, 2023. The Landlord testified that by profession he is a licensed registered pest control technician. As such, he immediately started to use bait weekly and seal holes. In May 2023, he contacted another pest control company to inspect the unit. The Landlord testified that in April 2023, the Tenant was satisfied with the Landlord’s efforts, as she messaged the Landlord on April 24, 2023, advising the Landlord that the holes were covered.

The Landlord also provided in evidence an email from the property standards officers from December 2023, that stated the Landlord is dealing with the pest issues reasonably. The Landlord testified that there was no report of activity between January 2024 to November 2024.

When asked whether a rat infestation persisted beyond January 2024, the Landlord testified that there was no activity. In the absence of corroborating evidence, such as maintenance records, pest control reports, or written communication, I am left with only the oral testimony of the parties.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely, appropriate and reasonable manner. I say this because at no time did the Landlord mention that he called for an exterminator or arrange for pest control treatment within the rental unit. There was no documentary evidence such as a pest control report before me to prove that the issue was rectified. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair in accordance with their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The Tenant testified that she was concerned that the rats would disturb the asbestos in the walls and track it throughout the apartment and she was unable to leave food out. The rats also caused damage to the Tenant’s property such as blankets, computer cables and groceries.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board and in assessing the impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenant, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $3,359.77. This amount represents a 10% rent abatement for the rat issue for the period of February 16, 2023, to December 31, 2023 ($1,415.72), a 10% abatement for the period of January 1, 2024, to December 31, 2024 ($1,660.38) and a 10% abatement of January 1, 2025, to February 28, 2025 ($283.66). Hole in the front porch

The Tenant testified that they raised the issue of holes on the front porch on June 24, 2022, by email to the Landlord. The Tenant testified that the Landlord was unresponsive to the complaints until property standards was notified on October 13, 2023. The Tenant testified that the at the front of the porch there was a large hole, the Landlord only put down plywood to prevent rodents from gaining access to the unit. The tenant testified that the hole continued to deteriorate and by the time the Tenant vacated the unit, the concrete had deteriorated, and new holes formed in other parts of the front porch.

The Landlord testified that they placed a plywood board to cover in the hole in 2022. The Tenant complained again in April 2023 that the plywood was not secured making it unsafe. The Landlord glued the board down. He also testified that the municipal property standards officer did not indicate that this was an issue when they attended the unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely, appropriate and reasonable manner I am satisfied that an area of front porch was in a state of disrepair, and the Landlord breached his obligations pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The next issue before me is the impact on the Tenant of this issue of disrepair. The Tenant says the repairs were superficial, but they did not specifically state that the front porch was unusable. As such, I find that the front porch issue had minimal impact on the Tenant and was essentially a cosmetic issue. As the small area of disrepair is merely cosmetic, I find that a nominal award of $50.00 accurately represents the impact on the Tenant. Damaged bathroom baseboard

The Tenant testified that the baseboard in her bathroom has a gap, and she told the Landlord on June 24, 2022. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not repair the issue until the property standards order was issued.
The Landlord testified that there was small gap between the baseboard and some of flooring in bathroom. He acknowledged that he did not do the repairs until April 25, 2023.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that an area of bathroom baseboard was in a state of disrepair and the Landlord breached his obligations pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The next issue before me is the impact on the Tenant of this issue of disrepair. The Tenant says the repairs were not done in timely manner and the issue created the opportunity for mould to appear but did not identify that the bathroom was unusable. As such, I find that the damaged bathroom baseboard had minimal impact on the Tenant and was essentially a cosmetic issue. As the small area of disrepair is merely cosmetic, I find that a nominal award of $50.00 accurately represents the impact on the Tenant. Missing rails on fire escape
The Tenant raised the issue to the Landlord on June 24, 2022, and the parties do not dispute that the issue was resolved on October 23, 2023.
The Tenant testified that they were not able to use the stairs without the rails in the event of a potential fire.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not follow up or bring the issue up to the Landlord after June 2022 and as such, it was repaired after property standards issued their order.

I am satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation in regard to the missing rails on the fire escape. Section 20 requires the Landlord to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair. The Landlord was notified there was missing rails on June 24, 20222 but did not take steps to address it until October 2023. I am not satisfied that waiting over one year to address the missing rails was either prompt or reasonable.

The missing rails on the fie escape did not affect the Tenant’s use or enjoyment of the rental unit itself. However, the missing rails were an annoyance and inconvenience. As such, the missing rails were a minimal interference with the [name] use of the residential complex.

Therefore, I find that an abatement of 2% is appropriate. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,350.00. I find that the abatement should apply for the period of June 24, 2022, to October 23, 2023, a total of 486 days. I calculate the abatement as follows: • 2% x ($1,350.00/month x 12 months ÷ 365 days/year) x 486 days= $431.37 • For a total of $431.37 Holes in the kitchen closest and in the living room wall

The Tenant testified that she reported the holes in the kitchen closest and living room wall to the Landlord in April 2022. The Tenant testified the Landlord made a hole in the kitchen closet to remove a racoon. However, the Landlord did not repair the hole until October 2023.

The Landlord testified that he could not fully repair the holes because he needed to access the traps placed for the racoons. The Landlord advised that the municipal property standards officer did not take issue with this approach. The Landlord submitted into evidence an email dated October 13, 2023, from a property standards officer who advised the Landlord that as long the pest issues are ongoing, it is reasonable to keep the holes accessible. However, once the pest control issues are dealt, the expectations are that the open areas of the wall are repaired. Therefore, the Landlord did not repair the holes in the walls.

I am satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation in regard to the hole in the kitchen closet and the living room wall. Section 20 requires the Landlord to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair. The Landlord was notified there was a hole in the kitchen and living room wall in April 2022 but did not take steps to address it until October 2023. I am not satisfied that waiting over one year to address the hole was either prompt or reasonable.

The holes in the unit did not affect the Tenant’s use or enjoyment of the rental unit itself. However, the holes were an annoyance and inconvenience. As such, the holes were a minimal interference with the Tenant’s use of the residential complex.

Therefore, I find that an abatement of 2% is appropriate. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,350.00. I find that the abatement should apply for the period of April 1, 2022, to October 31, 2023, a total of 578 days. I calculate the abatement as follows: • 2% x ($1,350.00/month x 12 months ÷ 365 days/year) x 578 days= $513.03 • For a total of $513.03 Stairwell water damage

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord on May 1, 2023 about a water leak from the roof into the stairwell. The Tenant testified that the water leak re-occurred on November 22, 26 and December 3, 2024.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord only addressed the damage superficially by painting over the affected drywall and the Landlord did not do the necessary repairs to the roof to prevent future leaks.

The Landlord submits that when the Tenant first reported the issue to them on May 1, 2023, the Landlord on the same day responded by repairing the leak on the roof and patching inside. After several months, the Landlord then replaced that section of the roof with steel. On November 24, 2024, a second leak occurred in a different area of the roof, and the Landlord again attended the unit and patched the area, and it was painted on February 2025.

Based on the evidence, I do not find that the Landlord has breached their obligations under section 20 of the Act. The Tenant had insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord refused to respond accordingly and make the requested repairs to the stairwell ceiling after she notified the Landlord. I accept that the Landlord was made aware of the issue, and they attempted to immediately find a resolution to the leak. [name] living room outlets

The Tenant testified that the two of the four electrical outlets in the living room were broken. The Tenant testified he told the Landlord on June 2022 and June 2023 and the Landlord did not repair the outlets.
The Tenant testified that the broken outlets prevented the Tenant from placing enough lamps in the living room to properly light the room and forced her to buy extension cords.
The Landlord testified that they did not repair the outlets because there were other working outlets the Tenant could rely on.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to living room outlet. I say this because I find that the Landlord’s failure to repair the rental unit, was unreasonable. Based on the testimony of the Landlord, refusing to fix the outlet was unreasonable in the context of the Landlord’s obligation under the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.
The Tenant testified that they relied on a lamp to provide lighting in the living room, although one plug was working, the Tenant was scared that plugging in a lot of plugs would lead it to overload.

I find that the Tenant experienced minimal disruption to their ability to normally reside in the unit. The Tenant was not prevented from using all electricity in her rental unit, there was just less electricity in the living room. I find that the effect of the disrepair on the Tenant was minimal and a nominal amount of $100.00 accurately represents the impact of this disrepair. [name] Stove

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord on October 4, 2023, by text message, that the large stove burner was not functioning and the oven took one hour to preheat. The Tenant testified that the Landlord never repaired the stove. The Tenant testified that her ability to prepare food was impacted as she could only cook small amounts of food at a time and was limited in the types of food she could make.

The Landlord testified that Tenant complained on November 17, 2022, and on November 24, 2022, the Landlord acquired the parts to repair the stove, and the stove was repaired on November 30, 2022. The Landlord maintains that the Tenant did not complain after it was repaired on November 30, 2022, and only did so after the application was filed.
The Landlord also argues that the Tenant still had three other elements to cook on.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to broken element on the stove. Based on the testimony of the Landlord, refusing to investigate and rectify was unreasonable in the context of the Landlord’s obligation under the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.
The Tenant testified that her ability to prepare food was impacted as she could only cook small amounts of the food at a time.

I find that the Tenant experienced minimal disruption to their ability to normally reside in the unit. The Tenant was not prevented from using the stove in her rental unit, there was just limited elements on the stove. I find that the effect of the disrepair on the Tenant was minimal and a nominal amount of $100.00 accurately represents the impact of this disrepair.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,371.25. This amount represents: • $5,803.45 for a rent abatement • $519.80 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026
