issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant sought an adjournment as they have not had an adequate opportunity to review and respond to evidence uploaded by the Landlord on the date of the hearing. However, the only new evidence uploaded by the Landlord was [name] 015040-23, which was an order from an L1 hearing for a non-payment of rent dispute between the Landlord and the Tenant that was issued on September 29, 2023, as well as the Sheriff’s notice to vacate.

Because the Tenant was a party to the proceeding that resulted in the order, I was not satisfied any prejudice would result from allowing the Landlord to rely upon it. I denied the request to adjourn. T2 Application

As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,548.00 which represents a rent abatement and the cost of filing this application. Illegal Entry

The Tenant alleges that within the 6 months prior to the filing of this application on May 31, 2023, the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on at least 47 separate occasions. 1. The Tenant entered into evidence videos of the Landlord entering the rental unit on December 26, 2022, April 13, 2023, May 20, 2023, and May 21, 2023.
It was undisputed that the Landlord entered the rental unit on the dates alleged by the Tenant.

The Landlord entered into evidence the following six notices of entry: 1. A notice of entry dated December 25, 2022 for entry on December 26, 2022 between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM for the purposes of inspecting the rental unit and to investigate a report of a water leak. 2. A notice of entry dated April 12, 2023 for entry on April 13, 2023 between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM to perform an inspection of the rental unit. 3. A notice of entry dated May 19, 2023 for entry on May 20, 2023 between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM to inspect the rental unit. 4. A notice of entry dated May 20, 2023 for entry on May 21, 2023 between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM to inspect the rental unit.
The Landlord also entered into evidence an entry log detailing their entry dates, reasons for entry and the date and time of the entry.

Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out the requirements for a Landlord to enter a rental unit with notice and states that a landlord may enter a rental unit with 24 hours of notice to carry out a repair or to inspect to determine if the rental unit is in a good state of repair and it is reasonable to carry out the inspection.

The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 19: The Landlord's Right of Entry into a Rental Unit provides the following guidance: Specifying the time of entry Where a specific time of entry is known, it should be stated in the notice. Where it is not possible to state a specific time of entry, the notice may provide a reasonable window of time for entry. What is a reasonable window of time will depend upon the facts and circumstances in each case. Where the landlord exercises control over the work being done and who is doing the work, the notice should be reasonably specific with respect to the time for entry. Where the landlord does not exercise control over the work being done or the person who is doing the work, the notice should set out a reasonable window of time for entry. For example, where the work is being done by a cable or telephone company and the company specifies a reasonable window of time when it will be at the rental unit, a landlord may reasonably specify that same window. Where the same or similar work is being done in a number of units on the same day, a reasonable window of time may be specified. In determining whether the specified window of time is reasonable, consideration should be given to the type and complexity of repair, replacement or work being undertaken, the location of the work and the extent to which the entry affects the tenant's ability to use the rental unit. The Divisional Court in Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation found that while a landlord is not required to specify the exact hour and minute of a required entry into a rental unit, a written notice providing for a nine hour period for entry to permit the landlord to carry out an annual inspection of smoke detector equipment does not comply with the requirements that the notice specify a time of entry between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.

The [name] is not binding upon me, but I see no reason to depart from it in this case. While I accept that the Landlord served notices of entry at least 24 hours in advance as required by section 27 of the Act, I am not satisfied that the 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. windows for entry were reasonable.

While in Wrona, the Divisional Court awarded $1,000.00 for a single entry, I was not satisfied that the breaches had a major impact on the Tenant. Rather, while the Landlord and his father are seen touching items in the rental unit, the impact of the entries were minor and I find, based on my knowledge of similar cases, that an abatement of $500.00, which is $100.00 for each of the five entries is sufficient to acknowledge the impact of the entries on the Tenant. [name]

The Tenant testified that on or about July 30, 2022, the Tenant received permission from the Landlord to change the locks of the rental unit to make the unit more accessible for the Tenant’s medical support workers. The Tenant testified that on December 26, 2022, the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit. The Tenant testified that during this time he was away from the rental unit due to ongoing medical treatment.

The Landlord did not dispute changing the locks and entered into evidence a text message from the Landlord to the Tenant dated December 26, 2022 stating, “I’m [sic] heading down to change the lock. You had changed the lock without permission. Grab the key off me next time you’re here.”

While the Tenant testified that conversations got heated regarding the changing of the locks, there was no supporting evidence from the Tenant of any discussion between the Landlord and the Tenant about obtaining the keys after the Landlord changed the locks.
The Landlord testified that due to the Tenant’s lack of response in obtaining the keys, he assumed the Tenant had vacated the rental unit.

While I accept, based on the uncontested evidence before me, that the Landlord changed the locks, the only supporting evidence before me was that the Landlord had informed the Tenant to obtain a copy of the key when the Tenant returned and there was no supporting evidence that the Landlord had refused to provide a copy of the key.

I was not satisfied that the Landlord’s failure to provide a key was the fault of the Landlord who had offered to provide the Tenant a copy of the key. Rather, I find that the failure to provide a replacement key was a result of the Tenant not taking reasonable steps to obtain a copy of the key.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. Harassment

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has engaged in threatening and coercive behaviour with the Tenant. The Tenant testified that the Landlord has threatened to remove the Tenant’s belongings and to change the locks. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord harassed the Tenant with repeated assertions that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit. The evidence submitted by the Landlord include photos of the text messages to the Tenant including a message dated December 21, 2022 stating “please let me know if you want to make a deal, or if you have abandoned your unit.” As noted above, in a December 26, 2022, the Landlord states “I’m [sic] heading down to change the lock. You had changed the lock without permission. Grab the key off me next time you’re here.” Later that day, the Landlord sent subsequent text messages to the Tenant stating “I am considering the unit abandoned. I will hold your belongings for 30 days.”

The Tenant entered into evidence a video dated March 2, 2023, in which the Landlord’s father is seen outside the entrance door to the Tenant’s rental unit measuring the door and stating “we’re trying to get rid of the tenant right now, he’s being a dick.”

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct constitutes harassment and coercion intended to pressure the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. I am satisfied that this pattern of conduct started between December 2022 and continued until at least March 2, 2023. I am satisfied by the Tenant’s testimony that tis pressure to vacate caused the Tenant undue stress. As a result, an order will issue for an abatement equal to 50% of the rent for the four months for a total of rent abatement of $3,000.00. Withholding Vital Services
The Tenant also asserts that the Landlord has interfered with vital services by blocking the Tenant from accessing his own parking space.

Section 2(1) of the Act defines vital services as “hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat.” Parking is not a vital service as defined under the Act. However, I considered whether the alleged interference with parking constituted substantial interference or harassment with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord has interfered with the parking.

The Tenant entered into evidence a video of him walking down the driveway at the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the video shows the Landlord’s car blocking his parking spot. However, it was unclear from the video whether the Tenant’s parking spot was blocked as there was ample space on the driveway. Further, the Tenant was unable to provide any specific date or time that the Landlord had parked on the driveway blocking his spot. Further, while the Tenant testified he incurred parking tickets as a result of being forced to park on the street, there was no supporting evidence such as communications with the Landlord about the parking spot or any of the alleged parking tickets, which I would have expected the Tenant to have had and produced. Given the vagueness of the Tenant’s claim and the lack of any supporting evidence, I was not satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant by blocking his vehicle.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services or care services and meals in a care home, nor did the Landlord interfere or harass by interfering with the Tenant’s parking. Remedies Abatement of Rent

As I have found above that the Landlord has entered the rental unit unlawfully and has harassed and coerced the Tenant into vacating the rental unit, the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $3,500.00. Cost to Repair or Replace Damaged, Destroyed or Disposed of Property
The Tenant testified that during their entries, the Landlord stole an ottoman, alarm system, central base system, keypad and security camera.
The Tenant further testified that during an unlawful entry, the Landlord caused damage to the Tenant’s security system, which cost the Tenant $1,500.00 to re-install.

I was not satisfied that the Tenant met the burden of proof to demonstrate the items were stolen or damaged as the Tenant suggests. No supporting evidence was provided to show that the Landlord stole or damaged the Tenant’s property and there was no supporting evidence of the alleged cost to repair or replace the item. If the Tenant is claiming the items were damaged or stolen, I would have expected some supporting evidence such as a police report, invoice for the items, communications with the Landlord about the missing items or other evidence to support the claim. As these items were not provided, I was not satisfied that the Tenant has met the burden of proof to demonstrate that these items were damaged, destroyed or disposed of as the Tenant asserts. The Tenant’s request for out-of- pocket expenses of $5,200.00 is denied. Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenant submits he incurred out-of-pocket expenses to stay elsewhere as a result of an N12 notice that was served on the Tenant. However, there was no T5 application before me, and I am not satisfied that the service of an N12 along constitutes substantial interference. As a result, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is denied. Order for the Landlord to Return the Tenant’s Property
I was not satisfied that the Landlord stole any property from the Tenant as they allege. As a result, the request for an order for the return of stolen property is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,548.00. This amount represents: • $3,500.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: Adrian Drinkwalter is not a party to the tenancy agreement and was always only an occupant of the rental unit. Therefore, on consent of the parties, he is removed as an applicant in these proceedings.
On September 16, 2025, the LTB combined LTB-T-080177-24 (T2, filed October 4, 2024) and LTB-T-043361-25 (T2/T6, filed May 30, 2025), to be heard together. Background

The Tenant T.N.P. took occupancy of the rental unit on August 1, 2022. The monthly rent was $2,550.00. She physically moved out of the townhouse on August 31, 2024 when she and her spouse separated. At that time, the monthly rent charged was $2,650.00. LTB-T-080177-24

The tenancy was terminated on November 25, 2024 by issuance of LTB order LTB-L- 073098-24 dated November 14, 2024. As of September 2024, the Landlord knew that the Tenant was residing elsewhere, as described in this order. The evidence is that the Tenant’s former spouse A.D. lived in the unit as an unauthorized, overholding occupant until he was evicted on April 3, 2025. T6 application

As explained below, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) to repair and maintain the rental unit and/or failed to comply with health housing and maintenance standards. Kitchen sink drainage issues
The Tenant T.N.P. testified that she had issues with the kitchen sink shortly after moving in and informed the Landlord; a few days later, the Landlord used a plumbing snake to unclog the drain.
She stated that in 2023 the issue recurred, but she simply hired a plumber to resolve it.

T.N.P. next informed the Landlord on June 25, 2024 of the kitchen sink again not draining properly and reported that there was water leaking under the sink, that the faucet was falling off and that she could not use the sink. She placed a bucket directly under the sink to catch the constant drips. She provided several videos to the Landlord showing the drain issues and leaking, which she had taken on June 23, 2024.
The Landlord bought over a chemical drain cleaner for her to use, with instructions. T.N.P. testified that this did not resolve the problem.

She reported the same issue again to the Landlord on July 4, 2024 and he left another chemical drain cleaner at her door for her to use. The morning after treating the apparent clog, she took a video and sent it to the Landlord showing a partially drained sink. The videos of the drainage issues were submitted as evidence.

T.N.P. testified that on August 17, 2024, when the Landlord came by to collect the rent, she showed him that the leak was still occurring. On August 19, 2024, he used a plumbing snake without success. A few days later he asked a plumber to make repairs. After that, T.N.P. says, the drain worked but still not properly, and water continued to drip down a pipe under the sink. She maintains that the issues were never satisfactorily resolved.

The Landlord A.H.T. agreed with the facts presented by T.N.P. up to July 4, 2024. However, he says, he heard no more about the sink issue until August 2024. He testified that when he inspected the sink on August 17th, he found that T.N.P. had “removed the drain”. He immediately hired a plumber to make repairs and the problem was resolved. Mould

On August 17, 2024, T.N.P. showed the Landlord significant mould that had appeared on the cabinet housing the sink. She took a video although she could not recall whether it was in July or August 2024 but she presented it to the Landlord at the time.

Her evidence is that the Landlord brought a piece of wood on the next visit to cover up the mould. She claims that he never conducted any further investigation and that the mould was never remediated. LTB-T-080177-24 Damage to the laundry room ceiling

T.N.P. explained that the water from the sink leaked into the ceiling of the laundry room directly below. She mentioned this to the Landlord, who responded that he would come by and check it out but, she says, he never did. Upstairs Toilet

When [name] moved into the unit, she discovered that the flush lever attached to the toilet was not working properly and so the toilet would not flush properly. She testified that a few days later she informed the Landlord by text message and in person. The Landlord tried to repair the handle, and she recalls that it did work for a couple of days.
T.N.P. indicated that when she informed the Landlord after it fell again into disrepair in July 2024, he did not respond to her texts.

She explained that, at that point, she had given up on trying to get things repaired having dealt with the Landlord’s non-responsiveness; he gave her the impression that he was bothering him and so she was hesitant to make further complaints.

T.N.P. testified that in September 2022, she hired a plumber to repair the flush lever but even then, the handle would fail sporadically, requiring multiple attempts. Her evidence is that it was not working properly up to the date when she moved out. Mice infestation

Shortly after moving in, T.N.P. heard rodents running in the walls of her bedroom. She saw mice darting under the fridge. Concerned, she says she immediately told the Landlord. Her former spouse A.D. – who was residing with her at the time – took videos on his phone. The videos submitted show a dog playing with a stunned or dead mouse on the kitchen floor and another shows a mouse running under the fridge. She recalls that the Landlord promised to bring a trap, but he did not. T.N.P. asserts that the infestation remained unresolved prior to her vacating.
A.D. testified that the Landlord never came by the unit or sent anyone to investigate the rodent issue. He described the Landlord’s attitude as typically “combative”.
The Landlord A.H.T. acknowledged what he deemed to be a minor mice infestation problem. He testified that T.N.P only informed him in August 2024 about the issue.

He stated that when he initially tried to inspect the unit in September 2024 with a contractor, he was prevented from doing so because T.N.P. or A.D. refused entry but also because the Tenant’s dog was aggressive towards him. This, he said, was captured in a video recording he took on that date.

When the Tenant's Legal Representative [name] replayed the video of the entry, [name] pointed out that the dog was silent and wagging its tail. He asked A.H.T. if he believed the dog’s behaviour in the video was indicative of an aggressive animal greeting a visitor. A.H.T. maintained that he was intimidated by the pet. Analysis
Subsection 20(1) of the Act requires a landlord to repair and maintain the rental unit and the residential complex in a good state of repair. LTB-T-080177-24

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance and repair obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the issue reasonably in the circumstances. Kitchen sink drainage issues

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the kitchen sink and faucet were in disrepair, that she informed the Landlord on multiple occasions about it and that the measures the Landlord took did not resolve the drainage issue. I believe the Tenant when she says that she continued to have issues with the drain up to the time she vacated the unit. This included a persistent water leak from the faucet down through the pipes and into the ceiling below. I am satisfied that, once the Tenant discovered the leak, she placed a bucket under the dripping water, manually emptying it as it became full.
The Landlord did not provide evidence of any professional inspection or of any effective plumbing repair.

I find that asking the Tenant to address a persistent plumbing problem herself using over-the-counter products does not satisfy the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. Responsibility for diagnosing and repairing underlying plumbing issues rests with the Landlord.
The evidence supports a finding that the drainage issue was ongoing for a significant period, was not adequately repaired, and contributed to water damage and mould. Mould
The photos the Tenant testified about as regards the existence of toxic mold were persuasive.

The unchallenged evidence is that it was never properly dealt with. Although he had the opportunity, the Landlord did not provide evidence of any professional inspection or remediation of the mould. What the Landlord did do was to hide the affected area with a board. The “repair” was consistent with a temporary or cosmetic fix.

It is well established that the presence of toxic mould is a serious maintenance and repair issue that requires investigation and remediation. Simply covering the affected area does not address the underlying problem.
I find that the Landlord failed to adequately investigate the source of the mould and to ensure the mould was eradicated. Ceiling disrepair
The Tenant testified that the leak also caused damage to the ceiling below, which was never repaired. The Landlord did not provide any evidence that this damage was addressed.
Given my findings regarding the unresolved leak, it is reasonable to conclude that resulting damage to the ceiling would require repair. LTB-T-080177-24
I find that the Landlord failed to repair water damage arising from a known plumbing issue, in breach of his obligations under section 20 of the Act. [name]
The Tenant testified that there was a mouse infestation in the unit and that the Landlord stated he would provide traps but failed to do so.
The Landlord did not provide evidence of any effective pest control measures being implemented.
Pest infestations fall squarely within a landlord’s maintenance obligations. A failure to take reasonable steps to address such conditions constitutes a breach of the Act.
I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence and find that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps in a timely manner to effectively resolve the rodent infestation. Prevention from making repairs
The Landlord submitted that he was unable to complete repairs on one occasion because the Tenant’s dog behaved aggressively. He provided a video in support of this position.

The Tenant’s representative pointed out that, in the recording, the dog appeared calm, wagged its tail, and did not bark or display aggressive behaviour. When asked about this, the Landlord stated that he nonetheless felt intimidated.
I find that the video evidence does not support the Landlord’s characterization of the dog as aggressive. The behaviour shown is consistent with a friendly interaction.

While I accept that a landlord may have subjective concerns about safety, those concerns must be objectively reasonable to justify a failure to carry out maintenance obligations. In this case, I do not find that the Landlord’s concerns met that standard or that they prevented him from access to the unit to complete necessary repairs. There is no evidence that the Landlord requested that the dog be secured during a scheduled repair time or asked the Tenant to make other arrangements for the dog.
I therefore do not accept that the Tenant’s dog was a valid reason for the Landlord’s failure to carry out necessary repairs. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant T.N.P. proved the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

On September 4, 2024, the Landlord’s former paralegal R.B. emailed T.N.P. to say: “I have been HIRED by your Landlord to now deal with this tenancy. YOU said you would leave, then you extended it, then you said you would leave August 31, 2024. Your landlord gave you an N111 to sign. … I left you a voice mail message. Please let’s talk. If you don’t want to talk, we will take this to the Landlord and Tenant Board and ask for immediate eviction as we have PROOF that you wrote in a text that you will leave. The Judge will give us an immediate 1 N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy (the ‘N11’). LTB-T-080177-24 eviction. I will give you until [September 5, 2024] to call… If not we go to a Judge to evict you…”.
On September 5, 2024, R.B. emailed T.N.P.: “Why are you ignoring me I guess you don’t want a deal We now go to court for immediate eviction If you can’t deal with it hire a paralegal”.

Without notice to T.N.P., on September 9, 2024 the Landlord filed an L3 application with the Board, for an ex parte eviction order. The application was based on an earlier text message that T.N.P. sent to the Landlord informing him that she would be moving out.
On September 12, 2024, the Board directed the L3 application to a hearing, which was subsequently scheduled for November 4, 2024.

T.N.P. testified that on the same day, the Landlord called her by phone to say that he knew A.D. had a criminal court date on September 17, 2024. Her evidence is that he told her that if she did not sign an N11 he would “get her involved” in that criminal charge (which related to an incident that occurred in the residential complex).

She understood this to mean that the Landlord would report to the police that she was also involved in the alleged criminal activity and “have her charged”. She stated that this was distressing because she had not engaged in any criminal conduct. 54. [name] was applying for Permanent Resident status; she said the Landlord also threatened to report her to immigration officials if she did not sign the N11. She contends that during the same call the Landlord acted in a blatantly threatening way: he told her that he knew where she worked and lived; he knew all her friends and family, and he would ‘defame’ her by disclosing personal information to them that would disparage her character. 55. There is no dispute that on or about September 15, 2024, the Landlord showed up unannounced at T.N.P.’s workplace. She testified that he “tried to make a scene” by demanding to talk with her in her office or outside and tried to give her an N11 form to sign. 56. There is no disagreement that [name] called the police. The police did not attend but, according to T.N.P., an officer called her by phone to inform her that they had cautioned the Landlord to not attend her workplace again. 57. She says she then discovered that the Landlord had indiscriminately posted her personal information to his Facebook account on a Vietnamese Community Group they belonged to. 58. T.N.P. also produced a voice message from R.B. left on the Tenant’s phone on September 19, 2024, at 8:09 p.m., R.B. states: “You have to talk to me. … Is [A.D.] really your husband?... Who is [A.D.]? … Do you know this is really bad and this is gonna be all over your record and all over the internet and your name will be completely run through the mud so get moving and phone me”. 59. On September 20, 2024, she received a text message from R.B., in which R.B. states, “See you in court.” On Saturday, September 21, 2024, R.B. again texted her:” Please hire a paralegal or this is going to be very stressful”. 60. The Landlord denies that his actions amounted to interference, harassment or coercion. LTB-T-080177-24 Analysis 61. I accept that on September 12, 2024, the Landlord telephoned the Tenant and demanded that she sign the N11 and that during that conversation, the Landlord threatened to report the Tenant to police for criminal activity. The Landlord led no evidence to support an allegation of criminal conduct. I find that this threat was baseless and was made for the purpose of pressuring the Tenant to comply with his demand to sign the N11. 62. The threat to contact immigration authorities, regardless of the Tenant’s actual status, was inherently intimidating and designed to exploit a perceived vulnerability. The Landlord’s statement that he knew where the Tenant lived was a clear message of intimidation, which would reasonably create ongoing discomfort and even fear. Posting the Tenant’s personal information on a community Facebook group was highly inappropriate. 63. This constitutes harassment and coercion within the meaning of section 23 of the Act. 64. In my view, attending at the Tenant’s workplace was a serious and unreasonable intrusion. The workplace is not an appropriate venue for the resolution of landlord-tenant disputes. 65. The Tenant relies on communications from the paralegal R.B. as further evidence of harassment and coercion. I find that those communications regarding the N11 misrepresented the legal process and likely outcomes; significantly pressured the Tenant to respond; and explicitly and implicitly threatened adverse outcomes. Particularly concerning are her assertions that “this is gonna be all over your record and all over the internet and your name will be completely run through the mud.” 66. An N11 Agreement must be voluntary. Efforts to secure such an agreement through intimidation or threats are contrary to the Act. 67. Therefore, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that he and his agent R.B. harassed, coerced and threatened the Tenant. Remedies 68. The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $7,552.00 and general compensation of $10,000.00 for each of the T2 and T6 applications. 69. A tenant’s entitlement to a remedy for a breach of the Act is directly tied to the date the tenant filed the application. The Board may only grant remedies for conduct that occurred within the prior 12 months; it cannot grant remedies for earlier incidents that fall outside the limitation period, although the facts may be considered as context. If it is an ongoing breach, remedies are limited to the conduct occurring within the 12 months prior to filing. 70. Some of the Tenant’s T6 claims fall outside the one-year limitation period. Therefore, the date for which the Board can grant remedies is limited to the period between May 30, 2024 and May 30, 2025. Rent abatement 71. A rent abatement is generally intended to compensate a tenant for loss of the use or enjoyment of the rental unit during the tenancy and occupancy of the rental unit. This remedy is usually associated with a tenant’s ability to make use of the unit. LTB-T-080177-24 72. The Tenant’s evidence is that she no longer physically occupied the unit after August 31, 2024 and, as such, did not benefit from its use after that date. Accordingly, any request in the T6 for an abatement after August 31, 2024 must reasonably be denied. 73. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $4,770.00 for the 3-month period beginning June 1, 2024 and ending on August 31, 2024, reflecting the serious impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit, as follows: (1) $1,987.50 for the rodent infestation, representing a 25% abatement; (2) $2,782.50 for the sink, faucet, mould issues and ceiling disrepair, representing a 35% abatement. 74. No remedy will be considered for the toilet’s flush lever issues. I am not satisfied that a remedy is sufficiently substantiated, as no documentary evidence was led to support this claim, though such evidence ought to have been capable of being presented. General compensation 75. The Tenant asks for general damages to compensate her for the trauma, expressed as distress and anxiety, that resulted from the Landlord’s unlawful conduct. Specifically, the Tenant explained that the Landlord’s non-responsiveness in relation to reported disrepair, his ineffective repairs, and his persistent harassment caused her considerable frustration. 76. The Tenant provided relatively few details of distress relating to the sink and water leak which would support compensation over and above the rent abatement awarded. However, there is no doubt that living with mould and mice elevated the level of the Tenant’s concern. The Landlord’s failure to prioritize those issues exposed the Tenant to potentially serious health problems. 77. The following factors also weigh in favour of a considerable award of compensation. The Landlord made baseless threats of police involvement, attended at the Tenant’s workplace (and during an ongoing conflict between them), threatened to interfere with her immigration status by reporting false information, and disclosed the Tenant’s personal information within her community which the Tenant perceived as maligning her character. 78. The Landlord’s agent R.B.’s improper threats of eviction and warnings to the Tenant that she would take certain actions to disgrace the Tenant publicly, including communicating directly to the Tenant’s social circle merit increased compensatory damages. 79. I have balanced this with the fact that the conduct relating to the N11 occurred over a relatively defined period, primarily in September 2024. However, the frequency and intensity of the pressure the Tenant was subjected to in that timeframe was remarkable and undoubtedly resulted in genuine emotional upset that affected her daily. 80. Having regard to all the circumstances, the Landlord shall pay general compensation to the Tenant in the amount of $7,500.00. Administrative fine 81. The Tenant requests that the Board impose an administrative fine to reflect the seriousness of the misconduct and to deter similar behaviour. 82. The Board generally reserves administrative fines for cases involving: LTB-T-080177-24 • serious or egregious misconduct; • repeated or escalating behaviour; • bad faith conduct; • deliberate disregard of the Act; and • conduct that demonstrates or establishes an abuse of Board processes. 83. The Board may consider whether the conduct reflects an intentional effort to circumvent the protections of the Act, rather than being an isolated or inadvertent breach. 84. In my view, the Landlord’s behaviour represents a deliberate pattern of conduct that was egregious in nature and scope; it reveals a blatant disregard for his obligations under the Act, of the Tenant’s statutory rights and for the LTB in general. The Landlord directed his paralegal to aggressively compel the Tenant to comply with his demands and a landlord is responsible for the conduct of their agent(s). 85. Overall, the Landlord’s ill-considered actions and statements were serious, targeted, repeated and inexcusable. His non-action in response to disrepair was unacceptable. 86. I find that, in this case, an administrative fine of $10,000.00 is appropriate. 87. Of note, had the Board been provided with proof that the Landlord actually carried out these threats (for example, reporting the Tenant to the police and to immigration authorities) the fine would be substantially higher.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,318.00. This amount represents: • $4,770.00 for a rent abatement. • $7,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $10,000.00 by July 10, 2026.* June 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Musial (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant in the amount of $1,100.60. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The parties agree that the last month the Tenant paid rent for was April of 2026.

The parties agree that: • On March 17, 2026 the Tenant asked the Landlord for permission to assign their lease. A specific individual was not specified. This was a general request. • The Landlord denied the Tenant’s request to assign on March 18, 2026. • The Tenant then served the Landlord with an N9 notice to terminate the tenancy on March 19, 2026 by email with a termination date of May 15, 2026.
The Tenant argues that she was entitled to terminate her lease on a minimum of 30 day’s notice under section 95(4)(a) of the Act due to the Landlord’s refusal.

The Landlord argues that in seeking out an assignment, the Tenant was intending to circumvent section 47 of the Act which requires that a tenant provide 60 days notice of their intention to terminate a monthly tenancy, with the notice ending on the last date of a rental period.

The Tenant’s motivations for ending her tenancy under section 95 of the Act are not relevant in this case. The Tenant was legally able to make use of this section because the Landlord refused to consider the possibility of an assignment. The consequence for refusing to consider an assignment is that a tenant is legally permitted to terminate their lease on 30 days’ notice, and this does not need to fall at the end of a rental period. This is in accordance with section 96 of the Act.

The Tenant seeks the return of $1,970.00 in last month’s rent deposit and $49.00 in interest owing to her. The parties agreed in the hearing that the Landlord is still holding these sums. The Tenant filed her application within one year of these sums being retained.
The Tenant is entitled to a pro-rated sum for the month of May 2026. The Tenant owes rent for the period of May 1, 2026 to May 15, 2026.
Accordingly, the Landlord shall return to the Tenant the sum of $998.60 representing a pro-rated last month’s rent deposit, $49.00 in interest, and the application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,100.60. This amount represents: • $998.60 for the last month's rent deposit. • $49.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the hearing, the parties clarified that there are two Landlords for the rental unit, whereas the application only names one, [name] [name] [name]. The parties requested on consent to add the second Landlord, [name] [name], to the application, and I found it appropriate to grant the request. The amendment is reflected in the style of cause of this order.

At the hearing, the Tenant also requested to amend the application to add harassment allegations against the Landlords. The Landlords opposed the request as they were not provided with an amended application and would not have been able to adequately respond to any additional allegations.

A request to amend an application is assessed under Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. Rule 15.3 requires that I consider factors such as whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known. The Tenant’s initial application was filed on June 3, 2024, and he had approximately 11 months to amend the application prior to the hearing. The Tenant also did not provide a satisfactory reason for the delay. Given these considerations as well as the prejudice to the Landlords and the need for fair and expeditious proceedings, the request was denied. Substantial Interference:
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The rental unit is described as a basement apartment with two bedrooms, two washrooms, and a den. The unit is located next to a common room with the utility panel and a shared dryer accessible to the other tenants in the residential complex (the ‘laundry room’).

The parties entered into a one-year fixed term lease agreement on March 6, 2018. The lease was to start on April 1, 2018, with the rent being $1,050.00 per month; however, the Tenant was allowed to take early possession on March 8, 2018 and paid a prorated amount of rent for that month.

The main issue in the application is whether the parties verbally amended the lease after signing to grant exclusive use of the laundry room to the Tenant, and if the Landlords substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by allowing other tenants access and usage of that room.

The parties do not dispute that the laundry room was a common area when the Tenant moved into the rental unit. However, the Tenant maintains that he and the Landlord, [name] [name] [name], made a verbal agreement in 2019 for the Tenant to have exclusive use of the laundry room to store his belongings and to use for exercise. The Tenant texted the Landlord on May 9, 2019, offering to increase the rent to $1,200.00 per month provided he could use the entire laundry room for storage. The other tenants in the residential complex would still have access to use the dryer, but the rest of the room would be for the Tenant’s sole use. A copy of the text message was submitted as evidence. The Tenant testified that the Landlord declined the offer and later that year verbally told the Tenant that he could keep using the laundry room for his own purposes at no extra cost provided he kept the room tidy. The Tenant further testified that he maintained personal use of the laundry room for five years before any issues arose with the other tenants regarding use of the room.

The Tenant submitted a text message exchange between himself and the Landlord from December 2020 wherein the Tenant asks the Landlord to review a draft text he was going to send the upstairs tenants regarding storing their bikes in the laundry room. The Tenant argued the exchange substantiates that the Landlord agreed the Tenant would have exclusive use of the laundry room for storage, and the other tenants could only use the room to access the dryer. The text reads as follows: “Hi [name], I noticed that someone upstairs parked their bike in the dryer room-are you aware of this? I’m not sure if you know, but I made a special arrangement with [name] at the start of my lease to park my bikes in the dryer room. I believe you did not. As a result, you can use that room for access to the dryer but you cannot store things there. You also have other areas you can put your bike. You have a large backyard, a shed, and also your entire lower floor area. Could you please put that bike in your designated areas at your earliest convenience? If you would like to discuss this matter further, let’s schedule a time.”

The Landlord sent the Tenant two edited versions of the Tenant’s draft text for consideration. The more recent edited text from the Landlord on December 4, 2020 reads as follows: “Hi [name], I noticed that someone upstairs parked their bike in the dryer room-are you aware of this? Did they receive permission from [name] to do this? Perhaps your roommate was unaware everyone upstairs uses the shed in the backyard? To my understanding, you all have a shed available in the backyard to store your bikes and other items. I received permission from [name] to park my bikes in the dryer room because I do not have any additional storage area, given that room was taken away to use as a shared dryer room. We want to try and keep the shared common areas as clutter free as possible. I understand you have other areas where everyone upstairs is able to store their personal items. You have a large backyard, a shed, and also your entire lower floor area. I would really appreciate if you could please ask your roommate to move that bike to the other designated areas at your earliest convenience. If you would like to discuss this matter, let’s schedule a time.” [substantive differences in the text are emphasized]

Neither the lease nor written amendment thereafter makes reference to the Tenant’s exclusive use of the laundry room for storage. The Landlords also submitted a copy of the Kijiji advertisement for the rental unit showing its availability for April 1, 2018, which explicitly states there is a separate shared laundry room with a dryer located on the same floor as the unit.

The Landlords submitted a text message from May 9, 2019, accepting the Tenant’s offer of $1,200.00 per month for added use of the laundry room for storage. They also submitted a text message from the Tenant on May 17, 2019 wherein the Tenant states he may no longer need the additional laundry room storage as it was likely insufficient, and he would let the Landlord know if his circumstances changed. The parties confirmed the Tenant did not pay the increased rent for added storage space in the laundry room. The Landlord does not dispute that the Tenant continued to use the laundry room; however, there was no verbal agreement between the parties to grant him exclusive use of the room for no added compensation.

The Landlords submitted an email from one of the other tenants in the residential complex dated October 29, 2020, complaining about the Tenant’s use of the laundry room as his personal workout space. The email states the other tenants’ discomfort in trying to use the dryer during the Tenant’s workouts, and their request that the laundry room revert to its common use for all to access the dryer and electrical panel. The Tenant could still store his bikes there but would have to cease exercising in the room. The Landlord testified the October 29, 2020 email was the first time he was informed that the Tenant was using the laundry room as a personal gym. This was also during the COVID pandemic when all gyms were closed. The Tenant told the Landlord that exercising assisted him with his mental health during that time, and the Landlords wanted to be understanding. The parties did not dispute that a zoom meeting was then held between the Landlords and all the tenants in the residential complex on November 1, 2020. During the meeting, it was agreed by all the parties that while the pandemic was ongoing the Tenant could use the space for exercising at certain times, and that all tenants would need permission from the Landlords to store any items in the laundry room. The Landlord testified this was only a temporary arrangement during the pandemic, and there was no intent for the arrangement to become permanent.

The agreement that resulted from the November 1, 2020 zoom meeting lasted until December 2020 when some of the upstairs tenants began to store their bikes in the laundry room; that was when the Tenant texted the Landlord his draft message to send to the upstairs tenants. The Landlord testified that his reply drafts to the Tenant emphasized the use of the laundry room as a communal area, but that the Tenant was permitted to store his bikes in that room. Anyone else would also require the Landlord’s consent to store items in the laundry room. The texts do not show or imply that the Tenant had exclusive use of the laundry room. The Landlords were not aware of any further issues regarding the use of the laundry room after December 2020 until 2024.

On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed that he attends the residential complex once every three months to collect the change from the dryer and would have seen the Tenant’s exercise equipment. The Landlord acknowledged that he should have told the Tenant to move the items and/or sent the Tenant an email revoking his use of the laundry room, but he did not. The Landlords maintain, however, that they were not aware that the issue was ongoing as they did not receive additional complaints during this time, nor did they want to escalate the situation since the Tenant can be intimidating at times. The Landlords also reiterated that in order to agree to the Tenant’s exclusive use terms, they would have needed the consent of the other tenants as it would have affected their access and use of a common area. Analysis:

Having considered the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. The Tenant is essentially stating that the parties amended the lease agreement verbally in 2019 and by their actions over five years. An amendment to an agreement may be done in writing, verbally, or be implied through the actions of the parties. As this is a tenant’s application, the burden of proof lies with the Tenant to show on the balance of probabilities that such an amendment was created, and that the Landlords breached the modified agreement to the point of substantial interference with the Tenant’s ability to reasonably enjoy the rental unit or residential complex.

There is no dispute that the Tenant has been using the laundry room for storage and exercise purposes over the years. The issue is whether both parties intended for that usage to be exclusive and permanent. The text messages between the parties on May 9 & 17, 2019, and the confirmation that the Tenant has not paid any compensation for an added facility shows there was no meeting of the minds at that time to amend the lease and add the laundry room as an exclusive storage facility for the Tenant.

The parties also dispute that there was a verbal agreement between them regarding this issue after May 2019; it is essentially the Tenant’s word against the Landlord’s, and I am not persuaded on the balance of probabilities that the Landlords agreed to give the Tenant exclusive use of the laundry room for storage or any other purpose for no added compensation, when their previous messages to the Tenant showed a negotiated increase to $1,200.00 per month.

With respect to a possible implied agreement between the parties, I am also not convinced. The Tenant did not dispute that an agreement was made on November 1, 2020 between the Landlords and the tenants at the residential complex for the Tenant to be able to use the laundry room to exercise at certain times while the pandemic was ongoing. Once again, there is no supporting evidence to show that the arrangement was to be permanent.

The draft messages between the Tenant and Landlord to be sent to the upstairs tenants in December 2020 also show that the Landlord still designated the laundry room as a common area, though the Tenant had permission to store his bikes. The Landlord’s draft message does not explicitly state or imply that only the Tenant can use the laundry room for storage or for any other purpose.

I am also not satisfied that because no one complained to the Landlord about the Tenant’s use of the laundry room for four years, that implied the Landlords agreed to a material change in the lease that affected the other tenants in the residential complex and their access to a common area without their consent. Ultimately, the Tenant argued that because no one stopped him from using the laundry room for his own purposes, the room became an added facility to his lease. I do not agree. The totality of the evidence does not support an implied agreement, but rather that the Landlord consented to the Tenant using the laundry room for exercise for a temporary period, and that the Tenant is permitted to store certain items in the laundry room, though other tenants would be able to do so as well provided they received permission from the Landlords.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 9, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord's Legal Representative raised that some of the issues raised on the T2 Application were outside of the limitation period, as many of the alleged illegal entries occurred outside of the one-year limitation period, she also noted that many of the issues alleged arose after the termination of the tenancy.

The Act imposes a one-year limitation period. The T2 Application was filed on October 29, 2024. Therefore, I have not considered those illegal entries which are alleged to have occurred outside the limitation period.
Additionally, some of the allegations raised on the T2 Application are alleged to have occurred after the tenancy had terminated and are also outside of the Board’s jurisdiction. & LTB-T-045512-25
Therefore, the hearing was limited to those allegations within the Board’s jurisdiction.

The T2 also appears to lack sufficient particulars with respect to the allegations of interference and harassment. It is sufficiently clear that the Tenant is framing the alleged illegal entries as interference. However, there are also allegations that the Landlord frequently threatened to evict the Tenant and used the Board as means of legal intimidation, charged illegal fines, delayed repairs to the rental unit, and removed the Tenant’s portal access. None of these allegations have clear dates and times attached to them. The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the only dates they were provided to go on and prepare their case were the dates and times related to the alleged illegal entry.

The Tenant indicated that she had provided a table of contents to the Landlord which contained additional dates and times. However, she confirmed that the dates and times were not contained in the Application itself. She testified that these allegations should still be considered because she needs the process to be over.

Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”).

MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct…”. While [name] involved a notice of termination served to a Tenant, in my view the general principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications. In [name], the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

Accordingly, I elected to limit the proceeding to those allegations which contain sufficient particulars, including dates and times and note that the Tenant has already been given an opportunity to amend her application after the adjudicative case conference which was held on April 29, 2025.

The Landlord's Legal Representative also sought clarity with respect to the remedies request by the Tenant on the T2 Application. The Tenant confirmed that she was seeking general compensation of $33,000.0. With Respect to the T6

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the T6 Application was filed on June 3, 2025, meaning that the limitation period was back to June 30, 2024 and that there were no allegations in the Application within that limitation period. Accordingly, she requested that the T6 be dimissed.

At the hearing the Tenant initially indicated that she was amenable to the T6 being dimissed and did not dispute the Landlord's Legal Representative request, before indicating that she would be prepared to go through with the T6. & LTB-T-045512-25
The most recent allegation raised in the T6 dates from May 5, 2024, and the Tenant was not able to point to any allegations that fell within the one-year limitation period.
Therefore, as the T6 does not contain allegations which fall within the one-year limitation period set out in the Act the T6 shall be dimissed. The T2
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,500.00

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on October 18, 2021 and vacated October 24, 2024. The rental unit is a single-family home converted into multiple rental units. The rental was located in the basement of the home. Illegal Entry

The Tenant’s Application identifies 108 alleged illegal entries, a small number of these appear to be duplicitous and all but 27 are outside the one-year limitation period. Additionally, the Tenant has noted that in many cases she was provided with adequate notice of entry. Therefore, I heard testimony from her only on the illegal entries which fell within the limitation period for which she alleged adequate notice of entry was not provided.

The Tenant testified that on November 9, 2023, she was sleeping in her bedroom when someone opened the door. She testified that she believed it was the water guy who was had come in to inspect the boiler and water tank for the complex, which is located in her unit. She testified that she did not receive a notice of entry from the Landlord prior to this entry.

During cross examination the Tenant was presented with an email dated November 10, 2024, that she had sent to the Landlord’s agent indicating that she had let someone in the day before, and she agreed that this contradicted her testimony that she was sleeping in her room at the time of the entry. However, she testified that there was an entry when she was sleeping.

The Tenant testified that a maintenance person came to her unit again on November 10, 2023. She testified that she initially received an email from an agent of the Landlord Ashley Neufeld on November 9, 2023, indicating that there would be an entry on November 10, 2023, to check the boiler system. It indicated the entry would occur between 8:00am and 12:00pm However, no one entered the rental during those times.

The Tenant then received a second email dated November 10, 2023, at 1:44pm from a Shefali Pandey indicating that they would be entering the rental unit on November 10, 2023 between 1:00pm and 5:00pm because there was no heat in the loft of the complex. She testified that the entry occurred around the time the email was sent.
The Tenant testified that people would attend daily and she was told she would be evicted if she refused entry so she allowed them to enter. & LTB-T-045512-25

The Tenant testified that on November 14, 2023, she was in a [name] appointment with her therapist, and an unidentified man entered her rental unit sometime between 10:00am and 11:00am. She testified that she had been provided with a notice of entry on November 13, 2023, indicating that someone would enter between 10:15am and 5pm on November 14, 2023. She testified that this entry was for a “fall (autumn) inspection”

She also described an entry on February 6, 2024, by who she believed to be electricians who attended to fix a faulty smoke alarm in her rental unit. She testified that she called the Landlord and Tenant Board and was informed that this did not constitute an emergency which would justify entry without notice. She indicated that she received an “emergency notice of entry” prior to the entry on February 6, 2024, indicating someone would enter her unit to repair the smoke alarm.

She testified that she reported a chirping smoke alarm to the Landlord and received a response on February 27, 2023, indicating that someone would attend between 10:00am- 5:00pm to rest the smoke alarms in her unit. She testified that an agent for the Landlord again subsequently attended the rental unit to fix the chirping smoke alarm in the Tenant’s rental unit. However, she indicated that by this time the alarm had already been fixed.

She testified that on February 29, 2024, her smoke alarm began chirping again and after she made the Landlord aware she received an email from the Landlord’s Agent on February 29, 2024 indicating that someone would attend to inspect and repair the smoke alarm and an agent of the Landlord subsequently entered to insect the alarm. However they were unbale to repair the alarm.

She testified that on February 29, 2024 she walked over to the fire department and described her chirping smoke alarm, and the fire department sent a truck and a fireman smashed her chirping alarm and told her to refer the Landlord to the fire department if they had a problem with the smashed alarm.

She indicated that she made the Landlord aware through the building portal that the fire department had smashed the alarm and on March 1, 2024, an agent for the Landlord attended the rental unit to replace the smashed alarm with a new smoke alarm. She also directed me to an email on February 29, 2024, indicating that someone would enter her unit on March 1, 2024. She testified that she did not know the purpose of this entry because at the time the email was sent, she had not made the Landlord aware of the smashed alarm.

The Tenant also testified that for her birthday on July 30, 2024, she submitted an N9 to the Landlord, and the next day on July 31, 2024, she received a notice of entry for August 1, 2024, to conduct an inspection and appraisal of the rental unit. She testified that this was an appraisal inspection of the unit.

She also testified that on August 8, 2024, she received an email from the Landlord’s Agent at 12:33pm indicating that there would be an entry between 9:00am and 5:00pm to inspect the rental unit. She testified that she replied to the email indicating that an agent for the Landlord named [name] had entered her rental unit at 10:44pm and to express that she was concerned at the large number of inspections which had occurred within her rental unit and requested that any move out inspection occurred closer to her move out date. & LTB-T-045512-25
The Tenant confirmed during cross examination that she had refused entry into the rental unit but was not too sure how many times.
She testified that she did not believe that a faulty fire alarm is an emergency, she indicated that a chirping smoke alarm could be an emergency, but it would be situational.
The Landlord’s Agent [name] testified at the hearing. She is a senior property manager for the Landlord.
She testified that a smoke alarm is an emergency, as in a residential property a fire can spread from one unit into others.

She explained that the Landlord’s portal uses a work order system which provides Tenant’s with a box they can check if they are making a request and do not need 24 hours notice of entry. If the box is checked notice of entry will not be provided if it is left blank notice is provided.

She also explained that the Tenant’s rental unit contained both the hot water tank and the heater, which would necessitate entry whenever either had issues. She testified that the Landlord would try to work with Reliance and other contractors to find time that works for entry but reliance will often show up late or not at all, and the Landlord has a has a duty to provide hot water to the complex.

She also testified that if Appliance repair is provided the Landlord would involve their contractor RTC who would coordinate directly with Tenants to schedule entry, and the Landlord would only become involved if RTC was unable to contact the Tenant to schedule entry. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that because of the excessive number of entries into her rental unit her life was severely impacted, and she lost her role assisting low-income families. She also testified that the stress caused her to have a seizure on September 12, 2024 and she lost her license as a result. Additionally, because the entries shad caused her to miss group therapy sessions, she was removed from her therapy program.

In support of this the Tenant relied on a letter from her pharmacist dated March 26, 2025 which asserts that the Tenant has been diagnosed with epilepsy which causes seizures which increase in frequency during emotionally overwhelmed periods, and asserts that the Tenant experienced repeated violations of her personal space which cased worsening PTSD symptoms and anxiety which led to more frequent seizures.

The Tenant testified that the number and purpose of the Landlord’s inspections was ridiculous and testified that she sent the Landlord an email on May 13, 2024, about the number of inspections and to remind the Landlord that they had already performed an annual inspection that year.

During cross examination The Tenant confirmed that the medical note that she relied on was written by her pharmacist rather than her doctor. However, she testified that she has & LTB-T-045512-25 this pharmacist forever and they have seen her conditions change. The Tenant denied that she had told her pharmacist what to write in the letter.

The Landlord’s witness [name] testified that the complex has an annual appraisal inspection which is booked by the bank and a series of annual inspections including an annual fire inspection, and an annual unit inspection and follow up.

She testified that not all entries alleged by the Tenant were entries as some were key audits, where the unit key would be tested but no one would enter the unit, and many of the notices of entry relied on by the Tenant were corrections or amendments sent by the Landlord.

She testified that no one who works for the Landlord has a grudge against the Tenant and they in fact did not know who she was when the Application was first filed, as she had been a good Tenant and not on the Landlord’s radar. . Harassment

The Tenant testified that by October 24, 2024, she was removing her belongings from the rental unit when she became ware that the Landlord had scheduled roof repairs for that day. She testified that when she arrived at the unit there was a plywood panel covering her door and she was hit by a shingle which was thrown from the roof by a contractor hired by the Landlord. She testified that she did not believe that this was deliberate, however she believed that the Landlord had deliberately scheduled roof repairs that day to interfere with her move and harass her.

A witness for the Landlord [name] testified at the hearing, He is the owner of Need a Roof. He testified that he did not remember the Tenant and had never met her but confirmed that his company performed repairs on the roof the day that the Tenant vacated. He testified that plywood panels were place around the worksite to protect from falling debris and explained that he would typically provide his clients with a variety of days during which work could be completed, but this would ultimately be contingent upon the weather. Analysis
Ultimately, I am satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord’s Agents have entered the rental unit illegally.

While I found the Tenant’s testimony to be credible, I did not find it to be reliable. It was at time inconsistent, such as when she indicated that she was sleeping during the November 9 2023, entry, only to later change this assertion, and when she revised her testimony around refusing entry. I am willing to attribute a portion of this to the Tenant’s anxiety and underlying conditions, and the stress of a hearing before the Board, however I am not satisfied this entirely accounts for the inconstancies in the Tenants testimony.

However, even in consideration of the reliability of the Tenant’s testimony, the documentary evidence indicates that illegal entries did occur. For example, on November 10, 2023 the Tenant received an email at 1:44pm indicating that someone would enter that day, and they entered the unit shortly thereafter. This is not 24 hours notice. Likewise, the notice of entry for November 14, 2023, does not provide a full 24 hours notice to the & LTB-T-045512-25 Tenant. Similarly, the Notice of entry issued for August 1, 2024, while provided the day before does not provide a full 24 hours notice to the Tenant.
Additionally, on August 8, 2024, the Tenant received an email advising her of an entry that day at 12:33pm.

Therefore, as the Landlord did not provide a full 24 hours notice for these entries, I am satisfied that they constitute illegal entry. I am also not satisfied that the Landlord has identified an emergency which would warrant entering without notice and note that the August 8, 2024, entry appears to be for an inspection.

While the Tenant also asserts multiple illegal entries related to her fire alarm between February 6, 2024, and March 1, 2024 I am satisfied that a faulty fire alarm within a multi- residential building does constitute an emergency which would warrant entry without notice. An undetected fire in the Tenant’s unit could easily spread throughout the complex, and I am satisfied that after the Tenant made the Landlord aware of her ongoing issues with the fire alarm it was appropriate for them to enter to remediate the issue.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord's Agent entered the rental unit illegally on November 10, 2023 Novembre 14, 2023, August 1, 2024 and August 8, 2024.
The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord interfered with her reasonable enjoyment both through the illegal entries and the sheer number of entries.

The Tenant’s Application lists 27 entries between November 2023 and September 2024. While this number seems excessive I am prepared to accept the testimony of the Landlord’s agent, that many of these entries were scheduled by a third part repair services after maintenance requests, and many are duplicates which represent the Landlord changing or amending a notice of entry, additionally I note that a some appear to have been requested by the Tenant herself and a large number of the entries were in response to the faulty fire alarm in the Tenant’s rental unit.

When these entries are subtracted it appears that the Landlord or their agents entered the rental unit approximately 11 times during the period of November 2023 to September 2024. However, even many of these entries appear to be for a legitimate purpose including to turn on the hear, conduct an annual unit inspection or audit, or to shut down the water or check the boiler system. Therefore, while the number of entries may at first appear excessive, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment by entering the rental unit an excessive number of times.

However, I am prepared to accept that the illegal entries substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyments, especially when I consider them in the overall context of the sheer number of entries during this period.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household

With respect to harassment, The Tenant’s assertion that the Landlord deliberately scheduled the roof repair during her move appears to be speculative, and I accept the testimony of the Landlord’s witness that he is the one who provides dates to clients and & LTB-T-045512-25 that those dates are weather dependant. Therefore, as the Tenant’s assertion that the roof repair was booked to interfere with and harass her is speculative and there is evidence before me to suggest that the dates were not selected by the Landlord alone, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that this constitutes harassment. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant sought general damages of $33,000.00. I am satisfied that a modest award is appropriate, however I am not prepared to order the quantum sought by the Tenant. I note that I have found only 4 illegal entries and while I have accepted that these illegal entries impacted her reasonable enjoyment, I am not satisfied that this warrants an award of $33,000.00

The Tenant testified that the entries caused her increased anxiety which worsened her PTSD and caused her to experience seizures which led to the loss of her licence and her employment. The Tenant relies on a letter from her pharmacist in support of this assertion. However I have placed little weight on the letter, and note that the Tenant’s pharmacist is not her doctor, and I am not pharmacists has assessed the Tenant to the extent that they are able to definitively assert that the Tenant’s medical conditions were caused or exacerbated by the Landlord’s actions, or were the primary cause of her conditions worsening.

Without a clear causal nexus, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the health effects she suffered were a direct result of the Landlord’s actions, and I therefore find the quantum sought excessive.

However, I am satisfied that general compensation of $1500.00 is appropriate. This represents $250.00 per illegal entry, and $500.00 for compensation for interference with reasonable enjoyment in recognition of the impact of the Landlord’s actions.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 Application is dimissed.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,500. This amount represents: • $1,500 for general compensation
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. & LTB-T-045512-25 June 3, 2026 ____________________________
