issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. An adjudicative case conference was heard by videoconference on January 19, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 12:45pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence and was heard uncontested.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the start of the case conference, the Tenant confirmed that she was ready to proceed uncontested. After giving evidence about the merits of the application, the Tenant advised that she wanted to upload additional evidence about remedies. I explained that evidence should have been filed and served before the hearing. At approximately 1:01 p.m., the Tenant left the videoconference. I waited until 2:00 p.m. and the Tenant did not return. I have decided the application based on the evidence filed and the evidence given before the Tenant left the hearing.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord and an unidentified man called and screamed at her and her family, threatened her family, and yelled at her children during the move-out process.

The Tenant’s application states that she moved out of the rental unit on May 27, 2025. The Tenant’s evidence was that the Sheriff enforced the eviction order on May 27, 2025. The Tenant’s evidence about the alleged harassment focused on events that occurred after that date, including June 2, 2025, when she attended at the rental unit to retrieve belongings.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant’s evidence about the relevant dates was inconsistent. The Tenant changed the date of the alleged events several times, and her evidence did not provide a reliable basis to determine what was said, who said it, or when the alleged conduct occurred. Further, the evidence focused on events after the Sheriff had enforced the eviction order and after the Tenant had vacated the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not prove that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
Subsection 41(2) of the Act requires a landlord to make an evicted tenant’s property available for retrieval during the 72-hour period after the enforcement of the eviction order.

The Sheriff enforced the eviction order on May 27, 2025. The Tenant’s evidence about being denied access focused mainly on May 31, 2025, June 2, 2025, and June 4, 2025. Those dates were after the 72-hour statutory retrieval period.

The text message evidence filed with the application also does not prove that the Landlord failed to provide the 72-hour retrieval period. The message advised the Tenant that she had 72 hours from the time of the eviction to remove her personal belongings, that access would be available daily between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. during that period, and that the belongings would not be considered abandoned or disposed of until June 4, 2025. The Tenant also testified that she attended at the rental unit on June 2, 2025 and was given 4.5 hours to pack. While the Tenant may have been dissatisfied with the arrangements after the 72-hour period, I am not satisfied that she proved the Landlord failed to make her property available during the 72-hour period required by the Act.

I also find that the Tenant’s evidence about this allegation was inconsistent. The Tenant changed the relevant date several times and did not provide reliable evidence that access was refused during the statutory 72-hour period. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not prove that the Landlord failed to give the Tenant 72 hours to remove her property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.

Because the Tenant did not prove the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities, no remedies are ordered. In any event, the Tenant did not provide reliable evidence identifying what property, if any, remained in the Landlord’s possession or control. Therefore, even if the Tenant had proven a breach of the Act, I would not have ordered the Landlord to return unspecified property.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Sections 30, 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: Upper 1, 14 DALHOUSIE ST Brantford ON [name] (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with their vital services. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was heard by videoconference on June 19, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 9:24 am the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence. The Landlord attended at 11:22 am. I advised him that this application was heard and that he can expect to receive an order I the near future. He claimed that he does not have a matter before the LTB. This argument is addressed below.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord argues that he is not a landlord. He did not participate in the hearing when the matter was heard but this issue was raised by the Tenant as the Landlord filed document 8114638 in Portal in which he claims that he is not a landlord.

S. 2(1) of the Act defines the Landlord as follows: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent;

The Tenant testified that the Landlord previously told them that he is not their landlord and they should check their lease. The Tenant’s lease is with a numbered company (document 8066865). It is not a standard Ontario residential lease as required by s. 12.1 of the Act.
Payments under the lease are to be made by e-transfer to [email]”. It is unclear who this email address belongs to but it would appear that the recipient has the same last name as the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord would contact them about rent payments when they were late. The lease was signed through email with the Landlord, and they always communicated with him. He is the one who showed them the rental unit and permitted occupancy of the rental unit when they moved in.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I find that the Landlord meets the definition of a landlord under the Act. It is possible that he is not the owner or the controlling mind of the corporate owner, but I find that he permits occupancy of the rental unit and meets the definition under s. 2(1). There may be more than one landlord under the Act.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence I find that it is more likely than not that they have been without power since May 21st, 2026. They contacted the Landlord, but he has done nothing to remedy the situation.
Under the lease the Landlord is responsible for paying the electric bill.
Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence I find that the Tenant’s stove is no longer in good working order. The Tenant’s contacted the Landlord who has failed to repair it.

The Tenant alleges breaches of ss. 21 and 20 of the Act: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), a landlord shall be deemed to have withheld the reasonable supply of a vital service, care service or food if the landlord is obligated to pay another person for the vital service, care service or food, the landlord fails to pay the required amount and, as a result of the non-payment, the other person withholds the reasonable supply of the vital service, care service or food.

It is unclear why there is no electricity supply to the rental unit. It is possible that the Landlord breached s. 21(1) of the Act, 21(2) of the Act or 20(1) of the Act. The Landlord may have intentionally interfered with electricity, failed to pay the bills or failed to maintain the unit resulting in electricity being disconnected. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord breached the Act by at the very least not taking any steps to address the issue of supply of electricity.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The Landlord was made aware of both issues and has not addressed them. I therefore find that he is in breach of the Act in accordance with Onyskiw even if he did not breach ss. 21(1) or 21(2).
The Landlord also breached s. 20(1) of the Act by failing to take any steps to repair or replace the stove.
The Tenant requested only a limited number of remedies, and I find that they are entitled to these remedies based on their uncontroverted testimony.

The Tenant lost many food items after they lost electricity, and the fridge stopped working. They testified that the property damaged, destroyed or disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s breach of the Act cost $203.89. I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $203.89, which is the reasonable cost that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of.

The Tenant has out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $279.85 because of the Landlord's actions. They had to pay these costs because the Landlord interfered with vital services or failed to restore electricity to the rental unit. The Landlord must pay the Tenant this amount.
The Landlord must also restore supply of electricity and provide a stove in good working order.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $483.74. This amount represents: • $203.89 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to replace property that was damaged / destroyed / disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $279.85 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred or will incur.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $483.74 from rent for August 2026.
The Tenant has the right to collect the full amount owing any time.
The Landlord shall immediately restore supply of electricity to the rental unit and shall not interfere with supply of electricity to the rental unit.
The Landlord shall immediately provide the Tenant a stove in good working order. June 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and Cameron [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex (T2 application); and. • failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application) This application was continued by videoconference on May 5, 2026. The Landlords and the Tenants attended the hearing. [name] [name] appeared as a witness for the Landlords. This was an FLS hearing. Board [name] provided French and English interpretation services.
reasons: The Tenants allege the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to a flood in the rental unit, which substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Landlord’s legal obligations to repair File Numbers : LTB-T-047067-25; LTB-T-058721-25

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

It is important to note that subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. Therefore, the reasons for a landlord’s breach are not relevant. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), however, the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem, then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it.

Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

In determining whether the Landlords have breached their obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. The Board must then consider when the Landlords were informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue and whether the steps taken by the Landlords to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstances.

There seems to be no dispute that the Tenants reported the basement flooded on July 15, 2024. As explained above, a disrepair issue is not an automatic breach of a landlord’s obligation under subsection 20(1). The issue to be determined is whether the steps the Landlords took to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstance. I am satisfied they were.

The evidence before me establishes that the Landlords immediately attended the rental unit on July 15, 2024 to assess the flood in the basement. The Landlords removed and replaced the carpets, flooring, and under pads and set up fans and dehumidifiers to dry out the basement. New flooring was installed in the bedroom and living room. In my view, the steps taken by the Landlords were appropriate and timely.

The Tenants seem to suggest that the Landlords ought to have known that the basement would have flooded because they had reported leaks from the basement ceiling, flooding File Numbers : LTB-T-047067-25; LTB-T-058721-25 in the laundry room due to the lack of an adequate drainage system, and a leak in the kitchen. As the applicants, the onus is on the Tenants to prove their claim on a balance of probabilities. I find the Tenants have failed to sufficiently establish that the basement flood was due to a leak in the basement ceiling, the lack of a drainage system in the laundry room, or a leak in the kitchen.

There is no dispute that there was a significant storm in the [name]-Burlington area and the region experienced severe flooding on July 15, 2024. The Landlords admitted into evidence several newspaper clippings and city documents indicating the sudden flood in the region was unforeseeable and overwhelmed municipal infrastructure. Landlord [name] testified that hundreds of homes in the region had been damaged in the storm and that the City was working to rectify the infrastructure.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the flooding in the basement was the result of storm waters and not due to an unresolved maintenance issue. I find the Landlords acted promptly and appropriately in addressing the flood. Accordingly, the Landlords have not breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Tenants’ applications are therefore dismissed.

The Tenants seem to take issue with the fact that their furniture and personal belongings were damaged in the flood waters. As the storm and resulting flooding was not reasonably foreseeable, the Landlords cannot be held financially liable for such damage and loss.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. June 09, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties did not dispute the following material facts: • The Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination under section 48 of the Act, which stated that they required vacant possession of their rental unit because the Landlord required the rental unit for personal use; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit on as a result of the N12 Notice; and • The Landlord continued to reside at the rental property as of the date of the hearing but did list the rental property for sale within 12 months after the Tenant vacated.
Therefore, the issues to be determined are whether the N12 Notice was given in bad faith.
The Landlord presented uncontested evidence that they have resided in the rental unit since April 3, 2025, and continue to reside at the unit as of the date of the hearing.

The Landlord testified that they gave the Tenant the N12 notice of termination for their own personal use because her medical condition and financial situation changed and she needed to move into the unit. She was living in a unit with stairs, and she needed a flat surface due to physical, mental and health issues. The Landlord testified that she lost her job, was struggling financially, and had to do testing for medical reasons, and it was recommended that she should live with someone, so she listed a room for rent online to share the unit with someone, but she was unable to rent out the room. Accordingly, she occupies the unit on her own.
The Landlord further testified that she did list the property for sale due to her financial situation changing but was unable to sell it.

The Landlord provided documentation evidence to support that she resides at the rental unit and continues to reside at the rental unit. These documents included, vehicle ownership and insurance, mail forwarding, her drivers license, her pension plan, T4A tax document from work, CRA documentation, loan details, and medical documentation. In addition, the Landlord provided photograph evidence to support that she moved into the rental unit by showing all her belongings within the unit.

The Tenant disputes that the Landlord provided the notice of termination in good faith and testified that the Landlord had the intention to rent it or sell it but was unable to do so within the 12-month period that Landlord claimed she was going to reside at the unit.
The Tenant during cross examination testified that he has no evidence that the Landlord is not actually living at the rental unit.

Given that it is undisputed that the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale, within one year of after the Tenant vacated, I find that the presumption of bad faith in section 57(5) is triggered. Therefore, the burden of proof shifted to the Landlord to prove that the N12 Notice was given in good faith. Based on the evidence presented by the Landlord, I am satisfied that the presumption was rebutted, and the Tenant has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord provided the notice in bad faith. The Landlord had an explanation as to why a bedroom was listed for rent, not the entire rental unit, in addition to why she listed the property for sale, which was an unforeseen financial circumstance, but the Landlord continues to reside at the rental unit as of the date of the hearing. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord met the burden of proof and did not serve the notice in bad faith.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act for “landlord’s own use” and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.

Therefore, the only issues in dispute are whether the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, and if the notice was given in bad faith. The other elements of the test in s. 57(1)(a) are not disputed.
The parties agree that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 30, 2025.

The Tenant testified that during the months from April 2025 to June 2025, the Tenant kept their mailbox keys to collect their mail and continued to use the mailbox after they vacated the rental unit and assumed the Landlord would get his own mail key, which would result in them no longer having access to the mailbox. The Tenant testified they had no knowledge of the Landlord getting their own key, but they maintained access to the mailbox until June 2025. The Tenant testified under cross examination that they kept accessing the mailbox after they vacated to prove their case and that the Landlord had no intention to move into the rental unit.

In addition, the Tenant testified that they drove past the rental property from April 2025 to June 2025 as they have to drive by to get their daughter to school, and the Tenant noticed the Landlord did not put garbage out on Fridays, as this was the day the garbage was collected. As well, the rental property looked vacant as the blinds were closed, no cars were in the driveway, and the grass was overgrown.
The Tenant testified that the hydro bill was still in their name as of May 15, 2025, and that the usage of hydro was significantly lower than a normal person, or their own usage.

The Tenant testified that it was not until sometime in July 2025, that the rental property showed signs of someone residing in the unit, which was after they filed this application. The signs were garbage being put out for garbage day, and one blind being opened.

The Tenant testified that she believed the Landlord only gave the N12 notice of termination due to The Tenant raising the issue that the 2 units within the building were not legal separate units, which did not meet fire and safety codes. The Tenant was to reside in the upper unit, and the basement unit was vacant when the Tenant moved in.

Under cross examination the Tenant testified that the Landlord rented them the entire home because the Landlord was not going to complete the work to address the fire and safety issues and turn the building into 2 separate units.
The Landlord testified that he and his spouse moved into the renal unit on April 5, 2025, and provided documentation from [name] to confirm that they rented a vehicle to move into the rental unit.

The Landlord also provided further documentation as evidence which was confirmation of their address change from Service Ontario which shows that on April 5, 2025, they changed the address on their driver’s license which took about 90 days for the new one to come in, bank statements to show the rental property as their residence, a doctor’s letter confirming they would be changing their family doctor from Mississauga where they previously resided to [name], which is where the rental unit is located. In addition, the Landlord provided photographs of work being completed at the rental property with the Landlord in the photographs, along with birthday parties, and other family gatherings that took place at the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that they changed their family doctor on April 25, 2025, as it made no sense for them to remain with their family doctor as it was a 2 hour drive away.

The Landlord testified in response to their garbage not being outside when the Tenant would drive by that garbage pickup is normally around 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., and the Landlord puts out the garbage around that time after his wife preps their meals.

The Landlord testified in response to the hydro usage, that they are a family of 3, whereas the Tenant was a family of 6, so the Tenant’s usage would be higher. In addition, the Landlords do not like to waste their money and are very cautious about their hydro usage, so they consume a lot less.

The Landlord testified in response to the lawn being overgrown, that the Tenants took the Landlord’s lawn mower when they vacated, and the Landlord did not want to purchase a new one, so the neighbour would cut the grass from time to time until they purchased a new one. The Law/Analysis:

While the Tenant offered reasonable suspicions, which are genuinely held by them, they remain however, mere suspicions. While I accept that the Tenant raised an issue with the Landlord about the fire and safety issues about the 2 separate units, the Landlord in return rented out the entire property to the Tenant to address this issue and did not turn the property into 2 separate units. The Tenant failed to provide any supporting documentation or evidence to support their suspicions and relied merely on garbage not being put out when they drove by the unit, the hydro usage, and the fact that the mailbox was not switched over.

The Landlord provided a great deal of documentation evidence to support that they moved into the rental unit in April 2025 and even provided documentation to support that they changed their family doctor to one that was closer to the rental property.

Ultimately, I find that the Landlord moved into the rental unit shortly after the Tenant vacated and continues to reside at the rental unit. Since the Tenant has not proved all of the parts of the test in s. 57(1)(a), the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background to the proceedings
The Tenant filed the initial T2 application on August 11, 2023.

The matter proceeded to an adjudicative case conference initially on July 3, 2025, following which an interim order was issued on July 14, 2025 which outlined the following determinations: “2.The Tenant’s reasons for this application are set out in “Schedule A” provided with the T2 application (DOC-1775211). During the ACC, the following allegations/issues were clarified/identified within those pleadings in order for the Landlord to be able to respond: • Tatiana, the Landlords’ daughter, who resides at the residential complex is the Landlord’s Agent. • The Tenant felt unsafe and harassed by the Landlords and/or their Agent(s) because: a) They failed to address threats to the Tenant of physical harm and death from another tenant in the complex; and b) The Tenant was under a threat of eviction if he was non-compliant with the Landlords and/or their Agent(s) set of rules. c) They called the Tenant names. d) They told the Tenant that they did not want him to live in the complex. e) They attempted and conducted malicious inspections of the rental unit; and f) They were disrespectful and inappropriate during encounters and exchanges with the Tenant. 3. The parties agreed that the disclosure of supporting evidence is complete between them.”

I note that this order does not attempt to refer to all the of documents, videos and photos filed and as uploaded that formulate the Board’s record. In making the decision below I have considered the entirety of the relevant parts of the record. T2 Application
The Tenant moved into the rental complex on January 1, 2022 and moved out December 31, 2022. The lawful rent was $920.00 and was inclusive of utilities.
The complex is comprised of four rental units.
The Landlords are [name] and [name]. They are the owners of a fourplex, “the residential complex.”
Their daughter Tatiana [name] (TA) lived in Unit 4 in the building.
The Landlord’s son, [name] [name] in Unit 2 in the building with his partner, [name] and their baby.

The Tenant became acquainted with the Landlord’s daughter Tatiana and her partner Christina Lugo through a chance meeting in the neighborhood, when a unit became available in the four-plex, the Tenant moved in.
The Tenant met [name] when they moved in sometime later, they decorated outside with plants and bonded over this activity.

The Tenant testified that at the outset of the tenancy, he was advised by (TA), that despite her father being the Landlord, he was to address any issues with her. The Tenant submits that (TA) was and functioned as a de facto superintendent and/or property manager for her parents, the Landlords.
The Tenant paid rent directly to (SA) the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that as soon as he moved in that Tatiana criticized his furniture and made comments about the cleanliness of his rental unit on a monthly basis. And that there were occasions that the Landlord (SA) also commented on the state of his rental unit.

The relationship took a turn when the Tenant submitted that he was called to come to the rental unit of Tatiana and Christina on August 11, 2022. The Tenant submitted that he sometimes blanks out and as he was suspect of something going down based on Tatiana’s mood that he recorded the conversation in which it was outlined that [name] – “Berto”, the Landlord’s son was going to kill him, will throw him off the balcony and that the two hour conversation also instituted rules for him to follow.

Here are some excerpts as contained in the audio recording (DOC-1775286): “my brother wants nothing to do with you, he is doesn’t want to look at you, he is like ready to throw you off the fucking balcony. You are meddling in something you shouldn’t be - Who the fuck are you to tell [name] her place is fine and clean when you can’t keep your own place clean. My parent and brother are up to here with your shit, I already told you don’t stress out my parents. Instead you come in and stir every fucking pot and play innocent. Why wont you let anyone in your apartment, you stress yourself out, …all of this is on your fucking head, you are on thin ice, on thin ice… [name] told Berto and Berto told mom, and I found out – Berto wants you to go. You are not ok to tell anyone anything period… you better write a letter to him, right now you are fucking dead to him, how dare you to involve yourself with their family. He wants nothing to do with you…. If my father has any health issues, I will lose it on you. The Tenant is heard asking “so two people are mostly mad at me, one person is really mad at me? The answer by Tatiana is “no, one person wants to kill you….”

As evident based on the above excerpts, Tatiana and Christina were addressing issues when becoming aware that the Tenant had been allegedly interfering with the personal affairs of her brother, the Landlord’s son [name] and his partner [name] who also resided in the complex.

Based on the evidence as before the Board, I find that the Landlords did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. And I find that the Landlords did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant for the reasons as follows. 39. For clarity, while the Tenant has made submissions that Tatiana [name] (TA), is a de facto superintendent and/or property manager for her parents, the Landlords, I can not arrive at the same conclusion on the basis of the evidence as before me. I say this as both (TA), and the Landlord (SA) submitted that the management and collections of rent are strictly done by the Landlord (SA). Further, the evidence was that inspections of the rental unit were also conducted by (SA). 40. Despite that (TA) was telling the Tenant to come to her with any issues, this was explained to be because her father was experiencing medical issues, and she wanted to shelter any complaints from him. And the evidence was that Tatiana took responsibility for vouching for the Tenant in his being accepted as a tenant in the complex, when issues arose, she is heard expressing to the Tenant that she was his supporter and was addressing issues of discord in the complex as expressed by the Tenant for the same reasons. 41. As the crux of the Tenant’s T2 filing rests with the events of August 11, 2022, as outlined to the parties at the time of the hearing I have reviewed the vast majority of the recorded conversation to get a better sense of the dynamics and the mood during the conversation to understand the context of the conversation. 42. In hearing the clips as shared at the time of hearing any audience can walkaway with a tainted view of the two plus hour conversation recording. I say this as the parts shared contain multiple explicit and implicit threats, including statements that [name]could kill” the Tenant and was “ready to throw him off the balcony,” along with warnings that the Tenant was “on thin ice.” These are reinforced by repeated assertions that the Tatiana would “lose it” if family members were affected. [name] together, the conversation reflects a pattern of intimidation and suggestions of potential physical harm. 43. However, on review of the entire record, I draw upon the mood and tone of conversation. Outside of the swearing and raised voices when addressing the allegations of threats as against the Tenant, most of the conversation is of normal tone, the voices are mostly calm; there is soft music in the background. Positive exchanges can be heard, where the tone was supportive and both Tatiana and Chritina express care and concern for the Tenant, noting that the relationship matters. For instance, they are heard saying: “I’m still willing… and like I said, I still somehow love you even though all the shit you’ve done…” “Will you be willing to come with me for a session?… I’m willing to help you… I’m still willing to go to your therapist…” This in support of the Tenant as it was testified that the Tenant was getting some assistance for his mental well being. 44. There are also tips provided to reduce conflict, including advice to give others space and avoid further involvement. And suggestions for better life balance in the form of improved routines by going to work, gym, social life improvements and seeking therapy. 45. It is at this juncture of the conversation that Chrsitina said let’s develop a practical plan to resolve issues and the list that the Tenant makes for himself is arrived at together. Which in summary addressed cleaning, limiting contact, and changing behaviour. The Tenant is heard responding with acknowledgement and willingness to improve. 46. It was undisputed that the mood and relationship between the parties in the complex was amended, so much so that on August 24, 2022, (TA) sent the Tenant a message in which (TA) outlines that: “….. today I am deeply saddened by the loss of our much treasured friendship. I was very excited for you to move in but I was also very clear with you when i gave you the opportunity to live in my family's apartment unit that i did not want you to cause stress to my parents, as we are fully aware of the stress and shit you caused with your other landlord, and all you have done is added stress to their lives. You quickly turned a beautiful apartment into a cluttered nightmare. You have been asked numerous times to clean up the disastrous hoarding storage unit you call a home, as it is a fire hazard, a breeding ground for vermin and bugs and you have not. What was once a beautiful, open, clean and spacious apartment is now an embarrassment that you yourself don't even want people to see. This is evident by the amount of people that you have not let in your apartment to use the bathroom or just see your place. When you moved in you said you needed multiple couches, so people had a place to crash if necessary but now you are too ashamed to even let us 'your closest friends' in to see the place. It is so beyond disrespectful what you have done as myself and my dad worked very hard to fix it up only for you to disrespect it. Your hoarding has now spread to the upper balcony/deck outside even though you have been told numerous times that it is not your personal space. It is cluttered and messy and once again you have been asked to stop putting things, and leaving your things outside, but instead of taking care of it you continue to just add more. I'm not sure why you felt the need to meddle in Berto and [name]'s relationship and try to advise her on her family. This has contributed to the position you are currently in. And how the fuck dare you try to accuse me and my brother of being any kind of violent people. Your life is not or has ever been in danger. I honestly thought you knew us better, and I'm saddened to even hear this coming from you. Always the victim never owning why he is in any situation. You stuck your nose where it didn't belong to a relationship you knew nothing about. You constantly ignore what other people say to do what is best for you. You don't care if it's inconvenient for them as long as its what’s best for you. You convince yourself that their requests are ridiculous and they don't matter. Those decisions aren't yours to make. It shows a complete lack of respect towards other people. And again instead of owning up to it you somehow manage to twist things in your head and throw the blame on anyone but yourself. I'm sorry if this is a hard truth but you don't seem to ever take responsibility for your actions. Do yourself a favour and put your money towards your mental health instead of trying 'fix' things with retail therapy. Happiness does not come from an object.” 47. The Tenant testified to having been staying out of the rental unit for some time after August 11, 2022 and when he replied to the message. 48. On September 10, 2022, the Tenant writes back advising that (TA) needs to take responsibility for her actions, and that he wanted an apology for himself and his mother for the in person conversation that took place on August 11, 2022, and outlines that he wants a written letter from the Landlord and co-signed by Tatiana and [name] confirming his safety and civil interactions if he’s to return to the building. He also notes “I need to move to safe accommodation starting tomorrow and I’ll be forwarding this cost to the [name] family. So far these costs are under $4,000.00.” …. “I am still willing to make this easy and less expensive. I still truly care about you all, but I’ve seen none of that care back to me in at least a month.” 49. No response was received from the Landlords nor the other occupants. 50. The Tenant decided to contact the police to report alleged threats from “Berto” on September 12, 2022, he testified that this was because of the conversations he had with Tatiana, Christina, [name], and because of Berto’s actions. Specifically, despite not being verbally nor physically threatened by [name] directly, the Tenant perceived him to be a threat by the way he was walking and driving aggressively into the complex, and as this was different than usual, the Tenant felt compelled to file the report. 51. The police report as evidence in DOC-3543630 was heavily redacted, the parts that are visible are as follow: “At 3:14 a.m. Police spoke to ALCARON-MAZZEY, who was cautioned and advised that he had no recollection of saying anything threatening to [redacted] as he has not seen him at the residence for the past 20 days. ALCARON-MAZZEY confirmed that there is an ongoing tenancy issue with [redacted], as well as a personal grievance due to meddling in his relationship. ALCARON-MAZZEY further advised he has absolutely no intention to harm or threaten [redacted] and that he will actively avoid him. Based on both parties recollection of events the comments allegedly uttered were not directed to or intended to be received by [redacted], as the comments occurred within a private conversation between family members. In addition, ALCARON-MAZZEY advised that he has no recollection of making any threatening remarks and has no intent to harm [redacted]. Pending further information becoming available there are no reasonable grounds to substantiate a criminal offence. This concludes police involvement in this matter.” Emphasis added … 52. Following this, the Tenant sent a text message to the second Landlord [name] on September 14, 2022 in which he asks for power to the rental unit to be turned on and advised that while he recognized things were tough at the time, that he “wants things to be peaceful enough so that I can feel comfortable enough to come and move out.” 53. The Tenant was referred to the first named Landlord (SA) to address this issue. In a recorded phone conversation with the first named Landlord (SA) as contained in DOC- 3588248, the Landlord is heard saying he was concerned about the Tenant being away from the apartment for some time and not being able to schedule an inspection. When asked if he wanted to address the issues as occurring at the residential complex, the Landlord (SA) said he did not want to address personal issues as pertaining to the Tenant and his friends Tatiana and Christina. The Tenant said this was despite being told that he left because he was scared for his safety and that he could not speak to him directly, given (TA’s) directions. The Landlord (SA) is then heard saying that this was a problem because he was the landlord. That lately Tatiana informed him of the interference he was causing with Berto and [name] and that he did not like this himself. 54. The Tenant then asked the Landlord about the words that were said to him by Tatiana and Christina. And told him that his own mom was very concerned about his own safety. The Landlord is heard again saying he did not have any involvement, and was not aware of the depth of the issues ongoing and apologised to the Tenant. The Tenant provided the Landlord with the option to be provided a letter outlining his safety and failing agreement he would be moving out. 55. It is not disputed that the Tenant record a threat that he internalized and believed to be real. Based on the characterization of the closeness of the relationship I prefer the evidence of Tatiana and Chritina and accept that when the conversation was taking place, this was what was assumed to be a private conversation between very close friends. These were not the words, messaging or otherwise as arising from the Landlords. The words stated were exaggerations, I accept that they were not meant to be threatening nor taken in a literal sense. In fact, I accept that Tatiana and Christian had good intentions in respect of the Tenant, and that the words stated were coming from a place of concern. 56. However, as there was tension in the residential complex and there was a shift in the relationship, and the relationship had been amended the perception of a nonexistent threat became a focus. And had the parties been in a positive phase of the relationships such conversation may have been shrugged off as a non-event. I say this as while the Tenant said this conversation felt different, the parties testified to having had similar conversations in the past, similar in that they were sharing guidance and advice about a variety of life issues inclusive of employment, health and habits to promote well being. 57. Further, based on the fact the family was being reported to the police, it is not surprising that the tone in the complex shifted, that is, Christina, Tatiana and the Tenant were no longer fiends. In a recording of October 14, 2022, (SA) the Landlord is heard saying “I thought you were moving out, I want you to leave.” This was in response to the Tenant having made suggestions of moving out prior. The Tenant provided the Landlords an N11 dated November 4, 2022 terminating the tenancy on December 31, 2022 when earlier attempts to terminate the tenancy were refused. And he testified that while not having resided in the unit for the last two months, he continued to pay the Landlords rent. 58. While the Landlord (SA) may not have taken the best approach here in that he was leaving the conflict to be resolved among his children, inclusive of his Tenant, Mr. [name]name], as much as he referred to the Landlord (SA) as his dad, I believe that up to the point of the police involvement that (SA) considered the Tenant as an extension of his own family. The non-involvement in what (SA) considered personal affairs/ issues between friends and his reluctance to become involved was not unusual. He was heard stating to the Tenant that he does not get involved in his son’s and daughter’s affairs. It appears that given the circumstances, this was the case with the Tenant. It is clear that the lines between family and any contractual and tenancy related responsibilities had been crossed. 59. Furthermore, I believe the testimony of (SA) that he was not entirely clear as to the severity of the impact upon the Tenant in respect of the interaction between the parties on August 11, 2022. I believe he was blindsided about the police involvement given the situation and having heard that the report rendered the matter as non-criminal and that [name] his son was not a threat to the Tenant, there was nothing more to be done. There was no actual threat uttered by “Berto” and there was no evidence so suggest he even knew what was being said about him in the conversion that took place, the root of all issues that followed. 60. Despite the Tenant staying away from the rental property and incurring costs while doing so, this was a unilateral decision that he undertook. Having been provided a police report indicating that the matter is closed and having assurances from the alleged individual “Berto” stating that despite never having threatened him, he would stay away, this should have been enough to put an end to what was a conversation taken out of context. I am satisfied, based on the evidence and testimony of the parties that there was no real threat to the Tenant at any point during his tenancy and that more likely than not that the reason he decided to move out was because of the demise and end of the relationship between the parities. A relationship that was deeply involved and extended to the Landlords’ and their families. Hearing the circumstances under which the parties parted their ways was undoubtedly difficult for all. 61. For the reasons as outlined, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. 62. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application  collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $11,668.00. Bad Faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Section 57(5) of the Act provides: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. [Emphasis added]

The uncontested evidence of the Tenants is that the Landlord issued an N12 notice which caused the Tenants to vacate the rental unit, after which the rental unit was listed for sale within weeks and sold within two months. Accordingly, the Landlord is presumed to have given the N12 notice in bad faith. Money retained illegally

The Landlord was required to pay the Tenant s compensation equivalent to one month’s rent when they issued the N12 notice. This was initially done by giving each of the tenants a cheque for an equal share of the compensation ($500 each). Two of the tenants ([name] and [name]) were able to cash their cheques, however when the remaining tenants attempted to do so, they were notified that the cheques had been retracted and were unable to deposit them. As a result, the Landlord has not paid the required compensation in full. The balance outstanding is $2,500.00 (5 x $500) Remedies
The Tenants agree that the to tal remedies awarded will be paid as one total payment and divided amongst them as they see fit.

The monthly rent for th e rental unit was $3,500.00 and was shared equally by the 7 tenants. After the N12 notice was issued, 4 of the 7 tenants ([name], [name], [name], and Catherin) moved into a new unit together with a monthly rent of $3,895.00, while the other 3 made alternate arrangements. The 4 that moved together are claiming compensation for increased rent. Both units are detached houses with yards and 2-car driveways. The new unit is slightly larger overall, but has fewer bedrooms, 1 kitchen instead of 2, and is further away from the Tenants’ school and work, making it overall less functional for the Tenants. Because it has fewer bedrooms, it accommodates fewer people and their per person rental costs have increased significantly. Based on this comparison, it is reasonable to compensate the Tenants for increased rent.

Therefore, I find that t he Landlord must pay the Tenants $4,740.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. ($395 x 12)

One of the Tenants, [name], testified to moving and storage expenses incurred as a result of the N12 notice. They moved home and had to put their belongings in storage at a monthly cost of $350.00 and spent $180.00 on a UHaul truck to move. While no receipts were submitted, these amounts are within the range of similar expenses which come before the Board frequently, so I am satisfied that they are reasonable. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $4,380.00 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $2,500.00 for the balance of the required N12 compensation.
ordered: The total amount the [name] ord shall pay the Tenants is $11,668.00. This amount represents:  $4,740.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025.  $4,380.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.  $2,500.00 for the balance of the required N12 compensation  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants t he full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Findings of Fact:

On consent the parties agreed to the following facts: a) The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination for “landlord’s own use” under s. 48 of the Act with a termination date of January 31, 2024; b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving that N12 notice on June 14, 2024; c) The property was listed for sale April 1, 2025; and d) The closing of the property was set for July 8, 2025 e) Renovations were completed within the rental unit. The Landlord gave the N12 Notice for own use in [name]:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

As the parties agreed that the Landlord had listed the rental unit for sale within 12- months after the Tenant vacated, 57(5)(c) of the Act applies and it is presumed that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith unless they rebut the presumption by proving on a balance of probabilities that they gave the notice in good faith. Landlord’s evidence [name] testimony

The Landlord testified that the N12 notice was provided to the Tenant as their family was going through a crisis, and her spouse along with their son were mentally unstable and going through extreme stress. At which point, police were called, and they were hospitalized. The decision was made for her spouse and their son to move into the rental unit permanently as this caused issues within their marriage resulting in a breakdown.

The Landlord testified that due to a police incident in the fall of 2023, her spouse could not reside at the property and due to the Tenant not vacating until June 14, 2024, her spouse was living with family and friends between the time the N12 was given and when the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that her spouse moved into the rental until July 1, 2024, and provided his driver’s license as evidence to support this. In addition, the Landlord provided further documentation evidence such as, the gas bills, property insurance, and photos taken while her spouse was living within the rental unit.

It is not disputed that [name] did renovations throughout the entire rental unit. The Landlord testified that the purpose of the renovations was for personal use, and not to upgrade and sell the home at the time the renovations were being completed.

The Landlord testified that it was not until March 2025, when their financials changed as [name] received a notice that he was permanently disabled and was not able to return to work which effected his income and his finances. The Landlord provided documentation evidence to support their financial struggles and the debt they were in.

The Landlord further testified that there was an attempt to reconcile their marriage after this, and they attempted to reconcile their marriage up to July 2024, and they realized that if they were going to reconcile, they did not need 2 residences. Their kids wanted to stay in their family home as they have resided there since 2009, and with [name]’s lower income due to disability, they sold the rental property as they could not afford both places.

The Landlord testified that when the N12 was given, it was their intent for [name] to move into the rental property and live there permanently and she was to remain in the family home with the kids and her parents would help out financially.

The Landlord testified that it wasn’t until July 2025 when [name] moved back into the matrimonial home, and that she now resides with her parents in their basement. [name] testimony 13. [name] testified that he moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2024, and that he did reside at the rental unit for a period of 12 months. 14. [name] testified that he did not have internet at the rental property and used his cell phone for internet usage so there was no proof to be provided by an internet provider, and that he did not change his address on everything as he still maintained joint ownership of the matrimonial home with [name], and they had joint debts and accounts, so he did not update his address, but he did change his address with the CRA and some of his banking, but could not confirm the date when these changes were made. 15. [name] testified that he did do renovations at the rental property, but it was for personal use and not to upgrade and sell the home. [name] testimony 16. [name] testified that she was aware that [name] moved out of the matrimonial home in July 2024 as she is neighbours with the Landlord. [name] testified that she attended the Landlord’s home to provide support to [name] while they were going through their separation, and she did not see [name] very often other than to visit the children from July 2024 to July 2025, when [name] moved back into the matrimonial home. Tenant’s evidence [name] [name] testimony 17. The Tenant testified that the entire home was renovated for the purpose of the Landlord to sell the property. 18. The Tenant testified that the Landlord attempted to sell her the rental property in 2002, but she was unable to obtain a mortgage which resulted in her not being able to buy the property, so she takes the position that the notice was given in bad faith. 19. The Tenant testified that she drove by the rental property all the time and there was never a vehicle in the driveway, and the lights were never on, in addition to the grass not being cut. The Tenant testified there were no signs of anyone residing in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided her a previous N12 notice that the Landlord’s spouse would be moving into the rental unit, but it was dismissed. 20. I have reviewed LTB-L-094368-23 order dated May 2, 2024, where an order was issued from the Board on a L2 application, pertaining to the N12 notice given to the Tenant, which the Board found the Landlord required the rental unit, and terminated the tenancy on June 30, 2024. There have been quite a few matters before the Board pertaining to these parties, and there are no orders from the Board dismissing the Landlord’s application for a N12 notice given. 21. Through the Tenant’s own documentation evidence, there is a letter dated November 20, 2023, from the Landlord’s legal representative, that explains that since the previous N12 notice was defective and it could not move forward and as such a new N12 notice was issued to the Tenant for the same reason. The new N12 notice is the notice that is the subject of the current application. 22. The Tenant testified there is a neighbour who can confirm that the grass was not cut and the lights were kept off, and that she spoke with the neighbour to confirm no one was there. This neighbour did not attend the hearing to provide any testimony. The Tenant further testified that she took photos but did not upload them, and that she did not have dates or times as to when she was driving by nor did she confirm that [name] was not living there. 23. Based on the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in good faith and her spouse resided at the rental property for 12 months beginning shortly after the Tenant vacated, and it was due to change in their financial circumstances that the property had to be sold, but it was not until after her spouse resided at the property for 12 months. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that her spouse moved into the rental unit and continued to live there until July 2025. The Tenant testified there was documentation and evidence within her possession but failed to upload them, nor serve them on the Landlord, and in addition the Tenant did not have any specifics about the dates and times she drove by the rental property. As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 in good faith. 24. As the Tenants did not establish the bad faith of the Landlord in serving the N12 notice, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Rowe (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that 189 Vaughan Inc. (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The original order, LTB-T-049815-22, issued on May 29, 2024, was dismissed because the Tenant did not participate in the hearing. LTB-T-049815-22-RV-IN2, issued May 7, 2025, cancelled the original order because it was determined that the Tenant was not reasonably able to participate at the previous hearing. As a result, a de novo hearing was ordered. The de novo hearing was heard by videoconference before me on November 13, 2025, January 16, 2026, and March 27, 2026. [name], [name], the Tenant, [name], the Landlord’s Representative, [name], and the Landlord’s Agent, [name] attended the hearings At the start of the first hearing, the parties consented to the amending of the application to change the name of the “landlord” from “[name]”, to “189 Vaughan Inc.” Since both sides are in agreement, I am satisfied that it would be fair to grant this amendment.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must allow the Tenant to pay rent by e- transfer starting July 1, 2026, and pay the Tenant $1,000.00 in compensatory damage. The Landlord is required to provide an email account to the Tenant on or before June 24, 2026, for the Tenant to make their e-transfer payment of their rent.

The Tenant has suffered a brain injury. As a result, she has several cognitive impairments. The Tenant is seeking, as an accommodation to her brain injury, to pay her rent via e- transfer, a method of payment in which the Tenant manually makes a payment online from her bank account and sends the payment via email to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that they were permitted to use e-transfer payments to the former landlord prior to the current Landlord’s purchase of the property, however, no written lease was provided that would show that this was an accepted form of payment.

The current Landlord has refused this form of payment and has provided the Tenant several other methods of payment: using the online portal system, set up for preauthorized payments, mail cheques to the Landlord, and pay in person at a local bank to the Landlord’s account.

It was not disputed that the Landlord used to allow the Tenant to drop cheques off in a mailbox at the building office. It is also not disputed that the Landlord discontinued this method of payment as of September 1, 2022. The Tenant regularly utilized this service until its discontinuance.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord wanted the Tenant to utilize the online portal system set up to manage all of tenant accounts within the Landlord’s portfolio. The Tenant testified that she was unable to utilize this method, in part due to cognitive function required to utilize the system was impaired due to the brain injury. Trying to use the online portal made her feel overwhelmed and confused. Secondly, utilizing the system required the Tenant to have payments ready to be withdrawn automatically on the 1st of every month. Due to the Tenant’s brain injury, the ability to remember dates and deadlines was affected to the point where she would be at risk of missing payments by not having the money in the account right on the 1st of the month. Besides the NSF charges and stigma of having defaulted on a payment, the stress of the consequences of the NSF charges and late payment created additional anxiety for the Tenant to such a degree that it was debilitating.

The Tenant stated that although they have been paying rent in person at the bank, the journey to the bank can be arduous at times and aggravates other injuries. The process, even at the best of times is time consuming.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was not very sympathetic to her circumstances, having told the Tenant, “Normal people can use the portal…” However, it should be noted that this statement was not corroborated or supported by any additional testimony or documentation.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (AZ), testified that they have extended the Tenant grace periods of 7 to 10 days to pay rent via the banking system or by mailing a cheque. The Landlord has also provided the following options: a) Auto pay, which is a form of preauthorized payment b) Manual payment, which would be a push-payment option through their portal software that would allow the Tenant to actively pay the rent through their digital portal system c) Mailing post-dated cheques: in which the Landlord also suggested the Tenant establish a notification system to remind her of rent payments coming due. d) Paying to the Landlord’s account directly at the bank.

The Landlord testified that since they utilize specific bank accounts for specific aspects of their portfolio, their accounting system does not allow for a party to make E-Transfer payments or wire transfers.

When asked if the Landlord investigated creating an option for a tenant to do so, AZ admitted that they had no evidence that they had discussed with their banking or accounting services the acceptance of E-Transfers or wire transfers. Analysis
The question before me is whether the Landlord sufficiently accommodated the Tenant’s disability.
Based on all of the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant has a disability that requires accommodation.

Pursuant to section 17(2) of the Ontario Human Rights Code (the ‘Code”) the duty to accommodate a disability requires that the person be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and safety requirements, if any.

The Tenant’s application claims that the Landlord breached section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by failing to accommodate the Tenant’s disability and as a result, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s right to enjoy the premises. By extension, by making comments regarding the Tenant’s disability, and by failing to accommodate the [name] needs, they breached section 23 of the Act by harassing the Tenant.

The Landlord made several concessions to the Tenant that they did not have to do: they are not bound to extend the due date to pay rent as this would be a contravention of the tenancy agreement, and a remedy is provided for in the Act for the Landlord to pursue eviction pursuant to section 58(1) paragraph 1 of the Act. However, the Landlord did make this offer to waive this right to a degree of an additional 10 days. This shows a willingness to accommodate.

The Landlord also looked into the Tenant’s difficulty in managing deadlines by offering to use a “push-payment” through their portal system which would allow the Tenant to control when a payment is made to the Landlord, eliminating the risk of incurring NSF fees.

However, the issue here is that the Tenant asked to be accommodated by allowing the Tenant to make rent payments to the Landlord via e-transfer. The Landlord did not provide any evidence that they had made any meaningful inquiry to their financial service providers in to making an exception to allow the Tenant to pay via e-transfer.

Although the Landlord had provided several ways to accommodate the Tenant, they are dictating to the Tenant how they will be accommodated and not making a serious consideration of the Tenant’s accommodation request.

Commerce means the taking in of money for the purpose of providing a service. I am not satisfied that the Landlord requires those funds to be transferred in a specific way or would not be permitted to accept a form of payment that is understood to be certified funds. If the system is not currently geared to accept this form of electronic payment, some form of evidence should have been presented to show the Board why they could not accept these funds as an e-transfer; either specific documentation or having a bank/financial service representative attend the hearing to explain why the Landlord is unable to accept an e- transfer.

For this reason, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to accommodate the Tenant. I am satisfied that failing to accommodate the Tenant has caused the Tenant both mental and physical anguish which would substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord has breached section 22 of the Act.

However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has met the burden require to prove that the Landlord harassed the Tenant. Harassment, as defined by the Code, is the engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct or conduct that is known or ought to be known to be unwelcome. I am not satisfied, based on the Tenant’s submissions, that the Landlord harassed the Tenant. The one incident testified to in the hearing (“normal people can use the portal”) was unsubstantiated, and even if this did happen once, could not be considered a “course of conduct”. Furthermore, the Landlord appears to have been well- meaning in their attempt to accommodate the Tenant, however, were blind to the fact that they had a duty as well to seriously consider the Tenant’s request. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking the ability to pay rent by e-transfer. Pursuant to section 31(1)(f) of the Act, the Board may make any other order that it considers appropriate. In this circumstance, the Landlord has not provided sufficient reason why they cannot accept an e-transfer. Financial institutions exist to take in money. Businesses survive by taking in money. I cannot think of one reason why the Landlord could not work with their accounting firm and set up an email account for the Tenant to e-transfer rent payments.

The Landlord is ordered to set up an email account in which the Tenant may make e- transfer payments to starting July 1, 2026. If the Landlord fails to do so, the Tenant will be allowed to withhold rent until the Landlord acts in accordance with this order. This does not mean that the Tenant is absolved of paying rent; once the method of e-transfer is established, the Tenant is liable for any rent owed.

It should also be noted that the Landlord is not being ordered to allow an additional buffer for when the rent is paid. The lease agreement states that rent is due on the 1st of the month, and the Landlord has a right to the rent as of the date rent is due.

The Tenant is seeking $1,963.20 in out-of-pocket expenses incurred because of the actions of the Landlord. The Tenant, in their application, states that the amount encompasses the cost of new medications required for sleep and the need to see an additional specialist. The Tenant did not bring forward sufficient evidence to satisfy me that they had incurred these out-of-pocket expenses. No receipts or evidence of payment were presented during the hearing.

The Tenant is seeking $7,500.00 in general damages. Although the term “general damages” is more consistent with a hearing in a civil court rather than an administrative tribunal, it should be noted that [name], [2007] OJ No. 437 (‘[name]”), confirms that section 31(1)(f) of the Act may also be interpreted as a means to award compensatory damages to a tenant for pain and suffering.

Based on the Tenant’s submissions, I am satisfied that the Tenant experienced pain and suffering that resulted from the Landlord’s failure to accommodate the Tenant. It is not that the Landlord did not try to accommodate to a certain degree, however, the Landlord took advantage of the balance of power in the landlord/tenant relationship to dictate terms without making a fulsome consideration of what the Tenant was requesting. In essence, the Tenant was never supplied with a sufficient explanation as to why they could not accept an e-transfer other than what one could perceive as “because I said so”. The Tenant stated that they could not use the portal system. Recommending that the Tenant use the portal system that the Tenant has stated that she was unable to use due to brain injury would knowingly cause frustration. The Tenant’s brain injury magnifies these emotions, as was apparent throughout the Tenant’s testimony.

However, it is noted that the Landlord was willing to work with the Tenant over this period of time, and although their method and philosophy throughout the negotiation may have had its faults, it was still an attempt to resolve the problem.

In acknowledgement of the pain incurred by the Tenant as a result, but also the mitigating factors from the Landlord’s attempt to resolve the issue, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to $1,000.00 for pain and suffering.
The Tenant is seeking an administrative fine of $10,000.00 to be paid to the LTB by the Landlord.

An administrative fine is issued as a deterrent to future breaches of the Act, especially if the remedy awarded to a tenant is not a sufficient deterrent on its own. I am not satisfied that an administrative fine is reasonable under the circumstances as the order should be sufficient to act as a deterrence to any future breaches of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,000.00. This amount represents compensatory damages for the pain and suffering of the Tenant as a result of the Landlord’s breach of the Act.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,000.00 from the rent due for July 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

By June 24, 2026, the Landlord is to provide the Tenant an email account in which the Tenant may make an e-transfer payment to for rent that comes due starting July 1, 2026. If the Landlord fails to provide an email address, the Tenant may withhold rent until an email account is provided to the Tenant. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
