issues: [name] under Sections 30, 31 and 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: B, 758 [address] THUNDER BAY ON Between: [name] Tenant And [name] [name] and [name]Landlords This amended order is issued to correct clerical errors in respect paragraphs 41 and 66 of the
reasons: The claim here is whether the overpayment of rent of $27.50 per month for the months of February 2024 and March 2024 should be returned to the Tenant.

The facts the parties were able to agree on were: a) The parties entered into a lease that was signed May 18, 2019 (Exhibit TT#1- signed lease). I note the signed lease was not in the Ontario standard from lease that became mandatory in April 2018, but it clearly stipulated that the Tenant was to pay $1,075.00 in monthly rent for the right to occupy the unit. The Tenant was required to pay for utilities separately, which were identified as his responsibility to pay. b) The Landlords served a Notice of Rent Increase (NORI) which set out that on April 1, 2024, the monthly rent would increase by $27.50 to $1,128.50 (exhibit LL#1- Jan 1/24 dated NORI and a copy of Feb 1/24 letter to the Tenant about overpayment and utilities owing). c) The Tenant paid the new rent of $1,128.50 in error for February and March 2024. This represented a total of $55.00 in overpayment for those two months. d) The Landlords sent a March 1, 2024 dated letter to the Tenant (exhibit LL#2) stating he paid the wrong rent again for March 2024 and set out again that the new increased rent would take effect on April 1, 2024. e) In both the February 1, 2024 and March 1, 2024 letters, the Landlords informed the Tenant they would apply his $27.50 overpayment against the utilities owing. At this hearing, the Landlords affirmed that it was the water bills specifically that the rent overpayments (totalling $55.00) were applied to. f) For completeness of record, the current monthly rent is $1,181.00.

This is a very simple clear case of the Landlords incorrectly transferring an overpayment of rent to some other tenancy cost that was not rent per se. The tenancy agreement (TT#1) clearly sets out monthly rent to allow occupancy by the Tenant, and it sets out utilities as something separate.

“Rent” is a defined term in section 2 of the Act. Based on that definition, the amount paid for the utilities under this tenancy is not rent. [name] simply, the Landlord may not take rent money paid and decide unilaterally to use that money and credit some other tenancy cost category. It was clear the Tenant never consented or agreed to having that overpayment accounted for elsewhere.
Consequently, the total rent overpayment of $55.00 in question here is to be returned to the Tenant.

I note that the parties were before Vice-chair [name] for an L1/L2-N5 application, case file no. LTB-L-065373-23. The hearing for that case was held on October 6, 2025 with an LTB order being issued on December 17, 2025.

In that order which I read post-hearing, the Tenant was ordered to pay the Landlords $1,215.48 in past-due water bills (utilities). That amount payable reflected to the penny the water bill information submitted by the Landlords; their statement of account was disclosed to the LTB on September 18, 2025 (TOP doc# 6423911). I reviewed that disclosure and found the rent overpayments of $27.50 in February 2024 and March 2024 were never applied to the statement of account in that disclosure.

Even if it had been applied, I still would have determined the unilateral transfer by the Landlords, to take $55.00 in rent overpayment and transfer it to a water bill account, as incorrect and unlawful. But as it turned out, the Landlords never applied the overpayment as they said they would do in LL#1 and LL#2, and which they had testified before me as having been done under this T1 claim. [name]

From the Interim Order, the T2 claims are: • Illegal entries on March 5, 2025 and March 6, 2025. • Harassment involving the Landlord repeatedly knocking on the Tenant’s door demanding the Tenant move and yelling at the Tenant in front of children. • Harassment involving the Landlord obstructing the plumber’s ability to make repairs on March 28, 2024. • Substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by applying portions of his rent payments towards unpaid water bills, failing to remove the washer and dryer, failing to provide snow removal service, and requiring the Tenant to pay the water tank rental.

Entries:- With regard to the Landlords’ entries on March 5 and 6, 2025, it was not disputed that MDL entered the rental unit on both those dates without any prior notice. I noted that the parties sometimes referenced March 4 and 5, 2025 concerning these two entry dates, but I used the “default” dates of March 5 and 6, 2025 as the two entry dates, which came from the Interim Order.

The Tenant testified that on March 5 and 6, 2025, his camera system showed MDL entered his unit on both dates and that he had no prior notice for the entries. As he affirmed he never consented to the Landlords entering, he stated these were unauthorized entries.

MDL testified that his reason for entering without notice was there had been a flood of water from a water tank leak in the upstairs unit of the fourplex (not the rental unit), but the water shut-off valve for the building is located in the rental unit. MDL state5d that because it was an emergency situation, he had to access the water shut-off valve without notice being given. He stated the repair work on March 5, 2025 could not be completed and so he had to return the next day to shut off the water again for the repairs upstairs to be continued and completed.

The parties did not provide me with any written communication between them or any other evidence that dealt with these two entry dates. The best evidence given me on what happened these two dates came from the direct testimony of MDL.

On a balance of probabilities, I accept MDL’s statement that an emergency situation stemming from a large water leak in an upstairs unit required the Landlords to shut-off water to the building. As a result, I do not find the March 5, 2025 entry (first entry) to be unlawful.

However, the second entry on March 6, 2025, in my view, was not an emergency but a follow-up repair visit to complete repairs from the day before. It was not established that the second entry was likely due to an emergency. I view that on the first day of repair, the Landlords were able to stop the leaking and at least stabilize the situation so that the water tank was stopped from leaking further. As a result, the Landlords should have been able to notify the Tenant that they would return the next day (on March 6, 2025) to access the shut-off valve or whatever else in the rental unit so as to complete repairs upstairs. Even a short text message or equivalent, had it been proffered, would have helped to understand what had happened during the two days of entry.
Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities, the Landlords entered the rental unit on March 6, 2025 without prior, lawful notice as set out in section 27 of the Act..

Substantial interference/harassment:- The Tenant stated that there was a pattern of harassment which has left his two children “terrified” of the Landlord MDL The Tenant testified about how the Landlords treated him or acted towards him over a number of tenancy issues such as a plumbing issue, a bathroom electrical issue and washing machine leak issue all in March 2024. He stated that MDL simply laughed at the idea the Tenant’s children were afraid of MDL, and that MDL made it clear the maintenance issues were the Tenant’s responsibility to repair.

Further, when the water bills became due every couple of months, the Tenant testified the Landlords knocked on his door, leading to insulting and rude demands about the money owing on the bills. The Tenant stated the Landlords would pass by the rental unit regularly which was done in his view to intimidate him. He recounted that once, MDL followed him when he went to the Giant Tiger store and started to yell at him in that public forum. He was told over and over that if he was not happy, he could leave the unit. The Tenant made mention of an alleged door-pushing assault that took place in July 2023 (MDL wanted to enter and the Tenant pushed back to disallow MDL’s entry).

The Tenant explained that due to his physical disability (he stated from a compression fracture to his L1 vertebra), he is unable to exert on or lift heavy things. He testified that at times, he has had to hire someone to clean snow at $60 per hour.

The Tenant stated that the Landlords have substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment by purposely digging up and removing his front-area garden in July 2025 (exhibit TT#4-statement and photo) and by not cutting grass around his cabana in the backyard. The Tenant indicated he had planted the garden in 2019 and believed the garden was his designated area. It was clear from the Tenant’s testimony, he was particularly fond of his Japanese lily garden and claimed MDL simply removed it to badger him.

During cross-examination, the Tenant admitted he did not provide dates and times of when his claims of harassment and substantial interference occurred so that the Landlords would have had a chance to prepare documented evidence for this hearing. The Tenant also acknowledged he did not submit any evidence related to costs incurred, and in particular the cost of $350.00 which he is seeking to recover for the Japanese lily plant.
When asked about his children, the Tenant stated he has “week on, week off” privileges with his children so that they may have seen the Landlords about once or twice a month.

Both Landlords testified they have never met or spoken with the Tenant’s children. Replying to a cross-examination question, the Landlords stated they never asked the Tenant’s children about water bills.

The Landlords explained they live about 2 or 3 minutes away from the rental unit building, so it is not irregular or uncommon that they pass by the building daily. As well, they stated that up to 2024 when the parties began communicating only by email or notes, they did knock on the Tenant’s door every month or two about water bills that had become due for payment. They testified that while their attendance at the door did not routinely result in the Tenant paying his water bills, they did not insult or abuse the Tenant verbally during those encounters. They said they did not enter the unit but spoke with the Tenant at the door about bill payments. For the past two years, the Landlords stated they have consistently posted on the Tenant’s front door all tenancy notices and requests for bill payments.

MDL testified he did recall the police being called about the alleged door-pushing incident, but he denied the police reprimanded him for any action or told him there had been any assault. As far as he could recall, the police came and went away without any ado.

With regard to snow clearing, MDL stated he has been taking care of snow clearing all along and LLR referenced there were invoices (paid to a third party) in disclosure that could be adduced if needed.

MDL testified he has cut the grass all along and confirmed that he has not cut the grass immediately inside the Tenant’s cabana located in the backyard. The stated reason was because he did not want to somehow be accused of damaging the structure. [name] is an August 2025 photo of the cabana and small area of uncut grass. MDL mentioned as well that in July 2025, he notified the Tenant in writing that the cabana should be taken down, but the structure still remains in place.

Finally, MDL confirmed he did remove the Tenant’s plants at the front of the building in July 2025. MDL was aware of these plants being planted and maintained by the Tenant but he denied that the Tenant was given that area as some sort of designated area under the lease/tenancy agreement. MDL stated that in the fourplex building, none of the tenants has any designated area. MDL explained the plants had overgrown, no annuals had been planted and the area had become infested with ants. He made a decision to clean out the unsightly area and plant something that made the front of the building look fresh and simple. In support of his testimony, MDL identified exhibit LL#5 which are “before” and “after” photos of the front-garden.

From the parties’ respective submissions, it was clear to me that the parties do not get along, and I was led to understand that since about early 2024, they have communicated very little and when they have, it has been done through the written word.

That being said, I do not believe that the list of claims raised by the Tenant point collectively to a planned or an intentional regime of harassment or substantial interference. Lack of particulars, and more so a lack of evidence, has led me to this conclusion on a balance of probabilities. Much of the Tenant’s claims for a pattern of harassment were denied/rebutted successfully by the Landlords in their viva voce submissions.

As well, I am of the view that in any tenancy, a landlord must retain the lawful right to pursue, for example, unpaid rents, unpaid utilities and repairs for damages clearly caused by a tenant. Such pursuit requires interaction between parties, and most often a tenant who is on the receiving end of such pursuit may not find the interactions welcomed or positive. In this case, the interactions I was given to consider between the parties appeared to be more of the Landlords lawfully seeking to collect water bill arrears than some pattern of harassment or substantial interference.

My finding is consistent with case law authority that relates to two parties who offer conflicting testimonies -- which is often referred to as a “he said, she said” case. As stated by [name], J. in a well-known criminal case before the Supreme Court of Canada, R. v. W.(D.), 1991 CanLII 93 (SCC), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742, “one must determine if, having considered the evidence as a whole, the burden of proof has been met by the party with that burden”. Here, it is evident to me the Tenant did not meet that burden whereas the Landlords’ reply testimony was more compelling.

However, when I consider two specific claims separately, the evidence was sufficient for a finding of harassment and substantial interference by the Landlords. Specifically, I find the Landlord’s actions of digging up the front garden (LL#5) that the Tenant had tended to since 2019 and of the omission of grass-cutting under the cabana (LL#6) as instances of harassment, but moreso of substantial interference.

The Landlords knew the Tenant had tended to a garden at the front for years and without any notice or any reason given to the Tenant, the Landlords simply removed the Tenant’s plantings. I accept the Landlords’ position that no one in the building has any designated area for themselves, but knowing the Tenant had tended that garden for years created an implicit understanding the Tenant had some vested interest in that garden. As well, no evidence was adduced by the Landlords to show there was an ant problem or any other adverse situation that would qualify the garden’s removal.

Further, I was not persuaded at all by the Landlords’ reason for not cutting grass under the cabana; the reasoning given to me to consider was rather paltry and glib. In my view, there was and is ample room under the open cabana to cut grass without difficulty or obstruction.

I note these two instances happened in July and August 2025, just as the parties were preparing for a review hearing of an earlier LTB order on this T2 and the Landlords’ L1/L2 applications. These actions took place when the parties were at an impasse on landlord and tenant issues in the tenancy at bar, their relationship was not good at all, and I believe it more likely the Landlords’ actions of digging up the garden and not cutting of the grass under the cabana were meant to make a point with the Tenant. In my view, these were not correct ways to make a point; in fact, I believe a reasonable person would see these actions as targeted, hurtful actions.

The other claims, also separately considered and relating to water bill collection (insults, abuse claim), harassing/scaring the Tenant’s children, snow clearing, and door-pushing assault are all denied. The reason for their denial is the same as given above for the collective pattern claim – lack of particulars, lack of evidence – and I found the Landlords’ submissions more persuasive. 38. [name] The amended T2 contains requests for non-monetary and monetary remedies. In respect of the non-monetary request, I am satisfied to order the Landlords stop entering the rental unit without proper notice. 39. As for monetary remedies, the Tenant requested an abatement of rent, a fine to the LTB and a number of other monetary remedies related to, inter alia, possible moving costs. These latter other remedies are not applicable here as the tenancy continues to be an active one. 40. The Tenant also sought to be reimbursed the cost of the Japanese lily planting, but as he did not provide any evidence to establish the cost he paid or incurred for that planting, that requested amount is not ordered below. 41. For the findings of illegal entry (March 6, 2025, second entry) and of harassment/substantial interference, I find that 15% of one month’s rent (i.e. $1,128.50 rent in March 2025 x 15% = $169.28) is reasonable tor the illegal entry and 50% of two months of rent (for July 2025 and August 2025) is adequate to address the targeted, hurtful nature of the Landlords’ harassing and substantial interfering actions. For the two months, therefore, the abatement to be ordered is $1,128.50. 42. With regard to the requested fine (ref: LTB Interpretation Guideline no. 16), I was not persuaded to any degree that the Landlords have or had a blatant disregard for the Act. Further, I believe the abatements of rent set out above will provide adequate deterrence and future Act compliance by the Landlords. T6 Application 43. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. This is the approach that I have taken for this T6 merits hearing. 44. From the Interim Order, the T6 claims are: • Washing machine - broken valve on the tap resulting in water leaks. Reported to the Landlord on March 11, 2024. Tenant had the issue repaired on April 5, 2024. • Bathroom electricity – issue with the power. Reported to the Landlord on March 11, 2024. Tenant had the issue repaired on March 28, 2024. • Toilet - leaks from the tank. Issue began February 2024 and reported to the Landlord on March 11, 2024. The issue is ongoing. • Door to the backyard storage broken. Repaired by Landlord sometime in 2025. • Front garden removed in 2025. [name] stopped cutting the Tenant’s grass in the summer of 2025. 45. At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed the backyard storage claim was resolved fully and no longer a claim under the T6. 46. I believe the front garden/removal and cabana/grass issues fall squarely into the tenant- right claims of the T2 application, which were heard fully during that part of this hearing. I do not view these two claims as maintenance issues per se. The front garden that had been tended to by the Tenant was removed in July 2025 and replaced by the Landlords’ own plantings – it was evident the Landlords have been maintaining that garden satisfactorily ever since. The back yard grass has been cut and continues to be cut by the Landlords, with the exception of a small rectangular patch of grass situated “inside” the [name]. The backyard grass, for all intents and purposes, has been nicely maintained by the Landlords except when in August 2025, the Landlords were shown to have stopped cutting that small section of grass. This is not a maintenance issue in my view, but a tenant-rights issue which has been disposed of by me in the T2 above. 47. The parties both agreed that on March 11, 2024, the Tenant notified the Landlords about three maintenance issues: the washing machine (leak), the bathroom light switch (not working, flickering) and the leaking toilet (leak). Exbibit TT#2 is a copy of the notice-letter dated March 11, 2024. In that letter, the Tenant “gave” the Landlords thirty days to make repairs or else the Tenant would arrange for the repairs and deduct the cost or repairs from upcoming rents. 48. The Tenant testified the Landlord basically refused to make repairs, stating those repairs were the Tenant’s responsibility. He acknowledged having received the Landlords’ March 17, 2024 letter of reply (exhibit LL#3) which told him there had been a February 9, 2024 inspection by a licenced plumber (accompanied by MDL). The Landlords’ letter stated the plumber found no leaks in the “water closet” inspection. 49. The Tenant stated apart from the March 17, 2024 letter, the Landlords in effect denied there was anything wrong with the plumbing or the on/off light switch, and they did nothing else. He then decided to arrange for the repairs himself. 50. The Tenant stated he hired a plumber who attended the washing machine leak on April 5, 2024 and repaired a “leaking seal” at the faucet. The Tenant led exhibit TT#3, which is an invoice for $178.77 by Thermal Mechanical Systems Inc., and which the Tenant affirmed he paid. 51. For the bathroom light switch issue, the Tenant stated he hired an electrician who attended the unit on March 28, 2024. The electrician replaced the faulty light switch with a new dimmer switch and charged the Tenant $288.43 for the repair. The Tenant led exhibit TT#4 into evidence (copy of the March 28, 2024 invoice) and stated he paid that invoice. 52. For the toilet leak issue, the Tenant first submitted the toilet itself sits 14 inches off the floor, which is unusually high and difficult to use. The Tenant testified that when the plumber he hired for the washing machine had a look at the toilet, the plumber told him that a new toilet was needed to be installed. After the Landlords refused to do anything, the Tenant stated he contacted a plumber last week when the toilet stopped flushing altogether. The Tenant testified he notified LLR directly on or about April 13, 2026 and was told by her that she forwarded his email to the Landlords, but that the Tenant should communicate directly with the Landlords on maintenance issues, not her. During cross- examination, the Tenant was able to identify a copy of the email exchanges between him and LLR on April 13, 2026 (led as exhibit LL#4). 53. As part of exhibit LL#4, there were photos taken on April 14, 2026 of a pill container, which the Tenant confirmed was his prescription bill box. 54. The Tenant testified that on April 14, 2026 when nothing was heard from the Landlords, he called a plumber (date not given) who attended the unit because the toilet was not flushing at all and needed immediate attention. He stated the plumber’s bill for that repair has yet to arrive. 55. For rebuttal evidence, MDL testified the Tenant never told him of any washing machine- valve issue, stating the first time he heard of the issue was on the Portal (TOP) when the Tenant provided disclosure. 56. With regard to the bathroom light switch issue, MDL acknowledged the Tenant’s notification of the problem (TT#2), but stated the Tenant ended up not waiting for the Landlords but instead, went about and upgraded the existing light switch with a dimmer switch. 57. With regard to the more recent toilet issue, MDL testified that after the Tenant’s April 13, 2026 email was forwarded to him by LLR, he entered the unit on April 14, 2026 with two plumbers. MDL confirmed in cross-examination he did not give notice for the April 14, 2026 entry since he took the Tenant’s maintenance issue to be a serious one. Nevertheless, he testified he instructed the plumbers to replace the tank (which was done) and then repair the blockage; they found the blockage in the toilet had been caused by the Tenant’s medicine/pill container that was pulled up by the plumbers (LL#4 photos). 58. Having considered the testimonies and documented evidence adduced by the parties, I find that the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act in respect of the washing machine leak and the bathroom light switch problem. As for the toilet issue, which seemed at this hearing to be more focused on the recent blockage (no- flushing possible) than the leaking tank, I do not find any breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations. My reasons follow below. 59. For the washing machine leak, MDL stated before me that he never knew of any such leak until he saw it in the LTB’s TOP. In my view, MDL’s statement contradicts the hard evidence of the March 11, 2024 letter by the Tenant (TT#2) and the Landlords’ reply letter of March 17, 2024 (LL#3). To me, TT#2 clearly identifies the washing machine leak issue and [name] responds specifically to TT#2. All considered, I do not find MDL’s testimony of no-knowledge of this maintenance issue to be credible or reliable. Most probably, the Landlords were aware of the Tenant’s complaint but simply took no action on it. This is where the breach lies. 60. Based on the evidence here, I believe the washing machine leak came from a faulty seal at the faucet, which was repaired by the Tenant’s plumber. This finding is based on a balance of probabilities… like all findings. Nothing was led into evidence that would show this to be caused by some Tenant negligent or inadvertent misuse. As a result, the responsibility for the resolution of this maintenance problem was the Landlords’ all along. 61. Whether or not the Tenant waited thirty days (as set out in his letter, TT#2) before taking matters into his own hands is of minor relevance in my view. A landlord’s reaction to address/repair a maintenance problem must be both reasonable and timely, neither of which was present here. The Tenant here “waited” 24 days (March 11 to April 5, 2024) before calling a plumber in, and I believe the Tenant was more than fair, considering the Landlords did nothing in that timeframe other than send their March 17, 2024 letter of reply. 62. For the bathroom light switch issue, there was no question the Landlords knew of the flickering/functional problem on March 11, 2024, but took no action to look into the problem. It was not wrong for the Tenant to contact an electrician to repair the light switch on March 28, 2024. This was over 2 weeks of no reasonable action by the Landlords. I find the Landlords breached their maintenance obligation because of this inaction. However, I do agree that the Tenant opted for a repair that gave him an improvement over that which was there before. Accordingly, the remedy to be awarded will be adjusted to account for this. 63. The most recent maintenance problem relating to the toilet tank and blocked toilet (which is what was focused mostly during the hearing), I find the problem has been resolved by the Landlords who were able to have a plumber attend the problem reasonably and timely. 64. T6 Remedies:- The amended T6 contains requests for non-monetary and monetary remedies. In respect of the non-monetary requests, there is no need to order repairs as all outstanding issues at the time of the amended-T6 filing have been resolved. As well, the Tenant requested no increases in rent to be permitted until the repairs were completed, and this too is no longer needed. 65. As for monetary remedies, the Tenant requested an abatement of rent, and reimbursement for the cost of repairs incurred by the Tenant because of the maintenance breaches. I note the Tenant checked off [name] (costs to repair), [name] 3 (out-of-pocket expenses) and [name] (Tenant did the repairs), but they all claim the same amount for the same set of costs to be recovered. t 66. For the findings of maintenance breaches in respect of the washing machine leak and the bathroom light switch problem, I believe that first, an abatement of 10% for the month of March 2024 (the material timeframe for the breaches) for each of the two breaches is to be ordered here. That means a total of 20% or $220.20 ($1,101.00 rent in March 2024 x 20% = $220.20) for a T6 abatement is to be ordered. 67. With regard to being reimbursed for costs incurred because the Tenant paid to repair the washing machine leak and the bathroom light switch, I am ordering below the Landlords to pay $178.77 (from exhibit TT#3-Thermal Mechanical Systems) and $265.70 (from exhibit TT#4- White Pine Electric Ltd). For the $265.70, I halved the material charges for the dimmer itself ($40.25 x 50%). I did this because the dimmer was an improvement over the on/off basic switch it replaced. Therefore, the labour cost of $215.00 is added to $20.13 for the basic on/off switch, plus 13% HST totalling $265.70.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $2,017.45. This amount represents: i. $55.00 for the illegal amount collected/retained respecting a rent overpayment (T1 application); ii. $169.28 for a rent abatement in respect of the Landlords’ illegal entry (T2 application); iii. $1,128.50 for a rent abatement in respect of harassment and substantial interference (T2 application); iv. $220.20 for a rent abatement in respect of the Landlords’ maintenance breaches (T6 application); v. $178.77 to reimburse the Tenant for plumbing costs incurred due to the maintenance breach (T6 application); and vi. $265.70 to reimburse the Tenant for electrician costs incurred due to the maintenance breach (T6 application).
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount of $2,017.45 owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent coming due on June 1, 2026 and similarly by deducting $500.00 from subsequent monthly rents up to when the full amount owing has been paid by way of this deduction.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agents'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application: The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the T6 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to the remedies identified below.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit is a three-bedroom townhome in a residential complex containing 97 rental units. T6 Application:

Section 20 of the Act states: Landlord’s responsibility to repair 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non- repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (2).

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has rejected the proposition that this provision ought to be interpreted such that a landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as soon as a maintenance issue arises. Rather, a contextual approach, including consideration of the “entirety of the factual situation”, must be applied to determine whether a landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act: Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, paras 58-60, 84-86; TST-98783-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 87665 (ON LTB).

Generally, landlords are not held liable for ma intenance issues that arise if the landlord addresses the issue of disrepair in a timely and effective manner once they become aware, or ought to have become aware, of the issue: TST-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB), para 33; LTB Interpretation Guideline #5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations.

This is the Tenant’s application, and the Tenant therefore bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53, paras 44-46.

In the T6 Application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to comply with its statutory obligation to maintain the rental unit in a state of good repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards relative to a hallway closet door, the rental unit’s furnace, two electrical outlets; and exterior fence posts. Closet Doors

The Tenant said that the first time the hallway closet door became an issue was in December 2021. She said this sliding closet door would not stay on the bottom track, and was hanging from the top rail. She said that the door was therefore free to “sway” [name] because it was not held in place by the bottom track.

The Tenant said that she informed the Landlord about this issue and requested repair on Decembre 28, 2021, and again on January 3, 2022. The Tenant said that on February 2, 2022 she was told the Landlord intended to install a bifold closet door, but that they were still awaiting approval.

The Tenant said that on February 13, 2022, the door was still not repaired, and after returning to the unit from a walk with her granddaughter, the door fell on her granddaughter’s head while she tried putting her coat in the closet.

When the Tenant informed the Landlord’s paralegal about this incident, she said the repair complaint was escalated. She said that the Landlord removed the closet door from the unit entirely, and there was no closet door until it was replaced after one or two weeks.

The Tenant said that despite the Landlord’s attempted repair, the replaced door still did not stay on the bottom track, and was still hanging from the top. She said she again complained to the Landlord’s paralegal about this issue, but the Landlord did not take any further action relative to the closet door as of the September 7, 2023 hearing date.

The Tenant said that she did not complain about the door again after this. She said that, unbeknownst to her, the Landlord’s paralegal had left the company. The Tenant said she was just waiting to hear back about the door, and did not want to be a nuisance.

The Tenant said that on August 31, 2023, an employee of the Landlord attended the unit do address a different issue, and while there, he said the Landlord would install a “box in closet door”, but that it would take a couple months.

BF acknowledged that the Tenant made maintenance requests relative to the closet door on December 28, 2021, January 3, 2022 and again in February 2022. She said that the Landlord repaired the door “several times”, but that they kept being broken. She said that these doors are “flimsy” and break easily, and that all units in the residential complex, except the remodelled units, have the same type of closet doors. She said that she has the same type of closet door in her own unit, and they come off the track frequently, and have to be repaired. She said that the Landlord’s contractor installed new closet doors in the Spring of 2022 after the repair attempts did not resolve the issue. BF said on September 7, 2023 that the Landlord is in the process of having the closet door repaired.

On cross-examination on February 26, 2024, BF acknowledged that the closet door had not been replaced, and she was not aware of the status at the time because the issue had been escalated above her role as superintendent.

The Landlord’s obligation is to ensure that the closet door is in a state of good repair. That this type of door is “flimsy” and breaks often does not excuse the Landlord from this responsibility. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the closet doors have been in disrepair since December 2021 because the door does not stay on the bottom track, and that the Landlord was first informed of the issue on December 28, 2021. Furnace

The Tenant’s evidence on September 7, 2023 was that she had lived in the unit for 8 years, so she knows what the furnace sounds like when it turns on. She said that the furnace kept turning on and off, so she made a maintenance request for the furnace on January 3, 2022. [name], who is BF’s husband and one of the superintendents, said that he would provide the Tenant with more furnace filters, but the Tenant told him that the issue is not the filter, and the furnace didn’t sound right.

The Tenant said that [name] then suggested getting the ducts cleaned, which was completed by the Landlord’s contractor on January 11, 2022, but the Tenant said this did not resolve the issue. The Tenant then called the Fire Department. No one from the Fire Department attended the unit, but the Teant believes they called the Landlord’s office, because the Landlord then sent someone to the unit to inspect the furnace. The Tenant could not recall the exact date, but said it was a week or to after the duct cleaning was completed.
BF denied that anyone from the Fire Department contacted the Landlord about this issue.

The Tenant said that the person who attended said the furnace was not “burning properly”, he completed the necessary repair, and the issue was resolved after that. The Tenant said that the furnace is operating properly, but the filters still come out “pretty black”, and that she changes the filter monthly. The Tenant said she complained to the Landlord about the issue with the filters on May 25, 2023, but the Landlord did not take any further action.
The Tenant presented as evidence a photo of one of the dirty furnace filters (DOC- 1692993). The photo shows a filter that is grey, but it is not black

BF said that the technician who attended the unit said that the filters come out they way they do because of carbon, which is normal for this type of furnace. BF said they come out grey and not black, which is consistent with the photo presented by the Tenant.
BF said that Tenants are given replacement furnace filters each year at the same time the Landlord has the smoke detectors checked.

The Tenant has not presented sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the furnace is not in a state of good repair because the filters come out grey. The technician who attended the unit to repair the furnace in January 2022 was not present at the hearing to give evidence. The Tenant’s evidence was that after the repair, the furnace functioned normally, and there was no evidence to contradict BF’s evidence that she was informed by the technician that the greyed filters are normal for this type of furnace.

The furnace was not functioning properly when the Tenant complained about it initially on January 3, 2023, but the Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlord failed to address this issue in a timely and effective manner. After having the ducts cleaned did not resolve the issue, the Landlord’s contractor attended and completed the necessary repairs. The Tenant did not present cogent evidence as to exactly when the furnace was repaired, so I cannot determine on the evidence before me that this was not completed in a timely manner after the Landlord was made aware of the issue.
The application is dismissed as it relates to the Tenant’s allegations about the furnace. Electrical Outlets

The Tenant said that when she moved into the unit there were two electrical outlets in the basement. She said she used one of the outlets for a treadmill. The Tenant said that one of these two outlets were removed by the Electrical Safety Authority (‘ESA’) in or about February or March 2022 because they were “not legal”. The Tenant does not know why the ESA attended the unit. She just received a notice that they would attend.
The Tenant said that the only remaining plug in the basement was used for a washing machine, and that she complained to BF about this, but nothing was done.

BF said the ESA insisted that the second outlet be removed, and that this was an issue in several units in the residential complex, because some tenants in the past had improperly installed additional basement outlets. BF said the outlet was removed by a licensed electrician.

While I understand that the removal of one of the electrical outlets in the basement may have been frustrating for the Tenant, I do not find that the evidence she presented establishes that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit or the residential complex in a state of good repair, fit for habitation, or in compliance with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
Although the Tenant did not know why the ESA attended, it appears more likely that the second outlet was removed in order to comply with safety standards. This is not an issue of disrepair.
The application is dismissed relative to the Tenant’s allegation about electrical outlets. Fence Posts

The Tenant said that on December 12, 2021 there was a windstorm that damaged a panel of the unit’s backyard fence. She said that she and her son spent hours repairing the fence, and that BF saw them working on it, but did not do or say anything.

The Tenant said that three of the fence posts were also broken at the ground level, and that two of these posts are the ones on either side of the gate. The Tenant said she implemented a temporary fix by installing “easy mend” to hold the posts up.

The Tenant said that she first requested that the posts be repaired on Apil 27, 2022, by making a maintenance request through the Landlord’s maintenance request app. The Tenant said there was no response until BF attended the unit in the Summer of 2022 with another person. The Tenant said that BF told her the posts would be repaired, but nothing was done after that time.

The Tenant later complained to the Landlord’s paralegal, but was told that the Landlord was not responsible to repair the fence posts because the Tenant erected the fence. The Tenant said that she hired a contractor to install the fence in 2017, but that the former landlord reimbursed her for the cost of the fence at the time.

The Tenant said that all of the townhomes in the residential complex now have fenced yards, but this was not the case when she initially moved in. She said the former landlord paid for the fence, and that at one point the Landlord painted it. She said the Landlord did not ask for her permission to paint the fence, because it belongs to the Landlord.

The Tenant presented as evidence four photos of the fence (DOC-1693015). The photos show that one fence post next to the gate is not straight, with pieces of wood propped against it, ostensibly in an attempt to hold it straight, and another post damaged near the bottom with a black brace on it.

The Landlord was not the landlord at the time the fence was constructed, but BF was the superintendent. The Tenant said that she had spoken with BF and another employee of the former landlord about the fence. BF said that she does not know if any “paperwork” was signed between the Tenant and former landlord relative to the fence, but said that the Tenant’s agreement about the fence was with another employee of the former landlord, and not BF.

BF acknowledged that the fence posts were not repaired as of September 7, 2023, but said that the Landlord had received the complaint and tried to determine whether it was responsible for the repair since the Tenant had the fence installed.

The Tenant was the only person who gave evidence who had direct knowledge of her agreement with the former landlord relative to the fence. I accept her evidence that she retained a contractor to install the fence, paid the contractor, but that the former landlord reimbursed her for the cost of the fence. The fence was the property of the former landlord, forming part of the rental unit and residential complex. When the Landlord became the landlord, the fence became the Landlord’s property. The Landlord is responsible to maintain the fence in a state of good repair.

Based on the evidence of both the Tenant and BF, the fence posts had not ben repaired as of the February 26, 2024 hearing date when the evidence on the T6 application was completed. The fence was not in a state of good repair because at least three fence posts are broken. T6 Application Remedies

The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement relative to the closet door for the period December 28, 2021 to February 26, 2024, a period of 26 months. I accept that the ongoing disrepair of the closet door is a nuisance, thought it is a relatively minor issue, requiring more careful use of the door.

The premise of a rent abatement is that if a tenant is obligated to pay 100% of the lawful rent, they are entitled to receive 100% of the value of what they pay for. A rent abatement is intended to account for the proportion of value of what is charged/paid for that the tenant did not receive as a result of the landlord’s breach of the Act. When considering this, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of 3% for 26 months relative to this issue.

In the application, the Tenant stated that her monthly rent was $852.83. There was no evidence of what, if any, rent increases were taken by the Landlord after the June 2, 2022 filing date. The Tenant is therefore entitled to a rent abatement of $665.08 [$852.83 x 3% x 26 months].

The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement relative to the fence posts for the 23-month period from April 27, 2022 to February 26, 2024. Although the fence was damaged, it was still standing, though I accept that the damaged posts would affect the operation of the gate. Considering the proportion of the value of what is charged/paid for that the tenant did not receive because of this breach of the Act, I find that a 3% rent abatement is also appropriate relative to this issue. The Tenant is therefore entitled to a rent abatement of $588.34 [$852.83 x 3% x 23 months].
The total rent abatement the Tenant is entitled to is $1,253.42 [$665.08 + $588.34].

The Tenant also sought recovery of $800.00 to compensate her for money she spent on temporarily repairing the fence. The Tenant did not present any receipts for the money spent, and her oral evidence was inconsistent with what was included in the application relative to her expenses. At the hearing she said she bought 6 braces, and believes the cost was $80.00 each, but she was only able to install 3 of the braces. In the application, the Tenant claimed to have purchased 5 braces, at a cost of $160.00 each. While I do not find that the Tenant was attempting to mislead the LTB, I do not find that her evidence about her expenses was reliable. I therefore decline to order compensation for these expenses.

As requested by the Tenant, I find that it is appropriate to order that the Landlord repair the closet door and fence so that both are in a good state of repair. If either or both of these things have not yet been repaired, the Landlord shall repair the fence and the closet door so that they are both in a state of good repair as soon as possible, but not later than August 3, 2026.

I do not find that it is appropriate to order that the Landlord cannot give a notice of rent increase until the repairs are completed, because such an order is limited to repairs related to “serious” breaches of the Act: ss. 30(1)7(ii), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. While I have found that the Landlord breached its obligations under section 20 of the Act, I do not find that the damaged fence posts or the closet door amount to serious breaches of those obligations.

This is because use of the word serious in the Act is a clear indication from the legislature that this remedy is to be reserved for orders requiring repairs of more serious issues, such as those, for example, that may render a unit uninhabitable, or that would have a significant and ongoing impact on a tenant’s ability to comfortably reside in a rental unit. The Tenant requested that the T2 application be amended, and the request to amend was granted on consent of the parties (DOC-3236705).

In the T2 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord and its agent and superintendent substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes, and that the Landlord and its agent and superintendent harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.

To prove that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent or superintendent substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, the Tenant must establish that the Landlord or its agent or superintendent did something, or failed to do something, that interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment in a substantial way. Conduct by a landlord that amounts to a mere annoyance or trivial incident will not normally amount to a breach of the Act. The enjoyment protected by s. 22 of the Act is qualified by the word reasonable. This means that the standard to be applied is an objective one. Even if some conduct, or lack thereof, is particularly annoying to the particular tenant before the LTB, the LTB must consider whether that conduct or lack thereof would amount to a substantial interference with enjoyment on the objective standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances: s. 22, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; TST-55210-14, 2014 CanLII 58631 (ON LTB), para 32.

Section 22 of the Act refers to the conduct of the Landlord, and not the behaviour of others in the residential complex. However, a landlord can be held liable for the conduct of others if they fail to respond reasonably to address complaints about such conduct: TST-55210- 14, 2014 CanLII 58631 (ON LTB), para 30.

For the Tenant to prove that the Landlord or its agent or superintendent harassed her, she must establish that the Landlord engaged in a course of vexatious comment or conduct toward the Tenant that the Landlord knew or ought to have known to be unwelcome: [name] v. Singh, 2023 ONLTB 13936 (CanLII), para 24. For comment or conduct to be vexatious, it must be pursued for no lawful or legitimate purpose. As an example, even if a tenant were in arrears of rent, the landlord would know, or ought to know, that issuance of a notice of termination of tenancy for rental arrears would be conduct that would be unwelcome by the tenant. This conduct, however, would not be vexatious because it would be conduct engaged in for a lawful, legitimate purpose (in accordance with the landlord’s rights under s. 59 of the Act).

[name] said that the Tenant’s conduct over the years had a significant negative impact on her family’s well-being. 109. When asked if she called the Tenant “psychotic”, MS did not explicitly acknowledge or deny saying this, but said that she would not just start calling another person names, and that whatever she said was provoked by the Tenant. MS also denied saying that it is “tacky” to get a gazebo from Facebook marketplace. She said that she would only communicate with the Tenant when the Tenant spoke to her child. 110. MS denied calling the Tenant a “fat face”, and said that is a comment that was directed at her by the Tenant. 111. [name] said that she was informed that the Landlord offered the Tenant a unit transfer, but the Tenant denied the offer. The Landlord then offered [name] and [name] a unit transfer, but they also declined, because by that time they already planned on moving out of the residential complex. 112. When asked on cross-examination, MS said the Landlord never suggested that the parties engage in mediation relative to their ongoing issues. 113. BF acknowledged that there was a period where the Tenant was not allowed to contact her directly, which made the situation more difficult to manage, because they would have to communicate through third parties. 114. BF said that both the Tenant and MS/Jason were offered transfers to other units, but that both declined their respective offers. BF said that this dispute has also caused her a lot of stress. She said the Tenant has made false accusations about her, it makes her feel nervous, and she ended up being prescribed medication. 115. On cross-examination, BF was asked how it works when a tenant makes a complaint. BF said that if it is a maintenance request, the work orders go to the Landlord, and they are then forwarded to BF. She said that if she receives any complaints, they are forwarded to the Landlord’s head office, and that if there is a dispute between tenants, she or [name] go to address the issue as soon as possible. She said the Landlord’s website includes pages to submit maintenance requests, and a separate page to submit other complaints. Complaints are then forwarded to BF and she is asked if she knows about the issue and if she can look into it. 116. When asked if the Tenant contacted her or [name] between 2021 and March 2024 to complain about any of the occupants of MS and Jason’s unit. BF said there were complaints during this period, for example a noise complaint. BF said she went to MS and [name]’s unit and told them that they cannot be too loud early in the morning, and cautioned them to be respectful to neighbours. BF said the last thing the Tenant complained about was a planter being put between the two units. BF did not say if she received complaints about the issues specifically identified in the application. 117. When asked on cross-examination, BF said she had no information about whether the Landlord suggested or offered that the Tenant and MS/Jason engage in mediation relative to their disputes. She said that is not the type of thing she would be involved in, and someone else from the Landlord’s office would handle that type of thing. Disposition – T2 Application 118. I find that the Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlord or its agent or superintendent substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes, or that they harassed, obstructed, coerced, interfered with, threatened the Tenant. 119. Although the Tenant testified that she made numerous complaints to the Landlord by email about the conduct of MS and [name], she did not provide any cogent, specific oral evidence to establish exactly what she complained about, to whom and when. There was oral evidence from the Tenant that she informed the Landlord by email of some specific incidents, but without explanation, there was no documentary evidence presented, such as copies of the emails, based on which this information can be determined or confirmed. 120. While the Tenant said she sent many emails and the Landlord was not responsive, she also gave evidence that, for a period of time, she was only complaining to the police. This was the case for the unacceptable comments made by [name] on October 6, 2022, for example. As set out above, I cannot find the Landlord breached the Act based on how they responded to this incident, because there was no evidence that the Landlord knew or ought to have known about the incident. 121. Similarly, I cannot determine that the Landlord failed to respond reasonably to the Tenant’s complaints about any of the other allegations about MS and [name], because there was not sufficient evidence to determine which incidents the Tenant informed the Landlord about, who she informed, or when. Without this information, it is not possible to determine if the Landlord responded appropriately. 122. The Tenant did present one email, dated May 26, 2025. These complaints were not issues included in the application, so no remedy can be awarded relative to them. Further, the issues in this email, including the installation of a bracket to hang flowers on and a dispute about where to keep garbage or recycling bins, are relatively minor issues. Without anything further relative to these allegations, they would likely not amount to more than mere annoyances or trivial incidents. 123. With respect to the allegation about the Tenant’s daughter’s mail, I do not find that the Tenant presented sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to prove it is more likely than not that the mail was actually received by MS/Jason. There was no explanation, for example, as to why a copy of the delivery confirmation was not presented as evidence. The only evidence before me was the Tenant and LT saying the mail was delivered to MS and Jason’s unit, and MS denying having received it. All of these witnesses’ evidence on this point was internally consistent, but it is only the Tenant who could have produced documentary evidence to support her allegation. MS could not, for example, be expected to produce a document stating that this piece of mail was not delivered to her unit. 124. Regardless of whether MS/Jason received the mail, the Landlord is only responsible for its own actions and that of its employees and agents. To that end, I find that BF’s response was reasonable. She spoke with MS/Jason to ask if they had the mail. Without any other evidence, there were no other reasonable steps for BF to take in the circumstances. There was no evidence that the Tenant, at the time, showed BF a copy of the delivery confirmation, for example. 125. As for the evidence that one employee of the Landlord told the Tenant she could use a specific garbage bin in the residential complex, and BF later telling her this [name] was only for contractors, there was no evidence that BF said or did anything inappropriate. At worst, the Tenant received conflicting information about use of a garbage bin from different employees. This may have been irritating for the Tenant, but I find that it was only a mere annoyance or trivial incident on the standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstancs. 126. For the foregoing reasons, on the evidence before me, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord or its agent or superintendent engaged in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that they knew or ought to have known would be unwelcome by the Tenant, nor did the Tenant prove the Landlord or its agent or superintendent’s acts or omissions amounted to more that a mere annoyance or trivial incident on the standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances. 127. The evidence was that there was an extended acrimonious dispute between neighbours, and that the Landlord delivered N5 notices to both of them. SF submitted that the Landlord should have offered to provide a mediator to try to help the parties resolve their issues. She said that there was instead no evidence of the Landlord doing anything, aside for issuing N5 notices. This is an accurate assessment (aside from some steps taken by BF, described above), but as set out above, the Tenant bears the burden of proof on this application, and I have found that there was not sufficient evidence to establish if and when the Landlord knew about, or ought to have known about, the specific incidents. General evidence of sending the Landlord emails, without more details and/or copies of the emails, is not sufficient clear, convincing and cogent evidence for the Tenant to discharge her burden. I can only determine that the Landlord had an obligation to respond to incidents where I am satisfied that they knew or ought to have known about them. 128. While offering mediation services is certainly a reasonable option, it is not necessary in order for there to be a finding that a Landlord responded reasonably to an issue. More importantly, the primary issue in this case is the lack of evidence about what the Landlord was informed about, how they were informed, and when. I cannot find the Landlord breached the Act because it did not offer mediation when I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved her case relative to when and how she informed the Landlord of the issues. 129. The T2 application is dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $453.00.

The Tenant testified that he and the Landlord had signed a tenancy agreement on April 20, 2025. On that same date, the Tenant paid to the Landlord a deposit of $400.00. The unit is question was a room in a rooming house.

On April 24, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that she would like to cancel the tenancy agreement as she needed to return to Korea and the Tenant never moved into the unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord had accepted her cancellation via text.

The Landlord and the Tenant began negotiating the return of the deposit on or about May 14, 2025, wherein the Landlord had agreed to repay the deposit but had also advised the Tenant that he may bring an action against her for lost revenue if the unit is not re-rented by June 1, 2025. Further e-mails were exchanged, and the Landlord rescinded their offer to repay the deposit.

The Landlord’s position is that a tenancy was never established and that he had found a new tenant as of June 22, 2025. The Landlord testified that the unit was listed for rent on April 24, 2025, but could not find someone to move into the unit as of June 1, 2025. Analysis

With respect to the last month’s rent deposit, s. 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) says: “A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

This provision has been interpreted to mean that the deposit must be repaid if the landlord refuses to give possession to the tenant on the date set for commencement of the tenancy. But neither a landlord nor a tenant can unilaterally decide the tenancy is not going forward. In other words, a tenant cannot simply decide not to move in after all and then expect the return of the deposit. (See: [name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923 (ON SCDC), [2008] [name] No. 1934 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), and Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., [2011] [name] ([name]. C.A.).)
In this case however, I am satisfied that the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to terminate the tenancy as of April 24, 2025.

Section 106(10) of the Act states: “A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.”

Pursuant to s. 134(1.1) of the Act: “No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit;”

So with the Tenant’s application, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant is entitled to the return of the deposit charged from June 1, 2025, to June 30, 2025, as the tenancy terminated as of April 24, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $453.00. This amount represents: • $400.00 for the return of the rent deposit; • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 29, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 30, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies. [name] [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-075706-25, LTB-T-056756-25-IN3 issued on February 4, 2026. On March 5, 2026, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On March 9, 2026, interim order LTB-L-075706-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on February 4, 2026. The review request was heard by videoconference on April 16, 2026. The Landlords, the Landlords’ Agent Spinghar [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s Legal Representative Vidy Matadeen attended the hearing. Although I find that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') does not apply, for ease of reference the parties are referred to as “Landlord” and “Tenant” for the purpose of this order.
reasons: In order LTB-L-075706-25 issued on February 4, 2025, the Member found that the Landlord resided in the residential complex prior to, and throughout the time that the Tenant resided there. The parties were required to share the kitchen. However, the Member found that the exemption under section 5(i) of the Act did not apply because the Landlord did not communicate to the Tenant that she resided there. The Member referenced [name] v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628, in the decision.

The Landlord’s Agent submitted that the Member misinterpreted the Act, adding an additional element of communication to the exemption under 5(i). The Landlord’s Agent also submitted that the Member misapplied Cowie, as it does not require advance communication. The Landlord’s Agent argued that, since the Landlord proved that she resided at the residential complex at all times of the Tenant’s occupancy and they shared a kitchen, the Act does not apply.

The Tenant’s Representative took the opposing position, submitting that the order did not contain a serious error. The Representative submitted that the Member thoroughly reviewed the evidence, the parties had a fair opportunity to participate, and the order contained sufficient reasons for the decision.
Section 5(i) of the Act does not require advance communication of the arrangement to the occupant. It states:

This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 5. Cowie does not add a communication requirement either. In Cowie, the tenant rented a room in a house with a shared kitchen and bathroom. The landlord moved in after the tenancy started. The Divisional Court found that the landlord could not unilaterally change the nature of the tenancy without communicating this to the tenant.

The facts of the current case differ, as the Member determined that the Landlord resided at the residential complex before and during the Tenant’s occupancy. Therefore, there was no change that needed to be communicated. The parties were required to share the kitchen from the beginning.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Member misapplied the Act and [name] by adding a requirement of advance communication to the test under section 5(i). This is a serious error, and the review request is granted.

However, I find no error in the remainder of the order determining that the Landlord resided in the house. The Member gave extensive reasons for her determinations, referencing both parties’ evidence. I am satisfied that the Member considered the parties’ evidence and submissions when making her determinations. The Member’s findings are therefore reasonable and entitled to deference. Therefore, I do not find it necessary for the entirety of the application to be re-heard. The order will be amended.
Given that the Act does not apply to these parties, the Tenant is not entitled to file an application to the Board. Therefore, application LTB-T-056756-25 must be dismissed.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-L-075706-25, LTB-T-056756-25-IN3 issued on February 4, 2026, is granted. The order is amended as follows.
The interim order issued on March 9, 2026, is cancelled.
The Act does not apply.
The Tenant’s application, LTB-T-056756-25, is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Masset (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] and [name] (the 'Purchasing Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations against the Landlord contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $8,390.46.

As also explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations against the Purchasing Landlords contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application against the Purchasing Landlords is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agreed that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 4, 2022 because of the N12 notice, and that no person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
The parties also agreed that the rental unit was rented to a third party as of June 1, 2022.

The Landlord testified that he served the N12 notice for purchaser’s own use on the Tenant because his real estate agent, [name], told him to do so. He said he was experiencing financial difficulty and just wanted to sell the building. He had no personal preference with respect to the Tenant vacating the rental unit or continuing the tenancy with the Purchasing Landlords. He said he did not draft or review the MLS listing for the property. He said that he did not personally know if the Purchasing Landlords intended to move into the rental unit. I found the Landlord’s testimony to be credible and reliable. I find that he had little knowledge with respect to this type of real estate transaction or with respect to the Tenant’s rights or his obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act in this type of situation. He clearly relied on [name] expertise in this matter and took direction from him. 7. [name] testified that the Purchasing Landlords’ real estate agent told him that the Purchasing Landlords were going to move into the rental unit. He did not produce any documentation to support this allegation. 8. [name], the Purchasing Landlords’ real estate agent, denied telling [name] that the Purchasing Landlords wanted to move into the rental unit. He testified that he told [name] that the Purchasing Landlords were investors and that they wanted to the rental unit as an investment property. 9. The Purchasing Landlord testified that they never intended to move into the rental unit and that they never communicated this to their real estate agent. They said they had their own home and purchased the rental unit as an investment property. 10. Neither the Landlord nor [name] produced any documentation to support the allegation that [name] or the Purchasing Landlords communicated that they intended to move into the rental unit. 11. I find on a balance of probabilities based on the evidence before me that there was no communication or other indication from the Purchasing Landlords or [name] to the Landlord or [name] that the Purchasing Landlords intended to move into the rental unit. The burden of proving that such a communication occurred rests on the Landlord and they have not met this burden. I find the Purchasing Landlord and [name] to be more credible than [name] and their testimony to be more consistent with the real estate transaction documents and correspondence. As a result, I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith and I find that the Purchasing Landlords had no involvement in the service of this notice. 12. I further find that [name] caused the Landlord to serve the notice in bad faith by communicating to him that the Purchasing Landlords intended to move into the rental unit. While it is possible, with the most generous interpretation, that [name] mistakenly confused the Purchasing Landlords desire for vacant possession to be an expression of a desire to move into the rental unit, I find it more likely that he simply disregarded the Tenant and their rights so that he could pursue this lucrative real estate transaction. 13. Although I find the Landlord acted on the information provided to him by [name], he still must bear responsibility for giving the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies 14. The difference in rent for a one year period between the rental unit and the Tenant’s subsequent rental unit is $7,290.00 per year. Although the subsequent rental unit is somewhat larger, I do not find the difference in size to be significant enough to reduce the rent differential to be awarded. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,290.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. 15. With respect to the claim for moving expenses, I am satisfied that the following expenses ought to be compensated: • new account set up fee for the electrical account in the amount of $58.50 • mail forwarding charge in the amount of $65.82 • moving expenses in the amount of $840.00 • [name] boxes in the amount of $33.95 • wrapping in the amount of $49.19 16. I do not find the remainder of the amounts claimed to be compensable under the Act. The payment of first and last month’s rent and (potentially unlawful) deposit at the Tenant’s subsequent rental unit is not compensable as these are housing expenses, not moving expenses, and the rent differential award covers the increase in housing expenses already. Similarly, the increased amounts the Tenant is paying for utilities is not compensable as these are related to usage rather than to moving. The remainder of the items claimed are either too remote (e.g. lawnmower, vet bills, pots and pans, home insurance), not substantiated (e.g. gas for moving/errands, cleaning expenses, chiropractic expenses), or unrelated to the move (e.g. handyman, water cooler and water expenses at new unit). 17. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,047.46 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. 18. I do not find it appropriate to impose a fine in this case as the amount ordered should be sufficient to ensure future compliance with the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $8,390.46. This amount represents: • $7,290.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after vacating the rental unit. • $1,047.46 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
