issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $3,348.00 $4,748.00 for excess rent collected and costs.
The Tenant alleges in their T1 application, filed on July 12, 2025, that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent which they have paid resulting in an overpayment of rent of $2,460.00.

It is uncontested that: a) T he Tenant and the Landlord signed a lease agreement for the period August 1, 2022 – August 1, 2024. The agreed-upon rent for this period was $2,800.00/month, payable on the first day of the month; b) T he Tenant and the Landlord signed a new lease agreement on June 20, 2024 for the period August 1, 2024 – July 31, 2026. The rent amount for this new lease was $3,100.00/month; and c) The Tenant and the Landlord agreed to reduce the rent to $3,000.00 on April 5, 2025, commencing with the May 1, 2025 rent payment. This reduced amount was to be in effect for the remainder of the lease period (until July 31, 2026). The Tenant paid this amount for three months (May 1, 2025 – July 1, 2025); and has paid this rent amount on an ongoing basis. d) The Tenant reduced their rent payment to $2,800.00 per month commencing August 1, 2025 and has paid that amount to the Landlord since.

The Tenant submits that there is nothing substantially different between the original lease agreement entered into between the Tenant and the Landlord and that the new lease agreement is an attempt by the Landlord to contract out of the Act to achieve an illegal above guideline rent increase.

The Landlord submits that his expenses for the unit rose, including a building-wide imposition of a $62.00/month TV and internet fee, necessitating an increase in the rent. The Landlord also indicated that the Tenant caused damages that he is seeking reimbursement for through an LTB application. Analysis

I find that the Landlord has collected rent more than the amount allowed by the Act and must pay the Tenant the illegally collected rent as sought in the Tenant’s T1 Application, for the reasons that follow.

The attempt to enter into a new lease agreement is an attempt to contract out of the Act, whether intentional or not. The new lease agreement attempts to circumvent the rent control provisions of the Act, in particular Section 110 of the Act which states that no landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with the Act’s rent increase rules.

Section 116 of the Act states that a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so using a Board approved form.
In this case the Landlord first increased the rent from $2,800.00 to $3,100.00, then reduced it to $3,000.00, without first serving the required Notice of Rent Increase (NORI).
In addition, even if the Landlord had given the Tenant a NORI, the increase would still have been illegal because the Landlord was limited to the 2024 guideline increase of 2.5%.

Subsection 120(1) of the Act provides: No landlord may increase rent charged to a tenant or to an assignee under section 85, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.

There was no evidence of any of the exceptions identified in section 120 under sections 121, 123, 126 or 127 applied – i.e. there were no Board orders permitting above guideline O rder Page 3 of 4 increases and there were no agreements entered into due to the provision of increased s ervices or because of additional capital expenditures undertaken.

The fact that the Tenant signed a new lease containing the illegal rent increase does not make it lawful. The Court of Appeal for Ontario addressed this very issue in Honsberger v. Grant Lake Forest Resources Ltd., 2019 ONCA 44. The Court found that while parties are free to enter into a new tenancy agreement at the expiry of their existing fixed term agreement, the landlord must also provide a written notice of rental increase in accordance with the RTA in order to increase the rent in the new tenancy agreement.
The rental amount of $3,100.00 (or ultimately $3,000.00) as contained in the new lease agreement is an illegal rent increase. The lawful monthly rent is $2,800.00.
The lawful rent the Landlord was entitled to for the period of August 1, 2024 to February 28, 2026 is $53,200.00 being 19 months at $2,800.00/month.

The Tenant has paid rent for this period as follows: Period Rent Paid/Month Total Rent Paid August 1, 2024 – April 30, 2025 (9 months) $3,100.00 $27,900.00 May 1, 2025 – July 31, 2025 (3 months) February 28, 2026 (10 months) $3,000.00 $9,000.00 $30,000.00 August 1, 2025 – February 28, 2026 (7 months) $2,800.00 $19,600.00 $56,500.00 $57,900.00

As the rent increase was unlawful, I find the Landlord collected $3,300.00 $4,700.00 of rent in excess of the amount permitted under the Act from the Tenant ($56,500.00 $57,900.00 paid - $53,200.00 owed).

The Tenant’s application was filed on July 12, 2025, which is less than one year before the rent was illegally rent increase took effect. Therefore, the Tenant’s application was filed within the one-year limitation period as set out under section 135(4) of the Act. In addition, the rent increase deeming provision contained in section 135.1 of the Act does not apply to this unlawful increase because the Tenant did not pay the unlawful increase for 12 consecutive months before filing this application.
As the Tenant was successful in their application, they are also entitled to the cost of the filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,348.00 $4,748.00. This amount represents: • $3,300 $4,700.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant submitted that they were given an N12 notice by the Landlord on or about May 31, 2024 with a date to vacate of July 31, 2024. That this notice was motivated by work completed to address mould remediation that had taken place, having commenced on or about November 2024 and concluded in May 2024. That the notice was a form of retaliation as when mould was discovered in the basement of the home, the Tenants called by-law enforcement, and the Landlord incurred a cost for repair. The cost was said to have been substantially more than the initial flood damage that was being addressed as resulting from a collapsed ceiling.
The N12 notice indicating that the Landlord’s child was moving into the rental unit, specifically her daughter [name] [name].

To avoid a hearing of the Landlord’s L2 application based on the N12 notice, the Tenant submitted that they signed an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy on July 11, 2024 with a termination date of July 31, 2024.
The Tenant’s agreed to accept $10,000.00 as part of the N11 agreement to vacate. This payment was confirmed to have been received by the Tenants once they moved out.

The Tenants believes that no one moved into the rental property after they moved out. This is based on (SW’s) mother’s confirming this as she resides a few doors down from the rental property and through other residents who the Tenants are acquainted with since residing on the street.
The Tenants lived in the property for 4 + years and prior the Tenant (SW) resided on the street as a child, in her family home as still occupied by her mother.

While the observations of the property are that while the property has been seen to have been maintained in terms of outdoor and lawn maintenance activities, that no one moved into nor resided at the rental property until November 2025.

In the Board’s record the Tenant relies on DOC-7510987, a handwritten note dated March 3, 2026 of [name], her mother and resident of 131 [address] Kitchener. In the note she details that on her nightly dog walks, she has not seen anyone residing at rental property from August 2024 to November 2025.

On cross examination, the Tenant confirmed that there was no evidence of the rental unit being re-rented or listed for sale nor any evidence to support the remedies sought. Specifically, while the Tenant claimed a rent differential, no copies of a new lease agreement in respect of the property they moved into on August 1, 2024 was evidenced. Landlord’s Evidence – J. [name] 12. (JH) submitted that she moved into the rental property at the end of August 2024 and that she continues to reside there, participating in the hearing from the rental property. Having moved in as she was having marital problems. 13. (JH) testified that her mom, the Landlord paid the Tenants $10,000.00 as part of the N11 agreement as they knew that it would take a long time for the matter to be scheduled for hearing. That the Tenants were not forced to sign the agreement and that they attempted to negotiate, seeking the payment of $20,000.00. 14. (JH) evidenced a variety of utility bills and photos of her at the rental property to support her residency and reliance on the utilities and her drivers license to confirm her residency. 15. Further, that she reconciled with her husband, sold their matrimonial home and that he moved into the rental unit on or about November 21, 2025, where they continue to reside together. Analysis: 16. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 17. There was no dispute between the parties that the N11 was proposed by the Landlord and that the Tenants accepted the payment of $10,000.00 in lieu of proceeding to a hearing in connection to the N12 notice, the Landlord’s L2 application filing was scheduled for hearing in November 2024. 18. In the T5 application, the Tenant while submitting that they “decided to sign an N11 anyway under significant stress,” at the time of the hearing the submission was the decision was made to avoid a hearing as understanding that it would be difficult to defend against the Landlord’s L2 application. The N11 was signed on July 11, 2024 prior to the expiration date of July 31, 2024 as outlined on N12 notice. 19. Effectively, the N11 agreement was superseded by the N12, resulting in a binding contract between the parties to end the tenancy on July 31, 2024 pursuant to the N11 notice, An Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy. 20. There are three elements necessary to form a binding contract. There must be: (i) An offer from one party to form a contract, which is accepted by the other party; (ii) An intention to create legal relations between the two; (iii) Consideration, or the exchange of something of value in exchange for the contract. 21. Here, I find the signing of the N11 was a binding agreement between the parties. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenants had a choice when signing the N11 notice, there was no evidence adduced to consider otherwise. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenants vacated the property pursuant to the N11 notice. 22. As outlined, to be successful on a T5 Application pursuant to Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 23. Here, it is not disputed that the Tenants were served an N12 notice however, they have not proven that they vacated the property because of the notice, rather, the evidence was that they signed an N11 agreement on July 11, 2024, accepted $10,000.00 and vacated pursuant to this agreement. 24. Given the above, as the Tenants did not prove that they vacated the rental unit pursuant to the N12 notice of termination the Landlord served them under section 48 of the Act it is not necessary to address the evidence led at the hearing relevant to the questions of bad faith and whether no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. 25. Accordingly, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed. 26. Alternatively, given the totality of the submissions, I am satisfied that the Tenants did not lead sufficient evidence to support that no one moved into the rental unit after they vacated. Therefore, the outcome of the T5 Application would remain unchanged. 27. This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-057838-25 issued on March 19, 2026. The Tenant did not attend the hearing on March 18, 2026. On March 19, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On March 23, 2026 interim order LTB-T-057838-25-RV-IN was issued.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that they were not reasonably able to participate in the scheduled hearing on March 18, 2026.

They stated that they could not participate due to a medical emergency. They were having a medical episode and had to go out to obtain medication. They confirmed that they did not see a medical practitioner, did not have a prescription or a receipt for the medications they purchased.
The Landlord opposed the request for a review submitting that the Tenant had not proven they could not participate in the prior hearing.

The Landlord’s daughter was not permitted to act as an interpreter for their parents to interpret from a Chinese language into English. They did not have a third party present to be able to interpret for them.

The Landlord’s daughter was not permitted to lead evidence. Although the Board’s Rules of Procedures at Rule 1.6 q, provides that the Board may exercise its discretion to permit a party’s representative (or agent) to give evidence, I determined that it would not be appropriate to do so.

The Landlord’s Agent could only provide hearsay evidence, that is what the Landlord or the Landlord’s spouse had told them. Although the Board could accept hearsay evidence, in my view there is significant prejudice to the Tenant, because they would not be able to cross-examine the person with direct knowledge of the issues. This prejudice outweighs any probative value that might be determined. Analysis
I was satisfied that the Tenant could not reasonably participate in the hearing on March 18, 2026. The request for review was granted and the re-hearing followed thereafter.

The Board’s power to review a decision may be exercised if a party to a proceeding was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. The case law from Divisional Court generally instructs the Board that the meaning of the phrase “not reasonably able to participate” should be interpreted broadly, to ensure natural justice, and where a party shows a genuine intent to participate in a hearing but was prevented from doing so, they should be entitled to a hearing through the review process. A party’s genuine intent to participate must be borne out by the evidence which clearly demonstrates the party’s intent to participate in the hearing. See [name] v. [name], 2011 ONSC 1557; King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., 2008 CanLII 60708, TSL-21992-11-RV (Re), 2012 CanLII 27914 (ON LTB); TEL-09087-10-RV (Re), 2011 CanLII 26960 (ON LTB); SWT-07158-10 (Re), 2010 CanLII 67967 (ON LTB).

In King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments 2008 CANLII 60708 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court stated: “Being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less”.

It would have been ideal had the Tenant produced a medical note, or prescription or receipt to show that there was a genuine medical emergency that precluded them from participating. However, I was satisfied with the genuine intent of the Tenant to appear and proceed with their own application. Therefore the request for a review was granted. Re-hearing
The re-hearing was heard after the request for a review was granted.
It was undisputed that there was a maintenance emergency that arose on July 4, 2026 while the Landlord’s were out of the country.

It was uncontested that the toilet in the Tenant’s unit had become clogged and was at risk of overflowing. The Tenant called a plumber for an emergency repair. (see DOC 7541799) the plumbing contractor notes in the receipt that the blockage was near 60 feet in the drain close to the main drain. They had to clear to 90 feet to clear the blockage properly.
It was uncontested that the Tenant had advised the Landlord about the plumbing emergency and had provided the invoice on July 5, 2026, after it was resolved. (See Doc 8083784 at page 5)
The Tenant was only seeking reimbursement of the emergency plumbing charges in the amount of $867.28.
The Landlord did not cross-examine the Tenant.

The Landlord in their closing submissions stated that this was not an emergency because the Tenant could have used a bathroom in the Landlord’s portion of the residence. They also submitted that the plumbing contractor was not reputable and expensive. They submitted that they had not prior notice of the emergency. They submitted that the plumbing emergency was the fault of the Tenant.
The Tenant responded by stating the powder room is not a part of the rental unit, it is in the Landlord’s unit. Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act, a landlord is responsible for: providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (Onyskiw) (CanLII), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.
It is undisputed that the Landlord’s were out of the country. It was also undisputed that the Landlord’s had not provided a local emergency contact in the event of an emergency.

In my view, it would be unreasonable in the circumstances to expect that the Tenant is required to take photos and send them to the Landlord and wait for a response from across multiple time-zones. Even if I accept that premise, the only response likely is that the Tenant would be authorized to resolve the problem. This would have only delayed getting a plumber in to resolve the problem. A delay may have led to additional damages if the toilet did overflow and flood the bathroom and rental unit.

The Landlord attempted to lay blame on the Tenant; however, they did not have their own plumber testify and did not summons the actual plumber that did the repairs to testify. Had the issue been in the toilet vice deep into the sewer line close to the main line, that might have been a possibility. In the absence of such testimony, I find that the receipt provides a reasonable description of the plumbing emergency and the efforts necessary to resolve it. In my view this does not amount to willfulness or negligence on the part of the Tenant.

Taking a contextual approach, I am satisfied that the Tenant has acted reasonably in the circumstances, knowing that the Landlord was out of the country, and most likely unable to resolve the plumbing emergency themselves, took the only logical action necessary to contact a plumber that came in after regular hours, around 10 p.m., at night to resolve the problem and thereby mitigate any further damages.

In my view the charges are reasonable. The Landlord may disagree with the charges, however beyond their bald statements that it was too expensive, the offered no testimony from anyone to show what might have been reasonable in the circumstances.

Therefore, I am satisfied that by failing to provide a local emergency contact while traveling outside the country, the Landlord failed in their general duty to maintain the rental unit. In the event of an emergency, the Tenant should have access to an emergency contact and be able to get an immediate response. In my view that was not possible in this case, because the Landlord was traveling outside the country.

The Tenant on July 4, at 5:51 p.m., had advised the Landlord that the power had been flickering and that that morning the fire alarm went off randomly. (DOC-8083784 at page 4) The Landlord did not respond to this email; however, they responded to the email about the plumbing emergency about 3.5 hours after they were sent the plumbing invoice.

Based on this, I can only presume that the Landlord was not concerned that the fire alarm had gone off or that the power had been flickering. These too could have been emergency situations where some electrical appliances may have been damaged by the flickering power or something more serious had caused the fire alarm to go off in the Tenant’s unit.
The Tenant’s acting in an emergency acted reasonably and in doing may have prevented more extensive damages.
The Tenant was seeking reimbursement for their out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $867.28.
I am satisfied that the plumbing charge is reasonable. The plumber came at night after regular business hours and spent 2.5 hours effecting the repair.
The Tenant also incurred an application fee of $48.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed that fee.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-057838-25 issued on March 19, 2026, is granted.
The order is amended as follows.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $915.28 which represents the following: a. Out of pocket expense of $867.28 and b. Application fee of $48.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the lawful rent commencing on August 1, 2026, until the full amount plus interest has been recovered.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord requested an adjournment of the matter to be combined with his L10 application.

Having reviewed the application, I had found that the issues raised in the Tenant’s application and the issues raised in the Landlord’s application were not overlapping and having considered Interpretation Guideline 1 – Adjourning and Rescheduling Hearings including the Board’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding and denied the Landlord’s adjournment request. Tenant’s Application.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,819.23.
The tenancy agreement signed by both the Landlord and the Tenant began on August 1, 2024, and was supposed to end on July 31, 2025. The monthly rent was $3,200.00.

The Tenant paid a $500.00 key deposit and had pre-paid 12 months of rent totalling $38,400.00 to the Landlord on June 23, 2023. This amount was applied to the first year of the tenancy and the lease was renewed as of August 1, 2024.

On July 5, 2024, the Tenant paid to the Landlord $19,200.00 which included 6 months of rent plus the last month’s rent deposit. On March 8, 2025, an agent for the Tenants sent an e-mail to the Landlord providing 60-day notice of the termination of the tenancy as of May 31, 2025. N9 notices were submitted into evidence.

On May 25, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that they were vacating the unit and asked where to leave the keys. The Landlord responded that her agent would retrieve the keys on her behalf, and a text message was sent to the Tenant the same date.

On June 16, 2025, the Landlord’s agent had advised the Tenant that the Landlord had intended to pay to the Tenant $3,200.00 for the last month’s rent deposit and the $500.00 key deposit. The Landlord’s agent advised the Tenant on July 14, 2025, that the funds would not be returned to the Tenant based on her instructions from the Landlord.
The Landlord testified that she believes that the tenancy was not terminated in accordance with the Act and the Tenants in fact do owe her the last month’s rent deposit.
The Landlord also seemingly blamed her agent [name] for agreeing to pick up the unit’s keys on her behalf without her instructions and that the unit was re-rented as of August 1, 2025. Analysis

Having considered the evidence of both parties, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected and retained an illegal key deposit, did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant, and that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected excessive rent from May 25, 2025, to May 31, 2025, as I find that the tenancy was terminated as of May 31, 2025.

The Tenant advised the Landlord and/or the Landlord’s agent in March of 2025 that they had intended on terminating the tenancy as of May 31, 2025. The Landlord simply did not respond and when asked about the return of the keys, the Landlord simply advised the Tenant to provide her agent the keys.

The N9 was served, and the Landlord never seemed to object to the termination of the tenancy. Further, despite the Landlord testifying that she never authorized her agent to accept the keys on her behalf, the Landlord’s recourse is not with the Tenant, it is with her former agent.
As such, I am satisfied that the tenancy was terminated as of May 31, 2025. The Tenants are owed the last month’s rent deposit, the interest on same and their key deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,819.23. This amount represents: • $500.00 for an illegal charge. • $3,200.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $71.23 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex (T2 application); and. • failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application) This application was continued by videoconference on May 5, 2026. The Landlords and the Tenants attended the hearing. [name] [name] appeared as a witness for the Landlords. This was an FLS hearing. Board [name] provided French and English interpretation services.
reasons: The Tenants allege the Landlords breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to a flood in the rental unit, which substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Landlord’s legal obligations to repair File Numbers : LTB-T-047067-25; LTB-T-058721-25

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

It is important to note that subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. Therefore, the reasons for a landlord’s breach are not relevant. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), however, the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem, then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it.

Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

In determining whether the Landlords have breached their obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. The Board must then consider when the Landlords were informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue and whether the steps taken by the Landlords to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstances.

There seems to be no dispute that the Tenants reported the basement flooded on July 15, 2024. As explained above, a disrepair issue is not an automatic breach of a landlord’s obligation under subsection 20(1). The issue to be determined is whether the steps the Landlords took to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstance. I am satisfied they were.

The evidence before me establishes that the Landlords immediately attended the rental unit on July 15, 2024 to assess the flood in the basement. The Landlords removed and replaced the carpets, flooring, and under pads and set up fans and dehumidifiers to dry out the basement. New flooring was installed in the bedroom and living room. In my view, the steps taken by the Landlords were appropriate and timely.

The Tenants seem to suggest that the Landlords ought to have known that the basement would have flooded because they had reported leaks from the basement ceiling, flooding File Numbers : LTB-T-047067-25; LTB-T-058721-25 in the laundry room due to the lack of an adequate drainage system, and a leak in the kitchen. As the applicants, the onus is on the Tenants to prove their claim on a balance of probabilities. I find the Tenants have failed to sufficiently establish that the basement flood was due to a leak in the basement ceiling, the lack of a drainage system in the laundry room, or a leak in the kitchen.

There is no dispute that there was a significant storm in the [name]-Burlington area and the region experienced severe flooding on July 15, 2024. The Landlords admitted into evidence several newspaper clippings and city documents indicating the sudden flood in the region was unforeseeable and overwhelmed municipal infrastructure. Landlord [name] testified that hundreds of homes in the region had been damaged in the storm and that the City was working to rectify the infrastructure.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the flooding in the basement was the result of storm waters and not due to an unresolved maintenance issue. I find the Landlords acted promptly and appropriately in addressing the flood. Accordingly, the Landlords have not breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Tenants’ applications are therefore dismissed.

The Tenants seem to take issue with the fact that their furniture and personal belongings were damaged in the flood waters. As the storm and resulting flooding was not reasonably foreseeable, the Landlords cannot be held financially liable for such damage and loss.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. June 09, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on June 15, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative, [name], and the Tenant, [name], attended the hearing. When the capitalized word “Landlord” is used in this order, it refers to all persons or companies identified as a Landlord at the top of the order. When the capitalized word “Tenant” is used in this order, it refers to all persons identified as a Tenant at the top of the order.
reasons: The Landlord submitted that the living arrangement between the parties is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the RTA”) under section 5(i) of the Act.
If the RTA does not apply, the Board lacks jurisdiction and the tenant’s application must be dismissed. [name]

Section 5(i) of the RTA provides that the RTA does not apply where: “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent, or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner or relative lives in the building.” Evidence Landlord’s Evidence

The landlord’s legal representative submitted that the property was owner-occupied and not a residential complex subject to the RTA. In support, the following evidence was provided: • A statutory declaration dated November 26, 2021, from [name] stating that no tenant claim existed on the property. • An affidavit from [name], Default Recovery Specialist at [organization], indicating that: a) A statement of claim was served on [name]. b) [name] stated he resided upstairs with the respondent, [name] [name]. • A statutory declaration from [name] [name] confirming the property is owner- occupied and not tenanted. • An appraisal dated August 5, 2025, describing the property as: A single-family residential dwelling; containing one kitchen; with a partially finished basement, consisting of a recreation room (used as a bedroom), and an unfinished area used for laundry, storage, and utilities. • The landlord asserted there is only one kitchen in the home, and that the basement area is not a self-contained rental unit. [name]

The Tenant submitted that: • The previous landlord was his mother, who resided upstairs; • He resided in the basement; • There are two rooms in the basement used by him; • His “kitchen” facilities consist of: a fridge, microwave, and hot plate located in the laundry room; • A two-piece bathroom was on the main floor and a Full bathroom was on the second floor. There were no bathroom in the basement. • He often ate out. • The Tenant maintains this constitutes a separate rental unit. Analysis
The determinative issue is whether the Tenant was required to share kitchen or bathroom facilities with the owner, thereby triggering the exemption under section 5(i).
The Landlord’s evidence is supported by multiple documents, including sworn declarations and third-party evidence.
The Tenant’s own evidence does not establish the existence of a self-contained rental unit but instead supports the conclusion that the basement was an extension of the family home.

The appraisal and other documentary evidence establish that the property is a single- family home with only one full kitchen. There is no evidence of a legally separate or fully equipped second dwelling unit in the basement.

As per the Tenant’s testimony, the basement does not contain a self-contained kitchen, but only limited food preparation appliances located in a laundry area, namely a hot plate, microwave, and fridge. This does not constitute a full kitchen.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant was required to share the only kitchen facilities in the home with the previous Landlord (his mother). The fact that the Tenant may have chosen to infrequently use the kitchen facilities does not effect the application of section 5(i).
It is undisputed that the previous Landlord (the tenant’s mother) resided upstairs and the Tenant lived in the basement.

A parent-child relationship clearly falls within the category of relatives identified in section 5(i) which states: living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I find that the Tenant resided in a portion of a single-family home; the previous landlord (his mother) resided in the same dwelling. The tenant did not have exclusive use of a fully self-contained kitchen facility, and any cooking arrangements were limited and informal. Accordingly, the living arrangement falls within the exemption set out in section 5(i) of the RTA.
As the RTA does not apply to this living arrangement, the Board does not have jurisdiction over this matter.
The Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 Application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-059565-25 issued on March 11, 2026. On April 1, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On April 2, 2026 interim order LTB-T-059565-25-RV-IN was issued. This review hearing was heard by videoconference on June 4, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant requested a review of order LTB-T-059565-25 issued on March 11, 2026 (the “Order”) on the basis of serious error.

The Tenant’s T1 application claims the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and the Landlord did not return the deposit to the Landlord.

In short, t he Tenant ’s review request (RTR) submit s the member seriously erred in not finding that the Landlord refused consent of the assignment of the tenancy . As a result of this error, the Tenant was not entitled to the return of the last month’s rent deposit(LMRD).

By way of background , the Tenant signed a year lease commencing October 1, 2024 . A LMRD of $1375.00 was given to the Landlord at that time and the Tenant vacated the rental unit only 6 months later on March 31, 2025.

At the merits hearing, the Tenant argued the Landlord refused consent of the assignment of the tenancy and consequently, the Tenant was entitled to terminate the tenancy on 30 days notice to the Landlord.

The pertinent facts are as follows: On February 17, 2025, the Tenant requested the Landlord’s permission to assign the lease for the remainder of the one -year term. The Landlord responded that any permitted assignee would have to sign “a new 12 month term lease.” When the Tenant requested that the Landlord agree to an assignment for only the balance of the remaining term, the Landlord advised on February 19, 2025 “I do not agree to the re-assignment then”.

The Tenant responded by giving the Landlord a Form N9 Notice to End Tenancy which I am satisfied was received by the Landlord on February 21, 2025 and which contained a termination date of March 31, 2025. As the Tenant paid the monthly rent for March 2025, the Tenant submits the Landlord was required to return the LMRD.

Section 95(4)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act , 2006 (the “Act”) provides that a tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination within 30 days after the date a request is made if, “the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent ”. Section 96(2) of the Act further provides that the date of termination specified in the notice shall be the lesser of the notice period otherwise required under the act or 30 days.

The [name] shows the member failed to consider the Landlord ’s refusal to consent to assignment for the balance of the one-year term. In doing so, the member found there was no refusal by the Landlord. Pursuant to sections 95(4) and 96(2) of the Act, I find the Tenant was entitled to treat the Landlord’s February 19, 2025 response as an assignment refusal . As I find the member made an unreasonable finding of fact on a material issue, the Tenant’s RTR was granted and the application was considered on its merits

The Tenant provided a Form N9 notice to terminate tenancy on March 31, 2025. The Tenant seeks the return of the LMRD, as the Tenant paid rent for the final month of occupancy (March 2025) and the Tenant testified the LMRD was never returned. As I am satisfied the tenancy was terminated on March 31, 2026 pursuant to the Form N9 notice, the Landlord must return the LMRD of $1375.00 to the Tenant.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-059565-25 issued on March 11, 2026 is granted and the order is cancelled
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,375.00 for the last month's rent deposit.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
