issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the Tenant indicated that he wished to proceed on an amended application filed with the Board on March 5, 2026.

Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure provides guidance on the Board’s discretionary authority to amend an application. It says that a request to amend an application must be in writing, served with the amended application to all parties, and be filed with the LTB with the amended application and completed certificate of service. The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. The request to amend will be decided considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors.

The Tenant served the Landlord with the amended application. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to raise opposition to the amendment, and I am satisfied that the amendment will not prejudice the Landlord. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $412.00.
The Tenant testified that on June 10, 2025 he contacted a realtor for the Landlord via text and inquired about renting a unit within the residential complex.

The Tenant further testified that he advised the realtor he wished to rent unit 950 commencing September 4, 2025 at the residential complex and on June 11, 2025 transferred $950.00 the equivalent of one month’s rent and $364.00 for a service to the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that they did not sign a tenancy agreement.

On June 13, 2025 the Tenant sent a message to the Landlord indicating that they wished to cancel the tenancy and sought the return of his rent deposit and service fee pursuant to the Landlord’s cancellation policy.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to return the rent deposit and service fee. [name]

With respect to a rent deposit s. 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') says: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

This provision has been interpreted to mean that the deposit must be repaid if the landlord refuses to give possession to the tenant on the date set for commencement of the tenancy. But neither a landlord nor a tenant can unilaterally decide the tenancy is not going forward. In other words, a tenant cannot simply decide not to move in and expect the return of the deposit. (See: [name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923 (ON SCDC), [2008] O.J. No. 1934 ([name]. Div. Ct.) (‘[name] v. [name]’), and Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., [2011] [name] ([name]. C.A.).)

Additionally in Opara v. Cook the Court upheld a decision of the Board dismissing a tenant’s application for a refund. The Court observed that a tenancy agreement came into effect the day the parties reached an agreement on the rental of a room and upon the rent deposit being paid.

Based on the text exchange between the Tenant and the Landlord’s realtor and the payment of a rent deposit I am satisfied that a tenancy agreement came into affect pursuant to [name] v. [name] and the Tenant would not be entitled to the return of the rent deposit paid as it was the Tenant’s act that prevented him from taking possession, not the action of the Landlord.

With respect to the service fee charged by the Landlord section 134(1)(a) of the Act states a landlord shall not: collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act when the Landlord collected a service fee from the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $412.00. This amount represents: • $364.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (‘T2 Application’).  failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (‘T6 Application’).
reasons: The Tenant delivered a request to am end the application on May 27, 2025 (DOC- 5692950). The request to amend the application is granted on consent of the parties. The Law Harassment

For the Tenant to prove t hat the Landlord harassed them, they must establish that the Landlord engaged in a course of vexatious comment or conduct toward the Tenant that the Landlord knew or ought to have known to be unwelcome: [name] v. Singh, 2023 ONLTB 13936 (CanLII), para 24. For comment or conduct to be vexatious, it must be pursued for no lawful or legitimate purpose. As an example, even if a tenant were in arrears of rent, the landlord would know, or ought to know, that issuance of a notice of termination of tenancy for rental arrears would be conduct that would be unwelcome by the tenant. This conduct, however, would not be vexatious because it would be conduct engaged in for a lawful, legitimate purpose (in accordance with the landlord’s rights under s. 59 of the Act). Maintenance

Section 20 of the Act states: Landlord’s responsibility to repair 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non- repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (2).

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has rejected the proposition that this provision ought to be interpreted such that a landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as soon as a maintenance issue arises. Rather, a contextual approach, including consideration of the “entirety of the factual situation”, must be applied to determine whether a landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act: Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, paras 58-60, 84-86; TST-98783-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 87665 (ON LTB).

Generally, landlords are not held liable for ma intenance issues that arise if the landlord addresses the issue of disrepair in a timely and effective manner once they become aware, or ought to have become aware of the issue: TST-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB), para 33; LTB Interpretation Guideline #5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations. Burden of Proof

This is the Tenant’s application, and they therefore bear the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53, paras 44-46. Evidence and Analysis T6 Application Cleanliness of Unit at Commencement of Tenancy

The tenancy agreement for t he rental unit commenced on June 1, 2024. The Tenant first said they moved in on June 2, 2024, but later said it was actually on June 3, 2024 after heaving visited the unit on June 2, 2024. Later, on cross-examination, the Tenant was referred to an email from their [name] to the Landlord’s Realtor, dated June 2, 2024 stating the Tenant’s had moved in that day, and all went well (DOC-5657718, p. 5). The Tenant’s evidence was that the unit was not ready on June 1, 2024 because it had not been cleaned, and she did not receive the keys for the unit until June 2, 2024.

The Landlord is a medical doctor, living in Winnipeg, Manitoba. She presented as evidence 8 photos of the unit that she said were sent to her by her cleaner on May 31, 2024 (DOC- 5657718, pp. 1-2). The photos do not show the whole unit, but the areas shown appear to be clean. The Tenant presented no documentary or photographic evidence to support their assertion that they could not move in on June 1, 2024 because the unit was dirty.

The T6 Application is dismi ssed as it relates to their claim about the unit not being ready on June 1, 2024 because it was dirty, because they failed to present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to discharge their burden of proof about this issue. Informing the Landlord about [name]

After moving in, the Tenant informed the Landlord about a number of maintenance issues by email on June 4, 2024 (DOC-7791871, p. 6). The email included the following list of issues, and also states that the Tenant had informed the Landlord about these issues previously, both before and after moving in: 1. One of the four stov e burners was not working; 2. There was a gap in the door which caused the unit to get very cold; 3. A light bulb was not working; 4. The “bathroom WC faucet” is old and rusted leading to the leakage in the bathroom; 5. The toilet flush lever was broken; 6. There was no cold water in the kitchen; 7. “[T[he paint chip off have already been sent” (sic); and 8. The fridge was missing a shelf “… and there is a crack below”.

The Tenant’s evidence was that their [name] also sent the Landlord an email identifying these issues on June 2, 2024 (DOC-5657718, p. 5). The Realtor’s email lists 5 issues that Tenant was asking to be repaired: the stove burner, the flush lever, the lack of cold water in the kitchen, the burned out light bulb, and the missing fridge shelf. The Tenant then said they discovered the bathroom water leak on June 3, 2024.

When KK, the Tenant’s adult child, gave evidence, they said that the issues identified in the June 4, 2024 email were all identified on June 2, 2025, and that KK helped to draft the email (DOC-7791871, p. 6). On cross-examination, after confirming all of these issues were identified on June 2, 2024, KK was asked about the fact that the water leak issue was missing from the Realtor’s June 2, 2024 email. KK then said that they went to inspect the unit on June 2, 2024, but the leak issue was not discovered until June 3, 2024.

The Tenant emailed the Landlord again on June 13, 2024 to follow up primarily on the issues about no cold water in the kitchen and the water leak in the bathroom, because these were the most pressing issues from the Tenant’s perspective (DOC-7791871, p. 11).

The Landlord said she was not aware of any issues in the unit because the former tenants who had moved out on May 29, 2024 did not complain about any issues, and none were identified by her cleaner who attended after that. Bathroom Leak and Toilet Lever

The Tenant said that when they moved into the unit there was a leak in a water line in the bathroom that supplies the toilet. The Tenant presented as evidence three photos of the water pipe from the wall that supplies the toilet, and a bowl with water under the pipe (DOC-7791871, p. 7). The Tenant’s evidence was that the bowl had to be emptied every couple hours.
The Tenant’s evidence was that there was a pipe that was old and rusted, causing the leak, and that the leak persisted for 14 days before it was fixed.
Specifically, the Tenant’s evidence was that the first plumber attended immediately, but after he left, the pipe was still dripping, and a second plumber came and repaired the leak 14 days later.

On cross-examination, the Tenant was referred to several photos, one of which shows the toilet with a bidet installed (DOC-5657718, p. 3). The Tenant acknowledged they had the bidet installed. When asked if the installation of the bidet may have caused the water leak, the Tenant said that the bidet was installed by the person the Landlord sent to fix the water leak on July 11, 2024, and this was not the cause of the leak.

The Tenant acknowledged the lease prohibits alterations to the unit without the Landlord’s consent, and the Landlord’s consent was not obtained relative to the installation of the bidet (5657406, p. 44).

The Landlord said that the Tenant actually installed bidets in both bathrooms in the unit without her consent. She said that the Tenant initially tried installing the bidets themselves, which caused leaks in both bathrooms, and it was after this that the Landlord’s handyman properly installed them, without the Landlord’s knowledge at the time. I note that the photos of the leak with a bowl under the pipe presented by the Tenant were close-up photos of the pipe from the wall, and it cannot be determined from the photos if a bidet was installed at that point.

The Landlord presented a transcript of a voicemail she received from the condominium supervisor stating there is a leak from the unit’s bathroom (DOC-5657718, p. 6). The Landlord said she immediately had Roto Rooter attend to address this issue. At the time the Landlord did not know the cause of the leak, but said her handyman later told her that it was caused by the Tenant tampering with the pipe to install their bidet.

The Landlord presented a June 3, 2024 invoice from Roto Rooter (DOC-5657410, pp. 6-7). Under “description of work”, the invoice states: “When I arrived the fill valve was cracked and the shut off valve was not working. I replaced everything. Now everything is working well”.
On cross-examination, the Landlord acknowledged the cleaner would not know how to conduct a maintenance inspection, but said they would tell her if there was a water leak.

The Landlord also said on cross-examination that her handyman informed her on August 1, 2024 that he had installed the bidets for the Tenant, and that the leak was caused because the Tenant had previously tried to install the bidets themselves.

I prefer the Landlord’s evidence relative to the water leak issue. Each witness for the Tenant gave inconsistent evidence about when the leak was discovered (June 2 or June 3, 2024), and both changed their evidence about when this was discovered only when confronted with the fact that this issue was missing from the Realtor’s June 2, 2024 email.

Further, the Tenant’s evidence was that the leak was so bad that the bowl they were using to catch water had to be emptied every couple of hours. The Landlord’s evidence was that it was so bad the building management became aware of it on June 3, 2024. If there was a water leak this significant on June 2, 2024, when the Tenant either moved in or inspected the unit, it is unlikely it would not have been identified at this time.

I also find it is unlikely that the water leak was active before June 3, 2024 because if there were a significant leak, the Landlord’s cleaner likely would have informed her about it, the former tenant likely would have informed her about it, and/or building management would have likely informed her about it if it was impacting the unit below.
I do not find the Tenant’s evidence about this issue to be reliable given the inconsistencies and the illogical conclusions that would be required to accept their evidence.

I find it is more likely than not that the leak was caused when the Tenant tried to install a bidet themselves on June 3, 2024. It is logical that the leak started on June 3, 2024 given that the voicemail the Landlord received from building management.

The Tenant’s evidence was also not logical because they claim to have discovered the leak on June 3, 2024, and they emailed the Landlord about it on June 4, 2024, which is after Roto Rooter had attended to address the issue.
To the extent that the leak persisted after June 3, 2024, I do not accept that it was an active, significant leak. The Tenant’s evidence was that the pipe continued “dripping” after this time.

Taking the entire factual matrix into account, I find that the Landlord addressed the water leak in a timely and effective manner once she became aware of it, regardless of whether the Tenant caused the leak. The Landlord sent [name] immediately when she was made aware of the issue, and was informed by Roto Rooter that the issue was resolved that same day. While a minor leak may have persisted after this, the Landlord had it repaired in a timely manner as well.

The Tenant also presented a photo of the toilet flush lever, which the Tenant said was broken and taped with scotch tape. The Tenant’s evidence was that the lever was broken, but it still worked (DOC-7791871, p. 7). This issue was effectively addressed by August 29, 2024 (DOC-7791871, p. 28).

Whether this was addressed in a timely manner must be considered in the context of the significance of the issue. Given that the lever worked, I find this to have been a primarily aesthetic issue. Given this and all of the other more significant issues at the time, I find that issue was addressed in a timely and effective manner.
The T6 Application is dismissed as it relates to the bathroom leak and the flush lever. [name]

The Tenant’s evidence was that upon move in, one of the four stove burners was not working. The Tenant presented a photo of the stove. The knobs for all four burners are on, and three of them are evidently working because they are red. One of the two larger burners is not rent and not working (DOC-7791871, p. 8).

The Landlord said that when she was informed that one of the stove burners was not working, she called her handyman to have the issue addressed. She said that the handyman ordered a part, but when it arrived, it did not fit. The Landlord considered ordering a new oven/stove, but there was an issue with it fitting through the unit door. She said that the initial repair attempt was on June 29, 2024 after the part arrived. She said that the burner was repaired on August 11, 2024, and that she was working on getting the correct part the entire time.
The Tenant acknowledged the burner was working in an August 14, 2024 email to the Landlord (DOC-5657410, p. 28).
The Landlord presented an email from “Partselect.ca” dated June 27, 2024 confirming an order, which the Landlord said was the initial part ordered that was no compatible (DOC- 5657410, p 24).

I accept that the Tenant made the Landlord aware of this issue on June 2, 2024 through their [name]’s email, and again informed the Landlord about this issue directly on June 4, 2024. While the Landlord eventually addressed this issue in an effective manner, the burner remained inoperative until August 11, 2024. The Landlord said she was working on getting this fixed during this whole period, but aside from ordering the wrong part on June 27, 2024, there was no specific detail provided by the Landlord as to exactly what she was doing during this time or why it took so long. For example, it is not clear why the Landlord could not have called an appliance repair person to inspect and repair the burner when she was informed of the issue.

The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period June 2, 2024 to August 11, 2024 relative to the stove burner, which is a period of 70 days. The monthly rent at the time was $2,400.00. The per diem rate would therefore be $78.90 [$2,400.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days]. The Tenants paid a total of $5,523.00 for these 70 days based on the per diem rate.

A rent abatement is a remedy based on the premise that if one pays 100% of the rent, they should receive 100% of the value of what they pay for. An abatement of rent is intended to account for the proportion of that value the tenant did not receive because of the Landlord’s breach of the Act.

This is issue related to one of four burners on the stove. It was one of the two larger burners. There was no specific evidence as to how this issue impacted the Tenant during the relevant period. Remedies ordered by the LTB are compensatory. They are not punitive or intended to penalize a party.
Given the evidence before me, I find that this was a minor issue warranting only a modest rent abatement of 1% for the relevant period, being $55.23 ($5,523.00 x 1%). Gap in Door

The Tenant’s evidence was that there was a gap in the sliding door leading to the balcony, and it was about two centimeters wide. The Tenant presented several photos of the door ([name], pp. 9-10). The Tenant said that the door could not close more than what is depicted in the photos. The Tenant’s evidence was that heat, dust, wind, and noise from outside were all issues because the door could not fully close.
The Landlord presented a photo sent to her by her cleaner on May 31, 2024 which includes the balcony door. The doors are fully closed in the photo, and there is no gap (DOC-5657718, p. 2).

The Landlord’s evidence was that there was no gap in the door. She said there was no issue at all with the sliding glass doors, and the only issue was that a screen door was off the track. This is consistent with the photos presented by both parties.

The Tenant’s evidence was that they believe this issue was finally repaired around October 10 or 11, 2024 (DOC-7791871, p. 51-52). The Landlord acknowledged that the issue was finally resolved on October 11, 2024.

I accept that there was an issue with the screen doors, but not the glass doors. The Tenant’s allegations and evidence on this issue were inconsistent and confusing. For example, there being an issue with the screen doors would not cause issues with wind, noise, dust, or temperature in the unit. These things would permeate a screen door whether it is in good repair or not. To prevent or attenuate issues relative to wind, dust, noise, or temperature, one would need to close the glass door, which I have found was not in disrepair.

The Tenant’s allegation in the application was that: “There was a significant gap in the door to the patio, resulting in a draft permeating throughout the unit”. Later in the application, the Tenant claims: “On October 11th, a technician came in to fix the gap in the screen door. The repair person explained to the Landlord on the phone that the coasters for the door were very old and would need to be replaced. He was told not to complete the repair. As a result the door must remain closed, and the Tenant has lost access to the balcony” [emphasis added]. The first allegation about the door is clearly not an allegation about the screen door, as a draft would permeate a screen door whether it is in disrepair or not. The second allegation was not consistent with the evidence at the hearing, which was that the screen door was repaired on October 11, 2024.
In the remedies section of the application, the Tenant seeks a remedy relative to the screen door.

The Tenant’s complaints to the Landlord about the patio door were ostensibly about the glass door, because they complained about the temperature issues it allegedly caused. There was no evidence about when the Tenant specifically complained about the screen door. The only allegation about it in the application was that it wasn’t fixed on October 11, 2024, but the evidence at the hearing was that it was repaired on this date.
The Tenant did not discharge their burden of proof relative to this allegation. The T6 Application is dismissed as it relates to the allegation about the gap in the patio door. [name]

The Tenant presented a photo of a light fixture that has three lights. The bulb in one of the lights is burned out. The Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord told them to buy light bulbs, so they did. A burned out light bulb is a minor issue, and does not warrant a rent abatement. The Tenant may have been entitled to recover the cost paid for the light bulb, but this was not claimed in the application, and no evidence as to the cost of the light bulb was presented.
In the application the Tenant claimed reimbursement for a fridge light bulb, but there is no allegation about a fridge light bulb in the application.
The T6 Application is dismissed as it relates to the light bulb. [name]

The Tenant presented a photo of the fridge. There is no shelf above the crispers (DOC- 7791871, p. 9). The Tenant said the shelf was replaced around August 19 or 20, 2024. The Landlord said it was hard to find the correct shelf for the fridge, but that she ordered it as soon as she found it online.
I do not need to consider whether this issue was addressed in a timely and effective manner, because no remedies is requested relative to the shelf in the application.

On July 23, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord, stating that they had reported an issue with the fridge on July 21, 2024, which had been “.. giving trouble since …” July 20, 2024. The Tenant’s complaint was that the fridge was not working properly, food could not be preserved, and the food that was in the fridge had gone bad (DOC-7791871, p. 13).

The lease contained a provision stating that the Tenant was to pay the first $75.00 toward repairs. On July 23, 2024, the Tenant sent the Landlord $75.00 for the fridge repair (DOC- 7791871, p. 17). The fridge was repaired on that day, for a total cost of $324.41 (DOC- 7791871, p. 18). The provision of the lease requiring the Tenant to pay the first $75.00 toward any repairs in the unit is void because it is inconsistent with the Act, which provides that the Landlord is obligated to maintain the unit in a state of good repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards: ss. 3(1) & 20, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Although the Tenant claimed this $75.00 in the application, the Tenant’s evidence was that they think the Landlord later paid them the $75.00 back. The Landlord acknowledged the Tenant paid the $75.00, but said she later returned it to them.

I find that the Landlord addressed the issue with the fridge in a timely and effective manner. The issue with the fridge is one that ought to be addressed expeditiously, and I find that it was. It was repaired the day after the Tenant’s July 23, 2024 email, and on the third day after the initial July 21, 2024 complaint. I note the July 21, 2024 email was sent at 6:24 p.m., which was a Sunday evening. In the context of this issue, I find that having the fridge repaired on July 24, 2024 amounts to a timely repair.

On October 8, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord stating that the fridge was again not working properly. The Tenant said that it was not cold and food was spoiling. According to the Tenant, the issue was with a sensor, and it was repaired by October 17, 2024 (DOC- 7791871, p. 52). The Landlord did not present any cogent evidence as to why it took 9 days to have the fridge repaired in October, after a much more expeditious repair of the fridge in July.

As noted above, a fridge not functioning is an issue that ought to be addressed expeditiously. Absent a reasonable explanation, I find that the issue with the fridge in October was not addressed in a timely manner. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for 9 days in October 2024 when the fridge did not function properly.
The Tenant’s request for a 10% abatement relative to this issue is reasonable. This amounts to $71.00 ($78.90 x 9 days x 10%).

The Tenant also claimed out of pocket expenses for takeout meals during the time the fridge was not functional, but there was no cogent evidence presented relative to these alleged expenses, so they will not be ordered. No Cold Water in Kitchen

The Tenant said that there was no cold water in the kitchen for the first 88 days after they moved into the unit. The Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord denied there was an issue, but when the property manager attended, they said there is an issue with the tap and it needed to be replaced. The replacement occurred after 88 days, according to the Tenant.
The Tenant’s evidence was that this was an issue because they only had hot water in the kitchen, and they could not use it for washing fruits or vegetables, or for drinking.

The Landlord’s evidence was that the previous tenant of the unit told her there was no issue with water temperatures in the kitchen. I do not give this evidence any weight because it is hearsay, except to the extent that I accept the former tenant did not complain about this issue, so the Landlord would not have been aware of it before the Tenant complained about it.

The Landlord said that when she was made aware of the issue, she called a plumber and her handyman. She said the faucet was changed on June 15, 2024, and changed again on August 27, 2024. This is supported by a text message from the Tenant to the Landlord dated June 15, 2024 where the Tenant wrote “[k]itchen faucet is changed and supply of cold and hot water both is operational” (sic) (DOC-5657410, p. 12).

The Tenant did not give any evidence about the June 15, 2024 repair that they had acknowledged by text message. It is apparent that as of June 15, 2024 the Tenant had cold water in the unit, but that the issue later recurred. The only evidence as to when the issue was recurred was that the Landlord spoke with her handyman on August 1, 2024 (when he informed her about the bidets) because the Tenant had complained about cold water.
The issue had been effectively addressed by August 27, 2024 according to the Landlord, which is consistent with an August 29, 2024 email sent by the Tenant to the Landlord (DOC-7791871, p. 28).

The Landlord also presented a text message from her plumber after the issue was repaired, which identified the issue as cold water pressure and flow having been “low”, not absent (DOC-5357410, p. 30).

Since the required repair was only to replace the faucet, it is unclear why this took 12 days in June, or at least 27 days in August. Cold water is defined in the Act as a “vital service”, and is an issue that ought to be repaired expeditiously once a Landlord is aware of the issue. There was no explanation from the Landlord relative to these timelines, and I therefore find that the issue was not addressed in a timely or effective manner in June or in August. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for 39 days relative to the cold water issue (12 + 27). The Tenant is not entitled to a remedy for the period from June 16, 2024 to July 31, 2024 because they did not present cogent evidence relative to when the issue recurred after the June 15, 2024 faucet replacement.

The Tenant sought a 20% rent abatement relative to the cold water issue. I find this to be excessive. I do not find it reasonable that the Tenant’s lost 20% of the value of what the paid for during this period because of a lack of cold water in the kitchen. I find that a 10% abatement is more appropriate in the context.
This amounts to $307.71 [$78.90 x 39 days x 10%]. Paint Chip

The Tenant said that there was paint chipping, and the Landlord was informed because they did not later want to be blamed. The Tenant said the paint was chipping in random places, but presented no photos of the issue.

In the June 2, 2024 email from the Tenant’s Realtor, the paint chip issue is identified “… just for the record of how the apartment was received and no action is expected to be taken” (DOC-5657718, p. 5).

The Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish it is more likely than not that any paint chipping amounted to anything more than a minor aesthetic issue. The Tenant also did not request any repair relative to paint chipping.
The application is dismissed relative to the paint chip issue. [name]

The Tenant presented an email from the Landlord dated July 24, 2024 where the Landlord states that the unit and appliances were “… in perfect working condition” before the Tenant moved in (DOC-7791871, p. 14). The Tenant believes this was inappropriate because they claim the issues complained of were all present before the tenancy began, and were reported the day after they moved in. I do not find that this email rises to the level of harassment because I do not find that it was vexatious for the purpose of the relevant legal test.

Landlord’s are not held to a standard of perfection, and I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she sincerely believe the unit and its appliances were in a state of good repair at the time the tenancy began.

The Tenant also presented an email from the Tenant to the Landlord dated July 24, 2024 where the Tenant accused the Landlord of shouting and using inappropriate language during a phone call, including calling the Tenant “Desis”, which the Tenant said is a derogatory term for a rural, rugged person. The Tenant’s evidence was that use of the term is pejorative in this context (DOC-7791871, p. 14).

The Tenant also presented a transcript of a text message from the Landlord on June 13, 2024. The Landlord refers to “multiple issues” since the Tenant moved in, and wrote “It will be better for you to move in to some other place. I will refund all your money” (the Tenant had prepaid one year’s rent). The Tenant replied that moving out was not an option for them ([name], pp. 39-40). There was no evidence that the Landlord raised this issue again.

The Tenant also referred to phone calls between them and the Landlord on June 30, 2024 and July 11, 2024. The Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord was harassing them, claiming they were responsible for all the damage to the unit, and calling the Tenant “Desi” and “Pagal”. The Tenant said that “Pagal” means “crazy”.

In the Tenant’s documentary evidence package, a transcript of text messages between the parties and record of phone calls was included (DOC-7791871, pp 36-52). The Tenant could not identify use of the words “Desi” or “Pagal” in the text messages, and said this happened on a phone call.

KK said that when this phone call occurred, KK and the Tenant were all present. KK said that the Landlord was shouting, and calling the Tenant “Desi” and “Pagal”, and KK then took the phone. KK said that this was in June 2024 in the evening, and it was a 7-minute phone call.

KK initially said that these insults were first made to her mother, then her father, then to KK, but on cross-examination, KK then said the phone call from the Landlord came to their mother’s phone, but she was too anxious so their father answered the call, and later passed the phone to KK.
KK said that these terms are not necessarily derogatory, but that context matters. In a friendly relationship they may not be pejorative, but would be in an acrimonious relationship.

The Landlord denied ever having called the Tenant names or using derogatory language. The Landlord said she had phoned the Tenant to talk about adjusting a knob on the fridge. She said the male Tenant began yelling at her about the state of the unit, and the Landlord was asking to talk to the female Tenant. Instead, the phone was passed to KK, who the Landlord said was also being rude to her. The Landlord said she just wanted to talk about getting the fridge repaired, but began to feel overwhelmed, and hung up.

The Tenant has failed to present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlord called the Tenant “Desi” and “Pagal”. Such language is not consistent with any of the significant amount of written communication between the parties that was presented as evidence, in which the [name] is civil. Although the Landlord did accuse the Tenant of causing the damage they were complaining about, this is in the context of a number of issues the Landlord was previously unaware of. This is not similar to or consistent with pejorative name-calling.

KK’s evidence about the call was inconsistent relative to this issue, in that KK first said that the Landlord first used these terms toward her mother, then her father, then to KK, but then later said that her mother did not actually speak with the Landlord that day.

The Landlord and Tenant gave conflicting evidence about what was said on the phone call, but it is the Tenant who bears the burden of proof. I find no reason to prefer the Tenant’s evidence over the Landlord’s on this point, so the Tenant’s burden of proof has not been discharged.

The Landlord sent a single text message stating that it would be better for the Tenant to move out, and that she would refund all the Tenant’s money. This is a communication that the Landlord knew or ought to have known would be unwelcome. The Tenant had a lawful right to continue the tenancy, and there was no evidence that the Tenant suggested they wanted to move. The comment was also vexatious in that it was not made for a lawful or legitimate purpose.

However, this was a single message, and there was no evidence that the Landlord ever made any similar comment of statement after the Tenant informed that they did not intend to move. This was not a course of vexatious comment or conduct, but was rather an isolated comment in the context of a landlord and tenant relationship that had become fraught, and one party suggested ending the relationship by mutual agreement. This single comment, in context, does not rise to the level of harassment.
The T2 Application is dismissed. Remedies
For the foregoing reasons, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $433.94 [$55.23 + $71.00 + $307.71] for a rent abatement relative to the T6 Application.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file this application and is entitled to recover this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $481.94. This amount represents:  $433.94 for a rent abatement.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by July 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

With respect to the Tenant’s T1 application, I find that the application does not disclose a valid basis for relief. The Tenant sought compensation on the basis of an alleged N12- related eviction; however, no N12 Notice was ever served. The undisputed evidence was that the Landlord advised the Tenant of an intention to sell the property, and the Tenant chose to vacate the rental unit proactively due to concerns about a potential future purchaser. The Tenant was not required to vacate and did so voluntarily. Accordingly, there is no entitlement to compensation under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), and the T1 application must be dismissed.

With respect to the Tenant’s T2 application, I find that it is not properly before the Board. The Tenant’s allegations primarily relate to an asserted bad faith eviction arising from the Landlord’s intention to sell the property and the subsequent re-rental of the unit. Such allegations, if properly advanced, fall within the scope of a T5 application, not a T2 application. There was no request to amend the application prior to or at the hearing.

Moreover, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment or any of the other grounds alleged. The Landlord’s communication of an intention to sell the property does not, in itself, constitute substantial interference. The Tenant’s decision to vacate was based on their own assessment of potential future circumstances, rather than any conduct by the Landlord that required the Tenant to leave.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has not established any of the grounds claimed in either the T1 or T2 applications on a balance of probabilities.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: After the hearing on April 2, 2025, interim order LTB-T-061138-24-IN was issued on April 10, 2025, resolving the T1 application.
At the hearing on March 31, 2026, the parties agreed that the Landlord complied with order LTB-T-061138-24-IN. T2 Application:
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants live in the basement of a house which is divided into two units. There is an upper unit where the Landlord’s sister and brother-in-law reside. There is only one thermostat, and it is located in the upper unit. The furnace is electric.
The monthly rent is $1,350.00, due on the first day of each month.
The utilities are divided between the parties with the upper paying 60% and the Tenants paying 40%.
The Tenants allege that the Landlord has failed to adequately respond to their complaints about insufficient heat in the winter and freezing air conditioning all summer.

The Tenants said that they first began to complain to the Landlord on December 28, 2023. They submitted into evidence a text written on December 28, 2023, in which they write to the Landlord, “….could you tell the upstairs tenants to please keep the heat on and have it set to a minimum of 21 degrees. The basement keeps getting super cold. We even went out and bought a thermometer verify (sic) if it’s below 21 degrees.” They include a photo of a thermometer reading of 18.2 degrees centigrade. The Landlord replied to them saying, “Yes on it.”

The Tenants said the temperature was all right for a while afterward. They said that they did not want to complain too much, and they started using their gas fireplace to supplement the heat. They said that the fireplace only heats the front room, not their bedroom, back room, kitchen or bathroom.

The Tenants submitted into evidence the Landlord’s response to their next complaint on March 13, 2024. He responds that the upstairs is set to 22, and “any higher and their new born baby is unable to sleep due to the heat upstairs. I hope you can understand due to these circumstances. It is a basement which will be colder than the rest of the house. I can offer you a heater if need be….”

The Tenants submitted into evidence a number of temperature readings from March 2024 and April 2024, which show temperatures between 17.7 and 19.5 degrees. They said that the upper tenants had the air conditioning running at times in April 2024. They said that the Landlord kept responding in a similar way, telling them the temperature upstairs was set above 21 degrees, or that they, the Tenants, should run space heaters. They said that as of April 8, 2024, the Landlord began to suggest that they leave. The Landlord wrote to them on April 8, 2024, saying “You are welcome to look for a new rental unit…As for temperature the house is set at 24. My hands are tied, you are welcome to find a new unit to rent please give me notice (sic).”

The Tenants said that the Landlord served them with a document on May 9, 2024, that informed them the City was evicting them because the unit was not up to fire code. They submitted into evidence an order to comply from the City of Pickering to the Landlord, dated May 7, 2024. The order to comply said that the Landlord had to obtain a building permit for an “accessory dwelling unit or restore the basement back to the original approved conditions by no later than June 20th, 2024.” They said the Landlord did not pursue them further until he served them with an N12 notice for Landlord’s own use in May 2025. The Landlord’s application based on that N12 notice was dismissed, as a result of a finding that the Landlord had not proved a good faith intention to reside in the rental unit. The order LTB-L-046516-25 dismissing the Landlord’s application was issued on January 7, 2026.

The Tenants said that, for the last two years, the Landlord has not done anything differently to address their concerns. They said that they asked him to move the thermostat to a communal area, but he failed to do it, and he refuses to install a second thermostat. They said that they have complained over 50 times in the last two years.

The Tenants said that in the winter of 2023-2024, the temperature was below 20 degrees about 80% of the time. This was also true, they said, in Spring and Summer of 2024 because the upstairs tenants were running the air conditioning very low. They said the temperature was all right between August 2024 and March 2025, but then from mid-March 2025 to mid-June 2025, the temperature was below 20 degrees 60% of the time. From June to September 2025, they said the temperature was all right and then September 2025 the temperature was too low 60% of the time. The Tenants said that October 2025 to February 2026 was all right, but by February 2026 they started suffering from freezing temperatures again, about 25% of the time, mostly at night.
The Tenants said that when the temperatures were very low, they had to sleep in warm clothing, use heating blankets, and it was so cold it sometimes woke them up at night.

The Tenants request a rent abatement for the substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of their unit. They also request that the Board order the Landlord to install a second thermostat.

The Landlord said that he has asked the upstairs tenants to set the thermostat at 24 degrees. He said that the Tenants refuse to use the gas fireplace in their unit, but he said that he has not been in their unit to check how much heat the fireplace emits.
The Landlord said that he got a quote for a second thermostat, and it was prohibitively expensive at about $3,000-4,000.00. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that the Tenants have proved the allegations in their application for the following reasons.

Subsection 21(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.
The City of Pickering bylaw on heating systems provides that every dwelling unit shall have heating equipment capable of maintaining a temperature of 20 degrees Celsius.
It is undisputed that the residential complex has only one furnace, and one thermostat, located in the upper unit. The Tenants have no control, nor access, to the thermostat.
The Tenants had extensive photographic and testimonial evidence that the temperature of their rental unit was frequently below 20 degrees Celsius since December 2023.

The Tenants informed the Landlord as of December 2023, that there was a problem in their unit. They did not have evidence of a repeat complaint until March 2024. However, the Landlord’s response was repeatedly the same. He either replied that he told the upstairs tenants to increase the temperature, or the upstairs tenants were unable to increase the temperature due to an issue with their baby, or that he would supply space heaters to the Tenants, or he told them to use their gas fireplace. Sometimes the Landlord alleged that the Tenants’ temperature readings were inaccurate. It is undisputed that the Landlord never attended the rental unit to take his own temperature readings, nor did he inspect the rental unit to see how much heat was provided by the gas fireplace. It is also undisputed that the Landlord never attempted to install a second thermostat over which the Tenants would have control.

I find that the Landlord was well aware by April 2024, that there was a problem with insufficient heat in the Tenants’ rental unit. The evidence is that by April 8, 2024, the Landlord attempted to have the Tenants vacate the unit rather than take more proactive steps to address the heat inadequacy. The Landlord first tried to get the Tenants to leave in May 2024 by showing them the City’s order to comply. Then he served them with at least two N12 notices of termination. On one of the N12 notices, the Landlord filed an application that was ultimately dismissed after a hearing before the Board.

The Landlord has an obligation to supply sufficient heat pursuant to subsection 21(1) of the Act cited above, and also by virtue of the municipality by-laws. The Landlord was informed by the Tenants that he was not providing sufficient heat, yet he did very little to either inspect, or to address the problem. The problem is ongoing. The Tenants have provided detailed dates when they suffered from the problem, and there are periods when they did not suffer from the problem as much, either because the upstairs tenants were keeping the thermostat at an adequate temperature or the outside temperatures were not as cold. I therefore find the Tenants’ evidence credible. Erratic periods of adequate temperatures, and then very inadequate temperatures are consistent with what the Landlord either did, or what he failed to do, which was occasionally telling the upstairs tenants to increase the thermostat, and not installing a thermostat system over which the Tenants had any control. While the Tenants said that most of the current winter has not been as problematic, they said that as of two months prior to the hearing, they were again suffering from the extreme cold at least 25% of the time. The last two months were, in general, very cold.

The Landlord was informed of the problem, the problem has been ongoing for almost 2 ½ years, the Landlord failed to adequately address the problem. It is the Landlord’s responsibility to ensure that there is adequate heat in the rental unit, and he has breached this responsibility. Therefore, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household by failing to provide adequate heat to the rental unit. The Tenants are entitled to a remedy for the substantial interference.

The Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement for the period January through August 2024, then mid-March through mid-June 2025, September 2025, and from February 2026 and ongoing until the issue is resolved. They will be entitled to an ongoing rent abatement until the Landlord installs a separately zoned thermostat system for the basement unit over which the Tenants have control.

I find that the Tenants are entitled to the 33% rent abatement they requested for the eight months from January through August 2024 (or $1,350.00 X 33% annual X 8 months)=$3,564.00. This substantial abatement takes account of the ongoing suffering and discomfort of the Tenants throughout this period. They were unable to sleep properly, they had to wear extra clothing, nor were they comfortable in their unit for a sustained period. For the period mid-March through mid-June 2025, the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of 20% or ($1,350.00 X 20% X 3)=$810.00. For September 2025, the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of 20%=$270.00. For the period commencing February 1, 2026, and ongoing until the Landlord installs a zoned thermostat system where the Tenants have control over their unit, the Tenants will be entitled to an ongoing 10% rent abatement, or $135.00 per month at the current rent amount. The total abatement is $4,914.00 to the date of the hearing, and then an ongoing 10% of the rent commencing April 1, 2026, until the Landlord installs a zoned thermostat for the Tenants’ unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,962.00. This amount represents: • $4,914.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

Commencing April 1, 2026, and continuing each month the Tenants have the right to deduct 10% from the monthly rent until the Landlord installs a zoned thermostat system with a thermostat to which the Tenants have access and control.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 23, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting it from the rent each month until the full amount is paid.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges the Landlord has collected or retained money illegally.

This application is brought under section 135 of the Act. Pursuant to subsection 135(4), such an application must be filed within one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of the Act.
The tenancy in question was for the period from September 1, 2023, to August 31, 2024, and a monthly rent of $2,650.00.
On September 2, 2023, the Tenant paid the Landlord $5,300.00, which represents the first and last month’s rent deposit.
On September 5, 2023, the Tenant paid the Landlord $26,800.00, which represents a $300.00 key deposit and 10 months of rent.
The Tenant filed her application on August 7, 2025, which is more than the one year after the Landlord collected the amounts referred to in paragraphs 4 and 5 above.

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. In this case, the last rent period would have been August 31, 2024, which is within the one-year limitation period. As such, the only issue we may consider is with respect to the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,650.00 as the parties agree the $300.00 key deposit has been returned. Did the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold consent to sublet?

The Tenant seems to argue that the money paid to the Landlord ought to be returned because the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant.

As noted above, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant (LTB- T-019340-24). That application was dismissed by the Board on April 7, 2026. MH attempted to argue that the Board made a finding that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the sublet and that the only portion of the decision that was reversed on review was the portion pertaining to the award of money. As explained several times during the hearing, this is incorrect.

The doctrine of res judicata operates to ensure finality of decisions and prevent abuse of process. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue. In effect, it prevents a “second kick at the can.” It has two aspects, issue estoppel, and cause of action estoppel. The test for issue estoppel has three elements, which must all be present: 1) The same question has been decided; 2) The decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and 3) The parties to the prior decision are the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised.

The Board has a residual discretion as to whether to apply the doctrine of res judicata even if all three of these criteria are satisfied. Further, res judicata or issue estoppel should not be applied in circumstances that would create an injustice.

We find that the question as to whether the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant has been decided in LTB-T-019340-24. The initial decision was issued on June 27, 2025. On September 5, 2025, the Member found that the order issued on June 27, 2025, contained serious errors. As such, the June 27, 2025, order was cancelled, and the matter was referred to a de novo hearing. The de novo hearing was held on November 10, 2025, and an order was issued on November 14, 2025, dismissing the Tenant’s application. That decision was upheld on April 7, 2025.
The April 7, 2025, decision is final. The parties to the prior decision are the same person as the parties to this proceeding and involve the same rental unit.

We do, however, find that the circumstances warrant an exercise of our residual discretion to not apply the doctrine of res judicata. Supreme Court of Canada addressed issue estoppel in [name], 2001 SCC 44, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 460 (‘Danyluk’), para 33: The rules governing issue estoppel should not be mechanically applied. The underlying purpose is to balance the public interest in the finality of litigation with the public interest in ensuring that justice is done on the facts of a particular case. … the court must still determine whether, as a matter of discretion, issue estoppel ought to be applied.

The Tenant’s application (LTB-T-019340-24) was dismissed because the Tenant failed to attend the de novo hearing on November 10, 2025. Given this, we feel that it is reasonable to make a determination as to whether the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to sublet the rental unit to the subtenant.

On February 8, 2024, MH emailed the Landlord to advise that the Tenant would be traveling to Iran for a family emergency for a couple of months and that the Tenant was seeking the consent of the Landlord to sublet the rental unit to her sister-in-law. On February 12, 2024, the Landlord’s agent, [name] (‘TC’), responded requesting additionally information as the email was not from the Tenant and MH’s connection to the Tenant was unclear. [name] requested that written notice come directly from the Tenant.

At 3:46 p.m. on February 12, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord to advise that she wanted to sublet the rental unit as she had to leave the country. Consent to sublet the rental unit was provided by the Landlord.

Email communication establishes that on February 19, 2024, [name] advised the Tenant that the potential subtenant’s application and document were under review. On February 20, 2024, MH advised [name] that he no longer represented the Tenant and the potential subtenant’s offer would expire 6:00 p.m. that same day. [name] reached out to the Tenant to determine whether she wanted TC to resolve the subtenancy issue directly. [name] testified that on February 21, 2024, the Tenant called him from the airport to advise that she was not going to sublease as she would be returning in a few months.

We are satisfied the Landlord consented to the Tenant taking the necessary steps to sublet the rental unit. We do not believe the Landlord is responsible for the first potential subtenant withdrawing their offer. Landlords are entitled to do their due diligence in approving a potential subtenant. We do not find the Landlord’s review and approval process was unreasonable. We also do not believe the Landlord refused to consent to the second potential subtenant as it is clear this offer was revoked by MH. There is no evidence before us establishing the Tenant made any further request to sublet. Is the Landlord obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit?

As the Landlord did not consent to a potential subtenant, the Tenant was bound to the terms of her tenancy agreement. There is no evidence before us establishing that the Tenant advised the Landlord that she had vacated the rental unit. This is supported by the fact that on July 15, 2024, [name] emailed the Tenant to remind her that her fixed-term tenancy expired on August 31, 2024, and was seeking confirmation as to whether she wished to remain in the unit. We further find that MH’s email to [name] on August 6, 2024, does little in establishing that the Tenant did not maintain possession of the rental unit. 21. [name] testified in July 2024, the Landlord learned that [name] (‘Reza’) was residing in the unit and apparently had been living there since February 2024 despite the Landlord advising the Tenant this his occupancy had not been approved. The Tenant’s tenancy terminated on August 31, 2024. 22. Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. The last month’s rent deposit was applied to the rent for August 2024, which was the last rent period. The Tenant presented no evidence establishing that [name] or another individual paid the Landlord rent for August 2024. As such, the Landlord was not obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenant. 23. As explained above, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. __________________________ [name] Vice-Chair, Landlord and Tenant Board June 3, 2026
