issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (the ‘T2 application’). This combined application was heard by videoconference on April 2, 2026, and May 14, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord attended the hearing. On April 2, 2026, the Tenant consulted with [name] prior to the commencement of the hearing. The Landlord was represented by [name].
reasons: This application is about a rural one and a half storey farmhouse that was built in the early 1900s. the Tenant and her family moved into it on January 1, 2022. The Tenant’s now former partner moved out in September of 2023, and the tenancy continued with the Tenant as the sole tenant. The Tenant and her children continued to live in the rental unit until the Landlord succeeded in obtaining an eviction order from the Board for demolition. (See Board order LTB-L-028175-25 issued November 4, 2025.) The Tenant returned vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord on or before December 1, 2025, and it was demolished sometime between April 2, 2026 and May 14, 2026.

The bulk of the Tenant’s application concerns disrepair. With some exceptions noted below, the Landlord does not deny that the rental unit was in a state of disrepair. She says that the disrepair was so extensive she could not afford to do many of the necessary repairs, so a few months into the tenancy she served the first of a number of notices of termination for demolition.

The T2 Application is somewhat duplicative in that it addresses the lack of heat issue, snow removal and yard maintenance which are covered by the T6 Application, but it also alleges the Landlord breached the Act with respect to attempts to evict the Tenant and refusing to allow the Tenant to put hydro in her name as stipulated in the tenancy agreement.

For the reasons set out below, the Tenant’s T2 Application is denied, the T6 Application is granted in part and denied in part, and the Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant a total of $12,800.00 for abatement of the rent, general compensation and out of pocket expenses. THE T2 APPLICATION
As I explained at the hearing, much of the Tenant’s T2 Application is out of time.

Pursuant to s. 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), no application can be made under s. 29(1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. On a T6 application the alleged conduct giving rise to the application is a landlord’s failure to effect repair, so the one-year limitation period does not start to run until the landlord does the repair. In contrast, a T2 application is about specific incidents that occur at identifiable points in time, so the Board has no jurisdiction to grant remedies with respect to incidents alleged that occurred more than one year prior to the filing of the tenant’s application.
The application here was filed with the Board on July 25, 2024.

The T2 Application complains the Landlord served multiple notices of termination for demolition and attempted or threatened to change the locks on the termination dates in the notices. All of the notices complained of in the T2 Application except one were served on the Tenant prior to July 25, 2023, so are beyond the Board’s jurisdiction. The one mentioned in the application that was issued during the period over which the Board has jurisdiction was issued on October 12, 2023. That was a notice of termination for demolition.

It is not harassment to issue a notice of termination to a tenant in good faith. Given that the Landlord did in fact demolish the rental unit once she obtained vacant possession it cannot be said the notice of termination in question was not issued in good faith. With respect to the threats to change the locks, the application fails to provide an in-time date for any such activity.
So the parts of the T2 Application that concern the notices of termination and attempts to change the locks are dismissed.

The T2 Application also complains that the tenancy agreement between the parties says that hydro was the Tenant’s responsibility and the account was to be put in the name of the Tenant’s former partner. According to the Tenant, her former partner did not put the account in his name at the beginning of the tenancy because there were outstanding electrical issues at the time that they were waiting to be fixed. So the Tenant would get the hydro bill from the Landlord and remit payment to her.

The Tenant’s former partner moved out in September of 2023. At some point after that the Tenant contacted Algoma Power about putting the account into her name and received a text confirming that the Landlord did not want the account transferred out of her name at that time. That text appears to be dated January 15th but no year is provided. Given the surrounding evidence, and lack of testimony to the contrary, I believe this denial occurred in January of 2024, which is basically just after the Tenant became the tenant of the rental unit and within the one-year limitation period over which the Board has jurisdiction.

The Tenant says this repudiation of the lease clause that said the hydro account was to be in the Tenant’s name impacted her negatively because it was a lost opportunity to build a credit record. With a better credit record she might have been able to find another place to live or even buy a property.

The difficulty that arises with this part of the T2 Application is that it is based on the right set out in section 22 which says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. [Emphasis added.]

Given the speculative and conditional nature of the impact the Tenant alleges occurred (being the opportunity to build a credit rating sufficient to find alternative housing) I am not satisfied the Landlord’s behaviour rises to the level of a substantial interference. It was definitely an interference as it was a lost opportunity that might have benefited the Tenant, but I am not satisfied it was a “substantial” one based on the scant evidence provided. So this part of the Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed.

The balance of the Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed as duplicative as it is about maintenance issues included in the T6 Application which are dealt with below: lack of heat; snow removal; and yard maintenance.
As a result, the T2 Application is dismissed in its entirety. THE T6 APPLICATION

To summarise in my own words, the Tenant’s T6 application alleges the Landlord breached s. 20(1) of the Act with respect to: • A lack of heat, issues with the wood stove and chimney, and problems with the exterior envelope resulting in the rental unit not being weathertight and permitting entry of pests; • Missing window screens; • Lead paint; • Damaged and missing doors; • Handrails on the exterior stairs were missing or in disrepair; • The interior stairwell had no railing and the stairs were damaged; [name] washing machine drainage; • Airborne particulates of insulation, interior water damage and closet problems; • Cabinets and drawers in the kitchen; • Electrical issues; • Laneway potholes, snow removal (which is mentioned in the remedies section of the T6) and yard maintenance; and • Septic system issues.
No evidence was led with respect to the presence of lead paint in the rental unit so that part of the Tenant’s T6 Application is dismissed for lack of evidence. The Legal Framework

The T6 Application rests on the rights and responsibilities set out in s. 20(1) of the Act which says: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

This provision imposes three separate obligations on the Landlord: to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair; ensure that the rental unit is fit for habitation; and comply with all health, safety and housing standards.

Pursuant to the Court of Appeal’s decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 47 a finding of liability is not automatic for every breach of maintenance as soon as it occurs. The Board is to consider the context including the landlord’s conduct and the surrounding circumstances to determine whether a breach has occurred. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 the context includes an exploration of whether the Landlord responded to the disrepair in a timely and effective manner.

With respect to the third of the obligations imposed by s. 20(1), the rental unit here is subject to the maintenance standards set out in Ontario Regulation 516/06 because the local township does not have a property standards by-law (see s. 224(1)(a) of the Act). The Evidence of Breaches of s. 20(1)

In response to the Tenant’s complaints the local township issued a Provincial Work Order on March 19, 2025. It says: • The foundation and the roof are not weathertight; • The foundation is deteriorating; • The upstairs washroom door cannot be locked from the inside; • The rental unit is not heated to 20 degrees Celsius; • Space heaters are being used as the primary source of heat; • The main entrance door is broken and not weathertight; • Exterior guardrails and handrails are in disrepair or lacking; • The interior stairs are missing the required handrail; • The interior stairs are in disrepair and not smooth; • The kitchen ceiling is cracking and is water damaged; • The kitchen cabinetry is in a state of disrepair; and • A pipe which is now capped came through into a bedroom upstairs.

The Tenant gave detailed evidence about the nature of the disrepair complained of (except for the allegation with respect to lead paint) and its impact on her that corroborates the contents of the Provincial Work Order and the other allegations in the application.

The Landlord did not lead evidence with respect to the majority of the Tenant’s disrepair complaints, nor did she refute any of the breaches described in the Provincial Work Order issued on March 19, 2025. And she also does not deny the Tenant complained to her about all of the issues listed in the application. The Insulation Issue

But the Landlord did testify that the insulation was never tested to determine if it was asbestos because the Tenant failed to provide an adequate sample. The Tenant denies failing to cooperate with the Landlord in providing a sample, but she did not test it either. According to the Tenant, a governmental authority told her that given the age of the building the insulation may or may not be made of a harmful material. That means I have no idea if the insulation was made of a hazardous material or not.

That being said, I am satisfied that insulation that is so old that it is decomposing and present as particles in the air as is the case here, is insulation that is not in a good state of repair. [name]
Pursuant to s. 26(1) of O.Reg. 517/06 the Landlord is responsible for removing “noxious weeds as defined in the regulations to the Weed Control Act”.

The Landlord states that she got a letter from a by-law officer about clearing “noxious weeds” in the yard, took photographs for him and asked for more detail about the area to be cleared, but got no response.

The Tenant’s evidence was with respect to burdock, but burdock is not a listed noxious weed in the regulations to the Weed Control Act and no evidence was led in support of the proposition that the plants the Tenant complains of are in fact “noxious weeds”. As a result, this part of the Tenant’s application must also be dismissed. The Washing Machine
With respect to the drainage from the washing machine the problem is that wastewater from it drains directly to the outdoors where it can enter a nearby creek.

The Landlord says she got a message from an unknown source telling her the plumbing had to be re-routed. She did not comply because laundry was not included in the tenancy agreement. Neither party produced the written lease agreement.

But the Landlord does not dispute that the laundry machines were present and in the unit when it was rented to the Tenant and capable of being used. The reason this is important is because s. 40(1) of O.Reg. 517/06 says any appliances supplied by the Landlord shall be maintained in a good state of repair and in safe operable condition so by leaving them in the unit the Landlord became responsible for ensuring they were in a good state of repair and incompliance with all housing standards.

That being said, although I strongly suspect there is some legal standard that says wastewater from a washing machine must be drained into a suitable septic system, I am not aware of any specific such legal standard and no evidence was led of one at the hearing. As a result, the evidence is insufficient to establish the way the washing machine operated and drained is a breach of s. 20(1). Therefore, the Tenant’s claim with respect to the drainage of the washing machine is also dismissed. Context: Did the [name] to Complaints in a Timely and [name]?

With respect to the other complaints raised in the T6 application, the Landlord led no evidence with respect to them. As a result, I accept the Tenant’s testimony in its entirety with respect to her descriptions of the nature of the disrepair issues.
That means the next issue for the Board is to determine whether the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints of disrepair in a timely and effective manner.

The Landlord did do some things in response to the Tenant’s complaints. • Electrical work was done that seems to have satisfied the Tenant although it is not clear when that was. (Absent evidence as to when the issue was resolved, it is impossible to determine if the disrepair existed during the one-year period prior to the filing of the application. That means I cannot determine if this issue is within the Board’s jurisdiction. As a result, no remedy shall flow to the Tenant with respect to electrical issues.) • The wood stove was replaced sometime in 2023, and an extension of the chimney was installed, but the Tenant continued to need to use space heaters as a primary source of heat and the lack of weathertightness of the building envelope continued. • When the Tenant complained about snow removal from the laneway the Landlord organised someone to do it, but the Landlord could not say when that was. Based on the Tenant’s evidence that was probably around December of 2024. • In the summer of 2024, the Landlord got a local company to put some gravel down on the laneway, but it did not grade or cover the entirety of the laneway area. • The Landlord did pump out the sewage tank on an unknown number of occasions but did not address the apparent failure of the septic bed.

Given all of the above I am satisfied that the rental unit was in a significant state of disrepair throughout the tenancy and the Landlord failed to respond to most of the Tenant’s complaints in a timely or effective manner.

The Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s disrepair application is two-fold. The Landlord says that when she discovered the depth of the disrepair problems shortly after the Tenant moved in, she served notice to terminate on the Tenant for demolition, and the Tenant should have moved out pursuant to the notice. Further the Landlord says the nature of the disrepair complained of was such that some, if not all, of the repairs would have been beyond the Landlord’s means.

With respect to the second of these positions, I am of the view that impecuniosity is not a defence to an application to the Board based on the rights and responsibilities set out in s. 20(1) of the Act. As set out in Interpretation Guideline 5 “Breach of Maintenance Obligations”: It is not a proper defence to such an application that the landlord needs the money for other purposes, even for other repairs. If there are many repairs necessary in a complex, the Member could take into account that some work should come first, and delay an order for other repairs. However, the obligation to maintain residential premises is not subject to whether the landlord has available funds. [Emphasis added.]

Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding on me, I agree with this statement. I say this because a landlord’s obligations under s. 20(1) are contractual in nature. Where there is a breach of contract, normal liability flows. If a contract cannot be fulfilled due to unforeseen outside circumstances, someone must bear the impact of that. In contract law the person who has contracted to provide something, and who now cannot do so, is the one who must suffer the loss. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s claims of limited means are not relevant to the question of whether or not the Landlord has breached s. 20(1) of the Act.

As for the argument that the Tenant should have moved out pursuant to the multiple notices of termination served on her, the problem with that argument is the Act enshrines the concept of security of tenure. The Tenant was entitled to live in the rental unit after notice of termination was served and after the termination date and continuing up to the date a Board order evicting her was enforced by the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff). Further, the tenant’s rights provisions in the Act continue throughout the occupancy of the unit. They do not cease to have effect just because a notice of termination has been served.

During the course of giving testimony the Landlord also remarked that the Tenant was aware of some of the issues prior to entering into the tenancy agreement. The Act specifically speaks to that issue. Subsection 20(2) says the rights and obligations set out in s. 20(1) apply even if the tenant is aware of the state of non-repair or contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

During final submissions the Landlord also argued that it should be expected that a house of the age of the rental unit would have major issues. There are many homes known to me that are more than a hundred years old that are in immaculate condition. More importantly, the Act applies to every rental unit regardless of the age of the rental unit.
As a result of all of the above, and with the exceptions noted, I am satisfied that the Landlord breached s. 20(1) of the Act. Remedies

The T6 Application seeks as remedies: abatement of the rent; compensation for damaged property; out of pocket expenses; an order for repairs, an order prohibiting a rent increase (‘OPRI’); and general compensation for “stress and mental anguish and injury to … dignity, feelings and self-respect”.
As the tenancy has terminated and the rental unit been demolished, the requests for an order for repairs and an OPRI are now moot and shall not be ordered.

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy. It is designed to address the idea that a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving those goods and services, the rent should be abated proportionate to the difference between what the tenant is paying for and what is actually received.

The Board will look at a number of factors when determining quantum of abatement including but not limited to: the proportion of the rental unit affected; the length of time the disrepair was ongoing; the seriousness and nature of the disrepair; and its impact on the Tenant.

The period for abatement under consideration here runs from July 25, 2023 (one year prior to the date the application was filed) to December 1, 2025 (when the Tenant returned vacant possession to the Landlord). I would point out at this juncture that during final submissions the Landlord submitted that the Tenant was claiming to have moved out in September of 2025, but the Landlord was taking the position vacant possession was not returned until December 1, 2025. The Tenant in fact did not refute the tenancy terminated on December 1, 2025, which is when vacant possession was returned to the Landlord. As a result, that is the appropriate end date for any abatement claim.
The rent charged throughout the tenancy remained at $800.00 a month. The T6 Application asks for abatement of the rent in the amount of $700.00 a month.

During final submissions the Tenant asked that the Board focus its monetary award on the request in the application for general damages in the nature of pain and suffering. Such an award is available to the Board pursuant to s. 30(1)9, but awards for pain and suffering for breach of contract are primarily appropriate in the situation where abatement alone does not recognize the true impact on the Tenant and her household with respect to the breach in question.

It seems to me that the Tenant’s complaints with respect to lack of heat, the lack of hand railings and disrepair to the stairs, are complaints appropriately addressed with an award for general damages. I say this because it is the uncontested evidence before the Board that the Tenant has a medical condition called postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (‘POTS’) which she told the Landlord about when she and her former partner were viewing the unit prior to renting it. They specifically discussed the need for hand railings which were missing from the interior stairs and wobbly or missing on the exterior stairs. The reason this is important is that because of her condition the Tenant is prone to fainting. Flare ups of her condition occur from stress or environmental factors like insufficient heat which causes difficulties with body temperature regulation and blood pressure dysregulation. This means that the Tenant was differentially impacted by the lack of heat, the disrepair to the stairs and the lack of railings due to her disability. I am therefore satisfied that abatement would not compensate her adequately for those impacts so the claims related to those disrepair items shall be excluded from the calculation of the abatement and dealt with by an award for damages for pain and suffering instead.
With respect to abatement of the rent, the Tenant was not receiving all of the goods and services being paid for throughout the relevant period.

There were vermin. The foundation was crumbling, at least one basement window was broken and there were multiple points of entry for vermin to enter which they did. The Tenant put out traps which caught mice, rats and weasels. The rodents would run up the walls and could be heard chewing things.

The wind lifted roofing nails resulting in leaking during rain in the mudroom and damage to the fascia which was also an entry point for vermin. The mudroom door was damaged and not weathertight. Rain and snow would penetrate five to six feet into the house.
The ceiling was water damaged in the kitchen and was opened when the pipes burst and never fixed. The kitchen cabinetry included a cracked cabinet door and drawer that did not close properly.

There was an open hole in a bedroom floor where a cook stove pipe had been removed. The Tenant and her former partner taped it up to prevent the particles of insulation from entering. None of the bedrooms had doors.

The laneway to the rental unit was shared by the Landlord, the Tenant, and the cell tower company that rented land from the Landlord. It also functioned as the Tenant’s driveway. The surface of the laneway was potholed and the culverts were damaged leaving sharp edges.

The lease agreement between the parties says the Tenant could use the tractor to remove snow if the Landlord was able to provide parts so it could be repaired. The Landlord determined providing parts and repairing the tractor was not feasible, so the tractor was never repaired. And pursuant to O.Reg. 516/07 s. 26(1)5 it was the Landlord’s responsibility to clear any unsafe accumulations of ice and snow.
The windows lacked screens, and if they were open the falling insulation would enter so the Tenant did not open them in the summer.

The property was served by a septic system. There was an access point to the septic system close to the house that had a wooden lid on it. Every spring that lid would be floating due to raw sewage escaping from the system. Sometimes it happened more than once a year. The Landlord would have someone pump out the septic tank but that did not address whatever problem was causing the septic system to malfunction in this manner. As a result, the Tenant did not let her children or the dog play in that part of the yard.

Behind the dining room was a closet that had a trap door leading to the basement. It was unlit and unventilated and covered with a black substance that smelt bad. The Tenant did not use it and as her ten year old has asthma, had an air cleaning system for her bedroom.

As can be seen from the narrative above, even excluding the issue of lack of heat and the stair and handrail issues, the disrepair to the rental unit was not insignificant. Given the nature of the disrepair, the impacts on the Tenant and her family, the seasonal or occasional nature of some of the disrepair problems complained of, the Landlord’s effort to remedy the snow removal issues late in the tenancy, and my knowledge of similar like cases, it seems to me a reasonable abatement of the rent would be about 25% of the rent charged for the relevant period which I fix at $5,600.00.
That brings me to the claim for damages for pain and suffering for the lack of heat issue and the condition of the railings and stairs.

Sometime in July of 2023 the Landlord replaced the wood stove and after that the chimney flue was lengthened. Given the totality of the evidence before me, I do not believe there was anything wrong with the stove. Rather, the rental unit was so lacking in proper insulation and weathertightness that it was impossible to heat the rental unit adequately with just the one wood stove. At the beginning of the tenancy the Landlord supplied some space heaters. At some point in time two of them caught fire and the others stopped working, so the Tenant replaced them herself.
Despite the wood stove and multiple space heaters, during the winter the rental unit was frequently cold. Multiple screen shots of temperature readings and the Provincial Work Order corroborate that.

Because of the cold in the winter, the Tenant’s children would keep their winter coats on, and crawl into bed with her at night. They told her they felt like they were camping. Approximately twice a week they would bathe elsewhere because of the cold in the bathroom and once a week the Tenant would go to the local swimming pool and shower there.

The cold meant the pipes were in danger of freezing so she had to let water drip constantly and use a blow dryer to prevent the pipes from freezing. That meant leaving home for any length of time was stressful. In January of 2025 the pipes burst.

With respect to the interior handrailing for the stairs, the Tenant told the Landlord when viewing the unit that she her condition means she faints quite often so she asked that the missing railing be replaced. It never was, so for both herself and her children, using the stairs was stressful. The children had to go down them on their bottoms. The exterior stairs were very steep and there should have been railings on both sides but there were not. The only section of railing present was wobbly and unsafe. The Tenant refused to let the children play there.

Given the seriousness of the problems associated with the lack of heat and the missing and unsafe hand railings, the particular vulnerability of the Tenant because of her disability, and taking into account that the heat issue was only relevant for half of each year, along with my knowledge of similar like cases, it seems to me a reasonable award for general compensation would be $6,000.00.
That leaves the claims for out of pocket expenses and damaged property.

The damaged property is a reference to a truck the Tenant was driving that had to be towed from the laneway and repaired in September of 2023. The Tenant blames the disrepair to the truck on the potholes in the laneway but she also says the mechanic told her the damage was likely caused by potholes and “wear and tear”. The vehicle was more than ten years old and had 100,000 kilometers on it. The receipt the Tenant located prior to the second hearing date did not describe the damage or its likely cause.

Although I would agree with the Tenant that the potholes on the laneway may well have caused or contributed to the truck breaking down, the Tenant’s evidence does not meet the burden of proof. The evidence must establish that it is more likely than not that the state of disrepair to the laneway caused the disrepair to the truck. Given the lack of evidence from a qualified mechanic, or information about driving habits and other roads regularly used, or the state of maintenance of the vehicle, the evidence does not rise to the level of proof necessary. As a result, that claim must be denied.
The application also claims $3,400.00 for out of pocket expenses for snow removal, laundromat costs, extra wood and rubber boots.
No evidence was led at the hearing with respect to these claims except for the snow removal costs.

With respect to snow removal, the Tenant says in November and December of 2023 the Tenant paid $150.00 on eight occasions to have the laneway snow removed. The Tenant produced no receipts but the Landlord also did not contest this evidence of the Tenant’s in any way and the cost claimed seems reasonable to me given the length of the laneway in question. As a result an order shall issue requiring the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant $1,200.00 for out of pocket expenses arising from the Landlord’s breach.
Given all of the above, the Tenant’s application is granted in part and denied in part. The Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant a total of $12,800.00.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $12,800.00, which represents: • $5,600.00 for abatement of the rent; • $6,000.00 for general compensation; and • $1,200.00 for out of pocket expenses.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application)
reasons: The Tenants filed the T2/T6 application on October 26, 2022. At the Adjudicative Case Conference on June 7, 2024, the matter was adjourned, and an interim order was issued as a result.

LTB-T-062734-22-IN, dated June 18, 2024, provided clear direction to the Tenants about steps to amending the application, as well as instructions with respect to submitting evidence to the LTB and the Landlord.
The matter was further adjourned on December 10, 2024.

At the hearing on February 11, 2026, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the allegations contained in the applications are unclear and there are no valid remedies sought being as the tenancy terminated. In addition, the Tenants have been given ample time to correct their application as this is the third time the parties have been before the Board. Accordingly, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant’s T6 application should be dismissed.

The Tenant admitted that they received the interim order and only filed an amendment with respect to the proper name of the Landlord, but did not file an amendment with the LTB to clarify the issues and/or the remedies. Analysis

Applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met and determine whether to raise a defence. Natural justice and procedural fairness require nothing less.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 that, “Particulars should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, in my view, the case supports the principles of procedural fairness regarding the need for particular and details to permit one to know the case against them, which applies equally to tenant applications.

These principles are confirmed in the Court which states that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

In the matter before me, the application was not only unclear as to what the Tenants’ issues were but did not include any remedies for which they were asking for, even after the Tenants were provided the opportunity to amend their application. I note that, the matter was adjourned 3 times previously so that the Tenants were provided an opportunity to amend the application to include further information and clarity.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application was not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at a hearing, or the remedies being sought. I also find that the Tenants have be given sufficient time to amend the application. As such, the Tenants’ T6 application will be dismissed. T2 application
At the hearing on June 4, 2026, the Tenants sought to withdraw the application, and I consented to the request.
ordered: The T6 application is dismissed.
The T2 application having been withdrawn, the LTB's file is closed. June 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $2,044.61.
The rental unit is a one-bedroom unit with a den , located in a basement of a single-family home. The tenancy commenced on January 1, 2022.
On July 16, 2024 , water from the bedroom window flooded the rental unit during a heavy downpour.

On July 19 or 20, 2024, an insurance company attended the unit for an assessment . The Landlord claimed that they asked the Tenant to move his belongings from the impacted areas, including providing access to the bedroom window. The Tenant denied the claim . Given the Landlord’s testimony that the insurance company was able to determine that a category three event affected the unit , I am satisfied that the y conducted a meaningful assessment without interference from the Tenant.
On July 23, 2024, the Landlord asked the Tenant to vacate the rental unit by July 26, 2024.
On July 26, 2024, the Landlord requested that the Tenant confirm if he vacated the unit.
On July 27, 2024, the Landlord informed the Tenant that demolition would be ongoing in the unit, and the Tenant should have vacated the day prior.

On July 28, 2024, the Tenant recorded a verbal communication between him and the female Landlord in which the Tenant was asked to vacate the rental unit for demolition work . This conversation included the Landlord saying professional movers were hired to remove the Tenant’s belongings from the unit the next day and the Tenant responding that they were welcome to do so, but he needed more information on how long he would have to be away from the unit. The Landlord then gave the Tenant a Notice to End your Tenancy for Causing Serious Problems in the Rental Unit or [name] (N7) with a termination date of August 6, 2024. The Landlord alleged in the notice that the Tenant prevented the insurance company from completing the cleanup of the unit on July 20, 2024, and failed to be out of the unit for the emergency cleanup on July 26, 2024.

On July 29, 2024, the Landlord stated that the insurance company returned to the unit to start the emergency cleanup and to carry out further assessment, but the Tenant did not properly prepare the unit to facilitate the assessment . A document from the insurance company dated July 31, 2024, stated that the required emergency cleanup included applying an anti-microbial agent to the affected floor; water extraction, and floor clean up. Nowhere in the document does it state that they were prevented from a meaningful assessment.

On August 9, 2024 , the Landlord informed the Tenant he could remain in the unit during renovations, and that they intended to remove the damaged floors and walls on August 12, 2024. The Landlord attached a document from their contractor stating that the Tenant would have to be available for the duration of the work to move his belongings from one spot to another.

On August 10, 2024, the Tenant requested a withdrawal of the eviction application which the Landlord filed based on the N7 notice. On August 11, 2024, the Landlord agreed to do so, if the Tenant permitted access to the unit. The Landlord withdrew the application in January 2025.

Between August 12 and August 14, 2024, the parties in emails tried to coordinate dates for the repairs. On August 12, 2024, for example the Landlord stated in an email to the Tenant that a date proposed by the Tenant was not feasible.
On August 31, 2024, - Landlord sent an email saying two walls in the unit would be demolished starting September 5, 2024, and failed to respond to the Tenant’s request for details.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not carry out any repairs and provided pictures taken on February 22, 2026, showing the damage the flooding caused to the window in the bedroom, living room floor, and the bathroom. On August 6, 2024, the Tenant ’s representative sent a letter to the Landlord about the state of the unit , and the Landlord’s conduct.

The Landlord stated that o n July 21, and 23, 2024, the Tenant agreed that the Landlord could go into the unit with movers to remove his belongings and store them somewhere else. On July 26, 2024, the Tenant postponed the entry and by July 28, 2024, refused entry completely.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant’s proposal to move his belongings from room to room was impractical given that the rental unit is a one-bedroom unit and a den. The Landlord has not visited the unit to address the flooding since July 29, 2024, and maintains that the Tenant has not made any complaints regarding disrepair. Analysis

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. I am satisfied that the Landlord neglected this responsibility by failing to maintain the rental unit.

Based on all the evidence, the flooding incident occurred on July 16, 2024. The parties agree that contractors hired by the insurance company attended the unit on July 19 or 20, 202 4, although the documentation from the insurance company indicates that an inspection did not take place until July 29, 2024. Following that date , the Landlord did not carry out any further inspections or repairs to the unit . T he pictures provided by the Tenant , dated February 22, 2026, demonstrates that the water damage significantly worsened over time so that the area surrounding the window, as well as the floor and wall of the unit, are severely impacted.

The Landlord based the lack of repairs on the Tenant’s alleged denial of meaningful entry to the unit. However, despite the earlier disagreement on whether the Tenant should remove his belongings from the unit or not, the evidence demonstrates that on August 9, 2024, the parties agreed that the Tenant could remain in the unit during the period of repair. As a result, the Tenant was no longer required to remove his belongings or temporarily vacate the unit. The Landlord did not provide any evidence to establish that at any time, the Tenant was given a Notice of Entry and subsequently denied access to either the Landlord or the Landlord’s contractors. In the absence of such evidence, I do not accept the Landlord’s claim that the Tenant prevented either an assessment or repairs from being carried out.

Furthermore, despite the Landlord’s repeated assertions that he was not informed of any damage to the window and wall, he was aware that the unit was impacted as a result of the flooding, as shown in the insurance company’s report. Despite this knowledge, the Landlord failed to carry out r epairs, and the natural consequence of the Landlord’s lack of diligence was the progressive worsening of the areas impacted by the flood as seen in the pictures from February 22, 2026.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The Landlord served the Tenant an N7 notice alleging that the Tenant prevented the completion of emergency clean up on July 20, 2024, and that the Tenant’s failure to vacate the unit on July 26, 2024, resulted in further damage to the walls and floor ing in the unit . However, these assertions are not supported by the evidence. The parties agree that contractors from the insurance company attended on July 20, 2024, for an assessment. The Landlord’s own testimony confirms that the incident was classified as a category three event on that date. The insurance report does not indicate that an emergency clean-up could not be completed on July 20, 2024, because of any actions by the Tenant.

Furthermore, there is no evidence to establish that the Tenant was legally required to vacate the rental unit on July 26, 2024. Accordingly, the Landlord’s claim that the Tenant’s failure to vacate the unit contributed to additional damage is unsupported by any evidence.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and sought to coerce the Tenant into vacating the unit by serving the N7 Notice.

Due to my findings above, a rent abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant a rent abatement equal to 10% of the monthly rent paid by the Tenant. The parties disputed the amount of the monthly rent in part, but rent abatement is awarded here based on the amount of rent paid by the Tenant . N o determination is made on the amount of the lawful monthly rent.

The Landlord will pay a total of $1,996.61 to the Tenant, for the period from August 1, 2024, when the repairs should have reasonably commenced to June 19, 2026, the date of this order: a. $360.00 (10% of $900.00 or $90 monthly) from August 1, 2024, to December 31, 2024; b. $1,107.00 (10% of $922.50 or $92.25 monthly) from January 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025; c. $470.90 (10% of $941.87 or $94.18 monthly) from January 1, 2026, to May 31, 2026; and d. $58.71 (10% of daily compensation of $30.96 or $3.09 daily) from June 1, 2026, to June 19, 2026.
The Landlord will be ordered to immediately inspect the rental unit and carry out the repairs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,044.61. This amount represents: • $1,996.61 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

In the alternative, if the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $ 500.00 from the rent each month from July 1, 2026, to September 1, 2026; and $544.61 on October 1, 2026.
The Landlord shall inspect the rental unit and carry out repairs to the area around the window, the wall and floor of the unit on or before July 10, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Preliminary Issue – Amending the Application

At the hearing, the Tenant sought to amend the remedies in their application to include the following: a. An order directing the Landlord not to harass the Tenant; b. A determination of the lawful rent moving forward; c. Compensation for the cost of installing CCTV d. Other monetary remedies that the Board deems appropriate.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord ought to be aware that the remedies were being sought as the Tenant’s case brief, which was served on the Landlord and the LTB on January 23, 2026, contained a description of the requested remedies.

At the hearing, the Tenant also sought to amend the remedies requested to include a 15% rent abatement and a return of the allegedly unlawfully collected rent amounts, which were not in the application or the case brief provided by the Tenant

The Landlord submits that as per the adjournment sheet issued on September 9, 2025 following the ACC hearing, the Tenant was directed to amend the remedy section of their application, with the presiding Member deciding whether to grant the amended application after hearing submissions from the parties.
The Landlord submits that they were not prepared to address an abatement of rent or return of unlawfully collected rent as these amounts were not claimed in the application.

The LTB’s Rules of Procedure provide guidance as to the factors that a Member ought to consider when considering whether to grant an amendment including the following: a. Whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. Any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. Whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. Whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. Any other relevant factors. 8. in the case before me, the Tenant was given clear direction at the hearing and in the adjournment sheet issued on September 9, 2025 to amend the application, particularly with regards to the remedies sought. The Tenant chose not to amend their application and the Landlord should not be unfairly prejudiced by the Tenant’s request to amend the application at the hearing. 9. The Tenant, who is represented, chose not to amend their application in spite of the direction from the Board. I find that it would be unfairly prejudicial to the Landlord to allow the Tenant to amend their application to include the rent abatement. As a result, the request to amend the application to claim a rent abatement is denied. 10. With regards to the request to amend to include a return of unlawfully collected rent under section 135 of the Act, not only has the Tenant filed the incorrect application for this remedy but the Tenant had not sought any amendment or indicated in their case brief any intention to seek a return of unlawfully collected rent. Rather, the Tenant only states in their case brief that they are seeking a determination on the amount of the lawful rent going forward. As a result, I find that it would be unfairly prejudicial to the Landlord to allow the Tenant to raise this issue in the application before me. As a result, the request to amend to include a claim for unlawfully collected rental amounts is denied. 11. With regards to the request to amend the application to claim an order requiring the Landlord not to harass the Tenant and for reimbursement of the CCTV footage, as the Landlord was aware the Tenant was raising issues with regards to substantial interference and harassment and these remedies flow from the claim in the original T2 application, I find it would not be unfair to allow the amendment to the application to include these remedies. [name] 12. The Tenant submits that the Landlord has given notices of rent increase that do not comply with sections 116 and 120 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). 13. The Tenant testified that on November 29, 2022, the Landlord called the Tenant seeking to increase the rent from $2,450.00 to $2,700.00. The Tenant denied the rent increase, citing the Guideline amounts set out in section 120 of the Act. 14. The Tenant testified that on December 3, 2022, the Landlord called the Tenant again to request a rent increase above the Guideline. The Tenant testified hat the Landlord stated that if the Tenant cannot afford the renal unit, the Tenant should move out of the rental unit. 15. The Tenant testified that on December 12, 2022, the Landlord and the Landlord’s cousin attended the rental unit and attempted to pressure the Tenant into vacating the rental unit as a result of the Tenant refusing to pay the proposed rent increase. 16. The Tenant also testified that on January 7, 2023, the Landlord emailed the Tenant indicating that he intended to sell the rental unit and requested the Tenant’s cooperation in allowing access to a prospective buyer and their agents and ensuring rental unit is in a clean and presentable condition. 17. The Tenant entered into evidence a number of emails between the Landlord and the Tenant between November 18, 2021 and October 17, 2024 regarding rent increases, sale of the property and alleged maintenance issues. 18. The Tenant testified that as a result of growing discomfort as a result of the entries scheduled by the Landlord that she installed a CCTV camera in her rental unit. 19. The Tenant testified that following the conversation on January 7, 2023, the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to a backdated rent increase of the rent from $2,450.00 to $2,511.25 effective April 10, 2023. 20. The Tenant testified that she received a subsequent N1 notice dated September 6, 2023 increasing the rent to $2,573.77 effective December 10, 2023. 21. The Tenant testified that she received a third N1 notice dated August 1, 2024, increasing the rent from $2,573.77 to $2,638.09 effective November 10, 2024. 22. The Tenant testified that at some point during their dispute with the Landlord, a mutual acquaintance of the Landlord and the Tenant became involved in the tenancy dispute which made the Tenant uncomfortable. 23. The Landlord testified he has only increased the rent per the guideline amount in 2023 and none of the subsequent N1 notices have been enforced or paid by the Tenant. The Landlord denies harassing the Tenant and testified that he has not been to the rental unit in 31 months as a result of the Tenant’s assertions of substantial interference and harassment. 24. The Landlord testified that due to financial hardship, the Landlord requested the rent increases and had considered selling the rental unit. The Landlord testified that they inevitably decided against selling the rental unit and gave the Tenant a proper 90-day notice for the guideline amount set out by section 120 of the Act in the form of the rent increase to $2,511.25 effective April 10, 2023. 25. The parties agreed the Tenant paid $2,511.25 from April 10, 2023 up to December 9, 2023 and paid the increased rent of $2,573.77 for the period of December 10, 2023 and February 10, 2024 through to August 9, 2024, when the Tenant contacted the LTB and learned that the rent increase to $2,573.77 was unlawful and stopped paying the increased rent. While the Landlord acknowledged collecting this amount, the Tenant reverted to paying the lower rent and there does not appear to be any pressure from the Landlord to obtain any additional rent since the Tenant reverted to paying $2,511.25. While I considered the rent increase for the purposes of determining whether there was substantial interference or harassment, as I indicated above, the Tenant’s request to claim unlawfully collected rent is denied and I make no determinations with regards to the amount of the lawful rent. 26. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Landlord’s behaviour constitutes substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or harassment. 27. With regards to the email evidence submitted by the Tenant, nothing in the communications provided as evidence by the Tenant suggests that the Landlord’s conduct rose to the level of substantial interference or harassment. While there may be some disagreement as to conversations about the amount of the lawful rent, I was not satisfied that the Tenant has discharged their burden of proof to demonstrate that these communications rose to the level of substantial interference or harassment. 28. While I am satisfied that the Landlord sought increases that did not comply with sections 116 and 120 of the Act, there was insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord’s requested rent increases amounted to substantial interference or harassment, coercion or intimidation as alleged by the Tenant. The Tenant only paid $2,511.25 as per their agreement with the Tenant in 2023 up to December 9, 2023. While the Tenant paid an increased rent for the periods of December 10, 2023 and February 10, 2024 through to August 9, 2024, there was no evidence that the Landlord pressured the Tenant to pay unlawful amounts. Rather, based on the evidence before me, it appears the Landlord continued to accept the lower rent once the Tenant decided not to pay the increased rent. 29. I am not satisfied that the Landlord attending the rental unit to discuss the rent on December 12, 2022 amounted to either substantial interference or harassment nor was I satisfied that the Landlord’s expression of an intent to sell rose to the level of substantial interference, harassment, coercion or intimidation as alleged by the Tenant. 30. As the Tenant has not established that the Landlord has substantially interfered with reasonable enjoyment nor have they harassed the Tenant, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to properly address a bed bug issue at the rental unit between June 2024 and August 2024.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or that the Landlord failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in early June 2024. The Tenant testified that on June 7, 2024, the Tenant discovered bed bugs and bites and immediately informed the property manager. I accept that the Tenant experienced bed bug activity and that the issue was upsetting and disruptive to the Tenant.

However, the evidence does not establish that the Landlord knew or ought reasonably to have known about a bed bug issue before June 7, 2024. The Tenant believed the issue must have existed before the Tenant moved in, given how soon the issue arose after moving into the rental unit. I do not find that this belief, without more, proves that the Landlord had prior knowledge of a bed bug infestation or failed to act before receiving notice from the Tenant.

After receiving the Tenant’s complaint, the Landlord arranged pest control. The Tenant acknowledged in cross-examination that they received a preparation sheet, and that the Landlord addressed the initial complaint promptly. The evidence before me shows that the Tenant reported the issue on June 7, 2024, received the preparation sheet on June 10, 2024, and that treatment was arranged for June 12, 2024.

The Tenant continued to report activity after the first treatment. The Landlord responded by relaying information from pest control that some activity may be expected between the first treatment and the follow-up treatment. The Landlord also advised the Tenant not to continue using an additional powder treatment because it could interfere with the pest control treatment already arranged by the Landlord. I find that these communications were consistent with the Landlord continuing to respond to the issue, not ignoring it.

The evidence also shows that a follow-up treatment was arranged for early July 2024. The Abell report dated July 3, 2024 records that a bed bug follow-up service was performed, that all areas of concern were inspected, and that pesticide was applied to the interior perimeter of the unit and hallway, as well as the legs and underside of the bed frame. The report also noted no sanitation concerns and no structural concerns at the time of service.

The Tenant relies on the opinion of the Tenant’s own pest control contractor, who inspected the rental unit on July 17, 2024 and indicated that there was moderate activity in the bedroom and that the prior treatment may not have been completed properly. I have considered that evidence. However, I am not satisfied that it proves the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations. The report does not establish that the Landlord failed to arrange the July follow-up treatment, particularly in light of the Abell report confirming that follow-up treatment was completed. The report also does not establish that the Landlord’s decision to use Abell, or the treatment plan being followed, was unreasonable.

I also find it significant that the Tenant decided to arrange private treatment and did not advise the Landlord after July 17, 2024 that the Tenant had arranged another treatment before it was completed. The Tenant later informed the Landlord on August 8, 2024 that the Tenant had hired a pest control company, paid for treatment, and continued to experience concerns. The Landlord then asked for the name of the company and arranged a reinspection. This further supports a finding that the Landlord continued to respond when new information was provided.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s response was delayed. I do not accept that the evidence establishes an unreasonable delay. The first report was made on a Friday, June 7, 2024. The evidence shows that the Landlord communicated with the Tenant, arranged pest control, provided preparation instructions, and scheduled the first treatment for June 12, 2024. The Landlord then arranged a follow-up treatment in early July. In the circumstances, I find that the Landlord’s response was reasonable.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not treat all units in the residential complex. The evidence shows that the Landlord arranged treatment for the Tenant’s unit and the hallway. The Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to establish that the other units were infested, that the Landlord had received complaints from other units, or that the Landlord’s decision not to treat all units at that time was unreasonable.

While I accept that the Tenant experienced bites and discomfort, the presence of bed bugs alone does not establish a breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. The issue is whether the Landlord responded reasonably after being notified of the problem. For the reasons above, I find that the Landlord did.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Tenant's Legal Representative requested an adjournment. She explained that one of the Tenant’s key witnesses was a former neighbour who the Tenant's Legal Representative intended to summons. However, she has been unable to reach this witness, and the Tenant’s whole case was based around this witness.

The Tenant's Legal Representative also explained that it had somehow been missed within her office that she was scheduled for an in person hearing in Belleville, which she only became aware of this morning, and she was not certain how long this proceeding would take to conclude.

The Tenant's Legal Representative explained that the Tenant originally retained the services of another paralegal who was no longer able to represent him. She testified that she had taken over this representative files, and had tried to reach out to the Tenant starting in March, but he believed her communications were spam, and she had only become retained the weekend prior to the hearing.
At the time of the adjournment request the Tenant was not present.

Interpretation Guideline one states: Parties are expected to make any necessary arrangement to proceed with a case management or merits hearing on the date set out in the Notice of Hearing. The granting of adjournments is at the discretion of the Member hearing the application or the Hearing Office conducting the case management. Pursuant to s. 21 of the SPPA, an adjournment will only be granted by the Board if it is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held. Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. The Member may consider the conduct of the party opposing the adjournment. For example, if the party opposing the request has shown bad faith or refused to provide information about their case to the other party which would allow them to prepare quickly for the hearing, this may affect the Member’s decision. Adjournment to Allow Representation Section 10 of the SPPA states that a party may be represented by a representative at a hearing. However, the right to representation is not absolute and an adjournment is not automatically granted when it is requested on this ground. The onus is on the party wishing to be represented to make all reasonable efforts to find a lawyer or paralegal able to represent them at the hearing once they become aware of the hearing date. A short adjournment may be allowed where a representative has been retained but is unavailable on the date set for the hearing, or where the party can demonstrate that they have made reasonable efforts to retain a lawyer or paralegal before the hearing but have not yet been able to do so.
While this guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. I am not satisfied that the Tenant's Legal Representative has demonstrated that an adjournment is necessary.

The notice of hearing was sent to the parties on January 12, 2026, and I am satisfied that the Tenant has been aware of the hearing since at least that date. As the Tenants initial representative was unable to proceed, and he was allegedly operating under the assumption that the messages from his new perspective representative were spam, I would expect that the Tenant would take reasonable steps to secure alternate representative, however, no evidence of such steps were put before me and the Tenant was not present to explain what steps if any were taken.

Additionally, this request for an adjournment appears to have arisen at least in part from a lack of due diligence on the part of the office of the Tenant's Legal Representative who were themselves unable to contact the Tenant, did not summons their key witness, and had mis-diarized another hearing on the same day as this proceeding.

I am also not satisfied that it is appropriate to adjourn the hearing to allow the Tenant's Legal Representative an opportunity to summons a particular witness. The Tenant's Legal Representative has clearly been aware of this proceeding since March and has had ample opportunity to request as summons, or coordinate with the witness to ensure their attendance. While I accept that this would have been complicated by the lack of a formal retainer, the Tenant's Legal Representative has nevertheless had ample time to summons or coordinate any potential witnesses.
I also accept that the Landlord has been waiting several months for the hearing and the Landlord’s witness has taken time off to attend the proceeding.

Therefore, I am satisfied that both the Tenant and Tenant's Legal Representative have had ample time to prepare for this proceeding, which is based on the Tenant’s own application and am not satisfied an adjournment is appropriate.

However, I elected to stand the matter down to allow the Tenant's Legal Representative to complete her other proceeding before the matter was heard on the merits. I also note that while the proceeding was stood down the Tenant’s proposed witness [name] was able to attend. Therefore I am satisfied that there was no prejudice to the Tenant in proceeding with the hearing. The T5
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant testified that he received an N12 Notice of Termination from the Landlord in August 2024 and vacated on the termination date in the notice, which he could not recall. He testified that after he vacated, he had difficulty securing a new rental unit and stayed in hotels, and lived in his van, and spent time staying with friends after he vacated as he had only been able to secure a new unit for his mother and daughter, not for himself.

He testified that after four months he realised that the N12 had been served in bad faith, as that was adequate time for the Landlord to perform any renovations, and in spite of this he had not yet observed any signs of occupation within the rental unit. He testified that he started to drive by the rental unit approximately every two weeks, but did not see any signs of occupation or renovation other than a rough repair conducted on the deck.
The Tenant confirmed that he never knocked on the door when he drove by, as he never saw a car in the driveway and typically passed the rental until in the afternoon or early evening.

A witness for the Tenant Sylvia Davey testified that she lived beside the Tenant for four years and he asked her to keep an eye on the unit after he vacated. She testified that she periodically saw people coming and going and doing sporadic restorations, but she never saw a vehicle parked there consistently or overnight.

She also testified that over the winter there was a foot or two of snow in the laneway of the rental unit and she began piling her own snow there and no one came to complain, and she did not see tire tracks in the snow from the rental unit.
She also testified that she spoke to the Landlord in March 2025 who informed her that he planned to sell the rental unit in August 2025.
She testified that as far as she knows the Landlord’s son is staying at the rental unit with his girlfriend a few nights a week but she did not see any furniture brought into the rental unit.
She testified that she is a stay-at-home mother with insomnia, whose office is in her garage, and she uses her front door everyday so it would be nice to her if someone were coming and going.

The Landlord testified that after the Tenant vacated, he and his son renovated the property and his son occupied the rental unit while the renovations were being performed. He testified that that Tenant vacated August 10, 2024, and his son moved into the rental unit immediately.

He testified that he and his son renovated the unit by replacing drywall, replacing a bathroom vanity, and replacing flooring within the unit among other changes. He testified that after his son moved into the rental unit the utilities were transferred into his name and his son paid those bills.
He also testified that approximately two weeks after his son moved in he brought him a bed from his own home.

He denied telling [name] that he intended the sell the rental unit and testified that all he told her was that he did not intend to re-rent the rental unit. He testified that his intention was always for his son to reside there.

The Landlord’s son [name] [name] testified that he moved into the rental unit in Mid to Late August 2024. He testified that he had been struggling financially and had been staying with his brother who was charging him rent, and it as more convenient to have an entire home to himself.
He testified that he moved into the rental unit with almost nothing and initially slept on an air mattress and accumulated belongings such as furniture over time.

He also referred me to extensive text conversations with his father where they discussed his transferring the utilities into his name, and messages wherein he asked his father to deliver various furnishings to the home or coordinate delivery or repair of appliances and the ongoing renovation work.

He also referred me to a text message from August 8, 2025, wherein the Landlord asked him to provide a picture of his bedroom and living room to provide to the Tenant to prove he was living in the rental unit. The metadata attached to this image demonstrates that he was able to send the pictures to the Landlord within one minute, and that they were taken contemporaneously.

He testified that he spent two weeks at his father’s house in February 2025 to take care of a dog, then returned to the rental unit, He testified that he leaves the unit around 5am and returns between 4pm and 7pm.
He also testified that he did not plow the driveway throughout the winter as his vehicle has four-wheel drive and only shovelled around the front door.

When questioned by the Tenant's Legal Representative as to why the utility usage in the rental unit was so low, he testified that he was trying to keep his usage low as he was on a budget. He confirmed that a gas bill from December 2024 depicted usage of 45m3.

He also explained that at some point the gas company had the wrong address and there was accredit applied to each bill. He also explained that he had the pilot light off during the winter and only used air conditioning for one month, all in an attempt to save funds. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated or that the N12 was served in bad faith.

Despite the assertion of the Tenant's Legal Representative, the onus is not on the Landlord to demonstrate that his son occupied the rental unit. Instead, the onus remains on the Tenant to demonstrate this. Much of the Tenant’s own testimony was speculative and amounted to an assertion that he did not observe occupation of the rental unit when he drove by every two weeks. The testimony of the Tenant’s witness is similar, while I can accept that she would have been well placed to observe the rental unit, I am not satisfied that an assertion that the rental unit did not appear to be occupied is itself determinative that the Landlord’s son did not occupy the unit, and I note that the witnesses own testimony was that she did see persons performing renovations on the home and that the Landlord’s son had begun staying there occasionally with his girlfriend.

With respect to her assertion that the Landlord informed her he intends to sell the unit, this was denied by the Landlord and has clearly not occurred as the rental unit was not listed for sale. Therefore, I place little weight on this assertion.

While the strongest evidence of occupation seems to date from the summer of 2025, I note that as the Landlord and his son were unaware of the Tenant’s Application until that time, they would not have had a need to document evidence of occupation prior to that date, and in spite of that there is strong evidence which suggests that the rental unit was occupied by the Landlord’s son by August 2024.

While there appears to have been minimal utility usage until the summer of 2025, I note that the Landlord’s son testified that he was on a low budget and was trying to keep utility usage to a minimum, which may account for the low usage and while I can accept that this low usage may suggest that the Landlord’s son did not occupy the rental unit ultimately there is other ample evidence to support that the Landlord’s son did occupy the unit by August 2024.

For example, there are text messages between the Landlord and his son from August 14, 2024 where the Landlord’s son asks for a key to be cut for him, and indicating that he will move his air mattress and desk into the rental unit as soon as a bedroom is ready for him. Additionally, there are texts confirming that the Landlord’s son had transferred the utilities into his name on August 16, 2024. There are also Texts discussing the renovations in the rental unit on October 1, 2024 and a text from December 11, 2025 which depicts the [name] son asking if his father has extra curtains he can have for the rental unit. All of these strongly suggest that the Landlord’s son had occupied and was renovating the rental unit and, supports his assertion that he moved into the rental unit with very little and accumulated his belongings over time.

Therefore, as the onus is on the Tenant to demonstrate that Landlord’s son did not occupy the rental unit, I am not satisfied that they have done so as there is ample evidence which supports a finding that he occupied the unit by August 2024 and remained in the rental unit in August 2025.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
