issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that the application should be dismissed on the grounds that the allegations were outside the statutory limitation period.
The application was filed on August 5, 2024.

Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states that the Tenant’s application can not be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. With the exception of one allegation from August 9, 2023, all allegations in the application were beyond the one-year limitation period. Therefore, only the events of August 9, 2023 were considered for the application.

The Landlord’s Representative then raised the issue that there were insufficient reasons and details for the Landlord to respond to the Tenant’s allegations from August 9, 2023, despite having ample time to amend their application prior to the hearing.

The application references the date of August 9, 2023 and to see the comments that were virtually pinned to the PDF document. Though there is a comment icon visible on the PDF application, the comment itself cannot be accessed.

The Tenant confirmed at the hearing that the application is only about the chemical fumes from the neighbouring unit that interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and/or the residential complex. All the allegations in the application (including those outside the limitation period) pertained to the same grievance but on different dates. The Tenant stated that the issue was resolved by August 31, 2023, and she seeks a rent abatement from August 8, 2023 to August 31, 2023 in light of the limitation period. The Tenant also reiterated her honest belief that she thought the Landlord and the Board would be able to see the pinned comments.

Having considered the parties’ evidence and submissions, I was satisfied there were sufficient details in the application to proceed with the hearing. The Landlord confirmed they were aware that the Tenant’s allegations included any grievance or complaint that arose from August 9, 2023, and a reasonable person having read the application would know that the Tenant’s issues stem from chemical fumes coming from renovations in a neighbouring unit.

I also note that after the oral decision was made, the matter was stood down for the Landlord to speak with their Legal Representative. The matter was then brought back approximately 3.5 hours later, providing the Landlord with additional time to prepare, and the hearing was completed. [name]:
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The rental unit is described as a one-bedroom unit in a mixed commercial and residential multistory building. Floors 1-5 are commercial with residential floors above. The Tenant’s unit is located on the 13th floor.

The Tenant testified that she began noticing a chemical smell coming from the neighbouring unit two doors down on July 20, 2023, when its floors were being renovated. The Landlord’s Agent confirmed that the neighbouring unit, a larger unit of approximately 1600 square feet, was being renovated for new tenant turnover. There was a work order from the new incoming tenants on July 17, 2023 to re-finish the floors. The renovations were completed from July 20-21, 2023. The floors were sanded on July 20, 2023, and the polyurethane stain was applied on July 21, 2023. The Landlord’s Agent also confirmed that the floor renovations would give off a paint-like smell that could be unpleasant, but there were no complaints from any other tenants in the residential complex regarding any odour.

The Tenant testified she spoke with a representative from the company doing the renovations on July 20, 2023, Royal Flooring (‘RF’), who told the Tenant that they do not use ventilation (fans, open windows, etc.) during floor renovations. The Tenant also noticed that none of the workmen were wearing protective equipment. The Tenant was also not aware of how long the renovations would take.

The Tenant informed the building concierge on July 20, 2023 about the chemical smell not having dissipated by the end of the day and of her inability to work in her unit as a result. The Tenant testified the concierge confirmed he could smell the chemical odour and gave the Tenant a standing fan, but that did not help much to alleviate the smell.
The Tenant then went to the building’s management office on July 21, 2023 and spoke with a Landlord agent, [name] (‘KM’), who said he would follow up with her but never did.

The Tenant testified that the chemical smell lingered for approximately 4-5 days. The issue did not resurface until August 9, 2023 when the Tenant noticed [name] had returned to the neighbouring unit to complete the floor renovations. The Tenant testified the chemical smell was as strong as before, causing her eyes to water, nasal passages to burn, persistent coughing, and severe headaches. The chemical smell did not begin to dissipate until August 11, 2023, though the Tenant continued to feel more acute side effects up to August 31, 2023. The Tenant stated she had opened the windows in her unit as well as the bathroom and kitchen vents to try and alleviate the smell. The Tenant then reported the matter to the concierge who then came up to the Tenant’s unit and confirmed there was a chemical smell that could be smelled on other floors as well. The Tenant further testified that the concierge then filled out one of several incident reports regarding this issue, but none were submitted at the hearing as evidence.

The Landlord’s Agent testified she had no knowledge of any follow-up work being done to the neighbouring unit on August 9, 2023. The floors were finished on July 21, 2023, so the Landlord’s Agent was not certain what subsequent chemical smell the Tenant was referring to.

The Tenant emailed the Landlord about the chemical smell on August 21, 2023, and testified that she followed up with the Landlord on October 6 & 11, 2023, November 17, 2023, December 13, 2023, February 13, 2024, and May 9, 2024 to no reply. The Tenant read the August 21, 2023 email into evidence at the hearing which described the chemical smell on July 20-22, 2023 and August 9, 2023, the Tenant’s symptoms, the impact on her health, and the concern that [name] did not use any ventilation during the renovations. The email went on to express the Tenant’s upset at the lack of response from the Landlord regarding the issue after she spoke with KM on July 21, 2023, and the minimal effect of the fan supplied by the concierge on July 20, 2023. The Tenant also inquired about the possible health risk from exposure to the fumes and if there are any ventilation issues in the residential complex.

The Tenant testified she does not believe she received a reply to her email, though the Landlord’s Agent confirmed the Tenant was sent a confirmation email on August 21, 2023 stating that the Landlord received the Tenant’s message and they would reply to her at a later time.

The Landlord’s Agent maintained that she was not aware of the issue until the Tenant’s email on August 21, 2023, well after any alleged chemical smell was gone. The Landlord’s Agent sent the Tenant’s email to her team to be addressed but can not say with certainty why a more detailed follow-up response was not sent to the Tenant. The Landlord’s Agent confirmed on cross-examination that she did not read or have access to any of the concierge’s reports regarding the issue, as the Landlord switched to a different reporting system in January 2024 and could not locate a copy of the report(s) on the new system. The Landlord’s Agent also apologized to the Tenant for MK not replying to her in a timely fashion and stated she will make efforts to ensure the Tenant is notified of renovations in the future. Nonetheless, the Tenant was met by the concierge both times when she complained and was provided with a fan to mitigate any purported smell. The Landlord’s Agent also met with the Tenant in May and June 2024 to discuss the matter and told the Tenant that it was safe to use the chemical for the floor staining process.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that each unit has a ventilation system that vents outside the residential complex, as do the vents in the corridors. It is possible that the RF workmen may have done some of the renovation with the unit door open, letting the paint-like smell enter the hallway, though that would have likely been by necessity to complete the portion of the floor by the entrance to the unit. However, it is the general practice when this type of renovation work is done for the vents in the unit to be turned on and the windows open.

The Landlord’s Agent further testified that the Landlord was not aware of any ventilation issues with either the Tenant’s unit, the unit being renovated, or for the residential complex in general. The Landlord also did not receive any complaints from other tenants regarding chemical fumes, nor was the Landlord made aware if the Tenant had any sensitivity to smells. The Tenant, however, denied any such sensitivity at the hearing.

Although the Landlord’s Legal Representative suggested that the Tenant may have mistaken flu or [name] symptoms for side effects from any chemical smell, the Tenant maintained that she knows the difference and did not have any flu or other virus at the time. The Tenant is a hospital pharmacist and testified that she used her professional knowledge to self-medicate with a nasal spray and puffer well into the autumn of 2023. However, the Tenant did not see a physician until November 9, 2023. Analysis:

The issue before me is the alleged resurgence of a chemical smell in the residential complex and into the Tenant’s unit on August 9, 2023, and the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s complaint about the problem.

The parties do not dispute that floor renovations were carried out in the neighbouring unit two doors down from the Tenant from July 20-21, 2023, and that chemicals were likely used to re-finish the floors. The Landlord also does not dispute that the Tenant likely sent a prior complaint about a chemical smell during that renovation period, and that the complaint was not followed up with in a timely manner. However, the Landlord’s Agent had no knowledge of any follow-up work completed in the neighbouring unit on August 9, 2023. The floors had been completed back in July 2023, thus there was no need for RF to return to the unit that day.

As this is a tenant’s application, the burden of proof lies with the Tenant to show, on the balance of probabilities, there was a chemical smell present on August 9, 2023 that was so strong, it, along with the Landlord’s inaction, rose to the level of substantial interference with the Tenant’s ordinary enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex to August 31, 2023. Having considered the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has met the evidentiary burden. The Tenant could have called supporting witnesses, such as MK or any other tenants from other affected units, to testify as to the presence and strength of the chemical smell that day but did not do so; nor did the Tenant submit any supporting documentation, such as photos or video of the floor renovations being done from the communal hallway, to illustrate that the RF workmen had returned to the unit on August 9, 2023 and were using chemicals that caused a strong disruptive odour. Neither the Tenant nor the Landlord could produce a copy of MK’s report regarding what happened that day. Though the Tenant did read-in her email complaint from August 21, 2023, I do not find that and the Tenant’s testimony alone to be sufficient proof of the allegations regarding whether there was a strong and disruptive chemical smell present August 9, 2023.

Though the Tenant claimed to have complained to MK about the issue on August 9, 2023, there was no proof of any complaint to the Landlord for that day until August 21, 2023, well after any such smell would have dissipated. There were also no follow-up incidents after August 9, 2023 regarding any strong and disruptive smells in the residential complex to compound the notion that there was a substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the unit. I am also not satisfied that there was sufficient evidence to show that the severity of the alleged chemical smell on August 9, 2023 alone rose to the level of substantial interference, given the above findings and that there were no complaints from other tenants and no reported or known issues with the ventilation system in the Tenant’s unit, the neighbouring unit or the residential complex. While the Tenant testified as to her physical symptoms beginning on August 9, 2023, there was also no supporting medical documentation submitted to help substantiate the presence and severity of those symptoms, or that they were directly linked to a chemical odour from August 9, 2023.

I will note, however, that the Landlord’s lack of response to the Tenant’s complaints was unreasonable. The Landlord’s Agent confirmed that she forwarded the August 21, 2023 complaint to her team but could not explain why there was no follow up with the Tenant after the initial confirmation of receipt email was sent to the Tenant that same day. Though the Landlord’s Agent herself did speak with the Tenant about her grievances in May and June 2024, that was at least 8 months after the Tenant sent her complaint email on August 21, 2023, which I find to be unreasonable. The Landlord’s Agent also could not explain why MK did not follow up with the Tenant after her July 21, 2023 complaint.

The issue here is that without the Tenant meeting the evidentiary burden to substantiate that the chemical smell on August 9, 2023 substantially interfered with her enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, the Landlord’s response to the issue is essentially irrelevant without a proven underlying interference for the purposes of this application. Consequently, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant, and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 3, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing it was agreed between the parties that the Landlords were [name] and [name], as such [name] was added to this application as a Landlord. T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $1,198.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agree that the Landlords served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act on September 1, 2024, and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 30, 2024. It is also not disputed that the Landlords listed the rental unit for sale and ultimately sold the property with a closing date of October 27, 2025. Bad Faith

Section 57(5) of the Act provided that in circumstances such as this there is a rebuttable presumption that the N12 notice was served in bath faith, if the Landlord pursuant to subsection c) advertises the rental unit or the building that contains the rental unit for sale.

Section 57(6) of the Act provides the time frame for section 57(5) as beginning on the day the landlord gives a notice of termination under section 48 and ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
For the following reasons, based on the evidence and testimony before me, I do not find that the Landlords have met the burden of establishing that the N12 notice was served in good faith.

The Landlords testified that they had been residing up north as the Landlord [name] worked for Orange Air Ambulance. On March 20, 2024 he found out he had received a transfer offer to work out of the City of [name] location effective January 5, 2025.
After the Tenant vacated the rental unit the Landlords moved into the rental unit on December 23, 2024.

While residing in the rental unit the Landlords discovered they were expecting their first child and determined they would need a larger home in June and reached out to a real estate agent who had scheduled a showing for them on June 25, 2025, but unfortunately the Landlords suffered a miscarriage and had to cancel the viewing.

They were able to reschedule the viewing in July and fell in love with the property and ultimately entered into an agreement of purchase and sale on a larger property in the country which closed on October 23, 2025. During the process the Landlords found out that the Landlord [name] was again pregnant.

The Landlords submit that they only listed the rental property for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating due to a changing in circumstances, that they were expecting a child and would need a larger home and property, additionally the Landlord explained that returning from up north to the City of Cambridge was a bit of a culture shock.
The evidence before me with respect to the rental property is that it is 2 ½ bedrooms and 1 bathroom and approximately 1050 square feet.

Based on the evidence educed at the hearing and the testimony of the parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlords gave the Tenants a notice in good faith. I find it is more likely than not that the Landlords initially had the intention of moving into the rental unit, but due to a change in mindset they decided a move to a more rural property would better suit their needs. The Landlords had no children prior to selling the 2.5 bedroom rental property, even if they were expecting a child the rental unit would have met their needs in terms of space. I am not satisfied that a change in mindset amounts to a change in circumstances that prevented the Landlords from remaining in the rental unit. I am satisfied that the tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Remedies
The Tenant in their application requests general compensation in the amount of $20,700.00 being 9 months of rent at $2,300.00.

The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3)(1.1), which states: An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. [Emphasis added].

The Tenant first moved into the rental property with her daughter on March 1 2024, she resided in the rental unit for 9 months before vacating and had intended to reside in the rental unit long term and stated she had put a lot of work into the property. After receiving the N12 notice of termination the Tenant entered into an agreement of purchase and sale and purchased a property of her own which closed on October 15, 2024, but did not move into the property until November 30, 2024 as the property required some work. Additionally, her daughter had to move schools.

Although the Tenant was impacted, by having to move from the rental unit as well as her daughter having to transition to a new school. The Tenant had only resided in the rental unit for 9 month prior to vacating. In consideration of all the circumstances I find that general compensation equivalent to half a months rent to be appropriate in being $1,150.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,198.00. This amount represents: • $1,150.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: le enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant; • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has wilfully or negligently caused damage to the premises The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlord's reasonable out- of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenant's failure to pay utility costs they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlord's reasonable out- of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 T6 Application: The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on May 27, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s legal representative, [name] (‘XL’), the Tenant, and the Tenant’s legal representative, [name] (‘SV’), attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant delivered a request to amend the T6 application on April 27, 2026. SV submitted that the amended application does not change the allegations made in the application, and is only an update relative to what has happened since the application was filed.
XL said the Landlord does not oppose the request to amend.

I accept that the request to amend was made in good faith, it was made in a timely manner in the circumstances, it was not cause delay pr prejudice to the Landlord, and it is therefore granted (see DOC-7844700). Limitation Period and Jurisdiction

The T6 application wa s filed pursuant to ss. 29(1)1 of the Act. Subsection 29(2) of the Act prescribes a one-year limitation period relative to this type of application. The LTB does not have jurisdiction to order a remedy relative to allegations about disrepair that occurred more than one year before the application was filed: s. 29, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; [name] v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2010 ONSC 1686.

The allegations in the T6 application about the stove in the rental unit occurred entirely outside of this limitation period, and the application is therefore dismissed as it relates to the allegations about the stove. Some of the other allegations about disrepair occurred outside the limitation period, but the disrepair is alleged to have continued into the limitation period. A remedy is only available for the period beginning one year before the application was filed on August 25, 2024.

The T6 application, filed under ss. 29(1)1, is grounded in the allegation that the Landlord breached an obligation under ss. 20(1) of the Act, which states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1).

The T6 application includes numerous allegations about the Landlord’s conduct, including, for example, allegations of harassment or a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. These types of allegations are not properly before me on a T6 application.

The Act provides for a different, specific ty pe of application for allegations about landlord conduct that may amount to harassment or a substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment (T2 application): see ss. 29(1)3 & 4, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. Where an issue raised in an application falls under a specific and applicable section of the Act, the issue should be determined in accordance with that specific and applicable provision: see, for example, Lise v. CLV Group Inc., 2022 CanLII 49901 (ON LTB), paras 12-13.

The T6 application is dismissed relative to the allegations made in the application that are not about the Landlord’s alleged failure to maintain the rental unit in a state of good repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards. Preliminary Issues: L2 Application:

The Landlord’s claim for compensation for undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex was withdrawn at a previous appearance before the LTB (see interim order [name], issued September 23, 2024).

The Landlord is not seeking termination of the tenancy in accordance with the N5 notice of termination. The Landlord only seeks compensation for unpaid utilities on the L2 application. T6 Application:
The Tenant alleges in the T6 that the Landlord breached her maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act relative to the following issues with the hot water, dishwasher, and pool.

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has rejected the proposition that this provision ought to be interpreted such that a landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as soon as a maintenance issue arises. Rather, a contextual approach, including consideration of the “entirety of the factual situation”, must be applied to determine whether a landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act: Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, paras 58-60, 84-86; TST-98783-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 87665 (ON LTB).

Generally, landlords are not held liable for maintenance issues that arise if the landlord addresses the issue of disrepair in a timely and effective manner once they become aware, or ought to have become aware, of the issue: TST-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB), para 33; LTB Interpretation Guideline #5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations. File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 Hot Water

The Tenant emailed the Landlord on April 24, 2025 informing the Landlord that there had been no hot water in the unit since the previous day. The Tenant also informed the Landlord that she had contacted Reliance, who had already sent a technician to the unit, but that they had determined the hot water heater could not be repaired and required replacement. The Tenant asked that the Landlord send someone to the unit to confirm if the hot water heater could be repaired or if it needed to be replaced (DOC-7844709, p. 8). On the same day the Tenant sent the Landlord a text message stating that she had sent the Landlord an email because the unit had no hot water. The Landlord replied to the text message on April 25, 2025, stating “[i]n the U.S. and will be back next week”. The Tenant then replied to the Landlord’s message by writing that she cannot go without hot water for a week, and asks the Landlord to either send someone, or allow the Tenant to call Reliance to replace the hot water heater (DOC-7844709, p. 21).

By April 28, 2025 the Tenant had not received a substantive response from the Landlord, so she sent an email to the provincial Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (‘RHEU’) (DOC- 7844709, pp. 9-10). Then, on April 29, the Landlord sent the Tenant a text message, asking the Tenant to get a quote for the cost of installation of a new rented water heater. The Tenant arranged for Reliance to attend that afternoon, and asked the Landlord to be available to receive and consider the quote while the technician was present.

Some alteration to duct work was determined to be needed for Reliance to install a new hot water heater, which required the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord was not responsive to communications from the Tenant or Reliance. Eventually, the technician found a “workaround” to replace the hot water heater without making any alterations. The hot water tank was replaced on April 30, 2025.

The Tenant was without hot water in the rental unit for 7 days (April 23 to April 30, 2025). A Landlord cannot be expected to remedy a maintenance issue they are not aware of. In this case, the Landlord was informed of the issue on April 24, 2025, and it was repaired in an effective manner 6 days later.
The issue was addressed in an effective manner by the Reliance technician on April 30, 2025, but I find that the Landlord failed to address the issue in a timely manner in the circumstances.

The issue was addressed at this time because of the Tenant’s diligence in contacting and coordinating with Reliance. The Landlord did not take reasonable steps to discharge her maintenance obligation by coordinating the repair or replacement of the hot water heater herself. Although the issue remained outstanding for only 6 days after the Landlord was made aware of the issue, this was not a minor or merely aesthetic issue. Hot water is a defined “vital service” under the Act: ss. 2(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

This issue ought to have been dealt with expeditiously by the Landlord. Instead, the Tenant was left to coordinate repairs herself, while at the same time having to actively seek the Landlord’s approval/consent for the repair. File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24

Considering the context and the entire factual situation, I find that the Landlord was in breach of her maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act relative to the hot water heater. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period April 24, 2025 to April 30, 2025.

A rent abatement is, in substance, a contractual remedy, based on the premise that if a tenant pays 100% of the rent, they ought to receive 100% of the value of what they have paid for. A rent abatement is intended to account for the proportion of the value that the Tenant did not receive because of the Landlord’s breach of the Act.

Given that hot water is a vital service and the impact of the lack of hot water on the Tenant, I find that a reasonable rent abatement is 15% of the rent for these days. The monthly rent at the time was $3,590.00. This amounts to an abatement of $106.23 [15% x ($3,590.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days x 6 days)]. Dishwasher

On May 6, 2025 the Tenant emailed the Landlord to inform her that the dishwasher was not draining properly, and has started leaking and caused water damage to surrounding cupboards and flooring in the basement bedroom, beneath the kitchen. Photos of the dishwasher and damaged cupboards were presented as evidence by the Tenant (DOC- 7844709, 13-19).
The Tenant’s uncontradicted evidence was that the dishwasher was eventually replaced about 7 weeks later.

On cross-examination, it was put to the Tenant that the dishwasher stopped working because of a “lack of maintenance”, according to the Landlord’s handyman. The suggestion was that it was a lack of ordinary cleanliness that caused damage to the dishwasher. The Tenant denied that this was the case, and there was no cogent evidence presented to support this assertion.

The Landlord’s handyman was not present to give evidence, but regardless, a “lack of maintenance” is not the same as ordinary cleanliness. If the dishwasher failed because of a “lack of maintenance” over time, it was the Landlord obliged to “maintain” the dishwasher. The Tenant’s obligation is to keep the unit in a state of ordinary cleanliness. Even the alleged words of the handyman that were put to the Tenant were not that a lack of ordinary cleanliness caused damage to the dishwasher.

In the absence of any evidence from the Landlord explaining this delay, I find that the broken dishwasher was not effectively addressed in a timely manner. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for 7 weeks relative to the dishwasher.

Being without a dishwasher for 7 weeks was surely frustrating for the Tenant, and I find that a 5% rent abatement is appropriate relative to this issue. It would have caused inconvenience for the Tenant to have to wash dishes by hand without the use of a dishwasher for this period. This amounts to a rent abatement of $289.17 [5% x ($3,590.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 x 49 days)]. File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 Pool

The tenancy agreement between the parties contains the following provision relative to the pool: “Tenant agrees to provide general maintenance for the swimming pool located on the premises, including cleaning, use of chemicals, opening and winterizing the pool. The Landlord shall be responsible for the upkeep of the equipment, including both chattels and fixtures associated with the operation of the pool.” (DOC-7989499, p. 7)

I find that cleaning and adding chemicals to a pool would fall within the Tenant’s responsibility to maintain the unit in a state of ordinary cleanliness: s. 33, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. The same may not be the case for winterizing and opening the pool, which may fall under the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. For the reasons that follow, whether this provision requiring the Tenant to winterize and open the pool is valid, or alternatively if it is void because it is inconsistent with the Act, given the Court of Appeal’s decisions in Crete v. Ottawa Community Housing Corporation, 2024 ONCA 459 (CanLII) and [name], 2009 ONCA 808 (CanLII), is not an issue I must determine on this application.

The Tenant said that a new pool heater was installed in 2018, but said it stopped working in 2021. The Tenant said that in July 2023, she sent a video to the Landlord showing that the pool heater was leaking water. The Tenant said she had a pool technician present at the time, and that it was an ongoing issue, but that the Landlord denied that the issue existed. I find that issues with disrepair of the pool heater, including a water leak from the pool heater, are responsibilities of the Landlord pursuant to the Act, and pursuant to the above-referenced clause in the tenancy agreement.

The Tenant said that she has not been able to use the pool at all in the years 2023, 2024, or 2025. The Tenant said that the Landlord attended the unit in December 2023, but it was cold and frozen outside, so the leak could not have been inspected at that time, nor could the state of repair of the pool heather have been reasonably inspected. She said the Landlord returned in May 2024 but did not look at the issue of the pool heater leak. The Tenant said that she had the leak repaired by a plumber in late 2024, for which she paid $186.45 (DOC-8029708, p. 2). The Tenant’s evidence was that the pool heater is still not working.

The Landlord said that she was not given evidence from the Tenant that there was a water leak, although the Tenant complains of a leak or a potential leak in several text message exchanges that were presented by the Landlord (DOC-7989499, pp. 72-78).
The Landlord said that she attended the unit in December 2023 with a handyman, and found a leak in the bathroom.

The Landlord said that she did not have this bathroom leak fixed because the Tenant would not let her in the basement, and the Tenant said she would repair it herself. The Tenant said the bathroom leak was minor and she had it repaired in December 2023. File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24

The Landlord said she then checked the pool heater for a leak on May 23, 2024, when she attended again with a handyman. The Landlord said no issue was found with the pool, and the Tenant would not allow her in the house to check on the bathroom leak. The Landlord said the Tenant told her that the bathroom leak had been repaired. The Tenant denied refusing entry to the Landlord, and said she only told the Landlord not to enter the bedrooms where children were sleeping.

The Tenant’s account of this is supported by a contemporaneous text message exchange presented by the Landlord (DOC-7989499, p. 62). The Tenant also said that since tension was high, she had phoned the non-emergency police line to request an officer’s assistance for the Landlord’s entry. The Tenant said she was concerned that the Landlord would not comply with her request to stay out of the bedrooms. She said that the Landlord left before the officer arrived.

The Tenant said that the company she contracted to discharge her obligations in the lease relative to the pool initially found the pool heater leak. She said this leak was substantial and the cause of the excessive water consumption. The Landlord presented an email from her pool contractor, however, this email was about leaves in the pool and potential issues that could be caused by that, and the chemical levels at the relevant time. The email does not address the water heater or the water heater leak (see [name], pp 82-83).

The Tenant presented a summary of her water bill history from 2019 to present. The Tenant’s evidence was that the household water usage did not change in any meaningful way during this period, however, the amount she was billed for water fluctuated significantly. According to this document, between 2019 and 2021 the Tenant was billed between approximately $3,000.00 and $3,800.00 annually for water. In 2022, the water bill increased slightly, to just over $4,000.00. In 2023 and 2024, the water bills increased substantially to $6,220.67 and $7,623.97 respectively. In 2025, after the Tenant had the water leak repaired, the bill returned to “normal”, at $3,555.56. This is consistent with the Tenant’s evidence that there was a water leak from the pool heater, which appears to have become progressively worse until it was repaired in November 2024, causing excessive water usage and bills (see DOC-8029708, p. 1). This is also consistent with the position that the excessive water consumption was not caused by the bathroom leak, because the water bills remained elevated after it was repaired.

In her application, the Tenant also claimed that the pool’s salt and sand filter was not in a state of good repair, but the Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to prove her allegations relative to this issue.

I am satisfied that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the pool heater has not worked since 2022. The Tenant’s evidence on this point was clear, cogent, and consistent. The Tenant also proved on a balance of probabilities that there was a leak in the pool heater until November 2024 when the Tenant had the leak repaired. This is consistent with the Tenant’s evidence about water consumption, and with the Landlord’s evidence about water consumption (see below).

Repair of the pool heater leak is the Landlord’s responsibility under the Act and the lease. While the Tenant ought to be entitled to recover any amounts she had to pay for excessive water use caused by this leak, this amount ought to be set off against the amounts added File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 to the Landlord’s property tax bills relative to water bill arrears (see below under L2 Application).

The pool heater not working is also the Landlord’s responsibility under the Act and the lease. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement as a result of the pool heater not working for the period August 25, 2023 (one year before the filing date) to present. I recognize that the pool heater not working may diminish enjoyment of the pool, but it is unclear from the evidence before me why the pool was not usable at all during the relevant period. An unheated pool can still be used.

I find that a 3% rent abatement for the months of September 2024, June to September 2025, and June 2026 is reasonable for the issue of the pool heater not working. This is a total of 151 days, and amounts to a rent abatement of $534.68 [3% x ($3,590.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 x 151 days)].

The Landlord is also ordered to inspect and ensure the pool heater is operational and in a good state of repair, including repairing or replacing the pool heater, if necessary, by July 31, 2026. L2 Application

While the Tenant claimed compensation for excessive water bills paid because of the water leak, the Landlord claimed compensation relative to costs incurred by the Landlord because the Tenant failed to pay the water bills she was required to pay under the tenancy agreement.
There was no dispute that the Tenant is responsible to pay the water bills under the tenancy agreement.
In the application, the Landlord claimed that the Tenant owes $9,008.64 for water bills that she failed to pay for the period November 23, 2021 to January 14, 2025.

The Landlord presented as evidence a letter from the Town of Oakville dated May 10, 2022. The letter states that $672.76 would be added to the property tax bill for the property for outstanding water arrears and an administrative fee of $80.00 (DOC-4024959, p. 27).

The Landlord also presented numerous other letters that she received from the Town of Oakville and the Region of Halton relative to the water bills (DOC-4024959, pp. 28-37). These letters are dated from September 15, 2022 to August 23, 2024. Each of these letters identifies that there are outstanding water arrears. Some state that the owner is responsible to pay the arrears, even if they relate to a tenant’s water use. Some state that the outstanding amounts would be added to the Landlord’s property tax bill.

The total amount set out in letters from the Town of Oakville that would be added to the Landlord’s property tax bills is $5,366.09. The letters from Halton Region do not provide specific amounts. Rather, they inform the Landlord that there are water arrears in excess of $500.00, and the Landlord is encouraged to contact [name] to pay the arrears. The exception to this is that the August 23, 2024 letter from Halton Region specifies $995.00 in water arrears. It is not clear from these documents on their face if the amounts referred to in the Halton Region letters are the same amounts referred to in the Town of File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 Oakville letters. The overlapping dates, and the fact that the letters from Halton Region state that if the amounts are not paid they would be added to the property tax bills by the Town of Oakville, suggest these are in fact the same amounts.

The Landlord also presented a Statement of Tax Arrears from the Town of Oakville, dated October 16, 2024. The statement identifies tax arrears totalling $8,609.87 for the year 2024, including $634.43 for penalties/interest. This statement does not identify what, if any, portion of this amount is by water arrears added to the property tax bill (DOC-7989499, p.36).

The Landlord also presented a copy of an interim property tax bill for the property, dated January 14, 2025. In addition to the interim 2025 taxes due, the bill shows a previous balance outstanding of $9,008.64 (DOC-7989499, p. 37). This appears to be where the number that the Landlord based the amount claimed in the application on came from, however, the bill does not identify whether all or a portion of the $9,008.64 previously owing are from water arrears, or if it is from previous unpaid property taxes. The Landlord was not able to provide a cogent explanation about this when asked on cross-examination.

Without any specificity or supporting documentary evidence, the Landlord claimed that the Tenant now owes over $10,000.00 in water arrears. Later, the Landlord presented a copy of an arrears statement from the Town of Oakville (DOC-7995052). The Landlord claims that entire “Balance Forward” amount shown of $14,246.92 is from water arrears. This is not specified on the bill, and the Landlord only claimed $9,008.64 in the application.

The Landlord then presented an email from Halton Region showing that a total of $6,669.52 was transferred to the Landlord’s property tax bill because of water arrears relative to billing dates from November 23, 2021 to July 24, 2024. This same document also says that $658.16 of the amount transferred had been paid by the Tenant. This means that a total of $6,011.36 was transferred to the Landlord’s property tax bills, and was not paid by the Tenant for the period ending May 8, 2024 (DOC-7989499, p. 44).

The Landlord claimed that the Tenant has not paid her water bill since 2020, and that since the Landlord was made aware of the non-payment in 2022, she has told the Tenant to pay. The Landlord presented as evidence a text message exchange from April 19, 2023 where the Landlord sent the Tenant a copy of a notice from the Town of Oakville about water arrears, and told the Tenant to pay the amount outstanding. In her response, the Tenant said she sometimes has to prioritize rent over utility bills, but that it would be paid. In this text message, the Tenant also wrote that there might be a water leak, as the bill was very high (DOC-7989499, p. 72). Several other similar text message exchanges during the relevant period were also presented by the Landlord (DOC-7989499, pp. 74-77).

After claiming that the Tenant had not paid any of the water bills, the Landlord later acknowledged on cross-examination that she does not know what the Tenant paid, she can only see what was not paid. The Tenant said she has always paid water bills, but when the bills started increasing, she struggled to keep up and was not able to pay the full amounts due. She said that the amount claimed in the T2 application is the amount that she thinks she overpaid.

The Landlord did not prove that the full amount claimed was added to her property tax bills. The Landlord only presented sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24 establish that it is more likely than not that $6,011.36 was added to her property tax bills during the relevant period (see email from Halton Region at DOC-7989499, p. 44). The Landlord did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to prove it is more likely that not that more than this was added to her property tax bill because of water arrears, and was not paid by the Tenant. The Landlord’s other evidence on this point was too vague and not sufficiently cogent.

As set out above in relation to the T6 application, the Tenant is not responsible to pay for the excess portion of the water bills that were caused by the pool heater leak for the period beginning one year before the T6 application was filed, being August 25, 2023 up to November 2024 when the Tenant had the leak repaired. This is a period of 16 months.

I do not accept the Landlord’s position that the excess water consumption was caused by the Tenant’s household’s overuse of water. The Tenant’s evidence, which I accept, was that there was no significant fluctuation in household water use during the relevant period. It is more likely than not that the excess consumption was caused by the pool heater water leak, given that the consumption was again reduced after the Tenant had the leak repaired.

In addition to the summary submitted by the Tenant of her escalating water bills for the years 2022 to 2024, the Landlord presented a water consumption report, showing consumption amounts in cubic meters together with billed amounts for each 60-day period from January 2019 to March 2026 (DOC-7989499, pp. 110-111). This report shows a clear and significant increase in consumption beginning with the bill dated July 21, 2022 up to the bill dated September 24, 2024, when consumption amounts were reduced significantly.

I find the Landlord’s consumption report to be the most reliable data showing consumption and billed amounts because it is a document provided by Halton Region, whereas the Tenant’s summary was a document that the Tenant created.

The average amount billed for water for each 60-day period from the bills dated January 18, 2019 to May 20, 2022 was $173.20. For each 60-day period from the bills dated September 22, 2023 to November 25, 2024 were $667.65. I find that it is reasonable to use these amounts to make a reasonable determination as to the amount that the Tenant was billed for excess water consumption caused by the leak. On average, the Tenant was billed an additional $494.45 for each 60-day period for excess water consumption caused by the leak.

As noted above, the Tenant is not responsible for the portion of the water bills attributable to excess consumption caused by the water leak for a total of 16 months (or eight 60-day periods). This totals $3,955.60.
The Tenant therefore owes the Landlord $2,055.76 for excess water bills for period November 23, 2021 to January 14, 2025 [$6,011.36 - $3,955.60].
The Landlord owes the Tenant a rent abatement in the amount of $930.08 with respect to the issues with the hot water ($106.23), dishwasher ($289.17), and pool ($534.68), as set out above
The Tenant therefore owes the Landlord $1,125.68 ($2,055.76 - $930.08). File Numbers: LTB-L-003712-24 LTB-T-068631-24
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $1, 125.68 for the the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Landlord has incurred or will incur as a result of the unpaid utility costs.
The Landlord shall inspect the pool heater, and ensure it is operational and in a state of good repair, including by repairing or replacing the pool heater as necessary, by July 31, 2026

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the fu ll amount owing on or before July 31, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant's application alleges that the Landlord unlawfully increased the monthly rent and seeks reimbursement of the alleged illegal rent increase paid between November 5, 2024 and August 4, 2025.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 2, 2025.
The monthly rent for the rental unit was $2,980.00 from October 2021 until November 4, 2024.

AA testified that the monthly rent increased to $3,500.00 effective November 5, 2024. AA submitted that the Landlord did not serve a Notice of Rent Increase pursuant to section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not obtain authorization from the Board for an above-guideline rent increase.

AA testified that the Tenants paid the monthly rent of $3,500.00 from November 5, 2024 until the tenancy terminated. AA further testified that no additional services or facilities were provided in exchange for the increase.
The Landlord acknowledged that he did not serve a Notice of Rent Increase and did not obtain an order authorizing an above-guideline rent increase.

The Landlord testified that the original tenancy agreement was entered into by four tenants. The Landlord further testified that, on November 4, 2024, a new tenancy agreement was executed by only two of the original tenants for a fixed term of seven months commencing November 5, 2024. The evidence before me was that the remaining two original tenants ceased to be tenants under the new agreement and instead remained in the rental unit as occupants.

AA acknowledged that he voluntarily signed the November 4, 2024 tenancy agreement. AA testified that the Landlord requested a new tenancy agreement because two of the original tenants no longer had income. There was no evidence before me that the Landlord threatened, pressured, misled, or coerced the tenants into entering into the new agreement.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the tenancy agreement executed on November 4, 2024 constituted a new tenancy agreement between the parties and reflected their intention to replace the existing tenancy agreement. The new agreement altered the composition of the tenant group by reducing the number of tenants from four to two and reflected that only the remaining two tenants would be legally responsible for the tenancy. The agreement also established a new fixed term of seven months commencing November 5, 2024. The reduction in the number of tenants, the change in legal liability, and the creation of a new fixed term are all factors that support the conclusion that this was not merely a continuation of the existing tenancy with unchanged parties. Rather, the parties entered into a new contractual arrangement with different parties and a new term.

In my view, where parties voluntarily enter into a new tenancy agreement involving a material change in the identity of the tenants, the parties may agree to a new rent for the new tenancy. In such circumstances, I find the rent charged under the new agreement is not a rent increase governed by sections 116 to 126 of the Act but rather the lawful rent established for the new tenancy.

I accept the Landlord's evidence that the November 4, 2024 agreement was entered into to reflect a change in who would be legally liable as tenants under the tenancy. I also accept AA's evidence that he voluntarily signed the agreement. There is insufficient evidence before me to conclude that the Landlord required the tenants to sign the new agreement through coercion or otherwise acted in bad faith.

As I have found that a new tenancy commenced on November 5, 2024, the increase in monthly rent from $2,980.00 to $3,500.00 was not an unlawful rent increase under the Act. Rather, it was the rent agreed upon by the parties for the new tenancy.
Accordingly, I find that the rent charged from November 5, 2024 onward was lawful, and the Tenant has not established that the Landlord collected or retained any illegal rent.
For these reasons, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $15,548.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination in accordance with section 48 of the Act. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2025 as a result of receiving the N12 notice of termination, and that the rental unit was listed for sale in or around August, 2025, within one year of the Tenants vacating the rental unit. [name]. Section 57(5) of the Act provided that in circumstances such as this there is a rebuttable presumption that the N12 notice was served in bath faith, if the Landlord pursuant to subsection c) advertises the rental unit or the building that contains the rental unit for sale. 5. Section 57(6) of the Act provides the time frame for section 57(5) as beginning on the day the landlord gives a notice of termination under section 48 and ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. 6. For the following reasons, based on the evidence and testimony before me, I do not find that the Landlords have met the burden of establishing that the N12 notice was served in good faith. 7. The Landlord testified that the N12 notice was served because the Landlord’s mother who was living with the Landlords wanted her own place. 8. The Landlord testified that his mother suffers from knee issues and she had suffered from these issues prior to the service of the N12 notice of termination on the Tenants and was told in October, 2024 that she would require a knee replacement. 9. The Landlord testified that after a few days of moving into the rental unit his mother began feeling scared and worried that if she were to trip or fall due to her medical condition she wouldn’t have any help. 10. The Landlord states his mother moved back in with himself and the other Landlord shortly after moving into the rental unit. The Landlords did not initially re-rent or list the property for sale as they wanted to see if things would get better with their mother and she would move back to the rental unit. 11. Eventually the Landlord’s mother had decided she would not be moving back into the rental unit and it was listed for sale and sold with a closing date of October 31, 2025. 12. The Tenants question the good faith intentions of the Landlord as in addition to the Landlord’s mother’s medical conditions regarding her knee condition, she is elderly and would not require a 5 bedroom, 4 bath house for herself. 13. Based on the evidence educed at the hearing and the testimony of the parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlords gave the Tenants a notice in good faith. I find it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s mother did not have a genuine intention to move in and that there was no change in circumstances that prevented her from remaining in the rental unit. The Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Remedies 14. The Tenants in their application request the following remedies: • Rent abatement totalling $7,800.00; • Rent differential totalling $7,800.00; • Moving expenses $7,345.00; • General Compensation $34,200.00; and • A fine to the Board. Rent Abatement 15. A rent abatement is a contractual remedy geared towards the premise that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent for a bundle of goods and services but is not receiving the full benefit of those goods or services, that they should be abated the difference for what they are not receiving but paying for. 16. At the hearing the Tenants testified that they were seeking a rent differential and not seeking an abatement of rent. As such no compensation for an abatement will be awarded. Rent Differential 17. The Tenants were renting the upper unit from the Landlord and had access to the entire house with the exception of the basement. The rental unit consisted of 3 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms approximately 1,800 square feet, a single car garage and two parking spots in the driveway. The Tenants were paying the Landlord $2,850.00 per month 18. The new rental unit was 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms approximately 1,500 to 1,600 square feet, with no garage but parking for two vehicles. The Tenants are paying $3,500.00 per month in rent. 19. The rent differential between the two similar units for a period of 12 months is ($3,500.00- $2,850.00 x 12) $7,800.00. The Tenants are entitled to the amount claimed for rent differential. Moving Expenses 20. The Tenants seek moving expenses in the amount of $7,345.00 and produced an invoice from a company Just Move It. The Landlords question the authenticity of the document produced. In addition to the high amount for the moving service the document is lacking in a GST number of the business, there is no address for the business and a google search of the phone number does not show that number belonging to Just Move it. The Tenants say the came across the business on Facebook and called the number. 21. Based on similar cases I am not satisfied that the moving expenses claimed are reasonable. In the circumstances the Tenants shall be awarded $2,000.00 for moving expenses. General Compensation 22. The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3)(1.1), which states: An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. [Emphasis added]. 23. The Tenants moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2022, and vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2025 the day after their third child was born approximately 2 years and 7 months later. The Tenants claim that at the time they vacated the rental unit the rental market was a nightmare and they were unable to find suitable housing in the City of [name] and only found suitable housing 80 km away in the City of Welland. This drastic move completely uprooted them from their established support networks, daycare and community ties raising three young children (newborn, 2 and 3 y/o) in a new City. Additionally the daily commute for Mr. [name]name] was greatly increased going back and forth from Welland to Mississauga. In the circumstances I find that general compensation equivalent to two months worth of rent to be fair $2,850.00 x 2 = $5,700.00. Administrative Fine 24. The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 25. In the circumstances I am satisfied that the other remedies awarded would provide an adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts in the future. As such, no fine shall be ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $15,548.00. This amount represents: • $7,800.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred or will incur for one year. • $2,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,700.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s rent deposit for the reasons stated below.
It is undisputed that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2018, and she moved out by July 11, 2025. The Landlord was holding a last month’s rent deposit.

It is undisputed that the Tenant sent a notice to the Landlord on June 18, 2025, that she would be moving out by July 31, 2025. The Landlord replied to the Tenant on June 19, 2025, acknowledging her notice. In fact, the Tenant left by July 10, and she returned the keys to the Landlord on July 11, 2025. It is undisputed that the Tenant paid rent for July 2025, so she requested the return of her last month’s rent deposit on July 20, 2025. The Tenant said that she paid the rent on July 1, 2025, in good faith, because she believed that the Landlord would return her last month’s rent deposit. She wrote again to the Landlord on August 2, 2025, repeating her request. The Landlord did not return the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant submitted into evidence an email sent to the Landlord on June 20, 2025, in which she said that she will probably leave earlier than July 31, 2025. She also wrote “Showings can be scheduled daily from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., if that is convenient. Kindly provide at least one hour’s notice prior to each showing to allow for preparation of the premises.”
The Tenant said that she received a reply from the Landlord on August 4, 2025, in which he said that he was deducting amounts from the last month’s rent deposit because he found damage in the unit.

At the hearing, the Landlord said that he did not return the last month’s rent deposit because he tried to rent out the unit, but he was unable to rent it before September 1, 2025. He said that he began to show the rental unit by July 20, 2025, after the Tenant had left. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s last month rent deposit for the reasons that follow.

It is undisputed that the Tenant provided insufficient notice to validly terminate the tenancy on July 31, 2025. She only gave notice on June 18, 2025, that she would be leaving on July 31, 2025, which was less than the 60 days required by subsection 44(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

Pursuant to subsection 88(1)1 of the Act, the Landlord might potentially be entitled to collect rent from the Tenant to August 31, 2025. However, the Landlord is also obliged, pursuant to section 16 of the Act, to mitigate his loss of the extra month of rent because of the insufficient notice provided by the Tenant.

For the following reasons, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to mitigate his loss, and he was therefore not entitled to the extra month of rent to August 31, 2025. The Landlord was aware by June 19, 2025, and he acknowledged, that the Tenant had provided her notice to leave by July 31, 2025. On June 20, 2025, the Tenant gave the Landlord full licence to start showing the unit at certain reasonable hours of the day provided he give her some notice, which notice he was obliged to provide in any case. Nevertheless, the Landlord chose to wait until July 20, 2025, a full month later, and almost 10 days after he knew that the Tenant had vacated, to start showing the unit. This delay in showing the unit indicates a lack of concern with mitigating his loss. The Landlord had the Tenant’s rent payment for July 2025, and he also had her last month’s rent deposit, so he was in no hurry to start showing the unit. I find that the Landlord’s behaviour demonstrates, on a balance of probabilities, a failure to mitigate the loss he suffered as a result of insufficient notice. Consequently, I find that the Landlord is not entitled to rent from the Tenant past July 31, 2025, after which date he could have had the unit re-rented if he had acted earlier to start showing the unit. The undisputed evidence is that the Landlord could have started showing the unit at the end of June for rental by August 1, but he waited until nearly the end of July 2025 to start showings.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $996.00. This amount represents: • $945.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination, that the Tenant’s vacated as a result of the notice, and that the Landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement in May 2025.

As the Landlord re-rented the unit in May 2025, subsection 57 (5) of the Act is engaged. This means that it is presumed that the N12 notice is given in bad faith unless the Landlord proves the contrary.

The Landlord, A. [name] testified that the intended occupants on the N12 did not move into the rental unit because after the N12 was issued, several things changed. The intended occupants on the N12 were his father, [name] [name], (the other Landlord), his mother (the other Landlord’s spouse) and his sister (the other Landlord’s child). 6. [name] testified that S. [name] and his spouse went to Turkey in May 2024. While in Turkey, S. [name]’s spouse had surgery on her wrist and legs. As a result of this, their return date was postponed until October 30, 2024. 7. [name] testified that S. [name] and his spouse could not move into the rental unit in October because the unit was damaged and required repairs. He testified that repairs were carried out and finished by December 20, 2024. 8. A. Baron testified that ultimately, S. [name] and his spouse did not move into the unit because S. [name]’s spouse was still recovering from her surgery and required assistance. As such, his parents stayed with family close to where the rental unit was located. 9. A. [name] testified that his sister, the other Landlord’s daughter, did not move into the rental unit because she was attending graduate school in Australia. He testified that she finished her undergrad in 2023 and wrote the MCAT exam in April 2024. A decision was made in August 2024 for her to attend medical school in Australia. 10. In [name] v. [name] [2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII)], the Court of Appeal found that in considering whether a notice of termination was given in bad faith, the LTB should not limit its analysis to the time the N12 was delivered. While Elkins involved a notice of termination given under section 49 of the RTA, I think that the case also applies where notice is given under section 48 and the LTB should not restrict its consideration of a landlord’s good faith to the point in time when the landlord delivered the relevant notice of termination. 11. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. While I accept that the Landlord’s spouse underwent surgery in Turkey in August 2024, I am not satisfied that this was a material change in circumstance that prevented the occupancy of the rental unit. I say this because there was nothing before me to confirm that the Landlord’s spouse’s condition was such that living in the rental unit became impossible. Further, but for the Landlord’s daughter attending medical school in Australia, it would be reasonable to presume that the Landlord and his spouse could move into the rental unit with her. The decision to go to medical school took place prior to the Tenant’s vacating the rental unit. As such, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies 12. The Tenant requested a rent differential. The Tenant’s rent at the old unit was $2,400.00. The rent for the unit the Tenant’s moved to is $3,500.00. 13. The Tenant testified that the old unit contained 4 bedrooms with a finished basement. The house they moved into was a much smaller 3-bedroom house about 10 minutes away from the rental unit. A copy of the lease was submitted confirming a monthly rent of $3,500.00 (DOC-7712632). 14. I am satisfied that the Tenant’s request for a rent differential is warranted and shall be awarded. The rent differential is calculated as $1,100.00 x12, totalling $13,200.00. 15. The Tenant requested costs associated with moving in the amount of $1,000.00. The Tenant produced a invoice from T.O. Roofing and Snowplowing dated September 9, 2024 in the amount of $1,000.00. The details confirmed in the invoice indicate that the Tenants rented a truck for the August 30, 2024- September 2, 2024 weekend and the September 6, 2024 – September 8, 2024 weekend (DOC-6279219, page 43). I am satisfied that this cost is directly associated with the Tenants moving out of the rental unit, is reasonable and it shall be awarded. 16. The Tenant is seeking general damages in the amount of $20,943.36. 17. Section 57 (3) 1.1 of the Act gives the authority to order the landlord to pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 (rent abatement). 18. The Tenant’s application bases the request for compensation on one of the Tenants losing an income source as a result of having to move. I take this into consideration as a factor when assessing whether a remedy for general compensation is appropriate. The Tenants testified that they lived in the rental unit in 2014. They lived in the unit with their two children, ages 15 and 22. The children did not need to change schools as a result of the move. V. [name] ran a home daycare from the unit, but as a result of the move, she lost families due to the new unit not being close to the school in which she serviced. 19. Based on the Tenant’s testimony and my knowledge of similar cases, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s are entitled to general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00. The Tenants were long term tenants having lived in the rental unit for 10 years prior to receiving the N12 notice. In coming to this determination, I note that the Tenant’s children were not overly impacted by the move, having heard that it did not result in having to change schools, etc. 20. The Tenant’s requested that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the LTB. 21. An administrative fine is a remedy used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter a landlord from breaching the Act in the future, if other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. In this matter, I am satisfied that the remedy provided to the Tenants is sufficient to deter the Landlord from breaching the Act with similar activity in the future. I therefore find that an administrative fine is not required to encourage the Landlord’s compliance with the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $19,248.00. This amount represents: • $13,200.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from September 1, 2024, to August 31, 2025. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
