issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. However, as the Tenant was partially successful in their claim but the only remedy sought by the Tenants was a rent differential and I have denied the request for the rent differential, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay $48.00 which is the cost of filing the application. Illegal Entry
The Tenants submit that the Landlord and the Landlord’s family would enter the rental unit without providing any notice of entry.

The Tenant, [name] (‘MC’) testified that as the Landlord or the Landlord’s family would enter randomly and without any prior notice, it was a general interference with her day-to-day living as they had to be prepared for entry at any given time and that the entries would occasionally interfere with her work meetings as she worked from home.
MC testified that the Landlord entered on an almost daily basis from the start of the tenancy on September 9, 2016, up to the date the Tenants vacated on August 30, 2025.

The Landlord did not deny that she and her family entered the rental unit on several occasions. The Landlord testified that the Tenant, [name] (‘WC’) is her cousin and that as WC had advised that he and MC would be moving back from the east coast to Ontario, the parties had come to an agreement for WC to occupy the basement. The Landlord testified that WC was advised prior to the commencement of the tenancy that the Landlord had either two bedrooms available upstairs or the basement unit available with the condition that the Landlord have access to the basement to access her freezer and the shared laundry machines. The Landlord testified that the Tenants chose to reside in the basement unit and consented to the condition that the Landlord have access to their freezer and the laundry room.

The Landlord testified that there was a breakdown in the relationship in August 2022, when the Landlord asked the Tenants to vacate the rental unit. The Landlord testified that due to her mobility issues, her sister would enter the rental unit to access the freezer on the Landlord’s behalf.

Based on the evidence before me, it appears the entries became contested as of approximately August 2022. The Tenants provided a list of 35 dates between September 4, 2023 to August 30, 2025 on which the Landlord or the Landlord’s sister entered the rental unit without giving prior notice. Regardless of any informal agreement to the contrary, the Landlord was obligated under the Act to comply with notice requirements. Section 26 of the Act allows the Landlord to enter without notice and section 27 of the Act sets out the circumstances in which a notice is required. The Landlord’s entry without notice or consent to access the freezer and laundry room did not comply with sections 26 or 27 of the Act. While I may have issued an order for a rent abatement, the Tenants withdrew their request for a rent abatement at the hearing. The Divisional Court’s decision in Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., [2012] O.J. No. 1052 ([name]. Ct.), essentially stands for the proposition that I am unable to order what is not specifically requested.

While the Tenants sought a rent differential pursuant to section 31(2) of the Act, I was not satisfied that the conduct of the Landlord induced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. Rather, I find that the Tenants continued to live in the rental unit and were minimally impacted by the entries. As a result, the request for a rent differential is denied. Harassment

The Tenants submit that the Landlord has harassed the Tenants by watching the Tenants vacate the rental unit on September 1, 2024 and laughing at the Tenants. The Tenants also submit that the Landlords have harassed the Tenants by giving [name] with various amounts owing.

The Landlord testified that she was under the impression there was initially no tenancy as the agreement was an informal arrangement between family. As a result, the Landlord filed an A1 application, LTB-L-081395-24, which was withdrawn when the Landlord became aware that there was a tenancy under the Act.

Subsequently as the agreement was an informal arrangement between family, the Landlord served N4 notices with incorrect amounts. However, I was not satisfied based on the Tenants’ testimony that the notices were excessive or were given for the purposes of harassing the Tenants. It was undisputed that the Tenants had not paid rent for a large portion of the tenancy and as a result, I was not satisfied that the notices were given as harassment but rather, find that these were notices given in accordance with the Act for non-payment of rent.
With regards to the Tenants’ assertion that the Landlord watched the Tenants vacate and laughed, I was not satisfied that this interference was substantial or amounted to harassment.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $48.00. This amount represents: • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application.

The Tenants allege that they began to suffer from excessive heat in the residential complex as soon as they moved in, and the Landlord failed to repair the problem. They also alleged that there was excessive cold in the winter. They allege that they informed the Landlord that there was a problem with the HVAC system in the residential complex, but the Landlord failed to respond to their maintenance complaint.
The Tenants moved into the residential complex in July 2022. It is a two-storey house with four bedrooms. The monthly rent was $5,637.50. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on July 1, 2024.
The application was filed on September 14, 2023. Therefore, the Tenants are only eligible for a remedy commencing as of September 15, 2022.

Both Tenants testified that they experienced excessive heat, particularly in the master bedroom, as soon as they moved in. They said the temperature was set at 22 degrees centigrade. Although they said that the HVAC worked, they said that the main problem was air flow, and they would get consistent temperature readings during the summer of between 26 and 28 degrees centigrade. They informed the Landlord. It is undisputed that a technician was sent by the Landlord on July 23, 2022, to inspect. It is also undisputed that the inspector told both the Landlord and the Tenants that there was no problem with the air conditioning.

The Tenants said that the hottest area was over the garage. Both parties testified about a technician opening the garage ceiling in August 2022 to inspect the duct system. Neither party was very clear about what happened as a result of opening the garage ceiling. The Tenants said that the Landlord informed them there was something wrong with the structure of the building. The Landlord said that they inspected the system infrastructure, and they concluded that the HVAC system was working well.

The Tenants said that after August 2022 it was not so hot. They said it was extremely cold by November 2022, and they told the Landlord verbally. They said that they had to use electric blankets and a portable heater in the master bedroom, and they had to shower in the basement where it was warmer.

The Tenants said that they did not further communicate anything about heat or cold to the Landlord until April 2023, when they told the Landlord’s husband during a visit that the summer heat issue had not been resolved. They said that he told them to purchase a new air conditioning system for the house and if it resolved the problem, he would reimburse them. They said that they did not do it as they did not believe they would be reimbursed.

The Tenants submitted into evidence the first written communication to the Landlord of that year, dated June 8, 2023. In it, they informed the Landlord that the HVAC is not working in the master bedroom, there was barely any air coming out, and it causes the room to go over 28 degrees in the summer and below 20 degrees in the winter. They attached photos of temperature readings they took the previous year that show a range of temperatures above 26 degrees.

The Tenants submitted into evidence the response from the Landlord, dated June 10, 2023, in which she states that three technicians “all agreed the high efficient HVAC worked well”. She continued that it’s “the house structure problem need a huge renovation, most houses here are the same.” The Landlord suggests that the Tenants can terminate the tenancy with an N11 notice, and/or that the Landlord can provide a portable air conditioner.

The Tenants said that the Landlord did nothing further, so they purchased a portable air conditioning unit. They submitted into evidence the receipt for the unit, dated April 28, 2023, for the amount of $440.69 including HST. They said that the unit was used in the master bedroom. There is no evidence that the Tenants sent the invoice to the Landlord for reimbursement. There is also no evidence that the Landlord ever made an effort to provide a portable air conditioner to the Tenants.

It is undisputed that the Landlord replaced the furnace in October 2023, and the Tenants did not complain about heat or cold to the Landlord after that time. The Tenants said that the situation was somewhat improved after the furnace was replaced, but they still used the heater.

The Landlord said that she investigated all complaints from the Tenants, and all the technicians found no problem with the HVAC system. She submitted into evidence a letter from [name], dated August 31, 2024, in which he writes that his company sent a technician to inspect the air conditioning in the rental unit on July 6, 2023, and the technician “didn’t find out any safety issues at that time, when he was in this property address.”

The Landlord said that the rental unit was a consistent 20 to 23 degrees, even though the thermostat was set at 24 or 25 degrees. She said that she told the Tenants to set it lower, but the Tenants did not want to because they said it would have a negative impact on their utility costs. She also said that she never heard anything from the Tenants about the temperature between August 2022 and June 2023. The Landlord said that everything had been resolved in the summer of 2022. She submitted a final text from the Tenants from August 14, 2022, in response to her information about the repair. They wrote, “Okay, thank you.” There is no further text from them in evidence until the following June of 2023.

The Landlord said that there was nothing wrong with the HVAC system, but she replaced the furnace in October 2023 as an “act of kindness”. She said that she also felt pressured by the Tenants, and she wished to avoid any future disputes. The Landlord submits that she responded to all maintenance complaints immediately, and she dealt with all of them.
The Tenants request a 15% rent abatement for the period September 15, 2022 through October 2023 when the furnace was replaced. Reasons and Analysis:

In accordance with section 20 of the Act, a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

As set out in the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards for the reasons that follow.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the documentary evidence supports the Landlord’s contention that both parties believed the matter had been dealt with in the summer of 2022. There is no written communication between the parties in evidence between September 2022 and June 2023. There is no documentary evidence to support the Tenants’ contention that they informed the Landlord about a continued problem in April 2023. However, by June 8, 2023, the Tenants communicate to the Landlord that they are suffering the same heat issues as the previous year. It is also only in this communication that the Tenants complain that they felt cold all winter. It is undisputed that the Landlord did not do anything about this complaint, nor did she provide an air conditioning unit as she offered, until she replaces the furnace entirely in October 2023.

I find that the Landlord breached her maintenance obligation, because she was well aware that the Tenants had a heat issue over the summer from the previous year, and she was well aware that nothing had been done to the HVAC system. In fact, the Landlord repeatedly told the Tenants that no one could find anything wrong with it. She did nothing further to investigate the matter until she fully replaced the furnace in October 2023. I find that there is no credible evidence to support the Tenants’ allegation that the Landlord knew anything about a cold issue until June 2023, when it was already summer time.

The Tenants said that the issue improved after replacement of the furnace, and they admit that they said nothing further to the Landlord about heat or cold after October 2023, until the time they vacated the rental unit in 2024.

On the basis of the above, I find that the Landlord’s response to the air conditioning problem, once informed about the issue in early June 2023, was not timely, effective nor appropriate. She did not even inspect the matter. She told the Tenants the HVAC was fully functional, but she would nevertheless provide them with an air conditioning unit, and she did not. She also implied that the Tenants could terminate the tenancy if they did not like how things stood. It is not credible that the Landlord completely replaced the furnace in October 2023 out of the kindness of her heart. She was aware by that point that there was an issue with the HVAC, or at least circulation of air in the rental unit, and she was aware that it was a problem with the Tenants because she had been informed about it in the summer of 2022. Although it is possible that the Landlord understood the problem to have been resolved in August 2022 as a result of the Tenants’ written responses in that month, when the Tenants complained again by June 2023, the Landlord could not have had any doubts that there was a problem. Remedies

The Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement for the months of June, July, August and September 2023, from the time they informed the Landlord about the problem, until the furnace was replaced in October 2023. They request a 15% rent abatement for the discomfort they experienced.

I find that it is not unfair to award the Tenants a 10% rent abatement for the four months of summer in 2023 for the following reasons. The Tenants said that the problem was primarily experienced in the master bedroom of the four bedroom rental unit. They said that it was an issue throughout the house, but particularly in that room. That is only a small area of the rental unit, though an important one for the Tenants when it was frequently very hot over the summer. The Tenants were experiencing a pregnancy and they had to sleep in the master bedroom. Therefore, I find that the Landlord will be ordered to reimburse the Tenants 10% X $5,637.50=$563.75 X four months=$2,255.00.

The Tenants purchased the air conditioning unit in April 2023, when they were aware that they were pregnant again, and they suspected the Landlord was not going to deal with the heat issue over the summer. They did in fact suffer hot temperatures over the whole summer because the Landlord took no action about the heat issue until October 2023. Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement of the $440.69 they spent on the portable air conditioning unit as it was their only relief for that summer.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $2,743.69. This amount represents: • $440.69 for purchase of the air conditioning unit • $2,255.00 rent abatement for the months of June through September 2023 • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination, the Tenant vacated as a result of the notice, no person indicated in the notice moved into the rental unit, and in fact, the rental unit was listed for sale within a year after the Tenant vacated.
As the rental unit was listed for sale, subsection 57 (5) of the Act is engaged. This means that it is presumed that the N12 notice is given in bad faith unless the Landlord proves the contrary.

The Landlord testified that when the N12 notice was served to the Tenant, it was her intention to reside there with her husband. In May 2025, the Landlord travelled to China to prepare herself and her husband for the move. She testified that her husband was unwell and spent two days in the hospital due to his diabetes. In June and into July, she testified that it was considered high risk for her husband to travel and he was advised to stay in China to continue to receive medical care. The Landlord submitted medical documents. (DOC-7681886). The documentation indicates that the Landlord’s husband was admitted to the hospital on May 26, 2025 and discharged on May 28, 2025. Discharge condition indicates that :
The Landlord testified that absent her husband’s illness, they would have returned to Canada to reside in the rental unit.

On cross examination, the Landlord testified that her husband was diagnosed with diabetes about five years ago and his condition deteriorated and got worse and worse. She testified that she made the decision to sell the house in July 2025 when she realized her husband’s condition was not improving. She testified that she wanted to focus on taking care of her husband. She testified that she did not advise the Tenant because she no longer wanted to be a landlord.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. The Landlord’s husband did not testify at the hearing. I am not satisfied that the contents of the medical documents support the Landlord’s position that the Landlord’s husband’s condition was an unforeseen change in circumstance that prevented the Landlord from moving into the rental unit. The Landlord’s husband was diagnosed with Diabetes five years ago. The medical documentation describes the Landlord’s discharge condition as essentially normal, with no immediate concerns. Follow up directions indicate to continue with medication after discharge, diet recommendations, blood-glucose monitoring 3 times a week, and to re-check diabetic complications every 6 months. The medical documentation alone does not support an unforeseen change in circumstance.

Further, and in the alternative, the Landlord testified that she made the decision to sell the house prior to the Tenant vacating, but did not inform the Tenant because she no longer wished to be a Landlord.

In [name] v. [name] [2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII)], the Court of Appeal found that in considering whether a notice of termination was given in bad faith, the LTB should not limit its analysis to the time the N12 was delivered. While Elkins involved a notice of termination given under section 49 of the RTA, I think that the case also applies where notice is given under section 48 and the LTB should not restrict its consideration of a landlord’s good faith to the point in time when the landlord delivered the relevant notice of termination.

The LTB may, depending on the circumstances, find that a landlord acted in bad faith where the circumstances that caused the landlord to deliver the N12 notice changed before the tenant vacated or found alternate accommodations and the landlord did not offer to allow the tenant to remain in or reoccupy the unit. This is the circumstance of the application before me.
As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies
The Tenant is requesting expenses related to moving and storage in the amount of $19,569.34.

The Tenant testified that the home he purchased after vacating the rental unit is half the size. This means that he does not have the same space for storage as he used to. He testified that he had access to 1/3 of an acre at the rental unit and had a heated garage. He testified that he has 10 vehicles/recreational vehicles along with a large amount of items that he has had to store since vacating. He testified that his current home only has a four car driveway with no outdoor storage space and cannot facilitate the space he needs for all his stuff and his cars.

The Tenant submitted receipts for his moving costs at $8,644.50. ([name] 29) The Tenant submitted receipts for storage totalling $10,924.84. This represents storage costs from August 2025 to July 2026 in the amount of $6,468.12.(DOC-7706523 Pg 30- 37) and from November 2025 to July 2026 for parking spaces and 1 storage unit in the amount of $4,456.72. ([name]).

Subsection 57 (3) 1.2 allows the Board to order the Landlord to pay the reasonable out of pocket moving, storage or other like expenses. I find that the amount the Tenant is asking for is reasonable. These expenses would not have been uncured but for the Tenant’s having to vacate the rental unit pursuant to the N12 notice. An order shall issue for reimbursement of $19,569.34.
The Tenant is requesting general compensation in the amount of $ 29,954.88.

The Tenant testified that he lived in the rental unit since 2017. He lived in the unit with his wife and two children. He testified that he purchased a home roughly 7 minutes away from the rental unit that is on a busier street. The Tenant testified that if the Landlord had informed him of the change of plans, he would have stayed at the rental unit. He testified that given the timeline, he had not closed on the house, and he would have preferred to have stayed.

Subsection 57 (3) 1.1 says that the Board can order the Landlord to pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. (rent abatement)

Based on my knowledge of similar cases, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00. I acknowledge that the Tenant lived in the rental unit for 8 years and would not have vacated but for receiving the N12 notice. The Tenant remained relatively close to the rental unit, and I did not hear of any adverse consequences not contemplated in the usual course of having to move. As such, an order shall issue for general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00.
The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay an administrative fine.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 23. n this case, as the Tenant has been awarded a substantial monetary remedy, I find that this provides sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $24,617.34. This amount represents: • $19,569.34 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has and will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.0 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T3 Application alleging the Landlord reduced usage of the washroom as of August 31, 2024 and reduced her ability to use the freezer found in the common area kitchen as of March 1, 2025. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant testified that the rental house is located inside a rooming house. The floor in which she lives used to have other tenants residing in rooms 2, 3, and 4 but as of the date of the hearing all the other rooms are unoccupied. The Tenant lives with a physical disability which makes it difficult to move around without assistance. At all relevant times the Tenant was paying $615.00 for monthly rent. [name]

There are two washrooms on the floor in which the Tenant resides. The first washroom, which contains a toilet and a sink, is located in the hallway just outside the rental unit. The second washroom, which contains a shower in addition to a toilet and sink, is down the hallway from the rental unit.

The Tenant’s testimony was that she first lost access to the washroom on August 31, 2024. The Tenant entered a picture into evidence taken September 16, 2024, the Tenant showing an “out of order” sign on the door of the first washroom. Subsequently, the Tenant discovered the door was locked and she could not gain access to it.

The Tenant testified that she did not gain access to the first washroom until “January or February 2026”. The Tenant confirmed in cross-examination that she always had full access to the second washroom. The Tenant is seeking a 25% rent reduction from September 16, 2024 onwards until access to the washroom was restored.

In cross-examination the Tenant was asked if there was a leak in the washroom which may have led to it being “out of order”. The Tenant originally was evasive with her answers, eventually admitting that there was a leak in the ceiling that needed to be addressed by the Landlord. [name]

The Tenant testified that when the tenancy began she had access to two fridges, both located in the common area. In 2024, the Landlord provided the Tenant a small fridge to use inside the rental unit. Subsequently, the Landlord removed one of the fridges from the common area. The Tenant’s evidence is that the small fridge has a freezer however it is not meant to store food such as meat in it.

On March 1, 2025, the Tenant was washing the fridge when the superintendent approached her and informed her she is not to use the freezer any longer. On March 17, 2025, the Landlord and Tenant met at the rental unit and discussed the issue. In a recording entered into evidence, the Tenant informs the Landlord that she wishes to have full use of the fridge/freezer in the common area. The Landlord replies that the Tenant should return the small fridge in her rental unit if she wishes to use the fridge in the common area. It is unclear from the recording whether the Tenant had use of the freezer moving forward.
The Tenant is seeking a 15% rent reduction from March 1, 2025 to the date of the hearing, and an ongoing rent reduction due to the lack of ability to use the freezer.

In cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed the freezer in the common area functions and is available, she is just fearful of the superintendent and does not want to go against his wishes. The Tenant confirmed she does not have documentary evidence regarding a police report or any complaints regarding the Landlord or superintendent. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord agreed with the Tenant that the first washroom was inaccessible due to a leaking ceiling. The Landlord admitted to locking the door and placing an “out of order” sign to prevent anyone from entering. The Landlord’s evidence is that the repair took approximately a week or two and the Tenant was allowed access to the washroom thereafter.

The Landlord also testified about the freezer, indicating that there is one common area freezer that the Tenant is allowed to use at any time. The Landlord was generally unaware that the Tenant had not been using the freezer. Analysis
The onus is on the Tenant to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that a service and/or facility was reduced.

In R.C. v. S.Y.S, 2026 ONSC 2799, the Court analyzed the credibility of parties and the role that is plays in the decision-making process. Paragraphs 38-40 state: [38] Credibility is a primary vehicle for determining the truth of alleged facts. Assessing credibility is not an exact science: [name] v. Berkovits, 2023 ONSC 497 (“Berkovits (ONSC)”), at para. 11, citing R. v. [name], 2006 SCC 17, [2006] 1 S.C.R. 621, at para. 20. [39] Traditional criteria used to assess witness evidence include witness demeanour, inherent probability in the circumstances, and internal and external consistency: Prodigy Graphics Group Inc. v. Fitz-Andrews, 2000 CarswellOnt 1178 (S.C.), at para. 46. [40] Where a party has the burden to discharge a legal onus, I must satisfy myself, on a balance of probabilities, of “the credibility and reliability of the evidence in order to be in a position to make the relevant findings of fact”: Berkovits (ONSC), at para. 9.

Overall, I found the Tenant’s evidence confusing, evasive, and contradictory. For example, the Tenant was asked at the beginning of the hearing when the washroom access was reduced, to which the Tenant confidently confirmed it was August 31, 2025. Subsequently, during her testimony, the Tenant alleged it occurred August 31, 2024. The Tenant then produced a photograph from September 16, 2024 showing the “out of order” sign without mentioning how she first came to learn of the washroom access being reduced.

Another example of the Tenant’s inconsistent testimony was surrounding the current occupants of the other units in the rooming house. The Tenant originally testified that units 2, 3, and 4 are unoccupied. In cross-examination, the Tenant changed her position, indicating it “is possible” there is an occupant of unit 4. On multiple occasions during cross- examination, the Tenant was evasive with her answers by refusing to answer simple questions put to her. Overall, after taking into account the evidence before the Board as well as the analysis in R.C. v. S.Y.S., I preferred the evidence of the Landlord over the Tenant as the Landlord was consistent, direct, and straightforward in his testimony.

It is undisputed that there was a temporary reduction of the washroom. I find that the duration of the temporary reduction was a few weeks as described by the Landlord rather than the unknown date provided by the Tenant. The Tenant was provided with multiple opportunities to present evidence of the date she re-gained access to the first bathroom but could not provide anything concrete to support her oral testimony.

Section 39(7) of O.Reg 516/06 states: 39(7) If the discontinuance or reduction is temporary and its duration is reasonable, taking into account the effect on the tenant or former tenant, there shall be no reduction of rent

Given the finding that access to the washroom was reduced for a short duration, it was temporary in nature, and the Tenant had access to another full washroom down the hall, I find that there shall be no reduction of rent for the washroom access. The reduction was reasonable in the circumstances and the effect on the Tenant was minimal.

Regarding the freezer, it is undisputed that there is a freezer located in the common area. The Tenant admitted they have access to the freezer however they were told by the Landlord and/or superintendent not to use it. I do not find that the kitchen amenities were reduced as contemplated by the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act). The freezer remains available to the Tenant for use. The T3 Application is not the proper application to allege harassment or substantial interference of reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit [name] complex. As a result, I find that the Landlord has not reduced a service as it relates to the freezer.
ordered: The T3 Application is dismissed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  entered the rental unit illegally.  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, [name] raised two preliminary issues.

JC first submitted that the LTB cannot adj udicate the Tenant’s allegations about illegal entry because the Tenant had moved out did not file supporting documentary evidence relative to this allegation. Whether the Tenant has moved out of the unit is not relevant to whether the LTB can adjudicate an allegation about illegal entry that is alleged to have occurred during the tenancy. Further, an allegation cannot be dismissed on a preliminary basis only because of a lack of documentary evidence. The Tenant is still entitled to present viva voce evidence to try to prove her allegation. 3. [name] also submitted that the Tenant has not cl aimed any “legal remedies”. [name] said that the rent abatement and administrative fine sought by the Tenant are not applicable because the Tenant has moved out. This is not correct. These remedies are available relative to allegations made in a properly filed application, provided that the alleged offensive conduct occurred during the tenancy: ss. 29(1)3/4 & 31(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 4. The application includes alle gations about the Landlord’s failure to clear ice and/or snow in the winter in the residential complex, causing her child to slip and fall, and the parties gave evidence relative to this issue. Although substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment is a broad and general claim, where there is another more specific and applicable provision of the Act relative to a specific issue, that issue should be addressed pursuant to that specific and applicable provision: CET-68554-17-RV (Re), 2017 CanLII 93918 (ON LTB), paras 19-20. 5. Clearing snow and ice is a maintenance issue covered by section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). That section of the Act requires landlords to maintain rental units and residential complexes in a state of good repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards (which would include, for example, local snow removal by-laws). This is a specific and applicable provision relative to snow and ice removal, and this issue ought to therefore be addressed on a T6 application under ss. 29(1)1 of the Act. There is no T6 application before me, and the T2 application is dismissed as it relates to the snow and ice removal allegations for this reason. Merits of the Application 6. This is the Tenant’s application, so she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53, paras 44-46. 7. The rental unit is a basement unit in a detac hed home. At the relevant time, the Landlord lives in the upstairs portion of the home with his spouse, Nina [name] (‘NK’) and his daughter, AK. 8. The relationship between the Landlord, NK, AK and the Tenant was initially cordial at the outset of the tenancy in December 2022. AK and the Tenant also spent time together socially, but the relationship between the parties later deteriorated, and conflict arose. Illegal Entry 9. The Tenant said that on September 3, 2023, the Landlord’s daughter, AK, entered the rental unit without notice to return keys to the Tenant’s roommate, [name] (‘SL’). The Tenant said that AK had SL’s keys because the Landlord’s guest had parked in the Tenant’s parking space, and [name] had asked them to move the car. AK asked [name] for her keys and said she would move the car for her once the Landlord’s guests left. 10. The Tenant was not present in the unit at the time, but said there was no notice of entry given, it was not an emergency, and no consent was provided at the time of entry. The next day, the Tenant said that she had a conversation with the Landlord, NK, and AK, where the Landlord, NK, and AK said that AK had seen SL smoking cannabis in the unit. The Tenant wondered how AK would have seen this since no notice of entry or consent to enter was given to AK. 11. The Tenant also said that [name] was not smoking cannabis at the time, and was in the shower. She also said that [name] did not permit AK to enter the unit at the time. 12. I note that the Tenant’s evidence relative to this issue is hearsay, except for her evidence that she did not give consent to the entry at the time and did not receive a notice of entry. There is no dispute that there was not an emergency warranting entry at the time. 13. The hearsay evidence is given limited weight. [name] was not present to given evidence, and there was no explanation as to why [name] could not have been called as a witness. I am therefore not satisfied that there was no other way to present this evidence to the LTB, aside from through hearsay evidence. I am therefore not satisfied that the hearsay evidence satisfies the principle of necessity. I also do not find that it satisfies the principle of reliability, because I am not satisfied that there is no concern about the truth of the evidence because of the circumstances in which SL gave this information to the Tenant: Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083 (CanLII), paras 29-31. 14. I do not doubt that this is what [name] told the Tenant, but the veracity of SL’s statements cannot be assessed through her own viva voce evidence, and could not be tested on cross-examination, which is why the hearsay evidence is given limited weight. 15. AK said that there is an interior staircase between the upper and lower units. She said that she knocked from upstairs, and someone yelled to come down. AK said she went downstairs, and SL’s sister was there. AK said she gave the keys to [name]’s sister, and went back upstairs. 16. I prefer AK’s direct evidence on this issue over the Tenant’s hearsay evidence. I accept that AK entered in accordance with verbal permission from a person who was permitted in the unit by [name] at the time of entry, returned SL’s keys, and left. 17. The Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to prove it is more likely than not that AK entered the unit in contravention of ss. 26-27 of the Act. [name] with Reasonable Enjoyment & Harassment 18. To prove that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, the Tenant must establish that the Landlord did something, or failed to do something, that interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment in a substantial way. Conduct by a landlord that amounts to a mere annoyance or trivial incident will not normally amount to a breach of the Act. The enjoyment protected by s. 22 of the Act is qualified by the word reasonable. This means that the standard to be applied is an objective one. Even if some conduct, or lack thereof, is particularly annoying to the particular tenant before the LTB, the LTB must consider whether that conduct or lack thereof would amount to a substantial interference with enjoyment on the objective standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances: s. 22, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; TST-55210-14, 2014 CanLII 58631 (ON LTB), para 32. 19. Section 22 of the Act refers to the conduct of the Landlord, and not about the behaviour of others in the residential complex. However, a landlord can be held liable for the conduct of others if they fail to respond reasonably to address complaints about such conduct: TST- 55210-14, 2014 CanLII 58631 (ON LTB), para 30. 20. For the Tenant to prove that the Landlord harassed her, she must establish that the Landlord engaged in a course of vexatious comment or conduct toward the Tenant that the Landlord knew or ought to have known to be unwelcome: [name] v. [name], 2023 ONLTB 13936 (CanLII), para 24. For comment or conduct to be vexatious, it must be pursued for no lawful or legitimate purpose. As an example, even if a tenant were in arrears of rent, the landlord would know, or ought to know, that issuance of a notice of termination of tenancy for rental arrears would be conduct that would be unwelcome by the tenant. This conduct, however, would not be vexatious because it would be conduct engaged in for a lawful, legitimate purpose (in accordance with the landlord’s rights under s. 59 of the Act). 21. The Tenant said that on December 8, 2022 a 5:30 a.m. and on December 19, 2022 at 12:47 a.m., she sent text messages to AK asking her to be quiet. She said that she made further complaints to AK about AK, the Landlord, and/or their guests were being too loud on the following dates and times: 1. January 5, 2023 (puppy barking); 2. January 29, 2023 – 11:24 p.m;
February 25, 2023 – 4:54 a.m.;
March 31, 2023 – 5:14 a.m. The Tenant said AK’s response was that she was playing with her dog;

July 19, 2023 – 11:21 p.m. [name] said that AK replied to this text message, saying sorry and that she would stop, but said that she had to text message AK about noise again at 12:14 a.m. on July 20, 2023;

September 1, 2023 – no time identified 22. The Tenant’s evidence about the noise complaints is problematic for several reasons. First, her evidence was that all of these complaints were made by text messages, but without reasonable explanation, none of the text messages at issue were presented as evidence. Further, although the Tenant claims there was excessive noise from the Landlord’s unit at these times, there was no evidence to support this assertion, such as any audio recording to demonstrate the noise is excessive. There was also no specific description of the noise presented by the Tenant that would amount to cogent evidence that the noise was excessive. 23. In any multi-unit housing context, one must expect to hear some noise from other units, including normal sounds of everyday life. The times referred to above are generally late at night or very early in the morning, but there was not sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence presented by the Tenant to prove that the noise at issue was excessive (i.e. loud music, yelling, or stomping), as opposed to sound generated by normal activities, like footsteps from walking in the unit. 24. Because the Tenant has not proven that there was excessive noise generated from the Landlord’s unit that amounted to more than a mere annoyance on the standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances, the application is dismissed relative to the noise complaint allegations. 25. The Tenant said that on February 1, 2023, police knocked on the unit door looking for someone with the same last name as the Landlord and AK. She said the Landlord and AK were home but did not answer the door for police. The Tenant said that the Landlord and AK them became upset with the Tenant for giving police their phone numbers. 26. On cross-examination a text message between the Tenant and AK after this happened was put to the Tenant. In the text message, AK wrote that police rang the doorbell, but went to knock on the rental unit door before she had a chance to answer the door. AK apologised for the incident, and the Tenant replied “It’s okay” (DOC-2662738, p. 48). 27. Police knocking on the unit door looking for someone with the Landlord’s last name would not, on its own, amount to anything more than a mere annoyance on the standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances. This is consistent with the Tenant’s reasonable response to AK’s apology, referred to above. 28. There was not sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that AK or the Landlord did or said anything inappropriate relative to the Tenant providing police with a phone number. Even if they were upset about this, the Landlord or AK simply being upset does not cross the threshold beyond a mere annoyance or trivial incident. 29. The Tenant said that on Augus 8, 2023 she sent a text message to AK to inform her that [name] would be using the shared laundry facility (which is in the Landlord’s unit). The Tenant said that carrying laundry baskets up the stairs was difficult for her because of a disability, so [name] was assisting her with this task. The Tenant said that AK then wrote that [name] is not permitted to use the laundry facilities, which the Tenant said interfered with [name]’s ability to assist the Tenant with this task. 30. The text messages referred to by the Tenant, without explanation, were not presented as evidence by the Tenant to support her oral evidence. AK said that she was never informed that the Tenant had a disability, and did not know the Tenant had a disability. The Tenant did not present cogent evidence to the contrary. 31. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord or AK knew or ought to have known that the Tenant suffered from a disability requiring accommodation relative to use of the laundry facilities, and I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord or [name] refused to allow [name] to use the laundry facilities while she lived in the unit. The Tenant did not discharge her burden of proof relative to this allegation. 32. The Tenant said that occupants of the Landlord’s unit parked in her parking space on September 2, 2023. The Tenant said that the parking space at issue is assigned to her in the tenancy agreement. The Tenant said that AK was confrontational with [name] when SL asked AK not to park in the space. 33. The Landlord said that there was an Indian festival on this day, and he had 20-25 people over at the time. He said that [name] came upstairs and insulted him after ringing the doorbell around 5:30-6:00 p.m. He said that [name] demanded the parking space, and yelled and swore at him. The Landlord said he then asked AK to handle the situation. He said he then saw SL give AK her keys, and AK moved cars around to get [name]’s car parked on the driveway. 34. The Landlord also said the Tenant was out of town, and had given permission to use her parking space that day. AK said an N5 notice was issued to the Tenant because of SL’s conduct. 35. As with the allegation about illegal entry, the Tenant’s evidence can only be given limited weight because she was not present at the time, and her evidence is hearsay. I prefer the Landlord’s direct evidence relative to this incident over the Tenant’s hearsay evidence. I find it is more likely than not that [name] spoke inappropriately to the Landlord relative to the parking issue, and AK then moved cars around so [name]’s car could be parked in the driveway. 36. Even if the Landlord did not have the Tenant’s consent to use her parking space, this single incident of a guest parking there while the Tenant was away is not more than a mere annoyance or trivial incident, particularly when AK immediately addressed the issue by moving cars around. 37. The Tenant said that on September 4, 2023, AK sent her a text message stating that she needed to enter the unit to inspect the electrical box, however, AK then entered the unit with an unidentified man, and they just looked around the unit. AK said the man was her uncle, who accompanied her because she did not know how to address the issue. AK said all he did was flip a breaker, and they left. AK said the Tenant was not upset at the time. AK’s evidence is supported by what is an ostensibly amicable text message exchange between AK and the Tenant on September 4, 2023 about this issue (DOC-2662738, p. 63). 38. I prefer AK’s evidence over the Tenant’s on this issue, because AK’s evidence is consistent with the civil tone of the contemporaneous text message referred to above. The Tenant has not proven that AK or her uncle did anything that would amount to a breach of the Act when the entered the unit on September 4, 2023. 39. The Tenant said that on September 5, 2023, AK text messaged her, demanding that the Tenant remove SL from the unit by September 12, 2023. This is supported by a text message chain between the Tenant and AK that was put to the Tenant on cross- examination (DOC-2662738, pp. 43-44). Notably, although there is discussion about [name] preparing to move, and AK writes “Yup as long as she’s out … by September 12, 2013”, in the same chain after these comments, there is a cordial conversation about AK starting school and the Tenant’s children. 40. As noted above, AK’s evidence was that an N5 notice had been given relative to [name]’s conduct days earlier. It appears that [name] moving was to resolve issues identified in the N5. 41. Tenants are permitted to have guests and occupants in rental units, and tenants are responsible for the conduct of any occupant or guest they permit in the residential complex. 42. The Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to prove that the comment made by AK would amount to a substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment or harassment. Although tenants are permitted to have occupants or roommates, there was not enough evidence about the surrounding facts and circumstances to determine that this was anything more than the parties agreeing that [name] would move out after an N5 was given relative to her conduct. 43. On September 6, 2023, the Tenant said that AK asked her by text message if she had given a unit key to SL, and wrote that the Landlord would not “tolerate that shit”. AK said the comment about not tolerating that shit” was about noise and disturbance being created by [name] and her guests. 44. In the context, it makes sense that AK would ask if [name] had a key, since [name] planned to move out. Using curse words is not appropriate, but in the context of the relationship between AK and the Tenant, I do not find this to be more than a mere annoyance when that language was used a single time in reference to a disturbance by [name]. 45. The Tenant’s evidence was that on September 9, 2023, AK was yelling that “there is a whore in the basement”. She said that AK sent her a text message shortly before this occurred demanding that the Tenant remove SL and her friend from the unit immediately, or the Landlord would take legal action for trespassing. 46. There was no corroborating evidence relative to the allegation about AK yelling about a “whore” in the basement. For example, there was no audio recording, and [name], who the Tenant said was present, was not at the hearing to give corroborating evidence about this. 47. A copy of the September 9, 2023 text message exchange was presented by AK (DOC- 2662738, p. 66). It is accurate that AK wrote there is an unknown person in the basement, that she/the Landlord had said they did not want “her” at the unit and asked that the Tenant have the people in the unit leave or the Landlord would take legal action for trespassing. The Tenant was not home at the time, but wrote in response “Hey they’re fine to be there, I don’t have great service. But I know she’s there with a friend”. After this, there is no further reference to [name] or SL’s guest in the unit in the text chain. 48. It appears that once the Tenant said [name] and [name]’s guest were in the unit with her knowledge and permission, AK did not demand any longer that the Tenant have them leave the unit immediately. There was no evidence of any further demand, or of any “legal action” relative to trespassing being taken. 49. I find that, in the context of all that was happening at the time, this was not more than a mere annoyance on the standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances. This is because once the Tenant confirmed the people in the unit were there with her permission, no other statements were made or action taken relative to this issue. 50. For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.

The Tenants filed their application pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act'). Since the Tenants filed their application, they bear the burden of proof of establishing on a balance of probabilities each of the following under this provision: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The presumptions of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act, are not applicable in this case.

There is no dispute between the parties, that the Landlord gave the Tenants a N12 Notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of a Board Order that was based on the N12 notice of termination (LTB-L-010725- 24). The Tenants vacated the rental unit on March 14, 2025.

The central dispute between the parties is whether the Landlord’s daughter occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, and whether the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenants claimed that they that on July 24, 2025, they send a text message to the Landlord advising him that it had come their attention that nobody had moved into the rental unit, to which the Landlord responded that the basement is being brought up to standards. The Tenants claimed that the Landlord’s response to this text message suggests that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit. The Tenants further claimed on September 8, 2025, and on September 24, 2025, they received text messages from various neighbours residing next/around the vicinity of the rental unit advising the Tenants that the rental unit was empty and that no one had moved in. The Tenants testified that from July 2025 to September 2025, they did not personally visit the rental unit to confirm whether the Landlord’s daughter had moved in. The Tenants also confirmed that they do not know who the Landlord’s daughter is and are not sure whether the neighbours next/around the vicinity of the rental unit recognize the Landlord’s daughter. Copies of these text messages were filed as evidence with the Board.

The Landlord claimed that this daughter moved into the rental unit in April 2025. He adduced photographs of his daughter at the rental unit in July 2025; photographs of his daughter taking some belongings inside the rental unit in July 2025; photographs of his daughter’s mail coming to the rental unit from June 2025; photographs of his daughter’s belongings inside the rental unit and of his daughter inside the rental unit with her friend; and photographs of his daughter with family/friends gathering at the rental unit in February 2026. With respect the text message dated July 24, 2025, the Landlord claimed that this text message does not reference that his daughter is not residing in the rental unit. The text message only references that the rental unit is being repaired. The Landlord claimed that the repairs were carried out intermittently at the rental unit while his daughter was in possession.
Considering the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants have established their claim.

The Tenants evidence relies primarily on text messages (from neighbours and the Landlord) and assertions made in those messages that they believe suggests that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit. This evidence is doubly problematic.

First, it is entirely speculative, and the absence of a seeing the Landlord’s daughter at the rental unit does not conclusively establish that the Landlord’s daughter does not reside in the rental unit/did not move into the rental unit. The Tenants did not personally attend the rental unit to confirm whether the Landlord’s daughter resides in the rental unit, and no other direct evidence was provided by the Tenants in support of their claim.

Second, the text messages relied on by the Tenants from the neighbours constitute uncorroborated hearsay evidence. The Tenants did not summons these witnesses to the hearing to confirm whether they know who the Landlord’s daughter is and how they arrived at the conclusion that the Landlord’s daughter does not reside at the rental unit/did not move into the rental unit. I would have reasonably expected the Tenants to summons these witnesses at the hearing to corroborate their claim. The Landlord also could not cross examine the reliability of the assertions made by these neighbours. For all these reasons, I place little weight on the Tenants’ evidence.

The Landlord provided direct, persuasive evidence of his daughter's occupancy of the rental unit. The Landlord adduced photographic evidence capturing his daughter moving belongings into the unit, as well as photographs documenting events hosted at the rental unit. While the daughter herself did not attend the hearing to testify, I do not find her absence fatal to the Landlord's defence. I find the Landlord’s testimony to be credible and reliable as the Landlord possesses direct, first-hand knowledge of his daughter's living arrangements. I accept the Landlord's direct evidence over the speculative evidence provided by the Tenants. I also accept the Landlord’s position that the text message dated July 24, 2025, does not specifically mention that his daughter does not occupy the rental unit. This text message only references that repairs needed to be conducted at the rental unit. I agree with the Landlord’s position that the Tenants’ evidence with respect to this text message was based on unfounded assumptions. The Landlord claimed the repairs were carried out intermittently while his daughter occupied the rental unit. The Tenants did not seriously challenge the Landlord’s claim. Thus, I find the Landlord’s evidence to be reliable in this regard. Accordingly, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s daughter occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, and that the notice of termination was not provided in bad faith.

Alternatively, even I do not accept the entirety of the Landlord’s evidence, for the reasons already noted above in this [name], the Tenants have failed their burden of proof of establishing on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s daughter did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, and that the N12 Notice of termination was served in bad faith.
Accordingly, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The hearing was held on April 21, 2026. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-073712-25 issued on April 27, 2026. On May 7, 2026, the Tenant the requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On May 8, 2026 interim order LTB-T-073712-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on April 27, 2026
reasons: The Tenant requested a review of the Board’s order on the ground that he was not reasonably able to participate in the hearing. The review of order LTB-T-073712-25 issued on April 27, 2026, is granted.

The Tenant says that on the date of the hearing, he was working as a forklift operator, dropped his phone, and ran it over and crushed it rendering it inoperable. The Tenant says he was unable to replace the phone in time for the hearing. The Tenant has since replaced his phone.

In King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., [2008] O.J. No. 4697 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court stated that, “being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less”.

The evidence as submitted by the Tenant is uncontested. As such, I am satisfied that the Tenant was not reasonably able to participate in the proceedings because his phone was inoperable and could not join the hearing.
As a result of my decision, I cancelled order LTB-T-073712-25 issued on April 27, 2026 and proceeded to hear the Tenant’s uncontested T5 application. T5 Application Determinations:

At the beginning of the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue concerning s. 57(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’), which states: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that although no formal notice of termination was given, the Tenant says that the Landlord told the Tenant that he needed to vacate the rental unit because the Landlord was selling it. The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on April 28, 2023.

This application is brought forth under section 57(1) of the Act. Under 57(2) of the Act, it is clear that the Tenant must file their T5 application within one year of the date they moved out of the rental unit.
As a result of the one-year limitation period in the Act, the Board has no jurisdiction to deal with the Tenant’s T5 application.
As such, the T5 application is dismissed.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-073712-25 issued on April 27, 2026 is granted. The order is cancelled and replaced with the following.
The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] De Vera and [name] De Vera (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. As a result, the Tenant is entitled to remedies under section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. The Facts

The parties agreed on the following facts: • The Landlords served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination on April 10, 2024, with a termination date of June 18, 2024. • The stated reason for termination was purchaser’s own use under section 49 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 7, 2024. • The Tenant vacated because of the N12. • The lawful monthly rent at the time was $2,100.00.

The Tenant testified that after vacating, they later learned that the agreement of purchase and sale did not close and that the property remained titled in the Landlords’ names. This evidence was not disputed.

The Landlord Andrew [name] De Vera (AD) testified that an agreement of purchase and sale existed and that the purchaser intended to move into the unit. He further testified that the agreement was mutually terminated on May 30, 2024, before the Tenant vacated.
I find as a fact that the Landlord knew on or before May 30, 2024 that the purchaser would not be moving into the rental unit.
Despite this knowledge, the Landlord did not inform the Tenant that the sale had failed, did not withdraw the N12, and did not offer the Tenant the opportunity to remain in the rental unit.
The Tenant vacated on June 7, 2024, unaware that the basis for the N12 no longer existed.
No purchaser, family member, or other qualifying person ever occupied the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. Analysis
The issuance of an N12 for purchaser’s own use creates a rebuttable presumption of bad faith where the intended occupant does not move in within a reasonable time.
The Landlords argued that the failure of the sale constituted a change in circumstances outside their control.

I do not accept that submission. While a failed sale can, in some cases, rebut bad faith, the evidence here shows that the Landlord became aware of the failed sale before the Tenant vacated and before the termination date.

At that point, the Landlord had an obligation to act honestly and in good faith. Reasonable options available to them included advising the Tenant that the N12 was no longer valid or permitting the Tenant to remain in the unit.
The Landlord chose to do neither and instead allowed the Tenant to vacate under false premises.
I find that permitting the Tenant to vacate while knowingly withholding material information that the N12 was no longer valid constitutes bad faith within the meaning of section 57 of the Act.
The Tenant’s evidence was consistent, supported by documentary evidence, and largely undisputed. By contrast, the Landlord’s evidence confirmed the critical facts establishing bad faith.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has satisfied all elements of subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act. Remedies

I find that the Landlord’s conduct was not a passive error or an unforeseen change in circumstances. The evidence establishes that the Landlord became aware on May 30, 2024 that the agreement of purchase and sale had been cancelled and that the purchaser would not be occupying the rental unit, yet the Landlord did not withdraw the N12 notice, did not advise the Tenant that the basis for the notice no longer existed, and did not provide the Tenant with any opportunity to remain in the rental unit before the termination date. Instead, the Landlord allowed the Tenant to vacate the rental unit on June 7, 2024, in reliance on a notice that the Landlord knew was no longer valid.

In my view, the Landlord’s omission was deliberate and material. The Tenant’s evidence establishes a clear causal connection between the N12 notice and the losses claimed. The Tenant would not have vacated the rental unit but for the N12, did vacate as a direct result of it, and immediately incurred higher rent and moving costs as a consequence. In these circumstances, I find it reasonable and proportionate to award remedies at the higher end of the range contemplated by the Act in order to fully compensate the Tenant for the losses flowing from the Landlord’s breach. Abatement of Rent

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement equal to six months of rent. Six months at the lawful rent of $2,100.00 totals $12,600.00. Given the seriousness of the Landlords’ conduct, the direct causal link between the bad-faith notice and the Tenant’s displacement, and the absence of any mitigating steps by the Landlords, I find this amount reasonable and proportionate.
I therefore order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $12,600.00 as compensation for bad-faith termination. Difference in Rent
The Tenant provided undisputed evidence that their new rental unit costs $2,670.00 per month, an increase of $570.00 per month over their prior rent.

I find this amount reasonable and directly attributable to the Landlords’ bad-faith conduct. The increase in rent of $570.00 per month for 12 months totals $6,840.00. I therefore order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $6,840.00 as compensation for the Tenant’s increase in rent. Costs and Expenses

The Tenant testified that they incurred $350.00 in moving-related expenses, including truck rental, fuel, and supplies. Although receipts were not produced, the Landlords did not credibly challenge the reasonableness of this amount. I accept the Tenant’s testimony and award $350.00.
The Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $19,838.00. This amount represents: • $12,600.00 for a rent abatement. • $6,840.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from June 2024 to May 2025. • $350.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant the amount of $420.00 on or before March 31, 2026.
The tenancy commenced in September 2024 and terminated on September 1, 2025, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
It was undisputed that at the onset of the tenancy, the Tenant provided the Landlord a key deposit in the amount of $500.00.
The parties agreed that due to the late return of the keys, the Tenant compensated the Landlord in the amount of $80.00.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord issued a payment of $374.38, representing the balance of the key deposit after deductions, including amounts the Landlord attributed to the cost of paint and paint brushes. The Tenant further testified that this payment was returned to the Landlord. The Landlord confirmed that the keys were ultimately returned.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the key deposit is governed by subsection 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), which permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit only in the amount of the reasonable cost of replacing keys.

Although the amount of the deposit may not be justified, I find that the $500.00 key deposit was a permissible deposit under the Act; however, the Landlord was only entitled to retain amounts corresponding to the reasonable cost of replacement keys or related key access items, not unrelated expenses such as paint or paint brushes.
The parties agreed that the Tenant is responsible for an $80.00 deduction arising from the late return of the keys.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord was entitled to retain $80.00 from the key deposit. After deducting this amount from the $500.00 deposit, the balance owing to the Tenant is $420.00. While the key deposit is not an illegal charge under the Act, I find that the remaining balance of the deposit must nevertheless be returned to the Tenant in accordance with the Act. I further find that the Landlord is required to return the remaining $420.00 to the Tenant, as there is no evidence before me that any additional deductions were agreed to by the Tenant.
The Tenant is therefore entitled to an order for the return of $420.00, being the balance of the key deposit.
At the hearing, the Landlord indicated that the amount owing to the Tenant could be paid by March 31, 2026, which I find to be reasonable.

The Tenant did not specifically request reimbursement of the application filing fee at the hearing. However, pursuant to the Act, the Board has the authority to order the reimbursement of the filing fee where a party is successful in whole or in part on an application.

In this case, the Tenant has been partially successful with respect to the return of the $420.00 balance of the key deposit. The Landlord’s obligation to return the balance of the deposit arises directly from the Act, and the Tenant was required to commence this application in order to obtain that relief. In these circumstances, I find it appropriate that the Landlord reimburse the Tenant for the filing fee.

At the hearing, the Landlord indicated that the amount owing to the Tenant could be paid by March 31, 2026, which I find to be reasonable. However, I have also considered that the issue of reimbursement of the filing fee was not raised or addressed at the hearing and the Landlord was not put on notice that costs would be sought. In these circumstances, I find that the standard compliance period appropriately accounts for the absence of prior disclosure regarding the filing fee issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $468.00. This amount represents: • $420.00 for the return of the key deposit balance. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 22, 2026 ____________________________
