issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants allege that they paid an illegal charge to the Landlord, and that the Landlord owes the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The tenancy commenced on March 15, 2023 and terminated on or about June 28, 2025. Illegal charge collected

It was undisputed that the Tenants paid the Landlord a key deposit of $200.00 at the commencement of the tenancy and that the keys were returned to the Landlord’s real estate agent on or about June 28, 2025.

The Landlord testified that he did not return the key deposit because the door lock had been damaged and there was damage to the kitchen cabinets that required repair before the rental unit could be re-rented. While the Landlord provided testimony regarding these alleged damages, he did not submit any documentary or photographic evidence in support of those claims. The Landlord further testified that he intended to file a separate application with respect to the alleged damages.
The Tenants testified that they left the rental unit in good condition upon vacating and denied causing any damage, including damage to the door lock.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the key deposit is governed by Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), which permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit only in an amount that is no more than the reasonable cost of replacing keys.

I find that the $200.00 key deposit was a lawful deposit under the Act. However, a key deposit may only be retained for purposes authorized by section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06, namely, to address the replacement costs of keys, remote entry devices, or access cards. A claim for compensation arising from alleged damage to the rental unit is a separate matter and cannot be satisfied by withholding a key deposit. While the collection of the key deposit did not contravene the Act, I find that the deposit must be returned to the Tenant in accordance with the Act.
The Landlord stated that he would return the key deposit to the Tenants on or before April 23, 2026. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Tenants paid a last month's rent deposit in the amount of $3,950.00 to the Landlord on March 3, 2023.

The Landlord testified that the rent was increased in March 2024. The Landlord further testified that he did not request that the Tenants pay any additional amount to top up the last month's rent deposit following the rent increase, either at the time of the increase or when the tenancy ended.

Subsections 106(6) and 106(7) state: Interest (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (6). Deduction applied to rent deposit (7) The landlord may deduct from the amount payable under subsection (6) the amount, if any, by which the maximum amount of the rent deposit permitted under subsection (2) exceeds the amount of the rent deposit paid by the tenant and the deducted amount shall be deemed to form part of the rent deposit paid by the tenant.

The last month's rent deposit was applied to the rent owing for June 2025. As the Landlord did not request that the Tenants pay an additional amount to top up the deposit following the March 2024 rent increase, I find it reasonable to conclude that the Landlord applied the annual interest owing on the deposit to offset any shortfall resulting from the rent increase. Accordingly, I find that interest on the last month's rent deposit was paid to the Tenants up to June 30, 2025.

For the above reasons, I do not find that the Landlord illegally retained money collected from the Tenants or failed to pay interest on the last month's rent deposit as required by the Act. This portion of the application is dismissed.

The Tenants did not specifically request reimbursement of the application filing fee at the hearing. However, pursuant to the Act, the Board has the authority to order the reimbursement of the filing fee where a party is successful in whole or in part on an application.

In this case, the Tenants have been partially successful with respect to the return of the key deposit. The Landlord’s obligation to return the deposit arises directly from the Act, and the Tenants were required to commence this application in order to obtain that relief. In these circumstances, I find it appropriate that the Landlord reimburse the Tenants for the filing fee.

At the hearing, the Landlord indicated that the amount owing to the Tenants could be paid by April 23, 2026, which I find to be reasonable. However, I have also considered that the issue of reimbursement of the filing fee was not raised or addressed at the hearing and the Landlord was not put on notice that costs would be ordered. In these circumstances, I find that the standard compliance period appropriately accounts for the absence of prior disclosure regarding the filing fee issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the return of the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') interfered with her rights, collected or retained money illegally, and gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant filed the combined application on September 22, 2023.
The matter has been adjourned on four other occasions and for various reasons. The July 15, 2025 adjournment was marked peremptory on both parties.

At the October 9, 2025 Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC), the Member noted that the Tenant requested to adjourn the matter because she was ill. However, the Member put the Tenant on notice of various deficiencies with the applications as filed, and directed the matter to a merit hearing. The Member also issued an interim order on October 15, 2025.

The interim order sets outs five areas at issue with the Tenant’s applications; jurisdiction and time limitations, missing documents, insufficient reasons and details, unlikely success with the T5 application and resolution to the T1 application.
The Member ordered the Tenant to amend the applications to clearly set out the allegations. The Member also ordered the amended applications to be served by January 9, 2026.
The Tenant did not comply with the interim order and did not amend the applications. The Adjournment Request

At the hearing, the Tenant preliminarily requested to adjourn the matter, stating she has a late-morning medical appointment. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support this claim.

While the Landlord initially said he would agree to the adjournment, he also said that the parties were advised at the last ACC that there would unlikely be any further adjournments granted. He said the Tenant did not comply with the interim order and the matter should not proceed.
When considering the request to adjourn, the interests of both parties have been considered including the relevant considerations under Guideline 1 and Rule 21.8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 Adjourning and Rescheduling Hearings, addresses the requirements for a request to reschedule the hearing and provides: “The party seeking the hearing's rescheduling should submit a written request to the Board at least five business days before the scheduled hearing, preferably in the form provided by the Board.”

Rule 28.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure provides: 21.8 A CMH or hearing may be adjourned at the discretion of a Hearing Officer or Member where satisfied that an adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held. Relevant factors the LTB may consider in deciding the request include: a. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; b. the issues in the application; c. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; d. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; e. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

The Tenant said that she was made aware of the medical appointment last Monday and did not have ample time to request to reschedule the hearing. Rather, she opted to attend the hearing to request and adjournment.

Aware of the lengthy history before the Board and the Board’s expectations for participation, I considered that the Tenant failed to provide any documentary evidence to support the proposition that she had a medical procedure that impacted her ability to participate at this hearing. In my view, it would have been reasonable for the Tenant to produce such evidence.
However, even had the Tenant provided medical documentation to support her request, I would have denied her adjournment request. I say this for the following reasons.
The Tenant was aware of the various deficiencies and challenges with her applications as per the October 9, 2025 ACC and subsequent October 15, 2025 interim order.
The Tenant failed to comply with the order to amend the applications by January 9, 2026. At this hearing, the Tenant provided no reasonable explanation for her failure to comply.

I have considered the nature of the multiple adjournments, and the prejudice to the Tenant as she has vacated the rental unit and this decision terminates her ability to move the matter forward with the LTB. However, I am not satisfied that a further adjournment would yield positive results. The ACC Member made it clear to the Tenant the challenges with her applications and the Tenant has made no effort to remedy the deficiencies, six months later.
Whether to grant or deny an adjournment is a discretionary decision to which considerable deference by the Court is given.

In the decision of the Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2015 ONSC 2556, the Court relied on s. 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) to concluded: "the Board member must take into account the public interest in resolving a case as soon as possible. The key question becomes how to balance the rights of the parties to ensure that matters are resolved quickly while not adversely affecting their respective rights to a fair hearing.”
The Courts consistently recognize that s.183 of the Act requires the Board to consider the public interest in dealing with applications in an expeditious manner.

In [name] v. Minto, 2005 ONSC2219, the Divisional Court found no denial of procedural fairness due the LTB’s refusal to grant an adjournment. The Court again relied on [name] with respect to consideration for the balancing the public interest, with parties’ rights.

I find it reasonable to apply [name] and [name] v. Minto in this case. The Tenant had the benefit of an ACC and an interim order to understand the shortcomings with her applications and was provided opportunity to amend the applications. The Tenant took no action to do so and did not provide any reasonable explanation for her failure to comply with the interim order. The Tenant filed the application in September 2023 and has been made aware of the challenges with the applications and has not made reasonable effort to move the matter forward.
Given the Tenant’s failure to comply with the Member’s oral direction and interim order, the Tenant’s adjournment request is denied and the applications are dismissed.
This order provides all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: The Landlord's Legal Representative requested an adjournment on the basis that she could not reach her instructing client [name], an employee of Landlord.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that she had last communicated with [name] on April 23, 2026, when they discussed the testimony [name] would provide at the hearing. She testified that she had attempted to both call and email [name] today and received no response, she also reached out to another employee of the Landlord who did not respond to her.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that she did not have experience with [name] but did have experience working with the Landlord and this conduct was uncharacteristic for them, and she believe that something out of the Landlord’s control ad occurred.
She was not sure who else from the Landlord would have information with respect to the proceeding to fill in for [name] and sought an adjournment.
The Tenant opposed the adjournment request and indicated that he wished to resolve the matter today as he did not want to have to take another day off work to attend a subsequent hearing.

While the matter was stood down to allow the Landlord's Legal Representative time to contact the Landlord and her instructing client, I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. Interpretation Guideline 1 states: Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. The Member may consider the conduct of the party opposing the adjournment. For example, if the party opposing the request has shown bad faith or refused to provide information about their case to the other party which would allow them to prepare quickly for the hearing, this may affect the Member’s decision.

While this guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. I am satisfied that the Landlord had adequate notice of the proceeding and was able to retain representation and prepare for the hearing. I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s Agent [name] was clearly aware of the hearing date as she had spoken with the Landlord's Legal Representative shortly before to prepare. While the Landlord's Legal Representative speculated that something outside the Landlord’s control had occurred to prevent [name] attendance no clear evidence of this assertion was provided and it remains speculation.

In short, the Landlord’s Agent has not attended and has provided no explanation for this failure to attend. Absent a compelling explanation, I note that the Board has a duty to be expeditious I am not satisfied that the Landlord's Legal Representative has demonstrated that an adjournment is appropriate. I also find that an adjournment would be prejudicial to the Tenant who would be required to miss another day of work in order to attend a new hearing when they have attended, prepared to have their matter heard. The T5
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,548.00

It was agreed by the parties that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 Notice of Termination under section 50 of the Act on the basis that the Landlord intend to demolish the rental unit. However, it was asserted by the Tenant that the intention of the Landlord was not to demolish the rental unit bit was to conduct repairs or renovations so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the Landlord was operating under the understanding that the project was a demolition but allowed the that rental unit was ultimately renovated and not demolished.
While the N13 served on the Tenant indicates that the Landlord intends to demolish the rental unit the scope of work outlined describes a renovation rather than a demolition.

Therefore, when I apply Section 212 of the Act to ascertain the true substance of the activities and the good faith of the parties I am satisfied that while the Landlord served an N13 for Demolition the actual intention was to do repairs or renovations to it that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit.

Therefore, I have considered the Tenant’s T5 Application on the basis that the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to reoccupy the rental unit after the renovations were completed, as had the Landlord filed the N13 under the correct ground the Tenant would have been permitted to exercise their right of first refusal.

The Landlord was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Act because the Tenant gave the Landlord written notice of the Tenant's intention to occupy the rental unit when the repairs or renovations are completed. The Landlord failed to allow the Tenant to occupy the unit after the repairs or renovations were completed.
The rental unit was a bedroom within a townhouse located in a townhouse complex.

The Tenant testified that he received the N13 Notice of Termination in mid-May 2024 and vacated on August 31, 2024, the Termination date specified on the N13. He testified that after he received the N13 he emailed the Landlord on August 18, 2024, to express that he intended to exercise his right of first refusal to reoccupy the rental unit. He testified that the Landlord replied indicating that the unit was being demolished so he could not exercise right of first refusal.
The Tenant ultimately provided an N9 and vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2024.

He testified that after he vacated, he searched for demolition permits issued for the rental unit but could not locate them. He testified that work was subsequently performed on the unit in accordance with the N13 Notice of Termination, which was renovated. However he believed that some Tenant’s remained within the complex.

He testified that he saw an advertisement for the complex in September 2025 and when he called the Landlord, he was informed that some units were ready to be rented. He testified that he believes that work on all the units in the complex has now been completed but was not sure if his former unit was one of those listed for rent.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord never reached out to him to honour his right of first refusal and failed to allow the him occupy the unit after the repairs or renovations were completed.
The Tenant confirmed that he moved into a new rental unit on September 1, 2024, and signed a fixed one year lease.

The Landlord's Legal Representative explained that it was her understanding that the Landlord was operating under the understanding that the project was a demolition at the time the N13 was served. She testified that the renovation work outlined on the N13 was completed.

She indicated that there was a misunderstanding, and there is still ongoing work being performed within the complex. She indicates that the work on the Tenant’s rental unit was completed in September 2025 and it was confused with another unit in which work is still ongoing. She indicated that the unit was not offered back to the Tenant because the Landlord was operating under the assumption that they did not have to offer it back to the Tenant.

She indicated that she believes the Tenant was offered a separate unit elsewhere that he could not accept because of his fixed term lease. She indicated that the Landlord did not act in bad faith but was misguided. Analysis

I am satisfied that the Landlord was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Act because the Tenant gave the Landlord written notice of the Tenant's intention to occupy the rental unit when the repairs or renovations are completed, and the Landlord failed to allow the Tenant to occupy the unit after the repairs or renovations were completed.

As described above I accept that while the N13 served on the Tenant indicated the unit was to be demolished, the true intention was to renovate the rental unit, as agreed by the parties. I also accept that the Tenant provided the Landlord with his right of first refusal in writing.

I also accept that the renovations on the rental unit were completed by September 2025 and the Tenant’s right of first refusal was not honoured. While the Landlord's Legal Representative attributes all of this to a misunderstanding on the part of the Landlord I am not prepared to accept this explanation. No one from the Landlord attended to provide direct testimony to explain why the unit was not offered back to the Tenant and I note that the Tenant’s email of August 18, 2025 explicitly outlines that renovations are being performed which affords him the right of first refusal, I find it would have been prudent for the Landlord to seek legal advice at that juncture with respect to whether the Tenant is entitled to his right of first refusal, rather than rely on their ongoing misconception that they were performing a demolition for which right of first refusal was not available.
I also note that the Landlord failing to understand that the Tenant had the right of first refusal does not absolve them of this responsibility.

I also note that with respect to the assertion that the Tenant would not have been able to excise his right of first refusal because he had signed a one year lease does not absolve the Landlord of their responsibility to make the unit available for the Tenant, and note that if the Tenant signed a one year lease starting September 1, 2024 it would have expired by September 2025. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent differential of $12,300.00. He confirmed that he was paying $400.00 per month for the rental unit which was a bedroom in a townhouse with 3 bedrooms sharing all common areas. He moved into a new unit on September 1, 2024, and paid $1425.00 per month. The new unit is a one-bedroom apartment. The Tenant testified that he was not able to find anywhere lese to move and was the cheapest available unit he could find.

I am not satisfied that the two units are comparable as the rental unit was a single bedroom and the new rental unit is a much larger, and provides more space within a newer building. However, I am satisfied that a differential of $200.00 per month is appropriate to recognise the increased costs incurred by the Tenant and recognise that even if the Tenant had been able to secure a bedroom it would likely come with increased rental costs. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,400 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant sought moving and storage expenses of $500.00 he testified that he did not have receipts because many of the items he purchased were from marketplace. He testified that the U-Haul was around $100.00, and he needed to buy furniture from marketplace for his new unit as the rental unit had been furnished. I am not satisfied that the purchase of new furniture constitutes moving and storage costs, and the Tenant has provided no receipts. However, I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony that he incurred costs of $100.00 to rent a U-Haul and note that this appears to be a reasonable cost for a budget move. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $100.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant sought general compensation of $1000.00 as compensation for increased electricity costs. The Tenant provided several electricity bills which were not served on the Landlord. I note that there are over 24 pages of bills, as the were not served on the Landlord I did not consider them. As the general compensation sought by the Tenant is only related to increased utility costs, I am not satisfied that this is the purpose of general compensation and decline to award this remedy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,548.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from September 1, 2024 to August 31, 2025. • $100.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $5,993.46
The Tenants ’ T2 Application alleges the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant s and thereby induced the Tenants to vacate the rental unit.

According to the Tenant [name] (MH), a meeting was scheduled with the Landlords in February 2024. The Tenants had resided at the rental unit long -term (8 years) and at the time of meeting, the parties were on good terms. In the discussion that followed, MH testified the Tenants were advised by the Landlord s that they were under “financial distress” and consequently, “had to list the property for sale ”. According to MH, the Landlords indicated they had children attending university and the associated tuition cost was “ out of their budget”. As such, the Landlord s sought to sell the property as soon as possible . Overall, MH stated the Landlords sounded “desperate” and urgently needed to sell the property. In an effort to assist, the Tenants subsequently vacated the rental unit in accordance with a Form N11 and an agreement to terminate the tenancy (the “Agreement”), which included a waiver of rent for April 1, 2024 (which the Agreement noted was being given due to a deck/shed built by the Tenants).

Soon thereafter, the Tenants discovered that the Landlords sought to re-lease the rental unit for nearly double the Tenants’ rent. Upon further investigation, the Tenants assert the Landlords misrepresented their financial situation for the purpose of “playing on our empathies” and simply, inducing them to vacate.

The Landlord YL denied making representations of having “ financial problems” during the February 2024 initial meeting , stating he merely advised the T enants that they were going through a “ difficult time”. At the hearing , YL elaborated the Landlords sought to sell the rental unit so as to purchase a condominium in Toronto for a family member who had health issues. YL stated that when the Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2024, the rental unit had dropped in market value by approximately $50,000.00 since the initial February 2024 meeting. While not a requirement to produce, no documentation was produced in respect of the purported market change. When the housing market did not change after a few weeks of regaining possession, YL advised the decision was made to clean-up and re- lease the rental unit. Although the property was never sold, YL confirmed he was still able to assist his family member in purchasing a home.
The onus to prove the allegations in the application rest with the Tenants.

Here, it is clear the Tenants vacated the rental unit at the Landlords’ request. I also find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit because of the Landlords’ representations of being in “financial distress”. While the Landlords denied making such representations, the Landlord YL admitted advising the Tenants they were going through a “ difficult time” which – in the absence of further particulars - could reasonably be construed as constituting financial problems. Moreover, the Landlord s’ real estate agent’s email correspondence to the Tenants in early March 2024 further support s the Tenants’ version of events , noting: “Understanding [name] and [name]’s financial situation , they were wondering if you guys could accommodate us to list the property before June 1…”[emphasis added].

Significantly, there was also no mention of any change in plans to the Tenants in the lead up to the June 1, 2024 termination date. Given the short period of time between the Tenants’ departure from the rental unit (May 31, 2024) and the time the property was re-listed for rent (late June-July 2024), I find it unlikely the Landlords experienced a change in circumstances as purported. In the circumstances, I find the Landlord s unduly pressured and interfered with the Tenants ’ housing situation. I also find the Landlords ’ actions r ose to the level of constituting a breach under the Residential Tenancies Act , 2006 (the “Act”) , namely that they “harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants”. Remedies

The Tenant MH testified the relocation came at an inconvenient time, resulting in them leaving their neighbourhood friends and the inconvenience of their child changing schools. MH also noted the relocation impacted the Tenants financially as a result of moving/storage costs and increased rent.

The Tenants claim out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $5,400.00 because of the Landlords' actions, consisting of utility/hydro deposits in the total amount of $350.00 ; cleaning costs of the new house in the amount of $700.00; as well as $4000.00 for painting the new house. The Tenants’ out-of-pocket expenses are denied, as the deposits used to set up the utility/hydro accounts will presumably be refunded to the Tenants at a later date. Moreover, insufficient evidence was given in respect of the cleaning/painting costs of the new location . In this regard, t he Tenants did not produce pictures o r other documentary evidence in support and I find such costs would only remotely relate to the Landlords’ breach.

The Tenants also claim moving and storage expenses in the amount of $ 2,345.46, consisting of portable storage pods in the amount $545.46; labour costs for movers in the amount of $600.00; and, 4 days of missed work for the Tenant [name] in the amount of $1200.00. The Tenants produced pickup/storage invoices in the total amount of $555.55 ($342.79 + $89.60 + 123.17) and thus, I find it appropriate to grant the requested amount of $545.46. The balance of the Tenants ’ moving and storage expenses are denied as the Tenants offered essentially no particulars or supporting documentation for the amount claimed.

The Tenants’ application also seeks a rent differential of $10,800.00, consisting of increased rent paid over the 12-month period after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. While no lease agreement for the new residence was provided, the Tenant MH testified that both residences were comparable in nature, consisting of 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms and approximately 1600 square feet . The Tenants paid approximately $1550/month in rent at the rental unit and MH, whom I found credible, testified the Tenants paid $2500/month in rent at the new residence. [name]’ new accommodations were thus an additional $ 900/month (approx.) and based upon the description of the new rental unit, I am satisfied the residences are comparable.

The Tenants , however, have a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses under Section 16 of the Act. While MH noted that moving was a “nightmare” with school- age children, relatively sparse details were provided of the Tenants’ housing search. In this regard, I note that notwithstanding the representations made by the Landlords, the tone of the parties’ communications leading up to the signing of the Agreement was quite amicable. While it appears the Landlords’ agent proposed the agreed upon termination date of June 1, 2024, the evidence did not establish that the Tenants sought additional time to locate more affordable housing - either at the time of signing the Agreement, or thereafter. In the circumstances, I do not find that the Landlord s should be re sponsible for the entire rent differential. More appropriately, I find a 50% rental differential is more reasonable and thus, $5,400.00 shall be awarded to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $5,993.46. This amount represents: • $5,400.00 for increased rent the Tenants has incurred for a one year period • $545.46 for part of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred. • $48 for the application filing fee
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 17, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith.
It was not disputed that the Tenant’s were served with an N12 Notice of Termination and vacated a result, and that the person identified in the N12 did not occupy the rental unit.

It was also agreed by the parties that the rental unit was listed for rent within one year of the Tenant vacating. Therefore, the presumption of bad faith in Section 57(5) applies and the onus is on the Landlord to rebut this presumption.

The Landlord testified that she served the Tenants with an N12 Notice of Termination on June 7, 2025 with a termination date of August 7, 2025. She testified that she served the N12 because she was facing difficult financial circumstances as her children were growing and her husband was working less. She explained that she was paying $3000.00 per month to rent her own unit and was thinking that she could save funds by leaving her rental and occupying the rental unit which had a mortgage which was less than her rent payment.

She testified that she was helping to assist her father-in-law who suffers from dementia, and that on July 14, 2025, he suffered a fall in the bathroom and hit his head causing a brain bleed. She testified that following this his care needs became extensive and he required someone with him at all times after he was discharged from the hospital on August 7, 2025 as he was at high risk of aspiration and infection.

The Landlord relied on medical progress notes and a discharge document which identifies her father-in-law as living with 10 medical conditions including advanced dementia, recurrent falls, right eye blindness, moderate to severe aortic stenosis and chronic kidney disease.

The Landlord testified that the unit she is renting is located on the same street as her sister in laws home where her father-in-law resides so she spent a lot of time there with the family providing support and caring for her father in law after his fall. The Landlord also explained the she is a nurse by trade which left her well equipped to care for her father in law.

She also testified that other members of the family attempted to get time off work to assist with her father in laws care but struggled to do so. She relied on a letter written by a [name] on September 16, 2025 in support of a Jaswanta Gill being permitted to take time off to care his father. The Landlord explained that in spite of this letter he was not permitted the time off to care for his father.

The Landlord also relied on an affidavit from her sister-in-law [name] outlining her father in laws fall and the care the Landlord provided to him and the family during this time, and on an ongoing basis.

The Landlord testified that after he fall in laws fall she decided to stay in her rental unit because it was very close to him and made it easier for her to provide her with the care that her required. She testified that she continued to struggle finically, which is why she subsequently listed the rental unit for rent after the Tenant’s vacated. She testified that she listed the rental unit for rent sometime in August 2025.

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit June 10, 2024 and vacated July 10, 2025 because they received the N12 Notice of Termination. They testified that they found an advertisement listing the rental unit for sale on July 24, 2025 at 8:00am. However, the screenshot uploaded by the Tenants to the portal was dated September 10, 2025. They also testified that they stopped by the rental unit and met the new Tenants, and confirmed the rental unit had been re-rented. Analysis

While I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the Tenant an n12 Notice of Termination, and the Tenant vacated as a result, and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, I am not satisfied that the N12 was given in bad faith.
As the rental unit was listed for sale the onus is on the Landlord to rebut the presumption of bad faith, and I am satisfied that they have done so.

I accept that the Landlord’s father-in-law who was living with dementia suffered a severe fall on July 14, 2025 after the service of the N12 Notice of Termination which left him hospitalized and in need of significant care when he was released. I am also prepared to accept that as the Landlord is a nurse and her current residence is close father in laws home, she was best placed within her family to provide him with the high level of care required after huis discharge, as supported by the Landlord’s testimony and the affidavit from [name]

Additionally, I am prepared to accept the medical documents relied on by the Landlord which confirm that her father-in-law had significant care needs stemming from his fall, which left him hospitalized and in need of increased care. The conditions described on the medical documentation support the assertion that he was unable to live alone after the fall and required a high level of care. I am prepared to accept therefore that after this deterioration he required a high level of care which the Landlord was best placed to provide, and that this has frustrated her intention to occupy the rental unit.

Therefore, I am satisfied that at the time the N12 was served the Landlord genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit, and this intention was pre-empted by her need to provide a high level of care for her father in law, which could best be accomplished by remaining in her own rental unit.
Therefore, while the rental unit was listed for sale and bad faith is presumed, I am satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted this presumption.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The parties agreed the Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 16, 2024. The Landlord only sought the rent arrears to the date the Tenants vacated. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit.
The lawful rent is $3,200.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants agreed they have not paid any rent for the period from August 1, 2024 to December 16, 2024.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to December 16, 2024 are $14,483.36.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,200.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $90.96 is owing to the Tenants for the period from October 28, 2023 to December 16, 2024. T6 Application - Maintenance

As explained below, the Tenants proved their claims on a balance of probabilities,. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $4,666.00 for a rent abatement, out-of- pocket expenses and the cost of filing both the T2 and T6 applications. These amounts shall be deducted from the amount of rent arrears owing by the Tenants to the Landlord.

The Tenant, [name] (‘OO’) testified that he initially viewed the house in October 2023. OO testified that he agreed to rent the rental unit with the expectation that the rental unit would be painted and cleaned before he moved into the rental unit. OO testified that when the tenancy commenced on November 30, 2023, the house had not been painted or cleaned.

OO testified about the following maintenance issues: a. The fridge had damage to a number of shelves and had not been cleaned prior to the Tenants moving into the rental unit. The fridge was also not properly cooling items and was not sealing properly. b. Cosmetic damage to surfaces including dents, holes and stains on the walls and main entrance door, washer and dryer and broken wall plate covers throughout the rental unit. [name] infestation in the rental unit. [name] in the backyard of the rental unit. e. Bathroom kitchen and sinks clogged. f. Non-functional electrical outlets in the rental unit. g. Smoke detector not functioning. Fridge

OO testified that the fridge was not repaired or replaced for the duration of the tenancy. OO testified that when they moved into the rental unit, the fridge contained food belonging to the prior Tenants of the rental unit and had not been cleaned. OO testified that several of the fridge shelves were damaged prior to the Tenants moving in and had not been repaired or replaced.

In an email from Tenants to the Landlord dated June 5, 2024, the Tenants state that the fridge is “not functioning well, is not cold, and the door is not locking properly. I think this was not showing for me earlier because it was winter. It is hot now, and water is dripping all over my food in the fridge…”
The Landlord testified that the fridge was two years old when the Tenants moved into the rental unit and was in working condition.

The Landlord testified that they sent multiple repair technicians to the rental unit to address issues with the fridge but that the technicians reported no issues in the operation of the refrigerator.

The Landlord further testified that on August 12, 2024, they sent a technician to inspect the refrigerator and, as per the invoice from [name] dated August 12, 2024, the technician noted that the freezer was packed too fully with food causing the drain to be blocked causing frost build-up in the freezer section. The invoice further states that the fridge and drain need to be cleaned.
There was no supporting evidence that the Landlord had sent any repair technician in before August 12, 2024, nor did the Landlord testify about any of the other dates repair technicians were sent.

I was satisfied based on the evidence before me, that the Landlord had been made aware that the Tenants were experiencing issues with the refrigerator on June 5, 2024 and there was no evidence provided as to why the Landlord would have waited two months to send a repair technician to address the issue.
OO testified that they incurred costs of $250.00 per week to replace food that spoiled as a result of not having a properly functioning fridge.

Further, there was no evidence that the Landlord ever repaired or replaced the broken shelving in the fridge during the tenancy. While the Tenants were able to clean out their own fridge and were able to use the fridge, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the fridge in good working order.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
In this case, I was not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the maintenance issue with the fridge reasonably in the circumstances.

While the Tenants requested compensation for the costs of replacing spoiled food, no supporting evidence was led of the Tenants’ expenses incurred as a result of the spoiled food. I also do not find it credible that the Tenants would continue to incur costs of $250.00 per week in spoiled food but would wait until June 2024 to put the issues with the fridge into writing to the Landlord. While I am satisfied that there were maintenance issues specifically related to the bins in the fridge since the outset of the tenancy based on OO’s testimony and photo evidence, I was not satisfied that there were cooling issues since the outset of the tenancy as the Tenants allege. Rather, I find it more likely, on a balance of probabilities, that the issue arose closer to June 2024 when the Tenants complained to the Landlord in writing.

As a result, I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to rent abatement of 5% for the period of December 2023 through to May 31, 2024 and a rent abatement of 15% for the period of June 1, 2024 through to August 31, 2024. The total rent abatement for the fridge issue is therefore $2,400.00. Holes in Surfaces Throughout the Rental Unit

OO testified that since the outset of the tenancy there were issues with holes and damage in the walls, doors and surfaces throughout the rental unit as the Landlord had not patched holes or painted the unit prior to the Tenants moving into the rental unit.
The Tenants’ email dated June 5, 2024 further addresses the ongoing cosmetic issues with surfaces throughout the rental unit.
The Tenants entered into evidence photos depicting the visible wear and damage to the walls, main entrance door, and fixtures such as wall plate covers throughout the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that while they were aware of the issues, they had not been able to access the rental unit as the Tenants were unwilling to cooperate with repairs to the walls, doors and fixtures of the rental unit.
While the Landlord testified they repaired the walls and surfaces of the rental unit, no supporting evidence was provided by the Landlord.

I preferred the evidence of the Tenants that the Landlord failed to repair and maintain the walls, door and fixtures such as wall plate covers throughout the rental unit for the duration of the tenancy. The Tenants’ evidence was supported by documentary evidence including their June 5, 2024 email and their photo evidence. I did not find the Landlord’s explanation to be reasonable or credible with regards to the repairs to surfaces throughout the rental unit.
I was satisfied that the Tenant has proven that there were a large number of holes, cracked wall plates and physical damage to the surfaces in the rental unit.

OO testified that due to these issues they were not fully able to enjoy the unit and felt embarrassment and were unable to have people visit or stay at the rental unit due to the condition of the rental unit.

I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of $1,920.00 which represents a 5% rent abatement for a 12-month period from December 1, 2023 to December 31, 2024 due to the ongoing deficiencies with the walls, door and wall plates throughout the rental unit. [name]

OO testified that in approximately March 2024, she began hearing the sounds of a bird inside the rental unit. OO testified that he informed the Landlord in approximately April 2024 that birds may have nested inside the house. OO testified that the Landlord sent somebody to inspect in May 2024 and was advised there were no birds inside the house. OO submits that birds were entering through the house’s external dryer vent cover. OO testified that the Landlord sent a second person to inspect the vent covers and that the issue was addressed by the Landlord in May 2024.
OO entered into evidence photos of the dryer vent cover covered in bird droppings.

The Tenants’ email dated June 5, 2024 states “in the bird’s situation that I messaged you about on the 17th of May with pictures, a gentleman came to the premises last week and said you sent him to see what was going on…”
OO testified that noises from the birds was ongoing throughout the night for the month of May 2024.
While the Tenants’ letter suggests the issue was ongoing as of the email dated June 5, 2024, OO’s testimony was that the issue was resolved in May 2024.

The Landlord testified that once they were informed about a potential bird or birds within the rental unit, they sent somebody to inspect the dryer vent and while they noted no birds had entered the dryer vent, they installed a net over the vent cover to prevent birds from entering or defecating on the vent cover in May 2024.

With regards to the alleged bird infestation, the Tenants’ evidence on dates they informed the Landlord of the bird issue were vague. I found neither the Landlord’s nor the Tenants’ testimony to be more credible than the others with regards to the timeline of the bird infestation issue. It was uncontested by the parties that the individuals sent to inspect the vent had reported no birds had entered the dryer vent. I was not satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenants have proven that the Landlord failed to maintain the dryer vent or address the alleged bird infestation in a timely manner. As a result, the Tenants’ request for an abatement on this ground is denied. Clogged Sinks

OO testified that the kitchen and bathroom sink were clogged since moving into the rental unit and that this as reported numerous times to the Landlord since moving into the rental unit. The Tenants did not provide any supporting evidence such as written complaints or photos of the clogged sink, nor did the Tenants provide any evidence about any dates and times they communicated these issues to the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that they were made aware of a clogged sink on January 18, 2024 and had advised the Tenants to use a drain cleaner. The Landlord testified that there were no further complaints about the drainage issues. The Landlord also testified that they sent a technician to inspect the sinks and that there were no issues noted by their technician. However, no supporting evidence was provided by the Landlord such as inspection reports or photos.

I was not satisfied that the Tenants established that there were any issues with the functioning of the sinks in the rental unit. As a result, the Tenants’ request for an abatement for this issue is denied. Non-functional Electrical Outlets

OO testified that most of the electrical outlets throughout the rental unit have not been working since the outset of the tenancy. The Tenants testified that a by-law officer had inspected the outlets in the rental unit.

The Tenants again did not provide any dates and times of any communications about issues with wall outlets either in their application or by way of verbal testimony. While OO testified that a by-law officer had inspected the outlets, no inspection report or supporting evidence was provided and the Tenants’ testimony about the by-law officer’s findings were hearsay evidence and given no weight.

The Landlord testified they were made aware on one occasion of issues with the wall outlets in the rental unit, but sent a certified electrician to inspect on December 9, 2024. The Landlord testified that the electrician had informed them that there were no issues with the electrical outlets.
An invoice from North York Electrical Contractors Inc dated December 9, 2024 was entered as evidence of the service call made for the electrical outlets by the Landlord.

While I accept, based on the evidence before me, that the Tenants complained of issues with the outlet at least once, I was not satisfied that the Tenants has established that the Landlord failed to maintain the electrical outlets in the rental unit in working condition. As a result, the Tenants’ request for an abatement on this ground is denied. [name]. OO testified the Landlord has failed to maintain the lawn at the rental unit. OO testified that the parties had agreed that the Tenants would be responsible for snow removal at the rental unit but that there was no discussion of who was responsible for lawn maintenance at the rental unit. 52. The Landlord did not deny that they had not maintained the lawn of the rental unit but testified that as per paragraph 18 of the lease agreement, which was entered into evidence by the Landlord, “[the] Tenant is responsible for snow removal, lawn and backyard maintenance.” 53. There was no evidence that the lawn maintenance clause in the lease was void under section 4(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The City of Brampton’s By- law 45-2025 states that lawn and garden maintenance are the responsibility of the “owner or occupant.” 54. The rental unit was the entire house and the lawn was for the Tenants’ exclusive use. The lease agreement stated that the Tenants were responsible for lawn and backyard maintenance. As the Tenants were responsible for the lawn maintenance, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have met the burden of proof to demonstrate that the Landlord has breached its maintenance obligations with regards to lawn maintenance. Smoke Detector 55. OO testified she informed the Landlord that there was no working smoke detector since the outset of the tenancy. The Tenants did not lead any evidence about dates or times this issue was reported to the Landlord or any supporting evidence such as photos or inspection reports. 56. The Landlord testified that they were made aware of the issue with the smoke detector and that the issue was addressed by the electrician from North York Electrical Contractors Inc., on December 9, 2024. 57. I was not satisfied that the Tenants have met the burden of proof to show that the Landlord did not properly maintain or repair the smoke detector in the rental unit. The Tenants did not provide any specific dates or times of any complaints. I found the Landlord’s evidence that the smoke detector was promptly addressed to be more credible. As a result, the request for an abatement on this ground is denied. T2 Application – Substantial Interference Cleanliness of the Rental Unit 58. OO testified that the Landlord’s failure to provide the rental unit in a state of ordinary cleanliness caused them to incur out-of-pocket expenses of $250.00 to clean the house when the Tenants took possession of the rental unit. 59. OO testified that the rental unit was not cleaned when they moved into the rental unit and as a result, they had to purchase cleaning supplies at the cost of $250.00 to clean the rental unit at the commencement of the tenancy. 60. Photos of the unit at the outset of the tenancy were provided into evidence by the Tenants. 61. The Landlord testified that as the Tenants as supposed to move into the rental unit on December 1, 2024 but asked for possession of the rental unit a day earlier, the Landlord was unable to clean the rental unit prior to the Tenants moving in. 62. I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to provide the rental unit in a state of ordinary cleanliness and that this substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I was further satisfied that the Tenants incurred out-of-pocket expense at the outset of the tenancy to clean the rental unit. While the Tenants did not provide any evidence of their costs, I find the requested amount of $250.00 for out-of-pocket expenses for cleaning products and equipment to be reasonable in the circumstances. An order will issue for the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $250.00 for the out-of-pocket cleaning expenses. Substantial Interference Due to [name] 63. While I am satisfied that maintenance issues may result in substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, as the maintenance issues were addressed in the T6 portion of the application above, the request for abatement as a result of substantial interference due to the maintenance issues is duplicative. As remedies were ordered above for the maintenance issues, the Tenants’ request for further abatement as a result of substantial interference for the maintenance issue is denied. Remedies 64. As stated above, I find that a rent abatement of $6,240.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. 65. I also find that the Tenants incurred the following costs and out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord's breach as a result of failing to clean the rental unit prior to providing possession to the Tenants. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $250.00 for these out-of-pocket expenses. 66. The Tenants are also entitled to the filing fees for the cost of filing both the T2 and the T6 application in the amount of $96.00.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated as of December 16, 2024, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $6,712.40. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit, the costs of filing the T2 & T6 applications, the out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Tenants, and the rent abatement awarded to the Tenants are deducted from the amount owing by the Tenants. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before June 20, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,200.00 for the last month rent deposit and interest on the last month rent deposit.
It was undisputed that the Tenant paid the Landlord $2,200.00 towards the last month rent deposit on June 22, 2025, and that the Tenant paid the Landlord for August 2025 rent.

It was undisputed that the Tenant provided the Landlord with notice on August 23, 2025, that he would be vacating the rental unit on September 1, 2025, and that the Landlord failed both to apply the last month’s rent deposit towards last month’s rent, and to provide the Tenant with interest on the last month rent deposit.
What is disputed is whether the Landlord is obligated to provide the Tenant with their last month rent deposit if the Tenant failed to give proper notice to terminate the tenancy.

Section 88(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), provides that where a tenant does not give notice in accordance with the Act or there is no agreement between the parties to terminate the tenancy, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with the Act. In this case, the Tenant could have given 60 days’ notice, therefore the Tenant would be obligated to pay rent up to October 31, 2025.

However, section 88(3) of the Act relieves the Tenant of the obligation to pay rent on the day a new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. A landlord is obligated to mitigate their losses pursuant to section 88(4) of the Act and consideration must be given to whether or not the Landlord took reasonable steps to do so.

The Landlord testified that he tried to rent out the unit as soon as he was notified that the Tenant was vacating but was unable to do so. The Landlord failed to provide any evidence or testimony as to his efforts to mitigate his loss, or when he rented out the unit to the new tenants.
The Tenant testified that when he attended the rental property on September 12, 2025, to retrieve mail, the unit had already been rented out to new tenants.

Upon review of documentation that was uploaded to the Portal, the Landlord messaged the Tenant on August 26, 2025, advising the Tenant that someone was going to look at the property and asked the Tenant to clean the basement.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Pursuant to section 106 (10) of the Act is states: A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

It is undisputed that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with their last month rent deposit. The Landlord failed to provide any evidence or testimony in relation to his efforts to mitigate the loss he faced due to the Tenant’s failure to provide notice in accordance with the Act, nor did the Landlord provide any evidence or testimony as to when he rented out the unit. I am satisfied that at some point in early September 2025; the unit was rented out to new tenants.

Therefore, I based on the evidence before me, the Landlord failed to provide sufficient evidence and testimony in relation to section 88(4) of the Act, and the Tenant provided testimony, which the Landlord did not challenge, that the unit was already rented out on September 12, 2025, when the Tenant attended the rental unit. It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 1, 2025, with a last month’s rent on deposit, in addition to rent being paid in full when the Tenant vacated.

It was undisputed the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, I find the Landlord is required to pay the Tenant their last month’s rent deposit, and the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,310.16. This amount represents: • $2,200.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $62.16 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $350.00.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). It was undisputed that the Tenant paid the Landlords $350.00 for an amenity pass.

The Tenant provided evidence of the rental property listing which outlines on the first page that excluded from the rent is a $350.00 charge for an amenity pass per person. The Tenant disputes this amount should have been paid to the Landlord as they argue that it is an illegal charge.

In addition, the Tenant provided evidence of the lease that was signed by the parties which outlines in paragraph 8, that the Tenant is to pay a one-time charge for $350.00, for the amenities access pass.
The Landlords’ agent testified that the Tenant agreed to pay this amount, and that the Tenant was provided access to the amenities located on site at the rental property.

Pursuant to section 4(1) of the Act, it states; Provisions conflicting with Act void 4 (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void.

In addition, section 134 of the Act states; Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; (b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord; or (c) rent any portion of the rental unit for a rent which, together with all other rents payable for all other portions of the rental unit, is a sum that is greater than the rent the landlord may lawfully charge for the rental unit.

T herefore, the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), as this was an additional charge for the amenities access pass, which is not exempt pursuant to section 17 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, Ontario Regulation 516/06 as the Landlord failed to provide any evidence or testimony to support the fee is exempt from the Act. While I acknowledge the parties agreed on this fee, for my reason stated in paragraph 6, this provision becomes void within the agreement as it is inconsistent with the Act and the regulations.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $398.00. This amount represents: • $350.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 filing fee
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
