issues: [name] (the 'Tenant) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant entered into a fixed-term tenancy commencing July 24, 2024, and ending on February 28, 2025, hereinafter referred to as the “first fixed-term tenancy”. The parties then entered into another fixed-term commencing March 1, 2025, and ending June 30, 2025, hereinafter referred to as the “second fixed-term tenancy”.
The Tenant paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,850.00. The Tenant paid the lawful rent for March 2025, April 2025, and May 2025.

On May 29, 2025, the Tenant wrote to the Landlord to advise that he would be vacating the rental unit on June 1, 2025. The Landlord objected as this was less than 60 days’ notice and before the expiry of the second fixed-term tenancy.
On June 8, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that he had vacated the rental unit. The Landlord instructed the Tenant to leave the keys in the rental unit.
The Landlord did not apply the last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. These facts are not in dispute. Analysis

The Tenant seems to take the position that he was not required to provide at least 60 days’ notice to end the tenancy because he left in accordance with the Landlord’s notice that they vacate at the end of the first fixed-term tenancy. For the reasons that follow, I do not agree.

The parties do not disagree that towards the end of the first fixed-term tenancy, the Landlord asked the Tenant to vacate by February 28, 2025, as the Landlord and his wife were uncertain whether they wanted to continue in the rental business. It is also undisputed that the Tenant explained to the Landlord that as his children were still in school, he would like to remain until June 30, 2025. The Landlord agreed to the Tenant’s request and the parties entered a new fixed-term tenancy.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied there was a meeting of the minds that the Tenant would remain in the rental unit with a fixed-term expiry date of June 30, 2025. As such, the Tenant was not entitled to end the tenancy before June 30, 2025, and was legally required to provide the Landlord with at least 60 days’ written notice. Accordingly, the Landlord was not obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenant.
The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application started to be heard on July 10, 2025, however there was insufficient time to hear the matter in its entirety.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, on July 10, 2025, the Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that this application ought to be dismissed as it is an abuse of process, and these issues have already been before the Board and the Divisional Court. Therefore, the Board is precluded from proceeding. The previous file number LTB-T-068206-22 involves the Tenant’s application regarding an eviction. This application was resolved in favour of the Tenant by order issued on March 29, 2023. In this application, the Tenant seeks to introduce claims against the Landlord that they knew about when filing their previous application, and those issues should have been addressed in the application.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative opposed the Landlord’s Legal Representative’s statements. The issue that was brought up in the previous application related to an illegal lockout, however in this application the Tenant is claiming issues against the Landlord that took place after the illegal lockout. These claims did not exist at the time of the Tenant filing the previous application. The order issued on March 29, 2023 did not make a determination on any issues that are before the Board in this application. Regarding the T6 Application, the Tenant agrees that those issues were ongoing at the time of filing the previous T2 Application, however the Tenant’s priority was the illegal lockout, and therefore urgently filed an application regarding that issue. However, the fact that the Tenant filed only a T2 Application and not a T6 Application should not prevent the Tenant from bringing up maintenance issues that were otherwise live.

After hearing the parties submissions, I am not satisfied that this application should be dismissed for the reason the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted. Regarding the T2 Application, I note that the issues in the application before me took place after the date the order was issued (March 29, 2023) and therefore they have not been before the Board. Regarding the maintenance issues, I do not find it appropriate that a party would be prevented from brining forward an application only because those issues were live while another application was filed. Therefore, the matter will proceed to be heard on the merits. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that she first notified the Landlord of the issues in the rental unit on or about a few months preceding October 2022. The Landlord did not respond to the Tenant, and no action was taken to repair anything in the rental unit. On or about the first week of October 2022, the Tenant followed up with the Landlord regarding the state of disrepair in the rental unit, however the Landlord did not address her complaints. The Tenant hired a contractor to perform the necessary repair to the rental unit at her own expense. The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement for the period of October 1, 2022 to October 31, 2022, the date that the contractor began the repairs.

The Tenant testified that on or about May 2022, she notified the Landlord of a crack in the dining room wall. The Landlord did not address this issue. She notified the Landlord again on or about first week of October 2022, and no action was taken. Due to the Landlord not repairing this, it resulting in mould forming around the crack and the window. A photograph of this crack was submitted to the Board as evidence. The Tenant is requesting a 5% rent abatement for the crack in the wall.

The Tenant stated that there was mould surrounding her entire window. This window is a single slide window that traps moisture and therefore the window allowed mould to infest the walls surrounding in the window. The Tenant submitted photographs of the mould as evidence to the Board. The Tenant is seeking a 15% rent abatement for the mould surrounding the window.

The Tenant stated that starting from 2021 and onward, there was a bedbug and cockroach infestation. The Tenant advised the Landlord of this issue however the Landlord refused to remedy it. When the Tenant hired the contractor, he remedied it in the first week of November 2022. The Tenant is seeking a 40% rent abatement for this issue. Legal Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act provides: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the act to repair and maintain the rental unit with respect to the crack in the wall, mould around the window, bedbugs and cockroaches in the rental unit. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response and evidence to the Tenant’s allegations made against them and I found the Tenant’s testimony credible and reliable, supported by documentation. T2 Application

The Tenant testified that per the order issued on March 29, 2023, the Landlord was ordered to put the Tenant back into possession no later than March 31, 2023, due to an illegal lockout that started in November 2022. When she received this decision, she was homeless and therefore was looking forward to being put back into possession by the end of March 2023. There unfortunately was a delay in moving back into the rental unit, which caused he significant stress and depression. The Tenant was forced to move into her mother’s two-bedroom apartment and share it with four adults and three children.

The Tenant stated that she was unable to return to the rental unit until July 15, 2023. The Landlord’s Legal Representative communicated via email that there were other tenants living in the rental unit, however they will be vacating in two weeks. A copy of this email dated June 30, 2023, was submitted as evidence to the Board.

When the Tenant returned to the rental unit, she testified that all of her belongings were not returned to her. When she was locked out, she had two couches (a three-seater couch and a love seat), a T.V, a rogers modem, LED lights, kids toys, coffee table, wallpaper, iPhone, bedroom rug and other miscellaneous items. These items were all in good and usable condition when she left them behind. The Tenant submitted photographs of these items dated November 4, 2022, the morning of the lock out. The Tenant did not have access to her belongings and only gained access to them when she returned to the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that when she returned to the rental unit, various items were broken and not in the same condition they were left in. Specifically, there were tears in the couch and love seat, the rogers modem was not returned, nor was the wallpaper. The Tenant stated that couches were in good condition, as she had to purchase new furniture in 2020 due to a bed bug infestation. the Tenant stated that the T.V was returned to her broken condition, as it did not work once the Landlord returned it to her. The Tenant submitted various photographs of these items as evidence to the Board.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord breached the Board order issued on March 29, 2023, when they did not preserve the Tenant’s belongings despite being order to do so. Legal Analysis
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord breached section 23 of the Act when the Landlord did not permit the Tenant to return to the rental unit as per the Order issued on March 31, 2023 and when the Landlord did not return the Tenant’s items in the same condition they were in when the lockout took place which is a breach of the preservation portion in the order. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response and evidence to the Tenant’s allegations made against them. I found the testimony of the Tenant credible and reliable and supported by documentation. Remedies Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenant claimed an amount of $5,728.34 for replacing the property that was disposed of by the Landlord. I find that it is reasonable for a tenant to estimate the cost of lost goods and that it would neither be reasonable or likely to expect someone to have receipts kept for every purchase made. I find it reasonable to provide an estimate, with photographs – where possible of the items that are lost or disposed of.

In Beauage v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 (CanLII), the Divisional Court stated, in part, as follows: “The Board heard evidence about the possessions of the respondent that were in the apartment unit, including two couches, a large television, a bed, two night tables, a stereo, a lap top, linen, clothes and many other items. The Board made an estimate of the reasonable replacement costs. It made no error of law in doing so. The estimate was a reasonable one in the circumstances, as broken down by the Board. [Emphasis added]

I accept the Tenant’s testimony as true and that the belongings, which were in the rental unit as of November 2022, are as outlined in Schedule A to her application. In accordance with Beauage, supra, in the absence of receipts or other third-party evidence about the value of the disposed items, I may estimate the reasonable replacement costs of the items at issue.

The Tenant presented cost estimates for a majority of the items she is seeking to claim replacement value for. I do not believe it is necessary to repeat, herein, each and every item claimed by the Tenant as same is concisely provided in Schedule A – Appendix A to the Tenant’s application and was reviewed during the hearing. I would note that for each and every item listed by the Tenant the corresponding estimated value is reasonable, and therefore this remedy will be awarded. Rent Abatement

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value.

The Tenant is requesting a 60% rent abatement for the period of 31 days, the month of October 2022. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find that a 35% rent abatement for the various maintenance issues is appropriate to award in this circumstance. I heard the Tenant’s evidence of the impact that these issues have had on them, and I further considered the documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony. I heard that Tenants evidence that these maintenance issues have been ongoing until she hired someone to repair them, and that the Landlord has refused to remedy them. Therefore, I find an amount of a 35% rent abatement for the month of October 2022 is appropriate in these circumstances, totaling to $525.00 ($1,500.00*35%=$525.00). General Damages

The Tenant is seeking a total of $7,000.00 in damages. The Tenant states that she is claiming $4,000.00 in general damages for the 106 days she was not permitted back into the rental unit. In addition, she is claiming $1,000.00 for each minor child that experience poor living conditions when they were not permitted back into the rental unit, totalling to $3,000.00. The Tenant testified that this was a very stressful situation, that had a negative impact on her and her children’s lives. Aside from being illegally locked out, the Landlord did not permit the Tenant back into the rental unit until approximately four months after the order.

I have considered the evidence of the Tenant and find that there was testimony provided of the direct impact on the Tenant due to the Landlord’s actions resulting in hardship to the Tenant. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide submissions and/or a response to this remedy that the Tenant is seeking. Having considered similar cases and impact, I find an amount of $3,000.00 in general compensation is appropriate in this circumstance.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,253.34. This amount represents: • $525.00 for a rent abatement. • $5,728.34 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace the property that was damaged, destroyed and/or disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $3,000.00 for general compensation
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord sublet the rental unit without the consent of the owner and charged her a monthly rent more than the amount of rent the Landlord was charged by the owner. The Tenant seeks $700.00, which is the amount of the excess rent the Landlord illegally collected and retained.
The Tenant also alleges the Landlord illegally collected and retained a damage deposit in the amount of $1,500.00. Illegal Excess Rent:
It is undisputed that the parties entered into a one-month fixed term tenancy commencing on July 31, 2025 and ending on August 31, 2025 for a monthly rent of $2,800.00.

The Tenant testified that she first learned the Landlord was not the owner of the rental unit from security staff at the residential complex. She maintains that the Landlord sublet the rental unit without the consent of the owner. It is the position of the Tenant that the owner of the rental unit charged the Landlord $2,100.00 in rent yet the Landlord has charged the Tenant $2,800.00.

The Tenant testified that she conducted a market survey of comparable rental units in the area and found that the monthly rents for a comparable rental unit was $2,100.00. The Tenant asked the Landlord what her monthly rent was for the rental unit, but the Landlord refused to provide this information to the Tenant.

The Landlord did not rebut the Tenant’s claim that she did not obtain the consent of the owner to sublet the rental unit or that she was paying a monthly rent of $2,100.00. Instead, the Landlord deferred to a contrived narrative that the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit until March 17, 2026, and owed her months of rent arrears.

I give little weight to the Landlord’s evidence in this regard as it was contrived and circumstantial, and her testimony was evasive and deceptive. During the Tenant’s cross examination of her evidence the Landlord was forced to admit to having fabricated evidence regarding the delivery of a filter to the rental unit in September 2026, in the [name] name. In contrast, I found the Tenant’s evidence throughout the hearing was informed, consistent, forthcoming and reliable.

Section 134. (3) (a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: (3)(a) Unless otherwise prescribed, no tenant and no person acting on behalf of the tenant shall, directly or indirectly, (a) sublet a rental unit for a rent that is payable by one or more subtenants and that is greater than the rent that is lawfully charged by the landlord for the rental unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the lawful monthly rent charged by the owner to the Landlord for the rental unit is $2,100.00. I am also satisfied the Landlord collected and retained $2,800.00 from the Tenant for the period from August 1, 2025 to August 31, 2025. This represents rent greater than the rent that is lawfully charged by the owner for the rental unit. As such, I find the Landlord has collected and retained money illegally from the Tenant and shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $700.00. Illegal Damage Deposit:

Section 105 (1) of the Act states that: The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. 2006, c. 17. The Landlord explained that the damage deposit was collected because the rental unit was furnished and the damage deposit applied to the furnishing. Notwithstanding the Landlord’s rationale for collecting a $1,500.00 damage deposit, it is an illegal rent deposit that was collected and must be returned to the Tenant. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $1,500.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to the reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,248.00. This amount represents: • $700.00 for excess rent illegally collected. • $1,500.00 for the last month's rent deposit illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 02, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant applied for a remedy on the basis that the Landlord failed to apply a last month's rent deposit to the final rental period of the tenancy and failed to return that deposit to her.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified she vacated the rental unit on July 3, 2025. At the time, the tenancy was continuing on a month-to-month basis. She further testified that a rent payment in the amount of $1,350.00 was withdrawn from her bank account on or about July 2, 2025,

Although the application refers to the Landlord's failure to apply or return a last month's rent deposit, it was clear from the application and the Tenant's evidence that she was seeking the return of the July 2025 rent payment. Accordingly, I amended the application to reflect the remedy actually sought by the Tenant. I am satisfied that no prejudice results from this amendment, as the Landlord was aware of the nature of the claim and was prepared to respond to it.
There was no evidence before me that the Tenant provided the Landlord with a last month's rent deposit at the commencement of the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that she verbally advised the Landlord on May 1, 2025 of her intention to terminate the tenancy. She further testified that she subsequently submitted a Tenant's Notice to End the Tenancy (N9) a few days later, which identified a termination date of July 3, 2025.

The Tenant testified that an on-site staff member amended the termination date on the N9 when it was submitted. The Landlord's representative testified that the Tenant was advised that the termination date contained in the notice did not comply with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') because it did not coincide with the last day of a rental period. The Landlord's representative submitted that the termination date was amended to July 31, 2025 in the Tenant's presence.

The Landlord's representative relied on a letter dated May 16, 2025, which confirmed that the tenancy would terminate on July 31, 2025 because the termination date identified by the Tenant did not comply with the Act. The letter also explained the basis for the correction and confirmed that the tenancy continued until the end of the July 2025 rental period.

Section 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.

Section 44 of the Act states: 44 (2) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.

Pursuant to subsection 44(2) of the Act, a tenant's notice of termination for a monthly tenancy must be given at least 60 days before the termination date and the termination date must be the last day of a rental period. I find that July 3, 2025, was not a valid termination date under the Act because it did not fall on the last day of a rental period.

Pursuant to section 47 of the Act, a tenancy terminates only in accordance with the Act. As the Tenant's proposed termination date was invalid, the tenancy continued until July 31, 2025, which was the earliest valid termination date arising from the Tenant's notice.

I find that rent was owing for the entire month of July 2025 because the tenancy continued until July 31, 2025. The fact that the Tenant chose to vacate the rental unit earlier in the month does not alter her obligation to pay rent for the balance of the rental period.

As the Tenant did not pay a last month's rent deposit at the commencement of the tenancy, there was no deposit available to be applied to the final rental period. The July 2025 payment withdrawn from the Tenant's account was therefore a rent payment for a period during which the tenancy remained in effect.

In these circumstances, I find that the Tenant is not entitled to reimbursement of the July 2025 rent payment. The rent was lawfully owing because the tenancy continued until July 31, 2025 pursuant to sections 44(2) and 47 of the Act.
For the above reasons, the Tenant's application, as amended, is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants alleged that the Landlord imposed an illegal rent increase.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2024 and vacated on April 26, 2026. She further testified that there were changes in ownership of the rental property during her tenancy, including a change in or about March 2025 when a third and final Landlord assumed control.

The Tenant testified that following the change in ownership, she signed a new tenancy agreement with the incoming Landlord in March 2025. The Tenant testified that under the prior arrangement her rent had been $1,600.00 per month, and that the rent under the new agreement increased to $2,000.00 per month. She further testified that the Landlord advised the increase was related to hydro charges and that the arrangement would be temporary until a separate hydro meter was installed, after which rent would return to $1,600.00 per month and the Tenant would become responsible for hydro costs. The Tenant testified that this arrangement did not ultimately occur.

The Tenant testified that she paid rent of $2,000.00 per month from May 2025 to July 2025. In August 2025, she paid $1,850.00 based on an agreement with the Landlord relating to a temporary hydro-related adjustment. From September 2025 onward, she paid $1,600.00 per month after being advised that the increased rent was unlawful.
Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord imposed an illegal rent increase contrary to the Act.

The evidence before me establishes that following the change in ownership, the Tenant entered into a new written tenancy agreement with the incoming Landlord in March 2025. The rent payable under that agreement was set at $2,000.00 per month. There was no evidence before me of a subsequent notice of rent increase within an ongoing tenancy or of a unilateral increase imposed by the Landlord beyond the terms of the agreement.

While the Tenant testified that she was told the increase was temporary and related to hydro costs, I find that these representations, even if made, relate to a collateral or future arrangement concerning utilities and do not establish that the rent charged under the tenancy agreement was unlawful under the Act.

The Tenant’s evidence indicates that she paid the agreed rent of $2,000.00 for a period of time, followed by a reduced payment in August 2025 pursuant to a separate arrangement, and thereafter resumed paying $1,600.00. However, these payment variations do not, on their own, establish that the Landlord unlawfully increased the rent.

In the absence of evidence demonstrating that the Landlord increased rent contrary to the Act or charged rent in excess of the amount agreed to in the operative tenancy agreement, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven an illegal rent increase and in my view, the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Illegal Charge

The Tenant testified that she paid first month’s rent and a last month’s rent deposit at the commencement of the tenancy. She further testified that following a subsequent change in ownership, the third and current Landlord requested an additional payment described as a “damage deposit.” Text messages entered into evidence confirm that the Landlord requested the “damage deposit,” and the evidence further confirms that a payment in the amount of $2,000.00 was made on April 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that she later requested that this “damage deposit” be applied to the March 2026 rental period, as she intended to vacate at the end of April 2026 and understood that her last month’s rent deposit would be applied to April 2026 rent. The Landlord refused.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected an unlawful security deposit contrary to the Act.

Subsection 134(1) of the Act prohibits a landlord from requiring or collecting any security deposit other than a rent deposit permitted under section 106 (last month’s rent) and a refundable key deposit limited to actual replacement cost.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that a last month’s rent deposit had already been paid at the outset of the tenancy. The subsequent $2,000.00 payment was requested and collected as a “damage deposit,” which is not authorized under the Act.

I find that the $2,000.00 payment constitutes an illegal security deposit within the meaning of subsection 134(1) of the Act, and that the Landlord collected a charge that is not permitted under the Act.
Accordingly, the Tenants are entitled to return of the unlawful deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,053.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The portion of the application alleging an illegal rent increase is dismissed.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 29, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 30, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The parties were before the Board on October 29, 2025, where they settled all, except one issue, in the Tenant’s application, by way of consent. An interim order capturing the terms of the consent was issued on November 13, 2025, by Member [name].

The parties were scheduled for a hearing to determine a single issue that was not settled by consent. The issue that is to be determined is whether the side area in dispute forms part of the Tenant’s rental unit with exclusive use as a patio or is it a common area walkway that provides access to the back yard. (Determinations- Para 3 of LTB-T-077558- 23-IN) Tenant’s position

The Tenant has lived in the rental unit since 2005. The Tenant testified that when she moved into the unit in 2005, she was told that the area directly outside her main entrance door is her patio area. The Tenant lives in a complex of town houses and her entrance is at the side and there is a unit in front of her unit and their entrance is at the front.

The Tenant testified that she is responsible for snow removal in her patio area. Over the years, the Tenant has used that area to set up a swing or other outdoor furniture. Periodically, the Tenant has stored stuff in that area.

The Tenant disagrees with the Landlord’s position that the area outside the Tenant’s main entrance is a common area walkway that provides access to other Tenants to the open green space behind the complex. The Tenant testified that the Landlord has structured access to the communal greenspace at the back side of her shared driveway. They built a railing so that it is accessible for people who may require mobility assistance. She testified that the area outside her main door is not accessible, as it has a step up and step down in the middle of the alleged walkway. Landlord’s position
The Landlord submitted a site plan (DOC-7405879). The Landlord submits that the site plan categorizes the area in question as an “asphalt walkway”. As such, it is a common area.

The Landlord’s property manager testified. She has been a property manager since October 2025. She testified that she has no knowledge of conversations that would have taken place at the commencement of the tenancy. The property manager did not know when the site plan was issued, and assumes it was when the complex was built. She does not know if the site plan has ever been modified. She testified that she has had no discussions with the Tenant about the use of the area in question. Analysis
Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the area in question is a common area walkway.

I am not persuaded by the Landlord’s submissions with respect to the site plan. The site plan describes the area in question as an asphalt walkway. I have no evidence to suggest that that means it is a common area walkway.

Section 202 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

In this circumstance, the Tenant has lived in the unit for 21 years. The Tenant testified, and it was not contested, that for the majority of those years, she used the area in question as her own space and that it was not a common area walkway that was used by others to access the shared greenspace. This is further supported by the Landlord’s action of constructing a railing at the rear of the Tenant’s driveway to facilitate access to the shared greenspace. Moreover, the area in question does not appear to be accessible as a common walkway as there is a step up and a step down, in front of the Tenant’s door, in order to pass through to get to the shared green space.
I am satisfied that the area in question forms part of the Tenant’s unit and is not a common area walkway.
ordered: The side area is part of the Tenant’s unit and is not a common area walkway. June 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant a total of $257.98, which represents the interest owing on the deposit and the Tenant’s filing fee.

The Tenant seeks the interest on his last month rent deposit that was collected and retained by the Landlord during his approximate 17 years tenancy at the rental unit. The Tenant also seeks return of the illegal rent that the Landlord collected and retained contrary to subsection 116 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’)

In his application, the Tenant also alleges that the Landlord gave him an N13 notice in bad faith and seeks remedies in connection to his moving costs and rent. The Tenant filed a T1 application under section 135 of the Act. The remedies sought by the Tenant in connection to bad faith can not be awarded under section 135. A claim for bad faith for a notice of termination under section 50 is brought under section 57 of the Act, which is a T5 application. As such, the portion of the Tenant’s application pertaining to the N13 notice will not be considered. Interest Owing on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit

It is undisputed that the Landlord did not pay the Tenant interest on his last month’s rent deposit as required in subsection 106 (6) of the Act which reads, A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 2006, c. 17.

The Landlord held that the Tenant was not entitled to interest because he had not increased the Tenant’s initial rent of $750.00 for 11 years and was not charged rent for the last 15 days of his tenancy. He also submits that the Tenant is not entitled to interest because he never charged the Tenant for utilities, internet, and television and because the Tenant was permitted to use the Landlord’s garage for storing personal items.

The Act does not permit a landlord to refuse to pay interest owing on a deposit for any reason. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $204.98 which is determined by adding the interests that accrued over the Tenant’s years of tenancy pursuant to subsection 106 (6) of the Act. llegal Rent Increases

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied the Landlord illegally collected and retained rent increases over the years of the tenancy without providing the Tenant with at least 90 days written notice. However, as the Tenant paid each rent increase for at least 12 months, the increase in rent is deemed to be valid pursuant to subsection 135.1 (1) of the Act.

The only exception to this relates to the rent increase on February 1, 2024, where the Landlord increased the rent from $950.00 to $1,100.00 without providing the Tenant with at least 90 days written notice. In accordance with subsection 116(4), the increase in rent is void as the Landlord did not give the Tenant the required notice. While the Tenant paid the illegal rent increase from February 2024 to August 2024, he did not file his application until September 13, 2025. In accordance with subsection 135(4), the Board cannot make an order with respect to an application filed more than one year after money was illegally collected or retained. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed as he is outside the time limitation.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the [Landlord, shall pay the Tenant is $257.98 which represents: • $204.98 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 02, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant requested, and I accepted, to remove the named Landlords 2789826 ONTARIO and [name] from the application and to proceed against only the Purchaser. The application is also amended to correct the spelling of the Purchaser’s name to [name].
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant alleges that the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and that the N12 notice was therefore given in bad faith. The Tenant sought remedies including a rent abatement, rent differential, moving and related expenses, general compensation, and a fine payable to the Board.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • no person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser’s own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord’s and the purchaser’s good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

The parties agreed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about December 10 or 11, 2024, and that the Purchaser and his family moved into the rental unit on or about October 2025. The central issue is whether the Purchaser failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and, if so, whether this supports a finding that the N12 notice was given in bad faith.

I find that the Tenant has not proven that the Purchaser failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time. The Purchaser testified that, before closing, he viewed the rental unit once and believed it was liveable and required only cleaning and painting. However, when the Tenant vacated, the unit was in a significantly worse condition than expected. The Purchaser’s evidence was that the unit contained garbage and personal items, damaged drywall, damaged doors and windows, missing or damaged fixtures, damaged appliances, missing cabinet components, damaged flooring, urine odour and staining, cat- related damage, and exterior waste and damage.

The Purchaser’s video and photographic evidence supported his testimony. The evidence showed extensive waste inside and outside the rental unit, damage to walls and ceilings, missing closet doors, missing electrical covers, damaged or missing trim and doors, dark paint and graffiti, dirty conditions, food waste, cat litter and excrement, damaged cabinets, and exterior debris and fence damage. The Tenant did not testify to dispute the Purchaser’s evidence about the condition of the unit when the Tenant vacated.

I also accept the Purchaser’s evidence that the rental unit required significant work before it could reasonably be occupied by the Purchaser and his family. The Purchaser’s evidence included receipts for materials, waste removal, repairs, and some contractor work, with receipt dates running from February 2025 to August 26, 2025. The Purchaser testified that he completed some of the work himself because of limited finances. The evidence also showed that after the work was complete, the unit had been substantially renovated, including repairs to the kitchen, floors, drywall, electrical fixtures, doors, bathrooms, yard, deck, and fence.

The former landlord, [name], testified that when the property was listed for sale, the rental unit was in decent and liveable condition, although it required some paint and had some missing cabinet doors. He testified that the condition shown in the Purchaser’s videos after the Tenant vacated was a significant change from the prior condition of the property. I find this evidence supports the Purchaser’s evidence that the condition of the unit after the Tenant vacated required substantial repair before occupancy.

I have also considered the Purchaser’s financial and personal circumstances. The Purchaser testified that during this period he had limited financial resources, was paying rent at his former residence while also carrying costs for the rental unit, was studying, working, caring for his children, and caring for his wife. The documentary evidence included bank statements and OSAP-related documents, which supported that the Purchaser had limited financial resources during the relevant period. The parties also agreed that the Purchaser was incurring expenses for both his apartment and the rental unit before he moved in.

The Purchaser also gave evidence that his wife had significant pregnancy-related medical issues. The medical evidence included documentation showing a history of pregnancy complications and hospital admission in August 2025. The Purchaser testified that his wife gave birth by C-section in September 2025 and required time to recover before the family could complete the move. I accept that these medical circumstances contributed to the timing of the Purchaser’s move.

The Tenant argued that the delay before the Purchaser moved in was unreasonable, particularly because the Purchaser had previously testified at the N12 hearing that he needed to move into the unit because of financial pressure. However, the evidence before the Board establishes that the Purchaser’s delay was caused by the unexpected poor condition of the rental unit, the extent of the repairs required, the Purchaser’s limited financial resources, and his wife’s medical circumstances. I find these explanations credible and reasonable.

I also find that the Purchaser’s eventual occupation of the rental unit supports his good faith intention. There was no evidence that the rental unit was listed for rent or sale after the Tenant vacated. The evidence establishes that the unit remained vacant while the Purchaser completed repairs and that the Purchaser and his family moved in once the work was completed and his family circumstances allowed. This is consistent with a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Purchaser occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time in the circumstances. I also find that the Tenant has not proven that the N12 notice was served in bad faith by either the former landlord or the Purchaser. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: pancham (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) • gave a notice of termination in bad faith. (T5 Application) • failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Former Tenant owes. (L10 Application) [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Former Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2, T5, or T6 applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s applications are dismissed.

The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed because it did not contain sufficient particulars to allow the Board to determine the allegations. The application lacked necessary details, including dates, times, names, and specific facts about the alleged substantial interference, harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats, interference, or withholding of vital services.

The Tenant’s T6 application is also dismissed because it did not contain sufficient particulars. The original and amended materials did not provide enough specific information about the alleged maintenance issues, including when the issues occurred, when the Landlord was notified, what response was provided, and how the Landlord allegedly failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Act.

The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed because there was no live T5 issue before the Board. The Tenant did not plead any facts supporting a claim that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. Rather, the Tenant agreed at the hearing that it was included in their application in error, and the pleadings for that claim were left blank. The Landlord’s L10 application
As explained below, the Landlord proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Former Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $314.22.
The Former Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 9, 2024.
The lawful rent was $1,950.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $64.11. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,950.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.

The parties agreed that the Former Tenant had moved out by November 1, 2024, but left belongings in the rental unit to be removed later. The parties also agreed that the Landlord permitted the Former Tenant to leave belongings in the rental unit for an additional 7 days, until November 7, 2024, without payment of rent. I reviewed the recording filed by the Former Tenant. In that recording, the Landlord did not object to the Former Tenant leaving belongings behind during that period and stated that the Former Tenant would not be charged for those days.

The Landlord claimed rent from November 1 to November 9, 2024. However, based on the parties’ agreement, I find that no rent or daily compensation is owing from November 1 to November 7, 2024. The Former Tenant acknowledged that, if any amount was owing, it would only be for November 8 and 9, 2024, which were outside the agreed 7-day period. I therefore find that the Former Tenant owes rent/daily compensation for November 8 and 9, 2024, in the amount of $128.22.

The Landlord’s claims for damage, cleaning, [name] rental, interference, by-law costs, bug screens, stove damage, drywall repair, and other out-of-pocket costs are dismissed. The Landlord did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Former Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex, or that the Former Tenant substantially interfered with the Landlord’s reasonable enjoyment, lawful right, privilege or interest.

The Landlord’s evidence did not sufficiently connect the claimed costs to compensable conduct by the Former Tenant. Several claims were unsupported by receipts, invoices, photographs, or other reliable evidence. Where photographs were referenced, they did not establish the extent of damage or cleaning claimed. The Landlord also claimed amounts for their own labour, but did not provide sufficient evidence to establish the work performed, the time spent, or the reasonableness of the amounts claimed.

I also find that some of the claimed costs were not recoverable on the evidence before me. The [name] rental was not incurred until January 2025, well after the tenancy ended, and I am not satisfied that it was required solely or primarily because of the Former Tenant’s belongings. The claims relating to by-law reports and the child-care-related complaint are dismissed because the Landlord did not prove that the Former Tenant made a false or improper complaint, or that those costs resulted from wilful or negligent damage or substantial interference. Therefore, the Landlord’s claims for out-of-pocket costs are dismissed.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2, T5, and T6 applications are dismissed.
The Landlord’s claims for damages and out-of-pocket costs are dismissed.

If the Former Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before July 5, 2026, the Former Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Vangeest (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,983.45 for a rent abatement and out of pocket costs.

The Landlord revoked the Tenants’ access to on-site laundry in April 2025 and revoked the Tenants’ access to two parking spots on approximately January 3, 2025. Previously the Tenants had access to these amenities and there was no reasonable justification for their removal. The Landlord’s agent acknowledged in a text message on March 12, 2026 that the Tenants were entitled to these amenities and they would be restored.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. Remedies
The Tenants have out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $779.20 because of the Landlord's actions. The Landlord must pay the Tenants this amount.

The Tenants had to do laundry at a public laundr omat, which cost an extra $1.00 per load. The Tenants estimate they averaged 5 loads per month. They also incurred transportation expenses, which they estimated using the jury guide rate of $0.34 per km x 15km each way x 2 trips per month. Over a 10.5 month period these extra laundry expenses total $266.70.

The Tenants have electric vehicles which t hey had to charge at public chargers when they did not have access to their regular parking spots at the residential complex. Public chargers have a higher cost than home charging, which the Tenants calculated to be an average of an extra $41.00 per month comparing home rates to public charger rates and the vehicle charging records. Over a 12.5 month period the extra charging costs total $512.50.

The Tenants request a rent abatement of 5% for the temporary loss of the on-site laundry. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, and the Tenants’ description of the inconvenience caused by the interruption, I find this to be a reasonable amount. The Tenants request an abatement 10% for the temporary loss of the 2 parking spots. This is $115.00 per month, which based on my knowledge of similar matters before the Board is a reasonable, if not low, estimate for the value of 2 parking spots. The Tenants were significantly inconvenienced by the Landlord’s actions in eliminating the parking spots. Accordingly, I find the requested abatement is not unreasonable.
Therefore, I find that a r ent abatement of $2,156.25 is appropriate in the circumstances. ($1,150.00 x 5% x 10.5 months for laundry access plus $1,150.00 x 10% x 12.5 months for parking)

The Tenants also requested the Board or der the Landlords and the Purchasers pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

In the present case, the Tenants have been awarded a monetary remedy, which provides a reasonable deterrent. Although the monetary remedy may not be objectively large, I am satisfied based on the evidence referred to in the hearing that the Landlord may be experiencing some financial difficulty and the remedy awarded may be significant in their circumstances. The Landlord acknowledged the Tenants’ entitlement to the previously included on-site laundry and parking and restored access to the services prior to the hearing. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,983.45. This amount represents:  $1,322.50 for a rent abatement.  $496.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants t he full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 20, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $750.00 from the rent each month from July to September 2026 and $733.45 from October 2026. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: On or about mid August 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlords for consent to sublet the rental unit to an individual, the potential subtenant.

On or about mid August 2025, the Landlords refused to consent to the sublet. The Landlords provided the following reason for the refusal: the Landlords advised the Tenant that because she had signed an N9 notice on July 30, 2025, stating she was vacating the rental unit on September 30, 2025, they were unable to now sublet their rent unit.

The application was filed within one year after the Landlords withheld consent. The Tenant requested to sublet their rental unit on or about mid August 2025 and filed their application with the Board on September 16, 2025, just one month after the Landlords had refused to consent to the subletting of the rental unit.

I find the Landlords did not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to the sublet of the rental unit to the potential subtenant. The Tenant stated they had found a subtenant to sublease the rental unit from September 1, 2025 to September 30, 2025. However, the Tenant did not adduce any documentary evidence at the hearing to support their position that they had found an individual to sublease the rental unit. I would have reasonably expected the Tenant to either call this individual forward to testify that they were willing to pay $1,300.00 to sublease the rental unit, or documentary evidence to support the Tenant had someone this individual.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application was scheduled for an adjudicative case videoconference on June 25, 2026. The Landlord’s representative [name] and the Tenant attended the case conference.
reasons: Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) establishes that no application that alleges the types of claims listed in section 29 of the Act can be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. This application makes claims pursuant to section 29 of the Act and is therefore subject to the limitation period established by section 29(2).

Order LTB-L-059072-24-RV issued on February 24, 2025, determined that this tenancy terminated on September 17, 2024. The Tenant filed their application on September 19, 2025. It is therefore out of time and must be dismissed.

The Tenant requested an adjournment because he is in the hospital and did not have access to any supporting documentation he sought to rely upon. The documents referred to by the Tenant are relevant to the merits of the application but not the question of whether the application was filed out of time. As such the adjournment request was denied.
The Tenant submits that the application should still be heard despite being filed out of time. I do not have the discretion to hear an application that was filed outside the limitation period.

The Tenant argues that his lease was set to run past September 17, 2024. Even if true, tenancies can be terminated before the end of a lease term for several reasons. Those reasons include rent arrears which was the subject of application LTB-L-059072-24.

The Tenant argues that his tenancy actually ended on a different date than what was determined in order LTB-L-059072-24. The issue of when the tenancy terminated has already been determined by the Board and the order was not successfully reviewed or appealed. I find that the issue of when the tenancy ended is subject to issue estoppel.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
