issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') for the following reasons. [name]:
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on October 15, 2024, and he vacated the rental unit on August 1, 2025.

The undisputed evidence is that the parties signed an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy on August 1, 2025. The N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy also had a signed addendum with further terms. It is also undisputed that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N5 notice of termination containing three allegations about the Tenant’s occupants creating a substantial interference to others, about the behaviour of the Tenant and his guests leading to police complaints, and it also alleges that there were complaints received about the Tenant’s smoking in the rental unit and on the balcony.

The tenancy began pursuant to a lease agreement that commenced the tenancy on October 15, 2024, for a period of 11.5 months, or 11 months and 15 days. The only rent amount mentioned was $25,000.00 for the entire term of 11.5 months. Although the documentary evidence showed the lease commenced on October 17, 2024, it was uncontested that the tenancy began on October 15, 2024, and I heard no evidence to the contrary.

Both parties provided testimony about how the lease agreement came about, and who chose to make the rent $25,000.00 for 11.5 months. However, that evidence was largely irrelevant to this matter. What is undisputed is that the Tenant paid $25,000.00 in total, up front to the Landlord for the 11.5 month lease.

The parties did not completely agree about the circumstances of how the tenancy terminated, either. However, they essentially agreed that they both decided to sign an N11 agreement to terminate on August 1, 2025, with its addendum, because it was quicker, easier and more amicable, rather than have to come before the Board to determine the merits of the Landlord’s N5 notice of termination.

The addendum to the N11 agreement to terminate states that the Landlord will refund the [name] 61 days of unused rent (by leaving August 1, 2025 rather than September 30, 2025), or a total of $4,357.23 if the Tenant leaves the “property as of August 1st in rentable/marketable condition. In other words, property is vacated with only normal wear/tear.” The addendum further states that 50% of refund will be issued after inspection last week of July 2025, and the other 50% when the property is vacated. The addendum concludes with the statement, “Both parties confirm this refund is agreed upon voluntarily and complies with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.”

The Tenant wrote to request his refund of $4,357.23 after he vacated on July 28, 2025. The parties had a series of text messages in evidence that show that the Landlord advised the Tenant that he did not believe that the rental unit had been left in “marketable condition”, and that he was going to subtract the repair costs from the money owed.
It is undisputed that the Landlord did not reimburse the Tenant the $4,357.23 owed. It is also undisputed that the Tenant cancelled any inspections that were scheduled prior to moving out.

The Tenant submits that he left the rental unit in marketable condition, and he is seeking the refund of the $4,357.23. He is not seeking the further three days of rent owed because he moved out on July 28, 2025, three days earlier than August 1, 2025. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that the Landlord shall reimburse the Tenant the $4,357.23, equivalent to 61 days of unused rent after the Tenant moved out for the following reasons.

The N11 agreement to terminate on August 1, 2025, signed by the parties is a contract agreed to by the parties upon their mutual decision to terminate the tenancy. However, in this case, the addendum to the N11 takes it out of the jurisdiction of the Board. By virtue of sections 37, 77, and 134(1.1) of the Act, taken together, the “conditions” in the addendum for the Landlord to refund the $4,357.23 of unused rent, render unenforceable the parties’ N11, taken as a whole together with the addendum. With the addendum, the apparent N11 agreement to terminate is not, in fact, what was intended by the Board’s N11 form. As a whole document it is not what was contemplated by an N11 agreement, and it would not have supported a valid N3 application for an ex parte eviction pursuant to subsection 77(1) of the Act. Merely because the parties agreed that the addendum “complies with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006,” does not make it so.
Consequently, I find that the Landlord is liable to reimburse the $4,357.23 to the Tenant for a different reason than the N11 agreement.

Pursuant to subsection 202(1) of the Act, the directive to “ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants….”, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the preponderance of the evidence demonstrates that the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to receiving the N5 notice of termination. The termination date on the N5 notice of termination was August 1, 2025.

The Landlord served the Tenant with an N5 notice which instructed him to vacate the rental unit by the termination date of August 1, 2025. According to subsection 134(1.1)(a), the Landlord is not entitled to rent payment past the termination date of August 1, 2025. The Tenant is therefore entitled to the per diem amount of rent that he overpaid the Landlord by paying the $25,000.00 for 11.5 months up front at the commencement of the tenancy.

The Landlord is not entitled to deduct from the amount that he owes the Tenant as a result of my finding above in paragraph #16, any amount owed for damage or any other illegal deposit amount. If the Landlord believes that he can prove negligent or wilful damage on the part of the Tenant, he can file the appropriate application with the Board in order to reclaim the amount owed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,405.23. This amount represents: • $4,357.23 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: This application is brought pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) and (b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; (b) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 49 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) or 49 (2) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that in order to be successful, the Tenants must first lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that they got a notice of termination under sections 48 or 49. Sections 48 and 49 read as follows: 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located. 49 (1) A landlord of a residential complex that contains no more than three residential units who has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by, (a) the purchaser; (b) the purchaser’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the purchaser, the purchaser’s spouse, or a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

It is undisputed the Landlord did not give the Tenants notice of termination on an approved form (N12 form). It is the Tenants position that emails received from the Landlord constitute as notice under sections 48 and 49. I do not agree.

O n September 16, 2024, the Tenants received an email from the Landlord advising that they would not be renewing the lease at the end of the term as they may be looking to sell the property or have their mother move back to Barrie. The Landlord requested the Tenants to confirm their move-out date.

T he Act provides a tenant security of tenure. Section 37(1) of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. Section 38 provides that a tenancy renews indefinitely unless it is terminated in accordance with the Act. And no landlord can unilaterally terminate a tenancy unless they have grounds to do so and follow the proper procedure which is set out in the Act.
This means that the Landlord’s email had no legal effect. The Tenants could have been free to ignore the email. If they had, the tenancy would have continued as is outlined within the Act.

In my view, the email falls short of notice under sections 48 or 49. There is no indication in the email that the Tenants are required to vacate the rental unit so that the Landlord’s mother can move in. The email also does not indicate that the Landlord has sold the property, and the purchaser intends to move in.

The Tenants testified that they received a second email from the Landlord on January 31, 2025, which reads as follows: “Hi Cathy, My mother & sister lives in bowmanville, so they want to move to Barrie so close for me, as I live in Etobicoke, as she own 50% of the property with me. Then few years later, if the market goes up, plan is to have them move close to me and sell [name].”

I find the above email to be vague and ambiguous as it does not clearly state the Tenants must move out and the reasons they must move out. This seemed to be shared with Tenant, [name] [name] (‘CC’) who requested clarification from the Landlord. There is no indication that the Landlord provided clarification as no such evidence was admitted at the hearing.
I am of the view that the Landlord’s emails suggest an intent to sell the property at some point. However, this does not constitute notice under section 49.

I am not convinced the Landlord advised the Tenants that they had to vacate by a certain date because their mother was going to move into the rental unit. I believe the Tenants acted prematurely and on assumptions. The Tenants clearly were aware of the proper forms required to terminate as evidenced from their communications with the Landlord. They could have waited for proper written notice, sought legal advice, or contacted the LTB. I find they have failed to sufficiently establish that they received notice under section 48 of the Act.
As the Tenants failed to establish they received notice under sections 48 or 49 of the Act, their application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 9, 2025.
Lawful rent is due on the first of each month in the amount of $1,000.00.
The Tenant filed the application with the Board on September 27, 2025.
The rental unit is a room in a rooming house with seven other rooms.
The Tenant alleges the Landlord did not use the last month rent deposit for the last month of the tenancy.
The Tenant filed evidence with the Board and provided copies to the Landlord.

The position of the Tenant is the Tenant found the rental unit listing on Facebook Market place. The Tenant reached out to the Landlord and inquired about renting the rental unit short term to see if it met his needs and if he could live with other tenants.
The Landlord and Tenant agreed and the Tenant occupied the rental unit from April 27, 2025 to April 29, 2025.
The Landlord drafted a tenancy agreement and both the Landlord and the Tenant signed the agreement. The tenancy agreement was to commence on May 1, 2025 on a month-to- month basis.
The Tenant informed the Landlord he changed his mind and did not wish to rent the room sometime in late April 2025.

After initially informing the Landlord he did not want to rent the room after his short stay, on May 4, 2025 the Tenant informed the Landlord he wished to rent the room and the Landlord and Tenant entered into an oral agreement with similar terms to the written tenancy agreement.
The Tenant stated he paid the Landlord a first and last month rent deposit in the amount of $2,000.00 and an additional $150.00 for a mini fridge for a total of $2,150.00.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit and paid rent for May 2025 June 1, 2025 and July 1, 2025. and the last month rent deposit.
The Tenant filed evidence with the Board to support the claim he had made the payments to the Landlord, (DOC-6655985) and (DOC-7079615) (DOC-6488906).
The Tenant informed the Landlord during a phone conversation that he wished to vacate the rental unit then sent a text on Jully 3, 2025 that he wished to vacate the rental unit.
The Tenant stated he vacated and helped the Landlord find a new tenant for the rental unit as of July 14, 2025.
The Tenant claims the Landlord owes the balance of the last month rent deposit since the Landlord had re-rented the rental unit, and the daily compensation from July 15, 2025 to July 31, 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute he offered the Tenant a two day trial in April 2025 and then agreed to rent the rental unit to the Tenant for May 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute he is still holding a last month rent deposit for July 2025.

The position of the Landlord is he offered the Tenant to split the last month rent deposit 50 / 50 and retain his portion for the inconvenience of the Tenant taking possession then requesting to terminate the tenancy without providing proper 60 day notice. Analysis

Section 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Rent deposit may be required 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (1).

Section 106(10) of the Act states: Rent deposit applied to last rent (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).

Section 88 of the Act states: New tenancy (3) Despite subsections (1) and (2), if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent that exceeds the lesser of the following amounts: 2. The amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 88 (3). [emphasis added]

Section 16 of the Act requires a landlord to mitigate losses and states: Minimize losses 16 When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. 2006, c. 17, s. 16.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Landlord did not apply the last month rent deposit to the Tenant’s last month of the tenancy.
I am satisfied that the Landlord and the Tenant ended the tenancy on an agreement and the Landlord was able to find a new Tenant to re-rent the rental unit on July 14, 2025.
In accordance with section 88(3) 2. the Landlord is not entitled to keep the balance of the last month rent deposit for July 2025 after the new tenant took possession.

Therefore, I find the Landlord owes the Tenant $525.92 calculated as follows: • $1,000.00 (lawful rent) x 12 (months) / 365 (days) = $32.87 x 16 days (July 25, 2025 to July 31, 2025) = $525.92 • $1,000.00 for the last month rent deposit the Landlord is still holding.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $573.92. $1,573.92. This amount represents: • $525.92 for the last month's rent deposit daily compensation of rent after the Landlord re-rented the rental unit from July 15, 2025 to July 31, 2025. • $1,000.00 last month rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026 June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026 June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 27, 2026 July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 15, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $1,292.72. T2 Application
The Tenant testified that on May 12, 2025, his neighbour’s son yelled at him and called him offensive names. The Tenant reported the incident to the Landlord who promised to speak with the neighbour.
On November 7, 2025, the neighbour’s drunk boyfriend screamed profanities at the Tenant. The Tenant also informed the Landlord of this incident.

On July 16, 2025, and July 30, 2025, the Tenant requested rent receipts from the Landlord, but the Landlord ignored the request until a legal clinic sent him a letter on August 26, 2025. In response, the Landlord sent an ‘INVOICE’ to the Tenant on August 28, 2025, showing both the Tenant’s and the Landlord’s names and addresses; the amount of the monthly rent, $500.00; the twelve-month period covered by the invoice, August 2024 to July 2025, and the total payments of $6,000.00. The Tenant stated that this was not a legal document.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Regarding the conduct of the neighbour , the Tenant has failed to demonstrate that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the unit and that the conduct persisted despite his complaint. The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord promised to speak with the neighbour following her son’s outburst toward the Tenant on May 12, 2025. Apart from the isolated incident involving the neighbour’s intoxicated boyfriend on November 7, 2025, the Landlord appears to have managed the situation appropriately. In this circumstance, I find that both incidents do not rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment.

Section 109 of the Act states that a landlord shall provide free of charge to a tenant or former tenant, on request, a receipt for the payment of any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent or any other amount paid to the landlord.
In addition, section 9 of the O. Reg. 516/06, provides: Receipt

A document constitutes a receipt for the purposes of section 109 of the Act if it includes, at a minimum, (a) the address of the rental unit to which the receipt applies; (b) the name of the tenants to whom the receipt applies; (c) the amount and date for each payment received for any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent, or any other amount paid to the landlord and shall specify what the payment was for; (d) the name of the landlord of the rental unit; and (e) the signature of the landlord or the landlord’s authorized agent. 9. The evidence here demonstrates that the Landlord provided a single document showing that the Tenant paid the rent for a 12-month period. Although the document does not specify the date of each individual payment, it substantially complies with section 9 of t he O’Reg. 516/06. However, going forward, the Landlord must provide the Tenant with a receipt for each rental payment at the time it is made.

Based on all the evidence , I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with the Tenant. T6 Application

Following the Landlord’s recommendation of a furnace repair company in November 2024, the Tenant contacted the company because the oil operated furnace in the rental home was dysfunctional. The company attended the residential complex on November 21, 2024, and recommended that the chimney needed to be unclogged before repairs to the furnace could commence. The company completed the work over several dates.

The Tenant provided an account statement dated September 24, 2025, from Hoover’s Home Energy Inc. indicating that he paid a total of $2,192.72 for furnace repair and chimney cleaning. The Tenant explained that although the services were performed in 2024, the statement date reflects the date on which it was printed and issued to him on request.

Section 20 (1) of the Act provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence demonstrates that at the direction of the Landlord, he hired a company to repair the furnace, and that the cleaning of the chimney was a necessary part of the service. The Tenant incurred a total cost of $1,292.72 for the repairs, which has not been reimbursed by the Landlord. As the responsibility for the maintenance of the rental unit rests on the Landlord, the Landlord is liable for the costs. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $1,292.72.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,292.72, in costs incurred for the furnace repair.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall provide monthly rent receipts to the Tenant. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: Adrian Drinkwalter is not a party to the tenancy agreement and was always only an occupant of the rental unit. Therefore, on consent of the parties, he is removed as an applicant in these proceedings.
On September 16, 2025, the LTB combined LTB-T-080177-24 (T2, filed October 4, 2024) and LTB-T-043361-25 (T2/T6, filed May 30, 2025), to be heard together. Background

The Tenant T.N.P. took occupancy of the rental unit on August 1, 2022. The monthly rent was $2,550.00. She physically moved out of the townhouse on August 31, 2024 when she and her spouse separated. At that time, the monthly rent charged was $2,650.00. LTB-T-080177-24

The tenancy was terminated on November 25, 2024 by issuance of LTB order LTB-L- 073098-24 dated November 14, 2024. As of September 2024, the Landlord knew that the Tenant was residing elsewhere, as described in this order. The evidence is that the Tenant’s former spouse A.D. lived in the unit as an unauthorized, overholding occupant until he was evicted on April 3, 2025. T6 application

As explained below, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) to repair and maintain the rental unit and/or failed to comply with health housing and maintenance standards. Kitchen sink drainage issues
The Tenant T.N.P. testified that she had issues with the kitchen sink shortly after moving in and informed the Landlord; a few days later, the Landlord used a plumbing snake to unclog the drain.
She stated that in 2023 the issue recurred, but she simply hired a plumber to resolve it.

T.N.P. next informed the Landlord on June 25, 2024 of the kitchen sink again not draining properly and reported that there was water leaking under the sink, that the faucet was falling off and that she could not use the sink. She placed a bucket directly under the sink to catch the constant drips. She provided several videos to the Landlord showing the drain issues and leaking, which she had taken on June 23, 2024.
The Landlord bought over a chemical drain cleaner for her to use, with instructions. T.N.P. testified that this did not resolve the problem.

She reported the same issue again to the Landlord on July 4, 2024 and he left another chemical drain cleaner at her door for her to use. The morning after treating the apparent clog, she took a video and sent it to the Landlord showing a partially drained sink. The videos of the drainage issues were submitted as evidence.

T.N.P. testified that on August 17, 2024, when the Landlord came by to collect the rent, she showed him that the leak was still occurring. On August 19, 2024, he used a plumbing snake without success. A few days later he asked a plumber to make repairs. After that, T.N.P. says, the drain worked but still not properly, and water continued to drip down a pipe under the sink. She maintains that the issues were never satisfactorily resolved.

The Landlord A.H.T. agreed with the facts presented by T.N.P. up to July 4, 2024. However, he says, he heard no more about the sink issue until August 2024. He testified that when he inspected the sink on August 17th, he found that T.N.P. had “removed the drain”. He immediately hired a plumber to make repairs and the problem was resolved. Mould

On August 17, 2024, T.N.P. showed the Landlord significant mould that had appeared on the cabinet housing the sink. She took a video although she could not recall whether it was in July or August 2024 but she presented it to the Landlord at the time.

Her evidence is that the Landlord brought a piece of wood on the next visit to cover up the mould. She claims that he never conducted any further investigation and that the mould was never remediated. LTB-T-080177-24 Damage to the laundry room ceiling

T.N.P. explained that the water from the sink leaked into the ceiling of the laundry room directly below. She mentioned this to the Landlord, who responded that he would come by and check it out but, she says, he never did. Upstairs Toilet

When [name] moved into the unit, she discovered that the flush lever attached to the toilet was not working properly and so the toilet would not flush properly. She testified that a few days later she informed the Landlord by text message and in person. The Landlord tried to repair the handle, and she recalls that it did work for a couple of days.
T.N.P. indicated that when she informed the Landlord after it fell again into disrepair in July 2024, he did not respond to her texts.

She explained that, at that point, she had given up on trying to get things repaired having dealt with the Landlord’s non-responsiveness; he gave her the impression that he was bothering him and so she was hesitant to make further complaints.

T.N.P. testified that in September 2022, she hired a plumber to repair the flush lever but even then, the handle would fail sporadically, requiring multiple attempts. Her evidence is that it was not working properly up to the date when she moved out. Mice infestation

Shortly after moving in, T.N.P. heard rodents running in the walls of her bedroom. She saw mice darting under the fridge. Concerned, she says she immediately told the Landlord. Her former spouse A.D. – who was residing with her at the time – took videos on his phone. The videos submitted show a dog playing with a stunned or dead mouse on the kitchen floor and another shows a mouse running under the fridge. She recalls that the Landlord promised to bring a trap, but he did not. T.N.P. asserts that the infestation remained unresolved prior to her vacating.
A.D. testified that the Landlord never came by the unit or sent anyone to investigate the rodent issue. He described the Landlord’s attitude as typically “combative”.
The Landlord A.H.T. acknowledged what he deemed to be a minor mice infestation problem. He testified that T.N.P only informed him in August 2024 about the issue.

He stated that when he initially tried to inspect the unit in September 2024 with a contractor, he was prevented from doing so because T.N.P. or A.D. refused entry but also because the Tenant’s dog was aggressive towards him. This, he said, was captured in a video recording he took on that date.

When the Tenant's Legal Representative [name] replayed the video of the entry, [name] pointed out that the dog was silent and wagging its tail. He asked A.H.T. if he believed the dog’s behaviour in the video was indicative of an aggressive animal greeting a visitor. A.H.T. maintained that he was intimidated by the pet. Analysis
Subsection 20(1) of the Act requires a landlord to repair and maintain the rental unit and the residential complex in a good state of repair. LTB-T-080177-24

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance and repair obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the issue reasonably in the circumstances. Kitchen sink drainage issues

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the kitchen sink and faucet were in disrepair, that she informed the Landlord on multiple occasions about it and that the measures the Landlord took did not resolve the drainage issue. I believe the Tenant when she says that she continued to have issues with the drain up to the time she vacated the unit. This included a persistent water leak from the faucet down through the pipes and into the ceiling below. I am satisfied that, once the Tenant discovered the leak, she placed a bucket under the dripping water, manually emptying it as it became full.
The Landlord did not provide evidence of any professional inspection or of any effective plumbing repair.

I find that asking the Tenant to address a persistent plumbing problem herself using over-the-counter products does not satisfy the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. Responsibility for diagnosing and repairing underlying plumbing issues rests with the Landlord.
The evidence supports a finding that the drainage issue was ongoing for a significant period, was not adequately repaired, and contributed to water damage and mould. Mould
The photos the Tenant testified about as regards the existence of toxic mold were persuasive.

The unchallenged evidence is that it was never properly dealt with. Although he had the opportunity, the Landlord did not provide evidence of any professional inspection or remediation of the mould. What the Landlord did do was to hide the affected area with a board. The “repair” was consistent with a temporary or cosmetic fix.

It is well established that the presence of toxic mould is a serious maintenance and repair issue that requires investigation and remediation. Simply covering the affected area does not address the underlying problem.
I find that the Landlord failed to adequately investigate the source of the mould and to ensure the mould was eradicated. Ceiling disrepair
The Tenant testified that the leak also caused damage to the ceiling below, which was never repaired. The Landlord did not provide any evidence that this damage was addressed.
Given my findings regarding the unresolved leak, it is reasonable to conclude that resulting damage to the ceiling would require repair. LTB-T-080177-24
I find that the Landlord failed to repair water damage arising from a known plumbing issue, in breach of his obligations under section 20 of the Act. [name]
The Tenant testified that there was a mouse infestation in the unit and that the Landlord stated he would provide traps but failed to do so.
The Landlord did not provide evidence of any effective pest control measures being implemented.
Pest infestations fall squarely within a landlord’s maintenance obligations. A failure to take reasonable steps to address such conditions constitutes a breach of the Act.
I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence and find that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps in a timely manner to effectively resolve the rodent infestation. Prevention from making repairs
The Landlord submitted that he was unable to complete repairs on one occasion because the Tenant’s dog behaved aggressively. He provided a video in support of this position.

The Tenant’s representative pointed out that, in the recording, the dog appeared calm, wagged its tail, and did not bark or display aggressive behaviour. When asked about this, the Landlord stated that he nonetheless felt intimidated.
I find that the video evidence does not support the Landlord’s characterization of the dog as aggressive. The behaviour shown is consistent with a friendly interaction.

While I accept that a landlord may have subjective concerns about safety, those concerns must be objectively reasonable to justify a failure to carry out maintenance obligations. In this case, I do not find that the Landlord’s concerns met that standard or that they prevented him from access to the unit to complete necessary repairs. There is no evidence that the Landlord requested that the dog be secured during a scheduled repair time or asked the Tenant to make other arrangements for the dog.
I therefore do not accept that the Tenant’s dog was a valid reason for the Landlord’s failure to carry out necessary repairs. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant T.N.P. proved the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

On September 4, 2024, the Landlord’s former paralegal R.B. emailed T.N.P. to say: “I have been HIRED by your Landlord to now deal with this tenancy. YOU said you would leave, then you extended it, then you said you would leave August 31, 2024. Your landlord gave you an N111 to sign. … I left you a voice mail message. Please let’s talk. If you don’t want to talk, we will take this to the Landlord and Tenant Board and ask for immediate eviction as we have PROOF that you wrote in a text that you will leave. The Judge will give us an immediate 1 N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy (the ‘N11’). LTB-T-080177-24 eviction. I will give you until [September 5, 2024] to call… If not we go to a Judge to evict you…”.
On September 5, 2024, R.B. emailed T.N.P.: “Why are you ignoring me I guess you don’t want a deal We now go to court for immediate eviction If you can’t deal with it hire a paralegal”.

Without notice to T.N.P., on September 9, 2024 the Landlord filed an L3 application with the Board, for an ex parte eviction order. The application was based on an earlier text message that T.N.P. sent to the Landlord informing him that she would be moving out.
On September 12, 2024, the Board directed the L3 application to a hearing, which was subsequently scheduled for November 4, 2024.

T.N.P. testified that on the same day, the Landlord called her by phone to say that he knew A.D. had a criminal court date on September 17, 2024. Her evidence is that he told her that if she did not sign an N11 he would “get her involved” in that criminal charge (which related to an incident that occurred in the residential complex).

She understood this to mean that the Landlord would report to the police that she was also involved in the alleged criminal activity and “have her charged”. She stated that this was distressing because she had not engaged in any criminal conduct. 54. [name] was applying for Permanent Resident status; she said the Landlord also threatened to report her to immigration officials if she did not sign the N11. She contends that during the same call the Landlord acted in a blatantly threatening way: he told her that he knew where she worked and lived; he knew all her friends and family, and he would ‘defame’ her by disclosing personal information to them that would disparage her character. 55. There is no dispute that on or about September 15, 2024, the Landlord showed up unannounced at T.N.P.’s workplace. She testified that he “tried to make a scene” by demanding to talk with her in her office or outside and tried to give her an N11 form to sign. 56. There is no disagreement that [name] called the police. The police did not attend but, according to T.N.P., an officer called her by phone to inform her that they had cautioned the Landlord to not attend her workplace again. 57. She says she then discovered that the Landlord had indiscriminately posted her personal information to his Facebook account on a Vietnamese Community Group they belonged to. 58. T.N.P. also produced a voice message from R.B. left on the Tenant’s phone on September 19, 2024, at 8:09 p.m., R.B. states: “You have to talk to me. … Is [A.D.] really your husband?... Who is [A.D.]? … Do you know this is really bad and this is gonna be all over your record and all over the internet and your name will be completely run through the mud so get moving and phone me”. 59. On September 20, 2024, she received a text message from R.B., in which R.B. states, “See you in court.” On Saturday, September 21, 2024, R.B. again texted her:” Please hire a paralegal or this is going to be very stressful”. 60. The Landlord denies that his actions amounted to interference, harassment or coercion. LTB-T-080177-24 Analysis 61. I accept that on September 12, 2024, the Landlord telephoned the Tenant and demanded that she sign the N11 and that during that conversation, the Landlord threatened to report the Tenant to police for criminal activity. The Landlord led no evidence to support an allegation of criminal conduct. I find that this threat was baseless and was made for the purpose of pressuring the Tenant to comply with his demand to sign the N11. 62. The threat to contact immigration authorities, regardless of the Tenant’s actual status, was inherently intimidating and designed to exploit a perceived vulnerability. The Landlord’s statement that he knew where the Tenant lived was a clear message of intimidation, which would reasonably create ongoing discomfort and even fear. Posting the Tenant’s personal information on a community Facebook group was highly inappropriate. 63. This constitutes harassment and coercion within the meaning of section 23 of the Act. 64. In my view, attending at the Tenant’s workplace was a serious and unreasonable intrusion. The workplace is not an appropriate venue for the resolution of landlord-tenant disputes. 65. The Tenant relies on communications from the paralegal R.B. as further evidence of harassment and coercion. I find that those communications regarding the N11 misrepresented the legal process and likely outcomes; significantly pressured the Tenant to respond; and explicitly and implicitly threatened adverse outcomes. Particularly concerning are her assertions that “this is gonna be all over your record and all over the internet and your name will be completely run through the mud.” 66. An N11 Agreement must be voluntary. Efforts to secure such an agreement through intimidation or threats are contrary to the Act. 67. Therefore, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that he and his agent R.B. harassed, coerced and threatened the Tenant. Remedies 68. The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $7,552.00 and general compensation of $10,000.00 for each of the T2 and T6 applications. 69. A tenant’s entitlement to a remedy for a breach of the Act is directly tied to the date the tenant filed the application. The Board may only grant remedies for conduct that occurred within the prior 12 months; it cannot grant remedies for earlier incidents that fall outside the limitation period, although the facts may be considered as context. If it is an ongoing breach, remedies are limited to the conduct occurring within the 12 months prior to filing. 70. Some of the Tenant’s T6 claims fall outside the one-year limitation period. Therefore, the date for which the Board can grant remedies is limited to the period between May 30, 2024 and May 30, 2025. Rent abatement 71. A rent abatement is generally intended to compensate a tenant for loss of the use or enjoyment of the rental unit during the tenancy and occupancy of the rental unit. This remedy is usually associated with a tenant’s ability to make use of the unit. LTB-T-080177-24 72. The Tenant’s evidence is that she no longer physically occupied the unit after August 31, 2024 and, as such, did not benefit from its use after that date. Accordingly, any request in the T6 for an abatement after August 31, 2024 must reasonably be denied. 73. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $4,770.00 for the 3-month period beginning June 1, 2024 and ending on August 31, 2024, reflecting the serious impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit, as follows: (1) $1,987.50 for the rodent infestation, representing a 25% abatement; (2) $2,782.50 for the sink, faucet, mould issues and ceiling disrepair, representing a 35% abatement. 74. No remedy will be considered for the toilet’s flush lever issues. I am not satisfied that a remedy is sufficiently substantiated, as no documentary evidence was led to support this claim, though such evidence ought to have been capable of being presented. General compensation 75. The Tenant asks for general damages to compensate her for the trauma, expressed as distress and anxiety, that resulted from the Landlord’s unlawful conduct. Specifically, the Tenant explained that the Landlord’s non-responsiveness in relation to reported disrepair, his ineffective repairs, and his persistent harassment caused her considerable frustration. 76. The Tenant provided relatively few details of distress relating to the sink and water leak which would support compensation over and above the rent abatement awarded. However, there is no doubt that living with mould and mice elevated the level of the Tenant’s concern. The Landlord’s failure to prioritize those issues exposed the Tenant to potentially serious health problems. 77. The following factors also weigh in favour of a considerable award of compensation. The Landlord made baseless threats of police involvement, attended at the Tenant’s workplace (and during an ongoing conflict between them), threatened to interfere with her immigration status by reporting false information, and disclosed the Tenant’s personal information within her community which the Tenant perceived as maligning her character. 78. The Landlord’s agent R.B.’s improper threats of eviction and warnings to the Tenant that she would take certain actions to disgrace the Tenant publicly, including communicating directly to the Tenant’s social circle merit increased compensatory damages. 79. I have balanced this with the fact that the conduct relating to the N11 occurred over a relatively defined period, primarily in September 2024. However, the frequency and intensity of the pressure the Tenant was subjected to in that timeframe was remarkable and undoubtedly resulted in genuine emotional upset that affected her daily. 80. Having regard to all the circumstances, the Landlord shall pay general compensation to the Tenant in the amount of $7,500.00. Administrative fine 81. The Tenant requests that the Board impose an administrative fine to reflect the seriousness of the misconduct and to deter similar behaviour. 82. The Board generally reserves administrative fines for cases involving: LTB-T-080177-24 • serious or egregious misconduct; • repeated or escalating behaviour; • bad faith conduct; • deliberate disregard of the Act; and • conduct that demonstrates or establishes an abuse of Board processes. 83. The Board may consider whether the conduct reflects an intentional effort to circumvent the protections of the Act, rather than being an isolated or inadvertent breach. 84. In my view, the Landlord’s behaviour represents a deliberate pattern of conduct that was egregious in nature and scope; it reveals a blatant disregard for his obligations under the Act, of the Tenant’s statutory rights and for the LTB in general. The Landlord directed his paralegal to aggressively compel the Tenant to comply with his demands and a landlord is responsible for the conduct of their agent(s). 85. Overall, the Landlord’s ill-considered actions and statements were serious, targeted, repeated and inexcusable. His non-action in response to disrepair was unacceptable. 86. I find that, in this case, an administrative fine of $10,000.00 is appropriate. 87. Of note, had the Board been provided with proof that the Landlord actually carried out these threats (for example, reporting the Tenant to the police and to immigration authorities) the fine would be substantially higher.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,318.00. This amount represents: • $4,770.00 for a rent abatement. • $7,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $10,000.00 by July 10, 2026.* June 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlords did not properly address septic fumes and a toilet/sewage backup into the bathtub.
Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $1,800.00.
I find that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords ' obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.

It was the uncontested evidenc e of the Tenant that when the Landlords were advised of concerns about septic fumes in the toilet room of the rental unit, instead of investigating and correcting the source of the problem they vented the fumes outside and screwed the bathroom door shut. Similarly, when the toilet backed up sewage into the bathtub, the Landlord blocked access to the toilet section of the room instead of fixing the problem.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the Landlords's maintenance obligations, including whether the Landlords responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a Landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant provided no evidence regarding no tifying the Landlord of the many problems referenced in the application, or that they were bothered by them. Instead they assert the problems were obvious and the Landlords must have been aware. There was no evidence regarding the frequency of the Landlords’ attendance at the residential complex to support a finding that they would have been present to be aware of the claimed issues. The only issues which I am able to infer the Landlords were aware of are the three to which some response was noted: septic fumes, toilet backup into bathtub, and bedbugs. Remedies

The septic fumes and plumbing issues had a significant impact on the Tenant’s use of the enjoyment. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find a rent abatement of 30% to be reasonable. The sewage backup into the bathtub occurred in February 2024. The timeline of the septic fumes is imprecise, however I am satisfied they were a problem as of February 2024 when the backup occurred. This represents an 8 month rent abatement period. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,800.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. ($750.00 x 8 months x 30%)

The evidence relating to the bedbugs was t hat the Landlord attended after receiving the Tenant’s complaint and attempted to treat the problem themselves. The Tenant thinks bedbugs cannot be successfully treated without specific knowledge or experience but provided no testimony or other evidence to confirm the level of success or failure of the treatments by the Landlord.

The Tenant did not prove the costs to repl ace property that was damaged or disposed of. In particular, the Tenant did not explain why they had to move to a smaller unit which could not accommodate his belongings, or why, if that was the case, the belongings couldn’t be either sold or placed in storage to mitigate the loss. While the Tenant disposed of a bed because they felt bedbugs were not properly treated, this was not supported by the evidence.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by June 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
