issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the parties requested that I adjourn only the T6 portion of the Application, as it was agreed that the front door must be replaced and the Landlord is in the process of facilitating this replacement. Accordingly, the parties requested that only the T6 portion be adjourned so that the Landlord can permitted time to replace the door and the Tenant can withdraw the T6 portion of the application if the door replacement is completed to their satisfaction.

When I canvassed the parties with respect to how they foresaw such a split adjournment working from a procedural standpoint the Tenant's Legal Representative revised his position to request an adjournment of the entire matter to allow him additional time to secure a witness.

I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. Interpretation Guideline 1 states: Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. The Member may consider the conduct of the party opposing the adjournment. For example, if the party opposing the request has shown bad faith or refused to provide information about their case to the other party which would allow them to prepare quickly for the hearing, this may affect the Member’s decision.

While this guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. I am satisfied that the Tenant’s have had adequate time to prepare for this proceeding and perfect their case, including having had the benefit of an adjudicative case conference.

I am also satisfied that the Tenant had had an adequate amount of time to summons any witnesses they intend to rely on. Therefore, I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. I also decline to split the Application and adjourn only the T6 portion of the Application, as I am not satisfied that this is an expeditious use of the Board’s time. The Request to Amend
At the hearing the Tenant requested an amendment to the Application. The Tenant filed two requests to amend on January 16, 2025, and September 26, 2025. However, neither was served on the Landlord.

The Request to amend filed on January 16, 2025, consists of 8 typed pages detailing the same issues raised on the original Application, and also raises new issues. The Request to amend filed on September 26, 2025, increases the abatement sought from $150.00 to $15,000.00.

In support of the request to amend the Tenant's Legal Representative referred me to the judicial principals of self represented litigants and the Tenants had been unrepresented at the time the request to amend was filed.

I agree that these principles provide useful guidance with respect to unrepresented litigants and recognise that the Tenant’s were unrepresented at the time the requests to amend were filed. However, I also note that the Tenant’s are now represented, and I would expect that the Tenant's Legal Representative would perform reasonable due diligence upon taking carriage of the file, including by ensuring that any request to amend had been served on the Landlord in accordance with the Board’s rules of procedure.

In this case, while it appears that the Landlord ultimately became aware of the September 26, 2025, request to amend, as this was identified as an issue at the Adjudicative Case Conference held on October 2, 2025. It does not appear the Landlord became aware of the January 16, 2025, request to amend which was simply filed to the Board as “submissions”

Ultimately, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to consider the increased quantum sought in the Tenant’s September 26, 2025 request to amend, while this increases the quantum sought significantly, the Landlord has clearly been aware of this since the Adjudicative Case Conference held on October 2, 2025 and as it does not add additional issues I am satisfied that there is minimal prejudice to the Landlord in this amendment.

However, I am not prepared to grant the request to amend filed on January 16, 2025. This request to amend was not filed in accordance with the Board’s rules, and while I accept that the Tenant’s were unrepresented at the time, I would expect the Tenant's Legal Representative to take reasonable steps, upon becoming retained to ensure that it had been served on the Landlord in accordance with the Boards rules. Additionally, it is clear that the September 26, 2025 request to amend was canvassed at the Adjudicative Case Conference, which would have also presented an opportunity for the Tenant to raise the January 16, 2025 request to amend. Finally, I note that this request to amend raise new issues, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s were ever made aware of it, therefore, I find it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to expect them to speak to these new issues on the day of the hearing, without adequate notice. The T2

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,548.00 and must complete the replacement of the unit door by May 31, 2026.
The Tenant [name] [name] testified at the hearing. She testified that the Tenant’s moved into the rental unit in 2016 and still reside there.

She testified that the door to the unit was warped and was letting in rainwater, ice, and drafts. She speculated that it was in this condition prior to the Tenant’s moving in because there was nothing around the framing, allowing her to see light coming through. She reported the door to the Landlord in November 2016 and sent an email about the door on December 16, 2016.

She testified that the Landlord made multiple attempts to repair the door, but the condition remained the same, she testified that the Landlord drilled holes in the framing, added two stripes of mohair, replaced and added new sweepers to the door, added leather stripping, added a threshold piece and did caulking work. However, none of these resolved the issues and there is still rainwear entering the unit, a draft, and ice buildup.
The Tenant relied on several videos taken in the summer of 2023, January 2024, November 2024, and December 2024, depicting rainwater entering and snow and ice buildup around the door within the unit.

The Tenant also testified that she had someone from [name] and Doors attend the rental unit and wrote a letter setting out the necessary repairs to the door. The letter is dated December 12, 2024, and indicates that they are not able to fix or replace the door as it is warped at the top and requires replacement including the frame down to the jamb extension. It indicates that weatherstripping will not help and indicates that the reason the Tenant is getting frost inside the room is because cold air is getting in and mixing with the warm moist air inside.

It was agreed by the parties that there have been 3-4 property standard orders issued with respect to the door including the most recent issued on [name] 4, 2026 which orders the Landlord to repair/replace the door for the rental unit to allow it to make proper contact with weather stripping and repair/replace weatherstripping to ensure airtight seal to prevent cold air from entering the rental unit. The Landlord is ordered r complete this work no later than Februray 20, 2026.
As of the date of the hearing the work had not yet been completed.
The Tenant testified that she continued to follow up with the Landlord throughout the tenancy to request an appropriate repair of the door. The Lockbox

The Tenant testified that her relationship with the Landlord was initially good, however the Landlord began to blame her for the issue with the door including claiming that it was caused by excessive clutter and humidity in the rental unit and exacerbated by the Tenant’s daily activities such as showering or doing dishes and using a dishwasher. The Tenant attributed this shift in behaviour to the Landlord becoming aware that the door was no longer under warranty and there would be cost associated with its replacement in 2017.

The Tenant also described an entry into the rental unit by the Landlord on January 15, 2024, where she blamed the Tenant for ventilation issues in the rental unit and attributed it to humidity in the Tenant’s apartment and indicated that she could vacate of she was not happy.

She testified that in 2023 the Landlord installed a lockbox on the humistat in the rental unit which prevented the Tenant from accessing or adjusting it. The Tenant testified that this caused the fans in the rental unit to run excessively, often 24 hours at a time because they were connected to the humistat controls. The Tenant testified that the content running of the fans interferes with her, and relied on a doctors note from a doctor [name].

She testified that when the Landlord installed the lockbox they had entered under the pretext of performing work on the range hood, and had not indicated they would be installing the lockbox, the Tenant testified that she allowed the installation because she did not understand her rights at the time.
The Tenant also testified that her unit is the only one in the complex with a lockbox installed on the humistat controls. The Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s Agent described the complex as a heritage building converted into 27 affordable units and rebuilt from scratch in 2010. She described it as [name] certified. She testified that it was built with ventilation because the certification required humistats connected to the range hoods and fans in the bathroom to prevent mold in the units.

She testified that she pointed out to the Tenant things that could cause moisture in the unit under the advice of her who had informed her that the door had no issues and it must be something inside the unit that causing condensation.

She testified that HVAC contractors attended the rental unit with a special device to measure humidity and noticed that the humidistat was off and speculated that the Tenant’s had turned it off to save money.

She testified that she also became aware that the Tenant had a dishwasher in the unit, and the building was not designed for dishwashers, and indicated that this could also be causing excess humidity within the unit.

She testified that she was informed that the only solution was to set the humistat between 30% and 50% and cover it so that the Tenant could not access it. She testified that she had been informed by contractors that the humistat had been turned off and the only solution was to install a lockbox. The agent noted that this unit is the only one with high humidity in the complex.

The Landlord relied on a printout of the invoices paid for the rental unit since 2016. This list indicates that the Landlord had a repair performed on the door on December 21, 2021, by a contractor who inspected and performed a temporary repair with caulking as they could not find anything else to do that day.
On January 24, 2023 Park Group again tested the humidity in the rental unit in response to a complaint about condensation around the frame and discovered that the humidity in the unit was very high.
On March 15, 2023 [name] attended the rental unit and installed new weatherstripping at the bottom of the door and installed new silicon on existing weatherstripping.

On September 2, 2023 Park Group Inc attended to check the air quality inside as condensation was reported by the Tenant, they also installed the humistat covers to prevent the Tenant from adjusting the humistat.
The Landlord also testified that on March 24, 2023 Park Group attended to check the humidity.
On October 20, 2023 Barton glass installed a new aluminum threshold and weatherstripping extrusion on the door.

On November 20, 2024 the entire door was stripped again top to bottom and another threshold was installed. She testified that she was there that day taking pictures and everything looked good. The Landlord relied on an invoice form this work indicating that new door weather seal and sills, and new weatherstrip and new mohair had been installed.

She testified the Landlord has now decided to replace the door completely to see of that causes the high humidity in the unit. She testified that she is not dealing with getting the new door but believes that the Landlord has spoken to the city of [name] and has ordered parts, and have completed some measurements for the door but need to perform additional measurements and send them to the manufacturer.
She testified that because of the heritage nature of the building the door must match all of the others within the complex which delays the replacement of the door,

She testified that the Landlord received a third property standards order from the city on January 20, 2025. This is a property standards order which directs the Landlord to repair/replace weatherstipping on the door. She testified that after receiving this order she contacted [name] who said there was no more they could do. She testified that she provided this information to the city who” kind of got over that letter” and changed the Landlord. She testified that she was not aware until the end of the year that the order had been cancelled and the money returned,
In support of this she relied on an email from [name] C.P.S.O from November 24, 225 indicating that the file had been closed.

The Landlord’s Agent also relied on a letter from Barton Glass dated January 31, 2025. The letter indicates that [name] has performed 3 repairs on the door describes the work performed on the door and indicates that nothing further can be done that would help the performance, air, or water seal.

The Agent also relied on photographs taken on November 24, 2024, depicting the repairs performed and testified that they depict that there is no light coming in from outside, that would indicate a draft.
She also testified that in between contractors attending the Landlord attende the add insulation to the door.

She also relied on an email from January 15, 2024 from [name] at Barton Glas expressing that there is a humidity issue within the rental unit which causes the window and door to condensate and freeze and indicates that they have sealed the door numerous times and this is not the issue. The email also includes a link to an apartment therapy website which indicates that dishwashers, washing machines and cooking can cause humidity within a renal unit.

The Agent also relied on an invoice from Park Group from January 17, 2024 after the lockbox was installed, which indicates that they tested the humidity and found 56% humidity upstairs and 52% downstairs. The incisive indicates that last year they attended and installed the lockbox and within two weeks humidity dropped to 35%. It indicates that nothing else can be done.

The Landlord also relied on a photograph from a window at the back of the unit which she testified is blocked by a dishware and has condensation on the bottom. She testified that this is preventing ventilation within the unit.

She testified that she has nothing personal with the Tenant. She testified that at one point she got frustrated because she understands her point of view but does not know how much more she can do. She also expressed that she was sorry if she had upset the Tenant. Analysis

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has both substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act.

With respect to substantial interference, it is undisputed that the Landlord installed a lockbox on the humistat controls on or about September 2, 2023. While the Landlord alleges that this was recommended by their contractors to control humidity in the rental unit, I accept that Tenant’s testimony that this installation was performed without the Tenant’s prior knowledge or consent, after the service of a notice of entry to preform work on the range hood. I also accept that the rental unit is the only unit with a lockbox over the humistat controls.

Further, I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony that this interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit as it caused the fans in the unto to run continuously, I also accept that being singled out by the Landlord for installation of the lockbox, and the insinuation that the condensation problems were caused by the Tenant’s own behaviour could reasonably be expected to interfere with the Tenant’s enjoyment.

While the Landlord suggest that the humidity and condensation were caused by the Tenant’s own actions, I am not satisfied this is the case. Most of the actions described by the Landlord as causing humidity and condensation, for example, washing dishes, and cooking, are simply actives of daily living performed in any rental unit. While I accept that the Tenant’s may have been using an unauthorised dishwasher, I find that the appropriate solution to this would be to request it be removed, or issue an N5, not to remove the Tenant’s access to the humistat. Additionally, I note that it appears that even after the installation of the lockbox humidity levels tested as high. This suggest to me that the humidity levels and condensation are connected to the problems with the door rather than the Tenant’s own activities.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicates that as the lockbox was installed on September 2, 2023, it is outside the one-year limitation period established by the Act, and the issue must be dismissed. However, I do not agree with this interpretation. While the Act does establish a one-year limitation period, where the breach is not a single event but is ongoing or recurring, such as the withdrawal of a vital service, the breach occurs over a period of time and the one-year limitation period runs from the date that the vital service is restored to the tenant.

I am satisfied that it is appropriate to consider this breach to be ongoing, as access to the lockbox has not been restored to the Tenant and continues to have an impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit. Therefore, I am not satisfied that this claim is outside the one-year limitation period.

I also accept that the door created ongoing issues with respect to air, water, ice, and condensation forming around it and entering the rental unit. While the Landlord suggests that their response was reasonable, I do not agree. I accept that the Landlord made several attempts to repair the door and were informed by their contractors that nothing more could be done. However, I also note that there were several property standards orders issued with respect to the door including one that is currently outstanding, this suggest that while the Landlord made efforts to mitigate the issue, they were ultimately unsuccessful. I also note that the Tenant privately engaged their own contractor who determined that the door required a complete replacement, a conclusion that the Landlord has apparently come to accept. However, I do not find it reasonable that it took the Landlord several years, and several property standards orders to reach this conclusion.

On balance, I find this is likely because the Landlord has employed cost effective stop gap measures, rather than address the issue by replacing the door as they have been ordered to do in the most recent property standards order, and I am not satisfied that such a response is reasonable.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Door Replacement

With respect to the T6 the Landlord indicated that they would not object to an order directing them to replace the door. The Landlord's Legal Representative suggested that it would be appropriate to order the Landlord to comply with the property standards order issued on January 28, 2026, by May 31, 2026.

While the parties were initially in agreement that I should order the Landlord to replace the door during their closing submissions the Tenant's Legal Representative suggested that I should defer jurisdictionally to the city and not issue an order for the Landlord to replace the door, as the city has already indicated that the Landlord should repair the door by Februray 20, 2026 and the city has their own enforcement mechanism.

I am not satisfied that the outstanding property standards order prevents the Board from issuing an order for the Landlord to replace the door and note that the Board will frequently order the Landlord to perform repairs when an outstanding property standards order exists.

I recognise that the complex has a heritage designation, and that this makes replacement of the door more complex as it must complex with certain appearance standards. However, I also recognise that the door has been an ongoing issue for years and that it is appropriate to strike a balance when setting a deadline for this replacement. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to replace the door by May 31, 2026. Remedies

I accept that an abatement is appropriate. Typically, an abatement is awarded in recognition that a Tenant is paying the full rent for a unit, and is not receiving full use or enjoyment of that unit. The Tenant in this case seeks an abatement of $15,000.00. While I am satisfied that an abatement is appropriate, I do not agree with the quantum sought.

The Tenant has provided a doctor’s letter from [name] expressing that that Tenant [name] has been under his care and that ongoing housing reacted stressor are affecting sleep, concertation and activities of daily living.

Based on this letter, and the Tenant’s testimony I accept that the lockbox and ongoing issues with condensation, drafts, water and ice have impacted her enjoyment of the rental unit. However, I note that the intrusions of water and ice appear to be intermittent and seasonally dependant rather than a constant, and while the doctors note is supportive it is also somewhat vague, simply mentioning ongoing stressors.

Ultimately, in recognition of the interference the Tenant has experienced I find that a flat abatement of $3,500.00 is appropriate, and recognisees the impact of the issues raised while recognising that the many of the impacts from the door are seasonal or intermittent.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $3,500.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also sought a fine. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that a fine is appropriate. While these steps were unsuccessful, the Landlord did make significant efforts to repair the door and address the issues raised by the Tenant, and while I accept that the Landlord has interfered with the Tenant by installing the lockbox, I accept that was done on the advice of the Landlord’s contractors, and, while inappropriate, was not intended to be a malicious action. Therefore, I am not satisfied that a fine is appropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,548.00. This amount represents: • $3,500.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent each month from July 2026 to January 2027, and $48.00 from the rent for February 2027.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall replace the door to the rental unit by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not do the replacement(s) by May 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $150.00 from the rent owing for the month(s) beginning June 1, 2026 until the replacement is complete. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.

As a preliminary issue, I found that the portions of the T2 application alleging substantial interference and harassment are defective as they contain no reasonable particulars of specific incidents or conduct. Those portions of the application are therefore dismissed without the need for further analysis.
The remaining allegation under the T2 application is that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with 72 hours to retrieve their belongings following the Sheriff’s eviction on October 13, 2023.

The evidence establishes that the Sheriff enforced the eviction on October 13, 2023, at approximately 10:00 a.m. [name] contacted the Landlord later that same day and was provided access to the unit. The Tenant acknowledged that they were provided access again on October 15, 2023, and remained in the unit for approximately 11 hours, until after 1:00 a.m.

While the Tenant alleged they were limited to insufficient access time, the Tenant did not provide any documentary or corroborating evidence to support the assertion that access was restricted to less than 72 hours overall. In particular, the Tenant referenced a recording but did not disclose or produce it at the hearing. The Tenant also did not provide any detailed inventory of belongings allegedly left behind.

In my view, the Tenant’s evidence regarding whether the Landlord provided 72 hours of access to retrieve their belongings was inconsistent and unreliable. Their testimony shifted repeatedly about when they contacted the Landlord, how much time was offered, and the number of opportunities they were permitted to attend.

The Tenant initially claimed they were told they would have only four hours on October 13, 2023, but then conceded that the Landlord offered eight hours on October 14 and ultimately allowed them to attend for approximately eleven hours on October 15, remaining in the unit until after 1:00 a.m. Despite stating that the Landlord refused them access on the 15th, they later confirmed they attended for an extended period that day. The Tenant also asserted they were limited to a single attendance but provided no corroborating evidence, and their own answers demonstrated multiple opportunities to retrieve their possessions. These internal contradictions, coupled with the absence of the alleged recording and any list of missing items, undermine the reliability of their account and do not demonstrate that the Landlord failed to provide the required 72‑hour access.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was provided with meaningful access to retrieve their belongings over multiple days following the eviction. The Tenant’s evidence does not establish that the Landlord denied access in a manner that breached the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the T2 application is dismissed. The Tenant’s T1 application - last month’s rent deposit

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 106 of the Act requires a landlord to apply the rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. Retaining the deposit in these circumstances is not permitted.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,402.94 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $51.31 is owing to the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,454.25. This amount represents: • $1,402.94 for the last month's rent deposit. • $51.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6 July 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6 July 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7 July 6 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed two requests to amend her application. The first was filed on May 27, 2025; the second was filed with the Board on March 16, 2026. The second amended application was served on the Landlord’s Representative on March 31, 2026. The Tenant was not initially represented. However, after obtaining representation, her Representative filed the second request to amend an application in March 2026.

The amended version added some remedies and removed others. For example, the Tenant no longer requested rent differential or an order terminating the tenancy but added the remedy of general compensation.

The Landlord did not offer any objections at the April 15, 2026, hearing but sought to clarify that this latest version superseded any prior applications or amendments. The Tenant’s Representative confirmed the March 16, 2026, amended version was the final iteration.

The Landlord was served with the amended application just over two weeks before the hearing, and while some remedies were added, some were also removed. The amendments largely sought to clarify the pleadings. Although remedies were added, I am not of the view that this would have prejudiced the Landlord because the same hearing preparation would have been necessary regardless of the requested remedies. When I consider the reasons for the amendments, I am satisfied that the amendments are appropriate and made in good faith, did not prejudice any party, and are consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. Tenant’s T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $4,200.00.

The Tenant says the problems began in December 2018. The Landlord asked for an illegal rent increase and said if the Tenant refused to pay this, she would put the unit up for sale. This was followed up with multiple messages from various agents of the Landlord, or the Landlord herself, asking the Tenant to help the Landlord pay the mortgage on the property. At one point, the Landlord withheld keys necessary for storage. The Tenant called the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit and was finally given the keys after they became involved. The Tenant also states that in 2020, the Landlord accused her of not paying her rent on time although she had provided the Landlord with post-dated cheques. In the summer of 2022, the Landlord refused to conduct repairs at the rental unit. The Tenant called bylaw officers, and only once bylaw became involved did the Landlord do the necessary repairs.

The allegations in this application have to do with the Landlord and the Landlord’s daughter (‘Nazanin’), coercing the Tenant to leave the rental unit. In September and October of 2023, the Tenant says the Landlord and Nazanin calling, e-mailing, and texting the Tenant relentlessly saying that the Nazanin wanted to move into the rental unit. The Tenant was told that the Landlord had “assigned” the property to Nazanin, and Nazanin now wanted to move into the rental unit. The Tenant’s testimony was that the Landlord also threatened to sue her if she did not leave, gave her less than the 60 days notice period, and tried to apply pressure to the Tenant to get her to leave. Eventually the Tenant was given an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of December 14, 2023.

Submitted into evidence were records the Tenant made of the calls and messages, and audio recordings from the Landlord and/or Landlord’s daughter. In total, between September 18, 2023, and October 13, 2023, the Landlord or her daughter contacted the Tenant by phone eleven times, five text messages, two e-mails and left five voice mails (Doc-4534225, Ex.1, pg 2). The Tenant ignored the calls. Nazanin would then call from blocked numbers or other numbers to try to engage her in the telephone calls.

By way of example, on September 14, 2023, Nazanin writes to the Tenant that the rental unit is not hers, and that it is her parent’s property and now hers (referring to Nazanin) and tells the Tenant she is unprofessional (Ex.1, pg 9) and that she did not want to involve the “legal” process (Ex. 1, pg 6). A voice message sent the same day by Nazanin says that her mother will “call the police.” On September 17, 2023, the Landlord left a voicemail which included a statement: “I know you believe in God, this is not good what you do.” A further message from Nazanin, sent on October 12, 2023, says that the Tenant can be evicted without notice and that they will not be paying the Tenant “anything” saying “I will sue you” (Ex. 1, pg 12). On October 14, 2023, the Landlord sent her an N12, with a termination date of December 14, 2023, (Ex. 1 pg 18, 19).

The Tenant says that this had a significant impact on her. She had a lot of anxiety about the interactions with the Landlord and Nazanin. She felt powerless and suffered from anxiety and depression and had other medical issues. It was difficult for her to concentrate and this impacted her work. She was taking care of a terminally ill parent during this, so the effect of these calls and threats compounded the stress she was already under. The Tenant said she did not feel safe, the interactions left her under heightened anxiety, and her routines were affected. She was not provided with the compensation under s.48.1 and was forced to bring a T1 application to get those funds.

In cross-examination, the Tenant admits she did not call back the Landlord or Nazanin, stating if they wanted the Tenant to vacate, then they should use the appropriate Board form rather than repeatedly call or message her.

In addition, the Tenant argues the Landlord substantially interfered because the Landlord did not attend the L2 hearing scheduled on June 4, 2024, pursuant to the N12 notice of termination. In her view, this was a waste of her time and shows the Landlord’s general lack of consideration. On November 13, 2023, the Tenant gave the Landlord an N9 notice terminating the tenancy effective December 1, 2023 (Ex. 1, pgs 21-23).

The Landlord does not deny that Nazanin contacted the Tenant but does deny that she was in any way inappropriate in her communications with the Tenant. Rather, she seemed to feel that the Tenant was to blame because the Tenant did not move out at the end of in February 2020, even though she had apparently “promised” the Landlord she would. Further, the Tenant did not respond to her messages, necessitating additional calls. Analysis

Section 22 of the Act, states: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

Section 23 of the Act, says: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.” 17. The term “harassment” is not defined in the Act, but in common with numerous other Board decisions, I accept the definition in subsection 10(1) of the Ontario Human Rights Code: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” 18. Although the parties’ relationship began to breakdown as early as 2018, the period in question before me is September 13, 2023, to December 1, 2023. The evidence with respect to the earlier issues helps to provide context, but no remedy can be awarded more than one year prior to the application having been filed. 19. I find that the Tenant, on a balance of probabilities, established that the Landlord harassed her during the period of September 18, 2023, though October 13, 2023. In my view, a reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that contacting a tenant about 18 times – not including voice mails – in a three-week period is unwelcomed, particularly when the Tenant has not replied to any of the messages. Further, references to the Tenant’s religious beliefs and threatening to sue the Tenant, is in my view, engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, would be unwelcomed. 20. I am also not persuaded that because some of the comments were made by the Landlord’s daughter, rather than the Landlord herself, that this alleviates the Landlord from responsibility. Nazanin acted as the Landlord’s agent, and the Landlord bears responsibility for the behaviour of her agents. 21. In the Divisional Court matter of Pinto v. [name] and White v Regan1, the Divisional Court at par. 39 refers to the obligations of landlords and tenants: [39] The Supreme Court of Canada in Bhasin v. Hrynew, 2014 SCC 71, [2014] 3 S.C.R. 494, established the organizing principle of good faith applicable to all contracts. This principle requires the performance of contractual duties and obligations honestly, not capriciously or arbitrarily, and with regard to the legitimate contractual interests of the other party: see [name], at paras. 63 and 65. The relationship between a tenant and a landlord is contractual in nature and requires that they discharge the obl igations they owe to one another in good faith. This duty of good faith includes how the parties conducted themselves toward each other at the end of that relationship. [Emphasis added] 22. What the Supreme Court of Canada has stated in Bhasin is that a landlord must still act in good faith and with honesty, even if the contract is coming to an end. As soon as it became apparent that the Tenant was not going to respond to the calls, the Landlord needed to explore other avenues rather than resorting to threats and intimidation, and to misleading the Tenant as to her rights. For example, giving the Tenant only 30 days to terminate rather than the 60 days’ termination required in s.48(2) of the Act, or by refusing to provide the required compensation. I cannot find that the continued calls, voice mails, e-mails, and texts, particularly given their content, demonstrates that the Landlord acted in good faith and honesty as required by Bhasin. 1 Pinto v. [name] and White v. [name], 2021 ONSC 5502 (CanLII) 23. Per the Divisional Court in Lorini v. [name] I am not of the view the Board has jurisdiction to order a remedy to the Tenant for the Landlord’s non-attendance at the L2 hearing because the tenancy had already terminated. Although the Landlord ought to have advised the Board that the hearing was no longer necessary, the tenancy had terminated by the hearing date, and the matter was moot. Remedies 24. By way of remedies, the Tenant seeks the following: • Rent abatement totalling $4,200.00; • General compensation of $7,500; and, • Board administrative fine totalling $35,000.00. 25. Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization]3 pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 26. The Tenant claims for the period of September 13, 2023, to December 1, 2023. However, aside from the Tenant’s general uneasiness given what had unfolded, there was no evidence adduced that the Landlord continued to threaten, harass, or interfere with the Tenant after October 13, 2023. As such, I do not find that this period ought to be considered in my determinations regarding remedies. Rent Abatement 27. The Tenant seeks two months’ rent abatement at 100 percent totalling $4,200.00. 28. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 29. There was no evidence to suggest that the rental unit could not be used or accessed between September 13, 2023, and October 13, 2023. However, I find that the Landlord and her agent’s behaviour negatively impacted the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment during this period. 2 Lorini v. Lombard, [2001] OJ No. 308(Ont. [name]. Ct.) 3 Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) 31. I am of the view that a 50% abatement for the period between September 13, 2023, and October 13, 2023, is warranted for the disruption to the Tenant. The Tenant’s testimony was that the persistent contact caused her unneeded stress and anxiety, and this interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 32. The Tenant’s rent was $2,100.00. I find the abatement is $2,100.00 for the thirty-day period between September 12 and October 13, 2023. General Compensation 33. General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered by the illegal eviction. 34. Although the matter of Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. Nazareth,4 (‘Biltmore Terrace’) a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], pertained to an application concerning disrepair, I find that Court’s guidance instructive nonetheless: “It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.” 35. When I consider the length of time where the Landlord was in breach of s. 22 and s.23 of the Act, and the impact this had on the Tenant, and the Court’s guidance in Offredi and Biltmore Terrace, I find that the Tenant is entitled to $2,100.00. Although I find the breach was serious, and negatively affected the Tenant, the duration of the breach was confined to a four-week period. Administrative Fine 36. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 sets out when an administrative fine can be imposed (in-part): A fine may be ordered in relation to the activities set out under: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant's occupancy of the rental unit; 4 Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881 37. The guideline also refers to the member considering the nature and severity of the breach, the effect the breach had on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors. It goes on to state that “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.” [Emphasis added] 38. In [name] v. Turnbull's [name], the Court of Appeal for Ontario summarized a line of previous case law involving residential tenancies and reaffirmed at paragraph 26 of its order that the Act is remedial legislation with “a tenant protection focus.” 39. When I consider the nature and severity of the breach, and the impact the breach had on the Tenant, I am of the view that the remedy granted to the Tenant sufficiently addresses the Landlord’s breach and considers the remedial nature of the Act. In my view, the remedy granted provides sufficient deterrence and encourages future compliance with the Act. 40. The Tenant paid $48.00 to file the application is entitled to reimbursement of this fee. 41. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony, and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 42. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $4,248.00. This amount represents: • $2,100.00 for a rent abatement. • $2,100.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 5 Price v. Turnbull's Grove Inc. (2007), 2007 ONCA 408 (CanLII), 85 O.R. (3d) 641 (C.A.)
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 9, 2026 ____________________________
