issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was uncontested that the Landlords served the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenant moved out because he received this notice. More specifically, the Tenant was ordered to vacate the rental unit pursuant to an order from the Board dated August 30, 2024, so that the Landlord’s son could move in. The Tenant vacated the unit September 30, 2024.

The central factual dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord’s son, who did move into the rental unit, did not have a good faith intention to remain in the rental unit for at least one year. [name]

The Tenant [name] (TL) testified that after he vacated the unit he found out through neighbors and by driving by the property that the Landlord ‘s son had moved out of the unit in July 2025, after his girlfriend had moved out, leaving one of the Landlord’s employees to reside in the unit himself.
TL testified that eventually the rental unit was sold.

TL referred to a copy of a summons for stunt driving, in the Landlord’s evidence, that the Landlord’s son [name] [name] received in September 2025, in which his address is stated to be that of his father’s address and not the address of he rental unit.
TL testified that through observing the unit and updates from neighbors, the unit appeared to be vacant in late August and early September 2025.

TL testified that the move resulted in a rent increase from $2,500.00 to $3,650.00 per month, moving expenses and he was seeking general compensation for having to move further north, adding additional time to his drive to work and for the eviction being in bad faith. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that he had bought the unit for his son and that is why the N12 notice was served on the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that they attended the unit on October 1, 2024, to clean and paint and then his son moved into unit on October 4, 2024, along with his girlfriend and a friend [name], who was also an employee of the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that his son had lived in the unit until his licence was suspended due to a stunt driving charge, at which time he stayed 30 days up north to be where his job was, and then when his licence was reinstated, he moved back into the unit.

The Landlord testified that around the same time, there was a downturn in business and although he wanted his son to stay in the unit, he couldn’t afford it and eventually the house was sold in January 2026.

The Landlord’s son [name] [name] (MC) testified that he is 23 years old and that he moved into the rental unit to start his independence. He believed he and his girlfriend were getting serious and it was his genuine intent to live in the unit long term. Copies of his bank statements showing the payment if the utility bills were submitted as evidence.
MC testified that his girlfriend moved out in July 2025, leaving just him and his friend [name] in the unit.

MC testified that he was charged with stunt driving in September 2025 and his licence was suspended for 30 days and during the time of the suspension he lived with his grandparents in [name] to be close to work.

MC testified that after his licence was reinstated, he moved back into the unit for a bit but then moved back in with his parents as he was financially crippled from the impound fees legal costs and loss of work.
Under cross-examination MC testified that he had never changed his address on his licence to the address of the unit because he had forgotten to. Analysis
The Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above.

The first and second elements of subsection 57(1)(a) are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2024, as a result of an N12 notice of termination served by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord's son moved into the unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated, I find that both the Landlord and his son provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that MC did move into the rental unit on October 4, 2024 and resided there until early October 2025.

The Tenant also gave straightforward and consistent evidence with respect to the little activity seen in the rental after late MC’s girlfriend moved out sometime in July 2025. I Find this testimony is consistent with the evidence of the Landlord and the Landlord's son that MC was not residing in the unit for one month in September due to losing his license and needing to be close to where he worked.

For these reasons, I find on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord's son did occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated but then experienced a change in circumstances that resulted in him moving back in with his parents in October 2024.
The Tenant has not proven all the elements of the test required for her application to be successful. Therefore, her application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. (T2 Application)
reasons: The residential complex is situated above a commercial premise and consists of 6 rental rooms on the 2nd floor and 6 rental rooms on the third floor. Each floor also contains two washrooms and a kitchen which are shared by the Tenants living on that floor.
The Tenant moved into the residential complex on March 1, 2022 and resided in a rental unit on the second floor until April 9, 2024.
The monthly rent was $850.00 due on the first of each month. T6 Application

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges that the Landlord failed to meet its maintenance obligation with respect to the following issues: a) bedbugs and cockroach infestation in the rental unit; b) inoperative heating system; and c) inoperative microwave Bedbug Infestation
The Tenant testified that an issue with bedbugs and cockroaches in the rental unit began in June, 2022 and that he had advised the superintendent [name] of the issue in July or August of that year.

The Tenant stated that the superintendent did not take any action. They did not bring in pest control or set traps and the Tenant dealt with the issue on his own, which continued until he was forced from the rental unit on April 9, 2024.
The Tenant stated that he observed cockroaches in his microwave, fridge and walls and that he would wake up with bites from bedbugs

The Landlord’s property manager [name] (the ‘Property Manager’) testified that the first time the Tenant raised the issue of bedbugs or cockroaches was on April 2, 2024 and that he offered the Tenant a steamer, but the Tenant advised him it was not his job to deal with the issue.

The Property Manager added that any issues regarding bedbugs and cockroaches that the Tenant experienced were related to his personal hygiene and cleanliness of his rental unit, and that any bedbugs were brought into the unit by the Tenant. 10. [name] (‘L.V.’) a tenant in the residential complex testified that he has resided in the residential complex for the past three years and that after the Tenant moved into the residential complex he began experiencing a bug problem and had to throw items away and put others in storage. He did not report the issue to the Landlord initially and stated that he purchased his own spray and that later the Property Manager gave him somethings to deal with the bugs, but that no exterminator was brought in. He further stated that after the Tenant left the residential complex the issue resolved. 11. Another tenant of the residential complex [name] (‘N.B’) testified that after about 4 months of the Tenant moving into the rental unit he began to experience bedbugs and cockroaches. He states that he advised the Property Manager of the issue and that the Property Manager would help him bag up his stuff and spray the rental unit, which resolved the issue. He did confirm that at no time did pest control attend the residential complex. 12. A third tenant [name] (‘P.O.’) who has resided in the residential complex for the past 6 years also provided testimony on this issue, but stated that he was not aware of any issue with bedbugs in the residential complex and when living downtown you can expect to see the odd cockroach here or there, but that it wasn’t an issue for him. Analysis 13. Pursuant to section 20(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’): 20(1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 14. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 15. Based on the testimony of the Tenant and the witnesses L.V. and N.B. who are also tenants residing in the residential complex it is clear that there was an issue with respect to bedbugs and cockroaches within the residential complex. By all accounts the Landlord through their property manager was aware of the issue. Additionally based on the evidence this issue started shortly after the Tenant moved into the residential complex and lasted until shortly after the Tenant left the residential complex. Notwithstanding that the issue may have originated with the Tenant’s occupation of the residential complex the Landlord still has a duty to address the issue once it is brought to their attention. On a balance of probabilities I am satisfied that the steps if any taken by the Landlord to address the issue were not reasonable in the circumstances, and that the Landlord breached its obligations under the Act and that this portion of the Tenant’s T6 application should be granted. Inoperative heating system 16. The Tenant testified that between December, 2023 and the spring of 2024 that although the heat was turned on, no heat was coming from the heating duct in his t. The Tenant states that during this time he would sleep in a jacket to stay warm. 17. The Tenant states that he told the Property Manager or the Landlord about the issue in December and was told that it would be addressed tomorrow, but the issue was never addressed, so he called City 3-1-1, but they did not do anything. 18. The Property Manager stated that he received one call from 3-1-1 regarding a heating issue in the residential complex and that the City attended and the system was rebooted and was working properly. 19. The Property Manager further states that he found pillows that the Tenant had stuffed in the heating duct in his room, which prevented the flow of heat. 20. L.V. and P.O. both testified that they did not experience any issues with respect to the heating system or any lack of heat in their units or the residential complex during this time. The tenant N.B. provided no testimony on this issue. Analysis 21. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. Based on the evidence before me I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet its maintenance obligations with respect to the heating system in the residential complex, and any lack of heat suffered by the Tenant was more likely than not caused by the Tenant stuffing pillows in his duct work. As such this portion of the [name] application is dismissed. Inoperative microwave 22. With respect to the allegation of a microwave being inoperative and in a state of disrepair the only evidence the Tenant provided with respect to a microwave was he had observed cockroaches in it. He did not provide any evidence as to is functionality or disrepair nor did he provide any testimony that an issue with the microwave was brought to the Landlord’s attention. As such I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached its obligations under the Act with respect to the repair of a microwave. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. Remedies 23. The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $3,400.00 being a 100% rent abatement for four months between October and January, 2024 due to the Landlord’s failure to address cockroaches and bedbugs in the rental unit and lack of heating during this time. 24. The Tenant was not successful in its allegation relating to the lack of heat in the rental unit, and the Tenant has also claimed an abatement under their T6 application with respect to cockroaches and bedbugs in the rental unit and residential complex. The rent abatement relating to this issue will be addressed under the remedies portion of the Tenant’s T6 application. 25. The Tenant seeks $100.00 to replace a microwave as a result of cockroaches and its state of disrepair, but led no evidence at the hearing in this regard. No compensation will be awarded to the Tenant with respect to the microwave. 26. The Tenant seeks out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $4,016.00 that the Tenant has incurred or will incur because the Landlord did not repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex. The Tenant’s explanation for this amount relates to potential moving expenses and transitioning into alternative housing and the Landlord to pay first and last month’s rent at market value. 27. I do not find the requested out-of-pocket expenses relate in anyway to expenses that the Tenant has or will incur because of the Landlord’s failure to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, and the Tenant is not entitled to any compensation for out-of- pocket expenses. 28. The other remedies sought by the Tenant relate to remedies that might have been imposed if the tenancy was continuing. Given that the tenancy has not continued no remedies requested by the Tenant relating to the treatment of cockroaches, bedbugs and compliance with municipal, provincial housing, health and safety standards will be imposed. [name] 29. The Tenant’s T2 application alleges that the Landlord or their agent entered the rental unit illegally, removed the Tenant’s possessions and locked the Tenant out and that he was not provided with 72 hours to remove his property, and that the actions of the Landlord or their agent leading up to and including the lock-out constitute harassment, obstruction, and substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 30. Additionally the Tenant’s T2 application also alleges substantial interference with respect to the Landlord’s failure to properly address the bedbug and cockroach infestation and heating issues. Lock-out and subsequent events 31. The Tenant testified that he received a phone call from the Landlord on April 1, 2024, telling him he needed to leave the rental unit if he didn’t pay rent. The following day the Landlord’s Property Manager told him he needed to get out of the unit by April 5, 2024. 32. The Tenant states that on April 5, 2024 he attended a community centre to get legal advice after being told to vacate the rental unit. A lawyer at the centre drafted him a letter to provide to the Landlord and he was provided three copies of that letter. The Tenant stated that he posted one copy on his door and the other two copies were in his room. 33. A copy of the letter was made an exhibit to the proceeding. The Letter is addressed to the Landlord and outlines the Landlord’s obligations under the Act regarding eviction. 34. The Tenant alleges that on April 5, 2024, the Property Manager removed the letter from his door and threw it in the garbage, and that the Property Manager then threatened him and took the other copies of the letter from the legal centre. 35. The Tenant testified that upon returning from work on April 8, 2024. He found a metal bar screwed to the door and the locks to his unit changed. Upon breaking into the unit the Tenant noticed about half of his belongings were thrown out or put in bags. 36. The Tenant further testified that the following day after returning from work he saw his belongings in the garbage on the street in front of the building including furniture. He was again locked out of his unit and upon gaining entry what was left of his belongings were missing. He states that he called the police. The Tenant stated that when police arrived they told him that it was a landlord and tenant issue and that they wouldn’t get involved in the dispute. Due to his fear of the Property Manager [name] left the residential complex and did not return and has resided in his car or shelters since that time. 37. The Tenant stated that the experience has affected him physically and mentally and he suffers from depression. He produced a medical prescription for Ach-Escitalopram a medication used to treat depression and anxiety disorders, prescribing 10mg once per day dated May 28, 2024 and containing 30 tablets. 38. The Landlord does not dispute that she contacted the Tenant as he was behind 2 months rent, but states that she did not tell him that if he didn’t pay rent he needed to get out of the unit, but instead asked him to pay the arrears and told him to go to a rent bank for assistance, but instead he went to a lawyer. 39. The Landlord further testified that the Tenant had broken doors in the past and was problematic. She was not aware of any locks being changed and that the Tenant had lost his key and kicked his door in. As far as she knew a latch was put on the door without a lock as it was the Tenant’s responsibility to obtain his own lock. The Landlord confirmed that she had not attended the residential complex between April 1 and 9, 2024 when the alleged incidents occurred and had never met the Tenant in person. 40. The Landlord’s Property Manager testified that he reached out to the lawyer who had written the letter for the Tenant and explained that he was not evicting him, but that he wanted the Tenant to clean his room as the Tenant was a hoarder and his room contained bottles of urine and feces and that due to health reasons he had put everything in the Tenant’s room into garbage bags. 41. The Property Manager states that on April 8, 2024 that when the Tenant had returned home he began kicking at the door and by the time he attended the Tenant’s unit the Tenant had kicked in the door, and was demanding to know why his items were in plastic bags. The Property Manager further stated that there was no lock on the door and that he had placed a latch on the door the last time the Tenant had kicked in the door and the Tenant had been told to put a lock on the latch. 42. A few hours later The Property Manager states that police and a sheriff attended the residential complex accusing The Property Manager of attempting to kick the Tenant out of his rental unit. However, after showing the sheriff the condition of the Tenant’s room, the Property Manager alleges that the sheriff told the Tenant he had 72 hours to vacate the unit. The Property Manager states that the Tenant did not return to the unit and that they kept his belongings for two weeks before sending them to the dump. 43. In cross examination the Property Manager admitted that he may be off by a day and his recollection of events occurring on April 8th could have been the 9th. 44. Both the Landlord and the Property Manager claim that they did not evict the Tenant and it was the sheriff who told the Tenant he had 72 hours to vacate the unit and pick-up his belongings. 45. The other tenant L.V. testified that he recalls the incident in April and that the Property Manager and the Tenant were arguing in the kitchen and he overheard that the Tenant was behind two months rent. The Property Manager told him that he couldn’t come in until he gave him the rent. He heard the police and sheriff attend the residential complex. He couldn’t see them but states that they talk very loudly and had identified themselves as police officers and the sheriff. They told the Tenant that he had 72 hours to get his things and go. In cross examination when asked about the Property Manager he stated that if you don’t pay rent there is a different side of him, that all the tenancies were month to month and if you did not pay your rent you knew your stuff is going to be moved out. 46. Another tenant [name] testified that he had seen the Tenant’s room in the past and that it seemed pretty destroyed. When asked if he recalls the Tenant kicking his door he stated that when the Tenant was kicked out for not paying rent for three months he was trying to get in and was kicking the door. He also recalled the incident with the police and sheriff, but was not sure of the specifics. Analysis Illegal entries 47. Neither party alleges that a notice was provided to the Tenant prior to the alleged entries into the rental unit. As such, I will deal with them in the context of entry without notice. 48. Section 26 of the act deals with entry without notice as follows: 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. (2) A landlord may enter a rental unit without written notice to clean it if the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to clean the rental unit at regular intervals and, (a) the landlord enters the unit at the times specified in the tenancy agreement; or (b) if no times are specified, the landlord enters the unit between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. (3) A landlord may enter the rental unit without written notice to show the unit to prospective tenants if, (a) the landlord and tenant have agreed that the tenancy will be terminated or one of them has given notice of termination to the other; (b) the landlord enters the unit between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; and (c) before entering, the landlord informs or makes a reasonable effort to inform the tenant of the intention to do so. 49. The Landlord through their Property Manager claims to have entered the Tenant’s unit due to health reasons. Based on the evidence provided at the hearing I am not satisfied that this reasoning falls under the category of an emergency under section 26(1)(a) or any other reason for entry without notice under the Act. 50. On a balance of probabilities I am satisfied that the Landlord’s Property Manager entered the Tenant’s unit illegally in contravention of the Act, as he testified that he had entered and bagged up the Tenant’s belongings due to health reasons. Lock-outs 51. Section 24 of the Act states: 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 52. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord had changed the lock to his rental unit on April 8 and 9, 2024 and that a metal bar was placed across the door of his unit and he was locked out and forced to break the lock to gain entry. 53. The Landlord states that the Tenant was not locked out of the rental unit as the Tenant’s door had no lock at the time and a latch was placed on the door as the Tenant had previously damaged the door and lock and that the Tenant had been told to place his own lock on the latch. 54. Based on the evidence before me I prefer the evidence of the Tenant to that of the Landlord. It is not reasonable that the Landlord would place a latch without a lock on the door to a rental unit and expect the Tenant to place their own lock on the door. If this were the case the Landlord would have no access to the unit in case of emergency without first obtaining a key from the Tenant. Even if I were to accept the Landlord’s evidence the actions of the Landlord in removing the pre-existing lock constitutes the altering of a locking system without giving the Tenant replacement keys. 55. Additionally N.B. another tenant in the rental unit testified that he recalls the Tenant kicking the unit door after the Tenant was kicked out for not paying rent for three months, and L.V. testified that he overheard The Property Manager tell the Tenant that he couldn’t come in until he gave him the rent. 56. Based on the totality of the evidence before me it is more likely than not that the Landlord did in fact change the lock on the rental unit, and find that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. [name] 57. The Tenant’s allegations of substantial interference relate to the illegal entries and lock- outs, the Landlord or their agent’s removal of the Tenant’s belongings, the infestation of bedbugs and cockroaches in the unit and lack of heat. 58. Pursuant to section 22 of the Act; 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. Illegal Entries/Lock-out 59. Based on the evidence before me the Landlord’s illegal entries and lock-outs of the Tenant from the rental unit constitute substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes pursuant to section 22. Removal of Possessions 60. Pursuant to section 41(1) of the Act: 41 (1) A landlord may sell, retain for the landlord’s own use or otherwise dispose of property in a rental unit or the residential complex if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with, (a) a notice of termination of the landlord or the tenant; (b) an agreement between the landlord and the tenant to terminate the tenancy; (c) subsection 93 (2); or (d) an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant. 61. None of the conditions under section 41(1) apply to this matter. The Landlord had no right to sell, retain, or otherwise dispose of the Tenant’s property in the rental unit and in doing so substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes pursuant to section 22. Bedbug and Cockroach Infestation 62. In terms of the T2 application, section 22 addresses a landlord’s action or inaction which substantially interferes with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. Here, it was the Landlord’s failure to respond to the bedbugs and cockroaches in a timely and adequate manner that result in substantial interference. Lack of Heat 63. In regards to the Tenant’s allegation of substantial interference related to a lack of heat in the rental unit, as addressed in the Tenant’s T6 application I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that any action or inaction by the Landlord led to a lack of heat in the Tenant’s rental unit and thus I am not satisfied that there was any substantial interference on the part of the Landlord in this regard. Harassment 64. Pursuant to section 23 of the Act a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 65. Based on the evidence before me the actions of the Landlord and or their agent the Property Manager constitute harassment under the Act. The Tenant was locked out of his unit on two occasions, the Landlord or their agent entered the Tenant’s unit illegally and removed his personal belongings from the unit and disposed of them. 66. The Landlord alleges that the Tenant was evicted by a sheriff who attended the rental unit on April 8th or 9th and gave the Tenant 72 hours to get his belongings and vacate the unit. 67. I do not find the evidence of the Landlord and their agent the Property Manager with respect to a sheriff attending the rental unit plausible. The role of a sheriff in the Province of Ontario is to enforce court orders under the Superior Court of Justice in the seizure and sale of property, serve legal documents and evict tenants in the enforcement of eviction orders under the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB). 68. No order had been issued by the LTB evicting the Tenant from the residential complex, that would have been enforceable by a sheriff. It is unfortunate that neither party were able to obtain any evidence in the form of an incident report or officer notes from the police officers in attendance that day. On a balance of probabilities I prefer the evidence of the Tenant and it is more likely than not that police attended the residential complex and advised the Tenant and the Property Manager that the matter was a landlord and tenant dispute and would not become involved. 69. I am further satisfied that the Landlord’s actions and/or the actions of the Landlord’s Property Manager directly led to the Tenant not returning to the rental unit after April 9, 2024. 72 hours not provided for property removal 70. Pursuant to section 41(2) of the Act, where an order is made to evict a tenant, the Landlord shall not sell, retain or otherwise dispose of the Tenant’s property before 72 hours have elapsed after the enforcement of an eviction order. 71. Section 41(2) of the Act does not apply to this matter before the Board as the evidence of both parties was that the Tenant was not evicted pursuant to the enforcement of an eviction order. As such this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Remedies Rent Abatement 72. The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $3,400.00 equating to a 100% rent abatement for a period of four months, due to the effects of living in a rental unit with cockroaches and bedbugs, illegal entry into the rental unit and lock-outs. The Tenant also seeks a portion of the rent abatement in relation to the traumatization, depression that he developed after this event. 73. The purpose of a rent abatement is to address and compensate a tenant when they can not fully use or enjoy the rental unit. I am not satisfied that the Tenants claim for an abatement due to the traumatization and depression that he developed after the event fits within the purposes and intent of a rental abatement and is better encapsulated under general damages, which the Tenant has claimed. 74. In relation to the cockroach and bedbug infestation in the rental unit and residential complex and the substantial interference and harassment on the part of the Landlord in relation to illegal entry into the rental unit and lock-outs an abatement would be appropriate in the cirucmstances. However, based on the uncontested evidence before me the Tenant was two months in arrears of rent and essentially already received an abatement. Having considered all the evidence before me and based on my knowledge of similar matters two months of rent would be an appropriate abatement of rent and no further amount will be awarded. [name]75. The Tenant seeks the costs associated with the replacement of their property that was disposed of by the Landlord in the amount of $8,750.00. 76. The Tenant included in their application a list of personal belongings and estimated values. 77. The Tenants evidence with respect to his belongings was largely uncontested. Landlord’s evidence through the Property Manager was that the Tenant was a hoarder and his room was in a state of disarray and a health hazard. 78. Additionally, the Landlord’s contractor [name] (‘[name]’) testified that he attended the residential complex to clean-up the Tenant’s room. He couldn’t recall the exact date he attended the unit, but his invoice to the Landlord was dated June 1, 2024. [name] states that the room was in a state of squalor with broken doors, holes in the wall and garbage about 3 feet high on the floor. He further described the unit as the filthiest place he had seen. He further testified that he removed approximately 3 – 4 trailer loads a mix of garbage and clothing from the rental unit. He does not recall observing any the items the Tenant described in his list of items disposed of by the Landlord or furniture. 79. The Property Manager testified that the Tenant’s bagged belongings were removed from the rental unit after two weeks. [name] did not indicate that he observed or removed any bagged belongings from the rental unit. I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant’s bagged belongings were already removed from the rental unit prior to H.R.’s attendance to clean-up the unit. 80. I accept the Tenant’s evidence as true and that the items as listed in his application were disposed of by the Landlord. The Tenant only provided a list of items that were disposed of and an estimated replacement value. The Tenant did not provide any further evidence with respect to the age or condition of the items. 81. In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 (CanLII), the Divisional Court stated, in part, as follows: “The Board heard evidence about the possessions of the respondent that were in the apartment unit, including two couches, a large television, a bed, two night tables, a stereo, a lap top, linen, clothes and many other items. The Board made an estimate of the reasonable replacement costs. It made no error of law in doing so. The estimate was a reasonable one in the circumstances, as broken down by the Board.” 82. In accordance with Beauage, supra, in the absence of receipts or other third party evidence about the value of the disposed items, I may estimate the reasonable replacement costs of the items and have done so as follows: Item Estimated reasonable replacement cost PC Tablet $100.00 2x Louis XV Chair $200.00 Samsung S20 $143.00 Samsung A70 $123.00 Mattress $100.00 Clothing $1000.00 3 x Watches $120.00 TV $75.00 TV stand $25.00 PlayStation 3 $50.00 Mini Fridge $50.00 Earrings $75.00 Air Pump $200.00 TOTAL $2,261.00 83. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,261.00, which is the reasonable cost that the Tenant will incur to replace property that was disposed of. Out-of-Pocket Expenses 84. The Tenant seeks out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $3,916.00 that the Tenant has incurred or will incur because of the actions of the Landlord. The Tenant seeks an amount related to potential moving expenses in transitioning into housing and the landlord to pay first and last month’s rent at market value. 85. I do not find the requested out-of-pocket expenses relate in anyway to expenses that the Tenant has or will incur because the Landlord’s actions, and these amounts have not been substantiated. The Tenant is not entitled to any compensation for out-of-pocket expenses. General Damages 86. The Tenant seeks general damages in the amount of $35,000.00, due to the impact on the Tenant of the illegal eviction, and disposal of the Tenant’s belongings. Section 31(2)(f) of the Act allows the Board to make any other order that it considers appropriate. 87. The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the tenancy. 88. In my review of similar cases the Board has awarded $3,000.00 to $5,000.00 in circumstances related to an illegal lock-out. Cases where awards have exceeded $10,000.00 such as Uzor v Islam, 2025 ONLTB 35419 (CanLII) and Conn v Equity Builders Ltd, 2024 ONLTB 16654 include the Landlord’s failure to adhere to an interim order and/or the Landlord’s conduct after the issuance of an interim order, which was not the case in the matter before me. 89. The evidence establishes that as a result of the illegal lock-out and the loss of all of his possessions the Tenant experienced depression, sought medical treatment, and was prescribed anti-depressants. In short, the Tenant was devastated and was forced to deal with homelessness staying in his car or shelters as he had no where else to go as a result of the Landlord’s actions. In the circumstances I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to $5,000.00. Administrative Fine 90. The Tenant also seeks an administrative fine although did not suggest an amount. 91. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline # 16 on Administrative Fines says: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 92. Illegally evicting a tenant and disposing of all of his or her worldly goods is behaviour that amply demonstrates a blatant disregard for the Act. The Landlord did not care whether the Tenant had rights or not. The Landlord locked out the Tenant and disposed of his possessions. 93. This is an appropriate case for an administrative fine. 94. In terms of quantum for a fine the Interpretation Guideline says: In setting the amount of the fine, the Member may consider: •the nature and severity of the breach •the effect of the breach on the tenant •any other relevant factors The amount of the fine should be commensurate with the breach. 95. Taking into account these factors and my knowledge of previous like cases an administrative fine of $2,000.00 is warranted and reasonable. An order shall issue accordingly. Stop Behaviour 96. The Tenant also sought an order that the Landlord and the Landlord’s Agent refrain from illegally entering the units and locking tenants out of their units and harassing them. 97. No evidence was produced during the hearing that this conduct occurred in relation to other Tenants of the residential complex as such no order in this regard will be issued. Return of Property 98. The Tenant sought an order that the Landlord return the Tenant’s property in its possession. It is clear from the testimony and evidence at this hearing that the Landlord no longer possesses the Tenant’s property and that it has been disposed of. As such no order will be issued in this regard.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,261.00. This amount represents: • $2,261.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace property disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions; and • $5,000.00 in general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,000.00 by June 13, 2026. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application based on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,150.00 which includes an unpaid balance of owed rental deposits and a refundable key deposit of $400.00.
The tenancy commenced on November 21, 2023 for a fixed-term ending on November 20, 2024. The monthly rent is $2,500.00 due on the 21st day of each month.
On November 19, 2023, the Tenants paid the Landlord a first month’s rent deposit of $2,500.00, last two months’ rent deposit of $5,000.00, and a key deposit of $400.00.

On or about, September 18, 2024, the Tenants told the Landlord that they would like to terminate the tenancy early on September 29, 2024. The Landlord agreed and the Tenants vacated the unit on September 29, 2024 and returned the key to the Landlord.

At the direction of the Landlord, the Tenants paid $2,500.00 on September 21, 2024. The Landlord explained that upon vacant possession, she would reimburse the unused portion of the rent to the Tenants, which she calculated as $1,750.00 for the period September 29 to October 20, 2024, along with the last two months’ rent deposit of $5,000.00 and the key deposit of $400.00.

The Landlord returned $4,000.00 to the Tenants, retaining $3,150.00 as costs to mitigate loss. The costs were for the services of a real estate agent hired in 2023 to assist the Landlord in assessing the Tenants’ application, and for the services of another service provider to assist in finding a new tenant for the rental unit after the Tenants vacated.
The above facts are not in dispute. Analysis

Pursuant to section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a landlord has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses resulting from a tenant’s unilateral repudiation of a tenancy agreement. I am not convinced, however, that the Tenants unilaterally refused the tenancy agreement.

The evidence before me establishes that on or about September 23, 2024, the Tenants contacted the Landlord by telephone to let her know that they wish to vacate the rental unit at the end of the lease period on November 20, 2024, because of a job prospect. The Landlord replied that she will start looking for another Tenant immediately and asked if they are prepared to vacate earlier. A day or so later, the Landlord called the Tenants to inform them that she had a new Tenant who wanted vacant occupancy of the rental unit on September 30, 2024, and asked if they could be out of the rental unit by September 29, 2024. The Tenants agreed to this because they were in good terms with the Landlord. As such, the Landlord is not entitled to charge the Tenants for her costs to re-rent the unit.

The Tenants paid the Landlord $2,500.00 for the rental period September 21, 2024, to October 20, 2024. As the Tenants vacated on September 29, 2024, they are entitled to the balance owing for the period from September 30, 2024, to October 20, 2024. In previous communication to the Tenants, the Landlord calculated this as $1,750.00. Accordingly, I find the Landlord is obligated to pay the Tenants $1,750.00.

The Tenants paid a two-months’ rent deposit totalling $5,000.00. In accordance with subsection 106(10) of the Act, this deposit is to be applied to the last two months of tenancy. As the Tenants paid the rent in full for the last two months of the tenancy, they are entitled to the return of this deposit.
The Tenants are also entitled to the return of the $400.00 key deposit as the keys to the rental unit were returned to the Landlord.

The total amount the Tenants are entitled to is $7,150.00. The Landlord paid the Tenants $4,000.00 in advance of the hearing. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $3,150.00 along with the Tenants’ cost of $48.00 for filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,198.00. This amount represents: • $1,750.00 for the rent charged for the period September 30, 2024, to October 20, 2024. • $5,000.00 for the last two months’ deposit illegally retained. • $400.00 for the key deposit illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application • Minus Credit of $4,000.00 that the Landlord has already paid the Tenants prior to the hearing.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant claimed that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, contrary to section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on March 1, 2022. The Tenant no longer lives in the rental unit and testified that he stopped residing there on or about August 27, 2024.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit was in a condominium building and that the alleged noise came from the occupants of a neighbouring unit. The Tenant testified that the neighbouring occupants were college students and that their gatherings interfered with his ability to enjoy the rental unit. The Tenant further states that on July 20, 2024, the occupants of the neighbouring unit hosted a party with approximately 15 people. The Tenant testified that there was loud music and shouting and that he, other occupants, and the concierge attempted to address the issue and that he then complained to property management.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the July 20, 2024, gathering disturbed him. However, the Tenant’s evidence was also that property management acted right away after the complaint and advised the occupants of the neighbouring unit that their behaviour was unacceptable.
The Tenant states that on August 21, 2024, there was a smaller gathering that was loud and that property management sent a letter to the owner of the neighbouring unit on August 22, 2024.

The Tenant also testified that there was another party on August 24, 2024, or August 25, 2024. However, the Tenant testified that he did not report this incident to the Landlord because he had lost faith in the Landlord and property management by that time.

In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2002] O.J. No. 5650, the Divisional Court confirmed that a landlord has a positive duty to take reasonable steps to respond to one tenant’s complaints where another tenant’s conduct may interfere with reasonable enjoyment. The issue is not whether the neighbouring occupants’ conduct is directly attributed to the Landlord. The issue is whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the Tenant’s complaints.

I find that the Tenant did not prove that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps. The Tenant’s own evidence was that property management responded promptly to the July 20, 2024, complaint and communicated with the occupants of the neighbouring unit. The Tenant’s own evidence was also that property management sent a letter to the owner of the neighbouring unit after the August 21, 2024, complaint.

The Tenant was clearly frustrated that the situation was not resolved to his satisfaction. However, the Act does not require a landlord to guarantee that a tenant will never be disturbed by another resident. The Landlord must take reasonable steps in response to complaints. I find that the Tenant’s evidence showed that property management did take steps after the complaints were made.

I also find that the Landlord was not given a reasonable opportunity to respond to the August 24, 2024 or August 25, 2024 incident before the Tenant decided to stop residing in the rental unit, because the Tenant did not report that incident to the Landlord at the time.
I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, based on the uncontested evidence, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Background
T he Tenants moved into the self-contained basement unit on November 1, 2019. The monthly rent was $2,000.00. The Landlord lived in a separate self-contained unit in the upper portion of the house.
The Tenants vacated the unit on August 31, 2022, after delivering an N9 notice to the Landlord on July 31, 2022. Service of the application

At the time of filing, the Tenants listed the Landlord’s address as the rental unit, which was the last known address where the Landlord resided. The Tenants also provided the Landlord’s email address. Following the filing of the application: • The Board served the Notice of Hearing and application materials on the Landlord by email on December 12, 2023, and further correspondence and notices on December 22, 2025 and February 6, 2026. • None of these emails were returned as undeliverable. • The Landlord did not attend any scheduled hearing or otherwise participate in the proceeding prior to this hearing date.

At the hearing held on May 16, 2024, the Tenants advised the hearing Member that the Landlord had vacated the property. Based on the Tenants’ submissions, the Member adjourned the hearing to ensure proper service of the application, authorizing the Tenants to serve the Landlord by email, which they did on or about May 31, 2024.
Having found that email remains the only reliable and available method of communicating with the Landlord, I find that it is fair and appropriate to validate the email service.
Since the Landlord did not attend this hearing, although properly served with the Notice of Hearing, the hearing proceeded in the Landlord’s absence. Substantial interference
The Tenants contend that the landlord-tenant relationship was initially good but in 2022 it deteriorated.
The alleged breaches of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) occurred primarily between May 2022 and early August 2022.
Based on the uncontested testimony, I find the following events occurred.
On November 3, 2021, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy, which the Tenants declined to sign.
In May 2022, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice, stating that the unit was going to be sold.

About three weeks later, the Landlord reported to police that the male [name] had assaulted her. E.P. testified that this was untrue and that the police did not lay charges or substantiate the allegation.

On July 12, 2022, the Landlord sent the following message to E.P.: “LOSER [name]. Your [spouse] has left you, she called me yesterday and told me what a liser (sic) you are … You pathetic piece of trash. You need to leave now. You are not welcomed here any longer… I will be going to court to get a restraining order on you…”
The Tenants’ evidence is that the female [name] did not contact the Landlord, contrary to the message.
E.P. submits that on July 15, 2022, the Landlord attended the rental unit, without proper notice, to show their unit to two prospective tenants.

On July 18, 2022, the Landlord lunged aggressively towards E.P. in the backyard. The next day, the Landlord turned off the air conditioning, which was included in their lease, and then never restored it.

There was another incident on July 27, 2022. When the Landlord’s adult daughter parked in the Tenants’ parking space, E.P. kindly asked her to remove the vehicle but the Landlord’s daughter began yelling at him, using profanity. The incident was the last straw; the Tenants decided the tenancy was no longer sustainable.

On July 31, 2022, when they gave an N9 Notice to End the Tenancy with 30 days’ notice to the Landlord, the Tenants posted a “Beware of dog” sign on the door, as a caution to realtors who were showing the unit to prospective tenants. The Landlord removed the sign. When E.P. complained in a text to her, the Landlord replied: “[name] my black ass”.

E.P. described how, on August 4, 2022, the Landlord attended the unit and banged aggressively on the door with an object E.P. described as like a hammer or axe. Although he called the police and attended, the police took no further action.

Over the course of July and early August 2022, the Landlord restricted access to the backyard (a previously shared space), exercised exclusive control over the shared mailbox and told the Tenants they could not dog-sit for friends because no pets were allowed in the residential complex.
The Tenants moved out on August 31, 2022, relocating to Calgary, Alberta. Analysis
The mere presentation of an N11, without more, is not in itself a breach of the Act. In any event, this claim is out of time pursuant to the limitation period in section 29(2) of the Act.

The Tenants also argue the N12 notice of termination was “fraudulent.” An N12 may be given by a landlord for purchaser’s own use if the landlord has entered into a purchase and sale agreement for the rental premises. The Tenants seem to think that the N12 must be given by the prospective purchaser but that is wrong. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether the N12 was invalid or whether it was an attempt to harass or otherwise interfere with the Tenants.

With respect to the Landlord’s text message dated July 12, 2022, I find that it is abusive, demeaning, and threatening – in a nutshell, it is a very offensive personal attack. The Landlord also threatened legal consequences and demanded that E.P. vacate. This was a clear instance of harassment, contrary to the Act.

The Landlord’s actions as described in the application and in the Tenants’ unchallenged testimony demonstrate a pattern of escalating hostility and intimidation over a relatively short but intense period. I am satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour more likely than not created a hostile living environment and contributed to the Tenants’ decision to vacate the rental unit prematurely.
I therefore find that the Landlord’s conduct as alleged constitutes substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, harassment and intimidation. Remedies

In their request for remedies, the Tenants ask the Board to order that the Landlord reimburse them for the following moving, storage and out-of-pocket expenses: • U-Haul truck rental – $339.03. • Storage costs in Ontario – $1,933.29. • The cost of shipping their belongings to Calgary – $1,456.90. • The cost of two flights to Calgary and travel costs to Pearson Int’l Airport - $637.69 (receipts for December 2022 or 2023; the ticket is partially illegible) and $414.85. • Mail forwarding – $81.93. • Driver’s Licence changes – $186.00.
The Tenants also ask for an order that the Landlord pay for the difference in rent for 12 months in the amount of $2,400.00 ($200.00/month). Expenses granted

I find that the Tenants are reasonably entitled to compensation for the following: • $339.03 for the U-Haul truck rental. • $350.00, for a portion of their short-term storage costs in Ontario which they incurred immediately upon vacating the unit. • $81.93 for mail forwarding costs. • $186.00 to update their address on their Drivers’ Licences. Expenses denied

The Act governs Ontario tenancies and, in my view, compensation for a rent differential is pertinent to Ontario tenancies. In assessing rent differential, the Board compares the rent paid for the former unit with that of a reasonably comparable unit in the same or similar Ontario market, having regard to size, type, and location of the unit.
Rental markets in Calgary may substantially differ from those in Scarborough, hindering the Board from determining whether an increase in housing costs is fair and reasonable.

The Tenants did not provide any evidence of securing or paying for a replacement rental unit, of the rental market in Calgary at the time, or explain why relocation to another province was necessary rather than a matter of personal choice.
Accordingly, I decline to award compensation for rent differential or for expenses relating to the interprovincial relocation. General Compensation
The Tenants seek $10,000 in general compensation.

This form of compensation addresses the unanticipated consequences of a premature and unplanned move, including stress, uncertainty, the disruption of daily routines and, in some cases, employment obligations. It also reflects the practical burdens of securing and transitioning to alternate accommodation, which may involve reliance on personal supports, acceptance of less suitable housing, and the assumption of unexpected costs.

The Board considers the severity and duration of misconduct and the impact on the Tenants. While medical documentation of harm is not strictly required, its absence – as is the case here - is a factor to be taken into account.
I find that compensation in the amount of $2,000.00 is reasonable and proportionate in all the circumstances. Administrative fine

The Board has authority to require a landlord to pay an administrative fine. In determining whether an administrative fine is appropriate, I have considered the intentional nature of the Landlord’s conduct; the pattern of escalating aggressive behaviour, as well as the need to deter similar conduct and reinforce that landlords must neither harass tenants nor resort to threatening eviction.

The Landlord’s conduct also reflects a serious lack of understanding of her obligations under the Act and, with respect to the particulars of the allegations, her conduct fell far below the standard the LTB expects of landlords.
The Landlord shall, therefore, be ordered to pay an administrative fine of $2,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,004.96. This amount represents: • $1,004.96 for part of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred. • $2,000.00 as general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $4,000.00 by July 10, 2026. June 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $4,848.00.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on August 15, 2025. Immediately they encountered problems caused by the tenants in the upper unit of the residential complex. Fire alarms went off multiple times a day preventing sleep. There was a constant flow of people in and out of the upper unit and drugs and drug paraphernalia were regularly present around the complex, including in the shared yard and patio. The Tenants reported their concerns to the Landlord immediately and repeatedly, but no action was taken until after the Tenants had given notice to end the tenancy.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household by failing to address the numerous issues caused by the other tenants in the residential complex in a timely manner.
I am satisfied that the T enants moved out of the rental unit because of the substantial interference; they were unable to sleep and had reasonable and valid fears for their personal safety.

The Tenants did not live at t he rental unit after October 1, 2025, however their possessions remained in the unit until October 15, 2025. The parties signed an N11 agreement to end the tenancy effective October 15, 2025. Remedies

The Landlord did not return the Tenants’ rent deposit or apply it to the last month’s rent as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’). When the Tenants moved in they paid $5,500, which represented the first and last month’s rent and the pro rated rent for the period of August 15 to August 31, 2025. They then paid $1,100.00 for the period of October 1 to October 15, 2025, expecting to receive the rent deposit back. The monthly rent was $2,200.00. In total, the Tenants paid three months’ rent but were only able to occupy the unit for two months. Therefore, the Landlord shall return the $2,200.00 representing overpaid rent or the not returned rent deposit.
The tenancy is confirmed to have ended on October 15, 2025.

The Tenants were unable to move into a new rental unit, so placed their possessions in storage. I accept their oral evidence that this costs $200.00 per month to be reasonable and within the range of costs presented to the Board in similar cases. At the time of the hearing, the storage costs were still ongoing with no known end date. I find it reasonable to award the maximum 12 months of storage. They rented a truck to move their possessions at a cost of between $200.00 and $250.00. This is also within the range of costs presented to the Board in similar cases. Because there is no receipt to confirm the amount paid, the lower range of their recollection ($200.00).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,848.00. This amount represents:  $2,200.00 for the return of overpaid rent  $2,600.00 for part of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred and will incur.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants t he full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The tenancy between the [name] ord and the Tenants is terminated as of October 15, 2025. June 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant described ongoing noise complain ts relating to tenants or occupants of another unit beginning May 13, 2025 and ending in mid-February 2026. The noise ended when the parties causing the noise were evicted.

The Divisional Court in Hassan v Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Div. Ct.) provides the premise that a landlord must take ‘the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment’ and ‘take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant’s right to quiet enjoyment.’
The terms ‘reasonably necessary’ and ‘reasonable steps’ must be assessed in the context of each situation.

In this case, the Tenant first reported problems to the Landlord on May 14, 2025. The Landlord sent a reminder notice a week later on May 22, 2026. After receiving additional complaints from the Tenant, the Landlord sent a second and final notice to the offending neighbours. Complaints continued and the Landlord advised the Tenant that an N5 notice had been issued by July 17, 2025. In July and August the Tenant reported continued noise, and requested updates on the status of the N5 process. On August 22, 2025 the Landlord advised that an L1 had been issued to the offending neighbours. When the Tenant asked for additional details of the legal processes against the offending neighbours in September, the Landlord advised that legal steps were being taken but no further details could be provided for privacy reasons. The Tenant reports that the offending neighbours were ultimately evicted in February 2026. Based on my knowledge of timelines of Board proceedings at this time, the length of time between initial complaint and eviction is not uncommon.

Based on the timeline report ed by the Tenant, I am satisfied that the Landlord took a reasonable course of escalating actions to address the ongoing noise. Initial attempts to correct the problematic behaviour were taken within a week of the initial report and an eviction notice was issued after approximately 2 months when less formal communication did not resolve the problem. While the Tenant would have preferred to receive additional details from the Landlord about the ongoing processes, I am satisfied that the Landlord provided an appropriate amount of information to assure the Tenant that appropriate steps were being taken while preserving some privacy relating to their own legal strategy and details of the offending neighbour’s situation which the Tenant may not have been entitled to. While the Landlord’s responsiveness and communication throughout may not have been perfect, I am satisfied that it was reasonable.
Therefore, I find that t he Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the amount of $194.32. Facts

The Tenancy began in 2021. In November 2022, the Landlord began annual communications via email with the Tenant with respect to the rent increasing. It was uncontested that the rent increased annually to the following: 1. December 1, 2022 - $2,460.00 2. December 1, 2023 - $2,584.53
December 1, 2024 - $2,671.50 3. The parties agreed that these increases were paid by the Tenant.
The parties agreed that the tenancy terminated on August 31, 2025, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that raised the issue of illegal rent increase with the Landlord after receiving an email during the year 2023 about the increase notice not being given within 90 days of the effective date and then requested an extension for the increase to begin on January 1, 2024, due to the short notice period.
The Landlord disputed that the rent was illegally increased.
The Tenant requested that the illegal rent increase amount for the previous year be returned to them for 2024 and the current year of 2025. Analysis
Section 110 of the Act states the following: No landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with this Part.

Subsection 116(1) of the Act states the following: A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so.

Subsection 120(1) of the Act states the following: No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.

Section 136(2) of the Act goes on to establish when an increase will be deemed lawful and provides: An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application.

The Tenant’s claim is limited by the Act both through a limitation period to make the claim to the Board in s. 135(4) and because of the deemed lawfulness under s. 136(2). It was uncontested that the Tenant did not file an application challenging the lawfulness of the increase for 2023, on or before December 1, 2024, and therefore the increase of the rent on December 1, 2023, in the amount of $2,584.53 is deemed lawful.

The Landlord increased the rent by 2.5% for the year 2024, and sent an email, with the N1 notice, to the Tenant on or about August 3, 2024, that the rent would be increasing to $2,671.50 effective December 1, 2024. The Landlord submitted the email to support his testimony.

Based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord provided 90 days’ notice to the Tenant, pursuant to the Act, the increase are in accordance with the Act, therefore lawful rent remains at $2,671.50 for December 1, 2024. There were no further increases in 2025, as the Tenant vacated the unit prior to the effective date of December 1, 2025.
Since the Tenant did not prove the allegations set out in the application, this portion of the application must be dismissed. Interest on rent deposit owing
The parties agreed that the Tenant paid a rent deposit in the amount of $2,400.00 on or around December 1, 2021.
The Tenant states that the Landlord did not pay him the interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the period of December 1, 2021, to the date he moved out of the unit on August 31, 2025.

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence and admitted that he did not pay the interest on the rent deposit. He testified that the Tenant owes him money because the rent was higher than the deposit paid.

Section 106(6) of the Act states: “a Landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due”

Landlords are required to pay interest on a last month’s rent deposit to a tenant annually pursuant to s. 106(6) of the Act so if the deadline for payment arrives and the Landlord does not pay the interest or use it to top up the deposit then at that point in time the Landlord starts to illegally retain the interest.

Based on the parties’ evidence and submissions at the hearing, I find that the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,400.00 on December 1, 2021, which was applied on December 1, 2022. Interest at 1.2% for that period is $28.80. Interest of 2.5% for the second period, which was applied on December 1, 2023, is in the amount of $60.72. Interest of 2.5% on the third period, which was applied on December 1, 2024, is in the amount of $62.24. And the final period is calculated at 2.5% to the date the Tenant moved out of the unit on August 31, 2025, which is the amount of $42.56.
The Tenant is entitled to interest on the last month’s rent deposit they provided to the Landlord.
As such, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant the total interest owing in the amount of $194.32.
This order contains all of the reasons, and no further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $194.32 This amount represents interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply with respect to this tenancy and the application must be dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Does the Act apply?
At the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue with respect to this tenancy – specifically, whether the Act applied.

The following facts are uncontested by the parties: a) The named Landlord are not the owners of the residential complex but rather are tenants who rent from the owner of the property; b) The Tenant paid the rent to the Landlord and rented a room; c) Throughout the Tenant’s tenancy, the Landlord has resided in the residential complex and shared the kitchen and bathroom with them; d) The Tenant moved into the residential complex on October 19, 2024; there was no timeline set by the parties on when the Tenant was to move out of the property; e) The Tenant did not sign a lease agreement with the owner Landlord.

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 defines a landlord, tenant and subtenant as follows: landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit; 2 (2) For the purposes of this Act, a reference to subletting a rental unit refers to the situation in which, (a) the tenant vacates the rental unit; (b) the tenant gives one or more other persons the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant’s term or period; and (c) the tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit after that specified date.

Based on the evidence and submissions between the parties, I do not find the Landlord falls into the definition of a landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 as they do not own the property and because they are tenants who pay rent to the owner in exchange for the right to occupy the premises.

I do not find the named Tenant to be a tenant under the lease agreement as I find the named Tenant in the application to be an occupant/roommate of the named Landlord and not a subtenant as they assert in their application. I say this because the evidence before the Board does not demonstrate the owner Landlord consented to add the Tenant to the lease agreement; as well I do not find the criteria outlined in subsection 2(2) of the Act applies to the living arrangement between the parties – the Tenant did not vacate the premises nor did the tenancy end on a specific date before the end of the Landlord’s term.
As such I find the Act does not apply and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s T5 Application

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Tenants received an N12 notice of termination under s. 48; • The Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of the notice; • The notice was given in bad faith; and • The person who was supposed to move into the rental unit failed to occupy the unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants moved out.

There is no dispute between the parties with respect to the first two elements of the legal test. The Landlord served an N12 notice on April 9, 2024, with a termination date of June 14, 2025 for the Landlord’s personal use, in accordance with section 48 of the Act. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on October 14, 2024, as a result of the N12 notice and consent order (LTB-L-033808-24).
