In the present case, the Tenant did not prove the remaining requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, whether the Landlord, or another person permitted under subsection 48(1) of the Act, occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith. The Sequence of Events

The Tenant testified that he began his tenancy on February 1, 2021. He further testified that he had no plans to move from the rental unit prior to receiving the N12 notice. The Tenant stated that the rental unit was well suited for his family and that he had established social, religious, and community connections in the neighbourhood.

The Tenant referred to his Agreement of Purchase of Sale dated September 8, 2024, in which the Tenant agreed to purchase a condo rather than renting a property because available rental units were expensive and unsuitable for his family’s needs. The property was purchased by the Tenant on October 14, 2024, which is also when the tenancy ended.

The Tenant testified that after vacating the rental unit, he was contacted by his former neighbour (Bilal [name]), who informed him that the Landlord was not residing in the rental unit. Based on this information and his own observations, the Tenant believed that the Landlord had not moved into the rental unit.

Bilal [name] testified that he lived “a few doors away from the rental unit.” He testified that he regularly attended in the area because he made deliveries nearby. He observed the rental property almost daily. [name] testified that he observed a younger couple with children residing at the property. [name] described the Landlord or the person he expected to see as an older woman and at one point referred to not seeing an “older Asian woman” at the property. He indicated that the individuals he observed appeared to be in their late 20s or 30s. During cross examination [name] acknowledged that he never met the Landlord, and it became apparent that he did not know what the Landlord actually looked like.

The Landlord testified that she experienced a breakdown of her marriage in late December 2023 and decided to separate from her husband. During her marriage she was living in the United States. The Landlord indicated that the rental unit was the only residence she owned in Canada, and she intended to permanently return to live in Canada after her separation. The Landlord referred to emails sent to the Tenant in January 2024 informing the Tenant that her circumstances had changed and that she would require possession of the rental unit.

On October 19, 2024, the Landlord testified that she returned to Canada and moved into the rental unit on the same day and that the property became her principal residence. The Landlord also stated that she travelled to the United States during part of the winter of 2025 for approximately two months, but the rental unit remained her principal residence.

The Landlord further testified that her nephew, [name], moved into the rental unit on October 19, 2024. [name] testified that he was experiencing financial difficulties and moved into the rental unit to provide emotional support to the Landlord following her separation. [name] stated that there was no tenancy agreement, he paid no rent, and the Landlord remained responsible for all household expenses. The Landlord also confirmed that she paid the property tax, utilities, and household expenses associated with the property. The Landlord’s documentary evidence included travel records, utility invoices, property tax records, delivery records, and shipping and storage records.

The Landlord also called [name] as a witness. [name] testified that she is the Landlord’s neighbour. She confirmed that the Landlord resided at the rental property, she also confirmed that the Landlord’s nephew, [name], his spouse Christina and their children also reside at the rental property.

The Landlord also called [name] as a witness. [name] testified that he attended the rental unit on a few occasions after the Tenant vacated and observed the Landlord residing there. [name] further testified that in October 2024 he observed the Landlord unboxing and attempting to assemble a bed frame in the rental unit. Analysis and Findings

In this case, the evidentiary burden rests with the Tenant. I find that the Tenant’s evidence is insufficient to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after he vacated. The Tenant’s evidence consisted primarily of information provided by his former neighbour ([name]). The Tenant also testified that on one occasion he visited the property, rang the doorbell and an occupant answer the door that was not the Landlord.

While [name] testified that he often observed the rental property and did not see an older woman residing there, his conclusion that the Landlord was not living in the unit was largely on assumption rather direct knowledge. I say this because [name] acknowledged that he did not know what the Landlord looked like. I therefore assign limited weight to his evidence. Further, the Tenant relied on the fact that other individuals, including [name] [name], his partner, and their children were residing at the property. However, the presence of additional occupants does not establish that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit. The evidence before me is that the Landlord also resided there and remained responsible for the household expenses.

I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she experienced a marital breakdown in late 2023 and that she decided to return to Canada because the rental unit was the only property she owned or was available to her in Canada. I also accept that the Landlord moved into the rental unit on October 17, 2024, which is three days after the Tenant vacated. I find the Landlord's testimony to be direct and supported by documentary evidence, including travel documentation and records relating to the moving of personal belongings into the rental unit shortly after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord also called witnesses who testified that they attended the rental unit and observed the Landlord residing there during the relevant period. While these witnesses were acquainted with the Landlord, this fact does not on its own render their evidence to be unreliable.

I have also considered the Landlord’s evidence that she travelled to the United States for approximately two months during the winter of 2025. In my view, this temporary absence does not establish that the rental unit ceased to be the Landlord’s primary residence. The evidence before me does not support a finding that the Landlord abandoned the rental unit or established a primary residence elsewhere. In addition, the Landlord continued to reside in the rental unit at the time of the hearing.

For these reasons, I am not satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. Rather, the evidence establishes that, at the time the N12 notice was served, the Landlord genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit for her own residential use and subsequently carried out that intention. Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenants did not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after the Tenant vacated or that the N12 notice was served in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was first before the Board on October 31, 2024. The matter was heard on an uncontested basis, as only the Tenants were present. Once the matter concluded, the Landlord signed in. The matter was adjourned to provide an opportunity for the Landlord to participate in the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of their claims on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on August 27, 2023, and vacated on September 7, 2023. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that when they first viewed the rental unit on or about August 24, 2026, it was under renovations. The Landlord advised them that the renovations would be completed by the end of the week, which was August 27, 2023. The Tenant stated that upon moving in, they realized that there a no kitchen countertops, no microwave, no working sink, no access to laundry, and no door to the bathroom. The only toilet that was working in the rental unit was not usable on a daily basis from 9:30am to around 5:00pm commencing August 31, 2023. On the morning of September 4, 2023 the Tenant was notified that there is no working shower in the rental unit, and the Landlord instructed the Tenants to shower at the gym nearby. Despite the Landlord agreeing to pay for the gym membership, the Tenants state that this is not a reasonable alternative.

On September 5, 2023 the Tenants expressed their concerns with the rental unit to the Landlord, specifically that the Landlord stated the renovations would be completed by the time the Tenants will be moving in. The Tenants therefore vacated from the rental unit on September 7, 2023.

The Tenant testified that there was no air conditioning provided in the rental unit despite it being very hot outside. The Tenant advised the Landlord on August 28, 2023 via text message at 9:01pm. The Landlord advised the Tenants to refer to the outdoor temperature and that the air conditioning will not turn on as it is on a factory setting. The Tenants stated that there was a heat warning in effect that lasted 3 to 4 days. The Tenant brought this issue back up to the Landlord on September 5, 2023. The Landlord responded that it has to be calibrated to every part of the house and due to him making new rooms, it is interfering with the thermostat. The Tenants stated that the Landlord turned on the air conditioning on September 6, 2023, which leads them to believe that the Landlord was withholding this service.

The Tenant stated that during an argument, the Landlord stated he will return half the amount of money he collected from the Tenant if they leave. The Tenant stated that staying in the rental unit given its state is not an option and therefore vacated on September 7, 2023. The Landlord did not return any money to the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that there was running water, they had access to a shower, the toilet was working and there was a sink to wash dishes in. The Tenants knew that the house was under construction and therefore should have been prepared and been respectful to the renovation process. He communicated the condition of the rental unit to the Tenant prior to them moving in, so they were aware of its current state and therefore is not responsible for the issues.

The Landlord stated that he cannot control the air conditioning. He states that part of the house may have been warmed than the other rooms, however they knew that the house was under construction. The air conditioner was working the entire time.

The Landlord stated that the Tenants can use the lower bathroom and shower, and he offered to pay for a taxi for them to go to the gym to shower. He reiterated that the Tenants knew about the stated of the rental unit and still decided to move in. He disagrees with all of the Tenant’s claims.
Upon cross examination, the Landlord stated that he advised the Tenants prior to them moving in that he rents it out as an Air Bnb. Legal Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act provides: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the act to repair and maintain the rental unit. The Landlord agrees that the rental unit was under construction, and although I note that the Landlord’s position is that the Tenant was aware of the state of the rental unit, I do not find that it absolves the Landlord of their obligations under the Act. I found the testimony of the Tenant credible and reliable, and it was support by documentation. The Landlord did not offer sufficient evidence to contradict that of the Tenants. T2 Application

The Tenant testified that the Landlord had a camera in the kitchen that was recording. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not advise them that there is a camera, and the Tenants were unaware that there was one, or that it was recording. This is a significant invasion of privacy. The Tenant submitted a photograph of the camera as evidence to the Board. The Tenant stated that this interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord threated the Tenant with immigration and permanent residency issues.

In addition, the Tenants were receiving communications from a new individual who was acting as the Landlord; however, the Landlord did not inform the Tenants of anyone else communicating with the Tenants. The Tenant received a communicate from this individual who stated that the Landlord was able to see what they are doing due to the camera that was in the kitchen. A copy of this text message was submitted as evidence to the Board.

The Tenant stated that the maintenance issues and the issues with the camera cause serious stress. It affected his sleep and therefore his ability to work resulting in his earnings going down. He had to look for a place overnight as the Landlord advised him to move out.

The Landlord testified that the camera was not recording and was there as a “dummy camera” to control the contractors going in and out of the rental unit. The camera was placed by the window, away from the washroom. The Landlord stated that the other individual the Tenants are referring to is his brother, who has shares in the rental property and he cannot comment to the text message that was sent to the Tenants. Legal Analysis

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord breached section 22 and 23 of the Act as a result of the camera that was in the rental unit and by making the comments about immigration to the Tenant. Although the Landlord stated that the camera was not on, I find the Tenant’s evidence credible that they believed the camera was on, which was further supported by the text message sent by the Landlord’s brother to the Tenant. I do not find that the Landlord provided sufficient evidence to disprove that of the Tenant’s that the camera was on. Furthermore, I find that the comments the Landlord made about the Tenant’s immigration status falls under the category of harassment, as it is conduct that the Landlord ought to have known to be unwanted. The Landlord did not offer sufficient evidence to contradict the Tenant’s statements about these allegations, and I note that the Landlord made comments about this subject during the hearing. Remedies Rent Abatement

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value.

The Tenant is requesting a rent abatement in the amount of $1,484.00. The monthly rent is $1,290.00. The Tenant calculated the daily rent and is requesting full compensation from August 27, 2023 to September 7, 2023, in addition to the amount paid to the Landlord before moving which is $2,000.00 making the difference $1,484.00.
The Landlord opposed this remedy as he stated that the Tenant saw the condition of the rental unit and decided to stay in it.

As I found that the Landlord breached sections 20, 22, and 23 of the Act, and based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find that a 20% rent abatement is appropriate to award in this circumstance. I heard the Tenant’s evidence of the impact that these issues have had on them, and I further considered the documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony. I heard that Tenants evidence that the maintenance issues began from when they moved into the rental unit which was on August 27, 2023 and therefore find it appropriate to award a rent abatement for the period of August 27, 2023 to September 7, 2023. A rent abatement totalling to totaling to $50.82($1,290.00*12/365=42.41. $42.41*12=508.92*20%=$101.78) will be awarded. Moving Expenses
The Tenant is requesting $49.75 that represents U-Haul charges they incurred for having to move out of the property due to the issues in the rental unit.
The Landlord opposed this remedy as he does not agree with what the Tenant is claiming.

I do not find that the Tenant offered sufficient evidence to demonstrate that this charge was incurred by them, and therefore I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities the Tenant proved this amount, and therefore will be denied. Out-of-pocket expenses

The Tenant is claiming $281.80 for out-of-pocket expenses incurred for having to buy take out food due to there not be a kitchen that works. The Tenant submitted credit card statements to demonstrate these amounts.
The Landlord opposed this remedy as he does not agree with the Tenant’s claims.

Upon considering the parties submissions, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant this remedy. The Tenant’s supported this amount by credit card statements, and I do not find it an unreasonable amount to order food over the course of twelve days. Other Remedies

The Tenant stated that they are requesting $5,000.00 due to the Landlord threatening the Tenant with immigration, and this is a level of harassment. He does not know what content was recorded on the video that the Landlord is still in possession of, as the Landlord was recording the Tenant without consent.
The Landlord does not understand what the Tenant wants this money for.

Upon hearing the submissions of both parties, and based on similar cases before the Board, I find an amount of $200.00 appropriate to award the Tenants for the twelve days there were in the rental unit.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $631.58. This amount represents: • $101.78 for a rent abatement • $281.80 for out-of-pocket expenses • $200.00 as general compensation • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant sought to raise issues related to substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment due to ongoing construction in the unit, lack of heat, withholding a vital service, failure to pay the compensation required under section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and unlawful entry. However, as these issues were not before me, the request to amend to claim these issues is denied. The Tenant may bring a separate application for these issues. T5 Application – Bad Faith
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The parties agreed that the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

Based on the uncontested submissions of the parties, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven the first two elements of the test under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. As a result, the issues before me were whether the person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated and the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that the residential complex is a duplex and the rental unit was the upper unit of the residential complex. The Tenant submits that the photos entered into evidence by the Landlord contain photos of the lower unit which was not occupied by the Tenant. The Tenant submits that based on the photos provided, it appears the Landlord does not reside in the rental unit. The Tenant also testified that he does not believe the Landlord has given the N12 in good faith as the Landlord has submitted into evidence a permit for renovations to the residential complex.

The Landlord testified that due to a breakdown in his marriage, he moved into the residential complex before the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that that since the Tenant vacated the rental unit nobody has occupied the upper unit and that he does not intend to re-rent the rental unit. The Landlord testified that he resides in unit 1 and uses the entire residential complex as his home and has used unit 2 for storage since the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that he has obtained a permit to install a door to the basement of the residential unit but that the renovation does not impact his ability or intention to use the entire property for his own residential occupation.

I found the Landlord’s testimony to be credible in that he moved into the residential complex prior to the Tenant vacating, he continues to reside in the residential complex and that he utilizes the entire complex for his own residential occupancy. I was not satisfied that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith or that the Landlord failed to move in within a reasonable amount of time.
As a result, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. An Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) was heard by videoconference on June 15, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 2:32 p.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, a hearing proceeded on the merits of the application with only the Tenant’s evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,401.97. Substantial interference
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on August 5, 2025. He occupied one of the bedrooms in the unit and another tenant (TO) occupied the other bedroom.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that he returned home from work on October 1, 2025 to find the power out in the rental unit and TO acting in a bizarre manner. TO was huddled in the front foyer of the rental unit and talking to people who were not there. The Tenant provided a video of this behaviour into evidence.
The Tenant testified that he reported TO’s behaviour to the Landlord and indicated that he didn’t feel safe in the rental unit due to the Tenant’s behaviour.

The Tenant provided into evidence copies of text chains and emails between himself and the Landlord, where the Tenant described TO’s behaviour and the fear and uneasiness he was feeling about staying in the rental unit. The Tenant indicated that he did not want to stay in the unit and that he wanted to leave and get his last month’s rent deposit back

In these texts, the Landlord indicated that he would contact the Tenant’s guarantor to get some assistance. There was some discussion about whether the Tenant would stay if the TO was removed, with the condition that the Tenant would either be responsible for the entire rent for the unit or would try to find another tenant for the unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was aware of TO’s behaviour and provided text messages from a previous tenant ([name]) which confirmed that TO had acted similarly when HM lived in the apartment, that one of the reasons HM left the rental unit was TO’s behaviour and that HM had filed an LTB application similar to this one (LTB-T- 061827-25) in an effort to get the Landlord to deal with TO’s behaviour.
The Tenant also provided into evidence a copy of a text chain with TO, where TO acknowledges and apologizes for his behaviour on October 1, 2025.
The Landlord did not attend the hearing to provide evidence on this matter. Analysis

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord interfered with his reasonable enjoyment by failing to address substantial interference by another tenant. To be successful in this application, the Tenant must establish that the other tenant substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or their rental unit by creating an unsafe and uncomfortable living environment. The Tenant must also establish that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to address the interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. Interference with Reasonable Enjoyment

It was uncontested that TO was acting oddly on October 1, 2025. The video provided by the Tenant clearly demonstrates TO’s behaviour and the uneasiness that was felt by the Tenant during the interaction.
The contemporaneous texts and emails to the Landlord clearly demonstrate that the Tenant did not feel safe or comfortable living in the rental unit as of October 1, 2025.
Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, the TO’s behaviour substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential unit. [name]

The Board must determine the following issues: a) when did the Landlord know or when was he reasonably expected to know about the disturbances to the Tenant caused by the other tenant TO; and b) once the Landlord knew about the disturbances to the Tenant, did he address the disturbances appropriately.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence is that he told the Landlord about TO’s behaviour as soon as it became sufficiently disturbing for him to fear for his safety. The Tenant claims that the Landlord dismissed his concerns and appeared to be more concerned about continuing to receive 100% of the rent from the two tenants.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence also indicates that the Landlord was aware of TO’s behaviour issues prior to the Tenant moving in, through the complaints of HM and the filing of HM’s LTB application on July 28, 2025, nearly 2 months prior to the October 1, 2025 incident.

As a result, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant contacted the Landlord on October 1, 2025 and notified the Landlord that TO was behaving in a disturbing manner that caused the Tenant to fear for his personal safety.

I further find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s concerns on October 1, 2025 was to minimize the Tenant’s concerns, with a focus on maintaining a 100% occupancy of the rental unit (with the associated rent).

I find that the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s concerns on October 1, 2025 was not adequate. The Landlord’s response demonstrated an unwillingness to involve himself in the situation involving the Tenant and TO. In light of the Landlord’s evident knowledge of previous concerns about TO’s behaviour, the Landlord’s dismissive response to the October 1, 2025 complaint constituted a failure to take reasonable steps to address the disturbances caused by TO.
I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant. Remedies
In his application, the Tenant is asking for a reimbursement of his $1,400.00 rent deposit and reimbursement of out-of-pocket costs of $344.00.

The Tenant effectively moved out of the unit on October 1, 2025 due to his perceived safety concerns and stayed with friends. He returned to the unit on October 2, 2025, gathered his belongings and did not return to the rental unit.
The lawful rent for the rental unit is $1,400.00. It is due on the 1st day of the month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $46.03. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,400.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.
T he Tenant produced a copy of his lease into evidence and it is uncontested that the Tenant provided the Landlord with a $1,400.00 rent deposit at the beginning of the tenancy.

Subsection 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires a Landlord to apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. The tenancy shall be terminated as of October 1, 2025, the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

As the Tenant effectively occupied the rental unit for one (1) day in October 2025, the Tenant should be responsible for paying the per diem rent due for that day. This amount shall be deducted from the last month’s rent deposit owing to the Tenant by the Landlord. Accordingly, there will be an order requiring the Landlord to refund the rent deposit, less this one day per diem, to the Tenant.

The Tenant’s out-of-pocket costs were constituted of $100.00 per night paid to a friend for accommodation ($200.00 total), $20.00 in parking fees and $124.00 in lost wages. No receipts were provided for the accommodation and parking costs, so I will not be ordering a reimbursement of these. Similarly, there was no evidence provided by the Tenant of any lost wages as a result of the October 1, 2025 incident; as such, no award will be given for this alleged expense either.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing this application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The tenancy is terminated as of October 1, 2025.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,401.97. This amount represents: • $1,353.97 reimbursement of the last month’s rent deposit ($1,400.00 rent deposit - $46.03 per diem for October 1, 2025 occupancy); and • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlords indicated that they were not notified in advance of the hearing that the Tenant intended to call any witnesses. The Tenant’s representative stated that there is no requirement in the Board’s Rules requiring the disclosure. I agree with the Tenant’s representative that there is no such requirement in the Board’s Rules.

I asked whether the Landlords knew the witness and whether they understood the issues raised in the application. The Landlords confirmed that they did. They also stated they were prepared to respond to the application. Therefore, I proceeded to hear the merits of the application. Whether the Landlord gave the N13 in bad faith
As explained below, the Tenant did prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $6,589.40.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under s. 50 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; c) The Landlord did not renovate/convert the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed that the Landlords served a “Notice to End your Tenancy Because the [name] to Demolish the Rental Unit, Repair it or [name] it to Another Use” (‘N13 notice’) on July 21, 2025, with a termination date of November 30, 2025, pursuant to s. 50 of the Act. It is also undisputed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2025, as a result of the N13 notice. Sequence of the Events

The Tenant testified that he occupied the basement unit of the property. The tenancy began in November 2023. The Tenant believes the Landlords served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith because the Landlords did not renovate or convert the rental unit after the Tenant vacated in accordance with the intended purpose set out on the notice.

On July 21, 2025, the Landlords served the Tenant with an N13 notice. The notice selected reason 2 and stated that the Landlords required the rental unit to be vacant to complete repairs or renovations. The N13 claims that the Landlords intend to “convert the home back to its previous approved use by removing all cooking facilities in the second unit.” The notice further claims: “The unit is being decommissioned in response to an order issued by the local Fire Department under Fire Protection & Prevention Act, 1997 on July 21, 2025 after the inspection on July 10, 2025. As part of this compliance process, cooking facilities will be removed to eliminate fire safety risks and ensure the space no longer operates as a separate dwelling. The renovation involves non-structural changes and does not affect plumbing or electrical systems. A building permit is not required for this scope of work, as confirmed by City guidelines.”

The City of Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services inspection order was attached to the N13 notice, the order states that the property contains two residential units and that the second unit was not registered with the City. The order directed the owner to comply with one of three options: “OPTION 1: [name] the home back to its previous approved use. By removing all cooking in the second unit. Note: this may require a building permit. OPTION 2: If the second unit was constructed after July 14, 1994, obtain a building permit for the construction of the second unit, which will require completion of the Second Unit Creation Date Affidavit attesting to the date of construction of the second unit, which must be notarized by a lawyer or Commissioner of Oaths, and register the second unit with the City of Mississauga. OPTION 3: If the second unit was constructed on or before July 14, 1994, complete the Second Unit Creation Date Affidavit attesting to the date of construction of the second unit, which must be notarized by a lawyer or Commissioner of Oaths and register the second unit with the City of Mississauga.”

The Tenant testified that shortly after receiving the N13 notice, he emailed the Landlords and informed them that the inspection order did not direct the Tenant to vacate the rental unit and did not require termination of the tenancy. The order only required the owner to bring the property into compliance by October 21, 2025.

During the hearing I inquired as to why the Tenant vacated the rental unit if he contested the N13 notice. There was no L2 application filed by the Landlords, and the Tenant vacated earlier than the termination date. The Tenant replied that after receiving the N13 notice, he believed he had no choice but to relocate. He was also concerned about uncertainty surrounding the tenancy, the possibility of having to move during winter, and disruption to his child’s schooling.

On August 2, 2025, the Tenant informed the Landlords by email that his family intended to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant later moved out at the end of September 2025. 12. [name] (‘Landlord’) testified on behalf of the Landlords. He acknowledged that when the N13 notice was served, he informed the Tenant the unit would no longer operate as a separate dwelling. 13. The Landlord testified that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2025, they reassessed their financial circumstances and by December 2025 realized that demolishing the kitchen and returning the property to a single-family dwelling would reduce the property value and create financial hardship. The Landlord testified that they rely on the rental income to pay a portion of their expenses. The Landlords then traveled to India and liquidated their assets to begin the legalization of the second unit. In early 2026, the Landlord testified that he rented a bedroom in the lower level to [name]. 14. [name] was summoned by the Tenant. [name] testified that he rents a bedroom in the lower level of the property and another occupant rented the second bedroom. He referred to his “Roomer/Landlord Agreement” which states that the tenancy commenced on March 1, 2026 and the term ended on April 30, 2026. [name] further testified that he was looking for rooms for rent on “Roomies” at the end of January and the beginning of February 2026. He viewed the rental unit on February 5, 2026. [name] stated that contractors were present performing work and he observed that the unit contained a functioning stove and kitchen facilities. He understood the lower level was being offered as residential accommodation and was never advised that the unit would cease operating as a separate dwelling. Analysis and Findings 15. In this case, I am satisfied that all parts of the test in subsection 57(1)(c) of the Act have been proven and that the Landlords gave the Tenant the N13 notice of termination under s. 50 of the Act in bad faith. 16. I accept that the Fire Department inspection required the Landlords to bring the rental unit into compliance because the rental unit was not properly registered. However, the inspection order did not require the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. The order expressly provided three separate compliance options, including two options that would have permitted the second unit to continue operating lawfully after registration. However, despite this, the Landlords served an N13 notice stating the unit was being “decommissioned” and would no longer operate as a separate dwelling. The Landlords selected reason 2 on the N13 notice and expressly required the unit to be vacant for the proposed work. 17. The evidence establishes that the Landlords did not carry out the purpose described in the N13 notice. Rather than converting the home back to its previous approved use by removing all cooking in the second unit, which did not require a building permit (option 1), the Landlords chose to legalize the rental unit and continue operating the unit as a rental. 18. The Landlords’ evidence is that they were under financial stress and initially believed they needed to terminate the tenancy in order to comply with the inspection order. The Landlords also indicated that they were unfamiliar with the legal process and were attempting to comply with the municipal requirements. I do not accept this explanation. It was the Landlord’s obligation to understand their legal obligations and options under the RTA before terminating the Tenant’s tenancy. Further, the Landlords’ lack of understanding of the process does affect the legal test that must be applied in this matter. I must consider whether the Landlords genuinely intended to carry out the intended purpose described in the notice at the time the N13 notice was served. 19. I find the Landlords’ evidence to be inconsistent and unconvincing on this point. I say this because while the Landlord acknowledged the purpose of the N13 notice was to convert the home back to its previous approved use by removing all cooking in the second unit, the Landlord also acknowledged the inspection order itself provided options that would permit the continued operation of a second unit. 20. In this case, I find the timing of events to be significant. According to the Landlords, they changed their mind and decided not to proceed with the work required to remove the rental unit in December 2025, which is three months after the Tenant vacated on September 30, 2025. Instead, the Landlord proceeded to legalize the second unit and advertised it for rent in February 2026, then re-rented the unit on March 1, 2026. The Landlords also confirmed that the rental unit continued to operate as a separate residential unit with shared cooking facilities. In addition, the Landlords confirmed that they did not offer the Tenant an opportunity to occupy the unit before renting it. 21. The Landlords’ explanation for this change in their plans was that they realized that the intended purpose set out in the N13 notice would not increase the value of their property. However, this was something that the Landlord could have easily determined before they served the Tenant the N13 Notice. The fact that the Landlord did not properly research the implications of serving an N13 Notice before serving it upon the Tenant and terminating the tenancy does not justify their actions. 22. I am also not satisfied with their explanation that they experienced financial difficulties and could not afford to operate the rental unit. I say this because shortly after the Tenant vacated the Landlords traveled to their home country and liquidated their assets to legalize the second unit so that the value of their property can increase. Thereafter they re-rented the property. The Landlord could have done all of these things without evicting the Tenant. 23. Therefore, I do not accept that any misunderstanding of the inspection order explains why the notice represented that the rental unit would be converted back to its previous use when the inspection order itself provided alternative compliance options that would have permitted the continued operation of the second unit. 24. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlords did not carry out the activity set out on the N13 notice after the Tenant vacated, and I also find that the Landlords served the N13 notice in bad faith. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is granted. Remedies 25. The Tenant requested to withdraw the following remedies requested in the application: [name] 1, (rent abatement of $25,200.00), and [name] 6 (other remedies) claimed on the application. The Landlords did not object, and I consented to the request. 26. The remaining requested remedies are $750.00 for moving and storage ([name] 4), for the Board to order a fine against the Landlords (Remedy 2), and General Compensation of $25,200.00 (Remedy 5). a) Expenses related to Moving and Storage The Tenant claimed $750.00 for moving and storage expenses. The Tenant referred to a U-Haul receipt in the amount of $241.40. I am satisfied that this is a reasonable expense which was incurred by the Tenant as a result of the bad faith termination. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the remaining amount claimed because the Tenant testified generally regarding disruption and inconvenience associated with the move, no numeration for those expenses or documentary evidence were provided. Therefore, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $241.40. b) General Compensation of $25,200.00 I accept that the Tenant moved out 2 months before the termination date set out in the N13 notice because he wanted to avoid searching for accommodation during the winter months while also minimizing disruption to his child’s schooling. I accept his explanation and find that the Tenant mitigated his losses. I also accept that the Tenant experienced stress, uncertainty, and inconvenience after receiving the N13 notice and that these concerns contributed to his decision to relocate from the rental unit. However, the Tenant did not provide a detail breakdown of his general damages, such as medical treatment, counseling expenses, lost income, childcare expenses, increased housing costs, or other significant financial losses arising from the move. I find the Tenant’s evidence regarding the impact of his circumstances to be limited. While I am satisfied that the Tenant suffered some inconvenience and disruption as a result of relying on the N13 notice, I find that the evidence does not support the amount claimed. Taking all of these circumstances into account, I find that general compensation equal to three month's rent is appropriate. Therefore, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $6,300.00 ($2,100x3). c) Fine against the Landlord Administrative fines are intended to promote compliance and deter future misconduct where other remedies are insufficient. Given the compensation award to the Tenant, I am satisfied that this order provides adequate deterrence. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $6,589.40. This amount represents: $6,300.00 for General Compensation, $241.40 for moving expense, and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026. If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent the Tenants owe (L1-Application-LTB-L-095227-24). [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application-LTB-T-086714-24). [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application-LTB-T-086714-24). These applications were heard on October 8, 2025 and June 3, 2026. The Landlords [name] and [name], the Landlords’ Legal Representative [name], the Tenants and the Tenants’ Legal Representative Sandra Askew attended the hearing.
reasons: The hearing of these applications originally began on October 8, 2025. On that date, the L1 application was heard. Shortly into the Tenants’ evidence concerning their issues under section 82 of the Act and their T2 and T6 applications, the Tenants requested an adjournment to amend the applications. The Landlords consented to the request and the applications were adjourned and I seized myself with the matters.

On October 16, 2025, I issued an interim order setting out deadlines for the service and filing of an amendment by the Tenants as well as deadlines for the disclosure of evidence for the parties. This order is meant to be read with LTB-L-095227-24&LTB-T-086714-24- IN, issued on October 16, 2025.

Paragraph 2 of my interim order reads as follows: No later than October 31, 2025, the Tenants shall serve the Landlord and file with the Board a request to amend the T2 and T6 applications. The request to amend shall provide the following information: a) A clear, succinct description of each issue the Tenants intend to raise, absent any irrelevant narrative. b) The date the issue occurred or began. c) The date the Tenants told the Landlords about the issue and the date the issue was resolved if it was. d) The remedy the Tenants are requesting for each issue.

In addition, paragraph 3 of my interim order also states: The request to amend shall include all of the issues the Tenants intend to raise at the hearing, including those that they had intended to raise under section 82 of the Act.

On October 30, 2025, the Tenants’ filed with the Board and served the Landlords, a request to amend the applications. The Landlords were not opposed to accepting the amended applications since they had been filed and served in accordance with the deadlines in the interim order. However, the Landlords were opposed to some of the contents of the amendment, particularly with respect to the T2 application. The Landlords took little issue with the amendment request relating to the T6 application and the remedies sought. The Landlords position was the amendment did not set out the dates and details for most of the allegations as required in the interim order.

The Tenants submitted their were 8 to 10 additional event or incidents they wanted to raise but agreed the dates and particulars of these events were not included in the amendment. The Tenants’ Legal Representative stated they misunderstood the wording of the interim order and as such, did not provide the Landlords with dates of when to account for their conduct. &LTB-T-086714-24

The amendment to the T2 application submitted by the Tenants provides the Landlords an eight-month window between May 21, 2024 and January 17, 2025 in which they are said to have substantially interfered with and harassed the Tenants. The amendment vaguely describes some of the events the Tenants seek to raise but does not fairly set out when incidents are said to have taken place or who was involved.

The Landlords are not required to look through the vast amount of the Tenants’ evidence to determine what the issues to be determined at the hearing will be. Despite this, the Landlords submitted they did attempt to understand the claims being made by reviewing the Tenants’ evidence and were only able to identify two specific complaints from May 21, 2024 and August 30, 2024.

The Tenants’ letter that accompanied the request to amend states: The issues we seek to amend and incorporate are not new or additional from those already identified in the original T2/T6 and s. 82 form but are directly related and provide further grounds to support the Tenant’s claim. All issues for the amended T2/T6 can be found in the Schedule A attached to the Amended applications. This request is being made in the interest of procedural fairness.

Having reviewed the request to amend and after considering the submissions of the parties, I did not find it would be procedurally fair to expect the Landlords to be able to respond to eight to ten vague and undated allegations that would only crystallize in real time while the Tenants testify. The Landlords are entitled to know the allegations and claims being made against them. Procedural fairness in my view, includes knowing when events and incidents are said to have occurred so that a party can look back to events of that day and examine their conduct and obtain witnesses or other evidence.

An eight-month date range between May 21, 2024 and January 17, 2025 falls very short in providing this notice to the Landlords such that they can know the case to meet and meaningfully respond. Essentially, the Tenants have put the Landlords to the burden of having to account for every day of the tenancy over an eight-month period in order to answer to the Tenants’ unspecified claims. This after already having been granted an adjournment to provide dates and particulars.

For all of these reasons, while I granted the amendment request itself, I did not consider the undated and vaguely worded allegations contained within it. In addition to the T2 claims, this determination also applied to a vague T6 claim concerning property maintenance.

Based on this decision, the Tenants requested an adjournment to further amend the application to particularize dates and details of event and incidents to the Landlords. The Landlords opposed the request citing the matter had already been adjourned for this reason, that it would require an additional appearance before the Board and additional preparation time that could only begin once another amendment was served to them.

When I considered the submissions of the parties alongside Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I did not find there was a sufficient basis to warrant adjourning the matters again. The Tenants already had the benefit of an adjournment and my clearly worded interim order. While the Tenants will be prejudiced by denying the request to adjourn, I find &LTB-T-086714-24 this prejudice largely avoidable had the Tenants followed the interim order and given the Landlords adequate notice of the 8 to 10 issues they wanted to raise. Given the circumstances and the history of the applications, the need for the Landlords to wait for another amendment to prepare before having to return before the Board a third time, I did not grant the request to adjourn the June 3, 2026 hearing. L1 Application

The Landlords served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit.
The lawful rent was $3,980.00 and increased to $4,054.50 on January 1, 2025. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to January 31, 2025 are $12,014.50. This amount was not disputed by the Tenants.
The Landlords incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlords collected a rent deposit of $3,980.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlords. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $149.39 is owing to the Tenants for the period from August 2, 2023 to January 31, 2025.
Once the rent deposit and interest owing on the rent deposit are deducted from the rent arrears owing and costs, the amount outstanding is $8,071.11.
While the Tenants filed issues under section 82 of the Act, these issues were incorporated into the Tenants’ amendment to the T2 and T6 application. T2 Application

The Tenant, [name], testified that on May 21, 2024, the Landlords sent them an email concerning the attendance of the police to the property, the shooting of firearms, the use of portions of the property leased for farming purposes, and the presence of permanent structures, trespassers and hunters. This email was submitted into evidence.

The Tenants responded in an email later on May 21, 2024, providing a response addressing each of the Landlords’ concerns, explaining no illegal activity was taking place &LTB-T-086714-24 and that no breach of the lease agreement had occurred. The Tenants asserted their legal rights to use the rented portion of the property legally and as how they see fit absent substantial interference and harassment from the Landlords. The Tenants state the email from the Landlords was unnecessary and that their activity is not the business of the Landlords.

The Landlords responded by explaining the intent of the initial email was not to disrespect the Tenants. The Landlords agree the Tenants have the right to reasonable enjoyment of the property and explain they have a responsibility to ensure the property will not be liable for damages or concerns raised by neighbours. The email thanks the Tenants for clarifying the issues the Landlords initially raised and states the email was sent to obtain clarification and not to insult the Tenants.

The Tenants respond by stating they did find the initial email disrespectful. For clarification, they also write they have not claimed anyone has interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit, harassed, obstructed, coerced or threatened them. Portions of the Act dealing with substantial interference and harassment referenced in the Tenants’ initial response to the Landlords was to explain the Tenants’ assertions. The email closes by stating the Tenants hope to have provided the clarification the Landlords’ sought on the issues.
The following morning on May 22, 2024, the Landlords respond by thanking the Tenants for their clarification and wish them a great day.

The Tenant testified that in August 2024, they erected some flags on the property that were of a political nature. The Landlords and the Tenants engaged in a conversation on August 29, 2024 concerning the flags and both parties agreed it was terse, unpleasant and involved screaming about the flags.

On August 29, 2024, the Landlords emailed the Tenants referencing the conversation held that morning. The Landlords write they understand the Tenants have the right to freedom of expression but state families with children drive by and it is offensive to see the ‘F-word’ on a flag. The Landlords explain they asked the Tenants to take the flag down or relocate it on the property so it does not offend the public. The email goes on to state it is the Tenants’ decision on how to raise their children but ask them to keep in mind that for some, the flag is offensive.

The Tenants responded by email on August 30, 2024 stating it is their right to have flags erected on the property and that whether or not the public may be offended is not the Landlords’ concern. The Tenants state the reference to raising their children was inappropriate and offensive.
The parties agreed the flags were not taken down.

The Tenant testified that the Landlords’ statement about how they raise their children was insulting and that how they raise their children is not any of the Landlords’ business. The Tenant described the interaction over the flags as politically motivated on the part of the Landlord and that the flag does not display the ‘F-word’ but only a possible suggestion of it.

The Landlord [name] testified that she was the one involved in the conversation and authored the August 29, 2024 email. She explained she did not tell the Tenants to remove the flags, just that she asked them to consider taking them down or relocating &LTB-T-086714-24 them. Ms. [name]name] testified that she agreed they had the right to expressions and stated she was not telling the Tenants how to raise their children and that the email states she agrees it is up to them as to how they choose to do so.

At the hearing on October 8, 2025, the Tenant testified about multiple inspections at the property as a result of a complaint concerning the water quality at the unit. It was at this time during the hearing on that date that the proceedings were adjourned. Prior to the closing of the Tenants’ evidence on the T2 application at the June 3, 2026 hearing, I asked the Tenants if there was more evidence they wanted to provide with respect to the September 2024 claims concerning inspections or if those issues were part of their T6 application. The Tenants confirmed the inspections would be incorporated into the T6 application.

This T2 application is based on sections 22 and 23 of the Act. These sections read as follows: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23. A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

There is no definition of “harassment” under the Act but generally speaking harassment is usually considered to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be most unwelcome.

Section 22 of the Act contains both a subjective and objective element. The interference must be substantial; that is a subjective element as not every tenant will be equally adversely impacted by various kinds of behaviour complained of. The objective element arises from the phrase “reasonable enjoyment” meaning the Board must ask itself whether or not the reasonable person would consider the behaviour to be unreasonable.

When I consider the evidence of the parties, I am not satisfied the email communications and conversations between the Tenants and the Landlords that took place in May 2024 and August 2024 rise to the level of substantial interference or amount to harassment. I say this for the following reasons.

The May 21, 2024 exchange resulted from a complaint by neighbours concerning the use of firearms and the attendance of the police at the property. In my view, the Landlords are entitled to investigate such a complaint and the Tenants are entitled to respond. This is what took place, in addition to the other issues raised by the Landlords’ being addressed.

The Landlords accepted the Tenants clarification email, assured the Tenants they did not mean any disrespect in making the inquiry, and finally, thanked the Tenants for their clarification. While I can appreciate the Tenants had to devote time in writing their responses, in my view, this is at most an irritation to the Tenants that I do not find rises to the level of substantial interference. &LTB-T-086714-24

The August 29, 2024 and August 30, 2024 conversations and communications concerning the flags on the property also do not amount to substantial interference in my view. The Landlords made a request to the Tenants to remove or relocate them. Nothing in the email from the Landlords show this was demanded or that any consequence would flow from the continued presence of the flags.

The mention of the Tenants’ children was unnecessary. However, it was singular offside comment that while annoying and upsetting to the Tenants, was also accompanied by acknowledgement the Tenants were within their rights to keep the flags. I am not satisfied this singular comment amounts to a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I am also not convinced these separate communications, taking place more than three months apart, are connected to each other. They relate to completely different issues and do not in my view, amount to a course of conduct taken by the Landlords against the Tenants. While no doubt an annoyance to the Tenants, I am not convinced the Tenants have established these interactions, taken alone or together, amount to harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference.

For the reasons above, I do not find the Tenants have established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords conduct considered in this application amounts to a breach of section 22 or 23 of the Act. As such, the T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application
The Tenants’ T6 application alleges the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations. The issues concern mold in the bathroom, excessive dust, and poor water quality.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. [name]

The Tenant testified that they had originally noticed mold in the master washroom in January 2024 and that after it had grown over time, told the Landlords about the issue on September 24, 2024 during an inspection because the issue had simply passed her by in comparison to other things.

The Tenant submitted a letter sent to them from the Landlords’ Legal Representative at that time on September 24, 2024 following the inspection. The letter acknowledges the presence of mold in the master bedroom washroom and advises the Tenants to open the washroom window and remove the indoor greenhouse and plants which is likely causing the mold issue. &LTB-T-086714-24

The Tenants submitted photos taken on September 30, 2024 showing the presence of mold on the ceiling of the washroom shower. The photos show several dark spots on the ceiling. I would describe the amount of mold as more than minimal but less than moderate.

On October 28, 2024, the Landlords emailed the Tenants advising them that a specialist will attend the unit on November 1, 2024 to assess the air quality and the presence of mold. The Landlords submitted the November 11, 2024 report from the specialist confirming the presence of mold and providing solution suggestions such as cleaning the affected areas, removing the greenhouse plant growing area and ensuring ventilation in the affected areas.

Ms. [name]name] testified that the report shows the presence of mold was essentially the fault of the Tenants. During cross examination, I asked Ms. [name] if any steps had been taken to address the mold in the washroom and she stated the Landlords had made three attempts to enter the unit in mid December 2024, January 15, 2025 and January 17, 2025 to assess what needed to be done to resolve the issue but that they were denied entry by the Tenants.

The Landlords submitted no notices of entry given to the Tenants showing they intended to enter the unit on these dates to assess or remediate the mold. In addition, Ms. [name] gave no explanation why the Landlords needed additional assessments in mid December 2024 given the recommended solutions provided in their November 11, 2024 report.

Based on the evidence presented, including the letter from the Landlords’ former Legal Representative on September 24, 2024 and the Landlords’ own email on October 28, 2024 acknowledging the presence of mold in the washroom, I am satisfied the Tenants have established there was mold in the master bedroom washroom.

The Landlords were aware of the mold issue on September 24, 2024 and provided no reasonable explanation as to why, despite this knowledge, they were still only sending people to assess the mold in mid December 2024, two and half months after they were originally notified of the issue, and more than a month after they received their own November 11, 2024 report. No explanation was provided as to why it took more than a month to have a specialist attend the unit to confirm an issue they had already acknowledged twice earlier in emails to the Tenants.

The amount of mold depicted in the Tenants’ photos was not extreme. In my view, the delay in taking any steps to address the problem does not amount to a reasonable response as contemplated in Onyskiw. As such, this portion of the Tenants’ application is granted.

The Tenants sought a rent abatement of $796.00 representing 5% of the monthly rent for the four-month period between October 1, 2024 and January 31, 2025 when the mold was present and unresolved. Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

The Tenant testified her family was sick with respiratory issues and the mold affected their breathing. However, the Tenant submitted no medical documentation showing a &LTB-T-086714-24 connection between their illnesses and mold. Without more, I am not convinced on a balance of probabilities the Tenants have shown the washroom mold made them sick or caused breathing issues.

The Tenants acknowledged they began moving out of the rental unit in December 2024 having purchased a home. The Tenant stated that while they continued to be at the rental unit until the tenancy ended, their belongings had been moved out by the beginning of January 2025. For these reasons, the Landlords position was that any rent abatement should be limited since there would be little impact to the Tenants once they stopped living in the rental unit. The Landlords also submitted the Tenants contributed to the mold issue by failing to open the window and having an indoor greenhouse.

The Landlords’ maintenance obligations are not suspended because they believe the Tenants have cause or have contributed to an issue. The Landlords were free to serve an N5 notice and file an L2 application seeking compensation for their claims.

The presence of mold in a home is a commonly known health risk. The Tenants were entitled to a home free of mold and the Landlords failed to provide this to them for the remedy period requested. I accept the area of the rental unit affected was minimal and I find the Tenants have proven minimal impact to them from the presence of mold, including the period they were not actively living in the unit. However, in my view, these circumstances are reflected in the minimal abatement sought by the Tenants for the issue and I find it reasonable. As such, the Tenants will be granted a $796.00 rent abatement because of the mold and this amount will be set off against the rent arrears owing. Water

The Tenant testified they noticed an oily film in the water and told the Landlords about the issue on August 27, 2024 in an email. This email was submitted into evidence. The Tenant explained their family had been ill and that animals on the property had died for no apparent reason.

The Landlords responded to the Tenants on August 29, 2024 acknowledging the Tenants’ concern and that the Tenants have sent a water sample for testing. The Landlords ask the results to be shared and advise the Tenants drink bottled water in the meantime.

The Tenants submitted the results of a water test performed by Public Health Ontario on August 21, 2024. The test shows 1 unit per 100ml of coliform. The test results explain that any amount of coliform may be indicative of water contamination. The water test showed no E. coli present. The test results were provided to the Landlord by email on September 4, 2024.

It was not disputed the parties discussed having the Tenant [name] install a UV filter system at the Landlords’ expense but ultimately decided the Landlords would have the installation done. The Landlords submitted an email from the Water Depot from September 9, 2024 confirming [name] had attended the property to assess installing the UV system and that the installation would take place on September 13, 2024. It was not disputed the UV filtration system was installed in the rental unit on September 16, 2024. The Landlords submitted an invoice from the Water Depot in the amount of $1,694.99. &LTB-T-086714-24

The Tenant testified they still noticed the oily film on the water after the UV system had been installed. The Tenants submitted photos taken on September 16, 2024, after the installation had been done showing a pot of water on the stove. The Tenant stated the photos show this oily film is present. I reviewed the photos both during the hearing and afterwards before writing this order and I could not discern an oily substance on the water in the pot. The Tenants submitted no other photos of the water after this date and acknowledged no other water tests had been done by them.

The Tenant testified they told the Landlords on September 24, 2024 that the issue with the water persisted. The Landlords had the water tested by Ontario Public Health based on a water sample taken on September 24, 2024. The water was analyzed on September 25, 2024 and show 0 units of coliform per 100ml. This test is identical to the one done by the Tenants on August 21, 2024, apart from the results now showing no coliforms present.

Based on the evidence presented, I am satisfied the Landlords responded to the water issue in a reasonable manner. Within 20 days the water had been tested, the rental unit had been assessed by the Water Depot for the installation of a UV system and the installation was completed. The emails show the Landlords also responded to the Tenants’ concerns in a timely manner and took their concerns seriously. With any issue, there is an inherent time requirement needed to assess and resolve it and I find the 20 days that elapsed here was not unreasonable in the circumstances considering what was done.

I also find on a balance of probabilities, the steps taken by the Landlords resolved the issue. While the Tenants claim otherwise, the best evidence I have to consider is the most recent evidence that was presented. This was the water test conducted by Ontario Public Health on September 25, 2024, showing no coliform detected.

This is the Tenants’ application and it is their burden to prove their claims. The Tenants had no other tests performed and submitted no other evidence showing the water was unsafe after the UV system was installed. While there may have been an oily film on the water, nothing was submitted showing the water was actually unsafe and an ongoing maintenance issue.
For all of these reasons, this claim is denied. Air Quality-Dust

The Tenant testified that she observed a significant amount of dust constantly coming from the furnace vents when it was operating. She stated this was seen in all areas of the home and the Tenants and their family had respiratory issues and were constantly getting sick. Concerned with the air quality, they put an air filtration system in the middle of the home. . The Tenants emailed the Landlords on August 27, 2024 advising them of their concern with the air quality in the rental unit.

The Tenant stated the Landlords had the furnace inspected on August 30, 2024 and the filter was changed however this did not resolve the issue. The Tenant’s testimony was they told the Landlords the issue persisted multiple times, including on September 9, 2024 and September 24, 2024. Despite this, the issue persisted until the tenancy ended. The Tenants did not submit any corroborating evidence showing follow up complaints were made to the Landlords. &LTB-T-086714-24

Ms. [name]name] acknowledged the Tenants complaint about the air quality in the rental unit. She agreed they sent a furnace technician on August 30, 2024 and that the filter was changed. Ms. [name]name] could not recall that further complaints were made about the air quality after the technician’s presence on August 30, 2024.

Again, this is the Tenants’ application and it is their burden to prove their claims. Despite the Tenant’s testimony about their experiences and concerns, no corroborating evidence was submitted showing the air quality in the unit was unsafe, falling below any health or safety standards. There were no photos of excessive dust in the air. The Tenants submitted no photos of dust or particle accumulation on furniture or other belongings over a defined period of time. There was no medical evidence provided linking any of the reported household illnesses to poor air quality.

While the Tenant was keen to review the air quality testing the Landlords had performed and provided in their evidence, I do not find this report assists the Tenants’ claim. While the inspector provided suggestions to improve air quality such as properly sized furnace filters, the November 11, 2024 report states: In conversation with the tenants they claimed that there was no one suffering from any health problems that may be affected by the quality of the air in the home. They did complain that some itchy throat and a mild case of dry Sinuses. Through our investigation there was no indication of airborne contaminates that may affect the occupants of the home. We would like to point out some areas of concern that may assist you in having an even more comfortable living environment for your family and assist you in maintaining your home.
