In the absence of some supporting evidence showing an abnormal amount of dust or particles were present in the rental unit, I am not satisfied the Tenants have shown on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords breach section 20 of the Act with respect to the air quality in the unit. Claiming an issue exists in not sufficient to support a finding it does exist, particularly when tangible evidence of the issue is easily obtainable for the Board’s consideration. For these reasons, this claim is denied.

The Tenants sought remedies for moving and storage expenses however, since I have already dismissed the T2 application, these amounts are denied. The rent abatement granted will be deducted from the amount the Tenants owe the Landlords in my order below.
ordered: The total amount the Tenants owe the Landlords pursuant to the L1 application (LTB-L- 095227-24) is $8,071.11. This amount represents the arrears of rent owing to January 31, 2025 and costs. The rent deposit and interest owing on the rent deposit have been deducted from this amount.

The total amount the Landlords owe the Tenants for a rent abatement pursuant to the T6 application (LTB-T-086714-24) is $796.00. This amount will be set off against the amount set out in paragraph 1 of this order. &LTB-T-086714-24
The total amount the Tenants owe the Landlords is $7,275.11.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlords the full amount owing by June 27, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlords the full amount owing by June 27, 2026, the Tenants will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants’ T2 application is dismissed. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the to Tenant the amount of $54.45. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that she paid a rent deposit in the amount of $750.00 on or about May 7, 2025, based on an assignment of a lease to the period ending August 31, 2025. She said that she vacated the unit on or about August 31, 2025, left the keys on the counter and notified the Landlord via text message. The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence.

The Tenant testified that she received the rent deposit from the Landlord in the amount of $750.00 since she vacated the unit, however, she is seeking the interest of $6.45 on the rent deposit, which was unpaid to the date of the hearing.
The Landlord admitted that she did not pay the interest owing on the rent deposit.
The Landlord testified that as a result of the damage to the rental unit, she did not owe any money to the Tenant, and in fact, the Tenant owed her money for the damages.

Although the Landlord alleges that there were damages in the rental unit as a result of the Tenant, this application is brough by the Tenant and not the Landlord, and no consideration was given to any alleged damages on part of the Landlord. The Landlord also testified that they did not file an application to obtain an order against the Tenant for damages to the rental unit.

Based on the evidence of the parties, and on the Landlord’s own testimony, I am satisfied that the Landlord retained money illegally when they failed to pay the Tenant the interest owing on the rent deposit on or about August 31, 2025, the date the Tenant vacated the unit.
As such, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant the interest on the rent deposit in the amount of $6.45.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $54.45. This amount represents: • $6.45 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. An Adjudicative Case Conference was held by video conference on May 14, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the case conference. As of 10:30 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the case conference although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. A hearing was held without the Landlord and the decision was based only on the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the tenancy terminated on November 1, 2025.

Unground parking garages are enclosed environments with constant vehicle traffic which makes them natural accumulation points for dirt and grime. As such, it is completely normal for an unground parking garage to have dust, sand and road salt. However, based on the uncontested evidence before me, which included videos of the parking garage, I am satisfied that there was excessive dust in the garage which created air that was visibly hazy that more likely than not was due to a lack of routine cleaning, such as sweeping and power washing.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2025. The Tenants reported their concerns to the Landlord on multiple occasions in September 2025 but received no response. When Tenant [name] (‘FJF’) complained to the Landlord that the excessive dust in the garage was affecting her breathing on October 16, 2025, the Landlord suggested she wear a mask. The Landlord made no indication that they believed the excessive dust was an issue or that they would take steps to address the issue.

I am satisfied the Landlord’s failure to address the excessive dust substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. FJF testified that as she is asthmatic and has several health issues, she was unable to enter the garage to access her car. I accept the Tenants had no alternatives but to vacate the rental unit as the Landlord refused to take necessary steps to address their concerns. As such, I find it reasonable to order the tenancy end on November 1, 2025, the date the Tenants gave vacant possession to the Landlord.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants ended on November 1, 2025.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $48.00 for the cost of filing their application with the Board.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Oluokun (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The parties agreed the Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 16, 2024. The Landlord only sought the rent arrears to the date the Tenants vacated. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit.
The lawful rent is $3,200.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants agreed they have not paid any rent for the period from August 1, 2024 to December 16, 2024.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to December 16, 2024 are $14,483.36.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,200.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $90.96 is owing to the Tenants for the period from October 28, 2023 to December 16, 2024. T6 Application - Maintenance

As explained below, the Tenants proved their claims on a balance of probabilities,. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $4,666.00 for a rent abatement, out-of- pocket expenses and the cost of filing both the T2 and T6 applications. These amounts shall be deducted from the amount of rent arrears owing by the Tenants to the Landlord.

The Tenant, [name] (‘OO’) testified that he initially viewed the house in October 2023. OO testified that he agreed to rent the rental unit with the expectation that the rental unit would be painted and cleaned before he moved into the rental unit. OO testified that when the tenancy commenced on November 30, 2023, the house had not been painted or cleaned.

OO testified about the following maintenance issues: a. The fridge had damage to a number of shelves and had not been cleaned prior to the Tenants moving into the rental unit. The fridge was also not properly cooling items and was not sealing properly. b. Cosmetic damage to surfaces including dents, holes and stains on the walls and main entrance door, washer and dryer and broken wall plate covers throughout the rental unit. [name] infestation in the rental unit. [name] in the backyard of the rental unit. e. Bathroom kitchen and sinks clogged. f. Non-functional electrical outlets in the rental unit. g. Smoke detector not functioning. Fridge

OO testified that the fridge was not repaired or replaced for the duration of the tenancy. OO testified that when they moved into the rental unit, the fridge contained food belonging to the prior Tenants of the rental unit and had not been cleaned. OO testified that several of the fridge shelves were damaged prior to the Tenants moving in and had not been repaired or replaced.

In an email from Tenants to the Landlord dated June 5, 2024, the Tenants state that the fridge is “not functioning well, is not cold, and the door is not locking properly. I think this was not showing for me earlier because it was winter. It is hot now, and water is dripping all over my food in the fridge…”
The Landlord testified that the fridge was two years old when the Tenants moved into the rental unit and was in working condition.

The Landlord testified that they sent multiple repair technicians to the rental unit to address issues with the fridge but that the technicians reported no issues in the operation of the refrigerator.

The Landlord further testified that on August 12, 2024, they sent a technician to inspect the refrigerator and, as per the invoice from [name] dated August 12, 2024, the technician noted that the freezer was packed too fully with food causing the drain to be blocked causing frost build-up in the freezer section. The invoice further states that the fridge and drain need to be cleaned.
There was no supporting evidence that the Landlord had sent any repair technician in before August 12, 2024, nor did the Landlord testify about any of the other dates repair technicians were sent.

I was satisfied based on the evidence before me, that the Landlord had been made aware that the Tenants were experiencing issues with the refrigerator on June 5, 2024 and there was no evidence provided as to why the Landlord would have waited two months to send a repair technician to address the issue.
OO testified that they incurred costs of $250.00 per week to replace food that spoiled as a result of not having a properly functioning fridge.

Further, there was no evidence that the Landlord ever repaired or replaced the broken shelving in the fridge during the tenancy. While the Tenants were able to clean out their own fridge and were able to use the fridge, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the fridge in good working order.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
In this case, I was not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the maintenance issue with the fridge reasonably in the circumstances.

While the Tenants requested compensation for the costs of replacing spoiled food, no supporting evidence was led of the Tenants’ expenses incurred as a result of the spoiled food. I also do not find it credible that the Tenants would continue to incur costs of $250.00 per week in spoiled food but would wait until June 2024 to put the issues with the fridge into writing to the Landlord. While I am satisfied that there were maintenance issues specifically related to the bins in the fridge since the outset of the tenancy based on OO’s testimony and photo evidence, I was not satisfied that there were cooling issues since the outset of the tenancy as the Tenants allege. Rather, I find it more likely, on a balance of probabilities, that the issue arose closer to June 2024 when the Tenants complained to the Landlord in writing.

As a result, I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to rent abatement of 5% for the period of December 2023 through to May 31, 2024 and a rent abatement of 15% for the period of June 1, 2024 through to August 31, 2024. The total rent abatement for the fridge issue is therefore $2,400.00. Holes in Surfaces Throughout the Rental Unit

OO testified that since the outset of the tenancy there were issues with holes and damage in the walls, doors and surfaces throughout the rental unit as the Landlord had not patched holes or painted the unit prior to the Tenants moving into the rental unit.
The Tenants’ email dated June 5, 2024 further addresses the ongoing cosmetic issues with surfaces throughout the rental unit.
The Tenants entered into evidence photos depicting the visible wear and damage to the walls, main entrance door, and fixtures such as wall plate covers throughout the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that while they were aware of the issues, they had not been able to access the rental unit as the Tenants were unwilling to cooperate with repairs to the walls, doors and fixtures of the rental unit.
While the Landlord testified they repaired the walls and surfaces of the rental unit, no supporting evidence was provided by the Landlord.

I preferred the evidence of the Tenants that the Landlord failed to repair and maintain the walls, door and fixtures such as wall plate covers throughout the rental unit for the duration of the tenancy. The Tenants’ evidence was supported by documentary evidence including their June 5, 2024 email and their photo evidence. I did not find the Landlord’s explanation to be reasonable or credible with regards to the repairs to surfaces throughout the rental unit.
I was satisfied that the Tenant has proven that there were a large number of holes, cracked wall plates and physical damage to the surfaces in the rental unit.

OO testified that due to these issues they were not fully able to enjoy the unit and felt embarrassment and were unable to have people visit or stay at the rental unit due to the condition of the rental unit.

I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of $1,920.00 which represents a 5% rent abatement for a 12-month period from December 1, 2023 to December 31, 2024 due to the ongoing deficiencies with the walls, door and wall plates throughout the rental unit. [name]

OO testified that in approximately March 2024, she began hearing the sounds of a bird inside the rental unit. OO testified that he informed the Landlord in approximately April 2024 that birds may have nested inside the house. OO testified that the Landlord sent somebody to inspect in May 2024 and was advised there were no birds inside the house. OO submits that birds were entering through the house’s external dryer vent cover. OO testified that the Landlord sent a second person to inspect the vent covers and that the issue was addressed by the Landlord in May 2024.
OO entered into evidence photos of the dryer vent cover covered in bird droppings.

The Tenants’ email dated June 5, 2024 states “in the bird’s situation that I messaged you about on the 17th of May with pictures, a gentleman came to the premises last week and said you sent him to see what was going on…”
OO testified that noises from the birds was ongoing throughout the night for the month of May 2024.
While the Tenants’ letter suggests the issue was ongoing as of the email dated June 5, 2024, OO’s testimony was that the issue was resolved in May 2024.

The Landlord testified that once they were informed about a potential bird or birds within the rental unit, they sent somebody to inspect the dryer vent and while they noted no birds had entered the dryer vent, they installed a net over the vent cover to prevent birds from entering or defecating on the vent cover in May 2024.

With regards to the alleged bird infestation, the Tenants’ evidence on dates they informed the Landlord of the bird issue were vague. I found neither the Landlord’s nor the Tenants’ testimony to be more credible than the others with regards to the timeline of the bird infestation issue. It was uncontested by the parties that the individuals sent to inspect the vent had reported no birds had entered the dryer vent. I was not satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenants have proven that the Landlord failed to maintain the dryer vent or address the alleged bird infestation in a timely manner. As a result, the Tenants’ request for an abatement on this ground is denied. Clogged Sinks

OO testified that the kitchen and bathroom sink were clogged since moving into the rental unit and that this as reported numerous times to the Landlord since moving into the rental unit. The Tenants did not provide any supporting evidence such as written complaints or photos of the clogged sink, nor did the Tenants provide any evidence about any dates and times they communicated these issues to the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that they were made aware of a clogged sink on January 18, 2024 and had advised the Tenants to use a drain cleaner. The Landlord testified that there were no further complaints about the drainage issues. The Landlord also testified that they sent a technician to inspect the sinks and that there were no issues noted by their technician. However, no supporting evidence was provided by the Landlord such as inspection reports or photos.

I was not satisfied that the Tenants established that there were any issues with the functioning of the sinks in the rental unit. As a result, the Tenants’ request for an abatement for this issue is denied. Non-functional Electrical Outlets

OO testified that most of the electrical outlets throughout the rental unit have not been working since the outset of the tenancy. The Tenants testified that a by-law officer had inspected the outlets in the rental unit.

The Tenants again did not provide any dates and times of any communications about issues with wall outlets either in their application or by way of verbal testimony. While OO testified that a by-law officer had inspected the outlets, no inspection report or supporting evidence was provided and the Tenants’ testimony about the by-law officer’s findings were hearsay evidence and given no weight.

The Landlord testified they were made aware on one occasion of issues with the wall outlets in the rental unit, but sent a certified electrician to inspect on December 9, 2024. The Landlord testified that the electrician had informed them that there were no issues with the electrical outlets.
An invoice from North York Electrical Contractors Inc dated December 9, 2024 was entered as evidence of the service call made for the electrical outlets by the Landlord.

While I accept, based on the evidence before me, that the Tenants complained of issues with the outlet at least once, I was not satisfied that the Tenants has established that the Landlord failed to maintain the electrical outlets in the rental unit in working condition. As a result, the Tenants’ request for an abatement on this ground is denied. [name]. OO testified the Landlord has failed to maintain the lawn at the rental unit. OO testified that the parties had agreed that the Tenants would be responsible for snow removal at the rental unit but that there was no discussion of who was responsible for lawn maintenance at the rental unit. 52. The Landlord did not deny that they had not maintained the lawn of the rental unit but testified that as per paragraph 18 of the lease agreement, which was entered into evidence by the Landlord, “[the] Tenant is responsible for snow removal, lawn and backyard maintenance.” 53. There was no evidence that the lawn maintenance clause in the lease was void under section 4(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The City of Brampton’s By- law 45-2025 states that lawn and garden maintenance are the responsibility of the “owner or occupant.” 54. The rental unit was the entire house and the lawn was for the Tenants’ exclusive use. The lease agreement stated that the Tenants were responsible for lawn and backyard maintenance. As the Tenants were responsible for the lawn maintenance, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have met the burden of proof to demonstrate that the Landlord has breached its maintenance obligations with regards to lawn maintenance. Smoke Detector 55. OO testified she informed the Landlord that there was no working smoke detector since the outset of the tenancy. The Tenants did not lead any evidence about dates or times this issue was reported to the Landlord or any supporting evidence such as photos or inspection reports. 56. The Landlord testified that they were made aware of the issue with the smoke detector and that the issue was addressed by the electrician from North York Electrical Contractors Inc., on December 9, 2024. 57. I was not satisfied that the Tenants have met the burden of proof to show that the Landlord did not properly maintain or repair the smoke detector in the rental unit. The Tenants did not provide any specific dates or times of any complaints. I found the Landlord’s evidence that the smoke detector was promptly addressed to be more credible. As a result, the request for an abatement on this ground is denied. T2 Application – Substantial Interference Cleanliness of the Rental Unit 58. OO testified that the Landlord’s failure to provide the rental unit in a state of ordinary cleanliness caused them to incur out-of-pocket expenses of $250.00 to clean the house when the Tenants took possession of the rental unit. 59. OO testified that the rental unit was not cleaned when they moved into the rental unit and as a result, they had to purchase cleaning supplies at the cost of $250.00 to clean the rental unit at the commencement of the tenancy. 60. Photos of the unit at the outset of the tenancy were provided into evidence by the Tenants. 61. The Landlord testified that as the Tenants as supposed to move into the rental unit on December 1, 2024 but asked for possession of the rental unit a day earlier, the Landlord was unable to clean the rental unit prior to the Tenants moving in. 62. I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to provide the rental unit in a state of ordinary cleanliness and that this substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I was further satisfied that the Tenants incurred out-of-pocket expense at the outset of the tenancy to clean the rental unit. While the Tenants did not provide any evidence of their costs, I find the requested amount of $250.00 for out-of-pocket expenses for cleaning products and equipment to be reasonable in the circumstances. An order will issue for the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $250.00 for the out-of-pocket cleaning expenses. Substantial Interference Due to [name] 63. While I am satisfied that maintenance issues may result in substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, as the maintenance issues were addressed in the T6 portion of the application above, the request for abatement as a result of substantial interference due to the maintenance issues is duplicative. As remedies were ordered above for the maintenance issues, the Tenants’ request for further abatement as a result of substantial interference for the maintenance issue is denied. Remedies 64. As stated above, I find that a rent abatement of $6,240.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. 65. I also find that the Tenants incurred the following costs and out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord's breach as a result of failing to clean the rental unit prior to providing possession to the Tenants. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $250.00 for these out-of-pocket expenses. 66. The Tenants are also entitled to the filing fees for the cost of filing both the T2 and the T6 application in the amount of $96.00.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated as of December 16, 2024, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $6,712.40. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit, the costs of filing the T2 & T6 applications, the out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Tenants, and the rent abatement awarded to the Tenants are deducted from the amount owing by the Tenants. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before June 20, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the to the Tenants the amount of $1,000.00
It was uncontested that the Tenants paid the Landlord a $1,000.00 refundable key deposit on April 30, 2025.
It was also uncontested that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on or about August 31, 2025, and that on the same day, the Tenants returned the keys and fob to the Landlord.
It was also uncontested that the Landlord did not return the refundable key deposit to the Tenants after they returned the keys and fob on August 31, 2025.
The Landlord testified that although she received the keys and the fob from the Tenants, she alleges there were damages to the fob, and the Tenants owe her money as a result.

S ection 135 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’), states the following: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act.

Based on uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected a charge in the amount of $1,000.00 when the Tenants paid for the key deposit on April 30, 2025. The Tenants returned the keys to the Landlord on August 31, 2025, when they moved out of the unit. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenants for the illegal amount retained in the amount of $1,000.00.

Although the Landlord alleges that there were damages to the fob when it was returned, this application is brough by the Tenants and not the Landlord, and no consideration was given to any alleged damages. The Landlord also testified that they did not file an application to obtain an order against the Tenants for any damages.
This order contains all of the reasons and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,053.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the illegal charge retained. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. This application was originally heard on April 7 ,2026. It was reconvened by videoconference on May 15, 2026. Only the Landlord’s representative, [name], attended the hearing on May 15, 2026. Mohnish Aggerwal appeared as a witness for the Landlord. The hearing was scheduled as a bilingual hearing, but as both the Landlord’s representative and the witness spoke English, the hearing on May 15, 2026 was conducted in English. The order will be published in both French and English. Tenant was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. The Landlord’s Representative advised the Member that the Tenant had emailed the Board to an outgoing mailbox only two days before the hearing to request an adjournment. There was no record of the request in the Portal. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Landlord’s evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Since the [name] is not Valid, the Act does not apply
At the hearing on April 7, 2026 the Landlord brought a motion to dismiss the application by alleging that the tenancy was not a bona fide tenancy.
The matter was reconvened on May 15, 2026 to address this issue.

The Landlord pointed to the following indicia in the lease (Exhibit 1) that cumulatively suggest the Tenant created the tenancy to undermine mortgage proceedings: • The length of the tenancy is 20 years, and was never registered on title, per Bank of Montreal v. Smith 2008 CanLii 28435 (ONSC) and s. 44 of the Land Titles Act RSO 1990 c. L 5. • The rent is $500 per month, which is well below market rent and insufficient to pay the mortgage on the property. • The Tenancy commenced on June 28, 2023 and is between 8557349 Canada Inc., as Landlord, the directors of whom are the Tenant’s son, [name] and daughter-in-law, [name], and the Tenant, his wife and daughter. • The property is a semi-detached townhouse and the same company signed a lease for market rent at $2,100 with the neighbouring tenants. This suggests family favouritism. • It appears the tenancy began on June 28, 2023 before the default judgment on March 22, 2024 against 8557349 Canada Inc and [name] and [name]. The Landlord suggested that creating the tenancy beforehand might have been a way for the Tenant and his son to attempt to undermine mortgage proceedings.

In addition to these concerns, I note the following irregularities in the lease: • There is an annual rent discount worth 3 months’ rent, which would make it difficult to pay the mortgage on the property • Rent was to be paid in cash 6. [name], the owner of Subhkin Management, which assisted the Landlord in preparing the property for seizure and sale, testified that he attended the property on May 13, 2024 to ascertain if there were any tenants or occupants on site. He was accompanied by his brother, Sandeep, who wrote the report that was admitted into evidence. (Exhibit 2). He testified that on that day, he knocked on the door and people who identified themselves as Mr. and [name] answered and confirmed they were not tenants but lived there with their son, [name]. [name] confirmed that these same people were present at the eviction on December 11, 2024. [name] further confirmed that the man he saw on both of those occasions was the same man who identified himself as the Tenant at the hearing on April 7, 2026. Therefore, I find Mr. and [name] to, in fact be [name] and his wife, Nadia Edmond. 7. I find that Mr. and [name] made representations to [name] that they were not tenants on May 13, 2024, that they merely lived with their son, [name]. 8. The Tenant did not attend the hearing to clarify any of these points on May 15, 2026 and did not file a rescheduling request on consent at least 5 days in advance of the hearing. Therefore, the evidence I have before me from the Landlord is uncontested. Analysis: 9. It is important to remember that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, is remedial legislation. Section 1 of the Act provides that: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. 10 Given the purpose of the Act, any claim that the Act does not apply has to be examined carefully to ensure that protections provided by the Legislature to residential tenants are not easily avoided (Grenadier (Tenants of v. We-Care Retirement Homes of Canada, [1993] O.J. No.1550 (Div. Court.)). A liberal interpretation of the exemptions from the Act would undermine the objectives of the Act. 11 In making findings on an application, section 202 of the Act requires me to determine the real substance of all transactions and activities pertaining to a rental unit with respect to this tenancy. 12 The onus or burden of proving the Act does not apply falls on the person claiming the exemption on a balance of probabilities. As the Landlord is claiming the exemption, the onus is on them to prove it on a balance of probabilities. 13 Individually, these aspects of the lease might not be enough to suggest the lack of a bona fide tenancy, but together they form a matrix of strong evidence. 14 At the original hearing on April 7, 2026, the Tenant was vague in his responses when it was put to him whether he had a valid tenancy, or if he had made representations to [name] about the purpose of the tenancy. 15 I find that re-examining the lease, in concert with [name] testimony leads me to conclude that the tenancy was not bona fide on a balance of probabilities. The fact that the Tenant failed to appear to explain is somewhat curious given that it is his application, the importance of the issue and the impending consequences, and the subsequent determination of the rest of his claims against the Respondent. 16 I therefore find that the Landlord has proven the allegation on a balance of probabilities and the Act does not apply. 17 As a result, the Board has no jurisdiction to hear the Tenant’s claims, so the matter shall be dismissed.
ordered: The application be dismissed. June 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: he Tenants or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (LTB-T-088565-23, hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’).1 The Landlord also applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenants because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owe (LTB-L-045503-24, hereafter referred to as the ‘L1 Application’).2 On September 18, 2024, the T2 Application and the L1 Application were directed to be heard together.3 The T2 Application and the L1 Application were heard by videoconference on April 20, 2026. Although the parties had not received a notice of hearing with respect to the L1 Application, both the Landlord and the Tenants confirmed that they were prepared to proceed with both applications on April 20, 2026. The Tenants [name], the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, Stuart [name], and the Landlord's Witness, [name], attended the hearing. 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 69 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 3 Rule 1.6c) of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. File Numbers: LTB-T-088565-23 LTB-L-045503-24
reasons: The T2 Application started to be heard by the Board on January 4, 2024.4

Pursuant to the Endorsement date October 21, 2024, the Tenants and the Landlord were advised that the Board Member who had started to hear the T2 Application on January 4, 2024, was unable to complete the proceedings.
The T2 Application was therefore directed to be heard de novo, alongside the L1 Application.

For greater clarity, a matter being heard de novo (i.e. heard anew) “is treated as if no previous decision had been made: there is no presumption of the correctness or validity of any prior finding, recommendation, or conclusion.”5
As such, the T2 Application would be considered independently, without deference to any earlier analysis about the matter.6 Board’s Jurisdiction

At the start of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue with respect to the Board’s jurisdiction, and ability to hear the applications , as they submit that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply to the relationship between the Landlord and the Tenants in light of the Landlord’s child and the Tenants living in accommodations requiring them to share a kitchen and bathroom.7 a) Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that they are the owner of the rental unit, which they acquired during the month of June 2001.

The Landlord described the rental unit , at the time of the purchase, as being a 2-bedroom unit, equipped with one (1) bathroom and one (1) kitchen. In 2019, the Landlord renovated the rental unit to add a bedroom.

The Landlord stated that they resided in the rental unit following its acquisition in 2001, and that their child, [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘M.N’) proceeded to move into the rental unit with them in 2004.
The Landlord indicated that since 2004, M.N has continuously resided in the rental unit. The Landlord, however, moved out at some point in 2019.

The Landlord stated that in addition to their child residing in the rental unit, they also rent the other two (2) bedrooms individually. 4 Interim order LTB-T-088565-23, issued on February 16, 2024. 5 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “de novo.” 6 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “de novo.” 7 Section 5i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. While the Landlord was travelling abroad, and as M.N was residing in the premises, they directed M.N to collect rent from the other Tenants, and deal with maters related to the tenancy and the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the agreement between the Landlord and M.N dated October 1, 2016 (DOC-5010015, page 36 of 74; Exhibit 1).

Under cross-examination, M.N did not recall the date that the Landlord moved out of the rental unit.

The Landlord submits that as the Landlord’s child was residing in the same accommodation as the Tenants , and as the Tenants and the Landlord’s child were required to share communal areas such as the kitchen and the bathroom, the Act does not apply to the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants. The Landlord clarified that they had only filed the L1 Application in the alternative that the Board concluded that the Act did apply. They expressed an intent to withdraw the L1 Application if the Board concluded that the Act did not apply. b) Tenants’ Evidence
S.G testified that they moved into the rental unit during the month of March 2020, and that M.N moved into the premises four or five months later.

S.G indicated that at the time they moved into the rental unit, another female tenant was also occupying one of the bedrooms. [name] proceeded to move into the unit upon the female tenant’s departure.

Under cross-examination, S.G reiterated that following M.N’s move into the rental unit, they were required to share communal spaces with them, such as a kitchen and a bathroom.
Under cross-examination, S.G agreed that they were unable to enter other bedrooms of the unit which were not assigned to them.
Under cross -examination, S.G did not recall ever seeing M.N move in any personal belongings into the rental unit.

Under cross-examination, S.G agreed that they had previously been residing in the same residential complex, and therefore knew the Landlord in passing as the Landlord also resided in the complex. File Numbers: LTB-T-088565-23 LTB-L-045503-24
Under cross-examination, S.G agreed that they knew that the Landlord had a child prior to moving into the rental unit.

The Tenants submit that, as a result of the time which has elapsed since the original filing of the T2 Application, here may have been some discrepancies with respect to the dates surrounding the events described by the Tenants.

Referring to [name] v. Bindlish , the Tenants indicated that the fact that the Landlord’s child moved into the rental unit after the Tenants had already moved in does not lead to the Act from ceasing to apply to the tenancy.8

Referring to [name] v. [name], the Tenants further state that the unilateral decision by the Landlord to have their child move into the rental unit does not lead to the Tenants losing their protections under the Act.9 c) Analysis

Section 5i) of the Act reads as follows: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

In Cowie v. Bindlish, the Divisional Court considered whether a landlord’s intention to and subsequent move into a property after the start of a tenancy, such that the tenant was then required to share a bathroom and kitchen with them, could oust the application of the Act. The Court determined that the relationship between the landlord and tenant was characterized from the beginning of the tenancy and that a unilateral action could not change the terms of the tenancy.

In [name] v. [name], the Divisional Court held that “occasional stays” did not equate to one using the premising as a “principal residence” and that such an occasional or transient occupation of the premises would not strip a tenant of their rights under the Act, as doing so would defeat the purpose of the Act.

I also note that in [name] v. [name], the Divisional Court held the law in Cowie had been correctly applied as the terms at the outset of the tenancy were examined and it was found the Act did not apply while the tenant was required to share a kitchen and bathroom with the landlord’s daughter.10 8 Cowie v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628 (CanLII), paragraph 16. 9 [name] v. [name], 2022 ONSC 3253 (CanLII), paragraphs 6 and 7. 10 McKnight v. [name], 2022 ONSC 3617 (CanLII). File Numbers: LTB-T-088565-23 LTB-L-045503-24
In this case, it is not in dispute that M.N is the Landlord’s child and that the Tenants and M.N resided concurrently in the premises and shared communal areas, such as a kitchen and a bathroom.
The questions before me therefore become, when M.N moved into the premises, and whether or not the Act applied at the inception of the tenancy between the Tenants and the Landlord.

I accept the Landlord’s position that the Landlord’s child, M.N, has been consistently residing in the rental unit since 2004, and that the premises has represented their principal residence since their move-in. Indeed, the testimony from the Landlord and M.N was consistent and credible and supported by contemporaneous documentary evidence which reflected M.N’s address throughout the years (Exhibits 2 to 6).

I note that the authenticity of these documents was not disputed (Exhibits 2 to 6), and while the Tenants sought to cast doubt as to their relevance, I find it unlikely that the Landlord and their child would have devised a plan to trick various companies and government agencies over the span of sixteen (16) years with the intent to retroactively seek to strip the application of the Act to the rental unit in case of a conflict or dispute.

Moreover, contrary to the Landlord and M.N, I note that the evidence led by S.G was riddled with inconsistencies, such as their account of their move in date changing no less than three (3) times ( June 1, 2020, according to their T2 Application filed on November 7, 2023; May 2021 based on their testimony in prior proceedings before the Board, and March 2020).
The Tenants could not provide a reasonable explanation for such discrepancies, beyond pointing to the passage of time between the filing of the application and the matter being heard anew.

Furthermore, I find that the part of the Tenants’ testimony with respect to never seeing M.N move belongings to the rental unit supports the Landlord’s assertion that M.N was residing in the premises prior to the Tenants’ move.

Although the Tenants sought to cast doubt with respect to M.N’s testimony surrounding their arrest and potential incarceration, they limited their submissions to general statements that were not supported by any evidence or details. I find that the Tenants failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim that M.N only moved into the premises after their release.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlord’s child was occupying the rental unit as their primary residence prior to the Tenants moving in. This matter is therefore distinct from the facts and circumstances set out [name] v. Bindlish and [name] v. [name].

As it was not in dispute that the Tenants were required to share communal areas such as a bathroom and a kitchen with the M.N, I find that – in accordance with section 5i) of the Act - the Act does not apply to the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants.
Accordingly, the T2 Application and the L1 Application cannot proceed and shall be dismissed. File Numbers: LTB-T-088565-23 LTB-L-045503-24

Subsidiarily, I note that the description of the use of the rental unit by both the Landlord and the Tenants reveals that the premises is being operated as a rooming house, with the Landlord renting each bedroom separately.

While S.G testified that they control the finances of [name], the fact that they each rent an individual bedroom , moved into their respective bedroom within the span of a few months and are each responsible for rent associated to a singular bedroom is indicative of separate and distinct tenancies.

Neither application was filed as a multi -unit application, and as such could not proceed on the merits regardless as they conflated more than one tenancy . With that said, in the spirit of the Board adopting the most expeditious method of determining questions arising in a [name], I found it appropriate, under the circumstances, to address the question of the Board’s jurisdiction.

The Landlord’s L1 Application, LTB-L-045503-24, is dismissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord's Legal Representative raised that some of the issues raised on the T2 Application were outside of the limitation period, as many of the alleged illegal entries occurred outside of the one-year limitation period, she also noted that many of the issues alleged arose after the termination of the tenancy.

The Act imposes a one-year limitation period. The T2 Application was filed on October 29, 2024. Therefore, I have not considered those illegal entries which are alleged to have occurred outside the limitation period.
Additionally, some of the allegations raised on the T2 Application are alleged to have occurred after the tenancy had terminated and are also outside of the Board’s jurisdiction. & LTB-T-045512-25
Therefore, the hearing was limited to those allegations within the Board’s jurisdiction.

The T2 also appears to lack sufficient particulars with respect to the allegations of interference and harassment. It is sufficiently clear that the Tenant is framing the alleged illegal entries as interference. However, there are also allegations that the Landlord frequently threatened to evict the Tenant and used the Board as means of legal intimidation, charged illegal fines, delayed repairs to the rental unit, and removed the Tenant’s portal access. None of these allegations have clear dates and times attached to them. The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the only dates they were provided to go on and prepare their case were the dates and times related to the alleged illegal entry.

The Tenant indicated that she had provided a table of contents to the Landlord which contained additional dates and times. However, she confirmed that the dates and times were not contained in the Application itself. She testified that these allegations should still be considered because she needs the process to be over.

Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”).

MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct…”. While [name] involved a notice of termination served to a Tenant, in my view the general principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications. In [name], the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

Accordingly, I elected to limit the proceeding to those allegations which contain sufficient particulars, including dates and times and note that the Tenant has already been given an opportunity to amend her application after the adjudicative case conference which was held on April 29, 2025.

The Landlord's Legal Representative also sought clarity with respect to the remedies request by the Tenant on the T2 Application. The Tenant confirmed that she was seeking general compensation of $33,000.0. With Respect to the T6

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the T6 Application was filed on June 3, 2025, meaning that the limitation period was back to June 30, 2024 and that there were no allegations in the Application within that limitation period. Accordingly, she requested that the T6 be dimissed.

At the hearing the Tenant initially indicated that she was amenable to the T6 being dimissed and did not dispute the Landlord's Legal Representative request, before indicating that she would be prepared to go through with the T6. & LTB-T-045512-25
The most recent allegation raised in the T6 dates from May 5, 2024, and the Tenant was not able to point to any allegations that fell within the one-year limitation period.
Therefore, as the T6 does not contain allegations which fall within the one-year limitation period set out in the Act the T6 shall be dimissed. The T2
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,500.00

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on October 18, 2021 and vacated October 24, 2024. The rental unit is a single-family home converted into multiple rental units. The rental was located in the basement of the home. Illegal Entry

The Tenant’s Application identifies 108 alleged illegal entries, a small number of these appear to be duplicitous and all but 27 are outside the one-year limitation period. Additionally, the Tenant has noted that in many cases she was provided with adequate notice of entry. Therefore, I heard testimony from her only on the illegal entries which fell within the limitation period for which she alleged adequate notice of entry was not provided.

The Tenant testified that on November 9, 2023, she was sleeping in her bedroom when someone opened the door. She testified that she believed it was the water guy who was had come in to inspect the boiler and water tank for the complex, which is located in her unit. She testified that she did not receive a notice of entry from the Landlord prior to this entry.

During cross examination the Tenant was presented with an email dated November 10, 2024, that she had sent to the Landlord’s agent indicating that she had let someone in the day before, and she agreed that this contradicted her testimony that she was sleeping in her room at the time of the entry. However, she testified that there was an entry when she was sleeping.

The Tenant testified that a maintenance person came to her unit again on November 10, 2023. She testified that she initially received an email from an agent of the Landlord Ashley Neufeld on November 9, 2023, indicating that there would be an entry on November 10, 2023, to check the boiler system. It indicated the entry would occur between 8:00am and 12:00pm However, no one entered the rental during those times.

The Tenant then received a second email dated November 10, 2023, at 1:44pm from a Shefali Pandey indicating that they would be entering the rental unit on November 10, 2023 between 1:00pm and 5:00pm because there was no heat in the loft of the complex. She testified that the entry occurred around the time the email was sent.
The Tenant testified that people would attend daily and she was told she would be evicted if she refused entry so she allowed them to enter. & LTB-T-045512-25

The Tenant testified that on November 14, 2023, she was in a [name] appointment with her therapist, and an unidentified man entered her rental unit sometime between 10:00am and 11:00am. She testified that she had been provided with a notice of entry on November 13, 2023, indicating that someone would enter between 10:15am and 5pm on November 14, 2023. She testified that this entry was for a “fall (autumn) inspection”

She also described an entry on February 6, 2024, by who she believed to be electricians who attended to fix a faulty smoke alarm in her rental unit. She testified that she called the Landlord and Tenant Board and was informed that this did not constitute an emergency which would justify entry without notice. She indicated that she received an “emergency notice of entry” prior to the entry on February 6, 2024, indicating someone would enter her unit to repair the smoke alarm.

She testified that she reported a chirping smoke alarm to the Landlord and received a response on February 27, 2023, indicating that someone would attend between 10:00am- 5:00pm to rest the smoke alarms in her unit. She testified that an agent for the Landlord again subsequently attended the rental unit to fix the chirping smoke alarm in the Tenant’s rental unit. However, she indicated that by this time the alarm had already been fixed.

She testified that on February 29, 2024, her smoke alarm began chirping again and after she made the Landlord aware she received an email from the Landlord’s Agent on February 29, 2024 indicating that someone would attend to inspect and repair the smoke alarm and an agent of the Landlord subsequently entered to insect the alarm. However they were unbale to repair the alarm.

She testified that on February 29, 2024 she walked over to the fire department and described her chirping smoke alarm, and the fire department sent a truck and a fireman smashed her chirping alarm and told her to refer the Landlord to the fire department if they had a problem with the smashed alarm.

She indicated that she made the Landlord aware through the building portal that the fire department had smashed the alarm and on March 1, 2024, an agent for the Landlord attended the rental unit to replace the smashed alarm with a new smoke alarm. She also directed me to an email on February 29, 2024, indicating that someone would enter her unit on March 1, 2024. She testified that she did not know the purpose of this entry because at the time the email was sent, she had not made the Landlord aware of the smashed alarm.

The Tenant also testified that for her birthday on July 30, 2024, she submitted an N9 to the Landlord, and the next day on July 31, 2024, she received a notice of entry for August 1, 2024, to conduct an inspection and appraisal of the rental unit. She testified that this was an appraisal inspection of the unit.

She also testified that on August 8, 2024, she received an email from the Landlord’s Agent at 12:33pm indicating that there would be an entry between 9:00am and 5:00pm to inspect the rental unit. She testified that she replied to the email indicating that an agent for the Landlord named [name] had entered her rental unit at 10:44pm and to express that she was concerned at the large number of inspections which had occurred within her rental unit and requested that any move out inspection occurred closer to her move out date. & LTB-T-045512-25
The Tenant confirmed during cross examination that she had refused entry into the rental unit but was not too sure how many times.
She testified that she did not believe that a faulty fire alarm is an emergency, she indicated that a chirping smoke alarm could be an emergency, but it would be situational.
The Landlord’s Agent [name] testified at the hearing. She is a senior property manager for the Landlord.
She testified that a smoke alarm is an emergency, as in a residential property a fire can spread from one unit into others.

She explained that the Landlord’s portal uses a work order system which provides Tenant’s with a box they can check if they are making a request and do not need 24 hours notice of entry. If the box is checked notice of entry will not be provided if it is left blank notice is provided.

She also explained that the Tenant’s rental unit contained both the hot water tank and the heater, which would necessitate entry whenever either had issues. She testified that the Landlord would try to work with Reliance and other contractors to find time that works for entry but reliance will often show up late or not at all, and the Landlord has a has a duty to provide hot water to the complex.

She also testified that if Appliance repair is provided the Landlord would involve their contractor RTC who would coordinate directly with Tenants to schedule entry, and the Landlord would only become involved if RTC was unable to contact the Tenant to schedule entry. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that because of the excessive number of entries into her rental unit her life was severely impacted, and she lost her role assisting low-income families. She also testified that the stress caused her to have a seizure on September 12, 2024 and she lost her license as a result. Additionally, because the entries shad caused her to miss group therapy sessions, she was removed from her therapy program.

In support of this the Tenant relied on a letter from her pharmacist dated March 26, 2025 which asserts that the Tenant has been diagnosed with epilepsy which causes seizures which increase in frequency during emotionally overwhelmed periods, and asserts that the Tenant experienced repeated violations of her personal space which cased worsening PTSD symptoms and anxiety which led to more frequent seizures.

The Tenant testified that the number and purpose of the Landlord’s inspections was ridiculous and testified that she sent the Landlord an email on May 13, 2024, about the number of inspections and to remind the Landlord that they had already performed an annual inspection that year.

During cross examination The Tenant confirmed that the medical note that she relied on was written by her pharmacist rather than her doctor. However, she testified that she has & LTB-T-045512-25 this pharmacist forever and they have seen her conditions change. The Tenant denied that she had told her pharmacist what to write in the letter.

The Landlord’s witness [name] testified that the complex has an annual appraisal inspection which is booked by the bank and a series of annual inspections including an annual fire inspection, and an annual unit inspection and follow up.

She testified that not all entries alleged by the Tenant were entries as some were key audits, where the unit key would be tested but no one would enter the unit, and many of the notices of entry relied on by the Tenant were corrections or amendments sent by the Landlord.

She testified that no one who works for the Landlord has a grudge against the Tenant and they in fact did not know who she was when the Application was first filed, as she had been a good Tenant and not on the Landlord’s radar. . Harassment

The Tenant testified that by October 24, 2024, she was removing her belongings from the rental unit when she became ware that the Landlord had scheduled roof repairs for that day. She testified that when she arrived at the unit there was a plywood panel covering her door and she was hit by a shingle which was thrown from the roof by a contractor hired by the Landlord. She testified that she did not believe that this was deliberate, however she believed that the Landlord had deliberately scheduled roof repairs that day to interfere with her move and harass her.

A witness for the Landlord [name] testified at the hearing, He is the owner of Need a Roof. He testified that he did not remember the Tenant and had never met her but confirmed that his company performed repairs on the roof the day that the Tenant vacated. He testified that plywood panels were place around the worksite to protect from falling debris and explained that he would typically provide his clients with a variety of days during which work could be completed, but this would ultimately be contingent upon the weather. Analysis
Ultimately, I am satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord’s Agents have entered the rental unit illegally.

While I found the Tenant’s testimony to be credible, I did not find it to be reliable. It was at time inconsistent, such as when she indicated that she was sleeping during the November 9 2023, entry, only to later change this assertion, and when she revised her testimony around refusing entry. I am willing to attribute a portion of this to the Tenant’s anxiety and underlying conditions, and the stress of a hearing before the Board, however I am not satisfied this entirely accounts for the inconstancies in the Tenants testimony.

However, even in consideration of the reliability of the Tenant’s testimony, the documentary evidence indicates that illegal entries did occur. For example, on November 10, 2023 the Tenant received an email at 1:44pm indicating that someone would enter that day, and they entered the unit shortly thereafter. This is not 24 hours notice. Likewise, the notice of entry for November 14, 2023, does not provide a full 24 hours notice to the & LTB-T-045512-25 Tenant. Similarly, the Notice of entry issued for August 1, 2024, while provided the day before does not provide a full 24 hours notice to the Tenant.
Additionally, on August 8, 2024, the Tenant received an email advising her of an entry that day at 12:33pm.

Therefore, as the Landlord did not provide a full 24 hours notice for these entries, I am satisfied that they constitute illegal entry. I am also not satisfied that the Landlord has identified an emergency which would warrant entering without notice and note that the August 8, 2024, entry appears to be for an inspection.

While the Tenant also asserts multiple illegal entries related to her fire alarm between February 6, 2024, and March 1, 2024 I am satisfied that a faulty fire alarm within a multi- residential building does constitute an emergency which would warrant entry without notice. An undetected fire in the Tenant’s unit could easily spread throughout the complex, and I am satisfied that after the Tenant made the Landlord aware of her ongoing issues with the fire alarm it was appropriate for them to enter to remediate the issue.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord's Agent entered the rental unit illegally on November 10, 2023 Novembre 14, 2023, August 1, 2024 and August 8, 2024.
The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord interfered with her reasonable enjoyment both through the illegal entries and the sheer number of entries.

The Tenant’s Application lists 27 entries between November 2023 and September 2024. While this number seems excessive I am prepared to accept the testimony of the Landlord’s agent, that many of these entries were scheduled by a third part repair services after maintenance requests, and many are duplicates which represent the Landlord changing or amending a notice of entry, additionally I note that a some appear to have been requested by the Tenant herself and a large number of the entries were in response to the faulty fire alarm in the Tenant’s rental unit.

When these entries are subtracted it appears that the Landlord or their agents entered the rental unit approximately 11 times during the period of November 2023 to September 2024. However, even many of these entries appear to be for a legitimate purpose including to turn on the hear, conduct an annual unit inspection or audit, or to shut down the water or check the boiler system. Therefore, while the number of entries may at first appear excessive, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment by entering the rental unit an excessive number of times.

However, I am prepared to accept that the illegal entries substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyments, especially when I consider them in the overall context of the sheer number of entries during this period.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household

With respect to harassment, The Tenant’s assertion that the Landlord deliberately scheduled the roof repair during her move appears to be speculative, and I accept the testimony of the Landlord’s witness that he is the one who provides dates to clients and & LTB-T-045512-25 that those dates are weather dependant. Therefore, as the Tenant’s assertion that the roof repair was booked to interfere with and harass her is speculative and there is evidence before me to suggest that the dates were not selected by the Landlord alone, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that this constitutes harassment. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant sought general damages of $33,000.00. I am satisfied that a modest award is appropriate, however I am not prepared to order the quantum sought by the Tenant. I note that I have found only 4 illegal entries and while I have accepted that these illegal entries impacted her reasonable enjoyment, I am not satisfied that this warrants an award of $33,000.00

The Tenant testified that the entries caused her increased anxiety which worsened her PTSD and caused her to experience seizures which led to the loss of her licence and her employment. The Tenant relies on a letter from her pharmacist in support of this assertion. However I have placed little weight on the letter, and note that the Tenant’s pharmacist is not her doctor, and I am not pharmacists has assessed the Tenant to the extent that they are able to definitively assert that the Tenant’s medical conditions were caused or exacerbated by the Landlord’s actions, or were the primary cause of her conditions worsening.

Without a clear causal nexus, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the health effects she suffered were a direct result of the Landlord’s actions, and I therefore find the quantum sought excessive.

However, I am satisfied that general compensation of $1500.00 is appropriate. This represents $250.00 per illegal entry, and $500.00 for compensation for interference with reasonable enjoyment in recognition of the impact of the Landlord’s actions.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 Application is dimissed.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,500. This amount represents: • $1,500 for general compensation
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 14, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (LTB-T-089836-24) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that 12728877 canada (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-089836-24 and LTB-T-105625-24)
reasons: By way of background the Tenant filed LTB-T-089836-24 on October 31, 2024, alleging that the Landlord both collected or retained money illegally and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations. On December 28, 2024, the Tenant filed LTB-T- 105625-24 which also alleged that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations.

Each Application was scheduled for a separate adjudicative case conference. At the adjudicative case conference for LTB-T-089836-24 the Tenant advised the Board they would not be proceeding with the T1 portion of their application as it was filed in error.

After the Adjudicative Case conference for LTB-T-105625-24 was completed the presiding Member became aware that the issues raised in LTB-T-105625-24 were largely duplicitous with those raised in LTB-T-089836-24 and the matters were combined to be heard together. Particulars

At the hearing before me I raised that neither T6 Application appeared to contain adequate particulars, including dates and times. However, as the Landlord had provided disclosure, I queried the Landlord's Legal Representative as to whether the Landlord had understood what was being alleged on the two applications.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that while the Landlord had done their best to provide disclosure, it was very difficult to determine the allegations and the case to be met, and it was very difficult to respond without knowing particulars such as dates and times.

As an example the Tenants T6 in LTB-T-089836-24 states: “my washer dont work dyer dont work dish washer dont work stover not working no fire alarm microwave fridge dose not get cold dyer vent missing lights dont work for switch shower heads gross and not working will sinks clogged staff dont want to fix anything rent is not rignt”

The Tenant indicated that dates and times were not provided within the Application, but he had provided evidence which contained dates, times, and details. He indicated that he was not going to write a book on each Application.
The only disclosure the Board received from the Tenant was a 109-page document titled LTB Tenant Evidence which only contains screenshots of emails between the Tenant and the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that he had served additional evidence on both the Landlord's Legal Representative and the Board 7 days prior to this hearing by email.
The Landlord's Legal Representative confirmed that the only disclosure she had received from the Tenant was the 109-page LTB Tenant Evidence package.

I note that the Interim order for LTB-T-089836-24 directed the parties to provide disclosure by May 23, 2025. The interim order for LTB-T-105625-24 ordered the parties to provide disclosure at least 15 days prior to the next hearing date and reply evidence at least 7 days prior.
The Tenant testified that he was told that disclosure was not due until 7 days prior to the next hearing date.

Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“[name]) is clear that Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.
MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct…”

While [name] involved a notice of termination served to a Tenant, in my view the same principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications. In [name], the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…

I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s Application provides sufficient particulars, while it is clear that the Tenant has maintenance concerns with respect to several appliances for example, there are no clear dates and times provided and very few details. I also note that the Tenant has had the benefit of two adjudicative case conferences, one for each Application, where the importance of particulars are discussed with the parties. However, in spite of this the Applications do not provide particulars and no request to amend has been filed by the Tenant.

With respect to the Tenant’s assertion that adequate particulars are contained in their disclosure I note that as of the hearing date this disclosure had not been received by either the Board or the Landlord's Legal Representative. Additionally, the two interim orders issued provided deadlines for disclosure which were not met. While the Interim order for LTB-T-105625-24 allowed parties to provide reply disclosure within 7 days of the hearing date I note that missing particulars should not be considered reply evidence, and it would not be reasonable to expect the Landlord to wait until 7 days prior to the hearing to receive clear particulars from the Tenant.

Finally, I also note that disclosure is not the Application, and even if the Tenant’s evidence were properly disclosed and provided the missing particulars this would not save the Tenant’s Application. In my view the Application is distinct from disclosure and disclosure cannot cure a flawed Application, as particulars must be included on the Application itself and it is inherently prejudicial to the Landlord to expect them to comb through often voluminous disclosure to ascertain the allegations made or the case to be met.

Therefore, As the Tenant’s applications are vague and failed to provide dates and specifics for the allegations made, I find that there are insufficient reasons and details to allow the landlord to know the allegations made or the case to be met. The applications must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
