issues: (“CP”) (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (T1 application) and gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants’ proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants one month’s compensation for the N12 notice that they served on July 27, 2023, interest on the last month rent deposit, and refund the pet deposit.
The Tenant claims that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Evidence and Analysis
The Tenants testified that the tenancy began on February 1, 2020. The Tenants stated the rent was $2,200.00 per month.

The Tenants stated they paid $4,400.00 for first month’s rent and a rent deposit and a $500.00 pet deposit prior to the tenancy commencing. The Tenants submitted a copy of the lease signed by themselves and the Landlord confirming that the Tenants paid these amounts.
The Tenants further testified that they never received any interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit from the Landlord.
The Tenants were advised that the pet deposit would be refundable at the end of the tenancy.
On July 27, 2023, the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice of termination pursuant to s. 49(1) of the Act for the Purchaser’s own use. The termination date was October 31, 2023.

Sections 49.1 and 55.1 of the Act state: 49.1 A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if, (a) the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy on behalf of a purchaser under subsection 49 (1) or (2); and (b) the notice of termination is given on or after the day the Protecting Tenants and Strengthening Community Housing Act, 2020 receives Royal Assent. 55.1 If the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55, the landlord shall compensate the tenant no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination of the tenancy given by the landlord under section 48, 49 or 50.

The Tenant testified that they vacated the rental unit on November 4, 2023, as a result of the N12. The Tenants testified that their pet deposit was never refunded by the Landlord when they moved out. In addition, the Tenants stated that the Landlord did not provide them the compensation required by section 49.1, nor did the Landlord return their last month’s rent deposit or pay interest owing on the deposit.

The Tenants submitted a copy of the agreement to terminate the lease as they did not feel comfortable signing a N11 form; this agreement was signed by both the Landlord and Tenant with specific terms. The main clause referred to in this agreement was that December 31, 2023, was the latest day that the Tenants can occupy the unit; moreover, if the Tenants were to leave prior to this date, they would be reimbursed that month’s rent.

The Tenants testified that they were initially given a cheque by the Landlord to compensate them for the N12, however, the cheque was null as it indicated it was for two different amounts. The Landlord mistakenly wrote a cheque for $22,000.00 and wrote out in words “twenty-two hundred”. When noticed by the Tenants, they immediately informed the Landlord, who told them they would issue a new cheque. Subsequently, when the Tenants followed up about a replacement cheque, the Landlord ultimately refused to write a new cheque to the Tenants for the N12 compensation.
As such, I find the Landlord did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by section 49 and pursuant to section 135(1.1), the Landlord is deemed to have retained this money illegally.

Furthermore, at the time the Tenants vacated the rental unit, their rent was paid in full, but the Landlord was still retaining their rent deposit. Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires the last month’s rent deposit to be applied to the last rental period, and it cannot be applied to offset the N12 compensation or used for any other purpose.

I find that the Landlord collected an illegal charge for a pet deposit, which was not returned to the Tenant as abovementioned. The parties agreed that the pet deposit was to be refunded upon the Tenants vacating the rental unit.
Subsection 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Subsection 105(2) of the Act defines “security deposit” as, money, property or a right paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition. Remedies:

As the pet deposit was to be refunded upon the Tenants vacating the rental unit, I find that this deposit meets the definition of “security deposit” in subsection 105(2) of the Act. I further find that it was not a rent deposit permitted under section 105 of the Act because the Tenants also provided a separate rent deposit for the last month of the tenancy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord contravened the Act when they collected a pet deposit from the Tenants that is in addition to the rent deposit, and they continue to contravene the Act by retaining the deposit.

Finally, I find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the rental deposit. Subsection 106(6) requires a landlord to pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline. The amount of interest owed on the rent deposit is $125.26. This is calculated by applying the amount of interest owed on the rent deposit from the date collected in January 2021 to the date the tenancy was terminated.
In total I find that the Landlord owes the Tenant $629.95 for money illegally collected or retained. T5 Application

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenants for the difference in rent they incurred or will incur for a 12-month period after they vacated and their moving expenses. Evidence and Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; and • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
The Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(b).

As noted, on July 27, 2023, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination for personal use pursuant to s. 48 of the Act. The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice on November 4, 2023.

The Tenants testified that they resided in the rental unit for 3 years and only started looking for a new rental after being served the N12 notice. The Tenants further stated that if not for this notice from the Landlord, they had no intention to leave the rental unit.
On a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination they were given under s. 49.

The Tenants testified that when the Landlord served the N12 that the property was sold. The Tenants were given multiple reasons by the Landlord as to who would be occupying the rental unit, but ultimately, were informed that the purchaser would be moving into the unit.

It was the uncontested evidence that the purchaser did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Furthermore, it was stated that the purchaser never moved into the rental unit at all as the property was never sold. The Tenants testified that they had friends in the area they visited often. They were told that the unit was re- rented and confirmed that the property was not sold. The new renters moved into the rental unit approximately two months after the Tenants had vacated rather than the purchaser personally occupying it in accordance with the N12 notice.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing to provide evidence, and therefore, they did not rebut the above information. Therefore, I find that the Tenants have established all three of parts of the test contained in s. 57(1)(b) of the Act. Remedies

At the hearing, The Tenants requested their rent differential for one year, out of pocket expenses for moving and storage, reimbursement for depreciation of their motor vehicle, and general compensation of $10,000.00.

With respect to rent differential, the Tenants are now paying $650.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. I see no reason not to grant the Tenants the remedy requested in this regard. The Tenants’ new unit is comparable to their old unit, and if anything, it is a smaller space. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $7,800.00 for their rent differential for a period of one year.

The Tenants also incurred reasonable out of pocket expenses in the amount of $1,845.35 for moving. The Tenant submitted receipts and bank statements to show how much expense they incurred for mail forwarding, U-Haul truck rentals, moving supplies and materials, gas for the truck rentals, Enbridge account set up, and utility changeover. I am satisfied the amount claimed reflects the reasonable moving expenses the Tenants incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach and an order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $1,845.35 for reasonable out of pocket moving expenses.

I am unable to award the Tenants depreciation costs as claimed to their motor vehicle. The Tenants testify that they moved to Barrie, and this significantly increased the use of their motor vehicle. As well, the Tenants testified that their commute time to work has increased due to this. The Tenants did not provide satisfactory evidence to substantiate the costs they were seeking in terms of depreciation of their motor vehicle. Therefore, I cannot assess the age and depreciation of the motor vehicle to determine whether the amount claimed is reasonable. In addition, I find it difficult to reconcile this claim with the Tenants’ evidence that the Tenants chose to move to Barrie and should have reasonably foreseen this increase in mileage and commute time as a result.

The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $10,000.00 due to pain and suffering. The Tenant, particularly TR, is an army veteran who suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder and has mental health issues due to his time in the military. It was the Tenants’ evidence that landscaping helps with TR’s therapy and is a coping mechanism for him, which he was regularly able to do at the rental unit prior to the N12 notice being served. As a result, the Tenants were unable to find a property with as much green space for TR to have therapeutic landscaping opportunities, and this has set back his treatment. In addition, due to the conduct of the Landlord in serving the N12 and the lack of communication with the Tenants, this worsened TR’s trust issues; moreover, it was the Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord was aware of TR’s mental health issues and the rehabilitation that landscaping gave him. Consequently, the Tenants testified that this entire process also gave them stress, anxiety, and uncertainty. The Landlord has no obligation under the Act to pay this amount, however, there is evidence before me that the Tenants have experienced pain and suffering from this termination of tenancy. As such, I find that the Landlord’s conduct resulted in a substantial disruption to the Tenants’ tenancy and personal life. Considering the circumstances and having regard to the nature of the breach and its impact, I find that an award of general compensation equivalent to two month’s rent is appropriate and just. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to pay the Tenant $4,400.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $19,118.61. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the pet deposit. • $2,200.00 for the one-month compensation from the N12 notice. • $2,200.00 reimbursement of the last month rent deposit. • $125.26 in interest on the last month rent deposit. • $7,800.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from November 4, 2023, to November 3, 2024. • $1,845.35 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $4,400.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] operating as WelGroup (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord is amended to reflect the corporate entity of [organization] operating as WelGroup and [name] is removed as a party, as he is simply employed by the corporate Landlord.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2026. Preliminary Issue – Request to Amend

On May 20, 2026, the Tenant served the Landlord and filed a request to amend this application to remove the original remedy requested of ordering the Landlord to complete necessary repairs and to add other remedies such as a rent abatement, costs for repairs completed, termination of the tenancy as of April 30, 2026, and return of the last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative opposed the Tenant’s request to amend. He submitted that none of the added remedies needed to wait until the Tenant vacated if the Tenant believed they were entitled to these additional remedies. He also submitted that the request to amend was only served eight days prior to today’s hearing although the Notice of Hearing was received over three months ago.

He further submitted that the Tenant was not prohibited from filing their request to amend prior to vacating and/or simply withdrawing this application and filing a fresh one as they knew when they would be vacating and had legal representation. In support of his submission, he relied upon LTB order, TET-98921-19 (Re), 2022 CanLII 97391 (ON LTB), wherein at paragraphs 15 and 17 of that order the LTB found that: “15. The reason for the adjournment was to amend; however, the Tenant knew or ought to have known what the procedure was for amending their T6 Application. In, fact, over the past 2 years, there were already 2 prior amendments submitted. 17. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that it would be highly prejudicial to the Landlord to allow a further amendment given the history of this matter. The Tenant was represented for most of the file. The Tenant’s side had already submitted two written amendments so they knew the process. The supporting evidence contained claims about lack of maintenance and additional damage claims with respect to the pool, gardening, and sprinkler – it would be unfair to allow the T6 application to be perfected at this late stage.” Emphasis Added

He also submitted that the original application was moot upon the Tenant vacating the rental unit as the only remedy requested for the Landlord to effect repair would be moot. He also submitted that therefore the request to amend is not appropriate and ought to be refused. In support of his submissions he relied on LTB order, CET-90776-19 (Re), 2021 CanLII 146737 (ON LTB), wherein at paragraph 6 of that order the LTB found that: “The Tenants’ Representative advised that the Tenants vacated the rental unit in July 2021. Given that the Tenants have vacated the rental unit, remedies 6, 7 and 9 indicated in the application are moot, except for the Tenants’ request that the Landlord reimburse them for the cost of filing the application.” Emphasis Added

He also relied on LTB order, Chanda v [name], 2021 CanLII 138944 (ON LTB), wherein at paragraphs 5 and 6 of that order the LTB found that: “5. As the tenancy terminated October 31, 2020 and that the only remedy which the Tenants sought in their T6 Application was for the tenancy to be terminated, this application is moot. 6. As there is no remedy to be granted in the T6 application the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.” Emphasis Added

He submitted that as per the above LTB’s jurisprudence a party cannot amend an application out of a moot nature. Additionally, he submitted that in [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 (CanLII), the Division Court held that the LTB erred when awarding remedies not claimed in the original application. As well, he relied on LTB order, TET-03961-19 (Re), 2022 CanLII 52527 (ON LTB), wherein at paragraphs 6 and 7 of that order, the LTB found: “6. The only remedies requested in the applications are no longer applicable because the Tenants have vacated the unit. The Tenants no longer have any interest in whether the repairs have been done and in how the Landlord conducts herself. 7. Because the only remedies requested are moot, and because I am bound by [name], I cannot order any remedies in this case. It is therefore not necessary to make determinations on all of the issues claimed in the application and for which the parties gave evidence at the hearing.” Emphasis Added

In closing, he submitted that how can the Tenant justify these amended remedies after vacating, nothing changed according to them with respect to the alleged issues. He also submitted that it would be incumbent on the Tenant to include these remedies at the outset. He requested that the request to amend be denied and the application dismissed with prejudice.

As per Rule 15.4 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure the LTB has discretion to grant a request to amend, and will only grant it if satisfied that the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

The matter was held down for some time to give the Tenant’s Legal Representative an opportunity to review the caselaw presented by the Landlord. She submitted that the Tenant moved out because of the issues raised in this application and that they have complied with Rule 15 with respect to the service and filing of the request to amend. However, she then requested to withdraw the application.
Therefore, the issue before me is whether the application is dismissed or withdrawn.

Based on the submissions before me, I was satisfied that the Tenant’s request to amend ought to be refused. The Tenant waited until after she vacated to amend the application and failed to provide any reasonably explanation as to why the amended remedies requested could not have been made in the original application or prior to vacating the unit.

I was satisfied that once the Tenant vacated the rental unit, this application as filed became moot as the only remedy requested was no longer of any interest by this Tenant as to whether the repairs are completed by the Landlord.

The application was filed on October 27, 2025, the Tenant had ample opportunity to request an amendment prior to vacating if she believed the issues in the application warranted different remedies, such as a termination of the tenancy, instead of just vacating and then seeking those remedies. I find that it would be unfair and prejudicial to the Landlord to permit the Tenant to amend the application at this point.
Consequently, since the application as filed is moot, it must be dismissed in accordance with the LTB jurisprudence presented.

Although, the Landlord requested that the matter be dismissed with prejudice, since the merits of this application were not determined by the LTB, I was not satisfied that the dismissal should be with prejudice. Costs

The Landlord’s request for costs were denied. As per Guideline 3 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guidelines, costs to a party are generally only awarded in cases of unreasonable conduct. [name] is unreasonable if it causes undue expense and delay. In this case, the Landlord’s Legal Representative requested costs for their attendance at today’s hearing and argued that they had to be in attendance all day and late in the day as the Tenant’s Legal Representative was away for periods of time addressing other matters that she had booked.

The Notice of Hearing for today advises the parties to “be ready to stay the whole day. There are many other hearings scheduled at the same time as your hearing, and your hearing may be later in the day.” In this case, although when I first called this matter the Tenant’s Legal Representative was not available, her assistant was present and advised when the Legal Representative would be available, approximately half hour later.

However, since there were other hearings still needing to be addressed at that time I was not satisfied that this conduct was unreasonable. This matter was heard although it was late in the day, and the parties ought to have expected that given the information provided in the Notice of Hearing.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the Tenants sought to amend the application to reflect [name] as the Landlord in accordance with an amended application previously filed with the Board and not Baytree Property Management. This amendment was on consent. T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

On or about July 31, 2025 the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 Notice of Termination (“N12”). The N12 states that the Landlord I good faith, required possession of the rental unit for their own use for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
In this case, it is undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 29, 2025 as a result of the N12 served by the Landlord.

With respect to the issue of bad faith, subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a) and (c), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or building that contains the rental unit, for sale;… 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
In other words, if section 57(5) of the Act applies, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish that they did not serve the N12 in bad faith.

In this case it was undisputed that the rental unit was advertised for sale in late October, 2025, a month after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. Based on the evidence before me and the Landlord’s admission of the rental unit being advertised for sale, I find that the presumption of bad faith under section 57(5) of the Act is engaged for this application. Therefore, the Landlord is required to prove their good faith on a balance of probabilities for the N12 served on the Tenants. DOES THE LANDLORD’S EVIDENCE ESTABLISH IT IS MORE LIKELY THAN NOT THE N12 WAS SERVED IN GOOD FAITH?

The Landlord testified that he is 75 years old and is on a fixed income. He was suffering financially. To alleviate his financial distress he had decided to sell his primary residence and move into the rental unit. He listed his primary residence for sale in June, 2025, and subsequently served the Tenants with an N12 for the rental property.

The Landlord further testified that after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Landlord’s financial issues continued and were exacerbated by the lack of a rental income, due to the Tenant’s vacating the rental unit. Additionally his primary residence hadn’t yet sold. Due to his dire financial circumstances the Landlord also listed the rental property for sale to see which property would sell first to address his financial burden.

The Landlord states that the rental property was only listed for sale for 11 days before the listing was cancelled. His primary residence eventually sold and he moved into the rental unit on December 10, 2025 where he still resides. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me I find that the Landlord did not act in bad faith when he served the N12 on the Tenants. The evidence established that at the time the Landlord gave the Tenants the N12, he genuinely intended to move into the rental unit due to financial issues he was dealing with.
I therefore find that the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith and additionally that the Tenants did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith.
Additionally, the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time, being a little over two months after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. After his primary residence sold.
As such, the Tenants have failed to establish each part of the test contained in section 57(1)(a) of the Act, and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

There are three prerequisites to a successful T5 application made pursuant to section 57(1)(b) of the Act: a. the Landlord gave notice of termination under s. 49 of the Act for “purchaser’s own use” in bad faith; b. the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice of termination; and c. no person set out in the in notice occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination under either section 48 or 49 of the Act. In other T5 applications the Board has found that the Landlord had served the Tenant with an N12 under section 49 even if a Board approved form had not been used where the Landlord communicated to the tenant the essential elements of an N12 notice. However, in this case the Tenant has not established, on the balance of probabilities, that Landlord communicated the essential elements of an N12 - i.e. that the Landlord wants to move in and it was necessary for the Tenant to vacate the rental unit in order to allow for the Landlord to occupy the unit for residential purposes.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit in 2024. The Tenant testified that on April 9, 2024, she spoke with the Landlord and the Landlord indicated that they wanted to sell their house. The Tenant entered into evidence exhibit 1.3 which is a text message dated April 11, 2024, in which the Landlord’s realtor indicated that the Landlord may be selling their home but they have to first make sure that they can get the amount they want and otherwise they would not be selling and the realtor offered his services if the house is listed for sale to help the Tenant re-locate.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s realtor attended the house on April 19, 2024, to evaluate the house for a potential sale. The Tenant provided that she started to look for alternative housing as she was unsure of whether the house would sell or not. The Landlord texted the Tenant on May 27, 2024, advising her that he intends to sell the house next spring and that would push the Tenant’s move out date to the end of February 2025. The Landlord told the Tenant that this would give her a reasonable time for her to find a place.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord inquired in December 2024 whether the Tenant would purchase the house and the Tenant declined their offer. The Landlord advised the Tenant at this point, that they plan to list the house for sale in May 2025, and they hope the Tenant can vacate by March 2025. The Tenant testified that she had exotic birds, and it would be difficult to find alternative housing that suited her needs to home her exotic birds.

The Tenant testified that she found new housing and provided notice to the Landlord on December 28, 2024, that she would vacate by January 31, 2025. She testified that she requested from the Landlord an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy and the Landlord refused. The Tenant testified she saw the rental unit listed for sale on April 2025.

The Landlord testified that he had not finalized the sale of the house, but he wanted to move in and strategize selling the house and if he had he would have served a formal N12 Notice of Termination and requested vacant possession at the end of March 31, 2025. This was clear in his communication to the Tenant on December 23, 2024. He testified that he often communicated to the Tenant she has till the end of March 2025 to vacate and was under no obligation to terminate earlier than that and she chose to vacate at the end of January 31, 2025.

The Landlord testified he moved into the unit and ultimately listed the home for sale on April 14, 2025, and then it was taken off the market in October 2025 and re-listed again on April 14, 2026, but he still lives in the rental unit. Analysis

Here, it is undisputed that the Landlord never served a formal N12 notice under section 48(1). The Landlord submitted that because the Tenant was never served with an N12 notice containing the essential element of that notice, this application should be dismissed.

However, section 202 of the Act requires me to consider the real substance of all transactions. In this case, the Landlord admitted they asked the Tenant to vacate to allow the Landlord to move in and eventually to sell the rental unit.

Based on the Landlord’s own testimony I find that the Tenant vacated because the Landlord told the Tenant that they had to vacate the rental unit by March 31, 2025, because he wanted to move in and sell the unit. I find that this communication contains the essential elements of a an N12 notice – a demand that the tenants vacate by a specific date because the landlord wanted vacant possession due to an anticipated sale of the rental unit.

It would be an absurd outcome for the Landlord to be allowed to rely on not serving a N12 as a means of circumventing the Act and avoiding the responsibilities under it when the whole basis for the termination is a reason contained within a landlord’s own-use notice.

Based on my above analysis, the first and second steps of the test have been met, namely that the Tenant was given a notice of termination under s. 48 of the Act for landlord’s own use and they vacated as a result of the notice. The only remaining issues to determine are whether the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and whether the N12 notice was given in bad faith.

Based on the evidence, the presumption of bad faith in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies to this situation. This provision states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, for sale

This provision means that, because there is evidence before me that during the one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale, it is presumed that the notice was given in bad faith. The onus then shifts to the Landlord to rebut the presumption and prove that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith.
I find that the Landlord did occupy the rental unit for at least 12 months as required when a landlord terminates the tenancy with a notice of termination served under section 48 of the Act.

The Landlord testified that shortly after the Tenant moved out, the Landlord moved into the rental unit and is currently still living there. The Landlord also testified that he listed the property for sale again on April 14, 2026. The Tenant did not present any concrete evidence to challenge the Landlord’s position on this point. Therefore, I cannot find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

The evidence was that rental unit was listed for sale on April 14, 2025, and it failed to sell. As a result, I find the evidence supports finding the true nature of the Landlord was to occupy the rental unit for the time required under the Act and at the end the Landlord re- listed the unit for sale on April 14, 2026.

Therefore, I find the Landlord has rebutted the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith and have proven on a balance of probabilities that their original intent was genuine. The Tenant’s application must therefore fail.
As the Tenant cannot establish all the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a)
The Tenant did not prove no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated

The Tenant testified that the rental unit is the top two floors in a 3-floor house, with a total of three bedrooms. He moved into the rental unit in 2010 and vacated October 31, 2024, because he was served an N12 notice of termination indicating that the Landlord’s son intends to occupy the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that after he vacated the Landlord’s son may have moved in, but he did not believe he lived there full time. He allowed it was possible the Landlord’s son had occupied one room and rented the two other rooms as he found two of the bedrooms within the rental unit listed for rent. The Tenant testified that at the L2 hearing for the Landlord’s N12 the Landlord’s son had testified that he required all three bedrooms for personal use.

The Tenant testified that he never saw the Landlord’s son at the rental unit and many of the rooms appeared to be empty. 8. [name] also testified at the hearing. He is a friend of the Tenant was enlisted to contact that [name] son through Kijiji after the Tenant discovered rooms in the rental unit listed for rent in June 2025. He testified that he tried to set up a date to view the rooms but this was delayed and ultimately abandoned because the witness left on vacation. He testified that the Landlord’s son sent him multiple text messages when they were trying to set up a viewing and confirmed that two rooms were available for rent. 9. The Landlord testified that his son moved into the rental unit in December 2024 and he (the Landlord) began performing renovations on the unit at the same time. Including flooring, drywall and electrical work which he classified as necessary because the Tenant had been living in the rental unit for 12 years. 10. He testified that in January 2025 his son moved to a different bedroom within the house. He testified that he believed his sons girlfriend also moved into the rental unit but vacated in Augus 2025. 11. He testified that all he knew was that his son had moved in and was very busy and in and out of the rental unit. He claimed not to be aware that his son had posted rooms in the rental unit for rent. 12. Harjinder [name] testified that he moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2024. He testified that he initially moved into a bedroom on the third floor while his father performed renovations on the second floor. He testified that after he and that his girlfriend broke up in August 2025 he moved to a different bedroom on the second floor as that floor had been renovated. 13. He testified that he used one room as a bedroom and had an office on the second floor and was leaving the third bedroom empty for his sister who moved in December 2025. 14. He testified that in June 2025 he was in a bind, and had lots of debt and elected to rent two of the bedrooms of the rental unit, while these were posted for rent he ultimately decided not to go through with this as he had always lived with family in the past. He testified that he never informed his father that he was intending to rent bedrooms within the rental unit. 15. Harjinder [name] testified that he was still residing in the rental unit, though he was considering a move to [name] to loge with a new girlfriend and his considering employment with a new employer there. He testified that he visited Halifax twice while residing in the rental unit, and stayed for a week each time. He testified that he was often out of the rental unit 6 or 7 days a week in explanation for why the unit did not appear to be inhabited, and had not updated his address on his personal documents which has always been his parents address. Analysis 16. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. {Apply s. 57(5) if applicable} 17. In this case I am prepared to accept that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination and the Tenant vacated as a result. I am also satisfied that the reverse onus in Section 57(5) applies, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord has refuted that the notice was served in bad faith. 18. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord’s son did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. 19. The Tenant’s evidence with respect to the Landlord’s son failing to occupy the rental unit was largely speculative and suggested that while the Landlord’s son may have briefly moved in, he did not reside in the rental unit in a manner consistent with residential occupation. 20. However, while the reverse onus applies to the burden of bad faith it does not apply with respect to occupation of the rental unit and the onus remains with the Tenant to demonstrate this, I am not satisfied they have done so. 21. In fact the Tenant’s own evidence seems to suggest otherwise, as the Landlord’s son was clearly advertising only two bedrooms for rent, suggesting that he himself was occupying the third, and I am not satisfied that the other evidence presented by the Tenant goes beyond speculation and is sufficient to demonstrated that the Landlord’s son failed to occupy the rental unit. 22. While the Landlord’s son offering two rooms for rent is certainly suggestive of bad faith, it does not demonstrate that the Landlord’s son failed to occupy the rental unit and I am satisfied that he did in fact occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated and remained in the unit as of the hearing date. I am not satisfied that son’s failure to update his address on official documents is demonstrative that he never occupied the unit, and accept that ultimately occupied the rental unit. 23. Therefore, as the Tenant has not demonstrated that the Landlord’s son failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time the Tenant’s Application must be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $901.88. The T1 Application

In a previous T1 application (LTB-T-018440-25), with an order dated October 3, 2025, Member [name] (the ‘Member’) found that (a) the Landlord was not entitled to rescind the rent discount applied to the Tenant’s rent for December 2024 and (b) the Tenant did not breach the lease or the Act.

The Member determined that, despite being entitled to the return of rent paid for the period December 6-31, 2024, the Tenant’s application only sought the return of $566.67, representing 10 days of rent calculated at a daily rate. Pursuant to [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 (CanLII), [2012] O.J. No. 1052 ([name]. Ct.), the Member found it was not open to the Board to order an amount in excess of that claimed in an application which has not been amended.

T his application seeks to get the remainder of December 2024 rent reimbursed to the Tenant in the amount of $853.88. This amount is calculated as: $1,700.00 monthly rent - $279.45 already reimbursed for a late move in - $566.67 from previous hearing = $853.88.
For the same reasons as the Member in LTB-T-018440-25, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $853.88 and that an order shall issue as such.
The Tenant also sought reimbursement for four (4) months of parking at the residential complex at the rate of $115.00/month ($460.00 total).

The Tenant testified that, because of her move-in being delayed by issues with the rental unit, the Landlord offered her six (6) months of free parking. She selected a parking space and provided into evidence a text from the Landlord’s staff indicating that the monthly charge for the space would be $115.00/month after the free six-month period was over.

The Tenant testified that she only used the parking space for two months (December 2024 and January 2025), after which she assigned her lease. The Tenant is seeking the value of the remaining four months of parking in this application and has claimed this amount as an illegal rent under Reason 1 on the T1 application.

I find that the Tenant is not eligible for a reimbursement regarding these four unused months of free parking. The Tenant did not pay for this parking, as it was not included in the Tenant’s monthly rent. As such, the failure of the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant for the unused parking neither constitutes an illegal rent, nor an illegal charge.This free parking was offered as a good faith gesture to the Tenant due to difficulties in the move-in process, with the understanding that the Tenant would become responsible for additional monthly payments for the parking spot after the six-month free period was complete.
The Tenant incurred costs in the amount of $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $901.88. This amount represents: • $853.88 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $11,538.98.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in August 2020. The rental unit was a one bedroom plus den condominium unit with two bathrooms and a storage locker. The rent was $1,700.00 per month when the Tenant vacated.

There is no dispute that the Landlords served the Tenant with an N12 notice on October 20, 2022. The N12 notice stated that the Landlords required vacant possession of the rental unit for residential occupation by first-named Landlord, Mr. [name]name].
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 30, 2022, after receiving the N12 notice. I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.
The remaining issues are whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith and whether Mr. [name] occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Bad Faith:

The evidence establishes that the rental unit was listed for sale on December 22, 2022, and sold in January 2023, less than one year after the Tenant vacated. In accordance with subsection 57(5) of the Act, there is a rebuttable presumption that the N12 notice was served in bad faith. The onus therefore shifts to the Landlords to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 notice was not served in bad faith.
I find that the Landlord has not met that onus.

The Tenant testified that, before the N12 notice was served, Mr. [name]name] sent her a text message on or about October 4, 2022, indicating that the Landlords intended to sell the rental unit because the property was causing financial hardship. Mr. [name]name] did not dispute that, before serving the N12 notice, he had considered selling the rental unit because of financial concerns.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the decision to purchase the condominium had caused tension in his marriage and that his wife blamed him for the financial difficulties associated with the property. He testified that, during an argument, his wife told him that he should go live in the rental unit. He stated that he then decided to serve the N12 notice because he intended to move into the rental unit.

Mr. [name]name] further testified that the decision was made during a period of marital stress and was short lived. He stated that, after the N12 notice was issued, the Tenant gave him an N9 notice on or about November 20, 2022, and vacated the rental unit by November 30, 2022. Mr. [name]name] testified that he and his wife mistakenly believed that, because the Tenant had given her own notice to terminate, he was no longer required to occupy the rental unit for one year.

Mr. [name]name] testified that he moved into the rental unit on December 1, 2022, and moved back to the family home on or about December 10, 2022, because being away from the home and children was not workable. He stated that he and his wife then decided to list the rental unit for sale.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal confirmed that the Board must consider all relevant evidence when determining whether an N12 notice was served in bad faith and should not restrict its analysis to the landlord’s stated intention at the time the notice was served.

Based on the evidence before me, I do not find the Landlords’ explanation persuasive. The evidence does not establish that the Landlords’ plan changed because of an unforeseen event that arose after the Tenant vacated. Rather, the circumstances relied upon by the Landlords existed before the N12 notice was served. The Landlords already had children, employment obligations, family responsibilities, financial concerns, and marital stress when the N12 notice was issued. Those circumstances were not new or unforeseen.

I also find the timing of the Landlords’ communications and conduct to be significant. On or about October 4, 2022, the Landlords communicated with the Tenant about selling the rental unit because of financial stress. On October 20, 2022, the Landlords served the N12 notice for Mr. [name]name]’s own occupation. The Tenant vacated on November 30, 2022. Mr. [name] testified that he stayed in the rental unit for approximately 10 days. The unit was then staged, listed for sale in December 2022, and sold in January 2023.

This sequence of events supports the Tenant’s position that the Landlords’ true objective was to obtain vacant possession so that the rental unit could be staged and sold. It is inconsistent with a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes for at least one year.
Considering all of the evidence before me, I find that the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Whether the Landlord Occupied the Rental Unit Within a Reasonable Time

The Tenant testified that, from the photographs posted for the sale listing, she believed that Mr. [name]name] never occupied the rental unit after she vacated. She stated that the unit appeared to be empty of ordinary personal belongings, including toiletries, towels, and other items that would normally suggest that someone was residing there.

Mr. [name]name] testified that he moved into the rental unit on December 1, 2022, and moved out on December 10, 2022. However, the Landlords did not provide reliable documentary evidence to support that assertion. The Landlords did not provide evidence that Mr. [name]name] changed his mailing address, transferred utilities, set up internet service, moved furniture into the rental unit, or otherwise took steps consistent with making the rental unit his residence. Mr. [name]name]’s evidence was that he brought only minimal personal items, such as bedding or a pillow.

I do not accept that this establishes residential occupation within the meaning of section 48 of the Act. Even if Mr. [name]name] briefly stayed in the rental unit for approximately 10 days, I find that this did not amount to genuine residential occupation for the purpose required by section 48.

The evidence before me is more consistent with the rental unit being prepared for sale than being occupied as a home. The listing photographs relied on by the Tenant show the unit staged for sale and largely absent of ordinary personal belongings.
In these circumstances, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that Mr. [name]name] did not occupy the rental unit for residential purposes within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
Accordingly, I find that all of the elements of the legal test in section 57 of the Act have been satisfied, and the Tenant is entitled to a remedy. Remedies
The Tenant requests the following remedies: • Rent differential, totaling $600.00. • Moving expenses, totaling $738.98 • General compensation, totalling $20,400.00.
The Landlord must pay a fine to the Board. The Rent differential:

The Tenant testified that her new rental unit is smaller, has less storage, and is located farther away. The new monthly rent is $1,750.00, which is $50.00 more than the rent charged for the rental unit.

I find that the two rental units are comparable. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to their request for a rent differential. The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted the new lease agreement as evidence during the hearing.
Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent differential for 12 months. The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $600.00, calculated as follows: $50.00 x 12 months = $600.00. Moving cost:
In the application, The Tenant claims $738.98 for moving and storage expenses.

The Tenant testified that she incurred these expenses because she had to move after receiving the N12 notice and because the new rental unit was smaller than the rental unit she vacated. She testified that she could not bring all of her belongings to the new unit, so some of her belongings were initially stored with a friend and later moved into paid storage. The Tenant provided receipts in support of these expenses.

I am satisfied that these expenses were incurred as a result of the move and that they are reasonable out of pocket moving and storage expenses within the meaning of paragraph 57(3)1.2 of the Act. General compensation: 32. he Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3) (1.1), which states: An order that the Landlords pay a specified sum to the former Tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former Tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former Tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 [Emphasis added] 33. The Tenant occupied the rental unit from August 2020 to November 2022. She had intended to continue living there and that she vacated because of the N12 notice. 34. The Tenant testified that being required to move caused financial, emotional, and personal hardship. She had difficulty finding another rental unit within her budget in the same area and ultimately moved to a smaller unit in Pickering. The Tenant further testified that the move occurred while she was going through a separation, which made the process more stressful and left her feeling overwhelmed and alone. She further stated that the move disrupted her connection to her community, including a nearby mosque that had been an important source of friendship and support, and made her workplace, friends, and community supports less accessible. 35. Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I accept that the move caused financial inconvenience, disruption to community connections, and emotional stress. I also accept that these impacts were more significant because the Tenant was already experiencing personal stress at the time she had to move. 36. Considering the length of the tenancy, the circumstances of the bad faith notice, the disruption caused by the move, the Tenant’s loss of community connection, and the fact that the Landlords’ conduct caused the Tenant to leave her home unnecessarily, I find that general compensation equivalent to six months of rent is fair in all the circumstances. 37. The last rent charged was $1,700.00 per month. The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $10,200.00 in general compensation, calculated as follows: $1,700.00 x 6 months = $10,200.00. Administrative Fine 38. The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 39. I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered. 40. This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,586.98. This amount represents: • $600.00 for increased rent the Tenant has for the one-year period from December 1, 2022, to November 30, 2023. • $738.98 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $10,200.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 31, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I make the following findings of fact: 1. The rental unit is a second-floor apartment in a house. Tenant moved into the rental unit on March 1, 2025, and is still living there. 2. There is a hole in the kitchen drywall around an electrical outlet between the counter and the cupboards. The Tenant first saw the hole in January 2025 when viewing the unit and immediately informed the Landlord of the issue.

The Landlord repaired the drywall himself in April 2025, however the underlying issue of water leaking through the wall was not resolved. The Tenant informed the Landlord that the roof was leaking on April 27, 2025.

The Tenant called the municipality, who inspected the unit and notified the Landlord that the electrical outlet was unsafe. The Landlord disconnected the outlet in October 2025. The Tenant covered it with tape.

The Landlord’s initial drywall repair has progressively worsened over time as the wall continues to be damaged from water leaking inside it. A repairman attended the rental unit in October 2025 and cut a hole in the drywall to look inside the wall, which has not been closed yet. The issue remains unresolved. The Tenant is concerned about possible mould growth in the wall. 3. I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints reasonably. The issue has been ongoing for over a year and is worsening, with insufficient action being taken to resolve it. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the application is granted. 4. On the application, the Tenant requested a rent abatement. However, at the hearing, the Tenant explained that she was only seeking a rent abatement if she needed to leave the unit during repairs, which is not the case here. This remedy is dismissed. 5. The Tenant also requested an order requiring the Landlord to replace the roof and kitchen wall. There was insufficient evidence to determine that there is mould in the wall or that the entire roof needs replacement. However, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to resolve the leak in the wall and the corresponding hole around the kitchen outlet, whatever repair that may require.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair the hole in the wall around the electrical outlet in the kitchen that has a leak. In particular, the Landlord shall: 1. Ensure no water leaks through the wall around the electrical outlet;
Ensure that the electrical outlet is connected and functional; and

Close the hole in the drywall around the electrical outlet. 2. If the Landlord does not complete the repair by July 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repair to be done and may recover the cost of the repair by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months after the repair is done until there is no longer any money owing.
