issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and/or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: As explained below, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed this application on October 31, 2025 alleging that the Landlord breached sections 21, 22, 23, and 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). In this application the Tenant requested that the LTB order the Landlord to refrain from these certain activities.

At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that she moved out of the rental unit on December 1, 2025. By vacating the rental unit, the remedies requested in this application are effectively moot as the Tenant no longer has any interest in the tenancy.

The Tenant submitted that she uploaded a request to amend the application and referred to a submission filed (DOC-8015915) wherein at page 12, the Tenant wrote the following paragraph: “I am pursuing legal remedies for rent abatement, harassment, privacy breach, interference with reasonable enjoyment and unsafe living conditions. I am also asking for reimbursement on my overpayment for the rent of November (**update: the November payment was (mostly) repaid) and any further restitution the court sees fit. I am also seeking protections from further harassment, unlawful restrictions and evictions on my unit as I seek new accommodation (**update: I have successfully moved)”

Rule 15.1 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure (the ‘Rules’) provides that: A request to amend an application before the hearing must be: a. in writing; b. served with the amended application to all other parties; and c. filed with LTB with the amended application and a completed Certificate of Service.

As per Rule 15.4 of the Rules, the LTB has discretion to grant a request to amend, and will only grant it if satisfied that the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

The Tenant confirmed that she had not provided the Landlord with a copy of this submission as she only uploaded to the Portal (‘TOP’) believing that the Landlord has access and would receive it there. There is no consent to service via TOP filed by the parties and therefore, I cannot find that the Landlord was served with this document.

Based on the submissions before me, I was not satisfied that the Tenant properly served and filed a request to amend this application in accordance with the Rules. Given this and the fact that the request to amend has only occurred at this hearing, I find that it would not be appropriate or fair to grant the request to amend.

The application was filed on October 31, 2025, the Tenant had ample opportunity to request an amendment prior to vacating or today’s hearing if she believed the issues in the application warranted different remedies, such as an abatement of rent or other compensation. I find that it would be extremely prejudicial to the Landlord to permit the Tenant to amend the application at this point.
I was satisfied that once the Tenant vacated the rental unit, this application as filed became moot as the only remedy requested was no longer of any interest to this Tenant.
Consequently, since the application as filed is moot, it must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: (MF) (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (AK) and [name] (GK), (the 'Landlord'), gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant’s evidence should be excluded as it was served/uploaded at 3:33 p.m. on April 5, 2026, not the required minimum 7 days prior to the hearing. The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted that the evidence should not be excluded as it is the same evidence filed with Schedule A attached to the T5 application, the only amendments are with respect to the calculation of expenses; the previously served evidence was included so it would all be in one file/document. The Landlord's Legal Representative responded it was fair to accept the Schedule A evidence but not the other.

The evidence was allowed; the Landlord's Legal Representative agreed it was fair to accept the Schedule A evidence and the amendment evidence was only the addition of 2 missed receipts for moving/storage. Merits

The tenancy was terminated October 31, 2026, pursuant to order LTB-L-053091-23 issued by the Board on September 18, 2024; the application was heard June 24, 2024. The member determined the Landlord satisfied the ‘good faith requirements pursuant to section 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The Tenant testified after receiving the order they panicked because she was on bed rest due to surgery on September 24, 2024; they asked the Landlord to extend the date but the Landlord refused. During their search for new housing, some landlords refused to look at them because they had been evicted, even though the eviction was not their fault. As there was no affordable housing in the area, they moved in with her mother on November 10, 2024, and stayed there approximately 1-year; this was the best option as she was unable to search for housing because of being unable to drive due to the operation. Her mother lived in a small house, therefore they had to share one room, which required 75% of their belongings to be thrown out and the balance being put into 2 storage units; 1 unit was not large enough. Their son was still in the same school, therefore, they were driving by the rental unit at least twice daily for 8-months; during this time they did not see anyone in the unit, or any signs that the unit was lived in such as tire tracks on the snowy driveway, foot prints, snow being shovelled, or salt being lain; the bag of salt they had left was in the same place on the porch all winter. In July 2025, a package of theirs was mistakenly delivered to the rental unit. The delivery company advised it was on the porch, therefore, about 2-days later they went to retrieve it. While there, they saw the salt bag still in the same place and it appeared the mail had not been collected in a while because the mailbox was overflowing with flyers. There were still no drapes in the living room window and upon peeking inside they noticed there was also no furniture in the living room.

The Tenant also testified it was very challenging having to live with her mother. Her mother was 81 years old and suffered from anxiety, therefore living with a 7-year-old was extremely stressful on her, which carried over to all of them; both hers and their son’s relationship with her mother was irreparably changed. Also, the drive to/from their son’s school took about 2 ½ hours per day. Further, her husband had to work longer hours because he is a contractor; all his tools were in one of the storage units and most of his clients were in Toronto. Essential she was a single mother the entire time they lived there. She ended up in therapy because of all the emotional issues associated to having to move and live in cramped accommodations. Her healing process was also negatively affected because of the stress. They found a new place in Whitby and moved ion November 7, 2025. Upon moving, they had to switch their son’s school, which was very upsetting to him. The Tenant further testified they had lived in the rental unit since the Landlord purchased it in 2010. It had a huge backyard with a beautiful garden; they loved living there.

On cross-examination the Tenant testified she did not think the hearing was an emergency situation; the surgery had not been scheduled, and they thought the process was just them having to wait for the Board’s decision as to whether they would be evicted; The surgery was scheduled approximately one month after the hearing. The Tenant also testified they had not advised the Landlord about their package or that they intended on going to the rental unit to pick it up.

The Tenant MF testified to being greatly affected by the move because his tools used to be in the garage, now they were stored in an outside facility that involved more driving time before and after jobs; therefore, he lost out on a substantial amount of family-time and the storage costs just added to the stress. [name] could not take on new jobs because of the extended travel-time resulted in jobs taking longer. Being crammed into her mother’s house affected everyone. The pressure just kept building, resulting in constant fighting between his wife and her mother; their son witnessed this, which also affected him. Also, it is not fair that because they stuck up for their rights, they now have an eviction on their record. He never believed that the Landlord intended to move in at all; first the Landlord wanted more money for rent then when told they were not lawfully entitled to an increase, they said they wanted to move in. Such a move also made no sense as their child was in school and the home they were living in was bigger. In cross examination the Tenant submitted the documentary evidence of his claims was presented at the eviction hearing, and he had no proof of bringing in less money/jobs because he works for himself.

The [name] testified that when the N12 notice was served he intended on moving into the rental unit with his wife and their 2 children. During this period his father was put on a trial drug which affected him psychologically and emotionally; he suffers from a kidney- related autoimmune disease. With all this going on, the Landlord was unable to start the outside work on the property until November 2024, it was during this time that he sought out a contractor for a quote on the inside work as the Tenant had been in the rental unit for 8 years. As set forth in the affidavit dated April 6, 2026, [name], of Tomaz Enterprises, found the unit in significant disrepair and not suitable for occupancy. According to the contractor, including replacing jammed and broken windows the work would take approximately 3 to 4 weeks. Unfortunately, he did not have sufficient financial resources to have the work done; his brother [name] was supposed to handle all the medical appointments but ended up being called back to work, therefore, his wife had to take over, which resulted in reduced workhours and less money coming in.

The Landlord also testified, they had no idea his father’s condition would worsen to such an extent when the N12 was served; his father ended up becoming more dependant on others and consequently became very angry, plus he had a lot of medications to take. His wife LK was qualified to administer the necessary medications he had to take at home because she was a nurse, therefore this made more sense than hiring someone else. Due to the anger issues that developed, his mother and the entire household was severely affected by the continual outbursts and stress. They did their best and made all reasonable efforts to move fully into the rental unit in timely fashion; he changed his driver’s licence in anticipation of the move and had mail redirected. He has never made any attempts to re- rent the property; he just did hos best, going back and forth from one house to theother, to get the unit ready for them. In November 2024, he did a lot of work in the backyard and started the inside work during December; however, he had to stop the interior work in January 2025, because of his father’s health. He did snow removal at the house in the evenings, as to the mailbox, it was small and would get jammed up quickly. The receipts for the utility bills show everything was changed to his name, and he paid them all along. The Landlord reiterated, they had no idea his father’s health would be in such a state or that all of these events would happen, including the affiliated financial hardship/stress.

On cross examination the Landlord testified he moved into the basement with his wife and children and his parents and brother lived upstairs, however, this was not the intention when the N12 was served; his family were supposed to move into the rental unit and his brother, father and mother were to stay in the house they were already living. As to his father’s care, it was best his wife stay at the house to care properly for his father’s needs; she had to stop work entirely by May 2025 because his father’s health was declining. His wife’s driver’s licence was not changed to the rental unit because of the children; their daughter was in grade 7 and the idea of changing schools for grade 8 was very upsetting, plus they did not want the children to change schools mid-year. Therefore, his wife’s driver’s licence had to stay as-is so the kids could remain registered at their school. The Landlord thought it would be fine to leave the rental unit vacant for a time to address everything else going on in their life; he was not thinking about any potential legal consequences of doing so. In respect of the work he has done at the rental unit, he confirmed not having any of the receipts in evidence.

LK testified she noticed her father-in-law’s health getting progressively worse in January 2025; his physical and mental symptoms worsened due to the new drug he was put on. The new medication also affected his blood sugars which required testing 3-times a day and increased his blood pressure and caused breathing issues. Therefore, they decided due to his medical needs and language barrier that she take care of him. Apart from the at- home care required, her father-in-law had to be taken weekly to his family doctor to manage/monitor his blood platelets and sugars. Therefore, they had a lot gong on come January 2025, and could not move into the rental unit as they had intended/wanted. All the care her father-in-law ended up needing could not have been done properly if she had to constantly drive back-and-forth from the rental unit to the house. Despite the stress involved, they had to focus on his health; the whole family came together to do this. In cross examination LK testified her-father-in-law was not capable of taking his own medications or able to monitor his own symptoms; he needed the special care. Once her father-in-law’s condition becomes stable, they will be moving into the rental unit. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved the first three elements of the above test under subsection 57(1)(a); the N12 was given pursuant to section 48 of the Act, the Tenant vacated because of a subsequent eviction order based on the N12 notice, and the Landlord did not move into the rental unit.
However, the Tenant did not prove the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith as is required by the fourth element of the test set out in subsection 57(1)(a).

There is no dispute the Landlord and his family did not move into the rental unit, despite the Tenant's Legal Representative’s assertion that the father’s health issue conveniently arose when the family was to move in, I find the Landlord and LK’s testimony to be reasonable considering the unexpected family circumstances they were faced with. When faced with an unexpected health crisis, I find focussing on that individual’s necessary care to be a normal and logical response. That the Landlord did not re-rent the unit, and it remains vacant, supports their intention to move in when the N12 was served. The pictures taken by the Tenant of the rental unit living room show construction material as well as what appears to be a new mattress leaning up against the wall; this further supports the Landlord’s good-faith intention. I also find it reasonable that the Landlord wanted to do repairs to make the rental unit suitable for them to move in and accept that these plans were thwarted because of his father’s deteriorating health. Although I am sympathetic to how the Tenant’s entire family was affected by the move, there was insufficient evidence presented to establish a bad-faith intention on the Landlord’s part. As to the Tenant’s testimony on their belief as to why the N12 was served, this was dealt with in the hearing order which found the Landlord did not give the notice in bad faith. For all these reasons, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, I was not satisfied that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) applies to this relationship.

The Tenant provided a copy of the agreement he had signed with the Landlord into evidence (DOC-8036223pg85). This agreement is titled “Sublet Agreement Form,” and provides that the Landlord is a Tenant and that [name] is the Owner/Landlord for the property. [name] is not a signatory to this agreement and the Tenant confirmed that he had no dealings with this person.
The Tenant also stated that he resided in the same rental unit as the Landlord and they shared common facilities including the kitchen.

Sect ion 2 of the Act provides that: A “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; Emphasis Added

Based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied that [name] is more likely than not a tenant occupying the unit and therefore does not meet the definition of a Landlord under the Act. I find it more likely than not that this was a roommate living arrangement which is not covered by the Act.
T herefore, the LTB has no jurisdiction to determine the dispute between these parties. Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: RH advised that [name] (GH) moved out of the rental unit in late 2024. Preliminary Issue – Payment Agreement

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that this application ought to be dismissed as the parties have signed a Payment Agreement (the ‘Agreement’) wherein they agreed all issues between them are resolved, the Landlord committed to withdraw their L2 application, LTB-L-100713-24, and the Tenants agreed to withdraw this application. In support of this submission, the Landlord’s Legal Representative provided a copy email correspondence between the Landlord and one of the Tenants, [name] (MH) on November 15, 2025 and November 26, 2025, into evidence (DOC-7507517pgs3-5). MH’s email read as follows: “Hi [name], you are correct the payment agreement did dismiss the hearing. We will not be proceeding with the hearing but with that being said we would really like the floors and baseboards in the basement to be replaced. The aftermath of the leak from last year has caused mold/mildew growth, leaving behind a very unpleasant odor. Sorry for the late reply as I was in the hospital for surgery.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative also provided into evidence a copy of the Landlord’s request to withdraw their L2 application dated April 2, 2025 (DOC-7507517pg26) and a copy of the Agreement, dated February 19, 2025 by the Landlord and February 25, 2025 by MH (DOC-7507517pgs30-31). The Agreement was to resolve application, LTB-L- 005870-25, the Landlord’s L1 application for non-payment of rent and was on the LTB’s standard “Payment Agreement” form. There is no addendum to this form confirming that all issues between the parties are resolved. The form itself lists the current agreed upon rent arrears and costs and sets out a series of payments to be made by the Tenants, failing which the Landlord may file a L4 application.

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the Agreement does not bind the parties to a resolution of all issues between them. She also submitted that the email correspondence from MH suggests they are only withdrawing if certain repairs are completed.

Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the parties’ Agreement amounted to a full and final resolution of all issues between them. The Agreement only speaks to rent arrears and costs, and provides a remedy only to the Landlord if not met. The Agreement makes no mention of the issues in this application or other issues raised by the Tenants. I find it likely that MH may have been referring to the Landlord’s hearing being dismissed after the Agreement was signed as that hearing did not proceed. He also speaks about maintenance issues in the email correspondence which are not the issues raised in this application. Therefore, I was not satisfied that the parties had reached a prior Agreement to resolve the issues in this application. Preliminary Issue - Amendment

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the Tenants filed with the LTB and served the Landlord a request to amend this application on February 27, 2026 (DOC- 7466991). The amendment reads: “ I am writing to formally request an amendment to my T2 application (File No: LTB- T-092641-24 ) pursuant to LTB Rule 15. Since the original application was filed, several significant incidents have occurred that further demonstrate a pattern of harassment and retaliatory behavior by the Landlord. The following additions have been made to the "Reasons for Application" section: ● October 11, 2024: The Landlord sent an "accidental" text message intended for her legal counsel, referring to the tenants as "this people" and expressing a desire to take legal action. This provides evidence of the Landlord's adversarial intent and bad faith. ● November 9, 2024: The Landlord served an N5 Notice regarding a pond and flower bed that have existed with her knowledge and consent since 2021. This notice was served immediately following my requests for maintenance and professional conduct, and I believe it is a retaliatory act intended to interfere with my reasonable enjoyment of the premises.”
The Landlord’s Legal Representative opposed the request to amend citing that the Landlord would be prejudiced as it infringes on the Landlord’s legal rights.

Rule 15.4 of the LTB Rules of Procedure provides that the LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. In this case, the allegations in the original application relate to harassment, the Tenants’ amendment asserts that there have been additional incidents of alleged harassment. The LTB must adopt the most expeditious method of determining the issues in an application affording the parties an adequate opportunity to know the issues.

The request to amend the application to include two additional allege incidents is granted. I was satisfied that the Landlord’s Legal Representative’s opposition to allowing the amendment was simply because the Landlord disputes those allegations not that she was not aware of them. The amendment request was served on the Landlord on February 27, 2026, I was satisfied that the Landlord knows the issues to respond to at this hearing and is therefore not prejudiced by their inclusion at the hearing today. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

In this application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord had breached sections 22 and 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Tenants allege that the Landlord had been aggressive and made several inappropriate/discriminatory comments which amount to harassment and rely on incidents of the Landlord’s conduct on October 10, 2024 and October 11, 2024, and the service of a notice of termination on November 9, 2024.

Section 22 of the Act provides: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act provides: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Harassment is not defined in the Act, however it is generally accepted that harassment is a course of conduct that a person knows, or should know, would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate, lawful purpose.

The Tenants’ Agent, [name] [name] (RH), who is MH’s daughter, and Power of Attorney, and GH’s sister, testified that although she was not present and believed it was October 10, 2024, her brother-in-law, who was present, had advised her that the Landlord and her partner were at the rental unit on that day speaking in Polish and made derogatory comments such as insinuating that the Tenants had brought in a mattress off the road. RH also testified that on this date the Landlord slammed open MH’s bedroom door and yelled at him.

Under cross-examination, [name] confirmed that she did not hear any of the comments by the Landlord, but her brother-in-law did and understood them as he also speaks Polish. She also confirmed that the date could have been October 11, 2024.

RH also testified that on October 11, 2024 after requesting maintenance at the unit, the Landlord sent an accidental text message to MH referring to him as “these people,” which she found discriminatory. RH provided a screenshot of the text message from the Landlord into evidence (DOC-7466993). The text message is undated and reads: “Can you please tell me what I have to do because I don’t have energy anymore for this people” “Sorry this was not for you for my lawyer”

RH further testified that on November 9, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenants with a N5 notice of termination (N5 Notice) requesting that they remove a flower bed which the Landlord has been aware of since 2021. RH asserted that the service of the N5 Notice left MH stressed out and panicked as he believed he had to immediately move out.

The Landlord testified that she would not have been at the rental unit on October 11, 2024 as this was a Friday and she was working. However, she did recall attending the rental unit about an issue with water leaking from the bathtub and it would have been on a Saturday or Sunday. She denied yelling at MH or speaking Polish with her partner as he does not speak Polish, he is Italian.

The Landlord also testified that she sent the text message to MH in error as the message was meant for her lawyer who she was seeking help from and when she realized she sent it to MH, she immediately apologized.

Under cross-examination, when asked what did you mean in the text message, the Landlord replied, it did not mean anything and nothing to do with the rental property or MH. Under redirect, the Landlord confirmed that English is her second language and that she never received any language schooling as she learned English from hearing others.

The Landlord further testified that she served a N5 Notice on October 30, 2024 to the Tenants and that it listed a number of items the Tenants have installed without her permission, not just the flower bed, as well as issues she was having accessing the rental unit.

Neither of the Tenants testified at this hearing nor did RH’s brother-in-law who provided RH with the assertions of the Landlord’s conduct on or about October 10 or 11, 2024. RH also had issues with confirming the specific dates of issues, the text message was not dated and the Landlord provided a different date for the service of the N5 Notice.

Therefore, the best evidence before me of the incident at the rental unit was from the Landlord. She denied the allegations made by RH of her conduct at the rental unit. The Landlord was not discredited under cross-examination and RH simply relied on hearsay evidence from her brother-in-law.

The Landlord did not dispute that she sent the text to MH in error as it was intended for her lawyer. [name] took offense with the use of the phrase “this people.” While I agree that there is a discriminatory tone when the phrase “these people” is being used, in this case since the Landlord’s first language is not English, it is also likely that the connotation of the phrasing of “this people” in the text message may have been a misapplication of the English language. Especially, given that the Tenants have not demonstrated a history of the Landlord using other derogatory or discriminatory to them in other text communications. Therefore, I was not satisfied that this one phrase in this particular text communication supports a finding of harassment toward MH by the Landlord.

A landlord is entitled to serve a notice of termination in accordance with the Act if they believed that a tenant has breached sections of the Act. In this case, RH asserted that the N5 Notice was simply retaliatory. [name] did not provide a copy of the N5 Notice into evidence, so it was not reviewed in its entirety. The issue [name] took with the N5 Notice was that it contained an allegation of an installation of a flower bed which the Landlord was aware of for the past three years. [name] because the Landlord was aware for years that the Tenants installed a flower bed at the rental unit, does not mean that she cannot assert that the installation was done without her permission.

A N5 Notice is a remedial notice which provides a tenant seven days to correct the issue and/or dispute the issue at a hearing before the LTB. I was not satisfied that the mere service of this N5 Notice to the Tenants in October or November 2024 amounted to harassment. There was no history presented of invalid notices of termination being served on the Tenants by the Landlord or that this notice was found to be without merit. Based on the Landlord’s testimony and not being able to review the N5 Notice itself, I was satisfied that there were other issues on the N5 Notice not just an issue about the flower bed. Therefore, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord was covering all possible grounds when serving this N5 Notice to the Tenants.
Since the Tenants have not proven that the Landlord breached the Act, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Did the Landlords give N12 for own use in bad faith?

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The facts were essentially undisputed.
The rental unit was a family home. It consisted of the main floor, basement, a yard, and a garage. The laundry facilities were located in the basement.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on February 11, 2024, and resided there with her 11-year-old son. The monthly rent was $2,500.00.

In February 2025, the Landlord informed the Tenant that the Landlords’ son would like to move into the basement. The Landlords offered to lower the Tenant’s rent by $500.00 to $2,000.00. The Tenant would retain the use of the main floor, and the Landlords’ son would reside in the basement. The Landlord offered to put a lock on the door separating the main floor and the basement. The Tenant, however, would have to share the kitchen on the main floor and the laundry facilities in the basement, with the Landlord’s son.

Not surprisingly, the Tenant was not willing to share her living arrangements with the Landlords’ son. The Tenant stated that she would feel uncomfortable sharing her living space with a strange man. As such, the Tenant refused the Landlords’ proposal.
As a result, on June 25, 2025, the Landlords served the Tenant a notice of termination N12 for their son’s use.

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit pursuant to the notice of termination on August 31, 2025. She purchased a new home. Her mortgage is comparable to the rent she had been paying in the rental unit.

The Landlords’ son ([name]) moved into the rental unit in September 2025, he continues to reside in the basement. In October 2025, [name], moved into the main floor of the home. He pays $2,000.00 per month. This is the same amount the Tenant would have paid, had she accepted the Landlords’ proposal to share the rental unit with the Landlords’ son.

According to the Landlord, the Landlords’ intention was not to re-rent the rental unit for a higher rent, but to provide living arrangements for their son. The Landlords did not mislead the Tenant about their son’s intention to move into the rental unit.

The fact that the Landlords’ son does not occupy the entire rental unit is not determinative. The determinative fact is that the Landlords’ son required the rental unit for the purposes of residential occupation for at least one year. The Landlords’ son moved into the rental unit and continues to live there. The rental unit is the entire home. The Landlords’ son chose to take in a roommate to share the living arrangements in order to offset his costs. The Act does not prohibit that.

There was some inconsistency in the Landlords’ evidence about the nature of the costs. However, whether the Landlords’ son makes mortgage payments or payments to his sister under an estate planning arrangement is not determinative.
The ownership of the house was transferred to the Landlords’ son in January 2026.

In the end, it was the Landlords’ son who was the person identified in the N12 notice of termination, as the person who required the rental unit for purposes of residential occupation for at least one year. The Landlords’ son moved into the rental unit and continues to live there.

In conclusion, in order for the Tenant to be successful in this application, she would need to prove all four requirements under s 57(1)(a). She did not. Although it was not disputed that the Landlords served the Tenant an N12 notice of termination and the Tenant moved out of the rental unit pursuant to the notice of termination. The evidence before me established that the person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; the Landlords did not mislead the Tenant, and did not serve the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
Based on the evidence before me, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant the difference in the monthly rent the Tenant has to pay for one year in the total amount of $6,000.00, and the cost of the application. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The rental unit was located in the basement of the Landlord’s home. The Tenant resided in the rental unit for 8 years.

On April 28, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination [name] for Landlord’s own use. The termination date set out the notice of termination was June 30, 2025. The Tenant moved out pursuant to the notice of termination on or about July 1, 2025.
The Landlord did not move into the rental unit.

About four months after vacating the rental unit, the Tenant discovered that the rental unit was advertised on Airbnb for short term rental. The rental unit continues to be advertised on Airbnb. The Tenant submitted into evidence screenshots of the advertisements on Airbnb.

The Tenant testified that after he moved out of the rental unit, his monthly rent increased by $500.00 every month. He had to find alternate accommodation quickly and there was a dearth of available rentals in the community. His current unit is smaller than the rental unit he had occupied for 8 years. Remedies

The Tenant requested compensation for the increased rent that the Tenant has and continues to incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit a rent differential for one year in the total amount of $6,000.00.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

As such, the Tenant is entitled to the difference in the increased rent that the Tenant has and continues to incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit in the total amount of $6,000.00 (12x $500.00).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,048.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has and continues to incur for the one-year period from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants’) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • Collected or retained money illegally (T1 application). • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application). This combined T1/T5 application was resolved by order LTB-T-094904-24 issued on September 9, 2025. On September 15, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On September 29, 2025 interim order LTB-T-094904-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 9, 2025. On December 2, 2025, [interim] order LTB-T-094904-24-RV [IN2] was issued granting the request for review and directing the application to be reheard. This application was reheard by videoconference on January 22, 2026 and April 7, 2026. The Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], the Tenants, [name] (MFC) and [name] (JFZ), the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Landlord, attended the hearing. The following witness testified at the hearing: [name] (JL), third tenant at rental unit, on behalf of Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $18,500.77 to the Tenants and an administrative fine of $10,000.00 to the LTB on or before July 4, 2026.

This tenancy commenced on September 1, 2023 for a fixed term ending on August 31, 2024 at a monthly rent of $3,050.00 due payable on the 1st day of each month. The parties signed a Residential Tenancy Agreement (Standard Form Lease) (the ‘Agreement’), a copy of which was provided into evidence (DOC-7164314pg1).

This application was filed pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') which requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination (N12 Notice) under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith. (a) Did the Landlord give a N12 Notice pursuant to section 48 of the Act?

Subsections 48(1) and (2) of the Act provides that: (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located. (2) The date for termination specified in the notice shall be at least 60 days after the notice is given and shall be the day a period of the tenancy ends or, where the tenancy is for a fixed term, the end of the term.

There was no dispute that the Landlord, on or about June 12, 2024, reached out to the Tenants through their group chat to see if the Tenants wanted to extend their tenancy (DOC-7164314pg19). The Tenants responded that they are still discussing it, but would let the Landlord know soon. The Landlord responded as follows: “Ok no problem. Just want to let you guys know as it stands right now I’m planning to use the property for myself after September so won’t be able to continue the lease. If you guys really want to keep living there I can see what I can do but I can’t guarantee.” 6. [name] stated that the Landlord then attended the rental unit on a Sunday night, June 23, 2024, and provided them with an Agreement to End the Tenancy (N11 Form) which MFC stated at the time he thought it was the correct form to sign. MFC also stated that the Landlord came at night around 9:00 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. and told them to just sign the N11 which gave them no time to speak with anyone or seek legal advice. [name] maintained that he had no reason to move out and that it would only be because the Landlord wanted the unit for his own use. A copy of the N11 Form was provided into evidence (DOC- 7164314pg39-40). The N11 Form is signed by the parties on June 23, 2024 and provided a termination date of August 31, 2024. 7. Under cross-examination, MFC confirmed that there was a possibility that they were not going to continue the tenancy but he does not remember why although they were discussing it amongst themselves. Under cross-examination, MFC also stated that the Landlord did not provide a reason for coming to the unit that Sunday night but they were not expecting any letter, and that he felt urged to sign the N11 when the Landlord gave it to them as the Landlord is the owner and had the power. 8. The Landlord stated that on June 7, 2024, he discovered that his in-laws were coming to Canada on August 31, 2024. In support, he provided a copy of text messages between his in-laws and himself (DOC-7128456pg1-2). The certified translation of this conversation is found on page 2 and the relevant portion read as follows: [name]: “Mom, we will book an Aug 31st flight ticket for you and [name]. Is that OK? [name]: “When you and [name] arrive, you can stay in my condo in Vaughan.” [name]: “OK” [name]: “Did you talk to the tenants?” [name]: “I will talk to them and tell them I need the unit back for you to live in.” [name]: “By the way, is our return flight in October 2025?” [name]: “yes, rest assured, if you guys can’t get used to life here, we will see” 9. The Landlord also stated that on June 12, 2024, he told the Tenants about his in-laws coming to Canada and that they will stay in the unit. 10. The Landlord’s witness, [name], JL, testified that he was one of the tenants residing in the rental unit. He confirmed that the rental unit is a two bedroom plus den and that he was occupying the den as his bedroom, which had no windows and only fit a twin bed. He recalled the Landlord’s text in June 2024 asking if they were staying or not. He stated that it was discussed with his roommates (Tenants), but personally he wanted to move out as he wanted a real bedroom. With respect to the N11 Form, JL testified that he asked one of his roommates to sign for him as he had a class to attend. 11. JL also testified that after they signed the N11 Form they were looking together for another rental unit and that he found an Agent to assist them. He further confirmed that they were looking for a three bedroom unit, looked at multiple listings, each one of them gave their input on a particular unit by saying yes or no, until mid-August and after a rejection, when they all felt rushed to find something and everyone just said “yes” to anything they found. JL further testified that it was only after August 24, 2026 and another rejection that he decided to find a place on his own. In support of this he provided a copy of the Tenants’ group chat messages into evidence (DOC-7164358pg1-2). 12. Under cross-examination, JL confirmed that as international students it was hard to find a new place, and that they needed to pre-pay at least half to one year of full rent to a new landlord. Also, under cross-examination, JL confirmed that he had not looked for another place on his own prior to June 2024. Further, under cross-examination, JL confirmed that it would not have been difficult for the Tenants to find another roommate and it would not have affected them if he had he just moved out. Under cross-examination, JL also confirmed that when the Landlord handed him the N11 Form, the Landlord said it was for personal use. 13. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenants signed the N11 Form because they wanted to terminate the lease which was supported by JL’s testimony. Also, she submitted that the Tenants signed the N11 Form without hesitation and although they knew and had retained a Legal Representative in the past, who is also a Real Estate Agent, they did not contact him when they received the N11 Form. 14. The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the N11 Form was effectively a notice pursuant to section 48 of the Act. He submitted that the Landlord first told them in a text message that he needed the unit for personal use and then presented them with a N11 Form that provided a termination date of August 31, 2024, which was the end of their lease term. He also submitted that pursuant to section 202 of the Act, the LTB must look at the real substance of this transaction and that in Pinto v. [name] and White v. [name], 2021 ONSC 5502 (CanLII), (‘Pinto’), the Divisional Court held that the LTB had a duty to consider the true nature of a transaction which in this case was having the Tenants agree to vacate without having to give the appropriate notice. 15. Subsection 202(1) of the Act provides that: In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 16. Based on the evidence before me I was satisfied that the Tenants were still considering whether to continue their tenancy as per the Landlord’s inquiry when the Landlord advised that he required the unit for his own use as evident by the text messages between the parties ([name]) at that time. This was even supported by JL’s testimony in that although he wished to end this tenancy for a better bedroom, nothing was initiated by him in support of that wish until the Landlord made the declaration that he wanted the unit for his own use and presented the Tenants with the N11 Form. Additionally, [name] maintained that he had no reason to move out of this rental unit which was also support by JL’s testimony confirming that the other two tenants would have no issues finding another roommate. 17. Additionally, given JL’s testimony on the difficulty they had in securing another rental unit as international students, I find it likely that the Tenants would have had a similar experience before securing this tenancy and would have been aware of this potential difficulty and additional costs of having to pay rent up front and that this would be a deterrent for them to terminate this tenancy. In any event, there was no evidence before me that all the Tenants collectively wished to terminate this tenancy or even contemplated that prior to the Landlord asking them about the renewal and making his declaration of wanting the unit for his own use. 18. In Pinto, that landlord had told the tenant he intended to renovate the building to build an addition on to it, and as the power and water would be shut off during construction the tenant would need to move out. That landlord also offered four months rent and the return of the final month’s rent if the tenant agreed to sign a N11 Form. The Divisional Court held in Pinto, that section 202 of the Act imposed a statutory duty on the LTB to determine questions of fact and to apply governing principals of law to ascertain the real substance of the transaction in a landlord having a tenant agreeing to vacate the premises (N11 Form) when the landlord has not given the appropriate notice of termination under the Act. 19. Given the evidence before me, and having regard to the real substance of the transaction between the parties pursuant to section 202 of the Act, I find that the N11 Form was given to the Tenants by the Landlord to effectively have them agree to terminate the tenancy without the Landlord having to give the proper notice of termination thus avoiding his obligations at law that come with giving a proper notice for landlord’s own use, such as compensation and the requirement for him or an immediate family member to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes for at least one year after the Tenants vacate. The Landlord confirmed that he also told the Tenants that his in-laws would be staying in the unit. 20. As well, although incorrect as a landlord cannot re-rent or sell a unit, the Landlord stated that he believed he could only sell the unit and not re-rent it after the Tenants vacated as per the N11 Form. This statement by the Landlord confirmed that he believed there is some obligation/deterrent when you give a tenant a notice of termination for your own use. 21. Finally, a landlord cannot escape liability because they do not provide the specific N12 Notice form to a tenant. In this case, it was clear that the Landlord’s purported intention was to terminate the tenancy for his own use, whether it was his in-laws moving in or he had some other plan. A tenancy can only be terminated by a landlord pursuant to a ground identified in the Act. 22. Consequently, I find that the Landlord’s text message, his stated intent, and the service of the N11 Form on the Tenants met the requirements of a N12 Notice pursuant to section 48 of the Act. The Landlord stated he required the unit for his own use, the termination date in the N11 Form was at least 60 days after the notice was given to the Tenants, and it was for the end of the term as required by subsection 48(2) of the Act. (b) Did the Tenants vacate the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice? 23. There was no dispute that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on or above September 10, 2024. [name] testified that he vacated the rental unit on September 1, 2024. [name] stated that they were in the process of vacating the rental unit on September 10, 2024 when the Landlord deactivated their key fobs to the premises. Additionally, the Tenants gave testimony that they were actively seeking a new rental unit after they received the N11 Form from the Landlord. (c) Did the Landlord or his in-laws occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated? 24. There was no dispute or evidence that either the Landlord nor his in-laws occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated and for a period of one year. The Landlord testified that since the Tenants did not vacate until September 10, 2024, he had to find his in-laws another place to stay when they arrived in Canada at the end of August 2024. He also testified that he ended up having to rent a place from a friend for the two months that his in-laws stayed in Canada. (d) Did the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith? 25. Based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied that the N12 Notice was given to the Tenants in bad faith. The Landlord had no intention of occupying the unit himself nor did his in-laws intend to occupy the premises for at least one year. There was no dispute that his in-laws only remained in Canada for two months. I was not convinced that his in-laws plan to occupy the rental unit only changed due to the Tenants not vacating on time (end of August 2024) and that this alone caused such a rift between the Landlord and his in- laws, that his in-laws were forced to go back to China. As well, I was not convinced that the Landlord had to sell the unit due to a lack of finances. 26. There was no dispute that on September 15, 2024, the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale. A copy of the listing was provided into evidence (DOC-7164314pg29). The rental unit was subsequently sold in December 2024 or January 2025 as per the Landlord. 27. Subsection 57(5)(c) of the Act provides that: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 28. In accordance with subsection 57(5) of the Act, it is presumed that the Landlord gave the N12 Notice in bad faith since the rental unit was listed for sale within the relevant period, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the onus switches to the Landlord to satisfy the LTB that the N12 Notice was not given in bad faith. 29. The Landlord stated that when his in-laws arrived on August 31, 2024 they could not stay with him as his place is only a one plus one unit which could not fit four people. He stated that they rented a friend’s condominium, which he had to pay two months rent of $4,080.00 up front, as that this was what he negotiated with his friend as September would have been a good time for his friend to rent the unit to someone else. In support, he provided a copy of the receipt for this payment dated September 1, 2024 into evidence (DOC- 5973972). 30. The Landlord also stated that not knowing when the Tenants would vacate was stressful on his wife, and his in-laws were angry with him as he had not set their stay up properly, which resulted in some fighting between them. He further stated that when he went to the in-laws to tell them the Tenants had moved out they were really upset that they had already paid two months rent at the temporary place, his friend’s condo. 31. The Landlord further stated that he could not afford to keep the rental unit vacant and believed that he could not re-rent the unit, but could sell it so he listed it for sale. He also stated that the unit was an investment property for him and at that time the condominium market was not good, as it took three to four months to sell the unit and he did not make any profit on the sale. 32. The Tenants were in the process of vacating the rental unit when the Landlord terminated their fobs on September 10, 2024. Given this, the Landlord had possession of the rental unit as this date. I find it unreasonable that if the Landlord’s in-laws were really intending to stay in Canada (and the rental unit) that they would not have just moved into the unit when it was available. The timeframe between their arrival and the Landlord having possession of the rental unit was only ten (10) days. I find it unlikely that a large plan like staying in Canada for a year would change in this short of a timeframe regardless of the alleged breakdown in the relationship. 33. Additionally, I did not find the Landlord’s evidence credible in that he could not afford to leave the rental unit vacant after September 10, 2024. While although, the Landlord asserted he paid two months rent for his in-laws to temporary house them elsewhere, he also stated that his in-laws were upset about having to pay to stay somewhere else during this time. Given this, it was not clear whether the Landlord or his in-laws paid the rent at the temporary condo. In any event, if the Landlord’s assertion, and supported by the receipt entered into evidence, was that he was responsible for his in-laws housing costs then this would have been no different if they occupied the rental unit as planned. Therefore, the Landlord ought to have expected to not have an income from this property after the Tenants vacated. 34. As well, the Landlord did not provide any evidence in support that he was experiencing financial hardship at the time he listed the rental unit for sale. Therefore, I was not satisfied that the rental unit was only listed for sale as a result in a significant change in the Landlord’s finances. 35. Finally, it is unlikely that the Landlord’s financial issues became so significant in the timeframe in question in this matter. The Tenants were supposed to vacated August 31, 2024, the Landlord took possession on September 10, 2024 by deactivating the Tenants’ key fobs, then listed the unit for sale on September 15, 2024. The entire timeframe was fifteen days. Given the above, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord’s plan all along was to sell the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. Remedies 36. Subsection 57(3) of the Act provides the following permitted remedies: 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 2. An order for an abatement of rent. 3. An order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 4. Any other order that the Board considers appropriate. 37. At the hearing, the Tenants requested a rent abatement of $500.00, rent difference of $4,896.18 for the one-year period after they vacated, general compensation of $15,000.00, and an order for the Landlord to pay an administrative fine of $10,000.00 pursuant to an amended application served on the Landlord and filed with the LTB on December 29, 2025 (DOC-7046975). The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not raise an objection to these amendments, so I was satisfied that the amendment was appropriate, did not prejudice any party and was consistent with a fair and expeditious hearing. 38. The Tenants request for an abatement of rent of $500.00 related to an issue with an internet disruption for about 4-5 hours during their tenancy. As this issue is not related to the Landlord providing the notice in bad faith, I cannot consider this remedy. 39. The Tenants also requested $4,896.18 as rent difference for the one-year period after they vacated due to a loss of square footage. The Tenants stated that their new rental unit was smaller two bedroom measuring only 600 square feet wherein the rental unit was a two bedroom plus den listed at 800-899 square feet as per the MLS listing. The rent at their new unit was $2,850.00 per month. 40. Subsection 57(3) 1 of the Act provides that the LTB may issue an order for the Landlord to pay any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the unit. In this case, there was no dispute that the Tenants’ rent for their new unit was less than the rent at the rental. Since the Tenants have not paid any increased rent for the one-year period after vacating, this request is denied. 41. The Tenants also requested general compensation of $15,000.00. They stated that they felt urged to find a new unit, were stressed, and lost sleep in August 2024. They also stated that they did not get their new keys until September 10, 2024, the day the Landlord deactivated their fobs. They had hoped for at least one more day to move out of the unit and into their new unit. They also stated it was harder for them as international students to find another rental unit as they are not working and do not have good credit and landlords were asking for 12 months up front which was financially hard as well. They felt deceived by the Landlord and maintained that it was very stressful for them to find another unit and move. 42. Subsection 57(3) 1.1 of the Act provides that the LTB may issue an order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former Tenants as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged, being $3,050.00 multiplied by 12 equals $36,600.00. 43. In this case, I was satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to general compensation of $15,000.00 as claimed. This amount is less than half of the maximum claim allowable and is reasonable given that there were two Tenants and their stated circumstances. As well, in accordance with subsection 57(3) 1.1 of the Act, an order can be made regardless of whether the former Tenants incurred any actual expenses. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $15,000.00. 44. The Landlord was aware that the former Tenants were international students. Given their status, I find it very likely that they had difficulties finding a new rental unit. They testified that they had been rejected for a couple of units and in the end they had to split up to find suitable affordable units. I was satisfied that this would have caused a great amount of stress to each of the Tenants given the current rental market and them not being able to demonstrate any income and/or a credit rating. I also find it likely that they would have had to prepay rent in advance as they had to do when renting this unit from the Landlord according to their Agreement (DOC-7164314pg3). 45. The Tenants further requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Guideline 16 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guidelines (the ‘Guidelines’) provides that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the LTB to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 46. Guideline 16 also provides the LTB with factors to consider with respect to quantum of the fine, which are: • The nature and severity of the breach • The effect of the breach on the tenant • Any other relevant factors 47. In this case, I find that an administrative fine of $10,000.00 is warranted to ensure compliance with the Act in the future especially given that the Tenants only met one of the three compensation remedies sought. The Landlord’s bad faith conduct and actions toward these Tenants showed a blatant disregard for the Act. 48. One of the primary purposes of the Act is to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful evictions. Therefore, in keeping with the spirt of the legislation the LTB has a great interest to deter landlords from in engaging in this type of behaviour in the future. 49. The effect of the Landlord’s breach on these Tenants was significant being an unlawful eviction which is the Act’s paramount purpose. The Tenants were already vulnerable being international students and uneducated regarding the laws in the province. The Landlord owns at least one other investment property (rented), and this behaviour must be deterred. T1 application 50. In this application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord failed to pay compensation to the Tenants in accordance with section 48.1 of the Act, failed to refund a key deposit collected, and did not pay any interest on the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit. Compensation 51. Section 48.1 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48. 52. Given the above findings, I was satisfied that the Landlord effectively gave the Tenants a notice to terminate their tenancy pursuant to section 48 of the Act as the real substance of the transaction of the N11 Form was to terminate the tenancy for the Landlord’s own use. There was no dispute that the Landlord did not compensation the Tenants one month’s rent as required by section 48.1 of the Act. Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to one month’s compensation. Consequently, the Landlord shall pay $3,050.00 to the Tenants. Key Deposit 53. There was no dispute that the Landlord collected a refundable key deposit of $500.00 from the Tenants. The Landlord stated that there were three Tenants and when [name] returned his keys he was refunded one third of the deposit being $167.00, this was confirmed by JL. The other Tenants testified that they returned the keys on September 20, 2024 and provided into evidence a copy of the UPS Express post receipt and photo of the keys (DOC-7164314pg51-52). 54. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenants have returned the keys to the Landlord and are therefore entitled to the full refundable deposit back. Since the Landlord already paid $167.00 of that deposit to JL, not contested, the Tenants are entitled to remaining amount of $333.00 which has been illegally retained by the Landlord. The Landlord shall pay $333.00 to the Tenants. Interest on the Last Month’s Rent deposit 55. There was no dispute that the Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit of $3,050.00 from the Tenants on August 31, 2023 as per the signed Agreement (DOC-7164314pg1). Subsection 106(6) of the Act provides that: A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 56. The Tenants last month’s rent deposit was applied to the month of August 2024 the last month of the tenancy. The guideline percentage for 2024 was 2.5. Interest is owing up to the date the deposit was applied, August 31, 2023 to July 31, 2024, being 334 days. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to interest on the last month’s rent is the amount of $69.77 ($3,050.00 x .025/365 x 334). 57. The Tenants are entitled to $48.00 for the costs of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $18,500.77. This amount represents: • $15,000.00 for general compensation. • $3,050.00 for the compensation owing • $333.00 for an illegally retained key deposit. • $69.77 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 4, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
