issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I find the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Preliminary Issues:

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative objected to the fact that the Tenant, [name], had named herself as a Tenant on the tenancy agreement. The Landlord’s Legal Representative relied upon the Lease Agreement found under [name] in DOCUMENT ID 7848416, Exhibit 1. This Lease Agreement signed in December 2018 only names [name] as the Tenant.

Furthermore, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that she had previously sent correspondence to the Tenant, as well as the Tenant’s former [name], stating very clearly, and I quote: “that Ms. [name] is not a tenant on the lease and the Landlord will not accept rent payments or instructions from her or any other occupant of the rental unit. Moreover, the landlord will not communicate wither her or any other occupant of the rental unit directly about tenancy matters. All requests for maintenance and all rent payments must be made directly by you, should Ms. [name] continue to attempt to interject herself onto the landlord as a tenant that interaction will be met with total rejection and denial.”

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that [name] was previously a tenant in one of the Landlord’s other units in the residential complex. She was evicted from that unit, after which at some point, she began to live in the basement unit, which was rented by her father, the named Tenant, in the Lease Agreement. Exhibit 1 shows that she attempted to pay the rent owed for the rental unit directly to the Landlord and communicate with him with respect to maintenance and other issues, from October 2022.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative also submitted that on all applications and Orders issued by the Landlord and Tenant Board with respect to this rental unit only name [name] as the Tenant and that [name] has not been named as a Tenant in any of the pleadings or Orders.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative also referred to an email exchange in Exhibit 1, between herself and the Tenants’ former [name], [name], where Kimberly confirmed in writing that “[name] is an authorized agent of [name] and will be acting on her father’s behalf for ALL issues moving forward, including sending the rent.”

Subsection 103(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: 103(2) A landlord does not create a tenancy with an unauthorized occupant of a rental unit by accepting compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit, unless the landlord and unauthorized occupant agree otherwise.

However, the Tenants’ Legal Representative disputed this under subsection 104(4) of the Act. Subsection 104(4) of the Act states: 104(4) A person’s occupation of a rental unit shall be deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if, a) a tenancy agreement is not entered into under subsection (1) or (2) within the period set out in subsection (3); b) the landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 for an order evicting the person within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy; and c) neither the landlord nor the tenant applies to the Board under section 101 within 60 days after the end of the subtenancy for an order evicting the subtenant.

No evidence was provided by either party that an application for eviction for unauthorized occupancy of the [name], had been brought before the Board. Therefore, by virtue of s. 104(4) of the Act I find [name] to have been a valid Tenant in the rental unit.

An issue was raised by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, who indicated she had not been served with the Tenant’s Evidence Brief. A review of the Portal (“TOP”) confirmed that no such brief had been uploaded. Following a brief recess, the Tenant’s Legal Representative uploaded two Evidence Briefs (Document IDs 8103674 and 8103696). Upon further review, the Landlord’s Legal Representative confirmed receipt of the brief identified as Document ID 8103674, which has been admitted into evidence as Exhibit 2. As there is no evidence that she or the Landlord were served with the brief identified as Document ID 8103696, that document is not admitted into evidence. Relevant Law, Burden of Proof and Admissions

On an application for service of a N12 Notice of Termination for landlord’s own use in bad faith, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires a tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 Notice of Termination under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice of Termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N21 Notice of Termination in bad faith.
The parties agree the Landlord gave the Tenant, [name], an N12 Notice on May 1, 2022, with a termination date of July 31, 2022.

However, the Tenants vacated the unit or around November 15, 2024. The Sheriff’s notice of vacant possession dated December 6, 2024, has been provided in page 25 of DOCUMENT ID 784816 and has been admitted into evidence as Exhibit 3. The Landlord testified that the Tenants never returned the keys of the rental unit to him.
The initial application brought by the Landlord to pertaining to the N12 Notice was resolved by Order LTB-L-027125-22 issued on March 20, 2024.

After the [name] was issued, the Tenant, [name], requested a review of it and that the Order be stayed until the request to review the [name] is resolved. On June 17, 2024, Interim Order LTB-L-027125-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the Order issued on March 20, 2024.

The review request was heard on August 1, 2024, during which the parties mutually agreed to resolve all matters at issue in the application and requested an [name] on consent. On consent of the parties, it was ordered that: • Order LTB-L-027125-22-RV-IN be cancelled and the stay of Order LTB-L-027125- 22 be lifted immediately; • Order LTB-L-027125-22 issued on March 20, 2024, be cancelled and replaced with the Order issued on August 21, 2024; and • The tenancy between the Landlord and Tenant be terminated and the Tenant must move out of the rental unit by November 15, 2024.

When the N12 Notice was served on the Tenant, [name], it identified the Landlord as the intended occupant of the rental unit. It was not denied at the hearing that the Landlord failed to move into the rental unit after the eviction of [name].
Consequently, I find this cannot satisfy the requirement that an individual indicated on the N12 Notice must have moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.
What remains disputed is whether the N12 Notice was served in bad faith.

Section 57(5) of the Act provides that if after a N12 Notice is given and within 12 months of the tenant vacating a landlord advertises the rental unit for sale (among other activities) then, unless the contrary of proven on a balance of probabilities, it is presumed that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith.

I find the evidence of the parties accorded insofar as the rental unit was listed for sale within one year of the time the Tenants vacated. As a result, it is the Landlord who bears the burden of demonstrating they genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit for a period of at least one year. The Landlord did not serve the N12 Notice in bad faith:

The Landlord had initially purchased a restaurant with a capacity to seat around 100 people, a few years ago. Along with the restaurant came a 2-bedroom residential unit and a 3-bedroom basement unit and the Landlord owns this entire complex. The Landlord’s intention was always to live in the rental unit at some point.

The Landlord’s position in essence is that he intended to move into the rental unit, acted in accordance with his intention, that circumstances prevented him from moving immediately and that it was only after increased financial pressures that he decided to sell the property.

The Tenants’ position is that the Landlord never intended to move into the rental unit and that he wished to evict the Tenants, so that he could sell the property and maximise his profits. The Landlord already has a much larger home and so there was no need to evict the Tenants and sell the rental unit.
The Landlord did not dispute that he owns a house, but he genuinely wanted to move into the rental unit as he wanted to live in the same complex as his restaurant.

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the rental unit was listed for sale on multiple occasions and evidence of the listings have been provided on pages 45 to 61 of Exhibit 2. These listings are dated April 11, 2025, and November 11, 2025, respectively in the Exhibit. Furthermore, the second listing shows that there was a price reduction of $100,000 from the original listing price. As of today, the Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the rental unit is still listed for sale with another price reduction.
As the rental unit was listed for sale in less than 12 months from the eviction date, there is automatically a presumption of bad faith on the Landlord, which now needs to be explored further.

The Landlord testified that he purchased the residential complex together with the restaurant and after some time, he decided it would be better for him if he moved into the rental unit so that he could run his restaurant and be close to it. Hence, he served the N12 Notice in May 2022.

Once the Landlord was in receipt of the Sheriff’s notice of vacant possession, he began renovations on the rental unit around December 15, 2024. The Landlord testified the Tenants had damaged the rental unit and left a lot of garbage behind. In order to be able to move into the rental unit, the Landlord needed to have the damages, as evidenced on pages 34-39 of Exhibit 1, repaired. Receipts for the renovations and repairs were not provided to the Tenants nor the Board.
The Tenants disputed the Landlord’s claims that extensive repairs and renovations had taken place in the rental unit and referred to pages 50 and 51 of Exhibit 2.

The Landlord testified that the repairs and renovations were carried out in the basement unit, which is the rental unit, but not in the residential unit upstairs. When asked why the Landlord didn’t move into the residential unit whilst the repairs were ongoing in the rental unit, he testified that the residential unit was occupied by his business partner, [name].

The Landlord testified that [name], although living in the residential unit, is not a tenant and does not pay rent. As a part of her partnership contract with the Landlord, she was able to live in the residential unit without having to pay rent. Even though the restaurant is now closed and they are no longer business partners, Connie currently still lives in the residential unit.

However, between the time the N12 Notice was served, and the Tenants vacated the unit, the Landlord testified that he saw a decline in his restaurant business. This decline was most noticeable during the fall of 2024. The restaurant used to have up to 15 employees but during the decline, the Landlord had to let some employees go and work on a reduced staff schedule consisting of 8-10 employees only. No evidence to support this claim was provided by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that in late January 2025, he made the decision not to live in the unit as he ran into financial difficulties and related mortgage issues and had to sell the property. The Landlord testified that he had to put his mortgage payments on hold for some time as is evidenced in Exhibit 1. Page 27 in Exhibit 1 provides evidence of the Landlord having taken out a second mortgage on the property on or around January 29, 2025. The condition placed on the second mortgage was that the property was to be listed for sale.
The Landlord testified that the restaurant closed around the same time the property was listed for sale. The Landlord then worked as a social worker from March 2025 to December 2025.

Due to stress, anxiety, the closing down of the restaurant, and this ongoing issue with the Tenants, the Landlord went on sick leave and started receiving Employment Insurance (“EI”) payments around January 2026. A statement of receipt of EI payments is provided on page 32 of Exhibit 1. The Landlord is not receiving any other form of income and is presently in the process of applying for Long Term Disability. The Landlord testified he now suffers from anxiety and depression.

When questioned by the Tenants’ Legal Representative, the Landlord testified that the intention was to sell his “St. Williams” property and move into the rental unit, but because of the financial challenges he faced with the restaurant, he decided to list the rental unit for sale as opposed to the St. Williams property.

The Landlord was asked by the Tenants’ Legal Representative why, when he knew he was not going to move into the rental unit, he did not offer it back to the Tenants whilst waiting for the property to be sold. Initially, the Landlord did not have a response to this question, but upon further questioning, the Landlord testified that his realtor advised him it would be worthwhile for him to sell the residential complex and the restaurant together as a package as this property is in a secluded location and for a potential restaurant owner, this would be a better sell.

The Landlord reiterated he had every intention to move into the rental unit, but due to a change in financial circumstances, he had no choice but close the restaurant down and sell the property in its entirety. Law and Analysis:

I find that there was evidence to support that the Landlord was faced with financial hardship pertaining to the restaurant and that it made practical and financial sense to sell the restaurant with the residential complex as a whole package. I also note that although conduct and motive may be considered as part of the good faith analysis, a landlord’s motivations or desire to move int a rental unit for 12 months need not be reasonable and are largely irrelevant – what is required is that the Landlord genuinely intend to live in the property for 12 months; [see [name], 2014 ONSC 3352 (CanLII) at para 17., citing Salter v. Belijinac, 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC)].

Further, I find that a deviation or change from a genuine intention to occupy a rental unit for a period of 12 months is insufficient to comply with the Landlord’s continuing duty of good faith unless the change takes place after the Tenants vacated.

The Tenants’ Legal Representative raised that this eviction process was just a means to sell the property and maximise his profits. Had the Landlord’s plan been to profit financially, I do not see why he would have let the rental unit sit empty until he found a buyer for it.

I am satisfied that the documents submitted by the Landlord’s Legal Representative together with the Landlord’s credible testimony supports the Landlord’s position that he was facing financial constraints and as a result, in these changed circumstances he felt he had no option but to close his restaurant. If the restaurant is closed, then there is no longer any purpose for him to move into the rental unit.
The fact that the rental unit is still unoccupied further supports that the Landlord’s sole purpose to evict the Tenants was to genuinely occupy the rental unit himself.

I find the Landlord has demonstrated it is more likely than not that she genuinely intended to move into the rental unit for a period of one year before the Tenants vacated. I therefore find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith and find that the N12 Notice was served in good faith.
As a result, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and Investfact Developments Inc. (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: The application is amended to add the corporate Landlord Investfact Developments Inc. as a respondent party, as they are listed on the residential lease agreement.

This matter was combined with LTB-L-071174-24, an L2 application based on a voidable N5 notice of termination. The Landlord indicated at the start of the hearing that they wished to withdraw the application. The request was not opposed. A separate order dismissing the L2 was issued on May 5, 2026. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Evidentiary background

The Tenants moved into the rental unit under a written residential lease agreement on September 1, 2022. The monthly rent was $2,395.00. The Tenant was responsible for electricity, heat, internet and water charges. They vacated the unit on December 31, 2024.

The lease submitted also states, at page 4, that “The tenant(s) is responsible for paying all the utilities including … Enbridge Gas including hot water rental … and setup an account directly in their name with them.”

The Tenant testified that at the time the lease was signed, the Landlord casually advised them that they could ignore the reference to the hot water tank rental, that it was standard language used in all their leases and that it did not apply to this tenancy. The Tenant stated that they relied on this representation and did not question the clause further.

The hot water tank stopped functioning on June 16, 2023. The Tenant promptly informed the Landlord. However, when the Landlord arranged to replace the tank, conflict between the parties arose, as evidenced in the following email exchanges: • June 19, 2023 at 12:23 - Landlord R.A. to Tenant: “This hot water tank is rental and usually it is bill through Enbridge, but Enbridge stop doing that and as per signed lease the tenant is responsible for paying the monthly rental. … They are sending the paperwork to you and me to sign it now for install today or tomorrow.” • June 19, 2023 at 13:44 - Tenant to [name]: “When the tank failed last Friday 1 am we called the emergency number on the tank. The people who answered were from Reliance and said the unit … was bought out by you or previous owners many years ago. As you are aware, we did not enter into a water tank rental agreement when we signed the lease. As you said in earlier communications, the lease ‘is standard lease for some other properties’ and the specific wording about a tank rental did not apply to us when we signed not have we had hot water rental payments since signing the lease. If there was an error in the original lease, please let us know and we may negotiate, otherwise this urgent repair cost shouldn't be ours to bear.” • June 19, 2023 at 16:35 - A. D. (Brilia Air Heating and Cooling Inc.) to Tenant, cc to the Landlord: “Please see attached landlord/tenant form that needs your signature. … [and] we will require a [name] cheque for pre-authorized payments …”. • June 20, 2023 at 23:45 - Tenant to Housing Help Ottawa: “We continue to receive threats and pressure from our landlord on this matter. It is extremely stressful to have these interactions with him continuously. He's previously used this tactic of "need to speak in person" to basically bully us. These text messages from him from hours ago, follow those from my previous email: The "I put on hold" he's talking about refers to him interfering with repairs by delaying them to force us to sign a hot water tank rental agreement before repairs would be started on the broken tank.” • June 21, 2023 14:21 - Tenant to A.D., cc to the Landlord: “Installation was completed… the broken water heater was a 20-year old unit owned by the landlord. It was his responsibility to repair his appliance when it broke.” • June 21, 2023 at 14:32 - Landlord R.A. to Tenant: “You are so wrong. Read the signed lease which clearly says hot water tank is rental and tenent is responsible for paying it. If you do not pay than the company who install it will remove it, or It may become a legal matter please advise.” • June 21, 2023 at 14:47 - Landlord R.A. to A.D., cc to the Tenant: “I will send you my paper work signed by tomorrow so that you can start billing me. If my tenent does not cooperate by this week and not meet me to sign the papers you needed I will serve him legal documents by early next week.”
The Tenant A.K-L. phoned R.A. on June 21, 2023 to discuss responsibility for the costs of the hot water tank rental. He submitted an audio recording he took of the conversation.

The Landlord did replace the tank with a rented appliance [name] supplied and, given the Tenant’s refusal to sign the contract, entered into an equipment rental lease with [name]. The Landlord then pursued the Tenant monthly for the rent instalment of $34.98 + HST. The Tenant refused pay for this cost. On August 7, 2023, the Landlords served a voidable N5 notice to collect the hot water tank arrears. The termination date was August 31, 2023.

On December 19, 2023 the Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice with a termination date of August 31, 2024 because the Landlord G.C. required personal use of the unit for her own residence. The Landlord filed L2 application LTB-L-007148-24 on January 26, 2024, based on the N12 but subsequently withdrew the application on June 17, 2024.

The Landlords served a second voidable N5 notice on July 31, 2024 with a termination date of August 31, 2024, again claiming that the Tenant was liable for and refused to pay the hot water tank arrears that had accumulated, despite repeated reminders. They filed an L2 application based on the N5 on September 3, 2024.

On October 29, 2024, the Tenant served and filed evidence in the Portal in response to the L2. They included land registry documents with a list of properties the Landlord owned. They appended LTB publications about the relevant law. The Landlord withdrew their application the next day.

The Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2024. They claim they were induced to move out because of the Landlord’s unrelenting pressure over 19 months to pay the hot water tank costs and repeated bullying which made it impossible to enjoy their home.

The Landlord denies any misconduct and disputes the Tenant’s version of events. The Landlord emphasizes that the Tenant was aware from the outset of the tenancy of their obligation to pay hot water tank rental charges. The Landlord's Legal Representative submits that, since the Tenant obstinately refused to comply, based on the plain wording of the lease it was appropriate for the Landlord to serve the N5 notices. The Law
Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes.
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The Act does not define “harassment.” However, the Board has consistently held that harassment involves conduct, or a course of conduct, which is known, or that ought reasonably to be known, to be unwelcome or vexatious. Analysis

The issues before the Board are: (1) Did the Landlord’s conduct by attempting to impose and enforce hot water tank rental charges substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit? (2) Did the Landlord’s conduct in pursuing multiple notices of termination substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit? (3) Did the Landlord engage in harassing conduct? (4) Was the Tenant induced to vacate the rental unit due to the Landlord’s conduct and, if so, what remedies should be granted? The lease terms relating to the hot water tank rental
A central issue is whether the Landlord was entitled to require the Tenant to assume responsibility for hot water tank rental charges after the original tank was replaced.

That is because the lease contained a clause that required the Tenant to pay for the “hot water rental”. I note that the lease includes multiple clauses that are contrary to section 4 of the Act, and that the inconsistent provisions cited below were void: • prohibiting the Tenant from allowing others to reside in the unit without the prior consent of the Landlord. • prohibiting pets. • prohibiting “wild parties”. • prohibiting the “usage of any unprescribed drug” on the premises. • prohibiting the use of medical marijuana, or any smoking on the premises outside of the unit. • requiring the Tenant to forfeit the “security deposit” if there is “any evidence of cannabis use on the premises”. • requiring the Tenant to acknowledge that the rental unit “comes as is”. • requiring the Tenant to maintain the HVAC equipment and the water softener. • requiring the Tenant to cleanse all appliances “once a week keep them tidy and clean”. • requiring the Tenant to make all “basic repairs” to the unit. • requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlord for any damage to the unit caused by normal wear and tear. • permitting the Landlord to charge for missed service calls for maintenance and repairs. • requiring the Tenant to use a professional cleaner to clean the unit at the end of the tenancy and to make repairs to holes in walls made by the Tenant (hanging pictures, shelving, etc.). • permitting the Landlord to attend the property to show the property to future “renters” of the property.

These additional terms tend to diminish the reliability of the lease as a legitimate statement of the parties’ legal rights and obligations, and so the lease the Landlord drafted and had the Tenant sign must be viewed with caution. [name]

The evidence establishes that the Tenant did not pay any hot water tank rental charges from the start of the tenancy to June 2023. The Landlord led no evidence to the contrary and, in fact, admitted in a recorded conversation that the original tank rental contract had expired and charges had ceased. This confirms no active rental agreement or fee existed at the start of the tenancy.

The evidence is that while the written lease referenced a hot water tank rental, the Landlord explicitly issued a verbal waiver, advising the Tenant to ignore the clause as it did not apply. The Tenant relied on this waiver to sign the lease. This representation, combined with the 10 months following without rental charges, established the lawful status quo: the hot water tank was landlord-owned equipment included in the rent.
Thus, when the tank failed in June 2023, it became a standard maintenance obligation under Section 20 of the Act. The Landlord was required to promptly repair this vital service.

Email evidence shows the Landlord instead used the disrepair as leverage, pressuring the Tenant to urgently sign a new rental agreement ("now for install today or tomorrow") and threatening legal consequences if they refused.

The Tenant’s contemporaneous communications reflect a justified concern that essential repairs were being delayed to force compliance with a new financial obligation. The Landlord’s decision to replace an owned tank with a rented unit was a personal business choice and the Landlord cannot unilaterally shift their capital replacement costs onto the Tenant mid-tenancy.
The supply of hot water is an essential service. Tenants are entitled to its restoration without unreasonable delay and without being forced to assume new contractual liabilities.

While the Landlord may advance a different interpretation of the lease, it must be supportable in law and fact. In this case, the Landlord ought reasonably to have known that the lease did not support imposing this obligation.

Because the Act prohibits landlords from unilaterally imposing such changes mid-tenancy, the Tenant was not required to enter the new tank rental agreement or pay the charges; the Landlord cannot retroactively enforce a written clause they had explicitly waived. Therefore, the arrears alleged in the N5 notices were not lawfully owing.

The Landlord’s cumulative conduct – insisting on levying unlawful charges and pursuing eviction remedies even up to the hearing date – undermined the Tenant’s security of tenure and caused them unnecessary ongoing stress and uncertainty.
Taken together, this conduct amounts to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Harassment

The Tenant contends that the Landlord R.A. frequently harassed them verbally and in emails. R.A. rebuts this by maintaining that the Tenant’s evidence is fabricated. He testified that his communications with the Tenant were never abusive because “we never operate like that at all”. He acknowledged he could be “curt” and may seem insensitive to tenants who are particularly sensitive individuals, but he was never harassing.

Besides the emails presented, the Tenant A.K-L. relies on an audio recording he took of the telephone call with R.A. on June 21, 2023, the day the replacement tank was installed. I have reviewed and accept this recording as reliable evidence of the parties’ interaction.

During the approximately five-minute call, the Landlord became increasingly agitated. He told the Tenant (5x) that they could “leave if they don’t like it” and that he would rent the unit to someone else. He stated it was a mistake to rent to the Tenant, complained (3x) that the Tenant was not sufficiently appreciative of his efforts to install the tank, and indicated (3x) that he would commence legal action on June 26, 2023.

I find the tone and content of these statements to be confrontational and dismissive. Repeated suggestions that the Tenant should vacate and referring to imminent legal action would reasonably be perceived as unwelcome, upsetting, and intimidating.

The Landlord’s persistence that the Tenant show appreciation is remarkable. Replacing a failed hot water tank is a basic maintenance obligation, not a favour. Framing it otherwise improperly suggests that the Tenant is beholden to the Landlord for fulfilling statutory duties, contributing to a dynamic in which the Tenant may feel pressured to comply to avoid the prospect of adverse treatment, including a refusal by the landlord to fulfill their obligations under the Act in future.

The Landlord also stated that the tank could be removed and, more significantly, threatened to remove it if the Tenant did not agree to the rental arrangement. The Tenant reasonably perceived this as a threat to enter the unit without authorization, engaging the Tenant’s rights to privacy and security.

Landlords are not entitled to communicate with tenants in a way that conveys intimidation or domineering attitude. They are expected to communicate neutrally and professionally; the tenant is a consumer. Without doubt, aggressive conduct plausibly creates a hostile or oppressive environment for tenants.

The Landlord’s conduct complained of was not an isolated incident. It formed part of a broader, sustained pattern of behaviour intended to coerce the Tenant into accepting a new financial obligation, despite the Tenant’s clear refusal. This pattern was reinforced by the imprudent service of N5 notices based on charges that were not lawfully owing.

The Tenant also submits that the N12 Notice of Termination was not issued in good faith, but rather as a means of pressuring them to vacate the unit. The Tenant points to the timing of the notice, the ongoing dispute, the Landlord’s ownership of multiple properties and the fact that the rental unit was likely not the most favorable living space.
The Landlord did not provide evidence addressing or rebutting this submission.

While a determination as to the good faith of an N12 notice is properly the subject of a separate proceeding, and I make no finding on the validity of the N12, I find that its service is not too remote and contributes to the overall pattern of conduct in assessing the [name] claims. The absence of any explanation from the Landlord further supports this inference.
I am sufficiently persuaded that the Landlord’s communications and notices of termination were coercive and harassing, contrary to section 23 of the Act. Inducement to vacate

The Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2024. I am satisfied in all the circumstances that it more probable than not that the Tenant was induced to vacate the rental unit as a direct result of the Landlord’s unlawful conduct. Remedies Rent Differential in the form of General Compensation

The Tenant purchased a home prior to vacating the rental unit. In their application they requested general compensation for 12 months based on the difference between the rent previously paid and the cost of their mortgage payments and property taxes.
The Tenant did not pursue this remedy at the hearing. In any event, the compensation sought by the Tenant, based on the difference between rent and the cost of home ownership, could not succeed.

Where a tenant establishes that they were induced to vacate the rental unit, subsection 31(2)(a) permits the Board to order compensation for “all or any portion of any increased rent which the tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period” after the tenant vacates. The Tenant’s claim does not fall within the scope of section 31(2)(a). The statutory language is specific and limited to “increased rent.” It contemplates a situation where a tenant leaves one rental unit and incurs higher rent for another rental unit. It does not extend to the costs associated with purchasing and owning a home. Moving Expenses

The following moving expenses of $430.00 are allowed: (i) $330.00 for U-Haul moving truck rental (per the reservation confirmation submitted), and (ii) $100.00 representing the reasonable cost of gas for the U-Haul truck.

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that they incurred these costs. I find that these expenses are reasonably connected to the events giving rise to the Tenant’s relocation and that the amount claimed is not unreasonable.

The Tenant claims $60.00 for the cost of renting blankets for moving but no invoice was submitted. Additionally, the Tenant requests reimbursement for TekSavvy’s internet service moving fee of $49.96. However, the billing the Tenant submitted shows that this fee was credited back to the Tenant. Costs including legal fees incurred
The Tenant seeks reimbursement of legal fees incurred in relation to this application and the Landlord’s L2 application based on the N12 notice.

Legal fees are not recoverable as damages under section 31 of the Act. However, as reflected in LTB Interpretation Guideline 3, the Board has a limited discretionary authority to award costs under Rule 23 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. Rule 23.2 permits granting reasonable representation or preparation fees, subject to a maximum of $100 per hour to a maximum of $700. It provides that such costs may be awarded where a party engages in unreasonable conduct that causes undue delay or expense in the proceeding.
As I have found, the Landlord maintained a position in their L2 that had no legal basis, up until the day of the hearing, at which time they withdrew the application.

In my view, requiring the Tenant to respond to two L2 applications that were ultimately withdrawn without adequate explanation and to pursue this T2 application resulted in significant unnecessary expense and a substantial investment of the Tenant’s time. I find that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable within the meaning of Rule 23.3.
Considering the time and effort realistically required to prepare and present this T2, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $700.00 in preparation and representation costs. Administrative fine

The [name] Interpretation Guideline 16 states that a fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter similar activity in the future. A fine is not normally imposed “unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

The Guideline provides that a Member may consider ordering a fine even though it has not been requested in an application. Although not requested in this application, the question of a fine was raised with the parties. The Landlord's Legal Representative questioned the Board’s discretion and opposes the imposition of a fine. The Tenant submits that a fine is warranted in the circumstances.

I agree. The Landlord’s conduct was serious: it included threatening to remove the hot water tank without intent to replace it; persistent unlawful demands for payment, and the giving of two invalid N5 notices – all carried out in the context of providing and maintaining an essential service the Landlord was obligated to provide.
This behaviour demonstrates a clear disregard for the Act and improper use of the Board’s processes by attempting to advance and enforce a claim that had no legal foundation.

The record shows that the Landlord operates multiple rental properties. A high standard of compliance is expected for professional and corporate landlords. The misconduct in this case raises concerns about a potential broader impact on other tenants who have entered into similar lease agreements with this Landlord.

While the Tenant has been granted other remedies, those remedies do not address the need for general and specific deterrence. Therefore, I find that an administrative fine is appropriate. The Landlord shall be ordered pay $2,500.00 to the LTB. Filing fee
Pursuant to Rule 23.1, the Landlord shall also reimburse the Tenant for the application filing fee.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of December 31, 2024.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,178.00. This amount represents: • $430.00 for moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $700.00 as costs. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.00 by July 6, 2026. June 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s application concerns an alleged issue with the bathtub in the rental unit and the Landlord’s repair of that issue. The Tenant testified that the bathtub was damaged, was not smooth, and this could be felt on the Tenant’s feet. The Tenant stated that the issue began approximately two years before the hearing, but the Tenant could not provide a specific date when the issue started, when the Landlord was first notified, or when the repairs were completed. The Tenant testified that they sent a picture to the Landlord and that the Landlord attended to repair the bathtub, possibly about two weeks later. The Tenant further testified that the repair came loose after about two weeks, but again did not provide specific dates.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord repaired the bathroom or bathtub more than once and changed contractors. The Tenant stated that one of the repairs was dusty and had an odour, which caused the Tenant to feel unwell and have a headache. The Tenant also testified that the issue was fixed approximately two months before the hearing. However, the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence identifying the type or source of the bathtub damage, when the Landlord was told of each problem, the details of the Landlord’s response, the dates of the repairs, or why the repairs were insufficient.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Applying that contextual approach, I find that the Tenant has not met the evidentiary burden required to establish a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. The Tenant’s own evidence was that the Landlord responded to the issue and performed repairs more than once. The Tenant did not provide enough detail or supporting evidence to establish that the Landlord’s response was unreasonable in the circumstances, that the Landlord failed to repair or maintain the rental unit, or that the Landlord failed to comply with any health, safety, housing or maintenance standard.

On the basis of the limited evidence before the Board, I cannot find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges the Landlord has illegally retained her last month’s rent deposit. As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The tenancy commenced on October 1, 2024 for a fixed-term ending on September 30, 2025. On September 30, 2025, the Tenant sent a text message to the Landlord advising that she would be moving out of the rental unit on October 1, 2025.

Subsection 38(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states as follows: 38 (1) If a tenancy agreement for a fixed term ends and has not been renewed or terminated, the landlord and tenant shall be deemed to have renewed it as a monthly tenancy agreement containing the same terms and conditions that are in the expired tenancy agreement and subject to any increases in rent charged in accordance with this Act.

What subsection 38(1) means is that the tenancy is deemed to have renewed as a monthly tenancy unless the tenancy was terminated in accordance with the Act. In accordance with subsection 44(4), the Tenant was required to give the Landlord at least 60 days notice before the expiration date specified in the fixed-term tenancy agreement.

The Tenant gave notice to the Landlord on September 30, 2025. As such, the earliest the Tenant could end the tenancy was November 30, 2025. The Tenant did not present any evidence as to whether the Landlord was able to mitigate their loss by re-renting the unit before November 30, 2025. The Tenant is therefore not entitled to the return of her last month’s deposit.
I find that the Tenant failed to prove the allegation on a balance of probabilities.
Therefore, the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 09, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant a rent abatement as described in the order below. Preliminary Issue: Limitation Period
The Tenant filed her application with the LTB on December 11, 2023.

Many of the issues identified in the Tenant’s amended application refer to periods more than one year before the Tenant filed her application. As such, per the limitation period set out in subsection 29(2) of the Act, the evidence presented at the hearing was restricted to those claims subsequent to December 12, 2022.

Some issues identified by the Tenant were first brought to the Landlord’s attention prior to the limitation period. While no remedy may be awarded for alleged disrepair prior to the limitation period described above, the Tenant’s testimony about disrepair and the Landlord’s previous responses provides relevant context for the Tenant’s in-time claims.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2024. Preliminary Issue: The Identity of the Landlord

The parties present at the hearing agree that [organization] is a property management firm hired by [name]. It is not an owner of the property and does not appear to otherwise meet the definition of “landlord” set out at section 2 of the Act.
Therefore, on the Board’s motion, [organization] is removed as a respondent Landlord from the Tenant’s application. [name] is the only Landlord of the rental unit. [name]
For the reasons set out below, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair and maintain the rental unit.

The Tenant testified about the following maintenance issues at the hearing: • The Tenant testified that when she moved into the unit in 2021, she began to notice various maintenance issues with the rental unit, including rotted deck boards, loose railings, and septic issues. Several other maintenance concerns were brought to the attention of the Landlord’s agent – a maintenance worker named [name] – throughout May 2022 to August 2022. No responses were received from the Landlord or [name]. • On December 24, 2022, the Tenant emailed [name] to report that the fridge inside the rental unit had broken. • January 16, 2023, [name] sent a follow-up issue regarding the condition of the roof. The Tenant testified that there have been various leaks from the roof that she has communicated to the Landlord or his agent throughout the tenancy. • On June 1, 2023, Pickering bylaw officers attended the rental unit at the Tenant’s request to inspect the condition of the unit. The Tenant provided photos of the business cards of the officers who attended. • On June 24, 2023, the Tenant emailed [name] to report a new roof leak into her child’s bedroom. A repair person attended to this leak on June 28, 2023, but per the Tenant, the leak resumed on November 21, 2023. • Also on November 21, 2023, the Tenant texted [name] to report that caulking around a recently repaired window had not dried and asked for a contractor to look into the issue. A contractor ultimately attended to inspect the issue on December 10, 2023, and added additional caulking, but was not confident in the repair due to concerns about rot surrounding the window.

The Tenant also testified about the following events, which would have occurred after the Tenant submitted her application: • April 14, 2024, the Tenant sent another letter to the Landlord to request the completion of various outstanding maintenance issues. • June 11, 2024, the Tenant received notification from [name] that roof repairs were to begin. • June 14, 2024, the Tenant notified the Landlord and [name] via text message that a worker had fallen through the roof and the ceiling of the rental unit. Per the Tenant, the resulting hole was left exposed and unrepaired through mid-July 2024. • On July 5, 2024, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord and [name] to follow-up on the holes in the ceiling reported on June 14, 2024. At this point, the Tenant gave the Landlord notice of their intent to vacate the rental unit as of August 31, 2024.

The Tenant directed the Board to the following documents during the hearing: • Emails dated May 5, 2022, and June 26 to 29, 2022, discussing the Tenant’s concerns about leaks from the ceiling in the bathroom and the living room. These emails include photos showing water damage and what appears to be mould and a video showing water falling into the living room. • Emails dated December 11-15, 2022, and December 24, 2022, discussing snow removal issues, the broken refrigerator, the identified roof leaks, and a leaking skylight. The response from the Landlord on December 24, 2022, shows the Landlord’s agent – [name] – denying responsibility for snow removal. • Emails dated April 12 through 15, 2023, requesting the Landlord to repair the lawn of the rental unit, which was damaged during a repair of the rental unit’s septic system. An email dated May 21, 2023, shows the lawn continuing to be in a state of disrepair. • An email dated April 16, 2023, from the Tenant to the Landlord and [name] with a video showing the leak in the bathroom into a light fixture. • An email dated May 27, 2023, regarding a dispute about previous tenant’s belongings in the shed. • An email dated June 1, 2023, which states that the fire inspector replaced all the smoke detectors in the home as they were expired and that the carbon monoxide detector was also expired and required replacement. • An email dated June 24, 2023, which details a new leak in her son’s bedroom and includes a video showing the damage. A photo shows the leak. Another photo shows mold growth on a panel of the ceiling that was removed as part of the repair of this leak in July 2024, nearly a year after the leak was first reported to the Landlord. • Emails dated June 27 to 29, 2023, demonstrating the parties’ dispute over yard maintenance. • Text messages from October 21, 2023, to November 28, 2023, showing communications between the Tenant and [name] regarding follow-up work to be performed on the roof of the rental unit and the front window leak. [name] responded. Per the Tenant, several repair persons attended to place temporary solutions over the roof, patching areas that were leaking. She testified that no roof replacement had taken place at this time. • An email from [name] to the Tenant, dated June 11, 2024, stating that roofers would be on site the next day repair the roof and that the work was estimated to take 2-3 days to complete. • An email dated July 5, 2024, from the Tenant to [name] discussing the holes in the roof that were exposed by the workers on the roof, including two holes created when workers fell through the roof into the kitchen and living room of the rental unit. • She clarified that a dog-sitter witnessed the contractor’s foot come through the ceiling of the kitchen, which the Tenant discovered on June 13, 2024, after returning from vacation. On June 14, 2024, the Tenant directly witnessed another worker falling through the living room ceiling. She testified that this was reported to the Landlord shortly after it happened and that the holes were exposed for about three weeks and not fully repaired for six weeks. • An N12 Notice of Termination served by the Landlord to the Tenant on July 12, 2024. • An email showing that the Tenant sent the Landlord and the Landlord’s agent an N9 form, declaring her intention to end the tenancy on August 31, 2024. The Landlord consented to the termination of the tenancy.

The Landlord’s legal representative cross-examined the Tenant on her testimony, and the Tenant was forthcoming and candid in her responses to his question. Having been tested under cross-examination, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s testimony is highly credible. She had a clear command of the details of the events disclosed in her application and was able to provide answers to follow-up questions without hesitation.

The Landlord appeared at the hearing on the Landlord’s behalf to present evidence. The Landlord testified to several invoices he paid in 2021 relating to various maintenance issues in 2021 and 2022, prior to the relevant period (i.e. more than one year prior to the Tenant’s application being filed with the Board).

The Landlord testified that his recollection of the events was uncertain, as several years had elapsed since the events in question. He testified that whenever he was notified of an issue, he notified HighGate Property Investments Inc. and that he was issued invoices by his property management company pertaining to several of the issues raised by the Tenant. He testified that he was generally not directly involved with the repairs in question.

The only substantive disagreement raised in the Landlord’s testimony was regarding the issue of the window caulking that would not set. He testified that his understanding was that the contractor attributed the issue to the window being disturbed, which is different than the explanation provided by the Tenant. I prefer the evidence of the Tenant at this point, as the Tenant testified that the contractor directly explained the issue to her, whereas the Landlord’s information is second-hand through the property management company.
Based on the totality of the evidence presented at the hearing, it is clear that the Landlord (and/or his agents) failed to keep the unit in a good state of repair.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Here, however, it is clear that the Landlord did not respond reasonably in the circumstances. The most significant issue in this respect is the state of the roof of the rental unit and the related leaks. The Tenant first emailed the Landlord about roof leak issues on May 5, 2022. The only evidence of attempts to address this issue took place in mid-2024. In fact, when the attempts to resolve the issue went underway, the damage had deteriorated to the point that two workers physically fell through the roof. Self-evidently, this could not occur where roof was in a state of good repair.
While the obligations under the Act do not demand perfection from landlords, they do require reasonable responses to maintenance issues brought to their attention by Tenants.

In my view, what happened in this case is that the Landlord offloaded day-to-day responsibility for the rental unit to his property management firm – [organization] – and their employee, [name], was the main point-of- contact for the Tenant. It appears, based on the correspondence provided and the Tenant’s testimony, that [name] was not diligent in ensuring maintenance issues were adequately addressed. This led to a culmination of maintenance issues that ultimately resulted in the Tenants vacating the rental unit in August 2024.

In his testimony, the Landlord testified that he was not “a professional landlord.” This is incorrect. Any individual who leases a rental unit that is governed by the Act to a Tenant is making the choice to enter into a highly regulated industry and assumes the legal liabilities and responsibilities associated with doing so. Many – like the Landlord in this case – choose to retain a property management company to help manage these obligations, but this does not displace the landlord’s statutory and contractual obligations.

With respect to the roof issues and the related leaks, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not reasonably respond to the Tenant’s communications about the disrepair. Therefore, he was in breach of section 20(1) of the Act.

The lease between the parties includes a provision that states that the Tenant agreed to maintain the front yard of the rental unit and remove snow. The Tenant takes the position that this term of the lease is void as it conflicts with the Landlord’s duty to maintain the rental unit pursuant to section 20 of the Act.
Per section 4 of the Act, a provision that is inconsistent with the Act or its regulations is void.

Whether or not the clauses relating to lawn maintenance and snow removal are inconsistent with the Act depends on whether there is an applicable legal standard that conflicts with the clause. The Tenant did not provide adequate information at the hearing about the legal standards applicable to the rental unit, which is located in Pickering. It is the Tenant’s obligation to provide the Board with a copy of the relevant standards being relied upon which was not done in this case. Therefore, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has shown the Landlord to be in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the yard work and snow removal. Remedies:
The Tenant amended her application in advance of the hearing to include a monetary remedy. This was served on the Landlord in advance of the hearing. I allowed the Tenant to amend her application.
Having found the Landlord to be in breach of section 20(1) of the Act, the Board must consider what remedy is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $14,452.50, the equivalent of a 100% abatement for 6 months. She testified that the extensive ongoing issues were exacerbated by the Landlord’s lack of diligence in response to maintenance issues. She also testified that the disputes over maintenance issues made her feel uncomfortable living in the rental unit during these disrepairs. She testified to experiencing stress, anxiety, and concerns about her child’s health.

As mentioned earlier, the Tenant showed evidence that establishes the roof and related leak issues were communicated to the Landlord on May 5, 2022, with several follow-up communications to the Landlord, [name], or both. Pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act, however, a remedy can only be awarded back to December 11, 2022.

The roof issues were not adequately addressed by the Landlord until near the end of the tenancy (i.e. in August 2024). Therefore, the period of remedy to be considered is December 11, 2022 through August 31, 2024 – a period of approximately 20 months.

While the roof issues and leaks did not render the rental unit uninhabitable – as evidenced by the Tenant’s continued habitation – they are a serious issue. It is obvious that when a Tenant signs a lease, a leakproof roof is part of the bundle of services being contracted for. While an 100% rent abatement would not be appropriate in the circumstances detailed in the Tenant’s evidence, a significant abatement is warranted.

The situation resulted in substantial disruption to the Tenant’s use of the rental unit for the relevant period. Based on my review of the evidence, I am satisfied that a 30% rent abatement for the period cited is an appropriate remedy.

Per the Tenant’s amended application, the monthly rent for the rental unit was $2,408.75. A 30% rent abatement for the rent paid from December 11, 2022, to August 31, 2024, amounts to $14,452.50. This is an appropriate remedy considering the scope of the issues identified by the Tenant, the Tenant’s diligence in attempting to get the Landlord or his agents to act, and the fact that the tenancy terminated – in large part – as a result of the maintenance issues with the unit.
The Tenant is also entitled to a reimbursement of the cost of filing this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $14,500.50. This amount represents: • $14,452.50 for an approximately 30% rent abatement from December 11, 2022, to August 31, 2024; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-097224-23 issued on March 10, 2026. On April 7, 2026, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On April 8, 2026 interim order LTB-T-097224-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on March 10, 2026
reasons: The Landlord’s review request (RTR) claims there is a serious error in Board order issued on March 10, 2026 (the “Order”).

The following grounds were considered at the review hearing: (i) That the member failed to maintain an impartial and focused environment required for a fair hearing; and, (ii) That the Board erred in making an objective mathematical contradiction in respect of the Tenant’s moving/storage expenses claim. Impartial and Focused environment

The Landlord’s RTR alleges the member “prioritized speed over a judicious review of the evidence and created a reasonable apprehension of bias”. The Landlord further alleges the member acknowledged being “tired” and “no longer interested in the merits of the case.”

In support of the RTR, the Landlord produced a transcription of the relevant portion of the proceeding: Adjudicator: Okay. The other question, the only other question I have, Mr. [name]name], before….because I want to make sure it’s procedurally fair hearing. Did you want to ask Mr, [name] any questions about any of his evidence? [name]: Yes, actually. Adjudicator: Okay, so that’s cross examination. I know we’re kind of going out of order, but um, I don’t really care at this point because I’m really tired, so let’s just get – get it done. So [name] – or, sorry, Mr. [name]name], go ahead and ask your questions, okay? I want to make sure you get a chance to do that?

In the lead up to the noted exchange, the transcript shows the Tenant had completed direct testimony and for a few minutes immediately thereafter , the member began asking the Landlord clarifying questions, namely regarding the identify of certain individuals.

Normally, when a part y has completed direc t testimony, the responding party is given an opportunity to immediately begin cross-examination. After a few minutes of questions, the member appeared to acknowledge the procedurally deviation and offered the Landlord the opportunity to cross-examine the Tenant.

In my view , the noted interaction does not support the Landlord’s submission that the member was “no longer interested in the merits of the case ”, or otherwise impaired due to being “tired”. While the member admittedly acknowledged being “tired”, such a comment appears to have been offered up as an explanation for the relatively m inor procedural change. I am not satisfied there was any substantive impact on the parties or outcome. In this regard, the Landlord was afforded a fulsome opportunity to cross -examine the Tenant and the [name] shows the member was attentive to the relevant issues raised at the hearing and provided fulsome reasons.

For completeness, I note that the Landlord additionally alleged the member inappropriately “intervened” by providing “a factual excuse” when the Tenant was challenged on cross - examination regarding the lack of written communications from May 25 through August 10. In this regard, the RTR alleges the member provided a factual excuse by offering up the Tenant had “grown tired” of texting and “switched to verbal complaints”.
At the review hearing, the L andlord prod uced a recording which showed the member acknowledging the lack of text messages after August

The recording excerpt produced did not support the Landlord’s assertion that the member had commented the Tenant had “grown tired” of texting and “switched to verbal complaints”. 10. With respect to whether the Tenant told the Landlord/Landlord’s agent through other means of communication, the recording shows the member acknowledged this possibility and noted there was “your (landlord) evidence and his ( tenant) evidence ” to consider . In the circumstances, I find the member’s interjection was made for the purpose of keeping the parties focused on the relevant issues and to ensure an orderly and efficient process. I do not find the member serious erred, or that an unfair hearing took place as a result. Mathematical Errors (i) Via / Uhaul Expenses
The Landlord states it is illogical for the member to include both truck (U-Haul) and train (Via Rail) costs as moving/storage expenses.

In considering the Tenant’s claim for moving/storage costs, the [name] shows the member considered the Tenant’s oral testimony and supporting documentary evidence adduced at the hearing which showed both truck and train expenses were incurred.
At the review hearing, the Landlord submit ted such expenses are “mutually exclusive”, however, the Landlord acknowledged that he did not question the Tenant as to the nature of such expenses.

While it is clear the Landlord disagrees with the member’s findings, the purpose of the review process is not to provide parties with an opportunity of relitigating the issues in the hopes of a better outcome. Here, the evidentiary foundation upon which the member’s finding of such moving/storage expenses is based appears to be rationally connected to the evidence adduced. I would thus not interfere with the assessment of the evidence by the hearing member, who was in the best position to assess the evidence and had the benefit and opportunity of hearing the evidence in its totality. In the circumstances, I find no error in the member’s inclusion of both such expenses. (ii) Mathematical Calculation

The Landlord submits the member seriously erred in awarding $2,500.00 in moving/storage costs, as a lesser sum was ultimately determined to be owing by the Member. In support, the Landlord points to paragraph 52 of the Order, whereby the member states “the Tenant’s claim is limited to the $2,000.00 as stated in the application…The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $2000.00 for moving and storage expenses” [emphasis added]
On its face , i t is clear the amount ultimately awarded for moving/storage expenses is inconsistent with the member’s reasoning and intent in paragraph 52 of the Order.

At the review hearing, however, I raised the issue of a possible clerical error as the [name] shows the member appears to have transposed the rent abatement amount with the moving/storage amount. In this regard, the member awarded $ ,2000.00 for a rent abatement, however paragraphs 54 and 57 of the [name] shows that the member sought to award a rent abatement of $2500.00, stating” “ The Tenant requests an abatement of $2500.00…I am of the view that an abatement of $2500. As requested, appropriate in the circumstances” [emphasis]

Overall, it is clear the member intended to award a total of $4,500.00 (2500 + 2000) for both moving/storage and rent abatement , however the member mistakenly transposed the intended amounts to the wrong head of damages. Although I am not satisfied that a serious error occurred as a result, the noted clerical issue will be addressed in my order below. (iii) $517.61 rent reimbursement / limited hearing re: rent reimbursement
Rule 26.15 of the Board’s Rules provide that a reviewing member may consider issues “not identified in the request but which the Member finds may amount to a seri ous error in the order.”
At the review hearing, it was acknowledged that the hearing member awarded $517.61 for “reimbursement” of rent paid after the termination date.

In Beauge v Metcap Living Management Inc., 20212 OCSC 1160 (“Beauge”), the Divisional Court held that it would be an error in law for the Board to award a claim in the absence of such a claim being included in the application and in the absence of the responding party being given adequate notice and opportunity to respond.

Here, the Tenant’s application makes no request for any overpayment of rent made to the Landlord after the termination date. In the circumstances I find the member seriously erred in its inclusion and thus, the review is granted for the limited purpose of amending the order and removing rent reimbursement award of $517.61.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant filed his application with the Board on January 10, 2025.
The Tenant provided testimony upon Board questioning, that the Landlord had sold the rental complex, which included the Tenant’s rental unit to the current landlord sometime in November 2024.

The Tenant further provided testimony that he and the current landlord had come to a settlement agreement regarding the issues in this application prior to the filing of this application and he did not wish to seek remedies from the current landlord and further did not wish to amend his application to add the current landlord. As the Tenant was under the impression he could seek remedies from the former Landlord.

Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) states: Covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made.

It is commonly accepted that what this provision means is that when a property is sold and there are sitting residential tenants, the tenancy agreements “run with the land” meaning they remain in place on the same terms and conditions as exited prior to the sale. The new owner steps into the shoes of the old landlord.

The primary purpose of the provision was to abolish the common law distinction between covenants in esse (which ran with the land) and covenants in posse (which did not). At common law, examples of covenants which have always been said to run with the land include the obligation to pay rent and the landlord’s obligation to provide the tenants with quiet enjoyment.

The definition of landlord in section 2(1) of the Act reads as follows: “(a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent;

The Act does not include “former landlord’ in the definition as landlord. The Tenant hence has no recourse against the former landlord in the case at hand, given he testified the rental complex was sold prior to him filing of this herein application.

Based on the evidence before the Board I find that the Respondent Landlord was not in fact the Landlord when the Tenant filed the application. While it is possible that a tenant may amend an application in circumstances such as these to add the current landlord as the proper respondent, the Tenant confirmed that he had no desire to do so. As a result, the Tenant’s application against the former Landlord cannot proceed and his application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,223.00 on or before June 22, 2026.

The Tenant and another tenant entered in a fixed term tenancy commencing January 5, 2025. The lawful monthly rent was $3000.00, the Tenant paid $1,550.00, while his roommate paid the remaining $1,450.00. There was also a $200.00 key deposit paid by the Tenant (his share).

The Tenant’s and the other tenant (who had settled her dispute with the Landlord) provided first and last month’s rent and prepaid rent for the last four months of the tenancy, September, October, November and December 2025, as was agreed upon between the parties. The Landlord’s Agent testified this was the Tenant’s offer given the rental market at the time. The Tenant did not dispute the same.
The Tenant testified that in early August 2025 he and his roommate decided to vacate the unit early and notified the Landlord.

The Landlord’s Agent testified the parties had a fixed term lease, but would be happy to oblige if the Tenant and the other tenant agreed they would be responsible for the cost of the Landlord’s realtor to re-rent the unit, cleaning of the rental unit if required, costs for any damages and an administrative fee for processing and coordinating an early eviction.

The Landlord’s Agent further testified that the other tenant advised this was not an issue, as the parties had a joint tenancy, the Landlord proceeded and retained a realtor and re- rented the unit as of September 1, 2025, and repaired the damaged balcony screen, towel bard and fridge handle, and issued a cheque for half of the funds as directed to the other tenant minus, the agreed upon expenses for a sum of $3,529.00 and that tenant executed a waiver. At this point the Landlord was advised by the Tenant he did not agree to this amount and some of the expenses and would not execute the waiver and accept the funds from the Landlord as he did not feel they were legitimate expenses. The Tenant sought roughly $4,800.00 to be reimbursed to him, which included his share of the last months rent deposit, which exceeded the lawful monthly rent as agreed upon at the commencement of the tenancy and his share of the key deposit.

The Tenant testified that he was owed four months of prepaid rent and four days in January 2026 which amounted to $6,200.00, half the key deposit and interest on the last month’s rent deposit of $15.00 for a total of $6,415.00.

The Tenant further testified he acknowledged that he agreed to real estate commission of his share of one months rent in the amount of $1,500.00 and half of the cleaning charge in the amount of $100.00, but did not agree that he should pay his share of the HST on the commission ($195.00) and half the costs to repair damages in the rental unit ($250.00) and half the costs for the administrative fee for the Landlord processing and coordinating an early termination of the tenancy ($200.00).

On a balance of probabilities, I am persuaded and prefer the Landlord’s evidence to that of the Tenant, regarding the agreement to terminate the tenancy prior to the end of the fixed term tenancy, and the expenses agreed upon. The Landlord’s Agent submitted documentary evidence of the expenses incurred, and thus from the abovementioned deductions the outstanding total amount owed to the Tenant by the Landlord is $4,170.00, which was calculated as follows: $6,415.00-$1500.00(half months rent for commission)-195.00(HST)-100.00 (cleaning charge)- $200.00(admin fee)-$250.00 (damages)

The Landlord’s Agent further testified this was never about withholding the last month’s rent and key deposit, but rather the Tenant not agreeing to the expenses incurred by the Landlord to mitigate his losses, and re-rent the unit, whilst assisting the Tenant in his request to mutually terminate the tenancy earlier, when originally agreed upon.
As the Tenant has been partially successful in his application, the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the costs of this application.

I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,223.00. This amount represents: • $2,655.00 for excess rent collected as agreed upon in lease agreement and key deposit. • $1,500.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $15.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 11, 2026 ____________________________
