issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and/or [name] and [name] (the ‘Purchasers') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the Landlord’s Legal Representative advised that the Landlord [name] had passed away, additionally the corporate owner of the property [organization] entered into the agreement of purchase and sale with the Purchasers and served the Tenants with the N12 notice of Termination.
The parties agreed that [organization] is the proper Landlord to this application.
On consent the Landlord in this application is amended to [organization] T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

There was no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act with a termination date of August 31, 2025 or that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice on August 19, 2025.
The Landlord and the Purchasers entered into an Agreement of Purchase and Sale on June 12, 2025 for the sale the rental unit with a scheduled closing date of September 2, 2025.
It was the Tenants belief that no one moved into the rental unit until January, 2026 at which time the rental unit was being rented by the Purchasers’ son-in-law.

The Tenants produced an audio recording taken by the Tenant [name] on January 10, 2026 at the rental unit. The recording is of [name] and another individual believed to be the Purchasers’ son-in-law. The Tenants’ claim that in the recording the other individual states he is renting from ‘[name]’ one of the Purchasers.

The audio recording was played at the hearing and the conversation regarding the rental of the property can be found at the 0:50 second mark and can be summarized as follows: [name] – “You guys renting this house from [name] or?” Son-in-Law – “No, I’m moving in here with [name].” [name] – “[name], oh yeah?” Son-in-Law – “Yeah [name] is my father-in-law.”

The Tenants further believe that the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith as they had raised maintenance issues to the Landlord, which were outstanding and the Purchaser [name] was a friend of the Landlords and did maintenance work at their properties. 13. [name] [name] Agent for the Landlord testified that she is the sole owner of [organization] after the passing of her husband [name] on January 9, 2026. She testified that the decision to sell the property came after [name] was diagnosed with cancer and health issues in late 2024, and they both decided to slow down and sell off assets. 14. The Purchaser [name] testified that he personally knew the Landlords and had worked for them for the past 12 years doing maintenance and other tasks on their properties. 15. He further stated that the Purchasers were planning to use inheritance they were set to receive after the passing of his brother, but his brother passed away without a will and they were waiting for probate on the estate, which delayed the sale of the rental property. 16. The Landlord and the Purchasers both testified that they entered into an escrow agreement where the Purchasers had access to the rental unit to perform renovations until the sale of the property was finalized, which occurred on February 13, 2026. 17. The Purchasers state that they began moving belongings into the rental unit in January of 2026, and that they along with their daughter, son-in-law and two grandchildren moved into the rental unit in February, 2026. Analysis 18. The evidence before me is that the closing on the sale of the rental unit was delayed due to the Purchasers first requiring a will of a deceased brother to be probated. The closing occurred on February 13, 2026, and the testimony of the Purchasers is that they moved into the rental unit shortly thereafter. 19. The evidence of the Tenants is that the Purchasers didn’t move into the rental unit, but instead rented the unit to their son-in-law. The Tenants relied upon an audio recording of a conversation between [name] and the Purchasers’ son-in-law in support of this claim. In the audio record the Purchasers’ son-in-law clearly says he is moving in with [name], one of the Purchasers. This supports the evidence of the Purchasers that they moved into the rental unit with their daughter, son-in-law and grandchildren. At no point in the recording does he state he is renting the unit from [name]. 20. I find on a balance of probabilities, the Tenants have not proven that the Purchasers did not move into the rental unit as required by section 57(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: SU (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Former Tenant owes. (LTB-L-096430-24) The Landlord applied for an order requiring [name] (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that are the result of the Former Tenant's conduct or that of another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex. This conduct substantially interfered with the Landlord's reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or another lawful right, privilege or interest. (LTB-L-096430- 24) The Former Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-098034-23)
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord proved the allegations related to non-payment of rent contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Former Tenant will pay to the Landlord $6,861.92 on or before July 11, 2026.

The Former Tenant was in attendance at the hearing. Therefore, I am satisfied in accordance with section 191(2) of the Act that the contents of the notice of hearing and application came to the attention of the Former Tenant and therefore are deemed to be properly given.

The Former Tenant informed the Landlord that they vacated the rental unit on December 1, 2023 by text message from [name]. While [name] testified that there had been discussions regarding the Former Tenant moving out of the rental unit before that date, it was acknowledged that the Former Tenant and [name] never gave the Landlord notice prior to December 1, 2023 in writing that the Former Tenant would move out on any particular date.
The application was filed within one year after the Former Tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent was $850.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Former Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.

The Former Tenant is no longer in possession of the rental unit. The tenancy was not lawfully terminated in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order or agreement to terminate the tenancy. The tenancy was a fixed term agreement which ended on August 31, 2024. In accordance with section 88 of the Act, if a tenant vacates without having given notice permitted by the Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the first termination date for which a notice of termination could have validly been served. Under section 44(4) of the Act, the earliest date to terminate a fixed term tenancy is the expiration date of that fixed term.
Therefore, subject to the Landlord’s obligations to minimize their losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act, the Former Tenant's obligation to pay rent ended on August 31, 2024.

The Landlord has an obligation to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. As the Former Tenant had not given a fixed date they would vacate the rental unit prior to confirming they had left the rental unit on December 1, 2023, I find the Landlord’s obligations in this regard start on this date.

The Landlord testified that after receiving this text on December 1, 2023 they listed the property for rent on Kijiji, and after it wasn’t rented in December also listed it on [name] starting in January, 2024. The Landlord provided a screenshot of their e-mail notifications from Kijiji as to communications with parties in regard to the Kijiji advertisements. While the majority of these start in March, 2024, they do include a message on December 15, 2023. I & LTB-T-098034-23 am satisfied based on these messages that the Landlord did list the rental unit on Kijiji in December, 2023 and throughout the period the room was not rented. I note the Landlord also provided a copy of an e-mail response from Kijiji sent in September 2024 asking about accessing older advertisements to state that they do not keep deleted or expired advertisements for more than 60 days as an explanation as to why the actual advertisement copies were not provided.
The Landlord also provided several text conversations with potential tenants, which the Landlord testified were all unsuccessful in resulting in tenancies.

The Landlord testified they were unable to successfully rent the room in question until July, 2024 when they entered into a lease with a party commencing in September, 2024. The Landlord provided a copy of the lease for this new tenancy, the term of which is listed as commencing September 1, 2024. The Landlord did testify they rented another room in the home starting in May, 2024, but that the party renting that room chose it as it was a smaller room that was cheaper than the room in question.

The Former Tenant challenged that the Landlord took adequate efforts to minimize their losses as: a. The Former Tenant had posted Kijiji advertisements and sent the Landlord several candidates for a sub-lease prior to leaving the rental unit; and b. The Former Tenant believed the Landlord’s requirements of potential new tenants were unreasonable.

As noted above, given that the Former Tenant did not provide the Landlord with a date on which they were moving, and as no application was commenced in relation to the refusal of a sublet, the actions of the Landlord in relation to potential sublets are not particularly relevant. However, by way of example as to why the Former Tenant believed the Landlord was acting unreasonably in their requirements of new tenants, the Tenant pointed me to an e-mail exchange in which a potential tenant was asked for proof of permanent residency in Canada, proof of employment, and a request about information showing they were waiting to get into the military (as the potential tenant had mentioned this in their e- mail to the Landlord). I do not find this to be indicative of unreasonable requirements – the requests seem to logically tie into a Landlord vetting a party for income, and that they are a party likely to remain in residence in the rental unit.

The Former Tenant also asserted that the Landlord was having difficulty in renting the unit as they were restricting what ethnicities they would rent to. The proof of this provided was a text exchange between [name] and the Landlord in August of 2023. After reviewing this exchange, I find that a plain reading of the message does not imply that the Landlord was restricting who they were renting to. I do not find there is evidence sufficient for me to conclude that the Landlord was restricting who they would rent to based on ethnicity or that the Landlord was otherwise acting unreasonably in their vetting of potential tenants.
The rent arrears and daily compensation owing to August 31, 2024 are $7,650.00.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs & LTB-T-098034-23

The Landlord also claimed compensation for the Former Tenant substantially interfering with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or interfering with their lawful rights, privileges or interests. However, the substance of what the Landlord was actually claiming for was lost time from work, stress and general compensation for having to deal with this claim and the related claim filed by the Former Tenant. These are not costs that can be recovered as out of pocket expenses related to substantial interference by the Former Tenant in the course of the tenancy. Therefore, this claim is dismissed and nothing will be awarded in regard to it.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $950.00 from the Former Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The amount of the rent deposit and interest on the rent deposit is applied to the amount the Tenant is required to pay. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $24.08 is therefore owing to the Former Tenant for the period from August 27, 2023 to August 31, 2024.

While the Landlord wished to amend the claim to reflect no rent deposit remains as it is applied to the last month of the tenancy, the deposit is deemed to be held and applied by virtue of this order, and so amending the application to remove it would be inappropriate. LTB-T-098034-23
The Former Tenant’s application is dismissed for the reasons outlined below.

The Former Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The 4 claims asserted were that: a. The Former Tenant was a minor and the Landlord promised assistance and care to him during the agreement, but was outside of Canada and not nearby during the tenancy; b. Between October 8 and 11, 2023 the temperature in the home dropped to 7 degrees Celsius as it was cold outside, but the Former Tenant did not know how to turn on the heat and the Landlord did not make time to walk the Former Tenant through the process to do so; c. The Landlord failed to provide adequate cleaning services as the Former Tenant asserts they were required to do; and d. There were a series of maintenance issues related to internet, air conditioning and the refrigerator in the first few weeks of the tenancy.

The claim under paragraph 22.a. cannot constitute a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. There is no obligation of a Landlord to live and be present nearby a rental unit under the Act, and there was no specific lease provision in this regard. Further, not doing so would not be properly characterised as a breach of maintenance obligations even if there was such an obligation. & LTB-T-098034-23
The claim under paragraph 22.d. was not sufficiently particularized with dates and details to expect the Landlord to be able to respond and defend against it and therefore could not proceed.

Evidence was taken in regard to the heating in the unit from October 8 to 11, 2023. There was no issue with the functioning of the heating system. The Former Tenant’s position was that turning it on was so complicated as an older system that there was an expectation that the Landlord would immediately make time to walk the Former Tenant through how to do so. When [name] was asked whether he had attended the unit to attempt to operate the system, [name] acknowledged he was not made aware of this issue until after the heat was on. It was determined after some questioning that all that was required to be done was that the temperature be set and switch turned to heat on the thermostat.

This is the usual and normal operation of a thermostat. If parties are sending a minor child to live on their own, they have some responsibility for ensuring that that minor is equipped with knowledge or resources to live independently, or a party to contact for help with items they may not have knowledge of. While the normal and usual operation of a thermostat may not have been in the knowledge of a minor, that does not impose additional obligations on the Landlord, and there was no failure of maintenance in this instance.

Evidence was received on whether there was any obligation of the Landlord to provide cleaning services under the lease. The Former Tenant pointed to a standard clause in the lease referring to the Landlord’s normal obligations under section 20 of the Act, and a text message translated by [name] that starts “It is possible that this sentence has ambiguity.” In support of their position that the Landlord was required to provide cleaning services under the tenancy agreement.

The language in the lease does not impose any obligations to provide cleaning services for the rental unit. 29. [name] acknowledged that the language in the text message was an auto-generated sentence from the translation program indicating there were multiple possible meanings that could be translated. The text message itself was not clear to establish the Landlord had an obligation to provide cleaning services in any event. Even if it were, given that auto- generated disclaimer, I find that I cannot find this text message is sufficiently reliable to accept this as evidence that the Landlord has an obligation to provide cleaning services under the lease. 30. I find instead that the best evidence I have of the agreement between the parties is in fact the written lease presented, and that its terms do not require cleaning services to be provided. 31. For the reasons above, the Former Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Former Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Former Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $7,650.00, which represents rent and compensation owing up to August 31, 2024. & LTB-T-098034-23
The Former Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord owes $974.08 which is the amount of the rent deposit and interest on the rent deposit, and this is deducted from the amount owing by the Former Tenant.
The total amount the Former Tenant owes the Landlord is $6,861.92*. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Former Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before July 11, 2026, the Former Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application shall be dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): • The Tenant received a notice under s. 48 on March 24, 2023 with a termination date of May 31, 2023. • She moved out of the unit on October 31, 2024 • Sometime afterward, the Tenant discovered that the unit was unoccupied because her mail had been misdelivered. • She hired a private investigator who confirmed the Landlord did not occupy the unit, but remained in her home at 85 Range Road, Ottawa, ON.

Under 57(5)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord: • a) advertises the unit for rent • b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; • c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit; or • d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit • e) takes any step to convert the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

I find that the Landlord did not engage in any of the activity outlined in s. 57(5). There were other tenants since October 2016 living in the rental unit, as evidenced by the lease in the Landlord’s materials, page 215. There have not been tenants since the Tenant vacated in October 2024. Why didn’t the Landlord move in?

The Landlord provided a brief and explained at the hearing the two reasons she did not move in: financial untenability and damage to the rental unit. She maintains that her interest and intention to move in were genuine at the time she filed the N12.
The Landlord filed an N4 and an N5 against the Tenant to recover arrears and damage.

The N4 was the subject of a Review by the Board on October 29, 2025 which was closed sine die. The arrears owing to the Landlord were suspended due to a stay of proceedings pursuant to the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act on February 13, 2025. (See LTB-L-056866- 24-RV)
Likewise, the N5, LTB-L-055116-24-RV, was also suspended pursuant to a stay of proceedings under the BIA.
On June 4, 2024 a Writ of Seizure and [name] was registered against the property at 237 Goulbourn Avenue.

The Landlord testified that she could not live in the house because of the extensive unfinished renovations by the Tenant, which I accept. She adds that she has had difficulty affording to fix the place and cannot afford a loan (Landlord’s brief, page 3)
However, it does not make sense that it would be cheaper not to occupy the house and pay for two houses.

Once the Writ of Seizure and Sale went into effect, I accept the Landlord could not occupy the property; the Tenant was still occupying the property until she vacated October 31, 2024. I find the Writ is a considerable change in circumstances that prevented the Landlord from moving in.
When asked whether she occupied the property after the Tenant left, the Landlord testified that she could not because it was being sold and has been under court order since.
Therefore, I find her intention to occupy the unit at the time of the N12 was genuine. She has been thwarted by the uninhabitable state of the house as well as the Writ of Seizure and Sale.
Therefore, I find she rebuts the Tenant’s allegation that she served the N12 in bad faith on a balance of probabilities.
As the Tenant has been unable to prove her claim on a balance of probabilities, her application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 09, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed his application on November 24, 2025. He was in possession of the rental unit when the application was filed and was still in possession on the hearing date.

His description of his complaint pursuant to [name], is as follows: « Plainte contre mon locateur harcèlement menaces et atteinte la jouissance paisible. Madame Monsieur les membres de la Commission Depuis le mois de juin 2025 je subis une série de comportements abusifs et intimidants liés la gestion de mon immeuble par le nouveau concierge et mon locateur. Ces comportements portent atteinte mes droits fondamentaux de locataire et compromettent [name] [name] . Promesses abusives concernant les garages : Le nouveau concierge a annoncé ses proches issus de sa congrégation religieuse qu’il leur attribuerait des garages dont j’occupe par des résidents depuis plus de dix ans dont [name]. Menaces d’éviction : Des lettres de menace ont t déposées devant les portes des locataires y [name] sans [name] respect des règles minimales d’ hygiène sur des tapis de couloir sales. Harcèlement et intimidations : Ces pratiques s’ajoutent un climat de harcèlement et de me pris visant nous pousser quitter nos logements ou nos espaces de stationnement. Insalubrit persistante : [name] couloirs et espaces communs sont laissés dans un état insalubre aggravant le sentiment d insécurité et de négligence. Ces faits démontrent un manquement grave aux obligations du locateur notamment en [name] concerne : le respect de la jouissance paisible du logement la protection contre le harcèlement [name] et l’hygiène des lieux. Je demande la Commission de constater ces manquements de mettre fin aux pratiques abusives et de garantir la protection de mes droits en tant que locataire. Je vous remercie [name]. [name]

The remedies sought include : To document the breaches committed by the landlord and his representative, the building superintendent. To order the immediate cessation of any acts of harassment, threats, or intimidation against me and the other tenants. To demand that my rights as a tenant be respected, in particular the peaceful use of the garage I have occupied for over ten years. Enforce the necessary measures to ensure the maintenance and cleanliness of the common areas. To comply with the terms of the garage occupancy agreement that the former building manager had provided me with

The application fails to mention specific events, dates, times, locations, when the Landlord was notified, or specific names of people, words or actions of the harassing behaviour. It fails to define the common areas, or the “necessary measures”
At the hearing, the lack of particulars was brought to the Tenant’s attention by the Member.

The Tenant replied that he did provide more details and pointed to the additional letters he wrote to the Landlord when he filed his application. The Landlord confirmed they received a copy of the additional letters with the application, so the Member reviewed it with the Tenant. (see DOCS-6852899 and DOC-6852904)

The letter dated October 27, 2025 (DOC-6852904)- alleged: • That the superintendent’ s conduct has deteriorated (no date, no specific behaviour, no dates of interactions) • Documents are routinely thrown onto the filthy hallway carpet (emphasis in original) and the tone of these documents is “aggressive, demeaning often targeting minor issues such as garage usage.” • The superintendent has taken unauthorized photographs of the tenants’ garages in violation of privacy norms and without consent. (no date no time, no name) • “persistent foul odour” “throughout the property, especially during warmer months” – no dates, no locations • Rodent and cockroach infestations that continue (no dates, no locations, no mention of when the Landlord was informed) [name] infestations – Tenant says he has spent $600 on treatments but gives no dates, or when the landlord was notified. • Clarification of garage rights - Tenant alleges garage is part of his tenancy agreement – does not indicate when the agreement was revoked or when the Landlord took back control of the garage.

Remedies requested include: • Cease all threatening communications by the superintendent (no name, no dates or times or communications listed) • All future communications be conducted in a respectful, professional and hygienic manner. This is unclear and not within the Board’s jurisdiction to order. • Property management to address the unresolved health and safety issues within the building. (these are not articulated clearly in the application or in the letter)
At the hearing, the Landlord did not dispute the particulars in the application. The Member raised them in order to better understand the case and ensure an adequate hearing could be held. Analysis:

In [name] v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (‘Ball’), the Divisional Court pronounced that applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” The Court went on to state that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

In my view, the Tenant’s application lacks sufficient details and the remedies are not clear or within the jurisdiction of the Board. He has had sufficient time to amend his application to provide sufficient details. I find on a balance of probabilities that his application contains vague allegations which frustrated the Landlord’s ability to know the specific allegations made and to be able to know the case that must be met. As such, the Tenant’s applications are dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants raised the issue of disclosure being provided to them by email. The Tenants acknowledged that they had received disclosure emailed from the Landlord’s Legal Representative, but they had elected not to open it. The Tenants stated that they had requested all disclosure be sent via registered mail/courier. The Landlord’s Legal Representative had filed Certificates of Service in the Portal (‘TOP’) confirming the disclosure was also sent by mail or [name]. Pursuant to section 191(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) a notice or document is deemed to have been validly given if it is proven that its contents actually came to the attention of the person for whom it was intended within the required time period. The Tenants received email correspondence from the Landlord’s Legal Representative but chose not to open it. Given that the Landlord’s disclosure was also mailed to the Tenants, I find the Landlord’s disclosure requirements have been satisfied.

The T5 application listed [name] only as the Landlord. The rental unit is jointly owned by [name] and her daughter [name]. The reason given on the N12 was for [name] Use by [name] only. Both Landlords were present at the hearing, and both were allowed to give evidence as parties to the proceedings.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove all the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Section 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Prior to the commencement of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative entered a statement agreeing to the first three elements of the test set out in section 57(1)(a) of the Act. There is no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice that resulted in the Tenants vacating the rental unit, and the Landlord did not move in. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenants gave evidence that having to vacate their rental unit came at a particularly difficult time for them, when they were dealing with a cancer diagnosis, the death of a family member, a workplace injury, and the loss of the family dog. Understandably, this caused them stress and anxiety.
The Tenants live in close proximity to the rental unit and seeing it remain vacant and under renovation since they moved out has been difficult for them.
The Tenants are of the opinion that the Landlord wanted them out of the rental unit and used the N12 to achieve this goal. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord led evidence of extenuating circumstances prohibiting them from moving into the rental unit. Extensive evidence was provided of issues with contractors hired to carry out repairs and renovations, and the Landlord’s serious medical issues. Contractor Issues
The Landlord testified to the challenges they faced in securing a dependable contractor to carry out the repairs and renovations required to make the house habitable after the Tenants vacated.
The repairs and renovations ended up being more extensive than originally anticipated, including the demolition and rebuilding of a wall between the kitchen and family room.

Initially, the repairs and renovations were supposed to be completed by April 2025 by contractor ‘[name]’ and the Landlord provided receipts for e-transfers totalling $45,500 that was paid to this contractor. 13. ‘[name]’ was unable to complete the work and after going back and forth for several months, another contractor ‘Adam’ was hired to complete the work, at a financial loss to Landlord. As of the hearing date, the work still is not complete. 14. The Landlord tendered evidence of letters written by both contractors, but the contractors were not called as witnesses, so I gave the letters little weight. 15. I did however assign more weight to the Landlord’s photographic and viva voce evidence. The Landlord moved their furniture into the rental unit and changed the address on their driver’s licence in anticipation of moving into the rental unit. The Landlord relied upon multiple photographs of the rental unit both prior to and during the renovation work. The Landlord also provided screen shots of multiple text conversations with both contractors, along with oral testimony. I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to hire a contractor and move the work along and the delay was due to an unforeseen change in circumstances. Medical Issues 16. The Landlord testified that she first experienced some neurological symptoms in or around the time of June 2024. However, it was not until September 2025 and three subsequent abnormal neurological events that she realized the seriousness of her condition. The Landlord provided medical records in support of this evidence. 17. The Landlord testified that due to the unpredictability of her neurological symptoms, her doctor had advised against living alone due to safety concerns. A doctor’s letter was tendered as evidence. 18. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held, in the context of a bad faith application, that the Board should not restrict itself to consideration of whether there was good faith at the time the N12 was served. I am satisfied that the Landlord’s medical issues were unanticipated, and the seriousness of these issues was not apparent until after the Tenants had vacated the rental unit. On her doctor’s recommendation, the Landlord and her family have decided that she should not live alone. 19. It is important for the Board to consider all relevant evidence in determining whether the notice was served in good faith. I find the evidence from the Landlord was credible and reliable and I accept their testimony that there was a material change in circumstances and that the N12 was served in good faith. On the other hand, the evidence from the Tenants was supposition and opinion, and I find the Tenants did not provide sufficient evidence that the N12 was issued in bad faith. Therefore, the application will be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove the requirement in subsection 57(1)(a). I say this for the following reasons.

The Tenant [name] (‘GW’) testified that on February 13, 2024, the Landlord provided an N12 for termination date of April 30, 2024. The N12 notice stated that the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit because the Landlord intends to move into the unit along with his family. The Tenant vacated as result of the N12 and moved out on November 29, 2024, pursuant to the LTB order (LTB-T-100385-25). The Tenant submitted that the Landlord’s utility bill shows a different address than the rental unit for the month of May 2025.

The Tenant provides that they have driven by the rental unit since they moved out and they only saw the Landlord’s car in the driveway occasionally. She also testified that she knows the family did not move in because their son does not attend the school in the area. She provided pictures of the Landlord’s car being parked but there was no garbage put out. She also provided pictures of the snow not being plowed. She testified that she saw the landlord and his family moving furniture on December 20, 2025.

The Landlord testified that he moved into the rental unit along with his family in December 2024 and is currently still occupying the property. The Landlord provided in evidence Ikea receipt of furniture that was ordered to the home on November 29, 2024, to be delivered to the rental unit. He also provided in evidence copies of utility, electricity and internet bills for the rental. He testified that the May 2025 utility bill contained a different address because it took some time to change the address but subsequently all the bills thereafter are in his name and the rental unit address. The Landlord provide pictures taken inside the rental unit with his family in October 2025. Analysis

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 and the Tenant vacated the rental unit in response to the eviction notice served by the Landlord. Given that the Tenant moved out the rental unit on the termination date of the N12, I am satisfied the Tenant vacated the rental unit due to the Landlord’s eviction notice and satisfied the second requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act. The only remaining issues to determine are whether the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and whether the N12 notice was given in bad faith.
In this case, the evidence from the Landlord was that they did move into the rental unit as of December 1, 2024, and they currently still occupy the unit.
I find that the Landlord did occupy the rental unit for at least 12 months as required when a landlord terminates the tenancy with a notice of termination served under section 48 of the Act.
There is no evidence before the Board to substantiate or corroborate the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The evidence of Tenant was that they occasionally pass through the neighbourhood and only occasionally see the Landlord’s car. I do not find that this alone establish that the Landlord did not occupy the unit. The Tenant also did not visit the rental unit after they vacated to confirm who moved into the rental unit.

Given it was not disputed that there are charges for internet, utilities, and the bills reflect usage. I also find the very fact that all their bills and accounts was placed in the Landlord’s name for approximately a year support a finding of residential occupation.

I find that for the utility bills show variation in electricity and water usage. Further, the utility bills show variability in thermal cooling charges in the spring, summer, and fall and thermal heating charges in the winter. Given the variable usage of utilities, I was not satisfied that no one resided in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not present any concrete evidence to challenge the Landlord’s position on these points. Therefore, I cannot find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

In these circumstances, the burden falls on the Tenant to establish that the Landlord did not move into rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Tenant has failed to lead sufficient evidence to establish the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. As such, the Tenant did not satisfy the third requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act. As the Tenant cannot establish all the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed their application on December 30, 2024. This application contained no specific details of dates/time of events that occurred which give rise to the grounds for the application and did not include any explanations as to how the Tenant arrived at their claim for their remedies. There was also no schedule attached to this application which included any detailed facts and explanation of remedies, and neither was there any evidence filed with the Board.

At the hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative requested an adjournment so he could amend the application to include detailed particulars of the issues that give rise to the application and provide details with respect to the remedies that the Tenant is seeking. He claimed that there was a break down in communication with the Tenant and that he recently reestablished contact with the Tenant 24 hours prior to the hearing. He also claimed that the Tenant could not attend the hearing due to a scheduling work conflict, and that at the time the application was filed no facts were provided because he was trying to “isolate the facts” – which I understand to mean that he was still gathering the facts and trying to put them together.

The Landlord legal representative opposed the adjournment. He claimed that the Landlord does not understand the grounds for the application and that the Tenant has had a reasonable amount of time (approximately two years) to amend their application and provide detail particulars to the Landlord. He also argued that the Tenant did not take any reasonable steps to even file/serve their evidence with respect to the application, and that the request for an adjournment is not reasonable given the amount of time that has elapsed.

An adjournment is not an automatic right. Considering the factors enumerated in the LTB guidelines pertaining to adjournments (No.1), and the submission of the parties, I declined the adjournment request. The Tenant had approximately two years to provide detailed particulars; an explanation of their remedies; and to file/serve their evidence to the Landlord. I take note that the application was also signed by the Tenant’s legal representative, and the representative did not provide a reasonable explanation as to why the facts and details pertaining to the remedies were not included with the application at the time it was filed. His explanation suggested that it was more likely than not, that the application was filed as a placeholder.
Given the lack of specific details on the application, I determined that the Landlord could not reasonably be expected to respond in these circumstances.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The rental unit is a condominium unit. Shortly after the Tenant moved in, in January 8, 2024, they caused a flood that resulted in significant damage to the rental unit. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not repair the unit within a reasonable period of time.

The parties also do not dispute the following facts: - There was an issue with the water pressure and hot water supply in the Tenant’s main bedroom ensuite bathroom. - The Tenant informed the Landlord of this issue on February 8, 2024 - The Landlord waited for the condominium management team to hire a contractor to commence repair work. - The repair work commenced on and was completed on December 10, 2024.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application.

The Tenant testified that she complained of the issue on February 8, 2024, by email. The Tenant testified that condominium’s care team attended the unit on March 15, 2024, to investigate. The Tenant testified that a lot of plumbers visited the unit until August 9, 2024. On August 9, 2024, the condominium’s care team discovered the wall had to be removed to investigate the issue and repair it. The Tenant testified that once the wall was removed and re-installed, the water pressure remained the same and the there was noise when the hot water was turned on. As such, the Tenant complained to the Landlord again on October 7, 2024, and as of November 12, 2024, there was no hot water. On December 2, 2024, the contractor broke down the wall and repaired the pipe on December 10, 2024.

The Tenant testified that during the repairs there was no proper hot water, and it was intermittent and extremely low pressure. She testified that there was another shower in the unit that she could share with her roommate. However, it was inconvenient as she preferred to have her own bathroom which she lost access to while the repairs were being conducted. There was also dust and coming into her room. She sometimes would work from home, and it was difficult to do so while repair work was being conducted.

The Landlord’s agent, [name] (‘SL’) testified that he is the property manager for the Landlord and that the condominium building is brand new, under warranty, and as such the condominium management hired their own contractors and technicians, and thus the Landlord could not hire their own contractor and had to rely on the condominium management. He does not dispute the dates provided by the Tenant in which contractors commenced repair work, which included removing the wall and repairing the pipes on December 2, 2024, and the work was completed as of December 10, 2024. Ultimately, he testified that he was not aware of the potential issue causing the delay which took approximately 10 months to resolve as he was notified of the issue that caused the delay. However, he testified that each time the Tenant complained he would reach out to management to get an update and persuade them to look into the issue. The Landlord Breached its Obligations by Failing to Properly Restore the Unit
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to repair the unit within a reasonable period of time, and in doing so breached their maintenance obligations.

On any application before the Board the person asserting a fact has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to prove that it is more likely than not that what they are claiming is true. This means that the Tenant bears the burden of proof with respect to the allegations in her application.

However, my concern with the Landlord’s evidence is not that it’s hearsay, but rather that I have so little evidence from the Landlord. I note that when I say that the Landlord provided insufficient evidence, I am not flipping the burden of proof onto the Landlord. However, I only have a few emails from the Tenant which to determine what the Landlord did and why it was reasonable. The Tenant must prove their claims on a balance of probabilities. Here I find that the Landlord failed to respond to the compelling evidence offered by the Tenant that there was issue with the ensuite shower in the rental unit for approximately 10 months, the Landlord was aware, and the problem was not fixed.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

There is no dispute that the Tenant notified the Landlord of the issue on February 8, 2024. The evidence before me is that all the Landlord did was follow up with the condominium management. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the condominium management was effectively the Landlord’s agent for the purpose of fulfilling their maintenance obligations and there was no evidence provided by the Landlord that explained why it took so long for the condominium management to fix the problem. I say this because I am unsure of what repairs were done by the condominium’s contractors. Neither the emails provided in evidence nor the Landlord’s witness provide a clear answer to that question. The best evidence I have before me is the Tenant who was in the unit observing the problem persisted for a period of approximately 10 months. As the repairs were not done until December 10, 2024, they were essentially ineffective. As such, I find the Landlord’s response was unreasonable. Remedies 9. The Tenant is seeking abatement of rent in the amount of $8,100.00 for the period between February 8, 2024, when the issue occurred and December 10, 2024, when they resolved the issue. 10. As I find that the Landlord’s breach caused some disruption to the Tenant’s ability to normally reside and enjoy the rental unit, a rent shall be awarded. This abatement is calculated as 10% due the amount of time the issue took to resolve and although the Tenant did not establish any specific losses as a result of not having her ensuite shower. The Tenant testified that it had negative effects on her such as having to share the main washroom with her roommate, not being able to work from home due to on-going construction and dust from the construction was spreading to her bedroom. There was no significant impact for health and safety as such a higher award would not be appropriate. 11. I find that a reasonable abatement of rent for this breach is about 10% of the rent charged from February 8, 2024, to December 10, 2024. This is a period of 306 days. At $2,700.00 per month, daily rent for the unit was $88.76. I therefore calculate the abatement as follows: 10% x $88.76 x 306 = $2,716.05.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,902.05. This amount represents: • $2,716.05 for a rent abatement for the period ending December 10, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario
