She sometimes would work from home, and it was difficult to do so while repair work was being conducted.

The Landlord’s agent, [name] (‘SL’) testified that he is the property manager for the Landlord and that the condominium building is brand new, under warranty, and as such the condominium management hired their own contractors and technicians, and thus the Landlord could not hire their own contractor and had to rely on the condominium management. He does not dispute the dates provided by the Tenant in which contractors commenced repair work, which included removing the wall and repairing the pipes on December 2, 2024, and the work was completed as of December 10, 2024. Ultimately, he testified that he was not aware of the potential issue causing the delay which took approximately 10 months to resolve as he was notified of the issue that caused the delay. However, he testified that each time the Tenant complained he would reach out to management to get an update and persuade them to look into the issue. The Landlord Breached its Obligations by Failing to Properly Restore the Unit
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to repair the unit within a reasonable period of time, and in doing so breached their maintenance obligations.

On any application before the Board the person asserting a fact has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to prove that it is more likely than not that what they are claiming is true. This means that the Tenant bears the burden of proof with respect to the allegations in her application.

However, my concern with the Landlord’s evidence is not that it’s hearsay, but rather that I have so little evidence from the Landlord. I note that when I say that the Landlord provided insufficient evidence, I am not flipping the burden of proof onto the Landlord. However, I only have a few emails from the Tenant which to determine what the Landlord did and why it was reasonable. The Tenant must prove their claims on a balance of probabilities. Here I find that the Landlord failed to respond to the compelling evidence offered by the Tenant that there was issue with the ensuite shower in the rental unit for approximately 10 months, the Landlord was aware, and the problem was not fixed.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

There is no dispute that the Tenant notified the Landlord of the issue on February 8, 2024. The evidence before me is that all the Landlord did was follow up with the condominium management. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the condominium management was effectively the Landlord’s agent for the purpose of fulfilling their maintenance obligations and there was no evidence provided by the Landlord that explained why it took so long for the condominium management to fix the problem. I say this because I am unsure of what repairs were done by the condominium’s contractors. Neither the emails provided in evidence nor the Landlord’s witness provide a clear answer to that question. The best evidence I have before me is the Tenant who was in the unit observing the problem persisted for a period of approximately 10 months. As the repairs were not done until December 10, 2024, they were essentially ineffective. As such, I find the Landlord’s response was unreasonable. Remedies 9. The Tenant is seeking abatement of rent in the amount of $8,100.00 for the period between February 8, 2024, when the issue occurred and December 10, 2024, when they resolved the issue. 10. As I find that the Landlord’s breach caused some disruption to the Tenant’s ability to normally reside and enjoy the rental unit, a rent shall be awarded. This abatement is calculated as 10% due the amount of time the issue took to resolve and although the Tenant did not establish any specific losses as a result of not having her ensuite shower. The Tenant testified that it had negative effects on her such as having to share the main washroom with her roommate, not being able to work from home due to on-going construction and dust from the construction was spreading to her bedroom. There was no significant impact for health and safety as such a higher award would not be appropriate. 11. I find that a reasonable abatement of rent for this breach is about 10% of the rent charged from February 8, 2024, to December 10, 2024. This is a period of 306 days. At $2,700.00 per month, daily rent for the unit was $88.76. I therefore calculate the abatement as follows: 10% x $88.76 x 306 = $2,716.05.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,764.05. This amount represents: • $2,716.05 for a rent abatement for the period ending December 10, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 1, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did prove the allegations contained in the T5 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must provide compensation to the Tenant as set out in this [name].

As explained below, I find that the Tenant met the burden of proof in a one of the issues raised in her maintenance application (T6) and therefore the Tenant’s T6 application is partly granted. Preliminary Issues

The Tenant raised some maintenance issues in the T5 application. I informed her that maintenance issues are properly raised in a T6 application. If the Landlord consents, then the Tenant may amend this application to be both a T5 and a T6 application. The Landlord consented, and subsequently, the Tenant’s application was amended to a T5/T6 application.

The Landlord served two N12 Notices on the Tenant. The 1st N12 Notice was served on July 1, 2025, with a termination date of August 31, 2025. The reason cited on the N12 Notice for terminating the tenancy was that the Landlord’s daughter was going to be moving into the rental unit. In accordance with s. 69(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), a landlord must file the application with the Landlord and Tenant Board within 30 days of the termination of tenancy date in order to evict a tenant. Since an L2 application was not filed within the 30-day period, this N12 is void.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord then served her with a 2nd N12 Notice on September 30, 2025. This 2nd Notice was not entered as evidence, but the Landlord did not dispute the 2nd N12 Notice was for the purpose of purchaser’s own use. He testified his son intended to purchase the unit. Again, the Landlord did not file an application to terminate the tenancy, but the Tenant vacated the rental unit prior to the termination date on the 2nd N12 Notice. Therefore, this is the N12 Notice upon which this [name] pertaining to the T5 application is based. Relevant Law, Burden of Proof and Admissions for T5 Application

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 Notice of Termination under section 49 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice of Termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 Notice of Termination in bad faith.
When questioned, the Landlord agreed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the N12 Notices that she was served with.
The parties disagreed whether the 2nd N12 Notice was given in good faith.

In her testimony, when describing the events that took place, the Tenant stated that when she was served with the 1st N12 Notice, her response to the Landlord was that even though she had been looking for a new rental unit for some time, she was unsure how quickly she could move out of the rental unit and that he should file an application with the Landlord and Tenant Board. The Landlord did not file an application with the Board.

When the Tenant went to pay her October rent on September 30, 2025, the Landlord then served her with a 2nd N12 Notice with a termination date of November 30, 2025. This time he said that the home had already been sold to his son. However, he did not provide any documentation to the Tenant nor to the Board to confirm this nor was any Declaration provided stating that the purchaser required the rental unit for their own use.

Section 49(1) states: “A landlord of a residential complex that contains no more than three residential units who has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by, (a) the purchaser; (b) the purchaser’s spouse; (c) a child or the parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the purchaser, the purchaser’s spouse, or a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.”

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

The Tenant referred to DOC ID 7740628, Exhibit 1, which was the Parcel Register for the house dated April 9, 2026. This register confirmed that the home was still in the Landlord’s name, and no transfer had taken place to his son in September of 2025.

When providing his testimony, the Landlord referred to DOC ID 7847600 – Exhibit 2, which he described was his timeline of the events and also, he included a Declaration signed by his daughter pertaining to the 1st N12 Notice that was served. No declaration was provided by his son. The Landlord testified he lived with his spouse in the upper unit of the complex whereas the Tenant lived in the basement unit. The Landlord’s written timeline does not identify if and when a 2nd N12 Notice was served to the Tenant, but there was no dispute from the Landlord the 2nd N12 was served on the Tenant. The Landlord described how after he got a new job out of town, his son and girlfriend sold their house and moved into the upper unit to live with him and his spouse. At the time the 2nd Notice was served on the Tenant, the Landlord’s son and girlfriend lived in the upper unit and the Landlord and his wife had moved out.

The Landlord testified that his son and girlfriend broke up and therefore his son, although living in the upper unit, did not complete the purchase of the property although there was no dispute about him having moved into it. Hence, the parcel register still shows that the complex belongs to the Landlord. The Landlord did serve the N12 Notice in bad faith
The Landlord testified that he served the 1st N12 Notice because his daughter was going to move into the rental unit.

Just over a year ago, the Landlord had accepted a position out of town and was leaning towards moving and buying a house near his job. The Landlord was travelling and would return to the rental complex on weekends. The Landlord claimed that before buying a second property, his son and girlfriend needed to sell their house and move into the Landlord’s unit.

The termination date of the 1st N12 Notice was August 31, 2025. The Landlord’s daughter intended to move into the rental unit on September 1, 2025. Both parties agreed the Tenant failed to vacate the rental unit by the end of August. Consequently, the Landlord’s daughter had to make other living arrangements.

In September 2025, the Landlord’s son and girlfriend sold their home moved into the Landlord’s home. The Landlord stated that in that same month, he had an oral agreement with his son and future fiancé with respect to purchasing the house in its entirety.
The Landlord agreed the Tenant had told him she would not be moving out of the unit and that he would need to file an application with the Landlord and Tenant Board.

Accordingly, the Landlord served the Tenant with the 2nd N12 Notice. The Landlord testified that he understood the Board process could take many months and he served the notice to have his bases could take Landlord made it very clear that his intent was always to have his daughter move into the rental unit.

After the Tenant vacated the rental unit, his daughter moved into it. She continues to live there. I find that the Landlord’s intent to have his daughter live in the rental unit to be a genuine one. The 1st N12 was served in good faith.

However, I find that the Landlord’s 2nd N12 Notice was not served in good faith. The reason I say this is because the at the time of serving the 2nd N12, no formal Agreement of [name] and [name] had been entered into between the Landlord and his son. The [name] son was already living in the upper unit. He never intended to move into the Tenant’s unit. If the purchase agreement had proceeded, the Landlord’s son would have owned the complex but not necessarily have moved into the Tenant’s lower unit. Even if I accept that there a material change in circumstances through the break-up, I am not satisfied the Notice of Termination for Purchaser’s own use included the couple moving into the basement suite. This explains why the Landlord’s daughter moved into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. In the absence of an agreement, either in writing or persuasive understanding, I am not certain the Landlord served the 2nd N12 Notice in good faith. It is not enough to simply say, “I was covering my bases.” An Agreement of Purchase and Sale is required by the Act when serving an N12 Notice for Purchaser’s Own Use.
Consequently, I find that the Tenant has demonstrated all the required elements under subsection 57(1)(b) and that the 2nd N12 Notice was not served in good faith. T6 Application Issues

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states that: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”
The T6 application must be made within one year of the date the alleged breach occurred.

The Tenant raised the following issues: a) The Landlord failed to plough the driveway snow in a timely manner; b) The Landlord failed to cut the grass on her side of the house; and c) The Landlord failed to address the sewage smell in the rental unit for several months.

The Landlord responded to the issue pertaining to ploughing the driveway. He testified that on December 5, 2024, he received a text from the Tenant (as he was out of town) at 8.51am after the snowfall and by 11.22am, the Landlord had taken care of this issue.
The Landlord did not respond to the grass and sewage smell issues that the Tenant raised and nor did he attempt to dispute them.

Therefore, I find that as a result of not having rectified the sewage issue for several months, the Landlord should pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of 25% for four months of rent. The key legal test here is whether this problem “seriously interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit.” A sewage smell cam ne a habitability and health issue as sewer gas exposure can cause headaches, nausea, and respiratory irritation. Other Issues
The Tenant raised harassment and intimidation issues during the hearing. These issues are not properly raised on a T5 or T6 application.

The Tenant raised an issue pertaining to internet services that the Landlord failed to provide her with internet that he was obligated to provide during the last 2 months of her tenancy. Again, this issue is not properly plead on a T5 or T6 application.

The Tenant raised an issue pertaining to her car being constantly blocked in the driveway thereby restricting her ability to get out of the driveway. This issue is not properly plead on a T5 or T6 application. Remedies

The Tenant was paying $1,550.00 per month in rent to the Landlord. The Tenant’s new rent is now $1,600.00 per month, which amounts to a $50.00 per month increase in rent. Therefore. I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $600.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant is incurring for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant had Wi-fi in the rental unit and since moving into a new rental unit, she needs to pay $67.80 per month for Wi-fi. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant one year’s worth of her Wi-fi fees which amounts to $813.60 ($67.80*12).

The Tenant had incurred moving costs of $600.00 as a result of having to vacate the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant $600.00 for the moving costs she incurred.

If the Tenant meets all 3 elements of the legal test in subsection 57(1) of the Act, then the Board may award a general compensation of up to 12 months rent last charged for the rental unit, which in this case was $1,550.00 per month. The tenant has asked for $14,387.00 in general compensation. The Landlord’s claim is that he did not serve the N12 Notice in bad faith and therefore, it would appear that his position would be that he does not owe any monies to the Tenant in the form of general compensation. Due to the fact that the 2nd N12 Notice to Terminate the tenancy was served in bad faith, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant some amount of general compensation. Having heard from both the Landlord and Tenant, I believe the general compensation should be equal to an amount of 3 months’ rent that was last charged for the rental unit which is a total of $4,650.00. This figure is reasonable, and I have based the amount on the stress and inconvenience put to the Tenant having to move and by the Landlord’s bad faith behaviour.

Covering your bases because of a lengthy process is not a satisfactory reason to serve a Tenant with an N12 Notice to evict them. I find the Landlord to have served the 2nd N12 Notice in bad faith and consequently, I believe the Landlord should pay a fine to the Board to deter him from engaging in such behaviour again. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay a fine to the LTB of $500.00.

As the Landlord did not respond to nor dispute the sewage smell issue the Tenant raised, I find the Tenant should be given some abatement of rent. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,550.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. I find this amount to be appropriate because exposure to sewer gas can cause several health issues and should not be considered as a simple or minor inconvenience.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $8,213.60. This amount represents: • $600.00 for increased rent the Tenant is incurring for the one-year period from November 1, 2025, to October 31, 2026; • $813.60 for the Wi-fi cost she is incurring for the one-year period from November 1, 2025, to October 31, 2026; • $600.00 for the reasonable moving costs that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit; • $4,650.00 for general compensation; • $1,550.00 for a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 by June 5, 2026. June 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: (CCHR) (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s T2 application alleges the Landlord’s agent has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed the Tenant by refusing to allow the Tenant to have an occupant in the rental unit.
The rental unit is a two-bedroom apartment on the seventh floor of a multi floor residential complex. Tenant submissions
The Tenant submitted evidence to support the claims in the application (DOC-7682002).
The position of the Tenant is her and her then husband moved into the rental unit February 1, 2009.

The Tenant stated she did not have the financial means to carry the lawful rent herself and brought in a roommate sometime around the end of 2012 or beginning of 2013. 7. sometime around February 2024 the Tenant reported issues to the Landlord regarding mice in the rental unit. During this time the Tenant had an occupant living in the rental unit to help subsidize her lawful rent. 8. The Tenant stated when the Landlord agent attended the rental unit to address the mice issue, the Landlord agent found out the Tenant had an occupant in the rental unit. 9. The Landlord agent filled out an A2 Board form and provided a copy to the Tenant holding the position the Tenant’s occupant was an unauthorized occupant and by having the occupant the Tenant was in breach of overcrowding in the rental unit. The Landlord agent then requested additional compensation for the additional occupant residing in the rental unit. 10. The Landlord agent also issued the Tenant a letter dated March 26, 2024 restating the Landlord’s position that the Tenant was subletting the rental unit which the Landlord stated was not authorized in accordance to the tenancy agreement. 11. On April 17, 2024 the Landlord also served the Tenant with an N5 notice alleging the Tenant was in breach of the tenancy agreement by having an occupant who was contributing to the rent. 12. After being served the N5 notice and prior to finding a new roommate, the Tenant obtained legal representation and on December 6, 2024 the Tenant’s legal representative sent a letter to the Landlord agent informing the Landlord agent that the Board has, “…consistently determined that tenants are allowed to have roommates can pay a portion of the rent to the tenant, who then pays the rent directly to you as the landlord. There is no contractual relationship between a tenant’s roommate and the landlord. Tenants are allowed to have guests, occupants, and/or roommates, even if they are not listed on the lease.” 13. The letter further goes on to inform the Landlord that overcrowding is determined by municipal by-laws and not by how many tenants sign the tenancy agreement. 14. Sometime after December 6, 2024 the Tenant and the Tenant’s legal representative attend the residential complex to speak to the Landlord agent and inform the Landlord agent that the Tenant would be seeking to have a replacement occupant live in the rental unit. 15. Sometime in late February 2025 or beginning of March 2025 the Tenant acquired a new roommate to occupy the rental unit and pay a portion of the rent. 16. The Tenant submits she lived in “fear” for attempting to exercise her rights. 17. The Tenant alleges that since the incident with the Landlord’s staff have ignored her when passing each other in the hallway and she feels this is intimidating behaviour. Landlord submissions 18. The Landlord agent has been the property manager for 29 years and manages the 2456 rental units in the residential complex. 19. The Landlord agent stated he attended the rental unit sometime in March 2024 after the Tenant made him aware of issues with mice in the rental unit. 20. The Landlord denies he entered illegally and stated the Tenant made a request for him to attend the rental unit to address the issue. 21. The Landlord agent does not dispute that he became aware of the Tenant’s occupant at this time and provided the A2 form to the Tenant and wrote the March 26, 2024 letter informing the Tenant that he believed she was on breach of the tenancy agreement. 22. The Landlord stated he served the Tenant with an N5 notice in April 2024 and filed an A2 application both of which he withdrew once he became aware that the Tenant was not in breach for having an occupant / roommate to subsidize her rent and the Landlord agent has taken no further action regarding this matter. 23. The Landlord agent stated sometime around late June 2024 the Tenant requested the Landlord agent’s assistance in removing the occupant. The Tenant had informed the Landlord agent that the occupant was harassing the Tenant. 24. The Tenant and the Landlord agent attended the rental unit and the Landlord agent told the occupant he had to leave and instructed the Tenant to call police. 25. The occupant eventually left and the Tenant requested the Landlord agent change the locks as the occupant did not leave his copy of the keys with the Tenant or the Landlord agent. 26. The Landlord agent changed the locks as the Tenant requested. 27. The Landlord’s position is the Tenant should not be granted an abatement since the Tenant was never actually prevented from having an occupant in the rental unit and his service of the letter, the A2 and the N5 were based on his belief he was operating within the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). 28. The Landlord’s legal representative points out that the removal of the roommate in June 2024 was at the request of the Tenant due to her allegations of harassment and the Landlord agent assisted the removal of the occupant at the Tenant’s request and not through any action imposed by the Landlord agent. Analysis 29. During her testimony the Tenant stated she was aware of her rights to have an occupant and even after the Landlord sent the March 2024 letter and the withdrawn applications the Tenant maintained her roommate until she requested the Landlord agent assist her with removing him in June 2024. 30. The Tenant stated she respects the Landlord agent and does not believe he has engaged in harassment. She further stated the Landlord’s staff have never done anything rude although they ignore her when passing by. 31. Substantial interference is not defined in a single fixed sentence in the Act, but it has been consistently interpreted through case law and other Board decisions using plain language meaning “more than trivial”, “ongoing” and / or “serious”. 32. Although the word harass is not defined in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines "harassment" as: “…engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” I do not find… 33. With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has not proved the Landlord agent’s actions have substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment or engaged in harassing behaviour. 34. Although I acknowledge the Landlord agent has shown a lack of education as to the Tenant’s right to have an occupant under the Act I do not find the Landlord agent’s and the service of the letter, the A2 and the N5 notice rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment. 35. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. 36. This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that he paid $1,600.00 to the Landlord on May 13, 2022, $841.64 of which was applied to the first partial rental period, and the balance still being held by the Landlord as a deposit.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that neither a last month’s rent deposit nor a key deposit was required. The Agent explained that the Tenant’s overpayment was applied to his account as a credit which was then used for months when the Tenant underpaid rent.

Having reviewed the tenancy agreement and the rent ledger, I am satisfied that the payment on May 13, 2022, was prepaid rent, not a deposit, and was properly applied to the Tenant’s account. The Landlord is no longer holding those funds. Therefore, this claim is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that he overpaid one month of rent on July 5, 2023, due to the month of May 2023 being a credit. The rent ledger has a note next to this payment entry stating, “keep payment until he moves out”, which the Tenant understood to mean that the Landlord is unlawfully holding these funds as a deposit.
The Landlord’s Agent testified that, despite the note, the overpaid rent was applied to subsequent months when the Tenant underpaid rent. The Landlord is no longer holding those funds.

Having reviewed the rent ledger, I am satisfied that the payment on July 5, 2023, was properly applied to the Tenant’s account and is not being held as a deposit. The Landlord is no longer holding those funds. Therefore, this claim is dismissed.

The Tenant also claimed that interest on the last month’s rent deposit has not been paid to him by the Landlord. Given that the Landlord is not holding any deposits for the Tenant, no interest is owing. This claim is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. (T2 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations regarding the key deposit and altering the locking system. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $463.80.

The Tenant claims the Landlord improperly collected and retained a damage deposit of $200.00 and improperly retained the last month’s rent deposit. She also claims the landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by locking her out, taking her property and failing to investigate the behaviour of the other Tenant. Key Deposit.
The Landlord collected a $200.00 damage deposit for the furniture when the tenancy began. The Tenant claims it was a key deposit. The conclusion here is the same.

A damage deposit is not permitted by section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). That section states that: [105] The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

A key deposit is permitted in certain circumstances. Ontario Regulations 516/06 set out circumstances when a key deposit can be collected and retained, such as to pay for replacement keys, for additional keys, or as a refundable deposit not greater than the expected direct replacement cost. This is not one of those situations. In no way is $200.00 the replacement cost of a single manual key to an interior door lock.
No damage deposit is permitted under the Act for any reason.
I note the Tenant returned the key to the rental unit door on December 7, 2024.
Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to return the $200.00 unlawful deposit to the Tenant. Last Month’s Rent Deposit

The Tenant also claimed the Landlord unlawfully retained last month’s rent deposit. She testified she was forced to vacate on November 30, 2024 and that the Landlord agreed he would return her rent deposit.

In contradiction, the Landlord submits the Tenant chose to vacate and did not give proper notice. The Tenancy agreement permits 30 days’ notice, but she gave four days’ notice. He informed her of this 30 day notice requirement and consistently refused to refund any deposit.

There were significant problems with the reliability of the Tenant’s testimony. Her testimony that she was forced to vacate, and that the Landlord agreed to return the last month’s rent deposit is directly contradicted by the text correspondence and the Landlord’s evidence. Instead, texts between the parties demonstrate the Tenant was not forced to vacate but instead proposed leaving as she felt the Landlord was not dealing with her dispute with the other tenant to her satisfaction. In addition the landlord consistently refused to give the last month’s rent deposit, insisting the Tenant is obligated to give 30 days’ notice, instead of 4 days.

Section 88 of the Act states that where a tenant vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with the Act, and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, the amount the rent owing is for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice had the notice been given properly.
In this case, the notice period was shortened to 30 days on consent of the Landlord.

Although the parties had come to some understanding that the Tenant would vacate on November 30, 2024, there was no agreement. I say this because the Tenant began asserting that since she paid rent up to December 4, 2024, she had the right to stay until then. There was no meeting of the minds and therefore no agreement between the parties to end the Tenancy. The Tenant therefore gave notice not in accordance with the Act and without agreement. There was no evidence before me that the Landlord gave the Tenant any notice of termination in any form, implied or written.
I find the Tenant owed rent to January 4, 2025, which is the earliest termination date she could have specified in the notice of termination.
Section 88(5) requires mitigation by the Landlord. I find he adequately attempted to mitigate his damages but failed to find a student to fill the rental unit room, midway through the academic year.
I find therefore that the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit. Unlawful Entry/Illegal Lockout.

The Tenant claimed that on December 1, 2024, the Landlord locked her out of the rental unit. The Tenant testified she had left on November 30, 2025, but came back on December 2, 2024 to pick up the remaining things.

The Landlord had remotely changed the code to the exterior door of the residential complex while he was out of the country on vacation. The Landlord testified he believed she had vacated both because of her notice to him that she would leave November 30, 2024, and her statement that she had taken all the possessions. This belief does not account for the Tenant’s later insistence that she paid rent and was entitled to stay until December 4, 2024. It is clear the Tenant had the right under the Act and expressed the intention to retain possession of the rental unit until December 4, 2024.
I find therefore that there was an unlawful lockout. A 100% rent abatement will be ordered for the period from December 1, 2024 to December 4, 2024.

However, the Tenant failed to prove unlawful entry. She provided no evidence that anyone entered the rental unit, and it is clear that only she had the key to her bedroom door, which she used to access the room on December 7, 2024 and which she then returned to the Landlord. [name].
The Tenant claims the Landlord failed to properly investigate the dispute between her and the other tenant. She also claims her property was taken by the Landlord when he entered unlawfully.
The Tenant’s testimony is problematic, contradicts her application and is prone to exaggeration. It is for this reason I prefer the documentary evidence and testimony of the Landlord.
The Tenant claims that the other tenant consistently took and used her possessions. She testified they were actually her kitchen utensils and dishes, which this tenant kept using.

However, evidence at the hearing is that these were communal dishes provided by the Landlord, dishes which the Tenant laid improper claim to for her exclusive use. The Tenant referred to this behaviour as ‘audacity’ and claimed the situation was ‘life and death’, in her texts to the Landlord. She felt the Landlord should terminate the other tenant. Given the Tenant’s failure to accurately recall recorded conversations, her lack of documentation, her hyperbole and looseness with detail, I find her evidence unreliable and prefer the testimony of the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that he did try to mediate between them on and around November 24, 2024. The Landlord reminded the parties the dishes were communal and tried to encourage them to get along. He offered to further discuss and mediate the situation when he returned from vacation. This was, in my view, a reasonable action given the triviality of the dispute. I find the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit with respect to the dispute she had with the other tenant.

Regarding her property, the Tenant claims she lost her driver’s license, student card, a sweater and a notebook. She claims the Landlord took them. However, she failed to provide any evidence of an application for a new driver’s license or student card, nor did she produce either of those cards with a new issuance dates. She provided no receipts for the sweater.

Other than speculation the Tenant has no supporting evidence. Her oral testimony is, as noted above, problematic and unreliable. It seems improbable that she would completely move all her possessions and not take her driver’s license, and more likely they were misplaced or she is mistaken. It is also improbable given only she had the key to the room and the Landlord was not in the country during the time period.

The evidence at the hearing was that the Tenant removed all her property completely on or before November 30, 2024. Text correspondence between the parties supports this conclusion. When the Landlord returned from vacation, on December 7, 2024, the Landlord allowed the Tenant inside, and she opened the rental unit door with her own key. Photos were produced at the hearing showing the rental unit to be completely bare. No personal items were within. The Tenant did not dispute these photos.
Based on the evidence provided at the hearing, I am satisfied the unit was empty, and none of the Tenant’s belongings were on a balance of probabilities, removed by anyone.
Remedy
I have discussed remedies for each matter above.
The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”.

In the present case, I do not find the Landlord has shown blatant disregard for the Act. I find the monetary award adequate deterrence in the circumstances given the confusion as to when the Tenant was in fact moving out and the evidence that she did actually vacate on November 30, 2024, despite retaining de facto possession. The evidence before me is that the impact to the Tenant was minimal. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $463.80. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the return of the unlawful key deposit. • $157.80 for rent abatement from December 1 to December 4, 2024 (39.45*4). • $106.00 for the cost of filing the applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $300.00.
The Tenant claims that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Evidence and Analysis

The Tenant testified that the tenancy began on July 1, 2025. The Tenant stated the rent was $850.00 per month and that they paid a key deposit of $300.00 prior to moving in. The Tenant submitted a copy of the lease signed by themselves and the Landlord confirming that the Tenant paid this amount.

The Tenant testified that they vacated the rental unit on October 2, 2025. The Tenant testified that they came to an agreement with the Landlord, and upon moving out of the unit, their key deposit was never refunded by the Landlord. The Tenant submitted a text message confirming that they vacated the unit and a request to obtain a refund of the key deposit which was replied to and acknowledged by the Landlord.

The Tenant further testified that they have tried to get into contact with the Landlord to get a refund of their key deposit, but there has been no response from the Landlord. The Tenant then stated that they reached out to their former housemates to connect to the Landlord, but this was ultimately unsuccessful.

The Tenant has filed a T1 application pursuant to section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The T1 is an application for an order that the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.

Section 134(1) of the Act states that unless otherwise provided, a landlord shall not directly or indirectly collect certain listed charges from a tenant in addition to rent. The provision specifically lists a key deposit as a prohibited charge, whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of the General regulation [name]. 516/06, provides a list of exemptions from section 134 of the Act, including a “payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”. According to this provision, a key or fob deposit must be refundable.

When read together, section 134 of the Act and 17 of the regulation prohibit a landlord from retaining a key deposit after the key has been returned at the end of the tenancy. Even if the key deposit was initially collected legally pursuant to section 17 of the regulation, the deposit must be refundable.

At the end of the tenancy, the Tenant did not receive a refund of this key deposit. While refundable key deposits are permissible pursuant to the Act, the Tenant never received the refundable key deposit upon terminating the tenancy, vacating the unit, and returning the keys even after requesting the same. Accordingly, the Landlord will be required to return the $300.00 key deposit the Tenant paid.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (T2 application). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenants pursuant to the terms of this order. T2 / Illegal Entry:

The Tenants testified that during their residential tenancy, the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, without serving the Tenants with proper notice pursuant to the Act. The Tenants testified to the Landlord entering the unit illegally on eight separate occasions.

On April 14, 2024, the Landlord and another individual entered the Tenants’ rental unit and performed an inspection of the unit. The Landlord walked through the rental unit and made a list of items that required the Landlord’s attention. The Tenants were not provided with a written notice of entry prior to the Landlord’s entry on this date. The Tenants did receive an email from the Landlord on or about April 11, 2024, letting them know that he will be attending the unit on April 14, 2024, between 12:00 p.m., and 12:30 p.m. The Tenants consented to the Landlord’s entry on this date.

On May 20, 2024, the Landlord’s father and another male individual entered the Tenants’ rental unit for the purposes of assessing and inspecting what work was required to have an outdoor water faucet installed. The Landlord’s father and individual inspected the basement and outside of the property, but no work was completed during this visit. The Tenants received a text message from the Landlord hours prior to the intended attendance and agreed/consented to this entry which was confirmed by their text communications.

On May 22, 2024, the Landlord’s father and another individual attended the Tenants’ rental unit unannounced and stated that they needed access to the basement for the purposes of taking additional photographs to start work on having an outdoor water faucet installed. The Tenants notified the Landlord of their concern that same evening, to which the Landlord responded by apologizing and confirming that in the future he would be providing the Tenants with a minimum of 24 hours’ notice as required. A copy of the email communications was tendered as evidence by the Tenants. The Landlord’s father made plans with the Tenants to return to the unit on the following day at 4:30 to drill a hole for the installation of the outdoor water faucet.

On May 23, 2024, the Landlord’s father and two unknown individuals attended the rental unit at approximately 3:45 p.m., prior to the time that the Landlord’s father and the Tenants had agreed upon. The Tenants were not at home at the time, with only the Tenants’ young daughter at home. The Landlord’s father was not permitted entry into the home on this date, and no work was completed. The Tenants emailed the Landlord to inform him of their concern regarding a lack of notice prior to attending or entering the unit.

On May 28, 2024, the Landlord attended the rental unit for the purposes of collecting a ladder from the backyard of the rental unit. The backyard was exclusively used by the Tenants. The Tenants received an email from the Landlord on May 26, 2024, informing the Tenants that the Landlord would be attending the property to pick up his ladder from the backyard between 2:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.

On May 28, 2024, the Tenants sent the Landlord an email informing the Landlord of their concerns with lack of notice for entries. The Tenants also requested the issuance of proper notices, and that the Tenants would not be accepting any text messages or calls asking to enter the unit moving forward.

On August 18, 2024, at 2:00 p.m., the Landlord’s agent attended the rental property with approximately five individuals who identified themselves as contractors. The Tenants testified that two of the men stayed outside during the visit, one of the men stayed in the living room, and two other men walked around and inspected the bathroom upstairs. No work was completed on this date or entry. The Tenants received an email from the Landlord on August 17, 2024, at approximately 10:00 a.m., notifying the Tenants that he will be sending contractors the following day between the hours of 2:00 p.m., and 4:00 p.m.

The Tenants responded to the Landlord email on August 17, 2024, by informing the Landlord that the notice he sent the Tenants was not legal and that the Landlord needed to get the work done rather than attending and inspecting the property multiple times with no results.

On September 5, 2024, at approximately 10:00 a.m., the Landlord attended the rental unit for the purposes of carrying out work inside of the unit. The Tenant was in the shower at the time of the Landlord’s entry and was startled by seeing him inside of the rental unit. The Tenant requested that the Landlord leave the rental unit which the Landlord complied with. The Landlord did email the Tenants a notification on September 1, 2024, informing the Tenants that the Landlord would be entering the rental unit between the hours of 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., for the purposes of carrying out electrical repairs. The Tenants did not expect to see the Landlord despite receiving this notice because the parties had a dispute the previous day.

On September 24, 2024, the Landlord and/or agent thereof, attended the rental unit at approximately 10:00 a.m., and proceeded to start drilling on the exterior wall of the rental property. The Tenants called the police department because the Landlord was banging on the Tenants’ front door aggressively. The police attended the rental property and asked the Landlord and contractor to leave the property. The Landlord sent the Tenants an email on September 22, 2024, informing the Tenants that the Landlord will be attending the property on September 24th, and 25th, 2024, between the hours of 9:00 a.m., to 7:00 p.m. The Tenants responded to the Landlord’s email communication informing the Landlord that they felt the notice was invalid and not legal. The Tenants did not consent to the Landlord’s entry on September 24, 2024.
The Landlord did not return to the rental unit on September 25, 2024, based on the recommendation of the police department.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord never obtained the Tenants’ consent for email service of documents and notices and sought compensation in the amount of $8,000.00 for the eight entries as described above.

The Landlord testified that he always provided the Tenants with notice in advance of the intended entry. The Landlord would often provide the Tenants with more than 24-hour notice as he would try to provide 48 to 72 hours’ notice when possible. The Landlord sent the Tenants these notifications of entry by way of email and text message. The Landlord did not have the Tenants’ consent for service of documents and notices by email communications. The Landlord was unable to serve the notices at the Tenants’ rental unit because he stated that he lived in Toronto, which was a far drive to the rental unit.

The Landlord also testified that the Tenants agreed to allow the Landlord into the rental unit for many of the entries raised by the Tenants. The Landlord testified to having the Tenants’ permission to enter the unit on April 14, 2024, and May 20, 2024.

The Landlord testified to serving the notices for the purposes of inspecting the rental unit and performing necessary repair work. The Landlord believed that serving the Tenants with notice of entry by email was an acceptable method of service if the notices were served a minimum of 24 hours in advance of the intended entry. The Landlord did not dispute his father attending the unit without notice of entry on May 22, 2024.

Section 191(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2026, reads as follows: (2) A notice or document that is not given in accordance with this section shall be deemed to have been validly given if it is proven that its contents actually came to the attention of the person for whom it was intended within the required time period. 2006, c. 17, s. 191 (2).

This means that a notice that is not served in accordance with the Act, or the Rules, shall be deemed to have been validly given if it is proven that its contents came to the attention of the person for whom it was intended within the required time period. I believe this section speaks directly to the Landlord’s service of the notices of entry by text and email communications because the Landlord did not have the Tenants’ consent for email service, but the notices did come to the attention of the Tenants within the required timeframe.

Based on the evidence, I find that the Landlord did not enter the unit illegally on April 14, 2024, and May 20, 2024. I make this finding because the Tenants permitted the Landlord’s entry at the time of the Landlord communicating his intent to enter the unit, and at the actual time of entry into the unit. I also do not find that the Landlord’s actions substantially interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment on these dates because the Tenants permitted entry at the time.

I find that the entry on May 22, 2024, was illegal because the Landlord failed to provide the Tenants with notice of entry as required. The Landlord’s father and a contractor attended the rental unit unannounced for the purposes of inspecting the unit for installation of an outdoor water faucet. I also find that this action would substantially interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit. I find the amount of $250.00 to be appropriate in these circumstances.

I do not find that the attendance on May 23, 2024, was an illegal entry. I make this finding because the Landlord’s father attended the unit prior to the time agreed upon with the Tenants. He was not permitted entry because the Tenants were not home. The Landlord’s father did not enter the unit on this date. The Tenants had agreed to allow the Landlord’s father entry at a certain time and were therefore aware he would be attending. Having said this, arriving at a time outside of the agreed hours is not appropriate and would substantially interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit. Therefore, I find it appropriate to award the Tenants $100.00 for this incident.

I do not find the entry or attendance on May 28, 2024, to amount to an illegal entry. The reason I make this finding is because the Tenants were made aware of the entry and Landlord’s intent to retrieve the ladder more than 24 hours in advance of the intended entry. Despite the Landlord sending this notification by email, the notice would still be deemed delivered as the information in the email came to the Tenants’ attention within the time required. Therefore, I find no compensation is appropriate for this incident.

I do not find the entry or attendance on August 18, 2024, to amount to an illegal entry. The reason I make this finding is because the Tenants were made aware of the entry and Landlord’s intent to enter the unit in advance of the entry. Despite the Landlord sending this notification by email, the notice would still be deemed delivered as the information in the email came to the Tenants’ attention within the time required. Having said this, I do find that the number of attendances for the purposes of inspecting the property without doing any work to be excessive and would substantially interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. Therefore, I find the amount of $100.00 to be appropriate to award for this incident.

I do find the entry or attendance on September 5, 2024, to be an illegal entry. The reason I made this finding is because the notice of entry was invalid. The Tenants were made aware of the entry more than 24 hours in advance of the intended entry. Despite the Landlord sending this notification by email, the notice would still be deemed delivered as the information in the email came to the Tenants’ attention within the time required. I do find the notice to be invalid because the time of entry is shown to be between the hours of 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., which the Courts have held to be unreasonable. I also find an eight hour window to be unreasonable, apart from certain circumstances which did not apply in this case. Therefore, I find compensation in the amount of $100.00 to be appropriate for this incident.

I also find that the entry on September 24, 2024, to be an illegal entry. The reason I made this finding is because the notice of entry was invalid. The Tenants were made aware of the entry more than 24 hours in advance of the intended entry. Despite the Landlord sending this notification by email, the notice would still be deemed delivered as the information in the email came to the Tenants’ attention within the time required. I do find the notice to be invalid because the time of entry is shown to be between the hours of 9:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., which the Courts have held to be unreasonable. I also find a ten hour window to be unreasonable. Therefore, I find compensation in the amount of $100.00 to be appropriate for this incident. T2 / Harassment:

The Tenants testified that the Landlord harassed the Tenants by way of serving multiple notices of termination without merit for the purpose of harassing the Tenants. The Tenants were served with an N5 notice of termination for damage to property and substantial interference. The notice was based on the Tenants installing security cameras without the Landlord’s consent and authorization. The Landlord claimed the installation of the cameras caused damage. The Tenants confirmed the installation of the camera did require a small hole for a screw to hold the camera in place.

The second notice was given to the Tenants for substantial interference because the Tenants were filming the Landlord and/or contractor when they attended the rental unit to perform inspections/repairs.

On December 27, 2024, the Tenants contacted the police to assist in having the Landlord removed from the property and claimed that the Landlord was harassing the Tenants. The Landlord was arrested and charged with criminal harassment. The Landlord was given a peace bond for the period of May 29, 2025, to May 29, 2026.

The Landlord testified that he served the Tenants with the notices of termination for substantial interference and damage because he believed that the actions taken by the Tenants warranted the issuance of a notice of termination. The Landlord testified that he did not issue the notices for the purposes of harassing the Tenants. The notices were defective due to errors.

Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord harassed the Tenants. I make thins finding because I do not have sufficient evidence do find that the notices of termination that the Landlord served the Tenants were without merit. Nor do I have sufficient evidence to find that the Landlord’s actions on December 27, 2024, amounted to harassment, criminal or otherwise. Therefore, I do not find it appropriate to award any compensation for these incidents. T6 / Bathtub / Bathroom Tiles:

The Tenants testified that the bathtub in the bathroom located on the upper level was leaking water. The water would weep below into the kitchen ceiling which caused the kitchen ceiling to begin bubbling, cracking, warping, and showing signs of water damage. The Tenants reported this issue to the Landlord in writing on February 28, 2024, by email communication. The Tenants testified that because of the leak, the Tenants were unable to take a bath or shower in this washroom. The Tenants were able to use the shower in the second bathroom but had to go to the basement to do so. The Tenants testified that this issue was never repaired or corrected by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that he did not ignore the issue of the upstairs bathroom and scheduled contractors do the work on September 24, 2024, but he was unable to do so, because the Tenants contacted the police department and had the Landlord and his contractor leave the property. The Landlord also testified that the Tenants did not feel comfortable having the walls removed in the bathroom. The Landlord completed the repairs required after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Landlord did not attempt to re-schedule the work to be completed after September 24, 2024.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act')., I make this finding because I find the Landlord’s attempt to have the repair work carried out in September 2024, unreasonable given the fact that he was initially made aware of the issue in February 2024, and either personally attended or had someone attend the rental unit multiple times in April, May, and August 2024. The Tenants did not cooperate with the Landlord’s efforts in September 2024, onward. This does not excuse the Landlord from having the repairs completed. Water leak / Kitchen Ceiling:

The Tenants testified that the water leak from using the bathtub upstairs caused water to leak down to the ceiling of the Tenants’ kitchen below. Because of this, the Tenants stopped using the bathroom upstairs for showering or bathing. The washroom was limited to washing hands and brushing teeth. The kitchen ceiling showed signs of water damage. The Tenants notified the Landlord of this issue in writing on February 28, 2024. The Tenants testified that the Landlord never repaired this issue during their tenancy.

The Landlord testified that he did not ignore the issue of the upstairs water leak and scheduled contractors do the work on September 24, 2024, but he was unable to do so, because the Tenants contacted the police department and had the Landlord and his contractor leave the property. The Landlord also testified that the Tenants did not feel comfortable having the walls removed in the bathroom. The Landlord completed the repairs required after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Landlord did not attempt to re-schedule the work to be completed after September 24, 2024.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act')., I make this finding because I find the Landlord’s attempt to have the repair work carried out in September 2024, unreasonable given the fact that he was initially made aware of the issue in February 2024, and either personally attended or had someone attend the rental unit multiple times in April, May, ang August 2024. The Tenants did not cooperate with the Landlord’s efforts in September 2024, onward. This does not excuse the Landlord from having the repairs completed. Mold:

The Tenants testified that they had black mold in their rental unit, more specifically inside of the closet in the master bedroom, cold room/storage space in the basement, on the floor in one of the bedrooms, inside another closet space, and linen closet. The Tenants had a technician attend the unit to assess the mold and found a substance that he identified as being mold and believed it may be possible that the material inside the walls may contain asbestos. The Tenants notified the Landlord of this issue in writing on February 28, 2024. The Tenants testified that the Landlord never repaired or corrected the issue.

The Landlord did not dispute the mold substance in the rental unit and testified that he attempted to have the mold removed and treated but the Tenants were unresponsive to his efforts. He testified in attempting to have the mold cleaned on April 3, 2025. The Landlord cleaned the mold and treated the areas on July 1, 2025, after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act')., I make this finding because I find the Landlord’s attempt to have the repair work carried out in April 2025, unreasonable given the fact that he was initially made aware of the issue in February 2024, and either personally attended or had someone attend the rental unit multiple times in April, May, ang August 2024. I do not have any evidence to support that the Tenants prevented the Landlord from carrying out the necessary repairs. [name] stairs and railing:

The Tenants testified that the steps leading to the deck and back entry of the rental unit were rotten, decaying, and uneven. The Tenants also testified that the railing for the deck stairs was loosely attached and required securing or replacement. The Tenants testified that the Landlord did have someone attend to the issue but only replaced one of the several steps that required replacement and never returned. When the Tenants informed the Landlord that the whole staircase required replacing, the Landlord stated that his contractor said it was safe and could survive another few years the way it was. The Tenants notified the Landlord of this issue on February 28, 2024, by email communication.

The Landlord testified that he had a contractor or handyman attend the rental unit on April 14, 2024. The Landlord agreed that he did not replace the entire stairway but argued that the stairway did not require replacement and that the replacement of the one step was sufficient. The Landlord did not replace or repair the railing because the Tenants did not make him aware of the issue. He also does not believe the issue was existent at that time because his contractor would have secured the railing.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). I make this finding because the Landlord’s response time in repairing the steps was approximately 1.5 months after being initially notified of the issue which is not reasonable given a Landlord’s obligations under the Act. I do however find the Landlord’s actions of repairing the one step to be sufficient, as I have no evidence before me to suggest that the remaining steps failed or malfunctioned during the remainder of the tenancy. [name] sod/mud:

The Tenants noticed that a large portion of their backyard had lost all its grass and became very muddy when it rained. The Tenants notified the Landlord of this concern and requested that the Landlord resod the area so that the Tenants can have grass in that part of the yard. The Tenants also notified the Landlord that the home did not have an outdoor water hose connection or faucet and requested the Landlord install a connection. The Tenants testified that the Landlord did not resod the backyard or install a water faucet outside. The Tenants tendered photographs of the backyard area as evidence.

The Landlord testified that he was willing to sod the backyard and have the area grassy for the Tenants. The Landlord ordered the sod sometime in May 2024, due to the availability and season for sod, but the Tenants informed the Landlord that the home had no outdoor water supply or [name], and the sod would simply die as it could not be maintained. The Tenants sent the Landlord an email to this effect on or about May 25, 2024. The same email also specifies the Tenants being concerned with the walls being opened, and the excessive noise from construction work due to one of the Tenant’s medical conditions.

Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). I am making this finding because I find the delay in ordering sod in May to be reasonable given the type of product that is required and its availability. I also find the Landlord’s response to the Tenants concern to be reasonable given the Tenants requested that the Landlord not install any sod as of May 2024. Therefore, I do not find it appropriate to order any compensation for this issue. Ceiling fans in bedrooms:

The Tenants testified that the ceiling fans in the bedrooms only had one of the two cords required to turn on the fan and light function. Because one of the cords was missing, the Tenants had to remove the light bulb to use the fan, if they wanted to use the fan alone. The Tenants testified that the fan and light both worked but the missing cord caused a great deal of inconvenience. The Tenants notified the Landlord of this issue on February 28, 2024, by email communication. The Tenants tendered pictures of the ceiling fans as evidence. The Tenants testified that the Landlord never addressed this issue.

The Landlord testified to repairing the ceiling fans after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. I was not provided with any compelling evidence as to why this repair could not have been done during the Landlord’s multiple visits in 2024.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord has failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord was notified of this issue in February 2024. Windows, window screens, and door:

The Tenants testified that they observed multiple windows in the rental unit that were missing screens or had ripped screens. The Tenants also testified that multiple windows were not properly sealed and caused a significant draft and increase in utility costs. The Tenants testified that some of the windows were jammed or gummed up and would not allow the Tenants to lock the windows when closed. The Tenants also testified that the windows not being properly sealed resulted in bugs and insects entering the rental unit. The Tenants tendered pictures of the windows, and window screens as evidence.

The Tenants testified that the front entry door had a large visible gap in it when the door was completely closed. The Tenants testified that the gap in the door allowed drafts through the home, as well as being less secure. The Tenants notified the Landlord of this issue by email on February 28, 2024. The Tenants testified that the issues were never addressed by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that that he did not ignore the issue of the windows and door, and scheduled contractors do the work on September 24, 2024, but he was unable to do so, because the Tenants contacted the police department and had the Landlord and his contractor leave the property. The Landlord is currently in the process of having the work completed. The Landlord did not attempt to re-schedule the work to be completed after September 24, 2024.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act')., I make this finding because I find the Landlord’s attempt to have the repair work carried out in September 2024, unreasonable given the fact that he was initially made aware of the issue in February 2024, and either personally attended or had someone attend the rental unit multiple times in April, May, ang August 2024. The Tenants did not cooperate with the Landlord’s efforts in September 2024, onward. This does not excuse the Landlord from having the repairs completed.
The Tenants testified that the Landlord did repair the basement bathroom fan and kitchen plug on September 5, 2024, and repaired the broken breaker fuse panel on September 30, 2024.

The Tenants sought a rent abatement in the amount of 30% and/or $8,820.00 for the period of twelve months from February 2024, through to February 2025, $150.00 for out- of-pocket expenses for mold testing, $2,500.00 in general compensation for mental and emotional duress.

Based on the evidence and the circumstances, I find that it is appropriate to award the Tenants the sum of $7,350.00, a rent abatement in the amount of 25% of the monthly rent for the period of March 1, 2024, through to February 28, 2025. I find that the reduction from the Tenants’ request of 30% to be reasonable because the Tenants were not cooperative in September 2024, and onwards. I do not find the Tenants’ position to be unreasonable given the number of entries the Landlord made prior to that date, and the amount of work that was completed during those visits. Having said this, I find that the Tenants’ reluctance and resistance in allowing entry would have impeded the Landlord’s ability to carry out the repairs in a timely manner. This does not excuse the unreasonable delay between the time that the Landlord was initially notified of the maintenance issues to the time of the Landlord attending and repairing the issues.
I also find it is appropriate to award the Tenants the sum of $150.00 for out-of-pocket expenses for the cost of having the unit inspected for mold.

Despite the issues between the parties and their feelings towards one another, I find that most of the issues and problems that arise in this case could have easily been avoided by better communication and organization of inspections and repairs. I am not satisfied that the Landlord intentionally or wilfully attended the property to upset the Tenants or harass them. I do not find it probable that someone would travel from Toronto to Sudbury, with the sole intent of causing someone a hard time. I believe the Landlord’s intentions were good, but he did not act within a reasonable time, nor did he effectively communicate with his Tenants. Therefore, I find that general compensation would not be appropriate in these circumstances. Remedies
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $7,350.00 is appropriate in the circumstances for the maintenance issues as described in the T6 application.
The Tenants incurred out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord's breach: Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $150.00 for these out-of-pocket expenses.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $650.00 for the Landlord’s conduct regarding the illegal entries and substantial interference as described in the T2 application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $8,198.00. This amount represents: • $8,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $150.00 for out-of-pocket expenses. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 22, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 10, 2026 ____________________________
