issues: LLP (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $1,263.00 on or before June 16, 2026.
By way of the background, the Tenant rented the unit on behalf of his daughter who occupied the rental unit. The Tenant’s daughter is [name] [name].

In the application, the Tenant claims that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit a habitable state since October 24, 2024, and this substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. The Tenant also claims that the Landlord entered the unit illegally and withheld or interfered with their vital services.

The parties do not dispute that the Tenancy lawfully terminated on October 31, 2024. However, the Landlord’s witness [name]’) testified that they took vacant possession of the unit on October 24, 2024, and began the process of turning over the unit.
The Tenant disputes that tenancy was lawfully terminated as of October 24, 2024.

Section 37(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act”) states that if a notice of termination is given in accordance with this Act and the Tenant vacates the rental unit in accordance with the notice, the tenancy is terminated on the termination date set out in the notice.

The Tenant RM testified that they provided the N9 notice to the Landlord to terminate the tenancy as of October 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that the Landlord accepted the N9 Notice. Therefore, in accordance with section 37(2) of the Act, I find that the tenancy ended October 31, 2024.

The Tenant’s agent AM testified that she attended the rental unit on October 24, 2024, and observed that the unit was destroyed. She also testified that all her belongings were removed from the unit and the vital services in the unit were no longer functioning. she testified that she left behind cleaning supplies, clothing items such as a wool coat, books, radio, packing material, bag pack and water bottle. She also left a sleeping bag in the event; she needed to stay over to sleep in between moving her items.

The Tenant RM testified that on December 6, 2024, that the Landlord returned their prorated rent that they paid in the amount of $771.99 for October 22 to 31, 2024 and interest owing the last month rent deposit held by the Landlord.

The Landlord’s witness VR who is a property manager testified that as of October 22, 2024, they entered the rental unit for inspection to commence turning over the unit. he does not dispute that they improperly commenced turn over prior to the termination date of October 31, 2024. VR testified that they noticed the Tenant’s agent AM was moving out However, VR maintains that the unit was empty, and there were no belongings left in the unit. The Landlord submitted in photos take on October 22, 2024. During cross examination, VR did confirm that that there was [name] holding a backpack in the [name] and there was bottle in the unit. VR also confirmed that the building manager who conducted the inspection did not check the bedroom closest to confirm whether there were belongings left behind.

He also testified that on October 15, 2024, they provided 24-hour notice to enter the unit on October 21, 2024; for the purpose of installing a water meter but subsequent notice of entries was not served to the tenant. He also submits that there were electricity and water in the unit but there was no heat in the unit.

In this case, I find that the Landlord acknowledges entering the rental unit a week before the Tenancy lawfully terminated and they began to do work in the unit which may have required them to turn off vital services such water to conduct plumbing repairs and he testified there was no heat in the unit for the 10 – day period from October 22, 2024 to October 31, 2024.

The issues raised in the application relate to an incident that occurred after October 23, 2024. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord illegally entered the unit and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit and the Landlord interfered with their vital services. Remedies

The Tenant claims that the Landlord improperly disposed of the following property when they unlawfully entered the rental unit during the tenancy: • Red Tivoli Radio valued at $300.00 • Brown Aritzia Wool Coat valued at $400.00. • Grey [name] valued at $60.00. • White S’well water bottle valued at $50.00. • [name] electric lamp valued at $140.00. • Navy blue sleeping bag valued at $100.00. • Personal mementos valued at $150.00.

I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven on a balance probability that the Landlord disposed of the above items when they unlawfully entered the rental unit. I say this because, VR confirmed the presence of some of these items in the pictures submitted from the unit inspection in late October 2024, and for the remaining items it was clear the Landlord’s agent did not inspect the unit and was not able to confirm or deny whether those items were in the closet. On the other hand, the Tenant’s evidence regarding these items was clear and consistent. The Tenant says the items were all purchased during their tenancy. They provided pictures of the items and in addition, the Tenant provided evidence regarding the replacement value of the items that they lost.
The Tenant did not have receipts for any of their items, but they provided enough details regarding the replacement value of their property.

As such, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,200.00 for the cost of replacing the Tenant’s property including the radio, Aritzia wool coat, backpack, water bottle, electrical lamp, sleeping bag and personal mementos that were improperly disposed of by the Landlord.

The Tenant also requested $30.00 for out-of-pocket expenses to compensate them for the Hydro bill that they paid for the month of October 2024 when the Hydro was cut off. The Landlord argues that only a partial amount should be refunded because the Tenant was able to use the Hydro in the unit until October 22, 2024. I find that the Tenant was able to use the unit until October 22, 2024, as such I find that the Tenant is only entitled to $15.00 for out-of-pocket expenses.

The Tenant also sought legal fees in the amount of $700.00. The Tenant would like to be re-imbursed for seeking legal counsel. This request is denied. Legal fees are a type of Costs. The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 3 regarding costs provides: While the Board may order a party to pay the costs of another party, costs to a successful party for the preparation/representation fees paid to a legal representative are generally only awarded in cases of unreasonable conduct.

Examples of unreasonable conduct listed in Interpretation Guideline 3 do include initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith or bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion. Although the Guidelines are not binding on me, I do find them persuasive and do not see any reason to depart from the Guideline in this matter.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,263.00. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $15.00 for the estimated reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment contrary to s. 22 of the Act. They also allege that the Landlord has harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with them contrary to s. 23 of the Act. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment by failing to respond to their complaints regarding another tenant’s actions. The complaints were primarily around noise disturbances, however, the Tenant also raised concerns over their safety due to the actions of another tenant. The noise was described by the Tenant as screaming, banging, and violent noises. Tenant Evidence

The Tenant testified that they first told the Landlord about issues with unit 504 in October 2023 and the issues persisted until March 2024, when the Tenant vacated. The Tenant states that their correspondence with the Landlord consists of approximately 226 emails, however, they were not relied upon at the hearing by the Tenant or raised by the Tenants representative. The Tenant testified that they sent three emails in October 2023, and some emails in November 2023, but did not provide specific dates.

The Tenant testified that because of the substantial interference, the Tenant had no choice but to vacate the unit. They are seeking to claim the difference in their new rent being charged in addition to their moving and storage expenses they incurred. The Tenant acknowledges that the Landlord was working with them to try and transfer them to another unit; however, this was not successful as the Tenants desire was to move to Toronto, not remain within London. The Tenant testified that they moved back to Toronto to be closer to their office, and their community supports there. The Tenant testified that she originally moved to London to be closer to her mother but had no desire to remain in the city after her experience in this unit.

The Tenant testified that unit 504 had their door missing, that the tenant of this unit would exhibit violent behavior, that he killed his dog, and that he refers to the “KKK” regularly, and that they feared for their life because of this tenant. Focusing on the behaviour that the Tenant is alleging, I asked the Tenant if she has experienced any of these incidents firsthand, and she stated “no”. When asked how she knew that the tenant in unit 504 killed their dog, she stated that she heard it from others, and that she also observed him mourning his dog on his Instagram. When asked about the “KKK” comment, the Tenant states that she can hear mumbled comments from the Tenant about the “KKK” and she believes he suffers from a mental illness. When asked if she has ever experienced violence from the tenant in unit 504, she stated “no”. When the Tenant was asked how the experiences were with the tenant in 504, she described it as “friendly small talk” while passing in the hallway or elevator.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N5 in November 2023 and January 2024 because of complaints received. That in February 2024, a [name] executive attend the Tenants rental unit to discuss their concerns and address them. During this discussion, the Tenant was offered the opportunity to relocate to another rental unit in London with the same lease terms. The Landlord offered the Tenant the same unit in a different building in London, at the same lease terms and with no penalty for terminating the lease early, but the Tenant rejected the offer. [name]7. The Landlord’s Representative presented evidence that in response to the Tenant’s complaints a first N5 was served to unit 504 November 28, 2023. The N5 notice was voided as there were no complaints received in the seven-day period following service of the notice. A second N5 was served based on additional complaints received on January 22, 2024. An N7 was served on February 8, 2026, including but not limited to, the Tenant removed their fire rated door from the hinges. The Landlord submitted a request to the Board to shorten the time to their hearing date. The N7 was heard on May 16, 2024, and the tenancy at unit 504 was terminated following the hearing. Analysis 8. Section 22 of the Act states: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22. 9. Section 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 23. 10. Guideline 6 also sets out factors the Board may consider in making a determination on whether or not a landlord is in breach of s. 22. Guideline 6 states: Sometimes it is other tenants living in the same building who are causing the disturbance, not the landlord. However, landlords have a positive obligation to provide quiet enjoyment and take reasonable action to address another tenant's conduct that disturbs the complaining tenant. If the landlord fails to reasonably respond to the complaints, the landlord may be in breach of section 22. While the landlord in such a situation is not directly responsible for the actions of the offending tenant, the landlord's responsibility is linked to a failure to take reasonably necessary actions to ensure that the complaining tenants could reasonably enjoy the premises: [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (On. [name]. Ct.), First Ontario Realty Corp. v. Appelrouth [2012] O.J. No. 3639 ([name]. [name]. Ct.). 11. In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, 2001 CarswellOnt 4890 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court held that a landlord must take reasonable steps to address allegations of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment by one tenant of another tenant. Failure to do so can result in the landlord being found to have substantially interfered with the complaining tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. 12. It may be that the Tenant heard terrible things from others about the occupant in unit 504, however, by their own admission, they described all personal encounters with this individual as positive. I have difficulty believing that the fear of this tenant was so extreme when all personal encounters were positive, and that the Tenant elected to follow this individual on social media. These circumstances do not rise to substantial interference or harassment such that the Tenant had no choice but to move. 13. The issue before me is to determine if the Landlord has satisfied their obligation to investigate and take reasonable steps to follow up with a Tenant’s complaints. The Tenant submitted several complaints to the Landlord, which were actioned by serving different notices of termination to the offending tenant, and following the processes laid out by the Board for terminating a tenancy. The Landlord attempted to speak with the offending tenant to correct their actions. I find that the Landlord acted promptly and professionally in addressing the issues and the continued efforts to work with the Tenant and preserve their tenancy in an alternative unit. The Landlord submitted a request for an expedited hearing and did what was in their power to address the Tenants concerns. 14. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and they did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $588.00 for an illegal rent increase and the application filing fee.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit in December 2023 and was paying $2,300.00 in rent. At the end of December 2024, the Landlord had a verbal conversation with the Tenant and told her that the rent would be increasing to $2,350.00 effective January 1, 2025.

The Tenant intended to pay $2,350.00 starting January 1, 2025, but for the month of January 2025, she paid $2,340.00. For the months of February 2025, through November 2025, she paid $2,350.00 in rent. The Tenant alleges that she paid $540.00 in an illegal rent charge because the Landlord did not give her 90 days’ notice, nor did he serve her any documentation regarding a rent increase. Analysis

When conducting an analysis of rent increases, the starting point is always section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which is supported by section 110 and sets out the mandatory requirements that must be met in order for a rent increase to be valid.

Section 116 says that, if a landlord intends to increase the rent, they must give the tenant a Notice of Rent Increase (‘NORI’) at least 90 days in advance and in writing. The NORI must be in the Board’s prescribed form. There must be at least 12 months between regular rent increases and, assuming the property is not exempt from the rent control guidelines, annual rent increases are limited to the annual guideline amount. Section 116(4) of the Act states that an increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by that section.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with a NORI in the Board’s prescribed form and did not give 90 days in advance and in writing. The rent increase was within the annual rent control guideline.

As the rent increase failed to comply with all the requirements set out in section 116, the next step in the analysis is found in section 135.1 which says: 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. [Emphasis added]

Essentially, these provisions ask two questions: Did the tenant pay the illegal rent increase for 12 consecutive months? Did the tenant file an application with the Board within that time which addresses the illegal rent increase?

If the Tenant did pay the illegal increase for 12 months and did not file an application with the Board, then the rent increase is deemed not to be void. In other words, the rent increase is deemed to be valid and can be enforced.

However in this case, based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Tenant paid the rent increase for 11 months, and filed the application with the Board on December 5, 2025 which is within the timeframe that addresses the illegal rent increase. As such, the rent increase is deemed to be unlawful and the Landlord shall return to the Tenant $540.00 which represents an illegal rent increase from the period starting January 1, 2025, up to and including November 1, 2025.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $588.00. This amount represents: • $540.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord delivered an N12 Notice to the Tenant which indicated that her father, [name] [name] ([name]), intended to occupy the rental unit which is one of 3 units in a modest home. The rental unit is located at the rear of the building facing the parking lot.
An [name] was made by the LTB on May 15, 2025 terminating the tenancy based on the N12 and the Landlord’s L2 application. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on July 26, 2025.
The Tenant was suspicious of [name]’s intention to occupy the unit and believes that the N12 was served in retaliation for his commencement of a T2 application against the Landlord.

The Tenant’s suspicion was heightened because of a telephone call with [name], which he recorded (DOC 6967382), in which [name] advised the Tenant that he was Barbados working and that he was “a hobo” with no fixed address. He told the Tenant that he would be using the rental unit only as a place to collect mail and that he “moves around depending on where the women are.” He stated, “I live in Barbados most of the time.” He stated that he comes to Toronto occasionally and would be at the unit approximately 1 week out of 2 months every year. [name], the Tenant was concerned and suspicious of the Landlord’s good faith intention to have her father occupy the unit.
The Tenant saw [name] on July 26, 2025 when he handed over the keys. The Tenant attended the rental property on 2 occasions in 2025 and on 3 occasions in 2026 and did not see [name].

The Landlord testified that her father is a delusional narcissist. Her parents are divorced and she, her sisters and her mother support her father. The Landlord testified that her father has an undiagnosed mental illness. She testified that her father does not spend lengthy periods of time in Barbados and produced a record of his out of country travel from the federal government (DOC 8101175) which shows that [name] has only been out of the country for 3 times during the period January 1, 2023 to April 13, 2026 each time for the period of one week.

The Landlord testified that her father “works” as a volunteer on community land in Stoney Creek. 9. [name], a former tenant in the residential complex, testified that she moved out in May of 2026. She stated that during the period July 2025 to the date on which she moved out she saw [name] at the complex 3 or 4 times per week and saw his car, a tan SUV, in the parking lot daily. 10. [name], a current tenant and resident since 2019 also confirmed that [name] is living in the Tenant’s unit. 11. The Tenant did not cross-examine either [name] or [name] but observed that they are the reason he filed a T2 and that he believes they are biased against him. 12. Finally, [name] himself testified. He stated that he has been living in the unit since shortly after the keys were given to him by the Tenant. He stated that he did not immediately move in as the unit was in deplorable condition. He stated “you lived like a rat or a homeless person.” [name] speculated that the Tenant had not seen him when the Tenant attended the property because he has an erratic work schedule. 13. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 14. The Tenant did not prove that [name], the intended occupant of the rental unit, failed to move in. To the contrary, the Landlord established that her father does occupy and has done so since the Tenant’s departure. 15. The Tenant has failed to establish bad faith by the Landlord in delivering the N12 Notice.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed, and the LTB file is closed. June 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the hearing the Tenant confirmed that she had vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2024. The T5 Application was filed December 9, 2025. The T5 Application was brought on the basis that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under Section 48 in bad faith.

Section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') states: Former tenant’s application where notice given in bad faith 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to i n clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; (b) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to i n clause 49 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) or 49 (2) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; or (c) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not de molish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 57 (1). Time limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 57 (2).

In short, the Act imposes a one-year limitation period, which the Tenant has not complied with as this Application was filed more than one year after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant testified that the Application was filed outside of the limitation period because her initial Application had been dimissed by the Board on a preliminary basis.
As the Tenant’s Application is outside the limitation period imposed by the Act, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Stenning (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit approximately 20 years ago and vacated on December 12, 2024, because she received an N12 Notice of Termination form the Landlord.
The rental unit is the basement and main floor of a home. The Tenant testified that she believed that the Landlord’s mother had moved into the upper floor of the complex in October 2024.

The Tenant testified that as of April 30, 2026, the Landlord’s have shown they have moved into the basement portion of the rental unit. She testified that at the hearing before the Board for the N12 Notice of Termination the Landlord said they were moving in immediately and have now elected to renovate the rental unit themselves which is taking a very long time, and they therfre have not occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time.

The Tenant testified that on October 28, 2025, she saw that her son’s bedroom was untouched, and noticed that the bedroom window was still open.During the winter she observed that the driveway had not been plowed.

The Tenant testified that believes that the Landlord’s own photographs depict renovations beginning on the unit starting in February 2026, with the bathroom and noted that the unit could not be inhabitable until after the bathroom was finished. The Tenant testified that the Main floor is still under renovation and is stripped down to plaster with no working bathroom in the unit as of May 2, 2026.

The Landlord [name] testified that they purchased the complex because they were looking for a duplex so that her mother who is an elderly refugee could could live close to them, but in separate units as the she is a nurse who cares for her mother.

She testified that they entered the rental unit the same day the Tenant vacated and found the unit in an unlivable condition. The locks were broken, the door wide open, and snow was inside the rental unit. She testified that there was also furniture garbage, and food left behind and explained that it took the Landlord’s until April 2025 to completely clear the waste from the home.

She testified that her husband works full time and has been renovating the rental unit himself. She explained that he began renovations in April or May 2025 as soon as he could stay in the rental unit. He would go to the unit after work and preform renovations then sleep on her mothers couch, until he had the basement portion of the unit prepared for habitation. He husband would return to their home on the weekend.

She testified that she attempted to move into the rental unit herself to stay with her husband but was unable to remain there due to allergies. The Landlord relied on a medical note to this effect. She testified that she was able to move into the unit full time in Februray 226 after the basement renovation was completed.
While her husband has performed the majority of the renovations himself to conserve funds she testified that a new roof was installed by subcontractors in August 2025.
She testified that they had listed their home for sale, but it still has not sold as it is not a sellers market and remains listed.

The Landlord [name] testified that he began renovations a soon as the belongings left behind by the Tenant were removed form the rental unit. He testified that he began to live there during renovations in Spring 2025. He testified that he first began renovations on the main floor before realising it would take longer to complete and switching to the basement. He relied on documentation detailing trips to the dump, the removal of furniture, the removal of a toilet. He testified that he was able to move into the basement full time in October or November 2025.He confirmed that the upper main level is still under renovations, and the flooring needs to be replaced. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I am satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord served a notice of termination and she vacated as result. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that no person moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time, or that the Notice of Termination was served in bad faith.

I accept that there was a delay in the Landlord moving into the rental unit, with the Landlord [name] moving in in October or Novembre 2025 after work on the basement was completed and the Landlord [name] not occupying the rental unit until Februray 2026. I also accept that it was the Landlord’s testimony at the eviction hearing that they had planned to move in immediately.

However, I also accept that after the Landlord’s regained possession of the rental unit they discovered that it required extensive renovations, and was both damaged and filled with refuse which needed to be removed. I accept that this may have delayed and prolonged the renovations on the rental unit, which were further complicated by the Landlord experiencing difficulty selling their prior residence. I also accept that renovations were begun, and completed on the basement portion of the rental unit, based on the testimony and supporting documentation of both Landlords.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct was reasonable they have clearly performed extensive renovations on the rental unit, and I accept that the delay in taking possession was due to this ongoing renovations, I also note that the basement which forms part of the rental unit was occupied by the Landlord [name] by November 2025, less than a year after the Tenant vacated.

I also note that an extensive delay in occupying the rental unit is not necessarily unreasonable and must be considered in context, and note that a prior decisions relied on by the Landlord's Legal Representative GREENHALGH v MILNER, 2024 ONLTB 32577, the priding Members determined a 17 month delay to be reasonable as the unit was undergoing renovations.
In this case, I am satisfied that the renovations to the rental unit were reasonable and account for the lengthy delay in the Landlord taking possession of the rental unit.

Even If I were not satisfied that the Landlord had occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, The Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 notice was given in bad faith.

I accept that the Landlord’s purchased the complex as they wanted a property similar to a duplex with an attached but separate unit for the Landlord’s mother so that they could provide care to her. This is exactly what has now occurred, both [name] now reside in the rental unit, providing care to the Landlord’s mother. I also accept that this remained the Landlord’s genuine intention from the time the N12 notice was given to today.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the N12 was given in bad faith. Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] TRICA- MAVRODIN (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, I made inquires as to whether the Tenant arranged for an interpreter as it appeared he struggled with English. The Tenant explained that he thought his English would be good enough and believed his counsel would provide translation services if needed. The Tenant’s representative indicated that she would not provide translation services to the Tenant. At this point the Tenant’s representative requested an adjournment for the purposes of securing an interpreter.
For the reasons that follow, the request is denied.
Rule 21.8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure provides an adjudicator may adjourn a hearing where such is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held. The decision is discretionary.

Among the factors to be considered include: the reason for the adjournment, the issues in the application, prejudice that may result in granting or denying the adjournment, the history of the proceeding and any previous adjournments, and the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious manner of adjudicating the matter through a fair proceeding.
Furthermore, Rule 21.9 states that adjournments will only be considered in exceptional circumstances.

The Tenant filed his application on February 3, 2025. A review of the LTB’s records indicates that on February 18, 2025, the LTB advised the Tenant that should he require the services of an interpreter at the hearing, he would be expected to arrange for someone to interpret for him. The LTB also advised the Tenant that he could submit a Financial Eligibility form for consideration for interpretation services to be provided. No request was made by the Tenant.

On June 30, 2025, an Adjudicative Case Conference was held in this matter. A review of the LTB records confirm that the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative participated in the case conference without the service of an interpreter. There was no record of the Tenant or the Tenant’s representative indicating an interpreter would be required. The Tenant filed a request to amend his application on December 29, 2025. Again, no request for an interpreter was made at that time. I am of the view that the Tenant had sufficient time to arrange for an interpreter if such a need was required.

I believe an adjournment would be prejudicial to the Landlord whose physical health is exacerbated by stress. The Landlord testified that she has been enduring struggles with her mental health for the duration of this case, including being ill the morning of the hearing.

The Tenant and his representative participated in the proceeding on June 30, 2025 without the need for an interpreter and gave no indication that such a service would be required at that time. They have had sufficient time to make the necessary arrangements and I believe an adjournment would result in an unnecessary delay and be prejudicial to the Landlord. [name]

Neither the Tenant nor the Tenant’s representative were prepared to present evidence or make submissions in support of the application. Given this, I find the Tenant has failed to establish the allegations and the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name], 2026 ONLTB 47162 Date: 2026-06-18 In the matter of: 1, 10 [address] Woodstock ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on May 13, 2026. The Landlord and the Prospective Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Prospective Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the funds illegally collected to the Prospective Tenants.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The parties agree that the Prospective Tenants never signed an agreement to rent the rental unit. In the process of negotiating a rental agreement, the Landlord’s agents demanded that the Prospective Tenants provide a payment of $1,800.00 to “secure the unit”. The parties understood that this amount would be applied to the first month’s rent if a tenancy agreement were entered into. The Prospective Tenants testified that they paid this amount to the Landlord, and it was never returned.
The Prospective Tenants decided to not enter into a rental agreement with the Landlord due to concerns about the unit’s condition. They never signed a lease and never moved into the unit.

The Landlord is of the opinion that the Prospective Tenants cost him a month of rent by not entering into an agreement to rent the unit from him. I disagree. There was no rental agreement between the parties. The Prospective Tenants did not, in any way, preclude the Landlord from renting the unit to someone else.

The Landlord charged money to Prospective Tenants that he had no right to charge. A rent deposit is permitted under the Act where a rental agreement has been entered into, but that is not the case here. Therefore, the $1,800.00 collected constitutes an illegal charge prohibited by section 134 of the Act and the Landlord must return it to the Prospective Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenants is $1,853.00. This amount represents: • $1,800.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenants the full amount owing by June 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Prospective Tenants the full amount owing by June 29, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 30, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Prospective Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] inc. (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (LTB-T-089836-24) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-089836-24 and LTB-T-105625-24)
reasons: By way of background the Tenant filed LTB-T-089836-24 on October 31, 2024, alleging that the Landlord both collected or retained money illegally and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations. On December 28, 2024, the Tenant filed LTB-T- 105625-24 which also alleged that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations.

Each Application was scheduled for a separate adjudicative case conference. At the adjudicative case conference for LTB-T-089836-24 the Tenant advised the Board they would not be proceeding with the T1 portion of their application as it was filed in error.

After the Adjudicative Case conference for LTB-T-105625-24 was completed the presiding Member became aware that the issues raised in LTB-T-105625-24 were largely duplicitous with those raised in LTB-T-089836-24 and the matters were combined to be heard together. Particulars

At the hearing before me I raised that neither T6 Application appeared to contain adequate particulars, including dates and times. However, as the Landlord had provided disclosure, I queried the Landlord's Legal Representative as to whether the Landlord had understood what was being alleged on the two applications.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that while the Landlord had done their best to provide disclosure, it was very difficult to determine the allegations and the case to be met, and it was very difficult to respond without knowing particulars such as dates and times.

As an example the Tenants T6 in LTB-T-089836-24 states: “my washer dont work dyer dont work dish washer dont work stover not working no fire alarm microwave fridge dose not get cold dyer vent missing lights dont work for switch shower heads gross and not working will sinks clogged staff dont want to fix anything rent is not rignt”

The Tenant indicated that dates and times were not provided within the Application, but he had provided evidence which contained dates, times, and details. He indicated that he was not going to write a book on each Application.
The only disclosure the Board received from the Tenant was a 109-page document titled LTB Tenant Evidence which only contains screenshots of emails between the Tenant and the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that he had served additional evidence on both the Landlord's Legal Representative and the Board 7 days prior to this hearing by email.
The Landlord's Legal Representative confirmed that the only disclosure she had received from the Tenant was the 109-page LTB Tenant Evidence package.

I note that the Interim order for LTB-T-089836-24 directed the parties to provide disclosure by May 23, 2025. The interim order for LTB-T-105625-24 ordered the parties to provide disclosure at least 15 days prior to the next hearing date and reply evidence at least 7 days prior.
The Tenant testified that he was told that disclosure was not due until 7 days prior to the next hearing date.

Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“[name]) is clear that Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.
MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct…”

While [name] involved a notice of termination served to a Tenant, in my view the same principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications. In [name], the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…

I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s Application provides sufficient particulars, while it is clear that the Tenant has maintenance concerns with respect to several appliances for example, there are no clear dates and times provided and very few details. I also note that the Tenant has had the benefit of two adjudicative case conferences, one for each Application, where the importance of particulars are discussed with the parties. However, in spite of this the Applications do not provide particulars and no request to amend has been filed by the Tenant.

With respect to the Tenant’s assertion that adequate particulars are contained in their disclosure I note that as of the hearing date this disclosure had not been received by either the Board or the Landlord's Legal Representative. Additionally, the two interim orders issued provided deadlines for disclosure which were not met. While the Interim order for LTB-T-105625-24 allowed parties to provide reply disclosure within 7 days of the hearing date I note that missing particulars should not be considered reply evidence, and it would not be reasonable to expect the Landlord to wait until 7 days prior to the hearing to receive clear particulars from the Tenant.

Finally, I also note that disclosure is not the Application, and even if the Tenant’s evidence were properly disclosed and provided the missing particulars this would not save the Tenant’s Application. In my view the Application is distinct from disclosure and disclosure cannot cure a flawed Application, as particulars must be included on the Application itself and it is inherently prejudicial to the Landlord to expect them to comb through often voluminous disclosure to ascertain the allegations made or the case to be met.

Therefore, As the Tenant’s applications are vague and failed to provide dates and specifics for the allegations made, I find that there are insufficient reasons and details to allow the landlord to know the allegations made or the case to be met. The applications must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. June 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $528.00 which represent an illegal security deposit and the application filing fee.

The parties agree that the tenancy began in May 2025 and that the tenancy ended on November 1, 2025. The parties also agree that on or about May 4, 2025, the Landlord collected from the Tenants a security deposit in the amount of $1,800.00. The Landlord testified she collected the security deposit for damages or if the Tenants did not pay the rent, she would use the security deposit for missed rent.

When the Tenants moved out, the Landlord gave back $1,320.00 from that security deposit and retained $480.00. The Landlord testified that she retained $480.00 for a cleaning charge and damages. Analysis
Section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) reads as follows: 1. The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act state: (1)Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act provides for the following exceptions to the prohibition of key deposit charges in s. 134: 1. Payment for additional keys, remote entry devices or cards requested by the tenant, not greater than the direct costs. 2. Payment for replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards, not greater than the direct replacement costs, unless the replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards are required because the landlord, on the landlord’s initiative, changed the locks. 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

Based on the evidence before me, I find the Landlord illegally collected a security deposit from the Tenants in the amount of $1,800.00 at the beginning of the tenancy, then illegally retained $480.00 of that security deposit when the Tenants vacated on November 1, 2025. This is contrary to section 134 of the Act and does not fall within any of the exceptions contained in section 17 of the Ontario Regulations 516/06.
As such, the Landlord shall refund the Tenants the security deposit in the amount of $480.00.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $528.00. This amount represents: • $480.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $2,444.66 on or before July 3, 2026. T1 Application

The Tenant entered into evidence a copy of the lease signed by both parties on August 8, 2021. Page 4 of the lease outlines that the Tenant is required to pay 2/3’s of all utility bills, which includes gas, water and electricity on the condition that the downstairs tenant does not have more than 2 residents.

The Tenant testified that this arrangement was agreed to as the Tenant’s unit has more space than the basement unit, which pays 1/3 of the utility costs. The Tenant testified that in January 2024, the downstairs Tenant had more than 2 residents.

There was no evidence put before me on whether the Tenant tried to renegotiate his share of the utility bills and had requested a fairer split of the utility expenses and whether the downstairs Tenant agreed to pay more based on this change in circumstance. As such I am unable to make a determination on whether the Tenan overpaid his portion of the utilities. As such, this claim is dismissed. T6 application

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord’s failure to repair the light switch, hot water in the bathroom was a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations, their failure to address the maintenance issue, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Light switch

The Tenant testified that there was light switch at the top of the stairs and at the bottom of the stairs. The Tenant testified it was supposed to work in conjecture, however, if the bottom light switch was turned on, the upstairs switch could turn off the light but the light switch at the bottom could not be turned back on. This would force the Tenant to go back upstairs to turn off the light. On March 17, 2024, the Tenant email the landlord about the light switch and the Landlord responded they have known about this issue for the past 10 years.
The Tenant testified this caused unnecessary trips going up and down on the stairs and the Tenant was worried that this could potentially cause an electrical fire as there may be a shortage.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to maintain the light switch in a good state of repair. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the issue impacted the Tenant’s ability to fully use and enjoy the rental unit during their tenancy. I find the response of the Landlord to address the issue to be inadequate as he did not investigate or attempt to repair the light switch. I also find that there was some substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because of the inoperable light switch.
The Tenant is seeking a 20% rent abatement.

A rent abatement is a contractual remedy geared towards the premise that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent for a bundle of goods and services but is not receiving the full benefit of those goods or services, that they should be abated the difference.

In this case, the light switch issue was not overly disruptive to the Tenant’s Day to day activities. As such, I find that a 20% rent abatement is excessive. The Tenant was not left without light. I can also appreciate that turning on the light or off at the stairwell required extra steps and that would substantially interference with one’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony, I find that since the lack of working light switch was an occasional issue, the Tenant should only be entitled to a 1% rent abatement from March 17, 2024, until October 31, 2024, or $204.81. Intermittent loss of hot water

The Tenant testified that there were issues with the hot water in which it took about ten to fifteen minutes for the water to heat up and the water pressure was inadequate. The Tenant testified he told the Landlord on March 1, 2024, and the Landlord responded that there was nothing he could do about it because of the age of the building. The Tenant testified that the Landlord suggested that he work out a schedule with the Tenant downstairs.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to have adequate hot water at the rental unit. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the issue impacted the Tenant’s ability to fully use and enjoy the rental unit during their tenancy. I find the response of the Landlord to address the issue to be inadequate as he did not investigate or attempt to address the hot water issue. I also find that there was some substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because of the lack of hot water.
The issue was unresolved as of the date the tenancy ended on October 31, 2024.
The Tenant is seeking a 20% rent abatement.

In this case, the hot water issue was intermittent. Based on the Tenant’s testimony, it sounds as though the hot water tank was too small for the rental complex and as a result, the hot water reservoir would be exhausted faster than it could be replenished. However, this also shows that the Tenant only had reduced access to hot water.

I find that a 20% rent abatement is excessive. The Tenant was not left without hot water all of the time, just during the high-usage periods. The Tenant was not left without hot water, but limited use. I can also appreciate that not having access to hot water on a regular or predictable basis would substantially interference with one’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony, I find that since the lack of hot water was an occasional issue, the Tenant should only be entitled to a 10% rent abatement from March 1, 2024, until October 31, 2024, or $2,191.85. T2 Application

The Tenant testified that the Landlord on October 2, 2024, had a friend staying with him and the Landlord was banging on the door aggressively. He also testified that the Landlord on August 12, 2024, called the Tenant a real selfish piece of work after the Tenant did not allow entry for the purpose of repair work on the air conditioner.

He also testified that the Landlord on July 21, 2024, threatened to report him to the credit bureau and did file with Front Lobby a collection company to get the Tenant to pay money. The Tenant testified that he felt unsafe living there because as the Landlord would look to see if his car was in the driveway.

This application is brought pursuant to section 22 and 23 of the Act, which states: Section 22: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. Section 23: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 23.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I do not find that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Tenant also claimed on their application that the Landlord harassed them. I have also considered whether or not the Landlord harassed the Tenant but as explained below, do not find that the Landlord harassed the Tenant.

The Act uses language like ‘substantial’ meaning not every disagreement or trivial event will lead to a cause of action. In considering these events, I do not find that they rise to the level of substantial interference. I come to the same conclusion when looking at these events globally. I say this because there are three isolated incidents in a 4-month period. I also do not find that it amounts to harassment as the Tenant stated at the hearing. As this portion of the T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,444.66. This amount represents: • $2,396.66 rent abatement from the period of March 1, 2024, to October 31, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants allege that the Landlord did not apply the last month's rent deposit to the final rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants.
The tenancy commenced on November 4, 2025. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on November 18, 2025, and returned the keys to the Landlord on November 24, 2025.

The Tenants submitted that they intended to enter into a one-year tenancy agreement; however, the Landlord did not execute a written lease. The Landlord testified that although the parties initially discussed a one-year term, the Tenants subsequently advised that they required the rental unit only on a short-term basis, and the parties agreed to a two-month tenancy.
It is undisputed that on October 28, 2025, the Tenants paid the Landlord $4,200.00 representing first and last month's rent.

The Tenant, [name] (‘PS’) testified that shortly after taking possession of the rental unit, the Tenants experienced excessive noise. PS testified that he works at a hospital and requires adequate rest and that the noise prevented him from sleeping. PS stated that, as a result, the Tenants vacated the rental unit shortly after moving in.

The Landlord testified that the Tenants advised him that they needed to return to India to attend a family wedding and requested the return of their money. PS did not dispute that such discussions occurred but maintained that the reason for vacating the rental unit was the excessive noise.

PS further testified that the Landlord agreed to return $3,200.00 of the $4,200.00 paid by the Tenants, retaining $1,000.00 to compensate for the period during which the Tenants occupied the rental unit. The Landlord denied that any such agreement was reached. No documentary evidence or other independent evidence was submitted to corroborate the existence of an agreement to return any portion of the deposit.
PS also testified that former occupants of the rental unit began moving belongings into the unit on November 16, 2025, with the intention of reoccupying the premises, in which the Landlord denied.

The Landlord testified that he did not consent to an early termination of the tenancy. The Landlord further testified that he attempted to mitigate his losses by advertising the rental unit through Kijiji and Facebook Marketplace in December 2025, but that the unit remained vacant as of the date of the hearing. No documentary evidence was submitted to confirm that the rental unit was advertised.

I find that the parties provided conflicting evidence regarding several aspects of the tenancy, including the agreed term of the tenancy, the circumstances surrounding the Tenants’ departure, and whether the Landlord agreed to return any portion of the monies paid. Having heard the testimony of both parties, I find each witness to be equally credible. Where the evidence conflicts, I am unable to prefer the evidence of one party over that of the other, particularly as the evidence before me consists solely of oral testimony and no documentary evidence was submitted to substantiate either party’s position.

Although the parties disagree as to whether the tenancy was intended to be for a one-year term or a two-month term, I do not find that issue determinative. In either case, the Tenants were not entitled to unilaterally terminate the tenancy without providing notice in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), unless otherwise agreed to by the Landlord. The evidence establishes that the Tenants vacated the rental unit approximately two weeks after taking possession and did not provide notice in accordance with the Act.

As this is the Tenants’ application, the burden rests with the Tenants to establish their claim on a balance of probabilities. While I accept that the Tenants vacated the rental unit shortly after taking possession, the evidence before me is insufficient to establish that the Landlord agreed to return the last month's rent deposit or otherwise release the Tenants from their obligations under the oral tenancy agreement. In particular, there is no documentary evidence confirming an agreement to refund any portion of the monies paid by the Tenants, and I am unable to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that such an agreement was reached.

I further note that the Tenants paid first and last month's rent in the total amount of $4,200.00 and occupied the rental unit for a portion of November 2025. Even accepting the Tenants’ position that the tenancy was intended to be short-term, the monies retained by the Landlord are consistent with the rent payable for the period of occupancy and, at a minimum, the period for which the Tenants remained liable after vacating without proper notice. Given the Tenants’ obligation to provide notice in accordance with the Act, and the absence of sufficient evidence establishing an agreement to refund any portion of the monies paid, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord improperly retained the last month's rent deposit. Accordingly, this application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants their moving expenses and an amount for general compensation.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It’s undisputed the Landlords advertised the unit for sale during the one-year period during which the Landlord’s mother, [name] [name], occupied the residential unit. Therefore the requirements in subsection 57(5))(c) were triggered meaning the Landlord bears the burden of proving that the N12 Notice was not served in bad faith.
The parties agreed to a number of facts prior to the commencement of the hearing. AGREED FACTS

The N12 Notice given to the Tenants by the Landlords under section 48 of the Act provided a termination date of November 30, 2024. The Tenants did not vacate the unit pursuant to the Notice and a hearing of the Landlord’s application to terminate the tenancy (LTB-L-080687-24) was scheduled for February 27, 2025. The matter was resolved by consent eviction order dated March 6, 2025. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice and the resulting eviction order on February 28, 2025.
Mrs. [name]name] Sr. moved into the rental unit on April 4, 2025.

The parties agree that the rental property was listed for sale on MLS as of June 2025. An Agreement of Purchase and Sale for the property was executed on April 30, 2026 and the date for closing of the sale is June 22, 2026. The MLS history is agreed to by the parties and is set out in DOC 8120085 at page 29. OTHER EVIDENCE

There is no dispute that this property had been listed for sale prior to the current sale and prior to the N12 which resulted in the Tenants vacating the property. It is also not in dispute that the previous potential sale did not close. The Landlords’ position is that it failed to close because the purchasers were concerned that the Landlords were not able to give vacant possession.

It is also not in dispute that Mrs. [name] did not immediately occupy the property after the Tenants vacated on February 28, 2025. Receipts for new flooring and a bathroom faucet were provided. I do not need to refer to this evidence in any detail because I do not find that the period of time between the Tenants vacating and Mrs. [name] moving into the rental unit to be out of the ordinary and it does not factor in my decision.

There is a dispute between the parties as to whether the property was listed on Facebook prior to Mrs. [name]name] moving in. The Tenants provided a picture from Facebook at page 22 of their book of documents (DOC 8109104) which purports to show the property for sale. The Tenants maintain that the property was listed for sale on Facebook outside the dates on which the Landlords say it was listed and beyond what was agreed to as a listing date in paragraph 7. They say that this is evidence that the property was always only going to be sold and that in effect Mrs. [name] was only a place holder occupant until the property could be sold. BAD FAITH

The undisputed evidence establishes that the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 Notice served by the Landlord. Therefore, the only remaining element of the test in subsection 57(1)(a) which needs to be addressed is whether it was served in bad faith.

My decision regarding the question of bad faith and the Landlords’ intention in delivering the N12 were delivered at the hearing following which we proceeded to consider the monetary remedies claimed by the Tenants. My decision on bad faith is set out below.

In my view, it is immaterial as to whether the property was listed for sale on Facebook as it Tenants allege it was. The fact that the property was listed for sale at all in the one-year period during which the Landlords’ mother occupied the property is sufficient to result in the rebuttable presumption that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith in accordance with section 57(5)(c) of the Act.

The Landlords did not dispute the MLS listing nor do they dispute their intention to sell the property during the one year period following the date the Tenants vacated. The Landlords provided no evidence establishing that after the Tenants vacated some unexpected event arose that required the Landlord to sell the unit less that a year after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord gave evidence about a medical condition that required her to alter her working hours from a full-time self-employed esthetician to a part-time one, reducing her pay from somewhere around $8000.00 per month to somewhere closer to $5000.00. The Landlord was not prepared with evidence to substantiate these numbers and was guessing at her pre and post illness earnings. Irrespective of the change in her earnings, I do not find that this change in circumstances affected the Landlords’ decision to sell the rental unit. Clearly, the evidence shows that the plan all along was to sell the unit as evidenced by the previous unsuccessful sale. As a result, I find that they have not rebutted the statutory presumption that the served the N12 Notice in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenants have claimed a rent abatement because of stress and substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit during the period May 2024 to February 2025. Counsel for the Landlord argued that as this application was filed in December 2025 complaints originating prior to December 2024 could not be considered by the LTB. Counsel for the Tenants conceded that this is the case and so no claim originating prior to December 17, 2024 will be considered in my calculation of damages.

The Tenants admit that there were no real estate showings between December 17, 2024 and when they vacated the unit in February 2025 and therefore there concerns about the showings do not properly form part of their claim for damages.

The Tenants complained that the Landlords posted notices of intention to enter the property on the front door of the home and that this caused them anxiety and distress because they were concerned about how their neighbours would view them.
I find that the evidence of stress and substantial interference arising from the notices to be exaggerated and not warranting of an award to damages.

The Tenants were required to pay $1395.55 in moving expenses to move to the new home that they purchased “around the corner.” The Landlords’ representative did not dispute that this was a valid charge, and I find that the Tenants should be reimbursed for this.

The Tenants also seek an order for the rent differential in the amount of $6540.00. This claim is made pursuant to paragraph 57(3) 1 of the Act which provides that the LTB can award: 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one- year period after vacating the rental unit.

On the question of Rental Differential, the Tenants’ application carefully phrased this as a “Higher Rate.” After lengthy questioning by me, the Tenant testified that in fact because of being forced out of the rental unit they decided to purchase their own home. The purchase was assisted by family and the Tenants testified that the decision to purchase was made much earlier than they wanted to and was at the height of the market following the inflation of prices following [name] and prior to the current market correction. In other words, the Tenants say they purchased at the height of the market. They are currently paying $2800.00 in a combined mortgage and property tax payment versus the $2255.00 in rent that they were paying. Further, of this mortgage payment $5667.00 is being paid to principal. So, in effect, the difference in monthly outlay rent vs. mortgage payment is being paid in equity on the home to the benefit of the Tenants; accordingly, there will be no order of compensation for rent differential.

The Tenants have also claimed $$27,060.00 in general compensation under paragraph 57(3)1.1 of the Act. It was no doubt stressful for the Tenants to move form a home that they enjoyed during a period where they were expecting the birth of their second child. The Landlords were engaged in a series of property renovations and flips during this time which clearly included the sale of this rental property. Their finances seemed to be in disarray but that is not the responsibility of the Tenants and the stress resulting from the bad faith eviction is something for which the Tenants should be compensated. I have exercised my discretion to award the Tenants $5000.00 in General Compensation for the Landlords’ unlawful conduct in delivering an N12 Notice in bad faith.

In so far as the Tenants’ much more substantial claim for damages, while I do find that they suffered stress resulting from this situation, I find their claims to be exaggerated and that they do not warrant what I consider to be the excessive amount claimed in the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $6,443.55. This amount represents: • $1395.55 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 7, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 26, 2026 ____________________________
