issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant testified that he applied to rent the unit through Rentals.com. Following discussions between the parties, and although no written tenancy agreement was executed, they reached an agreement by telephone whereby the tenancy would commence on December 21, 2025. The parties further agreed that the tenancy would be for a fixed term from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026, at a monthly rent of $1,447.00, with the Tenant responsible for the cost of electricity.
On December 13, 2025, the Tenant remitted $2,894.00 to the Landlord by [name] e- Transfer, representing the equivalent of first and last month’s rent.

The Tenant testified that, due to uncertainty regarding his employment and layoffs occurring at his workplace, he became concerned about his financial stability and ultimately decided not to proceed with the tenancy. On December 16, 2025, prior to taking possession of the rental unit, the Tenant advised the Landlord that he wished to withdraw from the arrangement .

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence and pursuant to section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), I find that the parties entered into an oral tenancy agreement respecting the rental unit. Although no written agreement was signed, the essential terms of the tenancy, including the commencement date, fixed term, monthly rent, and responsibility for utilities, had been agreed upon by the parties. The Tenant's application for the unit through Rentals.com, the subsequent discussions between the parties, and the payment of first and last month's rent further support the conclusion that the parties intended to enter into a tenancy agreement.

While a tenancy agreement was formed, the monies paid remain governed by the Act and are not forfeited automatically upon repudiation. The legal framework requires compensation based on actual loss, not penalty.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing and given the absence of evidence of damages or mitigation, the Landlord has not met the burden required to retain the funds. As such, I find the Tenant is entitled to a return of the deposit paid to the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,942.00. This amount represents: • $2,894.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name], [name], and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $7404.00, the full amount of compensation claimed in the application.

The Landlord gave an N12 for own use in bad faith. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
The Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 Notice in August of 2024 which claimed that the Landlords required the rental use for use by family members. That N12 did not result in an L2 being filed.

A further N12 Notice was served in November 2024 with Affidavits attached indicating that the Landlord’s parents and wife intended to occupy the rental unit (DOC 7014219). A hearing of the L2 application was scheduled to take place on May 21, 2025. On that date a mediated agreement was reached between the parties with an extended termination date of July 31, 2025.

The Tenant Dion Landon testified on behalf of all of the Tenants. He testified that he waited until December of 2025 to determine if the Landlords had moved into the rental unit. He looked through the windows and observed that there was no furniture. He drove by the home on numerous occasions to see the driveway piled high with snow. He spoke to the neighbour, [name], who advised him that no one lived at the home. He provided an email from [name] confirming this (DOC 8120572). I did not need to place any reliance on [name] email although I did not disbelieve it.

The Tenant believes that the N12 Notice was delivered in retaliation for his refusing to agree to pay the Landlord several above guideline rent increases in the period March 2022 to 2024. DOC 7014198 is a Notice of Rent increase seeing a $50.00 rent increase on a base rent of $2200.00 per month which the Tenant refused to pay. A second attempt to illegally increase the rent by $70.00 in June 2022 (DOC 7014195) was also rebuffed by the Tenant who then agreed to an increase of $27.00 per month. In 2023 a proper Notice of Rent Increase raised the rent to $2283.00. The Tenants did not receive a rent increase notice in 2024; rather, they received an N12 for each member of their household including their minor children.
The Tenant presented documentary evidence to show that the property was not being maintained after they vacated (DOC’s 8108851, 58, 62, 71 and 79).

The Tenant also produced photographs (DOC 8108889 and 8112071) of Notices from the City of Oshawa notifying the Landlord that the grass was too high and that the City would cut the grass and charge back the Landlord for this service if the grass was not attended to by June 5, 2025. On June 7 the grass was still not cut.
The Landlord did not cross examine the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that his father did not move into the house because he died in April 2025, a fact that was not revealed to the Tenants at the mediation. The Landlord testified that his mother did not move in because she was so overwrought by her husband’s death and then she needed knee surgery and could not manage the stairs of the home.

In the Landlords’ Book of Documents (DOC 8111640) at page 2 the Landlord produced proof of his wife’s change of address to the rental unit. On page 3 he showed a picture of a package with the rental unit address that had been delivered by UPS. He showed several very low Enbridge bills at pages 7 and 11 and evidence of snow shovelling at page 4. Finally, he showed a Certificate of Insurance at DOC 8112134 that purports to show that the unit is insured as being owner occupied.

The Landlord testified that he moved into the unit in August of 2025 and that the Tenants’ failure to see him could be attributed to his work schedule and a trip to India to observe the one year anniversary of his father’s death.

In response to questions by me, the Landlord admitted that his wife does not live in the rental unit rather she resides in the United States. Further questions by me caused the Landlord to show me where he sleeps as proof that he resides in the unit. The Landlord showed me an unmade single bed in the basement with a knapsack beside it.

I asked to see the upstairs of the home. The Landlord showed me the inside of the refrigerator which did not contain one ounce of food or liquid. The living room is devoid of any furnishings and the Landlord admitted there is no furniture on the upper floor either.

On the basis of the extensive evidence before me, some from the Tenant and some from the Landlord, I have reached the conclusion that neither the Landlord nor any of his family members have genuinely resided in the rental unit since the Tenants vacated on July 31, 2025..

Further, the Landlord has not provided me with any convincing evidence that unforeseen events arose after the Tenants vacated that prevented the Landlord from using the rental unit for residential occupation for at lease one year. In fact, the Landlord took the opposite approach and attempted to persuade me that he does live here which I have found to be untrue. 18. .Accordingly, I find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of an N12 Notice that was given in bad faith and the Landlord or his family members did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Remedies 19. The Tenants paid $2283 per month at the rental unit which is $617.00 less than the $2900.00 they are currently paying. 20. The evidence showed that on August 1, 2025, the Tenants moved into their current residence which is a 3 bedroom home. Despite having to pay more for the current rental unit, the Tenants 2 boys are required to share a bedroom because there are less bedrooms in the new rental. 21. The Tenant also described his stress and desperation in looking for a new rental because the couple has a low income and many potential landlords were reluctant to rent to them. 22. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenant $7,404.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants haves incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. 23. The Tenants did not claim any additional remedies.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $7,452.00. This amount represents: • $7,404.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 28, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 28, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. June 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $400.00 to the Tenant.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not fully return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant’s Agent, [name], testified that [name] passed away on March 17, 2025. As such, the application has been amended to reflect the Tenant as The Estate of [name], pursuant to [name]) of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. I was satisfied that the Agents who appeared on behalf of the estate has authority to do so. Evidence and Analysis

SL testified that the tenancy agreement at issue was between the Landlord and [name]. SL testified that the tenancy began on January 1, 2021. [name] stated the rent was $900.00 per month and that [name] paid the Landlord the first month rent and last month rent deposit of $1,800.00 prior to moving in. 5. [name] stated that on March 21, 2025, upon learning of the passing of the Tenant, the Landlord informed the Tenant’s Agent that they were terminating the tenancy. [name] stated that the parties consented to this earlier termination date. 6. SL testified that the property and belongings of the Tenant were removed from the unit on March 31, 2025. This also served as the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit. 7. SL further testified that when they spoke to the Landlord on March 23, 2025, while cleaning the rental unit, that she paid a last month rent deposit when the lease began. [name] then stated this amount was never used and should be applied to March 2025. The Landlord then returned $500.00 to SL. [name] further stated that the Landlord informed them when they returned the keys the remaining $400.00 will be refunded. 8. [name] testified that on March 31, 2025, she returned the keys to the Landlord; however, upon return of the keys, the Landlord did not refund the remaining $400.00 of the last month rent deposit. 9. The Tenant has filed a T1 application pursuant to section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The T1 is an application for an order that the Landlord illegally collected or retained money. 10. Section 105(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) states: The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit in accordance with section 106. 11. Section 106(2) of the Act states: The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. 12. Based on the uncontested testimony and evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a last month rent deposit equal to one month rent in the amount of $900.00 and did not apply this to the last month of the tenancy. This is prohibited by the Act. 13. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $400.00. This amount represents: • The remainder of the $900.00 for the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant’s Estate has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied in a T5 application seeking an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $8,871.00. The Landlords Gave N12 for Own Use in Bad Faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act for their own use; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
For the reasons explained below, the Tenants proved each of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities.

There was no dispute between the parties that the Landlords communicated by phone conversation to the Tenants during the summer of 2025 that they intended to move into the rental unit. The Tenants advised they wanted to stay and requested a formal N12 be served. The first N12 notice was provided around July 4, 2025 but was incomplete and not signed.

There was no dispute a signed version of the N12 Notice was served around August 8, 2025, which had checkmarks on the first page indicating the Landlord and spouse wanted to move into the rental unit themselves.

Both sides confirmed the tenancy had started approximately in September, 2020. The Tenants testified they had lived at the rental unit (2 bedroom apartment) for years and would have liked to keep staying while they saved for a downpayment to eventually buy a house. The Tenants testified they would not have moved out in the Fall of 2025 for any other reason other than their belief that the Landlords needed to move into the apartment themselves to downsize. The Landlords did not challenge the Tenants’ submission that the only reason they moved out was because of the N12 Notice.
The Tenants testified that they moved out of the rental unit on October 31, 2025 because they believed in good faith that the Landlords would move in.

There was no dispute that the Landlords never moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. As of the hearing date, the Landlords admitted they continued to live at their Lawrence Avenue house and they had remained living there the whole time since serving the Tenants with the N12 Notice.

It was undisputed that the Landlords listed the rental unit for sale within approximately 2 months after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord [name] is a licensed real estate broker so he conducted all the listings for both the [name] house and the rental unit himself. The Landlords did not recall the exact listing date, but they admitted around December 2025 the rental unit was listed for sale, and the listing expired after approximately 60 days without much interest (they only conducted 1 or 2 showings). They received not offers on the rental unit listing. After the sale listing expired, the Landlords admitted to listing the rental unit for rent, which was successful because a new tenant was scheduled to start on May 1, 2026.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this T5 application, the burden of proof typically falls on the Tenants to establish that the N12 Notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was listed for sale within a couple months after the Tenants vacated; and that it was then listed for rent a couple months after the failed sale listing; and that it was ultimately re-rented – all creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlords served the N12 Notice in bad faith. In other words, given the facts of this case, the burden shifts from the Tenants (to prove bad faith), and the burden falls on the Landlords to establish that they served the N12 Notice in good faith. Presumption of Bad Faith Not Rebutted

Subsection 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following grounds: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale… (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

The rebuttable presumption of bad faith is engaged in this application because there was no dispute (and the Landlords admitted) that they engaged in 3 of the behaviours referenced in subsection 57(5) of the Act – they listed the rental unit for sale; they listed the rental unit for rent; and they entered a different tenancy agreement with a new tenant – all within 1 year of the Tenants vacating the rental unit.
The Landlords testified that they had experienced a change in their circumstances, which explained why they could not move into the rental unit after the Tenants vacated.

The Landlords testified that at the time they served the Tenants with the N12 Notice, they were living at their 3 bedroom house on [name] (the ‘[name] house’) approximately 2 kms away from the rental unit. The Landlords testified their intention was always to sell the [name] house and downsize by moving into the rental unit apartment, which was why they had served the N12 Notice on the Tenants.

The Landlords testified they listed their [name] house for sale approximately September 26, 2025 for $899,000.00 but the market was so bad the listing expired after approximately 60 days. This listing was done after the N12 was served but before the Tenants vacated.

When questioned why the Landlords had not chosen to try and rent out the [name] house instead when it failed to sell, the Landlords testified that it would not have been feasible because the house was too old and required many touch-ups that would cost significant expense to bring it up to a state that was rentable.

The Landlords testified that to mitigate their losses after their [name] house did not sell, they decided to try to sell the rental unit instead. They listed it for sale within a few months of the Tenants vacating. When there were weak showings and no offers, the Landlords changed their strategy from trying to sell the [name] house to try to rent out the rental unit. That strategy was successful as evidenced by the new tenancy which was about to start a couple days after the hearing.

The Landlords testified that it was always their good faith intention to move into the rental unit themselves and to downsize. They admitted they did not previously know that a N12 could be given for a purchaser’s own use, or that a rental unit could be listed for sale and bought while remaining tenanted. If they had known this, they may have tried another course rather than asking the Tenants to move out. The Landlords also testified they recently learned about section 57 and the statutory requirements in the Act and the things that would cause a reverse onus and presumption of bad faith if a landlord did any of the items listed in subsection 57(5) within 1 year of the vacate date.

The Landlords testified they were not trying to do anything illegal or force the Tenants out of the rental lease on purpose. This may be true, but ignorance of the law is not a defence. The Landlords should have educated themselves on the business they are in, including the requirements of the Act.

The Landlords submitted that they genuinely tried to sell their [name] house but the market was so bad that they had to mitigate their loss by remaining in their [name] house while trying to sell or re-list the rental unit instead.

Based on the evidence before me and in light of the reverse onus that applies, I find that the Landlords failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish that they did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated due to a material change in circumstance. The Landlords alleged financial hardship and that they had to mitigate their losses; however, they provided no evidence how they were suffering any losses or experiencing any financial hardship after serving the N12 Notice.

The Landlords’ plan to eventually downsize by selling their [name] house and move into the rental unit apartment, existed before they served the N12 Notice, before the Tenants vacated, and continued after the Tenants vacated. Being a real estate agent, I would have expected the Landlord [name] to have more knowledge about the market conditions than a lay person.
The Landlords presented no evidence of how they were suffering any financial hardship. They admittedly let the [name] house listing expire without any downward price adjustments.
The Landlords presented no evidence how moving into the vacated rental unit would have caused financial hardship or that there was any change of circumstance preventing them from doing so.

The Landlords characterized the failure of the [name] house to sell at the price they wanted in the listing, as a material change in circumstance. However, I disagree with their characterization and find instead that their circumstances had not changed. It seems the Landlords were only willing to fulfil their downsize move to the rental unit, contingent on the sale of their [name] house for an appropriately acceptable price. But the failure to generate any acceptable offers existed before they served the N12 Notice and remained the same situation after the Tenants vacated. I find that the lack of offers at a price acceptable to the Landlords, was not a change in circumstance.

It may have been a different circumstance if the Landlords presented evidence that an agreement of purchase and sale for the [name] house had been signed, but that the closing had fallen through, causing them to have to take legal actions etc. A situation such as that may have proven some financial hardship and change in circumstance occurred for the Landlords.

Although the Landlords may have intended to downsize and move into the rental unit someday, they provided no evidence that any financial hardship or change in circumstance occurred after the Tenants vacated.

Further, the reverse onus would have applied even if only 1 of the elements listed in section 57(5) had been proven; however, I note in this case 3 elements admittedly occurred during the 1 year period after the Tenants vacated.
Since the Landlords failed to to rebut the presumption of bad faith, I find that the Tenants proved on a balance probabilities that the Landlords gave a notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenants sought remedies of an administrative fine (amount to be determined by the Board) and general compensation of $35,292.00 (calculated as 12 months of monthly rent which was $2,941.00 in October, 2025 when they vacated).

I do not find this an appropriate situation to impose any administrative fine on the Landlords. The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 16 discusses that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act. I believe the remedies awarded in this application are enough to deter the Landlords from engaging in bad faith conduct in the future, and to ensure they educate themselves on the obligations and responsibilities of landlords imposed by the Act and any applicable regulations.

The Tenants testified that they decided to buy a home in Markham because it was impossible to stay in Toronto (either to rent or buy) since the prices were extremely high in Toronto. The Tenants received help from family loans to buy their home. The Tenants were hoping to stay longer in the rental unit but were forced to buy a home far from Toronto faster than they had planned. [name]’s one-way commute to work used to be 25mins by TTC but now he drives 15 mins to the GO station, then takes a 40min transit ride. Their 3 children (ages 7, 4, 3) had to adjust to a move to another city. The whole family had loved Toronto and had intended to stay closer to Toronto if they had not been evicted in bad faith.

I acknowledge that the Tenants have faced some stress and hardship due to the unexpected move; however, the requested remedy for general compensation is not supported by evidence. The Tenants could have chosen to challenge the N12 Notice and argued their desire to stay in the rental unit at a L2 hearing. Instead, the Tenants chose to move out, to another city. Instead of continuing renting, the Tenants chose to accelerate their home-buying plans with the help of using all their savings and receiving loans from family.

The Tenants did not provide any evidence of what any rent differential might have been if they remained renting in Toronto, or what their increased expenses were for fulfilling their home-buying dreams (albeit sooner than planned).

I find it fair in the circumstances to award the Tenants 3 months of rent for general compensation. This amount is to acknowledge that the family experienced upheaval, increased commute, and similar stresses due to the bad faith eviction. The Tenants’ rent at the time of vacate was $2,941.00, so the total general compensation awarded is $8,823.00.
The Tenants also paid $48.00 to file the application and are entitled to be reimbursed for this cost.
ordered: 38. The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $8,871.00. This amount represents: • $8,823.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the filing fee. 39. The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026 (standard 11 days from the issuance date of this order). 40. If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 41. The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal Entry and [name]
It is the Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord entered illegally into the rental unit with less than 24 hours’ notice on September 14, 2025 and October 2, 2025.

The Tenants further allege that the Landlord served them an N5 and N7 notice and this substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and forced them to vacate the unit on November 30, 2025. September 14, 2025 entry

The Landlord testified and provided email proof that he was contacted by the Tenants on September 14, 2025 by text message concerning a leak under the sink in the powder room. The Tenants indicated that the leak was creating mold and that they had turned off the water valve.

The Landlord responded to Tenant [name] on September 15, 2025 that he booked a plumber to come look at the sink that evening at 6:00 p.m. and asked permission. He did not receive a response. Ms. [name]name] testified in redirect they were out that evening. The relations between the Tenants and the Landlord are strained, and the Landlord refuses to communicate with [name]. I understand this extends from an altercation in July 2025 between [name] and the Landlord when the police were called.

On September 16, 2025, the Landlord sent another email to Ms. [name]name] to inquire whether he should cancel the plumber’s visit because he had not received a response from the Tenants as to whether the visit was possible. On September 16, 2025 at 10:18 AM, the Landlord wrote that he canceled the plumber’s visit and would come by himself and inspect the problem between 5:00 PM and 7:00 PM. He signed his email, “Si ce temps ne vous convient pas, svp m’en aviser au moins une heure à l’avance. » (If this time is not convenient, please let me know at least an hour in advance) DOC-7943519 Exhibit 1.

The Landlord did not receive a reply, so he attended at the rental unit on September 16, 2025 between 5:00 PM and 7:00 PM. He testified he did not force the door or yell at anyone, and the Tenants let him in.

Section 25 states that a Landlord can only enter a rental unit in accordance with s. 26 or 27. Section 26(1)(b) further states, “A landlord may enter a rental unit ant any time without written notice, if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.”
I therefore find that the Tenants consented to the entry on September 16, 2025, and even if they had not, the written notice that the Landlord provided the day before was sufficient.
Therefore, there was no illegal entry on September 14, 2025. October 2, 2025 entry
The Tenants also allege that the Landlord made an illegal entry without 24 hours’ notice on October 2, 2025 to show the rental unit to prospective tenants.

The Landlord testified that he sent an email on September 21, 2025 at 10:17 a.m., and called Ms. [name]name] regarding various issues in her rental unit. She replied on September 22, 2025 at 10:17 p.m. The Landlord sent an email on September 23, 2025 that he would call her that evening.

The Landlord then testified that he had a conversation between September 24, 2025 and October 1, 2025 with Tenant [name] to fix the toilet in the powder room. He could not remember the exact date and it is not corroborated with email.
On October 1, 2025 at 12:27 p.m., he provided notice of entry on October 2, 2025 between 5:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. (DOC-7943659 Exhibit 2)

I find that the notice of entry was given with more than 24 hours’ written notice on October 1, 2025, and I accept the Landlord’s evidence that it was to fix the toilet in the powder room as this is explained in unaltered emails provided by the Landlord. I find the Tenants’ recollection of the issue to be inaccurate.
I therefore find that no illegal entry occurred on October 2, 2025. Substantial Interference Analysis:

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

The Divisional Court in Hassan v. Niagara Housing Authority [2000] O.J. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”) affirmed that a landlord has a positive obligation to take reasonably necessary actions to ensure that all tenants can reasonably enjoy the rental premises.

I find that in the case of September 14-16, 2025 and October 2, 2025, the Landlord was fulfilling his obligation to investigate a leak under the sink and of the toilet in the Tenants’ powder room. He sent emails and made phone calls and took reasonable steps to investigate the complaint about the leaks, so he cannot be said to be substantially interfering with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because he was responding to their request. I further find that on both occasions he gave 24 hours notice of entry and on September 16, 2026, the Tenants consented to his entry at the time he entered. Notice N5 and N7
The Tenants allege that the Landlord’s action to serve two eviction notices, an N5 and N7, that substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment.
It is not substantial interference to enforce one’s legal rights.
Just as the Tenants are able to enforce their rights under the Act, so is the Landlord, and he did so by bringing eviction notices to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenants.
I find that this does not amount to substantial interference, and to find otherwise would be counter to, or even undermine, the purpose of the Act. Harassment Analysis
The Tenants allege that the conduct of the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
Section 23 of the Act prohibits the Landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening or interfering with the Tenants.

“Harassment” is not defined by the Act, but is interpreted from the Ontario Human Rights Code, RSO 1990, [name] defines “harassment” as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”

In this case, I find no such conduct occurred. As mentioned above, the Landlord was contacted by the Tenants regarding a leak in their powder room. He emailed, telephoned and attended at their apartment with ample notice in order to fix the leak.
I further find that serving an N5 and N7 notice does not amount to harassing conduct because it is the enforcement of a legal right under the Act.
Therefore, I do not find that the Tenants have proven the allegations on a balance of probability that the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with them.
Having failed to prove the allegations of substantial interference and harassment, I find the application should be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. June 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Last Month’s Rent Deposit Interest

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlords have failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's deposit as required by section 106(6) of the Act. There is no dispute the Landlord has never paid interest to the Tenant. The Landlord acknowledged the Tenant paid $1,500.00 on September 1, 2017, as the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant claims the Landlord held a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,500.00 from September 17, 2017, to February 4, 2025. The Tenant testified that they vacated pursuant to N12 notice of termination with a termination date of October 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that they vacated on December 31, 2024. The Landlord filed the application with the board, and a hearing was held on February 4, 2025. The Tenant testified that at the hearing, there was an agreement to return the last month rent deposit back and as such the Landlord returned the last month rent deposit on the same day.
The Landlord claims that the Tenant used their last month rent deposit in May 2024 as they did not pay May’s rent. Therefore, the Landlord no longer held a last month rent deposit as of May 2024.
The parties do not dispute the Tenant vacated as of December 31, 2024.

With respect to the rent deposit, section 106 of the Act provides: (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. … (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

It is clear that the only deposit a landlord may collect is an amount equal to one month’s rent, and this deposit can only be applied to the rent owing for the last month of the tenancy. I find as of May 2024; the tenancy was on -going. Section 106(10) preclude a landlord from using a rent deposit for other purposes, including to satisfy any rent arrears while the tenancy is ongoing. Accordingly, it was improper for the Landlord to apply the Tenant’s rent deposit to the rent owing for May 2024.

The Landlord ultimately submitted that the last month rent was taken back by the Landlord because the Tenant was not moving out. I find it more likely that the Landlord retuned the Last month deposit back on February 4, 2025.
Section 29(2) of the Act states no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant is seeking interest from the date the deposit was allegedly collected in 2017 which is outside the one-year limitation period. Since the Tenants’ application was filed on December 29, 2025, the Board only has jurisdiction to order interest owing within the one year from the making of the application.
As such, interest is calculated for the period from December 29, 2024, to February 4, 2025, the date the Tenant received the Last month rent deposit back, in the amount of $3.91.

Section 207 (4) states the Board shall not make an order for the payment of an amount of money if the amount is less than the prescribed amount. [name]. 516/06, s. 58. States The amount prescribed for the purpose of subsection 207 (4) of the Act is five dollars.
Since the amount to be paid by the Landlord is under five dollars, I do not have jurisdiction to make an order for the payment. As such, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. June 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord retained monies paid by the Tenant for water utilities that were the Landlord’s responsibility under the tenancy agreement. The Tenant also claims that the Landlord failed to return the key deposit after the keys were returned at the end of the tenancy.
The tenancy commenced on October 26, 2021, and terminated on December 15, 2025, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant seeks reimbursement of water charges paid throughout the tenancy on the basis that such charges were the responsibility of the Landlord. The Tenant also seeks the return of the key deposit, which the Tenant alleges was not refunded upon the return of the keys to the Landlord at the end of the tenancy. Utility charges

Although the application indicates that the Landlord collected illegal rent, the details and particulars provided by the Tenant make it clear that the claim relates to water charges paid by the Tenant that were the responsibility of the Landlord under the tenancy agreement. In the circumstances, I find it appropriate to amend the application to reflect a claim for reimbursement of water charges paid by the Tenant on the Landlord’s behalf. I find that this amendment does not prejudice the Landlord, as the application clearly identifies both the nature of the claim and the remedy sought, thereby providing the Landlord with adequate notice of the allegations and an opportunity to respond.
The tenancy agreement provides that the Landlord is responsible for the payment of water charges.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord was responsible for the payment of water charges. However, the Tenant’s claim for reimbursement of water charges paid throughout the tenancy is subject to the limitation period prescribed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

Subsection 135(1) and (4) of the Act states: (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.; and (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
Pursuant to subsection (4) of the Act, the Tenant’s claim is limited to remedies arising on or after December 31, 2024, as the application was filed on December 31, 2025.
The Tenant testified that the utility account with Provident Energy was in the Tenant’s name and that the utility bills included charges for both electricity and water.
The Tenant testified that the utility bills were paid through automatic withdrawals from the [name] bank account and that those payments included the water charges.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord resided in China and that the Tenant communicated with the Landlord’s agent in Toronto regarding matters relating to the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that near the end of the tenancy, he realized that he had been paying the water charges since the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant advised the Landlord of the issue and provided a summary of the water charges paid in order to seek reimbursement. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s subsequent requests for reimbursement.

The Tenant submitted copies of the Provident Energy utility bills for the period from January 1, 2025, to December 15, 2025. Based on those bills, the water charges paid by the Tenant during that period totalled $1,453.73.

Based on the tenancy agreement, which provides that the Landlord is responsible for the payment of water charges, the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, and the documentary evidence consisting of the utility bills and payment records, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant paid water charges that were the responsibility of the Landlord. I therefore find that the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the water charges incurred during the period that falls within the limitation period prescribed by the Act, in the amount of $1,453.73. Key deposit

Although the Tenant’s application identifies a claim for interest on the last month's rent deposit, it is clear from the particulars provided in the application that the Tenant was seeking the return of a key deposit that the Tenant alleges was improperly retained by the Landlord.

As the application does not, in substance, seek interest on a last month's rent deposit, I find it appropriate to amend the application to reflect the Tenant’s claim for the return of the key deposit. I find that no prejudice results to the Landlord from this amendment, as the Tenant clearly described both the issue and the remedy sought in the application. As such, the Landlord had adequate notice of the claim and a fair opportunity to respond to and defend against the allegations.
The tenancy agreement required the Tenant to provide a key deposit in the amount of $250.00 at the commencement of the tenancy.
The Tenant submitted a receipt dated October 26, 2021, confirming payment of a key deposit in the amount of $250.00.

The Tenant testified that, despite making multiple attempts to obtain instructions from the Landlord regarding the return of the keys at the end of the tenancy, he received only a message from an individual claiming to act on behalf of the Landlord directing him to leave the keys in a lockbox. The Tenant testified that he was not comfortable relying on instructions from an unknown individual and requested confirmation directly from the Landlord. The Tenant testified that no such confirmation was received.

The Tenant further testified that, after making additional unsuccessful attempts to obtain instructions, he advised the Landlord that he would return the keys by [name] to the address at which the Landlord regularly received mail. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence confirming that the keys were mailed by [name] on December 31, 2025 and that the Landlord was notified by email on January 1, 2026, that the keys had been sent. The evidence further establishes that the package was delivered to the community mailbox on January 6, 2026, at 10:48 a.m.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant paid a key deposit in the amount of $250.00 and subsequently returned the keys to the Landlord. I find that the Tenant took reasonable steps to obtain clear instructions regarding the return of the keys and, when such instructions were not forthcoming, acted reasonably by returning the keys by [name] to the address at which the Landlord regularly received mail. I therefore find that the keys were returned to the Landlord on January 6, 2026, and that the Landlord is not entitled to retain the key deposit. Accordingly, the Tenant is entitled to the return of the key deposit in the amount of $250.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,751.73. This amount represents: • $1,535.34 for reimbursement of water charges paid by the Tenant. • $250.00 for the return of the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The tenancy commenced on December 1, 2021 for a twelve-month fixed term. The Tenant paid a monthly base rent of $1,950.00 and $50.00 a month for internet service.

In November 2022, the Landlord’s Agent advised the Tenant that their base rent will increase by $300.00 a month starting December 1, 2022. The Landlord did not give the Tenant a Notice of Rent Increase (‘NORI’) and instead required the Tenant to enter into a new lease agreement for another fixed length of time ending on November 30, 2023.
When the Tenant questioned the amount of the rent increase, the Landlord explained that the rental unit was exempt from the rules regarding rent.

The Tenant paid the Landlord $2,300.00 in base rent from December 1, 2022 to March 31, 2024. On April 1, 2024, the Landlord increased the base rent to $2,357.50 a month without a NORI and instead required the Tenant to sign a new lease. Analysis:

A tenancy continues month-to-month under the same terms following the expiry of a fixed- term unless the tenancy is terminated in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). What this means is that the Tenant was not required to enter into a new tenancy agreement at the conclusion of the fixed term on November 30, 2022.

Section 116 of the Act reads as follows: Notice of rent increase required 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the rent charged is increased in accordance with an order under section 126. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (2). Contents of notice (3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (3). Increase void without notice (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (4).

The Landlord did not give the Tenant written notice in accordance with section 116 of the Act. As such, the increase in rent is void pursuant to subsection 116(4). What this means is that the rent increase on December 1, 2022 is void and the lawful monthly rent is $2,000.00 ($1,950.00 base rent and $50.00 internet). Any amount of rent the Landlord collected and retained above $2,000.00 is illegal and must be returned to the Tenant.

The Tenant paid the Landlord $2,300.00 a month from December 1, 2022 to March 31, 2024, or 16 months. This represents $300.00 more a month than the Landlord was legally entitled to collect. The Landlord shall therefore be ordered to pay the Tenant $4,800.00 ($300.00/month x 16 months).

The increase on April 1, 2024 is also void as it was based on the illegal rent increase from December 1, 2022. The Tenant paid the Landlord $2,375.57, which was $375.57 more a month than the Landlord was legally entitled to collect. The Tenant paid the illegal increase from April 1, 2024 to April 1, 2026, or 25 months. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $9,389.25 ($375.57 x 25).

With each monthly rental increase, the Landlord demanded payment from the Tenant to top the last month rent deposit. The last month rent deposit was $2,000.00 before the illegal monthly rent was increased to $2,375.57. The Landlord will be required to return to the Tenant $375.57 of excess last month’s rent deposit collected.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant under the T1 application is $14,564.82 T2 Application
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord’s Agent substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed, threatened and interfered with them.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord’s Agent was very aggressive with respect to the illegal rent increase and threatened to throw them out of the unit immediately if they did not comply with the increase.

The Landlord’s Agent denied the Tenant’s allegations. 15. [name] (‘JDP’) appeared as a witness for the Tenant and testified that they were present during many telephone conversations between the Tenant and the Landlord’s Agent. [name] stated that he overheard the Landlord’s Agent speak to the Tenant in a disrespect and threatening manner. JDP described the Landlord’s Agent as being a bully and yelling at the Tenant. JDP described one phone call in late November 2022 when the Landlord’s Agent called to discuss a rent increase. JDP recalled having to intervene to remind the Landlord’s Agent to speak to the Tenant in a respectful manner. JDP indicated that the Landlord’s Agent them cursed at him and demanded that the Tenant move out immediately. 16. I prefer the Tenant’s evidence about the conversations with the Landlord’s Agent because it was corroborated by the oral testimony of their witness who described how the Landlord’s Agent used aggressive language and threats of eviction. The Tenant’s witness testified that the Tenant was emotionally distraught following the interactions. 17. While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, it is generally held that “harassment” is a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome. I find that a reasonable person would have known or ought to have known that yelling and threatening to kick someone out of their home would be unwelcome. 18. Landlords are entitled to enforce their rights by giving tenants proper notices when warranted and by filing applications at the Board. Landlords are not entitled to act in an abusive and aggressive manner towards their tenants. The Landlord Agent’s threats to the Tenant with respect to the rent increase were not only contrary to the Act, but do not fall within the realm of proper communications in a tenancy. Accordingly, I am satisfied the Landlord breached section 23 of the Act by harassing and threatening the Tenant. 19. The Tenant is claiming general damages for pain and suffering in the amount of $1,000.00, or what is commonly referred to as “non-pecuniary damages” because they are not damages directly related to a financial loss, but for pain and suffering. The object of non- pecuniary damages is to compensate a party’s pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life. In [name] v. Whitesands Apartments, [2009] O.J. No. 3198, the Court confirmed the Board’s authority to award general damages for mental distress under subsection 31(1)(f) of the Act. 20. I accept the Tenant’s testimony as to the profound stress they suffered because of the threats and harassment by the Landlord’s Agent. The Tenant explained that the harassment and threats were particularly difficult because they are an immigrant and transgender individual and feared losing their housing. 21. In considering the Tenant’s claim damages for pain and suffering, I must look at how the breaches have impacted the Tenant. I accept the Tenant’s testimony about the impact of the conduct of the Landlord’s Agent as credible and find that the Tenant experienced emotional anguish and stress. Given the evidence before me, I believe an award in the amount of $1,000.00 adequately compensates the Tenant for the mental distress they have endured. 22. The Tenant did not provide any specific details with respect to allegations the Landlord interfered with their internet service. The Tenant confirmed that all maintenance issues have resolved. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. 23. The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs. 24. The total amount the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant is $15,612.82.
ordered: The lawful monthly rent is $2,000.00, which represents $1,950.00 in base rent and $50.00 in internet.

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent.
reasons: The Landlord’s legal representative requested an adjournment because she said that the Landlord has a matter with the same parties in Superior Court, and the Landlord seeks to have the same legal representative as in Superior Court, to represent them at the LTB. The legal representative, [name], was not available to attend the Board for the hearing on June 29, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant did not consent to the adjournment. They submit that this is a “fraudulent application”.

The Landlord’s legal representative said that this application arises from the fact that they allege the Tenant, R. [name], sublet the rental unit to the unauthorized occupant, J. [name] (JP), in the past, and they only became aware of it when JP filed her application in Superior Court.

It is undisputed that JP has not lived in the rental unit for a number of years, and in fact, the Landlord has the current address of JP. The notice of hearing was sent to JP’s current address, which is not the address of the rental unit.
I denied the adjournment, and I dismissed the application for the reasons that follow.

JP does not live in the rental unit, and she has not lived in the rental unit for a number of years. Therefore, JP is not, by the Landlord’s own evidence, an unauthorized occupant of the rental unit. If she ever was an unauthorized occupant, it is historic. An application filed years after the alleged unlawful transfer has terminated, and after it has long ago reverted back to the Tenant’s occupation is not what is contemplated by section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

In fact, this application is an exact duplication of the issues that arise from JP’s Superior Court matter. It is not permitted to have a multiplicity of proceedings. The issues will be decided in that jurisdiction.
Since the Board does not have jurisdiction in this matter, I dismissed the application.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Corporation (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord did not file the application within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. However, the Landlord is a non-profit housing provider, and as such they qualify for the exemption from subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by virtue of subsection 7(1) of the Act.

The testimony of the Landlord’s witnesses, supported by documentary evidence, is that the Tenant requested, and she was granted, the right to add the Unauthorized Occupant, to her lease as an authorized occupant in 2024. The Landlord’s witness, [name] (ND) said that she explained to both the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant, M. [name] (MT) that an occupant does not have the same rights as a leaseholder. She said that they were both informed that when a Tenant vacates the rental unit, the occupant is obliged to vacate as well. ND also had a personal note, dated January 10, 2025, that she reminded MT on that date that if the Tenant moves out, he was also obliged to move out.

The Landlord’s evidence, supported by documentation, was that the Landlord learned that the Tenant had moved to long-term care in July 2025. ND said that she confirmed with the Landlord’s son that the Tenant was not going to return to the rental unit. She said that she informed MT about the implications of the Tenant moving out so he, too, could plan his own move. She said that she had a first conversation with MT about it in June 2025, after the Tenant went into hospital, and before she was transferred to long-term care.

ND submitted into evidence notes and correspondence with the Tenant’s son, and MT, about moving out the Tenant’s belongings from the unit. She said that she received a signed N11 agreement to terminate from the Tenant on July 22, 2025. ND said that she notified MT that he had until August 31, 2025, to move out of the rental unit. However, he did not move out.
The Landlord’s agent, [name] (LD), said that MT has not moved out to date. She also said that MT has not paid any rent at all since September 1, 2025.
The Landlord is seeking an eviction order as well as compensation from September 1, 2025. The market rent for the unit is $1,708.00. Reasons and Analysis:

The Unauthorized Occupant, MT, was an authorized occupant of the rental unit until the Tenant moved out. The Tenant moved out in July 2025, and she provided an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy. MT was provided an extra month to move out, and he failed to do so.

Consequently, MT became an Unauthorized Occupant of the rental unit on September 1, 2025. The Landlord had repeatedly informed MT that he did not have the rights of a leaseholder, and that he would have to move out when the Tenant moved out. He was well aware that the Tenant had moved out, and he even assisted the Tenant’s family in moving out her belongings. The Landlord had informed MT in writing that he had to move out by August 31, 2025.
MT has not moved out, nor has he paid any rent for the unit since September 1, 2025. Daily Compensation
Consequently, the Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $16,957.30 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from September 1, 2025 to the June 29, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $56.15. This amount is calculated as follows: $1708.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and they are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. In particular, the Unauthorized Occupant was informed almost a year ago that he was obliged to vacate the rental unit. He had been informed about it at the outset of his occupation of the rental unit. The Unauthorized Occupant did not attend the hearing to present any reasons to deny or delay the eviction. The Landlord is a non-profit housing provider and I find that it is prejudicial to the Landlord for the Unauthorized Occupation to continue.

The Tenant moved out in July 2025, she removed her belongings and she signed a valid N11 agreement to terminate. I find that payment of the compensation is solely the responsibility of the Unauthorized Occupant, MT.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 17, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by July 17, 2026, then starting July 18, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 18, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $16,957.30 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from September 1, 2025 to the June 29, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $56.15 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from June 30, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 17, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 17, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 18, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
