issues: ULC (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlord’s A1 Application seeks a determination as to whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”) applies to the named tenant [name] (ML)’s occupancy of unit # 207.
It is the Landlord’s position the Act does not apply.

The Landlord’s agent [name] (LJ) is the sole director, officer and owner of the residential complex and testified that ML unilaterally took possession of unit # 207 without the Landlord’s consent or authorization. In particular, no rental agreement was ever signed authorizing ML to take possession and upon taking possession, ML made no payments to the Landlord. LJ testified that she never authorized anyone to either grant ML possession of the rental unit or to enter into any tenancy agreement with ML. In support of their position, the Landlord produced a “Notice of Trespass” letter sent to the “Unauthorized Occupant” at unit 207, stating, in part: We have been advised that you have without authorization or consent of the owner been in occupation of the unit located at 207…..Under not circumstances are you or have you been a tenant of the subject property, in particular, there is no lease agreement and have been n exchange of rental payments, whatsoever…
The named tenant, ML, did not attend the hearing to dispute the Landlord’s uncontested evidence.

Section 2(1) of the Act provides that a “tenancy agreement” can be a written, oral or implied and that a “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit.Here, there is no evidence of the parties enter ing into a written, oral or implied agreement. While ML admittedly occupied the rental uni t, the Landlord’s uncontested evidence is that no payment of rent was ever made and that ML’s occupancy was unauthorized. Consequently, I do not find that the parties entered into a ny contractual arrangement or that ML is a tenant under the Act. The Act does not apply.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ULC (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlord’s A1 Application seeks a determination as to whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”) applies to the named tenant [name] ( the “tenant/occupant WC” or “WC”)’s occupancy of unit #301 (“Unit 301”).
It is the Landlord’s position the Act does not apply. Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord’s agent [name] ( [name]) is the sole director, officer and owner of the residential complex, which consists of 17 residential units.

The Landlord LJ submits WC unilaterally took possession of Unit 301 without the Landlord’s consent or authorization. In particular, no rental agreement was ever signed authorizing MJ to take possession and upon taking possession, WC made no payments to the Landlord . LJ testified that she never authorized anyone to either grant WC possession of the rental unit or to enter into any tenancy agreement with WC.

The Landlord LJ testified that WC was in prior units in the building and “moved around a lot” before taking possession of Unit 301. The Landlord LJ described WC as a “squatter” and testified she became aware of WC’s presence in Unit 301 so metime in 2024. Later, in October 2025 when the Landlord secured legal representation a “Notice of Trespass” was sent to the “Unauthorized Occupant” at Unit 301, stating, in part: We have been advised that you have without authorization or consent of the owner been in occupation of the unit located at 301…..Under not circumstances are you or have you been a tenant of the subject property, in particular, there is no lease agreement and have been n exchange of rental payments, whatsoever…

The Landlord’s project manager [name] (BI) testified he became involved in the Landlord’s operations in early 2025 and stated he reviewed the Landlord’s operational building records (or lack thereof). BI noted that there were “no records” for Unit 301 to support a tenancy agreement between the Landlord and WC. Neighbour’s Evidence

The named tenant/occupant’s witness [name] (NR) resides in the building and for a period of time, was WC’s neighbour. NR stated that WC previously lived in unit 205 until it was flooded and became unhabitable and in need of repairs. NR testified the t hen Landlord’s property manager/superintendent [name] (SC) authorized WC’s transfer to the current Unit 301. NR testified she overheard the Landlord LJ advise SC to move WC upstairs until the work is done.

Documentation from NR’s rental unit was produced in support of the Tenant’s position that SC had such authority to enter into tenancy agreements on the Landlord’s behalf. Some of the documentation included: - Page 1 of a document tiled Residential Tenancy Agreement, identifying NC as tenant and the Landlord LJ as landlord. This document appears to be initialed by SC, but not signed by the Landlord LJ. - Document titled “To whom it may Concern ” and dated March 15, 2025 , confirming NR has moved to unit 302 and con firming the r ental amount of $1750/month . The documents appears to be signed by NR (as tenant) and SC (as superintendent). The [name] name appears to be printed in the signing section for the Landlord but the Landlord LJ denies ever seeing this document. Named tenant/occupant’s evidence

The named tenant/occupant WC testified he initially moved into unit 201 with a roommate in the fall 2022, paying $1000/month. A few months later, WC testified he moved to unit 205 and a lease was signed whereby he paid rent in cash to SC in the amount of $1700/month.
As a result of the flood in Unit 205, WC testified his signed lease agreement for unit 205 was destroyed.

Regardless, WC acknowledged there were no writte n documents signed for Unit 301. According to WC, the relocation from unit 205 to Unit 301 was purportedly authorized by SC who received verbal approval from the Landlord LJ. WC testified he expected to reside in Unit 301 on a short -term emergency basis while repairs were undertaken in unit 205 and had no re ntal insurance. At the hearing, SC in dicated he would like to return to unit 205. There was no discussion of a rental amount for Unit 301, with WC suggesting Unit 301 was being provided as an “extension of 205 ” and as a form of “compensation for loss ” that occurred due to the flooding in unit 205.

The Landlord states SC had no authority to enter into any contractual relations on the Landlord’s behalf. LJ described SC as a “friend/handyman”, with no authority to collect any rent on the Landlord’s behalf. The Landlord LJ testified that SC lived across the street and would only help with painting and other odd maintenance jobs. As SC was “unreliable”, the [name] testified he ceased having any involvement with the building in 2024, when BI was hired to assist the Landlord. Analysis
The onus to prove the Act does not apply rests with the applicant, Landlord.

While the parties disagree as to whether or not SC was the [name] dlord’s agent with the requisite authority to enter a contract that binds the Landlord, in my view , the current application can be decided without a determination of SC’s authority, or lack thereof,

To find that a binding and enforceable agreement exists in respect of Unit 301, there must be a meeting of the minds of the parties on all essential tenancy terms. Here, irrespective of whether or not SC had authority to enter unto contractual relations on the Landlord’s behalf, I find there was no meeting of the minds.

At the time of possession of Unit 301 , or at any time there after, there does not appear to have been any discussion or agreement of essential terms. No lease documentation was signed by the parties when the tenant/occupant WC took possession of Unit 301. While I am mindful, that section 2(1) of t he Act provides a tenancy agreement can be written, oral or implied, there is also no indication that essential tenancy agreement terms, such as rental amount, lease term, due dates …etc., were orally discussed or agreed upon at the time of occupancy or thereafter.

In this regard, WC testified that Unit 301 was merely provided on an “emergency basis” and for a few months while unit 205 was returned to a habitable state. A rental amount was not agreed upon. Moreover, in the months that followed, no rent was paid for Unit 301, thus suggesting there was no subsequent implied other agreement of essential terms. As the parties also did not enter into an oral or implied tenancy at Unit 301, the Act does not apply.

Although I find the Act does not appl y to Unit 301, I make no determinations or findings as to whether or not a tenancy was created or exists at the present time between WC and the Landlord in respect of Unit 205, or any other unit in the residential complex. Such questions/determinations were not before the Board in the current A1 application.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply to Unit #301. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, [name] (ED) submitted that her parents, the Tenants, who are 84 and 86 years old respectively, have requested that she represent them in this proceeding. She also submitted that she had filed a request to reschedule this hearing as today is her parents’ 63rd wedding anniversary which they fear may be their last together as her father is very ill.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative objected to ED representing the Tenants without any authorization. He submitted that the Landlord has not had any communication with the Tenants for almost two years and they have also failed to attend this hearing. He also submitted that ED is the alleged [name] and has intercepted communications with the Tenants regarding the rental unit.

ED confirmed that she does not have Power of Attorney for either of her parents but submitted that her mother had given her written authorization previously to file a T2 application on her behalf and that as a result ED has access to her mother’s LTB portal.
The matter was held down to permit one of the Tenants to join the hearing and provide verbal authorization for ED to act on their behalf.

At approximately 10:47 a.m., [name] (GD) attended the hearing and provided verbal authorization permitting her daughter, ED, to act on her behalf in this proceeding. Therefore, I was satisfied that ED can act as the Tenants’ Agent in this proceeding. A2 application 6. [name] stated that their tenancy began in 2000 and that since October or November 2024 they have been living with family members because of health issues as a temporary measure. She also stated that she intended to move back into the rental unit when it is possible and that this information had been conveyed to the Landlord. She answered a couple of questions from the Landlord’s Legal Representative and then stated that her heart is pounding and she prefers not to continue and then chose to disconnect. 7. The Landlord’s Agent, [name], [name], testified that she has been the Property Manager for this unit for the last 17 years. She also testified that there is a signed tenancy agreement between the Landlord and the Tenants and provided a copy of it into evidence (DOC-8339787pgs3-6). She further testified that on January 12, 2026 another resident advised her that the Tenants had moved out of the unit and into a home. 8. [name] also testified that she has not communicated with the Tenants for some time despite several attempts as only ED would reply to her email and has stated that her parents are either not available or cannot talk at that time. [name] asserted that ED is residing in the rental unit as an unauthorized occupant. [name] testified that ED has advised that she is looking after her parents and has intimated in the past when asked where her parents are that they are simply unavailable or sleeping. [name] further testified that during an issue with a leak in June 2026, the Landlord discovered that there were two students residing in the unit who advised they were paying rent to ED and that ED was in Mexico during that time. 9. Under cross-examination, MA could not recall any specific dates or times that ED has denied access stating that her parents were at the unit sleeping. Under cross- examination, [name] was presented with an email that she recalled receiving from [name] dated March 5, 2025 wherein GD confirmed that they are staying elsewhere and that ED is the best point of contact, a copy of which was provided into evidence (DOC8339787pg23). Under cross-examination, [name] testified that she had been given false information from ED saying that her parents are still in the rental unit although every time MA has attended they are not there and most of their stuff is also not there. 10. ED testified that her parents experienced health issues around October 2024 and had to move in with their grandchild who’s home is located closer to other family members. She also testified that some of their belongings were moved there as well. She further testified that this had been communicated to the Landlord in November 2024, and again after the Landlord’s inquired in February 2025 when her mother emailed them. She testified that her father had a stroke in February 2025 and was still recovering. 11. ED also testified that her parents have entrusted her to house sit for them and that she is currently seeking permanent residency in Mexico. She testified that she has been the main contact for reporting maintenance concerns and assisting the Landlord with access to the unit. She further testified that her parents have not transferred the tenancy to her as they continue to pay the rent, the utilities are in their name, and they hope to return to the unit when possible. 12. Under cross-examination when asked if she recalled advising the Landlord that her parents were at the unit, ED testified that she remembered one time when her dad was there and sick but did not remember the date. Under cross-examination when asked if she had misled MA to believe that the Tenants were still living there, ED testified that she just stated this is their primary residence and that they are still receiving mail here. 13. This application was filed pursuant to subsection 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which provides that a landlord may apply to the LTB to terminate the tenancy if the tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an authorized assignment or sublet. Subsection 100(2) of the Act provides that the application must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. 14. There is no dispute that ED is residing in the rental unit when not in Mexico. She acknowledged being a house sitter and confirmed that her pet rats are kept at the unit, as she hired a pet sitter while she was recently in Mexico. There is also no dispute that the Tenants are currently not staying in the unit. They may stay in the unit on occasion when in the area but confirmed they are staying with family in another city which is closer to other family members and this is because of them requiring care for their health issues. 15. ED testified that the Tenants continue to pay the rent and utilities for the unit and plan to return to the unit when possible, and most likely it would just be GD after her husband passes. [name] also confirmed that she intended to return to the unit when possible. 16. In these circumstances, I was not satisfied that the Tenants have unlawfully transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to ED. I find it more likely than not that the Tenants continue to maintain their tenancy, through rental and utility payments, and their desire to return to the unit when and if their health improves. Additionally, ED has resided in Mexico for periods of time and testified that she is in the process of obtaining permanent residency there. Given this, I was satisfied that she does not intend to reside full-time in the unit and more likely than not is just looking after issues with the unit for her parents until they return. It is also not unlawful for ED to reside or stay in the rental unit with her parents. 17. As well, the Landlord bears the burden in this application to satisfy the LTB that the occupancy has been unlawfully transferred to ED. The Landlord did not provide any evidence to contradict that the Tenants are only staying elsewhere temporarily and not returning, or that it is not them continuing to pay the rent and utilities. The Landlord did not provide any specific evidence to support the assertion of the neighbouring resident that the Tenants have moved into a home, suggesting a long term care facility. 18. In any event, this type of application must be brought within 60 days of the Landlord discovering an unauthorized occupancy as per subsection 100(2) of the Act. There was no dispute that [name] emailed the Landlord on March 5, 2025, the contents of that email read as follows: “Dear Mr. [name]name] This is to confirm that [name] and I have in no way abandoned our home at 506- 2650 Marsdale [name], we are away due to ongoing health issues and will return to our home as able. We are continuing our excellent tenancy, paying our rent in a timely manner. [name] is currently in hospital with a very serious condition and cannot respond to any correspondence. our daughter [name] is still the best point of contact for day to day matters and is our trusted house sitter until we are able to be there. I ask you to please only contact her at her email address or [phone] for maintenance issues as further upset needs to be avoided at all costs. We will update you in the future. Sincerely” 19. Given the above, I was satisfied that the Landlord knew as early as March 5, 2025 that the Tenants were staying elsewhere due to health issues. The Landlord’s submission that an email from a neighbouring resident in January 2026 is when the 60 day limitation period should start was not credible. Especially because this neighbouring resident simply reported that the Tenants had moved out and into a home, which was not substantiated by the evidence. 20. If the unlawful transfer of the occupancy of the rental unit to ED occurred when the Tenants went to stay with family members, then the Landlord would have known this as early as March 5, 2025. Therefore, the application was not filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. 21. Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: d'Ottawa (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent (hereafter referred to as the ‘A2 Application’). The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. This A2 Application was heard by videoconference on June 10, 2026. The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘K.Q’), the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Unauthorized Occupant , [name] (‘M.N’) along with their witness [name] (‘J.K’), and their support individuals, [name] and [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: The parties agreed that [name] [name] passed away on November 11, 2025, as it appears from a copy of the Proof of Death from Kelly Funeral Home – Walkey Chapel, dated November 15, 2025 (DOC-8137138, “[name] M. - Proof of Death.pdf;” Exhibit 1).
The Landlord sought to amend the A2 Application to reflect the Tenant as being [name].
The parties agreed that M.N also represented the interests of [name].
M.N did not oppose the Landlord’s request to amend the A2 Application.

Pursuant to subsection 200(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I granted the amendment request. The style-of-cause was amended accordingly. Adjournment Request

At the start of the hearing, M.N requested that the matter be adjourned as they stated that they had only been made aware of the proceedings on June 8, 2026, and while they were previously receiving legal assistance, their representative was no longer retained.
M.N indicated that they require additional time to prepare for the proceedings , gather documents, and seek new legal representation.
M.N also indicated that they were ill and that their medical situation impeded their ability to participate in the proceedings.
The Landlord was opposed to the adjournment request. They submit that M.N was aware of the proceedings since the month of March 2026, and that they had legal representation until recently.

The Landlord submits M.N had previously filed a separate and distinct application (LTB-T-103361-25) through which they had raised similar issues to the ones brought forward by the Landlord through the current A2 Application.

The Landlord disputes that M.N was not aware of the current proceedings prior to June 8, 2026, as M.N had reached out to various levels of governments to seek assistance with respect to these proceedings, as it appears from a copy of the email sent to the Landlord by the Office of [name] ([name], Exhibit 2).

M.N recognized that they had indeed reached out provincial and municipal resources in advance of the June 10, 2026, hearing, in order to seek assistance. They reiterated that they are seeking additional time to prepare for the hearing.

Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 outline relevant considerations in determining whether or not an adjournment request should be granted, including: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.[Emphasis added]
On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, and having considered the factors outlined in Rule 21.8 of the Rules of Procedure, I denied the adjournment request.

Indeed, while section 10 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990, states that a party may be represented by a representative at a hearing, the right to representation is not absolute and an adjournment request based on this ground may be denied. The onus is on the party wishing to be represented to make all reasonable efforts to find a lawyer or paralegal able to represent them at the hearing once they become aware of the hearing.

In this matter, M.N had previously retained legal representation. They led no evidence as to when their previous representative ceased acting on their behalf and what steps they had taken to seek or secure new representation prior to the hearing. I therefore find that they were not diligent in this regard.

Furthermore, having reviewed M.N’s submissions related to the application LTB-T-103361-25, which they had filed with the Board on December 7, 2025 (hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’) , it is apparent that M.N was aware of the issues and circumstances which led to the filing of the Landlord’s A2 Application.

Indeed, while M.N ultimately elected to withdraw their T2 Application 1, they had originally alleged that the Landlord had harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them2 as the Landlord was seeking to evict them from the rental unit as the Landlord had a following the passing of [name] [name], as the Landlord had deemed that M.N was not a tenant. This forms the basis of the Landlord’s A2 Application.

While M.N also referenced that their medical situation impeded their ability to participate in the proceedings, they did not submit to the Board any medical notes (nor lead any evidence) that would provide an adequate description of their diagnosis or clarify the effect of any such diagnosis on their ability to participate in the proceedings in a fulsome manner.3

Based on the fact that M.N had previously retained legal representation, filed their T2 Application based on similar grounds and had sought assistance from various resources for matters directly related to the proceedings, I find that they are aware of the questions arising in the proceedings and therefore had a reasonable opportunity to know issues and respond accordingly. As such, I find that they had an opportunity to be heard on the matter.

Accordingly, I find that the adjournment request amounts to little more than an attempt by M.N to unduly delay the proceedings and perfect their litigation strategy . These are not appropriate grounds for an adjournment.

As the Board has an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding, 4 M.N’s adjournment request was denied, and the A2 Application proceeded to be heard. 1 Order LTB-T-103361-25, issued on January 6, 2026. 2 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 3 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028. 4 Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. A2 Application - Unauthorized Occupancy a) Landlord’s Evidence 23. [name] testified that they are an employee of the Landlord and act as a lease services manager. 24. K.Q described the rental unit as being a subsidized unit. 25. [name] stated that it is their understanding that M.N was the spouse of [name] [name] (‘S.N’), as it appears from a copy of the Mariage Certificate #003/87, dated March 8, 1984 ([name], “[name] M. - Marriage Certificate.pdf;” Exhibit 3) 26. K.Q indicated that S.N and the Landlord executed a tenancy agreement on April 30, 2024, prior to S.N moving into the rental unit on May 1, 2024. 27. K.Q stated that S.N was the sole individual listed as a tenant at the time the tenancy agreement was executed. 28. K.Q indicated that the Landlord was advised that M.N had moved into the rental unit on September 17, 2025, as it appears from a copy of the Change in Household Composition Form received by the Landlord on September 17, 2025 (DOC -8091151, page 2 of 3; Exhibit 4). 29. K.Q explained that tenants are required to submit such forms (Exhibit 4 ) on a yearly basis, and upon any changes to the makeup of the household, in order to continue to maintain their eligibility to their rent -geared-to-income assistance. Prior to September 17, 2025, S.N had provided the Landlord an update during the month of May 2025, which had confirmed that they were the sole individual residing in the rental unit at the time. 30. K.Q stated that while a change in the composition of the household may impact the subsidies that tenants receive, such a change does not change the terms of the tenancy agreement. Additional individuals moving into the rental units would be considered occupants or roommates, not tenants. 31. K.Q indicated that in the case of subsidized housing units such as the rental unit, prospective tenants are matched to the Landlord through a centralized waiting list which i s under the purview of the Housing Registry; which is a separate and distinct entity from the Landlord. The waiting list encapsulates all social housing providers in Ottawa. 32. K.Q stated that as prospective tenants are assigned to the Landlord through the aforementioned centralized waiting list, the tenancy could not be assigned to M.N. The Landlord also would not be eligible to enter into a market-rent tenancy with M.N. 33. K.Q indicated that f ollowing to the passing of S.N on November 11, 2025 (Exhibit 1), t he Landlord advised M.N that the tenancy would be ending on December 11, 2025, and that vacate possession of the rental unit would therefore need to be returned to the Landlord by that same date, as it appears for a copy of the letter dated November 13, 2025, sent by the Landlord to [name] (DOC-8091151, page 1 of 3; Exhibit 5). 34. [name] stated that they were advised by M.N that they did not intend to move out of the rental unit. 35. The Landlord therefore seeks to terminate the tenancy and evict M.N in order to maintain their eligibility to various subsidies and avoid losing their designation as a designated housing project. 36. Under cross-examination, K.Q reiterated that while M.N was the spouse of S.N, they are not eligible to remain in the rental unit. b) Unauthorized Occupant’s Evidence 37. M.N testified that they were the spouse of S.N (Exhibit 3). 38. M.N agrees that the tenancy agreement between the Landlord and S.N was executed on April 30, 2024, and that S.N was listed as being the sole Tenant at the time. 39. J.K testified that they are a relative of M.N. 40. J.K stated that at the time that S.N moved into the rental unit, M.N remained abroad (in Burundi). 41. M.N only joined S.N in the rental unit on April 24, 2025, as the latter was ill. They proceeded to advise the Landlord of this change on September 17, 2025 (Exhibit 4). 42. M.N seeks to remain in the rental unit and be recognized as a tenant. c) Analysis 43. Subsection 91(1) of the Act reads as follows: 91 (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant. 44. Section 3 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 reads as follows: 3. (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act unless the spouse vacates the unit within the 30- day period described in subsection 91 (1) of the Act. […] (4) Subsections (1) and (2) do not apply to, (a) a rental unit described in section 7 of the Act; (b) a rental unit that is in a care home to which Part IX of the Act applies; or (c) a rental unit to which section 6 of this Regulation applies. [Emphasis Added] 45. As the rental unit is part of a residential complex which is considered to be a designated housing project 5 under the Housing Services Act, 2011, the provisions of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 which would enable the spouse of a deceased tenant to be considered a “tenant” do not apply. 46. As it is not in dispute that M.N was not a tenant under the terms of the tenancy agreement executed between the Landlord and S.N, I find, on a balance of probabilities that the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant ended on December 11, 2025, i.e. thirty (30) days after the passing of S.N (Exhibit 1).6 47. As the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with M.N , I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the continued occupancy of the rental unit by M.N following the passing of S.N was done in a manner that was not authorized under the Act. 48. The Unauthorized Occupant shall therefore be required to move out of the rental unit. Daily Compensation 49. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. 50. The Landlord indicated that they were only intent on claiming the amount of $139.00 as the lawful monthly rent; which is due on the first (1st) of each month. 51. Based on the monthly rent, the daily compensation is $4.57. This amount is calculated as follows: $139.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 52. The Landlord stated that rent for the rental period starting December 1, 2025, and ending December 31, 2025, was paid in full. 53. The Landlord is therefore only claiming the amount of $735.77 in daily compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant for the rental period starting January 1, 2026, and ending the June 10, 2026. 54. It is not in dispute that following the passing of S.M, no additional payments were successfully completed by the Unauthorized Occupant to the Landlord for the rental period starting January 1, 2026, and ending the June 10, 2026 55. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 5 Ontario Regulation 368/11, Schedule 24. 6 Section 91 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. Postponement of the Eviction 56. The Landlord seeks for the Unauthorized Occupant to vacate the rental unit in order to ensure that the Landlord can continue to meet their funding requirements and that the rental unit can be used by eligible individuals who are waiting to secure housing accommodations. 57. In light of the Unauthorized Occupant’s circumstances following the passing of their spouse, the Landlord was amenable to delaying the eviction to August 31, 2026. 58. M.N seeks to remain in the rental in order to continue receiving the support from the neighbours and community members. In the alternative, they seek to continue the tenancy until at least the month of November 2026, which would align with the one-year anniversary of the passing of S.N. 59. J.K indicated that they live in a different province and would not be able to provide continued assistance to M.N. 60. As explained during the hearing, the Board does not have the jurisdiction to establish a new tenancy between a landlord and a prospective tenant.7 61. Having considered all of the disclosed circumstances, I find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until August 31, 2026. The delayed eviction will provide the Unauthorized Occupant additional time to search for new housing accommodations within an alleviated time constraint. 62. Considering the time which has elapsed since the start of the unauthorized occupancy and the hearing, I do not find it appropriate to postpone the eviction further. 63. The prejudice to the Landlord is minimized, as they were amenable to such a delay.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before August 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by August 31, 2026, then starting September 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.

Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after September 1, 2026. 7 Tataw v. Minto Apartment L.P., 2023 ONSC 4238.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord the total amount of $936.77 which represents: • $735.77 as daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from January 1, 2026, to the June 10, 2026, • $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $4.57 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from June 11, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 31, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 31, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from September 1, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (“PW”) (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord filed an A2 application on February 5, 2026, claiming the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there has been a transfer in the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Act.
As explained below, the Landlord having proven their application on a balance of probabilities, the tenancy is terminated and the Unauthorized Occupant will be ordered to vacate the rental unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

Marta Costa (“MC”), the Landlord’s Witness, is the Director of Residential Operations and has worked for the Landlord for around five years. She is responsible for managing the property and is familiar with [name] [name]’s tenancy. She said she has firsthand knowledge of the circumstances related to this matter.

MC testified that the Unauthorized Occupant is [name] [name]’s son, and to the MC’s knowledge, he has been living in the unit since she started managing the property and was living in the unit with [name] [name] before she passed away.
MC then testified that while she did not have the lease agreement for this unit on file, to her knowledge, [name] [name] was always the sole tenant of the unit based on the Landlord’s records.

MC further testified that all correspondence, documents, and notices that were sent to the rental unit were always sent to [name] [name] and not the Unauthorized Occupant as [name] [name] was the only listed tenant of the unit. MC also stated that there was no request made to the Landlord for the Unauthorized Occupant to be added to the lease and/or to have the lease assigned to them.

On January 28, 2026, which was the date of a hearing in respect of a separate application before the Board, MC was advised by Marsha [name], a family member who attended the hearing, that [name] [name] had passed away. Submitted into evidence was also the death certificate of the [name] [name], showing that she passed away on [name] 20, 2025. The Landlord was not notified prior to the January 28th hearing that [name] [name] had passed away.

The Unauthorized Occupant stated that he has been living in the rental unit since 2015. The Unauthorized Occupant stated that he is not an unauthorized occupant as his name is on the insurance documents for the unit. He did not submit the insurance documents into evidence. In any event, I am not satisfied that these documents would have proved that the Landlord consented to the assignment of the tenancy to the Unauthorized Occupant.

The Unauthorized Occupant also stated that he spoke to a legal clinic and was advised that he did not have to report [name] [name]’s passing to the Landlord. The Unauthorized Occupant further stated that he believes the Landlord wants him evicted so they can re- rent the unit for more rent.

The Unauthorized Occupant then stated that the address on his driver’s licence is that of the rental unit, and this is his address for most things; moreover, the Unauthorized Occupant stated that he paid bills for the unit while living there. Ultimately, the Unauthorized Occupant did not provide any evidence to establish that the Landlord consented to have occupancy or the tenancy transfer to him.

I am satisfied that the Tenant passed away and the Landlord became aware of her passing on January 28, 2026. This is pertinent as this when the Landlord discovered the unauthorized transfer of occupancy and whether the Landlord filed the application within 60 days of that date; moreover, the Landlord knew that the Tenant’s son was living in the rental unit with his mother. Therefore, I find that the Landlord discovered the unauthorized transfer of occupancy on January 28, 2026, and the Landlord filed the application within 60 days of that date.

Pursuant to subsection 91(1) of the Act, the tenancy terminated on February 27, 2026 (30 days after [name] [name]’s death): 91(1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $4,912.44 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from January 28, 2026, to the June 17, 2026, the hearing date.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $34.84. This amount is calculated as follows: $1059.65 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

The Landlord sought an eviction order as soon as possible, or in the alternative, if any relief from eviction was granted, that eviction be postponed for a brief time as there are rental arrears owing from September 2025.

The Unauthorized Occupant sought denial of eviction as he would have no where else to go and has health issues. In addition, Marsha [name] stated that the Unauthorized Occupant would face dire conditions such as homelessness if evicted. The Unauthorized Occupant then stated that he resided in the rental unit for several years and while there are rental arrears owing, he can afford the rent.

Although I have found that there has been an unauthorized transfer of occupancy, I still find that it would not be unfair to delay eviction to allow the Unauthorized Occupant some additional time to secure alternate housing.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until August 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before August 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by August 31, 2026, then starting September 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after September 1, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $4,912.44 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from January 28, 2026, to the June 17, 2026.

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent.
reasons: The Tenants transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Landlord is aware that the Tenant N.J. is deceased.

On December 15, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenant K.J. a voidable N5 notice of termination with a termination date of January 4, 2026. The Landlord alleged that the unit was “filthy with hording conditions” and there was an infestation of bedbugs as was reported to him by his pest control technicians after they tried to treat the unit on April 27, 2026. The Landlord took a series of photos depicting the “deplorable” state.

On December 20, 2025, the Landlord learned that the Tenant K.J. had died on or about December 5, 2025 and that their son [name] – who is not named as a tenant on the lease agreement but had been living with his parents – was the sole adult occupant. Analysis

Subsection 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that “If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant.” Since D.J. is not a tenant, the Act required him to move out within the 30-day period after the death of K.J.

The Landlord informed D.J. on December 20, 2025 that he was not authorized to continue living there but, in the circumstances, would allow him to stay until January 31, 2026. D.J. has not vacated the unit. The Landlord filed this application on February 5, 2026 for an order terminating the tenancy and for eviction.
I find that D.J. is an Unauthorized Occupant and that he was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
The Unauthorized Occupant was not present to speak about his personal circumstances.
The Landlord states that the bedbugs have travelled to other units in the multi-residential complex. Additionally, he fears that the clutter in the unit presents a serious fire hazard.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 28, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by July 28, 2026, then starting July 29, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 29, 2026.
On or before July 28, 2026, the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 28, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 29, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Inc (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: There is no dispute that the Unauthorized Occupant is the adult son of the second-named Tenant. For the following reasons, I find that the Tenants transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

First, I am satisfied that the Landlord entered into a valid tenancy agreement with the Tenants named in this application. I say this because the Landlord provided a copy of the lease agreement he signed with the Tenants. The lease agreement was signed by the Landlord and the Tenants on October 18, 2023, and was for a fixed one-year term ending October 31, 2024. The monthly rent the parties agreed to was $2,900.00 which included a parking space.

Next, I am satisfied that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on January 31, 2026. I say this because the Landlord says the Tenants served him with an N9 notice to terminate the tenancy at some point in December 2025. The Landlord says the Tenants then confirmed in writing that they had moved out and returned the keys to him.

At the hearing, the Landlord provided a series of text messages between himself and the Tenants dated January 31, 2026. These text messages state the following: Landlord: Hi [name], please let me know what time today you expect to have everything out of the apartment so I can arrange a time to come collect the keys. Thank you [name]: [name] has left the key and door beeper thing in the garage on a shelf you will see when u walk in. [name] moved 2 weeks ago. I look (sic) a lot last nite and today some time don’t know when and billy is leaving tonite that’s all I know Landlord: Thanks [name] [name]: Just push the garage door open

The Landlord then provided another series of text messages between himself and the Tenant informing them that the Unauthorized Occupant was still in the rental unit. These messages are dated February 22, 2026, and say the following: Landlord: Hi, the main floor reeks of smoke and there has been music blasting all weekend. Billy and his girlfriend are occupying the unit illegally. I need them out immediately. I need his contact info and would like your assistance to get him out. This isn’t right. [name]: I have no contact with him you’ll have to go see him there Landlord: You left him behind. This is your lease. [name]: I gave you proper notice and told him when we were leaving I’m not his sitter main reason I left get away from him. Serve an eviction notice on him

Based on the Landlord’s testimony and the supporting documentary evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on January 31, 2026, and left the keys in the unit for the Landlord to retrieve. The Tenants advised the Landlord they were terminating the tenancy and they left pursuant to the N9 they served the Landlord.

I am also satisfied that the Unauthorized Occupant remained in possession of the rental unit after the Tenants had moved out. I say this because the Unauthorized Occupant attended the hearing and admits that he still lives in the unit and has not signed a lease agreement with the Landlord.

I have also considered the testimony from the Landlord’s property manager who says that the Unauthorized Occupant has harassed him when he attended the residential complex and has been interfering with the remaining residents of the building.

Finally, I note that the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant on February 1, 2026, and filed the A2 application on February 6, 2026. I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord has met the 60 day deadline set out in subsection 104(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c. 17 (the ‘Act’).
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

Although the Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant, they provided no testimony or documentary evidence regarding this issue at the hearing. I can therefore not make any determination regarding what amount of compensation may be owing to the Landlord in this instance.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. I find that the Unauthorized Occupant should be responsible for these costs as he appears to be fully aware that he is not a named Tenant in the lease and he has not signed a new lease agreement with the Landlord. This means the Unauthorized Occupant knew or ought to have known that he should have vacated the rental unit along with the Tenants but he simply failed to do so. For these reasons, I therefore find that the Unauthorized Occupant is responsible for paying the costs of filing the application. An order will issue accordingly.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). In particular, I have considered that this portion of the Act relates to whether the Board to exercise its discretion and grant the Tenants relief from eviction. This portion of the Act does not give the Board any discretion to grant relieve from eviction for an Unauthorized Occupant. As the Tenants have already vacated the rental unit, I therefore find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenants is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before August 10, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by August 10, 2026, then starting August 11, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after August 11, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 10, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 10, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. The Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with the Tenant for a term ending on February 28, 2026. The Tenant advised the Landlord that they would be vacating early as of February 1, 2026, and proceeded to vacate on this date and transferred the utilities back into the Landlord’s name. The Landlord attended the rental unit on February 7, 2026 and discovered that the Tenant’s mother, the Unauthorized Occupant, and another individual were residing in the rental unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. The application was filed on February 18, 2026 approximately 11 days after the Landlord discovered the Unauthorized Occupant in the rental unit. Section 83 Considerations
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs from the Tenant. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act, and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: At the start of the hearing [name] testified that because she was only retained on June 8, 2026, she has not yet had opportunity to disclose the Landlord’s documentary evidence. As such, [name] asked for an adjournment to make disclosure. The Tenant opposed this request, asking instead that the hearing proceed today and that this evidence not be admitted because it was not disclosed. I recessed to allow the Tenant to review these documents, after which he testified that he had reviewed them to his satisfaction and the he was prepared to proceed with the hearing today with the admission of these documents. As such, I denied the Landlord’s request and proceeded with the hearing on the scheduled date.

The Landlord and [name] testified that the tenancy started on November 11, 2022 and ended on July 11, 2023. The residential complex is a three bedroom condominium apartment. The master bedroom includes an ensuite bathroom. As well, the apartment contains a common bathroom and a kitchen. During the tenancy the Landlord generally occupied the master bedroom, the Tenant occupied another bedroom and another person occupied the third bedroom. Though the Landlord was often away from the unit for work, he regularly used the kitchen when home. Because the other occupant prefers the master bedroom, at times the Landlord switched bedrooms with this person, during which times the Landlord used the common bathroom.

The Landlord and [name] further testified that the written tenancy agreement between the Landlord and Tenant is silent with respect to the Landlord and Tenant sharing a bathroom or kitchen but that at some point the parties orally agreed to amend the agreement to confirm the sharing of these facilities between them. 4. [name] testified that he is a friend of the Landlord. [name] visited the Landlord in the unit 4 times between 2022 on 2024, though he does not recall the dates of these attendances. At these times [name] shared meals with the Landlord in the kitchen. 5. The Tenant testified that the tenancy ended on June 12, 2024, the Landlord informed the Tenant that the Landlord lives in his parents’ home and that the apartment is exclusively a rental property. The Tenant mostly worked from home during his tenancy and so was able to consistently observe the goings on in the apartment. The Landlord never occupied any part of the apartment and only attended occasionally to conduct maintenance repair. At no time did the Landlord ever use the bathrooms or kitchen. As well, at no time did the parties amend the tenancy agreement to state that the parties share a bathroom or kitchen. 6. In my analysis, I find that neither party is generally more credible than the other with respect to the factual elements at issue. However, the principle of contra proferentem is a legal doctrine that calls on a decision-maker to resolve ambiguities in the interpretation of a contract in favour of the person who did not draft it (based on the presumption that the drafter would have been in the best position to avoid the creation of the ambiguity). With this principle in view, I find that the Landlord’s unexplained failure to include a provision in the tenancy agreement supportive of his assetion to be fatal to his claim. Moreover, neither the Landlord nor [name] had an explanation for why the parties would have allegedly chosen to orally amend a tenancy written tenancy agreement. 7. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that section 5(i) of the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.
ordered: Section 5(i) The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name], [name] [name] [name], and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] Occupants (the '[name] Occupants') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenants transferred the occupancy of th e rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the [name] Occupants.
The [name] Occupants were in posse ssion of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord said that the Tenants’ tenancy began on January 1, 2026. He believes that the Tenants moved out of the unit some time in March 2026, but he was not certain of the exact date, because he was not informed that the Tenants were moving out. He said the Tenants stopped paying rent after February 2026.

The Landlord discovered that the unit was being occupied by other individuals in or about late March 2026 or early April 2026 after a neighbour informed him that it appeared that a number of other individuals had moved into the unit.

The Tenant, [name] [name] [name] (‘DP’), acknowledged to the Landlord that he knew the people that moved in, but did not respond to the Landlord’s question about whether DP gave these people keys for the unit.

The Landlord presented a text message e xchange that he had with DP on April 2, 2026. Among other things, DP wrote that he “… talk ed them into paying something and that fell through so they gotta go unless you want to rent to them”. This supports the Landlord’s evidence that DP knew these people, though DP later contradicts himself in the text chain, stating that he does not know the [name] Occupants (DOC-7870481, pp. 2-4). The Landlord said that he was informed by police that the [name] [name] told police that they know DP and that DP let them into the unit. This happened when the Landlord contacted police and attended the unit with police around mid-April 2026.
The Landlord does not know the names of th e [name] Occupants, but said there are 6 or 7 people living in the unit.

Based on the Landlord’s communication with DP, the text message exchange between the Landlord and DP, and the information provided to the Landlord by police, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that DP transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. Daily Compensation

The Landlord requested in t he application that the [name] Occupants be required to pay compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit, but the Landlord did not present evidence about the lawful rent, and does not know the identities of the unauthorized occupants. I cannot therefore order that compensation be paid.
