issues: rminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupants') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants without the Landlord’s consent. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-038527-25 issued on January 29, 2026. Amended order, LTB-L-038527-25-AM, was issued on February 26, 2026 to correct a clerical error in the original order. On February 22, 2026, the Tenants requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On March 9, 2026 interim order LTB-L-038527-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on January 29, 2026. On May 28, 2026, interim order LTB-L-038527-25-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the review request, cancelling the January 29, 2026 order as amended on February 26, 2026, and directing the application be heard de novo (anew). The de novo hearing was held by videoconference on July 22, 2026. The Landlord’s Agent [name] [name], the Landlord’s Legal Representative [name], the Tenant [name] and the Tenant [name]’s Agent June [name] attended the hearing. June [name] also provided support to [name]. As of 2:02 p.m. the Unauthorized Occupants were not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the evidence of the Landlord and the Tenants.
reasons: On May 5, 2025, the Landlord filed this application with the Board to terminate the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants and evict the Unauthorized Occupants because the Tenants transferred the tenancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The tenancy agreement is for site 2A-16, 16 [address] in Erin, Ontario. The Tenants own a mobile home that is situated on the rented site. The definition of residential unit in section 2(1) of the Act includes a site for a mobile home. As such, for the purposes of clarity, in this order “rental unit” refers to this rented site, not the mobile home itself.

Section 95 of the Act permits a tenant to assign a rental unit to another person with the consent of the Landlord. Section 95(9) of the Act confirms the requirement to obtain the Landlord’s consent to transfer the tenancy applies to all tenants and there is no exception for tenants residing in a mobile home they own.

The Landlord’s evidence was that on March 11, 2025 it was discovered that the Tenants had transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants. [name] [name] testified upon discovering the unauthorized transfer, they attempted to negotiate a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized Occupants but did not succeed as the Unauthorized Occupants did not respond to them.

In the absence of a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized Occupants, the Landlord filed this application under section 100 of the Act on May 5, 2025. This is within 60 days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy as required by section 100(2) of the Act.

The Tenants did not dispute the basis for this application. They agreed they transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants and did not seek the Landlord’s consent to do so.

The Tenants acknowledged that in January 2025 they moved out of their mobile home and rented it to the Unauthorized Occupants. The Tenants collected rent from the Unauthorized Occupants and continued to pay the monthly rent to the Landlord. At the hearing, the parties agreed there are no arrears of rent owing.

The Tenants explained they misunderstood section 156(1) of the Act and as such, believed they could assign the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants without obtaining the consent of the Landlord. Section 156(1) states the Tenants has the right to sell or lease their mobile home without the consent of the Landlord but does not permit the transfer of the rental unit without consent.
The parties agreed the Unauthorized Occupants have now vacated the rental unit and no one is currently residing in the mobile home or using the rental unit for residential purposes.

Based on the undisputed evidence presented at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the consent of the Landlord and that this transfer was not authorized by the Act. I am also satisfied the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized Occupants and that this application was filed within 60 days of the Landlord discovering the unauthorized transfer. Section 83 Considerations

The Landlord sought termination of the tenancy citing their interest in having control of the unoccupied rental unit and who uses the unit for residential purposes. The Landlord acknowledged the Tenants own the mobile home situated on the rental and that termination in the standard time is not realistic.

The Tenants’ testimony was they now reside elsewhere and have since January 2025. They agreed no one lives at the rental unit and acknowledged the Landlord wants them to vacate and that they want to sell their mobile home. There was no evidence from the Tenants that they plan or wish to move back into their mobile home.

The Tenant gave evidence that they cannot afford to relocate the mobile home from the rental unit. They submitted an estimate showing the cost would be approximately $17,400.00 to move the mobile home.

The Tenants explained that an undertaking with the Landlord requires them to maintain and correct deficiencies at the unit and to the mobile home. This undertaking hinders their ability to sell the mobile home and assign the rental unit to a purchaser.

The Tenants do not believe the conditions in the undertaking are reasonable and want the Landlord to waive these conditions to facilitate a sale. The Landlord is not prepared to agree to waive the undertaking. [name] explained the requirements are based on park rules permitted under the Act and that they apply to all tenants at the mobile home park.

The Tenants also explained these conditions would result in costs that would reduce the amount of useable equity in the mobile home upon the sale of it. The Tenants state they need the proceeds from the sale to address unexpected costs at their current home and to avoid financial hardship.

The Tenants were asked about the financial details surrounding the mobile home and its approximate value. The Tenants purchased the home for approximately $160,000.00 and that it had been sold conditionally for $350,000.00. The conditions required the Tenants to pay the costs related to the undertaking with the Landlord and the sale did not complete. The Tenants submitted the market for the mobile home is now weaker but submitted no current market analysis showing the market is depressed or to what degree.

The Tenants also explained the situation has caused them a significant amount of stress and worry. The Tenant [name] suffers from anxiety and mental health issues that are exacerbated by the circumstances and concern for their finances.

The Tenants submitted that if the Landlord’s application for termination of the tenancy is granted, they would need 9 to 12 months to sell their mobile home. The home is not currently listed as the Tenants explained the difficulty in finding a buyer without finality in these proceedings. The Tenants intend to list the mobile home quickly as they are motivated to sell it. The Landlord was not opposed to a delay in the termination of the tenancy but submitted 9-12 months was not reasonable given the application was filed in May 2025.

In my view, there is no basis to deny termination of the tenancy in circumstances where the Tenants no longer live at the rental unit and have expressed no interest in returning. I find refusing termination in this case would be unfair to the Landlord.

However, I am satisfied that despite the Tenants’ actions in transferring the tenancy in an unauthorized manner, they should be given additional time to find a suitable buyer or make arrangements to move the mobile home if they are unable to sell. I note the Tenants have continued to pay the Landlord the monthly rent and as such the prejudice to them is therefore reduced.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the termination of the tenancy until February 28, 2027 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

This additional time amounts to just more than seven months. While longer than the Landlord submitted was reasonable and less than that requested by the Tenants, I find this additional time balances the interests of the Landlord while also providing the Tenants an opportunity to minimize any financial impact while keeping them motivated to sell or remove the mobile home from the rental unit. Lastly, the additional time is also meant to alleviate the impact to the mental health of both Tenants that a shorter period to termination would likely cause.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated effective February 28, 2027.
If the unit is not vacated by February 28, 2027, then starting March 1, 2027, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after March 1, 2027.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 10, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies (LTB-L-039347-26). [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order determining that the Landlord entered the unit illegally, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment, and harassed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with him. The applications were heard together by videoconference on July 28, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant rented a room from the Landlord from around 2020 to 2026. In 2025, the Landlord asked the Tenant to move out. She took the position that the tenancy was not governed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), and that she could therefore terminate it without following the processes set out in the RTA. The Tenant took the position that the RTA applied, and refused to move.
On May 1, 2026, the Landlord filed application LTB-L-039347-26, seeking a finding that the RTA did not apply.

On May 11, 2026, the Tenant filed application LTB-T-041140-26, seeking a finding that the Landlord had contravened his RTA rights by asking him to move in 2025, and that / LTB-T-041140-26-IN her subsequent conduct had also contravened the RTA. The application was premised on his position that the RTA applied to the tenancy.

At the time the applications were filed, the Tenant had temporarily moved out of the property to avoid ongoing conflicts with the Landlord. He hoped that the applications would resolve the conflicts so that he could move back in.

The two applications came before me on July 28, 2026. By that point, the Tenant no longer wished to move back into the unit. The parties agree that the tenancy has ended. The questions before me are therefore: whether the RTA applied to the tenancy in 2025 and 2026; whether the Landlord contravened the RTA; and what monetary remedies should be awarded for the contraventions.

At the July 28 hearing, I heard evidence and submissions on the threshold question of whether the RTA applied, and reserved my decision. This interim order sets out that decision. For the following reasons, I find that the RTA applied to the tenancy at the relevant times.
This order resolves the Landlord’s application to determine whether the RTA applied. The remaining issues in the Tenant’s application will be heard on a date to be scheduled. Facts
The residential complex is a house. The Landlord owns the house. The Tenant is the Landlord’s nephew.

The Landlord previously lived in the house with a different nephew. In 2020, that nephew moved out and the Tenant and another nephew moved in. The two nephews rented rooms in the house, and shared common spaces with the Landlord including the kitchen, one of the bathrooms, and laundry facilities.

The Landlord testified that in June 2024, she “evicted” both nephews. However, the Tenant then convinced her to let him stay on the basis that he would maintain and renovate the property. They agreed that the Tenant would pay a monthly rent of $800.00.

At some point, the Landlord stopped living in the property full-time. She was suffering from health issues, and started staying with her sister in order to be closer to medical supports and surgery. She left her furniture, and at least some belongings, in the house. She returned from time to time to pack up her belongings, and sometimes slept in a bed in the living room.

In August, 2025, the Landlord decided to put the house up for sale. At that point, she discovered that the Tenant had not maintained and renovated the property to her satisfaction. She told him to move out. The Tenant refused, taking the position that his tenancy could only be terminated in accordance with the RTA. / LTB-T-041140-26-IN Analysis

When the Tenant rented a room from the Landlord in 2020, the parties entered into a residential tenancy within the meaning of the RTA. However, the tenancy was exempt from the RTA pursuant to section 5(i), which provides that the RTA does not apply to: living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner…, and where the owner… lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.
In 2020, the Landlord lived in the building and the Tenant was required to share a kitchen and bathroom with her.

On the evidence before me, the original tenancy agreement ended in June, 2024. The Landlord testified that she “evicted” the Tenant, which I take to mean that she unilaterally ended his tenancy. She was entitled to do so, since the tenancy was not governed by the RTA. The parties then negotiated a new residential tenancy agreement with substantially different terms: the Tenant’s rent was changed to $800.00, and he was required to maintain and renovate the property as a condition of the tenancy.
The question before me is therefore whether the 2024 tenancy was exempt from the RTA pursuant to section 5(i).

As the party seeking the exemption, the Landlord bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that 2024 tenancy met the criteria set out in section 5(i). In other words, she must prove that she lived in the building when the 2024 tenancy was formed ([name] v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628 (CanLII)), and that the terms of the 2024 tenancy required that the Tenant share a bathroom or kitchen with her. Did the Landlord live in the building?

The Landlord argues that while she was staying with her sister, she was still living in the premises. Essentially, she argues that she was a temporary guest of her sister while receiving medical treatment, but that her home was always this property.

It is true that the Landlord maintained a connection to the property while staying with her sister. However, the evidence does not establish that the connection was sufficient to constitute “living” in the property within the meaning of section 5(i).
The Landlord’s belongings remained in the house, but at some point she packed them up for storage. She was unclear as to when she packed them up.

The Landlord visited the property from time to time, for the purpose of packing up her belongings and preparing the house for a sale. On those occasions, she slept at the property. When asked on cross-examination, she testified vaguely that she slept there “a couple of months, or a weekend, or a week or two.” She did not clarify or elaborate. / LTB-T-041140-26-IN
When she slept in the property, the Landlord slept in the living room, not in her own bedroom. She testified that this was because she slept on a hospital bed, which did not fit in her bedroom.
The Landlord kept some non-perishable food in the house, but brought fresh food with her on the nights that she slept in the property.

In sum, the Landlord primarily used the property to store her belongings. She occasionally visited for the purpose of packing her belongings and otherwise preparing the house for sale. When she visited, she stayed overnight, but brought food with her and slept in the living room. She did not maintain a bedroom for her own use. She has not established that her visits were at all frequent. In my view, she was not “living” in the property.

The evidence was unclear as to the date on which the Landlord stopped living in the property and started staying with her sister. The Landlord did not argue that the 2024 tenancy was formed before she left the property. She has not proved, on a balance of probabilities, that she was living in the property when the 2024 tenancy was formed. Did the 2024 tenancy agreement require that the Tenant share a bathroom or kitchen with the Landlord?
For similar reasons, the Landlord has also not proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the 2024 tenancy agreement required that the Tenant share a bathroom or kitchen with her.

When the parties negotiated the 2024 agreement, there is no evidence that they discussed the possibility that the Landlord would return to the property, either to live there or to stay briefly while packing up her belongings. There is no evidence that they agreed that the Landlord would continue to use any part of the building, including the bathroom or kitchen.

If the Landlord had still been living in the property, then the parties could be taken to have impliedly agreed that she would continue to use the bathroom and kitchen. However, as discussed above, the evidence does not show that the Landlord still lived in the property when the 2024 tenancy was negotiated. Result

The Landlord argues that the Tenant was a “boarder.” I take her to mean that he was living with her and sharing a kitchen and bathroom with her, and that the tenancy was therefore exempt from the RTA pursuant to section 5(i).

The Landlord is correct that the Tenant was a “boarder” between 2020 and 2024. However, in 2024 the Landlord ended that tenancy, negotiated a new tenancy with the Tenant, and moved out of the property. For the above reasons, she has not proved that the Tenant was still a “boarder” under the new agreement. / LTB-T-041140-26-IN
I therefore find that the RTA applied to the tenancy from June, 2024 onwards. The Tenant’s application concerns alleged conduct that occurred after June, 2024. The Tenant’s application may proceed.
ordered: The RTA applied to the tenancy from June, 2024 to the date the tenancy ended.
The hearing of the Tenant’s application is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB.
The parties shall provide their unavailable dates for the months of September, October, and November to the LTB by August 6, 2026.
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: LTD (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict Jacinda [name], [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord brings this A2 application pursuant to subsection 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.
Subsection 100(2) requires that an application of this nature must be filed within sixty days after the Landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. This application was filed on June 1, 2026.

The legal test on this type of an application is as follows: a) Did the Tenant transfer occupancy of the rental unit to another person without the Landlord’s consent as contemplated in subsection 100(1) of the Act? b) Did the Landlord file this application within sixty days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy as required by subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’)? c) If the Tenant did transfer occupancy and the Landlord filed the application in time, should the Tenant be granted relief from eviction pursuant to section 83 of the Act
The Landlord’s uncontested evidence was the Tenant passed away on April 29, 2026. The Unauthorized Occupant referred to in this application is the Tenant’s daughter.

The Landlord testified that the lease agreement named the Tenant as the sole leaseholder, who lived in the rental unit. The Landlord further testified that they had not entered into a new lease agreement with the Unauthorized Occupant after the Tenant’s death nor did they consent to the transfer of the tenancy during the Tenant’s lifetime or thereafter.
The Landlord seeks an order for eviction and compensation pursuant to subsection 100(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 as well as reimbursement of the application filing fee. ANALYSIS

I find that the application was filed within sixty days of discovery and thus, on time. I also find that the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized [name] on consent to a transfer of this tenancy.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the tenancy terminated on May 29, 2026 pursuant to section 91 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which states: 91 (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant.
This means the occupants of the rental unit became Unauthorized [name] as of May 30, 2026.

The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized [name] pursuant to subsection 100(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which states: (3) A landlord who makes an application under subsection (1) may also apply to the Board for an order for the payment of compensation by the unauthorized occupant for the use and occupation of the rental unit, if the unauthorized occupant is in possession of the rental unit at the time the application is made.
I find the Unauthorized [name] were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
As the tenancy here terminated on May 29, 2026, the Unauthorized Occupant is liable for daily compensation beginning May 30, 2026 to the date they vacate the rental unit.
Daily compensation is calculated as follows: [$1,673.56 x 12 months ÷ 365 days/year] x 40 days (May 30 2026 to the hearing date) = $2,200.85.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The total amount owing by the Unauthorized [name] is $2,401.85. Section 83 Considerations

The Landlord advised the Board they were aware that the Unauthorized Occupant suffered from mental health issues; as the Unauthorized Occupant was not present at the hearing to articulate their circumstances including the impact of eviction, I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated on May 29, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by July 31, 2026, then starting August 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after August 1, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $2,200.85 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from May 30, 2026 to the July 8, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $55.02 per day for compensation for the use of the unit starting July 9, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Group (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] et al (the 'Unauthorized Occupants') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] and other Unauthorized Occupants without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupants for the use of the rental unit. The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupants to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex.
reasons: The Landlord filed their application alleging that they first became aware that the Tenant, U. [name] (UR) had transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to unauthorized persons on April 8, 2025. They are seeking unpaid rent. They also filed an application seeking reasonable costs to repair property damaged by the Tenant or their unauthorized occupants in the amount of $30,000.00.
The rental unit is a two bedroom new-build condo. The monthly rent, or occupancy fee, is $3,685.45.
The parties agreed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale, dated June 22, 2019. Within that agreement, in [name], are the Terms of Occupancy Licence.

The Landlord’s agent, S. [name] (SJ), is in sales and customer care for the condo sales of the Landlord. She said that when purchasers buy a condo they have a right to live in the condo prior to the closing of the sale, under an occupancy agreement. The monthly rent is charged as an “occupancy fee”. She said that the Tenant first went into default in paying their occupancy fee in February 2025, and she submitted into evidence the letter sent by the Landlord to the Tenant about the default. The date on the letter is a clerical error. SJ said that it was sent to the Tenant in February 2025. SJ said that after a purchaser defaults in paying their occupancy fee, they get reminder letters, then they are given a period of time to leave, and then their purchase agreement is cancelled, and that is what happened in this tenancy. All this is outlined in the Agreement of Purchase and Sale submitted into evidence. It is dated June 22, 2019.

SJ said that the Landlord was notified of a leak in the rental unit on April 8, 2025, by one of the neighbours. She said that the occupants of the rental unit were not at home when the Landlord’s employees went to investigate, but the occupants arrived later. She said that the occupants kept referring to themselves as “tenants”. The only name communicated to the Landlord for the unauthorized occupants was “[name]”. [name] said that when the Landlord inspected, they found defrosting food in the sink, causing water to overflow and leak into the unit. She submitted into evidence a series of photos taken on April 8, 2025, that show water on the carpet in the hallway outside the rental unit, flooding water on the floor in the unit, water leaking inside the walls in the unit directly below the rental unit, and even water leaking into the unit below that one. She said that there was water leaking through ceiling vent into a unit four floors below the rental unit. SJ submitted into evidence a video of the leaking sink taken on the day of the flooding. The video showed a sink filled with defrosting items, and the sink was overflowing with water pouring into the entire unit.

SJ said that there were other reports about occupants of the unit causing problems. She submitted into evidence an incident report, dated September 5, 2025, in which children from the rental unit were observed causing damage to a light post outside the building.

The Landlord now seeks $20,329.08 for the cost of all repairs done by the Landlord as a result of the flood on April 8, 2025, which includes floor replacement costs, removal and disposal of damaged materials, wall replacement and painting to all the units affected by the flooding, replacement of carpet in the hallway, and replacement of a front door lock damaged by the Tenant or their occupants. The Landlord amended their application to request an extra $186.45 for the cost of replacing a damaged door lock (they submitted into evidence documentary evidence of this extra cost).
The Landlord is not seeking the compensation owed by the Tenants. The Landlord is only seeking reimbursement for the damage caused.

SJ said that the named Landlord is still responsible for the rental unit, and the Landlord continues to pay condo fees. She said that the Tenant asked to be reinstated, and the Landlord replied with terms and conditions. However, she said the Tenant did not respond to the terms and conditions. Reasons and Analysis:

This matter is within the jurisdiction of the Board for the following reasons. Pursuant to subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a “tenancy agreement” includes a licence to occupy a rental unit. Subsection 58(1)4 of the Act specifically contemplates this type of agreement as coming under the Act, as it provides that notices of termination under the Act may be given to a Tenant when the tenancy arose by virtue or “collateral to an agreement of purchase and sale of a proposed unit within the meaning of the Condominium Act, 1998 in good faith and the agreement of purchase and sale has been terminated.”

The Landlord had documentary evidence that the Tenant breached the terms of the collateral agreement of purchase and sale by failing to pay the occupancy fee, even after several reminders and opportunities to pay it. This terminated the agreement of purchase and sale, and the sale was never completed.

Since the Act applies to this relationship, and the Landlord had the right to serve the Tenant with a notice of termination, section 100 of the Act relating to unauthorized transfers of tenancy also applies.

For the reasons that follow, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to [name] and other Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person/these persons.

I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant, [name] and/or the other unauthorized occupants caused wilful or negligent damage in the rental unit, and they are responsible to pay the Landlord for the out-of-pocket expenses incurred to the Landlord to repair the damage for the following reasons.

The Landlord discovered on April 8, 2025, after responding to flooding in the rental unit, that the unit was occupied by unauthorized persons, not the Tenant. The Tenant had not asked the Landlord for authorization to install these people in the rental unit. According to the Agreement of Purchase and Sale, it was only the Tenant who had the right to occupy the rental unit prior to the closing of the purchase of the rental unit, as long as the Tenant paid the occupancy fee. The Tenant had a right to request authorization to install other people, but the Tenant never did so. The Tenant defaulted on paying the occupancy fee as of February 2025, and the sale never went through.

The Landlord had video evidence and testimonial evidence about the damage caused by the leak and subsequent flooding that originated in the rental unit on April 8, 2025. They had documentary evidence of the amount the Landlord had to spend to repair the flooding in the rental unit and the other units affected by the flooding.

The Landlord’s witnesses testified that they had communication with the Unauthorized Occupants when they came home after the flooding, referring to themselves as “tenants”, and they were therefore in possession of the rental unit on the date the damage was caused. They were still in possession on the date the application was filed.
The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and they are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord has incurred reasonable costs of $20,329.08 to repair the damage, or to replace property that was damaged and cannot be repaired. I find that both the Tenant and [name] and the other Unauthorized Occupants are jointly liable for this damage. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. In particular, the Tenant stopped paying their occupancy fees a long time ago, and it is prejudicial to the Landlord for this tenancy to continue. The Landlord has also suffered severe financial prejudice as a result of the unauthorized transfer of the tenancy to the unauthorized occupants. The unauthorized occupants caused extensive damage to the rental unit and other units in the building. Neither the Tenant nor the unauthorized occupants attended the hearing to explain any mitigating circumstances to delay or deny eviction.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Tenant, [name] and the Unauthorized Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 16, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 16, 2026, then starting June 17, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 17, 2026.
The Tenant, [name] and the Unauthorized Occupants shall pay to the Landlord $20,329.08, which represents the reasonable costs of repairing the damage or replacing the damaged property.
The Tenant, [name] and the Unauthorized Occupants shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Tenant, [name] and/or the Unauthorized Occupants do not vacate the rental unit on or before June 16, 2026, they shall also pay to the Landlord $121.17 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from June 17, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Tenant, [name], and/or the Unauthorized Occupants shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 16, 2026. June 5, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally. The Landlords applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) applies. These applications were resolved by order LTB-T-092542-25_ LTB-L-078767-25 issued on May 7, 2026. On May 18, 2026, the Landlords requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On May 19, 2026, interim order LTB-T-092542-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 7, 2026. The review request was heard by videoconference on July 16, 2026. The first named Landlord and the Landlords’ legal representative Taff Butters and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: By way of background, in the May 7, 2026 order, the presiding Member dismissed the [name] application having found that the Landlords did not serve a termination notice under section 48 or 49 of the Act and therefore not required to compensate the Tenant.

With respect to the Landlords’ A1 application, the Member found that the Act applies. Additionally, the Member imposed an administrative fine for the Landlords to pay the Tenants $1,000.00 and cited authority to do so under s.57(3) of the Act.

In the review request, the Landlords assert that Board lacked the jurisdiction to levy a fine in this circumstance and asks the Board to vary the order to remove the fine. Additionally, it was procedurally unfair of the Member to impose a fine without first identifying the statutory basis for the penalty and to seek submissions from the parties at the hearing.

For clarity, the Board form T1 application does not provide for a request for an administrative fine. However, the Member cites s.57(3) of the Act which allows for the Board to order “any other order that the Board considers appropriate” at paragraph 24 of the order.

The Member expressly found that the Landlords did not serve a termination notice to the Tenants under s. 48 or 49 and dismissed the application. Having made this determination, the Member should not have imposed a punitive fine against the Landlords. This finding leads to an internal contradiction and the Board lacked the jurisdiction to levy such a fine.
The Board is a statutory tribunal and it has the authority to consider claims that fall within its jurisdiction.

In the context of the A1 application, and as explained at the hearing, the only outcome of such application is a determination as to whether the Act applies. Therefore, the order to pay the fine was made outside of the Board’s jurisdiction.
The parties confirmed the balance of the order remains unchallenged. The order will be varied by removing the order related to the administrative fine.
On the basis of the submissions made in the request, I am satisfied that there is a serious error in the order when the Landlords were ordered to pay an administrative fine.
The parties were informed of my decision at the hearing.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-092542-25 issued on May 7, 2026 is granted. The order is varied in the following manner
Paragraph 2 of the May 7, 2026 order is varied to remove the order for the Landlords to pay the administrative fine.
The balance of the May 7, 2026 order remains in full force and effect.
The interim order issued on May 19, 2026 is cancelled and replaced with this order. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlord, [name] [name] (A.G.), testified that he and his wife are the legal owners/landlords of the rental property identified in this application.
A.G. testified that he entered into a residential lease agreement with an individual by the name of Harinder [name]. This individual was the sole named tenant on the lease agreement.

A.G. testified that [name] [name] occupied the rental unit on June 12, 2022. Mr. [name]name] occupied the rental unit with his two sons, [name] and [name] [name], as well as his daughter in law, [name], and his grandchild. A.G. confirmed that none of the three adults that occupied the unit with the Tenant signed the lease or were listed as tenants on the lease. A.G. was aware that [name] [name] would be occupying the unit with his family.

A.G. testified that he provided lock box access to the Tenant’s son, [name] [name]. A.G. also testified that most of the communications relating to the tenancy were by email or text and would be between the Landlord and either [name] or [name]. The communications included maintenance issues such as dishwasher and air conditioning repairs.

A.G. also testified that the rental payments would primarily be made by electronic transfer or cash payment, which were always paid by [name] or [name]. A.G. testified that the transfers made came from a corporation which was registered under the names of [name] [name] [name] and [name]. The Landlord uploaded copies of email communications, payment history, and incorporation documents as evidence.

A.G. testified that he believed and viewed [name] and [name] as tenants and not occupants or guests of the Tenant. [name] testified that both [name] and [name] used the rental unit as their primary residence.

A.G. was seeking an order which found [name] and [name] to be tenants by virtue of an implied tenancy between the parties. The Landlords’ Representative submitted that a lease can be oral, written, or implied.

On cross-examination, A.G. confirmed that the sole tenant identified in the residential lease agreement was [name] [name]. The lease was never amended to add or include any additional individuals as tenants. The individuals never requested to be added to the lease agreement in the capacity of tenants. A.G. also confirmed that [name] [name] occupied the rental unit for the duration of the residential tenancy.

A.G. also confirmed agreeing to sign the lease agreement with [name] [name], identified as the sole tenant. He also testified that this was common practice in his culture to have the eldest family member sign the lease as the head of the household.

The Tenant, [name] (T.S.A.), testified that he moved into the rental property with his spouse, child, brother and his father. He was not listed as a tenant on the lease agreement and understood that he was occupying the rental unit on the capacity of an occupant or guest of his father’s, the individual named as the sole tenant on the lease agreement.

T.S.A. confirmed that he communicated with the Landlord regarding all the issues as relating to the residential tenancy. He stated that this was done so that he could act as a go between his father and the Landlord because of a dispute that arose on or about September 2023, at which time the Landlord no longer wanted to communicate with T.S.A.’s father who was identified as the sole tenant on the lease.

T.S.A. testified that he moved to Canada on or about April 2022, and that his father was already living in Canada at that time. He never agreed to be added as a tenant to the lease and never requested to be added as a tenant.

On cross-examination, T.S.A. confirmed that the rental unit was his primary residence in Canada for the duration of the lease term. T.S.A. also confirmed that either he or his partner would make the rental payments to the Landlord on behalf of his father. T.S.A. confirmed that the payments were made on behalf of his father. T.S.A. also testified that the utility payments made to the Landlord were also made on behalf of [name] [name], the tenant named in the lease agreement.

The Landlord’s Representative argued that the Board should make a finding that [name] and [name] are Tenants by virtue of an implied tenancy agreement. The Landlord relied on the communications between the Landlord, and the named Tenants, rent and utilities being paid by the named Tenants, as well as the named Tenants occupying the rental unit in the capacity of their primary residence.

The Tenant’s Representative argued that the individuals listed in this application were residing in the rental unit in the capacity of guests or occupants of the Tenant, [name] [name]. The lease clearly identified one sole tenant. All rent and utility payments were made on behalf of their father, the tenant named in the lease. All communications were between these individuals and the Landlord because of a previous dispute between the Landlord and tenant named in the lease. They simply acted as a go between and never entered the tenancy in the capacity of tenants.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the relationship between the Landlord and the two individuals named in this application is that of a Landlord and Tenant relationship. I am making this finding because I am not satisfied that an implied tenancy exists between these parties. Despite the named tenants in this application paying the rent, utilities, and having communications with the Landlord throughout the residential tenancy, a written lease was executed at the commencement of this tenancy between AG and [name] [name]. Payments towards the rent or utility accounts do not create an implied tenancy. I find it is just as probable that the rental and utility payments and communications were done by these individuals on behalf of the Tenant in the capacity of occupants. I do not have sufficient evidence of these individuals having control or exercising their discretion with respect to any decisions made regarding the tenancy. Therefore, I do not find that the individuals named in this application to be tenants.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name]Wellington (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant passed away on August 19, 2025. This was established by the Statement of Death submitted into evidence.
The Landlord became aware that an unauthorized occupant was residing in the rental unit on September 18, 2025. The Landlord subsequently filed this application on November 7, 2025.

The evidence establishes that, during the period of unauthorized occupancy, a significant fire occurred in the rental unit on December 2, 2025. The fire destroyed the rental unit and its contents. As a result, the Unauthorized Occupant vacated the rental unit. The evidence further indicates that the rental unit remains under repair and is not presently habitable.

The rental unit is a rent-geared-to-income unit. The evidence includes an occupancy agreement entered into between the Landlord and [name] on May 16, 2025. The occupancy agreement provides that the occupant must vacate the rental unit on or before the date the Tenant vacates the rental unit, or upon the Tenant’s request.

Subsection 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that where a tenant dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy is deemed terminated 30 days after the tenant’s death.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant died on August 19, 2025 and that there were no other tenants named on the tenancy agreement. Accordingly, pursuant to subsection 91(1) of the Act, the tenancy was deemed terminated on September 18, 2025.

Following the termination of the tenancy, the Occupant no longer had any legal right to remain in possession of the rental unit. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the [name] was an unauthorized occupant and was in possession of the rental unit when the Landlord became aware of the occupancy and when this application was filed.

Although the Landlord has established that the [name] was unauthorized, the evidence also establishes that the Occupant has vacated the rental unit following the fire of December 2, 2025. In these circumstances, I do not find it necessary to issue an eviction order against the [name].

However, given that the tenancy was deemed terminated by operation of law on September 18, 2025 and that the Landlord seeks confirmation of its right to possession, I find it appropriate to issue an order terminating the tenancy and returning possession of the rental unit to the Landlord. Such an order will clarify the status of the tenancy and confirm the Landlord’s lawful entitlement to possession of the rental unit. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.

The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $823.50 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from September 18, 2025 to December 2, 2025, the date the Unauthorized Occupant vacated the rental unit.
The lawful monthly rent is $334.00.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $10.98. This amount is calculated as follows: $334.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 to file the application and is entitled to recover those costs. Based on the occupancy agreement, the Unauthorized Occupant knew or ought reasonably to have known that their right to occupy the rental unit ended upon the termination of the Tenant’s occupancy. Despite this, the Unauthorized Occupant remained in possession of the rental unit. Accordingly, I find it appropriate to hold the Unauthorized Occupant responsible for reimbursing the Landlord for the application filing fee of $201.00.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $823.50 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from September 18, 2025 to the December 2, 2025.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 13, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlords' consent. The Landlords also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to evict (the 'SubTenants') because the subtenancy ended and the SubTenants continue to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord testified that the tenancy commenced in June 2022 and that the Tenants did not provide notice to terminate the tenancy. On November 10, 2025, the Landlord observed three unknown individuals residing in the rental unit. The following day, he contacted the Tenants, who advised that they had sublet the rental unit and were no longer residing in Toronto, having relocated for employment purposes.

The Landlord testified that the Tenants never sought or obtained his consent to sublet the rental unit. He stated that he was prepared to consider entering into a tenancy agreement with the occupants, provided they supplied information regarding their identities.

The Landlord further testified that the Tenants had no intention of returning to reside in the rental unit and that the [name] residing in the unit had changed on at least two occasions since the Tenants vacated.
The Landlord testified that, notwithstanding their absence from the rental unit, the Tenants continued to remit the monthly rent to the Landlord on behalf of the [name].

The Landlord also testified that an L1 application, bearing Board file number LTB-L- 023269-26, was filed seeking termination of the tenancy for non-payment of rent. Following the hearing of this application and prior to the issuance of this [name], an order was issued in that proceeding on May 27, 2026.

The L1 Order was issued on consent and terminated the tenancy effective June 30, 2026. The L1 Order also addressed any rent arrears outstanding up to the date the Tenants were required to vacate and any per diem compensation thereafter. Accordingly, I find it unnecessary to make any further findings with respect to arrears of rent or termination of the tenancy, as those issues have already been determined.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants vacated the rental unit and transferred possession of the unit to other individuals without the Landlord’s consent. Given the Tenants’ admission that they had relocated outside of Toronto for employment and had no intention of returning to the rental unit, I find that the arrangement was not a lawful sublet but rather an unauthorized transfer of occupancy.

Although the tenancy has since been terminated pursuant to the L1 Order, the Landlord was required to commence this application as a result of the unauthorized transfer. The Landlord incurred a filing fee of $201.00. In the circumstances, I find that the Landlord is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee in the amount of $201.00.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenants is terminated in accordance with Board Order LTB-L-023269-26.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlords $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlords the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlords the full amount owing by July 13, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] Occupant(s) (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: At the hearing the [name] [name] wished to rely on and introduce documentary disclosure which had not been posted to the Portal (‘TOP’) as of the date of the proceeding.
Uploading materials to TOP does not mean documents have been provided to another party unless there is an agreement in place and, here, there was no such agreement.

The Landlord’s Representative objected to the [name] Occupant being permitted to rely on any documentary disclosure alleged to be in his possession as the Landlord or himself had not been served any of this alleged documentary disclosure.

Rule 19.1 of the LTB’s Rules provides that all materials on which a party intends to rely at a hearing must be provided to the other party and the LTB 7 days in advance of the hearing. Rule 19.7 provides, in part, that a party who fails to comply with Rule 19 may not rely on evidence that was not properly disclosed unless ordered otherwise.
To comply with the disclosure requirements the [name] [name] had to provide his materials on which he intended to rely to the Landlord on or before July 9, 2026. This was not done.
Absent a satisfactory explanation as to why the [name] [name] could not have done so, the [name] [name] is not able to introduce nor rely on any documentary materials that may be in his possession.

The Board’s records show the Notice of Hearing – which advises parties of their disclosure obligations mailed to the [name] Occupant on June 1, 2026. Approximately 1.5 months prior to the hearing. The [name] Occupant acknowledged receiving the same.
In the above circumstances I am not satisfied the [name] [name] could not have complied with the Rules.

As a result, the [name] [name] was not permitted to rely on materials he may have in his possession, as alleged. The [name] [name] remains free to seek legal advice and/or pursue any timely issues under the Act. Determination: [name] transfer of occupancy

For the reasons which follow, the Former Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with these persons.
The [name] Occupants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord’s Agent [name] (RB) testified that he is the regional manager for the Landlord and that the Landlord discovered that the Tenant, Mr. [name]name] was not residing in the rental unit on November 25, 2025, and the [name] Occupants were in fact in possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with these individuals. RB testified that the Landlord was not aware that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit until November 25, 2025, and the Landlord surmises the Tenant may have vacated in July 2025, as rent from August 1, 2025, to the date of this proceeding had not been paid, and previous to this had been paid by the Tenant.

The [name] Occupant [name] testified that he and his mother have been living in the unit since August 2021, when the previous Tenant vacated the rental unit, and he believed the necessary documents were completed and sent to the Landlord, that he and his mother were the Tenants and would pay the ongoing rent, as there was mutual agreement with the previous Tenant, but it seems the previous Tenant may have removed the [name] Occupants as tenants on his own accord.

On cross examination [name] testified that he has not provided any documentary evidence of his alleged agreement with the previous Tenant or the Landlord, nor has he provided any substantive evidence that he has paid any rent to the Landlord, and he acknowledged that the last payment received by the Landlord was made by the previous Tenant on August 8, 2025, and confirmed that he nor his mother have paid rent since that time as his mother is dealing with medical issues and he is currently unemployed. [name] continued to testify on cross examination that the previous Tenant secretly removed his information from the tenancy agreement, however, did not provide any documentary evidence to substantiate the same pursuant to the Board’s Rules, and that he had never applied for an assignment of the tenancy.

It is the Landlord’s Agent RB position that there was no agreement that the [name] Occupants could remain in the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, even if they were the Tenant’s occupants which the Landlord was unaware of and has just heard this evidence at this proceeding. Moreover, the [name] [name] had not sought an assignment of the tenancy, nor had they entered into a new tenancy agreement with the Landlord, nor had the Landlord received any payments of rent from the [name] [name] and it is the Landlord’s position these parties are [name] [name], and there is no tenancy agreement with them, nor have the [name] Occupants provided any documentary evidence to substantiate otherwise. Analysis

Subsection 100(1) of the Act stipulates the following: [name] occupancy 100 (1) If a Former Tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Former Tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.
Subsection 100(2) of the Act stipulates that an application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy.

I accept that the previous Tenant vacated the rental unit around the end of July 2025 as supported by the testimony of RB and the last payment received from the Tenant on August 8, 2025 and that the Landlord was not aware there were [name] Occupants in the rental unit until November 25, 2025, nor were they aware that the Tenant had vacated at that point, but surmise he did so around July 2025 after the fact by reviewing the rental ledger. I am not persuaded by the [name] Occupants testimony that the previous Tenant had vacated the rental unit on or about August 2021, and they had an agreement in place for them to take over the tenancy, and somehow the previous Tenant removed them from the tenancy agreement and documents with the Landlord, as there was nothing submitted pursuant to the Rules by the [name] Occupants which corroborates this.

The Landlord filed the A2 Application on December 3, 2025, which is less than 60 days after the Landlord discovered that the [name] Occupants were in the unit. I find this is supported by the evidence submitted and the oral testimony of the Landlord’s Agent RB, and I prefer his evidence to that of the [name] Occupant, [name], on a balance of probabilities. I further accept RB evidence that the Landlord had not entered into a new tenancy agreement with the [name] Occupants after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. This is supported by the [name] [name]’s [name] own testimony at the hearing in which he advised he had entered an agreement with the previous Tenant and somehow the Tenant had either not filed or removed his name from the Landlord’s records.

The [name] Occupants position that they have lived in the unit since prior to 2021 with the Tenant before he vacated as alleged by the [name] on or about August 2021 does not change their status as [name] Occupants. They did not pay rent directly to the Landlord and they did dispute that they are not named in any lease agreement but alleged there was an agreement with the Tenant and he must have removed them from the tenancy agreement, which the Landlord’s Agent RB vehemently denied.

For the above reasons and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Former Tenant [name] transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Act and that the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the [name] Occupants. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the [name] Occupants.
The [name] Occupants owe the Landlord $17,815.00 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from August 1, 2025, to the July 16, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $50.90. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,548.35 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the [name] [name], the Tenant and/or the [name] [name] paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
I have considered all the contested oral testimony and although I may not have referred to all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued
