issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Section 98 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply to the situation where a landlord is non- responsive to a request to assign a tenancy.
The Tenant’s filed an A2 application on December 22, 2025 which claimed that the Landlord arbitrarily refused consent for the Tenant’s to assign their 2-year fixed term tenancy. Facts
The parties entered into a two-year fixed term tenancy on August 5, 2024, commencing on August 23, 2024 through to July 31, 2026. Rent is due on the 23rd of the month.
The Tenant’s paid 1st and last months rent, along with an additional 2-months rent and a $150.00 key deposit to the Landlords.

On or about October 31, 2025, the Tenant, [name] sent the Landlord, [name] (‘TK’) a text message telling them they vacated on October 11, 2025 and asking for permission to consent to assign the tenancy agreement. No specific proposed assignee was mentioned.

The referenced text message can be found on page 24 of the Tenant’s Evidence Package (DOC-8183697) which stated: …Is it OK that we start to look for potential new renters ourselves to assign our lease…
BS testified that the Landlord did not respond to the text message.

As a result of the Landlord’s non-response to the request to assign the tenancy agreement, the Tenant gave notice to terminate in Form N9 to the Landlord via email on or about November 9, 2025, with a termination date of December 12, 2025.

On November 25, 2025, TK sent a text message to the Tenants’ realtor who informed her that the Tenants wished to return the keys and asking where the keys should be handed. TK sent two text messages which stated, “They are bound by the lease, so I am ok if they hold it.” and “Please tell them their last cheque bounced and to give me a new cheque.”

On November 25, 2025, the Tenants spoke with TK regarding the termination of the tenancy. BS stated that the Tenants were bound by the tenancy agreement and requested a replacement cheque for December 2025 rent payment. No resolution came from the conversation. Analysis

This application is brought pursuant to s. 98 of the Act which states: 98 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. [emphasis added]

Thus, this type of application can only be filed if a landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. With respect to assignments, s.95(5) states: A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of a rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3)(b). [Emphasis added.]

This reference in s. 95(5) to “clause (3) (b)” is to subparagraph 95(3)(b). Subsection 95(3) says: If a tenant asks a landlord to consent to the assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee, the landlord may, a. consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee; [name] consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee; or [name] consent to the assignment of the rental unit. [Emphasis added.]

These provisions to mean if a tenant asks a landlord to consent to an assignment to a potential assignee a landlord can refuse the particular proposed assignee or simply refuse permission to assign at all. More importantly, it is only where the landlord refuses consent to a particular proposed assignee that the right to make application to the Board under s. 98 is triggered.

In this case the Tenant did not propose a potential assignee who was refused by the Landlords. The Tenant made a general request to assign without identifying a specific potential assignee. What the Landlord did here was refuse consent to assignment by way of non-response. The Landlords did not respond to the text message of the Tenants. In other words, the Landlord chose paragraph 95(4)(c).
What this means is that s. 95(3)(b) does not apply to this situation. The consequence of that is that the right to file application under s. 98(1) and does not exist in this instance.

Subsection 98(1) is intended to address the situation where a arbitrarily or unreasonably refuses consent for a particular proposed assignee. The Tenants did not put forth a particular person to be the assignee and therefore the application cannot succeed and s. 98 does not apply.

Under s. 95(4)(b) of the Act a tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after an assignment request is made if the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days. This provision does not give rise to a right to file an application at the LTB – instead the tenant can directly give their landlord a notice of termination.

In this case the Tenant gave the Landlord a valid notice of termination after the Landlord failed to respond to the assignment request within seven days. The Tenant sent the Landlord and N9 Notice via email on or about November 9, 2025, with a termination date of December 12, 2025.
The tenancy lawfully terminated via the N9 notice on December 12, 2025. Even with this finding, given the above, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. S. 98 does not apply to this situation.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has not proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant filed an A2 Application alleging that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably denied consent for the Tenant to sublet her rental unit.

It was undisputed that the Tenant delivered an N9 Notice to Terminate her Tenancy (‘N9 notice’) on July 31, 2025 with a termination date of August 31, 2025. It was further undisputed that on July 31, 2025, the Tenant requested consent to sublet to Marthe Ntumba and the Landlord’s agent rejected the potential subletter on the basis that her income was not sufficient for the rental unit.

It was agreed by the parties, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2025 and handed the keys to the rental unit to the Landlord to the on-site office on September 2, 2025. As a result of the Tenant handing her keys to the rental unit the Landlord began showing the rental unit immediately upon receiving the N9 notice in an attempt to minimize any potential losses.
During the hearing, it was the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord rejected the potential subtenant arbitrarily and unreasonably and that the applicant put forward was a good candidate.

Further, the Tenant herself submitted an N9 notice and stated she had no intention to return to the rental unit as she was looking to terminate her tenancy due to a pest issue within the rental unit. As noted, the Tenant did in fact vacate the rental unit pursuant to that notice.

The Landlord’s agent testified that the Landlord uses preset qualification criterion when assessing a potential candidate for their buildings and where the applicant did not meet the criterion the Landlord would not rent the unit to that applicant. She further stated that the potential subletter presented by the Tenant would have been subject to that qualification criterion for the residential complex. Therefore, the potential subletter was not provided a tenancy for the rental unit.

It was the Landlord's legal representative submissions that the potential subletter put forward by the Tenants was not rejected arbitrarily and the reasons provided were in fact reasonable given the potential subletter did not make sufficient income to afford the monthly rent at the rental unit.

Further, the Landlord's legal representative submitted that the Landlord began immediately looking for an alternative tenant upon receiving notice that the Tenant was vacating in an attempt to minimize their losses. Finally, she stated that despite their best efforts which included viewings of potential renters, the Landlord was unable to re-rent the rental unit until December 1, 2025. Analysis

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to the sublet of the rental unit to the potential subtenants.

The evidence provided shows why the potential subtenant was denied and the reasons provided were, in my view, not arbitrary and were based on reasonable criteria related to income levels. It is not unusual or unreasonable for a landlord to have set criteria such as specific income requirements when assessing a suitable candidate.

Further, while the Tenant framed her request as a sublet, it was in fact a request for assignment under section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) as the Tenant made clear that she was not planning to return to the rental unit. In light of this, I find it reasonable for the Landlord to scrutinize the income of the potential subtenants put forward by the Tenant and the Landlord is not required to accept anyone the Tenant put forward.
In addition, I do not find that the Landlord failed to minimize their losses by refusing consent to sublet the rental unit to the applicants put forward by the Tenants.

It was agreed that the Landlord started advertising and showing the rental unit towards the end of July 2025 and continued to do so through November 2025. The Landlord was able to rent the unit 3 months after the Tenants vacated, which I do not find to be a lengthy period of time in the circumstances. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize their losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name] and Subsequent Damage

The Tenant [name] (OS) testified that on November 1, 2024 she notified the Landlord that there was a water pipe leaking on the second floor of the rental unit causing damage to the upstairs, main floor and basement flooring and drywall. Both parties testified that the Landlord had a restoration company attend the rental unit that same day and they removed the affected flooring, drywall and installed dehumidifiers for 3 days.

OS testified that the plumbing issue was fixed on November 23, 2024 and the water was turned back on. The Landlord testified that 2 plumbers attended the rental unit on November 4, 2024 and notified her that there was a blockage in the pipe. The Landlord then testified that the pipe was snaked on November 16, 2024 and the blocked portion of the pipe was cut out, showing that it was blocked with paper towels, baby wipes and sanitary products. The Landlord testified everything was fully repaired for the upstairs pipe on November 23, 2024. The Landlord testified the Tenant told her she did not flush anything except toilet paper; however, the Landlord’s daughter saw only paper towel in the bathroom when she attended on November 23, 2024.

OS testified that the full restoration and replacement of the flooring and drywall was not completed until February 25, 2025. OS testified that as the upstairs closest needed to be fixed, she needed to store items in the second bedroom that she would normally use as a reading room or for working from home. The Tenant testified that she lost all use of the second bedroom. The Tenant submitted photo evidence of the second bedroom from November 2024 as the photo includes a dehumidifier that was only in the rental unit for 3 days. The photo shows clothing on the couch and some shoes on the floor, but without the dehumidifier in the room, I could not identify how the second bedroom was unusable.

OS also testified that she could not use the living room, dining room or the kitchen as she did not want to set up furniture when she did not know when the repairs would be occurring. OS testified that from November 1, 2024 to sometime in December 2024 she did not have her furniture set up in these rooms. OS also testified that they could not use the partially finished basement as their recreation room because the table and the couch were stored in the basement from the main floor until sometime in December 2024 and January 2025. OS testified she did not think that the Landlord completed the renovations within a timely manner as it should have taken 2 to 3 weeks not 4 months.

The Landlord testified that she was going through TD insurance to have the damages assessed and repaired. The Landlord testified that she had contacted contractors about having the repairs completed before approved through insurance, however she could not find a contractor that was available in December 2024 and the plumber she used who was also contractor was not available until mid-January 2025. The Landlord testified that TD insurance started the process of measuring the damage by having contractors go to the rental unit on Jan 21, 2025. The Landlord testified she attended the rental unit for the first time on February 6, 2025 and all of the Tenant’s furniture had been placed back. The Landlord testified that the only time the Tenant would have needed to move her furniture was the first couple of days in November 2024 and from February 18, 2025 until February 25, 2025. The Landlord also testified that the Tenant asked her to claim the Tenant’s placements and table through insurance due to damage, however, on February 6, 2025 the Tenant was using the same table and chairs that she had previously said were damaged.

The Landlord testified that the only repairs done were the following: • Baseboards in the second floor laundry closet; • Drywall on the main floor ceiling; [name] and flooring replaced on the main floor; [name] in the basement laundry room, which was only partially finished previously.
The Landlord testified that she maintained open communication with the Tenant and sent update emails on November 26, 2024, December 16 and 23, 2024 and January 8, 2025. Analysis:
As the applicant, the Tenant has the onus to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their obligations under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
I am also mindful of both parties’ duty to mitigate found in section 16 of the Act. Specifically, section 16 imposes an obligation on each party to mitigate or minimize their losses.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations and I find that the Landlord responded within a reasonable time period. The Landlord sent contractors the day of the flooding and the affected ceiling and baseboards were removed November 1, 2024. The Landlord then had dehumidifiers installed for 3 days to remove any excess water. The repairs done to the rental unit because of the flood were not extensive and none of them required the Tenant to store her furniture for months as she alleged, and all repairs were finalized on February 25, 2025.

The Tenant only submitted 1 photo of the second bedroom when the flooding first occurred, and once the dehumidifier was removed, the Tenant did not provide any evidence about how the room could not be used. In addition, the only damage to the second floor was to the baseboards in the closest, and I find the Tenant did not provide a reasonable explanation why she could not have returned her clothing to the closest once the dehumidifiers were removed as there was no other damage besides the baseboards in the closet. OS testified she needed to store her couch and furniture from the dining room in the basement and she submitted photo evidence of this. However, none of the photos are date stamped, so while the Landlord acknowledged that the furniture would have needed to be removed for the 3 days following November 1, 2024 and for the week in February 2025, the Tenant did not provide any evidence to show that she needed to store her furniture in the basement outside of those time periods, or that they were stored. Section 16 of the Act requires the Tenant to minimize her losses, and I find that would include bringing her furniture back upstairs from the basement from when water was cleaned up by November 4, 2024, until the renovations fully started on February 18, 2025.
As I find that the Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenants allege that the Landlord breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the dryer.
The tenancy commenced on May 1, 2025. Tenants [name] and [name] vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2026 and CR and AM vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2026.

The dryer was an appliance included with the tenancy and it stopped working on December 12, 2025. The dryer was replaced on January 10, 2026, approximately four weeks later. These facts are not in dispute.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

As there is no dispute that the dryer was in a state of disrepair, the issue before me is whether the steps the Landlord took to address the disrepair issue were appropriate and reasonable in the circumstances.

The Landlord testified that a new dryer was purchased on December 17, 2025. He provided the Tenants with two options: quick delivery with charges or free delivery from Home Depot on January 3, 2026. The Tenants agreed to the free delivery option.
It was the evidence of the Landlord that on January 2, 2026, Home Depot advised him that the delivery would be delayed as the dryer was on backorder. He immediately advised the Tenants of the delay.
The Tenants did not challenge the Landlord’s evidence but took issue with the delay in order the new dryer.

The Landlord provided no persuasive explanation for why it took five days to purchase a replacement dryer after learning that the existing appliance had completely failed. During that period, the Landlord also failed to take any steps to lessen the impact on the Tenants. The Landlord did not offer a temporary replacement or any other accommodation, despite knowing that four adults occupied the rental unit and would incur additional expense to dry their clothing elsewhere.

I accept that the delivery delay was largely outside the Landlord’s control. However, I am not satisfied that the Landlord acted reasonably during the five-day period between December 12, 2025, and December 17, 2025, before purchasing the replacement dryer.

While the Landlord’s actions overall do not amount to neglect or wilful disregard, I find that that the Landlord’s response to the breakdown in December was not fully reasonable in the circumstances. Given that the dryer had required repairs only three months earlier, the Landlord knew the appliance had ongoing reliability issues. A prompter response was therefore warranted when it failed completely on December 12, 2025.

Considering the contextual approach required by Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord failed to respond reasonably to the maintenance issue and therefore breached the maintenance obligations imposed by section 20 of the Act. Remedies
The Tenants seek reimbursement of $350.00 for laundromat expenses, fuel and mileage incurred while the dryer was unavailable.

CR testified that she and AM attended a laundromat roughly 15 to 20 minutes away from the rental until, approximately twice each week and completed around five loads of laundry weekly during the period the dryer was not functioning. While no receipts were produced, I accept CR’s evidence regarding the number of loads completed and the cost per load. Based on that evidence, I find that the Tenants incurred approximately $70.00 laundromat costs, calculated as follows: • 5 loads x $3.50 = $17.50 per week • $17.50 per week x 4 weeks = $70.00

I also accept CR’s evidence that the Tenants travelled to and from the laundromat for each visit and therefore incurred transportation expense. Although receipts were not produced, I am satisfied that those expenses were necessarily incurred as a direct result of the Landlord’s failure to replace the dryer in a reasonable time. I have considered the Government of Canada’s prescribed mileage rate of $0.73 per kilometre, together with the evidence regarding the frequency of the trips to the laundromat in arriving at a reasonable estimate of the Tenants’ transportation expenses.

While the precise transportation costs cannot be determined from the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenants incurred out-of-pocket expenses beyond the $70.00 in laundry costs, the necessary transportation expenses, and the evidence as a whole, I find that an award of $250.00 fairly compensates the Tenants for the out-of-pocket expenses they incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach of section 20 of the Act.
The Tenants withdrew their requests for orders requiring additional maintenance work and prohibiting a rent increase.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $250.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenants have incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • Changed the locks or the locking system to rental unit or building without given replacement keys • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • Withheld or interfered with vital services
reasons: The Landlord testified that his property is a single-family home, that he purchased in September 2022 and it consisted of three bedrooms on the main level with two bathrooms and one main kitchen, and the basement was an open area with no egress to the outside originally, but he did build a graded exit from the basement to the outside, after he purchased the home, to add more sunlight and further to provide an exit to the yard. The basement also had a bathroom and a small bar fridge and counter area, which was not a kitchen and did not include a stove. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted photographic evidence to substantiate the Landlord’s oral testimony.

The Landlord testified he lived in a bedroom in the main level, and the Tenants lived in the basement and the shared the main kitchen, originally when they moved in late 2022, thereafter Ms. [name] went back to Iran for an extended period of time on or about April 2023 and Mr. [name]name] moved upstairs into one of the spare bedrooms, where they not only shared the kitchen but also the main floor bathroom.

The Landlord further testified that Mr. [name]name], had requested that upon the return of his spouse and his niece, in September 2023 if the Landlord was willing to move downstairs, to provide privacy given the Tenants niece was unmarried. The Landlord did not advise he would, but told Mr. [name]name] the Tenants should seek alternative arrangements, but the Tenants took it upon themselves to move the Landlord’s personal belongings to the basement without his consent.

The Landlord further testified that there was no separation between his space and the Tenants space, originally, but he installed an interior door between the spaces to increase the privacy as the Tenants requested only in late August 2023, anticipating the return of Mr. [name]name]’s spouse and their niece. Before this door was installed there was an opening allowing access from the main level to the basement. The Tenants vacated on or about October 10, 2023. Moreover, the parties certainly could open and close the interior door to get to the main level or the basement.
The Landlord further testified that the Tenants were acquittances of his father, and he sought to assist them in their time of need and allowed them to reside in his home.

The Landlord’s Witness [name] testified she was the realtor for the Landlord when he purchased the property and testified there was only one kitchen and three bathrooms in the property, with one of the bathrooms being in the basement. Moreover, [name] testified to her knowledge there was no tenancy agreement as the Landlord referred to the Tenants as family friends, and that she was aware that the Landlord built a graded exit from the basement to the exterior to allow for more light to get into the basement, and no other changes were made to the basement and to this date there was no kitchen in the basement.

The Tenants testified that there was in fact a kitchen in the basement but did not provide any documentary evidence to substantiate their claim and or to refute the Landlord’s testimony and documentary evidence that in fact there was not. The Tenants did testify at some point in time they moved upstairs and the Landlord moved downstairs, and they were adamant there were in fact two kitchens in the home.

On cross examination the Tenant Ms. [name]name] testified that they did move upstairs from originally residing downstairs and shortly after they vacated the Landlord’s property. Ms. [name] was adamant there was a kitchen in the basement, but on cross examination failed to describe the details of the same.

The Tenant’s witness [name] [name], the Landlord’s brother testified that he had seen a kitchen in the basement rental unit, and had visited his brother’s property on multiple occasions but could not describe the kitchen upon cross examination in detail, and further during cross testified that he and the Landlord were currently in a legal dispute over their father’s estate, where the Tenant’s witness is the estate trustee and being accused by the Landlord of fraud. The Tenant’s witness testified he attended as witness for the Tenants due to his civic duty and not in any course of retribution for other litigation between himself and the Landlord.

There are several general comments I would make about the exemption contained in section 5(i) of the Act. First the tenancy agreement between the parties must require the tenant to share the kitchen or bathroom with the owner or the owner’s immediate family. In addition, the Board must consider the living arrangements at the beginning of the tenancy and any unilateral change to the pattern of use by the Landlord after the tenancy begins will not cause a tenancy that is subject to the Act to be exempted by section 5(i) ([name] v. Bindlish, [2010 O.J. No. 2193 ([name]. [name]. Ct.)). In addition, and as with any exemption, the burden of proof rests on the person seeking to rely on the exemption. In this case, that is the Landlord. I note in the case at hand no tenancy agreement was submitted, by either party.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenants were required to share a kitchen facility with the Landlord, regardless of if they were residing upstairs or downstairs., which means this arrangement is exempt from this Act.
The Landlord and the Landlord’s Witness testimony was more credible to that of the Tenants and the Tenants’ witness on a balance of probabilities.
I am also persuaded by the documentary evidence, including photographic evidence submitted by the Landlord’s Legal Representative on the issue that there was only one kitchen in the property.

Based on the parties’ evidence and oral testimonies, including the parties’ witnesses. I am not satisfied that the Tenants space was ever self contained, even if an interior door was installed from the main level leading to the basement, a month or so prior to the Tenants vacating the property or that both spaced are outfitted with kitchen facilities as contemplated by Regulation 517/06 of the Act. As such, I find that the Tenants were required to share a kitchen with the Landlord on the main floor of the house and this arrangement is exempt from this Act. As the Act does not apply to this tenancy, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants T2 application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The Tenant has proven their application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $1,348.21 inclusive of costs on or before July 12, 2026.

The following facts are not in dispute: a. The tenancy commenced March 1, 2025. The tenancy agreement was for a one year fixed term ending February 28, 2026. The monthly rent was $1,550.00. b. The Landlord collected a last month rent deposit of $1,550.00 on or about January 31, 2025. c. On November 20, 2025, the Tenant requested consent to assign the remaining 2- months of his tenancy. Both the Tenant and Landlord began looking for a potential assignee. d. On December 2, 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord for consent to assign the rental unit to [name], the potential assignee. e. On December 4, 2025, the Landlord refused to consent to the assignment via email and did not provide any reason(s) for the refusal. f. On December 5, 2025, the Tenant served the Landlord with an N9 Notice to End the Tenancy (‘N9 notice’) with a date of termination of January 5, 2026. [name] vacated the rental unit on January 5, 2026 and returned the keys to the Landlord. h. The Tenant paid the December 2025 rent to the Landlord but not rent for January 2026.

The dispute before me is whether the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee. The Tenant sought a rental abatement in the amount of $1,348.21 for the period of January 5, 2026 until January 31, 2026.

The Tenant referred to pages 10, 11,19-26 and pages 40-41 of the Tenant’s Evidence Package (DOC-7090449) which included a completed OREA application, credit check, job letter, pay stubs and a criminal record check for the potential assignee. Further, on page 8, communications between the Landlord and assignee show a date and location for meeting between the Landlords agent and the potential assignee on December 3, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlords agent refused consent to assign the rental unit to the potential assignee. He specifically referred to page 8, an email dated December 4, 2025 from the Landlords agent where he stated they would not be accepting the potential assignee, it stated: “Hi [name]. The Landlord evaluates applications based on different factors. A specific reason can’t be given…”
The Tenant further testified that he spoke with the potential assignee, and he stated that he was not provided a reason for the refusal.

ZZ testified that after being notified by the Tenant that he wished to assign the remaining 2- months of his tenancy, he posted an ad attempting to locate a new tenant to assist the Tenant locate a suitable assignee. Further, after receiving legal advice and reading an LTB Brochure he believed that he did not need to provide the Tenant with a reason as to why he was not choosing the potential assignee.

However, at the hearing he stated that the request was refused because was concerned with the potential assignee’s ability to pay for the monthly rent as he worked for an agency and his term with the agency was ending February 28, 2026. Finally, he stated that he was able to re-rent the rental unit on February 1, 2026 so, he was able to save the Tenant one month of his responsibility for the remaining contract. Analysis

This application is brought pursuant to s. 98 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) which states: 98 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
The application was filed on December 30, 2025, which is within one year after the Landlord withheld consent.
Section 95(5) of the Act states: A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of a rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3)(b).

For the reasons that follow, I find that the Landlord arbitrarily refused consent to assign the rental unit to a specific assignee. The Landlord worked with the Tenant and potential assignee between December 2, 2025 until December 4, 2025 when the potential assignee was refused without reason. Although I can appreciate the Landlord believed that he did not have to provide a reason to the Tenant or the potential assignee of the reason for the refusal, I disagree. The Landlord has an obligation to inform the Tenant of the reason for the refusal, and that reason cannot be arbitrary or unreasonable. If no reason is provided, it is impossible for a Tenant to know whether they are entitled to file this type of application alleging that the refusal is arbitrary or unreasonable. In the absence of a reason being provided to the Tenant and the potential assignee at the time of the refusal, I find that the refusal was arbitrary. Remedies

The Tenant requested for the tenancy to be deemed terminated as of January 5, 2026 when he moved from the rental unit. Not only is this a remedy that can be granted for this type of application under s.98(3) of the Act, but the Tenant also served the Landlord with a valid N9 Notice under s. 95(4)(c) of the Act after the Landlord refused consent to the assignment. The termination date on that N9 Notice was also January 5, 2026.

As the tenancy lawfully terminated on January 5, 2026, the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent also ended on that date. In accordance with s.106(10) of the Act, a rent deposit must be used to satisfy the last rental period of a tenancy.
As noted, the Tenant paid the full rent for the month of December 2025, and the Landlord has not returned the Tenant’s rent deposit.

Tenant also sought a rental abatement of $1,295.21, being the amount of the rent deposit being held by the Landlord minus the 5 days the Tenant occupied the rental unit from January 1, 2026 to January 5, 2026. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $1,295.21.
As the Tenant is the successful party they are also entitled to reimbursement of the filing fee for this application.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of January 5, 2026.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,348.21. This amount represents: • $1,295.21 for a rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, I raised two preliminary issues with the Tenant: whether the Tenant named the correct Landlord on the application and whether the Landlord was properly served.
The Tenant conceded that the Landlord is Homestead and that [name] was an employee or agent of the Landlord that the Tenant communicated with during the tenancy.

Board records show that the Board mailed the Notice of Hearing package to [name] at 27 [address], [name], ON . This address was provided by the Tenant and the address is incomplete. 27 [address] is an apartment building with numerous units. The Tenant did not provide a suite or unit number on the application.

Board records show that the Board emailed the Notice of Hearing package to [name] at [email] on March 20, 2026. The Tenant was unable to confirm that [name] continued to be an employee of Homestead on March 20, 2026, had access to the email, and likely received the Notice of Hearing.

There is no evidence before the Board that the Landlord’s mailing address is 27 Cardigan Street and no evidence before the Board the Landlord agreed to receive notices or documents via email at [email].

There are no records that the Landlord accessed the Board file via the Tribunal Ontario Portal. Given this and the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant did not name the correct Landlord and the Landlord was not properly served with the Notice of Hearing.
Notwithstanding the above issues, the Tenant’s application, on its merits, must be dismissed for the following reasons.

The Tenant’s application was filed pursuant to section 98(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which states: Tenant application 98 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. [Emphasis added]

Section 98(1) of the Act is meant to address a situation where a landlord refuses consent with respect to the particular person that the Tenant has proposed as the new occupant. The Tenant is supposed to ask the Landlord to approve the proposed assignee and if the Landlord unreasonably or arbitrarily withholds consent to the proposed assignee, then that is the situation which gives the Tenant the right to file an application such as this one.

The Tenant acknowledged that no proposed assignee and no actual person or potential assignee was ever presented to the Landlord. The Tenant’s email to the Landlord on December 23, 2025 states: “Do you consent to the idea of me assigning my lease to another person?” This is a general request. While it may be true that the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant, the Landlord’s failure to respond, within seven days, to the Tenant’s request to assign the tenancy triggered the Tenant’s right to give 30 days notice of termination pursuant to section 96 of the Act; the Landlord’s non-response is not, in itself, equal to arbitrary or unreasonable refusal of consent to assign “to a potential assignee”.
As a result of the above, section 98 of the Act does not apply to the Tenant’s complaint concerning the Landlord and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The tenancy started on September 20, 2025, and was a one-year lease ending September 19, 2026.
In October 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord if she could assign the tenancy and began proposing various potential assignees to the Landlord.
Ultimately, the tenancy was assigned on February 24, 2026, with an effective date of March 1, 2026. Tenant’s Application
For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied that the Landlord unreasonably refused to consent to the Tenant’s potential assignee. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant a total of $4,392.60.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

This is an application for a determination that the Landlord unreasonably refused to consent to a specific assignment of the tenancy. The Tenant is seeking a 100% abatement of rent from January 20, 2026, to February 28, 2026.

The Tenant testified that she provided a total of 12 candidates for assignment to the Landlord and there were 3 that were unreasonably refused by the Landlord. The Tenant testified that she requested assignment to the first candidate that was unreasonably refused on November 13, 2025. The Landlord responded on November 13, 2025, refusing to consent to the assignment. Since the Landlord responded within 7 days, the Tenant could not terminate the tenancy under section 96(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') because none of the factors under 95(4) of the Act were triggered.

The Tenant testified that she provided another candidate that was unreasonably refused on December 15, 2025. The Landlord responded to the request on December 16, 2025, and there was some back and forth and ultimately a complete refusal on December 18, 2025, again within 7 days of the request.

The Tenant testified that she provided a third candidate that was unreasonably refused on December 31, 2025. The Landlord responded on January 1, 2026, and refused consent. Again, within 7 days of the request.
Tenant continued to provide prospective assignees to the Landlord until ultimately the tenancy was assigned effective March 1, 2026.

The question before me is if the Tenant is entitled to a 100% rent abatement for the period of January 20, 2026, through February 28, 2026, given the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord unreasonably denied consent to multiple potential assignees. First alleged unreasonably refused consent

In considering Landlord’s reasonableness of refusing consent, I considered that the Tenant only occupied the rental unit for roughly 6 weeks before she began requesting to assign the lease. I have also considered the cost implications to the Landlord from going from a sole occupant to the Tenant’s proposal to assign to a 5-member family.

The Tenant provided the email chain in which she provided basic information about the proposed assignee to the Landlord, and the possession date was December 1, 2025, a family of 5 composed of father, mother and 3 children, with a sufficient household income to cover rent. The email chain indicates the Landlord’s reply was “we are concerned about the size of the family and the age of the [c]hildren they have. Please be advised we would like to have a family not over 4 people and preferably growing up adults.”

Based on the evidence before me, cost implications were not a factor. It was undisputed that the rent was $3,300.00 and that was the same amount the potential assignee was going to pay. Furthermore, it is the Landlord’s own evidence that he was open to a 4- member family occupying the rental unit, it was just young children that the Landlord seemed to be opposed to.

I am satisfied that the Landlord was not concerned about cost implications as the Landlord was open to a family. The Landlord testified that he was concerned that young children may cause damage to the rental unit and that he did not think the rental unit was large enough for a family of 5. It appears from the Landlord’s own evidence that his concern was just families with young children, which I am satisfied with appears to be an arbitrary and unreasonable consideration.

The Landlord was then reminded of his obligation under the Human Rights Code R.S.O 1990 c. H.9, (the “Code”) to provide housing in manner that does not discriminate against family status. The Landlord testified that he did not intend to discriminate against the family based on their family status.

In any event, Landlord has an obligation to consider assignment in reasonable manner pursuant to the Act and the fact that a family has young children is simply not a reasonable consideration to refuse consent. Moreover, this unit is a 3-bedroom unit with an additional 1-bedroom suite in the basement, and I am satisfied the rental unit would be more than sufficient for a 5-member family.
Additionally, the Landlord testified that he was unaware of any municipal bylaws limiting occupancy.
Given the Landlord’s own evidence I find it was unreasonable and arbitrary to deny this application and assignment.

Having found that the Landlord unreasonably refused consent to the assignee proposed on November 13, 2025, I do not find it necessary to address whether the Landlord also unreasonably refused consent to the other 2 potential assignees. [name]

Section 98(3) of the Act provides that if the Board determines a landlord has unlawfully withheld consent to an assignment, then the Board may do one or more of the following: terminate the tenancy or order an abatement of the tenant’s rent, among other remedies.

The Tenant was asking that the tenancy be terminated as of January 19, 2026. The Tenant was not seeking to have the tenancy terminated any early and indicated that she was seeking the termination as of the end of the rental period for when the last unreasonable refusal occurred when the application was filed.
However, I am satisfied that the lease was ultimately assigned to new tenants and therefore the proper termination date is March 1, 2026, the date that assignment became effective.

Instead, what I believe Tenant is effectively seeking is an abatement of rent for the period of January 20, 2026, to February 28, 2026, which would have the same effect as a termination of the tenancy. The Tenant is seeking to not have further financial liability for the period after January 19, 2026, as the Landlord had unreasonably refused consent to multiple proposed assignees.

In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, the Divisional Court found that absent an amendment, the Board can only order what is claimed in the application (see paras 10 and 11). The Tenant did not request to amend the application to have a remedy commence from the first unreasonable refusal and as such, I do not find it appropriate to have the remedy go back to December 1, 2025, when the proposed assignees could have moved in. Therefore, the remedy will be limited to what the Tenant has requested and what the Landlord had notice of.

The Tenant testified that she was carrying the cost of her own mortgage on her own home as well as the cost of the rent on the rental unit. Additionally, the Tenant testified that she paid for the cost of listing the rental unit through the Multiple Listing Service that she could access as a Realtor.
The Landlord would have had no cost implications had he agreed to the assignment as there would have been new tenants as early as December 1, 2025.

The Landlord could have prevented costs to himself as well as costs to the Tenant. Instead, the Landlord’s unreasonable refusal of consent directly contributed to the Tenant’s continuing accrual of rental obligations after January 19, 2026. As such, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the full 100% rent abatement she is seeking for the period of January 20, 2026, to when the lease was assigned to the new tenants effective March 1, 2026.
It was undisputed that the rent was $3,300.00 per month due on the 20th day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $108.49. This amount is calculated as follows: $3,300.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.

Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement in the amount of $4,339.60. This amount is calculated as follows $108.49 x 40 = $4,339.60. There being 40 days between January 20, 2026, and February 28, 2026.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The assignment of the rental unit is effective March 1, 2026.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of March 1, 2026.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,392.60. This amount represents: • $4,339.60 for an abatement of rent for the period of January 20, 2026, to February 28, 2026. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord or the Tenant shall pay to the other any sum of money that is owed as a result of this order.

If the owing party does not pay the other the full amount owing by July 21, 2026, the owing will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 22, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $3,048.00.
The residential unit is a single detached dwelling. The Tenants resided in the house for 10 years and vacated on April 15, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name]

DJ testified that she and her family were given an N12 notice of termination in June of 2024 with a termination date of September 14, 2024. She stated that the Landlord was going through a separation and required the house for themselves. The parties attended a hearing in December of 2024 where the Landlord’s application was granted. The Tenants vacated the house on April 15, 2025.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not move into the rental house and it is vacant. She provided many dated pictures showing flyers stuck in the door, blinds in the same position she left them in, the Tenants’ garbage remaining at the front of the house, an unkempt lawn, weeds in front of the garage door and her son’s Sea-Doo which was left at the house. These pictures were dated from July 12, 2025 through January 21, 2026.

The Tenant also attended at the property several times personally to ensure that none of her mail had been sent there mistakenly and she provided the dates and approximate times for those visits. She stated that at each visit, she knocked and no one answered the door.

DJ stated that she and her husband were able to reside in the rental unit together because they had sufficient room to house their sons and granddaughter when it was required. DJ stated that due to her husband’s rheumatic arthritis and hip replacement, he has always required physical assistance from other family members.

The Tenant stated that the only place that they could afford was a basement, 1-bedroom apartment which is extremely difficult for her husband to move around the unit. She stated that the basement entrance has no railing. She provided a number of medical papers related to her husband’s condition.

DJ is seeking $1,300.00 in moving expenses, $26,400.00 (12 x $2,200.00) in compensation and $12,000.00 for pain and suffering. The Tenant stated that she had to give away many of her possessions and had to store many more due to the fact that she resided there for so many years. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I am satisfied that the Tenant’s pictures and testimony prove that no one is residing in the rental unit. I must determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.
Section 57(5) of the Act does not apply as the Landlord has left the rental unit vacant.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, the Landlord made no efforts to move into the rental unit and appeared to be content with having the unit unoccupied. Further, the Landlord failed to attend today to provide their information for me to consider. As such, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies
The Tenant requested moving expenses of $1,300.00 but provided no invoices to support that claim. As such, no amount will be awarded for moving expenses.

The Tenant requested compensation of $26,400.00 and $12,000.00 for pain and suffering due to the Landlord’s actions. The Tenant spoke about the issues that her husband was having with mobility in the basement apartment and she spoke about not having sufficient room for family members to stay over. This is of course unfortunate and I have no doubt that this move caused emotional upset and some financial hurdles. The Tenant provided an assortment of dated medical letters and/or medical results that spanned several pages. Although these pages were not helpful and no summary letter was provided, I accept that the Tenant suffers from rheumatoid arthritis and hip issues.

Having considered the circumstances in this case, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $3,000.00 to the Tenants in general compensation for the emotional distress, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $27,748.00. This amount represents: • $3,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants’ amended application corrects the spelling of the Landlord’s last name from [name] “Bibi” to [name] “[name].” The application refers to a Schedule “A” and seeks interest on the last months’ deposit. Mr. [name]name] acknowledged receipt of the amended application and was prepared to proceed with the hearing. Tenants’ Application for a Rebate of Money the Landlord owes (T1)

The tenancy commenced on December 22, 2021 and ended by mutual agreement on December 31, 2025. The parties renewed the tenancy annually. The monthly rent was $1,750.00 for the final lease term commencing January 1, 2025.

When the tenancy was renewed for 2024, the Landlords required the Tenants to pay: the first month’s rent; last month's rent deposit; and an additional security deposit equal to two months ($3,300.00).

After the rent increased on January 1, 2025, the Landlords required an additional $200.00, increasing the deposit to $3,500.00. 5. [name] testified that the lawful first and last month’s rent deposit are not in dispute because those amounts were applied to the rent as required by the Act. 6. The issue before the Board is with respect to the “additional security” deposit of $3,500.00 and the $400.00 key deposit. Following the end of the tenancy, the Landlords returned $2,633.40 on January 8, 2026 but retained $1,266.60. 7. The Landlord’s January 8, 2026 email states that they deducted repair costs of $1,266.60 from what they described as the total rent deposit of $3,900.00 before returning the balance to the Tenants. 8. Mr. [name]name] acknowledged at the hearing that he retained $1,266.60 because he believed the Tenants caused damage to the rental unit. He testified that he required the additional security deposit because the Tenants were international students and he was concerned he would be unable to recover compensation for damages. Analysis and Findings 9. The evidence establishes that the Landlords collected an “additional security deposit” of $3,500.00 which was prohibited by s.134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). This deposit was separate from the lawful last month’s rent deposit. 10. Although the Landlords returned part of that security deposit after the tenancy ended, I find that the Landlord unlawfully retained $1,266.60 as damage compensation. Accordingly, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $1,266.60. 11. A Landlord is not entitled to keep a rent deposit because they believe their Tenant caused damage. A Landlord must file an application at the Board claiming compensation for damages and the Board will decide if the Landlord is entitled to compensation after holding a hearing and considering the parties’ evidence on that issue. 12. I also find that the Landlords failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, interest for the period of November 1, 2023 to January 8, 2026, in the amount of $92.71 is applied to the outstanding balance owed by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,407.31. This amount represents: • $1,266.60 for the illegal charge collected; • $92.71 for interest on the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
