issues: order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 52674 Date: 2026-07-21 In the matter of: 1, 33 [address] Lindsay ON [name] (the 'Tenant') and [name] [name]-Huard applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord ’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application) This application was heard by videoconference on December 10, 2024 and June 5, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative, [name], the Landlord’s witness, [name], the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative, Nadine Little, attended the hearing on December 10, 2024. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative, Tayler Gerow, the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative, [name], attended the hearing on June 5, 2026.
reasons: The parties agreed that [name] [name]-Huard was an occupant within the meaning of the Act and that the application should be amended to delete [name] [name]-Huard as a tenant. The application was amended accordingly. T2 Application Background

The tenancy commenced on October 27, 2011. The Landlord took over the property in October 2020. The Tenant vacated the unit on September 15, 2023. The basement contained laundry facilities and a storage area.
The unit was located on the main floor of a Victorian home. There were two other units in the home, one on the second floor and one on the third floor.
At the time the Tenant vacated, the monthly rent was $1,098.61. Substantial interference

The Tenant claims that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by failing to adequately address maintenance issues as well as issues that arose between her and other tenants in the house, predominantly the second-floor tenant.
The Tenant testified she has had issues with the tenant above her (i.e. second-floor tenant) since the commencement of the tenancy but noise only became an issue in 2022.

On March 3, 2022, she emailed the Landlord about loud noise coming from the second-floor tenant (i.e. children, loud voices) . She admitted this was not a complaint but rather just to advise the Landlord that he should mention the lack of soundproofing to future tenants. The noise stopped thereafter.

On June 13 and 15, 2022, she had two disagreements with the second-floor tenant on June 13 and 15, 2022, one regarding items the Tenant left on the front step for a missing boy, the other because her acupuncturist parked in the second -floor tenant’s parking spot. She said that the Landlord dismissed her complaints about the two incidents [Doc 4621545, page 42] and ignored her suggestion of mediation.

In November 2022, the Tenant started parking her new car in the four-car garage (each tenant had an assigned parking spot) . The Landlord asked the Tenant if she could park her car a little closer to the house in the garage since the second-floor tenant said she was having trouble getting in an d out of her car. In response, the Tenant sent a detailed email to the Landlord identifying all the issues she was having with the second-floor tenant and asked the Landlord to tell the second-floor tenant to stop making noise and to stop harassing her [Doc 4621545, pages 26-28]. The Landlord told her he would talk to the second-floor tenant.
On January 7, 2023, the Tenant advised the Landlord that she was again having issues with noise caused by the second-floor tenant but said that the Landlord provided no feedback.

In April 2023, the Tenant met with the Landlord and his wife to discuss issues she was having with the second-floor tenant. It was the Tenant’s understanding from that meeting that if the second-floor tenant continued her disruptive behaviour, the Landlord would proceed with an LTB application.

In May 2023, the Tenant reported another incident to the Landlord and asked if he was going to move forward with an LTB application. Two weeks later that Landlord advised he had spoken with the second-floor tenant and would hold off on an LTB application.

In June 2023, the Tenant complained about noise from the upper tenant’s television . The Landlord responded, saying that he was out of the country and suggested that she should leave a note in the second-floor tenant’s mailbox. After she told him she was not comfortable doing so, he spoke with the second-floor tenant and the volume decreased.

The Tenant made further complaints about noise on July 9, July 31 and August 3, 2023. After the August 3, 2023 complaint, the Landlord told her he would send a note to the second-floor tenant and that she should call the police. Before she did so, police called her and threatened her with harassment charges because they received a call from the second-floor tenant. She emailed the Landlord to advise th at matters were escalating, after which he told her he did not think the unit would ever suit her need for quietness and that the second-floor tenant felt very intimidated by the Tenant. The Tenant believes his tone towards her changed because she was moving out.

On September 7, 2023, t he Tenant was in the process of movin g and she placed all of her garbage on the curb for pick up. She saw the third-floor tenant videotaping her garbage and when she approached her, the third-floor tenant was verbally aggressive. The Tenant called police and emailed the Landlord about the incident. He responded two days later thanking her for the keys and advising her to leave her keys in the mailbox. He did not comment , however, on the behaviour of the third -floor tenant but rather stated that it was in the hands of the police. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord testified that when he took over the property, he was not aware of any disputes between the tenants. He stated , however, that whenever he received a complaint from the Tenant, he made sure the other tenant was aware of the complaint (either through phone call, in person meeting, text message or email) and what he expected them to do to resolve the complaint. He produced some examples of how he dealt with complaints [Doc 4638936] , including having the second-floor tenant move her air-conditioner from her living room to the kitchen (i.e. given its previous proximity to the television, the second -floor tenant had increased the volume on her television so that she could hear it over the air-conditioner).

The Landlord stated that when he was repairing the Tenant’s dining room ceiling following a leak when he took over the property, he took advantage of the repairs (i.e. ceiling had been ripped out) by having the ceiling insulated with sound proofing insulation [Doc 4638924, page 17]. He did not insulate any other ceilings in the Tenant’s unit because 1) it would have required tearing out all of the ceilings and displacing the Tenant and 2) he had not received any noise complaints (i.e. he had just bought the property).

He confirmed that he spoke with the second-floor tenant about her behaviour stemming from the parking issue with the Tenant’s acupunc turist and removal of the Tenant’s property from the porch. He also met with the second-floor tenant after receiving the Tenant’s complaint about noise (stomping and banging) . The second -floor tenant denied any intentional stomping or banging, stating that she only vacuums her floors and goes around the house as usual.

He denied that he ever told any of the tenants in the home that he did not want to hear or deal with their issues. The only issue where he told the tenants they had to work things out themselves was the parking garage after the Tenant got a new car (i.e. larger). The second and third floor tenants resolved the situation by changing parking spots in the garage.

He did not deny that he told the Tenant he had no update for her after receiving complaints about the second -floor tenant but stated this was because he had already spoken with the second-floor tenant and asked her to cease any noises that might be extra loud.
He stated that the day he and his wife met with the Tenant for two hours, he and his wife proceeded upstairs and met with the second-floor tenant for the same amount of time.

He stated that he advised the Tenant that if she wanted him to proceed with an LTB application, he would need a written summary of all of the events so that he could issue an N5 notice. The Tenant did not provide him with same and told him an N5 notice was not her goal. He said that while he may not have responded to every message from the Tenant (they were prolific), he read all her messages and denied that there were any complaints from the Tenant which were not addressed. In support of this, he produced email and text messages with the Tenant [Doc 4638948].
The Landlord confirmed that since the Tenant vacated, he has received no complaints from any tenants in the residential complex.

On cross -examination, the Landlord confirmed that he did not serve an N5 notice on the second-floor tenant because the Tenant stated she did not one anyone evicted. He confirmed that he never attended the Tenant’s unit to listen to noise she complained about because the Tenant always sent her complaint after the incident. He did state, [name] wever, that he was in the Tenant’s unit many times during her tenancy and not once did he hear a noise or a television. There were many times when he would call the Tenant, rather than emailing or texting her, to confirm receipt of her complaint and to advise her that he would be speaking to the other tenant(s) about those complaints.
The Landlord stated that he did install vinyl flooring on the second floor which ha d better soundproofing than the original wooden floors. Landlord’s witness – [name] (‘JH’)

JH testified that she moved into the third -floor unit (i.e. unit 3) on September 1, 2021. She stated that in the summer of 2022, she was speaking with the second-floor tenant on the porch when the Tenant came and questioned the second-floor tenant. After the second-floor tenant refused to talk with the Tenant and started to return to her unit, the Tenant started yelling.

She stated that when the second-floor tenant asked to switch parking spaces with JH, they both went into the garage to measure JH’s parking spot to ensure it would fit the second-floor tenant’s car. The Tenant then came into the garage screaming so loudly they did not know what she was saying. The Tenant eventually returned to her unit.
JH denied that she v ideo-taped the Tenant’s garbage on September 7, 202 3, stating “ why would I do that”?

On cross-examination, JH confirmed that she exchanged phone numbers with the Tenant so they could deal with any disputes that arose between themselves. She said that while their exchanges were pleasant enough at the beginning of her tenancy, they were not near the end and that she would just say what she thought the Tenant wanted to hear to keep the peace [Doc 4621469, pages 30-33]. T6 application
In the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to repair or maintain the unit and residential complex with respect to a multitude of items.

Section 20 of the Act provides: (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non -repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

Section 29(1) of the Act provides: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 1. An order determining that the landlord has breached an obligation under subsection 20(1) or section 161.
Section 29(2) of the Act provides: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
The Tenant’s application was filed on January 13, 2024. Therefore, pursuant to Section 29(2), the Tenant was permitted to raise any issues that first arose on or after January 14, 2023.

After reviewing the eighteen (18) items raised by the Tenant’s [Doc 2577674], as well as considering the Tenant’s submissions with respect to the garage door, it was determined that sixteen (16) of those items were statute barred. As such, the T6 application dealt with the two remaining issues which were not statute barred, being storm damage and hot water heater. Storm damage
The Tenant testified that on August 3, 2023, there was a hailstorm in the area which damaged some windows in the home (i.e. the second-floor unit and the third-floor unit) and the garage door.

The Tenant stated that a window that was broken in the home (i.e. the second-floor unit above her) caused glass to fall onto the concrete outside the back entrance door and grass at the side of the house where the Tenant takes her dog. Given that the window was not “stabilized”, they presented an ongoing hazard to the Tenant and her family.

The Tenant produced photographs taken by her after the hailstorm [Doc 4620980] showing the following: Page 15: one small piece of glass on the concrete and one small piece of glass on the grass beside the concrete, taken on August 3, 2023 Page 16: Broken glass and/or white plastic in some of the window panels of four-car garage door and broken glass in one of the window panel’s of the second-floor tenant’s unit, taken on August 8, 2023 Page 17: Broken glass in the same window panel of the second -floor tenant’s unit and broken glass and/or white plastic in some of the window panels of the four -car garage door, taken on August 26, 2023 Page 18: Broken glass in one of the window panels of four-car garage door and broken glass in the same window panel of the second-floor tenant’s unit, taken on September 6, 2023 Page 19 Broken glass in the same window panel of the second-floor tenant’s unit, taken on September 13, 2023

The Tenant stated that she advised the Landlord about the broken glass on August 9, 2023 . He responded that the other tenants had already reported the damage and asked about the Tenant’s unit (it was undamaged). She raised concerns about the instability of the broken glass in the windows and was advised to steer clear of the area because he had people attending the property on August 11, 2023 to inspect the broken glass. When the Tenant vacated the unit on September 15, 2023, the windows had not yet been fixed, except for one window in the garage on September 9, 2023. The Tenant admitted that she was not using the garage during this point in time due to other issues . Had she been doing so, however, the broken glass in the garage door panels would have prevented her from being able to open and close the garage door.

The Tenant admitted that the broken windows in the upper units were not above her entrance way but maintained that pieces were continually falling and blowing onto the concrete beside her entryway and the area where she walked her dog. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord should have removed the broken glass from the windows in order to ensure everyone was safe and he did not do so. This left her feeling unsafe.
On cross-examination, the Tenant admitted that the storm did not affect her ability to access her unit via the shared entrance but did limit her use of her preferred entrance.

The Landlord confirmed that one window in the second -floor unit as well as three separate glass panes in the garage were damaged by the hailstorm. He testified that the other tenants in the home contacted him within one day told him that they had pick ed up all the glass, cleaned up and taped over the doors. As such, the Landlord believed damage at the rental property had been contained. In the meantime, he contacted his contractor (Harper Window and Doors) and attended the unit with them on August 11, 202 3. The contractor assessed the glass stability in the second -floor unit, deemed everything was fine, then took measurements for the replacement window. Given that the house is a heritage home, a replacement window had to be custom made. The replacement window was installed on September 27, 2023 at a cost of $4,034.10.

The Landlord stated that he did not observe any glass on the ground when he attended the unit on August 11, 202 3. He was not aware of any more glass falling from the second -floor unit after the storm . He said t he window contractor told him there was no danger of glass falling out and he relayed this assurance to the Tenant on August 11, 2023.

With respect to the garage doors, t he Landlord stated that after inspecting the damage, he personally replaced all of the windows in the garage doors with plexiglass that was cus tom ordered to size. The installation took place two weeks after the storm. Hot water tank

The Tenant stated that when she was moving out , she observed water on the floor in the basement around the hot water tanks (one tank for each unit). She texted the Landlord about the issue on September 3, 2023. On September 4, 2023, the Landlord asked the Tenant to take photographs of the water. Despite not staying at the property , the Tenant attended the property, took photographs of the three hot water tanks and sent them to the Landlord [Doc 4620980, page 20]. The Tenant does not know when the issue was resolved since the last time she was in the basement was on September 8, 202 3. She admitted that this issue did not affect her use of her unit, did not impede access to any of her personal items nor damage any of her personal belongings. She said it highlights the Landlord’s lack of communication in resolving issues.

The Landlord stated that after receiving the photographs of the water around the hot water tanks from the Tenant, he attended the property the evening of September 4, 2023 and inspected the tanks. After discovering a small leak in one of the tanks , he ordered a replacement tank from Home Depot, picked it up and installed it the evening of September 8, 2023. He said the replacement tank cost him $800.39.
He stated that the hot water tank that he replaced did not service the Tenant’s unit. As such, his communications regarding the tank and its replacement were with another tenant in the home. Analysis

In addition to section 20 of the Act , which is relevant to the T6 application , t he following sections of the Act are relevant to the T2 application: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 , the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to th e maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. Although Onyskiw deals with a breach regarding a maintenance obligation, I am satisfied that the Court of Appeal provides a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches in other situations, including substantial interference.

To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

With respect to the T2 application, I find that although the Landlords’ response to the Tenant’s complaints was not perfect, it was reasonable in the circumstances. I found the Landlord’s testimony to be credible, forthright and sincere and I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of his t estimony. Given that the second -floor tenant is elderly, I find it plausible that the Landlord’s communications with that tenant were mainly by phone call or in person. I am not persuaded by the submissions of the Tena nt’s representative that the lack of phone records or witnesses to corroborate those phone calls or visits means that they did not happen. I am satisfied that the Landlord responded promptly to the Tenant’s complaints after being notified of problematic behaviour by other tenants.

While the Landlord did not serve the second -floor tenant with an N5 notice, the Tenant admitted that she told the Landlord that she did not want to evict anyone and had responded that an N5 notice was not her goal. As such, I accept that the Landlord inte rpreted that to mean that the Tenant did not want him to initiate LTB proceedings. Furthermore, there is no evidence before me that the Tenant ever sent the Landlord a full written complaint documenting all issues since he took over as Landlord, as reques ted by him if she wished him to proceed with an LTB application.

I do not find the audio recordings produced by the Tenant to be particularly helpful. Given that they are audios recordings, I am unable to confirm, for the most part, where the Tenant was recording from (i.e. inside her rental unit, common hallway or out side of second -floor tenant’s unit) or whose television was on. Any audio I was able to hear was faint. Furthermore, the Tenant did not produce any audio recordings of stomping or banging coming from the second-floor tenant.

While the Landlord did admit that he told the tenants to sort out the parking issue themselves when he raised it with the Tenant, the evidence confirms that this was done almost immediately by the tenants in the second and third floor switching parking spots. There is no evidence before me that the issue was not resolved.

Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord acted unreasonably in responding to issues she had with other tenants in the building, in particular the second-floor tenant. As such, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

I also find the allegations above do not constitute harassment of the Tenant. While the Tenant claims the Landlord placed of poison (for pests) in or around the unit and ignored her pleas to keep her dog safe, no dates or specifics were provided regarding this incident in the application nor was this raised in the hearing. I find therefore that the Tenant has abandoned their claim related to this incident and the Tenant has failed to make out any claim related to harassment.
With respect to the T6 application, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.

With respect to the hailstorm, the Tenant confirmed that she only notified the Landlord about the broken glass from the hailstorm on August 9, 202 3. The Landlord and his window contractor attended the property two days later, on August 11, 2023. While he admitted that the other tenants had advised him about the storm damage earlier, they had also informed him that all glass had been cleaned up. Furthermore, his window contractor inspected the second-floor window and assured him that there was no danger of more glass falling to the ground below. The Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s evidence that he relayed this assurance to her after the window contractor’s inspection. The Tenant did not produce any photographs of additional glass on th e ground thereafter to corroborate her testimony that glass continued to fall. There was no evidence before me that the Landlord could have had a replacement window installed earlier than September 27, 202 3. As such, I find the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s complaint of August 9, 2023 was reasonable.

With respect to the broken glass in the garage door, the Landlord admitted that using the garage door before the broken glass was replace d could have dislodged further pieces of glass to fall. However, there is no evidence that more glass fell from the garage door after the storm and it is undisputed that the Landlord replaced all of the broken windows in the garage with plexiglass. Given that the Tenant admitted that she was not using the garage at the time because she did not trust the pulley system, I find the timeliness of the Landlord’s response in fixing the garage door was reasonable.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') were required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and have failed to do so. This application came before the Board by videoconference on June 16, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented by [name]. As of 9:45 a.m. the Landlords were not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the Board. There is no record of a request to reschedule the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant present.
reasons: The Tenant's application is brought pursuant to s. 57.1 of the Act and alleges that the Landlord has failed to restore the Tenant to possession as required after the Tenant vacated pursuant to an N13 notice of termination for extraordinary renovation and repairs.

The difficulty that arises here is that one could argue the application is premature. Section 57.1 is intended to address the situation where the landlord serves an N13, completes the renovations and repairs, and then fails to put the tenant back into possession. That does not appear to be what has happened here. The Tenant says no renovations or repairs appear to have been commenced let alone finished. The Tenant’s two-year limitation period was rapidly approaching so the Tenant filed this application in advance of the refusal to put the Tenant back into possession upon completion of the renovations in order to preserve the right of return.

It seems to me that the only way to preserve the Tenant’s right to go back into possession in these circumstances is to issue an interim order barring the Landlords from re-renting the unit to someone else. An order shall issue pursuant to s. 204(1) accordingly.
I am not seized.
ordered: This application is adjourned to a date to be set by the Board.

At the hearing of the application the Tenant should be prepared to speak to the following questions: a) Has the residential complex been sold or otherwise changed hands (for example, a mortgagee has gone into possession)? b) What building permits have been obtained if any from the local municipality? c) What communication, if any, has the Tenant had from the Landlords? d) Should the application be dismissed as premature (and taking into consideration the amendment to s. 57.1(2) of the Act scheduled to come into effect on September 26, 2026)?

The Landlords shall not re-rent the rental unit to another tenant or otherwise occupy the rental unit (except to do the repairs and renovations described in the N13) until this application is heard or the Board orders otherwise.

No later than 7 days before the hearing the parties shall give to the other and file with the Board a copy of any documents, receipts, photographs, recordings or like things the party intends to rely on at the hearing. All submissions must be uploaded on the Tribunals Ontario Portal (TOP) online. If a party is unable to use TOP, their evidence may be submitted via email at [email].
The parties may also consent in writing to the exchange of documents using the online TOP portal.
Pursuant to Rule 19.7 a party who fails to comply with an order for disclosure may not be permitted to rely on evidence that is not properly disclosed.

The Tenant shall notify the Board and the Landlords in writing immediately, if the hearing is no longer necessary and the Tenant wishes to withdraw or abandon the application. The LTB email address is [email]. July 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. And [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant filed her T2/T6 application with the LTB on December 30, 2023 and filed a request to amend on March 10, 2025.

The matter was initially scheduled to be heard on March 18, 2025, the matter was adjourned and an interim order was issued on March 28, 2025 providing the Tenant direction to amend her applications to include particulars by April 15, 2025.
The Tenant complied with the direction and submitted an amendment to the LTB and Landlord on April 15, 2025 as contained in the Board’s record in DOC-5503568.
Subsequently the Tenant made submissions to include further amendments to the T2/T6 application on January 5, 2026. Preliminary Issues: January 5, 2026 Amendment

The application has been amended a few times. An interim order required that the Tenant submit her amendments on or before April 15, 2025 however another amendment was done on January 5, 2026, the Landlord’s representative submitted that Board not consider the latest amended version.

The Tenant submitted that it has been difficult to get legal aid assistance, and that she no longer qualifies for their services. However, that she was subsequently advised to amend her application again as some of the issues are ongoing.

Amending application is outlined in LTB Rule 15 - Amending Applications where it is outlined that: 15.1 A request to amend an application before the hearing must be: a. in writing; b. served with the amended application to all other parties; and c. filed with LTB with the amended application and a completed Certificate of Service. 15.2 Where the request to amend requires the LTB to revise the Notice of Hearing, the applicant must serve the revised Notice of Hearing to all other parties and file a Certificate of Service within 7 days of receiving the revised Notice. 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors. 15.4 The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

In reviewing the Tenant’s request to amend the application as submitted on January 6, 2026, I refer to the considerations as outlined in rule 15.3. Specifically, I am mindful that the Interim Order was issued on March 28, 2025 providing the Tenant direction to amend her application by April 15, 2025 and that since there has been a prolonged period that has since passed.

As a result, the Tenant has attempted to raise new allegations, issues that have occurred since the last amendment was made and that may be more appropriately dealt with in a new application filing. I say this as I take into consideration the preliminary objection as raised by the Landlord in view of the prejudice the consideration of new issues would raise for the Landlord and that the amendments were only requested about 8 days prior to the hearing date of January 13, 2026.

On the basis of procedural fairness, in consideration of LTB rule 15 and in exercising my discretion, I denied the request to amend as received by the Board on January 6, 2026. Specifically, to limit any prejudice that the Landlord may experience as a result of the amendments where by virtue of the passage of time the issues as raised in the Tenant’s original application filed in December 2023 may have been amended to address newer issues and evolving issues precluding a finality to the proceedings. T6 lack of details/ particulars
While the Tenant amended the application pursuant to the direction of the interim order, the amended T6 application makes broad allegations that are not date specific.

The Landlord relies on Ball vs Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 ([name]. [name].) where the obligation to include “reasons and details” in a notice of termination was considered. MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of he alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct ...”

The Court went on to state that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal. Here, the Landlord states that the allegations are broad, providing date ranges and are not entirely clear.

From a procedural fairness perspective, I ruled that I am not prepared to dismiss [name] in its’ entirety based on lack of particulars until such time that I had a better sense of the totality of the issues raised. Some of the issues complained of had sufficient particulars. T2 allegations - lack of details/ particulars

Regarding the T2 application. While outlining claims of illegal entries, the Landlord’s representative submitted that entries did not occur, that the Tenant raises complaints as against other tenants which have been addressed by the Landlord and that the allegations concerning noise are lacking particulars. One such example was the date range of noise from July to December 2023. That while the Tenant has had ample opportunities to amend the application, that this was not done.

Further, in addressing the issues of noise that the Tenant raises, that the outlined timeframe was a period of capital repairs. That the Landlord does not dispute that there was noise, this was attributable to construction done with the aim to benefit the Tenant by making repairs and improvements, any noise created was within reason. That the way the Tenant described the events made it hard to respond to the particulars given a 6-month range.

The Tenant said that the construction was scheduled for June and July and did not began until November 2023. That lives of the tenants were not taken into consideration. She did not deny that plumbing capital improvements were required as there were issues ongoing with freezing pipes. T2/T6 Applications

The Tenant in her T2/T6 application as amended on April 15, 2025 seeks the same remedies in both applications as follows: • Rent Abatement $1,179.00 on the basis of $786.00 lawful rent (amended on date of the hearing due to clerical error). Calculated as: 25% of monthly rent ($786.00) portion ($196.50) for the period of July 1, 2023 –December 31, 2023 for the construction period and noise/ and or disruption and for “filth and sleep disturbance caused by pigeons, and filthy laundry room conditions.” • Out-of-Pocket Expenses $55.18 for hearing protection and stop payment of $10.00 as incurred by the Tenant. • Total monetary claim is $1,234.18.

The Tenant also make seeks non-monetary remedies as follows: o For the Landlord to stop miscommunication between management to ensure no further illegal entries o For the Landlord to stop making accounting errors in respect of the Tenant’s rent payment record. o For Landlord to explore where the Tenant’s February 2025 was lost. o Order the Landlord to include a maintenance schedule to ensure laundry machines are clean and usable.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. T6 Application

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

Specifically, the Tenant raises the following issues: • Safety concerns and odours from stairwell • Construction-related disruption (July–December 2023): o Significant noise and disturbance affecting livability. [name] infestation (2022–2024): o Resulted in unsanitary conditions and sleep disturbance. • Dirty laundry facilities: o Laundry room conditions allegedly unsanitary and unusable, causing:  Physical hardship  Need to use external laundromats Stairwell issues

The Tenant submitted that on occasion there have been non-tenants and or homeless people found in the stairwells of the residential complex. That she has encountered odours of rotting food, and cigarette smoke. That she had informed the property manager on December 8, 2023 and that despite this reporting, the trespasser being removed on the date, the issues have persisted.
The Tenant submits that despite CCTV cameras, she would like the building to be patrolled by staffing of onsite and for them to be present on weekends and late nights.
On cross examination it was not disputed the residential complex is not a smoke free building and that there are some tenants who are permitted to smoke in their rental units.

While the Tenant would prefer 24-hour security presence, the Landlord is a social housing provider with a limited operating budget. Given the location of the residential complex, while not desirable, there may be some occasions where other tenants do not close the door properly or permit someone to shelter from elements. As there was no further evidence of homeless individuals entering the rental complex, this may have been an isolated event. Further, this issue was said to have been addressed on the same date.

Given the above, the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord has failed in their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') no remedy will be considered. Pigeon Infestation

The Tenant submitted that since before summer 2022, the Landlord has failed to control a worsening pigeon infestation, resulting in droppings throughout the building exterior and causing persistent nighttime noise that disrupted her sleep.

It was not disputed that the Landlord took active measures to install netting and bird spikes between fall 2023 and May 2024. However, the Tenant feels these measures have been ineffective and these measures have not kept the pigeons away. A photo of a bench on the residential complex property was evidenced on page 45 of DOC 6278467, the photo was taken on November 28, 2023 and shows a bench covered in pigeon and or other bird droppings.
Another photo as taken on March 21, 2025 on page 51 shows that the spikes as installed to prevent pigeons from resting on the exterior of the building are shown and have partially fallen off.
It was the Landlord’s evidence that the issues concerning pigeons have been finally resolved as of the date of the hearing.

While not a perfect solution, the Landlord has demonstrated that they have taken steps to keep pigeons away from nesting and resting on the residential complex premises. The photo as evidenced from March 21, 2025 is the only evidence that the spikes are falling off, given the passage of time, there was no evidence led to suggest if these have been repaired or replaced. Nor any other evidence to suggest that this is an ongoing issue.

Given the above, and that the Tenant agreed that the issues concerning pigeons have been attempted to be mitigated by the Landlord through the installation of nets and spikes, and given the lack of evidence of any current outstanding issues, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the Landlord failed in their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') in respect of issues as alleged to have been created by pigeons. As such no remedy will be considered. Laundry Facilities

The Tenant alleges that the since the beginning of the tenancy in 2018, the Landlord has failed to maintain the onsite laundry facilities in a clean and usable condition. She submitted that the wash machines are frequently contaminated with feces, cigarette butts, and debris as found in the interior portion of the machine inside the rubber seal. Based on the condition of the machines she has opted to attend a laundromat and incurred additional costs and inconvenience.

It was submitted that when the Landlord became aware of the issue as reported by the Tenant that signage was put up advising users to check their pockets etc. and that the machines are checked and cleaned daily by the Landlord’s staff. And on cross- examination the Tenant submitted that she never reported the finding of feces in the machines.

Undated photos of the laundry room as evidenced on pages 53-54, show pieces of paper or bounce sheets scattered on the floor and something that resembles a child’s toy or hair tie in the rubber portion of the laundry machine tub. Aside from the scattered paper products, the room appears tidy, and the tile floors appear clean.

Given the above, the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord has failed in their maintenance obligations as pertaining to the conditions of the laundry room. Therefore, no remedy will be considered. Hot Water Issues

The Tenant alleges that throughout the tenancy and since 2018, the Landlord has failed to provide an effective maintenance reporting system and to resolve recurring service issues, particularly involving the loss or unreliability of hot water, as demonstrated by repeated incidents from September 28, 2023 through April 8, 2025, where water service was unavailable or inconsistent despite multiple documented complaints, resulting in a sustained disruption of essential services and a significant burden on the tenant to repeatedly report unresolved problems.
In her submissions, the Tenant summarizes these instances to be plumbing issues and she is frustrated when work orders are cancelled.
Given the lack of particulars and evidence to support the Tenant’s assertions of ongoing issues for the outlined period, this portion of the application is dismissed. Balcony - stucco surface

The Tenant submitted that sometime since August 2023, the Landlord applied a stucco upgrade to the balconies, this is non-slip surface coating that can not be cleaned effectively. The Tenant said that this upgrade did not need to be completed, and the coating cannot be effectively cleaned and damages cleaning tools, thereby reducing the usability of the balcony and diminishing the tenant’s enjoyment of the unit.

On cross examination it was outlined that there is a distinction between liking something and something being of quality. It was clear the Tenant would have preferred a balcony surface without the non-slip coating as applied to the surface.

The Tenant has not proven that the Landlord has failed in their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') in respect of the installation of the non-slip surface coating on the balcony. For this reason, no remedy can be considered. Plumbing Upgrade

The Tenant alleges that in November 2023, the Landlord installed defective plumbing components that reduced water flow, caused a malfunctioning toilet and a noisy faucet, and contributed to ongoing hot water instability. It was stated that although some fixtures were repaired on September 16, 2024, the hot water issue persists. Further, the Tenant was dissatisfied with the second toilet replacement in August 2024.

In their evidence, as contained in DOC-6257352 the Landlord evidenced two notices for water supply interruptions as connected to August 31, 2023 and February 23, 2024 during which the Tenants were advised that there would be an experienced water shutdown between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.to complete water supply repairs and upgrades. These are said to have been completed.

The Tenant submitted that access to hot and cold water is not of issue unless it is deliberately turned off for repairs, as it was done in September 2024. And while I appreciate it was the Tenant’s preference to keep the prior installed toilet, there has been insufficient evidence led to substantiate a remedy in respect of any alleged past or outstanding plumbing issues. For this reason, no remedy can be considered. [name]

In the T2 portion of the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord: • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services Illegal entries

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord’s staff entered her unit illegally on: August 28, 29, 2023, Nov 29, 2023, and September 25, 2024. Further that where notices were provided that they were improper. August 25, 2023

A general notice was taped to the Tenants door on August 25, 2023 which outlined that work in connection to balcony waterproofing and anti-slip coating was expected to begin on August 28, 2023 and that individual notices would be issued to inform of exact date of work her balcony.

Despite this, workers contracted to complete the balcony work showed to her unit on August 25, 2023 and that the notice was provided to her after the workers already attended at her unit. That the situation was distressing to her as she had a morning meeting and was unprepared.

The Landlord’s superintendent apologized to the Tenant in an email message of August 29, 2023 explaining that there was an oversight and that her unit was missed inadvertently in the notice communications for the August 25, 2023 entry. August 28, 2023

The Tenant was in the shower at approximately 8:00 a.m., that she had to jump out to find two contractors/ workers banging on her window advising her that she must clear the balcony. She stated that the notice of entry was only posted to the Tenant’s door at 2:30 p.m., on the same date.
That the late notice is wholly inadequate. November 27, 2023
Again, that a construction crew of workers attended at the Tenant’s unit and attempted to enter, as there was no notice entry was not granted. September 25, 2024

On the date, a vendor providing services attended at the Tenant’s unit. On September 26, 2024, Ana Moraru, the Tenant Engagement and Services Supervisor for the region in an email apologized to the Tenant for the vendors attendance indicating that there “had been a miscommunication between the building team and the vendor.”

Further, that there are three dates available as options during which balcony door and windows replacements would be done in her unit. The Tenant was provided 3 options of dates as follow: October 21-22-23 , 2024, October 23-24-25 , 2024, October 28-29-30, 2024 to choose from and that she would be provided minimum of 3 days in advance per her request.

On the basis of the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord’s agents entered the rental unit balcony illegally on one occasion of August 28, 2023. This was not disputed by the Landlord. The other outlined dates included situations where actual entries into the unit did not occur.
The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $200.00 for the entry on August 28, 2023. Substantial interference with Reasonable Enjoyment & Harassment Noise - construction and pigeons

The Tenant testified that she was subjected to unbearable construction noise above, below, outside as emanating from the balcony work and from exterior walls of the building. That the level of noise rose above 80 dB, and that as a result of the capital improvements being done she was subject to repeated interruptions from July to December 2023.

That the drilling noises and ongoing construction directly interfered with her online work and ability to connect with her clients. And that the noise complaints as raised with the Landlord were dismissive.

The Landlord did not dispute that the issues of noise that the Tenant raises were in connection to a period of capital repairs being conducted within the residential complex. [name] was attributable to construction done to make repairs and improvements. As noted at the outset, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue with the 6-month range between July and December 2023, this making it difficult to respond to the issues the Tenant raised.
Further that there was no reporting rendered to substantiate the claim that the noise levels rose above 80 dB.

Subparagraph 8(3)(b) of [name]. 516/06 outlines that unless the Tenant can establish the work done to repair the recreational complex could have been done in a more reasonable and less disturbing manner, the Board is statute barred from making a finding that what happened substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.

The issue for the Board is whether or not the work could have been done in a less disruptive manner during the period as outlined. There was no direct evidence to support this assertion other then the Tenant’s dissatisfaction that the repairs were protracted and noisy.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant was offered accommodation to work in the recreation room, which the Tenant declined. This was not disputed, and the Tenant was also offered compensation for hearing protection in the amount of $45.18 by the contractor of the Landlord where a release was to be signed. This option was declined by the Tenant, therefore the reimbursement was not provided. Payment of rent issues

The Tenant submits that due to multiple accounting errors in landlord's rent ledger in connection to the Tenant’s rental unit for the months of September through November 2024, she was accused of not paying rent and that these errors required her attention to correct. Specifically, that the ledger reflected the wrong cheque numbers for those months.

The issues commence in Dec 2023 when the Tenant provided the Landlord a payment for the wrong amount, however this was not raised to her attention until Feb 2025.That the cheque dated February 1, 2025 for $589.50 required a stop payment and incurred a bank charge of $10.00; and while the cheque went missing the landlord takes no responsibility for it. And that two cheques from Feb 2025 had not yet cleared her bank, which, in addition to the March 2025 rent cheque, if cashed at the same time would cause financial hardship.

As it was not disputed that the error concerning the initial issue arose with the Tenant providing the Landlord a payment for the wrong amount of rent, on the basis of the evidence, I can not determine that the landlord was responsible for the cost that the Tenant later incurred through her own banking institution. Further, I am not satisfied that this was not a voluntary option, one which the landlord should not bare the cost.

Given all of the above, I find that the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to establish that the carrying out of any capital improvement work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances and that the noises as created by pigeons have contributed to her lack of sleep. Further the Tenant opted to purchase her own hearing protection to address the noise issues complained of; in doing so she incurred a cost. As a reimbursement was offered to her, albeit contingent on a signed release, the landlord is not liable for any further claims for such reimbursement given the facts as before me. The Tenant’s application with respect to substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment must be dismissed. Withheld or interfered with vital services

The Tenant submitted that she was interrupted in her ability to conduct Zoom meetings on July 18, 2023 between the hours of 10:00 a.m. and 11:00 a.m., and again on July 19, 2023 from 10:00 to 11:00 a.m. by unexpected power outages without prior notice to her.

There is no disputed that there was a notice provided, the parties dispute when the notice was actually posted. The Tenant said that when she became aware of the expected outage, the Tenant rescheduled a [name] meeting for July 19, 2023.

On July 19, 2023, however that her rescheduled [name] meeting was interrupted by loud knocking and shouting at her door by the Landlord’s staff without notice. In her email to the Landlord’s superintendent (SC) the Tenant writes: “Do not phone or knock at my door without prior advanced warning. DO NOT DISTURB ME. Do not phone or knock at my door without prior warning. I am a writer, writing mentor (teacher), and editor. I often work with students online over zoom. Phone calls and door knocks are disruptive.”
Further, in the same communication the Tenant sought clarification of strategies the Landlord will put in place to avoid further disturbances. November 13, 2023

On November 13, 2023, the Tenant experienced another unexpected power interruption at approximately 10:00 a.m. as she was beginning work online with a client. That while the power was restored quickly, the outage shut down her computer causing her to be disconnect from meeting and causing closure to a number of computer files to be recovered. This created a delay in the meeting.

As outlined by the Landlord, unless there are planned power interruptions in connection to any work being performed in the complex the Landlord does not directly have control over any outages that are within the domain of the power service provider.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $200.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $100.00 from the rent each month August to September 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 03, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: At the outset , I enquired why there were two parties in the hearing room identified a s the Landlord when the application only specified one Landlord. The parties explained that while they both owned the property (i.e. were both Landlords), only one of them signed the tenancy agreement. Neither the Landlord nor the Tenant requested that the application be amended to include the second Landlord. I was satisfied, however, that [name] [name] [name], had standing to participate in the hearing as a Landlord. The Application

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application , namely that the Landlord discontinued her parking on December 6, 2025 , on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The tenancy commenced on May 1, 2022.

The unit is one of two units in townhouse. The Tenant rents a room in a four-bedroom unit on the second floor. There is one other unit in the home. It is located on the main floor with access to the basement. The Landlord stated it is occupied by her brother, [name]. While the two-bedroom basement unit used to be rented, the Landlord stated that it is now vacant.

There are only two parking spaces for the entire property, located at the back of the property. The Tenant stated that when she moved in, there was only one other person in the house with a car (i.e. one of her roommates) and that her roommate was using one of the parking spaces.

The Tenant admitted that she did not advise the Landlord that she had a car when she moved into the unit. She stated, however, that she has had continuous parking at the rental unit for the last four years, that the Landlord’s father visits the property at least once a week and he is well aware that the Tenant has always parked at the property. She said that when she signed her lease, the Landlord’s father told her she could park at the property but she could not recall if he actually assigned her a parking spot or just told her she could park in the second parking space if she needed to.

The Tenant stated that on December 6, 2025, she received a text from the Landlord stating that she had to remove her vehicle since she was parking in the space reserved for Airbnb guests. She said that she returned her car to the parking spot within two to seven days after December 6, 2025 and admitted that she continues to park in that spot as needed. She admitted that the December 6, 2025 text message is the only time she was ever told to move her car from the parking spot.

At my request, the Tenant emailed the Board a copy of her original tenancy agreement dated April 22, 2022. The Tenant confirmed that the lease is silent with respect to parking (i.e. does not state it is included or excluded). Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord testified that parking was never included in the Tenant’s lease because the parking space was always reserved for the main floor unit (i.e. her use when she lived there, her brother’s use or use by Airbnb guests) . She stated that she live d in the main floor unit until 2023. In July 2025, her brother moved in.

The Landlord stated that when the Tenant was applying for the unit, she asked the Tenant if she had a car and the Tenant said no. The Landlord stated that the Tenant did have an e- bike which she was allowed to store in the backyard.

The Landlord produced a copy of the updated tenancy agreement (i.e. Ontario standard form lease) [Doc 82555918] which the Landlord was ordered to provide to the Tenant by order LTB-T-071676-24 issued on November 5, 2025.

Page 1, paragraph 2 of the tenancy agreement states “Number of vehicle parking spaces and description – NA”. Page 2, paragraph 5 states “ parking (if applicable) – NA”. Page 3, paragraph 6 states “Guest Parking – No”. The Landlord said that the tenancy agreement was provided to the Tenant in November 2025 and the Tenant never disputed any of the terms in the lease, including that parking. Evidence of Landlord’s witness – [name] 13. [name] is the Landlord’s father. He testified that he sometimes spoke in English with the Tenant but never about anything important. He said he never discussed parking a car at the property when she moved in because she only had a bicycle. He said he never told the Tenant that she could park a car in one of the parking spaces at the back of the property when it was not in use. Analysis 14. I am not satisfied that there was a reduction or discontinuance of a service (i.e. parking) because I do not find that parking was included in the tenancy agreement. While the April 22, 2022 lease produced by the Tenant was silent on the issue of parking, the November 5, 2025 lease explicitly states that parking is not available . The Tenant did not produce any documentary evidence, such as emails or text messages to the Landlord, contesting the terms of the November 5, 2025 lease. The Tenant did not challenge the testimony of the Landlord’s father, namely that there was no discussion about the Tenant parking a car at the property and that he never told her she could park a car in one of the parking spaces when it was not in use. 15. While there was no dispute that one of the Tenant’s roommates utilized one of the two parking spaces, the Tenant did not produce her roommate as a witness to confirm whether parking was included in her roommate’s tenancy agreement or whether her roommate paid extra for the parking space. 16. The Tenant claimed she had parked at the property continuously for approximately four years with the Landlord's knowledge. In some circumstances, the Board has found that a service becomes part of the tenancy through the parties' conduct, even where the written lease is silent. In this case, however, the evidence of permission is disputed. T he Tenant had no corroborating documentary evidence to support that the Landlord was aware that she was previously parking at the property or that she was given permission to park at the property. 17. Even if I were satisfied that parking was included in the Tenant’s lease, I would not have found that there was a reduction or discontinuance of a service because the Tenant admitted that she was only ever asked to move her car once and that she continues to use the parking spot whenever she needs to.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
