issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [organization] Inc. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant. • The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. These applications were heard by videoconference on June 23, 2026. The first named Landlord [name] (EJ), the Landlords’ legal representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant spoke with Tenant Duty Counsel.
reasons: The Tenant filed the T2 application on December 30, 2025. On April 25, 2026, the Tenant filed a request to amend the application. At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative confirmed receipt of the amended application but said there are insufficient details in the application in order for the Landlord to defend the claims.

The Tenant said that she is unrepresented and not aware of the Board’s rules and requirements. She said that some of the issues directly related to claims made in the Landlord’s application and therefore they were well-aware of the issues claimed by the Tenant.

A detailed review of the claims was conducted at the hearing and I found that, while the Tenant failed to include various dates and specifics, the Landlord had sufficient information to know the case to be met. The hearing proceeded accordingly.
The power to amend an application does not permit the Board to add an entirely new application on a completely different ground.

While better suited to a T3 application, the Tenant understood that the claims related to the laundry facility must be considered under the legal test for substantial interference as also with the claims related to the stove versus the test for a T6 application. Disclosure

As part of pre-amble, I advise parties of their responsibilities related to evidence. They were put on notice to ensure they are ready to proceed to their hearing and have all evidence numbers ready to go in order to ensure an expeditious hearing.
At the onset of the hearing, I noted that the Tenant has uploaded to the Portal (TOP) in excess of 150 documents and those documents were not intuitively labelled.
The Landlord’s representative said that while he also received the Tenant’s voluminous disclosure, it was not organized and challenging to navigate.

The Tenant acknowledged that she has been before the Tribunal on around three previous occasions where the presiding Member’s flagged the Tenant’s disclosure as an issue which resulted in some dismissals.

In my view, the Tenant knew or ought to have known that continuing to overload TOP and the Landlord with evidence would be problematic. The Tenant did not describe any reasonable step taken to ensure her evidence related to this matter was presented in the required format. Nevertheless, the matter was stood down for around 40 minutes to allow the Tenant time to organize the evidence she intended to rely on at the hearing.
The Tenant requested and was afforded multiple breaks. As a result, and due to the volume of disclosure, the hearing took around six hours to complete.

At times throughout the hearing, the Tenant became frustrated, aggressive and refused to follow direction when I denied some of her evidence; having found it to be unnecessary and/or repetitive or not properly disclosed. At one point, the Tenant was put on notice that if her behaviour continues, I will consider costs in the amount of $50.00 for each interruption. The Tenant corrected course and no costs were levied.
The Landlords’ disclosure brief includes: photographs, the ledger and various communications and was referred to in its entirety (DOC8170368).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The T2 Application
The Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The tenancy began around July 1, 2015 at which time there was a different Landlord.
The original tenancy agreement was between the Tenant, a deceased Tenant and the former Landlord. I note, a copy of the original lease agreement was not provided to the Board.
The residential complex was sold and the new Landlord took over around December 2025.
The Tenant said that she lives in the rental unit with her partner who has not been added as a tenant to the lease.
The lawful rent is $1,121.50.
At the onset of the hearing, the process was explained, in detail to the Tenant.
I also explained how the Board determines the outcome of a matter on a balance of probabilities.

On a balance of probabilities means the applicant, in this case the Tenant must show that her version of events is the more probable and should succeed. Saying something is proven on a balance of probabilities simply means that it is more likely than not to have occurred. It means that it is probable, i.e., the probability that some event happened is more than 50%--indeed, 50.1% is sufficient. In all cases, the decision maker must weigh up the evidence and decide which version is most probably true. Consequently, the real truth may never be known. All that can be done is to decide which of the parties has presented the most probable version.

While I have dismissed the majority of the Tenant’s claims, as explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation related to the laundry service on a balance of probabilities. However, no further remedy is awarded to the Tenant as explained below.

The application claims the Landlord and agents substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, the Landlord and/or their agents obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant also asserts that the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit or building without giving the Tenant replacement keys.

The claims made by the Tenant relate to: • parking issues, • lock changes to the rental unit, residential complex and mailbox, • harassment from the Landlord and agents, • threats of eviction, • stove • laundry facility
By way of remedy, the Tenant seeks a rent abatement for the period December 2025 to April 2026 and a cease and desist order for various issues.
At the hearing, the application was amended to reduce the rent abatement claimed from $5,607.50 to $2,000.00. The Key Issues

The first issue in the Tenant’s application is brought under s.29(1)5 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which deals with situations where a Landlord and/or agent alters the locking system at rent rental unit or residential complex without giving the tenant a replacement key.

There is no dispute that the Landlord change the locks to the main door to the residential complex, the rental unit and the mailbox. There is also no dispute that the Tenant was provided replacement keys for the changed locks.

The issue raised by the Tenant is that she was not provided with two keys for each lock change. She said that she required a second key for her spouse and the Landlord levied a cost. So, the claim made in the application related to Reason 2, as selected by the Tenant cannot be successful.

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Considering the key issue through the lens of substantial interference, the Tenant’s claim is denied.

The lease agreement is between the Tenant and the Landlord. Her partner is not listed as a Tenant. She said that she is required to physically admit anyone at the door and this has become a nuisance. While she stated this inconvenience at the hearing, it was not pled in the application and therefore is not considered as part of the analysis.

While EJ was aware that the Tenant’s partner resides at the rental unit, the Landlord’s policy is to provide keys or replacement keys to the Tenant identified in the lease agreement, which is what happened here.

EJ explained the reason for the lock changes; to enhance building security and the new locking system and keys cannot be reproduced independently by the tenants. There is a cost to produce the “high security” key in the amount of $23.48. This cost was transferred to the Tenant for the additional key.

The Tenant’s application claims the interference is related to the cost of the second key. She believes the cost levied by the Landlord is an illegal charge. I note, this is not a T1 application. With respect to the key cost claim, pursuant to s. 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06, it is not illegal for a landlord to charge for additional keys not greater than the direct costs.

Again, I do not find the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex when the cost to produce the additional high security key was forwarded to the Tenant. The Parking Issues

To summarize, the Tenant takes the position that the lease provided her with a dedicated parking spot and starting around December 17, 2025 the Landlord permitted a large demolition bin to occupy her spot. The Tenant followed up multiple times with EJ to remove the [name]. The [name] was removed on December 22, 2025.
The Tenant said that on December 29, 2025 she notified EJ that a contractor was parked in her space and police were called.

It was also the evidence of the Tenant that she had issues with snow removal from her parking spot between January and February 2026. With the exception of the February 12, 2026 incident (described below), the Tenant did not provide further dates related to issues.

EJ testified that there was some confusion over the Tenant’s claimed parking spot in the transition to new ownership but it was rectified and recognized at the Tenant’s parking spot. EJ said that when she received complaints from the Tenant about the bin, others parking in the spot or snow issues, she responded promptly.

However, it was the evidence of the Landlord that the parking space was restricted to the Tenant’s car only and visitor parking was not permitted. This was supported by a photograph prohibiting visitor parking that was installed on the building by the former Landlord. This was later confirmed in email correspondence between EJ and the Tenant on January 21, 2026 in reference to a document provided to EJ by the Tenant where the Tenant noted visitor parking is prohibited.

On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed she does not have a personal vehicle and uses the spot for visiting family and friends. She said the no-visitor restriction was misunderstood by the Landlord and she could use her space as she pleases. The Tenant was unable to provide specific details as to whose parking was impacted on the dates claimed by the Tenant. I note, the Tenant did not call the former Landlord to provide testimony related to the visitor parking restriction. There was also insufficient evidence that the Tenant contacted EJ regarding visitor access on the dates described by the Tenant.

Nevertheless, EJ said that while the Tenant did not have a car to park, when she was made aware of various contractors using the Tenant’s space, they were promptly asked to relocate. Additionally, the Tenant was compensated by way of an abatement in the amount of $50.00 from December 2025 to January 2026 for snow related issues, despite the Tenant not using the parking spot as required.

With respect to the snow accumulation, EJ said that there was an unusual volume of snow during the period complained of by the Tenant. They took every measure possible to keep up with the heavy snow fall period but at times, it was challenging. EJ said the Tenant had no impact as she was not using the parking space as intended.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenant has not met the burden to prove that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment related to parking. I am satisfied that the Tenant was not using the parking space for the intended purpose and that visitor parking was prohibited.

The Tenant clearly was not using the reserved spot to park her car and her visitors were required to park off-site. It therefore cannot be said that there was any substantial interference over the brief six day period when the demolition bin was in her spot.
Even if I found that the Tenant’s spot was used by contractors or accumulation of snow, I would deny that claim through the lens of substantial interference.

The wording of s.22 of the Act indicates that not every disturbance is a breach of the Act. Rather, the disturbance must “substantially” interfere with “reasonable” enjoyment. This language indicates that for a disturbance to be a breach of the Act it must be a significant one from the perspective of the average, reasonable tenant.

The parking issues complained of by the Tenant cannot be construed a “substantial” as the Tenant did hot have a car to park in her designated spot and her visitors were restricted from parking their vehicles in the spot. So, the Landlord’s failure to move the [name] before six days and remove snow in a quicker fashion cannot be said to have caused any substantial interfered to the Tenant.
Given the above, all parking related complaints alleged by the Tenant are denied. The Verbal Altercation
It was the Tenant’s evidence that on February 12, 2026, she confronted the Landlord’s snow removal contractor regarding the accumulation of snow in her designated parking spot.

The Tenant relied on a video of the event where it can be seen that she and the contractor engaged in a verbal confrontation. The Tenant claims this encounter constitutes harassment from the Landlord’s agent.
EJ was aware of the confrontation and said they were trying to manage the heavy accumulation of snow.

Based on the evidence before the Board, while I acknowledge the Tenant was involved in a confrontational encounter with the Landlord’s contractor, I also find there was a lack of civility on the part of the Tenant. I am convinced that both parties engaged in banter and swearing and equally participated in the overall lack of civil discourse.

A definition of harassment can be found in section 10 of the Human Rights Code: engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. I find that an objective consideration of the circumstances surrounding the verbal altercation does not constitute harassment as much as it constitutes the contractors attempt to explain the situation to the Tenant. From the evidence, and in my view, the downward spiral of the conversation was instigated by the Tenant.

I find that the Tenant has not provided sufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord’s contractor spoke to the Tenant in any greater offensive and harassing manner as the Tenant spoke to the contractor. The contractor was explaining the pressures of his job and the conversation escalated as provoked by the Tenant. I cannot find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord/agent has harassed the Tenant and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. The Laundry Issue
There is no dispute that the Tenant had access to laundry services at the residential complex from the onset of the tenancy.

The Tenant had the option to file a T3 application for a reduction or discontinuation of a service or facility but chose to include the claim in her amended T2 application, where the legal test is distinct to s.22 of the Act.

The Tenant testified that around the end of December 2025 or the beginning of January 2026, the laundry room was closed for maintenance issues. She said that made it challenging for her as she has agoraphobia and used the onsite laundry during off-peak hours as not to encounter other tenants. The closure of the facility forced her to travel to off-site laundry facilities and incurred cost. From around January 8, 2026 to March 16, 2026 she made several attempts by email and phone to inquire about the status of the laundry facility and said she was often met with delay and lack of sufficient response.
The Tenant said that she complained to City of Kitchener and a by-law enforcement officer issued an Order to Comply to the Landlord by April 15, 2026.

The Tenant said she was compensated an abatement of $25.00 per month for January, February and March 2026 for the interruption in service. She appealed the abatement on March 2, 2026 and was successful and the amount increased to $112.00 per month effective April and continues until the service is restored.

The Tenant believes the amount is insufficient and should be retroactive to December 2025. The Tenant’s evidence [name] is an email from the Tenant to the EJ on March 11, 2026 where she indicated costs that total $26.06 for Uber Canada and DJ’s Laundry. I note, the Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence at the hearing to support the proposition that her costs have increased.

It was the position of EJ that the laundry facility is in a large space where around 95% is unoccupied space with no secured windows and doors. There was also a water/sewage backup around December 2026 and the Landlord is working with the City By-Law officer on the issue and to enclose a dedicated and secure laundry facility. They fully intend to restore laundry service at the complex and are currently subject to the City’s timeline for issuance of a permit. She is scheduled to review the project with the officer mid July 2026 with a target completion date of September 2026.

EJ said the Tenant was offered a $25.00 abatement which the Tenant accepted and in March 2026, she requested a greater abatement. Based on the information provided to the Tenant, EJ increased the abatement to $112.00 per month. The Tenant has not provided any documents to support a greater rebate. This rebate will continue until the laundry service is restored.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find the loss of the laundry facility has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment for all of the reasons cited by the Tenant.

An abatement is designed to address the idea that a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving them then the rent should be abated proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

The T2 application seeks a rent abatement for the interference and an order from the Board to restore the laundry facility. I am satisfied that the Landlord is working toward restoration of the laundry service and awaiting the required permits. As for the requested further rent abatement, I am satisfied the Landlord has already given a substantial rent abatement and will continue to do so until the laundry service is restored. In the absence of any documentary evidence to support the proposition that the abatement should be increased, I am not inclined to award anything further. The Camera Issue

There is no dispute that the Tenant has installed a doorbell camera at the rental unit and four additional cameras on the outside of the residential complex. The cameras were installed around 2022. There are two cameras affixed to the exterior of the building aimed at the parking lot and driveway and two cameras affixed to the building aimed at the back of the complex. Some of the exterior cameras capture both video and audio.

The Tenant states that she had permission from the former Landlord to install the various camera, including those in the common areas of the complex. It was the Tenant’s evidence that the former Landlord relied on the camera footage from time to time for various issues and this should be accepted as consent. Also, she said the neighbour across the hall is not bothered by the Tenant’s doorbell camera.
The Tenant said the cameras are imperative to her safety and she has been attacked in the past and endures bullying from other tenants.

EJ states that the new Landlord had serious concern about the cameras and privacy issues and issued to all units, notice to remove personally installed security cameras in common areas and building exteriors. The December 30, 2025 letter also states the Landlord’s intention to install professional security cameras and provided reasons for the requirement to remove personal devices.

EJ said the Tenant has failed to comply with both the December 30, 2025 letter and the February 10, 2026 N5 termination notice where the Tenant was reminded of the security camera policy and requirements.

EJ said that the cameras, in total are in invasion of privacy notwithstanding the neighbouring tenant’s acceptance of the doorbell camera. The exterior cameras are mounted on common areas, under the Landlord’s control and they need to be removed. There is no written confirmation from the former Landlord that the Tenant was permitted to install the cameras. Some of the exterior cameras breach the Criminal Code of Canada s.184 which restricts audio recording in common areas.
For clarity, section 184 of the Criminal Code of Canada prohibits the willful interception of private communication using any device without the consent of the communicating parties.

I note, there were no claims made by either party that there has been any reported violation in this regard. The issue of the cameras is also addressed in the context of the N5 termination notice. I am satisfied that the Tenant’s cameras place the Landlord in a precarious position with ensuring and protecting the privacy of other tenants at the residential complex.

However, I am not persuaded that the Tenant had permission from the former Landlord to install the cameras which is the focus of my analysis. In my view, the email evidence tendered by the Tenant is weak and does not constitute permission. The Tenant did not call the former Landlord to testify at the hearing to support her claim. I therefore cannot make a finding that the Landlord’s insistence in removing the cameras constitutes substantially interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex. The Stove/Oven

There is no dispute that when the Tenant complained to the Landlord about the oven control key issue around March 11, 2026, the Landlord replaced the oven. The Tenant said the replacement stove had temperature issues and it was also replaced around April 16, 2026. When delivered, it was covered in cockroaches. She complained on the same day and the unit was removed and again replaced. While she said it doesn’t work well, no further reports have been made to the Landlord. She said she feels intimidated to report other issues for fear of retaliation.

The Tenant relied on photographs that show the bag attached to the oven contained dead cockroaches. She did not see any live cockroaches. The Tenant believes the Landlord has the “pest-infested” oven sent in retaliation for the various issues reported to the Landlord and advocating for her rights.

Under cross examination, the Tenant confirmed that the various stoves were not delivered by the Landlord but a company hired by the Landlord. When the Tenant made the complaints, the Landlord had replacement units delivered.

EJ testified that when the Tenant issued the various complaints about the oven, she promptly contacted her vendor who replaced the units. She personally was not present nor aware of the condition of the deliveries but acted swiftly once reported by the Tenant.
EJ said that she is versed in aspects of the Act and understands the Landlord’s obligations in matters such as this. The Tenants claims of retaliation are not justified.

The wording of section 22 of the Act makes it clear that it is concerned with the behaviour of landlords. Here, the behaviour or conduct of the Landlord, which the Tenants claim caused a substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the unit, involves the Tenant’s belief that the Landlord had defective stoves delivered as a means of retaliation.
On the totality of evidence before the Board, I do not find the Landlord acted in a retaliatory manner in dealing with the stove issues. The Termination Notices
Next, there is the issue of the N5 termination notice(s) issued to the Tenant.
The Tenant believes the Landlord served termination notices because she attempted to assert her rights regarding the parking, snow, locks, contractors, stove, cameras and laundry issues.

The Landlord served an N5 notice to the Tenant on or around December 29, 2025. EJ said that she miscalculated the termination date and failed to sign the notice. Understanding this would be dismissed by the LTB, she did not file an L2 application.

On February 10, 2026 the Landlord served the Tenant a valid first N5 notice with a termination date of March 13, 2026. The schedule A attached details issues and correspondence related to the same issues addressed in the T2 application, this time from the Landlord’s perspective.

Essentially the Landlord takes issue with the volume and aggressive nature of the Tenant’s communications and her refusal to remove the security cameras that the Tenant has installed in the common areas.
As explained at the hearing, landlords and tenants are entitled to service notices and file application where they believe a breach has occurred under the Act.

Having reviewed in detail the Tenant’s claims in the application and the Landlord’s N5 notices, I do not find the N5 was made in retaliation to the Tenant asserting her rights. Rather, I am satisfied that the Landlord has legitimate reasons to put the Tenant on notice of concerns related to the volume and intensity of her communications and refusal to follow the Landlord’s policies regarding parking and the cameras.

I am therefore not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the reason for the Landlord’s termination notice and subsequent application being brought is that the Tenant has attempted to secure or enforce her legal rights.

For completeness, I will also state that I do not find this to be the case in considering the Tenant’s claims as they relate to s.83(3)(c) of the Act, where mandatory refusal of the application is required.

Subsection 83 of the Act states the following: 83(3) Without restricting the generality of subsection (1), the Board shall refuse to grant the application where satisfied that, (c) the reason for the application being brought is that the tenant has attempted to secure or enforce his or her legal rights;
I find the Tenant failed to meet the onus to show that the reason for the termination was the attempt to secure or enforce her legal rights. The Landlord’s Application
The Tenant made a preliminary motion to dismiss the Landlord’s application because of her efforts to enforce or secure her legal rights.
The Tenant’s motion was dismissed for the reasons cited above with respect to the termination notices.
When I attempted to further explain s.83(3)(c) of the Act, the Tenant interrupted as said that she did not need to hear any more on that issue.

It is the position of the Landlord that the Tenant did not void the order in accordance with s.64(3) of the Act. The voiding period was from February 18 to 24, 2026. On February 19, 2026, the Tenant emailed again and refused to remove the cameras.

EJ provided detailed testimony related to the Tenant’s volume, frequency and style of communications from the Tenant. She said the Tenant is aware of the Landlord’s policy related to the reporting of urgent and non urgent matters. She said it was not uncommon for the Tenant to file the same issue across platforms and by phone, multiple times in one day. At times, the Tenant was forceful, rude and unreasonably demanding. To support these claims, EJ reviewed the emails in the Landlord’s evidence brief.

EJ said that she takes tenant complaints seriously and acts on all complaints. The Tenant is aware of the Landlord’s 24-48 hour response policy yet refuses to wait until sending further and multiple inquires about the same reported issues. She said the Tenant “bombards” her and this impacts her ability to address the Tenant or other tenants’ issues and manage through her work obligations.
EJ pointed to several emails where she said the Tenant’s demands and threats impacted her personally and her ability to efficiently work.
The Landlord is not seeking a termination order if the Tenant agrees to conditions that she will follow the Landlord’s reporting policy and remove the cameras.
The Tenant declined to cross examine the Landlord’s evidence.

At the hearing I found that the Landlord met the burden of proof related to the volume, frequency and style of communications from the Tenant which substantially interfered with the Landlord’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex, lawful rights, privileges or interests.
Secondly, I found that the Tenant did not have the consent of the Landlord to install the cameras and her refusal to remove the cameras also constitutes substantial interference.

Having made this finding and denying the Tenant’s motion, she said that she would comply with a conditional order. However, multiple times the Tenant continued to argue her objection to my finding and said she felt pressured to consent. I told her that in the absence of a consent, I would proceed with the application.

I attempted to complete the Landlord’s application with a s.83 analysis and again the Tenant interrupted and asked me to stop. She said that she disagreed with the conditions but wanted to preserve her tenancy. After further discussion, I was satisfied that the Tenant understood the consequences of the consent, and willingly consented to the terms.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. LTB-L-020288-26 On consent of the parties is ordered that:
The tenancy is preserved subject to the following conditions.

For a period of one year from the date of this order, the Tenant shall comply with the Landlord’s protocols for reporting tenant-related issues with respect to urgent and non urgent matters. The Tenant is aware of the Landlord’s reporting systems.
The Tenant shall remove the doorbell camera at the rental unit and the four exterior cameras she installed at the residential complex on or before July 31, 2026.

If the Tenant breaches the terms in this agreement related to paragraphs 4 and/or 5 of this order, the Landlord may apply under section 78 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, without notice to the Tenant, for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant. The Landlord must make this application no later than 30 days after the Tenant’s breach. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative raised that that there was an order issued by the Board, LTB-L-009609-24, requiring the Tenant to pay rent arrears and that there were two other orders in relation to the appeal of the Board’s order requiring the Tenant to pay costs to the Landlord totalling $8,000.00. In addition, there was a Superior Court proceeding where the Tenant was required to pay costs to the Landlord in the amount of $18,000.00. To this end, the Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that set off ought to ordered if the Tenant was successful in their application.
The Tenant objected to any set off as he believed the matters were still active and before the courts and the enforcement of the orders were stayed.
The issue of set off was not determined on a preliminary basis and will be revisited in my analysis below.

Late disclosure was also raised as a preliminary issue. In this regard, the Tenant had filed evidence with the Board on January 21, 2026 but did not provide a copy to the Landlord or it’s representative until January 23, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative objected to the late disclosure.

Pursuant to Rule 19.1 of the LTB Rules of Procedure all parties to a matter that has been scheduled for a hearing must provide the other parties and the LTB with a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence that the party intends to rely upon at least 7 days before the hearing. The evidence must be provided to the other parties using one of the methods of service identified in the Act or Rule 3.

Pursuant to Rule 19.7 a party who fails to comply with Rule 19 or an order or direction for disclosure may not rely on the evidence that was not disclosed as directed or ordered, unless otherwise ordered.
The Tenant’s application was filed on January 12, 2023. The application had been scheduled previously for a hearing on May 3, 2023 and on November 17, 2025. On both dates, the hearing was adjourned.

The Tenant had ample time to organize, serve and file his evidence and was unable to provide a reason for filing this recent evidence late. Accordingly, the Tenant’s late evidence was not accepted and he was not permitted to rely on it at the hearing. The Application

On or about June 5, 2023, the Tenant filed a request to amend the application with the Board. The Landlord’s Legal Representative acknowledged having received a copy of the amended application and did not oppose the requested amendments. Accordingly, the request to amend the application was granted.
In summary, the Tenant’s application is about a cockroach infestation in his unit that he alleges the Landlord failed to properly address within a reasonable time and/or manner. [name] Evidence

A summary of the Tenant’s evidence is as follows: i. On or about November 4, 2022, the Tenant noticed cockroaches in the unit and filed a maintenance request with the Landlord. ii. The Landlord scheduled an inspection of the unit for November 24, 2022 and scheduled the unit to be treated on November 25, 2022. iii. In preparation for the treatment, the Tenant referred to the preparation sheet that he was provided, which asked the Tenant to complete various tasks such as emptying the cupboards and moving stuff away from the walls. The Tenant was concerned about the requirement to move things out from the wall because his unit was a small bachelor apartment and it was not possible to have the bed and his book cases pulled out from the wall because doing so would block the entry to the unit. iv. The Tenant contacted the property manager regarding his preparation concerns and was told by the property manager that it was probably okay if he could not move everything out from the wall but that it was up to the pest control company. v. When pest control attended on November 25, 2022, they refused to treat the unit because of the Tenant’s two bookcases. The Tenant requested that the pest control technician at least treat with gel and leave traps but the technician refused saying that they were not authorized to do so. vi. In December 2022, the Tenant went to see his doctor for anxiety and to obtain a letter because his unit was overrun with cockroaches and flies. The Tenant’s doctor recommended that the Tenant stay out of his unit until the pests had been eradicated and included this recommendation in the letter. vii. The Tenant advised the Landlord via email on December 2, 2022 that he was not staying in the unit at the advice of his doctor and would be staying in a hotel until the infestation was eradicated. viii. After the failed treatment on November 25, 2022, the Tenant requested that a different company treat the unit, specifically, [name]. The Landlord agreed to the request and a pest technician from [name] was scheduled to treat the unit on December 16, 2022. ix. [name] attended the unit as scheduled and did not raise any concerns with respect to the bookcases or the Tenant’s overall preparation of the unit and agreed to treat the unit. [name] treated the unit several times but the unit next door was not in sanitary condition and continued to attract cockroaches and pests. xi. The Tenant stayed in a hotel for 2 months, which was located near the airport. However, he still wanted to be notified of any entries to the unit and wanted to be present when the technician was coming in and out. xii. The Tenant moved back into the rental unit on February 2, 2023, before the infestation was fully resolved, as he could not afford the hotel any longer. The infestation was a little better when he moved back in but was not resolved until March 2024. xiii. The Landlord could have acted more responsibly and could have dealt with the infestation quicker. The infestation caused the Tenant anxiety as he was having to deal with constant pests while also trying to study for and take his final exams. Landlord’s Evidence

AS is a service manager with Orkin Canada and has been in that role for approximately 2 years. Prior to this, he worked as a pest control technician. He explained that, generally speaking, in an apartment building cockroaches like to hide in cracks and crevices such as drawers, seams, behind fridges and stoves. As they like tight spaces, it can be a challenge to get rid of them.
Prior to treating a unit, it must be prepared and a preparation sheet is provided in advance to tenants that explains what is required to prepare for treatment.

AS gave evidence with respect several treatments and/or inspections that were completed by [name] technicians in the rental unit from Dec 16, 2022 to March 12, 2024. He went through each service report, which were tendered as evidence. A summary of the service reports is as follows: i. On December 16, 2022, 2 live roaches were seen as well as 100 dead in the unit. The unit was treated with a chemical spray. ii. On January 10, 2023, no live activity was found but many dead roaches were found on the monitors. The monitors were replaced and a treatment known as a ‘flush and vacuum’ was performed, which involves a chemical treatment that fogs cracks and crevices, which is meant to force roaches out. iii. On January 30, 2023, no live activity was found in the unit or neighbouring units 103 and 107. The unit was treated using gel and dust. Under the status section of the report, the status is noted as resolved. iv. On August 10, 2023 there was evidence of roach activity but no live ones were seen. A flush and vacuum was completed. Clutter was noted as an issue in the unit. v. On Oct 13, 2023, a follow up inspection was conducted and minor roach activity was noted in the unit and another spray treatment was recommended. Access to the heating source and removal of the cover was also requested. vi. On October 25, 2023, a spray treatment was completed and significant improvement on the monitors was noted and there was minimal activity. vii. On November 23, 2023, a spray treatment was completed and less than a dozen roaches were found with only a few alive, which were trapped on monitors. viii. On December 15, 2023, a follow up inspection was conducted and a few roaches were found but they were mostly dead and trapped on monitors. A drastic decrease in activity was noted. The monitors were replaced and baited. ix. On January 3, 2024, a follow up inspection was conducted and minor activity was found in the unit with a few roaches found on the monitors. x. On March 12, 2024, a follow up inspection was conducted. Only one dead roach was found. The unit was considered clear of roach activity and no further treatments were recommended.

AS testified that reinfestation can happen and that something could have been missed on inspection or roaches could have been brought in from anywhere such as a box from the grocery store or dog food.

Regarding the state of the Tenant’s unit, AS stated that the technicians did what they could do in the Tenant’s unit and tried to work with the Tenant. In this regard, they explained what needed to be done to treat the unit more effectively. AS recalled speaking directly with the Tenant regarding the shelving units needing to be cleared so they could access behind them.

AS stated that the treatments take time to work and it is not uncommon for it to take several months to get rid of roaches, especially when there is a lot of stuff in the unit. AS was of the view that the issue could not have been dealt with faster and that the Landlord followed all the recommendations made by the [name] pest control technicians. Analysis
It was not disputed that there was a cockroach infestation that was reported on November 4, 2022 or that the issue was not finally resolved until March 12, 2024.
However, the presence of the infestation in itself does not automatically mean the Landlord is in breach of the Act and the tenant is entitled to remedies.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant complained to the Landlord regarding the cockroaches on November 4, 2022. It is unclear why it took the Landlord 21 days to have the unit inspected or why the unit could not be treated in some form on November 25, 2022. The Landlord later hired a different company at the request of the Tenant and had them treat the unit on December 16, 2022. In total, it took the Landlord 43 days to have the first treatment for cockroaches completed.

The evidence suggests that the Tenant was trying to comply with the preparation instructions of the first pest control company but was unable to do so fully because of the size of his unit and his furniture. The Tenant reached out to the property manager and made it a point to raise this issue and was not told he had to remove his bookcases or that no treatment could take place with the furniture in his unit. In light of this, I find it would not be fair to blame the inability to treat the unit on November 25, 2022 on the Tenant.

Based on my experience with similar cases and my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, 43 days is not a reasonable response time to a complaint of cockroaches. In this regard, it is common knowledge that cockroaches breed and can multiple quickly and so it is an issue that needs to be addressed relatively quickly. Most landlords are able to hire a technician and arrange for a first treatment within 2 to 3 weeks. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet its maintenance obligations under the Act as the Landlord failed to respond to the issue in a timely manner.
That said, thereafter the Landlord had the unit treated regularly by [name]. Based on the service reports provided, the cockroach issue was noted as resolved on January 30, 2023.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that he had to stay in a hotel because the infestation was severe and was giving him anxiety which was compounded by the fact that he had to study for and take university exams. He stated that he moved to the hotel at the recommendation of his doctor and provided a letter from his doctor in support of his testimony. The hotel receipts submitted as evidence show that the Tenant stayed in a hotel from December 2, 2022 to January 2, 2023. The Tenant sought a rent abatement as well as claimed out-of- pocket expenses for the hotel as well as travel costs.

The Tenant tendered photos of cockroaches stuck to monitors in support of his position that the infestation was severe. I also note that when the unit was finally treated for the first time on December 16, 2022 that the pest control report noted 2 live cockroaches and 100 dead ones. In my view, this suggests that the unit was heavily infested or would at least feel that way to the Tenant given it was a small bachelor unit. Given the level of infestation, the fact that the unit had still not been treated, and the recommendation of his doctor, I do not find the Tenant’s decisions to move to a hotel temporarily to be unreasonable in the circumstances. However, once the Landlord commenced treatment on December 16, 2022, the roach activity reduced and so it is unclear why the Tenant could not go back to living in the unit sooner. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to hotel costs from December 2, 2022 to December 17, 2022 in the amount of $3,203.84. The request for travel expenses is denied. The Tenant chose a hotel that was a far commute from the rental unit and his university and could have chose a hotel that was closer. The Tenant’s request for an abatement for this period is also denied as he is being compensated for hotel costs.

The unit was not treated again until August 2023 and there was no evidence to suggest that the Tenant complained of continued infestation in the interim. In light of this, I find it more likely than not that the unit experienced reinfestation as opposed to a continual ongoing infestation. There was no evidence to suggest that the reinfestation was a bad as the first infestation such that the unit was not livable.

The unit was then treated regularly from August 2023 to March 2024. Different treatment methods were used that provided results as the infestation was reduced and the roach activity decreased after the treatments. To this end, the treatments, although numerous, were effective. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord responded to the reinfestation within a reasonable time and in a reasonable and did not breach its obligations under the Act with respect to this time period. Therefore, the tenants claims for remedies for this time period are dismissed. Remedies / Set Off

The Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed by the Landlord in the amount of $3,203.84 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant incurred. However, the Landlord seeks set off with respect to monies owed to it by the Tenant which have been ordered by the Board, the Divisional Court, the Court of Appeal and the Superior Court of Justice.
The Tenant objects to any set off on the basis that the matters are still before the courts and the enforcement of the orders are stayed. For the reasons that follow, I disagree. Overview

The Board’s order, file no.: LTB-L-009609-24, was a voidable termination order which required the Tenant to pay $5,376.00 by October 26, 2024 to continue the tenancy. The Tenant filed a request to review the order and the request was denied. The review order, file no.: LTB-L-009609-RV was issued on November 14, 2024 and provided that the original order was confirmed and remained unchanged. In or around December 17, 2024, the Tenant filed an appeal to the Divisional Court, file no.: DC-24-00000781-0000. A copy of the Divisional Court’s Endorsement, released on September 22, 2025, was filed with the Board. In the Endorsement, it clearly indicates that the Tenant’s appeal was dismissed and costs of $4,000.00 were awarded to the Landlord. Thereafter, the Tenant brought a motion to the Court of Appeal to stay the enforcement of his eviction pending leave to appeal the order of the Divisional Court, file no.: COA-25-OM-0385. A copy of the Court’s disposition was filed with the Board. The Court of Appeal dismissed the Tenant’s motion finding that the test was not met for an interim stay. The motion was dismissed and costs in the amount of $4,000.00 were awarded to the Landlord.

In addition to the aforesaid proceedings, the Tenant filed a claim against the Landlord and several other parties in the Superior Court of Justice, file no.: CV-22-00688442-0000. A copy of the Court’s Reasons for Judgement was filed with the Board. The Tenant’s claim was dismissed and the Court awarded costs to the Landlord in the amount of $18,000.00. Thereafter, the Tenant filed an appeal of the decision to the Court of Appeal, file no.: COA- 25-CV-1057, in or around August 27, 2025 and this appeal has yet to be heard.

Unlike an appeal to the Divisional Court, an appeal to the Court of Appeal requires leave to appeal and does not result in an automatic stay. My understanding in reviewing the history of both proceedings is that no stay was issued by the Court of Appeal with respect to the appeal of the Board’s order or the Superior Court’s order or any of the orders for costs. Accordingly, I find that I am not prevented from ordering set off.
The principle of set off has been accepted by the Divisional Court in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (“Marineland”).

In Marineland, the Divisional Court determined that the Board erred when it failed to set-off the tenant’s rental arrears against compensation the landlord was required to pay under section 52 of the Act. The Divisional Court ruled that the Board should have dismissed the tenant’s application requiring the landlord to pay compensation, because the amount the tenant owed to the landlord exceeded the amount of compensation payable. The Divisional Court granted the landlord’s appeal and dismissed the tenant’s application.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord is entitled to set off the amount ordered for out-of- pocket costs in the amount of $3,203.84 from the amount still owing by the Tenant from orders LTB-L-009609-24, DC-24-00000781-0000, COA-25-OM-0385 and CV-22- 00688442-0000 (collectively the ‘Orders’).
After setting off the amount owed by the Landlord to the Tenant under this order against the amount owing by the Tenant to the Landlord in the Orders, the Tenant will still owe the Landlord.
ordered: The Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $3,203.84 as well as the costs of filing the application in the amount of $48.00. However, the Landlord is not required to pay these amounts to the Tenant as they are set off from the amounts owed by the Tenant to the Landlord. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlords illegally entered the rental unit on or about July 2022 and April 2023. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlords substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, and threatened her. The Tenant confirmed that these allegations occurred in 2022 and 2023.

Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’) states: “no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”

In this case, I find that the incidents relied upon by the Tenant occurred in 2022 and 2023, which is more than one year before the Tenant filed her application on January 10, 2025. Application of the one-year limitation period means the Board may only consider incidents which occurred on or after January 10, 2024. Retrieval of Tenant’s Property within 72 Hours

The tenancy terminated on October 31, 2024 by the Board’s order dated October 10, 2024 (LTB-L-093171-23). The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on December 11, 2024, when the Sheriff enforced the order.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not allow her to remove her belongings from the rental unit after the eviction.

Subsection 41(2) of the Act says, “despite subsection (1), where an order is made to evict a tenant, the landlord shall not sell, retain or otherwise dispose of the tenant’s property before 72 hours have elapsed after the enforcement of the eviction order.”

The Tenant testified that she was never given access to the rental unit or an opportunity to retrieve her belongings during the 72 hour period following the Sheriff’s enforcement. The Tenant subsequently testified that she left a voicemail advising [name] [name] that she would attend at the rental property approximately 4:00 p.m. on December 14, 2024 in order to retrieve her belongings. The Landlords acknowledged receiving that voicemail.
The Tenant testified that she attended at the rental property on December 14, 2024, but Fred [name] was not present.

Carly [name] testified that [name] [name] sent a text message to the Tenant on December 13, 2024, informing her that she can retrieve her belongings between 10:00 a.m. and 12:00 p.m. She also referred to [name] [name]’s message on December 14, 2024, in which he states he is at the property but the Tenant is not present. Carly [name] further testified that [name] [name] attended at the rental unit on December 14, 2024, she also referred to a video recording in which [name] [name] states that he is “at the rental property, it is 4:30, and nobody is here, nobody to move… yet again.” Analysis and Findings

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 titled “Tenant Rights” summarizes the relevant caselaw which provides that a Landlord has a positive obligation to make the Tenant’s property available during the 72 hour period. A Landlord must take reasonable, positive steps to facilitate the Tenant’s retrieval of their belongings.
The Tenant bears the burden of proof that the Landlords failed to take reasonable, positive steps to facilitate the retrieval of her belongings within the 72 hour period.

As noted, the Tenant initially testified that she was not contacted by the Landlords regarding the retrieval of her belongings but later stated that she left [name] [name] a voicemail message asking to retrieve her property at approximately 4:00 p.m. on December 14, 2024 and the Landlord acknowledged receiving that voicemail. In dispute is whether [name] [name] was in fact present at the rental unit at that time and date to allow the Tenant to retrieve her belongings.

The Landlords relied on a text messages exchanged on December 13 and 14, 2024 and the video recorded by [name] [name]. The text messages indicate that [name] [name] attended at the rental property after receiving the Tenant’s voicemail that she would attend at approximately 4:00 p.m. The video recorded by [name] [name] shows him at the rental property stating that no one had attended. Fred [name] also sent a text message to the Tenant in which he states: “It is now 5 p.m. You said in your message you would be here at 4. I have been waiting well over 45 minutes for you to show…. Sorry but I’m leaving.”

Although [name] [name] did not testify, I find the text messages and video establish that he likely attended at the rental property on December 14, 2024 after receiving the Tenant’s voicemail and left after approximately 45 minutes because the Tenant did not appear.

The Tenant testified that she attended the rental property on December 14, 2024 at approximately 4:00 p.m. but that [name] [name] was not present. However, there was no evidence that the Tenant attempted to contact [name] [name] or the Landlords to inform them that she was at the rental property or to arrange another opportunity to retrieve her belongings, which I would have expected she would have done if she was in fact present at the indicated time.

I acknowledge that the Landlord’s evidence concerning [name] [name] attendance at the property on December 14, 2024, is hearsay. However, I find it more credible and convincing than the Tenant’s unsupported testimony that went to the rental unit on December 14, 2024, and the Landlord did not show up.

For all the given reasons above, I am not satisfied that the Landlords failed to take reasonable, positive steps to facilitate the retrieval of the Tenant’s belongings. The Landlord was at the rental unit at the date and time requested by the Tenant and was prepared to provide the Tenant with access to the unit to remove her belongings. Therefore, based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant has not established a breach of s.41(2) of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I find the Tenant’s application does not contain sufficient particulars for the LTB or the Landlord to understand the allegations made against the Landlord.
In addition, I find the Tenant failed to comply with an interim order that outlined that the application was deficient, and the Tenant took no meaningful steps to correct those deficiencies.

In the circumstances, I find it would be procedurally unfair for the hearing to proceed, and the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Preliminary issue – Insufficient particulars 1. The Tenant filed her T2 application on January 17th, 2025. There were no allegations or remedies contained in the application at this time. 2. The T2 form explicitly sets out on page 4 that the Tenant is to describe the events that led them to apply, and include what happened, the dates and times of events and who was involved. Preliminary issue – failure to comply with Interim order 3. An Adjudicative Case Conference was held on March 9th, 2026.

At the ACC a member of the LTB explained to the Tenant that there were deficiencies in their application and was directed to amend their application and organize and file her evidence in an organized fashion in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence.

Following the ACC, Interim Order LTB-T-004667-25-IN was issued on March 12th, 2026. It states at paragraph 2: • The Tenant is aware of potential deficiencies in their application that that the discretion to accept amendments to the application rests with the adjudicator at the merits hearing.

I will also note that on the adjournment sheet that is an openly viewable document in the portal for all parties to access and view states, “the Tenant will need to seek an amendment to their application”.
At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative raised the issue that the Tenant had not complied with the interim order and was unsure of the case to be met.

The Tenant stated that she did comply with the interim order and provided an amended T2 application on March 20th, 2026, in accordance with the interim order. I will note that this was the deadline provided in the interim order and that the Tenant had submitted an “explanation for amendment” in the form of a PDF document.

While I accept that the Tenant took some steps to amend her application – in that they provided an overview of the events they are alleging occurred - the “explanation for amendment” still did not contain the particulars that are required in a T2 application.

In the “explanation for amendment”, the Tenant fails to provide specific dates, times or the individuals involved in the alleged conduct. Their “explanation for amendment” asserts various issues including illegal entries, failing to respond to maintenance requests, conduct relating to the parking area and harassment.

The Tenant’s explanation as to why there were no particulars in the “explanation for amendment” was that the dates and times were contained within the evidence. I do not accept this explanation. The application is what starts the proceedings and, if the application is devoid of particulars to the point where the Landlord or the LTB cannot discern the Tenant’s claims, the application cannot proceed.

Applications which make broad generalized claims and do not provide particulars do not allow a matter to be fairly heard. It is counter to the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness and would cause significant prejudice to the responding party if allowed to proceed.
As with all LTB applications, it is the applicant, the Tenant in this case, who must ensure their application meets the minimum requirements.

In my view, the Tenant has had the benefit of an ACC and an interim order, and their application still did not comply with setting out sufficient particulars. As a result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a condo located at [address]reet in Toronto, Ontario.
The Tenant commenced his tenancy on June 15, 2024 and vacated the unit on June 15, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (BC)

BC testified that he was very happy residing in the rental unit and it was very inconvenient having to move to another rental unit in June of 2025. He stated that he had to spend a lot of time applying for another unit, shopping for furniture because this unit was unfurnished and this time period (April – June) is his busiest time of the year in his job.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord was supposed to move back into the condo with his girlfriend, Sydney Perfound because she was accepted to dental school in Canada. He stated that the Landlord and his girlfriend lived in the United Kingdom.

BC stated that in December of 2025, he noticed that the Landlord’s social media presence still indicated that he resided in the UK and he discovered that [name] was accepted to dental school in British Columbia. He also noted on [name] that another person with the last name “[name]” appeared to be residing in his rental unit.

The Tenant directed me to DOC #8044022 which was a compilation of Ms. [name]’s pictures of the rental unit compared to his own pictures of the rental unit. He stated that [name] [name] provided many posts from July of 2025 through January of 2026 which show that she is residing in his previous unit. He believes that the Landlord rented the condo out to another person and that he gave the N12 notice in bad faith.

BC explained that with his employment contract, April to June of every year is their fiscal year end whereby the majority of his commissions are regularly earned. He stated that because he had to fill out rental applications, view different units, arrange for and move his possessions, he was not able to devote sufficient time to his job causing him to lose income. He estimated this monetary loss to be $6,000.00.

The Tenant is also seeking a rent differential of $3,660.00 ($305.00 x 12 months) as he had to pay for furniture for an unfinished unit, $600.00 for moving expenses and $6,000.00 for compensation. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] [name] (HW)

HW testified that on April 16, 2025, he gave the Tenant the N12 notice because he intended to move back to Toronto and reside there while his girlfriend (Sydney Perfound) attended dental school in British Columbia. He stated that they were residing together in the United Kingdom but that moving to Toronto would make it easier for their long-distance relationship based on the time difference between British Columbia and Ontario.

The Landlord stated that he attended the rental unit on June 5, 2025, met with the Tenant, arranged for all of the utilities to be transferred into his name and applied for technical jobs in the Toronto area while he was in Toronto. He then stated that on June 28, 2025, his girlfriend broke up with him.

HW stated that his girlfriend moved to British Columbia, he remained in the UK and no one moved into the rental unit. He stated that when he travels to Toronto to see his family approximately 4 times per year, he stays in the condo. Further, he stated that his younger sister, Zaida [name] who lives with their parents, visits the condo weekly but she does not reside there. He confirmed that he does not receive any rent from Zaida and no one else resides there or pays rent. Evidence of Sydney Perfound, (SP)

SP testified that she broke up with the Landlord on June 28, 2025 and that she continues to attend dental college in BC. She confirmed that their plan was for the Landlord to move to Toronto as that would be best for a long-distance relationship but that the plan changed after June 28, 2025. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord communicated to the Tenant that he wanted his rental unit back for himself, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice, and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord’s actions were made in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Although the Tenant provided several pictures of the Landlord’s sister appearing to be staying in the residential unit, I am not satisfied that she is residing in the condo or that the condo is being rented out. The Tenant’s pictures showed Zaida [name] in the condo on 10 different occasions from July 1, 2025 to January 11, 2026 which tells me that this young lady stays in the condo at times.
Based on the evidence provided, I believe that the condo is vacant and thus, subsection 57(5) does not apply.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12..

The Landlord’s actions prior to giving the N12 notice to the Tenant set out that he was preparing to move to Toronto so that he would be in the closest place to his girlfriend when she was in dental school. [name] confirmed that this was the plan prior to their unfortunate separation. After the relationship ended, the Landlord remained in the UK as he had no reason to move back to Toronto without his girlfriend. The Landlord testified that the condo has remained vacant since the Tenant left, his sister visits the condo regularly and he resides there when he returns to Toronto four times a year.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved the first three criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last criterion of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the sum of $1,698.00.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Landlord and the Tenant entered into a fixed term tenancy on February 1, 2025 for the term of February 1, 2025 to January 31, 2026. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $1,650.00 on February 1, 2025.

On December 2, 2025, the Tenant gave the Landlord an N15 notice of termination, together with a written statement in the form required by s. 47.1(4)(b)(ii) of the Act when an N15 notice is given. The termination date in the N15 notice was December 31, 2025. The Landlord acknowledged at the hearing that he received the N15 notice and [name], each signed by the Tenant, on December 2, 2025. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on December 31, 2025.
The Tenant paid the rent due for December, 2025 on December 3, 2025.

The Tenant has met the requirements of the Act for termination of the tenancy under the provisions of s. 47.1. The period of notice was at least 28 days as required by s. 47.1(3) and the notice meets the requirements of s. 43 of the Act. The notice was accompanied by a statement referred to in clause 47.3 (1) (d) of the Act and that statement meets the requirements of s. 47.3(5) of the Act. The Tenant therefore meets the deeming requirements set out in s. 47.3(1) and was entitled to terminate the tenancy in accordance with the provisions of s. 47.1 of the Act .

The final period of the tenancy was December, 2026. As the rent for December, 2026 was paid by the Tenant, the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit to cover the rent for December, 2026. Therefore, the Landlord must return the deposit to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,698.00. This amount represents: • $1,650.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. June 2, 2026 ____________________________
