issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Evidence:
The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on April 15, 2015. The rental unit was located in the basement of the residential complex.

The Tenant testified that there were two fires in January 2022. The first fire occurred on January 4, 2022, in Unit 17 on the third floor. The second fire occurred on January 15, 2022, and caused extensive damage to the residential complex. After the second fire, the building was unsafe and tenants were required to leave.

The Tenant relied on municipal records, Toronto Fire Services records, and the Office of the Fire Marshal report. The Tenant submitted that the residential complex had a history of maintenance and fire safety deficiencies. The Tenant also relied on a January 11, 2022, inspection record, which identified concerns relating to fire safety, electrical wiring, fire alarm testing records, smoke alarm testing records, emergency lighting records, fire extinguishers, closures, and combustible materials.

The Tenant testified that, on January 15, 2022, she woke up and saw or smelled smoke entering her unit. She left the rental unit and saw flames coming from an upper floor. The Tenant testified that firefighters used a large amount of water to fight the fire and that water entered the basement units. The Tenant testified that she was later unable to return to the rental unit freely because the building was unsafe.

The Tenant testified that she stayed in a hotel or motel after the fire and later moved into a new rental unit on or about March 1, 2022. She testified that some of her personal property remained in the rental unit and was lost when the building was demolished. She also testified that her cat died in the rental unit after the fire.
The Tenant claimed compensation for personal property. She provided an inventory of approximately 445 items and estimated the total replacement value at approximately $70,573.01.

The Landlords did not call evidence at the continued hearing. In submissions, the Landlords’ Legal Representative argued that the Tenant did not prove that the Landlords caused the fire or the claimed losses. The Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that the fire investigation did not find that the Landlords were responsible for the fire and that the cause of the fire was classified as undetermined.

At the hearing, the Tenant relied on a February 2022 letter from the Landlords or the Landlords’ representative. The Landlords’ Legal Representative objected to the use of the letter and submitted that it was a settlement proposal. I have not considered the contents of the settlement proposal as evidence that the Landlords admitted liability, caused the fire, or accepted responsibility for any particular amount. Settlement communications are generally protected and should not be used as admissions of liability. Law and Analysis:

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires a landlord to maintain a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal confirmed that a breach of subsection 20(1) is not established automatically whenever a defect, interruption, or maintenance issue exists. The Board must consider the entire factual context, including the nature of the problem, the Landlord’s knowledge of it, the steps taken by the Landlord, the time reasonably required to investigate or repair the problem, and whether the Landlord acted responsibly in the circumstances.
The Tenant relied on fires that occurred on January 4 and January 15, 2022, together with municipal and fire-safety records, as evidence that the Landlords failed to maintain the residential complex.

The evidence does not establish a connection between the January 4, 2022, fire and the January 15, 2022, fire. It also does not establish that the January 4 fire resulted from a breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations.

The Tenant also submitted a screenshot copied from a website concerning an inspection conducted on January 11, 2022. The screenshot appears to reproduce a City of Toronto Fire Services inspection record identifying eight violations.

I accept that the screenshot raises concerns about fire safety at the residential complex. However, it is not a formal Notice of Violation or Fire Code order. It does not identify the inspector by name or signature, the date of service, the corrective work required, any compliance deadline, or notice number. The screenshot does not establish when the Landlords received the inspection findings, whether a formal notice or order was served, or how much time the Landlords were given to comply. The evidence also does not establish what work required immediate attention or what steps the Landlords took between January 11 and January 15, 2022.

The inspection occurred four days before the fire. Without evidence concerning notice, the required corrective work, and the applicable compliance period, I cannot determine that the Landlords failed to respond within a reasonable time.

The earlier municipal records provide background concerning the residential complex. However, they do not establish that the conditions identified in those records continued to exist in January 2022. They also do not establish that the Landlords failed to comply with an outstanding order or deadline immediately before the fire.

The Tenant also relied on the Fire Marshal report concerning the January 15, 2022, fire. The report states that the cause of the fire was undetermined. I accept the report as evidence of the observations recorded during the post-fire investigation. However, it does not establish that the conditions observed after the fire existed before the fire or that they caused or contributed to it. It also does not establish that the Landlords knew or reasonably ought to have known of a specific condition before January 15, 2022. I therefore give the Fire Marshal report limited weight on the issues of prior notice, causation, and the reasonableness of the Landlords’ response.

The Tenant testified about the fire, smoke, water damage, displacement, the loss of personal property, and the loss of her cat. I accept that the fire caused the Tenant serious distress and significant loss.

However, the Tenant acknowledged that she did not know what caused the fire. She did not call the fire investigator, a fire-protection engineer, a municipal inspector, or another qualified witness to connect the fire or its spread to a maintenance condition for which the Landlords were responsible.

Applying the contextual approach set out in Onyskiw, the existence of fire-safety concerns does not, by itself, establish that the Landlords breached subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Tenant was required to establish a specific maintenance or safety condition for which the Landlords were responsible and that the Landlords failed to address within a reasonable time. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has done so on the evidence before me.
I therefore find that the Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords breached subsection 20(1) of the Act. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant the amount of $6,703.00 by July 14, 2026.
The residential unit is a condo located at 4009-295 Adelaide Street West, Toronto, Ontario.
The Tenant commenced his tenancy at the rental unit in November of 2020 and vacated the rental unit on January 25, 2025.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Preliminary Issue

The Tenant’s Legal Representative brought to my attention the amended application which was served and filed on June 1, 2026. The Landlords’ Legal Representative advised that he accepted the amendments except for the claimed abatement amount of $32,490.00 which will be excluded from the application. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (MP)

MP testified that he received an N12 notice in late September of 2024 from the Landlords (who reside in Turkey) stating that their son would be moving into the condo himself. The termination date was listed as November 30, 2024. The Tenant stated that he requested an extension of time which was granted and he moved out on January 25, 2025.

The Tenant stated that he was able to find another rental unit but his roommate was not able to move in with him as each of them worked in different locations in the city and they could not agree on a location. He stated that he rented his own unit which is $2,150.00 per month and he is now responsible for the full monthly payment. He also stated that he did not receive the one month’s compensation from the Landlord for this type of application.

MP stated that in March of 2025, he noticed that his rental unit was listed for rent at a price of $3,200.00 per month and he provided a copy of the listing with a date of March 14, 2025. He stated that he was angry and upset that he was forced to move out of his unit for the Landlord’s son’s occupancy and his son did not move in.

The Tenant is seeking a monthly rent differential of $777.50 for 12 months calculated as $9,330.00, moving costs of $910.00, one month’s compensation of $2,745.00 and general compensation of $32,940.00. Evidence of Landlord’s Son, Izzet [name] (IG)

IG testified that he and his fiancée separated on September 12, 2024 and he was very distraught and wanted to move to Toronto. He stated that his father let the Tenant know that he was going to move into the condo himself and that he wanted to start a new life there. He had every intention of moving to Toronto but he said that the Tenant took too long to move out.

IG stated that he was emotionally prepared to move and that he would not have to pay rent in the condo which was helpful. He stated that he had previously lived in Toronto from 2017 to 2020 and enjoyed his time there and wanted to return. He reached out to his former employer in Toronto but there were no jobs available for him.

IG stated that he purchased a ticket to Toronto on February 8, 2025 which was to depart on February 18, 2025. He stated that he had mental problems, he didn’t want to live alone and he was very emotional and depressed. He cancelled the flight but purchased another ticket on February 17, 2025 which was to depart on March 1, 2025.

IG stated that he met with a doctor on February 20, 2025 to deal with his emotional problems and the therapist told him that he did not have to move to Toronto and live alone. The Landlord’s son believed that this was his permission to stay in Turkey with his family so that he would not have to live alone. He stated that is when he decided to remain with his family and he started therapy sessions in March of 2025 to deal with his depression. Evidence of the Landlord, [name]

NG testified that after his son explained that he was depressed, had a panic attack and that he did not want to move to Toronto, he listed the condo for rent on March 14, 2025. He stated that he only became aware of his son’s mental health issue on February 20, 2025 when he saw the therapist. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord communicated to the Tenant that they wanted his rental unit back for their son, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord’s actions were made in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Not only did the Landlord fail to move his son into the residential unit, but the Landlord listed the unit for rent 6 weeks after the Tenant vacated the condo. The Landlord’s son’s explanation was that the Tenant took too long to vacate the unit and he became emotionally distraught causing him to decide to remain in Turkey. Of course it is unfortunate that IG and his fiancée broke up and that he was struggling with that separation. However, the Landlord’s decision to move his son into the condo was given to the Tenant in September of 2024 after the couple separated and 6 months later, IG decided not to move to Toronto.

The Landlord had an obligation to ensure that his son would be residing in the rental unit when he served the notice and displaced the Tenant. After serving the notice, the Landlord extended the termination date by 2 months which then resulted in the condo only being available on January 31, 2025. The Landlord and/or the Landlord’s son apparently had no concerns about the timing of the move-in which does not correlate with their evidence today.
Further, I was presented with no medical evidence to substantiate that the Landlord’s son was not in a sufficient state to travel to or move to Toronto in February of 2025.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12 or in this case, the email.

The Landlord served the N12 notice in September of 2024 as his son requested that he be able to move into the condo himself. After extending the termination date to January 31, 2025 and the Tenant vacating on January 25, 2025, the Landlord stated that on February 20, 2025 he then was informed of his son’s emotional troubles. On March 14, 2025, the Landlord listed the unit and rented it out to another tenant confirming the Landlord’s presumed bad faith.

The Landlord was represented by a legal representative and so I did not have to explain the presumption of bad faith in section 57(5) of the Act. As mentioned above, the separation date was in September of 2024 and 6 months later, the Landlord’s son decided not to move to Toronto for his own reasons. Both the Landlord and the Landlord’s son had an obligation to follow through on their actions which resulted in the unnecessary and costly displacement of the Tenant. The Landlord has not shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with his T5 application. Remedies

With respect to the Tenant’s request for a rent differential, the Tenant is now paying rent on his own of $2,150.00 as he no longer has a roommate. The rental unit’s cost was $2,745.00 per month which he shared with his roommate. Based on the above, I am denying a rent differential as the Tenant could have arranged to obtain another roommate.
With respect to the Tenant’s request for moving expenses, I will award $910.00 as set out on the invoice provided by the Tenant.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for the one month’s compensation that was required under the Act for this type of notice, I will award $2,745.00. Despite [name] argument that this amount should be decreased by half, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the whole amount as he was the only Tenant listed.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for compensation of $32,940.00, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $3,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith. I was not provided with any evidence or documents to substantiate a higher award.
The Tenant is entitled to the application fee as he was successful with his application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $6,703.00. This amount represents: • $910.00 for moving expenses; • $2,745.00 for the 1 month’s compensation; • $3,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] grand qresidential and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Upon Board questioning the Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application lack sufficient detail and particulars, and further the Tenant did not take the opportunity provided to him in the Board’s Interim Order dated October 10, 2025, to amend this herein application on or before October 31, 2025, to provide sufficient details for the application and the remedies sought.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that the application should be dismissed as the Tenant has not provided sufficient details and particulars of allegations and the remedies sought other than there were bed bugs, he was bitten and had some adverse effects. Moreover, the Landlords has been put in the unfair situation of having to defend itself to an application containing allegations that were general statement that the Landlords have no understanding of what the issues are other than generalities of the allegations that there were issues of bedbugs, nor the remedies sought by the Tenant. Accordingly, the Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant’s T6 application should be dismissed.
Upon Board questioning on why the Tenant had not provided sufficient details, he testified through his interpreter, that he had completed his application, and thought his application was fine.

The Board can assist parties by providing general information as needed, however the Board does not act as a legal representative for either party and consequently, it is the Applicant’s, in this case the Tenant responsibility to ensure that the application is complete and in compliance with the Act. It was further noted to the Tenant that he could have contacted Tenant Duty Counsel whose contact information was listed on the Notice of Hearing for this herein proceeding. The Tenant did not seek to amend his application during the proceeding, nor did he prior to this proceeding, even in the face of the Board’s Interim Order of October 10, 2025.

An application must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital [2022] O.J. No. 5931 that, “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, I am of the view the general principle regarding the need for particular and details apply equally to Tenant application. In this leading case, the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons an details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that they can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission….’’

The Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted the allegations toward the Landlords are lacking any semblance of details of said issues being pleaded by the Tenant. Moreover, evidence uploaded to the Portal by the Tenant was not introduced as evidence during the proceeding and hence did not provide sufficient particulars to support the Tenant’s allegations in his application, which the Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted was a general statement, and devoid of detail that simply there were issues with pests, specifically bed bugs.

I find the allegations in the Tenant’s application are vague and lack any context in terms of details. Specifically, the “Reasons for filing this Application” section of the application instructs the applicant to describe what each problem is, the date the problem started, whether the problem was repaired, and if so to provide the date, and explain who repaired it, further explain who or what caused the problem, and how the Tenant informed the Landlords for each problem listed, which the Tenant has not done in a way that the Landlords could properly comprehend the issues at hand.
On the T6 application there is simply a 12-line paragraph which is a general statement and description that the Tenant had issues with bedbugs, devoid of sufficient detail.

It is not for the Landlords or the Board to assist the Tenant in completing their application or correcting deficiencies. As with all applications before the Board, it is the applicant who must bring an application that meets minimum requirements. However, the undersigned noted to the Tenant, if he chooses to bring another application, if the issues alleged persist, he should seek out legal counsel whether privately or by contacting [name], if the time limitations of the Act permit.

The Landlords’ right to present a meaningful defence in a timely fashion must also be taken into consideration. The application does not contain sufficient details on the alleged grounds that would allow the matter to be fairly heard, nor does it contain sufficient details of the remedies sought.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application were not sufficient for the Landlords to understand the case to be met to and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at the hearing, and effectively would have experienced significant prejudice if expected to present a defence against unknown, generalized and unspecified allegations. Moreover, the Tenant did not seek an opportunity to adjourn the matter to amend said application and had not done so as of the date of this proceeding, even after the Board’s Interim Order dated October 10, 2025 provided him up to October 31, 2025, to amend his application.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, I shared on screen the T6 application as filed by the Tenant. The Tenant confirmed he recognized the application.

I explained to the Tenant that the problem with the application is that it does not contain a request for remedies related to the claims made in the application. For example, he did not request an abatement, costs or expenses. His request for repair is moot as the tenancy terminated around October 2022. The only other request is for a payment of $1,200.00 related to claims of fraud.
The Tenant said that the parties consented to disclosure using the Portal (TOP) and that he filed an amended application.

I shared by my screen and provided the Tenant with an opportunity to review his entries in TOP. He was unable to locate the consent related to using TOP and he could not locate the amended application he claimed. He then said that this was done verbally at a previous hearing.

I reviewed the March 17, 2025 interim order and the adjournment sheets for December 10, 2024 and February 17, 2026 in the Board record. I can confirm that there is no indication that the parties agreed to the Tenant’s amendment requests or to exchange evidence via TOP.

I also note that the Tenant has had since March 2025 to amend his order to include particulars and specifics going to remedies sought and corresponding monetary amounts and did not do so. Yet, as evident from the inordinate number of documents filed by the Tenant, he seemed resourceful and ready to argue his case. However, he provided no reasonable explanation as to why he was unable to amend the application and no evidence to support his claim that he had filed an amended application with the Board.

Given the Tenant’s failure to state what monetary remedies he is claiming, such as out-of- pocket expenses, rent abatement, et cetera, I am bound, by Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 (CanLII) (“Beauge”), where the Divisional Court decided that the Board cannot make an award if it is not requested by the applicant.
While I appreciate the Tenant’s challenging circumstances, I have no authority to correct the deficiencies in his application.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenants' T2 application is dismissed. Facts

The tenancy began on January 1, 2025. The Landlord permitted the Tenants to move into the rental unit early, on December 15, 2024, at no additional cost. The Tenants vacated the unit on December 31, 2025.

The Tenants filed their T2 application on January 25, 2026, claiming substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential unit, a failure to maintain the unit, harassment by third-party neighbours, and improper conduct connected to the ending of the tenancy. Gas Consumption and the Hot Water Tank.

The Tenants asked the Landlord, by email dated January 28, 2025, what gas consumption they should expect, noting they understood from earlier correspondence that costs were "not supposed to exceed $110" (Exhibit #1 – Gmail, "Gas Consumption," January 28, 2025). The Tenants' first Enbridge bill, for the period December 24, 2024 to January 24, 2025, totalled $230.81 for 384 m³ of gas (Exhibit #2 – “Enbridge Gas consumption bill”).

The Tenants attributed the high bill to a poorly maintained hot water tank and raised this with the Landlord. The Landlord arranged for [name], which owns and services the rented hot water tank, to attend. An initial technician suggested a part might need replacing, and the Landlord arranged an e-transfer of $225.00 (later corrected to $253.12 with HST) to cover the anticipated repair. A more experienced technician was consulted, found nothing wrong with the tank, and no charge was made; the Landlord's e-transfer was cancelled (Exhibit #3 – [name] service report relating to the inspection and maintenance of the hot water tank, receipt dated March 17, 2025, showing a $224.00 subtotal fully offset by a plan discount and an outstanding balance of $0.00). In January 2025 the Landlord also offered to contribute $33.42 toward the disputed bill and to cover the December portion attributable to the Tenants' early move-in; the Tenant confirmed in cross- examination that this was not necessary. [name] (March–August 2025)

Beginning March 21, 2025, the Tenants reported a series of disputes with two neighbouring unit owners (it is unclear if these were immediate attached dwellings or in the same complex), including a verbal altercation about the Tenants' dogs, animal feces left near the stairs, a note affixed to the Tenants' vehicle with construction-grade tape, and a garbage bag left at their door. The Tenants acknowledge, and I find, that the individuals involved in these incidents were not the Landlord's tenants, agents, or employees, and that the Landlord has no authority or control over them as well as the Landlord did not involve themselves in this dispute. Notice of Intent to Vacate

On August 18, 2025, the Tenant sent the Landlord an email titled "Notice of Intent to Vacate," stating that the Tenants "have made the difficult decision to vacate the condominium by the end of this year, with our final day of occupancy being December 31, 2025," and citing the neighbour disputes as the reason (Exhibit #4). The Landlord responded on August 22, 2025, offering to let the Tenants leave early without penalty if that was their goal, and asking them to clarify their objective. The Tenants replied that they wished to remain in the unit and instead pursue a complaint against the property management company. Condominium Authority Tribunal Consent Correspondence

On August 20, 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord for permission to file a complaint with the Condominium Authority Tribunal ("CAT") (Exhibit #5). Over August 22 and 23, 2025, the Landlord asked what the Tenants' ultimate goal was, confirmed she had no objection to the Tenants leaving early, and indicated she wished to consult her lawyer before consenting to a CAT filing made in her name; the Tenant clarified that his objective was not to end the tenancy but to pursue a complaint against the property manager, and the Landlord consented to the filing (Exhibit #6 – Gmail correspondence of August 22 and 23, 2025: "answer for permission for CAT," "explanation CAT," and "Consent for CAT").

On August 28, 2025, the Tenant sent the Landlord the full text of the proposed CAT complaint and asked for written consent in the specific form CAT required (Exhibit #7 – [name], "2nd Condominium Authority Tribunal consent," August 28, 2025). On September 2, 2025, the Landlord declined to consent, forwarding her lawyer's opinion that the CAT likely lacked jurisdiction over a harassment or discrimination complaint of this kind, and that the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario ("HRTO") was the more appropriate forum (Exhibit #8 – [name], "CAT consent rejection," September 2, 2025). The Tenant disputed this advice in later correspondence (see Exhibit #11, below). No CAT or HRTO application was ultimately filed, and no decision from either tribunal was placed in evidence.

October 18, 2025, the Tenant wrote to the Landlord disputing her lawyer's earlier CAT/HRTO advice, setting out the results of his own inquiries with [name] and the Condominium Management Regulatory Authority of Ontario and stating that the Tenants would provide formal notice of their move-out date using the N9 form once a new residence was secured (Exhibit #11 – [name], "CAT consent wrong advice and new moving date notification," October 18, 2025). The Landlord responded the same day, noting she had already accepted the August 18, 2025 email as notice and was expecting vacant possession on December 31, 2025. [name]12. The record confirms the Landlord generally gave notice of showings, with one instance falling short of 24 hours, which the Tenant characterized as an isolated administrative lapse rather than a pattern. On December 19, 2025, the Tenant emailed the Landlord to complain that, during a showing that day, a prospective buyer had opened drawers and furniture without permission and had used the bathroom without permission (Exhibit #9 – [name], "Unacceptable behavior during today's property visit," December 19, 2025). The Landlord responded the same day, apologized, and confirmed she had forwarded the complaint to her real estate agent. 13. The Tenants also relied on a broader compilation of text messages and photographs documenting the tenancy, including a further allegation that the real estate agent disturbed the cremated remains of a deceased pet during a showing, and that photographs of the unit's interior — in which the Tenants and their belongings incidentally appeared — were used in online listings without their express consent (Exhibit #10 – Support for Answer to Respondent's Statement). Mental Health Disclosure 14. On September 24 and October 1, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that he was undergoing medical treatment and asked that communications, including showing requests, be handled with greater sensitivity to his condition and availability (Exhibit #12 – [name], "Problems with REA and depression notification"). No official medical documentation was filed with the Board, and the Tenant confirmed in cross-examination that no doctor's note or clinical diagnosis had been disclosed to the other side in advance of the hearing, as the Rules of Procedure require. 15. The Landlord replied to the Tenant's October 18, 2025 letter the same day, clarifying that the CAT/HRTO legal advice she had shared had been obtained for herself, not for the Tenant, and had been forwarded only as a courtesy explaining her own position; she added that she was "a bit confused" by any suggestion that the move-out date remained open, noting that the Tenants' own August 18, 2025 email had given written notice, that she had accepted it, and that she was therefore expecting the unit to be vacated at the end of the Tenants' stated term. She reiterated that the option of leaving early had been offered solely to help ease the stress the Tenant had described (Exhibit #13 – [name], "answer 1 to CAT consent wrong advice and new moving date notification," October 18, 2025). 16. On January 1, 2026, the Tenant confirmed by email that the unit had been fully vacated the previous day, and identified, with photographs, several items left in the bathroom closet, the smaller bedroom closet, and the storage area — construction-related materials, a broom, and empty boxes — which he stated had been present at move-in and were not brought in by the Tenants. The Landlord replied the same day, thanking the Tenant for the confirmation and wishing the Tenants well in their new home, without raising any concern about the items noted or the condition of the unit (Exhibit #15 – [name], "Confirmation of vacant unit and items left on site," January 1, 2026). 17. The Tenants vacated the unit on December 31, 2025, no N9 provided by tenant. Analysis and Decision 18. The Tenants bear the burden of proving the allegations in their T2 application on a balance of probabilities. This means they must establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, or otherwise breached the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 19. My findings must be based on the evidence presented at the hearing. It is not enough that the Tenants genuinely believe the events occurred or that their concerns are understandable. I must determine whether the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the alleged conduct occurred and that it amounts to a breach of the Act. 20. The Tenants filed a significant volume of documents in support of their application. While I have reviewed and considered all of the evidence filed, my decision must be based on the allegations before me and on the evidence that is relevant to those allegations. Some of the materials relate to disputes involving individuals or organizations other than the Landlord or concern matters that are not directly relevant to the issues I must decide. Those materials have been given little or no weight in reaching my decision. 21. For the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have met their burden of proof. Gas Consumption and the Hot Water Tank 22. The Tenants did not establish, on the evidence, that the January 2025 gas bill was caused by any failure of the Landlord to maintain the rental hot water tank. Exhibit #3 confirms that when a technician raised a possible concern, the Landlord immediately arranged payment; when a second technician found nothing wrong, no charge was made and the payment was cancelled. That sequence is inconsistent with a landlord who neglected known maintenance obligations, and instead with one who responded promptly and reasonably to a tenant's concern. The Tenant's own evidence was that he had no documentation establishing that annual maintenance was in fact overdue, beyond his own inference from the timing of the service call. Nor did the Tenants separate the portion of the bill attributable to any tank issue from the delivery, transportation, and carbon charges shown on the face of Exhibit #2. Without that evidentiary link, I cannot find that the higher bill was caused by any act or omission of the Landlord, particularly where she offered, unprompted, to contribute toward it — an offer the Tenant declined. [name] 23. The individuals involved in the incidents beginning March 21, 2025 are not the Landlord's tenants, employees, or agents, and she has no authority to control their behaviour. Her obligation is limited to taking reasonable steps within her own control once she becomes aware of a problem. The evidence establishes that when the Landlord learned of the dispute, in December 2025, she promptly contacted the condominium board, which responded and addressed the issues raised. The Tenants were unable to establish, in cross-examination, an earlier date on which the Landlord had been made aware of the situation and failed to act. The repeated references throughout Exhibits #4 to #11 to CAT and HRTO confirms that the Tenants pursued, and were at times encouraged by the Landlord to pursue, other and more appropriate avenues for a dispute of this kind; no decision from any of those bodies finding fault on the Landlord's part was produced. I am not satisfied that the Landlord's conduct toward third-party neighbour disputes amounted to substantial interference. The CAT Consent Process 24. The correspondence at Exhibits #5 through #8 and #11 shows a landlord who engaged seriously and in good faith with an unusual request — consenting, in principle, to a legal proceeding being filed in her own name at her tenant's initiative — while reasonably seeking legal advice before finalizing that consent, given the personal stakes involved for her. A landlord's request for time to obtain legal advice, or her disagreement, informed by that advice, about the appropriate forum for a complaint, does not constitute harassment of or interference with the Tenants' reasonable enjoyment of the unit. No CAT or HRTO decision was filed establishing that the Landlord's position was legally incorrect or taken in bad faith. Showings and Privacy 25. The Tenants confirmed that the Landlord generally provided notice of showings, and the single occasion that fell short of 24 hours was, on this record, an isolated lapse rather than a pattern. The more serious allegations in Exhibits #9 and #10 — a prospective buyer going through drawers, use of the bathroom without permission, and disturbance of a deceased pet's remains — were not witnessed directly by either Tenant; the drawer and bathroom allegations rest on what the Tenants' mother and mother-in-law reportedly observed, and neither testified or provided a signed statement, so that evidence is hearsay to which I can give only limited weight. The allegation concerning "personal photographs," on closer examination of Exhibit #10, resolves to photographs already displayed on the unit's walls appearing incidentally in listing photographs — a materially different, and less serious, event than initially suggested. Being asked to keep dogs outside during showings may have been inconvenient, particularly in winter, but the Tenant could not identify any lease term or provision of the Act that this breached. The Landlord's prompt apology and referral of the December 19, 2025 complaint to her real estate agent further supports a finding that she took reasonable, responsive steps once made aware of a legitimate concern. Characterization of the Tenancy's End 26. The Tenants' own August 18, 2025 email, titled "Notice of Intent to Vacate," stated plainly that they had "made the difficult decision to vacate...with our final day of occupancy being December 31, 2025" (Exhibit #4). The Landlord's understanding that this reflected the Tenants' own decision, expressed in their own words, is a reasonable reading of its plain wording, and I find it was reasonable for her to rely on it, as she consistently and transparently did throughout the balance of the tenancy (Exhibits #13 and #14). She never filed an application to terminate the tenancy, never enforced an earlier deadline despite offering the Tenants that option more than once, and never denied them use or possession of the unit. 27. On the contrary, her November 10, 2025 email offered the Tenants a choice on how to apply their deposit, an unprompted letter of reference, and an assurance of flexibility on the move-out date if their search for new housing required it (Exhibit #14) — accommodations difficult to reconcile with the allegation that she was pressuring the Tenants to leave. The tenancy concluded on the date the Tenants themselves had proposed five months earlier, and did so amicably: the January 1, 2026 exchange confirming vacant possession and pre-existing items left in storage closed without any dispute over the unit's condition or the return of the deposit (Exhibit #15). The Tenant's evidence about the stress associated with moving (Exhibit #12) is understandable and I do not doubt it was sincerely felt, but in the absence of medical documentation properly disclosed before the hearing, and in the absence of any evidence that the Landlord pressured or coerced the Tenants into vacating, this falls well short of establishing coercion or constructive eviction. 28. Because the Tenants have not established a breach of section 22 of the Act on the merits, the question of an appropriate remedy or abatement under section 30(2) and Guideline 5 does not arise. I would in any event note that the Tenant's explanation of the claimed 35% abatement — an estimate reached by narrowing a range between 25% and 50% without reference to the specific issues raised — would not, on its own, have provided a reliable basis for quantifying compensation had liability been established.
ordered: The Tenants' T2 application is dismissed. _July 31, 2026__ ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants application is dismissed on the basis that their claim is beyond the statutory limitation period under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Tenants’ Claim is Really a Reduction/Discontinuance of a Service or Facility

The Tenants essentially allege that when they entered into a new tenancy with the Landlord in June 2024, the Landlord failed to provide laundry facilities as required by the tenancy agreement. The Landlord did not dispute that the lease provided for laundry facilities and that Tenants did not have access to any such facilities. The Landlord testified that it was included in the lease due to their own mistake.

Section 130 of the Act allows a tenant to apply to the LTB if their landlord has discontinued or reduced a service or facility. “Laundry facilities” are included in the definition of “services and facilities” in section 2 of the Act. Section 130(5) of the Act requires that the application be filed within one year of the reduction or discontinuance.

The Tenants did not file a T3 application. They filed a T2 application alleging that the Landlord’s failure to deliver laundry facilities substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. In my view, a T2 application alleging substantial interference was the wrong claim to make in the context of the Landlord’s failure to provide laundry services, which I consider to be a discontinuance within the meaning of section 130. The Legislature created a specific framework for addressing a Landlord’s discontinuance of laundry facilities—a Tenant may apply under section 130 of the Act for a rent reduction. It is a principle of statutory interpretation that where provisions in a statute address a specific subject, the statute’s general provisions should not be applied to address that subject (see for example, Danigelis v. [name], 2022 CanLII 843418 (ON LTB), at paras. 19 and 20). As a result, a tenant seeking a remedy for the discontinuance of laundry facilities should do so via a T3 application rather than a T2 application.

I am satisfied that the Landlord’s failure to provide laundry facilities was a discontinuance notwithstanding that they were never provided. In my view, it is unlikely that the Legislature intended that a landlord’s failure to provide services or facilities as required by the tenancy agreement would be treated differently depending on whether or not they were actually provided before being discontinued.

However, the Tenants’ use of the incorrect form is not fatal to their application. Section 212 of the Act provides that any error in the contents of forms and other documents substantially comply with the Act if the error does not significantly prejudice a party’s ability to participate in the proceeding. In my view, the Tenants’ use of a T2 application to plead a discontinuance did not cause prejudice to the Landlord because the Landlord’s case to meet was readily apparent from the application—the Tenants were clearly alleging that the agreement required the Landlord to provide laundry facilities (a service or facility), had failed to do so, and the Tenants were seeking a remedy as a result. The Landlord therefore knew or ought to have known the case to be met. I would therefore amend the Tenants’ application from a T2 application alleging substantial interference to a T3 alleging a discontinuance of a service or facility.

The bigger hurdle to the Tenants’ ability to pursue their claim however, is that a T3 application has a more restrictive limitation period than a T2 application. Section 29(2) of the Act provides that a T2 may not be brought “more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.” Thus, if the alleged interference is ongoing, the Tenant may apply more than one year after the conduct began, with the LTB’s ability to grant a remedy being restricted to the one-year period prior to the T2 being filed. Section 130(5) of the Act, on the other hand, provides that a T3 application shall not be “made under this section more than one year after a reduction or discontinuance in a service or facility”. I agree with and adopt the following non-binding statement of Vice- [name] in TST-79596-16-IN (Re), 2016 CanLII 88770 (ON LTB) regarding the differences between sections 29(2) and 130(5) 24. I find that the limitation period in subsection 130(5) should be treated differently from the limitation period in subsection 29(2). First, Guideline 6 only deals with the limitation period in subsection 29(2). However, it does say that when a breach is a single event, the limitation period begins on the day the event happened. In this case, the root of the T3 application is single event – the one-time removal of the on- site superintendent. Second, the wording of the limitation period in subsection 130(5) is clear that an application cannot be filed more than one year after the discontinuance of a service. This section seems to address, and render irrelevant, the notion that the unavailability of the discontinued service is ongoing. Therefore, I find that the limitation period in subsection 130(5) clearly bars the addition of the Potential Parties because the Tenant asked to have them added after April 21, 2016 when the limitation period expired.

As noted above, I am satisfied that the Landlord discontinued the laundry services notwithstanding that they were never provided. The discontinuance in this case occurred when the Tenants moved into the unit in June 2024 and it was apparent that the rental unit did not have laundry facilities. They filed this application on [insert here], well after the one-year limitation period prescribed by section 130(5) of the Act. To allow the Tenants to pursue their claim as a substantial interference claim would be contrary to the legislative intent behind section 130(5). Because the Tenants filed their application more than one year after the Landlord discontinued the laundry services, it must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The application is brought under section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), which states ‘A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere…’.

The parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Tenant paid a rent deposit, however a few days before the tenancy was to begin the Landlord unilaterally cancelled the agreement. As a result, the Tenant had to scramble to find new accommodations, which was especially difficult as they had just arrived in the country as an international student. In this application the Tenant seeks compensation for their out-of-pocket expenses incurred for two nights of temporary accommodations before securing a new unit, and general damages.
While I accept the Tenant’s evidence as credible, I find that their circumstances are not covered by section 22 of the Act because the Tenant did not at any time have occupancy of the rental unit.

The Tenant submits two cases in support of their application: TST-78326-16 (2017 CanLII 28574) and TST-79448-16 (2016 CanLII72026). Both are LTB cases which might be persuasive but are not binding. The first case is distinguished because the tenant received keys to the rental unit and moved some of their possessions into the rental unit. The facts in the second case are very similar to the present case; in both the landlord unilaterally cancelled the tenancy agreement and did not provide the prospective tenant with possession of the rental unit. In both cases the landlord returned the rent deposit to the tenant promptly.

With respect to the Member who issued the order in TST-79448-16, the order does not specifically address the wording of section 22 and whether it provides the Board with the authority to award remedies for interference with reasonable enjoyment to a tenant who does not occupy a unit. While many cases have grappled with scenarios where the named tenant doesn’t reside in the unit personally, but is found to occupy the unit by maintaining the tenancy for the benefit of a friend or family member, I am not aware of any other cases which have addressed the issue of whether a prospective tenant who does not get possession of the rental unit is entitled to remedies under sections 21, 22, or 24, all of which contain the same wording of ‘during the tenant’s occupancy’.

The phrase ‘during the tenant’s occupancy’ in these three sections is notable because it is unique to these sections, section 29 and 35 which refer to the same underlying issues, and sections 123 and 125 relating to the addition or removal of certain services. Other sections of the Act refer to when a tenancy begins or is terminated. Section 20 relating to maintenance obligations does not reference occupancy. Section 13 defines when a tenancy begins and when a tenancy agreement takes effect – whether or not the tenant actually occupies the rental unit. By using the phrase ‘during the tenant’s occupancy’ in some sections, the legislature chose to distinguish these sections by making occupancy a condition of entitlement to a remedy. Further, section 107 specifically addresses the situation where vacant possession is not provided to a prospective tenant. This section provides that in this circumstance the rent deposit shall be returned, but no other remedy is provided. In my view, theses choices by the legislature demonstrate an intention to distinguish between tenants who gain occupancy and prospective tenants who do not for the purposes of certain sections – most notably sections 22-24.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization]. (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: This is an application about whether a landlord can unilaterally alter a pre-existing parking arrangement without the consent of the tenant and whether attempts to do so constitute substantial interference with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. The Tenant seeks an order recognizing her entitlement to two parking spaces and prohibiting the Landlord from removing her use of one parking space without her consent and prohibiting the Landlord from further attempts to do so.

As explained below, I find that the Landlord is entitled to unilaterally change a pre-existing parking arrangement without the Tenant’s consent, subject to the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and that its attempts to effect such changes do not constitute a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. As such, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Is [name] a Tenant?

The Tenant’s application originally named herself and [name] as tenants. However, on review of the tenancy agreement entered into between the Tenant and the predecessor landlord, [name] is listed as an occupant, and not a tenant. The Landlord submitted that the only tenant of the rental unit known to them is the Tenant. The Tenant agreed that the tenancy agreement only lists her as a Tenant, but that [name] is a member of her household.

Based on my review of the tenancy agreement and the submissions of the parties, I find that only the Tenant is a properly named party. The application is amended accordingly to remove [name] as a party, which is reflected on the style of cause of this order. Background

The Tenant has resided in the rental unit since May 2016. Despite her lease agreement not allocating any parking spaces to her (Exhibit 1 (DOC-8235774), p. 5), since she moved in, she and members of her household have been parking two vehicles in the residential complex’s shared parking lot. The parking spaces favoured by the Tenant are located directly adjacent to a stairwell leading to her unit.

The Landlord purchased the residential complex in November 2021. On January 20, 2023, the Landlord gave notice to all tenants of the residential complex that the Landlord would be instituting a one-vehicle per unit policy (Exhibit 1, p.20). Shortly thereafter, the Tenant provided her vehicle information to the Landlord and advised the Landlord that she did not consent to this change to her pre-existing parking arrangement and having to remove one of her unit’s vehicles from the parking lot (Exhibit 1, p 22, 25). The Tenant maintains this position to this day and has continued to park two vehicles in the parking lot.

Since January 20, 2023, there has been intermittent correspondence between the parties regarding the parking issue. In July 2024, the Landlord sent out a reminder to tenants of the residential complex reminding all tenants that there were only ten parking spaces, and that the parking lot was “first come first serve”, meaning no tenant has an assigned space (Exhibit 1, p. 26). The Tenant alleges that in July 2024, the Landlord threatened to remove one of her vehicles from the parking lot.

On cross-examination, the Tenant admitted that she and her household continue to enjoy the use of two parking spaces, and that the Landlord has never sought to enforce its one- vehicle parking policy against her by having one of her household’s vehicles removed from the parking lot. The Tenant also admitted that on June 27, 2026, the Landlord offered her a rent reduction in exchange for moving one of her household’s vehicles to an offsite parking lot. The Tenant rejected this offer as it was a less convenient arrangement for her.

SK testified for the Landlord. He confirmed that the Tenant continued to enjoy the use of two spaces for her household vehicles in the parking lot and stated that there were no threats to remove one of the Tenant’s vehicles in the one-year period preceding the filing of the Tenant’s application, or since the application’s filing. He further confirmed the Landlord’s offer to reduce the Tenant’s rent in exchange for her moving one of her household’s vehicles to an offsite parking lot. Rent reduction only available remedy under the Act for loss of parking space

The Tenant seeks an order recognizing her entitlement to two parking spaces and prohibiting the Landlord from unilaterally changing what she refers to as the pre-existing parking arrangement for her unit without her consent, or from attempting to do so.

There are two main problems with the Tenant’s request. Firstly, her tenancy agreement as written does not entitle her to any parking rights, as she herself admits. The Tenant did not produce any documentation showing any amendments to her tenancy agreement adding any parking spaces authorized by either the Landlord or its predecessor.

Second, and more importantly, the Act allows for a landlord to discontinue a service or facility such as parking if there is a corresponding reduction of a tenant’s rent. Section 130 of the Act provides that a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for a rent reduction due to a landlord’s discontinuance or reduction of services or facilities within one year after the service or facility was first discontinued or reduced: 130 (1) A tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. (2) A former tenant of a rental unit may apply under this section as a tenant of the rental unit if the person was affected by the discontinuance or reduction of the services or facilities while the person was a tenant of the rental unit. …….. (5) No application may be made under this section more than one year after a reduction or discontinuance in a service or facility.

In this case, the Tenant has not had her services or facilities reduced or discontinued. The sole basis of her claim is that she has an implied right to two parking spaces because she has enjoyed such privileges for several years. However, should one day she lose the use of one parking space, the Act provides a remedy for her should the Landlord not reduce her rent accordingly. As such, I am unable to grant the remedy the Tenant seeks. Allegations statute-barred and do not constitute substantial interference

Moreover, as correctly pointed out by the Landlord, there are no allegations regarding any conduct of the Landlord within one year prior to the application’s filing. All the incidents cited by the Tenant as substantial interference by the Landlord took place in 2023 and 2024. Subsection 29(2) of the Act prohibits the granting of relief for any conduct of the Landlord more than one year prior to the filing of a tenant application (see Toronto Community Housing v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII)).
However, even if any of the incidents cited by the Tenant were timely, there is nothing that would constitute substantial interference by the Landlord.

The tenancy agreement between the parties does not grant the Tenant an entitlement to any parking spaces, notwithstanding her existing practice. Subsection 14.A.(i) of the tenancy agreement grants the Landlord the right to re-assign spaces from time to time as “the Landlord, in its sole discretion, may determine”. The subsection goes on to state that the Landlord has no obligation to provide parking for more than the number of automobiles specified in the first paragraph of the tenancy agreement (Exhibit 1, p. 7), which in the [name] case, is zero. While parking on site has been available to her, she has no contractual right to it.

Despite the clear terms of the tenancy agreement, the Landlord has stated that the Tenant and her household may use one parking space on a “first come first serve” basis, the same as other tenants of the residential complex. It has further attempted to resolve the issue of the Tenant using two spaces by offering the Tenant a rent reduction in exchange for her giving up one of the parking spaces and moving a vehicle to an offsite parking lot. As the Landlord is behaving in a manor expected of it by the Act, this cannot constitute substantial interference.

For the reasons set out in paragraphs 10-17, above, I find that the Tenant has failed to meet her burden under the Act on a balance of probabilities. As such, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all my reasons within it. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The basis of the Tenant’s application is that the Landlord failed to address their complaints regarding the lack of garage space and access to the garage was blocked by the downstairs tenant which substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The application must be dismissed.

In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2002] O.J. No. 5660, the Divisional Court affirmed that a landlord has a positive duty to address situations where one tenant substantially interferes with another tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. In that decision, the Court stated: “It is not that the other tenant’s actions are imputed to the landlord, but rather, the landlord’s legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives raise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant’s right to quiet enjoyment.”
Accordingly, the issue that must be determined in this case is whether the Landlord acted reasonably in response to the Tenant.

The Tenant first complained to the Landlord that they were having issues accessing the garage in November due to the downstairs tenant pulling their vehicle too far up the driveway. Following the complaint in November the Landlord addressed the complaint by speaking to the downstairs tenant which resolved the issue temporarily. The Tenant continued to complaint about the parking to which the Landlord offered to attend the property and mediate the situation however the Tenant declined.
Additionally, the Tenant testified that two vehicles would not fit in the garage as the rental unit is a one car garage with shelving and stairs.
The photographs provided by the Tenant show the garage to be a double car garage as stated in the lease agreement therefore I am satisfied that it is a double car garage.

The Landlord testified after the first incident he offered to mediate the situation between the tenants although it was declined. The Tenant confirmed this submission. I found the Landlords evidence to be credible.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely, appropriate and reasonable manner. The Landlord has spoken to the downstairs tenant, offered mediation and when requested removed items from the garage to give more space.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
As a result, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is granted as detailed below.
The Tenant brought a T5 Application claiming the Landlord gave them an N12 notice of termination in bad faith and it was filed on January 26, 2025.

On September 20, 2023, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination for personal use pursuant to s. 48 of the Act. The Landlord filed an application with the Board based on the N12 notice and the parties resolved that application by way of mediation agreement on May 7, 2024. The parties agreed that the Tenant would vacate the unit on January 31, 2025. Ultimately, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the mediation agreement (and the N12 Notice) on January 31, 2025. Evidence and Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

As noted, on September 20, 2023, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination for personal use pursuant to s. 48 of the Act. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice on January 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that they resided in the rental unit for 9 years and only started looking for a new rental after being served the N12 notice. The Tenant further stated that if not for this notice from the Landlord, they had no intention to leave the rental unit.

On a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination they were given under s. 48; however, even though there was a mediation meeting between both parties, this was ultimately based on the N12, so the Tenant was still acting as per the notice provided by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that when the Landlord served the N12, the Landlord’s intention was to occupy the property. The Tenant was given multiple reasons by the Landlord’s Agent, who was the person they communicated with throughout the tenancy, as to the Landlord’s desire to occupy the rental unit, but ultimately, testified that the rental unit was not occupied by the Landlord after the Tenant’s departure. In fact, the Tenant testified that after they vacated the unit, it was sold.

Prior to being served the N12, it was the Tenant’s testimony that they were approached by the Landlord’s Agent about a rent increase. Subsequent to this, the Tenant testified that they were advised that the Landlord was going to be doing renovations in the rental unit. In the end, the Tenant testified that they believed the Landlord had no genuine intention to occupy the rental unit and only stated this due to the Tenant’s refusal to acquiesce to a rent increase.

It was the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Furthermore, it was stated that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit at all as the property remained vacant and eventually was sold. The Tenant testified that they went back to the unit on multiple occasions to pick up mail and vote in government elections and was advised no one had moved into the rental unit.
On the basis of the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit.

With respect to the remaining issue of whether the N12 was served in bad faith, the Tenant testified that no person referred to in the N12 occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

Section 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Accordingly, s. 57(5)(a) of the Act applies and “it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that [the] landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith.” This presumption would also apply pursuant to s. 57(5)(b) of the Act as the Tenants also submitted that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with other tenants. When the presumption of bad faith is triggered, the burden of proof shifts to the landlord to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they gave the notice of termination in good faith. However, in this case, the Landlord did not attend the hearing to provide evidence, and therefore, they did not rebut the presumption of bad faith.
The Tenant has established all three of parts of the test contained in s. 57(1)(a) of the Act. I therefore find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies
At the hearing, the Tenant requested their rent differential for one year, out of pocket expenses for moving and storage, reimbursement of the filing fee, and general compensation of $28,000.00.

With respect to the rent differential, the Tenant is now paying $100.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. I see no reason not to grant the Tenant this remedy. The Tenant’s new unit is comparable to their old unit, and if anything, it is a smaller space. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $1,200.00 for their rent differential for a period of one year.

The Tenant also incurred reasonable out of pocket expenses in the amount of $1,152.61 for moving. The Tenant submitted receipts and bank statements to show how much expense they incurred for mail forwarding, U-Haul truck rentals, paying movers, and for moving supplies and materials. I am satisfied the amount claimed reflects the reasonable moving expenses the Tenant incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach and an order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $1,152.61 for reasonable out of pocket moving expenses.

The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $28,000.00, which is the equivalent of one year’s rent, pursuant to s. 57(3)1.1 of the Act. There is evidence before me that the Tenant has experienced impairment from this termination of tenancy. Accordingly, for this matter, and pursuant to s. 57(3)4 of the Act, I find that an award of general compensation equivalent to two month’s rent plus additional hydro charges that the Tenant has incurred over the 12-month period since vacating the rental unit appropriate and just. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to pay the Tenant $5,500.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,900.61. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from January 27, 2025, to January 26, 2026. • $1,152.61 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 5, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
