issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The Landlord’s Agent explained that the tenancy is a joint tenancy between the Landlord and 4 Tenants: [name], [name], [name] and Pascual Cole. Each Tenant occupied a bedroom and shared common arrears. All Tenants signed the same lease agreement. Only [name] and Pascual Cole were named on the Application and the Tenant’s Agent indicated that the Tenant Pascual Cole wished to be removed from the Application.

The Agent testified that the Tenants signed a one-year lease from September 1, 2025, to August 31, 2026. She testified that in September or October 2025 [name] and Cole decide that they wanted to sublet their bedrooms and informed their co-Tenants and their mothers. They intended to sublet from May 1, 2026 to August 31, 2026, and did not know at that time if they intended to return to the rental unit.

She testified that on December 10, 2025, she made a request to the Landlord that [name] and Cole be permitted to sublet their bedrooms. She relied on an email which states that [name] and Cole will not be staying on past August 26, and would like to sublet their rooms to two students over the summer.
She testified that Cole and [name] did not intend to return to the rental unit after the sublet.
She testified that the Landlord provided them with a sublet form to sign and indicated that all 4 joint tenants would need to sign.

However, there was a despite between the Tenants with respect to the allocation of bathrooms within the rental unit, and [name] and [name] had questions and were not prepared were not prepared to sign to sublet form. The Agent testified that she told the Landlord that [name] and [name] were not prepared to sign. The Landlord reiterated that all four Tenant were required to sign but indicated that they would have a meeting internally with their new general manager to discuss the situation. However, she received no response.

The Agent subsequently emailed the Landlord on January 12, 2026 asking for updates and received an email on January 27, 2026, indicating that all four Tenant’s would need to sign the request to sublet.
The Agent clarified that she did not complete the sublet form provided by the Landlord and return it because the other two Tenant’s would not sign.
The Agent confirmed that while she had identified prospective subtenants, they were not put before the Landlord due to the refusal of the other Tenant’s to sign.

The Agent testified that the other Tenant’s have since sublet their rooms, and she feels like she missed out on this opportunity because of a misunderstanding. She sought an end to the tenancy effective Apri, 30, 2026. Analysis
I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord arbitrary or unreasonable refusal consent to sublet the rental unit.
I note that the Tenant’s proposal does not appear to fall within the definition of a sublet.

The Act adopts the common law definition of subletting. Three conditions must be met: 1.The Tenant vacates the rental unit; 2.The Tenant gives someone the right to occupy for a term ending on a specified date that must be a date before the end of the fixed lease term or period; and 3.the Tenant has the right to resume occupancy after the specified date (called “the reversionary interest”).

In this case while the Tenant intended to vacate the rental unit, the end of the proposed sublet was August 31, 2026, which was also the same day as the end of the fixed term lease and the Tenant did not intend to resume occupancy of the rental unit at the conclusion of the sublet.

I also note that while on December 10, 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord for consent to sublet the rental unit to generally, they did not identify a potential subtenant at this time. However, the Landlord did not refuse this request and instead sent the Tenant the documentation required to request a sublet.

However, it appears the Tenant’s intent to sublet was frustrated primarily by the other joint Tenants within the rental unit who refused to sign the documentation provided by the Landlord and could not come to a consensus with respect to the request the sublet.

By xontrast it does not appear that the Landlord ever formally rejected the Tenant’s request to sublet and were in fact prepared to consider and possibly approve it, so long a sit was clear that this request came from all of the joint tenants.

Given that this is a joint tenancy where each Tenant is jointly and severally liable, I am satofsied that it was not unreasonable for the Landlord to ask all Tenant to indicate that they wished to sublet the rental unit.

While there was a delay in the Landlord’s responses to the Agent I am prepared to attribute a portion of this delay to the holiday period, and note that the Landlord remained consistent in their messaging that all four Tenant’s would need to sign the request to sublet.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to the sublet of the rental unit to the potential subtenant.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. July 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application – LTB-T-007746-26 [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 6, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant evidence. & LTB-T-007746-26
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant and complete repairs to the rental unit. [name]

The Tenant testified. They stated that the Landlord had illegally locked them out of the rental unit between February 2-5, 2026, with the assistance of police. The Sudbury Legal Aid clinic wrote to the Landlord and thereafter the Tenant was permitted back into the rental unit. See DOC-00991426 at pages 4 and 5.
The Tenant also testified that there is no heat, that he has had to purchase a portable heater to heat their room.
The Tenant also testified that there is no hot water in the rental unit. They stated that they use the facilities at the school they attend to shower and clean.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that the ceiling in their bedroom had collapsed into the room due to a leak or flooding in the ceiling on January 24, 2026. See DOC-7539090, photographs at pages 1-3. See also a video produced by the Tenant at DOC-7242164.
The Tenant stated that they changed rooms after this incident on January 24, 2026, and that the Landlord has not yet made any repairs to the ceiling.

The Tenant testified that the City of Greater Sudbury, Building Services Department had issued a “Order to Comply” to the Landlord because the residential complex had been converted into a multiplex without appropriate building permits. The Landlord had been directed to obtain building permits or to return the property to its original construction. See page 6 of DOC-7539090.
The Tenant also testified that the City of Greater Sudbury Fire Services had also issued an “Inspection Order” to the Landlord to bring the complex up to the fire code. See page 7 of DOC-7539090.
The Tenant testified that none of these repairs ordered by the City of Greater Sudbury had been completed.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. & LTB-T-007746-26

Therefore, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord obligations under subsection 20(1of the Act to repair maintain the rental unit or the residential complex and failed to comply with safety or housing or maintenance standards. Remedies
The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 40% of rent commencing January 24, 2026. The lawful rent is $500.00.

In Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.

I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. The Tenant did not provide case law on an appropriate remedy or to show what may have been ordered by the Board in past decisions. In my view a 40% abatement is reasonable in all of the circumstances. The Tenant has had to change rooms, has no heat provided by the Landlord and no access to hot water. In addition, it appears that the Landlord has not complied with City orders thereby jeopardizing the safety and security of the Tenant.
Therefore, an amount of 40% for the period January 24, 2026, to June 6, 2026, an amount of $2,214.00 shall be ordered.

In addition, commencing June 7, 2026, until the Landlord has repaired the ceiling and complied with the City of Greater Sudbury Orders the Tenant shall be entitled to a rent reduction of 40%. This is equivalent of 6.65 per day, or $200.00 per month.

The Tenant testified that some of their possessions had been damaged because of the ceiling collapse and flooding into their bedroom. They requested reimbursed for damaged items that they Tenant had to replace. These included a laptop, school materials, clothing, a mattress, and damaged documents, for a total amount of $11,000.00.

I have reviewed the list of items and the amounts claimed for each. In my view a reasonable amount of compensation is approximately $6,000.00. In my view the value of some items appears to be overestimated, therefore a reduction is appropriate.

The Tenant also claimed general damages for the emotional stress, loss of reasonable enjoyment, academic disruption arising from the loss of the Laptop. The Tenant requested an amount of $2,000.00 in the amended application. & LTB-T-007746-26
I am satisfied that in al of the circumstances that the amount of $2,000.00 is reasonable and shall be ordered.
The Tenant also requested an order that the Landlord repair the damaged ceiling in the bedroom, to restore heat and hot water. I find that this too is reasonable in all of the circumstances
The Tenant incurred applications fees in the amount of $96.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed those fees.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,310.00. This amount represents: • $2,214.00 rent abatement. • $6,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has or will incur to repair / replace property that was damaged / destroyed / disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $2,000.00 in general damages, and • $96.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $300.00 per month commencing September 1, 2026, until the full amount has been paid. The Landlord may deduct any arrears of rent owing from this amount.

The Tenant is entitled to a 40% rent abatement. This means that commencing August 1, 2026, the Tenant’s lawful rent shall be $300.00 per month until the Landlord has repaired the bedroom ceiling and complied with both City of Greater Sudbury orders. The Tenant is entitled to a $6.65 per day credit for the period June 7-30, 2026.
The Landlord shall restore heat to the rental unit.
The Landlord shall restore hot water to the rental unit.
The Landlord shall repair the bedroom ceiling that collapsed on January 24, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

This three-part test is one that must be met before the Board can order any of the remedies being requested by the Tenant. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In a T5 application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenant must establish all four parts of the test to succeed in their application. If one part of the test is not established, it is not necessary to determine if the other requirements have been met.
The main issues in dispute were parts three and four of the test, being that the N12 was served in bad faith and the specified person did not move in.
The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1) of the Act; however, the third and fourth requirements in subsection 57(1) of the Act have not been met.

There is no dispute to that the parties arranged to have a meeting about terminating the tenancy. During this meeting, which took place around October 2024 at the Landlord’s request, the Landlord outlined to the Tenant that she was going through a separation with her ex-partner and he would need the move into the rental unit if the relationship was not salvaged.

Furthermore, it was not disputed by the parties that a N12 notice was given by the Landlord to the Tenant and that the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12 notice. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 2, 2025. Per the N12, the Landlord’s spouse was to move into the rental unit.

The Tenant also confirmed that one month’s compensation was paid to them by the Landlord prior to vacating the rental unit. The Tenant then stated that they questioned whether or not the Landlord’s ex-partner actually moved in due to observations leading them to believe so, such as lights at the property being off and renovations happening.

The Tenant further testified that after she vacated the rental unit, she and her family would drive by the property and noted that it was not visibly occupied nor did they see anyone’s motor vehicle at the property.

To support this, the Tenant testified and relied on documentary evidence. The Tenant testified that they observed construction being done in the property for the purposes of renovation, and that they asked the workers if they have seen anyone move in. Additionally, the Tenant stated that her sons went to the property about 10 times and observed the same thing.

The Tenant testified that at any point in the year after they vacated the rental unit, they did not note the Landlord’s ex-partner living in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she was aware of the Landlord’s personal circumstances through meeting with the Landlord, as illustrated in paragraph 7. There was no other evidence provided by the Tenant, other than a few photos taken by the Tenant to show that there was snow accumulation in the driveway and what the neighbours told her.

The Tenant testified that she believes the Landlord served the N12 notice due to the amount of rent the Tenant paid not being sufficient to cover the cost of the rental property. The Tenant stated that there was a mutual agreement to increase the rent in the past but still believed that the renovations were happening to increase the property value so that the Landlord can obtain more rent from a new, prospective tenant. Moreover, the Tenant stated that even though she met with the Landlord and was informed about the need of her ex-partner, it was really about money and the amount of rent the Landlord was collecting from the Tenant.

The Landlord stated that she and her ex-partner were going through a separation. The Landlord then stated the reason why the N12 notice was served was so that her ex-partner can move into the rental unit to live.

The Landlord then testified that she intended on trying to reconcile with her ex-partner, and as such did not want to displace the Tenant and her family prematurely, and this is why the Landlord reached out to the Tenant about possibly terminating the tenancy in October 2024. As such, the Landlord stated that she informed the Tenant of what was happening and did not want to issue the N12 notice hastily, but instead, wanted to give the Tenant an indication on what her situation was.

The Landlord also testified that her ex-partner moved into the rental unit the same day that the Tenant vacated. This was corroborated by the Tenant in her testimony, with the caveat that the Tenant believed the ex-partner only moved in a small number of items into the property. As well, at the time of serving the N12, this individual was legally the Landlord’s spouse.

The Landlord then stated that the renovations in the property were being handled by her ex-spouse; however, the Landlord did pay for certain renovations. Moreover, it was testified by the Landlord that her ex-partner has been living at the rental property, on the lower floor and on his own, since the Tenant vacated. The Landlord further stated that her ex-partner is a firefighter, and his work schedule is based on rotating shifts of 24 hours.

The Landlord testified that she has been to the property since her ex-partner has been living there and noted that she did a walk around of the property on July 15, 2025, and observed the renovations being done. The Landlord’s ex-partner has been living on the lower floor of the property as the renovations are being completed on the main and upper floor of the property.

The Landlord also testified that the rental property has never been listed for sale or rent since the Tenant vacated the property. This is due to the fact that her ex-partner, by way of their separation agreement, is residing in the property, and is why the N12 was served on the Tenant as their relationship was not reconciled.

As noted above and based on the evidence that the Landlord did not list the rental unit after the N12 was given, this does not trigger the reverse onus on the Landlord and rebuttable presumption under section 57(5) of the Act that the N12 was served in bad faith.

While there is a question surrounding the nature of whether or not the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith, I accept the Landlord’s testimony and find their explanation for the events that followed service of the N12 to be reasonable. I am satisfied that up until the Tenant vacating the rental unit the Landlord had every intention to reconcile her marriage, but due to not being able to, her ex-partner as a result of a separation agreement had to move into the rental unit, and in fact moved into the rental unit. Furthermore, I find that the meeting from October 2024 to be vital as it relates to the allegation of bad faith. The parties both testified and agreed to the fact that they met for the purposes of the Landlord discussing her personal circumstances with the Tenant, and then outlined to the Tenant what her thought process looked like; moreover, this would have put the Tenant on notice that the Landlord’s ex-partner would have needed to move into the rental unit due to a potential separation.

I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s ex-partner moved into the rental unit on February 2, 2025, and still lives there as of the date of the hearing. While I accept the Tenant’s evidence that there were some days where renovations were occurring and there was snow accumulation in the driveway, it is not unreasonable to expect that the Landlord’s ex-partner may not have been home due to his job; moreover, there was no noted effort by the Tenant to go further into confirming whether someone was at the home or not. The fact that pictures were taken of the property from the Tenant’s motor vehicle, and the same for her sons, it would be unreasonable to expect that this alone would have simply indicated that the property was vacant and sitting empty.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant has failed to establish all of the test contained in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I am not convinced, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith nor the specified person did not move into the rental unit.

As such, based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I do not find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith nor that the person referred to in section 48(1) of the Act did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Therefore, the Tenant has not satisfied the third and fourth requirements of section 57(1)(a) of the Act.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (T1 application) and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). This combined application was heard by videoconference on May 7, 2026. The Landlord's legal representative, [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord's legal representative raised a preliminary issue regarding the sufficiency of the Tenant's application. The Landlord submitted that the T6 portion of the application was entirely blank and contained no allegations, particulars, or remedies sought. The Landlord further submitted that the T1 application appeared to challenge the amount of lawful rent payable based on alleged issues with the tenancy rather than alleging that the Landlord had collected or retained money contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Landlord's legal representative referred to the Interim Order issued by Member Quattrociocchi following the Adjudicative Case Conference held on March 27, 2025. Counsel submitted that the Interim Order specifically directed the Tenant to file and serve any amendments to the application by May 15, 2025, as the T6 application was deficient, and further directed the parties to exchange disclosure no later than seven days before the hearing. The Landlord submitted that, despite these directions, no amended application or disclosure had been received. Counsel further submitted that the documents uploaded by the Tenant to the Tribunal Ontario Portal consisted primarily of grievances and complaints rather than an amended application or properly disclosed evidence, leaving the Landlord unable to determine the allegations it was required to answer.

I reviewed the Board's record and confirm that an Adjudicative Case Conference was held on March 27, 2025. During the conference, the Tenant was advised that the T6 application was deficient because it contained no allegations or requested remedies. The matter was adjourned to provide the Tenant with an opportunity to amend the application before the merits hearing.

Following the conference, Member [name] issued an Interim Order directing the Tenant to file and serve any amendments to the application on or before May 15, 2025. The Interim Order also required both parties to exchange all evidence no later than seven days before the hearing. It expressly advised that, if the Tenant failed to amend the application, the Board may proceed only on the originally filed application and that evidence not disclosed in accordance with Rule 19.7 of the Board's Rules of Procedure may not be relied upon at the hearing.

As of the hearing date, the Tenant had not filed or served any amendments to the application as directed. The Board's records contain no amended application, and the Landlord confirmed that none had been received. Although the Tenant asserted that an amendment had been submitted, the Tenant was unable to identify when it had been filed, provide any confirmation of filing or service, or direct me to any document in the Tribunal Ontario Portal constituting the alleged amendment.

While the Tenant emailed a number of documents to the LTB, those documents do not constitute an amended application and were not filed or disclosed in accordance with the Board's Rules of Procedure or the Interim Order. It is not the role of the Board to review miscellaneous submitted documents in an effort to determine the allegations an applicant intends to advance. An application must clearly identify the claims being made and the remedies sought so that the responding party has adequate notice of the case to be met.

Despite being afforded an opportunity to remedy the deficiencies identified at the Adjudicative Case Conference, and despite the clear directions contained in the Interim Order, the Tenant failed to amend the application or provide disclosure in accordance with the Board's Rules of Procedure. The T6 application remains entirely blank and contains no factual allegations, dates, particulars, or remedies upon which the Board could adjudicate. Similarly, the T1 application does not clearly plead a claim that falls within the remedies available under that application.

During my attempts to explain these procedural deficiencies, the Tenant became agitated and argumentative, alleged that the Board was protecting the Landlord, stated an intention to sue the Board, and disconnected from the hearing before the preliminary issues were resolved. The Tenant did not return, and the hearing proceeded in the Tenant's absence.

The purpose of an application is to provide both the Board and the responding party with sufficient notice of the allegations to be determined at the hearing. In this case, the Tenant failed to comply with the Interim Order, failed to comply with the Board's Rules of Procedure respecting amendments and disclosure, and failed to file an application containing sufficient particulars to permit the Board to determine the issues in dispute. Proceeding with the application would be procedurally unfair to the Landlord and would require the Board to speculate as to the claims being advanced. Accordingly, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

This three-part test is one that must be met before the Board can order any of the remedies being requested by the Tenant. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In a T5 application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenant must establish all four parts of the test to succeed in their application. If one part of the test is not established, it is not necessary to determine if the other requirements have been met.
The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1) of the Act; however, the third and fourth requirements in subsection 57(1) of the Act has not been met.

There is no dispute to that there were communications between the parties about a potential sale of the unit to the Tenant as she as been a long-time occupant of the property. Both the Landlord and the Tenant testified to the fact that the Landlord communicated with the Tenant to discuss the nature of a sale of the unit to the Tenant based on the Landlord’s personal circumstances. However, due to the Tenant’s issues with phone storage and capacity issues, she could not see any of these correspondences sent by the Landlord until well after they were sent. The Tenant stated that she had to constantly clear the storage space on her phone to receive and review new messages and emails.

Furthermore, it was not disputed by the parties that a N12 notice was given by the Landlord to the Tenant and that the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12 notice. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025. The listed occupants per the N12 were going to be the Landlord and her parents.

The Tenant also confirmed that one month’s compensation was paid to them by the Landlord prior to vacating the rental unit. The Tenant testified that they doubted that the Landlord and her parents moved into the rental unit because they observed the blinds in the unit were in the same position when the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant testified that after she vacated the rental unit January 31, 2025, she went by the rental unit regularly and observed that no lights were on and her mechanic who also lives in the building said there was no motor vehicle in the parking spot assigned to the rental unit. The Tenant also stated that when she would go to pick up mail, there were numerous flyers in front of the rental unit door, and she assumed that no one moved in due to the untidy state of this area.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that when she served the N12 to the Tenant, it was her intention to go to Hong Kong and bring her parents back to live in the rental unit with her. The Landlord stated due to her personal circumstances, she moved in sporadically. The Landlord then stated that she went to Hong Kong on January 27, 2026, to bring her parents back to Canada; however, due to the medical status of her parents, her family refused to let the parents leave. The Landlord further stated that she was following her parents’ instructions when going back to bring them to the rental unit, but her other family members did not agree to this. The Landlord submitted her sister’s sworn [name] indicating her position was not to let the parents come to Canada.
The Landlord testified that due to this unforeseen change in circumstances, while she was moved into the unit, her parents did not move into the rental unit immediately.

The Landlord then testified and provided documentary evidence that she was preparing the unit for her parents’ arrival by getting furniture, installing handrail and bar devices, and keeping the unit in a clean and tidy manner.

The Landlord further admitted that her parents did not move into the rental unit, but it was due to her other family members preventing her parents from leaving Hong Kong. The Landlord then testified that this caused an additional delay to her bringing her parents back to Canada.

Based on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord has established that an unforeseen material change in circumstances resulted in the persons identified on the N12 being unable to occupy the unit.

The Landlord’s personal circumstances and her parents not moving into the rental unit was due to family issues arising after her trip to Hong Kong. The N12 was given with the intent of moving herself and her parents into the unit, and it is still the Landlord’s intention to do so; moreover, but for the resistance from her family in Hong Kong, the Landlord’s parents would have been occupying the rental unit already. I find this to be a reasonable explanation for the delay in the Landlord’s parents not immediately occupying the rental unit after the N12 was served on the Tenant.

Given the evidence before me, I am not persuaded by the Tenant that the Landlord acted in bad faith. I do not find that there is anything in the motives or conduct of the Landlord that leads me to conclude that the Landlord acted in bad faith or with ulterior motives when she delivered the N12, or at any time after that. I find that the Landlord occupied the unit and genuinely believed that her parents were going to move back to Canada and would reside in the rental unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant has failed to establish all of the test contained in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I am not convinced, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

As such, based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I do not find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. Therefore, the Tenant has not satisfied the third and fourth requirements of section 57(1)(a) of the Act.
Accordingly, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') and for an order to have the Tenant pay the rent they owe because the Tenant did not meet a condition specified in the order issued by the LTB on January 8, 2024 with respect to application LTB-L-075972-23-SA (‘the conditional order’). The Landlord's application was resolved by order LTB-L-007325-24, issued on February 12, 2024. This order was issued without a hearing being held (‘the eviction order’). The Tenant filed a motion to set aside the eviction order. T6 Application The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord also failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Hearing The Tenant’s motion and application were heard in person in Toronto, Ontario, on June 30, 2026. The Landlord and the Landlord’s representative attended in person. However, the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative [name] participated virtually. and LTB-T-008464-23-SA
reasons: Interim order LTB-L-007325-24 & LTB-T-008464-23-IN issued on July 3, 2024, indicates that another member was seized of these applications. However, after the order was issued the Member became unavailable and I was asked to hear the applications. I listened to the hearing recording from the previous appearance. The previous member only dealt with an adjournment. The hearing regarding the merits of the applications did not begin before the previous member. The interim order also reflects that the hearing did not began. As the hearing had not began having a different member step in did not impact the parties’ ability to prepare for the hearing or prejudice the parties in any way. Adjournment Request

The Tenant’s representative requested an adjournment on the Tenant’s behalf because anxiety prevented the Tenant from attending. The adjournment request was denied. The Board scheduled an in person hearing to accommodate the Tenant and help facilitate a fair hearing that was responsive to the Tenant’s accommodation needs. The day before the hearing the Tenant wrote to the Board and said he would be calling in by phone rather than attending in person. The Board accommodated that request and converted the hearing to a hybrid format. The Tenant did not provide any medical documentation that supports that he could not participate in the hearing at all regardless of hearing format. While a capacity assessment has been undertaken under the Law Society Act, that is related to the Tenant’s law licence and the findings of any such assessment are limited in scope and do not support that the Tenant cannot participate in proceedings at the Board. An adjournment would prejudice the Landlord who has been waiting a long time for the resolution of these matters.

After I denied the adjournment, I indicated that should the Tenant call in, I would accommodate his disabilities so that he could participate. The Tenant then called into the hearing and actively participated. Whenever the Tenant required a break, one was provided. That the Tenant was able to actively participate and provided testimony on all the relevant issues further supports that an adjournment was not necessary. L4 Application There was a breach of the previous order
The Tenant failed to meet a condition specified in the conditional order. Specifically, the Tenant failed to pay $7,500.00 towards the arrears on or before January 20, 2024.

The Tenant testified that he does not remember paying $7,500.00 to the Landlord at one time but he might have made other payments that added up to it. The Landlord testified that the payment was not made, nor were smaller payments made that added up to the required amount. I accept that the payment was not made. The Landlord’s testimony was forthright and confident about the non-payment. In contrast the Tenant did not appear and LTB-T-008464-23-SA confident that the payment was made. The Tenant provided no supporting documentation, such as a bank record etc, to demonstrate that the payment was made. The Surrounding Circumstances
After considering all of the circumstances, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the eviction order.
The arrears are astronomical. The Tenant owes $78,321.00 to June 30, 2026. However, the day before the hearing the Tenant filed a consumer proposal (DOC-8271817).

The Tenant argues that the bankruptcy necessitates that the set aside motion be granted. For the following reasons I disagree. However, I find the bankruptcy extremely relevant to whether it would not be unfair to set aside the eviction order.

Section 69.3 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (the ‘BIA’) creates an automatic stay that is intended to prevent creditors from taking steps to establish or recover a debt owed by the bankrupt outside of the process established by the BIA.

The Board has consistently held that it has no jurisdiction to order rent arrears or eviction based on any claims provable in bankruptcy. However, the eviction order that is the subject of the motion was issued prior to the bankruptcy and the motion is not a claim provable in bankruptcy.

The Court in Peel Housing Corporation v. Siewnarine, 2008 CanLII 31815 (ON SCDC) states at paragraph 24 that the remedy given to a landlord for a breach of a mediated settlement cannot fall within any definition of a claim provable in bankruptcy.

While not binding on me I find the reasons in LTB-L-069063-25-RV issued on January 19, 2026, persuasive. That order considers the application of section 78 of the RTA when a tenant becomes bankrupt. The Board says the following: “Application to L4 Applications 18. On an application under section 78—an L4 application—the basis for the LTB making an order terminating the tenancy is the failure of the tenant to meet or satisfy a condition in a previous order made by the LTB. [RTA, s. 78(1)] For that reason: (a) the application is not stayed by section 69.3 of the [name] because the application is not a proceeding to recover a claim provable [Peel Housing Corporation v. Siewnarine, 2008 CanLII 31815 (ON SCDC)]3; and (b) section 84.2 of the BIA does not apply because the termination is not based only on the failure of the tenant to pay pre-bankruptcy rent4. 19. The fact that section 84.2 if the BIA does not prohibit the LTB from making an order terminating a tenancy does not mean the LTB must terminate the tenancy. Where section 69.3 and section 84.2 of the BIA do not apply—which is the case on applications under subsection 74(3)—the LTB will apply the RTA. and LTB-T-008464-23-SA 20. Paragraph 74(11)(b) of the RTA says that the LTB may, having regard to all the circumstances, set aside a valid order terminating the tenancy on the basis of fairness. 21. In the case of a tenant who has become bankrupt, the circumstances the LTB must consider under paragraph 78(11)(b) include that any pre-bankruptcy rent is a claim provable against the (bankrupt) tenant and not recoverable by the landlord. The LTB is, in my view, also required to consider whether the tenant has paid rent post-bankruptcy as contemplated by section 84.2. 22. On an application under section 78 where the underlying application was for arrears or compensation, the landlord can—but is not required to—also request an order that the tenant pay arrears or other amounts owed to the landlord. [RTA, ss. 78(3) and (7)] 23. Where a landlord asks for an order that the tenant pay arrears or other compensation, section 69.3 of the BIA may apply to that application. The LTB is not able to make an order that the tenant pay any pre-bankruptcy amounts. The LTB is, however, able to order that the tenant pay post-bankruptcy amounts. 24. Where a tenant: (a) becomes bankrupt after an order is made under subsection 78 terminating the tenancy and ordering the tenant to pay arrears; and (b) applies under subsection 78(9) to have that order set aside, sections 69.3 and 84.2 of the BIA have little application. 25. Section 69.3 of the BIA applies to proceedings by a creditor to recover a claim provable in bankruptcy. A motion under subsection 78(9) is neither a proceeding by a creditor nor does it involve a claim provable in bankruptcy. 26. Section 84.2 of the BIA restricts the ability of a landlord or the LTB to terminate a tenancy. It does not apply to a motion to set aside the termination of a tenancy.”

I also find the Board’s reasons in LTB-L-069063-25-RV persuasive that despite the ruling in Forestwood Co-operative [name], [2002] OJ No 550 ([name]), which was not decided under the RTA, the termination of a tenancy under section 78 is not based on the existence of arrears and the request by a landlord for pre-bankruptcy arrears can be severed from the request that the tenancy be terminated.

All of which is to say that a tenant filing bankruptcy is not conclusive of a set aside motion under section 78 of the Act. The decision whether to grant the motion remains discretionary. However, in this case I find the bankruptcy largely favours that it would not be unfair to set aside the eviction order.

In LTB-L-069063-25-RV the Board determined that in the case of a tenant who has become bankrupt, the circumstances the Board must consider under paragraph 78(11)(b) include that any pre-bankruptcy rent is a claim provable against the (bankrupt) tenant and not recoverable by the landlord and the Board is also required to consider whether the tenant has paid rent post-bankruptcy. and LTB-T-008464-23-SA

The arrears are astronomical and have had a significant impact on the Landlord. However, the entirety of the arrears period in this tenancy is captured by the bankruptcy. The Landlord is not able to recover the pre-bankruptcy arrears from the Tenant. There are currently no post bankruptcy arrears. That there are no recoverable arrears is very relevant to whether it would not be unfair to set aside the eviction order.

During the hearing on June 30, 2026, the Tenant paid the upcoming rent for July 2026, and the Landlord confirmed that they received it. The Tenant testified that the bankruptcy will allow him to focus on paying new rent that comes due, that he has reduced his expenses, that he is receiving some income from working in a banquet hall, that he has court proceedings where he might receive compensation and he has a scheduled hearing to try and get Ontario Disability Support Program(‘ODSP’) payments. All these factors support that the Tenant will pay his rent going forward.

Another circumstance that supports that it would not be unfair to set aside the eviction order is that after the eviction order was issued on February 12, 2024, the Landlord’s husband signed a document on February 16, 2024, indicating that he received the rent for February 2024 and agreed to waive any current payment defaults by the Tenant (DOC- 8272763). Any current defaults would include the missed arrears payment from January 20, 2024, that is the subject of the [name] application.

While the Landlord’s husband is not listed on the application, the Landlord testified that her husband is also an owner of the property. Therefore, he also meets the definition of ‘landlord’ under the RTA.

The Landlord disputes that her husband signed the document. However, the version submitted by the Tenant has two signatures and the Landlord’s husband did not attend the hearing to provide any testimony.

I found the Tenant to be a very forthright witness. He was honest that he could not remember who put the other signature on the document but that he thought both landlords were present when the document was signed. The wording on the document “it is agreed between myself, my wife, and [name], supports that it was the Landlord’s husband who signed the document. That the Tenant was honest that he could not remember who signed the document leads me to find that he did not forge anyone’s signature.

While the Landlord texted the Tenant on February 17, 2024 saying that “we can’t sign this one for now”, the agreement reflects that it was signed the day prior and the agreement has two signatures on it.

For those reasons the motion is granted. Typically, when a set aside motion is granted, any outstanding arrears will be addressed with a new payment plan. However, in this case the entire arrears period is covered by the bankruptcy and therefore I cannot issue an order requiring the payment of the arrears. T6 Application

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. and LTB-T-008464-23-SA Plumbing in the Primary Bathroom

The Tenant testified that there are three bathrooms in the rental unit, but he only uses the bathroom connected to the primary bedroom. The Tenant testified that the tenancy began in May 2022 and that issues with the plumbing in the primary bathroom started within a few months.

The Tenant testified that the bathtub would not drain or would drain very slowly. The Tenant testified that this resulted in buildup in the bathtub. The Tenant testified that he fell in the bathtub on November 22, 2022. The Tenant testified that the fall resulted in physical issues, caused him to be depressed and lose motivation, and impacted his ability to work.
The Tenant testified that there was also an issue with the plumbing in the sink.

The Tenant testified that the toilet does not flush properly, that he must wait for things to break down to flush it, that the toilet now has a horrible stain, and that even clear liquid clogs the toilet. The Tenant testified that he does not put toilet paper in the toilet.

The Tenant testified that he has been in regular contact with the Landlord about the issue from the start of the tenancy. Later the Tenant said that he told the Landlord about the issue in the summer. The Tenant did not provide any copies of correspondence of him notifying the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that herself and the Tenant did an inspection prior to the tenancy starting and issues with the plumbing were not noted. The Landlord testified that she asked the Tenant in July if everything was ok and the Tenant did not mention any problems.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant sent her a list of problems that included the plumbing issues on September 11, 2023. Later the Landlord referred to this date as September 11, 2022. Unfortunately, neither party provided a copy of this correspondence. I find that September 11, 2022 is the most likely date that the Landlord was notified. It aligns with the Tenant’s testimony about notifying the Landlord closer to the start of the tenancy. Additionally, the T6 application was filed in December 2022 and the Landlord’s evidence package also includes emails about visits to the rental unit in January 2023 (DOC-8210845). I find that the Tenant provided insufficient evidence and his testimony was too vague to find that he notified the Landlord any earlier than September 11, 2022.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant told her that she cannot enter unless he is present, that she asked him when he is available for her to come and address the issues, but he never confirmed a time. The Landlord testified that eventually she told the Tenant a date she would be attending in January 2023. An email the Tenant sent to the Landlord on January 13, 2023 says that the Landlord cannot attend on the requested date (DOC- 8210845, page 62).

The Tenant denies that he impeded the Landlord’s ability to enter the rental unit. However, the emails provided by the Landlord support the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant wanted to be present for the visit and rejected some of the dates suggested by the Landlord (DOC-8210845, pages 62-66). The Tenant does suggest alternative times, however. and LTB-T-008464-23-SA

The Landlord testified that around February and March the Tenant stopped responding to her. The Landlord testified that during a hearing in May 2023 a mediator told her she can enter the rental unit without the Tenant present if notice is provided. The Landlord provided a notice of entry for May 30, 2023 (DOC-8210845, page 67).

The Landlord testified that on May 30, 2023 she entered the rental unit and drainage was done in the primary bathroom. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s husband put a long stick down the drain. The Landlord testified that in her own home she must regularly clear the drain. The Landlord testified that there is nothing wrong with the toilet other than a stain that was not there at the start of the tenancy. The Landlord testified that the toilet flushed properly during the May 30, 2023 visit. The Landlord testified that there have been no complaints since the visit.
The Tenant testified that both the sink and bathtub plumbing issues are resolved but then also that there are still occasional issues. The Tenant testified that the toilet issue is not resolved.

The Tenant indicated that he had not installed anything to stop hair and other debris from getting down the drains. The Tenant testified that he has short hair. The Tenant testified that the Landlord put something in the sink to catch hair and that he is now doing a more regular clean up. The Tenant testified that he is now trying to keep the bathtub cleaner so that he does not fall again.

The Tenant led insufficient evidence to support that there is an issue with the primary bathroom toilet. The parties provided conflicting testimony about whether the toilet adequately flushes. The Tenant says that even clear liquid clogs the toilet and yet did not provide a video of that. The Tenant provided no record of any complaints being made about the toilet after the May 2023 visit which I find inconsistent with the claim that the toilet not flushing is an ongoing issue.

While there may have been an issue with slow draining of the bathtub and sink, I’m not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that is because the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities. Hair and debris can build up around drains. The Tenant testified that he was taking no steps to mitigate that. The Tenant repeatedly referred to doing more cleaning now which left me with the impression that a lack of regular cleaning contributed to the issue. The tenancy started in May 2022 and the Tenant did not complain about the issue until four months later in September 2022 which also supports that something the Tenant did during the tenancy contributed to the issue.

I’m also not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant’s fall in the bathtub is related to a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. Bathtubs are a high-risk area for falls. The Tenant’s testimony supports that he was not regularly cleaning the area. The Tenant referred to a civil claim that he says made a finding that the Landlord is responsible for the fall, yet no copy of a judgement in that regard was entered into evidence.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably and LTB-T-008464-23-SA in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I also find that the Landlord responded reasonably to the issue once notified. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant wanted to be present for any entries and canceled some visits. That testimony is also bolstered by the emails presented by the Landlord. While the Tenant did propose some alternative dates, I also accept the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant eventually stopped responding to her in February and March 2023. Despite the Tenant’s objection to visits not in his presence, the Landlord served a notice of entry for May 2023 and the Landlord’s husband snaked the drain. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that no further complaints have been made since then. The Tenant provided no supporting documentation of any further complaints. Stovetop

The Tenant testified that that all four burners were not working on the stove top for 5-6 months but then also testified that it’s an ongoing issue that not all the burners work. The Tenant testified that the Landlord replaced two of the burners but provided no information about when.

The Landlord testified that one of the stove elements was not working before the Tenant moved in, so it was replaced, that you have to be careful because if you move it, because it stops working, and that when the parties did the house inspection before move in the burners were working.

I find that the Tenant led insufficient evidence to support this claim. The Tenant did not provide clear evidence about when the issue started or for how long it persisted. The Tenant provided no copies of any complaints and no photos or videos of the issue. The Landlord’s testimony conflicts the Tenant’s that there is an ongoing issue.

Even if I had found a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligation, the Tenant’s testimony was that he could function with only using two of the elements. As such any financial remedy awarded to the Tenant would be nominal. I’m not satisfied that this is an ongoing issue and therefore an order for repair also would not be awarded. Lawn Mower and [name]

The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided a lawn mower and weed whacker at the start of the tenancy, those items broke, the Tenant replaced the weed whacker himself, the Landlord replaced the lawn mower, the Tenant was not sure when this happened, and said that the items were probably not working for a couple months.

The Tenant led insufficient evidence to support this claim. The Tenant did not provide clear evidence about when the issue started, for how long it persisted, when the Landlord replaced the lawn mower or when the Tenant decided to buy a new weed whacker. Without more information I’m not satisfied that the Landlord responded unreasonably to the complaint.

The application does not make clear if the Tenant is raising an issue about the Landlord transferring lawn care to him. The application seems to concern the non-functioning of the and LTB-T-008464-23-SA weed whacker and lawn mower, not so much the delegation of responsibility for lawn care. As such this issue is dismissed for that reason. It is procedurally unfair to the Landlord to grant a remedy for a claim that did not make clear the case to be met.

Additionally, the issue about who is responsible for lawn care also would have been dismissed even if it had been sufficiently pled on the application. The Tenant led insufficient evidence to support that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations because the Tenant has undertaken lawn care. The Tenant led insufficient evidence about what areas he is doing the work on. Is it a private backyard that only the Tenant can access? Is it the front of the house or a shared area? What does the parties’ lease say about lawn care? Have the parties entered a severable contract from the tenancy for the Tenant to undertake lawn care? Without more information the Tenant did not prove the claim on a balance of probabilities.

Order LTB-L-007325-24, issued on February 12, 2024, is set aside and cannot be enforced.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This application was first before the LTB fo r an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) on March 18, 2026.

As set out in interim order LTB-T-009334-25-IN, issued on March 24, 2026 after the ACC, the Tenant was informed at the ACC that the application as filed lacked adequate particulars for the Landlord to know the case to be met. The interim order specifically states that particulars should include dates and times and a detailed description of the alleged issues, as well as a detailed description of the Landlord’s response to being made aware of the issues.

The interim order also stat es that the Tenant intended to request to amend the application, and that any request to amend must be made in compliance with rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. The interim order specifically encourages the Tenant to review this rule.

Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure requires a request to amend an application to be made in writing; served with the amended application on all other parties, and filed together with the amended application and a certificate of service: rule 15.1, LTB Rules of Procedure.

The Tenant filed an amended app lication on March 30, 2026, but it was not filed together with a certificate of service. The Tenant acknowledged at the hearing that she did not serve the amended application on the Landlord.

MC said that he had not seen, and was not aware of, the request to amend the application until the day of the hearing. I therefore do not find that the amended application is deemed to have been served pursuant to ss. 191(2) of the Act.

I denied the request to amend the applicatio n because it was not served and filed in compliance with rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure, as ordered. To grant the request to amend and proceed with hearing the application, as amended, would be procedurally unfair to the Landlord because the Landlord was not able to prepare to respond to the allegations in the amended application. Preliminary Issue – Request to Adjourn
After I denied the request to amend the appl ication, the Tenant requested an adjournment so that she could serve the request to amend the application, as required by the Rules of Procedure.
The Tenant said that she was not aware t hat she had to serve the amended application on the Landlord.

MC opposed the adjournment request, and submitted that the Tenant was already encouraged to review rule 15 in the interim order. He submitted that the Tenant’s failure to serve the amended application was the result of a lack of reasonable diligence, and an adjournment is not appropriate.

The Tenant acknowledged that she received the interim order, but said she was in the hospital, on unpaid sick leave from work for medical reasons, and that she spoke with a “non-profit lawyer” for an hour, who told her to upload the amended application to the Portal (‘TOP’). She also said that she has a “learning disability”. The Tenant did not present any supporting medical evidence to establish that the Tenant was not reasonably able to attend to reading rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure and sending the amended application to the Landlord when she filed it because of any medical issue.

In [name], 2023 ONSC 1028 (CanLII), the Divisional Court wrote about the adequacy of medical documentation in the context of requesting adjournments for medical reasons at paragraph 10: Further, the fresh evidence did not change the result. The doctor’s note is inadequate to justify an adjournment. Courts have made this point, repeatedly, about doctor’s notes. It is the court, not the doctor, who decides whether the adjournment will be granted. Thus, a doctor’s note must obtain sufficient information to enable the court or tribunal to exercise its own judgment as to whether the adjournment should be granted. This should, at a minimum, describe the diagnosis, the effect of the patient’s condition on their ability to attend and participate in the hearing, and a statement as to when, in the doctor’s opinion, the patient will be well enough to attend court and participate as required. In this case, the LTB reconsideration panel was not satisfied that the doctor’s note explained [name] inability to participate in the hearing – either by telephone or by [name] and did not further explain [name] failure to attend to request an adjournment. These are factual findings and are not amenable to appeal in this court. [emphasis added]

While this case refers to a request to adjourn a hearing because of a party’s alleged inability to participate in the hearing, I find it is instructive in the circumstances of this case. To warrant an adjournment because the Tenant claims that she did not know she had to serve the request to amend, and did not read rule 15 and learn about the service requirement because of medical issues, medical documentation describing the Tenant’s diagnosis and its impact on the Tenant’s ability to review rule 15 and serve the amended application on the Landlord during the relevant period is necessary.
It is not clear to me why the Tenant was able to prepare and file an amended application, but could not review rule 15 and serve the amended application, which was already prepared, on the Landlord.

The Tenant also did not present any evidence to support her assertion that she spoke with a “not-for-profit lawyer”, who told her only to upload the amended application to TOP. To the extent that she may have received flawed legal advice from a lawyer, this is an issue between the Tenant and the lawyer, and a matter for the Law Society of Ontario, and not the LTB, to consider. In my view, this does not justify the Tenant not reviewing rule 15 as she was encouraged to do my the Member presiding over the ACC.

I denied the Tenant’s request to adjourn so that she could serve the amended application. I am not satisfied that her failure to serve the amended application on the Landlord was caused by anything but the Tenant’s own lack of reasonable diligence in the circumstances. A lack of reasonable diligence in a legal proceeding is not an appropriate reason to grant an adjournment or delay a proceeding: Q Res Operating GP Inc. v. [name], 2017 ONSC 5541 (CanLII), para 8.

After the adjournment request was denied, the Tenant said that she also previously requested accommodation from the LTB. In the accommodation request emailed by the Tenant to the LTB on March 31, 2026, the Tenant stated that she needed accommodation due to an ADHD diagnosis, affecting her “… ability to process detailed written instructions, organize materials, and ensure that all required information is identified and submitted within strict timelines”. The accommodation requested was “[a] short grace period of [5-7] days to submit any additional or supplemental evidence, if needed; [p]ermission to provide additional documents if I later realize something relevant was missing due to these limitations; [and] [c]lear and structured communication or verbal communication via virtual meeting regarding requirements and expectations leading up to the hearing, to support my full participation” [emphasis added}.

The accommodation request does not specifically refer to the request to amend the application. I am also not satisfied that the interim order would not amount to “clear and structured communication … r egarding requirements and expectations” relative to the request to amend in the circumstances. The interim order was issued March 24, 2026, more than three months before the hearing before me. The April 1, 2026 deadline to request an amendment may have been relatively short given the date the interim order was issued, but the issue before me was not that the amended application was served after the imposed deadline, the issue was that it was not served at all.

I do not accept that an adjournment was necessary to accommodate a disability-related need, to the extent that this was the Tenant’s position, because there was no basis on the evidence before me that the Tenant’s failure to serve the amended application on the Landlord was caused, in whole or in part, by a disability as opposed to a lack of reasonable diligence. The information the Tenant provided about her request for accommodation does not change my decision to refuse to grant her requested adjournment. Preliminary Issue- Adequacy of Particulars
The hearing proceeding on the application as originally filed.
MC requested that the application be dismissed because it contains inadequate particulars.

When a party commences an application before the LTB, the application must contain details that are sufficient for the other side to know the case to be met. These details should include dates and times together with a detailed description of the alleged offensive conduct: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] OJ No 5931, paras 10 & 12; Tugui v. Miltowne Creek Investments Inc., 2021 CanLII 146888 (ON LTB).

The entirety of the factual allegations in the application are: “Water quality issue both kitchen and washroom brown water and sewage noise concern toilet leakage pest issue cockroaches spiders other unidentifable bugs etc.”
The Tenant said that because of a lack of legal support, she was not aware of the details she had to include, but that the details were included in the amended application.

The application does not include dates or a detailed description of the allegations being made. I find that the particulars included in the application are not adequate for the Landlord to know the case to be met.
The application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

This three-part test is one that must be met before the Board can order any of the remedies being requested by the Tenants. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In a T5 application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenants must establish all four parts of the test to succeed in their application. If one part of the test is not established, it is not necessary to determine if the other requirements have been met.
The Tenants proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1) of the Act; however, the third requirement in subsection 57(1) of the Act has not been met.

There is no dispute to that the parties agreed to mutually terminate the tenancy as the parties drafted and signed a settlement agreement. This settlement agreement contemplated the statutory requirement for one month compensation, an additional amount of money to be paid by the Landlord to the Tenants, returning the keys, and an inspection of the property at the time the Tenants vacated. This agreement was signed by the Landlord and Tenants on December 30, 2024. As a result, the connection between this settlement agreement and the N12 was to capture the date of termination for the Tenants and their last day of occupancy in the rental unit. Therefore, based on this, I find that the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 notice.

Furthermore, it was not disputed by the parties that a N12 notice was given by the Landlord to the Tenants and that the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 notice. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on February 2, 2025.

It was the evidence of the Tenants that they questioned whether or not the Landlord actually moved in due to snow accumulation in the driveway. The Tenants further testified that they noted the property was not visibly occupied nor did they see the Landlord’s motor vehicle at the property until April 6, 2025.

The Tenants then testified that at any point in the year after they vacated the rental unit they did not note the Landlord living in the rental unit. The Tenants testified that the Landlord’s Agent said they would be living there for a brief time, which is inconsistent with the information contained in the N12. There was no other substantial or considerable evidence provided by the Tenants, other than a few photos taken by the Tenants to show what they believed was inoccupation by the Landlord.

The Landlord’s Agent stated that he and the Landlord were going through a divorce. The Landlord’s Agent then stated the reason why the N12 notice was served was so that the Landlord can move into the rental unit to live with their two children.

The Landlord’s Agent also testified and submitted evidence that the Landlord paid utility and hydro bills at the rental property shortly after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord Agent also testified that the Landlord updated her address on her driver’s licence to that of the rental property. It is important to note that while the Landlord did this approximately six months later, no evidence was led to suggest anything other than the Landlord taking an unusually long time to update the Ministry of Transportation records.

The Landlord’s Agent further stated that he helped the Landlord move into the rental property and that the Landlord moved in after the Tenants vacated. It was then submitted by the Landlord’s Agent that the Landlord could not afford to keep the rental property vacant, and so the Landlord moved in as soon as possible; moreover, with the Landlord having two young children, the Landlord had to take their time and move into the rental unit incrementally, which took approximately two weeks. In addition, the Landlord’s Agent referenced the N11 agreement that was signed by both parties and indicated the terms of the settlement agreement.

While there is a question surrounding whether or not the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, I find the Landlord’s explanation for the two-week delay to be reasonable. I am satisfied that the Landlord had every intention to move into the rental unit, and in fact moved into the rental unit, and the delay in moving in has not, on a balance of probabilities, established that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit in a reasonable amount of time.

The Landlord’s Agent provided clear and consistent evidence about the Landlord’s intentions and actions after the N12 Notice was served. On the other hand, the Tenants’ evidence did not provide a clear and objective basis to find that the Landlord failed to move into the rental unit and/or that the N12 Notice was given in bad faith.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenants have failed to establish all of the test contained in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I am not convinced, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s delay in moving into the rental unit was unreasonable and/or that the N12 was given in bad faith. 16. , Therefore, the Tenants have not satisfied the third and fourth requirements of section 57(1)(a) of the Act. 17. Accordingly, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed. 18. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant took possession of the rental unit on January 1, 2026, and vacated on January 31, 3026. The term of the tenancy was for the period from January 1, 2026 to August 31, 2026.

The Landlord was provided $100.00 as a key deposit that was returned to the Tenant on February 3, 2026, and the Tenant no longer sought to have this issue heard as it was resolved between the parties.
The Tenant provided the Landlord with a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $750.00 on December 19, 2025.
The Tenant paid the Landlord January 2026 rent.
The Landlord rented out the unit on February 1, 2026, to new tenants. T1 Application

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the Tenants the last month’s rent that is on deposit.

The Landlord testified he made an agreement with the Tenant on January 25, 2026, in relation to terminating the tenancy, which was for the Tenant to find someone to take over the lease, or if he wanted to terminate the tenancy early the Tenant would have to provide the Landlord with 1 month rent compensation because of the short notice provided to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that the reason for terminating the tenancy early was due to allergies within the rental unit, and that he did not agree to provide the Landlord with 1 month rent compensation to terminate the lease before the end of the tenancy.

It is not disputed that the Landlord re-rented out the unit February 1, 2026. Therefore, I find that the Tenant’s interest in the tenancy effectively ended on January 31, 2026, along with their obligation to pay rent.

In accordance with s. 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a landlord can only use a rent deposit to cover the rent for the last rental period. Since the rent for the last rental period was already paid, the deposit must be returned to the Tenant.

I find that the Tenant would have been responsible for rent up to and including the rental period of January 2026, as the Landlord re-rented out the unit on February 1, 2026. The Tenant’s obligation to pay rent ended because their interest in the unit ended when the new tenancy began. Since January 2026 rent was already paid by the Tenant, the Landlord is required to provide the Tenant with the last month’s rent deposit as it was not applied to January 2026 rent.

Section 134(1.1) of the Act states: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.
Therefore, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $798.00. This amount represents: • $750.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
