issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application – LTB-T-007746-26 [name] [name] frank (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 6, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant evidence. & LTB-T-007746-26
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant and complete repairs to the rental unit. [name]

The Tenant testified. They stated that the Landlord had illegally locked them out of the rental unit between February 2-5, 2026, with the assistance of police. The Sudbury Legal Aid clinic wrote to the Landlord and thereafter the Tenant was permitted back into the rental unit. See DOC-00991426 at pages 4 and 5.
The Tenant also testified that there is no heat, that he has had to purchase a portable heater to heat their room.
The Tenant also testified that there is no hot water in the rental unit. They stated that they use the facilities at the school they attend to shower and clean.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that the ceiling in their bedroom had collapsed into the room due to a leak or flooding in the ceiling on January 24, 2026. See DOC-7539090, photographs at pages 1-3. See also a video produced by the Tenant at DOC-7242164.
The Tenant stated that they changed rooms after this incident on January 24, 2026, and that the Landlord has not yet made any repairs to the ceiling.

The Tenant testified that the City of Greater Sudbury, Building Services Department had issued a “Order to Comply” to the Landlord because the residential complex had been converted into a multiplex without appropriate building permits. The Landlord had been directed to obtain building permits or to return the property to its original construction. See page 6 of DOC-7539090.
The Tenant also testified that the City of Greater Sudbury Fire Services had also issued an “Inspection Order” to the Landlord to bring the complex up to the fire code. See page 7 of DOC-7539090.
The Tenant testified that none of these repairs ordered by the City of Greater Sudbury had been completed.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. & LTB-T-007746-26

Therefore, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord obligations under subsection 20(1of the Act to repair maintain the rental unit or the residential complex and failed to comply with safety or housing or maintenance standards. Remedies
The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 40% of rent commencing January 24, 2026. The lawful rent is $500.00.

In Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.

I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. The Tenant did not provide case law on an appropriate remedy or to show what may have been ordered by the Board in past decisions. In my view a 40% abatement is reasonable in all of the circumstances. The Tenant has had to change rooms, has no heat provided by the Landlord and no access to hot water. In addition, it appears that the Landlord has not complied with City orders thereby jeopardizing the safety and security of the Tenant.
Therefore, an amount of 40% for the period January 24, 2026, to June 6, 2026, an amount of $2,214.00 shall be ordered.

In addition, commencing June 7, 2026, until the Landlord has repaired the ceiling and complied with the City of Greater Sudbury Orders the Tenant shall be entitled to a rent reduction of 40%. This is equivalent of 6.65 per day, or $200.00 per month.

The Tenant testified that some of their possessions had been damaged because of the ceiling collapse and flooding into their bedroom. They requested reimbursed for damaged items that they Tenant had to replace. These included a laptop, school materials, clothing, a mattress, and damaged documents, for a total amount of $11,000.00.

I have reviewed the list of items and the amounts claimed for each. In my view a reasonable amount of compensation is approximately $6,000.00. In my view the value of some items appears to be overestimated, therefore a reduction is appropriate.

The Tenant also claimed general damages for the emotional stress, loss of reasonable enjoyment, academic disruption arising from the loss of the Laptop. The Tenant requested an amount of $2,000.00 in the amended application. & LTB-T-007746-26
I am satisfied that in al of the circumstances that the amount of $2,000.00 is reasonable and shall be ordered.
The Tenant also requested an order that the Landlord repair the damaged ceiling in the bedroom, to restore heat and hot water. I find that this too is reasonable in all of the circumstances
The Tenant incurred applications fees in the amount of $96.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed those fees.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,310.00. This amount represents: • $2,214.00 rent abatement. • $6,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has or will incur to repair / replace property that was damaged / destroyed / disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $2,000.00 in general damages, and • $96.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $300.00 per month commencing September 1, 2026, until the full amount has been paid. The Landlord may deduct any arrears of rent owing from this amount.

The Tenant is entitled to a 40% rent abatement. This means that commencing August 1, 2026, the Tenant’s lawful rent shall be $300.00 per month until the Landlord has repaired the bedroom ceiling and complied with both City of Greater Sudbury orders. The Tenant is entitled to a $6.65 per day credit for the period June 7-30, 2026.
The Landlord shall restore heat to the rental unit.
The Landlord shall restore hot water to the rental unit.
The Landlord shall repair the bedroom ceiling that collapsed on January 24, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') was required to allow the Tenants to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant, HSS testified he understood they were required to vacate the rental unit so that repairs could be completed. The Tenants’ position is that the Landlord failed to provide them with a right of first refusal to return to the rental unit after the renovations were completed.

The Landlord’s challenged the Tenant’s testimony and argued the tenancy terminated by agreement as supported by the N11 Agreement signed by the Tenants. The Landlord denied that the N11 Agreement was intended to operate as a temporary vacancy for the purpose of repairs.

Section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), states, a tenant who receives notice of termination of a tenancy for the purpose of repairs or renovations may [emphasis added], in accordance with this section, have a right of first refusal to occupy the rental unit as a tenant when the repairs or renovations are completed.

Section 57 (1) (C) of the Act states, the Board may make an order on a application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.
Section 57.1 allows the Board to make an order if it is determined that the landlord was required to afford the former tenant a right of first refusal under section 53 and failed to do so.

Section 37(1) of the Act also states that a tenancy may be terminated only by notice given by the tenant or the landlord, an agreement between the landlord and tenant to terminate the tenancy, or an order of the Board.

A claim under section 57(3) or 57.1 of the Act must establish that the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the notice or order; the notice was given in bad faith; and the Landlord did not follow with the reasons for terminating within and reasonable time after termination.

The Landlord did not terminate the tenancy by servicing any Notice of Termination. Therefore the tenancy did not terminate by either notice or board order. The tenancy terminated by agreement based on the N11 Agreement the Tenants’ signed.

The N11 Agreement also can not be treated as an N13 Notice or that it gives rise to the remedies available under section 53 of the Act related to rights of first refusal. The N11 Agreement ended the tenancy by mutual agreement. It did not notify the Tenants that the Landlord was terminating the tenancy for repair or renovations, did not identify a right to first refusal and did not contain the essential features of the N13 Notice. The N11 Agreement was also consistent with the Tenants signed declaration stating, “We [name] and [name] [name] hereby inform that treat Dec 2023 as our last month at 50 Horseley Hill [name]. Please adjust our advance as rent for Dec 2023 ie the last month. We will vacate the apartment on 31st Dec 2023. Thank you”.

Since the tenancy terminated by mutual agreement and not by a notice of termination or Board order, the Tenants have not proven a claim of bad faith that the Landlord denied them the right of first refusal.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $2,884.68 which represents: $2,836.68 for the remaining compensation owed to the Tenant. $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. Compensation for N13 Notice Owing
The Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 50 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act.
The Tenant’s application alleges the Landlord did not pay the compensation required pursuant to section 52(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Evidence

The Tenant testified that in late July 2025 she was served with an N13 notice from the Landlord. After following up with the Landlord on her intention to comply with the N13 and vacate the unit, she was informed by voicemail that she was only entitled to one month of compensation as per the N13 notice.
The Tenant testified that she was paid one month’s compensation in the amount of $1,418.34.
The Tenant’s position is that they are entitled to three months of compensation pursuant to s. 52(1) of the Act because the residential complex contains at least five residential units.

The Tenant testified that the buildings of 230 and 232 [address] are related and should be considered one residential complex based on the following testimony: • 230 [address] has 2 residential units and 232 [name] has 4. [name] and operations of the buildings was handled collectively – snow removal and lawn maintenance was done collectively by one team. • The property manager handles all matters concerning both buildings. • The buildings shared garbage collection facilities, and the Tenant was never advised of garbage bins that were designated for a specific building. • One driveway goes between the buildings and there is one common parking lot behind the buildings. The Tenant relied on a video showing the parking lot that is shared between both buildings and located at the rear of both buildings. • There are no markings designating where to park and residents park where they can find space in the shared parking lot • Payments made for parking were made to 230 [name] and the Tenant resides in 232 [name].

The Tenant states that the Landlord is relying on government and accounting principles to define the property but submit that the definition under the Act is applied differently and when applied to these circumstances, both buildings would meet the definition of a residential complex.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledged that she was advised payments for the parking would be separate from her rent and this is why payments were made to 230 [name]. She agreed that there are in fact two laneways to the parking area, but states that all residents only use the main driveway located between the two buildings. The Tenant stated that there was no barrier between the properties and that both buildings shared the garbage area under the front awning of 230.

The Landlord’s Agent testified the following: • Both buildings are titled and deeded separately • Both buildings are treated separately for accounting and tax purposes • Both buildings were purchased by them at certain times • There are 2 residential units in 230 [name] and there are 4 residential units in 232 [name]. • They testified that once they owned both properties, they removed a fence that separate the buildings for ease of movement between the two properties and because it was in a state of repair. • They were not aware of any shared garbage facilities Analysis

Section 52(1) of the Act states the following: 52 (1) A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if, (a) the tenant receives notice of termination of the tenancy for the purposes of demolition or conversion to non-residential use; (b) the residential complex in which the rental unit is located contains at least five residential units; and (c) in the case of a demolition, it was not ordered to be carried out under the authority of any other Act. 2006, c. 17, s. 52. [underlining added]

Section 2(1) of the Act defines “residential complex” and states: [name], except in Part V.1 means, a) A building or related group of buildings in which one or more rental units are located. b) A mobile home park or land lease community, c) A site that is a rental unit d) A care home, and, Includes all common areas and services and facilities available for the use of its residents. [underlining added]

In this case, I find that the buildings of 230 and 232 were a “residential complex” as contemplated by the Act. I say this because the Landlord owns both buildings, the buildings share a common area parking lot, and they primarily use a shared driveway that is located between both the building. Despite there being evidence of another driveway available, the evidence before me supports that the residents of the building commonly use the driveway between the buildings to access the shared parking lot. Despite the Landlord not being aware that the residents of both buildings use a shared garbage facility in front of 230 [name], the evidence before me is that the residents do share common garbage facilities. The residents of both buildings were required to report issues to the same property manager and residents of 232 [name] were required to make their parking payments to 230 [name]. I am satisfied that these are a related group of buildings and should be defined as such under the Act.

The residential complex contains 6 residential units. Therefore, pursuant to section 52(1) of the Act the Landlord was required to pay three months compensation to the Tenant. Since the Tenant was only paid one month’s compensation, the Tenant is owed the remaining two months of compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,884.68. This amount represents: • $2,836.68 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing the Landlord indicated that the rental unit is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the Act”) as the Tenant was required to share a kitchen and bathroom with the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024. The agreement between the parties was verbal and there was no written lease agreement.
She testified that complex was a 6-bedroom home with 2 bathrooms, the rental unit was one bedroom within the house.

The Tenant testified that the kitchen and bathroom were not shared with the Landlord as they The Landlord’s had their own bathroom only for their use and the Tenant’s had another bathroom for their exclusive use.

She testified that that the kitchen was divided between the Landlord and the Tenants with the Tenants having a separate section for pots and pans and a separate fridge and dining area. She testified that the stove was shared with separate burners for the Tenants and the Landlord, however she did not have access to the oven portion of the stove.

Section 5 (i) of the Act states that the Act does not apply with respect to: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

I am satisfied based on the Tenant’s own testimony that she was required to share a kitchen with the Landlord. While certain portions of the kitchen appear to have been divided between the parties, with an additional fridge for the Tenants and separate storage space and shelving, this is common within shared living situations. It is clear that despite these rules surrounding usage of the kitchen, that the complex contains one single divided kitchen, rather than a separate kitchen for the sole use of the Landlord and the Tenant.

Additionally, I note that the divisions within the kitchen support the notion that it is shared, as they demonstrate that the Landlord exercises control over the kitchen. If the Tenants had their own kitchen, they would be permitted to allocate storage as they saw fit and would not be excluded from using the oven portion of the stove.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant is required to share a kitchen with the Landlord. Accordingly. I find that the rental unit falls within the exemption in Section 5(i) and the Act does not apply. Therefore, the application is dismissed
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. July 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Myriad Property Management (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he has lived in the rental unit since approximately February 2010. The Tenant gave evidence that he discovered bedbugs that were coming out from the baseboards in the unit.
The Tenant also testified that he discovered the baseboards were wet and contacted “Adrijan”, the Landlord’s agent, to report yellow and black mold.

The Tenant explained that Adrijan disputed that the photographs depicted mold and when the Tenant asked that a baseboard be removed to inspect for mold the Tenant was advised that any unapproved baseboard removal would be the Tenant’s responsibility to repair.

The Tenant gave evidence that he removed the baseboard and discovered the baseboards were “soaked”. The Tenant testified that he found black mold that caused him to investigate the issue further by moving the dresser in the bedroom. The Tenant found that the floor was peeling and sent pictures to Adrijan.

The Tenant further testified that a property manager had come to his rental unit and both the mold, and the Tenant’s repairs. The Tenant’s position is that the property manager complimented the Tenant’s work and offered to partially pay for the repairs.
The Tenant also gave evidence that after the repairs were complete, he requested paint to match the colour in the rental unit and Adrijan took two months to deliver paint.
The Tenant also recalled leaving an envelope with a sealed letter requesting payment for the repairs that the Tenant asserts was improperly intercepted by Adrijan.
The Tenant did not submit any correspondence, photographs, or invoices to corroborate his testimony. The Tenant’s evidence is that the contractor’s invoice totaled $4,412.22.

During cross examination the Tenant testified that his unit was dry throughout the winter and presently remains dry. The Tenant also recounted his work in the rental unit which included the floors, drywall, and baseboards. The Tenant’s evidence is that any tradesperson or contractor that did work in the rental unit was licensed.

The Tenant gave evidence in relation to other repairs and improvements he performed in the rental unit including updating electrical service, kitchen cabinets, painting the bedroom, bathroom, and doors, and kitchen repairs. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s agent [name] (AA) testified that the Tenant did not request permission from the Landlord to do repairs. AA confirmed that the Tenant asked him to inspect the rental unit and during the inspection he found no evidence of water leaking or mold in the Tenant’s rental unit.

AA also explained that there are no pipes or water that runs inside the wall where the Tenant asserts the baseboards and drywall were moldy. AA denied performing any repairs or waterproofing in the Tenant’s rental unit.

AA also gave evidence about the Landlord’s procedure for submitting work orders and testified that despite receiving work orders from the Tenant for other issues including bedbugs, a stove and fire alarm, there was no associated work order submitted in relation to the water leaking or mold in the Tenant’s rental unit.

AA testified that their assistant “[name]” was the property manager that the Tenant asserts offered to pay his invoice however, AA’s evidence is that [name] would not have had the authority to approve payment, and AA would have needed to be informed of any payment agreement for repairs. Analysis
The Tenant’s application is brought pursuant to paragraph 1 of subsection 29 (1) alleging that the Landlord has breached their obligations under subsection 20 (1).

The Tenant must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has breached their obligation to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. A remedy can only be considered once the Tenant has proven the Landlord has breached their obligations under section 20(1).

The Tenant testified that there was yellow and black mold in the rental unit that resulted from some sort of water intrusion. The Tenant’s evidence is that they repaired the baseboards, drywall, and floors in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not submit any photographs or correspondence that would corroborate their testimony. In the absence of any reports, notes, or photographs, it cannot be definitively determined whether there was mold in the rental unit, whether there was water intrusion that would engage the Landlord’s maintenance or repair obligations, or the severity of any alleged mold or water damage.

Further, AA recounted various historical work orders submitted by the Tenant and the absence of a work order or request for reimbursement relating to the issues alleged by the Tenant in this application does not support their narrative of events.

It is also noted that the Tenant has performed various other repairs or improvements and there was insufficient evidence to distinguish this issue from an improvement undertaken by the Tenant voluntarily, and an issue of disrepair attributable to the Landlord.

Accordingly, I am not satisfied the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing, maintenance standards.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • collected or retained money illegally. The Landlord applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Tenant owes. These applications were heard by videoconference on June 15, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord, the Landlord’s legal representative, [name], and the Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘AD’) attended and participated in the hearing. The Tenant’s witness, D. Cordaie, attended but did not participate in the hearing because the evidence he declared he would give, about the Tenant telephoning him on February 9, 2024, was not necessary to determine the Tenant’s applications.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant agreed he was aware of the Landlord’s L10 application under section 87 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) before the June 15, 2026 File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24 hearing date. Indeed, the Tenant disclosed to the Landlord and filed material with the Board to respond to the Landlord’s claim that the Tenant did not pay rent and compensation for the period July 1, 2023 to January 31, 2024. I accordingly ruled that the parties were aware of the issues arising in the L10 application and that the application was properly before the Board. I therefore directed the L10 hearing to proceed with the Tenant’s applications. The Tenant’s Applications – The Landlord Retained the Tenant’s Rent Deposit
The Landlord agreed at the hearing that he continues to hold a $1,400.00 rent deposit from the Tenant.

The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s evidence that the Landlord paid the Tenant interest owing on the rent deposit after the Board held an Adjudicative Case Conference on July 15, 2025 for this proceeding.

Based on the evidence introduced at the June 15, 2026 hearing, I find the Landlord retained the Tenant’s $1,400.00 rent deposit but paid the Tenant interest on the deposit. The amount of $1,400.00 shall accordingly be set-off against the amount the Tenant must pay the Landlord for unpaid rent. The Landlord Substantially Interfered With the Tenant’s Reasonable Enjoyment of the Property and Illegally Entered the Unit

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord evicted the Tenant from the rental unit on February 9, 2024. The Landlord agreed that he did not have a Board order that actively permitted the Landlord to evict the Tenant: the Board did not issue an order evicting the Tenant from the rental unit until March 5, 2024. The Landlord therefore did not have the right to recover possession of the rental unit from the Tenant, pursuant to section 39 of the Act. Doing so substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental property.

The Landlord further agreed that contrary to section 141 of the Courts of Justice Act, the Landlord personally evicted the Tenant from the rental unit. The Landlord did not contest the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not ask the Sheriff to enforce a Board order pursuant to section 85 of the Act, which states that a Board order shall be enforced in the same manner as a civil writ of possession.

To explain his actions, the Landlord described a history of Board proceedings between the parties. The Landlord testified that in Board order LTB-L-070997-22, issued on March 5, 2024, the Board found that the Tenant substantially interfered with the Landlord’s lawful rights, privileges and interests by, among other things, sending threatening and harassing messages to the Landlord and to his employer. The Board found the Tenant’s explanation for writing to the Landlord’s employer – that the Tenant was concerned for the Landlord’s health and safety – was not credible. The Board accordingly terminated the tenancy and directed the Sheriff to enforce the eviction on or after April 1, 2024.

The Board denied the Tenant’s request to review the March 5, 2024 order in review order LTB-L-070997-22-RV, issued on April 9, 2024. The Tenant subsequently appealed the File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24 order to the Divisional Court, pursuant to section 210 of the Act. The Tenant’s appeal resulted in a stay of the March 5, 2024 eviction order.

At the June 15, 2026 hearing for this proceeding, the Landlord described frustration with delays and other barriers to ending the tenancy. The Board, for example, issued the March 5, 2024 hearing order LTB-L-070997-22 approximately six months after the September 21, 2023 hearing date. The Landlord testified that the Tenant’s behaviour continued after the Board hearing. Citing concerns for his and his household’s safety and security, on February 9, 2024, the Landlord evicted the Tenant and instructed the Tenant’s roommate not to permit the Tenant to return to the property.

Based on the evidence introduced at the hearing, I find that the Landlord illegally locked the Tenant out of the rental unit and that this substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and complex. The Landlord’s frustration with the legal process to end a tenancy and evict a tenant did not permit the Landlord to disregard the law and personally evict and prevent the Tenant from returning to the property. Evidence of a conversation between the Landlord and the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing’s Rental Housing Enforcement Unit confirms that the Landlord acted wilfully and was aware of the significance of his actions.

I also find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit when he removed and stored the Tenant’s personal property. Evidence that the Tenant’s roommate AD permitted the Landlord to enter the rental unit on February 9, 2024 is in the circumstances inadequate and does not support a contrary finding. The Landlord did not enter the rental unit in response to an emergency as contemplated in section 26 of the Act, and of course nothing in section 27 of the Act permits a landlord to give a notice of entry for the purpose of enforcing an illegal eviction. Remedies

Having proven that the Landlord illegally retained money and entered the rental unit, and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the property by evicting the Tenant from the rental unit in a manner the Act does not authorize, I find it is appropriate to order remedies under subsection 135(1) and 31(1)(d) of the Act. As described in the following paragraphs, however, concerns about the Tenant’s credibility and the reliability of his evidence led me to deny other remedies the Tenant claimed in his T2 application. Compensation for Personal Property is Denied

Based on evidence introduced at the June 15, 2026 hearing, I find that the Tenant already claimed compensation for most of the personal property listed in this application in Board file number LTB-T-018444-22. That application was resolved by an order issued on September 16, 2025. In his pleadings for file number LTB-T-018444-22, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord damaged his personal property by improperly storing it outside and under a tarp. The Board denied the Tenant’s claim for compensation in Board order LTB-T-018444-22 in the September 16, 2025 order. File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24

The Tenant did not dispute evidence of Board order LTB-T-018444-22, or dispute the Landlord’s legal representative’s submission that the order resolves most of the Tenant’s claims in this proceeding for damaged or missing personal property. The Tenant declined to introduce reply evidence about Board order LTB-T-018444-22, and he did not respond to the Landlord’s legal representative’s submission on this issue, when afforded an opportunity to do so.
The Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord damaged the Tenant’s personal property, including a mattress, a television set and clothing.

The Landlord and his witness AD introduced independent and consistent evidence that the Landlord removed the Tenant’s belongings from the rental unit and stored them in a storage locker at the Landlord’s expense. Both witnesses testified the Landlord offered the Tenant a key giving access to the locker on February 10, 2024. The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s evidence about the storage locker and the Tenant agreed he collected his property one-week after vacating the rental unit. The Tenant did not explain delaying to collect his items, or prove that items, such as a mattress, television and clothes, were damaged because of the illegal eviction. By contrast, the Landlord and AD again gave independent and consistent evidence that these, and other, items were already damaged before February 9, 2024.

The Tenant’s wilful or negligent attempt to mislead the Board by pleading and introducing issues unrelated to the February 9, 2024 illegal eviction brings the Tenant’s overall credibility into question. A photograph of mould on a mattress was also of little probative value: the Tenant’s assertion that the amount of mould shown in the photograph appeared in such little time is improbable. Even if the mould did develop while the mattress was in storage, without evidence or a submission to explain why the Tenant did not collect his items promptly, I am not satisfied the Tenant acted reasonably to minimize his losses and damage to his personal property.

In the circumstances, I prefer the Landlord’s and AD’s evidence that the Tenant’s personal property was already damaged by the Tenant’s lack of care. I also find that the Landlord safely stored the Tenant’s personal property and that the Tenant had access to the property as of February 10, 2024. The Landlord testified that he removed the Tenant’s items and AD confirmed that the Landlord stored all the Tenant’s items – except for a fire extinguisher and a mould-covered soap dispenser – in a storage locker, making a key available to the Tenant on February 10, 2024.
Again, the Tenant did not dispute or challenge the Landlord’s and AD’s evidence about these matters. Their evidence about storing the Tenant’s personal property is therefore reliable and credible.

The Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence that the Landlord, or his family member or any other person, retained and/or sold any of the Tenant’s belongings. Declarants were not present to be cross-examined on the contents of the declarations the Tenant submitted as exhibits at the June 15, 2026 hearing, and the declarations are accordingly of little probative value.

I am therefore not satisfied the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, his claim for damaged or missing personal property, or that the Landlord continues to retain the File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24 Tenant’s property. There shall accordingly be no order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant compensation for damaged or missing property or for the Landlord to return personal property to the Tenant. Compensation for Out-of-Pocket Moving and Storage Costs is Denied

There was similarly no reliable evidence, such as receipts or any other evidence of payment or cash withdrawal, to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant paid $4,000.00 to move his items to his temporary or current accommodation.

Also, the Tenant’s evidence of storage fees lacked basic information, including the rental period for which the storage company allegedly charged the Tenant $535.00. The receipt the Tenant submitted at the hearing as an exhibit was altered or incomplete and of no evidentiary value. The Tenant placed a business card over the top part of the receipt in a location where one would expect to find relevant information related to the storage company and the date and nature of the transaction. A note claiming the Tenant paid $6,500.00 for storage costs similarly lacks details and is also of no probative value.

In the circumstances, the Tenant’s evidence of out-of-pocket storage costs is not reliable and therefore not credible evidence to merit a remedy under subsection 31(2)(b) of the Act. Compensation for Out-of-Pocket Temporary Accommodation Costs is Denied

The Tenant did not introduce reliable and reasonably available evidence to support his claim that he was unable to find alternative accommodation that cost less than $100.00 a night for the period February 9, 2024 to May 10, 2024. The Tenant did not introduce evidence of local motel rates or rates from online, short-term vacation rental providers such as Airbnb to support his assertion that it is not possible to find temporary accommodation for less than that amount.

I am unable, and accordingly decline, to take judicial notice of daily rental rates in or around [name], Ontario. I am therefore not satisfied that the Tenant’s decision to stay with a friend who required the Tenant to pay $100.00 a night was reasonable. Additionally, without evidence of the Tenant’s efforts to look for permanent accommodation in the three-month period from February to May 2024, I am not satisfied that he attempted to minimize his out-of-pocket temporary accommodation costs, per section 16 of the Act.
There shall accordingly be no order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant’s temporary accommodation costs from February 9, 2024 to May 10, 2024. Claim For Increased Rent is Denied

The Tenant introduced evidence of a written tenancy agreement that requires the Tenant to pay his new landlord $2,100.00 a month to possess and occupy new, permanent accommodation. This amount, like the rent the Tenant paid at the rental unit, includes utilities. There was no evidence that the Tenant’s former rental unit and current accommodation are substantially dissimilar. File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24

The Tenant’s monthly rent at the rental unit was also $2,100.00. Since there is no difference between the rent the Tenant paid at the rental unit and the amount he now pays at his new accommodation, there shall be no order under subsection 31(2)(a) of the Act. Claim For Abatement of Rent is Denied

The Tenant did not introduce evidence that he was unable to use and enjoy the rental unit for all usual purposes before being illegally evicted on February 9, 2024. There shall therefore be no order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant an abatement of rent pursuant to subsection 31(1)(c) of the Act. The Tenant’s obligation to pay rent, however, shall end as of February 9, 2024, the date the Landlord illegally evicted the Tenant. No Claim for General Damages

The Tenant did not apply to the Board for an order for general damages pursuant to subsection 31(1)(f) of the Act and as the Divisional Court described in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801. The Tenant did not ask to amend his applications, and the parties did not discuss this remedy at the June 15, 2026 hearing. In the circumstances, I find it is not appropriate to amend the application on my own initiative, and there shall accordingly be no order for general damages. The Landlord Shall Pay an Administrative Fine
The Tenant did, however, apply for an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine pursuant to subsection 31(1)(d) of the Act.

The Landlord admitted to wilfully disregarding the Act’s provisions that permit a landlord to recover possession only under strict conditions. Here, the Landlord acted before the Board issued its March 5, 2024 order, LTB-L-070997-22, evicting the Tenant from the rental unit. Because of the appellate stay of the order, the Landlord was not entitled to enforce – and certainly not by his own personal action – the eviction set out in that order. Given the Landlord’s blatant disregard for the Act, the Landlord’s actions merit ordering an administrative fine to discourage and deter similar future behaviour from this and other landlords.

The Act, however, is remedial and not punitive legislation. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines, for example, does not include demonstrating the Board’s disapproval as an appropriate factor when determining the amount to fine a landlord.

With the Act’s remedial purpose in mind, I find it is appropriate to order the individual Landlord to pay an administrative fine of $8,000.00. This is a substantial amount. It is intended to remind this and other landlords that they must comply with legal processes in place to resolve civil disputes, including eviction proceedings. The Landlord’s claim that he was concerned about his and his household’s safety and security does not relieve the Landlord of his duties and responsibilities under the Act and Courts of Justice Act, and his actions were accordingly not reasonable. I decline to order the Landlord to pay more than $8,000.00, as I believe doing so would be unduly punitive. File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24

I note here that the Tenant’s evidence of minor injuries to his hand was not persuasive. The Tenant’s photograph showing small scratches was not consistent with his description of having a door slammed on his fingers or the self-reported information in a hospital admission report the Tenant submitted at the hearing. The Tenant’s evidence on this issue therefore did not contribute to assessing an appropriate fine. The Landlord Shall Return the Tenant’s Rent Deposit

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,400.00 for retaining the Tenant’s rent deposit. This amount shall be set-off against the rent and compensation the Tenant owes the Landlord. The Landlord’s L10 Application

As noted in paragraph 29, above, lawful rent for the rental unit was $2,100.00 a month. In the July 25, 2025 interim Board order LTB-T-011826-25-IN, issued after the July 15, 2025 Adjudicative Case Conference, the Board determined that the Tenant’s claim the Landlord increased the rent illegally was statute-barred because of a limitation period. The Tenant withdrew the claim at the Adjudicative Case Conference and accepted that lawful rent was $2,100.00.

At the June 15, 2026 hearing, the Tenant, the Landlord and AD all agreed that the Tenant and AD paid the rent by paying $1,050.00 each directly to the Landlord. The Landlord claimed at the hearing that the Tenant did not pay any of the Tenant’s usual $1,050.00 payment for the period July 1, 2023 to February 8, 2024, or $[name] ($276.16 is the pro rated amount of compensation payable from February 1 to 8, 2024).

The Tenant denied the Landlord’s claim and submitted copies of text messages purportedly between the Tenant and the Landlord. The text messages suggest that the Tenant paid the Landlord the amount owed when the Tenant personally met with the Landlord and tendered cash. At the hearing, the Landlord denied meeting with the Tenant and receiving cash payments. The Landlord introduced evidence that he was not in Canada and therefore unable to meet as the Tenant described.

The Tenant’s overall lack of credibility, and the altered or incomplete receipt claiming to show the Tenant’s out-of-pocket storage costs, factor into my assessment of the Tenant’s evidence of rent payments. I note that, like the Tenant’s evidence of his alleged storage costs, his evidence of text messages lacks relevant information, including dates and times. Moreover, I agree with the Landlord’s legal representative that evidence of the Landlord’s flight plans is inconsistent with the Tenant’s evidence of a text message which, on a plain reading, claims the parties met on December 30, 2023 to pay and collect rent.
The text messages the Tenant submitted as exhibits are therefore not reliable evidence of cash payments to the Landlord.

I prefer instead the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant did not pay the Landlord $[name] in rent and compensation for the period July 1, 2023 to February 8, 2024. Contrary to the Tenant’s assertion, the Landlord’s material confirms the Landlord was not in Canada on December 30, 2023 to accept cash from the Tenant. File Numbers: LTB-T-011826-25 LTB-L-038774-24

Based on all the evidence related to this issue, I find the Tenant’s claim he paid rent to the Landlord in person is not credible. The Tenant shall therefore be ordered to pay the Landlord $[name] and the Landlord’s Board filing costs, less the rent deposit the Landlord continues to hold.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Tenant shall pay the Landlord $6,412.16. This amount represents $[name] for rent and compensation payable for the period July 1, 2023 to February 8, 2024 and $186.00 for the Landlord’s cost of filing the application, less $1,400.00 the Landlord must pay the Tenant for retaining the Tenant’s rent deposit.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Tenant will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord and/or Tenant may set-off the amount set out in this order against any other Board order.
The Landlord or Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this and any other order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $8,000.00 by August 2, 2026. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant [name] testified that the Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord on November 11, 2025, commencing December 1, 2025 for a fixed term of one year.
Pursuant to the tenancy agreement the Tenants are responsible for electricity in the rental unit and the Landlord is responsible for heat.

The Tenants testified that the rental unit is heated by electric baseboard heaters, and that they have had to pay for the heating of the rental unit, which is the responsibility of the Landlord pursuant to the tenancy agreement.

The Tenants tendered two hydro bills in the amount of $140.72 and $358.46. They seek reimbursement of 80% of two hydro bills from January and February, 2026 which the Tenants estimated was the percentage associated with heating the rental unit.

Although the Tenants believe the baseboard heater is part of their hydro bill and not connected to the hydro for the common areas of the residential complex, which the Landlord is responsible for, but were unable to confirm this. Analysis

Section 134(1) of the Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; (b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord; or (c) rent any portion of the rental unit for a rent which, together with all other rents payable for all other portions of the rental unit, is a sum that is greater than the rent the landlord may lawfully charge for the rental unit.

Section 135(1) of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit to apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of the Act.
The hydro bills tendered are in the Tenant, [name] name and are issued by Utilities Kingston. The Tenants paid the service provider Utilities Kingston directly.
Based on the evidence before me no money was collected or retained by the Landlord in contravention of section 134(1) of the Act. As such, the Tenants application shall be dismissed.
