issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $198.00.

The Tenant [name] testified that he came across the rental unit on Facebook Marketplace and entered into rental discussions with the Landlord. He further stated that he and the other Tenant viewed the unit in mid January, 2026.

The Tenants submitted a rental application to the Landlord along with a $150.00 application fee. The Tenants received confirmation via a text message from the Landlord that their application had been approved.

The Landlord subsequently sent a lease agreement to the Tenants for signature through Docusign. The Tenant [name] testified that he advised the Landlord that he wanted to wait for his father to sign the lease agreement as he wanted his father to be a guarantor, but his father was on vacation.

Notwithstanding wanting to wait for his father to return from vacation the Tenants signed the tenancy agreement via Docusign on January 28, 2026. The [name] agreement was previously signed by the Landlord on January 27, 2026.

The [name] agreement indicated that the tenancy was set to being on February 15, 2026 for a fixed term ending on February 28, 2027. It indicated a monthly rent amount of $1,495.00 due on the 1st of each month. The tenancy agreement did not contain any provisions for a guarantor.

The Landlord sent the Tenants a request for payment of $1,495.00 for last months rent on January 29, 2026 and January 30, 2026. The Tenants sent an e-transfer to the Landlord in the amount of $1,495.00 on January 30, 2026.

After having discussions with his father on January 31, 2026, [name] testified that his father didn’t want to proceed with the lease. The Tenant [name] then sent a message to the Landlord on January 31, 2026 that he no longer wanted to proceed with the Tenancy, and requested the return of the deposits paid to the Landlord.
The Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord refused to return the rent deposits.

The Landlord’s Legal representative submitted that the Board does have jurisdiction to deal with the Tenant’s application as the tenancy did not being and the Tenants did not receive possession of the rental unit or keys. Analysis

With respect to a rent deposit s.107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') says: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

This provision has been interpreted to mean that the deposit must be repaid if the landlord refuses to give possession to the tenant on the date set for commencement of the tenancy. But neither a landlord nor a tenant can unilaterally decide the tenancy is not going forward. In other words, a tenant cannot simply decide not to move in and expect the return of the deposit. (See: [name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923 (ON SCDC), [2008] O.J. No. 1934 ([name]. Div. Ct.) (‘[name] v. [name]’), and Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., [2011] [name] ([name]. C.A.).)

Additionally in Opara v. Cook the Court upheld a decision of the Board dismissing a tenant’s application for a refund. The Court observed that a tenancy agreement came into effect the day the parties reached an agreement on the rental of a room and upon the rent deposit being paid.

Based on the evidence before me the Tenants and the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement and the Tenants made a payment of a rent deposit. I am satisfied that a tenancy agreement came into affect pursuant to [name] v. [name] and the Tenant would not be entitled to the return of the rent deposit paid as it was the Tenants’ act that prevented them from taking possession, not the action of the Landlord.
With respect to the application fee paid to the Landlord in the amount of $150.00 the Landlord’s Legal Representative suggests that this was a deposit to be applied towards first month’s rent.
Pursuant to section 105(1) of the Act the only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit in accordance with section 106.
Section 106(2) of the Act states: The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.
The amount being held by the Landlord is $1,645.00 which is excess of the rent for one month.

Section 134(1) of the Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no Landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) Collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Based on the evidence before me I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the collection of $150.00 by the Landlord from the Tenants in addition to a last month’s rent deposit is a charge which is not allowed under the Act, and the Tenants are entitled to the return of that payment.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $198.00. This amount represents: • $150.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the sum of $640.94.

The Tenants allege that the Landlord collected a charge for a hot water tank rental and solid waste management fees which were not agreed upon pursuant to the tenancy agreement. Additionally the Tenants allege that the Landlord charged the Tenants 100% of gas and hydro and water expenses for a two month period in contravention of the lease agreement.

The Tenants testified that they moved into the rental unit being the basement of 721 Brimley Road on October 1, 2024 and pursuant to the tenancy agreement the Tenants were responsible for 40% of utilities being gas, hydro and water.
The utilities for the residential complex were split 60/40 between the upstairs tenants and the Tenants who resided in the basement.

The Tenants further testified that when the upstairs Tenants moved out of their unit the Landlord charged them 100% of the utilities for May and June 2025 at the residential complex being $608.56 until the unit was re-rented to another tenant in July.
The Tenants 40% portion of utilities for May and June should have been $243.42 which resulted in an overpayment of $365.14
The Landlord testified that she had approached the Tenants regarding the utilities for May and June 2025 and that the Tenants had agreed to pay 100% of the utilities during this period.
The Tenants dispute that they agreed to pay 100% of the utilities during this time period and submit that they are only responsible for 40% pursuant to the lease agreement.

The Tenants further testified that they were charged for additional fees being a hot water tank rental and solid waste management fees, which they were not responsible to pay pursuant to the lease agreement.

The Tenants produced evidence at the hearing that since the commencement of the tenancy in October 2024 they have paid $149.94 to the Landlord towards a hot water tank rental and $157.86 for solid waste management fees.

The Landlord testified that at the commencement of the tenancy she sent an email to the Tenants with a copy of the utility bills being Toronto Hydro, [name] and Enbridge explaining how she sends the bills for utilities and the Tenants ought to have been aware which bills they were responsible for.
Additionally the Landlord testified that Toronto Hydro sends one combined bill for water and solid waste management fees, although the bill has a separate breakdown for each fee. Analysis

It is clear based on the lease agreement that the Tenants were responsible for 40% of utilities being gas, hydro and water. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there was an agreement between the Landlord and the Tenants for the full payment of 100% of the utilities at the residential complex for the months of May and June, 2025. In additional any additional charges paid to the Landlord were not the responsibility of the Tenants pursuant to the lease agreement.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Tenants overpaid utility charges to the Landlord for May and June, 2025. I am further satisfied that the Tenants have paid charges not contemplated by the lease agreement to the Landlord and were not reimbursed.

Section 135(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act , 2006 (the 'Act') explicitly states that the Tenants must file their application to the Board within one-year after the Landlord collected or retained money in contravention of the Act. The Tenants’ application was filed on February 7, 2026.

The Landlord collected the additional charges from the Tenants. This money was not retained. The Board only has jurisdiction to order a remedy for the Tenants starting from February 7, 2025 being one-year prior to the filing of the Tenants’ application. This reduces the amount claimed by the Tenants for a hot water tank rental to $113.94 and the claim for solid waste management fees to $113.86.

The Tenants shall be entitled to reimbursement of $592.94, which consists of an overpayment of utilities for May and June in the amount of $365.14 and the collection of an illegal charge for a hot water tank rental in the amount of $113.94 and a charge for solid waste management fees in the amount of $113.86.
The Tenants also incurred the expense of $48.00 for the filing of this application and are entitled to that amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $640.94. This amount represents: • $592.94 for the illegal charges collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that ACO Enterprise and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,660.00.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I make the following findings of fact. 1. The rental unit is a main floor apartment in a four-plex. The monthly rent is $995.00. 2. In 2021, the Tenant [name] (‘KP’) began experiencing severe allergic reactions including lesions. She visited medical specialists who believed the lesions were caused by environmental factors. On August 29, 2023, the Tenants realized that KP’s allergic reactions were caused by bedbugs and immediately informed the Landlord.
The Landlord’s repairman inspected the rental unit within a week of the Tenants’ complaint. Two pest treatments were done on October 15, 2023, and October 26, 2023, which resolved the issue.

From November 2023 to February 2024, the Landlord consistently failed to clear the snow from the front entryway and steps of the building and failed to maintain the laundry room and other common areas.

The parties initially had an agreement that the Landlord would compensate the Tenant $100.00 per month for snow removal. The Landlord did not compensate the Tenant for the months of November 2023 to February 2024.

The parties did not have an agreement for cleaning the entryway and other common areas. The Tenants cleaned the common areas of the building three times each month from June 2023 to March 2024 for 2-3 hours at a time. 3. The Tenant testified that the bedbug issue started much earlier, in 2021. However, the Tenant only realized what the issue was and informed the Landlord on August 29, 2023. After being informed, the Landlord arranged for an inspection within a week and resolved the issue entirely within two months. I find that the Landlord acted reasonably in responding to the bedbug issue; therefore, it is dismissed. 4. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the residential complex in accordance with subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the snow removal and common areas of the complex. 5. In the amended application, the Tenants requested only the costs of damaged property, out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants incurred due to the Landlord’s lack of maintenance, and costs for repairs or other work the Tenant did to maintain the residential complex. 6. No evidence was provided to support a finding that the Tenant’s property was damaged due to the lack of snow removal and common area maintenance. Therefore, this request is dismissed.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the parties had an agreement for the Landlord to compensate the Tenant $100.00 per month for snow removal. The Landlord will be required to pay the Tenants $400.00 for the months of November 2023 to February 2024.

The Tenants also requested $45.00 for each clean they conducted in the common areas of the residential complex from June 2023 to March 2024, which included hourly wages and cleaning supplies. I find this amount to be reasonable. The Landlord will be required to pay the Tenants $1,260.00 for the work the Tenants did on the residential complex as well as their out-of-pocket expenses.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,660.00, representing the work the Tenant did on the residential complex and the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation contained in the application on a balance of probabilities relating to substantial interference from the water issues. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,809.68. Illegal entry:

The Tenant testified that on December 26, 2024 the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice to identify what was causing the water and heating issues. On this date, the Tenant was staying in a hotel with his family due to issues with e-coli in the rental unit.

The Tenant then testified that Landlord attended the rental unit on January 1, 2025 without notice, and the Tenant denied him entry. The Tenant testified that on January 3 and January 4, 2025 the Landlord asked for access with only 2 hours notice, so the Tenant denied entry. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord asked for access to the rental unit on February 9, 2025 but did not provide a specific time, so the Tenant said he could attend on February 10, 2025 at 1:00p.m., but when the Landlord attended early than 1:00p.m. the Tenant denied entry and said he was not available.
The Tenant sought to raise incidents of illegal entries from March and April 2025, however these were not included in the original or the amended application, therefore I denied the Tenant’s request.

On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. Based on the Tenant’s testimony, the Landlord did not enter the unit on January 1, 3, or 4th, 2025, February 9th or 10th of 2025 as the Tenant denied, therefore there was no illegal entry on these dates and the claims for these dates must be dismissed. On December 26, 2024, the Landlord attended the property as the Tenant notified him there was no water or heat to the property. Interpretation Guideline 19 and section 26 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), states that a landlord may enter a rental unit without notice in cases of emergency. Given that it was alleged that the property did not have heat in the winter and the Landlord needed to determine the cause, I would find it reasonable that this would be classified as an emergency case requiring entry as soon as possible to prevent potential lasting and severe damage to the rental unit. As I find the entry on December 26, 2024 would qualify as an emergency, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally, and the claim for this date would also be dismissed. Substantial interference:

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The Tenant testified when they moved into the unit on September 15, 2024 there were dogs on the property that were not supposed to be there, and the Landlord told him they would be removed on September 16, 2024. The Tenant testified that on September 24, 27, and 28, 2024 there were goats on their portion of the lawn that ate their dog’s food and pooped on their lawn, and the Tenant testified cleaning up the poop was a nuisance. The Tenant then testified that on November 7, 2024 goats were loose on the road for a few hours at night, which was a safety hazard. The Tenant then testified on January 4 and 25, 2025, a German shepherd broke free from its leash and could have put the Tenant and his children at risk. The Tenant testified that the impact was the fear that his children could have been injured or that his chickens could have been killed. After each incident, the Tenant testified he contacted the Landlord to address the issue, which did happen, though not always promptly.

While there were 4 incidents where goats got loose and 2 incidents where a dog broke free from a leash that were inconvenient over a 6-month period, I am not satisfied that these amount to substantial interference. The Tenant provide minimal evidence relating to how his reasonable enjoyment was substantially interfered with by the 6 incidents. As I find the incidents with the dog and goats did not substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, these claims are dismissed.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord promised to provide a shed, however the Tenant testified he was only provided a greenhouse for storage and a lot of personal items were damaged. The Tenant testified the promise occurred in November 2024, though no documentary evidence was provided to support the claim. In the application, the Tenant alleged that approximately $1,500.00 worth of personal belongings were damaged from the lack of storage, which was the ground for the substantial interference, yet the application did not identify any specific belongings, there were no photographs of what was damaged, and the Tenant did not provide receipts to substantiate the amount claimed. At the hearing, the Tenant testified that a BBQ, smoker, golf clubs, snowblower and kid’s toys were damaged, however he also said he still has the snow blower and the smoker, the [name] was very old and not worth much, and the Golf club bag was a limited edition that was 10 years old.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant established on a balance of probabilities that a shed was specifically promised, or that only having the greenhouse as storage substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment. The Tenant claimed the substantial interference was due to belongings being damaged because they had to be stored in the greenhouse, but the Tenant provided no evidence of any damage occurring, and 2 of the more expensive items alleged as damaged he still has. As such, this claim is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that there were worker’s that lived on the property and when in the common areas, they would leave the doors open and let cold air into the rental unit. The Tenant also testified that there was a situation where a worker asked him for chicken feed at 8:30 p.m. The Tenant testified that the workers would play loud music outside until 11:00 p.m. or 1:00 a.m. and he called the police once or twice. The Tenant testified he would notify the Landlord, but the Landlord would not do anything. The Tenant did not testify to specific times this occurred or when or how the Landlord was contacted.

The Tenant’s allegations relating to substantial interference from worker’s living on the property and the noise they caused is vague and lacks any specifics relating to frequency, timing, and impact. To find that the worker’s leaving the door open and causing noise so significant as to substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment would require the Tenant to provide detailed information on what was happening, how often was it happening, if he notified the Landlord, and what the Landlord’s response was. The Tenant testified he made reports to the police, however he did not identify when this occurred and no report was provided as documentary evidence. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant provided sufficient information to establish that the worker’s substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment, therefore these claims are dismissed.

The Tenant also testified there was a mice infestation from when they moved into the rental unit, and he notified the Landlord immediately. The Tenant testified that the mice ruined pieces of clothing, towels, and he had to purchase pest control supplies. The Tenant did not provide any evidence of the cost of items damaged, the presence of mice, that pest control supplies were purchased, or when the Landlord was notified of the issue.

Again, as the Tenant has the burden of proof establishing that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, I would expect the Tenant to provide some proof to support his claims that are general in nature. The Tenant testified there was a mice infestation that damaged a lot of personal property; however, no pictures were submitted to show an infestation and no photos were submitted of damage that occurred. As such, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established that there was a mice infestation or that damaged occurred as to substantially interfere with his reasonable enjoyment. [name], Threats and Intimidation:

Section 23 states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. While the term “harassment” is not defined in the Act, it is generally held that “harassment” is a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.. Interpretation Guideline 6 states: To determine whether a landlord's conduct harasses, obstructs, coerces, threatens or interferes with a tenant, the LTB will generally consider the cumulative effect of the landlord's conduct upon the tenant in the context of the landlord-tenant relationship. This is a very fact specific determination, and each application involves unique circumstances and considerations.

The Tenant wanted to raise issues of harassment that occurred in April 2025, however these issues were not identified in the original application or the amended application, therefore the request was denied.

The Tenant testified that on November 28, 2024 the Landlord threatened him and his family in a phone call. The Tenant also submitted a phone conversation from December 2024 or January 2025 that he testified showed the harassment from the Landlord (DOC- 5932651). During this phone call the Landlord tells the Tenant that their rental unit is disgusting and uninhabitable, that the heating is appropriate based on the square footage, and that the Tenant can still do laundry and drink the water despite testing positive for e- coli. The Tenant also testified that in the phone call the Landlord threatened to call public health or the Children’s Aid Society, and that the Tenant had not cleared items off the heaters as instructed.

The Tenant testified that when the Landlord entered the rental unit on December 26, 2024, the Landlord took pictures without consent and threatened to use the pictures against them in court. The Tenant also alleged that the times the Landlord attended the rental unit without proper notice was harassing as well. The Tenant also testified that he felt that the illegal entries alleged were harassing as well. As I found that no illegal entries occurred, I find that the claim that the entries were harassing is also dismissed.

The phone call recording submitted as evidence was related to ongoing issues with heat and water availability. While the phone call was not always friendly in nature, and both parties engaged in raised voices, I would not classify one phone call about the ongoing maintenance issues harassment or that anything within the phone call was threatening. Same with the pictures taken on December 26, 2024. While the Tenant did not consent to the pictures, there was nothing inherently harassing, threatening or intimidating in the action. As such, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was harassing, threatening or intimidating, and these claims must be dismissed. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care service:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord withheld vital services by not providing heat from September 1 to June 15, and by not providing sufficient water. The Tenant also alleged that the issues with the heat substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment.

Section 21(1) of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. Water Issues:

The Tenant testified there were ongoing issues with the water in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the cistern ran empty on October 9, 2024, and November 3, 2024, which required the Landlord to fill the cistern. The Landlord did refill the cistern within 24 hours.

The Tenant also testified that his water supply was frequently cut off. The Tenant testified he did not have access to water on the following dates: • December 13 and 14, 2024 • January 3 to January 5, 2025 • January 9 and 10, 2025 • January 15, 2025 • January 21 to 23, 2025 • February 9 to 11, 2025

The Tenant testified that he assumed that for all the above noted incidents the water stopped due to frozen pipes, and the Landlord tried to put insulation around the pipes, but the freezing continued. The Tenant also testified that on one occasion the Landlord put a propane heater under the house to warm the pipes, but it was not effective. The Tenant also testified that the pump for the cistern was on the opposite side of the property and he was not sure if the Landlord was purposely turning off the water.

The Tenant also testified that on December 18, 2024, the cistern tested positive for e-coli, which meant none of the water was usable and the Tenant went to a hotel from December 22, 2024 to December 30, 2024. The Tenant testified that the City did not confirm a negative e-coli test until January 3, 2025. The Landlord needed to properly clean the cistern as the Tenant said it had not been properly maintained as the rental unit was empty for a year prior to the Tenant moving in.

While the issues with the water and frozen pipes would be grounds for a maintenance application, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord withheld water. When the cistern was empty, the Landlord filled it within 24 hours. When the water was not working, the Tenant’s own testimony was that he assumed it was due to frozen pipes. The Landlord failed to properly maintain the pipes, which impacted the flow of water when they froze, but there was no evidence that the Landlord intentionally or deliberately withheld water.

The Tenant did not identify the issue of the water as grounds for substantial interference, however, in his amended application dated May 26, 2026 the Tenant sought a full rent abatement for the period of his tenancy and cited the lack of essential utilities as a reason for his claim. In addition, the application clearly identified the lack of water on specific dates as one of the main issues of the application. While the water issues were not claimed under substantial interference, I am satisfied that the Landlord would know or ought to have known that part of the rent abatement claimed was for substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment due to the recurring water issues.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony of the Landlord’s limited attempts to address the freezing pipes, and the lack of maintenance in the cistern that led to the Tenant and his family needing to stay in a hotel until there was a negative test for e-coli, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenant testified to a total of 14 days where there were frozen pipes that prevented him from accessing water in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the rent was $3,500.00, and the daily compensation would be $115.07 per day. I find that a reasonable rent abatement for the days the pipes were frozen and the rental unit did not have access to running water would be 50%. The total for the 14 days is a rent abatement of $805.49.

The Tenant also testified that he did not have access to water for about 17 days from December 18, 2024 to January 3, 2025 due to e-coli in the cistern, and during this period he went to a hotel for 9 days. I find that due to the e-coli in the water, the rental unit would not have been habitable during this period, and would warrant a full rent abatement for the 17 days. The total rent abatement for the 17 days would be $1,956.19. Heat Issues:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord withheld sufficient heat and also substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment due to the insufficient heat. The Tenant testified that the indoor temperature on the main floor was normally below 20 degrees Celsius and it was cold and uncomfortable. The Tenant testified that they had 2 baseboard heaters and the Landlord provided 3 plug-in heaters in January 2025, but the main floor was still so cold that his children needed jackets and blankets. The Tenant testified that the upper floor was fine because of the baseboard heaters. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord blamed the Tenant for the heating issues and claimed they had clutter preventing the heat from circulating. This claim was heard on the Phone recording referenced above between the Tenant and the Landlord. On this phone call, the Tenant asked specifically for a heat pump as he was worried the baseboard heaters would burn his children, and the Landlord was heard telling the Tenant the baseboard heating is sufficient, it will not burn the children, and he was not going to install a heat pump.

The Tenant did not provide any evidence of the temperature on the main floor being below 20 degrees Celsius. The Tenant did not provide any evidence of the temperature from before the Landlord provided 3 plug-in heaters and the temperature after, and I find it highly unlikely that the addition of 3 heaters would have no impact at all on the temperature. On the phone call recording referenced above, the Tenant’s primary concern seemed to be that the heat could not be provided through baseboard heaters as his children could hurt themselves, and that he only wanted a source of heat off the ground. On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlord withheld sufficient heat or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment as I find that the Tenant has not established that the heat in the unit fell below the appropriate temperature. I find that the Tenant was unhappy with the source of the heat and that the Landlord would not provide a heat pump in place of the baseboard heaters, as evidenced through the Tenant’s phone call with the Landlord. Due to the lack of evidence, I find that the Landlord did not withhold the heat or substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, and these claims must be dismissed. Remedies Sought for Issues not Identified in the Application:

The Tenant submitted amended remedies for issues that were not outlined in the original or the amended application. Specifically, the Tenant sought a rent abatement for the length of the tenancy from September 16, 2024 to June 2, 2025 as he testified the rental unit was found unfit for habitation from March 6, 2025 to April 4, 2025. The Tenant sought reimbursement of gas for the period of March 6, 2025 to April 4, 2025 for driving his son to school daily. The Tenant also sought for reimbursement of storage costs for 11 months following the Tenant vacating the rental unit on June 2, 2025.

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (‘Ball v. Metro Capital’). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established.
The Court held in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...”

In [name], the Court stated that the responding party must be able “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…

As none of these issues were addressed within the application itself, I find that I am unable to order remedies where the issues were not mentioned or alluded to within the application. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established that the application had sufficient details of the events sought in the remedies for the Landlord to know the case to meet and whether he was going to dispute the allegations. As such, these remedies are dismissed as they are not issues that have been identified within the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,809.68. This amount represents: • $2,761.68 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Amending the application

The Tenant’s initial request to amend his application was granted at the hearing on April 3, 2024. Though the matter was ultimately adjourned, the amendment was granted via the Member’s Interim Order dated April 16, 2024.

The Tenant made a further request to amend the application dated September 2, 2025 to adjust the remedies claimed for inflation. The request was addressed at the hearing on September 11, 2025. As it is not Board practice to adjust remedies for inflation, the request was denied. T6 Application:

The Tenant signed a one-year lease with the Landlord (September 1, 2022 – August 31, 2023) for one bedroom in a four-bedroom apartment within a 12-floor student residential complex. The Tenant’s bedroom was unit 606A (the ‘unit’), and he shared common facilities with three other students who signed separate leases for their respective bedrooms in apartment 606.

The Tenant moved into the unit on September 7, 2022. Tenant A moved into their unit in September 2022 as well. However, two other Tenants in the apartment moved in before the Tenant. For purposes of this order, they will be referred to as Tenant B and [name] B moved into the apartment around 2020 and [name] moved into the apartment in May 2022. Tenant’s Evidence:

The Tenant testified that the day he moved into the unit, he immediately noticed it was dirty, and the apartment kitchen and bathroom had a large number of cockroaches. The Tenant verbally notified the Landlord’s Agent that same day of both issues. The Landlord’s Agent replied that the issues would be dealt with.

The Tenant testified that both his unit and the apartment were treated for cockroaches on October 14, 2022 and October 20, 2022. The Tenant was not certain when, but he believed a third treatment was done between November 1-4, 2022. However, the Tenant continued to see cockroaches throughout the apartment and in his unit until the day he vacated in December 2022.

The Tenant stated that although he left the unit on November 14, 2022, he returned to the unit on two occasions thereafter and had fully vacated the unit by December 22, 2022. The Tenant testified that he had followed up on numerous occasions with [name] (‘SM’), another Landlord Agent, who was the primary contact person for the Tenant. The Tenant stated he could no longer live in the unit because of the pests and gave the Landlord a signed N9 Notice on November 30, 2022 to end the tenancy for January 31, 2023. However, the Landlord did not accept the Tenant’s notice.

The Tenant testified that SM sent all four of the Tenants in the apartment the same email on October 14, 2022, after the pest control treatment was done, stating that the state of the apartment was not at an appropriate level of cleanliness and was contributing to the pest problem which was now spreading to other apartments on the floor. The Tenant submitted SM’s email into evidence which further stated that the Tenants were given until October 21, 2022 to thoroughly clean the apartment and their respective rooms for another inspection. If the unit was not clean, then all pest control treatments for the apartment would be charged back to the Tenants going forward.

The Tenant argued, however, that the Landlord was aware of the cockroach issue prior to him moving into the unit and was improperly shifting the responsibility to the Tenant when SM specifically mentioned in her October 27, 2022 email to the Tenant that the Landlord was aware that Tenants B & C were likely the main cause of the uncleanliness of the apartment. The Tenant felt he was receiving misleading information regarding the treatment plan for the unit and threats that he could be made to pay for the treatments. However, the October 27, 2022 email submitted at the hearing also stated that because SM believed that Tenants B & C were likely responsible for the pest issue, the Tenant and Tenant A would not be charged for any treatments.

The Tenant reiterated that he and his father, the Tenant’s Representative Marious [name] (‘MI’), persistently followed up the Landlord about the ineffectiveness of the treatments, and submitted a copy of MI’s October 26, 2022 email complaint to the Landlord as an example. The Tenant testified that although SM highlighted the uncleanliness of the unit as the cause of the pests, the Tenant had lived in another apartment in the residential complex (unit 706) a year prior and there were no pests despite that unit being in a similar state of cleanliness. Landlord’s Evidence:

The Landlord’s Agent and Assistant General Manager, [name] (‘JM’), testified that when the Tenant informed him upon moving in that the room was dirty, JM arranged for a cleaner to specifically clean the room. JM did not provide a date for when the cleaning occurred, but the Tenant did not contest that it was done.

The Landlord did not dispute that there was a pest issue on the same floor at the Tenant’s apartment as of September 2022, but the Landlord argued they had taken swift action to address the issue and have all units on the 6th floor of the building treated multiple times by late October 2022. JM testified that as a precaution, the pest control company recommended treating all apartments in the residential complex ending in “06” earlier in May 2022, which included the Tenant’s apartment. The Landlord implemented the recommendation, though no pests were reported in the Tenant’s unit prior to September 7, 2022.

The Landlord submitted a Service Inspection Report from Homepro Pest Control dated September 12, 2022, showing that a treatment was done to the Tenant’s apartment within five days of receiving the Tenant’s initial complaint. The report also states that only light cockroach activity was found in the apartment, in contrast to the Tenant’s allegation of a heavy presence. When the Tenant was asked about this treatment date on cross- examination, he could not recall the apartment being treated that day though he confirmed that he had reviewed the treatment reports.

The Landlord submitted that Homepro Pest Control informed them that at least three spray treatments were needed to effectively deal with pests in the affected areas of the residential complex. The Tenant was made aware of this in paragraph 3 of SM’s October 27, 2022 email, and therefore knew that the issue would not be able to be resolved immediately.

JM testified that the Tenant’s apartment underwent pest control treatment on September 12, 2022, October 14, 2022, October 20, 2022, and November 3, 2022. Homepro Service Inspection Reports for each date were submitted at the hearing as evidence. The reports confirmed a light presence of cockroaches and concerns over the uncleanliness of the apartment. The Landlord also submitted a November 9, 2022 email from SM informing the tenants that the Landlord hired a professional cleaning service to attend the unit on November 14, 2022 to clean the common areas of the apartment in preparation for the next pest control treatment. The Tenants were told they were responsible for cleaning their individual rooms, and if a tenant’s room was not prepared for the treatment in accordance with the instruction sheet provided with the email, then that tenant would face a chargeback. A copy of the invoice from Steam Force Ltd. for cleaning services for the apartment on November 14, 2022 was submitted as evidence at the hearing.

While the Tenant was in the process of vacating the unit, the Landlord attempted to have the unit treated again for cockroaches on December 15, 2022, but the technicians were denied entry. A copy of the treatment report for that date was submitted as evidence confirming the denial of entry. JM testified that regardless of the Tenant moving out of the unit, the Landlord continued pest control treatment for the apartment but was denied entry on several more occasions. Consequently, the pest issue was not fully resolved until September 2023. Analysis:

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name], clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, below.

Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The parties do not dispute that there was a cockroach problem in the apartment; however, the Tenant claims that the Landlord was aware of the problem before he moved into the unit and unfairly shifted blame onto the tenants in the apartment. Nevertheless, the Tenant did not provide any supporting documentary evidence showing that the Landlord was aware that there were cockroaches in the Tenant’s apartment prior to the Tenant moving in. The emails between SM and the Tenant only show that the Landlord was aware of a pest problem on the 6th floor of the residential complex in September 2022, and the Landlord was already in the midst of treatment plans for all units on that floor beginning that same month. The emails also explicitly state that the Landlord did not place the blame on the Tenant himself, but that the cockroaches were likely the result of uncleanliness in the apartment from two other tenants.

The issue before me is how the Landlord responded once the Tenant informed them about the state of his unit and the presence of cockroaches in the apartment. I accept that the Landlord had the Tenant’s room cleaned after the Tenant submitted his complaint upon moving in on September 7, 2022. The Tenant also did not dispute this was done and made no submissions regarding any unreasonable delay regarding the timing. Consequently, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the state of the Tenant’s unit upon moving in.

I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that a first pest treatment was done in the apartment within five days of receiving the Tenant’s complaint. The Landlord informed the Tenant that at least three separate treatments would be needed to resolve the issue, and that was dependent upon the apartment being in an ordinary state of cleanliness. Therefore, if the apartment was not clean after each treatment or attempted treatment, as noted in the Inspection Reports submitted, the process would be drawn out. The Landlord consequently arranged for at least five different treatment appointments because of the unclean state of the apartment, which resulted in the problem persisting over the original three-treatment estimate. The Landlord also sent the tenants several emails directing the Tenants to clean their respective rooms and the common areas, the latter for which the Tenant bears joint responsibility. The apartment was not sufficiently cleaned, so the Landlord then hired a professional cleaning service for the apartment on November 14, 2022 to address the issue before the next pest treatment.

The Tenant disputed the Landlord’s claim about the effect of cleanliness causing or exacerbating a cockroach infestation as he had lived in another apartment in the residential complex a year prior and there were no pests despite that unit being in a similar state of cleanliness. I do not find this argument persuasive given that there was no supporting visual evidence regarding the state of cleanliness in the prior unit nor if there was a pest issue in other units on the same floor at that time. Whereas, in this instance, cockroaches were found by the Landlord in other units on the same floor around the same time, and it is not unreasonable to assume unclean living accommodations would likely attract or exacerbate pests in the apartment.

While the presence of pests may be distressing to some tenants, the Landlord can not be said to automatically be in breach of their maintenance duties under the Act once pests are found in the rental unit. In this instance, the Landlord acted in a reasonable and timely manner once they were informed by the Tenant of cockroaches in the apartment. Treatments began within five days of the initial complaint, and the Landlord’s agents responded to the Tenant and MI about issues with the treatments and the necessity of keeping the unit in a clean state. The Landlord also treated all other units on the same floor of the residential complex around the same time in an effort to keep the pest problem from spreading. Furthermore, the Tenant was never charged for any treatments or professional cleaning. The Tenant vacated the unit of his own accord before the issue could be resolved, and I am not satisfied there was sufficient evidence to show that vacating the unit was necessary because of the Landlord’s actions. Consequently, I find that the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application, and the application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 28, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application).
reasons: As explained below, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that section 5(i) the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies to the rental unit and therefore the relationship is exempt from the Act.
As a preliminary issue, I addressed whether the Landlord lives in the same living accommodation.

Section 5 of the Act sets out certain living arrangements where the Act does not apply. Subsection 5(i) of the Act which reads as follows: 5.This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

The Tenant testified that the Landlord lives at the residential complex but upstairs in a completely separate rental unit and that the downstairs is a separate rental unit from the Landlord’s rental unit. The Tenant testified that the downstairs has its own kitchen and bathroom and that neither was shared with the Landlord and instead was shared with the other tenants downstairs. The Tenant testified that there were other people renting downstairs, but he did not know who they were.

The Landlord’s Representative testified that he is the Landlord’s husband and there were 4 other people living downstairs including himself. He testified that they run the house as a room share house and the downstairs tenants all share a kitchen and bathroom. The [name] testified that the Landlord, his wife, and their children live upstairs. The Landlord’s Representative testified that it was made clear at the time the Tenant entered into the agreement that the Landlord’s Representative lived downstairs and it was a shared kitchen and washroom. The Landlord’s Representative testified that he lives his day-to-day life downstairs and eats his meals downstairs, all in order to keep an eye on the rooming situation.

Based on the evidence before me, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord’s Representative as it was more consistent and detailed. As such, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s husband lives primarily in the downstairs unit and therefore shared a kitchen and bathroom with the Tenant. Therefore, section 5(i) of the Act applies, and this rental unit is exempt from the Act.
Since I am satisfied that the rental unit is exempt from the Act, I do not need to address the remainder of the Tenant’s claims as the Act does not apply and the Board does not have jurisdiction.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') does not apply. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
