issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It is uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice and the Tenants moved out because of this notice.
The Tenant [name] Di [name] (SD) testified that the Landlord sent them a notice of rent increase at the end of 2024 and only a few months later she served them with the N12 notice.
SD testified that the Landlord claimed that she and her partner were having issues so she required the unit for her own personal use.
SD testified that she believes the Landlord and her partner may have gotten back together and that the Landlord is not residing in the unit.

SD testified that she was disabled at the time of the move and they have a dog so it was hard for them to find an alternative unit. She further testified that the unit was partially furnished so she had sold some of her own belongings and whren having to move, they were forced to buy new.
SD testified that the Landlord has always used the address of the rental unit as her mailing address, as her partner’s unit is just above the rental unit.
SD submitted photos of the unit from January 31, 2026 to March 23. 2026 showing no light on and no activity in the unit. She also testified that the backyard had not been cleared.
The Tenant [name] (VA) testified that they had shared a mailbox with the Landlord and that the furniture in the unit was the furniture that was always there.
VA testified that the Landlord may be using the unit as an office, but has not moved back into the unit.
The Landlord testified that she and her partner had broken up and she had moved back in with her parents waiting to regain possession of the unit.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant moved out of the unit on May 10, 2025, she had a cleaning service clean the unit on May 15, 2025v, she then moved furniture into the unit and moved in.

The Landlord testified that on May 26, 2025 internet was hooked up in the unit and she changed the insurance on the unit from having a tenant to herself living in the unit. Copies of the insurance and the wi-fi bill were submitted as evidence. A copy of her driver’s licence with the unit’s address was also submitted as evidence.
The Landlord testified that she and her partner have reconciled but they keep separate residences. She further testified that the unit has never been listed for rent or rented out or listed for sale.
The Landlord also submitted proof of parcel deliveries to the unit. Analysis

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the Landlord did not move into the unit and that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In this case, the evidence is that the Landlord did move into the unit in May 2025, shortly after the Tenants vacated the unit. Her testimony is supported by the wi-fi bill, the change in insurance and the parcel delivery to the unit.
Although the Tenants do not believe that the Landlord has moved into the rental unit, their testimony did not provide any evidence to the contrary or contradict the Landlord’s evidence.

Based on the evidence before me, I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of the Landlord’s testimony. I am therefore satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenants vacated and that the Landlord did not serve the N12 notice in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord’s nieces S.S. and T.S. informed the Board that the Landlord R.S. is deceased, having passed away on November 27, 2024. They are the joint executors of his estate. The application is therefore amended to name the Estate.

The Tenant A.H. asked the Board to amend the application to include a T1 claim, in which she requests an order requiring the Landlord to return the last month’s rent deposit the Landlord collected from her on or about April 3, 2020. S.S. and T.S. acknowledge that R.S. may have collected the deposit. They take no position about its disposition. Accordingly, I find it fair and appropriate to grant the amendment to include the T1 claim. T2 application
For the reasons below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on the balance of probabilities.

The Tenant A.H. alleges that: • the Landlord R.S. harassed her and pursued an unwanted romantic relationship, which escalated in March 2023; • maintenance deficiencies in the rental unit contributed to her temporary departure from the unit as of July 31, 2023; • R.S. illegally locked her out of the rental unit on October 22, 2023; • R.S. misrepresented to the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit ("RHEU") that she had moved out and had given her property left in the unit to him; and • her belongings in the Landlord’s control and possession were subsequently improperly retained, lost and/or damaged. Background 5. [name]’s largely uncontested testimony was that R.S. persistently engaged in behaviour that was unwelcome. He pursued her romantically and harassed her over the course of the tenancy. She stated that she communicated to him, verbally, in writing and through her conduct, that she was not interested in a relationship with him. 6. Between March 2023 and June 2023, [name] sent him multiple letters by registered mail requesting rent receipts, a copy of the lease and confirmation of R.S.’s legal name and address. She specifically raised disrepair issues in a letter dated June 24, 2023, all of which A.H. then reported to the Township of Brock Property Standards department. 7. [name] stated that, by April 17, 2023, she ceased all verbal communications with R.S. but he continued to contact her. She sent a letter to him dated May 1, 2023, “to reiterate that you stop contacting me by phone” and to put all communications in writing in future. She explained, “I don’t feel safe in my home because of these unwanted phone calls”, the most recent call being April 29, 2023. She wrote: “You have used abusive language and tone. You have said things to put me down. You’ve invited me to have “drinks” in spite of my repeated refusals. You have made unfair accusations. You have called me while intoxicated. You have called to take your anger out on me. You are argumentative and insist on going over old ground repeatedly. This has been going on since the start of my tenancy. It’s beyond professional and totally unacceptable. I feel harassed. It makes me afraid and exacerbates my health conditions.” 8. [name] lives with PTSD and an anxiety disorder. She testified that R.S.’s conduct caused her enormous discomfort and made the tenancy emotionally difficult to maintain. She was also concerned about ongoing disrepair in the unit, which presented health and safety issues. 9. There was conflict about rent. R.S. did not cash her May 2023 rent cheque. She withheld the June and July 2023 rent because R.S. would not provide receipts, a copy of the lease agreement and notice of his legal name and address for service when asked. 10. In mid-June 2023, municipal Property Standards by-law officers inspected the unit for maintenance deficiencies and disrepair (Report 23-254) at A.H.’s request. They found the unit unsafe and recommended that she stay elsewhere until repairs were completed. [name] also understood this as an opportunity for respite from the harassment. She contacted a moving company for a quote to move “mostly boxes”. They refused because there were physical obstacles impeding their large truck from safely accessing the premises. 11. On July 17, 2023, by-law officers informed A.H. that R.S. was being uncooperative about the repairs, restating that [name] should secure alternative housing for the time being. [name] arranged for interim housing and rented a U-Haul truck that could park at the building. 12. On July 18, 2023, R.S. served [name] with an N4 notice of termination for non-payment of rent with a termination date of July 31, 2023. 13. On July 19, 2023, [name] left the unit to stay with her father in Toronto. She maintains she did not vacate and intended to return to live in the unit once repairs were completed and she felt emotionally capable of doing so. As of July 31, 2023 she had moved items she needed or wanted out of the unit. She left furniture, clothing, pots, pans, tools, a Rogers modem and other household and decorative items in the unit. She retained the keys. 14. On August 10, 2023, A.H. emailed by-law officer L.J. about the status of repairs. [name] wrote “I have not moved out. I’m staying with my dad in Toronto, until the safety issues are addressed by my landlord.” She stated that she had someone “check the apartment once a week to make sure there is no flooding” and invited L.J. to meet her at the unit if needed. 15. While she claimed in the application that she did not access the unit personally after July 31, 2023, the parties clarified at the hearing that [name] did go there in August 2023. The claim of an illegal lockout 16. [name] contacted R.S. by phone on October 22, 2023 to ask about the repairs. She went to the unit the same day and was surprised to discover that her key no longer worked in the lock. She was therefore unable to enter or to access her personal belongings. 17. While at the unit, A.H. called the police to investigate (Incident Report 23-276129). They tried but were unable to reach R.S. The attending officer noted that R.S. lived outside of their jurisdiction and referred A.H. to the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (‘RHEU’). On October 23, 2023 A.H. reported the lockout to RHEU. 18. S.S. and T.S. became estate trustees after R.S.’s death in November 2024. They had no idea that anyone had been renting A.H.’s unit until they became the executors. They do not believe that [name] was illegally locked out. They rely on the N4 Notice and on an undated handwritten note allegedly written by their uncle, in which he was resolute that [name] had either moved out voluntarily on July 31, 2023 or abandoned the unit. Their position is that R.S. was entitled to change the locks to prohibit [name] from further access. RHEU evidence 19. [name] made a complaint to RHEU on July 17, 2023 about R.S.’s refusal to provide her with rent receipts and other information she requested. [name] then filed another complaint, relating to R.S. locking her out of the rental unit. 20. RHEU investigator [name] testified pursuant to a summons. She confirmed that RHEU had opened two cases relating to the rental unit and these parties. She was assigned to further investigate the lockout complaint on January 23, 2024. 21. [name] relied upon partial records submitted by the parties in Complaints #23-774955227 and 23-74955257. For the first complaint, R.S. provided the required information on August 23, 2023 and the complaint was closed. The record shows that A.H. informed RHEU that day that she “was living with others”. 22. On October 23, 2023, the day after the alleged lockout, RHEU compliance officer L.Z. completed A.H.’s intake. She noted that Property Standards by-law informed [name] on July 17, 2023 that the unit was unsafe, that R.S. was being uncooperative with repairs, and that [name] was advised to stay elsewhere temporarily. 23. L.Z. reported that on July 19, 2023, [name] left to stay with her father and that [name] returned to the unit with her father about one month later to “check the lease”, the “state of repairs”, and to “grab some personal items” as repairs had not yet begun. L.Z. also documented A.H.’s claim that R.S. “would get angry and harass her, yell at her”. 24. She then interviewed R.S., who explained that he had served a first N4 notice and filed an L1 with the LTB but it was found premature. He served a second N4 notice in July, and a few days later he observed A.H. moving items into a U-Haul truck. Then, on July 31, 2023 he saw [name] and her father loading a car with items; they were also transporting a cat. He didn’t hear from [name] again until October 14, 2023. 25. L.Z. included in the file R.S.’s assertion that he advised [name] that she could retrieve her property but he refused her demand that he deliver the items. He claimed that [name] “left the items for him” to use or dispose of as he saw fit. [name] disagreed with these statements. The records also show that, on September 20, 2023, R.S. informed by-law officer L.J. that [name] “took all her personal belongings and clothes but left furniture and dishes” in July 2023. 26. On October 14, 2023, A.H. phoned R.S. directly to inquire about the status of the unit repairs but he “scoffed and hung up” as soon as he realized who it was. R.S. changed the locks to the rental unit on October 22, 2023. 27. On October 24, 2023, L.Z. terminated the initial investigation due to insufficient evidence. 28. On October 26, 2023, A.H. emailed by-law officer L.J. to ask whether she could reoccupy the unit. L.J. advised that the unit was safe for occupancy. [name] then forwarded that email to L.Z., and stated to L.Z.: “My unit is now safe for occupancy. I believe I have the right to move back in. Can you shed some light on this? … The [Landlord] has not gone through the proper channels to evict me. He just expects me to walk away. Unfortunately, I can't walk away from all my personal possessions. I'm living in a precarious situation now.” 29. L.Z. recounted a subsequent phone conversation with [name] on October 31, 2023. She wrote: “[A.H.] did not move out, [[name]] just left because she felt it was unsafe” and “due to conversation with by-law, she left”, and, finally, that “[A.H.] wants items back and expects [R.S.] to pay to move but [[name]] would like to live there”. 30. On November 8, 2023, L.Z. gave a letter to R.S. strongly encouraging him to replace the new lock with the original lock immediately or else face enforcement action. 31. L.Z. was not present to give testimony or to be cross-examined. 32. [name] advised RHEU on November 23, 2023 that she no longer wanted to live in the unit. On December 13, 2023, A.H. applied for rent-geared-to-income Toronto housing based on her eligibility as an ODSP recipient. 33. M.G.’s further investigation resulted in finding insufficient evidence to merit enforcement. She closed the file on March 4, 2024. Four months later, [name] filed the T2.3 Medical evidence 34. [name] submitted a letter from Dr. [name], of CAMH, dated March 7, 2025. Dr. [name], a psychiatrist, referred to an appointment with [name] on May 29, 2023, in which A.H. described in detail how her landlord “had propositioned a relationship with her, now wants her gone and is using indirect ways to have her feel unwelcome”. 35. The letter states that [name] self-reported that “she felt she had no choice but to leave her apartment in July 2023, she later came to regret the decision as she subsequently experienced abuse from her father”. 36. Dr. [name] was not present to testify and the letter could not be tested on cross-examination. Personal property claims 37. [name] claims in her T2 filed on July 26, 2024 that R.S. (and later S.S. and T.S.) unlawfully disposed of or retained her property that remained in the rental unit as of August 1, 2023, except for those items she personally removed from the premises. 38. The total compensation A.H. requests for property loss and damage as set out in particulars is $7,310.27. However, she seeks an order for the maximum monetary compensation available through the LTB. 39. In January 2025, S.S. and T.S. contacted A.H. regarding belongings found at the property, advised that they were preparing the house for sale, and offered to arrange for or to facilitate the return of her possessions. According to S.S. and T.S., [name] told them that she preferred to continue with the LTB proceeding to resolve the issues. 40. In May 2025, S.S. and T.S. relocated the contents of the rental unit to a storage shed in preparation for realtors listing the property. In June 2025, they notified [name] that they had transferred her items to a different shed. 41. After an LTB hearing on September 22, 2025, S.S. and T.S. delivered A.H.’s property to her on October 6, 2025. The parties also exchanged coordinated lists of the stored items, identifying that which was allegedly damaged and missing. 42. [name] testified that damaged items included non-perishable food, linen, a pillow, a mattress, a duffel bag, a futon and a sentimental art print. S.S. and T.S. assert that they returned the futon hardware but [name] disagrees. There is no dispute that [name] did not receive various small kitchen appliances, cookware, footwear, and clothing. S.S. and T.S. testified that they did not see these items and did not believe that they stored any of them. 43. They do allow that A.H.’s tool collection may have been mistaken for the Landlord’s tools. In an email to A.H. dated October 2, 2025, T.S. stated that an individual who was helping “may have moved your tools along with other things” in July 2025. She explained that A.H.’s belongings were “relocated again to a different shed on another property”. She wrote: “I guess we assumed your tools belonged to our uncle. So unfortunately, it's very possible that we no longer have them and that they may have been sold.” 44. S.S. and T.S. acknowledged that some of the items were damaged as A.H. described. They did not think it likely that someone purloined A.H.’s items by gaining access to the rental unit or sheds without their permission. They photographed the contents of the unit on January 28, 2025 and sent the photos to A.H. – the missing items were not captured in the photos. 45. They suggest that perhaps [name] had forgotten or misremembered about where she had, herself, stored the items. They also submit that [name] did not take reasonable steps to recover her personal possessions between August 1, 2023 and September 2025 and, as a result, bears partial responsibility for any loss or damage to those possessions. Analysis 46. S.S. and T.S. pointed to inconsistencies in A.H.’s evidence. While some inconsistencies exist, I do not find that they undermine the core allegations. Considering the evidence as a whole, I find the inconsistencies relate primarily to chronology and peripheral details which do not impact the substance of A.H.’s evidence. Harassment 47. I found [name]'s evidence regarding harassment, the deterioration of the landlord-tenant relationship, and the circumstances leading to her departure from the unit to be detailed and honestly given and, therefore, reliable and credible. 48. Dr. [name] March 7, 2025 letter is important. Although the letter does not independently establish that the harassment occurred, it provides professional evidence of A.H.'s state of mind contemporaneous to the harassment claimed. It corresponds with A.H.'s evidence that she left because an authority had recommended it, and because it would benefit her mental health, and that she did not intend to permanently renounce her tenancy. 49. S.S. and T.S. confirmed that they had no personal knowledge of the events giving rise to this application. They did not present any witnesses with firsthand knowledge capable of contradicting the evidence of harassment or of giving context to the tenancy. Their own testimony is necessarily restricted to matters within their own knowledge, primarily concerning the handling/storage of A.H.'s belongings from January 2025 onward. 50. I accept that the Landlord R.S. harassed A.H. from at least March 2023 to June 2023, contrary to section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The illegal lockout 51. There is no dispute that R.S. changed the locks to the rental unit on October 22, 2023 and did not provide [name] with replacement keys. [name] testified that, before the lockout, the tenancy had not been terminated by notice, agreement, or order of the Board. 52. R.S. appears to have treated A.H.'s departure on July 31, 2023 as proof that the tenancy had ended: after receiving the N4 notice, [name] rented a moving truck, removed the belongings she wanted, and vacated by the N4 termination date. His evidence does not seem to be that [name] abandoned the unit itself. Rather, the more reasonable inference is that R.S. believed she had abandoned the belongings she left behind. 53. I am not satisfied that A.H.'s conduct demonstrated a clear intention to permanently relinquish possession of the unit. When the N4 notice was served, she was already arranging temporary accommodation with a relative at the recommendation of the by-law officers. R.S. was aware of those circumstances. 54. The evidence instead supports the conclusion that A.H.'s departure was a temporary relocation during the repairs. Between August 10 and October 22, 2023, she contacted Property Standards regarding the repairs and twice attempted to contact R.S. about their status. Four days after the lockout, she asked whether the unit was safe for occupancy and was advised that it was. The same day, she advised the RHEU that she believed she had the right to move back into the unit. A.H.'s unchallenged evidence is that she did not decide to end the tenancy until November 23, 2023. This evidence is inconsistent with an intention to terminate the tenancy on July 31, 2023. 55. Nor am I satisfied that R.S. took reasonable steps to determine whether A.H. had in fact surrendered possession before changing the locks. The evidence suggests that he disregarded information inconsistent with his assumption that the tenancy had ended. [name] retained her keys, left furniture and personal effects in the unit, maintained throughout that she had not vacated, and contacted R.S. about a date when she could resume occupancy because she could no longer stay at her father’s home. 56. I also attach significance to what R.S. did not do. After July 31, 2023, he did not recover A.H.'s keys, obtain written confirmation that the tenancy had ended, address the rent deposit, seek an order terminating the tenancy, or apply for relief under section 79 of the Act based on abandonment, if that was the case. Despite receiving information that cast doubt on whether the tenancy had ended, he continued to treat it as if it had. 57. I find the most probable explanation for the lockout is that, by October 2023, R.S. became concerned that [name] might return to the rental unit and resume occupancy. When R.S. gave A.H. the N4 notice, it was evident that the parties' relationship had become strained and adversarial. [name] had stopped paying rent, complained to municipal authorities about the condition of the unit, accused R.S. of harassment, and demanded that only contact her in writing about tenancy matters. In these circumstances, I might reasonably conclude that it was in R.S.'s interest to deem her departure as permanent rather than temporary. 58. The situation changed in October 2023 when [name] began directly contacting him about the availability of the unit for occupancy. This presented a practical problem for R.S. – A.H. still regarded herself as a tenant entitled to return and she still possessed the keys. It seems that he then moved quickly to change the locks before she could regain possession. 59. I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that R.S altered the locks on a door giving entry to the rental unit without providing [name] with replacement keys, contrary to section 24 of the Act. This was an illegal eviction, interfering with her rights as a tenant. 60. A.H.’s ultimate decision on November 23, 2023 to reside elsewhere does not alter the fact of the illegal lockout and cannot retrospectively validate it. She made that decision after the lockout and after the landlord-tenant relationship had irretrievably broken down. Property loss and damage 61. There is no dispute that S.S. and T.S. returned many of A.H.’s belongings to her and that some items were damaged while in the possession and control of the Landlord. They submit that several items merely require laundering. Except for a duvet cover [name] thought might be cleaned, I do not find this will properly resolve the issue given the length of time the items were left stored in sheds that were infested with rodents and exposed to excess moisture. [name] also gave explicit details of missing items, which I find determinative. 62. Based on the evidence and submissions presented, I am persuaded that the Landlord failed to return certain of the Tenant’s personal possessions and that some returned items were irreversibly damaged while in the Landlord’s care. Therefore, the Landlord is liable for the reasonable costs of repair or replacement of those items. T1 application 63. [name] contends, without strong opposition, that she paid a last month’s deposit of $700.00 to R.S. on April 3, 2020 upon entering into the residential tenancy agreement. 64. There is no evidence before the Board establishing that R.S. applied the deposit to the last month of the tenancy as required by the Act, that he returned the deposit to the Tenant or that he paid the required interest to [name] Her evidence is that the Landlord did none of those things. As a result, the Landlord has unlawfully retained funds owed to the Tenant. Remedies Rent abatement 65. In her amended application filed on October 28, 2025, the Tenant seeks $8,514.00 as an abatement of rent, which represents a 100% abatement for the 12 months preceding the illegal lockout. The monthly rent charged at the time was $711.30. 66. Section 29(2) of the Act provides that no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. This means that the Board may only grant remedies in respect of conduct that occurred within the 12-month period immediately preceding the filing date of the application. 67. In this case, the Tenant filed the application on July 26, 2024 and so the Board may only grant remedies for breaches of the Act that occurred on and after July 26, 2023. Earlier incidents are outside the limitation period and no remedies can be awarded for them, although they are considered context in support of the facts alleged. 68. I find that the Tenant is entitled to $2,297.63, representing a 100% rent abatement for the period July 15, 2023 to October 22, 2023. It is evident that, due the Landlord’s conduct, she was unable to reside in the unit during this period. Having decided the tenancy had ended on October 22nd, the Landlord could not then continue to charge and collect rent. Property damage and loss 69. The Board's monetary jurisdiction sets the maximum amount that may be awarded for compensation where the evidence justifies such an award. It does not entitle an applicant to the maximum amount merely because they have proven a breach of the Act or simply because the landlord's conduct was reprehensible. 70. Compensation is based on evidence of actual loss. There is no evidentiary basis before the Board upon which I could increase the amount to the Board's monetary maximum. 71. The Tenant stated that on October 6, 2025 she received the damaged items listed below, noting replacement costs: • non-perishable food items, with evidence of mouse feces - $132.78 • fitted double sheet, which was torn and had fecal matter on it - $50.00 • pillow, damaged by water - $136.45 • mattress, damaged by water - $300.00 • duvet cover, damaged by water - $68.50 (cost to launder) • duvet, damaged by water - $450.00 • blue duffel bag with water stains and covered in a sticky substance - $500.00 • futon (3-seat), stained and absent hardware - $565.00 • print of sailboat (sentimental value), restore damaged print and mat - $675.00 72. There is no dispute that the Tenant did not receive the following items from S.S. and T.S., listed below with their estimated replacement costs: • tools - $1,000.00 • coffee maker - $39.99 • tea kettle - $15.00 • Henkles pots and lids - $160.00 • saucepan - $48.58 • vintage wool winter coat from Etsy (receipt submitted) - $220.00 • Chanel brand purse (irreplaceable gift) - $100.00 for imitation product • work blazers and swimsuit - $450.00 • Croc brand shoes - $73.44 73. No receipts were provided for the duvet or duffel bag, or evidence of the product quality. The Tenant is entitled to a replacement of similar quality, estimated at $300.00 each. 74. I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven that she incurred a total of $4,634.74 to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of, as listed above. Moving and storage expenses 75. The Tenant requests $1,000.00 for moving and storage expenses. No receipts for the moving costs were submitted and the need for a public storage unit was not sufficiently demonstrated. As is the Board’s practice where receipts for moving costs are unavailable, I will allow the Tenant reasonable costs in the amount of $750.00. Out-of-pocket expenses 76. The Tenant seeks reimbursement for the out-of-pocket expenses of $1,514.63 for mail forwarding and renting a post office box, meals, lockable bins, locksmith services, a sleeping bag and pillow, and miscellaneous household items. 77. There is no question that her need to obtain alternative accommodation resulted in unplanned expenses and that these were foreseeable consequences of the Landlord's conduct. I find that the Tenant is entitled to the costs of (i) $68.37 for mail forwarding and (ii) $136.45 to purchase a sleeping bag and pillow, for a total of $204.82. The remaining expenses were not proven to be sufficiently connected to the Landlord's breaches of the Act or adequately explained and justified. 78. She also seeks to recover $602.00 representing an increased automobile insurance annual premium incurred while residing at her father’s Toronto residence. While this is a cost the Board may consider, the Tenant bears the burden of proving the loss and that she took reasonable steps to mitigate. 79. Mitigation means that a party cannot sit back and allow avoidable costs to accumulate and then expect the other party to pay for them; they must act prudently to reduce the financial impact where they can. That is because all the financial consequences relating to where a tenant chooses to live are not automatically offloaded to the landlord. 80. The Tenant's insurance document submitted shows that the increase took effect on February 12, 2024. She explained that she had to notify her insurer that the address of the principal residence where she kept her vehicle had changed. This resulted in the policy being re-rated from a rural community to a higher-risk urban location. 81. The evidence does not establish that the Tenant sought a more favourable insurance rate from another insurer, that she explored accommodation in the Beaverton area or in a comparable rural area where the insurance consequences may have been reduced, or that she otherwise attempted to minimize the additional cost. 82. The Board cannot determine how long the increased premium would apply if the Tenant relocated somewhere else with cheaper rates within the 12 months post-eviction, either. Accordingly, I am not persuaded that the increased premium amount is recoverable. Last month’s rent deposit 83. The Landlord shall reimburse the Tenant $700.00, representing the last month’s rent deposit, and $25.67, representing the interest owing on the deposit, for a total of $725.67. General compensation 84. In the Tenant’s amended T2 application served and filed, she requested that the Board consider “any appropriate remedies” under section 31 of the Act. She clarified at the hearings that she seeks an order for general compensation for mental distress. I am satisfied that the Landlord had adequate notice of this claim and the reasons for it. 85. Along with her testimony and description in the T2 of the impact of the breaches, the Tenant relies on the uncontroverted evidence of the mental health supports and treatment she accessed, including the letter from Dr. [name], to establish the claim. 86. I find that the Landlord's premature termination of the tenancy caused the Tenant significant stress. She lost her home without adequate notice, disrupting both her living arrangements and those of her father, who was providing temporary accommodation. She suffered financial and personal consequences inherent to these kinds of situations. She experienced difficulties recovering her belongings, and the loss and damage of possessions with significant sentimental value further compounded her distress. In my view, the Tenant suffered more than ordinary upset or inconvenience. 87. An aggravating factor is that the Landlord R.S. made no meaningful effort to return the property for 15 months, unnecessarily prolonging the consequences of the illegal lockout. 88. Compensation amounts for breaches of section 23 of the Act are determined on a case by case basis, with consideration given to the seriousness and impact of the breach. As regards illegal lockouts pursuant to section 24 of the Act (often linked to an illegal entry under section 25 of the Act where the tenant’s property is interfered with upon or after a lockout), the Board has consistently applied a base amount of $2,500.00, which is adjusted upward or downward as the circumstances dictate. 89. In this case, the evidence supports an award of general compensation in the amount of $4,000.00, which I find is proportionate and responsive to the proven claims. Administrative fine 90. Administrative fines may be imposed where a landlord shows an obvious disregard for the Act. The LTB generally treats illegal lockouts as among the most serious breaches because forcing a tenant out of their home without an LTB order demonstrates an intention to circumvent the LTB eviction process. 91. Tenants are entitled to the procedural protections provided by the Act, including a determination of tenancy rights before being unjustly deprived of possession of the rental unit. In the circumstances, the Landlord ought to have sought a determination from the Board regarding the status of the tenancy rather than unilaterally resolving that issue by changing the locks. 92. In assessing the seriousness of the Landlord’s breaches and the appropriate amount of any fine, I have considered the broader course of conduct. The harassment, the unresolved disrepair, the rent issues, the Tenant's temporary departure from the unit, and the eventual lockout are not isolated incidents. 93. Any liability arising from R.S.'s conduct survives his death and is properly recoverable from the Estate. However, the death of the Landlord is a mitigating factor; fines are generally imposed on living persons. That said, fines are not just about specific deterrence, they also serve the larger objective of promoting compliance with the Act. 94. Here, the Landlord’s misconduct shows indifference for his legal obligations and disdain of the Tenant’s rights. His casual, unfiltered approach to the tenancy and the Tenant clearly fell short of what the Act requires of landlords. 95. With respect to the Tenant’s property, I recognize that S.S. and T.S. took prompt, diligent action once becoming the executors. Regardless, property was damaged and some went missing under their watch. They were accountable for preserving the Tenant's belongings and they were required to take reasonable steps to protect them from loss and damage. 96. Therefore, the Board imposes an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.001.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,660.86. This amount represents: • $2,297.63, as an abatement of rent. 1See, for example, Laczi-bencze v. Cheung, 2024 ONLTB 66824 (CanLII); [name] v. [name], 2025 ONLTB 94190 (CanLII); and [name], 2026 ONLTB 1460 (CanLII). • $4,634.74, for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to repair/replace property that was damaged/destroyed/disposed of because of the Landlord's actions. • $750.00, for the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has reasonably incurred. • $204.82, for out-of-pocket expenses. • $4,000.00, as general compensation. • $725.67, representing reimbursement of the last month’s rent deposit and accrued interest owing on the deposit. • $48.00, for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.00 by August 3, 2026*. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

As a preliminary issue the Tenant indicated that her evidence had been served via email to the previous Landlord's Legal Representative on September 26, 2025; the Landlord's Legal Representative submitted that she checked the previous counsel’s email and there is no record of receiving the Tenant’s evidence. The Tenant produced an email to the previous legal counsel dated September 26, 2025, however, at the top of the email it said it had bounced back.

The Landlord's Legal Representative requested that the Tenant’s application be dismissed: the Tenant sent the disclosure to an inaccurate address, and despite it bouncing back did not attempt to resent it or send to either the Landlord Agent’s or the company’s general email; according to interim order LTB-T-013683-25-IN issued by the Board on August 26, 2025, any amendments to correct deficiencies in the application and compilation and service of her evidence were to be done no later than September 26, 2025; the Tenant did not amend the application, therefore it lacks sufficient particulars to proceed, and did not compile/serve her evidence as order; the application still contains incidents outside the limitation period; and, the application was filed February 28, 2025, therefore, the Tenant had more than enough time to correct any application or evidentiary deficiencies. For all these reasons, the Tenant’s application should be dismissed; to adjourn it prejudices the Landlord and ultimately rewards the Tenant for a lack of due diligence.

The Tenant submitted she did not realize the email had bounced back; she thought everything was fine because shortly after she received the Notice of Hearing. As to the application and evidence issues, she does not have legal counsel and has been preparing everything herself; she thought she had done what was necessary. She currently lives in Australia which makes it difficult to get legal help/direction. In respect of the limitation period, she kept the dates in the application to go towards a pattern of behaviour and indicated that remedy is not being sought for them. The matter should be adjourned so she can address/fix the deficiencies.

Based on the testimony/submissions before me, I find the Tenant did not act diligently; therefore, the application shall be dismissed. Interim order LTB-T-013683-25-IN is clear that any amendments to correct deficiencies in the application were to be done no later than September 26, 2025. It is also clear from the submissions and the adjournment sheet that the Tenant was also to compile and served her in accordance with the Board’s rules; the Tenant did not do this. Even after receiving the Landlord’s intial evidence brief on August 11, 2025, and a final package prior to the hearing, the Tenant took no steps to compile and serve hers in the same fashion. Although the Tenant indicated she did her best and was unable to find legal assistance, that she did not ensure she complied with what was ordered of her or consider the consequences of non-compliance demonstrates a lack of due diligence on her part. In in Q Res IV Operating GP Inc. v. [name], 2017 ONSC 5541 the Divisional Court said at paragraph 8 that, “Lack of due diligence in dealing with court proceedings is a reason for refusing to set aside an order where a party failed to appear”; logically, acting with due diligence is applicable to a party’s actions throughout the legal proceeding. The Tenant has had over a year to ensure the application and evidence were properly prepared so the hearing could proceed. For all these reasons, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not meet his maintenance obligations.
reasons: The Tenant put in her evidence at the March 11, 2026 hearing. The matter was adjourned due to insufficient time, with the Landlord to put in his evidence at the next hearing date. However, the Landlord and his representative did not attend the next hearing date, and there was no record in the Landlord and Tenant Board’s (LTB) files of any request to reschedule the matter. I waited until 9:46am, and then proceeded to hear the rest of the matter, which consisted only of the Tenant’s closing arguments. I have decided this case based on the Tenant’s evidence. Hot and cold temperatures

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has caused the unit to be too hot and too cold. She testified that her unit is at times too cold during the day, and at times too hot. She believes that the unit gets cold because the Landlord deliberately turns the heat off. It is not clear why the unit gets too hot.

The Tenant’s testimony was vague and general in nature. She did not testify as to what the specific temperature was on any specific date. She testified that she had taken photos of thermometer readings, but only put one photo into evidence. The photo, apparently taken on or about January 14, shows a temperature of 25 degrees Celsius. I am not persuaded that that is an excessive temperature. She did not adduce any photos of any cold temperatures.

The Tenant also relies on a text message exchange with the Landlord on November 19, 2025. She asked the Landlord to tell her how to turn the heat down. He replied “the heart is trons off.” She asked for clarification, and he said “I tron the heat off from my end.” She took him to mean that he had a practice of deliberately making the unit excessively cold by turning off the heat.

I do not see how the text message could bear the meaning the Tenant ascribes to it. She specifically asked the Landlord how to turn down the heat, presumably because she was too hot. In reply, the Landlord said that the heat was off, and seemed to say that he had turned it off. That would seem to be a reasonable reply to the Tenant’s question. I do not see any basis for concluding that he meant that he also turned the heat off on other days when the Tenant was too cold.

There is only evidence of one specific time the Tenant complained to the Landlord about excessive temperatures. On January 14, 2026, she sent the Landlord’s representative a photo of her thermostat. The Landlord responded promptly by sending a contractor the next morning.
The evidence does not establish that the Landlord is responsible for excessively hot or cold temperatures or has not met any obligation in respect of the unit’s temperature. Hot water
The Tenant testified that for roughly three months starting in December, 2025, there was no hot water supply to the unit.

The Tenant did not testify that she had ever reported the problem to the Landlord. The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance. He was not obligated to repair issues that he could not reasonably have known about. Absent any evidence that the Landlord knew about the hot water issue, I do not find that he failed to meet his obligations.
The Tenant eventually made a complaint to a property standards officer. She testified that the Landlord promptly repaired the issue one the officer made him aware of it. Dishwasher

The Tenant testified that the dishwasher was leaking when she moved in on September 3, 2025. The Landlord replaced it, but the new one also leaked. The Landlord told her to use it anyway. I conclude from her testimony that the Landlord was aware of the leak but failed to fix it.

The Tenant’s testimony was uncontradicted, and I accept it as true. I will award a rent abatement of 10% from September 3, 2025 to July 6, 2026. The Landlord will also be ordered to repair the dishwasher. Washer and dryer
The Tenant testified that the clothes dyer does not get hot and the washing machine does not start. She informed the Landlord at the end of November, 2025, but he did not repair the problems.

On the basis of the Tenant’s uncontradicted testimony, I will award a rent abatement of 10% from December 1, 2025 to July 6, 2026. The Landlord will also be ordered to repair the washer and dryer. Mail

The Tenant testified that on December 16, 2025, she caught the Landlord accessing her mailbox and taking her mail out. She did not provide any details or say what mail was taken or what the Landlord was doing with it.

Absent more detailed evidence, I will award a $50.00 rent abatement for substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Landlord will also be ordered not to access the Tenant’s mailbox. Result

The monthly rent is $2,350.00. I am awarding a 10% rent abatement for 306 days, a 10% rent abatement for 217 days, and a $50.00 rent abatement, for a total of $4,090.71. An order will issue accordingly.
ordered: The Landlord shall forthwith inspect the dishwasher, washer, and dryer, and conduct all needed repairs to ensure that the are fully functional.
The Landlord shall not access or interfere with mail in the Tenant’s mailbox.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant a total rent abatement of $4,090.71

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 13, 2026 ____________________________
