issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith
It was uncontested that the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenants moved out because they received this notice.

The central dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord did not move into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. The Tenants state the Landlord renovated the property and then listed it for sale.
There is no dispute that the Tenants moved out of the unit on August 10, 2025. It was also uncontested that the rental unit was listed for sale in February 2026.

The reverse onus provision in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies to this situation. This provision states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, for sale; …

This provision means that, because there is evidence before me that during the one year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale, the Landlord bears the burden of proof to establish that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith. For the following reasons I find that the Landlord has met this burden. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] (CL) testified that they moved out based on the N12 notice and believing that the Landlord and their family was moving into the unit.

The Tenant testified that she became aware in February 2026that the house was listed for sale and sold that month. She further testified that renovations had been done to the unit before being sold and submitted before and after pictures of the kitchen, the flooring, the stairs and the bathroom.
The Tenant testified how the move has greatly affected her family, uprooting them from their community and having to move into a much smaller unit.
The Tenants are seeking $30,000.00 in general compensation. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord that the home was purchased in April 2021 and was rented out and then in April 2025, they were ready to move into the unit.

The Landlord testified that in May 2025 her workplace went on strike and that continued until July 5, 2025. Due to the financial hardship caused by the strike, her children were taken out of the private school they had attended.

The Landlord testified that they moved into the unit the week of August 10, 2025, right after the Tenants moved out, and this is when they started seeing issues within the house. A receipt for the furniture they needed for the home was submitted as evidence.

The Landlord testified that due to the Tenants having pets, they hired a company to clean the vents and during that cleaning they were informed that there was a carbon monoxide issue and they needed the furnace serviced.
The Landlord testified that the company hired to repair the furnace told them that the furnace needed to be replaced.

The Landlord testified that they also became aware of water issues in the basement and although they tried to repair the bathroom themselves, there were still issues with the water caused cracked tiles and visible stairs in the downstairs bathroom.

The Landlord testified that they had to take a loan and a second mortgage to afford the repairs and at the same time, their mortgage was up for renewal and the increase due to the higher interest rates were more than they could afford.
The Landlord testified that they did not know there were going to be these issues with the home and that they would no longer be able to afford to live in the house.

The Landlord testified that they were forced to sell the home before they lost it and as a result they were forced to move back in with their parents and store their belonging in a storage unit. She further testified that they lost money in the sale of the home due to the repairs they had to make. Analysis
The Tenants must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above.

The first and second elements of subsection 57(1)(a) are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on August 10, 2025, as a result of an N12 notice of termination served by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord moved into the unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenants vacated, I find that the Landlord provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that they moved into the rental unit the week of August 10 2025, right after the Tenants moved out.
The Tenant also gave straightforward and consistent evidence but I do not find that the Tenant’s testimony provided any evidence that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith, as noted above there is a statutory presumption of bad faith given that the Landlord advertised the unit for sale in the year following the Tenants’ departure.

The Landlord did not dispute the unit was listed for sale but testified that this was due to the unforeseen financial circumstances they found themselves in after having to make necessary repairs to the unit.

The Landlord's testimony on this point was consistent and I find that her evidence is credible and reliable. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the renovations and replacement of the furnace were not known before moving into the unit. Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did move into the unit within a reasonable time but then experienced of change in circumstances which resulted in them having to sell the home.

Therefore, I find the Landlord has rebutted the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith and has proven on a balance of probabilities that their original intent was genuine. The Tenants’ application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and/or RADHA SANGARAJU, SRIDHAR SANGARAJU and ROHIT SANGARAJU (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing, the named purchasers in the application (collectively, the “Purchasers”) requested, on consent with the Tenants, that they be removed as parties in the application.

Prior to granting the request, the Tenants were reminded that in the event the Purchasers were removed as parties, the Board would have no authority to award a remedy as against the Purchasers, irrespective of any factual findings made in the application. The Tenants advised they were not pursuing a ny remedies as against the Purchasers and sought only remedies as against the Landlord.
In accordance with the Purchasers’ request and on consent with the Tenants, the purchasers [name], Sridhar Sangaraju and Rohit Sangaraju were removed as parties in the application. T5 Application
The Tenant’s T5 Application was filed January 11, 2023 and claims the Landlord gave them an N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice, and no person referred to in clause 49 occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. To be successful in their T5 application, the Tenant must establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(b) on a balance of probabilities: First, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act (the N12 notice) in bad faith; Second, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or Board order based on the N12 notice; Third, that the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

The Tenant [name] Popovich-Ignjic (IP) testified the tenancy commenced in March 2019 and that they were good tenants, paying rent on time and looking after the property. At the relevant time, IP resided at the rental unit with her spouse and two children, ages 7 and 22. The monthly rent was $2000/month.

In July 2022, the Tenants received a form N12 (the “Form N12”) from the Landlord by way of text communication from the Landlords’ agent. The Form N12 stipulated that the Landlord entered into an agreement of purchase and sale (the “Agreement”) and that the purchasers in good faith require possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by the purchaser. No declaration/affidavit was received from the Purchasers at this time, or anytime thereafter. The Tenant IP testified the Tenants vacated the rental unit on October 15, 2022, being a few months after receiving the Form N12 notice. When the rental unit was not occupied by the Purchasers in the months that followed, IP testified it became clear that the Form N12 was given in bad faith by the Landlord in order to help facilitate a sale to the Purchasers as the Landlord “wanted to sell no matter what”

It is not disputed that the Purchasers did not move into the rental unit. The purchaser Sridhar Sangaraju (SS) testified the Purchasers sought vacant possession from the Landlord, as the property was to be used for “investment p urposes”. SS further explained that the Purchasers did not represent to the Landlord, or any other person, that they would be moving into the rental unit for their own personal use . While SS conceded being aware that the property was tenanted when the Agreement was signed, SS testified he was unaware of how vacant possession was ultimately achieved by the Landlord.

The purchaser’s real estate agent [name] (SB) testified - somewhat surprisingly - that he was unsure as t o the Purchasers’ intended purpose for the property. Regardless, SB denied ever communicating to the Landlord/Landlord’s agent that the Purchasers sought vacant possession for the purpose of residential occupation . Interestingly, SB acknowledged receiving an email on July 29, 2022 from the Landlord’s real estate agent which enclosed a copy of a Form N12 purportedly given to the Tenants by the Landlord. SB testified he forwarded the email and Form N12 attachment to the Purchasers, however, the purchaser Rohit Sangaraju (RS) testified he did not recall receiving this email. Analysis

The evidence is clear the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice given by the Landlord and that the Purchasers did not move into the rental unit. The issue in this application is whether the Form N12 was served in bad faith.
The onus to prove the allegations on a balance of probabilities rest with the Tenant s. For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied the Tenant has satisfied the requisite onus.

As a starting point, I note it is somewhat suspicious that the Purchaser’s agent, SB, received an email from the Landlord’s agent which enclosed a Form N12 - and which SB had purportedly forwarded to the Purchasers (for which the Purchasers denied having any knowledge). Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Purchasers are not a party to this application and the uncontested evidence presented does not support the Landlord’s ultimate decision to serve the Form N12 upon the Tenants. In this regard, the purchaser did not sign a declaration/affidavit indicating they would be moving into the property, nor does it appear from the uncontested evidence that the Landlord was given any other written or oral indication that the Purchasers would be occupying the rental unit. In the absence of any alternative explanation, I interpret the Landlord’s service of the Form N12 as an attempt to obtain vacant possession, without the requisite grounds for termination under the Act. I therefore find the Form N12 was given to the Tenants in bad faith. Remedies
The next issue to be determined is remedies.

The Tenant’s application seeks a one-year rent differential of $12,000.00, as the Tenants new accommodations costed $3000/month, as opposed to $2000/month at the rental unit. IP testified alternative accommodations were sought after receiving the Form N12, however the Tenants’ housing options were limited as “nothing was available” . Eventually, after viewing approximately 5 -6 places, the Tenants secured alternative accommodations and vacated the rental unit on October 15, 2022

Both places are townhouses, comprising 3 bedrooms and 4 bathrooms . I am satisfied the new accommodations were somewhat comparable to the rental unit and that the Tenants took reasonable steps to secure appropriate accommodations . I therefore find it is reasonable for the requested sum of $12,000.00 to be awarded to the Tenants.

The Tenant’s application also seeks moving and storage costs of $3178.00. This claim is denied as many of the expenses clamed relate to such things such as deposits and betterments at the new home. The Tenants also produced no documentation in support of the alleged costs incurred; in the circumstances, I find that insufficient evidence was led in support of this claim.
ordered: 1. [name], Sridhar Sangaraju and Rohit Sangaraju are removed as parties. 2. The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $12,053.00. This amount represents: • $12,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after leaving the rental unit; and, • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application. 3. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant filed their application with the Board on February 18, 2025. The Tenant filed a request to amend the application on or about August 7, 2025. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not oppose the amendments requested and acknowledged having received a copy of the amended application. Accordingly, the request to amend the application was granted.
It was not disputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 16, 2026.

The maintenance issues and/or allegations of disrepair as claimed in the application are as follows: • the freezer in the fridge stopped working and the replacement fridge leaked; • there were mice in the unit; • the dryer did not function properly and/or safely and this resulted in a fire; and • the Landlord failed to maintain the yard and/or gardens.

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities one of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlords must compensate the Tenant in accordance with the order below. Freezer / Fridge

The Tenant testified that she lived in the rental unit with her mother. Her mother has serious health issues and the Tenant is her primary caregiver. The Tenant also gave evidence regarding her own health issues and explained that she has mobility issues.

As a result of the Tenant’s and her mother’s health issues, they kept the fridge fully stalked with food at all times as getting out to shop was difficult and/or challenging. In addition, they asked people entering the unit to wear a mask.

The fridge became an issue for the Tenant in January 2025. In this regard, the Tenant stated that she emailed the Landlord, [name] (‘SV’), on January 11, 2025 to advise that the freezer portion of the fridge was not working. The next day she sent a follow up email to SV about the freezer because items were beginning to perish and to advise that she would be reaching out to a technician to have the fridge serviced. A copy of the aforesaid emails were tendered as evidence.

After not hearing from SV, on or about January 13, 2025, the Tenant had an appliance repair contractor attend the rental unit to inspect the fridge. The Tenant was told that a compressor needed to be ordered to fix the issue. The Tenant paid the contractor a deposit of $800.00 to order the compressor and make the necessary repairs. The contractor said they would order the compressor and come back and do the repairs. However, he never returned and kept the Tenant’s money. A copy of the receipt for the deposit was tendered as evidence.

The Tenant stated that she and her mother were not able to eat all the food from the freezer and the fridge and so a lot of food had to be thrown out because it had gone bad. The Tenant estimate the value of the food lost was approximately $3,000.00.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that the fridge was not replaced until sometime in February 2025 and that this was due to her legal representative contacting the Landlords. The fridge that was ultimately delivered was an old fridge of lesser value as it was smaller and did not fill the space and was leaking and smelled. A photo of the replacement fridge was tendered as evidence.

The Landlords were advised that the replacement fridge was leaking and a repair person was sent toward the end of February 2025 to address the leak. However, the fridge continued to leak and the Tenant emailed the Landlords regarding this on April 14, 2025. A copy of the email was tendered as evidence.

Komanthi [name] (‘KS’) testified on behalf of the Landlords. It was her evidence that the Tenant was given the Landlords’ phone number when she moved in and also both of the Landlords’ emails. She stated that the Landlords did not receive the Tenant’s complaint about the freezer not working in the fridge on January 10, 2025 because the Tenant only sent it to SV’s email and that email was no longer active. The Landlords later learned of the freezer not working through their legal representative on January 24, 2025.

A summary of KS’s evidence with respect to the steps taken by the Landlords to address the freezer/fridge issue are as follows: • On January 24, 2025 an email was sent to the Tenant’s Legal Representative advising the Landlords would inspect the fridge on January 25, 2025; • A fridge technician was scheduled for January 26, 2025 and did attend the unit on this date; • After being advised by the fridge technician that the freezer was not fixable, the Landlords advised the Tenant by email that they were looking for a replacement fridge. • A new fridge was purchased from Leons on January 28, 2025 and it was to be delivered by Leons. The new fridge was to be delivered on January 31, 2025. [name] of the fridge did not occur on January 31, 2025 because the Tenant insisted the delivery people where masks in the unit and the delivery people were not comfortable with this. They asked if the Tenant and her mother could wait upstairs while the fridge was being delivered. The Tenant refused and the fridge was returned to Leons. • The Landlords contacted Leons again to reschedule the delivery with different delivery people. A new delivery date of February 4, 2025 was scheduled. • Delivery of the fridge did not occur on February 4, 2025 as the Tenant was wearing personal protective equipment that gave the delivery people the impression that she was sick. The Tenant refused to wait elsewhere while the delivery was completed and so the delivery people did not feel comfortable entering the rental unit to deliver the fridge. A copy of screen shots of the delivery comments from Leons were tendered as evidence. • The Landlords contacted Leons again regarding delivery of the fridge and the fridge was supposed to be delivered on February 6, 2025. However, the delivery was cancelled due to severe weather. As a solution, the Landlords decided to personally deliver their fridge, that was less than 2 years old and in good working condition, to the Tenant. The Landlords’ fridge was delivered successfully and was clean and working when they left the unit. However, approximately 30 minutes after leaving the Tenant claimed it was leaking. The Landlords responded right away that it was likely snow or ice from outside that had stuck to the bottom and was melting and asked if they could come back to inspect it. However, the Tenant did not respond. • No further complaints were received about the fridge until April 14, 2025. The Landlord had the fridge repaired on April 18, 2025. A copy of the invoice from the appliance technician was tendered as evidence. Mice

It was the Tenant’s evidence that there was an ongoing rodent issue in the home that was never resolved. The Tenant filed a T2 application with the Board and obtained an order, LTB-T-072704-23 (the ‘[name]’), for a rent abatement from August 15, 2022 to August 13, 2024. The Tenant tendered a photo of a dead mouse and a box full of mouse feces taken on or about April 23, 2025 as evidence. The Tenant advised the Landlords of the ongoing rodent issue by email on April 14, 2025 and January 2, 2026.

It was the Landlords’ evidence that a technician was hired and treated the rental unit on April 18, 2025 and on June 13, 2025. A copy of the invoices from the pest control company for the aforesaid treatments were tendered as evidence. No further complaints regarding rodents were received until January 2, 2026. Dryer

It was the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord had been made aware that the dryer was operating in an unsafe condition. Specifically, that smoke was coming from the dryer. The Tenant sent the Landlords an email regarding this on April 14, 2025. The Tenant stated that the Landlords took the position that the dryer was still drying the clothes and so they were not prepared to replace it despite smoke coming from it.

On or about June 13, 2025, there was a fire in the dryer. The Tenant described hearing a loud pop at approximately 4:00 am. She was using the dryer at this time to dry a towel. She then started to smell smoke and heard the smoke detector go off. The Tenant called the fire department and they attended shortly after. The Tenant obtained a copy of the fire report, which was tendered as evidence. The report stated that the fire department personnel investigated the scene and noted the smell of electrical burning in the basement, light smoke and no flames. The dryer was unplugged upon arrival. When the dryer was plugged back in smoke came out of the dryer. The power to the dryer was isolated as it could not removed at the time and a fan was set up to remove the light smoke in the house.

The Tenant testified that the impact of the fire was profound as she and her mother feared for their lives. The Tenant expressed concerns of being able to escape a fire as she uses a cane and her and her mother are unable to move swiftly.

It was the Landlords’ evidence that they had the dryer inspected on April 18, 2025. A copy of the invoice was tendered as evidence. In the invoice the technician describes the complaint as the dryer making a grinding metallic sound and started smoking. The invoice indicates that the work performed by the technician on the dryer was the cleaning of the vent. The Landlords denied receiving another complaint about the dryer until the alleged fire incident on June 13, 2025. KS stated that she went to the rental unit the same day to find out what was going on and arranged for an electrician to attend the next day. The electrician advised that nothing was wrong with the electrical connection. After this was ruled out, the Landlords purchased a new dryer the next day and had it delivered to the rental unit on June 20, 2025. A copy of the receipt for the new dryer was tendered as evidence. Yard/Garden Maintenance

It was the Tenant’s evidence that the yard and garden maintenance was the responsibility of the Landlords under the lease. Despite this, she had to pay for lawn maintenance out of her own pocket. The Landlord purchased a lawnmower and extension cord and told the Tenant that it was her job to maintain the grass. The Tenant advised the Landlord that she would not be cutting the grass and would have to hire someone to do it. This issue was also addressed in the [name] but it only covers the period up to June 1, 2024. The parties reached an agreement regarding the grass cutting in interim order LTB-T-014324- 25-IN, issued on August 26, 2026 (the ‘Interim Order’). Accordingly, the Tenant was only seeking remedy for the period of June 2, 2024 to August 26, 2025.
The Tenant tendered a video of the grass being mowed by someone else on June 9, 2025 as evidence. The Tenant stated that she paid the person $50.00 to mow the lawn.

No direct evidence was given by the Landlords regarding the yard maintenance. However, the Landlords’ Legal Representative challenged the frequency of the grass cutting and actual costs incurred by the Tenant during cross examination. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act places an obligation on the landlord to maintain a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and in compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.
The existence of disrepair or non-compliance with standards does not in itself automatically mean there has been a breach of the Act and entitle a tenant to remedies.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the Landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the Landlords responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a Landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Freezer / Fridge

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find it more likely than not that the Landlords did not become aware of the freezer issue until January 24, 2025. The Tenant did not deny that her first two emails were sent to only one of the Landlords and that she did not try calling the Landlords or emailing the other Landlord when she received no response from SV.

Section 16 of the Act requires parties to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. I do not find that the Tenant did so in this case. In this regard, the Tenant should have tried contacting the other Landlord by email and tried calling the number provided for the Landlords to alert the Landlords of the issue. However, she did not do so and, instead, she hired an appliance technician to try and fix the fridge without the Landlords’ permission.

Upon learning of the freezer issue on January 24, 2025, the Landlords moved swiftly to inspect the fridge, hired a technician and ordered a replacement fridge. The Landlord attempted to have a new fridge delivered three times. Two of the deliveries were canceled because the Tenant insisted that the delivery personnel wear masks and the third was cancelled due to the weather.

I understand that the Tenant had concerns about her and her mother’s health that made the Tenant hesitant to allow people in the unit without a mask on. However, I do not find the Tenant’s actions reasonable in the circumstances and find that this delayed resolving the issue.

The Landlords did not have control over the actions of the Leon’s delivery personnel and the testimony of KS and the documentation provided suggests that the Landlords made Leon’s aware that the Tenant wanted delivery personnel to be masked. In any event, on both occasions when [name] attempted to deliver a reasonable suggestion was made for the Tenant and her mother to go to another area of the home to wait while the fridge was being delivered but this was refused by the Tenant. I understand that this may not have been the accommodation that the Tenant wanted but, in my view, it was a reasonable form of accommodation and there was no evidence to suggest that it would have caused hardship to the Tenant or her mother.

The replacement fridge provided by the Landlord was not as esthetically pleasing as the previous fridge as it was not stainless steel and did not fill up the same space in the kitchen fully. However, this is not disrepair. The Tenant suggested that the fridge was in poor condition and smelled. However, the photos tendered as evidence by the Landlords show a clean fridge that appears to be relatively new. The Tenant’s testimony regarding the alleged odour was vague and does not appear to be mentioned to the Landlord until April 14, 2025. In response, the Landlord had the fridge serviced on April 18, 2025 to address leaking. There was no mention of smell in the invoice from the contractor and there were no further reports of odour after this date.

For the reasons provided above, I find that the Landlords responded to the Tenant’s complaints regarding the freezer and the replacement fridge within a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner. The Tenant did not make all reasonable efforts to notify the Landlords of the issue with the freezer when it first began and did not have permission from the Landlords to hire a fridge technician or to authorize the fridge technician to do any work to the fridge. Accordingly, no remedies shall be granted in relation to this issue. Mice

The evidence provided demonstrates that the Tenant complained to the Landlord on April 14, 2025 and on January 2, 2026 regarding mice in the unit. The Landlord had the unit treated for mice in April and June 2025 and the Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord had the unit treated again shortly after the email was sent in January 2026.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the Landlords failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the mice issue. In this regard, when the Tenant complained, the Landlords responded within a reasonable time and arranged for the unit to be treated for rodents. There was no evidence to suggest that this response was unreasonable in the circumstances. Accordingly, no remedies shall be granted in relation to this issue. [name]

The Tenant suggested that the Landlords knew or ought to have known that the dryer was smoking and unsafe and that their negligence led to the alleged fire on June 13, 2025. I disagree. The evidence shows the Tenant complained to the Landlords about the dryer on April 14, 2025 and that the Landlords had it inspected and had the vent cleaned on April 18, 2025. There were no other complaints about the dryer smoking or being unsafe until June 13, 2025 when the fire department came. On that same date, the Landlords attended the unit and made arrangements for an electrician to inspect the issue. After electrical was ruled out, the Landlord proceeded to purchase a dryer and have it delivered within a week.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached their obligations under section 20 of the Act. In this regard, I find that the Landlords responded to the Tenant’s complaints regarding the dryer within a reasonable time and within a reasonable manner. Accordingly, no remedies shall be ordered in relation to this issue. Yard/Garden Maintenance
It was not necessarily disputed by the Landlords that they were responsible for the yard maintenance under the lease or that the Tenant had to arrange for the grass to be cut from time to time.

The Tenant’s evidence with respect to the yard/garden maintenance issue is very vague and mainly consisted of allegations of the grass not being cut regularly and that she was unable to do so because of her health issues and so she had to hire someone to do it. However, it was not clear how many times she arranged to have the grass cut and how much it cost her. The Tenant testified to paying the person in the video tendered as evidence $50.00 to cut the grass. She said that she did not have receipts because they only accepted cash. The video tendered as evidence shows the grass to be fairly long and the area of grass being cut as relatively small.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that the Landlords failed to have the grass cut on a regular basis and that this is a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act.

The Tenant requested a 10% rent abatement for the spring and summer months during which the yard and garden maintenance was not performed but later narrowed this period to June 2, 2024 to August 26, 2025, having considered the [name] and the Interim Order. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I do not find the percentage of abatement requested to be appropriate in the circumstances.

Abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that rent is charged in exchange for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving those goods and services then the rent should be abated in a sum proportional to the difference between what is being charged and what is being received.

In other words, an abatement of rent can be viewed as compensation to the tenant for the inadequate state of repair and any inconvenience or actual loss of use of the rental unit. In determining the amount of an abatement of rent, I have to consider the impact on the Tenant.

Limited evidence was given with respect to how the Landlords’ failure to maintain the lawn impacted the Tenant. That said, I accept that the Tenant was burdened with having to arrange for grass cutting when it was not her responsibility and I accept that it was frustrating for her as she was not in a position to do it herself and likely had to pay someone something for grass cutting services.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, my experience with similar cases, and review of other decisions of the Board, I find an abatement $282.02 to be appropriate in the circumstances. This represents a 2% rent abatement for approximately an 8 month period, being for the periods of June 2, 2024 to September 30, 2024 (121 days) and May 1, 2025 to August 26, 2025 (118 days)/. The abatement is calculated as follows: $1,800.00 x 12 / 365 = 59.18 per diem rent x 2% = $1.18 per day x 239 days = $282.02. The aforesaid periods of time are based on my review of the [name], the Interim Order and when grass typically starts to require regular cutting in Ontario.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $330.02. This amount represents: • $282.02 for a rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
It is undisputed that the Tenant was evicted by the sheriff.

The Tenant alleges that he was “illegally” locked out. He claims that he was never provided any notice, nothing was ever explained to him, no lease agreement was ever signed, and he was generally unaware of any proceeding against him. His theory is that the agents claiming to be the sheriff showed up out of the blue and evicted him without proper authority or documentation. These agents called the police, and they helped the sheriff escort him out of the building.
The LTB terminated this tenancy by order LTB-L-010817-24 issued on May 23, 2024, effective June 30, 2024 (the ‘Eviction Order’). The Tenant did request a review of this order but was not successful.

The Tenant denied receiving the Notice of Vacant possession. He claimed that the sheriff office also did not have a record if other than the paperwork filed by the Landlord to seek termination of the tenancy. The Tenant provided in evidence the documents retrieved from the Sheriff’s office that demonstrate the Landlord had filed for eviction. I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant was properly served with the Eviction Order. He may have chosen to ignore the documents, but this is inconsequential.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant received the notice of the upcoming eviction by the sheriff in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). It was properly served in accordance with the Act and the Rules. The Tenant’s denials of receipt are unpersuasive.

I find that the Landlord did not act contrary to the Act when the locks were changed. The locks were changed by a sheriff pursuant to an eviction order. S. 39(b) states that a landlord is not entitled to recover possession of the rental unit without an eviction order from the LTB. The Landlord had an eviction order and I find that they were entitled to recover possession of the rental unit.

Under s. 24 a landlord may not alter the locking mechanism during a tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit. The Landlord changed the locks after the tenancy was terminated by the LTB, and the Tenant was evicted. The locks were therefore not changed during the [name] occupancy.
The Tenant’s claim of illegal lockout is therefore dismissed.

The Tenant undisputed evidence was also that the Landlord allowed access into the unit for the Tenant to collect their medicine. The Tenant confirmed that he was given a brief opportunity to return to the rental unit after the eviction and that entails him the status of being a tenant. 11. 41(2) and 41(3) require the Landlord to retain the property for 72 hours and to make it available to the Tenant. As such, I find that the Landlord was only allowing the Tenant to enter the rental unit for the purpose of retrieving their belongings. 12. The Tenant’s claim that the Landlord allowed the Tenant to re-enter the unit and as such, he is a tenant is therefore dismissed as well. 13. The Tenant didn’t claim any interference with his reasonable enjoyment or harassment independent of the Landlord’s alleged illegal lockout. The Landlord carried out the eviction in accordance with the Act. The Landlord didn’t call the police – the Sheriff did. He is also claimed that unknown people entered his unit (referring to the sheriffs). The Landlord has no control over OPP officers. The Tenant’s interactions with the police, if there was anything improper about them at all, are entirely unrelated to the Landlord and are outside my jurisdiction. 14. The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $11,988.74

On or about November 12, 2024 the Landlords served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination (“N12”) via mail. The N12 stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 and the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 served by the Landlords. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2025.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord [name] did not move into the rental unit as indicated in the N12 and supporting declaration. The Tenant [name] testified that she is friends with the neighbours of the rental unit and she was told that no one had moved in since they vacated the rental unit.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In a T5 application, the burden typically falls on the tenants to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith. However, with respect to the issue of bad faith, subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith as follows: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a) and (c), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
In other words, if section 57(5) of the Act applies, the burden falls on the Landlords to prove it is more likely than not that he served the N12 in good faith.

The presumption applies here because the rental unit was listed for sale on December 8, 2025 with a listing expiry of June 30, 2026. DOES THE LANDLORDS’ EVIDENCE ESTABLISH IT IS MORE LIKELY THAN NOT THE N12 WAS SERVED IN GOOD FAITH?
For the reasons that follow I am not satisfied the Landlords have met their burden of proof.
The Landlord [name] testified that he was having financial troubles and that after doing some renovations the Landlords listed the property for sale.

He further testified that his son [name] had a co-op near the rental unit in the fall until January and that he would spend his time between his residence and [name], the rental unit and the Landlord [name]’s residence. 12. [name] [name] states that his son would use the rental unit for the pool or when on vacation with his friends. 13. The Landlords offered no corroborating documentation of any alleged financial difficulties that required them to list the unit for sale. 14. I find it more likely than not that the Landlords listed the rental unit for sale at the Landlord [name]’s co-op placement was nearing an end and he would no longer require the rental unit. 15. I am not satisfied that it is more likely than not that the Landlords served the N12 in good faith. The Landlords’ evidence is insufficient to rebut the presumption in s. 56(5). 16. Additionally I am not satisfied that the Landlord [name] moved into the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of least one year. On the evidence before me the Landlord [name] would use the property occasionally during a co-op placement and when he wanted to use the pool or for vacation. Remedies Rent Differential 17. The Tenants testified that the rent for the rental unit was $3,997.50 per month, and the Tenants moved into another rental unit for $5,000.00 a month starting July 1, 2025. The rent differential sought is $1,002.50 per month for a period of one year. The Tenants testified that their new rental unit has an additional bedroom and bathroom and is larger than the rental unit. 18. With respect to quantum, some of the increase in rent that occurred here is attributable to the rise in market rent but some of it is also arguably attributable to the fact that the new rental unit has an additional bedroom and bathroom. The Tenants are entitled to rent differential for an equivalent unit but not for a bigger one. Therefore, the rent differential claimed per month of $1,002.50 should be reduced given that the number of bedrooms and bathrooms increased. It seems to me a fair rent differential would be $500.00 per month totalling $6,000.00 for the period of one-year. 19. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenant $6,000.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. Moving Expenses 20. The Tenants seek their reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit as follows: • $1,130.00 to relocate security camera’s; • $190.00 for cleaning; • $4,250.00 for movers; • $350.00 to have televisions removed and re-mounted at the new rental unit; and • $1,046.72 to have furniture re-assembled. • $110.74 to have mail forwarded to their new address with Canada Post. 21. The Tenant’s provided receipts for their alleged out-of-pocket expenses associated with moving, storage and other like expenses. 22. In the circumstances I am not satisfied that cleaning in the amount of $190.00 and furniture re-assembly in the amount of $1,046.72 is reasonable. 23. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $5,840.74 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Compensation 24. The Tenants seek $2,088.00 in general damages and their new rental unit is further from work and school and has added to commute times. The compensation sought is based on the increase time and distance travelled. 25. The Act specifically indicates that general compensation does not require proof of out of pocket expenses, meaning it is intended to capture the non-tangible impact of having to leave one’s home. But here, the Tenants led little to no evidence of the impact on them of having to move except that the Tenants commute for work and school has been increased. As a result, in the absence of further evidence of impact on the Tenants of the move, I am of the view that only a nominal amount for general compensation should be ordered which I fix at $100.00. Administrative Fine 26. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline # 16 on Administrative Fines says: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 27. I am not satisfied on the evidence before me that an administrative fine against the Landlords is appropriate in the circumstances as the other remedies in this order will provide an adequate deterrence to the Landlords.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $11,988.74. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for increased rent the Tenants have or will incur for the one-year period from July 1, 2025. • $5,840.74 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $100.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a duplex located at [address]nue in Toronto, Ontario. The Tenants resided in the rental unit from June 4, 2025 to August 10, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (DA)

DA testified that he and his wife moved into the duplex on June 4, 2025. He stated that after they moved in, the Landlord wanted to change the terms of their lease and the Tenants were not agreeable to that. He stated that the Landlord started harassing them, blackmailing them, using aggressive and hostile language and calling them occupants instead of Tenants.

DA stated that on June 24, 2025 they were served with an N12 notice stating that the Landlord, her spouse and a care provider would be moving into the rental unit with a termination date of August 31, 2025. The Tenant believed that the Landlord was retaliating and that the Landlord, who lived in Nova Scotia, would not be moving into the rental unit.

The Tenant stated that they vacated the rental unit on August 10, 2025 and they do not believe that the Landlord moved into the unit or is residing there now. He referred me to DOC #7396430 which included text messages from his wife to the Landlord’s full-time handyman, [name]. The Landlord’s Legal Representative objected to the entering of this document because of the number of redactions and lack of contact information. Based on my review,the document was not entered as an exhibit. 7. [name] testified that she texted the Landlord’s handyman, [name] and asked if [name] or her husband moved to Rosemount and Jorge replied that people from Spain were residing in both floors of the rental. The Tenant stated that [name] response was on November 8, 2025. Procedural Issue – Lack of Direct Evidence 8. At this time, I asked the Tenants if they had any direct evidence to suggest that the Landlord was not residing in the rental unit and [name] brought up the Landlord’s request to review a previous order. [name] stated that the Landlord told the Board in March of 2026 that no one was home at [address]nue (to receive the Notice of Hearing) and requested that it be sent to her Nova Scotia address. 9. [name] also stated that the Landlord operates a hotel in Nova Scotia and could not possibly do this and reside in Toronto at the same time. Further, he stated that the Landlord’s driver’s license states that she resides at 3 [address]nue not 5 [address]nue which is the rental unit. 10. Although I provided many opportunities for the Tenants to provide some type of document to substantiate their application, they had no such documents or testimony. 11. This is the Tenants’ application and they bear the onus of providing sufficient information to satisfy me that their version is more believable on a balance of probabilities than the Landlord’s version. 12. The Tenants’ text message document was a 27-page document with no verifiable identifiers for the parties involved. The document was also heavily redacted, so much so that full pages were blank causing me to reject this as an exhibit. 13. As this document represented the crux of their case, [name] read out the text message between herself and the Landlord’s handyman. However, the Tenants did not arrange for the Landlord’s handyman to attend the hearing to be a witness which would have been direct evidence. 14. Based on the fact that the only evidence that the Tenants had to support their case was [name] brief conversation with the Landlord’s handyman, I dismissed the application. Analysis 15. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 16. The Tenants proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a condo in a multi-condo building and the Tenant resided in Apt.# 1501 from June 20, 2018 until March 31, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (RR)

RR testified that he was given an N12 notice of termination on February 25, 2025 with a termination date of April 30, 2025. He stated that the Landlord was going to move into his unit and he understood that [name] would be moving in because the form was signed by [name].

The Tenant stated that he vacated the rental unit at the end of March of 2025 and he moved into a rental unit directly across the street. He stated that he works remotely and because he is home all of the time, he saw that a woman moved into his unit and noted that she was sitting on the balcony regularly. He stated that a friend of his who resides in his original building on the same floor advised him that the person who moved in is from the [name] area and that his friend sees her in the gym.

RR does not believe that the Landlord moved in after he left and he stated that in January of 2026, a couple moved into the unit. He stated that this couple has also been seen by his friend who resides on the same floor and that they are regularly seen in the gym.

The Tenant believes that the Landlord gave him the N12 notice in bad faith because the Landlord wanted him to sign a new lease when she realized that he had a new girlfriend. RR stated that the Landlord gave him a new lease with the rental amount blank, she wanted to increase the rent above the guideline and because he would not agree, he believed that the Landlord gave him this N12 notice.
RR is seeking one month’s compensation that he did not receive from the Landlord, the return of a $500.00 security deposit and his application fee. Evidence of Dawn Duesbury, [name] (DD)

DD testified that she is a tenant of the condo building located at 225 Sackville Street and she resides in Apt. #1503 which is just a couple of doors down from the residential unit. She stated that she has met a 35-40 year old woman a few times who has been apparently living in Apt. #1501 and she provided that information to the Tenant.

DD stated that she met the new tenant in May of 2025 and saw her throughout 2025. However, she stated that in January or February of 2026, she noted that a new couple had moved into Apt. #1501. Evidence of Landlord, [name] (TC)

The Landlord was very adamant that she did move into the rental unit herself on April 1, 2025 and that she shares her time between her house (with her children and abusive husband) and her condo which she uses as a safehouse. She stated that she is regularly beaten by her spouse, she often has black eyes and bruises and she emails pictures of herself to the Board. She stated that she has been living in this abusive relationship for years but she cannot leave her children. She stated that is why she called into the hearing by phone today rather than appear on video. 12. [name] stated that she felt that she had every right to require the Tenant to sign a new lease as his previous girlfriend moved out and a new girlfriend moved in. She stated that she had not approved the new girlfriend which is why the Tenant had to sign a new lease. However she stated that is not why she gave the Tenant an N12 notice. 13. The Landlord stated that she has been wanting to remove herself from this abusive relationship for years but her husband threatens her and her children. She stated that this is the only way that she could ensure that she has a safe area to escape when her husband attacks her. 14. [name] stated that the Tenant’s witness’ testimony was actually about [name] meeting her for the first time. Ms. [name]name] stated that she is the person who shows up at the condo, sits on the balcony and resides there for periods of time. Ms. [name]name] stated that she and her friend both reside in the condo and that her friend stays there all of the time. 15. The Landlord asked me if she had the right to request that the Tenant sign a new lease when the Tenant’s girlfriend changed and I explained the responsibilities of each party. She asked if she was supposed to pay the Tenant something for moving out and I responded that one month’s compensation was required to be paid to the Tenant. The Landlord then stated that if she had known about that responsibility, she would have paid the $1,943.66 to the Tenant. The Landlord requested that I tell her when that amount had to be paid to the Tenant because she intended to pay that amount to him. Analysis 16. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 17. The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. I am not persuaded that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. 18. The Tenant’s testimony included that he saw a woman in his old apartment who also sat out on the balcony. He was able to see this from his new apartment which was across the road from his old building. 19. The Tenant’s witness, who resides on the same floor as Apt. #1501, stated that she spoke with a woman who resided in that unit a few times. 20. The Landlord attended the hearing by phone and stated that she has been residing in the unit since April 1, 2025. 21. This is the Tenant’s application and he has the onus of providing sufficient information to convince me on a balance of probabilities that his story is more believable than the Landlord’s story. 22. The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed.

Based on the consent between the parties regarding the compensation for the N12 notice, I am ordering that the Landlord pay the amount of $1,943.66 to the Tenant by July 17, 2026. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
