issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord 's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (LTB-T-015201-25) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and, withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (LTB-T-027528-25) The applications were heard by videoconference on July 8, 2026. The Landlord [name], the Landlord [name]’s representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,396.00.

The Tenant’s T6 Application was brought pursuant to s.29(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and alleges the Landlords breached an obligation under s.20(1): and LTB-T-027528-25 A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards

In addition to the T6 Application, the Tenant filed a T2 Application pursuant to s.29(1) of the Act, alleging the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them, and/or substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, or with the reasonable supply of a vital service the Landlord is obligated to supply.
The T2 and T6 applications were filed, respectively, on April 2, 2025 and March 5, 2025.
The residential complex is comprised of 3 floors, with the Landlords residing in an upper unit and the Tenant residing in one of the two lower units.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024 and and vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025. The monthly rent was $2000/month. Lack of Heat
The Tenant [name] (the “Tenant” or “Tenant JT”) alleges that inadequate heat was provided to the rental unit.

The Tenant JT testified the Landlord was notified of the cold temperature towards the end of October 2024. A text message was produced from November 10, 2024 whereby the [name] advised the Landlord as follows: …I noticed it gets very cold before midnight through the entire morning, I’m trying like you said with my heater but its not enough, If you want I get a smart thermostat today that records all the information 24/7….

According to JT, the lack of heat concerns were ignored by the Landlord and remained unresolved, as supported by subsequent text communications. For instance, on January 23, 2025, the Landlord text: “ Hi [name], I received your message, and I understand you’re asking for cooperation. However, I feel that there hasn’t been much cooperation on your side either…” Later, on January 29, 2025, the Tenant texted the Landlord “Turn off the cold ac blowing in the basement…I need hot air not cold please”, to which the Landlord responded “stop….imagining stuff”.

In an effort to address the lack of heat, t he Tenant purchased two electric heaters . The Tenant also installed 3 thermostats in the kitchen, bedroom and hallway areas. Thermostat readings from February 15, 2025 were produced, showing temperatures of 15.9 C, 16.8 C and 17.5 C. According to the Tenant JT, the temperatures would consistently be around 16- 17 C and would get down to 13 C. Overall, the lack of heat resulted in an uncomfortable and stressful living environment which the Tenant stated impacted his sleep. and LTB-T-027528-25

The Landlord’s [name] (the “Landlord” or “Landlord SG”) lived in the upper unit and testified there was no issue with heat, stating the building has central heating and the other basement tenant never complained . While the Landlord SG testified her spouse [name] (MG) investigated the Tenant’s concerns, MG was not in attendance at the hearing or otherwise called to testify.

Upon hearing all the evidence, I find the Tenant’s oral testimony as sup ported by text communications and temperature readings, to be more reliable than the Landlord’s general denial. I therefore find the heat was inadequate in the rental unit and find the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations as a result. At the hearing, the Tenant indicated he sought only a $2 ,150.00 abatement in respect of the T6 Application (as opposed to the $5,375.00 abatement in the application). Here, I find there was some disruption to the Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit from November 2024 onwards. Accordingly, I find a rent abatement of approximately 20% from November 2024 through to March 2025 to be reasonable in the circumstances, for a total abatement of $2,150.00. Stove-top element/hood fan

The Tenant alleges one of four stove-top elements, including the oven hood fan stopped working. While the Tenant acknowledged having use of the remaining three stove-top elements, the Tenant stated the non -functioning element was unsafe and posed a safety concern. Furthermore, with respect to the hood fan, the Tenant testified he was often reluctant to cook due to fog that would arise as a result.
The onus to prove the allegations rest with the Tenant.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477 (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding breach and/or remedy and that this is consistent with the Board’s Interpretation Guideline #5

While not a requirement to produce , the Tenant did not produce any supporting documentation, pictures or messages in support of the maintenance issues. The Landlord, in response, produced a video whereby the Tenant acknowledges that the stovetop is working. The Landlord SG also testified that the purported non -functioning hood fan was never brought to the Landlords’ attention. Here, I am not satisfied the Tenant clearly communicated the purported maintenance issues to the Landlords, nor am I satisfied based upon the limited evidence provided that such issues impacted the Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit. These allegations are dismissed. and LTB-T-027528-25 Garage Door Keypad

The Tenant alleges the garage door [name] did not function as intended, stating the problem became worse over time . As such, in order to enter the garage and access the doorway leading to the rental unit, the Tenant had to use the garage door opener remote.

The Landlord submits there was no breach, as the Tenant always had an alternative means to access the rental unit. Regardless, the Landlord submits that the garage code was changed upon being advised of the issue, so as not to utilize the non-functioning button/number on the keypad.

Based upon the evidence presented, I do not find that the Tenant’s maintenance concern rises to the point of constituting a breach under the Act. Here, there is no suggestion that the Tenant was ever deprived of access to the rental unit and very little evidence was presented as to any inconvenience suffered by the Tenant as a result of having to use the garage door remote. This allegation is accordingly dismissed. Threat of eviction and accusations

The Tenant alleges that on January 28, 2025, the Landlord falsely accused the Tenant “taking drugs” and threatened to evict the Tenant without cause. In support, the Tenant produced a text communication which stated the following: You brought drink people in drugs to our house in the middle of the night many times. Its very easy to evacuate you immediately especially if we add negligent to pay rent Choice is yours

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $500 as a result of the eviction threat and false accusation. Although the Landlord’s text communication appears to be an isolated incident, I do find the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental. It is clear that the Tenant was made to feel unwelcome and that the Tenant was troubled by the accusation which the Tenant asserts was false. In the circumstances, I find a rent abatement of $150 to be reasonable in the circumstances.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $2,300.00.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $96.00 for the cost of filing both applications.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $2,396.00. and LTB-T-027528-25

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026 the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the outstanding balance. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $684.00.

The Tenant testified that she had moved into the residential complex in 1987 and that during most her time in the residential complex she had been sick. The Tenant once drove a scooter but now has a walker.

The Tenant testified that the residential complex does not possess any disability buttons in order to open doors. She testified that the doors are very heavy and that she was advised that by 2025, all buildings were required to have disability buttons to open doors in compliance with new measures to ensure disability accommodation. As of the date of the hearing, despite repeated requests by the Tenants for these buttons to be installed, nothing has been done by the Landlord.

Therefore, based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord and Landlord's Agent substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $684.00 and an order that the Landlord install disability buttons at each access and egress into the residential complex. The Tenant further requested updates about their installation.

While I had agreed to give the Landlord until May 31, 2026 to install this equipment, due to the age of this order and the fact that I am unsure what sort of timeline would be required to conduct this work, the Landlords will be given until August 31, 2026, to produce a timeline of work to be done in order to install the disability buttons.
Should the Landlord not provide the Tenant with an update of same on or before August 31, 2026, the Tenant will be permitted to deduct 10% of her lawful monthly rent until the work is complete.
I further find that a rent abatement of $684.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord and the Landlord's Agent shall pay the Tenant is $737.00. This amount represents: • $684.00 for a rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord and the Landlord’s agent shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026.

If the Landlord and the Landlord’s agent do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 29, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 29, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $684.00 from the lawful, monthly rent for August 2026
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
On or before August 31, 2026, the Landlord and the Landlord’s agent must develop and provide the Tenant with a plan to install disability buttons in the residential complex.

Should the Landlord fail to do so by this date, the Tenant is permitted to reduce her lawful monthly rent by 10% ($114.00) per month until a plan has been developed and provided to the Tenant. July 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, a preliminary issue was raised that the residential complex has sold, and the new Landlord is Homestead Land Holding Limited. The Tenant’s application lists both Homestead Land Holding Limited (new Landlord) and [organization] (former Landlord).

The Landlord parties agreed that despite any provision of the Act, including section 18 which provides that “covenants run with the land”, the appropriate party to be listed as the Landlord on the Tenant’s application is “[organization]”.

Both representatives for the named Landlord parties agreed that because of the contractual obligations set out in the purchase agreement for the property, the former Landlord remains responsible for liabilities arising during their ownership of the property.
Based on the submissions at the hearing, I am satisfied that [organization] is the appropriately named Landlord and Homestead Land Holding Limited is removed from the application. Limitation Period

The Board’s adjudicative record shows that the Tenant’s application was filed on February 24, 2025. Section 29(2) of the Act sets out a one-year limitation period after the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurs: (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
Accordingly, the earliest date from which the Tenant’s allegations may be considered is February 25, 2024. T2 Application- Substantial Interference
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that they were sent a notice from the Landlord to commence major repairs in December 2023. The Tenant also testified that they left the rental unit in December 2023 and stayed with their mother out of the country because they did not feel safe remaining in the rental unit.
The Tenant gave evidence that the repairs required her to move belongings, and she could not use her kitchen or bathroom during this time.
The Tenant submitted 13 black and white undated photographs showing the Tenant’s belongings not in closets or cupboards and various large holes in walls throughout the rental unit.

The Tenant gave evidence that because of the holes in the walls and ceiling she did not feel safe standing under the stove or cooking. The Tenant also testified that plastic covering taped over the holes in the rental unit would fall off, and the floor in the rental unit was dusty and dirty with work debris.
The Tenant further testified that the dust and debris was so unsafe that a piece of the ceiling fell on her head.
The Tenant also gave evidence that she was pregnant at the time and because the work required her to empty storage spaces in the rental unit, she was unable to use her bed or living spaces.
The Tenant did not specify an exact time period during which the work was being completed, when she was able to move her belongings back into the storage spaces, or when the work was completed.

The Tenant’s unspecific testimony was that the work commenced in December 2023 and persisted for months up to March 2024. The Tenant’s evidence is that even after she was permitted to use storage spaces in the rental unit the Landlord was still coming to the rental unit to complete plastering, sanding, and painting.

The Tenant also testified that during this time there were multiple water interruptions every time there was work being performed. The Tenant submitted notices from the Landlord advising that there would be work performed and water interruptions beginning September 3, 2024 (for six weeks), another interruption on October 21, 2024 (completion date April 2025), and January 9, 2025 (interruptions between January 13, 2025-January 17, 2025, during the hours of 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m.)
The Tenant testified that her water would be cut every single day that there was work being performed which was especially difficult during her recovery after her child’s birth.

The Tenant acknowledged during cross examination that she did not know when the photographs of the rental unit she submitted were taken. The Tenant testified that the holes in her ceiling were not repaired until some time in March or April, 2024.

The Tenant was also unspecific in her evidence testifying that if the Landlord advised that there would be a water interruption the water was cut off during the specified times. The Tenant’s evidence is that the water was cut “every single day” including September 3, 4, 5, and 6.
The Tenant testified that their water would be interrupted daily between September 2024 up to April 2025 during the specified work hours of 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s agent [name] (SC) testified that he is a property manger, and the residential complex consists of two towers with 117 units in each building. The towers are connected by one boiler system in the basement of the interconnected buildings.

SC testified that it was not possible the Tenant was without water daily between September 2024 and April 2025. SC’s evidence is that any water disruptions were in “different zones” and different areas of the residential complex.
SC acknowledged that there were intermittent water interruptions but testified that notice was always provided to the Tenant unless it was an emergency situation.

SC gave evidence that the issues raised in the Tenant’s application arise from a substantial work project undertaken by the Landlord. SC testified that notice was provided to all tenants about the scope of work, duration, and anticipated impact. The work was required due to leaks in the “upper zone” of the building’s risers because of non-functional valves.

The work required entire risers to be shut down to complete repairs and it was not possible to isolate specific rental units. Once work began in the upper zone of the risers it was determined that the whole building required pipe replacement. This project was completed and a subsequent project to replace the underground garage piping then began.
During the repairs there were complications involving sediment being dislodged and causing emergency issues that sometimes required additional unplanned water interruptions.

SC also testified that contractors would tape plastic garbage bags over holes in the rental unit until final drywall repairs and painting could be completed but denied ever receiving a complaint from the Tenant about the coverings coming down or debris falling.
SC disputed that the Tenant’s rental unit was dusty and dirty testifying that contractors would clean daily after performing work and did their best to clean and vacuum tenant’s units.
SC submitted copies of the scope of work document dated October 19, 2023, and the invoice for the work completed to the risers and pipe replacement dated February 12, 2024.
An invoice for the work completed underground in the garage dated September 19, 2024, was submitted, and the final invoice for all the work to the building’s risers was rendered on July 16, 2025.
SC submitted various photographs of the work being completed and explained that the project was significant affecting the entire residential complex.

SC also submitted copies of notices of entry for the Tenant’s rental unit requesting entry on March 12, 2024, and March 21, 2024. The first entry relates to an emergency entry for plumbing repairs, and the second entry is to repair the holes from the original work undertaken by the Landlord.

SC acknowledged that there were subsequent water disruptions between January 13 and January 17, 2025, but that there were individual risers being turned off during this time and the work was completed in “zones”.

During cross examination SC reiterated much of his initial testimony and explained that during the garage project the water interruptions would have been specific to individual risers, and the water was not turned off during the entire period. SC also acknowledged that despite providing an estimated completion date, the project did have some unanticipated delays. Analysis

The Tenant filed a T2 application pursuant to section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit while work was being completed in the rental unit.

Section 8 of Regulation 516/06 (O. Reg 516/06) sets out considerations applicable to the fact scenario advanced by the Tenant: 8. (1) In this section, “work” means maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex. (2) For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances. (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.

The earliest date from which the Tenant’s issues can be considered begins on February 25, 2024, and the Tenant’s evidence was unspecific as to whether the work to the pipes and risers was ongoing at this time, or whether it was simply the holes in the rental unit that required repair.

The evidence before me shows that the holes in the Tenant’s walls and ceiling were repaired some time in March 2024, and the only conclusion that can be reached based on the vague evidence from the Tenant is that the pipe work was completed by this time and the only repairs remaining were to the holes in the walls and ceiling.

The photographs depicting the walls and ceiling submitted by the Tenant do not show unsafe conditions and the Tenant did not submit evidence to support her position that the rental unit was uninhabitable.

There was no evidence that the rental unit was deemed uninhabitable by the City or municipal authority, and the Tenant’s assertion that there was dust and other safety concerns was not supported by corroborating evidence.

The holes in the walls and ceiling were aesthetically unpleasing however, based on the work being performed it took approximately one month from the completion of the pipe work to repair the walls which is not unreasonable in the circumstances.

There is insufficient evidence to conclude that there was any substantial work ongoing in the rental unit after February 25, 2024, and the Tenant’s rental unit was entirely repaired on or around March 27, 2024.

The Tenant did not provide testimony about when they could put their belongings back in the cupboards and storage area to determine whether it was an unreasonable length of time the Tenant was deprived of their storage areas.
Section 8 (3) of [name]. 516/06 requires that an interference during work is only substantial if it is unreasonable in the circumstances.

Based on the period from February 25, 2024, to March 27, 2024, I am not satisfied that any work being carried out by the Landlord was unreasonable in the circumstances, and therefore, it cannot be determined to be a “substantial” interference.

When considering the Tenant’s allegations in relation to water interruptions at the building, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that the risers were not all shut down daily since September 2024 up to April 2025.

The Tenant’s evidence in relation to this allegation is unsupported by evidence. The Tenant submitted notices from the Landlord that tells the Tenant when an interruption in water could be expected however, there was no definitive evidence proving the number of times the water was shut off, the dates of water interruptions, or the duration of any interruptions.

While it was acknowledged by CS that during this time there were water interruptions due to the work being performed, the Tenant has the burden to prove their allegations on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant’s evidence about the number and duration of water interruptions was speculative and lacked specifics or corroboration.

Accordingly, I do not find that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as a result of water interruptions during the work project.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on Sept ember 15, 2025, two days before a sheriff was to attend pursuant to an eviction order in LTB-L-034626-25 issued on July 2, 2025 (“L1 Order”). The Tenant, as of the date of this hearing, still owes the Landlords over $20,000.00 in arrears of rent as per the L1 Order.
It is not contested that t he Tenant returned the keys to the rental unit to the Landlords at the end of the tenancy, and as such were requesting the $200.00 key deposit be refunded.
The Landlords did not return the $200.00 key deposit to the Tenant. Instead, they indicated their intent to apply the amount against the arrears outstanding.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act provides a prohibition on additional charges to Tenants with narrow exceptions. Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulations”) provides an exception to allow refundable key deposits so long as they do not exceed the expected direct replacement costs. In this case, the tenancy agreement specified this key deposit would be returned to the Tenant upon the Tenant returning the keys to the Landlords.
The Landlord failed to return the key deposit to the Tenant as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

However, in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522, the Divisional Court found that when a tenant is entitled to compensation from a landlord but the tenant also owes the landlord rent arrears, the Board must off-set these amounts: [18] . . . While the tenants were entitled to $3,000.00 in compensation because of the N13 Notice, the landlord was owed more than $3,000.00 by them at the time of their application. The amount owing for arrears of rent should have been taken into consideration in determining the amount of compensation owing. Had that been done, the Board would have had to conclude that the tenants were owed nothing in compensation at the time of the application because of the set-off. [18] This conclusion is in keeping with the purposes of the Act set out in s. 1, which include “to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.” I note that counsel for Marineland acknowledged that should it seek to pursue any remaining amounts owing from the tenants, it would be required to set off the $3,000.00 of compensation that it owed to the tenants.
Therefore, while the [name] ds owe the Tenant $200.00, this amount shall be awarded to the Tenant and will instead be applied to the arrears of rent still owing by the Tenant.
ordered: A credit of $200.00 sha ll be applied to the amount of rent arrears owing by the Tenant to the Landlord in order LTB-L-034626-25. July 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.

The Tenant’s evidence was not compiled/organized as ordered; on June 28 and 29, 2026, the Tenant uploaded approximately 29 documents with attachments on the portal; a Certificate of Service to the Landlord was not provided/posted on the portal. Although the documents submitted June 28, 2026, included a table of contents (DOC #8245596), it was a reference to the document numbers on the portal not a proper document brief. Rule 19.7 says “A party who fails to comply with Rule 19 or an order or direction for disclosure may not rely on the evidence that was not disclosed as directed or ordered, unless otherwise ordered.” The interim order also set out the potential consequence of non-compliance and the requirements. It was ordered:
If a party does not comply with the deadlines in this order, the Member may refuse to accept the evidence or consider the issues not disclosed.

All evidence shall be organized in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence. The Tenant was aware of the evidence requirements and the potential consequences of non-compliance and did not seek legal advice to ensure her evidence was submitted properly. To adjourn the matter under these circumstances would essentially be rewarding her for a lack of due diligence. 4. Further, there is a second preliminary issue is with respect to the Tenant having filed T6 application LTB-T-013861-25 that was heard by the Board on June 2, 2026; the order is pending. The concept of ‘res judicata’ is a common law doctrine meant to ensure the finality of judicial decisions, preventing the same parties from re-litigating the same issue in future proceedings; it is crucial for maintaining judicial efficiency and protecting parties from the burden of repeated litigation. Although this doctrine specifically references matters that have already been ‘judged’, I consider the concept to be applicable here considering the facts and remedies are identical; the Board cannot order remedies twice.
For all these reasons the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application is filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and claims the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.
The Tenant’s claim for the return of rent paid due to an illegal rent increase is dismissed as the rent increase is deemed lawful.

The Tenant’s claim for one month’s rent compensation owing as a result of the Landlord having served the Tenant with an N12 Notice to Terminate is dismissed as the Tenant did not file her application within one year of having vacated the rental unit.
The Tenant’s claim for interest payable on the last month’s rent deposit is granted.
As the Tenant is successful on a portion of her application, the Tenant is awarded her costs of filing this application. T1 Application – Determinations:

The Tenant claims the Landlord: a) Charged her illegal rent from October 15, 2023, to July 14, 2024; b) Owes her interest on her last month’s deposit; and c) Failed to pay her one month’s compensation when she was served with an N12 Notice of Termination as required under section 48.1 of the Act.

Subsections 135(1) and (4) of the Act provide: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant ant money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. The October 15, 2023, rent increase of $100.00 is deemed lawful:
The Landlord and Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement effective October 15, 2022.

The Tenant testified rent was $3,000.00 a month and that during a verbal conversation between the Landlord and Tenant, the Landlord had said that effective October 15, 2023, the monthly rent would be increased to $3,100.00, which amounted to an increase of $100.00 per month.

The Landlord testified that the rent increase was effective as of November 15, 2023, and not October 15, 2023. However, the Landlord did not dispute the fact that the required 90 days notice of a rent increase was not provided and nor did she dispute the fact that the Notice of Rent Increase was not provided to the Tenant using the prescribed form by the Board.

When asked why she increased the monthly rent above the guideline increase, the Landlord responded that because the Tenant had another person move in with her during her tenancy, which was strictly prohibited in the lease agreement, the Landlord increased the monthly rent by more than the prescribed guideline.

Section 120 (1) of the Act provides: 120 (1) No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.
The guideline increase in 2023 was 2.5% which would be equivalent to $75.00 a month on a monthly rent of $3,000.00. The $100.00 rent increase on October 15, 2023, was above the guideline increase.

Above guideline increases are permitted where the Landlord has made an application to the Board under section 126 of the Act and the increase has been granted by an order of the Board. Parties are also entitled to agree to above guideline rent increases so long as the agreed upon increase accords with sections 121 or 123 of the Act.

There was no evidence this increase was authorized by an order of the Board, nor a suggestion the rent was increased because parking or a new prescribed service was added as provided for in section 123 of the Act, nor was there an agreement reached under section 121 of the Act.

The Tenant also testified she was not provided with a Notice of Rent Increase. Sub- sections 116(1) and (4) of the Act provide: 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.
In the above circumstances, I find the increase in monthly rent from October 15, 2023, from $3,000.00 to $3,100.00 was in excess of the guideline.
Nonetheless, there are sections of the Act that provide for circumstances under which an unlawful rent increase will be deemed lawful.

Section 135.1 addresses when an increase in rent that would have been void under section 116(4) for failure to serve a Notice of Rent Increase does not apply. 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116(4) is deemed not to be vid if the tenant has paid the increased in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. (3) For greater certainty, if subsection (1) applies wit respect to an increase in rent, section 116 is deemed to have been complied with. (4) For greater certainty, nothing in this section limits the application of section 136.

The Tenant did not file an application disputing the increase within one year of when it was first charged. Therefore, I find the monthly rent of $3,100.00 to be deemed lawful in accordance with section 135.1 of the Act.
Consequently, the Tenant’s claim for illegally charged rent is dismissed. Interest on the last month’s rent:
The parties agree that the Tenant paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $3,000.00.
The Tenant seeks interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the period October 15, 2022, to July 14, 2024.

Interest on a last month’s rent deposit is due once a year. The Tenant testified interest on her last month’s rent deposit was due October 15, 2023, and July 14, 2024. If a Landlord fails to pay interest to the Tenant on the annual anniversary date, then an illegal retention has begun.

The illegal retention is deemed to be an ongoing action. 626114 & [organization] V. Tirado, 2005 CanLII 36461 (ON SCDC) tells us that a tenant is allowed to assert their eights under s118 of the Tenant Protection Act, 1997 with respect to interest owed on an annual basis and that there is no one year limitation period in which a tenant can bring forward their claim.

Therefore, the Tenant’s claim for interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the period October 15, 2022, to July 14, 2024, is granted, and the Landlord shall be ordered to pay same. One month’s compensation under section 48.1 of the Act:
The parties agree the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination on April 15, 2024, with a termination date of July 15, 2024.
There is no dispute by the Tenant that the N12 Notice was served in good faith.
The issue being raised by the Tenant is that the Landlord failed to compensate her in accordance with section 48.1 of the Act.

Section 48.1 of the Act provides: 48.1 A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48.

Section 55.1 of the Act provides: 55.1 If the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54, or 55, the landlord shall compensate the tenant no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination of the tenancy given by the landlord under section 48, 49 or 50.
The Tenant testified that she did not receive a cheque from the Landlord for one month’s rent and the Landlord admitted she had not provided the Tenant with one month’s compensation.

The Landlord testified that the compensation did not form a part of the Lease Agreement, and she was not aware that she had to make this payment to the Tenant. The Tenant responded by saying that even though the Landlord may not have been aware of the compensation owed to the Tenant when serving the Tenant with the N12 Notice, the Tenant did bring this to her attention on several occasions.
The Tenant further testified that she provided the Landlord with a few options to resolve the compensation owed, but the Landlord refused.

When asked why she refused the options suggested by the Tenant, the Landlord testified that she told the Tenant that the Tenant first needed to fix the damages she caused in the rental unit, and only then would she pay the Tenant the one month’s compensation owed to her.
In the above circumstances, I find the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant one month’s compensation for termination of tenancy as required under section 48.21 of the Act.
Nonetheless, the Tenant failed to file her application in the time period as provided under subsection 135(4) of the Act.

Subsection 135(4) of the Act provides: 135(4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

When the question was put forward to the Tenant why she waited over 18 months after she vacated the rental unit to file her application with the Board, she responded by saying she “needed time to get things settled and then needed time to fill out the form.”
As the Tenant waited over a year from the date of vacating the rental unit to file her application, the Tenant’s claim for one month’s rent compensation is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $156.00. This amount represents: • $108.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: AU (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application)
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative requested to withdraw the T2 application, and the Board consented to the requested.

As explained below, the Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. The Tenant filed their application on February 26, 2025, claiming that the Landlord charged illegal rent from November 15, 2023, to December 14, 2024.

Rent increase took effect on November 15, 2023. The Landlord’s legal representative claimed that no valid Notice of Rent Increase (NORI) was provided to the Tenant under subsection 116 of the Act Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’). There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant paid their increased rent amount to the Landlord for a period of 12 consecutive months from December 15, 2023, to November 15, 2024.

With respect to rent increase, subsection 116 of the Act requires that: (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the rent charged is increased in accordance with an order under s. 126. (3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.

However, under subsection 135.1 of the Act, an increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. Furthermore, subsection 135.1(2) of the Act stipulates that subsection 135.1 (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. Subsection 135.1(3) of the Act reads that if subsection 135.1(1) applies with respect to an increase in rent, subsection 116 is deemed to have been complied with.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on balance of probabilities that the rent increase is deemed not void pursuant to subsection 135.1 of the Act. The Tenant paid the increased rent amount to the Landlord for a period of twelve consecutive months from December 15, 2023, to November 15, 2024, thus 135.1(1) of the Act applies. Since the rent increase took effect in November 2023, and the Tenant filed their application in February 2025, I find that the Tenant did not file their application within one year after the date the increase was first charged (November 2023). Thus, subsection 135.1(2) of the Act does not apply. As 135.1(1) of the Act applies in this case, pursuant to subsection 135.1(3), section 116 of the Act is deemed to have been complied with by the Landlord. Thus, the rent increase is deemed not void.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owe (L1 application). The lawful rent is $1,207.99. It is due on the 1st day of each month.

Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $56.79 is owing to the Tenant for the period from June 1, 2024, to July 8, 2026.
The Landlord attempted to negotiate a payment plan with the Tenants prior to the hearing.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

This Tenant application under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) claims the Landlord collected a first and last month rent deposit and did not return the unused rent portion or the last month rent deposit. Tenant submissions

The Tenant filed evidence with the Board to support the claims in the application consisting of the tenancy agreement the first and last month rent deposit amount paid and text communications with the Landlord. DOC-7441583, DOC-7441822, DOC-7989872, DOC- 7989875, DOC-7441699 and DOC-7441701.
The Tenant signed a tenancy agreement for a fixed term commencing on September 2, 2025 for a fixed term of one year.
Lawful rent is $2,200.00 due on the 2nd of each month.
The Tenant provided proof of her payment to the Landlord for first and last month rent deposit in the amount of $4,400.00.

The Tenant had texted the Landlord asking about an alternative parking spot. The issue was regarding the parking situation with the other Tenant in the residential complex. Both tenants had a shared space that required one Tenant to park behind the other and the tenants were constantly moving each other’s vehicles to move out of the way of the first parked vehicle.
The Tenant sent a follow up text to the Landlord to inquire about her request.

The evidence shows the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s texts on September 12, 2025 where the Landlord states: Good day [name], Before you move in you were able to walk the property and see the conditions. If it wasn’t fit for you, you shouldn’t have rent on our property. If you still no happy you can always move out and find a better place for you and your family, we’ll be happy to reimburse your rent.

The Landlord texted the Tenant on September 19, 2025 to follow up with the Tenant and the Tenant responded she was moving out on Sunday September 21, 2025 and the Landlord can meet her at the rental unit for the keys.
The Landlord responded by informing the Tenant to Just leave the keys under the carpet or at the box in front at the entrance of the building. Thank you.
The position of the Tenant is the Landlord had never indicated he required 60 days’ notice, and she believes the Landlord gave her an invitation to leave at her discretion which she did.
The Tenant is seeking a remedy for a return in full of her last month rent deposit and unused rent for September 2025. Landlord submissions
The Landlord’s position is the Tenant did not give her 60 days’ notice as required under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).
The Landlord filed evidence to support his position, DOC-7500290.
The Landlord stated he advertised on Facebook Marketplace late September 2025 and was able to find new tenants for November 15, 2025.

The Landlord stated in one of his response texts to the Tenant he indicates “let me know” with regard to her move out date and this was his request for 60 day notice to terminate. The Act and Analysis

Section 202 of the Act states: Findings of Board 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 202.

Section 37 of the Act states the termination of a tenancy can only be in accordance with the Act. The termination can be done by a notice, Board order or on an agreement between the landlord and the tenant, either written or oral.

I find the Tenant credible and consistent in her testimony and evidence to support her claim the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy and reimburse the Tenant’s rent and did not indicate a requirement of 60 days’ notice.
I prefer the evidence of the Tenant, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord put the Tenant on notice and gave clear direction he required 60 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has proved the allegations in the application.
Therefore, the Landlord owes the Tenant unused rent from September 22, 2025 to October 1, 2025 and the last month rent deposit.

The Landlord owes the Tenant $2,923.20 calculated as follows: • Daily compensation for unused rent: $2,200.00 x 12 months / 365 = $72.32 • Tenant occupied rental unit September 22, 2025 to October 1. 2025 (10 days) = $723.20 • Last month rent deposit $2,200.00 • $732.20 (daily compensation) + $2,200.00 (last month rent deposit) = $2,923.20.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord pay the Tenant is $2,971.20. This amount represents: • 723.20 for the unused rent from September 22, 2025 to October 1, 2025 • $2,200.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

On June 24, 2024, the Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination with the termination date of August 31, 2024. The Landlords claim that they require vacant possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by their child. 24.Section 71.1 and 72 under the Act states: 71.1 (1) A landlord who, on or after the day subsection 11 (1) of [name] to the Protecting Tenants and Strengthening Community Housing Act, 2020 comes into force, files an application under section 69 based on a notice of termination given under section 48 or 49 shall file the affidavit required under subsection 72 (1) at the same time as the application is filed. 2020, c. 16, [name]. 4, s. 11 (1). (2) The Board shall refuse to accept the application for filing if the landlord has not complied with subsection (1) 72 (1) The Board shall not make an order terminating a tenancy and evicting the tenant in an application under section 69 based on, (a) a notice of termination given under section 48, unless the landlord has filed with the Board an affidavit sworn by the person who personally requires the rental unit certifying that the person in good faith requires the rental unit for his or her own personal use for a period of at least one year; or (b) a notice of termination under section 49, unless the landlord has filed with the Board an affidavit sworn by the person who personally requires the rental unit certifying that the person in good faith requires the rental unit for his or her own personal use ; LTB-T-017673-24; and LTB-L-051019-24 25. Although the application was accompanied by a declaration it was not sworn by the Landlords’ child and therefore, I have no jurisdiction to consider the merits of this application because the statutory requirements under sections 71.1 and 72.1 have not been met. 26. On cross examination the Landlords’ child testified he did not sign the declaration that the Landlords submitted when the application was filed. The Landlords testified it was sworn by the Landlords’ representative on behalf of his child. I find the declaration to be invalid because of the following: 27. Section 72 of the Act states that the affidavit must be sworn by the person who personally requires the rental unit. In this case the declaration was not prepared nor sworn by the Landlords’ child and there was no evidence that the child authorized the Landlords’ representative to do so on his behalf; The Landlords indicate their child has cognitive disability which is consistent with the manner in which he presented at the hearing. However, there was no evidence to believe that the child couldn’t have sworn his own declaration.

I considered if the declaration substantially complies when accompanied by testimony, but it doesn’t apply under these circumstances. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the Act) or failed to comply with health, safety or maintenance standards
reasons: The Tenants application alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by interrupting vital services, specifically heat and water.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit in April 2024. She stated that interruptions to water service began shortly after she moved into the building and continued throughout her tenancy. Initially, she believed the interruptions were isolated maintenance events and therefore did not keep detailed records.
However, by late 2024 she concluded that the interruptions had become a recurring problem and began documenting the interruptions.

The Tenant submitted a chronology (DOC 7445256, p. 2) identifying dates on which she alleged water and heat services were interrupted. With respect to water service, she identified numerous shutdowns throughout January 2025 and additional interruptions in February, March, April, May and June. She testified that many of these interruptions occurred with little or no advance notice. She explained that because her apartment was situated between other occupied units, prolonged water shutdowns created unpleasant living conditions, including toilets that could not be flushed for extended periods.

The Tenant testified that the heating problems became particularly severe during February 2025. She stated that the apartment was without heat for extended periods during the coldest part of the winter and that she was forced to leave the rental unit because, as a senior with medical issues, she could not safely remain in the apartment. She testified that she stayed at a nearby hotel on two occasions and otherwise stayed with her daughter until the heat returned.

The Tenant further testified that she contacted property management regarding the lack of heat and was advised that recurring failures involving the building's heating system were responsible for the interruptions. The Tenant provided that management informed her that contractors had been retained and that repairs were expected to be completed quickly. She stated, however, that despite those assurances, the heating interruptions continued.

The Tenant also relied upon evidence from the City of Guelph. She testified that Property Standards attended the rental unit after she complained about the lack of heat and measured the temperature inside the unit. She submitted a photograph of a household thermometer (DOC 5149829), which she testified was taken during the period of the municipal inspection and reflected the temperature in the unit at that time. She stated that the inspector confirmed that the temperature recorded on her thermometer was generally consistent with the inspector's own equipment. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord relied on the evidence of [name] ('NR'). NR was the Senior Property Manager responsible for the residential complex during the period relevant to the application.

NR testified that the residential complex consists of approximately ten storeys and more than one hundred residential units. She explained that the building is heated through a hydronic radiator system, meaning that hot water circulates through radiators located in each apartment. As a result, repairs to the heating system frequently require temporary interruptions to the building's water supply.

NR acknowledged that the building experienced significant heating problems during the winter of 2025. She explained that the heating system suffered recurring circulation issues that prevented hot water from flowing evenly throughout the building. She testified that some units received heat in one room while radiators in other rooms remained cold because air had accumulated within portions of the heating system. Maintenance staff repeatedly bled radiator lines and cleaned components to restore circulation.

NR acknowledged that the building experienced significant heating problems during the winter of 2025. She explained that the heating system suffered recurring circulation issues that prevented hot water from flowing evenly throughout the building. She provided that some units would receive heat in one room while radiators in other rooms remained cold because air had accumulated within portions of the system. Maintenance staff repeatedly bled radiator lines and cleaned components to restore circulation.

She further testified that the Landlord retained multiple plumbing contractors in an effort to diagnose and repair the recurring problems. Whenever management received a complaint of inadequate heat, staff attended the affected unit, measured radiator temperatures using a heat gun, documented their findings and immediately arranged for plumbing contractors to attend the building. NR testified that the repairs continued until the heating system was functioning properly. Analysis

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) says the landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.
The Landlord’s witness does not dispute the Tenant experienced interruption to water and heating services. However, that does not automatically mean the Landlord has breached section 20 the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 the Court of Appeal held that it is necessary to take a contextual approach to determining whether a landlord breached his maintenance obligations under the Act and a landlord will not be found liable for such a breach.

I found NR to be a credible and reliable witness. She readily acknowledged facts that were not favourable to the Landlord, including that the building experienced recurring heating problems during the winter of 2025.

NR did not dispute that tenants experienced interruptions to heating service. Rather, she disputed the Tenant's characterization of those interruptions. She testified that the interruptions were intermittent, not continuous. According to her evidence, the heating system would fail, repairs would be undertaken, heat would be restored, and then additional circulation problems would develop, requiring further repairs. She maintained that, while individual tenants may have experienced periods of several hours, or in some cases approximately one day, without heat, the building did not remain entirely without heat for multiple consecutive days.

I find portions of the Tenant's evidence to be less reliable. In particular, her testimony regarding the duration of the heating interruption was inconsistent with the chronology she prepared. While she initially described an approximately twelve-day period without heat, her chronology and subsequent testimony demonstrated that heat was restored on several occasions before failing again. Likewise, her recollection concerning the date of the thermometer photograph changed during cross-examination.

Taking a contextual view of the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably to recurring mechanical problems affecting the building's heating system. The evidence establishes that the Landlord retained multiple contractors, investigated tenant complaints, attended affected units, measured radiator temperatures, supplied portable heaters where appropriate, and continued repair efforts until the problems were resolved. I also accept that the City of Guelph, after inspecting the property, was satisfied that the Landlord was actively addressing the issue and did not issue a compliance order.

I am also persuaded by the Landlord's evidence that, while the heat and water services were intermittently disrupted, the interruptions were temporary and arose from necessary repair work affecting the building's infrastructure. I do not accept the Tenant's evidence that there were prolonged, continuous disruptions to her heat and water service as alleged.

Although the interruptions undoubtedly caused inconvenience and frustration to the Tenant, I am not satisfied that they resulted from neglect or a failure by the Landlord to maintain the residential complex. Rather, I find that the interruptions occurred while the Landlord was actively undertaking reasonable and ongoing repairs to an aging heating system. Applying the contextual approach described in Onyskiw, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Tenant filed an application alleging, among other things, illegal entries, substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment, harassment and other breaches of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord brought a preliminary motion seeking dismissal of the application on the basis that it failed to disclose sufficient particulars to permit the Landlord to know the case it was required to meet.
As explained below, I the Landlord’s motion is granted and the application is dismissed. Background
An adjudicative case conference was held August 18, 2025. Although no interim order was issued the Adjournment Sheet notes the Tenant planned to file an amended application within 30 days.

Although the Tenant subsequently filed amendments, many of those amendments related to new allegations arising after the original application was filed. At the commencement of this hearing, the Tenant withdrew the majority of those amendments.
The Landlord submitted that the remaining allegations continue to lack sufficient factual particulars and therefore fail to satisfy the requirements of procedural fairness.

Having reviewed the application, the amendments, and the parties' submissions, I am satisfied that the remaining allegations do not contain sufficient particulars to permit the matter to proceed fairly. Illegal Entry Allegations

The Tenant submits that the application identifies specific dates, including March 3, 2024, and another alleged entry recorded as March 11, 2025, which the representative submits was intended to refer to March 11, 2024.
I accept that some dates appear within the application. However, in my view the existence of dates alone does not satisfy the requirement of procedural fairness.

The difficulty here is that the Tenant acknowledges she was not present during the alleged entries. Instead, the application relies upon information allegedly received from another individual who, in turn, obtained the information from three unnamed friends.

The application does not identify these individuals, describe their relationship to the tenancy, explain precisely what they observed, or provide sufficient information to permit the Landlord to investigate the allegations or determine whether those individuals should be summoned as witnesses.

In my view, without that information, the Landlord cannot reasonably know the factual basis upon which the allegations are made. While the Tenant may well have intended to lead direct evidence of the alleged misconduct of the Landlord or his agents through witness testimony or other evidence at the hearing, the problem lies in the actual text of the originating document – their application – which is the document against which the respondent Landlord must craft his answer. I find on the balance of probabilities that the vague allegations contained in this application frustrate the Landlord’s ability to fully and properly respond to the application. Remaing Allegations
The remaining allegations containing similar deficiencies.
Several allegations refer generally to harassment, intimidation, parking disputes, and other conduct without identifying the material facts relied upon.

In a number of instances, the application identifies when the Tenant learned of an event rather than when the event itself allegedly occurred. Other allegations refer to unnamed third parties or unidentified witnesses without explaining their involvement.

While pleadings should be read generously, they must nevertheless contain sufficient material facts to permit the opposing party to know the case it must answer. The remaining allegations do not meet that standard. Request to Amend
The Tenant submits that deficiencies in the pleadings resulted, in part, from memory issues associated with her disability.

I accept that the Tenant alleges she experiences medical and memory-related difficulties. However, even accepting those submissions, I am not persuaded that the deficiencies can be remedied at this stage.
The application has been before the Board for over a year. During that period, the Tenant attended an adjudicative case conference at which the deficiencies in the pleadings were identified.

The Tenant subsequently retained legal representation and filed amendments to the application. Despite those opportunities, the application still fails to provide the material particulars necessary to permit the Landlord to understand and respond to the allegations remaining before the Board.
In these circumstances, I find permitting the hearing another change to amend the application would result in procedural unfairness to the Landlord.

I find that the Tenant’s allegations were not properly plead as filed with the Board. I find that it would be improper to “craft” pleadings from the Tenant’s oral and documentary evidence led in the course of the hearing. I further find that it is not sufficient for the Tenant to expect the Landlord to piece together the case to be met.
As the Tenant’s application does not meet the requirements of the law, it must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] DeLua, [name] [name] and TSCC 2565-Imperial Plaza (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • charged the Tenant illegal charges • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. • gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant filed two applications arising from the same tenancy. The applications are essentially duplicative applications made against two different landlords. One application names TSCC 2565 – Imperial Plaza as the respondent. The second names [name] and [name] [name], the owners of the rental unit (the 'Landlords').

As explained below, I find that TSCC 2565 – Imperial Plaza is not a landlord within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Accordingly, the application against the condominium corporation is dismissed.

Common law establishes that there is no legal relationship between a condominium corporation and a tenant who occupies an owner’s unit within the residential complex and who pays rent to the owner of the unit for that privilege. A condominium corporation has no legal standing before the Board. A series of cases confirms this principle. (See, for example, TEL-96466-18 /TET-97624-18, 2019 CANLII 126965 (ON LTB); Chimel v. MacLachlan, 2020 CANLII 118438 (ON LTB); TSL-09662-19; K.G. v. J.D.L.R. 2019 CANLII 87771 (ON LTB); TST-95268-18; TNT-99110-17)

The courts have reached the same conclusion. In Carleton Condominium Corporation No. 555 v. Legacé, 2004 CanLII 26137 (ON SC), the Court explained that the condominium corporation's legal relationship is with the unit owner rather than the tenant. Where issues arise concerning a tenant's occupancy, the corporation looks to the owner for compliance, and the owner in turn enforces the tenancy agreement with the tenant.

Accordingly, I find that TSCC 2565 – Imperial Plaza is not a landlord within the meaning of the Act. The application against the condominium corporation is therefore dismissed. The hearing proceeded only against [name] and [name] [name]. Preliminary Issue – Date the Application Was Filed

A further preliminary issue concerns the date on which the Tenant commenced the application against the Landlords. The Board's records indicate that application LTB-T- 017945-25 was filed on March 2, 2025.

The Tenant submits that she originally filed an application in December 2023 and that the Board subsequently misplaced it. She relies primarily on Canada Post tracking information demonstrating that an envelope was delivered to the Board during that period. (DOC- 7589638 pg.42) She testified that the application had been prepared by family members while she was recovering from surgery and that she no longer possesses a copy of the documents that were allegedly mailed.
I am not persuaded, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant filed an application in December 2023.

The Canada Post tracking information establishes only that an envelope was delivered to the Board. It does not establish what documents were contained in that envelope. More importantly, there is no copy of the alleged application, no acknowledgement of receipt from the Board, and no correspondence demonstrating that the Board received or processed such an application. LTB-T-017945-25

I accept that administrative errors can occur and that documents may occasionally be misplaced after being received. However, there is insufficient evidence before me to conclude that such an error occurred in this case.

I also find it noteworthy that there is no persuasive evidence of any meaningful follow-up by the Tenant after the alleged December 2023 filing. While some delay in processing applications is not unusual, I find it unlikely that a reasonable person would wait well over a year without obtaining confirmation that an application had been received or without retaining a copy of the documents allegedly filed.

Had a copy of the alleged December 2023 application been produced, the Board could have compared it with the present application to determine whether they were substantially the same. In the absence of that evidence, I am unable to conclude that the Tenant commenced proceedings before March 2, 2025.

I therefore find that the filing date of the application is March 2, 2025. Pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act, the Board may only grant a remedy for conduct occurring within one year before that date unless the alleged conduct constituted a continuing breach extending into the limitation period. T5 Application

At the outset of the hearing the Tenant withdrew their allegation that the Landlords served a notice of termination in bad faith. Accordingly, the Tenant presented evidence surrounding the remainder the allegations set out in their application that are within the applicable limitation period. [name]

The Tenant alleges that the Landlords substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by illegally changing the locks, harassing her, unlawfully entering the rental unit, and withholding vital services.

The Tenant testified that the Landlords changed the locks to the rental unit on several occasions without her consent. She testified that the Landlords caused the condominium corporation to change the locks while she remained hospitalized following thoracic surgery. According to the Tenant, the Landlords already had access to the rental unit because the condominium corporation maintained master keys and had previously changed the locks in December 2023. The Tenant believes, there was no legitimate reason for another lock change.

The Tenant relied upon email correspondence dated March 25, 2024, (DOC-7589638 pg.131) which demonstrates that a locksmith attended the building and that replacement keys would be available following the lock change. She submits this correspondence establishes that the Landlords requested the lock change and that the condominium corporation acted at their direction.

The Tenant testified that members of her family attempted to obtain replacement keys while she remained hospitalized but were unsuccessful because the condominium corporation required her to attend personally. She testified that she was therefore required LTB-T-017945-25 to temporarily leave the hospital to obtain replacement keys, causing pain, inconvenience and disrupting her recovery. Although she ultimately regained access to the rental unit before vacating the premises on June 30, 2024, she maintains that the temporary inability to access the unit constituted an illegal lockout.

The Tenant further testified that the repeated lock changes formed part of a broader pattern of harassment and intimidation. She submits the Landlords' communications, together with the ongoing dispute concerning the heating system, caused her to feel unsafe in the rental unit and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. Landlords' Evidence

The Landlords deny ever illegally locking the Tenant out of the rental unit. [name] testified that, beginning in the fall of 2023, the Landlords were attempting to obtain access to the rental unit to investigate the Tenant's complaints regarding the HVAC system and to facilitate an insurance inspection. He testified that, despite serving notices of entry, the Landlords were unable to gain access because they possessed neither a working key to the unit nor a building fob. 21. [name] testified that the condominium corporation re-keyed the locks in December 2023 after it was determined that neither the replacement key nor the condominium's master key functioned properly. He denied that either he or [name] De Luca tampered with the lock and stated that the condominium corporation concluded the lock had been altered, necessitating another re-keying. 22. VD provided similar evidence. She testified that the March 2024 lock change occurred solely to permit lawful access so the HVAC system could be inspected and repaired and denied that the purpose of the lock change was to interfere with the Tenant's occupancy or enjoyment of the rental unit. Analysis 23. I have already determined that the application was filed on March 2, 2025. Accordingly, pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act, I may only grant a remedy for conduct occurring on or after March 3, 2024. Much of the Tenant's evidence concerning lock changes, and communications between the parties occurred during 2023. While I have considered that evidence to provide context, I have not relied upon it as a basis for granting the Tenant’s application. 24. With respect to the March 2024 lock change, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord illegally locked her out of the rental unit. 25. I do not accept the Tenant's submission that the March 2024 lock change constituted an illegal lockout. An e-mail from the condominium corporation to the Tenant (DOC-7589638 pg.131) confirms that the Tenant received notice from the condominium corporation advising that the locks had been changed and that a replacement key was available for collection. LTB-T-017945-25 26. Although the Tenant was unable to personally collect the key because she remained hospitalized, there is no persuasive evidence that either Landlord directed the condominium corporation to withhold the key from the Tenant or otherwise attempted to obstruct her from possession of the rental unit. 27.
