I accept the Tenant's evidence that the condominium corporation declined to release the replacement key to members of her family while she remained hospitalized. However, I am not satisfied that this decision can properly be attributed to the Landlords. Nor do I find it unreasonable that the condominium corporation required confirmation that the individual requesting the key was authorized to receive it on the Tenant's behalf. 28. While I accept that the Tenant experienced inconvenience and frustration as a result of having to personally retrieve the replacement key, I am not satisfied that those circumstances establish an illegal lockout under the Act. 29. I also reject the Tenant's allegation that the Landlords harassed or substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. Much of the evidence relied upon by the Tenant relates to communications occurring in 2023 and therefore falls outside the applicable limitation period. 30. I find the communications occurring within the relevant period primarily concern attempts to arrange inspections, obtain access to the rental unit and facilitate repairs to the HVAC system. Although the relationship between the parties had clearly deteriorated, I am not satisfied that those communications amount to harassment, coercion or substantial interference within the meaning of the Act. T6 Application 31. The Tenant testified that the heating system serving the rental unit stopped functioning in approximately February 2023. She stated that she repeatedly notified the Landlords through emails, text messages, telephone calls and WhatsApp messages that the rental unit had no heat. According to the Tenant, despite her repeated complaints, the Landlords failed to investigate the issue or arrange for repairs. 32. The Tenant testified that she also contacted the condominium corporation and various enforcement authorities in an effort to have the issue addressed. She stated that she was advised the HVAC unit serving the rental unit was the responsibility of the unit owner rather than the condominium corporation. 33. The Tenant testified that the lack of heat significantly affected her ability to use and enjoy the rental unit. She stated that she purchased a portable heater, but it was incapable of adequately heating the unit and she was later advised not to leave it operating unattended because of the potential fire risk. She further testified that the prolonged absence of heat and air conditioning damaged clothing, furniture and other personal belongings and contributed to the deterioration of her health. Landlords’ Evidence 34. The Landlords do not dispute that the heating system was not functioning properly. [name] acknowledged that the Tenant first reported problems with the heating system in early LTB-T-017945-25 2023 and candidly admitted that the Landlords did not respond as promptly as they should have. He testified the Landlords initially believed responsibility for the HVAC unit rested with the condominium corporation and that, shortly after the complaints were received, the Landlords experienced a significant family tragedy that diverted their attention from the issue. 35. [name] testified that he became directly involved in approximately October 2023 when it became apparent that the issue had not been resolved. He testified that, from that point forward, the Landlords actively attempted to inspect the HVAC system and arrange repairs. [name] submitted those efforts included serving notices of entry, retaining contractors, communicating extensively with the condominium corporation and attempting to obtain lawful access to the rental unit. 36. [name] further testified that, after the Landlords finally regained access to the rental unit in March 2024, the HVAC system was inspected. He stated that the inspection revealed the repair required removal of the ceiling-mounted heat pump and portions of the surrounding drywall. He further testified, large clothing racks and other belongings stored beneath the unit prevented the contractor from safely performing the work. 37. [name] testified that he requested the Tenant move those belongings so that the contractor could complete the repairs. Although he was unable to locate the email making that request during the hearing, he maintained that the request was made and that the Tenant never responded. [name] submitted, the Landlords received no further communication from the Tenant until June 30, 2024, when they were advised that she had vacated the rental unit. Analysis 38. Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. There is no dispute that the HVAC unit serving the rental unit was the Landlords' responsibility. 39. I accept the Tenant's evidence that she notified the Landlords of the heating issue in early 2023. I also accept [name]’s candid admission that the Landlords did not respond as promptly as they should have. Although I accept that the Landlords were dealing with significant personal circumstances and initially misunderstood who was responsible for the HVAC unit, those circumstances did not relieve them of their maintenance obligations. 40. Had the application been filed within the limitation period prescribed by subsection 29(2) of the Act, the evidence would have supported a finding that the Landlords failed to take reasonable steps to investigate and address the heating issue for several months after first receiving notice of the problem. 41. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 the Court of Appeal held that it is necessary to take a contextual approach to determining whether a landlord breached his maintenance obligations under the Act and a landlord will not be found liable for such a breach. 42. In applying a contextual analysis to this application, I find the circumstances in this case changed in October 2023. I accept [name]’s evidence that, from that point onward, the LTB-T-017945-25 Landlords made genuine and ongoing efforts to obtain access to the rental unit, inspect the HVAC system and arrange for the necessary repairs. 43. I also find the evidence of the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (DOC-7382699, pp. 33– 38) to be relevant. In an email dated July 21, 2025, the inspector confirmed that the file had been closed and noted that the Tenant had been difficult to reach and that there were challenges arranging access to conduct an in-unit inspection. I find this to be consistent with the Landlords' submission that they experienced ongoing difficulties obtaining access to the rental unit. Viewed together with the balance of the evidence, I find it supports the Landlords' position that access to the rental unit presented an ongoing challenge. 44. I also accept that, once access was finally obtained in March 2024, the required repair was more extensive than initially anticipated. [name]'s evidence that the ceiling-mounted heat pump had to be removed and that the work required unobstructed access beneath the unit was not contradicted by the Tenant. 45. Although the Landlords were unable to produce the email requesting that the Tenant move her belongings to facilitate the repair, I found [name]’s evidence in this regard to be credible. I I therefore accept that the Landlords continued attempting to complete the repair after regaining access to the rental unit. 46. In considering the totality of the evidence, I find that, after approximately October 2023, the Landlords took reasonable steps to investigate and repair the HVAC system. Any continuing delay thereafter cannot fairly be attributed solely to a failure on the part of the Landlords. 47. More importantly, subsection 29(2) of the Act prevents the Board from granting a remedy for conduct occurring more than one year before the application was filed. I have found that the application was filed on March 2, 2025. Consequently, any failure by the Landlords to respond promptly to the Tenant's complaints during the period before October 2023 occurred well outside the applicable limitation period. 48. Since I am satisfied that the Landlords acted reasonably after approximately October 2023, I find the Tenant has not established any maintenance breach within the period for which the Board may grant relief under the Act. 49. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. T1 Application 50. The Tenant seeks the return of the $150.00 key and fob deposit paid at the commencement of the tenancy. 51. The Tenant testified that she returned the keys at the conclusion of the tenancy through the building concierge after vacating the rental unit on June 30, 2024. Although the Landlords initially questioned the precise date on which the keys were returned, they ultimately acknowledged that the keys were recovered from the concierge shortly thereafter. The Landlords also acknowledged collecting a $150.00 refundable key and fob deposit from the Tenant at the commencement of the tenancy. LTB-T-017945-25 52. Subsection 134(3) of the Act permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit provided it does not exceed the expected direct replacement cost of the keys or access devices. Once the tenant returns the keys at the end of the tenancy, the landlord must refund the deposit unless it has been properly applied toward replacement costs. 53. There is no evidence that the Landlords incurred any replacement costs or that they had any lawful basis for retaining the deposit. I am therefore satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the return of the $150.00 key and fob deposit. 54. The Tenant also seeks interest on the deposit. Unlike a rent deposit under section 106 of the Act, the Act does not require a landlord to pay annual interest on a refundable key deposit. Therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to interest on the key deposit. 55. I therefore find it appropriate to set off the $150.00 refundable key and fob deposit against the outstanding amount owing by the Tenant under the previous Board order. 56. While the Tenant was partially successful in their application, the Boards records indicate the cost of filing the application was waived by Board. As such the Tenant is not entitled to be reimbursed that cost.
ordered: The application against the Landlord, TSCC 2565-Imperial Plaza, is dismissed.
The Tenant is awarded $150.00 which represents the return of her key deposit.
The total amount of $150.00 will be used to offset the rent arrears sought by the Landlords in LTB-L-016001-24. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,048.00. Illegal entry

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on June 19, 2024, and moved out on January 31, 2025. The rental unit is a one-bedroom condominium apartment. The monthly rent was $2,500.00.

The Tenant testified that on July 17, 2024, at approximately 11:00 a.m., the Landlord attended at the rental unit with the building manager. The Landlord did not knock, did not provide written notice, and did not announce her entry. Instead, the Landlord used a master key to open the door and entered the rental unit with the building manager.

The Tenant testified that the female Tenant and three young children were inside the rental unit at the time. The female Tenant was in the bathroom when the Landlord and the building manager entered. The female Tenant testified that she felt shocked, embarrassed, and unsafe because she did not expect the Landlord to enter the rental unit without notice or permission.
The Tenant further testified that when she complained to the Landlord about the entry, the Landlord responded that it was her property and that she had the right to enter the rental unit at any time.

Section 26 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), sets out the circumstances in which a landlord may enter a rental unit without written notice, including where the tenant consents to the entry or where there is an emergency. In most other circumstances, section 27 of the Act requires a landlord to give the tenant at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering the rental unit.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord, with the assistance of the building manager, entered the rental unit on July 17, 2024, without giving prior written notice. I am further satisfied that there was no emergency and that the Tenant did not consent to the entry. I therefore find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit. Substantial interference and Harassment

The Tenant further testified that on July 9, 2024, two police officers attended at the rental unit and questioned the Tenant about their legal right to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the police informed them that the Landlord had called the police and alleged that the Tenant did not have a legal right to occupy the unit, that they were only guests, and that they should vacate the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that they showed the police their tenancy documents and payment records to establish that they were tenants of the rental unit. After reviewing the documents and speaking with the Tenant, the police left the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that this incident caused them anxiety and stress. They had three young children in the rental unit, had recently arrived in Canada, and did not understand the legal process. The Tenant testified that they felt frightened and overwhelmed when police officers attended at their home because of the Landlord’s false allegation.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not, at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an eviction order is executed, substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by the tenant or members of the tenant’s household.
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The Act does not define “harassment.” However, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines harassment as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. In the landlord and tenant context, harassment is generally understood as conduct that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome, inappropriate, or intimidating in the circumstances.
Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act.

The Landlord’s conduct on July 9, 2024, must be assessed in context. The Tenant’s evidence establishes that the Landlord called the police and made a false allegation that the Tenant had no legal right to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord did so despite the existence of a tenancy agreement and payment records. I find that the Landlord attempted to use the authority of the police to pressure or intimidate the Tenant into leaving the rental unit outside the statutory process under the Act.

Security of tenure is a fundamental protection under the Act. When a landlord attempts to remove a tenant, or pressure a tenant to leave a rental unit, without following the statutory process, that conduct strikes at the core purpose of the Act.

Although the incidents occurred over a short period of time, I find that the seriousness of involving the police to challenge the Tenant’s lawful occupation of the rental unit elevates the conduct beyond a minor dispute. A reasonable tenant in these circumstances would feel intimidated, unsafe, and uncertain about their right to remain in their home.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant, contrary to sections 22 and 23 of the Act. Remedies
At the hearing, the Tenant sought moving costs. The Tenant submitted that they moved out of the rental unit because they felt unsafe and because of the Landlord’s conduct.
I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the Landlord’s conduct on July 9, 2024, and July 17, 2024.

Subsection 31(2)(b) of the Act provides that if the Board determines that a tenant was induced by the conduct of the landlord, the superintendent, or an agent of the landlord to vacate the rental unit, the Board may order the landlord to pay the tenant reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage, and other similar expenses.

The Tenant testified that this was a sublease arrangement. The Tenant stated that the Landlord rented the unit from the building management and paid $2,150.00 per month to the management office but charged the Tenant $2,500.00 per month. The Tenant testified that after they discovered in August 2024 that they were paying more than the amount the Landlord paid to the building, they decided to find another place to live. The Tenant gave notice to vacate in January 2025 and moved out on January 31, 2025.

Based on the Tenant’s own evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s decision to vacate the rental unit was directly caused by the Landlord’s conduct on July 9, 2024, or July 17, 2024. Rather, I find that the Tenant chose to move out because of the rent dispute and the amount being charged by the Landlord.

Therefore, I find that the Tenant was not induced to vacate the rental unit because of the Landlord’s breach of sections 22 and 23 of the Act. The claim for moving costs is denied. General Damages: Pain and Suffering

The Tenant sought general damages for the distress caused by the Landlord’s conduct. The Board has authority to award general damages pursuant to paragraph 31(1)(f) of the Act. See [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name]. Ct.).

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord’s unauthorized entry into the rental unit, together with the Landlord calling the police and making a false allegation about the Tenant’s right to occupy the rental unit, caused the Tenant shock, stress, anxiety, and distress.

I also accept that the impact of the Landlord’s conduct was heightened by the Tenant’s circumstances. The Tenant had three young children in the rental unit, had recently arrived in Canada, and was unfamiliar with the legal process. In those circumstances, it was reasonable for the Tenant to feel frightened and overwhelmed when police officers attended at the rental unit because of the Landlord’s allegation.

I am satisfied that the Tenant’s distress was reasonably foreseeable and does not require medical evidence to establish. The Tenant gave direct evidence about the emotional impact of the Landlord’s conduct, and I accept that evidence.
Based on the seriousness of the Landlord’s conduct, the impact on the Tenant, and the evidence before me, I find that an award of $1,000.00 in general damages is appropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 in general damages for pain and suffering. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $1,401.88 on or before July 18, 2026.

The Tenant filed this application on March 4, 2025, claiming the landlord has charged them a rent increase that does not comply with Part VII of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act”) and is therefore unlawful.
The Tenant testified that they have been paying rent in the amount of 1,400.00 since December 1, 2022.

By operation of sections 135.1 and 136 of the Act, any rent increase that would otherwise be unlawful is deemed to be lawful if a tenant pays it for 12 consecutive months before brining an application to the Board challenging the validity of that rent increase within on year after the date the increase was first charges. As a result, this portion of the T1 application must be dismissed.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord has failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's deposit as required by section 106(6) the Act.
Section 29(2) of the Act states no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant is seeking interest from the date the deposit was collected on December 1, 2021, which is outside the one-year limitation period. Since the Tenant’s application was filed on March 4, 2025, the Board only has jurisdiction to order interest owing within the one year from the making of the application. As such, interest is calculated for the period from March 4, 2024, to April 14, 2024, the date the Tenant moved out, in the amount of $3.88.

On March 27, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), claiming the Landlord required possession of converting the unit or complex to non-residential use. The termination date in the N13 notice was July 31, 2024.
The monthly rent was $1,350.00
The Tenants submitted to the Board a copy of the signed N13 notice as evidence.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 14, 2024. The Tenant submit that the Landlord did not pay the required one month’s rent compensation.

Section 55.1 of the Act states: If the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55, the landlord shall compensate the tenant no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination of the tenancy given by the landlord under section 48, 49 or 50.

The Act is clear that a landlord is required to pay a tenant compensation equal to one month’s rent if the landlord serves the tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act. Since the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants compensation for termination of the tenancy, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), I find that the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the one month’s rent compensation that is properly owed in this matter. T6 & T2 application

The Tenant testified that the unit had a flood in July 2023. As a result of the Landlord did not take the reasonable steps in ensuring that the unit was properly dried and as a result there was mould in the unit and that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance and repair obligations under the Act. The Tenant relies largely on the same factual allegations in their T2 application, alleging that the Landlord’s response to these issues substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and harassed the Tenant to induce them into vacating.

The Tenant testified that there was mould growth behind the walls and under the floor in the living room, entryway and kitchen. the Tenant testified that she advised the Landlord on January 31, 2024. The Landlord responded asking whether the Tenant had a dehumidifier that the Tenant can use to dry up the moisture, after the Tenant said no. The Landlord sent two people with a bowl and soap on the same day to clean up the mould.

On February 3, 2024, the Tenant discovered more mould and advised the Landlord on the same day. The Landlord completed a mould and air quality assessment test and found that there was mould in the unit, and the report was provided in evidence. On March 5, 2024, the Landlord opened the walls to conduct remediation. The Tenant provides that the Landlord did not hire a third party but did the work himself. The Tenant submitted that due to mold toxicity syndrome, the Tenant re-located temporarily on February 1, 2024, and moved out of the unit as of April 14, 2024.

The Tenant testified that on March 15, 2024, the Landlord was forcing her to sign the N11 to mutually terminate the tenancy and in the alternative serve her an N13 Notice of termination. The Tenant provided that the Landlord wanted his brother-in-law to move into the unit instead. The Tenant refused to the sign the N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy.
The Tenant also testified that the Landlord called the police in March 2024 on the Tenant, and the police spoke with Tenant on the phone and advised her to abide by the law.
On April 10, 2024, the Landlord sent an email to the Tenant advising that the Tenant was making frivolous and vexatious claims against them.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The simple presence of a maintenance issue in itself is not sufficient to find the Landlord liable and additional factors must be considered. The Landlord in this case may not be found in breach of section 20(1) of the Act solely because water damage and mould were alleged. The Court emphasized that a contextual approach must be taken, focusing on whether the Landlord responded reasonably once aware of the issue.

Here, it was the Tenant’s own evidence, once the Landlord became aware of the mould in the unit, the Landlord set out to first clean it and later did a mold and air test to confirm. Thereafter took reasonable steps to begin remediation.

There is no conclusive evidence that the steps taken by the Landlord were inadequate as confirmed by professionals, and there is no evidence before me that the issue persisted past the date of March 5, 2024, as the Tenant had re-located and did not attend the unit to confirm whether the issue had been resolved.

As such, I find that the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s maintenance complaint regarding the mould was both timely and appropriate. While the Tenant may have perceived the response time as inadequate, the objective facts demonstrate that the Landlord acted with due diligence and in a manner consistent with their legal obligations.

The Tenant provided their testimony on the Landlord forcing the Tenant to move out. So, he can have his brother-in-law move into the unit. However, no corroborative evidence was led about the Landlord forcing the Tenant to vacate to re- rent the unit for to his brother-in- law. Instead, I find that the Landlord and Tenant had a breakdown in communication that led to disagreements.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to terminate the tenancy as of April 14, 2024. I find that it is more likely than not, the Tenant was already actively seeking alternative housing. The Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to establish that they did not understand that they were agreeing to terminate the tenancy or that they were coerced or under duress by the Landlord to terminate the tenancy.

On any application before the Board the person who wants to establish a certain fact or version of events has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to prove it is more likely than not that version of events is true. The Tenant has failed to meet their burden of proof.

In this context, I find that there was no breach of maintenance obligations, and I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Accordingly, the Tenant’s T6 and T2 application must be dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,401.88. This amount represents: • $3.88 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $1,350.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant claims two illegal charges: 1. $540.10 for water utility charges paid; and 2. $200.00 key deposit that has not been returned. Water Utility Charges

The Tenant paid $540.10 in water utility c harges to the Landlords when the water was included in the rent. The Landlords did not return the amount but instead allocated the amount towards the arrears owing.

The Tenant was responsible to pay for r ent from March 1-14, 2026, due to not having given notice in accordance with the Act, and the Landlords having mitigated their costs by re-renting the unit on March 15, 2026.
The Tenant notified the Landlords of their intent to vacate the rental unit on February 28, 2026. The Tenant thereafter vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2026.

The Landlords, having received the notice to vacate, notified the Tenant that it was short notice, and that based on the Act, the earliest date to vacate was March 31, 2026. There was no agreement to accept short notice or to terminate the tenancy on February 28, 2026.
The Landlords re-rented the unit on March 15, 2026.

The Landlords’ oral evidence confirm that the Tenant’s monthly rent was $2,950.00. The Landlords charged rent for the period from March 1-14, 2026, in the amount of $1,332.26. From this amount, the Tenant was credited $600.00 for the utility compensation that was erroneously paid.

In Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522, the Divisional Court found that when a tenant is entitled to compensation from a landlord but the tenant also owes the landlord rent arrears, the Board must off-set these amounts: [18] . . . While the tenants were entitled to $3,000.00 in compensation because of the N13 Notice, the landlord was owed more than $3,000.00 by them at the time of their application. The amount owing for arrears of rent should have been taken into consideration in determining the amount of compensation owing. Had that been done, the Board would have had to conclude that the tenants were owed nothing in compensation at the time of the application because of the set-off. [18] This conclusion is in keeping with the purposes of the Act set out in s. 1, which include “to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.” I note that counsel for Marineland acknowledged that should it seek to pursue any remaining amounts owing from the tenants, it would be required to set off the $3,000.00 of compensation that it owed to the tenants.

Therefore, while the Landlords owed the Tenant $540.10, the Landlord’s credited $600.00 against the arrears of rent still owing by the Tenant leaving a balance for the arrears in the amount of $732.26. Key Deposit
It is not contested that the Tenant returned the keys and fobs to the rental unit to the Landlords at the end of the tenancy, and as such is requesting the $200.00 key deposit be refunded.
The Landlords did not return the $200.00 key deposit to the Tenant.
As of the date of the hearing the arrears of rent are $732.26.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act provides a prohibition on additional charges to a Tenant with narrow exceptions. Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulations”) provides an exception to allow refundable key deposits so long as they do not exceed the expected direct replacement costs. In this case, the tenancy agreement specified this key deposit would be returned to the Tenant upon the Tenant returning the keys to the Landlords.
The Landlords failed to return the key deposit to the Tenant as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
However, in accordance with Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522, I am obligated to off-set this amount from rent arrears owed to the Landlord.
Therefore, while the Landlords owe the Tenant $200.00, this amount shall be awarded to the Tenant and will instead be applied to the arrears of rent still owing by the Tenant.

There was no evidence that the Landlords communicated to the Tenant that the key deposit amount of $200.00 was being credited against the arrears owing. As such, the cost to file the application is granted and the Landlords shall also apply the cost of this application, $48.00, against the arrears of rent still owing by the Tenant.
ordered: A credit in the aggregate amount of $248.00 (representing the $200.00 key deposit and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application) shall be applied to the amount of rent arrears owing by the Tenant to the Landlords. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants were seeking to remove [name] and [name] as applicants. The Landlord opposed removing them as applicants as this could allow them to seek an order against the Landlord in the future.
The Tenants’ Legal Representative stated he only had the authority to represent the Tenants present.

I was satisfied that [name] and [name] [name] did not need to be removed as parties for the application to proceed. I was aware that only [name] and [name] were represented by [name]. Preliminary Issue: Late Disclosure by the Tenants

The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the Tenants had served and filed disclosure on June 11, 2026, not in accordance with the Rules. The evidence that was late served was 2 pictures. The Landlord confirmed having seen the pictures. When asked what the prejudice would be to consider the 2 pictures, the Landlord’s Legal Representative stated they would have been able to provide photos contradicting the evidence. When asked, the Landlord’s Legal Representative did acknowledge that the Landlord could provide oral testimony refuting the photo evidence.

As I was satisfied that the Landlord had seen the pictures and there would be no prejudice in allowing the Tenants to refer to the pictures given the Landlord could provide oral testimony about the photos, I allowed the documentary evidence to be submitted. Preliminary Issue: Insufficient Details in the application

The Landlord’s Legal Representative sought for the application to be dismissed as she found that there were insufficient details in the application. The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that there were no specific dates in the application for when they found the Landlord had not moved into the rental unit and when there was an advertisement for rent.

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (‘Ball v. Metro Capital’). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established.
The Court held in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...”

In [name], the Court stated that the responding party must be able “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…

While the Tenants’ application does not have a specific date, the application clearly identifies that they found that the Landlord had not moved into the rental unit in May 2025 and that the rental unit was advertised for rent. I am satisfied that the Landlord was aware of the case that must be met as the allegation is that she did not move in and that she advertised the unit for rent. The Landlord also submitted evidence in relation to the allegations in the application, which I find indicates she understood to case to be met and was able to respond. As I find that the Landlord was able to understand and to respond to the allegations, I find the application has sufficient particulars. Therefore, the application proceeded. T5 Application:

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. The Tenants did not Prove that the Landlord was not Occupying the Rental Unit

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute that the Landlord served an N12 notice on January 27, 2025 with a date of termination of March 31, 2025 for her own occupation of the rental unit, and that the Tenants vacated on March 1, 2025 as a result of the N12 notice.

Tenant [name] (LJ) testified that the Landlord posted an advertisement on March 6, 2025 for a lease starting May 1, 2025, and that the advertisement does not mention the Landlord living on site. On cross-examination, LJ did acknowledge that the rental unit has 4 bedrooms and that the advertisement was only looking for 3 tenants.

The Landlord testified that she served an N12 notice because the rental unit needed extensive renovations, she was not sure how long it would take, and she was moving into the rental unit to manage the contractors that would arrive early and on the weekends. The Landlord testified that there was a leak in the ceiling of the kitchen which required the ceiling to be removed, the upstairs bathroom to be renovated, and the main floor was renovated to blend in with the kitchen and pot lights were added. During this time, the Landlord testified that all furniture was placed in the middle of the room, which was demonstrated by the photo evidence submitted by the Tenants on June 11, 2025. The Landlord testified that when she took possession of the rental unit in March 2025, she needed to clean up things left by the prior Tenants, and she then moved into the rental unit on April 9, 2025 into one of the upstairs bedrooms. The Landlord testified she moved into the upstairs bedroom first as the mudding and sanding was finished. The Landlord testified that she did not receive the final approval from the City of Guelph for the framing and plumbing as required by the building permit until July 29, 2025, and drywall could not be installed until after this date. The Landlord testified that the electrical permits were signed on August 8, 2025 and she moved into the basement bedroom where she has her own bathroom before the end of August 2025 when the roomers moved in.

The Landlord testified that she did list an advertisement for 3 roomers to help her offset her mortgage and the costs of the renovations, however, the Act does not apply as she shares a kitchen with them. The Landlord testified that she did not contact the prior Tenants as there were 4 of them as joint tenants with only 3 rooms available and their lease was pursuant to the Act, while the rooming situation would be exempt. The Landlord further testified that she still resides in the rental unit and was participating in the hearing from the rental unit. I had the Landlord show the main floor of the rental unit, and the Tenants confirmed that it was the rental unit they resided in. I also had the Landlord show on zoom her bedroom, office area and her bathroom to confirm she was residing in the rental unit. The Landlord also testified that she has changed her identification to the address of the rental unit, the utilities are in her name, the insurance for the property is for personal use and not a rental unit, and she had to notify the Canadian Revenue Agency about her new address.

Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have proven on a balance of probabilities that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, pursuant to section 57(1)(a) of the Act. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she moved into the rental unit on April 9, 2025, which was within 6 weeks of the Tenants vacating the rental unit. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that she continues to live in the rental unit, which was supported by the Landlord providing a walk-through of her living space in the rental unit on zoom at the hearing. The Landlord acknowledged that she posted an advertisement for roomers and that as they share a kitchen, the roomers are exempt from the Act, while the prior Tenants were not exempt from the Act, and there were more Tenants than rooms available once the Landlord moved into the unit. As the Landlord did move into the rental unit and the advertisement was for a rooming situation exempt from the Act, I find that section 57(5)(c) of the Act is not invoked, and if it were, I would find that the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith.

As the Tenants did not establish the no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the amount of $9,966.37 by July 21, 2026.
The residential unit is a townhouse located at [address]nue, St. Thomas, Ontario.
The Tenants commenced their tenancy at the rental unit in March of 2024 and vacated the rental unit on January 13, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Preliminary Issue

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that this matter must be dismissed due to the fact that the parties signed Terms of Settlement on October 29, 2025. [name] read out clause 6.1 which stated “This Agreement constitutes a full and final settlement of all issues, applications, claims or complaints between the parties arising from or relating to the tenancy or the residential premises up to and including February 28, 2026.”

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the Agreement resolved issues up to February 28, 2026 and it cannot waive actions in the future. The Tenants were given an N12 notice of termination because the Landlord wanted to move into their rental unit and the Landlord failed to move in and listed the house for sale.

Firstly, I note that section 6.2 sets out that “rights or obligations arising after that date (February 28, 2026) are unaffected unless expressly stated herein.” This agreement makes no mention of rights or obligations relating to the Landlord’s stated intention to move into the house. Secondly, this is a private agreement between parties, it has not been ratified by the Board so it is not binding on the parties. Finally, an agreement cannot bar or attempt to waive future actions of the parties.

This agreement does not absolve the Landlord of his obligation to move into the rental unit as set out on his N12 notice. Although [name] requested an adjournment of the matter so that he could amend his defence, I denied that request as that was an insufficient reason for an adjournment. Evidence of Tenant, [name] ([name]) 9. [name] testified that she and her husband moved into the house on March 1, 2024 and they have 5 children together. She stated that the Landlord is dating [name]’s (other Tenant) mother and so the relationship between [name] and the Landlord is very tense. 10. The Tenant stated that the Landlord gave them 3 separate N12 notices and the last one was given to them on October 16, 2025 with a termination date of December 31, 2025. She stated that one of those N12 applications was dismissed by the Board in October of 2025 due to the Landlord not disclosing that he had served previous N12 notices. 11. [name] stated that the Landlord attempted to force the Tenants to pay for utilities in the rental unit which were not set out in their lease and they refused to pay those expenses. Ms. [name] provided text messages dated March 12, 2025 between [name] and the Landlord confirming [name] demand for the Tenants to pay utilities. These text messages were found in the Tenants’ Document Brief, DOC #8072581 at pages 28 and 29. 12. The Tenant stated that she was told on October 17, 2025 that she was trespassing in the house and that the Landlord would be arranging for the police to attend to remove the Tenants. This occurred one day after she received the third N12 notice. This text message was from her previous representative to herself and it was found in the Tenants’ Document Brief. 13. [name] confirmed that she signed the Terms of Settlement as she was fed up with the harassment and bullying from the Landlord. She stated that although they could have remained in the unit until February 28, 2026, they felt so threatened that they moved out 1.5 months early on January 13, 2026. 14. The Tenant stated that the Landlord listed the house for sale on March 1, 2026, 7 weeks after they vacated the rental unit and she was incredibly frustrated and felt betrayed. She is seeking a rent abatement of $7,500.00, moving and storage expenses of $1,843.80, a rent differential of $4,524.00 ($377.00 x 12), utilities of $10,069.93 because their previous rent included the utilities, compensation of $7,500.00 (if abatement is not granted) and an administrative fine. 15. In cross-examination, [name] asked the Tenant whether she had paid rent for October, November and December of 2025 and the Tenant confirmed that she did not pay for November and December’s rent. The Tenant explained that arrangement was part of the settlement agreement between the parties. Evidence of Landlord, [name] Kirsten (FK) 16. FK testified that he did not move into the rental unit when the Tenants moved out because he had to complete renovations/repairs and so it was not ready for him. The Landlord stated that he intended to move into the unit and would have if it was in a proper condition. 17. The Landlord stated that he had to sell the rental unit because he required sufficient funds to prepare for his separation battle with his common law spouse. He confirmed that he listed it for sale in March and the house has since been sold. 18. FK stated that he felt that the agreement that he signed with the Tenants resolved all issues between them and he stated that he paid funds to the Tenants as set out in the agreement. 19. In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked if he signed a declaration stating that he would be moving into the rental unit for at least one year. [name] answered for his client by saying “not for the last N12” and I instructed [name] to allow Mr. [name]name] to reply. [name] then replied with the same answer. A further question was asked by [name] and [name] spoke for his client again. [name] was warned again about speaking for his client and he became increasingly argumentative. 20. [name] chose to end her cross-examination of the Landlord due to the actions of [name]. Analysis 21. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 22. There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord communicated to the Tenants that he wanted their rental unit back for himself, the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of this N12, no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord’s actions were made in bad faith. 23. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 24. Not only did the Landlord fail to move into the residential unit, but the Landlord listed it for sale 7 weeks after the Tenants vacated the house. The Landlord stated that he could not move into the house because it was not in a move-in condition and then sold the house so that he would have sufficient funds for his legal separation. 25. However, the Landlord did not provide any corroborating materials to support his reasons for not moving into the rental unit and he provided no financial disclosure to support his claim that he required the funds for his separation, I would have expected to see pictures of the state of the rental unit when the Tenants left, invoices for repairs or renovations to the unit and documentation to support his need for funds. 26. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12 or in this case, the email. 27. The Tenants’ testimony regarding the Landlord’s attempt to force the Tenants to pay for utilities and the Landlord’s trespassing threat were not challenged by the Landlord. These actions demonstrate to me that the Landlord willingly contravened the Act prior to serving the N12 notice. After the Tenants vacated, the Landlord made the decision to renovate the rental unit and list it for sale 7 weeks after the termination of the tenancy which puts the Landlord in a situation where he is presumed to be acting in bad faith. 28. The Landlord was represented by a legal representative and so I did not have to explain the presumption of bad faith in section 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord has not shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act. Based on the above, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith. 29. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies 30. With respect to the Tenants’ request for an abatement of rent from October of 2025 to February of 2026, I am not granting an award under this head of damage. I was not provided with sufficient evidence to substantiate that the Tenants did not receive the full benefits of their tenancy during those months. 31. With respect to the Tenants’ request for a rent differential, the Tenants are now paying $377.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. The Tenants provided a copy of their new lease which confirmed the rent of $1,877.00 per month. Based on the fact that this evidence was not questioned by the Landlord, I accept that this is a comparable unit and will grant the rent differential of $4,524.00 ($377.00 x 12). 32. The Tenants requested that the Landlord pay for their utilities which are not included in their new rent and they provided a copy of the utilities paid so far at the new house. These Entegrus invoices (electricity and water) included previous, unpaid balances and a required deposit that was not apparently paid. The calculated, average prices for water and hydro were exaggerated due to these extra fees rendering these invoices unreliable. As such, I will not be awarding any amount for utilities. 33. With respect to the Tenants’ request for moving and storage expenses, I award $394.37 for the Read-Bin which was used to assist the Tenants with moving. An invoice was provided for same dated November 7, 2025. I was not provided with sufficient information as to why storage expenses were necessary and as such, I will not award those storage costs. 34. With respect to the Tenants’ request for compensation of $7,500.00, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $5,000.00 to the Tenants. I am satisfied that the Tenants suffered emotional distress, a serious disruption and inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith. 35. The Tenants are also requesting that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 36. Administrative fines are generally ordered where there is egregious conduct by a landlord. Although the Landlord acted in bad faith, I am satisfied that the total award of $9,966.37 in other remedies is sufficient to provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 37. The Tenants are also entitled to their application fee of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,966.37. This amount represents: • $4,524.00 for rent differential; • $5,000.00 for compensation; • $394.37 for moving expenses; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] [name][name], [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes (the “L1 Application”). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (the “T2:T6 Application”)
reasons: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $5,959.11 on or before July 13, 2026 for the reasons detailed below. L1 Application

The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2024. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit
The lawful rent is $2,150.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant has paid $8,600.00 to the Landlord since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to March 31, 2024 are $10,750.00. The parties acknowledged this was the amount owing, subject to a dispute as to whether the Landlord also held a last month’s rent deposit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,150.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord.

The Landlord disputed that he still held the last month’s rent deposit as he stated that he never received the last month’s rent deposit from his property management company. The lease acknowledges the rent deposit was paid, and the Landlord does not dispute its receipt by the property management company. The Landlord took the position that this amount must have been applied to the last month of the first year’s term, which the Landlord states was paid upfront as a payment of twelve month’s rent. The Landlord provided no proof to substantiate this such as bank records or a ledger tracking payments in the tenancy to corroborate this position.

Given the above, and that by operation of law the last month’s rent can only be applied to the last month of the tenancy in any event, I find that the Landlord did continue to hold this rent deposit. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated. Interest in the amount of $75.45 from July 1, 2022 to February 28, 2024, the day before the last month’s rent deposit is deemed to be applied to the last month of the tenancy, is also deducted from the arrears owing. and LTB-T-020157-24 T2:T6 Application/Section 82 Issues
The Tenant raised issued pursuant to section 82 of the Act and as part of the T2;T6 application. Laundry/Alteration of the Locking System

The Tenant claims they were entitled to have access to laundry services in accordance with their lease and were denied this access from February, 2023 to September 30, 2023 when the Landlord’s Witness, [name] (“[name]”), who was the basement tenant, locked the Tenant out from being able to access the laundry some time in February, 2023 following a disagreement between the Tenant and [name]. This also constitutes the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord altered the locking systems of the unit.

The Landlord took the position that laundry was not included in the lease, despite it being listed as included in the lease. The Landlord testified that the rent was reduced on this basis from $2,500.00 to $2,150.00 as the Tenant stated they could do laundry at their parent’s home. The Landlord was not able to provide any corroborating evidence for this testimony to support the assertions that the written lease did not accurately reflect the agreement between the parties.

I note that the Landlord later in his testimony stated that his property manager at the time and not himself was responsible for the discussions with the Tenant as to lease terms when the Tenant rented the unit. It is therefore unclear as to when this supposed conversation with the Tenant related to a reduction in rent for laundry not being included would have occurred.

While the Landlord acknowledged that the Tenant was able to use laundry for a prolonged period, the Landlord states that this was because the Tenant had a good relationship with [name], but they no longer had access when the relationship between the Tenant and [name] soured. The Landlord’s position is they are not responsible for this.

The Tenant, [name] [name][name] (“Mr. [name]name][name]”) acknowledged that once [name] moved in they negotiated access to the laundry with him and paid for internet that was shared in return, but the Tenant’s position is that despite this the Landlord remained responsible for providing laundry as specified by the lease as this formed part of their agreement.

I find given this conflicting version of events the best evidence I have as to the agreement between the parties is the lease itself. This supports the Tenant’s position, and I note that given the Landlord acknowledged that it was his property manager and not himself that was responsible for discussing lease terms with the Tenant, I find the Tenant’s account more reliable in this regard. This is also supported by the Landlord giving access to the Tenant to do laundry after [name] moved out. If laundry was not intended to be included, it is unclear why the Landlord would have done so.

In relation to the changing of the locks, the Landlord’s position is that the locking system was never changed and that [name] merely locked the door to the basement after the dispute between [name] and the Tenant. The Tenant had not been provided with a key to the basement as it did not form part of the rental unit. and LTB-T-020157-24

The Tenant’s position is not that the locking system was altered, but that the basement door was locked, and that this deprived the Tenant of access to the laundry area, which in their position formed part of the services that were to come with the rental unit.

I find based on the above that the Landlord failing to provide or arrange for access to laundry as specified in the agreement is a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I do not find this constitutes an alteration of the locking system.

Mr. [name]name][name] testified that after being denied access to the laundry he had to take his laundry to his parents’ house or the laundromat and he would have to incur costs of Ubers and costs at the laundromat to do so.

While there was some confusion as to the date in the hearing, I find the best evidence before me in respect to when the Tenant got access to the laundry in the basement is the video shown during the testimony of the Tenant, [name] (“[name]”) that it occurred on September 30, 2023 when the Landlord attended to give the Tenant this access following [name] moving out within a few days from the stove being cracked.

The Tenant seeks a 6% rent abatement per month for the period in which they were restricted from using the laundry facilities. I find this to be an appropriate abatement in this respect based on the interference caused and on that basis order a total abatement for this issue in the amount of $554.17 for the period between May 23, 2023 to September 30, 2023 calculated as ([4 x $2150.00] + [$2150.00 x 12 / 365 x 9]) x 0.06. Stove

The Tenant sent the Landlord an e-mail on September 28, 2023 that stated the glass top of the stove had cracked, the Tenant presumes from wear and tear, and is functionally unsafe to use as an electrical hazard.

I note that the Tenant states in the e-mail that the issue is not a rush to deal with as the Tenant understands it may be financially difficult. The Tenant followed up with the Landlord several times after this date. This includes that when the Landlord attended the rental unit on September 30, 2026, the Tenant asked the Landlord to take a look at the stove for the purposes of repair and the Landlord refused to do so.

The Landlord takes the position that the stove in the rental unit was a good quality stove purchased in 2021 and worked fine until the incident that happened between the Tenant and [name]. The Landlord asserts that the Tenant purposefully damaged the stove in order to put pressure on the Landlord, who the Tenant knew had a lack of funds. The Landlord asserts that the Tenant declined the solution provided by the Landlord of moving the downstairs stove upstairs after [name] moved a few days after this damage occurred.

The Landlord acknowledged that he never inspected the stove for the purposes of seeing if it could be repaired. The Landlord also acknowledges he never replaced the stove or served a notice to enter the unit for the purposes of replacing the stove. and LTB-T-020157-24

Ultimately, regardless of the cause of the damage to the stove, the Landlord has an obligation to repair or replace the stove if the stove was non-functional. If the Tenant in fact caused damage, the Landlord could have brought a claim against the Tenant in respect this damage. The Landlord’s evidence was also not that the Tenant attempted to physically prevent the Landlord from replacing the stove with the downstairs stove, but that they told the Landlord they wanted a repair to that stove or a new stove. I find the Landlord was not prevented from providing a replacement or repairing the stove and took no steps to do so. On that basis the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance responsibilities under section 20 of the Act.

The Tenant claimed a rent abatement of 6% for the period they were without a stove, and out-of-pocket expenses for food deliveries and the purchase of a hot plate since the stove was not repaired or replaced.

The Tenant purchased a hot plate on October 15, 2023 at a cost of $127.66, and the best evidence before me was that it was delivered on October 19, 2023. I find this is a reasonable out of pocket expense to have incurred in the circumstances directly caused by the Landlord’s failure to maintain the stove, and I award the Tenant this cost.
The Tenant also provided a number of receipts for meal deliveries from September 28, 2023 to the end of the tenancy.

The Tenant acknowledged they ordered meal deliveries prior to the stove breaking, but Mr. [name][name] testified this was more frequent after the stove broke, and was much more frequent during the period prior to purchasing the hot plate.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant presented a receipt for a meal delivery on September 28, 2023. This is the same day the Landlord was informed about the issue of the stove. I find that in accordance with the principles articulated in Onyskiw, it is not reasonable to expect the Landlord could have had the stove repaired or replaced on the same day, and so no award is made in respect of this amount.

The next meal delivery receipt presented was for October 1, 2023. Given the Landlord never took any steps to inspect the stove, or repair or replace it, including that the Landlord declined to even look at the stove when in attendance at the rental unit on September 30, 2023, I find that the Landlord was in breach by this time. It is unreasonable when already in attendance at the rental unit to inspect the broken appliance for the purposes of identifying whether it can be repaired or requires replacement.

Mr. [name]name][name] testified that when he had a functional stove he ordered food deliveries 1-2 times a week, but that this increased to 3-4 times a week when he did not. and LTB-T-020157-24 He testified that it took much longer to cook things on the hot plate and so he made the choice more often to order food even after receiving it as he works often to midnight.

Meal delivery receipts presented for the period from October 1, 2023 to October 15, 2023 total $443.05. They appear to be in an increased frequency as described by [name] [name], but I note that Mr. [name]name][name] acknowledged he would have incurred some of these costs in any event. I find it appropriate to award $200.00, on the basis that it represents a little less than half of these costs incurred during this time period. I find this amount is appropriate as it appears food deliveries were ordered about twice as frequently, but that a nominal amount should be deducted given the Tenant’s grocery bill would have been correspondingly reduced by at least a small amount during this period. I find on a balance of probabilities that this represents the additional out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant incurred during this period due to the breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations.
The Tenant is awarded a total of $327.66 for reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred due to the Landlord’s breach of maintenance obligations in relation to the stove on this basis.

The Tenant presented a further 19 receipts for food deliveries that occurred during the approximately 10-week period between October 21, 2023 and January 1, 2024 after the hot plate had arrived. I find that this average of approximately 2 food deliveries a week falls within the range of meal deliveries that Mr. [name]name][name] testified he would normally order. I am not satisfied on this basis that the Tenant incurred additional out-of-pocket expenses related to this period on the basis of the evidence provided and therefore decline to make an award related to these amounts.

In relation to a rent abatement, Mr. [name]name][name] testified that even after having the hot plate, they cooked less, particularly when he returned from work, as the hot plate took much longer to cook food than the stove had. Given his hours of work, this wasn’t always feasible for him, and was inconvenient at all times.

The Tenant requested a 6% rent abatement for this period, and I find this to be a reasonable estimate for the loss of use of the stove. I award a total abatement of $774.00 for the period of October 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024 based on the calculations as follows 6 x $2150.00 x 0.06. [name]

The Tenant submits that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations by failing to adequately clear the snow and that this was the Landlord’s responsibility to do so in the common outdoor areas of the rental unit.
The lease contains no provisions that allocate the responsibility for snow clearing. The lease provides for one parking spot in the driveway.
The Landlord’s position was that the Tenant was responsible for snow clearing. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord is responsible for snow clearing. and LTB-T-020157-24
There is a driveway near the back of the house that fits one car, and common pathways from the sidewalk to the entrance to the house that serve both the upstairs and downstairs rental unit.

In accordance with the principles articulated in Crete v Ottawa Community Housing Corporation, 2024 ONCA 459, I find that to determine responsibilities for snow clearing I must first look to the appropriate maintenance standards bylaw for the region. For the City of Oshawa, Consolidated By-law 127-2007 of the Corporation of the City of Oshawa (the “By-Law”) applies, and section 4.5 states: “4.5. Parking Areas, Walkways and Safe Passage: Owners shall maintain driveways, ramps, parking areas, exterior walkways, exterior passages, exterior stairs, exterior landings and similar areas on the Property – with the exception of a Sidewalk as defined in Sections 2.1 and 3.0 of the City’s Winter Access By- law 92-2009, as amended – so as to provide for safe passage under normal use and weather conditions (e.g. snow and ice), day or night. (96-2022, 188-2022)”

The definition of Owner in the By-Law includes both an owner and occupier of a property. Therefore, this does not specify whether the Landlord or Tenant would be responsible. Given this and that the lease is silent on the responsibility, I must make a determination as to whether the obligation falls under the Landlord’s maintenance responsibilities under section 20(1) of the Act, or the under the Tenant’s obligations for ordinary cleanliness under section 33 of the Act. This will depend in part of whether the areas in question are common areas or exclusive use areas.

The Landlord’s position is that the areas to be cleared were for the exclusive use of the Tenant. The Tenant’s position was that these were common areas of the property given the multiple units in the building.

From the evidence of the Landlord and the Tenant, I am satisfied that there were common pathways from the road and sidewalk to various entrances to the rental unit, including for access to the building and for access to the backyard. Despite the Landlord’s testimony that these were each excusive areas for the downstairs and upstairs tenants, I find these did in fact constitute common areas given that there are no specific provisions in the tenancy agreement allotting certain areas or paths to be exclusive to each tenancy.

I find on this basis that the snow clearing of common areas does fall into the maintenance responsibilities of the Landlord under section 20(1) of the Act given the silence in the lease on this point.

The Tenant provided evidence that during the 2022 to 2023 winter [name] shovelled parts of the path in a manner that piled up the snow behind the gate and made the backyard inaccessible. This period however is prior to the available period for a remedy in relation to snow removal and I make no award in respect of this.

Mr. [name]name][name] testified that through the entirety of the winter they complained to the Landlord once to twice every week or two about the Landlord not clearing the snow or providing salt, but that the Landlord did not take any steps in that regard. The Tenant testified that this occurred from the period of October or November, 2023 to about April, and LTB-T-020157-24 2024. I note that while the Landlord attempted to provide evidence in the middle of closing submissions that he had taken care of the snow and ice in an adequate manner, the Landlord had already declined an opportunity to cross-examine Mr. [name]name][name] on his testimony, or to provide any rebuttal evidence on the issue of snow clearing when given the opportunity to do so following the Tenant’s testimony. On this basis, I take [name] [name]’s testimony to be accurate and accept it in this regard.

The Tenant testified that during this 2023 to 2024 winter season the front steps of the rental unit were difficult to maintain as there was ice build up and that it was slippery due to poorly maintained areas on the front porch.

While I am satisfied from Mr. [name]name][name]’s testimony both that these issues occurred and that they did notify the Landlord of them throughout the season, I find given this evidence was unclear as to the exact dates the issues occurred within the season, and the exact dates the Landlord was notified as to the occurrence of these issues, I am only satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was in breach and that a remedy is appropriate for the time period of December 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024. I am satisfied that this time period encompasses a time in which these issues occurred and the Landlord was on notice of them as the time period starts on a date after the latest start date in the time period referred to Mr. [name]name][name]’s testimony, and ends prior to the earliest date they would have ceased based on Mr. [name]name][name]’s testimony.

The Tenant seeks a 2% rent abatement, or $43.00 per month. I find this to be reasonable based on the interference caused, and award a total abatement of $172.00 for the period of December 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024 based on the calculations as follows 4 x $2150.00 x 0.02. [name]

The Tenant submits that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to take adequate action in respect of the noise complaints they made in relation to [name] use of the basement unit.

The Tenant testified that [name] would purposefully leave an unreasonably loud alarm going off at 4:00 a.m., waking up the Tenant on a daily basis. This occurred both when [name] was present in the rental unit and occasionally when he stayed elsewhere, leaving the alarm to go off for long periods of time and disturb the Tenant’s sleep.

Mr. [name]name][name] testified that while the alarm was set at 4:00 a.m. to wake [name] for work, and most of the time was for a short period of approximately 15 seconds, there originally had not been an issue when the Tenant and [name] had gotten along as [name] had used an alarm that did not wake the Tenant after being told that [name] louder alarm disturbed the Tenant’s sleep. Following the Tenant and [name] having a falling out, [name] resumed using the disturbing alarm, and would then further make a lot of large banging sounds to purposefully disturb then Tenant. Mr. [name]name][name] testified he knows that this banging sounds were purposeful for the disturbance of the Tenant as [name] had not previously made them prior to their falling out. This resulted in the Tenant’s complaints to the Landlord. and LTB-T-020157-24

The Tenant testified that they made complaints to the Landlord about this, but that they didn’t adequately respond. An e-mail from the Tenant to the Landlord dated April 13, 2023 summarises the complaints previously made on February 16 and 24, March 13, 14, 17, 18, 21, and 30, April 7, 9, 10, and 13 – all of 2023.
