This e-mail directly asks the Landlord to serve [name] an N5 notice of termination. The Tenant complained again on April 17, 2023. While these dates are prior to the compensable period due to the limitation periods discussed above, they are relevant and establish the Landlord was on notice of this issue and that it was ongoing by this time.

The Landlord’s position is that each of [name] and the Tenant were pointing fingers at each other as to who was at fault for these incidents. The Landlord testified that he told [name] he would have to leave the property given these issues and did serve an N5 notice of termination, though a copy of this was not provided to the Board for consideration. The Landlord could not identify when they served the N5 notice of termination, but stated it was after the incident that occurred between the parties in August, 2023. The Landlord states he did not file an application pursuant to that N5 notice of termination. 62. [name] attended as a witness on behalf of the Landlord and testified that he did not actually at any time receive an N5 notice of termination, but that the Landlord had contacted him to ask him to keep the noise down when he could. [name] testified that he moved out voluntarily at the end of September, 2023. 63. I find it should have been clear to the Landlord by the beginning of April that he was required to take action in regard to these complaints beyond sending e-mails to [name] in regard to them. I find it was unreasonable to take no further action given the volume and nature of complaints. I also find that given [name] testimony and the lack of any corroborating evidence from the Landlord that they ever actually served an N5 notice of termination, that they did not do so. 64. The Landlord could have taken further action to solve this issue by serving an N5 notice of termination on [name] if he believed it to be appropriate, or alternatively to investigate options for sound proofing to alleviate the issue. The Landlord did not do either of these things. 65. On this basis, I find that the Landlord did substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by failing to take action in this regard to the noise issue for the period of April 1, 2023 to September 30, 2023. As the earliest date a remedy is available is May 23, 2023, I find it is appropriate to award an abatement from May 23, 2023 to September 30, 2023 in regard to this issue. 66. The Tenant testified that the issues with [name] caused a significant disturbance to their sleep and was highly disruptive to their lives. I accept this evidence, which was accompanied by recordings of the sound emitted by the alarm. The Tenant’s claimed a 10% rent abatement in relation to this interference. I find that to be an appropriate award during the period in which the Tenant was interfered with and for which a remedy can be awarded based on the impact on the Tenant. I calculate this sum to be $923.61 based on this 4 month and 9-day period as follows ([4 x $2150.00] + [$2150.00 x 12 / 365 x 9]) x 0.1. and LTB-T-020157-24 67. The Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent totalling $2,423.78 and $327.66 for reasonable out-of-pocket expenses based on the above. This amount will be deducted from the amount owing to the Landlord.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of March 31, 2024, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $5,959.11. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit, interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit, the abatement of rent and the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses have been deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before July 13, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The application was heard on August 28, 2025 and resolved—dismissed—in an order issued on September 18, 2025. [DOC-6376327] The Tenants requested that the LTB review the Hearing Order. The Request to Review is 74 pages long and raises various issues, including that. (a) it was a serious error for the Member to have relied on the evidence of the Landlords; daughter—[name]—without there being a power of attorney or written authorization; (b) the [name] contradicted an order made on February 2, 2025 in LTB-L-051482- 24; and (c) the Member made a procedural error that raises issues of natural justice in relying on an uncertified translation of certain communications between the parties. [DOC- 6600225] In an interim order issued on October 16, 2025 (the ‘Interim Order’), the LTB directed to the Tenants’ request to a hearing; and (b) stayed the Hearing Order. [DOC-6600697] I heard the review via videoconference on July 6, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. [name] represented the Tenants. [name] represented the Landlords
reasons: The review of an LTB order is a two-stage process.

The first stage of the process is a preliminary analysis of the request to review the hearing order. At this stage, the LTB determines whether, based only on the written request made by the party seeking to have the order reviewed, the request has sufficient merit to proceed to a review hearing. The Member decides at this stage only whether the hearing order may contain a serious error or whether the requester may not have been reasonably able to participate . The Member does not determine whether to grant the request that the order be reviewed.

If the Member determines that it has sufficient merit, the request to review will be scheduled for a hearing to determine whether the hearing order contains a serious error or that a party was not reasonably able to participate.

The second stage of the review process involves the LTB hearing submissions from the parties and determining the request on the merits —whether in fact: (a) the hearing order contains a serious error; or (b) the requester was not reasonably able to participate. If at this stage the Member determines that: (a) there was a serious error; or (b) the party requesting the review was not reasonably able to participate, they will direct that the application be heard again on the merits.

This case is somewhat unique. I am granting review and directing that the application be heard again not because I find that there is a serious error in either the Hearing Order or the conduct of the hearing on August 28, 2025, but to prevent an abuse of process.

It came to light on July 6, 2026, that the unofficial transactions filed by the Landlords were generated by [name] using AI —Google—and the accuracy of those transactions was not verified by him before filing them with the LTB.

The Member was not advised on August 28, 2025 that the transactions filed by the Landlord had been generated by [name] using AI and that he had not taken steps to verify the accuracy of the AI-generated translations.

I have no hesitation in finding that: (a) the Member place at least some reliance on the AI -generated transactions filed by the Landlords; and (b) there are ‘discrepancies’ between the official transactions filed by the Tenants and the AI-generated translations filed by the Landlords which call into question the accuracy of the translations.

In my view, it constitutes an abuse of the LTB’s processes for a party to rely on an inaccurate AI-generated translation as evidence in an application before the LTB. [See [name], 2024 BCSC 285 (CanLII)]

The use of generative AI to translate documents can be a valuable legal research tool. [name] can, for example, allow un ilingual English lawyers and licensed paralegals to understand decisions or academic articles written in French.

AI-generated translations can be accepted by the LTB. [Statutory Powers Procedures Act, s. 15] However, the use by lawyers or licensed paralegals of generative AI to produce documents upon which a Member is asked is fraught with issues. Similar to is the case with AI-generated hallucinated legal content, the use of AI-generated translations engaged the obligation of the lawyer or licensed paralegal to ensure that documents filed with a tribunal are accurate and truthful.

Where lawyers or licensed paralegal s rely on AI-generated translations as evidence before the LTB they have, in my view, an obligation to: (a) disclose to the Member that the translations are AI-generated; and (b) take appropriate steps to ensure the accuracy of the translations.

The Paralegal Rules of Conduct, for example, say: 4.01 (1) When acting as an advocate, the paralegal shall represent the client resolutely and honourably within the limits of the law while, at the same time, treating the tribunal and other licensees with candour, fairness, courtesy and respect. (emphasis added)
And it is an offence under the RTA for any person to furnish false or misleading information in any material filed with the LTB. [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 234(v)]
The LTB has broad jurisdiction to make orders to prevent abuse of its processes. [Statutory Powers Procedures Act, s. 23(1)]

In my view, the most appropriate way to address the abuse of the LTB’s process caused by the filing by [name] of inaccurate AI -generated translations is to have the application reheard based on official translations.

At the (re)hearing of the application, the following issues will be determined: (a) whether the Tenants vacated the unit ‘as a result’ of the N12 notice of termination delivered by the Landlords; (b) whether the Landlord acted in bad faith in delivering the N12 notice; and, assuming I find the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 and the Landlords acted in bad faith, (c) The compensation, if any, to which the Tenants are entitled.
The Landlord may, should they not agree with the transactions filed by the Tenants, file their own official—certified—translations.

The Landlords and their son should be at the next attendance to provide evidence. The failure of the Landlords and their son to attend will result in an adverse inference being drawn as to their good faith—genuine intent.
At the (re)hearing of this application, [name] should be prepared to address whether he should personally be required to pay the costs associated with the hearing on August 28, 2025.
ordered: The review is granted and the Hearing Order is set aside.
The application will be reheard by me on a date to be fixed by the LTB based on the available dates provided by the parties. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order to evict [name] (the ‘Subtenant’) because the [name] continued to occupy the rental unit after the subtenancy ended. The Tenant also claimed compensation for each day the Subtenant remained in the unit after the subtenancy ended.
reasons: A subtenant is defined in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 as a “… person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit”: ss. 2(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
Section 97 of the Act provi des that a tenant may sublet a unit to another person with the consent of the landlord: ss. 97(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Subletting a rental unit for the purpose of t he Act refers to a situation where the tenant vacates the rental unit, the tenant gives one or more other persons the right to occupy the unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant’s term or period, and the tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the unit after the specified date: ss. 2(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

In this case, the Tenant’s evidence was that his tenancy at the rental unit began in 2014, and he was the sole tenant of the unit. He said that the Subtenant moved into the unit in 2021 as a roommate, but the Tenant then moved out of the unit that same year, leaving the [name] occupying the unit.

The Tenant said that there was no consent s ought or received from the Landlord to sublet the unit. He also said there was no specific date agreed to on which the subtenancy was to end. He said that he and the Subtenant agreed that whenever the Tenant needed the rental unit back, he would give the Subtenant 60 days’ notice, and she would have to vacate.
This is an application m ade under section 101 of the Act, where the Tenant alleges that the [name] continues to occupy the unit after the subtenancy ended.

The Tenant’s evidence, however, is inconsistent with a subtenancy for the purposes of the Act. The Landlord’s consent was not sought or received, contrary to section 97 of the Act. There was no agreement that the purported subtenancy was to end on a specified date, or before the end of the Tenant’s term or period. This was a monthly tenancy at the relevant time, meaning that the specified would have had to be before the end of the monthly period in which the subtenancy is alleged to have began.

I therefore find that his was not a subtenancy, and the [name] is not a “subtenant” for the purposes of the Act. I cannot therefore determine that the [name] continued occupying the unit after the end of the subtenancy, and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The rental unit consisted of the main and upper floors of a house, with the tenancy commencing on August 31, 2021 and it terminating on May 5, 2024 when they were allegedly forced to vacate.
At the time the tenancy terminated the lawful rent was $2,700.00.
The Tenant filed their initial application on March 27, 2025 and their amended application on September 26, 2025.
As explained below, the Tenant proved in part the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that on May 25, 2026, May 26, 2026 and May 30, 2026 the Landlord without providing notice attended and accessed the rental unit, initially refusing to leave then returning a few hours later. The Tenant’s witnesses all corroborated the Tenant’s testimony, as they were all living at the rental unit at the time.

The Tenant also supported there testimony with a video, entered in evidence, of the May 26 2026 incident, showing the Landlord crawling under the garage door to gain entry and the May 30, 2026 incident showing the Landlord entering the unit with police.
It was the Tenants testimony that the police refused to assist them as the Landlord claimed they were squatters.
Section 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states that a LAndlrod may enter a rental unit only in accordance with sections 26 or 27.

Section 26 of the Act states a Landlord many enter at any time in case of an emergency or when the Tenant gives consent whereas section 27 states they may enter upon providing proper written notice. Based on the uncontested testimony, namely that no notice was given, along with the video evidence, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on May 25, 2024, May 26, 2024 and May 30, 2024. Substantial interference and harassment

It was the Tenant’s testimony, corroborated by their witnesses and supported by video evidence entered, that on May 15, 2024 and May 16, 2024, the Landlord attended the property and harass them by yelling and banging on the door for them to “get out of their house.”

The Tenant’s witnesses all testified that this behaviour caused significant anxiety and stress and contributed to them vacating the property. It was also [name] [name]’s testimony that this behaviour led her to seek ongoing medical treatment. This was supported by a letter from a medical professional entered in evidence.

The Tenant them testified, supported by pictures entered in evidence, that the Landlord, over a 14 month period, removed the laundry machines, along with the door separating their unit from that of the lower level, representing a safety and security issue. It was also their testimony that during the same time the Landlord prevented their use of the parking spot pursuant to the lease agreement.

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Given the uncontested testimony and video evidence, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. That said, given the Tenant failed to provide a copy of the lease to support their claim, the remedy sought shall be affected.
Section 23 of the Act states A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

For the same reasons, I further find, that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Specifically, based on the video evidence and testimony I am satisfied that was their intent and the effect that the banging and yelling had on the Tenant. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services

The Tenant testified that in March 2025 the Landlord began cutting off the electricity and gas services to the rental unit, forcing them to place the service under their name. In both cases they also testified the services were restored within 24 hours. This was supported by copies of the bills entered in evidence.

Section 21(2) of the Act states a landlord shall be deemed to have withheld the reasonable supply of a vital service, care service or food if the landlord is obligated to pay another person for the vital service, care service or food, the landlord fails to pay the required amount and, as a result of the non-payment, the other person withholds the reasonable supply of the vital service, care service or food.

Therefore, based on the uncontested testimony and evidence I find that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant's vital services by failing to maintain the electric and gas bills in good standing. However, given the interruption lasted only 24 hours, and no lease was entered to support their claim, the remedy awarded will be limited. Remedies

The remedies sought are as follows: a. A 20.00% abatement over a period of 14 months for each instance of interference totalling 60.00% or $19,440.00; b. A 100.00% abatement for the 16 days without vital services totalling $1,393.60; c. A difference in rent of $3,000.00; d. Moving and storage costs totalling $3,778.00; e. Out of pocket expenses totalling $2,700.00, for the last month’s rent that the Landlord did not apply to May 2024; and f. General compensation totalling $12,000.00.

An abatement is a monetary award expressed in terms of a portion of past or future rent. It may be in the form of an order: (a) directing that the landlord pay the tenant a fixed amount—return rent paid by the tenant; or (b) allowing the tenant to pay less rent going forward by a fixed amount or percentage of the rent the tenant pays.

A rent abatement is meant to compensate the tenant to the degree that the tenant was deprived of what was bargained for or what is prescribed by legislation or minimum housing standards. It is only when a tenant is completely deprived of all of the benefits of a tenancy—where the rental unit in uninhabitable—that a 100% abatement is appropriate. [See 22001839 (Re), 2022 ABRTDRS 15 (CanLII)] As noted by the Vice Chair in TST- 56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘[abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

In determining the appropriate abatement, the LTB will consider, among other things: a. what percentage of the ‘package’ of shelter and services the landlord contracted or was otherwise obliged to provide was not available to the tenant; b. the length of time the problem existed and the severity of the problem in terms of its effect on the tenant; c. whether the tenant told the landlord about the issue(s) in a timely manner; d. whether the landlord responded to the issues raised by the tenant within a reasonable time and the landlord’s response was appropriate and effective. e. whether the tenant is wholly or partially responsible for the issue(s); and f. whether the tenant hindered or interfered with the landlord’s efforts to address the issue(s).

The LTB will consider the impact the breach has on the average tenant or the impact a reasonable person would expect this problem to have on a tenant. If the tenant has a particular susceptibility to the problem, the landlord can only reasonably be liable to the tenant for a more significant abatement if it can be shown that the landlord knew of the particular condition of the tenant.

The ultimate objective is to grant an abatement that is fair considering all of the circumstances. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name] [[1997] O.J. No. 1881 (Gen Div)] the Court said, “It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the no- repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.”
Similarly, in Offredi v. [organization] [1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC)] the Court said that there is no mathematical way in which to determine an appropriate abatement.

In the case before me, the Tenant only provided evidence to support three instances of harassment, May 25, 2024, May 26, 2024 and May 30, 2024.Furthermore they failed to provide a copy of the original lease, denoting their entitlement to the parking space, or the Landlord’s alleged obligation to provide laundry services or pay the utilities. Furthermore, I cannot overlook that they testified that the utilities were restored within 24 hours, Similarly, they also failed to provide a copy of their new lease, to support the alleged difference in rent or the receipts for the alleged moving costs.

That said, the testimony and video evidence is compelling, and I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that behaviour directly contributed to them vacating. Accordingly based on these factors I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of $2,700.00 representing 100.00% compensation for the month of May 2024.

I am also satisfied based on the Tenant’s testimony that they are entitled to the return of the $2,700.00 representing the last month’s rent deposit. 30. [name], given the above determination I am also satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed the $48.00 representing the cost of filing the application. 31. As stated above in the absence of either the original or new lease I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that they should be awarded the amounts sought for the disruption in utilities, or difference in rent. 32. Regarding the general compensation sought, I cannot overlook that the letter provided, substantiating the effects on [name] [name] dates back to September 2024. However, given their oral testimony along with that of the Tenant and their siblings I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities they did experience anxiety as a result of the Landlord’s behaviour and are entitled to general compensation totalling $4,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,448.00. This amount represents: • $2,700.00 in abatement of rent for May 2024. • $2,700.00 in out-of-pocket expenses, representing the last months rent. • $4,000.00 in general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act), to repair or maintain the rental unit.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $348.00.

The Tenant testified that the refrigerator stopped working on November 29, 2023. She testified that she notified the Landlord of the problem that same day. The refrigerator remained unusable until it was replaced on December 28, 2023.

The Tenant testified that, on or about December 1, 2023, she hired a repair company to assess and repair the refrigerator because she had not received a response from the Landlord. The Landlord initially objected to the repair company selected by the Tenant and advised that she preferred to use another company. However, the Landlord did not arrange for another repair company to attend the rental unit. The Tenant subsequently proceeded with the company she had selected. The attempted repair was unsuccessful because the refrigerator was later determined to require further work to the compressor.

The Landlord then decided to replace the refrigerator. Although a replacement refrigerator was ordered, it was not delivered until December 28, 2023. The Tenant was therefore without a functioning refrigerator for approximately one month.
Subsection 20(1) of the Act requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord was advised of the problem on November 29, 2023, and did not provide the Tenant with a functioning refrigerator within a reasonable time. I accept that a landlord must be given a reasonable opportunity to investigate a maintenance problem and arrange an appropriate repair. The fact that an appliance stops working does not, by itself, establish a breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act.

However, in this case, the Tenant remained without a functioning refrigerator for approximately one month and continued to communicate with the Landlord about the problem during the holiday season. The Landlord did not promptly repair the refrigerator or arrange for a replacement. Although the Landlord ultimately replaced the appliance, I find that the time taken to provide the Tenant with a functioning refrigerator was unreasonable in the circumstances.
I therefore find that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act. Remedies Repair Expense:

The Tenant seeks reimbursement of $848.46 for the service call, labour, and parts associated with the unsuccessful attempt to repair the refrigerator. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established entitlement to reimbursement of this amount.

The Tenant contacted the repair company and began arranging the repair on December 1, 2023, before the evidence clearly established that the Landlord had authorized her to incur the expense. Although the Tenant testified that the Landlord later agreed that she could proceed with the company she had selected, the evidence concerning the timing and scope of that authorization was not sufficiently clear for me to find that the Landlord agreed to be responsible for the full amount of $848.46 before the expense was incurred.

The Tenant submitted email correspondence exchanged with the Landlord during the material period. However, the emails do not establish that the Landlord consented to or authorized the Tenant to hire her own repair company and incur the claimed expense.

I accept that the Tenant incurred the expense. However, proof that an expense was incurred does not, by itself, establish that the Landlord must reimburse it. The documentary evidence does not support the Tenant’s oral testimony that the Landlord authorized the expense. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant has not established that she obtained the Landlord’s consent or authorization before incurring the cost.

I must also be satisfied that the expense was reasonably incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach and that the amount claimed is an appropriate remedy. The evidence was not entirely consistent as to whether the Tenant first contacted the Landlord on November 29 or November 30, 2023. In either case, the Tenant arranged for the repair company to attend on or about December 1, 2023. I am not satisfied that the Landlord had already failed to respond within a reasonable time when the Tenant committed to the repair expense.
The Tenant’s claim for reimbursement of $848.46 is therefore denied. Food Loss:
The Tenant also seeks compensation for food that spoiled while the refrigerator and freezer were not functioning.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that she had refrigerated and frozen food in the appliance when it stopped working. I also accept that food spoilage was a reasonably foreseeable consequence of being without a functioning refrigerator and freezer for an extended period.
Although the Tenant did not provide receipts for every item that was lost, I found her evidence concerning the nature of the food and the circumstances of the loss credible.

Considering the Tenant’s evidence as a whole, I find that $300.00 is reasonable compensation for the food that spoiled as a result of the Landlord’s failure to provide a functioning refrigerator within a reasonable time.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $348.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
As per the lease agreem ent, the monthly rent is $2,900.00 and is payable on the 15th of each month. The Tenant paid first and last month rent at the commencement of the tenancy.
The Tenant did not provide notice that they were vacating t he rental unit. They vacated the unit on January 23, 2026.
The rent for the period from December 15, 2025, to January 14, 2026, was paid on December 22, 2025.
The Landlord learned that the Tenant vaca ted the rental unit on January 24, 2026. The Landlord applied the last month rent deposit to the rental period from January 15, 2026, to February 14, 2026.
There was no agreement to terminate the tenancy on short notic e or on January 23, 2026. Therefore, rent for the period from January 15, 2026, to February 14, 2026, remained owing.

Section 106(10) of t he Act provides that, a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

Section 88(1) of the Act provides that, If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. 2. If the tenant abandoned or vacated the rental unit without giving any notice, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a notice of termination had the tenant, on the date that the landlord knew or ought to have known that the tenant had abandoned or vacated the rental unit, given notice of termination in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.

The Landlord’s use of the Tenant’s last month rent deposit to pay for the rental period from January 15, 2026, to February 14, 2026, is not prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant’s rent deposit. The Tenant’s claim for an illegal rent charge in the amount of $2,900.00 is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Downey-Thomas (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed for failing to provide the Landlord with particulars as to events that gave rise to the application.

The Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931).

Although the [name] case related to the details required in a landlord’s notice of termination, it reflects the general principles of procedural fairness, which include a party’s right to know the case to be met. I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as I find it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient details of the issues to determine whether to defend the claim.
As it pertains to the Tenant’s T2 application, the Tenant’s claimed an illegal entry, substantial interference, and harassment and coercion, but provided no dates any of the alleged conduct occurred.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s application contains sufficient details regarding an illegal entry, as their claim just states the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, but fails to specify when. Next, the claim for substantial interference also lacks particulars as the claim alleges that the Landlord installed a surveillance camera directly facing the rental unit entrance but does not specify when this occurred. Lastly, the claim for harassment states that the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to have overnight guests, but again, does not specify when this occurred.

I find that by failing to include particulars regarding the dates and times the alleged conduct occurred, the Landlord is not in a position to know the case to be met and I must dismiss the Tenant’s application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the amount of $14,004.71 by July 19, 2026.
The residential unit is a single detached house located at [address]reet, London, Ontario.
The Tenants commenced their tenancy at the rental unit in June of 2020 and vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Preliminary Issue
Despite the fact that the Landlord’s Legal Representative did not bring this up as a preliminary issue when asked, I will address [name] submission now.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted in her final submissions, that due to the fact that the Landlord did not serve an N12 notice to the Tenants, that this application should be dismissed.

There is no dispute that an N12 notice was not given to the Tenants. The issue before me was whether the communication between the parties amounted to a notice of termination under section 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”).

Subsection 37(1) of the Act states “a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act which means that a tenancy can only be terminated by proper notice, by way of an agreement between the Tenants and the Landlords, or by way of an order issued by the Board.

Section 43(1) of the Act states “Where this Act permits a landlord or tenant to give a notice of termination, a proper notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall, a) identify the rental unit for which the notice is given; b) state the date on which the tenancy is to terminate; and c) be signed by the person giving the notice or the person’s agent.”

Section 212 of the Act provides that substantial compliance with the Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. Therefore, in some circumstances it may not be necessary for a landlord to use a Board approved version of the forms in order for a notice to be valid so long as the specific information required on the notice, such as the address, length of notice period, termination date, etc. substantially complies with the statutory requirements.

The Tenants submitted that the communications between the Tenants and the Landlord substantially complied with the notice required under section 48 of the Act as the Landlord indicated that the Tenants had to move out in accordance with a timeline because the Landlord’s parents would be moving into the rental unit.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenants always wanted to move to Ottawa and they did this on their own initiative.

I have reviewed the email correspondence between the Landlord and the Tenants from February 19, 2024 to February 29, 2024. The Landlord advised the Tenants that her parents wanted to move to Canada the following year and she proposed a short 10-month lease ending April of 2025. The Tenants requested a 12-month lease instead and on March 8, 2024, the Landlord refused. Based on those communications, the Tenants moved forward with finding alternate accommodations for their family of 7. The Landlord then confirmed that the lease would end on July 31, 2025, after the Tenants’ further request for an extension.

Based on these conversations and the fact that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the Tenants what amounts to a notice of termination under section 48(1) of the Act. Evidence of [name] [name] (OV)

OV testified that he received emails from the Landlord in February of 2024 where the Landlord refused to provide another 12-month lease as she stated that her parents would be moving to Canada in 2025. He stated that normally the lease was renewed every year by the Landlord, he was not aware of his rights under the Act and he normally signed a new lease at the end of each term.

The Tenant stated that he and his wife have 5 children who attended grade school, high school and post secondary institutions. He stated that when he was advised that their tenancy would be terminating in the spring of 2025, he had to plan accordingly. He stated that he and his family loved residing in their home and the children were happy and doing well in school.

OV stated that he understands the importance of family and understood that the Landlord’s parents would be moving to Canada so he found another place for his family to reside in Ottawa. He stated that although they resided in London, it had always been a dream of theirs to move to Ottawa but they had not planned on relocating until their daughters graduated university. The Tenant stated that he moved his family out of their home because the Landlord advised him that they had to vacate the unit for her own parents’ occupation.

The Tenant stated that his children were settled in London and had to move away from their friends which was very difficult for them. He stated that his daughter, who was completing a degree in London, had to stay in London to complete her studies. He stated that keeping his family together has always been the most important thing for him and it was breaking his heart that his daughter had to stay in London by herself.

The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $6,960.00(difference in rent of $580.00 per month), moving expenses of $1,996.71 and compensation of $32,640.00 ($2,720.00 x 12). He said that this move has caused severe and ongoing harm to his family due to the fact that the family is now separated from their eldest daughter who is completing her studies in London. His daughter was unable to transfer to a program in Ottawa so she now resides in a basement apartment in London, studying full time and working full time. He stated that this was incredibly difficult on themselves and all of their children and it did not need to happen.

OV stated that in September of 2025, the rental house was listed for sale at almost one million dollars and was eventually sold in March of 2026. He was very angry and upset that the Landlord’s parents did not end up moving in and that his family had to suffer for no reason. Evidence of [name] (XZ)

XZ testified that she told the Tenants that she would not offer a 12-month lease whether or not her parents moved in. She stated that every February, she and the Tenants would sign a new lease and that at this time, her parents planned to reside in Canada in 2025. She stated that her whole family resides in Canada and that her parents retired in 2024. She wanted her parents to be able to experience summer in Canada in 2025.

The Landlord stated that the Tenants had always wanted to move to Ottawa and they chose to move there after leaving the rental unit. She stated that she cannot be held responsible for the family breaking up.

XZ stated that she renovated the rental unit in mid-August of 2025 after her grandmother became ill. She stated that her grandmother passed away but she could not provide a date when that occurred. She also stated that her father became ill with cancer in early 2026 and he had to remain in China to complete his recovery with the hospitals there which is why they could not move into the unit in 2026.
The Landlord stated that she had no choice but to sell the rental unit with her family situation and she confirmed the listing dates that the Tenant provided. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord communicated to the Tenants that they wanted their rental unit back for her parents, the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of these communications, no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord’s actions were made in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Not only did the Landlord fail to move her parents into the residential unit, but the Landlord renovated the house and listed it for sale 5 weeks after the Tenants vacated the house. The Landlord stated that she listed the house because her grandmother became ill and unfortunately passed away some time in 2025 – 2026 and that her father was battling a cancer diagnosis. These are of course terrible events to deal with and these events can significantly alter personal plans.

However, the Landlord did not provide any corroborating materials to support her reasons for not moving her parents into the rental unit. I would have expected that the Landlord would provide medical documentation to support her grandmother’s illness and/or documentation to substantiate her father’s condition.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12 or in this case, the email.

In February and March of 2024, the Landlord advised the Tenants that they must vacate the unit by April of 2025 so that her parents could move into the unit. Although the Tenants repeatedly requested an extension of the lease, the Landlord refused to renew the lease for another 12 months. The Landlord clearly stated to the Tenants that their lease would be terminating whether or not her parents moved into the rental unit. This demonstrates to me that the Landlord was not serving this notice in good faith as she intended to terminate the lease in whatever method was necessary which was contrary to the Act. The Landlord’s actions 5 weeks after the Tenants vacated the rental unit confirm that the Landlord was acting in bad faith when she listed the house for sale. The Landlord testified that her father’s illness in early 2026 prevented them from moving to Canada in 2026 as he had to continue his treatment in China. However, this testimony contradicts the fact that the house was renovated in mid-August and was listed for sale in late August of 2025.

The Landlord was represented by a legal representative and so I did not have to explain the presumption of bad faith in section 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord has not shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies

With respect to the Tenants’ request for a rent differential, the Tenants are now paying $580.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. The Tenants provided a copy of their new lease in Ottawa which confirmed the rent of $3,300.00 per month and their evidence was not questioned by the Landlord. The rental unit apparently had 5 bedrooms and 4 bathrooms according to the sale listing and so I am accepting the Tenant’s evidence that this unit is comparable to the rental unit. Based on these facts, I will award the requested rent differential calculated as $6,960.00 ($580.00 x 12).
With respect to the Tenants’ request for moving expenses, I will award $1,996.71 which is the invoice from Big Box that was provided to me by the Tenants.

With respect to the Tenants’ request for compensation of $32,640.00, the Tenants were both very emotional during their testimony and the hearing itself and I have no doubt that the family has suffered emotional distress. Mr. [name]name] detailed how important it was to have their family physically together so that the parents could support their children financially and emotionally. The Tenant also spoke about how the move affected their children who had to leave their familiar schools and neighbourhood friends. But I was not provided sufficient evidence to warrant an award of this amount.

Having considered the circumstances in this case, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $5,000.00 to the Tenants in general compensation for the emotional distress, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $14,004.71. This amount represents: • $6,960.00 for the rent differential; • $1,996.71 for the moving expenses; • $5,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application); • substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex (T2 Application); and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). These applications were heard by videoconference on June 23, 2026. Only the Tenants legal representative, [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 1:02pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $[name] and shall make the necessary repairs on or before August 31, 2026. Preliminary Issue: T1 Application

The Tenant filed a T1 application alleging the Landlord charged illegal rent for April 1, 2024 through to February 1, 2025. Additionally, the Tenant alleged that the Tenant paid an illegal charge to the Landlord on March 1, 2025.

The Tenant’s legal representative submitted that the T1 application was filed as an alternative to the T2/T6 applications to capture the Tenants entitlement to a rebate of $790 which was a $250 rent abatement that the Tenant was entitled to from January 31, 2025 onward under a prior LTB Order (LTB-T-049402-22) and $540 for snow removal work the Tenant performed for the Landlord in January and February as per the agreement between the Landlord and Tenant.

I found the remedies being sought within the T1 application were captured within the T2/T6 application and could be found to be duplicative with remedies. The Tenant’s legal representative agreed the T1 application should be withdrawn. As such the T1 application is withdrawn. T2/T6 Applications Prior LTB Order

The Tenant’s applications stem from a prior LTB order (LTB-T-049402-22) where the Landlord and Tenant entered into a consent order where the Landlord was ordered to repair interior water damage and complete mold remediation in the unit, and the Landlord would pay an ongoing $250.00 rental abatement until the work was completed. The Tenant’s legal representative submits that the work has not been completed within the requisite period of time and in addition there are issues not previously covered by the consent order that give rise to remedy.
Within the Consent Order at paragraph 2 it stated: On or before January 31, 2025, the Landlord shall repair the interior water damage and mold remediation, in the rental unit

The Tenant’s legal representative submits that the Landlord has failed to complete the work as agreed and therefore seeks remedy for the Landlord to complete the repairs as ordered that have not been completed as well as additional remedies as set out within the T2/T6 applications. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant’s T2 application alleging substantial interference is on the basis of failure of the Landlord to respond to maintenance requests and/or that the Landlord has failed to repair the rental unit and therefore has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. As the basis for the T2 application stems from the actions/inactions of the Landlord, I find it most appropriate to address the applications together.
The residential complex contains 10 rental units.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2019. The Tenant’s monthly rent is $800.00.

It was the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that her rental unit has been leaking since she moved in, in 2019. She stated that water comes in through the windows and ceiling when the snow melts. Further she stated that there is visible mold in unit and the Landlord has not completed mold remediation.

The Tenant stated that after the prior [name], the Landlord sent an individual by the name of [name] (‘[name]’) to complete repair work in the bedroom. The Tenant’s legal representative referenced the Tenant’s Evidence Package (DOC-8173877) at page 46 & 48 to demonstrate that [name] removed a piece of the drywall and placed a new piece of drywall overtop of the hole and painted it, the Tenant stated that no mold remediation was completed at that time.

Further the Tenant’s legal representative referenced page 55, where the Landlord was alleged to have completed the work. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not attend to check the work. The Tenant testified that [name] left debris and dust throughout the room and when the Tenant contacted the Landlord, the debris was thrown out the window of the rental unit, which stayed outside the rental unit until the Tenant and her husband cleaned it from outside.

The Tenant testified that she did not believe the work was completed as per the prior [name] and reached out to her legal representative to obtain the information and qualifications regarding the individual who attended the home as well as receive the anticipated time frame for the remaining work to be completed. She referenced page 95, an email from her representative on December 6, 2024 at 3:07pm seeking the information from the Landlord. The Landlord responded the same day at 8:25pm stating that the re- insulation and drywall replacement had been completed, the contractor sent photos as confirmation and stating the contractor would be back Monday.

Further correspondence on page 94 through to 98 of the Tenant’s evidence demonstrate correspondence between the Tenant’s legal representative and the Landlord regarding the allegation that the Landlord did not complete the necessary repairs inclusive of mold remediation and the Landlords belief that no mold existed and the work had been completed.

In February 2025, the Tenant testified the entire front of building collapsed, including but not limited to the soffit & facia which was supported by the Tenant’s evidence at page 70. Further, on February 24 2025 the eaves troughs collapsed and fell off the building.

The Tenant stated that in February 2025 the Landlord attempted to fix the front of the building. The Tenant testified that a company by the name of [name] attended and completed the work. The Tenant was informed that their work was guaranteed.

The Tenant further testified that in March 2025, the front of the building collapsed again, she referred to page 83 of the evidence package to show the state of the front of the residential complex. The Landlord responded via email on April 14, 2025 stating that [name] would be attending the property the property to look into the issues. Additionally, the Landlord inquired regarding the roof and if the Tenant was experiencing leaks after the snow melted. The Tenant’s representative provided an update via email which included ongoing leaking, interior repairs needing completion and the furnace.

The Tenant stated that she reached out to [name] and they informed her that they could not get a hold of the Landlord, this statement was supported by the Tenant at page 118 of the Tenant’s evidence package, an email chain dated April 18, 2026. The Tenant stated that the front of the building remains in the same condition.

The last response from the Landlord was noted on page 102 an email dated April 24, 2025 in which the Landlord stated that [name] would be starting the next week. The Tenant testified that no further work was completed by [name] or the Landlord.

As the Tenant had not heard from the Landlord, she testified that she contacted By-law in December 2025. By-law attended and completed an inspection, the Tenant was informed By-law provided the Landlord with an Order to Comply for the repairs to be fixed by May 5, 2026 or they would complete the necessary repairs. This supported on page 116 of the Tenant’s evidence, a follow-up letter from property standards. The Tenant stated that she was informed that the time lapsed, and the Landlord did not submit an appeal.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord has not been accepting her rent since December 2025, the Tenant referenced page 120 of the evidence package which she states was a text from a neighbouring Tenant where he informed her that he had heard from the Landlord on May 4, 2026. The Tenant provided the following dates she had attempted to reach the Landlord without receiving a response: a. December 2025 - 17, 19, 22, 26 & 31 b. January 2026 – 2 & 17 c. March 2026 - 2, 7, 18 & 23, d. April 2026 - 14 e. May 2026 - 9, 17 & 28 f. June 2026 - 3 & 13

The Tenant testified that the impact of the Landlord’s actions and/or inactions caused her to feel that she was not being treated as a human being and her home is falling apart. Furthermore, this affects her mental health and her husband’s physical health as he has experienced COPD flare ups.

The Tenant’s legal representative submits that the Landlord has neglected the issues at the rental unit since 2022. He submitted that while he agreed to a consent order including agreeing to complete the repairs, the Landlord had completed some but not all of the work, such as the mold remediation. Furthermore, the work that was completed was not completed to industry standard. He further submitted that the Landlord’s actions are deliberate in that the Landlord has refused to response to By-law. Finally, he submitted that while there is an order to comply, the Tenant is unsure of the scope of work that will be completed by the By-law and therefore seeks an order from LTB. Analysis T2 Application

Section 22 of the Act states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant.

Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Although the word harass is not defined in the Act, harassment has been found by this Board to generally be a course of conduct or behaviour that the reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.

It was the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that since moving into the rental unit she has repeatedly and continually contacted the Landlord about the maintenance issues at the residential complex and within her rental unit. Further, she stated that the Landlord had been reasonably responsive at times as well as completed some repairs, with this said, the Landlord often did not and does not respond. Furthermore, based on the evidence before me the Landlord has not completed the maintenance at the rental unit and is now refusing the Tenants rent as a result of her contacting By-law. I find that the actions of the Landlord have substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of her dwelling. T6 Application

Section 20(1) of the Act, states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

On the basis of the evidence provided and on a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s actions during the period of January 31, 2025 to June 23, 2026, constitute a failure to repair or maintain the rental unit and residential complex. The actions of the Landlord were not timely under the circumstances, and ultimately ineffective. I find that the Landlord failed to work with the municipal by-law office to resolve the maintenance issues raised. Additionally, the Landlord did not complete the work as ordered as per the order to comply. Accordingly, I find the Landlord breached their responsibilities during this period, pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act.

Furthermore, and in contemplation whether a fine is warranted in this case, I find the Landlord’s actions in refusing to respond to the Tenants 17 text messages over a period of 7-months and refusal to accept the Tenant’s rent to be a retaliatory action as a result of the Tenant contacting By-law. The Tenant contacted By-Law in December 2025 and the Landlord began refusing the Tenant’s rent the same month, the timing of the events is proximate and cannot be ignored. As a result, the Landlord will pay a fine to the [name]. Remedies

The Tenant sought the following remedies for the T2/T6 application: a. Requiring the Landlord for 12 months to reply to the Tenant’s communication regarding interference with reasonable enjoyment and maintenance requests and repairs within 14 days. b. If the Landlord fails to respond the Tenant may choose to: i. Arrange for an inspection quote for the repairs required by a qualified professional; ii. Provide the resulting information to the Landlord in writing; iii. If the Tenant provides the information to the Landlord, the Landlord must reply to the quote within 7 days. iv. If the Landlord does not reply ‘on time’ the Tenant is entitled to compensation, should she arrange for the work to be completed in accordance with the quote provided. c. $250.00 rental abatement until the work is completed. d. Repair: i. All damage and perform all maintenance to the exterior common elements of the residential complex that are causing leaking and resulting in water damage or mold in the Tenants rental unit; ii. Arranging for a mold inspection by a qualified professional and where necessary complete mold remediation; and, iii. Maintain the common interior areas of the residential complex in a state of ordinary cleanliness including regular removal of garbage from the laundry room and hallways as needed. e. Fine to the Board Request for Communication from the Landlord

While I understand the Tenant’s reasoning for this remedy, I find that any order written would be unenforceable. Therefore, I will not be ordering this requested remedy. Should the Tenant have sought the remedy to complete the repairs herself, this was a remedy available within the T6 application. [name] for the Landlord to Complete Necessary Repairs

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord has not completed the repairs and has not maintained the rental unit/residential complex. The Tenant has requested the Landlord be ordered to complete the necessary repairs, I find it appropriate for the Landlord to complete the repairs as requested. The Landlord is therefore ordered to complete the following: a. Complete maintenance or repair the exterior common elements of the residential complex, including the roof, exterior facia, soffit and eavestroughs; [name] any repairs to the Tenants rental unit regarding leaking to the Tenants windows or water damage to the walls; and, c. Arrange for a mold inspection by a qualified professional, where deemed necessary complete mold remediation to the Tenants rental unit.

If Landlord fails to meet this condition, the Tenant may deduct 25% of the total monthly rent from the lawful monthly rent starting September 1, 2026 until the above work is completed and/or repaired. Rent Abatement

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

Determining appropriate remedies is often described as more of an art rather than a science. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], the Court remarked: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.

I find that an abatement of $250.00 per month for the period January 31, 2025 – June 23, 2026 for the disrepair of the residential complex common areas, rental unit and lack of response is appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant provided substantial evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord has failed to make the repairs as agreed and the disrepair has been ongoing until the date of the hearing.
Therefore, the amount owing to the Tenant’s is $ ($250.00 x 17 months = $[name]). Administrative Fine

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine. The Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16 provides guidance about the Board’s use of fines. It states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It further provides that the remedy is not usually imposed “unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”. I find that the Landlord in this case were afforded the opportunity via consent order to complete the repairs alleged in this application in a prior Board order and did not comply with that order. I find based on the uncontested evidence that the Landlord made minimal efforts to complete the repairs.

The Landlord was not at the hearing to present evidence or submissions. Based on the evidence before me I find that the Landlord has showed blatant disregard for a prior Board order and a fine is necessary to discourage this type of conduct. Even though the previous orders directed the Landlords to repair the rental unit and maintain the common arears and the Landlord has failed to comply with the prior Board’s order. Therefore, I am imposing an administrative fine of $250.00.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $[name] by August 6, 2026. This amount represents: • $4,250.00 for a rent abatement.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

Should the Landlord fail to make the payment in accordance with paragraph 1, the Tenant’s shall be permitted to deduct $500.00 from the rent starting on September 1, 2026 and continuing until the amount has been satisfied.

The Landlord shall also ensure that the following work will be completed by August 31, 2026: a. Complete maintenance or repair the exterior common elements of the residential complex, including the roof, exterior facia, soffit and eavestroughs; [name] any repairs to the Tenants rental unit regarding leaking to the Tenants windows or water damage to the walls; and, c. Arrange for a mold inspection by a qualified professional, where deemed necessary complete mold remediation to the Tenants rental unit.

If the repairs, maintenance, mold contractor contacted and remediation is not completed by August 31, 2026, the Tenant may deduct 25% from their monthly rent for 12-months from September 1, 2026 to August 31, 2027 or until the work is completed, whichever is earliest. When the work and repairs are completed, the Tenant must cease deducting any amounts from their lawful monthly rent.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $250.00 by August 6, 2026. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Very (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: I noted that after reviewing the Tenant’s Application regarding Tenant’s Rights (‘T2 application’) there was a lack of detail in the application regarding the alleged illegal entries. The application only stated “on numerous occasions” without dates, years or how many alleged illegal entries occurred.

The Adjournment Sheet prepared on September 11, 2025 after the parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference states the “Tenant to amend application to include specific dates and details for Reason 1 and to clarify the claims in Reason 5.”

I sought submissions from the Tenant regarding his choice not to amend his application to provide sufficient details such as dates, times and alleged illegal entries which was outlined within the Adjournment Sheet. The Tenant refused to provide any response. I cautioned the Tenant that he would need to participate in the hearing for the application to be heard, I asked an additional time for submissions, the Tenant replied and stated that the Landlords “know the dates” and “it’s all there”.
The Landlord stated they were unaware of the dates and times the Tenant was referencing and stated that they deny any illegal entries to the rental unit.

I find that the Tenant’s allegations surrounding illegal entries lacks sufficient details to hold a procedurally fair hearing for all parties. The Tenant has had over 10-months to amend their application to include sufficient details, so the Landlord and the LTB know when the alleged breaches occurred. Therefore, I am not considering the illegal entry allegations. T2 Application
The application alleges the Landlord withheld their vital services, specifically, heat and water.

On any application before the Board the person making an allegation bears the burden of proof. This means the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlords did what they were alleged to have done. In this case, I am not satisfied based on evidence presented at the hearing that the Landlord deliberately interfered with or withheld vital services.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2018 and was removed by Sheriff eviction on July 26, 2025.
The Lease Agreement stated that the Tenant was responsible for payment of utilities including water, heat and hydro for the rental unit.

The Tenant referenced a letter from the City of [name] dated November 23, 2023 (DOC-5261339) which noted that “Effective January 1, 2024 billing will commence at the property noted above for fixed charges only”. Specifically, the Tenant stated that as of January 1, 2024, the bills would be in the Landlords name.

The Tenant further referred to water bills (DOC-5245826) that were supplied to him by the Landlords which he submits demonstrates that there was no running water to the property, the bills show no water consumption. The Tenant testified that prior to the water bills being changed into the Landlords name, the bills were paid in full and while he did not have hot water, he did have running water. After the bills were changed to the Landlords name on January 1, 2024 he no longer had running water, cold or otherwise. The Tenant further alleged that the furnace was not in working order and the Landlords refused to supply him with heat.

On cross examination, the Tenant acknowledged that he was responsible for payment of the utilities, such as water and heat at the rental unit. Additionally, he acknowledged that the bills had been sent to him from the Landlords for payment. He further acknowledged the furnace was in fact in working order and stated that if he paid the bill, he would have heat at the rental unit.

The Landlord, [name] (‘DAR’) testified that he was informed that in 2023 the water was shut off to the rental unit due to lack of payment by the Tenant. DAR testified that they saw the Tenant twice a week and communicated via text, and the Tenant did not raise any issue with the water and heat at that time.

DAR stated that it was not until September 2024 after an LTB hearing that they became aware the Tenant did not have water or heat. DAR stated this caused him and his wife great concern and they completed an inspection to see if there was in fact heat and water. DAR explained that the obligation for payment of the water had not shifted from the Tenant to the Landlord, the fact was that with the City of Niagara sent the bills to him and his wife and would then be sent to the Tenant for payment. DAR stated he found that as the bills were not paid, the water and heat had been turned off. DAR further testified that they did not look at consumption of the water on the bill, simply provided the bills to the Tenant and awaited payment, which never came. DAR stated that the furnace was in working order, the bills just needed to be paid for the Tenant to have heat. Finally, DAR testified that despite the Tenant being responsible for payment of the water bills, the Landlord’s paid the water bills from January 1, 2024 until the Tenant vacated the property 2025 to ensure the Tenant had water. Analysis

Subsection 21(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. [emphasis added]

The difficulty with the Tenant’s application and submissions concerning the water and heat is that the evidence is insufficient to establish the Landlord deliberately or intentionally withheld the water and heat. Rather the evidence supports the conclusion that the supply of the water or heat at the rental unit was interrupted because he did not pay the bills for these utilities, as he was required to do so under the tenancy agreement.

The parties agreed that the rental property’s furnace was in working order and could supply heat should the Tenant have paid the bills. Further, the Landlords supplied water as soon as they became aware the Tenant did not have running water. The issue here is not one where the Landlords withheld or interfered with the Tenants water or heat.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name], and [name] (the ‘Respondents'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: This application concerns a tenancy that ended in January, 2025. [organization] was the Tenant’s landlord. [name] and [name] managed the premises, and may also have been landlords, or agents of the landlord.
