The Tenant brings this application alleging that all three of them contravened his rights under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA).

For the following reasons, the Tenant has not proved any contravention of the RTA. Consequently, I do not need to determine whether Mr. [name]name] or Mr. [name]name] were landlords or agents of the landlord. I will refer to them and [organization] collectively as the “Respondents.” Substantial interference and harassment during the tenancy
The Tenant rented the unit from 2019 until January, 2025. His application alleges that throughout the tenancy, other tenants in the building harassed him.

The Tenant gave very little testimony regarding harassment by his neighbours. More importantly, he did not testify that he ever reported the problem to the Respondents. Without knowing that there was an issue with other tenants, the Respondents could not have taken any action and had no obligation to do so.

The application also alleges that various maintenance issues existed during the tenancy. The most significant of these was a bedbug infestation. The application also alleges that in June, 2024, the Tenant’s ceiling fell in. These are maintenance issues that ought to have been raised in a T6 application, but I will assume for the sake of argument that I can consider them in this T2 application.

The Tenant did not testify regarding the ceiling incident. He testified that bedbugs and other maintenance issues existed during the tenancy, but did not testify as to whether or when he reported the issues to the Respondents. The Respondents testified that the Tenant never reported any maintenance issues to them.
The Respondents’ obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance. They were not required to repair issues they were not told about and were unaware of.

The Tenant has not proved that the Respondents contravened any of their obligations during the tenancy. His testimony regarding the issues was extremely vague, but more importantly, he has not established that he ever informed the Respondents about the issues. Rent receipts

The application alleges that the Respondents did not provide adequate rent receipts during the tenancy. However, it does not allege that the Tenant ever asked for better receipts. Moreover, the Tenant did not testify regarding any issue with receipts.
The Tenant has not proved that the Respondents failed to provide him with receipts on request in accordance with section 109 of the RTA. Mailbox

The application also alleges that the Respondents did not provide the Tenant with an adequate mailbox. He did not give any testimony regarding this claim either, and has therefore not proved the claim. Lockout

The Tenant testified that on Friday, January 10, 2025, he came home and discovered that his key did not work. A neighbour told him that “two guys” had changed the lock. The neighbour phoned the two guys and, in response, a person named [name] arrived at the unit. [name] asked the Tenant for his unit key, and the Tenant gave it to him. [name] told the Tenant to call him on Monday and he would “deal with it.” The Tenant started staying at a shelter.

The Tenant testified that the following Monday, a social worker named [name] phoned [name]. [name] told her that he no longer worked for the landlord, and that she should call someone named [name] instead. There is no evidence that [name] or the Tenant called [name].

The Tenant does not appear to have taken any further steps, and did not regain possession of the unit. He lost all his belongings which had been stored in the unit. He seeks an order for compensation for the lockout and for the lost belongings.

The Tenant’s evidence is hearsay. He did not call the neighbour, [name], or Victoria as witnesses. The neighbour’s assertion that “two guys” had changed the lock is hearsay. [name] assertion that [name] had asserted that he had formerly worked for the landlord is double hearsay.

Moreover, even if I were to accept truth of the hearsay evidence, it would be insufficient to prove that the Respondents or an agent of the Respondents locked the Tenant out. There is no evidence as to who the “two guys” were who changed the locks, and no evidence that they worked for the landlord.

Even if the Respondents did not change the locks, they would have been obligated to change them back and restore the Tenant to possession if he had informed them of the issue. However, there is no evidence that he did so. He only communicated with [name], a person who may have worked for the landlord at some unknown point in the past. [name] told him to contact [name], but the Tenant did not contact [name]. There is no evidence that he ever contacted any of the Respondents, or anyone who worked for or represented them, to tell them that he had been locked out and ask to be let back in.
Similarly, there is no evidence to establish what happened to the Tenant’s belongings, and no evidence that he ever contacted the Respondents to retrieve his belongings.
The Tenant has not proved that the Respondents contravened the RTA in respect of the January 10, 2025 lockout. Result
The Tenant has not proved any of the allegations raised in the application. The application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 25, 2025. In their application, the Tenant states that he vacated the rental unit on August 16, 2025.
Rent was due on the 1st of the month. When the Tenant vacated, the Landlord was holding a last month rent deposit of $600.00.

The Tenant testified that he first gave notice to the Landlord by text message and email on July 23, 2025, that he would be vacating the rental unit on August 16, 2025. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not respond at all to their notice.
The Tenant testified that she paid $50.00 for the key deposit on June 25, 2025. A copy of the e-transfer to the Landlord was submitted into evidence.

The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on August 16, 2025. The Tenant testified that the Landlord wanted the Tenant to return the key but they did not do so because the Landlord refused to return the key deposit amount back.

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.
Section 17 of O.Reg. 516/06 under the Act states that a Landlord can collect payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord did not receive the keys originally provided to the Tenant. Since the Tenant did not return the keys to the Landlord, they effectively forfeits the reimbursement of that deposit.

A tenancy can terminate in any one of three ways: notice of termination, agreement to terminate or by an order of the Board. Pursuant to section 37 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. Here, there is no evidence before me that the tenancy between the Tenant and the Landlord was terminated via any of the three ways permitted by the Act.

The Tenant’s notice to the landlord on July 23, 2025 was not valid as it failed to comply with section 44(2) of the Act, which states that to terminate a tenancy, a tenant must give notice at least 60 days before the date of termination specified in the notice and the termination date must be on the last day of a rental period. Here, those requirements were not met as the termination date was not on the last day of a rental period. There was certainly no agreement between the parties to terminate the tenancy on August 16, 2025.
The Tenant did not provide any evidence on whether the unit was re-rented.

The scenario in this case is expressly addressed in section 88 of the Act. The relevant portions read as follows: 88 (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. (3) Despite subsections (1) and (2), if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent that exceeds the lesser of the following amounts: 1. The amount of arrears of rent determined under subsection (1) or (2). 2. The amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. (4) In determining the amount of arrears of rent owing under subsections (1), (2) and (3), consideration shall be given to whether or not the landlord has taken reasonable steps to minimize losses in accordance with section 16.

Basically, what this provision means is that where a tenant gives improper notice to vacate, the tenant is liable for the rent up to the date the tenancy could have been terminated if proper notice was given—here, that would be September 30, 2025. The Landlord is under a legal obligation to attempt to mitigate their losses by trying to re-rent the unit.

In this application, the burden of proof falls on the Tenants to establish that first, the Landlords held a last month’s rent deposit and second, the Landlord did not use said deposit for the last month of the tenancy. Based on the evidence before Board, I find that the Tenant has failed to establish that the Landlord re-rented the unit as of August 17, 2025. I say this because at the hearing the Tenant gave no evidence as whether the unit was re-rented out or any evidence of any efforts made to re -rent out the unit for August 17, 2025.

Based on the Tenants’ uncontested evidence, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not apply the rent deposit to the rent for the last month of the Tenants’ tenancy. I find that the Tenant were responsible for the rent from August 17, 2025, to September 30, 2025, just under two months. As the rent owing for this period exceeds the amount of the payment being claimed by the Tenant, the Tenant is not entitled to a return of the last month rent deposit.
ordered: The T1 Application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issues: Summons and Request for Adjournment

The Tenant requested an adjournment at the outset of the hearing. The Tenant submits that she has been unable to affect service of her summonses prior to the hearing date, this as a result of her mother passing is March 2026. The Tenant submitted that she would be unable to adequately present her application without the individuals present.

The Landlord's legal representative opposed the request as the adjournment would be highly prejudicial to the Landlord as this matter has already been to an Adjudicative Case Conference on November 27, 2025, the Tenant was well aware of the steps she was required to take and has had 7-months to prepare.

The Tenant submitted and received 10 issued summonses on October 16, 2025 for an Adjudicative Case Conference that was scheduled for November 27, 2025. The Tenant requested a second set of 6 summonses before the hearing. The first set of summonses were submitted and approved on May 19, 2026 & May 29, 2026 for the hearing.

The Landlord's legal representative submitted that the summonses were not appropriately served with the requisite compensation. Additionally, specific summonses contained either no information regarding what would be expected from the witnesses to bring with respect to documentation and/or included documentation they also included information that would be barred by limitations such as “key stored info when take over happen from [name]”. He stated this event occurred many years prior and he is unaware of the relevance of the [name] transfer to the Tenants application. Finally, he stated that Tenant appeared to be using the summonses to build her application via a ‘fishing expedition’, he submits this is not the purpose for summonses, conversely, any witnesses summonsed should be in attendance to support the claims already alleged within the application.

I asked the Tenant if she appropriately served the summonses in accordance with the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. She admitted she did not provide the accompanying compensation and was also unable to physically serve each of the individuals, she stated that due to her mothers passing she was unable to serve the summonses.

In the hearing, I reviewed in detail each requested summons, the individual and the purpose for their attendance. After reviewing the list with the Tenant, there was only one individual who may have assisted in speaking to the dates within the Tenant’s application, namely [name]. With this said, the Tenant was unable to serve Sivasothy [name] and sought alternative service, which was denied by the LTB on June 1, 2026.
For the reasons that follow, the Tenant’s request is denied.
In determining whether to grant the adjournment I have considered the factors set out in LTB Rule of Procedure 21.8.

I have also considered s. 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which directs the Board to "adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and to be heard on the matter." Parties should assume that the hearing will proceed on the date stated in the Notice of Adjourned Hearing. This means that the parties should be prepared to present their evidence, call and question witnesses and make their submissions.

The Board’s record reflects that the Tenant was served the Notice of Hearing (‘NOH’) on May 3, 2026 at 1:59pm. I am satisfied the Tenant has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date.

I turned my mind to LTB Guideline 1 and whether a further adjournment would be appropriate, I do not believe it would be appropriate or a good use of the Board’s resources in the circumstances. While the Tenant submits that she was unable to serve the summonses due to her mother’s passing, the Tenant had 4-months prior to her mother’s passing to serve the summonses, or she could have hired a process server as she did on the first occasion to serve the summonses. This is the first merits hearing, but second appearance for the parties. I do not find an adjournment would assist in ensuring the Tenant’s summons issue could be addressed, nor did she have a reasonable explanation as to why she did not pay the individuals whom she did serve their summonses.
I denied the Tenant’s request for an adjournment Should the Tenants application be dismissed?

The Tenant filed a T2 application on March 25, 2025. The T2 form sets out clear instructions including ‘what were the dates and times of the events’ with this in mind the reasons within the application must contain sufficient particulars needed for the other party to know the case they must meet and for the Board to determine the issues.

The T2 application, which was later amended on April 30, 2026 adds further vague narration of events, including allegations about a turbulent relationship with the Landlord’s agents. However, the reasons set out certain challenges the Tenant may have been experiencing with specific individuals, without specific dates or identifiable time periods.

Without dates or timeframes for the specific incidents relied on, it is not possible to determine from the application which allegations, if any, fall within the one-year limitation period in subsection 29(2) of the Act for T2 application, and which may be out of time. The absence of dates and timeframes therefore affects both fairness to the Landlord and the Board’s ability to assess its jurisdiction.

I noted that I was having difficulty understanding the details of the applications, as the only dates included in the T2 application June 26, 2026 and February 20, 2025. Additionally, this subject was addressed within the Adjournment Sheet which stated “T2 lacks particulars except for June 24, 2024 and February 20, 2025” and the Tenant was to “obtain legal advice”.

I asked the Tenant to make submissions regarding the lack of dates and details in the T2 applications. Additionally, I sought clarity on if the Tenant sought legal advisement. The Tenant referred to the amendment which was provided to the LTB. I asked the Tenant to direct me to the dates in their applications the Tenant stated that “the dates are there”. Further she stated she spoke with legal aid, but they would not assist as this was not an application pertaining to eviction proceedings.
I turned to the Landlord's legal representative for submissions regarding his understanding of the details in the T2 application.

The Landlord's legal representative stated he did not understand the Tenants applications, as it contained a long spanning narrative. Additionally, even where the Tenant provided dates within the application, he submits the dates do not point to any alleged interference in the Tenant’s tenancy and requested for the application to be dismissed.

Given the two dates regarding allegations in the applications, I sought submissions on whether the Landlord's legal representative would be able to proceed to the hearing on the two dates presented within the application. The Landlord's legal representative repeated that he did not believe the Tenant sufficiently outlined the allegations against the Landlord and sought for the application to be dismissed.

I declined to dismiss the Tenant’s application, as the Tenant has 2 dates that are sufficiently detailed for the parties to have a hearing on the merits of the application. I proceeded to hear the matter specifically outlining that the merits hearing would be solely on the two dates and incidents outlined in the Tenant’s application, specifically June 26, 2026 and February 20, 2025. [name] June 6, 2024 - Broken Glass in Refrigerator

The Tenant’s uncontested testimony was that the superintendent attended the rental unit on June 6, 2024, looked in the fridge and alleged that the Tenant’s daughter had intentionally broke the glass. She stated that the superintendent informed her that there would be a charge for the broken glass in the amount of $320.00. The Tenant further stated that after an investigation by the Landlord she was not required to pay the $320.00 for the glass in the fridge.

The Tenant further testified that there were allegations made during the inspection regarding her cleanliness and has been “constantly harassed” on how her rental unit should be kept. The Tenant further testified that due to the interaction she experienced stress and was uncomfortable in her unit after this encounter and with each encounter in her rental unit with the Landlord’s agents, as a result she is required to take medications.

The Tenant stated that her concern stems from the Landlord not completing inspections according to the requirements for ‘modified inspections’. She stated she filed a complaint regarding the interaction and the superintendent’s conduct but did not hear back from the Landlord. She stated she followed up with the resolution manager who stated that it was handled internally.
The Tenant presented no evidence regarding the impact to her medical or physical health as a result of the inspection that occurred on June 6, 2024. February 20, 2026 – Inspection

The Tenant’s uncontested testimony was that there was no one specific issue regarding the conduct of the individuals who attended the inspection on February 20, 2026. The issue stems from improper ‘modified inspections’ relating to her accommodations such as a hospital bed, walker and electric scooter. The Tenant stated that the inspection caused a high level of stress.

The Tenant further testified the Landlord is required to send a letter addressing concerns regarding her rental unit after the inspection, but she did not receive a letter, and this caused her depression. Furthermore, the Tenant stated that she filed a complaint regarding the inspection and did not hear back from the Landlord and did not follow-up regarding this complaint.
The Tenant presented no evidence regarding the inspection or impact to her medical or physical health as a result of the inspection that occurred on February 20, 2025.

On cross examination, the Landlord's legal representative referenced a letter that was uploaded by the Tenant as her evidence. The referenced letter was sent to the Tenant on February 27, 2026 (DOC-8215046) regarding Toronto Community Housing Corporation (‘TCHC’) and their attempts to work with the Tenant, obligations and action items that would be completed in the future. The Tenant stated that she did not receive it or “did not see it within her mailbox”.

The Landlord's legal representative submitted that the while the Tenant has provided substantial testimony the Tenant has failed to establish the Landlord has acted improperly. Further, he submitted that the actions of the Landlord do not rise to the level of substantial interference. He further submitted the Tenant has failed to provide evidence regarding the modified inspections or the inspections were in contravention of the Act. He further submitted that the requested damages would be excessive and punitive. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states that a “landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant”.

The Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”.

Black’s Law Dictionary (https://thelawdictionary.org/) defines harassment as “a course of conduct directed at a specific person that causes substantial emotional distress in such person and serves no legitimate purpose”.
Harassment in the landlord and tenant context is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate.

Regarding the allegations of harassment, obstruction and substantial interference, in effect, I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterrence for egregious conduct, beyond whatever deterrent effect simple damages might provide, is an over-riding factor.

The Tenant testified that the inspections substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of her rental unit. The Tenant further submitted as a result of this failure it impacted her ability to feel comfortable or calm within her rental unit. The Tenant led no evidence that the Landlord harassed her during the hearing, the Tenant’s sole claim was with respect to substantial interference. Additionally, the Tenant did not supply evidence that the Landlord failed to provide lawful notice to enter, that the Landlord did not complete the inspection pursuant to a modified inspections or that would support her claim regarding what if any impact there was to her physical or mental health. The Tenant’s application is with respect to 2 specific inspections 8-months apart from each other. I am not satisfied the behaviour of the Landlord amounts to substantial interference. While it may have been uncomfortable or inconvenient for the Tenant, I do not find it rises to the level of substantial interference.

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine. The Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16 provides guidance about the Board’s use of fines. It states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It further provides that the remedy is not usually imposed “unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”. I find a fine would not be appropriate in this case, the Tenant has failed to lead sufficient evidence that would warrant a fine in this case.

I find the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof required under the Act in their T2 application. As the Tenant’s allegations simply do not meet the burden of proof; it is not necessary for the Landlord to call any evidence. The Tenants application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove all of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the claim for excess rent collected is dismissed, however, as the Landlord consented to paying the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit, this portion of the application shall be granted on consent.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord charged him and his mother illegal rent by serving a N1 notice of rent increase via email and that the Tenant never consented to service by email. The Tenant also testified that the N1 is invalid due to the notice only containing the [name] name, and not the name of his mother, who is also a listed as a tenant on the lease.

The Tenant further stated that the Landlord’s Agent acted in bad faith when serving the N1 notice as it was sent shortly after the Tenant served the Landlord notice, via email, of their own T2 and T6 applications.
The Tenant also sought payment of the interest on the last month’s rent deposit that has accrued throughout the duration of the tenancy. The Landlord did not dispute that this amount is owing.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that he did act in bad faith when serving the N1 notice as he sent the notice via email as he had no other means of serving this on the Tenant. The Landlord’s Agent further stated that the timing was not an act of retaliation as he believed that due to being served the notices for the T2 and T6 applications, the rental increase conversation between himself and the Tenant were on pause due to the matters to be scheduled before the Board.

With respect to the ways in which a document or notice can be served, sections 191(1) and (2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) set out the following: 191(1) A notice or document is sufficiently given to a person other than the Board, (a) by handing it to the person; (b) if the person is a landlord, by handing it to an employee of the landlord exercising authority in respect of the residential complex to which the notice or document relates; (c) if the person is a tenant, subtenant or occupant, by handing it to an apparently adult person in the rental unit; (d) by leaving it in the mail box where mail is ordinarily delivered to the person; (e) if there is no mail box, by leaving it at the place where mail is ordinarily delivered to the person; (f) by sending it by mail to the last known address where the person resides or carries on business; or (g) by any other means allowed in the Rules. 2006, c. 17, s. 191 (1). 191(2) A notice or document that is not given in accordance with this section shall be deemed to have been validly given if it is proven that its contents actually came to the attention of the person for whom it was intended within the required time period. 2006, c. 17, s. 191 (2).

I find that given the acknowledgment by the Tenant that on July 30, 2025, he received the email, saw the N1 notice, and paid the rent increase starting on November 1, 2025, that it came to the attention of not only himself, but his mother as well, as there was no evidence led by the Tenant to show that the contents of the email were not intended for them; moreover, there was no issues with or evidence to suggest that the N1 notice was improper in terms of the time needed to serve and notify the Tenant of the increase in rent. I find that this is compliant with section 191(1) and (2) of the Act.

With respect to the Tenant’s argument that the N1 notice is invalid because they did not indicate his mother’s name, I must consider section 212 of the Act which provides for when substantial compliance with a form is sufficient. Sections 212(1) and (2) of the Act set out the following: 212 (1) Substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. 2006, c. 17, s. 212. 212(2) For greater certainty, an error in the contents of a form, notice or document still constitutes substantial compliance with this Act, as long as the error does not significantly prejudice a party’s ability to participate in a proceeding under this Act. 2024, c. 28, Sched. 24, s. 1.

The Tenant acknowledges they knew that the rent was increased with service of the N1 notice and opted to pay increase from the date it was received on July 30, 2025. In addition, I find that there is no prejudice to the Tenant and his mother with this issuance as both parties were aware of the increase, and thereby not prejudiced, in their ability to participate in this hearing. As such, I find there was no confusion as to what the rent was and by how much it increased, thereby not invalidating the N1 notice as it substantially complied with the Act.

I also find that it is rather peculiar that the Tenant deemed it proper service for serving his documents on the Landlord via email when there was no evidence or consent given by the Landlord for this method of service. As this was the main issue raised by the Tenant as he did not provide consent to transact with the Landlord via email, the Tenant has done the same exact thing.

Ultimately, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the notice of rent increase is invalid by virtue of invalid service or otherwise. Therefore, I am also not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that any rent paid by the Tenant pursuant to that rent increase was illegally collected or retained.
As it pertains to the interest on the last month’s rent deposit, the Landlord agreed to pay the Tenant $137.50 for interest owing on the rental deposit.
ordered: T he Landlord shall pay to the Tenant the interest on the last month’s rent deposit in the sum of $137.50.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before July 31, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
Because this is the Tenant’s application, the Tenant bears the burden of proof relative to each element of this legal test on a balance of probabilities.

To prove something on a balance of probab ilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), paras 44-46.

I am satisfied that the T enant was given an N12 notice of termination asserting that the Landlords required vacant possession of the unit because one of their parents intended to move into the unit. I am also satisfied that the Tenant moved out of the unit because of the N12 notice.

The Tenant has not presented sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the parent did not move into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, and I am also not satisfied that the N12 notice was given in bad faith.

The termination date on the N12 notice was February 28, 2026, but the Tenant moved out on February 1, 2026. The Tenant was entitled to do so, but the termination date in the notice is a relevant factor in considering if the intended occupant moved into the unit within a reasonable time.

The intended occupant was KF’s mother, who was living in Saskatchewan when the N12 notice was given. The Tenant said that KF’s mother’s house in Saskatchewan was not listed for sale until February 25, 2026. The Tenant said that KF’s mother attended the unit on February 24, 2026 to help with some “unnecessary renovations” at the rental unit, and then returned to Saskatchewan on March 9, 2026.
On cross-examination, the Tenant said that KF’s mother moved into the unit on April 9, 2026.

KF said that after the Tenant moved out, the Landlords were working out of town between about February 1-17, 2026. She said that after February 17, 2026 they began doing some work on the unit to make it more suitable for her mother to move in. KF said her mother’s condominium in Saskatchewan was not listed for sale until February 25, 2026 because she did not want to list it until she was sure the Tenant had vacated the unit.
KF’s mother came to Ontario around February 24, 2026, and helped with the work on the unit until March 8, 2026.
KF said that her mother’s condominium was sold on March 5, 2026, and that her mother went to Saskatchewan on March 9, 2026 to finalize that transaction.

KF’s mother moved into the unit on April 9, 2026, and still lives there. This was one month and 9 days after the termination date. In the circumstances, I find that KF’s mother moved into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant moved out.

Further, I find that the N12 notice was not given in bad faith, because there was a genuine intention on the part of the Landlords and KF’s mother that KF’s mother would move into the unit and live there for at least one year when the N12 was given: see [name], 2014 ONSC 3352 (CanLII), para 17; Salter v. Beljinac, 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), paras 18-20; [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC).
For these reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. (T2 application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application)
reasons: This member queried whether the Landlord had been served the Tenant’s evidence package. The Tenant responded that to the best of their knowledge their social worker who helped them complete the application, [name], served the Landlord. Based on the uncontested testimony before me, I am satisfied the Landlord was served the Tenant’s evidence; the application was served by the Board.

The Tenant described the rental complex as a small Care Home; the staff give meals and distribute the residents’ daily medications. The Tenant also testified that the residence was not short-term respite care. Based on the uncontested testimony/submissions before me, I find the residential complex does not fall under any exemptions covered by section 5 of the Residential Tenancy Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’); therefore, the Act applies. Merits
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant as set out below.

The Tenant testified thewy moved into the residence on December 27, 2023. The Tenant signed an agreement to rent and paid the Landlord a last month rent deposit of $1,250.00 and the first month’s rent; as indicated by the receipts, ODSP paid the Landlord direct and the Tenant paid any difference. The last month rent deposit was paid January 9, 2023. On March 19, 2024, the Tenant returned from an AA meeting to find his personal property all damage; he asked the Landlord to call the police so he could report the incident. After asking, the Tenant left to speak to a worker at the Brantford Regional Indigenous Support Centre (BRISC); when he returned to the residence the Landlord said he was no longer welcome to stay and had to move immediately; this was an illegal eviction. As seen by the email in evidence, the Tenant emailed BRISC that he was illegally evicted; BRISC found and paid for temporary accommodation at the Galaxy Motel March 19, 2024 through March 28, 2024, and then arranged permanent housing. The Landlord did not return the last month rent deposit or the balance of [name] 2024 rent.

The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord retained the full rent for the month of March 2024, despite illegally evicting the Tenant on March 19, 2024; the Tenant is entitled to return of the monies illegally withheld.

An order shall issues requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant $493.15, calculated as follows: monthly rent X 12 months in a tear, divided by 365 days X 12 days for the period March 19, 2024 through March 31, 2024.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord retained the Tenant’s last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,250.00 after evicting him on March 19, 2024. An order shall issue for same.

Based on the uncontested testimony and evidence before me, I find the Landlord illegally evicted the Tenant on March 19, 2024, thereby substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex.

The Tenant requested an abatement of $1,075.00 because he was illegally evicted and forced to move into a hotel until permanent housing could be found. The Tenant also requested $1,000.00 for his damaged personal property and an award of $5,000.00 fotr pain and suffering.
The Tenant did not testify to the specific property that was damaged or go into detail about how being illegally evicted affected him; therefore, these remedies are dismissed.
I consider the requested abatement of $1,075.00 to be reasonable considering the Tenant was illegally evicted by the Landlord and forced to live in a hotel until placed in permanent housing.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,816.13. This amount represents: • $491.13 for excess rent collected. • $1,250.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $1,075 rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit was a one-bedroom unit in a rental home where the Tenant shared communal areas with other residents.
The parties agreed that the furniture in the rental home belonged to the Landlord who offered them to the residents for free if they vacated their units in January 2022. Illegal Lockout
The Tenant alleged that on April 21, 2022, the Landlord illegally locked him out of the rental unit and failed to provide a replacement key.

As part of his evidence, the Tenant presented, a copy of a tenancy agreement for his new unit. The agreement showed that the tenancy for his new unit commenced on March 1, 2022, for a one-year period ending on February 28, 2023. The Tenant argued that , although a charitable organization paid the first and last month's rent deposit on his behalf, he did not immediately move into the new unit due to ongoing repairs. As a result , he remained in possession of the rental unit during that time.

The Tenant testified that the last month's rent deposit was paid on February 14, 2022, the same date the tenancy agreement was signed. Despite that, the Tenant claimed that he did not receive the keys to the new unit until May 5, 2022.

The Tenant also presented bank statements in support of his position regarding the dates on which he paid rent for the new unit. However, the evidence consisted of multiple versions of the same bank statements which contained discrepancies. The Tenant acknowledged that he possessed different versions of the statements and claimed that the inconsistencies were caused because of the dates on which the statements were printed, page formatting, or errors made by the bank. I did not find the Tenant’s explanation persuasive and relying on multiple, conflicting versions of the same banking records undermined his testimony. As a result, I do not find the Tenant to be a credible witness on this issue, and I do not assign any weight to the bank statements.

The Landlord denied locking the Tenant out of the rental unit. In March 2022, the Landlord was alerted by the condominium management that the Tenant had been observed removing belongings from the rental unit. The Landlord attended the unit, and observed the refrigerator was empty and it appeared the Tenant had vacated the unit.

In April 2022, the Landlord entered the rental unit and observed that the Tenant had set up a ‘spy camera’ in the unit, and left behind some old clothing, and a laptop. The Landlord's Legal Representative contacted the Tenant, and they subsequently met at a plaza where he handed the items to the Tenant. The Landlord proceeded to change the locks on April 21, 2022.

Based on all the evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant vacated the rental unit prior to the changing of the locks. The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant entered into a new tenancy agreement with a commencement date of March 1, 2022, and was observed removing his belongings from the unit that month.

The Tenant failed to provide any documentary evidence that would lead me to believe that he was unable to occupy th e new unit until May 2022 despite the commencement date of March 1, 2022, and his payment of the f irst and last month's rent deposit . In addition, the Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s evidence that his representative handed the Tenant’s computer and other items to the Tenant. The Tenant simply claimed that the computer was broken without providing any documentary evidence to substantiate the claim.

During his testimony, the Tenant also argued that the Landlord disposed of the furniture in the rental unit. However, the evidence demonstrates that the furniture belonged to the Landlord who offered it to the Tenant on the condition that he vacates the rental unit in January 2022. As the Tenant remained in the rental unit well after that date, the offer was rescinded and the Tenant, therefore, had no ownership claims over the furniture.

Given the evidence , I find the Tenant’s testimony is not substantiated by any reliable documentary evidence and I prefer the Landlord’s version of events. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit before the locks were changed and that the Landlord returned the Tenant’s remaining belongings to him.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally ; alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys; substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant; or obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Vital Services

While the Tenant claimed that the Landlord failed to provide adequate heat in the communal areas of the rental unit, the Landlord argued that each unit had its own thermostat which the residents could control.

The Tenant testified that the heat was shut off in the entire unit from January 2, 2022, to January 29, 2022. The Tenant contacted the police who visited the unit on January 3, 2022, and informed the Tenant that the Landlord w ould restore the heat. The Landlord then set the thermostat at 15 degrees Celsius until the Tenant contacted the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (RHEU) who were misled by the Landlord into believing that it was set to 22 degrees Celsius. On January 17, 2022, the RHEU told the Tenant that the thermostat was set at 22 degrees Celsius. On January 28, 2022, an inspector measured the temperature at 15.3 and 16 degrees Celsius.
The Tenant also stated that the heater had a remote control which was not provided to him until January 28, 2022.

In an email from the Tenant to the RHEU dated January 4, 2022, the Tenant informed them that the Landlord’s personal assistant, MS, shut off the only heater in the communal areas. In another email on January 11, 2022, after the RHEU requested an update, the Tenant stated that the Landlord maintains the unit at 16 degrees Celsius at night and 17 degrees Celsius during the day.

The Landlord testified that [name] was a resident of the rental home and was not his employee. The thermostat in the communal areas could be controlled by any of the residents and although set at 20 degrees Celsius, it sometimes went below that . The RHEU told the Landlord to increase the temperature which was already set to 20 degrees Celsius. The Landlord further stated that January 2022 was a very cold month, and the heater struggled to maintain that temperature. As a result, the thermostat was increased to 24 degree s Celsius. The Tenant never made a complaint directly to the Landlord.

Section 21 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the land lord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. Section 4(1) of [name]. 516/06 of the Act states September 1 to June 15 is prescribed as the part of t he year during which heat is a vital service and that heat shall be provided so that the room temperature at 1.5 metres above floor level and one metre from exterior walls in all habitable space and in any area intended for normal use by tenants, including recreation rooms and laundry rooms but excluding locker rooms and garages, is at least 20 degrees Celsius

The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant’s complaints regarding insufficient heat in the unit were made directly to the RHEU in January 2022 rather than to the Landlord. This deprived the Landlord of the opport unity to address the Tenant’s concerns prior to the RHEU's involvement. Once the issue was brough t to the Landlord’s attention , it would appear that the Landlord addressed it. On January 17, 2022, for example, the RHEU was satisfied that the temperature in the communal area was 20 degrees Celsius. The Tenant’s claim that the Landlord misled the RHEU was not supported by any meaningful evidence. There was also no evidence to support the Tenant’s assertion that the temperature was found to be 15.3 degrees Celsius on January 28, 2022, or that the re was insufficient heat for the most of that month.

Furthermore, the Tenant’s own evidence undermines his claim that the Landlord was responsible for the alleged lack of heat. The Tenant’s email to the RHEU dated January 4, 2023, demonstrates that the heat was turned down by MS whom he referred to as the Landlord’s assistant, but the Landlord disputed the assertion and claimed that she was also a tenant. Based on the evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that all residents had access to the thermostat in the communal area, and it would appear that MS chose to reduce the temperature. There was no evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord authorized MS’s conduct or that it was reported to the Landlord at the time of its occurrence.
Accordingly, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord withheld or deliberately interfered with the reasonable supply of a vital service.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord asked that the application be dismissed because the Tenant had not complied with the Landlord and Tenant Board’s (LTB) directions. For the following reasons, the request is granted and the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed the application on March 14, 2025. The application, as filed, was not ready to be heard because the allegations raised in it were not clearly set out. The application listed a very large number of incidents. Most of the alleged incidents appeared to involve conflicts with other tenants in the complex, not with the Landlords. The application did not appear to set out any instances in which the Tenants had complained to the Landlords about the other tenants’ conduct, thereby triggering any obligation on the Landlords’ part to take any action. The lack of reference to contraventions by the Landlords or complaints to the Landlords, combined with excessive detail including irrelevant details, made it impossible to know what claims the Tenant was making against the Landlords.
The application did, however, properly set out the date on which each incident was alleged to have occurred.

Over the course of March through June, 2025, the Tenant uploaded more than 50 images to the LTB’s online portal, which she presumably intended to disclose as evidence. The images were not organized or labelled.

An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held on February 2, 2026. One of the primary purposes of an ACC is to identify steps an applicant needs to take so that their application can be heard. The Member who conducted the ACC directed the Tenant to narrow and clarify the issues, and to file a consolidated evidence brief.

On June 16, 2026, the Tenant filed a letter asking to amend her application. The letter stated that attached were: [name] particulars of the T2 application. • Consolidated evidence brief. • Supporting exhibits.

This was not accurate. In actual fact, the Tenant uploaded roughly 27 unlabelled pdf files with her amendment request. None of them was an amended set of particulars or a consolidated evidence brief. It is not clear what a “supporting exhibit” would be, but in any event, none of the pdfs contained anything called a supporting exhibit.

Particulars of the Tenant’s allegations were not contained anywhere in the pdfs. Instead, each pdf contained a general written overview of an issue, and copies of evidence related to that issue with handwritten annotations. The Landlords and the LTB were expected to piece together the allegations by going through all the evidence and reading the annotations.
The allegations were also undated. In that respect, the amended application was in a worse state than the original application, which had included dates.

The Tenant’s evidence was interspersed with other materials spread over 26 pdf files, rather than being contained in a consolidated evidence brief. Furthermore, the evidence did not have a table of contents, as required by the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence. One of the files contained a table of contents of sorts, but it only provided the topics of each of the other 26 files, and did not assist in organizing the evidence so that it could be referenced during a hearing.

In short, the application was still not in a state where the Landlords could know the case against them or respond to it, and in some respects it was in a worse state than it had been prior to the amendments.
The Tenant argued that she had complied with the LTB’s direction. For the above reasons, I do not agree.
Since the application does not properly set out any allegation against the Landlords, the application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to maintain the carpets within the rental unit. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Preliminary Issues: Issues and Remedies not properly before the LTB

In addition to alleging the carpets need to be replaced, the Tenant has raised two further issues within her application. The first is a claim that an issue with the smoke detector was not rectified until 2023 and the second was a request for an order requiring the Landlord to issue rent receipts on or before February 28th of each year. For clarity I will address each issue below separately. Smoke Detector

The Tenant raised an issue regarding the smoke detector in the rental unit stating that the Landlord failed to respond to her request to repair the smoke detector. It was uncontested that the issue with the smoke detector was rectified in April 2023. The application was filed on March 18, 2025, which is more than a year after the issue was rectified. Therefore, the issue is barred by s. 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which provides that no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. Therefore, this issue is dismissed, and no remedy will be ordered. Rent Receipts

The Tenant also sought remedy under [name] 9, seeking an order to compel the Landlord to provide proper rent receipts on or before February 28th of each year. The Tenant filed a T6 application, the issue regarding rent receipts is not a maintenance issue, therefore, I have no jurisdiction to order this remedy. T6 Application
The rental unit is a single-family home, with 3 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms. The monthly rent is $1,443.99.

The Tenant’s primary complaint in this application is that the carpets within the living room carpets need to be replaced. She asks that she be permitted to complete the repairs or replacement and order the Landlord to pay the associated costs. The Landlord denies that the carpets need replacing.

For the reasons that follow, on a balance of probabilities I find that there is insufficient evidence to prove that the carpets are damaged and need to be replaced. Does the carpet need to be replaced?

The Tenant testified that for several years, she has had problems with a smell emanating from the carpet and now has issues with the carpet lifting within the living room within the rental unit. The carpet lifting causes concern for the Tenant as she has grandchildren that crawl within the rental unit and the lifting causes a safety hazard.

The Tenant testified that she first notified the Landlord that the carpets needed to be repaired or replaced via email on October 16, 2022. She stated while the Landlord replied to the email promptly, the Landlord has taken no steps to inspect, repair or replace the carpets since notifying him of the issue.

The Tenant referred to 2 quotes from SacWal Flooring Canada. The Tenant testified that after calling other companies SacWal was the most economical and therefore she had them attend to provide quotes.

The Tenant first referred to Quote #11537 (DOC-5264677) dated January 25, 2025, for $1,354.49 which the Tenant stated is for ‘entry level carpet’ and not preferred option as it is a temporary solution and not for long-term use. The quote stated that it is a “Rough Quote – Carpet not Chosen by Customer yet” and outlines the quote is for the removal, disposal of the existing carpet and install the new carpet. Finally, the quote stated “The existing carpet was installed incorrectly. The seam was 6” off the kitchen reducer, Pictures show the seam as well as the scrim heat tape under Photos were taken”.

The Tenant also referred to a second Quote #11546 (DOC-5264678) dated January 27 2025 for $1,551.11 which mirrors Quote #11537 with respect to the statements within the Quote. The Tenant stated that this would be the most economical choice and would last longer than the entry level carpet in the prior Quote.
The Tenant stated that both quotes are now outdated.

There are significant problems with the Tenant’s evidence. The quotes provided by the Tenant, where it stated the carpet was improperly installed is hearsay, and I give it little weight. The Tenant did not adduce any photos of the carpet within the hearing; she solely provided viva voce testimony to describe the condition of the carpet.

The Landlord testified that the rental unit is a brand-new 10-year-old home. The Tenant is only the 2nd tenant within the property. He stated that he had a professional cleaner attend the rental unit within 2-days of the Tenants original request to have the carpets cleaned and stated that he understood this issue had been rectified. Further, he provided his opinion that the carpets should be in good condition minus regular wear and tear. He supplied no documentary evidence to support these claims such as pictures or quotes of his own to corroborate his testimony or refute the testimony of the Tenant. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act, states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

On a balance of probabilities, the Tenant has failed to prove that the living room carpet has fallen below acceptable maintenance standards and needs to be replaced. I say this because the Tenant failed to adduce corroborating evidence such as pictures of the living room carpet nor did the Tenant have any supporting witnesses to testify to her allegations relating to the carpets within the proceeding. Additionally, the quotes are not strong, the quotes provided by SacWal, who are in the business of installing carpets have a vested interest in suggesting that a carpet should be replaced.

The Landlord testified and provided solely his opinion that the carpet should be in good condition minus regular wear and tear. He stated that he nor an agent of his attended the property to examine if the carpet needed to be repaired or replaced despite the Tenant complaining the carpets need to be replaced.

I find the Landlord’s testimony speculative, and he failed to set out any basis for his assertion that the carpet is in good condition minus regular wear and tear. The Landlords testimony did not assist me in determining whether the carpet is lifting or requires replacing. Further the Landlord admitted that he has noted inspected the carpet nor did he send a contractor to the home to provide any corroboratory evidence to his testimony. I must give little weight to his testimony as he has not attended the rental unit after the Tenant informed him that the carpet needed to be repaired or replaced.

The quotes submitted by the Tenant do not, on their own, substantiate the claim that the carpet needs to be replaced or that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation. The burden of proof rests with the Tenant, and I am not persuaded by their testimony along with the 2 quotes supplied within the hearing. The lack of readily available supporting evidence, such as pictures of the state of the living room carpet being in disrepair and requiring to be replaced leads me to conclude that the Tenant has not met this burden. The Tenants application is therefore dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenants application is dismissed. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
