issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has not proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.

This case involves an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 Notice’) delivered under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which says, in part: 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord's spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord's spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord's spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord's spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

On March 1, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant with the N12 Notice. The N12 Notice stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for their parent (‘mother’), for the purposes of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of th e Act, the LTB may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, 57 (1) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

For a tenant to obtain a remedy under section 57 based on a n N12 notice of termination (‘N12 Notice’) delivered under section 48, the LTB must be satisfied on the balance of probabilities that: • the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or LTB order based on the N12 Notice; and • the person named in the N12 Notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; • the notice was given in bad faith.

It was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 Notice and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice served by the Landlord. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2024.
It is also undisputed that the Landlord’s mother never moved into the rental unit.

As stated above, s ection 48 of the Act permits a landlord to terminate a tenancy where possession of the unit is required for the purpose of residential occupation. The requirement that a person have occupied the unit within a reasonable time in paragraph 57(1)(a) must be interpreted in that context. In my view, paragraph 57(1)(a) requires the person identified on the N12 Notice to have occupied the unit for purposes of residential occupation within a reasonable period. That means that the person must have moved into the unit and engaged in activities or conduct that is residential in nature.

On a T5 application, the burden of establishing bad faith, or perhaps more precisely lack of good fai th, typically falls on the tenant. However, subsections 57(5) and (6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith where the application is based on section 48. Those subsections say: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a) and (c), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
In other words, if section 57(5) of the Act applies, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish that they did not serve the N12 in bad faith.

What the LTB must consider on an application under section 57 based on an N12 notice of termination delivered under section 48 is whether: (a) the landlord genuinely intended that the person identified on the N12 notice of t ermination would occupy the unit; and (b) the person identified on the N12 notice of termnat ion genuinely intended to occupy the unit. [See [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SCDC) and [name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC)]

It is difficult to determine a person’s subjective intent. The LTB will typically make inferences concerning the subjective intent of the person identified on the N12 notice of termination based on the evidence, including the testimony of that person. [See [name], 2014 ONSC 3352 (CanLII)].
The LTB has broad discretion in terms of the evidence it may consider in determining whether a notice of termination under section 48 was delivered in good faith. [RTA, s. 72(3)]

The fact that the person identified as wanting to occupy the rental unit did not move into or occupy the unit and that the landlord advertised the unit for rent or sale are not the sole considerations when determining the landlord’s good faith. A landlord may be able to establish that an unforeseen change in circumstances resulted in the person identified on the N12 notice of termination being unable to occupy the unit. All other things being equal, this would be sufficient to rebut the presumption of bad faith arising under subsection 57(5) and (6) of the Act. [See, for example, [name], 2021 CanLII 141438 (ON LTB)]

The Landlord testified that he spoke with the Tenant in February 2024 about his mother moving into the rental unit and, once he determined she would need to do so, he served the N12 Notice on March 1, 2024. He stated that on March 10, 2024, his mother suff ered a fall resulting in a hip fracture, leaving her incapacitated and unable to move into the unit. Her health continued to decline thereafter: she experienced a heart attack on August 29, 2024, and by March 5, 2025, she was being monitored for lung cancer.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘L.F’) testified that she has worked as a Personal Support Worker for fifteen years and had been contracted by the Landlord to care for his mother for approximately six or seven years. She explained that before the Landlord’s mother sustained a hip fracture, the mother was living independently and could have moved into the rental unit. L.F. stated she would have continued providing care, but the severity of the hip fracture, combined with the mother’s advanced age, left her unable to move or live on her own. She also confirmed that she is no longer employed by the Landlord.

The Landlord’s representative submitted several medical reports 1 as evidence. These reports confirm the Landlord’s mother’s hip fracture on March 10, 2024 however the balance of the reports show she was not in Canada. The Landlord testified h is mother departed for Lebanon in June 2024 as has not returned to Canada as medical clearance from her doctor to return has not been provided.

The Landlord testified that once he learned his mother could not move into the rental unit, he contacted the Tenant to offer additional time to relocate. The Tenant informed him that he had already secured a new home. The Landlord maintained that, despite his mother’s inability to occupy the unit, he understood that the unit could not be rented for one year. As a result, the unit remained vacant from May 1, 2024 until it was rented in the fall of 2025.

The Landlord testified that although the Tenant provided an advertisement 2 listing the unit for rent, he did not authorize anyone to post such a listing and only became aware of it on March 7, 2025 after receiving an email from the Tenant’s representative. He recalled meeting with [name] (‘A.G.) to discuss his rental units generally but stated that he never entered into any agreement with A.G. to rent this unit. The Landlord maintained that the listing was false and that A.G. had no authorization to advertise the unit.

The Landlord’s witness, A.G. testified he has been a real estate agent for approximately ten years and is currently working with Royal LePage. He explained that he made a cold call to the Landlord about the Landlord’s rental properties and later met him at the rental unit. A.G. stated that, without the Landlord’s consent and without having a contract with him, he listed the rental unit on PadMapp er and [name], identifying himself as the point of contact. He testified that the Landlord never instructed him to advertise the unit and that his sole purpose in doing so was to assess its market value. He further stated that in March 2025, the Landlord contacted him and directed him to remove the advertisements, which he did immediately.

The Landlord’s wi tness, [name] ( ‘A.D.’) testified that she has served as the Landlord’s real estate agent for approximately four and a half years. She stated that she was unaware of the rental listing until she discovered it during an online search. She further testified that she does not know A.G. but understood that he had contacted the Landlord by telephone. A.D. explained that, in order to list a unit for rent, both the agent and the client must execute a binding contract before the property can be posted on the Multiple Listing Service (M.L.S.). It was her understanding that no such contract existed between the Landlord and A.G., and that A.G. committed fraud by listing the unit without authorization. She also testified that the listings were removed immediately after the Landlord instructed A.G. to do so. She added that at no time was the unit listed for rent. 1 Reply Submission of Landlord – DOC-6313152 – Pages 18 to 36 2 Tenant’s Schedule A – DOC-5270980 – Pages 12 to 13

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Analysis and Legislation

In this case, it is undisputed that the Landlord’s mother did not move into the rental unit. Based on the evidence before me and the Landlord’s admission that his mother did not move into the rental unit, I find that the presumption of bad faith under section 57(5) of the Act is engaged for this application. Therefore, the Landlord is required to prove their good faith on a balance of probabilities for the N12 Notice served to the Tenant.
This is a case where the Landlord has, in my view, rebutted the presumption of bad faith and I find that the N12 notice was given in good faith.
I am satisfied that when the N12 Notice was delivered, the Landlord genuinely intended that his mother would, within a reasonable time, move into and occupy the unit for at least one year.

In many other cases, the LTB has found that an unforeseen change in circumstances that results in the person listed in an N12 notice of termination being unable to occupy the rental unit does not constitute bad faith (see, for example, TST-66921-15, TST-87559-17, TST- 80046-16). I agree that this is a case where an unforeseen change of circumstances resulted in the Landlord’s mother failing to take occupancy of the rental unit.

The Tenant’s representative submits that the Landlord had no intention to have his mother move into the rental unit. She further notes that the injury occurred only nine days after service of the N12 Notice, and that the Landlord did not advise the Tenant until the end of March 2024 that his mother would be unable to occupy the rental unit. By that time, the Tenant had already arranged to purchase a home and was no longer in a position to return to the rental unit. The Tenant’s representative maintains that the Landlord’s sole purpose in serving the N12 Notice was to regain possession of the unit for the purpose of re‑renting it.

A landlord acts in good faith in delivering an N12 notice of termination where there is a genuine intent to move into and occupy the unit. In [name] v. Noble [1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC)], the Divisional Court found that whether a landlord’s intention in retaking possession of a unit under what is now section 48 was reasonable is not the test that the LTB is to apply to determine good faith.

In this case, I am satisfied that the Landlord genuinely intended to retake possession of the unit for purpose of residential occupation by his mother but an unforeseen change in circumstances prevented the Landlord’s mother from moving in.

In [name] v. [name] [2014 ONSC 3352 (CanLII)], the Divisional Court found that the LTB can consider a landlord's conduct and motives to infer whether the landlord acted in good faith in delivering the relevant notice of termination.

In this matter, there is nothing in the Landlord’s motives or conduct that supports a finding of bad faith or any ulterior purpose in delivering the N12 Notice, or at any time thereafter. I find that the Landlord genuinely believed his mother would occupy the rental unit, and that her unforeseen health complications ultimately prevented her from doing so. I further accept the Landlord’s evidence that the unit was listed for rent without his authorization and that it remained vacant from May 1, 2024 until the fall of 2025. No documen tary evidence was presented to contradict this conclusion.

The Tenant’s representative contends that, although it was argued the Landlord had an obligation to offer the rental unit back to the Tenant once it became apparent that his mother would not be able to occupy it, no statutory authority or case law was provided in support of that proposition, nor was any such authority identified for my consideration.

In [name] v. [name] [2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII)] (‘Elkins’), the Court of Appeal found that in considering whether a notice of termination was given in bad faith, the LTB should not limit its analysis to the time the N12 notice of term ination was delivered. While Elkins involved a notice of termination given under section 49 of the Act, I think that the case also applies where notice is given under section 48 and the LTB should not restrict its consideration of a landlord’s good faith to the point in time when the landlord delivered the relevant notice of termination. The LTB may, depending on the circumstances, find that a landlord acted in bad faith where the circumstances that caused the landlord to deliver the N12 notice of termi nation changed before the tenant vacated or found alternate accommodations and the landlord did not offer to allow the tenant to remain in or reoccupy the unit.

In this matter, the Landlord did not become aware that his mother would be unable to occupy the rental unit until after the Tenant had secured alternative accommodations. In these circumstances, I do not find that the Landlord acted in bad faith by failing to offer the Tenant an opportunity to reoccupy the unit.

In conclusion, I appreciate the Tenant’s frustration at being forced to vacate their long-time home in circumstances where, in retrospect, it might not have been necessary for them to vacate. However, in my view, the Landlord delivered the N12 Notice in good faith, and the Landlord genuinely wanted to retake possession of the unit for purposes of residential occupation by his mother. In those circumstances, no remedy is available to the Tenant, and this application must, as a result, be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $426.55.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord collected an illegal charge by charging the Tenant $378.55 for plumber’s invoices after the Tenant complained to the Landlord about having issues with hot water.

Section 34 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that a Tenant is only responsible to repair undue damage to a rental unit that is caused by wilful or negligent conduct. Section 89(1) provides that a landlord may apply to the Board to have a tenant pay for reasonable costs that the landlord has incurred for repair of undue damage wilfully or negligently caused by the tenant.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that no landlord shall directly or indirectly collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

The Tenant testified that there was an issue with his hot water that started on approximately October 30, 2025, and he was not getting a proper supply of hot water to his unit, he would only get luke warm water after running the water for 5 minutes. The Tenant testified that he notified the Landlord and the Landlord sent a plumber out to investigate and the plumber found nothing and said it was fine. The Tenant testified the issue persisted and again notified the Landlord.

The Tenant testified there was back and forth and ultimately after multiple visits from plumbers, the Landlord advised that the recirculation pump was reset on November 12, 2025. The Tenant testified that this appeared to have rectified the issue and his supply of hot water was restored.

The Tenant then testified that the Landlord provided him with two invoices for plumbers’ visits that occurred prior to the November 12, 2025, resolution in which the Landlord had claimed the issue was resolved and sought reimbursement from the Tenant. The Tenant did not pay and was served an N5 notice of termination claiming the amounts of the unpaid plumbers’ invoices.

The Tenant testified that he paid the invoices under the N5 notice and provided a letter to the Landlord indicating that he only did so to avoid eviction and that he did not believe he was responsible. The Tenant provided a copy of the letter at the hearing.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant did not wilfully or negligently cause undue damage to the recirculation pump of the hot water tank. The Tenant testified that the hot water tank is not in his unit and not under his control. The Landlord can only collect costs from the Tenant for repairs that are a result of undue damage wifully or negligently caused by the Tenant.

Here, I am satisfied that the Tenant had a legitimate concern about the supply of his hot water that he continually reported to the Landlord who had an obligation to investigate and ultimately was found not to have been due to the Tenant’s wilful or negligent conduct, but due to an issue with the recirculation pump that was under the Landlord’s control. The Tenant was therefore not responsible for the plumbers’ invoices from the Landlord’s investigations into why the Tenant was having issues with the hot water.

Here, I am satisfied that a charge for plumbers’ invoices can be equated to a fee or penalty, a “other like amount of money”, under section 134(1)(a) of the Act, to which the Landlord was not entitled to charge to the Tenant as the Tenant did not wilfully or negligently cause undue damage.

I am also satisfied that the Tenant notified the Landlord that the Tenant was paying the amounts claimed on the N5 notice under protest and simply to avoid eviction. While the more optimal approach may have been to not pay the amount and have the matter proceed to a hearing under a Landlord’s application, the Tenant clearly communicated with the Landlord that the Tenant did not agree with the amount owing.

As such, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act and therefore the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the amounts paid to the Landlord representing the $378.55 paid for the plumber’s invoices.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $426.55. This amount represents: • $378.55 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 26, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $426.55 from the rent for August 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the outset of the hearing the Landlord Representative requested that the applications be dismissed pursuant to the Tenant failing to provide a cause of action or lacked sufficient detail, specifically, dates and times of alleged events as required by s.43(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and addressed by the Divisional Court in [name] v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”).

It was also their submission that these deficiencies were identified at an adjudicative case conference (ACC) held between the parties on October 2, 2025, yet despite this, the Tenant failed to correct the deficiencies when filing their amended application. As such they requested that in addition to the application being dismissed, that no further adjournments be granted and that costs also be ordered against the Tenant.

Canvassing the Tenant Representative, it was their submission that an amended application, pursuant to the issues identified at the ACC had been filed and that they would be relying upon the Tenant’s Viva voce evidence. It was also on this basis and the submission that they were acting in good faith that if required an adjournment should be granted and no costs ordered. Analysis.

Reviewing the amended application, I am satisfied that all that was pled was a series of broad allegations regarding another Tenant and the Landlord’s alleged lack of response covering the period of December 3, 2024 to December 2, 2025 with no other details, such as detailed events, dates or times.

Similarly, having reviewed the adjournment sheet from the ACC, it was noted that this was an issue identified by the parties and the Tenant was advised to correct this issue by way of filing an amended application by December 2, 2025. Adjournment denied.

Given the time that has passed since the ACC, the fact that the adjournment sheet from the ACC identifies the same issues, I am satisfied that the Tenant has had more than ample opportunity to correct these deficiencies. Accordingly, I am not granting an adjournment to further amend the application. Application dismissed.

As held by the Supreme Court of Canada: • The duty to comply with the rules of natural justice and to follow rules of procedural fairness extends to all administrative bodies acting under statutory authority. Moreau-Bérubé v. New Brunswick (Judicial Council), 2002 SCC 11 (CanLII), [2002] 1 SCR 249, at para. 75; and, • the purpose of the participatory rights contained within the duty of procedural fairness is to ensure that administrative decisions are made using a fair and open procedure…with an opportunity for those affected by the decision to put forward their views and evidence fully and have them considered by the decision-maker. Baker v Canada (Ministry of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC), 1999 2 S.C.R. 817, the Supreme Court of Canada stated, at para. 22

Further, the Divisional Court has held that for administrative powers to, “be exercised in a procedurally fair way require[s] that notice be given which set[s] out the allegations sufficient to enable the parties to know the case they had to meet” and further, that, “[t]he applicants’ legitimate expectation was …to know the case that they had to meet.” In Fox North Bay Inc. v. Ontario (Alcohol and Gaming Commission, Registrar), 2022 ONSC 5898), at paras. 58 and 61.

Applications which make broad generalized claims and do not provide basic particulars do not allow a matter to be fairly heard. It is counter to the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness and would cause significant prejudice to the responding party if allowed to proceed. I do not find the Landlord or the LTB can discern what the Tenant’s claims are and I find that it is not now for the LTB or the Landlord to correct deficiencies in the Tenant’s application, nor for the LTB or the Landlord to interpret, infer or imagine what the Tenant’s allegations might be. Accordingly for this reason and those above I am dismissing the Tenant’s application. Costs

As to the request that costs be ordered, section 204(3) of the Act states the Board may order that its costs of a proceeding be paid by a party or the party’s paid representative. Rule 23.4 of the Landlord Tenant Board Rules states a party, or a paid representative may be ordered to pay the LTB for its costs of a proceeding. Hearing costs will not exceed $100 per hour to a maximum of $700.00.

As identified above, one of the core principles of procedural fairness is the right to notice of the claims made and matters being considered. I find that the Tenant was advised that the application lacks sufficient detail at the original hearing and they were given the opportunity to amend the application. The Tenant ignored the advice given to amend the application and chose to re-attend the hearing with the materials unchanged. The Tenant Representative asserting that the issues would be clarified by way of oral evidence presented at the hearing is not acceptable. This does not provide adequate notice to the other party to have the opportunity to prepare to defend the claim. I find that disregarding advice received at the ACC and attending the hearing, having taken no action to correct the deficiencies in the application, constitutes an abuse of process and also resulted in the ineffective use of the Boards time.

Furthermore, having considered the submissions of the Tenant’s Legal Representative, I still find that it was unreasonable to take no action to correct the deficiencies in the application and to proceed without adequate notice to the other party. Accordingly, for this reason I am satisfied that the ordering of costs against the Tenant Representative is warranted in the amount of $350.00.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant Representative shall pay into the Board $350.00 in costs by July 31, 2026. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $9,616.03.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I make the following findings of fact. 1. The tenancy started on July 1, 2022, and ended on December 31, 2024. The rental unit is an apartment on the second floor of a Victorian house. The lawful monthly rent was $1,400.00 in 2022, increased to $1,435.00 on July 1, 2023, and to $1,470.00 on July 1, 2024. 2. On August 21, 2022, the parties had a telephone conversation where the Landlord called the Tenant a “cheeky bloody woman.” On September 17, 2022, the parties had a telephone conversation where the Tenant complained about maintenance issues and the Landlord said she has a “compulsive behaviour to clean” and a “mental disorder.”

There were bedbugs in the rental unit since the start of the tenancy. The Tenant informed the Landlord of the issue on July 19, 2022. The Landlord conducted a pest treatment on July 20, 2022, which was ineffective. The Tenant informed the Landlord that the issue was not resolved. The Landlord conducted a second pest treatment on August 12, 2022, which was also ineffective. The bedbugs persisted until the Tenant moved out.

There were cockroaches in the rental unit starting in September 2022; the Tenant notified the Landlord as soon as she saw them. The Landlord conducted a pest treatment in September or October 2022, which was effective. The cockroaches returned on January 27, 2024; the Tenant notified the Landlord immediately. The Landlord responded to the Tenant the next day and brought gel traps to the unit four days later. This treatment was also effective until the cockroaches returned on October 3, 2024. The Tenant notified the Landlord, but no further action was taken until the Tenant moved out.

There were mouse droppings in the rental unit starting in December 2022 and continuing throughout the tenancy. The Tenant closed a hole in the wall behind the kitchen cabinets and notified the Landlord of the repair on May 28, 2023.

There was no electricity in the washroom outlet. The issue started on September 17, 2022. The Tenant notified the Landlord on September 18, 2022, who sent a contractor to inspect it on September 26, 2022. The issue was resolved in May 2023.

There was a locked common area on the main floor of the house where all the tenants would store their bicycles. However, the lock on the main door was not fully functional. In mid-September 2022, the Tenant’s bicycle accessories were stolen, including a helmet, saddle, and lights.

On December 19, 2024, the Tenant was in the process of moving out and returned to the rental unit to find it open and some of her belongings missing. The Landlord informed the Tenant that he instructed a neighbouring tenant to clean out her unit. The Landlord disposed of the Tenant’s vacuum cleaner but later reimbursed the Tenant in the amount of $175.00. The Tenant testified that the vacuum was almost new, costing $203.37. 3. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 4. The Landlord was notified of the bedbug issue on July 19, 2022, and conducted treatments which were ineffective. This issue remained unresolved until December 31, 2024, which is an unreasonable amount of time. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached his maintenance obligations with respect to the bedbugs. 5. The Landlord responded reasonably to the Tenant’s first two complaints about the cockroaches. The Landlord conducted treatments within days of the Tenant’s complaints which were effective for significant periods. However, the Landlord failed to take any action regarding the Tenant’s final complaint on October 3, 2024, and therefore breached his maintenance obligations from that date to December 31, 2024. 6. I am not satisfied that the Landlord was in breach of his maintenance obligations regarding the mice. Although the Tenant testified that this was a persistent issue, she did not indicate when she first notified the Landlord of the issue. The only communication presented as evidence was the text message about the Tenant conducting repairs. I am not satisfied that the Landlord was aware that the issue persisted past that date. 7. The Landlord was notified of the washroom outlet issue on September 18, 2022, and did not resolve it until May 2023. This is an unreasonable delay; therefore, the Landlord breached his maintenance obligations with respect to this issue. 8. The Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” I am satisfied that the Landlord’s comments to the Tenant during their phone calls on August 21, 2022, and September 17, 2022, were offensive to the Tenant. Therefore, I find that the Landlord harassed the Tenant.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant by failing to maintain the residential complex, by failing to secure the common area on the main floor, and by entering the rental unit on December 19, 2024, before the tenancy terminated, and disposing of the Tenant’s belongings.
Therefore, the application is granted. Remedies

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s refusal to maintain the rental unit had a significant impact on her wellbeing. After the Tenant disclosed her disability to the Landlord, he used that against her in their conversations when she complained about maintenance issues. The Tenant could not sleep because of the bedbug bites and had to move to the floor to avoid them. However, the Tenant has chronic back pain, which was exacerbated by sleeping on the floor. The Tenant attempted to mitigate her damages by purchasing a mattress encasement; however, it did not stop the bedbugs.

The Tenant works from home as an art teacher, but lost clients because she could not conduct classes at the bedbug-infested rental unit. The Tenant felt isolated from her friends, who did not feel comfortable having her over because of the risk of a bedbug infestation. The Tenant’s mental health was affected by the ongoing issues, and she fell behind in her work and education. The Tenant is now living farther from her work and community.

Based on the duration that the issues remained unresolved and the Tenant’s inability to fully use the rental unit, I find a 30% rent abatement to be appropriate for the period of July 19, 2022, to December 31, 2024. However, the Tenant only requested an abatement of $6,720.00. The LTB cannot award an amount greater than what is requested on the application; therefore, the rent abatement is limited to $6,720.00. Given the impact on the Tenant’s life and the negative effects of these issues on her mental health, I find an award of $2,000.00 in general damages to be appropriate.

The Tenant provided a breakdown of the items she had to dispose of when moving out but only provided two receipts to substantiate these costs. I find it appropriate to award the costs to replace the mattress, pillows, mop, nightstand, shelf, and hamper, totalling $761.66, which were supported by receipts. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine the cost of the remaining items. I also find it appropriate to award the difference between the cost of the replacement vacuum and the amount the Landlord paid, in the amount of $28.37. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $790.03, which is the reasonable cost that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was damaged or disposed of.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,616.03. This amount represents: • $6,720.00 for a rent abatement. • $790.03 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was damaged or disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $2,000.00 in general damages. • $106.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the amounts ordered below to the Tenant. Illegal Charge

Per the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, the Tenant paid the Landlord a $500.00 refundable key deposit at the beginning of the tenancy. The Tenant testified that he returned the keys upon moving out of the unit on February 26, 2026, and that $350.00 of the deposit was never returned to him. He testified that he instructed the Landlord to apply $150.00 to an outstanding utility bill and to return the rest. The Landlord sent an e-transfer to the Tenant for the remaining $350.00, but due to a technical issue the payment was never processed. The Tenant testified that he asked the Landlord to send another transfer to complete the transaction, but the Landlord never did.
I found the Tenants to be credible in his testimony, and his testimony was consistent with the terms of the lease provided at the hearing.
By not returning the balance of the refundable key deposit, the Landlord has illegally retained the funds. These funds must be paid to the Tenant. Deposit Interest
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

Per the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, he paid the Landlord a deposit for the final two months of his tenancy at the beginning of the tenancy on October 28, 2023. He testified that he was never paid interest on this deposit.

Half of the deposit – $ 2,900.00 – was held by the Landlord form October 28, 2023, to January 1, 2026, when it was applied to the Tenant’s rent. The interest owing on this amount is $158.13. This interest must be paid to the Tenant.

The other half of the deposit – $ 2,900.00 – was held by the Landlord form October 28, 2023, to February 1, 2026, when it was applied to the Tenant’s rent. The interest owing on this amount is $163.30. This interest must be paid to the Tenant.
I found the Tenants to be credible in his testimony, and his testimony was consistent with the terms of the lease provided at the hearing.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants the amounts ordered below.
The Landlords collected excess rent which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant [name] testified that the Tenants paid a $7,400.00 rent deposit to the Landlords’ real estate broker when they signed a lease for the rental unit on September 4, 2025. The term of the lease was scheduled to commence on October 1, 2026.

On September 10, 2026, the Tenants informed the Landlords’ agent of their intention not to proceed with the lease because one of the Tenants got a job offer and the Tenants were relocating immediately to the United States.

Section 88(1) of the Act provides that where a tenant does not give notice in accordance with the Act or there is no agreement between the parties to terminate the tenancy, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with the Act. In this case, the Tenant could have given 60 days’ notice, therefore the Tenants would be obligated to pay rent up to November 9, 2025.

However, section 88(3) of the Act relieves the Tenants of the obligation to pay rent on the day a new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. A landlord is obligated to mitigate their losses pursuant to section 8(4) of the Act and consideration must be given to whether or not the Landlords took reasonable steps to do so.

The Landlords, per the Tenants’ evidence, listed the rental unit for rent again on September 13, 2025. On October 14, 2025, the Landlords’ agent informed the Tenants’ agent that the property had been rented to a new tenant scheduled to take possession on October 20, 2025.

Since a new tenant took possession of the rental unit on October 20, 2025, the Landlords’ loss is limited to the period from October 1, 2025, to October 19, 2025. Beyond that time, the Landlord experienced no losses.
Ms. [name]name] testified that the Tenants and their agent attempted to contact the Landlords and their agent to arrange for a partial refund of the deposit paid and received no response.

I find that pursuant to section 88(3) of the Act, despite the inadequate notice, the Tenants were no longer liable to pay rent to the Landlords for any period of time after October 19, 2025. As such, any rent paid with respect to the use of the rental unit after this date ought to be returned to the Tenants.

The deposit paid by the Tenants to the Landlord was $7,400.00. Per section 88(1), the Tenants owe the Landlords $2,311.23 in rent for the period of October 1, 2026, to October 19, 2026. Section 134(1.1) of the Act prohibits the Landlords from collecting rent in respect of any period after the Tenants’ tenancy terminated and the Tenants vacated the rental unit. Therefore, the excess amount of rent paid by the Tenants – $5,088.77 – should be returned to the Tenants by the Landlords.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $ 5,136.77. This amount represents: • $5,088.77 for the illegal rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the sum of $657.37.

The Tenant testified that he entered into an oral tenancy agreement with the Landlord to rent a room at the residential complex on December 23 2024, with the tenancy commencing on January 1 2025. He states that at the time of entering into the tenancy agreement he paid the Landlord $100.00 as a security deposit and $1,000.00 for first and last months rent.

The Tenant further testified the Landlord approached him in October, 2025 and asked him to vacate the rental unit, which the Tenant agreed to do at the end of the month. The Tenant states that he vacated the rental unit on October 31 2025 and left the keys in the rental unit and sent a text message to the Landlord confirming his move out.
On November 6 2025 the Tenant sent a text message to the Landlord requesting the return of his deposits, but as of the date of this hearing the Landlord has failed to do so. Analysis Security Deposit
Section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Section 106 of the Act goes on to say: 106(1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.
The amount of $100.00 collected by the Landlord was in addition to a last month’s rent deposit of $500.00, which was also paid to the Landlord.

Additionally, Section 134(1) of the Act states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;
The charge collected by the Landlord was not a permitted charge under Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the ‘Regulation’)
Based on the uncontested evidence before me the Landlord collected an illegal charge in contravention of the Act. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The parties mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy at the end of October, 2025. The Tenant had previously paid the Landlord rent for October, 2025 and still held a last months rent deposit on behalf of the Tenant, which was not returned.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act. Interest on Rent Deposit

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant is entitled to pro-rated amount from January 1, 2025 to October 31, 2025 in the amount of $9.37.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $657.37. This amount represents: • $100.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $500.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $9.37 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) This applications were heard by videoconference on June 30, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Tenant’s Legal Representative, Cassia Gomes, and the Tenant attended the hearing. Witnesses attended the hearing for both the Landlord and the Tenant but did not appear before the Board to provide evidence.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative raised several preliminary issues relating to the Tenant’s request to amend the applications, late disclosure, and the lack of particulars in the applications.

By way of background, the Tenant’s applications were filed on March 23, 2025 and an Adjudicative Case Conference (“ACC”) was held on December 9, 2025. The Tenant, the Landlord, and the Landlord’s Legal Representative attended the ACC. Interim order [name] was issued on December 15, 2025 requiring the Tenant to amend the applications and provide all evidence to the Landlord by January 30, 2026 and the Landlord to provide all evidence to the Tenant by February 27, 2026.
The Tenant filed their amended applications and their evidence with the Board on June 23, 2026 and provided the Landlord the same a week before the hearing.

Given that the Tenant’s applications were filed in March 2025 and the parties were before the Board at the ACC in December 2025, I find that the Tenant has had ample time to amend the applications and serve disclosure to the Landlord. I note that the Tenant had a Legal Representative as of at least March 2, 2026, almost four months before the hearing when the Tenant’s Legal Representative requested the Board to add them on record.

In my view, there is no reasonable explanation why the Tenant only filed the amended applications and served disclosure a week before the hearing. While the Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant had health issues that prevented the Tenant from gathering evidence or sitting down to prepare the applications with the Representative, the Tenant elected not to disclose any specific health issues or symptoms related to the health issues and I am unable to assess whether the delay was reasonable due to these vague submissions. To amend the applications at this point is prejudicial to the Landlord. It is unreasonable to expect the Landlord to be able to respond to the [name] amended applications and review almost 100 pages of disclosure with only a week’s notice. The request to amend is denied.
Even if I grant the Tenant’s request to amend the applications, the Tenant’s amended applications and original applications have the same issue; that is, they lack particulars.

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (“Ball v. Metro Capital”). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case are tenant applications instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established.

A review of both the amended and original applications show that the Tenant did not provide any specifics, such as dates and times, of the allegations. For example, the Tenant alleges that since 2020, the Landlord has made derogatory and insulting comments toward the Tenant; however, the Tenant does not indicate what comments were made, how these comments were made, and when these comments were made. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord permitted other individuals to park in the Tenant’s designated parking space but does not indicate who and when these occurrences happened. On the T6 application, the Tenant alleges unresolved maintenance issues but does not indicate what exactly is in disrepair.

I also note that the Board’s jurisdiction is subject to the time limitation provision of subsection 29(2) of the Act but the Tenant seems to be alleging some issues and asking for remedies beyond the time limitation.

Based on the submissions before the Board, I find the Tenant’s applications lacked sufficient details and particulars to clearly establish the Tenant’s claims on its face and there is insufficient detail in the applications to allow the Landlord to know the case being alleged against them. As such, the Tenant’s applications must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the Tenant’s Agent raised an issue with respect to the late service and filing of a document, being an interim order under LTB-L-049864-25, which was deemed served on the Tenant by the Landlord’s Legal Representative on June 3, 2026 and filed on June 10, 2026 the day before the hearing.

The document in question is an interim order under LTB-L-049864-25, which was issued on October 2, 2025 and had been sent to the parties by the Board via email on the same date of issuance including the Tenant and the Tenant’s Agent. Additionally, the Tenant’s Agent acknowledges that the order was previously received from the Board.

Based on the evidence before me I see no prejudice to the Tenant in permitting the use of the interim order under LTB-L-049864-25 at this hearing as it had been in the possession of the Tenant and the Tenant’s Agent for a number of months prior to this hearing. Preliminary Issue: Res Judicata

At the commencement of the hearing the Landlord raised the issue of res judicata alleging that the issues raised in the Tenant’s T1 application were previously decided by the Board in the interim order issued under LTB-L-049864-25 on October 2, 2025.

The Tenant’s Agent confirmed that the T1 application deals with an alleged overpayment by the Tenant to the Landlord in February 2025 in the amount of 0.01 cent; and an alleged overpayment by the Tenant to the Landlord in April 2025 in the amount of $1.00 and the retention of those funds by the Landlord.
The matter of LTB-L-049864-25 is an L1 application commenced by the Landlord against the Tenant for alleged rental arrears
On August 28, 2025 the matter came before Member [name] who dealt with preliminary issues and seized himself of the matter as there was insufficient time to complete hearing the matter on its merits.

Member [name] issued an interim order with respect to the preliminary issues raised, including the validity of the Landlord’s N4 notice of termination, wherein he addressed the issue of the overpayment of 0.01 cent by the Tenant in February 2025 and $1.00 in April 2025.

With respect to these issues the order states as follows in paragraphs 5 and 6: 5. The Landlord testified that the one cent overpayment from February 2025 had been returned to the Tenant. In support of this the Landlord relied on a photograph of an e transfer showing that an electronic transfer was sent to the Tenant on February 20, 2025, in the amount of one cent. 6. The one-dollar overpayment from April 2025 was not returned and has instead been allocated towards the rent deposit as there were no arrears outstanding in April 2025. The Landlord’ Legal Representative testified that when the lease began the lawful monthly rent was $1300.00 however the rent has since increased to $1350.00. At the time that the April payment was made there were no existing arrears, and the Landlord allocated the additional one dollar to the last month rent deposit.

In his analysis of the evidence before him Member [name] states in paragraphs 13 to 19: 13. I am satisfied that the N4 is valid. Under the circumstances I am satisfied that the Landlord attempted to return the over payment of one cent, and while this may have been erroneously sent to an old email address no longer in use by the Tenant, I am satisfied that it was returned on February 20, 2025. I am also satisfied that at the time the N4 was created the Landlord believed the refund had ben accepted by the Tenant and drafted the N4 on this basis. 14. With respect to the discrepancies, I have also applied Section 212 of the Act. 15. Section 212 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: Substantial compliance sufficient 212 (1) Substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. 2006, c. 17, s. 212. When error still constitutes substantial compliance (2) For greater certainty, an error in the contents of a form, notice or document still constitutes substantial compliance with this Act, as long as the error does not significantly prejudice a party’s ability to participate in a proceeding under this Act. 2024, c. 28, Sched. 24, s. 1. 16. When I canvassed submission on section 212 of the Act from the Tenant’s Agent, she testified that everyone has a duty to follow the rules and this Landlord has a history of making errors, and the Act requires the N4 to be accurate and even a small discrepancy will render the N4 invalid. 17. Ultimately, I am satisfied that it was reasonable for the Landlord to allocate the one-dollar overpayment towards the last months rent as there were no arrears outstanding. However, even if I were not satisfied, I would still find the N4 valid after applying Section 212 of The Act. 18. The Tenant’s agent was unable to articulate any significant prejudice that the Tenant would experience if the N4 were deemed valid. Ultimately the discrepancy in question is one dollar and one cent, and the Tenant has clearly been aware of this since June 2025 and has been able to prepare and present robust submission with respect to the discrepancy. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is prejudiced and find the N4 would be saved by Section 212 of the Act. 19. I also note that the Tenant’s agent has not provided a satisfactory explanation for the over payment of one dollar and one cent, which to my mind lends credence to the suggestion made by the Landlord’s Legal Representative that the overpayment was a deliberate attempt to frustrate any future N4. To my mind this would support an Application of Section 212 of the Act in the case of this N4.
The Tenant’s Agent submits that the interim order issued under LTB-L-049864-25 on October 2, 2025 is an interim order and not a final order and is not in full force and effect. Analysis

An issue is res judicata if it has already been settled by a prior order. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue. In effect, it prevents a “second kick at the can”. Three elements must be present for res judicata to apply. First, there must be an earlier decision on the issue. Second, that decision must be final in that it has not been reviewed or appealed. Third, the same parties must be involved.

In assessing the elements that must be present for res judicata to apply I am satisfied that there was an earlier decision on the same issues as raised in the Tenant’s T1 application by Member [name] in his interim order issued on October 2, 2025 under LTB-L- 049864-25.

I am further satisfied that the decision of Member [name] was final with respect to these issues. Although the order is an interim order a final determination had been made with respect to the alleged overpayment and retention of 0.01 cent in February 2025 and $1.00 in April 2025. The interim order has not been reviewed or appealed and is in full force and effect.
Lastly, I am also satisfied that the same parties are involved in both LTB-L049864-25 and this matter.

The Tenant’s application will be dismissed as based on the evidence before me the issues of the Tenant’s T1 application have previously been decided by the Board and the [name] application is an attempt to relitigate the issues and constitutes res judicata.
After making my oral determination on the issue at the hearing the Tenant’s Agent disconnected from the hearing at 11:09 a.m. Request for Costs
After the Tenant’s Agent disconnected from the hearing the Landlord’s Legal Representative sought costs in the amount of $750.00.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submits that notwithstanding the Board had issued an order on the Tenant’s issues on October 2, 2025 the Tenant attempted to have these issues relitigated and filed a T1 application on March 19, 2026 when the Tenant knew, or ought to have known they were estopped from doing so, requiring the Landlord to incur expenses to defend himself.

The Board’s Guideline on costs indicates that while the Board may order a party to pay the costs of another party, costs to a successful party for the preparation/representation fees paid to a legal representative are generally only awarded in cases of unreasonable conduct.

In the circumstances I am not satisfied that the conduct of the Tenant or their Agent rise to the level of unreasonable, or that that the Tenant and/or their Agent fully understood the principal of res judicata prior to the hearing as such no costs will be awarded in favour of the Landlord.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
