issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord’s Agents raised the concern that the details of the T1 application were lacking and did not set out the minimum information required for either the Landlord/Respondent or the Board to understand the claims being made. The first deficiency was understanding what specific issues were being raised since they were not clearly written in the T1 application, such as not in a list format as requested on the form.

By going through what had been provided in the application, Part 2 and the additional typed details, the Tenant did not make any submissions to clarify what the issues were and stated that he did the paperwork himself. As well, the Tenant stated that if he had to redo the application and file it properly, he would do so.

None of the issues contained sufficient details to adequately set out or explain the claim being made. For example, none of the issues had a start date (except the first issue, but this was a general statement about a cable charge starting on February 1, 2026).

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (“Ball v. Metro Capital”). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established.

The types of particulars expected in notices and applications include dates, times, and a detailed description of the alleged conduct or behaviour. This allows the responding party to know the case they have to meet and to prepare their defence.

The Board’s tenant application forms have been developed with written instructions to elicit the necessary details required. For example, the T1 form states at page 3: “Shade the box completely next to each of your reasons for applying to the Board” and from that point on has important information on how to fill out each reason; moreover, on page 5, it states that “for reasons 1 - 7 you must explain in the table below why you are filing this application. List the number of each reason you chose on pages 3 and 4. Then describe the events that led you to apply to the Board and explain why you believe the landlord owes you money as a result of those events”.

The Tenant did not provide any other submissions other than what was provided in paragraph 2. There was nothing provided to the Board to show that his evidence and disclosure for the hearing contained all the necessary details.
The main issue is that the details are insufficient because they do not describe why the amounts the Tenant is claiming are contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’).

In the application the Tenant claims that the Landlord collected $498.00 in illegal rent for the period February 1, 2026, to February 28, 2026. The Tenant explains the reason for their claim as follows: due to an unfair charge and conflict, the Tenant no longer has enjoyment of the unit.

These details are insufficient as the T1 Form states that if the tenant is applying for Reason 1 (charged an illegal rent), the tenant is expected to explain why they believe the landlord charged an illegal rent and to show how they calculated the amount they were overcharged. In this case, there was no real substance or particulars provided other than what was alleged in the above paragraph.

I find that a responding party should not have to look for the supporting disclosure filed with the application to try to piece together the claims that are being made against them. Often times, some of the supporting evidence is irrelevant. In this case, the Landlord’s Agents pointed out that there was no supporting evidence, thus making it difficult for both the Landlord and the Board to understand what issues were being alleged.
There was no request by the Tenant for an adjournment of the matter to amend the T1 application to include the necessary details.
Therefore, the Tenant’s T1 application as-is does not contain basic details about the alleged tenant-related issues for a rebate of money.
Since there are insufficient particulars provided to the Landlord to which to respond to the allegations, the rebate issues cannot be adjudicated, and the Board cannot make any determinations.
For the reasons given above, the T1 Application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not meet his maintenance obligations. • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This application concerns a very short tenancy. The Tenant moved into the unit on February 15, 2025, but only stayed there for one night. On February 16, she moved to a hotel. She removed her belongings on February 28.

The Tenant brings this application alleging that she was induced to move because of issues with the rental unit. She seeks remedies including retroactive termination of the tenancy, return of the rent she paid, compensation for her expenses, and a rent abatement.

For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant decided move out without giving the Landlord a reasonable opportunity to address her complaints. She is not entitled to retroactive termination of the tenancy, or compensation for her expenses. She is entitled to some compensation for the issues, in the form of a small rent abatement.
The Landlord re-rented the unit as of April 1, 2025. He is permitted to retain funds to cover the rent to the March 31, 2025, and must return the remaining amounts the Tenant paid. Facts
The residential complex is a house divided into three rental units. The Tenant rented the main floor unit. The other two units were in the basement and on the upper floor.

The tenancy was to commence on February 15, 2025, at a monthly rent of $1,250.00, payable on the first of each month. Before signing the lease, the Tenant paid the Landlord $625.00 in pro-rated rent for February, a rent deposit of $1,250.00, and a key deposit of $25.00, in a lump sum of $1,900.00.

The Landlord’s property management company then told the Tenant that her payment was going to take too long to clear. It required her to pay by a different method prior to signing the lease. The Tenant then made a second payment of $1,900.00.

The Tenant then signed the lease, and moved into the unit on February 15, 2025. She immediately noticed three problems: there was noise from occupants of the upstairs unit; the toilet did not flush properly; and there was mold in the bathroom.

The Tenant also says that there were other maintenance issues – dust and debris on the vent covers, a crack in the bathroom wall, and detached molding in the bathroom – but these were minor and she never brought them to the Landlord’s attention. They have no bearing on the issues before me.

On February 16, the Tenant emailed the Landlord and the property management company. She said that she had heard loud noise from the upstairs unit throughout the first two days of her tenancy, including late at night and early in the morning. She said that if the noise were to continue for another day or two, she would like to agree to end the tenancy.

The Landlord did not immediately reply. The same day, the Tenant started staying in a hotel. She says that she could not stay in the unit because of the noise, because the toilet did not flush, and because of mold in the bathroom.

On February 18, the Tenant emailed the Landlord again. She said that the constant noise from the upstairs unit had been unbearable, and that the toilet was not working and there was mold in the bathroom. She said that she was moving to a hotel that day. What she told the Landlord was not accurate, since in fact she had moved to the hotel on February 16. It is not clear how she would have continued to hear noise on February 17 and 18, when she was no longer staying in the unit on those dates.
The parties then spoke by phone on February 18. They attempted to negotiate a solution, such as moving the Tenant to a different unit, but were unable to reach an agreement.

On February 21, the Tenant followed up by email, reiterating her complaints. The Landlord’s property management company then gave her notice that it would enter the unit immediately to assess the toilet, which it considered to be an emergency.
The property management company assessed the toilet on February 21, and scheduled and carried out a repair on February 25, with notice to the Tenant.

On February 28, the Tenant moved her belongings out of the unit and put them in storage. She gave the Landlord a 60-day notice to end her tenancy effective April 30, 2025. The Landlord returned her $25.00 key deposit.

The Tenant then made a complaint to the municipal bylaw enforcement office. An officer inspected the property and, on March 4, issued an order to repair the toilet, provide ventilation to the bathroom, and carry out other minor repairs. The Landlord complied with the order. The evidence does not establish when he complied, but the date does not matter since by then, the Tenant had already vacated the unit.
The Landlord testified that he re-rented the unit as of April 1, 2025. Issues

The Tenant argues that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment by failing to address the noise from the upstairs unit, and did not meet his maintenance obligations in respect of the toilet and the bathroom mold. She seeks a rent abatement for those contraventions.

More importantly, the Tenant argues that the contraventions reasonably induced her to vacate the unit. She seeks an order retroactively terminating her tenancy, which would also result in an order that the Landlord return the rent she paid. She also seeks compensation for her hotel, storage, and other expenses, and general damages for the impact that staying in a hotel had on her.
In the alternative, even if the tenancy is not retroactively terminated, the Tenant seeks the return of the extra amounts she paid at the start of the tenancy.

Finally, the Tenant argues that the property management company’s entry to assess the toilet on February 21 was contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). She seeks a rent abatement for the contravention.
I will consider each issue in turn. Noise complaint

The Tenant testified that when she viewed the unit, the property management company told her that the upstairs unit was not occupied, and was only used for storage. She testified that she would not have rented the unit if she had known that anyone would be living upstairs. She argues that she was induced by misrepresentation to enter into the tenancy.

I am not persuaded by that argument. Even if the Tenant was told that the upstairs unit was being used for storage when she viewed the premises, there is no evidence that the property management company promised her it would never be used as a residence. It was not reasonable for the Tenant to expect that a residential unit would be left unoccupied indefinitely. When renting in a building with multiple residential units, a person should expect that the other units will be used for their normal purpose.

Nonetheless, if the upstairs occupants were making excessive noise, the Landlord was obligated to address the issue. I am satisfied that he did not adequately respond to the [name] noise complaint. Her February 16 email described a severe, ongoing disruption. The Landlord should have addressed it urgently. Instead, he did not respond for two days.

The Landlord argues that he was not required to address the noise complaint, because the Tenant had not provided recordings to prove to him that the issue was genuine. There is no merit to that argument. The Landlord’s obligation was to investigate the complaint. In any case, the Landlord did not ask the Tenant for recordings of the noise. Instead, he simply did not respond to her email.

Given the uncontradicted evidence of the severity of the noise issue, I will award a rent abatement of 50% for February 16, 17, and 18. The total abatement comes to $61.64. I will not award the Tenant’s hotel expenses for those days, as I am not satisfied that it was reasonable for the Tenant to stay in a hotel simply because of noise.

The parties spoke by phone on February 18. The Landlord testified that the Tenant was adamant that she could not live in the unit, that she would move out, and that the tenancy should be terminated. On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that after one day in the unit, she was already “certain” that she could not live there. Her emails to the Landlord also indicate that she was only interested in terminating the tenancy.

The Landlord argues, and I agree, that in the circumstances he had no further obligation to address the Tenant’s noise complaints after the February 18 phone conversation. The Tenant was not living in the unit, and was not going to return even if the noise was resolved. I therefore find no substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment from February 19 onwards. Toilet
I accept the Tenant’s testimony that the toilet was unusable because it did not flush.

However, on the evidence before me, the Tenant did not tell the Landlord about the toilet issue until February 18. The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance, which did not include repairing an issue that he did not know about. His obligation to repair the toilet began on February 18.
The unit only had one toilet. In the normal course, the non-functioning toilet would have been an emergency. It would not have been reasonable for the Landlord to delay repairs until February 25.

However, as discussed above, on February 18 the Tenant told the Landlord that she would not, under any circumstances, move back into the unit. In my view, it was therefore not necessary for the Landlord to treat the non-functioning toilet as an emergency. He met his maintenance obligations by repairing the toilet on February 25. I do not find that he contravened the RTA in respect of the toilet. [name]
Similarly, the Tenant also did not tell the Landlord about the mold in the bathroom until February 18.

The Landlord was still obligated to investigate and remediate the mold, but I do not find that he did so on an unreasonable timeframe, given that the Tenant was not going to live in the unit anyway. Retroactive termination

I have found that the Landlord contravened his obligation to respond to the Tenant’s noise complaint from February 16 to 18. He did not contravene his obligations to rectify the toilet and mold issues. I must therefore consider whether the Landlord’s contravention in respect of the noise issue reasonably induced the Tenant to move within the meaning of section 31(2) of the RTA.

On the evidence before me, I am not persuaded that the Landlord’s slow response to the noise complaint reasonably induced the Tenant to move. Although the Landlord ought to have responded sooner, the slow response was not sufficient reason to end the tenancy. When the parties spoke on February 18, the Tenant had already decided to move, and did not give the Landlord any further opportunity to address the noise.
I will therefore not retroactively terminate the tenancy. This means that the tenancy ended on April 1, 2025 when the Landlord re-rented the unit.

Similarly, I will not award compensation for the Tenant’s hotel and storage expenses, related expenses, and damages. It was not reasonable for the Tenant to vacate the unit and stay in a hotel based on two days of noise, without giving the Landlord any further opportunity to address the noise. February 21 entry

The Landlord’s property management company entered the unit on February 21 to assess the toilet, without having given 24 hours’ notice under section 27(1) of the RTA. The Landlord argues that the property management company was permitted to enter without notice under section 26(1)(a) of the RTA, because the non-functioning toilet was an emergency.

In the normal course, I would agree that the non-functioning toilet would have been an emergency which would have warranted immediate entry under section 26(1)(a). However, as discussed above, in this case the Landlord did not treat the toilet issue as an emergency. Consequently, I find that entry was not permitted without 24 hours’ notice.

There is no evidence that the illegal entry had any impact on the Tenant, who was not staying in the unit at the time. I will award a nominal rent abatement of $5.00 for the illegal entry. Return of rent paid

The Tenant paid a key deposit of $25.00, rent of $625.00 for February 15-28, a rent deposit of $1,250.00, and an additional payment of $1,900.00. The Landlord has already returned the $25.00 key deposit.
After applying the rent abatements awarded above, the Tenant only owed $558.36 for February 15-28. The Landlord will be ordered to refund $66.64 in abatements.
The Landlord properly applied the rent deposit to the rent for March, 2025, the last month of the tenancy.
The final $1,900.00 is an overpayment which the Landlord must return.
Since the Tenant was partially successful in her application, she is also entitled to her filing fee of $48.00.
An order will issue accordingly.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,014.64, which represents a rent abatement, the return of overpaid rent, and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, CY submitted that the Landlord should not be permitted to rely on the documentary evidence they served and filed, because the documentary evidence was disclosed only the day before the hearing.
The Landlord’s position was that they were waiting to receive the Tenants’ evidence before providing their own disclosure, but the Tenants did not serve any disclosure.
The Tenants’ disclosure was filed on May 31, 2026, but CY acknowledged it was not served on the Landlord because the Tenants did not know this was required.
The Landlords did not open and view the Tenant’s disclosure before the hearing. [name] said they checked the Portal (‘TOP’) on May 1, 2026, but not thereafter.

The LTB’s Rules of Procedure require that if a party intends to rely on documentary evidence, it must be both served and filed at least 7 days before the hearing, or 5 days before the hearing if it is reply disclosure: rr. 19.1 & 19.2, LTB Rules of Procedure.

Since neither party complied with the requirements of the Rules of Procedure relative to disclosure of evidence, I declined to permit either party to rely on the documentary evidence they filed in TOP. Merits of the Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

This is the Tenants’ application, and they bear the burden of proof relative to each element of this legal test on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. [name], 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), paras 44-46.

I am satisfied that the Tenants were given an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, and that they moved out of the unit on March 27, 2025 because of that notice and a consent order on an application based on the N12 (LTB-L-085388-23). I find, however, that the Tenants did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that no person identified in subsection 48(1) of the Act moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.
CY said that after moving out of the unit, they visited the unit about once or twice per month, when they were in the area, to try to determine if the Landlord had moved in.

CY’s evidence was that the Tenants did not ever believe that the Landlord intended to move into the unit, and instead believe the Landlord’s intention was to sell or re-rent the unit to someone else. CY believes that there was a clear financial incentive for the Landlord to do this because the Tenants’ monthly rent was far below market rents at the time they moved out.

CY’s evidence was that after the Tenants moved out in late March 2025, there was a dumpster in the driveway from April to June 2025, leading the Tenant to believe the unit was being renovated. CY also said that there were no vehicles in the driveway when they attended the unit. CY said the Landlord’s family has two vehicles, and the garage would only fit one.

CY said that the only person they ever saw at the unit when they passed by after they moved out was the Landlord’s spouse by himself with a toolbox. CY said that the blinds were closed and there was no indication that anyone was living there.

CY said that they then started seeing a vehicle in the driveway that is not the Landlord’s vehicle. CY speculated that this may have been a new tenant’s vehicle or the vehicle of a neighbour renting a parking space.

While I did not permit either party to rely on the documentary evidence they filed for the reasons set out above, CY said the Tenants requested disclosure from the Landlord of reliable evidence to establish the Landlord moved into the unit. CY said that the Landlord filed personal records including a driver’s license and a notice of assessment from the Canada Revenue Agency, but said the Landlord could easily lie to obtain these documents. CY took issue, in particular, with the fact that the Landlord did not provide a copy of a gas bill in her name.
On cross-examination, CY acknowledged that they did not ever see any advertisement listing the unit for rent or sale, and did not ever see a sign at the house that the house was for rent or sale.

The Landlord’s evidence was that she did move into the unit, and that she started moving in the weekend after the Tenants moved out. The Landlord acknowledged there were some renovations taking place, but that she lived in the unit during the renovations. The Landlord said three bathrooms were renovated, one at a time.
The Landlord said she still lives in the unit. The Landlord turned her camera on during the hearing and CY acknowledged that it looked like the inside of the rental unit.
On cross-examination, the Landlord said that after she and her family moved into the unit, one vehicle was parked in the garage, and the other was parked in the driveway.

The Landlord’s evidence was cogent and consistent. That the Landlord was in the unit during the hearing, and that the Tenant acknowledged seeing a driver’s license and notice of assessment from the Landlord with the rental unit identified as the Landlord’s home address, supports the Landlord’s evidence that she moved into the unit after the Tenant moved out.

The Tenant’s evidence that this did not happen was circumstantial and speculative, based only on observations made by the Tenants once or twice per month when they happened to be in the area after having moved out. This is not sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did not move into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, particularly in the context of the evidence to the contrary, described above.
Because I am not satisfied that the Tenants have proven that the Landlord did not move into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants moved out, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord’s Agent advised he did not receive a copy of the application from the Board due to an incorrect address listed on the Tenant’s application which was later received, along with the disclosure, from the Tenants through WhatsApp. The Tenants also indicated they did not receive the Landlord’s disclosure. The Tenants were provided additional time to review the Landlords disclosure and additional time to prepare for the proceedings. The parties confirmed they were prepared to proceed. Adjournment Request mid-hearing

After the hearing started, approximately one hour into the proceedings the Tenants requested an adjournment so that they could better organize their documents because one of the Tenants had difficulty accessing their documents on the portal on the day of the hearing. I denied this request because only one of the two Tenants had difficulty accessing the portal, and the Tenants were already provided time to organise their documents prior to the hearing. It is the Tenants’ application, and the Tenants had ample time to organize and prepare for their case. T6 Application
This application involves a single-family dwelling containing three separate units. The Tenants reside in one of the basement units.
The monthly rent is $1,300.00.
The Tenants allege that the Landlord has failed to meet their maintenance obligation in relation to mice inside the residential unit, missing bug screens, and a missing fridge handle.

As explained below, on the evidence before the Board I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to reasonably respond to the mice issue and in relation to a missing bug screen in VS’s bedroom.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Mice issue

JS testified that she noticed a mouse in the unit in October 2025, which she immediately reported to the Landlord. She stated that the Landlord attended the unit at different times between October and mid-November to lay traps and fill possible entry points inside the residential unit. However, the Tenant said the mouse infestation became worse and by mid-November 2025 the Landlord started ignoring the WhatsApp communications.

The Tenants provided supporting evidence, including photos and videos showing mice caught in traps, a dead mouse in the ceiling air duct, a video of a mouse in their kitchen, items on top of the refrigerator, mice scratching behind the wall of the bedroom, and video of chewed areas outside a bedroom door. They also provided copies of their communications to the Landlord complaining about the issue.

VS testified that the mouse infestation was everywhere in the unit that they had to throw away food from their kitchen, would find mice droppings in their drawers and clothes, and mice in their beds. VS testified they did not feel comfortable in their home because of the mice.

The Landlord’s agent (SS) stated that he placed traps and sealed holes inside the residential unit prior to property standards involvement. He testified that he did all that he could and on February 3, 2026, he hired an exterminator and provided an image of an invoice attached to an email with Toronto Property Standards.

While neither Tenant provided evidence regarding property standards bylaw involvement the Landlord provided an 11-paged email chain with a Toronto Property Standards Officer with dates raging from February 6,2026 to May 6, 2026. The Landlord summarised each page indicating that he was working with the officer to rectify the mouse infestation.

While there was some question regarding the dates exterminators attended, both parties agreed that exterminators attended the rental unit in February 2026 and April 2026. It was provided that sometime in April, the exterminator sealed outside portions of the residential home and placed poison for the mice.
Both SS and the Tenants further agree that the mice infestation is improved greatly since May 2026, and, as of the date of the hearing, mice have not been seen in the unit for approximately a month.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that from mid-November 2025 to March 31, 2026, there was a mouse infestation in the residential unit that the Landlord failed to reasonable address. As such, I find the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations.

While the Landlord took some action early on, including setting traps, I find the Landlord’s efforts fell short of being reasonable. The evidence demonstrates a significant mouse presence in the unit in mid November 2025, and in my view the extent of the infestation by that point required more action that simply laying traps and removing dead mice.

Despite this, the Landlord failed to hire an exterminator to deal with the infestation for approximately 3 months. The Landlord’s own evidence shows as late as March 27, 2026, the Toronto property standards officer had emailed the Landlord stating “Please ensure a more aggressive approach is taken as the Tenant are regularly finding or coming across rodents daily. I do have an inspection sometime next week to ensure everything is done to address this matter.” I do not find the Landlords explanation regarding accumulated snow to be a reasonable explanation as to why they waited until 2026 to retain an exterminator despite that the Tenants had been informing the Landlord that the rodent issue had persisted.

Although it is inferred that an issue may continue past a period for abatement claimed in the Tenants application, I am satisfied that the Landlord took adequate steps to address the mouse issue in April 2026 with exterminator’s treatment. Therefore, I decline to order an ongoing abetment for the months of April and May 2026.
Given all of the above, I find that the landlord failed to reasonably respond to the Tenants complaints about mice in a timely and effective manner and the Tenants are entitled to compensation.
The Tenants requested a 100% abatement for the period beginning November 2025 and ending March 2026.

An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that rent is being paid for a bundle of goods and services and where a tenant does not receive 100% of what is being paid for then the tenant is entitled to an abatement of the rent proportional to the difference. Here, the Tenants are paying for a rental unit and the expectation that the Landlord will ensure the home is free from rodents.

Based on my knowledge of similar cases and considering that I accept the infestation had a significant impact on the Tenants’ enjoyment of the unit, I find a 25% abatement to be warranted for the period between November 15th, 2025, and March 31, 2026, which totals $1,474.00. due to the Landlord failure to effectively maintain the residential unit. [name] screens

The Tenants testified that when they moved into the property, screens were missing from both bedrooms as well as other windows in various rooms of the residential unit. The Tenants requested that the Landlord install the screens.

It was undisputed that JS’s bedroom screen was installed sometime in October 2025. I find that the Landlord installed a screen in the Tenant JS’s bedroom within a timely manner and therefore this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The screen for VS’s bedroom was not installed until sometime between February 6th and February 8, 2026. She stated that she was unable to use her window because of the missing screen, and I find that there was a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligation in failing to install a screen in VS’s bedroom. However, I find based on the evidence before me, that the impact was minimal and a minimal abatement of 2% is warranted.

The Tenants’ evidence regarding when the other screens were installed was vague, and they were unable to provide specific dates or time frames. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that they have established a breach in relation to the other screens in the residential unit.

I find the Tenants are entitled to an abatement of 2% for a period from October 1, 2025, to February 6, 2026, in the amount of $104.92, for the Landlord’s failure to provide a screen for the bedroom window. [name]

The Tenants testified that when they moved into the unit the refrigerator supplied by the landlord was missing the handle and that this issue still existed as of the hearing date. The Tenants lead no evidence of the impact this issue has or whether this causes the fridge to not function properly, such as the lack of handle made it difficult or impossible to open the fridge or resulted in an improper internal temperature.

SS testified he is actively seeking a replacement part for the handle but that the missing handle does not cause any deficiency in the intended function of the refrigerator. The Landlord’s Agent states he would be happy to replace the fridge if a replacement part is not available.
There is no evidence presented to warrant a breach due to the lack of the fridge handle. Therefore, the tenants claim regarding the fridge handle is dismissed. Request for General Compensation

The Tenants also requested $500.00 in their application for the Landlord’s failure to maintain the residential unit. Essentially, the Tenants are requesting compensation for the same issues in addition to the abatement. I find the abatement I ordered appropriately compensates the Tenants for the impact of the maintenance issue and decline to award the additional lump sum requested. The Tenants request for additional compensation is dismissed.
The Tenants paid an application filing fee of $48.00 and are entitled to reimbursement of the fee.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $1,626.92. This amount represents: • $1,474.00 rent abatement due to the mouse infestation • $104.92 for a rent abatement due to a missing bedroom screen • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 27, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing until there is no longer any money owing.

The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. 15 Grosvenor Street, [name] Toronto ON If you have any questions about this order, call [phone] or toll free at 1-[phone]. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
