issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenants testified that they were not joint tenants as this was a rooming house. The original lease was with 2 tenants, and then the 4 Tenants were assigned the lease agreement from them.

The Tenants testified that they all paid different rent amounts therefore it was not a joint tenancy. The Tenants submitted an excel spread sheet that named each Tenant and their portion of rent. The Tenant [name] (SS) testified they all moved in on different dates and vacated on different dates, so that is also why it is not a joint tenancy. SS testified that one person would pay the whole amount of the rent to the Landlord. When asked who told the Tenants how much each of them were required to pay, the Tenants said one of the prior tenants told them. [name] (VB) testified that he was originally responsible for $385.00 per month, but when tenants left the house in January 2025, he started paying $450.00 to make up the shortfall.

The Landlord testified that the original lease was a joint tenancy, and when the lease was assigned to the Tenants, it continued as a joint tenancy. The Landlord testified that the Tenants submitted a lease where SS signed but none of the other Tenants had, and testified the second lease submitted by the Tenants was not valid as the Tenants refused to sign, therefore the original lease governed the tenancy. The Landlord further testified that the Tenants moved into the rental unit before the prior tenants had vacated, which further demonstrates that the prior tenants lease governs the tenancy and this was an assignment of the prior lease. The Landlord testified that rent was a lump sum and he did not dictate how rent was paid; rather the Tenants decided amongst themselves their portions of the rent.

The lease does not explicitly state what kind of tenancy agreement was created, however it identifies that the tenants that signed the lease were collectively responsible for the monthly rent. In the circumstances, I am satisfied that this is a joint tenancy that was collectively entered into by the Landlord and the prior tenants, and this is the lease that was assigned to the Tenants. Therefore, the Tenants are joint tenants. Preliminary Issue: Amended Application not filed in accordance with [name]. The Tenants were given until October 17, 2025 to file their amended application. The Tenants filed their amended application on May 24, 2026. The Tenants testified they filed late because they were busy with other things. 6. As the Tenants did not file their amended application according to the Interim Order, I proceeded based on the original application only. Preliminary Issue: Landlord claimed the T2 and T6 application is too vague 7. The Landlord sought to have the T2 application be dismissed as there was no information contained in the application or remedy sought. The Tenants were supposed to amend the T2 application to address the deficiencies. As this was not done, the T2 application was dismissed. 8. The Landlord also sought to have the T6 application dismissed as there said the allegations were too vague, did not include specific dates and the Tenant sought a rent abatement under [name] 9 instead of Remedy 1. 9. I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (‘Ball v. Metro Capital’). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established. 10. The Court held in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” 11. In [name], the Court stated that the responding party must be able “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission… 12. While the Tenants’ application does not have specific dates, the application clearly identifies the issues that they were addressing with general time periods, and the remedy was identified as a rent abatement, despite not being addressed under [name] 1. I am satisfied that the Landlord was aware of the case that must be met as the allegation is that he did not address the ongoing cockroach infestation, denial of shower access, failure to install door locks, and the exterior was not maintained. The Landlord also submitted evidence in relation to the allegations in the application, which I find indicates he understood to case to be met and was able to respond. As I find that the Landlord was able to understand and to respond to the allegations, I find the application has sufficient particulars. Therefore, the application proceeded. T6 Application: 13. As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Cockroach Infestation: 14. The Tenants alleged that from September 9, 2024 to February 2025 there were cockroaches in the kitchen and bedrooms, and the Landlord failed to address the issue. 15. SS testified that he called the Landlord and texted him on approximately Sept 29, 2024 about the issue with the cockroaches. SS testified that there was no pest control and the issue continued until he vacated the rental unit. SS testified that the cockroaches were mostly in the kitchen, would fall onto his plate, and he got ill from the cockroaches, though no documentary evidence was provided to support this claim. SS testified he would stay with his family 3 days a week to be away from the cockroaches. 16. VB testified the cockroaches were an existing problem before them moved in as the Landlord had done pest control previously, and that the first round of pest control happened on December 12, 2024 after they complained on September 29, 2024. VB testified that the Landlord told them in February 2025 that they could not do anything further unless the Tenants vacated the rental unit, and the Landlord brought an N11 notice and an N9 notice for the Tenants to sign, which they declined. VB testified he was admitted to the hospital the first week of May 2025 for an appendix issue, but thought the issues were related to the cockroaches. 17. Tenant [name] (AM) testified that there were cockroaches in the unit from the day he moved into the rental unit and he would only cook food at his friend’s house due to the insects in the kitchen. AM testified that the LL treated the cockroaches in December 2024, but no further actions were taken, so the Tenants called bylaw. 18. The Landlord testified that he had pest control completed in May 2024, June 2024 and December 2024. The Landlord testified that the pest control report stated that there was not proper cleanliness in the kitchen and the insect shells were not being cleaned up, so the property would need to be vacated to fully address the issue. The report also stated that the activity in the basement kitchen was light and the activity in the kitchen on the main floor was light to medium. The Landlord provided the report as documentary evidence. The Landlord testified that normally a second round of pest control happens 8 days after the first treatment, however the Tenants said they were busy with school from December 12, 2024 until March 2025. 19. The Landlord testified a second round of pest control occurred on March 22, 2025 where it was reported the activity in the kitchen on the main floor was heavy and the activity in the basement kitchen was light to medium. The report stated that the cabinets in the kitchen were not emptied as instructed, there was rotten food in the kitchen, and a general issue with cleanliness. 20. The Landlord testified that a bylaw officer, [name], contacted him on February 5, 2025 about the complaint from the Tenants about the cockroaches. The Landlord testified he sent pictures from the March 22, 2025 treatment to show the state of the rental unit, and the bylaw officer responded on March 26, 2025 that the file would be closing as the Tenants were not doing the minimum required to ensure the treatments worked. The Landlord submitted a copy of the communication with [name] and the email closing the file. 21. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 22. Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s have proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that when notified of the issue he provided pest control treatments, and the Tenants did not provide any documentary evidence to support their claim that they repeatedly notified the Landlord of issues with cockroaches. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that the delay in the second treatment was due to the Tenants asking for a time that did not interfere with their education. I further accept the Landlord’s photo evidence and email from bylaw that the Tenants’ contributed to the pest control treatments not working by not maintaining proper cleanliness and failing to prepare the rental unit as required for treatment. 23. As I find that the Landlord did respond to the cockroach issue within a reasonable time period, and that the Tenants were the cause of the delay in the second treatment and the treatment not being effective, this claim must be dismissed. Issue 2: Exterior Maintenance 24. The Tenants testified that in October 2024 there were leaves on the lawn and the lawnmower provided by the Landlord did not work. The Tenants testified that this affected their studies, but nothing specific was identified as being impacted. VB testified that he hurt his back during the winter from shovelling the driveway after a snowstorm. VB testified he requested the Landlord to provide clarity on snow removal multiple times, though no documentary evidence was provided. 25. The Landlord testified that when he was notified about the lawnmower not working, he told the Tenants to purchase a lawnmower on Facebook Marketplace and he would reimburse them. The Landlord also testified he provided yard waste bags and tools to pick up the dead leaves. The Landlord did not provide documentary evidence of having told the Tenants he would reimburse the cost of a lawnmower. The Landlord testified that he hired a contractor twice for grass cutting and twice for snow removal after snowstorms in December 2024 and January 2025. 26. Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied the Tenants’ have proven that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. The allegations provided by the Tenants were vague and lacked details about what days they were referring to for the snow removal, and the Tenants did not provide any evidence on how the leaves and snow impacted them. As the Tenants did not provide evidence to establish how the Landlord failed to maintain the exterior of the rental unit, as I find the oral evidence was very limited and no documentary evidence was submitted, the claim must be dismissed. Issue 3: Door Locks 27. SS testified that there were no locks on the individual bedrooms, and an appraiser walked into his bedroom without notice. VB and AM testified that the bedroom doors had locks, however they were broken and did not actually lock, which was why they framed the issue as the doors did not have locks. VB testified they notified the Landlord of the issue in October 2024 after the appraiser walked into their bedroom without notice. 28. The Landlord testified that the rooms had a simple lock where the bedrooms could be locked from the inside not the outside. The Landlord testified that the Tenants requested he change the locks to ones that had a key on the door. 29. Based on the evidence provided by both parties, I am satisfied that the doors did have locks, though they were not the type of locks that the Tenants preferred. I find that the Tenants have not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the unit. There is no requirement that the Landlord must provide key locks to each bedroom in the rental unit, and while the Tenants stated the locks were broken, they did not provide any evidence to support this allegation. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the locks worked from the inside of the room, and I find that the Tenants have not proven the locks did not work, only that they were not the type of lock that they wanted. As I find that there was no breach in the Landlord’s maintenance obligations, this claim must be dismissed. Issue 4: Shower was Unusable 30. SS testified that from December 21, 2024 to January 7, 2025 he could not use the shower and had to get a gym membership to shower. SS testified that the shower head was dripping. VB testified that they notified the Landlord in mid October that the shower head was dripping and falling outside of the shower, but the Landlord did not respond to the notification. VB testified he did not have access to the shower and bathroom for 20 days. VB testified he asked for the Landlord to ask the basement tenants to use their bathroom or to have them stay in a hotel. The Tenants testified that work started on December 21, 2024 and was completed on January 7, 2025. 31. The Landlord testified that he was notified by AM that the shower head was leaking and spilling over the sides of the shower. The Landlord testified he was working with a contractor and said the repairs would take 2 weeks, however, neither the upstairs Tenants not the tenants in the basement unit notified the Landlord when the issue started, so the damage was more extensive than he thought. The Landlord testified he notified the Tenants on December 20, 2024 that the work would start at the end of December 2024 and the shower area would not be available for approximately 10 days. The Landlord testified that his contractor notified him that the work started in the shower area on December 31, 2024 and the work was finished by January 6, 2025, and the contractor confirmed that the Tenants had been notified prior to January 8, 2025. The Landlord submitted the text messages with the contractor as documentary evidence. 32. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 33. Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied that the Tenants’ have proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he was notified around mid October of the issue, and while the shower head was leaking until the flooring was fixed in December 2024, the Tenants still had full use of the bathroom and there was no impact identified. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenants only had restricted access to the shower in the bathroom from December 31, 2024 to January 6, 2025, a total of 7 days, not the 20 days as claimed by the Tenants. The Landlord’s evidence was supported through the text messages from the contractor submitted as documentary evidence that outlined the day work started and the day it was finished. I find that the Landlord responded to the maintenance issue within a reasonable period of time, and the Tenants were impacted for a maximum of 1 week while the issue was fixed. As the Landlord acted within a reasonable period of time, I am satisfied that they did not breach their maintenance obligations. As a result, the claim must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants application be dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants claimed the Landlord illegally increased the rent from $1,296.00 to $1,727.00 as of October 1, 2025. The Tenants paid the increased rent for the period starting of October 1, 2025, to March 1, 2026. In total the Tenants sought the return of $2,586.00 as this represents the excess rent the Tenants believed they paid.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2025, and are still in possession of the rental unit. [name] (“HRO”) represented all the Tenants and testified the monthly rent was increased within the first twelve months of the tenancy. Entered into evidence was a copy of the tenancy agreement dated January 1, 2025, which shows that the tenancy was to commence on April 1, 2025, and that it was to be for a one-year term ending March 31, 2026.

HRO further testified that when the Tenants received the notice of rent increase from the Landlord, the Tenants did not understand why there was an increase in rent since the tenancy had only begun a few months prior. HRO stated there was no reason as to why the rent was increased.

With respect to the Tenants’ claim that the Landlord collected rent illegally, the Landlord’s Agent provided viva voce evidence and testified that the unit is under a regional rent assistance program. According to the criteria of the program, the rent for the unit may increase when there is a change in the household composition, and that if there is a change, it must be reported by the Tenants within thirty days of the change.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that the Tenants’ rent was increased as HRO was added to the household composition effective April 1, 2025. This change in the household composition for the rental unit was the Landlord’s reason for serving notice that the rent increasing to$1,727.00.

The Landlord’s Agent further testified that the Landlord is obligated to complete annual renewals every year for this month of October, and this mandates the use of most recent income tax returns. The renewals are based on the Tenants’ income and their continued qualification for the rental price of the unit. As such, it was the Landlord Agent’s testimony that due to a new lease being created in April 2025, and there was an interim review, the annual review was completed in October 2025.
The Tenant opted not to cross-examine the Landlord’s Agent. Analysis
The Tenants led insufficient evidence to prove the allegations contained in the application.

The Tenants led no supplemental or documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s claim that there is no legal basis for the increase in rent. HRO’s testimony was simply that due to there being a lease for twelve months, the rental amount was locked in for that year. Nothing other than this assertion by HRO was presented at the hearing for the Board to consider.

The Tenants also led insufficient evidence regarding any steps the Tenants took to attempt to retrieve the alleged illegal rent collection from any time during the tenancy to the date of the hearing. In this regard, the Landlord’s Agent testified and provided credible and credible testimony as to why the rent was increased.

The Landlord’s Agent presented the argument that the unit is exempt from certain rules related to rent in the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) and do not apply. This is stated in various sections of the tenancy agreement that was entered into evidence. 1.01 You acknowledge that the Unit is subsidized and was developed under the Canada-Ontario Affordable Housing Program (the "AHP Program"), and/or the Investment in Affordable Housing Program (the "IAH Program") an eligible initiative, and is subject to a housing services agreement with The Regional Municipality of York (the "Region Agreement"), with the result that the Unit is exempt from specific provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"). Schedule B-2 A The Region provides funding to the Housing Provider through the Rent Assistance Program (the "Program") to enable the Housing Provider to make some apartments more affordable for lower income tenants. The Housing Provider must follow the Program rules as set out in an agreement with the Region and in the Program guidelines as may be amended from time to time without notice to the Tenants. Tenants participating in the Program receive a rent assistance benefit (the "Rent Benefit") based on the household's total gross income, calculated according to the Program guidelines as may be amended from time to time without notice to the Tenants. The Rent Benefit is paid by the Region to the Housing Provider. The Rent Benefit will be recalculated every year based on the updated financial and household information that the Tenant(s) must provide to the Housing Provider. The Tenant(s) is/are responsible to pay the Housing Provider an amount equal to the difference between the market rent and the Rent Benefit (the "Tenant Contribution"). The Tenant Contribution will be adjusted every year to reflect the new Rent Benefit amount. Schedule B-2 D (1) Under the terms of the Lease, the Tenant(s) are always responsible to pay the market rent owing for the Rented Apartment and all rent increases permitted by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. As long as the [name] is eligible to receive a Rent Benefit, the Tenant(s) is only required to pay the Housing Provider the Tenant Contribution which is the difference between the market rent and the Rent Benefit. The Region will pay the balance. The Tenant(s) will pay the Housing Provider the Tenant Contribution on or before the first day of each month. Schedule B-2 D (2) In the event that the [name] is no longer eligible to receive a Rent Benefit the Tenant(s) must pay market rent to the Landlord. Schedule B-2 D (4) If the Tenant(s) want someone else to move into the Rented Apartment: the Tenant(s) will request and receive the Housing Provider's approval of the new person BEFORE that person moves in; and the Tenant(s) will give the Housing Provider eligibility and income information and supporting documents for the new person; and every adult who lives in the apartment will sign a new [name]; and the Tenant(s) will pay the new Tenant Contribution based on a new Rent Benefit calculation.

While s.119 of the Act states that a Landlord cannot increase the rent until at least 12 months have elapsed since the day the rental unit was first rented to the tenant, there is evidence that s.7(2) of the Act, which is an exemption to s.119, applies in this case. Therefore, I find that the rental unit in this case falls within this provision as the Tenants are occupying a rental unit and pays rent in an amount geared-to-income due to public funding.

In this case, the onus is on the Tenants to prove on a balance of probabilities that there was illegal rent collected by the Landlord. Due to insufficient evidence, I find the Tenants did not meet their onus. Therefore, this application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenants the amount set out below. Agreed Statement of Facts

At the hearing, the parties agreed that: • the tenancy commenced October 1, 2023; • the parties signed a standard form lease, with an expiration date of September 30, 2024; • the lawful rent was $1,825.00; • the Tenants moved out May 1, 2024.
I will further note that the Landlords did not serve a termination notice to the Tenants and the Tenants did not give proper notice to the Landlords that they were moving out. The Applications
The Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications are predicated on the same facts and seek essentially identical remedies and were considered together.

The Tenants filed their applications on April 2, 2024 and claims that the Landlords’ breached s.20 of the Act related to the Landlords’ maintenance obligations and s.22 of the Act related to substantial interference with respect to: • stairs to the parking area; • washing machine; • leak and bathroom light; • floors; • asbestos
The rental unit is a two bedroom apartment in a complex with six units.
The Tenants filed a request to amend the applications and the Landlords’ representative confirmed receipt of the amendment requests.
The Tenants’ disclosure includes: Board forms, tenancy agreements, maintenance requests, photographs and various communications (DOC8335313 – pgs. 60,63, 65-70, 72-77, 83-85,87,89, 91-95, 100-108).
The Landlords’ disclosure includes: lease agreement, work order, reports and various communications (DOC8359645 – pgs. 40-43, 45-48,50-140, 149-151, 153, 156,159-160, 228-246)

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The Tenants’ Evidence The Stairs:

The Tenant testified that on October 11, 2023, they submitted a request through the property management reporting system that the stairs to the parking area and main entrance for the Tenants were uneven and dangerous. They received a response that the issue would be addressed in 10 to 12 days.

The Tenant reviewed three photographs she took on October 11, 2023, February 16, 2024 and March 2, 2024, which showed the stairs in disrepair and uneven. She said this was dangerous for her family including two minor children.

The Tenant said that she followed up with [name], who is head of maintenance on several occasions and nothing was done. In fact, the Tenant noted that the maintenance request they had filed on October 11, 2023 was marked as closed on the same day. To the date they moved out, the stairs had not been repaired.

The Landlord’s representative called Alysia Hyde (AH) to testify for the Landlords. She is the current [name] but was not in the role at the material times of this application. Her knowledge was limited to reviewing and recounting various reports and communications but has no first hand knowledge of the issues.

With respect to the stairs, AH had little to contribute as to if the Tenants’ complaint was reasonably responded to and if the stairs had been repaired during their tenancy. She said she believed the stairs were repaired but had no further evidence. The Washing Machine:

It was the Tenants’ evidence that they reported issues related to the washing machine to the Landlord via telephone and filing a maintenance request on January 12, 2024. The Landlord’s maintenance staff attended the unit on January 15, 2024 and later reported that someone would be in touch later in the week to rectify the issue. There was some back and forth communication and on January 23, 2024, the Tenants were advised that a replacement part had been order and later told there was some delay with the part. On February 6, 2024 the Tenants were advised that the washing machine would be replaced. To the date they moved out, the washing machine had not been replaced. As a result, the Tenants had the inconvenience of doing laundry offsite and at an expense of around $295.00.
AH did not lead any evidence that the washing machine had been replaced during the tenancy. She said that it can take time in the [name] area to replace appliances. The Water Leak:

On January 26, 2024, the Tenants reported a leak coming from the ceiling of the bathroom and an electrical issue to the Landlord’s emergency line. [name] attended the unit a short time later and said the leak was a result of a hole in the roof. [name] advised that the electrical could not be fixed until January 29, 2024. The matter was not inspected and [name] told the Tenants to “just flip the breaker.” The Tenant said that when she plugged things into the receptacle, it would crackle and pop. It made her nervous so she did not use the plug in the bathroom. To the date they moved out, the matter was not attended to by the Landlord.

AH did not lead any evidence that the electrical issue in the rental unit had been attended to by the Landlord. While they may have been working on the reparations to the roof, AH did not state that the records show the reported electrical issue was reasonably investigated by the Landlord. The Flooring:

The Tenant said that, on February 1, 2024, the Tenants advised [name] while he was at the rental unit, that the flooring in the unit was lifting. The Tenant reviewed various photographs to support their claim. On February 12, 2024, the Tenants were advised that a contractor had been contacted about the flooring issue. To the date the Tenants vacated, no further steps were taken by the Landlord with respect to the flooring.
AH led no evidence that the floor issue had been reasonably attended to by the Landlord. They contacted the insurance company who investigated the issue. The Asbestos Issue:

On February 13, 2024, the Tenants were advised that the Landlords’ insurance company was performing building inspections related to air quality testing. On February 17, 2024, they received a notice to vacation due to “traces of asbestos”.

The Tenants temporarily vacated on the same day and returned within 48 hours. On February 19, 2024, while retrieving personal items at the rental unit, they were advised by a contractor that there was no asbestos in their unit and it was safe for them to return. The Tenants believed this information to have come from a “trustworthy” source so they returned to the unit on February 19, 2024 and remained there until they moved out.

The Tenant said that the Landlord continued to issue notices to vacate stating the presence of asbestos. However, they opted to remain in the unit based on the trusted information from the contractor. Their repeated attempts to get information from the Landlord related to a status update and information for the Tenants’ insurance went unanswered by the Landlord.

While AH provided testimony related to the impact of asbestos and the safety of tenants based on her experience, this testimony had little value to the issue at hand. There was no dispute that the Tenants’ unit was not impacted by any traces of asbestos in the residential complex. The Tenants acknowledged this and stayed in the unit, notwithstanding the numerous notices to vacate.

In cross examination, the Landlords’ representative requested to introduce a document from the Tenants’ disclosure that was not led during examination in chief. The Tenants’ representative opposed the request. Ultimately, I denied the submission as it was unnecessary to further explore the safety of the unit and the release of reports based on the Tenant’s submission that they did not believe the unit to be unsafe. No further exploration on this matter was necessary. Law and Analysis

Pursuant to s. 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 22 of the Act states that “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

As noted above, the Tenants alleged identical facts in both the T2 and the T6 applications. With the exception of the asbestos issue, the remedies claimed by the Tenants more appropriately lie in the T6 application and the remedies of the Tenants will be addressed in the T6 application.

On a balance of probabilities means the applicant, in this case the Tenants must show that their version of events is the more probable and should succeed. Saying something is proven on a balance of probabilities simply means that it is more likely than not to have occurred. It means that it is probable, i.e., the probability that some event happened is more than 50%--indeed, 50.1% is sufficient. In all cases, the decision maker must weigh up the evidence and decide which version is most probably true. Consequently, the real truth may never be known. All that can be done is to decide which of the parties has presented the most probable version.

In this case, I am satisfied that the Landlord is in breach of their obligations under s.20 of the Act related to the stairs, washing machine, bathroom electrical and floors. The Landlord was unsuccessful in challenging the Tenants’ claims that the issues were reported and not attended to. The Tenants’ evidence supports their claim that to the date they vacated, the matters were not resolved by the Landlord.

While the Landlord takes the position that they did reasonably respond to the various issues and further investigation, remediation and/or replacement was underway, I find they failed provide sufficient evidence to support this claim.
With respect to the stairs, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not attend to the issue and repair the stairs and they remained in disrepair to the date the Tenants vacated.

With respect to the electrical issue, while the Landlord undertook to repair the roof, the Landlord led insufficient evidence that they attended to the concerns related to the electrical issue and this was not investigated and/or repaired to the date the Tenant’s vacated. Telling the Tenant’s to “flip the breaker” does not constitute a proper investigation.

With respect to the floors, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not reasonably address the Tenants’ complaint of the unsafe nature of the flooring throughout the rental unit to the date the Tenants vacated.

With respect to the washing machine, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenants; complaints in a reasonable manner. I find it unlikely that it takes almost four months to either repair or replace an appliance. The Landlord did not provide any other steps taken to remedy the issue in a timely manner.

I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached either s.20 or s.22 of the Act with respect to the claims related to asbestos. I say this for the following reasons. The evidence of both parties shows that the rental unit was not subject to any issues related to asbestos and what may have been present in the residential complex was at minimal and did not represent a health risk to the Tenants. It was the Tenant’s own testimony that they moved back into the rental unit based and the “trustworthy” account of the contractor and did not feel unsafe in doing so. So, the Tenants have not satisfied the test for s.20 of the Act.

Considered thru the lens of substantial interference, I cannot find that the Landlord is in breach under s.22 of the Act. The Tenants willingly moved back into the unit, stating their belief that it was not unsafe. While they may have found the numerous notices to vacate a nuisance, there is insufficient evidence to support the proposition that this substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. They received the notices and chose to disregard them, believing that their safety was not at risk. In my view, the actions of the Tenants suggest that the conduct of the Landlord was not “substantial” as contemplated by the Act.
The Tenant, herself, stated that their choice to unilaterally terminate the tenancy was related to the unresolved maintenance claim and not for their safety concerns.

Pursuant to subsection 37(1), a tenancy may only be terminated in accordance with the Act. In other words, one party cannot unilaterally terminate a tenancy. In this instance, the tenancy can only be terminated three ways: a valid 60-day written given by tenant with a termination date being the last day of the lease, an agreement by the parties to terminate or an order of the Board. Neither of these things occurred.

What that means is that to claim rent differential and moving costs, the Board must be satisfied that it was the conduct of the Landlord that induced the Tenants to terminate their lease earlier that permissible.
I am not persuaded that this is what occurred here. I say this because, the Tenant confirmed that they contemplated ending their tenancy as early as March 7, 2024.

I appreciate that the Tenants were frustrated by the Landlord’s poor communication and slow response to repair the various issues and supply reports. However, I do not find the issues complained of would warrant an early termination of the tenancy. Rather, the Tenants made a choice to end their lease early and without proper notice. In this case, it would be inappropriate to award costs related to their moving expenses and difference in rent.
I also find that the remedies awarded below reasonably compensate the Tenants under s.20 of the Act and s.22 related to the interference they endured as a result of the Landlord’s breaches.

In making this finding, I considered Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, where the Court of Appeal held that a landlord will not be held liable for breaching its maintenance obligations if it responds to a maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances.
For the reasons give above, I do not find that the Landlord responded reasonably when addressing the Tenants’ maintenance issues. Remedies
As the tenancy terminated, some of the requested remedies are moot.
The Tenants did not provide receipts related to the costs claimed related to laundry expenses and a remedy will not be awarded.

The Tenants seek a 60% rent abatement in the amount of $7,240.84 related to the unresolved maintenance issues from October 11, 2023 to April 30, 2024. I find it would be inappropriate to award this remedy as a whole as some of the breaches occurred after October 11, 2023. For that reason, I find it appropriate to award the following. The Stairs:

The Tenants said that the stairs were in disrepair and posed a safety hazard from October 11, 2023 to April 30, 2024. The filed required was closed by the Landlord on the same date without addressing the issue. Based on my knowledge of similar like cases, I am satisfied that a reasonable abatement would be 15% for the period claimed. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $1,818.00. $1,825.00 x 12/365 = $60.00 per [name] 15% x 202 days = $1,818.00 The Washing Machine:

The Tenant said that they had to use off site laundry service which was costly and inconvenient. Based on my knowledge of similar like cases, I am satisfied that a reasonable rent abetment would be 15% for the period claimed, January 12, 2024 to April 30, 2024 (109 days). The total amount the Landlord will be ordered to pay is $981.00. The Floors:

The Tenants said they were concerned for the safety of their minor children as a result of the condition of the floors in the rental unit. Based on my knowledge of similar like cases, I am satisfied that a reasonable abatement would be 15% for the period claimed, February 1, 2024 to April 30, 2024 (89 days). The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $801.00. The Electrical Issue:

When the Tenant heard crackling and popping sounds from the bathroom plug, they were concerned for their safety and did not use the plug. While it may have been somewhat of a convenience, I am satisfied that a reasonable remedy would be a 5% abatement for the period claimed, January 26, 2024 to April 30, 2024 (95 days). The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $285.00.
Having been successful with their application, the Tenants are entitled to costs related to the filing fee.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants are $3,933.00. This amount represents: • $3,885.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 7, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 7, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $5,257.20.

The Tenant testified that he and his family moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2023, and prior to moving into the rental unit he paid the Landlord a last month rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $2,750.00 on June 20, 2023.

The Tenant further testified that on March 6, 2026 the Sheriff attended at the rental unit to enforce a Writ of Possession issued under file #CV-25-00001265-0000 on December 9, 2025. A copy of the Notice of Vacant Possession was entered into evidence at the hearing of the matter.
The Tenant states that he and his family vacated the rental unit on March 6, 2025, as a result of the [name]’s attendance and Notice of Vacant Possession.
The Tenant believes that the Writ of Possession was due to the Landlord’s failure to pay the mortgage on the property.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Amendment to Application

At the hearing the Tenant sought to amend the application to include a claim that the Landlord has illegally collected and retained a key deposit, and that the Landlord failed to return a portion of rent for March, 2026 after the Tenant’s were forced to vacate the rental unit due to the Sheriff’s enforcement of a Writ of Possession.

Rule 15.4 of the LTB Rules of Procedure address requests to amend an application at a hearing stating: The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

In the circumstances I am satisfied that the amendment sought is an appropriate request, it would not prejudice the Landlord and the amendment is consistent with a fair an expeditious proceeding. Additionally the Landlord failed to attend the hearing to raise any opposition to the amendment request. As such the request to amend shall be granted. Return of Key Deposit
The Tenant testified that in addition to paying the Landlord a last month rent deposit on June 20, 2023 he also paid a key deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $250.00.

The Tenants states that when he vacated the rental unit on March 6, 2026, as a result of the Sheriff enforcing the Writ of Possession he left the keys in the unit. The Landlord did not return the key deposit to the Tenants after the end of the tenancy.

Section 134(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; …
Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the ‘Regulation’) provides a list if exemptions to Rule 134(1) which includes a refundable key deposit.

The Regulation is clear that a key deposit is refundable. Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied that the Landlord did not return the key deposit to the Tenant. Retention of Rent after the tenancy ended

The Tenant testified that rent for the month of March, 2026 in the amount of $2,800.00 had been paid to the Landlord and when the Sheriff enforced the Writ of Possession on March 6, 2026 the Landlord retained the balance of March’s rent.
The Tenant submits that the Landlord ought to have returned the balance of March’s rent from March 7 to March 31, 2026 to the Tenant as the tenancy had ended.

Pursuant to Section 135 of the Act: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied that the Landlord retained money in contravention of the Act.
The Tenant is entitled to the return of rent paid and retained by the Landlord after the tenancy ended for the period of March 7, 2026 to March 31, 2026 being 24 days.
Based on the monthly rent of $2,800.00 the daily rent is $92.05. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,800.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenant is entitled to $2,209.20 being $92.05 x 24.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,257.20. This amount represents: • $2,750.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • $250.00 for a key deposit not returned; • $2,209.20 for money illegally retained; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved one of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $106.38 in rent abatement.
The rental unit is a one-bedroom unit in a shared two-bedroom rental home. The tenancy commenced on October 30, 2021, and ended on July 29, 2024.
The parties gave evidence regarding the following issues raised in the application: Illegal Entry; Bedbug Infestation
The Tenant testified that on June 21, 2024, the Landlord sent an email informing him about an intended entry into the rental unit for an inspection on June 24, 2024.

The Landlord stated in the email: ‘This email is to notify you that on Monday between 2-4 pm pest control company will be visiting the unit and will probably need to access your room and treat the rest of the apartment’.

According to the Tenant, it was not a proper notice, and the Landlord did not provide any information on the treatment process. The Landlord also repeatedly refused to provide the name of the pest control company when the Tenant requested it.

On June 24, 2024, the pest control technician arrived at the unit and refused to identify himself. He did not inspect the unit prior to administering harsh chemicals but simply told the Tenant that he could not return to the unit until approximately 7:00 p.m. The Tenant claimed that the treatment was ineffective because he found bedbugs in the rental home later that day, and the next.

On June 27, 2024, the Tenant received an email from the Landlord about an upcoming follow up treatment on July 5, 2024, between 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m. The Tenant stated that the email did not provide details such as information on the identity of the pest control company, and how to prepare for the treatment.

On July 5, 2024 , the pest control technician identified himself as [name] n from China. The Tenant stated that he found the treatment ineffective and although he also stated that he informed the Landlord about the ineffective treatment on July 10, 2024, no documentary evidence was provided to substantiate the claim. The Tenant did provide a picture of an alleged bedbug taken between July 15, 2024, and July 20, 2024.

The Landlord testified that he had the unit treated on June 24, 2024, and July 5, 2024, to rid it of bedbugs and hired a pest control company for that purpose on the recommendation of the building’s condominium management. The Landlord denied receiving any further complaints from the Tenant.

Section 27 (1) of the Act provides: Entry with notice 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. Contents of notice (3) The written notice under subsection (1) or (2) shall specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord gave the Tenant written Notices of Entry on June 21, 2024, and June 27, 2024 , both more than 24 hours before the intended time of entry. The notices advised the Tenant that a pest control company would be attending the unit and specified a reasonable time frame for the treatment. I am satisfied that the notices complied with the requirements set out in sections 27(1) and 27(2) of the Act. The Landlord neither served defective Notices of Entry nor entered the rental unit unlawfully.

Regarding the bedbug infestation, section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd ., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence, there was no dispute that the unit was infested with bedbugs, and that the Landlord arranged for the unit to be treated on two separate occasions. Although the Tenant questioned whether [name] from China was employed by a certified pest control company, the Landlord argued that he was. Whether or not the technician was certified, the evidence indicates that the bedbugs were eradicated from the unit following the second treatment as the Tenant did not make any further written complaints to the Landlord.

In addition, bedbug treatments are usually repeated multiple times and the date of the first treatment or the day after , would be too premature to assess the effectiveness of the treatment. Although the Tenant provided a picture of what was alleged to be a bedbug, taken between July 15, 2024, and July 20, 2024, the absence of a formal complaint to the Landlord undermines the claim that the infestation continued. I am not satisfied that the bedbug activities continued in the rental unit after July 5, 2024. [name]

The Tenant alleged that he was illegally locked out of the rental unit on June 28, 2024. The rental unit door has a keypad entry system which requires a passcode for entry. In an email sent to the Landlord on the same date, the Tenant requested the password, stating that the keypad was either changed or was broken and needs repair. The Landlord responded that he did not change the pa sscode. The parties subsequently realized that the batteries were depleted, and at the instruction of the Landlord, were replaced by another resident that day.

I find the Tenant’s characterization of th e problem as an illegal lockout misleading and unsupported by the evidence. The evidence demonstrates that the depleted battery caused the keypad to malfunction, and that the Tenant was allowed into the rental unit by another resident prior to the battery change. There was no evidence to show that the Landlord denied the Tenant entry into the rental home or changed the locks or passcode.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex. Internet and Lights

The Tenant testified that on April 7, 2024, he informed the Landlord that there was no internet connection in the rental home, and there was a problem with the lights in his unit. The Tenant contacted the city over the issue between April 8, 2024, and April 12, 2024 , because the Landlord did not appear ready to fix it.
On April 24, 2024, the Landlord contacted the Tenant to inquire about the issue so he could send an electrician to fix it. The issue was subsequently resolved on May 3, 2024.

The Landlord testified that while there was originally a problem with the electrical outlet which the internet modem was connected to, the internet service was immediately restored when a resident connected the modem to a different electrical outlet. As for the lights in the rental unit, the Landlord denied there was a problem with it because he never had to repair it.
On cross-examination, the Landlord acknowledged that he sent an email to the Tenant on May 2, 2024, regarding entry into the unit by an electrician on May 3, 2024.

Based on all the evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the issue with the internet was resolved on April 7, 2024, when a resident relocated the modem to a different out let. However, the Tenant continued to experience the light problem in his unit, and the Landlord did not send an electrician to investigate or resolve the issue until May 3, 2024. Given the unnecessary delay in addressing the problem, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant.
The lawful monthly rent was $800.00.

The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant a rent abatement equal to 15% of the daily rent, in the amount of $106.38, for the period from April 7, 2024, to May 3, 2024. The daily rent for the rental unit was $26.30, resulting in a daily abatement of $3.94. The interruption lasted 27 days, calculated as $3.94 x 27 days, for a total abatement of $106.38. Harassment

The Tenant testified that on [name] ly 15, 2024, another resident confronted him in the laundry room, kicked the laundry room door, and threatened him with a knife. The Tenant contacted the police who instructed the resident to stay away from the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that the police contacted him over the incident and he in turn contacted the other resident to understand what occurred. The Landlord did not contact the Tenant because they had a strained relationship.

While the Landlord’s evidence demonstrated a clear preference for the other resident and showed a limited understanding o f his responsibility to address and resolve disputes between tenants, I am not satisfied that the Landlord harassed, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. The police resolved the dispute on July 15, 2024 , and the Tenant did not report any further incidents.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $106.38 for a rent abatement.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The residential unit includes one commercial unit and 6 separate, residential units. The Tenant resided in Unit #2 which was an apartment directly above the commercial store and he resided there since 2019.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Evidence of [name] (NS)

NS testified that he was given an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on January 25 or 26 of 2025 and it had a termination date of March 31, 2025. He stated that the Landlord told him that she was going to move into his unit.

NS stated that he did not have a good relationship with the Landlord because he had too many visitors, he was letting people in at night and that the Landlord called the police about potential drug dealing in the rental unit. He admitted that he did not remember that time period well as he was drunk and high most of the time.

The Tenant stated that he was in an alcohol and drug treatment centre when he received the N12 notice as he had been coughing up blood and was not well. He stated that the timing was fine because he had to get himself healthy and he was getting help.

NS stated that he continued to reside in the treatment centre on March 31, 2025 and his mother had arranged to have all of his possessions removed from the rental unit. He stated that he has been in another men’s residential treatment facility for 3 months now and will continue to reside there for a further 9 months.

The Tenant does not believe that the Landlord moved into his rental unit because a friend of his, who resides in Unit #1 of the same building, told him on January 19, 2026 that the Landlord did not move into his unit. NS stated that his friend told him that he has walked past Unit #1 and no one is residing there.

The Tenant is very stressed knowing that he does not have a home to return to and he suffers from depression with one suicide attempt. He is seeking $7,800.00 in rent abatement, $5,000.00 in compensation and that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Evidence of Priscilla [name] (PL)

PL testified that she is the daughter of the Landlord and that her mother is elderly and not well which is why she is unable to attend the hearing. She stated that her 76-year-old mother decided to move into the Tenant’s unit so that she would have easy access to the commercial store where she worked every day. PL stated that her mother and father resided in a residential house a few miles away from the downtown business centre where the residential complex was located.

Ms. [name]name] stated that her mother walked everywhere as she was fearful of driving and after working in the store every day, she would walk back to her residence at the end of the day. She said that her mother would often receive calls from her vendors who required access to the store after hours and she would have to walk back to the store multiple times in a day. She stated that she spoke to her mother about this decision and felt that it made sense in the situation.

PL stated that the Landlord moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2025 and resided in the unit during the week and went back to her residence on the weekends to care for her father. The Landlord’s daughter stated that she continued residing in the unit during the week until the end of April of 2026. PL stated that her father died on April 8, 2026 and that her mother moved all of her belongings out of the rental unit by April 30, 2026.

In cross-examination, the Landlord’s daughter was asked about the frequency of her mother’s occupancy at the rental unit and she responded that during the winter, her mother would stay at the rental unit a minimum of 3-4 nights a week. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. I am not persuaded that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant’s testimony was vague and he confirmed that his memory was not clear due to his alcohol and drug addiction issues. NS stated that on January 19, 2026, he spoke to a neighbour who resides in Unit #1 of the same building and that neighbour told him that he does not believe that the Landlord moved into the rental unit. The neighbour did not attend as a witness to provide direct evidence of what he saw when he walked past Unit #2 and no evidence was produced to suggest how many times that he walked past this unit’s door.
This is the Tenant’s application and he has the onus of providing sufficient information to convince me on a balance of probabilities that his story is more believable than the Landlord’s story.
The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Lascelles, [name] [name], [name] [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') entered the rental unit illegally., substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $8,953.65. [name]
The Tenant testified that she moved into the unit on April 1, 2022, and had vacated the unit as of April 30, 2023. The lease signed by both parties was entered into evidence.
The Tenant testified that in February of 2023, the Landlords had asked the Tenant if she intended on remaining in the unit beyond March 31, 2023, the date the fixed-term lease was to expire.

The Tenant testified that once she advised the Landlords that she did intend to stay that the Landlords intended on increasing the rent by 9%. The Tenant had agreed that the residential complex was not subject to rent control and that the Landlords could legally increase the rent by this amount.

The Tenant testified that she requested time to consider this and on February 9, 2023, she had e-mailed the Landlords and advised them that she would be vacating the unit. On February 16, 2023, the Tenant sent an e-mail to the Landlords advising them that she would like to vacate the unit on May 1, 2026, and that if anything changed, she would let the Landlords know.

On February 18, 2023, the Landlords e-mailed the Tenant again, stating that they would agree to the Tenant vacating the unit by the end of the day on May 1, 2026, and that the Landlords intended on showing the unit.

The Tenant responded that same date, stating: “…And just so you’re aware, I will need as much notice as possible for entry and showings will not be available when I’m sleeping post call, etc. I’m willing to work the with agent to accommodate as much as possible but people cannot come in whilst I’m sleeping. I hope you can understand that.

The Tenant is a doctor who would work 24-hour and overnight shifts. She testified that it was important that her rest time not be disturbed so that she may be able to recover between shifts. The Tenant testified that she understood the agreement with the Landlords regarding showings would be at least 24-hours notice.

The Landlords’ realtors SM and MP acted as the Landlords’ agent in showing the unit. The Tenant testified that there had been a request for a showing less than 24-hours on February 23, 2023, however, the time worked for the Tenant, and she permitted the showing but reminded the Landlords about keeping proper communication regarding same.

The Tenant testified that on February 24, 2023, at 7:42 am, she received a showing booking for 4:45 pm that afternoon. The Tenant rejected this showing as she was not available to be in the unit and needed time to get ready to leave for the airport.

The Tenant testified that on March 18, 2023, an agent walked into her unit without knocking. On March 24, 2023, one of the Landlords’ agents accused the Tenant of damaging the unit’s window blinds. On March 24, 2023, the Landlords’ agents permitted a booking with less than 24-hours notice.

On February 24, 2023, the Landlords requested that the Tenant now vacate the unit on April 30, 2023, as a potential tenant wanted to move in on May 1, 2023. SM sent the Tenant an N11 to terminate the tenancy as of April 30, 2023. The Tenant responded the same date, stating that she would like the document to reflect what we had discussed concerning vacating on May 1, 2023, and stated that she didn’t believe she had the capacity to amend it.

SM responded saying that the Landlords could not accommodate May 1, 2023, as this would lose a potential month of rent for the Landlords. The Tenant responded the same date, reminding SM that the Landlords has already agreed in writing to May 1, 2023, and that her and MP could show the unit as often as they wanted the next seven days as the Tenant was out of town. The Tenant completed an N9 and forwarded it to MP. On February 27, 2023, MP e-mailed the Tenant confirming that 24-hours notice will be given however, MP stated that the 24-hour period starts when the Landlords send the e-mail, not when the Tenant reads the e-mail.

On March 16, 2023, a showing was booked with less than 24-hours notice. MP advised the Tenant that the booking should have never been approved without 24-hours notice and that the Tenant cane refuse the showing if she wished.
On March 17, 2023, the Tenant e-mailed MP, SM and the Landlords reminding them that she needs 24-hour notice of showings.

On March 24, 2023, the Tenant received a request for a showing at 3:03 pm that day for a showing for 2:30 pm on March 25, 2023. PM responded on March 24, 2023, advising the Tenant that he would ensure there is a buffer so that the Tenant may receive requests in enough time and that, “Please be advised that there will be no days without showings going forward. If it’s 24 hours notice, it will be confirmed. This is final. No need to e-mail back as it will be a further waste of everyone’s energy”. The Tenant responded that no one may enter her unit while she is sleeping.

That same date, MP responded with the following e-mail: “If you aren’t willing to cooperate and give leniency on things like an extra 30 minutes it takes a text to get to you then I’m done being accommodating. Your choice – some small flexibility and its easier for everyone or 24 hours no exceptions doesn’t matter if you’re sleeping, awake, working or performing surgery on your dining room table. In this case, the agent can go at 3:04 pm as that’s when the time you were notified. Flexibility or not, it’s your choice going forward.”
Bothe SM and MP e-mailed that same date, stating that they would e-mail the Tenant with notice from here on in in order to avoid delays.

In total, the Landlords booked 32 showings in 44 days, of which 20 led to actual showings of the unit prior to the Tenant vacating. The Tenant rejected showing requests on February 23, 2023, twice on March 17, 2023, and once on March 25, 2023. The Landlords had also cancelled booked showings on February 28, 2023, March 5, 2023, March 13, 2023, March 21, 2023, March 27, 2023, and March 30, 2023.

The Tenant testified that she had been cooperating with the Landlords and their agent by providing them a copy of her work schedule so that showings may be booked accordingly. On March 28, 2023, the Tenant had been involved in an incident where two individuals dressed as construction workers had entered her hospital attempting to serve documents upon her. This issue, along with MP’s statement that showings would be happening regardless put the Tenant on edge. The Tenant ended up vacating the unit on April 30, 2023. Landlords’ Evidence

AB testified that she had agreed with the Tenant that she could vacate the unit on May 1, 2023, however, after speaking with SM and MP she had been advised that she would be short a month of rent and as such, agreed to renege on her agreement.
AB testified that she was aware of the issues her real estate agents were having with the Tenant and agreed that she and the Tenant would generally get along.
AB testified that any issues between the Tenant and the Landlords is the fault of her agents SM and MP.

MP also testified and largely confirmed most of the Tenant’s evidence. Potential tenants would call the brokerage who represents the listing and may book online. MP testified that he knew he could show the unit while the Tenant was out of town and that he knew about the 24-hour requirement once she was back. He testified that the booking program would not permit a booking with less than 24-hours notice. Analysis

Based on the evidence of the parties, I am satisfied that the Landlords and their agent entered the Tenant’s illegally, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit and also harassed the Tenant.

Once the Tenant rejected the Landlord’s rent increase and had agreed to vacate the unit on May 1, 2023, the Tenant had made it clear that she would require specific notice based upon her employment as a Doctor and required the notice so as not to overly disrupt her busy schedule. AB had agreed to May 1, 2023, as the termination date and the Tenant had started providing the Landlords a copy of her work schedule in order to facilitate showings.

In my view, the issues began once SM and MP became involved and began interfering with the arrangement that AB and the Tenant had come to. And yes, while it would absolutely make more sense for the Tenant to have vacated on April 30, 2023, the Landlords should not have attempted to unilaterally change that date by telling the Tenant that the Landlords cannot accommodate that.

Further, the Landlords’ agents continued to press the issue of the showings with the Tenant. The Tenant in my view responded reasonably and firmly with both SM and MP that her time needed to be respected and that she just needed 24-hours notice.

MP then began to blame a “delay” between when he would send the Tenant text messages and when they would be received. MP knew or ought to have known that his method of communication was insufficient in providing proper notice yet never took responsibility for same and had agreed to e-mail notice only.

When the Tenant attempted to assert her rights, this clearly upset and frustrated MP causing him to essentially lash out with passive-aggressive language such as asking the Tenant to not e-mail back as it would be a waste of energy and that the Tenant will accept his notices despite whatever the Tenant is doing, including performing surgery on the dining room table.

Quite frankly, the actions and behaviour of SM and MP served to further antagonize the Tenant. As well, neither agent was able to explain why they required so many showings of the unit. No insight was provided as to why the unit needed to be shown daily as MP threatened as if the renting of this unit was a matter of life or death. Even AB blames her own agents for this behaviour. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement for the period beginning February 24, 2023, until April 30, 2023, in the amount of $958.36, a Board fine, $1,947.29 moving expenses and $6,000.00 for pain and suffering.
I find the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement within the period requested is reasonable and will be ordered to be paid by the Landlords.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative challenged the Tenant’s request for moving expenses on the basis that the Tenant had signed an N9 termination of tenancy and agreed to vacate the unit. While that may be the case, the Tenant and AB had agreed to a vacate date of May 1, 2023. Both SM and MP advised AB that the Landlords should not have agreed to same and attempted to renege on this agreement.

While the Tenant did sign an N9 notice of termination, I am satisfied that the document was signed as a result of the actions of the Landlords’ and their agents and the Landlords will be ordered to pay the Tenant’s moving expenses in the amount of $1,947.29.

The Tenant also seeks a Board fine. While a fine would likely be appropriate in these circumstances, I find AB to be less at fault than SM and MP in this case and considering that these remedies will have to be bourn by AB and likely sorted out between herself and MP and SM in another forum, I don’t find a Board fine to be reasonable in these circumstances.

The Tenant is also seeking $6,000.00 in general compensation due to the constant attention she needed to put to these showings in light of the fact of her occupation as a doctor and dealing with her schedule. Both MP and SM unreasonably reacted to the Tenant asserting her rights and despite this, continued attempting to book showings with less than 24-hours notice. As such, I find an award of $6,000.00 in general damages to be reasonable.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $8,953.65. This amount represents: • $958.36 for a rent abatement. • $1,947.29 for part of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $6,000.00 for general damages • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 29, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): This application came before the Board by videoconference on June 16, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented by [name]. As of 10:50 a.m. the Landlords were not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the Board. There is no record of a request to reschedule the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant present.
reasons: The Tenant's application is brought pursuant to s. 57.1 of the Act and alleges that the Landlord has failed to restore the Tenant to possession as required after the Tenant vacated pursuant to an N13 notice of termination for extraordinary renovation and repairs.

The difficulty that arises here is that one could argue the application is premature. Section 57.1 is intended to address the situation where the landlord serves an N13, completes the renovations and repairs, and then fails to put the tenant back into possession. That does not appear to be what has happened here. The Tenant says no renovations or repairs appear to have been commenced let alone finished. The Tenant’s two-year limitation period was rapidly approaching so the Tenant filed this application in advance of the refusal to put the Tenant back into possession upon completion of the renovations in order to preserve the right of return.

It seems to me that the only way to preserve the Tenant’s right to go back into possession in these circumstances is to issue an interim order barring the Landlords from re-renting the unit to someone else. An order shall issue pursuant to s. 204(1) accordingly.
I am not seized.
ordered: This application is adjourned to a date to be set by the Board.

At the hearing of the application the Tenant should be prepared to speak to the following questions: a) Has the residential complex been sold or otherwise changed hands (for example, a mortgagee has gone into possession)? b) What building permits have been obtained if any from the local municipality? c) What communication, if any, has the Tenant had from the Landlords? d) Should the application be dismissed as premature (and taking into consideration the amendment to s. 57.1(2) of the Act scheduled to come into effect on September 26, 2026)?

The Landlords shall not re-rent the rental unit to another tenant or otherwise occupy the rental unit (except to do the repairs and renovations described in the N13) until this application is heard or the Board orders otherwise.
