No later than 7 days before the hearing the parties shall give to the other and file with the Board a copy of any documents, receipts, photographs, recordings or like things the party intends to rely on at the hearing. All submissions must be uploaded on the Tribunals Ontario Portal (TOP) online. If a party is unable to use TOP, their evidence may be submitted via email at [email].
The parties may also consent in writing to the exchange of documents using the online TOP portal.
Pursuant to Rule 19.7 a party who fails to comply with an order for disclosure may not be permitted to rely on evidence that is not properly disclosed.

The Tenant shall notify the Board and the Landlords in writing immediately, if the hearing is no longer necessary and the Tenant wishes to withdraw or abandon the application. The LTB email address is [email]. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord 's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (LTB-T-015201-25) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and, withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (LTB-T-027528-25) The applications were heard by videoconference on July 8, 2026. The Landlord [name], the Landlord [name]’s representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,396.00.

The Tenant’s T6 Application was brought pursuant to s.29(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and alleges the Landlords breached an obligation under s.20(1): and LTB-T-027528-25 A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards

In addition to the T6 Application, the Tenant filed a T2 Application pursuant to s.29(1) of the Act, alleging the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them, and/or substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, or with the reasonable supply of a vital service the Landlord is obligated to supply.
The T2 and T6 applications were filed, respectively, on April 2, 2025 and March 5, 2025.
The residential complex is comprised of 3 floors, with the Landlords residing in an upper unit and the Tenant residing in one of the two lower units.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024 and and vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025. The monthly rent was $2000/month. Lack of Heat
The Tenant [name] (the “Tenant” or “Tenant JT”) alleges that inadequate heat was provided to the rental unit.

The Tenant JT testified the Landlord was notified of the cold temperature towards the end of October 2024. A text message was produced from November 10, 2024 whereby the [name] advised the Landlord as follows: …I noticed it gets very cold before midnight through the entire morning, I’m trying like you said with my heater but its not enough, If you want I get a smart thermostat today that records all the information 24/7….

According to JT, the lack of heat concerns were ignored by the Landlord and remained unresolved, as supported by subsequent text communications. For instance, on January 23, 2025, the Landlord text: “ Hi [name], I received your message, and I understand you’re asking for cooperation. However, I feel that there hasn’t been much cooperation on your side either…” Later, on January 29, 2025, the Tenant texted the Landlord “Turn off the cold ac blowing in the basement…I need hot air not cold please”, to which the Landlord responded “stop….imagining stuff”.

In an effort to address the lack of heat, t he Tenant purchased two electric heaters . The Tenant also installed 3 thermostats in the kitchen, bedroom and hallway areas. Thermostat readings from February 15, 2025 were produced, showing temperatures of 15.9 C, 16.8 C and 17.5 C. According to the Tenant JT, the temperatures would consistently be around 16- 17 C and would get down to 13 C. Overall, the lack of heat resulted in an uncomfortable and stressful living environment which the Tenant stated impacted his sleep. and LTB-T-027528-25

The Landlord’s [name] (the “Landlord” or “Landlord SG”) lived in the upper unit and testified there was no issue with heat, stating the building has central heating and the other basement tenant never complained . While the Landlord SG testified her spouse [name] (MG) investigated the Tenant’s concerns, MG was not in attendance at the hearing or otherwise called to testify.

Upon hearing all the evidence, I find the Tenant’s oral testimony as sup ported by text communications and temperature readings, to be more reliable than the Landlord’s general denial. I therefore find the heat was inadequate in the rental unit and find the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations as a result. At the hearing, the Tenant indicated he sought only a $2 ,150.00 abatement in respect of the T6 Application (as opposed to the $5,375.00 abatement in the application). Here, I find there was some disruption to the Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit from November 2024 onwards. Accordingly, I find a rent abatement of approximately 20% from November 2024 through to March 2025 to be reasonable in the circumstances, for a total abatement of $2,150.00. Stove-top element/hood fan

The Tenant alleges one of four stove-top elements, including the oven hood fan stopped working. While the Tenant acknowledged having use of the remaining three stove-top elements, the Tenant stated the non -functioning element was unsafe and posed a safety concern. Furthermore, with respect to the hood fan, the Tenant testified he was often reluctant to cook due to fog that would arise as a result.
The onus to prove the allegations rest with the Tenant.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477 (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding breach and/or remedy and that this is consistent with the Board’s Interpretation Guideline #5

While not a requirement to produce , the Tenant did not produce any supporting documentation, pictures or messages in support of the maintenance issues. The Landlord, in response, produced a video whereby the Tenant acknowledges that the stovetop is working. The Landlord SG also testified that the purported non -functioning hood fan was never brought to the Landlords’ attention. Here, I am not satisfied the Tenant clearly communicated the purported maintenance issues to the Landlords, nor am I satisfied based upon the limited evidence provided that such issues impacted the Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit. These allegations are dismissed. and LTB-T-027528-25 Garage Door Keypad

The Tenant alleges the garage door [name] did not function as intended, stating the problem became worse over time . As such, in order to enter the garage and access the doorway leading to the rental unit, the Tenant had to use the garage door opener remote.

The Landlord submits there was no breach, as the Tenant always had an alternative means to access the rental unit. Regardless, the Landlord submits that the garage code was changed upon being advised of the issue, so as not to utilize the non-functioning button/number on the keypad.

Based upon the evidence presented, I do not find that the Tenant’s maintenance concern rises to the point of constituting a breach under the Act. Here, there is no suggestion that the Tenant was ever deprived of access to the rental unit and very little evidence was presented as to any inconvenience suffered by the Tenant as a result of having to use the garage door remote. This allegation is accordingly dismissed. Threat of eviction and accusations

The Tenant alleges that on January 28, 2025, the Landlord falsely accused the Tenant “taking drugs” and threatened to evict the Tenant without cause. In support, the Tenant produced a text communication which stated the following: You brought drink people in drugs to our house in the middle of the night many times. Its very easy to evacuate you immediately especially if we add negligent to pay rent Choice is yours

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $500 as a result of the eviction threat and false accusation. Although the Landlord’s text communication appears to be an isolated incident, I do find the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental. It is clear that the Tenant was made to feel unwelcome and that the Tenant was troubled by the accusation which the Tenant asserts was false. In the circumstances, I find a rent abatement of $150 to be reasonable in the circumstances.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $2,300.00.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $96.00 for the cost of filing both applications.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $2,396.00. and LTB-T-027528-25

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026 the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the outstanding balance. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenants’ T2 Amended Application was filed January 14, 2026 and was brought pursuant to s .29(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) . The Tenants allege the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them. Illegal entry

The Tenants’ application alleges that “In early Feb 2025 while police was on call to unit, the Landlord entered the unit without permission”. No other pertinent particulars were provided at the hearing in support of the allegation. The Landlord [name] (CS) denies ever illegally entering the rental unit , stating the only time entry was made was at the commencement of the tenancy.
The onus to prove this allegation rests with the Tenant s. Here, due to a lack of evidence of any illegal entry by the landlord, this allegation is dismissed. Landlord’s agent/hot water tank

The Tenants’ application alleges “The Landlord’s sister lives upstairs in the unit above the tenants and acts as her agent. She was repeatedly and deliberately on the floor day and night to harass & annoy the Tenants and “Repeatedly the Landlord’s sister turned off the hot water during the evening hours.”

With respect to the general allegation of “harass & annoy ” by the “Landlord’s sister”, the Tenants’ application provided no further details of the alleged harassment such as dates or times - nor did the Tenant ’s testimony at the hearing supplement such missing details. In the circumstances, I find insufficient particulars were provided so as to enable the Landlord to know the case to be met and/or to decide whether or not to dispute the allegation before the Board.

With respect to the hot water allegation, at the hearing the Tenant BP initially testified the hot water tank malfunctioned for approximately 1 week until it was resolved by the Landlord’s contractor. When questioned further as the allegation of deliberate interference, the Tenant recalled an incident where the upstairs tenant arrived home late at night and the hot water was subsequently turned off. N o further particulars were provided to corroborate the Tenant’s suspicion of deliberate interference. In the circumstances, I do not find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant s have established an interference or other contravention under the Act with respect to this allegation.

The allegations are accordingly dismissed. In the alternative, I do not find the Tenants have established that one of the upper unit residents was acting as the Landlord’s “agent” , as alleged. In this regard, it was unclear from t he evidence how the “Landlord’s sister” was acting – or held out as acting - on the Landlord’s behalf, authority or control. The Landlord testified that a friend occupied one of the upper units - and not her sister as alleged by the Tenants. The Landlord further advised that her friend did not collect rent or perform any other activities on behalf of the Landlord . In the circumstances, I find that insufficient evidence was led to establish that the Landlord’s friend was acting as the Landlord’s agent. Service of Form N7/N12

The Tenant’s application alleges the Landlord illegally served a Form N12 on March 1, 2025 by posting it on the rental unit door; and, that the Landlord illegally served a Form N7 on February 28, 2025 and March 7, 2025 by posting it on the front door.
The onus to prove this allegation rests with the Tenants.

At the hearing, the Tenant sought to dispute the merits of the notices served. While the substance of the Landlord’s Forms N7 and N12 are not before me, the Landlord submits the notices did not lack merit and noted the Form N7 was served twice as a result of a defect in the initial service attempt . It was also noted that an application for eviction was not required/pursued, as the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025. While it is clear the Tenants dispute the contents of the notices, the Board’s notices advise the Tenant that the allegations may be disputed in the event of disagreement: “You do not have to move out if you disagree with what the landlord has put in this notice….the landlord will have to prove the claims they made in this Notice …and you can respond to the claims your landlord makes.” Moreover, while posting of the notices on the Tenant’s door is not a permitted method of service under the Act, it is unclear from the evid ence how the Landlord’s attempted mere method of service adversely impacted the Tenant. Here, I do not find that the service of the Board’s notices rise to the level of constituting a breach under the Act. General Harassment

Lastly, the Tenants’ application alleges that on March 8, 2025, the Landlord “harassed the Tenants (see video)”. No other pertinent particulars were provided in the application, or at the hearing. While the Tenants produced two videos showing discussions between the Tenant BP and the Landlord, the Tenant BP was unclear as to when such recordings or events took place, nor was it submitted that such recordings related to the general March 8, 2025 harassment allegation. In the circumstances, I find that insufficient evidence was led to establish that the Landlord “harassed” the Tenants on the date in question.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a single-family dwelling located at [address] Street in Picton, Ontario. The Tenants moved into the unit on June 1, 2024 and they vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2025.

The Tenants were served with an N12 notice of termination in March of 2025 with a termination date of May 31, 2025. This application alleges that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (SC)

SC testified that he was notified by the Landlord in March of 2025 that the Landlord was needing to take the property back for his wife’s parents. After some confusion from the Landlord, the Landlord provided an N12 notice and that was provided to him on March 20, 2025 with a termination date of May 31, 2025.

SC stated that he and his wife were very stressed about receiving this and immediately began trying to find another unit in Prince Edward County. He was unable to find another rental that they could afford in the County so they rented a home in Milford which is much more remote than their previous home. SC explained that he has to travel frequently for work and now has to drive 2 hours to get to the train station to get to Toronto and his wife now has to drive him. The Tenants only have one car and that was all they needed in Picton where everything was close by.

SC also stated that the new house that they rented was not furnished (as this rental unit had been) and so this caused extra time and money to arrange to find all of their furniture for their unfinished rental unit. Evidence of [name] (JC) 7. [name] also commented on how Picton was the perfect place for them to live as she and her son were able to walk to the grocery stores, the library and other stores and that at their new house, she does not have the ability to walk to any stores as Milford is a very small hamlet. She said that the family is suffering with only having one vehicle and so when her husband goes away for work, she has to drive her husband to the train station, 2 hours one way and then returns so that she has access to the car. 8. [name] stated that in October of 2025, she was looking through the paper and noticed that the rental house was up for sale. She said that she was very upset to see this because they had just moved out 5 months earlier so that the Landlord’s parents could move into the house. She provided a copy of the listing showing that the house was put up for sale on October 28, 2025. 9. [name] stated that they are seeking that the Board issue a fine against the Landlords, they are seeking $4,410.36 in out-of-pocket expenses including moving expenses and furniture that they had to purchase, they are seeking 12 months of their previous rent of $2,900.00 per month, totalling $34,800.00 and they are seeking general damages of $10,789.64. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (WD) 10. WD testified that despite the guidance that his realtor provided him, he realized that he did have to provide an N12 notice of termination to the Tenants and he did serve same to them. The Landlord advised the Tenants that his wife’s parents would be moving into the rental unit as soon as the Tenants vacated. 11. WD stated that his wife’s parents wanted to live closer to their family so that they could assist the Landlords with their child and be closer to the family. He said that he and his wife were thrilled that her parents would be moving into the rental house and they agreed to live there for at least one year. He stated that he was very hopeful that his in-laws would make this area their permanent home. 12. The Landlord stated that his in-laws moved into the rental house on May 3, 2025 and remained there until June 1, 2026. The Landlord provided a document, [name] that included dated pictures of the in-laws, the Landlords and the child throughout the time period that the in-laws were residing there. The Landlord also provided copies of the hydro bill in his father-in-law’s name and water bills again in his father-in-law’s name. 13. He stated that in October of 2025, his in-laws advised him that they would not be staying in Picton permanently but told him that they would stay for the full year as agreed. He stated that both he and his wife were disappointed that they were not going to stay in the area. 14. WD stated that based on his in-laws’ decision to return to Huntsville in June of 2026, he and his wife decided to put the rental house up for sale to test the market. He said that he made it clear to his realtor that the sale could not close until after June of 2026 and that they wanted to see what the market result would be. He listed the house for sale on October 29, 2025 and removed the listing in December 2025 after getting an idea of what the market was like. 15. The Landlord stated that his in-laws vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2026 to return to [name] and that he and his wife are considering their options with the house. The Landlord stated that they have not done anything in bad faith and that they simply wanted to get an idea of how long it would take to sell the rental house. Analysis 16. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 17. The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlords served an N12 notice on the Tenants and the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. 18. Based on the evidence that I have heard from the parties, I am satisfied that the Landlords’ parents resided in the rental unit from May 1, 2025 to June 1, 2026. A number of dated pictures that included the Landlords, their child and their in-laws were provided as well as utility bills that were in the name of the in-laws. As such, the Tenants proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but they did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. 19. The presumption of bad faith set out in section 57(5) states: “For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6), the landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 20. As the Landlords listed the house for sale in October of 2025 which was within the period of time set out in section 57(6) of the Act, there is a presumption of bad faith on the part of the Landlords. 21. Based on the fact that the rental house would be empty after June 1, 2026, it is reasonable that the Landlords were concerned about whether or not they would be able to sell the house and how long that process might take. Both Landlords stated that the house would not have been sold prior to June 1, 2026 and that they were considering their options with the house. The house was not sold during the time it was listed and the Landlords’ parents continued to reside in the rental unit until June 1, 2026. Further the Landlords confirmed that they removed the house listing in December of 2025. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords have rebutted this presumption under 57(5) of the Act. 22. The Tenants proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: We find it more likely than not that the Landlord breached their responsibilities to maintain the residential complex and/or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, maintenance standards when they failed to warn the Tenant about the risk of butternuts falling into the parking lot or otherwise protect her car from resultant damage.

The Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,954.80 for costs she will incur to repair the damage to her car and the cost of filing this application. As no evidence was presented in support of the Tenant’s claim for $250.00 to rent a car, we have not considered or awarded this amount. Background

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2024. The parking lot behind the apartment building contains 6 unassigned parking spots and one outdoor parking spot was included with the Tenant’s lease [Exhibit 5 – EVID ID 8250312].
Three butternut trees, including one that is on the Landlord’s property, overhang the parking lot. There is no overhead barrier between the cars and the butternut trees [Exhibit 2 – EVID ID 7665765].

It was admitted that every fall, over a period of a few weeks, nuts fall from the butternut trees and the Landlord was aware of this. It was also not disputed that the nuts are hard and large – being about the size of a small orange or apple [Exhibit 3 – EVID ID 7665769].

The Landlord’s Agent admitted they did not consider or take any steps to trim the trees as he understands the trees are an endangered species. He also admitted they have not erected signage or some form of protection in the parking lot. Instead, the Landlord’s Agent testified it was his standard practice to warn prospective tenants of the issue and suggest they not park under the trees when the nuts are dropping.

The issues to be determined before us were whether the Landlord warned the Tenant about the risks posed by the falling butternuts, whether the Tenant’s car was damaged, and whether the Tenant will incur costs to repair their car. Relevant Law

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides: 20(1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The Landlord did not warn the Tenant about the falling butternuts

The parties’ evidence as to whether the Tenant was warned that butternuts would fall into the parking lot diverged. We find the Tenant’s evidence she was not warned credible and decline to draw an inference from the Landlord’s standard practice that she was.

We find support for this finding in the fact that the Landlord’s Agent admitted both that he did not have a specific memory of warning the Tenant and admitted that there is no warning signage. Additionally, we found the Tenant’s evidence about the importance of her car and parking and that she would not have moved in had she known of the issue accorded with the steps she has taken since discovering the issue.

In the above circumstances, we find the Landlord did not warn the Tenant and so find the Landlord was in breach of their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. The Tenant’s car was damaged by falling butternuts

We accept the Tenant’s evidence that her car was damaged by falling butternuts as it accords with the pattern of dents indicated in photographs taken at the Acura collision centre and an estimate was provided to repair these dents.

We accept that the Tenant did not notice any damage to her car right away as she left early in the morning and returned late at night. The Tenant testified, and it was not disputed, that she spoke with the Landlord upon discovery of the issue.

The Tenant submitted photographs of her car [Exhibit 4 – EVID ID 7665786, 7665779, 7665798 and 7665812] that she testified were taken at the [name] collision centre. The Tenant was forthright that dents are not clearly visible in the photographs. She submitted this is due to the glare from the paint and the Acura collision centre identified where there were dents on her car with blue masking tape so that the extent of damage could be seen. That the dents had been marked by professionals at the collision centre was not disputed.

The pattern and distribution of the blue tape accords with what might be expected to result if items were falling on a car from above as the tape is primarily on the roof, hood, and trunk. Where there is tape on the side of the car only areas that protrude such as the body that extends over the wheel are marked. No damage is marked on the bumpers.

The estimate [Exhibit 1 – EVID ID 7665758] is dated September 26, 2025. It reflects that the work to create the estimate was started on September 23, 2025. It was also not disputed that the estimate for repair was authentic. We do not give any weight to the Landlord’s submission that the lack of a description of the damage on the estimate suggests there was none. We find an estimate need not describe damage so much as the work that will be done.

We also do not find whether the Tenant offered to show the Landlord the damage first- hand relevant nor do we accept that the time the Tenant took to commence this application is any indication of whether there was damage.
In the above circumstances, we find it more likely than not that the car was damaged by falling butternuts. Costs that will be incurred for repair are authentic

Under subpara 1, para 5 of subsection 39(1) of the Act the reasonable costs a tenant will incur to repair property damaged due to a breach of the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) may be awarded.

The Tenant relied on the estimate, testified she intended to have her car repaired, and that she has not received any funds to repair the car. The estimate indicates the costs to repair the damage to her car will be $4,906.80 [Exhibit 1 – EVID ID 7665758].

We find these costs reasonable as they are from an estimate provided by a collision centre, and do not find they are speculative as suggested by the Landlord’s Representative. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant these costs.

The Tenant also claimed $250.00 on her application for the cost to rent a replacement car while her car is repaired. No evidence was presented in support of this claim at the hearing and so it is dismissed.
The Tenant was largely successful on her application and so is entitled to her costs of filing this application in the amount of $48.00.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,954.80. This amount represents: • $4,906.80 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to repair property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 1, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) after the repair(s) are done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: It was undisputed that the Landlord returned the Tenants’ key deposit on April 24, 2026. As such, the Tenants’ claim was resolved.
The only issue that the parties could not agree on was whether or not the Tenants were entitled to their filing fee of $48.00.

The Tenants provided that they promptly returned the keys when they moved out on March 28, 2026, and then followed up with the Landlord about return of the deposit. However, instead of returning the deposit, the Landlord began responding about damage claims. The Tenants indicated that they waited for a few days before filing the claim. The Tenants said that the Landlord began sending bills for alleged damage instead of the key deposit, so they filed the claim for the key deposit on April 6, 2026.

NN provided that since the parties were able to resolve the substantive issue well in advance of the hearing, each party should bear their own costs. NN provided that the key deposit was returned to the Tenants within 24 days which was a reasonable amount of time. NN provided that the key deposit was returned to the Tenants within a reasonable amount of time after the moveout process was complete and the refund process could be completed.
The Board charges Landlords and Tenants a filing fee when an application is filed with the Board.

This fee is a discretionary decision to be granted to a successful application under the Board’s Rules of Procedures section 23 Costs that states: Ordering the Application Fee as Costs 23.1 If the applicant is successful, the LTB may order the respondent to pay the application fee to the applicant as costs.

Here, if the Landlord would have returned the key deposit promptly when the keys were returned the Tenants would not have felt the need to file an application. The purpose of the refundable key deposit is to cover the reasonable replacement cost of keys in case they are not returned. As soon as a tenant returns the keys, the deposit is to be refunded to the tenant.

I am not persuaded that it takes 24 days to process a refund of a key deposit when the keys have been returned, especially when there have been requests from the Tenant that were met with not responses about the refund of the key deposit but conversations about alleged damages.
As such, I am satisfied that the Tenants had a valid claim when the application was filed and as such are entitled to their filing fee.
Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the $48.00 filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $48.00. This amount represents: • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants filed their application in May 2022, alleging that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on March 11, 2022, and that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the residential complex, and that she harassed them to leave the rental unit.
The Tenants, M. [name] (MD)(daughter), and D. [name] (DD)(mother), moved into the rental unit in August 2018.
The rental unit is a one bedroom condo apartment, and the rent was $800.00 per month when they vacated the unit in May 2022.
It is undisputed that the parties got along amicably until 2021. Tenants’ Evidence:

The Tenants allege that after October 2021, the Landlord’s pattern of conduct towards them became intimidating and deceptive, and she harassed them to leave, culminating in an alleged egregious illegal entry on March 11, 2022.

MD said that the Tenants made a number of maintenance complaints about their oven that the Landlord failed to respond to. She submitted into evidence a series of emails she sent to the Landlord asking her to fix the oven. There were emails dated July 13, 2021, September 2, 2021, September 15, 2021, October 14, 2021.

MD said that prior to July 2021, the Landlord had mostly responded to all the Tenants’ maintenance complaints. MD admits that the Tenants, at one point, owed the Landlord a substantial amount of arrears, over $15,000.00, but they were paid off in full by June 2021.

The Tenants allege that, instead of the Landlord responding to their complaint or repairing the oven as requested, she decided to evict them. They submitted into evidence a letter from the Landlord, dated October 15, 2021, the day after an oven complaint. The letter from the Landlord informed the Tenants that the rental unit was sold “through a private sale”. The letter then gave them 60 days to vacate “no later than 11:59 p.m. on Friday, December 31, 2021.” It gave them the required 24 hours advance notice that the Landlord and the new owner would view the property on October 21, 2021.

The Tenants allege that the entry on October 21, 2021, was an illegal entry because there was never a “new owner”. They did not make this allegation in their application, so I did not consider that date for an illegal entry.
It is undisputed that, in December 2021, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination, for Landlord’s own use, to vacate the rental unit on or before February 28, 2022.

MD said that the October 2021 letter, followed by the N12 notice made it apparent to the Tenants that the Landlord would do “anything” to get them out. She said that the Tenants had begun looking for an alternative accommodation in October 2021, and they did not stop looking.

MD submitted into evidence an interac history from her account in late December 2021 and early January 2022. There was a payment for rent on January 1, 2022, that was declined. The message recorded on the statement was “Declined due to unauthorized monetary amount and illegal tenant occupancy at 303-429 Somerset St. W, Ottawa, ON. Formal eviction action and related procedures are in progress as of 2022-01-01.”
MD said that the message made her feel horrible because it called her an “illegal tenant”, it increased her level of stress, and it frightened her by speaking about “formal eviction action”.

The Tenants allege that the Landlord’s substantial interference and harassment to pressure them to leave culminated in an illegal entry on March 11, 2022. DD testified that she was alone in the unit on that date when she heard the dog “screaming”. She said that she had never heard a knock. She said that she was shocked to see a lady with a mask and a suitcase, and DD asked her what she was doing in the home. DD said that the lady replied “get out of my house” and the lady went crazy yelling at her. DD said that she then informed the lady that she would call the police. 16. [name] said that she called MD, and the lady was still screaming when she called. MD confirmed that testimony. MD said that her mother was in a “complete panic”. DD said that she had seen the Landlord before, but she did not recognize her on that day because she was wearing a mask. DD admits that the lady told her she was the Landlord. DD said that the incident left her shocked and sick, and she is still scared when a door is left unlocked. MD also said that her mother is still traumatized by the incident, and she asks every night if the doors are locked. DD provided contradictory evidence about whether she heard her dog bark before, or after, the Landlord entered the rental unit. 17. MD said that the Landlord never apologized for the incident on March 11, 2022. She said that the Tenants decided to leave as quickly as they could, and they left at the end of May 2022. 18. The Tenants said that they moved to a larger two bedroom apartment. It is undisputed that the Tenants served the Landlord with N9 notice of termination for termination by the end of May 2022. There was no new lease entered into evidence to support the allegation of the 150% increase in the monthly rent. 19. The Tenants request their moving costs of $1,065.03, a rent abatement of 50% from October 2021 through May 2022, and the rent differential of $1,267.68 for 12 months. Landlord’s Evidence: 20. The Landlord said that she responded to the oven complaint, and she said there were email exchanges between the parties about the oven, however she did not submit these into evidence. The Landlord said that she attempted to come and inspect in October 2021, but she was denied entry because it was during the COVID period. The Landlord said that perhaps a light had blown in the oven, but it was always working and fully functional. 21. The Landlord said that she had a private buyer for the unit in October 2021, but the sale fell through because the Tenants would not confirm that they would leave by December 31, 2021. 22. The Landlord said that after the sale fell through, she then served an N12 notice of termination for Landlord’s own use because she was going to renovate her home and she wanted to move into the rental unit while the renovations were taking place. She said that she did move into the rental unit in November 2022. 23. It is undisputed that the Landlord entered the rental unit on March 11, 2022. She said that she went to inspect the unit because she heard from the condo management that there were complaints about a dog barking. The Landlord did not submit into evidence any communications from the condo management about dog barking. She said that she did not serve a notice of entry, nor did she communicate with the Tenants because she “assumed” they had already moved out by February 28, 2022, the termination date. She said that she believed she was making an “emergency” entry because of the dog complaints. Nevertheless, the Landlord said she knocked a few times and heard the dog. When there was no response, she said that she entered and saw DD, who began to scream and yell at her. The Landlord said that she identified herself, and she entered as far as the kitchen, but it did not stop DD yelling at her. The Landlord said that she did not have a suitcase with her but rather a shoulder bag. After DD yelled and threatened the police, the Landlord said that she left and waited in the lobby for MD to show up. However, after 90 minutes or so she said that she left. 24. The Landlord admits that she declined the January 2022 rent payment because she had already told the Tenants to leave by December 31, 2021, and she believed they were illegal tenants. She said that she never communicated with the Tenants about whether or not they had left because there was a bad relationship between the parties. She said that rent payments had stopped in 2019. 25. The Landlord said that she called the private purchaser the “new owner” in her letter of October 2021 because that is how she viewed the purchaser, although she admits that no money changed hands. 26. The Landlord submits that the N12 notice for landlord’s own use was served in good faith, she believed that the Tenants had moved out, and service of an N12 notice is not, in itself, harassment. In any case, the Landlord submits that the Tenants did not move out by the termination date, and they only moved when they had, at their own leisure, found a place to live. Reasons and Analysis: 27. For the following reasons, I find that the Tenants proved some of the allegations in their application. 28. The Landlord mentioned, a number of times, the Tenants’ failure to pay rent for a substantial period of time. The Landlord’s repeated mention of failure to pay rent, I find, demonstrated her annoyance about it. The Tenants admitted that they had substantial arrears until at least June 2021. MD said that it was all paid off by the summer of 2021, but those dates also coincide with the dates when the Tenants started to complain about the oven. The Landlord had no documentary evidence to support that she ever responded to the oven complaints, nor that she ever dealt with the oven complaints. Even in her testimony, the Landlord minimized the oven issue, rather than asserting that she had fully dealt with the maintenance issue. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the series of events, taken together, prove the Tenants’ allegation that the Landlord entered into a campaign of harassment, and she decided to take steps from October 2021, to get them to leave, when she sent the letter on October 15 to tell them she had sold the unit. It was sent one day after their fourth maintenance request. 29. My finding above is also supported by the other evidence, or lack thereof, namely, that there is no documentary evidence at all to support the Landlord’s testimony that she had a “private purchaser” and the purchase fell through because the Tenants did not leave. The sequence of events, the lack of documentary evidence to support a sale of the unit, combine together to lead to my conclusion that the letter of October 15, 2021, from the Landlord to the Tenants was her attempt to illegally evict them. She never served the Tenants with a valid N12 notice for purchaser’s own use. The Landlord was well aware of the law with respect to serving N12’s, because she later served the Tenants with a valid N12 notice for landlord’s own use. 30. When it became apparent to the Landlord that her first, illegal attempt was not going to work, she served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination for landlord’s own use. The Landlord said that she moved into the rental unit within nine months after the termination date of February 28, 2022. While that is arguably not a reasonable amount of time between termination date and moving in (nine months), this application is not a T5. Since the Landlord’s evidence that she moved into the rental unit in November 2022 is against her own interest, I find that it lends her evidence more credibility, and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord actually did move into the rental unit in November 2022. 31. Although I find that the Landlord engaged in a campaign of harassment, I find that the Tenants did not leave as the result of an illegal eviction. They did not leave on or before either of the termination dates, and they took a further two months after the March 11, 2022, entry to vacate the rental unit. In addition, as stated above, there is no evidence that the Landlord did not occupy the unit for her own use. That is why they will not be awarded their rent differential or their moving costs (see below). 32. However, service of a valid N12 notice of termination in December 2021, was insufficient to stop the Landlord’s campaign of harassment. She declined the rent payment for January 2022, and then she wrote, on the declined payment message, that the Tenants were occupying the unit illegally. The Landlord said that she wrote this because she honestly believed that they were illegal at that time, however, I find that testimony has no credibility. By January 1, 2022, the Landlord was well aware of the difference between a letter asking the Tenant’s to move out by December 31, 2021, and a formal N12 notice for Landlord’s own use, because she had already served the N12 notice. She was aware of legal eviction procedures. The Landlord further wrote in the message that “formal eviction action and related procedures are in progress”. I see no point to writing all that on a declined payment message unless the Landlord intentionally wanted to intimidate and frighten the Tenants. 33. It is the Landlord’s own evidence that she did not provide a notice of entry to the Tenants for the March 11, 2022, entry. She gave a number of contradictory, and not very credible, reasons for this. She said that she had received complaints about a dog barking from the condo management. She had no documents to support this contention. She said that she believed it was an “emergency” entry, and therefore it did not require a notice of entry, yet she said that she waited four days from first hearing about the complaints to the date she entered. She also said that she believed the Tenants had already moved out by the termination date of February 28, 2022, but she had not communicated with them, nor had she asked them if they vacated. None of the reasons provided by the Landlord for entering on March 11, 2022, make sense. It cannot be an emergency if one waits four days before checking into it, and she could not have believed the Tenants had already moved out if their dog was barking incessantly. 34. As a result of the sequence of events recounted above, I find, on a balance of probabilities, the testimony of DD about what happened on March 11, 2022, far more credible than the [name]. That is, the Landlord decided to enter the unit with her key and a suitcase to further intimidate the Tenants. Consequently, the entry by the Landlord on March 11, 2022, was an egregious illegal entry. 35. The Landlord’s harassment and substantial interference, as well as the illegal entry entitle the Tenants to the following remedies. Remedies 36. The Tenants request a 50% rent abatement for the months of October 2021 through May 31, 2022. I find that a rent abatement of 25% for the eight months is an appropriate abatement. The Tenants were not being bothered by the Landlord every day. There were only a few communications from the Landlord during this period, but they were quite substantive. It is credible that the pressure to leave, reiterated a number of times, and in different ways by the Landlord, combined with the Landlord’s intimidating message on her refusal to accept the January 2022 rent, would significantly interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit. Therefore, they are entitled to 25% abatement, or $200.00 per month for 8 months=$1,600.00. 37. The Tenants failed to provide their new lease with an alleged rent differential of $1,267.68, to support their claim for 12 months of this amount. It is undisputed that the new rental unit was larger and not comparable to the old unit. However, in any case, I find that the Tenants are not entitled to the rent differential because they ultimately left the unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and I have found above that the Landlord did, in fact, move into the rental unit for her own use. The Tenants did not feel so intimidated that they left prior to the termination date. They did not vacate the rental unit until three months after the termination date. For similar reasons, I find that the Tenants are not entitled to their moving costs. More appropriate is the remedy of a one-off payment for the egregious illegal entry of March 11, 2022. I find that I am entitled to grant such a remedy pursuant to subsection 31(1)(f) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). 38. It is undisputed that the entry on March 11, 2022, was without notice. I have found above that it was not an emergency, nor in compliance with any of the requirements of sections 25 through 27 of the Act. 39. In Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, (January 24, 2007), 2007 CanLii 3228 (ON SCDC), one of the foundational cases for illegal entry awards, the Divisional Court awarded the Tenant $1,000.00 rent abatement for a single illegal entry. The Court in that case called it a “rent abatement”, but the Board has repeatedly imposed a one-off, single payment amount of $1,000.00 as an appropriate amount for an illegal entry. 40. The Tenants explained the surprise and shock of the entry on March 11, 2022. The evidence is that the Landlord did not retreat immediately after seeing DD, but she remained in the rental unit, having entered unannounced with her own key, for several minutes, shouting back and forth. DD gave contradictory evidence about whether she knew that it was the Landlord who had entered. I find that DD could have, at first, been confused because, as she said, the Landlord was wearing a mask. It is undisputed that the Landlord had not provided a notice of entry, so it is not surprising that DD would be shocked and terrified to suddenly find a person, carrying a suitcase, in her kitchen, and then be further shocked that the person would not leave, but rather engage in a shouting match with her. I find that the Landlord must have remained several minutes, because it is the testimony of both DD and MD that DD had enough time to call MD in the midst of the shouting, and MD heard some of the argument. Both Tenants testified that DD remains traumatized by this incident. Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a larger payment than $1,000.00 because of the understandable trauma they suffered as a result of this entry. The Wrona decision awarding $1,000.00, was also almost 20 years old. Taking into account the length of time, almost 20 years, since that decision and inflation, as well as the traumatic nature of the entry, I find the payment should be larger then $1,000.00. I find that a one-off payment of $2,500.00 for the illegal entry is appropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,148.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00 for a rent abatement. • $2,500.00 for the illegal entry. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Eshanzada and [name] [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (the ‘first T2 application’). In file number LTB-T-053843-23, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the reasonable supply of a vital service (the ‘second T2 application’). In file number LTB-T-028322-24, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the [name] failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 application’). These applications were heard by videoconference on June 29, 2026. The Landlord [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: These related applications were scheduled together and on having case management discussions with the parties, I determined it would be fair and expeditious to hear them together as the evidence of both parties would be common to all applications.

In the first T2 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord played loud music on October 16, 2022 that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit. That application adds that on October 27, 2022 and again on November 3, 2022, someone illegally entered the rental unit.

The second T2 application adds the Tenant was without electricity for two days in July 2023 putting her to hotel and restaurant expenses which she seeks to recover. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord declined to reset the fuses when they tripped and thereby unreasonably withheld the supply of electricity.

In the T6 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to fix a persistent water leak and faulty wiring that caused the fuses to trip. The T6 application further alleges the Landlord deliberately ignored her maintenance obligations as a form of harassment calculated to drive her out of the rental unit. The Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2023 and seeks her moving expenses and difference in rent.

Nearly all of the Tenant’s issues were already resolved by the Board’s order LTB-L- 056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 and therefore could not be relitigated in these applications. Of those that remain, the Tenant was only able to prove one, as detailed below. Therefore, the rest of the claims must be dismissed.

Before discussing the substance of the claims, I pause to make a note about the quality of the evidence. I had misgivings about the Tenant’s testimony because I found the Tenant was prone to exaggeration and equivocation where she perceived it to be needful. While this manner of presentation no doubt stemmed from a desire to forcefully advocate for her cause and not a deliberate attempt to mislead the Board, it still gives me serious concerns about its reliability. Furthermore, much of the materials the Tenant relied on in support of her claims were her own communications voicing her complaints either directly to the Landlord or to third parties such as municipal inspectors. These prior consistent statements are not proof of the truth of their contents.

The Tenant carries the burden to prove her allegations on a balance of probabilities. Where I find the evidence to be evenly balanced, I must dismiss the claim because the Tenant has not discharged her burden. Leaks, [name] and Property Loss

The Tenant says that almost immediately after moving into the unit in October of 2021, she discovered persistent leaking into the rental unit that the Landlord failed to remediate leading to an infestation of mould. She raised those concerns in response to the Landlord’s application to collect rent arrears heard on May 23, 2024 and received compensation by order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024.

The Tenant seeks to enlarge her recovery, relying on a report from Safetech Environmental Limited dated October 27, 2023 that says personnel from that company visited the unit on October 17, 2023 to assess water damage and identify potential mould. They tested samples and reported their readings. The report contains no opinion about an infestation of mould nor a finding that the rental unit is unsafe for habitation. Rather, it contains a specific disclaimer that the author is not qualified to give such an opinion. The photographs relied on show dampness and mildew but no visible mould growth, much less anything that could be called an infestation.

The Tenant says the Landlord ignored the findings of the mould experts. She says she sent the Landlord this report by email on November 6, 2023 but did not include a copy of that particular email in the package of emails and text messages filed. The Landlord testified she was only given the report as the Tenant was vacating the rental unit on December 31, 2023.

The Tenant testified that a further major leak event occurred in the month of December 2023 as the Tenant was preparing her move. Her packed belongings were soaked through with water and had to be discarded by a specialist waste management firm qualified to handle toxic mould as her regular movers refused to touch them for fear of injury. No photographs were produced showing the Tenant’s personal property to be damaged, or infested with mould.

The Tenant gave no explanation for why she did not seek this additional relief when the Board heard her concerns about leaking on May 23, 2024. The Tenant offered no principled reason why this claim should be litigated again on a different evidentiary record. The Tenant would have had in her possession or control all the facts and documents, including the Safetech report, and particulars of her lost property as of the hearing of May 23, 2024. [name] that the doctrine of cause of action estoppel is discretionary and must not be mechanically applied in all cases, I find it bars the Tenant’s disrepair claims in this case because it would undermine the objectives of finality and certainty in Board decisions if issues finally decided between the same parties were litigated again. Therefore, I find the claims in relation to leaks, mould, and concomitant property loss must be dismissed as res judicata. Electrical issues

The Tenant testified that on innumerable occasions, the fuses would trip because they were faulty and, because the Tenant had no access to the electrical panel, she could not reset them leaving her with no power for hours, sometimes days, at a time. The Tenant says she later discovered that the electrical supply and the wiring was inadequate for servicing two separate households and the Landlord’s failure to fix it is a breach of section 20 of the Act. The Board’s reasons for decision in order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 disclose that the Tenant advanced the same claim in those proceedings. For reasons detailed above, I find this claim is res judicata and cannot be raised again in new applications. [name]

The Tenant says that although the tenancy agreement shows laundry is not included, the written agreement is not consistent with the true agreement because she was orally promised laundry. The Tenant testified that she signed the written agreement under duress, as she needed housing urgently and was therefore not in a position to negotiate or seek alternatives.

The Board’s order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 has already found that laundry facilities were not included in this tenancy. I find this claim must be dismissed because the issue has finally been decided by the Board and I was given no persuasive reason why the Board should allow it to be relitigated. Parking

The Tenant seeks compensation because she was only given one parking spot when she was promised two. I find this claim must be dismissed because the tenancy agreement specifically speaks of only one parking spot. Guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the Tenant’s testimony that she felt compelled to sign the agreement is insufficient to prove that the substance of the contract was anything other than what it says. The Tenant led no evidence of having lodged any complaints about having only one spot and led no evidence of the Landlord ever having granted her the use of two spots. Illegal Entries

The Tenant testified that the door separating her unit from the main floor unit where the Landlord lived was not adequately secured, such that members of the Landlord’s family and her guests would wander into her private space. She presented a text message of October 27, 2022 where the Landlord contacted the Tenant to tell her a child had entered the rental unit and to apologize for the intrusion. The Tenant also wrote the Landlord on November 3, 2022 stating that someone tried to enter her rental unit. The Landlord responded that it was her brother sliding the mail under the door but promised to put a lock on that door to safeguard against any future intrusions.

I find the child inadvertently entering the rental unit on October 27, 2022 cannot be characterized as an illegal entry within the meaning of section 25 of the Act because that entry was not instigated by the Landlord or done at her behest or by anyone acting on her behalf. In any case, the Tenant admitted this entry caused no impact.

I find the evidence insufficient to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s brother actually entered the rental unit on November 3, 2022 because I find it at least equally probable that he merely slid the mail under the door as the Landlord says. That would be consistent with the Tenant’s description of the event as an attempted entry.
Although the Tenant spoke of countless other intrusions on her privacy by strangers, she offered no details in her evidence. Loud Music

I find the Tenant was unable to prove this incident on a balance of probabilities because, given the Landlord’s denial of the event, and the lack of any confirmatory evidence (such as a recording), I must find the evidence equally balanced and therefore insufficient to discharge the burden of proof. Harassment, Obstruction and Threats

The Tenant claims that once she voiced her concerns about disrepair, the Landlord embarked on a campaign of harassment that involved blocking her access to her parking spot, making constant complaints by phone and email, serving notices of termination, deliberately shutting off the electricity and enlisting her brother to redouble the illegal entries into the rental unit. The Landlord denied each of these allegations in turn but allowed that she did serve N4 notices for arrears of rent and an N12 notice to repossess for her own use. This Board has consistently held that attempting to enforce one’s rights under the Act, even unsuccessfully, cannot be characterized as harassment: [name] v 6891799 Canada Inc., 2023 ONLTB 25933 at para. 70; TST-49807-14 (Re), 2015 CanLII 34298 (ON LTB), at para 68.

As discussed above, the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that anyone illegally entered the rental unit at any time. The Tenant filed a text message where the Landlord cautions that if the Tenant does not advise in advance of her guests using the driveway for parking, she will assume these are trespassers and will have their car removed. I would not characterize this communication as harassment or a threat within the meaning of section 23. I agree that the tone is somewhat unprofessional but there is no evidence it happened more than once and critically, the Tenant led no evidence of how it impacted her warranting any recovery for what, even if proven, would be a trivial breach. [name]

The Tenant has proven the claim contained in the second T2 application that the Landlord deliberately shut off electricity for some 8 days in July 2023 by reference to an entry in a municipal inspector’s notes that says: Attended location and spoke with property owner on the phone and advised them that they need to turn the power back right away. They kept saying they turned it off because of no payment from tenant.

I accept this hearsay evidence and the Tenant’s testimony because the Landlord did not deny it and in fact, explained at length about how the Tenant’s choice to withhold rent caused her financial hardship. The Landlord did not say that the utility provider had discontinued service for want of payment. The evidence suggest that the Landlord restored power after learning of her mistake as the municipal inspector closed his file when the Tenant did not renew her complaint. Still, withholding the supply of a vital service for non-payment, in these circumstances, is unreasonable within the meaning of section 21 of the Act which means this claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities. Remedies

Having established that the Landlord unreasonably withheld the supply of electricity in July 2023, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies she can prove on a balance of probabilities in relation to that breach. That claim is pleaded in the second T2 application that claims out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $1,000.00 and an administrative fine. Hotels and Meals

The Tenant has delivered hotel bills totalling $1,240.22 and proof of payments made to restaurants totalling $526.46 to substantiate this claim. The Tenant testified that living in the rental unit without power was impossible so she relocated herself and her child to hotels and ate at restaurants. The Tenant filed an invoice for a stay at the Pickering Casino Hotel for July 9 to July 14, 2023 issued to herself. She also relied on another invoice for Sheraton Centre Hotel in Toronto spanning the period July 15 to July 18, 2023 issued to [name] of Villa Park, California. I was not told why the Tenant’s hotel invoice is drawn up in the name of that person. That invoice speaks of additional pages which weren’t filed.

The Tenant explained that having experienced an abusive relationship, she was unable to take lodgings in the same locality as the rental unit for fear that her abuser might find her. So the Tenant decided to stay at a hotel in Toronto. She has filed four POS printouts from various restaurants in Toronto for July 15 and July 16, 2023. The Tenant did not explain why she was not fearful of staying at the Pickering Casino Resort between July 9 and July 15, 2023 which is in the same locality as the rental unit.

I find that the Tenant has failed to prove either causation or the quantum of damages claimed on a balance of probabilities because her documentary proof is unreliable on its face and contradicts her testimony. I recognize that as trier of fact I must assess a fair and reasonable amount of compensation even where that task is made difficult by frailties in the evidence. However, in this case, I find the evidentiary record is so lacking that the task is impossible. I find the Tenant’s choice of hotels and restaurants is not consistent with an emergency. Accordingly I can only award nominal damages. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $100.00 for deliberately depriving her of electricity. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not binding on me but I accept it as the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

This remedy is not normally granted unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and ensure future compliance. The objectives of deterrence involve both specific and general deterrence. I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act or to deter future breaches. The Landlord has already been ordered to compensate the Tenant in respect of the disrepair claims adjudicated in file number LTB-L-056337-23 and I find that no further deterrence is required in respect of the one claim that has been proven in these proceedings.
The Tenant incurred no filing fee in respect of the second T2 application which is the only one that was successful.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $100.00 on or before August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Morley (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This application is about the responsibility for cleaning up fallen tree branches and repairing the damage caused by them. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has failed to meet his obligations under s. 20 of the Act by failing to remove three large branches which fell during a winter storm in December 2025 and in failing to repair damage to the backyard of the rental unit caused by the fallen branches.
For the reasons set out below, I find that the Landlord failed to meet his obligation under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit. Background
The facts of this case are largely not in dispute.

On the night of December 27, 2025, an ice storm caused three large tree branches to fall into the backyard of the rental unit, which damaged planter boxes and a fence separating the rental unit from neighbouring properties.

The Tenant referred me to several photographs taken by him which show the extent of the issue. In one taken on December 27, 2025 (DOC-7675917), the fallen branches take up most of the visible area of the backyard and there is a large hole in the fence separating the rental unit and a neighbouring property. There is also damage to a planter box in the right side of the photograph.
The Tenant first notified the Landlord via email on December 28, 2025, and again on January 2, 2026. In both cases, the Tenant attached photographs of the fallen branches.

Despite emailing the Landlord on December 28, 2025, and again on January 2, 2026, the Landlord took no action to fix the issue and commence repairs to the backyard. As such, the Tenant undertook the repairs himself.

When the Landlord and the Tenant attended before the Board on a separate matter in March 2026, the Tenant again raised the issue of the tree branches to the Landlord. The Landlord laughed at the Tenant, told him it was the neighbours’ problem and not the [name], and asked why the Tenant fixed the problem himself.

The Tenant states that he spent 2-3 half days in January 2026, 3-4 half days in March 2026, and approximately 10 hours over 4-5 days in May 2026. The work involved cutting the branches down into smaller pieces with a chainsaw, taking the pieces to a local dump, and repairing the hole in the fence. Tenant has a disability which made him unable to work more than a half day at a time on the repairs.
The Tenant referred me to a photo taken on June 21, 2026 ([name]), which shows the repairs have been completed, including the repair to the fence.

The Landlord testified on his own behalf. He did not dispute the fact that the tree branches had fallen into the yard and caused damage, that he had been put on notice by the Tenant on December 28, 2025, and again on January 2, 2026, that the Tenant had effected the repairs himself, or the time expended by the Tenant effecting repairs.

Instead, the Landlord testified that as the branches came from a tree in the neighbours’ yard, it was the neighbours’ problem to fix, and not his. However, the Landlord also admitted that he had not spoken to the neighbours about the issue nor asked them to fix it. In fact, the Landlord does not know the neighbours at all.

The Landlord testified that it is not fair that the Tenant is “trying to charge me” for repairs that are not the Landlord’s responsibility. He referred me to the second page of a purported contract between the parties entered into at the time the tenancy commenced in October 2017 (DOC-8245085). The document states, among other things: • That the Tenant “agrees to maintain property for safety and repairing something inside and outside the house for day move in [sic]”; • “…if tenants is not happy to live in the property and then feel free to find yourself new place to live for yourself and your family [sic]”; and • “don’t bother Landlord or call Landlord anything, Landlord is not your babysitter[sic]”. The Tenant disputes the validity of this agreement and states that he does not remember signing it. He says he thinks the document is fraudulent. He also disputes the Landlord’s characterization of the tree as being the neighbours’, and states that it is on the Landlord’s side of the property line. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the Board should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Landlord did absolutely nothing to fix the issue identified by the Tenant once being made aware of it. Instead, the Landlord seeks to shift his legal responsibilities onto others, including the Tenant and the neighbours. I will address both these issues in turn.

Section 20 of the Act makes it clear that it is the responsibility of the Landlord and not the Tenant to maintain and repair the rental unit: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Sections 3 and 4 of the Act make clear that the Act prevails despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary, and that provisions in tenancy agreements that conflict with the Act are void: 3 (1) This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. 4 (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void. What this means is that, even if the Landlord and the Tenant did agree to shift the responsibility for maintenance and repair to the Tenant, such an agreement would be worthless. The responsibility to maintain and repair always remained with the Landlord.

It is also irrelevant whether the tree branches originated from the neighbours’ property or not. While, given the Tenant’s extensive photographic documentation, I accept on a balance of probabilities that the branches were from a tree located within the boundaries of the rental unit and not the neighbours’ yard, even if the opposite were true, it does not absolve the Landlord of the responsibility to maintain and repair under the Act. Once the tree branches fell into the backyard of the rental unit and the Tenant notified the Landlord, the Landlord’s obligations under s. 20 of the Act were engaged.
