During the hearing, I referred the Landlord to sections 4 and 20 of the Act. In response, the Landlord made it clear that he does not feel he is bound by the Act and that it would be unfair to hold him to his responsibilities under it.

I do not find expecting the Landlord to comply with his responsibilities under the Act to be unfair in any way whatsoever. I do however find that it would be unfair to the Tenant to allow the Landlord to escape his responsibilities under the Act by shifting them onto other persons; in any event, I am bound to apply the Act as it is written.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord has failed to meet his obligations under s. 20 of the Act. Remedies

The Tenant claimed $1,465.00 in out-of-pocket expenses. This claim covers both purchases related to the removal of the tree branches, as well as time lost effecting repairs that the Landlord failed to do.

The Tenant claimed the amount of $200.00 for additional gas expenses resulting from attending at the local dump multiple times to dispose of the tree branches, as well as for the purchase of batteries for an electric chainsaw used to cut the tree branches to a manageable size prior to removal. This amount was not disputed by the Landlord, and I find the amount to be reasonable in the circumstances

The Tenant spent 2-3 half days in January, 3-4 half days in March, and approximately 10 hours over 4-5 days in May 2026. In this context, I take “half day” to mean half of an ordinary 8-hour working day, i.e. 4 hours. Combined, this means that the Tenant spent 38 hours fixing a problem that was properly the Landlord’s to fix.

Additionally, I have also considered the fact that the Tenant is a person with a disability, who cannot work more than a half day without his muscles cramping up. I also take note of the fact that the bulk of the time spent by the Tenant effecting these repairs took place in the winter to early spring, outside and in cold temperatures.
Given the above factors, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant an additional $1,265.00 for the time spent effecting repairs that were the Landlord’s responsibility to undertake and complete.
Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,465.00 for out-of-pocket expenses.
This order contains all my reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,465.00. This amount represents the reasonable out- of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for any future rent periods until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application); • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services (T2 Application); and, • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant requested to amend her application to request that the tenancy be terminated effective December 24, 2024, the date the Tenant left the rental unit. She further requests that the Board issue an administrative fine to the Landlords in the amount of $10,000.00.
The Landlord did not contest the request for the amendment to the application to the termination date. The Landlord did contest the request for a Board administrative fine; however.

With regard to the request to terminate the tenancy effective December 24, 2025, I did not find any prejudice to the parties in granting the amendment particularly as the Landlord did not contest the Tenant’s amendment request. Therefore, I consented to the Tenant’s amendment request to include a request to terminate the tenancy on December 24, 2024.

With regard to the amendment to include a Board administrative fine, the purpose of Board administrative fines is discussed in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline #16 (LTB | Administrative Fines) and includes instances where vital services have been withheld and unlawful entries, both of which are allegations in the Tenant’s applications. The purpose of an administrative fine is to deter landlords from engaging in similar behaviour in the future and other remedies do not adequately address deterrence and compliance with the Act. The Landlord was also given an opportunity to make submissions on the Tenant’s request.

Based on the submissions before me, and the seriousness of the allegations, and considering whether the Tenant’s requested remedies would adequately act as deterrent, and I am persuaded that amending the Tenant’s application to include a request for a Board administrative fine is appropriate in the circumstances. Tenant’s Application
As explained bel ow, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $250.00.

By way of background, the tenancy was a two-bedroom basement unit. The upper rental unit was also tenanted. The tenancy began on September 1, 2024, and terminated on December 24, 2024. At the beginning of the tenancy, the tenancy was a joint tenancy with a second Tenant, ‘HS’, who is not named as a party to this tenancy. However, this individual left the tenancy after about one month. The Landlords were aware of this change. T1 Application 6. The Tenant states that the Landlords did not refund her $1,650.00 last month’s rent deposit or $250.00 security deposit which she paid at the beginning of the tenancy. 7. The Landlord does not deny collecting or retaining these funds. He adds that there were cleaning fees which he incurred as a result of the Tenant. Security Deposit

Section 105(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’), states that: “The only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.” Section 106(2) sets out that a security deposit may be no more than the rent for one month.

Section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’), states: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; [Emphasis added]

Per s.106(2), the Landlord was entitled to collect the last months’ rent deposit. Per s.134 of the Act; however, the Landlords were not entitled to collect or require a tenant to pay any kind of security deposit such as a fee, etc. Therefore, the Landlords were not entitled to collect the $250.00 security deposit nor are the Landlords entitled to a fee for cleaning as these are prohibited by s.134(1)(a). As such, I find that the Landlords collected an amount of money which they were not entitled to and the Tenant must be reimbursed for this charge. An order shall issue. Rent Deposit

The Tenant also seeks the return of her last months’ rent deposit. However, the Tenant says she did not pay rent for the month of December 2024 as her last month’s rent deposit was applied to that month.

Given that the Tenant did not pay rent for the month of December, her last months’ rent deposit was applied to the month of December. Section 106(1) of the Act states that a landlord shall apply a rent deposit to the last period before the tenancy terminates. The Landlords applied the last month’s rent deposit to December, the month the tenancy terminated. Therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to reimbursement of the deposit paid. T2 Application

The Tenant also claims that the Landlords substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the tenancy, withheld vital services, harassed or interfered with the Tenant, and unlawfully entered the rental unit. Power Cut-Off

The Tenant submits that the Landlords withheld power from the rental unit despite the cost of utilities being included in the cost of the monthly rent. A copy of the tenancy agreement was submitted into evidence corroborating this. However, the Tenant says that on October 3 through October 11, 2024, the power was “cut-off”. 16. The Landlord does not disagree that the Tenant was without power, although he disputes the dates stating that the period was from October 12 through November 1, 2024. Regardless, I do not find this discrepancy material to my determinations. The Landlord states that he provided a gas-powered generator to the Tenant, with extra fuel, extension cords, and a heater. This was in place until the power was restored to the rental unit. 17. The Landlord explained that the power was being paid for by the tenant in the upper rental unit because the units did not have separate power meters. The upper tenant, who had been living in the rental unit for about 12 years, stopped paying for the power utility in September. Electra, the utilities provider, withdrew service after the upper tenant failed to pay the utility bill. He called Electra, but they would not discuss the file with him because he was not the account holder. 18. The Tenant was able to restore the power to the rental unit herself. She agreed to pay the outstanding utility bills and Electra turned the power back on. The outstanding utility bills the Tenant paid totalled $307.53. However, the Tenant states that she withheld rent for the month of November, in part, because of having to pay to have the power restored. 19. Section 21(1) of the Act specifies that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service. Vital services are described in s. 2(1) of the Act and includes electricity. Section 22 of the Act states that landlord shall not interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental property. 20. Given the specific wording found in s.21(1) of the Act, I am not persuaded that the Landlords withheld the supply of any vital service. He was not the account holder, nor did he have the power shut off to the rental unit. The utility bill was not paid by the upper tenant, and the utility company turned the power off as a result. For the same reason, I am not persuaded that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment because the Tenant did not have utility-supplied power between October 3 and October 11, 2024. 21. Although the case of Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd.1 referred to a Landlord’s obligation to maintain a rental unit in accordance with s.20(1) of the Act, I find the Court of Appeal’s analysis applicable to the situation at hand, stating at par. 80: [80] [name] illustrates that tenants do not bargain for a particular service or facility that can never be changed or interrupted. Looking at the jurisprudence as a whole, it appears that [page315] a landlord ought to provide something in exchange for a significant interruption or discontinuation of a particular facility or service. The adequacy of what is provided is to be adjudged by regard to the legislation and regulations under the RTA, the board's Guidelines and the particular factual circumstances, including the reasonable expectations of the parties viewed objectively. 1 Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) 22. In this case, the Landlords took immediate steps to try to rectify the loss of power by contacting the utility company, and providing a generator, fuel, and extension cords, power bars, and a heater. In my view, the Landlords acted in an appropriate, timely, and reasonable fashion. 23. Even if I am wrong and the Landlords are in breach of the Act, the only remedy sought by the Tenant was $570.06 for the cost of lost groceries. The Tenant led no evidence to substantiate the claim for lost groceries. As such, no order shall issue. Unlawful Entries 24. The Tenant also alleges three instances of unlawful entries: October 7, 12, and December 8, 2024. The Tenant states that on October 7, 2024, she discovered the extension cords and heater in the rental unit, but she was not informed the Landlords would be attending the rental unit. On October 12, 2024, she found these same items removed from the rental unit. Again, no notice was given that the Landlords would attend the rental unit. 25. The third instance was not the Landlords who are alleged to have unlawfully entered the rental unit. Rather, it was a new tenant, who was going to be moving into the rental unit to occupy the second bedroom which had been previously occupied by HS. The Tenant says she was taken aback by this person who was at the door saying she was going to move into the rental unit. The Tenant says she did not agree to the new roommate moving in. The new tenant just “showed up.” 26. The Landlord provides a different picture of the situation. He says that on October 7, 2024, HS was still in possession of the rental unit. When he arrived with the generator, HS provided verbal consent for his attendance to sort out the power needs. The Landlord states there was no additional entries and denies that anyone attended the rental unit on October 12, 2024. 27. With regard to the December 8, 2024, entry, he says after HS moved out, the Tenant said she could not afford the rent. She was going to look for a new roommate. The Landlord offered that he could also look for a new roommate to assist. The Tenant agreed but stipulated that she would not feel comfortable with a male roommate. 28. The Landlord then set about finding a renter and told the Tenant that he found someone and that it was a female. This new tenant was to move in on December 1, 2024, although there was conflicting testimony about the date she actually moved in. However, he says the Tenant was aware there was new tenant moving in. 29. Section 26(1) of the Act provides that a landlord may enter without notice if there is an emergency or if the tenant consented to the entry at the time of entry. 30. I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that HS gave consent on October 7, 2024, and that the Landlord did not reattend the rental unit on October 12, 2024. I say this because, I found the Tenant’s evidence lacked reliability and credibility during the hearing. 31. In R. v. Morrissey2, (1995), 1995 CanLII 3498 at p. 205, the Court of Appeal addressed the reliability of testimonial evidence, and the interaction between credibility and reliability: Testimonial evidence can raise veracity and accuracy concerns. The former relate to the witness's sincerity, that is, his or her willingness to speak the truth as the witness believes it to be. The latter concerns relate to the actual accuracy of the witness's testimony. The accuracy of a witness's testimony involves considerations of the witness's ability to accurately observe, recall and recount the events in issue. When one is concerned with a witness's veracity, one speaks of the witness's credibility. When one is concerned with the accuracy of a witness's testimony, one speaks of the reliability of that testimony. Obviously a witness whose evidence on a point is not credible cannot give reliable evidence on that point. The evidence of a credible, that is, honest witness, may, however, still be unreliable. … 32. In this case, I found the Tenant left out pertinent details when testifying. In other words, her sincerity to speak the truth, as stated in Morrissey, above, calls into question her credibility. The Tenant did not tell the Board that she had been provided with a generator while she was without power. She did not explain that she had agreed to allow the Landlord to assist her with finding a new roommate. Lastly, at the beginning of the hearing, she explained she paid the rent in December. However, later in the hearing she then said that her last month’s rent deposit had been applied to December’s rent despite her application clearly stating that the Landlords withheld the funds unlawfully. 33. Further, the evidence does not demonstrate that the new tenant, who came to reside in the rental unit in December, unlawfully entered the rental unit. Rather, the Tenant expressed her surprise at finding the new tenant at the door ready to move in after she says she told the Landlord she objected. 34. Section 26 refers to the “landlord’s” unlawful entry. In this case, there is no question the person who attended December 8, 2024, was not one of the Landlords. I am also not persuaded that the new tenant was an agent of the Landlords. Typically, an agent is acting on a landlord’s behalf, such as a realtor or property manager. There is no evidence to suggest this new tenant was acting on behalf of the Landlords. 35. The Tenant did not provide any evidence, beyond her oral statement, which could demonstrate that she had objected to this individual moving in. Further, the Tenant did not testify that she refused to allow the new tenant into the residence. In my view, this supports the Landlord’s version of events that the Tenant was aware there was a new roommate move in. I also accept the Landlord’s testimony that this arrangement was made to assist the Tenant and was not done maliciously. No order shall issue. 2 R. v. Morrissey, (1995), 1995 CanLII 3498 at p. 205 Termination of the Tenancy 36. The Tenant seeks an order to terminate the tenancy on December 24, 2024, the date she left the rental unit. She states that the situation became untenable, as a result of the three alleged unlawful entries, renting the unit to another tenant, and the power issue. 37. The Landlord states that he was not given proper notice nor did the Tenant terminate the tenancy in accordance with the Act. Therefore, he objects to the Board terminating the tenancy on the date the Tenant left the rental unit. 38. The Tenant did not terminate her tenancy in accordance with the Act. She had signed a fixed-term tenancy agreement to end on August 31, 2025. Despite this, she terminated the tenancy on December 24, 2024, notifying the Landlord the same day she left. 39. I am not persuaded that the issues the Tenant experienced were sufficient to warrant terminating the tenancy early. I say this because although there was an interruption in power, the Landlord’s evidence, which I accept, is that as soon as he was made aware of the problem, he immediately addressed it. Further, by the time the Tenant left the rental unit, the power had already been restored by the utility company for about six weeks. When she left, this was no longer a live issue. 40. I am also not persuaded that the alleged unlawful entries were sufficient to warrant terminating the tenancy early. The first two entries took place in early October. If the Tenant was so distressed by these alleged entries, it does not accord that it was not until after the new tenant moved in, in December, that she decided to leave. I find it is more likely than not that the Tenant did not wish to live with the new roommate and that is why she terminated the tenancy early. No order shall issue. Board Administrative Fine 41. The allegations of the lack of power, unlawful entries, and the new tenant being moved in are relevant to the Tenant’s request for a Board fine of $10,000.00. She says the situation made her feel unsafe and interfered with her mental and physical health. 42. The Landlord says that he does not believe a fine is warranted in the circumstances. He took all reasonable steps to address the power issue. Further, he says he did not unlawfully enter the rental unit, and the new tenant was only brought in to help the Tenant because she could not afford the rent on her own after [name] left. 43. While not binding on me, I have considered the Board’s Guideline 16, and I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is warranted in the circumstances. I am not satisfied that the Landlords showed a blatant disregard for the Act which requires an order to deter future behaviour or ensure future compliance with the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $298.00. This amount represents: • $250.00 for the return of unlawfully collected funds, and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 27, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order. Substantial interference:
The Tenant, [name] (D.K.), testified that she moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2020, and continues to reside in the unit as of the date of the hearing.

D.K. testified that on February 22, 2024, she notified the Landlord of a mold issue in her rental unit and requested that the Landlord address the issue. The mold issue related to observations of surface mold around a bedroom windowsill. The Tenant notified the Landlord of this concern by way of text communications. A screenshot of the text communication was tendered as evidence by the Tenant.

D.K. testified that despite the Landlord acknowledging and responding to her text message on February 24, 2024, the Landlord did not make any effort to attend the unit or inspect the problem until March 9, 2024. The Tenant did not believe this was a timely response.

D.K. testified that the Landlord attended the rental unit on March 9, 2024, inspected the mold around the windowsill in the bedroom and stated that it would have to be cleaned and repainted. The Landlord did not remove the visible surface mold on this date but did other repair work inside the rental unit.

The Landlord informed the Tenant that she would also be reaching out to the Condominium Corporation and Management Company to determine whether the issue was the responsibility of the Landlord or Condo Corporation. D.K. testified that the Landlord failed to contact the Condo Corporation or Management Office until approximately March 21, 2024, a delay that the Tenant also felt was also unreasonable.

D.K. testified that on March 27, 2024, she contacted the Landlord and informed the Landlord that the issue was getting worse, and a mold specialist was required to inspect the area. The Landlord retained the services of a mold company to attend and inspect the rental unit on March 30, 2024. The inspection took place on March 30, 2024.

D.K. followed up with the Landlord on April 1, 2024, at which time the Landlord informed the Tenant that no above normal moisture levels were detected in the unit, and that there was some surface mold observed on the windowsill. This surface mold was identified as safe to clean with household cleaners from time to time as needed. D.K. testified that the inspection did not include any removal of the walls or baseboards that had signs of water damage to determine if any mold is a concern deeper than the surface. Based on the inspection of the mold technician, the Landlord was not prepared to take any further steps. The surface mold was not cleaned by the technician or Landlord at this time.

On April 2, 2024, the Tenant contacted the management company directly and informed them of her issues and concerns. The management company replied by stating that they would have someone attend and inspect the unit on April 9, 2024.

D.K. testified that because she was concerned about her health and about the quality of the inspection performed by the Landlord’s technician, the Tenant retained the service of a third-party mold technician who attended and inspected the rental unit on April 3, 2024. The report of the technician indicated findings of surface mold and notes of there being a high probability of mold growth behind the baseboards and wall beneath the windowsill. The recommendations included having the mold professionally removed by sealing of the area, opening the areas that could have been exposed, inspecting, removing mold, and treating said areas as necessary. D.K. incurred costs of $584.21 for the mold inspection. The Tenant tendered a copy of the mold report as evidence.

D.K. testified that the management company sent a contractor to inspect the unit using thermal imaging equipment which revealed significant areas showing moisture and concern. Based on the inspection and observations of the inspection, the management company determined that a section of the wall below the windowsill must be removed to be properly inspected and re-installed after being treated for mold if necessary. The Tenant was informed the work would take approximately one day to complete.

D.K. testified that the repair work in the bedroom started on April 15, 2024, and was not completed until April 18, 2024, being an unexpected delay of two days. D.K. testified that she was negatively impacted by this work because she was required to move all her belongings in and out of the bedroom and also maintain all of the items in the living room while still living in the unit. The Landlord refused to provide the Tenant with alternative housing during the period which the work was being carried out.

D.K. was not satisfied with the work done by the management company and attend Parkdale Legal Clinic and had a letter written to the Landlord requesting that the repair work be properly completed as per the suggestions and recommendations of the mold technician she hired. The Landlord responded by confirming the work required was completed.

D.K. testified that between the period of April 19, 2024, through to March 12, 2025, the Tenant did not experience or observe any mold on the windowsill that had been previously repaired by the Landlord.

D.K. testified that on March 13, 2025, she notified the Landlord that she has started noticing mold again on the windowsill and requires someone to inspect the issue. D.K. also informed the Landlord that the mold was now also visible on another window located near the balcony in the living room area.

D.K. testified that the management company sent another contractor to attend the unit on May 8, 2025, and inspect the window with mold issues. D.K. testified that the contractor cleaned the mold from the balcony window but wanted to wait until winter to inspect where the issue was as the Tenant stated it would primarily only leak during the winter/spring.

D.K. testified that on February 3, 2026, she contacted the Landlord and the management company to determine when someone would be coming into the unit to re-inspect as she was previously informed. The management company had a contractor attend and inspect the rental unit on February 10, 2026. The management company observed that the window weather stripping required replacement. The replacement of the window weather stripping was completed on March 26, 2026.
D.K. testified that since completion of the window weather stripping, she has not observed any signs of visible surface mold or otherwise.
D.K. testified that she believed that the Landlord’s delayed actions of addressing the concern resulted in the substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenant was seeking a rent abatement of one month’s rent, out of pocket expenses in the amount of $584.21 for the cost of having the mold test completed, and $5,000.00 in general damages for loss of income.
On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she is not a mold expert. The Tenant also confirmed that the Landlord is not a mold expert.
The Tenant confirmed that the work done in 2024 was completed by the management company between the period of April 15, 2024, through to April 18, 2024.
The Tenant also testified that she did not recall the Landlord having the unit re- inspected by a mold technician in 2025.
The Tenant also confirmed that she did not provide any documentation to support her claim for general compensation and loss of income.

The Landlord, [name] (J.W.), testified that she lived in the rental unit with her husband between the period of February 2014, through to 2020, at which time the unit was occupied by the Tenant. 26. [name] testified that she never experienced any issues regarding mold or water leakage during the time in which she occupied the property. 27. [name] testified that the Tenant informed her of concerns regarding condensation, humidity, and mold on February 22, 2024. The Landlord informed the Tenant that she would be attending the unit personally to do a visual inspection. The Landlord attended the unit on March 9, 2024. 28. [name] testified that on March 9, 2024, she attended the unit and observed some discoloration around the windowsill and some water damage, but she did not believe the issue was serious in nature. 29. The Landlord contacted the property management company for the condo corporation approximately one week after inspecting the rental unit. The purpose of contacting the property management company was to try and determine if this was an issue the Landlord would have to repair or an issue the condo corporation would address. The Landlord attributed the one-week delay in contacting the management company because she was going out of town and would contact them upon her return. 30. [name] testified that she had a mold technician inspect the rental unit on March 27, 2024. The Landlord testified that the mold technician observed some surface mold in the bedroom windowsill and also noted that the humidity in the bedroom was approximately 71% and the norm should be between 30% to a maximum of 50%. No elevated levels of moisture were detected at the time of the inspection. The Landlord tendered a report dated March 30, 2024, as evidence. 31. The report made recommendations such as running the exhaust fans after showering and cooking for at least 30 minutes, using a dehumidifier when necessary, and not storing any items to close to the window allowing airflow and circulation. The mold was not cleaned from the windowsill at the time of this inspection. The Tenant was simply informed that it was safe to clean same with the use of household cleaners. 32. [name] testified that the property management company had informed her that they were also in the process of sealing areas outside of the residential complex that may be impacting the rental unit. 33. J.W. confirmed that the work was done between April 15, 2024, and April 18, 2024, and that the work took longer than initially predicted due to the contractor wanting to allow some time for the area to settle before completing the work. [name] also testified that the work was initially planned for April 11, 2024, but the Tenant requested a short delay. 34. [name] testified that the next time she heard from the Tenant regarding this issue was not until March 13, 2025, when the Tenant contacted the Landlord and informed her that she was experiencing further problems around the windowsill area in the bedroom again. The Tenant also informed the Landlord that there was now also visible mold around the window near the balcony in the living room. 35. The Landlord responded by notifying the Condo Management Company, who arranged to inspect the unit on the week of March 17, 2025. The management’s contractor attended the unit and observed visible signs of surface mold due to the high humidity levels in the rental unit. No leaks or high moisture levels were found at the time of inspecting the unit. 36. [name] testified that she also arranged to have the unit re-inspected by the mold technician that previously attended the unit. The mold technician attended the unit on April 14, 2025. The mold technician observed sign of surface mold around the windowsill but did not identify any high or abnormal levels of moisture. He informed the Landlord that the surface mold was safe to clean with household cleaners. 37. [name] attended the unit after receiving the report from her mold technician and proceeded to clean the area in which the surface mold was observed. J.W. also painted the areas with mold-resistant paint. 38. [name] testified that the management company also sent a contractor to inspect the [name] concerns regarding the mold on the windowsill. The contractor attended the unit, observed and cleaned the mold but informed the Tenant that any actual fault with the windows could not be found until such time that they were leaking. This normally only occurred in the winter, and the management company informed the Tenant that they would return in the winter to see if the windows have any problems. 39. [name] testified that the Tenant contacted her on February 3, 2026, asking when the follow up inspection to determine if the window was faulty would take place. The Landlord contacted the property management company immediately and asked for them to have the window inspected by the same contractor who previously attended the unit. 40. [name] testified that the contractor attended the unit on February 10, 2026, at which time he observed that the weather stripping around the window was no longer effective and required replacement. The weather stripping was replaced on March 19, 2026. 41. [name] testified that she has not received any further complaints or concerns regarding this issue since the replacement of the weather stripping. 42. On cross-examination, the Landlord testified that the unit had no pre-existing damage when rented to the Tenant. The Landlord also tendered photographs of the unit prior to the Tenant occupying as evidence. 43. The Landlord testified that she felt waiting one week to initially contact the management office was reasonable because she was going out of town and would deal with it upon her return. 44. The Landlord testified that she asked that the Tenant run a dehumidifier but never offered to provide the Tenant with one to use. 45. Based on the evidence, the unit had mold around the windowsill throughout the duration of the residential tenancy, and the presence of this mold would have substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of an individual. The questions that must be addressed are did the Landlord act reasonably when notified by the Tenant and was the Landlord able to take different steps or do different repairs to reduce any substantial interference. 46. I find that the Landlord’s initial response to the Tenant’s concern on February 24, 2024, to be reasonable timing. I do not find the Landlord’s initial inspection of the unit on March 9, 2024, to be reasonable or timely as it was approximately two weeks after the Tenant’s initial concern to the Landlord. I also take issue with the Landlord failing to clean or remove the surface mold from the windowsill at the time of that inspection. 47. I find that the Landlord’s delay in contacting the condominium corporation and/or management company to be unreasonable. The Landlord testified that she was going on a trip for a week and planned to address the issue upon her return. Given today’s technology and the ability to communicate electronically almost anywhere in the world, I find the delay of one week to be unreasonable under the circumstances. 48. I am mindful that the Landlord retained an independent mold technician who found surface mold but simply suggested running the exhaust fans for longer and using dehumidifier when necessary. The technician also recommended the surface mold be cleaned with household cleaners as necessary. I do not find it unreasonable for the Landlord to rely on this individual’s findings. The Tenant had an independent inspection completed because she was unsatisfied with the quality of findings of the Landlord’s technician’s inspection. The management company also had an inspection of the unit performed with thermal imaging equipment. 49. The management company determined that the wall beneath the windowsill required removal and further inspection. This work was completed between April 15, 2024, through to April 18, 2024. I am also mindful that the Tenant was responsible for moving all their personal belongings in and out of the room for the work to be completed. The scope of work had to be done and could not be done in a more convenient manner for the Tenant. I also find the completion time of three days to be reasonable given the scope of work and time required for drying if necessary. 50. I am satisfied that the issue was addressed and no concerns were present between the period of April 19, 2024, through to March 12, 2025. On March 13, 2025, the Tenant notified the Landlord of a concern regarding the presence of surface mold on the bedroom windowsill and additional surface mold on the window near the balcony. The management office had the unit inspected the week of March 17, 2025, and the Landlord had the unit re-inspected by their mold technician in April 2025. The surface mold was removed from the windowsill, and the area was treated and painted with mold-resistant paint. The inspection report tendered by the Landlord indicated no findings of high or abnormal moisture readings but did observe very high levels of humidity. The mold was identified as surface mold, safe to clean with household cleaners. 51. I find it reasonable to delay any further inspections until winter of 2026, because any fault with the windows would not be visible or detectible until such time that the issue exists. The window did not appear to be showing any signs of problem or concern during the summer or fall. I also find the Landlord’s response time and steps taken to be reasonable given the circumstances. 52. The management company re-inspected the unit on February 10, 2026, and the contractor observed that the window weather sealing around the window was starting to become frail and required replacement. This window weather stripping work was completed on March 19, 2026. The Landlord did not receive any additional concerns from the Tenant regarding any mold issues since this repair. I was not given any information or reasoning as to why the replacement of the window weather stripping would have taken over a month to complete and as such find that this delay is unreasonable. 53. The Landlord failed to initially inspect the issue, failed to report the issue to the condominium corporation after inspection in a timely manner and failed to initially take steps to have the surface mold cleaned; therefore, I find that this substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. I am satisfied that the Landlord did take adequate steps to remove the mold when notified and observed by the Landlord in 2025. 54. The Tenant has not proven any general compensation in the form of lost wages or otherwise. Therefore, the claim for general compensation is denied. Remedies 55. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant’s out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $584.21. This amount represents the Tenant’s costs incurred in having an independent mold inspection conducted in the rental unit. I find that this cost was reasonable given the Tenant’s concerns and that the Landlord’s technician determined the issue to be limited to surface mold without examining or taking any steps to determine if there is an underlying issue or deeper concern. 56. Therefore, I also find that a rent abatement of $552.75 is appropriate in the circumstances. This abatement represents a 15% abatement for the period of February 22, 2024, through to April 18, 2024 ($251.25), and 10% abatement for the period of February 3, 2026, through to March 19, 2026 ($301.50). I find these amounts to be a reasonable abatement due to the unreasonable delay in having the work completed and substantial interference resulting from the same. I am satisfied that the Tenant having to constantly clean the mold from the windowsill and have concern for their health and well-being to substantially interfere with one’s reasonable enjoyment. These amounts also consider that the mold found was determined to be surface mold which on a balance of probabilities would have no negative health effects or otherwise.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,259.21. This amount represents: • $552.75 for a rent abatement. • $584.21 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 2. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026. 3. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 4. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,259.21 from the rent for the period of August 2026. 5. The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T1 application which included a claim for money paid to a utility company which the Tenant disputes he should have been responsible for. In addition, the Tenant was seeking reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses that he paid.

T1 applications are filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which states A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act.

I suggested that the Tenant may wish to seek legal advice or file a separate tenant application to address these two issues, and that I would only be proceeding on the claim regarding the collection of an illegal security deposit, and a claim for interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. Agreed Facts
The parties do not dispute that at the start of the tenancy, the monthly rent was $3,500.00.

The Landlord and the Tenant do not dispute that the Tenant paid the Landlord a total of $9,000.00 at the start of the tenancy. This amount was for first month’s rent, the last month’s rent deposit, and a $2,000.00 security deposit. The Tenant paid this amount in 3 separate transactions. On August 17, 2023, the Tenant paid $1,500.00, on August 21, 2023, the Tenant paid $2,500.00, and on August 31, 2023, the Tenant paid $5,000.00.
The tenancy was terminated on December 31, 2025, and the Landlord applied the last month’s rent deposit to the rent for the last month of the tenancy. Merits of the Application

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the security deposit and interest on the last month’s rent deposit, in addition to the filing fee. Illegal charge collected
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
It is not disputed by the parties that the Landlord collected a security deposit of $2,000.00 from the Tenant, which the Tenant agreed to pay.

The Landlord disputed that he was required to pay this amount back to the Tenant as the Tenant agreed to pay the security deposit and failed to leave the unit in the same condition as to when he moved into the rental unit.
Subsection 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Subsection 105(2) of the Act defines “security deposit” as, money, property or a right paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition

I am satisfied that the $2,000.00 security deposit was not a rent deposit permitted by s.105(1) of the Act because the Tenant provided a separate rent deposit, which was to be applied to the last month of the tenancy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord contravened the Act when they collected a security deposit from the Tenant in addition to the last month’s rent deposit and they continue to contravene the Act by retaining that deposit. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act.
It is not disputed that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
The Landlord took the position that within the agreement to rent, the parties consented to waive any interest owing to the Tenant on the last month’s rent deposit.
Section 3(1) of the Act states that the Act applies to rental units in residential complexes despite any other Act and any agreement or waiver to the contrary.
Section 4(1) of the Act states that a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void.

Section 106(6) of the Act states a landlord shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at the rate equal to the guideline in effect at the time the payment becomes due.
Therefore, I find that the part of the tenancy agreement which effectively waives interest owing on the rent deposit is void.
It was undisputed the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant any interest on the last month's rent deposit during the tenancy, as required by the Act.
Therefore, I find the Landlord is required to pay the Tenant their security deposit, and the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit which is broken down below.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,245.31. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the illegal charge collected. Time Period From (DD-MM- YY) To (DD-MM-YY) or Anniversary Date Deposit Amount # of Days Interest Due • $197.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, I raised the issue that the Tenant's application did not contain any particulars of the claim. The application was blank and did not identify the factual basis for the application, the dates or times of any alleged incidents, the nature of the Landlord's alleged conduct, when the Landlord was notified of any concerns, or the remedies sought. As filed, the application provided no meaningful notice of the case the Landlord was required to meet.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing. There was no evidence before me that the Landlord had knowledge of the allegations the Tenant intended to raise at the hearing beyond the blank application that had been served. Permitting the Tenant to advance allegations that were not disclosed in the application would be procedurally unfair and would deny the Landlord a reasonable opportunity to know and respond to the case against them

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that her assigned parking space had been given to another individual. However, that allegation was not set out in the application, nor were any particulars provided regarding when the issue arose, when the Landlord was notified, the Landlord's response, or the remedy sought. I therefore decline to consider this allegation, as it was not properly pleaded in the application.

In any event, based on the Tenant's evidence, I am not satisfied that the alleged parking dispute is appropriately addressed in this application. The issue appears to concern the Tenant's use of an assigned parking space and does not fall within the scope of the claims available in the application.

In [name] v. Metro Capital Property., [2002] O.J. No. 5931 ([name]. [name]. [name].) the Court explained that “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” The Court went on to state that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal”.

The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Although the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long recognized.

The Board must ensure that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the principles of procedural fairness. An application that contains no particulars does not provide a responding party with sufficient notice of the allegations to enable them to prepare a response. In the circumstances, I find that the application cannot fairly proceed. I find there is insufficient detail in the Tenants’ application to allow the Landlord to know the case being alleged against them.

The Tenant submitted that English is not her first language and that she was unsure how to complete the application. I have considered that explanation. However, it does not relieve the Tenant of the obligation to file an application that contains sufficient particulars to notify the Landlord of the allegations to be addressed.

The application was filed on April 1, 2026. The Tenant had ample opportunity before the hearing to review the application, seek assistance in completing it, or otherwise ensure that it contained the necessary particulars. Despite that opportunity, the application remained entirely blank and did not provide the Landlord with any notice of the case to be met.

While I accept and have considered that the Tenant may have experienced difficulty completing the application, the Board must also ensure that proceedings are conducted fairly. Proceeding on the basis of a blank application would be procedurally unfair to the Landlord, who was not provided with notice of the allegations or the remedies sought. In these circumstances, the Tenant's explanation does not remedy the fundamental defect in the application and does not cure the complete absence of particulars or override the Landlord's right to procedural fairness.
In the circumstances, I find that the application is fundamentally deficient and cannot be fairly adjudicated. Accordingly, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Position
The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord collected or retained money in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

The monthly rent was $870.00 and was due on the first day of each month. On March 30, 2026, the Tenant’s father emailed the Landlord requesting consent to assign the tenancy to another person (DOC-7695924). The Tenant selected the proposed assignee and vacated the rental unit on April 25, 2026. The new occupant moved into the rental unit on May 3, 2026.

Before moving out, the Tenant made a payment of $623.50 on April 1, 2026. This was the Tenant’s final payment to the Landlord. The Landlord’s ledger also contained an administration charge of $250.00 and a subsequent credit of $150.00.
The Tenant submits that he is entitled to a refund of rent for the period after April 25, 2026 and that the administration charge was illegal. Landlord’s Position
The Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant had not paid the full rent owing for the period during which he remained in possession of the rental unit in April 2026.

The Landlord further submitted that the administration fee had not actually been paid. Although the charge appeared on the ledger, the Tenant did not make any payment in addition to the $623.50 paid on April 1, 2026. The Landlord therefore requested that the application be dismissed. Analysis
The Tenant bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected or retained money in contravention of the Act. In this case, the Tenant has not met that burden.
It is undisputed that the Tenant’s final payment before vacating the rental unit was $623.50, paid on April 1, 2026. The Tenant remained in possession of the rental unit until April 25, 2026.
Even if the Tenant was entitled to vacate the rental unit on April 25, 2026, the amount he paid was less than the rent attributable to the period during which he remained in possession.

The Tenant cannot recover rent that he did not pay. I therefore find no basis for the Tenant’s claim that he overpaid rent for April 2026 or that he is entitled to a refund for the period after he vacated. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.

With respect to the administration charge, I find that the Tenant did not prove that he paid the fee. The Landlord’s ledger showed a $250.00 administration charge and a later credit of $150.00. However, the presence of a charge on a ledger is insufficient to establish that the Landlord collected that amount from the Tenant.
The Tenant’s only payment in April was $623.50, made on April 1, 2026. Given that rent was due on the first day of the month, I find that this payment was made toward the rent due April 1, 2026.

The Tenant did not produce evidence of a separate payment of $250.00 or any additional payment that could reasonably be attributed to the administration fee. I find no legal basis to order repayment of an amount that was entered as a charge on the Tenant’s ledger but was never actually paid.
I am therefore not satisfied that the Landlord collected or retained any money in contravention of the Act. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2848.00 Background
Before the commencement of the tenancy, the Tenant paid the Landlord $2,800.00 in two instalments. The first payment was $800.00, and the second payment was $2,000.00.

The parties entered into a written tenancy agreement for a was for a fixed term of one year commencing on April 1, 2026. The Tenant attended the rental unit on April 1, 2026, intending to move in. However, she did not take possession of or remain in the rental unit that day. The Tenant filed this application on April 2, 2026 seeking the return of the $2,800.00.

On or about April 15, 2026, the Tenant returned to the rental unit and moved some of her belongings into it. She made a further payment of $800.00 on April 15, 2026 and another payment of $1,400.00 on April 30, 2026.

The Tenant submits that the parties entered into a new tenancy commencing on April 15, 2026. Consequently, she seeks the return of the rent deposit paid in connection with the original tenancy. The Landlord submits that the original written tenancy continued and that the parties delayed the move-in date and adjusted the amount of one payment. Tenant Evidence

The Tenant testified that she attended the rental unit on April 1, 2026 with the intention of moving in. When she entered the unit, she discovered that it was dirty and heavily infested with cockroaches.

The Tenant submitted photographs showing the condition of the stove, kitchen counters and cupboards. The photographs show insects and extensive black markings that the Tenant identified as cockroach droppings.

The Tenant stated that she attempted to address the problem but concluded that the unit could not reasonably be occupied in its existing condition. She advised the Landlord that the unit was not habitable, that she could not move in and that she wanted her money returned.

The Tenant did not stay in the rental unit on April 1, 2026. She placed her belongings in storage and went to stay with her sister. Two weeks later, the Landlord advised the Tenant that the unit had been cleaned or treated and invited her to inspect it again.

The Tenant paid $800.00 on April 15, 2026. She testified that this represented a new tenancy with a new rental period from April 15 to May 15, 2026, because of the condition of the unit and the delay in moving in. The Tenant paid an additional $1,400.00 on April 30, 2026. She testified that this was an advance payment for the rental period beginning May 15, 2026. [name]

The Tenant’s sister, [name], testified at the hearing. She confirmed that the Tenant stayed with her between April 1 and April 15, 2026, and did not reside in the rental unit during that period. She also testified that the Tenant stored her belongings because she could not move into the rental unit.

DM attempted to communicate with the Landlord on the Tenant’s behalf. However, the Landlord declined to discuss the tenancy with her because her name was not on the tenancy agreement. Evidence from the Landlord’s Spouse

The Landlord’s spouse, [name] (“HN”), testified on the Landlord’s behalf. She acknowledged that the previous tenant moved out of the rental unit on April 1, 2026, the same day the Tenant was scheduled to move in.

HN acknowledged that the Landlord had not had sufficient time to inspect or properly clean the rental unit before the Tenant arrived. She accepted that the unit had not been properly cleaned and acknowledged that this was the Landlord’s responsibility.

HN acknowledged that the Tenant did not move into the rental unit on April 1, 2026. She testified that the Landlord asked the Tenant to allow additional time for cleaning and pest- control treatment before moving in.

HN acknowledged that the Landlord sent the Tenant a text message on April 1, 2026 referring to finding another tenant and transferring the Tenant’s money back. She maintained that the promise to refund the money was conditional on the Landlord finding a replacement tenant.

HN testified that the Tenant returned on April 15, 2026, accepted the condition of the unit and moved in. She denied that the parties created a new tenancy on April 15. She maintained that the original tenancy remained in effect and that the move-in date was merely delayed. Analysis
Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) requires a landlord to repay a rent deposit where vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The Landlord acknowledged that the Tenant was unable to move into the rental unit on April 1, 2026, because of its condition and the cockroach infestation. The issue to be determined is whether the parties merely postponed the commencement of the original tenancy or entered into a new tenancy agreement commencing on April 15, 2026.

The Tenant filed this application on April 2, 2026. I find that the timing of the application supports her evidence that she understood that the original tenancy had not commenced and that she expected the $2,800.00 to be returned.

I also find that the text messages sent by the Landlord support the Tenant’s position. Specifically, the chain of messages exchanged on April 1, 2026 (DOC-8210834, pages 31- 32) confirms that the Landlord intended to find another tenant and return the Tenant’s deposit.
I find this evidence more consistent with an acceptance that the April 1 tenancy would not proceed rather than an agreement to postpone the move-in date under an otherwise continuing tenancy.

Moreover, the Landlord accepted a further payment of $800.00 on April 15, 2026. If the parties had merely postponed the commencement of the original tenancy, it would have been reasonable for the Landlord to account for the $2,800.00 already held and credit the Tenant for the period during which the rental unit could not be occupied, rather than collect an additional payment.

I find the April 15 payment, together with the further payment made on April 30, supports the Tenant’s evidence that the parties entered into a new tenancy arrangement under which the rental periods commenced on the 15th day of each month.

Accordingly, I find on a balance of probabilities that the original tenancy scheduled to commence on April 1, 2026, did not proceed and that the parties entered into a new tenancy arrangement commencing April 15, 2026.

I further find that the Landlord did not give the Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit on April 1, 2026. The Landlord was therefore required under section 107 of the Act to return the $2,800.00 rent deposit.
For greater certainty, this order relates only to the written tenancy agreement that was scheduled to commence on April 1, 2026, and the $2,800.00 paid in connection with that agreement.

I make no determination regarding the payments made on or after April 15, 2026, or whether the Tenant is entitled to the return of any of those payments. I understand that the Tenant has filed a separate application concerning the later tenancy arrangement, and those issues may be determined in that proceeding.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,800.00. This amount represents: • $2,800 for return of the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant resided in the rental unit while the original tenant was alive and continued to reside there after the original tenant died on June 5, 2024.

Following the original tenant’s death, there was a dispute between the parties about the Tenant’s legal status. The Landlord maintained that the Tenant was an unauthorized occupant and described the payments it accepted from him as compensation for his use and occupation of the rental unit.

In a previous proceeding, the Board considered whether the Tenant was an unauthorized occupant. In order LTB-T-055856-25, the Board determined that the tenancy had been legally assigned to DC and that he was subject to the terms of the tenancy agreement signed by the deceased tenant.

Following the original tenant’s death, there was a dispute between the parties about the Tenant’s status. The Landlord maintained that the Tenant was an unauthorized occupant and described the payments it accepted from him as compensation for his use and occupation of the rental unit.

The Tenant now submits that the payments described by the Landlord as compensation for his use and occupation of the rental unit did not constitute rent and therefore amounted to an illegal charge contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence and Submissions
The Tenant testified that the Landlord began accepting payments from him in approximately April 2024. He stated that the payments were $600.00 per month and continued until April 1, 2026.

The Tenant relied on the descriptions contained in the Landlord’s ledger. He submitted that the Landlord consistently recorded the payments as compensation rather than rent. The Tenant argued that the Landlord could change its legal position after he was found to be a tenant but could not retroactively change the purpose for which it had originally accepted the payments.
The Tenant therefore submitted that the payments were collected for a purpose other than rent and constituted an illegal charge. Landlord’s Evidence and Submissions
The Landlord’s representative submitted that the payments were accepted in exchange for the Tenant’s continued use and occupation of the rental unit.

The Landlord initially described the payments as compensation because it maintained that the Tenant was an unauthorized occupant. The Landlord submitted the description was intended to preserve the Landlord’s legal position while the Tenant’s status remained unresolved.

Once the Board determined that the Tenant was a tenant, the Landlord treated the payments as rent and provided the Tenant with a rent receipt. The Landlord further submitted that the terminology used in its accounting records did not alter the substance of the transaction. Analysis

Section 135 of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant to apply for an order requiring a landlord, superintendent or landlord’s agent to repay money collected or retained in contravention of the Act.

I find it is not sufficient for the Tenant to establish that the Landlord used the word “compensation” in its accounting records. The Tenant must establish that the Landlord was not legally entitled to collect or retain the payments.
Section 103(1) of the Act provides that a landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of a rental unit by an unauthorized occupant.
The Landlord was therefore legally entitled to accept compensation from Tenant for his use and occupation of the rental unit while maintaining its position that he was an unauthorized occupant.

Section 2 of the Act defines rent to include the amount of any consideration paid or required to be paid by a tenant to a landlord for the right to occupy a rental unit. I find once the Board determined that the tenancy had been assigned to DC, the monthly payments he made in exchange for his continued occupation of the rental unit fell within that definition.

I do not accept the Tenant’s submission that the description of the payments in the Landlord’s ledger made them illegal. Whether the payments constituted compensation or rent depended on the Tenant’s status, not the terminology used by the Landlord.

The Board has jurisdiction to ascertain the real substance of all transactions between the parties under section 202 of the Act. In doing so, I have considered that the Tenant continued to reside in the rental unit, received the benefit of that occupation and paid monthly amounts in exchange for it. He has also received a rent receipt for the payments. As such, I find the payments made by the Tenant constitute rent, despite the Landlord’s initial characterization of the payments.

I find further find it is unreasonable for the Tenant to rely earlier uncertainty about his status in attempt to obtain the return of payments that he was legally obligated to make once his status as a tenant was determined. In my view, it was appropriate for the Landlord to provide the Tenant with a rent receipt once the Board determined that the tenancy had been assigned to him.

Ordering the Landlord to return the payments would effectively allow the Tenant to occupy the rental unit during the relevant period without paying either rent or compensation for his use and occupation of the unit. Such a result would be inconsistent with the Act.

I am therefore not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the payment made by the Tenant were collected or retained in contravention of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $3,448.00.
The Landlord gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 49 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by the Act.

JP testified that the Landlord had told the Tenants a few weeks prior to serving the N12 notice of termination (“N12 notice”) that there was an offer coming on the rental unit and as of January 22, 2026, the Landlord told the Tenants the rental unit had sold. JP testified that the Tenants wanted to be prepared so they had started looking for another rental unit, knowing that an N12 notice was coming.

JP testified that an N12 notice was served to the Tenants the morning of January 29, 2026, with a termination date of March 31, 2026. The Tenants asked to have February rent waived in lieu of compensation, but the Landlord said that she would pay compensation to the Tenants on March 31, 2026, and the Landlord wanted rent for February 2026. The Tenants then decided to exercise their right to serve an N9 Tenant’s Notice to end the [name] (“N9 notice”) and provided a termination date of February 28, 2026.

JP testified the Landlord told the Tenants that since they were moving out “early” that they were no longer getting the compensation. JP testified that the Tenants never received the one month’s compensation required under the Act. JP testified that the Tenants never would have moved out of the rental unit or been looking for a new rental unit had the Landlord not sold the rental unit they were in.

Here, I am satisfied the Landlord served a notice under section 49 of the Act thereby triggering the Landlord’s obligation to provide compensation to the Tenants no later than the termination date on the notice of termination per section 55.1 of the Act. The Landlord’s obligation to compensate the Tenants is not voided or otherwise negated by the Tenants service of the N9 notice. In fact, the Tenants had the right to an earlier termination date on minimum 10 days’ notice as set out by section 49(4) and (5) of the Act. The fact that the Tenants opted for an earlier termination date does not change the obligation of the Landlord to pay compensation under section 49.1 of the Act.
As such, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenants one months rent per section 49.1 of the Act, which is $3,400.00.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,448.00. This amount represents: • $3,400.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed the application seeking an order that the Landlord had arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to sublet the rental unit.
On March 1, 2026, the Tenant asked the Landlord for consent to sublet the rental unit to [name] (“AG”), the potential subtenant, from May 1, 2026 to August 31, 2026.

There is no dispute that the Landlord had previously consented to the Tenant subletting to AG from November 16, 2024 to April 30, 2025 and again from May 1, 2025 to April 30, 2026. AG has resided in the rental unit since November 2024 and is currently residing in the rental unit.
It is also undisputed that the tenancy commenced on September 1, 2019 and is now a month-to-month tenancy.

Subsection 2(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) defines a sublet as follows: Interpretation, sublet (2) For the purposes of this Act, a reference to subletting a rental unit refers to the situation in which, (a) the tenant vacates the rental unit; (b) the tenant gives one or more other persons the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant’s term or period; and (c) the tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit after that specified date.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 21 explains: For a subtenancy to exist under the RTA, the tenant (the "head tenant") must: a. vacate the rental unit; b. give one or more other persons the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant's term or period; c. retain the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit at the end of the tenancy; and d. obtain the consent of the landlord.

Guideline 21 further states: In addition, there is a requirement that the right to occupy given to the potential subtenant must be for a period of time that is less than the term of the head tenant's lease. This indicates that there must be a tenancy agreement between the landlord and the head tenant for a specific term. Therefore, in the ordinary case, there cannot be a sublet of a month to month tenancy. It is, however, theoretically possible to create a subtenancy for one month less one day in the case of a month to month tenancy.

In the case of a month-to-month tenancy, the period of the tenancy is a calendar month. Therefore, to comply with subsection 2(2) of the Act, a request to sublet a rental unit in the case of a month-to-month tenancy cannot exceed one month less a day so as to enable the Tenant the ability to resume occupancy before the end of the rental period.

Here, the Tenant asked the Landlord’s consent to sublet the rental unit to AG for four months, from May 1, 2026 to August 31, 2026. The proposed sublet of four months would therefore not have been valid under the Act and as the Tenant’s request was not lawful, the Landlord has not unlawfully withheld consent to sublet the rental unit.

Even if the Landlord had previously conceded and agreed to the Tenant subletting longer than one month less a day and the Tenant has indicated that she plans to return to the rental unit on September 1, 2026, this does not change the fact that the current sublet request is invalid under the Act and the parties cannot contract out of the Act pursuant to subsection 3(1) of the Act. As such, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
