issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $1,500.00 for the last month’s rent deposit, interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit and rent collected in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.

The parties were before the Board on April 17, 2025, on a different matter, which resulted in an order being issued on June 4, 2025, terminating the tenancy for the Landlord’s own use (LTB-L-103436-24). The tenancy was terminated effective June 10, 2025. The order did not address a last month’s rent deposit or daily compensation.
The Tenant testified he vacated the rental unit despite the short notice, on June 13, 2025, because of the Board’s order terminating the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that prior to vacating the unit, he paid the rent for June 2025 in full, and the Landlords were holding, and continue to hold, a rent deposit in the amount of $1,500.00. The Tenant paid the rent deposit to the Landlords on March 1, 2014. Excess Rent Collected

The Landlords collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant is responsible for rent from June 1, 2025, to June 13, 2025, when the tenancy was terminated. The Landlords were paid for the entire month of June 2025, which the Landlords are not entitled to as the Landlords received an order from the Board terminating the tenancy and the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the order.

The lawful rent is $1,500.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $49.32. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,500.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.

Pursuant to section 134(1.1) of the Act it states: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit;

Therefore, I am satisfied by the uncontested testimony from the Tenant, that the Tenant is responsible for the rent from June 1, 2025, to June 13, 2025 (13 days), when the tenancy ended, which is $641.16. The Tenant paid the Landlords $1,500.00 for the month of June 2025, therefore, the Landlords are required to pay the Tenant from June 14, 2025, to June 30, 2025 (17 days), which is rent that was collected in excess of the amount allowed by the Act as the tenancy was terminated for the Landlords’ own use. Therefore, the Landlords are required to pay the Tenant $858.84, for rent that was collected in excess of the Act. Rent Deposit Illegally Retained

The Tenant provided uncontested testimony that he paid a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,500.00 to the Landlords on March 1, 2014, which is reflected in the Board’s order that was issued for the Landlord’s previous L1 application (LTB-L-105627-24 issued April 24, 2025). The Tenant testified that the Landlord failed to apply the last month’s rent deposit to the last month’s rental period and has failed to return this amount to the Tenant.

In accordance with s. 106(10), a landlord can only use a rent deposit to cover the rent for the last rental period. Since the rent for the last rental period was already paid, the deposit must be returned to the Tenant.

Therefore, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act. Interest Owing on the Rent Deposit
The Tenant testified that the Landlord failed to pay an interest on the last month’s rent deposit that was paid to the Landlord March 1, 2014.
Therefore, I find that the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants’ representative requested to withdraw the Tenants’ claim for illegal rent charged (Reason 1) in the Application. I granted the Tenants’ request. Tenants’ Application for a Rebate of Money the Landlord owes (T1)

It is undisputed that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement commencing January 1, 2026 and its term ending on December 31, 2026. It is also undisputed that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on March 31, 2026.

The Tenant testified that he paid $1,525.00 directly to a realtor at the Landlord’s direction. However, the Tenant did not identify the realtor, provide documentary evidence confirming the transfer, or call the realtor as a witness.

The Landlord denied directing the Tenant to make any payments to a realtor. The Landlord testified that he did not have a realtor and that he advertised the rental unit on Facebook Marketplace and located the Tenants himself.

Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlord directed the Tenants to pay $1,525.00 to a realtor on his behalf. I find that the Tenants paid $1,525.00 to the Landlord as the last month's rent deposit.

The written lease agreement provides a last month's rent deposit of $3,050.00; however, $1,525.00 was actually paid to the Landlord. The Landlord referred to email transfers dated December 29, 2025 from [name] in which the Tenant transfers the first month’s rent of $3,050.00 and separate transfer for $1,525.00.
The Landlord did not pay interest on the last month's rent deposit. Accordingly, interest for the period of January 1, 2026 to March 31, 2026 in the amount of $7.89 shall be paid to the Tenants.

The Landlord does not dispute that the Tenants also paid rent for March 2026. He stated that he is entitled to keep the last month's rent deposit because he was not provided with 60 days’ notice. The Landlord testified that the Tenants entered into a fix term tenancy from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 and vacated on March 31, 2026 after providing 21 days’ notice of their intention to leave. Although the Landlord accepted the Tenants’ request to terminate the tenancy earlier because of [name]’s health issues, he believed the Tenants intended to vacate at the end of April 2026 rather than on March 31, 2026. The Landlord testified that the Tenants did not provide a precise date in their initial communication as to when they intended to move out.

The Tenant testified that he informed the Landlord verbally on March 9, 2026 that he was moving out on March 31, 2026. The Tenant also testified that on March 9, 2026 he had not located a new accommodation or signed a new tenancy agreement. The Tenant confirmed that he located his new accommodation on March 15, 2026.

The Landlord testified that he began searching for a new Tenant and re-rented the rental unit on April 5, 2026. The Landlord further testified that he should be entitled to retain the last month's rent deposit because the Tenants did not provide 60 days’ notice and because he incurred expenses associated with re-renting the unit, including realtor costs.

I do not find that the March 9, 2026 communication constituted a valid notice under s. 44 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Even if the communication provided an intention to vacate the rental unit on March 31, 2026, it would be insufficient because it is less than 60 days’ notice.

In these circumstances, the Tenants were required to either: enter into an agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy in accordance with s. 37(3) of the Act; or serve a notice to terminate his tenancy at least 60 days in advance in accordance with s. 44(3). The Tenants did neither.

Subsection 88(1)1 of the Act addresses how much rent a tenant may owe if they vacate a rental unit without having served a valid notice of termination or entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy: “(1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.”

In accordance with subsection 88(3) of the Act, a Tenant’s liability for rent arrears can end earlier if the landlord re-rents the unit. In this case, the Landlord re-rented the unit on April 5, 2026. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord’s actual loss was limited to four days of rent, being from April 1, 2026 to April 4, 2026.

Based on the evidence before me, I have considered whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize its losses, as required by subsection 88(4) of the Act. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord fulfilled their obligations as required by subsection 88(4) of the Act in reasonably attempting to re-rent the unit and to mitigate its losses.

For all the reasons given above, I am satisfied that the Landlord was entitled to deduct $406.67 from last month's rent deposit ($3,050/30x4). However, the remainder $1,118.33 shall be returned to the Tenants.
The Tenants are also entitled to $48.00 for the costs of this application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,174.22. This amount represents: • $1,118.33 for the last month's rent deposit; • $7.89 for interest on the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenant $3,611.35.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 30, 2016, and the monthly rent was $1,150.00.

There is no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 Notice in July 2022 under section 48 of the Act. The notice stated that the Landlord required the rental unit for his own residential occupation. The termination date was September 30, 2022.

The Landlord filed an L2 application based on the N12 Notice. At the hearing on March 20, 2023, the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy. Under the consent settlement, the Tenant received $7,788.65 as compensation for storage and moving costs and vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2023.
There is no dispute that the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12 proceeding and that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit.
The remaining issue is whether the Landlord gave the N12 Notice in bad faith. Bad Faith:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord advertised the property for sale on May 10, 2023, only ten days after he vacated the rental unit. He also testified that the Landlord had attempted to sell the property several times before he vacated.

The Tenant stated that the property was marketed for sale in October and November 2022 and again in January 2023. The Landlord’s real estate agent contacted him during those periods to arrange access for showings. The property was removed from the market approximately one week before the March 20, 2023, hearing and was advertised for sale again on May 10, 2023.

The Tenant submitted text messages exchanged with the Landlord’s real estate agent in November 2022 and January 2023, together with a copy of the later sale advertisement. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord did not genuinely intend to occupy the rental unit and used the N12 process to obtain vacant possession and facilitate a sale.

The Landlord acknowledged that the property had been marketed for sale before the Tenant vacated. His position is that material changes in circumstances caused his original plan to collapse and that selling the property was necessary to reduce his financial losses.

The Landlord testified that he purchased the property in February 2022 and initially intended to move into it with his wife and children. He stated that the process of obtaining possession took longer than expected and that his family had to establish itself elsewhere. He acknowledged that the property was listed for sale in October and November 2022 and again in January 2023.

The Landlord also testified that, after obtaining possession, he discovered that the property required more work than expected. He stated that the cost of the work made it financially impractical for his family to move into the property.

The Landlord relied on a photograph of a tent in the basement. He believed that the Tenant had grown marijuana in the rental unit and stated that he was concerned about the possible effect on his family’s health. He testified that this concern contributed to his decision not to move into the property.
The Landlord further testified that the property did not sell after being marketed for several months and that he eventually rented it to another tenant.

The Landlord also stated that his former Legal Representative advised him during the March 20, 2023, settlement process that the tenancy would end and that he would then be free to decide what to do with the property. The Landlord stated that he understood this advice to mean that he could sell the property after the tenancy ended. Analysis:

The evidence before me is that the rental unit was advertised for sale 10 days after the Tenant moved out, and the Landlord did not move in the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. In these circumstances, the N12 Notice is presumed to have been given in bad faith pursuant to section 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord has the opportunity to rebut the presumption of bad faith. Once the presumption of bad faith is triggered, the burden of proof then shifts to the Landlord to prove on a balance of probabilities that they gave the Tenant the N12 notice in good faith.

The Landlord did not rebut this presumption. In the Court of Appeal’s decision in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the court held that the LTB should consider all relevant evidence when determining whether the N12 was served in bad faith and should not restrict itself to consideration of whether there was good faith at the time the N12 was served.

In this case, the Landlord acknowledged that the property was listed for sale in October, November 2022, after the N12 Notice had been given. It was marketed again before the March 20, 2023, hearing. Despite this, the N12 proceeding continued and the tenancy ended in the context of that proceeding.

I place significant weight on the sequence of events. The property was marketed for sale several times before the tenancy ended. It was removed from the market shortly before the March 20, 2023, hearing. The Tenant then agreed to vacate on April 30, 2023. The Landlord did not move into the rental unit, and the property was advertised for sale again on May 10, 2023.

I do not find persuasive the Landlord’s explanation that the decision to sell arose only after he obtained possession and discovered the condition of the property. That explanation is inconsistent with the earlier attempts to sell the property while the Tenant remained in possession.

The Landlord’s evidence that his family circumstances changed is relevant. However, it does not adequately explain why he continued to rely on an N12 Notice for personal occupation after the property had already been marketed for sale on several occasions. The Landlord did not advise the Tenant that his intentions had changed, withdraw the N12 Notice, or discontinue the L2 proceeding.
I find it more likely than not that the Landlord continued to use the N12 process to obtain vacant possession and facilitate the sale of the property.

I have also considered the Landlord’s reliance on [name], 2007 ONCA 491, and Biancaniello v. DMCT LLP, 2017 ONCA 386. Those cases confirm that a written settlement must be interpreted objectively, having regard to its language and the surrounding circumstances. However, they do not assist the Landlord in rebutting the presumption of bad faith. There is no dispute that the March 20, 2023, settlement was valid and binding, but it did not state that the Landlord could obtain possession through the N12 proceeding and then immediately sell the property. It also did not determine whether the N12 Notice had been given or pursued in good faith. The Landlord’s personal understanding of the legal advice he received cannot add a term that is not contained in the settlement.

The events after the settlement are also significant. The Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated on April 30, 2023. The property was advertised for sale only ten days later. Those events are directly relevant to the inquiry under section 57 of the Act.

I have also considered the Landlord’s evidence concerning the alleged marijuana growing area. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that [name] was present in the rental unit when the Tenant vacated. The Tenant testified that he had previously received medical authorization to grow marijuana and had set up a tent, but that the tent was empty when he left. The Landlord’s photograph also showed an empty tent.

The Landlord did not provide expert evidence establishing that [name] cultivation had damaged the rental unit, created an environmental concern, or made the property unsuitable for occupation. He also did not provide evidence of any inspection, testing, repair, or remediation undertaken to address the alleged concern before deciding not to move in. More importantly, the alleged condition does not explain why the Landlord had already marketed the property for sale before the Tenant vacated. I therefore give this evidence limited weight and find that it does not rebut the presumption of bad faith.

Considering the evidence as a whole, I find that the Landlord has not rebutted the statutory presumption. I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave and pursued the N12 Notice in bad faith, that the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12 proceeding, and that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time.
Accordingly, I find that all of the elements of the legal test in section 57 of the Act have been satisfied, and the Tenant application is granted. Remedies
The Tenant request the following remedies: • $4,500.00 for moving and storage expenses. • $30,500.00 for gentle compensation;
The Tenant also requested the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine to the LTB. Moving expenses:
There is no dispute that the Landlord paid the Tenant $7,788.65 under the previous consent settlement. The Tenant now seeks $4,500.00 for moving and storage expenses.

I find that the Tenant has already been compensated for those expenses. A further award would result in duplicate recovery. The claim for additional moving and storage expenses is therefore denied; General compensation:

The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3)(1.1) of the Act, which states: • An order that the Landlords pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 [Emphasis added]

The Tenant testified that losing the rental unit had a significant personal impact. He experienced periods of homelessness and stayed with friends, in his vehicle, and periodically with his former wife. His son moved to his grandmother’s home, and the Tenant’s family relationships were adversely affected.

The Tenant also testified that he operated an art and production business from the rental unit. The space allowed him to create sculptures, paintings, and other work. After he lost the rental unit, he could no longer operate the business in the same manner. He further testified that the loss of the tenancy and resulting housing instability aggravated his anxiety and other mental health concerns.

I also accept that the loss of the tenancy caused significant disruption. The Tenant experienced housing instability, his son moved to his grandmother’s home, and the Tenant was unable to immediately secure comparable accommodation that he could afford.

Considering the length of the tenancy, the impact of the displacement on the Tenant, I find that compensation equal to six months of the last monthly rent is appropriate. The monthly rent was $1,150.00. Six months of rent equals $6,900.00. Of the $7,788.65 previously paid, $4,500.00 compensated the Tenant for moving and storage expenses. I find that the remaining $3,288.65 must be credited against the general compensation award to avoid duplicate recovery. The amount payable is calculated as follows: $6,900.00 less $3,288.65 equals $3,611.35.
The Landlord shall therefore pay the Tenant $3,611.35 as general compensation. Administrative Fine:

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines, states that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter Landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlords in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered.
This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,611.35. This amount represents: • $3,611.35 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (LTB-T-031104-25 and LTB-T-031512-25). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (LTB-T-032117-25). • reduced or discontinued a service or facility at the residential complex (LTB-T-034044-25). This applications were heard by videoconference on July 9, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Landlord’s agent [name] and the Landlord’s witness [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: By way of background, the parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on September 22, 2025, where the matter did not resolve. The Tenant’s applications were combined and directed to a merit hearing. LTB-T-031512-25 LTB-T-032117-25 LTB-T-034044-25

The Member noted in the Adjournment Sheet ([name]) that the Tenant was put on notice of various deficiencies in his applications such as insufficient reasons and details, limitation periods and duplication of issues. The Member advised that the Tenant shall amend the applications and provide disclosure by October 10, 2025 and the Landlord’s due by October 24, 2025.
The Member issued an interim order on October 2, 2025 where the Tenant was provided with direction should he intend to amend the applications and set the due dates as described above (DOC6497291).
The parties were also ordered to comply with all disclosure requirements with specifics provided.
The parties were put on notice that the failure to comply with the terms of the interim order may result in the refusal of the Tenant’s evidence.

At this hearing, The Tenant acknowledged that he received and read the interim order. He said that he opted not to undertake to amend his applications as he believed the original applications were accurate and sufficient. I did note that the Tenant filed a Request to Amend an Application on January 16, 2026 (DOC7198680). However, this email was unrelated to relevant amendments.

The Tenant did not provide any reasonable explanation for his failure to comply with the interim order which was based on the Member’s assessment of the validity of the Tenant’s applications at the ACC. Rather, he believed the applications were sufficient as filed.

With respect to the Board’s order for disclosure, the Tenant believed that the parties consented to disclosure using the Portal (TOP). A close examination of the Tenant’s various files was conducted and the Tenant was unable to locate or provide documentary evidence of this consent. The Tenant was afforded time to review the various files and was unable to produce the consent form. I am not satisfied that the parties mutually agreed to exchange disclosure via TOP.

The Landlord’s legal representative said that he did not believe such consent was given and no documentation was signed. Additionally, he said the Tenant has not complied with the interim order, did not organize and provide his evidence as required by October 10, 2025.

The Landlord asks the Board to dismiss the Tenant’s applications for failure to comply with the interim order and that they are defective on their face. The T1 applications are duplicative and seek a determination of the lawful rent which was previous adjudicated in LTB-L-038852-25. The Tenant’s request to review that order was denied on September 29, 2025. As the lawful rent has already been determined, the doctrine of [name] prevents another hearing on the claims made in the Tenant’s T1 applications.

The Landlord’s representative said that the claims made in the T6 application are about the amount of rent and amenities; these do not fit the legal test as per s.20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and discloses no cause of action as per s.197(1) of the Act. LTB-T-031512-25 LTB-T-032117-25 LTB-T-034044-25
Finally, the Landlord’s representative points out that the Tenant’s T3 application is out of time. I note, this was also an issue explained to the Tenant at the ACC.

Given all of the above, I dismissed the Tenant’s application at the hearing. As explained to the Tenant, he had the benefit of an ACC, where a Member identified the issues of concern. This was followed up by and interim order which the Tenant acknowledged receipt. However, the Tenant failed to take any steps to comply with the interim order. He did not undertake to amend the applications and he did not organize and provide his evidence as ordered.

Additionally, I agree with the Landlord representative’s position. The Tenant’s applications are plagued with deficiencies which renders them defective on their face. In my view, it was reasonable to dismiss the applications without hearing the merits of the applications.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. July 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Respondent, [name], raised a preliminary issue that the Board does not have jurisdiction to hear the matter because he has a “roommate agreement” with the Applicants. [name] referred to the agreement and his tenancy agreement with the Landlord/owner of the property. He stated that he rented a room to the Applicants; however, he is a Tenant himself and not the Landlord or owner of the property.

The Applicants acknowledged that they entered into a roommate agreement with the Respondent and that the rent was paid directly to him. The Applicants also testified that they shared the basement with another individual who was also renting a room from the Respondent. Analysis and Findings

The definition of a Landlord in subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’) expressly excludes another Tenant in the residential complex. Subsection 2(1) of the Act says “a Landlord includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”)”

In this case, I am not satisfied that [name] meets the definition of a “landlord” in s.2(1)(a) of the Act because I find that he is not the owner of the residential complex or an individual who can permit occupancy of the basement unit or any part of the residential complex. I also find that the Applicants were occupants and were not Tenants within the meaning of s. 2(1) of the Act.

T he evidence establishes that [name] is a Tenant himself, with the right to occupy the entire residential complex through his tenancy with the owner/Landlord. Therefore, while he may satisfy a part of the definition of a Landlord by permitting the Applicants to occupy bedrooms in the basement of the residential complex, his status as a Tenant in the residential complex means he cannot be the Applicant’s Landlord. In addition, the Applicants’ evidence was that they shared the basement with another occupant supports the conclusion that the arrangement was a shared accommodation or rooming arrangement rather than a tenancy of a separate rental unit.
Given all of the above, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (LTB-T-031104-25 and LTB-T-031512-25). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (LTB-T-032117-25). • reduced or discontinued a service or facility at the residential complex (LTB-T-034044-25). This applications were heard by videoconference on July 9, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Landlord’s agent [name] and the Landlord’s witness [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: By way of background, the parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on September 22, 2025, where the matter did not resolve. The Tenant’s applications were combined and directed to a merit hearing. LTB-T-031512-25 LTB-T-032117-25 LTB-T-034044-25

The Member noted in the Adjournment Sheet ([name]) that the Tenant was put on notice of various deficiencies in his applications such as insufficient reasons and details, limitation periods and duplication of issues. The Member advised that the Tenant shall amend the applications and provide disclosure by October 10, 2025 and the Landlord’s due by October 24, 2025.
The Member issued an interim order on October 2, 2025 where the Tenant was provided with direction should he intend to amend the applications and set the due dates as described above (DOC6497291).
The parties were also ordered to comply with all disclosure requirements with specifics provided.
The parties were put on notice that the failure to comply with the terms of the interim order may result in the refusal of the Tenant’s evidence.

At this hearing, The Tenant acknowledged that he received and read the interim order. He said that he opted not to undertake to amend his applications as he believed the original applications were accurate and sufficient. I did note that the Tenant filed a Request to Amend an Application on January 16, 2026 (DOC7198680). However, this email was unrelated to relevant amendments.

The Tenant did not provide any reasonable explanation for his failure to comply with the interim order which was based on the Member’s assessment of the validity of the Tenant’s applications at the ACC. Rather, he believed the applications were sufficient as filed.

With respect to the Board’s order for disclosure, the Tenant believed that the parties consented to disclosure using the Portal (TOP). A close examination of the Tenant’s various files was conducted and the Tenant was unable to locate or provide documentary evidence of this consent. The Tenant was afforded time to review the various files and was unable to produce the consent form. I am not satisfied that the parties mutually agreed to exchange disclosure via TOP.

The Landlord’s legal representative said that he did not believe such consent was given and no documentation was signed. Additionally, he said the Tenant has not complied with the interim order, did not organize and provide his evidence as required by October 10, 2025.

The Landlord asks the Board to dismiss the Tenant’s applications for failure to comply with the interim order and that they are defective on their face. The T1 applications are duplicative and seek a determination of the lawful rent which was previous adjudicated in LTB-L-038852-25. The Tenant’s request to review that order was denied on September 29, 2025. As the lawful rent has already been determined, the doctrine of [name] prevents another hearing on the claims made in the Tenant’s T1 applications.

The Landlord’s representative said that the claims made in the T6 application are about the amount of rent and amenities; these do not fit the legal test as per s.20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and discloses no cause of action as per s.197(1) of the Act. LTB-T-031512-25 LTB-T-032117-25 LTB-T-034044-25
Finally, the Landlord’s representative points out that the Tenant’s T3 application is out of time. I note, this was also an issue explained to the Tenant at the ACC.

Given all of the above, I dismissed the Tenant’s application at the hearing. As explained to the Tenant, he had the benefit of an ACC, where a Member identified the issues of concern. This was followed up by and interim order which the Tenant acknowledged receipt. However, the Tenant failed to take any steps to comply with the interim order. He did not undertake to amend the applications and he did not organize and provide his evidence as ordered.

Additionally, I agree with the Landlord representative’s position. The Tenant’s applications are plagued with deficiencies which renders them defective on their face. In my view, it was reasonable to dismiss the applications without hearing the merits of the applications.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 9, 20 18, and moved out on December 1, 2024, due to an Order Prohibiting Use or Occupancy of Unsafe Building issued on November 28, 2024, by the city. T2 Application

The Tenant alleged that on July 6, 2024, he returned home to find the Landlord’s handyman exiting the rental uni t. The handyman informed the Tenant that he was investigating an electrical problem following a complaint from another unit. The Tenant was not given a Notice of Entry prior to this incident. The Landlord denied any knowledge of the entry.

In support of his evidence, the Tenant presented a typed document which he allegedly sent to the Landlord, titled ‘Email Septembre 2nd, 2023. The Tenant informed the Landlord that the handyman entered his unit on ‘July 6th last,’. The Tenant also presented the Landlord’s response titled ‘ Response 6 septembre 2023 ’. The Tenant stated that the year in both documents should indicate 2024 rather than 2023.

Section 27 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) permits a landlord to enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry. Except in cases of emergency, entry into the unit without first providing a valid Notice of Entry is illegal.

In this case, the Landlord failed to provide a Notice of Entry to the Tenant and in the ir response letter, appeared to be unaware of the handyman’s activities. The Landlord stated that they were addressing the complaint with the handyman . While I am satisfied that the handyman illegally entered the rental unit , I am unsure from the evidence whether the incident occurred on July 6, 2023, or on July 6, 2024 . In any event, as the Tenant did not report any further incidents of illegal entry , a rent abatement is not warranted in the circumstance.

The Tenant further testified that there was no hot water in the residential complex for one week from about July 10, 2024, to July 18, 2024, when the residents made a complaint to the city. The city inspected the residential complex on July 18, 2024, and the hot water was restored on the same date after the city hired a plumber. Following their inspection, on August 12, 2024, they issued an Order to [name].

I found the Tenant ’s evidence inconsistent as to when the issue with the hot water started and when it was resolved by the city. The Tenant’s oral evidence contradicts the contents of the application. In the application, the Tenant states that there was no hot water for about one week from July 18, 2024, and at the hearing, contradicted that statement by saying that the period was from July 10, 2024.

In addition, the order from August 12, 2024, indicates that the date of inspection was August 8, 2024, and not July 18, 2024, as claimed, which means that the issue was not resolved by a plumber on July 18, 2024. Due to these inconsistencies, I am unable to determine when the problem was resolved and for how long rent abatement should be calculated. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that on February 13, 2023, he informed the Landlord that there was approximately two inches of standing water and mold present in the basement of the residential complex. Although the rental unit was not located in the basement, the Tenant stated that the furnace room was in the basement and that the poor air circulated from the basement into his unit through the vents. As a result, the Tenant was hospitalized with breathing problems on January 2, 2024, August 6, 2024, August 9, 2024, and September 19, 2024.
The evidence demonstrates that the city found that the basement at the rear of the building contained a significant amount of water.

Section 20 (1) of the Act, provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and ma intenance standards.

Based on all the evidence, there is no dispute that the Landlord failed to maintain the rear basement of the residential complex. Although the Tenant testified that his breathing was negatively affected by mold in the basement, no documentary evidence was provided to establish either that mold was present in the basement or that the Tenant’s breathing problems are a result of the air quality in the basement. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s breathing issues were caused by the condition of the rear basement unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The named tenant [name] filed a T2 Application as against the Landlord on April 13, 2026.

A preliminary issue of standing was raised concerning the named tenant [name] (“[name]”). The Landlord submits that the Occupant Danny is not a Tenant and at most, was a mere occupant with no legal right to bring the current application as against the Landlord.
By way of background, it is not disputed that in or about May 2017 a lease agreement (“Lease”) was signed by the Landlord and [name] (“[name]”), as tenant.

The Occupant Danny and [name] are brothers. It is the Occupant Danny’s position that [name] and other family members moved into the rental unit in 2017 and that approximately 4 years later (October 2021), [name] simultaneously moved out and transferred the tenancy to the Occupant Danny. The Landlord denies there was any transfer of tenancy and submits [name] remains the sole tenant of the rental unit.

Since the tenancy began in 2017, it was noted that the Landlord and [name] have each commenced LTB proceedings as against the other . Recently, on August 25, 2025, the Landlord and [name] were in attendance at the Board for the Landlord’s L1/N4 Application in LTB-L-010464-25 (the “L1/N4 Order”). A voidable eviction order was rendered on October 28, 2025 as against [name], the sole named tenant. In accordance with paragraph 2 of the L1/N4 Order , the member found that the tenant [name]“… was still in possession of the rental unit.” The L1/N4 Order has not been reviewed or appealed.

While the Occupant [name] advised he was unaware of the L1/N4 proceeding s, the [name] admittedly assisted [name] in other applications before the Board concerning the existing tenancy; i n such applications, [name] was named as the sole tenant.

In the current proceeding, the Occupant Danny is alleging there was a transfer of tenancy in October 2021 . Given the prior member’s finding that [name], as tenant, was still in possession of the rental unit as of August 2025, the question was raised whether the issue being raised concerning a purported transfer of tenancy in October 2021 was already decided. In the circumstances, I find it has. Here, the [name] confirmed he is not alleging that a transfer of tenancy took place at any time after August 25, 2025. In my view, the member’s finding that [name] was still in possession of the rental unit in his capacity as Tenant as of August 25, 2025 is thus dispositive of the current application. In other words, a finding that a transfer of tenancy from [name] to the Occupant Danny had taken place in October 2021 – as requested by the Occupant Danny in the current application - would result in an inconsistent finding being made to the L1/N4 Order.
As I do not find that the Occupant Danny is a tenant, t he [name] application must therefore fail due to a lack of standing to bring such an application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining the Landlord did not comply with an agreement to increase the rent above the guideline. (T4 Application)
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw the application and I consented to the request. Request for Costs

The Landlord did not object to the Tenant’s withdrawal request but requested costs for the time spent at the hearing. The matter was originally called at 10:01 a.m. and the matter was stood down until 1:48 p.m. when the parties appeared before the Board again.

An award of costs is discretionary. Rules 23.2 and 23.3 of the Landlord and Tenant Board Rules (the “Rules”) provide for ordering another party’s costs. Under Rule 23.2 costs are limited to representation/preparation fees and out of pocket costs. The hourly rate for a paid representative is capped at $100.00 to a maximum of $700.00. Rule 23.3 does not specify the types of costs that may be awarded but does provide a party must have engaged in unreasonable conduct that caused undue delay or expense.

The Board’s Costs: Interpretation Guideline 3 provides costs to a successful party will generally only be awarded where conduct is unreasonable. Unreasonable conduct is discussed, in part as follows: Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes the following: 1. Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; 2. Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith; 3. Taking unnecessary steps in a proceeding; … 11. Maligning another party or unreasonably slurring the character of the other party.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant ought to have known that the application was flawed and that the Tenant not withdrawing earlier caused the Landlord to incur undue expense of retaining a legal representative. The Tenant’s Legal Representative objected the request for costs citing that the parties were expected to be at the hearing until 4:00 p.m. when the hearing block ends and that the Landlord responding to tenant applications is part of the job of being a landlord.

While I do agree that there was some delay in the proceedings due to the Tenant’s disorganization, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has established that the Tenant has engaged in unreasonable conduct. This is the first appearance before the Board for the merits hearing. The matter was concluded on the hearing date. When the matter was stood down, the parties engaged in private discussions. In my view, it is not uncommon that a party elects to not proceed with the proceedings after engaging in settlement or private discussions with the other side.

Considering Guideline 3 which states that the Board should not use its power to order costs in a way which would discourage landlords and tenants from exercising their statutory rights, I do not find the circumstances here warrant costs. As such, the Landlord’s request for costs is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed as withdrawn. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 14, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative, [name], the Landlord, and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the parties negotiated and executed a mutual settlement agreement, the terms of which were intended to fully and finally resolve the Tenant’s applications.

The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the Landlord complied with their obligations under the settlement agreement prior to appearing before me. At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that the Landlord had complied with the terms of the agreement. Notwithstanding the Landlord’s compliance, the Tenant refused to withdraw the applications.

The Landlord’s representative requested that the applications be dismissed as an abuse of process. The parties had previously been advised of the Board’s jurisdictional limitations at the Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) on September 4, 2025.

Following the ACC, the matter was scheduled for a brief hearing for the limited purpose of hearing submissions with respect to the possible application of section 197(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which provides: “The Board may dismiss an application without holding a hearing or refuse to allow an application to be filed if, in the opinion of the Board, the matter is frivolous or vexatious, has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action.”

The hearing on July 14, 2026, proceeded for the limited purpose of determining whether the Tenant’s applications should continue in light of the settlement agreement and whether section 197(1) of the Act ought to be applied.

I also note that Rule A8.1 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure provide the LTB the power to make such orders or give such directions in proceedings before it as it considers proper to prevent an abuse of process.

The Tenant testified that, although she agreed the Landlord had complied with the terms of the mutual release, she wished to proceed with her applications because new issues arose after the settlement agreement was executed. In support of this position, the Tenant referred to a CBC News article that had been uploaded to the Board's portal by the Landlord.

I do not accept that this issue is properly before the Board in the context of these applications. The evidence before me establishes that the article relied upon by the Tenant was uploaded to the Board's portal on September 4, 2025. The mutual release was executed by the Tenant on September 4, 2025, at 12:03 p.m. and by the Landlord on September 4, 2025, at 12:04 p.m. Although the Tenant suggested that the issue arose after the Attendance and Case Conference, the documentary record does not support that assertion.

In any event, the issue raised by the Tenant was not included in the applications before the Board. The Tenant did not amend her applications following the execution of the mutual release and did not serve the Landlord with an amended application, additional claims, or supporting documentation alleging new issues. Therefore, the Landlord did not have notice of the new issue(s) that the Tenant intended to raise. Accordingly, any alleged new issue is not properly before me and cannot be considered in determining whether these applications should proceed.

The evidence establishes that the parties entered into a written settlement agreement containing a broad mutual release. The release provides that the parties release one another: "...from all matters arising from, raised (or which could have been raised) in, or as a consequence of the landlord/tenant [name]/occupant relationship, any lease executed between the parties, the term of the lease or occupancy until termination, and/or events that transpired during the course of the occupancy, lease or tenancy or thereafter including but not limited to LTB File Number LTB-T-031872-25."

From the evidence adduced at the hearing, the tenancy was already over at the time the settlement agreement was signed. It would be reasonable to expect that the release would then account for all existing and potential claims arising out of the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that she signed the settlement agreement voluntarily, had an opportunity to read the agreement prior to signing, understood its terms, and did not feel pressured, coerced, or induced into entering the agreement. The Tenant also acknowledged that the Landlord complied with their obligations under the settlement agreement.

I find that the parties voluntarily entered into a valid and binding settlement agreement intended to fully and finally resolve the disputes arising from the tenancy. There is no persuasive evidence that the agreement was obtained through fraud, duress, misrepresentation, or any other circumstance that would justify setting it aside. Nor is there any evidence that the Landlord failed to perform their obligations under the agreement.

In these circumstances, permitting the Tenant's applications to proceed would amount to an attempt to relitigate matters that have already been resolved by agreement between the parties. I am satisfied that continuing the applications would constitute an abuse of the Board's process within the meaning of section 197(1) of the Act. Accordingly, the applications are dismissed.

The Landlord's representative requested an order for costs arising from attendance at this hearing. While I have dismissed the applications pursuant to section 197(1) of the Act, I am not satisfied that this is an appropriate case for the exercise of the Board's discretion to award costs. Although the applications have been dismissed, there is insufficient evidence that any party acted unreasonably, frivolously, vexatiously, or in a manner that unnecessarily prolonged the proceeding. The circumstances do not warrant such an order, and the request for costs is therefore denied.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1, T2 and T6 applications are dismissed. July 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-032107-25 issued on January 15, 2026. On February 13, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review hearing was held on April 13, 2023 where the Tenant’s review request was granted and the matter directed to a de novo hearing as per the April 23, 2026 interim order. The de novo hearing was heard by videoconference on July 21, 2026. The Tenant, her support persons [name], [name], [name] and [name], the Landlord and the Landlord’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, I reviewed the April 23, 2026 interim order with the parties. Specifically, at paragraph 8 the Member writes: The Tenant’s application lacks sufficient particulars as it is currently drafted. For example, there are no dates contained in the allegations. It is strongly recommended the Tenant seek legal advice.
I note, I have reviewed the Tenant’s application and concur with Member [name]’s findings that the application lack sufficient details.
Further, I reviewed at the hearing the portion of the order related to amending the application and disclosure requirements.
While the Landlord complied and provided to the Tenant and the LTB their disclosure by June 15, 2026 the Tenant neither requested to amend the application or provided disclosure as ordered.

When asked if she received, read and understood the interim order, I found the Tenant to be inconsistent with her response. She said that she received two orders and was confused. The Tenant also said that she “did not take a good look at it.”

The Tenant also said that she was victim of a cyber attack on May 18, 2026 and essentially lost her apps and functions with her devices. However, she regained access around two weeks ago. She was not able to comply with the April 23, 2026 order as a result of the technical issues.

I then asked the Tenant why she had not filed a request to amend the application or her disclosure as ordered once her technology was stabilized. She believed she had complied and directed me to various files she uploaded to the Portal (TOP); DOC8384819. DOC8384829, DOC8380154. I shared my screen and reviewed each document, as directed by the Tenant and confirmed that the documents were not related to an amended application or disclosure as ordered.

Additionally, the Tenant said that she sought legal counsel and due to the short notice, was unable to have her filed reviewed. The Tenant was asked multiple times to provide steps taken to secure counsel, including the name, date and agencies she attempted to contact. The Tenant asked for time to consult her assistant and she was granted time. The Tenant then proceeded to play an audio statement from her phone which cited various historical dates she contacted [name]. The Tenant confirmed that her assistant was AI. While the Tenant was asked multiple times for the specific inquiries made, she was unable to do so.

Well into the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw her application. I denied her request and explained that her late-stage request in not an opportunity to perfect her application, particularly in light of the April 23 interim order which noted the deficiencies in the application and afforded time for the Tenant to remedy the issue.

The Landlord’s representative sought a dismissal of the Tenant’s application for failure to correct the deficiencies in the application, failure to comply with the interim order and failure to comply with order LTB-T-070960-25, issued July 10, 2026 where the Tenant was ordered to pay both party costs and Board costs. As of the date of the hearing, the Tenant has not paid the ordered costs. As per s.196 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Landlord’s representative said that the Tenant’s application, in the least, should be stayed until the Tenant pays the ordered Board costs.
The Landlord’s representative said the Tenant requested a review of the July 10, 2026 order and that request was denied by the Board on July 17, 2026.
The Tenant confirmed she received the July 10, 2026 order, was aware of the ordered costs and said she has no intention of paying the costs.
Due to the Tenant’s failure to remedy the issues with her application, I determined there was no reason to stay her application.

At the hearing, I dismissed the Tenant’s application and while attempting to provide reasons, the Tenant disconnected from the hearing. I canvassed her support persons as to the Tenant’s intention to return to the hearing. [name] appeared on camera and confirmed that the spoke with the Tenant and said she will rejoin the hearing.

I explained to the Tenant that based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I was not satisfied that the Tenant took reasonable steps to comply with the April 23, 2026 interim order. She was aware of the deficiencies and steps required to further her application. She had almost three weeks, before the claimed cyber issue and took no reasonable steps to do so. I also explained that once her technology was restored and to the date of the hearing, she neither sought to amend her application nor provide her evidence as ordered by the Board.

I also explained that I was not satisfied that she took reasonable steps to seek legal counsel as she claimed. She led insufficient evidence to support her claims that she was denied service due to the time to hearing.
Overall, I found the Tenant, while put on notice that her application was defective, took no steps to address the issue or comply with the interim order which she received. The Request for Costs

The Landlord’s representative requested costs related to this hearing. He said the Tenant has experience before the Board and is aware of the process. She has filed applications, attended hearings and reviewed Board orders. The Tenant received the interim order and has no regard for orders of the Board. She was aware that her application was defective and the Landlord had no option but to attend this hearing to defend their position. The Landlord seeks $350.00 for costs related to time spent at this hearing.

The Landlord’s representative also requested Board costs related to the Tenant’s behaviour. She knowingly pursued a defective application and wasted Board time. She has a blatant disregard for Board orders and processes and refused to pay the costs already ordered. The Tenant, through the proceedings has had support and resources and yet continues to waste the Board’s time and resources.
The Landlord said that the Tenant, in previous hearings, has also voluntarily left the hearing when a ruling was not made in her favour.

I asked the Tenant to respond to the costs claimed by the Landlord. She asked for some time to prepare her response and was afforded time. The Tenant then attempted to play another AI generated response which she said she had “prepared in advance”. The Landlord objected to the Tenant’s formulated response.

I explained to the Tenant that I found the use of artificial intelligence to be inappropriate in this circumstance. I asked the Tenant to provide a response as to why she believes costs should not be levied and AI cannot replace her testimony.
The Tenant then provided a response that costs don’t “make much sense”.

While out of the normal course of a proceeding, the Tenant’s support [name], who was not called as a witness, implored the Board to exercise compassion due to the Tenant’s medical condition and not impose further costs. The Landlord’s representative was afforded opportunity to respond to these submissions and maintains their position that costs should be levied.

Based on the submissions of the parties, I find that costs are warranted in this circumstance. The Tenant was put on notice by the LTB that her application, as filed, was defective. However, she chose to advance her application. I was not persuaded that it was her inability to secure legal counsel nor the cyber attack that prevented her from complying with the interim order. Rather, in my view, the Tenant has little regard for Board orders or process. She acknowledges the costs previously levied, challenged the finding of the Board, was denied a review and asserts that she will not pay the costs.
The maximum amount of costs the Board can award per proceeding or application pursuant to the commentary to Rule 23.2 of the Board’s Rules of Practice is $700.00.

As explained to the parties, as per Guideline 3, generally fees relate to time spent at the hearing by a party’s legal representative are considered. However, in some cases, further costs for preparation time may be allowed if the unreasonable conduct led to the need for the party’s legal representative to spend additional time preparing for the hearing.

The Guideline provides examples of situations where Board costs may be appropriate. Essentially the question is: has the Tenant behaved in an unreasonable manner in how she dealt with this application in her behaviour before the Board. An unreasonable manner is where a party consciously makes choices that unnecessarily delay the proceeding or otherwise frustrate the hearing process.
Due to the behaviour of the Tenant, the Landlord was required to attend the hearing to defend their position.

In this case, the Landlord’s representative, aware of the defective application was not require to spend additional preparation time. The matter was called at 3:33 pm and concluded around 4:45 pm. Part of the reason for the delay was the Tenant’s voluntary exit from the hearing and delay for her return. In this case, I am satisfied that an award of $200.00, represents the costs incurred to attend the hearing.

With respect to Board costs, I am of the view, that the Tenant has experience before the Board and is aware of the process, yet took no reasonable steps to remedy the problems with her application. She chose to advance her application, knowing there was no successful outcome. The Tenant took around 1.25 hours of Board time to advance her defective application, time that might well have been better devoted to the many other matters the Board is required to resolve.

I am also mindful of the Tenant’s behaviour at the hearing and that she comes to the Board without clean hands and has willingly put herself in this position. The Tenant received the interim order and took no required action. At the hearing, the Tenant chose to leave mid-hearing when I found her application could not proceed as per the interim order. Her behaviour does not appear to be an isolated occurrence. The Tenant did not challenge the Landlord representative’s assertion that this is a pattern of disruptive behaviour.

Subsection 204(3) of the Act provides a Member with discretion to order a party or their agent or legal representative to pay the costs of the Board. Needless to say, such discretion should be used economically. The Legislature intended that such Board power be used to recover some of the public’s monies which funded the proceedings and, further, to discourage inappropriate practices and conduct by parties and parties’ agents and legal representatives.
In my view, considering the conduct of the Tenant globally, I find Board costs appropriate in this circumstance.
As per s.204(3) and (4) of the Act, I find it appropriate to award Board costs in the amount of $150.00 for hearing time.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $200.00 on or before August 14, 2026.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before August 14, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant shall also pay costs of $150.00 to the Board on or before August 14, 2026. July 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenants filed their application on April 28, 2025, alleging that the pool heater was not functioning, but did not include specific dates in the application. At the hearing, the Tenants confirmed that the issue started in October 2023, and that they repaired the pool heater on April 26, 2024. The Tenants explained that, although the initial issue was repaired by April 26, 2024, the Landlord failed to reimburse the bill the Tenants sent them on April 30, 2024.
Pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act, “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”

The cause of action in this application is the pool heater disrepair, which occurred past the limitation period under subsection 29(2) of the Act. The Tenant’s repair costs are a remedy arising from the initial disrepair, not a new maintenance issue. Therefore, the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear the application, and it must be dismissed.

The Tenants submitted that the issue reoccurred again later. However, they did not amend their application to include later events despite being made aware of the limitation period issue at the Adjudicative Case Conference held on January 7, 2026. An application must contain sufficient details for the opposing party to know the case to be met and prepare accordingly. The description of the issue in the application does not indicate that it reoccurred. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord was aware that the Tenant intended to claim that the disrepair continued past the first period indicated, and the application could not proceed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not meet their maintenance obligations
reasons: The Tenant filed this application on April 20, 2025. An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held on February 17, 2026. At the ACC, the parties and Member discussed potential issues with the application including missing or incorrect dates, and the option for the Tenant to amend the application.

On July 1, 2026, the Tenant filed three documents intended as an amendment to his application. The documents were confusing and poorly organized. They consisted of: • A 20-page document titled “request to amend application” which included a cover letter, a one-page “amended particulars,” a one-page “amended remedies,” and a copy of the original application with annotations listing amendments to remedies; • A 194-page document titled “Hearing Brief – Part 1” which included 20 pages of particularized allegations, legal argument, and an evidence list mixed together, and 174 pages of evidence without a usable table of contents; • A 94-page document titled “Hearing Brief – Part 2” consisting of further evidence without a usable table of contents.
It was impossible to tell, from the documents, which of the pages were meant to constitute the particulars of the Tenant’s claim against the Landlord.
The Landlord opposed the amendment request. They asked that the amendment be denied and that the application be dismissed for lack of particulars.

I asked the Tenant’s representative to identify which pages of the documents contained the particulars of the facts the Tenant would seek to prove in this proceeding. The Tenant’s representative identified page 2 of the “request to amend application” document, titled “amended particulars.”

I granted the Tenant’s request, and amended the application to consist of the claims set out on page 3 of the “request to amend application” document, without prejudice to the Landlord’s right to argue that the amended particulars were still insufficient. Prior settlement
The Tenant argues that the amended claims raised in this proceeding are barred by a settlement the parties reached in a prior proceeding, LTB-L-105833-24.

LTB-L-105833-24 was an application by the Landlord to terminate the tenancy for rent arrears. On March 10, 2025, the Tenant filed an “Issues a Tenant Intends to Raise at a Rent Arrears Hearing” form, indicating that he intended to raise the following issues pursuant to section 82 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA): unrepaired windows and frames; basement foundation leakage; ongoing plumbing issues; harassment and property damage; and rent increase dispute.
The form indicated that the Tenant did not intend to seek monetary remedies for his issues. He intended to seek orders that the Landlord carry out repairs and cease the alleged conduct.

The application was heard on April 2, 2025. At the hearing, the parties engaged in mediation. The Landlord’s representative says that during mediation, the Tenant was asked whether there were any outstanding issues. He said that there were not. The Landlord argues that this means the Tenant agreed that the maintenance and harassment issues he filed on March 10 had, by April 2, been resolved.

The parties then requested a consent order to resolve the Landlord’s application about rent arrears. The order stated that the parties agreed that “the Tenant did not raise any s. 82 issues.” 12. 18 days later, on April 20 the Tenant filed the present application alleging issues which include all the issues previously identified in his section 82 form, other than the rent increase dispute. The application alleges that the issues were ongoing as of April 20. 13. The Landlord argues that the Tenant is barred from raising those issues, because he previously agreed that as of April 2, the issues had already been resolved. The Landlord also argues that the Tenant should not be able to allege that any other issues existed as of April 2, since he agreed at that time that there were no outstanding issues. 14. I am not persuaded by the Landlord’s argument. The consent order did not state that the Tenant agreed that there were no issues, or that he was settling any existing claims he might have. It only stated that he was not raising any claims in that proceeding. 15. If the Tenant admitted, during mediation, that the Landlord had resolved the issues, the admission might be protected by settlement privilege. If it is not privileged, the admission can be put into evidence and used to attack the Tenant’s credibility if it contradicts his current testimony. That, in my view, is the proper use of a prior admission that contradicts a party’s claim. A prior admission does not legally bar a claim, absent an agreement to settle that claim. 16. I therefore held that this application was not barred by a prior settlement or admission. Sufficiency of particulars 17. The Landlord then moved that the application be dismissed on the basis that, as amended, it did not contain sufficient particulars of the Tenant’s claim. 18. I granted the motion. The amended application contains almost no dates setting out when the issues occurred. For example, the application alleges “basement leaks and flooding” but only says that they occurred on “April 10, 2025 and continuing.” It does not say what, specifically, happened on April 10, nor what leaks or floods occurred on any subsequent dates. 19. Several of the issues also state “exact dates to be confirmed.” The amended application was filed more than a year after the original application was filed, and only two weeks before the hearing. It is unclear why the dates of the incidents were still not available, nor when they would be provided. 20. Most of the issues also lacked sufficient description. For example, one of the issues was “kitchen flooding” but said nothing about whether the flood was caused by a plumbing leak, a broken appliance, a roof leak during rainstorms, or something else. 21. The lack of dates was identified as an issue at the ACC, yet the amended application failed to address the issue. 22. I agree with the Landlord that the amended application does not set out sufficiently particularized claims for the Landlord or the LTB to know what is being alleged. The application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
