issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. An adjudicative case conference was held by videoconference on April 16, 2026. Only the Tenant attended. As of 11:27am, the Landlord was not present or represented although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

T he Tenant testified that on March 18, 2025, at approximately 8:10 p.m., the Tenant returned to the rental unit and was unable to access their room because the battery in the electronic door lock had died.

The Tenant contacted ‘[name]’, the property manager, at approximately 8:32 p.m. Jeff advised the Tenant that he was attempting to find someone to assist. After waiting approximately one hour without assistance, the Tenant asked whether they could contact a locksmith and was advised that they could do so.

A locksmith attended at approximately 10:20 p.m., and the Tenant regained access to the room at approximately 10:30 p.m. The Tenant paid the locksmith $339.00. The battery in the lock was replaced the following day.

The Tenant testified that they had been working and studying and wanted to return home to relax. I accept that being unable to access the room for approximately two hours was frustrating and inconvenient. However, the evidence established that this was an isolated incident caused by a dead battery. The property manager responded to the Tenant, attempted to obtain assistance and ultimately authorized the Tenant to contact a locksmith.

There was no evidence that the Landlord intentionally prevented the Tenant from accessing the room, knew before the incident that the battery was about to fail or failed to correct the problem after becoming aware of it. There was also no evidence that the problem was repeated or ongoing.

The Act uses language like “substantial,” meaning that not every inconvenience or isolated event will lead to a cause of action. I accept that the Tenant was inconvenienced by being unable to access their room for approximately two hours. However, considering the isolated nature and limited duration of the incident, together with the property manager’s response, I do not find that it rises to the level of substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $14,730.60 on or before August 3, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant with a Notice of Termination (‘N12 Notice’) under section 48 of the Act on February 21, 2023 with a termination date of April 30, 2023 and that the Tenant moved out on June 1, 2024 because they received this notice.
Both parties agree that in the N12 Notice, the Landlord claimed that they required vacant possession of the rental unit for their own residential occupation.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord is using the rental unit as a temporary residence. She submitted pictures she took of the unit on August 12, 2024 which show that the kitchen, living room and bathroom are gutted. She testified that the unit is still in this condition.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord uses the rental unit as a temporary residence and that she lives and works in Toronto. The Tenant maintains that the Landlord evicted her because they did not want to do maintenance work and wanted to take the unit to do renovations and live there. The Tenant provided in evidence a text message from the Landlord around May 2022, which stated that the house needs improvements, and they can not be done while the Tenant lives there.

The Landlord testified that she wanted to live in Flesherton but she lost her job around February 15, 2024 and had to re-locate to Toronto. As such, she resides at the rental unit from Friday to Sunday and then she lives mostly in Toronto along with her son in her other home. She also testified that she undertook to do repairs at the rental unit once she moved in because she discovered asbestos and mold. She testified that she can only do the renovations now while she is still working.

She testified that she only occupies the main floor of the rental unit, and the upper unit is rented out to another tenant. She did agree that she demolished the walls and kitchen on the main floor. The bathroom is also under renovation as such she only has a sink and toilet. She stated that she does not cook or shower at the rental unit and only takes sponge baths. She stays mainly in her bedroom.

However, she testified in three years she plans to retire and live full time at the rental unit. She also testified that in November 2021, the she was hemorrhaging money as such, she made the decision to move into the rental unit and as it would be less expensive for her.

I find that Landlord made no effort to confirm if the property was suitable for her to live in prior to serving the N12. I am also not satisfied by the evidence presented that the Landlord genuinely experienced a change in circumstances after the Tenant vacated that prevented her from moving into the rental unit on a full-time basis.

Finally, even if I accept the Landlord’s evidence that they were occupying the rental unit, I find their “sporadic” occupation does not constitute “residential occupation” for the purpose of section 48. In numerous decisions of this Board and the Divisional Court (see [name] [1994] O.J. No. 2737; and McDonald v. Smith [1993] O.J. No. 1680) it has been established that casual or intermittent use of the rental unit, as was described by the Landlord, does not meet the standard of “residential occupation” for the purposes of section 48 of the Act. In this case, I find that the Landlord’s sporadic or part- time occupation of the rental unit does not constitute “residential occupation” under section 48(1). I see no reason not to apply the same principle to the phrase “occupied the rental unit” in section 57(1)(a). In other words, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant moved out.

Accordingly, the Tenant has proven all of the elements of the test in section 57(1)., I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith and the Tenant’s application must be granted. Remedies

The monthly rent at the end of the tenancy was $860.20. The Tenant requested a 100% rent abatement equivalent to 365 days of rent, in the amount of $10,322.40. I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent.

An abatement of rent is based on the principle that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. There was evidence before me that the Tenant was not able to utilize the rental unit in its entirety after the service of the notice. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not do adequate repairs to the unit or there were lengthy delays in doing repairs. The Tenant did not produce any documentary evidence to corroborate that the Landlord was harassing the Tenant to move out. However, I do find that the Tenant was packing and preparing to move and as such, they lost any kind of enjoyment at the rental unit. The Tenant submitted that the process of looking for another rental unit and moving caused them to experience a high level of stress. I find that any tenant who has to move due to a landlord’s request would experience stress and their use of the unit would have been diminished when they had to look for a new place to live, instead of enjoying their unit. The rent was $860.20, and the Tenant received the notice on February 21, 2023. The Tenant moved out June 1, 2024. I find that an abatement of 100% for the for the month of May 2024, to be reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $860.20. 30. The Tenant requested the rent differential they incurred for one year after moving out of the rental unit, based on $860.20 per month for a total of $10,322.40 for the year. The Tenant moved into a house which consisted of two bedrooms, and one-bathroom as of March 1, 2025, paying $2,350.00 for the monthly rent. The parties agreed that the monthly rent for the rental unit was $1,489.80 at the time the Tenant vacated. The rental unit was a ground floor of the house and consisted of 2 bedrooms and 1 bathroom and basement for storage. 31. I find that the rental units are comparable, I do find that the Tenant is entitled to the rent differential because the Tenant had to move as a result of the N12 notice they received. I find that awarding an increased rent in the amount of $860.20 to be fair in the circumstances. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $10,322.40 for rent differential for a period of one year. 32. The Tenant incurred reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses as a result of the Landlord’s breach in the amount of $1,000.00 According to the testimony of the Tenant, the Tenant paid for a moving truck and gas and paid for four men to help her move. She did not submit documentary evidence in support of the claim, but I find her testimony is sufficient and this to be a reasonable amount. 33. The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $10,322.40. 34. Section 57(3) (1.1) of the Act authorizes the Board to order general compensation in the amount of up to 12 months rent the Tenant last paid should it be determined the Landlord gave an N12 notice in bad faith. 35. The Tenant testified that the move had a detrimental effect on their financial and emotional well being. She testified that she lived next door to her kid’s grandmother who assisted her with childcare. To find alternative housing, it depleted their life savings. 36. The Landlord’s actions had a significant impact on the Tenant. Given the inconvenience faced by the Tenant by the N12 having been served in bad faith, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $2,500.00 in general compensation. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,500.00 for general compensation. 37. The Tenant is requesting that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 38. In light of the other remedies awarded, I do not find that this is an appropriate case for an administrative fine for deterrence. The other remedies ordered do provide sufficient deterrence to the Landlord. [name] for Costs 39. The Landlord’s legal representative requested an order requiring the Tenant to pay costs. Pursuant to Rule 23.3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, an order for party costs will usually only be awarded when one party engages in unreasonable conduct during the proceedings which causes undue delay or expense. I am not satisfied the Landlord has established that the Tenant engaged in this kind of conduct. The request for compensation of costs is therefore denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $14,730.60. This amount represents: • $860.20 for a rent abatement. • $10,322.40 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from June 1, 2024, to May 30, 2025. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

On March 21, 2025 a contractor for the Landlord entered the rental unit to carry out repairs in the bathroom. The contractor engaged in small talk with the Tenant asking if she had any single friends and stated he “wasn’t looking to mingle, if you know what I mean”. The Tenant testified his body language was suggestive and this comment made her uncomfortable. The contractor later apologized for the comment and acknowledged it was inappropriate. As the contractor was leaving, he inserted himself into a conversation the Tenant was having with her son about their upcoming birthdays.

In the morning of March 24, 2025, the Tenant called the Landlord’s office and left a message requesting that the contractor not return to the rental unit. When the Tenant drove into the parking lot that morning she was surprised to see the contractor in the parking lot. The contractor asked the Tenant what time he should return to the rental unit to finish the work. The Tenant responded to the contractor advising him to contact the office.
It is undisputed the contractor did not return to the rental unit.
On April 9, 2025 the Tenant saw the contractor in the common area of the residential complex. The contractor did not interact with the Tenant.
The property manager [name] testified that after April 9, 2025 the contractor no longer was employed by the Landlord. Analysis Harassment
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Harassment is not defined in the Act; I turn to the Ontario Human Rights Code’s definition of harassment: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”

It is uncontested the contractor did not return to the rental unit after March 21, 2025. It is likely that, given the timing of the Tenant advising the Landlord of the issue, that the contractor was not aware of the issue when he spoke to the Tenant on March 24. The contractor and the Tenant did not communicate on April 9, 2025.

Therefore, the only issue to consider is the allegation on March 21, 2025. Based on the uncontested testimony of the Tenant, I am not satisfied that the single event on March 21, 2025 rises to a level of harassment.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: nitially heard by videoconference on May 8, 2026 as part of an urgent block with the initial focus on the allegation of interference with vital services. [name] on behalf of both tenants attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented by Charmaine [name] (‘CP’) who is the sister of JP and his Power of Attorney. [name] [name] (‘EP’), the son of JP and DP, attended the hearing as a witness for the Tenant. [name] [name] (‘DS’) attended the hearing on behalf of the Landlord. The Board found that the Landlord interfered with supply of vital services. The balance of the application was adjourned to be heard on a future date. Interim order LTB-T-033979-26-IN2 was issued on May 11, 2026 requiring the Landlord to restore supply of vital services. The rest of the application was heard on July 24, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was again represented by CP. EP attended the hearing as a witness for the Tenant. As of 9:20 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $15,053.00.
Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence I find that they established their claims on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant’s application contains some allegations that fall outside of the one-year limitation period contained in s. 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’): No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. I advised the Tenant of this provision and the Tenant did not pursue these allegations at the hearing.

On November 21, 2025, the Tenant was at home. [name] had just put [name] [name], who had been unwell for a long time, to bed. She heard loud banging and yelling at her door. Looking outside, she saw [name], and other individuals, one of whom she believed to be the property manager.

They demanded that she open the door and threatened to break it down if she did not comply. DP told them their actions were not legal, but they continued aggressively banging on the door with the goal of forcing it open. The Landlord seriously damaged the door in the course of this interaction. The Tenant described the incident as extremely frightening and testified that she feared what would happen once they entered. DP stated that she had never seen anyone behave in such an aggressive manner and was particularly intimidated by the property manager. JP, who had been asleep, was awakened by the disturbance.
EP was also home. He came out during the incident to confront the Landlord and demand that he stops. The Landlord threatened to call the police, and EP invited him to do so, which he then did.
DP also testified about the prolonged loss of hot water, which caused significant hardship for her and JP.

Because there was no hot water, she was unable to properly bathe or care for JP. She described the effect the Landlord’s actions had on her as humiliating, embarrassing, and deeply distressing. She stated that these conditions negatively affected her family relationships and social life, as she felt unable to invite family members or guests into the home. According to DP, JP was largely confined to staying downstairs because of his health and poor living conditions.

The tenant further testified that the gas service providing heat and hot water was disconnected on April 8, 2026. As of the date of her testimony, she stated that the hot water issue remained unresolved and that the landlord had failed to remedy the situation.

EP testified as well. On November 21, 2025, he observed the landlord, [name], and unidentified people including a property manager at the door, holding crowbars and trying to break down the door. He believes two other individuals were associated with a construction or demolition company working on the Landlord’s lot nearby. They were very agitated, rude and confrontational. They were seeking access to the property to obtain drywall samples for asbestos testing related to a planned demolition.

The Landlord accused the occupants of squatting and asserted that no one was supposed to be living in the upper level of the property. EP replied that DS had permitted them to live upstairs and that he has a recording to prove it. DS did not dispute it. The Landlord became irate and contacted the police, falsely alleging that EP had threatened to shoot or stab him. The landlord stated that he has the right to enter his property and threatening to cut off water, power, and other services.

Police attended and mediated the situation. After the Landlord left, the son permitted the contractors to enter the property. He stated that he never learned the identity of the property manager and that the front door remains visibly damaged as a result of the attempted forced entry.
EP recorded part of the interaction using his cellphone. The recording (Document ID 7901592) is consistent with EP’s testimony.
With respect to utilities, EP testified that the Landlord only made things worse after the Board’s interim order requiring him to restore supply of vital services.

On or about May 11, 2026, after returning from a medical appointment for his father, EP observed Enbridge crews working in the area and initially believed they were reconnecting the gas service. However, he subsequently learned that the gas line had instead been capped at the homeowner’s request, resulting in the gas service being permanently disconnected. EP was advised that the work was completed pursuant to a shut-off request by the owner and that the gas could not simply be reconnected. He was informed that a new account would need to be established before gas service could be restored. The supervisor also indicated that he had not been aware that anyone was residing at the property.
I find that it is morel likely than not that the Landlord has harassed and coerced the Tenant and has interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence, I find that the Landlord breached ss. 21(1), 22 and 23 of the Act. 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The Landlord persistently harassed the Tenant by showing up at the property with crowbars and attempting to break in, and by intentionally interfering with supply of vital services in an apparent attempt to intimidate the Tenant and force them to leave after threatening to do so in November 2025.

The Tenant’s application requests only one remedy: general damages in the amount of $50,000. Other remedies, such as ongoing remedies and/or fines until the Landlord complies, may have been appropriate but won’t be awarded as they weren’t requested.

This would be a particularly appropriate case for a fine payable to the LTB for the Landlord’s blatant disregard for the law, the Act, and the LTB. The application does not request it, and I will not order it at this time but the Landlord should consider this order to be his notice that the Board may order a fine against them on its own motion next time the Landlord is a party before the LTB.
The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $50,000 for the serious impact the Landlord’s misconduct has had on their mental, physical and emotional well-being.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment.
Some recent cases award higher damages. Havill v Equity Builders Ltd, 2024 ONLTB 19914 for example, ordered a landlord to pay $15,364 in general damages.

I find the amount of $15,000 to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s actions had on them, their mental health and their ability to live their lives. I found the Tenant’s evidence to be persuasive and compelling. The Landlord did not illegally evict the Tenant but did everything they could to force the Tenant to leave short of locking them out. They intentionally interfered with supply of three vital services. They intimidated and harassed the Tenant. The misconduct was not one isolated incident on November 21 2025 – it was a campaign that started in November of last year and intensified in April 2026. It didn’t stop even after the Board issued its interim order requiring the Landlord to restore supply of vital services. I find that this high award is required to restore the Tenant into the same position they would have been in had the Landlord not interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. I find it appropriate to award an amount substantially higher than the “usual” award for general damages in serious cases.
This amount represents general damages up to July 24th 2026.
This order is without prejudice to the Tenant’s right to seek other remedies, including fines, abatement, expenses, damages, et c. for the Landlord’s misconduct if it continues beyond July 25, 2026.
The Tenant incurred the cost of $53.00 in filing this application and is entitled to reimbursement of this cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,053.00. This amount represents: • $15,000.00 for General Damages. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Howell (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Landlord is amended to reflect the correct corporate name, [organization]. [name] is removed as a party as he is only an employee of the corporate Landlord.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must take reasonable steps to address the noise complained of by the Tenant.

In this application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of her rental unit and the residential complex by failing to address issues of noise disturbances from another unit in the complex.

The Tenant has resided in the rental unit since July 1, 2014. She described the residential complex as a 5 storey property built in 1967. There are 5 units per floor with 3 on one side (where her unit is located, #402) and 2 on the other side. She stated that around November 2024 a family, 2 adults and one child, moved into unit #406 which is on the same floor and side as her unit, but that they are separated by another unit between them.

She stated that the tenants of 406 leave the door to their rental unit open and the noise from their unit resonates down the hallway. She also stated that in December 2024 they had a second child who has been continuously crying, fussing, and/or screaming since that time and that she has regularly complained to the Landlord about this. She provided a copy of an email sent to the Landlord dated June 2, 2025 as one example of a complaint she made into evidence (DOC-7909774) and maintained that she has complained monthly to the Landlord about these noise issues.

She also provided a video recording of an incident involving the noise into evidence (DOC- 8024784). In the recording, which is approximately one minute and forty-eight seconds, and taken from inside the Tenant’s unit, but near the main entrance door, you can hear an infant crying in the hallway creating an echo. The Tenant had uploaded a number of video recordings but maintained that they are all same regarding the type of noise disturbance she is experiencing. She maintained that the noise disturbance of a baby crying, screaming, continues every day, multiple times a day, even now that their second child would be a toddler, it is still the same type of crying. She stated that she has contacted the City and the Police who have advised her that it is a civil matter.

There was no dispute that this Landlord took over from a previous landlord in April 2025. The Landlord’s Agent stated that he first corresponded with unit 406 by phone regarding the noise issue in April 2026 and was in their unit during an annual inspection on May 15, 2026 where the Tenant’s complaints were discussed. He stated that the tenants of 406 advised they are doing their best to keep the noise at a minimum. He also stated that no other tenants in the complex have complained about any noise coming from unit 406.

Under cross-examination, the Landlord’s Agent recalled a complaint by the Tenant as early as December 7, 2025 and then also confirmed an email complaint received on April 6, 2025 (DOC-7909782) that he replied to on April 7, 2025 that he would speak to unit 406 despite only speaking to unit 406 in April 2026. The Landlord Agent’s also stated that in early December 2025 he was in hospital and then in/out of the hospital from then until March 2026 due to a diagnosis of an auto-immune disease.

A landlord’s duty to address substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a tenant by another tenant was affirmed by the Divisional Court in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”). The Court held, inter alia, as follows: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.”

In other words, a landlord has the positive obligation to provide the Tenant with quiet enjoyment and take the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of his premises.

Based on the evidence before me, I find it more likely than not that the Tenant’s quiet enjoyment of the rental unit has been affected by continuous on-going noise emanating from another unit in the complex for an extended period of time. Additionally, I was satisfied that the Tenant had repeated reported this issue to the Landlord, the first time being as early as April 6, 2025 yet the Landlord has only spoken with the offending tenant over the telephone in April 2026 and attended the offending unit in May 2026. I was not satisfied that these actions amounted to reasonable steps required to taken pursuant to [name].

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by failing to take reasonable necessary steps to address the Tenant’s complaints of noise disturbance. Remedies

The Tenant stated that all she wants is for the Landlord to address/resolve the noise issues from unit 406. She also stated that she is willing to assist if necessary by being transferred to another unit. Although, she feels that she should not have to move.
The Board does not have the authority to force a Landlord to transfer the tenancy of any tenant.

However, I was satisfied that the Landlord shall be ordered take reasonable steps to address the noise disturbances complained of by the Tenant. In my view, the courts have held that a landlord, faced with complaints about offending conduct by one tenant against another tenant, must take reasonable steps, within a reasonable amount of time, to investigate the offending conduct, appropriately address the conduct and, where the conduct does not cease, issue a notice of termination to the alleged offending tenant(s). The service of a N5 notice of termination by a landlord is a significant, and an often effective first step when the offending conduct does not cease as is alleged here. If the offending conduct continues even after the N5 step is taken, a next step might be the filing of an application with the Board to terminate that tenancy.
ordered: The Landlord shall take reasonable steps to address any noise complaints made by the Tenant. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. N12 Notice not Given in Bad Faith:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified he received an N12 notice on March 25, 2024 with a date of termination of May 31, 2024 because the Landlord was moving into the rental unit. The Tenant testified he vacated on April 30, 2024. It is not disputed that the Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice, and Landlord [name] (PDS) testified she could not speak on whether the Tenant vacated due to the N12 notice. Based on the Tenant’s testimony, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established that he vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.
The Tenant testified that on September 6, 2024, he saw the rental unit advertised for rent, therefore he believes that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Landlords acknowledged that the rental unit was advertised for rent within 1 year of serving the N12 notice. Accordingly, s. 57(5)(c) of the Act applies and “it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that [the] landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith.”

The Landlord [name] (RR) testified that when he served the N12 notice he and his wife had been separated and he had been living with his brother for 2 months. PDS also testified that she and her husband has been separated when the N12 notice was served. RR further testified that he did not foresee reconciling with his wife, so he served the N12 notice as he had nowhere else to live except with his brother. RR testified he moved into the rental unit on May 4, 2024 and lived in the rental unit until October 30, 2024. RR testified he changed his driver’s license to the rental properties address. The Landlords did not provide documentary evidence that RR moved into the rental unit, however the Tenant did not seriously contest this fact.

RR then testified that he and his wife continued working on their marital issues and in September 2024 he contacted a real estate agent to re-list the property as the plan was for RR to move back into the matrimonial home in November 2024 as he had reconciled with his wife.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario found that in determining bad faith, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant the termination notice.

In [name] v. Belijinac, 2001 CanLii 40231 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court determined that a Landlord satisfied the “good faith” requirement to terminate a tenancy where the person identified in the notice of termination genuinely intends to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes

Based on the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the Landlords have rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I am satisfied that the Landlords served an N12 notice in good faith, and that RR genuinely intended to reside in the rental unit for at least 12 months, and did reside there for 6 months. I accept RR’s evidence that he and his wife separated which led to the N12 notice being served, and I accept RR’s evidence that the rental unit was listed for rent due to him and his wife reconciling, which was an unforeseen circumstance as he had already been separated from his wife and living outside the matrimonial home for 2 months when the N12 notice was served. I accept that the Landlords decided to re- rent the rental unit as a result in the change of circumstances and not based on bad faith. As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in good faith.
As the Tenants did not establish the bad faith of the Landlord in serving the N12 notice, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must complete the necessary repairs and pay the Tenant $3,298.85 by August 31, 2026.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I make the following findings of fact. 1. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2024. The rental unit is a one-bedroom apartment, with one washroom and an open kitchen and dining area. The lawful monthly rent is $2,400.00. 2. When the Tenant moved in, the rental unit was in a poor state of repair from the previous tenants. The walls had drawings on them, the cupboards were coming off their hinges, the window screens were ripped, the blinds were not functioning, there was water damage under the washroom sink, the baseboards were not properly secured, the carpet was stained, the microwave vent was clogged, the lights in the entryway were not working, and the kitchen sink was slanted to one side and not draining properly.
The Tenant informed the Landlord of all the issues when he went to view the rental unit two weeks prior to the tenancy starting.

The Landlord started conducting repairs in the rental unit in April 2026. The sink was reinstalled on June 12, 2026. All of the walls in the rental unit were painted in April and May 2025, finally being completed on June 4, 2026. The carpet was replaced on June 26, 2026. The loose baseboard was painted over but not secured on May 24, 2026.

The entrance lights were repaired on May 22, 2026, but the electrical issue moved to the bathroom and then the bedroom. The Tenant has not had a functioning light in the bedroom since June 5, 2026. 3. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 4. In this case, the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s complaints reasonably. The Landlord was informed of the issues in October 2024, before the tenancy started, but only began repairs in April 2026, over a year later. Therefore, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit. Although the Tenant suspected that there may be mould in the unit, there was insufficient evidence for such a finding. 5. The Tenant requested a rent abatement from November 1, 2024, to March 31, 2026, and for the repairs to be completed within a firm schedule. The Tenant explained that, while most of the issues were cosmetic, the sink was a concern because it would turn black at the corners if it was not cleaned on a daily basis. The Tenant became frustrated from having to repeatedly ask for repairs, to no response. Based on the number of issues and the significant length of time they remained unresolved, I find an 8.00% abatement to be appropriate. The Landlord will be required to repair any outstanding issues.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair the following items in the rental unit by August 31, 2026. The Landlord shall ensure that: • the kitchen cupboards are properly secured; • the window screens and window blinds are fully functional and not damaged; • the water damage under the washroom sink is repaired; • the baseboards are properly secured; • the microwave vent is cleaned; • the light in the bedroom is functional and the underlying electrical issue is resolved.

If the Landlord does not do the work by August 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the work to be done and may recover the cost of the work by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months after the repairs are done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,298.85. This amount represents: • $3,250.85 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from September 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 31, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months after repairs are done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

A T1 application is brought under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which permits a Tenant or former Tenant of a rental unit to apply for an order that the Landlord pay to the tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of the Act by the Landlord. Preliminary issue – wrong type of application
With respect to the Tenant’s T1 application, The Tenants claimed the towing charges and the refund of monies associated with the tow.

At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal representative raised the issue that this application was in relation to the towing of a vehicle and the fees associated with the tow. At no time did the Landlord take possession of the vehicle or sell the vehicle. [name] took the position that this is the wrong application for the remedy that the Tenants are seeking.

In response, the Tenants stated that they had called the LTB and they were the ones to tell them what kind of application to file. The Tenants did confirm that their vehicle was never sold by the Landlord and that the amount requested in the application was the amount in connection with the tow and the associated fees. The Tenants also confirmed that they had not sought legal advice prior to the hearing date.

I am in agreement with the Landlord that this is the wrong application. What the Tenants are seeking are out-of-pocket expenses allegedly caused by the Landlord’s conduct. Out- of-pocket expenses is not a remedy that is available in a T1 application but is available in other applications available to the Tenants.
As the Tenants are seeking a remedy that I cannot order with the type of application before me, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order, LTB-T-037450-25, determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order, LTB-T-034661-25, determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 15, 2026 at 09:00 am. Only the Tenant Representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 09:30 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenancy commenced on February 6, 2023 and terminated on July 30, 2025 when the Tenant moved out.
The rental unit consisted of an apartment with two bedrooms and one bathroom. The lawful rent was $1,460.63.
The Tenant field their applications on April 29, 2025.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the applications: LTB-T-034661-25

The Tenant alleged the Landlord failed to address the following maintenance issues: [name] windows; b. Washing machine c. Pests in form of mice and flies; d. Kitchen sink backing up; e. Bathroom tub chipping and peeling; f. Stove exhaust connection; and g. Electrical

It was the Tenants testimony that the broken windows and bathroom tub peeling were identified as part of their walkthrough prior to commencing the tenancy in February 2023 and that despite promises to have them fixed, the Landlord never did. Same was their testimony regarding the stove vent, having never been connected, and the kitchen sink backing up, having reported both issues in March 2023 by text, entered in evidence.

It was also their testimony that they were required to pay an additional $50.00 a month for use of a washing machine inside the unit, which they continued to pay, despite it not working, specifically, leaking, as of February 2023, until it was removed in February 2024 and never replaced.

They then testified that they had identified a mice and fly problem to the Landlord by a phone call at the same time in March 2023 and despite this a pest technician did not attend the property until June 2023, who in turn only provided traps and tape to catch the pests. It was their testimony that they would routinely have to place both to keep up with the problem.
As to the electrical, it was their testimony that due to faulty wiring they were limited in the number of outlets they could use at one time, for fear of tripping the breaker.

Upon completion of the Tenant’s testimony, the Tenant Representative entered in evidence, pictures, correspondence and a property standards order to comply, dated April 9, 2024, to substantiate the Tenant’s claims.

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested testimony, and evidence above I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with health safety housing and maintenance standards.

Specifically, the photographic evidence entered clearly showed the windows to be broken and nonfunctional to include missing panes. Similarly, the pictures of the bathtub show that the paint was in fact peeling, exposing metal and rust throughout while there were clear signs of a mice and fly issue by way of traps and feces.
The pictures entered, also showed the kitchen sink to have been backed up and the vent to the stove not connected.

That said, the Tenant failed to provide any evidence of the electrical outlets not working, other than their oral testimony. However, given it was uncontested, I am satisfied they also proved the Landlord has failed in this regard as well.

It is also clear by the text messages entered that as early as February 7, 2023 the Tenant had started to communicate these issues and to continue to do so up to February 20, 2024 whereas the property standards order proves that these issues were still extant as of April 9, 2024.This is not reasonable behaviour on part of the Landlord a clear breach of section 20 of the Act. LTB-T-037450-25

The Tenant testified that the Landlord withheld vital service by way of failing to ensure that the rental unit and complex had sufficient heat. They testified to complaining about this issue to the Landlord in February 2023 and that it was unresolved when they moved out. The Tenant Representative referred to the property standards order to support this claim.

The Tenant then testified that that they were substantially interfered with by way of the Landlord’s failure to address the maintenance issues and the installation of security cameras, which in their submission violated their privacy as they pointed in such a way that they could see into their rental unit. They supported their testimony with pictures of the camera entered in evidence.
On my own questioning, they testified that the door to their unit was a few feet back along the same wall that the [name] was angled along.

The Tenant then testified to the impact the Landlords failure to address the maintenance issues and withholding of vital service had. Specifically, the stress and additional effort required to maintain the unit in a habitable state, whilst resorting to family and friends to do their laundry which combined resulted in them moving out.

Section 21(1) of the Act states a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.
Given the Tenant’s uncontested testimony and the property standards ordered, I am satisfied that the Landlord did breach this section of the Act regarding the provision of heat.

Section 22 of the Act states a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Given my determinations above regarding the Landlord’s breach of section 20 of the Act, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven their claim for substantial interference regarding the Landlord’s failure to address maintenance issues.

That said, I am not satisfied this is the case regarding the installation of security cameras. Specifically, by the camera’s location and the Tenant’s own testimony I am not satisfied that it could see inside the unit, only who was entering and leaving which does not constitute a violation of privacy under the Act. Remedies sought.
Pursuant to the Tenant’s applications the remedies sought are: a. Rent abatement of $36,269.32; b. The Landlord ordered to pay a fine; c. Reimbursement of the filing fee of $48.00 Remedies awarded.

An abatement is a monetary award expressed in terms of a portion of past or future rent. It may be in the form of an order: (a) directing that the landlord pay the tenant a fixed amount—return rent paid by the tenant; or (b) allowing the tenant to pay less rent going forward by a fixed amount or percentage of the rent the tenant pays.

A rent abatement is meant to compensate the tenant to the degree that the tenant was deprived of what was bargained for or what is prescribed by legislation or minimum housing standards. It is only when a tenant is completely deprived of all of the benefits of a tenancy—where the rental unit in uninhabitable—that a 100% abatement is appropriate. [See 22001839 (Re), 2022 ABRTDRS 15 (CanLII)] As noted by the Vice Chair in TST- 56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

In determining the appropriate abatement, the LTB will consider, among other things: a. what percentage of the ‘package’ of shelter and services the landlord contracted or was otherwise obliged to provide was not available to the tenant; b. the length of time the problem existed and the severity of the problem in terms of its effect on the tenant; c. whether the tenant told the landlord about the issue(s) in a timely manner; d. whether the landlord responded to the issues raised by the tenant within a reasonable time and the landlord’s response was appropriate and effective. e. whether the tenant is wholly or partially responsible for the issue(s); and f. whether the tenant hindered or interfered with the landlord’s efforts to address the issue(s).

The LTB will consider the impact the breach has on the average tenant or the impact a reasonable person would expect this problem to have on a tenant. If the tenant has a particular susceptibility to the problem, the landlord can only reasonably be liable to the tenant for a more significant abatement if it can be shown that the landlord knew of the particular condition of the tenant.

The ultimate objective is to grant an abatement that is fair considering all of the circumstances. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name] [1997] O.J. No. 1881 (Gen Div) the Court said, “It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the no- repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.”
Similarly, in Offredi v. [organization] 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) the Court said that there is no mathematical way in which to determine an appropriate abatement.

In this case, I believe that a lump sum abatement is appropriate in terms of compensating the Tenant for the impact the Landlord’s failure to address maintenance issues and the resulting substantial interference which I am satisfied contributed to them moving out of the rental unit.

That said, I also cannot overlook the fact the Tenant was able to reside in the unit for over two years, despite the issues present. Accordingly, on this basis I set the abatement at $14,825.00 based on a 35.00% abatement from February 2023 until July 2025.
I am also satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed the $50.00 month paid for the washing machine that was inoperable for a period of 12 months totalling $600.00.
Given the Tenant has proven their case they are also entitled to reimbursement for the cost of filing their application, totalling $48.00.
Given the remedies already awarded and the fact that the LAndlrod was not present, I am not satisfied a fine is appropriate.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,473.00. This amount represents: • $14,825.00 for a rent abatement for the period of February 2023 until July 2025. • $600.00 for use of the washing machine that was inoperable. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed as it fails to contain sufficient dates, times and details.

There is no dispute that the Tenant appeared before the Board for an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) on January 13, 2026. During that ACC, the Board explained to the Tenant that his application lacks sufficient dates, times and details. The application also fails to claim any remedies other than a vague request for various kinds of “damages”, but the application does not request any specific monetary amounts.

At the hearing, the Landlord requested that the application be dismissed because it fails to include sufficient dates, times and details. I agree with the Landlord on this point. While I recognize that the application lists at least 4 possible issues of alleged disrepair in the rental unit and mentions three dates when the Tenant complained to the Landlord about mice, I remain satisfied that the application contains insufficient details and cannot proceed.

It is a fundamental principle of law that the parties are entitled to know “the case they have to meet”. This means that each party is entitled to know the precise allegations being raised so they can prepare an adequate defence against those allegations. If the allegations contain insufficient information, the responding party is at a loss to know how to adequately prepare their defence. That is precisely what has happened here.

The Tenant failed to include dates, times or details for any of the four issues he intends to raise. The Tenant also failed to include any requests for remedies or provide any guidance about the alleged impact he experienced as a result of the disrepair. This is despite the fact that the Tenant filed this application on May 6, 2025, and had an ACC on January 13, 2026, during which the Board explained these problems to him.

The Tenant has already had many months to submit a request to amend his application to address the many problems described above, but he has failed to take any action in this regard. I would also note that, pursuant to section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Board is compelled to complete its hearing process in the most expeditious manner possible.

As there are deficiencies in the application and the Tenant has taken no steps to address those deficiencies despite being advised of them and being given additional time, I find that the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $213.35. Illegal Charge Collected:

The Tenant testified when he moved into the rental unit, the Landlord required him to pay a $600.00 refundable key deposit on July 11, 2025. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord clarified that his last name is [name] and not [name]. It appears the Landlord’s last name was submitted on the Tenant’s application although was not listed within the Board’s Notice of Hearing. All parties consented to the Landlord’s last name being added to the application. Therefore, the application shall be amended to include the Landlord’s last name. T5 Application

This application is brought pursuant to section 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that in order to be successful, the Tenant must first lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that they got a notice of termination under section 48. Section 48 reads as follows: 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

It is undisputed the Landlord did not give the Tenant a notice of termination on an approved form (N12 form). It is the Tenant’s position that a verbal conversation with the Landlord constituted a notice under sections 48. I do not agree.

The Tenant testified that on September 29, 2024, she and the Landlord met to ‘renew’ the Lease Agreement and the Landlord advised he would need the rental unit for his parents. Further, during the conversation the Tenant stated the Landlord chose an end date for the Lease Agreement of August 31, 2025. The Tenant stated that while the Landlord did not express a date that his parents would be moving into the home, she took the end date of the Lease term as the date his parents would be moving into the rental unit. Finally, the Tenant stated there were no further conversations regarding the Landlord’s parents occupying the home, but she began searching for a new rental unit.

The Act provides a tenant security of tenure. Section 37(1) of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. Section 38 provides that a tenancy renews indefinitely unless it is terminated in accordance with the Act. No landlord can unilaterally terminate a tenancy unless they have grounds to do so and follow the proper procedure which is set out in the Act.

This means that the verbal conversation with the Landlord had no legal effect. The Tenant was free to ignore the conversation. If she had, the tenancy would have continued as is outlined within the Act.

I find that a conversation a year prior to the alleged date the Tenant was required to vacate falls short of notice under sections 48. There was no indication the Tenant was required to vacate the rental unit so that the Landlord’s parents could move in.

Looking to section 202 of the Act, it requires the Board to ascertain the substance of the conversation between the parties, and in doing so it may disregard the outward forms of a transaction and have regard to the parties’ pattern of activities. In this case, I am not convinced the Landlord advised the Tenant that they had to vacate by a certain date because his parents were going to move into the rental unit. I believe the Tenant acted prematurely and based on assumptions. The Tenant could have waited for proper written notice, sought legal advice, or contacted the LTB. I find the Tenant has failed to sufficiently establish that they received notice under section 48 of the Act.
As the Tenant failed to establish she received a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • did not meet his maintenance obligations. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenant has proved that the Landlord is illegally retaining a rent deposit which was not used to pay the rent for the last month of the tenancy. The Tenant has not proved the other allegations raised in his application. Disposal of furniture

The Tenant moved into the unit on September 1, 2022. He testified that he brought some furniture to the unit, such as a bed and dresser. The Landlord allowed him to move the bed into the unit, but did not let him move in the dresser or other furniture. The Tenant left the furniture outside instead. Some time later, the furniture was no longer outside, and the Landlord told the Tenant that he had disposed of it. However, the Tenant later saw the furniture in the Landlord’s garage, and concluded that the Landlord had stolen it. He asks that the Landlord reimburse him for the value of the furniture.

The Landlord testified that he did not refuse to let the Tenant move his furniture in. When the Tenant moved in, he left some broken furniture outside because he was disposing of it. The Landlord helped him put some of it on the curb for garbage pickup. He did not take or dispose of the furniture.

Both parties’ testimony lacked detail. Neither party’s testimony corroborated by any other evidence. The testimony was largely untested on cross-examination, except that when the Tenant asked the Landlord the date the garbage was collected, the Landlord’s answer was consistent with his other testimony.

The Tenant bears the onus of proving the allegations raised in this proceeding. I have no reason to prefer the Tenant’s testimony over the Landlord’s, and the Tenant has therefore not proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord threw out or stole his furniture in September, 2022. Cockroaches

The Tenant testified that throughout the tenancy, there was a severe cockroach infestation in the shared kitchen. He testified that the cupboards and fridge were infested. The cooking area was so badly infested that cockroaches sometimes fell into his food while he was cooking.

The Tenant adduced a video he took in the kitchen, which shows roughly three cockroaches on different parts of the counter. The video does not show the inside of the cupboards, the fridge, or the area above the stove. The video is not consistent with the Tenant’s testimony that the infestation was severe.

The Tenant also adduced an image which he says is a copy of a text message he sent the Landlord on October 27, 2022. The message says “I will start searching for a new place next month… I can’t live in these conditions. Roaches everywhere.” The image consists entirely of text, and does not look like a screenshot of a text message. The Tenant was unable to explain why the image did not look like a text message.
The Landlord testified that he was not aware of any cockroaches in the unit, and that the Tenant never told him about the cockroaches.

In light of the Tenant’s exaggerated testimony about the severity of the cockroaches, and my concerns about the purported text message, I find the Landlord’s testimony to be more credible than the Tenant’s. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant never complained to him about cockroaches.

The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance. He was not obligated to remedy a cockroach issue that he did not know about. That is particularly true since, as it appears from the Tenant’s video, the issue was not so severe that the Landlord ought to have known about it without being told.
The Tenant has not proved that the Landlord failed to follow a reasonable program of maintenance in respect of cockroaches. Eviction

On March 22, 2023, the Landlord filed application LTB-L-021140-23. The application alleged that the parties had signed an agreement to terminate the tenancy. On March 22, 2023, the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) issued an order granting the Landlord’s application and terminating the tenancy effective April 2, 2023.
The Tenant says that he did not sign an agreement to terminate the tenancy. He says that he was never given notice of the proceeding, and did not know that the order had been issued.
On May 1, 2023, the Court Enforcement Officer (Sheriff) enforced the order and evicted the Tenant.

In this proceeding, the Tenant seeks to argue that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment by forging an agreement to terminate the tenancy, filing it with the LTB, and obtaining and enforcing an eviction order.

In my view, the Tenant’s proposed argument would be an impermissible collateral attack on order LTB-L-021140-23. In that order, the LTB made a finding of fact that the parties had entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant did not file a motion to set the order aside, a review, or an appeal. The order is binding on the parties.

The Tenant argues that he did not have an opportunity to challenge the finding in LTB-L- 021140-23, because he had already been evicted. I am not persuaded by that argument. Where a party has been evicted through an abuse of process, the LTB has the authority to grant a review and reinstate a tenancy. The Tenant did not pursue that remedy.

I therefore find the Tenant to be barred from claiming, in this proceeding, that he did not agree to terminate the tenancy or that the Landlord improperly evicted him. He was evicted pursuant to a lawful order of the LTB. Disposal of belongings
The Landlord was required to make the Tenant’s belongings available to him in the 72- hour period following the eviction.

The Tenant testified that he arranged with the Landlord to retrieve his belongings on May 3, 2023. On that day, the Landlord let him into the unit and he started packing his belongings. However, the Landlord then demanded that he withdraw this application, which he had filed the previous day. The Tenant refused. The Landlord then falsely reported to the police that the Tenant had threatened him with a weapon. The police attended, but the Tenant showed them a video he had taken of his interaction with the Landlord, which did not show any threats or weapons. The police did not charge the Tenant, but directed him to leave the unit and make arrangements to pick up his belongings another day.
The Tenant testified that he tried to follow the police’s instructions, but the Landlord told him that because 72 hours had elapsed, he was no longer required to return the belongings.
The Landlord and his representative both testified that the Tenant did in fact collect his belongings on May 3, and that the Landlord did not prevent him.

I do not find the Tenant’s testimony to be credible. His video shows that he was in the unit and able to retrieve his belongings on May 3. There is no subsequent evidence to corroborate his testimony regarding his interaction with the police. He has not adduced a police report, although one ought to have been available. He has not explained why the police would have required him to leave the unit even though they concluded that he had not committed a crime. He has not adduced any subsequent written or recorded communication with the Landlord seeking to retrieve his belongings.

I do not find the Landlord’s and his representative’s testimony to be credible, either. They both testified, baldly, that the Tenant had retrieved his belongings. They provided no details of their recollection of the incident. I repeatedly invited the Landlord’s representative to provide details, but he was unable to do so.

The Tenant bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to make his belongings available as required during the 72-hour period. Since neither side presented credible evidence of what happened on May 3, the Tenant has not proved that he was unable to collect his belongings when he attended the unit on that date. Return of deposit

The monthly rent was $1,250.00. When the Tenant moved in, he paid a rent deposit of $1,250.00 in addition to his first month’s rent. He testified that he paid rent through April, 2023, but the Landlord refused to return his deposit after he was evicted on May 1.

The Landlord and four witnesses all testified that at 8:00am on May 1, the Landlord offered the Tenant $2,500.00 by cheque. The Tenant refused, and demanded cash. The Landlord then gave him $2,500.00 in cash and asked him to sign a receipt. The Tenant refused to sign the receipt.
I do not find the Landlord’s and his witnesses’ testimony to be credible, for several reasons.

First, the witnesses’ testimony did not have an air of reality. None of them described any details of what they observed on May 1. They did not explain why the five of them were all at the unit at 8am that day, or what was happening at the time. They simply testified, baldly, that they saw the Landlord give the Tenant $2,500.00 in cash.
Second, the witnesses all gave strikingly similar testimony, using nearly identical words.

Third, the witnesses all attended the hearing through the Landlord’s device, which did not have a working camera. Consequently, I could not see the witnesses. Specifically, I could not see whether they were reading their testimony or otherwise being prompted. Further, I directed that the witnesses be excluded prior to giving their testimony, but I could not see whether they had actually been excluded. These were significant concerns in light of the similarity between the witnesses’ testimony.

Fourth, the Tenant testified that the Sheriff evicted him around noon on May 1. I find that testimony to be plausible. I do not know the Sheriff’s schedule, but it seems unlikely that the Tenant would have already been evicted prior to 8am as the Landlord’s witnesses suggested.

Fifth, the Landlord did not owe the Tenant $2,500.00. He owed him $1,250.00, the amount of the rent deposit which had not been used. The Landlord did not explain why he would have paid the Tenant twice as much as he owed him.

Sixth, the Landlord did not adduce corroborating documents that ought to have been available, such as a copy of the cheque he says he tried to give the Tenant, the receipt he says he asked the Tenant to sign, or bank records showing that he had withdrawn $2,500.00 in cash.

For all those reasons, I find the Tenant’s testimony that his deposit was not returned to be more credible than the Landlord’s and the Landlord’s witnesses’ testimony. The Tenant has proved that the Landlord is illegally retaining the $1,250.00 deposit. The Landlord will be ordered to return it.
Since the Tenant was partially successful in his application, the Landlord will also be required to reimburse him for the filing fee for this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,298.00, which represents the return of a rent deposit and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 13, 2026 ____________________________
