issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was first before the LTB on April 15, 2025, however, was adjourned for the application to be amended to add the Landlord, MSW Inc. to the application.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023, and moved out on April 24, 2024. He stated that his was a student residence unit, with four bedrooms and a shared kitchen and living room. His monthly rent was $911.00 and he signed a one year lease agreement from September 1, 2023 to August 31, 2024.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord substantially interfered with his enjoyment of the rental unit due to an issue that arose with the toilet which caused there to be a foul smell throughout the rental unit resulting in the Tenant not being able to stay there. On or about April 4, 2024, the Tenant stated that he went back home to Barrie to study for exams. On or about April 15, 2024 he received a message from a representative of the property manager that there was an issue with the toilet, it leaked and caused damage to the apartment below.

The Tenant stated that he went back to the rental unit on or about April 20, 2024 to prepare for upcoming exams. When he came back to the rental unit, he noticed that the toilet was removed and there was a big hole on the floor with a very strong sewer gas smell emanating from it. He stated that this was the only bathroom with a shower, so he had to use it despite the awful smell. The smell was going through the bedroom, and it was hard to study and live there. On or about April 21, his mother sent an email to the property manager regarding the living conditions, and they stated they would inform the owner. On or about April 24, 2024 after 10 days the toilet was reinstalled however it did not look like the Landlord took proper precautions to block the hole and prevent sewer gases from entering the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord engaged in harassing behaviour. On or about April 23, 2024 the Landlord served an N5 Notice of Termination (“N5 Notice”) to the Tenant stated that he owed money for the repair and cleaning of the toilet. The Tenant stated that was not properly filled out, and that it was not clear as there were no invoices for damages, cleaning and an explanation as to why the Landlord believes the Tenant is responsible. This had a significant impact on the Tenant as he was a student who was living on his own for the first time, did not know his rights and the Landlord was trying to take advantage of students. The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on April 24, 2024 as he could not live there due to the conditions of it.

The Landlord opposed the Tenant’s claims of interference with reasonable enjoyment. There was another working toilet in the rental unit that he could use. However, the Landlord agrees that the smell may have interfered with the Tenant’s ability to use the shower without the smell. According to the Landlord, this issue commenced around April 15, 2024 and was resolved within a week and a half to two weeks. The reason for the smell was due to there being a hole that was not covered during this time.

The Landlord further opposes the Tenant’s claim that there was harassing behaviour. The Landlord exercised their rights and served the Tenant with a N5 Notice as the Tenants caused the damage to the toilet.
The Tenant does agree that once the toilet was fixed there was no more smell throughout the rental unit when he vacated, which was on April 24, 2024. Legal Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit of the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes.
Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case, the burden falls on the Tenant.

After hearing the parties submissions, I do not find that Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I note that the Tenant did not file an application pursuant to s. 20 of the Act claiming a maintenance breach. I find that to allow a remedy under s. 22 of the Act would “place the provisions of s. 20(1) and s. 22 in conflict or disharmony with one another and disregard the intent of the legislature that where, as here, there is an overlap...” [ See Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 at paragraph 55].

I acknowledge that there may be circumstances where a maintenance issue could be a substantial interference with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit or residential complex. However, in my view, it is not appropriate to permit that type of claim to be filed under a T2 application so that a tenant may circumvent section 20 of the Act.

Substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment is very broad and general claim and could potentially encompass any number of issues that could arise during a tenancy. However, when an issue raised in an application falls under a more specific and applicable section of the Act, Onyskiw confirms that the Board must interpret the general claim in harmony with the more specific provision. I find that this applies to the issue relating to the toilet in the rental unit. I find that this claim ought to have been brought under section 20 of the Act, rather than section 22. Therefore, this claim is dismissed.

Regarding the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord harassed and substantially interfered with the Tenant by serving an N5 Notice, I do not find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed and/or interfered with the Tenant. Although I heard and considered the Tenant’s evidence, I find that the Landlord exercised their right by serving a notice of termination on the Tenant, and the Tenant could have contested the N5 Notice before the LTB and did not have an obligation to vacate until there is an order terminating the tenancy from the LTB. I note that this could have been a stressful situation for the Tenant, as they were a student and had their exams that they needed to study for, however, I did not find the actions of the Landlords rose to the level where I would find the Landlord contravened section 22 and 23 of the Act. The Tenant’s claims are therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that another tenant verbally abused her, failed to clean the common areas, secretly recorded her, followed her, and otherwise harassed her. She submits that the Landlord failed to intervene appropriately and, by siding with the other tenant, substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant further alleges the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that the rental unit was a four-bedroom house occupied by unrelated individuals who shared the kitchen, bathroom, and other common areas. She explained that the Landlord resided in another portion of the property but had access to the tenants' living space through an interior doorway that did not have a lock.

The Tenant testified that shortly after moving into the rental unit she began experiencing ongoing conflict with another occupant of the house. According to the Tenant, the other tenant regularly failed to clean the common areas, allowed her dog to interfere with the Tenant's use of the shared space, verbally abused her, secretly recorded her, followed her throughout the house, and engaged in a pattern of intimidating behaviour.

The Tenant testified that she repeatedly reported these concerns to the Landlord by text message, email, and in person. She stated that she maintained a written chronology of events and provided the Landlord with photographs, videos, audio recordings, and other documentary evidence in support of her complaints. The Tenant maintained that, despite these repeated complaints, the Landlord failed to adequately investigate the incidents or

The Tenant testified that on March 15, 2026, she was involved in a verbal altercation with the other tenant after attempting to spend time alone in the living room without the other tenant’s dog being present. She testified that other tenant called her offensive names. The Tenant stated that she reported the incident to the Landlord, who subsequently served the other tenant with an N5 notice.

The Tenant testified that additional confrontations occurred on March 26 and April 15, 2026. She stated that the other tenant continued verbally abusing her, removed a cleaning schedule the Tenant had prepared for the shared areas, contacted the police after the Tenant sang inside the house, and repeatedly recorded the Tenant using a cellular telephone. The Tenant testified that the attending police officers concluded she had done nothing wrong and advised the other occupant that she could simply remove herself from the situation if she was bothered by the Tenant's singing.

The Tenant testified that, rather than addressing the other occupant's conduct, the Landlord began relying upon the other tenant’s complaints and video recordings. She stated that the Landlord subsequently served her with two N5 notices and later commenced eviction proceedings before the Board. The Tenant testified that she believed the Landlord and the other tenant were working together against her and that the Landlord accepted the other tenant’s version of events without fairly considering the Tenant's evidence.

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by relying upon video recordings made by the other tenant. She testified that those recordings constituted unlawful surveillance and invaded her privacy. The Tenant argued that, by accepting and relying upon those recordings, the Landlord effectively endorsed the other tenant’s harassment [name]

The Tenant called [name] as a witness. She testified that she was present at the rental property on April 20, 2026, as the Tenant's guest. CM testified that while visiting the property she observed the other occupant using a cellular telephone to record the Tenant while the Tenant was in the kitchen. CM further testified that she herself was also recorded and advised the other tenant that she did not consent to being audio or video recorded.

CM also testified regarding the events of April 20, 2026. She stated that, despite requests to stop recording, the other tenant continued filming the Tenant. [name] testified that the other tenant positioned herself in a manner that made it appear as though the Tenant was approaching or threatening her and, at one point, stumbled behind a staircase while continuing to record. CM further testified that the Landlord attended during the incident but did not intervene to stop the recording. CM believes the Landlord appeared to agree with the other tenant’s actions rather than attempting to de-escalate the situation. Landlord Evidence

The Landlord testified that throughout the tenancy he received frequent complaints from both tenants of the house. He stated that he attempted to remain neutral and investigate each complaint as it arose.

The Landlord submitted, the Tenant consistently portrayed herself as entirely blameless while attributing all responsibility for the conflict to the other Tenant. However, the Landlord testified that the video recordings and other evidence provided to him by the other tenant did not support the Tenant's description of the events.

The Landlord relied heavily upon several video recordings created on April 15, 2026. He testified that the recordings showed the Tenant standing outside the other tenant’s bedroom singing loudly and directing the lyrics toward her. Although he acknowledged that the Tenant was singing lyrics from commercially available songs, the Landlord testified that, in his view, the Tenant was intentionally directing those lyrics toward the other occupant in an effort to intimidate or provoke her.

The Landlord testified that, after reviewing the complaints and video recordings, he concluded that the Tenant's conduct had escalated beyond an ordinary disagreement between roommates. As a result, he served the Tenant with an N5 notice dated April 18, 2026, followed by a second N5 notice dated April 26, 2026, before commencing an L2 application before the Board.

The Landlord acknowledged that he also served the other tenant with an N5 notice following the Tenant's complaints. However, he testified that the other tenant remedied the behaviour identified in the notice within the statutory remedial period and, in his opinion, her conduct did not subsequently warrant eviction.

The Landlord further testified that he communicated with both tenants throughout the dispute, attempted to mediate their disagreements, and encouraged them to avoid one another in an effort to preserve the living arrangement.

Finally, the Landlord testified that he attempted to resolve the dispute by offering the Tenant alternative accommodation at another property he owned. He stated that he offered the Tenant the opportunity to move into a vacant room either temporarily or permanently and further offered her approximately $2,000.00, together with the return of her last month's rent deposit, to assist her in securing alternate accommodation. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit by a tenant. A landlord also has a positive obligation to take reasonable steps to address conduct by one tenant that substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of another tenant. See [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Ct.).

A landlord is not automatically liable whenever tenants sharing accommodation are unable to coexist peacefully. The Landlord's obligation is to take reasonable steps once complaints are brought to his attention. The Act does not require a landlord to guarantee harmonious relationships between unrelated tenants, nor does it require a landlord to evict one tenant simply because another tenant requests that result.

I have considered the evidence of CM I accept that she testified honestly about what she personally observed during her visit to the rental property and about the Tenant's emotional state. However, she was present for only a limited number of incidents and did not reside at the residential complex. While her evidence confirms that conflict existed between the tenants, it does not assist in determining whether the Landlord failed to respond reasonably to that conflict.

I accept that the relationship between the Tenant and the other tenant deteriorated significantly and that the Tenant experienced genuine distress as a result of the ongoing conflict. However, I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to hold the Landlord responsible for the conflict between the tenants

I accept that the Landlord took the Tenant's complaints seriously and responded reasonably in the circumstances. Although the Tenant disagreed with many of the Landlord's decisions, I find the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord investigated complaints from both tenants, communicated with each of them, attempted to mediate the dispute, and served notices of termination if he believed they were warranted. The Act requires a landlord to respond reasonably to disputes between tenants; it does not require the landlord to guarantee a particular outcome.

A significant portion of the hearing focused on several video recordings created during the parties' disputes. Having reviewed those recordings, I find they undermine the Tenant's assertion that she was merely the passive victim of the conflict. Rather, the recordings demonstrate that the conflict became reciprocal, with both tenants contributing to the deterioration of their relationship.

The recordings depict the Tenant repeatedly singing immediately outside the other occupant's bedroom while directing portions of the songs toward her. Although the Tenant testified that she was simply singing lyrics from popular songs and that the police determined she had committed no criminal offence, I accept the Landlord's evidence that, in the context of the ongoing conflict, the Tenant intentionally directed the lyrics toward the other tenant in an effort to provoke or intimidate her.

While the other tenant occasionally responded with insulting language, I accept the Landlord's evidence that many of those exchanges occurred only after the Tenant deliberately engaged or directed her conduct toward the other tenant. I therefore find that the conflict was not one-sided. Rather, both tenants contributed to the escalating tension within the household. Accordingly, I am unable to conclude that the evidence establishes the Tenant alone was subjected to harassment or substantial interference by the other tenant.

The recordings were created by the other tenant rather than the Landlord. The Landlord testified that the forwarded the recordings to him while he was at work. I accept that evidence. The video evidence relied on at the hearing was taken in the common areas of the residential complex where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord's decision to review and subsequently rely upon those recordings while investigating complaints between two tenants does not amount to harassment or substantial interference under the Act.

The Landlord subsequently served the Tenant with two N5 notices after receiving complaints concerning her conduct and reviewing the available evidence, including the video recordings. I find that serving N5 notices on both tenants at different stages of the dispute demonstrates that the Landlord attempted to address complaints from each tenant rather than automatically accepting one person's version of events.

The service of notices of termination and the commencement of an L2 application are remedies expressly contemplated by the Act. Whether those notices are valid, and whether the allegations they contain are proven, are matters to be determined in a separate proceeding. The mere fact that a landlord serves a notice of termination or files an application with the Board does not, without more, constitute harassment, coercion, or substantial interference.

I also accept the Landlord's evidence that he attempted to resolve the dispute by offering the Tenant alternative accommodation at another property together with approximately $2,000.00 and the return of her last month's rent deposit to assist her in securing alternate accommodation. The Tenant acknowledged that these offers were made but declined them because she no longer trusted the Landlord. While the Tenant was entitled to refuse the proposal, I find the offer itself demonstrates that the Landlord was attempting to resolve the conflict rather than ignoring it.

The Board's role is not to determine which tenant was more difficult to live with or whether the parties liked one another. Rather, the issue before me is whether the Landlord breached obligations imposed by the Act. On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that he did.

Having considered the evidence in its totality, I am not satisfied that the Landlord ignored the conflict or failed to respond reasonably. Instead, the evidence demonstrates that he investigated complaints from both tenants, attempted to mediate the dispute, served N5 notices where he believed appropriate, monitored the situation as it evolved, offered the Tenant alternative accommodation together with financial assistance to relocate, and ultimately commenced an application before the Board after concluding the conflict could not be resolved. I am therefore not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit contrary to section 22 of the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant's application is dismissed.

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit. Much of the Tenant's evidence concerned the Landlord's movement through the common areas of the house and an interior doorway separating portions of the residence. However, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord entered the Tenant's bedroom or any other area over which the Tenant had exclusive possession contrary to the Act. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenat’s application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application); • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application); • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys (T2 Application); • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application); • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application); • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application); • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant (T2 Application); and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). The Tenant also filed a blank T5 Application, which is an application that the Landlord gave a Notice of Termination in Bad Fatih. The application was heard by videoconference on July 20, 2026. The Landlords and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue regarding the timeline surrounding the Tenant’s tenancy. The Tenant submitted in her application that she moved into the rental unit on September 10, 2017, and moved out of the rental unit on December 23, 2017. The Landlords confirmed these timelines. The application was filed on May 2, 2025.

Th e [name] application is filed pursuant to section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Subsection 135(4) of the Act states that “No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.”

The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are filed pursuant to section 29(1) of the Act. Subsection 29(2) also states that “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”

The Tenant’s T5 application was blank and as such is dismissed. Even if it did contain details, a T5 application is filed pursuant to section 57(1) of the Act or section 57.1(1) of the Act. 57(2) of the Act states that “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.” Section 57.1(2) of the Act states that “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than two years after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.”

Ontario Regulation 516/06 subsection 56(2) states that the Board cannot extend the deadlines for filing applications, other than those which the Board is expressly permitted to extend or shorten under subsection 190(1) of the Act. The deadline for filing an application is not one of those listed under s.190(1) and so there is no flexibility on the part of the Board to extend it.

On this basis, I find that the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred more than one year after the Tenant filed their application and that the application must be dismissed. Any issues that arose during this tenancy are statute barred and the Tenant can no longer file an application with the Board. I have no discretion to extend the timeline to allow the application to proceed.
Therefore, this application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1, T2, T5, and T6 applications are dismissed. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s served the Landlord with an N9 notice to terminate the tenancy on February 26th, 2026, with a termination date of April 30th, 2026 (DOC7897658). The Landlord accepted the N9 notice and stated in their response that the Tenant’s Last month rent deposit in the amount of $2,450.00 would be applied to the last month of the tenancy – April 2026.

On February 18th, Mr. [name]name] emailed the Landlord and requested to assign their lease (DOC7836641). The email states, “we are the tenants of unit 603 at 15 [address]. We are requesting consent to assign out tenancy”.

The Landlord responded to the request stating that as there are three leaseholders, any changes would need to be agreed in writing by all three and that the approval is subject to management review and income qualification.

Mr. [name]name] responded to the Landlord’s response on February 24th, 2026, stating that all tenants are in agreement with making this request and reiterated the request is for consent from the Landlord to assign the tenancy in accordance with s.95 of the Residential Tenancies Act.

On March 4th, 2026, the Tenants provided a second N9 notice of termination with a termination date of April 3rd, 2026. The Tenants vacated the unit on April 2nd, 2026, and confirmed that the Tenants did not pay rent for April 2026.

Mr. [name]name] testified that because the Landlord did not respond to the Tenants request to assign their unit, under s.95(4) of the Act, they were entitled to give the Landlord 30 days notice as opposed to the 60 days notice provided in the first N9 notice and would thus be entitled to their last months rent deposit back.

Section 95(4) of the Act outlines several criteria that a Tenant must meet in order to engage the right to serve notice within 30 days as opposed to 60 days: Refusal or non-response (4) A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if: (a) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent; (b) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made; (c) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord refuses consent to the assignment under clause (3) (c); or (d) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made.

The Landlord’s position is that they did respond to the Tenant’s request when they informed [name] that any potential assignee is subject to management review and income qualification. As the Tenants did not provide any information for a potential assignee, the Landlord did not refuse the request. Analysis
In the case before me, Mr. [name]name] confirmed that, at no point, did the Tenants ever provide contact information for any potential assignee.
In addition, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenants request to assign the unit but were not provided any additional information with respect to a potential assignee.

As noted above, the only way for s.95(4) to be engaged is if the Landlord arbitrarily refuses consent to assign a unit or does or does not respond to the Tenants request within 7 days of the request being made – neither of these criteria were met in the case before me. As such, the Tenant has not established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord refused or did not respond to the request to assign the Tenants unit.

As I find that the Tenants were not permitted to provide the Landlord with 30 days notice in accordance with S.95(4), the earliest the Tenants could terminate their tenancy would be April 30th, 2026, which is in line with the termination date in the first N9 notice that was served correctly on February 26th, 2026. As such, the Tenants are not entitled to receive their last months rent deposit back as it was applied correctly to the rent for April 2026.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $819.43. Illegal rent collected

The Tenant testified that his tenancy stared on November 1st, 2023, with an initial rental amount of $745, and that the Landlord increased his rent to $873.19 on September 1st, 2024. He also testified that he paid this new rental amount until he vacated the unit on April 1st, 2026. He testified that there was no written notice to increase the rent.

There are two issues with this portion of the Tenants application. Firstly, S.29(2) of the Act provides that a Tenant must file their application within one year from the date the money was collected or retained illegally.

The second issue is that the Tenant has paid the increase of rent since September 1st, 2024. Even if a Landlord increased the rent without serving a tenant with a notice of rent increase, the otherwise lawful rent increase is deemed to be valid if the tenant pays the increased rent amount for a year without filing an application with the Board challenging the lawfulness of the increase.

In this case, the Tenant stated that he had paid the increased rent for more than 12 months, meaning the unlawful amount is deemed lawful. The intent of S.136 is to prevent those who knowingly pay more than their lawful rent for longer than 12 months from commencing proceedings on that account. Here, the claim goes back to September 1st, 2024, when the purported unlawful was first charged.

Section 136(2) of the act states: Increase deemed lawful (2) An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application.

Accordingly, because the unlawful rent was first charged back in September 2024, more than one year before the Tenant filed this application in April 2026 and the Tenant made the increased rent payments for more than 12 months, the unlawful amount is deemed lawful pursuant to S.136(2) of the act and thus, this portion of the Tenants application will be dismissed: Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy
As noted above, the tenancy began on November 1st, 2023, and the Tenant stated that he provided a rent deposit to the Landlord on October 31st, 2023, in the amount of $745.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord gave him notice to vacate the rental unit on March 8th, 2026, with a termination date of April 8th, 2026, and that he vacated the unit on April 1st, 2026, in accordance with the notice give by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that he asked the Landlord for his last months rent deposit back on March 8th, 2026, when the Landlord gave notice to the Tenant to vacate but that this request was refused without reason. He requested the last months rent deposit back because he stated he paid rent for the month of March 2026.
In accordance with S.106(10) of the Act, a Landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the Landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

Due to the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord has no right to retain the last months rent deposit and, since the Tenant paid the monthly rent for the last month of his tenancy in accordance with the Landlord’s notice to vacate. The Landlord shall return the last months rent deposit of $745 to the Tenant. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not pay any interest on his last months rent deposit. The period for which interest should accrue would be from October 31st, 2024, through April 1st, 2026, when the Tenant vacated the unit.
The interest rate on the last months rent deposit between October 31st, 2024, through December 31st, 2025, was 2.5%. The total amount of interest owed during this period is $21.79.
The interest rate between January 1st 2026 and April 1st, 2026, was 2.1%. The total amount owed during this period is $4.64.
The Total amount of interest owed on the last month rent deposit between October 31st, 2024, and April 1st, 2026, is $26.43.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Landlord owes interest on the last months rent deposit and shall pay to the Tenant a total of $26.43 for interest owing on the last months rent deposit. Proceeds from sale of property owing
The Tenant testified that on or around February 27th, 2026, the Landlord entered the rental unit and stole his kettle but provided no evidence that the Landlord actually sold the stolen item.
As the Tenant was unable to establish that the Landlord sold any property of the Tenants, this portion of the application is dismissed. Order prohibiting rent increase
There was no evidence before me that the Landlord was prohibited from increasing the rent for the rental unit. As such, this portion of the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $$819.43. This amount represents: • $745.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $26.43 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the commencement of the hearing the Landlord’s Legal Representative raised two preliminary issues: a) The named landlord [name] was incorrect and that the properly named Landlord should be [organization]; and b) There is no merit to the Tenant’s application as the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with a notice to termination under section 50 of the Act, and the tenancy was terminated pursuant to a Board order under LTB-L-086858-25.

Based on the evidence before me I am satisfied that [name] is an employee and not the landlord and that the proper Landlord is [organization] The application will be amended to reflect the proper Landlord.

In reviewing the Board’s order under LTB-L-086858-25 issued on February 26, 2026, I am satisfied that a hearing occurred on February 5, 2026 in the absence of the Tenant and the tenancy was terminated pursuant to that order effective March 3, 2026.
Additionally based on the evidence of the Landlord, the Sheriff enforced eviction on April 16, 2026 and provided the Landlord with vacant possession the rental unit on that date.
The Tenant confirmed that she received a copy of the order under LTB-L-086858-25, and that she vacated the rental unit on April 16, 2026, due to the Sheriff’s enforcement of that order.

The Tenant’s application is brought pursuant to section 57.1(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which states: 57.1 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection 57 (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that the landlord was required to afford the former tenant a right of first refusal under section 53 and failed to do so.

Section 53 of the Act states: 53 (1) A tenant who receives notice of termination of a tenancy for the purpose of repairs or renovations may, in accordance with this section, have a right of first refusal to occupy the rental unit as a tenant when the repairs or renovations are completed.

Based on the evidence before me there is no basis for the Tenant’s application, as the Landlord did not give a notice of termination for the purpose of repairs or renovations under section 50 of the Act. Additionally, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the enforcement of a Board order. As such the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges in his Application that he entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord, but the Landlord did not permit him to move into the rental unit and did not return his rent deposit in the sum of $2,500.00. Background

The Tenant, his spouse and a friend decided to jointly rent a rental unit from the Landlord with a monthly rent of $2,500. The Tenant and his spouse viewed the rental unit on May 7, 2025, and decided to sign a lease with the Landlord. The lease was to commence on May 15, 2025, and the Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $2,500.00.

After signing the lease, the friend refused to join the Tenant and his spouse in renting the rental unit. This was financially catastrophic news for the couple as they would be unable to afford the monthly rent alone. The Tenant notified the Landlord of their financial predicament on May 11 and asked to cancel the lease and to return their rent deposit. The Landlord advised that he had found an individual willing to share the rental unit with the Tenant and his spouse. The Tenant, however, did not find this option acceptable.

The Tenant did not move into the rental unit. The Landlord immediately advertised the rental unit for rent, but it was not rented until June 8, 2025, so it sat vacant for 24 days. The Landlord did not refund the Tenants for 7 days of their rent deposit because he alleged he paid to advertise the rental unit for rent and took time of work to get the rental unit rented. 3. For deciding the matter, it is necessary for me to consider subsection 107(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) that requires a landlord repay the amount received as a rent deposit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. In Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 5425 (CanLII), the Court found that the word “not given” suggests that it is the refusal or inability of a landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. Here, it was the Tenant’s inability to pay the first month’s rent and key deposit and afford the monthly rent that prevented him from taking possession of the rental unit. As such, he is not entitled to the return of the rent deposit pursuant to subsection 107(1) because it was his act of repudiation of the agreement that prevented him from taking possession of the unit, not the action of the Landlord. 4. However, the analysis is not complete. Pursuant to Section 6 of the Act, the Landlord also has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses resulting from the Tenant’s unilateral repudiation of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord was able to re-lease the rental unit on June 8, 2025. As the rental period would have run from May 15, 2025, to June 14, 2025, the Landlord mitigated some of his losses as he did not lose any rent from June 8 – 14, 2025.

I have also considered the costs the Landlord incurred to mitigate his losses by re-renting the rental unit after the Tenant’s repudiation. The Landlord did not lead any evidence as to his costs to advertise the rental unit or the time missed from work. In the absence of any evidence, I find that $50.00 is reasonable for the Landlord’s costs to mitigate his losses..

The Landlord was entitled to retain the Tenant’s deposit to cover the rent owed from May 15 – June 7, 2025. As the rental unit was re-rented on June 8, 2025, the Landlord must return $525.33 to the Tenant. This is calculated as follows: $2,500/month x 12 months/365 days = $82.19/day x 7 days = $575.33 - $50.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord must pay the Tenant is $573.33. This amount represents: • $525.33 from the deposit paid to the Landlord • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act. However, the Tenant did not establish entitlement to the remedy sought. Accordingly, the application is dismissed. [name] and termination of the tenancy

There is no dispute that the Tenant suffered a serious leg injury in November 2024 and temporarily resided with his brother while continuing to maintain his tenancy and his belongings at the rental unit.

The evidence establishes that on February 1, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord of his intention to vacate the rental unit effective March 31, 2025. There is no dispute that the Tenant paid January 2025 rent late and did not pay rent for February 2025.

The Tenant submitted text messages, WhatsApp communications, and video recordings in support of his application. The evidence shows that throughout February 2025 the Landlord advised the Tenant that his last month's rent deposit would be applied to February's rent and that she intended to re-rent the room effective March 1, 2025. The communications further indicate that the Landlord intended to remove the Tenant's belongings and permit a new occupant to take possession of the room before March 31, 2025. During the text communication the Tenant indicated he was not ok with the Landlord touching his belongings and removing them for the rental unit.

While the Tenant testified that he provided notice on February 1, 2025, of his intention to terminate the tenancy effective March 31, 2025, in his amended application the Tenant identified February 28, 2025, as the termination date of the tenancy. The Tenant's position was that the tenancy effectively ended on February 28, 2025, because the Landlord re- rented the room to a new occupant effective March 1, 2025.

The evidence establishes that the Tenant did not pay rent for February 2025 and did not pay rent for March 2025. The Landlord applied the last month's rent deposit to February 2025 and re-rented the room effective March 1, 2025. There is no dispute that a new tenant took possession of the rental unit on that date.

In these circumstances, I find that both parties treated February 28, 2025, as the effective termination date of the tenancy notwithstanding the Tenant's earlier indication that he intended to vacate on March 31, 2025. Accordingly, I find that the tenancy ended on February 28, 2025. Illegal entry, Locking system and Interference

The Tenant testified that the Landlord advised him that a new tenant would be moving into the rental unit on March 1, 2025. The Tenant's video evidence shows individuals entering the rental unit and handling the Tenant's belongings on February 27, 2025, and again on March 1, 2025. The evidence also establishes that when the Tenant and his brother attended at the property on February 27, 2025, they were unable to gain access to the rental unit using the Tenant's key.

The Landlord acknowledged that the Tenant's belongings were removed from the room and put into the garage before the intended move-in date of a new occupant. The Landlord's support, [name], (RZ) submitted that the Landlord’s maintenance worker. [name], mistakenly removed the belongings on February 27, 2025, rather than February 28, 2025. RZ testified that any issue relating to access to the room was subsequently corrected and that the Tenant's belongings were returned to the room the same day.

I accept that the Tenant's belongings were returned to the rental unit on February 27, 2025, after the error was brought to the Landlord's attention. I also accept that the Tenant regained access to the room later that day. However, I find that the Landlord's evidence demonstrates that she intended to regain possession of the room and re-rent it effective March 1, 2025, notwithstanding that the Tenant had advised that he intended to vacate on March 31, 2025.

Even if the initial removal of the Tenant's belongings on February 27, 2025, occurred in error, the evidence establishes that the Landlord subsequently proceeded to remove the Tenant's belongings from the room on March 1, 2025, and place them in the garage in anticipation of a new tenant taking possession. The Landlord does not dispute that this occurred.

The Tenant remained entitled to possession of the rental unit until the tenancy was lawfully terminated. The Landlord had no authority to remove the Tenant's belongings from the rental unit before February 28, 2025, or otherwise interfere with the Tenant's possessory rights prior to the end of the tenancy.
Regardless of whether the Tenant was temporarily residing elsewhere due to his injury, he remained a tenant and retained the right to exclusive possession of the rental unit until February 28, 2025.

I therefore find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment and lawful rights under the Act when she removed the Tenant's belongings from the rental unit and attempted to recover possession of the room before the tenancy had lawfully ended. The appropriate remedy for this breach is addressed below. Locking system
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord changed the lock or locking system to prevent him from accessing the rental unit.

While I accept that the Tenant was temporarily unable to access the rental unit on February 27, 2025, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord intentionally changed the lock for the purpose of denying the Tenant access. The evidence supports a finding that there was a temporary access issue that was corrected later the same day.

Accordingly, I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant's rights by deliberately changing the locking system or permanently denying the Tenant access to the rental unit. Harassment, Coercion and Obstruction

The Tenant and his brother testified that the Landlord repeatedly contacted the Tenant regarding overdue rent and contacted the Tenant's sister in January 2025 regarding the rent arrears. The Tenant also relied upon communications in which the Landlord advised that she intended to use the last month's rent deposit and re-rent the room. The Tenant submitted that these were harassing.

I accept that the Tenant may have found these communications upsetting, particularly given his medical condition and financial circumstances. However, the communications primarily concerned the payment of rent, the proposed use of the last month's rent deposit, and the Landlord's intention to re-rent the unit. While some of the communications were inappropriate and reflected a misunderstanding of the Tenant's continuing right to possession of the rental unit, I am not satisfied that they rise to the level of harassment, coercion, threats, or obstruction contemplated by section 23 of the Act.
Accordingly, this portion of the application is dismissed. Remedies

As set out above, I have found that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant's rights under section 22 of the Act. In determining the appropriate remedy, I have considered the nature and duration of the interference, the fact that the Tenant was temporarily residing elsewhere due to his injury, and the fact that the Tenant did not pay rent for February 2025 in the amount of $1,000.00.

While the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant's lawful right to possess the rental unit, the interference was limited to a relatively brief period at the end of the tenancy and does not justify the three-month rent abatement sought by the Tenant. However, I find that a rent abatement equivalent to one month's rent, or $1,000.00, is an appropriate remedy to compensate the Tenant for the loss of enjoyment and interference with his rights resulting from the Landlord's conduct.

I have also considered that the Tenant owes the Landlord $1,000.00 for unpaid rent for February 2025. Consistent with the principle that mutual debts between parties may be set off against one another (see Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (CanLII), at para. 17), I order that the $1,000.00 rent abatement be applied against the $1,000.00 rent owing for February 2025.
As a result, the amounts owing by the parties offset each other in full. Accordingly, neither party shall be required to make a payment to the other with respect to these amounts.

The Tenant also requested that the Board order the Landlord to cease the impugned conduct. As the tenancy has ended and the Tenant no longer resides in the rental unit, that remedy is unnecessary and no order will issue.

The Tenant also requested compensation based on an alleged higher market rent for a replacement rental unit. The Tenant did not provide a lease agreement, rent receipts, or other documentary evidence establishing the rent paid for his current accommodation. Accordingly, I decline to award this remedy.

The Tenant further sought reimbursement for moving and storage expenses in the amount of $67.17. However, no receipts, invoices, or other supporting documentation were submitted. I therefore decline to award compensation for these alleged expenses. Further, it was the Tenant who chose to vacate the rental unit.

Finally, the Tenant requested compensation of $160.00 for a day's lost wages allegedly incurred by his brother. No evidence was submitted regarding the brother's earnings, any wages actually lost, or whether any loss was incurred as a result of the Landlord's conduct. Accordingly, this claim is also dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the circumstances warrant an administrative fine. While the Landlord improperly interfered with the Tenant's possession of the rental unit, the evidence indicates that the movement of the Tenant's belongings was corrected the same day and does not establish the type of deliberate, serious or recurring conduct that would justify the imposition of an administrative fine.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $1,000.00 for substantially interfering with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment of and lawful right to possess the rental unit, contrary to section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
The Tenant owes the Landlord rent arrears of $1,000.00 for February 2025.
The Tenant's entitlement to a rent abatement of $1,000.00 shall be set off against the rent arrears of $1,000.00 owing to the Landlord.
After set-off, neither party owes any amount to the other with respect to the abatement and the February 2025 rent arrears. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to pay the Tenant $2,215.95 on or before July 31, 2026.

The Tenant filed this application under subsection 57(1) (a) of the Act, which establishes a three-part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenant must establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: First, that the Landlords gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 notice) in bad faith; Second, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or Board order based on the N12 notice; Third, that the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord Gave the Tenant a N12 Notice of Termination Under s. 48 of the Act
The rental unit is one of two residential units located in a duplex. The Tenant resided in the rental unit from May 5, 2023, to May 12, 2024.

The Landlord served an N12 Notice to End your Tenancy (‘N12 Notice’) on the Tenant which stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for herself, for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year. The N12 Notice stated a termination date of June 30, 2024. The N12 Notice was given under s. 48 of the Act. The Tenant Vacated the Rental Unit as a Result of the N12 Notice

It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 12, 2024. However, it was disputed the Tenant vacated the rental unit because the Landlord gave the Tenant a N12 Notice claiming the Landlord required possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that he gave the Landlord an N9 Notice to End the Tenancy (“N9 Notice”) in response to receiving the N12 Notice. The Tenant testified that, because he understood the Landlord was moving into the rental unit, he believed there was no reason to continue the tenancy through the summer when university classes were not in session. The Tenant further testified that he would not have given the N9 Notice if the Landlord had not first served the N12 Notice.

The Landlord’s position was that the Tenant vacated in accordance with the N9 Notice because the Tenant left before the termination date set out in the N12 Notice and vacated by the termination date in the N9 Notice.

While the Landlord’s position is that the Tenant vacated due to the N9, I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he vacated the rental unit because of the N12 Notice. Although the Tenant ultimately vacated on the termination date set out in the N9 Notice, I find that the N9 Notice was given in response to the Landlord’s N12 Notice. The Tenant’s evidence was that he had no intention of permanently vacating the rental unit and intended to return to school in [name] in September. This is a plausible explanation for the sequence of events, and it is consistent with the timing of the N9 Notice. In these circumstances, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice. The N12 Notice Was Given in Bad Faith
It was also undisputed that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent on December 28, 2024.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was advertised for rent within one year of the Tenant vacating triggers the presumption of bad faith in section 57(5) of the Act. The burden of proof then shifted to the Landlord to rebut the presumption of bad faith by proving on a balance of probabilities that they served the N12 in good faith.

The Landlord disputes that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith. The Landlord testified that she moved into the rental unit in August 2024 to oversee the repairs for multiple rental properties she owns in the area and because travelling to and from the area was difficult. The Landlord testified that she resided in the rental unit from August 2024, up to and including May 15, 2025, when the new tenancy began with the new tenants.

The Landlord testified that the rental unit was advertised for rent because it is located near McMaster University and is typically rented to students. The Landlord testified that rental units in the area are commonly advertised around December because students make housing arrangements in advance for the upcoming school year. The Landlord further testified that only two rooms were advertised because the other rooms were already rented for a tenancy beginning May 15, 2025.

I find the Landlord has not rebutted the presumption of bad faith. Although the Landlord did move into the rental unit in August 2024, the Landlord did not reside there for 12 months as required by section 48 of the Act. The Landlord did not provide sufficient evidence of a genuine change in circumstances that caused her to vacate the rental unit before the end of the required one-year period.

The Landlord testified that she did not move into the rental unit until August 2024 because she did not have a mattress and because work needed to be completed in the rental unit. However, the evidence was that the Tenant vacated on May 12, 2024. The Landlord also testified that, before August 2024, she was able to travel to and from the area to address and supervise repairs at multiple rental properties. In my view, this evidence does not explain why the Landlord could not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated or why she did not remain in occupation for at least one year. In all of the circumstances, and in light of the reverse onus that applies, I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith.

I also find it significant that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent on December 28, 2024, and entered into a new tenancy agreement on January 8, 2025, for a tenancy beginning May 15, 2025. This evidence demonstrates that, within the first year after the Tenant vacated, the Landlord was taking steps to re-rent the rental unit to students for next academic year. Although the new tenancy did not begin until May 15, 2025, the Landlord’s decision to advertise and enter into a new tenancy agreement before completing one year of occupation is inconsistent with the intention under section 48 of the Act.
For all these reasons, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith and the Tenant’s application must be granted. Remedies Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines is intended to assist parties in understanding the Board’s usual interpretation of the law, and to provide guidance to Members to promote consistency in decision-making.

The Interpretation Guideline explains that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Although the Landlord’s conduct in this case does show a blatant disregard for the Act, I am of the view that the other remedies awarded should provide adequate deterrence and promote future compliance with the Act. Therefore, this remedy is denied. Moving Costs

The Tenant claimed $1,835.90 in moving expenses. He testified that he incurred the following costs: • U-Haul truck rental: $590.99 • Gas: $275.09 • U-Haul truck rental Milage readjustment: $51.87 • Return to [name] estimation expense: $917.95

The Tenant is seeking the costs that he incurred from moving from the rental unit back to his family home in Pembroke. The Tenant is also seeking an additional cost of estimated return expense as he testified that because he was attending school in the fall he would have to move back to [name] from Pembrook. The Tenant claimed that the U-Haul rental was made under the name of his girlfriend’s father, however he incurred the costs.

The Landlord opposed the request for the estimation as the Landlord noted that no expenses were incurred and that this remedy is only intended to compensate tenants for moving costs that were incurred.

The Tenant provided receipts and bank statements of gas used on that day, I find the costs of $917.95 which represents the U-Haul truck rental, the gas and the U-Haul adjustment reasonable for moving one adult from a one-bedroom rental unit. The Landlord will be ordered to compensate the Tenant for these expenses.

The Tenant's claim for $917.95 in estimated costs for a return move to [name] is denied. The claim is based on estimated future expenses rather than actual costs incurred, and the Tenant did not provide updated figures or supporting evidence despite having had an opportunity to amend the application. General compensation

The Tenant seeks general compensation in accordance with section 57(3)(1.1), in the amount of $7,500.00. It is important to note that as referenced in the Act, an order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the Tenant has incurred any actual expenses. However, in determining a reasonable quantum I must consider the impact this bad faith eviction had on the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that the bad faith eviction caused him stress during a period when he was completing school exams and looking for alternate accommodations. The Tenant was required to secure alternative housing sooner than anticipated and to make arrangements for future accommodations while continuing his studies during an already stressful period. However, I am not satisfied that the requested amount of $7,500.00 is warranted in the circumstances.

In determining the amount of general compensation, I have considered the Tenant’s evidence about the impact of the bad faith eviction, including the stress caused during his school exams, the disruption and need to move back to Pembroke, and the need to secure future accommodations to return to school in [name]. I have also considered the tenancy was a joint tenancy and that the parties understood each tenant’s share of the monthly rent was $635.00 each. In my view, compensation equivalent to two months of the Tenant’s share of rent, $1,250.00, is reasonable in the circumstances. I find the amount recognizes the disruption, inconvenience, and loss of housing stability caused by the bad faith eviction.
The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant in the amount of $1,250.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant of $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,215.95. This amount represents: • $917.95 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $1,250.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $14,400.00. Did the Landlord serve the N12 Notice in bad faith?

It was the uncontested testimony of the Tenant, [name] (‘JTM’) that on August 24, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenants a notice of termination (‘N12 notice’) under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) claiming that he required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of their parents’ residential occupation. The termination date on the N12 notice was October 31, 2025.
It was further uncontested that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on October 22, 2025 as a result of the service of the N12 notice.
JTM testified that on May 8, 2026, the Landlord listed the property for sale on Realtor.ca for $649,000.00 (the listing can be found at DOC-7931609 in the Portal).

The Tenants testified that they faced significant challenges and strain including 2 moves, the first to JTM’s father’s basement into a single bedroom and then to an apartment in [name] on Pitt Street. Further, the Tenants testified that they faced significant stress and mental health challenges as a result of the service of the N12 notice. The Tenant, [name] [name] testified that she is still undergoing counselling as a result of this process. [name]6. Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Act, the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice … and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith 7. Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establishes a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. 2017, c. 13, s. 10. The Tenant’s application asserts that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith as they had listed the house for sale and never had the intention of residing in the rental unit for residential purposes, for a period of at least one year; it was always the Landlord’s intention to sell the house. Analysis 8. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenants to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith. 9. It was undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenants, the Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice, and the Landlord placed the property for sale within 1year of serving the Tenants the N12 notice. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not intend to move into the rental unit for residential purposes for a period of at least one year. On a balance of probabilities, I therefore find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith 10. It was also uncontested that the rental unit was placed for sale on May 8, 2026, just over 7 months after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. As a result, there is a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden would ordinarily fall to the Landlord to establish that they served the N12 in good faith. As the Landlord was not present to provide testimony or supporting evidence regarding why the Landlord chose to place the rental unit for sale, I find that the Landlord has acted in bad faith. Remedies Moving Expenses 11. The Tenants also sought $1,360.00 for moving expenses they incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach; however, while they stated that they paid $200.00 for a moving truck and $250.00 to each of three movers, they did not have any supporting documentation such as receipts. In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have established it is more likely than not that she incurred the moving expenses sought, as a result I decline to award moving expenses. General Damages 12. I am prepared to award $14,400.00 in general compensation relating to the impact the Tenants faced as a result of the actions of the Landlord. The Tenants were forced to vacate their rental unit and reside with their father in a single room in his basement until they moved after 5-6 months to an apartment in Cornwall. when they located a new rental unit, they stated this required multiple moves. The Tenants also testified they suffered mental health challenges and experienced a large amount of stress as a result of the Landlord’s service of the N12 notice. Considering the significant impact the Landlord’s conduct had on the Tenant, I consider an award of $14,400.00 in general compensation to be reasonable and appropriate. Administrative Fine 13. The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s purpose of fines. It states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It further provides that the remedy is not usually imposed “unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”. I have awarded the Tenants a substantial monetary remedy, and I am satisfied that the amount will act as a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is therefore denied 14. This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.
