issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-037172-23 issued on January 12, 2026. On April 15, 2026, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On April 16, 2026, interim order LTB-T-037172-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on January 12, 2026. The review request was heard by videoconference on June 30, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord, and the Landlord’s Legal Representative [name] [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: Application LTB-T-037172-23 was heard by videoconference on December 3, 2025. The Landlord did not attend. The Board granted the application on an uncontested basis.

The Landlord testified that he did not receive the Notice of Hearing by mail or e-mail. He does not have access to the Portal. The Landlord’s Representative submitted that he left his firm to an associate and went to work at a different firm from February to June 2025. However, when he returned to his firm in July 2025, he had trouble regaining access to his files. The current application had been assigned to a different legal representative, Justin Timms-Fryer, whose license is currently suspended. As a result, the current file was not recorded in the Landlord’s Representative’s calendar, which caused him to miss the hearing.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord was properly served with the adjourned Notice of Hearing and should have been aware of it. The Tenant also submitted that the Landlord ought to have contacted the Board to obtain a status update on his file.

In King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., 2008 CanLII 60708 (ONSC Div. Ct.) though the tenant received proper notice of a hearing, the tenant made a mistake about when the hearing was to be held. A new hearing was ordered. At para. 3, the court said “[b]eing reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less.”

The Board’s records show that the Landlord was not sent the Notice of Hearing directly. The Landlord’s Representative was e-mailed the Notice of Hearing but admitted to losing track of the file. I do not find it appropriate to penalize the Landlord for the actions of his representative. Although the Landlord could have obtained access to the file himself, I do not find it unreasonable that he relied on his representative to keep track of it.
Accordingly, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was not reasonably able to participate in the hearing held on December 3, 2025.
The Landlord’s request to review the order is granted. The Tenant’s application was heard de novo on June 30, 2026. T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,087.15 on or before August 7, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; 3. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the ‘N12 Notice’), and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice.

The Tenant testified that he went by the rental unit several times in the year after he moved out. The Tenant provided photographs from May and June 2023 showing the lawn unkept, the garbage bin empty, the lights off in the evening hours, and no vehicles in the driveway. The Tenant submitted that the Landlord may have attended the unit occasionally to cut the lawn but was not actually living there.

The upstairs unit has two bedrooms, the main floor has two bedrooms, and the basement is a bachelor apartment. The Landlord testified that he started renovating the main floor first and moved there in late 2022, around 3-4 months after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord then continued the renovations in the upstairs unit. However, he was only at the rental unit around 40% of the time, spending the majority of his time taking care of his elderly and sick parents. The Landlord still spends more time at his mother’s house than at the unit.

In Kohen v. Warner, 2018 ONSC 3865 (‘Kohen’), the landlord intended to occupy the unit on weekends and during the summer months. The Divisional Court found that indefinite part-time occupancy was insufficient to justify termination under section 48(1) of the Act. [name] is directly applicable here, as the Landlord also occupies the unit only part-time.

While I am sympathetic to the Landlord’s circumstances, I find that this level of occupancy does not constitute “residential occupation” under section 48(1). Therefore, the Landlord did not move into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Landlord testified that he served the N12 Notice because he wanted to renovate the house and move in. However, the Landlord was aware of his parents’ health conditions when he served the N12 Notice; therefore, he would have been aware of how much time he would spend at the rental unit. Given that the Landlord served the N12 Notice while being aware he would only occupy the rental unit part-time, I find that the notice was served in bad faith.

The Tenant requested general compensation, which is awarded for a tenant’s mental distress or hardship that resulted from their landlord’s actions. In my view, it applies where the hardship the tenant experienced goes beyond the normal inconvenience of changing residences.

The Tenant found it challenging to find a similar unit at a reasonable price. Consequently, the room the Tenant moved to is smaller, and so he had to rent storage separately. The Tenant also had to sell some of his belongings to accommodate the smaller space. I am not satisfied that the circumstances the Tenant described amount to significant mental distress or hardship that goes beyond the normal inconvenience of changing residences. Therefore, the request for general compensation is denied.

However, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant incurred moving and storage costs totalling $1,087.15 as a result of the Landlord’s actions. The Landlord will be required to reimburse the Tenant for these costs.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that she paid a $200.00 key deposit to the Landlord at the outset of the tenancy, and that she returned the keys to the Landlord when she vacated. Section 17 of Ontario regulation 516/06 under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 allows a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit.

Because the Landlord retained the refundable key deposit after the Tenant returned the keys, I am satisfied that the Landlord unlawfully retained the $200.00 refundable key deposit.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the difference in the illegally collected rent increase.
The parties agree that the tenancy began on May 1, 2024, under a fixed term tenancy ending on April 30, 2025, that lawful rent was $2,950.00, and was due on the 1st day of each month.

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not serve a N1 notice of rent increase and instead called the Tenant in late April 2025. As a result of the phone call the rent increased from $2,950.00 to $3,075.00 effective May 1, 2025, and that the increase was above the guideline. Is the Rent Increase [name] to Section 135.1?

The Landlord submitted that because the Tenant paid the increased amount for 12 straight months, the increase was deemed valid due to section 135.1 of the Act, which provides as follows: 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. 135.1(2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue.

At the hearing I shared my screen with the e-transfer document filed by the Tenant showing each e-transfer rent payment made from April 30, 2025, to June 27, 2026. The Tenant testified that he could only send a maximum of $3,000.00 per day so the payments reflect two payments made to cover the rent either on two last days of the month or the last and first day of the month.

I am satisfied the Tenant paid the increased rent from May 1, 2025, to April 1, 2026, which is consecutively 12 months of payment of the increased rent. In my view, the rent was first charged on May 1, 2025, the date the increased amount first came due.

The Tenant filed their application challenging the validity of the rent increase on April 28, 2026, which is 11 months and 28 days after the increased rent was first charged. As a result, I find the Tenant challenged the increase within one year of it being first charged, and section 135.1(1) does not apply. Even if I considered April 30, 2025, the date the Tenant first sent the increased amount to the Landlord, the Tenant still would have filed their application within one year it was first charged. Did the Landlord Unlawfully Increase the Rent?

The Tenant submitted that they verbally agreed to the increase because they did not understand their rights at the time and were nervous about having to find another place and possible housing insecurity. They sought legal advice after speaking to their neighbours and subsequently filed the T1 application for the illegal rent increase.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant agreed to the increase, The Landlord testified that the Tenant in the second unit moved out of the property on or about August 2025 and a new Tenant moved into the unit in or around October 2025. The Landlord added that with the new Tenant and the rent increase in this application he has not raised the rent in 2026.

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) is clear that rent may only be increase in accordance with sections 111 and 116 of the Act, which state: 111 (1) No landlord shall charge rent for a rental unit in an amount that is greater than the lawful rent permitted under this Part.

In my view, the fact that the Tenant agreed to the increase in and of itself cannot result in a finding that it was a lawful increase because section 3(1) of the Act prohibits parties from contracting out of the Act’s provisions: 3 (1) This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.
For all of the above reasons, I find there was no agreement in accordance with the Act, and that the increased rent was unlawful.
I find the Tenant is entitled to the illegal rent amounts charged from May 1, 2025, to April 1, 2026, in the amount of $1,500.00.
The Tenant incurred a cost of $48.00 for filing their application and are entitled to the cost of filing the application.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,548.00 from the rent each month until all funds are paid.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order, LTB-T-037450-25, determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order, LTB-T-034661-25, determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 15, 2026 at 09:00 am. Only the Tenant Representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 09:30 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenancy commenced on February 6, 2023 and terminated on July 30, 2025 when the Tenant moved out.
The rental unit consisted of an apartment with two bedrooms and one bathroom. The lawful rent was $1,460.63.
The Tenant field their applications on April 29, 2025.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the applications: LTB-T-034661-25

The Tenant alleged the Landlord failed to address the following maintenance issues: [name] windows; b. Washing machine c. Pests in form of mice and flies; d. Kitchen sink backing up; e. Bathroom tub chipping and peeling; f. Stove exhaust connection; and g. Electrical

It was the Tenants testimony that the broken windows and bathroom tub peeling were identified as part of their walkthrough prior to commencing the tenancy in February 2023 and that despite promises to have them fixed, the Landlord never did. Same was their testimony regarding the stove vent, having never been connected, and the kitchen sink backing up, having reported both issues in March 2023 by text, entered in evidence.

It was also their testimony that they were required to pay an additional $50.00 a month for use of a washing machine inside the unit, which they continued to pay, despite it not working, specifically, leaking, as of February 2023, until it was removed in February 2024 and never replaced.

They then testified that they had identified a mice and fly problem to the Landlord by a phone call at the same time in March 2023 and despite this a pest technician did not attend the property until June 2023, who in turn only provided traps and tape to catch the pests. It was their testimony that they would routinely have to place both to keep up with the problem.
As to the electrical, it was their testimony that due to faulty wiring they were limited in the number of outlets they could use at one time, for fear of tripping the breaker.

Upon completion of the Tenant’s testimony, the Tenant Representative entered in evidence, pictures, correspondence and a property standards order to comply, dated April 9, 2024, to substantiate the Tenant’s claims.

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested testimony, and evidence above I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with health safety housing and maintenance standards.

Specifically, the photographic evidence entered clearly showed the windows to be broken and nonfunctional to include missing panes. Similarly, the pictures of the bathtub show that the paint was in fact peeling, exposing metal and rust throughout while there were clear signs of a mice and fly issue by way of traps and feces.
The pictures entered, also showed the kitchen sink to have been backed up and the vent to the stove not connected.

That said, the Tenant failed to provide any evidence of the electrical outlets not working, other than their oral testimony. However, given it was uncontested, I am satisfied they also proved the Landlord has failed in this regard as well.

It is also clear by the text messages entered that as early as February 7, 2023 the Tenant had started to communicate these issues and to continue to do so up to February 20, 2024 whereas the property standards order proves that these issues were still extant as of April 9, 2024.This is not reasonable behaviour on part of the Landlord a clear breach of section 20 of the Act. LTB-T-037450-25

The Tenant testified that the Landlord withheld vital service by way of failing to ensure that the rental unit and complex had sufficient heat. They testified to complaining about this issue to the Landlord in February 2023 and that it was unresolved when they moved out. The Tenant Representative referred to the property standards order to support this claim.

The Tenant then testified that that they were substantially interfered with by way of the Landlord’s failure to address the maintenance issues and the installation of security cameras, which in their submission violated their privacy as they pointed in such a way that they could see into their rental unit. They supported their testimony with pictures of the camera entered in evidence.
On my own questioning, they testified that the door to their unit was a few feet back along the same wall that the [name] was angled along.

The Tenant then testified to the impact the Landlords failure to address the maintenance issues and withholding of vital service had. Specifically, the stress and additional effort required to maintain the unit in a habitable state, whilst resorting to family and friends to do their laundry which combined resulted in them moving out.

Section 21(1) of the Act states a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.
Given the Tenant’s uncontested testimony and the property standards ordered, I am satisfied that the Landlord did breach this section of the Act regarding the provision of heat.

Section 22 of the Act states a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Given my determinations above regarding the Landlord’s breach of section 20 of the Act, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven their claim for substantial interference regarding the Landlord’s failure to address maintenance issues.

That said, I am not satisfied this is the case regarding the installation of security cameras. Specifically, by the camera’s location and the Tenant’s own testimony I am not satisfied that it could see inside the unit, only who was entering and leaving which does not constitute a violation of privacy under the Act. Remedies sought.
Pursuant to the Tenant’s applications the remedies sought are: a. Rent abatement of $36,269.32; b. The Landlord ordered to pay a fine; c. Reimbursement of the filing fee of $48.00 Remedies awarded.

An abatement is a monetary award expressed in terms of a portion of past or future rent. It may be in the form of an order: (a) directing that the landlord pay the tenant a fixed amount—return rent paid by the tenant; or (b) allowing the tenant to pay less rent going forward by a fixed amount or percentage of the rent the tenant pays.

A rent abatement is meant to compensate the tenant to the degree that the tenant was deprived of what was bargained for or what is prescribed by legislation or minimum housing standards. It is only when a tenant is completely deprived of all of the benefits of a tenancy—where the rental unit in uninhabitable—that a 100% abatement is appropriate. [See 22001839 (Re), 2022 ABRTDRS 15 (CanLII)] As noted by the Vice Chair in TST- 56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

In determining the appropriate abatement, the LTB will consider, among other things: a. what percentage of the ‘package’ of shelter and services the landlord contracted or was otherwise obliged to provide was not available to the tenant; b. the length of time the problem existed and the severity of the problem in terms of its effect on the tenant; c. whether the tenant told the landlord about the issue(s) in a timely manner; d. whether the landlord responded to the issues raised by the tenant within a reasonable time and the landlord’s response was appropriate and effective. e. whether the tenant is wholly or partially responsible for the issue(s); and f. whether the tenant hindered or interfered with the landlord’s efforts to address the issue(s).

The LTB will consider the impact the breach has on the average tenant or the impact a reasonable person would expect this problem to have on a tenant. If the tenant has a particular susceptibility to the problem, the landlord can only reasonably be liable to the tenant for a more significant abatement if it can be shown that the landlord knew of the particular condition of the tenant.

The ultimate objective is to grant an abatement that is fair considering all of the circumstances. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name] [1997] O.J. No. 1881 (Gen Div) the Court said, “It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the no- repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.”
Similarly, in Offredi v. [organization] 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) the Court said that there is no mathematical way in which to determine an appropriate abatement.

In this case, I believe that a lump sum abatement is appropriate in terms of compensating the Tenant for the impact the Landlord’s failure to address maintenance issues and the resulting substantial interference which I am satisfied contributed to them moving out of the rental unit.

That said, I also cannot overlook the fact the Tenant was able to reside in the unit for over two years, despite the issues present. Accordingly, on this basis I set the abatement at $14,825.00 based on a 35.00% abatement from February 2023 until July 2025.
I am also satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed the $50.00 month paid for the washing machine that was inoperable for a period of 12 months totalling $600.00.
Given the Tenant has proven their case they are also entitled to reimbursement for the cost of filing their application, totalling $48.00.
Given the remedies already awarded and the fact that the LAndlrod was not present, I am not satisfied a fine is appropriate.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,473.00. This amount represents: • $14,825.00 for a rent abatement for the period of February 2023 until July 2025. • $600.00 for use of the washing machine that was inoperable. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Pursuant to 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.
Pursuant to section 57(2) of the Act. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.
The evidence before the Board is that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 28, 2025 returned the keys to the Landlord and received a refund for a key deposit being held by the Landlord.

The Tenant’s application was filed on April 29, 2026, more than one year after the Tenant vacated the rental unit in contravention of the on-year limitation period established by section 57(2) of the Act.

As made clear in the Divisional Court case of Sharma v. Sandhu, 2020 ONSC 6536, which is binding authority, the principal of discoverability is derived from the Limitation Act, 2002, which can in some cases conflict with the one-year limitation period outlined in section 57(2) of the RTA. However, section 3(4) of the RTA provides that if a provision of the RTA conflicts with another statute, the RTA applies.

At paragraph 20 of Sharma v. Sandhu the court also notes that the Supreme Court of Canada has in Peixeiro v. Haberman, 1997 CanLII 325 (SCC), referred to the discoverability rule as an interpretive tool for construing of limitations statutes and that: “…when time runs from the ‘accrual of the cause of action’ or from some other event which can be construed as occurring only when the injured party has knowledge of the injury sustained, the judge-made discoverability rule applies. But, when time runs from an event which clearly occurs without regard to the injured party’s knowledge, the judge-made discoverability rule may not extend the period the legislature has prescribed.”
The Tenant was required to file their application within one year of vacating the rental unit and failed to do so. The Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the sum of $2,728.00 by August 10, 2026.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit in an amount equal to rent for two rental periods or two months, which is contrary to s. 106(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Landlord applied a portion of that rent deposit, equal to one month’s rent, to the last rental period of the tenancy, as set out in s.106(10) of the Act. The Landlord did not return the remainder of the deposit to the Tenant, which is prohibited by the Act.

The parties entered into a tenancy agreement on July 11, 2024 for a fixed term commencing September 1, 2024 and ending August 31, 2025. Effective September 1, 2025, the tenancy became a month to month tenancy.
The lawful rent was $2,580.00. It was due the first of each month.

The Tenant paid a voluntary rent deposit of $5,160.00 to the Landlord on July 11, 2024 and a part of this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the rent deposit, as required by the Act. Tenant’s Notice of Termination

The Tenant vacated the unit on April 15, 2026. The Tenant sent the Landlord a text message on February 13, 2026, advising that he bought a house and was applying for a loan which, if approved, meant that he would “probably” move out around April 15, 2026.

Then, on February 27, 2026, the Tenant texted the Landlord again, advising that his loan had been approved and he would move out on April 15, 2026. I am satisfied that the Landlord received this text as he sent a responding message in the text chain.
The first issue for the Board to consider is whether the Tenant gave proper notice of termination in accordance with the Act. For the reasons that follow, I find that he did not.

Section 47 of the Act says a tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44. Subsection 44(2) says for a monthly tenancy a tenant must give a minimum of 60 days’ notice and the date of termination on the notice shall be the last day of a period.

Subsection 43(1) of the Act says: 43 (1) Where this Act permits a landlord or tenant to give a notice of termination, the notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall, (a) identify the rental unit for which the notice is given; (b) state the date on which the tenancy is to terminate; and (c) be signed by the person giving the notice, or the person’s agent.

As this was a month to month tenancy, the Tenant was required to provide a minimum of 60 days notice to the Landlord of his intention to terminate the tenancy. The period here was monthly starting on the 1st day of each month so the date of termination on any notice of termination needed to be the last day of a month. When the Tenant texted the Landlord on February 13, 2026, it was unclear whether he would be vacating the unit as he was still waiting for an answer on his loan application. However, by February 27, 2026, his loan had been approved and he was in a position to confirm his intention to vacate the unit. Based on the evidence before me, the Tenant’s notice to terminate the tenancy on February 27, 2026 did not meet the requirements of the Act. Section 88 of the Act Applies

The next issue for the Board to consider is the proper application of s. 88 of the Act, which reads in part as follows: 88 (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.

Basically, what this provision means is that where a tenant moves out of a rental unit after giving notice of termination that does not comply with the requirements of the Act, the tenant is liable for the rent for the period ending on the date the tenant could have properly terminated the tenancy.

The evidence before the Board is that, on February 27, 2026, the Tenant advised the Landlord that they would be vacating the premises and the Landlord confirmed receipt of this notice. Pursuant to s. 88(1) of the Act, I am satisfied that April 30, 2026 is the earliest date of termination the Tenant could have put on a notice to terminate that met the requirements of the Act and that he vacated the unit on April 15, 2026.
As such, the Tenant is liable for the rent only up to the period ending April 30, 2026. Rent Deposit

The Tenant paid a voluntary deposit of $5,160.00 to the Landlord in July 2024, representing two months of rent. Pursuant to s. 106(2) of the Act, the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. As such, the amount of the deposit paid to the Landlord was contrary to the Act.

The Tenant submitted to the Board that the Landlord applied a part of the deposit to the last month’s rent in April, for the period of April 1 to 15, 2026, but then failed to return the remainder of the deposit to the Tenant. The Tenant claims $3,870.00 from the Landlord, representing the last 15 days in April 2026 after he vacated the premises, plus one additional month which as I noted above was collected contrary to the Act.

Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. As the Tenant is liable for rent up to the period ending April 30, 2026, I am satisfied that a rent deposit equal to one month’s rent was properly applied to the month of April 2026.

However, as the second month’s deposit was not permissible by the Act, and the Tenant vacated the premises before April 30, 2026, the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of the remaining deposit of $2,590.00 which continues to be held by the Landlord. Interest
The Tenant claims $100.00 in interest on the deposit collected by the Landlord in July 2024. He calculates this amount using ChatGPT with reference to market stocks.

Pursuant to s. 106(6) of the Act, a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under s. 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

The uncontested evidence before the Board is that the Landlord collected a deposit in the amount of $5,160.00 on July 11, 2024 and the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on that deposit, as required by the Act.

Interest on the deposit would have come due in July 2025, using the applicable guideline amount of 2.5% for 2025, in the amount of $129.00. As this amount exceeds the amount sought by the Tenant on this application, and there was no request before me to amend the application, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven entitlement to interest in the amount of $100.00 as claimed. Costs
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $2,728.00. This amount represents: • $2,580.00 for the remainder of the rent deposit owing. • $100.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') for the month of March 2026. The legal monthly rent continues to be $1,315.63 and therefore the Landlord must refund the tenant the $25.66 for the excess rent collected in March 2026.
There is no dispute as to the lawful rent for the period of January 1 to December 31, 2024 – the rent during this period was $1,283.54, payable on the first of each month.

On September 27, 2024, the Landlord served a N1 notice on the Tenant (the “original N1”) purporting to increase the monthly rent in accordance with the guideline to $1,315.63 per month, effective January 1, 2025. The Tenant does not dispute the validity of this N1 notice and she commenced paying rent in the amount of $1,315.63 effective January 1, 2025 and continued to pay that monthly amount for at least 12 months thereafter.

On January 15, 2025, the Landlord served another N1 notice on the Tenant (the “revised N1”), purporting to increase the monthly rent by 5.5%, subject to approval by an [name] under the Act. The Landlord advised that they had applied to the Board for a rent increase above the guideline and advised the Tenant that her rent would increase to $1,354.13 effective May 1, 2025. Page 2 of the N1 Notice sets out “Important Information about the Law” including the following: N1 dated January 15, 2025 for Rent Increase Effective May 1, 2025 is Invalid

The Tenant disputes the validity of the revised N1 notice. She relies on s. 119(1)(a) of the Act which states that a Landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase. The Tenant states that, as her rent was already increased effective January 1, 2025, this revised N1 purporting to increase the rent effective May 1, 2025 is an illegal increase.

The Landlord submits that the original N1 notice was served in error and that they then cancelled it and served the revised N1 in January 2025. The Landlord relies on their email of January 22, 2025 in which they advised the Tenant that they wished to make a correction regarding the rent increase, noting as follows: Upon review, we realized that the notice did not include the proposed 3% rent increase above the guideline. As a result, the January 2025 rent increase notice will be considered invalid and is thereby canceled. A new notice reflecting the correct rent increase will be issued, and the rent increase will now take effect starting May 1, 2026 . Please note that the proposed 3% rent increase above the guideline is still subject to approval. Until it is approved, you are not required to pay that portion of the increase. However, once it is approved, the 3% increase will be applied retroactively to the effective date stated in the notice.

The Landlord’s position is that, as the original N1 notice was canceled or rescinded by them, they are not in contravention of the 12 month rule set out in s. 119(1) of the Act. By virtue of canceling the original N1, their position is that the clock essentially reset and when they served the revised N1, this would have been 16 months following the day of the last rent increase. For the reasons set out below, I do not accept this argument.

In the circumstances before me, the evidence is that the original N1 notice was served on the Tenant in accordance with the Act, proposing a rent increase in writing and on 90 days notice, and after at least 12 months had elapsed since the last rent increase. The Tenant did not dispute the validity of the notice and she conducted herself in accordance with the Act and her obligations as a tenant. Effective January 1, 2025, she paid rent at the new amount, in accordance with this notice, and the Landlord accepted this payment.

The Act contains no provision which would permit a landlord to unilaterally rescind a notice of rent increase after it was served. Had the legislature intended to empower the Board to permit the cancellation of N1 notices in circumstances of this kind, it would have set that out clearly in the Act. In the absence of any authority presented to me by the Landlord to permit them to rescind a N1 notice and in light of the clear language of section 119(1)(a) of the Act, such a claim cannot succeed. The Tenant here clearly did not consent to the rescission explicitly or by her actions; on the contrary, she has disputed the revised N1 notice before the Board and has continued to pay rent in accordance with the original N1 notice that she received.

As the Tenant received the original N1 notice and the parties conducted themselves in accordance with that notice, with the Tenant paying the new rent amount on the date that it was due, and the Landlord accepting said payment, s. 119(1)(a) of the Act effectively worked to prohibit the Landlord from serving another N1 notice less than a month since the day of the last rent increase.

Putting aside the invalidity of the revised notice as a result of the 12 month rule, the revised N1 notice fails on a second ground. The revised N1 notice purports to increase the rent by 5.5%, subject to approval by an order under the Act of a rent increase above the guideline. However, the Landlord relies on an AGI Order issued by the Board on December 5, 2025 [LTB-L-096141-23] which does not in fact permit such an increase. Rather, that [name] permitted the Landlord to increase the rent charged for this unit by an additional 2% within the specific time period of March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025.

Pursuant to s. 33(2) of [name]. 516/06 General, increases pursuant to an AGI order must be taken within the period specified in that order and the Landlord cannot apply the increase to subsequent periods. 33. (1) If an order with respect to a rental unit that increases the lawful rent is made under section 126 of the Act with respect to capital expenditures or operating costs for security services before the time for taking any rent increases under one or more previous orders has expired, the landlord may annually increase the lawful rent being charged by no more than the guideline rent increase plus 3 per cent of the previous lawful rent, until such time as no rent increase with respect to capital expenditures or operating costs related to security services ordered under section 126 of the Act remains to be taken. 33 (2) If a landlord fails to take a rent increase in accordance with subsection (1) in any 12-month period in which the landlord was entitled to take such a rent increase, the landlord may not take that rent increase in any subsequent time period.

For the reasons set out above, I find that the revised N1 notice is invalid and the lawful monthly rent continued to be $1,315.63 for the disputed period of May 1, 2025 onward. N1 dated January 26, 2026 for Rent Increase Effective May 1, 2026 is Invalid

On January 26, 2026, the Landlord served a N1 notice on the Tenant purporting to increase the monthly rent in accordance with the guideline to $1,369.46 per month, effective May 1, 2026. The Tenant disputes the validity of this N1 notice on the basis that it is an above guideline increase.

Having found that the lawful monthly rent for the period preceding this most recent N1 increase was $1,315.63, and as this rental unit is not exempt from s. 120 of the Act, the most the Landlord could have increased the rent, effective May 1, 2026 was to $1,343.25 per month, which represents a guideline increase of 2.1%. As the proposed rent increase for the period commencing May 1, 2026 is above the guideline amount, it is not permitted by the Act and the N1 notice of January 26, 2026 is therefore invalid.

Pursuant to s. 110 of the Act, a landlord is not permitted to increase the rent charged for a rental unit except in accordance with the Act. Until such time as the Landlord serves a valid N1 notice in accordance with the Act, the lawful monthly rent continues to be $1,315.63. March 2026 Overpayment

The evidence before the Board is that the Tenant, in response to emails from the Landlord, made an e-transfer payment of $1,341.29 on March 1, 2026, $25.66 more than her lawful monthly rent. She subsequently sought that the Landlord return to her the overpayment amount. Having found the lawful monthly rent is $1,315.63, I am satisfied that there was an overpayment in the amount of $25.66 in March 2026.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $73.66. This amount represents: • $25.66 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $73.66 from the monthly rent which comes due on September 1, 2026. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Kipling Residential Management 11 (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally, namely a $2750.00 credit of one month’s rent upon signing a 13-month lease.
reasons: This T1 Application is brought under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”), which permits a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit to apply for an order that the landlord pay to the tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of the Act. Subsection 135(4) of the Act provides that no order shall be made under that section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained the money in contravention of the Act.

At the hearing the daughter of the Tenant explained that the rent credit was supposed to be applied to their account in September 2023. It was not applied and they did not ask for it back until March 2026, when they were planning to move out.

The Landlord’s representative argued that the credit was to be applied in either September 2022 or September 2023 and the Application was out of time, as it has been more than one year since the money was retained.

Given the Tenant’s T1 application relates to a credit that was to be applied in either September 2022 or September 2023, I am satisfied that even if I accept the more recent date of September 2023, more than one year has passed since the Landlord retained the money. As such, this Application is out of time pursuant to s. 135(4) of the Act and must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
