issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This application was commenced on January 6, 2026, and heard to completion by videoconference on June 1, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Landlord’s agent [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant required Spanish interpretation services provided by [name].
reasons: As background, the Tenant filed this T2 application alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by either failing to take action against another tenant who was causing serious issues in the residential complex, or by taking insufficient action to address the issues.

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s representative raised a preliminary issue that another tenant in the residential complex had filed an application in LTB-T-060898-22. The application in LTB-T-060898-22 was dismissed and raised the same issues alleged by the Tenant in this T2 application.

The Tenant made submissions that her position is distinguishable from the order in LTB-T- 060898-22 because the Landlord failed to take adequate and diligent steps to screen potential applicants or potential future tenants and should be responsible for the ensuing disturbances caused by the other tenant.

Without recounting all of the parties’ evidence and submissions on the preliminary issue I determined it was appropriate to hear the Tenant’s application on its’ merits and the prior determination in LTB-T-060898-22 does not bind my determination in this matter.

Further, the Tenant was permitted to advance their position in relation to the Landlord failing to adequately screen applicants or new tenants since it was plead in the Tenant’s attached “explanation form” that accompanied their T2 application. Specifically, the Tenant writes, “I highly suspect they knew S.W.’s record and mental state before he moved in. Nonetheless, no safety precautions were provided to me or my neighbours.”. Limitation Period

Section 29(2) of the Act sets out a one-year limitation period for a Tenant to file an application after an event or alleged conduct occurs: (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
The Tenant’s application was filed on May 7, 2023, and accordingly, the earliest period from which a remedy can be considered is May 8, 2022. [name] Evidence

The Tenant [name] (LC) testified that she moved into her rental unit on January 1, 2006, and began having issues with another tenant in the residential complex immediately upon the other tenant taking possession of their rental unit on July 1, 2020.

LC’s evidence is that the other tenant (SW) would speak loudly, use profanities, play loud music, and talk loudly to himself. LC testified that between July 2020 and May 2022, SW would get furious and break things in his rental unit causing LC to stop doing things in her rental unit such as using the blender for fear it would trigger an outburst by SW.

LC also testified that SW became aware that she was making security reports and would call her names including “whore”, and make statements like, “Call the police, call security, I’m ready!”. LC’s evidence is that on one occasion the other tenant was walking around with a sharp object but was assured by security that it was only a cane SW uses for mobility.

During the relevant period of consideration for the Tenant’s application beginning in May 2022, LC testified that there were incidents involving the other tenant on May 5, 2022, May 6, 2022, and May 18, 2022.

LC gave evidence that on May 18, 2022, SW was “out of control” and broke all the windows in his rental unit eventually cutting a hole between his rental unit and LC’s unit. LC testified that during this time SW said he would, “kill me”, and “kill anyone who had a computer cell phone or camera.”.
LC testified that there was an e-mail sent to the Landlord’s Agent [name] (SD) on June 26, 2022, wherein LC requests hotel accommodations and SD failed to reply to LC’s e-mail.

LC also testified that whenever she would contact the Landlord’s security personnel, she would receive a response acknowledging receipt of her report and that every time she would call security they would investigate.

While each individual report submitted at the hearing has not been noted in this order, LC did submit security reports and corroborating evidence about the issues she experienced with SW. LC also submitted evidence to corroborate the number of complaints made about SW, which were numerous.

LC also submitted a copy of a decision from the Ontario Review Board (ORB) dated November 1, 2022, that relates to SW. LC submitted this decision in support of the proposition that the Landlord ought to have better screened SW prior to entering into a tenancy with him.

LC noted that the decision references challenges faced by SW since childhood and also refers to psychiatric and criminal history of SW which she submits was information the Landlord should have been able to access when considering SW as a tenant.

LC further testified that the Landlord did not provide sufficient supports to SW or provide him with referrals to services that could have assisted him. LC’s evidence that despite the Landlord having a social worker available to tenants of the residential complex she did not receive any calls or offers of support.
LC also gave evidence that the Landlord did not advise her about the steps being taken to address her concerns with SW which resulted in her belief that the Landlord was not taking adequate measures.

LC’s testimony is that the last time she saw SW at the residential complex was on July 1, 2022. LC concluded her direct testimony by expressing her belief that she was treated unfairly and had to do a lot of the work herself to gather the evidence to ensure action was taken against SW.
LC testified during cross examination that after the serious incident with SW on or around May 18, 2022, the Landlord sent the Tenant to a hotel for three days to escape the situation.

LC also confirmed that she was offered a transfer to unit 1008 on the 10th floor however, LC’s evidence conflicted in relation to the transfer. LC first testified that she was unhappy that the Landlord offered her a rental unit in the same building as SW, and she did not know anyone on the 10th floor. LC then testified that despite wanting to change buildings, she preferred to stay in the same building but transfer to the rental unit opposite SW and not directly beside him.
LC expressed her discontent that she was being asked to consider moving despite SW causing the issues. LC felt that SW was being protected and she was being punished.

Two pieces of correspondence from May 2022 were also put to LC on cross examination showing that the Landlord’s agent [name] followed up with LC about supports and reached out to respond to LC’s complaints.

LC acknowledged that there were times that SW got arrested but would return to his rental unit days later. LC also testified on cross examination about her knowledge of the process through which the Landlord receives new tenants and reiterated her belief that the Landlord ought to have done more to screen SW and resolve her issues.

The issues caused by SW resulted in LC seeking professional treatment for symptoms of anxiety and depression. [name], a psychotherapist, testified about her work with LC, the cause of LC’s issues, and the subsequent stress caused by these proceedings. Landlord’s Evidence 27. [name] (SD) testified that she is a tenancy support worker for the Landlord and her role includes investigating complaints, making referrals, liaising with tenant supports, and preparing LTB documents. 28. SD acknowledged receiving complaints about SW and testified that she reached out to SW’s supports. Ultimately, the decision was made to serve an N5 notice of termination to SW on or around May 8, 2021. 29. SD gave evidence that after service of the N5 notice, SW was being assisted by a support worker and the complaints “quieted down”. The Landlord did not file an application believing that the first N5 served to SW was voided. 30. SD recalled receiving additional complaints in May 2022 and another N5 notice was served to SW. During that time SD reached out to a mental health worker and the Ottawa police department to try to resolve the issues with SW. 31. SD also noted that the issues alleged by LC span between July 2020 and July 2022 which was during the height of the [name] pandemic. SD’s evidence is that during this time there was a moratorium on evictions and because of the pandemic there was a delay at the LTB in scheduling hearing dates. 32. SD also explained that during the pandemic police were not holding individuals in custody and it was difficult to find resources to assist individuals with mental health challenges. 33. SD confirmed that LC was not informed about the steps being taken to address her concerns with SW because of privacy restrictions. SD’s evidence is that she explained to LC that there was a process that the Landlord is required to follow but she could not disclose the specific steps being taken to resolve LC’s issues. 34. SD acknowledged that despite the serious issues being reported about SW, the Landlord must follow the LTB’s process to seek an eviction, and the Landlord cannot arbitrarily lock out a tenant. 35. SD recounted that an N5 notice to terminate was served to SW on June 9, 2022, and subsequently on June 24, 2022, the Landlord served a second N5, N6, and N7 notice of termination to SW on June 24, 2022. 36. The Landlord filed L2 applications based on the first N5 notice, and the subsequent N5/N6/N7 notices. The Landlord also filed a request to shorten time to a hearing on July 5, 2022. 37. SD testified that SW was arrested on July 1, 2022, and SD worked with SW’s support worker to execute an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy. SD confirmed that SW did not return to the rental unit after July 1, 2022. 38. SD gave evidence that she was contacted by LC in May 2022 which is when she explained that the Landlord must follow the LTB’s process. SD also testified that she asked community and safety services to reach out to LC and that despite it being during the pandemic LC would often speak to “Chad”. 39. SD also explained that during the long weekend in May 2022, the Landlord anticipated lower staffing levels and the potential for issues with SW, so the Landlord arranged for LC to stay at a hotel. 40. SD’s testimony is that despite offering LC a transfer of rental units, the Landlord would not approve a transfer for LC to a rental unit on the same floor. SD’s evidence is that because of the pandemic there were lower vacancy rates which made it difficult to offer other transfer options to LC. 41. SD summarized her efforts to resolve LC’s issues as doing everything possible to help including working with mental health workers, security, and police. 42. SD also explained that since the Landlord is a social housing provider, there is a process by which the Landlord obtains new tenants. The Landlord is required to select tenants from the “housing registry” in chronological order based on the date of their application for social housing. The Landlord is not provided information about the prospective tenants and does not have the ability to “vet” individuals on the housing registry. 43. During cross examination LC asked why she wasn’t given the opportunity to have an in- person meeting about her issues like other tenants and SD gave evidence that she would have met with LC if she made the request. 44. SD was also asked about why an e-mail from LC on June 26, 2022, did not receive a reply and SD expressed remorse for the lack of reply testifying that the Tenant was requesting another hotel stay which SD did not have authority to authorize. SD believed one of the other 4 e-mail recipients who did possess that authority would reply. Analysis 45. In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority (February 5,2001), [name] No.99- 002412-DV [2000] O.J. No.5650 ([name]) the Court held that a landlord who fails to take reasonable steps to address substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment by one tenant of another tenant can be found to have substantially interfered with the complaining tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. 46. This means that the Landlord has the positive obligation to take reasonable, timely, and appropriate steps to address the Tenant’s complaints. 47. Based on the evidence before me, the following is the chain of events and timelines of the various pertinent considerations: • SW moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2020; • The first evidence of LC making a complaint to the Landlord is July 17, 2020; • LC’s complaints about SW continued between July 2020 and June 2022. • The Landlord served a first, voidable, N5 notice of termination to SW on May 8, 2021 (SW voided); • The Landlord served a “second” first, voidable, N5 notice of termination on June 9, 2022, and filed an L2 application on June 23, 2022; • The Landlord served a second N5, N6, and N7 notice of termination on June 24, 2022, and filed an L2 application on July 4, 2022; • The Landlord filed a request to shorten time to a hearing on July 5, 2022. • SW was removed from the rental unit on July 1, 2022, and did not return; • Based on the limitation period, the issues raised in LC’s application are considered from May 8, 2022 (one year prior to the application being filed), up to July 1, 2022 (the date SW was removed). 48. It should be made clear in this order that the evidence submitted by LC shows that the issues she experienced with SW were severe, traumatizing, and impactful. There was no dispute that the actions of SW were disruptive and caused serious safety issues. 49. Despite the clear impact to LC, the determination in this matter rests on whether the Landlord failed to take reasonable, timely, and appropriate steps to address LC’s complaints. 50. There was significant evidence at the hearing about the issues that predate the limitation period and when considering this evidence contextually, the Landlord was taking active steps since 2021 when the first N5 notice was served around May 8, 2021. The issues with SW also began during an unprecedented time when there was a global pandemic and a moratorium on evictions. 51. During the relevant period between May 2022 to July 2022, the Landlord discharged their obligation to take reasonable, timely, and appropriate steps to resolve the situation by: offering LC a transfer, making arrangements for LC to stay at a hotel, working with SW and his supports, engaging with onsite security and police, serving multiple notices of termination, filing applications, requesting to shorten time to a hearing, and working with SW to negotiate an agreement to terminate the tenancy. 52. LC’s submission that the Landlord should have done more to screen or “vet” SW prior to the commencement of his tenancy falls outside of the limitation period since SW’s tenancy commenced in July 2020. 53. However, even if this issue were to be considered I accept the Landlord’s evidence and submissions that the Landlord is not privy to information about potential tenants and must simply choose the next name from the housing registry. 54. In these circumstances, I do not find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with LC’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the Landlord took reasonable, timely and appropriate steps to resolve LC’s issues. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $848.00.

The Tenant testified that in October 2025, the parties signed a residential lease agreement (the ‘lease’). The monthly rent was $1,500.00 due on the 30th of each month. The tenancy began on November 1, 2025. On October 11, 2025, the Tenant paid the Landlord $3,000.00 for first and last month’s rent and an additional $500.00 for a refundable damage deposit.
The Tenant claims she was unaware that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not allow landlords to charge tenants for damage deposits.

The Tenant further claims that after she moved in, she advised the Landlord that all the parking spaces were occupied by other occupants in the building and she needed a space for her car. The Landlord advised her that she must pay an additional amount for a parking space. The Tenant paid an additional $50.00 per month for a parking space for the months of December 2025 through to May 2026, for a total of $300.00. At paragraph 7 of the lease signed by the parties, it includes, “one parking spot in the driveway”. No additional fee for the parking space is stated in the lease.

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on July 1, 2026. The Tenant requested a refund of $300.00 for parking and $500.00 for the damage deposit from the Landlord. As of the hearing date, the Landlord had not returned any of those funds to the Tenant.
The Landlord collected charges which are not allowed by the Act. Analysis Damage Deposit

Together, sections 105 and 106 of the Act state that the only security deposit a landlord may lawfully collect is a rent deposit equal to one month's rent, which must be applied to the last month of the tenancy.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act explicitly prohibits landlords from collecting or attempting to collect any fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or similar amount, whether refundable or not, unless otherwise prescribed.

Section 135 of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant to apply to the Board for an order requiring the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord to return any money that was unlawfully collected or retained.

The damage deposit collected by the Landlord is an additional security deposit beyond the last month’s rent deposit. As section 105 of the Act permits only a last month’s rent deposit, the collection of this damage deposit is contrary to the Act and constitutes an illegal charge. The Landlord must return this money to the Tenant. Parking Charges

Subsection 2(1) of the Act defines “rent” as follows: “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing… “services and facilities” includes, (b) parking and related facilities…
I find that parking is rent as subsection 2(1) of the Act clearly includes the amount that is paid for parking facilities in the definition of rent, whether or not a separate charge is made for it.

Pursuant to subsection 119(1)(b) of the Act “a landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed… (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply.”

I find that the lease included a parking space in the rent of $1.500.00 per month. Given the tenancy only began on November 1, 2025, the Landlord was not entitled to increase the rent, as 12 months had not elapsed since the day the rental unit was first rented to the Tenant.

This is not a situation where the parties agreed to a rent increase because the landlord added a parking space to the Tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit. According to the tenancy agreement, the Tenant had access to a parking spot and parking was included in the rent from the start of the tenancy. Therefore, the rent increase was not authorized by section 123 of the Act.
The additional $50.00 per month collected by the Landlord for parking is contrary to the Act and constitutes an illegal charge. The Landlord must return this money to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $848.00. This amount represents: • $800.00 for the illegal charges collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). These applications were heard by videoconference on July 22, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.
The Tenant, [name] (S.H.A.) moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2024. The rental unit was one of two fully furnished self-contained bachelor units located in the basement.

S.H.A. testified that on April 3, 2025, she was contacted by another resident and informed that her unit had flooded and that she would need to return to the unit as soon as possible. S.H.A. was in [name], Ontario, for her birthday at the time the unit flooded.

S.H.A. testified that the Landlord also contacted her and arranged to enter the rental unit to inspect the sate of the unit and start removing the water from the unit. The Tenant tendered videos of the unit being flooded by water and videos of the Landlords attempting to remove the water with a mop and paper towels. S.H.A. did not believe that the steps taken by the Landlord were appropriate or reasonable given the circumstances.

S.H.A. returned to her rental unit on the evening of April 3, 2025. She immediately contacted her insurance company. S.H.A. testified that the unit was unhabitable due to the flooding and that she was unable to reside in the rental unit as of April 3, 2025, the date of the flooding.

S.H.A. also testified that the Landlord brought a fan and dehumidifier to the rental unit the same day as the flood and asked the Tenant for them to be kept running for the next several days to dry out the unit.

On April 9, 2025, the Tenant’s insurance provider attended the unit to perform an inspection of the unit and damaged items belonging to the Tenant. The Tenant’s undamaged items were removed at this time and placed in a secure storage facility. The Tenant tendered a report provided by the Tenant’s insurance company as evidence. The report contains multiple photographs that show multiple areas with moisture in the rental unit, six days following the flooding.

S.H.A. testified that she continued to contact the Landlord asking for update status on her rental unit and when she could anticipate completion of the repair work. The Landlord assured her the unit would be repaired and brought back to its original state prior to the flooding. No completion date or timeline was provided for the Tenant.

S.H.A. testified that on or about April 12, 2025, she provided the Landlord with a copy of the rental unit key in a lockbox and full access to the rental unit as necessary to ensure that repairs are carried out as fast as possible. The Tenant was not living in the unit at the time and only had her damaged items remaining in the unit.

S.H.A. testified that the Landlord did not take any steps to repair the rental unit between April 4, 2025, through to April 28, 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit and returned the keys to the Landlord on or about April 27, 2025. The Tenant testified to vacating the unit because of the Landlord failing to conduct the repairs in a reasonable or timely manner.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord applied her rent deposit to the month of April 2025, and that the Landlord also charged her $100.00 for utilities for the month of April 2025. The Tenant was seeking the return of the rent deposit and $100.00 utility payment made to the Landlord. Alternatively, the Tenant was seeking an abatement in the amount of one month’s rent of $1,550.00 for the month of April 2024. The Tenant was also seeking her $1000.00 insurance deductible and rent differential of $350.00 per month for twelve months, and $2,000.00 as out of pocket expenses for the Tenant having to purchase new furniture because her new unit was not furnished. The Tenant also sought general compensation for loss of funds paid for a course that she was unable to complete due to the circumstances.
On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she moved into the unit on May 1, 2024, and that her one year lease was ending on April 30, 2025.

The Tenant also confirmed telling the Landlord that she may not want to remain in the unit at the end of the lease term unless the Landlord could reduce her rent so that she can purchase a motor vehicle to drive to work.
The Tenant confirmed that she stayed at three separate locations between April 3, 2025, through to April 30, 2025. The cost of the accommodation was covered by her insurance provider.
The Tenant also confirmed that she initially viewed and secured her new rental unit on or about April 25, 2025, after the flooding had occurred in her rental unit.

The Landlord, [name] (M.G.), testified that the Tenant’s lease was expiring on April 30, 2025, and that the Tenant had no intentions of remaining in the rental unit at her current rental rate. [name] also testified that the Tenant did not pay rent for April 2025, meaning the Landlord was to use the rent deposit as the last month of the lease. 17. [name] confirmed that the unit flooded on April 3, 2025. The Landlord testified that the cause of the flooding was because of the amount of rainfall experienced on this date. 18. [name] testified that she attended the unit with her property manager on the same day that the flood occurred. [name] testified to immediately taking steps to remove the water from the rental unit by using a wet/dry vacuum, paper towels, and a mop. The Landlord did not contact any professional remediation contractors to assist or inspect the unit or damage at this time. 19. [name] testified that she had her property manager attend the property after their initial attendance to monitor the situation and determine the status of the water. 20. [name] testified that she agreed to adjust the Tenant’s rent for the month of April 2025 but did not refund any money to the Tenant. 21. [name] also testified that on or about April 12, 2025, the Tenant left a key to the rental unit for the Landlord in a lock box, allowing the Landlord to come and go as they please to carry out the necessary work. 22. [name] testified that the Tenant returned vacant possession of the unit and the keys to the Landlord on April 29, 2025. 23. The Landlord confirmed that no additional work or steps to repair the unit were taken between April 4, 2025, through to April 30, 2025. The Landlord testified that she was waiting for the unit to dry out entirely prior to doing any work so that she could have a better understanding of what exactly needed to be completed. 24. The Landlord argued that the Tenant should not be entitled to the insurance deductible because they elected to maintain a policy with a deductible or high deductible. The Landlord also argued that the Tenant should not be entitled to any rent differential because the Tenant’s new unit was in a condominium and not one of two units in a basement and had prime location when compared to her previous unit. The Tenant’s new unit also had the amenities of the condominium which were not available at her previous unit. The Landlord did not believe that she should be liable for the Tenant’s additional expenses for renting out a much nicer unit. 25. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s failure to address or repair the rental unit after the flooding within a timely and reasonable manner would have substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. I find the Landlord’s actions of attending the unit the same day to be reasonable and timely. What I find unreasonable and untimely is the Landlord’s failure to complete any additional work as required in the unit between April 4, 2025, through to April 30, 2025. 26. I am also satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) repair the rental unit. This finding is based on the Landlord’s failure to address the repairs in a timely and reasonable manner. Remedies 27. The Tenant has out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $1,000.00 because of the Landlord's actions. The Landlord must pay the Tenant this amount. This amount represents the Tenant’s insurance deductible paid to her insurance company. I am not satisfied that the out-of-pocket expense sought for the Tenant’s new furniture or loss of funds paid for a course to be appropriate. I did not have sufficient evidence of the funds claimed for schooling and found the cost of new furniture to be more appropriately incurred by the Tenant. The Landlord should not have to pay for the Tenant’s new furniture because the Tenant decided to occupy an unfurnished unit. The Tenant also has the benefit of using the furniture and selling it after they no longer require it. Accordingly, I find the amount awarded to be appropriate in the circumstances. 28. I also find that a rent abatement of $1,397.15 is appropriate in the circumstances. This is equal to a 100% abatement of rent for the period of April 4, 2025, through to April 30, 2025. I find this amount reasonable given the Tenant was unable to use the rental unit due to the flooding. 29. I find that an administrative fine is not warranted under these circumstances. The Tenant did not address this issue at the time of the hearing. 30. The tenancy will end on April 30, 2025, as agreed by the parties at the hearing. 31. I also find that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions or inactions. I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred an additional $350.00 and/or $4,200.00 per year in rent differential between the Tenant’s previous rental unit and new rental unit. The new rental unit is in a much nicer, central, and sought-after area of the GTA. The new unit is also bigger and located in a condominium versus a basement apartment. I find that units are not comparable and any additional amount spent on rent would be accounted for by way of the Tenant’s improved or upgraded living accommodations. The Landlord should not be liable for a Tenant’s upgraded living accommodation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,445.15. This amount represents: • $1,397.15 for a rent abatement. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of April 30, 2025. July 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant LTB-T-039397-23 [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearings and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. LTB-L-008418-23

As explained below, the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy. Therefore, the tenancy is terminated, and the Tenant must vacate the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

On January 13, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant a first, voidable N5 notice of termination. The Tenant is substantially interfering with another tenant or the Landlord’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or a lawful right, privilege, or interest by engaging in altercations with other residents and failing to clean up her dog’s urine in common areas of the residential complex. Therefore, the Landlord was allowed to give the Tenant a second, non-voidable N5 notice of termination under section 68 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act).

On January 26, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant a second N5 notice of termination. The notice of termination contains the following allegations: The Tenant is substantially interfering with another tenant or the Landlord’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or a lawful right, privilege, or interest by engaging in altercations with other residents.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (“MK”) testified that she is the Residential Administrative Manager for the Landlord and has been for the last three years (as of the first hearing in 2024). [name] testified that there were several complaints from other tenants about the Tenant that came to her attention that were essentially the same, confrontations between the Tenant and other tenants that would escalate to yelling and screaming. [name] testified that a first N5 was issued and it was not voided and the issues continued as of the date of when [name] first testified.

MK testified that the Landlord addressed the issue with all parties, not just the Tenant and all parties were advised to leave each other alone. [name] testified that the Landlord has reached out to Canadian Mental Heath Association about educating residents on bullying but seminars have not rolled out.

MK testified that the same process is followed for all tenants involved in these types of incidents. There are warning letters, followed by N5 Notices, followed by applications to the Board if necessary. MK testified that there are other tenants where there are Board orders in place after following through with N5 Notices.

One of the other tenants, [name] (“LK”) testified that she has lived in the residential complex for 7 years and she testified about several incidents with the Tenant. LK testified and LTB-T-039397-23 that she has seen the Tenant confronting employes of the Landlord and has witnessed confrontations between the Tenant and other tenants. LK testified about one incident on January 22, 2023, when the Tenant appeared to loiter in the area around the gazebo outside to attempt to engage LK in a confrontation and when LK was walking away the Tenant told her to “take the snarky look off your face” and called her a “loser, a f***ing loser”.

LK testified that she is fearful of the Tenant and she has sought a peace bond against the Tenant because of this. LK testified that the Tenant has flipped her off, screamed derogatory words at LK, and records LK. LK testified she has witnessed the Tenant yelling at other tenants and cornering other tenants in confrontations. LK testified that living in the residential complex is uncomfortable because of the Tenant’s unpredictable reactions. LK testified that she tries to avoid the Tenant if at all possible.

The Tenant testified that she voided the first N5 Notice but then someone came up with other incidents. The Tenant testified that for the January 22, 2023, incident, she did not say “snarky” she said “smarmy”. The Tenant denied all of the allegations in the second N5 Notice and maintained that what is contained in the N5 Notice is being grossly exaggerated.

A lot of time was then spent on incidents that were either the subject of the first N5 notice or that occurred after the second N5 notice. However, section 68(1) of the Act provides that a second notice of termination may be given if 1) the landlord has already given the tenant a notice of termination under section 62, 64 or 67; and 2) more than 7 days, but less than six months after the first notice was given, an activity takes place, conduct occurs or a situation arises that constitutes grounds for a notice of termination under section 60, 61, 62, 64 or 67.

Pursuant to section 68(1), the second N5 could only raise new incidents/conduct that occurred more than 7 days after the first N5 was given, i.e. beginning January 21, 2023. As such, I am only concerned with allegations of new incidents / conduct alleged on the second N5 Notice arising after January 21, 2023, of which there are 2, one on January 22, 2023, and one on January 25, 2023.

In this case, the Tenant admitted that she reacts, however, she denied that it is threatening or aggressive. The problem is that the Tenant reacts. The Tenant claims that her reaction is to the “abuse and harassment” that the Landlord and other tenants have put her through, which is discussed more fully below.

However, the Tenant’s reaction cannot be condoned, especially as it pertains to the January 22, 2023, incident where it appears the Tenant made unprovoked comments to LK that were unnecessarily inflammatory. The Tenant wants me to believe that the Landlord’s claims on the second N5 were grossly exaggerated, but it is the Tenant herself who corrected the Landlord’s evidence in that the Tenant said it was a “smarmy” look and not a “snarky” look.

I find that LK’s version of events more persuasive as I find that the Tenant appeared to be downplaying her accountability in matter. The Tenant appeared to be loitering around the gazebo in an attempt to engage a confrontation and when LK did not engage, the Tenant and LTB-T-039397-23 made unprovoked comments. The Tenant confirmed some of the comments which included taking the “smarmy” look of LK’s face.
The Landlord did not present any evidence regarding the incident that took place on January 25, 2023, at the hearing.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s behaviour is substantially interfering with other tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.

While I understand that the Tenant feels her actions are not threatening or aggressive, the problem is that her reactions are still interfering with other tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. The Tenant’s reactions by making unnecessary comments and engaging in confrontations is what is causing the interference with the other tenant’s reasonable enjoyment which is not permissible. Even though there are only two incidents noted on this N5 notice and only one with sufficient evidence provided during the hearing, I am satisfied based on the evidence presented that it is a pattern of behaviour demonstrated by the Tenant that has been ongoing and persisting for some time and therefore is substantially interfering with the reasonable enjoyment of other tenants.
The Tenant claims that her reactions are due to the Landlord’s failure to address bullying by other tenants, so I now turn to the Tenant’s claims.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. LTB-T-039397-23 Preliminary Issue
At the start of the September 6, 2024, hearing the Tenant requested to amend her application.

The Tenant wanted to amend to include two additional incidents that were not included in the initial application. The Tenant’s Representative provided that to not allow the amendment would be prejudicial and would bias the Tenant’s ability to fully present her case.

The Landlord’s Representative objected as the Tenant had retained [name] by July 1, 2024, who should have been aware of the need to amend well in advance of the July 30, 2024, hearing. To proceed with the hearing on July 30, 2024, and not bring up the request at the first hearing or the subsequent hearing in August but then at the third hearing in September and an hour and a half into the Tenant’s testimony was too prejudicial to the Landlord.

The request to amend was granted as the prejudice was minimal to the Landlord, since the Landlord’s witness was present and available to testify if necessary. Furthermore, the incidents were known to the Landlord, and the Landlord was aware of and ready to discuss and LTB-T-039397-23 the specific incidents and had discussed some of the incidents during their evidence already. Therefore, the amendment would be an efficient use of Board resources.
As such the Tenant’s application was amended to add an incident from May 24, 2024, and an incident from June 27, 2024. The Application

As explained below, the Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

Tenant’s application alleges substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and harassment. The Tenant alleges that she is being targeted by [name] ("LM"), the Landlord’s superintendent, as well as other tenants in the residential complex. The Tenant alleges that she is being wrongly accused of incidents and the Landlord and their staff are doing nothing to de-escalate the situations that arise.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord has created a negative environment and has encouraged other tenants through the Landlord’s staff to surveil and make reports about the Tenant thereby harassing and substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.
The Tenant focused her allegations on incidents that occurred on the following dates, July 20, 2022, August 22, 2022, September 10, 2022, November 19, 2022, May 24, 2024, and June 27, 2024.

Much of the Tenant’s evidence was focused on either responding to the Landlord’s allegations on the Landlord’s application or incidents on dates not included in the Tenant’s application. However, the evidence that did cover the Tenant’s incidents is essentially the same in that the Tenant feels targeted by an incident that is started by another tenant or LM and this will trigger the Tenant into responding.

The Tenant testified that LM will laugh at and mock her or will just standby while incidents are occurring and do nothing to de-escalate or intervene. The Tenant testified that LM will start shouting at her out of nowhere to “get away”.

The Tenant testified that she has reached out to the Landlord on numerous occasions including, July 20, 2022, September 10, 2022, December 13, 2022, and December 15, 2022, about what she perceives as bullying and either receives no response or an unsatisfactory response. The Tenant testified that she eventually stopped communicating with the Landlord completely because she felt that she was having the blame placed solely on her and felt intimidated and threatened by letters sent from the Landlord’s Representative. and LTB-T-039397-23

As discussed above, MK testified that the Landlord addressed the issue with all parties, not just the Tenant and all parties were advised to leave each other alone. [name] testified that the Landlord has reached out to Canadian Mental Heath Association about educating residents on bullying but seminars have not rolled out. 35. [name] testified that the same process is followed for all tenants involved in these types of incidents. There are warning letters, followed by N5 Notices, followed by applications to the Board if necessary. MK testified that there are other tenants where there are Board orders in place after following through with N5 Notices. 36. MK also testified that the Landlord completes Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act training for all staff within 5 days of hiring new staff and does diversity and inclusion training yearly. [name] testified that the Landlord also completes quarterly townhall meetings with onsite staff and has conversations as issues arise. [name] testified that the Landlord completes one on ones with staff to assist with dispute resolution. 37. [name] (“JW”) testified that he is a Property Manager with the Landlord and the residential complex is one of the buildings he manages. He testified that he investigated each complaint that was sent to him from the Tenant. JW testified that he had a conversation with the Tenant on December 5, 2022, and it was difficult conversation because the Tenant would not let him get a word in. JW testified that the Tenant constantly interrupted, would not listen, and would not take suggestions. 38. JW testified that all incidents brought to the Landlord’s attention were investigated but the Tenant does not listen or follow rules and she continues to act out. JW testified that he has often had to remove himself from situation with the Tenant. 39. JW testified that all the Landlord’s staff is trained on diversity and inclusion and bullying but tenants are not given that. JW testified that each situation is dealt with individually and other tenants have been given warnings or notices where appropriate or further legal action has been taken if called for. 40. LM testified that she is currently the residential complex building manager and as been since June 26, 2023. LM testified that she was never told about any particular tenants before starting in her position. LM testified that her first interaction with the Tenant was when she accidentally called the Tenant’s dog the wrong name and the Tenant corrected LM, the Tenant then began calling a few other tenants names like “fatso” and that they would “brainwash” LM. LM said she would make her own decisions about people. 41. LM testified that other tenants had approached her to say the Tenant was a problem and LM told them she would not discuss tenants with other tenants. LM then went to JW and discussed not engaging if possible. LM then testified about various incidents she has had with the Tenant and how LM is now afraid of the Tenant and how security has been hired for LM while LM is working. LM said there is always a lot of yelling, swearing, and name calling when the Tenant is involved. LM has said she no longer attempts to intervene and just tries to get people to move along. and LTB-T-039397-23 42. Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 43. Section 23 of the Act states “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.” 44. Although the word “harass” is not defined in the Act, the Board often applies the definition from the Ontario Human Rights Code, which defines “harassment” as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. 45. On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden rests with the Tenant. 46. Here, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord harassed the Tenant or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. The Tenant assert that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of harassment and substantial interference by failing to adequately address her concerns and issues as raised by the Tenant and encouraging other tenants to file complaints about the Tenant. That the Landlord has encouraged a toxic environment of bullying. 47. But what this really appears to be is that the Landlord was not addressing the Tenant’s concerns in the way the Tenant wanted. A tenant does not get to dictate how a landlord addresses an issue or concern and as long the landlord reasonably addresses or investigates the issue, the landlord’s response is not harassment or substantial interference. 48. Here, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord as it is more consistent than the vague allegations provided by the Tenant. Both MK and JW testified about the training that all the Landlord’s staff receive on diversity and inclusion. MK and JW also testified that all complaints are equally investigated, and all tenants are warned, provided notices, and have Board applications pursued if necessary. I am satisfied that the Tenant has not been singled out or targeted by the Landlord or any of the Landlord’s staff. 49. I am also not persuaded by the Tenant’s allegations that the Landlord has convinced their staff or other tenants to surveil her and file complaints. Other than the allegations, the Tenant provided no corroborating evidence that this is the case and not other tenant’s filing complaints of their own free will based on the Tenant’s own admittedly reactive behaviour. 50. I am satisfied that the Landlord has taken reasonable steps to address the Tenant’s concerns in a timely manner and the Tenant is simply unhappy with the answers she is receiving which does not rise to the level of substantial inference or harassment. and LTB-T-039397-23 51. I do accept that these incidents have had an impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit, however I am not persuaded that it is due to the any substantial interference or harassment from the Landlord. 52. As such, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Relief from eviction 53. The Tenant testified that she is on a fixed income and would not be able to afford rent at another rental unit. The Tenant testified that an eviction would further traumatize her more than this whole experience already has. The Tenant testified that she has panic attacks because of this and has fallen behind in her housework. 54. The Landlord’s Representative provided that the incidents have continued even after the N5 notice because the Tenant continues to engage instead of removing herself so the Landlord does not believe a conditional order is appropriate. The Landlord’s Representative provided that the Landlord has taken all reasonable steps to address the issues and nothing has worked so the Landlord is seeking an immediate eviction. 55. Here, I am not satisfied that a conditional order is appropriate. The N5 notice was issued on January 26, 2023, and there was testimony regarding many incidents that occurred after the issuance of the N5 notice. I am not satisfied that the Tenant will be able to adhere to a conditional order given that she has continued to engage in the same or similar behaviours. The Tenant continues to fail to recognize or take accountability for her role in the interactions and how it interferes with other tenants’ reasonable enjoyment and as such I do not see a conditional order being appropriate. 56. However, given the circumstances as presented by the Tenant, I find it fair in the circumstances to postpone eviction until July 31, 2026, to allow the Tenant a little more time to make the necessary arrangements to find alternate living accommodations. 57. As such, I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until July 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated on or before July 31, 2026, then starting August 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord on or after August 1, 2026.
The Tenant shall also pay to the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application. and LTB-T-039397-23
The total amount the Tenant must pay the Landlord is $186.00.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before July 31, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application); and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $318.00 on or before August 10, 2026.

It was undisputed that the Landlord unlawfully increased the rent on July 1, 2024. The Tenant was overcharged $550.00 over 11 months. The Landlord already reimbursed the Tenant $525.00. The Landlord will also be required to pay the Tenant the balance of $25.00.

It was undisputed that the rental unit is one of two residential units located above a store on the main level. There is a shared garbage bin for the two residential units located at the back of the building. The garbage bin needs to be moved to the front near the street for pickup once a week.

The Tenant, [name], testified that upon move in he was told it was his responsibility to move the garbage bin to the front bi-weekly, alternating with the other unit. Later, the Tenant stated that he did not remember a specific instruction to remove the garbage, and that it was not included in the tenancy agreement. The Tenant requested the Landlord to handle the garbage multiple times, which the Landlord failed to do. The Tenant stated he took the garbage to the front for the full duration of the tenancy and was now seeking a rent abatement for this service.

The Landlord testified that it was the Tenant’s responsibility to move the garbage to the front bi-weekly, and that this was communicated at the start of the tenancy. In April 2025, the Tenant decided not to take the garbage to the front anymore. The Landlord responded to the Tenant’s e-mails and arranged for the neighbouring tenant to move the garbage to the front from April 2025 to the end of the tenancy.

Section 20(1) of the Act states that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Ontario Regulation 517/06 provides maintenance standards for landlords. Pursuant to subsection 45(2) of the regulation, it is the Landlord’s responsibility to place the shared garbage container for pick-up in a multi-unit building.

In [name] v. Van, 2009 ONCA 808 (‘Montgomery’), the Court of Appeal found that a landlord may delegate their snow removal responsibilities to a tenant. However, such a clause must constitute a contractual obligation severable from the tenancy agreement in order not to be void. Although Montgomery dealt with snow removal, not garbage, I find that the reasoning is applicable here.

Neither party presented a written tenancy agreement. However, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that they agreed it would be the Tenant’s responsibility to move the garbage to the front of the building on a bi-weekly basis as part of the tenancy agreement. As this provision is part of the tenancy agreement, not a severable contract, it does not meet the requirements of Montgomery and is void under section 3(1) of the Act. Therefore, it was the Landlord’s responsibility to move the garbage bin to the front of the building.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to comply with maintenance standards by failing to move the shared garbage bin to the front of the building. I prefer the Landlord’s testimony over the Tenant’s regarding the arrangements the Landlord made for the garbage removal in April 2025, as the Tenant contradicted himself in his testimony regarding the communications between the parties at the start of the tenancy. I therefore find that the Landlord met his obligations to remove the garbage from May 2025 to the end of the tenancy. I find a rent abatement of $20.00 per month to be appropriate for the bi-weekly garbage removal the Tenant did from May 2024 to April 2025, totalling $240.00.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $318.00. This amount represents: • $25.00 for the return of illegal rent charged. • $240.00 for a rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
