issues: Haimove (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenancy began on or about November 1, 2021, although the Tenant moved out on February 28, 2026.

The Tenant filed a T6 application on May 16, 2025, alleging that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under s.20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (‘the Act’) stemming from problems relating to a cockroach infestation, alleged electrical issues light fixtures and light bulbs issues.

The Tenant served and uploaded to the Portal (TOP) an amended application on December 15, 2025. The application contained further issues alleged regarding a toilet not functioning, a broken fence, and a nonfunctioning microwave, but not all of the above were brought up during this proceeding by the Tenant.
The amendments to the application were granted to proceed at this herein matter, as the majority which dealt with the remedies sought.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not object to the amendments sought to the [name] application

The Tenant was seeking a rent abatement in the amount of $49,581.82. The lawful rent was $4,080.50, the Tenant was further seeking costs to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlord’s pest control contractor in the amount of $14,236.45, out of pocket expenses in the amount of $500.00, as well as the Landlord do the necessary repairs regarding pest control and electrical issues, as well as the Board ordering that Landlord cannot raise the lawful rent until the maintenance issues are remedied, and unspecified general damages, for emotional distress.

The Tenant claims for more than the $50,000.00 the LTB has jurisdiction to order a person to pay under section 207 of the Act. The Tenant testified that the Tenant has agreed to proceed with his application at the LTB understanding that this would result in the extinguishment of his right to file a claim for the matters in issue on this application in the Superior Court of Justice. Testimony and Evidence

The Tenant submitted into evidence various photos and documentary evidence to support the claims in the application and his testimony at the hearing. Pest issue: cockroaches, electrical issue, microwave not functioning

It was the testimony of the Tenant, that on May 14, 2025 the Landlord came to inspect the rental unit, after the Tenant raised concerns of the pest issue, specifically the cockroach infestation, and the Landlord seemed dismissive, regarding the same and the electrical issue, which the Tennat believed was related to the pest issue, as his lightbulbs would not function past a few months and the lighting fixtures seemed to have pest infestation, which could affect the electrical system.

The Tenant further testified on or about May 16, 2025 he was advised that an exterminator or pest technician would attend, this contractor attended on May 19, 2025 and commenced spraying a white substance in the rental unit, and he was not told by the Landlord this would be occurring, There were two more pest treatments, the Tenant believes on or about August 2025 and September 2025, hence there was three treatments over a 4 month span to deal with the pest issue, which was resolved, however the treatments destroyed property in the Tenant’s kitchen and his business products in his basement, as he was running a day care for special needs children and he had to remove and purchase new toys/games, and child related materials, due to the damage caused by the pest treatments. The Tenant provided photographic evidence of kitchen utensils such as plates, pots that had a white film on them as well as various children’s items in his basement. The Tenant further submitted a receipt of various items purchased for his business and alleged these amounted to the claim abovementioned for damaged property. The Tenant further testified to issues with the electrical which an electrical tech was brought and claims there was no issue and further testified to an issue with a microwave not functioning.

On cross examination, the Tenant testified that he told the Landlord in mid May 2025 regarding the pest issue, and that the pest technician/specialist attended on three occasions, and the issue of cockroaches had resolved by September 2025, and that he was told that the had to prepare for the treatment, leave the premises for three hours, and that the treatment was not harmful to kids and his personal belongings.

The Tenant further testified on cross examination that he had not provided time stamped photographs of the damaged property as alleged and the residue left on his kitchen materials and it was inferred by the Landlord’s Legal Representative that the kitchen materials/utensils may simply have needed to be washed, or this white residue could have been soap residue. The Tenant did not have a reasonable response to the questioning by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, other than to say the pest treatment caused the damage, even though he did not have any before or after pictures related to the alleged damaged property.

The Landlord’s testified and provided documentary and photograph evidence with respect to an HVAC service maintenance request on October 30, 2025, where the HVAC tech serviced the furnace, humidifier, and changed the filters, cleaned the furnace and flame sensor, and tested the heating systems, although the Tenant did not testify to this issue, the Landlord testimony is to show there were no issues with pests in the HVAC system.

The Landlord further testified there were three fumigations/pest treatments regarding cockroaches after he had attended the Tenant’s residence regarding another issue and noticed the pest issue, which the Tenant had advised he had under his control by using borax. The Landlord testified he acted swiftly and reasonably related to the issue and the issue was dealt with in two treatments, but a third treatment by the pest control technician was completed and the reporting email was submitted as evidence that no live cockroaches were found on October 24, 2025 which was consistent with the Tenant’s own testimony.

The Landlord further testified there was no electrical issue, and to date there is no issue, it is the Landlord’s understanding the Tenant used less expensive bulbs and further used the incorrect bulbs (non dimmer bulbs, rather than dimmer bulbs), and the electrician advised the Landlord there were no electrical issues, and to his knowledge no issue with the microwave appliance.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted, that in his opinion, the Tenant’s application was simply a feeble attempt to set off approximately $15,000.00 in rent arrears owed to the Landlord via another [name], which remain unpaid as of the date of this proceeding. Analysis and Determinations Section 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence adduced by the Tenant, either in part or taken in its entirety, suffices to meet the burden of proof upon the Tenant to demonstrate that the Landlord has breached his obligations as they pertain to the T6 application. In fact the documentary evidence and testimonies, point to the timely rectification of these issues by the Landlord and or the Landlord’s Agents.

After considering all of the evidence, I cannot find that the Landlord breached s.20 of the Act with respect to the aforementioned issues as alleged by the Tenant. I acknowledge that the presence of some of these issues such as the pest issue as described by the Tenant, would be unpleasant, I find that the Tenant were not able to identify any breach. Based on the testimony before me, I also find that the Landlord acted reasonably following the reporting of the issues by the Tenant. Various experts were contracted, and multiple steps taken in attempts to identify and isolate any cause related to the pest or electrical issue as alleged.

In the matter before me, I find that the Landlord acted reasonably and relied on the various experts contracted to investigate the particular issues in regard to the pest issues of the rental unit, and the electrical issues. As such, the Tenant is not entitled to a remedy for this application.
The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord’s Agent’) substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord’s Agent’) failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 9, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative, Bruce Parsons, the Landlord, the Tenant’s legal representative, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: The rental unit is a townhouse that includes an unfinished basement. The Tenant testified that, notwithstanding its unfinished condition, she regularly used the basement as a playroom for her child and as a workspace for her home office.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed a T2 application about Tenant rights on November 4, 2024, alleging that the Landlord or an agent of the Landlord committed the following breaches of the Act substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
The Tenant also filed a T6 application, alleging that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act.

Section 20 (1) states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Tenant’s evidence regarding maintenance Bathroom Issues

The Tenant testified that in April 2024 she reported several maintenance concerns to the Landlord through maintenance request forms submitted electronically. These concerns included alleged mould beneath the bathtub caulking, mould on the bathroom ceiling, peeling paint on the ceiling, and an ineffective bathroom exhaust fan.

The Tenant testified that mould was present beneath the bathtub caulking and on the bathroom ceiling. However, the Tenant did not provide objective evidence establishing that the substance observed was in fact mould. No inspection report, laboratory testing, expert evidence, or other independent documentation was submitted. Although photographs were provided, photographs alone are insufficient to establish the nature of the condition depicted. On the evidence before me, I am unable to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that the condition constituted mould rather than mildew, staining, or another form of discolouration.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord acknowledged receipt of the maintenance request on April 15, 2024, and advised he would attend the rental unit on April 19, 2024, to inspect the concerns. The Tenant testified that no further action was taken by the Landlord and that she ultimately completed the work herself.

The Tenant testified that she removed and replaced the silicone caulking, treated and repaired the ceiling, and purchased a dehumidifier because she believed the bathroom fan was inadequate. However, the Tenant did not seek reimbursement for these expenditures in her application and provided limited evidence regarding the costs incurred. As such, no monetary remedy is available with respect to these expenses.

The Landlord testified that he did not recall receiving the maintenance request relating to the bathroom issues. However, he acknowledged that after becoming aware of the concerns through the application, he did not investigate or take steps to address them.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord was made aware of the Tenant’s concerns and did not address them within a reasonable period of time. However, the primary remedy sought by the Tenant was an order requiring the Landlord to perform repairs. By the time of the hearing, the Tenant had already completed the work herself, and the conditions complained of no longer existed. Accordingly, that remedy is no longer available and is therefore moot.

The Tenant also requested an order prohibiting the Landlord from increasing the rent. Pursuant to subsection 30(1) of the Act, such a remedy is generally reserved for serious breaches of maintenance obligations. While I accept that the Landlord failed to respond adequately to the Tenant’s concerns, the evidence does not establish a serious maintenance deficiency warranting the extraordinary remedy of prohibiting a rent increase. I therefore decline to grant that relief. Basement Flooding and Repairs

The parties do not dispute that water entered the basement of the rental unit on or about December 30, 2024. The issue before me is whether the Landlord responded reasonably to the problem once notified.

The Tenant notified the Landlord of flooding from a floor drain in the basement laundry area by email on December 30, 2024. The evidence establishes that the Landlord responded within minutes of receiving the notification and arranged for a contractor to attend the property the same day.

The contractor recommended that a plumber be retained. Due to the holiday period, the earliest available attendance by Doyle Plumbing was January 2, 2025. An invoice dated January 2, 2025, confirms that a blocked sewer line was identified and addressed. Further recommendations were made to remove and replace the existing building trap.

The Landlord subsequently retained another plumbing contractor to complete the recommended work. Documentary evidence establishes that additional plumbing repairs were undertaken on January 15, 2025, including replacement of sections of old cast-iron piping with PVC piping. The repair process also involved restoration work in the basement following completion of the plumbing repairs.
The Landlord submitted that all repair work was completed by February 8, 2025. The Tenant confirmed that no further flooding occurred after the repairs were completed.

The Court of Appeal in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, held that the Board must consider the entirety of the circumstances when determining whether a landlord has complied with section 20 of the Act, including whether the landlord responded reasonably to the maintenance problem after becoming aware of it.

Having considered the evidence as a whole, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded to the flooding issue reasonably and within a reasonable period of time. The Landlord arranged for contractors to attend promptly, obtained professional assessments, authorized the recommended repairs, and completed the work within a reasonable timeframe given the nature of the repairs and the holiday season.
Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act with respect to the flooding issue. Quality of Repairs

The Tenant testified that certain restoration work that was performed following the flooding repairs was unsatisfactory. In particular, the Tenant testified that she was required to clean dust and residue, perform additional sanding, repaint portions of the basement wall, and address what she believed were deficient wall repairs.

The Tenant provided an email dated January 31, 2025, identifying several outstanding concerns, including finishing of wall repairs, painting, cleaning of residue, and replacement of damaged stair treads. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not respond to the email.

The Landlord acknowledged that he did not respond to the email, explaining that he was travelling outside Canada at the time and was experiencing communication difficulties. However, he testified that he understood the contractor was nearing completion of the project.

I have considered the parties’ evidence regarding the quality of the repair work. The evidence establishes that the Tenant was dissatisfied with the appearance and finish of certain portions of the basement wall and believed inappropriate materials had been used. The Tenant subsequently elected to remove the material, complete additional finishing work herself, and purchase supplies for that purpose.

Significantly, the Tenant acknowledged in a text message dated February 8, 2025, that she was satisfied with the flooring repairs and that her remaining concerns related primarily to the appearance of the wall repairs.

While I accept that the Tenant was dissatisfied with the aesthetics and finish of certain restoration work, the evidence does not establish that the rental unit was left in a state that contravened section 20 of the Act. The evidence before me demonstrates that the flooding issue was repaired, the underlying cause of the problem was addressed, and the basement was restored to a usable condition.

On the totality of the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the maintenance obligations imposed by section 20 of the Act. Accordingly, the Tenant's T6 application is dismissed. Substantial Interference – T2 Application

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because she was unable to use the basement for approximately one month while repairs arising from the flooding were being completed.

The Tenant testified that she used the unfinished basement as a play area for her child and as a home office. As a result of the flooding and subsequent repair work, she was temporarily unable to use that space.

I accept that the Tenant experienced inconvenience and some loss of use during the repair period. However, not every inconvenience experienced during a tenancy constitutes substantial interference within the meaning of the Act.

The evidence establishes that the basement was unfinished and that the interruption was temporary while necessary repairs were being undertaken to address a plumbing and flooding issue. The Landlord responded reasonably to the flooding, retained contractors, and completed the repairs within a reasonable period of time. The work was necessary to restore the rental unit following the flooding. There was no evidence before me that the work was carried out unreasonably or that it could reasonably have been completed in another manner that would have significantly reduced the impact on the Tenant.

Pursuant to section 8(3) of Ontario Regulation 516/06, interference resulting from necessary work does not constitute substantial interference with a tenant's reasonable enjoyment unless the tenant establishes that the work was carried out in an unreasonable manner or could have been undertaken in a less intrusive way. On the evidence before me, the Tenant has not established either circumstance. In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the temporary loss of use of the unfinished basement amounted to substantial interference with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the temporary loss of use of the unfinished basement amounted to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit contrary to the Act. Conclusion

The Tenant has not established that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act in a manner warranting relief under the T6 application, nor has the Tenant established substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment under the T2 application.
Accordingly, the Tenant's T2 and T6 applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 application is dismissed. July 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for purchaser's use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (“Elkins”), the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

There was no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenants the N12 notice of termination for purchaser’s use with a termination date of October 31, 2023. The first N12 notice, served August 11, 2023, had an invalid termination date and the Landlord served a second N12 notice on August 18, 2023 with the correct termination date.

I find based on the testimony of Tenant [name] Parsalidas (AP), the Tenants prepared to vacate the rental unit as a result of receiving the N12 notice. AP testified that over a period of time, they looked for another unit but found that they were unable to afford increased rents in the downtown area. They began to move some of their smaller items to their parents’ homes by car, to change addresses for identification, to notify their employers of address changes, and to prepare themselves to move. They submitted evidence that they booked a UHaul truck in early October to move the final items at the end of the month.

There was no evidence that the Tenants had already planned to move or that they would have done so had they not received the N12 notice. I therefore find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving the N12 notice of termination.

The Tenants did not prove the following requirements in subsection 57(1)(b): that the purchaser did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated, and that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. Tenants’ evidence

AP testified that the Landlord sent the Tenants an email on August 11, 2023, attaching the first N12 notice. In that email, the Landlord that for financial reasons, he couldn’t keep the rental unit (DOC 8322177, p. 2]. A new N12 notice was served with a correct date of termination on August 18, 2023. After speaking with the LTB helpline, AP testified that he asked the Landlord by email for a copy of the Agreement of Purchase and Sale on October 16, 2023.

AP testified that he spoke with the Landlord’s real estate agent on October 17, 2023 and that he was told that the rental unit was never for sale. Even though the agent offered for them to stay in the unit, they had already finalized their arrangements to move out as it was only two weeks prior to the termination date on the N12 notice.

AP spoke with the Landlord on October 23, 2023, at which time the Landlord told him that he jointly owned the rental unit with his brother [name] (listed as the Purchaser on the N12 notice). AP testified that the Landlord said that the plan for the brother to move in fell through and that he was not moving in.

AP further testified that in his opinion, the N12 notice was served in bad faith and the Purchaser never intended to move into the rental unit since it was listed for rent in late November. The Tenants submitted several rental listings for the rental unit dated approximately between November 24 and 29, 2023. The Tenants also submitted a further rental listing for January 14, 2025 into evidence. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord testified that he and his brother [name] [name] (“Samnit”) co-owned two condominium units in the same residential complex: the rental unit and Unit 1209. The Landlord was responsible for everything with respect to the rental unit, including all interactions with the Tenants. The Tenants never had contact with Samnit and were unaware that he co-owned the property. Samnit had exclusive responsibility for Unit 1209, a slightly smaller unit with lower carrying costs.

For financial reasons and because Samnit was getting married, the brothers agreed to exchange responsibilities for the two units, and that Samnit and his new wife (with two household incomes) would move into the larger, more expensive rental unit after their wedding. The first (incorrect) N12 notice was served August 11, 2023 based on the brothers’ verbal agreement.

Samnit got married on August 12, 2023, and it was not until August 23, 2023 that they finalized a written agreement (“the Agreement” – DOC 8321317, p. 4) which codified their verbal agreement. The Agreement stated in part: 1.1 Property 1: Sam shall assume full ownership, control, and responsibility for Property 1 [the rental unit], including all associated liabilities, pending the successful refinancing of Property 1. 1.2 Property 2: Sehaj shall assume full ownership, control, and responsibility for Property 2 [Unit 1209], including all associated liabilities, pending the successful refinancing of Property 2. 1.3 The actual transfer of ownership of Property 1 and Property 2 from one Party to the other shall occur only after each respective Property has been refinanced in a manner acceptable to both Parties.

The Landlord testified that he and Samnit chose to enter into the Agreement because a full legal title transfer would have cost over $5,000.00. Because they were brothers with a good relationship, they felt that the Agreement was sufficient to cover their intentions for the properties. The actual legal title transfer never occurred due to lack of suitable refinancing. He testified that the termination of the tenancy on October 31, 2023, Samnit took over all responsibility for the rental unit.

The Landlord explained that he checked Reason 2, Purchaser’s Use, on the N12 notice because Reason 1 did not apply, and Reason 2 was the closest option which reflected the brothers’ arrangement and intention for Samnit to move in. He listed himself on the N12 notice as the only Landlord because the Tenants had never dealt in any way with Samnit and would not have known who he was if he was listed as a Landlord. He testified that he served the N12 notice for the sole purpose of giving effect to the Agreement so that Samnit could occupy the rental unit after his marriage.
The Landlord testified that his understanding at the time he served the N12 notice was that Samnit and his wife would move into the rental unit and occupy it for more than one year.

In cross-examination, he agreed that during the October 23, 2023 phone call with the Tenants [DOC 4844513], he told them that he co-owned the rental unit with Samnit, the “deal fell apart” and that they would likely sell the unit. He explained that Samnit and his new wife were “back-and-forth” about whether living in the rental unit would be convenient for his wife’s job, but the Landlord believed at the time the N12 notice was served that they intended to move in.

He testified that Samnit and his wife moved into the rental unit on November 2 or 3, 2023 and he was aware of this because he saw them packing and helped them move in. He visited them numerous times after they moved in because they were family.

Samnit [name] testified that the property report dated June 2, 2024 (at page 27 of the Tenant’s documents) which shows that both brothers still have legal ownership of the rental unit is correct. Title was not transferred because suitable anticipated refinancing did not occur. He confirmed the Landlord’s testimony that the intention of the Agreement was to capture the brothers’ intention that after Samnit was married, he would take over the rental unit, and the Landlord would take over Unit 1209. He confirmed the Landlord’s testimony that they did not do a formal legal transfer of title in order to save costs.

Samnit also testified that he and his new wife had discussions immediately before moving into the rental unit about whether it would be suitable, but in the end, they moved into the rental unit in early November 2023 after the Tenants vacated. He no longer lives in the rental unit but lived in the unit for over one year and did not list it for rent until January 2025. It is currently rented.

Samnit testified that he authorized the real estate listings in late November 2023 because he and his wife were having difficulty deciding whether they could remain in the rental unit since his wife was working in Georgetown and finding the commute difficult. He stated that it was an “emotional decision” to list the unit for rent, but they only left the posting up for a few days before taking it down, and after reflection they remained in the unit.

The Landlord submitted letters into evidence (pages 30-32 of the Landlord’s book of documents) from a company which stated they provided services to set up Samnit’s home office on November 7, 2023. He also submitted letters from kitchen cabinet installers who stated that they installed cabinets in May 2024 and that Samnit and his wife were living in the unit in September 2024, and from painters who stated that Samnit and his wife were living in the unit in November and December 2023. Analysis

As there was no dispute that the Landlord served the N12 notice, and as I have found that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving the N12 notice, only two elements of the test remain.

The Tenants have the burden of proof to establish that, on a balance of probabilities, the person on the N12 notice did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated and that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

As I noted at the hearing, had the Landlord brought an L2 application based on the N12 notice, it would not have been successful. The fundamental issue is that the Landlord did not name both legal owners as Landlords on the N12 notice. The N12 notice was effectively intended to be for the use of a Landlord (Samnit) rather than a purchaser. There was no Agreement of Purchase and Sale at the time that the N12 notice was served, and Samnit was not a purchaser, but the brothers had agreed to transfer responsibility for the unit and for Samnit to live there.

The Landlord’s testimony was clear, however, that in his mind, the Tenants would not have known who Samnit was, so he didn’t name him as a Landlord. Reason 1 on the N12 notice did not apply to the situation as he understood it, because he, the Landlord, did not intend to occupy the unit himself.
Whether or not the N12 notice was valid or a Landlord application based upon it would have been successful is not relevant to the current application except in the context of assessing good faith.

The Landlord and Samnit provided direct testimony that after the Tenants vacated the unit and turned over keys on October 31, 2023, Samnit and his wife moved into the rental unit in early November. Despite the temporary advertisements, they did not move out of the rental unit until early 2025. The Landlord submitted documentary evidence that offers some third-party support to the claim that Samnit resided in the rental unit, but the Landlord did not call witnesses to testify about the letters. I am, however, able to accept these documents as hearsay evidence and can accord the evidence some weight, although the authors were not available for cross-examination. The Tenants did not raise any evidence to challenge the truth of the content of the letters.

The Tenants rely on the rental listings from late November 2023 as evidence of bad faith but agreed on cross-examination that they have no evidence of how long the listings were active or whether the advertisements resulted in a rental.

Samnit’s explanation of why the rental unit was advertised for rent in late November 2023 was plausible and there was no evidence to challenge this version of events. It is not relevant that the unit was re-rented in January 2025, as this was more than one year after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

The Tenants did not lead evidence to counter the Landlord’s evidence that Samnit moved into the rental unit and resided in the unit. The mere suspicion that he did not move in or live in the unit is not evidence, and I find that based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, it is more likely than not that Samnit did move into the rental unit and reside there. I therefore find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in good faith.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: For the reasons explained below, the Tenant’s application must fail as the named Landlord in this application does not meet the definition of landlord as defined by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).
The Tenant submitted a lease (DOC-8030068) which names Thushatha [name] (“TK”) as the landlord. The Tenant testified she paid the lawful monthly rent to the e-mail address belonging to TK.

The Tenant named [name] (“SS”) as Landlord to this application because, throughout the tenancy, SS: 1. Posted the rental unit ad on Facebook; 2. Advised the Tenant when non-tenants would be entering the unit (i.e. technicians, house tours, etc.); 3. Accepted maintenance complaints from the Tenant to be addressed; and
Sent reminders regarding utility costs due. 4. It is undisputed that SS did not stay at the residential complex more than a few times between September 2025 and April 2026.
SS testified she is the niece of TK. Because TK lives in Toronto, SS spoke with tenants of the residential complex on TK’s behalf. Analysis

Subsection 2(1) of the Act provides a definition for landlord: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”)
The submissions provided by the Tenant confirm that SS acted as an employee for TK. I find that TK is the Landlord for the rental unit and not SS.

Based on the submissions made at the hearing, there is enough evidence to deduce that the Act does apply to the relationship between the Tenant and TK. However, since SS is named as the Landlord in this application and not TK, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply to the Tenant and the named Landlord to this application. July 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  entered the rental unit illegally.  altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.  withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.  did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.  did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: At the outset of the heari ng, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue about whether the Act applies to the tenancy. The Landlord claimed that the Act does not apply because it was living accommodation where the Tenant was required to share kitchen or bathroom facilities with the Landlord, who owned the unit, and the Landlord also lived in the building: see ss. 5(i), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

I heard evidence from the parties about t he preliminary issue on November 16, 2023. There was dispute as to whether the Tenant was required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord. The Landlord said there was only one kitchen in the house, and both the Landlord and Tenant used it. The Landlord said the home has 4 bathrooms, which were also shared by the Landlord and Tenant. The Tenant said there were two kitchens in the house, she was not required to share a kitchen with the Landlord, and the basement bathroom was only shared by basement tenants, and not the Landlord. Neither party presented any documentary evidence relative to this preliminary issue, such as photographs of the unit to support their respect evidence about how many kitchens were in the house.

I reserved my decision on this issue, but proceeded to hear evidence from the parties about the Tenant’s allegation that she was illegally locked out of the unit. The intention was to conclude the hearing about this issue, as the matter had been scheduled in an urgent hearing block because of the allegation about an illegal lockout.

After this evidence was complete, the Tenant informed me that she does not wish to seek repossession of the unit, and seeks only compensation as a remedy on the application. Because of this, the hearing was adjourned, and I directed the parties to prepare to present further and better evidence relative to the preliminary issue about whether the Act applies on the next hearing date, because I found the evidence before me to be inadequate to make a determination. I suggested that photographs and oral evidence from another person who occupied the house during the relevant time may be helpful.

When the matter returned before me on January 10, 2024, neither party had served or filed any additional disclosure, and no additional witness was present to give evidence. It became apparent that the parties were not ready to proceed with the hearing on the balance of the merits of the application. I orally directed the parties to serve and file the documentary evidence they intended to rely on at least 7 days before the next hearing date. Both parties were to serve each other by email. This direction was documented in the adjournment sheet, which was accessible to the parties through the Portal (‘TOP’) (DOC-2562750).

When the matter returned before me on June 12, 2024, the Landlord had filed a copy of a lease agreement, but nothing in the lease was helpful relative to the determination about whether the Act applies. The hearing was again adjourned because it became apparent that the hearing relative to the preliminary issue was not proceeding in an expeditious manner, and because there was inadequate time remaining in the hearing block to complete the hearing.

Interim order LTB-T-042614-23-IN was issued on July 2, 2024. This interim order included specific directions that the Tenant serve and file all documentary evidence she intended to rely on by July 31, 2024. The Tenant was to serve the Landlord by email. The Landlord was also ordered to disclose any documentary evidence on which she intended to rely by July 31, 2024. The order specifically cautioned that if the parties failed to comply with these deadlines, then I may refuse to accept evidence not disclosed as required.
On November 4, 2025, the hearing was adjourned for scheduling overflow.
On June 10, 2026, I heard the balance of the Tenant’s application Preliminary Issues Does the Act Apply?
When a party argues that the Act does not apply because a rental unit is exempt from the Act, the party alleging that the Act does not apply bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), paras 44-46.

The Landlord’s evidence was that the rental unit is a room in the basement of a house. The house has 5 total bedrooms, including 3 upstairs and 2 in the basement. The Landlord lived in the house during the relevant period as her primary residence in one of the 3 upstairs bedrooms. She said that she had also rented out the other rooms in the house, including the other two upstairs bedrooms, and the two basement bedrooms (one of which was the Tenant’s unit).
The Landlord said she owns the house, together with her partner.
The Landlord said the house has only one kitchen, which she shared with the Tenant and the other tenants. She said that the house has 4 bathrooms, which were also shared.
The Landlord’s evidence was that the only kitchen was in the basement, and there was no kitchen on the main floor.

On cross-examination, the Landlord said she does not cook breakfast, and she would sometimes go to the kitchen in the basement to prepare lunch at about 1:00 p.m. The Landlord also said she had cookware stored in a cupboard in the basement.

The Landlord said she has an “extra” fridge upstairs, but also kept items in basement fridge. The Landlord said she had a microwave upstairs, but there was no stove or oven. The Landlord said the stove/oven had been moved to the basement before the Tenant moved into the unit.

The Landlord said that she would only use the basement kitchen when necessary, and often used a barbecue. She said that while the Tenant lived in the unit, she used the basement kitchen about 3 times per week, on average.

The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord lived in the house during the relevant time, but said there was a kitchen on the main floor and one in the basement. She said that the main floor had a full kitchen, including a dishwasher, microwave, oven/stove, and fridge, and that she did not share a kitchen with the Landlord.
The Tenant also said she shared a bathroom with the other basement tenant, but not with the Landlord. The Tenant said that only the washer and dryer were shared by everyone living in the house.

Neither party presented any relevant documentary, photographic, video, or other evidence to support their respective evidence on this preliminary issue. Despite evidence that a number of other people lived in the unit during the relevant time, neither party brought any of those other people to act as witnesses, and neither party requested a summons to compel any other person to attend as a witness.

Both parties’ evidence relative to whether the Tenant was required to share kitchen or bathroom facilities with the Landlord was internally consistent. Neither party has satisfied me that their evidence on this issue ought to be favoured over the other party’s. Because of this, I find that the Landlord has failed to discharge her burden of proof: see [name]Gibbs, 2019 ONSC 3355 (CanLII), para 27
The Act applies. Disclosure

Despite the previous oral directions and interim order relative to disclosure, referred to above, as of June 10, 2026 neither party had served or filed any documentary evidence (aside from the copy of the tenancy agreement previously filed by the Landlord).

On June 10, 2026, the Tenant said that she needs more time to serve and file documents. She said that she has documents she wants to rely on, but has been too overwhelmed to disclose those documents in advance of the hearing.
The Tenant also said that police are withholding evidence from her.

This application was filed on May 29, 2023, more than three years before the June 10, 2026 hearing. The Tenant could have served and filed any documentary evidence that she wishes to rely on at any time after May 29, 2023.

Further, the Tenant was given specific direction that she could serve the Landlord with any documents she intends to rely on by email to a specifically identified email address. This direction was initially given orally on January 10, 2024, documented in an adjournment sheet that has been available to the parties in TOP since January 11, 2024, and again by interim order, issued on July 30, 2024.

The Tenant has had more than 3 years since the application was filed; approximately 2.5 years since the January 10, 2024 oral direction and January 11, 2024 adjournment sheet, and approximately 23 months since the interim order was issued to serve and file her documentary evidence.

There was also no cogent explanation from the Tenant as to why the time and direction already provided was inadequate, or why it would be reasonable to grant yet another adjournment to allow her to serve and file documentary evidence.
The Tenant also did not present any cogent evidence to establish that police are improperly withholding any relevant evidence from the Tenant.

The hearing has already been adjourned several times to give the parties a chance to organize their evidence and submissions. I declined to consider another adjournment in the circumstances. Parties are not entitled to repeated adjournments to prepare for hearings, particularly when the parties have not taken advantage of the years since this application was commenced to serve and file documents. Adequacy of Particulars

When a party commences an application before the LTB, the application must contain details that are sufficient for the other side to know the case to be met, and so they can be able to prepare to respond to the allegations being made. These details should include dates and times together with a detailed description of the alleged offensive conduct: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] OJ No 5931, paras 10 & 12; Tugui v. Miltowne Creek Investments Inc., 2021 CanLII 146888 (ON LTB).

In the application, the Tenant alleges: a) The Landlord entered the rental unit after the Tenant went on vacation to Saskatchewan on April 4, 2023, and packed up and moved all the Tenant’s belongings out of the rental unit; b) When the Tenant arrived home on [name] y 10, 2023, the locks had been changed and the Tenant was locked out of the unit. Police attended but were not able to get the Tenant back into the unit, and the Landlord had stolen the Tenant’s belongings; c) The Landlord “… continually took out light bulbs. Unlpugged dehumidifier/heater against numerous requests. Continued to enter room without 24 hour written notice.” (sic); d) The Landlord “[y]elled, threatened to call police on my guests if they didn’t leave. Wouldn’t allow me to have anyone at house. Continually moved my personal belongings around kitchen, bathroom and dining area” (sic); and e) The Landlord “withheld me from my home. My belongings have been stolen from me and I was put on the street. [The Landlord] made agreement with police to move my belongings back to me and has not made any attempt and has me blocked from calling her” (sic).

There is no issue with the adequacy of particulars relative to the allegations about the illegal lockout, recited at paragraph 34(a) and (b) above. Paragraph 34(e) is essentially a repetition of those allegations.

I asked the parties for submissions as to whether the allegations recited at paragraph 34(b) and paragraph 34(c) contain adequate particulars. The parties’ submissions on this issue were not particularly helpful to making a determination about the adequacy of the particulars with respect to these allegations.
I find that the allegations recited at paragraph 34(b) and 34(c) contain inadequate particulars. The allegations in these paragraphs are relatively vague and do not include any dates or timelines.

As an example, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord “… cont inued to enter room without 24 hour written notice”. Since there are no dates related to this allegation, the Landlord would not know the case to be met, and could not reasonably prepare to respond to the allegations. If there were dates attached to the allegation, then the Landlord would be able to look at her records, find if she entered the unit on the relevant day, if she gave a 24-hour notice of entry, and/or if she was even home at the time.
Without dates, the Landlord cannot reasonably be expected to know the case that she has to meet.
Since these allegations contain inadequate particulars, I dismissed the application as it relates to these allegations. Merits of the Application
I heard evidence about the alleged illegal lockout on November 16, 2023.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on February 1, 2023.

On April 4, 2023, the Tenant went to Saskatchewan, and returned to the unit on May 10, 2023. Upon her return, she went to the house but her key did not work. She left her suitcase in the garage and went to a friend’s house.
The Tenant went back to the house the next day, but her suitcase was gone and her key still did not work. The Tenant tried phoning and emailing the Landlord, but could not get in contact with her.

Eventually, the Landlord pulled into the driveway, and told the Tenant to get into the car. The Tenant told the Landlord she had called police, and the Landlord said to call them back to meet at a different address. The Landlord drove to another address, where police met the Landlord and Tenant.

The Tenant’s personal property was in a garage at this address. The Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord said at the time that the Tenant was not stable and she did not want the Tenant at the residential complex. The Landlord had changed the lock on the door giving access to the residential complex, and did not offer the Tenant a replacement key.

The Landlord acknowledged at the November 16, 2023 hearing that she changed the lock and there was no order of the LTB terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant. The lock was not changed pursuant to a lawful eviction procedure involving the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff).

When asked for final submissions at the June 10, 2026 hearing, the Landlord said that the tenancy ending pursuant to an N11 agreement, disputed that the Tenant was illegally locked out, and said the application ought to be dismissed.

This change in the Landlord’s position is confounding. The Landlord did not lead any evidence that the parties ever signed an N11 agreement, and never served and filed a copy of an N11 agreement where the parties agreed to end the tenancy. It strains credulity to suggest that the Landlord decided to initially acknowledge she changed the lock in the absence of an LTB order or a process involving the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff), would not mention that there was an agreement to end the tenancy at any other point across 5 hearing dates, and would not serve and file a copy of the N11 agreement.
I reject the Landlord’s assertion that the parties signed an N11 agreement.

The Landlord illegally locked the Tenant out of the rental unit by changing the locking system on the door giving entry to the residential complex during the Tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without offering a replacement key, contrary to s. 24 of the Act: s. 24, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

In the application, the Tenant sought a rent abatement of $5,850.00; $9,350.00 for the cost to repair or replace damaged, destroyed, or missing personal property; $4,800.00 for rent differential ($400.00 x 12 months); $3,365.00 for moving and storage expenses; $950.00 for out-of-pocket expenses; and $5,000.00 for general compensation.

While the burden of proof was born by the Landlord relative to the issue of whether the Act applies, the Tenant bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities to prove the allegations in her application, and this includes the requirement to prove entitlement to the remedies sought.

The Tenant was given the opportunity to present evidence relevant to the remedies being sought on June 10, 2026. The Tenant did not present any cogent evidence based on which I can determine what, if any, personal property of the Tenant was lost, damaged, or destroyed, or what cost was incurred by the Tenant to repair or replace that property; what rent was paid for the new living accommodation the Tenant moved to after being locked out of the unit, or how the new accommodation compared to the rental unit (relative to the claim for rent differential); what, if any moving or storage expenses were incurred by the Tenant; or what, if any, other out-of-pocket expenses were incurred by the Tenant.

A rent abatement is a remedy premised on the concept that if a person pays 100% of the rent for a rental unit, they ought to receive 100% of the value of what is paid for. An abatement is intended to account for the proportion of the value of is paid for that a tenant did not receive because of a landlord’s breach of the Act.

The Tenant would, of course, be entitled to a rent abatement of 100% for any period for which she paid rent that was after the day the Landlord changed the locks, however, there was no cogent evidence as to what, if any period the Tenant had paid rent for that was after the lock was changed.

It is clear from the Tenant’s evidence that being locked out of the unit was understandably very distressing for her. The Landlord locked her out of the unit without legal justification, and the Tenant then had to quickly and unexpectedly move her belongings, and find other living accommodation. The Tenant said that there were some specific items she lost in this process that cannot be ascribed monetary value, including artwork made by her mother, her father’s ashes, and baby pictures.

The LTB has found in other cases involving illegal lockouts that it is appropriate to order general compensation to account for the inherent indignity in having one’s home taken away, as well as the time, effort, frustration, and stress involved in unexpectedly having to arrange for food and accommodation while seeking new accommodation, as well as the inconvenience and displacement caused in this type of situation. The amount the LTB has generally awarded for illegal lockouts is $2,500.00: see, for example, HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), para 35-36, and [name] v. Tahir, 2025 ONLTB 94190 (CanLII), para 51.

While the $2,500.00 general compensation award is not automatic, I do not find that either party has established that the lockout had an unusually minimal or significant impact on the Tenant, and I therefore find this to be an appropriate amount of compensation.
The Tenant paid $53.00 to file this application and is entitled to recover this amount.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $2,553.00.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2, 553.00 for general compensation and costs.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by August 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $3,825.33

The Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance and repair obligations under the Act. The Landlord did not respond in a timely manner to the Tenants’ complaints of mould in the kitchen and bathrooms of the rental unit. The Landlord also did not repair the damage in the kitchen pipe sink.

The Tenant relies largely on the same factual allegations in their T2 application, alleging that the Landlord’s response to these issues substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and harassed the Tenant by making threats.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that, when the tenancy began on March 5, 2024, he noticed the presence of mould in the rental unit. the Tenant testified that he advised the Landlord of his concern on March 6, 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord hired a contractor attend around November 2024 but there was nothing done. The Tenant testified the mould was visible in the kitchen and bathroom. Since there were no steps taken, the Tenant called the City of Brampton on December 5, 2024. After inspecting the property, the city of Brampton issued an order on January 23, 2025. The Tenant submitted a copy of the order and a letter from the By- law office dated stating the sections of the By-law that has not been complied among some of the items were: rotten kitchen countertop and [name]. The letter indicates that inspection noted mould in the kitchen and bathroom. The order states that Landlord has until March 31, 2025, to comply. The Tenant therefore proved the presence of mould at the property.

The basis of the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord harassed him is based on that the Landlord authorized a collections agency to collect a debt owed by the Tenant to the Landlord. He testified that Landlord harassed him by filing with Front Lobby a collection agency in regard to the Tenant not paying rent and other lease charges. The Tenant testified he received emails from this company on December 27, 2024, January 2, January 28, 2025, and February 26, 2025.

The Landlord testified that the condition of the unit of the unit was good when the Tenant moved in. He testified that the Tenant told him of the issue in March, and he never mentioned it again. After which, the Tenant provided 60 days notice on at the end of August 2024 to move out by October 2024. As such, he did not address the maintenance issues. He testified that he did try to enter the unit along with the city inspector and provided 24-hour notice around January 2025, but the Tenant refused the Landlord entry and only allowed the city inspector to enter his unit.

He submitted that the Tenant did ask to do the repairs himself, but the Landlord wanted to use his own contractors. The Landlord also testified that he was also afraid to enter the Tenant’s unit because of safety issues but did not identify any specific incidents that would entail it would be a safety issue. The Landlord ultimately testified that after the Tenant moved out on March 22, 2025, he began the repair work, and the issues were fixed as of May 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute that he used a collection agency to collect debt owed by the Tenant. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I find the Landlord is in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. I say this because I find that the Landlord did not take any steps to address the Tenant’s complaint and investigate his complaints. The Landlord testified that once the Tenant complained of the maintenance issues, he waited until the Tenant moved out to begin repairs. The Property Standards Order is clear evidence that the Landlord failed to comply with a safety, housing or maintenance standard as required by subsection 20(1). The fact that the Landlord did not take appropriate steps to address the issue until the Property Standards Order was issued—almost nine months after the Tenant identified the issue to the Landlord—resulted in the Landlord breaching subsection 20(1) of the RTA.

There is overlap between subsection 20(1) and section 22 of the RTA. A breach by a landlord of subsection 20(1) can result in a substantial interference with a tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises. In this case, I am satisfied that the failure of the Landlord to react in a timely manner to the issues raised by the Tenant substantially interfered with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit insofar as the Tenant was deprived of the use and enjoyment of the unit because the Landlord failed to comply with subsection 20(1) of the RTA.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period of March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. This finding contributes to the total rent abatement calculated below.

Seeking recovery of a debt is clearly not harassment. No evidence presented by the Tenant suggests that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable in the circumstances. It is the Tenant’s obligation to prove the merits of their case on a balance of probabilities, and he has failed to do so.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. The Tenant’s application must, therefore, be dismissed. Remedies Rent Abatement

With respect to the issue of mould and kitchen pipe sink, the Tenant sought a $13,875.00 rent abatement, at 100% rent abatement for 9 months. I considered the Tenant’s testimony that the mould made the Tenant sick. However, the Tenant did not provide any medical documentary evidence to prove that is the case. In this case, I find the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement is not reasonable. However, it is evident that the presence of mould and issue the kitchen faucet has interfered with the Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the basement for all usual purposes.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if the tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of the services; and should a tenant receive any reduction in services, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support how the Tenant arrived at the numerical figure of 36% so I must consider the appropriate method to calculate a fair and reasonable value of the rent abatement. I find a 36% rent abatement for the 383-day period is excessive as I find that the space, while potentially uncomfortable and unsanitary due to the mould and the kitchen faucet was in disrepair, it was not fully unusable. Therefore, based on similar circumstances from other matters, I find that a 15% rent abatement is fair and reasonable, meaning the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $3,777.33. This amount represents a 15% abatement of the daily compensation for the period March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. Daily compensation is calculated as ($2,000.00 x 12)/365 = $65.75.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,825.33. This amount represents: • $3,777.33 for a rent abatement for the period ending March 22, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
