issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. The amount of $3,825.33 is set-off against the amount still owing by the Tenant to the Landlord under order LTB-L- 0047232-25, issued by the Board April 28, 2025.

The Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance and repair obligations under the Act. The Landlord did not respond in a LTB-T-042715-25-AM timely manner to the Tenants’ complaints of mould in the kitchen and bathrooms of the rental unit. The Landlord also did not repair the damage in the kitchen pipe sink.

The Tenant relies largely on the same factual allegations in their T2 application, alleging that the Landlord’s response to these issues substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and harassed the Tenant by making threats.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that, when the tenancy began on March 5, 2024, he noticed the presence of mould in the rental unit. the Tenant testified that he advised the Landlord of his concern on March 6, 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord hired a contractor attend around November 2024 but there was nothing done. The Tenant testified the mould was visible in the kitchen and bathroom. Since there were no steps taken, the Tenant called the City of Brampton on December 5, 2024. After inspecting the property, the city of Brampton issued an order on January 23, 2025. The Tenant submitted a copy of the order and a letter from the By- law office dated stating the sections of the By-law that has not been complied among some of the items were: rotten kitchen countertop and [name]. The letter indicates that inspection noted mould in the kitchen and bathroom. The order states that Landlord has until March 31, 2025, to comply. The Tenant therefore proved the presence of mould at the property.

The basis of the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord harassed him is based on that the Landlord authorized a collections agency to collect a debt owed by the Tenant to the Landlord. He testified that Landlord harassed him by filing with Front Lobby a collection agency in regard to the Tenant not paying rent and other lease charges. The Tenant testified he received emails from this company on December 27, 2024, January 2, January 28, 2025, and February 26, 2025.

The Landlord testified that the condition of the unit of the unit was good when the Tenant moved in. He testified that the Tenant told him of the issue in March, and he never mentioned it again. After which, the Tenant provided 60 days notice on at the end of August 2024 to move out by October 2024. As such, he did not address the maintenance issues. He testified that he did try to enter the unit along with the city inspector and provided 24-hour notice around January 2025, but the Tenant refused the Landlord entry and only allowed the city inspector to enter his unit.

He submitted that the Tenant did ask to do the repairs himself, but the Landlord wanted to use his own contractors. The Landlord also testified that he was also afraid to enter the Tenant’s unit because of safety issues but did not identify any specific incidents that would entail it would be a safety issue. The Landlord ultimately testified that after the Tenant moved out on March 22, 2025, he began the repair work, and the issues were fixed as of May 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute that he used a collection agency to collect debt owed by the Tenant. Analysis LTB-T-042715-25-AM

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I find the Landlord is in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. I say this because I find that the Landlord did not take any steps to address the Tenant’s complaint and investigate his complaints. The Landlord testified that once the Tenant complained of the maintenance issues, he waited until the Tenant moved out to begin repairs. The Property Standards Order is clear evidence that the Landlord failed to comply with a safety, housing or maintenance standard as required by subsection 20(1). The fact that the Landlord did not take appropriate steps to address the issue until the Property Standards Order was issued—almost nine months after the Tenant identified the issue to the Landlord—resulted in the Landlord breaching subsection 20(1) of the RTA.

There is overlap between subsection 20(1) and section 22 of the RTA. A breach by a landlord of subsection 20(1) can result in a substantial interference with a tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises. In this case, I am satisfied that the failure of the Landlord to react in a timely manner to the issues raised by the Tenant substantially interfered with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit insofar as the Tenant was deprived of the use and enjoyment of the unit because the Landlord failed to comply with subsection 20(1) of the RTA.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period of March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. This finding contributes to the total rent abatement calculated below.

Seeking recovery of a debt is clearly not harassment. No evidence presented by the Tenant suggests that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable in the circumstances. It is the Tenant’s obligation to prove the merits of their case on a balance of probabilities, and he has failed to do so.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. The Tenant’s application must, therefore, be dismissed. Remedies Rent Abatement

With respect to the issue of mould and kitchen pipe sink, the Tenant sought a $13,875.00 rent abatement, at 100% rent abatement for 9 months. I considered the Tenant’s testimony that the mould made the Tenant sick. However, the Tenant did not provide any medical documentary evidence to prove that is the case. In this case, I find the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement is not reasonable. However, it is evident that the presence of mould and LTB-T-042715-25-AM issue the kitchen faucet has interfered with the Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the basement for all usual purposes.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if the tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of the services; and should a tenant receive any reduction in services, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support how the Tenant arrived at the numerical figure of 36% so I must consider the appropriate method to calculate a fair and reasonable value of the rent abatement. I find a 36% rent abatement for the 383-day period is excessive as I find that the space, while potentially uncomfortable and unsanitary due to the mould and the kitchen faucet was in disrepair, it was not fully unusable. Therefore, based on similar circumstances from other matters, I find that a 15% rent abatement is fair and reasonable, meaning the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $3,777.33. This amount represents a 15% abatement of the daily compensation for the period March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. Daily compensation is calculated as ($2,000.00 x 12)/365 = $65.75.
The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Set-off

The Landlord raised that he filed a L1 application with the Board and obtained an order against the Tenant, file no. LTB-L-004732-25 (the ‘L1 Order’). In the L1 Order, I note that the Tenant was ordered to pay the Tenant $8,157.21. The Tenant filed a request to review of the order. However, that request was denied and so the L1 Order stands.

The Landlord requested that any rent abatement ordered be set off by the amount owing to the Landlord under the L1 Order. If granted, the set-off would essentially allow the Tenant to reduce the arrears claim by using the rent abatement the Landlord owes to the Tenant.

This approach is consistent with the Divisional Court’s decision in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 which directs the Board to set off any amount one party owes against the amount owing by the other party.

The Board cannot ignore an order, especially one of its own orders, for the payment of money that remains outstanding and is obligated to apply the doctrine of set-off. As such, the amount owing to the Tenant shall be deducted from the amount owing to the Landlord as ordered below.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,825.33. This amount represents: LTB-T-042715-25-AM • $3,777.33 for a rent abatement for the period ending March 22, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The amount of $3,825.33 owing from the Landlord to the Tenant for rent abatement and the costs of filing this application pursuant to this order shall be set-off against the previous amount owed by the Tenant to the Landlord pursuant to Order LTB-L- 004732-25 issued on April 28, 2025. July 3, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] [name] (a.k.a. [name] Poscente) (the 'Landlords ') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’). This T2 Application was heard by videoconference on March 23, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlords attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant filed their T2 Application with the Board on July 29, 2022.
The T2 Application was originally scheduled to be heard on April 4, 2024, and subsequently adjourned five (5) times between April 4, 2024, and January 15, 2026.
Pursuant to the interim order LTB -T-042775-22-IN3, issued on January 28, 2026, the appropriate respondents and named Landlords were found to be [name] and [name] [name] (a.k.a. [name] Poscente).
At the conclusion of the hearing on March 23, 2026, the parties were directed to submit to the Board their written closing submissions, in accordance with the Endorsement dated March 24, 2026.

The written submissions provided by the Tenant on April 10, 2026 ( DOC-7743433) and May 15, 2026 (DOC-7975070), and the written submissions provided by the Landlords on April 28, 2026 ( DOC-7857077) complied with the Endorsement dated March 24, 2026. They were therefore read and considered in arriving at my determinations. Allegation of Apprehension of Bias

Through their closing submissions submitt ed to the Board in accordance with the Endorsement dated March 24, 2026, the Tenant claim ed that I displayed a bias in favour of the Landlords with respect to both the assessment of the evidence presented during the hearing and the limitations imposed to some of the Tenant’s lines of questioning.

The fact that an oral ruling with respect to certain elements of the testimony and evidence presented during the hearing may have been seen as being favourable to the Landlords and therefore unfavourable to Tenant , is not – in my view – in and of itself, sufficient to establish a reasonable apprehension of bias.

Similar to what was discussed by the Divisional Court in Turner v. Northview Apartment Reit, 2019 ONSC 2204 at paras. 18-20, an argument that there is bias because the evidence or submissions of one party has been preferred over another, or even where there have been several adverse decisions does not establish bias and is circular.

As confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada, the test with respect to a reasonable apprehension of bias is objective , not subjective. The test, “ is what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically —and having thought the matter through—conclude. Would [they] think that it is more likely than not that [the presiding member], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly.”1

There is also a strong presumption of judicial impartiality; i.e. that the state of the mind of the decision maker is disinterested in the outcome and they are open to being persuaded by the evidence and submissions. This means the threshold to establish a reasonable apprehension of bias is high and the onus of demonstra ting bias lies with the person who is alleging its existence. “Mere suspicion” is not enough, and a real likelihood or probability of bias must be demonstrated.2

Furthermore, with respect to limiting certain questions by the Tenant through thei r cross- examination of the Landlords, I find that there is nothing untoward about a presiding Member controlling the process before the Board by stopping repetitive and meandering questions3, or for the Board to refuse to admit evidence which is not relevant to the proceedings.

Indeed, a presiding Member has authority to control the hearing room process, can decide how a matter will [name], can limit or exclude unduly repetitious evidence5, and has the mandate to proceed in an expeditious manner.6 1 Committee for Justice and Liberty et al. v. National Energy Board et al., 1976 CanLII 2 (SCC), [1978] 1 SCR 369, page 394. 2 See also R. v. S. (R.D.), 1997 CanLII 324 (SCC), [1997] 3 SCR 484. 3 [name] v. Shim, 2024 ONSC 6450. 4 Rule 1.4 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. 5 Rule 1.6 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and section 15 Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990. 6 Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Ultimately, the Tenant did not bring a motion for reasonable apprehension of bias and so I find that their submissions in this regard were not relevant to the matters in issue and, in any event, reflected hypotheses not based in evidence before me or reflective of what transpired during the hearing.

In the above circumstances, I am satisfied a reasonable and informed person would conclude it was more likely than not that I would decide the issues in the T2 Application fairly and based solely on the evidence, submissions and legal framework before me without any interest in the outcome. Request to Amend the T2 Application

At the start of the hearing, the Tenant sought the permission of the Board to amend their T2 Application, in accordance with the amended application they filed with the Board on March 26, 2024 (DOC-3039431).

The Tenant’s proposed amendments included changes to their requested remedies as they sought a rent abatement of $3.003.00 for a period of ninety -one (91) days between the months of December 2021, and October 2023, along with an additional claim that the Landlords had substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant , by allegedly violating the Tenant’s privacy on January 23, 2023.

Pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) a tenant can file an application, such as the T2 Application, no later than one (1) year “after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”

The purpose of an amendment to an application is not to do indirectly what the Tenant could not do directly. Indeed, if the Tenant wanted to amend their T2 Application to include claims related to an event that would have occurred on January 23, 2023, they ought to have sought to amend their T2 Application within one (1) year of this alleged event.
By filing their r equest to amend the T2 Application on March 26, 2024, the Tenant did so more than one year after the alleged event they now seek to also present.

Accordingly, I denied the Tenant’s request to amend the T2 Application to include the claim related to the January 23, 2023, incident. To do otherwise would allow the Tenant to circumvent the limitation periods set out in the Act 7 and would enable the Board to forego the restrictions related to altering time requirements set out in the Ontario Regulation 516/06.8

The Landlords were not opposed to the Tenant’s request to amend their remedies to include a rent abatement in the amount of $3,003.00. They intended to dispute the merits of the request for a rent abatement.

On the basis of the submissions before me, I granted the Tenant’s request to amend their remedies to include a rent abatement in the amount of $3,003.00. In my view, the Board must provide a self -represented party the benefit of the doubt and permit reasonable 7 Sections 29 and 190 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 8 Section 56 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06. amendments in order to give meaningful application of the Act’s objectives of remedial legislation with a tenant protection focus. The amendment to the remedies , which the Landlords were not opposed to, is not prejudicial to the Landlord s, as the grounds of the T2 Application, which were well known to them, remained the same. [name]

As explained below, the Tenant partially proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant the amount of $750.00 by July 20, 2026. a) [name] Evidence

The Tenant tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenant started on May 1, 2008, as it appears from a copy of the tenancy agreements executed between the parties on April 10, 2008 ([name], pages 21 to 28 of 78; Exhibit 1). i) Pictures and Recordings During Visits and Inspections of the Rental Unit

The Tenant testified that during the month of September 2009, they had sent the Landlords a letter asking that the Landlords, along with their agents ensure that they “refrain from invading [the Tenant’s] privacy” when entering the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the letter sent by the Tenant to the Landlords during the month of September 2009 ([name], page 28 of 78; Exhibit 2).

The Tenant indicated that the present T2 Application does not equate to the first time that the Tenant has raised concerns with respect to the Landlords’ behaviour and conduct. The Tenant had previously filed another application which led to the Landlords being ordered not to “engage in conduct that substantially interferes with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, including but not limited to yelling and uttering obscenities at the Tenant,” as it appears from a copy of the order TST-22510-21, issued on July 13, 2022 ([name], pages 15 to 18 of 78; Exhibit 3).

The Tenant stated that during the month of December 2021, the Landlords advised the Tenant of their intent to conduct an inspection of the rental unit on December 7, 2021, despite the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, and corresponding public health mandates , as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on December 1, 2021 ([name], page 31 of 78; Exhibit 4).

The Tenant indicated that in light of the upcoming inspection, the Tenant sent the Landlords an email requesting that the Landlords be mindful of public health recommendations , and that they “refrain from brin ging any recording devices ” into the rental unit , in addition to refraining from “making any video or audio recordings” while in the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Tenant to the Landlords on December 6 , 2021 ([name], page 30 of 78; Exhibit 5).

The Tenant stated that despite their request ( Exhibit 5 ), the Landlord [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘E.C’) entered the rental unit on December 7, 2021, with their smartphone in hand, through which they could take videos.
The Tenant indicated that E.C had insisted to record their dealings with the Tenant on December 7, 2021, based on their prior interactions.
The Tenant stated that they do not know if the Landlords actually proceeded to record anything on the mobile device on December 7, 2021, or what any such recording would depict.

The Tenant indicated that the Landlords sent them a notice of entry on December 19, 2021, as the Landlords intended to enter the rental unit along with their real estate agent in order to “prepare for a property appraisal .” The Tenant replied to the aforementioned email on December 20, 2021. and reiterated that they do no consent for pictures, audio or video recordings to be taken by the Landlords or their agents while within the rental unit , as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on December 19, 2021, and the reply sent by the Tenant to the Landlords on December 20, 2021 ([name], pages 32 and 33 of 78; Exhibit 6, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that following their reply to the Landlords ( Exhibit 6 ), the Landlords suggested that, if the Tenant had any safety concerns, they could leave the rental unit during the scheduled inspection time, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on December 20, 2021 ([name], page 32 of 78; Exhibit 7). The Tenant submitted that this was not a reasonable request in light of the ongoing pandemic.

The Tenant indicated that they proceeded to file a complaint with the Toronto Police Service on December 21, 2021, on or around 9:13am (i.e. prior to the scheduled visit by the Landlords), which led to both the Tenant and the Landlords being directed to “keep the peace during further visits” at the rental unit, as it appears f rom a copy of the General Occurrence Report #2021-1445839, dated December 21, 2021 ([name], pages 35 to 39 of 78; Exhibit 8).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they had no knowledge or documentary evidence of the Landlords, their agents, or prospective purchasers actually taking pictures or videos within the rental unit. ii) Lock Checks

The Tenant testified that the Landlords conducted multiple lock check related to the locking mechanism associated to the doors of the rental unit , specifically on December 7, 2021 (Exhibit 4), February 25, 2022, and March 13, 2022.
The Tenant did not express concerns with respect to the lock check conducted by the Landlords on December 7, 2021.
The Tenant stated that the further lock check conducted on February 25, 2022, and March 13, 2022, were done with the Landlords providing the Tenant with less than a twenty-four (24) hours’ notice.

The Tenant indicated that these checks were conducted to facilitate the sale process of the rental unit, in order to ensure that the Landlords their agents, and various real estate agents could access the rental unit to conduct showings of the rental unit to prospective purchasers.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlords’ repeated checks of the locking mechanism within a short period of time equate to a lack of competence from the part of the Landlords and their agents and substantially interfered with the Tenant. iii) Conduct During Scheduled Entries
The Tenant submitted that providing them with a notice of entry does not dispense the Landlords and their agents from acting in a respectful manner.

The Tenant testified that the entry to the rental unit is comprised of two (2) doors. The first exterior door leads to a vestibule and staircase which are of the exclusive use of the Tenant. At the top of the staircase, there is a secondary door which leads to the residential premise occupied by the Tenant.

The Tenant indicated that at times, including on December 7, 2021, the Landlords or their agents would enter the rental unit a few minutes prior to the scheduled time as set out in the prior notices of entries provided by the Landlords to the Tenant.

The Tenant disputed that they were intentionally interfering with the sale process, and rather only requested that individuals entering the rental unit were diligent with respect to public health guidelines and recommendations and mindful of respecting the Tenant’s space and privacy, after prior visitors had left muddy shoe prints on the floor of the rental unit , failed to wear a mask before entering the rental unit , and opened cabinets or drawers in the kitchen area, as it appears from screenshots of video recordings taken by the Tenant showing a prospective purchaser opening a drawer in the kitchen on February 22, 2022, and an agent or prospective purchaser failing to wear a mask prior to entering the rental unit on April 1, 2022, and a copy of a picture of the floor of the rental unit taken by the Tenant on March 6, 2022, showing a dirty shoe print ([name], pages 47 to 49 of 78; Exhibit 9, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that despite their prior requests, prospective purchasers entered the rental unit without a mask on February 23, 2022, all while holding a phone in their hand which could have been recording, as it appears from a screenshot of the video recording taken by the Landlords on February 23, 2022 ([name], page 50 of 78; Exhibit 10).

The Tenant indicated that during a scheduled visit of the rental unit on March 12, 2022, the Landlords’ agent and prospective purchasers sought to enter through the exterior door without knocking on the door , as it appears from a copy of the security camera footage dated March 12, 2022 (DOC-3077961; Exhibit 11).

The Tenant approached the agent and prospective purchasers and asked them to be respectful of their privacy and their space. All the individuals can be seen wearing a face mask and removing their shoes prior to entering the premises (Exhibit 11).

The Tenant stated that they tested positive for COVID -19 on April 2, 2022, and were therefore required to isolate in accordance with Ontario Public Health mandates and guidelines. The Tenant proceeded to advise the Landlords of their positive diagnostic, but was advised that the Landlords were intent on continuing with the already -scheduled viewings of the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the email exchanges between the Tenant and the Landlords between March 31, 2022, and April 4, 2022 ( [name], pages 68 to 75 of 78; Exhibit 12, in bundle).

The Tenant had sent links related Ontario Public Health guidelines to the La ndlords and reiterated their need to isolate during a period of five (5) days, and therefore that viewings of the rental unit ought not to take place during this time (Exhibit 12).

The Tenant indicated that they felt that the Landlords were again blaming them for their inability to complete the sale of the rental unit , all while they were looking to ensure their health and well-being (Exhibit 12).

The Tenant stated that the Landlords had advised them that two (2) viewings of the rental unit were scheduled to take place on June 21, 2022. Despite receiving such notice, neither of these two showings took place.

The Tenant indicated that the Landlords’ failure to advise the Tenant of the cancellation of these previously scheduled viewings interfered with them, as they had carved out time in their day to accommodate the Landlords.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that if they were located in their office within the rental unit, they may not hear someone knocking on the door. This may depend on the force applied by the individual knocking on the door. iv) N5 Notice of Termination

The Tenant indicated that the Landlords blamed them for their inability to sell the rental unit and proceeded to serve them with an N5 Notice of Termination dated June 6, 2022, as they alleged that the Tenant’s behaviour substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyments of the residential complex or their lawful rights, privileges, and interests, as it appears from a copy of the N5 Notice of Termination (hereafter referred to as the ‘N5 Notice’; [name], pages 62 to 64 of 78; Exhibit 13).

The Tenant is of the position that the N5 Notice was served without merit and fits within a pattern of harassment, which includes: • Someone knocking on the door of the rental unit and leaving before the Tenant had an opportunity to meet them at the entrance of the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the security camera recording dated March 12, 2022 (DOC-3077947; Exhibit 14); • Failed attempts by agents of the Landlords to conduct a viewing of the rental unit on August 22, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the security camera recording dated August 25, 2022 (DOC-4117987; Exhibit 15)
The Tenant stated that they were unaware as to whether or not the Landlords blamed the Tenant for failed viewings following the service of the N5 Notice.

The Tenant indicated that their conduct during viewings of the rental unit to prospective purchasers did not change following the service of the N5 Notice, as it appears from copies of the recordings or exchanges between the Tenant and agents or prospective purchasers at the rental unit on March 19, 2022, and September 4, 2022 ( DOC-4128564 and DOC-4128568; Exhibit 16, in bundle).
The Tenant described the N5 Notice as being frivolous and points to the Landlords’ refusal to withdraw the N5 Notice as being indicative of their bad faith.

The Tenant submitted the Landlords’ difficulties in selling the rental unit was likely related to fluctuations of the housing market, as opposed to the Tenant’s behaviour and conduct, as it appears from a copy of the Canadian Real Estate Association news release dated July 15, 2022, and CBC News dated July 15, 2022, and titled “Pace of real estate slump quickens, with sales and average prices down from last year” ([name], pages 51 to 62 of 78; Exhibit 17, in bundle).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they had no knowledge of the Landlords taking further legal action against the Tenant, beyond serving them with the N5 Notice (Exhibit 13). v) Requested Remedies

The Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of $3,003.00, as: • they found it extremely stressful to be accused of interfering with a sale value at one million dollars, • they felt that their tenancy was jeopardized by being unduly served the N5 Notice, • they felt harassed by having to repeatedly address the Landlords’ request to have pictures or videos taken within the rental unit.

The Tenant stated that the La ndlords’ behaviour and conduct led them to sleepless nights and a constant sense of dread due to the spectre of the Landlords threatening them with legal action; which in turn impacted their health.

The Tenant also sought for the Board to impose an administrative fine to the Landlords . They described the Landlords as being experienced in their field as they also own other residential complexes, and submitted that the Landlords knew or ought to have known that their conduct was designed to intimidate the Tenant.

Although the Tenant had also claimed the amount of $847.50 as out-of-pocket expenses they would have incurred as a result of the Landlords ’ conduct, they sought – during the hearing – to withdraw their request for such a remedy, along with their request for the Landlords to stop certain activities.

As I was satisfied that the Tenant understood that – if they were successful , the T2 Application could only result in the Tenant being awarded a rent abatement of up to $3,003.00, and a fine payable to the Board, 9 I granted the Tenant ’s further request to amend their remedies. 9 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160. b) Landlords’ Evidence
The Landlord [name] [name] Poscente (hereafter referred to as ‘N.C .P’) testified that the residential complex is comprised of three (3) residential units.
The Landlords agreed that they have been landlords since 2001, and have owned up to seven (7) residential units.

The Landlords submitted that their conduct would not warrant awarding any remedied to the Tenant, and therefore sought for the T2 Application to be dismissed. i) Pictures and Recordings During Visits and Inspections of the Rental Unit

N.C.P stated that the Landlords did not proceed in taking any audio or video recordings of the rental unit throughout the course of their inspection of the r ental unit on December 7, 2021. They stated that while E.C did in fact have their phone in their hand, their camera was not recording, as it appears from the side- by-side comparison of the pictures of E.C’s phone screen during the viewing on December 7, 2021, and phone screen during a recording taking place on a separate and distinct date ( DOC-3049341, page 2 of 7; Exhibit 18).

N.C.P indicated that the Landlords sent an email to all the tenants of the residential complex on December 1, 2021, in order to advise them of the Landlords’ intent to conduct an inspection of each unit, in accordance with the recommendations set out by their insurance provider (Exhibit 4).

Under cross-examination, N.C.P agreed that the Tenant has reiterated their request that the Landlords refrain from taking any recordings while within the rental unit. They did not recall the request to outright refrain from bringing any such device within the rental unit. ii) Lock Checks 72. [name] stated that the Landlords did indeed conduct multiple check of the locking mechanisms associated to the doors of the rental unit , including on December 7, 2021, February 25, 2022, and March 13, 2022. 73. N.P.C indicated that the Landlords had provided a notice of entry to the Tenant on February 22, 2022, advising them of their intent to access the rental unit on February 25, 2022, in order to take various measurements within the rental unit. They intended to use this opportunity to also ensure they had the adequate set of keys for the residential and rental unit in order to facilitate the process of the sale of the residential complex, by installing a lock-box on the premises, that realtors and agents of the Landlords could access with ease when required, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on February 22, 2022 (DOC-3006201, page 14 of 23; Exhibit 19). 74. N.P.C agreed that a third lock check took place on March 13, 2022, as there had been a mix-up with the keys by one of the real estate agents that had conducted a viewing of the rental unit. N.P.C stated that they personally check the keys by testing them on the exterior door leading to the vestibule and the secondary interior door. 75. N.P.C recognized that the Landlords had not given the Tenant a twenty -four (24) hours’ notice with respect to the third lock -check N.P.C indicated that they did not have any interactions with the Tenant on that occasion and left after ensuring that the keys were adequately labelled. iii) Conduct During Scheduled Entries 76. N.C.P stated that the Landlords were mindful of the ongoing pandemic throughout the course of their dealings with the Tenant during the sale process of the residential complex, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on December 19, 2021 (DOC-3006201, page 14 of 23; Exhibit 20). 77. N.C.P indicated that despite the email sent to the Tenant on February 22, 2022 (Exhibit 19), the Landlords had a conversation with their real estate agent to advise them that no pictures or videos could be taken within the rental unit, and that all measurements would nee to be taken manually with a tape measurer, as opposed to other technological means, in order to ensure that the Tenant’s concerns with respect to their privacy being impeded were alleviated. 78. N.C.P disputed that the Landlords or their agents failed to knock on the Tenant’s door or announce themselves prior to entering the rental unit for a scheduled entry. 79. N.C.P stated that it is the Landlords’ common practice to knock on the door and wait prior to entering occupied residential units. 80. N.C.P indicated that the Landlords ought not to be held liable for the conduct of various real estate agents, as they claimed that they had no control over the real estate agents with respect to any such alleged conduct. 81. [name] stated that the Landlords took reasonable steps to ensure that any prospective purchaser, as the online listings reflected that 1) the Landlords would provide a notice of entry to the Tenant, 2) the prospective purchasers and their agents were required to “always knock” before entering the rental unit , and 3) the individuals visiting the rental nit were not to take any photos or “touch anything,” as it appears from a copy of the Re/Max Realtron listing of the rental unit ( DOC-3049561, page 3 of 5; Exhibit 21 ). These instructions were provided at the beginning of the listing process. 82. [name] recognized that the viewings scheduled on June 21, 2022, did not take lace as originally intended. They stated that they were unaware of the intended cancellation prior to being advised by the Tenant on June 21, 2022, and proceeded to apologize for any inconvenience that the Tenant may have incurred, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences between the Tenant and the Landlords between June 21, 2022, and June 22, 2022 (DOC-3006201, page 16 of 23; Exhibit 22). 83. With respect to the Tenant testing positive for COVID-19, [name] recognized that exchanges between the parties between March 31, 2022, and April 4, 2022 (Exhibit 12). 84. [name] stated that despite the back and forth between the parties, the Landlords proceeded to cancel the viewing scheduled on April 4, 2022, and had advised their real estate agent that no viewings of the premises could take place between April 2, 2022, and April 7, 2022. 85. N.C.P further indicated that no viewings were actually booked or conducted between April 2, 2022, and April 7, 2022, after the Tenant advised the Landlords of their positive diagnostic (Exhibit 12). 86. Under cross-examination, N.C.P stated that the Landlords did not install a doorbell to the rental unit after the Tenant had raised concerns about individuals entering the rental unit for a scheduled entry without knocking on the door. They explained that they had never received any such request from the Tenant. iv) N5 Notice of Termination 87. The Landlords did not dispute that they served the Tenant with the N5 Notice (Exhibit 13) on June 6, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on June 6, 2022 (DOC-3006201, page 18 of 23; Exhibit 23). 88. [name] stated that the Landlords had received – through their real estate agent – feedback from other real-estate agents that had conducted viewings of the rental unit , with respect to the Tenant’s conduct impeding the process of the sale, as it appears from a copy of the emails sent to the Landlords by their real estate agent [name], on March 7, 2022, March 16, 2022, and June 3, 2022 (DOC-3006201, pages 17 and 18 of 23; Exhibit 24). 89. N.C.P indicated that the concerns related to the Tenant’s “rude” behaviour impeding the sale process were relayed to the Tenant prior to the service of the N5 Notice, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on March 10, 2022 (DOC-3006201, page 18 of 23; Exhibit 25). c) Analysis 90. Section 22 of the Act reads as follows: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. [Emphasis Added] 91. Section 23 of the Act reads as follows: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 92. Although the term “harassment” is not defined anywhere in the Act or its Regulations, the Board generally adopts the definition from the Human Rights Code, 1990 that defines harassment as “ engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”10 93. As the applicant, the Tenant bears the burden of the proof – on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present “ sufficiently clear, 10 Subsection 10(1) of the Human Rights Code, 1990. convincing, and cogent”11 evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened, or a fact is true. This is particularly important to note as the Tenant ’s written submissions suggests that the Landlords bore the burden of demonstrating that they had not harassed or interfered with the Tenant. 94. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I a m satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlords harassed the Tenant by repeatedly requesting to take pictures or videos within the rental unit. 95. Indeed, while a landlord is entitled t o take pictures or photographs of a rental unit for legitimate purposes, such as but not limited to, gathering evidence for an upcoming Board hearing12, they do not have an inherent right to take such pictures or videos, or to have their agents or prospective purchasers take them either. 96. As the tenancy agreement executed between the parties (Exhibit 1) does not set out that the Landlords may seek to enter the rental unit in order to take pictures or videos for marketing purposes in light of a prospective sale of the residential , the Landlords had no authority to do so in the absence of the Tenant’s consent.13 97. I accept that the Tenant had repeatability asked the Landlords to refrain from taking pictures or videos. Their testimony in this regard was consistent and credible and corroborated by contemporaneous documentary evidence (Exhibits 2, 5, 6, and 7); which was not disputed by the Landlords. 98. While it may not be reasonable to expect a landlord to outright refrain from brining a “recording device” within a rental unit in this day and age in light of the fact that smart phones may also serve such a purpose, the Landlords ’ own evidence (Exhibit 18) supported the Tenant’s testimony that they had their camera app open on their phone upon entering the rental unit on December 7, 2021. 99. Although the Landlords may not have been actually recording at the time (Exhibit 18), they ought to have known , in light of the previous communications they had with the Tenant , that such a conduct was unwelcome, and unnecessarily antagonistic. 100. Furthermore, the Landlords continued to send communications to the Tenant suggesting that they would need to enter the rental unit multiple times to take pictures of the premises (Exhibit 19). While I can appreciate that these communications equated to messages sent by the Landlords to all the tenants of the residential complex, they ought to have been more mindful of the communications sent directly to the Tenant , and ought to have known that messages of this nature were vexing to the Tenant. 101. Moreover, while the Landlords had a right to serve the Tenant with a notice of entry and enter the rental unit for legitimate purposes, 14 the contemporaneous context of the pandemic cannot be ignored. 11 F.H. v. [name], 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), [2008] 3 SCR 41, paragraph 46. 12 Nickoladze v Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management, 2015 ONSC 3893. 13 Juhasz v Hymas, 2016 ONSC 1650, paragraph 29. 14 Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 102. While I accept that the Landlords did not ultimately proceed in conducting viewings of the rental unit between March 31, 2022, and April 7, 2022, they had sent the Tenant no less than seven (7) messages in the span of less than three (3) days, between April 2, 2022, and April 24, 2022, suggesting that – despite the Tenant’s medical situation - they intended to continue with thei r viewing on April 4, 2026, and that the Tenant ought not to interfere with their “ right to show [the] property ” (Exhibit 12). Based on the clear information conveyed by the Tenant through their messages, the Landlords ought to have known that continuing to insist on conducting non-urgent showings of the rental unit, who had for sole purpose to facilitate the process of a potential sale, were unwelcome. 103. With that said, I do not find that the service of the N5 Notice equated to harassment , or substantial interference (Exhibits 13 and 23). Indeed, while a notice seeking the termination of a tenancy is likely to be unwelcome by a tenant as a result of the very nature of such a notice, a landlord remains entitled to serve them in accordance with the Act. In this case, the Landlords proceeded to serve the N5 Notice to the Tenant after having concerns regarding the behaviour and conduct of the Tenant, during showings of the rental unit , relayed to them (Exhibits 24 and 25). 104. Although I note that the Landlord sought to justify their conduct by stating that they were following the instructions or directions provided to them by the Landlord and Tenant Board or the Landlord's Self -Help Centre, I note that the Board does not provide parties or prospective parties legal advice and that regardless of the information of advice provided by the Landlord's Self-Help Centre, the Landlords ought to ensure that they act reasonably and diligently in their dealings with the Tenant. 105. As the application before me (i.e. the T2 Application) was not one which could lead to the termination of the tenancy, I do not find it appropriate nor expedi tious to address the grounds for the termination of the tenancy reflected in the N5 Notice in a similar fashion as if this matter was an application brought forward by the Landlord s under section 69 of the Act. 106. I will, however, say that the Landlords appeared to have reasonable grounds to serve the Tenant such a notice based on the information relayed to them (Exhibits 24 and 25); and while the Tenant had sought to have this notice withdrawn , such a request was not necessary nor relevant as the N5 Notice was deemed to be void, pursuant to subsection 64(3) of the Act. 107. Although I am satisfied that some of the Landlords ’ conduct described herein equated to harassment, I am not satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant ’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant. 108. Indeed, even though the Landlords needed to ensure that the keys to the residential units were adequately labelled and stored within the appropriate lock-box within a relative short period of time (between December 7, 2021, and M arch 13, 2022) due to administrative lapses between themselves and their agents, such conduct from the Landlords caused little to no impact to the Tenant, who – I note – did not allege that the Landlords entered into the rental unit illegally.15 While this may have bothered the Tenant to an extent, I find that this 15 Section 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. conduct from the Landlords equates more to being a “minor inconvenience,”16 as opposed to “substantial interference.” 109. Similarly, I accept that the Landlords took reasonable steps to ensure that their agents and prospective purchasers abided by the Tenant ’s preferences, such as not taking any pictures or videos in the rental unit and removing their shoes prior to their entry (Exhibits 9, 11 and 21). The simple fact that an individual entered the unit with their phone in their hand is not synonymous of them recording anything (Exhibit 10). Again, such conduct is not necessarily uncommon nowadays, and the Tenant led no evidence as to any pictures or videos being actually taken and or used for illegitimate purposes. 110. Likewise, I do not find that cancelled or missed showings (Exhibits 14, 15, 22) or some unknown individual knocking on the Tenant’s door and leaving prior to the Tenant’s arrival to reach the level of substantial interference. While perhaps annoying to the Tenant, such occurrences cannot reasonably be considered more than minor inconveniences.17 d) Remedies 111. As I have found that the Landlords have harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, the next matter to be addressed pertains to the remedies being requested by the Tenant. i) Rent Abatement 112. While the Tenant sought the amount of $3,003.00, which represented a one hundred percent (100%) rent abatement for a period of ninety -one days, I do not find such an amount be appropriate under the circumstances. 113. Indeed, a rent abatement equivalent to one hundred percent (100%) for a defined period of times implies that the rental unit was uninhabitab le over the course of such a rental period. This was not the case for the mat ter before the Board, as t he evidence led by the Tenant did not suggest that they were unable to occupy the premises. 114. Although the Tenant referenced that the Landlords’ conduct impacted their health they did not provide any details with respect to their condition, nor any medical documentation for the Board to consider a description of their diagnosis, the effect of any such a diagnosis on the Tenant, and how their medical situation stemmed from t he Landlords ’ actions and conduct (by analogy [name], 2023 ONSC 1028). 115. Pursuant to the evidence and submissions before me, and having knowledge of similar cases, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement in the amount of $750.00, with respect to the harassing behaviour they encountered from the Landlords. 16 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975. 17 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975. ii) Administrative Fine 116. Subsection 31(1)(d) of the Act provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlords pay a fine of up to $50,000.00, which is equivalent to the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.18 117. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the [Act] and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 118. In effect, I should consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors, such as the conduct of the Landlords. 119. Deterrence for egregious conduct, beyond whatever deterrent effect simple damages might provide, is an overriding factor. 120. Considering the time which has elapsed since the events giving rise to the T2 Application, that the Landlords no longer act in such a capacity with respect to the tenancy in question, that the Tenant was awarded other monetary remedies and that no evidence was led with respect to ongoing issues pertaining to the Landlords’ conduct, I do not find that this is an appropriate case in which an administrative fine ought to be imposed. 121. Accordingly, the Tenant’s request for an administrative fine to be imposed to the Landlords is denied. iii) Filing Fee 122. The Tenant also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the T2 Application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the total amount of $798.00, which represents: • $750.00 for the rent abatement, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 20, 2026. 18 Subsection 207(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, and Section 1 of the Ontario Regulation 626/00.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord submitted that the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application lack sufficient detail and particulars, and further the Tenant did not take the opportunity provided to her in the Board’s Interim Order dated February 4, 2026, to amend this herein application on or before March 4, 2026.

The Landlord submitted that the application should be dismissed as the Tenant has not provided sufficient details and particulars of allegations other than there were various issues of disrepair since she moved into the rental unit. Moreover, the Landlord has been put in the unfair situation of having to defend itself to an application containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are other than generalities of the allegations that there were issues of disrepair, nor the remedies sought by the Tenant. Accordingly, the Landlord submitted that the Tenant’s T6 application should be dismissed.

Upon Board questioning on why the Tenant had not provided sufficient details, she testified that it was her understanding she could amend if she wished, and she thought her application was fine, as she was a layperson.

The Board can assist parties by providing general information as needed, however the Board does not act as a legal representative for either party and consequently, it is the Applicant’s, in this case the Tenant responsibility to ensure that the application is complete and in compliance with the Act. It was further noted to the Tenant that she could have contacted Tenant Duty Counsel whose contact information was listed on the Notice of Hearing for this herein proceeding. The Tenant did not seek to amend her application during the proceeding, nor did she prior to this proceeding.

An application must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital [2022] O.J. No. 5931 that, “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, I am of the view the general principle regarding the need for particular and details apply equally to Tenant application. In this leading case, the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons an details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that they can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission….’’

The Landlord submitted the allegations toward the Landlord are lacking any semblance of details of said issues being pleaded by the Tenant. Moreover, evidence uploaded to the Portal by the Tenant was not introduced as evidence during the proceeding and hence did not provide sufficient particulars to support the Tenant’s allegations in her application, which the Landlord submitted was a general statement, and devoid of detail that simply there were issues with disrepair.

I find the allegations in the Tenant’s application are vague and lack any context in terms of details. Specifically, the “Reasons for filing this Application” section of the application instructs the applicant to describe what each problem is, the date the problem started, whether the problem was repaired, and if so to provide the date, and explain who repaired it, further explain who or what caused the problem, and how the Tenant informed the Landlord for each problem listed, which the Tenant has not done in a way that the Landlord could properly comprehend the issues at hand.
On the T6 application there is simply a seven-line general statement and description that the Tenant had various maintenance issues, devoid of sufficient detail.

It is not for the Landlord or the Board to assist the Tenant in completing their application or correcting deficiencies. As with all applications before the Board, it is the applicant who must bring an application that meets minimum requirements. However, the undersigned noted to the Tenant, if she choose to bring another application she should seek out legal counsel whether privately or by contacting [name], if the time limitations of the Act permit.

The Landlord’s right to present a meaningful defence in a timely fashion must also be taken into consideration. The application does not contain sufficient details on the alleged grounds that would allow the matter to be fairly heard.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application were not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met to and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at the hearing, and effectively would have experienced significant prejudice if expected to present a defence against unknown, generalized and unspecified allegations. Moreover, the Tenant did not seek an opportunity to adjourn the matter to amend said application and had not done so as of the date of this proceeding, even after the Board’s Interim Order dated February 4, 2026 provided her up to March 4, 2026 to amend her application pursuant to Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. July 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Peterborough Housing Corporation (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant’s applications were heard by videoconference on February 3, 2026 and May 28, 2026. The Tenant, The Tenant’s Legal Representative, Tiffany Badour, the Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘RV’), the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘ZH’), attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the applications are dismissed. The Applications
The Tenant’s applications, being a T2 Application about Tenant Rights (the ‘T2 Application’) and a T6 Tenant Application about Maintenance (the ‘T6 Application’), were filed on May 30, 2024.

The Tenant filed a request to amend the applications on or about October 15, 2025. The amendments were completed to narrow the issues in the applications and were done in accordance with the LTB Rules of Procedure and/or as directed by the Board. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not oppose the amendments. Accordingly, the request to amend the applications was granted.

In summary, the applications alleged the following: T2 Application • the Landlord, Landlord’s agent or superintendent substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by failing to adequately address the Tenant’s complaints of second-hand smoke; • the Landlord, Landlord’s agent or superintendent harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by failing to address various maintenance issues and failing to provide the Tenant with a copy of security footage she required for an investigation after being assaulted by an ex-partner; T6 Application • the Landlord failed to resolve the following issues/items in the rental unit that were in a state of disrepair and/or required maintenance: - bathroom fan was not strong enough which allowed moisture to remain and led to mould growth; - rusted plumbing fixtures and/or bathroom accessories and jewelry; and - cracks in the ceiling. Tenant’s Evidence

At the hearing, the Tenant only gave evidence on two main issues in her applications, being second-hand smoke and the bathroom ventilation. Accordingly, the other allegations are dismissed. Second-hand Smoke

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in or around February 2021. The residential complex was supposed to be a smoke free building. However, approximately 3 months after moving in, she started experiencing second-hand smoke coming from a neighbouring unit and contacted RV to report it. The Tenant stated she was asked to continue to make her complaints in writing and to provide dates and times when she would smell smoke. The Tenant did so for about a year. However, she ultimately stopped sending complaints as RV began to accuse the Tenant of abusing her. The Tenant believed that the last complaint that she sent regarding second-hand smoke was in early 2024. However, she continued to smell smoke until she moved out in September 2025.

In response to the Tenant’s complaints of second-hand smoke, the Landlord gave the Tenant an air purifier. However, the Tenant found that it did not remove the second-hand smoke from the air and was not helpful. In addition, the Tenant was aware of the Landlord sending a letter to the tenant that was smoking and posting a notice to all tenants in the residential complex about not smoking in the building. The Tenant noted that she learned the Landlord gave the smoking tenant two N5 notices of termination through the disclosure of evidence process but that the Landlord never communicated this to her at the time they were served.

In addition to her neighbour smoking, the Tenant stated that other tenants or residents of the building would congregate around her parking spot outside and smoke, which she reported to the Landlord in 2023. In response, the Landlord offered the Tenant a different parking spot. However, the Tenant declined this as she is a person with a disability and her spot was close to the entrance of the residential complex. The Landlord also moved the bench that was close to the Tenant’s vehicle. However, this did little to help the situation as many of the smokers were in wheelchairs and did not use the bench.

Tenant stated that she experienced chronic migraines due to the second-hand smoke and that she obtained a doctor’s letter regarding this and provided it to the Landlord. She also testified that she required a puffer the last year that she lived in the unit due to the second- hand smoke. Bathroom Ventilation

The bathroom in the rental unit did not have any windows. The Tenant stated that, initially, there was no bathroom fan that she could turn on or off. Rather, there was some sort of air exchange system that she did not have any control of and there was a vent with a grate over it in the bathroom. The Tenant recalled noticing not long after moving in that her bathroom walls were sweating and that her jewelry was corroding and so she reported this to the Landlord. Later, in January 2024, after complaining to the Landlord on multiple occasions, the Tenant contacted the City of Peterborough (the ‘City’) to file a complaint. After this, a booster fan was finally installed. However, it did not work very well and accumulated dirt and debris. This also occurred with the vent to the air exchange system. The Tenant testified that she did not vacuum out or otherwise clean the vent or booster fan as this was the Landlord’s responsibility.

The Tenant obtained a copy of the complaint record through a freedom of information request, which was tendered as evidence at the hearing. According to the records obtained, a complaint was received by the City on January 8, 2024. The Tenant stated that she met with someone from the City on January 17, 2024 regarding the bathroom ventilation not working properly. In the comment section of the records obtained, the City staff wrote that it appeared that the exhaust fan in the bathroom was not functioning and photos were shown of mold and that the shower rod, soap hanger, etc. were rusted. It also stated that the shower [name] was damaged and the exhaust fan was filled with dirt and debris. The aforesaid complaint was noted as closed on August 21, 2024 in the records obtained and stated that all repairs requested had been completed. Landlord’s Evidence Second-hand Smoke
RV is the Resident Services Manager for the residential complex.

RV acknowledged receiving complaints about second-hand smoke from the Tenant. She described the complaints as sporadic and stated that it was very difficult getting information about the smoking from the Tenant and that often things like the dates, times or where the smoke was coming from would be missing from the Tenant’s complaint.

RV recalled providing the Tenant with an air purifier and stated that it was specifically for smoke. She testified that community wide notices were given regarding smoking not being permitted in the residential complex and that the tenant who was believed to be smoking was served with a total of three N5 notices of termination. The notices of termination being served on the smoking tenant were not initially shared with the Tenant due to privacy reasons.

RV testified that she believed that the issues with the smoking tenant had been fully and finally resolved based on inspections done in that unit and feedback from other tenants. In addition, no further complaints were received from the Tenant.

With respect to smoking that was taking place close to the Tenant’s parking spot, RV stated she did not receive complaints about this issue until April 2024 and explained that it was a smoke free building but not a smoke free property. In this regard, tenants could smoke outside provided that they were far away enough from the building, which is approximately 9ft or 30 meters. RV testified that, in response to the Tenant’s complaints of smoking near her parking spot, RV moved the cigarette disposal to another spot, removed the park bench that was near the Tenant’s parking spot, and offered her two different parking spots that were close to the building entrance. Bathroom Ventilation

ZH is a Technical Service Coordinator for the Landlord. He stated that the Residential Complex is equipped with an ERV system, which is a mechanical ventilation system that exchanges indoor air with fresh outdoor air. This system runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

ZH testified that there was a grill in the bathroom ceiling of the rental unit and its purpose was to continuously draw air out of the unit. The more dust and dirt that accumulates on the grill, the less air can go through it. If air is not being evacuated, moisture is held in the air. ZH stated that tenants are required to clean the grills and that this does not form part of his regular duties. Tenants can simply vacuum the grill to clean it and are not required to take the grill off.

ZH stated that a complete bathroom fan was installed, which had an independent duct system that was vented outside directly, as a specific accommodation for the Tenant’s unit. He explained that, similar to the ERV grill, if the bathroom fan becomes clogged with dirt, it would become less effective.
ZH was present when the by-law officer from the City attended and ZH testified that he did not see any mould present in the unit at the time.

RV stated that there was no mould in the rental unit and that property standards did not advise that there was mould in the unit. Rather, that is what the Tenant told the property standards inspector.

RV testified that, the results of unit inspections indicated a lack of cleaning the grills to the vents as causing reduced ventilation and that this is something that the Tenants are expected to clean and are aware of. However, she did arrange for a contractor to clean the bathroom grate on February 2, 2024 because of the Tenant’s complaints.

RV testified that she ultimately had a very expensive ventilation system installed in the bathroom, after enduring several months of email attacks from the Tenant. In this regard, she received approximately 84 emails from the Tenant wherein the Tenant used profanity and threatened RV’s employment. RV stated she installed the fan hoping that it would appease the Tenant. However, it did not and so the Tenant was issued a warning letter and later N5 notices of termination. The intent was not to stop the Tenant from complaining but rather to stop her from being abusive and threatening toward RV. Ultimately, the matter was scheduled for a hearing before the Board but it was resolved through a consent order wherein the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy. Analysis T2 Application

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that the Landlord did not: i) substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; or ii) harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.

The evidence suggests that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint of second- hand smoke in a reasonable time and manner. The Landlord contacted the smoking tenant, sent warning letters and served them with notices of termination. The Landlord also provided the Tenant with an air purifier. The Tenant acknowledged that she stopped making complaints about the smoking tenant in early 2024 and so I do not find it unreasonable for the Landlord to assume that the issue had resolved.

Although the Tenant argues that she stopped complaining because the Landlord accused her of abusing RV and tried to have her evicted, in reviewing LTB file no. LTB-L-043633- 25, it does not appear that the Landlord took any steps to commence eviction proceedings until service of the first N5 notice of termination in February 2025. In light of this, the timelines do not appear to overlap or align with the Tenant’s version of events.

With respect to the outdoor smoking issue, the evidence suggests that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints in a reasonable time and manner and offered the Tenant a reasonable accommodation. It was unclear why the Tenant would not accept a different parking spot as a solution when that parking spot would have been just as close if not closer to the building than the one she had. T6 Application
Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet its obligations under section 20 of the Act.

There was no evidence to suggest that the Landlord’s ERV system was in a state of disrepair or not functioning properly. In this regard, a report from the Landlord’s contractor was tendered as evidence and put to the Tenant during cross examination. The report stated that the unit was inspected on January 11, 2024 and it was determined that the ERV system was running at 100%. Thereafter, the Landlord had the grills and/or vent covers in bathroom cleaned on February 2, 2024 to try and increase the ventilation.

Although additional moisture or humidity was noted in the unit by the Tenant and by one of the Landlord’s contractors when the unit was inspected on July 11, 2024, there was no evidence of it causing mould or rust as alleged by the Tenant. In this regard, the Tenant did not provide any photos or reports to support her position that there was mould or rust in the unit. Moreover, the contractor’s email that was tendered as evidence regarding the inspection on July 11, 2024 specifically stated that there was no mould visible.

To try and resolve the Tenant’s complaints and reduce the humidity levels in the unit that were noted by the Landlord’s contractor, the Landlord had a complete bathroom fan system installed in or around July 23, 2024 that was independent of the ERV system. Although the Tenant stated that the addition of the bathroom fan did not improve her situation she did not provide any reports, photos or any other documentary evidence to support her position that it was not working properly or was in a state of disrepair.

During the hearing it was suggested by the Tenant that the Landlord failed to maintain the ERV system and bathroom fan because the Landlord did not clean the grills and/or vent covers which resulted in reduced efficiency. I disagree. Vacuuming and/or wiping off dust and dirt from a grill and/or vent cover is part of ordinary cleanliness which the Tenant is responsible for under section 33 of the Act.
For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 application) • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) [name] was held by videoconference on February 3, 2026. Only the Tenant and the Tenant’s legal representative, [name], attended the hearing. As of 1:47pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenant moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2024. The monthly rent was $550.00.

The Tenant testified that on or about March 5, 2025, the Landlord told him that he would have to vacate the rental unit because renovations were required. The Tenant understood that he would only be required to leave temporarily and that the renovations would take approximately 15 days.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 16, 2025. The Tenant stated that the renovations were not completed within the anticipated period and that he was not subsequently permitted to return to the rental unit.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. However, the Tenant provided limited evidence concerning the discussions that occurred before he vacated. The Tenant did not provide detailed evidence about the renovations that were proposed, the terms upon which he agreed to leave, or the specific representations made by the Landlord concerning his return.

The Tenant also did not provide detailed evidence concerning any attempts he made to return to the rental unit, the Landlord’s response to those attempts, or the circumstances in which the Landlord allegedly refused to permit him to resume occupancy.

Although the Tenant expected to return to the rental unit, the evidence did not sufficiently establish whether the tenancy was intended to continue while the renovations were completed or whether the parties had reached an agreement that the Tenant would permanently vacate the rental unit.

The Tenant’s evidence primarily established that he left the rental unit after the Landlord asked him to do so and that he was disappointed when he was not subsequently permitted to return. Without further evidence about the parties’ agreement and the Landlord’s conduct after the Tenant vacated, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant did not prove the allegation contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. The T2 application is dismissed. T1 application
The Tenant paid $550.00 on March 1, 2025 for the full month of March 2025.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 16, 2025 after the Landlord directed him to leave. The Tenant was unable to occupy the rental unit for the remainder of March 2025.
The Landlord retained the rent paid for the second half of March 2025. I find that the Landlord must return $275.00 to the Tenant, representing one-half of the monthly rent.

The Tenant also paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit of $550.00. Since the Tenant separately paid the full rent for March 2025, the Landlord did not apply the rent deposit to the last rental period of the tenancy. The Landlord also did not return the deposit to the Tenant.
The Landlord must pay the Tenant $825.00, consisting of $275.00 for the unused portion of the March 2025 rent and $550.00 for the last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The T2 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $873.00. This amount represents: • $550.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $275.00 for rent retained for the second half of March 2025 • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
