issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant testified that she had amended her T2;T6 application [name], B, D on March 4, 2026, and served the Landlords via email correspondence on March 4, 2026. The original T2:T6 application was issued on January 21, 2024.
The Tenant testified that she required these amendments due the passage of time to get to this herein proceeding.
The Landlords objected to these amendment requests.

The relevant parts of Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure state the following: 15.1 A request to amend an application before the hearing must be: a. in writing; b. served with the amended application to all other parties; and c. filed with LTB with the amended application and a completed Certificate of Service. 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors. 15.4 The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

Rule 15.3 specifically requires that a Board Member consider and then grant or deny any requested amendments. The Tenant did provide the aforementioned amended schedules to the contents of the Tenant’s Schedule A, B bad D and had served the Landlords the amended schedules via email correspondence, both on March 4, 2026, just a week prior to this herein proceeding. I note the Tenant did not file a complete Certificate of Service, as required under Rule 15.1.

Amendments are intended to correct an error, not include new issues that were not included in the original application. In my view, an amendment to include new issues that were not included in the original application and did not form the basis of the original application is an improper attempt to circumvent the established process in which parties advance their claims before the Board.

As a result of all of the above, I denied the Tenant’s request to amend her application. Moreover, to permit these amendments, which included further both new details and new claims, which were effectively new instances of causes of action not all as originally claimed, and if I was to allow them it would be an abuse of process effectively attempting to curtail the limitation period, by seeking amendments which included the new causes of action. Preliminary [name] did not provide timely disclosure denied
The Tenant had uploaded evidence labeled LTB-T-044448-23 Disclosure onto the Ontario Tribunals Portal on March 4, 2026, at 11:29 p.m., and further evidence on March 10, 2026.

Uploading materials to TOP does not mean documents have been provided to another party unless there is an agreement in place and, here, there was no such agreement. Moreover, there was no evidence submitted that this disclosure had been served upon the Landlords provided during the proceeding.

Similarly, Rule 19.1 of the LTB’s Rules provides that all materials on which a party intends to rely at a hearing must be provided to the other party and the LTB 7 days in advance of the hearing. Rule 19.7 provides, in part, that a party who fails to comply with Rule 19 may not rely on evidence that was not properly disclosed unless ordered otherwise.

The Board’s records show the Notice of Hearing – which advises parties of their disclosure obligations - emailed to the parties November 14, 2025, as well as mailed on February 11, 2026. Approximately 4 months prior to the hearing.

In the above circumstances I am not satisfied the Tenant could not have complied with the Rules. The Tenant had a period of at least 4 months to complete and provide her materials to the Landlords and LTB.

Absent a satisfactory explanation on why the Tenant could not comply with the disclosure requirements of the Rules of the Board and even further as mentioned in the Notice of Hearing which the Tenant acknowledged receiving for this herein proceeding. The Tenant may not rely on their materials/evidence uploaded to TOP, on and after March 4, 2026, which was not served on the Landlords.
Moreover, the Landlords were not permitted to rely on any evidence that did not comply with rule 19 as well. T2;T6 Application Determination:
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2;T6 application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed a T2/T6 Application about Tenant Rights (T2) with the Board on January 21, 2024. The T2 indicated that the grounds for the notice are substantial interference and that the Landlords, harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened of interfered with the Tenant. Further the T6 alleged that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under s.20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (‘the Act’) stemming from problems relating to issues with water leaks on November 20, 2023, December 5, 2023 and January 21, 2024 and no heat on the date the application was filed.

The Tenant’s requested remedies for the T2 application were an $1,566.20 abatement of rent, an LTB Fine, out of pocket expenses of $1,000.00 and for the T6 application an $1,566.20 abatement of rent, out of pocket expenses of $500.00, as well as general damages of $2000.00.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2007, and the lawful rent is $581.05, as testified to by the Tenant, which defers from $522.20 as stated in this herein application. [name]

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The Tenant testified that on November 20, 2023, November 30, 2023, December 5, 2023, and January 21, 2024, she contacted the Landlords via email and telephone regarding water leaks in her rental unit, which seemed to be related to radiator and boiler system of f of the residential complex.

The Tenant further testified that [name] (BS) who dealt with maintenance in the residential complex, attended on November 30, 2023, shut down the boiler and it seemed to solve the water leak on that date.

The Tenant further testified, that on December 5, 2023, there was another water leak and she left a telephone message with the Landlord, and as of December 13, 2023, she had not been provided any details on what caused the leak and how and if it was repaired.

The Tenant further testified that on January 21, 2024, there was further leak where the Landlords responded immediately. The Tenant testified that the residential complex is three floors, and the heating of the residential complex is via a 100-year-old steam boiler. The Tenant asserts there was smoke emanating from the building because of the boiler malfunction that caused three separate leaks that day, and the boiler system was shut down on January 21, 2024 to repair the issues, and while the Landlords did remedy the situation by late evening on the same date, they did not cooperate regarding responding to email correspondence sent to them seeking clarification, which negatively interfered with the Tenant, and due to the leaks, caused her knee injury to aggravate, hence her seeking $1000.00 in out of pocket expenses for physiotherapy, which was not substantiated by any documentary evidence by the Tenant.
The Tenant testified to issues with her cabinet door which was not completed as well.

On cross examination by the Tenant, the Tenant testified required time and accommodation regarding moving items in her rental unit, so the cabinet repair could be completed, but she had not asked for the same, it was further acknowledged there was another L2 application regarding this same issue. Further it was clear from the cross examination that there was animosity between the parties related to various issues in this herein tenancy.

The Landlord [name] (NJ) testified that the Landlords had owned the residential complex for 40 years, and everything related to building maintenance was completed by [name], with assistance from NJ when needed, and outside professional when required.
NJ testified that in fact the heating system of the residential complex was a boiler system, which included radiators in each rental unit, the number of radiators, varied with each rental unit.

NJ further testified there were in fact leaks on November 30, 2023, and December 5, 2023, related to the radiator nipples, and the feed lines from the boiler system, which were both repaired in a reasonable time upon notification from the Tenant. The December 5, 2023, leak was repaired instantly, as it just required further tightening of various parts of the radiator in the rental unit. The November 30, 2023, leak seemed to have gone unnoticed for a few weeks as it was a small drip, that seemed to have saturated from one rental unit to another, however, upon notice from the Tenant, and other tenant, it was remedied as well.

NJ further testified on January 21, 2024, there was a serious pressure leak related to the boiler system. NJ was already onsite dealing with another tenant complaint, when the Tenant notified him of the issue as well. The boiler was required to be shut down, as the whole system in the residential complex required to be drained for several hours prior to the repair. The boiler system is cast iron piping, with radiators, and it works via steam, water and forced air.

NJ testified the issues with the boiler system persisted from 6am however was back in operation by 6pm on January 21, 2024. NJ testified that the heat effectively in the residential complex, was off for 12 hours, as it required himself, [name] and a gas technician to repair the same. NJ testified that the Tenant, did send multiple emails and calls that day seeking clarification and updates, to the Landlord, [name] [name], as he was onsite and did not receive the emails and or telephone calls, and could not properly advise the other Landlord what was transpiring, every second of the day. However, the Landlord, [name] [name] notified the Tenant she would be advised as soon as possible.

NJ further testified, that the Tenant was aware the problem was getting repaired on site, as staff and the gas technician were working on the boiler system, with NJ and once completed the Tenant was advised.

NJ testified he and the professional gas technician retained as well as [name], worked as quickly as possible to get the heat back on, and he admits it took close to 12 hours, but the ambient temperature of the residential complex, had not declined to a state where space heaters, were required, nor did the Tenant allege this.

NJ further testified that there was nothing to prevent this from happening, as this issue on January 21, 2024 was unrelated to the previous leak issues, and the response time regarding all issues was immediate, prudent and rational and since that time to the date of this proceeding, the boiler system has been monitored without an issue.

NJ testified the issue alleged by the Tenant related to the cabinet, was more of an issue with her not being able to close the cabinet door, and the lack of the ability of the Landlord to repair the same given the condition of the Tenant’s rental unit and getting to the cabinet. The Landlords have requested the Tenant declutter for safety reasons, and even have mentioned previously they could help, however given the number of applications brought forward and the tension between the parties.

NJ further testified on cross examination that the Tenant had been notified all the time regarding repairs and maintenance issues with the boiler system, it was just not to her liking, but it was reasonable and certainly not delayed, and it certainly did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenant nor did the Landlords interfere with the Tenant in his opinion.

The question to be determined by the Board is whether the aforementioned issues were a substantial interference of reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant and whether the Landlords harassed, obstruct, coerced, threaten or interfere with a tenant. The Tenant emphasized it was inference during the proceeding.

The Tenant alleged the Landlords behaviour and delay in actions to repair the leak and cabinet interfered with her. Although, the word interfere is not defined in the Act, interfere generally would be a course of conduct or behaviour that the reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome, similar to harassment, as has been found by the Board.

The Act further states that: 29(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: (3) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household. (4) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit.

On the evidence before me, I find the Tenant’s claims of substantial interference, and harassment, obstruction, coercion, threatening or interference were not met. I find that the Landlord took all reasonable steps to attempt to rectify the situation and ultimately on a balance of probabilities did so. On a balance of probabilities, I prefer the Landlords’ evidence to that of the Tenant’s, and thus I find there was no substantial interference or interference as alleged by the Tenant. T6 Application Analysis and Determinations

Section 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence adduced by the Tenant, either in part or taken in its entirety, suffices to meet the burden of proof upon the Tenant to demonstrate that the Landlords have breached their obligations as they pertain to the T6 application.

After considering all of the evidence, I cannot find that the Landlord breached s.20 of the Act with respect to the leaks from the boiler system, or the testified to cabinet issue as alleged by the Tenant. I acknowledge that these water leak issue would be unpleasant and may have been an annoyance, I find that the Tenant was not able to identify any breach of section 20 of the Act. Based on the testimony before me, I also find that the Landlord acted reasonably following the reporting of the issues by the Tenant on three occasions. Various in-house or outsourced experts were contracted to identify and isolate any cause related to the issue, and to find the best solution for the repair, which ultimately led to the repair of the water leaks as they related to the boiler system on three separate occasions. I further note from the testimony provided these three incidents while all relate to water leaks and the boiler system, were not related and could not be predicted or prepared for in advance by the Landlords as alleged by the Tenant, on a balance of probabilities.

In the matter before me, I find that the Landlord acted reasonably and relied on the various staff and experts contracted to investigate the leak issues particularly in regards to January 21, 2024, leak, and the ultimate repair of the issues related to pressure in the boiler system. As such, the Tenant is not entitled to a remedy for this application.

I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2; T6 application is dismissed. July 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Peterborough Housing Corporation (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant’s applications were heard by videoconference on February 3, 2026 and May 28, 2026. The Tenant, The Tenant’s Legal Representative, Tiffany Badour, the Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘RV’), the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘ZH’), attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the applications are dismissed. The Applications
The Tenant’s applications, being a T2 Application about Tenant Rights (the ‘T2 Application’) and a T6 Tenant Application about Maintenance (the ‘T6 Application’), were filed on May 30, 2024.

The Tenant filed a request to amend the applications on or about October 15, 2025. The amendments were completed to narrow the issues in the applications and were done in accordance with the LTB Rules of Procedure and/or as directed by the Board. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not oppose the amendments. Accordingly, the request to amend the applications was granted.

In summary, the applications alleged the following: T2 Application • the Landlord, Landlord’s agent or superintendent substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by failing to adequately address the Tenant’s complaints of second-hand smoke; • the Landlord, Landlord’s agent or superintendent harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by failing to address various maintenance issues and failing to provide the Tenant with a copy of security footage she required for an investigation after being assaulted by an ex-partner; T6 Application • the Landlord failed to resolve the following issues/items in the rental unit that were in a state of disrepair and/or required maintenance: - bathroom fan was not strong enough which allowed moisture to remain and led to mould growth; - rusted plumbing fixtures and/or bathroom accessories and jewelry; and - cracks in the ceiling. Tenant’s Evidence

At the hearing, the Tenant only gave evidence on two main issues in her applications, being second-hand smoke and the bathroom ventilation. Accordingly, the other allegations are dismissed. Second-hand Smoke

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in or around February 2021. The residential complex was supposed to be a smoke free building. However, approximately 3 months after moving in, she started experiencing second-hand smoke coming from a neighbouring unit and contacted RV to report it. The Tenant stated she was asked to continue to make her complaints in writing and to provide dates and times when she would smell smoke. The Tenant did so for about a year. However, she ultimately stopped sending complaints as RV began to accuse the Tenant of abusing her. The Tenant believed that the last complaint that she sent regarding second-hand smoke was in early 2024. However, she continued to smell smoke until she moved out in September 2025.

In response to the Tenant’s complaints of second-hand smoke, the Landlord gave the Tenant an air purifier. However, the Tenant found that it did not remove the second-hand smoke from the air and was not helpful. In addition, the Tenant was aware of the Landlord sending a letter to the tenant that was smoking and posting a notice to all tenants in the residential complex about not smoking in the building. The Tenant noted that she learned the Landlord gave the smoking tenant two N5 notices of termination through the disclosure of evidence process but that the Landlord never communicated this to her at the time they were served.

In addition to her neighbour smoking, the Tenant stated that other tenants or residents of the building would congregate around her parking spot outside and smoke, which she reported to the Landlord in 2023. In response, the Landlord offered the Tenant a different parking spot. However, the Tenant declined this as she is a person with a disability and her spot was close to the entrance of the residential complex. The Landlord also moved the bench that was close to the Tenant’s vehicle. However, this did little to help the situation as many of the smokers were in wheelchairs and did not use the bench.

Tenant stated that she experienced chronic migraines due to the second-hand smoke and that she obtained a doctor’s letter regarding this and provided it to the Landlord. She also testified that she required a puffer the last year that she lived in the unit due to the second- hand smoke. Bathroom Ventilation

The bathroom in the rental unit did not have any windows. The Tenant stated that, initially, there was no bathroom fan that she could turn on or off. Rather, there was some sort of air exchange system that she did not have any control of and there was a vent with a grate over it in the bathroom. The Tenant recalled noticing not long after moving in that her bathroom walls were sweating and that her jewelry was corroding and so she reported this to the Landlord. Later, in January 2024, after complaining to the Landlord on multiple occasions, the Tenant contacted the City of Peterborough (the ‘City’) to file a complaint. After this, a booster fan was finally installed. However, it did not work very well and accumulated dirt and debris. This also occurred with the vent to the air exchange system. The Tenant testified that she did not vacuum out or otherwise clean the vent or booster fan as this was the Landlord’s responsibility.

The Tenant obtained a copy of the complaint record through a freedom of information request, which was tendered as evidence at the hearing. According to the records obtained, a complaint was received by the City on January 8, 2024. The Tenant stated that she met with someone from the City on January 17, 2024 regarding the bathroom ventilation not working properly. In the comment section of the records obtained, the City staff wrote that it appeared that the exhaust fan in the bathroom was not functioning and photos were shown of mold and that the shower rod, soap hanger, etc. were rusted. It also stated that the shower [name] was damaged and the exhaust fan was filled with dirt and debris. The aforesaid complaint was noted as closed on August 21, 2024 in the records obtained and stated that all repairs requested had been completed. Landlord’s Evidence Second-hand Smoke
RV is the Resident Services Manager for the residential complex.

RV acknowledged receiving complaints about second-hand smoke from the Tenant. She described the complaints as sporadic and stated that it was very difficult getting information about the smoking from the Tenant and that often things like the dates, times or where the smoke was coming from would be missing from the Tenant’s complaint.

RV recalled providing the Tenant with an air purifier and stated that it was specifically for smoke. She testified that community wide notices were given regarding smoking not being permitted in the residential complex and that the tenant who was believed to be smoking was served with a total of three N5 notices of termination. The notices of termination being served on the smoking tenant were not initially shared with the Tenant due to privacy reasons.

RV testified that she believed that the issues with the smoking tenant had been fully and finally resolved based on inspections done in that unit and feedback from other tenants. In addition, no further complaints were received from the Tenant.

With respect to smoking that was taking place close to the Tenant’s parking spot, RV stated she did not receive complaints about this issue until April 2024 and explained that it was a smoke free building but not a smoke free property. In this regard, tenants could smoke outside provided that they were far away enough from the building, which is approximately 9ft or 30 meters. RV testified that, in response to the Tenant’s complaints of smoking near her parking spot, RV moved the cigarette disposal to another spot, removed the park bench that was near the Tenant’s parking spot, and offered her two different parking spots that were close to the building entrance. Bathroom Ventilation

ZH is a Technical Service Coordinator for the Landlord. He stated that the Residential Complex is equipped with an ERV system, which is a mechanical ventilation system that exchanges indoor air with fresh outdoor air. This system runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

ZH testified that there was a grill in the bathroom ceiling of the rental unit and its purpose was to continuously draw air out of the unit. The more dust and dirt that accumulates on the grill, the less air can go through it. If air is not being evacuated, moisture is held in the air. ZH stated that tenants are required to clean the grills and that this does not form part of his regular duties. Tenants can simply vacuum the grill to clean it and are not required to take the grill off.

ZH stated that a complete bathroom fan was installed, which had an independent duct system that was vented outside directly, as a specific accommodation for the Tenant’s unit. He explained that, similar to the ERV grill, if the bathroom fan becomes clogged with dirt, it would become less effective.
ZH was present when the by-law officer from the City attended and ZH testified that he did not see any mould present in the unit at the time.

RV stated that there was no mould in the rental unit and that property standards did not advise that there was mould in the unit. Rather, that is what the Tenant told the property standards inspector.

RV testified that, the results of unit inspections indicated a lack of cleaning the grills to the vents as causing reduced ventilation and that this is something that the Tenants are expected to clean and are aware of. However, she did arrange for a contractor to clean the bathroom grate on February 2, 2024 because of the Tenant’s complaints.

RV testified that she ultimately had a very expensive ventilation system installed in the bathroom, after enduring several months of email attacks from the Tenant. In this regard, she received approximately 84 emails from the Tenant wherein the Tenant used profanity and threatened RV’s employment. RV stated she installed the fan hoping that it would appease the Tenant. However, it did not and so the Tenant was issued a warning letter and later N5 notices of termination. The intent was not to stop the Tenant from complaining but rather to stop her from being abusive and threatening toward RV. Ultimately, the matter was scheduled for a hearing before the Board but it was resolved through a consent order wherein the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy. Analysis T2 Application

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that the Landlord did not: i) substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; or ii) harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.

The evidence suggests that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint of second- hand smoke in a reasonable time and manner. The Landlord contacted the smoking tenant, sent warning letters and served them with notices of termination. The Landlord also provided the Tenant with an air purifier. The Tenant acknowledged that she stopped making complaints about the smoking tenant in early 2024 and so I do not find it unreasonable for the Landlord to assume that the issue had resolved.

Although the Tenant argues that she stopped complaining because the Landlord accused her of abusing RV and tried to have her evicted, in reviewing LTB file no. LTB-L-043633- 25, it does not appear that the Landlord took any steps to commence eviction proceedings until service of the first N5 notice of termination in February 2025. In light of this, the timelines do not appear to overlap or align with the Tenant’s version of events.

With respect to the outdoor smoking issue, the evidence suggests that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints in a reasonable time and manner and offered the Tenant a reasonable accommodation. It was unclear why the Tenant would not accept a different parking spot as a solution when that parking spot would have been just as close if not closer to the building than the one she had. T6 Application
Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet its obligations under section 20 of the Act.

There was no evidence to suggest that the Landlord’s ERV system was in a state of disrepair or not functioning properly. In this regard, a report from the Landlord’s contractor was tendered as evidence and put to the Tenant during cross examination. The report stated that the unit was inspected on January 11, 2024 and it was determined that the ERV system was running at 100%. Thereafter, the Landlord had the grills and/or vent covers in bathroom cleaned on February 2, 2024 to try and increase the ventilation.

Although additional moisture or humidity was noted in the unit by the Tenant and by one of the Landlord’s contractors when the unit was inspected on July 11, 2024, there was no evidence of it causing mould or rust as alleged by the Tenant. In this regard, the Tenant did not provide any photos or reports to support her position that there was mould or rust in the unit. Moreover, the contractor’s email that was tendered as evidence regarding the inspection on July 11, 2024 specifically stated that there was no mould visible.

To try and resolve the Tenant’s complaints and reduce the humidity levels in the unit that were noted by the Landlord’s contractor, the Landlord had a complete bathroom fan system installed in or around July 23, 2024 that was independent of the ERV system. Although the Tenant stated that the addition of the bathroom fan did not improve her situation she did not provide any reports, photos or any other documentary evidence to support her position that it was not working properly or was in a state of disrepair.

During the hearing it was suggested by the Tenant that the Landlord failed to maintain the ERV system and bathroom fan because the Landlord did not clean the grills and/or vent covers which resulted in reduced efficiency. I disagree. Vacuuming and/or wiping off dust and dirt from a grill and/or vent cover is part of ordinary cleanliness which the Tenant is responsible for under section 33 of the Act.
For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 57 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: [address] Ottawa ON [name] (the 'Tenants ') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was heard by videoconference on June 17, 2026. The Tenants and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenants the total amount of $10,048.00 on or before August 20, 2026. Agreed Facts

The following facts are agreed upon by the parties: • On July 31, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 Notice of Termination, with a termination date of September 30, 2024, as they claimed that the Landlord needed the rental unit for the purposes of their own residential occupation (hereafter referred to as the ‘N12 Notice’), as it appears from a copy of the N12 Notice (DOC-6076331; Exhibit 1). • The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on September 15, 2024, as a result of being served the N12 Notice. • The Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent within one year of the Tenants moving out of the rental unit and proceeded to enter into a tenancy agreement with respect to the rental unit with someone other than t he Tenants , as it appears from the screenshots of the online advertisements of the rental unit taken by the Tenants on March 5, 2025 ( [name], DOC -5738406, DOC -5738410, DOC -5738415, DOC-5738354, DOC-5738360, DOC-5738368; [name], in bundle). • The rental unit was built and occupied for residential purposes, for the first time, prior to November 15, 2018. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

As stated above, the Landlord is not disputing that they advertised the rental unit for rent within one year of the tenants moving out as a result of being served an N12 Notice. The Landlord’s position, however, is that the N12 Notice was served in good faith to the Tenants and that a change of circumstances led to the property being advertised for rent.

Pursuant to subsection 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice … and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1) (a) of the Act establishes a three-part test. In order to be successful in their application, the Tenants must establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • First, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 Notice) in bad faith; • Second, that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice or Board order based on the N12 Notice; and • Third, that the person named in the N12 Notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant s to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was advertised for rent - within one (1) year of the Tenants vacating the rental unit - creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith.1 1 Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Accordingly, on the basis of the undisputed evidence and submissions before me, I find that the presumption of bad faith pursuant to subsection 57(5) of the Act is engaged and that the Landlord is therefore required to prove their good faith on a balance of probabilities. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that they purchased the rental unit in 2022. They had visited the premises on a few different occasions, and were aware of the layout of the rental unit, prior to serving the N12 Notice to the Tenants.

The Landlord indicated that after serving the Tenants with the N12 Notice, the Tenants provided the Landlord with an N9 Notice of Termination with a termination date of September 15, 2025 (hereafter referred to as the N9 Notice), as it appears from a copy of the N9 Notice ([name]; Exhibit 3).
The Landlord stated that they accepted the N9 Notice and proceeded to pay the Tenants compensation equal to one month’s rent.

The Landlord indicated that upon the Tenants vacating the rental unit, they proceeded to clean the premises and use the rental unit intermittently , between one (1) to two (2) nights per weeks, based on their need to be closer to their clinic (which is located between three and five kilometres away from the rental unit) during nights shifts where they were on-call.

The Landlord explained that they always intended to use the rental unit intermittently, based on their work requirements and commitments. They never intended to have their family move into the premises with them, nor did they intend to permanently relocate from their primary residence.

The Landlord stated that they conducted minor renovations to the rental unit as of the month of January 2025, such as painting and cleaning the basement. These renovations lasted a “couple of months.”
The Landlord indicated that the rental unit was not up to the “standard” they were looking for when considering a longer-term occupancy.
The Landlord stated that they elected to proceed with renovating the rental unit when they deemed the premises to be inconvenient to their needs.
The Landlord clarified that the aforementioned inconvenience was related to the fact the laundry facilities were located in the basement area, as opposed to the upper-level.
The Landlord indicated that upon the completion of their renovations , the rental unit was subdivided into two (2) distinct residential units, namely an upper-level unit and a basement unit.
The Landlord stated that between the months of January 2025, and March 2025, they would alternate between using the upper -level and the basement based on the ongoing status of the renovations.

The Landlord asserted that they stopped using the basement unit for their own use during the month of April 2025. At that point, they started occupying the upper -level unit until the month of October 2025.

The Landlord clarified that their use of the premises had to change as they proceeded to rent the basement unit to new tenants towards the end of the month of April 2025. They then also rented the upper-level unit to new tenants as of October 16, 2025.
The Landlord indicated that prior to moving out of the rental unit, the Tenants’ lawful monthly rent was in the amount of $2,665.00.

The Landlord stated that the lawful monthly rent for the new basement tenants was in the amount of $2,100.00 as of the month of April 2025, and that the lawful monthly rent for the new tenants of the upper -level unit was in the amount of $3,300.00 as of the month of October 2025.

The Landlord submits that they did not act in bad faith and that their acceptance of the N9 Notice and the fact that they provided the Tenants with compensation equal to one month’s rent is demonstrative of them acting in good faith.

Under cross -examination, the Landlord indicated that while the online advertisements suggested that new tenants could move into the rental unit as of April 1, 2025 (Exhibit 2), they were still using the basement at that time.
Under cross -examination, the Landlord stated while new tenants took possession of the upper-level unit on October 1, 2025, their official move-in date was October 16, 2025.
Under cross-examination, the Landlord indicated that they stopped using the upper -level premises towards the end of September 2025.
Under cross -examination, the Landlord stated that their idea to renovate the rental unit materialized towards the end of 2024. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenant [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘V.D’) testified that during their tenancy, they had access to both the upper-level and the unfinished basement of the rental unit. They described the rental unit – during their tenancy - as having three (3) bedrooms in the upper- level, along with one (1) bedroom in the basement and two and half bathrooms, as it appears from the pictures of the rental unit taken by V.D during the month of September 2024 (DOC-7274709; Exhibit 4).

V.D indicated that when comparing pictures taken in September 2024 (Exhibit 4) to the screenshots of the online advertisements taken in March 2025 (Exhibit 2), it is apparent that the premises were significantly different.

V.D stated that they are a building inspector by trade, and have experiences with renovations such as the one undertaken by the Landlord. They characterized the work done by the Landlord as being fairly exhaustive.

V.D indicated that as the Tenants had ties to the community, they would visit the neighbourhood surrounding the rental unit after moving out. They noticed that renovations to the rental unit had begun during the month of December 2024.

V.D stated that as they were hoping to find alternate housing accommodations in the same neighbourhood, they were conducting online searches in this regard, which led them to finding that the Landlord had separated the rental unit into two separate units (Exhibit 2).

V.D indicated that prior to being served the N12 Notice, the Landlord had asked to meet with the Tenants on July 25, 2024. During this meeting, the Landlord had requested to increase the monthly rent from $2,665.00 to $3,500.00.

V.D stated that the Tenants had advised the Landlord that they would refuse a rent increase to $3,500.00, as it appears from a copy of the text message sent by the Tenants to the Landlord on July 30, 2024, at 4:13pm (DOC-7274702; Exhibit 5).

The Tenant [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘E.G.D’) testified that the Tenants occupied the rental unit with their two (minor children). They had been residing in the same neighbourhood since 2020, and moved into the rental unit in 2022.
E.G.D indicated that the Landlord gave them the N12 Notice in close proximity to the start of their children’s new academic term.

E.G.D stated that they were unable to secure alternate housing accommodations in the same neighbou rhood based on their budget requirements. The Tenants were therefore required to leave their community, move to Gatineau, and find a new school for their children at the last-minute. These were not things they were expecting nor intending to do prior to being served the N12 Notice.
E.G.D indicated that based on the different school requirements between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, they had to change their children’s schooling arrangements.

E.G.D stated t hat to accommodate their younger child’s school needs , they required the intervention of a psychologist to justify their admittance in a Quebec -based kindergarten. They were able to obtain a spot in a kindergarten for their child, at the onset of the academic year.
E.G.D indicated that they faced a lot of stress and anxiety in relation to having to change the schools, and other provincial services, such as driver licences, and health cards.

E.G.D stated that the Tenants also lost their family physician as a result of their move to [name]. They are currently on a waitlist to obtain a family doctor in the province of Quebec, which has impeded their ability to follow-up with their child’s asthma diagnosis.
V.D further indicated that the cost of life in Quebec , along with the taxes , are higher in Quebec than they are in Ontario.

V.D stated t hat prior to their move as a result of the N12 Notice, they were working on construction projects, between Kanata and Ottawa. Due to the long commute stemming from their move to Gatineau, they were required to change jobs.

The Tenants submit that they were served the N12 Notice in bad faith as the Landlord’s true intention was to increase the rent beyond the requisite guideline. The Tenants’ long-term intent is to return to the province of Ontario.

The Tenants therefore seek general compensation in the amount of $ 31,980.00 (which represents the equivalent of the monthly rent of $2,665.00 for twelve months) as a result of the stress and non-pecuniary they have endured as a result of their move related to the N12 Notice.

Under cross -examination, V.D reiterated that the Tenants’ intent was to continue their tenancy, and that they only proceeded to move to Gatineau due to budgetary constraints following the Landlord providing them with the N12 Notice.
The Landlord did not seek to ask any question to E.G.D under cross-examination. Analysis

It is not in dispute that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of being served the N12 Notice by the Landlord, pursuant to subsection 48(1) of the Act, which reads as follows: 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located. [Emphasis added]

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Landlord did not serve the Tenants the N12 Notice in good faith. Indeed, the Landlord’s own testimony revealed that they never intended to relocate to the rental unit with their family on a permanent basis, and instead only sought to use the rental unit in order to reduce the costs of their temporary stays in the neighbourhood to accommodate their work schedule.

The Landlord’s recognition that they only used the rental unit for one (1) to two (2) nights per week for less than one year draws a stark contrast to what one would consider “residential occupation.” In fact, the Landlord’s use and occupation of the rental unit until the month of September 2025 can only be considered as being “infrequent” or “occasional” rather than a residential2.

Furthermore, while the Landlord may have originally sought to increase the Tenants’ rent to alleviate their financial burden related to their work commitment s, I find that the Landlord 2 Kohen v. Warner, 2018 ONSC 3865. sought to terminate the tenancy as a direct result of the Tenants refusing to comply with the Landlord’s proposed illegal rent increase, through which they sought to increase the rent from $2,665.00 to $3,500.00 which would have represented an increase of over 31% . For context, the rent increase permitted under the Act in 2024 was equivalent to 2.5%.3

The Landlord did not dispute the authenticity of the test message sent to them by the Tenants on July 30, 2024 (Exhibit 5) and served them with the N12 Notice the very next day (i.e. July 31, 2024). The extreme proximity between the date that the Tenants sought to exercise their lawful rights ( i.e. not to be subjugated to an unlawful rent increase) and the date the Landlord served the Tenants the N12 Notice does not lend any credence to the Landlord’s self-proclaimed intent they were acting in good faith.

Indeed, while the Landlord suggested that the application ought to be dismissed as their good faith would have been demonstrated by them accepting the N9 Notice which reflected an earlier termination date than the one listed on the N12 Notice, and by providing the Tenants with compensation equal to one month’s rent, I note that the Landlord actually has a statutory obligation to provide such compensation to the Tenants 4, and that the Tenants were within their rights to seek to terminate the tenancy prior to the date specified in the N12 Notice.5 The Landlord abiding by these mandatory statutory requirements does not automatically translate to them acting in good faith. I afford no weight to the Landlord’s submissions in this regard.

Moreover, I did not find credible that the Landlord only came to discover that the rental unit was not suitable to their needs after the Tenants had vacated the rental unit. Indeed, the Landlord anchored their inability to continue occupying the rental unit to the fact that the laundry facilities were located in the basement area. The Landlord had recognized that they acquired the rental unit in 2022 (on or around two years prior to serving the Tenants with the N12 Notice) and that they were familiar with the layout of the premises. If they had genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit for their residential occupation, they ought to have been far more diligent in ensuring that the premises were suitable to their needs prior to seeking to terminate the Tenants’ tenancy through no fault of their own.

Pursuant to the Landlord’s submissions, I do not find that the location of the laundry facilities, which were well-known to the Landlord prior to them serving the N12 Notice, to equate to a change of circumstances that would lead the Landlord successfully rebut the presumption under subsection 57(5) of the Act.

In fact, by proceeding with their renovations and converting the premises into two (2) separate and distinct unit s which were subsequently rented to new tenants, the Landlord increased their rental income from $2,665.00 to $5,400.00, which represents an increase of over 200% per month.

Pursuant to the evidence and submissions before me, I find that i t is more likely than not that the Landlord served the Tenants with the N12 Notice as part of a scheme that they had 3 Section 120 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 4 Sections 48.1 and 55.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 5 Subsections 48(3) and 48(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. devised to unduly enrich themselves upon the Tenants seeking to exercise their lawful rights under the Act.
Accordingly, I find that t he Landlord failed to meet the burden of proof to rebut the presumption of bad faith, and therefore conclude that the N12 Notice was given in bad faith.
Consequently, I find that the Tenants are entitled to compensation. Remedies

Paragraph 57(3)1.1) of the Act authorizes the Board to order general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of twelve (12) months of the last rent charged to the Tenants, should it be determined the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. In this instance, the Tenants claimed the amount of $31,980.00. This amount was calculated as follows: $2,665.00 x12 months.

Although the term “general compensation” is not defined under the Act, such compensation is understood as being related to “damages that cannot be measured in money,” 6 and therefore that “cannot be easily ascertained because there is no fixed pecuniary standard of measurement.”7
For further clarity , and contrary to administrative fines, 8 general compensation is not a remedy intended to be punitive in nature.
I found the Tenants’ testimony with respect to the impact of the move to be cogent, consistent, and credible.

While the Landlord did not dispute the Tenants’ testimony, they submitted that they ought not be held liable for the Tenants’ administrative hurdles and complications related to a move between different provinces, I disagree. Indeed, the cascade of inconvenience faced by the Tenants, such as the stress and anxiety of moving in close proximity to the start of an academic term, the loss of a family physician treating a chronic illness, the change of employment due to unexpectedly longer commutes , and leaving behind a neighbou rhood and community that the Tenants had called their own for close to four (4) years, are a direct result of the Landlord serving the N12 Notice in bad faith in order to enact their scheme to unduly enrich themselves.

Although I find that general compensation in the amount of $31,980.00 would not be justified under the circumstances, having considered the evidence and submissions before me, including the length of the tenancy and the impact that the move had on the Tenant s and members of their household, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants compensation in the amount of $10,000.00.

The Tenants also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 6 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “nonpecuniary damages.” 7 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “irreparable damages.” 8 Paragraph 57(3)3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the total amount of $10,048.00, which represents: • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 2 0, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant for the moving costs and general damages.

In order to succeed on this application, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires the Tenant to prove the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The criteria set out above with respect to the legal test is an “and” list, meaning that each and every element of the list must be proven on a balance of probabilities.

There is no dispute between the parties about the first two elements of this test. The parties agree that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of that notice.
In response to that N12 notice, the parties negotiated an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy and the tenancy was terminated effective July 31, 2025.

The Landlord testified that he did not occupy the rental unit at any time after the Tenant vacated, although that was initially his intention when he served the Tenant with the N12 notice in January 2025.

The Landlord testified that he found the premises uninhabitable due to the presence of odors from cigarette smoke and the Tenant’s dogs. He wanted to clean the property and paint the home. The Landlord also identified deficiencies in the home that he wanted to remedy prior to moving in, including issues with the ceiling and cracks in the tiles. He initial plan was to replace the flooring, and renovate the bathrooms and kitchen in order to make the home more to his liking before he moved in.

The Landlord’s evidence was that, by September 2025, he had discovered even more deficiencies with the property, including puddling around the furnace and plumbing issues, as a result of which his renovation expenses would increase significantly. It was at this point, owing to a delayed move-in timeline and with potential additional renovation costs looming, that the Landlord decided he could no longer move into the home. He hired a realtor and put the home up for sale in the fall of 2025. The home sold a few weeks later. Presumption of Bad Faith

Pursuant to subsection 57(5)(c) of the Act, it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith if at any time during the period beginning on the day the landlord gives the said notice of termination and one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit, the landlord advertises the rental unit or the building that contains the rental unit for sale.

I would observe at this point, given the parties’ evidence, that the reverse onus provision in subsection 57(5)(c) of the Act applies to this situation. This provision means that, because there is evidence before me that, during the one year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit (the “Mariner property”), the Landlord advertised the said property for sale, the Landlord bears the burden of proof to establish that he did not serve the N12 notice in bad faith. For the following reasons, I find that the Landlord has not met this burden.

The Landlord served the Tenant with the N12 notice personally in January 2025, with a termination date of March 31, 2025. At the time of the N12 notice, the Landlord was living on his own in a home in the University Downs neighbourhood in [name]. He states that his intention was to downsize from his current home and move into the Mariner property.
He had been attending home shows for about a year at this time, in contemplation of renovating the Mariner property and had already started upgrades to his current home.

He testified that he lost his job about two and a half years ago (early 2024) at which point his income was cut off. His former employer paid him for a year and a half after that but he has not worked since and is now retired. The Landlord testified that the loss of his job, changes in his health and his overall age led him to want to downsize.

I am not persuaded, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord intended to downsize by relocating from his current home in University Downs to the Mariner property. The homes are similar in size, offered similar amenities, and are close in proximity to one another such that I am unable to accept that there would have been any meaningful reduction in space, maintenance or costs.

The Landlord testified that the Mariner property is similar to his current home, although the garage, kitchen and bedrooms in his current home are a little bit bigger. Both homes have 3 bedrooms. There are bathrooms on the main floor of each home with additional bathrooms on the upper level. There is one big open space in the basement of the Mariner property, while at his current home the big open space is found in one of the bedrooms. The space on the main floor of both homes is open concept. He lives alone and this was not expected to change in the future.

The scope of the renovations undertaken at the Mariner property, and the anticipated reasonable cost of such renovations, is inconsistent with the Landlord’s testimony that he was downsizing for financial reasons after having lost his job. He testified that he was relying on his payout money and a line of credit to fund the renovations.

Between January 2025 and May 2025, when the N11 agreement was signed by the parties, the Landlord attended at the Mariner property approximately 2-3 times to inspect the unit and determine what renovations were needed. He identified issues with the ceiling and determined that the kitchen, bathrooms and flooring needed to be replaced. His evidence was that he set an initial renovation budget of $25,000.00 at that time.

I am not persuaded on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord believed $25,000.00 was sufficient to complete the initially contemplated renovations at the Mariner property which included replacing the upstairs and downstairs bathrooms, a complete gut of the kitchen, replacing the flooring in the main room and painting the entire home. The selection of high- end materials for the renovation, including quartz in the kitchen and bathrooms, is also inconsistent with the initial budget and the Landlord’s reported financial constraints.

The Landlord testified that, by September, he realized he would need another $40,000.00 to $45,000.00 to finish the renovations. He had already replaced the patio stones and driveway which were not initially contemplated but he felt that there was value in doing the additional work. However, when he realized that more work was needed, he decided he did not want to put more money into a property where other unknown issues may be present and he decided to sell. He listed the property in October and sold it in November.

The Landlord did not advise the Tenant that he intended to list the property for sale. He did not attempt to contact the Tenant to discuss the possibility of the Tenant re-renting the unit. Such a step on the part of the Landlord would have demonstrated good faith. The Landlord testified that he did not consider this because he knew that the Tenant had purchased their own home by that point in Wingham. Earlier in the hearing, the Landlord raised concerns about the [name] address listed in the Tenant’s application and questioned the Tenant on whether they were renting at that property. I found this to be inconsistent with the Landlord’s explanation as to why he did not contact the Tenant when his circumstances changed and before he decided to list the Mariner property for sale.

I am similarly not persuaded that the Landlord planned to sell his University Downs property in order to move into the Mariner property. He testified that he had already began upgrading the University Downs home a few years before. He had been asked about his intentions to sell it, but he had not taken any proactive steps in this regard, including listing the property or speaking with a realtor to explore his options. His evidence was that he would have tried to sell his current home privately. I find this to be inconsistent with his decision to hire a realtor for the purpose of selling the Mariner property.

The Landlord testified that when he decided to sell the Mariner property, the market had turned. This too is inconsistent with the evidence before the Board that the Mariner property sold within a relatively short time.

Based on the evidence before me, and in light of the reverse onus that applies, I find that the Landlord has failed to provide sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption that he served the notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith. The Landlord never moved into the Mariner property; he did not take any meaningful steps to show that he was seriously contemplating selling his current home in order to downsize as alleged; he commenced renovations on the Mariner property almost immediately upon the Tenant vacating and listed the Mariner property for sale within less than 3 months thereafter. The order in which these events took place, the value which was added to the Mariner property by virtue of the renovations, the relative speed and efficiency within which the property was renovated, listed and sold, all work in tandem to support my conclusion.

For all of the reasons set out above, I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith and he has breached subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be granted. The Remedies

The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to award to the Tenant. The remedies the Tenant is requesting in the application are: an abatement of rent in the amount of $14,862.72, a rent differential for one year amounting to $14,862,72, out of pocket expenses for moving and storage costs and general compensation.

At the hearing, the Board sought to clarify the Tenant’s claim for a rent abatement, noting that abatement may be available for the period of time between when the Tenant received the N12 notice and when they vacated the unit, provided that the Tenant can show that they paid rent for a bundle of goods and services but they did not receive everything they paid for in which instance they may be entitled an to abatement proportional to the difference between what they paid for and what they received. Upon clarifying what this remedy was, the Tenant confirmed that they did not intend to seek a rent abatement and the Board consented to their request to withdraw that portion of the claim.

The Tenant also seeks $14,862.72 for a rent differential on the basis that they were paying monthly rent of $1,550.00 at the Mariner property whereas now they pay $2,788.56 per month in satisfaction of a mortgage at their current property. The amount they seek is the difference between the two monthly payments ($1,238.56) over a period of 12 months.
The Tenant confirmed that they own their current home and in fact make monthly mortgage, as opposed to rent, payments.

Section 57(3) of the Act sets out the types of orders that the Board may make on a Tenant’s successful application where notice was given in bad faith. This includes an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one year period after vacating the rental unit. The available remedies do not include a mortgage differential.

The relevant terms and their definitions are found in section 2 of the Act, including: “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, acc ommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, “rental unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises,

The Tenant was asked to provide submissions in support of their claim for a differential in the circumstances. In response, the Tenant said that they should be compensated for the significant disruption to their lives and the extra costs they are now incurring as part of their daily living, including the fact that they had to relocate 80 kms away and the additional expenses that come with that. While these considerations may be relevant to the Tenant’s claim for general damages, they do not support the claim for a differential.

I am not satisfied that the Board has authority to order the Landlord to pay any part of the [name] monthly mortgage payments. Had the legislature intended to empower the Board to compensate tenants for mortgage expenses in circumstances of this kind, it would have set that out clearly in the Act. In the absence of any caselaw permitting such a claim and in light of the clear language of section 57 and the relevant definitions set out in section 2 of the Act, such a claim cannot succeed.

The Tenant is not currently making monthly payments toward “rent” as contemplated by the Act; rather they are making monthly payments toward the satisfaction of their mortgage and each principal payment is equity in their home. The money is not being spent; rather it is being converted into real property and these amounts are something that the Tenant will be able to recover if and when they sell their current home.

To require the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant for mortgage payments would be unfair and would result in a windfall to the Tenant. Accordingly, there will be no order requiring the Landlord to pay any differential.
The Tenant also claims $2,178.75 for moving and storage related expenses.

The Tenant testified that their family of 6 had accumulated many items throughout the 8 years they lived at the Mariner property. The home had 3 bedrooms, a basement and a garage that they used for storage. When they were advised that they had to vacate, they did not initially know where they would move. The Tenant rented 24-foot storage units in order to store their possessions while they got ready to vacate and searched for a new place to live. The Tenant provided an invoice from Dundee Storage in the amount of $1,553.75 which confirmed storage fees charged between April and August 2025.

The Tenant also provided a U-Haul Equipment Contract which confirmed a one day truck rental to be picked up in [name] and dropped off in Wingham on July 31, 2025, which corresponds to their moving date. A charge of $425.72 was noted to the Tenant’s debit. As this was a different amount than what was claimed on the Tenant’s application, the Tenant was asked to provide submissions in this regard. The Tenant testified that the amount reflected as the charge to their debit was the amount that they paid for the truck rental.

I am satisfied based on the evidence before that the Tenant incurred reasonable moving expenses as a result of the N12 notice in the amount of $1,979.47, as supported by the invoice for the storage units and the debit charge for the truck rental. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant for those reasonable out of pocket expenses.

Finally, the Tenant claims $5,000 in general compensation on the basis that they experienced frustration and emotional distress, they had to relocate 82 km away from [name] and their jobs, their lives were disrupted and their living expenses increased as a result of the move.

Under the Act, the maximum that can be claimed is an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former Tenant. An order for this remedy may be made regardless of whether the Tenant has incurred any actual expenses.
I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the move was very stressful for their family.

The Tenant’s family lived at the Mariner property for 8 years. The evidence before me is that they all worked in the [name] area. The Tenant’s wife had worked in [name] for approximately 20 years; her employment was a 3 minute drive from the Mariner property. She still works at the same place but now commutes 5 days per week from Wingham to [name] and back, a daily distance of approximately 160 kms in total.

The Tenant claims for expenses relating to this commute, including the additional gas and mileage costs that they would not be incurring but for the relocation, the wear and tear on the vehicles and the loss of time which is now spent in the daily commute.

The Tenant’s daughters, who do not drive, left their jobs in [name] and found new jobs in [name] and Blyth respectively. Their son, who was commuting to Cambridge for work, also left to find a job closer to their current address. I accept that this move caused a reasonable disruption in the Tenants’ lives and resulted in distress at least in the initial period following the move given the significant changes in their location and their jobs.

The Tenant gave evidence that the family began looking for a new rental unit as soon as they received the N12 notice but they struggled to find a place to rent in the [name] area at a comparable price. Their evidence was that they were out looking at potential places every weekend, up to 3-4 times per day. Whatever rental options they did find, the Tenant testified were for double the rent compared to what they paid at the Mariner property.

They considered other options and met with a mortgage consultant who found them their current home. The Tenant testified that this was not an ideal situation as the house was a significant distance from where they had been living and it needed some work, but it was what they could afford. They had trouble securing a mortgage which is why the sale did not close until July 31, 2025, the same date that they were to vacate the Mariner property. The Tenant described stress associated with this situation as well, stating that the family was literally sitting in the garage of the Mariner property waiting to see if the sale on their new home had closed when the Landlord came to make sure that the unit had been swept up.

As a result, and for the reasons set out above, the Tenant has satisfied me that an award of $5,000.00 for general damages is reasonable for the stress, disruption to their lives and increased living expenses that the move has caused them.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,027.47. This amount represents: • $1,979.47 for the reasonable moving and storage expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
