issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
Upon Board questioning the Landlord submitted that the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application lack sufficient detail and particulars.

The Landlord’s position was that the application should be dismissed as the Tenant had not provided sufficient details and particulars of allegations other than generalities of spreading rumours and misinformation in the community about the Tenant’s and threats by the Landlord’s partner directed at the Tenant’s partner and an issue with the internet service. The Tenant had moved out of the rental unit in July 2025. Moreover, the Landlord has been put in the unfair situation of having to defend itself to an application containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are other than generalities of the allegations abovementioned, nor were there any remedies sought by the Tenant. Accordingly, it was submitted that the Tenant’s T2 application should be dismissed.

Upon Board questioning on why the Tenant had not provided sufficient details, she testified that she could not afford private counsel, and he was a layperson, but had reached out and received help from her local Legal Clinic.
The Tenant testified that she had amended her T2 application on or about November 27, 2025. The original T2 application was issued on June 13, 2025.

The Landlord testified that she never received the amended T2 application from the Tenant, the Tenant then testified it was in the evidence documents she provided the Landlord, and in any event, she had uploaded the email amending the T2 application to the Portal (TOP).

Uploading materials to TOP does not mean documents have been provided to another party unless there is an agreement in place and, here, there was no such agreement. On a balance of probabilities from the oral testimonies provided by the parties, I am of the view the Landlord had not been served the amended T2 application/email

It was determined upon Board review that the Tenant had emailed the Board on November 27, 2025, the email stated as follows: AMENDED T2 November 27, 2025 * Reason for filing this application… -entered our unit illegally on more than one occasion without ANY notice at all -changed the locks without contacting US or giving US a new copy of the key -Substantially interfered with my reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by disconnecting the internet (May) and shutting off the electricity (June) -Harassed and threatened to shut off hydro -Shut off hydro June 14, 2025 (day before unfiled N4 date would have been due) * We were forced to leave the apartment June 18th by the City as landlord refused to turn power back on * Hired moving company July 10th to move everything to Access Storage Unit as we still had no new apartment * Landlord served [name] an N11 to serve my husband [name] and I on moving day. * Landlord drilled through our lock to change locks on us June 18, 2025 to gain access to our apartment. Then landlord delivered new key to [name] and not us. No contact was made to us by landlord about any of this. * Loss of food in fridge and chest freezer pictures uploaded. Approx value $500 * Requesting that the landlord pay a fine to the LTB and RHEU. * Requesting the landlord pay our storage unit, moving costs which total $7066.26 * Requesting landlord reimburse us for food loss due to her shutting off power. $500 (pictures included) * Requesting landlord to pay for new door lock that she drilled through. $300 * Requesting landlord pay for the lodging we required from June 18th to August 11, 2025. $6853.74

The relevant parts of Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure state the following: 15.1 A request to amend an application before the hearing must be: a. in writing; b. served with the amended application to all other parties; and c. filed with LTB with the amended application and a completed Certificate of Service. 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors. 15.4 The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

Rule 15.3 specifically requires that a Board Member consider and then grant or deny any requested amendments. The Tenant did provide the aforementioned email requesting amendments be made to the contents of the Tenant’s T2 application and remedies to be included to the Board only on November 27, 2025 but had not served the Landlord an amended application nor filed with the LTB the amended application and nor did she file a completed Certificate of Service, as required under Rule 15.1.

Amendments are intended to correct an error, not include new issues that were not included in the original application. In my view, an amendment to include new issues that were not included in the original application and did not form the basis of the original application is an improper attempt to circumvent the established process in which parties advance their claims before the Board.

As a result of all of the above, I denied the Tenant’s request to amend the application. Moreover, even if I had accepted the Tenant’s amendments sought to the reasons of her T2 application, the reasons would still be devoid of sufficient details.

The Board can assist parties by providing general information as needed, however the Board does not act as a legal representative for either party and consequently, it is the Applicant’s, in this case the Tenant responsibility to ensure that the application is complete and in compliance with the Act. It was further noted to the Tenant that she could have contacted Tenant Duty Counsel whose contact information was listed on the Notice of Hearing for this herein proceeding. The Tenant did not seek an adjournment of this proceeding so that she could properly amend her T2 application pursuant to the Board’s Rules.

An application must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital [2022] O.J. No. 5931 that, “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, I am of the view the general principle regarding the need for particular and details apply equally to Tenant application. In this leading case, the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons an details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that they can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission….’’

The allegations toward the Landlord are lacking any semblance of details of said issues being pleaded by the Tenant. Moreover, evidence uploaded to the Portal by the Tenant was not introduced as evidence during the proceeding, but for the denied amendment request abovementioned, and hence did not provide sufficient particulars to support the Tenant’s allegations in her application, which the Landlord submitted were general statements, and devoid of detail.

I find the allegations in the Tenant’s application are vague and lack any context in terms of details. Specifically, the “Reasons for filing this Application” section of the application instructs the applicant to describe what happened, the dates and times of the events, who caused the problem and the names and titles of all people involved, which the Tenant has not done in a way that the Landlord could properly comprehend the issues at hand.

On the T2 application there are simply statement and description that the Tenant and her partner had been threatened by the Landlord’s partner, and further the Landlord and her partner were spreading misinformation about them in the community and further the internet service had ceased for a time being, devoid of sufficient detail.

It is not for the Landlord or the Board to assist the Tenant in completing her application or correcting deficiencies. As with all applications before the Board, it is the applicant who must bring an application that meets minimum requirements. However, the undersigned noted to the Tenant if she chooses to bring another application she should seek out legal counsel whether privately or by contacting [name], if the time limitations of the Act permit.

The Landlord’s right to present a meaningful defence in a timely fashion must also be taken into consideration. The application does not contain sufficient details on the alleged grounds that would allow the matter to be fairly heard.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application were not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met to and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at the hearing, and effectively would have experienced significant prejudice if expected to present a defence against unknown, generalized allegations. Moreover, the Tenant did not seek a further opportunity to adjourn this herein matter to properly amend said application.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $444.76.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I make the following findings of fact. 1. The rental unit is a room in a second-floor apartment of a house, with a shared kitchen, living room, and bathroom. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2026. 2. At 5:00 AM on June 4, 2025, the Tenant was in the shared bathroom. A neighbouring tenant came to the bathroom as well and started an argument. The Tenant left the building and called the police, who did not take action against the neighbouring tenant.

When the Tenant returned to the rental unit around 7:00 AM, he found that the locks to his room door were changed. The Tenant went to buy a new lock around 8:30 AM and had to make arrangements at work to arrive late. The Tenant regained access to the rental unit around 10:00 AM that same day after changing the room lock. The Tenant purchased a new lock for $32.76.
On September 19, 2025, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice to unclog the kitchen sink.
On December 20, 2025, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice.

During the months of January and February 2025, the Landlord did not sufficiently clear the snow. The Tenant had to clean the snow himself regularly so avoid the driveway and parking lot becoming obstructed. 3. On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on June 4, 2025, September 19, 2025, and December 20, 2025. I find that, on June 4, 2025, the Landlord altered the locking system on the rental unit door without giving the Tenant replacement keys. I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by failing to clean snow in January and February 2025. Therefore, the application is granted. 4. The Tenant testified that the illegal lockout and entries negatively affected his peace of mind. He felt uncomfortable living in the rental unit because he was unsure of when someone may show up unannounced. The lack of snow removal caused blockages and conflicts between the tenants and forced the Tenant to clean the snow himself. 5. I find a 10% rent abatement for two months to be appropriate for the snow removal issue as this affected the Tenant’s use of the parking area. I find a $200.00 rent abatement to be appropriate for the lockout and illegal entries. Although the Tenant indicated that he felt uncomfortable living in the unit, he was able to regain access to the unit quickly on June 4, 2025. The Landlord’s entries to the common areas did not appear to cause a significant disturbance for the Tenant. 6. The Tenant requested $60.00 for lost wages, which are not an out-of-pocket expense. This request is dismissed. However, I am satisfied that the Tenant purchased a new lock for $32.76, which the Landlord will be required to reimburse.

The Tenant also requested $1,000.00 in general compensation. This request is dismissed as the Tenant did not lead sufficient evidence to support a finding that he experienced distress above and beyond the loss of reasonable enjoyment.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $444.76. This amount represents: • $364.00 for a rent abatement. • $32.76 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the amount of $2,648.00 by July 24, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of Tenant, [name] [name] (AC)

AC testified that she was notified on April 16, 2026 through the Landlord’s realtor that the Landlord would be listing the rental house for sale. The Tenant stated that they moved into the unit on November 1, 2024 and that the lease was for a period of 2 years.

The Tenant stated that she was asked if she wanted to purchase the house in April of 2026 but she was not in a financial position to do so as she and her husband were expecting their second child in September of 2026. The realtor also advised her that he would assist her with finding another rental unit.

Ms. [name]name] stated that she began looking for another residence as she did not want to have to relocate after their second child was born. Further on April 20, 2026, the Landlord’s realtor stated to her “I would say find something and move and I will convince the Landlord to sell when you are out so that you don’t have to deal with showings.”

The Tenant stated that she continued to look for another residence and then on May 12, 2026, the realtor stated that the Landlord wanted to list the house for sale “sooner rather than later”. She stated that she had a telephone call with the realtor the following day who confirmed that if she moved out by May 31, 2026 she would not have to pay June’s rent and would receive her last month’s rent deposit.

Ms. [name]name] stated that after moving out, the Landlord refused to return the last month’s rent after she emailed him and the Landlord’s realtor. She provided a copy of text messages between the Landlord’s realtor and herself. Evidence of Landlord, [name] (CS)
CS testified that the Tenant only advised him that she would be vacating the unit on May 13, 2026 and that he had not been given 60 days’ notice which was why he retained the last month’s rent.
The Landlord stated that despite the fact that he was selling the house, the Tenant could have stayed until November of 2026 or later and that she did not have to leave. Analysis

Section 134(1.1) of the Act provides: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit, or b)any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.

The text messages between the Tenant and the Landlord’s realtor confirmed that the Landlord provided notice advising that he would be listing the house for sale. The Landlord’s realtor and the Tenants had an agreement whereby the Tenant could vacate by the end of May and the last month’s rent deposit would be returned. As such, the tenancy terminated on May 31, 2026.

Further, the Landlord provided notice to the Tenant that he would be listing the house for sale and the realtor encouraged the Tenant to vacate the house as early as possible. This could be interpreted as the Landlord serving an N12 notice of termination to the Tenant but fortunately for the Landlord, the Tenant did not push that interpretation. It is however unfortunate for the Tenant that this application was necessary in the circumstances.
Based on the Landlord’s notice of termination and the agreement between the Landlord’s realtor and the Tenant, the tenancy terminated on May 31, 2026.
As such, the Tenant is entitled to the return of her last month’s rent deposit and her application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,648.00. This amount represents: • $2,600.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The parties had been before the Board on a prior occasion on a T2 application (File LTB- T-017094-22). The hearing was held on October 16, 2023, and the Board issued the order on November 7, 2023. The order dismissed the Tenants’ application finding that the Landlord had acted reasonably in the circumstances.

At paragraph 3, the order refers to the Tenants’ T5 application and notes that the two applications contained identical remedies, stating: “The Tenants’ Legal Representative requested to withdraw the other remedies and proceed with only the claim for the property the Landlord allegedly disposed of….No change to the substance of the allegations in the application was made and no new evidence was submitted. The application proceeded with the Tenants’ claim for costs to repair or replace the Tenants’ property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlord.”
The Tenants’ Legal Representative submits that the Tenants’ request to withdraw the claim for property, and plans to move forward on a Board fine, rent differential, and general compensation.
The Landlord did not make any submissions.
Given that the request does not prejudice the Landlord, I granted the Tenants’ request to amend their application to remove the request for property-related claims. Tenants’ T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 8. [name] states that in 2018, he was a university student attending school in Ontario. He received word from the Saudi government that he and his family would have to return to Saudi. Returning would have resulted in AAS being unable to finish his university degree. Rather than do that, he chose to explore other options which would allow him to remain in Canada. 9. Sometime around September or October of 2019, the Landlord advised AAS that he wanted to move back into the rental unit, and in December 2019, the Landlords told them that they needed to leave in January 2020. 10. However, [name] and his family did not move out. It was not until April 1, 2021, that the Tenants finally moved. [name] says that between September/October 2019, through March 2021, the Landlord persistently asked them to move out and sent them countless listings during this time for other properties. 11. The Tenants submit that although they were not given an N12 notice of termination, the persistent bothersome listings and the demand the Tenants leave in January 2020 equated to the Landlord giving the Tenants an N12 notice of termination. Were the Tenants given an N12 notice of termination? 12. Typically, when a landlord wants to reoccupy a residential rental unit, they are required to use a Board-approved form pursuant to s. 43 of the Act. There is no dispute that the Landlord did not give the Tenants the Board approved notice known as an N12. 13. However, I must consider what information ought to be present in the form. Pursuant to s.43, the information that must be contemplated is that the rental unit is identified, the date on which the tenancy is to terminate must be specified, and it must be signed by the parties or agents. 14. The problem here is that there is no equivalent document. AAS’s verbal testimony was that the Landlord told the Tenants they needed to leave “in January.” I can find that this is clear enough to identify the rental unit as it would be absurd that this statement would be attributed to any other rental unit in this case. However, there is no written document nor is there a specific date on which the tenancy was to terminate. In my view, this statement does not meet the test as found in s.57(1)(a) of the Act. 15. Further still, even if I was to find that the oral statement constituted a notice to terminate the tenancy, the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit until well over a year later in April 2021. This then challenges the second part of the test found in s.57(1)(a), because there is no clear nexus between the Landlord’s oral statement made in December 2019 and the Tenants vacating the rental unit 17 months later. 16. [name] pointed to multiple listings of rental housing and properties for sale that he was sent by the Landlord to support the submission that the test in s.57 was “triggered” by the oral statement in December. 17. I am not persuaded by this argument. The Landlord testified that he is a realtor and that AAS frequently asked him about purchasing and renting property. He also brought prospective tenants to the Landlord. This statement was corroborated by AAS’ own testimony. So the Landlord was sending listings because, as a realtor, he had set up automatic delivery to AAS of properties that met his desired factors. It was not, as AAS suggested, that the Landlord sat there pestering him every time any kind of rental property was available. Further still, many of the properties the Landlord sent were for purchase, not rent. This contradicts the Tenants’ evidence that he was being bombarded by listings for other rental units. 18. The Landlord submitted copies of text messages between the parties which corroborated that many of the listings sent were in response to AAS’s requests. Therefore, I do not find that the Landlord was attempting to put undue pressure on the Tenants to move out by sending them various realtor listings. Rather, I find that the Landlord was acting in a way consistent with being a realtor and sending information to interested parties. 19. I am also of the view that the Landlord’s oral statement, which was contested, amounts to giving the Tenants a notice of termination. An oral statement with a vague termination date does not constitute notice either as required pursuant to s.43 or s.48 of the Act. 20. The Tenant provided several pieces of caselaw to the Board. However, none are binding, and most do not fit the circumstances before me. For example, omitted details can form part of the notice if they were provided verbally. However, there is no written notice in this case at all (CET-74019-18). Other cases made distinct reference to a specific termination date (SOT-0241819; TET-84356-17). None of the cases suggested that an oral statement without a termination date constitutes notice under the Act. 21. In closing submissions, the Tenants also requested that I consider amending the Tenants’ T5 application to include a T2 application for substantial interference because of the Landlord having peppered the Tenants with listings and having told the Tenants he wanted to occupy the rental unit. 22. The Landlord contests this request because no notice was provided in advance that the Tenants would be seeking to amend their application. 23. I am not of the view it is appropriate to amend the Tenants’ application. The Tenants were before the Board with a T2 application based on the same facts. The Tenants’ Legal Representative opted at that time to withdraw all claims except for the furniture claim. In my view, it is an abuse of process to now allow the Tenants a second chance to bring forward a claim that ought to have been included and adjudicated on at the original T2 hearing. Further, I find it would be prejudicial to allow the Tenants to amend their application given that the Tenants did not amend their application nor provide any notice of their intention to request an amendment until closing submissions.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,050.00

The T1 application alleges that the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord, but the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to move into the rental unit and did not return the Tenant’s deposit money.

The Tenant testified that in response to the Landlord’s advertisement for the rental unit, he called the Landlord, entered into a tenancy agreement and provided the last month’s rent deposit of $1,050.00 in installments on May 1, 2025, April 6, 2025, and April 17, 2025. The Tenant submitted financial documentation as evidence to substantiate the same.

The Tenant testified that when he arrived to move into the rental unit on April 30, 2025, the date they parties agreed the Tenant could move into the rental unit, even though the tenancy was to begin on May 1, 2025, the Landlord was not there as had been agreed upon between the parties. The Landlord did not pick up her telephone nor did she answer her door.

The Tenant further testified that he was able to contact the Landlord by telephone later that evening, and he was advised she was no longer responsible for the rental unit and that he should forget about his last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant testified he was an internationally student, had gone to the police who advised to bring an application to the Board, and that he felt bamboozled by the Landlord. The Tenant further demanded his deposit returned and the Landlord refused on multiple occasions.
The Tenant testified that he has never received his deposit of $1,050.00 back from the Landlord. Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') states: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The Tenant provided compelling testimony and corroborating evidence of his deposit payment and his dealings with the Landlord. I am satisfied, based on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not give vacant possession to the Tenant and failed to return the Tenant’s deposit in the amount of $1,050.00. This is prohibited by the Act.
The Landlord shall be ordered to return the Tenant’s deposit forthwith.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,050.00. This amount represents the deposit paid by the Tenant which was not returned by the Landlord.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 20, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
T he Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: The Landlord requested an adjournment to seek legal representation. He attempted to speak to a lawyer, but his lawyer had retired. He then reached out to a different lawyer one day before the hearing. He argued that this application is complex and that it would be difficult for him to have a fair hearing without representation. When asked to explain the complexity, he claimed that he was losing thousands of dollars because the Tenant is only paying rent for one room and he has the rest of the apartment empty. He also suggested that he didn’t receive the notice of hearing until the week before the hearing but didn’t explain how this happened. His evidence was that paperwork was dropped off in his mailbox the week before. Board records indicate that the notice of hearing was sent on or about June 22, 2026. The Landlord may have been referring to the Tenant’s evidence package that was in fact dropped off the week before.

The Tenant opposed the request. She argued that this is an urgent application. The Tenant was illegally locked out and while she was restored in possession after the interim order was issued, the Tenant remains uncertain about her rights and fearful of what the Landlord may do if the status of her LTB application remains uncertain.

I have considered the Landlord’s request in light of the Board’s obligation to “adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and to be heard on the matter.” Contained in s. 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the parties’ arguments, and the factors the Board usually considers when deciding whether to grant an adjournment including: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; and 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling.

I denied the request. The matter remains somewhat urgent, and parties will be prejudiced by delay. The Landlord himself complained that the status quo costs him money. The issues in the application are not particularly complex, and most facts were not in dispute. The Landlord did not act with any diligence or urgency in seeking representation. He only spoke to one lawyer the day before the hearing. Evidence and factual findings
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,654.85 and $500 fine to the LTB.
Many facts were ultimately undisputed. The findings below are based on parties’ agreement or on the Tenant’s uncontroverted testimony which I found to be credible.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in November 2025. She found it through a third party, [name] (‘Dereje’), who was the tenant at the time. Dereje misled her. He led her to believe that he was the landlord. She moved into the rental unit and Dereje left shortly thereafter. She occupied one room. She paid first and last month’s rent to Dereje.

She then realized that Dereje was not the landlord. She met with the Landlord in December 2025. He signed a document entitled Rental Promissory Note found on page 6 of 8301621 in Portal (‘TOP’). It indicates that the Tenant is renting one room for $650 a month starting December 1, 2025 and indicates that the Landlord requires a payment of $1,400. The document was prepared in order for the Tenant to receive $1,400 in social assistance from ODSP, which she did. She then provided these funds to the Landlord. The document is dated December 18, 2025 and bears the parties’ names. The Landlord did not dispute its authenticity and referenced it in his testimony.

The Tenant then stayed in the room and paid $650 a month to the Landlord. The Tenant provided proof of payment for two other months. Document 8281347 contains a rent receipt the Landlord provided to the Tenant in January 2026. Page 4 of 8301621 contains a rent receipt for April 2026. The Landlord did not deny signing these rent receipts. It is not entirely clear whether she is fully current on rent but this issue is not before me in this application.

The Landlord obtained an eviction order from the LTB in LTB-L-009877-26 after an uncontested hearing that took place on April 9, 2026. The order was obtained against Dereje without notice to the Tenant. The Landlord claims that at the time he commenced this proceeding he was not aware of the Tenant’s existence and that he only discovered her when he served the N4 notice of termination. According to the Landlord’s certificate of service, he served the N4 on November 2, 2025. The rental promissory note the Landlord signed and the first rent receipt predate the hearing and the eviction order. The Landlord ought to have informed the Landlord and Tenant Board of the Tenant’s existence during the April 9 hearing.
The Landlord enforced LTB-L-009877-26 with the Sheriff’s assistance on June 8th, 2026.

The Tenant was completely locked out of her unit between June 8 and June 11. She was then able to get back into the unit on June 11th after work. It is unclear who unlocked the door for her but she found the door unlocked after making many attempts to contact the Landlord. It would appear that the door was unlocked on the Landlord’s instructions. The Tenant testified that she felt humiliated, degraded and embarrassed. She was homeless and had to sleep in a shelter. She was unable to shower before work.
The Tenant continued to reside at the property between June 11 and July 8th without a key. She was able to leave and enter the rental unit, but she didn’t feel certain or safe.
The Landlord provided her a key on July 8th. Law, analysis and remedies

Section 1 of the Act sets out its purposes as follows: “The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.” [emphasis added]

S. 2(1) provides some definitions, including: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;

Under s. 24: “A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

Under s. 202(1), the Board is to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit: “In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.”

The Landlord argued that the Tenant is not a tenant because he does not have a lease with her. His intention was always to rent the entire unit and he is losing money because she is only renting one room. I disagree with the Landlord that the applicant is not a tenant.

Based on the totality of the evidence, based on the definition of a tenant and a tenancy agreement in the Act, and in accordance with s. 202(1), I find that it is more likely than not that the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit does was a tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant effective at least December 2025. The Tenant paid $650 a month for the right to occupy one bedroom and use the common areas. The lease was not written but under the Act an oral or implied lease is valid. The Landlord may rent out the other room in the apartment but there is a valid tenancy for the room he agreed to rent to the Tenant after he discovered her.

There is no dispute that the Landlord caused the locks to be changed on June 8, 2026 and that he did not provide the Tenant replacement keys until a month later. I find that the Landlord breached s. 24 of the Act.
The Tenant’s application requests the following remedies: 1. rent abatement of $106.85, 2. a fine payable to the LTB, and 3. $25,000 for general damages.

Remedy 1 is granted in full. The Tenant was completely locked out of her unit and lost 100% of her enjoyment of the rental unit between June 8th and June 11th. She was then inconvenienced and stressed as a result of not having a key to her unit for almost 30 days. 24. [name] is granted in the amount of $500.00. 25. Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $50,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant: The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 26. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provide that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 27. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 28. I should therefore consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor. 29. The Tenant was seriously impacted by the Landlord’s actions. 30. The Landlord chose to ignore requirements of the Act and obtained an eviction order without informing the Board that there was another tenant at the property. He then caused the locks to be changed. On the other hand, the Landlord apparently allowed the Tenant to get back into the unit within 4 days. It would appear that the Landlord is more ignorant and confused than he is malicious or deliberate in his breaches of the Act. A future violation may well warrant a much steeper fine if it happens again, but I trust that this order, including this fine, will case this Landlord and any similar landlords to familiarize themselves with their obligations under the Act before causing locks to be changed contrary to s. 24 of the Act. 31. The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $25,000 for the serious impact this eviction had on her mental, physical and emotional well-being. 32. The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment. 33. The Board has previously found in cases of harassment and illegal lockouts that an amount for the illegal lockout is appropriate under general damages. See for example HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), the LTB reasoned that:…it seems to me that the quantum of general damages normally awarded to compensate a tenant for an illegal lockout is $2,500.00. That sum takes into account the inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodations while also seeking legal assistance; and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home. 34. I find the amount of $2,500 to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s actions had on her, her work and her mental health. This evidence was uncontroverted. I found it to be persuasive and compelling. A higher award may have been appropriate had the Tenant been locked out in a more permanent manner or for a longer period of time. I find that the “usual” award for “inconvenience and displacement” inherent in an illegal lockout case is appropriate in all of the circumstances. 35. The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application and I find that she is entitled to a reimbursement of this cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,654.85. This amount represents: • $106.85 for a rent abatement. • $2,500 for general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $650.00 from the rent each month from August 2026 until the amount owing is fully repaid.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 by July 25, 2026. July 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name] the Rental Unit and [name] in the Pipes

The residential complex is a 100-year-old property that is split into 2 rental units, unit A & B respectively. The heating system for the residential complex is located within the Tenant’s rental unit.

RP testified that he first notified the Landlord verbally in approximately October 2024, that there was a ‘screeching’ noise in the rental unit’s pipe and requested that the Landlord rectify the issue. He stated he notified the Landlord for the first time in writing via email on January 19, 2025 of the noise ([name]).

RP testified that this noise was occurring repeatedly on a daily basis, generally heard in the evening and he believed the noise is coming from the bedroom, he suggested that the noise is likely due to air in the pipes.

RP further testified that he notified the Landlord on several dates which included: a. March 13, 2025; b. March 13, 2025 through to March 20, 2025 – provided a recording to the Landlord; c. May 27, 2025; d. June 2, 2025; and, e. June 20, 2025 – via the Property Manger
RP presented a video taken on April 5, 2025 of the noise (DOC-586031), and he stated that this was an accurate representation of the noise.

RP stated that he received an email on June 2, 2025 from the Landlord which stated they had hired a property management company, [name] (‘[name]’). After June 2, 2025, RP stated that all communication occurred with the [name]. RP further stated that neither the Landlord nor [name] attended the rental unit at this time to investigate the noise.

On August 26, 2025, the Tenants attended [name]’s office with the recording of the noise and was able to present the issue to staff at Genedco. RP stated the Landlord, [name] or a technician attended the rental unit after he attended [name]’s office. RP stated he was informed that as it was late summer the complaint would not be addressed until heating season started.

RP testified that on September 15 & 16, 2025, he contacted [name] via email requesting the issue be rectified. [name] responded requesting RP stop contacting them as they considered the communication to be ‘borderline harassing’.

RP stated that on October 3, 2025, the Landlords sent the first technician to the property. RP stated that he had requested a copy of the inspection report, which he was not provided. Further, he stated that the technician that attended the rental unit was not aware of the sound, had not been shown the video of the noise and was there to check the heating.
RP referenced an email from [name] (DOC-8227918) sent on October 20, 2025 at 11:03am which stated:

Additionally, RP submitted a witness statement from his colleague [name] which stated that he was at the property on November 25, 2025 during a visit of a technician from [name] Refrigeration and Heating where he assisted in translating with the technician. Further, the statement referenced that the technician discussed the noise and “Appeared to understand that the concern was the specific pipe creaking/screeching issue, not merely whether the heating system was operating” and “…the technician indicated that the issue is related to air in the heating system, or that air in the system was a likely cause requiring further attention, such as bleeding the system”.

RP further referenced an email sent to [name] on December 11, 2025 at 4:14pm (DOC-7989763) regarding recent plumbing work that had been completed at the rental unit. The email outlines that the expansion tank had fallen and was unsupported, and RP requested that a technician attend as soon as possible as he believed it to be an urgent matter. A Rental Management Administrator from [name] responded at 4:27pm on the same day and advised that the email had been forwarded to the Landlord, additionally stating that the Landlord had contacted Simpson’s heating and was attempting to have someone attend the rental unit before they closed.
RP testified that the noise has persisted and the Landlord has not yet rectified the issue as of the hearing. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord, [name] (‘AB’) submitted that the Landlords responded to the [name] concerns reasonably and promptly. He stated they are unsure of what is causing the noise and as a result have engaged various companies, technicians and experts to investigate the complaints of the Tenants. Further, he stated there were a total of 13 service calls and RP was present for almost all of the calls and the work that performed.

AB submitted a timeline which he confirmed is a true accounting of the dates and times regarding the Tenants complaints and when and how the Landlords responded; it outlines the following: a. January 11, 2025 - RP reported noise from the heating system. Landlords responded and arranged for an HVAC inspection on January 17, 2025. b. January 17, 2025 - Technician inspected the system, confirmed it was operating safely and within normal parameters, checked the radiator for air pockets. As the technician noted one circulation pump could benefit from oiling this was completed on the same day. Total cost to the Landlords - $342.28. c. January 19, 2025 - RP advised that the circulation pump remained noisy and requested a replacement. d. January 22, 2025 – Circulation pump was replaced. RP suggested the noise may instead be related to a sediment filter. The technician advised no such component exists within the system. Cost to the Landlords - $621.52. e. February 12, 2025 - Landlords consulted Genedco Property Management. f. On February 21, 2025 – Received an email from RP to stating the new pump had reduced the noise, but that some noise remained. RP suggested possible causes, including air in the lines and flooring related factors. g. February 24, 2025 – [name] attended the rental unit with the Landlords. During the visit, RP discussed concerns. h. May 5, 6, 15, 19, 21 of 2025 - Hoover's Home Energy Inc. attended the property in relation to a separate thermostat and zone valve issue affecting the other rental unit at the residential complex. As unit A and B share the same boiler, the technicians also addressed the heating system serving the Tenants rental unit. RP was present for the visit involving unit a period the technicians bled the radiators; there was no air in the heating system and advised that the reported noises were consistent with normal expansion and contraction of a boiler system. Total costs to the Landlords were $508.50 and $484.50. i. June 1, 2025 – [name] assumed management of the property. The Tenants were notified of Genedco’s involvement on June 2, 2025. j. July 30, 2025 - Genedco advised Tenants a second HVAC contractor would inspect the heating system during the heating season to ensure an accurate assessment. k. October 2, 2025, [name] and [name] attended the rental unit to assess the system. RP was present for the inspection. The technician inspected the system and was unable to replicate the reported noise, technician concluded the boiler and circulation pumps were operating normally. Summary report was provided to the Tenants on October 9, 2025. l. November 6, 2025 – [name] Refrigeration and Heating (‘[name]’) was contacted by Landlords. [name] was provided a copy of the videos from the Tenants. m. November 11, 2025 – RP emailed informing that noise concerns were still present and requested a service call. Landlords booked a service call with [name]. n. November 25, 2025 – Technician from [name] attended the rental unit, RP was present. The technician found the system to be operating safely and within normal parameters and recommended certain upgrades to further optimize system performance and reduce potential noise. o. December 9, 2025 – [name] attended the rental unit and completed the recommended upgrades, RP was present during the work. The work included installation of a micro bubbler to reduce air in the system, relocation and upgrade of the expansion tank and water feed, and bleeding of radiators. Total costs to the Landlords were $2,031.28. p. December 11, 2025 – RP emailed and advised there was an issue with the tank. Landlords called [name] and were advised that there was no immediate concern. The Landlords arranged for [name] to attend the rental unit the next day. q. December 12, 2025 – [name] secured the tank and advised that there was no impact to the system, including no air getting in the lines. r. December 30, 2025 – RP emailed [name] advising of a different noise and requested a service call. A service call was booked for January 5, 2026 due to the holidays. s. January 22, 2026 – [name] HVAC technician attended the rental unit, RP was present. The radiator lines were bled. Total costs to the Landlords were $168.50. t. On February 6, 2025 – Email to the Tenants advising of the results of the service call and confirming the system was operating normally and no further service calls were recommended for the concern based on the assessment that was completed. u. March 6, 2026 – [name] provided the Landlords with a final report confirming the system was operating normally.

AB testified that he was informed that the residential complex has a hydronic radiant heat system and as a result there will be natural noise when the pipes contract and expand. Further, he stated that he does not believe that there is anything further they could do as Landlords to remedy the Tenants complaints. [name]

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out the Landlord’s maintenance obligations and states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Analysis

I find that the Tenants have failed to establish that the Landlords have breached their obligations under s. 20(1) of the Act or failed to act within a reasonable period of time to investigate or repair the noise reported by the Tenants.

While I accept the Tenant’s testimony that they hear a noise within the rental unit, I find it likely due to the age of the property and not for the Landlords’ lack of response or attempts to investigate or repair the complaint. Further, I find the Tenant’s testimony contradictory to the supporting documentary evidence supplied by the Landlords, which included reports, invoices, receipts and communications from the technicians who attend the rental unit. As an example, the Tenant testified that the Landlord did not send technicians to the property until October 3, 2025, the Landlord provided evidence of technicians attending the home on no less than 10 occasions prior to this date.

I am persuaded by the testimony and evidence of the Landlord. The Landlord has taken exceptional measures to address the Tenant’s complaints of the noise in the rental unit. 23. [name] in addition to approximately 3 companies have visited the rental unit on more than 13 occasions to investigate the complaints of the noise and have taken steps to address the possible source of the noise. The Landlords steps included installation of a micro bubbler to reduce air in the system, relocation and upgrade of the expansion tank and water feed, and bleeding of radiators. The Landlords have completed all recommendations of the technicians and companies who attend the rental unit, at a cost of $4,439.05. 24. I find the Landlords have been proactive and addressed each complaint the Tenants raised reasonably in the circumstances Based on the evidence before me, I cannot find that any resulting noise represents a maintenance problem in the unit. 25. On the basis of the testimony and evidence provided by both parties I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations pursuant to s. 20 of the Act with respect to this issue. 26. As noted above, I find that the Landlords did not breach their obligations under s. 20(1) of the Act. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. 27. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. She also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant and • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,970.00. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that she rented a room in the rental unit effective May 1, 2026. Monthly rent was $900 and it was payable on the first of every month. She paid the Landlord first and last in the amount of $1,800.
She paid June rent to the Landlord on May 31st.

On or about June 11, 2026 the Landlord kicked her out. She was forced to return her key and was not permitted to return. She was confronted and yelled at. She was accused of stealing. She was prohibited from returning to the rental unit without police escort. She initially collected a few of her belongings and was unable to collect the rest on June 11th.

She was eventually permitted to return on June 22nd with police escort. She found her belongings packed by the Landlord. The Landlord clearly went through her belongings. She says some of her items are now missing including expensive shoes.

She was seriously affected by the eviction. She has been homeless for 3 weeks. She has been staying with friends from Belleville and commuted back and forth from Oshawa. The Landlord didn’t refund her, and this made it difficult for her to find a new place to live. She had to go through [name]. She lived on the streets and in homeless shelters. She had preexisting conditions that were exacerbated by the Landlord’s misconduct. I do not find that it is necessary for me to describe the Tenant’s evidence about her health in detail in this publicly available order.
The Tenant filed proof of payment of rent (documents 8171036 and 8171043 in Tribunals Ontario Portal). The Landlord didn’t dispute that rent was paid.

She filed copies of some messages exchanged by the parties. One set of messages was sent by a roommate. Conflict between the Tenant and another roommate is not before me in this application. Document 8171050 was a message sent by the Landlord in which he refuses to refund her and tells her to take him to court. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord argues that he is not a landlord. He described himself as an agent for the house. He deals with several properties. He makes sure the landlord receives his money and secures the property.
He argues that there was no tenancy agreement. The Tenant is not on the lease. She was permitted to move into the property on a trial basis. The occupancy was tentative and there was no lease.

The Tenant had issues and caused many issues at the property. The Landlord makes serious allegations against the Tenant, but these allegations are not before me in this application. Because of the Tenant’s alleged misconduct, the Landlord made the decision to cause her to leave.
The Landlord denies locking the Tenant out. The locks were never changed. The Tenant still had the passcode that would allow her to access the property.
The Landlord did not withhold her property – he told the Tenant that she can only collect it with police escort because he did not trust her to be at the property without police being present.
B.Y. testified that she provided the Tenant a code on May 1, 2026. On cross-examination she confirmed that the Tenant was told not to return without police escort. [name] and analysis
The Landlord argues that the Act does not apply, that he is not a landlord, and that the Tenant is not a tenant. I disagree.

Section 1 of the Act sets out its purposes as follows: “The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.” [emphasis added]

S. 2(1) provides some definitions, including: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;

Under s. 202(1), the Board is to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit: “In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.”

Based on the totality of the evidence, based on the definitions of landlord, tenant and tenancy agreement in the Act, and in accordance with s. 202(1), I find that it is more likely than not that the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit does was a tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant effective May 1, 2026. The Tenant paid $900 a month for the right to occupy one bedroom and use the common areas. The lease was not written but under the Act an oral or implied lease is valid. The Landlord is the only person she interacted with. He permits occupancy at the rental unit. He collects rent. He may not be the owner, but multiple landlords may exist simultaneously under the Act. The Landlord bears the burden of proof in establishing that the Act does not apply and fell far short from meeting this burden. To the contrary, the preponderance of the evidence is that the Act applies.
The application invokes ss. 22, 23, 24 and 135 of the Act.

Under s. 135(1), A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Section 22 prohibits landlords from interfering with tenants’ reasonable enjoyment: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”
Section 23 deals with harassment and coercion: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

Section 24 addresses illegal lockouts: “A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

I do not find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord breached s. 24 of the Act. I accept his evidence that the locks were never changed. This does not change the outcome of this application, however, as the Landlord’s conduct nevertheless caused the Tenant to permanently vacate the rental unit and to temporarily lose access to her belongings. The effect on the Tenant was identical to what she might have experienced had the locks been changed.
I find that the Tenant established the rest of her allegations on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord breached ss. 22 and 23 of the Act.

The Landlord coerced the Tenant into permanently vacating the rental unit. She was forced to leave and was prohibited from ever returning other than to collect her belongings with police escort. The Landlord believed he was justified in these actions because of the Tenant’s alleged misconduct, but the Act does not allow self-help in this manner. The Landlord could have contacted the police and/or applied to the LTB to have the tenancy terminated and may have requested an urgent hearing if he believed the matter to be sufficiently urgent. Simply forcing the Tenant to leave and keeping her rent payments was not an option permissible under the Act.
It is undisputed that the Landlord collected a deposit and collected rent for June 2026 and failed to return these funds to the Tenant. This is contrary to the Act.

The Tenant’s application requests the following remedies: a. Return of her last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $900.00, b. 100% rent abatement/refund of rent she paid for the days when she was unable to stay at the rental unit for the total of $570.00, c. A fine payable to the LTB, d. $350.00 for out-of-pocket expenses, e. Return of her belongings, and f. $5,000.00 for general damages.

Remedies ‘a’ and ‘b’ are granted in full. The Tenant is entitled to a 100% refund for rent she prepaid for June and July because she lost 100% of enjoyment of the rental unit during this period. A last month’s rent deposit may only be applied to last month’s rent. It cannot be withheld for any other reason.

The Tenant did not seriously pursue remedies ‘c’ and ‘d’ at the hearing. There is no evidence to corroborate any out-of-pocket expenses she may have incurred. These remedies are therefore not granted.

Remedy ‘e’ is also denied. The Tenant regained possession of most of her belongings on June 22, 2026. She claims that a couple of pairs of shoes was lost but provided no further detail. It is unclear what may have happened to them, when she last saw them, etc. I am unable to find that it is more likely than not that these shoes are now in the Landlord’s possession. I don’t find that the Tenant’s extremely brief and uncorroborated testimony on this issue is sufficient to establish entitlement to this remedy. The application does not request compensation for cost of property lost, damaged or destroyed. Even if it did, the Tenant did not provide sufficient detail to allow the Board to quantify this remedy.
Remedy ‘f’ is granted in the amount of $2,500.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. The Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment.

The Board has previously found in cases of harassment and illegal lockouts that an amount for the illegal lockout is appropriate under general damages. See for example HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), the LTB reasoned that:…it seems to me that the quantum of general damages normally awarded to compensate a tenant for an illegal lockout is $2,500.00. That sum takes into account the inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodations while also seeking legal assistance; and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home.

I find the amount of $2,500 to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s actions had on her and her mental health. This evidence was uncontroverted. I found it to be persuasive and compelling. I find that the “usual” award for “inconvenience and displacement” inherent in an illegal lockout case is appropriate in all of the circumstances considering the relatively short duration of this tenancy, the amount of monthly rent, and the Tenant’s own evidence that she agreed to vacate the property by the end of June.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,970.00. This amount represents: • $900.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $570.00 for rent abatement. • $2,500.00 for general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 14, 2026 ____________________________
