issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v CIBC, 2026 ONLTB 54398 Date: 2026-07-16 In the matter of: [address] OSHAWA ON Between: [name] [name] Tenant And CIBC Chaitons LLP [name] [name] Landlord [name] and [name] (collectively, the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that CIBC, Chaitons LLP (collectively, the 'Respondent'), [name] and [name] (collectively, ‘Mortgagors’): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application was heard by videoconference on July 10, 2026. The Respondent and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Respondent was represented by [name]. The Tenant was represented by [name]. [name] interpreted to and from Tamil for the Tenant. The Mortgagors were not present or represented at the hearing. It is undisputed that they had no notice of the hearing and were not properly served with a notice of this hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities as against the Respondent. Therefore, the application against the Respondent is dismissed. The Tenant provided no valid contact information for the Mortgagors and they were therefore not present at the hearing and had no notice of this hearing. The Tenant did not request to adjourn the hearing in order to ensure the mortgagors could receive a proper notice of hearing and requested that the application be dismissed without prejudice to the Tenant’s right to bring a similar application against the Mortgagors if they can find address for service for them. This request is granted.
Most facts are not in dispute. The legal question before me is whether or not the Respondent is a proper party to this proceeding.

The Respondent argues that they are not a proper respondent in this application. Th is application is brought because utilities were disconnected. They were disconnected due to non-payment by the Mortgagors. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (‘CIBC’) and Chaitons LLP (CIBC’s legal representative) did nothing to interfere with vital services. After the Board issued interim order LTB-T-052148-26-IN requiring the Respondent and the Mortgagees to restore vital services, the Respondent restored vital services on a without prejudice basis in order to comply with the order and in order to preserve the value of their security.

CIBC is the mortgagee of the landlord Mortgagors who defaulted on payments. CIBC filed a statement of claim against the landlord and subsequently obtained a default judgement against them on March 13th, 2026. The judgement entitles them to possession of the rental unit, but they argue that they have not taken possession yet.
It is undisputed that the Respondent has not changed the locks, demanded rent, nor served a notice of attornment of rent.

The Tenant relies on two documents to demonstrate that the Respondent started acting as a mortgagee in possession or a as a landlord within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

First, they sent a letter to the Mortgagors dated April 16th, 2026 in which they indicate that CIBC is entitled to immediate possession of the property. The letter is addressed to the landlord/Mortgagors, not the Tenant. A copy of the letter can be found in Portal under document ID 8322021.

Second, they sent a letter to the Tenant on May 6th, 2026 demanding particulars of the tenancy. This letter can be found on page 5 of document 8182154. In its letter the Respondent indicates that they intend to enforce on its security against the property. Law and analysis

The Tenant relies on section 47(1) of the Mortgages Act, 1990: 47(1) A person who becomes the mortgagee in possession of a mortgaged residential complex which is the subject of a tenancy agreement between the mortgagor and a tenant or who obtains title to the residential complex by foreclosure or power of sale shall be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement. (2) A person who is the landlord under the tenancy agreement ceases to be the landlord while another person is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1). (3) A person who is deemed to be a landlord is subject to the tenancy agreement and to the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which apply to residential complex.
The Tenant is not relying on any case law.
The Respondent argues that they are not a mortgagee in possession within the meaning of s. 47(1) of the Mortgages Act.

They rely on s. 50 of the Mortgages Act: 50(1) Despite section 42, a mortgagee may at any time after the default under a mortgage on a residential complex make inquiries of the mortgagor regarding the existence of any tenancy agreement and require the mortgagor to provide a list of tenants, if any. 50(2) Despite section 42, a mortgagee at any time after default under a mortgage on a residential complex which is the subject of a tenancy agreement may, (a) enter into the common areas of the residential complex for the purpose of inspection; (b) demand production from the mortgagor or the mortgagor’s tenant of a copy of the tenancy agreement if it is written; and (c) demand from the mortgagor or the mortgagor’s tenant any particulars of the tenancy agreement. 50 (3) The mortgagee does not become a mortgagee in possession of the residential complex by any of the acts described in subsection (1) or (2). [emphasis added]

They rely on Bank of Montreal v. [name], 2008 CanLII 28435 (ON SC) (‘[name]’). [name] to 43 address whether the bank was deemed to be a landlord as follows: [30] Section 44 (1) (4) of the Land Titles Act states as follows: 44. (1) All registered land, unless the contrary is expressed on the register, is subject to such of the following liabilities, rights and interests as for the time being may be subsisting in reference thereto, and such liabilities, rights and interests shall not be deemed to be encumbrances within the meaning of this Act: 4. Any lease or agreement for a lease, for a period yet to run that does not exceed three years, where there is actual occupation under it. [31] The Land Titles Act provides that a party takes title to a property subject only to leases less than three years in duration or to registered encumbrances. However, Section 47 of the Mortgages Act provides as follows: 47.(1)A person who becomes the mortgagee in possession of a mortgaged residential complex which is the subject of a tenancy agreement between the mortgagor and a tenant or who obtains title to the residential complex by foreclosure or power of sale shall be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement. 1997, c. 24, s. 215 (5). (2) A person who is the landlord under the tenancy agreement ceases to be the landlord while another person is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1). 1991, c. 6, s. 3; 1997, c. 24, s. 215 (6). (3) A person who is deemed to be a landlord is subject to the tenancy agreement and to the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which apply to residential complex. 1997, c. 24, s. 215 (7); 2006, c. 17, s. 252 (7). (4) A person shall no longer be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement when the person ceases to be a mortgagee in possession. 1991, c. 6, s. 3; 1997, c. 24, s. 215 (8). (5) Despite subsection (4), a person who is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1) continues to be liable for the obligations of a landlord that were incurred while the person was deemed to be a landlord. 1991, c. 6, s. 3 (6) A person who is deemed to be a landlord shall serve notice to all tenants of the change in landlord. 1991, c. 6, s. 3. (7) The notice shall be in writing and shall provide the person’s name and address. 1991, c. 6, s. 3. (8) The notice may be in the form prescribed by the regulations made under this Act. 1991, c. 6, s. 3. [32] A question in this case is whether the respondent tenant is entitled to any protection as a result of s. 47 of the Mortgages Act. In my view, the Bank correctly states the issue: Is the Bank deemed by the Mortgages Act to be a landlord and thereby subject to the 10 year lease? [33] The case of [organization] v. Pieckenhagen and the judgments of the Divisional Court (reported at 1999 CanLII 19930 (ON CTGD), [1999] O.J. 2711) and the Court of Appeal (reported at 2000 CanLII 17044 (ON CA), [2000] [name]) are illustrative of how the relevant provisions of the Land Titles Act and the Mortgages Act impact on one another. [34] In [organization] v. Pieckenhagen, the Ontario Divisional Court held that a lease with a term longer than three years was unenforceable against a purchaser without notice. The Court found that because the lease was not registered, and because the applicant had no knowledge of its terms, the applicant was not bound by the lease by virtue of s. 44 of the Land Titles Act. [35] Pieckenhagen was reversed by the Ontario Court of Appeal on the basis that the Mortgages Act deems a party who acquires title by power of sale to be a landlord with the result that the purchaser is bound to the terms of the lease. In Pieckenhagen the Court of Appeal said as follows (paras. 14 - 20): [14] In my view, it is apparent that the "mischief" addressed by the Mortgages Amendment Act, 1991 was the vulnerability of tenants in residential complexes to being disrupted in their tenancy by changes in possession and title resulting from mortgage default by the landlord or owner of the property. Before the Mortgages Amendment Act, 1991, tenants lacked security of tenure as against mortgagees in possession, those who obtained title by foreclosure, and subsequent purchasers who acquired title in power of sale proceedings. It was held in Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Hurst (1989), 1989 CanLII 4222 (ON HCJ), 71 O.R. (2d) 294 (H.C.J.) that a mortgagee in possession was not a party to and was not bound by the terms of a tenancy agreement between the mortgagor and the tenant. It followed that a mortgagee in possession was not a "landlord" and, accordingly, was not caught by the terms of the Landlord and [name] (see now the Tenant Protection Act, 1997, S.O. 1997, c. 24) protecting tenants by restricting the right of the "landlord" to terminate a residential tenancy. Accordingly, a party who obtained possession or title by virtue of mortgage default could obtain vacant possession despite the existence of a landlord and tenant relationship between the mortgagor and its tenants. [15] The purpose and intent of the Mortgages Amendment Act, 1991 was to overcome this state of affairs and to provide tenants with security of tenure in the event of mortgage default by the landlord. The Mortgages Act, s. 47 specifically puts those persons described in the position of the landlord under the tenancy agreement. [16] The section embraces three classes of persons who are to be subject to the rights and obligations of a landlord, namely: (1) a "mortgagee in possession", (2) a person "who obtains title . . . by foreclosure", and (3) a person who obtains title by "power of sale". The specific issue raised in this appeal is the meaning to be given the words "a person . . . who obtains title by power of sale". [17] It is my respectful view that in light of the language and purpose of this legislation, the Divisional Court erred in its interpretation of the words "a person . . . who obtains title by power of sale". While I agree that it would have been possible for the legislature to use more precise language, as I read the words of the section, the language is adequate to embrace a party who acquires title by purchasing lands from a mortgagee exercising a power of sale. If the words of the legislation do not convey that meaning, it is difficult to see what they do mean. A mortgagee who exercises a power of sale does not "obtain title by power of sale". If these words include anyone, the only candidate seems to be a person who purchases the property through the exercise of the power of sale. A court should strive to give some meaning to the words of a statute rather than interpret [it] in a way that renders it meaningless: Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Co. v. Dearborn (1919), 1919 CanLII 47 (SCC), 58 S.C.R. 315 at pp. 320-21, 47 D.L.R. 27; [name] (1910), 1910 CanLII 42 (SCC), 44 S.C.R. 1 at p. 24. [18] I accept the contention that a purchaser under the power of sale is in a different, perhaps more vulnerable, position than a mortgagee. However, as noted by the appellant, such purchasers are not bereft of protection. The mortgagee exercising power of sale has the right to obtain a copy of the lease (s. 50(2)) or to set aside tenancy agreements entered into after default with the object interfering with the mortgagee's rights (s. 52(1)). It would be open to the purchaser under power of sale to insist that these rights be exercised as a condition of the agreement to purchase the property. As noted, the respondent chose to purchase the property on a "no vendor representations" basis. [19] The respondent relies on the statutory heading "Mortgagees in Possession of Rental Residential Premises" to Part V of the Mortgages Act, the part of the Act containing ss. 46 and 47. I do not accept the respondent's submission that this heading restricts the reach of the section. Headings may be resorted to as an interpretive aid, but they do not trump the actual language of the section, nor should they frustrate its purpose. In my view, the language of the section indicates a legislative attempt to deal comprehensively with the security of tenure of tenants in the event of mortgage default and consequent change in possession or title. The section should be given "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as will best ensure the attainment of the object of the Act according to its true intent, meaning and spirit": Interpretation Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.11, s. 10. [20] I conclude, therefore, that the Divisional Court erred in finding that the respondent was not bound by the terms of the appellant's lease. The Mortgages Act, s. 47 applies and, in accordance with s. 46, prevails to the extent there is any conflict with the Land Titles Act in the absence of any explicit provision to the contrary. It follows that it is not necessary to consider the alternative submission advanced by the appellant that the Divisional Court erred in finding that the renewal clause rendered this lease subject to the Land Titles Act. [36] The Bank, in the case at bar, did not obtain title to the residential complex by foreclosure or power of sale. The issue therefore is whether the Bank is a mortgagee in possession. If the Bank is a mortgagee in possession, then the applicant is deemed by [name] of the Mortgages Act to be a landlord under the tenancy agreement. [37] Falconbridge on Mortgages (5th ed., May 2007), at pp. 31-32, states that a mortgagee becomes a mortgagee in possession where the mortgagee: ... deprives the mortgagor of the control and management of the mortgaged property. A mere token taking of possession such as erecting a barricade is not sufficient to place the mortgagee in possession, especially where the mortgagee does not contemplate any advantage from the taking of possession. [38] [name] asserts that because the Bank’s agent attended at the property and attempted to secure any vacant units, the Bank has become a mortgagee in possession. The fact is, as [name] agreed in cross-examination, the locks have not been changed. There is no evidence that the Bank has interrupted or interfered with the mortgagor's control and management of the property by preventing the mortgagor from selling the property. [39] Have the rents been attorned by the mortgagee? As Falconbridge states in the excerpt noted above, the mortgagee “may if it is entitled to possession as between itself and the mortgagor take possession by requiring the tenant to pay the rents and profits to the mortgagee or its agent instead of paying them to the mortgagor.” In this case, the Bank has not attorned rent. [name], in his cross-examination, confirmed that he is not paying rent to the Bank. [40] The cases relied on by [name], namely, Premier Trust Co. v. [name], 37 R.P.R. (2nd) 165; Unican Development Corp. v. Settlers Savings & Mortgage Corp., [1984] A.W.L.D. 139, are all distinguishable. They are cases where the mortgagee attorned rents or otherwise asserted control over the lands and premises. Sun Life Trust Co. v. R., [1998] G. S.T.C. 63, another case relied on by the respondent, is a case decided by the Tax Court of Canada. Sun Life Trust Co. involved the appellant’s entitlement to a tax credit which turned on whether the appellant mortgagee had taken possession of property before November 1990. If the appellant mortgagee was in possession prior to that date, it was not entitled to a tax credit. The headnote accurately and succinctly sets out the ratio of the case as follows: Appeal dismissed. A mortgagee takes possession by taking such steps as are necessary to deprive the mortgagor of the control of the property. In this case, the mortgagee instructed its lawyers to take control of and manage the property to the exclusion of the mortgagor. That is, the mortgagee had intercepted the owner’s right to manage its property by November 1990, which was before the window period during which subsection 183(7) could have provided a credit. [41] In this case, there is no evidence that the mortgagee has taken out of the mortgagor’s hands the control and management of the mortgaged premises. It has neither entered into actual occupation nor obtained the receipt of the rent of the mortgaged premises. [42] I am satisfied on the evidence before me that the applicant mortgagee is not and has not been in possession. The cases noted and the authorities cited therein provide ample support for this conclusion. [43] I therefore conclude that the applicant, not being a mortgagee in possession, is not deemed to be the respondent's landlord pursuant to section 47 of the Mortgages Act? The respondent’s unregistered 10-year lease is not protected by virtue of s. 47 of the Mortgages Act.
I agree with the Respondent in accordance with BMO v Smith and ss. 47 and 50 of the Mortgages Act. The Respondent has not become a mortgagee in possession.

When a mortgagor defaults on a mortgage, the mortgagee has options. They can avoid “going into possession” or they can become a “mortgagee in possession” with all corresponding rights and obligations. They can then sell the property subject to the existing tenancy agreement, or they can attempt to set it aside pursuant to s. 52 of the Mortgages Act or to terminate the tenancy in accordance with the Act. They may not simply obtain vacant possession.

In the case at bar, I find that the Respondent has avoided becoming a mortgagee in possession. The actions they undertook are expressly enumerated in s. 50(3) of the Mortgages Act as steps a mortgagee may take without becoming a mortgagee in possession.

The Respondent did not undertake any of the steps that would make them a mortgagee in possession such as collecting rent, changing the locks, serving a notice of termination or permitting occupation of the unit. They simply requested and obtained information about tenancies before deciding how to proceed. They did not serve a notice of attornment of rents. Notice demanding possession the Respondent sent was addressed to the landlord/ Mortgagors, not to the Tenant.

The Respondent may become a landlord within the meaning of the Act at a later date. The Tenant’s rights are protected in the meantime. The Respondent may not obtain vacant possession without following the procedures set out in the Act or in the Mortgages Act.
The application is dismissed as the Respondent is not a proper party before the Board and not a landlord within the meaning of the Act at this time.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Eshanzada and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (the ‘first T2 application’). In file number LTB-T-053843-23, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the reasonable supply of a vital service (the ‘second T2 application’). In file number LTB-T-028322-24, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the [name] failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 application’). These applications were heard by videoconference on June 29, 2026. The Landlord [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: These related applications were scheduled together and on having case management discussions with the parties, I determined it would be fair and expeditious to hear them together as the evidence of both parties would be common to all applications.

In the first T2 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord played loud music on October 16, 2022 that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit. That application adds that on October 27, 2022 and again on November 3, 2022, someone illegally entered the rental unit.

The second T2 application adds the Tenant was without electricity for two days in July 2023 putting her to hotel and restaurant expenses which she seeks to recover. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord declined to reset the fuses when they tripped and thereby unreasonably withheld the supply of electricity.

In the T6 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to fix a persistent water leak and faulty wiring that caused the fuses to trip. The T6 application further alleges the Landlord deliberately ignored her maintenance obligations as a form of harassment calculated to drive her out of the rental unit. The Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2023 and seeks her moving expenses and difference in rent.

Nearly all of the Tenant’s issues were already resolved by the Board’s order LTB-L- 056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 and therefore could not be relitigated in these applications. Of those that remain, the Tenant was only able to prove one, as detailed below. Therefore, the rest of the claims must be dismissed.

Before discussing the substance of the claims, I pause to make a note about the quality of the evidence. I had misgivings about the Tenant’s testimony because I found the Tenant was prone to exaggeration and equivocation where she perceived it to be needful. While this manner of presentation no doubt stemmed from a desire to forcefully advocate for her cause and not a deliberate attempt to mislead the Board, it still gives me serious concerns about its reliability. Furthermore, much of the materials the Tenant relied on in support of her claims were her own communications voicing her complaints either directly to the Landlord or to third parties such as municipal inspectors. These prior consistent statements are not proof of the truth of their contents.

The Tenant carries the burden to prove her allegations on a balance of probabilities. Where I find the evidence to be evenly balanced, I must dismiss the claim because the Tenant has not discharged her burden. Leaks, [name] and Property Loss

The Tenant says that almost immediately after moving into the unit in October of 2021, she discovered persistent leaking into the rental unit that the Landlord failed to remediate leading to an infestation of mould. She raised those concerns in response to the Landlord’s application to collect rent arrears heard on May 23, 2024 and received compensation by order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024.

The Tenant seeks to enlarge her recovery, relying on a report from Safetech Environmental Limited dated October 27, 2023 that says personnel from that company visited the unit on October 17, 2023 to assess water damage and identify potential mould. They tested samples and reported their readings. The report contains no opinion about an infestation of mould nor a finding that the rental unit is unsafe for habitation. Rather, it contains a specific disclaimer that the author is not qualified to give such an opinion. The photographs relied on show dampness and mildew but no visible mould growth, much less anything that could be called an infestation.

The Tenant says the Landlord ignored the findings of the mould experts. She says she sent the Landlord this report by email on November 6, 2023 but did not include a copy of that particular email in the package of emails and text messages filed. The Landlord testified she was only given the report as the Tenant was vacating the rental unit on December 31, 2023.

The Tenant testified that a further major leak event occurred in the month of December 2023 as the Tenant was preparing her move. Her packed belongings were soaked through with water and had to be discarded by a specialist waste management firm qualified to handle toxic mould as her regular movers refused to touch them for fear of injury. No photographs were produced showing the Tenant’s personal property to be damaged, or infested with mould.

The Tenant gave no explanation for why she did not seek this additional relief when the Board heard her concerns about leaking on May 23, 2024. The Tenant offered no principled reason why this claim should be litigated again on a different evidentiary record. The Tenant would have had in her possession or control all the facts and documents, including the Safetech report, and particulars of her lost property as of the hearing of May 23, 2024. [name] that the doctrine of cause of action estoppel is discretionary and must not be mechanically applied in all cases, I find it bars the Tenant’s disrepair claims in this case because it would undermine the objectives of finality and certainty in Board decisions if issues finally decided between the same parties were litigated again. Therefore, I find the claims in relation to leaks, mould, and concomitant property loss must be dismissed as res judicata. Electrical issues

The Tenant testified that on innumerable occasions, the fuses would trip because they were faulty and, because the Tenant had no access to the electrical panel, she could not reset them leaving her with no power for hours, sometimes days, at a time. The Tenant says she later discovered that the electrical supply and the wiring was inadequate for servicing two separate households and the Landlord’s failure to fix it is a breach of section 20 of the Act. The Board’s reasons for decision in order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 disclose that the Tenant advanced the same claim in those proceedings. For reasons detailed above, I find this claim is res judicata and cannot be raised again in new applications. [name]

The Tenant says that although the tenancy agreement shows laundry is not included, the written agreement is not consistent with the true agreement because she was orally promised laundry. The Tenant testified that she signed the written agreement under duress, as she needed housing urgently and was therefore not in a position to negotiate or seek alternatives.

The Board’s order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 has already found that laundry facilities were not included in this tenancy. I find this claim must be dismissed because the issue has finally been decided by the Board and I was given no persuasive reason why the Board should allow it to be relitigated. Parking

The Tenant seeks compensation because she was only given one parking spot when she was promised two. I find this claim must be dismissed because the tenancy agreement specifically speaks of only one parking spot. Guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the Tenant’s testimony that she felt compelled to sign the agreement is insufficient to prove that the substance of the contract was anything other than what it says. The Tenant led no evidence of having lodged any complaints about having only one spot and led no evidence of the Landlord ever having granted her the use of two spots. Illegal Entries

The Tenant testified that the door separating her unit from the main floor unit where the Landlord lived was not adequately secured, such that members of the Landlord’s family and her guests would wander into her private space. She presented a text message of October 27, 2022 where the Landlord contacted the Tenant to tell her a child had entered the rental unit and to apologize for the intrusion. The Tenant also wrote the Landlord on November 3, 2022 stating that someone tried to enter her rental unit. The Landlord responded that it was her brother sliding the mail under the door but promised to put a lock on that door to safeguard against any future intrusions.

I find the child inadvertently entering the rental unit on October 27, 2022 cannot be characterized as an illegal entry within the meaning of section 25 of the Act because that entry was not instigated by the Landlord or done at her behest or by anyone acting on her behalf. In any case, the Tenant admitted this entry caused no impact.

I find the evidence insufficient to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s brother actually entered the rental unit on November 3, 2022 because I find it at least equally probable that he merely slid the mail under the door as the Landlord says. That would be consistent with the Tenant’s description of the event as an attempted entry.
Although the Tenant spoke of countless other intrusions on her privacy by strangers, she offered no details in her evidence. Loud Music

I find the Tenant was unable to prove this incident on a balance of probabilities because, given the Landlord’s denial of the event, and the lack of any confirmatory evidence (such as a recording), I must find the evidence equally balanced and therefore insufficient to discharge the burden of proof. Harassment, Obstruction and Threats

The Tenant claims that once she voiced her concerns about disrepair, the Landlord embarked on a campaign of harassment that involved blocking her access to her parking spot, making constant complaints by phone and email, serving notices of termination, deliberately shutting off the electricity and enlisting her brother to redouble the illegal entries into the rental unit. The Landlord denied each of these allegations in turn but allowed that she did serve N4 notices for arrears of rent and an N12 notice to repossess for her own use. This Board has consistently held that attempting to enforce one’s rights under the Act, even unsuccessfully, cannot be characterized as harassment: [name] v 6891799 Canada Inc., 2023 ONLTB 25933 at para. 70; TST-49807-14 (Re), 2015 CanLII 34298 (ON LTB), at para 68.

As discussed above, the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that anyone illegally entered the rental unit at any time. The Tenant filed a text message where the Landlord cautions that if the Tenant does not advise in advance of her guests using the driveway for parking, she will assume these are trespassers and will have their car removed. I would not characterize this communication as harassment or a threat within the meaning of section 23. I agree that the tone is somewhat unprofessional but there is no evidence it happened more than once and critically, the Tenant led no evidence of how it impacted her warranting any recovery for what, even if proven, would be a trivial breach. [name]

The Tenant has proven the claim contained in the second T2 application that the Landlord deliberately shut off electricity for some 8 days in July 2023 by reference to an entry in a municipal inspector’s notes that says: Attended location and spoke with property owner on the phone and advised them that they need to turn the power back right away. They kept saying they turned it off because of no payment from tenant.

I accept this hearsay evidence and the Tenant’s testimony because the Landlord did not deny it and in fact, explained at length about how the Tenant’s choice to withhold rent caused her financial hardship. The Landlord did not say that the utility provider had discontinued service for want of payment. The evidence suggest that the Landlord restored power after learning of her mistake as the municipal inspector closed his file when the Tenant did not renew her complaint. Still, withholding the supply of a vital service for non-payment, in these circumstances, is unreasonable within the meaning of section 21 of the Act which means this claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities. Remedies

Having established that the Landlord unreasonably withheld the supply of electricity in July 2023, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies she can prove on a balance of probabilities in relation to that breach. That claim is pleaded in the second T2 application that claims out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $1,000.00 and an administrative fine. Hotels and Meals

The Tenant has delivered hotel bills totalling $1,240.22 and proof of payments made to restaurants totalling $526.46 to substantiate this claim. The Tenant testified that living in the rental unit without power was impossible so she relocated herself and her child to hotels and ate at restaurants. The Tenant filed an invoice for a stay at the Pickering Casino Hotel for July 9 to July 14, 2023 issued to herself. She also relied on another invoice for Sheraton Centre Hotel in Toronto spanning the period July 15 to July 18, 2023 issued to [name] of Villa Park, California. I was not told why the Tenant’s hotel invoice is drawn up in the name of that person. That invoice speaks of additional pages which weren’t filed.

The Tenant explained that having experienced an abusive relationship, she was unable to take lodgings in the same locality as the rental unit for fear that her abuser might find her. So the Tenant decided to stay at a hotel in Toronto. She has filed four POS printouts from various restaurants in Toronto for July 15 and July 16, 2023. The Tenant did not explain why she was not fearful of staying at the Pickering Casino Resort between July 9 and July 15, 2023 which is in the same locality as the rental unit.

I find that the Tenant has failed to prove either causation or the quantum of damages claimed on a balance of probabilities because her documentary proof is unreliable on its face and contradicts her testimony. I recognize that as trier of fact I must assess a fair and reasonable amount of compensation even where that task is made difficult by frailties in the evidence. However, in this case, I find the evidentiary record is so lacking that the task is impossible. I find the Tenant’s choice of hotels and restaurants is not consistent with an emergency. Accordingly I can only award nominal damages. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $100.00 for deliberately depriving her of electricity. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not binding on me but I accept it as the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

This remedy is not normally granted unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and ensure future compliance. The objectives of deterrence involve both specific and general deterrence. I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act or to deter future breaches. The Landlord has already been ordered to compensate the Tenant in respect of the disrepair claims adjudicated in file number LTB-L-056337-23 and I find that no further deterrence is required in respect of the one claim that has been proven in these proceedings.
The Tenant incurred no filing fee in respect of the second T2 application which is the only one that was successful.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $100.00 on or before August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Respondent'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Applicant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the application is dismissed.
The Applicant claims that he is a tenant.
The Respondent disagrees.
The Respondent is a mortgagee in possession. They enforced a writ of possession against the owner of the property, [name]. She was not a party to this proceeding and did not attend the hearing.
Based on the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing I find that it is more likely than not that the Applicant is not a tenant. Evidence

The Applicant provided brief testimony. He explained that he returned from a business trip on Sunday June 14th and discovered that one of the locks had been changed. There was a lockbox on the front door. He entered the unit through the backdoor and continued living at the rental unit.

On June 17 the Respondent’s contractors saw him at the unit and called the police to have him removed as a trespasser. He spoke with the police and was not charged. He describes this incident as a false arrest. He called the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

The Applicant testified that he has been living at the unit since September 2025. His possessions are still in the unit. He had to leave with nothing but the clothes on his back and most of his stuff is in the Respondent’s control.
He has his record collection, a suitcase, and a modem at the property.
According to the Applicant, his tenancy agreement is oral or implied.

He filed 3 pieces of corroborating evidence: a. Document 8192425 in Portal is proof of delivery of an Amazon package to the residential complex on May 22, 2026. b. Document 8192427 is proof of delivery of an Amazon package to the residential complex on May 16, 2026. c. Documents 8192351 and 8192353 are pages 1 and 2 of a document purporting to be an N4 notice of termination for non-payment of rent.
The Applicant claims that he was never notified about any enforcement proceedings. He has been sleeping outside since the lockout and wishes to be compensated.
The Applicant’s evidence was seriously shaken and undermined by cross-examination. His evidence was inconsistent with documentary evidence, self-contradictory, and his explanations defied belief.
He reiterated that he moved into the property in September 2025.

He was asked to explain why the N4 document he relies upon claims that he owes rent for August 2025. He replied that he was allowed to occupy the unit in the end of August. This does not explain why he would be charged rent for the entire month of August. It is also inconsistent with his prior testimony.

He confirmed that he was asked to provide a copy of his lease by the Respondent on more than one occasion and hasn’t provided it. He says he has an implied tenancy with [name] and her assistant, whose name he was unable to pronounce but whose name would appear on the N4 document. When asked to elaborate, he explained that the implied tenancy is borne out by the N4, that he has had his possessions at the rental unit since September 2025 and that [name] and her assistant have known about his presence.

The Respondent introduced evidence of correspondence they received from ‘Bo Gu’, a stager who claims that the furniture in the residential complex is theirs. The Applicant explained that he never had any of his own furniture in the rental unit – the unit was furnished, and he didn’t need to bring anything. His possessions consisted of a suitcase, clothes, records and a few pairs of headphones. He confirmed that there is nothing else.

He was confronted with issues in the document he claims to be an N4 he received for [name]. He was asked to explain why it is dated October 31st but gives the tenant until October 5th to repay the arrears owing. He couldn’t explain it and said that [name] would be in the position to explain this mistake.

He was asked whether he actually paid rent to [name]. He replied that he eventually paid it. He was asked if he had proof of payment. He confirmed that he didn’t and complained that he was unable to locate [name] or her assistant. It is unclear why this would be necessary as proof of payment can usually be obtained without cooperation from the landlord.

I also note that the deliveries are not addressed to what the Applicant claims to be his rental unit (being the basement) and the N4 has additional issues not brought up during cross-examination. It does not show the total amount owing on page 2. It shows the third rental period as 01/10/2025 to 31/09/2025. The signature field is filled out as “YZ” only. It is not actually signed by [name] or by the person named as her representative on page 2. The notice of termination is defective in the sense that [name] would be unable to rely upon it to obtain an eviction order from the LTB.
The Respondent provided evidence of their efforts to confirm occupancy of the rental unit. The Applicant was never mentioned or found despite the Respondent’s multiple attendances at the rental unit.

Document 8231961 deals with attempted service and claims that the property was used as a short-term rental. The Applicant did not deny this and explained that his occupancy started through Air BNB. He usually stays in short-term rentals because he travels. He then entered into an implied tenancy with [name]. He was shown an expired piece of ID from [name] listing the residential complex as her address. He explained that there was a tenant on the first floor and a tenant on the second floor and [name] didn’t live there. He had not heard from her nor seen her for 7 months.

His application claims $5,000 for moving costs and storage. He confirmed that he provided no evidence of incurring such costs. He explained that he has very little money and will incur these expenses once receives his paycheque. He was asked to confirm that he has not incurred any such moving and storage costs. He replied that he had to purchase bus tickets and had to walk.

He similarly filed no evidence to corroborate his claim that he incurred out-of-pocket expenses of some $25,000. He replied that he has huge expenses in terms of trying to find a place to stay but has filed no corroborating evidence.

The Respondent relies on their motion record before the Superior Court before they obtained writ of possession (8231927). There is affidavit evidence that they arranged for people to attend at the property multiple times and never discovered the Applicant. The locks were changed on May 25 and the Applicant didn’t file their application until June 17th. Document 8231884 is an email the Respondent received from the person claiming to be a stager.
The Respondent had no notice that the Applicant occupied any part of the residential complex until June 17th. Law and Analysis

When the Respondent enforced their writ of possession, they became the Applicant’s landlord to the extent that the Applicant was a genuine tenant. Section 47(1) of the Mortgages Act, 1990, states inter alia: 47 (1) A person who becomes the mortgagee in possession of a mortgaged residential complex which is the subject of a tenancy agreement between the mortgagor and a tenant or who obtains title to the residential complex by foreclosure or power of sale shall be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement. (2) A person who is the landlord under the tenancy agreement ceases to be the landlord while another person is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1). (3) A person who is deemed to be a landlord is subject to the tenancy agreement and to the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which apply to residential complex

S. 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides some definitions, including: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;

Under s. 18, covenants run with the land: “Covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made.”

Under s. 24: “A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

Under s. 202(1), the Board is to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit: “In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.”

Based on the totality of the evidence, and in accordance with s. 202(1), I find that it is more likely than not that the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit does not include a tenancy between the Applicant and [name] or any other person.

Overall, I did not find the Applicant to be a credible and reliable witness. His story contained self-contradictions and inconsistencies. It was inconsistent with his own documentary evidence and his own application. His explanations lacked the ring of truth and defied belief at times.
The Applicant’s evidence was unpersuasive and implausible on its face. It was then seriously undermined by cross-examination.

He testified that he moved into the rental unit in September 2025 but also testified that he moved in in August and that he initially occupied the unit through Air BNB. These other dates were only provided during crosse-examination in order to explain inconsistencies between his testimony and other evidence.

The Applicant’s proof of Amazon deliveries does not prove a tenancy – at most, they may support a finding that he occupied the rental unit in May 2026. An Amazon delivery could be arranged to anyone’s address. The deliveries are addressed to the residential complex, not to what the Applicant claims to be his unit. The address listed on his deliveries does not include any reference to a basement unit.

The main piece of evidence that could establish a tenancy is the N4 but the document purporting to be an N4 is unreliable at best. It raises more questions about the Applicant’s claim than it answers. The dates don’t make sense. Rental periods are wrong, and it was signed after the termination date. The amounts claimed for arrears are inconsistent with the Applicant’s testimony. The document does not bear anyone’s actual signature. The document is deficient in other ways as well. Such document could not be relied upon to terminate a tenancy as the notice fails to comply with legal requirements.

I draw a negative inference from the Applicant’s failure to produce more persuasive evidence of his tenancy. There are no IDs, no mail addressed to him at the actual rental unit, no messages with [name] or her assistant – only two deliveries and an N4 that is full of contradictions and mistakes and doesn’t bear anyone’s signature. There are no witnesses who would corroborate the Applicant’s self-serving testimony.

There is no documentary evidence to confirm that the Applicant ever paid rent. I draw a negative inference from the Applicant’s failure to produce such evidence. He did not provide satisfactory explanation for failure to produce it. At least some of the evidence should have been easy to obtain given the Applicant’s claim that the occupancy commenced through a short-term rental platform. He could have provided proof of e- transfers or deposits/withdrawals. He did not testify that he paid rent in cash but even if he did, some evidence could have been obtained.

There are multiple other issues with the Applicant’s evidence. It is difficult to understand how one’s primary residence can have no food or kitchen items whatsoever. The Applicant’s testimony was that the complete list of his belongings was limited to a suitcase, clothes, records and a few pairs of headphones. This claim is also difficult to reconcile with the Applicant’s application document which claims that he has incurred or will incur storage expenses and exorbitant out-of-pocket expenses. It would appear that his belongings were always meant to be easy to move on short notice.

The Respondent produced some evidence that they undertook efforts to ascertain occupancy and that they never discovered the Applicant. This does not necessarily establish that it is more likely than not that the Applicant was not simply missed, but it goes some way towards establishing that the Applicant was not a tenant on a balance of probabilities.

It is possible that the [name] was never even an occupant of the rental unit until June 17th. It is possible that he was. He may have been a squatter, a short-term rental guest who overstayed his welcome, or he may have stayed at the rental unit in some other capacity. I find that it is more likely than not that he was never a tenant within the meaning of the Act.
The application is dismissed.
ordered: The Application is dismissed.
Interim order LTB-T-052690-26-IN issued by the LTB on June 22, 2026 is cancelled. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] 2565-[name] [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • charged the Tenant illegal charges • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. • gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant filed two applications arising from the same tenancy. The applications are essentially duplicative applications made against two different landlords. One application names [name] as the respondent. The second names [name] and [name], the owners of the rental unit (the 'Landlords').

As explained below, I find that [name] is not a landlord within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Accordingly, the application against the condominium corporation is dismissed.

Common law establishes that there is no legal relationship between a condominium corporation and a tenant who occupies an owner’s unit within the residential complex and who pays rent to the owner of the unit for that privilege. A condominium corporation has no legal standing before the Board. A series of cases confirms this principle. (See, for example, TEL-96466-18 /TET-97624-18, 2019 CANLII 126965 (ON LTB); Chimel v. MacLachlan, 2020 CANLII 118438 (ON LTB); TSL-09662-19; K.G. v. J.D.L.R. 2019 CANLII 87771 (ON LTB); TST-95268-18; TNT-99110-17)

The courts have reached the same conclusion. In Carleton Condominium Corporation No. 555 v. Legacé, 2004 CanLII 26137 (ON SC), the Court explained that the condominium corporation's legal relationship is with the unit owner rather than the tenant. Where issues arise concerning a tenant's occupancy, the corporation looks to the owner for compliance, and the owner in turn enforces the tenancy agreement with the tenant.

Accordingly, I find that [name] is not a landlord within the meaning of the Act. The application against the condominium corporation is therefore dismissed. The hearing proceeded only against [name] and [name]. Preliminary Issue – Date the Application Was Filed

A further preliminary issue concerns the date on which the Tenant commenced the application against the Landlords. The Board's records indicate that application LTB-T- 017945-25 was filed on March 2, 2025.

The Tenant submits that she originally filed an application in December 2023 and that the Board subsequently misplaced it. She relies primarily on Canada Post tracking information demonstrating that an envelope was delivered to the Board during that period. (DOC- 7589638 pg.42) She testified that the application had been prepared by family members while she was recovering from surgery and that she no longer possesses a copy of the documents that were allegedly mailed.
I am not persuaded, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant filed an application in December 2023.

The Canada Post tracking information establishes only that an envelope was delivered to the Board. It does not establish what documents were contained in that envelope. More importantly, there is no copy of the alleged application, no acknowledgement of receipt from the Board, and no correspondence demonstrating that the Board received or processed such an application. LTB-T-017945-25

I accept that administrative errors can occur and that documents may occasionally be misplaced after being received. However, there is insufficient evidence before me to conclude that such an error occurred in this case.

I also find it noteworthy that there is no persuasive evidence of any meaningful follow-up by the Tenant after the alleged December 2023 filing. While some delay in processing applications is not unusual, I find it unlikely that a reasonable person would wait well over a year without obtaining confirmation that an application had been received or without retaining a copy of the documents allegedly filed.

Had a copy of the alleged December 2023 application been produced, the Board could have compared it with the present application to determine whether they were substantially the same. In the absence of that evidence, I am unable to conclude that the Tenant commenced proceedings before March 2, 2025.

I therefore find that the filing date of the application is March 2, 2025. Pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act, the Board may only grant a remedy for conduct occurring within one year before that date unless the alleged conduct constituted a continuing breach extending into the limitation period. T5 Application

At the outset of the hearing the Tenant withdrew their allegation that the Landlords served a notice of termination in bad faith. Accordingly, the Tenant presented evidence surrounding the remainder the allegations set out in their application that are within the applicable limitation period. [name]

The Tenant alleges that the Landlords substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by illegally changing the locks, harassing her, unlawfully entering the rental unit, and withholding vital services.

The Tenant testified that the Landlords changed the locks to the rental unit on several occasions without her consent. She testified that the Landlords caused the condominium corporation to change the locks while she remained hospitalized following thoracic surgery. According to the Tenant, the Landlords already had access to the rental unit because the condominium corporation maintained master keys and had previously changed the locks in December 2023. The Tenant believes, there was no legitimate reason for another lock change.

The Tenant relied upon email correspondence dated March 25, 2024, (DOC-7589638 pg.131) which demonstrates that a locksmith attended the building and that replacement keys would be available following the lock change. She submits this correspondence establishes that the Landlords requested the lock change and that the condominium corporation acted at their direction.

The Tenant testified that members of her family attempted to obtain replacement keys while she remained hospitalized but were unsuccessful because the condominium corporation required her to attend personally. She testified that she was therefore required LTB-T-017945-25 to temporarily leave the hospital to obtain replacement keys, causing pain, inconvenience and disrupting her recovery. Although she ultimately regained access to the rental unit before vacating the premises on June 30, 2024, she maintains that the temporary inability to access the unit constituted an illegal lockout.

The Tenant further testified that the repeated lock changes formed part of a broader pattern of harassment and intimidation. She submits the Landlords' communications, together with the ongoing dispute concerning the heating system, caused her to feel unsafe in the rental unit and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. Landlords' Evidence

The Landlords deny ever illegally locking the Tenant out of the rental unit. [name] testified that, beginning in the fall of 2023, the Landlords were attempting to obtain access to the rental unit to investigate the Tenant's complaints regarding the HVAC system and to facilitate an insurance inspection. He testified that, despite serving notices of entry, the Landlords were unable to gain access because they possessed neither a working key to the unit nor a building fob. 21. [name] testified that the condominium corporation re-keyed the locks in December 2023 after it was determined that neither the replacement key nor the condominium's master key functioned properly. He denied that either he or [name] tampered with the lock and stated that the condominium corporation concluded the lock had been altered, necessitating another re-keying. 22. VD provided similar evidence. She testified that the March 2024 lock change occurred solely to permit lawful access so the HVAC system could be inspected and repaired and denied that the purpose of the lock change was to interfere with the Tenant's occupancy or enjoyment of the rental unit. Analysis 23. I have already determined that the application was filed on March 2, 2025. Accordingly, pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act, I may only grant a remedy for conduct occurring on or after March 3, 2024. Much of the Tenant's evidence concerning lock changes, and communications between the parties occurred during 2023. While I have considered that evidence to provide context, I have not relied upon it as a basis for granting the Tenant’s application. 24. With respect to the March 2024 lock change, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord illegally locked her out of the rental unit. 25. I do not accept the Tenant's submission that the March 2024 lock change constituted an illegal lockout. An e-mail from the condominium corporation to the Tenant (DOC-7589638 pg.131) confirms that the Tenant received notice from the condominium corporation advising that the locks had been changed and that a replacement key was available for collection. LTB-T-017945-25 26. Although the Tenant was unable to personally collect the key because she remained hospitalized, there is no persuasive evidence that either Landlord directed the condominium corporation to withhold the key from the Tenant or otherwise attempted to obstruct her from possession of the rental unit. 27. I accept the Tenant's evidence that the condominium corporation declined to release the replacement key to members of her family while she remained hospitalized. However, I am not satisfied that this decision can properly be attributed to the Landlords. Nor do I find it unreasonable that the condominium corporation required confirmation that the individual requesting the key was authorized to receive it on the Tenant's behalf. 28. While I accept that the Tenant experienced inconvenience and frustration as a result of having to personally retrieve the replacement key, I am not satisfied that those circumstances establish an illegal lockout under the Act. 29. I also reject the Tenant's allegation that the Landlords harassed or substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. Much of the evidence relied upon by the Tenant relates to communications occurring in 2023 and therefore falls outside the applicable limitation period. 30. I find the communications occurring within the relevant period primarily concern attempts to arrange inspections, obtain access to the rental unit and facilitate repairs to the HVAC system. Although the relationship between the parties had clearly deteriorated, I am not satisfied that those communications amount to harassment, coercion or substantial interference within the meaning of the Act. T6 Application 31. The Tenant testified that the heating system serving the rental unit stopped functioning in approximately February 2023. She stated that she repeatedly notified the Landlords through emails, text messages, telephone calls and WhatsApp messages that the rental unit had no heat. According to the Tenant, despite her repeated complaints, the Landlords failed to investigate the issue or arrange for repairs. 32. The Tenant testified that she also contacted the condominium corporation and various enforcement authorities in an effort to have the issue addressed. She stated that she was advised the HVAC unit serving the rental unit was the responsibility of the unit owner rather than the condominium corporation. 33. The Tenant testified that the lack of heat significantly affected her ability to use and enjoy the rental unit. She stated that she purchased a portable heater, but it was incapable of adequately heating the unit and she was later advised not to leave it operating unattended because of the potential fire risk. She further testified that the prolonged absence of heat and air conditioning damaged clothing, furniture and other personal belongings and contributed to the deterioration of her health. Landlords’ Evidence 34. The Landlords do not dispute that the heating system was not functioning properly. [name] acknowledged that the Tenant first reported problems with the heating system in early LTB-T-017945-25 2023 and candidly admitted that the Landlords did not respond as promptly as they should have. He testified the Landlords initially believed responsibility for the HVAC unit rested with the condominium corporation and that, shortly after the complaints were received, the Landlords experienced a significant family tragedy that diverted their attention from the issue. 35. [name] testified that he became directly involved in approximately October 2023 when it became apparent that the issue had not been resolved. He testified that, from that point forward, the Landlords actively attempted to inspect the HVAC system and arrange repairs. [name] submitted those efforts included serving notices of entry, retaining contractors, communicating extensively with the condominium corporation and attempting to obtain lawful access to the rental unit. 36. [name] further testified that, after the Landlords finally regained access to the rental unit in March 2024, the HVAC system was inspected. He stated that the inspection revealed the repair required removal of the ceiling-mounted heat pump and portions of the surrounding drywall. He further testified, large clothing racks and other belongings stored beneath the unit prevented the contractor from safely performing the work. 37. [name] testified that he requested the Tenant move those belongings so that the contractor could complete the repairs. Although he was unable to locate the email making that request during the hearing, he maintained that the request was made and that the Tenant never responded. [name] submitted, the Landlords received no further communication from the Tenant until June 30, 2024, when they were advised that she had vacated the rental unit. Analysis 38. Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. There is no dispute that the HVAC unit serving the rental unit was the Landlords' responsibility. 39. I accept the Tenant's evidence that she notified the Landlords of the heating issue in early 2023. I also accept [name]’s candid admission that the Landlords did not respond as promptly as they should have. Although I accept that the Landlords were dealing with significant personal circumstances and initially misunderstood who was responsible for the HVAC unit, those circumstances did not relieve them of their maintenance obligations. 40. Had the application been filed within the limitation period prescribed by subsection 29(2) of the Act, the evidence would have supported a finding that the Landlords failed to take reasonable steps to investigate and address the heating issue for several months after first receiving notice of the problem. 41. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 the Court of Appeal held that it is necessary to take a contextual approach to determining whether a landlord breached his maintenance obligations under the Act and a landlord will not be found liable for such a breach. 42. In applying a contextual analysis to this application, I find the circumstances in this case changed in October 2023. I accept [name]’s evidence that, from that point onward, the LTB-T-017945-25 Landlords made genuine and ongoing efforts to obtain access to the rental unit, inspect the HVAC system and arrange for the necessary repairs. 43. I also find the evidence of the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (DOC-7382699, pp. 33– 38) to be relevant. In an email dated July 21, 2025, the inspector confirmed that the file had been closed and noted that the Tenant had been difficult to reach and that there were challenges arranging access to conduct an in-unit inspection. I find this to be consistent with the Landlords' submission that they experienced ongoing difficulties obtaining access to the rental unit. Viewed together with the balance of the evidence, I find it supports the Landlords' position that access to the rental unit presented an ongoing challenge. 44. I also accept that, once access was finally obtained in March 2024, the required repair was more extensive than initially anticipated. [name]'s evidence that the ceiling-mounted heat pump had to be removed and that the work required unobstructed access beneath the unit was not contradicted by the Tenant. 45. Although the Landlords were unable to produce the email requesting that the Tenant move her belongings to facilitate the repair, I found [name]’s evidence in this regard to be credible. I I therefore accept that the Landlords continued attempting to complete the repair after regaining access to the rental unit. 46. In considering the totality of the evidence, I find that, after approximately October 2023, the Landlords took reasonable steps to investigate and repair the HVAC system. Any continuing delay thereafter cannot fairly be attributed solely to a failure on the part of the Landlords. 47. More importantly, subsection 29(2) of the Act prevents the Board from granting a remedy for conduct occurring more than one year before the application was filed. I have found that the application was filed on March 2, 2025. Consequently, any failure by the Landlords to respond promptly to the Tenant's complaints during the period before October 2023 occurred well outside the applicable limitation period. 48. Since I am satisfied that the Landlords acted reasonably after approximately October 2023, I find the Tenant has not established any maintenance breach within the period for which the Board may grant relief under the Act. 49. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. T1 Application 50. The Tenant seeks the return of the $150.00 key and fob deposit paid at the commencement of the tenancy. 51. The Tenant testified that she returned the keys at the conclusion of the tenancy through the building concierge after vacating the rental unit on June 30, 2024. Although the Landlords initially questioned the precise date on which the keys were returned, they ultimately acknowledged that the keys were recovered from the concierge shortly thereafter. The Landlords also acknowledged collecting a $150.00 refundable key and fob deposit from the Tenant at the commencement of the tenancy. LTB-T-017945-25 52. Subsection 134(3) of the Act permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit provided it does not exceed the expected direct replacement cost of the keys or access devices. Once the tenant returns the keys at the end of the tenancy, the landlord must refund the deposit unless it has been properly applied toward replacement costs. 53. There is no evidence that the Landlords incurred any replacement costs or that they had any lawful basis for retaining the deposit. I am therefore satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the return of the $150.00 key and fob deposit. 54. The Tenant also seeks interest on the deposit. Unlike a rent deposit under section 106 of the Act, the Act does not require a landlord to pay annual interest on a refundable key deposit. Therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to interest on the key deposit. 55. I therefore find it appropriate to set off the $150.00 refundable key and fob deposit against the outstanding amount owing by the Tenant under the previous Board order. 56. While the Tenant was partially successful in their application, the Boards records indicate the cost of filing the application was waived by Board. As such the Tenant is not entitled to be reimbursed that cost.
ordered: The application against the Landlord, [name] 2565-[name] [name], is dismissed.
The Tenant is awarded $150.00 which represents the return of her key deposit.
The total amount of $150.00 will be used to offset the rent arrears sought by the Landlords in LTB-L-016001-24. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
