issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Eshanzada and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (the ‘first T2 application’). In file number LTB-T-053843-23, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the reasonable supply of a vital service (the ‘second T2 application’). In file number LTB-T-028322-24, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the [name] failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 application’). These applications were heard by videoconference on June 29, 2026. The Landlord [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: These related applications were scheduled together and on having case management discussions with the parties, I determined it would be fair and expeditious to hear them together as the evidence of both parties would be common to all applications.

In the first T2 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord played loud music on October 16, 2022 that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit. That application adds that on October 27, 2022 and again on November 3, 2022, someone illegally entered the rental unit.

The second T2 application adds the Tenant was without electricity for two days in July 2023 putting her to hotel and restaurant expenses which she seeks to recover. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord declined to reset the fuses when they tripped and thereby unreasonably withheld the supply of electricity.

In the T6 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to fix a persistent water leak and faulty wiring that caused the fuses to trip. The T6 application further alleges the Landlord deliberately ignored her maintenance obligations as a form of harassment calculated to drive her out of the rental unit. The Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2023 and seeks her moving expenses and difference in rent.

Nearly all of the Tenant’s issues were already resolved by the Board’s order LTB-L- 056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 and therefore could not be relitigated in these applications. Of those that remain, the Tenant was only able to prove one, as detailed below. Therefore, the rest of the claims must be dismissed.

Before discussing the substance of the claims, I pause to make a note about the quality of the evidence. I had misgivings about the Tenant’s testimony because I found the Tenant was prone to exaggeration and equivocation where she perceived it to be needful. While this manner of presentation no doubt stemmed from a desire to forcefully advocate for her cause and not a deliberate attempt to mislead the Board, it still gives me serious concerns about its reliability. Furthermore, much of the materials the Tenant relied on in support of her claims were her own communications voicing her complaints either directly to the Landlord or to third parties such as municipal inspectors. These prior consistent statements are not proof of the truth of their contents.

The Tenant carries the burden to prove her allegations on a balance of probabilities. Where I find the evidence to be evenly balanced, I must dismiss the claim because the Tenant has not discharged her burden. Leaks, [name] and Property Loss

The Tenant says that almost immediately after moving into the unit in October of 2021, she discovered persistent leaking into the rental unit that the Landlord failed to remediate leading to an infestation of mould. She raised those concerns in response to the Landlord’s application to collect rent arrears heard on May 23, 2024 and received compensation by order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024.

The Tenant seeks to enlarge her recovery, relying on a report from Safetech Environmental Limited dated October 27, 2023 that says personnel from that company visited the unit on October 17, 2023 to assess water damage and identify potential mould. They tested samples and reported their readings. The report contains no opinion about an infestation of mould nor a finding that the rental unit is unsafe for habitation. Rather, it contains a specific disclaimer that the author is not qualified to give such an opinion. The photographs relied on show dampness and mildew but no visible mould growth, much less anything that could be called an infestation.

The Tenant says the Landlord ignored the findings of the mould experts. She says she sent the Landlord this report by email on November 6, 2023 but did not include a copy of that particular email in the package of emails and text messages filed. The Landlord testified she was only given the report as the Tenant was vacating the rental unit on December 31, 2023.

The Tenant testified that a further major leak event occurred in the month of December 2023 as the Tenant was preparing her move. Her packed belongings were soaked through with water and had to be discarded by a specialist waste management firm qualified to handle toxic mould as her regular movers refused to touch them for fear of injury. No photographs were produced showing the Tenant’s personal property to be damaged, or infested with mould.

The Tenant gave no explanation for why she did not seek this additional relief when the Board heard her concerns about leaking on May 23, 2024. The Tenant offered no principled reason why this claim should be litigated again on a different evidentiary record. The Tenant would have had in her possession or control all the facts and documents, including the Safetech report, and particulars of her lost property as of the hearing of May 23, 2024. [name] that the doctrine of cause of action estoppel is discretionary and must not be mechanically applied in all cases, I find it bars the Tenant’s disrepair claims in this case because it would undermine the objectives of finality and certainty in Board decisions if issues finally decided between the same parties were litigated again. Therefore, I find the claims in relation to leaks, mould, and concomitant property loss must be dismissed as res judicata. Electrical issues

The Tenant testified that on innumerable occasions, the fuses would trip because they were faulty and, because the Tenant had no access to the electrical panel, she could not reset them leaving her with no power for hours, sometimes days, at a time. The Tenant says she later discovered that the electrical supply and the wiring was inadequate for servicing two separate households and the Landlord’s failure to fix it is a breach of section 20 of the Act. The Board’s reasons for decision in order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 disclose that the Tenant advanced the same claim in those proceedings. For reasons detailed above, I find this claim is res judicata and cannot be raised again in new applications. [name]

The Tenant says that although the tenancy agreement shows laundry is not included, the written agreement is not consistent with the true agreement because she was orally promised laundry. The Tenant testified that she signed the written agreement under duress, as she needed housing urgently and was therefore not in a position to negotiate or seek alternatives.

The Board’s order LTB-L-056337-23 issued on July 22, 2024 has already found that laundry facilities were not included in this tenancy. I find this claim must be dismissed because the issue has finally been decided by the Board and I was given no persuasive reason why the Board should allow it to be relitigated. Parking

The Tenant seeks compensation because she was only given one parking spot when she was promised two. I find this claim must be dismissed because the tenancy agreement specifically speaks of only one parking spot. Guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the Tenant’s testimony that she felt compelled to sign the agreement is insufficient to prove that the substance of the contract was anything other than what it says. The Tenant led no evidence of having lodged any complaints about having only one spot and led no evidence of the Landlord ever having granted her the use of two spots. Illegal Entries

The Tenant testified that the door separating her unit from the main floor unit where the Landlord lived was not adequately secured, such that members of the Landlord’s family and her guests would wander into her private space. She presented a text message of October 27, 2022 where the Landlord contacted the Tenant to tell her a child had entered the rental unit and to apologize for the intrusion. The Tenant also wrote the Landlord on November 3, 2022 stating that someone tried to enter her rental unit. The Landlord responded that it was her brother sliding the mail under the door but promised to put a lock on that door to safeguard against any future intrusions.

I find the child inadvertently entering the rental unit on October 27, 2022 cannot be characterized as an illegal entry within the meaning of section 25 of the Act because that entry was not instigated by the Landlord or done at her behest or by anyone acting on her behalf. In any case, the Tenant admitted this entry caused no impact.

I find the evidence insufficient to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s brother actually entered the rental unit on November 3, 2022 because I find it at least equally probable that he merely slid the mail under the door as the Landlord says. That would be consistent with the Tenant’s description of the event as an attempted entry.
Although the Tenant spoke of countless other intrusions on her privacy by strangers, she offered no details in her evidence. Loud Music

I find the Tenant was unable to prove this incident on a balance of probabilities because, given the Landlord’s denial of the event, and the lack of any confirmatory evidence (such as a recording), I must find the evidence equally balanced and therefore insufficient to discharge the burden of proof. Harassment, Obstruction and Threats

The Tenant claims that once she voiced her concerns about disrepair, the Landlord embarked on a campaign of harassment that involved blocking her access to her parking spot, making constant complaints by phone and email, serving notices of termination, deliberately shutting off the electricity and enlisting her brother to redouble the illegal entries into the rental unit. The Landlord denied each of these allegations in turn but allowed that she did serve N4 notices for arrears of rent and an N12 notice to repossess for her own use. This Board has consistently held that attempting to enforce one’s rights under the Act, even unsuccessfully, cannot be characterized as harassment: [name] v 6891799 Canada Inc., 2023 ONLTB 25933 at para. 70; TST-49807-14 (Re), 2015 CanLII 34298 (ON LTB), at para 68.

As discussed above, the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that anyone illegally entered the rental unit at any time. The Tenant filed a text message where the Landlord cautions that if the Tenant does not advise in advance of her guests using the driveway for parking, she will assume these are trespassers and will have their car removed. I would not characterize this communication as harassment or a threat within the meaning of section 23. I agree that the tone is somewhat unprofessional but there is no evidence it happened more than once and critically, the Tenant led no evidence of how it impacted her warranting any recovery for what, even if proven, would be a trivial breach. [name]

The Tenant has proven the claim contained in the second T2 application that the Landlord deliberately shut off electricity for some 8 days in July 2023 by reference to an entry in a municipal inspector’s notes that says: Attended location and spoke with property owner on the phone and advised them that they need to turn the power back right away. They kept saying they turned it off because of no payment from tenant.

I accept this hearsay evidence and the Tenant’s testimony because the Landlord did not deny it and in fact, explained at length about how the Tenant’s choice to withhold rent caused her financial hardship. The Landlord did not say that the utility provider had discontinued service for want of payment. The evidence suggest that the Landlord restored power after learning of her mistake as the municipal inspector closed his file when the Tenant did not renew her complaint. Still, withholding the supply of a vital service for non-payment, in these circumstances, is unreasonable within the meaning of section 21 of the Act which means this claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities. Remedies

Having established that the Landlord unreasonably withheld the supply of electricity in July 2023, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies she can prove on a balance of probabilities in relation to that breach. That claim is pleaded in the second T2 application that claims out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $1,000.00 and an administrative fine. Hotels and Meals

The Tenant has delivered hotel bills totalling $1,240.22 and proof of payments made to restaurants totalling $526.46 to substantiate this claim. The Tenant testified that living in the rental unit without power was impossible so she relocated herself and her child to hotels and ate at restaurants. The Tenant filed an invoice for a stay at the Pickering Casino Hotel for July 9 to July 14, 2023 issued to herself. She also relied on another invoice for Sheraton Centre Hotel in Toronto spanning the period July 15 to July 18, 2023 issued to [name] of Villa Park, California. I was not told why the Tenant’s hotel invoice is drawn up in the name of that person. That invoice speaks of additional pages which weren’t filed.

The Tenant explained that having experienced an abusive relationship, she was unable to take lodgings in the same locality as the rental unit for fear that her abuser might find her. So the Tenant decided to stay at a hotel in Toronto. She has filed four POS printouts from various restaurants in Toronto for July 15 and July 16, 2023. The Tenant did not explain why she was not fearful of staying at the Pickering Casino Resort between July 9 and July 15, 2023 which is in the same locality as the rental unit.

I find that the Tenant has failed to prove either causation or the quantum of damages claimed on a balance of probabilities because her documentary proof is unreliable on its face and contradicts her testimony. I recognize that as trier of fact I must assess a fair and reasonable amount of compensation even where that task is made difficult by frailties in the evidence. However, in this case, I find the evidentiary record is so lacking that the task is impossible. I find the Tenant’s choice of hotels and restaurants is not consistent with an emergency. Accordingly I can only award nominal damages. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $100.00 for deliberately depriving her of electricity. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not binding on me but I accept it as the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

This remedy is not normally granted unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and ensure future compliance. The objectives of deterrence involve both specific and general deterrence. I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act or to deter future breaches. The Landlord has already been ordered to compensate the Tenant in respect of the disrepair claims adjudicated in file number LTB-L-056337-23 and I find that no further deterrence is required in respect of the one claim that has been proven in these proceedings.
The Tenant incurred no filing fee in respect of the second T2 application which is the only one that was successful.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $100.00 on or before August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes (LTB-L- 097744-25). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (LTB-T-054173-25).
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

It was undisputed that the Tenant informed the Landlord several months in advance and vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2026. The Landlord sought rent arrears to May 24, 2026, the day the Landlord changed the locks, due to the Tenants’ failure to return the keys.

Possession of a rental unit is not defined solely by who holds the keys; rather, it is assessed by who has control over the unit, including access to, use of, and occupation of the unit. The Landlord was aware that the Tenant was vacating on April 30, 2026, and had the opportunity to change the locks on May 1, 2026, if the keys were not properly returned. I am not satisfied that the Landlord mitigated their damages as required by section 16 of the Act by waiting until May 24, 2026, to change the locks, despite the various negotiations the parties had about the key return. Accordingly, rent arrears are calculated up to April 30, 2026, the date the Tenant vacated the unit, not May 24, 2026.
The lawful rent is $3,200.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.

It was undisputed that the Landlord collected six months of rent at the start of the tenancy, which included the last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant submitted that the collection of four additional months of rent was an illegal charge. The Landlord submitted that these additional months were prepaid rent. Either way, the funds have now been properly applied as payments toward the arrears in paragraph 7, below. There is no further remedy as the Landlord is no longer holding these funds for future rent payments.
The Tenant has paid $18,925.00 to the Landlord since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to April 30, 2026, are $3,475.00.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,200.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $107.98 is owing to the Tenant for the period from November 30, 2024, to April 30, 2026.

It was undisputed that the Landlord collected a key deposit of $300.00 at the start of the tenancy. The parties made arrangements to hand over the keys on May 2, 2026. However, the Tenant did not return the keys to the Landlord’s Agent because the document confirming the number of keys was incorrect. The parties made arrangements to meet again on May 16, 2026. The Tenant requested the Landlord’s Agent to sign a document confirming that they do not owe any rent. The Landlord’s Agent declined, as the Landlord did not believe that statement to be true, and the Tenant refused to return the keys. As of the hearing date, the keys have not been returned.

It is not appropriate for a tenant to make the return of keys to a rental unit conditional on a landlord signing a document confirming a lack of rent arrears. The appropriate time to dispute a rent arrears claim is at an LTB hearing. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Tenant acted reasonably in withholding the keys. Given that the keys were ultimately not returned, the Landlord is entitled to keep the deposit. The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application, LTB-T-054173-25, is dismissed.
The Landlord’s application, LTB-L-097744-25, is granted.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of April 30, 2026, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $353.02. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit is deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before July 31, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. September 23, 2025 – Hearing

At the hearing on September 23, 2025 the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant’s application ought to be dismissed on the ground that the individual who filed it, [name], is not a tenant, rather he is the representative of [name] as she passed away and therefore does not have jurisdiction to bring the application forward and the LTB does not have the jurisdiction to hear this matter.
The parties were directed to provide written submissions regarding this preliminary matter as there was extensive submissions regarding this preliminary matter.

As per interim order LTB-T-054966-24-IN issued on November 12, 2025, I did not find, on a balance of probabilities that [name] was not permitted to file an application on behalf of the Tenant. Therefore, the matter was adjourned for the merits of the application to be heard. Per section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) it provides that “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives. Therefore, I find that the Board has the jurisdiction to hear this matter, as Mr. [name]name] is a representative of [name]. June 24, 2026 – Hearing Adjournment Request

At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative requested an adjournment of this matter as their key witness was unavailable to attend the hearing due to a prior commitment that he is unable to reschedule.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative opposed this adjournment request as he is not overly familiar with this individual, and believes that this witness was only briefly involved in this matter. They are prepared to proceed on the matter today and find that an adjournment would be prejudicial to the Tenant.

Upon hearing the parties submissions and in consideration of the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1, I did not find it appropriate to grant the adjournment request. I find that the Landlord had ample opportunity to prepare for the next hearing and to ensure that their witnesses are available and find that granting an adjournment would not be consistent with the LTB’s mandate to hear matters on an expeditious basis. Preliminary Matter

The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the Tenant’s application pertains to a complex where there are multiple buildings owned by the Region of Waterloo. Some of these buildings are part of community housing which fall under the LTB’s jurisdiction however some are [name] buildings, which are exempt under the Act. Therefore, the Landlord is requesting that the LTB does not hear the claims pertaining from the Long- Term Care Homes as they are exempt from the Act. The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the claims pertain to building units 239 and 247. Building 239 is a residential unit however building unit 247 is the Long-Term Care facility. The Tenant, [name] [name] lived in the residential building for one month for the time of December 2023 to January 2024 and May 2, 2024, to May 28, 2024.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative did not dispute that the Act did not reply, and that the claims are not against the Long-Term Care Facility, but it would be impossible for separate them as the communications were going back and forth, from the Long-Term Care Facility to the residential units. Unfortunately, Ms. [name] passed away during the transition from the Long-Term Care to the Residential building and the communications are going back and forth with a individual, who interfered with the discharge of Ms. [name]name] from hospital. In addition, the issue of Mr. [name]name] being trespassed involved the entire complex, another reason why it would be difficult to separate.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the individual who the Tenant’s Legal Representative is referring to was only part of the Long-Term Care home.

Upon hearing the parties submissions, I find on a balance of probabilities that the claims that arise from the Long-Term Care Home are exempt from the Act as per section 5 of the Act. Therefore, I declined to hear the claims that made part of the Tenant’s application that arose from communications from the Long Term Care Home. Tenant Evidence

Mr. [name]name] testified that he was trespassed by the Landlord, and that this was a violation of the Trespass to Property Act, 1990. A copy of the trespass notice was submitted as evidence to the Board. He stated that the Landlord had no legal basis to trespass him, and that by receiving a trespass notice it significantly interfered with his ability to visit his mother as he was unable to drive into the complex to get to his mothers unit. A copy of a map of the complex was submitted as evidence to the LTB.

Mr. [name]name] testified that [name] interfered with his ability to care of his mother, as she was making it impossible for him to see his mother and she prepared a series of letters that kept changing regarding his ability to visit his mother. Mr. [name]name] states that [name] did not have the jurisdiction to interfere the way she did and made it impossible for him to be there.

He stated that since December 2023, he was with his mother constantly, as she required a lot of care at this time. The trespass notice restricted access to his mother’s care. During this time, he was requesting evidence as to why he was trespassed, however he did not receive any reasons. The trespass notice restricted his access to visit his mother and therefore impacted his ability to get for her.

Mr. [name]name] testified that his mother’s hospitalization was prolonged as the hospital staff stated that the trespass notice is still in effect and therefore his mother was discharged later than she should have been.

In addition, the Landlord did not respond to Mr. [name]name]’s application to be a tenant. He stated that he sent in his application, however, did not hear back from the Landlord despite following up.

Mr. [name]name] stated that this had impacted his mother as she was stressed that she was not able to come home due to the trespass notices. Her health deteriorated due to the stress and her blood pressure was elevated. His mother’s health continued to decline and she eventually passed on May 28, 2024. A copy of his mother’s medical records was submitted as evidence to the Board.

Upon cross examination, he stated that the first time his mother entered the Long-Term Care facility was on May 31, 2023. He stated that other than him, there is another Power of Attorney, who was his cousin’s wife. Mr. [name]name] further stated that the trespass notice dated December 22, 2023 prevented him from attending building 239, despite not explicitly stating it as she cannot access the parking lot. He believed the ambiguity in the trespass notice was intentional. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s witness, [name] who is the Region of [name] and Community Specialist testified at the hearing. She stated that the Region of [name] owns the entire campus. There are four buildings in total, building 239 and 233 are under the Region of [name] and 245 and 247 are under Sunnyside Senior Services. Her role entails addressing tenant concerns, and any filings with the LTB. [name] stated that she has never met [name], who is the director of Sunnyside Senior Services. 21. [name] testified that the reason the trespass notice encompassed buildings 233 and 239 was because if it was served for staff safety, it would cover the who campus. She has served trespass notices to unauthorized guests. 22. Regarding Mr. [name]name] being added to the lease, they received an application from him on May 30, 2023 requesting to be added to his mother’s lease. However, his mother moved into the Long Term Care Facility a day later, on May 31, 2023. Therefore, there was no reason to add him to the lease. In addition, the application was incomplete. 23. [name] testified that she was only aware of the one trespass notice that she served, as the senior services are governed by a different body and bound by confidentiality. She was unaware that she was directed to serve the trespass order until she was instructed to do so. She served the trespass order on February 26, 2024. She was not aware of any restraints from Waterloo Regional Housing for the period of December 14, 2023 to January 14, 2024. 24. From May 2, 2024 to May 28, 2024, the period that Ms. [name] was back in her residence from the hospital, she was unaware of any contact made to the Police, or any other trespass notices that came from the Landlord. 25. During cross examination [name] stated that she has never met [name]. She stated that building 239 has support workers and nurses, which is why she has the ability to go to the other buildings. She was instructed to provide the trespass notice by her manager. Based on the previous trespass orders form Sunnyside Senior Services, she believes it was giving due to safety concerns. She further stated that she did not communicate with Mr. [name]name] regarding his application to become a tenant from May 2023 until December 2023 and is not sure why she did not follow up. Legal Analysis 26. Section 22 of the Act states that the landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 27. Section 23 of the Act states that the landlord shall not harass, obstruct, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 28. After hearing the parties submissions, and based on a balance of probabilities, I do not find that the Tenant proved that the Landlord contravened section 22 and section 23 of the Act. I find that a substantial amount of evidence that Mr. [name]name] provided related to how the trespass notice impacted his ability to visit his mother and take care of her. Mr. [name]name] represented the [name] of the Tenant, and therefore he does not have rights against the Landlord as he was not a party to the Landlord and Tenant relationship. Therefore, Mr. [name] does is not able to bring claims forward against the Landlord. I heard that the Mr. [name] made an attempt to become a tenant, and that the Landlord did not respond to his application in a timely manner, however Mr. [name]name] did not lead any evidence to demonstrate that he became a tenant at any point. Therefore, any claims that are made from Mr. [name]name] against the Landlord are denied. 29. On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true 30. Mr. [name]name] testified that the Landlord’s actions had a negative impact on his mother, her health deteriorated as a result of the way the Landlord treated her, and that by the Landlord trespassing Mr. [name]name], her Power of Attorney, impacted the care she was able to receive. I note that the evidence that Mr. [name]name] provided was hearsay. 31. The Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990 permits administrative tribunals to allow hearsay evidence. In Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083, the Divisional Court stated that administrative tribunals must first assess whether the hearsay evidence is necessary and reliable. 32. While certain elements of the testimony and evidence presented or submitted by Mr. [name]name] certainly amount to hearsay evidence, I found them to be necessary as Ms. [name] was unable to attend the proceedings. However, I did not find their testimony to be reliable, as it was not detailed, clear and sufficient to establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord interfered and/or harassed Ms. [name]name]. Although the Mr. [name]name] submitted medical documentation, I do not find that these documents were sufficient to prove the Tenant’s application on a balance of probabilities, as the documents did not provide sufficient information on how the Landlord’s actions directly affected Ms. [name]’s health. After hearing the submissions I do not find that Mr. [name]name] provided sufficient evidence to establish his mother’s state of mind during these incidents to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant, and/or harassed her. Therefore, the Tenant’s claims are denied. Costs 33. The Landlord’s Legal Representative requested that the LTB order costs that the Landlord incurred reviewing a substantial amount of disclosure that was not presented before the LTB due to a lot of the claims being out of the LTB’s jurisdiction to hear and there being two legal representatives involved on this matter. 34. The Tenant’s Legal Representative stated that having to review disclosure is not an appropriate reason for costs to be awarded. In addition, an individual has the right to change counsel at any time and should not be penalized for it. 35. With regard to Landlord’s Legal Representative’s request for costs, the authority limits for a Member to consider awarding costs of another party come from subsection 204(2) of the Act, Rule 27.2 of the Board’s Rules of Practice and the Board’s Interpretation Guideline #3 entitled “Costs”. 36. Having review the Board’s Rules, and in consideration of the Board’s Guideline, I do not find it appropriate to award costs against the Tenant. I heard the Landlord’s Legal Representative’s submissions and although they may have spent a significant amount of time reviewing the disclosure, I do not find there to be grounds for costs in this matter. The claim for costs is denied. 37. The Tenant’s Legal Representative also requested costs on the grounds that the Landlord called a witness to only address one issue is an insult to Mr. [name]name] and his late mother. The Tenant’s Legal Representative stated that they spent almost twelve hours preparing for this matter, and the Landlord only addressed a narrow issue. 38. The Landlord’s Legal Representative opposed the costs, stating that it is the Tenant’s application and the Landlord does not have to have a reason to respond. The key witness was not available, and therefore she called the other witness they had for the residential Landlord. 39. Upon considering the parties submissions, and in consideration of the Board’s Rules and Guideline # 3, I do not find it appropriate that costs be awarded against a party for only having one witness to address the issues. Indeed, it is the Tenant’s application and therefor they bear the burden of proof, how the Landlord responds to the application is not, in my view, grounds for costs to be awarded. The claim for costs is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Respondent'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Applicant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Applicant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Applicant.
reasons: For the reasons below I find that the Act does not apply to the relationship between these parties. The Respondent was a tenant and the Applicant was their roommate. Any dispute they may have will need to be resolved outside of the LTB.
The application is therefore dismissed. Evidence
The residential complex is a house with two kitchens and multiple washrooms.
The Respondent is not the owner of the property. She is a tenant who rented the entire house from the property owner.

Document 8357840 in the Portal is a copy of the standard Ontario lease between the Respondent and the property owner, [name]. The tenants are listed as the Respondent, Meiqi Hao and [name], who are the Respondent’s children. The lease was signed in June 2025. Monthly rent was $3,500.

The Applicant and the Respondent signed a “Room Rental Agreement”. The original agreement was in Mandarin. The Applicant translated it into English and uploaded the translation to the Portal under document ID 8329673. Parties agree that the translation is accurate.

The room rental agreement was entered into on November 6, 2025. It names the parties as a landlord and a tenant. The rented areas include one small bedroom on the second floor and access to the basement kitchen and dining area. Rent is set at $630.00 a month.

There is no dispute that the Respondent and her son lived at the property at material times. There is no dispute that other people lived there as well. Parties disagree about the room the Respondent occupied but this dispute is immaterial.

There is no dispute that parties used the same kitchen on the main floor to cook their meals. Parties disagree about the reason why the Applicant was using the upstairs kitchen instead of the basement kitchen but this dispute is also immaterial.
The Respondent vacated the property on June 20, 2026. The Applicant alleges that he was locked out of his room shortly thereafter and that his belongings were disposed of.
The Respondent argues that the relationship between the parties is not governed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and the application ought to be dismissed.
For the reasons below, I agree. [name] and analysis
The Respondent claims that the Act does not apply and bear the burden of proof in establishing same on a balance of probabilities.

Section 2(1) of the Act provides the following definitions inter alia: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; [emphasis added] “rental unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and “rental unit” includes, (a) a site for a mobile home or site on which there is a land lease home used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and (b) a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home; “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; (“convention de location”) “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;
Under s. 95(1), a tenant may assign a rental unit: “95 (1) Subject to subsections (2), (3) and (6), and with the consent of the landlord, a tenant may assign a rental unit to another person.”

The consequences of assignment are outlined in s. 95(8): (8) If a tenant has assigned a rental unit to another person, the tenancy agreement continues to apply on the same terms and conditions and, (a) the assignee is liable to the landlord for any breach of the tenant’s obligations and may enforce against the landlord any of the landlord’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act, if the breach or obligation relates to the period after the assignment, whether or not the breach or obligation also related to a period before the assignment; (b) the former tenant is liable to the landlord for any breach of the tenant’s obligations and may enforce against the landlord any of the landlord’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act, if the breach or obligation relates to the period before the assignment; (c) if the former tenant has started a proceeding under this Act before the assignment and the benefits or obligations of the new tenant may be affected, the new tenant may join in or continue the proceeding.
It is clear that no assignment has occurred in the case before me and the Applicant didn’t argue that the unit was assigned to them.
Under s. 97(1) A tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord.

Under 97(4) If a tenant has sublet a rental unit to another person, (a) the tenant remains entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the landlord for the breaches, of the tenant’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act during the subtenancy; and (b) the subtenant is entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the tenant for the breaches, of the subtenant’s obligations under the subletting agreement or this Act during the subtenancy. 2006, c. 17, s. 97 (4).
Under 97(5), A subtenant has no right to occupy the rental unit after the end of the subtenancy.

In accordance with subsection 202(1) of the Act, in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 21 titled “Landlords, Tenants, [name] and Residential Tenancies” states in part: There is no definition of "occupant" in the RTA. For the purposes of proceedings at the LTB, an "occupant" may be considered to be a person who is not a tenant but who lives in a rental unit as their principal place of residence. An occupant may be authorized or unauthorized depending on the facts of each case… If a tenant does not vacate the rental unit but allows another person to live in the rental unit with them, a sublet is not created within the meaning of the Act. In such a case there is no landlord and tenant relationship between the tenant and that person or between that person and the landlord. In that case, no consent of the landlord is required and the other person is a roommate of the tenant and/or an occupant of the tenant's rental unit. A tenant can allow people to occupy the rental unit with the tenant but the tenant cannot subdivide the rental unit into more than one rental unit. For example, if a tenant rents an entire home, the tenant may permit a person to live in and have exclusive use of the basement of that home, however, the home, including the basement, remains the rental unit. That person would be a roommate of the tenant or an occupant of the rental unit and the roommate/occupant has no protection under the Act…. [Emphasis Added]

In some circumstances a tenant may be a landlord within the meaning of the Act. In [name] v. Ogunfeibo, 2019 ONSC 7423 (CanLII) (‘Tremblay’) Divisional Court found a tenant to be a landlord. A person who rented a rental unit from a landlord who was not a party to the proceeding was named as the landlord. The Divisional Court held that the tenant was not a subtenant, but rather a tenant of [name] who herself rented the rental unit. [36] The relationship between [name] and [name] falls squarely within the words of the statute. She is a landlord because she is a “person who permits occupancy of a rental unit”. She is not permitting [name] to occupy her unit with her, so the exemption in the definition of “landlord” in paragraph (a) of the definition does not apply. [37] Similarly, [name] is “a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit.” He pays that rent directly to [name] and he gave evidence that he believed she was the landlord. So, he fits the definition of “tenant”. [38] The bedroom, kitchen, common area, and bathroom are “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises” so they meet the definition of a “rental unit.” Although [name] shares the bathroom, kitchen and common area with others, the premises are akin to a boarding house or a rooming house, both of which are expressly included in the definition of “rental unit” above. Finally, because the bathroom and kitchen are shared with other occupants and are not required to be shared with the “owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent” the exclusion from the Act in s.5(i) does not apply. [emphasis added]
The facts before me are different from Tremblay.

The Respondent lived at the property when the relationship commenced with full knowledge of the Applicant. She continued living at the property until she moved out as her 12-month lease ended on or about June 20th, 2026. The Applicant was always aware that the Respondent is herself a tenant. The Respondent permitted the Applicant to occupy the rental unit with her which distinguishes this case from Tremblay. The definition of a ‘landlord’ in the Act expressly excludes people like the Respondent.

I find that the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the residential complex was always a roommate agreement between the parties despite them apparently using Mandarin language equivalents to ‘landlord’ and ‘tenant’ in their roommate agreement. There was no sublet or assignment. There was never a tenancy within the meaning of the Act. The [name] was always the Respondent’s roommate. The Respondent was never a ‘landlord’ within the meaning of the Act. She was always “a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex”.
The Act does not apply.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subTenants.
reasons: At the hearing, I raised the issue that the substance of the Tenant’s application concerns the Landlord’s requirement that the Tenants pay a fee of $1,252.55 as a condition of approving the assignment of the tenancy. The Tenants allege that they advertised the rental unit, conducted showings, and prepared the rental unit for turnover, and therefore submit that the amount charged does not reflect the Landlord’s reasonable out-of-pocket expenses. The relief sought is a determination as to whether the fee charged exceeded the amount permitted by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and, if so, an order requiring repayment of the excess.

The application was filed as an A2 application under subsection 98(1) of the Act. However, subsection 98(1) applies where a landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to a proposed assignment or sublet. The issue before the Board is not whether the Landlord unreasonably withheld consent, but whether the fee collected by the Landlord exceeded the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses permitted by subsection 95(7) of the Act. A claim seeking repayment of money allegedly collected contrary to the Act is properly brought under section 135 of the Act by way of a T1 application.

Rule 15.3 of the Board's Rules of Procedure permits the Board to amend an application where appropriate. In determining whether to amend an application, the Board considers whether doing so would cause prejudice to any party that cannot be remedied.

I find it appropriate to amend the application from an A2 application to a T1 application. Although the application was filed under the incorrect application type, the Tenants' application is detailed and clearly sets out the factual allegations, the statutory basis for their complaint, and the remedy sought, namely, a determination that the assignment fee exceeded the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket expenses and an order for repayment. In my view, the Landlord was fully apprised of the case to be met and had a fair opportunity to respond to the allegations. I am satisfied that amending the application to reflect the appropriate application type does not alter the factual issues in dispute or the relief sought and does not result in any prejudice to either party that cannot be addressed at the hearing. As such the A2 application filed under 98(1) of the Act is amended to a T1 application pursuant to section 135 of the Act. The T1 application
The Tenant, [name] ('EH'), testified that the Tenants entered into a fixed-term tenancy commencing August 15, 2024, with a term ending August 31, 2025.
EH testified that the Tenants purchased a home during the winter of 2024 and, as a result, sought to have another person take over the remainder of their fixed-term tenancy.

EH testified that the Tenants initially considered subletting the rental unit. However, after discussions with the Landlord, they were advised that any subtenant would be required to vacate the rental unit at the end of the fixed term and would be required to apply for a new tenancy if they wished to remain. The Tenants therefore elected to pursue an assignment of the tenancy, to which the Landlord agreed to.

EH testified that the Tenants first advised the Landlord of their intention to assign the tenancy in early March 2025. The documentary evidence shows that the formal request for consent to assign was made on March 25, 2025, although the Landlord had been aware beforehand that the Tenants were purchasing a home. The assignment was ultimately completed at the end of May 2025.

As a condition of approving the assignment, the Landlord required the Tenants to pay an assignment fee of $1,252.55, which the Tenants paid on May 6, 2025. EH testified that the Landlord initially requested an amount equal to one month's rent but later reduced the fee to $1,252.55. EH testified that the Tenants understood there would likely be costs associated with processing the assignment; however, they believed the amount charged was excessive and requested a breakdown of the fee.
EH testified that before proceeding with the assignment, the Tenants reviewed the assignment provisions of the Act, conducted their own research, and discussed the process with the Landlord.

During cross-examination, the Landlord's representative referred to subsection 95(4) of the Act and questioned why the Tenants did not give notice to terminate the tenancy after the Landlord failed to respond to the assignment request within seven days. EH testified that the Tenants wished to proceed cooperatively because the Landlord ultimately consented to the assignment and they did not want to leave the Landlord with a vacant rental unit. EH further testified that the Tenants believed they had no practical alternative but to pay the assignment fee, as they understood the Landlord would not process or approve the assignment unless the fee was paid.

EH’s uncontested testimony was that the Tenants advertised the rental unit in early April 2025, paid to promote the advertisements, screened prospective applicants, selected a suitable assignee, conducted the showing of the rental unit and building amenities, and prepared the rental unit for turnover. After the Landlord approved the assignee on May 27, 2025, the Tenants completed the cleaning and turnover of the rental unit before the assignee took possession on June 1, 2025. EH testified that the Landlord did not advertise the rental unit, conduct showings, locate prospective assignees, or prepare the rental unit for occupancy.

EH acknowledged that the Act permits a landlord to recover reasonable out-of-pocket expenses associated with an assignment. However, the Tenants maintained that the amount charged by the Landlord greatly exceeded those expenses.

The Landlord's witness, [name] Fischer (EF) is the Landlord’s leasing and building administrator. EF testified that a large portion of her job duties include application reviews, creation of lease documentation, assisting with move in/out inspections, and processing assignments.

EF testified that the Landlord generally charges an assignment fee equivalent to one month's rent, however reduced the fee for the Tenants in order to accommodate them. She stated that the fee is intended to recover costs associated with marketing, advertising, conducting showings, reviewing applications, creating tenant accounts, obtaining credit reports, preparing lease documentation, and using various software platforms. EF testified that in addition to her wages, the Landlord incurred nominal third-party costs, including a charge of a few dollars for the JOT platform, approximately $9.25 for a credit report, and approximately $10.00 for the use of DocuSign.

EF testified that her role in the assignment process included reviewing the proposed assignee's application, verifying employment and references, obtaining a credit report, preparing the assignment documentation, ensuring the required forms were completed, confirming tenant insurance, coordinating the transfer of the hydro account, and distributing the executed documents to the parties. EF estimated that these responsibilities represented approximately 80% of the assignment process and required approximately 10 hours to complete. EF testified that her hourly wage is approximately $28.00. EF further testified that the remaining aspects of the assignment process, including the administration of the last month's rent deposit, the receipt and processing of the first month's rent, and the collection and administration of the key deposit, are completed by the Landlord's accounting department.

Subsection 95(7) of the Act permits a landlord to charge only reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred in connection with giving consent to an assignment. The onus rests with the Landlord to establish that the amount charged reflects expenses actually incurred.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord has established that the fee of $1,252.55 represents its reasonable out-of-pocket expenses. Much of the justification advanced by the Landlord relates to services that were not provided in this case, including advertising the rental unit, marketing the unit, conducting showings, and locating a suitable assignee. The evidence before me establishes that these tasks were completed by the Tenants on their own time and at their own expense.

While I accept that the Landlord incurred administrative costs in reviewing the proposed assignee, preparing the assignment documentation, conducting reference and credit checks, coordinating utility changes, and completing the necessary administrative work, those costs do not reasonably support a fee of $1,252.55. EF testified that she spent approximately 10 hours completing her portion of the assignment process at an hourly wage of $28.00, representing labour costs of approximately $280.00, together with nominal third-party expenses for the credit report, DocuSign, and the JOT platform.

I also accept EF's evidence that the remaining 20% of the assignment process included the Landlord's accounting department and the administration of the last month's rent deposit, the processing of the first month's rent, and the collection and administration of the key deposit. However, the Landlord did not lead any evidence regarding the amount of time spent by accounting staff completing these tasks, the hourly wages of those employees, or any other evidence from which I could determine the actual out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Landlord in relation to that work. As a result, I am unable to conclude that the accounting functions materially increased the Landlord's recoverable out-of-pocket expenses beyond the evidence that was presented.

Having considered all of the evidence, I find that a fee of $350.00 reasonably reflects the Landlord's out-of-pocket expenses incurred in processing the assignment. That amount accounts for EF's labour, the Landlord's nominal third-party expenses, and reasonably recognizes the additional administrative work performed by the accounting department, despite the absence of evidence quantifying those costs. It also recognizes that the Tenants undertook the substantial work associated with advertising the rental unit, locating a suitable assignee, conducting the showing, and preparing the rental unit for turnover. I am satisfied that $350.00 represents the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket expenses within the meaning of subsection 95(7) of the Act.
As the Landlord collected $1,252.55 from the Tenants, I find that the Landlord collected $902.55 in excess of the amount permitted by subsection 95(7) of the Act.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $955.55. This amount represents: • $902.55 for the excessive amount not permitted pursuant to subsection95(7) of the Act • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing on or before July 21, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: -Louis (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (hereafter referred to as the ‘T6 Application’).
reasons: At the start of the hearing, the Tenant sought that the matter be adjourned in order to have the T6 Application heard alongside the application LTB-L-089364-25, through which the Landlord applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant because the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit, or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex, has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant (hereafter referred to as the ‘L2 Application’).
The Landlord was opposed to the Tenant’s request, and sought for the T6 Application to proceed as originally scheduled, on May 26, 2026.

Rule 1.6c) of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reads as follows: In order to provide the most expeditious and fair determination of the questions arising in any proceeding the LTB may: […] join applications or hear applications together where it is fair to do so.

Having reviewed both the T6 Application and the L2 Application, I do not find that that it would be fair, in all of the circumstances, to have these applications heard at the same time. While they certainly involve the same part ies, these applications pertain to separate and distinct material facts.

As the parties do not risk facing inconsistent outcomes by having the T6 Application and the L2 Application heard separately, and as the Board as an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding, 1 I denied the Tenant’s request to have the T6 Application and the L2 Application heard together.
Accordingly, the T6 Application proceeded to be heard. T6 Application Amendment

The Tenant sought to amend the T6 Application in order to clarify the remedies they were requesting. Specifically, the Tenant was seeking: • A thirty percent (30%) rent abatement from July 2024 to the date of the hearing, • The amount of $6,436.70 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair or replace the property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions.
The Landlord was not opposed to the Tenant’s amendment request. Instead, they intended to dispute the merits of their claim.

Accordingly, on the basis of the submissions before, and pursuant to subsection 200(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, I granted the Tenant’s request to amend their T6 Application. Agreed Facts
The parties agreed that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2026.

The parties agreed that the lawful monthly rent was in the amount of $964.45 until December 31, 2025, and was duly increased to $984.70 as of January 1, 2026. 1 Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. T6 Application

As explained below, the Tenant partially proved some of the allegations contained in the T6 Application on a balance of probabilities . Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the total amount of $4,408.75, on or before August 15, 2026. a) [name] Evidence
The Tenant testified that they first noticed the presence of cockroaches in the rental unit on September 20, 2023.

The Tenant stated that they proceeded to advise the Landlord of the cockroach issue either during the month of September 2023, or October 2023, after another tenant of the residential complex had also discussed similar issues with the Tenant.

The Tenant contacted a pest control company in order to confirm if the insects they were seeing throughout their rental unit were indeed cockroaches, as it appears from a copy of the estimate from Herb’o’Dem , dated November 6, 2023 (DOC -5974681, page 12 of 36; Exhibit 1).
The Tenant indicated that the Landlord advised them that they could proceed in moving out of the rental unit if they so chose, due to the cockroach infestation.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord, thought their Superintended, provided the Tenant with traps for cockroaches, which they believe were bought at Canadian Tire.

As they felt that the Landlord had failed to take adequate measure to address the cockroach issue, the Tenant indicated that they proceeded to contact the City of Hawkesbury’s by-law enforcement services (hereafter referred to as the ‘City’) to advise them of the ongoing infestation.

The Tenant indicated that following their complaint to the City, the City proceeded to investigate the matter, as it appears from a copy of the complaint form, service request and occurrence report #89507 from the Corporation of the Town of Hawkesbury obtained by the Tenant through their FOI request #A17-269 (DOC-5974681, pages 3 to 11 of 36; [name], in bundle).

The Tenant indicated that the City’s internal investigation led them to issuing an [name] to Remedy Violation of Maintenance and Occupancy against the Landlord, following an inspection of the residential complex on November 16, 2023, as it appears f rom a copy of the Order to Remedy Violation of Maintenance and Occupancy, dated November 29, 2023 (DOC-5974681, pages 1 and 2 of 36; Exhibit 3).
The Tenant stated that as the Landlord continued to fail to duly address the ongoing infestation, the City proceeded to secure the services of a pest control company and invoiced the Landlord.
The Tenant recalled that the pest control company secured by the City proceeded to conduct two (2) treatments of the residential complex (which includes the rental unit).
The Tenant suggested that the treatments were not necessarily efficient, as the Tenant occupying the lower-level unit had refused to allow the treatments to take place in their unit.

Despite the two (2) aforementioned treatments, the Tenant continued to notice the presence of cockroaches throughout the rental unit. They therefore advised the Landlord that the issue was not resolved.

The Tenant indicated that, as the Landlord had continued to ignore or adequately treat the cockroach infestation, they were required to purchase new appliances such as refrigerators, and a stove as excrement from the cockroaches were found within the appliances (Exhibit 2).

The Tenant stated that they incurred expenses in the amount of $6,436.70, which represents: • $1,412.49 for a stove, as it appears from a copy of the invoice #18547158 from Tanguay, dated May 14, 2024 (DOC-5974681, page 13 of 36; Exhibit 4). • $1,569.40 for a mattress, as it appears from a copy of the invoice #09064GBDUEZ, from The Brick, dated September 6, 2024 (DOC-5974681, page 15 of 36; Exhibit 5), • $3,454.81 for a refrigerator and bedframe, as it appears from a copy of the invoice #03155GBYQTG, from The Brick , dated March 15, 2025 (DOC-5974681, page 14 of 36; Exhibit 6).

The Tenant therefore sought for the Board to award them a rent abatement of thirty (30%) between the month of July 2024, and the date of the hearing, along with the amount of $6,436.70 for the costs incurred to replace their belongings. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord described the residential complex , which they purchased in 2021, as being comprised of two (2) residential units, with the Tenant residing in the upper-level unit.

The Landlord stated that they were aware that the tenant occupying the lower-level unit had health issues , as it appears from a copy of the medical note dated June 28, 2007 (DOC-8027711; Exhibit 7) . They took this into consideration when considering treatment options to address the cockroach infestation.

The Landlord agreed that there was an ongoing cockroach infestation between September 20, 2023, through the month of July 2024. They submit that they were never advised by the Tenant that the issue was ongoing following the month of July 2024.

The Landlord indicated that after the Tenant advised them of the cockroach issue during the month of September 2023, they arranged to have bait -traps delivered to the rental unit on September 30, 2023, as it appears from a copy of the note signed by the Tenant on September 30, 2023, acknowledging the receipt of such traps (DOC -8027672; Exhibit 8 ) The Landlord elected to use such traps to address the Tenant’s concerns in order to limit potential health risks to the lower-level tenant.

The Landlord indicated that they had been cooperating with the City throughout 2023 and 2024. They were under the impression that the City would complete the required pest control treatments and that the issue was resolved.
The Landlord recognized that the City had indeed contracted a pest control company on behalf of the Landlord, and had proceeded to send the corresponding invoices to the Landlord.

The Landlord stated that the City had facilitated six (6) treatments of the rental unit, through their chosen pest control contractor. The Landlord contacted the assigned by-law officer and was advised, during the month of July 2024, that the tenant occupying the lower -level unit would need to allow access to their unit for adequate treatments of the cockroach infestation to take place.

The Landlord indicated that they cannot control the way that tenants live, nor can that control their level of cooperation with pest control treatments. They submit that they could not have acted differently.

Under cross -examination, the Landlord agreed that they had advised the City on July 11, 2024, that they were trying to facilitate access to the lower-level unit for pest-control treatments to take place, which led them to serving the tenant residing in the lower-level unit an N5 notice of Termination, as it appears from a copy of the N5 Notice of Termination dated July 12, 2024 (hereafter referred to as the ‘N5 Notice’; DOC-8027701; Exhibit 9).
Under cross-examination, the Landlord reiterated that despite serving the N5 Notice, they were unaware of ongoing cockroach issues in the rental unit.
Under cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that they had offered the tenant of the lower- level unit alternate accommodations to facilitate the pest control treatments.

Under cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that they did not appeal the [name] to Remedy Violation of Maintenance and Occupancy (Exhibit 3) . The Landlord stated that they could not abide by the deadlines set out in the order as they were abroad at the time.

The Landlord's Witness, [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘F.L’) testified that they are a friend of the Landlord, whom they assist with respect to the management of the residential complex and the dealing of maintenance issues, which includes the cockroach infestation forming the basis of the T6 Application.

F.L stated that they visited the lower -level unit of the residential complex twice since the month of July 2024. They found the unit to be very clean and never saw any cockroaches or other pests within the unit. The tenant occupying the lower -level unit had never complained to them about cockroach issues.

F.L indicated that the Tenant advised them on or around the month of January 2026 that they were once again experiencing a cockroach infestation. Prior to that, the Tenant had not advised them of any ongoing infestation between the month of July 2024 and December 2025. They were under the impression that the cockroach issue was resolved as they had been to the rental unit a few times, and the Tenant had not reported any ongoing pest issues.
F.L stated that the Tenant had not advised them of their need or intent to replace their appliances.

F.L indicated that they were aware that the tenant residing in the lower-level unit had refused certain pest control treatments in their unit due to certain chemical products being used impacting their medical situation.

Under cross-examination, F.L stated that they had only conducted summary inspections of the lower-level unit. They had not opened the appliances or closets to check for the presence of cockroaches. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the tenants2.

While the intervention of the City and the issuance of the Order to Remedy Violation of Maintenance and Occupancy, dated November 29, 2023 (Exhibits 2 and 3) are certainly indicative of the Landlord’s failure to take reasonable steps to address the cockroach issue of their own accord, it is important to note that the Tenant filed their application with the Board on July 4, 2025, and that pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act "no application may be made […] more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”
As such, the events that occurred prior to July 4 , 2024, may be contextual in nature, but would not be subject to any remedies.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to take reasonable steps to treat and eliminate the cockroach infestation.

Indeed, the testimony from the Tenant was cogent, consistent, and credible, and supported by independent and contemporaneous documentary evidence (Exhibits 1, 2, and 3) . I also note that the Landlord themselves recognized that there was an ongoing cockroach infestation between September 20, 2023, through the month of July 2024. 2 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name].

Although the Landlord claimed that they were not notified of any issues following the month of July 2024 and were therefore unaware that the issue had not been resolved, I did not find them to be credible. Indeed, their testimony was contradicted by their prior communications with agents of the City (Exhibit 2) – the authenticity of which they did not dispute – through which the Landlord acknowledges on July 17, 2024, that they were unable to complete treatments as the tenant of the lower -level units had been refusing to cooperate with the intended contractor.

The Landlord’s subsequent service of the N5 Notice to the tenant of the lower-level unit, on the basis that they had refused “treatments […] designed by [an] exterminator” and that this refusal had “impacted [the] the reasonable enjoyment ad [rights] of the other tenants and landlord” is further demonstrative of the Landlord’s own recognition that further treatments were required to resolve the cockroach issue.
Yet, the Landlord did not attempt to schedule any further treatments within the residential complex, and allowed the N5 Notice to be voided3 with no further action.
Such conduct from the Landlord is antonymous to their obligation to take reasonable steps to address the ongoing pest control issue.

As I am satisfied that the Tenant has faced an ongoing cockroach infestation and that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to address the aforementioned infestation, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement.

Pursuant to the evidence and submissions before me, and having knowledge of similar cases, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of twenty percent ( 20%) from July 4, 2024, to May 26, 2026, which equates to a total of $4,408.75. This amount takes into consideration the length of the delay, the Landlord persistent failure to address the cockroach, and the inconvenience faced by the Tenant.

Although the Tenant found the presence of cockroaches within the stove and oven range (Exhibit 2) and on or around their refrigerator, bed, and mattress , I do not find that the replacement of these appliances and furniture items to be reasonable under the circumstances (Exhibits 4, 5, and 6).

Indeed, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, the Tenant had a duty to mitigate their damages. While the presence of cockroaches within such appliances and furniture items can certainly be distressing, there was no evidence that these appliances ceased to operate as intended due to the presence of the cockroaches, or that the furniture could no longer be used.

The Tenant provided no reasonable explanation as to why these appliances and furniture items could not be cleaned as opposed to needing to be replaced. I am therefore not satisfied that the Tenant had to incur costs of $6,436.70 (Exhibits 4, 5, and 6).

Accordingly, the Tenant’s request for the Landlord to pay the Tenant the amount of $6,436.70 as reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair or replace the property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions, is denied. 3 Subsection 64(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

While I note that the Tenant had also raised concerns regarding bedbugs in their application, they led no evidence during the hearing with respect to this issue. As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations with respect to an alleged bed bug issue. Therefore, no remedies were awarded in this regard.
ordered: The Landlord shall p ay the Tenant the total amount of $4,408.75, which represents a rent abatement for the period ending May 26, 2026.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 28, 2026 ____________________________
