issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was uncontested that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12. It was also uncontested that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent within one year of the Tenant vacating the rental unit and that the rebuttable presumption of bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies in this case.
Although the Tenant took the position that the Landlord’s father, the intended occupant, did not move into the rental unit, the Tenant did not lead any evidence in this regard.

The Landlord’s father testified that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2021, he moved in around July 20, 2021. He said that the rental unit was purchased in 1986, he never lived there previously, and that he had always intended to move into the rental unit as a retirement home. He said that after moving in, he had difficulties with the underground parking. More specifically, he felt there was not enough space in the underground parking and he had difficulty negotiating the turns near the ramp. He said that he scraped his car against one of the pillars and that he got into a verbally abusive altercation with another Tenant in the underground parking lot in relation to them both trying to negotiate driving there. He said that he moved out at the end of March 2022 because of the difficulties with the parking and that the rental unit was subsequently rented out to another tenant.

Initially, after the first hearing date, I was not satisfied that the Landlord had provided sufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord’s father had moved into the rental unit. Of particular concern to me was the lack of documentary evidence to show that the Landlord’s father had moved into the rental unit. More specifically, the only documentation provided was a letter from the condominium management stating that the Landlord’s father had moved in and correspondence from his auto insurer addressed to the Landlord’s father at the rental unit. I had indicated at the hearing that I was prepared to make an adverse inference because of the lack of the plethora of evidence that ought to have been available to show the Landlord’s father had moved into the rental unit (e.g. driver’s license, health insurance card, other correspondence), however, drawing an adverse inference is discretionary and upon further reflection and consideration of this case, I do not find it appropriate to do so. Ultimately, I find the Landlord’s father’s testimony regarding moving into the rental unit and why he moved out to be genuine and credible. Moreover, the Tenant did not meaningfully challenge the Landlord’s father’s testimony on these points.

Although I find it distasteful that the Landlord has profited (by being able to rent the rental unit out at a significantly increased rent) and the Tenant has suffered significant loss from what transpired, the law as it currently stands does not provide a remedy to the Tenant when the intended occupant genuinely moves into the rental unit, but moves out because of a change in circumstances.

I am mindful of the Tenant’s argument that the Landlord’s father did not reside in the rental unit for 12 months, however the requirement that an intended occupant intends to reside in the rental unit for 12 months relates to a Landlord’s application to terminate a tenancy rather than to a tenant’s application regarding bad faith. While it can sometimes be inferred from an occupancy of less than 12 months that the intended occupant did not genuinely occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time (the third part of the test identified in paragraph two above), the failure to reside in the rental unit for a full 12 months does not necessarily mean that the intended occupant did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time.

In conclusion, the Tenant’s application is dismissed because the Tenant was unable to prove the third part of the test for this application (i.e. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated).
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord’s Agent is not a [name] of the Law Society of Ontario. The Landlord’s Agent acted as the Landlord’s legal representative under an exemption in the Law Society Act that allows unpaid friends to act as a representative for a small number of matters annually.

The Landlord’s Agent previously acted for the Landlord at the July 25, 2024 Adjudicative Case Conference. The Landlord’s agent confirmed this is the only matter for which he has appeared before any court or tribunal, and that he is not being paid to assist the Landlord.
In the circumstances, the Landlord’s Agent was permitted to continue acting as the Landlord’s representative. The Tenant’s Application

The Tenant conceded at the June 15, 2026 hearing that no loss, injury or other adverse result arose from the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord harassed and interfered with the Tenant by accusing the Tenant of: making the property difficult to sell; making false claims to police; stealing a mattress; and causing the Landlord to lose another tenant. The Tenant similarly conceded that nothing resulted from an October 6, 2024 message from the Landlord that identified the Tenant’s IP address.
In the circumstances, the Tenant’s claims with respect to the above allegations are dismissed.

The Tenant agreed that he was able to use the rental unit bathroom for all usual purposes, despite there being no towel bar. The Tenant therefore did not prove that the Landlord’s failure to replace the towel bar interfered with the Tenant or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.

Similarly, the Tenant did not prove that missing stovetop knobs interfered with the Tenant or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the property. The Tenant’s testimony that two burners did not function was inaccurate and the testimony exaggerated the nature of the issue.

By contrast, the Landlord introduced reliable evidence – which the Tenant did not contest – that two knobs for two of the stovetop burners had broken. The Landlord attempted to replace the knobs, but the model was discontinued and the replacement knobs he had ordered and received did not fit. The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant could operate all stovetop burners by simply moving the remaining knobs. The Tenant’s assertion at the hearing – that he feared being electrocuted or otherwise injured by moving the stovetop knobs – was not reasonable and not evidence of substantial interference for the purpose of subsection 29(1)3 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The Tenant confirmed that the residential complex was built after November 15, 2018. Pursuant to subsection 6.1(2) of the Act, the Landlord was accordingly entitled to give the Tenant a notice of a rent increase in an amount greater than the annual guideline amount. Although the Tenant described being shocked when he discovered the exemption in subsection 6.1(2) of the Act, the Tenant’s lack of knowledge does not merit a finding of interference or harassment as contemplated in section 23 of the Act.

I agree with the Landlord that a July 22, 2023 message from the Tenant to the Landlord does not advise that the key fob giving access to the residential complex was broken other otherwise unable to open entry doors. The Tenant’s message only reads: “the key holder of my fob is damaged.”

It was not until September 2, 2023 that the Tenant informed the Landlord: “The fob is not working and I am not having access.” The Tenant asserted in the same message: “I had highlighted to you previously and you had agreed to provide a new one.” I find, however, that the Landlord’s reply later that day accurately reflects the contents of the Tenant’s earlier, July 22, 2023 message. At 9:45AM on September 2, 2023, the Landlord wrote to the Tenant: “You never said the fob is not working all you said [sic.] you broke the clip part of it, you never mentioned [sic.] is not working.”

The Tenant obtained a replacement key fob shortly after the September 2, 2023 email message exchange with the Landlord. In the circumstances, I find the Tenant did not prove the Landlord interfered with the Tenant, or changed the locking system giving access to the rental property, as pled in the application.

The Tenant did not prove that the Landlord on May 5, 2024 harassed, threatened, intimidated or otherwise interfered with the Tenant in any way by laying “siege to my room as I was vacating. Did not get to rest and finish packing my belongings. Police involved.”

Overall, the Tenant’s description of events that evening is not credible. The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant had promised to vacate the rental unit and return the keys to the Landlord at 8:00PM on May 5, 2024. When the Landlord attended at the rental unit at 8:00PM to collect the keys, the Tenant had emptied only part of the rental unit, including the bedroom. The Landlord waited in the empty bedroom for the Tenant to conclude packing and vacating. When it became apparent after 10:30PM that the Tenant needed more time, the Landlord agreed to the Tenant’s request to continue occupying the rental unit until May 12, 2024. The Tenant paid the Landlord a pro- rated amount to compensate the Landlord for the Tenant’s use and occupancy of the rental unit from May 5, 2024 to May 12, 2024.

When afforded an opportunity to respond to the Landlord’s evidence about the events of May 5, 2024, the Tenant chose not to do so and accepted the Landlord’s version of events. I accordingly find the Tenant’s pleading in his application and his testimony are not credible.

Having exaggerated his complaints throughout his written pleadings and June 15, 2026 testimony, I am not satisfied that the Landlord caused the Tenant’s relationship with another occupant of the rental unit to deteriorate. Other than the Tenant’s vague description of a temporary period of friction with his roommate, there was nothing to support the Tenant’s claim. The Tenant’s roommate did not attend the hearing. There was no other reliable evidence, such as text or email messages, to suggest that the roommate took seriously the Landlord’s text message, sent on or about August 3, 2023, for the roommate to “slap [the Tenant’s] week [sic.] ass out or punch him in the face”, or that the Landlord otherwise interfered with their relationship.

The Landlord, however, agreed that language he used in the August 3, 2023 text message to the Tenant’s roommate, and language in another message thread in which the Landlord repeatedly called the Tenant an “asshole”, was inappropriate. Although there was evidence that the Landlord later apologized to the Tenant, I find that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, that these messages were improper. The result is that I find the Landlord harassed the Tenant with these messages, contrary to section 23 of the Act.

Given the paucity of evidence that the Landlord’s text messages caused material loss or injury to the Tenant, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant a nominal amount of $100.00 in general damages, pursuant to subsection 31(1)f of the Act.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $148.00. This amount represents $100.00 for general damages and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to adequately address maintenance issues and failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $836.75.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2022, and still lives in the rental unit. The rental unit is part of a house and includes one bedroom, a kitchen, a bathroom and a living room. The monthly rent is $1,669.18.

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair. The Tenant also referred to issues involving the Landlord’s conduct, entry, privacy and alleged threats. However, those issues relate more closely to a tenant rights application and are not the main issues in this T6 maintenance application.

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) requires a landlord to provide and maintain a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain parts of the rental unit in a good state of repair. The Tenant testified that she reported maintenance concerns to the Landlord in July 2024, including ceiling cracks, damaged or uneven flooring or tiles, and other deficiencies. The Landlord and a contractor attended in mid July 2024, but the Tenant testified that the repairs were minimal and did not resolve the issues.

The Tenant testified that she again reported the outstanding maintenance issues to the Landlord on October 30, 2024. The issues included ceiling cracks, unfinished painting, damaged flooring or tiles, kitchen cupboard repairs, a broken or missing towel rack, and an electrical outlet near the stove that was not functioning properly.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord and his contractor attended on November 4 and November 6, 2024. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that some work was performed, but the work was incomplete. The Tenant stated that putty was applied to some ceiling and wall cracks but was not fully sanded and painted. She also testified that the kitchen walls were painted over without primer, causing the pink marker stains to reappear. The Tenant further testified that the front entry door was shaved down but left unfinished and unpainted.

I also accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the Landlord did not meaningfully complete the outstanding repairs during 2025. The Tenant testified that she continued to raise the issues, but the Landlord’s communications were mainly about the heating system and not the outstanding repairs. The Tenant testified that repairs were not completed until after the February 2026, and completed some drywall repairs, sanding, and painting. Even then, the Tenant testified that not all work was completed, including the bedroom ceiling
At the hearing, the Tenant submitted photographs and correspondence between the parties about the maintenance complaints from 2024.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair and maintain the rental unit. The evidence supports a finding that the Landlord knew about the issues by July 2024 and again by October 2024, but did not reasonably complete the repairs until February 2026, and some issues remained incomplete. Remedy:

In the application, the Tenant requested $788.75 as a rent abatement. I find that amount is reasonable in the circumstances. The amount recognizes the Landlord’s delay in completing repairs and the impact on the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit from August 2024 to February 2026.

The Tenant also requested that the tenancy be terminated early. I am not satisfied that termination of the tenancy is warranted under section 30 of the Act. Termination is a significant remedy. The evidence establishes delayed and incomplete repairs, but it does not establish that the rental unit was unfit for habitation, unsafe to occupy or so substantially affected that termination is appropriate. The Tenant’s request to terminate the tenancy was also based partly on allegations of privacy concerns, entry issues, harassment and threats. Those issues are not properly before me in this T6 maintenance application.
Therefore, the request to terminate the tenancy is denied.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $ 836.75. This amount represents: • $788.75 for a rent abatement for the period ending February 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 27, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. These applications were heard over the course of three hearing days, which were July 29, 2024, October 30, 2025 and June 10, 2026. The Landlord, [name], the Landlord’s witnesses, [name], [name], [name], the Tenant’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Tenant [name] [name] attended the hearing. L1 Application
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed. LTB-T-062405-22
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 18, 2021. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit
The lawful rent is $1,650.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to December 18, 2021 are $12,526.50.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord proved that the Tenant owes $12,526.50, which represents the rent until the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit. However, the Tenant states that they do not owe that full amount to the Landlord due to the ongoing maintenance issues in the rental unit. Section 82 Issues Issues Raised by the Tenant – Section 82 of the Act

The Tenant sought to raise issues under section 82 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), which could result in a rent abatement that would be set off against the arrears of rent owing to the Landlord and therefore reduce the amount the Tenant owed. The issues the Tenant intends to raise pertain to allegations that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the Tenant. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that there were maintenance issues with the sewage, and that this was an ongoing issue in the rental unit. The first message he sent the first text message to the Landlord about this issue was on or about October 4, 2020. A copy of the text LTB-T-062405-22 message was submitted as evidence to the Board. The Tenant testified that around that time, one of the seals on the trash pump were leaking and he observed a lot of liquid coming out of the septic tank. To his text message, the Landlord responded and told the Tenant to plug the pump in directly, which temporarily fixed it.

In February 2021, the Tenant stated that he still smelled the septic tank. On or about February 1, 2021, the septic tank started spraying sewage all over the basement. The Tenant testified that he had sentimental belongings that were also damaged as a result of this. The Tenant does not believe that the Landlord repaired the septic tank properly. On or about March 26, 2021, the Tenant advised the Landlord that there is a leak again. The Landlord advised him to call [name], and provided him a phone number.

The Tenant took photographs of the basement. The Tenant believes that the trash pump tank should have been a septic tank, and it should have had a septic pump instead of a trash pump. The Tenant stated that when other tenants who lived in the rental unit would use the washroom, everything would overflow in the basement. Photographs that were taken on or about May 2021 were submitted to the Board as evidence.

On or about October 7, 2021, there was an inspection done in the rental unit. The Tenant stated that from October 2020 to October 2021 the septic issue was only fixed temporarily, and that the Landlord sent someone named [name] on one occasion fix it. As a result of the septic tank leaking, he had to throw out approximately $7,500.00 worth of belongings, as it leaked all over his items in the basement. The Tenant stated that the basement had a dirt/stone floor, not a finished floor.

The Tenant stated that on or about November 17, 2021, while [name] was at the rental unit, there was another issue with the septic tank. As it was blocked, it was not working and started spraying sewage all over the place. The Tenant stated that he received a 24- hour notice however no one showed up at the rental unit.

At this time, he lived with his wife, son and daughter. His daughter would refuse to stay the night because of the smell and her asthma. The Tenant stated that this had a significant impact on him, and that he would have to sleep on the porch because the smell was so bad. The septic tank was not repaired properly, which resulted in ongoing issues with it throughout the year. The Tenant is therefore requesting a 20% rent abatement for the period of October 2021 to December 2021, when he vacated the rental unit.

Upon cross examination, the Landlord asked the Tenant if he recalls being advised to not store his belongings in the basement however the Tenant stated that did not happen. The Tenant stated that this is an illegal septic tank. He stated that his now ex-wife had asked the Landlord to clean the floors, and the Landlord dropped off some cleaning products. The Tenant stated that the septic tank started working after [name] advised him to fix the trash pump however it started spraying all over the place shortly after.

When the Landlord asked if there were any allegations of damages made prior to the Tenant leaving, he stated that he had a verbal discussion with the Landlord in May 2021, and advised him that he lost about $7,500.00 worth of personal belongings due to the septic tank overflowing. LTB-T-062405-22 Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that when the Tenant moved into the rental unit, he specifically told him not to put any of his belongings in the basement. The rental unit is an old stone house, with a stone floor. It is not bad for moisture, but it does get wet as stone floors and stone basements are damp. He provided a dehumidifier and a working sump pump in the basement. He stated that over the year, there were issues with the septic tank three or four times, and every time the Tenant advised him that there was an issue, he ensured that [name], a licensed plumber, attended the rental unit within 24 hours. The Landlord stated that it was inspected by the Fire Marshall and the Building Inspector, and it was deemed to be proper with no issues. The Tenant did not mention any damages to the Landlord until the L1 application was filed. He did not conduct inspections related to the septic pump. The Landlord stated that the Tenant kept the rental unit in a messy state, and that the Tenant may have caused the damage to the septic tank which caused issues.

During cross examination, the Tenant’s Legal Representative ask him if he is aware that it is unlawful to pump raw sewage onto the surface of the ground with a sump pump, and that Landlord stated that he is not and that is it normal to remove sewage from a basement with the sump pump. The sump pump is in the floor and would pump out any sewage that is on the floor. The Landlord stated that although he has documents that the septic system is complying with health and safety standards, he did not provide any of these documents as proof to the Board.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] testified at the hearing. [name] is the Landlord’s head secretary, and she believes that the Tenant contacted her approximately two times. When the Tenant contacted her, she sent a licensed plumber, [name], to remedy the issue. Both times this was repaired and there were no more leaks. The plumber did not indicate to her that anything would need to be replaced. [name] testified that [name] attended the rental unit on multiple occasions, however does not remember what he told her as it was approximately three years ago. [name] stated the Tenant did not ask her to clean the place nor did he request cleaning products. When she did an inspection of the rental unit, she noticed animal smells, not a septic smell. Legal Analysis

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, in regard to the septic tank. Indeed, the Landlord was aware of the issue since the septic tank and stated that there were issues with it. I heard the Landlord’s submission regarding the state of the rental unit and allegations that it was the Tenant who caused damage, however I find that the Landlord did not lead sufficient evidence regarding these allegations to discredit the Tenant’s testimony.

While the Landlord claims that the repairs were done and there were no further issues, and that the septic tank was repaired, the Landlord did not offer sufficient evidence to convince me that this issue was resolved. I do not find that the Landlord offered sufficient evidence to contradict that of the Tenant’s, that there was an ongoing septic issue. Although a LTB-T-062405-22 maintenance issue does not automatically constitute a breach, the Landlord did not provide sufficient information that they repaired the issue. The Landlord themselves stated that there was an ongoing issue, however did not provide sufficient evidence to convince me that they did everything they could to have this issue resolved.

I found the Tenant’s submissions to consistent and credible, while the Landlord’s testimony was more limited to general statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details. Indeed, the Landlord did not provide specifics with respect to the scope of work conducted with the septic tank nor an exact date as to when the repair were completed. I therefore find that the Landlord failed to establish their response to the Tenant’s maintenance issue was reasonable. Remedies
The Tenant is requesting a rent abatement of 20% for the months of October, November and December 2021.

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. In the case before me, I do not find that a 20% of abatement of rent is an appropriate remedy to award. Based on the Tenant’s submissions of the issues with septic tank, the impact it had on them and based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find a rent abatement of 8% appropriate in these circumstances. Therefore, a rent abatement totaling to $396.00 (8% of $1,650.00=$132.00*3 months=$396.00) will be awarded. T2 Application Determinations:

The Tenant testified that he did not think he was going to get locked out as there was a hearing scheduled before the Board on January 11, 2022, and as hopeful this would all get resolved.

The Landlord would make posts on Facebook that were harassing in nature. A copy of the Facebook posts from November 2021 were submitted as evidence to the Board. The Tenant stated that some of the posts were shaming him and stated that this constitutes public harassment.

Regarding the ownership of the vehicle, he stated that he owned it for approximately four years and when he purchased it there was around 32,000 km on it. The Tenant testified that he had to put some items in the storage unit, and those items are still there. He submitted a Storage Agreement from Box Me Up Storage dated April 28, 2021, with a total monthly rate of $246.96.

The Tenant stated that as he was locked out, he has been living in a travel trailer. He has no plumbing, and it was very difficult to sleep as it was winter time, and it was really cold. The Tenant further stated that there was an interim order, LTB-T-062405-22 issued on November 30, 2022, regarding the return of the Tenant’s property. He further does not have a copy of the Notice of Entry for November 2021 or December 2021, however he must have given the Tenant notice. It was the Tenant who changed the locks, and he was able to enter the rental unit as the door was unlocked. [name] – [name] LTB-T-062405-22

The Landlord’s witness, [name] testified at the hearing. She is a property manager who looks over and manages everything for the Landlord. [name] testified that prior to April 2021 the rental unit was in good condition. She recalls receiving some calls regarding plumbing in June 2021, regarding some kind of sewer damage. [name] sent an employee to the rental unit who stated that there was a full sump pump, another time it was due to a water heater. The employee was [name], a licensed plumber. She got another call from the Tenant stating that there was no water, and when [name] attended the rental unit, he noted that the water was shut off. [name] testified that that she did not get a call for the entire year regarding heat or lack thereof. In the rental unit, there is propane, a woodstove to heat the rental unit. She further testified that when she tried to connect with the Tenant, he would ignore some of her text messages. 70. [name] testified that she never entered the rental unit without provide a proper 24 hour Notice of Entry, nor did she break into the rental unit or remove any of the locks. 71. [name] stated that she attended the rental unit to see if the Tenant had vacated. The door was unlocked, there was garbage everywhere and there was no bed. It looked like no one was living there. She believes she contacted the Tenant but there was no response. When she was walking through the rental unit, she noticed that there was garbage everywhere, a terrible smell, animal feces and junk all over the place. She tried to contact the Tenant approximately five or six times however the Tenant did not respond and there was no notice from the Tenant. They put the items in the storage so that the Tenant can come and take back his belongings. The Landlord called the Police to arrange a date to pick up the items, however he only came once with a pickup truck and did not gather anything that she is aware of. The Tenant did not come back. She testified that they did everything possible to give the Tenant a chance to pick up their belongings and does not know what else they could have done. Cross-Examination of [name] 72. When asked about when the employee showed up to fix the septic tank, [name] stated that she did not keep any records of when the plumber came. 73. [name] testified that she does not recall the exact date she entered the basement, however when she attended the rental unit there was a bad smell. 74. [name] testified that she was not present on December 15, 2021 and does not know who was there. She was not present on the date the locks were removed. She was present when the workers attended the rental unit and removed the Tenant’s property, and was aware of the trespass notice. Landlord’s witness – [name] 75. The Landlord’s witness [name] who lived in the rental unit testified at the hearing that in December 2021 he felt that the situation in the rental unit had changed. There was a lot of neglect in the property. [name] testified that the Landlord had asked him to assist in cleaning out the rental unit, and to remove the Tenant’s belongings and not to LTB-T-062405-22 destroy or damage anything. The conditions of the items were not good, and there was food leftover that they had to throw out. The were cracked lamps, a lot of garbage few bags of old clothes that were in the basement, nothing of value. 76. [name] further stated that the condition was relatively clean where the sump pump was, it was all in a corner with clothes and other garbage. He stated that the items were off to the side would have not been damaged from any moisture. There was no sign at sewage. He did notice that there was a bad pet odour, and there was no bed in the property, no cutlery, dishes or T.V was in the rental unit. Cross Examination & Redirect – [name] 77. During cross examination, [name] stated that he did not drill out the locks in December 2021 and he did not open any doors. He stated that he was not involved in the clean up of the septic tank in November 2021. 78. [name] testified that some of the Tenant’s items were put into an outbuilding and some put into a trailer. Any items that were outside he was told to put in the corner of the same property. Regarding the Chrysler 300, he stated it would have been with the trailer and does not recall if it had license plates on it. 79. Upon redirect, [name] stated that since the Tenant vacated there has been no issue with the sewage. Landlord’s witness – [name]80. The Landlord’s witness, [name] who is a licensed plumber with 25 years of experience testified at the hearing. He stated that the electrical main power came through the back unit ([name] unit) and then it was transferred under the house. He stated that the sewage pump and the furnace are all controlled in the Tenant’s unit. 81. He does not recall the exact date that he attended the rental unit, however he remembers there were some issues with the sewage or with the water. He stated that when he was at the rental unit, he was there to repair sewage pumps that sprung a leak. He stated that the pipe looked deliberately damaged. He stated that there were multiple occasions where there was no water to [name] unit. Cross Examination & Redirect – [name]82. [name] testified that he has work for the Landlord for approximately six or seven years. He stated that [name] is his partner and they live together. 83. The first time there was an issue with the septic pump there was a serious repair conducted. He has done general maintenance on the trash pump and believes it was replaced one time before. [name] does not recall the dates it was replaced however the Tenant was living in the rental unit. When the pipe was broken, he determined that the Tenant broke it as faulty pipes do not snap in half, which was the case here. He stated that there was issues with the septic tank from the beginning, and it was not possible that the LTB-T-062405-22 pipe was frozen as it was not winter time. In addition, the Tenant may have been driving over the septic bed that is under the driveway. 84. [name] stated that he is not a licensed septic installer nor a licensed inspector. 85. Upon redirect, the [name] stated that if the trash pump started to spray, it I highly unlikely that it would reach the Tenant’s items are stored. [name] stated that his relationship with [name] did not affect his testimony in any way. Legal Analysis 86. On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. 87. Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“ the Act”) permits landlord to enter the rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under. 88. After hearing the parties submissions, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord entered the rental unit without providing 24-hour notice. I heard and considered the Landlord’s and their witnesses’ testimony that there was a 24-hour notice provided every time there was an entry, however the Landlord provided insufficient evidence to contradict that of the Tenants. The Landlord did not provide any specifics regarding the notices or any copies of the notices to enter. Therefore, I find the Tenant proved their allegations in this regard. 89. Section 24 of the Act states that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 90. After hearing the submissions of the parties I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord altered the locking system which prevented the Tenant from accessing the rental unit. I heard the Landlord’s testimony that there were some dead bolt locks that were not altered, however I found the Tenant credible and consistent when he stated that the locks were altered and he was unable to access the rental unit. The Landlord provided insufficient evidence to contradict that of the Tenant’s. I found the Tenant credible when he stated that he did not give notice to vacate the rental unit, and there was no evidence led by the Landlord that the Tenant intended to move out of the rental unit. 91. Section 22 of the Act states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 92. Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. LTB-T-062405-22 93. After hearing the parties submissions, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached section 22 and 23 of the Act, by posting the Facebook posts, various attempts to have the Tenant vacate the rental unit, changing the locks, serving a trespass notice when the Tenant did not give notice that he was vacating and disposing of the Tenant’s belongings. I heard and considered the Landlord’s evidence, that there were reasons for the Facebook posts and serving the trespass notice, however I do not find that the reasons the Landlord provided were sufficient for me to dismiss the Tenant’s claims against the Landlord in this regard. I further considered the Landlord’s evidence regarding the Tenant not retrieving his belongings, however I find the Landlord did not offer sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they permitted the Tenant to obtain their belongings and the Tenant refused. As such, I prefer the evidence of the Tenant, that the Landlord breached the interim order and did not provide access or return the Tenant’s property by December 30, 2022. Remedies 94. The Tenant is seeking $3,000.00 for the illegal notices of entry, claiming $1,000.00 per entry. The Landlord opposed this remedy as they stated there was no illegal entry. Upon hearing the submissions, the impact that it had on the Tenant, I find it’s appropriate to award the Tenant $100.00 per entry, totalling to $300.00. 95. The Tenant is claiming a total of $10,000.00 for an illegal lockout to the rental unit. He stated that this has had a negative impact on him, caused significant stress and depression as he had no where to go. The Landlord opposes this remedy as his position is that he did not alter the locking system. After hearing the submissions of the Tenant, and based on similar cases before the Board, I find it is appropriate to award the Tenant $5,000.00. 96. The Tenant is requesting general damages for the Landlord’s actions. The Tenant is claiming an amount of $35,000.00 for replacing the property that the Landlord disposed of. The Landlord contested the Tenant’s claim for their belongings and stated that I should not accept the Tenant’s evidence going to the value of the missing items because most of the items were not in good condition, and therefore the amount that the Tenant is seeking is not accurate. I find it reasonable for a tenant to estimate the cost of lost goods and that it would neither be reasonable or likely to expect someone to have receipts kept for every purchase made. I find it reasonable to provide an estimate, with photographs – where possible of the items that are lost or disposed of. Therefore, upon considering the submissions of the Tenant, I find an amount of $4,000.00 appropriate to award in these circumstances. 97. The Tenant is seeking $10,000.00 for general damages for refusing to return the property and comply with the interim order. I do not find that the Landlord demonstrated that they made sufficient efforts to comply with the interim order and return the property to the Tenant. However, I do not find an amount of $10,000 to be appropriate in these circumstances. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find an amount of $1,500.00 to be appropriate in these circumstances. LTB-T-062405-22 98. The Tenant is requesting that the LTB order the Landlord to return any Tenant’s personal property that the Landlord possesses. I find it appropriate to order that the Landlord returned to the Tenant any personal property that the Landlord possesses, or that the Landlord can get back from other people. 99. The Tenant is seeking $4,981.04 for out of pocket moving and storage expenses. This amount represents $382.72 for the initial storage fee, plus $400.00 to move items back into storage plus $246.96 for 17 months of storage, all totalling to $4,981.04. The Landlord opposed this remedy as the Tenant did not provide receipts to demonstrate the amount paid. After considering the parties submissions, I do not find that the Tenant proved that he incurred this full amount on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant submitted an agreement or storage, with a monthly amount of $246.96, however did not provide any invoices to demonstrate that amount that they incurred. In addition, I find the Tenant offered insufficient evidence to prove the initial storage amount of $382.72 and $400.00 of moving costs. Therefore, this amount is denied. 100. The Tenant is claiming a rent abatement in the amount of $13,480.00. The Landlord opposes this remedy as they did not do anything wrong. Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. In the case before me, I do not find that a 100% of abatement of rent is an appropriate remedy to award as the Tenant was living in the rental unit, despite the issues that arose between the Landlord and Tenant. The Tenant has been awarded compensation for the Landlord’s actions, and therefore the request for a rent abatement is denied. Administrative Fine 101. The Tenant requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. 102. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine equivalent to the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 103. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 (‘the Guideline’) outlines relevant considerations in determinate the appropriateness of an administrative fine. 104. The Guideline provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 105. In determining whether to order a fine, I have considered the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such as the conduct on the Landlord. Deterrence for egregious conduct, beyond whatever deterrent effect simple damage might provide, is an overriding factor. While the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded LTB-T-062405-22 a monetary remedy for pain and suffering, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of December 18, 2021, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $12,316.50. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit, the cost of filing the application, less the rent abatement in the amount of $396.00. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from September 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: Sharma (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

To succeed on this application, the Tenant must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Act on a balance of probabilities: (1) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (an N12 notice); (2) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice; (3) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (4) The Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. 2. The Act also contains a reverse onus in subsection 57(5) that says if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 and then puts the unit up for rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. What this means is that the Landlords must prove it is more likely than not they were not acting in bad faith in giving the N12 notice to the Tenant.

In some situations, the Board may determine that an unforeseen change in circumstances which prevents the person named in the N12 notice from taking possession is sufficient to show that the Landlord did not act in bad faith.

The parties agreed that the Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice appointing December 27, 2021 as the date of termination, that the Tenants vacated as a result of it and that the person identified on the N12 did not take up residence in the unit within a reasonable amount of time. The parties also agreed the Landlords advertised the unit for sale within the time specified in 57(6) of the Act and so they carry the burden to prove that they did not give the N12 notice in bad faith.

Around October of 2021, the Landlords persuaded [name] (mother to the Landlord [name]) to move to Toronto and live in the rental unit so she could be nearer to the Landlords and their child. [name] was living in Vancouver with her spouse but she would travel to Toronto often to visit the Landlords. It made sense for [name] to relocate to Toronto and avoid the constant travel.

Still, [name] and the Landlords knew this would not be a permanent move because [name] father had been diagnosed with a terminal illness and it was expected that he had some 2 to 3 years to live. While as of 2021, [name] father was living fairly independently with his spouse and his son in Vancouver, it was expected that he would eventually require [name] help once his illness advanced. Accordingly, [name] and the Landlords determined this was a fleeting but opportune moment for [name] to live in rental unit. They expected she could stay for 2 to 3 years at least before she would be needed back in Vancouver.

To that end, the Landlord [name] instructed his realtor to prepare an N12 notice which he signed and delivered on October 27, 2021. By agreement of the parties, the Tenants stayed on until January 31, 2022.

The Landlords’ plans were upset because by the end of January 2022, near the time the Landlords regained vacant possession of the unit, it became apparent to Maria and to the Landlords that [name] window of opportunity for making the move to Toronto was closing sooner than they had hoped. Her father’s terminal illness progressed more quickly than expected as did his Alzheimer’s. He could no longer be left alone. He would assault nurses and try to escape from care, meaning that [name] and her sister [name] had to care for him personally. On top of that, [name] spouse also became seriously ill, needing almost around-the-clock care. So [name] found herself stuck in Vancouver as a full-time caregiver to her father and her spouse and thus unable to make the move to Toronto. Therefore the Landlords advertised the unit for rent in March of 2022 and re-rented it in May.

I find the Landlords’ detailed explanation is incapable of displacing the presumption of bad faith on a balance of probabilities because it depends on a very precise chronology of events which has not been proven. Specifically, the Landlords filed nothing to establish the various illnesses and hospitalizations that upset their well-laid plans. [name] testified that she has all of these records but neither she nor the Landlords offered an explanation for their failure to produce them. The only document produced was a death certificate showing [name] father died in Vancouver on August 4, 2024 which suggests to me that the Landlords appreciate the evidentiary value of independent documentary confirmation. I draw an adverse inference from their failure to produce documents necessary to establish chronology. Furthermore, I found the Landlords and their witnesses were unable to give precise dates for when they came to be in possession of the facts that precipitated their decisions, or even when those decisions were taken.

Except where expressly prohibited by law, an adverse inference is discretionary. The trier of fact may, where it is warranted upon consideration of all the circumstances, draw an inference against the party who is in possession or control of relevant evidence but fails to produce it without adequate explanation. The inference that may be drawn is that the evidence would be contrary to the party’s case or at least would not support it. This is neither a rule of law nor a rule of evidence. It is an expression of logic and human experience that may in appropriate cases inform the fact-finding exercise. In this case, I infer that the documentary records relating to [name] father and [name] spouse would not support the Landlords’ detailed chronology of events.

In any case, even if the Landlords had proven their chronology of events, I would reach the same result. Although the Landlords had hoped, and possibly even expected that [name] would live in the rental unit for at least 12 months, that was based on a speculative assumptions. The Landlords were candid that they never intended for Maria to make her home in the unit permanently, but to live there temporarily, for an uncertain duration. That the window of opportunity closed sooner than the Landlords had hoped is not an unforeseen change in circumstances. On the contrary, I find it was foreseeable given that it depended on factors outside of the Landlords’ control or their ability to predict with any accuracy. In short, I find the Landlords dispossessed the Tenants knowing there was a real risk they could not carry out their plans, which I find to be inconsistent with their duty of good faith.
Having established the grounds for their application, the Tenants are entitled to those remedies they can prove on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants’ testimony, supported by a tenancy agreement, proves on a balance of probabilities that they incurred an increase in rent of $275.00 per month. The Tenants will be awarded $3,300.00 for the increased rent they incurred for a one-year period because I find this amount to be fair and reasonable based on the Tenants’ testimony that the two units are essentially similar.

The Tenants have delivered a table particularizing their claimed rent difference in the amount of $9,214.84 together with hydro costs and legal fees. Those heads of damages are not recoverable under subsection 57(3) of the Act. In any event, the Tenants were asked, but declined, to seek an amendment to their application. The Board cannot make an award greater than what was pleaded: Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 at paras 10-11.

The Tenants will be awarded $100.00 for their reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses because I find that claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities and it is fair and reasonable in the circumstances.

The Tenants seek general compensation in the amount of $26,400.00. This head of damages is intended as compensation for intangible non-pecuniary losses suffered by the Tenants as a result of being unlawfully evicted. The Tenants testified that searching for apartments and organizing their move during the COVID-19 pandemic was particularly challenging. They pointed to no other evidence warranting the quantum they claim which is the maximum allowed by law. Still, I accept that being unlawfully evicted is stressful, inconvenient and an affront to one’s dignity which are compensable losses. Based on the evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess $2,500.00 as the fair and reasonable award for general compensation.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not binding on me but I accept it as the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act or to deter future breaches. The damages awarded should be sufficient to demonstrate to the Landlords and to landlords generally that evicting tenants in bad faith carries consequences.

The parties agreed that the compensation required by section 48.1 of the Act was not given in contravention of subsection 135(1.1) and consented to an order adding that prayer for relief and awarding the Tenants $2,200.00.
ordered: The application is amended to include a claim under section 135 of the Act for $2,200.00.

The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $8,153.00. This amount represents: • $3,300.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period after vacating the rental unit. • $100.00 for the reasonable moving costs. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $2,200.00 for money illegally retained. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') has collected money illegally. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord gave a notice in bad faith. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $23,048.00.
The tenancy began on July 1, 2020, and amended on January 1, 2022. The unit was a farmhouse with out buildings and pastures.
On April 4, 2022, the Landlord had sent to the Tenant written notice to terminate the tenancy “for cause”. No cause was given and the Landlord dropped his request.
On August 13, 2022, the Landlord issued a no trespassing notice to the Tenant. Police were called and the notice was never enforced.

On September 14, 2022, the Tenant arrived at the unit and had found that the front gates had been padlocked. After police were called, the Landlord was forced to remove the lock and allow the Tenant onto the property.

The Tenant testified that from April until October 31, 2022, he had been harassed by the Landlord, almost struck by the Landlord in his vehicle and would yell and scream at the Tenant’s children. Videos were entered into evidence.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and also harassed the Tenant. [name]

The Tenant testified that the unit’s main house had electrical issues in which the Landlord had been informed about many times. The issues included outlets that were damaged and not working, and also outlets that were exposed causing a potential fire hazard. A property standards order was issued to Landlord in September of 2022.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit is accordance with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. N12 Compensation & Last Month’s Rent Deposit

The Tenant was issued an N12 notice of termination by the Landlord, alleging that the Landlord required the unit for a caregiver. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2022, in accordance with that notice. The Landlord never paid the Tenant the required compensation.
The Tenant testified that to the best of his knowledge, a caretaker never moved into the unit after he had vacated.
The Tenant testified that he moved into a mobile home in the same area and is now paying $2,599.00 a month in new rent. The Tenant testified that he lived at that unit until 2024.
The Tenant testified further, that the Landlord never applied the last month’s rent deposit to the month of October 2022 prior to him vacating.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave a notice in bad faith, failed to pay the Tenant the required compensation and failed to apply the last month’s rent deposit to October of 2022. Remedies

Within respect to the Tenant’s claim regarding substantial interference and harassment, the Tenant is seeking a 25% rent abatement for 4 months from August to October 2022 totalling $2,000.00. I find this amount to be reasonable, and it will be ordered. The Tenant also requested $1,000.00 in moving expenses, which I also find to be reasonable in the circumstances.
The Tenant is also seeking a $2,000.00 rent abatement with respect to the lack of maintenance by the Landlord. I also find this amount to be reasonable, and it will be ordered.
Further, the Tenant is entitled to $2,000.00 for compensation having been issued an N12 notice, and a further $2,000.00 as the Landlord did not apply the last month’s rent deposit to October of 2022.

Further, the Tenant is requesting $14,000.00 in general damages for the behaviour of the Landlord in his dealings with the Tenant and his family, the fact that no caregiver moved into the unit after the Landlord issued his N12 notice, and the impact of the move in his family, as well as the impact of the maintenance issues on the Tenant’s family. I find this amount to be reasonable and will also be ordered.
The Tenant is also requested the return of the $48.00 filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $23,048.00. This amount represents: • $4,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $1,000.00 for moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $2,000.00 for the N12 compensation • $2,000.00 for the last month’s rent deposit • $14,000.00 in for General Compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 27, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $100.00. Evidence:

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2024. He was incarcerated from January 2025 until approximately April 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that he lived alone and did not give anyone permission to enter the rental unit or remove his belongings while he was incarcerated.

The Tenant testified that, when he was released, he did not return to the rental unit because he was told that his belongings were gone. He testified that he lost items including televisions, a laptop, clothing, bedding, furniture and other personal belongings.

The Tenant’s witness, [name], testified that she assisted the Tenant after his release. She testified that she spoke with a person named [name], who identified himself as the property manager. [name] testified that [name] told her that some of the Tenant’s belongings had been stored and that he needed time to complete an inventory. She further testified that [name] later told her by text message that the Tenant’s belongings had been taken to the dump. 5. [name] also stated that she did not personally attend the rental unit and did not personally see the Tenant’s belongings in the rental unit. She also testified that outreach workers attended the property while the Tenant was incarcerated, but they did not enter the unit. 6. The Landlord’s evidence was that the unit had been occupied by unauthorized people while the Tenant was incarcerated, that the police were involved, and that the Landlord did not regain possession until after those people were removed in June 2025. 7. The Landlord denied that [name] was an employee, property manager or agent of the Landlord. The Landlord testified that [name] was another tenant in the building. The Landlord also denied removing or disposing of the Tenant’s personal property. 8. The Landlord testified that, when staff entered the rental unit in June 2025, there were no valuable items in the unit. The Landlord testified that only garbage, debris and damaged items remained. Law and Analysis: 9. Section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) says: A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 10. Section 26 of the Act sets out circumstances under with a landlord may enter a rental unit without giving written notice of entry, including where the Tenants consent to the entry and in the cases of emergency. In most other cases, a landlord is required to give a tenant at least 24 hours’ notice before entry in accordance with section 27 of the Act. Altered locks: 11. At the hearing, the Landlord acknowledged that the Landlord did not file an application with the Board to determine that the rental unit had been abandoned and did not obtain an order terminating the tenancy. The Landlord also acknowledged that the locks were changed in June 2026. The Landlord’s position was that the unit had been occupied by other people while the Tenant was incarcerated, that the police were involved, and that the Landlord did not regain possession until after those people were removed. 12. I accept that the Landlord may have had concerns about unauthorized people being in the unit and about the condition of the unit. However, the Tenant remained the tenant of the rental unit. The Landlord did not obtain an order from the Board terminating the tenancy or determining that the rental unit had been abandoned. In the circumstances, the Landlord was not entitled to take possession of the rental unit or change the locks without following the proper legal process. 13. Therefore, I find that the Landlord illegally locked the Tenant out of the rental unit. Illegal entry: 14. In the application, The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit while he was incarcerated. I am not satisfied that this allegation was proven. The Tenant did not personally observe the Landlord enter the unit. The Tenant was incarcerated during the relevant period and did not provide direct evidence of when the Landlord entered the unit, who entered the unit, or what occurred inside the unit between January 2025 and May 2025. I therefore dismiss the illegal entry claim. Remedies 15. The Tenant also claimed compensation for personal property. I accept that the Tenant lost access to the rental unit and may have lost personal belongings. However, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord removed, disposed of, or caused the loss of the Tenant’s valuable personal property. 16. The difficulty with the Tenant’s evidence is that the Tenant did not prove that [name] was an employee or agent of the Landlord. The Landlord denied that [name] was the property manager and testified that [name] was only another tenant in the building. The Tenant did not call Wade as a witness. There was also evidence that other people were in the rental unit while the Tenant was incarcerated. The Tenant did not return to the unit after his release to verify what remained in the unit. 17. Therefore, the claim for property compensation is dismissed. 18. In deciding the appropriate remedy, I have considered that the Landlord failed to use the proper legal process before taking possession of the rental unit and changing the locks. 19. In all of the circumstances, I find that a nominal award of $100.00 is appropriate for the illegal lockout.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $100.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
