issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord raises that the Tenant’s claim includes claims which are beyond the one- year limitation period, and that the Tenant’s allegations are insufficiently plead such that the Landlord could not know the case to be met.

In review of the Tenant’s application, I see that the Tenant amended her application June 25, 2026. During the hearing, the Tenant explained that she would only be pursuing a claim only for the porch leak and ceiling leaks. All other claims were being withdrawn.

In my review of this material, I am not persuaded that the Landlord could not know the case to be met. [name] are noted and the claims are listed clearly under appropriate headings. A chart referring to the key evidence with document ID numbers which correlate to the Portal was included.

Although remedies are discussed, the amending document does not include specific details about the request for a remedy nor the amount claimed. However, the originating document included this information.

I am not persuaded that the Landlord could not understand the case to be met. The issues were listed in the amending document. Further, dates are included if only the month. Regardless, I find that this should be sufficiently clear to be understood what the Tenant was complaining of.

The Tenant’s request to amend her application to remove the balance of claims, except for the leaks to the kitchen ceiling, is granted. Of note, the Tenant also sought to advance a claim regarding the porch roof. However, per my findings below, this was not properly pled.

The Landlord’s request to dismiss the Tenant’s application because of claims made beyond the limitation periods is dismissed. The Tenant’s claims, where the issue pertains to maintenance and had not been repaired specific to the ceiling falls within the one-year limitation period.
For the reasons already stated, the Landlord’s request to dismiss the Tenant’s application because it lacks sufficient particulars is also dismissed.
The hearing proceeded. [name] Porch Roof
The Tenant alleges that the porch had been damaged. Specifically, the fascia had come away from the roof over the porch area. This led to her inability to use the front door.

Despite my preliminary ruling at the hearing that the Tenant could advance a claim for the damaged porch rood, I am no longer of the view that this was properly pled such that the Landlord could reasonably understand the case to be met. Pursuant to s.17(1) of the Statutory Powers and Procedures Act, a tribunal shall give its final decision in any proceeding in writing.

In reviewing the Tenant’s amending document, I find that stated in section 8, entitled “Secondary Issues and Side Allegations” the Tenant says the following in par. 2. “Other issues, such as porch, stove, electrical, lock/code disputes...are not the main claim. I refer to them only if necessary as context or response to the Landlord’s allegations.”

Based on the Tenant’s own statements in the amending document, the Tenant did not intend to proceed with this claim. As such, the Landlord would not reasonably been aware that it would still be necessary to defend against this allegation. I find that the statement that the porch was not the “main claim” and that it being referenced only for contextual purposes would reasonably lead a the Landlord to conclude that the Tenant was not pursuing a claim for the allegation of the porch.

Given this, I am not of the view it would be appropriate or fair to allow the Tenant to advance a claim for the damage to the porch. In my view, to do so would be prejudicial to the Landlord who would reasonably have concluded, based on the Tenant’s amending document, that this claim was no longer being advanced. [name]
I do not find that the Landlord was in breach of their obligations pursuant to s. 20(1) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s application was filed with the LTB on August 23, 2023.

By way of background, the rental unit was a single-family home. It is not precisely clear when the tenancy terminated, because the Tenant’s evidence was unclear. However, she says she left sometime after August 20, 2024. At the time the issues began which lead to the Tenant bringing this application, the Tenant, her spouse, and her adult daughter, lived in the rental unit. The Tenant’s adult daughter had exclusive use of the master bedroom and ensuite bathroom located on the second floor of the home.

The Tenant states that the shower in the ensuite of the master bedroom was leaking. She discovered a puddle on the floor in the kitchen, which was directly below the master bathroom. She told the Landlord on January 9, 2022, that it was need of repair.
The repair to the master bathroom was not completed until December 6, 2023. During this period, repair people attended, but no one actually fixed the leak and kitchen ceiling.

The Landlord states that he had sent someone over shortly after the Tenant notified him of the issue. However, he says that the Tenant asked him to delay the repairs in-part because she wanted to encourage her adult daughter to move out. The Tenant does not dispute this but says she told the Landlord that her daughter moved out in March 2022, so he was free to attend to conduct the repairs.

The Landlord says he did send in several contractors over that period to quote the repairs needed to the washroom and kitchen ceiling. He also alleges the Tenant herself interfered with the Landlord’s right to enter including changing the locks and calling police on his agent who was attending to deliver a notice of entry. The agent was subsequently assaulted by the Tenant’s husband. A police report submitted into evidence corroborates the Landlord’s version of events.

Additionally, the Landlord says the Tenant just wanted the ceiling to be plastered and painted. However, that would not have addressed the problem if the leak persisted. As the Landlord tried to send contractors to assess the problem, he was met with refusals and cancellations from the Tenant.

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), states that it is the Landlord’s responsibility to keep the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.
The Court of Appeal in Onyskiw1 directed the Board to look at, “…the entirety of the factual situation” before determining whether or not the Landlord committed a breach of s.20 (para. 84).

In my view, the Tenants’ own conduct led to the delays in repairs. For example, on September 17, 2022, when the Landlord’s agent attended to provide a notice of entry so that the Landlord could have repairs conducted, the agent was assaulted by the Tenant’s husband.

Further, the Tenants told the Landlord that they would not allow him to repair, cancelled appointments, called the police on the Landlord and his agent, assaulted the Landlord’s agent, and changed the locks.

It seems to me that if Tenants wish to allege that their Landlord has not followed through with maintenance and repairs in a timely, effective, or reasonable manner, then Tenants cannot also put up persistent roadblocks to hamper the Landlord’s efforts. Given the contextual analysis required by the Court of Appeal in Onyskiw, I am not persuaded that the Landlord was in breach of the Act.
Even if I was persuaded that the Landlord was in breach of s.20(1) of the Act, I am not persuaded that the Tenant suffered any damages.

The Tenant’s testimony was that her daughter had the exclusive use of the master bedroom and ensuite bathroom. The Tenant says that she wanted the bathroom fixed because the plan was to have her daughter move back in as soon as the repairs were complete. This is disputed by the Landlord who says the Tenant never told him that the plan was to have her daughter move back in. Rather, he says that the Tenant did not want her daughter living with her any longer, and this was a convenient way to have her leave. The Tenant testified her daughter was “very private” and did not wish to share another washroom.

In this case, I find the Landlord’s evidence to be as believable as the Tenant’s. The Tenant was asked in cross-examination, more than once, about the circumstances surrounding the initial delay between January and March, to repairing the bathroom, but did not answer the question. Her daughter was not called to give evidence to support the Tenant’s position that her daughter was going to move back in after the renovations were complete.

Lastly, the Tenant did not give evidence that she personally used the washroom and thus lost the use of that washroom while awaiting a repair. In other words, the disrepair did not result in any actual loss or harm.
ordered: T he Tenants’ application is dismissed. 1 Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant’s application revolves around the roof top patio and allegations regarding the safety of the patio because there was bare asphalt on a flat-top roof without proper railings surrounding the area and there was at least a two metre drop off the patio to the ground below.

He submits that at the onset of his tenancy in on October 1, 2022, the Landlord promised to replace the patio and induced the Tenant into accepting this unit on that basis. Despite the promise, not only did the Landlord not reconstruct the patio, but they failed to ensure that the area was safe for the use of the Tenant until on or about the end of September 2025 when they installed a metal grate outside of the patio door.

With respect to the submissions regarding the loss of the patio space, this part of the application must be dismissed. The true substance of this allegation ought to have been submitted on a T3 application pursuant to section 130 of the Act regarding a discontinuation or reduction of a service or facility. Subsection 130(5) of the Act requires that such an application be made within one year of the date the reduction or discontinuance in a service or facility occurred. On this basis, the Tenant ought to have filed the T3 application by no later than September 30, 2023 and they did not. They are not entitled to a remedy on this basis.
The only lenses in which the application may be viewed is with respect to whether or not the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act.
Since the Tenant filed their T6 application on August 17, 2025, pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act, I can consider a remedy starting August 18, 2024.

The Tenant submitted into evidence several emails that they had with the Landlord regarding the patio. Mostly the correspondence is with respect to the Tenants assertions that the patio was included in the rent when the tenancy began and the Landlord stating that they would look into the issue. However, some of the correspondence is with respect to safety concerns of the patio and the two metre drop on each side.

For instance, when the Tenant inquired with the Landlord about the patio space on may 27, 2024, the Landlord replied on June 11, 2024 that the owner is going to send someone for an estimate pending the Tenant’s availability. The Tenant testified that someone came for an estimate the following week.
Then, on June 26, 2024 the Landlord responded that they never promised a patio and that it is not included in the rent.

On July 14, 2025 the Tenant followed up by email putting forth another argument about the patio being included with the rental unit. On July 20th the Tenant sent a follow up email to the Landlord. In this email the Tenant specifically addressed the safety issue with the unguarded patio because the patio door has unobstructed access to the area and cites that the unguarded patio violates the Ontario Building Code because it has a drop of over two meters.

In reply by the Landlord on July 21, 2025 the Landlord finally tells the Tenant that the space is not included in their rent and that the area should not be considered or used as an outdoor living space, as it is not intended for that purpose.

Prior to the Landlords correspondence, I accept the Tenants testimony that they would use the outdoor patio space regularly to sit outside. They would not use the space if it was covered in ice in the winter as they did not want to risk a slip and fall.

I also accept that the Tenant advised the Landlord of the safety issue on July 14, 2025 and that because the Landlord had not adequately responded about their intentions with the outside space, on August 17, 2025 the Tenant filed both this T6 application and a T2 application under LTB-T-068228-25. For completeness, the T2 application was withdrawn at an Adjudicative Case Conference on February 19, 2026.

I also accept that on or about September 11, 2025 the Landlord informed the Tenant that they had decided to move forward with repairing the damaged metal rail and installing a new one for safety reasons. I further accept that the railing was put up outside the Tenant’s patio door by September 24, 2025.

Based on the evidence before me, based on a breach of maintenance, I do find in favour of the Tenant regarding the unsafe rooftop patio and find that the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Although the Tenant did not advise the Landlord of their position regarding it being unsafe until July 14, 2205, the Landlord ought to have known that the Tenant had full unimpeded access to the patio since their tenancy began and they took no steps to either investigate or resolve the issue until on or about September 24, 2025, after the Tenant filed their applications.

This is evidenced by the Landlord finally installing a metal barrier at the patio door so the Tenant could not longer access the rooftop space. Prior to the installation, the unobstructed use of the space and the approximate two metre drop one either side of it did pose a serious safety risk for the Tenant. I accept that the unguarded space was not in compliance with the City of Ottawa Property Standards bylaw regarding railings and patios. More specifically, Subsection 24(1) of the bylaw states that: A guard shall be installed and maintained in good repair on every surface to which access is provided, including but not limited to exterior landings, porches, decks, balconies, mezzanines, galleries, raised walkways and roofs, on each side which is not protected by a wall and where there is a difference in elevation to adjacent surfaces of more than 60cm (23 5/8 in.).

Had the Landlord not intended for the Tenant to use the space, then they ought to have installed the barrier sooner or ought to have taken steps to ensure the space was safe for the Tenant’s continued use of it and they did not. The patio otherwise did not comply with housing and maintenance standards in accordance with the City’s bylaws.

The Tenant requested a 25% abatement for the one year period prior to filing their application. They had originally requested this abatement for the period since the tenancy began, however, that is more than the one year period that subsection 29(2) of the Act allows.

Further, the Tenant in their application did not specify an abatement as a particular remedy under [name] 1 of the application, however, under [name] 9, under “Other” remedies, the Tenant clearly states what they are seeking. They based their remedy on the loss of space which they submit was approximately 25% of the overall floor space.

However, I find that a 25% abatement is excessive regarding the maintenance aspect of the application as I have dismissed the application regarding the loss of use of the space. I find a 10% abatement for the period of August 18, 2024 to the date the railing was installed on September 24, 2025 to be reasonable which is a period of 13 months.

The Tenant testified that their rent for the period of August 2024 to October of 2024 was $1,458.12 and a 10% abatement for three months is $145.81x3 or $437.43. The rent increased to $1,492.07 on November 1, 2024 through to September of 2025 and a 10% abatement for ten months is $149.21x10 or $1,492.10. The total abatement is therefore $1,929.53.
Since the Tenant is successful on their application, the Landlord shall also reimburse the Tenant the $48.00 application filing fee.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,977.53 This amount represents: • $1,929.53 for a rent abatement for the period of August 18, 2024 to September 24, 2025 for the unsafe patio. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Tenant may alternatively recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent owing for August, September and October of 2026 and the balance of $477.53 from the rent owing for November 2026. July 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenants did not Vacate as a Result of the N12 Notice:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant [name] (SJ) testified that on January 9, 2025 the Landlord sent an email that she would be raising the rent above the guideline amount and that she will be listing the property for sale. SJ testified that they responded that they intended to stay as tenants even with the sale of the rental unit and that the rent increase was high and required 90 days notice. SJ testified that the Landlord responded on March 5, 2025 that the increase would only be 2.5%, she would calculate the 90 days from the initial email, and asked that the Tenants work with the real estate agent to accommodate viewings. I noted that [name] (AP) sent an email on March 10, 2025 that stated if the new owners want to move in, the Landlord could give them an N12 notice when the sale is finalized and they would vacate within 60 days.

SJ then testified that the Landlord sent another email on April 14, 2025 that viewings would start at the end of April 2025 and she offered a $1,000.00 discount for May 2025 rent for the Tenants to move items to allow for painting. At this time, SJ testified that the Landlord also offered an extra month of rent-free living if they agreed to move out by June 2025. The Landlord sent another email on April 17, 2025 stating that she had received a tenant referral request and asked if the Tenant’s are agreeing to move by June 2025.

SJ testified she responded on April 17, 2025 saying that nothing had been finalized and she did not want to accept the Landlord’s offer. On April 24, 2025 an email was sent stating that the Tenants would ideally prefer to stay on as Tenants, but they were willing to do a cash for keys arrangement. The Landlord then gave notice on April 30, 2025 that she intended to move into the rental unit. The Tenants submitted the entire email chain as documentary evidence.
The Tenants testified that they received an N12 notice on April 30, 2025 with a date of termination of June 30, 2025.
The Tenants also submitted a copy of their new lease which was originally dated April 17, 2025 and finalized on April 22, 2025 that their new tenancy commenced on April 24, 2025.

Based on the evidence provided by the Tenants, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants did not prove that they vacated as a result of the N12 notice as required in section 57(1)(a) of the Act. The Tenants evidence clearly identifies that they signed a lease and their new tenancy commenced on April 24, 2025, 6 days prior to the N12 notice being served on April 30, 2025. The Tenants testimony also confirms that the N12 notice was served on April 30, 2025, and as such, I find that the Landlord had not yet served an N12 notice when the Tenants signed their new lease, which I find is an indication that their desire to vacate the rental unit was not as a result of the N12 notice.

While the Tenants did not hand in the keys until June 30, 2025, I find it unreasonable that the Tenants would continue holding a lease for both rental units given that SJ testified that it was difficult that they held a lease for 2 rental units for 2 months. SJ also testified that they waited until June 30, 2025 to give back the keys because it took time to move their belongings to their new rental unit, which was the neighbouring unit.

I also find that the Tenants were aware that they did not have to vacate the rental unit or find a new rental unit because the Landlord was planning to list the property for sale. The Tenants mentioned their intention to stay in the rental unit in multiple emails, and on March 10, 2025 AP stated that the Landlord could serve an N12 notice if the property was sold and the purchaser’s intended to move in. I am satisfied that this shows that the Tenants were aware that they did not have to vacate the rental unit when they signed a new lease on April 24, 2025, and they decided to sign a new tenancy agreement anyways.
As the Tenants did not establish that they vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The A1 application at issue seeks a determination as to whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) applies to the parties’ lease arrangement.
The named tenant [name] (KA) submits the Act applies because she is a “tenant” and [name] (“TT”) is a “landlord”. TT states the Act does not apply because KA was a mere occupant or roommate.

The facts are not largely in dispute. TT testified she leased the entire rental unit from a family friend for $2000/month. TT subsequently posted an online advertisement which provided, in part, as follows: “…Looking for a female roommate for a long term….I will be your roommate…$1250 per month including Wi-Fi and hydro…”

Shortly thereafter, a standard form lease agreement (“Lease”) identifying KA as the Tenant, and TT as the Landlord was signed. From May 1, 2025 through to August 30, 2025, KA occupied one of the bedrooms/bathrooms in the rental unit and paid $1350/month in rent . TT occupied the other available bedroom, and the parties shared a kitchen. During this time, KA testified TT assumed topical Landlord responsibilities, collecting rent and responding to maintenance issues raised.

TT denied being an owner/landlord, stating she is a tenant who leased the entire rental unit, as evidenced by her own lease agreement with a 3rd party. As TT never vacated the rental unit and only leased a portion of the rental unit to KA, TT submits that KA was a mere occupant or roommate.
For the reasons that follow, I find the Act does not apply to the parties’ lease arrangement.

Section 2(1) of the Act speaks to such circumstances and defines a “Landlord” as explicitly excluding “…a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit… ” Section 2(2) of the Act is also informative and specifically identifies three requirements for a “sublet” to occur, as follows: For the purposes of this Act, a reference to subletting a rental unit refers to the situation in which, (a) the tenant vacates the rental unit; (b) the tenant gives one or more other persons the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant’s term or period; and (c) the tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit after that specified date. [emphasis added\

Here, it is clear that TT, herself, was a tenant who continued to reside in the rental unit while leasing out only a portion of the rental unit to KA. In such circumstances, I find that TT does not meet the definition of a “Landlord” under the Act.

I also find the parties did not enter int o a “sublet” arrangement. Given TT’s continued possession of the rental unit, the necessary prerequisite to “vacate the rental unit” is not satisfied. Consequently, I find that KA was a mere roommate or occupant. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 21 provides that the Act does not apply to such lease arrangements, stating “a finding that a person is an occupant means that the occupant has no protection or rights in proceedings at the LTB under the RTA”.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. July 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit in December 2019 and vacated Februray 28, 2023. The lawful monthly rent was $800.00. The Parking

The Tenant testified that he had problems with parking during the tenancy. He testified that there were no real parking arrangements when he first moved into the rental unit. However, this changed during the tenancy when he purchased gravel and spread it beside the complex to create a space for his vehicles.
He testified that he spoke to the Landlord first then purchased the gravel and he and the Landlord spread it out to create a parking space for his scarp vehicles and his truck.

The Tenant testified that his relationship with the Landlord started out well but deteriorated after he approached the community advocacy centre who issued a letter to the Landlord indicating that he could park on the complex and could pay by cheque, the letter also requested the Landlord provide rent receipts. The Tenant testified that the relationship deteriorated after this occurred. The Tenant also testified that after he gave the Landlord this letter the Landlord tried to give him two months notice to end the tenancy, and the Landlord would no longer talk to him.

The Tenant testified that after this he began to have difficulties with his vehicles including scratches on his vehicles, and the Landlord blocking him in. He testified that during the winter the Landlord would plow snow around his vehicles and up against the side of his vehicles and into the bed of his truck. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord would also frequently block his vehicles in. and would sometimes block off the entrances to the complex including on the day that he was moving out of the rental unit.

In most cases the Tenant could not recall specific dates and times for the incidents reacted to parking however, he did rely on a video (DOC-6452707) in support of theses assertions. The video depicts the Landlord blowing snow using a snow blower and a small portion of the snow landing in the bed of the Tenants truck and on a trailer attached to the truck. I do note that on either side of the Landlord there are two other vehicles, so that any way the blower was turn a portion of the snow would land on a vehicle within the parking lot.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was using a snow blower and directing the blown snow so that it faced into the box of his truck and performed 3 or 4 passes. The Tenant testified that when he was doing the rest of the parking lot, he would ensure the snow was directed away from other vehicles but when blowing snow around the Tenants vehicle he would angle the blown snow so that it landed in the bed of the Tenants truck and make 3 or 4 passes. He testified that the Landlord would also use a snowplough and would angle the blades so that snow ended up right under and around his truck. He testified this occurred all winter during the last year of the tenancy when the Landlord cleared the snow.

The Tenant testified that the video was probably taken in January 2022. The Tenant could not recall any of the exact dates that the Landlord had blown snow into his truck bed or ploughed snow around his vehicles.

The Tenant testified that he spent 4 or 5 minutes recording the video of the Landlord blowing snow on his truck before taking it to the police station. When asked why he didn’t move his truck when the Landlord was blowing snow, he testified that he could have but he instead chose to record the Landlord harassing him by blowing snow on his vehicles. He testified that after he recorded the vehicle, he did go outside.
The Tenant denied that the Landlord had told him not to park scarp vehicles within the complex but allowed that he had some scrap vehicles in and out.
The Tenant testified that he was aware that the Landlord ran a U-Haul business from the complex, and customers could drop of the vehicles anywhere at any time.

The Landlord testified that the agreement between himself and the Tenant was that the Tenant was to park his cobalt-coloured truck and trailer out front alongside a ditch and park his other truck along the left side but no other vehicles were supposed to be there.

He testified that he was aware that the Tenant had purchased a load of gravel and claimed that the Tenant had informed him he had purchased the gravel and asked the Landlord where he wanted it, and the two spread it out. However, the Landlord denied that this was done to create a parking spot for the Tenant.

The Landlord indicated that he was not intentionally interfering with the Tenant’s parking and would move things as soon as he became aware of any blockage, the Landlord also testified that there were three driveways in and out of the complex, so there was always a way for the Tenant to get in and out.

He described that his snow blowing method as going straight through with a gas snow blower then up the side of the building before going across the front to move snow away from that area, He testified that he had to direct the snow towards the road, not directly towards the Tenants vehicle.

The Landlord denied blocking the entrances to the complex when the Tenant vacated and indicated that he runs a U-Haul rental company from the complex, so there are always multiple driveways for Tenant’s and customers to use to enter and exit the complex. The Landlord did allow that there were two occasions when the Tenant had called the OPP claiming the Landlord had blocked him in, but indicated that on both occasions there was a clear path for the Tenant, who had not asked him to move the U-Haul trucks before contacting the OPP directly. The Heat

The Tenant also testified that the heat was not turned on in December 2022, he testified that spoke to the Tenant’s upstairs who indicated that they had heat and were on the same circle as the Tenant so he should have heat as well. The Tenant testified that he asked the Landlord to turn on the heat and received no reply, so he began to heat his rental unit using the stove. He subsequently contacted the fire department seeking advice and they instructed him to turn off his stove and to text his Landlord and tell him it was illegal to keep his heat of. He testified that about three hours later he saw the Landlord walk by and enter the basement and then he had heat. He testified that the heat, which is controlled by a water boiler, was constant, and he had no control over it and it cold not be shut off.

The Tenant could not recall how long he was without heat, he testified that he just knew it was in the middle of December. He estimated that it took about 4 or 5 days from his first message to the Landlord for the heat to be turned on.

With respect to the heat, the Landlord explained that each unit has is own thermostat. He testified that the Tenant had his window open all winter and never informed him that he had no heat, or that the heat in his rental unit was too high, or unable to be shut off. Analysis

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord entered his rental unit illegally, interfered with his reasonable enjoyment, harassed him, or withheld or interfered with vital services.

The Tenant’s testimony was vague and general in nature and largely lacked specific dates for the allegations made. It also at times conflicted with the dates in the Application itself. For example, the Application alleges a lack of heat in November, and the Tenant testified this occurred in the month of December. While this discrepancy is minor on its own when combined with the Tenant’s inability to recall specific dates for the allegations made during the hearing, it causes me to question the reliability of his testimony.

Additionally, while I am prepared to attribute a portion of the inconsistency and lack of specifics in the Tenants testimony to the time that has passed since the Application was filed, even in after doing so I am not satisfied that the Tenant has identified clear dates for his allegations, and what remains are general allegations of interference and harassment related to parking without clear details or specifics.

While the Tenant has provided a video of the Landlord blowing snow within the parking lot, and a portion of that blow snow does appear to land on the Tenant’s vehicle, it is not clear from the video that this is done with malicious intent, and could as easily depict the Landlord attempting to blow snow towards the road and a portion landing on the Tenant’s vehicle as the Landlord claimed in their testimony. I also note that the video clearly depicts the Landlord stopping before they get too close to the Tenant’s truck and note that there are vehicles on both sides of the Landlord, so no matter which way the snow is blown a portion of it would land on a vehicle.

With respect to the allegation that the Landlord blocked the driveways of the complex when the Tenant was attempting to vacate, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven this on a balance of probabilities, I accept that the complex also houses a U-Haul rental business owned by the Landlord and contains several driveways, and I find it unlikely that the Landlord would block all entrances and exits given the disputation this would cause to their bruises, simply to disrupt the Tenant’s move. While I am prepared to accept that the Landlord or customers of the Landlord’s may have parked or returned U-Haul trucks in positions around the complex which were inconvenient for the Tenant, I am not satisfied that he has demonstrated that this deliberate or part of pattern of harassment or interference.

I note that this is a Tenants Application and the balance rests with the Tenant to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has entered his rental unit illegally, interfered with his reasonable enjoyment, harassed him, or withheld or interfered with vital services, and given the vague nature of the Tenant’s testimony and the lack of supporting evidence presented, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has done so with respect to his allegation surrounding parking.

With respect to the heat, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord failed to turn the heat for the rental unit on, or that once it was restored it was too warm and could not be controlled by the Tenant. Each unit appears to be controlled by its own thermostat, which would allow the Tenant to adjust the heat to their liking once it had been turned on, and the Tenant has not provided any supporting documentation which would confirm his assertion that the Landlord was ever made aware of a lack or overabundance of heat within his rental unit.

Given my concerns with respect to the reliability of the Tenant’s evidence, I am not satisfied that his testimony alone has satisfied me the Landlord was ever made aware of a problem with the heat in the rental unit.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that that the Landlord has interfered with their reasonable enjoyment or withheld vital services with respect to heat.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally. I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant, and I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Post-hearing submissions

At the conclusion of the hearing on March 27, 2026, I invited the parties’ Legal Representatives to serve and file closing submissions on or before April 17, 2026. The submissions came to my attention on April 29, 2026.

The Tenant filed his own submissions on April 16, 2026. It is unclear whether he alerted his representative of his intent to make independent submissions, and whether he served these submissions on the Landlord or the Landlord's Legal Representative M.Z.
Given the Tenant is represented by a licensee, I am not prepared to consider the Tenant’s submissions as filed on April 16, 2026. T6 application
The Tenant moved into the studio apartment in the multi-residential building on February 4, 2015. The current monthly rent is $1,343.58.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to effectively and promptly resolve disrepair in the rental unit. The Tenant’s primary concerns were about alleged mould contamination, particularly within the fan coil unit (“FCU”) in the living area and in a kitchen vent, and about a water damaged ceiling.

The Landlord contends that they responded reasonably to resolve the disrepair issues. The Landlord's Legal Representative M.Z. submits that there are only a few factual disputes and no disagreement regarding the steps the Landlord took in response to the Tenant’s complaints. I accept that there is little dispute about the sequence and details of events.

The issue before the Board is whether the actions taken by the Landlord to address maintenance and repairs in the rental unit were sufficient to meet its obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Landlord’s witnesses S.H.(M.) and [name]

The Landlord’s Regional Manager [name]) spoke about her role in managing the 157 unit residential complex. She testified that the Landlord spends considerable funds to maintain the building. They have three superintendents on site and unlimited access to contractors to ensure timely responses when maintenance and repairs are needed. 10. [name], the Senior Property Manager, explained that in her role she would receive work orders from tenants. She became familiar with the Tenant’s mould complaint on August 1, 2024, when S.H.(M.) asked her to assist. She arranged ceiling repairs, which contractors assessed as cosmetic in nature. She facilitated mould remediation processes in the unit as well as the Tenant’s access to a guest suite while the work was being done. She received and reviewed remediation reports prepared by their contractor. Ceiling disrepair 11. I find that the Landlord failed to address ceiling repairs in a timely and effective manner. 12. On July 8, 2023, the Tenant filed a work order asking the Landlord to inspect the ceiling in the living room, dining room and bedroom due to “upper leak - “ceiling is soaking wet (mold)”. A notation was added to the document: “DONE 7/8/2023” and “PUT 1 ELEC FAN”. There is no dispute that the in-built radiator or fan coil unit (“FCU”) located in the unit above the Tenant’s unit was the source of a water leak at the time. 13. On September 3, 2023, the Tenant reported to the Landlord that “a water overflow is draining down from an upper unit on the main bathroom/kitchen”. In an email to the Landlord’s agent S.D.V., he added, “This can be the perfect breeding ground for black mold. … I’d look into this.” He also noted, “Btw my ceiling from the last leak is still a mess.” 14. The Landlord arranged for a plumber to repair a broken pipe in the unit above on September 14, 2023 and for a contractor to repair and repaint the Tenant’s bathroom. 15. An undated work order from Manny’s Painting and Decorating shows that the contractor was to repair the bedroom ceiling. However, in the notes section, the author refers to the bathroom. An invoice dated November 24, 2023 shows only that bathroom repairs were completed. No mention was made of repairs to the kitchen or living room ceilings. 16. The Tenant had retained S.D.C. to represent him on another matter. On October 7, 2023, he emailed S.D.C. photos he had taken on September 27, 2023 depicting the ceiling condition. The photos show bubbling and flaking paint on the living area ceiling plus visible reddish-brown stains on the ceiling in various locations in the unit. In his email, the Tenant described these as “water damage to ceiling from leaking radiator in [Unit] 813”. 17. S.D.C. emailed S.H.(M.) and M.S., the acting property manager, the same day, pointing out that the water damaged ceiling was the result of two incidents of water leaking into the Tenant’s ceiling from the unit directly above the Tenant’s unit. There was no response. 18. On July 26, 2024, the Landlord gave a Notice of Entry for July 31, 2024 “to inspect the state of repair of the rental unit”. On July 31, 2024. [name], the Senior Property Manager, attended with a maintenance team to examine the ceiling and to assess necessary repairs. 19. On August 1, 2024, maintenance people attended at the unit to take measurements. The photos taken that day, as presented by the Landlord, show that the edge of the ceiling near the balcony doors was uneven and had bubbling and peeling paint. 20. On August 2, 2024, S.H.(M.) emailed S.D.C. stating that, “we had previously attended to the complaint made by your client and had determined previously that nothing further needed to be done.” She continued: “It was only recently that a further complaint was made which precipitated an inspection in the rental unit and a determination that some remedial work was required to resolve what appeared to be cosmetic issues.” 21. The Landlord gave a Notice of Entry for August 6, 2024 to complete repairs. However, the repairs were not completed that day. Instead, they were paused while the Landlord inspected whether mould was present in the unit and determined next steps. 22. The evidence is that the ceiling repairs were completed on October 22, 2024. The Law 23. Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.” 24. Section 3 of O.Reg. 517/06 states that “All repairs to and maintenance of a rental unit or residential complex shall be carried out in a manner and with the materials that are accepted as good workmanship in the trades concerned.” 25. The Toronto Municipal Code, Chapter 629, Property Standards demands work that is “free from defects” and “made of materials that are sufficient to ensure maintenance in good repair, including compatible in design to adjoining finished materials; …” (§ 629-1.1). The landlord must also “ensure all repairs are made and completed with appropriate skill” (§ 629-3.4). The Municipal Code also provides that: § 629-27. Every wall and ceiling shall be maintained clean and free of holes, cracks and damaged and deteriorated surface material, and each repair shall be finished to reasonably match the existing walls or ceilings. 26. Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) is binding caselaw relating to disrepair. The Court of Appeal confirmed that compliance with subsection 20(1) of the Act must be assessed using a contextual, fact-specific approach, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. Analysis 27. I find that Landlord’s contractor left the ceiling in the rental unit in an objectively unreasonable condition on September 3, 2023. 28. After the Tenant reported the issue on October 7, 2023, the Landlord did not take meaningful steps to resolve it, considering it a cosmetic issue that did not engage their repair obligations under the Act. It was not until July 2024, approximately 9 months after the Tenant’s initial request, that the Landlord took any proactive steps to address it. 29. The Landlord acknowledged that the ceiling condition was unacceptable in communications to the Tenant between July 31, 2024 and August 3, 2024. They agreed to have a contractor fix the issue. Still, the repairs were not completed for about another 3 months because the Landlord decided to first address mould issues discovered in the unit. 30. I agree with the Tenant that the Landlord’s delay was excessive. The Landlord provided insufficient explanation as to why mould concerns prevented the completion of the ceiling repairs, or why the two issues could not be addressed independently. I was therefore left without a satisfactory account, justifying the failure to complete the repairs sooner. 31. The Tenant asserts that living with the disrepair daily affected his enjoyment of his home. Tenants are entitled to occupy a unit that has not been visibly degraded by lack of repair or substandard repair work. They are not entitled to aesthetic perfection – but while landlords are not required to replicate the exact original finish, they must ensure the work is properly finished so that it is uniform, reasonably blends with the surrounding surface, and is not visually objectionable. 32. I am amply persuaded that the Landlord’s failure to make proper repairs in a timely manner contributed to the persistence of the disrepair and negatively impacted the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit. Mould 2022 – 2023 33. On or about April 27, 2022 the Tenant observed mould on the fibreglass cover of the FCU. 34. On September 3, 2023, the Tenant mentioned his suspicions and concerns about mould growth to the Landlord in relation to a water leak from the unit above his into his unit. 2024 35. The Tenant testified that he suffered from breathing issues for a good part of the 2023- 2024 winter. He acknowledged that he did not have proof that he reported any further mould complaints directly to the Landlord either verbally (as audio recorded) or in writing between October 2023 and January 2024, although he maintains that he did. 36. He stated that on February 2, 2024, he again observed “black fuzz” inside the fiberglass cover of the FCU in the living area. He recalls reporting this in a text message to the Landlord, with a photo. He did not produce a copy of the text for the Board to consider. 37. On April 5, 2024, the Tenant underwent endoscopic sinus surgery. He testified that he continued to experience respiratory difficulties throughout the spring/summer of 2024 and believed these were caused or exacerbated by the indoor environment in the rental unit. 38. It is unclear to me what event(s) preceded the Landlord’s Notice of Entry on July 26, 2024, but as earlier noted, on July 31, 2024 the Landlord inspected the unit. 39. On August 1, 2024, S.D.C. emailed M.S. requesting details of the planned repairs and to ask if mould testing would be performed. M.S. forwarded the email to S.H.(M.), who then emailed S.D.C. on August 2, 2024. S.H.(M.) stated in the email that they disagreed there was evidence of mould but “in an effort to accommodate your client”, the Landlord would have their environmental contractor assess the unit condition, “including testing for mould.” 40. On August 3, 2024, S.D.C. emailed both S.H.(M.) and M.S: “The 2023 leakage was never properly inspected and addressed, which is what has led to our concern of mould forming in the area. It has been ignored for almost a year.” 41. The Landlord consequently retained S2S Environmental Inc. (“S2S”) to investigate. On August 8, 2024, S2S’s Project Scientist P.M. collected tape-lift samples from the ceiling and other areas which were discoloured or appeared to have water staining. No evidence was led that the HVAC ducts, including in the kitchen ceiling, were inspected. 42. S2S advised the Landlord on August 16, 2024 that mould was present in the FCU. On August 22, 2024, S.D.C. emailed S.H.(M.), asking for a copy of the mould test results. S.H.(M.) did not immediately respond. 43. On August 28, 2024, the Landlord scheduled S2S for a single-day, professional remediation on September 10, 2024. The same day, the Tenant filed the T6 application and S.D.C. again asked the Landlord for a copy of the mould assessment results. 44. On August 30, 2024, S.H.(M.) informed S.D.C. that the Landlord declined to release internal reports “but rather will be following the recommendations made by our experts and moving forward with repairs based on that.” 45. The remediation work was not completed on September 10, 2024 because the Tenant wanted temporary use of a guest suite during the remediation. He expressed to the Landlord his concern about toxic spores being disturbed and released into the air, triggering not only his asthma but that, in all likelihood, these would negatively impact the health of his pets. Since a guest suite was not available, the remediation was rescheduled. 46. On September 21, 2024, the Tenants engaged Mold Solutions Canada to inspect for mould. A.D., a Certified Mold Remediator, conducted the testing. On September 23, 2024, S.D.C. emailed S.H.(M.): “We have retained our own expert and have conducted our own [name]. The results were very disturbing as not only was [name] detected in Mr. [name]’s unit but it is spreading and growing. It was also discovered that water continues to leak into the ceiling from leaky pipes behind the walls. This is a serious health risk. Mr. [name]name] has been experiencing continuing medical issues that may be related to the existence of the [name] he has been forced to live with in his unit. Moreover, both his pets have suffered from medical problems that may be directly related to the existence of mould spores in the air in Mr. [name]name]’s unit.” 47. The Landlord scheduled the remediation work for October 21, 2024. They arranged a guest suite for the Tenant, at the Landlord’s expense, for the duration of the process. Mould abatement was completed that day by Dry-It Inc. (retained by S2S on behalf of the Landlord) after which S2S deemed the unit acceptable for occupancy. 48. On October 23, 2024, S.D.C. shared with S.H.(M.) the Tenant’s concern that not all the mould was removed. She explained that the Tenant had his own surveillance camera footage from inside the unit showing that the technicians wore no PPE “and the only process that appears to have been used to remove the mould is vinegar in a spray bottle.” S.D.C. asked the Landlord to provide proof the mould was removed and “that you didn’t just instruct your team to sand and paint over the problem.” 49. S.H.(M.) replied that their team “followed all necessary protocols for the assessment, treatment, and repair.” 2025 50. On February 13, 2025, S.D.C. emailed S.H.(M.) noting that the Landlord had not confirmed in writing that the mould was successfully removed, despite S.D.C.’s numerous requests, and that mould was a “health hazard” that needed to be addressed immediately. [name] replied the next day asserting that “there are no current issues” relating to maintenance. 51. The Tenant testified that his dog began to exhibit severe respiratory symptoms in March 2025, requiring veterinary treatment. On May 16, 2025, the Tenant found more mould growth in the FCU. On May 18, 2025, he videorecorded the FCU interior to capture the presence of rust and black mould. He purchased air purifiers to use as a precaution. 52. The Tenant’s evidence is that the veterinarian and his doctor had each recommended he test the air quality within his unit for mould. 53. The Tenant’s veterinarian, Dr. [name], advised him that euthanasia was the only option to reduce his dog’s respiratory suffering. This procedure occurred on August 11, 2025. The Tenant provided a letter dated September 3, 2025 from the Rosedale-Moor Park Veterinary Clinic, explaining that the dog showed severe respiratory symptoms in the spring of 2025 and, “While a final diagnosis was never made, mould such as Aspergillus…could well have been a contributing factor” to the dog’s poor health. 54. On August 8, 2025, the Tenant hired F.H. of Bionic Environments Inc. (also operating as Verify Air Quality Ltd.) to conduct a more thorough mould assessment. 55. On August 14, 2025, F.H. inspected the unit and took surface samples by swab as well as moisture readings. [name] reported to the Tenant that he observed mould inside the kitchen vent and on the surrounding drywall, water damage in the vent and heavy mould on a kitchen cutting board. He recommended professional Level 3 mould remediation. 57. He wrote: “Molds such as Aspergillus species can definitely be involved in causing these kinds of nasal and sinus symptoms. His symptoms subsequently recurred post surgery. These are again troublesome and it is my medical opinion that exposure to mold species is particularly problematic for this patient.” 58. S.D.C. informed the Landlord’s representative M.Z. on September 3, 2025 that the Tenant had discovered mould in the common laundry room and asked for an emergency meeting. The Tenant’s evidence is that when the property managers met him at the unit, they initially advised him that the FCU had been properly cleaned in 2024 and they left; however, they then returned to the unit and stated that the FCU needed to be replaced because of “appearance” issues, namely the rust – not because the FCU was in disrepair. 59.
