Then, because of his respiratory issues, he suspected mould was growing in the unit and thought it prudent to have a specialist check it out before reporting it again to the Landlord. 61. On September 11, 2025, the Landlord retained S2S to inspect the unit and conduct testing. 62. When the test results came back, S2S confirmed with the Landlord that there was mould in the FCU. The Landlord arranged for another Level 1 remediation of the FCU and, as a precaution, to clean the plaster around the kitchen vent. 63. On September 16, 2025, [name] contacted the FCU manufacturer about a replacement, which was a customized model. The Landlord authorized the purchase and instalment on September 17, 2025 and [name] submitted the order right away. 64. The City of Toronto inspected the unit on September 18, 2025, finding the HVAC system was “not free of” damaged or deteriorated materials”, including rust, and issued a compliance order obligating the Landlord to replace the FCU. 65. S2S retained Ferro Environmental Inc. to complete Level 1 remediation and vent cleaning in the unit on October 6, 2025. The Landlord arranged for the Tenant to use a guest suite from October 6, 2025 to October 8, 2025. 66. On October 8, 2025, S2S took post-remediation air samples and removed air [name] that the technicians had left running in the unit for two days. The new FCU arrived, and the Landlord’s contractor installed it on October 27, 2025. 1 High-efficiency air filtration equipment. 67. The Tenant confirmed that as of October 28, 2025, the mould issues seemed addressed. 68. S2S completed a final inspection on December 4, 2025. They looked for signs of mould growth in the abated spaces; used a borescope to view the interior of the kitchen air vent and operated a thermal camera to assess moisture levels. 2026 69. S2S provided a final report and Clearance Certificate to the Landlord on January 15, 2026, confirming the air quality, temperature and humidity were all satisfactory and did not favour mould growth. The Tenant has not made any further complaints about mould issues. 70. The Landlord appealed the compliance [name] to the City of Toronto Property Standards Committee because they had replaced the FCU and the [name] was rescinded. The Landlord’s witness K.M. 71. K.M., B.ES, GIS and Remote Sensing Certificate, is a Microbial Remediation Technician (AMRT)2, and is the Manager of Health, Safety and Compliance with S2S. He has 14 years’ experience managing projects related to identifying and abating mould, asbestos and other substances. 72. He confirmed that he was not personally involved in the testing or mould abatement but he approved reports authored by other individuals directly engaged in the processes. 73. He testified that S2S determined that Level 1 remediation3 would be appropriate because the mould in the FCU was confined to less than 10 ft2. He noted that no mould was identified in the kitchen ceiling “but it could have been leaking”. The information he received from the Landlord was that they deemed the ceiling issue to be “an esthetic problem for the Landlord to fix” and not related to mould contamination. 74. When asked by M.Z. to comment on the differences between the Tenant’s report by Verify Air Quality and S2S’s reports, [name] stated that the only real difference was the Tenant’s results showed mould in the kitchen vent. He noted that, “If there was mould there, we didn’t find it”, adding that they didn’t open the kitchen wall or ceiling for testing. 75. On cross-examination, S.D.C. asked him if mould exposure would be more harmful to pets. He replied that an answer was not within his expertise. The Scientific and Technical Reports September 24, 2024 – Report of Mold Solutions Canada [Tenant] 76. A.D., a Certified Mold Remediator inspected for mould in the unit on September 21, 2024. His report includes photos he took of water damage on the ceiling, evidenced by bubbling, flaking paint. He did not detect excess moisture when using a moisture meter. He observed “visible mold growth in the HVAC enclosure” and suggested “it’s possible that the mold growth occurred from the previous leak and the impacted material dried out”. 2 Consultant member in good standing with the Environmental Abatement Council of Canada (EACC). 3 According to technical evidence, mould abatement may proceed by different levels relating to the size of the area being abated. Generally, Level 1 is less than 10 sq. ft; Level 2 is 10 -30 sq. ft. Levels 3 and above require more intensive remediation practices. October 21, 2024 – S2S Field Assessment Report [Landlord] 77. S2S acknowledges in this report that mould growth and “potential growth” in the FCU were visually confirmed. The mould found in the laboratory results based on the August 8, 2024 test samples consisted of “moderate to abundant [name]”. 78. The report states that the Level 1 abatement of the FCU was done on October 21, 2024 by workers wearing PPE, using a HEPA-equipped vacuum, and by applying [name] disinfectant4 to clean the FCU’s concrete floor. [name] noted that the ceiling was “reportedly cleaned and fixed” by the Landlord’s contractor the next day. A final visual inspection verified the “identified suspect mould impacted area was clean”. October 24, 2024 Mould Air Sampling relating to permitting occupancy [Landlord] 79. S2S reported that the results of the subsequent airborne mould sampling taken October 23, 2024 were that “the airborne spore concentrations … were considered to be within normal ranges for similar-type residential units”. The unit was “acceptable for occupancy”. November 22, 2024- S2S Summary of Mould Abatement [Landlord] 80. K.M.’s report summarizes the work completed by Dry-It Inc. on October 21, 2024. He recommended that buildings and surfaces be maintained to prevent conditions favourable for mould growth and to guard against mould reoccurring. He notes that S2S did not evaluate health risks associated with mould exposure, nor did they perform “a detailed building envelope investigation to assess the potential cause of the water infiltration that created an environment favourable to mould proliferation”. August 14, 2025 - Verify Air Quality Ltd. (the ‘Verify Report’) [Tenant] 81. [name], BA, BB, BBEI, CMC, CIHM, of Bionic Environments Inc./Verify Air Quality Ltd. is a Certified Indoor Environmental Inspector.5 In his report, F.H. discusses mould types, levels, impacts and abatement processes. He explains that “Mould growth can create thousands to hundreds of thousands of spores that, if disturbed, can become airborne and affect occupant health as well as lead to mould growth in unaffected areas.” 82. Along with photos he took of extensive mould contamination, he observed “[r]ust and visible water damage inside radiator”. He reported that the FCU did not appear to have been serviced or cleaned “in quite some time.” 83. On August 12, 2025, F.H. took swab samples of affected surfaces. The Axxon Lab report he subsequently received confirmed mould growth in the FCU and kitchen vent. 84. [name] recommended Level 3 remediation. He wrote that, while there are numerous guidelines published, “We prefer the more stringent approach to health and safety when dealing with mould remediation.” He did not recommend using “biocides, bleach, chemicals and anti-microbial solutions” (such as Bad Axe MMR, which is corrosive) to remove mould. The only effective solution was for a specialist to remove the growth as well as airborne and settled spores. He emphasized that adequate PPE was always required 4 Commercial grade mould and mildew stain remover. 5Certified Indoor Environmental Inspector, Council Certified Microbial Investigator, Certified Industrial Hygiene Manager, Master Trainer - Approved Certification Course Provider – ACAC and Past Founding Director-Indoor Air Quality Association - Toronto Chapter. during the remediation process. The minimal necessary PPE included full-face respirators with HEPA P-100 filters, Tyvek clothing covering the head and shoes, and gloves. 85. Additionally, [name] warned, “Any moisture sources that led to the mould growth will need to be successfully stopped in order to avoid a recurrence.” He also advised that “hidden or developing problems may be missed” without an exhaustive inspection. [name] points to the necessity of performing Post Remediation Verification (Clearance Testing). September 11, 2025 – Pre-abatement [name] Testing [Landlord] 86. S2S collected tape-lift samples inside the unit in the FCU and kitchen vent areas. October 6, 2025 S2S Field Assessment Report [Landlord] 87. S2S retained Ferro Environmental Inc. to perform the mold abatement. This time, in addition to steel-toe boots and gloves, the contractor wore PPE which included a Tyvek suit and a full-face respirator equipped with P-100 filters. Using an EPA-equipped vacuum, he removed rust and mould from the metal finishes in the FCU covering about 8ft2. He cleaned the kitchen air vent, removed and cleaned <1ft2 of “suspect mould” from plaster around the kitchen air vent, and applied a layer of anti-fungal primer and paint to the vent area. He also installed an air scrubber to run for the next 48 hours. October 8, 2025 S2S Post-abatement Field Assessment [Landlord] 88. S2S conducted air sampling within the unit following the remediation. October 9, 2025 - EMC Scientific Lab (S2S) [Landlord] 89. The October 9, 2025 lab report results show the total concentration of airborne spores identified in the sample collected within the unit the day before was acceptably lower than the outdoor level. The spores consisted of [name], Ascospores, Aspergillus/Penicillium, Basidiospores, and Cladosporium, but no presence of Chaetomium or Stachybottys which, like Cladosporium, are commonly associated with water damaged materials. October 14, 2025 – S2S Summary of the Mould Assessment and Abatement [Landlord] 90. D.K. also of S2S, summarized the Landlord’s second request for an assessment “following concerns raised regarding suspect mould growth on the kitchen ceiling and within the HVAC fan coil unit”. 91. Moisture measurements and tape-lift samples were taken pre-abatement and air sampling was performed post-abatement. Based on the findings from visual observations and tape- lift sampling, S2S recommended Level 1 abatement within the FCU and, as an added precaution, Level I cleaning of the plaster finishes around the kitchen air vent. 92. S2S conducted a final visual inspection, finding the unit acceptable for occupancy. D.K. noted that the Landlord advised that the FCU was being replaced in the near future. December 5, 2025 - EMC Scientific Inc. (S2S) [Landlord] 93. Testing of the unit by S2S showed “a few spores” of Cladosporium but no mould growth. The claims of a latent defect, failure to report the disrepair, and failure to mitigate 94. M.Z. claims that the mould in the FCU was a latent defect for which liability should not be imposed upon the Landlord. He submits that the Landlord could not reasonably have known about the defect prior to the mould complaint first being made. He also submits that the Landlord cannot be held responsible for the mould disrepair between May and September 2025 because the Tenant failed to report it in a timely way. 95. Finally, he asserts, the Tenant’s refusal to leave the unit for remediation scheduled on September 10, 2024 interfered with the Landlord’s ability to reasonably perform the work in a timely manner and, since the Tenant did nothing to mitigate, the Landlord should not be held responsible for failing to complete the first mould abatement sooner. The Law 96. In addition to the application of subsection 20(1) of the Act, Section 3 of O.Reg. 517/06, the Toronto Municipal Code § 629-3.4, the Municipal Code provides the following: § 629-38. Every heating and air-conditioning system or unit shall be kept in good repair and maintained in good working condition at all times relevant to the operation of that system. 97. The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 5 gives guidance to parties and refers to the importance of a landlord having reasonable program of maintenance, including preventative maintenance.6 Additionally, the Guideline notes that a tenant “has no right to insist upon a standard of perfection regarding repairs. By the same token, a landlord is not entitled to rely upon repairs that were improperly done as a complete answer to the need for repairs, especially if the repairs had no effect or resulted in a need for further repairs.” Analysis Hearsay evidence 98. Each representative submitted that little or no weight should be given to hearsay evidence. 99. The Board is not bound by strict rules of evidence and may admit hearsay evidence. However, the weight assigned depends on factors such as reliability, first-hand knowledge, and whether the evidence can be tested through cross-examination. 100. I accept that the parties’ expert reports are business records reflecting professional work. 101. [name]'s qualifications and role with S2S enabled him to review, interpret, and approve S2S's reports. I therefore find his testimony relevant and generally reliable. However, some of the reports are based on observations and data collected by individuals who did not testify. As a result, those portions of the reports could not be tested through cross-examination. It is unclear whether K.M. personally discussed those findings with the individuals. I have taken this into account when assessing the evidence. 102. Neither of the Tenant's experts attended the hearing. Nevertheless, I am satisfied that their reports were prepared in the ordinary course of professional practice and contain findings based on identified inspection and testing methods. 103. The Mold Solutions Canada report prepared by A.D. on September 24, 2024, was created close in time to the events in issue. Its findings are consistent with the Landlord's own pre- abatement findings and are broadly corroborated by F.H.'s later assessment. The Landlord 6 See Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON CTGDDC) (also cited in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII). did not specifically challenge the report's findings. Although A.D. did not testify and the report could not be tested through cross-examination, I am satisfied that the report is relevant and sufficiently reliable to be considered. 104. I find that F.H.'s 2025 report is generally consistent with the other evidence presented. It reflects F.H.'s own assessment and contains conclusions supported by the methodology described in the report. Although F.H. did not testify, I am satisfied that the report is sufficiently reliable to be considered as part of the evidentiary record. 105. The Tenant filed letters from his physician and veterinarian. Although neither testified, the letters were prepared by qualified professionals and are admissible despite being hearsay. Both were prepared contemporaneously to the Tenant reporting mould concerns. This supports their reliability and is consistent with the Tenant’s evidence that he was experiencing ongoing health concerns that he associated with mould exposure. 106. The physician’s letter as evidence of the Tenant’s health vulnerability warrants moderate weight. However, I give reduced weight to the physician’s opinion on causation because it does not specifically link the Tenant’s condition to mould in the unit, and the opinion could not be tested at the hearing. And while I have no reason to doubt the sincerity of the veterinarian’s opinion, its conclusion regarding a causal connection between mould and the dog’s condition is speculative. I therefore assign it limited weight. The competing expert reports 107. A central dispute between the parties concerns the interpretation and consideration to be given to the expert evidence about the mould contamination. 108. Both [name] and K.M. possess qualifications relevant to mould issues. However, by comparison, I find that [name]'s qualifications are significantly more extensive and specialized. This enhances the reliability of the Verify Report. 109. S2S’s reports contain testing results and briefly describe the remediation work undertaken but provide minimal analysis linking their findings to their conclusion that the mould issue had been appropriately investigated and effectively resolved. 110. On the other hand, F.H.’s conclusions are consistent with A.D.'s findings and with aspects of the Landlord's own evidence. Where the expert evidence differs, I prefer the evidence of [name] and so place greater weight on his report. [name] testing results 111. The Tenant relies on the Verify Report. It explains that buildings with no indoor mould source generally have indoor mould levels that are like, or lower than, outdoor levels. It notes that buildings with an indoor mould source may also show mould types that are not commonly found outdoors. 112. The report states that, unlike air sampling which measures airborne spores, surface sampling examines fungi on surfaces; to accurately detect the presence of mould spores and hyphal fragments7, surface testing is more dependable and conclusive. 113. The [name] laboratory results from the surface sampling found the presence of: 7Commonly known to disperse by the thousands into the air if disturbed. • heavy Cladosporium in the FCU and moderate amounts on the kitchen ceiling. • heavy Aspergillus/Penicillium in the FCU and moderate to heavy levels in the kitchen ceiling. 114. [name] says this “implies a moderate to high level of contamination” and “suggests active growth”. Under “Mould Growth Conditions”, he described the FCU and kitchen ceiling vent/duct as areas that have actual mould growth and water damage. He stated that Cladosporium spores are typically found with water damage and that he observed such damage in the FCU and in the kitchen vent. Cladosporium is known to be a cause of severe allergic reactions, and it can trigger asthma. 115. He describes the professional action to be taken: all FCU components must be dismantled, cleaned and disinfected and the pipe insulation must be replaced if it cannot be cleaned; the drywall in the kitchen vent area must be replaced and the ducts cleaned and disinfected. 116. The Landlord's expert S2S agreed that there was abundant mould growth within the FCU. S2S did not confirm mould growth on the kitchen ceiling but admit they did not inspect the vent. Nevertheless, they acknowledged that some spores may have settled on the ceiling surface and recommended precautionary mould cleaning around the vent. 117. I accept the Landlord's evidence that airborne mould levels inside the unit were lower than outdoor levels. However, it is clear from the reports that air sampling and surface sampling measure different things. The relevant concern F.H. raised was that the contamination was present within an HVAC component which circulated air throughout the rental unit. 118. Where the expert opinions diverge, I find the Verify Report to be the more reliable and persuasive. It was more thorough, provided a clear explanation of its findings and explained in great detail the necessary remediation process. It also set out detailed recommendations and explained the basis for those recommendations. In contrast, the S2S Reports did not provide the same level of analysis and did not adequately explain the basis for their preferred treatment of the mould contamination or why alternative remediation measures were not required. The Tenant’s reporting of the mould issue 119. The Landlord maintains that the Board cannot hold them liable for the mould issue because the Tenant did not complain directly to the Landlord about it in 2024 or 2025; he knew work orders were required and neglected to submit any to the Landlord. 120. I agree that timely notice is generally required. However, notice must be assessed in context. I find that the Tenant’s delay in, or lack of, notice is understandable given the Landlord’s documented history of minimizing or denying mould issues, leading to the Tenant’s doubt that a further complaint would be effective. 121. The Tenant reasonably believed that further complaints without evidence would result in similar dismissal of his concerns. He was experiencing his own illness while caring for a seriously ill pet. In his view, arranging independent testing before escalating the issue was done in good faith; he did not want to engage in another prolonged dispute with the Landlord without first securing compelling evidence of mould. He prudently used air purifiers to minimize the impact. In the circumstances, the Tenant’s decision was not unreasonable. 122. With respect to the Landlord’s complaint that the issues were not reported “directly” to them but were communicated through the Tenant’s paralegal, I do not find the distinction relevant. There is no requirement under the Act that a tenant personally provide notice. Notice given through an authorized representative is valid and sufficient where it clearly communicates the issue to the landlord. Here, the notice requirement was satisfied. 123. The LTB’s Guideline 5 states that if a tenant failed to notify the landlord of the disrepair issue before filing a T6 application, “it does not mean that the application must be dismissed … However, failure to advise the landlord will affect the remedies to be ordered, unless the landlord knew about the problem already or should have known”. 124. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord performed an inspection of or maintenance to the FCU prior to August 2024, during which the mould would have been visible. This reduces the reliance to be placed on strict notice requirements. The Tenant’s denial of access to the unit for remediation and failure to mitigate 125. Section 16 of the Act provides that, “When a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses.” 126. The Landlord submits that Board must consider that the Tenant unreasonably interfered with the Landlord’s attempts to complete remediation scheduled for September 10, 2024 by demanding – with little lead time – the use of a guest suite, thereby delaying the work. Their position is that they ultimately agreed to book a guest suite so they could complete the work in a timely manner and avoid breaching subsection 20(1) of the Act. 127. This submission does not assist the Landlord. First, the Landlord has not identified what reasonable steps the Tenant ought to have taken to mitigate. Neither did they demonstrate that they explored other reasonable options to proceed with the remediation sooner. 128. Second, the Tenant’s request for temporary accommodation must be considered in the context of the work being carried out. It was reasonably foreseeable that the Tenant would be unwilling to remain in the unit during mould remediation that required extensive PPE. 129. I am satisfied that the Tenant did not refuse the remediation date in bad faith but merely conditioned it on the Landlord providing a safe interim residence. 130. This is a large, corporate landlord operating a multi-unit residential complex. While the legal obligation under the Act is the same for all landlords, corporate landlords with greater resources and operational capacity may reasonably be expected to anticipate foreseeable issues. They were in a position to proactively to inquire about necessary, alternative accommodation during the remediation rather than waiting for the Tenant’s request. 131. In my view, this forms part of the Landlord’s obligation to carry out repairs and their assertion that they felt compelled to bend to tenant pressure does not alter that obligation. Latent Defect 132. The Landlord argues that the mould in the FCU was a latent defect, and the Landlord could not reasonably have known about it. To succeed, the Landlord must show the alleged defect was hidden and not reasonably discoverable by routine maintenance. 133. The Tenant’s expert [name] and the City Order directly challenge that claim by stating the FCU showed significant rust and other evidence of long-term lack of maintenance. 134. The Landlord led no evidence to show that they performed FCU maintenance prior to August 2024. Had they inspected the FCU earlier, the moisture, rust and mould would have been revealed. Accordingly, I do not find that the issue constitutes a latent defect, but accept it was a condition that developed over time from a lack of routine maintenance. The failure to comply with subsection 20(1) of the Act regarding the mould 135. M.Z. submits that once the Landlord became aware of the Tenant’s complaints, they reasonably responded and completed the work in a manner consistent with Onyskiw. 136. I find that the Landlord responded promptly and diligently to the Tenant’s mould complaints in August 2024 and August 2025. 137. However, the Onyskiw analysis extends beyond reasonableness and timeliness of the response to certain disrepair and includes an assessment of whether the Landlord maintained an adequate preventative HVAC maintenance program, whether regular FCU inspections were scheduled and completed, whether the Landlord ensured water leak issues had been adequately resolved – verifying the unit condition was not favourable to mould growth – and whether the Landlord properly investigated the cause of the mould. 138. The evidence does not establish that the underlying cause of the mould contamination was identified or addressed. The 2024 remediation focused on cleaning the FCU rather than determining why mould had developed. Had the issue been fully resolved in October 2024, it is unlikely that the Landlord’s own expert would have found abundant mould growth in the same FCU less than a year later. Although active growth in the vent was not conclusively established, the area ultimately required remediation. 139. The evidence further shows that the initial remediation did not permanently resolve the problem and the FCU was ultimately replaced. The replacement supports the conclusion that cleaning alone was not an effective long-term solution. 140. The Tenant plausibly questions why the FCU was not assessed and replaced after his initial complaint. Doing so may have avoided the costs of remediation and reduced the impact on the Tenant. 141. I also note the significant disparity between the Tenant’s expert recommendation for Level 3 remediation and the Landlord’s repeated use of Level 1 remediation. In addition, the decision to replace the FCU occurred only after mould was discovered in a common area and at the Tenant’s insistence. The Landlord presented no evidence addressing whether a broader moisture or building-wide problem existed even though the FCU in the unit above the Tenant’s unit had caused water leaks and the common laundry room had mould. 142. The Landlord called two witnesses who could speak to maintenance procedures, but no evidence was led regarding FCU maintenance policies, inspection schedules, servicing history, or post-remediation monitoring. 143. The issue is not that the Landlord failed to respond – they did. The problem is that they failed to establish that they investigated and addressed the source of the contamination, reasonably monitored the unit for recurrence or verified that their efforts were effective. Impact on the Tenant 144. The Tenant described the inconvenience, distress, health issues and trauma he suffered because of the ongoing mould issue. 145. The Tenant’s evidence confirms that he suffers from chronic respiratory issues. The letter from his doctor describes how mould exposure could affect his health as the allergenic nature of the mould heightens the impact on this Tenant. The Tenant was certain his beloved dog was a casualty of the mould contamination, and he described the significant emotional devastation he suffered as a result. 146. F.H. presented as a scientific fact that mould contamination may remain even after S2S’s treatment because dead mould spores and fragments can remain present despite some or many being rendered non-viable. In light of his health issues, the Tenant is not wrong to fear that the presence of mould within a FCU that distributes air through the unit would negatively affect him and his pets on an daily basis. 147. The Tenant was assured by the Landlord’s expert after the first remediation that the unit was “acceptable for occupancy”. A Clearance Certificate was not produced. Neither the Landlord nor their expert provided sufficient explanation of the standard applied in reaching that conclusion or whether the assessment considered the particular circumstances of the Tenant. If the unit environment was acceptable, it was not so for long. 148. The Tenant was also compelled to deal with two remediation processes. The Landlord was dismissive about his legitimate concerns, and it was only after concerted efforts by his paralegal S.D.C. and filing his T6 application that movement began to rectify the disrepair. 149. Accordingly, the application being granted, the Tenant is entitled to a remedy. Remedies 150. The Tenant's Legal Representative S.D.C. points to several LTB mould and ceiling disrepair cases in support of a compensatory remedy. For example, in SWT-96898-16 (Re), 2017 ONLTB 28841 a segmented rent abatement was ordered at 25% and 75% for the relevant periods. In [name] v. [name], 2025 ONLTB 33839 (CanLII), the Board granted a 15% abatement of rent for 6 months.8 151. The Landlord submits that, if a breach is found, a rent abatement should not exceed 5%. 152. Regarding the ceiling disrepair, I find that a 5% abatement is appropriate for the period from September 15, 2023 to October 22, 2024 for a total of $955.97. 153. For the failure to maintain the FCU properly, which facilitated mould contamination, and for the impact of having to live in a mould-contaminated environment, the Tenant is entitled to $8,599.22, representing an abatement of 30% for the following periods: • $4,388.52 – September 3, 2023 to July 31, 2024, 8 See also [name] v. [name], 2024 ONLTB 67936 (CanLII); TNT-82027-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72020 (ON LTB) [15%]; TST- 95268-18 (Re), 2018 CanLII 123260 (ON LTB); [name], 2025 ONLTB 93213 (CanLII); [name] v. Adeoye, 2025 ONLTB 13799 (CanLII), [25%]; [name], 2025 ONLTB 46161 (CanLII) [30%]; SOT-96678-18 (Re), 2018 CanLII 145063 (ON LTB); [name] v. City Blox Property Management, 2025 ONLTB 68271 (CanLII) [40%]; [name] v. [name], 2024 ONLTB 81090 (CanLII); Flowers v. Fahel & Co Property Management, 2025 ONLTB 97413 (CanLII) (similar fact) [50%]; [name], 2025 ONLTB 43736 (CanLII), (not habitable) [90%]. • $556.54 – September 10, 2024 to October 21, 2024 and • $ 3,654.16 – December 1, 2024 to September 2, 2025.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $9,603.19, representing: • $ 9,555.19 as a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If at the time this order is issued the Tenant continues to occupy the rental unit, the Tenant may elect to deduct the amount from rent owing to the Landlord as follows: (a) up to the full amount of monthly rent until the total amount has been credited; (b) any remaining balance after a full rent deduction may be deducted from subsequent rent payments; and (c) once the full amount has been deducted, the Tenant shall resume paying the lawful monthly rent in full.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Tenant sought an adjournment of this application as she was having trouble accessing the portal as of the hearing date and said this was due to a recent cyber attack against her.

For the reasons outlined below, I did not feel the need to grant an adjournment on this basis as adjourning the matter would not perfect the deficiencies with the application. Preliminary issue – Validity of the application
At the onset of the hearing, both the Landlord’s Legal Representative and I raised a preliminary issue with respect to the type of application that was filed – the A1 application.
An A1 application has a very specific purpose: to determine whether the Residential Tenancies ACT, 2006 (the ‘Act’) applies to all or part of a rental unit or residential complex.

In the Tenant’s application, the Tenant is seeking clarification with respect to a rental arrears order that was levied against her and why she was unable to, to my understanding, raise S.82 issues during the rental arrears hearing.

It was explained to the Tenant that the purpose of an A1 application is not to review or appeal a previous order. The purpose of the A1 application is to determine whether the Act applies in certain situations.
As this is the wrong application, the application is dismissed. The Landlord’s requests for costs
The Landlord’s Legal Representative seeks cost against the Tenant in the amount of $200.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that there has been an extensive history of litigation between the parties, and they together have been to the Board on 7 previous occasions. Although the Tenant is self-represented, she has received support with respect to her litigation against the Landlord and, in the opinion of the Landlord’s Representative, she understands the various types of applications and has filed both review and appeal requests. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submits that the Tenant understands the system and this application amounts to an abuse of process as she ought to have known there was no basis for filing an A1.

The Tenant argues that she has represented herself entirely on her own and has not done anything that she hadn’t been advised to do. She stated that she did not remember filing this application and had issues accessing the portal due to a cyber attack. She also stated that she suffers from mental health issues but did not elaborate on how this impacted her ability to file righteous applications. The Tenant did not dispute the claim that various applications have been properly before the board in the past involving the parties.

Pursuant to Guideline 3, the Board does not normally award costs (aside from the applicant’s filing fee in certain circumstances) unless the conduct of the party is unreasonable causing undue expense or delay. Although the guideline is not binding on the Board, I see no reason not to follow it in this instance.

In the matter before me, the Tenant provided no rationale explanation as to why an A1 application was filed in this instance. The explanation was that the Tenant did not remember filing it. If there was a dispute about the extensive litigation between the parties, I may have been more inclined to agree with the Tenant that this may have simply just been an error due to the unfamiliarity with Board proceedings, but I am in agreement with the Landlord’s Legal Representative that the Tenant has an understanding of the various types of applications at the LTB and their intended purposes. I will also note that when filing an application of this type, it is quite clear in what the application is about: “Use this form to apply to have the Board determine whether all or part of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the RTA) applies to the rental unit or residential complex”. This application is not like other applications at the LTB that can have multiple purposes. An A1 has only one purpose and I fail to see how the Tenant could have been confused about its intended purpose when it was filed.
The maximum amount of costs the Board can award per proceedings or application pursuant to the commentary to Rule 23.2 of the Boards Rules of Practice is $700.00.

As per guideline 3, generally, fees relate to time spent at the hearing by a party’s Legal Representative are considered. However, in some cases, further costs for preparation time may be allowed if the unreasonable conduct led to the need for the party’s legal representative to spend additional time preparing for the hearing.

I am satisfied that the Tenant filed a frivolous application that, in my view, should not have been filed in the first place. The Tenant wasted the Board and the Landlord’s time. The Landlord incurred undue expense in attending the hearing for this application. I will also note however, that the Landlord’s Legal Representative did not have to prep for this file as there were no actionable allegations contained within the application – the only action, in my view, the Landlord’s Legal Representative had to take was to attend the hearing.

On the day of the hearing, the matter was called at 10:12am and concluded shortly before 10:30am. As I note that no prep had to be completed for this matter, I will award costs for one hour in the amount of $100.00.

I find that the Tenant’s A1 application is frivolous and was initiated in bad faith. The Divisional Court has commented that the Board has an obligation to use its powers to address what it sees to be an abuse of process under the Act. The mere fact that the Tenant didn’t even remember filing this application is a clear indicator to me that it was initiated in bad faith and resulted in a waste of the Boards time and resources.
As such, I will also order the Tenant to pay $100.00 in costs to the Board for the frivolous application and wasting the Boards time and resources.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $100.00 in costs on or before July 21st, 2026.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before July 21st, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 22nd, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance owing.
The Tenant shall pay costs of $100.00 to the Board on or before July 21st, 2026. July 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $20,342.63.
The Tenant’s evidence included photos, videos, lease agreements and receipts.
The Landlord’s evidence included photos, bills, estimates and travel receipts.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations.

This application is brought pursuant to s.57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was uncontested that the Landlord served an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy for his own personal use, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice and the required compensation was paid to the Tenant. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant [name] [name] (CM) testified that they found an alternative rental only 2 blocks away, the rent was $3,700.00 per month, plus utilities and they lost approximately 1000 sq. ft. of living space and 2 parking spots.

CM testified the new unit[name] is approximately 1/3 the size, her daughter’s bedroom is only 10’ x 10’, they lost 2 parking spots which resulted in parking tickets and they had to either sell or throw away a lot of their belongings because they would not fit in the new unit and due to the higher rent ($2,500.00 to $3,700.00), they were unable to afford storage.

CM testified that the Landlord repeatedly asked them when they were moving out and then he did not even move into the unit after they left. She further testified that throughout the 4- year tenancy they never seen the Landlord, he never did any inspections of the unit throughout the entire time they were in the unit.

CM testified that they drove past the unit multiple times throughout the period of November 2024 and February 2026, when they were told by neighbors that new tenants were moving into the unit, and at no time during this period did the Landlord move into the unit.
CM testified to the photos showing the driveway not cleared of snow, no footprints or tire marks in the snow and a notice issued from bylaw on May 23, 2025, because the lawn was not being maintained.

CM also testified to photos and videos taken during this period, at the Landlord’s mailing address provided on their original lease, showing the Landlord and his family appearing to still be residing at this address in [name].
CM testified that neighbors of the rental unit also told her that the Landlord never moved in and the only activity at the unit was for renovations.
CM testified to the moving costs from MovingHelp and [name] totaling $894.63.

The Tenant’s witness [name] (KG) testified that he lives directly across the street from the rental unit since 2021, and he can see the unit’s front door and driveway from his porch. 17. [name] testified that since the Tenant vacated the unit, he has seen the Landlord 3-4 times, but he never saw the Landlord moving into or out of the unit. 18. KG testified that he works from home, and he sees the unit multiple times everyday, including when he is walking his children to and from school. 19. [name] testified that after the Tenant moved out, he used the unit’s driveway to park in during the summer weekends because no one was living there or using the driveway, but he was unable to use the driveway in the winter because it was never cleared. 20. [name] testified that he had occasionally seen workers coming and going from the unit and then in February 2026 he seen people, not the Landlord, moving into the unit. 21. [name] testified that he was an observant person, that no one moved in after the Tenant moved out until the new tenants moved in February 2026, during that period no one was living in the unit, the house was empty, the grass was almost 12’ high, no garbage was ever put out and no children were ever playing outside. Landlord’s Evidence 22. The Landlord testified that he has served the N12 notice because he and his family were moving into the unit. 23. The Landlord testified that throughout the 4-year tenancy he had never attended the unit and expected when the Tenant moved out, the unit would be in a livable condition but found the unit smelled because the Tenant had pets, there were stains in the carpet and mice in the master bedroom. 24. The Landlord testified that the Tenant moved out of the unit on September 14, 2024, and he and his family moved into the unit on September 23, 2024. 25. The Landlord testified that his belongings were moved to the unit by multiple car trips and some friends with pickup trucks. 26. The Landlord testified that 2-3 days after moving in, his children started getting sick and he contacted a contractor and was provided a quote of $60,000.00 to remove the carpets. 27. The Landlord testified that they started doing renovations on the unit but resided in it while they were being done. He testified that he had lost his job in October, which had a financial impact on getting the renovations completed. 28. The Landlord testified that he and his family resided in the unit until January 7, 2026 and the renovations were completed the first or second week of February. 29. The Landlord testified that the neighbor may not have seen him or his family there because on March 24, 2025, his grandmother passed away and they spent 3-4 days per week at his parents’ helping with the Indian traditions, his family had gone on vacation from June 3 to June 10, 2025, his wife’s father had passed away and she left back to India the first week of August until the second week of October. 30. The Landlord testified to the series of pictures submitted showing pictures of the unit, some with his family included, between February and July 2025. Many of the photos showing the renovations being completed. 31. The Landlord testified to the gas and hydro bills being in his name and for the address of the unit. 32. Under cross-examination the Landlord testified that in September 2025, his daughter was registered and attended school at a school in [name], despite there being 3 schools within walking distance of the rental unit and other than the utility bills, he had not submitted any other evidence such as a driver’s licence to support that he had lived in the unit. He further testified that they had moved out of the unit because his wife had lost her job and after the cost of the renovations they needed to downsize. Analysis 33. Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord issued as N12 notice without a genuine intention to occupy the unit. 34. I find the Tenant’s evidence to be credible and consistent with the neighbor KG. 35. I find the evidence of KG to be credible and his testimony to be believable and consistent. He testified that he lives directly across the street from the unit and had never seen the Landlord move in or out of the unit. 36. I do not find the testimony of the Landlord to be credible. Despite being away from the unit due to a death in the family and a vacation, I do not find it reasonable that a neighbor would not see a family of 4 at the unit at anytime within an entire year. 37. I further do not accept that moving into the unit on September 23, 2024, and being lived in by a family of 4, there would be no gas usage for the month of October and almost no usage for the months of November and December. Additional, hydro bills averaging approximately $40.00 per month are not consistent with a family of 4 residing in the unit. 38. Although the Landlord submitted photos of his family at the unit, the unit did not appear to be lived in and the photos seem to support that the Landlord and his family may have attended the unit to observe and/or participate in the renovations of the unit. 39. For all of these reasons, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time and served the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies 40. The Tenant is requesting an abatement of the rent in the amount of $14,400.00, an administrative fine, rent differential for one year in the amount of $14,400.00, out of pocket expenses for moving and storage in the amount of $5411.79, and general compensation of $9,325.40. Abatement 41. Although the Tenant is requesting an abatement of rent in the amount of $6,400.00, I do not find that remedy to be warranted here. Abatement recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. At the hearing, the Tenant led no evidence that she was prevented from using a portion of the rental unit at any time before she moved out. For this reason, the Tenant is not entitled to an abatement of the rent. Rent Differential 42. With respect to rent differential, the Tenant is now paying $1,200.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. I see no reason not to grant the Tenant the remedy requested in this regard. The Tenant’s new unit is smaller than this unit and no evidence was led that the rent they are now paying is in any way unreasonable. An order will issue requiring the Landlords to pay to the Tenant $14,400.00 for rent differential for a period of one year. Moving and Storage 43. On the evidence before me I find the Tenant has also incurred reasonable out of pocket expenses in the amount of $894.63 for moving. The Tenant submitted the receipt for the moving company and truck. I am satisfied the amount claimed is reasonable and an order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $894.63 for the reasonable out of pocket expenses. General Compensation 44. The Tenant requested compensation in the amount of $9,325.40 for the hardships and emotional distress caused by the Landlord’s service of the N12 notice in bad faith. The Tenants further claim the loss of their property which they had to sell or throw away as their new unit was not large enough to storage their belongings and they could not afford to pay for storage after the significant increase in rent they were now paying. 45. I accept that moving is stressful, however I find that the Tenant’s request for general compensation in the amount of $9,325.40 is excessive. The Tenant did not establish with significant details how the stress of finding and moving to a new unit resulted in significant hardships and emotion distress. Nevertheless, I am satisfied that the Tenant suffered some distress, hardship and loss of property because of the move. I find it reasonable and appropriate to grant the tenant $5,000.00 in general compensation for the hardship, emotional distress and loss of property due to the move. Administrative Fine 46. Pursuant to s. 57(3)3 of the Act, the Tenant is seeking an order for the Landlord to pay an administrative fine to the Board as a result of the Landlord’s breach of s. 57(1)(a) the Act. 47. An administrative fine is a remedy used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter a landlord from breaching the Act in the future, if other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. In this matter, I am satisfied that the remedies provided to the Tenant are sufficient to deter the Landlord from breaching the Act with similar activity in the future. I therefore find that an administrative fine is not required to encourage the Landlord’s compliance with the Act. Accordingly, the Tenant’s request for the Board to issue an administrative fine to the Landlord, pursuant to s. 57(3)3 of the Act, is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $20,342.63. This amount represents: • $14,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from September 14, 2024. • $894.63 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (“ACC”) was held by videoconference on March 9, 2026. Only the Tenants and the Tenants’ Representative, [name], attended the ACC. As of 1:45 p.m. the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, the ACC proceeded with only the Tenants' evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $6,232.40.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the ACC and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The Tenants’ application raises the following issues: a) Microwave b) Stove/Oven c) Toilet d) Flood e) Key Fob

Subsection 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations, clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, as explained below. Microwave

The Tenants testified that the microwave did not work from the time they moved into the rental unit. They sent messages and emails to the Landlord about it and were told the Landlord had a replacement microwave, but the Tenants had to go and pick it up. So the Tenants went and picked up the microwave but it waws too big and was not an appropriate replacement. The Tenants testified that the Landlord never found an appropriate replacement microwave for them and they ended up replacing getting their own smaller replacement microwave because they had been waiting over a year. Stove / Oven

The Tenants testified that 2 months before the flood they messaged the Landlord that the oven and 3 elements on the stove were not working. The Tenants testified that they first notified the Landlord on October 15, 2024, and a technician was not sent for over a month. The Tenants testified that a new stove was not delivered until December 20, 2024. The Tenants testified that they could not cook and were limited to using an air fryer for cooking. Toilet and flood

The Tenants testified that they reported an issue with the toilet in April 2024 and no one was sent to look at it. The Tenants then testified that there was a flood on December 20, 2024, and the Landlord came right away. The Tenants testified that the leaking toilet contributed to the flood. The Tenants testified that they could not stay at the rental unit and when they came back on January 29, 2025, they found their belongings all packed into garbage bags. The Tenants testified that the floor was removed, walls were removed, and they had not been given any notice of the work to be done, but the Landlord was claiming that the Tenants were going to have to pay for the work.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord at some point said that they were not going to do any more repairs and then the Landlord also stopped cooperating with the Tenants insurance to confirm if the rental unit had been repaired so the Tenants insurance stopped covering the Tenants expenses. Key Fob

The Tenants testified that their key fob to gain access to the rental unit worked on January 29, 2025, but then it stopped working on January 30, 2025. When they contacted the Landlord about why the keys were not working the Tenants were not provided an explanation. Analysis

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord has failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair.

I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenants’ complaints regarding the microwave, oven, and key fob in a timely and reasonable manner and therefore breached their obligation under the Act as it pertains to those issues. Specifically, requiring the Tenant to pick up a replacement microwave that is not a suitable size that took almost one year is not a reasonable or timely response. Furthermore, taking a month to arrange for a technician to inspect the stove is also not timely or reasonable response. Additionally, taking an additional month after sending a technician to inspect the stove/oven to finally replace it without explanation is also unreasonable. Finally, no explanation for the key fob not working is also unreasonable.
As such, as it pertains to the stove / oven, microwave, and key fob, I am satisfied the Landlord breached their obligation under section 20 of the Act.

As it pertains to the toilet and the flood. I am satisfied that responding immediately to the flood is reasonable, however the Landlord’s actions after responding to the flood were not reasonable in the situation. The Landlord did not communicate with or repair the damage in a timely manner. As of January 29, 2025, the rental unit still had significant damage with no estimate from the Landlord as to when it would be repaired. Furthermore, it appears that a contributing factor was the toilet which the Landlord was notified about in April 2024 and ignored. Again, not a reasonable response. Finally, it appears that the Landlord had told the Tenants that he did not intend to finish repairs which was unreasonable.
Therefore, I am also satisfied that the Landlord breached their breached their obligation under section 20 of the Act as it pertains to the toilet and the flood. Remedies
The Tenants are seeking a 100% rent abatement for the period of April 2024 through January 2025.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy that is meant to compensate a tenant for the portion of the “bundle of goods and services” that they contracted for under the tenancy agreement but were denied as a result of the landlord’s breach of the Act.

Here, I am not satisfied that a 100% abatement of rent for the requested period is appropriate. First, the Tenants had full functionality of their rental unit for all of April 2024 until December 20, 2024, when the flood occurred. Second, the maintenance breaches, were inconveniences and for the most part may have caused some disruption to their ability to reside in the unit, they were however, not deficiencies such that it caused substantial disruptions, other than the flood.

For the period of December 20, 2024, to January 31, 2025, I do agree that the rental unit was effectively rendered uninhabitable by the flood and ensuing remedial work and therefore the Tenants should be entitled to a 100% rent abatement for that period.

However, for the stove issue I find that a 15% rent abatement for the period of 2 months is more appropriate as it was approximately 8 weeks from the time the Tenants informed the Landlord of the issue to when the replacement stove was delivered. Not having a working stove causes some disruption and inconvenience to the Tenants’ ability to reside in the unit but they were still able to use the rest of the kitchen.

I find that a 5% rent abatement for the unreasonable response to repairing the microwave and the toilet from April 1, 2024, to December 19, 2024, is appropriate as these were minor disruptions to the Tenants. The Tenants found their own replacement microwave, which they should not have had to do so they were not out a microwave, but were inconvenienced in having to find their own replacement and the Landlord never fulfilled their obligation. Furthermore, the Tenants testified that although the toilet was always running, it continued to work. So, another minor inconvenience. As such, 5% is appropriate.
The rent was $2,416.00 per month. The per diem compensation is $79.43. This is calculated as follows: $2,416 x 12 divided by 365.

For the period of December 20, 2024, to January 31, 2025, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants a rent abatement for a total of 43 day, a total of $3,415.49 calculated as follows: $79.43 x 43 = $3,415.49.
For the stove/oven, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants a rent abatement of $724.80. Calculated as $2,416.00 x .15 = $362.40 x 2 = $724.80.

For the period of April 1, 2024, to December 19, 2024, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants a rent abatement of for a total of 263 days, a total of $1,044.11 calculated as follows: $79.43 x .05 = $3.97 x 263 = $1,044.11.
The total rent abatement the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants is $5,184.40.

The Tenants were also seeking an additional $5,000.00 for the cost of damaged furniture, clothes, and other personal items. The Tenants testified that when they attended the rental unit on January 29, 2025, all of their items had been packed into garbage bags. The Tenants testified that they had not packed the items, that someone else had. The Tenants testified that they found people hired by the Landlord in the rental unit and were guessing it was them who packed the items at some point. The Tenants also testified that they were reimbursed by insurance for what they took from the rental unit. However, the Tenants testified that the Landlord stopped cooperating with insurance, so the insurance stopped paying.

While I do believe that the Tenants did lose personal possessions and property as a result of the flood and the way the Landlord or the Landlord’s repair people packed the Tenants belongings. I am not satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenants have established their claim of $5,000.00. The Tenants provided no supporting documentation of replacement receipts, itemized damage logs, or what was not covered by their already paid insurance claim, to support the claim of $5,000.00.

As such, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have established the value of the costs to repair or replace the property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of. In the absence of evidence of the value, only a nominal amount can be awarded with respect to these items, which I fix at $500.00.

Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $500.00 for the costs to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed, or disposed of because the Landlord did not repair or maintain the rental unit or the residential complex.

The Tenants also claimed out of pocket expenses in the amount of $4,6000.00 and testified that they spent $3,000.00 for Airbnb. However, the Tenants did not provide any receipts or other documentary evidence to establish whether or not any portion of this was covered by insurance before their insurance stopped covering their claims. Again, in absence of evidence of the value, only a nominal amount can be awarded, with respect to out-of-pocket expenses. I am satisfied that the Tenants would have had to pay for a hotel or Airbnb as temporary accommodation immediately after the flood and fix this cost at $500.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,232.40. This amount represents: • $5,184.40 for a rent abatement. • $500.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenants have incurred to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions • $500.00 for out-of-pocket expenses. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: On August 27, 2025 , the Tenant filed a T1 application with the LTB claiming the Landlord has charged the Tenant an illegal rent, which the Tenant paid.

In the application, the Tenant’s agent states: On Jan 1 2022 the rent increased to $1315.00 per month. I had a hearing for rent arrears in Jan 2025 wheee [sic] the landlord was claiming I owed $1382 per month based on illegal rent increases. My representative was prepared to argue the monthly rent was $1315 and not $1382 however she decided to ultimately make a consent agreement. At the hearing for the L1 a consent ageement [sic]was made that the rent would be $1350.00 however a review on another matter that was agreed upon determined that a term on a consent agreement is not enforceable if it’s unrelated to the application being heard. In this case tha [sic] application was for an L1 therefore the consent term to change the rent is unenforceable. Also a rent increase from $1315 to $1350 is above the rent increase guideline which would mean the consent agreement is void as the increase violates the ltb rules a nd the rta. Also the original amount the landlord claimed I owed which was $1382 is based on illegal rent increases given to a tenant that he admitted was not in possession of the unit at the time the increase was given. Since the consent order was issued in Jan 2025 I paid paid $175 additional for rent. The current rent should be $1315 per month instead of $1382 as stated on the L1 and instead of the $1350 that was consented on. Furthermore the landlord attempted to get more rent illegally and has caused financial hardship from his actions

The Tenant’s application states that consent order LTB-L-084085-23, issued on January 29, 2026, is not enforceable and therefore the [name] dlord is charging an illegal monthly rent amount. The Tenant believes review order LTB-L-084085-23-RV, issued on April 23, 2025, contains information that the consent order is unenforceable, and this includes the monthly rent of $1,350.00.

Consent order LTB-L-084085-23 includes conditions not related to the original L1 application and are therefore not enforceable. The review order, LTB-L-084085-23-RV, at paragraph 11 states: 11. The Landlord’s L1 application is based on an N4 notice of termination for non - payment of rent. As the conditions at paragraphs 2 and 3 in the order relate to grounds other than non payment of rent and as stipulated at paragraph 4(v) in the order issued on January 29, 2025, I find these conditions are not enforceable pursuant to section 78 of the Act and the Board lacks jurisdiction to terminate the tenancy should these conditions not be met by the Tenant.

The Tenant’s assertion that the consent order is unenforceable in its entirety, based on paragraph 11 above, is without merit. At the hearing held on January 17, 2025, the Tenant’s agent expressly agreed that the monthly rent was $1,350.00, and the consent order was issued on that basis. The review order issued on April 23, 2025 confirms that the issue of the lawful monthly rent was not before the LTB on review and, therefore, was neither reconsidered nor varied. The Tenant’s request for review was limited to a claim relating to bankruptcy. The request for review was ultimately denied.

An oral decision dismissing the application was delivered to the parties at the conclusion of the hearing. For the reasons set out above, and as indicated during the hearing, I find that the Tenant has failed to establish any basis upon which the relief sought in the T1 application could be granted. I am not persuaded that the application has merit. Accordingly, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue – Amended Application

The Tenant’s T6 application was filed on August 30, 2024 and amended on July 28, 2025. The application was amended to remove five of the nine allegations in the application and reduce the requested reme dies. The representatives for the Landlords confirmed they received the amended application at the hearing and were prepared to proceed. Background

The rental unit is a four -bedroom house which has a finished basement containing two of the four bedrooms, bathroom, laundry room and furnace room. The Tenant moved into the rental unit with her two daughters on September 21, 2023 and vacated the unit on August 21, 2024.

The Tenant raised the f ollowing f our issues in the amended application and alleges the Landlords did not act reasonably after being notified of the issues: • Caulking required in basement bathroom – tub/shower • Basement bedroom door does not close properly • Main floor bathroom exhaust fan leaking • Water intrusion in the basement Caulking in basement bathroom

The Tenant testified that on or about September 28, 2023, she emailed the Landlord, [organization] ( ‘B.P.’), to report maintenance issues in the unit. When no action was taken, she contacted B.P. again on November 20, 2023. In that email 1, she included the phrase “Ca lking [sic] in the basement bathroom.” The Tenant recalled that someone attended to inspect the issue however, she stated that the caulking was never repaired. She added that she was unsure whether she followed up with B.P. again regarding the matter.

B.P.’s witness testified that an employee of the Landlord, [name], looked at the caulking in the tub/shower in the basement bathroom and determined that since the tub and shower was a new install, he did not find it necessary to put any more caulking around the area. He could not recall if the Tenant was notified but added no further complaints regarding the issue were received from the Tenant. Basement Bedroom Door

The Tenant testified that she first notifi [name] by [name] on October 2, 2023 regarding an issue with the basement bed room door not closing pro perly. When she did not receive a response, she included the issue on the second email sent on November 20, 2023.

The Tenant further testified that B.P. did send someone to look at the door. She explained that they shaved a portion of the door, but it did not fix the issue. She could not recall if she contacted B.P. again.

B.P.’s witness testified that the Tenant was correct , the door had been planed to remove a portion of the wood so it could close properly. To the best of his knowledge and given that the Tenant did not raise the matter again, he believed the issue had been resolved. Main Bathroom Exhaust Fan

The Tenant testified that she observed water coming from the exhaust fan in the main bathroom. She stated that she contacted B.P. by telephone to report the issue but was told it was not a significant concern and was likely caused by condensation. She further testified that she consulted a friend, a firefighter, who advised her that her concerns were valid and 1 Tenant’s evidence – DOC-6243508 – Page 5 2 Tenant’s evidence – DOC-6243508 – Pages 5 and 6 that action should be taken. The Tenant explained that when she spoke with B.P. again by telephone, it was only after mentioning her conversation with her friend that the matter was taken seriously. She stated that [name], an employee of the Landlord, instructed her to turn off the breaker to the exhaust fan and unplug it, which she did. She reiterated the substance of her telephone communications to B.P. in a follow‑up email.3

The Tenant testified that on October 11, 2023, [name] attended the rental unit to repair the exhaust fan. She stated that the initial repair resulted in a loud, unpleasant noise, prompting B.P. to send someone to return on October 13, 2023 to replace the fan. However, she testified that the noise persisted even after the replacement. The Tenant submitted several photographs and a video4 of the exhaust fan and the repairs as evidence.

B.P.’s witness testified the issue with the e xhaust fan could have b een condensation but after observing how the first repair was done, a second contractor was called who repaired the exhaust fan properly. He stated that no other complaints were received from the Tenant regarding the issue. Water Intrusion in the Basement

The Tenant testified she first contacted the Landlords on October 6, 2023 regarding a water issue in the basement. She stated that when she stepped on the floor, water became visible between the seams of the flooring. The Tenant submitted several photographs5 as evidence, which depict water in multiple areas of the basement, including the laundry room, furnace room, and hallway. She explained that the water issue existed prior to her moving into the unit and that the Landlord had informed her the weeping tile required replacement. The Tenant testified that although the Landlords attempted to address the problem on several occasions, water continued to be present in the basement despite her use of a dehumidifier and industrial fans. She stated she ultimately had no choice but to vacate the unit and believes the issue remains unresolved.

B.P.’s witness testified that, upon receiving the Tenant’s report of water infiltration in the basement, Underground Solutions attended the rental unit to assess the matter. He stated that the weeping tile was blown out on three separate occasions, the sum p pump was replaced, and the sump pipe was rerouted. He further testified that, following the Tenant’s vacating of the premises, CPR Construction was retained to undertake repairs to the foundation. He added that the portion of the basement affected by water was limited in scope and was situated primarily within non ‑habitable areas, including the furnace room and laundry room.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 3 Tenant’s evidence – DOC-6243508 – Page 7 4 Tenant’s evidence – DOC-6243508 – Pages 8 to 10 5 Tenant’s evidence – DOC-6243508 – Pages 11 to 15 Analysis and Legislation

This application is being brought pursuant to section 20 (1) of the Act which states that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Landlords responded promptly and reasonably to the concerns raised by the Tenant. The evidence establishes that, once notified of the issues, the Landlords took steps to arrange for repairs and remediation. Although the Tenant questioned th e adequacy and effectiveness of those efforts, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlords acted in a manner that was both timely and reasonable in the circumstances. While the water issue in the basement remained unresolved at the time the Tenant vacated the premises, I am further satisfied that the Landlords undertook reasonable measures to mitigate the impact of the issue on the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord s did not fail to meet the Landlord s’ obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards
Accordingly, the T6 application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________
