issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant, [name] (‘MB’) testified that he began noticing bedbugs in his rental unit on or about November 10, 2022. MB testified that between November 10, 2022 and September 14, 2023, the Landlord did not adequately treat the rental unit for bedbugs. MB testified that while he informed the Landlord of bedbugs on several occasions and the Landlord treated the unit, the bedbugs were not eliminated until the Tenants engaged their own pest control company to perform a heat treatment of the rental unit in September 2023.

MB testified that he complained of bedbugs on November 10, 2022, November 16 2022, January 4, 2023, June 23, 2023, June 28, 2023, July 23, 2023, August 21, 2023, August 22, 2023, August 23, 2023, August 25, 2023, August 28, 2023, September 3, 2023, September 4, 2023, September 5, 2023, September 6, 2023, and September 7, 2023. MB testified that he subsequently hired Just Bugs Inc to perform a heat treatment at the rental unit on September 14, 2023, which he alleges resolved the bedbug issue.

MB also testified that the Landlord had treated the rental unit on November 15, 2022, November 29, 2022, December 19, 2022, January 16, 2023, July 4, 2023, July 21, 2023, August 30, 2023, and September 11, 2023.

MB testified that an inspection was performed on September 26, 2023 and confirmed that there were no signs of active bedbugs in the rental unit. The Tenants submit that based on an email dated September 21, 2023 from [name] (‘AS’), a pest control technician from Just Bugs, the unit was effectively treated via the heat treatment done by Just [name] on September 14, 2023. The Tenants also rely upon a statement made by AS in his September 21, 2023 email stating that bedbugs “were present before the heat treatment. These are photos to prove it your landlord will see from all the fecal marks around your apartment.”

The Tenants’ Witness, [name] (‘EB’) testified that the residential complex previously had a bad bedbug unit and that her unit had been treated for bedbugs in August 2022. However, the mere presence of bedbugs in 2022 does not establish the Landlord’s failure to adequately treat the rental unit. [name]’s testimony was largely unrelated to the issue alleged in this application as it was related to a pest control issue in the residential complex which was not claimed in the Tenants’ application which focused primarily on a pest control issue within the Tenants’ rental unit.

The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (‘RC’), who is the Landlord’s pest control consultant, testified that the Landlord’s standard practice is to perform chemical spray treatments. RC testified about the Landlord’s process for performing spray treatments. RC testified that heat treatments often do not prevent future proliferation of bedbugs as chemical treatments do.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘MM’) testified that the Landlord has an arrangement for monthly pest control within the common areas of the residential complex. MM confirmed that the Landlord had engaged [name] to perform treatment on the rental unit on the dates alleged by the Tenants above.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case it was undisputed that the Landlord had engaged a professional pest control company to perform chemical spray treatments of the rental unit within two weeks of each complaint, often within a few days of the Tenants’ reports of pest control issues. The unit was professionally treated each time the Tenants complained of bedbugs. As a result, I was not satisfied that the Tenants have proven that the Landlord did not respond reasonably to the Tenants’ requests for treatment. Rather, it appears the Landlord acted with reasonable due diligence to address the bedbugs in a timely manner each time the Tenants reported bedbugs in the rental unit.

With regards to whether the unit was effectively treated by the Landlord’s spray treatment on September 11, 2023 or the Tenants’ subsequent heat treatment, I find the Landlord’s witness testimony to hold more weight than the email provided by the Tenants which could not be cross-examined.

While the email from AS states that bedbugs were present based on fecal material found in the unit, even if I were to accept this hearsay evidence, I am not satisfied that the mere presence of bedbug fecal matter was sufficient to show that the Landlord had not effectively treated the unit for bedbugs on September 11, 2023. It was not clear whether there was any live activity or whether the fecal matter pre-existed the Landlord’s September 11, 2023 treatment and AS was not present to testify about any presence of live bedbugs.

Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the Tenants have met the burden of proof to demonstrate that the Landlord has breached its maintenance obligations. As a result, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application); and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application).
reasons: The Tenant’s Legal Representative sought to amend the T2/T6 application to add in more details in the application. The Tenant’s Legal Representative also sought to amend the remedies requested in both applications: the T2 application for rent differential, storage and moving expenses, and other expenses concerning an air quality test, and the T6 application for the amount requested for damaged property, out of pocket expenses, and request court fees.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative indicates she served the amended application to the Landlord by placing them in a secure drop box at the Landlord’s place of work on April 26, 2026. The Tenant’s Legal Representative filed a certificate of service with the Board.
The Landlord says he never got the amended applications. However, the Landlord says he had an opportunity to review the amended application on the Portal and is ready to proceed with the hearing.

I am satisfied the Tenant’s Legal Representative complied with Rule 15 of the LTB Rules and Procedures. As such, the amendment is granted. It is appropriate and necessary, not prejudicial to the Tenant, and was filed in a timely manner. T2/T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The parties agree that the Tenant moved in on March 1, 2025 and that the Tenant moved out on or about December 1, 2025. The rental unit is a bungalow, and the Tenant rents it in its entirety.

The T6 application alleges the Landlord failed to repair or maintain the rental unit, and that it has not complied with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards and because of that, the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful enjoyment of the rental unit (T2 application). Both allegations contained the same attached summary and are summarized as follows: 1. That prior to her tenancy which began on March 1, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord there was mould beneath the shower and around two basement windows, and that the Landlord did not resolve these issues in a timely manner which lead to the Tenant experiencing health issues and moving out because of it. Also, that on July 13, 2025, water was entering the basement window and the Landlord failed to do anything about it.
The Tenant requested various remedies including rent abatement, damaged property, out of pocket expenses, court costs, rent differential, and moving and storage costs. Testimony of the Tenant

The Tenant testified that she first viewed the rental unit on or about January 31, 2025 and observed black spotting which she believed to be mould in the basement ceiling, which was directly underneath the main floor bathroom, as well as inadequate caulking around the main floor shower area. The Landlord told her that there was a prior water issue, but that it was remedied.

The Tenant moved in on March 1, 2025 and the mould was cleaned by the Landlord, and she did not note any mould upon move in. However, the Tenant stated that the mould issue reappeared. The Tenant did not offer any further testimony as to when the mould issue reappeared, where, and when.

On July 13, 2025, the Tenant observed water leaking in one of the basement windows. The Tenant says she notified the Landlord the same day, and the following day the Landlord’s janitor attended the rental unit and caulked around the windows. The Tenant says that the Landlord did not repair the issue properly because it subsequently rained and the leaking persisted. The Tenant says she told the Landlord about the subsequent leaking but does not remember when that was. The Tenant says the Landlord did nothing about her subsequent complaint.

The Tenant says that she was experiencing health problems in that she was having difficulty breathing and that she took it upon herself to hire [name], who specialize in mould and air quality testing, to conduct and air quality test. This test was conducted on August 26, 2025.

The Tenant says that the sample obtained on the basement ceiling for moisture was noted at a level that was three times superior to the exterior samples which meant that the air quality was contaminated. A copy of the report was submitted as evidence.
The Tenant believes that there was an issue with the main floor bathroom shower, that the shower caulking was inadequate and water would leak into the basement ceiling causing a mould issue.

The Tenant says that she called the Property Enforcement Standard Officer shortly after she received the air quality report to report her concerns. The Tenant says she did not provide the Landlord with a copy of the air quality report, nor did she tell the Landlord about the ongoing issues and decided to notify the municipality about them instead.

The Tenant says that she had to throw out several personal items due to the mould and moisture issues. The Tenant did not provide into evidence any evidence, such as pictures, to demonstrate her items were damaged due to mould.

The Tenant says that she had to attend the hospital due to the mould issue because she was having difficulty breathing. The Tenant provided into evidence a medical report of two dates where she attended the hospital on September 4, 2025 and 23, 2025.

The Tenant says that because of the mould and moisture issues, she needed to vacate her rental unit and began to look for a new rental unit on or about September 17, 2025. The Tenant says that since she moved out of the rental unit, she no longer has any health issues. Testimony of Rheal Pilon

The Tenant summonsed [name] who is the Property Standard Enforcement Officer for the City of Hawkesbury. [name] says that he received a complaint about the rental unit on September 8, 2025 regarding mould and moisture issues. [name] attended the rental unit on September 11, 2025 and noted violations in contravention of the municipal bylaw. This report was submitted into evidence. The report (summarized) required the Landlord to remove mould from the basement ceiling which [name] described as a black spot 5-6 inches in size, to repair the ventilation system so that it is clean and sanitary, to inspect the bathroom shower area for water accumulation, and to inspect the air quality in the rental unit. 20. [name] testified that he returned to the rental unit with ESCO, who are a disaster cleanup company, on October 17, 2025 to inspect the work they did. ESCO was hired by the Landlord once the Landlord became aware of potential issues within the rental unit. During that inspection, amongst other things, the rear of the shower was inspected and there was no trace of water leaks or evidence of mould or water damage. The black spot was cleaned by ESCO and was now lighter in colour. [name] stated that the Landlord investigated all the issues in the order in a timely manner and that the file was closed on December 16, 2025. Landlord’s Evidence 21. The Landlord testified that the rental unit is a new build in 2017. The Landlord says that there was water damage from the previous tenant with regards to the shower, but that that issue was rectified at the time it occurred. The Landlord does not deny there was a small area of black-like substance that remained on the basement ceiling prior to the Tenant moving in, but that the Landlord cleaned it prior to the Tenant taking possession of the rental unit. 22. With regards to the water leaking in the Tenant’s basement, the Landlord says the Tenant contacted him on July 13, 2025, and that his janitor attended the following day to caulk the window and fix the issue. The Landlord says that he never heard about any leaking since that incident and thought the issue was resolved. 23. The Landlord says that the Tenant did not pay rent that was due on August 1, 2025 and that shortly thereafter, served the Tenant with an N4 Notice of Termination (‘N4 Notice’) for unpaid rent, and the Landlord says once he served her with the N4 Notice, is when all the issues started with the complaints of the mould and moisture commenced. The Landlord subsequently filed an application with the Board and the matter was heard on November 20, 2025 where an eviction order was issued as well as rent arrears owing to the Landlord. 24. The Landlord says that the Tenant never told him about any mould or moisture issue until out of the blue she provided him with a copy of the air quality control test sometime after August 29, 2025, as well as being notified that there was a complaint filed to the Property Standard Officer who subsequently attended the rental unit to conduct an inspection. 25. At that point, the Landlord hired ESCO as soon as he got the report, and ESCO attended the rental unit on September 18, 2025 to clean and disinfect the rental unit and provided recommendations to the Landlord. The Landlord says that he did all the recommendations as suggested by ESCO. The ESCO report was submitted into evidence. The Landlord feels that the moisture issue was caused by the Tenant who failed to properly clean and maintain the rental unit. 26. The Landlord submits that [name] confirmed there was no water leaks, mould, or moisture issues and that they opened the wall behind the shower and none were observed. 27. The Landlord says that he completed all the requirements in a timely manner as required by the report from [name]. 28. The Landlord says that the Tenant never complained to him about any health related issues such as breathing difficulties due to the alleged mould and moisture issue. The Landlord says the Tenant spoke to him about other personal and sensitive medical issues that had nothing to do with breathing issues. 29. The Landlord says that he conducted his own air quality control test by hiring Lakeside Green Environmental Consulting on January 22, 2026 and that there were no mould issues identified in the report. This report was submitted into evidence. Analysis 30. This application is bought under s. 64(1) and s. 20 of the Act. Section 64(1) of the Act states: A landlord may give a tenant notice of termination of the tenancy if the conduct of the tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant is such that it substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex for all usual purposes by the landlord or another tenant or substantially interferes with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the landlord or another tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 64 (1) 31. Section 20 of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1) 32. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. 33. With regards to the leaking basement window issue, the evidence before me is that the Tenant reported the problem to the Landlord on July 13, 2025 and that the Landlord’s janitor attended the following day to repair the issue. The Tenant says that the issue was not resolved and that subsequent leaking occurred, that she told the Landlord about it, but the Landlord did not do anything about it. The Landlord denies ever receiving any further complaints about subsequent leaking in the basement window. 34. There is no evidence in front of me, such as an email or text message, to establish that the Landlord failed to respond to a subsequent maintenance request from the Tenant. A landlord is not generally liable for any disrepair they had no knowledge of and could not reasonably have known about. (see: the LTB Interpretation Guideline #5 Breach of [name]; [name] (1975), 8 O.R. (2d) 249 (C.A.); and s. 16 of the Act.). As such, this claim is dismissed. 35. The same can be said about the issue with mould and moisture. The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord prior to moving in that there was some mould in the rental unit, and that upon move in the mould was no longer present. The Tenant says that the mould reappeared but did not provide testimony as to when she noticed the mould issue again. Through the Tenant’s own testimony, she did not tell the Landlord about the mould and moisture issues. The Landlord was unaware until the Landlord became aware of the air quality report of the Tenant’s and when the Property Standard Bylaw Officer was called by the Tenant about it. 36. Although I recognize that the report as submitted by [name] did contain some issues to be investigated or remedied, in the decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances. 37. Once the Landlord was made aware of the report from the Property Standard Officer, the Landlord took all reasonable steps to inspect and rectify the issues identified in the report. [name] indicated that the Landlord completed all the requirements in the order in a timely manner. Because of this, and for the reasons stated above, the Tenant’s claims are dismissed. 38. The Tenant claims that she became sick due to the mould and moisture and vacated the rental unit because of it. However, there was no medical evidence to support the Tenant’s breathing issues were directly caused by mould in the rental unit. There is also no evidence, such as pictures, to support that the Tenant’s contents were damaged due to the mould. It appears based on the evidence provided, and on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant vacated because she was in arrears of rent as she failed to pay rent from August 2025 to the date she vacated which was December 1, 2025. 39. Having failed to meet her burden of proof, the Tenant is not entitled to any remedies. 40. As such, the application is dismissed. 41. Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations. 42. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name]) (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-072708-24 issued on March 12, 2026. The adjudicative case conference was held March 10, 2026. As of 9:30 a.m., the Tenant was not present nor represented. On April 13, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On April 14, 2026, interim order LTB-T-072708-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on March 12, 2026. This request to review was heard by videoconference on June 23, 2026. The Landlord, [name], and the Tenant attended the review.
reasons: The Tenant requested a review of order LTB-T-072708-24 issued on March 12, 2026, because the Tenant was not reasonably able to participate at the adjudicative case conference held on March 10, 2026.

In support of this submission, the Tenant provided medical documentation which showed that on March 10, 2026, between 2:00-3:00 a.m., the Tenant was taken to the hospital. Of note, the Tenant was living in British Columbia. Thus, there was a three-hour time difference between the provinces on that date. The Tenant states that he was not discharged until about 10:00 a.m. local time as they had to wait for cardiology before being discharged. The Tenant’s phone was not charged because of the long visit at the hospital. By the time it was charged, the adjudicative case conference, which was held at 9:30 a.m. EST, was over.
The Landlord submits that this is typical behaviour from the Tenant who “always has an excuse.”

The phrase “not reasonably able to participate” has been considered by the Divisional Court on several occasions. In King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., [2008] O.J. No. 4697 (Ont. [name]. Ct.) the tenant argued she did not attend the hearing because she misread the Notice of Hearing and got the dates mixed up. The Divisional Court ruled the Board should have granted her request to review on the grounds of not reasonably able to participate because the evidence suggested that the tenant genuinely intended all along to participate and otherwise, she would be denied the right to be heard. The Court stated: “being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less.”

In Sutherland v. [name], [2008] O.J. No. 5763 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) the tenant had dialled into the telephone hearing five minutes late and was not able to join the hearing. The Court held the tenant was not reasonably able to participate.

Similarly, in Decosse v. Isles of Innisfree Non Profit Homes, [2012] O.J. No. 964 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) the tenant attended multiple hearing dates but on the final day arrived 20 minutes late and was not able to join the hearing. Again, the Court found they were not reasonably able to participate. In all of these cases there was some evidence that the individual had made attempts to participate.

In my view, the Tenant intended to participate but after being released from the hospital, and by the time they were able to get home and have their phone functioning, the adjudicative case conference was over. There is documentary evidence to support the Tenant was being seen by emergency physicians in the early hours of the date of the adjudicative case conference. Given the Court’s guidance in King-Winton, Sutherland, and Decosse, and the principles of natural justice, I am satisfied that the Tenant intended to participate in the March 3, 2026, adjudicative case conference.
Therefore, I granted the Tenant’s request. The matter was heard de novo. [name]

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord unlawfully entered the rental unit without notice, failed to respond appropriately to a request by the Tenant to sublet or assign the Tenant’s lease, failed to provide appropriate notice of entry for pest control treatment, and misrepresented an agreement to terminate the tenancy. 11. For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord unlawfully entered the rental unit without notice. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $250.00. 12. However, I do not find that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, the remaining allegations which are dismissed. Unlawful Entry 13. The Tenant states that on August 27, 2024, they were sleeping in their bedroom at about 7:30 p.m. They say that even though they had locked the door, they were awoken by the Landlord yelling “Hello” in the apartment. They had to scramble to make themselves presentable. When they exited their room, the Landlord was there. The Tenant alleges the Landlord then began to berate them for not having paid the rent, refused to leave even after being asked, threatened to cut off the power to the rental unit, and said he would make the Tenant’s life a “living hell.” 14. The Landlord agrees that he attended the rental unit on August 27, 2024. The Landlord was already in the residential complex. He says he knocked on the door of the rental unit, but no one answered. Then he tried the door which he says was not locked. He opened the door, and yelled inside, but remained in the vestibule. 15. The Landlord says he attended the rental unit out of concern for the Tenant’s well-being. He says he had not seen the Tenant for a long time, and because significant rental arrears had amassed, he decided to knock on the door. He says he had a tenant die in a fire in a rental unit in the past. Further, the Tenant needed to remove their vehicle from the parking area because this space was reserved for another tenant. He also said he did not threaten or berate the Tenant during the visit. 16. Section 26 of the Act speaks to entry without notice in situations where there is an emergency or where the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. 17. The first question I must determine is whether the Tenant consented to the entry at the time of entry. There is no evidence to support they did. Rather, the Tenant’s uncontested evidence was that they asked the Landlord to leave several times. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant did not consent to the entry. 18. There is conflicting testimony from both parties pertaining to whether the Landlord was physically inside the rental unit. The Tenant states that the Landlord was in an area which was located within a locked portion of the rental unit under the Tenant’s control. The Landlord states he remained in the vestibule and did not go inside the Tenant’s rental unit. 19. Whether or not the Landlord remained in the vestibule, I find that opening the door constitutes entry. The Landlord knocked on the door; the Tenant did not respond, so the Landlord opened the door. In my view, a tenant has a reasonable expectation to privacy when their door is closed, locked or not, particularly when there was no notice given to them in advance. The parties disagree about whether the door was locked or not. However, I do not find that to be germane to my analysis. 20. The next question I must determine is whether there was an emergency which warranted the entry. I am not of the view there was. The Landlord’s prior experience with a tenant perishing in a fire does not constitute an emergency, nor does the Tenant failing to answer the door, or because the Tenant had not been seen in a long time. In my view, an emergency warranting an entry might be reports of flooding or other serious mechanical issues warranting an immediate unit inspection. 21. Rather, I find the Landlord’s attendance was precipitated because of rental arrears and because the Tenant needed to arrange to move their vehicle. Nothing in the Landlord’s evidence suggests the Landlord even asked about the Tenant’s well-being. In my view, if the Landlord possessed a genuine concern for the Tenant’s well-being, then it does not accord he did not even ask the Tenant this. 22. I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and unlawfully entered the rental unit on August 27, 2024. 23. Although not binding upon me, I find the order of Vice-Chair [name] to be helpful in considering my analysis to the situation before me1: “In Wrona the Divisional Court ordered the landlord to pay to the tenant $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry. In Wrona the application before the Board involved a large non-profit landlord and a vulnerable tenant. It was a second application by the tenant about the same complaint – notices of entry that had a very broad range of entry for a scheduled inspection. The first application resulted in an order telling the landlord that a range of entry of more than six hours made its notice of entry invalid. But the landlord did not alter its practice despite the prior order. The second application involved an incident where the tenant received a notice of entry the same as the first one. I believe it is fair to say that the remedy in Wrona took into account the landlord’s refusal to change its illegal practice despite a prior finding that it was illegal. That is not the situation here.” 24. Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization]2 pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 25. There is no evidence to support that this was a persistent issue which had been adjudicated before the Board on a prior occasion such as found in Wrona above. However, the Tenant reports feeling anxious having been woken up and was traumatized by this incident. 1 Bosch v Cerino, 2025 ONLTB 62674 (CanLII), par.48 2 Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) 27. By way of remedy, the Tenant seeks an abatement. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 28. When I consider the impact, this had on the Tenant and given my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find a lump sum abatement of $250.00 is warranted. The Tenant was sleeping and undressed only to be awoken by someone calling into their rental unit. An order shall issue. Failing to [name] to [name] to Amend Lease 29. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with his tenancy because he failed to respond to his request to sublet or assign his lease. However, I find that what the Tenant requested was not to sublet or assignment the lease. Rather, the Tenant sought to add another name to the lease as they wished to have a roommate to offset the rent payments. They explain that he asked this second person be added to the lease several times over an 11-month period. However, the Landlord did not reply. 30. The Landlord agreed that he did not respond to the Tenant’s e-mail, stating that he did not care who lived in the rental unit and that there was nothing preventing the Tenant from having a roommate. He was not obliged to form a new lease agreement with a new party which constitutes a material change to the terms of the lease. 31. The Landlord is correct. There is no provision in the Act which prohibits a tenant from having a roommate and landlords are not permitted to increase the rent because a tenant has a roommate. Unlike the requirements found for assignment or subletting, where there are statutorily required responses from a landlord, there is no such requirement for the purposes of having a roommate. Further, there is no requirement for the Landlord to agree to a material change in a lease which in effect is beginning a new lease with new parties to the lease agreement. 32. I understand the Tenant wished to have a roommate to offset the rent payments. However, there was nothing in the Act preventing the Tenant from taking on a roommate. As such, I do not find that the Tenant held a reasonable expectation that the Landlord ought to respond. No order shall issue. Parking Arrangements 33. The Tenant says that the Landlord caused unnecessary issues by failing to address parking issues at the rental complex. The only tenant in the building who had parking was the “middle floor” tenant. Where the middle floor tenant did not require the parking space, the Tenant had a private agreement with them to use the spot. This arrangement worked fine until the middle floor tenants moved out and new tenants moved in, and the new tenants did want to use the parking space. 34. However, the Tenant was in the middle of conducting an in-depth repair to his vehicle and had dismantled it. The Landlord then demanded that the Tenant move the vehicle. They say in order to exit their rental unit, they had to climb through the vehicle for a period of about 4-6 weeks until it was in a sufficient enough state that they could push the vehicle on to the road. The Tenant contends that this should not have happened had the Landlord properly assigned parking spaces and dealt with the issue. 35. The Landlord states that he did ask the tenants to sort the problem of parking out themselves because only the middle floor tenants were entitled to a parking space as part of their lease. But if those tenants did not need their spot, he did not mind if they let another tenant use it but left it to the parties to sort out. New tenants took over the middle floor unit tenancy, and they wanted to have the use of the parking space. The Landlord then told the Tenant he needed to move his vehicle and says he was being pressured by the new tenants to access the space which belonged to them under their lease. 36. It is not clear to me why the Tenant believes that the Landlord substantially interfered with their tenancy in this regard. The Tenant made a private agreement with the middle floor tenants to use their parking space. It was unfortunate timing that when they moved out, the Tenant had just dismantled their vehicle. However, the Landlord had an obligation to the middle floor tenants to provide the parking space that they were not only lawfully entitled to as a term of their lease but were paying for. 37. I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes because the Landlord allowed tenants to privately loan out their parking space. The Tenant had no expectation to occupy a parking space that was not included as a term of their lease and for which they did not pay. Further, there is no evidence the Landlord placed the Tenant’s vehicle in such a way that blocked the Tenant’s exit from his rental unit. No order shall issue. Letter for Parking 38. The Tenant also submits that the Landlord dragged his heals in providing a letter to them which would outline that parking was not included in their rental agreement. The Tenant says it took a month to get the letter they requested. 39. The Landlord denies this saying it took only one week to provide the requested letter. He explained that he contacted the City about the Tenant’s request and was told the Tenant simply needed to make an application for a street parking permit. The Tenant clarified that when they did this, the City requested verification in the form of a letter from the Landlord. The Tenant reports that they did not get any tickets or fines as a result of not having the parking permit in the period of time between requesting the documentation and submitting this to the City. 40. The plain and ordinary meaning of substantial is of considerable importance, size, or worth. Given the Tenant did not receive a fine or penalty because they did not have the permit while they waited for the Landlord to provide the requested documentation, I am not of the view that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. In my view, the delay in providing the requested document did not result in an interference which rises to the level of considerable importance, size, or worth. No order shall issue. Pest Control Attendance 41. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord sent pest control to the rental unit on August 26, 2024, without first having provided 24-hour notice. The Tenant states that he did allow the pest control technician to treat the rental unit. 42. As I noted earlier, s.26 states that entry can be made without notice if the Tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. The Tenant’s own evidence was that he consented to pest control entering the unit to conduct pest control treatment. As such, the Landlord is not in breach of s.26 of the Act. No order shall issue. Misrepresentation of Agreement to Vacate 43. The Tenant says that the Landlord, when he attended on August 27, 2024, agreed that if the Tenant paid him $6,000.00, they would be allowed to stay in the rental unit. Although it is not entirely clear to me how much the arrears were at that time, I understand that the rent arrears were greater than $6,000.00. The Tenant did pay the Landlord the requested funds. 44. The Tenant submitted into evidence an e-mail, dated October 9, 2024, in which the Landlord states he was willing to “…accept your previous payment as full payment up until October 31, 2024, can you resume regular rent payments from Nov. 1, 2024?” However, the Tenant states that despite this agreement, the Landlord did not honour this agreement and on October 22, 2024, served the Tenant with an N4 notice of termination for non-payment of rent. 45. The question before me is whether on August 27, 2024, the parties agreed that the Landlord would waive a portion of the rental arrears due and owing to the Landlord. 46. Although not binding on me, I find the follow excerpt3 helpful in the analysis of an agreement in pars. 26 and 27, in-part: “26. A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more persons for a particular purpose. In order to be valid, a contract requires an offer, an acceptance of that offer and consideration…. 3 Shantiaee v [name], 2025 ONLTB 88643 27. An offer must be clear and unequivocal and must occur before a specified time limit on the offer expires. The acceptance must be clear, unequivocal, unconditional, and made by the person to whom the offer is intended….” 47. As for whether there was an agreement to waive the collection of the unpaid rent, I do not find that there was. Rather, I find it was a gratuitous offer to waive a portion of rent. It is not clear to me whether there was acceptance as the e-mail in evidence is framed as a question, and there was no reply confirming acceptance. More importantly, though, is that there was no evidence that there was any consideration that flowed between the parties. 48. Consideration is defined as the “…mutual exchange of promises or obligations of the parties to a contract.”4 There was no evidence before me that the parties exchanged any mutual exchange of promises or obligations. The e-mail does refer to the Tenant continuing to pay ongoing rent as of November 1, 2024. However, I do not find this amounts to consideration, because the Tenant was already statutorily obligated to pay the rent. 49. As such, I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, or otherwise harassed or interfered with the Tenant, because the Landlord issued the Tenant an N4 notice of termination for non-payment of rent. The Landlord is statutorily entitled to collect rent in exchange for providing an exchange of good and services, and I am not persuaded that the parties formed a legal contract in which the Landlord agreed to waive the collection of a portion of the rent arrears. 50. The Tenant also seeks other remedies, for example, moving costs, rent differential, and an administrative fine, and orders which, as the tenancy has ended, are now moot. Pertaining to the remedies sought for moving costs, etc., I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because they were harassed or their tenancy was substantially interfered with to the extent that the Tenant left the rental unit. 51. Rather, based on the facts before me, I find it is more likely than not that the Tenant vacated the rental unit after the Landlord issued the N4 notice of termination (‘N4’). The Tenant was served with an N4 notice of termination on October 22, 2024, with the earliest termination date which would have been November 5, 2024. It is not entirely clear the precise date the tenancy ended, but the Tenant’s evidence shows they entered into a new lease overseas on November 1, 2024. 52. When I consider the Board’s Guideline #16 on Administrative Fines, I am not satisfied an administrative fine is warranted in the circumstances. The purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act generally reserved for situations where a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act. In my view, although an unlawful entry is a serious breach of the Act, there was no evidence that this was an ongoing issue and at best there was conflicting evidence about the Landlord’s behaviour during the entry. As such, I am not satisfied that there is sufficient evidence of the Landlord’s behaviour which would give rise to an administrative fine in these circumstances. 4 https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/consideration 53. Lastly, the Tenant brought forward issues regarding a lack of maintenance to the rental unit, that the rental unit was unfit for habitation, and that the Landlord corresponded with the Tenant in an unprofessional, rude manner. However, these allegations were not stated in the Tenant’s T2 application nor was the application amended. I am of the view it is prejudicial to allow the Tenant to raise issues that were not stated within the application because the Landlord cannot be expected to know the case to be met. Therefore, these allegations have not been addressed in this order. 54. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $3,584.52.
The second named tenant, [name], wa s referenced in the application but not listed as an applicant. The application is amended to include both affected Tenants.

The Tenants viewed a two-bedroom unit, paid a rent deposit of $1,300.00 to the Landlord AD. When they went to move into the unit as planned on August 1, 2025, there was another group of people moving in. The Landlords offered the Tenants this rental unit instead while the problems at the first unit were corrected. They were initially told there was a problem with bed bugs that would be corrected by September 1. Although the Tenants had agreed to rent a 2-bedroom unit, they had only 1 bedroom in this unit. Despite the reduced size of the new unit, the Tenants still paid the initially agreed upon amount of $1,300.00 for the month of August.

On August 30, 2025, the Landlord SG told the Tenants he was the owner of the house, and they needed to move out on September 1, 2025. On the same day, the Landlord AD threatened that the Tenants would have a car accident and suffer in the house. As a result of the threats from the Landlords, the Tenants got temporary accommodations and did not remain in the house after September 4, 2025. Between September 1, 2025 and September 4, 2025, the Landlords changed the lock to the rental unit and prevented the Tenants from collecting some of their furniture and possessions.
Therefore, I find that t he Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants. Remedies

The unit the Tenants were provided with was appr oximately half of the size of what they agreed to rent. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of 50%, of $650.00, is reasonable for the month of August. The Landlords did not return the rent deposit, despite insisting that the Tenants move out. The Tenants are entitled to the return of the unused portion of the rent deposit. The daily rent for the 4 days in September, reduced by the 50% abatement, is $85.48. Therefore, the unused portion of the rent deposit which shall be returned to the Tenants is $1,214.52. The total the Tenants are entitled to for a rent abatement and the return of the unused portion of the rent deposit is $1,864.52.

The Tenants have out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $1,590.00 because of the Landlord's actions. The Landlord must pay the Tenant this amount. A receipt for $1,150.00 for temporary accommodations was provided and the Tenants described items which they were unable to retrieve from the rental unit and their approximate cost at $440.00. Although no documentation was provided to support the replacement cost of the lost items, I am satisfied that the amount of $440.00 is less than the total actual cost to replace multiple pieces of furniture, a mattress, a tv, clothes, and shoes, so the amount is not unreasonable.
The Tenants incurred moving costs of $130.00, comprised of $110.00 to rent a UHaul truck and $20 for gas. I am satisfied that this amount is reasonable to relocate from one unit to another.

The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlords pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”
In the present case, as the Tenants have been awarded a substantial monetary remedy, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the [name] ords shall pay the Tenants is $3,584.52. This amount represents:  $1,864.52 for a rent abatement and return of the unused portion of the rent deposit.  $130.00 for the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred  $1,5900.00 for the estimated reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 17, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 17, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected money illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-075658-25 issued on March 26, 2026. On April 22, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On April 30, 2026, interim order LTB-T-075658-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on March 26, 2026.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that despite having been e-mailed the Notice of Hearing for the March 24, 2026, hearing date on November 24, 2025, the Tenant submitted that he had mistaken the hearing date to be March 26, 2026. When the Tenant was pressed for further details, none were provided.
While I would acknowledge that the Tenant mis-diarized the hearing date, I do not find that the Tenant has provided a reasonable explanation other than that he simply mis-diarized the hearing date.
The Tenant submitted that he has cognitive issues but never provided any medical documentation to show how this issue may have affected his ability to reasonably participate in the process.

As such, on the basis of the submissions made by the Tenant, I am not satisfied that the Tenant was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding and the Tenant’s request to review is dismissed. Jurisdiction
The Tenant filed this application October 5, 2025, after having vacated the unit on January 1, 2024, according to his application. The Tenant confirmed this at the hearing.
Section 29(2) of the Act states: (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

Section 135(4) of the Act states: (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
As such, even if I would have granted the Tenant’s request to review, the Tenant’s application was out of time to file his applications.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-075658-25 issued on March 26, 2026, is denied. The order is confirmed and remains unchanged.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The Tenant sought for the Board to terminate their tenancy on October 1, 2025, as they allege that the Landlord unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee.
As explained below, the Tenant failed to establish their claim on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application must be dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that in between the months of June 2025 and July 2025, they asked the Landlord, in a more general sense, for their permission to assign.

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord consented to the Tenant’s request and provided them with details with respect to the process they would need to follow once they wanted the Landlord to review the application of a specific potential assignee.
The Tenant stated that they found a potential assignee, Jelena, during the month of August 2025, who sought to move into the rental unit on an expedited basis.

The Tenant indicated that they, along with their potential assignee, were unable to meet with the Landlord’s agents on August 30, 2025, as the offices were closed. They therefore returned to the Landlord’s offices on August 31, 2025, in order to complete the required documents and submit their application.

The Tenant stated that, based on their prior exchanges with the Landlord’s agents, the potential assignee had brought multiple documents with them to facilitate the application process and the Landlord’s review of their assignment request.

The Tenant indicated that they spent around two (2) hours in the Landlord’s office in order to submit their application and were advised that additional documents were needed, such as a reference check from the potential assignee’s two (2) prior landlords.

The Tenant opined that the Landlord was suggesting that the potential assignee would not meet the required criteria to successfully complete the assignment, without ever providing a concrete reason as to why that would be the case.

The Tenant stated that the potential assignee expressed an intent to move into the rental unit on August 31, 2025, but was advised that as the Landlord had to conduct a review of their documents and materials, the earliest move in date – if the application w ere to be successful – would be either on September 3, 2025, or September 4, 2025.

The Tenant indicated that once they left the Landlord’s office, their potential assignee felt discouraged and proceeded to send a message to the Tenant, on August 31, 2025, that they were no longer intent with moving forward with the assignment.

The Tenant stated that as they felt that the Landlord had unduly complicated the assignment process, they gave the Landlord , on September 1, 2025, a Tenant’s Notice to End the Tenancy, with a termination date of September 30, 2025 (hereafter referred to as the ‘N9 Notice’; DOC-8015322; Exhibit 1).
Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they had entered into a fixed-term tenancy with the Landlord, which was scheduled to end on April 30, 2026.

Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that while they themselves submitted an application to move into the rental unit, they did not receive an immediate response. They claimed to not know the purpose of t he delay between the moment they applied and the moment they were approved.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant stated that they assumed that the assignment process was different than the process undertaken by prospective new tenants.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the Landlord did not decline their request to assign the rental unit to their potential assignee, Jelena. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord submits that they never denied the Tenant’s request to assign their rental unit to the potential assignee, Jelena.

Instead, the Landlord submits that they received a formal request from the Tenant to assign the rental unit specifically to Jelena on August 31, 2025, and that their request was in the process of being reviewed prior to receiving the N9 Notice from the Tenant. Analysis
It is not in dispute that, on August 31, 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord for consent to assign the rental unit to Jelena, the potential assignee.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refused to consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee.

Indeed, the Tenant’s own testimony reveals that the potential assignee, of their own accord, elected not to proceed with the assignment process, and withdrew their intent to take over the rental unit from the Tenant on August 31, 2025 (i.e. the same day that they submitted their request to the joint request to the Landlord).

While the Tenant may have found the Landlord’s assignment process to be exhaustive, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’)1, in compliance with the Human Rights Code, 1990 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Code) , and its corresponding regulation2, allows landlords to request certain documents and references, which include a prospective tenant’s prior rental history, in order to review and assess such a tenant’s application to move into a residential unit.

By providing landlords seven (7) days to respond to a tenant’s request to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee, it is apparent that the legislative intent was to allow landlord s sufficient time to conduct their due diligence in order to review and assess a potential assignee’s application to move into the rental unit.3

Accordingly, the simple fact that the Landlord requested documents allowed under the Act and the Code from the potential assignee cannot be interpreted as being synonymous with “arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment,” 4 especially when taking into consideration that the Landlord requested these documents on the same day as the application was presented to them. The Landlord’s conduct therefore did not unduly delay the review of the assignment request.

As I have found that the potential assignee, Jelena, elected of their own accord to not complete the assignment process, as opposed to the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refusing to consent to the assignment, the Tenant was not entitled to seek to terminate their fixed-term tenancy within thirty (30) days, in accordance with section 96 of the Act.

Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. 1 Section 10 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Ontario Regulation 290/98 Business Practices Permissible to Landlords in Selecting Prospective Tenants for Residential Accommodation. 3 Subsection 95(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 4 Subsection 95(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') or [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay to the Tenant a total of $10,904.40. [name]:

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit in February 2019, and the monthly rent was $1,900.00.

There is no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice on April 13, 2023, for the Purchaser’s own use. The termination date in the notice was June 30, 2023. There is also no dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2023, as a result of the N12 notice.

The remaining issues are whether the Landlord or the Purchaser acted in bad faith and whether the Purchaser occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. Tenant’s evidence:

The Tenant testified that, after he and his family vacated the rental unit, he drove past the property on several occasions and did not observe anyone living there. A friend who lived in the area later advised him that for lease sign had been placed on the property. The Tenant also observed the sign when he drove past the rental unit.
The Tenant stated that the Purchaser never occupied the rental unit and that a new tenant later moved in. He learned that the new occupant was an employee of his mechanic and was not the Purchaser.

The Tenant further testified that the rental unit was advertised for rent at $2,395.00 per month on September 14, 2023, approximately two and one half months after he vacated. The Tenant submitted a copy of the rental advertisement. The photographs included in the advertisement showed the rental unit vacant and unoccupied. Landlord’s evidence:
The Landlord did not dispute that the N12 notice was served or that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice.

The Landlord testified that the agreement of purchase and sale required vacant possession because the Purchaser intended to occupy the rental unit for personal use. The Landlord stated that she served the N12 notice after receiving instructions through the Purchaser’s real estate agent. She relied on the agreement of purchase and sale, which stated that the Purchaser intended to occupy the property.

The Landlord testified that the information concerning the Purchaser’s intended occupancy was communicated through the real estate agents involved in the transaction. A copy of the agreement of purchase and sale was submitted at the hearing.

The Landlord did not communicate directly with the Purchaser concerning the intended use of the property. The sale was handled primarily through the Landlord’s real estate agent and lawyer, and the Purchaser was represented by a separate real estate agent.

The Landlord testified that title transferred and the sale closed on July 6, 2023. After the sale was completed, she did not know whether the Purchaser moved into the rental unit. Her evidence concerning the Purchaser’s intended occupancy was based on the agreement of purchase and sale and the information provided through the real estate agents. Analysis:

Based on the uncontested evidence of the parties, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Purchaser did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. I also find that the rental unit was advertised for rent approximately two and one half months after the Tenant moved out.

I am satisfied that the Landlord honestly believed that the Purchaser intended to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord’s belief was supported by the written agreement of purchase and sale and the information communicated through the real estate agents. I therefore find that the Landlord did not act in bad faith when she served the N12 notice.
The next issue is whether the Purchaser genuinely required the rental unit for residential occupation.

The evidence establishes that the Purchaser signed the agreement of purchase and sale on April 10, 2023, and represented that the property was required for personal occupancy. However, the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit after the sale closed. Instead, the rental unit was advertised for rent in September 2023.

The Purchaser did not attend the hearing or provide evidence explaining why the stated intention to occupy the rental unit was not carried out. In the absence of any explanation, and considering the short period between the Tenant’s departure and the rental advertisement, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Purchaser did not genuinely intend to occupy the rental unit when the N12 notice was served.

I therefore find that the Purchaser did not in good faith require the rental unit for residential occupation. The Tenant has established a bad faith termination under section 57 of the Act and is entitled to remedies against the Purchaser. As confirmed in Elkins, where a landlord did not act in bad faith, but the purchaser did, paragraph 4 of subsection 57(3) authorizes the Board to make an appropriate order against the purchaser. Remedies 12. The Tenants request the following remedies:  Rent differential, totaling $2,999.37  Moving expenses totaling $2,000.00  General compensation, totalling $35,000.00 13. The Tenant requested that the Purchaser also be ordered to pay a fine to the LTB. Rent differential: 14. The Tenant testified that he and his family purchased another home after receiving the N12 notice and before vacating the rental unit. The monthly mortgage payment for the new property is $4,899.37. The Tenant sought the difference between the former monthly rent and the mortgage payment. 15. In this regard, the Board must consider section 57(3) of the Act which references section 57(1) of the Act: The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: i. all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit; and ii. reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 16. Paragraph 1 of subsection 57(3) authorizes the Board to award all or part of any increased rent incurred by a former tenant during the one-year period after vacating the rental unit. A mortgage payment is not rent within the meaning of that provision. 17. Because the Tenant purchased a property rather than renting another unit, the Board does not have authority under paragraph 1 of subsection 57(3) to award the difference between the former rent and the mortgage payment. This claim is therefore denied. Moving expenses: 18. The Tenant claimed $2,000.00 for moving expenses, including the cost of moving vehicles, temporary storage, a rental trailer, and equipment required to tow the trailer. The Tenant submitted an itemized summary and supporting invoices establishing direct expenses of $1,351.40. 19. The Tenant explained that the balance of the claim represented the value of his own time, time taken away from work, and assistance provided by friends. However, these amounts are not reasonable out-of-pocket expenses because the Tenant did not establish that he paid those amounts or incurred an obligation to do so.
I find that the Tenant incurred reasonable out-of-pocket moving and storage expenses of $1,351.40. The Purchaser shall pay that amount to the Tenant. General Compensation:

The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3)(1.1), which states: An order that the Landlords pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 [Emphasis added]

The Tenant testified that the move was stressful and disruptive. At the time, he was employed full time as an engineer and was also completing a master’s degree. He stated that the time and effort required to arrange the move adversely affected both his work and academic performance. He further testified that the effect on his work was reflected in his performance review and may have affected his salary progression and bonus opportunities.

The Purchaser’s conduct caused the Tenant and his family to lose a long-standing tenancy and required them to arrange alternative housing within a limited period. The Tenant also lost the benefit of a monthly rent that was substantially below the market cost of comparable accommodation. Considering the length of the tenancy, the disruption caused by the move, I find that general compensation equivalent to five months of rent is fair and appropriate.
The monthly rent was $1,900.00. Five months of rent equals $9,500.00. The Purchaser shall therefore pay the Tenant $9,500.00 as general compensation. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines, states that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”
The Act does not authorize the Board to impose an administrative fine against a purchaser in these circumstances. The Tenant’s request for an administrative fine is therefore denied.
This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.

This amount represents: • $1,351.40 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $9,500.00 for general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

This matter was initially before me on January 27, 2026. Following that hearing, I issued interim order LTB-T-077595-25-IN, which indicated that I required additional evidence to determine whether there had been a reduction in the number of parking spots the Tenant is given access to and use of in the tenancy agreement. On April 8, 2026, the matter was brought back before me, specifically to give the parties the opportunity to present evidence and testimony in relation to how many vehicles can park in the driveway at the residential complex and whether it is possible to park three vehicles there. This question is relevant for determining whether there has been a reduction in the services or facilities provided to the Tenant in the tenancy agreement.

The Tenant testified at the first hearing that, that when she moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2019, she was given 2 parking spots on her lease. This is confirmed by the tenancy agreement which was submitted the Tenant. In addition, the Tenant testified that the parties agreed that the tenant(s) of the basement unit would park off to the side of the driveway, so the Tenant could get in and out of the driveway any time that she needed, and this agreement worked for 5 years. The Tenant testified that there was previously a tenant living in the basement unit who had a vehicle, and they parked off to the side of the driveway where there is a dug-out spot that was used for the basement tenants until the current basement tenants moved into the property.

The Tenant further testified at the first hearing date, that since the new tenants have moved into the basement unit, her vehicle is blocked in the driveway as they do not park off to the side as of September 4, 2025. As a direct result of this, the Tenant has been late picking up her child from school as the basement tenants sometimes do not answer the door to move their vehicle when she needs to leave. The Tenant provided photograph evidence of the driveway.

The Landlord testified at the first hearing date, that there is nowhere in the lease to show that the basement tenant will park in the dug-out spot, as it was always assumed they would share the driveway, and the tenants between both units would make the accommodation to move their vehicles back and forth and would move their cars as needed. The Landlord further testified that she did try and find a tenant for the basement unit who did not own a vehicle, but the unit was empty for a few months, and she finally decided to rent to someone with a vehicle.

The Tenant testified at the reconvened hearing date that there is space within the driveway for four vehicles comfortably. The only issue is that you cannot access the vehicles at the front of the driveway and that you would be only able to access the vehicle at the end of the driveway and they would have to be moved around.

After considering the evidence and testimony of the parties, I find that the Tenant has been provided with 2 parking spaces, and that within the lease it does not specifically state the location of the parking spaces, nor does it state the Tenant has exclusive use of the parking spaces within the driveway. The Tenant still has access to two parking spaces at the residential complex and the only thing that may have changed is that the other Tenant is no longer able to park in the dugout area on the side of the driveway, which has caused inconvenience for the Tenant.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven the allegations within their application for the reasons noted above.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
