issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-077897-24 issued on June 12, 2025. The Landlord did not attend the hearing. The Board granted the Tenant’s application. On July 18, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On July 22, 2025, interim order LTB-T-077897-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on June 12, 2025. The review request was heard by video conference on August 6, 2025. Interim order LTB-T- 077897-24-RV-IN2 issued on August 14, 2025, granted the review request and directed that the application be heard de novo. The de novo hearing was held on June 2, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord, the Landlord’s Legal Representative Giuseppe Rizzuto, and the Landlord’s Witness Nealon Soltanpour attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $612.08 on or before July 13, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the ‘N12 Notice’), and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2024, because of the N12 Notice. It was undisputed that the Landlord’s son did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The only contested issue before me is whether the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states that, if a landlord advertises the rental unit for rent or enters into a new tenancy agreement for the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant within one year after the tenant vacates, it is presumed that the landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord did not dispute that she re-rented the unit in July 2024. Therefore, the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act applies in this case. The onus is on the Landlord to show, on a balance of probabilities, that she served the N12 Notice in good faith.

The Landlord’s son, [name] (‘NS’), testified that, in early 2024, he was taking his last semester of undergraduate courses at the University of Toronto, expecting to graduate in June 2024. NS’s plan was to move into the rental unit after graduation because he wanted to be closer to his family and he did not like living in downtown Toronto. However, NS was struggling with his mental health at the time which led him to drop one of his courses in April 2024, shortly before the final exam. Because NS dropped the course, he was unable to graduate in June 2024 and move in as expected.

The Landlord testified that she served the N12 Notice with a June 30, 2024, termination date, because she believed NS would graduate and move into the rental unit. The Landlord explained that NS had hidden his failed courses from her in the past, which happened again in 2024. The Landlord only learned that NS dropped one of his courses in June, after the Tenants vacated. When the Landlord realized NS would not move in, she re-rented the unit because she needed to maintain the large mortgage.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s son experienced a change in circumstances which prevented him from moving into the rental unit; rather, the N12 Notice was given prematurely. Given NS’s history of mental health concerns and failed courses, his graduation in June 2024 was not a certainty. I also do not find it credible that NS would occupy a three-bedroom house by himself. While NS explained that he wanted to be close to the university to complete his final course in order to avoid commuting, I do not find this reason to be sufficient for him not to move in. Given that NS only had one course left to finish after his winter 2024 semester, and considering the serious consequences of serving an N12 Notice, he could have moved into the rental unit and commuted downtown.

The Landlord has not rebutted the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act. Therefore, I find that the N12 Notice was given in bad faith. The Tenant proved all of the requirements under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act and the application is granted. Remedies

The Tenants requested the difference in rent between their new unit and the rental unit for the year after they moved out. The Tenant, [name], testified that the rental unit was the main floor of a house with three bedrooms, one bathroom, two outdoor parking spaces, a backyard, and a shed, with a total area of around 900 square feet. The Tenants’ new unit also has three bedrooms but is a full house with a garage and a total area of around 2000 square feet. The Tenants’ new unit is not comparable to the rental unit, but rather a substantial improvement. I am not satisfied that the Tenants’ rent increased because of the Landlord; therefore, this remedy is dismissed.

The Tenant provided a U-Haul receipt showing $214.08 was paid for the rental. The Tenant also testified that he spent $150.00 on boxes and other packing materials and $200.00 on gas for the 30-minute drive when moving. Although there were no receipts for the other expenses, I find them to be reasonable. The Landlord must pay the Tenant $564.08 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenants also requested general compensation. General compensation is awarded for a tenant’s mental distress or hardship that resulted from their landlord’s actions. In my view, it applies where the hardship the tenant experienced goes beyond the normal inconvenience of changing residences.

The Tenant testified that he has a 12-year-old daughter who was nine at the time of the move. She was enrolled in various summer camps and classes in [name]; however, the Tenant could not take her there anymore after the move because the new unit was too far. The Tenants looked at many other units in the area, which were too expensive, before moving farther away. The Tenants had friends in the neighbourhood, and their daughter had to change schools in the middle of the school year. The Tenant’s daughter did not handle the move well and had to take therapy.

However, the Tenants vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2024, when they had until June 30, 2024, to find a new unit. The Tenant explained that he was told by the LTB that he needed to serve an N9 notice of termination to the Landlord in order to receive the one month’s rent compensation owing to him. The Tenant explained that he also had a surgery coming up at the time, which required him to move out earlier. The Tenant did not provide any details about the surgery, and I do not find it credible that the LTB would advise the Tenant that an N9 notice was necessary to receive compensation. As such, I am not satisfied that the Tenants were required to move as early as they did. They could have taken their time up to June 30, 2024, to find a closer, more affordable unit to mitigate their damages and allow their daughter to finish the school year in the same school. Therefore, the request for general compensation is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $612.08. This amount represents: • $564.08 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the a llegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $2,037.94 to the Tenant [name] [name] and $1,465.60 to the Tenant [name]. Issues in Dispute

The Tenants raised many concerns, which fe ll into seven categories and occurred over a period of several years. Although the testimony and evidence relating to all concerns was considered, for brevity, the issues are summarized in this order. Many of the incidents which the Tenants referred to were not disputed by the Landlord. It was largely agreed that the tenant in unit 306 behaved in a way that impacted others around him, including causing noise disturbances, making messes in the hallways and elevators, having numerous guests and visitors who caused messes and disturbances, and not properly disposing of pet waste. The primary issue was whether the Landlord’s response to the incidents was adequate.

A landlord’s duty to address substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a tenant by another tenant was affirmed by the Divisional Court in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”). The Court stated: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.”

In other words, a landlord has a positive ob ligation to provide a tenant with quiet enjoyment and take the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of their premises.

In [name] and many subsequent cases whic h have relied on [name], the Board and the Courts have grappled with what constitutes reasonable steps to address an interference with reasonable enjoyment by another tenant. The assessment of what is reasonable is contextual, similar to the leading case addressing a landlord’s responsibility to address maintenance concerns.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Factual Analysis

The Tenants reported their concerns relating to unit 306 - loud music, dogs, the behaviour of visitors, garbage in the halls, and pet waste in the halls - on multiple occasions and provided copies of email communication dating back to October 27, 2023 which referenced earlier conversations and communications dating back to 2021.

The most notable problems and dates reported to the Landlord are as follows:  [name] – ongoing from Febr uary 18, 2024 until October 2024  [name] in stairwell – Jan 6, 2024  Feces in stairwell – Jan 16, 2024  [name] doorbell camera – March 8, 2024  Racial slurs and death th reats – March 24, 2024  Garbage in hallway – April 8, 2024  Dog feces – June 6, 2024  Loud altercation – June 23, 2024  Garbage in hallway – July 2, 2026  Blood in hallway – July 12, 2024  Blood in elevator – July 30, 2024

Many of the reported issues included non-residents accessing the residential complex under the guise of visiting the tenant in 306, and these individuals causing noise, mess, sleeping in stairwells and hallways, and urinating and defecating in stairwells and hallways.

The Landlord first came to the Board with regards to the tenant in unit 306 with an L1 application which resulted in a payment plan in June 2023 and an L2 based on an N8 notice for persistent late payment of rent which resulted in a conditional order in November 2023. The Landlord submits that these applications were the most likely to result in an eviction because other application types were taking longer to resolve due to scheduling and adjournments. Ultimately the tenancy in unit 306 was terminated as a result of a breach of the conditional order relating to the L2/N8.

The Landlord also gave the tenant in 306 4 notices of termination related to their behaviour: an N5 and N7 issued January 25, 2024, an N5 issued June 19, 2024, and an N5 issued July 23, 2024. The notices which were issued on January 25, 2024 related to actions of the offending tenant towards the Landlord and did not include the issues which the Tenant had raised.

The Tenants acknowledge that the Landlord did take some steps to address concerns both specifically and generally. In most circumstances, messes – including urine and feces – were cleaned up by the Landlord, but not always in a manner the Tenants considered to be timely. The Landlord increased the cleaning staff from external contactors to include two full-time staff cleaners in July 2024, which the Tenants acknowledge improved the cleanliness problems. Security was hired in March 2024 to remove unauthorized persons from the premises and deter the unwanted behaviours of both authorized and unauthorized visitors, such as sleeping, urinating, and defecating in hallways and stairways. The Tenants submit that the hourly rounds by one security guard assigned to two 18-storey buildings were inadequate to curb the interfering behaviour.

The Tenants reported that cumulatively, these issues caused sleep disruptions and concerns about sanitation and personal security when accessing common areas such as hallways and stairwells, which caused anxiety generally.

The Tenants also reported that the tenant in 306 was causing a fire risk with hoarding conditions in their rental unit. I make no finding in this regard; there was inadequate evidence to support a finding that this alleged behaviour caused a substantial interference with the Tenants’ enjoyment of their rental units or the residential complex.

The Tenant [name] [name] described discomfort around being asked to testify at the N7 hearing regarding the behaviour of the tenant in 306. While I appreciate that the hearing may have been a stressful experience for the Tenant, the hearing was a necessary step for the Landlord to take in addressing the problems in the residential unit. It would be unfair and contradictory to penalize the Landlord for taking the very steps the Tenants asked them to.

While the Landlord took some steps to address the Tenants’ concerns, the actions were delayed and there was no clear explanation for those delays. Most notably, the Landlord waited at least five months to serve a notice of termination for the issues which were impacting the Tenants. Remedies

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by failing to adequately address the behaviour of the tenant in unit 306 which was interfering with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their units and the residential complex. An abatement is warranted from the beginning of the limitation period, October 23, 2023, until the Landlord hired additional cleaners in July 2024, a period of 8 months. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, a 20% rent abatement is appropriate. 18. [name] [name]’s monthly rent was $1,243.71 which translates to a rent abatement of $1,989.94 for 8 months. [name]’s monthly rent was $916.00 which translates to a rent abatement of $1,465.60 for 8 months. 19. An application filing fee of $48.00 was paid by [name] [name]; he is entitled to compensation for this cost. 20. The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlords and the Purchasers pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” In this case, the evidence does not support a finding that there was a blatant disregard of the Act. Rather, the Landlord fell short in their attempts to comply with the Act. Therefore, the request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.

The total amount the [name] d shall pay the Tenant [name] is $824.40. This amount represents:  $1,465.60 for a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay each Tenant the full amount owing to them by August 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant [name] the full amount owing to them by August 8, 2026, the Tenant [name] may recover this amount by deducting the amount owing from the rent which becomes due on September 1, 2026. July 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 Application)  interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. (T2 Application)  failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved so me of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $298.00.

At the hearing the Tenants advis ed that they were no longer seeking some of the remedies originally listed on the application, and were only pursuing the following:  compensation for legal fees and similar costs  a rent abatement of 1 month fo r the non-provision of a lease  a rent abatement of $100/m onth for reduced use of the balcony as a result of the claimed maintenance issue  $300.00 for items lost or dam aged by the maintenance issue Provision of Landlord address for service

The tenancy first began in 2017 between the T enants and a prior landlord. The unit was sold to this Landlord around 2020. There was a written lease between the Tenants and the initial landlord, however the Tenants assert that they were not provided with an address for service for the current Landlord for more than 30 days despite making multiple requests for the information.

The Tenants’ position refers to sections 12 and 12.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) interchangeably. These sections refer to similar issues but have different remedy provisions. Section 12 requires that every written tenancy agreement provide a legal name and address for service for the landlord. If this is not provided, the tenant may withhold rent until the required information is provided, after which the landlord can require the repayment of all withheld rent. Section 12.1 requires that a written lease in the prescribed form and signed by the landlord be provided. If a tenant requests a lease which complies with this section and the landlord does not comply within 21 days, the tenant may begin to withhold rent up to one month’s rent. If the landlord does not provide the required lease within 30 days of the request, the tenant is not required to repay the withheld rent.

A written lease was provided to the Tenants at the start of the tenancy in compliance with s.12.1, therefore the Tenants are not entitled to retain any withheld rent. They acknowledge that they now have an address for service for the Landlord via her legal representative. The Tenants obtained the address information in September 2024 when the legal representative became involved and issued an N4 Notice of Termination for arrears of rent. Text messages and emails entered into evidence show that the Tenants first requested the address information in 2020 and then again in June 2024.

I am satisfied that the c ontinued failure of the Landlord to provide the required address information over an extended period of time and after multiple requests for the information caused the Tenants inconvenience and frustration and interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, a rent abatement of $250.00 is reasonable. [name] and water on balcony

The rental unit is a condo unit, which means that certain maintenance in the residential complex is the responsibility of the condo corporation. This does not absolve the Landlord of all obligations but is a factor which must be considered the overall context of the application.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenants assert that excess water has been overflowing from the eavestroughs onto their balcony/raised porch, reducing their ability to use and enjoy the balcony and damaging their personal possessions. In some instances the Tenants believe the misdirection of water was caused or contributed to by blocked eavestroughs. The water has been an issue since approximately 2017 with little change through the end of the tenancy in October 2025.

Two examples of complaints were submitted into evidence. On July 13, 2022 the Landlord sent an email to property management advising that the Tenants had complained about water overflowing from plugged eavestroughs at the beginning of June but she had missed the email. The Tenants replied on July 24 that they had already fixed the problem themselves. On July 29, 2023 the Tenants emailed the Landlord again about the issue. The Landlord forwarded the concern to the condo property management on August 2, 2023. Property management replied to the Landlord on August 16, 2023 that there a high number of similar complaints and they would be addressed with the reserve fund in the next few years, but in the mean time blockages would be cleared and spot repairs done.

The Landlord testified that the property management company cleaned the eavestroughs on multiple occasions to address clogs. Because the eavestroughs are part of the common elements which the condo corporation is responsible for, the Landlord had limited control over the repair timeline. The Landlord says that she consistently forwarded the complaints to the property management and pushed for a repair, but there were other issues prioritized by the condo corporation, including serious leaks into the unit. The documentary supports this position for the most part.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. While the repairs would ideally have completed sooner, I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the issues with the condo corporation and the delays were beyond her control.

Even if the Landlord could have taken additional steps, I am not satisfied that the water which was directed onto the balcony or raised porch would result in a significant remedy. As an outdoor space, a certain amount of water is to be expected. The video evidence did not, in my view, show a significant volume of water being directed into an area that would otherwise be expected to be dry to make a significant difference in the Tenants’ use of the outdoor space. Although the Tenants claim compensation for items damaged by water, in my view it is not reasonable to expect compensation for items damaged by water when stored outside – even in a location which would usually be somewhat sheltered. In particular, as the problem had been ongoing since 2017, the Tenants should have been aware of the conditions and mitigated their risk by not storing items in a location which they knew by then would experience some water. Remedies
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $250.00 for a rent abatement as discussed above.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 to file this application and they are entitled to be compensated for this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $298.00. This amount represents:  $250.00 for a rent abatement.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 54383 Date: 2026-07-17 In the matter of: [address] LONDON ON [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was initially heard on March 13, 2026. The Landlord argued that the Act did not apply. The Board made a final determination that the Act applies and that the Tenant is a tenant within the meaning of the Act and the Landlord is a landlord within the meaning of the Act in LTB- T-081009-25-IN (the ‘Interim Order’). There is no appeal or request for review of this final determination. The merits of the application were heard by videoconference on July 10, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented by Candice Fogarty. The Landlord was represented by [name]
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Tenant’s evidence
Only [name] testified at the hearing. I will refer to her evidence as the Tenant’s.

She testified that the rental unit was very messy when she took possession of the property. The property had been vacant for a long time and needed a lot of cleaning and repairs. She agreed to move into the property and to clean, paint and remove some garbage from the property.
The repairs were never completed. The Landlord has always known about the issues.

The Tenant testified about the items that remained outstanding. The testimony was supported by photographs. They can be found on pages 80-84 and 108-115 of the Tenant’s document package 7486608. The authenticity of these photos was not disputed. I note however that photos 80-84 were taken before the tenancy commenced in September 2025.

There is no sink in the main floor kitchen, and the Tenant has had to go downstairs to wash dishes. Lower level of the house is not part of the Tenant’s unit other than the shared laundry area, so the Tenant’s unit does not have a functioning kitchen sink at all.

The back door has no lock on it, and the Tenant secured it with a latch. The shower doesn’t work properly. The handle/faucet was never installed so the Tenant needs to use pliers to operate the shower. The third bedroom window is missing and is currently boarded up. The Landlord never installed a proper window although one was purchased. The Landlord similarly never installed an interior door to the third bedroom. Smoke alarms are missing and/or not properly installed. There are cracks on one of the photos where walls connect to the ceiling. The Tenant briefly mentioned mold issues. Garage is full of garbage, and the Tenant argues that the garage needs to be emptied so that the Tenant can park her car in the garage as the Landlord had promised her.
The Tenant was extensively cross-examined about her agreement to do repairs herself and her ability to do so. I don’t find this line of questioning to be relevant as addressed below.

She admitted that she didn’t separately notify the Landlord of any issues but argued that the Landlord has always been aware of the issues as he was planning to do this work himself until the relationship deteriorated.
She confirmed that the Tenant applied for a peace bond against the Landlord and that this application was later withdrawn.

On or about February 18th the Tenant lost gas supply to her unit. She immediately informed the Landlord. Gas was restored 10 days later. It was very cold and the Landlord did nothing to ameliorate the situation. They promised to provide space heaters but didn’t actually provide any.

Cross-examination revealed that the Landlord acted quickly when he was notified of furnace issues. The Tenant confirmed that someone attended at the property the next day on February 19th and then again the following day. She confirmed that gas was shut off by the city and that it was restored on February 27th.

She was asked about her rent and what is included in it. She disagreed that she pays $600 for one bedroom. According to the Tenant, they pay $1,200 for the house excluding the basement because the basement wasn’t done. She was asked to explain why she thought the garage was included if it contained the Landlord’s belongs. She explained that it did not contain the Landlord’s property but instead contained garbage left behind by previous tenants. The Landlord started emptying it but never finished. He told her that she would eventually be able to use the garage to park her vehicle. The garbage she initially agreed to remove from the property was limited to what was in the house and did not include the garage.
She confirmed that she filed no evidence to corroborate her claim that there is mold at the property. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord has owned the property for over 20 years. The lot contains two houses: 265 and 267 [address]. The properties are visually on the same plot of land and are attached to each other. The garage is detached and not attached to either property. It is behind and to the side of the buildings closer to the rental unit than to 267 Springbank.

According to the Landlord the agreement was for 2 bedrooms, kitchen and family room. It did not include the basement and did not include the garage. He hired the Tenant to fix his property and the adjacent property, but they never finished the work.
The Landlord claimed that he purchased supplies himself using his ATM card.

He has not been at the rental unit since September 1st 2025. He is not aware of what is and what isn’t done at the rental unit. He refuses to go back to the property because the Tenant allegedly harasses him. The Tenant’s alleged misconduct is not before me in this application.
There was a summons for him to appear before a judge. The judge confirmed to him that he was able to go to his property, which the Landlord was previously unsure about.

In response to the Tenant’s claim, he testified that everything has been fixed. Bedrooms were fixed, showers were fixed, and the kitchen sink is still outstanding because he hasn’t found one yet. The shower was working fine when he rented the property, and he believes the Tenant broke it or at the very least the Tenant failed to fix it. Garage was never part of the tenancy – it is just a storage unit. The back door has a new lock on it.

He has not received any notices of maintenance issues since September. He is not aware of any mold issues. He spent approximately $2,000 to fix the furnace. He repaired it as soon as he could. He spent the 10 days when there was no heat at the property trying to find people who can get the work done. He had someone attend right away. He claims that the smoke alarm was broken by the Tenant.
The Landlord did not present any supporting or corroborating evidence.
On cross-examination the Landlord confirmed that parties were communicating through their respective representatives. There is no dispute that the Landlord received the Interim Order.
He complains that he couldn’t fix things because there was a peace bond and because he has no money to fix things.
On cross-examination he did not dispute that there were still issues at the property and argued that the Tenant was hired to fix them.

He was asked why he didn’t file evidence to corroborate his claim that he paid for various supplies. He replied that he used his ATM card and didn’t have receipts. He explained that he thought the Tenant were his friends and didn’t expect the relationship to deteriorate. He then said that the Tenant was not a contractor. On re-direct he said that they were not a contractor, but they were hired to do some work that they were capable of doing. Law and analysis
This is the Tenant’s application, and they bear the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

At the outset of the second hearing the Landlord briefly argued that it is “unclear” that [name] is a tenant and provided very brief submissions on the issue. The [name] determined that the applicants were tenants. The order was not appealed and there was no request to review. The issue has been determined by the LTB in a final manner. Even if it weren’t the Landlord’s brief submissions were unpersuasive. [name] has lived at the property and has paid rent. The history of the tenancy is further addressed in the Interim Order.

Section 20(1) requires landlords to maintain and repair rental units: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”
Under 20(2) subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

Under s. 3(1) the Act applies despite any agreement to the contrary: “3(1) This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.”

I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant established the following issues on a balance of probabilities: [name] furnace for 10 days in February 2026, [name] shower, [name] lock on the back door, d. Missing sink in the kitchen, [name] or missing smoke detectors, and f. Missing window and door in the third bedroom.
There is no dispute that the furnace was broken for 10 days. The issue of whether the Landlord responded reasonably is addressed below.

The claims about shower, lock, sink, smoke detectors, and third bedroom are established on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant provided credible testimony that was supported by photographic evidence. The Landlord disputes that these issues existed but simultaneously maintains that the Tenant was supposed to address them, that everything has been repaired, and also denies having been at the property since September. His denials are therefore unreliable at best. To the extent the parties may have contracted out of the application of the Act and required the Tenant to maintain the property, this agreement became void effective September 1, 2025 when this tenancy commenced by virtue of s. 3(1) of the Act. The Tenant’s knowledge of the issues is irrelevant under s. 20(2) of the Act. The Landlord’s allegation that the Tenant may have broken the smoke detector and/or the shower was vague and uncorroborated. Even if it were the case, it would not necessarily matter for the purposes of this application. A tenant causing an issue does not absolve a landlord of their responsibility to repair (see CET-10108-11, 2011 LNONLTB 214 ([name]. L.T.B.) affd Gouge v EQB Ltd. (2011), Brampton Court File No. DC- 11-0009-0000 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), leave to appeal denied by the Ontario Court of Appeal). I also find that the rental unit includes the third bedroom on the balance of probabilities.

I do not find that the claim of mold has been established on a balance of probabilities. The evidence consisted solely of self-serving uncorroborated testimony. The testimony was extremely brief, and it is unclear what the Tenant’s belief that there is mold is based on, even if the belief is genuine. It is unclear where the mold was found and the extent of alleged issues. The Tenant failed to meet the requisite burden of proof.

I also do not find that the Tenant established that there is any issue related to the garage because I do not find that it is part of the rental unit. The garage is detached. It is closer to 265 than to 267 but it is not obviously connected to either property. The Tenant only rented the upper level of 265. Her photographic evidence does not include photos of the inside of the garage. It is unclear whether she even has access to the garage of whether she was ever given a key. It is undisputed that she never used it. The Landlord denies that the garage was part of what the Tenant rented. This seems at least as consistent with the totality of the record and as likely to be the case as the Tenant’s version of the events. As the Tenant bears the burden of proof, this is fatal to this part of the Tenant’s claim.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I find that the Landlord acted reasonably when dealing with the furnace. The totality of the evidence is that the service interruption was caused by a third party or a leak. The Landlord then arranged for someone to attend at the property right away and everything was repaired and heat was restored within 10 days. The Tenant did not lead evidence about any unreasonableness or delay. Cross-examination of the Landlord did not reveal any misconduct or lack of diligence. While unfortunate, this interruption in service does not entitle the Tenant to any remedies in accordance with Onyskiw.

I do not find that the Landlord acted reasonably dealing with other issues. The Landlord advanced multiple mutually exclusive arguments. He claimed that he didn’t know about the issues, that he couldn’t attend at the property, that the Tenant was supposed to repair everything and that there were no issues at all. Overall, he has done absolutely nothing to address the issues since September 2025. This lack of action stands in stark contrast with the Landlord’s furnace repairs.

The Landlord has undeniably been aware that issues exist since no later than this application was filed in late September 2025. He admitted that he has done nothing to even investigate, let alone repair. He arranged for furnace repairs in a timely manner despite any alleged issues with peace bond or with communicating with the Tenant or with attending at the rental unit. This was before the Board made a determination that the Act applies. This strongly suggests that the issues the Landlord blamed for his failure to address maintenance issues were not in fact preventing him from dealing with the property.

I find that the Tenant is entitled to their remedies starting October 1 2025 in accordance with Onyskiw and based on the totality of the record. The Landlord has likely been aware of the issues since before the tenancy even commenced but I find that he behaved reasonably in relation to these issues until this application clearly put him on notice of the Tenant’s position. The parties’ relationship was previously unclear, and the Landlord could reasonably believe that the Tenant was carrying out the repairs themselves in accordance with their previous business arrangement between the parties. The Tenant was clearly doing some work at the property and the Tenant’s own photos show a dramatic improvement to the rental unit due to their work at the property. There is no record of the Tenant notifying the Landlord of any issues before this application was filed and I will not award abatement of rent in relation to these issues before October 1, 2025 in accordance with Onyskiw and s. 30(2) of the Act.

The Tenant requests the following remedies: a. An order for the landlord to address maintenance issues as follows: 1. Installation of a functioning kitchen sink on the main floor; 2. Repairs to the shower; 3. Repair of the rear door locking mechanism; 4. Installation of functioning smoke alarms; 5. Repair and waterproofing of windows; 6. Correction of dryer venting deficiencies; and 7. Installation or repair of the third bedroom door. b. 25% abatement of rent until repairs are carried out for maintenance issues. c. Additional rent abatement of $200.00 for the loss of vital services for 10 days. d. Reimbursement of the Tenant’s out-of-pocket expenses incurred to repair the property. e. An order that rent can’t be increased until repairs are carried out.
Remedy ‘e’ is granted.

Remedy ‘a’ is granted for issues that were established on a balance of probabilities. ‘a.2’ and ‘a.5’ are limited in scope to the issues that were established at the hearing. The only window that the Landlord is required to repair is the third bedroom window. Shower repairs are limited to the shower faucet. ‘a.6’ is denied as the Tenant did not lead any evidence about any dryer venting deficiencies.

Remedy ‘’b’ is granted in part. Based on the totality of the record I find that a 15% abatement is appropriate in all of the circumstances. Abatement is a contractual remedy intended to compensate the Tenant for the loss of enjoyment of the bundle of goods and services they were paying for. Some issues such as a missing lock are relatively minor. Others are relatively major, such as the lack of a proper kitchen sink, but it was somewhat mitigated by the Tenant’s ability to access a sink in the basement of the residential complex. Overall, based on Board practice and based on my experience hearing similar cases, I find that a 15% abatement starting October 1, 2025 is appropriate. The abatement awarded to July 10th 2026 is calculated as 9 months and 10 days times $1,200 times 15% for the total of $1,679.18. The abatement is ongoing until all of the repairs are completed. 46. [name] ‘c’ is denied as I find that the Landlord acted reasonably in relation to the furnace. 47. Remedy ‘d’ is granted but limited to expenses incurred after commencement of the tenancy. As determined in the Interim Order, the Tenant first paid rent or attempted to pay rent in September 2025. I find that the tenancy commenced at that time. The previous arrangement between the parties was not a tenancy. No rent was paid and parties had some business arrangement for the Tenant to do some work. The Tenant complains that the Landlord failed to reimburse them for expenses they incurred to update the property. The Landlord argues that the Tenant breached their contract and failed to carry out the repairs/work they promised to carry out. Any disputes parties have about issues that predate the tenancy are outside of LTB jurisdiction. 48. Expenses the Tenant incurred to repair the property after the tenancy commenced ought to be reimbursed by the Landlord as reasonable out of pocket expenses incurred by the Tenant. Document 8278885 summarizes these expenses on page 12. The expenses the Tenant incurred after September 1 2025 were: $39.85, $9.70, $9.47, $15.74, $12.42, $5.64 for the total of $92.82. Corresponding invoices can be found in document 7486608. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a reimbursement of these costs. 49. The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application and find that they are entitled to a reimbursement of this cost as the substantially successful party.
ordered: The Landlord shall immediately carry out the following repairs/work: 1. Installation of a functioning kitchen sink on the main floor;

Repair/install a shower faucet in good working order; 3. installation of a locking mechanism on the rear door; 4. Installation of functioning smoke alarms; 5. Installation of a proper window in the third bedroom; and 6. Installation of the third bedroom door. 2. If the Landlord does not do the work by July 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the work to be done and may recover the cost of the work by deducting the amount from the rent owing until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant is authorized to deduct $180 a month or $5.92 per day starting July 11, 2026 from monthly rent owing until the work is complete. This represents an ongoing rent abatement of 15%.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,820.00. This amount represents: • $1,679.18 for a rent abatement for the period ending July 10, 2026. • $92.82 for repair or replacement work the Tenant was authorized to do. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing starting in August 2026 until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord is not authorized to increase rent until all of the work listed in paragraph 1 is complete. July 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,050.00 for the last month’s rent deposit, and $500.0 for the cleanliness deposit collected that was not permitted to be collected.

The Tenant testified they moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023, and vacated the rental unit August 31, 2025. The Tenant paid the Landlord $550.00 for a last month’s rent deposit on August 1, 2023, which was not applied towards the last month’s rent, and paid rent for August 2025 to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that they contacted the Landlord for the last month’s rent deposit back, and they were directed to another party as the Landlord claimed she does not take care of payments. The Tenant further testified that they were advised they would be given the last month’s rent deposit back within 15 days, but the Landlord has failed to provide this amount to the Tenant.

Upon review of text messages between the Landlord and the Tenants, the Landlord messaged the Tenants on September 1, 2025, to confirm that the Tenants vacated the rental unit and left the keys within the unit. Therefore, I am satisfied that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on August 31, 2025, which would be the date the Tenants would be responsible for rent.

Therefore, based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified on August 1, 2023, a security deposit in the amount of $500.00 was paid to the Landlord to ensure the cleanliness of the unit. The parties agreed that this deposit was to be refunded on the Tenant vacating and the rental unit being in a clean condition.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
Subsection 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Subsection 105(2) of the Act defines “security deposit” as, money, property or a right paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.

As the $500.00 cleanliness deposit was to be refunded upon the Tenant vacating the rental unit and the unit being in clean condition, I find that this deposit meets the definition of “security deposit” in subsection 105(2) of the Act. I further find that it was not a rent deposit under section 105 of the Act because the Tenant provided a separate deposit for the last month of the tenancy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord contravened the Act when they collected the $500.00 deposit for cleanliness, and they continue to contravene the Act by retaining the deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,098.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $550.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  entered the rental unit illegally.  altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.  withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Garage and Basement

Most of the Tenants’ claims relate to the usage of the garage and basement at the rental unit. The Tenants say the lease covers the entire property; the Landlord says the lease does not include the basement or the garage and is limited to the main and upper floor of the house.

Three versions of the lease were entered into evidence. The key characteristics of each version are summarized in the following chart: DocID Unit Identification Landlord Signature Date Tenant Name Tenant signature 5536408 None June 20, 2023 [name] None 5535428 None June 20, 2023 [name] None 5457972 Ground and upper July 31, 2023 [name] July 31, 2023

Of the three versions, only one is signed by any of the Tenants. This is also the most recently dated version which is signed by the Landlord. As the most recent document, and the only one which is signed by any of the Tenants, I find the version dated July 31, 2023 and filed as DocID 5457972 is the most reliable. This version clearly identifies the unit as ‘ground and upper’ which logically excludes the basement. None of the versions mention the garage. In the absence of any other corroborating information, I find it likely that as the two areas were presented as a package of issues – that is both were taken away at the same time – either both were included in the lease, or neither were.
Having determined that the basement and the garage are not included in the lease agreement, the portions of the application relating to these areas must be dismissed. Harassment
During the hearing the Tenant gave evidence about an incident of harassment, however as the issue was not referenced anywhere in the application, it is not properly before the Board. Remedies

The Tenants claimed compensat ion for a rug in their application but provided no evidence relating to what happened to the rug or why compensation would be appropriate. As a result, this portion of the claim must be dismissed.

The Tenants requested an order for the Landlord to return monthly withdrawals from one of their paycheques. Few details of these withdrawals were provided, however based on the information obtained during the hearing it is likely these withdrawals are a garnishment for another legal matter. The Board does not have the authority to vary a garnishment or any order of any other legal authority.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the Tenants the last month’s rent that is on deposit.

The Tenants testified that they paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,300.00 on July 29, 2024, and the Landlord failed to apply this amount to the last month of their tenancy.

The Tenants testified that they provided their Landlord with notice on September 5, 2025, to terminate their tenancy effective September 30, 2025, to which the Landlord agreed. The Tenants testified that they paid September 2025’s rent before providing their Landlord with notice to terminate the tenancy.
Based on the Tenants’ uncontested evidence I find that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2025.

I find that the parties agreed that the tenancy would terminate on September 30, 2025, as the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant disputing the termination date of September 30, 2025, bur rather responded to the Tenant accepting termination of the tenancy on October 1, 2025, which is only 1 day prior to the date the Tenant vacated. Therefore, I find there was a clear meeting of the minds to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2025. The Tenants vacated the rental unit pursuant to the agreement between the Landlord and the Tenants. At the time the Tenants vacated the rental unit and the tenancy ended, the rent was paid in full, and the Landlord was still holding the rent deposit.

In accordance with s. 106(10), a landlord can only use a rent deposit to cover the rent for the last rental period. Since the rent for the last rental period was already paid, the deposit must be returned to the Tenants.

Therefore, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,800.00. Compensation for N12 Notice owing

The Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act. The Tenant testified that the Landlord served an N12 Notice to End the Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit in July 2025. A copy of the N12 was filed as Document #6524136.

After receiving the N12, the Tenant exercised the right provided by section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') to terminate the tenancy by serving an N9 notice on July 25, 2025, with a termination date of August 31, 2025. A copy of the N9 was filed as Document #6524139. The Tenant testified that they vacated the rental unit on September 1, 2025.
The tenancy agreement (Document #6524145) establishes that the monthly rent was $1,800.00. Analysis

Section 48.1 of the Act requires a landlord who gives a tenant an N12 notice to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one month's rent or offer another rental unit acceptable to the tenant. The compensation must be provided on or before the termination date specified in the N12 notice.

The Board accepts the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the Landlord did not pay the required compensation. The Tenant subsequently contacted the Landlord by text message requesting the compensation. The Landlord responded that he did not believe he was required to pay it. The text message exchange was filed as Document #6524176.

The Landlord's belief that compensation was not required does not relieve the Landlord of the statutory obligation imposed by section 48.1 of the Act. The requirement to pay compensation is mandatory where a landlord gives an N12 notice and the tenant vacates the rental unit pursuant to that notice.

The Board finds that the Landlord failed to comply with section 48.1 of the Act. The Tenant is entitled to compensation equal to one month's rent in the amount of $1,800.00. As the Tenant was successful in the application, the Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,848.00. This amount represents: • $1,800.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 19, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
