issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $791.00. The parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord did not give the Tenant access to the rental unit

The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit. The evidence regarding the material facts was not disputed.

The parties entered into a tenancy agreement for the specific rental unit identified in the lease. Prior to the commencement of the tenancy, the Landlord was unable to make that rental unit available for occupancy as agreed.

The Landlord acknowledged that the rental unit was not ready for the Tenant to move into on the agreed commencement date. As a result, the Landlord arranged alternate accommodation for the Tenant and provided complimentary storage while the Tenant waited for the rental unit to become available. The Tenant paid the agreed market rent for the alternate accommodation, and the Landlord confirmed that the storage was provided at no cost.

The evidence establishes that the rental unit remained unavailable for an extended period. The Tenant ultimately advised the Landlord that she could not continue waiting for possession of the rental unit and elected to terminate the tenancy agreement. I find that the Tenant's decision was a direct consequence of the Landlord's inability to provide possession of the rental unit that was the subject of the lease.

The parties further agreed that the Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $7,250.00. The Landlord refunded the balance of that deposit but retained $791.00, representing a fee the Landlord had paid to a third-party property management company that introduced the Tenant to the Landlord.

The Landlord submitted that it should not bear the cost of the introduction fee because the tenancy did not proceed. The Landlord stated that it provided an alternate accommodation to the Tenant and storage for the Tenant’s belongings. I do not accept this submission. Analysis

Section 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 limits the purposes for which a landlord may collect and apply a rent deposit. A rent deposit is to be applied only to the rent for the last rental period of the tenancy. The Act does not authorize a landlord to deduct its own business expenses, including leasing commissions, referral fees, or property management fees, from a tenant's rent deposit.

Moreover, the evidence establishes that the tenancy did not proceed because the Landlord was unable to provide the rental unit in accordance with the parties' agreement. The Landlord's payment of a fee to a third-party property management company was a business expense voluntarily incurred by the Landlord. The financial consequences of that expense cannot be transferred to the Tenant, particularly where the Tenant's decision to terminate the agreement arose from the Landlord's inability to make the agreed rental unit available for occupancy.

Section 106(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit to be applied to the rent for the last rental period before the tenancy terminates. The Act restricts both the collection and the use of a rent deposit. A last month's rent deposit is not a security deposit that may be applied toward any loss or expense a landlord incurs in connection with a tenancy.

In this case, the $791.00 retained by the Landlord did not represent rent for the last rental period. Rather, it represented a business expense incurred by the Landlord when it chose to engage a third-party property management company to locate a tenant. While the Landlord may have incurred that expense, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 contains no provision authorizing a landlord to recover a leasing commission, referral fee, or similar business expense by deducting it from a tenant's last month's rent deposit.

The Landlord identified no provision of the tenancy agreement or the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) authorizing the deduction of the $791.00 from the Tenant's rent deposit. I therefore find that the Landlord improperly retained that amount.

Accordingly, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of $791.00. As the Tenant has been successful in the application, the Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $791.00. This amount represents: • $791.00 for the balance of the rent deposit retained by the Landlord • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 19, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Section 57(5) of the Act provides: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. [Emphasis added]
The Tenant moved out of the rental unit in January 2025 and the unit was listed for sale in September 2025, thus engaging the reverse onus provisions of Section 57(5).

The Landlords say they sold their former hom e in Lucan and moved into this unit on March 26, 2025 after completing some renovations. In support of this they submitted an invoice from a moving company for a move from their former address to the rental unit on March 26, 2025.

The Landlords acknowledge listin g the home for sale but says they included a closing date more than a year after the Tenant moved out to ensure that they lived in the unit for at least one year. Further, the home was not sold, and they continue to live there. The Tenant agrees that the Landlords still reside at the unit.

Based on the evidence before the Board, the Landlords have proven on a balance of probabilities that they issued the N12 notice in good faith. After issuing the notice, the Landlords did in fact move into the rental unit and continued to live there for more than a year. While it is possible that they intended to occupy the rental unit for only the minimum one-year period required under the Act, that would not constitute a breach of the Act.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

This application is brought pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that in order to succeed on this application the Tenants must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that they got a notice of termination under s. 48, they moved out of the rental unit because of the notice, and that the person noted in the notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time.

It is undisputed that the Landlords gave the Tenants a N12 Notice of Termination on November 3, 2024, with a termination date of February 1, 2025. The N12 notice indicated that the Landlords required possession of the rental unit for residential occupancy by their family and parents. The Tenants vacated their rental unit on April 11, 2025 because of the notice.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Pursuant to subsection 57(6), the period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that begins on the day a landlord gave the notice of termination and ends one year after a tenant vacated the rental unit. In this case, the period began on November 3, 2024 and ended on April 11, 2026.

The Landlord did not dispute that they entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant during the prescribed period. Accordingly, it is presumed the notice was given in bad faith. The Landlords must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that at the time the N12 was given to the Tenants, they genuinely intended to reside in the rental unit. Landlords’ evidence

It was the evidence of the Landlords that they intended to relocate from British Columbia to Ontario and move into the rental unit. They stated that their home in British Columbia was inadequate to accommodate their growing family and parents, who were coming from abroad to reside with them.

On November 3, 2024, the Landlords gave notice to their landlord in Abbotsford, British Columbia indicating that they will be ending their tenancy on January 31, 2025 as they planned to move back to Ontario.

The Landlords testified that they were forced to change their plans because the Tenants refused to vacate the rental unit in accordance with the N12 notice. They explained that they could not risk moving their business and personal belongings from British Columbia only to find themselves homeless in Toronto with their toddler and newborn child. Given this, the Landlords advised the Tenants and the Board on March 27, 2025 that they no longer intended to move into the rental unit. Tenants’ evidence
The Tenants believe that what the Landlords really wanted to do was to re-rent the unit for a higher monthly rent. Analysis

The Ontario Divisional Court in [name] v. Salter 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), [2001] O.J. No. 2792 ([name]. Ct.), stated that: “…the test of good faith is a genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the landlord’s proposal.” Moreover, in Kennealy v. [name], the English Court of Appeal pronounced that a landlord need only establish a bona fide wanted and immediate intention to occupy the premises as a residence.
In this case, I find the Landlords have established that they genuinely intended to move into the rental unit for at least twelve months at the time the N12 notice was given to the Tenants.

The Tenants did not sufficiently challenge the Landlords’ evidence that their year family required a larger home to meet the needs of their growing family and the need to provide care to their parents. I accept the Landlords were concerned with the Tenants’ unwillingness to vacate the rental unit in accordance with the N12 notice. This was a legitimate source of concern for the Landlords who needed certainty as to when they could reliably move forward with their plans.
The Tenant did not present any compelling evidence to support their belief that the Landlords never intended to move into the rental unit and wanted to charge a higher monthly rent.

I am of the view that the Landlords had every intention of relocating from British Columbia to move into the rental unit. I accept they felt uneasy with proceeding with such a big move given the Tenants’ refusal to vacate. They advised the Tenants before they vacated that their intentions had changed. I find the Landlords’ failure to move into the rental unit was reasonable given the change in their personal circumstances.
Having found the N12 was given in good faith, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ Application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: d the parties, or their representatives, will be advised of the rescheduled hearing date by way of a new notice of hearing. If the Board does not grant the request, the hearing will proceed on the originally scheduled date and the parties or their representatives must attend. Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. 4. The parties did not receive a confirmation from the Board that the hearing was re- scheduled. Therefore, they should have been prepared to proceed on the set date. The Board sent the parties the Notice of Hearing on May 4, 2026. The parties had sufficient time to prepare for the hearing. I was not satisfied that there were exceptional circumstances requiring an adjournment. Accordingly, the adjournment request was denied. The matter was stood down for one hour and fifteen minutes for the Landlord to prepare their case. The Landlord was also permitted to submit documentary evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Former Tenant proved that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations with respect to the smoke detector. The Landlord proved that the Former Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit. Therefore, the Former Tenant must pay the Landlord $6,173.37 on or before August 31, 2026.

It was undisputed that the Former Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 17, 2025, but was still storing some belongings there after that date. The tenancy terminated on September 30, 2025. Smoke Detector

It was undisputed that, on July 23, 2025, the smoke detector on the main floor of the rental unit was beeping every 45 seconds. The Former Tenant immediately notified the Landlord, who responded stating that they are coordinating with a technician. The Former Tenant hired a technician on July 24, 2025, who changed the battery in the smoke detector. However, the smoke detector was still beeping and had to be removed. The Former Tenant incurred costs of $145.00 for this service. The Former Tenant informed the Landlord on July 25, 2025, that the smoke detector was removed. The smoke detector remained disconnected until the end of the tenancy, September 30, 2025.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations with respect to the smoke detector from July 23, 2025, to July 25, 2025. The Landlord’s internal communications between their employees indicates that they were making arrangements to resolve the issue on July 25, 2025. The Former Tenant hired her own technician before the Landlord had the chance to attend the unit. I do not find a delay of two days to be unreasonable for this issue. However, I do find that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations after that date because they failed to reinstall the smoke detector after being notified that it was removed.
This portion of the Former Tenant’s application is granted. The Former Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 to file this application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Former Tenant requested a $250.00 rent abatement due to the interference from the smoke detector beeping, which interfered with her sleep, and the safety risk caused by the non-functioning smoke detector after July 25, 2025. I find this rent abatement to be reasonable; therefore, it is granted. The Former Tenant also requested reimbursement for the costs she incurred to hire a technician on July 24, 2025. I do not find it appropriate to award these costs because the Former Tenant acted prematurely and could have avoided these costs by waiting for the Landlord one additional day. The request for out-of-pocket costs is dismissed. Water Leak

It was undisputed that the Former Tenant notified the Landlord of a water leak from the main floor toilet on August 25, 2025. The water leak caused considerable mildew and mould as well as a musty odour in the garage, basement, and storage area of the rental unit.

The Landlord’s Agent [name] inspected the unit on August 26, 2025, made sure the water was off, placed a dehumidifier, and made arrangements for repairs. By September 11, 2025, all the mouldy drywall was removed. The Landlord’s contractors continued to conduct repairs on an almost daily basis until September 26, 2025, when the work was completed.

I am satisfied that the Landlord responded to the water leak reasonably. The Landlord’s Agent inspected the issue the next day after the Former Tenant complained, and the repairs were completed within a reasonable time. Therefore, the Landlord did not breach their maintenance obligations with respect to the water leak. This portion of the Former Tenant’s application is dismissed. [name]. The Landlord’s Agent submitted that the water leak was caused by the Former Tenant and requested that the Former Tenant reimburse the Landlord for the subsequent disposal and repair costs. 12. The Landlord’s Agent provided photographs he took during his inspection of the rental unit on August 26, 2025, which showed that toilet tank had a large crack from the top corner. The Landlord’s Agent submitted that it was extremely unlikely for a ceramic toilet tank to crack that way on its own. The photographs also showed patches of dark mould over large areas of the walls and ceiling in the basement. The Landlord’s Agent submitted that such substantial mould growth could not have occurred over a short period and was likely several weeks old. 13. The Former Tenant denied damaging the toilet. The Former Tenant testified that she had visited the rental unit on August 23, 2025, at which point the toilet was functioning normally. When she returned on August 25, 2025, she discovered the leak and immediately turned the water off. However, at that point, the whole main floor was already flooded. 14. The crack in the toilet tank is large, which in my view constitutes undue damage. It is unclear how such a crack could be caused by reasonable use, and I find it highly likely that the tank cracked spontaneously. The Former Tenant is responsible for undue damage regardless of whether she, an occupant, or another person she permitted in the unit caused the damage. 15. Based on the severity of the mould growth in the photographs, I do not find the Former Tenant’s timeline of events to be credible. Even to an untrained eye, the extent of the mould suggests that it was left unchecked for more than a day or two. It was the Former Tenant’s responsibility to inform the Landlord of the leak immediately. I find it more likely than not that the Former Tenant vacated the unit on August 17, 2025, and did not return until August 25, 2025, at which point the water leak had spread and mould had grown. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Former Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit. 16. The Landlord’s Agent provided a breakdown of the costs the Landlord incurred, which included disposal of the toilet and damaged drywall, restoration work for the water damage and mould, installing new drywall, and painting it. The Landlord’s Agent also provided receipts to support the costs claimed. I am satisfied that the Landlord incurred reasonable costs of $6,285.37 to repair the damage. Although the Landlord claimed the disposal costs as being related to substantial interference and not damage, I do not find this to be a fatal error. The application is clearly about the water leak and the related costs incurred. Therefore, the Landlord’s application is granted. 17. There is no last month's rent deposit.
ordered: The Landlord owes the Former Tenant $298.00. This amount represents $250.00 for a rent abatement and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Former Tenant owes the Landlord $6,471.37, which represents $6,285.37 for the reasonable costs the Landlord incurred as a result of the damage, and $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The total amount the Former Tenant owes the Landlord is $6,173.37.

If the Former Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before August 31, 2026, the Former Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from September 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenants sought to rely on their amended application. This was referenced in order LTB-T-086310-25-IN, issued on May 21, 2026, after an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) failed to resolve the matter between the parties on May 19, 2026. The amended application was filed with the Board on May 12, 2026, and the Landlord was served.
The amended application reduced the Tenants’ abatement claim from $22,572.00 to $14,256.00 and withdrew the claim for out-of-pocket expenses and reimbursement for work done by the Tenant.

In reviewing the Tenants’ request, I considered Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. In my view, the amendment is appropriate, does not prejudice the parties, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. Therefore, I granted the Tenants’ request to amend the application to claim $14,256.00 for a rent abatement. Service of Evidence

The Landlord submits that the Tenants did not serve evidence in accordance with the Board’s Interim Order. Specifically, paragraph 5 states that the Tenants are to provide a copy of their evidence to the Landlord on or before June 1, 2026. Paragraph 7 indicates that failure to comply with paragraph 5 of the interim order may result in the presiding member refusing to accept the evidence.
The Landlord states that the Tenants provided evidence by way of a USB stick on June 17, 2026. However, the Landlord was unable to open the majority of the documents enclosed.

The Tenants say that they did try, on more than occasion, to provide the evidence to the Landlord, but that she was – referring to the Landlord’s legal representative – never at her desk. They further submit that most of the documents were already in the portal prior to the last hearing date.

The Landlord explained that the office in which she works has a front desk with several customer relations representatives (‘CRR’). When someone attends the office, the staff will alert the individual. In this case, the CRR placed the envelope containing the USB stick on the Landlord Representative’s desk and sent an e-mail advising of same at 3:08 p.m. on June 17, 2026.

The Landlord submits it is prejudicial to the Landlord to allow the Tenants to rely on the evidence which was submitted late. She says the Tenants were advised very clearly of the service requirements at the ACC on May 19, 2026. This is why an order to serve was included in the Interim Order.

In my view, it is prejudicial to allow the Tenants to rely on the evidence which was not served in accordance with the Board’s Interim Order and Rules of Procedure. Although the evidence may have been uploaded to the Portal ('portal'), this is not considered service unless both parties consented to service via the portal. Further, the materials served were not actually accessible.

Therefore, the Tenants were not permitted to rely on evidence which was not served in accordance with the Interim Order. However, the Tenants were able to give oral testimony to the contents of that evidence. In addition, if evidence was referred to which was critical to making a relevant finding, I was able to seek submissions from the Landlord as to whether it was appropriate for me to do so. Tenants’ T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.

By way of background, the rental unit is a townhome built sometime in the 1970’s. The rental unit has one washroom, which is located on the second floor. The tenancy began in November 2024. Of note, the Tenant’s testimony was the tenancy began in November 2024. However, the entirety of the evidence dealt with events that took place in September and October 2024. Given the evidence and testimony, it is my understanding that the tenancy actually began in September 2024, rather than November 2024.

The Tenants’ allegation is that the Landlord failed to provide maintenance to the rental unit in a timely, effective, and reasonable manner. The Tenants’ report that their toilet was “rocking” such that it was moving when in use, and that it was leaking. The leaking led to raw sewage, known as “black water”, to permeate the ceiling and drywall of the floor below.

The first floor of the rental unit consists of a living room area on one side, and on the other side is the kitchen area. The kitchen is a galley style. The foundation wall has cabinetry, a stove and sink, while the opposite side has additional cabinetry and the fridge. Unusually, the “refrigerator” side is not against an exterior wall. Rather, there are two walls midway in the room forming an L shape. The first part of the L is a 6-foot-wide wall adjacent to the refrigerator (‘refrigerator wall’). The second wall forming the “longer” part of the L (‘hallway wall’) is the wall which has the cabinetry affixed to it. It is about 15 feet long.

On the exterior wall which houses the sink and stove, there is a bulkhead running along the wall (‘bulkhead wall’) from the living room area to the kitchen. I have included a diagram for ease of understanding (note: not to scale/proportion).

The Tenant states that a portion of the drywall fell from the bulkhead. He alleges it was wet and the toilet running was the reason the drywall came away from that area. In addition, the Tenant reports that the drywall adjacent to the refrigerator had become saturated to the extent that it was sagging. He explains he knows that the toilet was the issue because whenever the toilet was flushed, raw sewage could be seen running down the walls moments later. He states that the sewage was observed along the hallway wall, the refrigerator wall, and the bulkhead wall.

The Tenant says he told the Landlord right after he moved in on approximately November 14, 2024. Again, I believe the Tenant misspoke and meant to specify September 14, 2024, rather than November 14, 2024. The Tenants say the toilet was fixed on September 28 or 29, and it was not until October 24, 2024, that repairs were completed to the walls. During this time, the Tenants say they could not use their kitchen and that it was unsanitary and unsafe.

The Tenants did access their own insurance who provided compensation for items which were ruined by the sewage and also sent in their own team to conduct a proper cleaning of the biohazardous materials and mold remediation. The Tenant said this was done on about October 1, 2024.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘JJ’), testified that he is the Capital Projects Supervisor for the Landlord. He does not personally oversee the assignment of work orders but would interact with the staff who not only assign the work orders but carry out the repairs needed to the rental units.

Submitted into evidence was a copy of a workorder from the Tenants (Doc-8120449, Ex.1, pg. 2). It is dated September 26, 2024. JJ explains that the workorder was created after the Tenant called into the after-hours emergency line the night before. Within the body of the document, it states: “Ongoing toilet issue that’s leaking to livingroom [sic] below. Not urgent but wants someone there asap.”

The workorder was given to the maintenance fellow, ‘[name]”, who attended the unit that day along with another maintenance worker, ‘Dwayne.’ At that time, the maintenance workers did not observe any active leaks despite running the tub and flushing the toilet. However, they did observe a hole in the ceiling where the bulkhead was and the drywall which had fallen onto the floor. They offered to clean up the area, but the Tenants were not satisfied with this because they were concerned about raw sewage which would require proper biohazard protocols.
The maintenance workers reattended on September 26, 2024, and did not observe any active leaks.

It is not clear to me the exact date, however, sometime between September 26 and September 29, 2024, the Tenant again called the after-hours emergency line to demand that the Landlord have the mess cleaned up and the biohazards addressed. A second work order was submitted into evidence.

The Landlord attended the next day with cleaning supplies for the Tenants. On September 30, 2024, the Landlords attended with a plumber. The plumber snaked the drain, replaced the flange and the wax seal. The plumbers did not find any sources of active leaks, but replaced the seal, which is necessary every time you remove a toilet, and snaked the drain and replaced the flange as a precaution. They also noticed some cracking around the bathtub caulking which was also addressed.

I note that there is a discrepancy in the evidence about date of the plumbers’ visit. JJ’s testimony was that the plumbers attended on September 29, 2024. However, the invoice indicates it was September 30, 2024. Regardless, I accept that the plumbers attended on one of these two dates. 27. [name] (‘MM’) also testified. He attended the rental unit on September 29, 2024, with the plumbers. He says he was in the living room and could see the bulkhead during the repair work. During this time, he did not see any visible signs of water although he observed a large hole in the bulkhead which accords with the Tenant’s evidence. 28. A large amount of cross-examination, particularly of JJ, focused on the refrigerator area. JJ and MM both testified that they believe that the area at the bottom of the refrigerator wall had been soaked in urine by the Tenants’ dogs, both of which are large breed. The only photo submitted into evidence appears to show that only 2 feet were affected at the bottom of the wall. 29. JJ’s testimony was that the joists in the refrigerator wall were no longer affixed to the floor. He believes this was due to age. So the drywall had to be removed because it had been wet and saturated with urine, but also because the joists needed to be repaired for the wall to be structurally safe. The same repairs were conducted to the hallway wall. JJ also submits that “spot tests” were done in other areas of drywall, for example, the wall nearest the kitchen which butted up against the bulkhead (see diagram above). Moisture readings were done and no moisture was detected. 30. The Tenant made a point of asking why there had been a yellow puddle underneath the fridge if there had not been a sewage issue. JJ’s testimony was that he believed the dogs had been urinating on the refrigerator wall and hallway wall because the damage and dampness was only observed on the bottom portion of the walls, and because the Tenant himself had stated, on September 29, 2024, that the dogs had been peeing in that area. Additionally, he reports that the plumber had commented to him that the rental unit smelled of animal waste. 31. The Tenant did clarify that he had said this, but that he also said it was because they already smelled urine in the area from the black water leak. 32. JJ also testified that the concern of a leak could not have affected the bulkhead area because there were no pipes over that area. However, the Landlord acknowledges there had been an area where plaster fell away from the ceiling. 33. JJ testified that this repair to the Tenants’ walls happened to coincide with an ongoing project to renovate the kitchens of multiple tenancies which included the Tenants’ unit. This work began on October 6 and concluded on October 10, 2024. The Landlord also sent a professional cleaning company to the Tenants’ home to clean it after the renovation was over. Analysis Date Service Was Requested 34. When I review the evidence before me, I am not persuaded that the Tenants told the Landlord of the need for maintenance for the toilet on September 14, 2024. Rather, I find that the first time the Tenants brought this to the attention of the Landlord was on the evening of September 24, 2024. The Tenant stated that the Landlord’s Representative understood he requested maintenance on September 14, 2024. However, even when he was given an opportunity to provide this evidence, with the Landlord’s consent, he was unable to point the Board to any documentary evidence to support his statement that he told the Landlord of the need for repairs as of September 14, 2024. 35. The best evidence available to me is the copy of the Landlord’s work orders. The Tenants did not submit any documentary evidence, such as a work order, that could corroborate the Tenant’s statement. The Tenant alluded to the fact he had told MM that the rental unit needed repairs but did not put this to him in cross-examination. JJ’s testimony was that the Tenants did not tell the Landlord about the leaking toilet nor submit a work order to that effect until September 24, 2024. 36. The work order itself is somewhat telling. The Tenant states that he was living with raw sewage flowing down the walls every time someone used the bathroom for weeks. However, when I review the work order, it says “not urgent but wants someone there asap.” This notation is important, because it was made contemporaneously, and I assign it significant weight. Effective, Timely, and [name] 37. Given that I find that the first time the Landlord was made aware of the requested maintenance was September 24, 2024, the next part of the analysis is whether the Landlord responded in a timely, effective, and reasonable manner. I find that they did. 38. The Landlord sent maintenance persons on September 25, 2024, to check the site. They did not observe any active leaks and offered to clean up the mess. They reattended on September 26, 2024, and again did not observe any active leaks. They provided cleaning supplies on September 27, 2024. On September 29, 2024, they attended again with plumbers. The repairs conducted were precautionary as the plumbers did not observe any active leaks. 39. Multiple individuals attended the rental unit. First, it was [name] and [name]. Then JJ and MM and then two plumbers. None of them observed any sewage nor any wet drywall or leaking. MM testified he was in the room looking at the ceiling while the plumbers flushed the toilet about 30 times. He did not observe any water. JJ testified there are no pipes in that area. 40. The only area that did appear to be damaged and wet was the hallway and refrigerator walls. However, based on the photo and the area of the damage, the lower 2 feet of the wall, the evidence is consistent with the Landlord’s theory that the dogs may have caused the damage. If the saturation was significant enough, it is also possible that the yellow liquid under the Tenants’ fridge was urine from the dogs. The spot tests, done on the wall which was just a few feet away from the refrigerator wall showed no signs of moisture. 41. Even if I am wrong and the Tenants’ dogs did not cause the damage to the hallway and refrigerator walls, and the problem was due to the toilet leaking, the Landlord still repaired the toilet, repaired the joists, and replaced the drywall. 42. The Tenants’ evidence was they were able to procure biohazard clean up through their insurance company who attended on or about October 1, 2024. However, the Tenants did not submit any evidence to support whether any testing was conducted, or which explained any of the insurers findings. Thus, I do not find the Tenants led sufficient evidence to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the toilet leaked and that this led to raw sewage running down the Tenants’ walls. 43. The Landlord had contractors attend to repair the damaged walls and bulkhead. The kitchen renovation was then done and completed in early October, after which the Landlord sent a professional cleaning company to clean the Tenants’ unit. JJ also testified that the Tenants’ fridge and stove were working throughout the entire period. Although it may have been challenging to use the kitchen during the renovation period, especially, there is no evidence to support that the Tenants could not continue to use their kitchen. 44. It is not disputed that there was some sort of problem involving the Tenants’ bulkhead, although it is unclear what caused it. There was a fairly large hole observed by MM. I do not doubt that there was some sort of problem in the Tenants’ rental unit. But the Landlord’s sent maintenance staff to check the area and offered to clean the area up. They then brought cleaning supplies to the Tenants and re-attended with plumbers. If there had been a leak with the toilet, it was repaired within four business days. The Tenants told the Landlord on the evening of September 24th; the problem was fixed on September 29, 2024. 45. In my view, and given the Divisional Court’s guidance in Onyskiw, the Landlord responded in a timely, effective, and reasonable manner. 46. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute that the Tenant received a notice of termination pursuant to section 48 of the Act. The Landlords served the notice indicating that they require the rental unit for their child’s residential occupation for a period of at least one year. The Tenant vacated December 31, 2022, as a result of that notice.

For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant did not prove that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Reverse Onus:
As explained below, I do not find that the rebuttable presumption is engaged pursuant to subsection 57(5) of the Act. Therefore, the burden of proof remains the Tenant’s.

Subsection 57(5) says that it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection 6 the landlord: (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

There is no dispute that the Landlords own multiple apartment buildings- the Tenant relied on advertisements during the prescribed period, however, none of them were the rental unit subject to this application. There was no reliable evidence presented by the Tenant to establish that the Landlords engaged in any of the activities described above. Therefore, I do not find that the rebuttable presumption applies in this case.

The Tenant’s legal representative [name] testified at the hearing that while in the role of the Tenant’s legal representative, they did some of their own “research” to determine whether or not the Landlords’ child moved into the rental unit. They testified that within the year after the Tenant vacated, there were packages delivered to the rental unit to a person named [name]. [name] also testified that she had a call with [name] on July 23, 2024, who confirmed that she resided in the rental unit, that the Landlords’ son’s belongings were also stored there, but that he never really resided there. [name] did not attend the hearing to provide testimony and the package was dated in April 2024, which was outside of the prescribed period.

The Tenant relied on a series of text messages between their spouse and another Tenant who also resided in the same residential complex. That person did not testify at the hearing. The entire conversation was entered into evidence for consideration. Essentially the text message conversation was over the period of several months and it described that there were 2 females who were predominantly staying and/or residing in the rental unit and that they never witnessed the Landlord’s son at the residential complex.

The Tenant also called A.G as a witness, who is a paralegal that completed a series of searches of the Landlord’s son drivers abstract and licence plate registration with the Ministry of Transportation. The searches show that the Landlord’s son did not change the address registered to their vehicle or plates from the Landlords address. The date of these searches was July 8, 2024 (outside of the prescribed period).

M.S who was the person in which the notice was given on behalf of. They attended the hearing to provide testimony. They stated that they moved in sometime in January 2023, after the Tenant vacated. They painted and got the place ready to occupy. He stated that they needed the rental unit to stay with their girlfriend and it was close to the go station and needed it to commute to a post secondary trades program. The Landlords relied on receipts that were purchased for the rental unit (different furnishings like beds, mattresses etc).

M.S testified that Cristabell was his partner’s friend who would stay with them from time to time to keep his partner company due to his busy schedule. M.S also testified that his vehicle was used only for work and that the corporation business address was registered to the Landlords residence, which is why it was not changed when he moved. He stated that although he no longer resided with the Landlords, the company’s address did not change- therefore, there was no need to update his plates or vehicle registration.

M.S was subject to a rigorous cross examination. They provided reasonable explanations with respect to the other people residing or being present in the rental unit (partner and partner’s friend, guests and roommates), their vehicle registration not being updated (work), why the other Tenant may not have seen him around the rental unit (work schedule). Therefore, I find his testimony creditable and reliable.

Although there was evidence presented that may put into question whether M.S actually resided there- that evidence is at best indirect or circumstantial- it was either outside of the prescribed period or the people involved in the different conversations either with the Tenant, their spouse or [name], were not called to present direct evidence.

Based on the above I find that the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to find on a balance of probabilities that no person referred to in the notice moved into the rental unit or that the notice was given in bad faith. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed because the Tenant did not follow the Interim Order issued on May 12, 2026, which directed the Tenant to serve the Landlord with a Notice of Hearing and the Tenant failed to do so.
The matter was heard on April 9, 2026. Only the Tenant, and the Tenant’s Agent, attended the hearing.

At that hearing, an Interim Order was issued on May 12, 2026. Under the determinations, the Member stated that she was not satisfied the Purchaser nor Landlord were served with the Notice of Hearing. In paragraph 4 of the Order, the Tenant was ordered to serve the Landlord with the new Notice of Hearing along with any attached information sheets, within five (5) days of its receipt. Under paragraph 5 of the Order, the Tenant was ordered to file a Certificate of Service indicating the Tenant served the Notice of Hearing to the Landlord.

At this hearing, the Tenant says that he has not been able to locate the Purchaser. The Tenant says that the original Landlord disappeared and that he was served with the N12 from “[organization]”. Since the last hearing held on April 9, 2026, he was able to locate who he believed to be the Landlord, [name], from CMI Group. The Tenant says on May 14, 2026, he emailed the Landlord his evidence including the application.
The new Notice of Hearing for this hearing, was mailed and emailed to the Tenant on May 20, 2026.

In paragraph 11 of the Interim Order, it states that: If the Tenant fails to serve the Landlord and submit the corresponding Certificates of Service in accordance with paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 of this order, the Board may dismiss the Tenant’s application.

There is no evidence before me that the Tenant emailed or mailed the new Notice of Hearing to the Landlord in accordance with paragraph 4 of the Interim Order, nor did the Tenant file a certificate of service in accordance with section 5 of the Interim Order.

As the Tenant failed to serve the Landlord with the new Notice of Hearing and failed to file a certificate of service in accordance with paragraphs 4 and 5 of the Interim Order, in accordance with paragraph 11 of the Interim Order, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. The Tenant offered no reasonable explanation as to why the Tenant failed to serve the Landlord with the new Notice of Hearing.
