issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven that the water appearing on the bathroom floor or the alleged mold resulted from the Landlord’s failure to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The application is therefore dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence:

The Tenant testified that she has lived in the rental unit since April 2014. She testified that she began experiencing water around the bathtub and on the bathroom floor and submitted numerous work orders concerning the issue beginning in 2022.

The Tenant stated that water would sometimes appear near the corner of the bathtub and, on some occasions, pool toward the middle of the bathroom floor. She also observed discoloration around the bathtub, on the bathroom ceiling, and in the closet adjoining the bathroom, which she believed was mold.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord generally responded after she submitted work orders between 2022 and June 2026. Contractors repaired and painted bathroom walls, re-caulked the bathtub, repaired the adjoining closet, opened part of the bathroom wall to investigate the source of the water, and installed splash guards. However, the Tenant maintained that the source of the water was never identified and that the condition continued.

The Tenant also testified that she took precautions when using the shower, including ensuring that the shower curtain was properly closed and reducing the length and temperature of showers. She also attempted to clean the areas where she observed discoloration but stated that the condition returned.
With respect to the alleged mold around the bathtub, the Tenant submitted photographs showing black staining or spots around the faucet area. The Tenant did not obtain a professional mold assessment.

The Tenant relied on photographs and videos showing water on the bathroom floor and discoloration around the bathtub. She testified that she showed some of this material to the Landlord’s contractors. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord repeatedly repaired the visible damage without identifying and repairing the underlying source of the water. Landlord’s Evidence: 8. [name], the Property Manager for the residential complex, testified at the hearing. [name] stated that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints and sent contractors to the rental unit on numerous occasions. 9. Between 2022 and 2026, the Landlord’s contractors repaired drywall and baseboards, re- caulked the bathtub, repaired the adjoining closet, painted the bathroom, opened part of the wall to inspect the plumbing, and installed splash guards on the bathtub. 10. The Landlord also retained GTA Plumbing, a third-party contractor, to investigate the alleged leak. [name] testified that the plumbing company ran water from the bathtub and shower and inspected the plumbing, including while part of the wall was open. No active plumbing leak, spraying, or dripping was observed. 11. The Landlord also relied on a City of Mississauga inspection conducted on April 11, 2024. The municipal inspector did not observe water leaking in the bathroom. The City identified repairs required to the bathroom wall and the adjoining closet wall. [name] testified that those repairs were subsequently completed. 12. The Landlord’s position is that the water was more likely escaping from the bathtub during shower use. The Landlord relied on the location of the water, the shower curtain, the handheld shower device, and the absence of any plumbing defect identified by the contractors, GTA Plumbing, or the municipal inspector. 13. With respect to mold, [name] testified that the Landlord’s staff and contractors did not observe mold in the bathroom. The Landlord’s position is that the discoloration around the bathtub was surface mildew associated with moisture and ordinary bathroom use. Law and Analysis: 14. Subsection 20(1) of the Act requires a landlord to maintain a residential complex and the rental units within it in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with applicable health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards. 15. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health or maintenance standards. 16. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 17. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that water repeatedly appeared on the bathroom floor during showers and that she made numerous complaints to the Landlord. I also accept that the Tenant observed recurring discoloration around the bathtub areas that she believed to be mold. 18. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the water resulted from a plumbing defect or another maintenance condition for which the Landlord was responsible. 19. The evidence establishes that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaints on numerous occasions within a reasonable time. The Landlord inspected the bathroom, repaired damaged walls and baseboards, re-caulked the bathtub, repaired the adjoining closet, opened the wall to inspect the plumbing, and installed splash guards. 20. The Landlord also retained a professional plumbing company to investigate the alleged leak. The plumbing was inspected while water was running from the bathtub and shower, and no active leak was identified. The municipal inspector also did not observe water leaking from the location identified by the Tenant. 21. The Tenant’s photographs and videos establish that water was present on the bathroom floor. However, they do not establish the source of that water. On the question of whether there was an active plumbing leak, I prefer the evidence of the plumbing investigations and the municipal inspection. 22. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the discoloration she observed was mold caused by an unresolved maintenance defect. The Tenant did not provide a professional mold assessment or other evidence identifying the substance or connecting it to a plumbing defect. The municipal inspector did not identify an active leak or require mold remediation in the bathroom. 23. Considering the evidence as a whole and applying the contextual approach in Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord responded reasonably to the Tenant’s complaints. The Landlord investigated the alleged leak, retained a professional plumbing company, completed repairs, complied with the municipal inspector’s requested repairs, and took additional steps to address water escaping from the bathtub area. 24. I therefore find that the Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that the water appearing on the bathroom floor or the alleged mold resulted from the Landlord’s failure to meet the maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] VadWeerd (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’). • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential • complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (the ‘T2 Application’). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’).
reasons: For the reasons provided below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $4,424.46 to the Tenant. Evidence and Submissions

The tenancy began on or about October 18, 2024. The Tenant rented the basement unit at the residential complex. The Tenant testified that he was attending Mohawk College and working multiple jobs at the time he entered into the tenancy. He stated that it was convenient for him to reside at the rental unit while he was attending school.

The Tenant signed the Landlord’s agreement called “Basic Agreement”. The parties agreed that the monthly rent would be $850.00. It is undisputed that the Tenant paid $1,700.00, for the first and last month's rent.

Shortly after moving into the rental unit, the Tenant informed the Landlord regarding the following issues: the shower door would not close properly; flickering lights; inadequate ventilation; defects with the window and ceiling; and dampness, humidity and temperature issues in the unit. The Landlord acknowledged that the shower door was defective but informed the Tenant that replacing the door would be expensive.

Further, the Tenant alleges that during the tenancy: The Landlord entered the rental unit without notice approximately on three or four occasions; and the Landlord repeatedly complained about the Tenant’s cooking, stating that it smelled “gross” and informed him to keep the window open. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s comments caused him stress and interfered with his enjoyment of the rental unit.

On October 25, 2024, the Tenant removed some of his belongings from the unit and went to stay temporarily with his mother while he was working. The Tenant testified that he left his personal property in the unit because he intended to return back to the unit. The Tenant stated that he had not moved out or informed the Landlord that he was terminating his tenancy. However, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant stating: “Apt repairs R completed it seems U’ve moved out ….plz confirm” We’ve removed the very smelly garbage…”
On October 26, 2024, the Tenant replied: “I worked last night I worked today, working tonight, and working tomorrow. I won’t be able to see you till Monday the earliest. I’ll talk to you soon.”
The Landlord responded: “Uve completely abandoned the Apt; locks R changed.”

The Tenant testified that he occupied the rental unit for approximately one week. On October 26, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks and denied the Tenant access to the rental unit. The Landlord did not provide replacement keys or a new access code to the Tenant. The Landlord also did not return the Tenant’s rent deposit or the remaining three weeks of rent for October 2024 that he had paid the Landlord. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25

On October 27, 2024, the Landlord alleged that the Tenant’s father threatened her. The Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant which states: “provided a police report in anticipation of a restraining order against U, as might be required if U try access w/o prior permission to commit further property theft.”

During the hearing, the Landlord did not produce a restraining order or a police report. The Tenant testified that he believed the Landlord had contacted the police and obtained a restraining order so he did not attempt to return to the rental unit. He later learned that no restraining order had been obtained. Analysis and Reasons for the Decision
I am not satisfied that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit on October 26, 2024.

Pursuant to s.2(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’), “a tenant has not abandoned a rental unit if the tenant is not in arrears of rent.” Here, the Tenant had paid both first and last month’s rent and was not in arrears. Further, even though the Tenant removed some of his belongings from the unit, he left personal property behind, expressly advised the Landlord that he would speak to her on Monday, and never served a notice terminating his tenancy. The evidence before me does not establish an intention on the part of the Tenant to permanently give up possession of the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not abandon the tenancy.

Section 24 of the Act says that “a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

In the present case, the Tenant never regained possession of the rental unit. There is no evidence that the tenancy had terminated or that the Tenant had surrendered possession of the rental unit. The Landlord did not challenge the fact that locks were changed on October 26, 2026. Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on October 26, 2026, when the Landlord changed the locks and never provided the Tenant with replacement keys or a new access code.
I also find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful right to occupy the rental unit by illegally locking the Tenant out contrary to s. 24 of the Act.

The Tenant paid the Landlord $[name], for the first and last month's rent. The Tenant occupied the rental unit for approximately one week. The Landlord was not entitled to retain the last month's rent deposit after unilaterally terminating the tenancy and preventing the Tenant from continuing his occupation of the rental unit. Therefore, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant the last month's rent deposit of $850.00.

I also find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to interest for the period of October 18, 2024 to October 26, 2024 in the amount of $0.46. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25 Tenant’s T2 Application

Section 22 of the Act provides that “a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

The Tenant referred to his text messages with the Landlord, he testified that throughout the first week that he resided in the unit, the Landlord repeatedly commented on his cooking, warned him about damage to the unit, and informed him to keep the windows open because of his cooking. The Tenant testified that these comments were made on multiple occasions during his short tenancy and made him feel unwelcome in the rental unit. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord repeatedly complained about the Tenant’s cooking and warned him about causing damage to the unit, which substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I also accept that the Landlord’s comments made the Tenant feel stress and anxiety. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit contrary to s. 22 of the Act.

With respect to the Tenant’s claim for illegal entries, the Tenant testified that the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice on three or four occasions between October 18, 2024 to October 25, 2024. However, the Tenant was unable to provide dates or sufficient details regarding those alleged entries. As for the Landlord’s conduct on October 26, 2024, when the Landlord changed the locks and denied the Tenant access to the rental unit, I have addressed the Landlord’s conduct above in paragraphs 12-16. In the absence of sufficient particulars regarding the alleged entries between October 18-25, 2024, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, this portion of the application is dismissed.

During the hearing the Tenant requested to withdraw remedies 5, 6, and 9 from the T2 application. I granted the Tenant’s request. The Tenant indicated that he is claiming the following remedies under the T2 application: [name] 1: Rent Abatement I find it reasonable to award the Tenant $850.00 in rent abatement given the reasons in paragraphs 19 and 20. I am satisfied that this amount is appropriate because the Tenant resided in the unit for only one week and during the week the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedy 3: Administrative Fine to the Board Administrative fines are intended to promote compliance and deter future misconduct where other remedies are insufficient. Given the compensation award to the Tenant, I am satisfied that this order provides adequate deterrence. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25 Remedy 4: Termination of Tenancy Reasons given in paragraphs 12 to 15. [name] 7: Moving and Storage Expenses The Tenant claims $80.00 for car expenses and gas. The Tenant testified that he incurred travel expenses as a result of the lockout. The Tenant testified that he incurred these expenses travelling between his mother's residence, work, and the rental unit in an attempt to address the lockout and recover his belongings. While the Tenant did not have receipts for these expenses, I found his testimony to be credible. I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred these expenses as a direct result of the Landlord's unlawful conduct. Accordingly, I find it reasonable to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant moving expenses of $80.00. Remedy 8: Out of pocket expenses The Tenant claims that he incurred $50 at “local laundry mat because the supplied washer and dryer didn't work which was part of the monthly rent.” The Tenant testified that the washer dryer advertised as part of the tenancy was not operational, as a result he was required to use a laundry mat during his tenancy. I find there was insufficient evidence to establish that the washer or dryer did not work. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established this claim on the balance of probabilities. This remedy is denied. Remedy 11: Other Remedies The Tenant seeks compensation for anxiety, loss of employment income, tuition/textbook expenses, and losses associated with his studies. The Tenant alleges that the illegal lockout caused him significant emotional distress, required him to move further away from Mohawk College, and resulted in reduced work hours and eventually caused him to lose his employment. The Tenant referred to his evidence in which he seeks $6,371.00 for income loss and $2,500 for tuition loss. Although I accept the Landlord's unlawful lockout caused the Tenant stress and anxiety, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established the full amount claimed under this remedy on a balance of probabilities as a direct result of the Landlord’s conduct. However, having regard to the distress, convenience and uncertainty caused by the Landlords unlawful lockout, I find that an award of $2,500.00 in general damages is appropriate. [name]

The Tenant amended his T6 application, he seeks a rent abatement of $164.52 for “loss of use/rental value for specific days.” “Due to severe interference with reasonable enjoyment and loss of essential (vital) services and facilities including heat and loss of use of amenities.” File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25

The Tenant testified that the shower door did not properly close, causing water to escape onto the floor. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that shortly after moving into the rental unit he informed the Landlord regarding the shower door, flickering lights, inadequate ventilation, dampness, humidity and temperature issues. I further accept that the Landlord acknowledged that the shower door was defective and informed the Tenant that replacing it would be expensive. A shower curtain was used to address the issue.

Although there was limited evidence regarding the maintenance issues, I am satisfied that at least some of the conditions complained of existed and that the Landlord failed to adequately address them during the tenancy. However, I declined to award a further rent abatement of $164.52 because the Tenant has been awarded the full abatement of the rent paid for the period that he occupied the rental unit, see paragraph 22 ([name] 1). Accordingly, no further rent abatement can be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,424.46. This amount represents: • $850.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • 0.46 Interest on the last month’s rent deposit; • $850.00 for rent abatement; • $80.00 for moving expenses; • $2,500.00 for general compensation or other remedies; and • $144.00 ($48.00 [name]) for the cost of filing the T1, T2, and T6 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, this application is dismissed as withdrawn.
The Tenants filed this herein T2 application on November 8, 2023, and testified they moved out of the rental unit on November 1, 2024, upon Board questioning.
The Tenants sought to amend their application and uploaded an amended T2 application to the Portal on February 2, 2026.

The relevant parts of Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure state the following: 15.1 A request to amend an application before the hearing must be: a. in writing; b. served with the amended application to all other parties; and c. filed with LTB with the amended application and a completed Certificate of Service. 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors. 15.4 The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

Rule 15.3 specifically requires that a Board Member consider and then grant or deny any requested amendments. The Tenants did provide the aforementioned email requesting amendments be made to the contents of the Tenants’ T2 application and remedies to be included to the Board on February 2, 2026, and had provided a copy of an email that the amended T2 application was allegedly emailed to the Landlord on February 3, 2026 (which is not proper service pursuant to the Board’s Rules), nor was a completed Certificate of Service filed as required under Rule 15.1.

That being said, amendments are intended to correct an error i.e. to discreet event and instances and or to add further sufficient details, not to include new issues/causes of action and new monetary remedies that were not included in the original application, over two years after the original application was filed. In my view, an amendment to include new causes of action and remedies that were not included in the original application and did not form the basis of the original application is an improper attempt to circumvent the established process in which parties advance their claims before the Board, and further an attempt to curtail the limitation period for the new causes of action and remedies sought.
As a result of all of the above, I denied the Tenants’ request to amend their application.

The Tenants argued that they were laypersons and were not aware of the requirements of Rule 15 until their appearance in front of the Board on November 12, 2025. I note even if this was the case, they took an additional 2.5 months to seek to file and allegedly serve an amended T2 application.

The Board can assist parties by providing general information as needed, however the Board does not act as a legal representative for either party and consequently, it is the Applicant’s, in this case the Tenants responsibility to ensure that the application is complete and in compliance with the Act. I note that the Tenants could have contacted Tenant Duty Counsel prior to or after this first appearance in front of the Board on October 23, 2024, and to argue the reason for the delay in preparing an amended application was a result of both not being aware and Board scheduling delays is not sufficient nor proper.

It is not for the Board to assist the Tenants in completing their application by adding new causes of action and remedies or correcting deficiencies via an amendment request. As with all applications before the Board, it is the Applicant who must bring an application that meets minimum requirements. Although, the Tenants original T2 application does meet the minimum requirements, it would seem that 20 months after vacating the rental unit they seek to include new causes of action and monetary remedies not sought initially.

The Tenants amendments to their T2 application were not granted for the above- mentioned reasons. The Tenants were provided the opportunity to proceed with their original T2 application as filed, but instead sought to withdraw this herein application, and I consented to the withdrawal of the same, which the Landlord’s Legal Representative did not oppose.
ordered: The Tenants T2 application is dismissed as withdrawn. July 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] VadWeerd (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’). • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential • complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (the ‘T2 Application’). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’).
reasons: For the reasons provided below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $4,424.46 to the Tenant. Evidence and Submissions

The tenancy began on or about October 18, 2024. The Tenant rented the basement unit at the residential complex. The Tenant testified that he was attending Mohawk College and working multiple jobs at the time he entered into the tenancy. He stated that it was convenient for him to reside at the rental unit while he was attending school.

The Tenant signed the Landlord’s agreement called “Basic Agreement”. The parties agreed that the monthly rent would be $850.00. It is undisputed that the Tenant paid $1,700.00, for the first and last month's rent.

Shortly after moving into the rental unit, the Tenant informed the Landlord regarding the following issues: the shower door would not close properly; flickering lights; inadequate ventilation; defects with the window and ceiling; and dampness, humidity and temperature issues in the unit. The Landlord acknowledged that the shower door was defective but informed the Tenant that replacing the door would be expensive.

Further, the Tenant alleges that during the tenancy: The Landlord entered the rental unit without notice approximately on three or four occasions; and the Landlord repeatedly complained about the Tenant’s cooking, stating that it smelled “gross” and informed him to keep the window open. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s comments caused him stress and interfered with his enjoyment of the rental unit.

On October 25, 2024, the Tenant removed some of his belongings from the unit and went to stay temporarily with his mother while he was working. The Tenant testified that he left his personal property in the unit because he intended to return back to the unit. The Tenant stated that he had not moved out or informed the Landlord that he was terminating his tenancy. However, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant stating: “Apt repairs R completed it seems U’ve moved out ….plz confirm” We’ve removed the very smelly garbage…”
On October 26, 2024, the Tenant replied: “I worked last night I worked today, working tonight, and working tomorrow. I won’t be able to see you till Monday the earliest. I’ll talk to you soon.”
The Landlord responded: “Uve completely abandoned the Apt; locks R changed.”

The Tenant testified that he occupied the rental unit for approximately one week. On October 26, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks and denied the Tenant access to the rental unit. The Landlord did not provide replacement keys or a new access code to the Tenant. The Landlord also did not return the Tenant’s rent deposit or the remaining three weeks of rent for October 2024 that he had paid the Landlord. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25

On October 27, 2024, the Landlord alleged that the Tenant’s father threatened her. The Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant which states: “provided a police report in anticipation of a restraining order against U, as might be required if U try access w/o prior permission to commit further property theft.”

During the hearing, the Landlord did not produce a restraining order or a police report. The Tenant testified that he believed the Landlord had contacted the police and obtained a restraining order so he did not attempt to return to the rental unit. He later learned that no restraining order had been obtained. Analysis and Reasons for the Decision
I am not satisfied that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit on October 26, 2024.

Pursuant to s.2(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’), “a tenant has not abandoned a rental unit if the tenant is not in arrears of rent.” Here, the Tenant had paid both first and last month’s rent and was not in arrears. Further, even though the Tenant removed some of his belongings from the unit, he left personal property behind, expressly advised the Landlord that he would speak to her on Monday, and never served a notice terminating his tenancy. The evidence before me does not establish an intention on the part of the Tenant to permanently give up possession of the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not abandon the tenancy.

Section 24 of the Act says that “a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

In the present case, the Tenant never regained possession of the rental unit. There is no evidence that the tenancy had terminated or that the Tenant had surrendered possession of the rental unit. The Landlord did not challenge the fact that locks were changed on October 26, 2026. Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on October 26, 2026, when the Landlord changed the locks and never provided the Tenant with replacement keys or a new access code.
I also find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful right to occupy the rental unit by illegally locking the Tenant out contrary to s. 24 of the Act.

The Tenant paid the Landlord $[name], for the first and last month's rent. The Tenant occupied the rental unit for approximately one week. The Landlord was not entitled to retain the last month's rent deposit after unilaterally terminating the tenancy and preventing the Tenant from continuing his occupation of the rental unit. Therefore, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant the last month's rent deposit of $850.00.

I also find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to interest for the period of October 18, 2024 to October 26, 2024 in the amount of $0.46. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25 Tenant’s T2 Application

Section 22 of the Act provides that “a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

The Tenant referred to his text messages with the Landlord, he testified that throughout the first week that he resided in the unit, the Landlord repeatedly commented on his cooking, warned him about damage to the unit, and informed him to keep the windows open because of his cooking. The Tenant testified that these comments were made on multiple occasions during his short tenancy and made him feel unwelcome in the rental unit. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord repeatedly complained about the Tenant’s cooking and warned him about causing damage to the unit, which substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I also accept that the Landlord’s comments made the Tenant feel stress and anxiety. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit contrary to s. 22 of the Act.

With respect to the Tenant’s claim for illegal entries, the Tenant testified that the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice on three or four occasions between October 18, 2024 to October 25, 2024. However, the Tenant was unable to provide dates or sufficient details regarding those alleged entries. As for the Landlord’s conduct on October 26, 2024, when the Landlord changed the locks and denied the Tenant access to the rental unit, I have addressed the Landlord’s conduct above in paragraphs 12-16. In the absence of sufficient particulars regarding the alleged entries between October 18-25, 2024, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, this portion of the application is dismissed.

During the hearing the Tenant requested to withdraw remedies 5, 6, and 9 from the T2 application. I granted the Tenant’s request. The Tenant indicated that he is claiming the following remedies under the T2 application: [name] 1: Rent Abatement I find it reasonable to award the Tenant $850.00 in rent abatement given the reasons in paragraphs 19 and 20. I am satisfied that this amount is appropriate because the Tenant resided in the unit for only one week and during the week the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedy 3: Administrative Fine to the Board Administrative fines are intended to promote compliance and deter future misconduct where other remedies are insufficient. Given the compensation award to the Tenant, I am satisfied that this order provides adequate deterrence. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25 Remedy 4: Termination of Tenancy Reasons given in paragraphs 12 to 15. [name] 7: Moving and Storage Expenses The Tenant claims $80.00 for car expenses and gas. The Tenant testified that he incurred travel expenses as a result of the lockout. The Tenant testified that he incurred these expenses travelling between his mother's residence, work, and the rental unit in an attempt to address the lockout and recover his belongings. While the Tenant did not have receipts for these expenses, I found his testimony to be credible. I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred these expenses as a direct result of the Landlord's unlawful conduct. Accordingly, I find it reasonable to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant moving expenses of $80.00. Remedy 8: Out of pocket expenses The Tenant claims that he incurred $50 at “local laundry mat because the supplied washer and dryer didn't work which was part of the monthly rent.” The Tenant testified that the washer dryer advertised as part of the tenancy was not operational, as a result he was required to use a laundry mat during his tenancy. I find there was insufficient evidence to establish that the washer or dryer did not work. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established this claim on the balance of probabilities. This remedy is denied. Remedy 11: Other Remedies The Tenant seeks compensation for anxiety, loss of employment income, tuition/textbook expenses, and losses associated with his studies. The Tenant alleges that the illegal lockout caused him significant emotional distress, required him to move further away from Mohawk College, and resulted in reduced work hours and eventually caused him to lose his employment. The Tenant referred to his evidence in which he seeks $6,371.00 for income loss and $2,500 for tuition loss. Although I accept the Landlord's unlawful lockout caused the Tenant stress and anxiety, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established the full amount claimed under this remedy on a balance of probabilities as a direct result of the Landlord’s conduct. However, having regard to the distress, convenience and uncertainty caused by the Landlords unlawful lockout, I find that an award of $2,500.00 in general damages is appropriate. [name]

The Tenant amended his T6 application, he seeks a rent abatement of $164.52 for “loss of use/rental value for specific days.” “Due to severe interference with reasonable enjoyment and loss of essential (vital) services and facilities including heat and loss of use of amenities.” File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25

The Tenant testified that the shower door did not properly close, causing water to escape onto the floor. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that shortly after moving into the rental unit he informed the Landlord regarding the shower door, flickering lights, inadequate ventilation, dampness, humidity and temperature issues. I further accept that the Landlord acknowledged that the shower door was defective and informed the Tenant that replacing it would be expensive. A shower curtain was used to address the issue.

Although there was limited evidence regarding the maintenance issues, I am satisfied that at least some of the conditions complained of existed and that the Landlord failed to adequately address them during the tenancy. However, I declined to award a further rent abatement of $164.52 because the Tenant has been awarded the full abatement of the rent paid for the period that he occupied the rental unit, see paragraph 22 ([name] 1). Accordingly, no further rent abatement can be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,424.46. This amount represents: • $850.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • 0.46 Interest on the last month’s rent deposit; • $850.00 for rent abatement; • $80.00 for moving expenses; • $2,500.00 for general compensation or other remedies; and • $144.00 ($48.00 [name]) for the cost of filing the T1, T2, and T6 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the Tenants the last month’s rent that is on deposit.

The Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord was provided with notice to terminate their tenancy effective September 30, 2025, but the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 17, 2025. The Tenants had provided the Landlord with a last month’s rent deposit at the start of the tenancy on July 27, 2021, in the amount of $1,195.00.

The Tenants uploaded and provided an email from the Landlord dated July 28, 2025, where the Landlord states the Tenants need to provide 60 days notice, but if the Landlord is able to find a new tenant, then the Landlord would be agreeable to terminate the tenancy with the notice the Tenants have provided.

The Tenant [name] testified that on September 12, 2025, an email was sent to the Landlord to arrange for the keys for the rental property to be dropped off, and the Landlord responded for the Tenants to just mail the keys to the Landlord directly. In addition, the Tenants emailed the Landlord on September 14, 2025, advising the Landlord they would be attending the rental unit to do a final inspection.

The Tenants uploaded and provided a response email from the Landlord dated September 15, 2025, confirming the Landlord re-rented out the unit and that the new tenants were already in possession of the rental unit.
I find that the Landlord re-rented out the unit sometime in September 2025, therefore the Landlord would have accepted the Tenants’ notice to terminate the tenancy.

In accordance with s. 106(10) of the Act, a landlord can only use a rent deposit to cover the rent for the last rental period. Since the rent for the last rental period was already paid, the deposit must be returned to the Tenants.

I find that the Tenants would have been responsible for rent up to and including the rental period of August 2025, as the Landlord re-rented out the unit in September 2025. The Tenants obligation to pay rent ended because their interest in the unit ended when the new tenancy began. Since August 2025 rent was already paid by the Tenants, the Landlord is required to provide the Tenants with their last month’s rent deposit as it was not applied to August 2025 rent.

Section 134(1.1) of the Act states: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.

Therefore, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Interest on rent deposit owing
The Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord failed to pay any interest on the last month’s rent deposit that was paid to the Landlord July 27, 2021.
Therefore, I find the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
I find that the Landlord owes the Tenants $70.40 for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit, and the calculation is noted below.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,320.13. This amount represents: • $1,195.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $77.13 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 5, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') - Collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) and; - Entered the rental unit illegally. - Substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. - Harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must T1 Application

It is undisputed that the Landlord collected a total of $3,100.00 from the Tenants for the lease that was set to begin September 1, 2025 for a fixed term of one year. The total amount is calculated as follows: i. $1,400.00 first month rent payment (September 2025) ii. $1,400.00 last month rent deposit iii. $300.00 refundable key deposit
As of the date of the hearing, the Landlord returned $2,400.00 to the Tenants.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 16, 2026.

The Tenants testified that on or about August 29, 2025 the Landlord advised the Tenants that there had been a change in their family’s circumstances and the Landlord would need vacant possession of the rental unit by November 2025. There is no dispute that the Landlord offered the Tenants a “rent free” period for September 2025 to entice the Tenants to move out as soon as possible. Analysis

Section 17 of O.Reg. 516/06 under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') permits a landlord to collect: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs

On the basis of the evidence provided I find that the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Act. The Landlord was entitled to collect the key deposit and the Landlord subsequently returned the key deposit albeit not until after the first hearing.

Subsection 106(1) of the Act permits a landlord to collect a rent deposit. Subsection 106(10) requires the rent deposit be only applied to the last month of the tenancy. In this case, the last month of the tenancy was September 2025. Since the Landlord waived the rent for September 2025, I find that the Landlord ought to have returned the rent deposit and therefore, the Tenants are owed $1,400.00 for the period of September 1, 2025 to September 30, 2025.

The amount owing from the total amount collected by the Landlord from the Tenants is $700.00. The Tenants are entitled to this amount and the Landlord will be ordered to return that amount to the Tenants. T2 Application Illegal entry

On September 3, 2025 the Landlord attended the rental unit and demanded the Tenants remove their belongings from the rental unit due to an inspection by the city. The Tenant JS testified that he opened the door to the Landlord but the Landlord did not enter the rental unit. Since the Landlord did not enter the rental unit, the Tenants’ claim for illegal entry must be denied. Substantial interference

JS testified that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Specifically: a. On August 29, 2025 when the Landlord advised the Tenants of the change of plans for the rental unit and reneged the year term lease agreement. b. On September 3, 2025 when the Landlord attended the property and demanded the Tenants remove their belongings from the rental unit into the garage in advance of a city inspection.

When the Tenants signed the lease agreement, they understood there would be a fixed term lease for one year. The Landlord almost immediately reneged the agreement which, JS testified, left the Tenants in a state of disarray and anxiety of not having stable housing.

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit … substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Based on the undisputed testimony of the Tenants, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenants. But for the Landlord’s actions, the Tenants would have had stable housing for at least one year. Harassment, etc.

JS testified that on August 29, 2025 during a phone call with the Landlord, the Landlord raised his voice while discussing the need for the Tenants to vacate the rental unit. 16. [name] testified that on September 10, 2025 during a phone call with the Landlord, the Landlord raise his voice while pressuring the Tenants to vacate the rental unit. 17. I have reviewed the audio evidence provided by the Tenants. Based on the audio recordings I am not persuaded that the Landlord was raising his voice. Rather it was two parties having discussions regarding terminating a lease. 18. Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 19. [name] is not defined in the Act; I turn to the Ontario Human Rights Code’s definition of harassment: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” 20. Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am not satisfied the conduct of the Landlord rises to a level of harassment. Therefore, the Tenants claim for harassment is denied. Remedies 21. I am satisfied the Tenants have proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Furthermore, the actions of the Landlord forced the Tenants to move out of the rental unit on short notice. 22. The Tenants testified the rent at their new rental unit is $200.00 more per month. Therefore, the Tenants will incur increased rent of $2,400.00 for a one-year period after the Tenant left the rental unit. 23. The Tenants submit they paid $28.20 for transportation rental from Home Depot to move to the new rental unit and paid a “local” mover $40.00 cash to help with the move. I find this amount to be reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses of $68.20.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants are $3,221.20. This amount represents: • $700.00 for the remaining amount of the last month's rent deposit. • $2,400.00 in increased rent at the new rental unit. • $68.20 in moving expenses. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by August 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlords’) and [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords Agents') entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application – LTB-T-089267-23) The Landlord, [name], applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes (L1 Application – LTB-L-084769- 23).
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant reiterated her accommodation request to remove observers. LTB-L-084769-23-IN-2 Vice [name] directed the matters be heard in the absence of other matters. I found the request to be reasonable and therefore permitted a closed hearing. and LTB-L-084769-23

In LTB-L-084769-23-IN-2 the question of a publication ban and anonymization of an order is raised and is deferred to the hearing member. The Tenant did not raise these issues at the hearing, although she raised the request for a closed hearing, I find the request for publication ban and anonymization of an order was abandoned. [name]

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, a rent abatement in the amount of $600.00 has been deducted from the arrears owing as well as the filing fee associated with the cost of the Tenant’s Application. Rental Unit Description
For the reasons below, I find the Rental Unit is a bedroom with shared accommodations between tenants in the basement unit.

The Tenant testified she rented a “unit” from the Landlord in 2019 and submitted a lease (DOC-4845685, pages 295 – 314). In the lease the rental unit is described as “Basement Unit #3”. The lease has an addendum (page 313) and one condition in the addendum, specifically part 6 which states “The Tenant acknowledges the premises are video surveillance in public area.”. It is undisputed there was a video camera in the kitchen area of the residence which pointed toward the entrance to the basement.

Throughout her testimony, the Tenant asserted there were three bedrooms. She occupied one bedroom at the start of the tenancy in April of 2019 and then moved to a different bedroom in 2022. The other two bedrooms were otherwise rented to other tenants or were vacant throughout the tenancy.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony and the lease agreement provided, I find on a balance of probabilities the Rental Unit is a bedroom and the kitchen and bathroom were shared accommodations. Tenant’s Evidence

Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’) states: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant’s application was filed on November 26, 2023. The application claims allegations dating back to June 9, 2022. Pursuant to subsection 29(2) the only allegations the Board can consider are from November 26, 2022 and onward. As such, the allegations that predate November 26, 2022 were not heard or considered. The Tenant provided oral testimony and documentary evidence in support of her allegations.

On December 5, 2022 the property manager [name] (“[name]”) texted the Tenant at 3:33PM (DOC-4845685, page 59): and LTB-L-084769-23 “During the coming Christmas vacation period, we will have some one to do minor repairs in the basement. Not wanting to interrupt you, if you could advise me your going away/vacation time, if any, that will be greatly appreciated! Thank you in advance! [name]”

The Tenant testified this line of questioning was confusing to her as she had never requested any repairs. She confirmed with her roommate at the time that [name] had not asked him the same question. This made the Tenant feel uncomfortable.
The Tenant testified sometime between December 10 and December 16, 2022 someone entered the basement and did repairs in the bathroom.

On December 22, 2022 around 1:00PM as she was exiting the bathroom after having a shower, she heard someone attempting to open the basement door. She yelled for the person to not come in. When she got into the Rental Unit, she saw [name] was standing there. She texted [name] at 1:03PM “You can go back in” (DOC-4845685, page 62). [name] did not enter the basement and did not respond to the Tenant’s text message.
The Tenant testified she believed that [name] had access to the video camera in the shared accommodations and planned to be in the basement to intercept the Tenant while she was only in a towel.

On December 27, 2022 [name] ([name]) and [name] entered the basement and knocked on the Tenant’s door. The Tenant did not open the Rental Unit door. [name] and [name] inquired about her plans of staying in the Rental Unit for the holidays and she responded yes. They provided her with verbal notice that someone would be entering the basement the following day for washroom repairs.

The Tenant provided a text message exchange between herself and [name] on December 28, 2022 at 11:24AM (DOC-4845685, page 63): TT: What time is the person arriving to repair the washroom? [name]: In the afternoon. TT: What exact [time]? [name]: If you need to take a shower, please do now. He could come anytime.
The Tenant testified this comment from [name] about her taking a shower made her uncomfortable and confused.

On December 31, 2022 at 8:30PM [name] entered the basement and knocked on the Tenant’s bedroom door. Prior to knocking on her door, the Tenant heard [name] unplug the video camera in the basement. When the Tenant opened the door, [name] was holding a bottle of wine and stated it was a holiday gift for the Tenant. The Tenant testified [name] was making inappropriate comments and gestures of a salacious nature. She told [name] having alcohol is against her religion and closed the door. The Tenant testified this incident left her feeling very shocked and confused given the time of day and the advances made by [name]. and LTB-L-084769-23
In January 2023 a new roommate moved into one of the bedrooms in the basement. From then, any concerns regarding the basement went through the roommate to [name].

On May 5, 2023 at 7:53AM the Tenant texted [name] that there was an issue with a lightbulb and including a video of the light fixture above the stove in the kitchen (DOC-4845685, page 79). The Tenant asked [name] to come repair the issue between 10AM and 1PM. She then texted [name] the light fixed itself and no longer needed repair. [name] responded he will come to replace it “in a moment”. The Tenant again asked if he could come later. [name] responded “Why? Is it in the kitchen? Or your room?”. She confirmed it was the kitchen and [name] responded, “so you don’t have to dress up, no interruption to you.”.

The Tenant testified she wanted to be out of the basement when [name] was there as his presence made her uncomfortable. She felt [name]’s insistence to come right away, when he knew she would be in the basement, made her feel uncomfortable. She felt his comment about her dressing up was unwarranted. Ultimately, to her knowledge, the lightbulb was not replaced.

On May 22, 2023 at 5:35AM the Tenant texted [name] advising the electricity to the kitchen was not working (DOC-4845685, page 89). She testified that around 7:30AM [name] attending the basement and had a coffee for the Tenant. [name] was insistent that she take the coffee. [name] directed the Tenant to the circuit board and instructed her on how to flip the breaker. When the Tenant placed her finger on the breaker to confirm if that was the correct switch, [name] placed his finger on hers and confirmed that was the correct switch. The Tenant moved away and [name] continued to follow her while asking her questions about if she had intentions to vacate, about her studies, and continued to follow her as she exited the basement.

On May 30, 2023 at 9:40AM the Tenant texted [name] advising her that she wishes to only be in contact with [name] and cease communication with [name] (DOC-4845685, page 95). [name] did not respond to the message.
On June 19, 2023 at 9:44PM the Tenant texted [name] asking to have 24 hours notice before anyone enters the basement. (DOC-4845685, page 96). [name] did not respond to the message.

In the afternoon on July 3, 2023 the Tenant woke up from a nap and heard someone in the shared laundry room. She opened the door and saw [name] who asked if she just woke up. [name] started walking toward the Tenant and the Tenant continued to back away to keep distance between them. The Tenant headed toward the Rental Unit when [name] commented on the length and healthiness of the Tenant’s hair. These comments made the Tenant uncomfortable and she felt were unwarranted.
On July 15, 2023 at 8:35PM the Tenant texted [name] asking if they can meet to discuss “something urgent”. [name] did not respond to the message.

On August 20, 2023 at 4:50PM the Tenant left her rental unit to have a shower. Shortly after entering in the bathroom, the Tenant heard someone working in the vacant bedroom. She confirmed with her roommate that [name] was in the vacant bedroom (DOC-4845685, page 112). The roommate asked [name] to leave and come back later as the Tenant was in and LTB-L-084769-23 the shower. [name] first refused to leave but eventually left. The Tenant then left the basement apartment and went to the park until her roommate confirmed [name] left.
The Tenant testified she believed [name] was using access to the video camera in the basement unit to enter when she was going into the bathroom in just a towel.

On August 21, 2023 at 3:03PM the Tenant texted [name] advising again she wanted to meet in person to discuss “[name]’s behaviour”. In this message exchange, the Tenant tells [name] “I need a few pieces of information with respect to my tenancy and the property before I make the payment for the month of September”.
In the evening on August 21, 2023 [name] hurriedly walked into the basement apartment and seemed anxious. [name] kept asking “What happened?”.
On August 22, 2023 [name] entered the basement holding painting supplies and left after 5- 10 minutes.
On August 27, 2023 [name] entered the basement and stood in the kitchen. The Tenant remained in her bedroom until he left.

On September 5, 2023 at 10:50AM the Tenant was alone in the basement and saw two unknown men enter the main door and into the laundry room. The two men told her [name] and [name] would be coming. At 11:10AM [name], [name], and the two men entered the basement. The Tenant testified she heard [name] walked toward the video camera to plug it in. Prior to that, the Tenant had unplugged the camera as she was feeling increasingly unsafe assuming [name] had access to the camera. [name] then knocked aggressively on the Tenant’s door 2-3 times asking her to open the door while turning the doorknob. The Tenant asked them to come to the window of her rental unit to talk. She attempted to speak with [name] about the unanswered messages but [name] said she didn’t receive any. [name] then told the Tenant he is the property manager and any conversations should go through him. [name], [name], and the two men left by 11:30AM.

At 1:13PM the Tenant sent an e-mail to [name] (DOC-4845685, page 291). The Tenant repeated her requests to only speak with [name] and detailed the previous requests she had made to [name] regarding the same. The Tenant advised she would be contacting the police about the incident. [name] responded at 12:04PM on September 6, 2023 “Message noted, please let the police follow up”. Four minutes later at 12:09PM [name] again e- mailed the Tenant advising “The landlord approved that I will be your contact person”.
On September 7, 2023 [name] texted the Tenant at 1:06PM asking her to remit payment for September’s rent. The Tenant responded asking what e-mail to send the rent to. [name] provided her e-mail.

The Tenant testified that due to her anxiety surrounding the circumstances she began to believe that the Landlord was not aware of her tenancy and that [name] and [name] were “pocketing” the money. I find this speculation to be unreasonable. The Tenant has paid the rent to [name]’s e-mail since 2019 and never received any N4 Notice or otherwise that would make her believe the Landlord was not receiving the money.

On September 12, 2023 [name] texted the Tenant at 11:38AM advising that the Landlord intends to sell the residential complex and there would be a showing the following day and LTB-L-084769-23 (DOC-4845685, page 44). The Tenant responded to [name] detailing the issues that she has with [name] and the interactions that have taken place between them. This was the first time the Tenant made [name] aware of the allegations (DOC-4845685, pages 46-48). In these messages the Tenant also asks that [name] not be present for any showings. The showing was cancelled the next
On September 29, 2023 [name] texted the Tenant advising of another showing. The Tenant again responded asking [name] not to be present. The showing scheduled was cancelled.

On October 3, 2023 the Tenant received a text message from the Landlord [name] (XL) advising he has been made aware of the Tenant’s complaints and request to meet and offered the same (DOC-4845685, pages 211-213). The Tenant responded that she would only meet under certain conditions and encouraged XL to speak with [name] about what those demands were. The Tenant had previously demanded an affidavit sworn and notarized about who the Landlord is, where his home and business addresses are, the contact of the lawyer who notarized the document, two pieces of government ID, among other things (DOC-4845685, pages 206-207). The parties never met for a meeting.

On November 30, 2023 the Tenant heard someone in the basement apartment. She was introduced to someone who claimed to be the new property manager and they were showing a new prospective roommate the vacant bedroom and advised he would be staying there. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord, XL, testified only he has access to the camera in the basement – [name] nor [name] had access to the camera.
XL first became aware of the allegations of [name]’s behaviour on October 2, 2023. Shortly after, [name] and [name] were fired and a new property manager was hired. Analysis Illegal Entry

Based on my findings in paragraph 6 of this order, and the Tenant’s testimony that [name], nor anyone associated with the Landlord entered the Rental Unit, I find that the Landlords’ Agents did not enter the rental unit illegally. Harassment
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Harassment is not defined in the Act; I turn to the Ontario Human Rights Code’s definition of harassment: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” and LTB-L-084769-23

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence about the behaviour of [name], I find that these incidents can be seen as conduct that is known or ought to reasonably be known to be unwelcome: December 31, 2022, May 22, July 3, August 20, 21, 22, 27, September 5, and 12, 2023. It is evident from the Tenant’s testimony that the Tenant was becoming increasingly uncomfortable with the presence of [name]. [name]

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit … substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony and evidence about the behaviour of [name] on the same dates provided in paragraph 45, I find the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex were substantially interfered with. The Tenant testified she felt unsafe in the residential complex and would hide herself in her bedroom anytime [name] was present in the residential complex.

Furthermore, the Tenant first made [name] aware of her desire to no longer communicate with [name] on July 15, 2023. The Tenant made further requests to cease communication with [name] which went unanswered. There was no evidence put forward to suggest that [name] did not receive these messages. It wasn’t until September 6, 2023 that finally the Tenant was “approved” to speak directly with [name] rather than [name]. I find this almost two months of unresponsiveness from [name] to be unreasonable and therefore, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex.

However, based on the Landlord’s testimony, once the Landlord was made aware of the Tenant’s despair with the Landlord’s Agents, the Landlord fired [name] and [name]. Once their employment was terminated, the complaints from the Tenant ceased. I took this submission in consideration when determining a rent abatement. Remedies

The Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of $4,291.00 which equals to 100% rent abatement for the months of December 2022, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, and December 2023.

An abatement recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. and LTB-L-084769-23

Based on the 9 incidents in paragraph 45 and the two months the Tenant repeatedly requested communication between her and [name] cease, I find a lump sum rent abatement of $600.00 to be reasonable given the circumstances.
The Tenant also requested $33,115.00 in “Non-Pecuniary Damages”. I am not satisfied the Tenant has provided sufficient evidence to support this request and as such, this remedy will not be awarded.

The Tenant is also entitled to the cost of filing this application. L1 Application 54. The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed. 55. As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $549.30. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $18.06. This amount is calculated as follows: $549.30 x 12, divided by 365 days.

The parties agreed the Tenant has paid $14,951.90 to the Landlord since the application was filed. The parties agreed the rent arrears owing to June 30, 2026 are $3,228.00. As such, the arrears reflected in this order are based on the parties’ agreement.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $520.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $43.97 is owing to the Tenant for the period from January 1, 2023 to June 15, 2026. Relief from Eviction

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until July 31, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
The Landlord sought a standard order terminating the tenancy in 11-days from the date of this order should the Tenant not pay the arrears owing.

The Tenant requested a payment plan to repay the arrears. Upon review of the Tenant’s financial disclosure, it appears the Tenant is in a deficit each month due to her low income. However, the Tenant testified her parents are able to help her financially. If termination of and LTB-L-084769-23 tenancy was to be ordered, the Tenant asked for four months to move due to her strong ties in the community.

The Landlord provided insufficient evidence to support the need for an 11-day termination order. No financial documents or otherwise were provided to suggest the Landlord is at a high risk of foreclosure or financial despair should a longer termination date be given.

Since the Tenant is a deficit each month, I find granting a payment plan to be unreasonable. However, the Tenant did not provide any evidence to suggest she has contacted local agencies to help pay the arrears; I find it reasonable that the Tenant may access these resources to help pay the arrears. Failing which the Tenant will have to move out of the rental unit on or before July 31, 2026.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] & [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $1,048.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). It is not disputed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit as a result of an N12 notice of termination on October 31, 2025, and as of the date of the hearing the person named in the notice ([name] [name]) has moved into the rental unit.

The Landlords’ agent is the son of the Landlords. He testified that his father is living with him until renovations on the rental unit are complete, and another tenant in the residential complex with whom his father may have arguments with has been evicted. He says the renovations have taken longer than planned because the contractor they use was delayed on a prior job is now injured. The contractor did not attend or provide a statement.

In August 2025, prior to issuing the N12 not ice, the Landlords wrote to the Tenant and advised that they were thinking of moving [name] into the rental unit if the Tenant didn’t agree to an increase in rent from $1,200.00 to $1,400.00. The Tenant responded that they had agreed to an above guideline increase in the past but could not afford to do so again. The N12 notice was issued approximately 1 week later. While the Landlords’ attempt to negotiate an above guideline increase immediately prior to issuing the N12 notice is not conclusive of bad faith, it is one factor to be considered.

In my view, the statement by the Landlords’ agent that his father would not be moved into the rental unit until another tenant in the complex was evicted to avoid arguments between them is not indicative of a well settled and definite intention for their father to occupy the rental unit – rather the intention is conditional on the outcome of other Board proceedings involving another tenant in another unit. Remedies
The Tenant requested general compensation to compensate her for the stress of not knowing where she would end up living. I find this is a reasonable remedy.

General compensation is no rmally awarded for pan and suffering, where there is evidence of impact and the other remedies awarded are insufficient to account for the psychological impact on the Tenant. In this case the only remedy requested is general compensation. Although no specific documentation was provided, the Tenant referenced stress associated with having to move as a result of the N12 notice and not knowing where she would end up. This is a reasonably anticipated consequence of receiving a notice of termination. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, in the absence of specific documentation to quantify the amount of general compensation, $1,000.00 is a reasonable amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents:  $1,000.00 for general compensation  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by July 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by July 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
