issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’). • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential • complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (the ‘T2 Application’). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’).
reasons: For the reasons provided below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $4,424.46 to the Tenant. Evidence and Submissions

The tenancy began on or about October 18, 2024. The Tenant rented the basement unit at the residential complex. The Tenant testified that he was attending Mohawk College and working multiple jobs at the time he entered into the tenancy. He stated that it was convenient for him to reside at the rental unit while he was attending school.

The Tenant signed the Landlord’s agreement called “Basic Agreement”. The parties agreed that the monthly rent would be $850.00. It is undisputed that the Tenant paid $1,700.00, for the first and last month's rent.

Shortly after moving into the rental unit, the Tenant informed the Landlord regarding the following issues: the shower door would not close properly; flickering lights; inadequate ventilation; defects with the window and ceiling; and dampness, humidity and temperature issues in the unit. The Landlord acknowledged that the shower door was defective but informed the Tenant that replacing the door would be expensive.

Further, the Tenant alleges that during the tenancy: The Landlord entered the rental unit without notice approximately on three or four occasions; and the Landlord repeatedly complained about the Tenant’s cooking, stating that it smelled “gross” and informed him to keep the window open. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s comments caused him stress and interfered with his enjoyment of the rental unit.

On October 25, 2024, the Tenant removed some of his belongings from the unit and went to stay temporarily with his mother while he was working. The Tenant testified that he left his personal property in the unit because he intended to return back to the unit. The Tenant stated that he had not moved out or informed the Landlord that he was terminating his tenancy. However, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant stating: “Apt repairs R completed it seems U’ve moved out ….plz confirm” We’ve removed the very smelly garbage…”
On October 26, 2024, the Tenant replied: “I worked last night I worked today, working tonight, and working tomorrow. I won’t be able to see you till Monday the earliest. I’ll talk to you soon.”
The Landlord responded: “Uve completely abandoned the Apt; locks R changed.”

The Tenant testified that he occupied the rental unit for approximately one week. On October 26, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks and denied the Tenant access to the rental unit. The Landlord did not provide replacement keys or a new access code to the Tenant. The Landlord also did not return the Tenant’s rent deposit or the remaining three weeks of rent for October 2024 that he had paid the Landlord. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25

On October 27, 2024, the Landlord alleged that the Tenant’s father threatened her. The Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant which states: “provided a police report in anticipation of a restraining order against U, as might be required if U try access w/o prior permission to commit further property theft.”

During the hearing, the Landlord did not produce a restraining order or a police report. The Tenant testified that he believed the Landlord had contacted the police and obtained a restraining order so he did not attempt to return to the rental unit. He later learned that no restraining order had been obtained. Analysis and Reasons for the Decision
I am not satisfied that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit on October 26, 2024.

Pursuant to s.2(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’), “a tenant has not abandoned a rental unit if the tenant is not in arrears of rent.” Here, the Tenant had paid both first and last month’s rent and was not in arrears. Further, even though the Tenant removed some of his belongings from the unit, he left personal property behind, expressly advised the Landlord that he would speak to her on Monday, and never served a notice terminating his tenancy. The evidence before me does not establish an intention on the part of the Tenant to permanently give up possession of the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not abandon the tenancy.

Section 24 of the Act says that “a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.”

In the present case, the Tenant never regained possession of the rental unit. There is no evidence that the tenancy had terminated or that the Tenant had surrendered possession of the rental unit. The Landlord did not challenge the fact that locks were changed on October 26, 2026. Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on October 26, 2026, when the Landlord changed the locks and never provided the Tenant with replacement keys or a new access code.
I also find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful right to occupy the rental unit by illegally locking the Tenant out contrary to s. 24 of the Act.

The Tenant paid the Landlord $[name], for the first and last month's rent. The Tenant occupied the rental unit for approximately one week. The Landlord was not entitled to retain the last month's rent deposit after unilaterally terminating the tenancy and preventing the Tenant from continuing his occupation of the rental unit. Therefore, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant the last month's rent deposit of $850.00.

I also find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to interest for the period of October 18, 2024 to October 26, 2024 in the amount of $0.46. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25 Tenant’s T2 Application

Section 22 of the Act provides that “a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

The Tenant referred to his text messages with the Landlord, he testified that throughout the first week that he resided in the unit, the Landlord repeatedly commented on his cooking, warned him about damage to the unit, and informed him to keep the windows open because of his cooking. The Tenant testified that these comments were made on multiple occasions during his short tenancy and made him feel unwelcome in the rental unit. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord repeatedly complained about the Tenant’s cooking and warned him about causing damage to the unit, which substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I also accept that the Landlord’s comments made the Tenant feel stress and anxiety. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit contrary to s. 22 of the Act.

With respect to the Tenant’s claim for illegal entries, the Tenant testified that the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice on three or four occasions between October 18, 2024 to October 25, 2024. However, the Tenant was unable to provide dates or sufficient details regarding those alleged entries. As for the Landlord’s conduct on October 26, 2024, when the Landlord changed the locks and denied the Tenant access to the rental unit, I have addressed the Landlord’s conduct above in paragraphs 12-16. In the absence of sufficient particulars regarding the alleged entries between October 18-25, 2024, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, this portion of the application is dismissed.

During the hearing the Tenant requested to withdraw remedies 5, 6, and 9 from the T2 application. I granted the Tenant’s request. The Tenant indicated that he is claiming the following remedies under the T2 application: [name] 1: Rent Abatement I find it reasonable to award the Tenant $850.00 in rent abatement given the reasons in paragraphs 19 and 20. I am satisfied that this amount is appropriate because the Tenant resided in the unit for only one week and during the week the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedy 3: Administrative Fine to the Board Administrative fines are intended to promote compliance and deter future misconduct where other remedies are insufficient. Given the compensation award to the Tenant, I am satisfied that this order provides adequate deterrence. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied. File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25 Remedy 4: Termination of Tenancy Reasons given in paragraphs 12 to 15. [name] 7: Moving and Storage Expenses The Tenant claims $80.00 for car expenses and gas. The Tenant testified that he incurred travel expenses as a result of the lockout. The Tenant testified that he incurred these expenses travelling between his mother's residence, work, and the rental unit in an attempt to address the lockout and recover his belongings. While the Tenant did not have receipts for these expenses, I found his testimony to be credible. I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred these expenses as a direct result of the Landlord's unlawful conduct. Accordingly, I find it reasonable to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant moving expenses of $80.00. Remedy 8: Out of pocket expenses The Tenant claims that he incurred $50 at “local laundry mat because the supplied washer and dryer didn't work which was part of the monthly rent.” The Tenant testified that the washer dryer advertised as part of the tenancy was not operational, as a result he was required to use a laundry mat during his tenancy. I find there was insufficient evidence to establish that the washer or dryer did not work. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established this claim on the balance of probabilities. This remedy is denied. Remedy 11: Other Remedies The Tenant seeks compensation for anxiety, loss of employment income, tuition/textbook expenses, and losses associated with his studies. The Tenant alleges that the illegal lockout caused him significant emotional distress, required him to move further away from Mohawk College, and resulted in reduced work hours and eventually caused him to lose his employment. The Tenant referred to his evidence in which he seeks $6,371.00 for income loss and $2,500 for tuition loss. Although I accept the Landlord's unlawful lockout caused the Tenant stress and anxiety, I am not satisfied that the Tenant established the full amount claimed under this remedy on a balance of probabilities as a direct result of the Landlord’s conduct. However, having regard to the distress, convenience and uncertainty caused by the Landlords unlawful lockout, I find that an award of $2,500.00 in general damages is appropriate. [name]

The Tenant amended his T6 application, he seeks a rent abatement of $164.52 for “loss of use/rental value for specific days.” “Due to severe interference with reasonable enjoyment and loss of essential (vital) services and facilities including heat and loss of use of amenities.” File Numbers: LTB-T-089372-24 LTB-T-087817-25 LTB-T-087043-25

The Tenant testified that the shower door did not properly close, causing water to escape onto the floor. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that shortly after moving into the rental unit he informed the Landlord regarding the shower door, flickering lights, inadequate ventilation, dampness, humidity and temperature issues. I further accept that the Landlord acknowledged that the shower door was defective and informed the Tenant that replacing it would be expensive. A shower curtain was used to address the issue.

Although there was limited evidence regarding the maintenance issues, I am satisfied that at least some of the conditions complained of existed and that the Landlord failed to adequately address them during the tenancy. However, I declined to award a further rent abatement of $164.52 because the Tenant has been awarded the full abatement of the rent paid for the period that he occupied the rental unit, see paragraph 22 ([name] 1). Accordingly, no further rent abatement can be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,424.46. This amount represents: • $850.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • 0.46 Interest on the last month’s rent deposit; • $850.00 for rent abatement; • $80.00 for moving expenses; • $2,500.00 for general compensation or other remedies; and • $144.00 ($48.00 [name]) for the cost of filing the T1, T2, and T6 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

This application was filed on October 10, 2025. Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) limits tenant applications to incidents or issues which occurred within the 1 year prior to the application being filed. In this case, the application is limited to incidents which occurred on or after October 10, 2024.

The Tenant alleges that the actions of the Landlord’s agent, [name], were harassing and interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. In support of these allegations, the Tenant referred to four incidents within the one-year limitation period. In October 2024 the Landlord’s agent sent a text message or email to the Tenant asking him to make room in the shed so they could put some of their items on their side of the shed, and ten days later sent another message asking if some floor panels in the shed belonged to the Landlord or the Tenant. Neither of these communications are inappropriate or unreasonable. The shed appears to be a shared space which both parties have access to and some communication about accessing and utilizing the shared space is expected.

Between February 12, 2025 and March 1, 2025, the Landlord’s agent sent two emails advising that they would refer what they believed to be costs owing by the Tenant to third- party debt collection rather than pursuing options available through the LTB. This is not generally the preferred method for parties to approach issues; however, I am not satisfied based on the limited excerpts provided by the Tenant that the communications rise to the level of harassment or substantial interference. A disagreement between parties about what constitutes damage or who is responsible for a certain item is inherently uncomfortable and not automatically a breach of the Act. I am not satisfied that the communications presented had any greater impact on the Tenant than if the Landlord had used LTB approved notices to navigate the dispute.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1698.00.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on October 5, 2026, and signed a one year lease agreement ending September 30, 2026. The HVAC

He testified that from the day he moved in he became aware of a noise from the HVAC system, he described it as a grinding noise which could be heard all over the unit even when the HVAC was off. He explained that the noise made it hard to sleep and impacted the functioning of the HVAC system which left the rental unit too hot during the day and too cold at night. The Tenant also testified that the lights would flicker whenever the HVAC system was in use.

The Tenant testified that he made the Landlord aware of the issues with the HVAC system on October 6, 2025, and the Landlord kept insisting someone would be dispatched to repair the system. He testified that someone did come to assess the system but could not recall when this occurred. The Tenant testified that the HVAC system was finally repaired on November 24, 2025, after he had followed up with the Landlord 5 or 6 times. The Laundry Room Door

The Tenant testified that the laundry room door did not close properly because the latch was loose. He testified that this defect was present when he moved in and he made the Landlord aware on October 6, 2025, but the latch was never repaired. The Tenant described this issue as having no impact on him. The Balcony Door

The Tenant testified that he could not open the door to the balcony of the rental unit as the jamb was not sliding. He testified that he made the Landlord aware of this on October 6, 2025, and it was not repaired for 4 or 5 months until April 2026 shortly before he vacated the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he was unable to access the balcony until the door was repaired. The Toilet Paper Holder

The Tenant testified that the toiler paper holder in the bathroom was broken, he testified that he informed the Landlord on October 6, 2025, and it was repaired after approximately two months after he had followed up two three times. He testified that he was required to place the toilet paper on the sink which would cause it to become wet every time he used the sink. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I am satisfied that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations. The Tenant reported all of the issues in the rental unit by October 6, 2026, and the HVAC was not repaired for a month and half despite the impact on the Tenant, the balcony door was not repaired for upwards of 5 months, and the laundry room door was never repaired by the Landlord. While the Landlord may have an explanation for this delay they did not attend and thus I did not have an opportunity to hear evidence from them on the issue.

I note that the HVAC system was central to the heating and cooling of the rental unit and also impacted the electrical system of the rental unit, therefore a timely repair would be appropriate, the issues with the balcony door and laundry room door as described by the Tenant appear to be simple repairs, which are unlikely to take months to accomplish. Therefore, absent evidence from the Landlord to support the delay in repair I am not satisfied they responded to the issues raised responsibly in the circumstances.
Therefore, I am satisfied Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent abatement of 40%. I am satisfied that an abatement is appropriate but find that the quantum claimed is excessive. While I am prepared to accept that the HVAC system had a significant impact on the Tenant this only persisted until November 24, 2025, approximately a month and a half, I also accept that the Tenant lost use of their balcony for several months, I accept that theses issue meaningfully impacted the Tenants use of the rental unit while they were ongoing. However, the impact of the other maintenance issues appears to have been less significant. In consideration of the issues raised I find that an abatement of one month $1650.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also sought unspecified general compensation. In this circumstance I am satisfied that the abatement awarded is sufficient compensation and note that several of the issue described by the Tenant (the laundry room door and the toilet paper holder) had only a minimal impact on them. I am not satisfied that general compensation is appropriate.

The Tenant also sought termination of the tenancy effective April 30, 2026, the date that he vacated the rental unit. He testified that his status in Cananda expired, and he needed to leave the country. The Tenant testified that the Landlord informed he was responsible for securing someone to take over the lease and he has been sending the Landlord candidates but they have not been responding to them.

The maintenance issues raised by the Tenant are not serious enough to justify termination of the tenancy, and with the exception of the laundry room door which had no impact on the Tenant all were resolved by the time the tenancy was terminated and were not the cause of the end of the tenancy. Therefore, I am not satisfied that termination of the tenancy April 20, 2026 is appropriate.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,698.00 This amount represents: • $1650.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending April 2026 • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T2 Application about Tenant Rights (T2 application) with the Board on November 7, 2024. The T2 application indicates that the grounds for the notice are substantial interference, harassment and illegal entry by the Landlord, withholding of vital services, and the Landlord did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement.

The parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference on March 3, 2025, where the parties agreed the tenancy had terminated on November 30, 2024, and an interim order was issued regarding the timelines for the Tenant to amend her application.

The Tenant filed and served her Amended Application upon the Board and the Landlord on March 17, 2025, where she amended her reasons for the application, specifically removing Reason 7 and amended reason 5, to only include the withholding/interfering of vital services claim, and adding further sufficient details to her application to support her claims. Moreover, the Tenant amended her remedies sought to include a $4,800.00 rent abatement, which she sought $400.00 a month for 12 months, which corresponding to a 33.3% abatement of rent for a year, the Tenant also sought an LTB fine to be ordered against the Landlord, and further a rent differential of $400.00 per month for a total of $4,800.00 sought for rent differential.
Upon the submissions of the parties the amendments to the Tenant’s Reasons and Remedies sought in her Application were granted, as the amendments had limited prejudice to the Landlord.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the amended application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Facts
The Tenant resided in the rental unit from February 1, 2023, to November 30, 2024, when she vacated the rental unit.
The Tenant paid a monthly rent of $1,200.00.

Section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) governs tenant applications, including applications for substantial interference, harassment and illegal entry, withholding of vital services. Subsection 29(2) of the Act states that no application can be made under this provision more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. In Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich, [2010] O.J. No. 1463, the Divisional Court held that a remedy cannot go back further than the one-year limitation period in subsection 29(2). In other words, a remedy cannot go back further than one year before the application was filed.

In the present case, as above noted the T2 application was filed on November 7, 2024. Therefore, pursuant to Vlahovich, the Board does not have jurisdiction to order remedies that go back further than November 7, 2023. This prevents me from making determinations regarding incidents of substantial interference, harassment and illegal entry, withholding of vital services and all other claims that occurred prior to November 7, 2023, one year before the T2 application was filed. Therefore, I find that the Tenant’s claims in her application prior to November 7, 2023, are out of time to seek remedies for and these claims are dismissed, specifically the claims regarding the noises of the lavatory and alleged temperature issues related to withholding vital services. Furthermore, the claims regarding the lavatory noises upon flushing that amounted to a groaning noise as pleaded may be a maintenance issue, and this herein is not the proper application for this issue, and hence the issue was not heard as it related to maintenance other than potential issue related to the substantial interference to the Tenant as a result of the alleged noises from the lavatory upon flushing.

The Tenant testified that the following events occurred: a) On or about October 8th, 2024, the Tenant testified that the temperature in her rental unit dropped to 15 degrees Celsius as the heat was not yet turned on by the Landlord, who also resided in the rental complex. b) On or about October 9th, 2024, the Tenant testified she requested the Landlord deal with the temperature issues and she was met with immediate hostility resulting in verbally being evicted on the spot. The Tenant further testified she returned to her rental unit, locked her rental unit door and contacted her father. The Tenant alleged the Landlord listened to her conversation through her door and then forcibly entered the rental unit by breaking the lock on the door, and the yelling and hostility from the Landlord continued, which caused the Tenant to change the lock and bring a friend home with her to feel safe that evening. c) On October 11, 2024, the Tenant testified she made maintenance requests and was served an N12 notice by the Landlord on the same date and was met with the Landlord inebriated on her front door upon her return from grocery shopping, yelling slurs and threatening to tow her vehicle from the mutual driveway. The Tenant noted she was aware that’s this was not a T5 application, but wished to illustrate the constant issues with the Landlord. d) On October 12, 2024, the Tenant testified that the Landlord restricted the internet services, that were included in her rental agreement, and it affected her work. e) On October 13, 2024, the Tenant testified that the police were called regarding tenancy rights, and both parties were advised to contact the Board, and thereafter internet service was restored by the Landlord. f) On November 1, 2024 the Tenant testified that the Landlord was making loud banging and slamming noises outside of the rental unit in front her rental unit door for an hour, which she deemed as an intimidation tactic, the police were called, and as the Landlord was inebriated and the Tenant did not feel safe. g) On November 4, 2024, the Tenant testified the temperatures again was below what was required under the Act, forcing the Tenant to purchase a space heater. h) On November 6, 2024, there was an issue with the kitchen drain falling out and a whole going straight from the rental unit to the basement unit. There were also issues with the smoke detector and carbon monoxide which were replaced upon the Tenant contacting the Fire Department. i) The Tenant testified that she did not feel safe in her rental unit, and anytime maintenance issues were brought up they were unanswered and when it was related to the heating, she was met with screaming from the Landlord, and an illegal entry on October 9, 2024 and an altercation with the Landlord, and the ongoing threats and hostility, caused her a constant state of fear.

The Tenant testified that she was very distressed, upset, her anxiety and mental health and wellbeing was suffering due to the Landlord’s alleged illegal entry into the rental unit, the threatening and harassing and intimidating behaviors, all caused the Tenant substantial to interfere with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Finally, the withholding of vital services caused her great distress.
The Tenant testified that due to the above incidents, the Tenant terminated the tenancy on her own accord.

The Tennat submitted evidence of the heating and cooling issues, specifically some text messages regarding heating and cooling requests to the Landlord and some photographs of her thermostat, with some being time and date stamped. The documentary evidence submitted as a whole, did not illustrate that the Landlord withheld vital services, on a balance of probabilities, in my opinion, but rather showed communication of remedying the issues as alleged by the Tenant.

There was a thermostat photograph of 26.1 degrees Celsius, which alleged to be August 20, 2024, alleging the AC was off, there was a date stamped thermostat reading of 17.3 degrees Celsius on October 9, 2024, at 10:35 a.m., and further reading of 19.9 degrees Celsius of 19.9 degrees Celsius on November 4, 2024, at 2:54 p.m. The Tenant claimed there were further incidents of temperature issues in 2023, but she did not have the readings of the same. The Landlord testified the fall of 2024, was unusually warm, and often the AC was still on.

The Landlord testified the Tenant is his niece and allowed her to rent his rental unit as a favour to his sibling. That being said, there were never issues with heating and cooling of the residence, and the temperature was always kept to provincial standards as required. The Landlord is not sure how two readings only during the tenancy indicated the opposite. Moreover, the Landlord resided in the rental complex, which was an older home, with dual thermostats, and would keep the home at the legal temperatures, as he himself wanted to be comfortable.

The Landlord further testified on October 9, 2024, the Tenant, did ask him to purchase a space heater to make her rental unit even warmer than the provincial standards, and the Landlord told the Tenant that was fine as long as she paid any excess hydro costs associated, with the same in an initial discussion. That is when the Tenant lost it, began slamming doors to the point items were being knocked off walls, screaming and yelling and the Tenant assaulted the Landlord in his dining room, which was witnessed to by the Landlord’s Support Person. The Landlord submitted evidence of the same. The Tenant then ran to her unit and locked the door.

The Landlord notified her that given the assault she needs to move out, and the Landlord provided evidence of the same. The Landlord testified that she was abusing him and the situation of the relationship, and when she was told to vacate due to her assault, she commenced the application.

The Landlord denied the illegal entry as alleged, and further put the Tenant to strict proof of her claims, the majority of which were not substantiated with documentary evidence, even the police reports were just incident reports of her calling the police and then cancelling the need for the police to attend, as the Tenant alleged the activity had stopped which the Landlord denies occurred in first place but for the pausing of the [name], which is not a vital service in his opinion.

The Landlord did testify he did pause the Wi-Fi on October 12,2024 and reinstated the same October 13, 2024. Moreover, the reason for the pausing was the noise was so excessive, from the Tenant’s devices, it seemed as though this was retaliation for telling the Tenant she was required to vacate, after the Tenant assaulted the Landlord as he alleged.
The Landlord further testified that the Tenant’s application is without merit and should be dismissed, as she did not meet her evidentiary burden on a balance of probabilities. Legal Analysis

Section 21 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant…
Section 23 of the Act states “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”
Section 25 of the Act established a Tenant’s right to privacy and states that a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27.

Pursuant to section 26 of the Act a landlord is permitted to enter a rental unit without notice: in emergencies; where the tenant consents at the time of entry; where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to enter at regular intervals in order to clean; and to show the unit to prospective tenants.

Section 27 of the Act outlines entries that are permitted with written notice and sets out the minimum requirements for entry notices, including that written notice of entry must be delivered at least 24 hours prior to the entry.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence was adduced by the Tenant, nor the Tenant’s oral testimony either in part or taken in its entirety, suffices to meet the burden of proof upon the Tenant to demonstrate that the Landlords have breached their obligations as they pertain to the T2 application and allegations made therein.

On the evidence before me, I find the Tenant’s claims of substantial interference, harassment, one instance of illegal entry, and withholding of vital services by the Landlord were not met. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord’s behaviour on a balance of probabilities substantial interfered with or harassed the Tenant. Furthermore, there is no evidence before me on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord illegal entered the rental unit or withheld vital services. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that there was an altercation on or about October 9, 2024, that effectively soured the relationship with the Tenant, and that these claims brought by the Tenant are without merit on a balance of probabilities.

I have considered all the contested evidence presented at the hearing and although I may not have referred to each piece of documentary evidence or referenced all of the oral testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
