issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally. The Landlords applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) applies. These applications were resolved by order LTB-T-092542-25_ LTB-L-078767-25 issued on May 7, 2026. On May 18, 2026, the Landlords requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On May 19, 2026, interim order LTB-T-092542-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 7, 2026. The review request was heard by videoconference on July 16, 2026. The first named Landlord and the Landlords’ legal representative Taff Butters and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: By way of background, in the May 7, 2026 order, the presiding Member dismissed the [name] application having found that the Landlords did not serve a termination notice under section 48 or 49 of the Act and therefore not required to compensate the Tenant.

With respect to the Landlords’ A1 application, the Member found that the Act applies. Additionally, the Member imposed an administrative fine for the Landlords to pay the Tenants $1,000.00 and cited authority to do so under s.57(3) of the Act.

In the review request, the Landlords assert that Board lacked the jurisdiction to levy a fine in this circumstance and asks the Board to vary the order to remove the fine. Additionally, it was procedurally unfair of the Member to impose a fine without first identifying the statutory basis for the penalty and to seek submissions from the parties at the hearing.

For clarity, the Board form T1 application does not provide for a request for an administrative fine. However, the Member cites s.57(3) of the Act which allows for the Board to order “any other order that the Board considers appropriate” at paragraph 24 of the order.

The Member expressly found that the Landlords did not serve a termination notice to the Tenants under s. 48 or 49 and dismissed the application. Having made this determination, the Member should not have imposed a punitive fine against the Landlords. This finding leads to an internal contradiction and the Board lacked the jurisdiction to levy such a fine.
The Board is a statutory tribunal and it has the authority to consider claims that fall within its jurisdiction.

In the context of the A1 application, and as explained at the hearing, the only outcome of such application is a determination as to whether the Act applies. Therefore, the order to pay the fine was made outside of the Board’s jurisdiction.
The parties confirmed the balance of the order remains unchallenged. The order will be varied by removing the order related to the administrative fine.
On the basis of the submissions made in the request, I am satisfied that there is a serious error in the order when the Landlords were ordered to pay an administrative fine.
The parties were informed of my decision at the hearing.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-092542-25 issued on May 7, 2026 is granted. The order is varied in the following manner
Paragraph 2 of the May 7, 2026 order is varied to remove the order for the Landlords to pay the administrative fine.
The balance of the May 7, 2026 order remains in full force and effect.
The interim order issued on May 19, 2026 is cancelled and replaced with this order. July 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 Application) [name] and [name] (the ‘Tenants’) also applied for an order determining [name] (the ‘Landlord’) failed to meet his maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) These applications were heard by videoconference on June 16, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have proven some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $1,869.68 which includes reimbursing the filing fee. [name]
The rental unit was a furnished, 3-bedroom house.
The lawful monthly rent was $2,300.00.
The tenancy began on July 12, 2023 and ended on September 1, 2024.
The Application was filed on October 22, 2024. Rent Deposit

At the outset of the hearing, the Tenants and the Landlord disputed whether 12 months’ rent was paid up front, or 4 months’ rent deposit was made. The Tenants have not filed a T1 and so this issue is beyond the scope of the applications before me and will not be considered. [name]. The Tenants allege the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed them by making illegal entries into the rental unit and sitting in the driveway of the rental unit on July 17, 2024. 8. Section 22 of the Act states: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.” 9. Further, section 23 states: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.” 10. Substantial interference must rise to the level of more than trifling or passing; it must be substantial. 11. While there is no definition of harassment in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code, RSO 1990 CH-19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. The Ontario Human Rights Code is paramount legislation to the Residential Tenancies Act, which means it takes precedence over the Act. 12. Tenant [name] (‘SY’) testified that the Landlord entered the rental unit multiple times in April 2024 to collect the rent. She does not remember the time or dates, but remembered specifically that he entered on April 22, 2024 to pick up winter tires from the garage. She also said that he accused her of running drugs and called the police on her. 13. The Landlord testified that it was explicit in the lease that he had unfettered access to the garage for the duration of the tenancy, and that he always gave notice of entry ahead of time by text, phone or email. He did not produce any text messages or the lease as an exhibits to confirm notice or the terms. He also denied that the entry took place on April 22, 2024, and denied that he accused the Tenants of being drug runners or ever called the police on them. 14. As the applicant, the Tenants bear the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities. I had issues with the reliability of SY’s evidence in that it was vague and lacked specifics such as dates and details of the alleged entries. Given this, I find the Tenants failed to sufficiently establish that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit. 15. There seems to be no dispute that the Landlord sat in the driveway of the rental unit in his truck on July 17, 2024 for several hours until told to leave by police. 16. SY testified that on July 16, 2024, the Landlord advised her that he wanted to sleep in the driveway as he had nowhere else to stay. SY stated that she told the Landlord he could not stay and phoned police. 17. The Landlord maintains that he sat in the driveway of the rental unit because the Tenants had not paid rent for several months and he was afraid they were going to steal the furniture in the house. He acknowledged that he did not provide them notice that he would attend the rental unit and that he sat in the driveway in his truck until police advised him to leave. 18. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the Landlord’s conduct on July 17, 2024 constitutes harassment and that it substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. 19. In my view, a reasonable person knows or ought to know that the course of conduct of sitting in a driveway uninvited for hours would be unwelcome. I find the Landlord’s conduct constitutes harassment. The Landlord’s conduct made the Tenants feel intimidated and caused them stress. I am satisfied the Landlord’s conduct had a substantial impact on the Tenants’ ability to normally reside and enjoy the rental unit. 20. The only remedy sought by the Tenants in their T2 Application is that the Board impose an administrative fine on the Landlord. The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 21. As this was a single incident where no illegal entry was made, no criminal charges were laid and the incident only lasted a few hours, I do not find it appropriate or reasonable to impose an administrative fine with respect to the driveway incident. I do not find the Landlord’s conduct amounted to “blatant disregard” and am satisfied other remedies would provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Fines are reserved for egregious conduct and that threshold was not met in this incident. T6 Application 22. The Tenants allege that the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the refrigerator, septic water system, water pump, mold, snow removal and railing, and grass cutting. 23. Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 24. Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act. 25. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord. 26. To find the Landlord breached his obligations, I must first be satisfied a disrepair issue existed. I must then consider whether the Tenants reported the issue to the Landlord and whether the steps the Landlord took to address the issue were timely, appropriate and reasonable in the circumstances. Refrigerator 27. For the reasons that follow, I find the Tenants have failed to sufficiently establish that the Landlord breached his maintenance obligations with respect to the refrigerator. 28. The parties disagree as to the date the disrepair issue with refrigerator was reported. SY testified that she notified the Landlord on July 12, 2023 that the refrigerator stopped working while the Landlord maintains he was notified on July 17, 2023. What is not in dispute is that a new refrigerator was delivered to the rental unit on July 21, 2023. 29. As explained above, the fact the refrigerator was in a state of disrepair is not an automatic breach. Even if I accept the issue was reported on July 12, 2023, I find that the Landlord addressed the issue in a timely and appropriate manner, having replaced the fridge on July 21, 2023. Septic water system 30. It is undisputed that sometime in August 2023, the septic water system leaked near the washing machine. SY testified that the leak was resolved within three days by a technician. I find that Landlord addressed the leak in a timely and appropriate manner. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Water pump 31. It was the evidence of the Tenants that in February 2024, the water pump began malfunctioning. They described it as “stopping and starting”. By March 1, 2024, no water was available. The Tenants reported the issue to the Landlord, who was traveling abroad. 32. The Landlord testified that he returned to Canada on March 5, 2024 and immediately contacted a technician who repaired the issued on March 7, 2024. 33. While the Landlord responded immediately upon his return to Canada, I do not believe it was reasonable that he did not provide the Tenants with an alternative point of contact for emergencies during his absence. 34. The evidence before me further establishes that there was no potable water supply to the rental unit throughout the tenancy. Water is a vital service. Landlords are required to provide continuous access to an adequate supply of clean, drinkable water and running hot and cold water as a mandatory vital service under provincial and municipal standards. The fact that the Landlord advised the Tenants that there was no potable water at the rental unit does not recuse him of his obligations under the Act and municipal standards. As such, I am satisfied the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to water. Mold 35. There seems to be no dispute that there was a presence of mold in the rental unit. The Tenants indicated they first noticed mold in November 2023 but did not report the issue to the Landlord until January 30, 2024. The Landlord maintains that any presence of mold is the result of the Tenants refusing to run a dehumidifier or hanging clothes in the hallway. 36. The Tenants did not admit evidence establishing the type of mold present in the rental unit. There were no third-party reports confirming whether the mold was surface mold or toxic mold. Given the lack of evidence establishing the mold was toxic black mold, I am of the view the mold was surface. I say this because the mold was cleaned within four days after the Tenants vacated and has not returned. 37. Subsection 30(2) of the Act provides that a landlord should not be held financially liable if they do not know about a particular disrepair problem. The Tenants did not report the issue to the Landlord until nearly three months after first discovering the issue. The delay of the reporting was an impediment to the Landlord’s ability to address the issue. 38. Additionally, section 16 of the Act provides that a tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize loss. It is widely known that mold grows in damp or wet areas with high humidity. As such, it would have been prudent for the Tenants to run a dehumidifier. In my view, their failure to do so resulted in creating an environment prone to the growth of mold. The Tenants also should have taken appropriate steps to mitigate any loss, including the cleaning or removal of their bed in the basement and properly storing coats and clothing. 39. For these reasons I am not satisfied the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1). Snow Removal and Railing 40. The Tenants allege that the Landlord failed to put salt on the porch to remove snow and ice and did not install a railing on the stairway resulting in MY falling and injuring himself. 41. There seems to be no dispute that the Tenants are responsible for the removal of snow and ice on the walkway and driveway for which they have exclusive use. The Landlord provided the Tenants with two large shovels and an electric snow blower. As such, any issues with the removal of snow or ice lies with the Tenants and not the Landlord. 42. The Tenants seem to suggest that MY slipped and fell on January 25, 2024 because the Landlord failed to install a railing on the steps leading to the rental unit. The issue to be determined is whether the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) because a railing was not installed for the stairway. 43. It is the Tenants’ position that a railing ought to have been installed as there were more than seven steps leading to the rental unit. The Tenants, however, made no submissions as to the municipal or provincial bylaw relied upon to make such a finding. I find the Tenants have failed to sufficiently establish that the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) with respect to the railing. [name] cutting 44. It is undisputed that the Tenants were responsible for lawn maintenance. They allege the Landlord provided them with unsafe and insufficient equipment to maintain the lawn. 45. The Tenants acknowledge that they are responsible for the lawn maintenance as per the lease agreement. In my view, this responsibility includes having the necessary equipment. I am not convinced the Landlord was obligated to provide the Tenants with the equipment necessary to maintain the lawn. The Landlord provided the Tenants with an electric mini tractor and a push lawn mower. The Tenants had the option of using the push lawn mover if they felt uncomfortable operating the electric mini tractor. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied the Landlord is in breach of his maintenance obligations. Remedies 46. As noted above, I am satisfied the Landlord’s failure to provide safe, drinking water is a breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. The remedy sought by the Tenants in connection to the water issue is a rent abatement. 47. Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that rent is for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving everything he or she is entitled to then the tenant is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference. Assessing quantum is something of an art and will vary based on a number of factors including the nature of the problem, the length of time or frequency of the breach, and the impact on the Tenants. 48. The Tenants did not have potable water throughout their 14 ½ month tenancy. MY testified that they preferred bottle water so the fact the rental unit did not have potable water was not a significant issue. The biggest impact was during the seven-day period when they were without any running water due to the water pump issue. 49. In relation to the lack of water from March 1-March 7, 2024, I find that it is appropriate and reasonable to award the Tenants a rent abatement of $259.68, which is calculated at 50% of the rent for one week, March 1-7, 2024. 50. The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant a rent abatement of 5% of the monthly rent of $2,300.00 for the period of July 2023 to September 2024, which amounts to $1610.00. Administrative Fine 51. As water is a vital service, Guideline 16 provides that a fine can be levied where the Landlord withheld a vital service in such a way as to demonstrate blatant disregard for his obligations to the Tenants. 52. SY testified that she and her husband and five children occupied the house for 14 months. In that time, they had no access to drinking water and bought bottled water at their own expense. This is unthinkable. Even though they testified that they preferred bottled water and knew about the lack of drinking water when they signed the lease, it does not absolve the Landlord from fulfilling his obligations. 53. I find that the Landlord’s failure to uphold his obligation amounted to blatant disregard for the Tenants and their rights. He had an obligation to provide a habitable rental unit in compliance with provincial and municipal standards and failed to meet those standards. Therefore a fine is reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances in order to deter such behaviour. He shall pay the Board a fine of $3220. 54. The amount of the fine reflects the seriousness of failing to provide a vital service like water, the protracted length of time the service was unavailable, and represents a 10% portion of the rent the Landlord collected during that period. Consideration was given to the fact that the Landlord is an independent landlord and not a large, for-profit corporation. The amount is also intended to deter similar future behaviour by this Landlord and others.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,869.68 This amount represents: • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application, • Rent abatement for $259.68, for March 1-7, 2025 • Rent abatement for July 2023-September 2024, $1610.00
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $3220.00 by July 28, 2026. July 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring Chritstina [name] and [name] (the 'Former Tenants') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Former Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex. T1 Application [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T5 Application [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. These applications were heard by videoconference on May 4, 2026. The Landlord’s legal representative [name], the Landlord and the Former Tenants attended the hearing. LTB-T-093611-24
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Compensation for Damage
The Landlord’s application alleges the Former Tenants caused wilful or negligent damage to the rental unit or residential complex and claims $11,634.42 to repair the damage.
The Landlord alleges the following damage: • Driveway repair (oil spill) • Camera Installation • Wall Damage • Painting • Eavestrough repair. [name]

The Landlord submitted colourless photographs of the driveway and parking area that purport to show damage caused by the Tenants’ vehicle. The Landlord’s evidence is that the Tenants’ vehicle caused oil stains on the driveway and the Tenants drove over the oil spill causing further staining.

The Landlord gave evidence that she sent text messages to the Tenants about repairing the driveway. The Landlord testified that Christina advised her that it was power-steering fluid and not oil however, the Landlord’s evidence is that power-steering fluid is still oil- based and requires steam cleaning.

The Landlord also testified that the Tenant was having problems with their vehicle for two weeks and despite this the Tenant failed to put down an oil pan or other basin when draining fluids asserting that the Tenant let the fluids drain onto the driveway.

The Landlord submitted an estimate from “Shack Shine” dated September 23, 2024, and Action Paving Inc. dated September 19, 2024. The estimate from Shack Shine shows a cost of $1,015.87 to wash, degrease, and spot clean the entire driveway. The Shack Shine estimate recommends sealing or painting the driveway after the cleaning service is performed.

The Action Paving Inc. estimate shows a cost of $5,751.70 to seal the driveway using an oil-based product. The Landlord testified that the entire driveway has to be cleaned and sealed otherwise it will look patched in the areas requiring repair. LTB-T-093611-24

The Tenant’s evidence is that the power-steering line broke in their vehicle and it was not during a time when work was being performed. A text message submitted by the Tenants reads, “I already discussed the mishap with the car. It was an act of God.. [name] working on it and have done a few things since ..”

The Tenant briefly testified that they did their best to clean up the oil spill and should not be responsible for cleaning and sealing the entire driveway. The Tenants also submitted photographs of the oil spill, photos depicting the Tenant making attempts to clean the spill, and one photo after the spill had been cleaned.

The Landlord must prove that the Former Tenants either wilfully (intentionally), or negligently (through a lack of reasonable care) caused damage to the driveway. The Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant was working on their vehicle in the two weeks leading up to the spill is insufficient to establish that the Tenant wilfully or negligently damaged the driveway.

The Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant failed to put down an oil pan and let fluids drain from the vehicle is speculative and without corroboration. The Landlord’s understanding of the circumstances surrounding the oil spill was based on information given to her by the tenant in unit 1, and I give little weight to this hearsay evidence.

Further, I am persuaded by the photographs submitted by the Tenant showing their efforts to remediate the issue, and the completed work. Accordingly, based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Former Tenants wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the driveway. Camera Installation
The Landlord’s application requests reimbursement for installing cameras in the residential complex in the amount of $1,285.94.

The Landlord testified the cameras were necessary because when the Tenants put their vehicle up for sale, there were a number of “random” individuals coming to look at the vehicle which the Landlord asserts was concerning for her other tenant residing in unit 1. The Landlord further testified that she did not regularly monitor the cameras on a regular basis.

The Landlord’s evidence is that audio recording features were added to the cameras because one of the Tenants was using profanities and would be loud while being on the back deck. The Landlord testified that she lives next door to the Tenants and could clearly hear the Tenant making disparaging remarks.
During cross examination the Landlord acknowledged that the cameras are still installed, and the cameras are her personal property.

The Tenants testified in relation to their displeasure with the camera installation and their concerns about privacy. The Tenants disputed being responsible for the cost to install the cameras. LTB-T-093611-24

The Landlord’s application for compensation is brought pursuant to section 89 of the Act, which requires the Landlord to prove that the Tenants caused wilful or negligent damage resulting in costs to the Landlord. The installation of cameras is not attributable to any wilful or negligent damage caused by the Tenants as contemplated by s. 89 of the Act.

The Landlord did not claim the camera expense as costs owing for substantial interference pursuant to section 88.1 of the Act however, the Landlord’s own evidence is that the cameras were installed out of concern to provide greater security for Unit 1 because of the Tenants listing their vehicle for sale.

Even if the Landlord had claimed the cost of camera installation on the basis of substantial interference, the Landlord’s reason for installing the cameras was because the Tenants were selling their vehicle which does not substantially interfere with the Landlord.

Accordingly, the installation of the cameras was not as a result of damage caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenants. The camera installation cost was not claimed as a substantial interference, nor would I find that there was a substantial interference entitling the Landlord to claim this expense. Wall Damage/Painting
The Landlord submitted 16 colourless photographs purporting to show damage to the walls in the rental unit attributable to the Tenants hanging various pictures, decorations, and wall hangings.

Many of the holes appear to be patched in the photos, and none of the holes appear to be caused by anything other than pictures, wall hangings, and decorations. The Landlord did not submit any evidence that baseboards or trim were damaged.

The Landlord submitted an invoice showing a cost of $1,780.91 to paint the entire rental unit including baseboards and trim, and paint costs of approximately $2,064.59. The Landlord did not submit an invoice to repair holes in the walls.

The Board considered a claim for damage where there are holes in the wall from tenants hanging pictures or shelves in Malik v Cleaver, 2021 CanLII 119221 (para 9): With respect to the shelves and frames, I am satisfied by the Landlord’s testimony and photographic evidence that the Tenant wilfully or negligently caused damage to the unit. Section 62 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that the damage must be undue. It is recognized that some damage will occur over the regular course of time, due to regular wear and tear in a residential complex. Reasonable wear and tear would not normally constitute “undue damage” ([name] Housing Corp. 2005 O.J. No. 3911). Reasonable wear and tear may include a few small holes from screws or nails during the course of hanging pictures or shelves in a unit. [Emphasis added]
While prior decisions of the Board are not binding, the decision in Malik v Cleaver is persuasive and I adopt the reasoning in relation to what constitutes “reasonable wear and tear”. LTB-T-093611-24

The Landlord’s evidence does not show the Tenant’s caused damage wilfully or negligently, and the holes in the walls are normal wear and tear caused by hanging pictures and wall decorations. Eavestrough
The Landlord testified that the Tenants installed privacy lattice by affixing the lattice to the eavestrough with nails and cut into the handrails causing damage.

The Landlord submitted photographs showing the area of the eavestrough where the privacy lattice was affixed, and a section of a handrail that had been cut to accommodate a post to secure the lattice. The photographs submitted show the installed privacy lattice, but fail to show the resulting damage alleged by the Landlord.

The Landlord also submitted a copy of an e-mail from “PPM Systems Home Improvement” dated December 20, 2024, providing a quote to remove and replace eavestrough, remove and replace siding, and remove and replace the handrail at a cost of $1,500.00 plus HST.

The Landlord’s evidence is that the lattice came down during a windstorm in November or December and disputed giving the Tenants permission to install the lattice. The Landlord testified that the Tenants installed the lattice without asking permission and without the Landlord’s knowledge.

The Tenant testified that they asked the Landlord if they could install the lattice for privacy because of a neighbouring retirement home. The Tenant gave evidence that the Landlord’s “boyfriend” told the Tenants how to install the lattice, they spent their own money and ensured that the installation was solid and professional.
The Tenants acknowledged installing the lattice and assert that they had permission from the Landlord. The Landlord’s unequivocal evidence is that the Tenants did not have permission.

The Tenants did not submit any correspondence with the Landlord showing the Tenants either requested or obtained permission to install the lattice. There was no evidence that the Landlord’s partner assisted the Tenants with installing the lattice or that he provided installation instructions.

Accordingly, in the absence of evidence from the Tenants to corroborate their assertion that they had permission from the Landlord to install the lattice, I am satisfied that the Tenants caused wilful damage to the residential complex by installing privacy lattice.

Despite this finding, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has proven that the out-of-pocket expenses claimed are reasonable. There was no testimony from a contractor or PPM Systems Home Improvement to substantiate the estimate submitted, nor was there evidence proving that both eavestrough and siding require replacement.
Further, based on the photographs submitted I am not satisfied that that the issues require replacement and could not be repaired. LTB-T-093611-24
Therefore, the Landlord did not prove the reasonable costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur as a result of the installation of the privacy lattice.
The Landlord did not prove that the Tenants caused wilful or negligent damage, nor the reasonable out of pocket expenses for the damage that was proven.
Accordingly, the Landlord has not proven the allegations of damage and the Landlord’s application is dismissed. T5 Application/T1 Application

The Tenants filed a T5 application alleging that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith, and a T1 application that alleges the Landlord failed to pay compensation as required by section 48.1 of the Act. The Tenant’s T1 application also alleges that the Landlord failed to return the unused portion of their rent deposit. [name] for Own Use in Bad Faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that the relationship between the Landlord and the Tenants began deteriorating in September 2024. The Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of January 31, 2025. The N12 notice lists the Landlord’s child as the intended occupant.

The Tenant testified that after receiving the N12 notice they began looking for a new residence and the Landlord failed to pay compensation as required by section 48.1 of the Act. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 29, 2024.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord’s son did not move into the rental unit because after the Tenants moved out, the Landlord listed the property for rent three days later. The Tenant submitted a copy of the rental advertisement with a listing date of October 3, 2024. The Tenants submitted another rental listing showing the Landlord had again re-listed the property for rent on May 20, 2025.

The Tenants gave evidence that they paid first month’s rent and a rent deposit at the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant testified that they also paid rent for the month of September 2024. LTB-T-093611-24

The Landlord did not dispute serving the Tenants an N12 notice and rationalized service of the N12 notice by stating that she told the Tenants she would not be renewing the lease in February 2025. The Landlord testified that she needed the property for her son who was going to move in around March 2025.

The Landlord further testified that she has two children, and her son told his sister that he needed a place to live around August 2024. The Landlord did not directly answer whether she actually spoke to her son about plans to move into the rental unit testifying that she and her son are, “not on good terms” and do not have a good relationship.

The Landlord testified that her son moved into the rental unit in June 2025 and submitted a copy of a redacted driver’s license listing the address of the rental unit, and an issuance date of June 27, 2025.
The Landlord also testified that if her son and his girlfriend did not separate after moving in together in March 2025, her son probably would not have moved into the rental unit at all.
The Landlord’s son did not testify at the hearing, and I am without evidence from him about any conversations he had about his plans, needs, intention or desire to move into the rental unit.

It was undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination. While there were ancillary events contemporaneous to service of the N12 notice (including service of an N5 notice of termination), I am satisfied that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.

The Tenant’s testimony is that they began looking for a new residence after receiving the N12 notice and vacated the rental unit on September 29, 2025. The determination that the Tenants vacated the rental unit because of the N12 notice is supported by the fact that the Tenants had already began looking for a new residence prior to service of the N5 notice.

The Tenants have also proved that no person listed in the N12 notice moved into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time. The Landlord’s testimony confirms that the [name] son did not move into the rental unit until June 2025- approximately 9 months after serving the Tenants with the N12 notice.

It is also noted that, while speculative, the Landlord acknowledged that her son would likely not have moved into the rental unit except for his separation from his partner. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s son moved into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time.

When considering the final part of the requirements set out in section 57 of the Act, the facts here trigger the reverse onus clause in s. 57(5). That provision says that if a landlord gives a notice under s. 48 and then puts the unit up for sale or rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. What this means is that the Landlord must prove it is more likely than not that when she gave the N12 to the Tenants she and her son genuinely intended that her son would move in. LTB-T-093611-24

The Landlord testified vaguely that she became aware that her son needed a place to live in August 2024 through her daughter. The Landlord did not submit any correspondence with her son about plans to move into the rental unit contemporaneous to service of the N12 notice. The actions of the Landlord’s son moving in with his girlfriend around March 2025 are indicative that he had no genuine intent to occupy the rental unit.

The Landlord’s evidence about her son’s intention to occupy the rental unit was specious and I draw a negative inference from his lack of participation at the hearing. Generally, a Landlord will adduce evidence of a material change in circumstances to rebut the presumption of bad faith however, I am without evidence that there was any change in circumstances.
The Landlord’s testimony and evidence is insufficient to rebut the presumption of bad faith in these circumstances. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

Further, since the Landlord served an N12 notice pursuant to section 48 of the Act, sections 48.1 and 55.1 require the Landlord to compensate the Tenants in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the Tenants another rental unit.

The Landlord’s justification for serving the N12 notice being that she did not intend to renew the lease does not negate the Landlord’s obligations pursuant to section 48.1 and 55.1. Further, there is no basis in the Act for the Landlord to terminate a tenancy on the basis of not renewing the lease. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant compensation in the amount of one month’s rent.
In relation to the rent deposit, the Landlord served both an N12 and N5 notice of termination. The Tenants vacated the rental unit after receiving the notices of termination.

Section 37(2) of the Act provides: (2) If a notice of termination is given in accordance with this Act and the tenant vacates the rental unit in accordance with the notice, the tenancy is terminated on the termination date set out in the notice.

Further, section 86 of the Act sets out a Landlord’s entitlement to compensation if a tenant fails to vacate the rental unit after the tenancy is terminated by notice: 86 A landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of a rental unit by a tenant who does not vacate the unit after his or her tenancy is terminated by order, notice or agreement.

Finally, section 134(1.1) precludes a Landlord from collecting any amount of money purporting to be rent after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant vacates, or after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy terminated: LTB-T-093611-24 (1.1) No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. 2017, c. 13, s. 24 (2).
There was no dispute that the Landlord collected a rent deposit, and the Tenants paid rent for the month of September 2024.

The Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 29, 2024, pursuant to notices of termination and therefore, the Landlord is only entitled to rent up to the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Tenants are entitled to the return of the rent deposit paid. T2 Application

The Tenants also filed a T2 application alleging that the Landlord harassed, threatened, or interfered with the Tenants by serving an N5 notice of termination, sending multiple text messages in relation to the driveway cleanup, and installing security cameras that included audio and video recording. N5 Notice

The Landlord was entitled to serve the Tenants with an N5 notice in relation to the driveway cleanup and I do not find that this can be considered in the context of advancing the allegation of harassment in relation to the driveway cleanup. Text Messages

The Tenants also testified that the Landlord sent numerous text messages in relation to their broken-down vehicle, the driveway cleanup, and individuals being observed at the back of the residential complex.

The first few text messages submitted demonstrate typical correspondence about tenancy issues however, the Landlord continues to send text messages to the Tenants in relation to the driveway cleanup and persists in attempting to illicit a response from the Tenants.

While it may have been more reasonable for the Tenants to respond to the Landlord and provide an estimated timeline to clean the driveway, the Tenants were unequivocal in their request for the Landlord to stop sending text messages and reiterated that request multiple times.

There is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome” LTB-T-093611-24

The Landlord persisted in sending text messages to the Tenants despite being made aware that those messages were unwelcome. Accordingly, I find that the text messages sent to the Tenants from the Landlord in relation to the driveway cleanup were harassing. Security Cameras/Audio Video Recording

The Tenants testified that the Landlord had installed video cameras, and the Tenants were unaware that the cameras could move and swivel. The Tenants gave evidence that the Landlord eventually upgraded the cameras to include audio recording and asserted that the cameras were a breach of their privacy because the cameras were situated 10 feet from their balcony where their private conversations could be recorded.

The Landlord testified that the first-floor tenant had made complaints that there were individuals in the rear of the residential complex that were not friends of the Tenants, and the Tenant would “verbally abuse” the Landlord.

The Landlord’s evidence is that the cameras were installed for everyone’s safety and that the cameras served their purpose because the Tenant’s yelling, screaming, and profanity stopped after the cameras were installed.

When considering the Tenant’s submission that the cameras were a breach of their privacy, it is not necessary to examine the issues typically associated with privacy (collection, retention, and dissemination). The cameras do not appear to be directed towards the Tenants’ balcony and there was no evidence that the cameras observed any areas other than the common areas of the driveway and parking lot.

The Tenants’ application alleges that the Landlord harassed, threatened, or interfered with the Tenants, and not substantial interference. There was no evidence that the use of the cameras with audio constitutes harassment, threats, or interference as contemplated by the Act.
Even if the cameras and audio recording were considered in the context of substantial interference, I would not find that the cameras were a substantial interference.

The Tenant testified that they could not have a private conversation on their balcony because their discussion would be audio recorded by the cameras. The Tenants’ belief that the cameras could capture the Tenants regular conversations on their balcony is unsupported and speculative.
The Tenants have a full expectation of privacy inside their rental unit however, the expectation of privacy on an outdoor balcony that overlooks a common area would not attract that same expectation.

Given that conversations on an outdoor balcony can reasonably be overheard by others, the Tenants must demonstrate that the recordings captured audio beyond what would normally be audible to a person outside. Absent such evidence, it cannot be concluded that the recordings infringed the Tenants’ privacy. LTB-T-093611-24 Remedies T1 Application
As decided above, the Tenants are entitled to compensation pursuant to section 48.1. The Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $2,100.00 for compensation owed.
Further, the Tenants are entitled to the return of the rent deposit being held. The Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $2,100.00 for the rent deposit.
The Tenant’s application also seeks interest on the rent deposit from January 3, 2024. The Landlord owes interest on the rent deposit in the amount of $183.55. T2 Application
The only allegation proven by the Tenants in relation to their T2 application is harassment relating to the text messages and correspondence pertaining to the driveway cleanup.

The Tenants testimony in relation to the duration of the harassment was unclear. The text messages submitted at the hearing were undated and it cannot be determined whether the harassment persisted over a period of hours, days, or weeks.

The text messages from the Landlord did not contain insults or profanities. The issue was determined to be the persistence and ongoing communications despite the Tenants’ protests. Therefore, I find that a lump sum abatement in the amount of $140.00 is appropriate, which is the equivalent of approximately a 2-day abatement ($2,100.00 x 12 / 365 x 2). T5 Remedies
The Tenant’s T5 application requests a fine in the amount of $5,000.00.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative fines provides: “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

While this order makes findings that there were breaches of the Act by the Landlord, I do not find that these breaches constitute a blatant disregard for the Act attracting the imposition of a fine. The remedies ordered herein should suffice to encourage compliance and provide deterrence.
The Tenants’ application requests reimbursement for moving and storage expenses in the amount of $11,836.00. LTB-T-093611-24

The Tenants submitted a U-haul invoice in the amount of $179.07, and claimed fuel expenses of $159.86. I am satisfied that the Tenants have proven the reasonable out of pocket expenses incurred for moving and the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $338.93.

The balance of out of pocket expenses claimed for moving and storage consists of lost wages for both Tenants, and one of the Tenants’ additional travel costs to and from work. These expenses are not moving and storage expenses as contemplated by the Act and I find these alleged damages are too remote.

The Tenants also request general compensation in the amount of $25,200.00 pursuant to section 57(3) 1.1 which entitles a Tenant to seek an amount up to the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged: 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2.

Section 57(3)(1.1) offers little guidance on how to determine the amount of general compensation that should be awarded in any particular case. General compensation is compensation for the non-pecuniary impacts of the loss of the Tenants’ home, such as pain and suffering, inconvenience, and loss of enjoyment of life. In setting a high maximum amount for general compensation, it would appear that the Legislature intends s.57(3)(1.1) to indicate that the loss of a person’s home should be taken to be a very serious loss.

Section 57(3)(1.1) was enacted relatively recently, and the LTB has not yet arrived at a consistent approach to calculating general compensation. In Conde- Jahnel v. Tatone, (2024 February 22), File No. LTB-T-009158-23 (unreported, cited in Fleming, Ontario Landlord and [name], 2025), the LTB awarded general compensation of 5.2 months’ rent for a bad-faith eviction. In that case, there were some factors suggesting that the move was difficult for the tenants, but nothing out of the ordinary course of what one would expect from being forced to move.

The present case is similar in that the loss of the Tenants’ home impacted their lives in significant ways, but not beyond what one would expect from the loss of a family’s home. However, in these circumstances, 5.2 months’ rent would be a somewhat low award given that the maximum award is more than twice that amount.

In light of the above considerations and recognizing that in some respects assessing non- pecuniary compensation is more art than science, I find that general compensation equivalent to 8 months of the last rent charged is appropriate. Accordingly, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $16,800.00.
ordered: The Landlord’s L10 application is dismissed. LTB-T-093611-24 T1 Application

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was scheduled for an adjudicative case conference on June 25, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the adjudicative case conference. The Landlord was not present or represented at the case conference although properly served with notice of this case conference by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the case conference. As a result, the case conference proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities regarding a hole and leaks in the rental unit ceiling.

The Tenant testified that on July 20, 2025, water began dripping from the bedroom ceiling onto his bed. The water was significant and lasted for approximately 40 minutes. The Tenant testified that he notified the Landlord, but the Landlord did nothing.

The Tenant testified that on September 4, 2025 a huge portion of the bedroom ceiling collapsed. The Tenant testified that he notified the Landlord, the Landlord said he was in Europe, and that he would send someone. The Tenant testified that the roof was not addressed until sometime in October 2025.
The Tenant provided videos of the incidents (DOC-6759348, DOC-6759349, DOC- 6759365).

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable. The Landlord did nothing about the first leak and then took a significant time to address the collapsed ceiling.

The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on October 15, 2025. The Tenant requests the return of his last months rent. The Tenant testified that he pre-paid his rent but then did not get to live in the rental unit for the month he paid for. I find that request to be reasonable because the Tenant only vacated as a result of the maintenance issues. While the Tenant testified that his last month’s rent was $1,800.00, in the application the Tenant only requested $1,625.68 so that is what will be awarded.

The Tenant also requests a rent abatement from when the ceiling collapsed on September 4, 2025. The Tenant testified that the roof was fixed sometime in October 2025 but was not sure of the date. As such the Tenant led insufficient evidence to get a rent abatement for more than one month. I find a 30% rent abatement for the month to be reasonable. There was substantial disruption to the tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit. The rent abatement is $540.00.

The Tenant’s new rental unit is more expensive by $224.00 a month. The Tenant requests the difference in rent for one year. While I accept that the Tenant only moved because of the maintenance issues, I do not find the units entirely comparable. The Tenant testified that both units are one-bedroom units, but that the new unit is bigger, has a fancier kitchen, and the flooring is better. As such, I’m not satisfied that the entirety of the rent differential is related to the Landlord’s conduct. I find a $50.00 monthly rent differential for a total of $600.00 for one year to be reasonable.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and should be reimbursed by the Landlord for those costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,813.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 15, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the Tenants the last month’s rent that is on deposit.

The Tenants testified and provided text messages as evidence that there was a flood that occurred in their rental unit on July 31, 2025, which they advised the Landlord of, and they advised the Landlord of mold concerns. The Tenants further testified that on August 5, 2025, they still had not received a response from the Landlord and continued to follow up through to August 11, 2025, which ultimately led them to terminate their tenancy effective September 1, 2025.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord thanked them when they advised they would be vacating the rental unit due to flooding issue, and that the Landlord failed to apply their last month’s rent deposit to August 2025 rent.

The Tenants provided uncontested oral testimony and evidence in relation to providing the Landlord notice to terminate the tenancy, which the Landlord did not dispute but rather thanked them for providing notice to terminate the tenancy on September 1, 2025.

I find that the parties agreed that the tenancy would terminate on September 1, 2025, as the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant disputing the termination date, but rather thanked them. The Tenants vacated the rental unit pursuant to the agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant. At the time the Tenants vacated the rental unit and the tenancy ended, the rent was paid in full and the Landlord was still holding the rent deposit.

In accordance with s. 106(10), a landlord can only use a rent deposit to cover the rent for the last rental period. Since the rent for the last rental period was already paid, the deposit must be returned to the Tenants.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant’s T2 application alleges that the Landlord improperly refused a request to sublet and failed to respond within the required time period.

At the beginning of the hearing, the Landlord’s representative objected to the matter proceeding as a T2 application. He submitted that the allegations related to an assignment or sublet provision under the Act and should proceed as an A2 application pursuant to ss. 95 and 97 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant requested for her application to proceed as a T2 because she seeks compensation for moving and out of pocket expenses because of the Landlord's conduct.

Based on the submissions, I find that the allegations and the remedy sought fall within the scope of a T2 application alleging interference with the Tenant’s rights under the Act. Here, the Tenant is not seeking an order authorizing a specific assignment or sublet. In addition, the Tenant confirmed that she did not identify or propose a specific subtenant and was refused to sublet by the Landlord. Therefore, I was satisfied to proceed with the Tenant’s T2 application. Preliminary issue - Tenant’s evidence

During the hearing the Tenant referred to her evidence. The Landlord’s representative who was on the phone advised that he only received materials up to page 13 and had not received the additional documents referenced by the Tenant. The Tenant testified that she delivered the materials to the management office located at the residential complex. The Landlord’s representative objected to the method of service because it was not delivered to the “Landlord’s address for service” as set out on the lease agreement.

I directed the Tenant to email the evidence package to the Landlord’s management office for the attention of the Landlord’s agent and representative. The hearing was held down to permit the Landlord’s representative an opportunity to review the materials. When the matter was reconvened the Landlord’s representative indicated that he does have the Tenant’s evidence but was not referring to the PDF page numbers. I proceeded to hear the merits of the application. Evidence and Submissions
The Tenancy agreement between the parties began on March 1, 2024, for a fixed term of one year ending on February 28, 2025.

The Tenant referred to her evidence and testified that on October 11, 2024, she emailed the Landlord requesting permission to sublet the unit from November 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025. In her email she indicated that the tenancy will remain in her name and the rental payments will continue to be paid from her account. A “follow up” email was sent to the Landlord on October 16 and 18, 2024. On October 19, 2024, the Tenant received a letter from the Landlord dated “October 11, 2024.” She testified that the letter was placed under her door. The Landlord’s letter stated that her sublet request was denied.
On October 21, 2024, the Landlord emailed the Tenant stating: “as per the property manager's direction, we have notified you already. We do not do sublets and your request has been rejected.”

On October 25, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord, she quoted the lease provision stating that “the Landlord cannot arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold consent to a sublet or assignment.” In her email she asked the Landlord to identify any concerns so she could address them. The Tenant did not receive a response from the Landlord explaining the refusal. Therefore, on November 1, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord giving notice that she would vacate at the end of November 2024. She requested for the last month’s deposit to be applied to November 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord unreasonably withheld consent so she provided a 30 days’ notice to terminate her tenancy. The Tenant stated that it is her understanding that if the Landlord arbitrarily withholds consent to sublet she can serve a 30 days’ notice to terminate her tenancy.

On November 6, 2024, the Landlord sent the Tenant a letter stating that her notice was improper and that she remained legally responsible for the unit until February 28, 2025, unless the unit was re-rented or another person took over the tenancy.

The Tenant returned the keys and gave vacant possession on November 29, 2024. 13. [name] (Landlord’s regional manager) testified that the Landlord does allow sublets, including at the rental property. She indicated that the email to the Tenant stating “we do not do sublets” should not have been sent. 14. [name] explained that the Tenant’s request was denied because the Tenant requested to sublet the unit until February 28, 2025. She indicated the Tenant was not returning after the end of her lease term. The Tenant’s request was treated as an assignment than a sublet. However, after the Landlord reviewed the circumstances, the Landlord decided “not to hold the Tenant responsible/liable” and applied the last month’s rent deposit to November 30, 2024. Analysis and Findings 15. Pursuant to s. 2 of the Act, a “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit.” Subsection 97 of the Act states “a tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord.” In this case, the Tenant requested permission to sublet the rental unit from November 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025, which was to the end of the Tenant’s fixed term lease. 16. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 21, titled Landlords, Tenants, [name] and Residential Tenancies states “for a subtenancy to exist under the Act, the tenant must retain the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit before the end of the tenancy term.” Therefore the arrangement proposed by the Tenant did not technically meet the definition of a sublet under the Act because the Tenant would not have resumed occupancy before the end of the tenancy term. However, the issue before me is not limited to whether the Tenant properly characterized her request. The issue is whether the Landlord’s communication substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, which includes the ability to exercise her rights under the Act. 17. The evidence before me establishes that Tenant repeatedly attempted to communicate with the Landlord and asked whether there were concerns for the refusal, which could be addressed. Instead, the Landlord communicated an outright refusal stating that it “does not do sublets.” The Landlord’s agent acknowledged that the communication sent to the Tenant should have not been sent because the Landlord allows sublets at the property. 18. I also note that section 97(2) of the Act provides that a landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant. A complete refusal by a landlord to consider any sublet is a breach of section 97(2). 19. I accept [name] evidence that the Landlord's concern was related to the duration of the proposed arrangement and the fact that the Tenant would not be returning to occupy the unit before the end of the lease term. However, none of this was ever communicated to the Tenant, despite her repeated attempts to seek clarification and resolve the issues. 20. I also accept the Tenant’s evidence that she attempted to understand and comply with the process by communicating with the Landlord, reviewing her lease agreement, and asking whether there were concerns that could be addressed. Instead of receiving clarification, she was advised that the Landlord simply does not do sublets. 21. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlords inaccurate and misleading communications substantially interfered with the Tenant’s rights under the Act because it deprived the Tenant of a meaningful opportunity to address the landlord’s concerns, clarify the nature of the request, or make an informed decision regarding her tenancy. I also find that the Landlord's subsequent conduct supports this conclusion. Remedies 22. During the hearing, the Tenant testified that she incurred $60.00 for gas, $100.00 for U- Haul and she claimed $880.00 for her boyfriend's lost wages. The Tenant provided limited testimony regarding the out of pocket expense of $2,888.00. The Tenant did not file documentary evidence in support of these expenses or provide a sufficient testimony explaining how the amounts were calculated or how they were incurred as a result of the Landlord’s conduct. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to these remedies. 23. I also find that the Tenant had an intention to vacate the rental unit by the end of her term and she would have incurred expenses associated with the move. I say this because the evidence before me establishes that the Tenant sought permission to sublet the rental unit until February 28, 2025, which is to the end of her fixed term tenancy and there was no evidence before me that she intended to resume occupancy of the rental unit thereafter. 24. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved entitlement to the remedies claimed in the application or that the remedies claimed were incurred as a result of the Landlord’s conduct.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
On or about September 11, 2025, the parties entered into a tenancy agreement for a rental period commencing on December 1, 2025, for a fixed term ending on December 31, 2026.

On October 2, 2025, the Tenant learned that the residential complex included mixed income subsidized housing and advised the Landlord that they would not take possession of the rental unit. The Landlord explained to the Tenants that they could assign the tenancy or agree to end the tenancy with forfeiture of the last month’s rent deposit.
On October 14, 2025, the parties executed an Agreement to End the Tenancy (N11 notice) ending the tenancy on December 1, 2025. The above facts are not in dispute.
Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I am not convinced the Tenants are entitled to the return of the last month’s rent deposit.

Subsection 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires that a landlord repay the amount received as a rent deposit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. In Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 5425 (CanLII), the Court found that the word “not given” suggests that it is the refusal or inability of a landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. In the present case, however, it was the Tenants’ action in refusing to take the unit that prevented them from taking possession, not any act of the Landlords. As such, the Tenants are bound by the agreement with the Landlords and would not be entitled to the return of the rent deposit pursuant to subsection 107(1) because it was their act of repudiation of the agreement that prevented them from taking possession of the unit, not the action of the Landlords.

Rather than bind the Tenants to the agreement, the Landlords agreed to end the tenancy with forfeiture of the last month’s rent deposit. In my view, this was reasonable given the alternative. That is, the Tenants would have been financially liable until December 31, 2026.

However, that is not the end of the analysis. Pursuant to section 16 of the Act, the Landlords also have a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses resulting from the Tenants’ unilateral repudiation of the tenancy agreement. Despite efforts, the Landlords could not re-rent the unit for December 1, 2025. Accordingly, I find the Landlords were entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. July 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-096530-25 issued on May 1, 2026. On May 5, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On May 5, 2026, interim order LTB-T-096530-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 1, 2026 The request to review was heard by videoconference on July 9, 2026.
reasons: The order issued May 1, 2026, found the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant which is prohibited by s.106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The hearing Member ordered the Landlord to repay the rent deposit, together with the applicable interest. However, the Member deducted $345.20 from the amount owing because the Tenant remained in possession of the rental unit for seven days in May 2025.
For the reasons set out below, I find that the original order erroneously deducted $345.20, representing seven days of rent for May 2025, from the amount owing to the Tenant.

Although the hearing Member asked the Tenant when he vacated the rental unit and reviewed the final rent payments, neither party was advised that the Member was considering deducting rent for May 2025. The parties were not invited to make submissions concerning the applicable rental period, the daily rent calculation, or whether any rent remained payable for the period ending May 7, 2025.
The deduction was therefore made without giving the parties a meaningful opportunity to address the issue. I find that this amounted to a serious error and a denial of procedural fairness.

Moreover, it was clear from the evidence adduced at the hearing that each monthly rental period began on the third day of the month and ended on the second day of the following month. Therefore, even if it had been appropriate to deduct a daily amount for the period during which the Tenant remained in possession, I find the original order erred by including May 1 and May 2, 2025, in the calculation.

Included in the Tenant’s request to review (DOC-7897752 page 6) was an email from the Landlord in which the Landlord advised that he had decided to waive the rent payable for the period from May 3 to May 7, 2025.
Accordingly, I find there was no basis to deduct $345.20, or any other amount for May 2025 rent, from the rent deposit and interest owing to the Tenant.

I am satisfied that the original order contains a serious error and that a serious error occurred in the proceeding. Therefore, the Tenant’s request to review is granted, and the order shall be varied accordingly.

At the hearing, the Landlord also disputed the original finding that the Tenant had paid a last month’s rent deposit. Although the Landlord did not file the request to review, he submitted that the hearing Member erred by accepting the Tenant’s evidence concerning the deposit. I do not agree with the Landlord’s submission.

The hearing Member considered the parties’ evidence and accepted the Tenant’s testimony that he provided the Landlord with $3,000.00 before moving into the rental unit, of which $1,500.00 represented the last month’s rent deposit.

Although the Landlord disagrees with the weight given to the Tenant’s evidence, he has not established that the hearing Member’s finding was unreasonable based on the evidence presented at the hearing.

A review hearing is not an opportunity for a party to reargue the case merely because the party disagrees with the hearing Member’s findings of fact, assessment of credibility, or weighing of the evidence.

I therefore find no serious error in the hearing Member’s determination that the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit, and the Landlord did not apply deposit to the rent for the last month of the tenancy. Accordingly, the balance of the order issued May 1, 2026, will remain unchanged.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-096530-25 issued on May 1, 2026, is granted.

Paragraph 1 of the order is varied to read as follows: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,630.73. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for the return of the last month's rent deposit. • $82.73 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 3. [name] and 3 of the order remain unchanged. 4. The interim order issued on May 5, 2026, is cancelled. The stay of order LTB-T-096530- 25, as varied, is lifted immediately. 5. The Board shall refund to the Tenant the $58.00 filing fee that he paid with respect to the request for review. July 31, 2026 ____________________________
