issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed [name]

The Tenant alleges that: 1. On February 22, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of entry for February 23, 2024 but did not attend on February 23, 2024 as per their notice of entry. 2. On February 28, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of entry for February 29, 2024. The Landlord did not adhere with the time of entry contained in the notice of entry, entering the rental unit after the time period specified in the notice of entry.

On October 29, 2024, the Landlord entered the rental unit with her son pursuant to a notice of entry for inspection and the Landlord’s son took photos and video of the LTB-T-098138-24 Tenant without the Tenant’s consent. The Landlord and the Landlord’s son also harassed the Tenant while conducting the inspection of the rental unit. The Landlord did not Enter Pursuant to Notice of Entry 3. The Tenant’s Witness, [name] [name] (‘QQ’), who is the husband of the Tenant, testified that on February 22, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of entry for February 23, 2023 but did not attend on February 23, 2023. The Tenant did not lead any evidence that the notice of entry was given for any improper purpose. Rather, QQ’s testimony was simply that the Landlord had failed to attend on this single instance pursuant to their notice of entry.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (‘FS’), the Landlord’s son-in-law, acknowledged that the Landlord had given the notice of entry for February 23, 2023 to the Tenant but asserts that the Landlord had to attend to her ill father and was not able to enter as per the notice of entry. I found the FS’s explanation for the missed entry to be credible and reasonable.

I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord substantially interfered by serving a single notice of entry for which the Landlord did not attend by either failing to attend on a single instance pursuant to the notice of entry or by giving the notice in bad faith to harass or interfere with the Tenant. Unlawful Entry

QQ testified that on February 28, 2024, the Landlord gave a notice of entry for February 29, 2024, indicating that the Landlord would enter between the hours of 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m. QQ testified that the Landlord did not attend the rental unit between the hours specified in the notice of entry but sent a text message to the Tenant at approximately 7:00 p.m., indicating that they were on their way to the rental unit. QQ testified that at approximately 7:19 p.m., the Landlord attended the rental unit with her son. QQ testified that as the Tenant was not aware of their legal rights with regards to notice of entry, they allowed the Landlord and her son to enter the rental unit.

Subsection 26(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that “a landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice…if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.”

While the Landlord did not give a proper notice of entry pursuant to the Act, based on the uncontested testimony of the Tenant, I find that the Tenant consented to the request to entry. As a result, I find that pursuant to subsection 26(1)(b) of the Act, that the entry was a lawful entry. Substantial Interference & Harassment by Landlord During Entry on February 29, 2024

QQ testified that on February 29, 2024, the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed the Tenant by taking photos and behaving aggressively towards the Tenant. LTB-T-098138-24
QQ testified that during the Landlord’s entry on February 29, 2024, the Landlords delivered baseless notices of termination and began recording personal items within the rental unit.

The Tenant entered into evidence a video of the Landlord’s entry on February 29. 2024. In the video, the Landlord’s son handed the Tenant an N12 notice of termination. took photos of the Tenant’s wall indicating that the Landlord would be serving an N5 for the damage to the wall, and engaged in a brief argument with the Tenant and QQ about whether QQ is a Tenant. The video also contains footage of another of the Landlord’s sons taking video of the Tenant’s clothing inside of the Tenant’s hallway closet, which the Landlord’s son alleges was for the purposes of inspecting the electrical panel within that closet.
The Tenant also entered into evidence a video of the Landlord’s son filming one of the Tenant from the common hallway of the residential complex upon leaving the rental unit.

The Tenant, [name] (‘MQ’) testified that the purpose of the February 29, 2024 inspection was to perform repairs but the Landlord did not perform repairs on that date but harassed the Tenant during their entry.
FS testified that the Landlord’s sons had filmed the rental unit to take video of items that needed to be repaired in the rental unit.

In Nicoladze v. Bloor Street Investments/Advent Property Management, 2015 ONSC 3893, the Divisional Court clarified that taking photos or video during an inspection is not, on its own, a breach of the tenant’s privacy rights. It may become so if done for an improper purpose.

In this case, the Tenant did not lead any evidence that the videos were taken for any improper purpose. FS’s submissions were that the video was taken for the purposes of documenting items of disrepair within the rental unit. Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenant has established that the photos were taken for any improper purpose.

Section 22 of the Act states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant o the tenant’s household.
Section 23 of the Act states that “a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

In considering breaches of s. 22 of the Act, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 states: The interference must be substantial in nature before it constitutes a breach of section 22 of the RTA. A minor inconvenience or disruption for a brief period of time does not normally result in an abatement of rent: Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. Herbold, [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC).

With regards to the Landlord’s sons’ conduct during the inspection, I was not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or constituted harassment. While the Landlord’s son gave an N12 notice of termination, LTB-T-098138-24 stated he would be serving an N5 notice for damage, and engaged in an argument with the [name] occupant, QQ about whether he was a tenant, I was not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct rose to the level of “substantial” interference nor did it constitute harassment. The Landlord is entitled to give notices of termination and I was not satisfied that the notice was given for any improper service. I was also not satisfied that the Landlord’s son stating he would serve an N5 for the alleged undue damage constituted substantial interference or harassment. With regards to the argument about whether QQ is a Tenant, while the parties disagreed about QQ’s status as either a Landlord or a Tenant, I was not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct or the Landlord’s sons’ conduct rose to the level of harassment or substantial interference.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household nor did the Landlord harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. As a result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application came before the Board for an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’), which was heard by videoconference on June 1, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 12:50 p.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, a hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: On November 20, 2025, the Tenant filed a T6 application alleging that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by failing to adequately address leaking/flooding in the rental unit, perform pest control, deal with mold/mildew and various plumbing-related concerns.

Pursuant to Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (ONSC DC), applications must contain sufficient particulars. Notwithstanding that the present case is a tenant application instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established.

The types of particulars expected in notices and applications include dates, times, and a detailed description of the alleged conduct or behaviour. This allows the responding party to know the case they have to meet and to prepare their defence.

The Board’s tenant application forms have also been developed with written instructions to elicit the necessary details required. For example, the T6 form states at page 3: Explaining your Reason: What is the problem? If there is more than one problem, list each problem. Give the date each problem started. Has the problem been repaired? If so, give the date it was repaired and explain who repaired it. Explain who or what may have caused the problem. How did you inform the landlord about the problem?
In short, it is not enough to rely on the dates and time contained in evidence; the pleadings themselves must identify the alleged breaches and their timing.

After reviewing the application, I find that the application does not clearly state when the alleged maintenance failures occurred. On the application, the Tenant indicates that April 12, 2025 was “The date I first told the landlord about the maintenance problems”, but there are no dates/times associated with any of the specific (and numerous) maintenance concerns identified.

For example, in the application the Tenant writes: ”I have lived in this unit for 5 years this past year it went through a massive flood in the bathroom. For 3 months it was raining they onlyBand Aidthe ceiling it’s now November and this all started in April and the ceiling is still raining.”
This lack of specificity leaves the Landlord and the Board to infer timelines by piecing together the evidence.

Pursuant to section 197 of the Act, the Board may dismiss an application, or a portion of an application, without holding a hearing, if, in the opinion of the Board the matter discloses no reasonable cause of action.
Accordingly, I find the Tenant’s application lacks the particulars in the application in order to procced to a hearing and the application should be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: Parties attended the Case Management Hearing for this matter on February 10, 2026; the matter did not resolve. Interim order LTB-T-098767-24-IN issued on March 16, 2026, set out the following requirements: • Paragraph 3: Should the Tenant wish to amend their application, they must do so in accordance with Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure on or before March 23, 2026. A copy of the amended application must be served to the Landlord and the LTB and proof of service in the form of a “Certificate of Service.” must be provided to the Board on or before the above-mentioned date. • Paragraph 4: Evidence that has not already been disclosed/does not comply with the Practice Direction and relates to the original application, including documents, receipts, photographs, recordings or like things intended to be relied on, shall properly disclosed by the following dates: Tenant’s disclosure on or before March 23, 2026; Landlord’s disclosure on or before March 30. 2026; any reply evidence from the Tenant on or before April 4, 2026. • Paragraph 5: Specified the requirements for disclosure of evidence pursuant to Rul 19 of the Rules of Procedure. • Paragraph 6: Set out disclosure cannot be done via the portal unless the parties have agreed to exchange documents via TOP. • Paragraph 7: Advises, pursuant to [name], a party who fails to comply with an order for disclosure may be permitted to rely on the evidence improperly disclosed.

At the start of the hearing, this Member raised as preliminary issues: a) The Tenant’s disclosure documents were all received well-past the date set out in the Interim Order. b) There is no amended T2 on file. c) Document #4613780, titled ‘[name]’ dated November 27, 2024, is for the Landlord’s L1 application LTB-L-096307-24 that was adjourned April 29, 2026, with a pending hearing date. The document notes: the Tenant vacated; the Tenant is raising section 82 issues; and if the section 82 issues overlap with the T2 application, the TT shall file a Request to Combine (RTC). No RTC was filed.

The Tenant testified she noticed that document #7637580 was missed when she did her first upload of evidence, therefore she resubmitted it. The COS and video were not included because she was unable to attach them; the evidence list was attached. When raised by this Member that the ‘evidence list’ was not the proper format as set out in the interim order and the T1 issues intended to be raised as under section 82 were not on the proper form that would be required for the L1 application, the Tenant submitted she intended on testifying to the evidence at the hearing and requested an adjournment of the T2 application until the L1 application proceeds in case of how it goes. The Tenant also mentioned being in Superior Court but then advised this is a matter being filed in Family Court against her husband that the Landlord is not party to.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted the Landlord has not been served any court documents and is not a party to any family law issues being pursued. The previous Member went through the evidence and disclosure requirements in great detail for approximately 45 minutes; there is no reason/excuse for the requirements not to be followed. As to service of documents, the Landlord never consented to service via the portal. Further, there was an A1 application where [name] was found to be a Tenant, and the L1 application is in respect of arrears not paid by her; the L1 was adjourned February 9, 2026, to give the Tenant time to properly submit/disclose these issues and evidence. This is the 7th hearing/time that evidence/disclosure and been an issue and the matter has been adjourned for the Tenant to properly address them. The Tenant’s application should be dismissed.

The Tenant replied: she served a well-organized list of documents on March 23, 2026; the T2 application is important; there is new evidence because of the way the case is advancing; document #4613780 is for the Landlord’s application and the section 82 issues; the L1 should be proceeding first; and she was unable to attach the 6 videos therefore they should be allowed to be submitted late.

The Tenant’s application is dismissed. The evidence was not submitted in accordance with the timeline ordered in LTB-L-096307-24-IN issued on March 16, 2026, or with the Rules of Procedure. A ‘document list’ that points to the document number on the portal, no matter how detailed, is not sufficient; this is not a ‘document brief’. As to new documents or those that could not be attached to submitted emails, the Tenant uploaded to the portal the following: 2 documents April 7, 2026; 1 document June 29, 2026; 29 documents June 30, 2026; 11 documents July 1, 2026; 1 document July 2, 2026; 1 document July 3, 2026; 2 documents July 4, 2026; 4 documents July 6, 2026; and, 3 documents July 3, 2026. Most of these documents were uploaded well after the ordered date(s) and none were properly served/disclosed. The Tenant’s behaviour in respect of ordered amendment and evidentiary requirements shows a blatant disregard of the LTB’s rules and procedures. Costs

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted costs should be ordered against the Tenant for failing to follow the requirements in the interim order; the Landlord has been greatly prejudiced because they have paid for representation for each hearing. Between all matters, there have been 9 to 11 appearances, therefore $400.00 is being requested.
The Tenant submitted this is prejudicial to her because it goes against her being told $50.00 in costs was going to be awarded because of her behaviour.

Interpretation Guideline 3 gives the Board the discretion to award the costs of another party and the costs of a proceeding to be paid by a party or their representative when a party’s conduct is unreasonable, including but not limited to failing to take necessary steps such as those required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). Examples of failing to comply with the RTA or Rules include: • Failing to follow a procedural order or direction such as an order to serve another party with a document; • Serving another party in a way which was not appropriate; • Delaying the hearing by not taking actions required in the Rules.
There does not appear to be any written reference to previous costs of $50.00, even if such was contemplated verbally, none were ordered, therefore this point is irrelevant.

The Tenant shall be ordered to pay $225.00 in costs to the Landlord. The Landlord's Legal Representative’s requests included costs for other proceedings which cannot be included in this order. I consider $225.00 to be reasonable as: the Landlord/Landlord's Legal Representative had to prepare for the hearing; approximately one hour was spent on the hearing because of the Tenant’s lack of compliance; and, the Landlord/Landlord's Legal Representative was required to be in attendance by 9:00 a.m.; this amount included $75.00 preparation time and $150.00 for hearing time at $50.00 per hour.
Although I consider the Tenant’s behaviour to be deserving of cost awarded to the LTB, as she did not have the opportunity to make submissions on same, as such, they have not been ordered.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $225.00 costs on or before August 10, 2026.

reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. These facts are not in dispute.
It is the Landlord’s position that a portion of the last month’s rent deposit was retained because of alleged damage to the rental unit.

Subsection 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies, Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires that a rent deposit be applied to the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. The Act does not permit a landlord to retain a deposit for damages.

T he last rent period was November 1 – 16, 2025 and the rent owing for this period was $946.88 ($1,800.00 x 12/365 = $59/18/day x 16 days). Accordingly, the Landlord was required to return $853.12 of the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants. As the Landlord has returned $137.66, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $715.46, which represents of the balancing owing.

It is also undisputed that the Landlord has failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month’s rent deposit in accordance with subsection 106(6) of the Act. As such, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $151.71. This is interest owing from February 1, 2023, to the date of this [name]. This was calculated as follows: • February 1, 2023, to August 31, 2023 (212 days): $1,700, 2.5% • September 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024 (395 days): $1,750, 2.5% • October 1, 2024, to September 30, 2025 (366 days): $1,795, 2.5% • October 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025 (93 days): $1,800,2.5% • January 1, 2026, to July 9, 2026 (190 days): $1,800, 2.1%

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,902.48 which is broken down in the order below.
The parties agree that the Tenants vacated the rental unit September 30, 2025. Illegal rent increase

The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord failed to provide the Tenants with 90 days written notice of the intention to increase the rent in accordance with section 116(1) of the Act, which states: A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so.

It was not disputed by the parties that on September 16, 2024, the Landlord provided the Tenants with a written notice that the rent would increase effective December 1, 2024, which is equivalent to 76 days notice. The increase was for an additional $125.00 per month, making the total monthly rent $5,125.00, from the previous $5,000.00 monthly rent that the Tenants were previously paying.
The Tenants testified that they paid the increase amount from December 1, 2024, to August 1, 2025, even though they did not receive notice in accordance with the Act.

Section 116(4) of the Act states that an increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given notice in accordance with section 116(1). Under s. 135.1 of the RTA, a rent increase that would otherwise be void due to lack of proper notice under s. 116(4), is deemed not void if the tenant has paid the increased rent each month for at least 12 consecutive months.

In this case, the Tenants did not pay the increase for a period of 12 months, which is not disputed by the parties. Therefore, I find that the increase was void and the Landlord illegally increased the rent and collected an excess of $125.00 per month from December 2024 to August 2025, which totals $1,125.00. Damage deposit

The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act. It was not disputed by the parties that the Landlord collected a $500.00 damage deposit from the Tenants on December 1, 2023, which was paid to the Landlord with the first and last months rent deposit.
The Landlord testified the reasoning behind collecting the $500.00 damage deposit was due to the Tenants having a dog.

As the $500.00 damage deposit was to be refunded upon the Tenants vacating the rental unit and the rental unit being in good condition, I find that this deposit meets the definition of “security deposit” in subsection 105(2) of the Act. I further find that it was not a rent deposit permitted under section 105 of the Act because the Tenants provided a separate deposit for the last month of the tenancy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord contravened the Act when she collected a damage deposit from the Tenants that is in addition to the last month’s rent deposit and she continues to contravene the Act by retaining the deposit.

I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act, as it was undisputed that the Tenant paid a $500.00 deposit to the Landlord for a pet damage deposit, which is not in accordance section 106(2) of the Act. Interest owing on the rent deposit

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. It is not disputed that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants any interest on their last months rent deposit of $5,000.00 that was collected on December 1, 2023. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord owes the Tenants interest which is calculated below.
ordered: T he total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,902.48. This amount represents: • $1,125.00 for excess rent collected. • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $229.48 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The evidence before me establishes the Landlord collected a $1,200.00 security deposit from the Tenants on February 1, 2025. The Basic Rental Agreement that was admitted into evidence explains this deposit as follows: “SECURITY DEPOSIT: The total of the above deposits shall secure compliance with the terms and conditions of the terms and conditions of this agreement and shall be refunded to RESIDENT within 30 days after the premises have been completely vacated less any amount necessary to pay OWNER; a) any unpaid rent, b) cleaning costs, c) key JULY 3, 2026 replacement costs, d) cost for repair of damages to premises and/or common areas above ordinary wear and tear, and e) any other amount legally allowable under the terms of this agreement. A written accounting of said charges shall be presented to RESIDENT within 30 days of move-out. If deposits do not cover such costs and damages, the RESIDENT shall immediately pay said additional costs for damages to OWNER.”
For the reasons that follow, I find the Landlord illegally collected a security deposit for which he has failed to return to the Tenants.

Subsection 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. Subsection 106(2) states that the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the rent for one month.

The term “security deposit” is defined in subsection 105(2) as follows: “security deposit” means money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.

Further, subsection 134(1)(a) says: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

“Unless otherwise prescribed” is a reference to section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 which lists permissible fees and deposits. Section 17 does not list damage or cleaning deposits. Section 17 does allow for a key replacement deposit, but such deposit shall not be greater than the direct replacement costs. I do not believe it could be argued that the direct replacement costs of the keys is $1,200.00. Additionally, the keys were returned to the Landlord.

I am satisfied the Landlord illegally collected a security deposit from the Tenants in the amount to $1,200.00, for which he has failed to return. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $1,200.00.

The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs. Based on the facts and the legislation, I find on a balance of probability that the Landlord illegally collected and retained an illegal security deposit and will be ordered to return the $1,200.00 security deposit to the Tenants. The Landlord will also be ordered to pay the Tenants for their filing fee in the amount of $48.00 for a total of $1,248.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,248.00. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 3, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This application is brought under section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which reads as follows: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (1).

The basis of the Tenant’s claim is that she paid the utility bills for the rental unit for approximately 11 months even though the lease agreement indicates the Landlord is responsible for the utilities.

The issue with the Tenant’s claim is that these payments were made directly to the utility company as the utility accounts were in her name. There is no indication the Landlord collected these payments from the Tenant. Given this, it can not be said the Landlord illegally collected or retained money illegally. As such, the Tenant’s claim is not properly brought under section 135(1) and must be dismissed.
Even had I considered the Tenant’s claim under section 135(1), I would have dismissed as I am not convinced the Landlord is responsible for the utility bill.

The Tenant’s representative admitted into evidence a copy of the lease agreement indicating the Tenant is responsible for setting up the utility accounts in her name and the Landlord is responsible for paying for utilities.

The Landlord denied that they are responsible for the utilities explaining that all tenants in their 50 residential tenancies pay for their own utilities. The Landlord believes the Tenant has altered their copy of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord, however, did not admit into evidence the original, signed lease agreement supporting their suspicions.

I believe it is more likely than not the checkmark in the box indicating the Landlord was responsible for the utilities was a clerical error rather than an agreement between the parties. I say this because the Tenant was required to set up the utility accounts in her own name. I do not believe this would have been a requirement had the agreement been the Landlord would be responsible for the utilities as bills are issued and sent to the account holder. Furthermore, the Tenant paid the utility bills for 11 months. I am of the view that had the parties agreed that the Landlord was responsible for the utility bills, the Tenant would have contacted the Landlord immediately upon receiving the first bill.
For the foregoing reasons, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-099972-24, issued on May 4, 2026. On July 1, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on July 13, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the review hearing. The Tenant and the Landlord attended the subsequent new hearing.
reasons: The Landlord did not attend the review hearing. At 1:22pm, I heard the review and decided it based on the Tenant’s submissions, for the following reasons.

The tenancy was to end on November 15, 2024. On November 14, 2024, the Landlord retook possession of the unit. The Tenant brought this application arguing that the Landlord had illegally locked him out of the unit before the tenancy ended. The Landlord argued that the Tenant had already vacated before the Landlord retook possession on November 14.

The Member found that when the Landlord retook possession, the unit was “mainly empty” despite still containing a few items including a moving box and cleaning supplies. On that basis, the Member found that the Landlord had not “changed the locks prior to the termination of the tenancy.” Although not clearly articulated, the Member appears to have reasoned that the Tenant had vacated the unit on or before November 14; that the tenancy had terminated when the Tenant vacated; and that as a result, when the Landlord changed the locks, the tenancy had already ended.

Section 39 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) provides that a landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit less the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit. The Member was correct to consider whether the Tenant had vacated the unit prior to the Landlord retaking possession. However, I find that the Member erred by failing to apply the correct legal test to determine whether the Tenant had vacated.

Possession of a rental unit refers to some form of control over the unit as demonstrated by factors such as access to, use of, or occupation of the unit ([organization] v. [name], 2004 CanLII 59995 (ON CA)). In this case, in considering whether the Tenant had vacated, the Member only considered one factor: that the Tenant had removed most of his belongings. The Member did not consider any other factors, including evidence that the Tenant still had a few belongings in the unit; had not returned the keys; and was actively asserting to the Landlord his right to continue accessing the unit to remove his remaining belongings.

It was a serious error for the Member to find that the Tenant was not in possession solely on the basis that he had removed most of his belongings the day before the end of the tenancy. If she had considered all the factors pursuant to [name], she might have reached a different conclusion.
I therefore granted the review, and directed that a new hearing of the application would be held. New hearing

At 1:38pm, just before the new hearing commenced, [name] joined the virtual hearing room. He stated that he was assisting the Landlord, and had been waiting in the virtual waiting room since the start of the 1:00pm hearing block.

I was not satisfied that [name] had been waiting in the waiting room. This was a Member-moderated hearing block, meaning that the waiting room was visible to me at all times so that I could admit participants to the room as they arrived. [name] was not in the waiting room when the review was heard at 1:22pm. He only arrived there shortly before 1:38pm.
Nonetheless, I waited for the Landlord to arrive before commencing the new hearing.

Partway through the hearing, the Tenant asked that the matter be adjourned because a witness he intended to call had been hospitalized unexpectedly. I granted the request. The new hearing will therefore continue on a date to be scheduled.
ordered: Order LTB-T-099972-24, issued on May 4, 2026, is cancelled.
The LTB shall hold a new hearing of the Tenant’s application. The new hearing has commenced, and will continue on a date to be scheduled.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') did not meet their maintenance obligations (LTB-T-055660-23). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords entered the unit illegally, substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with her, and withheld or interfered with vital services (LTB-T-100550- 23). The applications were heard together by videoconference on July 8, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlords attended the hearing. The Landlod [name] was assisted by [name].
reasons: The Tenant filed these applications in 2023. The applications as filed were not sufficiently clear or organized.

From May 22, 2024 onwards, the Tenant uploaded a large number of documents to the Landlord and Tenant Board’s (LTB) online portal. Some of them appeared to be intended as evidence, while others were amendments to her applications or further particulars of her applications. Many of the documents had cryptic filenames such as “attachment amended,” “attachment support,” and “submitted document.” File Number: LTB-T-055660-23-IN / LTB-T-100550-23

The applications came before the LTB on May 29, 2024, and were adjourned on consent because the Tenant had recently retained a paralegal. An interim order was issued which indicated that the paralegal planned to file amended applications. However, no legible amendment was filed, and the paralegal subsequently ceased to represent the Tenant.

The applications were adjourned on consent a second time on October 28, 2024, and came before the LTB again on March 4, 2026. The Tenant requested an adjournment to seek legal counsel, even though her previous paralegal had apparently withdrawn in 2024. The Member granted the request, noted that the Tenant appeared to have a language barrier, and recommended that she request an interpreter.

The applications came before me on July 8, 2026. By that point, the files contained many different versions of amended applications, books of evidence, and other documents. I asked the Tenant to specify which documents were the current ones. Some of the documents the Tenant identified as current had not been uploaded. I held the matter down while the Tenant uploaded the following documents: a. A 75-page document titled “submit application” which the Tenant intended as an amended application LTB-T-055660-23. It contained interspersed pages from the LTB’s application form, photos, emails, and other evidence, with some written descriptions of allegations scattered throughout. It was not in a useable format as an application, as it did not set out the allegations in an organized or legible way. b. A 91-page book of documents containing the Tenant’s evidence for both applications. It was properly formatted, with page numbers and a table of contents. c. A 12-page document which the Tenant described as a “summary” of application LTB-T-055660-23. The document was not in fact a summary. It thoroughly set out the particulars of the allegations against the Landlords in that application, and the remedies requested.

The Tenant insisted that she had a similar “summary” document respecting application LTB-T-100550-23, but despite being given repeated opportunities, was unable to either identify it on the portal or upload a new copy to the portal. I eventually concluded that no such document exists.
Given the state of the file, I raised, on my own motion, the question of whether the applications could be heard. Sufficiency of LTB-T-055660-23

LTB-T-055660-23 is a T6 application about maintenance. As discussed above, the application form itself is not in a useable state. However, the “summary” document serves as a suitable application, because it properly and succinctly sets out the allegations raised and remedies requested.
The Tenant’s book of evidence is also properly organized.

It appears that the book of evidence may not contain all the photographs and documents the Tenant wants to rely on. However, in 2024 she was directed, by interim order, to File Number: LTB-T-055660-23-IN / LTB-T-100550-23 organize her evidence in a book of documents. She has had two years to do so. At this point, it is fair to limit her evidence to what is included in her book of documents.

I therefore find that application LTB-T-055660-23 can be heard. The “summary” document shall be taken to be the full application setting out the allegations and remedies requested. The Tenant may only adduce documentary evidence contained in the book of evidence. No other documents the Tenant has filed will be considered, including the “submit application” document or any prior versions of any documents. The Tenant may not file any further pleadings or evidence in this matter. Sufficiency of LTB-T-100550-23

LTB-T-100550-23 is a T2 application about illegal entries, substantial interference, harassment, and vital services. The file does not contain any document that clearly sets out the allegations against the Landlord. The Tenant was given repeated opportunities to identify or produce such a document, but was unable to do so.
Since the application does not properly plead allegations against the Landlords, the application will be dismissed. Adjournment
On May 4, 2026, the presiding Member noted that the Tenant had a language barrier and recommended that she request an interpreter. The Tenant did not do so.

At the July 8, 2026 hearing, the Tenant struggled to understand and communicate in English. At several points in the hearing, I raised my concern that she might not be able to understand the proceeding. In each case, she insisted that her English was sufficient and that the case could proceed. The matter proceeded very slowly due to a frequent need to restate and rephrase questions.

After making the above findings, I tried to commence hearing the evidence, by swearing in the Tenant as a witness. However, when asked whether she promised to tell the truth, the Tenant did not understand the question.

I am satisfied that the Tenant will be unable to testify without an interpreter. Since she does not have any other witnesses, the only way for her to prove her case is to testify. I therefore adjourned the matter. The Tenant will be ordered to arrange for an interpreter for the next hearing date. She has the option of filing a request that the LTB provide an interpreter. If she does so and the request is denied, she will have to provide her own interpreter. If she does not, her application will be dismissed on the basis that she is unable to adduce any evidence to prove her case. Costs

At the next hearing, the Landlords may make a request for costs of the July 8, 2026 appearance on the basis that it was unreasonable for the Tenant to attend the hearing File Number: LTB-T-055660-23-IN / LTB-T-100550-23 without an interpreter. I did not hear that request on July 8, because it is preferable that the Tenant have an interpreter when replying to the costs request.
ordered: Application LTB-T-100550-23 is dismissed.
Application LTB-T-055660-23 is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB.
The parties shall provide their unavailable dates for the months August, September, October, and November to the LTB by July 20, 2026.
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.
The allegations raised and remedies sought in the application shall be limited to those set out in DOC-8305777 on the LTB’s portal.
The Tenant’s documentary evidence shall be limited to the evidence contained in DOC- 8305392 on the LTB’s portal.
The Tenant may not file any further amendments or evidence in this matter.
The Tenant shall take all necessary steps to ensure that an interpreter is present at the next hearing date to assist her.
The parties shall come to the next hearing prepared to make submissions about whether the Tenant should be ordered to pay costs to the Landlords.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $20,048.00 on or before August 9, 2026.

This T5 application was filed on November 30, 2025. The T5 is based on the assertion that the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of an N13 notice delivered by the Landlord under section 50 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’) and that notice was delivered in bad faith.

On July 17, 2023, the Landlord delivered an N13 notice with a termination date of January 31, 2024. That N13 indicated that the unit would be demolished. The Landlord filed an L2 application based on this N13. That application was heard by the Board on August 8, 2024. On September 11, 2024, the Board issued an order terminating the tenancy on November 30, 2024.
The Tenant vacated the unit on December 5, 2024.

Section 57 of the RTA says, in part: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, … … (c) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. … (3) The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 2. An order for an abatement of rent. 3. An order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 4. Any other order that the Board considers appropriate.

The Tenants must establish: (a) the Landlord gave the N13 notice in bad faith; (b) they vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13; and (c) the Landlord did not demolish the rental unit—within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

There is no dispute that: (a) the Tenants vacated the unit as a result of the N13— they would not have vacated were it not for the N13; and (b) the Landlord has not demolished the unit. This application comes down to whether the Landlord gave the N13 in bad faith.

In this case, I am satisfied that the conduct and actions of the Landlord demonstrate that it is more likely than not that the intention of the Landlord when the N13 was served was not to demolish the rental unit, but to induce the Tenant to vacate the unit.

The Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord did not keep true to their testimony at the August 2024 hearing in which the Landlord’s agent submitted that once they receive vacant possession that the Landlord will demolish the unit. the Tenant provided in evidence the recording of the August hearing.
The Tenant also submits the rental unit is still not demolished and that commercial unit in the building is still being occupied/used and that unit was never provided notice to vacate.

The Landlord’s agent asserted that the unit was not demolished for several different reasons. He testified that while the Tenant vacated in December 2024, some of his belongings remained in the unit and vacant possession was not provided until March 2025. The Landlord has provided that their intention was to build an 18-storey high rise condominium consisting of 217 residential units and 3 commercial unit. The Landlord’s agent testified that they launched sales for the units in 2023 to get the units sold by 2024. As a result of the delay of the Tenant moving out by March 2025, this delayed the Landlord being able to deliver on the sold units.

The Landlord’s agent also testified that ultimately, they decided to add additional height to the building, and pre-application consultation meeting with the City of [name] was held in May 2024. They made an application in and around October 2024, to increase the height of the building. In March 2025, the city approved the Landlord’s application to increase the height of the building. He testified that the decision to move forward with increasing the height of the building was made in February 2026.

The Landlord noted that the corner of Bathurst was deemed a heritage site, and the building was within proximity to this area. As such, the Landlord is required to take extra steps to move the development project forward such as obtaining special permits to demolish and, they are in the process of obtaining these permits.

The Landlord submits that they are expecting to demolish after they receive the site plans and it will mostly be at the beginning of 2027. During cross examination, the Landlord’s agent submitted that the plan to change the scope of work came to fruition on May 2, 2024, as an alternative in the event the Tenant delayed moving out. He also testified that they were aware of the extra permits required to preserve heritage but did not obtain them at the time notice of termination was served. Analysis
In this case, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith.

In the decision of [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (“Elkins”), para 45., the court makes it clear that under s. 202(1) of the Act, the Board is required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit and the good faith of the participants. The court in Elkins in para 43., also made it clear that it was an error of law for the Board to restrict their analysis of the evidence to the point in time when the landlord served a tenant a notice of termination. While the analysis in [name] is centred upon notices of termination served for “purchaser’s own use” under section 49 of the Act, the legal principles can be applied in the context of notices provided pursuant to section 50 of the Act for demolition.

In applying the legal principles in Elkins, I find that the Landlord did not take reasonable steps to demolish the rental unit after vacant possession was provided by the Tenant. I say this because, I find that the Landlord was still in the process of making a decision of which site plans were better suited for their financial goals. The evidence of the Landlord was that prior to the hearing held in August 2024, the Landlord was considering a change in their scope of work for the site plans. This meant that the Landlord was required to make additional applications and require further permits to demolish the rental unit. It was further evident that until February of 2026, the Landlord had not yet made the decision about which site plan they were going to be proceeding on and that demolition was to take place after vacant possession was provided.

In addition, subsection 73(1) of the RTA contemplates that a landlord will have obtained all necessary permits to carry out the activity on which an N13 is based or, if it has not, will have taken all reasonable steps to obtain all necessary permits. The fact that the Landlord did not take steps to obtain the heritage site demo permits to be required to demolish the rental unit after delivering the N13 and getting vacant possession and until today’s date, supports a finding that Landlord did not genuinely intend to demolish the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.

In conclusion, I find on a balance of probabilities that all of the elements of section 57(1)(c) were satisfied, including that the Landlord did not demolish the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the rental unit and the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies

Subsection 57(3) of the Act provides that the Board can order the landlord to pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant’s evidence was that they moved into their partner’s home from December 4, 2024, to present and paid $1,500.00 a month in rent. This is less than the monthly rent the Tenant paid for the rental unit. There is no increased rent for the Board to order.
The Tenant withdrew their claim for moving costs.

Pursuant to s.57(3) (1.1), the Landlord may be ordered to pay the Tenants general compensation in an amount not exceeding 12 months’ rent. The only other remedy claimed by the Tenant is general compensation in the amount of $37,200.00.

Section 57(3) (1.1) offers little guidance on how to determine the amount of general compensation that should be awarded in any particular case. General compensation is compensation for the non-pecuniary impacts of the loss of the Tenants’ home, such as pain and suffering, inconvenience, and loss of enjoyment of life. In setting a high maximum amount for general compensation, it seems to me that the Legislature intends s.57(3) (1.1) to indicate that the loss of a person’s home should be taken to be a very serious loss.
By way of background, the Tenant testified that the rental unit was a 2-story building and the Tenant occupied the whole second floor.

He testified that he is a carpenter by trade and that he had ample workspace in the rental unit and eviction caused him to lose a lot of space. He had to move into a smaller house and was no longer able to do his woodworking as his tools were in storage. 27. [name], [name], [name] and [name] each provided oral testimony for the Tenant. Each of these individuals are occupants of the rental unit and gave evidence with respect to the impact the eviction had on them. 28. [name] testified that that the eviction disrupted his lifestyle as he used the rental unit as his studio and shared the space with other artists to work on projects and after moving, he was no longer able to do so. 29. [name] testified that living at the rental unit she was able to utilize the space for work. As a result of the eviction, she was uprooted from work situation and lost her dance studio and as such she had to spend out of her pocket for studio spaces. She testified that she still does not secure housing as she is currently subleasing. 30. [name] testified that having to move out affected their mental health as she was no longer able to stay connected to her former roommates and it negatively affected her romantic relationship due to lack of stability and being able to function due to lack of housing. 31. [name] Philips testified that the eviction order impacted him financially and he had to re- coup the costs of moving and had to pay for extra storage. As the rental unit had enough space to store his deceased father’s belongings. He testified that he is in a lot of small space and can fit all of his belongings. 32. The Tenant testified that they had lived in the rental unit since 2003, so the move was very stressful, and they were not prepared to pay a significant amount more in rent plus the additional expense of storage. He testified that where he moved to, he could no longer conduct his woodworking as he did not have enough space. 33. . The Landlord’s actions had a substantial impact on the Tenant. They were not able to find anything in the area and with enough space to conduct their trade/ hobbies and faced the difficult choice of having to alter his lifestyles and community and face the inconvenience of seeking additional storage to store their belongings. The Tenant had lived in the unit for quite some time, and the move put additional financial pressures on him. Considering the impact on the Tenant due to the N13 having been served in bad faith, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $20,000.00 in general compensation. Administrative Fine 34. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, an administrative fine is intended to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. I find that this is an appropriate case for an administrative fine for deterrence, and I say this for the following reasons. 35. The Tenant testified that the Landlord prematurely evicted the Tenant. Considering the Landlord experience and their behaviour in leading the Tenant to believe they would be demolishing the rental unit; I do not believe the remedies awarded will be sufficient deterrence. 36. Regarding the quantum of the fine, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline states: In setting the amount of the fine, the Member may consider: 1. The nature and severity of the breach 2. The effect of the breach on the tenant 3. Any other relevant factors 37. The amount of the find should be commensurate with the breach. 38. Here, the impact on the Tenant was considerable because he was forced to move from a home he has lived in for approximately twenty-three years. The move caused unexpected expense as well as adjustment to their lifestyle and loss of enjoyment. This kind of behaviour on the part of the Landlord must be strongly condemned. A substantial fine is necessary for its general deterrence effect. Given all of the above, I find that a fine of $2,000.00 is reasonable in the circumstances. 39. The Tenant was successful on the application and are entitled to recover from the Landlord the $48.00 he paid to file the application.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant general compensation of $1,000.00 and the $48.00 application filing fee by July 13, 2026.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord engaged in a series of harassing and coercive behaviours on or about October 10, 2025 to November 30, 2025 which induced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit during their mid-term exams for nursing school.

The Tenant testified that on or about October 10, 2025 the Landlord served them with a First N5 Notice of Termination. They alleged that the Tenant had been interfering with the cupboards and personal belongings of other residents in the rooming house. The Tenant read the notice and disagreed with it and submits that they had already spoken with the other residents and the issue was already resolved prior to the service of the notice.

The Tenant further submits that when they raised the issue with the Landlord, that the Landlord would refuse to respond or would otherwise pressure the Tenant into vacating the rental unit. Specifically, on or about October 18, 2025 the Tenant sent and email to the Landlord stating that less than 30 days was too short of notice and that they requested additional time if the Landlord insisted they vacate. The Landlord responded on October 20th with a message insisting the Tenant vacate the rental unit by the 14 days required by law and that they had already been considerate in extending the deadline to October 31st based on the Tenant’s circumstances. The Landlord, or their agent further stated that they already had the Tenant’s unit rented for November 1st and that the Tenant must leave.

Additionally, the Tenant submits that the Landlord targeted him on the basis that he is an international student and the Landlord made reference to “I don’t know how monthly tendencies work in whatever country you come from but in Canada, monthly rent covers from the first of the month to the last day of the month”… “if you want to live in MY country, I recommend you educate yourself.”

The Tenant submits that this message was received on or about November 30, 2025 or December 1, 2025. They submit that this is discriminatory, and they felt offended and hurt by the Landlords remarks. The Tenant finally acquiesced to the Landlords demands and vacated the rental unit and signed an N11 agreement on December 1, 2025 after they found alternative short term housing on short notice.

They left the unit because their father secured them a space to sleep on a friend’s floor in order to finish their mid-terms and while waiting to find alternative stable housing. They could only access the internet by hot-spotting this kind persons phone.

The Tenant submits that all of the correspondence from the Landlord caused them to barely pass their mid-terms because they could not focus on their education while also being unreasonably pressured to vacate the rental unit. They submit they were unable to enjoy their housing or focus on much else between October 10th and December 1st. They had only just moved into the unit on or about September 1, 2025 and had just settled in before being harassed to leave the unit.

I accept, based on the uncontradicted evidence of the Tenant, that they were harassed by the Landlord and inducted to vacate the rental unit without due legal process by the Landlord and I also find the Landlord email correspondence discriminatory.

Although the Landlord asserted that they had every right to evict the Tenant in their correspondence, I disagree. I find that the Landlord either knowingly or ought to have know that they were misguiding the Tenant.

Firstly, there is no record that the Landlord ever filed the N5 Notice with the LTB. Secondly, if I accept the Tenants evidence that the issue was resolved, then arguably the Tenant voided the notice by correcting the behaviour or omission within the 7 days after receiving the notice. On this basis, the Landlord had no lawful ability to proceed with termination of the tenancy based on the service of the single notice. Even if the Tenant had not voided the notice, then the Landlord still cannot evict a tenant without an order from the Board or without an agreement to terminate the tenancy.

While I accept that the parties did enter into an agreement to terminate the tenancy on December 1, 2025, and the Landlord returned to the Tenant the last month’s rent deposit of $850.00, this does not negate the harassment caused by the Landlord which I believe is the real reason the Tenant vacated the unit. Indeed, based on their agreement to terminate the tenancy the Landlord would be obligated to return the unused portion of the last months rent deposit anyways. The Tenant had paid the rent for the months of September, October and November to the Landlord in addition to their first and last month’s rent.

Accordingly, having found that the Landlord and or their agent harassed and coerced the Tenant, I find it appropriate to grant the Tenant general compensation for the harassment and discrimination they endured during their tenancy for the period of October 10, 2025 to December 1, 2025. I find a lump sump of $1,000.00 is reasonable under the circumstances.

I accept that even though the Tenant was aware that they did not have to vacate the unit pursuant to the N5 Notice that was given, I also accept that the Landlord’s conduct and insistence that they vacate citing incorrect law and applying persistent pressure to leave based on the Tenant’s international student status warrants a financial remedy under the circumstances.
Since the Tenant is successful on their application, I also find it appropriate to order the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant their application filing fee costs of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 in general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Ke [name] and [name] [name] (the Landlords) collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlords failed to pay the three month’s compensation due to her pursuant to subsection 52 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act). As explained below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Background

On July 1, 2025, the Landlords gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination with a termination date of November 30, 2025. The N13 stated that Landlords intend to convert the rental unit to a non-residential space.

It was the Landlords’ evidence that they served the N13 notice because the Municipality identified the rental unit as being non-compliant with the Fire Code as it lacked a second means of egress. Rather than carry out renovations necessary to make the unit compliant with the Fire Code, the Landlords opted to convert the rental unit to a non-residential space.

Section 52(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: 52 (1) A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if, (a) the tenant receives notice of termination of the tenancy for the purposes of demolition or conversion to non-residential use; (b) the residential complex in which the rental unit is located contains at least five residential units; and (c) in the case of a demolition, it was not ordered to be carried out under the authority of any other Act.

I am satisfied the Tenant received a notice of termination of the tenancy for the purpose of conversion to non-residential use. The fact the Landlord chose not to carry out renovations required by the Fire Code does not remove his obligation under section 52(1).

Subsection 52(1) of the Act requires a landlord to compensate a tenant in the amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if, (a) the tenant receives notice of termination of the tenancy for the purposes of demolition or conversion to non-residential use; (b) the residential complex in which the rental unit is located contains at least five residential units; and (c) (c) in the case of a demolition, it was not ordered to be carried out under the authority of any other Act.

The Landlord maintains that there are less than five units in the residential complex. According to the Landlord’s Agent, there are four units located in a basement with a separate entrance, four units in an attached shed, two units on the first floor, and two units of the third floor.

The Act defines a “residential complex” as a building or related group of buildings in which one or more rental units are located and including all common areas and services and facilities available for the use of its residents. The fact that the units are located in an attached shed, are serviced by a separate entrance, or are on a floor closed by the fire department means little in establishing they are part of the residential complex as defined by the Act. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the residential complex contains at least five residential units. As such, the Landlord was required to compensate the Tenant an amount equal to three months rent.
The lawful monthly rent is $1,600.00. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $4,800.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,848.00. This amount represents: • $4,800.00 for compensation owing under section 52(1); and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5628.80 on or before July 14, 2026.
By way of background the Tenant remains in possession of the rental unit. The residential complex is an apartment building. The rental unit has two bedrooms, and the lawful monthly rent is $2,124.00.

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges the following disrepair claims: a mouse infestation and an ant infestation both of which began on May 11, 2025 and while the mouse infestation issue resolved on January 30, 2026, the ant infestation remained.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that because she had a fear of rodents, she had asked the Landlord when they viewed the unit on March 21, 2025 whether there were any infestation issues – to which the Landlord responded there were not. The Tenant moved in on April 25, 2025. Shortly thereafter, the Tenant recalls spotting a live mouse running in the kitchen and making noises in the bottom drawer of the stove. Photos and videos were submitted in support of these assertions.

The Tenant submits that while she complained about seeing mice in the unit in May 2025, November 2025, December 2025, it was only in January 2026 that the issue was completely resolved by the Landlord’s technician when they sealed all the entry points in the rental unit, instead of just those where the mice were found. Further, the Tenant submits that it was only through the Landlord’s technician that they discovered this issue existed prior to them moving into the rental unit, and that the Landlord misrepresented this fact.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act as it relates to the rodent infestation in the rental unit. I say this because while the issue was first reported in May 2025, days after the Tenant moved into the rental unit, the Landlord’s technicians attended on multiple occasions to seal the same holes where the mice were being observed coming out of– namely in the kitchen and bedroom but it was only on January 30, 2026 that the mice infestation issue resolved completely. So, while the Landlord’s response was timely, it was not effective until eight months later.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case it is unclear why it took the Landlord eight months to resolve the issue of a mouse infestation, particularly where the infestation was minor to moderate in nature. What appears to be the case is the Landlord’s ineffective resolution of only sealing some of the entry points – which wasn’t very strong - until January 2026 when the remainder were sealed.
With respect to the ant infestation, I find the evidence to be insufficient to establish this claim and therefore it is dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a nine-month rent abatement in the amount of 65% of their rent for the paranoia, discomfort and inconvenience due to the mouse infestation as well as the aggravation of their rodent phobia. The Tenant also submits they should be reimbursed for their out-of-pocket expenses of purchasing their own sticky traps and having to replace their food due to the infestation.

Abatement of the rent is the most common remedy awarded to tenants in these kinds of situations. It is intended to reflect the idea that if a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving everything being paid for, then the tenant is entitled to abatement of the rent proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

With respect to the rent abatement, given my knowledge and experience in other similar matters, and considering the level of infestation, the time it took to rectify the issue (264 days), and the impact on the Tenant given her phobia I find it appropriate to award a 30% rent abatement for the period May 11, 2025 to January 30, 2026 or $5,530.80.

With respect to the request for out of pocket expenses, given the failure to provide any receipts for these expenses and considering the testimony and photographs of the Tenant using their own sticky traps which were more effective than the bait stations provided by the Landlord’s technician, I find it appropriate to award $50.00.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,628.80. This amount represents: • $5,530.80 for a rent abatement for the period ending January 30, 2026; • $50.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 14, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months of August, September and October 2026 until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 3, 2026 ____________________________
