issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
This matter was called and stood down at 2:15 p.m., 2:18 p.m., 2:30 p.m., 2:45 p.m., and 2:49 p.m., so that the Tenant had an opportunity to log into the hearing.

When the matter was called, I canvassed with the Tenant’s Legal Representative how they were going to proceed with the matter. She advised that she did not want an adjournment even though she had no access to the Portal and no client present, as the Tenant had the documents with her.

I repeatedly to stood the matter down so that the Tenant could login to provide evidence and testimony to support their application, but the Tenant’s Legal Representative did not want it stood down because she wanted to proceed without her client, and to give submissions on his behalf.

When I addressed my concerns with the Tenant’s Legal Representative in relation to the Tenant being required to attend to provide evidence and submissions to support their application as I was not satisfied it was appropriate for her to provide the only evidence in support the application, she then requested an adjournment.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not consent to the adjournment given that the parties had been waiting all day for the matter to be called, and at no time did the Tenant’s Legal Representative previously seek an adjournment.

I was not satisfied it was appropriate to adjourn the matter and provided ample opportunity for the Tenant to login to the hearing as the hearing docket commenced at 9:00 a.m., and at no time before the matter was called, was the Tenant logged into the hearing room.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative sought to have the matter stood down until after 3:00 p.m., as the Tenant was at work, and would login when he was available to do so. The Tenant’s Legal Representative thought she could have the hearing without the Tenant present as divorce proceedings are done without the applicant.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative wanted to proceed based on written submissions and to provide evidence on behalf of her client, which I advised her that she cannot provide evidence to support the Tenant’s application as the Tenant was required to attend. The Tenant’s Legal Representative then proposed that she deliver opening statements and call the Landlord’s witnesses first to allow the Tenant further opportunity to login to hearing room.

I declined to allow the Tenant’s Legal Representative to start with opening statements as it is not required and I declined to allow the Tenant’s Legal Representative to start with asking the Landlords’ witnesses questions as this was a Tenant’s application before me, and the Tenant was required to provide evidence and testimony to support their application, which would then provide the Landlord an opportunity to respond to the Tenant’s evidence and testimony thereafter.

Under the LTB rules of procedure, section 1.6(q), it states that the LTB may exercise its discretion to permit a party’s legal representative to give evidence where appropriate. This rule is typically applied on L1 hearings where only the landlord’s legal representative attends and gives evidence about the ledger and the rent amount owing. In this circumstance, in which I anticipate that there may be credibility issues/assessments given the nature of the allegations and the Tenant’s Legal Representative does not have any direct knowledge of the events, but rather second-hand knowledge provided by her client. Therefore, the Tenant’s Legal Representative would not be in a good position to speak to the events or to be questioned on them by the Landlord/ Landlord’s Legal Representative.
Therefore, I was not satisfied to allow the Tenant’s Legal Representative to provide any evidence or oral submissions on behalf of her client to support the Tenant’s application.
With the Tenant not present to support their application, I am not satisfied the matter could be proven on a balance of probabilities.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,907.78.
By way of background, the rental unit is a multi-storey building. The Tenant lives in the rental unit with a child who is disabled and requires supportive services. Tenant’s T6 Application

The Tenant states that the unit had a bed bug infestation and that the Landlord failed to respond to her request for pest control in a timely, effective, or reasonable manner. She told the Landlord on August 5, 2025, about the infestation. The Landlord arranged treatment. Although the date is not clear, the Tenant’s evidence was that she was given 24 hours notice of entry shortly after advising the Landlord of the problem, and the unit was treated.

On August 20, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that the first treatment had been insufficient to address the problem and the infestation persisted. The Landlord again sent pest control to the rental unit at “the end of August.” The Tenant told the Landlord again about two or three days afterwards in early September, that the pest control treatment was insufficient as the problem continued, and asked for a further treatment. The Landlord responded that there was a building-wide issue that they were trying to manage. However, the Tenant’s evidence was the Landlord made no further arrangements to continue treatment in her rental unit.

The Tenant purchased her own treatment solutions in September and was able to successfully remedy the bed bug problem in her unit. She also purchased new furniture including mattresses, a couch, blankets, and pillows. She explained that she had to do this for safety and that of her child as recommended by her doctor.

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), states that the Landlord is obligated to provide and maintain a residential complex in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd.1 the Ontario Court of Appeal rejected a long-standing presumption that a landlord may be deemed immediately in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act once a defect arises. To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, I find that the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenant’s request for pest control in a timely, effective, or reasonable manner. Although initially the Landlord did respond appropriately by sending pest control in early August and again in early September, the Landlord did not continue to treat the rental unit despite the request for additional treatments. In my view, and in keeping with the Court of Appeal’s guidance in Onyskiw, the Landlord breached s.20(1) of the Act because they did not arrange for additional pest control even after being advised the problem was not rectified. 1 Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) Tenant’s T2 Application

The Tenant says that the Landlord has failed to provide adequate parking facilities to the Tenant. The Tenant states there are no disabled parking spaces at the rental complex. The Tenant’s child has complex medical needs, and the Tenant uses a specialized vehicle which has been modified to accommodate necessary medical equipment. The Tenant requested a designated parking space, but the Landlord told the Tenant she needed to park at the rear of the building. She reports that she must park at the rear of the building, and even though she pays for a parking space, sometimes there are none. Further, when the Tenant has to manage her child’s care without the benefit of a designated disability parking space causes her significant stress while she is trying to maneuver in and out of the building.

The Tenant advises she used to be able to park at the front of the building. However, about one year earlier, the Landlord designated the parking spaces at the front of the building as visitor parking. She reports they were mandated to do so, although it is not clear to me precisely by whom. After this change, the Tenant could still park there, but it is almost always full. What is unusual; however, is that the building which a multi-storey residential dwelling does not have any permanently designated disability parking spaces, given the Human Rights Code2 has paramountcy over all other provisional legislation including the RTA.

When the Tenant requested a designated parking space, she was told to park at the rear of the building. In addition to an abatement of rent, the Tenant seeks a designated disability parking space at the front of the building.

Section 22 of the Act, states: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, the lack of adequate parking space(s), particularly one designated as a disabled parking space, has caused substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant’s evidence is that she is not always able to find parking and it is difficult to manage her child’s safety and equipment, particularly in the winter. As such, I find this to be a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedies

By way of remedy, the Tenant seeks: • a rent abatement of $5,000.00; • $2,138.04 for the cost of replacing the furniture which she disposed of because of the bed bug infestation; and, • a designated disability parking space. 2 Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19 | ontario.ca Abatement of Rent

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

In Offredi v. [organization]3, the trial judge considered complaints made by a group of tenants concerning a lengthy power outage, lack of parking due to garage repairs, poor maintenance of common arrears and lack of adequate security. These problems extended over a two-year period. Justice [name] held at page 15 of that judgment: It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances.

In considering a remedy, I have considered the Tenant’s evidence about the impact of the lack of an appropriate parking, the pest infestation, and the lack of a designated parking space to accommodate the Tenant’s specific needs for her child.

In reviewing other similar cases before the Board, I can find no consensus amongst the orders. However, I find a reasonable abatement to be 10% for the lack of parking space is appropriate because there was some disruption to the Tenant’s normal use and enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant’s testimony was the issues with the parking began one year earlier which I find to be June 2025. Therefore, I find the period the abatement to apply is for the period of June 2025, to June 2026. An order shall issue.
The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,805.00, and I calculate the abatement to be $2,166.00 ($1,805.00 x .10% = $180.50 x 12 months).

As for the lack of adequate pest control, I accept the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that she was advised by her doctor to replace the furniture. Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to $1,603.53 for the cost of replacing her belongings that were disposed of because of the pest infestation. The Tenant’s evidence was that the furniture she replaced was about 5 years old. As such, I find that these items would have depreciated and estimate this at 25%. This is consistent with similar orders of the Board (See EAT-94453- 21; TNL-28525-20; [name] v Lecky, 2025 ONLTB 80396).
I calculate this amount to be $1,603.53 ($2,138.04 x .75%). An order shall issue.

I find an abatement of 5% is appropriate for the period of September 2025. I say this because the Landlord did make attempts to rectify the problem, and only after the Landlord refused further treatments is the Tenant eligible for an abatement. Further still, the Tenant was able to mitigate the Landlord’s damages, as is required per s. 16 of the Act, by treating the unit herself which corrected the problem at the end of September. An order shall issue. 3 Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC)
I calculate the 5% abatement for September to be $90.25 ($1,805.00 x .05).
The total the Landlord owes the Tenant is $3,859.78. Designated Disability Parking Space

The Tenant requests a designated disability parking space for her personal use. However, I find that the Tenant did not plead the request for a designated parking space in her claim. Rather, the Tenant’s application seeks an abatement of rent for the interference of not having a designated disabled parking space.

The application says: “Parking accessibility Parking is often full or not accessible. Very difficult and unsafe to load my disabled child and her equipment especially when the school bus is waiting.” There is no specific request for an assigned disabled parking space or to provide a designated disability parking space at the front of the building. In my view, to amend the application to include this remedy can only be done on notice to the Landlord and the Landlord was not in attendance. No order shall issue.

Of note, the Landlord has a duty under the Code to accommodate to the point of undue hardship. Section 17(2) of the Code, states: “(2) No tribunal or court shall find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and safety requirements, if any.” If the Landlord does not explore accommodations, where a tenant has requested one, they may be found to be in breach of the Code and the Act, and they may also be in breach of their obligations pursuant to the municipality’s bylaws.

The Tenant also submits that the elevator in the building is inadequate to accommodate a stretcher and this causes problems when it is necessary for emergency services to attend to her child. However, it is not clear what the Tenant would request by way of remedy. There was no evidence that the Tenant asked for a reasonable accommodation, for example a first-floor rental unit, which would then negate the need for using the elevator. Therefore, the Landlord is not necessarily in breach of the Act because of this issue. No order shall issue.

The Tenant also seeks an order about the AGI increase which she states is incorrectly stated on an N4 Notice. However, I do not find that this is a matter which is properly before the Board on a T2/T6 application. If the AGI amount is incorrect, this will be dealt with by way of either an AGI order or the Tenant can raise this at an L1 hearing if the Landlord has filed an application with the Board. If there is an error on an order, the Tenant may consider filing a review. No order shall issue.

The Tenant also seeks an administrative fine against the Landlord. The Board’s Guideline LTB | Administrative Fines says that “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

Although it is clear that the impact on the Tenant has not been minimal, I do not find that the breaches rise to the level contemplated by the Board’s Guidelines. In my view, the Landlord’s behavior falls just short of a blatant disregard for the Act. I believe that the abatement awarded is sufficient to deter the Landlord from further breaches in the future.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,907.78. This amount represents: • $2,256.25 for a rent abatement. • $1,603.53 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 10, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,500.00 from the rent each month commencing September 2026 and October 2026, and $907.78 from the rent due and owing for the month of November 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the Landlord’s Legal Representative raised the issue that 4 of the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application are statute barred as the limitation period has expired as per section 29(2) of the Act as the application was filed December 18, 2024, with 2 issues arising from 2022, one from September 2023, and one from November 2023.

The Tenant filed their application under section 29(1) of the Act. The limitation period set out in s. 29(2) applies and it states that no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

This means the Tenant is limited to raising issues that occurred beginning 12 months before that date, which is December 18, 2023. Any claims from before December 18, 2023, will not be considered, except as a matter of background only, where appropriate.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference & Harassment, etc.

I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. In addition, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that on December 15, 2024, the Landlord served an N4 notice of termination on her due to rent that was 16 days late. The Tenant testified this was because she asked him for a copy of a recent water test to ensure the water was not toxic.

The Tenant testified that on December 17, 2024, after receiving the N4 for rent arrears and mentioning her recent suspected kidney concerns, the Landlord then served a N5 notice of termination which was full of false accusations, lacked details, and contained inconsistent information in relation to smoking complaints.

Under cross examination, the Tenant confirmed and did not dispute that on December 15, 2024, her rent was 16 days late. Furthermore, under cross examination the Tenant testified that she received an email from the Landlord on December 15, 2024, and rather than explain to the Landlord that she didn’t smoke, she responded about the water testing she wanted to have completed. The Tenant confirmed that the Landlord did not proceed with filing an application with the LTB based on the N5 notice of termination.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant provided the Landlord with a N9 notice to terminate her tenancy instead of disputing the N5 notice of termination, which was not disputed by the Tenant.

After considering the Tenant’s evidence and testimony, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or harassed the Tenant by providing the Tenant with a N4 notice of termination, and a N5 notice of termination as it is the Landlord’s right to serve on the Tenant notices of termination for non-payment of rent, or if they believe the Tenant is interfering with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex if they receive complaints from other tenants. In this case, there was nothing unreasonable about the Landlord serving notices of termination based on grounds that are specified in the Act and based on the information the Landlord had at the time.
Therefore, the Tenant has failed to prove the allegations contained within their application.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act, nor am I satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The allegations of lack of maintenance and substantial interference arise from the same facts/incidents related to the way in which the Landlord addressed flooding in the rental unit. As explained below, I find that the Landlord acted promptly in addressing the issues related to the floods, that these issues were out of the Landlord’s control, and the Landlord made reasonable attempts to resolve the issue in a timely manner.

The Tenant testified she moved into the rental unit sometime in April 2014, and that throughout her tenancy when it would rain, her unit would suffer from some flooding. The Tenant testified that in December 2023, there was a major flood within her unit and that she discussed this issue with the Landlord in December 2023 and into January 2024.
The Tenant testified that due to the flooding in the rental unit, which caused her to vacate the rental unit, the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
The Tenant further testified that sometime in January 2024, a contractor attended the rental property to complete some of the emergency repairs within the unit.

The Tenant testified that she received a N13 notice of termination from the Landlord, claiming that the Landlord required vacant possession of the unit in order do extensive repairs or renovations and this work was to be completed within the unit in May 2024. The Landlord provided her with 1 month’s rent compensation in relation to the N13 notice, as required by the Act.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord started the repairs while she was still residing in the rental unit and could not provide her a timeline as to when the repairs would be completed but was forthcoming about when the contractors would be entering the unit.

The Tenant testified that from the date of the flood that took place sometime in December 2023, she had to move all of her personal belongings out of her bedroom, which was located in the basement, to the kitchen/dining room area on the main floor of the rental unit. There was a bedroom and a bathroom located in the basement of the rental unit.

Under cross examination the Tenant testified that while she was living in the unit, the flooding was sporadic, and agreed the circumstances were outside of the Landlord’s control. Further, the Tenant testified that the Landlord had various contractors going in and out of the unit to attempt to remedy the flooding issue, and that the Landlord would continuously keep her updated on the status of the repairs.

The Landlord testified that he has been the Landlord since 2009, and that the rental property was over 100 years old and he did his best to maintain the property and rectify all issues when they arose and acted in a prompt manner.
The Landlord testified that in relation to the flood issue, he had Winmar attend the property to rectify the issue as soon as possible, and that the remediation took place right after that.
The Landlord testified that he was not aware of the serious issues within the rental property until the contractors attended to look at the remedial work that was required to rectify the flood issue.

The Landlord testified that the work commenced in January 2024 and was not completed until November 2025, and the timeline was out of his control given the severity of the work that was required to be completed.

The Landlord testified there was a delay with the insurance company processing the claim for the damages as the Tenant needed to remove her belongings to get the significant repairs completed, and these repairs could not have been completed with the Tenant in the unit.
The repairs included the lower half of the unit being demolished, foundation work , and there was a draining issue between the sewer of the property and the city sewer line that had to be addressed.
The Landlord testified that he was aware of the flooding issue and always rectified it, but in December 2023, this flood was extreme and out of his control.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant was not residing in the unit from January 2024 to April 2024 and he was appealing to the insurance company to rectify the issues properly, as the insurance company was only willing to put the unit back to its original state and was refusing to remedy the underlining issues, which delayed the process.

The Landlord testified that he discussed with the Tenant the issues he was having with the insurance company to keep her informed of the status of the rental unit and when the repairs would be completed. Furthermore, the Landlord testified that it was not his intention to evict the Tenant but rather rectify the issues within the rental unit properly as he was not aware of the seriousness of the issues until the contractors attended and started to assess where the flooding issue was coming from.

The Landlord further testified that once the work commenced, further issues were found which resulted in further delays and work that was required to be completed. It was found that a tree root destroyed and impacted the drainage system. As a result, the concrete in the basement bathroom was required to be removed and the yard had to be dug up to address the issue. In addition, foundational issues were found which was not part of the original issues.

Under cross examination the Landlord testified that he tried his best to accommodate the Tenant, but due to financial issues that arose, and having to argue with the insurance company to properly rectify the issues, there were significant delays with the repairs that were out of his control. In addition, he became unemployed and lost his own living arrangements during this period.

Furthermore, the Landlord testified under cross examination that the delays were out of his control as the insurance company was the one delaying the process and would work at their own pace. The Landlord testified he was trying to find a permanent solution to the issue rather than having a temporary solution that would require him to address the issues again in the future.

After considering all the evidence and testimony from the parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations, nor did the Landlord substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because it was clear from the evidence and testimony that the repairs needed to rectify the flooding issue were substantial that the Tenant was required to vacate the rental unit in order for the repairs to be completed, resulting in the Landlord providing the Tenant with a N13 notice to complete such repairs.

While I can appreciate it was inconvenient and caused the Tenant unwanted stress and disturbance, I find that the repairs were necessary and that due to the delay from the insurance company and having the work completed, which is out of the control of the Landlord, the Landlord acted promptly to rectify the issue.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
Applying the decision in Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord’s response to the flooding issues in the rental unit was reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Tenant's Legal Representative made a request to amend the Application. The request to amend increases the general compensation sought to $35,000.00 from $10,000.00 and adds a request for a fine. The Request to amend was submitted to the Board on May 11, 2026, two days prior to the hearing, and did not comply with Rule 15. However, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to grant the request, I note that it does not significantly alter the substance of the Tenant’s allegations or add news claims, rather it increases the remedies sought by the Tenant. Accordingly, I find there is little prejudice to the Landlord as they had already prepared for example to depend against a claim for general compensation.

I also note that a large portion of the general compensation sought would place the total quantum sought over the Board’s jurisdictional limit and could not be ordered by the Board. The Monetary Jurisdiction

The Application sought by the Tenant is more than the LTB's monetary jurisdiction. Under subsection 207(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') the LTB may order payment up to $50,000.00. Proceeding with this application at the LTB extinguishes any rights the Tenant may have to claim the full amount owing at the LTB or a court. The Tenant was made aware of the LTB's monetary jurisdiction and chose to proceed with this application.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $27,235.71.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
The rental unit was listed for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating the rental unit. Therefore Section 57(5) of the Act applies, and bad faith is presumed.

It was not disputed that the Landlord served an N12 Notice of Termination, and the Tenant vacated as a result, and the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit. Therefore, my determination hinges on the good faith of the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that he had planned to move back into the rental unit with his partner and her daughter. He testified that he gave his own Landlord an N11 to Terminate his tenancy effective April 30, 2025, and gave two weeks notice to his employer to end his employment April 4, 2025. This letter indicates that the Landlord is resigning as he has made the decision to move back to his home in Belleville.

The Landlord testified that when he attended the unit on April 7, 2025 it was a mess with the walls and the floor covered in animal waste. He testified that [name] – Property Remediation Specialists attended the property on April 28, 2025, and produced a report deeming the rental unit uninhabitable. The report was prepared by [name] Mascotto. The executive summary of the report indicates that the severity of animal fecal matter and urine throughout the property presents an immediate and serious risk to the health and safety of any living being.
The Landlord also relied on photographs and videos depicting the state of the rental unit after the Tenant had vacated.

The Landlord testified that his intent was initially to have the rental unit restored, and to occupy it, however the costs of the repair were estimated by Winmar at $32,728.70. These were funds the Landlord did not have, accordingly he secured a loan of $30,000.00 and [name] a downpayment of $14,481.73 The Landlord relied on banking records in support of this assertion which depict a debit of $14,481.73 on May 9, 2025 and a payment of $18,296.97 on September 6, 2025. The Landlord confirmed that he had not provided a copy of the receipt from or cheque to Winmar and confirmed that the banking records were produced after the Tenant has raised discrepancies related to the Winmar Report relied on by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that after he became aware that the unit was uninhabitable he asked his Landlord if he could withdraw his N11, which he was permitted to do in exchange for the signing of the new lease agreement with a $100.00 rent increase.

The Landlord testified that on August 4, 2025 he received a letter from a lawyer indicating that he was in default of his mortgage on the rental unit. He called the lawyer and was effectively informed that he would have to sell the unit or it would be repossessed. The Landlord testified that the rental unit was subsequently listed for sale, however a realtor noticed a large cracked in the ceiling of one of the bedrooms and he was informed that the crack must be assessed before he could proceed.
He testified that it was determined that two ceiling joists had fractured and removed from the wall seem and he received a quote for $2,825.00 for this repair.

The Landlord confirmed that Mishar Holdings Inc was listed as the mortgagee on the letter he received from the lawyer regarding his mortgage default, he described Mishar Holdings as the people who provided the loan for the mortgage and described them as the mortgage holders. He denied having any relationship to the company beyond owing them money. When asked if any of his family members worked for Mishar Holdings he testified that he was not exactly sure the employment of his family members. The Landlord testified that he was not aware of whether it was a family business.
The Landlord also initially testified that he had no relationship with [name] who had also joined the hearing as a witness for the Landlord, beyond a work capacity and denied that she was his sister.

When asked who [name] was, he described him as the father of [name], who managed the property for Mishar Holdings before he retired. When pressed further on this issue the Landlord confirmed that [name] was also his father but testified that he did not have a relationship with him.

The Landlord also allowed that [name] was in fact his sister, who he described as a half sister that he did not really know and testified that the only relationship he had with her was with respect to the property. He testified that they did not have a sibling relationship, and as if they were not related in that regard. 20. [name] also testified at the hearing. She testified that she was the property manager for the rental unit and had taken part in the remediation of the rental unit, she testified that she called some nearby companies including one in Kingston and one in Belleville. 21. She testified that she performed a walkthrough of the rental unit approximately one week after the Tenant vacated and the unit smelled of urine and ammonia and the surfaces felt disgusting with lots of urine stains on surfaces and walls within the rental unit. She also testified that she observed cat feces on top of a cabinet. She testified that she felt disorientated after entering and was informed she should be wearing a mask before entering the rental unit. 22. She also testified that she had previously conducted an inspection of the rental unit while it was occupied by the Tenant. She testified that she mainly focused on safety precautions during the inspection, and smelled ammonia, but none of the rooms were open and the rental unit was crowded and the Tenant did not permit her access to much of the rental unit. She did not issue any notices as a result of this inspection and did not complete a written report. 23. The Tenant testified that there was no move out inspection completed when she vacated the rental unit, she agreed that she vacated on March 30, 2025, without informing the Landlord but denied that this was done to avoid a walkthrough inspection as one was not requested. 24. The Tenant testified that the last inspection, which was on December 27, 2024 when the Landlord’s witness [name] attended the rental unit, She testified that she asked to go upstairs and the Tenant permitted this but asked her not to startle her son in his room. She testified that no concerns were raised as a result of this inspection. 25. The Tenant also testified that the flooring in rental unit was laminate and claimed that the photographs and videos relied on by the Landlord depicted a hardwood flooring. In support of this the Tenant relied on her own video of the rental unit. 26. The Tenant testified that she did not believe the report relied on by the Landlord from Winmar depicted the rental unit. She testified that she contacted Winmar and asked for a copy of the report herself by emailing the email address on the report. She testified that a [name] responded and informed her that he did not see anything for the address and would forward the Tenant’s query to [name] who was named as the person who had prepared the report. 27. He subsequently sent the Tenant an email indicating that he had spoken with [name] who did not believe he had ever inspected the rental unit and did not prepare the report and expressed that [name] was very concerned that someone had fraudulently created a document using the company name and the estimators name. He also indicated that if the Tenant knew who had created the document they would be very interested in that information. 28. The Tenant denied knowing [name] prior to this exchange. 29. [name] also testified at the hearing, he is the Office Manager for Winmar Kingston and Brockville, who handles the books and record keeping and works with the technicians .He testified that there was previously a separate Belleville branch of Winmar, but it closed two or three years ago, and he believed it had closed prior to 2025. 30. He testified that he was emailed by the Tenant seeking more information on the Winmar report relied on by the Landlord. He testified that all documents bearing Winmar’s name were a forgery, he testified that they had nothing to do with the property and had never been inside the rental unit. 31. He also testified that the owner of Winmar had a conversation with the Landlord’s daughter and her brother the day prior during which they had admitted that they had forged the documents bearing Winmars logo. 32. He testified that he was in attendance at the hearing because he is the one who documents everything and that [name] was not present because he was conducting estimates. He testified that [name] did not respond to the Tenants initial email because it was sent to him to handle as office manager. 33. He testified that the Belleville office of Winmar closed down around April 2025 and believed they handled their own paperwork while they were open and that the Kingston office only took over new files when the Belleville office close down. his testimony was somewhat inconstant with respect to the closure of the Belleville office, ranging from 2-3 years ago to April 2025. However during re-examination he reaffirmed that it has closed prior to 2025. Analysis 34. I accept that the Tenant has demonstrated that they were served an N12 Notice of Termination and vacated as a result, I also accept that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. 35. I am not satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I place very little weight on the testimony of the Landlord or his sister, and little weight on the documentation relied on by the Landlord for the reasons that follow. 36. I found the Landlord to be evasive when he was initially asked about his relationship with Mishar Holdings and [name]. The Landlord initially attempted to deny that he was related to [name] or that his father also had an interest in the priority and appeared prepared to maintain this assertion until the Tenant's Legal Representative sought to introduce evidence which would confirm they were related. This causes me to have serious concerns regarding the credibility of the Landlord, and accordingly I place little weight on his testimony. 37. With respect to the documentation relied on by the Landlord, in particular the Winmar report. I prefer the evidence of [name], who asserted that the Winmar report relied on by the Landlord was fraudulent, I find [name] testimony to be confident, credible and reliable, and note that he would appear to have no reason or motive to falsely claim that the report was fraudulent. I also note that it would likely be harmful to Winmar’s reputation if they were to falsely assert that a former client had fabricated a report, and that his decision to appear and provide testimony was likely not taken lightly. While the Landlord asserts that there may be some prior relationship between him and the Tenant, no clear evidence of this was introduce during the proceeding, and I find it more likely that there was no relationship prior to the hearing and [name] has simply attended as a represenative for Winmar after they were contacted by the Tenant. 38. While it is possible, as the Landlord seems to suggest, that the report was produced by a Belleville office of Winmar, which subsequently closed, this seems unlikely, while [name] testimony was somewhat inconsistent with respect the exact closing of the Belleville office, he did reaffirm that it had close dripper to 2025 and I note that the estimator involved still remains with Winmar, and the report relied on by the Landlord bears the logo of [name]. Additionally, were this a real possibility I find it very unlikely that Winmar would involve itself in these proceedings, and level such accusations against a potential former client. 39. While I would have preferred to hear evidence directly from the estimator [name] who completed the report, I am prepared to accept the explanation provided by Mr.[name] that he was in attendance at the hearing because he is the one who documents everything and deals with theses issues, and accept this as a reasonable explanation for his attendance and testimony. I also note that given his role within the organization, that while he may not have been named on the report he would be in a position to testify to whether it was genuine. 40. With respect to the Landlord’s position that his banking records are proof of payment to [name] and proof of the legitimacy of the report, I note that the records simply indicate a debit in the amount of $14,481.73 on May 9, 2025 and a payment of $18,296.97 on September 6, 2025. There is no clear indication within the bank records that indicates that the funds were paid to Winmar. 41. Therefore, I find that the report relied on by the Landlord was not produced by Winmar. This determination also causes me to question the other documentation relied on by the Landlord such as the request to his Landlord to end his tenancy and the letter to his employer, and the banking records relied on by the Landlord and I place little weight on the documentation presented by the Landlord. 42. Given my concerns regarding the documents relied on by the Landlord and with the Landlord’s testimony, I am not satisfied they have rebutted the presumption of bad faith. Therefore, I am satisfied that the N12 Notice of Termination was served in bad faith. Remedies 43. The Tenant sought a fine, primarily on the basis of the Landlord relying on fraudulent documentation from Winmar. While I recognise the deterrent effect of a fine, I am satisfied that the other remedies order will already have a sufficient deterrent effect, and am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that a fine is warranted. 44. The Tenant sought a rent differential of $15,600.00. She relied on a lease agreement indicating that she moved into a new rental unit at a monthly rent of $2500.00 per month. The Tenant testified that the new tenancy began March 7, 2025. Based on the Tenants testimony the new rental unit is larger containing 4 bedrooms rather than 3 and 2 bathrooms. Therefore, while I am satisfied that a differential is appropriate, I have reduced it to $1000.00 per month in consideration of the fact that the Tenant is now in a larger unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $12,000.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. 45. The Tenant sought moving and storage expenses of $171.56 she testified that she had to rent a moving truck, and a trailer, and had to pay for gas for the move. While the Tenant has not provided receipts or invoices for these expenses, they are modest, and I am prepared to accept that the Tenant had to spend this amount to secure a rental truck and trailer. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $171.56 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. 46. The Tenant also sought general compensation of $35,000.00 she testified that she is a mental wreck now, and it has been hard for her. She also testified that the false accusation the Landlord levelled at her using the documentation from Winmar will make it hard to secure a new rental. I accept that the eviction has had a significant impact on the Tenant and note that she had resided in the rental unit for many years. Given the impact on the Tenant and the Landlord’s use of what appear to be false documents to defend the Tenant’s Application, I am satisfied that general compensation is appropriate. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $15,000.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $41,435.71. This amount represents: • $12,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026. • $171.56 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $15,000.00 for general compensation. • $64.15 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
