issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord refused to give her access to the rental unit and did not return her last month rent deposit of $1,450.00. Background

The tenancy was scheduled to commence on December 1, 2025. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit and was required to pay the first month’s rent deposit and provide proof that she had set up the hydro account in her name prior to the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant failed to pay the first month’s rent deposit and failed to provide proof of the hydro account. Given this, the Landlord refused to provide the Tenant with the keys to the rental unit. These facts are not in dispute.
The Tenant seeks the return of her last month’s rent deposit.

Subsection 107(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires that a landlord repay the amount received as a rent deposit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. In Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2010 ONSC 5425 (CanLII), the Court found that the word “not given” suggests that it is the refusal or inability of a landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. Here, it was the Tenant’s action in refusing to pay the first month’s rent and provide proof of the hydro account as required in the agreement that prevented the Tenant from taking possession of the rental unit. As such, she is not entitled to the return of the rent deposit pursuant to subsection 107(1) because it was her act of repudiation of the agreement that prevented her from taking possession of the unit, not the action of the Landlord.

However, that is not the end of the analysis. Pursuant to section 16 of the Act, the Landlord also has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses resulting from the Tenant’s unilateral repudiation of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord took immediate steps to advertise the rental unit for rent and was able to re-lease the rental unit to another tenant on/around March 1, 2026. As the unit was not re-rented until that time, the Landlord was entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed [name]
The tenancy began on December 1, 2022.
The Landlord received a rent deposit of $1,250.00 on October 1, 2022. [name].
The Tenants occupied the rental unit when the application was filed and were in occupation on the day of the hearing.
As of May 1, 2026, the lawful rent is $1,340.25. At the time of filing the application, the lawful rent was $1,313.25.

The Tenants rent a unit in a triplex and have a backyard that is big enough for a play structure, chairs, table and a shed. They did not disclose the dimensions of the backyard but provided pictures in DOC-6971361 (Exhibit 1). It is not shared and is fenced with gates for access.
When the Tenants moved in, the neighbouring unit (311) was unoccupied, so there was no issue.
The lease does not stipulate an easement or right of way for neighbouring tenants. DOC- 6971376 (Exhibit 2).
When the tenant in 311 moved in, the Landlord asked the Tenants to allow her to pass through their yard to access her unit if she was carrying heavy things.

The Tenants agreed at the time, but now say that during Summer and Fall 2025, the traffic to unit 311 was so busy from the tenant’s family and friends that they felt it substantially interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenants complained to the Landlord about the high traffic through their yard. The specific date they informed the Landlord was requested twice in the hearing, but the Tenants were vague and could not remember when in the Fall 2025 they told the Landlord. They directed me to an email on the portal, however, there is no such email in their evidence.
The Tenants stated that they took matters into their own hands and put locks on the gate to prevent their neighbour from passing through.
They testified that the Landlord asked them to remove the locks and served them with an N5 notice of termination on November 21, 2025 DOC-6971359 (Exhibit 3).
They testified and stated in their application that they told the Landlord that they would not remove the locks unless he lowered the rent.
The Tenants filed their application November 24, 2025.
The Landlord did not attend the hearing, so the Tenant’s evidence is unchallenged. [name]

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, states: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

There are two parts to assessing a claim that the Landlord substantially interfered in the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. First, it must be grounded in “interference” that is more than trifling or passing; it has to be substantial. Second, it must be found that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps in addressing the complaints.

The Divisional Court in Hassan v. Niagara Housing Authority [2000] O.J. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”) affirmed that a landlord has a positive obligation to take reasonably necessary actions to ensure that all tenants can reasonably enjoy the rental premises: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.
I find that the first part of the test is met: frequent traffic in one’s yard is a substantial interference on one’s right to quiet enjoyment of the rental unit.

However, I find there is no evidence that the Tenants informed the Landlord about the situation until they put locks on the gate and he asked them to remove them and subsequently served them with an N5. Without knowledge, the Landlord does not have an opportunity to take reasonable steps to uphold his obligation. Landlords are not held to a standard of perfection; they are held to a standard of reasonableness, and in this case I find the Landlord was not given an opportunity to act reasonably.

Furthermore, the Board does not find that the service of a single N5 Notice constitutes substantial interference. It is a legitimate exercise of a legal right of landlords to serve notices. To find otherwise would undermine the purpose and function of the Act.

Therefore, the Tenants have not proven the allegation that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of property on a balance of probabilities, and so the application shall be dismissed. Harassment
The Tenants further allege that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them by asking them to remove the locks on the gate.
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (The Act) states: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known as unwelcome.”

A review of the Tenants’ application indicates no claim for harassment, no date of any particular behaviour or activity or event, nor describes any harassing act, behaviour, or words on the part of the Landlord.

In [name] v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (‘Ball’), the Divisional Court pronounced that applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to meet the case.

MacDougall J. wrote in [name] that, “Particulars should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” The Court went on to state that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

At the hearing, the Tenants did not elaborate any specific events of harassing behaviour, other than the Landlord asking them to remove the locks, which they did. I find the Landlord was within his rights to ask the Tenants to remove the locks and that this does not constitute harassment as it is not “a course of vexatious comment or conduct.. that is unwelcome.”
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with or harassed them, and so the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. July 02, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; • The Landlord did not demolish the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.
This is the Tenant’s application, and the Tenant therefore bears the burden of proving each of these conjunctive elements of the legal test on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(c).

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2012, and vacated December 31, 2024 after the tenancy was terminated by the Landlord and Tenant Board pursuant to an L2 Application based on an N13 Notice of Termination.
The Tenant clarified that she had left some belongings in the home into January 2025 and did not formally vacate until January 18, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the N13 she received from the Landlord indicated that they intended to demolish the rental unit so that the space could be used as a turnaround area for tandem trucks because at their current location the trucks had been vandalised.

The Tenant testified that she went by the rental unit every month and the home was still standing in December 2025. She testified that it was subsequently removed from the foundation and moved to a new location with the garage and breezeway left behind.
The Tenant testified that the house was moved approximately 10 minutes away to 525 Fennel Road Kawartha Lakes, Ontario. The Tenant did not know if the house had been sold when it was moved.

The Tenant testified that she would consider a demolition to result in the unit being completely done away with and did not consider the removal to be a demolition. She testified that the evidence provided by the Landlord suggested that a company hired to perform the demolition back out in 2025 due to weather conditions, but the Landlord had not provided any other evidence regarding any company hired to perform the demolition.

She testified that there was an 11-month delay before the rental unit was technically demolished, and that the Landlord had everything set in place for a proper demolition. She testified that she believed the Landlord never intended to demolish the rental unit and instead intended to sell it for a profit.

The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord had obtained a quote for demolition, and that they had always maintained that the rental unit was to be demolished. She also agreed that it would have been impossible for her or anyone else to occupy the unit as of December 2025.
The Landlord testified that he served the N13 for demolition in November 2023 and an eviction order was ultimately issued by the Board terminating the tenancy effective December 31, 2024.

The Landlord testified that they waited until the Tenant had removed all of her belongings on January 18, 2025 then contacted [name] to have the electricity to the unit disconnected. The Landlord relied on documents form [name] showing zero usage at the property.

The Landlord testified that there intent had been to have La Rue perform the demolition of the home after the electricity was disconnected however they had to wait until the winter ended to bring the excavator to the rental unit and remove the debris and were further delayed by weight restrictions on the spring roads until April 30, 2025 which would have prevented the machinery from accessing the rental unit.
After encountering this delay the Landlord testified that they approached an individual named [name] who said they could assist with the removal of the unit by removing the home as a single unit.

The Landlord relied on a series of text messages between themselves and [name] discussing the removal, in one such text message Curvin indicates to the Landlord that they have been delayed because they are waiting in permits to be issued. The text messages also depict the Landlord following up with [name] on October 14, 2025 and November 21, 2025 as they were concerned that the demolition permit would expire. The Landlord ultimately renewed the permit on November 21, 2025, and the unit was placed on piles in Novembre 2025.

The Landlord testified that on or about December 15 2025 [name] attended and demolished the breezeway and the garage and removed the debris, and [name] removed the remaining structure in January 2026. The Landlord testified that they attempted every month to move the project forward. The Landlord testified that they were not paid by [name] and there was no transfer of title and they have had no further dealing with the structure since its removal. Analysis
As noted above, the elements of the legal test are conjunctive. I accept that the Tenant has demonstrate that they received the N13 notice and moved out of the rental unit because of the notice.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that Landlord did not demolish the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated or that the Notice of Termination was served in bad faith.

The Act does not define the word demolish. When interpreting the meaning of the word “demolish”, I am required to apply the modern principal of statutory interpretation, which is that the words of the Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of the Legislature.

Demolish is variously defined as “pull down, completely destroy or break” and “destroy, pull down, or do away with something”: [name], 2021 CanLII 139751 (ON LTB) at para. 13; TEL- 6389315 (Re), 2016 CanLII 38366 (ON LTB) at para. 11. Accordingly, the grammatical and ordinary sense of the word “demolish” suggests that the proposed work should be something akin to the irrevocable destruction of the rental unit.

In Two Clarendon Apartments Limited v. Sinclair, 2019 ONSC 3845 (CanLII), the issue was whether the work proposed by the landlord constituted a renovation or a demolition for the purposes of section 50(1) of the Act. The Board had found that it was a renovation, and not a demolition, because the unit would be available in the same floor space, albeit reconfigured and extensively rebuilt.

At paragraph 10, the Court held that the Board’s approach to the definition of demolition was reasonable and consistent with the Act and modern principles of statutory interpretation. The following portions of the Board’s reasons were quoted by the Court: 13. In a situation where the rental unit continues to exist, albeit in an extremely altered form, it is possible for the tenant to exercise a right of first refusal, because the rental unit is still there: the tenant may move back and continue the tenancy. In a situation where the rental unit is gone, it is not possible for the tenant to exercise a right of first refusal: the rental unit is no longer there and so the tenant cannot move back. The fact that the Act distinguishes renovations and demolitions by the tenant’s right of first refusal shows that the intention of these sections of the Act is to preserve tenancies where it is possible to do so. [Emphasis added] 14. Accordingly, a project will be defined as a renovation under the Act in a case where it is possible for the tenant to move back into the unit and a project will be defined as a demolition where it is not possible for the tenant to move back into the unit.

In this case I am satisfied that the work perfumed by the Landlord constitutes a demolition. A portion of the rental unit, being the garage and breezeway was pulled down, and removed in a manner that is entirely consistent with demolition. Additionally, the remainder of the structure was removed and could not be inhabitable. While a portion of this structure continued to exist, it could not be said that the Tenant could exercise a right of first refusal and move back into the rental unit. Therefore, I am satisfied that the removal of the structure was consistent with the definition of demolition and the intent of the Act.

I also accept the Landlord’s testimony with respect to delays caused by the Tenant’s belongings, the winter season, and the road conditions, and accept that the Landlord made reasonable efforts to move the project forward. Including by renewing the demolition permit. Therefore, I am satisfied that the demolition occurred within a reasonable time when I consider the context and surrounding circumstances.

Even if the removal of the structure did not constitute a demolition, The Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the N13 notice was given in bad faith. I accept the evidence of the Landlord that their intention was always to demolish the rental unit, and note that the Landlord took clear steps towards this purpose, including renewing the demolition permit until the structure was demolished and removed, additionally the Tenants own evidence was that the Landlord had always maintained that the property would be demolished. While the Tenant asserted that the Landlord was paid to have the structure removed, there is no definitive proof of this, and I am prepared to accept the Landlord’s testimony that no funds changed hands and they had no further involvement with the structure after it was removed.

Therefore, I am satisfied that there was always a clear consistent pattern of the Landlord intending to demolish the rental unit and taking appropriate steps to follow through with this intention. Therefore, I am not satisfied the Tenant has demonstrated that the N13 was served in bad faith.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. July 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background to the tenancy and the application.

The tenancy began on January 1, 2025, on a fixed one-year term. The monthly rent period was from the 1st of the month to the end of the month. The Tenants testified that they moved out of the rental unit on or about November 30, 2025. The monthly rent was $2,350.00. The Tenants provided documentary evidence that the last month’s rent was in this amount and submitted she had paid the Landlord the first and last months rent upon commencement of the tenancy.

The Tenants testified they were model Tenants and just wished to leave the rental unit and move into their other home early and sought $850.00 the remaining funds of their last month’s rent deposit plus interest on their last month’s rent deposit.

On December 12, 2025, the Tenants filed a T1 Application with the Board, alleging, the Landlord did not use his last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to them nor provided interest on said deposit. The Tenant’s Legal Representative clarified that the Landlord had provided $1,500.00 of the deposit, hence the Tenant sought the remainer of $850.00

The Tenants testified that they notified the Landlord on or about October 10, 2025 that they would be vacating the rental unit on November 30, 2025, even though this was a fixed term tenancy to December 31, 2025, and the Landlord seemed genuinely open to working with the Tenants to find a replacement tenant for the rental unit and the parties executed an N11 for November 30, 2025, and that the Landlord provided them $1,500.00 of the last month’s rent deposit.

Upon Board questioning the Tenants acknowledged they provided the Landlord with less than 60 days notice of their intention to vacate the rental unit, and further that this was a fixed term tenancy to December 31, 2025, and they could not vacate prior to the end of the term, but still wished the return of the remainder of their last month’s rent deposit which the Landlord had not returned.

The Landlord testified that the Tenants entered a fixed term lease, and while he did provide $1,500.00 of the last months rent deposit to the Tenants in good faith and wanted the couple to succeed in their next endeavour, they left the unit, prior to the termination of the tenancy and there was an agreement that’s all they would receive due to the early termination, which from the evidence in front of the Board both oral and documentary seems to be the case on a balance of probabilities. Moreover, the Landlord could not re- rent the rental unit until after the termination of the fixed term tenancy, as work had to be done to prepare the unit for re-rental from his testimony.

It was quite apparent from the testimonies that the Tenants vacated the rental unit one month early in a fixed term, with short notice as agreed upon between the parties, and the Landlord had not consented to the early termination of the tenancy, however had negotiated the same.

Based on the evidence before the Board I find that the Tenants had not met the burden of proof for this herein application. As the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Moreover, the reason that the full amount of the Tenants’ last month rent deposit was not returned to them seems to be from the short notice, provided to the Landlord and an agreement between the parties, on a balance of probabilities from the testimony of the parties and evidence submitted. On a balance of probabilities, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence to that of the Tenants. Hence the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ T1 application is dismissed. July 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $3,825.33

The Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance and repair obligations under the Act. The Landlord did not respond in a timely manner to the Tenants’ complaints of mould in the kitchen and bathrooms of the rental unit. The Landlord also did not repair the damage in the kitchen pipe sink.

The Tenant relies largely on the same factual allegations in their T2 application, alleging that the Landlord’s response to these issues substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and harassed the Tenant by making threats.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that, when the tenancy began on March 5, 2024, he noticed the presence of mould in the rental unit. the Tenant testified that he advised the Landlord of his concern on March 6, 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord hired a contractor attend around November 2024 but there was nothing done. The Tenant testified the mould was visible in the kitchen and bathroom. Since there were no steps taken, the Tenant called the City of Brampton on December 5, 2024. After inspecting the property, the city of Brampton issued an order on January 23, 2025. The Tenant submitted a copy of the order and a letter from the By- law office dated stating the sections of the By-law that has not been complied among some of the items were: rotten kitchen countertop and [name]. The letter indicates that inspection noted mould in the kitchen and bathroom. The order states that Landlord has until March 31, 2025, to comply. The Tenant therefore proved the presence of mould at the property.

The basis of the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord harassed him is based on that the Landlord authorized a collections agency to collect a debt owed by the Tenant to the Landlord. He testified that Landlord harassed him by filing with Front Lobby a collection agency in regard to the Tenant not paying rent and other lease charges. The Tenant testified he received emails from this company on December 27, 2024, January 2, January 28, 2025, and February 26, 2025.

The Landlord testified that the condition of the unit of the unit was good when the Tenant moved in. He testified that the Tenant told him of the issue in March, and he never mentioned it again. After which, the Tenant provided 60 days notice on at the end of August 2024 to move out by October 2024. As such, he did not address the maintenance issues. He testified that he did try to enter the unit along with the city inspector and provided 24-hour notice around January 2025, but the Tenant refused the Landlord entry and only allowed the city inspector to enter his unit.

He submitted that the Tenant did ask to do the repairs himself, but the Landlord wanted to use his own contractors. The Landlord also testified that he was also afraid to enter the Tenant’s unit because of safety issues but did not identify any specific incidents that would entail it would be a safety issue. The Landlord ultimately testified that after the Tenant moved out on March 22, 2025, he began the repair work, and the issues were fixed as of May 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute that he used a collection agency to collect debt owed by the Tenant. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I find the Landlord is in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. I say this because I find that the Landlord did not take any steps to address the Tenant’s complaint and investigate his complaints. The Landlord testified that once the Tenant complained of the maintenance issues, he waited until the Tenant moved out to begin repairs. The Property Standards Order is clear evidence that the Landlord failed to comply with a safety, housing or maintenance standard as required by subsection 20(1). The fact that the Landlord did not take appropriate steps to address the issue until the Property Standards Order was issued—almost nine months after the Tenant identified the issue to the Landlord—resulted in the Landlord breaching subsection 20(1) of the RTA.

There is overlap between subsection 20(1) and section 22 of the RTA. A breach by a landlord of subsection 20(1) can result in a substantial interference with a tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises. In this case, I am satisfied that the failure of the Landlord to react in a timely manner to the issues raised by the Tenant substantially interfered with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit insofar as the Tenant was deprived of the use and enjoyment of the unit because the Landlord failed to comply with subsection 20(1) of the RTA.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period of March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. This finding contributes to the total rent abatement calculated below.

Seeking recovery of a debt is clearly not harassment. No evidence presented by the Tenant suggests that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable in the circumstances. It is the Tenant’s obligation to prove the merits of their case on a balance of probabilities, and he has failed to do so.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. The Tenant’s application must, therefore, be dismissed. Remedies Rent Abatement

With respect to the issue of mould and kitchen pipe sink, the Tenant sought a $13,875.00 rent abatement, at 100% rent abatement for 9 months. I considered the Tenant’s testimony that the mould made the Tenant sick. However, the Tenant did not provide any medical documentary evidence to prove that is the case. In this case, I find the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement is not reasonable. However, it is evident that the presence of mould and issue the kitchen faucet has interfered with the Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the basement for all usual purposes.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if the tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of the services; and should a tenant receive any reduction in services, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support how the Tenant arrived at the numerical figure of 36% so I must consider the appropriate method to calculate a fair and reasonable value of the rent abatement. I find a 36% rent abatement for the 383-day period is excessive as I find that the space, while potentially uncomfortable and unsanitary due to the mould and the kitchen faucet was in disrepair, it was not fully unusable. Therefore, based on similar circumstances from other matters, I find that a 15% rent abatement is fair and reasonable, meaning the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $3,777.33. This amount represents a 15% abatement of the daily compensation for the period March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. Daily compensation is calculated as ($2,000.00 x 12)/365 = $65.75.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,825.33. This amount represents: • $3,777.33 for a rent abatement for the period ending March 22, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. July 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. The amount of $3,825.33 is set-off against the amount still owing by the Tenant to the Landlord under order LTB-L- 0047232-25, issued by the Board April 28, 2025.

The Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance and repair obligations under the Act. The Landlord did not respond in a LTB-T-042715-25-AM timely manner to the Tenants’ complaints of mould in the kitchen and bathrooms of the rental unit. The Landlord also did not repair the damage in the kitchen pipe sink.

The Tenant relies largely on the same factual allegations in their T2 application, alleging that the Landlord’s response to these issues substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and harassed the Tenant by making threats.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that, when the tenancy began on March 5, 2024, he noticed the presence of mould in the rental unit. the Tenant testified that he advised the Landlord of his concern on March 6, 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord hired a contractor attend around November 2024 but there was nothing done. The Tenant testified the mould was visible in the kitchen and bathroom. Since there were no steps taken, the Tenant called the City of Brampton on December 5, 2024. After inspecting the property, the city of Brampton issued an order on January 23, 2025. The Tenant submitted a copy of the order and a letter from the By- law office dated stating the sections of the By-law that has not been complied among some of the items were: rotten kitchen countertop and [name]. The letter indicates that inspection noted mould in the kitchen and bathroom. The order states that Landlord has until March 31, 2025, to comply. The Tenant therefore proved the presence of mould at the property.

The basis of the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord harassed him is based on that the Landlord authorized a collections agency to collect a debt owed by the Tenant to the Landlord. He testified that Landlord harassed him by filing with Front Lobby a collection agency in regard to the Tenant not paying rent and other lease charges. The Tenant testified he received emails from this company on December 27, 2024, January 2, January 28, 2025, and February 26, 2025.

The Landlord testified that the condition of the unit of the unit was good when the Tenant moved in. He testified that the Tenant told him of the issue in March, and he never mentioned it again. After which, the Tenant provided 60 days notice on at the end of August 2024 to move out by October 2024. As such, he did not address the maintenance issues. He testified that he did try to enter the unit along with the city inspector and provided 24-hour notice around January 2025, but the Tenant refused the Landlord entry and only allowed the city inspector to enter his unit.

He submitted that the Tenant did ask to do the repairs himself, but the Landlord wanted to use his own contractors. The Landlord also testified that he was also afraid to enter the Tenant’s unit because of safety issues but did not identify any specific incidents that would entail it would be a safety issue. The Landlord ultimately testified that after the Tenant moved out on March 22, 2025, he began the repair work, and the issues were fixed as of May 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute that he used a collection agency to collect debt owed by the Tenant. Analysis LTB-T-042715-25-AM

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I find the Landlord is in breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act. I say this because I find that the Landlord did not take any steps to address the Tenant’s complaint and investigate his complaints. The Landlord testified that once the Tenant complained of the maintenance issues, he waited until the Tenant moved out to begin repairs. The Property Standards Order is clear evidence that the Landlord failed to comply with a safety, housing or maintenance standard as required by subsection 20(1). The fact that the Landlord did not take appropriate steps to address the issue until the Property Standards Order was issued—almost nine months after the Tenant identified the issue to the Landlord—resulted in the Landlord breaching subsection 20(1) of the RTA.

There is overlap between subsection 20(1) and section 22 of the RTA. A breach by a landlord of subsection 20(1) can result in a substantial interference with a tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises. In this case, I am satisfied that the failure of the Landlord to react in a timely manner to the issues raised by the Tenant substantially interfered with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit insofar as the Tenant was deprived of the use and enjoyment of the unit because the Landlord failed to comply with subsection 20(1) of the RTA.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period of March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. This finding contributes to the total rent abatement calculated below.

Seeking recovery of a debt is clearly not harassment. No evidence presented by the Tenant suggests that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable in the circumstances. It is the Tenant’s obligation to prove the merits of their case on a balance of probabilities, and he has failed to do so.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. The Tenant’s application must, therefore, be dismissed. Remedies Rent Abatement

With respect to the issue of mould and kitchen pipe sink, the Tenant sought a $13,875.00 rent abatement, at 100% rent abatement for 9 months. I considered the Tenant’s testimony that the mould made the Tenant sick. However, the Tenant did not provide any medical documentary evidence to prove that is the case. In this case, I find the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement is not reasonable. However, it is evident that the presence of mould and LTB-T-042715-25-AM issue the kitchen faucet has interfered with the Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the basement for all usual purposes.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if the tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of the services; and should a tenant receive any reduction in services, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support how the Tenant arrived at the numerical figure of 36% so I must consider the appropriate method to calculate a fair and reasonable value of the rent abatement. I find a 36% rent abatement for the 383-day period is excessive as I find that the space, while potentially uncomfortable and unsanitary due to the mould and the kitchen faucet was in disrepair, it was not fully unusable. Therefore, based on similar circumstances from other matters, I find that a 15% rent abatement is fair and reasonable, meaning the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a rent abatement of $3,777.33. This amount represents a 15% abatement of the daily compensation for the period March 4, 2024, to March 22, 2025. Daily compensation is calculated as ($2,000.00 x 12)/365 = $65.75.
The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Set-off

The Landlord raised that he filed a L1 application with the Board and obtained an order against the Tenant, file no. LTB-L-004732-25 (the ‘L1 Order’). In the L1 Order, I note that the Tenant was ordered to pay the Tenant $8,157.21. The Tenant filed a request to review of the order. However, that request was denied and so the L1 Order stands.

The Landlord requested that any rent abatement ordered be set off by the amount owing to the Landlord under the L1 Order. If granted, the set-off would essentially allow the Tenant to reduce the arrears claim by using the rent abatement the Landlord owes to the Tenant.

This approach is consistent with the Divisional Court’s decision in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 which directs the Board to set off any amount one party owes against the amount owing by the other party.

The Board cannot ignore an order, especially one of its own orders, for the payment of money that remains outstanding and is obligated to apply the doctrine of set-off. As such, the amount owing to the Tenant shall be deducted from the amount owing to the Landlord as ordered below.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,825.33. This amount represents: LTB-T-042715-25-AM • $3,777.33 for a rent abatement for the period ending March 22, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The amount of $3,825.33 owing from the Landlord to the Tenant for rent abatement and the costs of filing this application pursuant to this order shall be set-off against the previous amount owed by the Tenant to the Landlord pursuant to Order LTB-L- 004732-25 issued on April 28, 2025. July 3, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Region Non- Profit Housing Corporation (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them. • was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and failed to do so. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. T2 & T6 Applications

The Tenant was before the Board on May 22, 2025 for an adjudicative case conference. At the ACC, the Member also discussed with the Tenant the adequacy of the particulars and an interim order was issued on May 29, 2025 stating at paragraph 3 that: If the Tenant wishes to request that the application be amended, a written request to amend the application shall be served and filed in compliance with rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure on or before June 22, 2025.
The Tenant did not submit any request to amend the application or provide any dates and times as per the interim order.

At the hearing, I addressed the lack of particulars, particularly the lack of any dates and times in the Tenant’s application as the Tenant’s applications contain broad allegations without any accompanying identifying dates or times and canvassed as to whether the Tenant was able to provide any accompanying dates or times. The Tenant testified that she is unable to provide any identifying dates or times.

Administrative tribunals are bound by the duty of fairness and the duty of procedural fairness includes the right of a party to know the case they have to meet. Absent this, the right to a fair hearing is denied and generally, as with any lack of procedural fairness, the resulting decision is compromised.

As I was not satisfied that the Landlord or the LTB can discern the particular dates and times of the Tenant’s claim, I find that it would be procedurally unfair to permit a hearing on the merits. As a result, I find that the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. T5 Application
At the adjudicative case conference, the Tenant confirmed that she was not served with an N12 or N13 notice and indicated she did not intend to pursue the T5 portion of this application.
The Tenant did not lead any evidence at the hearing that she was served an N12 or N13 notice. As a result, this application was dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegation contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation and costs in the amount of $1,748.00 to the Tenant. T6 Application

On December 29, 2024, the Tenant filed a T6 application alleging that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by failing to adequately address leaking/flooding in the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that: a) On August 5, 2024, he noticed a leak in the basement and immediately verbally notified the Landlord that water was pooling and damaging the floor; b) Nothing was immediately done to address the leaking issues; c) Approximately one (1) week later, the Tenant noticed that mold was forming in and around the water-damaged areas. He notified the Landlord of the mold issue and the Landlord immediately called their insurance company; d) A contractor attended the rental unit and tore up the floor, cut out water-damaged drywall and removed the doors from the affected areas of the unit (the bedroom and bathroom). The Tenant provided photographs of this demolition; e) The Landlord issued him a handwritten eviction notice (submitted into evidence), dated August 25, 2024, indicating that the Landlord wanted him to leave by December 1, 2024 as they believed the unit was uninhabitable. No offer was made by the Landlord to fund any moving or relocation expenses; f) The Tenant arranged for alternate accommodations for he and his son, but he left his possessions in the rental unit and continued to pay rent. He stayed in these alternate accommodations from approximately August 25, 2024 to December 14, 2024, when he returned to live in the rental unit; g) As of December 14, 2024, the rental unit had not been repaired. The Tenant submits that he incurred expenses to purchase carpets and curtains to cover the torn up floor and replace the removed doors respectively; and h) The Tenant submits that he moved out of the rental unit on or about December 31, 2024.

The Tenant is requesting the following remedies: a) Rent abatement for five months totalling $6,550.00; b) Out-of-pocket expenses of $1,500.00 for additional transportation and food costs incurred due to having to live elsewhere; c) Repairs/replacement of $280.50 for the purchase of carpets and curtains to replace torn up floor and removed doors; d) An order for the Landlord to repair the rental unit; and e) General damages of $35,000.00. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act states: 20(1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the uncontested evidence of the Tenant is that there was leaking/flooding in the rental unit that required a significant remedial response, including the floor and doors being removed and drywall cut back. This demolition work was completed within several weeks of the being reported (in August 2024), but the reconstruction of the rental unit was not completed by the time the Tenant vacated the unit on December 31, 2024.

The evidence submitted by the Tenant indicates that the Landlord sought to terminate the [name] tenancy due to the repairs required. This attempted termination was not done through an LTB form or process, but via a handwritten letter. No compensation was offered to the Tenant as part of the attempted termination process.

Based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under s. 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. While there appears to have been demolition work undertaken on the rental unit, the uncontested evidence before me shows that there was little work undertaken on repairing the rental unit after the demolition was completed, and that the Landlord instead sought to terminate the Tenant’s tenancy. The Landlord’s response to the maintenance issues was neither reasonable nor effective. Remedies

Given that the rental unit was not fully habitable once the demolition was undertaken, I find that a rent abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. The demolition appears to have been confined to the areas in and around the bedroom and bathroom of the rental unit. As such, I find that a 50% rent abatement for the months of September – December 2024, totalling $1,700.00 ($850 monthly rent x 4 months x 50%) is reasonable.

I do not find the Tenant’s request for $1,500.00 in out-of-pocket expenses related to transportation and food costs to be reasonable in the circumstances. The Tenant did not provide any detail or receipts regarding these claimed expenses and I find that the Tenant would have had to incur some of these expenses regardless of where he was living.

I further do not find the Tenant’s request for $280.50 in repair/replacement expenses to be reasonable in the circumstances. Again, no receipts were provided and the nature of the expenses incurred (curtains and carpets) do not truly constitute repairs/replacements.
As the Tenant has already vacated the rental unit, I will not be ordering the Landlord to undertake any repairs.

Finally, I do not find the Tenant’s request for $35,000.00 in general damages to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant’s basis for this request is more akin to something that would be adjudicated through a T2 or T5 application, not a T6 application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,748.00, which represents: • $1,700.00 for a 50% rent abatement (rent = $850.00/month) for the months September – December 2024; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by July 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and Medallion Corporation (the 'Landlords'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: On consent, the application is amended to include Medallion Corporation as the Landlord.

The Tenant indicated that she had filed an amended application. I informed the Tenant that the Board’s record does not reflect that an amended application was filed. The Landlord’s representative also stated that an amended application was not served on the Landlord in advance of the hearing. I identified the allegations contained in the application before the Board and asked the Tenant whether those were the issues she wish to proceed with. The Tenant confirmed that they were. Accordingly, I have considered the allegations contained in the application filed with the Board on December 30, 2024. T2 Application
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act’) states “a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

The Tenant bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord engaged in conduct that falls within s. 23 of the Act. For the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has met that burden. a) Proof of insurance

The Tenant testified that the Landlord requested proof of Tenant insurance on three occasions despite her evidence that she had already submitted proof of insurance. The Tenant stated that she submitted her insurance certificate on June 27, 2024, before the deadline. The Tenant further testified that she received notices dated June 14, July 3, 2024 and an N5 notice in October 2024 alleging that she had failed to provide insurance. The Tenant testified that the repeated requests and the N5 caused her stress and amounted to harassment because they threatened eviction despite her having already provided proof of insurance. 6. [name] acknowledged that the Landlord received the Tenant’s proof of insurance. [name] indicated that the requests for proof of insurance were made as part of verifying compliance with the tenancy agreement and were administrative in nature. She denied that the requests were intended to harass or intimidate the Tenant. 7. While the Tenant testified that she submitted proof of insurance on June 27, 2024, the evidence does not establish when the Landlord received the proof of insurance. As the Tenant bears the burden of proving the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities, I am unable to conclude that the repeated requests for proof of insurance or the service of the N5 amounted to harassment, coercion or substantial interference within the meaning of s. 23 of the Act. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. b) Noise complaints 8. The Tenant testified that beginning in December 2023, she heard repeated drilling, hammering and other excessive noise originating from the neighbouring unit. She testified that the noise continued through March 2026, including outside permitted construction hours. The Tenant testified that she repeatedly reported the noise to the Landlord, its after- hour line, and municipal bylaw officers regarding drilling, hammering, banging and other loud noises. The Tenant further testified that she provided recordings of noise, maintained a log of incidents, and submitted written complaints, but the Landlord failed to adequately investigate or resolve the issue. 9. The Landlord denied failing to address the Tenant’s noise complaints. The Landlord’s evidence was that management investigated the complaints on several occasions, including attending at the neighbouring unit and speaking with its residents on February 27, March 1 and March 2, 2026. 10. [name] testified that the Landlord distributed notices to neighbouring residents asking them to report excessive noise. 11. The evidence does not establish that the Landlord’s investigation discovered unreasonable or excessive noise from the neighbouring occupants. The Landlord referred to evidence in which they responded to the Tenant’s complaints by attending the neighbouring unit on multiple occasions and speaking with residents. The Landlord also offered the Tenant a transfer into another unit, which she declined. 12. I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to investigate or respond to the Tenant’s noise complaints. The evidence establishes that the Landlord responded reasonably to the complaints in the circumstances. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. c) Door kicking 13. The Tenant testified that on January 30, 2025, the superintendent kicked her apartment door. She filed a written complaint the following day and considered contacting the police but ultimately did not do so. 14. [name] testified that the superintendent denied this allegation. 15. I find the evidence before me is insufficient to make a finding that the incident occurred as alleged by the Tenant. The superintendent did not testify, and the Tenant did not summon the superintendent or other witnesses with direct knowledge of the incident. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. d) Hot water temperature 16. The Tenant testified that she experienced issues with the hot water temperatures with repeated periods of no hot water. The Tenant further testified that the superintendent attended the rental unit on or about January 13, 2025 but dismissed her concerns regarding insufficient hot water temperatures. The Tenant stated that she was required to involve the City of Toronto, bylaw officer, who directed the Landlord to address the issue. 17. The Tenant testified that despite repeated attendances by the Landlord, the issues with the hot water temperature continued and several attempts were required before the issue was resolved. 18. The Landlord denied failing to address the Tenant's hot water complaints. The Landlord stated that it first became aware of the issue on December 17, 2024, after being contacted by a municipal bylaw officer. The management immediately attended at the rental unit to verify water temperature and continued monitoring temperatures throughout December 2024 and January 2025. The Landlord also inspected the neighbouring units, replaced the bathroom faucet, hired plumber and boiler system contractors, who investigated the boiler system and determined that the issue was caused by malfunctioning boiler component. 19. The necessary repairs were completed by the Landlord on January 22, 2025, after which temperature readings confirmed that the hot water was within required range. 20. The evidence establishes that the Landlord investigated the complaint, monitored the hot water temperature on numerous occasions, retained contractors, perform repairs and communicated with municipal bylaw officer throughout the investigation until the issue was resolved in a timely manner after the Landlord became aware of the issue. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant’s vital services. Accordingly, the Tenant has not established this allegation on a balance of probabilities. 21. For the given reasons above, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that the residential complex is comprised of nine (9) residential units, and that they have been facing ongoing noise issues stemming from the unit located directly above them (i.e. unit #6).

The Tenant stated that the noise issues related to unit #6 started during the month of May 2025, and have been ongoing since then, with regular noise disturbances taking place during the weekends for a period of one (1) to two (2) hours between 6:00am and 1:00am.

The Tenant indicated that they have advised the Landlord of these ongoing noise disturbances on multiple occasions, as it appears from the screenshots of the Tenant’s email’s “sent folder” showings a list of emails sent by the Tenant to the Landlord between February 17, 2024, and February 15, 2026, which include the terms “noise complaint” (DOC-8178088, DOC-8178099, and DOC-8178112; Exhibit 1, in bundle).
The Tenant stated that the Landlord them advised that they would speak with the tenants of unit #6 regarding their concern, but that the issue never ceased.

The Tenant described the noise disturbances they have encountered as being akin to stomping, screaming, and items being dropped on the floor, as it appears from the video recordings taken by the Tenant on their cellphone on or around 7:00am on August 29, 2025 ([name] and DOC-8178198; [name], in bundle).
The Tenant submits that the Landlord has failed to take reasonable steps to address the noise disturbances related to the conduct of the tenants of unit #6. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) reads as follows: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority , the Divisional Court held that a landlord who fails to take reasonable steps to address the conduct of a tenant of the residential complex which impedes on the reasonable enjoyment of the premises by another tenant can be found to have substantially interfered with the complainant t enant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.1

Therefore, the general expectation of a landlord, when dealing with tenant -on-tenant complaints, is for the landlord to first investigate the complaint in question. If the complaint is found to be well founded, the landlord then is expected to take increasingly serious steps to deal with the behaviour complained of in order to stop it.

As such, for the Landlord’s obligation to take reasonable steps to stop the conduct of the tenants of unit #6, the Tenant’s complaint must first be well founded, with the disturbances rising beyond what one would consider to be normal and ordinary sounds within the context of a communal living environment, such as a multi-unit residential complex.

In the matter before the Board, the Tenant mostly limited their submissions to superficial, vague and accusatory statements, which were supported by little to no detail as they were only able to provide the date of a singular incident which would have occurred on August 29, 2025 (Exhibit 2) . Indeed, while the Tenant shared screenshots of various outgoing communications sent to the Landlord between February 17, 2024, and February 15, 2026 (Exhibit 1), they did not actually submit into evidence any of the actual complaints, nor the contents of these email communications. 1 [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650, paragraphs 16 to 18.

Furthermore, while the Tenant characterized the sound heard on the video recordings dated August 29, 2025 (Exhibit 2) as being equivalent to the ongoing level of noise they have been “forced to endure,” I note that the sound emanating from a different residential unit is imperceptible and seemingly does to depict any stomping, screaming, or dropping of various items on the floor.
I therefore find that the Tenant has failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim.

Although some level of noise may very well be emanating from unit #6, the Tenant is “not entitled to absolute silence from their neighbours.”2 As such, I find that the noise emanating from unit #6 would amount to little more than minor inconveniences,3 which - in turn - would not engage the Landlord’s obligation to take increasingly serious steps to deal with the behaviour being complained of, within the context of a multi-unit residential complex.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord is amended to [organization] [name] is removed as a party as she is an employee of the corporate Landlord.
At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant advised that she vacated the rental unit on February 15, 2026.

In this application, the only remedies requested by the Tenant were the following: • the Landlord’s Building Manager to not come to the unit for any reason that for a maintenance request or emergency such as flood or fire; and • the Landlord will only contact the Tenant via email correspondence moving forward and will stop harassing the Tenant.
Since the Tenant has vacated the rental unit, the remedies requested in this application are no longer of any interest to the Tenant and therefore are moot.

A s per Rule 15.4 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure the LTB has discretion to grant a request to amend, and will only grant it if satisfied that the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

The Tenant has not filed a request to amend the application and requested an adjournment to do so at this hearing. The Tenant submitted that she vacated the rental unit due to the allegations raised in the application. If this were the case then it would be incumbent on the Tenant to include these remedies she now seeks at the outset of filing the application or at the very least filed a request to amend the remedies prior to vacating the rental unit.

I was satisfied that the Tenant has had ample opportunity to file a request to amend. The Tenant waited until after she vacated to amend the application and failed to provide any reasonable explanation as to why the amended remedies requested could not have been made in the original application or prior to vacating the unit.

Additionally, since once the Tenant vacated the rental unit, this application as filed became moot I find that it would be unfair and prejudicial to the Landlord to permit the Tenant to amend the application at this point. Therefore, I was satisfied that the Tenant’s request to amend ought to be refused.
Consequently, given that the application as filed is moot, it must be dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application. For the reasons below I find that res judicata applies to this application and the application is therefore dismissed. Procedural History

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant has improperly brought this herein T1 application claiming illegal rent was charged by the Landlord, the application was filed with the Board on December 16.2025.

File LTB-L-042115-25 was an L1 application filed by the Landlord to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owed. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted paragraph 11 of the Board’s Order dated August 13, 2025, for said application listed what the lawful rent was. The Tenant voided said order of the Board by bringing a motion to void under section 74(4) of the Act, which was granted by Board Order dated, August 28, 2025.

Thereafter, the Tenant brought a review of the Order in file LTB-L-042115-25, in which Vice [name] enumerated in paragraph 5 and 6 of the review order, dated September 8, 2025: …By summarizing the evidence that guided the Member’s decision, the order shows that the Tenant was aware of the issues to be determined at the hearing, and the Tenant exercised the right to address those issues. The Tenant was therefore afforded procedural fairness, and no error occurred in the proceeding. The order also shows that there was sufficient evidence for the Member to find that the Tenant had not paid the Landlord $26,982.18 in rent for the period ending August 31, 2025. The order notes that the Tenant agreed with the Landlord’s evidence of rent owing. The Member’s material finding of fact is therefore rational. [Emphasis added]

Thereafter the Landlord brought an L2 application (LTB-L-098690-25) based on an N8 notice for persistent late payments that resulted in the consent order after the parties engaged in mediation. I note the Tenant had reputable legal counsel attending to her matter. The result of the consent order, dated January 23, 2026 was that for a period of 12 months commencing February 2026 up to including January 1, 2027, the Tenant would pay lawful monthly rent to the Landlord in full and on time, on or before the first day of each month, subject to s78 of the Act.
The decision in order LTB-L-098690-25 was final. It was not appealed as of the date of this proceeding, and the Tenant did not file a request to review that decision.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant on two occasions did not dispute the lawful rent, in an L1 application which she had reviewed and further in an L2 application, where with the benefit of counsel she consented to the lawful rent.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative further submitted the Tenant would be statue barred from bringing this herein T1 application, even if issue estoppel was not the reason for this application being dismissed. [name] estoppel

The doctrine of res judicata operates to ensure finality of decisions and prevent abuse of process. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue. In effect, it prevents a “second kick at the can”. It has two aspects, issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. The test for issue estoppel has three elements, which must all be present: (1) the same question has been decided; (2) the decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and, (3) that the parties to the prior decision were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised.

The Board has a residual discretion as to whether to apply the doctrine of res judicata even if all three of these criteria are satisfied. Further, res judicata or issue estoppel should not be applied in circumstances that would create an injustice.

I find that the question before me to determine in this application is the same as that considered by the Board in orders related to the Landlord’s L1 and L2 applications: where the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owed the Landlord, and the Tenant had been persistently late in paying the Tenant’s rent.

It now seems the Tenant is attempting to obtain a third kick at the can in regard to what lawful rent is, by alleging the Landlord charged her in an illegal rent from May 1, 2019, the commencement of the tenancy to August 24, 2025. Even if the Landlord’s applications had not dealt with the issue of what lawful rent was, the Tenant would have issues with the limitation period in relation to her application, which there is no need to make a ruling on given I have determined res judicata applies.
The parties to the prior decisions are the same people as the parties to this proceeding. The Landlord, the Tenant, and the rental unit are all the same.
I therefore find that issue estoppel res judicata applies to this application as all three of the requirements are met.

The Supreme Court of Canada addressed issue estoppel in [name], 2001 SCC 44, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 46, para. 33: The rules governing issue estoppel should not be mechanically applied. The underlying purpose is to balance the public interest in the finality of litigation with the public interest in ensuring that justice is done on the facts of a particular case. … the court must still determine whether, as a matter of discretion, issue estoppel ought to be applied.
I do not find that the circumstances warrant an exercise of my residual discretion to not apply the doctrine of res judicata.
I am not persuaded by the Tenant’s submissions that the Landlord’s operating entity did not exist and on why the doctrine of res judicata does not apply to this situation at hand.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determination and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. July 8, 2026 ____________________________
