issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The parties do not dispute that the Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $2,900.00 on October 30, 2025.
The parties do not dispute that the Tenant did not move into the rental unit.
The parties do not dispute that they entered into a tenancy agreement that was to commence on December 1, 2025.

The parties do not dispute that there was an agreement to delay the move in date due to a death in the Tenant’s family along with the Landlord still needing additional time to complete the renovations within the rental unit.
The parties do not dispute that they agreed the new move in date would be January 1, 2026.

The Landlord is disputing that she is required to return the deposit as the Tenant did not provide enough notice to her to terminate the tenancy, and although the rental unit was undergoing renovations, it was available for the Tenant to move in.

The Tenant testified that she had a death in her family, which required her to go to Nova Scotia, and that she did not return to Ontario until December 18, 2025. The Tenant testified that on December 19, 2025, the Landlord’s husband showed up at her current residence unannounced to discuss the plans for the Tenant moving in as the Tenant did not respond to a text from the Landlord.

In addition, the Tenant testified that when the Landlord’s husband showed up at her residence, he advised her that she needed to get her phone and respond to the Landlord and she needed to confirm December 30, 2025, was the move in date.

The Tenant testified that after the Landlord’s husband showed up at her property unannounced, she was scared and was not comfortable with moving into the rental unit and felt it was not going to work, so she contacted the Landlord by telephone on December 20, 2025, or December 21, 2025 and sent a follow up email to the Landlord on December 22, 2025 confirming the conversation.

The Landlord does not dispute that her husband attended the Tenant’s residence, but she testified that the purpose of the visit was to confirm the move in date, along with setting up a scheduled walk through of the rental property. The Landlord testified that the rental unit was not ready for the Tenant to move in and they were on a tight schedule to have it completed and they would have it ready for the Tenant to move in on January 1, 2026.

The Landlord testified that the only outstanding work was the back deck and that the permit was not completed, and that when the Tenant confirmed she was not moving into the rental unit she did not push for the permit to get issued for the back deck.

The Landlord testified that the back deck is an entrance/ back sliding door to the kitchen and that there were alternative means for the Tenant to access the rental unit, but the unit would have been ready for the Tenant to move in for January 1, 2026. Law & Analysis Valid Tenancy Agreement

The first issue for me to consider is whether the parties had a tenancy agreement. Only if there is a valid tenancy agreement, is it necessary to consider whether the Tenant complied with the notice requirements in the Act.

In Fuamba et al. v. [name], 2024 ONSC 4587, the Court reiterates that “a valid tenancy agreement must contain certain basic elements,” and that the following are considered to be essential elements of a valid tenancy agreement: the parties; a description of the premises to be rented; the commencement of the term; the duration of the term; the rent (if any); and all the material terms of the contract not being matters incident to the relation of landlord and tenant, including any covenants, exceptions, or reservations.

After considering all the testimony from the parties, I find that there was a valid tenancy agreement because it is not disputed by the parties that a lease was signed, the commencement of the term was to start January 1, 2026, the duration of the term, and the rent.
Section 13(1) of the Act states: The term or period of a tenancy begins on the day the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit under the tenancy agreement.
Section 13(2) of the Act states: A tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit, whether or not the tenant actually occupies it.

Therefore, I find that the Tenant was required to provide the Landlord with notice pursuant to the Act as I find there was a valid tenancy agreement, and although the Tenant did not take possession of the rental unit, the Tenant could have moved into the rental unit on January 1, 2026. Subsequently I find that the Landlord collected a rent deposit and provided the Tenant with vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord is not required to repay the rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. July 16, 2026 ____________________________
